docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
AS-REP Roasting is fundamentally a Kerberos configuration and password-strength issue.

The critical distinctions are:

AS-REP Roasting != Kerberoasting

AS-REP != NT hash

AS-REP != NetNTLMv2

AS-REP obtained != Password recovered

Password recovered != Administrator

The attack path is:

Known username
      |
      v
Kerberos pre-authentication disabled
      |
      v
Unauthenticated AS-REQ
      |
      v
AS-REP returned
      |
      v
Password-derived encrypted material
      |
      v
Offline password cracking
      |
      v
Credential recovery
      |
      v
Privilege analysis
      |
      v
Minimum impact validation

The most effective defensive control is to remove the condition that enables the technique:

Require Kerberos pre-authentication

combined with:

Strong passwords
      +
Least privilege
      +
Configuration monitoring
      +
Kerberos authentication monitoring

A mature assessment should therefore identify not only whether AS-REP material can be obtained, but why the affected account has pre-authentication disabled, whether its password is realistically recoverable, what privileges it possesses, whether defenders can detect the activity, and how the legacy configuration can be removed safely.

docs.title: Active Directory Authentication Coercion
docs.text:
Authentication coercion is the process of causing a Windows user, computer, server, or service to initiate authentication to a destination chosen or influenced by an attacker.

The fundamental concept is:

Attacker
   |
   v
Trigger Remote Behaviour
   |
   v
Victim
   |
   v
Outbound Authentication
   |
   v
Attacker-Controlled Destination

Authentication coercion is important in Active Directory because the resulting authentication can potentially be:

Captured

or:

Relayed

to another service.

A complete relay chain may therefore look like:

Coercion
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
Target Service
   |
   v
Victim Privileges
   |
   v
Impact

The distinction is essential:

Coercion
   !=
Relay

Coercion answers:

How can authentication be triggered?

Relay answers:

Where can that authentication be forwarded?

MITRE ATT&CK tracks forced authentication as:

T1187 - Forced Authentication

Authorised testing only

Authentication coercion can cause production systems, including servers and Domain Controllers, to authenticate to an assessment host. Perform active coercion only when it is explicitly permitted by the rules of engagement. Prefer controlled test systems and identities, avoid broad or repeated triggering, and do not automatically relay captured authentication into privileged actions.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text:
Consider a Windows server:

APP01$

An attacker interacts with a remote service on APP01 and provides a path referencing another host.

Conceptually:

Attacker
   |
   | RPC / Service Request
   v
APP01
   |
   | Access Remote Resource
   v
\\ATTACKER\share
   |
   v
Authentication Attempt

If the operation executes under the computer's security context, the authentication may originate as:

CORP\APP01$

The attacker has not necessarily:

Stolen APP01$ Password

or:

Obtained APP01$ NT Hash

Instead, the attacker caused APP01 to authenticate.

docs.title: Authentication Coercion Is a Primitive
docs.text:
Authentication coercion should usually be treated as one component of a larger attack path.

Coercion Primitive
        |
        v
Authentication
        |
        +--> Capture
        |
        +--> Relay
        |
        +--> Detection / Validation

The coercion primitive by itself may have limited impact.

The importance depends on what can be done with the resulting authentication.

docs.title: Coercion vs Credential Theft
docs.text:
Do not automatically interpret forced authentication as:

Credential Theft

The attacker may receive:

NTLM Authentication

without obtaining the underlying:

Password

or:

NT Hash

The authentication may instead be relayed immediately.

docs.title: Coercion vs NetNTLM Capture
docs.text:
If the attacker receives NTLM authentication and stores the challenge-response:

Victim
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Capture
  |
  v
NetNTLM Challenge / Response

the captured material may potentially be used for offline password guessing.

This is different from relay:

Victim
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Relay
  |
  v
Target

See:

NTLM

NTLM Relay

docs.title: Coercion vs Kerberos Relay
docs.text:
Authentication coercion does not inherently mean NTLM.

Depending on:

Target Name
SPN
DNS
Service
Protocol
Windows Authentication Behaviour

the victim may attempt:

Kerberos

or:

NTLM

Therefore:

Coercion
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   +--> Kerberos
   |
   +--> NTLM

See:

Kerberos Relay

docs.title: Why Windows Systems Authenticate Automatically
docs.text:
Windows environments are designed to provide transparent access to domain resources.

A user accessing:

\\FILE01\Finance

should not normally need to type credentials repeatedly.

Windows can automatically use the current security context.

This behaviour enables seamless enterprise authentication but also creates security-sensitive situations where applications or services are instructed to access attacker-controlled resources.

docs.title: UNC Paths
docs.text:
A UNC path commonly looks like:

\\SERVER\share

For example:

\\FILE01\Finance

If a Windows process attempts to access:

\\ATTACKER\share

Windows may attempt authentication to the remote system.

The exact behaviour depends on:

Security Context
Protocol
Network Configuration
NTLM Policy
Kerberos Availability
WebClient
Zone Configuration
Service Behaviour

docs.title: Computer Account Authentication
docs.text:
One of the most important coercion scenarios involves a Windows service running as:

SYSTEM

or:

NETWORK SERVICE

When such a service accesses a remote resource using the machine identity, authentication may occur as:

DOMAIN\COMPUTER$

Example:

CORP\APP01$

This is known as:

Computer Account Authentication Coercion

docs.title: Machine Accounts Are Security Principals
docs.text:
A machine account should not be treated as:

Just a Computer Name

It is an Active Directory security principal.

Examples include:

WS01$
APP01$
SQL01$
DC01$

Machine accounts can have:

Group Memberships
Directory Permissions
Local Administrative Rights
Service Permissions
Kerberos Keys
Certificates
Delegation Rights

Therefore machine authentication can be highly valuable.

docs.title: Domain Controller Authentication
docs.text:
A particularly sensitive coercion target is a Domain Controller.

Example:

CORP\DC01$

A Domain Controller computer account participates in privileged Active Directory operations.

Therefore:

DC Authentication
       |
       v
Potential High-Value Relay Source

depending on the destination.

docs.title: Do Not Equate DC Authentication with Domain Compromise
docs.text:
The following is incorrect:

Coerce DC
   |
   v
Domain Compromise

The complete chain still requires:

Coercion
   +
Authentication Protocol
   +
Relay-Compatible Target
   +
Missing Protection
   +
Useful Privilege

docs.title: Authentication Coercion Families
docs.text:
Several Windows components have historically provided coercion primitives.

Common names encountered in Active Directory security research include:

PrinterBug
PetitPotam
DFSCoerce
ShadowCoerce
MSEven
WebDAV-Based Coercion
Application-Specific Coercion

These are not all equivalent.

Each relies on different:

RPC Interfaces
Services
Functions
Permissions
Network Paths
Windows Versions
Mitigations

docs.title: Coercion Methodology
docs.text:
A useful methodology is:

Identify Target
      |
      v
Identify Exposed Services
      |
      v
Identify Potential Coercion Interface
      |
      v
Determine Required Authentication
      |
      v
Determine Resulting Security Context
      |
      v
Determine Authentication Protocol
      |
      v
Determine Relay Destination
      |
      v
Controlled Validation

docs.title: RPC and Authentication Coercion
docs.text:
Many well-known coercion techniques involve:

MS-RPC

Remote Procedure Call allows Windows systems to expose functions remotely.

Conceptually:

Client
  |
  v
RPC Endpoint
  |
  v
Remote Function
  |
  v
Service Performs Operation

If the function accepts a remote path:

\\ATTACKER\resource

the remote service may attempt to access it.

docs.title: Named Pipes
docs.text:
RPC interfaces may be reachable through named pipes over SMB.

Examples encountered in Windows environments include:

\PIPE\spoolss
\PIPE\lsarpc
\PIPE\efsrpc
\PIPE\netdfs

Availability and access depend on the service and Windows configuration.

The presence of a named pipe alone does not prove coercion is possible.

docs.title: RPC Endpoint Enumeration
docs.text:
From Windows, RPC-related information can be investigated with built-in administrative and diagnostic tooling.

From Linux, Impacket and other assessment utilities can enumerate RPC interfaces.

For example:

impacket-rpcdump 10.10.10.20

Authenticated environments may require credentials depending on the target and interface.

Check:

impacket-rpcdump -h

for current syntax.

docs.title: RPC Endpoint Mapper
docs.text:
RPC commonly uses:

TCP/135

for endpoint mapping.

Some RPC interfaces are subsequently reached through:

Dynamic RPC Ports

while others may be transported over:

SMB Named Pipes

Network filtering therefore matters.

docs.title: PrinterBug
docs.text:
One of the classic authentication-coercion techniques is commonly called:

PrinterBug

or:

SpoolSample

The technique abuses behaviour exposed through the Windows Print Spooler RPC interface.

At a high level:

Attacker
   |
   v
Print Spooler RPC
   |
   v
Victim
   |
   v
Printer Change Notification
   |
   v
Remote Path
   |
   v
Victim Authentication

docs.title: PrinterBug Concept
docs.text:
The Print Spooler supports remote printer-related operations.

A notification mechanism can cause the target to communicate with a specified system.

Conceptually:

RPC Request
    |
    v
Victim Spooler
    |
    v
Notification Destination
    |
    v
Attacker Host

The resulting connection may authenticate using the victim computer account.

docs.title: Print Spooler Service
docs.text:
On Windows:

Get-Service Spooler

Example output:

Status   Name     DisplayName
------   ----     -----------
Running  Spooler  Print Spooler

A running Spooler service does not automatically prove that remote coercion is possible.

docs.title: Remote Spooler Exposure
docs.text:
The relevant questions include:

Is Spooler Running?
Is the RPC Interface Reachable?
Can the Caller Access the Interface?
Does the Target Permit the Relevant Operation?
Can the Target Reach the Listener?

docs.title: Domain Controllers and Print Spooler
docs.text:
Domain Controllers generally should not provide unnecessary print services.

If printing is not required on a Domain Controller, disabling the Print Spooler can reduce attack surface.

Before changing production systems, confirm operational requirements.

docs.title: PetitPotam
docs.text:
Another important coercion technique is commonly called:

PetitPotam

PetitPotam demonstrated authentication coercion through the:

Encrypting File System Remote Protocol

commonly:

MS-EFSRPC

docs.title: PetitPotam Concept
docs.text:
The simplified model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
EFSRPC Request
   |
   v
Victim
   |
   v
Attempts Remote File Operation
   |
   v
\\ATTACKER\resource
   |
   v
Authentication

The attack became particularly important when combined with NTLM relay to certificate enrollment services.

docs.title: EFSRPC
docs.text:
EFSRPC provides remote functionality related to:

Encrypting File System

operations.

Security research demonstrated that certain EFSRPC operations could cause a remote system to access an arbitrary network path.

That network access could trigger authentication.

docs.title: PetitPotam Is Not an AD CS Vulnerability
docs.text:
This distinction matters.

PetitPotam

provides:

Authentication Coercion

It does not itself provide:

Certificate Enrollment

A complete historical attack path could be:

PetitPotam
     |
     v
DC Authentication
     |
     v
NTLM Relay
     |
     v
AD CS Web Enrollment
     |
     v
Certificate

The relay portion is commonly associated with:

ESC8

when the AD CS web enrollment configuration is susceptible.

docs.title: PetitPotam Is Not NTLM Relay
docs.text:
Likewise:

PetitPotam
    !=
ntlmrelayx

The first can trigger authentication.

The second can relay suitable authentication.

docs.title: DFSCoerce
docs.text:
Another coercion technique is commonly called:

DFSCoerce

It involves the:

Distributed File System Namespace Management Protocol

or:

MS-DFSNM

The underlying concept is again:

Remote RPC Operation
       |
       v
Victim Accesses Remote Resource
       |
       v
Authentication

docs.title: DFSCoerce Security Model
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Attacker
   |
   v
DFS RPC
   |
   v
Victim
   |
   v
Remote DFS-Related Operation
   |
   v
Attacker-Controlled Path
   |
   v
Authentication

As with other coercion techniques, success depends on:

Interface Availability
Caller Permissions
Patching
Service Configuration
Network Reachability
Authentication Policy

docs.title: ShadowCoerce
docs.text:
Security research has also identified coercion paths involving Microsoft File Server Shadow Copy functionality.

These are often referred to as:

ShadowCoerce

The high-level pattern remains:

RPC Operation
    |
    v
Victim
    |
    v
Remote Path
    |
    v
Authentication

Do not assume every Windows server exposes every coercion primitive.

docs.title: MSEven
docs.text:
Other research has demonstrated forced-authentication behaviour involving Windows event-related RPC functionality.

The important lesson is not to memorise one tool name.

Instead understand the generic pattern:

Remote Interface
      |
      v
Attacker-Controlled Path
      |
      v
Victim Accesses Path
      |
      v
Authentication

New coercion primitives may continue to be discovered.

docs.title: Coercer
docs.text:
A commonly used assessment tool for identifying and testing Windows authentication-coercion methods is:

Coercer

The project consolidates multiple known coercion techniques.

Always review the installed version and project documentation before testing.

Start with:

coercer --help

The exact supported interfaces and syntax can change between versions.

docs.title: Why Coercer Is Useful
docs.text:
Instead of manually testing each historical coercion primitive:

PrinterBug
PetitPotam
DFSCoerce
ShadowCoerce
...

a framework can help determine which known RPC methods are reachable.

However:

Tool Says Vulnerable
      |
      X
Complete Relay Attack Proven

You must still analyse the resulting authentication and target protections.

docs.title: Safe Coercer Usage
docs.text:
On a production assessment, avoid immediately testing every coercion method against every host.

Prefer:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Select Test Host
   |
   v
Select Listener
   |
   v
Run Minimal Test
   |
   v
Confirm Authentication
   |
   v
Stop

docs.title: Impacket and Coercion
docs.text:
Impacket provides RPC and authentication tooling used by many coercion research projects.

Useful supporting utilities include:

rpcdump
rpcmap
ntlmrelayx

Modern installations commonly expose commands such as:

impacket-rpcdump

and:

impacket-ntlmrelayx

Check:

impacket-rpcdump -h
impacket-ntlmrelayx -h

before using version-specific options.

See:

Impacket

docs.title: Authentication Listener
docs.text:
For safe validation, the assessment host can simply observe whether authentication occurs.

The initial objective may be:

Trigger
   |
   v
Observe Connection

rather than:

Trigger
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
Modify Target

docs.title: Responder Analyze Mode
docs.text:
Responder can be useful for observing local authentication behaviour.

When the objective is discovery rather than active poisoning, use the project's passive or analysis capabilities where appropriate.

Always inspect the installed version:

responder --help

Avoid broad poisoning when the assessment only requires confirmation of a specific coercion path.

docs.title: Packet Capture
docs.text:
Network capture can provide lower-impact evidence.

For example:

sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 host 10.10.10.20

A more focused filter can be applied based on the expected protocol.

This can confirm:

Victim
   |
   v
Assessment Host

communication without automatically attempting relay.

docs.title: SMB Authentication
docs.text:
A common coercion result is:

Victim
   |
   v
SMB
   |
   v
TCP/445
   |
   v
Assessment Host

The authentication may be NTLM depending on naming and environment configuration.

docs.title: HTTP / WebDAV Authentication
docs.text:
Forced authentication can also occur over:

HTTP

through Windows WebDAV behaviour.

This matters because:

SMB Coercion

and:

HTTP Coercion

can interact differently with relay targets and security controls.

docs.title: WebClient Service
docs.text:
Windows WebDAV functionality is associated with the:

WebClient

service.

Check locally:

Get-Service WebClient -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

A running WebClient service can expand the available authentication paths.

It does not automatically prove a useful coercion-and-relay chain.

docs.title: WebDAV UNC Syntax
docs.text:
Windows can represent WebDAV destinations using UNC-style paths.

Conceptually:

\\SERVER@PORT\DavWWWRoot\resource

or other WebDAV-compatible path forms depending on the application and service.

This allows some coercion paths to generate HTTP-based authentication instead of direct SMB authentication.

docs.title: Why HTTP Coercion Matters
docs.text:
Consider:

Victim
  |
  v
HTTP Authentication
  |
  v
Relay Host
  |
  v
LDAP

The relay characteristics may differ from:

Victim
  |
  v
SMB Authentication
  |
  v
Relay Host
  |
  v
LDAP

This is why the resulting authentication transport must be identified.

docs.title: WebClient and Relay Analysis
docs.text:
A useful model is:

WebClient Running?
       |
       v
Can HTTP Authentication Be Triggered?
       |
       v
Can Authentication Reach Relay Host?
       |
       v
Can It Be Relayed?
       |
       v
Does Victim Have Useful Rights?

docs.title: Authentication Protocol Selection
docs.text:
After triggering authentication, determine whether the victim uses:

NTLM

or:

Kerberos

Do not assume.

Factors include:

Destination Name
DNS
SPN
IP Address vs Hostname
Protocol
Authentication Policy
Service Configuration

docs.title: IP Address vs Hostname
docs.text:
Kerberos generally relies on SPNs associated with names.

An authentication attempt to:

10.10.10.50

may behave differently from:

relay01.corp.example

This can influence whether authentication uses:

Kerberos

or falls back to:

NTLM

docs.title: Coercion Listener Naming
docs.text:
Listener naming can therefore matter.

A relay host might be referenced through:

IP Address
NetBIOS Name
FQDN
DNS Alias

Each can produce different authentication behaviour.

During an assessment, record the exact name used.

docs.title: NTLM Coercion
docs.text:
The classic attack chain is:

Victim
   |
   v
Forced NTLM Authentication
   |
   v
Relay Host

The relay host can potentially forward the authentication to:

SMB
LDAP
LDAPS
HTTP
HTTPS
MSSQL

depending on target protections and tool support.

See:

NTLM Relay

docs.title: Kerberos Coercion
docs.text:
A victim may instead authenticate using Kerberos when the destination name and SPN conditions support it.

The resulting attack surface is more constrained because Kerberos tickets are service-bound.

See:

Kerberos Relay

docs.title: Coercion to SMB Relay
docs.text:
One possible chain is:

Coercion
   |
   v
Victim NTLM
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
SMB Server

For SMB, a key target-side control is:

SMB Signing

If SMB signing is required, common NTLM relay scenarios to SMB are mitigated.

docs.title: Coercion to LDAP
docs.text:
Another important chain is:

Coercion
   |
   v
Victim Authentication
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
LDAP
   |
   v
Active Directory

The resulting impact depends on:

LDAP Signing
Channel Binding
Authentication Transport
Victim Directory Rights

docs.title: Coercion to AD CS
docs.text:
A historically significant attack chain is:

Coercion
   |
   v
Machine Authentication
   |
   v
NTLM Relay
   |
   v
AD CS HTTP Enrollment
   |
   v
Certificate

This is associated with AD CS relay exposure such as:

ESC8

when the relevant prerequisites are present.

docs.title: AD CS Changes the Impact Model
docs.text:
Without a relay target:

Coercion
   |
   v
Authentication Attempt

may be limited.

With a vulnerable certificate enrollment path:

Coercion
   |
   v
Machine Authentication
   |
   v
Certificate Enrollment
   |
   v
Certificate-Based Authentication

the resulting certificate can become reusable authentication material.

This is why AD CS must be included in relay assessments.

docs.title: Coercion to RBCD
docs.text:
Another possible downstream chain is:

Coercion
   |
   v
Relay to LDAP
   |
   v
Write Computer Object
   |
   v
Configure RBCD
   |
   v
S4U

This requires the relayed principal to have the necessary directory rights.

See:

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: Coercion to Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
If the relayed identity can modify:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

a downstream path may involve Shadow Credentials.

Coercion
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
Directory Write
   |
   v
Key Credential

See:

Active Directory Shadow Credentials

docs.title: Coercion and Machine Account Quota
docs.text:
Some relay chains may combine:

Machine Account Creation

with:

RBCD

Machine Account Quota can therefore become one supporting primitive.

However:

MAQ > 0
   |
   X
Authentication Coercion Vulnerability

These are separate security conditions.

See:

Active Directory Machine Account Quota

docs.title: Coercion and Directory ACLs
docs.text:
A relayed identity may have useful rights because of an Active Directory ACL.

Examples include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
WriteProperty
AddMember

Therefore:

Coercion
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
ACL Abuse

may form a complete attack path.

See:

Active Directory ACL and ACE Abuse

docs.title: Coercion and BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can help model attack paths involving coercion and relay.

Modern BloodHound versions can represent relationships where authentication from a computer can potentially be coerced and relayed under particular conditions.

Exact edge support depends on:

BloodHound Version
Collector Version
Collected Data
Target Configuration

Do not assume a graph edge replaces validation.

docs.title: CoerceAndRelay Relationships
docs.text:
A BloodHound path may conceptually represent:

Authenticated Users
        |
        v
Can Coerce Computer
        |
        v
Computer Authentication
        |
        v
Relay
        |
        v
LDAP / AD CS / Other Target

The graph should be treated as:

Attack Path Hypothesis

that must be verified against the environment.

docs.title: BloodHound Workflow
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Collect
   |
   v
Identify Coercible Systems
   |
   v
Identify Relay Paths
   |
   v
Review Victim Permissions
   |
   v
Review Target Protections
   |
   v
Controlled Validation

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: Coercion Target Selection
docs.text:
Do not begin with:

Coerce Every Host

Instead identify high-value or representative systems.

Examples:

Test Workstation
Test Member Server
Application Server
Management Server
Domain Controller
Certificate Server

Use the least sensitive system capable of demonstrating the condition.

docs.title: Identify the Victim Context
docs.text:
Before coercion, determine what identity is expected to authenticate.

Possible identities include:

Logged-On User
Computer Account
Service Account
Application Identity

This dramatically affects impact.

docs.title: SYSTEM Context
docs.text:
If a remote operation runs as:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

network authentication normally uses the computer's domain identity when appropriate.

Conceptually:

SYSTEM
   |
   v
Network Authentication
   |
   v
DOMAIN\COMPUTER$

docs.title: NETWORK SERVICE Context
docs.text:
Services running as:

NETWORK SERVICE

can also authenticate to remote resources using the machine account in common domain scenarios.

Again, verify actual behaviour.

docs.title: User Context
docs.text:
Some coercion primitives may cause an operation to execute using:

Logged-On User

or another impersonated context.

The resulting authentication could therefore belong to a user rather than the machine.

docs.title: Service Accounts
docs.text:
Applications running under domain service accounts may generate authentication as:

CORP\svc-application

These identities may have significant access to:

Databases
Shares
Servers
Applications
Directory Objects

docs.title: Determine Expected Privilege
docs.text:
Before active testing, answer:

If this identity authenticates, what can it do?

This can often be answered through:

BloodHound
Group Membership
Local Administrator Mapping
Directory ACL Analysis
Application Permissions

docs.title: Reachability
docs.text:
A successful coercion primitive is useless if the victim cannot reach the listener.

Assess:

Victim
  |
  v
Outbound Network
  |
  v
Listener

Potential controls include:

Host Firewall
Network Firewall
Segmentation
Egress Filtering
SMB Blocking
HTTP Restrictions

docs.title: SMB Egress
docs.text:
Blocking unnecessary outbound:

TCP/445

from sensitive servers can significantly reduce SMB-based forced-authentication exposure.

This is particularly valuable for:

Domain Controllers
Certificate Authorities
Management Servers
Application Servers

where business requirements permit.

docs.title: Internet SMB Egress
docs.text:
Organisations should generally prevent internal Windows systems from sending SMB authentication directly to the Internet unless there is an explicit requirement.

A useful boundary is:

Internal Host
     |
     X
Internet TCP/445

docs.title: Internal Segmentation
docs.text:
Internet filtering alone is insufficient.

An attacker may already have:

Internal Network Access

Therefore consider:

Workstation -> Server
Server -> Workstation
Server -> Server
Server -> DC

communication requirements.

docs.title: Authentication Coercion Enumeration
docs.text:
A practical assessment can begin with:

1. Identify Windows hosts
2. Identify sensitive roles
3. Enumerate RPC
4. Identify Spooler
5. Identify WebClient
6. Identify SMB reachability
7. Identify NTLM use
8. Identify relay targets
9. Map privileges
10. Validate selectively

docs.title: Windows Service Enumeration
docs.text:
Check Print Spooler:

Get-Service Spooler -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Check WebClient:

Get-Service WebClient -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Check multiple relevant services:

Get-Service Spooler,WebClient -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object Name,Status,StartType

docs.title: Remote Service Enumeration
docs.text:
With appropriate administrative access:

Get-Service -ComputerName SERVER01 -Name Spooler -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Support for remote service enumeration depends on environment configuration and PowerShell version.

Avoid requiring privileged access merely to enumerate when lower-impact methods are available.

docs.title: Service Configuration
docs.text:
Inspect locally:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object { $_.Name -in @('Spooler','WebClient') } |
    Select-Object Name,State,StartMode,StartName

docs.title: SMB Reachability
docs.text:
From PowerShell:

Test-NetConnection SERVER01 -Port 445

For RPC endpoint mapper:

Test-NetConnection SERVER01 -Port 135

These checks demonstrate reachability only.

They do not prove a coercion primitive is available.

docs.title: Linux Reachability
docs.text:
From Linux:

nmap -Pn -p 135,445 10.10.10.20

For multiple authorised targets:

nmap -Pn -p 135,445 -iL targets.txt

docs.title: RPC Enumeration with Impacket
docs.text:
impacket-rpcdump 10.10.10.20

For an authenticated query where required, inspect the current help:

impacket-rpcdump -h

Avoid embedding real passwords in shell history.

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec can help inventory:

Windows Hosts
SMB
Signing
Domain Information
Authentication

Example:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24

This can help identify systems relevant to subsequent relay analysis.

See:

NetExec

docs.title: Check SMB Signing
docs.text:
The coercion and relay workflow should include:

Coercion Source

and separately:

Relay Target

A relay target using SMB should be assessed for signing requirements.

Do not assume the coercion victim must also be the relay target.

docs.title: Coercion Source vs Relay Target
docs.text:
Example:

DC01
 |
 | Coerced Authentication
 v
ATTACKER
 |
 | Relay
 v
FILE01

Here:

DC01

is the:

Coercion Source

and:

FILE01

is the:

Relay Target

They are different roles.

docs.title: Coercion Listener vs Relay Target
docs.text:
Similarly:

Assessment Host

receives the authentication.

It may then connect to:

Relay Target

The architecture is:

Victim
  |
  v
Listener / Relay Host
  |
  v
Target

docs.title: Safe Validation Without Relay
docs.text:
The lowest-impact active test is:

Coercion
   |
   v
Connection to Assessment Host
   |
   v
Stop

Evidence can include:

Timestamp
Source IP
Victim Hostname
Expected Security Context
Network Trace
Listener Log

No authentication needs to be relayed.

docs.title: Safe Validation with Relay
docs.text:
If relay validation is required:

One Victim
   |
   v
One Controlled Authentication
   |
   v
One Approved Target
   |
   v
Non-Destructive Authentication
   |
   v
Stop

Avoid broad:

MultiRelay

testing against production systems.

docs.title: Coercion Tools Are Not Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
A report should not state:

Server Is Vulnerable to Coercer

Instead describe the actual condition:

Remote Authentication Can Be Forced Through the Print Spooler

or:

Server Can Be Induced to Authenticate to an Arbitrary SMB Destination

or the complete validated path:

Forced Machine Authentication Can Be Relayed to an Unsigned SMB Service

docs.title: Tool Success Is Not Impact
docs.text:
Likewise:

[+] Exploit worked!

from a research tool does not automatically mean:

Privilege Escalation

The result may only mean:

Authentication Triggered

Always determine what happened after the trigger.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Authentication coercion can produce telemetry across:

RPC
SMB
HTTP
Authentication
Network
Directory
Endpoint

No single event universally identifies every coercion method.

docs.title: Detection Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Unusual RPC Request
       |
       v
Sensitive Server
       |
       v
Outbound Authentication
       |
       v
Unexpected Host
       |
       v
Possible Relay Activity

docs.title: Event 4624
docs.text:
A relayed authentication may produce:

4624

on the destination.

Useful fields include:

Account Name
Account Domain
Logon Type
Source Network Address
Workstation Name
Authentication Package

docs.title: Detect Machine Authentication from the Wrong Host
docs.text:
One useful relay detection idea is:

Account:
APP01$

Source IP:
10.10.10.50

when:

APP01

actually uses:

10.10.10.20

This discrepancy can indicate that APP01's authentication was relayed through another system.

It is not conclusive by itself.

docs.title: Event 4776
docs.text:
For NTLM domain credential validation:

4776

may provide useful context.

Correlate:

Account
Workstation
Time
Target

docs.title: Event 4768 and 4769
docs.text:
If Kerberos is involved, review:

4768

and:

4769

for TGT and service-ticket activity.

See:

Kerberos

docs.title: Network Detection
docs.text:
Network telemetry is particularly useful.

Look for:

Sensitive Server
      |
      v
Unexpected Workstation / Host

over:

SMB
HTTP
HTTPS

immediately after unusual RPC traffic.

docs.title: Coercion Timing
docs.text:
A coercion attack may produce a sequence such as:

20:10:01 ATTACKER -> DC01 RPC
20:10:01 DC01 -> ATTACKER SMB
20:10:01 ATTACKER -> TARGET LDAP

Correlating these flows can provide strong evidence of coercion and relay.

docs.title: Print Spooler Detection
docs.text:
Monitor unexpected remote interactions with the Print Spooler on systems where remote printing is unnecessary.

Particularly sensitive systems include:

Domain Controllers
Certificate Authorities
Management Servers

docs.title: EFSRPC Detection
docs.text:
Monitor unusual EFSRPC-related network behaviour when possible.

The useful behavioural pattern is:

Remote RPC Request
      |
      v
Server Initiates Unexpected SMB / HTTP

rather than relying solely on a particular PetitPotam signature.

docs.title: DFS Detection
docs.text: Likewise, monitor unusual DFS management RPC activity followed by unexpected outbound authentication.

docs.title: Endpoint Detection
docs.text:
Endpoint telemetry may expose:

Service Activity
RPC Calls
Network Connections
Authentication
Process Context

Correlating these can identify coercion even when the tool or method changes.

docs.title: Detect Relay After Coercion
docs.text:
If coercion is followed by relay, additional events may appear.

For LDAP relay:

5136

may show directory changes.

For computer creation:

4741

may be relevant.

For group changes:

4728
4732
4756

may be relevant depending on group scope.

docs.title: Detect RBCD Changes
docs.text:
Monitor:

msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity

for unexpected modification.

A chain may look like:

Coercion
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
5136
   |
   v
RBCD Attribute Change

docs.title: Detect Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Monitor changes to:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

on sensitive objects.

Unexpected changes may indicate Shadow Credentials abuse following relay.

docs.title: Detect AD CS Relay
docs.text:
For certificate-based relay paths, monitor:

Certificate Requests
Requester
Template
Source
Authentication
Certificate Issuance

and correlate with preceding forced authentication.

docs.title: Authentication Coercion Hardening
docs.text:
There is no single:

Disable Authentication Coercion

switch.

Defence should address:

Coercion Source
+
Authentication
+
Network Reachability
+
Relay Destination
+
Victim Privilege

docs.title: Hardening Model
docs.text:
Remove Unnecessary Coercion Interfaces
              |
              v
Restrict Network Reachability
              |
              v
Reduce NTLM
              |
              v
Enforce Relay Protections
              |
              v
Reduce Victim Privilege

docs.title: Disable Unnecessary Print Spooler
docs.text:
If a system does not require printing:

Stop-Service Spooler

and:

Set-Service Spooler -StartupType Disabled

may be appropriate administrative actions.

Warning

Do not disable production services during a penetration test unless configuration changes are explicitly authorised.

For Domain Controllers and other sensitive servers, review whether the Print Spooler is required at all.

docs.title: Group Policy for Print Spooler
docs.text:
Organisations can centrally manage printer-related security settings through Group Policy.

A particularly important defensive objective is:

Prevent Unnecessary Remote Print Spooler Access

while preserving legitimate printing where required.

See:

Active Directory Group Policy

docs.title: Restrict RPC
docs.text:
Network controls can restrict unnecessary RPC access to sensitive systems.

Consider:

Who Actually Needs RPC Access?

for:

Domain Controllers
Certificate Authorities
Management Servers
Database Servers

Do not block required Active Directory traffic without understanding dependencies.

docs.title: Restrict SMB Egress
docs.text:
Where operationally feasible:

Sensitive Server
      |
      X
Untrusted SMB Destination

can prevent many forced SMB authentication paths.

docs.title: Restrict HTTP Egress
docs.text:
HTTP-based coercion may use WebDAV or other mechanisms.

Sensitive servers should not have unrestricted outbound access merely because:

TCP/80

or:

TCP/443

is commonly allowed.

Apply destination-aware controls where practical.

docs.title: Disable WebClient Where Not Required
docs.text:
If WebDAV functionality is unnecessary on a sensitive server, review whether the:

WebClient

service should be available.

This can reduce HTTP/WebDAV-based authentication paths.

docs.title: Reduce NTLM
docs.text:
A major defensive objective is reducing reliance on:

NTLM

Use a staged process:

Audit
  |
  v
Identify Dependencies
  |
  v
Remediate
  |
  v
Restrict

Do not disable NTLM blindly in production.

docs.title: Restrict Outgoing NTLM
docs.text:
Windows provides policy controls for restricting outgoing NTLM authentication.

These controls can significantly reduce forced-authentication risk.

Deploy through a staged process:

Audit
  |
  v
Identify Required Destinations
  |
  v
Remediate
  |
  v
Restrict

docs.title: Restrict Incoming NTLM
docs.text:
Services can also be hardened to reduce acceptance of NTLM.

This reduces relay destinations.

Again, inventory dependencies before enforcement.

docs.title: Require SMB Signing
docs.text:
For SMB relay targets:

Require SMB Signing

where appropriate.

See:

NTLM Relay

docs.title: Require LDAP Signing
docs.text:
Domain Controllers should be hardened according to current Microsoft LDAP signing guidance.

The objective is to prevent insecure LDAP authentication and relay paths.

docs.title: LDAP Channel Binding
docs.text:
Configure LDAP channel binding according to current Microsoft guidance.

This is especially important for LDAPS authentication.

docs.title: Extended Protection for Authentication
docs.text:
Enable:

EPA

for supported Windows-authenticated HTTP services.

This is particularly important for sensitive services such as certificate enrollment endpoints.

docs.title: AD CS Hardening
docs.text:
For AD CS:

Use HTTPS
Enable EPA
Review NTLM
Review Web Enrollment
Review Certificate Enrollment Web Services
Review Templates
Review Enrollment Permissions

A later AD CS section should cover these controls in detail.

docs.title: Reduce Computer Account Privilege
docs.text:
A coerced computer account becomes more dangerous when it has broad permissions.

Review:

Computer -> Computer ACLs
Computer -> Group Rights
Computer -> Local Administrator
Computer -> Application Permissions
Computer -> Directory Writes

docs.title: Protect Domain Controller Authentication
docs.text:
Domain Controllers should have particularly restrictive outbound communication.

A useful principle is:

DC
 |
 +--> Required Infrastructure
 |
 X
Untrusted Workstations

where operationally feasible.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Segmentation can break coercion and relay chains.

Example:

DC01
 |
 X
Assessment / Workstation VLAN TCP/445

Even if a coercion primitive exists, the victim cannot authenticate to an unreachable listener.

docs.title: Host Firewalling
docs.text:
Host-based firewall rules can provide additional protection.

Consider restricting outbound:

SMB
WebDAV
HTTP

from sensitive servers to only required destinations.

docs.title: Administrative Tiering
docs.text:
Privileged accounts should not authenticate unnecessarily to lower-trust systems.

Although computer-account coercion does not depend on interactive administrator activity, tiering still reduces user-authentication coercion and downstream relay impact.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Relay impact depends on the coerced identity.

Therefore:

Coercible Identity
       +
No Useful Rights
       =
Limited Impact

while:

Coercible Identity
       +
Sensitive Rights
       =
High Impact

Review the rights assigned to:

Computer Accounts
Service Accounts
Management Servers
Domain Controllers

docs.title: Authentication Coercion and SCCM
docs.text:
Management infrastructure can create particularly sensitive machine-to-machine trust relationships.

For example, Microsoft Configuration Manager environments may include:

Site Servers
SMS Providers
Site Databases
Management Points
Clients

Machine accounts associated with these systems can have powerful rights on other site systems.

As a result:

Coercion
   |
   v
Site Server Authentication
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
Another Site System

can become significantly more impactful than coercion of an ordinary workstation.

Always assess the resulting identity privileges.

docs.title: Application-Specific Coercion
docs.text:
Do not limit coercion testing to famous RPC techniques.

Applications may perform operations such as:

Fetch File
Import URL
Read UNC Path
Load Configuration
Validate Share
Access Backup Path
Retrieve Template
Query Remote Resource

If these operations run under a privileged Windows identity, they may trigger authentication.

docs.title: Example Application Path
docs.text:
Internal Application
        |
        v
"Import configuration from UNC"
        |
        v
\\ATTACKER\config.xml
        |
        v
Application Service Account Authentication

This is conceptually an authentication-coercion condition even if no named exploit is involved.

docs.title: SQL Server
docs.text:
SQL Server functionality may interact with network resources depending on:

Features
Stored Procedures
Service Account
Permissions
Configuration

Any server-side operation that accesses an attacker-controlled UNC path should be reviewed for forced-authentication risk.

docs.title: Backup Software
docs.text:
Backup products frequently access:

Network Shares
Remote Repositories
UNC Paths

under privileged service identities.

A path-injection or configuration weakness could potentially trigger service-account authentication.

docs.title: Monitoring Software
docs.text:
Monitoring and management systems may similarly:

Fetch Remote Files
Query UNC Paths
Connect to Agents
Load Scripts

under powerful identities.

These systems deserve special attention because their service accounts may have broad administrative access.

docs.title: Reporting Authentication Coercion
docs.text:
A finding should explain:

What Trigger Exists?
Which Identity Authenticates?
Where Can It Authenticate?
Which Protocol Is Used?
Can It Be Relayed?
What Is the Resulting Impact?

docs.title: Finding Titles
docs.text:
Possible titles include:

Remote Authentication Can Be Forced from Domain Controllers

Print Spooler Allows Forced Machine Authentication

EFSRPC Allows Forced Authentication to Arbitrary Network Hosts

Application Functionality Exposes Service Account Authentication

Forced NTLM Authentication Can Be Relayed to Internal Services

Authentication Coercion and Relay Enable Active Directory Modification

Choose the title that matches the validated condition.

docs.title: Example Finding - Coercion Only
docs.text:
Finding:
Remote Authentication Can Be Forced from APP01

Affected System:
APP01.corp.example

Description:
The affected server exposes a remote Windows service that can be
instructed by an authenticated domain user to access an arbitrary
network path.

During controlled testing, APP01 was instructed to access a resource
hosted on the assessment system.

APP01 subsequently initiated authentication to the assessment host
using its domain computer identity:

CORP\APP01$

No authentication was relayed and no credential material was cracked.

Impact:
An attacker with suitable domain access and network positioning may be
able to cause APP01 to authenticate to an attacker-controlled service.

Depending on protocol configuration elsewhere in the environment, this
authentication could potentially be captured for offline password
guessing or relayed to another service.

The final impact depends on the privileges of APP01$ and the security
controls implemented by potential relay targets.

Recommendation:
Disable unnecessary services capable of triggering outbound
authentication.

Restrict SMB and WebDAV egress from sensitive servers.

Reduce NTLM usage and enforce relay protections such as SMB signing,
LDAP signing, LDAP channel binding, and Extended Protection for
Authentication where applicable.

docs.title: Example Finding - Coercion and Relay
docs.text:
Finding:
Forced Machine Authentication Can Be Relayed to Internal SMB Services

Affected Authentication Source:
APP01.corp.example

Affected Relay Target:
FILE01.corp.example

Description:
APP01 can be remotely induced to initiate NTLM authentication to an
assessment-controlled system.

FILE01 accepts SMB connections without requiring SMB signing.

During controlled validation, a single authentication attempt from the
APP01$ computer account was relayed to FILE01.

No command execution or credential dumping was performed.

Impact:
An attacker able to reach both systems may be able to authenticate to
FILE01 using APP01$ without knowing the computer account password.

The resulting impact depends on the privileges assigned to APP01$ on
FILE01.

Recommendation:
Require SMB signing on FILE01 and other applicable SMB servers.

Restrict unnecessary outbound SMB authentication from APP01.

Review why APP01$ requires access to other systems and remove
unnecessary privileges.

Reduce NTLM usage and remediate the coercion primitive where
operationally possible.

docs.title: Example Finding - High-Impact Chain
docs.text:
Finding:
Authentication Coercion and NTLM Relay Enable Active Directory
Computer Object Modification

Authentication Source:
MGMT01$

Relay Target:
Domain Controller LDAP Service

Description:
MGMT01 can be induced to authenticate to an attacker-controlled
network endpoint.

The resulting NTLM authentication can be relayed to an Active
Directory LDAP service under the tested configuration.

MGMT01$ possesses write permissions over the designated computer
object.

During controlled validation, the assessment confirmed an approved
non-persistent directory modification and immediately reverted it.

Impact:
An attacker with internal network access and suitable domain
credentials could potentially use the MGMT01$ identity to perform
directory operations without obtaining the underlying machine account
password.

Depending on the affected ACL, this could enable additional attack
paths such as resource-based constrained delegation or credential
persistence.

Recommendation:
Remove unnecessary directory permissions from MGMT01$.

Enforce LDAP signing and applicable channel-binding requirements.

Restrict outgoing NTLM authentication from sensitive servers.

Remediate the authentication-coercion primitive and restrict
unnecessary RPC access.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity should reflect the complete path.

A useful model is:

Coercion Accessibility
        +
Victim Identity
        +
Authentication Protocol
        +
Relay Feasibility
        +
Victim Privilege
        +
Target Sensitivity
        =
Severity

docs.title: Low-Impact Example
docs.text:
Test Workstation
     |
     v
Forced Authentication
     |
     X
No Relay Target

This may primarily represent a hardening issue.

docs.title: Higher-Impact Example
docs.text:
Management Server
       |
       v
Forced Machine Authentication
       |
       v
NTLM Relay
       |
       v
Server Where Machine Is Admin

This may provide lateral movement.

docs.title: Critical-Path Example
docs.text:
Privileged Server / DC
        |
        v
Forced Authentication
        |
        v
Relay
        |
        v
Sensitive AD / AD CS Service
        |
        v
Reusable Privileged Authentication

Depending on the exact result, this may represent a severe domain-level attack path.

docs.title: Evidence Checklist
docs.text:
Record:

Coercion Target
Coercion Method
Required Privilege
RPC / Service Interface
Victim Identity
Victim IP
Listener IP
Listener Name
Authentication Protocol
Authentication Transport
Timestamp
Relay Target
Relay Protection
Resulting Privilege
Resulting Action
Cleanup

docs.title: Protect Sensitive Evidence
docs.text:
Do not place reusable authentication material in reports or repositories.

Avoid storing:

NetNTLM Captures
NT Hashes
Kerberos Tickets
Certificates
Private Keys
Passwords

unless required by the engagement.

If stored temporarily:

Restrict Access
Encrypt
Track
Delete Securely

after the engagement.

docs.title: Authentication Coercion Testing Model
docs.text:
The basic model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
Trigger
   |
   v
Victim
   |
   v
Outbound Authentication

The capture model is:

Coercion
   |
   v
NTLM Authentication
   |
   v
Capture
   |
   v
Offline Password Guessing

The relay model is:

Coercion
   |
   v
NTLM Authentication
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
Target

The computer-account model is:

Remote Service
     |
     v
Runs as SYSTEM
     |
     v
Remote Resource Access
     |
     v
DOMAIN\COMPUTER$

The user-context model is:

Application
    |
    v
Runs / Impersonates User
    |
    v
Remote Resource
    |
    v
DOMAIN\User

The service-account model is:

Application Service
       |
       v
DOMAIN\svc-app
       |
       v
Remote Resource
       |
       v
Service Account Authentication

The RPC model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
RPC Function
   |
   v
Victim Service
   |
   v
Attacker-Controlled UNC
   |
   v
Authentication

The PrinterBug model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
Print Spooler RPC
   |
   v
Victim
   |
   v
Notification Destination
   |
   v
Authentication

The PetitPotam model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
EFSRPC
   |
   v
Victim
   |
   v
Remote File Path
   |
   v
Authentication

The DFSCoerce model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
DFS RPC
   |
   v
Victim
   |
   v
Remote Resource
   |
   v
Authentication

The WebDAV model is:

Coercion
   |
   v
WebClient
   |
   v
HTTP / WebDAV
   |
   v
Authentication

The protocol-selection model is:

Authentication
      |
      +--> Kerberos
      |
      +--> NTLM

The complete NTLM attack path is:

Coercion
   |
   v
Victim NTLM Authentication
   |
   v
Relay Host
   |
   v
Relay-Compatible Target
   |
   v
Victim Privilege
   |
   v
Impact

The AD CS model is:

Coercion
   |
   v
Machine Authentication
   |
   v
NTLM Relay
   |
   v
AD CS Enrollment
   |
   v
Certificate
   |
   v
Authentication

The RBCD model is:

Coercion
   |
   v
Relay to LDAP
   |
   v
Computer Object Write
   |
   v
RBCD
   |
   v
S4U

The detection model is:

Inbound RPC
    |
    v
Sensitive Server
    |
    v
Immediate Outbound Authentication
    |
    v
Unexpected Destination
    |
    v
Possible Coercion

The relay detection model is:

Victim Authentication
        |
        v
Unexpected Source Host
        |
        v
Sensitive Target
        |
        v
Privileged Operation

The hardening model is:

Reduce Coercion Interfaces
         +
Restrict Egress
         +
Reduce NTLM
         +
Enforce Relay Protections
         +
Least Privilege
         =
Reduced Risk

The most important distinction is:

Authentication Coercion
        |
        X
Credential Compromise

A system can be forced to authenticate without exposing its plaintext password.

Another important distinction is:

Authentication Coercion
        |
        X
NTLM Relay

Coercion generates authentication.

Relay forwards authentication.

Another important distinction is:

Coercion Successful
       |
       X
Privilege Escalation Successful

The victim still requires useful rights on a compatible relay destination.

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Can PetitPotam or Coercer trigger this host?"

Ask:
"Which identity can be forced to authenticate,
which protocol will it use, where can that
authentication be relayed, and what can the
identity do there?"

For defenders:

Do Not Ask:
"Did we patch PetitPotam?"

Ask:
"Which systems can be forced to authenticate,
where are they permitted to authenticate,
which protocols are available, and which
relay protections prevent that authentication
from becoming useful?"

The complete relationship is:

Remote Interface
      |
      v
Service Context
      |
      v
Outbound Authentication
      |
      v
Authentication Protocol
      |
      v
Network Reachability
      |
      v
Relay Protection
      |
      v
Identity Privilege
      |
      v
Impact

Authentication coercion should therefore be assessed as an end-to-end identity and network trust problem rather than as a collection of individual exploit names.

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Authentication coercion is best understood as:

Attacker-Controlled Authentication Trigger

rather than:

Password Theft

The attacker exploits legitimate Windows behaviour:

Service
  |
  v
Access Remote Resource
  |
  v
Authenticate Automatically

The resulting authentication becomes dangerous when combined with another weakness.

The complete relationship is:

Coercion Primitive
        |
        v
Victim Identity
        |
        v
Authentication
        |
        v
Relay Opportunity
        |
        v
Target
        |
        v
Victim Privilege
        |
        v
Impact

This means that fixing only one named coercion technique does not necessarily remove the overall attack class.

For example:

PetitPotam Mitigated
        |
        X
All Authentication Coercion Eliminated

Other:

RPC Interfaces
Applications
Management Platforms
UNC Functions
WebDAV Workflows

may still cause outbound authentication.

Likewise:

Print Spooler Disabled
        |
        X
NTLM Relay Eliminated

because other authentication sources may remain.

The defensive objective is therefore broader:

Reduce Coercion
     |
     v
Restrict Outbound Authentication
     |
     v
Reduce NTLM
     |
     v
Enforce Relay Protections
     |
     v
Reduce Identity Privilege

For penetration testers, the preferred workflow is:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Understand the Primitive
   |
   v
Identify the Victim Identity
   |
   v
Determine the Protocol
   |
   v
Map Relay Targets
   |
   v
Map Privileges
   |
   v
Validate Minimally
   |
   v
Stop

rather than:

Run Every Coercion Tool
        |
        v
Against Every Server
        |
        v
Relay Every Authentication

The central assessment questions are:

Can this system be forced to authenticate?

Which identity authenticates?

Which protocol does it use?

Where can that authentication go?

What can that identity do there?

For defenders, the equivalent questions are:

Which systems expose coercion-capable interfaces?

Which systems can send SMB or WebDAV authentication
to untrusted destinations?

Where is NTLM still required?

Which services accept relayable authentication?

Which computer and service accounts have powerful
rights on other systems?

Which protocol protections are enforced?

The final model is:

Trigger
  |
  v
Service
  |
  v
Security Context
  |
  v
Authentication
  |
  v
Network Path
  |
  v
Relay Protection
  |
  v
Authorisation
  |
  v
Impact

Authentication coercion is therefore not merely an RPC problem.

It is a Windows authentication, network segmentation, service configuration, identity privilege, and protocol-hardening problem.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound is an identity security and attack-path analysis platform used to model relationships between users, groups, computers, permissions, sessions, trusts, certificate services, and other identity objects.

During an authorised Active Directory assessment, BloodHound helps answer questions such as:

What can this user control?

Who can administer this computer?

Which principals can modify this group?

Who can reach Domain Admin?

Which systems contain privileged sessions?

Which ACLs create privilege escalation paths?

Which delegation relationships are dangerous?

Which certificate services relationships create attack paths?

Which paths become available after obtaining a new credential?

What should be investigated next?

BloodHound should not be treated simply as:

Run collector
    |
    v
Click "Shortest Path to Domain Admin"
    |
    v
Exploit everything

A better methodology is:

Collect
   |
   v
Build Identity Graph
   |
   v
Understand Relationships
   |
   v
Identify Interesting Paths
   |
   v
Verify Prerequisites
   |
   v
Validate Safely
   |
   v
Re-Collect / Re-Analyse
   |
   v
Evidence
   |
   v
Report

docs.title: Authorised Use
docs.text:
Use BloodHound and related collectors only for:

Authorised penetration testing
Internal security assessments
Red team exercises
Purple team exercises
Identity security assessments
Training environments
CTFs
Security research

Collection can generate:

LDAP queries
SMB connections
RPC activity
Session enumeration
Local group enumeration
Registry access
Kerberos activity
DNS queries
Authentication events
Endpoint telemetry

Always remain within the agreed scope and rules of engagement.

docs.title: BloodHound Ecosystem
docs.text:
BloodHound is better understood as an ecosystem rather than a single executable.

                    Active Directory
                           |
          +----------------+----------------+
          |                |                |
          v                v                v
      SharpHound      BloodHound.py      NetExec
          |                |                |
          |                |                |
          +----------------+----------------+
                           |
                           v
                    Collection Data
                           |
                 JSON / ZIP / Graph
                           |
             +-------------+-------------+
             |                           |
             v                           v
       BloodHound CE                 BloodBash
             |                           |
             v                           v
       Graph Analysis              Offline Analysis
             |
             v
       Attack Paths

Depending on the environment, collection may be performed using:

SharpHound CE
BloodHound.py CE
NetExec BloodHound ingestor
Other compatible collectors

Analysis may then be performed using:

BloodHound CE
BloodHound / Neo4j legacy environments
BloodBash
Custom graph analysis

docs.title: BloodHound Community Edition
docs.text:
BloodHound Community Edition (BloodHound CE) is the current community platform from SpecterOps.

It provides:

Graph-based identity analysis
Attack path visualisation
Active Directory analysis
AD CS relationships
Hybrid identity analysis
Cypher-based graph querying
Data ingestion
Attack path exploration

The basic architecture is:

Collector
   |
   v
JSON / ZIP
   |
   v
BloodHound CE
   |
   v
Graph Database
   |
   v
Web Interface
   |
   v
Attack Path Analysis

docs.title: BloodHound CE Installation
docs.text:
Current BloodHound CE deployments commonly use the BloodHound CLI and containerised services.

Follow the official BloodHound CE documentation for the current installation process.

After installation, the interface is commonly exposed locally through:

http://localhost:8080

Do not expose a local BloodHound instance to untrusted networks without appropriate authentication and network controls.

docs.title: Data Collection
docs.text:
BloodHound is only as useful as the data supplied to it.

Incomplete Collection
        |
        v
Incomplete Graph
        |
        v
Missing Relationships
        |
        v
Potentially Missed Attack Paths

Collection strategy therefore matters.

docs.title: Collection Options
docs.text:
A practical AD assessment may use several collection methods.

Windows foothold
     |
     +--> SharpHound CE
     |
Linux foothold
     |
     +--> BloodHound.py CE
     |
     +--> NetExec
     |
Existing JSON / ZIP
     |
     +--> BloodHound CE
     |
     +--> BloodBash

The collector should be chosen based on:

Operating system
Network position
Credentials
Privileges
Endpoint controls
Available protocols
Assessment scope
Required data
Operational impact

docs.title: SharpHound CE
docs.text:
SharpHound CE is the official Active Directory collector for BloodHound CE.

It is written in C# and collects information through mechanisms including:

LDAP
Windows APIs
SMB
RPC
Registry access
Session enumeration
Local group enumeration

depending on the selected collection methods.

docs.title: Basic SharpHound Collection
docs.text:
From a domain-joined Windows system:

.\SharpHound.exe

Without additional collection flags, SharpHound uses its default collection method.

The resulting data is normally written into a ZIP archive containing BloodHound-compatible JSON.

docs.title: Specify a Domain
docs.text:
.\SharpHound.exe --Domain example.local

Short form:

.\SharpHound.exe -d example.local

DNS must be able to resolve the target domain correctly.

docs.title: SharpHound Collection Methods
docs.text:
Important collection methods include:

Default
All
DCOnly
ComputerOnly
Session
LoggedOn
Group
ACL
GPOLocalGroup
Trusts
Container
LocalGroup
LocalAdmin
RDP
DCOM
PSRemote
ObjectProps
UserRights
CARegistry
DCRegistry
CertServices

Always check the current SharpHound documentation because collection capabilities evolve.

docs.title: Default Collection
docs.text:
A default SharpHound CE collection gathers important information including:

Group memberships
Domain trusts
AD object permissions
AD CS object permissions
OU structure
Group Policy links
Object properties
Local group relationships
User sessions

depending on accessibility and permissions.

docs.title: DCOnly
docs.text:
For a lower-impact directory-focused collection:

.\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods DCOnly

Conceptually:

SharpHound
    |
    v
Domain Controller
    |
    +--> Groups
    +--> Trusts
    +--> ACLs
    +--> AD CS objects
    +--> OUs
    +--> GPO links
    +--> Object properties

DCOnly avoids directly querying every domain-joined workstation/server for computer-specific data.

This can be useful when:

Reducing endpoint connections
Performing initial collection
Working under restrictive ROE
Performing directory-only analysis

docs.title: Session Collection
docs.text:
Sessions are more dynamic than many directory relationships.

.\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods Session

Sessions can reveal relationships such as:

User
 |
 v
Logged onto
 |
 v
Computer

These relationships may change frequently.

docs.title: Session Loop
docs.text:
SharpHound can repeatedly collect session information:

.\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods Session --Loop

A custom loop duration can be supplied:

.\SharpHound.exe \
    --CollectionMethods Session \
    --Loop \
    --LoopDuration 03:00:00

Session looping can significantly increase network and endpoint activity.

Use it only when authorised.

docs.title: Stealth Collection
docs.text:
SharpHound provides:

--Stealth

for supported collection workflows.

Example:

.\SharpHound.exe \
    --CollectionMethods Session \
    --Stealth

"Stealth" should not be interpreted as:

Undetectable

It changes collection behaviour but still generates observable activity.

docs.title: Scope Collection
docs.text:
Limit collection where possible.

For example, collection can be constrained using:

Domain
Distinguished Name
Computer list
LDAP filter

This is useful for:

Large environments
Restricted assessment scope
Sensitive networks
Phased assessments
Testing specific OUs

docs.title: Track Computer Calls
docs.text:
SharpHound can track computer collection attempts.

This can help answer:

Which systems were contacted?

Which requests failed?

Which systems were unreachable?

This is useful for both troubleshooting and evidence.

docs.title: SharpHound Workflow
docs.text:
Windows Access
      |
      v
Confirm Domain
      |
      v
Confirm DNS
      |
      v
Choose Collection Method
      |
      v
Run SharpHound
      |
      v
Collect ZIP
      |
      v
Transfer Securely
      |
      v
BloodHound CE

docs.title: BloodHound.py
docs.text:
BloodHound.py is a Python-based BloodHound ingestor originally developed for performing BloodHound collection from Linux systems.

It is based heavily on Python Active Directory protocol implementations and is useful when:

No Windows foothold exists

You are testing from Kali Linux

LDAP and SMB are reachable

You possess domain credentials

SharpHound cannot be executed

A Linux-native collector is preferable

docs.title: BloodHound.py Legacy vs CE
docs.text:
This distinction is important.

The primary BloodHound.py branch targets legacy BloodHound versions.

For BloodHound Community Edition, use the CE-compatible version.

Conceptually:

BloodHound Legacy
       |
       +--> bloodhound-python

BloodHound CE
       |
       +--> bloodhound-ce-python

Do not assume data generated for one version is automatically correct for another.

docs.title: Install BloodHound.py for BloodHound CE
docs.text:
Using pipx:

pipx install bloodhound-ce

Check:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

docs.title: Install BloodHound.py Legacy
docs.text:
For legacy BloodHound:

pipx install bloodhound

Command:

bloodhound-python

Do not confuse this with the CE collector.

docs.title: BloodHound.py Authentication
docs.text:
BloodHound.py supports authentication using mechanisms including:

Username + password
NTLM hash
AES key
Kerberos TGT / ccache

The exact options depend on the installed version.

Always inspect:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

before running a collection.

docs.title: BloodHound.py Basic Context
docs.text:
Set useful variables:

export DOMAIN="example.local"
export DC="dc01.example.local"
export DC_IP="10.10.20.10"
export USER="alice"

Verify DNS:

dig "$DC"

Verify LDAP SRV:

dig SRV "_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.$DOMAIN"

Verify Kerberos:

dig SRV "_kerberos._tcp.$DOMAIN"

docs.title: BloodHound.py Collection
docs.text:
The exact command should always be based on the installed CE version.

General structure:

bloodhound-ce-python \
    -u <username> \
    -p '<password>' \
    -d <domain> \
    -ns <dns-server> \
    -c <collection-methods>

Check:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

for current options.

docs.title: Collection Methods
docs.text:
BloodHound.py supports many BloodHound collection categories.

Examples include:

Group
LocalAdmin
Session
Trusts
ACL
Container
RDP
DCOM
PSRemote
ObjectProps
All

Support may not be identical to SharpHound.

When complete coverage matters, understand the limitations of the collector being used.

docs.title: BloodHound.py Workflow
docs.text:
Kali
 |
 v
Domain Credential
 |
 v
DNS
 |
 v
LDAP / SMB
 |
 v
bloodhound-ce-python
 |
 v
JSON Collection
 |
 v
BloodHound CE

docs.title: Kerberos with BloodHound.py
docs.text:
Kerberos collection requires correct:

DNS
Time
Domain
KDC
FQDN
Credential cache

Check:

date

dig "$DC"

If using a ccache:

export KRB5CCNAME=/path/to/user.ccache

Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

docs.title: NetExec BloodHound Ingestor
docs.text:
NetExec can also perform BloodHound-oriented LDAP collection.

This is particularly useful when NetExec is already being used during an internal assessment.

Conceptually:

NetExec
   |
   v
LDAP Authentication
   |
   v
BloodHound Collection
   |
   v
JSON / ZIP
   |
   v
BloodHound

This can reduce tool switching during an assessment.

docs.title: NetExec LDAP Context
docs.text:
Start by validating LDAP access:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

Check the current BloodHound options:

nxc ldap --help

NetExec syntax changes over time, so use the installed version's help output rather than assuming older command syntax.

docs.title: NetExec BloodHound Collection
docs.text:
The NetExec LDAP protocol contains BloodHound collection functionality.

Before collection, confirm:

Domain
Domain Controller
DNS
Credentials
BloodHound edition
Collection scope

Then inspect:

nxc ldap --help

for the current BloodHound collection options.

docs.title: NetExec BloodHound Workflow
docs.text:
nxc smb
   |
   v
Discover Environment
   |
   v
Validate Credential
   |
   v
nxc ldap
   |
   v
Directory Access
   |
   v
BloodHound Collection
   |
   v
BloodHound CE

This integrates naturally with the broader NetExec methodology.

docs.title: Choosing a Collector
docs.text:
Where am I?
    |
    +--> Windows
    |      |
    |      +--> SharpHound CE
    |
    +--> Linux / Kali
           |
           +--> BloodHound.py CE
           |
           +--> NetExec

Then consider:

Need maximum official compatibility?
        |
        +--> SharpHound CE

Need Linux-native collection?
        |
        +--> BloodHound.py CE

Already using NetExec heavily?
        |
        +--> NetExec BloodHound ingestor

Only have collected JSON/ZIP?
        |
        +--> BloodHound CE
        |
        +--> BloodBash

docs.title: Collector Comparison
docs.text:
Collector Platform Best Use SharpHound CE Windows Official BloodHound CE AD collection BloodHound.py CE Linux / Kali Linux-native AD collection NetExec Linux / Kali Integrated LDAP/BloodHound collection during NetExec workflows

Collection capabilities are not necessarily identical.

docs.title: Importing Data into BloodHound CE
docs.text:
SharpHound and compatible collectors generate:

JSON
ZIP

BloodHound CE can ingest collection data through the web interface.

Typical workflow:

BloodHound CE
     |
     v
Administration
     |
     v
Data Collection
     |
     v
File Ingest
     |
     v
Upload JSON / ZIP

The exact interface may change between releases.

docs.title: BloodHound Graph Model
docs.text:
BloodHound represents identity relationships as a graph.

Node
 |
 +--> User
 +--> Group
 +--> Computer
 +--> Domain
 +--> OU
 +--> GPO
 +--> Certificate Authority
 +--> Certificate Template

Relationships are represented as edges.

User
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
Group

or:

User
 |
 | AdminTo
 v
Computer

docs.title: Nodes and Edges
docs.text:
A graph contains:

Nodes = objects

Edges = relationships

Example:

ALICE
  |
  | MemberOf
  v
HELPDESK
  |
  | GenericAll
  v
SERVER ADMINS
  |
  | AdminTo
  v
APP01

The value of BloodHound comes from chaining relationships.

docs.title: Attack Paths
docs.text:
An attack path is a sequence of relationships that may allow one identity to influence another security object.

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
Computer
 |
 v
Privileged Session
 |
 v
Tier-0 Identity

BloodHound helps identify these relationships.

It does not automatically prove that every path is exploitable.

docs.title: Edge Interpretation
docs.text:
For every interesting edge ask:

What does this edge mean?

What security control creates it?

What permissions are required?

Is the relationship current?

Can I independently verify it?

Does exploitation require state changes?

What is the impact?

Is validation authorised?

docs.title: Common Relationships
docs.text:
Important relationships may include:

MemberOf
AdminTo
HasSession
CanRDP
CanPSRemote
ExecuteDCOM
GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
ForceChangePassword
AddMember
Owns
DCSync-related rights
AllowedToDelegate
AllowedToAct
GPO relationships
AD CS relationships
Trust relationships

The exact BloodHound edge model evolves over time.

docs.title: MemberOf
docs.text:
Example:

ALICE
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
HELPDESK

Nested membership matters.

ALICE
 |
 v
HELPDESK
 |
 v
SERVER ADMINS
 |
 v
ADMINISTRATORS

Do not only examine direct memberships.

docs.title: AdminTo
docs.text:
User / Group
     |
     | AdminTo
     v
Computer

This indicates an administrative relationship.

It does not necessarily mean:

The user is currently logged on

The host is reachable

Remote administration is enabled

Execution is authorised

Those conditions should be verified separately.

docs.title: HasSession
docs.text:
User
 |
 | HasSession
 v
Computer

Session data is highly useful but dynamic.

A session discovered earlier may no longer exist.

Treat session information as:

Potentially Time Sensitive

docs.title: CanRDP
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | CanRDP
   v
Computer

This indicates an RDP-related relationship.

Still verify:

RDP reachable
Account permitted
Network path
Authentication restrictions
MFA / NLA controls

docs.title: CanPSRemote
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | CanPSRemote
   v
Computer

Verify:

WinRM reachable
Authentication works
Remote management rights
Network controls

docs.title: ExecuteDCOM
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | ExecuteDCOM
   v
Computer

This represents a DCOM-related relationship.

Actual usability depends on:

Permissions
Firewall
RPC
DCOM configuration
Endpoint controls

docs.title: ACL Relationships
docs.text:
BloodHound is particularly useful for finding dangerous ACL relationships.

Examples include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
ForceChangePassword
AddMember

These may form paths such as:

User
 |
 | GenericAll
 v
Group
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
Privileged Group

docs.title: GenericAll
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Principal
   |
   | GenericAll
   v
Object

This represents broad control over the target object.

The exact security impact depends on the object type.

For example:

User
Group
Computer
OU
GPO

can each produce different attack possibilities.

docs.title: GenericWrite
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | GenericWrite
   v
Object

This represents permission to modify certain properties.

Do not automatically equate:

GenericWrite

with:

Full Control

The exploitable effect depends on the target object's writable attributes.

docs.title: WriteDacl
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | WriteDacl
   v
Object

This can allow modification of the object's access control list.

This is often a high-impact relationship because new permissions may be introduced.

docs.title: WriteOwner
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | WriteOwner
   v
Object

Ownership changes can affect the ability to alter permissions.

Treat validation carefully because changing ownership modifies directory state.

docs.title: ForceChangePassword
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | ForceChangePassword
   v
User

This indicates a password reset relationship.

Do not validate against real users without explicit approval because it can disrupt access and business operations.

docs.title: DCSync Relationships
docs.text:
BloodHound can identify principals with directory replication rights.

Conceptually:

Principal
   |
   +--> GetChanges
   |
   +--> GetChangesAll
   |
   v
Domain

These relationships may indicate DCSync capability.

Treat them as high impact.

Validation should be explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify:

Unconstrained delegation
Constrained delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

Graph relationships should then be analysed together with:

SPNs
Accounts
Computers
Privileges
Protocol transition
S4U configuration

docs.title: RBCD
docs.text:
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation relationships may appear as paths involving control over:

Computer objects
msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity

BloodHound can help reveal who controls the objects involved.

Detailed analysis belongs in:

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: Group Policy
docs.text:
BloodHound models:

OU
 |
 v
GPO
 |
 v
Computers / Users

and potentially permissions over the GPO itself.

Interesting questions include:

Who can modify the GPO?

Where is the GPO linked?

Which computers receive it?

Which users receive it?

Can a low-privilege identity influence it?

docs.title: AD CS
docs.text:
Modern BloodHound collection includes Active Directory Certificate Services relationships.

This can help identify relationships involving:

Certificate Authorities
Certificate Templates
Enrollment permissions
Template permissions
Certificate services configuration

BloodHound should complement, not replace, dedicated AD CS analysis.

Use tools such as Certipy where detailed certificate-service enumeration is required.

docs.title: Trusts
docs.text:
BloodHound can model trust relationships between domains.

Domain A
   |
   | Trust
   v
Domain B

Analyse:

Direction
Transitivity
Trust type
SID filtering
Selective authentication
Cross-domain group membership
Cross-domain ACLs

docs.title: High-Value Targets
docs.text:
High-value objects commonly include:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Domain Controllers
Tier-0 systems
Certificate Authorities
Privileged service accounts
Identity management infrastructure

But environment-specific critical systems may be equally important.

Do not rely solely on BloodHound's default high-value marking.

docs.title: Owned Principals
docs.text:
When a credential or identity has been confirmed under the assessment scope, mark it appropriately in BloodHound.

Conceptually:

Known Controlled Identity
        |
        v
Mark as Owned
        |
        v
Analyse Outbound Paths

This helps answer:

What can I reach from here?

docs.title: Re-Analyse After New Access
docs.text:
New Credential
      |
      v
Mark Owned
      |
      v
Search Outbound Paths
      |
      v
New Relationships
      |
      v
Validate

docs.title: Shortest Paths
docs.text:
Shortest paths can be useful for triage.

Owned User
    |
    v
Shortest Path
    |
    v
High Value Target

However:

Shortest
   !=
Best

Shortest
   !=
Safest

Shortest
   !=
Most Reliable

A longer path may be more realistic or less disruptive.

docs.title: Path Prioritisation
docs.text:
Evaluate paths using:

Path length
Required privileges
Operational impact
Detection likelihood
Credential requirements
Network reachability
State changes
Business risk
Rules of engagement

A useful model:

Candidate Path
      |
      v
Technically Possible?
      |
      v
Reachable?
      |
      v
Credentials Available?
      |
      v
Safe?
      |
      v
Authorised?
      |
      v
Validate

docs.title: Neo4j
docs.text:
BloodHound historically used Neo4j directly as its graph database, and legacy BloodHound deployments are often encountered with Neo4j.

This remains relevant when:

Using legacy BloodHound

Reviewing older assessment environments

Working with existing Neo4j databases

Performing custom Cypher analysis

Conceptually:

BloodHound Data
      |
      v
Neo4j
      |
      v
Graph
      |
      v
Cypher

BloodHound CE architecture has evolved beyond the older "BloodHound desktop application + manually managed Neo4j" model.

Do not assume modern BloodHound CE installation instructions are identical to legacy BloodHound.

docs.title: Cypher
docs.text:
Cypher is a graph query language associated with Neo4j and graph-based BloodHound analysis.

Conceptually:

MATCH (n)
RETURN n
LIMIT 10

This returns graph nodes.

docs.title: Find Users
docs.text:
Example conceptual query:

MATCH (u:User)
RETURN u
LIMIT 25

docs.title: Find Computers
docs.text:
MATCH (c:Computer)
RETURN c
LIMIT 25

docs.title: Find Groups
docs.text:
MATCH (g:Group)
RETURN g
LIMIT 25

docs.title: Find Domain Admin Members
docs.text:
A conceptual relationship query may look like:

MATCH (u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)
WHERE g.name CONTAINS 'DOMAIN ADMINS'
RETURN u,g

Schema and query behaviour can vary between BloodHound versions.

Validate queries against the installed version.

docs.title: Find Administrative Relationships
docs.text:
Conceptually:

MATCH (u:User)-[:AdminTo]->(c:Computer)
RETURN u,c

docs.title: Find Sessions
docs.text:
Conceptually:

MATCH (u:User)-[:HasSession]->(c:Computer)
RETURN u,c

docs.title: Custom Queries
docs.text:
Custom graph queries are valuable when investigating:

Specific groups
Specific users
Specific servers
Delegation
ACL relationships
Cross-domain relationships
Privileged sessions
Certificate services

Do not rely only on pre-built queries.

docs.title: BloodBash
docs.text:
BloodBash is an open-source offline analyser for SharpHound and AzureHound data.

It is useful when you want to:

Analyse SharpHound data quickly

Avoid running a BloodHound server

Avoid maintaining Neo4j

Perform offline triage

Analyse collected JSON or ZIP files

Generate prioritised findings

Inspect attack paths from the terminal

Conceptually:

SharpHound
    |
    v
