docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Constrained delegation limits Kerberos delegation to explicitly configured backend services.

The fundamental configuration is:

Delegating Account
        |
        v
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
        |
        v
Destination SPN

The main authentication models are:

Kerberos Only

and:

Protocol Transition

Protocol transition introduces:

TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

and makes the S4U flow particularly important:

Front-End Service
      |
      v
S4U2Self
      |
      v
User Representation
      |
      v
S4U2Proxy
      |
      v
Configured Backend Service

The central security question is not merely:

Does constrained delegation exist?

It is:

Who controls the delegating account?
        |
        v
Which SPNs are permitted?
        |
        v
Which users can be represented?
        |
        v
What privileges do those users
have at the destination?

A complete attack path therefore looks like:

Account Compromise
       |
       v
Delegation Capability
       |
       v
S4U
       |
       v
User Impersonation
       |
       v
Configured Service
       |
       v
User's Permissions

Constrained delegation is safer than unconstrained delegation because the delegation scope is restricted, but it should still be treated as a sensitive Active Directory trust relationship.

The defensive objective is:

Remove Unnecessary Delegation
          +
Minimise Destination SPNs
          +
Protect Delegating Accounts
          +
Protect Sensitive Users
          +
Harden Account ACLs
          +
Segment Backend Services
          +
Monitor Delegation Changes
          +
Monitor Kerberos Activity

A mature assessment should therefore combine delegation enumeration, SPN analysis, account-control analysis, ACL analysis, BloodHound attack-path analysis, minimum-impact S4U validation, Kerberos telemetry, and application context rather than treating msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo as an isolated vulnerability.

docs.title: Active Directory Credential Access
docs.text:
Credential Access is the process of identifying, obtaining, or recovering authentication material that can be used to authenticate as users, computers, or services within an Active Directory environment.

Active Directory environments contain many different forms of authentication material.

Examples include:

Passwords
NT Hashes
Kerberos Keys
Kerberos Tickets
Certificates
Private Keys
Service Account Credentials
Computer Account Credentials
Managed Service Account Secrets
Cached Credentials
LSASS Credentials
DPAPI-Protected Secrets
NTDS.dit Credential Data
Group Policy Preference Credentials
LAPS Passwords
Application Credentials
Configuration File Secrets

From an attack-path perspective:

Initial Access
     |
     v
Credential Access
     |
     v
Additional Identity
     |
     v
Additional Permissions
     |
     v
Lateral Movement
     |
     v
Privilege Escalation

Credential Access is therefore not a single technique.

It is a collection of techniques for discovering and obtaining authentication material from:

Active Directory
Endpoints
Domain Controllers
SYSVOL
Memory
Registry
Files
Applications
Certificates
Backups
Management Platforms

A useful assessment model is:

Identity
   |
   v
Accessible Credential Source
   |
   v
Credential Material
   |
   v
Authentication Capability
   |
   v
Resulting Access

Authorised testing only

Credential-access testing can expose highly sensitive authentication material and may affect many systems beyond the original test target. Prefer read-only enumeration and dedicated test identities wherever possible. Do not dump production credentials merely to demonstrate that a permission exists when the exposure can be proven through ACLs, metadata, configuration, or controlled test credentials. Treat hashes, tickets, certificates, private keys, passwords, credential databases, and memory dumps as sensitive evidence and securely remove temporary copies after the engagement.

docs.title: Credential Access Is Broader Than Passwords
docs.text:
A common mistake is to think:

Credential
    =
Password

In Active Directory, many objects can function as credentials.

For example:

Password
   |
   +--> Interactive Authentication
   |
   +--> NTLM
   |
   +--> Kerberos Key Derivation

But authentication may also occur using:

NT Hash
Kerberos AES Key
TGT
Service Ticket
Certificate + Private Key
Computer Account Password

Therefore:

No Plaintext Password

does not mean:

No Credential Compromise

docs.title: Credential Material Model
docs.text:
A useful classification is:

Credential Material
      |
      +--> Knowledge
      |
      |     +--> Password
      |
      +--> Password-Derived Material
      |
      |     +--> NT Hash
      |     +--> Kerberos AES Keys
      |
      +--> Tickets
      |
      |     +--> TGT
      |     +--> TGS
      |
      +--> Certificates
      |
      |     +--> Certificate
      |     +--> Private Key
      |
      +--> Managed Secrets
      |
      |     +--> LAPS
      |     +--> gMSA
      |
      +--> Stored Credentials
            |
            +--> DPAPI
            +--> Credential Manager
            +--> Configuration Files

docs.title: Credential Sources
docs.text:
During an Active Directory assessment, credentials may exist in several layers:

Domain
 |
 +--> NTDS.dit
 +--> AD Attributes
 +--> LAPS
 +--> gMSA
 +--> Certificates
 |
Endpoints
 |
 +--> LSASS
 +--> SAM
 +--> LSA Secrets
 +--> Cached Logons
 +--> DPAPI
 +--> Credential Manager
 |
SYSVOL
 |
 +--> GPP
 +--> Scripts
 +--> Configuration Files
 |
Applications
 |
 +--> Service Credentials
 +--> Database Credentials
 +--> API Secrets
 +--> Deployment Credentials

docs.title: Credential Access Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
A structured workflow is:

Enumerate Identity
      |
      v
Enumerate Accessible Sources
      |
      v
Identify Credential Material
      |
      v
Determine Access Requirements
      |
      v
Assess Resulting Identity
      |
      v
Map Attack Path
      |
      v
Validate Safely
      |
      v
Collect Minimum Evidence
      |
      v
Cleanup

docs.title: Start with the Controlled Identity
docs.text:
Before searching for credentials, understand the identity already controlled.

Record:

Username
Domain
SID
Group Membership
Privileges
Local Rights
Directory ACLs
Computer Access
Share Access

Example:

whoami

whoami /user

whoami /groups

whoami /priv

PowerShell:

[System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()

docs.title: Why Identity Context Matters
docs.text:
Suppose the controlled identity is:

CORP\alice

The correct question is not:

Can credentials be dumped somewhere?

Instead:

What credential sources can Alice legitimately reach?

For example:

Alice
 |
 +--> Read SYSVOL
 |
 +--> Read Deployment Share
 |
 +--> Read LAPS Password for CLIENT01
 |
 +--> Read gMSA Password
 |
 +--> Local Admin on SERVER01

Each relationship creates a different credential-access opportunity.

docs.title: Credential Access and BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify credential-related attack paths.

Examples include relationships involving:

AdminTo
HasSession
ReadLAPSPassword
ReadGMSAPassword
AddKeyCredentialLink
DCSync
Certificate Relationships

depending on BloodHound version and collected data.

A useful model is:

Controlled User
      |
      v
BloodHound
      |
      v
Credential-Relevant Relationship
      |
      v
Target Identity / System

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: Credential Access and Active Directory ACLs
docs.text:
Many credential exposures are fundamentally authorization problems.

Examples:

User
 |
 v
Read LAPS Password
 |
 v
Computer

User
 |
 v
Read gMSA Password
 |
 v
Service Account

User
 |
 v
Replication Rights
 |
 v
Domain
 |
 v
DCSync

User
 |
 v
Write Key Credential Link
 |
 v
Target Account

Therefore credential-access testing should be closely connected to ACL analysis.

See:

Active Directory ACL and ACE Abuse

docs.title: Credential Access Categories
docs.text:
A practical Active Directory credential-access review can be divided into:

1. Directory-Stored Credentials
2. SYSVOL Credentials
3. Managed Passwords
4. Endpoint Credentials
5. Domain Controller Credentials
6. Kerberos Credentials
7. Certificate Credentials
8. Application Credentials
9. Backup Credentials
10. Cloud / Hybrid Credentials

docs.title: Directory-Stored Credential Material
docs.text:
Active Directory contains information that may directly or indirectly expose authentication material.

Examples include:

LAPS Password Attributes
gMSA Managed Passwords
Password-Related Metadata
Certificate Credentials
Key Credentials
Replication Secrets

Access is normally controlled through directory ACLs.

docs.title: SYSVOL Credential Sources
docs.text:
SYSVOL is intentionally accessible to domain members because Group Policy must be distributed throughout the domain.

Typical location:

\\corp.example\SYSVOL

Potentially sensitive content includes:

Group Policy Preferences
PowerShell Scripts
Batch Scripts
VBScript
Configuration Files
Deployment Scripts
Legacy Passwords
Service Credentials

docs.title: Enumerate SYSVOL
docs.text:
Windows:

dir \\corp.example\SYSVOL

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem \
    '\\corp.example\SYSVOL' \
    -Recurse \
    -File \
    -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Search SYSVOL for Credential Keywords
docs.text:
A read-only search:

Get-ChildItem \
    '\\corp.example\SYSVOL' \
    -Recurse \
    -File \
    -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String \
        -Pattern 'password|passwd|pwd|secret|token|apikey|cpassword' \
        -CaseSensitive:$false \
        -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Matches require manual validation.

A string containing:

password

does not automatically contain a real credential.

docs.title: Group Policy Preference Passwords
docs.text:
Historical Group Policy Preferences could store passwords using:

cpassword

inside XML configuration.

Potential files include:

Groups.xml
Services.xml
ScheduledTasks.xml
Drives.xml
DataSources.xml
Printers.xml

Example path:

\\corp.example\SYSVOL\corp.example\Policies\
{GPO-GUID}\Machine\Preferences\Groups\Groups.xml

A dedicated page should cover this issue:

active-directory/gpp-passwords.md

docs.title: Search for cpassword
docs.text:
Windows:

findstr /S /I "cpassword" \\corp.example\SYSVOL\corp.example\Policies\*.xml

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem \
    '\\corp.example\SYSVOL\corp.example\Policies' \
    -Recurse \
    -Filter '*.xml' \
    -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String \
        -Pattern 'cpassword'

This is read-only.

docs.title: LAPS
docs.text:
Local Administrator Password Solution technologies provide managed local administrator passwords.

Two broad implementations may be encountered:

Legacy Microsoft LAPS
Windows LAPS

The security question is:

Who can read the password?

Conceptually:

Computer
 |
 v
LAPS Password Attribute
 |
 v
Directory ACL
 |
 v
Authorised Reader

An excessive read permission can become:

Controlled User
      |
      v
Read LAPS Password
      |
      v
Local Administrator
      |
      v
Target Computer

LAPS should be covered in detail in:

Active Directory LAPS

docs.title: Legacy LAPS Attributes
docs.text:
Legacy Microsoft LAPS commonly uses attributes including:

ms-Mcs-AdmPwd
ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime

The password attribute is sensitive.

Do not retrieve production LAPS passwords unless required for authorised validation.

docs.title: Windows LAPS Attributes
docs.text:
Windows LAPS introduces attributes including:

msLAPS-Password
msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime
msLAPS-EncryptedPassword
msLAPS-EncryptedPasswordHistory

depending on configuration.

Windows LAPS can also protect password information through encryption.

docs.title: LAPS Enumeration
docs.text:
Where the Windows LAPS PowerShell module is available, administrators and authorised testers can inspect configured rights using supported LAPS cmdlets.

Always inspect the installed module:

Get-Command *Laps*

and:

Get-Help Find-LapsADExtendedRights -Full

where available.

The goal during assessment is initially:

Identify Readers

not:

Retrieve Every Password

docs.title: gMSA
docs.text:
Group Managed Service Accounts provide automatically managed service-account passwords.

They are commonly used for:

Windows Services
Scheduled Tasks
IIS Application Pools
Enterprise Applications

The relevant credential material is represented through:

msDS-ManagedPassword

for authorised principals.

docs.title: gMSA Security Model
docs.text:
gMSA
 |
 v
msDS-ManagedPassword
 |
 v
Directory ACL
 |
 v
Authorised Computer / Principal

If an attacker controls a principal authorised to retrieve the managed password:

Controlled Principal
        |
        v
Read Managed Password
        |
        v
Derive Authentication Material
        |
        v
Authenticate as gMSA

A dedicated page should cover:

Group Managed Service Accounts - gMSA

docs.title: Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Key Credential Link abuse involves the:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

attribute.

This is different from stealing an existing password.

Instead, an attacker with sufficient write permissions may be able to introduce alternative key-based authentication material for a target account.

Conceptually:

Controlled User
      |
      v
Write msDS-KeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
Target Account
      |
      v
Attacker-Controlled Key Credential
      |
      v
Certificate-Based Authentication

This should be treated as credential-access and persistence-related behaviour.

A dedicated page should cover:

Active Directory Shadow Credentials

docs.title: Endpoint Credential Sources
docs.text:
Windows endpoints may contain credentials or credential-derived material in:

LSASS
SAM
SECURITY Hive
Credential Manager
DPAPI
Registry
Configuration Files
Browser Data
PowerShell History
Application Files
Scheduled Tasks
Services

The ability to access these sources depends heavily on local privilege.

docs.title: Local Administrator Context
docs.text:
Credential access changes substantially when the controlled principal becomes:

Local Administrator

Conceptually:

Domain User
    |
    v
Local Administrator
    |
    v
Protected Local Resources
    |
    v
Potential Credential Material

This is why local administrative relationships are important during Active Directory attack-path analysis.

docs.title: LSASS
docs.text:
The Local Security Authority Subsystem Service:

lsass.exe

plays a central role in Windows authentication.

Depending on:

Windows Version
Authentication Packages
Credential Guard
LSA Protection
Logged-On Sessions
Security Configuration

LSASS may contain authentication material useful to an attacker.

docs.title: LSASS Credential Exposure
docs.text:
Potential material historically associated with LSASS includes:

NT Hashes
Kerberos Tickets
Kerberos Keys
Authentication Package Data

The exact material available depends on system configuration and current sessions.

Do not assume plaintext passwords will be available.

docs.title: LSASS Testing Safety
docs.text:
Dumping LSASS is intrusive and frequently triggers endpoint security controls.

During an assessment:

Local Admin Confirmed
       |
       v
Is Credential Dump Required?
       |
       +--> No
       |     |
       |     v
       |   Stop
       |
       +--> Yes
             |
             v
      Explicitly Authorised?
             |
             +--> No -> Stop
             |
             +--> Yes
                   |
                   v
             Controlled Validation

Often the existence of local administrative access is already sufficient evidence for the primary finding.

docs.title: Credential Guard
docs.text:
Windows Defender Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to help isolate secrets.

Credential Guard can reduce exposure of certain credential material.

Its presence should be recorded during endpoint security assessment.

PowerShell/system configuration methods can be used to determine whether virtualization-based security protections are configured and running.

docs.title: LSA Protection
docs.text:
LSA protection can run LSASS as a protected process.

This raises the barrier for unauthorized access to LSASS memory.

Credential Guard and LSA protection are complementary but distinct controls.

docs.title: SAM
docs.text:
The local Security Account Manager database stores local account password hashes.

Relevant registry hive:

SAM

Access to the raw hive normally requires elevated privileges.

The associated boot/system key material is required to interpret protected secrets.

docs.title: Local SAM Model
docs.text:
Local User Password
       |
       v
NT Hash
       |
       v
SAM

This is separate from domain credential storage.

docs.title: Local vs Domain Credentials
docs.text:
A local account:

.\Administrator

is different from:

CORP\Administrator

Likewise:

Local SAM Hash

is not automatically:

Domain NT Hash

This distinction is essential during reporting.

docs.title: LSA Secrets
docs.text:
Windows can store system and service-related secrets protected by the Local Security Authority.

Potential examples include:

Service Account Secrets
Machine Account Secrets
Cached Authentication Material

Access normally requires elevated privileges.

docs.title: Cached Domain Logons
docs.text:
Windows may cache information that allows users to log on when a domain controller is unavailable.

These cached values are not equivalent to reusable NT hashes.

Conceptually:

Cached Domain Credential
       |
       v
Offline Logon Verification

They are designed differently from normal NTLM credential material.

Do not report cached domain logon values as:

NT Hashes

docs.title: DPAPI
docs.text:
Windows Data Protection API:

DPAPI

protects many user and system secrets.

Applications can use DPAPI to encrypt data tied to:

User Context

or:

Machine Context

Potential DPAPI-protected data includes:

Credential Manager Secrets
Browser Credentials
Application Secrets
Certificates
Private Keys
Wi-Fi Credentials

depending on application and system configuration.

docs.title: DPAPI Model
docs.text:
User Credential / Machine Secret
          |
          v
DPAPI Key Hierarchy
          |
          v
Master Key
          |
          v
Protected Application Secret

Obtaining a DPAPI blob does not necessarily mean the plaintext secret has been recovered.

docs.title: Credential Manager
docs.text:
Windows Credential Manager can store:

Windows Credentials
Generic Credentials
Application Credentials

Native enumeration:

cmdkey /list

This shows stored credential targets but does not normally reveal plaintext passwords.

docs.title: PowerShell History
docs.text:
PowerShell command history may reveal sensitive information if administrators entered secrets directly on the command line.

Common location:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Review:

Get-Content \
    (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

where authorised.

Search carefully for:

-password
-credential
token
secret
key

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Common credential locations include:

web.config
appsettings.json
app.config
*.ini
*.xml
*.yml
*.yaml
*.conf
*.config
.env

Searches should be targeted rather than indiscriminately copying entire file systems.

docs.title: Example PowerShell Search
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem \
    'C:\inetpub' \
    -Recurse \
    -File \
    -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String \
        -Pattern 'password|passwd|pwd|secret|token|connectionString' \
        -CaseSensitive:$false \
        -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Use application-specific paths whenever possible.

docs.title: Service Credentials
docs.text:
Windows services may run under:

LocalSystem
LocalService
NetworkService
Domain User
gMSA
Virtual Account

Enumerate:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        StartName,
        State,
        PathName

Domain user service accounts deserve further review.

docs.title: Scheduled Task Credentials
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks may run under domain or local identities.

Native enumeration:

schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask |
    Select-Object \
        TaskName,
        TaskPath,
        State

The presence of a privileged task does not mean its password is directly retrievable.

docs.title: IIS Application Pools
docs.text:
IIS applications may use:

ApplicationPoolIdentity
NetworkService
LocalSystem
Domain Service Account
gMSA

Review application-pool identities when assessing Windows web servers.

Avoid extracting secrets unless required.

docs.title: Network Shares
docs.text:
Credential material frequently appears on administrative or deployment shares.

Examples:

Software
Deployment
Scripts
Backups
IT
Install
Config
DevOps

The attack model is:

Domain User
     |
     v
Readable Share
     |
     v
Configuration / Script
     |
     v
Credential

docs.title: Share Enumeration
docs.text:
NetExec can help identify accessible SMB shares.

General pattern:

nxc smb <TARGET> \
    -u '<USER>' \
    -p '<PASSWORD>' \
    --shares

For a domain account:

nxc smb fileserver.corp.example \
    -d corp.example \
    -u alice \
    -p '<PASSWORD>' \
    --shares

Check:

nxc smb --help

for the installed version.

docs.title: Impacket smbclient
docs.text:
Impacket can also be used:

impacket-smbclient \
    'corp.example/alice:<PASSWORD>@fileserver.corp.example'

This can support manual inspection of authorised shares.

See:

Impacket

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Backups may contain highly sensitive Active Directory data.

Potential sources include:

System State Backups
Domain Controller Images
VM Snapshots
NTDS.dit Copies
Registry Hives
Configuration Backups
Application Backups

A backup containing domain-controller state should be treated as Tier 0 material.

docs.title: NTDS.dit
docs.text:
The Active Directory database is stored in:

NTDS.dit

on domain controllers.

It contains directory information including password-derived credential data.

Conceptually:

Domain Controller
      |
      v
NTDS.dit
      |
      +
SYSTEM Secrets
      |
      v
Domain Credential Material

Access to this data represents severe credential exposure.

A dedicated page should cover:

NTDS.dit and Active Directory Credential Extraction

docs.title: NTDS Access Is High Impact
docs.text:
Obtaining credential material from NTDS can potentially expose:

Domain Users
Service Accounts
Privileged Accounts
Computer Accounts
Historical Password Material

depending on the technique and data.

This should not be performed merely to prove domain administrative access.

docs.title: DCSync
docs.text:
DCSync is conceptually different from copying:

NTDS.dit

Instead, a principal with the required directory replication permissions can request password-related data through domain replication protocols.

Conceptually:

Controlled Principal
       |
       v
Replication Rights
       |
       v
Domain Controller
       |
       v
Directory Replication
       |
       v
Credential Data

docs.title: DCSync Rights
docs.text:
Important replication rights commonly include:

DS-Replication-Get-Changes
DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All

Additional rights may matter depending on the data and domain configuration.

These permissions should be tightly restricted.

docs.title: DCSync Attack Path
docs.text:
Alice
 |
 v
Replication Rights
 |
 v
Domain
 |
 v
DCSync Capability
 |
 v
Domain Credential Material

This is generally a high-impact or critical attack path.

docs.title: DCSync Validation
docs.text:
In many assessments, it is unnecessary to retrieve every domain credential.

A safer model is:

Confirm Replication Rights
       |
       v
Confirm Attack Path
       |
       v
If Required:
Request Dedicated Test Account

Avoid dumping all domain credentials when a test identity can demonstrate the issue.

docs.title: secretsdump
docs.text:
Impacket provides:

secretsdump.py

commonly exposed as:

impacket-secretsdump

It supports several credential extraction scenarios involving Windows systems and Active Directory.

Because its use can retrieve highly sensitive credentials, it should only be used where specifically authorised.

Inspect current options:

impacket-secretsdump -h

before use.

docs.title: Scope secretsdump Validation
docs.text:
Where DCSync validation is explicitly required, prefer targeting a dedicated account rather than retrieving the complete domain credential set.

The objective is:

Prove Replication Capability

not:

Collect Maximum Credentials

docs.title: Kerberos Tickets
docs.text:
Kerberos tickets are credentials.

Important types include:

TGT
TGS

A stolen or otherwise controlled valid ticket may permit authentication without knowing the user's plaintext password.

See:

Kerberos Tickets

and:

Pass-the-Ticket

docs.title: Kerberos Keys
docs.text:
Long-term Kerberos keys can also function as reusable authentication material.

Examples include:

RC4 / NT-derived Key
AES128
AES256

See:

Pass-the-Key

docs.title: NT Hashes
docs.text:
The NT hash can be security-sensitive because it may be used by authentication protocols or to derive/use Kerberos-compatible key material in appropriate circumstances.

Relevant techniques include:

Pass-the-Hash

and:

OverPass-the-Hash

docs.title: NetNTLM Challenge-Response
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

NT Hash

with:

NetNTLMv2 Challenge-Response

The relationship is:

NT Hash
   |
   v
Used Internally in NTLM Authentication

while:

Captured NetNTLMv2
   |
   +--> Offline Guessing
   |
   +--> Potential Relay

A captured NetNTLMv2 response is not itself an NT hash.

See:

NTLM

docs.title: Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Kerberoasting is a credential-access technique involving Kerberos service tickets for accounts with SPNs.

Conceptually:

Domain User
    |
    v
Request Service Ticket
    |
    v
TGS
    |
    v
Offline Password Guessing
    |
    v
Service Account Password

See:

Kerberoasting

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting
docs.text:
AS-REP Roasting applies to accounts where Kerberos pre-authentication is disabled.

Conceptually:

Account
 |
 v
Pre-Authentication Disabled
 |
 v
AS-REP
 |
 v
Offline Password Guessing

See:

AS-REP Roasting

docs.title: Password Spraying
docs.text:
Password spraying attempts a small number of candidate passwords across multiple accounts.

Conceptually:

One Password
    |
    +--> User A
    +--> User B
    +--> User C
    +--> User D

It differs from credential extraction but may provide the initial identity required to reach other credential sources.

See:

Password Spraying

docs.title: Certificates as Credentials
docs.text:
In Active Directory environments using AD CS, certificates can become authentication credentials.

Conceptually:

Certificate
    +
Private Key
    |
    v
Authentication

Therefore:

Certificate + Private Key

should be protected similarly to passwords, hashes, and Kerberos keys.

docs.title: Certificate Credential Model
docs.text:
Certificate Template
       |
       v
Certificate Issued
       |
       v
Private Key Controlled
       |
       v
Authentication Capability

AD CS misconfiguration can therefore become a credential-access and privilege-escalation path.

docs.title: Private Keys
docs.text:
A certificate without the associated private key generally does not provide the same authentication capability as possession of both.

Therefore evidence should distinguish:

Certificate Only

from:

Certificate + Private Key

docs.title: PFX / PKCS#12
docs.text:
Certificates and private keys may be stored in containers such as:

.pfx
.p12

These files may themselves be password protected.

Treat them as highly sensitive.

docs.title: Credential Access and Delegation
docs.text:
Kerberos delegation can expose authentication capability under specific conditions.

Relevant areas include:

Unconstrained Delegation

Constrained Delegation

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

S4U

Delegation should be understood as an authentication relationship rather than simply a credential dump.

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
A compromised unconstrained delegation host may become particularly sensitive when privileged users authenticate to it.

Conceptually:

Privileged User
      |
      v
Delegation Host
      |
      v
Delegated Kerberos Material
      |
      v
Potential Reuse

See:

Unconstrained Delegation

docs.title: Credential Reuse
docs.text:
Once a credential is obtained, determine:

Where is it valid?

Do not automatically attempt it against every system.

A safe process is:

Credential
   |
   v
Identify Intended Scope
   |
   v
Identify Authorised Targets
   |
   v
Validate Minimum Necessary Access

docs.title: Credential Blast Radius
docs.text:
Credential value depends on:

Identity
 +
Privilege
 +
Reuse
 +
Reachability
 +
Authentication Protocol
 =
Blast Radius

Examples:

Local Administrator Password

may affect one system if unique.

The same password reused across 100 servers can create a much larger risk.

docs.title: Local Administrator Password Reuse
docs.text:
A common historical weakness is:

SERVER01\Administrator
        |
        v
Same Password
        |
        +--> SERVER02
        +--> SERVER03
        +--> SERVER04

LAPS is designed to reduce this risk by providing unique managed local administrator passwords.

docs.title: Service Account Password Reuse
docs.text:
Service accounts may be used across:

Services
Scheduled Tasks
Applications
Servers
Databases

A compromised service account can therefore have a broad blast radius.

During assessment, determine:

Where is this account used?

rather than indiscriminately authenticating everywhere.

docs.title: Privileged Credential Exposure
docs.text:
Prioritise credentials belonging to:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Administrators
Backup Operators
Server Administrators
Certificate Administrators
Virtualisation Administrators
Management Platform Accounts
High-Privilege Service Accounts
Tier 0 Operators

But avoid retrieving such credentials unless necessary.

docs.title: Privileged Sessions
docs.text:
A compromised server may become more significant when privileged administrators log on to it.

Conceptually:

Compromised Server
       |
       v
Privileged Admin Logs On
       |
       v
Credential / Ticket Exposure
       |
       v
Privilege Escalation

This is one reason administrative tiering is important.

docs.title: BloodHound HasSession
docs.text:
Session information can help identify where users are currently or recently authenticated.

However:

HasSession

should not automatically be interpreted as:

Credential Available

It is an indicator that requires further validation.

docs.title: Credential Hunting Priorities
docs.text:
A useful prioritisation model is:

1. Directory ACL-Based Credential Access
2. Managed Password Exposure
3. SYSVOL / Share Secrets
4. Service Configuration
5. Endpoint Credential Exposure
6. Domain Controller Credential Access

Start with lower-impact sources.

docs.title: Low-Impact Credential Discovery
docs.text:
Prefer:

Directory Enumeration
ACL Analysis
Configuration Review
Metadata
Group Membership
BloodHound

before:

Memory Dumping
Registry Hive Extraction
NTDS Extraction
Mass Credential Collection

docs.title: Credential Access Validation Levels
docs.text:
A useful hierarchy is:

Level 1
Identify Potential Credential Source

Level 2
Confirm Read Permission

Level 3
Read Metadata

Level 4
Retrieve Dedicated Test Credential

Level 5
Authenticate with Test Credential

Level 6
Retrieve Production Credential

Level 7
Use Production Credential for Lateral Movement

Use the lowest level that proves the issue.

docs.title: Example - LAPS
docs.text:
Instead of:

Read Every LAPS Password

prefer:

Identify Excessive Reader
       |
       v
Confirm ACL
       |
       v
Retrieve One Approved Test Password
       |
       v
Validate Test Computer

where active proof is required.

docs.title: Example - gMSA
docs.text:
Instead of:

Dump Every gMSA Secret

prefer:

Identify gMSA
     |
     v
Identify Password Readers
     |
     v
Confirm Controlled Principal Has Read Access
     |
     v
Retrieve Only if Required

docs.title: Example - DCSync
docs.text:
Instead of:

Replicate All Domain Hashes

prefer:

Confirm Replication Rights
       |
       v
Request Dedicated Test Account
       |
       v
Replicate Only Test Account

where tooling and scope permit.

docs.title: Example - LSASS
docs.text:
Instead of:

Dump LSASS from Production Server

prefer:

Confirm Local Administrator
       |
       v
Confirm Privileged Session
       |
       v
Document Potential Exposure

unless credential extraction is explicitly required.

docs.title: Credential Evidence Handling
docs.text:
Credentials should not be placed unnecessarily in:

Screenshots
Tickets
Chat Messages
Email
Git Repositories
Plaintext Notes
Final Reports

Use redaction.

Example:

Password:
Sup3rSecretPassword!

should become:

Password:
[REDACTED]

docs.title: Hash Redaction
docs.text:
Instead of storing:

Administrator:500:<FULL_HASH>

use:

Administrator:500:[REDACTED]

or, where correlation is necessary:

NT Hash:
8846f7... [truncated]

Do not retain more credential material than required.

docs.title: Ticket Handling
docs.text:
Files such as:

.ccache
.kirbi

may contain reusable authentication material.

Treat them as credentials.

Cleanup should include:

Delete Test Tickets
Unset KRB5CCNAME
Purge Test Sessions
Remove Temporary Files

docs.title: Certificate Handling
docs.text:
Files such as:

.pfx
.p12
.pem
.key

may contain private keys.

Treat them as credentials.

Do not commit them to:

Git
Documentation
Shared Repositories

docs.title: Memory Dumps
docs.text:
Memory dumps may contain far more information than the credential being tested.

They can expose:

Other Users
Tokens
Keys
Application Data
Personal Data
Secrets

This makes them particularly sensitive evidence.

docs.title: Credential Storage During Assessment
docs.text:
Use:

Encrypted Storage
Restricted Permissions
Minimum Retention
Controlled Evidence Directory

Avoid:

World-Readable Files
Shared Folders
Public Git Repositories
Cloud Sync Without Approval

docs.title: Credential Cleanup
docs.text:
At the end of testing:

Credential Artefacts
      |
      +--> Password Notes
      +--> Hash Files
      +--> Kerberos Tickets
      +--> PFX Files
      +--> Private Keys
      +--> Memory Dumps
      +--> Registry Hives
      +--> NTDS Copies
      +--> Temporary Scripts

should be handled according to the agreed evidence-retention policy.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Credential Access detection should combine:

Identity Telemetry
     +
Endpoint Telemetry
     +
Directory Auditing
     +
Kerberos Events
     +
NTLM Events
     +
File Access
     +
Process Activity

No single event detects all credential-access techniques.

docs.title: Credential Access Detection Model
docs.text:
Credential Source
      |
      v
Access Attempt
      |
      v
Collection
      |
      v
Authentication
      |
      v
Lateral Movement

Detection opportunities exist at each stage.

docs.title: Detect Directory Credential Access
docs.text:
Monitor unusual access to:

LAPS Attributes
gMSA Password Attributes
Replication Rights
Key Credential Link
Certificate Configuration

especially from principals that do not normally perform administrative operations.

docs.title: Event 4662
docs.text:
Security event:

4662

can record operations performed on Active Directory objects when the appropriate auditing and SACL configuration is enabled.

This can be useful for detecting certain directory credential-access techniques, including replication-related activity.

docs.title: Event 5136
docs.text:
Event:

5136

can record directory object modifications.

Relevant examples include changes to:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink
msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity
Delegation Configuration
Sensitive ACL-Related Attributes

depending on auditing configuration.

docs.title: Kerberos Events
docs.text:
Important Kerberos events include:

4768
4769
4770
4771

These can help identify:

TGT Requests
Service Ticket Requests
Ticket Renewals
Pre-Authentication Failures

depending on the event.

docs.title: NTLM Events
docs.text:
Useful authentication events include:

4624
4625
4648
4776

depending on the authentication path and audit configuration.

See:

NTLM

docs.title: Event 4688
docs.text:
Where process creation auditing is enabled:

4688

can help identify processes associated with credential-access activity.

Command-line logging can significantly improve context.

docs.title: Endpoint Detection
docs.text:
EDR telemetry can help identify:

Unexpected LSASS Access
Memory Dump Creation
Registry Hive Access
Credential Tool Execution
Suspicious PowerShell
Unusual Certificate Export
DPAPI Access

Detection should focus on behaviour rather than only tool names.

docs.title: Do Not Detect Only Mimikatz
docs.text:
A weak detection model is:

Process Name = mimikatz.exe

Attackers can:

Rename Tools
Use Different Tools
Use Native APIs
Use Remote Techniques
Use Custom Implementations

Prefer behavioural detections.

docs.title: LSASS Detection Model
docs.text:
Process
 |
 v
Opens LSASS
 |
 v
Requests Sensitive Access
 |
 v
Reads Memory
 |
 v
Credential Material

Investigate unusual processes obtaining sensitive handles to LSASS.

docs.title: DCSync Detection Model
docs.text:
Non-DC Principal / Host
       |
       v
Directory Replication Request
       |
       v
Replication Rights Used
       |
       v
Credential Data

Replication activity originating from unexpected systems or identities deserves investigation.

docs.title: LAPS Detection Model
docs.text:
User
 |
 v
Reads LAPS Password
 |
 v
Is User an Expected Reader?
 |
 +--> Yes -> Baseline
 |
 +--> No -> Investigate

docs.title: gMSA Detection Model
docs.text:
Principal
 |
 v
Retrieves gMSA Managed Password
 |
 v
Expected Host / Service?
 |
 +--> Yes -> Baseline
 |
 +--> No -> Investigate

docs.title: Credential Reuse Detection
docs.text:
The second half of credential-access detection is:

Was the credential subsequently used?

Correlate:

Credential Access
      |
      v
Authentication Event
      |
      v
New Source Host
      |
      v
Privileged Access

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
Credential Access prevention requires multiple layers.

A useful model is:

Reduce Stored Credentials
        |
        v
Protect Credential Stores
        |
        v
Restrict Credential Readers
        |
        v
Protect Privileged Sessions
        |
        v
Use Strong Authentication
        |
        v
Segment Administration
        |
        v
Monitor Credential Access

docs.title: Use LAPS
docs.text:
Use Windows LAPS or another approved solution to provide unique, managed local administrator passwords.

This reduces:

Local Administrator Password Reuse

and therefore reduces lateral-movement blast radius.

docs.title: Use gMSA
docs.text:
Where compatible, use:

gMSA

instead of long-lived manually managed service-account passwords.

Benefits include:

Automatic Password Management
Long Random Passwords
Reduced Human Knowledge of Password
Controlled Retrieval

docs.title: Protect gMSA Readers
docs.text:
A gMSA is only as secure as the principals authorised to retrieve its password.

Review:

PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword

and related directory permissions.

docs.title: Protect LAPS Readers
docs.text:
Restrict LAPS password access to the minimum required administrative identities.

Avoid unnecessarily broad groups.

docs.title: Protect LSASS
docs.text:
Consider controls such as:

Credential Guard
LSA Protection
EDR
Attack Surface Reduction
Administrative Tiering

where compatible with the environment.

docs.title: Reduce Privileged Logons
docs.text:
Avoid logging privileged identities onto lower-trust systems.

The model should be:

Tier 0 Account
      |
      X
Workstation

and:

Tier 0 Account
      |
      v
Tier 0 Administrative System

where practical.

docs.title: Privileged Access Workstations
docs.text:
Privileged Access Workstations can reduce exposure of administrative credentials to compromised endpoints.

Conceptually:

Privileged Identity
       |
       v
Dedicated Administrative Device
       |
       v
Privileged Resource

docs.title: Protect Service Accounts
docs.text:
Service accounts should have:

Minimum Privilege
No Interactive Logon Where Unnecessary
Long Random Passwords
Managed Rotation
Limited Host Scope
Limited Network Access
Monitoring

Prefer gMSA where compatible.

docs.title: Remove Credentials from Scripts
docs.text:
Do not store credentials in:

PowerShell
Batch Files
VBScript
XML
YAML
JSON
INI

where domain users can read them.

Use appropriate secret-management mechanisms.

docs.title: Protect Deployment Shares
docs.text:
Deployment infrastructure frequently contains highly privileged secrets.

Restrict:

Read Access
Write Access
Administrative Access

and monitor access to sensitive files.

docs.title: Protect Backups
docs.text:
Treat:

Domain Controller Backup

as equivalent in sensitivity to:

Domain Controller

because it may contain Active Directory credential material.

docs.title: Protect Replication Rights
docs.text:
Review principals with:

DS-Replication-Get-Changes
DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All

and related replication permissions.

Only legitimate replication and tightly controlled administrative identities should possess them.

docs.title: Protect Certificate Infrastructure
docs.text:
Treat:

CA Private Keys
Enrollment Agent Certificates
Authentication Certificates
Certificate Templates

as security-sensitive identity infrastructure.

docs.title: Use Strong Passwords
docs.text:
Offline credential attacks such as:

Kerberoasting
AS-REP Roasting
Cached Credential Cracking

become substantially harder when accounts use long, randomly generated passwords.

Service accounts are particularly important.

docs.title: Reduce NTLM
docs.text:
Where operationally feasible, reduce unnecessary NTLM usage.

This can reduce exposure to:

Pass-the-Hash
NTLM Relay
Captured Challenge-Response

Migration should be carefully planned and monitored.

docs.title: Prefer Kerberos AES
docs.text:
Modern Kerberos environments should prefer stronger AES encryption types where compatible.

Legacy RC4 dependencies should be identified and remediated carefully.

docs.title: Credential Access Incident Response
docs.text:
A credential-access incident should answer:

What credential was exposed?
       |
       v
Which identity?
       |
       v
How was it obtained?
       |
       v
Where was it stored?
       |
       v
Where can it authenticate?
       |
       v
Was it used?
       |
       v
What did it access?
       |
       v
How do we invalidate it?

docs.title: Credential Invalidation
docs.text:
Different credentials require different response actions.

Example:

Password
   |
   v
Password Reset

NT Hash
   |
   v
Password Reset

Kerberos Key
   |
   v
Password / Key Rotation

TGT / TGS
   |
   v
Ticket Expiration + Credential Rotation Where Required

Certificate
   |
   v
Revoke Certificate + Protect / Rotate Key

Computer Account
   |
   v
Reset Machine Password

The exact response depends on the credential type and compromise scenario.

docs.title: Domain Credential Compromise
docs.text:
If highly privileged domain credentials are compromised, response may require significantly more than:

Reset One Password

Investigate:

Persistence
Replication Rights
Certificates
Delegation
Scheduled Tasks
Services
New Accounts
ACL Changes
Kerberos Tickets
Domain Controller Access

docs.title: krbtgt
docs.text:
The:

krbtgt

account is fundamental to Kerberos ticket signing in an Active Directory domain.

Compromise of its key material is a severe incident.

Recovery procedures may involve controlled rotation of the krbtgt password according to Microsoft's guidance.

Do not casually rotate krbtgt during testing or incident response.

docs.title: Credential Rotation Order
docs.text:
Where multiple credentials are compromised, rotation order matters.

Conceptually:

Contain Attacker
      |
      v
Remove Persistence
      |
      v
Secure Administrative Plane
      |
      v
Rotate Credentials
      |
      v
Monitor Reauthentication

Rotating credentials before removing attacker persistence may allow credentials to be stolen again.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Credential-access findings should identify:

Credential Source
Credential Type
Affected Identity
Required Access
Exposure Mechanism
Resulting Authentication Capability
Privilege
Scope
Evidence
Remediation

Avoid unnecessarily including the credential itself.

docs.title: Finding Titles
docs.text:
Examples include:

Excessive Permissions Allow Reading LAPS Passwords

Domain User Can Retrieve gMSA Credential Material

Credentials Exposed in SYSVOL Script

Service Account Password Stored in Readable Configuration File

Excessive Replication Rights Enable DCSync

Privileged Credentials Exposed on Lower-Trust Server

Domain Controller Backup Exposes Active Directory Credential Material

docs.title: Example Credential Exposure Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Service Account Credential Stored in Domain-Readable SYSVOL Script

Affected File:
\\corp.example\SYSVOL\corp.example\scripts\deployment.ps1

Affected Account:
CORP\svc_deploy

Description:
A PowerShell deployment script stored in SYSVOL contains reusable
authentication material for the CORP\svc_deploy service account.

The script is readable by ordinary authenticated domain users through
the normal SYSVOL share.

The credential was identified during read-only review of domain policy
and deployment files.

The credential value has been omitted from this report.

Impact:
A compromised domain user able to read the script could obtain the
service-account credential and authenticate as CORP\svc_deploy.

The resulting impact depends on the account's privileges and the
systems on which the credential is accepted.

Recommendation:
Immediately rotate the exposed credential.

Remove the credential from SYSVOL and replace plaintext credential
storage with an approved secret-management mechanism.

Review the privileges and authentication history of CORP\svc_deploy,
search for other copies of the credential, and review SYSVOL for
additional exposed secrets.

docs.title: Example LAPS Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Excessive Directory Permissions Allow Reading LAPS Passwords

Source Principal:
CORP\helpdesk-user

Affected Scope:
OU=Servers,DC=corp,DC=example

Description:
The CORP\helpdesk-user account has directory permissions that permit
access to managed local administrator password information for systems
within the Servers OU.

The permission was confirmed through Active Directory ACL analysis.

Where active validation was required, access was tested only against
an approved test computer.

Production LAPS passwords were not collected.

Impact:
Successful abuse could provide local administrative access to affected
systems.

The resulting impact depends on the systems within scope and whether
additional credential or privilege-escalation opportunities exist on
those hosts.

Recommendation:
Restrict LAPS password retrieval to dedicated administrative identities
that require access.

Review delegated permissions throughout the directory and monitor
access to LAPS password attributes.

docs.title: Example DCSync Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Excessive Active Directory Replication Rights Enable Credential Replication

Source Principal:
CORP\svc_backup

Affected Scope:
DC=corp,DC=example

Description:
The CORP\svc_backup account possesses Active Directory replication
permissions that can allow it to request sensitive directory
credential data using domain replication protocols.

The relevant directory permissions were independently confirmed.

The complete domain credential database was not retrieved during
validation.

Impact:
Successful abuse could expose password-derived credential material for
domain identities, potentially including privileged accounts.

This could result in domain-wide compromise.

Recommendation:
Remove unnecessary directory replication permissions from the affected
account.

Restrict replication rights to Domain Controllers and explicitly
approved identity-management services.

Investigate the authentication and directory activity of the affected
account and monitor replication operations originating from unexpected
systems or identities.

docs.title: Severity Assessment
docs.text:
Credential findings should not be rated solely according to:

Credential Exists

Consider:

Credential Type
     +
Credential Privilege
     +
Ease of Retrieval
     +
Number of Readers
     +
Authentication Scope
     +
Credential Reuse
     +
Network Reachability
     =
Actual Risk

docs.title: Example Severity Model
docs.text:
Readable Password
      |
      v
Low-Privilege Test Account
      |
      v
Single Non-Sensitive System

may have relatively limited impact.

Compare:

Readable Credential
      |
      v
Tier 0 Service Account
      |
      v
Domain-Wide Administrative Access

which can be critical.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Confirm credential-access testing is authorised
  • [ ] Confirm whether credential extraction is permitted
  • [ ] Confirm whether memory dumping is permitted
  • [ ] Confirm whether NTDS access is permitted
  • [ ] Confirm whether DCSync validation is permitted
  • [ ] Confirm whether production credentials may be retrieved
  • [ ] Define credential evidence handling
  • [ ] Define credential retention period
  • [ ] Prepare encrypted evidence storage

docs.title: Identity Enumeration
docs.text:
• [ ] Identify controlled user
  • [ ] Record SID
  • [ ] Enumerate groups
  • [ ] Enumerate privileges
  • [ ] Enumerate directory ACLs
  • [ ] Enumerate local administrative access
  • [ ] Identify accessible systems
  • [ ] Identify accessible shares

docs.title: Directory Credentials
docs.text:
• [ ] Review LAPS readers
  • [ ] Review Windows LAPS configuration
  • [ ] Review legacy LAPS configuration
  • [ ] Review gMSA readers
  • [ ] Review replication rights
  • [ ] Review msDS-KeyCredentialLink
  • [ ] Review certificate-related permissions
  • [ ] Review computer-account control

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
• [ ] Enumerate SYSVOL
  • [ ] Search for cpassword
  • [ ] Review scripts
  • [ ] Review XML files
  • [ ] Review configuration files
  • [ ] Search for credential keywords
  • [ ] Review referenced external resources
  • [ ] Review file permissions

docs.title: Shares
docs.text:
• [ ] Enumerate readable shares
  • [ ] Review deployment shares
  • [ ] Review backup shares
  • [ ] Review script repositories
  • [ ] Review configuration shares
  • [ ] Review administrative shares where authorised
  • [ ] Search targeted locations for secrets

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
• [ ] Identify local administrative access
  • [ ] Review logged-on users
  • [ ] Review services
  • [ ] Review scheduled tasks
  • [ ] Review application configuration
  • [ ] Review PowerShell history
  • [ ] Review Credential Manager metadata
  • [ ] Review DPAPI-relevant artefacts where authorised
  • [ ] Determine Credential Guard status
  • [ ] Determine LSA protection status
  • [ ] Avoid LSASS dumping unless required

docs.title: Kerberos
docs.text:
• [ ] Review available tickets
  • [ ] Review service accounts
  • [ ] Review Kerberoasting exposure
  • [ ] Review AS-REP roasting exposure
  • [ ] Review delegation
  • [ ] Protect collected .ccache
  • [ ] Protect collected .kirbi

docs.title: Domain Controllers
docs.text:
• [ ] Review replication rights
  • [ ] Review DCSync paths
  • [ ] Review DC administrative access
  • [ ] Review backup access
  • [ ] Review NTDS exposure
  • [ ] Avoid mass credential extraction
  • [ ] Use dedicated test account where possible

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
• [ ] Enumerate authentication certificates
  • [ ] Review private-key access
  • [ ] Review certificate templates
  • [ ] Review certificate enrollment rights
  • [ ] Review key credential links
  • [ ] Protect PFX/P12 files
  • [ ] Protect private keys

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Use lowest-impact validation
  • [ ] Prefer ACL proof
  • [ ] Prefer metadata proof
  • [ ] Prefer dedicated test credentials
  • [ ] Retrieve minimum necessary credential material
  • [ ] Validate only authorised targets
  • [ ] Avoid broad credential reuse testing
  • [ ] Record resulting privilege

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• [ ] Monitor directory credential access
  • [ ] Monitor 4662
  • [ ] Monitor 5136
  • [ ] Monitor Kerberos events
  • [ ] Monitor NTLM events
  • [ ] Monitor process creation
  • [ ] Monitor LSASS access
  • [ ] Monitor registry hive access
  • [ ] Monitor DCSync
  • [ ] Monitor LAPS reads
  • [ ] Monitor gMSA retrieval
  • [ ] Monitor certificate export
  • [ ] Correlate credential access with authentication

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:

docs.title: Credential Access Testing Model
docs.text:
The basic model is:

Controlled Identity
       |
       v
Credential Source
       |
       v
Credential Material
       |
       v
Additional Identity
       |
       v
Additional Privilege

The directory model is:

User
 |
 v
Directory Permission
 |
 v
Sensitive Attribute
 |
 +--> LAPS
 +--> gMSA
 +--> Replication
 +--> Key Credential

The endpoint model is:

User
 |
 v
Local Administrator
 |
 v
Protected Credential Source
 |
 +--> LSASS
 +--> SAM
 +--> LSA Secrets
 +--> DPAPI

The SYSVOL model is:

Domain User
    |
    v
SYSVOL
    |
    v
Readable Script / XML
    |
    v
Stored Credential

The DCSync model is:

Controlled Principal
       |
       v
Replication Rights
       |
       v
Domain Controller
       |
       v
Directory Replication
       |
       v
Credential Material

The Kerberos model is:

Kerberos Credential
       |
       +--> Password-Derived Key
       |
       +--> TGT
       |
       +--> Service Ticket
       |
       v
Kerberos Authentication

The certificate model is:

Certificate
    +
Private Key
    |
    v
Authentication

The credential-reuse model is:

Credential
    |
    v
Where Is It Valid?
    |
    +--> One Host
    |
    +--> Multiple Hosts
    |
    +--> Domain
    |
    +--> Tier 0

The validation model is:

Potential Exposure
       |
       v
Confirm Permission
       |
       v
Confirm Source
       |
       v
Retrieve Minimum Evidence
       |
       v
Validate Minimum Access

The detection model is:

Credential Source
      |
      v
Suspicious Access
      |
      v
Credential Retrieval
      |
      v
Authentication
      |
      v
Privilege / Lateral Movement

The defensive model is:

Reduce Credential Storage
        |
        v
Restrict Credential Readers
        |
        v
Protect Credential Stores
        |
        v
Protect Privileged Sessions
        |
        v
Rotate Credentials
        |
        v
Monitor Access and Reuse

A mature credential-access assessment should answer:

What credential sources exist?
       |
       v
Who can access them?
       |
       v
What credential type is exposed?
       |
       v
Which identity does it represent?
       |
       v
Where is it valid?
       |
       v
What privilege does it provide?
       |
       v
Can the exposure be proven safely?

The most important principle is:

Can Access Credential Source
        |
        X
Must Dump Everything

Instead:

Identify Exposure
      |
      v
Confirm Permission
      |
      v
Retrieve Minimum Necessary Evidence
      |
      v
Determine Resulting Impact

Credential-access testing should therefore optimise for:

Minimum Collection
        +
Maximum Evidence Quality
        +
Clear Attack-Path Analysis

rather than:

Maximum Number of Credentials Collected

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Credential Access should be treated as an identity-expansion problem.

The fundamental model is:

Controlled Identity
       |
       v
Credential Source
       |
       v
Additional Credential
       |
       v
Additional Identity
       |
       v
Additional Access

The most important question is not:

How many credentials can I dump?

It is:

Which credential can this identity access,
and what additional privilege does that provide?

A mature assessment therefore follows:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Identify Exposure
   |
   v
Confirm Permission
   |
   v
Understand Credential Type
   |
   v
Map Authentication Scope
   |
   v
Determine Resulting Privilege
   |
   v
Validate Minimally

Different credential types should remain clearly separated:

Password
   !=
NT Hash
   !=
NetNTLMv2 Response
   !=
Kerberos Key
   !=
Kerberos Ticket
   !=
Certificate
   !=
Private Key

Even though several of them may ultimately provide authentication capability.

The Active Directory credential-access landscape can be visualised as:

                   Active Directory
                          |
        +-----------------+-----------------+
        |                 |                 |
        v                 v                 v
     Directory          SYSVOL          Endpoints
        |                 |                 |
        v                 v                 v
      LAPS              GPP              LSASS
      gMSA              Scripts           SAM
    DCSync              Config            DPAPI
 Key Credentials                         Secrets
        |
        +-----------------+-----------------+
                          |
                          v
                  Credential Material
                          |
                          v
                     Authentication
                          |
                          v
                  Effective Privilege

For penetration testing:

Credential Source
       |
       v
Can I Access It?
       |
       +--> No
       |     |
       |     v
       |   Document Boundary
       |
       +--> Yes
             |
             v
      Can I Prove It Safely?
             |
             +--> Yes
             |     |
             |     v
             |   Minimum Evidence
             |
             +--> No
                   |
                   v
             Stop and Document

For defenders:

Where Are Credentials Stored?
        |
        v
Who Can Read Them?
        |
        v
Who Can Modify Authentication?
        |
        v
Where Are Privileged Users Logging On?
        |
        v
Can Credential Access Be Detected?
        |
        v
Can Compromised Credentials Be Rotated Quickly?

The strongest defensive strategy combines:

Least Privilege
      +
Managed Credentials
      +
Administrative Tiering
      +
Credential Guard
      +
LSA Protection
      +
Strong Kerberos Configuration
      +
Reduced NTLM
      +
Protected Backups
      +
Directory Auditing
      +
Endpoint Detection

Credential Access should ultimately be analysed as part of the complete Active Directory attack graph:

Identity
   |
   v
Credential
   |
   v
Identity
   |
   v
Privilege
   |
   v
Credential
   |
   v
Higher Privilege

Breaking any link in that chain can prevent a small credential exposure from becoming domain compromise.

docs.title: Active Directory DCOM - Remote Administration and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM) is Microsoft's technology for allowing Component Object Model (COM) objects to communicate across process and network boundaries.

DCOM is used by legitimate Windows components and management technologies for:

Remote Administration
Distributed Applications
Management Services
Enterprise Software
WMI
Microsoft Management Console
Application Automation
RPC-Based Communication

During an Active Directory security assessment, DCOM is important because an identity with sufficient remote permissions may be able to activate or interact with COM objects on another Windows system.

Some COM objects expose methods that can indirectly start processes or applications.

The resulting relationship can become:

Compromised Identity
        |
        v
Remote DCOM Access
        |
        v
Remote COM Object
        |
        v
Exposed Method
        |
        v
Process / Application
        |
        v
Target System

DCOM should therefore be understood as a legitimate Windows infrastructure technology that can become a lateral-movement mechanism when combined with excessive privileges and network reachability.

Authorised testing only

DCOM can invoke functionality on remote Windows systems and may create processes or applications. Begin with configuration and permission review. Only perform remote activation or execution testing against systems explicitly included in the assessment scope, and stop after sufficient evidence has been collected.

docs.title: DCOM at a Glance
docs.text:
The basic architecture is:

Client
  |
  v
COM Request
  |
  v
RPC
  |
  v
DCOM
  |
  v
Remote COM Object
  |
  v
Windows Component

From a lateral-movement perspective:

Identity
   |
   v
Network Reachability
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
DCOM Permissions
   |
   v
Remote Activation
   |
   v
COM Method
   |
   v
Remote Action

docs.title: COM
docs.text:
COM stands for:

Component Object Model

COM allows software components to expose:

Objects
Interfaces
Methods
Properties

to other applications.

Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
COM Object
    |
    +--> Method A
    +--> Method B
    +--> Property A

docs.title: DCOM
docs.text:
DCOM extends COM across machine boundaries.

Conceptually:

COM
 |
 v
Local Component Interaction

becomes:

DCOM
 |
 v
Remote Component Interaction

docs.title: COM vs DCOM
docs.text:
A useful distinction is:

COM
=
Component interaction

while:

DCOM
=
Distributed COM interaction over RPC

A COM object may support local activation without being remotely usable through DCOM.

docs.title: DCOM and Active Directory
docs.text:
DCOM is not an Active Directory protocol itself.

However, in domain environments it frequently relies on:

Domain Identities
Kerberos
NTLM
Windows Groups
Local Administrators
Group Policy
RPC

This makes it relevant to Active Directory lateral movement.

docs.title: DCOM and RPC
docs.text:
DCOM uses:

RPC

for remote communication.

A simplified network flow is:

Client
  |
  v
TCP 135
  |
  v
RPC Endpoint Mapper
  |
  v
Dynamic RPC Port
  |
  v
DCOM Server

docs.title: TCP 135
docs.text:
The RPC Endpoint Mapper commonly listens on:

135/TCP

Test from Windows:

Test-NetConnection srv01.corp.example -Port 135

From Linux:

nmap -Pn -p135 srv01.corp.example

docs.title: TCP 135 Does Not Prove DCOM Access
docs.text:
An open:

135/TCP

only indicates that the RPC Endpoint Mapper is reachable.

Successful DCOM interaction still depends on:

Dynamic RPC Reachability
Authentication
Launch Permissions
Activation Permissions
Access Permissions
Object Availability
Object-Specific Security

docs.title: Dynamic RPC
docs.text:
After contacting the RPC Endpoint Mapper, the client may be directed to another TCP port.

Conceptually:

Client
  |
  v
135/TCP
  |
  v
Endpoint Mapper
  |
  v
Dynamic Port
  |
  v
Remote COM Server

This is why allowing only:

135/TCP

is generally insufficient for full DCOM functionality.

docs.title: DCOM Authentication
docs.text:
DCOM uses Windows authentication.

Depending on the environment, authentication may involve:

Kerberos
NTLM

docs.title: Kerberos
docs.text:
In a properly functioning domain environment:

Domain Identity
      |
      v
Kerberos
      |
      v
RPC / DCOM
      |
      v
Remote Host

may be used.

Correct:

DNS
SPNs
Time Synchronisation
Domain Trust

remain important.

docs.title: NTLM
docs.text:
Where Kerberos cannot be used and NTLM remains available:

Identity
   |
   v
NTLM
   |
   v
RPC / DCOM

may occur.

This makes DCOM relevant to broader:

NTLM Reduction
Credential Reuse
Pass-the-Hash
Lateral Movement

analysis.

See:

NTLM

docs.title: Hostnames vs IP Addresses
docs.text:
When Kerberos is expected, prefer:

srv01.corp.example

instead of:

10.10.10.25

Using an IP address can alter authentication behaviour because Kerberos normally depends on service names rather than raw IP addresses.

docs.title: DCOM Security
docs.text:
DCOM access is controlled through several permission categories.

Important concepts include:

Access Permissions
Launch Permissions
Activation Permissions

docs.title: Remote Access
docs.text:
Remote Access determines whether a principal can access a running COM server remotely.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Remote Access Permission
 |
 v
Running COM Object

docs.title: Remote Launch
docs.text:
Remote Launch determines whether a principal can remotely start the COM server.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Remote Launch
 |
 v
COM Server Starts

docs.title: Remote Activation
docs.text:
Remote Activation determines whether a principal can remotely activate a COM object.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Remote Activation
 |
 v
COM Object Instance

docs.title: Permission Model
docs.text:
The effective DCOM path can therefore resemble:

Identity
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Remote Launch
   |
   v
Remote Activation
   |
   v
Remote Access
   |
   v
COM Object

Object-specific security can add further restrictions.

docs.title: Local Administrators
docs.text:
Members of:

Administrators

typically have broad remote management capabilities.

A compromised account with local administrator rights on another Windows host should therefore be evaluated for multiple lateral-movement mechanisms, including:

SMB
WinRM
WMI
DCOM
RDP

depending on network and system configuration.

docs.title: DCOM Is Not the Root Cause
docs.text:
If a domain group has:

Local Administrator

rights across hundreds of servers, the primary issue is usually:

Excessive Administrative Privilege

rather than:

DCOM Exists

DCOM is one mechanism through which that privilege may be exercised.

docs.title: DCOM Configuration
docs.text:
Windows provides:

Component Services

for viewing COM and DCOM configuration.

The graphical path is commonly:

Component Services
  |
  v
Computers
  |
  v
My Computer
  |
  v
DCOM Config

docs.title: DCOMCNFG
docs.text:
The Component Services interface can be opened with:

dcomcnfg.exe

During an assessment, use it for inspection rather than modifying permissions.

docs.title: Registry Locations
docs.text:
COM and DCOM registrations are represented in the Windows Registry.

Important areas include:

HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\CLSID
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Classes\CLSID
HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\AppID
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Classes\AppID

docs.title: CLSID
docs.text:
A:

CLSID

identifies a COM class.

Example format:

{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}

The actual value uniquely identifies a registered COM class.

docs.title: AppID
docs.text:
An:

AppID

can associate COM classes with configuration including DCOM security settings.

Conceptually:

CLSID
  |
  v
COM Class
  |
  v
AppID
  |
  v
DCOM Configuration

docs.title: Enumerate COM Registrations
docs.text:
PowerShell can inspect registered COM classes through the Registry.

Example:

Get-ChildItem 'Registry::HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\CLSID' |
    Select-Object -First 20

This is local enumeration.

Do not treat every registered COM class as remotely exploitable.

docs.title: Why COM Enumeration Is Difficult
docs.text:
Windows contains a very large number of COM registrations.

Most are:

Not Useful for Remote Execution
Not Remotely Activatable
Restricted
Application-Specific
Version-Specific

Therefore:

Enumerate Every CLSID

is usually less useful than:

Understand the Target
Review Permissions
Identify Known Administrative Components
Validate Only Relevant Objects

docs.title: DCOM Lateral Movement
docs.text:
DCOM lateral movement generally requires:

Valid Credential
      +
Network Reachability
      +
Remote DCOM Permissions
      +
Suitable COM Object

Conceptually:

Credential
   |
   v
Remote Authentication
   |
   v
DCOM
   |
   v
COM Object
   |
   v
Execution-Capable Method

docs.title: Commonly Discussed DCOM Objects
docs.text:
Security research has historically identified several COM objects that can expose methods useful for remote execution in certain Windows versions and configurations.

Examples include objects associated with:

MMC20.Application
ShellWindows
ShellBrowserWindow

Availability and behaviour can vary significantly between:

Windows Versions
Desktop vs Server
Installed Components
Session State
Security Configuration

Do not assume that an object documented in an old technique is present or remotely usable on a current target.

docs.title: MMC20.Application
docs.text:
One historically well-known DCOM lateral-movement technique uses:

MMC20.Application

The conceptual chain is:

Remote DCOM
    |
    v
MMC20.Application
    |
    v
Document.ActiveView
    |
    v
ExecuteShellCommand
    |
    v
Process

This technique should only be validated where remote execution testing is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: PowerShell DCOM Object Creation
docs.text:
PowerShell can request a COM object on another system using the .NET System.Activator class.

Conceptually:

Get COM Type
      |
      v
Remote Activator
      |
      v
COM Instance

A common pattern is:

$type = [type]::GetTypeFromProgID('MMC20.Application', 'srv01.corp.example')

Then:

$object = [Activator]::CreateInstance($type)

This attempts remote activation.

Do not invoke execution-capable methods unless required by the approved test plan.

docs.title: Safe DCOM Validation
docs.text:
A safe sequence is:

Confirm RPC Reachability
        |
        v
Confirm Identity
        |
        v
Attempt Remote Object Activation
        |
        v
Determine Whether Activation Succeeds
        |
        v
Stop if Evidence Is Sufficient

Remote object activation itself may already demonstrate excessive DCOM permissions.

docs.title: Execution Validation
docs.text:
If command execution must specifically be proven, use a harmless command.

For example, in an authorised lab:

cmd.exe /c echo authorised-dcom-test > C:\Windows\Temp\dcom-test.txt

Do not use:

Reverse Shell
Credential Dumper
Security-Control Disablement
Persistence Payload

when a harmless marker provides sufficient evidence.

docs.title: MMC ExecuteShellCommand
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised, the relevant MMC object exposes functionality conceptually similar to:

Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand

A lab-only PowerShell example is:

$type = [type]::GetTypeFromProgID('MMC20.Application', 'srv01.corp.example')
$object = [Activator]::CreateInstance($type)
$object.Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand(
    'cmd.exe',
    $null,
    '/c echo authorised-dcom-test > C:\Windows\Temp\dcom-test.txt',
    '7'
)

This changes the target by creating a process and marker file.

Use only when remote execution validation is explicitly required.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Where authorised administrative SMB access exists:

Remove-Item '\\srv01.corp.example\C$\Windows\Temp\dcom-test.txt'

Do not assume failure to access:

C$

means the DCOM execution failed.

SMB and DCOM have separate network and authorisation requirements.

docs.title: Why DCOM May Be Non-Interactive
docs.text:
DCOM execution generally does not provide:

Interactive Shell

by itself.

The model is closer to:

Remote Method
     |
     v
Remote Process

Tooling may add command-output handling around this mechanism.

docs.title: Impacket DCOMExec
docs.text:
Impacket provides:

dcomexec

for authorised DCOM-based remote execution testing.

Check current syntax:

impacket-dcomexec -h

Depending on installation, the script may also be available as:

dcomexec.py

docs.title: DCOMExec Password Authentication
docs.text:
For an approved test account:

impacket-dcomexec 'CORP/audit-admin:PASSWORD@srv01.corp.example'

Avoid placing production credentials directly in shell history where possible.

docs.title: DCOMExec Pass-the-Hash
docs.text:
Where pass-the-hash testing is explicitly authorised:

impacket-dcomexec -hashes ':NTHASH' 'CORP/audit-admin@srv01.corp.example'

See:

Pass-the-Hash

docs.title: DCOMExec Authentication Model
docs.text:
Credential
   |
   +--> Password
   |
   +--> NTLM Hash
   |
   +--> Kerberos where supported/configured
   |
   v
DCOM
   |
   v
Remote COM Object
   |
   v
Command Execution

Always verify options against:

impacket-dcomexec -h

because tool syntax can change.

docs.title: DCOMExec Object Selection
docs.text:
Impacket's DCOMExec implementation can support different DCOM object approaches depending on the installed version.

Do not assume an older object's availability.

Review:

impacket-dcomexec -h

before testing.

docs.title: Pass-the-Hash with DCOM
docs.text:
If NTLM is available and the account has sufficient remote rights:

NTLM Hash
    |
    v
Authentication
    |
    v
DCOM
    |
    v
Remote Object
    |
    v
Remote Execution

may be possible.

The underlying security weakness may be:

Reusable Administrative Credential

rather than DCOM itself.

docs.title: Local Administrator Reuse
docs.text:
Example:

WS01
 |
 v
Local Administrator Hash
 |
 v
Same Credential on WS02
 |
 v
DCOM
 |
 v
Remote Execution

This is another reason to deploy:

Windows LAPS

See:

LAPS

docs.title: DCOM and Kerberos
docs.text:
Where Kerberos authentication is supported by the client and environment, ensure:

DNS
Time
Domain
SPNs
Credential Cache

are correct.

Linux:

klist

Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

docs.title: DCOM vs WMI
docs.text:
WMI commonly uses DCOM for traditional remote communication.

The relationship is:

WMI
 |
 v
DCOM
 |
 v
RPC

But DCOM can expose many COM objects unrelated to WMI.

Therefore:

WMI Lateral Movement

and:

DCOM Lateral Movement

are related but distinct.

See:

WMI

docs.title: DCOM vs SMB
docs.text:
SMB lateral movement commonly involves:

445/TCP
Administrative Shares
Named Pipes
Service Control Manager

DCOM commonly involves:

135/TCP
Dynamic RPC
Remote COM Activation

See:

SMB

docs.title: DCOM vs WinRM
docs.text:
WinRM:

5985 / 5986
      |
      v
WS-Management
      |
      v
PowerShell Remoting

DCOM:

135 + Dynamic RPC
      |
      v
RPC
      |
      v
Remote COM

See:

WinRM

docs.title: DCOM vs PsExec
docs.text:
PsExec-style execution:

SMB
 |
 v
ADMIN$
 |
 v
Service Control Manager
 |
 v
Temporary Service

DCOM execution:

RPC
 |
 v
DCOM
 |
 v
COM Object
 |
 v
Method
 |
 v
Process

docs.title: DCOM vs WMIExec
docs.text:
WMIExec:

RPC / DCOM
      |
      v
WMI
      |
      v
Win32_Process

DCOMExec:

RPC / DCOM
      |
      v
COM Application
      |
      v
Application-Specific Method

Both may ultimately create remote processes, but the execution path differs.

docs.title: DCOM vs RDP
docs.text:
DCOM:

Remote Object Invocation
Non-Interactive
RPC-Based

RDP:

Interactive Desktop
GUI Session
3389/TCP

For simple execution validation, creating an interactive desktop session is often unnecessary.

docs.title: DCOM and Microsoft Management Console
docs.text:
Microsoft Management Console:

MMC

is used by many Windows administrative tools.

Examples include:

Computer Management
Event Viewer
Services
Certificates
Group Policy

The existence of MMC-related COM components is therefore expected.

The security concern arises when:

Remote Activation
+
Execution-Capable Method
+
Excessive Privilege

are combined.

docs.title: DCOM and Office
docs.text:
COM automation is also heavily used by Microsoft Office and other desktop applications.

Do not treat:

Office COM Object Exists

as evidence of a lateral-movement path.

Remote usability depends on:

Object Registration
Remote Activation
Session Context
Permissions
Application Behaviour
Windows Version

docs.title: DCOM and Server Core
docs.text:
Some COM-based lateral-movement techniques depend on components that may not exist on:

Server Core

or may behave differently from full desktop installations.

Always validate the actual environment.

docs.title: Version Dependence
docs.text:
DCOM techniques can be highly:

Version Dependent

A method that works on:

Windows 10

may not behave identically on:

Windows 11
Windows Server 2022
Windows Server 2025

or later releases.

Do not build findings around assumptions from old offensive-security documentation.

docs.title: Object Availability
docs.text:
Before considering an object useful, establish:

Is It Registered?

Can It Be Remotely Activated?

Does the Identity Have Permission?

Does the Required Method Exist?

Does the Method Behave as Expected?

Is the Technique Necessary to Prove the Finding?

docs.title: DCOM Network Exposure
docs.text:
A weak network model may allow:

Any Workstation
      |
      v
RPC / DCOM
      |
      v
Every Server

A stronger design may restrict:

Privileged Admin Workstation
          |
          v
Management Network
          |
          v
RPC / DCOM
          |
          v
Managed Server

docs.title: Workstation-to-Workstation DCOM
docs.text:
Where not operationally required:

WS01
 |
 v
DCOM
 |
 v
WS02

should be restricted.

This can reduce lateral-movement opportunities after endpoint compromise.

docs.title: Windows Firewall
docs.text:
Windows Firewall should be used to restrict remote administration.

During an assessment, inspect existing firewall rules rather than enabling new ones.

Example:

Get-NetFirewallRule |
    Where-Object Enabled -EQ 'True' |
    Select-Object DisplayName,Direction,Action

Filter as needed for the specific RPC/DCOM service under review.

docs.title: Remote Address Restrictions
docs.text:
Firewall rules should ideally limit management traffic to approved source systems.

Review:

RemoteAddress

rather than checking only:

Enabled

docs.title: Do Not Enable DCOM for Testing
docs.text:
Do not modify DCOM settings merely to demonstrate a technique.

If DCOM is disabled or restricted:

The Control Is Working

and that should form part of the assessment evidence.

docs.title: DCOM Hardening
docs.text:
A practical DCOM hardening strategy includes:

Restrict RPC Network Exposure
Apply Least Privilege
Restrict Remote Launch
Restrict Remote Activation
Restrict Remote Access
Reduce Local Administrators
Deploy Windows LAPS
Separate Administrative Identities
Use Privileged Administrative Workstations
Reduce NTLM
Monitor RPC and DCOM
Use EDR
Use Application Control

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Review which principals genuinely require:

Remote Access
Remote Launch
Remote Activation

Remove unnecessary rights.

docs.title: Administrative Group Review
docs.text:
Review:

Local Administrators
Server Administrator Groups
Helpdesk Groups
Application Support Groups
Service Accounts

for unnecessary administrative rights across large numbers of systems.

docs.title: Windows LAPS
docs.text:
Unique local administrator credentials reduce the ability to reuse credentials for DCOM lateral movement.

See:

LAPS

docs.title: Reduce NTLM
docs.text:
Where possible:

Prefer Kerberos
Reduce NTLM

as part of a broader domain-hardening programme.

See:

NTLM

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Restrict RPC/DCOM traffic between security zones.

Examples:

User VLAN
   |
   X
   |
   v
Server Management RPC

while allowing:

Management VLAN
      |
      v
Server Management RPC

where required.
