docs.title: Help
docs.text:
Every Impacket tool has its own options.

Always check:

impacket-GetADUsers -h

or, from the source tree:

python3 examples/GetADUsers.py -h

This is particularly important because Impacket evolves and command-line options can change.

docs.title: Target Syntax
docs.text:
Many Impacket tools use a target format similar to:

domain/username:password@target

Example:

example.local/alice:Password@dc01.example.local

Other tools use:

domain/username

with the target or Domain Controller supplied separately.

Always check:

<tool> -h

docs.title: Authentication Models
docs.text:
Impacket supports several authentication models.

                   Authentication
                         |
       +-----------------+-----------------+
       |                 |                 |
       v                 v                 v
    Password            NTLM            Kerberos
                          |                 |
                          v                 |
                        Hash                |
                                            |
                             +--------------+-------------+
                             |              |             |
                             v              v             v
                          Password         TGT          AES Key
                                           |
                                           v
                                         ccache

docs.title: Password Authentication
docs.text:
Many tools accept:

domain/user:password@target

Example:

impacket-smbclient \
    example.local/alice:'Password'@file01.example.local

Be careful with:

Shell history
Process listings
Terminal logs
Screenshots
Evidence files

when supplying plaintext credentials.

docs.title: NTLM Hash Authentication
docs.text:
Many Impacket tools support:

-hashes LMHASH:NTHASH

A commonly used format when only the NT hash is known is:

-hashes :NTHASH

Example structure:

impacket-smbclient \
    example.local/alice@file01.example.local \
    -hashes :<NT-HASH>

This represents NTLM hash-based authentication.

The dedicated Pass-the-Hash note should cover the technique and its prerequisites in detail.

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication
docs.text:
Many Impacket tools support:

-k

for Kerberos authentication.

Depending on the tool, Kerberos authentication may use:

Password
NTLM hashes
AES key
Kerberos credential cache

Kerberos workflows depend heavily on:

DNS
FQDNs
SPNs
Time synchronisation
Domain configuration
KDC reachability

docs.title: AES Keys
docs.text:
Where supported, Impacket tools commonly expose:

-aesKey

for Kerberos authentication using an AES key.

Always verify the tool's help:

<tool> -h

before using key-based authentication.

docs.title: Kerberos Credential Cache
docs.text:
Kerberos tickets are commonly stored in a credential cache:

.ccache

Set:

export KRB5CCNAME=/path/to/ticket.ccache

Verify:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

Then use a Kerberos-aware Impacket tool with its supported Kerberos options.

docs.title: Kerberos Ticket Inspection
docs.text:
If Kerberos utilities are installed:

klist

can be useful for reviewing the current credential cache.

The important relationship is:

Ticket
  |
  v
Identity
  |
  v
Service
  |
  v
Validity

docs.title: Kerberos Requirements
docs.text:
Before troubleshooting Impacket itself, verify:

DNS
Domain
FQDN
Domain Controller
KDC
Clock
SPN
Ticket

Check time:

date

Check the DC:

dig dc01.example.local

Check Kerberos:

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.local

Check LDAP:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

docs.title: Core Impacket Tool Map
docs.text:
A useful operational map is:

ENUMERATION

GetADUsers
GetNPUsers
GetUserSPNs
lookupsid
findDelegation
samrdump
rpcdump
net


KERBEROS

GetNPUsers
GetUserSPNs
getTGT
getST
ticketer
ticketConverter


SMB

smbclient
smbserver


CREDENTIAL ACCESS

secretsdump


REMOTE ADMINISTRATION

psexec
wmiexec
smbexec
dcomexec
atexec


RELAY

ntlmrelayx

docs.title: GetADUsers
docs.text:
GetADUsers.py queries Active Directory through LDAP and retrieves information about domain users.

It is useful during authenticated enumeration.

Typical information can include:

Username
Email
Last logon
Password last set

docs.title: GetADUsers - Basic Usage
docs.text:
Current upstream syntax uses a target of:

domain[/username[:password]]

Example:

impacket-GetADUsers \
    example.local/alice:'Password' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.20.10 \
    -all

docs.title: GetADUsers with NTLM Hash
docs.text:
Check the current help:

impacket-GetADUsers -h

The tool supports hash-based authentication.

General pattern:

impacket-GetADUsers \
    example.local/alice \
    -hashes :<NT-HASH> \
    -dc-ip 10.10.20.10 \
    -all

docs.title: GetADUsers with Kerberos
docs.text:
General pattern:

impacket-GetADUsers \
    example.local/alice \
    -k \
    -no-pass \
    -dc-host dc01.example.local \
    -all

This assumes an appropriate Kerberos authentication context exists.

docs.title: GetADUsers Workflow
docs.text:
Domain Credential
       |
       v
GetADUsers
       |
       v
User Inventory
       |
       +--> Active users
       +--> Service identities
       +--> Stale users
       +--> Password age
       |
       v
Further Analysis

docs.title: GetNPUsers
docs.text:
GetNPUsers.py is used to identify accounts that do not require Kerberos pre-authentication and can support AS-REP roasting analysis.

Conceptually:

Domain Users
     |
     v
Kerberos Pre-Authentication?
     |
 +---+---+
 |       |
Yes      No
 |       |
 |       v
 |   AS-REP Candidate
 |
 v
Normal Kerberos Flow

docs.title: AS-REP Candidate Enumeration
docs.text:
A common authorised assessment workflow is:

Enumerate Users
      |
      v
Identify Accounts
Without Pre-Authentication
      |
      v
Determine Whether
Configuration Is Intended
      |
      v
Controlled Validation

The detailed technique belongs in:

AS-REP Roasting

docs.title: GetNPUsers Help
docs.text:
Always inspect:

impacket-GetNPUsers -h

because output and request options should be selected deliberately.

docs.title: GetUserSPNs
docs.text:
GetUserSPNs.py queries the domain for Service Principal Names associated with user accounts.

This makes it useful for Kerberoasting analysis.

Conceptually:

Active Directory
       |
       v
Accounts with SPNs
       |
       v
Service Accounts
       |
       v
Privilege / Password Analysis

docs.title: Enumerate SPNs
docs.text:
Example:

impacket-GetUserSPNs \
    example.local/alice:'Password' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.20.10

Enumeration alone can reveal:

Service account
SPN
Service
Password age
Delegation-related information

depending on the directory data returned.

docs.title: Cross-Domain SPN Queries
docs.text:
Current versions support:

-target-domain

for querying a domain different from the authenticating user's domain.

Check:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

before using cross-domain options.

docs.title: Kerberoasting
docs.text:
GetUserSPNs.py can also request service tickets.

That moves beyond simple SPN enumeration into Kerberoasting validation.

The workflow should therefore be separated:

SPN Enumeration
      |
      v
Identify Candidate
      |
      v
Assess Account Context
      |
      v
Authorised Ticket Request
      |
      v
Offline Password Strength Assessment

See:

Kerberoasting

docs.title: lookupsid
docs.text:
lookupsid.py performs SID lookup/enumeration through MS-RPC.

It can help enumerate:

Users
Groups
Domain SID
RID relationships

docs.title: lookupsid Syntax
docs.text:
Current upstream target syntax is similar to:

[[domain/]username[:password]@]<target>

Example:

impacket-lookupsid \
    example.local/alice:'Password'@dc01.example.local

docs.title: Why the Domain SID Matters
docs.text:
A SID looks conceptually like:

S-1-5-21-111111111-222222222-333333333-1105

The domain portion is:

S-1-5-21-111111111-222222222-333333333

The final value:

1105

is the RID.

Understanding this helps with:

Identity mapping
Trust analysis
SID history
Group analysis
Kerberos research

docs.title: findDelegation
docs.text:
findDelegation.py enumerates delegation relationships in Active Directory.

Current upstream functionality covers:

Unconstrained delegation
Constrained delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: Basic Delegation Enumeration
docs.text:
Example:

impacket-findDelegation \
    example.local/alice:'Password' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.20.10

docs.title: Delegation Analysis
docs.text:
The result should be interpreted as:

Principal
    |
    v
Delegation Type
    |
    v
Target Service
    |
    v
Prerequisites
    |
    v
Potential Security Path

Do not treat every delegation relationship as automatically exploitable.

See:

Unconstrained Delegation

Constrained Delegation

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: rpcdump
docs.text:
rpcdump.py enumerates RPC endpoints.

This can help identify:

RPC services
Interfaces
Protocol sequences
Endpoints

It is useful when investigating Windows services exposed through RPC.

Check:

impacket-rpcdump -h

docs.title: samrdump
docs.text:
samrdump.py queries the Security Account Manager Remote Protocol.

Depending on access, it can provide information about:

Users
Groups
Account properties
Domain information

Check:

impacket-samrdump -h

docs.title: net.py
docs.text:
Impacket also includes a remote alternative to portions of the Windows net.exe functionality.

It uses RPC and can interact with:

Users
Groups
Local groups
Computers

Some operations can modify remote state.

Enumeration and modification should therefore be clearly separated.

docs.title: smbclient
docs.text:
smbclient.py provides an interactive SMB client.

It is useful when a share has already been identified and needs focused review.

Example:

impacket-smbclient \
    example.local/alice:'Password'@file01.example.local

docs.title: SMB Client Workflow
docs.text:
NetExec
   |
   v
Interesting Share
   |
   v
Impacket smbclient
   |
   v
Focused Review

This avoids manually reviewing every share on every system.

docs.title: SMB Client Commands
docs.text:
Once connected, use:

help

to review commands supported by the installed version.

Common operations include:

List shares
Change share
List directories
Change directories
Download files
Upload files

Only write or upload files when explicitly required and authorised.

docs.title: SMB Share Analysis
docs.text:
Review shares for:

Configuration
Scripts
Deployment files
Backups
Credentials
Certificates
Keys
Connection strings
Service configuration
Administrative documentation

Do not indiscriminately download entire shares.

docs.title: smbserver
docs.text:
smbserver.py creates an SMB server from the assessment system.

General syntax:

impacket-smbserver SHARE /path/to/directory

Example:

mkdir -p /tmp/share

impacket-smbserver SHARE /tmp/share

Modern environments should use appropriate SMB versions and authentication where required.

Review:

impacket-smbserver -h

before use.

docs.title: SMB Server Security
docs.text:
An assessment SMB server can expose files to the network.

Consider:

Interface binding
Firewall rules
Authentication
Share contents
Network exposure
Cleanup

Never expose sensitive client material unnecessarily.

docs.title: getTGT
docs.text:
getTGT.py requests a Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket for a supplied identity.

Conceptually:

Credential
    |
    v
KDC
    |
    v
TGT
    |
    v
Credential Cache

docs.title: getTGT Workflow
docs.text:
Use:

impacket-getTGT -h

to confirm the syntax for your installed release.

A resulting ticket may be stored as:

user.ccache

Set:

export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/user.ccache"

Then inspect:

klist

docs.title: Why getTGT Is Useful
docs.text:
It allows a workflow based around Kerberos tickets rather than repeatedly supplying credentials.

Credential
   |
   v
getTGT
   |
   v
.ccache
   |
   v
KRB5CCNAME
   |
   v
Kerberos-Aware Tools

docs.title: getST
docs.text:
getST.py is used for obtaining Kerberos service tickets in supported Kerberos workflows.

It is particularly relevant to topics such as:

Constrained delegation
RBCD
S4U
Service-specific Kerberos access

Because the options depend heavily on the technique, detailed commands belong in the relevant delegation notes.

Always begin with:

impacket-getST -h

docs.title: S4U
docs.text:
Service-for-User Kerberos extensions are important in delegation attack paths.

Conceptually:

Service Account
      |
      v
S4U2Self
      |
      v
User-to-Service Ticket
      |
      v
S4U2Proxy
      |
      v
Delegated Service

See:

Kerberos S4U

for the detailed security model.

docs.title: ticketConverter
docs.text:
ticketConverter.py converts between common Kerberos ticket formats.

Common formats include:

ccache
kirbi

Conceptually:

Windows Tool
   |
   v
.kirbi
   |
   v
ticketConverter
   |
   v
.ccache
   |
   v
Linux Kerberos Tooling

and the reverse direction when required.

docs.title: Ticket Format Matters
docs.text:
Linux tooling commonly works with:

ccache

while Windows Kerberos tooling frequently uses:

kirbi

Ticket conversion does not change the identity or privileges represented by the ticket.

It changes the storage format.

docs.title: ticketer
docs.text:
ticketer.py can create Kerberos tickets from appropriate cryptographic key material.

This is advanced functionality associated with topics such as:

Golden Tickets
Silver Tickets
Trust Tickets
Kerberos persistence

It should not be treated as routine enumeration.

See the dedicated Kerberos persistence notes before using it.

docs.title: Credential Access Tools
docs.text:
Impacket includes tools capable of accessing credential material.

The primary example is:

secretsdump.py

This functionality is substantially more intrusive than normal enumeration.

docs.title: secretsdump
docs.text:
secretsdump.py can retrieve credential-related secrets from Windows systems and Active Directory under appropriate privilege conditions.

Depending on the target and access, this may involve sources such as:

SAM
LSA Secrets
Cached domain credentials
NTDS

docs.title: secretsdump Security Model
docs.text:
Think in terms of:

Administrative Access
        |
        v
Credential Material Accessible?
        |
        v
Collection Method
        |
        v
Sensitive Secrets
        |
        v
New Identities

This is a major security boundary.

docs.title: Authorisation Before secretsdump
docs.text:
Before using it, confirm:

[ ] Credential dumping is in scope
[ ] Target is approved
[ ] Account is approved
[ ] Sensitive-data handling is defined
[ ] Evidence storage is protected
[ ] Cleanup requirements are understood

Do not run credential dumping simply because administrative access exists.

docs.title: NTDS
docs.text:
Domain Controller credential extraction represents particularly high-impact testing.

Conceptually:

Domain Controller
       |
       v
NTDS
       |
       v
Domain Credential Material
       |
       v
Potential Domain-Wide Impact

See:

NTDS.dit and Active Directory Credential Extraction

for detailed methodology.

docs.title: Remote Administration
docs.text:
Impacket includes several remote command-execution examples.

Common tools include:

psexec
wmiexec
smbexec
dcomexec
atexec

These tools use different Windows mechanisms.

docs.title: Remote Execution Comparison
docs.text:
psexec
   |
   +--> SMB
   +--> Service Control Manager

smbexec
   |
   +--> SMB
   +--> Service-based execution

wmiexec
   |
   +--> DCOM
   +--> WMI

dcomexec
   |
   +--> DCOM

atexec
   |
   +--> Task Scheduler

The correct tool depends on:

Privileges
Firewall
Available services
Operational impact
Detection considerations
Rules of engagement

docs.title: psexec
docs.text:
psexec.py implements remote execution using SMB and Windows service-management mechanisms.

Because it can create and interact with a service, it should be considered intrusive.

Check:

impacket-psexec -h

before use.

docs.title: psexec Workflow
docs.text:
Administrative Credential
          |
          v
SMB Reachability
          |
          v
Service Control Access
          |
          v
Remote Execution

Use only after administrative access has been established and remote execution is authorised.

docs.title: wmiexec
docs.text:
wmiexec.py executes commands through WMI/DCOM.

Current upstream documentation notes that the account must have appropriate administrative access and that DCOM connectivity is required.

Conceptually:

Administrative Identity
        |
        v
DCOM
        |
        v
WMI
        |
        v
Remote Process

docs.title: WMI Requirements
docs.text:
Typical considerations include:

RPC Endpoint Mapper
Dynamic RPC ports
DCOM
Firewall
Administrative rights

A successful SMB authentication does not guarantee WMI access.

docs.title: smbexec
docs.text:
smbexec.py uses SMB and service-management mechanisms for remote command execution.

It should be treated as intrusive because service-based execution creates observable host activity.

Check:

impacket-smbexec -h

docs.title: dcomexec
docs.text:
dcomexec.py performs remote execution using DCOM.

This can be relevant when:

SMB-based execution is unavailable
DCOM is reachable
The identity has sufficient rights

Check:

impacket-dcomexec -h

docs.title: atexec
docs.text:
atexec.py uses the Windows Task Scheduler interfaces to execute a command remotely.

Conceptually:

Administrative Identity
        |
        v
Task Scheduler RPC
        |
        v
Scheduled Task
        |
        v
Command

This creates different telemetry from WMI or service-based execution.

docs.title: Choose Remote Administration Deliberately
docs.text:
Do not randomly cycle through:

psexec
wmiexec
smbexec
dcomexec
atexec

Instead:

What access do I have?
        |
        v
What protocol is reachable?
        |
        v
What mechanism is permitted?
        |
        v
What operational impact is acceptable?
        |
        v
Choose One Technique

docs.title: Remote Execution Is Not Enumeration
docs.text:
Keep these phases separate:

ENUMERATION
     |
     v
ACCESS VALIDATION
     |
     v
PRIVILEGE CONFIRMATION
     |
     v
REMOTE EXECUTION

Do not jump directly from discovering a credential to remote execution.

docs.title: ntlmrelayx
docs.text:
ntlmrelayx.py is Impacket's major NTLM relay framework.

It is used for controlled testing of authentication relay scenarios.

Conceptually:

Victim Authentication
        |
        v
Attacker
        |
        v
ntlmrelayx
        |
        v
Target Service
        |
        v
Target Validates
Authentication

docs.title: Capture vs Relay
docs.text:
These are different concepts.

CAPTURE

Client
  |
  v
Attacker
  |
  v
Authentication Material

versus:

RELAY

Client
  |
  v
Attacker
  |
  v
Target Service

Therefore:

Capture != Relay

docs.title: Relay Prerequisites
docs.text:
Relay depends on the protocol and target configuration.

Potential factors include:

SMB signing
LDAP signing
LDAP channel binding
Authentication protocol
Target service
Identity privileges
EPA
Network reachability

A single missing hardening control does not prove a successful relay path.

docs.title: Relay Methodology
docs.text:
Use:

Identify Potential Target
        |
        v
Review Security Controls
        |
        v
Identify Authentication Source
        |
        v
Confirm Rules of Engagement
        |
        v
Controlled Relay Validation
        |
        v
Record Exact Impact

See:

NTLM Relay

for the full technique.

docs.title: Responder and ntlmrelayx
docs.text:
Responder and Impacket are commonly used together in authorised relay testing.

Conceptually:

Responder
    |
    v
Name Resolution / Authentication
    |
    v
Authentication Attempt
    |
    v
ntlmrelayx
    |
    v
Target

But remember:

Responder Capture
       !=
Successful Relay

docs.title: BloodHound and Impacket
docs.text:
BloodHound helps identify relationships.

Impacket can help validate selected relationships.

BloodHound
    |
    v
Potential Path
    |
    v
Understand Edge
    |
    v
Impacket
    |
    v
Controlled Validation

Do not automatically exercise every BloodHound edge.

docs.title: NetExec and Impacket
docs.text:
The tools complement each other.

NetExec
   |
   +--> Broad host discovery
   +--> Credential validation
   +--> Share enumeration
   +--> Access mapping
   |
   v
Interesting Target
   |
   v
Impacket
   |
   +--> Focused LDAP
   +--> Focused RPC
   +--> Kerberos
   +--> SMB
   +--> Delegation
   +--> Remote administration

docs.title: PowerView and Impacket
docs.text:
PowerView provides directory-oriented enumeration from Windows.

Impacket provides protocol-oriented operations from Linux.

Windows
   |
   v
PowerView
   |
   v
Directory Relationships

Linux
   |
   v
Impacket
   |
   v
Protocol Relationships

Using both can provide different perspectives on the same environment.

docs.title: Impacket Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Impacket is commonly used after gaining access to another network segment.

Kali
 |
 v
Pivot
 |
 v
Internal Network
 |
 v
Domain Controller
 |
 v
Impacket

Before assuming a tool is broken, verify:

Routing
DNS
Kerberos
RPC
SMB
LDAP
Dynamic RPC ports

docs.title: SOCKS vs Routed Pivoting
docs.text:
Some Impacket operations are straightforward through SOCKS.

Others become more complicated because Windows protocols may use:

Multiple connections
Dynamic RPC ports
Hostname resolution
Kerberos

A routed/TUN-based pivot can therefore be more convenient for broad AD testing.

See:

Active Directory Pivoting - Tunnelling, Port Forwarding and Network Access

docs.title: DNS During Pivoting
docs.text:
Check:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Resolve the DC:

dig dc01.example.local

Check LDAP:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

Check Kerberos:

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.local

docs.title: Common Error - Clock Skew
docs.text:
Kerberos is time sensitive.

Check:

date

If Kerberos authentication fails unexpectedly, compare the assessment system's time with the Domain Controller.

Do not immediately assume the credential or ticket is invalid.

docs.title: Common Error - DNS
docs.text:
A common failure pattern is:

IP connectivity works
        |
        v
Hostname resolution fails
        |
        v
Kerberos fails

Correct DNS rather than permanently replacing hostnames with IP addresses.

docs.title: Common Error - SPN Mismatch
docs.text:
Kerberos authenticates services through SPNs.

Using:

10.10.20.10

where the ticket expects:

dc01.example.local

can cause unexpected authentication problems.

Prefer correct FQDNs for Kerberos workflows.

docs.title: Common Error - Wrong Domain
docs.text:
Always distinguish:

EXAMPLE\alice

from:

FILE01\alice

A local account and a domain account with the same username are different security principals.

docs.title: Common Error - NTLM Hash Format
docs.text:
Impacket frequently expects:

LMHASH:NTHASH

When only an NT hash is available, the format commonly becomes:

:NTHASH

Always check the individual tool's help.

docs.title: Common Error - Wrong Ticket
docs.text:
A valid Kerberos ticket does not mean it is valid for every service.

Understand:

TGT

versus:

TGS

and the service principal represented by a ticket.

docs.title: Common Error - KRB5CCNAME
docs.text:
Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

Then:

klist

Make sure the expected cache is actually being used.

docs.title: Common Error - RPC Blocked
docs.text:
Tools such as:

lookupsid
samrdump
wmiexec
dcomexec
atexec

may rely on RPC-related connectivity.

Check:

135/tcp
445/tcp
Dynamic RPC ports
Firewall rules

depending on the technique.

docs.title: Common Error - Authentication Works but Tool Fails
docs.text:
This can occur because:

Authentication succeeded
        |
        v
Required Authorisation Missing

For example:

SMB authentication
        !=
Remote Registry access

SMB authentication
        !=
Service Control Manager access

SMB authentication
        !=
WMI access

SMB authentication
        !=
Domain Admin

docs.title: Common Error - Using Old Blog Syntax
docs.text:
Impacket changes over time.

When an old command fails:

<tool> -h

Then verify:

python3 -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('impacket'))"

Compare the installed version against the matching upstream release.

docs.title: Operational Security
docs.text:
Impacket tools can create very different levels of telemetry.

Low-impact examples may include:

LDAP enumeration
RPC enumeration
SMB browsing

More intrusive operations may include:

Kerberos ticket requests
Credential dumping
Remote service creation
Remote task creation
WMI execution
DCOM execution
NTLM relay

Use the least intrusive operation that answers the assessment question.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Create a structured evidence directory:

mkdir -p evidence/impacket

Suggested structure:

evidence/
└── impacket/
    ├── ldap/
    ├── kerberos/
    ├── smb/
    ├── rpc/
    ├── delegation/
    ├── credentials/
    ├── remote-access/
    └── relay/

docs.title: Save Enumeration Output
docs.text:
Example:

impacket-GetADUsers \
    example.local/alice:'Password' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.20.10 \
    -all |
    tee evidence/impacket/ldap/users.txt

Be careful that commands containing passwords may themselves be captured by:

Terminal logging
Shell history
Screenshots

docs.title: Evidence Naming
docs.text:
Useful names include:

users.txt
spns.txt
delegation.txt
sid-enumeration.txt
shares.txt
kerberos-tickets.txt
remote-access.txt
relay-validation.txt

docs.title: Credential Evidence
docs.text:
Avoid putting actual:

Passwords
NTLM hashes
AES keys
Kerberos tickets
Private keys

into reports unless strictly required.

Prefer evidence that demonstrates the security condition without unnecessarily reproducing sensitive secrets.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Report the security condition rather than the tool.

Avoid:

secretsdump worked.

Prefer:

The tested administrative account was able to access credential
material stored by the target Windows system.

Avoid:

GetUserSPNs found an account.

Prefer:

A domain service account was configured with a Service Principal
Name and was therefore eligible for Kerberos service-ticket
requests.

docs.title: Reporting Delegation
docs.text:
Avoid:

findDelegation says constrained.

Prefer:

The service account was configured for constrained delegation to
the identified service.

Then explain:

Principal
Delegation type
Target service
Prerequisites
Potential impact

docs.title: Reporting Remote Administration
docs.text:
Avoid:

wmiexec worked.

Prefer:

The tested account possessed sufficient administrative privileges
to execute commands remotely on APP01 through WMI.

docs.title: Detection Perspective
docs.text:
Impacket activity may create telemetry across:

Windows Security logs
Kerberos logs
SMB logs
LDAP logs
RPC telemetry
Service creation
Task Scheduler
WMI
DCOM
Network monitoring
EDR
Domain Controller logs

Different tools produce different indicators.

docs.title: Purple Team Use
docs.text:
Impacket is useful for controlled purple team exercises because individual protocols and behaviours can be tested separately.

Example:

Technique
   |
   v
Execute Controlled Action
   |
   v
Observe Host Telemetry
   |
   v
Observe Network Telemetry
   |
   v
Detection?
   |
 +---+---+
 |       |
Yes      No
 |       |
 v       v
Tune    Create
Rule    Detection

docs.title: Tool Selection
docs.text:
A practical decision tree:

What do I need?
      |
      +--> Domain users
      |       |
      |       +--> GetADUsers
      |
      +--> SPNs
      |       |
      |       +--> GetUserSPNs
      |
      +--> AS-REP candidates
      |       |
      |       +--> GetNPUsers
      |
      +--> SID / RID information
      |       |
      |       +--> lookupsid
      |
      +--> Delegation
      |       |
      |       +--> findDelegation
      |
      +--> SMB files
      |       |
      |       +--> smbclient
      |
      +--> Kerberos TGT
      |       |
      |       +--> getTGT
      |
      +--> Kerberos service ticket
      |       |
      |       +--> getST
      |
      +--> Ticket conversion
      |       |
      |       +--> ticketConverter
      |
      +--> Credential material
      |       |
      |       +--> secretsdump
      |
      +--> WMI administration
      |       |
      |       +--> wmiexec
      |
      +--> Service-based administration
      |       |

docs.title: Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Kerberoasting is an Active Directory credential attack that targets accounts associated with Service Principal Names (SPNs).

An authenticated domain user can normally request Kerberos service tickets for services they are permitted to access. Parts of those service tickets are encrypted using key material associated with the account running the service.

If that account uses a weak password, the captured service ticket can be subjected to offline password guessing.

Domain User
    |
    | Request service ticket
    v
KDC
    |
    | TGS-REP
    v
Service Ticket
    |
    v
Password-derived encrypted material
    |
    v
Offline password cracking
    |
    v
Service account credential

Kerberoasting does not exploit a vulnerability in Kerberos itself.

The practical risk usually results from a combination of:

SPN-enabled account
        +
Password-derived Kerberos key
        +
Weak or predictable password
        +
Excessive account privileges

Authorised testing only

Kerberoasting obtains password-derived authentication material that can be subjected to offline password cracking. Only perform this testing against accounts and domains explicitly included in the assessment scope. Protect collected tickets and recovered credentials, use controlled cracking strategies, and validate only the minimum impact necessary.

docs.title: Kerberoasting at a Glance
docs.text:
A typical assessment workflow is:

Identify Active Directory domain
          |
          v
Obtain authorised domain access
          |
          v
Enumerate SPNs
          |
          v
Identify user-based service accounts
          |
          v
Review account characteristics
          |
          v
Request service tickets
          |
          v
Export cracking material
          |
          v
Identify encryption type
          |
          v
Offline password assessment
          |
     +----+----+
     |         |
     v         v
 Not cracked  Cracked
     |         |
     v         v
Record        Validate minimum
exposure      required impact
     |         |
     +----+----+
          |
          v
Detection and remediation

docs.title: Kerberos Refresher
docs.text:
Kerberoasting occurs during the service-ticket stage of Kerberos authentication.

A simplified Kerberos workflow is:

User
 |
 | AS-REQ
 v
KDC
 |
 | AS-REP
 v
TGT
 |
 | TGS-REQ
 | Request service ticket
 v
KDC
 |
 | TGS-REP
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Target Service

The important distinction is:

TGT
 |
 +--> Represents authentication to the domain
 |
 v
Used to request service tickets


Service Ticket
 |
 +--> Intended for a specific service
 |
 v
Protected using service-account key material

For detailed Kerberos architecture, see:

Kerberos

docs.title: What Is an SPN?
docs.text:
A Service Principal Name identifies a service instance for Kerberos authentication.

Conceptually:

Service
   |
   v
SPN
   |
   v
Active Directory account

Common SPN forms include:

service/hostname
service/hostname:port

Examples include:

MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433
HTTP/web01.corp.example
CIFS/fileserver.corp.example
LDAP/dc01.corp.example

The SPN allows Kerberos to determine which account represents the requested service.

docs.title: SPN Components
docs.text:
A simplified SPN can be viewed as:

MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433
    |            |            |
    |            |            +--> Port
    |            |
    |            +--> Host
    |
    +--> Service class

Not every SPN includes a port.

docs.title: SPNs and Accounts
docs.text:
SPNs can be associated with:

Computer accounts

or:

User accounts

For Kerberoasting assessments, user-based service accounts are usually particularly interesting because they may use administrator-selected passwords.

Conceptually:

SPN
 |
 +--> Computer Account
 |       |
 |       +--> Machine-managed password
 |
 +--> User Service Account
         |
         +--> Potentially human-managed password

This distinction is important when prioritising targets.

docs.title: Why Service Accounts Are Attractive Targets
docs.text:
Traditional service accounts can have characteristics such as:

  • long-lived passwords
  • passwords that rarely change
  • PasswordNeverExpires
  • human-generated passwords
  • predictable naming conventions
  • access to servers
  • database permissions
  • application privileges
  • local administrator rights
  • delegated Active Directory rights
  • membership in privileged groups

A service account might therefore look like:

svc_sql
   |
   +--> SPN
   +--> Password never expires
   +--> Password unchanged for years
   +--> SQL administrative access
   +--> Local administrator on SQL servers

If the password is weak enough to recover, the resulting impact may extend beyond the individual service.

docs.title: Kerberoasting Requirements
docs.text:
The typical requirements are:

Valid domain account
       |
       +
Reachable domain controller
       |
       +
Kerberos access
       |
       +
Target SPN

Unlike AS-REP Roasting, Kerberoasting generally starts from authenticated domain access.

The requesting user does not normally need administrative privileges.

docs.title: Why Any Domain User Can Be Relevant
docs.text:
Kerberos is designed so authenticated users can request tickets for services they need to access.

Conceptually:

Authenticated User
        |
        v
Request ticket for MSSQLSvc/sql01
        |
        v
KDC
        |
        v
Service Ticket

The KDC cannot require the requesting user to know the service account's password because that would defeat the Kerberos service-ticket model.

The defensive objective is therefore not to prevent legitimate ticket issuance.

Instead, organisations should ensure service accounts use credential material that resists offline recovery and have only the privileges they require.

docs.title: Kerberoasting vs AS-REP Roasting
docs.text:
These techniques target different parts of Kerberos.

AS-REP Roasting
      |
      v
AS-REQ
      |
      v
AS-REP
      |
      v
Pre-authentication disabled


Kerberoasting
      |
      v
TGS-REQ
      |
      v
TGS-REP
      |
      v
Account has SPN

Comparison:

Property AS-REP Roasting Kerberoasting Target User without pre-authentication Account with SPN Common account type User Service account Authentication required Not necessarily Generally yes Ticket stage AS-REP TGS-REP Offline cracking Yes Yes Password strength important Yes Yes

For detailed AS-REP coverage, see:

AS-REP Roasting

docs.title: Kerberoasting vs Password Spraying
docs.text:
Password spraying performs online password guesses:

Password
   |
   v
Many accounts
   |
   v
Authentication service

Kerberoasting instead obtains service-ticket material:

SPN
 |
 v
TGS request
 |
 v
Service ticket
 |
 v
Offline password guessing

The offline stage avoids repeated password authentication attempts against the target account.

For password-spraying methodology, see:

Password Spraying

docs.title: Enumerating SPNs from Windows
docs.text: Windows provides several ways to identify SPNs.

docs.title: setspn
docs.text:
The native setspn.exe utility can query SPNs.

Query SPNs associated with a specific account:

setspn -L <ACCOUNT>

Example:

setspn -L svc_sql

Query registered SPNs within the domain:

setspn -Q */*

This can generate substantial output in large environments.

docs.title: Query a Specific Service Class
docs.text:
For example:

setspn -Q MSSQLSvc/*

HTTP:

setspn -Q HTTP/*

CIFS:

setspn -Q CIFS/*

This can help focus enumeration on particular service types.

docs.title: PowerShell - Active Directory Module
docs.text:
Enumerate users with SPNs:

Get-ADUser `
    -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=*)' `
    -Properties ServicePrincipalName

Display usernames and SPNs:

Get-ADUser `
    -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=*)' `
    -Properties ServicePrincipalName |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,ServicePrincipalName

docs.title: Useful Service Account Properties
docs.text:
Expand enumeration:

Get-ADUser `
    -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=*)' `
    -Properties `
        ServicePrincipalName,
        Enabled,
        PasswordLastSet,
        PasswordNeverExpires,
        MemberOf |
    Select-Object `
        SamAccountName,
        Enabled,
        PasswordLastSet,
        PasswordNeverExpires,
        ServicePrincipalName

This helps prioritise accounts based on actual risk.

docs.title: Enabled SPN Accounts
docs.text:
Filter disabled accounts:

Get-ADUser `
    -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=*)' `
    -Properties ServicePrincipalName,Enabled |
    Where-Object Enabled -eq $true |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,ServicePrincipalName

docs.title: Password-Never-Expires SPN Accounts
docs.text:
Identify accounts where passwords never expire:

Get-ADUser `
    -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=*)' `
    -Properties `
        ServicePrincipalName,
        PasswordNeverExpires,
        PasswordLastSet |
    Where-Object PasswordNeverExpires -eq $true |
    Select-Object `
        SamAccountName,
        PasswordLastSet,
        ServicePrincipalName

This configuration is not automatically exploitable.

It can, however, increase the practical risk of weak service-account passwords remaining valid for long periods.

docs.title: LDAP Enumeration
docs.text:
SPN-bearing users can be identified using:

(servicePrincipalName=*)

A more focused LDAP filter for user objects is:

(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))

docs.title: ldapsearch
docs.text:
Where LDAP access is available:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://10.10.10.10 \
    -D 'CORP\testuser' \
    -W \
    -b 'DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))' \
    sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName pwdLastSet userAccountControl

The exact bind format depends on the environment.

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView can enumerate SPN-enabled user accounts where its use is authorised.

A commonly used command is:

Get-DomainUser -SPN

Useful properties may include:

Get-DomainUser -SPN |
    Select-Object `
        samaccountname,
        serviceprincipalname,
        pwdlastset,
        useraccountcontrol

Exact functionality depends on the PowerView version.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify service accounts and determine their significance.

A useful workflow is:

SPN-enabled account
       |
       v
BloodHound
       |
       +--> Group membership
       +--> Local administrator rights
       +--> Remote management rights
       +--> ACL relationships
       +--> Sessions
       +--> Paths to privileged assets

This is valuable because not every roastable account has the same risk.

For detailed BloodHound coverage, see:

BloodHound

docs.title: Impacket GetUserSPNs
docs.text:
Impacket's GetUserSPNs.py is commonly used for Kerberoasting assessments.

Depending on installation, it may be available as:

GetUserSPNs.py

or:

impacket-GetUserSPNs

Check:

which impacket-GetUserSPNs

Review current options:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

docs.title: Enumerating SPNs with GetUserSPNs
docs.text:
With authorised domain credentials:

impacket-GetUserSPNs \
    'corp.example/testuser:<PASSWORD>' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

This can enumerate accounts associated with SPNs.

Output may include information such as:

ServicePrincipalName
Name
MemberOf
PasswordLastSet
LastLogon
Delegation

depending on the tool version and directory information available.

docs.title: Requesting Service Tickets
docs.text:
To request roastable service-ticket material:

impacket-GetUserSPNs \
    'corp.example/testuser:<PASSWORD>' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 \
    -request

Conceptually:

GetUserSPNs
    |
    v
Enumerate SPNs
    |
    v
TGS-REQ
    |
    v
Domain Controller
    |
    v
TGS-REP
    |
    v
Cracking format

docs.title: Requesting a Specific Account
docs.text:
Where a specific service account has already been identified, use targeted requests where supported by the installed version rather than requesting tickets for every account.

This reduces:

  • authentication noise
  • unnecessary ticket requests
  • evidence volume
  • cracking workload

Review:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

for the installed version's targeting options.

docs.title: Output to a File
docs.text:
Where supported:

impacket-GetUserSPNs \
    'corp.example/testuser:<PASSWORD>' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 \
    -request \
    -outputfile kerberoast.hashes

Protect this file as credential-sensitive assessment evidence.

docs.title: Password Prompting
docs.text:
Avoid placing plaintext passwords directly in shell history where possible.

Instead of:

impacket-GetUserSPNs 'corp.example/testuser:Password123!'

prefer authentication methods that allow interactive prompting where supported by the installed tool.

If credentials must be supplied through a command during a controlled lab, ensure shell-history and evidence-handling requirements are understood.

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication with Impacket
docs.text:
If Kerberos authentication is already available, Impacket tools may support options such as:

-k
-no-pass

depending on the current credential and ticket environment.

For detailed Impacket authentication methods, see:

Impacket

docs.title: NetExec Enumeration
docs.text:
NetExec can also contribute to Active Directory and LDAP enumeration.

With authorised credentials, start by identifying available protocols and domain information.

Example:

nxc ldap 10.10.10.10 \
    -d CORP \
    -u '<USER>' \
    -p '<PASSWORD>'

NetExec modules and protocol functionality evolve, so inspect the installed version:

nxc ldap --help

and available modules:

nxc ldap -L

before relying on a particular Kerberoasting-related command.

For detailed usage, see:

NetExec

docs.title: Service Ticket Output
docs.text:
Kerberoasting material commonly appears in a format beginning with:

$krb5tgs$...

The exact format depends on the Kerberos encryption type.

Treat this material as sensitive.

Do not commit real ticket material to:

Git
GitHub
Documentation repositories
Issue trackers
Public notes

docs.title: Kerberos Encryption Types
docs.text:
Kerberos service tickets may use different encryption types.

Commonly encountered types include:

RC4-HMAC
AES128
AES256

The encryption type has a major effect on offline password-cracking cost.

A useful model is:

Service account
      |
      v
Supported encryption types
      |
      v
Ticket encryption type
      |
      v
Offline cracking characteristics

Do not assume every Kerberoasting ticket uses RC4.

docs.title: RC4 and Kerberoasting
docs.text:
RC4-based Kerberos service tickets have historically been especially relevant to Kerberoasting because password guessing against RC4-HMAC service-ticket material is comparatively efficient.

Conceptually:

SPN account
   |
   v
RC4 service ticket
   |
   v
Offline candidate password
   |
   v
Derive candidate key
   |
   v
Test ticket

Modern environments should reduce unnecessary RC4 dependencies where compatibility permits.

docs.title: AES and Kerberoasting
docs.text:
AES-enabled Kerberos does not eliminate Kerberoasting.

Service-ticket material protected using AES can still potentially be subjected to offline password guessing.

However, the computational characteristics differ from RC4.

Therefore:

AES
 |
 X
Not automatically immune to Kerberoasting

Strong service-account credentials remain essential.

docs.title: Do Not Force Downgrades Unnecessarily
docs.text:
During an assessment, avoid manipulating encryption types merely to obtain easier-to-crack ticket material unless downgrade testing is explicitly part of the authorised scope.

Prefer observing and reporting the environment's natural authentication configuration first.

This provides a more representative assessment.

docs.title: Identifying the Ticket Type
docs.text:
Hashcat can list supported Kerberos modes:

hashcat --help | grep -i kerberos

The captured value itself can also indicate the format:

$krb5tgs$...

Select the cracking mode that corresponds to the actual encryption type.

Do not blindly reuse a mode from an old write-up.

docs.title: Hashcat
docs.text:
Hashcat can perform authorised offline password-strength testing against Kerberos service-ticket material.

General pattern:

hashcat \
    -m <MODE> \
    kerberoast.hashes \
    wordlist.txt

Show recovered results:

hashcat \
    -m <MODE> \
    kerberoast.hashes \
    --show

Determine the correct mode from:

hashcat --help | grep -i kerberos

or the current Hashcat example-hash documentation.

docs.title: John the Ripper
docs.text:
John the Ripper can also support Kerberos service-ticket formats.

List Kerberos-related formats:

john --list=formats | grep -i krb

General workflow:

john \
    --wordlist=wordlist.txt \
    kerberoast.hashes

Show recovered results:

john --show kerberoast.hashes

Verify compatibility with the installed version before beginning the assessment.

docs.title: Controlled Password Cracking
docs.text:
Password cracking should answer a security question.

For example:

Does this privileged service account
use a realistically recoverable password?

A sensible progression is:

Small common-password list
        |
        v
Organisation-relevant candidates
        |
        v
Approved rule set
        |
        v
Larger dictionary if required

Do not automatically run extremely large cracking campaigns when a smaller controlled test already demonstrates the weakness.

docs.title: Password Rules
docs.text:
Password mutation rules can model predictable human password changes such as:

word
  |
  +--> Capitalisation
  +--> Number suffix
  +--> Year suffix
  +--> Special character

For example, a weak organisational password pattern may evolve as:

Service
Service1
Service2026
Service2026!

The security issue is the predictable construction, not a particular cracking tool.

docs.title: Cracking Strategy
docs.text:
A useful assessment workflow is:

Ticket
  |
  v
Identify account
  |
  v
Review password age
  |
  v
Review account purpose
  |
  v
Review password policy
  |
  v
Select realistic candidates
  |
  v
Controlled cracking

This is generally preferable to blindly applying enormous wordlists to every service ticket.

docs.title: Password Age
docs.text:
Old passwords can increase practical Kerberoasting risk.

PowerShell:

Get-ADUser \
    -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=*)' \
    -Properties PasswordLastSet |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,PasswordLastSet

Look for service-account passwords that have remained unchanged for unusually long periods.

Do not assume age alone means the password is weak.

A long randomly generated password can remain resistant to offline guessing.

docs.title: Password Never Expires
docs.text:
Review:

Get-ADUser \
    -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=*)' \
    -Properties PasswordNeverExpires |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,PasswordNeverExpires

The risk is:

PasswordNeverExpires
        +
Weak password
        +
SPN

rather than PasswordNeverExpires by itself.

docs.title: Privilege Analysis
docs.text:
After identifying a roastable account, determine what the account can actually do.

Questions include:

Is it a Domain Admin?

Is it a local administrator?

Can it use WinRM?

Does it control another AD object?

Can it modify groups?

Does it have delegation rights?

Can it access databases?

Does it own sensitive shares?

Does it have a path to Tier 0?

BloodHound is particularly useful for this analysis.

docs.title: High-Value Service Accounts
docs.text:
Potentially high-impact accounts can include:

  • SQL service accounts
  • backup service accounts
  • application deployment accounts
  • monitoring accounts
  • automation accounts
  • web application service accounts
  • privileged middleware accounts
  • legacy domain service accounts

The account name alone does not determine risk.

Validate actual privileges.

docs.title: Domain Admin Service Accounts
docs.text:
A service account should rarely require Domain Admin membership.

If an SPN-enabled service account is a Domain Admin:

SPN
  +
Domain Admin
  +
Weak password
  |
  v
Potential domain compromise

This represents both:

Credential weakness

and:

Excessive privilege

These may warrant separate remediation considerations.

docs.title: Managed Service Accounts
docs.text:
Windows provides managed service-account technologies designed to reduce dependence on manually managed service passwords.

These include:

sMSA

and:

gMSA

A major security advantage is automated password management.

docs.title: Group Managed Service Accounts
docs.text:
A gMSA uses a long, automatically managed password maintained through Active Directory.

Conceptually:

Active Directory
      |
      v
Managed password
      |
      v
gMSA
      |
      v
Authorised hosts

This substantially improves resistance to traditional password cracking compared with weak human-generated service-account passwords.

docs.title: gMSA Is Not a Universal Fix
docs.text:
gMSAs introduce their own security considerations.

The organisation must still protect:

  • permissions to retrieve managed passwords
  • hosts authorised to use the account
  • Active Directory ACLs
  • service configuration
  • account privileges

Therefore:

gMSA
 |
 +--> Strong managed password
 |
 +--> Reduced manual rotation
 |
 X
Not automatically risk-free

docs.title: Service Account Migration
docs.text:
A useful remediation process is:

Traditional service account
         |
         v
Identify application requirements
         |
         v
Can gMSA be used?
      +--+--+
      |     |
     Yes    No
      |     |
      v     v
 Migrate   Generate strong
           random password
              |
              v
        Automated rotation

docs.title: Validating a Recovered Password
docs.text:
If a password is recovered and credential validation is authorised, use the minimum necessary test.

Example:

nxc smb 10.10.10.25 \
    -d CORP \
    -u 'svc_sql' \
    -p '<PASSWORD>'

This can confirm credential validity.

Do not automatically test the credential against every domain system.

docs.title: Authentication Success vs Privilege
docs.text:
Always maintain:

Valid password
      |
      X
Administrator

A successful service-account login only confirms authentication.

Privilege requires separate validation.

docs.title: BloodHound Impact Analysis
docs.text:
BloodHound can help minimise unnecessary active testing.

Recovered account
       |
       v
BloodHound
       |
       +--> MemberOf
       +--> AdminTo
       +--> CanRDP
       +--> CanPSRemote
       +--> ACL relationships
       +--> Session relationships
       +--> Paths to high-value targets

This helps answer:

What could this credential provide access to?

before attempting broad lateral movement.

docs.title: Kerberoasting and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
A recovered service-account credential may later support:

SMB
WinRM
WMI
RDP
SQL
Application authentication

depending on privileges and environment configuration.

These are post-compromise activities and should not be conflated with Kerberoasting itself.

Kerberoasting
      |
      v
Credential recovery
      |
      v
Privilege analysis
      |
      v
Potential lateral movement

docs.title: Kerberoasting and NTLM
docs.text:
The password recovered through Kerberoasting may subsequently be used through:

Kerberos

or:

NTLM

depending on the service and environment.

If the account's NT hash becomes available through another authorised technique, Pass-the-Hash may also become relevant.

Kerberoasting itself does not return an NT hash.

For NTLM fundamentals, see:

NTLM

docs.title: Kerberoasting and Pass-the-Hash
docs.text:
Maintain the distinction:

Kerberoast ticket
       |
       v
Offline password cracking
       |
       v
Plaintext password

versus:

NT hash
   |
   v
Pass-the-Hash

A $krb5tgs$ value cannot simply be used as an NT hash.

docs.title: Ticket Request Scope
docs.text:
Avoid requesting every available service ticket simply because the tool permits it.

A targeted approach is preferable:

Enumerate SPNs
      |
      v
Prioritise accounts
      |
      +--> Privilege
      +--> Password age
      +--> Service type
      +--> Business importance
      |
      v
Request selected tickets

This reduces unnecessary noise and sensitive data collection.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Kerberoasting produces Kerberos service-ticket requests that can be visible on domain controllers.

A central event is:

4769 - A Kerberos service ticket was requested

docs.title: Event 4769
docs.text:
Event 4769 can provide information such as:

Account Name
Service Name
Service ID
Ticket Options
Ticket Encryption Type
Client Address
Status

Field availability can vary with Windows versions and logging enhancements.

This event is useful for identifying unusual service-ticket request patterns.

docs.title: Detecting Bulk Ticket Requests
docs.text:
A basic Kerberoasting pattern may look like:

Single user
    |
    +--> MSSQLSvc/service1
    +--> HTTP/service2
    +--> custom/service3
    +--> MSSQLSvc/service4
    +--> HTTP/service5

within a short period.

Detection logic can correlate:

Requesting account
        +
Source host
        +
Unique SPNs
        +
Time window

docs.title: Targeted Kerberoasting
docs.text:
A sophisticated or cautious assessment may request only one or two high-value service tickets.

This means:

High volume detection

alone is insufficient.

Defenders should also consider:

  • unusual requesting hosts
  • unusual requesting users
  • unusual service-ticket encryption types
  • sensitive SPNs
  • service accounts with weak configurations
  • baseline deviations

docs.title: Encryption-Type Monitoring
docs.text:
Ticket encryption type can be useful detection context.

A useful model is:

4769
 |
 +--> Requesting user
 +--> Service account
 +--> Service
 +--> Client IP
 +--> Encryption type

Unexpected use of legacy encryption types may warrant investigation.

However, encryption type alone should not be treated as proof of Kerberoasting.

docs.title: RC4 Detection
docs.text:
Where an environment normally uses AES, unexpected RC4 service tickets may deserve attention.

Conceptually:

Environment baseline
       |
       +--> Mostly AES
       |
       v
Unexpected RC4 ticket
       |
       v
Investigate

Possible legitimate compatibility requirements must be considered.

docs.title: Configuration-Based Detection
docs.text:
Defenders should maintain an inventory of SPN-enabled user accounts.

PowerShell:

Get-ADUser \
    -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=*)' \
    -Properties \
        ServicePrincipalName,
        PasswordLastSet,
        PasswordNeverExpires,
        Enabled |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        Enabled,
        PasswordLastSet,
        PasswordNeverExpires,
        ServicePrincipalName

Review:

Is the account required?

Is the SPN required?

How old is the password?

Is the password managed?

What privileges does the account have?

Can it be migrated to gMSA?

docs.title: Monitor SPN Changes
docs.text:
Changes to SPNs can also be security relevant.

An attacker with sufficient permissions could potentially modify an account's SPNs as part of other Active Directory attack paths.

Monitor changes to:

servicePrincipalName

especially on privileged accounts.

docs.title: Directory Change Monitoring
docs.text:
Useful monitoring can include:

Account modified
       |
       v
SPN added or changed
       |
       v
Review actor
       |
       v
Review target
       |
       v
Validate change request

Directory auditing should be configured appropriately before relying on these events.

docs.title: Offline Cracking Detection
docs.text:
Once the service ticket has been obtained:

Domain Controller
       |
       X
No interaction required for cracking

The password-cracking stage happens offline.

Therefore defenders should focus on:

Strong service passwords
       +
Secure account configuration
       +
Service-ticket monitoring

rather than expecting to detect the cracking process itself through Active Directory logs.

docs.title: Post-Credential Detection
docs.text:
If the service-account password is recovered and used, additional events may appear.

Examples include:

4624 - Successful logon
4768 - Kerberos authentication ticket
4769 - Kerberos service ticket
4776 - Credential validation where NTLM is used

Correlate:

Unusual service-ticket request
       |
       v
Service account credential use
       |
       v
New source host
       |
       v
Administrative activity

docs.title: Purple Team Validation
docs.text:
Kerberoasting can be tested safely using a dedicated service account.

Example:

PT-Kerberoast
      |
      +--> Controlled SPN
      |
      +--> Known test password
      |
      +--> No production privilege

The red team requests a service ticket while the blue team validates telemetry.

docs.title: Purple Team Exercise Flow
docs.text:
Red Team
   |
   | Enumerate controlled SPN
   v
Domain Controller
   |
   | TGS request
   v
Event 4769
   |
   v
SIEM
   |
   v
Blue Team
   |
   +--> Identify requester?
   +--> Identify source?
   +--> Identify target SPN?
   +--> Identify encryption type?
   +--> Recognise Kerberoasting pattern?

docs.title: Purple Team Metrics
docs.text:
Useful measurements include:

Time to detect
Time to triage
Requesting account identified?
Source host identified?
Service account identified?
SPN identified?
Encryption type identified?
Technique correctly classified?
Response correctly escalated?

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
Kerberoasting should be addressed using layered controls.

Kerberoasting
      |
      +--> Strong service credentials
      |
      +--> gMSA
      |
      +--> Remove unnecessary SPNs
      |
      +--> Least privilege
      |
      +--> Modern encryption
      |
      +--> Password rotation
      |
      +--> Ticket monitoring

docs.title: Strong Service Account Passwords
docs.text:
Because Kerberoasting enables offline guessing, service-account passwords should be resistant to large-scale guessing.

Prefer:

Long
Random
Unique
Machine-generated

over:

Company2026!
SQLService1!
ServicePassword!

Password complexity alone does not guarantee sufficient resistance.

Length and unpredictability are critical.

docs.title: Use gMSA Where Possible
docs.text:
Where applications support them, group Managed Service Accounts can substantially reduce Kerberoasting password-recovery risk.

Benefits include:

  • automatically managed passwords
  • long random passwords
  • automatic rotation
  • reduced administrative handling
  • reduced password reuse

docs.title: Remove Unnecessary SPNs
docs.text:
Review SPNs periodically.

SPN
 |
 +--> Is service still present?
 |
 +--> Is account still used?
 |
 +--> Is duplicate SPN present?
 |
 +--> Is user account required?

Remove obsolete service registrations through controlled change management.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Service accounts should have only the permissions required by their applications.

Avoid:

Service Account
      |
      v
Domain Admins

unless an exceptional, documented technical requirement exists.

Review:

  • domain groups
  • local administrator rights
  • delegated AD permissions
  • database privileges
  • application roles
  • remote logon rights

docs.title: Prefer Modern Kerberos Encryption
docs.text:
Where compatibility permits:

Reduce RC4 dependency
       |
       v
Support AES

This improves Kerberos security more broadly.

However, AES does not make weak passwords acceptable.

docs.title: Rotate Legacy Service Passwords
docs.text:
Where gMSA cannot be used:

Generate strong random password
       |
       v
Store securely
       |
       v
Automate rotation where possible
       |
       v
Monitor service health

Avoid manually constructed passwords.

docs.title: Remove Password-Never-Expires Where Possible
docs.text:
Review whether:

PasswordNeverExpires = True

is genuinely required.

If not, migrate to an appropriate managed credential solution.

Do not simply enable password expiration without understanding how the application receives updated credentials.

docs.title: Protect Privileged Service Accounts
docs.text:
High-value service accounts should receive additional controls.

Consider:

  • dedicated service identity
  • gMSA
  • minimal privileges
  • restricted logon rights
  • network segmentation
  • monitoring
  • protected administrative tiers
  • denial of interactive logon where appropriate

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
The finding should describe the actual weakness demonstrated.

Possible titles include:

Weak Service Account Password Permits Kerberoasting

Kerberoasting Permits Offline Recovery of Privileged Service Account Credentials

Legacy Service Accounts Use Weak Passwords Vulnerable to Offline Kerberos Attacks

If the password was not recovered, a more accurate title may be:

Kerberos Service Accounts Expose Password-Derived Material for Offline Guessing

depending on the organisation's risk model.

docs.title: Avoid Overstatement
docs.text:
Do not report:

SPN exists = Vulnerable

An SPN is a normal Kerberos feature.

The meaningful risk is determined by:

SPN
 |
 +--> Account type
 +--> Password strength
 +--> Encryption
 +--> Password age
 +--> Privileges
 +--> Monitoring

docs.title: Severity Considerations
docs.text:
Consider:

Can ticket material be obtained?
       |
       v
Which encryption type?
       |
       v
How strong is the password?
       |
       v
Was the password recovered?
       |
       v
What privileges does the account have?
       |
       v
What business systems can it access?

A low-privilege service account with a strong random password has a different risk profile from a Domain Admin service account with a predictable password.

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Weak Service Account Password Permits Kerberoasting

Affected Account:
svc_sql

SPN:
MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433

Password Age:
Approximately 3 years

Password Expiration:
Disabled

Validation:
An authenticated standard domain user was able to request a Kerberos
service ticket for the affected SPN.

Offline Password Assessment:
The account password was recovered using an approved password dictionary.

Privileges:
The account had administrative access to the SQL server.

Impact:
An attacker with standard domain credentials could obtain password-derived
Kerberos ticket material and recover the service account password offline,
potentially gaining the privileges assigned to the service account.

Recommendation:
Migrate the service to a gMSA where supported. Otherwise use a long,
randomly generated service password with managed rotation. Remove
unnecessary privileges and review legacy Kerberos encryption requirements.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful evidence includes:

Domain
Domain controller
Requesting account
Target service account
SPN
Service class
Target hostname
PasswordLastSet
PasswordNeverExpires
Account enabled/disabled
Group membership
Ticket encryption type
Request timestamp
Source assessment host
Tool
Command
Password recovered?
Validated privileges

docs.title: Protect Sensitive Evidence
docs.text:
Kerberoasting output is credential-sensitive.

Protect:

$krb5tgs$...
Recovered passwords
Credential files
Kerberos tickets
Screenshots
Tool output

Use:

  • encrypted assessment storage
  • restricted access
  • evidence retention procedures
  • password redaction
  • secure deletion after the engagement

docs.title: GetUserSPNs Cannot Resolve the Domain
docs.text:
Check:

DNS
Domain name
Domain controller
VPN routing
/etc/resolv.conf
/etc/hosts

Where appropriate:

-dc-ip 10.10.10.10

can explicitly identify the domain controller.

docs.title: KDC Unreachable
docs.text:
Check:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 88

Review:

Routing
Firewall
VPN
Domain controller address

docs.title: LDAP Authentication Fails
docs.text:
Check:

Username
Password
Domain
Bind format
LDAP port
TLS requirements
Account state

docs.title: Clock Skew
docs.text:
Kerberos requires reasonably synchronised clocks.

Check:

date

Large time differences between the assessment host and domain controller can cause authentication errors.

docs.title: No SPNs Found
docs.text:
Possible explanations include:

  • insufficient directory access
  • incorrect domain
  • LDAP problems
  • no user-based SPNs
  • only computer-account SPNs
  • incorrect query
  • tool configuration issue

Verify using multiple methods where appropriate.

docs.title: Ticket Obtained but Password Not Cracked
docs.text:
This does not mean the test failed.

Record:

Service ticket obtained
Password not recovered within approved effort

This is materially different from:

Credential compromised

Do not claim password compromise without evidence.

docs.title: Recovered Password Does Not Authenticate
docs.text:
Possible reasons include:

Password changed after ticket issuance
Account disabled
Authentication restrictions
Incorrect domain context
Service-specific restrictions
Credential parsing error

Validate carefully before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: Mistake 1 - Treating Every SPN as a Vulnerability
docs.text:
SPNs are required for normal Kerberos service authentication.

SPN != Vulnerability

The surrounding account configuration determines risk.

docs.title: Mistake 2 - Confusing Kerberoasting with AS-REP Roasting
docs.text:
Remember:

Kerberoasting
     |
     +--> SPN
     +--> TGS


AS-REP Roasting
     |
     +--> Pre-auth disabled
     +--> AS-REP

docs.title: Mistake 3 - Calling a Kerberos Ticket an NT Hash
docs.text:
A Kerberoasting value is not an NT hash.

$krb5tgs$
    |
    X
NT hash

docs.title: Mistake 4 - Assuming Kerberoasting Requires Administrator Rights
docs.text:
A normal authenticated domain user can generally request legitimate service tickets.

Administrative rights are not inherently required.

docs.title: Mistake 5 - Assuming the Password Will Be Recovered
docs.text:
Offline cracking is not guaranteed.

A sufficiently strong random password may remain impractical to recover.

docs.title: Mistake 6 - Ignoring Encryption Type
docs.text: Always identify the ticket encryption type before evaluating cracking feasibility.

docs.title: Mistake 7 - Ignoring Account Privilege
docs.text:
A cracked password matters in the context of what the account can access.

Analyse:

Credential
    +
Privileges
    =
Impact

docs.title: Mistake 8 - Requesting Every Ticket
docs.text: Targeted enumeration and prioritisation generally provide a cleaner assessment.

docs.title: Mistake 9 - Immediately Using the Password Everywhere
docs.text:
A recovered credential does not justify unrestricted lateral movement.

Validate only the required impact.

docs.title: Mistake 10 - Recommending Only Password Rotation
docs.text:
Changing the password may address the immediate credential compromise but not the underlying service-account management problem.

Review:

Password generation
Rotation
gMSA compatibility
Privileges
SPNs
Encryption
Monitoring

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Confirm Kerberoasting is authorised
  • [ ] Identify domain
  • [ ] Identify domain controllers
  • [ ] Confirm Kerberos connectivity
  • [ ] Confirm DNS
  • [ ] Confirm time synchronisation
  • [ ] Establish evidence-handling requirements

docs.title: SPN Enumeration
docs.text:
• [ ] Enumerate user-based SPNs
  • [ ] Identify service accounts
  • [ ] Identify service classes
  • [ ] Identify target hosts
  • [ ] Remove disabled accounts where appropriate
  • [ ] Record SPNs
  • [ ] Identify duplicate or obsolete SPNs

docs.title: Account Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Review PasswordLastSet
  • [ ] Review PasswordNeverExpires
  • [ ] Review group membership
  • [ ] Review delegated privileges
  • [ ] Review local administrator relationships
  • [ ] Review BloodHound paths
  • [ ] Identify gMSA opportunities

docs.title: Ticket Requests
docs.text:
• [ ] Prioritise targets
  • [ ] Avoid unnecessary bulk requests
  • [ ] Record requesting account
  • [ ] Record source host
  • [ ] Record timestamp
  • [ ] Record encryption type
  • [ ] Store ticket material securely

docs.title: Password Assessment
docs.text:
• [ ] Identify correct cracking format
  • [ ] Identify correct Hashcat/John mode
  • [ ] Use approved wordlists
  • [ ] Use realistic rules
  • [ ] Record cracking duration/effort where relevant
  • [ ] Record whether password was recovered
  • [ ] Stop when sufficient evidence exists

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• [ ] Validate recovered credential only if authorised
  • [ ] Determine actual privileges
  • [ ] Review BloodHound relationships
  • [ ] Avoid unnecessary lateral movement
  • [ ] Record minimum demonstrated impact

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• [ ] Review Event 4769
  • [ ] Correlate requesting account
  • [ ] Correlate source host
  • [ ] Review unique SPNs requested
  • [ ] Review encryption types
  • [ ] Monitor SPN changes
  • [ ] Correlate post-compromise authentication

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• [ ] Use strong random service credentials
  • [ ] Migrate to gMSA where possible
  • [ ] Rotate compromised passwords
  • [ ] Remove unnecessary SPNs
  • [ ] Remove excessive privileges
  • [ ] Review password-expiration configuration
  • [ ] Reduce legacy RC4 dependencies
  • [ ] Monitor service-ticket activity

docs.title: Kerberoasting Testing Model
docs.text:
A useful mental model is:

                    Active Directory
                           |
                           v
                     Domain Users
                           |
                           v
                    SPN Enumeration
                           |
                 +---------+---------+
                 |                   |
                 v                   v
          Computer Account      User Account
                 |                   |
                 v                   v
          Machine-managed      Service account
            credential              |
                                     v
                              Prioritise target
                                     |
                                     v
                                  TGS-REQ
                                     |
                                     v
                                    KDC
                                     |
                                     v
                                  TGS-REP
                                     |
                                     v
                              Service Ticket
                                     |
                                     v
                           Identify encryption
                                     |
                                     v
                           Offline password test
                                     |
                           +---------+---------+
                           |                   |
                           v                   v
                     Not recovered         Recovered
                           |                   |
                           v                   v
                    Record exposure       Credential
                                             |
                                             v
                                      Privilege analysis
                                             |
                                             v
                                      Minimum validation

The defensive model is:

Kerberoasting
      |
      +--> Credential strength
      |       |
      |       +--> Long random passwords
      |       +--> gMSA
      |
      +--> Reduce exposure
      |       |
      |       +--> Remove unused SPNs
      |       +--> Remove stale accounts
      |       +--> Modern encryption
      |
      +--> Limit impact
      |       |
      |       +--> Least privilege
      |       +--> Restricted logon
      |
      +--> Detect
              |
              +--> Event 4769
              +--> Ticket-request patterns
              +--> Encryption-type monitoring
              +--> SPN change monitoring

The assessment should answer:

Which user accounts have SPNs?
        |
        v
Are those SPNs still required?
        |
        v
How are the service credentials managed?
        |
        v
How old are the passwords?
        |
        v
Which Kerberos encryption types are used?
        |
        v
Can service-ticket material be obtained?
        |
        v
Is the password realistically recoverable?
        |
        v
What privileges does the account possess?
        |
        v
Can defenders detect the ticket requests?
        |
        v
Can the account migrate to a managed identity?
