docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Active Directory persistence should be treated as a:

Trust Problem

rather than simply an:

Account Problem

A compromised administrator can potentially influence:

Accounts
Groups
ACLs
Kerberos
Certificates
Delegation
Group Policy
Trusts
Management Infrastructure

This means:

Reset Password

may address only one layer.

A useful persistence review asks:

Who Can Authenticate?

Who Can Become Privileged?

Who Can Modify Privileged Objects?

Who Can Replicate Directory Secrets?

Who Holds Authentication Certificates?

Who Can Modify Key Credentials?

Who Controls Kerberos Delegation?

Who Controls GPOs?

Who Controls Certificate Authorities?

Who Controls Federation?

Who Controls Tier 0 Management Systems?

The strongest persistence mechanisms often rely on legitimate Active Directory functionality.

For example:

ACL
Certificate
Group Membership
Delegation
Replication

may all be normal features.

The security issue is:

Who Controls Them?

A complete recovery model is therefore:

Compromise
    |
    v
Identify Initial Access
    |
    v
Identify Escalation
    |
    v
Identify Persistence
    |
    v
Identify Exposed Trust Material
    |
    v
Remove Unauthorised Control
    |
    v
Rotate Affected Secrets
    |
    v
Revoke Affected Certificates
    |
    v
Restore Known-Good Configuration
    |
    v
Monitor for Re-entry

For security assessments, the preferred approach is:

Discover
   |
   v
Analyse
   |
   v
Validate Minimally
   |
   v
Report

rather than:

Install Persistence
   |
   v
Prove It Works

In many environments, demonstrating that an unauthorised principal possesses:

WriteDacl
DCSync
GPO Control
Certificate Control
Key Credential Control

already provides sufficient evidence of the persistence risk without introducing a durable production backdoor.

The final objective is not merely to ensure:

No Attacker Account Exists

but to ensure:

No Unauthorised Path Back to Privilege Exists

docs.title: Active Directory Pivoting - Tunnelling, Port Forwarding and Network Access
docs.text:
Pivoting is the process of using an already accessible system as an intermediary to reach another network, host or service that cannot be reached directly from the operator's current position.

In an Active Directory assessment, a compromised or authorised foothold may have access to:

Internal Subnets
Management Networks
Server VLANs
Domain Controllers
Database Networks
Backup Networks
Legacy Networks
Cloud-Connected Networks
Isolated Application Segments

that are not directly reachable from the testing system.

The basic relationship is:

Operator
   |
   X
   |
Internal Target

but:

Operator
   |
   v
Pivot Host
   |
   v
Internal Target

may be possible.

Pivoting does not inherently provide additional privileges.

It provides:

Network Reachability

which may allow other authorised assessment techniques to operate across previously inaccessible network boundaries.

Authorised testing only

Pivoting can extend testing into network segments that were not directly reachable from the original assessment system. Confirm that every destination network and target remains within the authorised scope. Use restrictive routes and listeners wherever possible, avoid exposing tunnels to unnecessary interfaces, and remove all temporary forwarding configuration when testing is complete.

docs.title: Pivoting at a Glance
docs.text:
A simple pivot is:

Kali
 |
 v
Host A
 |
 v
Host B

A more realistic Active Directory path may be:

Assessment Host
      |
      v
Workstation
      |
      v
Server Network
      |
      v
Application Server
      |
      v
Management Network
      |
      v
Domain Controller

The security assessment should determine:

Why Is the Path Possible?

Which Network Boundary Was Crossed?

Which Host Provided the Route?

Which Services Became Reachable?

Was the Access Intended?

docs.title: Pivoting vs Lateral Movement
docs.text:
These concepts are related but different.

Lateral movement normally means:

Identity / Credential
        |
        v
Remote Service
        |
        v
Another Host

Pivoting normally means:

Network Position
      |
      v
Intermediate Host
      |
      v
Previously Unreachable Network

For example:

WMI to SRV01

may be lateral movement.

Using SRV01 to reach:

10.20.30.0/24

may be pivoting.

docs.title: Pivoting vs Remote Execution
docs.text:
Remote execution answers:

Can I execute something on the remote host?

Pivoting answers:

Can I route or proxy traffic through the remote host?

A host may provide one capability without the other.

docs.title: Pivoting vs Tunnelling
docs.text:
Pivoting is the overall objective.

Tunnelling is one mechanism for achieving it.

Pivoting
   |
   +--> Port Forwarding
   |
   +--> SOCKS Proxy
   |
   +--> Reverse Tunnel
   |
   +--> TUN Interface
   |
   +--> Native Routing

docs.title: Pivoting vs Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Port forwarding exposes or redirects a specific network connection.

Example:

localhost:8445
      |
      v
Pivot
      |
      v
10.20.30.10:445

This provides access to one destination service.

Pivoting can be broader and may provide access to:

Multiple Hosts
Multiple Ports
Entire Subnets

docs.title: Pivoting vs SOCKS
docs.text:
A SOCKS proxy provides application-level proxying.

Example:

Tool
 |
 v
SOCKS5
 |
 v
Pivot
 |
 v
Internal Network

Applications that support SOCKS directly, or that can operate through ProxyChains, can use the tunnel.

docs.title: Pivoting vs TUN
docs.text:
A TUN interface creates a virtual Layer 3 network interface.

Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
Operating-System Routing Table
    |
    v
TUN Interface
    |
    v
Tunnel
    |
    v
Pivot
    |
    v
Internal Network

This can be more transparent than SOCKS because many tools can use the operating system's normal routing table.

docs.title: Why Pivoting Matters in Active Directory
docs.text:
Active Directory environments are rarely flat.

A typical architecture may contain:

User Network
Server Network
Domain Controller Network
Management Network
Database Network
Backup Network
DMZ
Cloud Network

A compromised system may have access to several of these zones.

Example:

Internet
   |
   v
DMZ
   |
   X
   |
Internal Network

But a DMZ host may itself have:

DMZ Host
   |
   +--> Internal DNS
   +--> Database Server
   +--> Domain Services
   +--> Management Server

These relationships should be carefully evaluated.

docs.title: The Pivot Host
docs.text:
A pivot host is an intermediate system through which traffic passes.

Examples include:

Windows Workstation
Windows Server
Linux Server
Jump Host
Application Server
Web Server
Management Server

The host does not necessarily need to be domain joined.

docs.title: Identify Network Interfaces
docs.text:
Before creating any tunnel, understand the pivot's existing network connectivity.

Windows:

Get-NetIPConfiguration

Alternative:

ipconfig /all

Linux:

ip addr

docs.title: Windows Routing Table
docs.text:
Get-NetRoute

Focused output:

Get-NetRoute |
    Select-Object DestinationPrefix,NextHop,InterfaceAlias,RouteMetric

Legacy view:

route print

docs.title: Linux Routing Table
docs.text:
ip route

Example:

default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0
10.20.30.0/24 dev eth1 proto kernel scope link
192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link

This host may provide a path between:

192.168.1.0/24

and:

10.20.30.0/24

depending on firewall and routing controls.

docs.title: Identify Listening Services
docs.text:
Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen |
    Select-Object LocalAddress,LocalPort,OwningProcess

Linux:

ss -lntup

This helps identify:

Existing Management Services
Potential Tunnel Ports
Unexpected Exposures

docs.title: Identify Reachable Networks
docs.text:
Do not immediately perform broad scanning through a pivot.

Start with:

Interfaces
Routes
DNS Configuration
Known Application Dependencies
Active Directory Information
Configuration Files
Approved Architecture Documentation

Then perform targeted validation.

docs.title: Windows DNS Configuration
docs.text:
Get-DnsClientServerAddress |
    Where-Object ServerAddresses |
    Select-Object InterfaceAlias,AddressFamily,ServerAddresses

This can reveal internal DNS infrastructure accessible from the pivot.

docs.title: Linux DNS Configuration
docs.text:
Depending on the system:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

or:

resolvectl status

docs.title: Active Directory Context
docs.text:
On a domain-joined Windows host:

$env:USERDNSDOMAIN

$env:LOGONSERVER

nltest /dsgetdc:corp.example

These can help identify domain infrastructure visible from the pivot.

docs.title: Basic Pivoting Decision Model
docs.text:
Before selecting a tool, determine:

What Can the Operator Reach?

What Can the Pivot Reach?

What Must Be Reached?

Which Direction Can Connections Be Established?

Which Protocols Must Traverse the Tunnel?

The decision flow is:

Destination
    |
    v
Single Service?
    |
    +--> Yes --> Port Forward
    |
    v
Multiple TCP Services?
    |
    +--> Yes --> SOCKS
    |
    v
Need Broad IP Routing?
    |
    +--> Yes --> TUN

Then determine:

Can Operator Connect to Pivot?

or:

Can Pivot Connect Back to Operator?

This determines whether a:

Forward

or:

Reverse

tunnel is more suitable.

docs.title: Pivoting Method Selection
docs.text:
Requirement Common Approach One remote TCP service Local port forwarding Expose one service from pivot side Remote port forwarding Multiple TCP destinations SOCKS proxy SOCKS-aware tooling SOCKS5 Broad Layer 3 access TUN interface Outbound-only pivot Reverse tunnel Existing SSH access SSH forwarding Complex multi-hop routing Ligolo-ng or chained tunnels

The correct approach depends on:

Scope
Network Controls
Available Software
Privileges
Protocols
Operational Risk

docs.title: Local Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Local forwarding maps a local port to a remote destination.

Conceptually:

Operator
localhost:8445
      |
      v
Tunnel
      |
      v
Pivot
      |
      v
10.20.30.10:445

The operator then connects to:

127.0.0.1:8445

while the pivot reaches:

10.20.30.10:445

docs.title: SSH Local Port Forwarding
docs.text:
If legitimate SSH access to the pivot already exists:

ssh -L 8445:10.20.30.10:445 user@pivot.example

The mapping becomes:

127.0.0.1:8445
      |
      v
SSH
      |
      v
Pivot
      |
      v
10.20.30.10:445

docs.title: Bind Locally Only
docs.text:
By default, prefer forwarding listeners bound to:

127.0.0.1

rather than:

0.0.0.0

unless there is a specific authorised reason to expose the listener to other systems.

This reduces accidental exposure.

docs.title: SSH Forward Without Interactive Shell
docs.text:
Where supported:

ssh -N -L 8445:10.20.30.10:445 user@pivot.example

-N tells SSH not to execute a remote command.

This is useful when only forwarding is required.

docs.title: Remote Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Remote forwarding works in the opposite direction.

Conceptually:

Remote Side
localhost:8080
      |
      v
SSH Tunnel
      |
      v
Operator-Side Destination

Example:

ssh -N -R 8080:127.0.0.1:8000 user@pivot.example

The exact exposure of the remote listening port depends on the SSH server configuration.

docs.title: Remote Forwarding Security
docs.text:
Do not assume a remote forwarded port is bound only to loopback.

Review:

GatewayPorts
Bind Address
Firewall
SSH Server Configuration

before using remote forwarding in sensitive environments.

docs.title: Dynamic SSH Forwarding
docs.text:
SSH can provide a SOCKS proxy using:

ssh -N -D 1080 user@pivot.example

This creates a SOCKS listener on:

127.0.0.1:1080

The flow becomes:

Application
    |
    v
127.0.0.1:1080
    |
    v
SSH
    |
    v
Pivot
    |
    v
Destination

docs.title: SOCKS Proxy
docs.text:
SOCKS provides a flexible way to proxy multiple TCP connections.

Example:

Browser
   |
   v
SOCKS
   |
   v
Pivot
   |
   +--> Web Server
   |
   +--> SMB Server
   |
   +--> LDAP Server
   |
   +--> Database

Tool compatibility varies.

docs.title: SOCKS4 vs SOCKS5
docs.text:
SOCKS5 provides capabilities beyond SOCKS4 and is generally preferred where supported.

Important differences can include:

Authentication Support
Addressing
DNS Handling
Protocol Features

Always verify which version the selected tunnelling tool provides.

docs.title: ProxyChains
docs.text:
ProxyChains can force many TCP client applications through a SOCKS proxy.

Common configuration file:

/etc/proxychains4.conf

A typical SOCKS5 entry is:

socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

docs.title: Test ProxyChains
docs.text:
For a known authorised HTTP service:

proxychains4 curl http://10.20.30.20/

This provides a low-impact connectivity test.

docs.title: ProxyChains and Nmap
docs.text:
Nmap does not behave transparently through ProxyChains for every scan type.

Raw packet techniques such as:

SYN Scan
ICMP Discovery
OS Detection

cannot simply be proxied through a normal SOCKS TCP proxy.

Where TCP connect scanning is explicitly required:

proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -p80,443 10.20.30.20

Keep scans tightly scoped.

docs.title: Why -sT Matters
docs.text:
A SOCKS proxy operates at a higher level than raw packet generation.

Therefore:

SYN Scan

requires packet-level access that SOCKS does not provide.

TCP connect scanning:

-sT

uses normal socket connections and is more compatible with SOCKS proxying.

docs.title: Why -Pn Matters
docs.text:
Host discovery mechanisms such as ICMP may not traverse a SOCKS proxy.

Using:

-Pn

tells Nmap to treat the target as online and test the specified ports directly.

This does not mean:

The Host Is Definitely Online

It simply skips normal host discovery.

docs.title: DNS Through a Proxy
docs.text:
DNS deserves special attention during pivoting.

A tool may resolve:

srv01.corp.example

on the operator's system rather than through the pivot.

If the internal DNS name is only resolvable inside the target network, this can fail.

docs.title: Proxy DNS
docs.text:
ProxyChains supports proxy-based DNS behaviour depending on configuration.

Review:

proxy_dns

in:

/etc/proxychains4.conf

before relying on internal hostnames.

docs.title: DNS Leakage
docs.text:
A common operational mistake is:

Internal Hostname
      |
      v
Operator's Normal DNS Resolver

instead of:

Internal Hostname
      |
      v
Tunnel
      |
      v
Internal DNS Resolver

This can:

Fail Resolution
Leak Internal Names
Produce Misleading Results

docs.title: Chisel
docs.text:
Chisel is a TCP tunnelling tool that operates over HTTP and uses SSH internally for transport security.

It can provide:

Port Forwarding
Reverse Port Forwarding
SOCKS

and is useful where an authorised pivot can make outbound HTTP connections.

Project:

Chisel

Always verify current syntax with:

chisel --help

docs.title: Chisel Architecture
docs.text:
A common reverse-pivot architecture is:

Operator
Chisel Server
    ^
    |
    | Outbound Connection
    |
Pivot
Chisel Client
    |
    v
Internal Network

This can be useful when:

Operator -> Pivot

connections are blocked but:

Pivot -> Operator

connections are permitted.

docs.title: Start a Chisel Server
docs.text:
In an authorised lab, a server capable of reverse tunnels can be started with:

chisel server --reverse --port 8080

Check the installed version first:

chisel server --help

docs.title: Chisel Reverse SOCKS
docs.text:
From the pivot:

chisel client OPERATOR_IP:8080 R:socks

The exact SOCKS listener behaviour and defaults should be verified against the installed Chisel version.

The conceptual flow is:

Internal Target
      ^
      |
Pivot
      |
      | Outbound Tunnel
      v
Operator
      |
      v
SOCKS

docs.title: Chisel Security
docs.text:
Treat the Chisel server as temporary assessment infrastructure.

Restrict:

Source Addresses
Listening Interfaces
Firewall Rules
Assessment Duration

where possible.

Do not leave an unrestricted tunnelling server running after the engagement.

docs.title: Chisel Authentication
docs.text:
Where appropriate, configure Chisel authentication rather than exposing an unauthenticated tunnelling service.

Check current options:

chisel server --help

because authentication and configuration options may change between versions.

docs.title: Ligolo-ng
docs.text:
Ligolo-ng provides a tunnelling approach based around:

Agent
Proxy
TUN Interface

Project:

Ligolo-ng

Its major advantage is that many tools can interact with the routed network without requiring ProxyChains.

docs.title: Ligolo-ng Architecture
docs.text:
Assessment Host
      |
      v
Ligolo Proxy
      |
      v
TUN Interface
      |
      v
Encrypted Tunnel
      |
      v
Ligolo Agent
      |
      v
Internal Network

docs.title: Why TUN Is Useful
docs.text:
With a TUN interface:

Tool
 |
 v
Operating-System Route
 |
 v
TUN
 |
 v
Tunnel
 |
 v
Pivot

Many applications can operate normally because the routing occurs at the operating-system level.

This can simplify use of tools that do not support SOCKS.

docs.title: Check Ligolo-ng Version
docs.text:
Before using syntax from notes:

./proxy -h

and:

./agent -h

Ligolo-ng has changed its interface across versions, so current built-in help should be treated as authoritative for the installed release.

docs.title: Ligolo-ng Proxy
docs.text:
A typical assessment begins by starting the proxy component on the operator system.

The exact command depends on the installed release.

Verify:

./proxy -h

and identify:

Listen Address
Listen Port
TLS Options
Authentication Options

before starting the service.

docs.title: Ligolo-ng Agent
docs.text:
The agent is started on the authorised pivot and connects to the proxy.

Conceptually:

Pivot Agent
    |
    | Outbound
    v
Operator Proxy

Verify current connection syntax using:

./agent -h

docs.title: Ligolo-ng Route
docs.text:
Once the tunnel interface and session are established, a route is added on the assessment host for the network reachable through the pivot.

Conceptually:

sudo ip route add 10.20.30.0/24 dev ligolo

The interface name must match the interface actually created for the assessment.

docs.title: Check Routes
docs.text:
ip route

Verify that only the intended in-scope networks are routed through the tunnel.

docs.title: Route Specificity
docs.text:
Prefer:

10.20.30.0/24

over:

0.0.0.0/0

when only one internal network is required.

This reduces accidental routing of unrelated traffic through the pivot.

docs.title: TUN vs SOCKS
docs.text:
SOCKS:

Application
    |
    v
Proxy Configuration
    |
    v
SOCKS

TUN:

Application
    |
    v
Normal Network Stack
    |
    v
Routing Table
    |
    v
TUN

docs.title: TUN Advantages
docs.text:
Potential advantages include:

Broader Tool Compatibility
Normal Routing Semantics
No ProxyChains Requirement
Simpler Multi-Service Access

docs.title: TUN Considerations
docs.text:
Potential considerations include:

Route Conflicts
Local Privileges
DNS Configuration
Overlapping Networks
Accidental Traffic Routing
Cleanup

docs.title: Overlapping Networks
docs.text:
A common problem is:

Operator Network:
10.0.0.0/24

Target Internal Network:
10.0.0.0/24

The local operating system may route traffic to the wrong interface.

Possible solutions depend on the tunnelling technology and environment.

Do not blindly replace the operator's normal route.

docs.title: Route Inspection
docs.text:
Before adding routes:

ip route

Record existing entries.

After adding routes:

ip route

confirm the intended result.

After testing, remove only the routes created for the assessment.

docs.title: Remove a Linux Route
docs.text:
Example:

sudo ip route del 10.20.30.0/24 dev ligolo

Use the actual interface and route configured during testing.

docs.title: SSH as a Pivot
docs.text:
SSH is often the simplest option when legitimate SSH access already exists.

Supported approaches include:

Local Forwarding
Remote Forwarding
Dynamic SOCKS

This avoids introducing another tunnelling utility when SSH already provides the required functionality.

docs.title: SSH Local Forward
docs.text: ssh -N -L 8445:10.20.30.10:445 user@pivot.example

docs.title: SSH Dynamic SOCKS
docs.text: ssh -N -D 1080 user@pivot.example

docs.title: SSH Remote Forward
docs.text: ssh -N -R 8080:127.0.0.1:8000 user@pivot.example

docs.title: SSH Bind Address
docs.text:
A local forward can explicitly bind to loopback:

ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:8445:10.20.30.10:445 user@pivot.example

This is preferable to unnecessarily exposing the listener externally.

docs.title: SSH Keepalive
docs.text:
Long-running assessment tunnels may benefit from SSH keepalive configuration.

For example:

ssh -N -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -L 127.0.0.1:8445:10.20.30.10:445 user@pivot.example

This can help detect broken sessions.

docs.title: Windows SSH
docs.text:
Modern Windows systems may have:

OpenSSH Client
OpenSSH Server

installed as optional capabilities.

Check:

Get-Command ssh.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Do not install additional Windows features without explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Windows Portproxy
docs.text:
Windows includes:

netsh interface portproxy

which can configure TCP forwarding.

This modifies persistent operating-system configuration and should therefore be used carefully.

docs.title: View Existing Portproxy Rules
docs.text:
netsh interface portproxy show all

This is safe for inspection.

docs.title: Portproxy Concept
docs.text:
Client
 |
 v
Pivot:8445
 |
 v
Windows Portproxy
 |
 v
10.20.30.10:445

docs.title: Portproxy Modification Warning
docs.text:
Creating a portproxy rule changes the host configuration and may persist after the assessment.

Prefer temporary tunnelling mechanisms unless:

Portproxy Testing Is Explicitly Required

docs.title: Example Portproxy Rule
docs.text:
In a controlled lab:

netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=127.0.0.1 listenport=8445 connectaddress=10.20.30.10 connectport=445

This requires suitable privileges.

docs.title: Verify Portproxy
docs.text: netsh interface portproxy show all

docs.title: Remove Portproxy
docs.text:
netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 listenaddress=127.0.0.1 listenport=8445

Always verify cleanup:

netsh interface portproxy show all

docs.title: Windows Firewall and Portproxy
docs.text:
Creating a portproxy rule does not automatically guarantee that the listener is reachable through Windows Firewall.

Do not weaken firewall rules merely to make a pivot work unless firewall changes are explicitly part of the approved test.

docs.title: Native Linux Forwarding
docs.text:
Linux can route traffic between interfaces when:

IP Forwarding
Routing
Firewall

are configured appropriately.

Check current forwarding state:

sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward

docs.title: Do Not Enable Routing Automatically
docs.text:
Changing:

net.ipv4.ip_forward

modifies the host's networking behaviour.

Do not enable it on a production pivot merely to facilitate testing unless explicitly authorised.

A user-space tunnel may be less intrusive.

docs.title: Socat
docs.text:
Socat can relay connections between network endpoints.

Project documentation:

Socat

It can be useful for simple single-port forwarding where already installed.

docs.title: Socat Forwarding Concept
docs.text:
Client
 |
 v
Pivot:8445
 |
 v
socat
 |
 v
10.20.30.10:445

docs.title: Socat Example
docs.text:
In an authorised lab:

socat TCP-LISTEN:8445,bind=127.0.0.1,reuseaddr,fork TCP:10.20.30.10:445

This keeps the listener on loopback.

docs.title: Verify Socat Listener
docs.text: ss -lntp

docs.title: Stop Socat
docs.text:
Terminate the assessment process when testing is complete.

Do not leave forwarding listeners running.

docs.title: Reverse Tunnels
docs.text:
A reverse tunnel is useful when:

Operator
   |
   X
   |
Pivot

but:

Pivot
   |
   v
Operator

is permitted.

The pivot initiates the connection outward.

docs.title: Reverse Tunnel Model
docs.text:
Internal Network
      ^
      |
Pivot Host
      |
      | Outbound Connection
      v
Assessment Host

The established connection is then used to carry traffic back through the pivot.

docs.title: Why Reverse Tunnels Work
docs.text:
Network security frequently permits:

Outbound Connections

more broadly than:

Inbound Connections

A reverse tunnel uses that asymmetry.

This does not mean the control is automatically vulnerable.

The security question is whether the allowed outbound path enables an unintended trust-boundary bypass.

docs.title: Egress Filtering
docs.text:
Strong egress controls can restrict:

Pivot -> Internet

or:

Server -> Arbitrary External Host

connections.

Assess:

Allowed Destinations
Allowed Ports
Proxy Requirements
TLS Inspection
DNS Restrictions
Application Controls

docs.title: Do Not Bypass Controls Unnecessarily
docs.text:
If a tunnel is blocked by:

Firewall
Proxy
Application Control
EDR
Egress Filtering

do not immediately attempt increasingly evasive techniques.

First determine whether the control itself answers the assessment question.

docs.title: Double Pivoting
docs.text:
Sometimes the desired target is reachable only through multiple systems.

Example:

Operator
   |
   v
Pivot A
   |
   v
Network B
   |
   v
Pivot B
   |
   v
Network C
   |
   v
Target

This is commonly called:

Double Pivoting

or:

Multi-Hop Pivoting

docs.title: Multi-Hop Risks
docs.text:
Every additional pivot increases:

Complexity
Latency
Detection Surface
Cleanup Requirements
Route Conflicts
Failure Points
Scope Risk

Use the minimum number of pivots required.

docs.title: SSH Multi-Hop
docs.text:
SSH supports jump hosts through:

ProxyJump

Example:

ssh -J user@jump01.example admin@srv01.internal.example

This is often cleaner than manually creating several forwarding layers when SSH access already exists.

docs.title: SSH Config
docs.text:
For repeated authorised administration:

Host jump01
    HostName jump01.example
    User audituser

Host srv01
    HostName srv01.internal.example
    User auditadmin
    ProxyJump jump01

Then:

ssh srv01

Do not store passwords in SSH configuration.

docs.title: ProxyChains Multi-Hop
docs.text:
ProxyChains can chain proxies depending on configuration.

However, each additional proxy adds complexity and can make:

DNS
Timeouts
Authentication
Tool Compatibility

harder to troubleshoot.

docs.title: Routing Through Multiple Pivots
docs.text:
For complex networks, a TUN-based solution may be easier to reason about than multiple application-level SOCKS proxies.

The important principle is:

Understand Every Route

before adding another one.

docs.title: Pivoting and SMB
docs.text:
Suppose:

10.20.30.10:445

is reachable only from the pivot.

A tunnel may make SMB accessible to the assessment system.

However, SMB tools can depend on:

Hostname Resolution
Kerberos SPNs
Multiple Connections
RPC
Named Pipes

so a single forwarded port may not reproduce full native network access.

See:

SMB

docs.title: Pivoting and Kerberos
docs.text:
Kerberos can be particularly sensitive to tunnelling configuration.

Requirements may include:

Correct DNS
Correct Hostname
Reachable KDC
Reachable Service
Correct SPN
Time Synchronisation

docs.title: Kerberos Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Assessment Host
      |
      +--> KDC
      |
      +--> Target Service

Both paths may need to be available.

Forwarding only:

Target:445

may not be sufficient if the assessment host also needs access to:

Domain Controller:88

docs.title: Kerberos Ports
docs.text:
Common Kerberos-related connectivity includes:

88/TCP
88/UDP
464/TCP
464/UDP

depending on the operation.

DNS may also require:

53/TCP
53/UDP

docs.title: LDAP Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Active Directory enumeration may require:

389/TCP
636/TCP
3268/TCP
3269/TCP

depending on whether the workflow uses:

LDAP
LDAPS
Global Catalog
Global Catalog over TLS

docs.title: DNS Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Internal Active Directory names often require the domain's DNS servers.

A useful architecture is:

Assessment Tool
      |
      v
Tunnel
      |
      v
Internal DNS
      |
      v
AD Name Resolution

Incorrect DNS configuration is one of the most common reasons that:

IP Connectivity Works

but:

Active Directory Tooling Fails

docs.title: Pivoting and BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound data collection can require access to multiple services across domain systems.

See:

BloodHound

Before collecting through a pivot, determine which protocols the selected collector requires.

Avoid unnecessarily routing the entire assessment system through the target network.

docs.title: Pivoting and NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec can operate against multiple protocols.

See:

NetExec

When using it through a pivot, verify whether the tunnel supports the required:

TCP Connections
DNS
Kerberos
RPC
SMB
LDAP

behaviour.

docs.title: Pivoting and Impacket
docs.text:
Impacket tools can require different combinations of:

SMB
RPC
Kerberos
LDAP
HTTP
DNS

See:

Impacket

Do not assume that because one Impacket tool works through a tunnel, every Impacket tool will.

docs.title: Pivoting and WMI
docs.text:
Traditional remote WMI requires:

135/TCP
+
Dynamic RPC

A single port forward to:

135/TCP

does not provide the dynamic RPC connectivity required for normal WMI operation.

See:

WMI

docs.title: Pivoting and DCOM
docs.text:
DCOM has the same general RPC consideration:

135/TCP
      |
      v
Dynamic RPC Port

A route-based tunnel is often easier to use for RPC-heavy protocols than a collection of individual port forwards.

See:

DCOM

docs.title: Pivoting and WinRM
docs.text:
WinRM commonly uses:

5985/TCP
5986/TCP

Because these are fixed ports, simple forwarding may be sufficient for some WinRM workflows.

See:

WinRM

docs.title: Pivoting and RDP
docs.text:
RDP commonly uses:

3389/TCP

A local forward can expose an internal RDP service to the assessment host.

Conceptually:

127.0.0.1:13389
      |
      v
Tunnel
      |
      v
10.20.30.20:3389

Interactive logon should only be used when required by the test objective.

docs.title: Pivoting and Web Applications
docs.text:
Internal web applications are often straightforward to access through:

SOCKS
Port Forwarding
TUN

For example:

Browser
   |
   v
SOCKS
   |
   v
Internal Web Application

Browser proxy configuration may be preferable to routing all system traffic through the pivot.

docs.title: Browser SOCKS
docs.text:
A browser can be configured to use:

127.0.0.1:1080

as a SOCKS proxy.

Where internal DNS is required, ensure DNS requests are also resolved through the intended network path.

docs.title: Burp Suite Through a Pivot
docs.text:
A useful assessment chain can be:

Browser
   |
   v
Burp Suite
   |
   v
SOCKS Proxy
   |
   v
Pivot
   |
   v
Internal Web Application

Burp Suite supports upstream SOCKS proxy configuration.

This allows:

Browser -> Burp -> Pivot -> Internal Application

while preserving normal web-testing functionality.

docs.title: Do Not Expose Internal Services Publicly
docs.text:
Avoid creating:

0.0.0.0:445
      |
      v
Internal SMB

or similar public listeners.

Prefer:

127.0.0.1

for local assessment forwarding whenever possible.

docs.title: Bind Address Matters
docs.text:
Compare:

127.0.0.1:8445

with:

0.0.0.0:8445

The first is reachable only locally.

The second may be reachable from other network interfaces.

This can unintentionally expose internal services.

docs.title: Privilege Requirements
docs.text:
Some pivoting techniques require elevated privileges.

Examples can include:

Creating TUN Interfaces
Changing Routes
Enabling IP Forwarding
Changing Firewall Rules
Configuring Windows Portproxy

Others may operate entirely in user space.

Prefer the least invasive method that satisfies the test objective.

docs.title: User-Space Tunnels
docs.text:
User-space tunnelling can avoid modifying:

Kernel Forwarding
NAT
Persistent Routing
System Firewall

on the pivot.

This often simplifies cleanup.

docs.title: Network Address Translation
docs.text:
Some native routing designs require:

NAT

to allow return traffic.

However, adding NAT rules changes network behaviour and may affect other traffic.

Do not modify production NAT or firewall configuration unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Return Routes
docs.text:
Routing requires bidirectional communication.

Suppose:

Assessment Host
      |
      v
Pivot
      |
      v
10.20.30.10

The destination must have a valid return path.

Tunnelling tools often solve this by carrying responses back through the established connection.

Native routing may require explicit:

Routes
NAT

depending on the topology.

docs.title: Tunnel Direction
docs.text: Determine connection direction before selecting the tool.

docs.title: Forward Connection
docs.text:
Operator
   |
   v
Pivot

Useful options may include:

SSH Local Forward
SSH Dynamic Forward
Direct Agent Connection

docs.title: Reverse Connection
docs.text:
Pivot
   |
   v
Operator

Useful options may include:

Reverse SSH
Chisel Reverse Tunnel
Ligolo-ng Agent

docs.title: Firewall Considerations
docs.text:
Ask:

Can Operator Reach Pivot?

Can Pivot Reach Operator?

Which Ports Are Allowed?

Is an HTTP Proxy Required?

Is DNS Allowed?

Is TLS Inspection Present?

Are Unknown Binaries Blocked?

The answers determine the appropriate pivoting design.

docs.title: Application Proxies
docs.text:
Some enterprise environments require outbound traffic through:

HTTP Proxy

A tunnelling tool may not automatically inherit system proxy configuration.

Do not modify enterprise proxy configuration merely to force a tunnel through it.

docs.title: TLS Inspection
docs.text:
Outbound TLS may be inspected by enterprise security controls.

This can affect:

Certificate Validation
Unknown Protocols over TLS
Tunnel Reliability
Detection

Do not disable enterprise TLS controls during an assessment unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Pivoting OPSEC
docs.text:
Pivoting can produce significant network telemetry.

Potential indicators include:

Long-Lived Connections
Unusual Outbound Connections
High Fan-Out Internal Connections
Unexpected SOCKS Traffic
Unusual SSH Connections
New Listening Ports
TUN Interfaces
Route Changes
Portproxy Rules
Unknown Tunnel Processes

docs.title: High Fan-Out Traffic
docs.text:
A tunnel may transform:

One Connection to Pivot

into:

Pivot
 |
 +--> Host 1
 +--> Host 2
 +--> Host 3
 +--> Host 4
 +--> Host 5

From the internal network's perspective, all traffic may appear to originate from:

Pivot Host

This is important for detection and evidence interpretation.

docs.title: Source Attribution
docs.text:
When traffic is proxied:

Assessment Host
      |
      v
Pivot
      |
      v
Target

the target may log:

Pivot IP

rather than:

Assessment Host IP

Document this clearly in the assessment timeline.

docs.title: Pivoting Detection
docs.text:
Detection should combine:

Process Telemetry
Network Telemetry
Firewall Logs
Route Changes
Listening Ports
Authentication
EDR
Proxy Logs
DNS

docs.title: Process Detection
docs.text:
Potential processes requiring context can include:

ssh.exe
ssh
chisel
socat
Custom Tunnel Agents

These tools can also be legitimate.

Do not detect solely by executable name.

docs.title: Command-Line Telemetry
docs.text:
Where process command-line auditing is enabled, look for unusual use of:

-L
-R
-D

with SSH or unusual forwarding parameters in other networking tools.

docs.title: Network Detection
docs.text:
Look for:

Long-Lived External Connections
Unexpected Outbound Server Connections
Unexpected High-Volume Internal Connections
New Listening Ports
Unusual Destination Networks

docs.title: Route Changes
docs.text:
Unexpected changes to:

Routing Table
IP Forwarding
Network Interfaces

may indicate tunnelling or unauthorised network bridging.

docs.title: Windows Portproxy Detection
docs.text:
Review:

netsh interface portproxy show all

Unexpected entries should be investigated.

docs.title: Linux Forwarding Detection
docs.text:
Check:

sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward

and review:

ip route

as part of system-baseline monitoring where appropriate.

docs.title: New Network Interfaces
docs.text:
TUN-based tunnelling may create interfaces.

Linux:

ip link

and:

ip addr

Unexpected interfaces should be investigated in context.

docs.title: Firewall Telemetry
docs.text:
Network and host firewalls can identify:

New Outbound Connections
Unexpected East-West Traffic
RPC Fan-Out
SMB Fan-Out
LDAP Access
RDP Connections

originating from systems that normally do not perform administrative activity.

docs.title: EDR Telemetry
docs.text:
Modern EDR platforms may detect:

Tunnel Tools
Unusual Process Execution
Network Connections
Port Listeners
Route Modification
Persistence
Binary Introduction

Pivoting should not be assumed to be invisible.

docs.title: Detection Correlation
docs.text:
A useful model is:

New Process
    |
    v
Long-Lived Connection
    |
    v
New Internal Fan-Out
    |
    v
Previously Unusual Network Segment

This correlation is stronger than any single signal.

docs.title: Pivot Host Context
docs.text:
Compare:

Network Management Server
       |
       v
Many Internal Connections

with:

User Workstation
       |
       v
Many Server-Segment Connections

The second pattern is usually more suspicious.

docs.title: Pivoting Hardening
docs.text:
A strong defensive model includes:

Network Segmentation
Host Firewalls
Egress Filtering
Least Privilege
Administrative Tiering
Application Control
EDR
Proxy Restrictions
Network Monitoring
DNS Monitoring
Restricted Management Paths

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Segmentation should control:

Which Source
Can Reach
Which Destination
On Which Port
For Which Purpose

rather than simply creating VLANs.

docs.title: Segmentation Is Not Just VLANs
docs.text:
A network may contain:

User VLAN
Server VLAN
Management VLAN

but if:

User VLAN -> All Server Ports

is permitted, the security boundary may provide limited protection.

docs.title: Host Firewalls
docs.text:
Host-based firewall policy remains important even when network firewalls exist.

Example:

Server
 |
 +--> Allow WinRM from Admin Network
 |
 +--> Allow Monitoring from Monitoring Network
 |
 +--> Deny Workstation Network

docs.title: Egress Filtering
docs.text:
Servers should not automatically be permitted to connect to:

Any Internet Address
Any Port

unless required.

Restricting outbound connectivity can make reverse tunnelling more difficult and improve detection.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Application control can reduce the ability to introduce arbitrary tunnelling binaries.

Examples include:

WDAC
AppLocker

This should complement rather than replace network controls.

docs.title: Administrative Tiering
docs.text:
A strong administrative model limits:

Who Can Administer What

and:

From Which Systems

Example:

Privileged Identity
       |
       v
Privileged Workstation
       |
       v
Management Network
       |
       v
Tier 0 System

docs.title: Restrict Peer-to-Peer Traffic
docs.text:
Where not required:

Workstation
    |
    X
    |
Workstation

can significantly reduce lateral-movement and pivoting opportunities.

docs.title: Restrict Server Egress
docs.text:
Application servers often need only specific outbound destinations.

Example:

Application Server
      |
      +--> DNS
      +--> Database
      +--> Update Service
      +--> Monitoring
      |
      X
      |
      +--> Arbitrary Internet

docs.title: Safe Pivoting Workflow
docs.text:
A controlled assessment should follow:

Understand Topology
      |
      v
Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Identify Pivot Interfaces
      |
      v
Inspect Routes
      |
      v
Identify Required Destination
      |
      v
Choose Minimum Tunnel
      |
      v
Restrict Listener
      |
      v
Validate One Service
      |
      v
Expand Only if Required
      |
      v
Collect Evidence
      |
      v
Remove Tunnel
      |
      v
Verify Cleanup

docs.title: Step 1 - Understand the Pivot
docs.text:
Windows:

Get-NetIPConfiguration

Linux:

ip addr

docs.title: Step 2 - Understand Routes
docs.text:
Windows:

Get-NetRoute |
    Select-Object DestinationPrefix,NextHop,InterfaceAlias,RouteMetric

Linux:

ip route

docs.title: Step 3 - Identify the Required Destination
docs.text:
Avoid:

Tunnel Entire Internal Network

when the objective requires only:

10.20.30.10:443

docs.title: Step 4 - Select the Minimum Mechanism
docs.text:
Example:

One Web Service
      |
      v
Local Port Forward

rather than:

Full TUN Route

docs.title: Step 5 - Bind Safely
docs.text:
Prefer:

127.0.0.1

for assessment listeners.

docs.title: Step 6 - Validate Connectivity
docs.text:
For HTTP:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/

For a direct routed target:

curl http://10.20.30.20/

Use the least intrusive validation appropriate for the target service.

docs.title: Step 7 - Record Traffic Path
docs.text:
Document:

Assessment Host
      |
      v
Pivot Host
      |
      v
Target Host

including IP addresses and tunnel type.

docs.title: Step 8 - Remove Tunnel
docs.text:
Stop:

SSH Forward
Chisel
Ligolo-ng
Socat
Other Tunnel Processes

and remove temporary routes or configuration.

docs.title: Step 9 - Verify Cleanup
docs.text:
Check:

Listening Ports
Processes
Routes
Portproxy Rules
Temporary Files
Network Interfaces

docs.text:

  • [ ] Restore modified forwarding only if it was explicitly changed

docs.title: Evidence Checklist
docs.text:
Record:

Assessment Host
Assessment IP
Pivot Host
Pivot IP
Pivot Interfaces
Pivot Routes
Destination Network
Destination Host
Destination Port

Tunnel Direction
Tool

docs.title: Sensitive Evidence
docs.text:
Do not unnecessarily include:

Passwords
NTLM Hashes
Kerberos Tickets
Private Keys
Tunnel Authentication Secrets

in screenshots or reports.

Where sensitive material must be retained:

Restrict Access
Encrypt Storage
Minimise Retention
Redact Reports

docs.title: Reporting Pivoting Findings
docs.text:
Do not report:

Pivoting Is Possible

without explaining the underlying security weakness.

The actual issue may be:

Insufficient Network Segmentation

or:

Unrestricted Server Egress

or:

Workstation-to-Server Administrative Access

or:

Management Network Reachable from Lower-Trust Host

or:

Broad East-West Connectivity

docs.title: Example Finding - Insufficient Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Finding:
Compromised Workstation Can Reach Restricted Server Network

Description:
A workstation in the standard user network had direct network
connectivity to management services within the server network.

The workstation could therefore be used as an intermediary to access
systems that were not directly reachable from the external assessment
position.

A temporary assessment tunnel was used to validate the network path.
No persistence was created.

Impact:
Compromise of a standard workstation could provide an attacker with a
network foothold from which additional internal systems and
administrative services could be reached.

This reduces the effectiveness of network segmentation as a
lateral-movement control.

Recommendation:
Restrict workstation-to-server connectivity to explicitly required
application services.

Administrative protocols should be reachable only from approved
management networks, jump hosts and privileged administrative
workstations.

docs.title: Example Finding - Unrestricted Server Egress
docs.text:
Finding:
Internal Server Permits Unrestricted Outbound Internet Connectivity

Description:
The tested server was able to establish arbitrary outbound network
connections to Internet-hosted systems.

The server's documented application role did not require unrestricted
Internet access.

Impact:
If the server is compromised, unrestricted outbound connectivity may
facilitate command-and-control communication, reverse tunnelling and
data exfiltration.

Recommendation:
Apply egress filtering based on the server's documented business
requirements.

Permit only required destinations, protocols and services and monitor
blocked outbound connection attempts.

docs.title: Example Finding - Management Network Reachability
docs.text:
Finding:
Lower-Trust Application Server Can Reach Management Network

Description:
An application server in a lower-trust network segment had network
connectivity to systems within the administrative management network.

The application did not require this connectivity for normal business
operation.

Impact:
Compromise of the application server could provide an attacker with a
network pivot into a higher-trust management segment.

This may expose administrative services and increase the impact of an
initial application compromise.

Recommendation:
Block lower-trust systems from initiating connections into the
management network.

Permit management traffic only from explicitly approved
administrative systems.

docs.title: Example Finding - Workstation-to-Workstation Connectivity
docs.text:
Finding:
Unrestricted Peer-to-Peer Workstation Connectivity

Description:
Standard workstations were able to initiate connections to
administrative and file-sharing services on other workstation systems.

Impact:
Compromise of one workstation may provide an attacker with direct
network paths for credential reuse, remote administration and lateral
movement to additional endpoints.

Recommendation:
Restrict unnecessary peer-to-peer workstation traffic using host and
network firewall controls.

Allow only explicitly required workstation-to-workstation services.

docs.title: Example Finding - Excessive Internal Reachability
docs.text:
Finding:
Application Server Has Excessive East-West Network Reachability

Description:
The tested application server could initiate connections to multiple
internal networks unrelated to its documented application
dependencies.

The reachable networks included administrative and infrastructure
services.

Impact:
Compromise of the application server could allow an attacker to use
the host as a network pivot and significantly expand access within the
internal environment.

Recommendation:
Implement application-specific network allowlisting.

Permit the server to communicate only with systems and ports required
for its documented function.

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Pivoting should be understood as:

Network Reachability

rather than:

Privilege Escalation

The key question is not:

Can I Start a SOCKS Proxy?

It is:

What Additional Security Boundary
Does This Host Allow Me to Cross?

A good assessment starts with:

Interfaces
Routes
DNS
Network Architecture
Scope

before creating any tunnel.

Choose the smallest mechanism that satisfies the test objective:

One Service
    |
    v
Port Forward

Several TCP Services
    |
    v
SOCKS

Multiple Protocols / Broad Routing
    |
    v
TUN

Do not unnecessarily route:

0.0.0.0/0

through an assessment tunnel.

Prefer explicit routes such as:

10.20.30.0/24

or even narrower destinations where possible.

Pay particular attention to Active Directory dependencies:

DNS
Kerberos
LDAP
SMB
RPC

because a tunnel that provides basic IP connectivity may still be insufficient for domain-aware tooling.

Finally, treat cleanup as part of the assessment rather than an optional final step.

Verify:

Processes
Listeners
Routes
Interfaces
Portproxy Rules
Temporary Files
Proxy Configuration

after the tunnel is removed.

The defensive goal is not merely:

Block Chisel

or:

Block Ligolo-ng

It is to build an architecture where compromise of one system does not automatically provide:

A Route to Everything Else

A mature design should look more like:

User Network
     |
     X
     |
Management Network

Application Server
     |
     +--> Required Database
     +--> Required DNS
     |
     X
     |
Unrelated Internal Networks

Privileged Workstation
     |
     v
Management Network
     |
     v
Administrative Services

The next section moves from network reachability into one of the most important Active Directory security boundaries:

Domain and Forest Trusts

docs.title: Active Directory Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Active Directory privilege escalation is the process of moving from a lower-privileged identity or security context to one with greater control over:

Users
Groups
Computers
Servers
Applications
Domain Controllers
Active Directory Objects
The Domain
The Forest

Privilege escalation in Active Directory is rarely limited to a single technique.

A typical path looks like:

Initial User
    |
    v
Local Access
    |
    v
Credential / Configuration Discovery
    |
    v
Additional Identity
    |
    v
Delegated AD Permission
    |
    v
Privileged Group / System
    |
    v
Domain or Forest Control

The important concept is:

Privilege Escalation
!=
Only Exploiting Software Vulnerabilities

Active Directory privilege escalation frequently results from legitimate functionality combined with excessive permissions, credential exposure, weak delegation or poor administrative architecture.

Authorised testing only

Active Directory privilege escalation testing can affect identities, computers and domain-wide security controls. Prefer read-only path discovery first. Do not modify privileged groups, ACLs, delegation, Group Policy, certificates, directory replication permissions or production credentials unless the assessment scope explicitly authorises active validation.

docs.title: Why Privilege Escalation Matters
docs.text:
A normal domain account may initially have limited privileges:

Domain User

but still have relationships with other objects.

For example:

Domain User
    |
    v
Helpdesk Group
    |
    v
Reset Password
    |
    v
Server Administrator
    |
    v
Management Server
    |
    v
Domain Administration

No software vulnerability is required.

The weakness is the:

Privilege Path

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Is a Graph Problem
docs.text:
Active Directory contains relationships between:

Users
Groups
Computers
OUs
GPOs
Domains
Certificates
Sessions
Credentials
ACLs
Trusts

These relationships form a graph.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
ACL
 |
 v
Computer
 |
 v
Session
 |
 v
Administrator

Tools such as BloodHound are useful because they model these relationships as attack paths.

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: Direct vs Indirect Privilege
docs.text:
Direct privilege:

User
 |
 v
Domain Admins

Indirect privilege:

User
 |
 v
Group A
 |
 v
Group B
 |
 v
Local Admin
 |
 v
Server

Indirect relationships are often more difficult to identify manually.

docs.text:

docs.title: Start With the Current Identity
docs.text:
Before looking for escalation paths, understand the current security context.

Windows:

whoami

whoami /groups

[System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().Name

$env:USERDOMAIN

Get-ADDomain

For focused output:

Get-ADUser -Identity $env:USERNAME -Properties MemberOf,PrimaryGroupID |

Recursive group relationships should also be considered.

Permissions
Network Reachability
Authentication
Endpoint Controls
Object State

docs.title: Shortest Path Analysis
docs.text:
A conceptual path may look like:

USER01
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
HELPDESK
 |
 | GenericAll
 v
SERVER-ADMINS
 |
 | AdminTo
 v
MGMT01
 |
 | HasSession
 v
DOMAIN-ADMIN

The graph reveals the relationship.

The assessor still needs to determine whether the path is practically valid.

docs.title: Privileged Groups
docs.text:
Important groups can include:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Schema Admins
Administrators
Account Operators
Server Operators
Backup Operators
Print Operators
Group Policy Creator Owners
DnsAdmins

The actual security impact depends on:

Domain
Operating System
Configuration
Delegation
Group Usage

Do not assume every historical escalation technique still works on every modern environment.

docs.title: Domain Admins
docs.text:
Membership of:

Domain Admins

normally provides extensive administrative control within the domain.

Review:

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Domain Admins' -Recursive

docs.title: Enterprise Admins
docs.text:
In a forest root domain:

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Enterprise Admins' -Recursive

Enterprise Admins have forest-wide significance.

docs.title: Schema Admins
docs.text:
Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Schema Admins' -Recursive

Schema administration is highly privileged and should normally have minimal standing membership.

docs.title: Built-In Administrators
docs.text:
Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Administrators' -Recursive

Interpret this group in the correct domain and built-in container context.

docs.title: Group Nesting
docs.text:
Privilege can be hidden through nested groups.

User
 |
 v
Group A
 |
 v
Group B
 |
 v
Group C
 |
 v
Privileged Group

Recursive enumeration is therefore important.

docs.title: Group Management Rights
docs.text:
A user does not need to already belong to a privileged group if they can control the group.

Example:

User
 |
 | WriteMembers
 v
Privileged Group

This can represent an escalation path.

See:

Groups

and:

ACL and ACE

docs.title: ACL-Based Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Active Directory objects are protected by:

Access Control Lists - ACLs

An ACL contains:

Access Control Entries - ACEs

Misconfigured permissions can allow lower-privileged users to control sensitive objects.

docs.title: Common Dangerous Rights
docs.text:
Security-relevant rights include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
WriteProperty
AllExtendedRights
ForceChangePassword
WriteMembers

Specific object types may expose additional security-sensitive extended rights.

docs.title: GenericAll
docs.text:
Conceptually:

User
 |
 | GenericAll
 v
Target Object

This can provide broad control over the target object.

The exact security consequence depends on whether the target is a:

User
Group
Computer
OU
GPO
Domain

docs.title: GenericWrite
docs.text:
User
 |
 | GenericWrite
 v
Target

GenericWrite can allow modification of writable attributes.

Whether that becomes privilege escalation depends on which attributes can be changed and how they are used.

docs.title: WriteDacl
docs.text:
User
 |
 | WriteDacl
 v
Object
 |
 v
Modify Permissions

Control over an object's DACL can allow the attacker to grant additional permissions.

docs.title: WriteOwner
docs.text:
User
 |
 | WriteOwner
 v
Object
 |
 v
Ownership
 |
 v
Potential Permission Control

Ownership can provide a path toward modifying the object's permissions.

docs.title: ForceChangePassword
docs.text:
An identity may have the extended right to reset another user's password.

Conceptually:

Helpdesk User
      |
      v
Reset Password
      |
      v
Privileged User

This is security-sensitive when the target has greater privilege.

docs.title: ACL Enumeration
docs.text:
See the dedicated:

ACL and ACE

page for detailed enumeration.

With PowerView loaded, common discovery commands include:

Get-DomainObjectAcl -ResolveGUIDs

Always confirm syntax against the PowerView version being used.

docs.title: BloodHound ACL Edges
docs.text:
BloodHound may represent rights such as:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
ForceChangePassword
AddMember

Use these edges as leads for validation rather than automatic findings.

docs.title: Credential-Based Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Privilege often follows credentials.

Low-Privilege User
      |
      v
Credential Discovery
      |
      v
Privileged Credential
      |
      v
Privileged Context

See:

Credential Access

docs.title: Common Credential Sources
docs.text:
Examples include:

Configuration Files
Scripts
Scheduled Tasks
Services
Registry
Credential Manager
Shares
Backups
Deployment Systems
Service Accounts
PowerShell History
Application Configuration

docs.title: Credential Reuse
docs.text:
A password may belong to an ordinary domain user but provide administrative access elsewhere.

Example:

USER01
 |
 | Same Password / Credential
 v
Local Administrator
 |
 v
SERVER01

The resulting server may contain additional privileged credentials.

docs.title: Local Administrator Reuse
docs.text:
A common historical escalation pattern is:

Compromised Workstation
       |
       v
Local Admin Credential
       |
       v
Same Credential on Server
       |
       v
Server Compromise

Unique local administrator passwords reduce this risk.

See:

LAPS

docs.title: LAPS
docs.text:
Windows LAPS or legacy Microsoft LAPS can reduce local administrator password reuse.

However, the key security question becomes:

Who Can Read the Managed Password?

If a low-privileged identity can read LAPS credentials for a sensitive system:

User
 |
 v
Read LAPS Password
 |
 v
Local Administrator
 |
 v
Sensitive Server

See:

LAPS

docs.title: gMSA
docs.text:
Group Managed Service Accounts can reduce static service-account password management.

However:

Who Can Retrieve the Managed Password?

remains important.

Conceptually:

User / Computer
      |
      v
Allowed to Retrieve gMSA Secret
      |
      v
Service Identity

See:

gMSA

docs.title: Service Accounts
docs.text:
Service accounts frequently have:

SPNs
Server Access
Database Access
Application Rights
Delegated AD Permissions

A service account should therefore be assessed based on:

Credential Exposure
Privilege
Reachability
Delegation
Group Membership

docs.title: Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Accounts with Service Principal Names may be relevant to Kerberoasting.

See:

Kerberoasting

Conceptually:

Domain User
    |
    v
Request Service Ticket
    |
    v
Offline Password Analysis
    |
    v
Service Account

The escalation occurs only if the recovered service identity provides greater privilege.

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting
docs.text:
Accounts without Kerberos preauthentication may expose material suitable for offline password analysis.

See:

AS-REP Roasting

Again:

Roastable Account
!=
Privilege Escalation

The account must provide meaningful additional privilege.

docs.title: Kerberos Tickets
docs.text:
Existing Kerberos tickets can represent valuable authentication material.

See:

Kerberos Tickets

and:

Pass the Ticket

docs.title: Pass the Hash
docs.text:
NTLM hash material can sometimes be used for authentication without recovering the plaintext password.

See:

Pass the Hash

The security impact depends on:

Target
Privileges
Protocol
Endpoint Controls

docs.title: Pass the Key
docs.text:
Kerberos keys can also be used in authentication workflows.

See:

Pass the Key

docs.title: Overpass the Hash
docs.text:
See:

Overpass the Hash

for the relationship between NTLM-derived key material and Kerberos authentication.

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
Kerberos delegation is another major privilege-escalation area.

Common models include:

Unconstrained Delegation
Constrained Delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
See:

Unconstrained Delegation

A system trusted for unconstrained delegation can create significant credential exposure when privileged users authenticate to it.

docs.title: Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
See:

Constrained Delegation

The security impact depends on:

Delegating Principal
Allowed Services
Protocol Transition
Target

docs.title: Resource-Based Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
See:

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

RBCD shifts delegation configuration to the target resource.

Control over the relevant computer-object attributes can therefore become security-sensitive.

docs.title: S4U
docs.text:
Kerberos Service-for-User extensions are central to several delegation workflows.

See:

S4U

docs.title: Machine Account Quota
docs.text:
Historically, Active Directory domains commonly allowed ordinary authenticated users to create a limited number of computer accounts through:

ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota

See:

Machine Account Quota

Check the current value:

Get-ADDomain |
    Select-Object DistinguishedName

Then:

Get-ADObject -Identity (Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName -Properties ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota |
    Select-Object ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota

A non-zero value is not automatically a vulnerability.

Its relevance depends on other privilege relationships.

docs.title: Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Control over key credential attributes can enable certificate-backed authentication paths.

See:

Shadow Credentials

The important relationship is:

Attacker
 |
 v
Write Relevant Key Credential Attribute
 |
 v
Target Identity

This is particularly important when the target identity is privileged.

docs.title: Group Policy
docs.text:
Group Policy can control:

Security Settings
Scripts
Scheduled Tasks
Services
Registry
Local Groups
Software

Control over a GPO linked to sensitive systems can therefore represent substantial privilege.

See:

Group Policy

docs.title: GPO Privilege Path
docs.text:
User
 |
 | Can Modify
 v
GPO
 |
 | Linked To
 v
Servers OU
 |
 v
Privileged Servers

The existence of GPO write access should be evaluated together with:

Link Scope
Security Filtering
WMI Filtering
Target Computers

docs.title: OU Control
docs.text:
Delegated control over an Organisational Unit can create escalation opportunities.

Example:

User
 |
 | Delegated Rights
 v
Servers OU
 |
 +--> SERVER01
 +--> SERVER02

Review the exact ACEs inherited by objects within the OU.

docs.title: Computer Object Control
docs.text:
Control over a computer object can matter because computer objects contain security-sensitive attributes.

Potentially relevant areas include:

Delegation
SPNs
Key Credentials
Group Membership
DNS Relationships

The exact escalation path depends on the permissions granted.

docs.title: User Object Control
docs.text:
Control over another user may include:

Password Reset
Attribute Modification
ACL Modification
Key Credential Modification
Group Relationships

Prioritise targets with higher privilege.

docs.title: Group Object Control
docs.text:
Control over group membership can directly change authorisation.

Example:

User
 |
 | AddMember
 v
Server Admins

The target group's effective privilege determines impact.

docs.title: Domain Object Control
docs.text:
Permissions on the domain root can be extremely sensitive.

Particularly important are replication-related extended rights.

docs.title: Directory Replication Rights
docs.text:
The rights commonly associated with directory replication include:

DS-Replication-Get-Changes
DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All

and, in some environments and scenarios:

DS-Replication-Get-Changes-In-Filtered-Set

Accounts with sufficient replication rights may be able to request sensitive directory replication data.

docs.title: DCSync
docs.text:
DCSync refers to abusing directory replication permissions to request credential data from a domain controller.

Conceptually:

Account
 |
 | Replication Rights
 v
Domain Controller
 |
 v
Directory Secrets

This is a high-impact capability.

Do not perform DCSync in production merely to prove that the required rights exist unless explicitly authorised.

Permission evidence can often establish the finding.

See:

NTDS

docs.title: Backup Operators
docs.text:
Backup-related privileges can provide access to data that ordinary file permissions would otherwise protect.

On sensitive systems this can expose:

Registry Hives
System State
Application Data
Directory Data

Membership should therefore be reviewed carefully.

docs.title: Server Operators
docs.text:
Server Operators can possess significant server-management capabilities on domain controllers in applicable environments.

Do not assume the group is harmless simply because it is not:

Domain Admins

docs.title: Account Operators
docs.text:
Account Operators can manage certain users and groups subject to Active Directory protections and object scope.

Assess what the group can actually control in the current environment.

docs.title: DNS Administrators
docs.text:
DNS administration can be highly sensitive on domain controllers and AD-integrated DNS infrastructure.

Review:

DnsAdmins

membership and actual DNS server permissions.

See:

Active Directory Integrated DNS

Historical DNS privilege-escalation techniques are configuration and version dependent, so validate current behaviour before reporting exploitability.

docs.title: AD CS
docs.text:
Active Directory Certificate Services can introduce powerful authentication paths.

See:

Active Directory Certificate Services

Common areas include:

Certificate Templates
Enrollment Rights
CA Configuration
Certificate Mapping
Web Enrollment
RPC Enrollment
CA Security

docs.title: ESC Paths
docs.text:
The AD CS section contains detailed notes for:

ESC1
ESC2
ESC3
ESC4
ESC5
ESC6
ESC7
ESC8
ESC9
ESC10
ESC11
ESC12
ESC13
ESC14
ESC15
ESC16
ESC17

Do not assume every ESC condition is exploitable merely because a scanner reports it.

Validate:

Enrollment Rights
Template State
CA State
Authentication Mapping
Patch Level
Certificate Purpose
Target Privilege

docs.title: AD CS Privilege Model
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Low-Privilege Identity
       |
       v
Certificate Misconfiguration
       |
       v
Certificate for Higher-Privilege Identity
       |
       v
Authentication
       |
       v
Privilege Escalation

The exact path depends on the specific ESC condition.

docs.title: NTLM Relay
docs.text:
NTLM authentication can sometimes be relayed to another service when protections are insufficient.

See:

NTLM Relay

The privilege impact depends on:

Relayed Identity
Target Service
Signing
Channel Binding
EPA
Target Permissions

docs.title: Authentication Coercion
docs.text:
Authentication coercion can cause a system or identity to authenticate to another location.

See:

Authentication Coercion

Coercion alone is not privilege escalation.

A full path may be:

Coercion
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
Privileged Target

docs.title: Kerberos Relay
docs.text:
See:

Kerberos Relay

Kerberos relay scenarios depend heavily on:

Protocol
SPN
Target
Signing
Authentication Context

docs.title: NTLM Relay Path
docs.text:
A conceptual path is:

Privileged Machine
      |
      v
Authentication
      |
      v
Relay
      |
      v
Target Service
      |
      v
Privilege

Do not treat captured NTLM authentication as equivalent to successful relay.

docs.title: Trusts
docs.text:
Active Directory trusts can extend authentication relationships across domains or forests.

See:

Trusts

A trust itself is not a vulnerability.

Review:

Direction
Transitivity
Authentication Scope
SID Filtering
Foreign Principals
Privileged Group Membership

docs.title: Cross-Domain Privilege
docs.text:
A conceptual cross-domain path may look like:

DOMAIN-A\User
      |
      v
Foreign Security Principal
      |
      v
DOMAIN-B Group
      |
      v
Resource Administration

This may be completely intentional.

The assessment should determine whether the resulting privilege is appropriate.

docs.title: SID History
docs.text:
SID History can affect authorisation decisions across migrations and trust relationships.

A dedicated page should evaluate:

SIDHistory Population
Migration Requirement
Privileged Historical SIDs
Trust Controls
Monitoring

Do not assume the presence of SID History is malicious.

docs.title: Trust Tickets
docs.text:
Inter-domain Kerberos trust material is highly sensitive.

Compromise of trust secrets can create authentication risks across trust boundaries.

This should be assessed separately from ordinary user-level privilege escalation.

docs.title: Local Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Active Directory escalation frequently depends on first escalating privileges on a Windows endpoint.

Conceptually:

Domain User
    |
    v
Workstation
    |
    v
Local Administrator
    |
    v
Credential Discovery
    |
    v
Domain Identity

Local Windows privilege escalation should therefore be analysed alongside Active Directory relationships.

docs.title: Local Administrator Enumeration
docs.text:
From the target:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'

Remote administrative rights can also be modelled with BloodHound.

docs.title: Privileged Sessions
docs.text:
A low-value server can become important when a privileged user logs into it.

SERVER01
   |
   v
Domain Admin Session

If another identity controls SERVER01, the server may become part of a privilege path.

docs.title: Session Exposure
docs.text:
The security model is:

Control Computer
      |
      v
Privileged User Uses Computer
      |
      v
Credential / Session Exposure

Modern credential protections can significantly affect practical exploitability.

Do not assume that every administrative session exposes reusable credentials.

docs.title: Administrative Tiering
docs.text:
A strong administrative model separates:

Tier 0
Tier 1
Tier 2

or equivalent modern privileged-access tiers.

Conceptually:

Tier 0
 |
 X
Must Not Log Into
 |
 v
Tier 2 Workstation

This prevents lower-trust systems from becoming credential stepping stones.

docs.title: Privileged Access Workstations
docs.text:
Dedicated administrative workstations reduce exposure of privileged credentials.

A privileged administrator should avoid using high-value credentials from ordinary endpoints.

docs.title: Credential Guard
docs.text:
Windows Defender Credential Guard can reduce exposure of certain credential material.

Its presence can change the practicality of credential-based escalation paths.

Do not assume:

Local Administrator
=
All Credentials Available

docs.title: Protected Users
docs.text:
The:

Protected Users

group provides additional authentication protections for high-value accounts.

Assess whether appropriate privileged identities use modern protections.

docs.title: Authentication Policies
docs.text:
Authentication Policies and Authentication Policy Silos can further restrict where sensitive accounts authenticate.

These controls can reduce credential exposure.

docs.title: Protected Objects
docs.text:
Some privileged Active Directory objects are affected by:

AdminSDHolder

and:

SDProp

These mechanisms help protect permissions on certain privileged accounts and groups.

docs.title: AdminCount
docs.text:
Protected accounts may have:

adminCount = 1

but do not treat this attribute alone as definitive proof of current privilege.

Historical privileged membership can leave adminCount set.

docs.title: Enumerate adminCount
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -LDAPFilter '(adminCount=1)' -Properties adminCount |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,Enabled,adminCount

Review results manually.

docs.title: AdminSDHolder
docs.text:
AdminSDHolder provides a protected security descriptor used for certain privileged objects.

A simplified model:

AdminSDHolder
     |
     v
Protected ACL
     |
     v
Privileged Objects

Permissions on AdminSDHolder are therefore extremely sensitive.

docs.title: AdminSDHolder Assessment
docs.text:
Review:

Unexpected ACEs
Delegated Control
Non-Administrative Principals
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
GenericAll

Do not modify AdminSDHolder during ordinary assessment.

docs.title: Domain Controller Access
docs.text:
Any path that results in administrative control of a domain controller should be considered highly significant.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Server Admin
 |
 v
Domain Controller
 |
 v
Domain Control

However, establish exactly what administrative rights exist rather than assuming them from network reachability.

docs.title: Domain Controller Services
docs.text:
Sensitive services include:

LDAP
LDAPS
Kerberos
SMB
RPC
DNS
WinRM
RDP

Availability of these services is normal.

The security question is:

Can the Current Identity Perform Privileged Operations?

docs.title: Infrastructure Privilege Paths
docs.text:
Active Directory environments often depend on management infrastructure such as:

SCCM
WSUS
MDT
SCOM
AD FS
AD CS
Backup Platforms
Virtualisation
Monitoring
Deployment Systems

Compromise of these systems can indirectly affect large numbers of domain computers.

docs.title: SCCM
docs.text:
Systems management platforms may have extensive access to managed endpoints.

A privilege path can conceptually be:

SCCM Administrator
      |
      v
Managed Servers
      |
      v
Privileged Systems

See:

SCCM

docs.title: WSUS
docs.text:
WSUS is part of the software-update trust chain.

See:

WSUS

Assess:

Administrative Rights
Transport Security
Update Approval
Server Security

docs.title: MDT
docs.text:
Deployment infrastructure may contain:

Deployment Credentials
Scripts
Configuration
Images

See:

MDT

docs.title: SCOM
docs.text:
Monitoring infrastructure can possess broad visibility and agent relationships.

See:

SCOM

Review whether its administrative model creates paths to higher-value systems.

docs.title: AD FS
docs.text:
Federation infrastructure is highly trusted.

See:

AD FS

Administrative control over AD FS or federation signing material can have consequences across relying-party applications.

docs.title: RODC
docs.text:
RODCs intentionally limit the impact of branch-domain-controller compromise.

See:

RODC

Important questions include:

Which Credentials Can Be Cached?
Which Credentials Have Been Cached?
Who Administers the RODC?

docs.title: Shares
docs.text:
File shares can reveal:

Credentials
Scripts
Configuration
Backups
Deployment Files
Keys

Review:

Shares

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Through Scripts
docs.text:
Administrative scripts can contain:

Passwords
API Keys
Service Credentials
Mapped Drive Credentials
Deployment Credentials

Search only locations authorised within scope.

docs.title: PowerShell History
docs.text:
On a system where access is authorised:

Get-Content (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Treat any discovered credentials as sensitive evidence.

Avoid unnecessarily reproducing them in reports.

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Review:

Get-ScheduledTask

Look for:

Privileged Run Context
Writable Scripts
Writable Executables
Credentials
Weak Paths

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Review:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

Relevant questions include:

Who Runs the Service?
Who Can Modify the Binary?
Who Can Modify the Directory?
Who Can Modify the Service Configuration?

docs.title: Writable Administrative Paths
docs.text:
A generic privilege relationship is:

Low-Privilege User
      |
      v
Writable File
      |
      v
Privileged Process

This is a local privilege escalation concept but may become part of an AD escalation chain.

docs.title: Software Deployment
docs.text:
Determine whether lower-privileged identities can modify:

Software Packages
Deployment Scripts
Installation Sources
Login Scripts
Management Packages

that execute on higher-value systems.

docs.title: Login Scripts
docs.text:
Active Directory logon scripts can be referenced through user or Group Policy configuration.

If a low-privileged user can modify a script executed by privileged identities, a privilege relationship may exist.

Validate:

Script Location
ACL
Execution Context
Affected Users

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
SYSVOL contains domain-wide policy and script information.

Normal users generally have read access.

The key security question is:

Who Can Write?

Unexpected write access to security-sensitive SYSVOL content can create substantial risk.

docs.title: Group Policy Preferences
docs.text:
Historical Group Policy Preferences deployments could expose recoverable passwords through:

cpassword

in SYSVOL XML files.

Modern environments should not create new GPP password entries.

Existing legacy artefacts may still be present.

docs.title: GPP Search
docs.text:
A read-only authorised search can identify legacy references:

Get-ChildItem "\\$env:USERDNSDOMAIN\SYSVOL" -Recurse -Filter '*.xml' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'cpassword'

Finding a cpassword value warrants investigation.

Do not expose recovered credentials in reports.

docs.title: Password Spraying
docs.text:
Password spraying can sometimes identify additional accounts, but it carries:

Account Lockout
Detection
Operational
User Impact

risk.

See:

Password Spraying

Do not use spraying as the default escalation technique.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Through Password Reuse
docs.text:
If credentials are obtained legitimately within scope, determine where they are authorised rather than blindly attempting them across the domain.

A safer workflow is:

Credential
    |
    v
Identify Account
    |
    v
Determine Group Membership
    |
    v
Determine Known Administrative Scope
    |
    v
Minimal Validation

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec can help assess administrative access across authorised systems.

See:

NetExec

Avoid uncontrolled domain-wide authentication attempts.

Use a scoped host list.

docs.title: Impacket
docs.text:
Impacket provides many tools relevant to Active Directory assessment.

See:

Impacket

The presence of an Impacket technique in a playbook does not mean it should automatically be executed.

Use the least invasive validation method that establishes the security impact.

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView can help enumerate:

Users
Groups
Computers
ACLs
Trusts
Sessions
Delegation

Verify commands against the specific PowerView version loaded into the assessment environment.

docs.title: Native Tools First
docs.text:
Where possible, use:

ActiveDirectory PowerShell Module
whoami
nltest
dsquery
repadmin
Group Policy Tools
Windows Event Logs

for read-only validation.

This often produces cleaner evidence than immediately using offensive tooling.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Methodology
docs.text:
A structured methodology is:

Establish Context
      |
      v
Enumerate Identity
      |
      v
Enumerate Groups
      |
      v
Enumerate ACLs
      |
      v
Enumerate Credentials
      |
      v
Enumerate Delegation
      |
      v
Enumerate GPOs
      |
      v
Enumerate AD CS
      |
      v
Enumerate Trusts
      |
      v
Model Paths
      |
      v
Validate Safely
      |
      v
Report

docs.title: Phase 1 - Establish Current Context
docs.text:
Record:

Username
SID
Domain
Groups
Privileges
Host
Network
Authentication Context

docs.title: Phase 2 - Identify High-Value Targets
docs.text:
Examples:

Domain Controllers
Certificate Authorities
AD FS
Management Servers
Backup Servers
Virtualisation Platforms
Tier 0 Systems
Privileged Groups

docs.title: Phase 3 - Enumerate Group Paths
docs.text:
Look for:

Direct Membership
Nested Membership
Group Management Rights
Foreign Group Membership

docs.title: Phase 4 - Enumerate ACL Paths
docs.text:
Review:

Users
Groups
Computers
OUs
GPOs
Domain Root
AdminSDHolder

for rights held by the current identity and its groups.

docs.title: Phase 5 - Enumerate Credential Paths
docs.text:
Review authorised sources such as:

Shares
Scripts
Configuration Files
Services
Scheduled Tasks
Deployment Infrastructure
Managed Credentials

docs.title: Phase 6 - Enumerate Kerberos Paths
docs.text:
Review:

SPNs
Kerberoasting

docs.text:

Sessions
Computers
Trusts

Continuous or periodic path analysis is therefore valuable.

docs.text:

      |
      v
