docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials demonstrates an important Active Directory security principle:

Authentication Security
        |
        X
Only Password Security

An account may have:

Strong Password
MFA Elsewhere
Password Rotation

and still be compromised if an attacker can modify authentication-related directory attributes.

The core relationship is:

Principal
   |
   v
Write msDS-KeyCredentialLink
   |
   v
Target

That write permission can potentially become:

Directory Permission
      |
      v
Authentication Credential
      |
      v
Kerberos TGT
      |
      v
Target Identity

This is why Active Directory ACL analysis is critical.

A seemingly simple:

GenericWrite

relationship can represent much more than the ability to change harmless metadata.

For privileged identities:

GenericWrite
      |
      v
Authentication Attribute
      |
      v
Privilege Escalation

may represent a severe attack path.

The technique also highlights why password resets are not a complete incident-response strategy.

Password Reset
      |
      v
Password Credential Changed

does not necessarily affect:

KeyCredentialLink

Therefore incident response must review alternative authentication mechanisms.

For penetration testers, the preferred workflow is:

Enumerate ACL
      |
      v
Identify AddKeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
Determine Target Privilege
      |
      v
Validate PKINIT
      |
      v
Use Controlled Test Object
      |
      v
Modify Only If Necessary
      |
      v
Restore Exact Original State

For defenders:

Restrict ACLs
      |
      v
Monitor msDS-KeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
Correlate Directory Changes
      |
      v
Monitor PKINIT
      |
      v
Investigate Unexpected Authentication

The central question is:

Who can add authentication material
to which Active Directory identity?

The second question is:

What can that identity access?

Together:

Write Permission
      +
Target Privilege
      =
Attack Path

Shadow Credentials should therefore be analysed as part of the broader Active Directory relationship:

ACL Control
   |
   v
Identity Control
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Privilege

rather than as an isolated certificate technique.

docs.title: Windows and Active Directory Shares
docs.text:
Windows file shares are one of the most important sources of information during an Active Directory security assessment.

Organisations commonly use SMB shares to store:

Documents
Scripts
Software
Configuration Files
Deployment Packages
Backups
Administrative Tools
User Profiles
Department Data
Application Files

From a security perspective, shares frequently reveal information that connects otherwise separate Active Directory attack paths.

A share may expose:

Credentials
Configuration Secrets
Deployment Scripts
Private Keys
Certificates
Connection Strings
Passwords
API Keys
Administrative Scripts
Sensitive Documents

The assessment model is:

Active Directory Identity
        |
        v
SMB
        |
        v
Share
        |
        v
Files and Directories
        |
        v
Permissions / Secrets / Information
        |
        v
Potential Security Impact

Authorised testing only

File-share enumeration can expose confidential business information and credentials. Access only systems and shares within scope. Prefer metadata and targeted searches over bulk downloading. Do not modify, delete or upload files unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Shares at a Glance
docs.text:
A Windows file share exposes a directory through SMB.

Example:

Server:

FILE01

Local directory:

D:\Departments\Finance

Share:

Finance

UNC path:

\\FILE01\Finance

Users access:

SMB
 |
 v
FILE01
 |
 v
Finance Share
 |
 v
NTFS Directory

docs.title: SMB
docs.text:
Modern Windows file sharing primarily uses:

SMB

Common port:

TCP 445

Older environments may also expose NetBIOS-related services such as:

TCP 139
UDP 137
UDP 138

See:

SMB

docs.title: Share Permissions vs NTFS Permissions
docs.text:
Windows file access commonly involves two permission layers:

Share Permissions
       +
NTFS Permissions
       |
       v
Effective Access

These should not be treated as the same control.

docs.title: Share Permissions
docs.text:
Share permissions apply when accessing a directory through SMB.

Common permissions include:

Read
Change
Full Control

docs.title: NTFS Permissions
docs.text:
NTFS permissions apply to the underlying file-system objects.

Common rights include:

Read
Read and Execute
Write
Modify
Full Control

docs.title: Effective Permissions
docs.text:
When a resource is accessed through a share, both permission sets matter.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Share ACL
 |
 v
NTFS ACL
 |
 v
Effective Permission

A permissive share ACL does not automatically mean that every user can modify the underlying files.

docs.title: Common Administrative Shares
docs.text:
Windows commonly creates administrative shares such as:

C$
ADMIN$
IPC$

Additional drives may appear as:

D$
E$

These normally require administrative privileges.

docs.title: C$
docs.text:
\\HOST\C$

maps to the system drive.

Example:

C:\

docs.title: ADMIN$
docs.text:
\\HOST\ADMIN$

normally maps to the Windows directory.

Typically:

C:\Windows

docs.title: IPC$
docs.text:
\\HOST\IPC$

is used for inter-process communication and SMB-related operations.

It is not a conventional file-storage share.

docs.title: Domain Controller Shares
docs.text:
Domain controllers normally expose important shares including:

SYSVOL
NETLOGON

These are expected and necessary for Active Directory.

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
SYSVOL contains domain-wide data used by:

Group Policy
Logon Scripts
Startup Scripts
Administrative Templates
Policy Distribution

Typical path:

\\corp.example\SYSVOL

or:

\\DC01\SYSVOL

docs.title: NETLOGON
docs.text:
NETLOGON commonly exposes logon-related scripts and files.

Typical path:

\\corp.example\NETLOGON

docs.title: SYSVOL Security Relevance
docs.text:
SYSVOL is intentionally readable by domain users in normal Active Directory environments.

The security question is therefore not:

Can Domain Users Read SYSVOL?

That is generally expected.

Instead ask:

What Sensitive Information Is Stored There?

docs.title: Common SYSVOL Findings
docs.text:
Potentially interesting content includes:

PowerShell Scripts
Batch Files
VBScript
Configuration Files
Legacy GPP Files
Deployment Scripts
Mapped Drive Scripts
Printer Scripts
Application Installers
Hard-Coded Credentials
Service Account Names
Internal URLs

docs.title: Group Policy Preferences
docs.text:
Historically, Group Policy Preferences could contain passwords encrypted using a publicly documented key.

The relevant value is commonly:

cpassword

Potential file names include:

Groups.xml
Services.xml
Scheduledtasks.xml
DataSources.xml
Printers.xml
Drives.xml

Modern Windows versions no longer allow administrators to create new GPP password configurations through the normal Group Policy interface, but legacy files may still remain.

If your dedicated page exists, see:

docs/active-directory/gpp-passwords.md

docs.title: Search SYSVOL for cpassword
docs.text:
Windows:

Get-ChildItem '\\corp.example\SYSVOL' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'cpassword'

This is a read-only search.

docs.title: Search for Password Keywords
docs.text:
A targeted search can identify suspicious configuration content.

Get-ChildItem '\\corp.example\SYSVOL' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','passwd','pwd','secret','credential'

Expect false positives.

Do not report keyword matches without examining context.

docs.title: Enumerating Shares from Windows
docs.text: Native Windows provides several methods for share enumeration.

docs.title: net view
docs.text:
Enumerate shares on a server:

net view \\FILE01

docs.title: PowerShell Get-SmbShare
docs.text:
When executed locally with appropriate permissions:

Get-SmbShare

This displays locally configured SMB shares.

docs.title: Get-SmbShareAccess
docs.text:
Inspect share-level permissions:

Get-SmbShareAccess -Name 'Finance'

docs.title: UNC Access
docs.text:
Test an approved share:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance'

docs.title: Directory Listing
docs.text: dir \\FILE01\Finance

docs.title: Recursive PowerShell Enumeration
docs.text:
For a small approved directory:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Avoid recursive enumeration across very large production shares without considering performance and data volume.

docs.title: Search by Extension
docs.text:
Example:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.Extension -in '.xml','.ini','.config','.ps1','.bat','.cmd','.vbs' }

docs.title: Search Interesting File Names
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Name -match 'password|credential|secret|backup|config|connection'
    }

docs.title: Search File Contents
docs.text:
For approved text-based files:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','passwd','secret','apikey','connectionstring' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Use targeted extensions or directories where possible to reduce unnecessary access to business data.

docs.title: Enumerating Shares from Linux
docs.text:
Common tools include:

smbclient
NetExec
Impacket
rpcclient

docs.title: smbclient
docs.text:
List shares:

smbclient -L //10.20.30.40 -U 'CORP/audituser'

docs.title: Hostname
docs.text:
Prefer hostnames when Kerberos or domain context matters:

smbclient -L //files01.corp.example -U 'CORP/audituser'

docs.title: Connect to Share
docs.text:
smbclient //files01.corp.example/Finance -U 'CORP/audituser'

Inside the interactive client:

ls

docs.title: Browse Directory
docs.text:
cd Reports
ls

docs.title: Download a Specific Approved File
docs.text:
Inside smbclient:

get example.txt

Do not bulk-download a share simply because access is available.

docs.title: Kerberos with smbclient
docs.text:
Where Kerberos is configured, current smbclient versions provide Kerberos-related authentication options.

Because syntax can vary between Samba releases, verify the installed version:

smbclient --help

and use the supported Kerberos option for that version.

docs.title: NetExec Share Enumeration
docs.text:
NetExec is particularly useful for evaluating SMB access across authorised systems.

See:

NetExec

Check the installed syntax:

nxc smb --help

docs.title: Enumerate Shares with NetExec
docs.text:
nxc smb files01.corp.example -u audituser -p 'PASSWORD' --shares

This can show:

Share
Permissions
Description

depending on the server and permissions.

docs.title: Multiple Hosts
docs.text:
Against an explicitly authorised subnet:

nxc smb 10.20.30.0/24 -u audituser -p 'PASSWORD' --shares

Large-scale enumeration can generate substantial authentication and network telemetry.

Use scope-specific target lists where possible.

docs.title: Domain Credentials
docs.text: nxc smb files01.corp.example -d corp.example -u audituser -p 'PASSWORD' --shares

docs.title: Avoid Passwords in Shell History
docs.text:
Where possible, avoid placing production credentials directly in command-line arguments.

Prefer:

Dedicated Assessment Accounts
Environment-Specific Secure Credential Handling
Kerberos Tickets
Tool-Supported Prompts

according to the engagement environment.

docs.title: Null Session Testing
docs.text:
Some legacy or misconfigured SMB servers may expose information without authenticated credentials.

Example:

smbclient -L //files01.corp.example -N

Modern Windows environments normally restrict meaningful anonymous access.

docs.title: Guest Access
docs.text:
Anonymous and guest access are different concepts.

Possible states include:

Anonymous
Guest
Authenticated User
Domain User
Administrative User

Record which security context actually provided access.

docs.title: rpcclient
docs.text:
rpcclient can query certain SMB/RPC information.

Check options:

rpcclient --help

Anonymous connection attempt:

rpcclient -U '' -N files01.corp.example

Whether useful information is exposed depends on server configuration.

docs.title: Share Enumeration Through Active Directory
docs.text:
Active Directory itself may reveal systems likely to host shares.

Potential sources include:

Computer Objects
DFS Configuration
Group Policy
Logon Scripts
User Home Directories
Profile Paths
Application Configuration

docs.title: User Home Directory Attributes
docs.text:
Active Directory user objects may contain:

homeDirectory
homeDrive
profilePath
scriptPath

PowerShell:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties homeDirectory,homeDrive,profilePath,scriptPath |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,homeDirectory,homeDrive,profilePath,scriptPath

These values can reveal important file servers.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
User:
alice

homeDirectory:
\\FILE01\Users\alice

profilePath:
\\FILE02\Profiles\alice

This identifies:

FILE01
FILE02

as potential infrastructure of interest.

docs.title: Group Policy Drive Maps
docs.text:
Group Policy can map network shares to users.

Example:

Finance Users
      |
      v
GPO
      |
      v
\\FILE01\Finance

This provides useful information about:

Share Purpose
Target Users
File Servers
Department Boundaries

See:

Group Policy

docs.title: Logon Scripts
docs.text:
Logon scripts frequently contain:

net use

commands.

Example:

net use F: \\FILE01\Finance

or PowerShell equivalents.

Searching SYSVOL can reveal these mappings.

docs.title: Distributed File System
docs.text:
Organisations may use:

Distributed File System

or:

DFS

to provide a unified namespace.

Example:

\\corp.example\Shares

may redirect users to several backend servers.

docs.title: DFS Model
docs.text:
User
 |
 v
DFS Namespace
 |
 +--> FILE01
 +--> FILE02
 +--> FILE03

docs.title: Why DFS Matters
docs.text:
A single visible path may hide:

Multiple File Servers
Replication
Alternative Targets
Different Network Segments

Enumerating the namespace can therefore reveal additional infrastructure.

docs.title: Share Discovery Through SYSVOL
docs.text:
Search scripts for UNC paths.

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem '\\corp.example\SYSVOL' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern '\\\\[A-Za-z0-9._-]+\\[A-Za-z0-9$._-]+'

Review results manually.

docs.title: Share Discovery Through Local Configuration
docs.text:
Mapped drives:

net use

PowerShell:

Get-SmbMapping

These can reveal resources already used by the current user.

docs.title: PowerShell Drives
docs.text:
Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Mapped network drives may appear alongside local drives.

docs.title: File Share Access Model
docs.text:
For each discovered share:

Share
 |
 v
Can List?
 |
 v
Can Read?
 |
 v
Can Write?
 |
 v
Can Modify Existing Files?
 |
 v
Can Delete?

Do not treat all accessible shares as equivalent.

docs.title: Read Access
docs.text:
Read access can expose:

Confidential Information
Credentials
Configuration
Internal Architecture
Source Code
Backups

docs.title: Write Access
docs.text:
Write access may create additional risk if other users or systems consume content from the share.

The important question is:

What Uses This Directory?

docs.title: Writable Share Risk Model
docs.text:
User Can Write
      |
      v
Shared Directory
      |
      v
Another User / Service Reads File
      |
      v
Security-Relevant Behaviour

Write permission alone does not prove code execution.

docs.title: Write vs Modify
docs.text:
A user may be able to:

Create New Files

without being able to:

Modify Existing Files

or:

Delete Files

Always identify the actual effective permission.

docs.title: Safe Write Test
docs.text:
If write testing is authorised, use a uniquely named temporary text file.

PowerShell:

$path = '\\FILE01\TestShare\pentest-write-test.txt'
'Authorised write validation' | Set-Content -Path $path
Test-Path $path
Remove-Item $path

Use only an explicitly approved test location.

docs.title: Verify Cleanup
docs.text:
Test-Path '\\FILE01\TestShare\pentest-write-test.txt'

Expected:

False

docs.title: Linux Write Validation
docs.text:
Within an approved smbclient session, a harmless uniquely named local text file can be uploaded and immediately removed.

Do not perform write validation in:

Software Deployment
Logon Scripts
Startup Scripts
Application Executable Directories
Backup Locations

unless the specific impact test is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Sensitive File Types
docs.text:
During targeted review, pay attention to files such as:

*.ps1
*.bat
*.cmd
*.vbs
*.xml
*.config
*.ini
*.conf
*.yml
*.yaml
*.json
*.kdbx
*.rdp
*.ppk
*.pem
*.key
*.pfx
*.p12
*.cer
*.crt
*.sql
*.bak
*.zip
*.7z

A file extension alone does not make the file sensitive.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Potentially useful configuration files include:

web.config
appsettings.json
connectionStrings.config
database.ini
settings.xml
config.yml

Search carefully and avoid bulk collection.

docs.title: Connection Strings
docs.text:
Applications may store:

Database Server
Database Name
Username
Password
Integrated Security Settings

inside configuration files.

Example conceptual structure:

Server=SQL01
Database=AppDB
User ID=appsvc
Password=<secret>

If discovered, protect the evidence and avoid testing the credential outside scope.

docs.title: PowerShell Scripts
docs.text:
Administrative scripts may contain:

Credentials
Service Accounts
Server Lists
Remote Commands
Backup Paths
API Tokens

Search:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Scripts' -Recurse -Filter '*.ps1' -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','credential','secret','token','key'

docs.title: Batch Files
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Scripts' -Recurse -Include '*.bat','*.cmd' -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','pass=','pwd=','net use','runas'

docs.title: XML Files
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Config' -Recurse -Filter '*.xml' -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','cpassword','credential','connectionString'

docs.title: INI Files
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Config' -Recurse -Filter '*.ini' -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','passwd','pwd','secret'

docs.title: Backup Files
docs.text:
Backups may expose older copies of:

Configuration
Credentials
Databases
Scripts
Certificates
Keys

Potential names include:

backup
old
archive
copy
previous
.bak

docs.title: Password Databases
docs.text:
Files such as:

*.kdbx

may contain password vaults.

Their existence is not automatically a vulnerability.

Assess:

Who Can Read It?
Why?
How Is It Protected?
Is It Intended to Be Shared?

docs.title: Private Keys
docs.text:
Files such as:

*.pem
*.key
*.ppk

may contain private cryptographic material.

If a private key is discovered:

Do Not Immediately Use It

First determine:

Owner
Purpose
Scope
Protection
Associated System

docs.title: PFX and P12 Files
docs.text:
Files such as:

*.pfx
*.p12

can contain:

Certificate
Private Key
Certificate Chain

They may be password protected.

Treat them as sensitive credential material.

docs.title: RDP Files
docs.text:
.rdp files may reveal:

Hostnames
Gateways
Usernames
Connection Settings

They do not normally contain a reusable plaintext password.

docs.title: Deployment Shares
docs.text:
Software deployment shares deserve particular attention.

Examples:

\\DEPLOY01\Software
\\SCCM01\Packages
\\MDT01\DeploymentShare$

These may contain:

Installers
Scripts
Configuration
Task Sequences
Drivers
Credentials

docs.title: Deployment Share Risk
docs.text:
The security model is:

Writable Deployment Share
          |
          v
Package / Script
          |
          v
Automated Deployment
          |
          v
Many Systems

This can produce substantial impact if inappropriate write permissions exist.

Do not modify deployment content during normal testing.

docs.title: SCCM
docs.text:
Microsoft Configuration Manager environments may expose:

Packages
Applications
Content Libraries
Scripts
Task Sequences

through network infrastructure.

See the planned page:

Microsoft Configuration Manager - SCCM

docs.title: MDT
docs.text:
Microsoft Deployment Toolkit commonly uses deployment shares.

A typical share might resemble:

\\MDT01\DeploymentShare$

See:

Microsoft Deployment Toolkit - MDT

docs.title: WSUS
docs.text:
Windows Server Update Services can also introduce infrastructure and content-management relationships relevant to Active Directory assessments.

See:

Windows Server Update Services - WSUS

docs.title: Backup Shares
docs.text:
Backup shares can be particularly sensitive.

Potential content:

System Backups
Database Backups
VM Images
Configuration Exports
Directory Backups
Private Keys

docs.title: Active Directory Backups
docs.text:
Backups containing:

NTDS.dit
SYSTEM Registry Hive
Domain Controller Images

should be treated as Tier 0 material.

See:

NTDS

docs.title: Database Backups
docs.text:
Files such as:

*.bak
*.sql
*.dump

may expose application data and credentials.

Do not restore or process production databases unless authorised.

docs.title: User Home Shares
docs.text:
User home directories may expose:

Documents
Scripts
SSH Keys
RDP Files
Configuration
Browser Exports
Developer Files

Privacy and proportionality are especially important.

Do not indiscriminately search user documents.

docs.title: Department Shares
docs.text:
Examples:

Finance
HR
Legal
Engineering
IT
Security

These can contain highly sensitive business information.

A penetration test should minimise access to unrelated content.

docs.title: Data Minimisation
docs.text:
A good assessment follows:

Find Permission
      |
      v
Identify Relevant File
      |
      v
Collect Minimum Evidence
      |
      v
Stop

rather than:

Download Everything

docs.title: File Metadata
docs.text:
Often sufficient evidence can be collected using:

File Name
Path
Owner
Size
Modification Date
ACL

without opening the file.

docs.title: PowerShell Metadata
docs.text:
Get-Item '\\FILE01\Finance\sensitive-config.xml' |
    Select-Object FullName,Length,CreationTime,LastWriteTime

docs.title: NTFS ACL
docs.text:
Get-Acl '\\FILE01\Finance\sensitive-config.xml' |
    Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Directory ACL
docs.text:
Get-Acl '\\FILE01\Finance' |
    Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: icacls
docs.text:
Native Windows:

icacls "\\FILE01\Finance"

This can provide a compact view of NTFS permissions.

docs.title: Permission Inheritance
docs.text:
NTFS permissions may be inherited.

Conceptually:

Parent Directory
      |
      v
Inherited ACE
      |
      v
Child Directory
      |
      v
File

Identify whether an excessive permission originates from:

Direct ACE

or:

Inherited ACE

docs.title: Group-Based Permissions
docs.text:
A user may gain access through nested groups.

Example:

Alice
 |
 v
Finance Users
 |
 v
All Employees
 |
 v
Share ACL

See:

Groups

docs.title: Domain Local Groups
docs.text:
File-server permissions are commonly assigned through Domain Local groups.

Example:

User
 |
 v
Global Group
 |
 v
Domain Local Group
 |
 v
Resource ACL

This is a normal Active Directory design pattern.

docs.title: AGDLP
docs.text:
A common permissions model is:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

Often abbreviated:

AGDLP

docs.title: AGUDLP
docs.text:
Multi-domain environments may use:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Universal Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

Often abbreviated:

AGUDLP

docs.title: Why Group Resolution Matters
docs.text:
A share may appear restricted to:

FS-Finance-RW

but that group may contain:

Finance
Helpdesk
Legacy Migration Group
Foreign Security Principal

The full membership chain determines exposure.

docs.title: Foreign Principals
docs.text:
Trusted-domain users can potentially receive share access through:

Domain Local Groups
Foreign Security Principals
Direct ACL Entries

See:

Trust Relationships

docs.title: SID History
docs.text:
Legacy share permissions are a common reason organisations retain:

sIDHistory

See:

SID History

A migrated user may continue accessing a share because the ACL references the old SID.

docs.title: Share Permissions and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Writable or administratively accessible shares can contribute to lateral movement.

See:

Lateral Movement

However:

Share Access
!=
Remote Code Execution

Additional conditions are required.

docs.title: Administrative Shares and Remote Execution
docs.text:
Some Windows remote-management techniques use administrative shares as part of their workflow.

For example:

Administrative Access
      |
      v
ADMIN$ / C$
      |
      v
Remote Service Mechanism

The security weakness is usually:

Excessive Administrative Privilege

rather than the existence of ADMIN$.

docs.title: Impacket and SMB Shares
docs.text:
Impacket includes SMB-related tooling.

See:

Impacket

When testing remote administration, distinguish:

Share Enumeration

from:

Remote Execution

and use the least intrusive method needed.

docs.title: Share Access with Kerberos
docs.text:
SMB supports Kerberos authentication when:

DNS
SPN
Realm
Ticket

are correctly configured.

Prefer hostnames over raw IP addresses when intentionally validating Kerberos.

docs.title: Share Access Across Trusts
docs.text:
A trusted-domain identity may access a share when:

Trust Allows Authentication
        |
        v
User Authenticates
        |
        v
Group / ACL Authorises Access

The trust itself does not automatically grant access.

docs.title: Share Access and SID Filtering
docs.text:
For cross-domain access, SID filtering and SID History can influence the SIDs accepted across the trust.

See:

SID History

and:

Trust Tickets

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
SMB signing protects SMB message integrity and is particularly important when considering NTLM relay.

See:

NTLM Relay

Share enumeration and SMB-signing assessment should be considered together when evaluating SMB security.

docs.title: SMB Encryption
docs.text:
Modern SMB supports encryption.

This can protect SMB traffic from network interception.

Whether it is required depends on:

Server Configuration
Share Configuration
Data Sensitivity
Windows Version
Operational Requirements

docs.title: Share Discovery Workflow
docs.text:
A structured assessment can follow:

Active Directory
      |
      v
Identify File Servers
      |
      v
Enumerate Shares
      |
      v
Determine Access
      |
      v
Review Permissions
      |
      v
Identify Interesting Paths
      |
      v
Targeted Content Review
      |
      v
Validate Security Impact
      |
      v
Report

docs.title: Step 1 - Identify File Servers
docs.text:
Sources can include:

Active Directory Computer Objects
User Home Directories
Group Policy
Logon Scripts
DFS
DNS
Existing Drive Mappings
BloodHound

docs.title: Step 2 - Enumerate Shares
docs.text:
Windows:

net view \\FILE01

Linux:

smbclient -L //files01.corp.example -U 'CORP/audituser'

NetExec:

nxc smb files01.corp.example -d corp.example -u audituser -p 'PASSWORD' --shares

docs.title: Step 3 - Determine Access
docs.text:
Record whether the current identity has:

No Access
List
Read
Write
Modify
Full Control

Do not infer permission solely from a tool's abbreviated output if direct validation is required.

docs.title: Step 4 - Review ACLs
docs.text:
Where accessible:

Get-Acl '\\FILE01\Finance'

and:

Get-SmbShareAccess -Name 'Finance'

if querying locally with appropriate permissions.

docs.title: Step 5 - Identify Interesting Files
docs.text:
Prefer metadata first.

Example:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Extension -in '.ps1','.bat','.cmd','.xml','.ini','.config','.json','.yml','.yaml','.kdbx','.pfx','.p12','.pem','.key','.bak'
    } |
    Select-Object FullName,Length,LastWriteTime

docs.title: Step 6 - Search Targeted Content
docs.text:
Only after identifying relevant files:

Select-String -Path '\\FILE01\Scripts\deploy.ps1' -Pattern 'password','credential','secret','token'

docs.title: Step 7 - Validate Impact
docs.text:
For a discovered credential:

Credential Found
      |
      v
Identify Owner
      |
      v
Identify Intended Use
      |
      v
Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Minimal Authentication Validation

Do not automatically test credentials against every reachable service.

docs.title: Step 8 - Preserve Evidence
docs.text:
Record:

Share
Path
File
Permission
Relevant Content
Identity Used
Timestamp

Redact sensitive values where possible.

docs.title: Step 9 - Cleanup
docs.text:
If a write test was performed:

Verify Test File Removed

If no modification was required:

No Cleanup Necessary

docs.title: Searching Large Shares
docs.text:
Large recursive searches can create:

Network Load
File Server Load
EDR Telemetry
Large Result Sets
Privacy Exposure

Use targeted filtering.

docs.title: Better Search Strategy
docs.text:
Instead of:

Search Every File

prefer:

Identify Interesting Directory
        |
        v
Filter Extensions
        |
        v
Filter Names
        |
        v
Inspect Metadata
        |
        v
Read Relevant Files

docs.title: File Age
docs.text:
Old files can be highly relevant.

Examples:

Old Deployment Script
Old Backup
Old Password File
Old Configuration

But age alone does not prove that the content is still usable.

docs.title: Credential Validation
docs.text:
If a credential is found:

Found Credential
      |
      v
Is It In Scope?
      |
      v
Is Validation Permitted?
      |
      v
Identify Intended Service
      |
      v
Minimal Test

Avoid password spraying with discovered credentials unless explicitly part of the assessment.

docs.title: Secret Handling
docs.text:
Never place discovered production secrets into:

Public Notes
Screenshots Without Redaction
Git Repositories
Chat Logs
Unencrypted Reports

Use redaction.

Example:

Password:
P***********3

docs.title: Evidence Screenshot
docs.text:
A screenshot should show enough context to establish:

Share
Path
Permission
Relevant Finding

while hiding unnecessary confidential information.

docs.title: Writable Share Validation
docs.text:
A safe proof is:

Test Identity
     |
     v
Approved Directory
     |
     v
Create Harmless Text File
     |
     v
Verify
     |
     v
Delete
     |
     v
Verify Cleanup

docs.title: Avoid Executable Uploads
docs.text:
If the finding is simply:

User Can Write to Share

there is normally no need to upload:

EXE
DLL
Script Payload
Macro Document

A text file proves write access.

docs.title: Deployment Directory Validation
docs.text:
For a sensitive deployment directory:

Write Permission

may already be enough evidence.

Do not replace or modify deployment packages to demonstrate theoretical execution.

docs.title: Share Detection
docs.text:
Defenders should monitor:

Share Enumeration
Sensitive File Access
Unusual Recursive Reads
Administrative Share Access
File Creation
File Modification
File Deletion
Permission Changes

docs.title: Event 5140
docs.text:
Windows Security event:

5140

records:

A network share object was accessed

when the relevant auditing is enabled.

docs.title: Event 5145
docs.text:
Event:

5145

provides more detailed share access information and can include:

Share
Relative Target Name
Access Requested
Source Address
Account

when Detailed File Share auditing is enabled.

docs.title: Event 5142
docs.text:
Event:

5142

indicates:

A network share object was added

docs.title: Event 5143
docs.text:
Event:

5143

indicates:

A network share object was modified

docs.title: Event 5144
docs.text:
Event:

5144

indicates:

A network share object was deleted

docs.title: Event 4663
docs.text:
Event:

4663

can record access attempts against file-system objects when:

Object Access Auditing

and appropriate SACLs are configured.

docs.title: Authentication Events
docs.text:
Correlate SMB activity with:

4624
4625

and other relevant authentication telemetry.

docs.title: SMB Network Telemetry
docs.text:
Monitor:

TCP 445 Connections
Source Host
Destination Host
Connection Volume
Authentication Identity

A workstation suddenly enumerating many file servers can be worth investigating.

docs.title: Administrative Share Monitoring
docs.text:
High-value patterns include unusual access to:

C$
ADMIN$

especially from:

User Workstations
Unexpected Servers
Non-Administrative Accounts

docs.title: Recursive Enumeration Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

One Account
    |
    v
Many Shares
    |
    v
Many Directories
    |
    v
Large Number of Reads

This can indicate:

Inventory
Backup
Indexing
Security Scanning
Adversary Discovery

Context is required.

docs.title: Sensitive File Monitoring
docs.text:
Consider monitoring access to locations containing:

Deployment Scripts
Configuration Secrets
Private Keys
Backups
Password Vaults
Tier 0 Documentation

docs.title: Share Hardening
docs.text:
A strong file-share security model includes:

Least Privilege
Group-Based Access
NTFS ACL Review
Share ACL Review
SMB Signing
SMB Encryption Where Required
Legacy Protocol Removal
Sensitive Data Protection
Monitoring
Lifecycle Management

docs.title: Remove SMBv1
docs.text:
SMBv1 is obsolete and should generally be disabled unless an unavoidable legacy dependency exists.

Modern environments should use supported SMB versions.

docs.title: Require SMB Signing Where Appropriate
docs.text:
SMB signing can reduce exposure to certain relay and tampering scenarios.

See:

NTLM Relay

docs.title: SMB Encryption
docs.text:
Consider SMB encryption for:

Sensitive Data
Untrusted Network Segments
Administrative Traffic

where operationally appropriate.

docs.title: Restrict Anonymous Access
docs.text:
Avoid unnecessary:

Anonymous Share Enumeration
Anonymous File Access
Guest Access

docs.title: Use Security Groups
docs.text:
Prefer assigning permissions to:

Security Groups

rather than individual users.

Example:

Finance Users
      |
      v
FS-Finance-Read
      |
      v
Finance Share

docs.title: Separate Read and Write Groups
docs.text:
Example:

FS-Finance-RO
FS-Finance-RW

This makes access easier to understand and audit.

docs.title: Avoid Everyone Full Control
docs.text:
A common design may use broad share permissions combined with restrictive NTFS permissions.

This is not automatically vulnerable.

However, effective permissions should still be reviewed carefully.

docs.title: Review Authenticated Users
docs.text:
Broad groups such as:

Authenticated Users
Domain Users
Everyone

should not receive unnecessary access to sensitive directories.

docs.title: Protect Deployment Shares
docs.text:
Deployment shares should use particularly restrictive write permissions.

A good model is:

Deployment Administrators
          |
          v
Write

Deployment Systems
          |
          v
Read

Ordinary Users
          |
          X

depending on operational requirements.

docs.title: Protect Backup Shares
docs.text:
Backup data should be isolated from ordinary users and ideally from standard administrative compromise paths.

Consider:

Separate Credentials
Restricted Network Access
Encryption
Immutable Copies
Offline Copies
Monitoring

docs.title: Protect Credential Files
docs.text:
Avoid storing:

Plaintext Passwords
Reusable Tokens
Private Keys
Unprotected PFX Files

on broadly accessible shares.

docs.title: Use Managed Identities
docs.text:
Where possible, replace embedded service passwords with technologies such as:

gMSA
Managed Identity
Integrated Authentication
Secret Management Platforms

See:

gMSA

docs.title: Share Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
When:

Project Ends
Department Changes
Server Migrates
Application Retires

review:

Share
ACLs
Groups
Data
DNS
Backups

docs.title: Stale Shares
docs.text:
Old shares can expose:

Historical Data
Legacy Credentials
Old Scripts
Forgotten Backups

even when the associated application is no longer active.

docs.title: Hidden Shares
docs.text:
A share ending with:

$

is hidden from some casual browsing.

Example:

DeploymentShare$

This is not an access-control mechanism.

If a user knows the name and has permission, the share can still be accessed.

docs.title: Hidden Does Not Mean Secure
docs.text:
Hidden Share
    !=
Protected Share

Security must come from:

Authentication
Authorisation
ACLs
Network Controls

docs.title: Reporting Share Findings
docs.text:
Do not report:

SYSVOL Is Readable

as a vulnerability by itself.

Do not report:

ADMIN$ Exists

as a vulnerability by itself.

Do not report:

Share Exists

as a vulnerability.

Report the actual security condition.

docs.title: Potential Findings
docs.text:
Examples include:

Sensitive File Share Accessible to All Domain Users

Plaintext Service Credentials Stored on Shared Drive

Deployment Share Writable by Low-Privilege Users

Legacy Backup Share Exposes Active Credentials

Anonymous SMB Share Exposes Internal Information

Excessive NTFS Permissions Permit Unauthorised Modification

Legacy GPP Credential File Remains in SYSVOL

docs.title: Example Finding - Sensitive Share
docs.text:
Finding:
Sensitive Department Share Accessible to Unauthorised Domain Users

Description:
A low-privilege domain account was able to read files from a network
share intended for a restricted business department.

The accessible content included documents containing information not
required for the assessment account's business role.

Impact:
Any domain identity with equivalent access may obtain confidential
business information from the affected share.

If a low-privilege account is compromised, the share may therefore
increase the amount of sensitive data exposed to the attacker.

Recommendation:
Review the share and NTFS permissions associated with the affected
directory.

Grant access through dedicated role-based security groups and remove
broad groups that do not require access.

Periodically review group membership and effective permissions.

docs.title: Example Finding - Plaintext Credential
docs.text:
Finding:
Reusable Service Credential Stored in Plaintext on Network Share

Description:
A configuration script stored on an accessible network share contained
a plaintext username and password for a service account.

The file was readable by users who did not require access to the
credential.

Impact:
An attacker who compromises any account with access to the share may
recover the service credential.

The resulting impact depends on the privileges and systems accessible
to the affected service account.

Recommendation:
Immediately rotate the exposed credential after confirming dependent
services.

Remove plaintext credentials from scripts and configuration files.

Use a managed service account, integrated authentication or an
approved secret-management platform where technically appropriate.

Restrict access to the configuration files to identities that require
them.

docs.title: Example Finding - Writable Deployment Share
docs.text:
Finding:
Low-Privilege Users Can Modify Software Deployment Share

Description:
A low-privilege domain identity had write permission to a directory
used to store software deployment content.

No production package was modified during testing.

Impact:
If systems or administrators consume files from the affected directory,
an attacker may potentially influence the deployment process.

The exact impact depends on which files are trusted and how deployment
integrity is validated.

Recommendation:
Restrict modification of deployment content to dedicated deployment
administrators and service identities.

Separate read and write permissions and implement package integrity
validation where supported.

docs.title: Example Finding - Anonymous Share
docs.text:
Finding:
Network Share Accessible Without Authentication

Description:
The SMB server allowed unauthenticated access to a network share from
the assessment network.

The share exposed internal files and directory names without requiring
a domain identity.

Impact:
Any system with network access to the SMB service may obtain the
exposed information.

The information may assist infrastructure reconnaissance or disclose
sensitive business data.

Recommendation:
Disable unnecessary anonymous or guest SMB access.

Require authenticated access and apply least-privilege share and NTFS
permissions.

docs.title: Example Finding - Legacy Backup
docs.text:
Finding:
Legacy Backup Files Expose Sensitive Configuration Data

Description:
A shared backup directory contained historical copies of application
configuration files.

The backup files were readable by a broad domain group and contained
security-sensitive configuration values.

Impact:
Historical backups can preserve credentials or secrets even after the
live application configuration has been remediated.

An attacker may therefore recover previously exposed credentials from
older copies.

Recommendation:
Restrict access to backup repositories, remove obsolete backups
according to retention requirements and rotate any credentials exposed
in historical copies.

Include backup locations in future secret-scanning and access reviews.

docs.title: Share Testing Model
docs.text:
The basic model is:

Identity
   |
   v
SMB Server
   |
   v
Share
   |
   v
Directory
   |
   v
File

The permission model is:

Identity
   |
   v
Share ACL
   |
   v
NTFS ACL
   |
   v
Effective Access

The group model is:

User
 |
 v
Global Group
 |
 v
Domain Local Group
 |
 v
Resource Permission

The read-risk model is:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Readable Share
       |
       v
Sensitive File
       |
       v
Information / Credential Exposure

The write-risk model is:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Writable Share
       |
       v
Trusted File or Directory
       |
       v
Another User / Service
       |
       v
Potential Security Impact

The important qualification is:

Writable Share
     !=
Automatic Code Execution

The credential model is:

Share
 |
 v
Configuration File
 |
 v
Credential
 |
 v
Account
 |
 v
Accessible Service
 |
 v
Potential Privilege

The migration model is:

Legacy Share ACL
      |
      v
Historical SID
      |
      v
SID History
      |
      v
Current User
      |
      v
Access

The cross-domain model is:

Trusted User
     |
     v
Trust Authentication
     |
     v
Group / ACL
     |
     v
Share

The detection model is:

Authentication
      |
      v
SMB Connection
      |
      v
Share Access
      |
      v
File Access
      |
      v
Potential Modification

The defensive model is:

Least Privilege
      +
Group-Based Access
      +
NTFS Security
      +
SMB Security
      +
Secret Management
      +
Sensitive Data Protection
      +
Monitoring
      +
Lifecycle Management
      =
Reduced Share Risk

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"How much can I download?"

Ask:
"What is the minimum evidence required
to demonstrate the access-control or
secret-management weakness?"

For defenders:

Do Not Ask:
"Who can connect to the file server?"

Ask:
"Which identities can access each
sensitive dataset, why do they need
that access, and would we detect
unexpected use?"

The complete model is:

Identity
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Share Permission
   |
   v
NTFS Permission
   |
   v
File / Directory
   |
   v
Sensitive Information or Trusted Content
   |
   v
Security Impact

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Windows shares are much more than file-storage locations.

In Active Directory they often connect:

Users
Groups
Servers
Applications
Deployment
Backups
Credentials

The basic assessment model is:

Discover Share
      |
      v
Determine Permission
      |
      v
Understand Purpose
      |
      v
Identify Relevant Content
      |
      v
Validate Minimum Impact
      |
      v
Report

The presence of:

SYSVOL
NETLOGON
ADMIN$
C$

is not itself a vulnerability.

Likewise:

Readable Share

does not automatically mean:

Security Finding

The important question is:

Can an identity access or modify
information that it should not?

For readable shares, focus on:

Sensitive Data
Credentials
Configuration
Backups
Private Keys

For writable shares, focus on:

Who Consumes the Content?

The most important distinction is:

Write Access
    !=
Automatic Code Execution

A strong assessment demonstrates the actual dependency rather than assuming impact.

The defensive objective is:

Least Privilege
      |
      v
Role-Based Groups
      |
      v
Secure SMB
      |
      v
Protected Sensitive Data
      |
      v
Secret Management
      |
      v
Monitoring

The next page moves into enterprise endpoint and software-management infrastructure:

Microsoft Configuration Manager (SCCM)

docs.title: Active Directory SID History
docs.text:
SID History is an Active Directory migration feature that allows an account to retain security identifiers from a previous account or domain.

The attribute is:

sIDHistory

Its legitimate purpose is to preserve access during migrations.

Conceptually:

Old Domain
   |
   v
Old Account SID
   |
   v
Migration
   |
   v
New Domain Account
   |
   +--> New SID
   |
   +--> Old SID stored in sIDHistory

This allows resources that still contain access control entries for the old SID to continue recognising the migrated identity.

From a security perspective, SID History is important because Windows authorisation decisions can consider SIDs carried in an access token.

A high-value SID appearing in sIDHistory can therefore create privileges that are not obvious from normal group membership alone.

Authorised testing only

SID History analysis can reveal relationships with migrated, legacy or trusted domains. Do not modify sIDHistory, trust settings or SID filtering during an assessment unless the rules of engagement explicitly permit it. Read-only enumeration is normally sufficient to identify risky configurations.

docs.title: SID History at a Glance
docs.text:
Normal account:

User
 |
 v
Current SID
 |
 v
Group Membership
 |
 v
Access Token
 |
 v
Resource ACL

Migrated account:

User
 |
 +--> Current SID
 |
 +--> sIDHistory
          |
          v
       Old SID
 |
 v
Access Token
 |
 v
Resource ACL

The resource may still contain:

Allow OLD-DOMAIN\User

and the migrated user can continue accessing it because the old SID is represented through SID History.

docs.title: Security Identifier
docs.text:
A Security Identifier, or SID, uniquely identifies a Windows security principal.

Examples include:

User
Group
Computer
Domain
Local Account
Service

A typical domain account SID resembles:

S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-1105

The structure can be viewed as:

S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-1105
|-----------------------------------------|  |
               Domain SID                   RID

docs.title: Domain SID
docs.text:
Accounts belonging to the same domain share the domain portion of the SID.

Example:

Domain SID:

S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333

User:

S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-1105

Group:

S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-2101

The final component is the:

Relative Identifier

or:

RID

docs.title: Why SIDs Matter
docs.text:
Windows authorisation is fundamentally based on security identifiers rather than account names.

An ACL may visually display:

CORP\alice

but the security descriptor ultimately references Alice's SID.

This matters during migrations because:

Account Name

can remain similar while:

SID

changes.

docs.title: Migration Problem
docs.text:
Suppose an old domain contains:

LEGACY\alice

with SID:

S-1-5-21-100-200-300-1105

A file server ACL contains:

Allow S-1-5-21-100-200-300-1105 Read

Alice is migrated to:

CORP\alice

with a new SID:

S-1-5-21-400-500-600-2107

Without migration handling:

New SID
   |
   X
   |
Old ACL

Alice may lose access.

docs.title: SID History Solution
docs.text:
The migrated account can contain:

Current SID:
S-1-5-21-400-500-600-2107

sIDHistory:
S-1-5-21-100-200-300-1105

The effective model becomes:

CORP\alice
   |
   +--> Current SID
   |
   +--> Legacy SID
           |
           v
       Old Resource ACL

This allows access to continue while ACLs are migrated.

docs.title: SID History Lifecycle
docs.text:
SID History should normally be considered transitional.

A healthy migration lifecycle is:

Migration Begins
      |
      v
SID History Added
      |
      v
Legacy Access Continues
      |
      v
Resource ACLs Migrated
      |
      v
Dependencies Validated
      |
      v
SID History Reviewed
      |
      v
Legacy Values Removed When No Longer Required

A common problem is:

Migration Completed
      |
      v
SID History Never Reviewed
      |
      v
Legacy Access Persists

docs.title: Why SID History Is Security Sensitive
docs.text:
The security significance comes from the relationship:

SID
 |
 v
Access Token
 |
 v
ACL
 |
 v
Privilege

If an account possesses a SID associated with a privileged identity, authorisation may treat that SID as relevant when evaluating access.

Therefore:

Current Group Membership

does not always reveal the complete privilege picture.

docs.title: Privilege Visibility Problem
docs.text:
Consider:

CORP\migration-user

Normal group enumeration may show:

Domain Users
Migration Users

Nothing appears privileged.

But:

sIDHistory

could contain a SID that maps to a privileged legacy principal.

The actual security path becomes:

Migration User
      |
      v
sIDHistory
      |
      v
Privileged SID
      |
      v
Resource ACL
      |
      v
Unexpected Access

docs.title: SID History Is Not Automatically a Vulnerability
docs.text:
The existence of:

sIDHistory

is not inherently a vulnerability.

It is legitimate Active Directory functionality.

A meaningful finding requires additional context such as:

Unexpected Privileged SID
Stale Migration Data
Unnecessary Legacy Access
Weak Trust Configuration
Missing Migration Cleanup
Unexpected Cross-Domain Privilege

docs.title: Assessment Questions
docs.text:
During an authorised assessment, ask:

Which Accounts Have SID History?

Which Groups Have SID History?

Which Domains Do Those SIDs Belong To?

Are Those Domains Still Active?

Was SID History Created for Migration?

Are the Legacy Permissions Still Required?

Do Any Historical SIDs Represent Privileged Identities?

Does SID Filtering Protect the Trust Boundary?

Has the Migration Been Completed?

docs.title: Enumerating SID History
docs.text:
The safest starting point is read-only directory enumeration.

Using the ActiveDirectory PowerShell module:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties SIDHistory |
    Where-Object { $_.SIDHistory } |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,SID,SIDHistory

docs.title: Scoped User Enumeration
docs.text:
In large environments, avoid retrieving every user unnecessarily.

Example:

Get-ADUser -LDAPFilter '(sIDHistory=*)' -Properties SIDHistory |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,SID,SIDHistory

This directly requests users containing SID History.

docs.title: Enumerate Groups
docs.text:
Groups can also contain SID History.

Get-ADGroup -LDAPFilter '(sIDHistory=*)' -Properties SIDHistory |
    Select-Object Name,SID,SIDHistory

Do not limit the assessment to user objects.

docs.title: Enumerate All Relevant Objects
docs.text:
LDAP can be used when broader object coverage is required.

Example:

Get-ADObject -LDAPFilter '(sIDHistory=*)' -Properties sIDHistory,objectSid |
    Select-Object Name,ObjectClass,ObjectSid,sIDHistory

docs.title: Query a Specific User
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -Identity 'migration-user' -Properties SIDHistory |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,SID,SIDHistory

docs.title: Query a Specific Group
docs.text:
Get-ADGroup -Identity 'Legacy-App-Users' -Properties SIDHistory |
    Select-Object Name,SID,SIDHistory

docs.title: LDAP Enumeration from Linux
docs.text:
SID History can also be queried through LDAP.

Example:

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
  -D 'audituser@corp.example' -W \
  -b 'DC=corp,DC=example' \
  '(sIDHistory=*)' \
  sAMAccountName objectSid sIDHistory

Binary SID values may require additional conversion before they are human-readable.

docs.title: LDAP Filter
docs.text:
The important LDAP filter is:

(sIDHistory=*)

This can significantly reduce unnecessary directory retrieval.

docs.title: Raw LDAP Representation
docs.text:
LDAP tooling may return SID values in binary or escaped form.

Therefore:

LDAP Result
    |
    v
Binary SID
    |
    v
Convert SID
    |
    v
Readable S-1-5-21-...

Do not mistake binary output for malformed data.

docs.title: PowerShell SID Conversion
docs.text:
A binary SID can be converted using .NET.

Example:

$sid = New-Object System.Security.Principal.SecurityIdentifier($bytes,0)
$sid.Value

where $bytes contains the binary SID value.

docs.title: Current User SID
docs.text:
To inspect the current identity:

whoami /user

docs.title: Current Group SIDs
docs.text:
whoami /groups

This is useful when understanding the SIDs present in the current security context.

docs.title: Complete Token Context
docs.text:
whoami /all

This can display:

User SID
Group SIDs
Privileges
Integrity Information

docs.title: Domain SID Enumeration
docs.text:
Using PowerShell:

Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot,DomainSID

Example:

DNSRoot   : corp.example
DomainSID : S-1-5-21-400-500-600

docs.title: Identify SID Origin
docs.text:
Suppose SID History contains:

S-1-5-21-100-200-300-512

Separate:

Domain SID:
S-1-5-21-100-200-300

RID:
512

This helps determine the possible origin and significance.

docs.title: Well-Known Domain RIDs
docs.text:
Some commonly encountered domain-relative RIDs include:

RID Typical Group 500 Administrator account 501 Guest account 512 Domain Admins 513 Domain Users 514 Domain Guests 515 Domain Computers 516 Domain Controllers 517 Cert Publishers 518 Schema Admins 519 Enterprise Admins 520 Group Policy Creator Owners 521 Read-only Domain Controllers

These values provide useful context when analysing historical SIDs.

Note

A RID alone does not prove effective privilege. Confirm the SID's domain, object type, trust context and resulting authorisation before assigning impact.

docs.title: Example Privileged SID History
docs.text:
Suppose:

Current Account:
CORP\migration-user

Current SID:
S-1-5-21-400-500-600-2107

SID History:
S-1-5-21-100-200-300-512

RID:

512

commonly corresponds to:

Domain Admins

in the domain represented by:

S-1-5-21-100-200-300

This requires investigation.

docs.title: Do Not Infer Impact from RID Alone
docs.text:
The correct process is:

Historical SID Found
      |
      v
Identify Domain SID
      |
      v
Identify Original Principal
      |
      v
Determine Trust Context
      |
      v
Determine Whether SID Is Accepted
      |
      v
Identify Resource / ACL
      |
      v
Validate Actual Access

docs.title: SID Resolution
docs.text:
Windows can resolve a SID when the corresponding authority is reachable and trusted.

PowerShell example:

$sid = New-Object System.Security.Principal.SecurityIdentifier(
    'S-1-5-21-100-200-300-1105'
)

$sid.Translate([System.Security.Principal.NTAccount])

This may return something such as:

LEGACY\alice

Resolution can fail when:

Domain No Longer Exists
Trust Removed
Network Unreachable
SID Unknown

docs.title: Unresolved Historical SIDs
docs.text:
An unresolved SID should not automatically be dismissed.

It may represent:

Retired Domain
Removed Account
Old Migration
Disconnected Forest
Deleted Group
Legacy Resource

Document the unresolved value and investigate using approved data sources.

docs.title: SID History and Groups
docs.text:
SID History on a group can be especially important.

Conceptually:

New Group
   |
   v
Old Group SID in sIDHistory
   |
   v
Legacy ACL
   |
   v
Access for All New Group Members

A single historical group SID can therefore affect multiple users.

docs.title: Group Migration
docs.text:
Example:

LEGACY\File-Admins

is migrated to:

CORP\File-Admins

The new group may retain:

LEGACY\File-Admins SID

in:

sIDHistory

This preserves access to resources still secured using the legacy group.

docs.title: SID History and ACLs
docs.text:
SID History becomes meaningful when the SID intersects with an ACL.

Example:

Historical SID
      |
      v
NTFS ACL
      |
      v
Sensitive Directory

or:

Historical SID
      |
      v
Active Directory ACL
      |
      v
Privileged AD Object

docs.title: File System Permissions
docs.text:
A legacy file server may contain:

Allow LEGACY\File-Admins Full Control

After migration:

CORP\File-Admins

may continue receiving access through SID History.

The long-term fix is generally to migrate the ACL rather than retain historical dependencies indefinitely.

docs.title: Active Directory ACLs
docs.text:
Historical SIDs can also remain relevant to directory permissions.

Review:

Users
Groups
OUs
GPOs
Computers
Service Accounts
Domain Objects

See:

ACL and ACE

docs.title: SID History and Group Policy
docs.text:
Legacy SIDs may appear in:

GPO Security Filtering
Delegation
Restricted Groups
User Rights Assignments
File Permissions
Registry Permissions

See:

Group Policy

docs.title: SID History and Local Groups
docs.text:
A historical domain group may still appear in:

Local Administrators
Remote Desktop Users
Remote Management Users
Backup Operators

on member systems.

Example:

Legacy Group SID
      |
      v
Server Local Administrators
      |
      v
Migrated Group via SID History

docs.title: SID History and SMB
docs.text:
Legacy file permissions are one of the most common reasons SID History exists.

Review:

Share ACL
NTFS ACL
Historical Group SID
Current Migrated Group

See:

SMB

docs.title: SID History and Trusts
docs.text:
SID History becomes especially important when it crosses domain or forest boundaries.

See:

Domain and Forest Trusts

and:

Trust Relationships

docs.title: Trust Boundary
docs.text:
Consider:

Domain A
   |
   v
Trust
   |
   v
Domain B

A user token may contain:

Current SID
Group SIDs
Historical SIDs

The receiving domain must decide which SIDs should be accepted across the trust.

This is where:

SID Filtering

becomes important.

docs.title: SID Filtering
docs.text:
SID filtering is designed to prevent inappropriate SID information from being honoured across certain trust boundaries.

Conceptually:

Security Token
      |
      +--> Current SID
      +--> Group SID
      +--> SID History
      |
      v
Trust Boundary
      |
      v
SID Filtering
      |
      +--> Allowed
      |
      X
      |
      +--> Filtered

docs.title: SID Filtering Is Context Dependent
docs.text:
The exact filtering behaviour depends on factors including:

Trust Type
Trust Attributes
Forest Relationship
SID Namespace
Migration Configuration

Do not reduce SID filtering to:

Enabled
=
Everything Safe

or:

Disabled
=
Automatically Exploitable

Analyse the actual trust and authorisation path.

docs.title: Intra-Forest Context
docs.text:
Domains inside the same forest have a much stronger trust relationship than separate forests.

The forest should generally be treated as the primary Active Directory security boundary.

Therefore:

Child Domain

should not be assumed to provide strong isolation from:

Forest Root Domain

simply because they have different domain SIDs.

docs.title: Cross-Forest Context
docs.text:
Separate forests provide a stronger security boundary.

For cross-forest relationships, carefully review:

SID Filtering
Selective Authentication
Foreign Group Membership
Cross-Forest ACLs
Administrative Dependencies
Network Reachability

docs.title: External Trust Context
docs.text:
External trusts connect specific domains rather than entire forests.

SID filtering is particularly relevant because the receiving domain should not blindly accept arbitrary SID information from another security boundary.

docs.title: Forest Trust Context
docs.text:
Forest trusts provide broader authentication relationships.

The security assessment should evaluate:

Forest Trust Direction
Forest Transitivity
Selective Authentication
SID Filtering
Foreign Privilege

docs.title: Selective Authentication
docs.text:
Selective authentication and SID filtering solve different problems.

SID filtering asks:

Which SIDs should be accepted?

Selective authentication asks:

Where may this foreign identity authenticate?

docs.title: Combined Model
docs.text:
Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Trust
      |
      v
SID Filtering
      |
      v
Selective Authentication
      |
      v
Resource Authorisation

Both controls can contribute to reducing cross-boundary risk.

docs.title: SID History and Migration Trusts
docs.text:
Migration environments may intentionally configure trusts to support:

Account Migration
Resource Migration
SID History
Temporary Legacy Access

These environments require careful interpretation.

A configuration that appears unusual may be:

Temporary Migration Requirement

rather than:

Security Misconfiguration

docs.title: Migration Exceptions
docs.text:
Temporary migration exceptions should have:

Documented Purpose
Business Owner
Technical Owner
Start Date
Expected End Date
Cleanup Plan

docs.title: Migration Completion
docs.text:
Once migration is complete:

Old ACLs

should ideally be replaced with:

Current SIDs

and unnecessary historical dependencies removed.

docs.title: SID History and BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can help reveal privilege relationships involving historical identities and cross-domain paths.

See:

BloodHound

A useful analysis model is:

Account
   |
   v
Historical Identity
   |
   v
Group / ACL
   |
   v
Privilege

Do not rely on a graph alone.

Confirm the underlying directory attributes and effective access.

docs.title: SID History and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
SID History can contribute to lateral movement when it provides access to:

Local Administrators
Remote Management Users
File Shares
Applications
Administrative Services

See:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: SID History and WinRM
docs.text:
Example:

Migrated Account
      |
      v
Historical Group SID
      |
      v
Remote Management Permission
      |
      v
WinRM Access

See:

WinRM

docs.title: SID History and RDP
docs.text:
A historical SID may also map to a principal that remains authorised for Remote Desktop access.

The assessment should distinguish:

Authentication

from:

Actual RDP Authorisation

docs.title: SID History and WMI
docs.text:
Administrative permissions derived through historical SIDs may indirectly enable remote WMI access.

See:

WMI

docs.title: SID History and DCOM
docs.text:
The same applies to DCOM where the resulting identity has the required permissions.

See:

DCOM

docs.title: SID History and Privileged Accounts
docs.text:
Pay particular attention when historical SIDs correspond to:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Schema Admins
Administrators
Server Administrators
Backup Administrators
Application Administrators

The question is not simply:

Does the SID look privileged?

but:

Does the SID create effective privilege?

docs.title: High-Value RID Review
docs.text:
Historical SIDs ending in values such as:

-500
-512
-518
-519

deserve additional investigation.

However:

Interesting RID
!=
Confirmed Vulnerability

docs.title: Current Group Membership
docs.text:
For a specific user:

Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership -Identity 'migration-user' |
    Select-Object Name,GroupScope,GroupCategory

Compare this with:

SIDHistory

to identify privilege that may not be apparent from current group membership.

docs.title: Current User Token
docs.text:
On a controlled test system:

whoami /groups

can help confirm the SIDs represented in the user's current token.

docs.title: Token Validation
docs.text:
A safe validation sequence is:

Directory Attribute
      |
      v
Historical SID Identified
      |
      v
Relevant Resource Identified
      |
      v
Controlled Logon
      |
      v
Token Inspected
      |
      v
Minimum Access Tested

docs.title: Do Not Modify SID History for Testing
docs.text:
Avoid changing:

sIDHistory

merely to prove that Windows uses SIDs for authorisation.

This introduces unnecessary directory changes and can create privilege.

Read-only evidence is usually sufficient.

docs.title: Do Not Disable SID Filtering
docs.text:
Similarly, do not modify:

SID Filtering

during normal penetration testing.

Changing trust security controls can affect authentication across entire domains or forests.

docs.title: Avoid Destructive Migration Tests
docs.text:
Do not:

Delete SID History
Modify Trust Attributes
Change Resource ACLs
Remove Migration Groups

during assessment unless explicitly approved.

These changes may break production access.

docs.title: Safe Validation Example
docs.text:
Suppose:

CORP\migration-user

contains an old SID associated with:

LEGACY\File-Readers

and an approved test share still grants:

Read

to that old SID.

A safe test can be:

Authenticate as CORP\migration-user
      |
      v
Access Approved Share
      |
      v
Read Approved Test File
      |
      v
Stop

There is no need to:

Modify Files
Execute Code
Change ACLs

to demonstrate the relationship.

docs.title: Safe Administrative Validation
docs.text:
If a historical SID appears privileged:

Do Not Immediately Perform Administrative Actions

First establish:

Original SID
Current Account
Trust Context
Target Permission

Then use the least intrusive approved action capable of demonstrating impact.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each relevant SID History entry, record:

Current Account
Current SID
Historical SID
Historical Domain
Historical Principal
Object Type
Current Group Membership
Trust Relationship
SID Filtering Context
Affected Resource
Permission
Validation Performed
Timestamp

docs.title: Example Evidence Table
docs.text:
Current Principal Current SID Historical Principal Historical SID Resource Access CORP\migration-user S-1-5-21-400-500-600-2107 LEGACY\App-Users S-1-5-21-100-200-300-2201 APP01 Read

Use:

Redacted

or:

Representative

values where appropriate in public reports.

docs.title: Evidence Quality
docs.text:
Strong evidence should establish:

SID History Exists
      |
      v
Historical SID Identified
      |
      v
Permission Identified
      |
      v
Effective Access Confirmed

Weak evidence is merely:

Account Has SID History

docs.title: SID History Detection
docs.text:
Defenders should monitor:

SID History Changes
Unexpected Migration Activity
Privileged Historical SIDs
Cross-Domain Authentication
Foreign Privileged Access
Trust Changes

docs.title: Directory Service Auditing
docs.text:
Changes to Active Directory attributes can be visible through Directory Service Changes auditing.

Event:

5136

can record modifications to directory objects when the relevant auditing and SACL configuration are present.

docs.title: Event 5136
docs.text:
Event 5136 indicates:

A directory service object was modified

Relevant details can include:

Object
Attribute
Actor
Operation

Monitoring should look for unexpected changes involving:

sIDHistory

where sufficient audit detail is available.

docs.title: Account Migration Events
docs.text:
Windows provides security events associated with SID History migration activity.

Depending on the operation and auditing configuration, events such as:

4765
4766

may be relevant.

docs.title: Event 4765
docs.text:
Security event:

4765

is associated with:

SID History being added to an account

This should normally correspond to authorised migration activity.

docs.title: Event 4766
docs.text:
Security event:

4766

is associated with an attempt to add SID History that failed.

Unexpected occurrences may warrant investigation.

docs.title: Authentication Events
docs.text:
Correlate SID History observations with authentication telemetry such as:

4624
4625
4672
4768
4769

where relevant.

docs.title: Privileged Logons
docs.text:
Event:

4672

indicates that special privileges were assigned to a new logon.

If a migrated identity unexpectedly generates privileged logons, investigate:

Current Groups
SID History
Local Groups
ACLs
Trust Relationships

docs.title: Trust Monitoring
docs.text:
Relevant trust events can include:

4706
4707
4716

See:

Trust Relationships

docs.title: Detection Model
docs.text:
SID History Change
       |
       v
Account
       |
       v
Authentication
       |
       v
Privileged Resource
       |
       v
Unexpected Access

Correlation provides more value than monitoring a single event in isolation.

docs.title: Baseline SID History
docs.text:
Organisations using SID History legitimately should maintain an inventory of:

Expected Accounts
Expected Groups
Source Domain
Migration Project
Migration Date
Business Owner
Cleanup Date

This makes unexpected values easier to detect.

docs.title: Detect Privileged Historical SIDs
docs.text:
Defenders can periodically enumerate SID History and identify values corresponding to privileged domain-relative RIDs.

Example read-only review:

Get-ADObject -LDAPFilter '(sIDHistory=*)' -Properties sIDHistory |
    Select-Object Name,ObjectClass,sIDHistory

The resulting SIDs should then be correlated with known domains and migration records.

docs.title: Do Not Alert on Every SID History Entry
docs.text:
In migration-heavy environments:

SID History Present

may be normal.

Better detection focuses on:

New SID History
Unexpected Source Domain
Privileged SID
Account Outside Migration Scope
Post-Migration Changes
Unusual Administrative Access

docs.title: SID History Hardening
docs.text:
A strong defensive model includes:

Controlled Migration
SID Filtering
Least Privilege
Migration Inventory
ACL Migration
SID History Cleanup
Trust Review
Monitoring

docs.title: Restrict Migration Privileges
docs.text:
Only authorised migration systems and administrators should be capable of performing operations related to SID History.

Protect:

Migration Accounts
Migration Servers
Domain Controllers
Trust Configuration

docs.title: Use Dedicated Migration Accounts
docs.text:
Migration activities should use:

Dedicated
Controlled
Audited
Time-Bounded

administrative identities.

Avoid using normal daily administrative accounts for migration operations.

docs.title: Protect Migration Infrastructure
docs.text:
Migration tooling can be highly privileged.

Treat migration servers as sensitive systems.

Apply:

Network Restrictions
Privileged Access Controls
Logging
EDR
Credential Protection
Administrative Separation

docs.title: Maintain SID Filtering
docs.text:
Appropriate SID filtering should remain in place across trust boundaries.

Any migration-related exceptions should be:

Documented
Approved
Temporary
Monitored
Removed

docs.title: Migrate Resource ACLs
docs.text:
The long-term objective should generally be:

Legacy SID ACL
      |
      v
Current SID ACL

rather than indefinitely depending on:

sIDHistory

docs.title: Remove Stale Dependencies
docs.text:
After migration:

Find Legacy ACLs
      |
      v
Replace with Current Principals
      |
      v
Validate Applications
      |
      v
Review SID History

docs.title: Review Privileged SID History
docs.text:
Historical SIDs associated with privileged groups require particular attention.

Examples include SIDs corresponding to:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Schema Admins
Administrators

These should have a clear documented migration justification.

docs.title: Review Legacy Domains
docs.text:
If SID History references a domain that:

No Longer Exists

determine whether the historical SID still provides access through existing ACLs.

A retired domain does not automatically make the SID harmless.

docs.title: Review Trust Lifecycle
docs.text:
Migration trusts should not remain indefinitely without justification.

The lifecycle should be:

Create Trust
    |
    v
Perform Migration
    |
    v
Migrate Permissions
    |
    v
Validate
    |
    v
Remove Legacy Dependency
    |
    v
Review / Remove Trust

docs.title: Reporting SID History Findings
docs.text:
Do not report:

SID History Enabled

as a vulnerability.

SIDHistory is an attribute and migration capability, not a simple global feature that is either safely enabled or disabled.

Report the actual weakness.

Examples:

Privileged Legacy SID Remains Assigned After Migration

Stale SID History Preserves Unnecessary Access

Migration Account Retains Historical Administrative Privileges

Legacy ACLs Continue to Depend on SID History

Unnecessary Cross-Domain Privilege Persists Through SID History

docs.title: Example Finding - Privileged SID History
docs.text:
Finding:
Migrated Account Retains Privileged Legacy SID

Description:
A migrated account in the corporate domain retained a historical SID
associated with a privileged group in the legacy domain.

The migration project had already been completed and no documented
requirement for the historical administrative access was identified.

Impact:
The account may retain access to systems or resources that continue to
authorise the historical privileged SID.

This can provide privileges that are not apparent from the account's
current group membership.

Recommendation:
Identify all resources that still reference the historical SID and
replace those permissions with current role-based groups where access
remains required.

After validating that no legitimate dependencies remain, remove the
obsolete SID History value through the organisation's approved Active
Directory migration and change-management procedures.

docs.title: Example Finding - Stale Migration Access
docs.text:
Finding:
SID History Preserves Legacy Resource Access After Migration

Description:
Multiple migrated accounts retained SID History values associated with
the previous domain.

Several production file-system ACLs continued to reference these
legacy SIDs even though the migration had been completed.

Impact:
Legacy access relationships remain active and increase the complexity
of permission management.

Access may persist even when current group membership suggests that an
account should no longer have access.

Recommendation:
Inventory resources that continue to reference legacy SIDs.

Replace legacy ACL entries with current domain groups, validate
application and user access, and remove unnecessary SID History values
after dependencies have been eliminated.

docs.title: Example Finding - Missing Migration Cleanup
docs.text:
Finding:
Historical SIDs Remain Without Documented Migration Requirement

Description:
SID History was present on accounts migrated from a legacy domain.

The organisation could not identify an active migration project,
business requirement or remaining resource dependency requiring the
historical values.

Impact:
Unnecessary historical security identifiers can preserve access paths
that are difficult to identify through standard group-membership
reviews.

Recommendation:
Establish an inventory of accounts containing SID History and map each
historical SID to the resources that continue to depend on it.

Remove obsolete permissions and historical SID values through a
controlled migration-cleanup process.

docs.title: Example Finding - Privileged Group SID History
docs.text:
Finding:
Migrated Group Retains Historical Administrative Group SID

Description:
A current domain group retained the SID of an administrative group
from the legacy domain in its SID History.

Members of the current group could therefore potentially inherit
permissions assigned to the historical administrative SID.

Impact:
Adding a user to the current group may grant access to legacy
administrative resources that is not obvious from the group's current
name or documented purpose.

Recommendation:
Identify every permission associated with the historical SID.

Replace required access with explicitly named current administrative
groups and remove the historical dependency after validation.

docs.title: SID History Testing Model
docs.text:
The SID model is:

Domain
  |
  v
Domain SID
  |
  +--> RID
  |
  v
Principal SID

The migration model is:

Old Account
    |
    v
Old SID
    |
    v
Migration
    |
    v
New Account
    |
    +--> New SID
    |
    +--> Old SID in sIDHistory

The compatibility model is:

New Account
    |
    v
SID History
    |
    v
Old SID
    |
    v
Legacy ACL
    |
    v
Access

The privilege model is:

Current Account
      |
      v
Historical SID
      |
      v
Privileged ACL
      |
      v
Unexpected Access

The group model is:

Current Group
      |
      v
Historical Group SID
      |
      v
Legacy Permission
      |
      v
All Current Group Members

The trust model is:

Identity
   |
   v
SID Set
   |
   v
Trust Boundary
   |
   v
SID Filtering
   |
   v
Authorisation

The selective-authentication model is:

Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Trust
      |
      v
SID Filtering
      |
      v
Allowed to Authenticate
      |
      v
Resource ACL

The migration lifecycle is:

Migration
   |
   v
SID History
   |
   v
Temporary Compatibility
   |
   v
ACL Migration
   |
   v
Validation
   |
   v
Cleanup

The unhealthy lifecycle is:

Migration
   |
   v
SID History
   |
   v
Migration Completed
   |
   v
No Cleanup
   |
   v
Legacy Permissions Persist

The detection model is:

SID History Change
       |
       v
Account
       |
       v
Authentication
       |
       v
Historical Permission
       |
       v
Sensitive Resource

The defensive model is:

Controlled Migration
       +
SID Filtering
       +
Migration Inventory
       +
ACL Migration
       +
Least Privilege
       +
Monitoring
       +
Cleanup
       =
Reduced SID History Risk

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Does this account have SID History?"

Ask:
"What access does the historical SID
still provide?"

For defenders:

Do Not Ask:
"Can we delete every SID History value?"

Ask:
"Which resources still depend on each
historical SID, and how can those
dependencies be safely removed?"

The complete model is:

Historical Identity
       |
       v
SID History
       |
       v
Current Identity
       |
       v
Authentication
       |
       v
Historical ACL
       |
       v
Effective Access
       |
       v
Security Impact
