docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
SID History exists to solve a legitimate migration problem:

Identity Changes
      |
      v
SID Changes
      |
      v
Existing ACLs Break

SID History temporarily bridges that gap:

New Identity
      |
      v
Old SID Preserved
      |
      v
Legacy Access Continues

The security problem appears when:

Temporary Compatibility

becomes:

Permanent Hidden Privilege

A proper assessment therefore follows:

Find SID History
      |
      v
Identify Historical SID
      |
      v
Identify Historical Principal
      |
      v
Understand Migration Context
      |
      v
Understand Trust Context
      |
      v
Find Remaining Permission
      |
      v
Validate Effective Access
      |
      v
Determine Security Impact

The presence of sIDHistory alone should not be reported as a vulnerability.

The important question is:

What does this SID still authorise?

Defenders should work toward:

Migration
   |
   v
Temporary SID History
   |
   v
Resource ACL Migration
   |
   v
Validation
   |
   v
Removal of Legacy Dependencies

while maintaining:

SID Filtering
Least Privilege
Migration Monitoring
Trust Governance
Administrative Separation

The next page covers the Kerberos side of Active Directory trust relationships:

Trust Tickets

docs.title: Active Directory SMB - Enumeration, Authentication and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Server Message Block (SMB) is one of the most important protocols encountered during Windows and Active Directory security assessments.

SMB is used for:

File Sharing
Printer Sharing
Named Pipes
Remote Administration
Administrative Shares
Group Policy Distribution
SYSVOL
NETLOGON
Service Management
Remote Registry
RPC Transport

In Active Directory environments, SMB is especially important because it frequently provides the connection between:

Identity
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Remote Windows Host
   |
   v
Files / Shares / Administration

SMB can therefore appear during:

Enumeration
Credential Validation
Share Discovery
Sensitive File Discovery
Lateral Movement
Remote Administration
NTLM Relay
Authentication Coercion
Domain Controller Enumeration

Authorised testing only

SMB authentication and remote administration can generate significant security telemetry and may affect production systems. Only test hosts and credentials included in the assessment scope. Prefer read-only enumeration before attempting file writes or remote execution.

docs.title: SMB at a Glance
docs.text:
The basic model is:

Client
  |
  v
TCP 445
  |
  v
SMB Server
  |
  +--> Authentication
  |
  +--> Shares
  |
  +--> Files
  |
  +--> Named Pipes
  |
  +--> Remote Administration

In an Active Directory environment:

Domain Account
      |
      v
Kerberos / NTLM
      |
      v
SMB
      |
      v
Windows Host

docs.title: SMB Ports
docs.text:
Modern SMB primarily uses:

TCP 445

Older environments may also expose:

TCP 139

which is associated with SMB over NetBIOS.

During modern Active Directory assessments, the primary port is normally:

445/TCP

docs.title: Check SMB Connectivity
docs.text:
From Windows:

Test-NetConnection srv01.corp.example -Port 445

Example:

ComputerName     : srv01.corp.example
RemoteAddress    : 10.10.10.25
RemotePort       : 445
TcpTestSucceeded : True

From Linux:

nmap -Pn -p445 srv01.corp.example

For a defined subnet:

nmap -Pn -p445 10.10.10.0/24

docs.title: SMB Versions
docs.text:
The major SMB generations are:

SMBv1
SMBv2
SMBv3

SMBv1 is obsolete and should generally be disabled.

Modern Windows environments should use:

SMBv2
SMBv3

docs.title: Why SMBv1 Matters
docs.text:
SMBv1 lacks many protections available in later SMB versions and has historically been associated with serious security weaknesses.

During an assessment, the important question is usually:

Is SMBv1 Enabled?

rather than:

Can I exploit SMBv1?

docs.title: Check SMBv1 on Windows
docs.text:
On a Windows server:

Get-SmbServerConfiguration |
    Select-Object EnableSMB1Protocol,EnableSMB2Protocol

Example:

EnableSMB1Protocol EnableSMB2Protocol
------------------ ------------------
False              True

docs.title: Check SMB Client Configuration
docs.text:
Get-SmbClientConfiguration

Useful properties include:

EnableSecuritySignature
RequireSecuritySignature
EnableInsecureGuestLogons

docs.title: Check SMB Server Configuration
docs.text:
Get-SmbServerConfiguration

Useful properties include:

EnableSMB1Protocol
EnableSMB2Protocol
EnableSecuritySignature
RequireSecuritySignature
EncryptData
RejectUnencryptedAccess
EnableAuthenticateUserSharing

Exact properties can vary by Windows version.

docs.title: SMB Authentication
docs.text:
SMB commonly uses:

Kerberos

or:

NTLM

in Active Directory environments.

Conceptually:

SMB Client
    |
    v
Authentication
    |
    +--> Kerberos
    |
    +--> NTLM
    |
    v
SMB Server

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication
docs.text:
When the client accesses a domain host by its hostname and Kerberos requirements are satisfied:

Client
  |
  v
KDC
  |
  v
CIFS Service Ticket
  |
  v
SMB Server

The service principal typically resembles:

cifs/srv01.corp.example

docs.title: SMB and SPNs
docs.text:
Kerberos authentication to SMB normally uses the:

CIFS

service class.

Example:

cifs/fileserver.corp.example

You can inspect Kerberos tickets on Windows:

klist

Look for:

cifs/

service tickets.

docs.title: Hostnames vs IP Addresses
docs.text:
When Kerberos is expected, prefer:

\\srv01.corp.example\share

rather than:

\\10.10.10.25\share

Using an IP address may prevent normal SPN matching and can result in NTLM authentication or authentication failure.

docs.title: NTLM Authentication
docs.text:
When Kerberos cannot be used, SMB may fall back to NTLM if NTLM is permitted.

Conceptually:

Client
  |
  v
NTLM Challenge / Response
  |
  v
SMB Server

This becomes important for:

Pass-the-Hash
NTLM Relay
Credential Exposure
Legacy Authentication

docs.title: Identify Authentication Protocol
docs.text:
Do not assume that successful SMB authentication means Kerberos was used.

Determine whether the session used:

Kerberos

or:

NTLM

using:

Windows Event Logs
Kerberos Ticket Cache
NTLM Operational Logs
Network Telemetry

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
SMB signing protects the integrity of SMB messages.

Conceptually:

SMB Message
    |
    v
Cryptographic Signature
    |
    v
Receiver Verifies Signature

This helps prevent an attacker from modifying or relaying SMB authentication in certain scenarios.

docs.title: SMB Signing States
docs.text:
A system can broadly be considered:

Signing Supported

and:

Signing Required

These are not the same thing.

The important security question for relay resistance is usually:

Is SMB Signing Required?

docs.title: Why SMB Signing Matters
docs.text:
Without required SMB signing:

Victim
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Attacker
  |
  v
Relay
  |
  v
SMB Target

may become possible if the other relay requirements are satisfied.

With signing required:

Victim
  |
  v
Attacker
  |
  X
  |
  v
SMB Target

the classic SMB relay path is substantially restricted because the attacker cannot produce the required message signatures without the appropriate session key.

See:

NTLM Relay

docs.title: Check SMB Signing with PowerShell
docs.text:
Server configuration:

Get-SmbServerConfiguration |
    Select-Object EnableSecuritySignature,RequireSecuritySignature

Client configuration:

Get-SmbClientConfiguration |
    Select-Object EnableSecuritySignature,RequireSecuritySignature

docs.title: SMB Signing with NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec can help identify SMB hosts and their signing configuration.

Check your installed version:

nxc --version

SMB help:

nxc smb -h

Basic discovery:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24

Example conceptual output:

SMB  10.10.10.10  445  DC01   Windows Server
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  Windows Server
SMB  10.10.10.30  445  WS01   Windows

Depending on the NetExec version, output may also show:

signing
SMB version
domain
hostname

docs.title: NetExec SMB Signing Enumeration
docs.text:
NetExec provides SMB modules and options that can help identify systems where signing is not required.

Because command options can change between releases, first use:

nxc smb -h

Do not rely on an old CrackMapExec command without confirming that the equivalent exists in the installed NetExec release.

docs.title: Nmap SMB Security Modes
docs.text:
Nmap SMB scripts can provide additional protocol information.

For example:

nmap -Pn -p445 --script smb2-security-mode srv01.corp.example

This can help determine SMB signing behaviour.

docs.title: SMB Dialect Enumeration
docs.text:
Nmap:

nmap -Pn -p445 --script smb-protocols srv01.corp.example

This can help identify supported SMB dialects.

docs.title: SMB Encryption
docs.text:
SMB 3 supports encryption.

Conceptually:

SMB Data
   |
   v
Encryption
   |
   v
Network

SMB encryption protects SMB data confidentiality in transit.

docs.title: Signing vs Encryption
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

SMB Signing

with:

SMB Encryption

Signing primarily provides:

Integrity
Authentication Protection

Encryption provides:

Confidentiality

Modern SMB configurations can use both.

docs.title: SMB Share Enumeration
docs.text:
One of the first authenticated SMB activities should normally be:

Enumerate Shares

rather than:

Remote Execution

docs.title: Windows Share Enumeration
docs.text:
Local system:

Get-SmbShare

Traditional command:

net share

docs.title: Remote Share Enumeration
docs.text:
From Windows:

net view \\srv01.corp.example

Depending on permissions and system configuration, this may list accessible shares.

docs.title: NetExec Share Enumeration
docs.text:
nxc smb srv01.corp.example -u 'audit-user' -p 'PASSWORD' --shares

Example conceptual result:

Share        Permissions
-----        -----------
IPC$         READ
Shared       READ
Projects     READ,WRITE

docs.title: smbclient
docs.text:
List available shares:

smbclient -L //srv01.corp.example -U 'CORP/audit-user'

The password can be entered interactively.

This is preferable to placing production passwords directly in shell history.

docs.title: Connect to a Share
docs.text:
smbclient //srv01.corp.example/Shared -U 'CORP/audit-user'

Useful commands inside smbclient include:

ls
cd
pwd
get

Only upload or modify files when explicitly required.

docs.title: Anonymous SMB Access
docs.text:
Some SMB servers may permit:

Anonymous

or:

Guest

access.

Test carefully:

smbclient -L //srv01.corp.example -N

-N means:

No Password

docs.title: Null Sessions
docs.text:
Historically, Windows systems sometimes exposed significant information through:

Null Sessions

Modern Windows environments are generally more restrictive.

However, third-party SMB implementations, appliances and legacy systems may still expose anonymous information.

docs.title: Anonymous Access Is Not Automatically a Vulnerability
docs.text:
If anonymous access exists, determine:

What Is Actually Accessible?

For example:

Public Software Share

may intentionally allow read access.

Whereas:

HR Documents
Credentials
Backups
Configuration Files

would represent a much more serious issue.

docs.title: Common SMB Shares
docs.text:
Typical shares include:

IPC$
ADMIN$
C$
NETLOGON
SYSVOL
Shared
Users
Software
Backups
Projects

docs.title: IPC$
docs.text:
IPC$

is used for inter-process communication and named pipes.

It is frequently involved in:

RPC
Remote Administration
Authentication
Enumeration

docs.title: ADMIN$
docs.text:
ADMIN$

normally maps to the Windows directory.

Typically:

C:\Windows

Access generally requires administrative privileges.

docs.title: C$
docs.text:
C$

is the administrative share for the system drive.

Access generally indicates significant local administrative rights.

docs.title: Administrative Share Model
docs.text:
Administrative Credential
        |
        v
SMB
        |
        +--> ADMIN$
        |
        +--> C$

This can provide:

File Access
File Write
Remote Administration Support

docs.title: NETLOGON
docs.text:
Domain controllers commonly expose:

NETLOGON

The share contains scripts and files associated with domain logon processes.

Example:

\\dc01.corp.example\NETLOGON

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
Domain controllers expose:

SYSVOL

which contains:

Group Policy
Logon Scripts
Domain-Wide Configuration

Example:

\\dc01.corp.example\SYSVOL

docs.title: SYSVOL Security Review
docs.text:
During an authorised assessment, inspect SYSVOL for:

Scripts
Configuration Files
Hardcoded Credentials
Legacy Passwords
Deployment Commands
Mapped Drive Scripts
Software Installation Parameters

docs.title: GPP Passwords
docs.text:
Historically, Group Policy Preferences could expose encrypted passwords through:

cpassword

values in SYSVOL.

See:

GPP Passwords

docs.title: Search SYSVOL
docs.text:
Using smbclient:

smbclient //dc01.corp.example/SYSVOL -U 'CORP/audit-user'

Navigate read-only and inspect relevant files.

docs.title: NetExec SYSVOL Review
docs.text:
NetExec functionality changes between releases.

Inspect available modules:

nxc smb -L

and SMB options:

nxc smb -h

Use only modules relevant to the authorised assessment.

docs.title: Sensitive Files in SMB Shares
docs.text:
Common high-value file types include:

.ps1
.bat
.cmd
.vbs
.xml
.ini
.config
.conf
.txt
.csv
.xlsx
.docx
.kdbx
.rdp
.ppk
.pem
.key
.pfx
.p12

The presence of these files is not itself a vulnerability.

Review:

Content
Permissions
Business Need
Sensitivity

docs.title: Common Credential Indicators
docs.text:
Search authorised copies or accessible shares for terms such as:

password
passwd
pwd
credential
secret
token
apikey
api_key
connectionstring
username
user=
pass=

Avoid downloading large volumes of unrelated user data.

docs.title: Share Permissions
docs.text:
SMB access is controlled by multiple permission layers.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Share Permissions
 |
 v
NTFS Permissions
 |
 v
Effective Access

Both must be considered.

docs.title: Share Permissions vs NTFS Permissions
docs.text:
A user may have:

Share = Full Control

but:

NTFS = Read

Result:

Read

Similarly:

Share = Read
NTFS = Full Control

still results in:

Read

for network access.

The effective access is constrained by both layers.

docs.title: Enumerate Local SMB Shares
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-SmbShare |
    Select-Object Name,Path,Description

docs.title: Review Share Access
docs.text:
Get-SmbShareAccess -Name Shared

Example:

Name    ScopeName AccountName       AccessControlType AccessRight
----    --------- -----------       ----------------- -----------
Shared  *         CORP\Domain Users Allow             Read

docs.title: Review NTFS ACL
docs.text:
Get-Acl 'D:\Shared' |
    Format-List

More focused:

(Get-Acl 'D:\Shared').Access |
    Select-Object IdentityReference,FileSystemRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited

docs.title: Writable Shares
docs.text:
Writable shares are important because they may allow:

File Modification
Script Replacement
Configuration Modification
Software Replacement
Data Tampering

But:

Writable Share

does not automatically mean:

Remote Code Execution

The security impact depends on how files in the share are consumed.

docs.title: Safe Write Testing
docs.text:
If write permission must be validated, use an approved temporary file.

Example from an authorised Windows client:

$path = '\\srv01.corp.example\Shared\write-test.txt'

'Authorised security test' | Set-Content -LiteralPath $path

Test-Path -LiteralPath $path

Remove-Item -LiteralPath $path

Record:

Creation
Verification
Cleanup

Do not overwrite an existing file.

docs.title: Safe smbclient Write Test
docs.text:
If explicitly authorised:

put

can upload a temporary test file.

Use a uniquely named harmless file and remove it immediately after validation.

docs.title: Dangerous Writable Share Patterns
docs.text:
Writable shares become especially important when they contain:

Logon Scripts
Deployment Scripts
Application Binaries
Scheduled Task Scripts
Service Executables
Configuration Files
Web Content
Software Packages
Administrative Tools

docs.title: Example Attack Path
docs.text:
Domain User
    |
    v
Write Access
    |
    v
Deployment Share
    |
    v
Script Executed by Administrators

The real vulnerability is:

Untrusted User Can Modify
Privileged Execution Content

not simply:

SMB Share Is Writable

docs.title: Named Pipes
docs.text:
SMB transports many Windows named pipes.

Examples can include:

svcctl
samr
lsarpc
netlogon
spoolss

Named pipes are used by Windows RPC services and remote administration mechanisms.

docs.title: Named Pipe Model
docs.text:
SMB
 |
 v
IPC$
 |
 v
Named Pipe
 |
 v
RPC Service

This relationship explains why SMB appears in many Windows remote-management techniques.

docs.title: Service Control Manager
docs.text:
The Service Control Manager can be remotely accessed through RPC.

Conceptually:

SMB / RPC
    |
    v
svcctl
    |
    v
Service Control Manager

Administrative access can enable:

Service Enumeration
Service Management
Remote Service Creation

docs.title: PsExec
docs.text:
PsExec-style lateral movement commonly uses:

SMB
+
Administrative Share
+
Service Control Manager

Conceptually:

Attacker
   |
   v
SMB
   |
   v
ADMIN$
   |
   v
Upload Component
   |
   v
SCM
   |
   v
Temporary Service
   |
   v
Execution

docs.title: Impacket PsExec
docs.text:
Check syntax:

impacket-psexec -h

Authorised example:

impacket-psexec 'CORP/audit-admin:PASSWORD@srv01.corp.example'

Prefer password prompting or another secure credential-handling method where supported.

docs.title: PsExec with NTLM Hash
docs.text:
Where pass-the-hash testing is explicitly authorised:

impacket-psexec -hashes ':NTHASH' 'CORP/audit-admin@srv01.corp.example'

See:

Pass-the-Hash

docs.title: PsExec Is Intrusive
docs.text:
PsExec-style execution can create:

Temporary Executable
Temporary Service
Service Events
File Events
Process Events
SMB Events

Do not use it simply because:

Pwn3d!

appears in NetExec output.

docs.title: SMBExec
docs.text:
Impacket also provides:

smbexec

Check syntax:

impacket-smbexec -h

Example:

impacket-smbexec 'CORP/audit-admin:PASSWORD@srv01.corp.example'

Hash authentication:

impacket-smbexec -hashes ':NTHASH' 'CORP/audit-admin@srv01.corp.example'

docs.title: PsExec vs SMBExec
docs.text:
Conceptually:

PsExec
  |
  +--> SMB
  +--> File Transfer
  +--> Service Creation

while:

SMBExec
  |
  +--> SMB
  +--> Service Control
  +--> Command Execution

Exact implementation and artifacts depend on the tool version.

docs.title: ATExec
docs.text:
Impacket:

impacket-atexec -h

Example:

impacket-atexec 'CORP/audit-admin:PASSWORD@srv01.corp.example' 'whoami'

ATExec uses Task Scheduler mechanisms rather than the same service workflow as PsExec.

docs.title: WMIExec
docs.text:
Although WMIExec is primarily a WMI/DCOM technique, SMB may still be involved in retrieving command output depending on tool behaviour.

Check:

impacket-wmiexec -h

Example:

impacket-wmiexec 'CORP/audit-admin:PASSWORD@srv01.corp.example'

docs.title: NetExec Credential Validation
docs.text:
Password:

nxc smb srv01.corp.example -u 'audit-user' -p 'PASSWORD'

Hash:

nxc smb srv01.corp.example -u 'audit-admin' -H 'NTHASH'

docs.title: Target Lists
docs.text:
Prefer:

nxc smb targets.txt -u 'audit-user' -p 'PASSWORD'

over unnecessarily scanning:

Entire Corporate Network

docs.title: Local Accounts
docs.text:
When validating a local account rather than a domain identity, inspect the current NetExec options:

nxc smb -h

Typical versions support:

--local-auth

Example:

nxc smb srv01.corp.example -u 'Administrator' -p 'PASSWORD' --local-auth

docs.title: Domain vs Local Authentication
docs.text:
Domain account:

CORP\audit-user

Local account:

SRV01\Administrator

Always document which security authority owns the account.

docs.title: Pass-the-Hash
docs.text:
SMB is one of the classic protocols associated with:

Pass-the-Hash

Conceptually:

NTLM Hash
    |
    v
NTLM Authentication
    |
    v
SMB

The plaintext password is not required.

See:

Pass-the-Hash

docs.title: Local Administrator Password Reuse
docs.text:
Suppose:

WS01\Administrator

and:

WS02\Administrator

use the same password.

Their NTLM hashes will also match.

This creates:

Compromise WS01
      |
      v
Local Admin Hash
      |
      v
Authenticate to WS02
      |
      v
Lateral Movement

docs.title: Windows LAPS
docs.text:
Windows LAPS mitigates this problem by maintaining unique local administrator passwords.

See:

LAPS

Conceptually:

WS01 -> Password A
WS02 -> Password B
WS03 -> Password C

rather than:

WS01 -> Shared Password
WS02 -> Shared Password
WS03 -> Shared Password

docs.title: SMB and NTLM Relay
docs.text:
SMB is also a major NTLM relay target.

See:

NTLM Relay

The basic path is:

Victim
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Relay Host
  |
  v
SMB Target

docs.title: Relay Requirements
docs.text:
Successful SMB relay depends on multiple conditions, including:

NTLM Authentication Available
Attacker Can Receive Authentication
Target Accepts Relayed Authentication
SMB Signing Not Required
Victim Identity Has Useful Target Rights
Authentication Is Not Reflected Back Improperly
Other Protocol Protections Do Not Block the Path

Do not report:

SMB Signing Not Required

as equivalent to:

Domain Compromise

docs.title: Relay Target Identification
docs.text:
The assessment question is:

Which Hosts Do Not Require SMB Signing?

Then:

Which Identities Could Authenticate?

Then:

What Rights Would Those Identities Have?

docs.title: ntlmrelayx
docs.text:
Impacket provides:

ntlmrelayx

for authorised NTLM relay testing.

Check current syntax:

impacket-ntlmrelayx -h

The complete relay workflow is covered in:

NTLM Relay

docs.title: Authentication Coercion
docs.text:
SMB frequently appears in authentication coercion scenarios.

See:

Authentication Coercion

Conceptually:

Target
  |
  v
Coerced Authentication
  |
  v
Attacker Listener
  |
  v
Relay

docs.title: Responder
docs.text:
Responder can interact with SMB-related authentication during authorised name-resolution and credential-capture testing.

A dedicated page will cover:

docs/active-directory/responder.md

Always distinguish:

Capture

from:

Relay

docs.title: Capture vs Relay
docs.text:
Capture:

Victim
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Attacker
  |
  v
Capture Challenge / Response

Relay:

Victim
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Attacker
  |
  v
Target Service

These are different attack paths.

docs.title: SMB and Domain Controllers
docs.text:
SMB is particularly important on domain controllers because DCs expose:

SYSVOL
NETLOGON
IPC$

and provide RPC services used throughout Active Directory.

docs.title: Do Not Disable SMB on Domain Controllers Blindly
docs.text:
Active Directory relies on SMB functionality.

Hardening should focus on:

SMBv1 Removal
Signing
Encryption Where Appropriate
NTLM Reduction
Firewalling
Least Privilege
Monitoring

rather than simply disabling SMB everywhere.

docs.title: SYSVOL Permissions
docs.text:
SYSVOL should normally be readable by domain users because Group Policy requires access.

Therefore:

Domain Users Can Read SYSVOL

is normally expected.

The security question is:

Can Unauthorised Users Modify Sensitive SYSVOL Content?

docs.title: NETLOGON Permissions
docs.text:
Similarly:

NETLOGON

may legitimately expose logon-related content.

Review the content and modification permissions rather than reporting normal read access as a vulnerability.

docs.title: SMB Enumeration with rpcclient
docs.text:
Samba's:

rpcclient

can communicate with Windows RPC services over SMB.

Example:

rpcclient -U 'CORP/audit-user' dc01.corp.example

Enter the password interactively.

docs.title: rpcclient Commands
docs.text:
Depending on permissions, useful read-only commands may include:

srvinfo
enumdomusers
enumdomgroups
querydominfo

Modern Active Directory environments may restrict some enumeration.

docs.title: rpcclient Anonymous Test
docs.text:
Where anonymous SMB/RPC access is in scope:

rpcclient -U '' -N dc01.corp.example

Do not assume anonymous connection means useful information is exposed.

docs.title: enum4linux-ng
docs.text:
enum4linux-ng can automate SMB/RPC enumeration.

Check:

enum4linux-ng -h

Example:

enum4linux-ng -A srv01.corp.example

Use authenticated enumeration where appropriate rather than relying only on anonymous access.

docs.title: NetExec Host Information
docs.text:
A basic NetExec SMB connection may reveal:

Hostname
Domain
Operating System
SMB Signing
SMB Version

depending on target and tool version.

Example:

nxc smb srv01.corp.example

docs.title: SMB Session Enumeration
docs.text:
On a Windows SMB server:

Get-SmbSession

This can show active SMB client sessions.

Useful properties include:

ClientComputerName
ClientUserName
NumOpens
Dialect
Encrypted
Signed

depending on Windows version.

docs.title: SMB Open Files
docs.text:
Administrators can inspect open SMB files:

Get-SmbOpenFile

This can provide useful defensive visibility.

docs.title: SMB Connections on Client
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-SmbConnection

This can reveal:

ServerName
ShareName
UserName
Dialect
Signed
Encrypted

depending on system version.

docs.title: Windows net use
docs.text:
Existing network connections:

net use

Connect to a share:

net use \\srv01.corp.example\Shared

Disconnect:

net use \\srv01.corp.example\Shared /delete

docs.title: Explicit Credentials
docs.text:
Windows can establish an SMB connection using explicit credentials.

Avoid placing sensitive passwords directly into command history when alternatives are available.

PowerShell:

$cred = Get-Credential

For administrative scripting, use secure credential-management mechanisms rather than embedding passwords in scripts.

docs.title: SMB Credential Conflicts
docs.text:
Windows may return errors when multiple connections to the same server are attempted using different credentials.

Review existing sessions:

net use

Remove only your own test connection when necessary.

Do not disrupt legitimate user mappings.

docs.title: SMB Enumeration with PowerShell
docs.text:
Remote share discovery can also use CIM or management interfaces where authorised.

However, do not assume that:

SMB Access

automatically grants:

Remote WMI

or:

WinRM

Each management protocol has its own authorisation requirements.

docs.title: SMB and Firewalling
docs.text:
SMB should generally not be exposed:

Internet -> TCP 445

unless an exceptional architecture specifically requires and securely protects it.

Internally, access should also be restricted.

docs.title: East-West SMB
docs.text:
A common weak architecture is:

WS01
 |
 +--> WS02:445
 |
 +--> WS03:445
 |
 +--> WS04:445

This creates unnecessary workstation-to-workstation lateral-movement opportunities.

docs.title: Better Workstation Segmentation
docs.text:
Where operationally possible:

WS01
 |
 X
 |
 v
WS02:445

Peer workstation SMB administration should be restricted.

docs.title: Server Administration
docs.text:
A stronger model is:

Privileged Admin Workstation
          |
          v
Management Network
          |
          v
Server:445

rather than:

Any Workstation
      |
      v
Server:445

docs.title: SMB Hardening
docs.text:
A practical SMB hardening strategy includes:

Disable SMBv1
Require SMB Signing Where Appropriate
Use SMB Encryption Where Appropriate
Restrict TCP 445
Reduce NTLM
Deploy Windows LAPS
Remove Credential Reuse
Apply Least Privilege
Restrict Administrative Shares
Monitor Remote Service Creation
Protect Privileged Accounts

docs.title: SMBv1
docs.text:
Verify:

Get-SmbServerConfiguration |
    Select-Object EnableSMB1Protocol

Expected modern configuration:

False

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
Review:

Get-SmbServerConfiguration |
    Select-Object EnableSecuritySignature,RequireSecuritySignature

The desired configuration depends on Windows version, organisational requirements and compatibility.

For systems where relay resistance is required:

Require Signing

is the important property.

docs.title: SMB Encryption
docs.text:
Review:

Get-SmbServerConfiguration |
    Select-Object EncryptData,RejectUnencryptedAccess

Do not enable organisation-wide encryption without considering compatibility and performance.

docs.title: NTLM Reduction
docs.text:
SMB hardening should form part of a broader:

NTLM Reduction

strategy.

See:

NTLM

docs.title: Local Administrator Passwords
docs.text:
Deploy:

Windows LAPS

to reduce reusable local administrator credentials.

See:

LAPS

docs.title: Administrative Rights
docs.text:
Review membership of:

Administrators

on servers and workstations.

Avoid broad groups such as:

Domain Users
Authenticated Users
Large Helpdesk Groups

having unnecessary administrative access.

docs.title: Share Permissions
docs.text:
Review shares for:

Everyone
Authenticated Users
Domain Users
Anonymous
Guest

permissions.

These principals are not automatically inappropriate.

The decision depends on:

Share Purpose
Data Sensitivity
Write Capability
Execution Context

docs.title: Everyone Read
docs.text:
Example:

Everyone -> Read

may be acceptable for:

Public Software Distribution

but inappropriate for:

HR
Finance
Backups
Secrets
Administrative Scripts

docs.title: Everyone Write
docs.text:
Broad write access deserves much closer review.

Especially dangerous:

Everyone -> Modify

on content later executed by:

Administrator
SYSTEM
Deployment Service
Scheduled Task

docs.title: Detection - Logon Events
docs.text:
SMB authentication commonly creates:

4624

successful logon events.

Network logons commonly use:

Logon Type 3

docs.title: Failed Authentication
docs.text:
Failed SMB authentication can generate:

4625

Repeated failures may indicate:

Password Spraying
Credential Guessing
Stale Credentials
Misconfigured Services

docs.title: Explicit Credentials
docs.text:
Event:

4648

can indicate use of explicit credentials in relevant Windows authentication workflows.

docs.title: Special Privileges
docs.text:
Event:

4672

may occur when a privileged account receives special privileges during logon.

docs.title: Share Access Auditing
docs.text:
Windows can audit network share access.

Relevant events include:

5140
5145

docs.title: Event 5140
docs.text:
5140

indicates that a network share object was accessed.

Useful fields can include:

Account Name
Source Address
Share Name

docs.title: Event 5145
docs.text:
5145

can provide detailed share-access checks.

This can help identify access to:

ADMIN$
C$
Sensitive Shares

docs.title: Service Creation
docs.text:
PsExec-style lateral movement may generate:

7045

for service installation.

With suitable auditing:

4697

may also provide service-installation visibility.

docs.title: File Creation
docs.text:
Monitor unexpected executable or script creation in:

ADMIN$
C$
Windows
Temp
ProgramData

especially when correlated with remote SMB access.

docs.title: Named Pipe Detection
docs.text:
EDR products may provide visibility into unusual named-pipe activity.

Named-pipe telemetry should be correlated with:

Source Host
Account
Process
Remote Connection
Service Creation

docs.title: Detect Administrative Share Access
docs.text:
High-value pattern:

User Workstation
       |
       v
ADMIN$
       |
       v
Server

Ask whether the source system is an approved administrative workstation.

docs.title: SMB Relay Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

Unexpected NTLM Authentication
Unusual Source Systems
Authentication to Systems Not Normally Used
SMB Connections Following Coercion Activity
Privileged Machine Account Authentication

Detection should be correlated with:

NTLM Relay

and:

Authentication Coercion

docs.title: Network Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

445/TCP

for unusual:

East-West Connections
Workstation-to-Workstation SMB
User VLAN-to-Server SMB
High Fan-Out Authentication

docs.title: High Fan-Out SMB
docs.text:
Example:

WS01
 |
 +--> SRV01
 +--> SRV02
 +--> SRV03
 +--> SRV04
 +--> SRV05

within a short period may indicate:

Enumeration
Credential Validation
Lateral Movement

although legitimate management tools can create similar patterns.

docs.title: Baseline Administrative Systems
docs.text:
Defenders should know which systems legitimately generate large amounts of SMB administration traffic.

Examples:

SCCM
Backup Servers
Software Deployment
Monitoring
Patch Management
Administrative Jump Hosts

docs.title: Reporting SMB Findings
docs.text:
Avoid reporting:

Port 445 Open

as a vulnerability by itself.

SMB is required for many Windows and Active Directory functions.

Report the actual weakness.

Examples:

SMBv1 Enabled

SMB Signing Not Required

Shared Local Administrator Credentials Permit SMB Lateral Movement

Sensitive SMB Share Accessible to Unauthorised Users

Unprivileged Users Can Modify Privileged Deployment Scripts

Workstation Network Can Reach Administrative SMB Services on Servers

docs.title: Example Finding - SMB Signing
docs.text:
Finding:
SMB Signing Is Not Required on Multiple Windows Systems

Description:
Multiple Windows systems accepted SMB connections without requiring
SMB message signing.

SMB signing provides integrity protection for SMB sessions and is an
important mitigation against NTLM relay attacks targeting SMB.

The identified systems may therefore be usable as SMB relay targets if
an attacker can obtain or coerce suitable NTLM authentication from an
identity with useful privileges on those systems.

Impact:
An attacker positioned to receive NTLM authentication may be able to
relay that authentication to an affected SMB service.

The actual impact depends on the privileges of the relayed identity and
the availability of other relay prerequisites.

Recommendation:
Require SMB signing on systems where compatible with the organisation's
Windows environment and security baseline.

Prioritise domain controllers, servers and administrative systems.

In addition, reduce NTLM usage, restrict SMB network access and address
authentication-coercion paths.

docs.title: Example Finding - Sensitive Share
docs.text:
Finding:
Sensitive Information Exposed Through Excessive SMB Share Permissions

Affected Host:
files01.corp.example

Affected Share:
Finance

Description:
The tested standard domain user could access files within the Finance
SMB share despite having no documented business requirement for this
access.

The accessible content included information classified as sensitive by
the organisation.

Impact:
Any compromised standard domain account with equivalent permissions
could access the affected information through SMB.

Recommendation:
Review both share-level and NTFS permissions and restrict access to the
minimum groups required for the business function.

Periodically review share permissions and remove stale or overly broad
group assignments.

docs.title: Example Finding - Writable Deployment Share
docs.text:
Finding:
Unprivileged Users Can Modify Files Used by Privileged Deployment Process

Affected Host:
deploy01.corp.example

Affected Share:
Software

Description:
Standard domain users had modification rights to files within an SMB
share used by an administrative software deployment process.

Files from the share are subsequently accessed or executed by systems
operating with elevated privileges.

Impact:
An attacker compromising a standard domain account could potentially
modify deployment content and influence code or configuration consumed
by privileged systems.

This may provide a path from a low-privileged domain account to
privileged code execution depending on the deployment workflow.

Recommendation:
Restrict modification rights to dedicated deployment administrators and
service identities.

Separate read-only software distribution paths from administrative
staging locations and implement integrity validation for deployed
content.

docs.title: Example Finding - Local Administrator Reuse
docs.text:
Finding:
Shared Local Administrator Credentials Enable SMB Lateral Movement

Description:
The same local administrator credential was valid on multiple Windows
systems.

The credential provided administrative SMB access to more than one
approved test endpoint.

Impact:
Compromise of one affected endpoint may expose reusable administrative
credentials that permit lateral movement to other systems.

Recommendation:
Deploy Windows LAPS or another centrally managed mechanism providing
unique local administrator passwords per endpoint.

Restrict remote SMB administration between peer systems and monitor
administrative share access.

docs.title: Evidence Checklist
docs.text:
Record:

Target Host
Target IP
Domain
Operating System
SMB Port
SMB Dialect
SMBv1 Status
Signing Supported
Signing Required
Encryption
Authentication Protocol
Account
Account Type
Accessible Shares
Share Permissions
NTFS Permissions
Anonymous Access
Guest Access
Administrative Share Access
Sensitive Files
Write Access
Remote Administration Rights

Timestamp
Commands Used

Never place:

NTLM Hashes
Private Keys
Sensitive File Contents

directly into a report unless strictly necessary and appropriately protected.

docs.title: SMB Testing Model
docs.text:
The protocol model is:

Client
  |
  v
TCP 445
  |
  v
SMB

The authentication model is:

Domain Identity
      |
      +--> Kerberos
      |
      +--> NTLM
      |
      v
SMB Server

The Kerberos model is:

User
 |
 v
KDC
 |
 v
cifs/server
 |
 v
SMB

The share model is:

Authenticated User
       |
       v
Share Permission
       |
       v
NTFS Permission
       |
       v
Effective Access

The administrative model is:

Administrator
      |
      v
SMB
      |
      +--> ADMIN$
      |
      +--> C$
      |
      +--> IPC$
      |
      v
Remote Administration

The PsExec model is:

Administrative SMB
       |
       v
ADMIN$
       |
       v
Service Control Manager
       |
       v
Temporary Service
       |
       v
Execution

The Pass-the-Hash model is:

NTLM Hash
    |
    v
NTLM Authentication
    |
    v
SMB
    |
    v
Remote Host

The relay model is:

Victim
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Attacker
  |
  v
Unsigned SMB Target

The signing model is:

SMB Signing Required
        |
        v
Message Must Be Signed
        |
        v
Classic SMB Relay Restricted

The sensitive-share model is:

Domain User
    |
    v
SMB Share
    |
    v
Sensitive File

The writable-share model is:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Writable SMB Share
       |
       v
Privileged Script / Binary
       |
       v
Privileged Execution

The lateral-movement model is:

Compromised Host
      |
      v
Reusable Credential
      |
      v
SMB
      |
      v
Second Host
      |
      v
Administrative Access

The defensive model is:

SMBv1 Disabled
      +
SMB Signing
      +
NTLM Reduction
      +
Unique Local Credentials
      +
Least Privilege
      +
Network Segmentation
      +
Monitoring
      =
Reduced SMB Attack Surface

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Can I get a shell through SMB?"

Ask:
"What access does this identity have
through SMB, and what security boundary
does that access cross?"

For defenders:

Do Not Ask:
"Is port 445 open?"

Ask:
"Who can authenticate to SMB,
what can they access, is signing required,
and which systems are allowed to administer
each other?"

The complete SMB relationship is:

Identity
   |
   v
Kerberos / NTLM
   |
   v
SMB
   |
   +--> Shares
   |
   +--> Files
   |
   +--> Named Pipes
   |
   +--> Administrative Shares
   |
   +--> Remote Administration
   |
   v
Potential Lateral Movement

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
SMB should not be treated simply as:

Port 445

It is a major Windows infrastructure protocol connecting:

Authentication
File Access
RPC
Administration
Group Policy
Domain Services

The most useful SMB assessment sequence is:

Discover SMB
     |
     v
Determine Version
     |
     v
Check Signing
     |
     v
Determine Authentication
     |
     v
Enumerate Shares
     |
     v
Review Permissions
     |
     v
Identify Sensitive Access
     |
     v
Determine Administrative Rights
     |
     v
Assess Lateral Movement

For many assessments, the most important SMB questions are:

Is SMBv1 enabled?

Is SMB signing required?

Is NTLM still accepted?

Which shares can this user access?

Which shares can this user modify?

Can this identity access ADMIN$ or C$?

Are local administrator credentials reused?

Can workstations directly administer each other?

Can an attacker relay authentication to this host?

Do not assume:

SMB Signing Not Required
=
Immediate Compromise

The complete relay chain still requires:

Authentication Source
       +
Relay-Compatible Target
       +
Useful Victim Privileges

Similarly:

Writable Share

does not automatically mean:

Code Execution

The critical question is:

Who Consumes the Writable Content?

A writable public-document share may have limited security impact.

A writable share containing:

SYSTEM Deployment Script

may provide a serious privilege-escalation path.

For lateral movement, SMB frequently becomes dangerous when combined with:

Reusable Administrative Credentials

because:

Compromise One Host
      |
      v
Recover Local Admin Credential
      |
      v
Credential Reused
      |
      v
Authenticate Through SMB
      |
      v
Compromise Additional Hosts

Windows LAPS, administrative separation and network segmentation can significantly reduce this blast radius.

During authorised testing, begin with:

Read-Only Enumeration

and escalate validation only when necessary.

If:

ADMIN$ Access

already proves administrative access, a remote shell may provide little additional evidence.

The purpose of SMB testing is not to execute as many remote administration techniques as possible.

It is to determine:

Identity
   |
   v
SMB Access
   |
   v
Effective Permission
   |
   v
Security Impact

and provide the organisation with a clear explanation of how to reduce that attack path.

The next page examines another major Windows remote-management protocol:

WinRM

docs.title: Active Directory Trust Relationships
docs.text:
Active Directory trust relationships define how authentication can cross domain and forest boundaries.

The general trust model is:

Identity
   |
   v
Source Domain
   |
   v
Trust Relationship
   |
   v
Target Domain
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Authorisation
   |
   v
Resource

Trust relationships are commonly encountered in environments containing:

Parent and Child Domains
Multiple Domain Trees
Multiple Forests
Mergers and Acquisitions
Legacy Domains
Partner Organisations
Resource Forests
Migration Environments
Kerberos Realms

Understanding the existence of a trust is only the beginning.

A complete assessment should determine:

Source
Target
Direction
Type
Transitivity
Authentication Scope
SID Filtering
Trust Attributes
Foreign Principals
Cross-Domain Groups
Cross-Domain ACLs
Network Reachability
Actual Resource Access

Authorised testing only

Discovering a trusted domain or forest does not automatically place that environment within the penetration-testing scope. Treat every newly discovered domain, forest and organisation as a separate scope boundary until the rules of engagement explicitly confirm otherwise.

docs.title: Trust Relationships at a Glance
docs.text:
Suppose two domains exist:

CORP.EXAMPLE
PARTNER.EXAMPLE

A trust might connect them:

CORP.EXAMPLE
      |
      | Trust
      |
      v
PARTNER.EXAMPLE

But the security implications depend on:

Who Trusts Whom?
Is It One-Way or Two-Way?
Is It Transitive?
Is It Intra-Forest or Cross-Forest?
Is Selective Authentication Enabled?
Is SID Filtering Applied?
Which Foreign Principals Have Permissions?

docs.title: Trusting and Trusted Domains
docs.text:
Trust terminology can initially appear backwards.

If:

DOMAIN-A
trusts
DOMAIN-B

then:

DOMAIN-A
=
Trusting Domain

and:

DOMAIN-B
=
Trusted Domain

DOMAIN-A accepts authentication originating from DOMAIN-B.

docs.title: Authentication Direction
docs.text:
Therefore:

DOMAIN-A trusts DOMAIN-B

allows the relationship:

DOMAIN-B User
      |
      v
DOMAIN-A Resource

subject to authorisation.

A useful mental model is:

Trust Arrow:
Resource Domain -> Identity Domain

Potential Access:
Identity Domain -> Resource Domain

docs.title: One-Way Trust
docs.text:
A one-way trust establishes trust in one direction.

Example:

CORP.EXAMPLE
      |
      | trusts
      v
PARTNER.EXAMPLE

The potential authentication path is:

PARTNER.EXAMPLE\User
          |
          v
CORP.EXAMPLE\Resource

CORP trusts identities from PARTNER.

PARTNER does not automatically trust identities from CORP.

docs.title: Two-Way Trust
docs.text:
A two-way trust establishes both directions:

CORP.EXAMPLE
      <---->
PARTNER.EXAMPLE

Potential authentication relationships exist in both directions:

CORP User
    |
    v
PARTNER Resource

and:

PARTNER User
      |
      v
CORP Resource

Actual access still depends on authorisation.

docs.title: Trust Direction from the Querying Domain
docs.text:
Tools commonly report:

Inbound
Outbound
Bidirectional

The meaning must be interpreted relative to the domain being queried.

This is one of the most important details to record correctly during trust enumeration.

docs.title: Inbound Trust
docs.text:
From the perspective of the current domain, an inbound trust generally means that the current domain trusts identities from the other domain.

Conceptually:

Other Domain
     |
     | Identity
     v
Current Domain

Foreign identities may therefore be able to access resources in the current domain if authorised.

docs.title: Outbound Trust
docs.text:
From the perspective of the current domain, an outbound trust generally means the other domain trusts the current domain.

Conceptually:

Current Domain
     |
     | Identity
     v
Other Domain

Users from the current domain may therefore be accepted by the other domain.

docs.title: Bidirectional Trust
docs.text:
A bidirectional trust combines both relationships:

Current Domain
      <---->
Other Domain

docs.title: Why Direction Matters
docs.text:
Suppose an assessment identifies:

CORP.EXAMPLE

and:

ADMIN.EXAMPLE

A trust exists.

That alone does not answer:

Can CORP users access ADMIN resources?

The direction must first be understood.

docs.title: Trust Type
docs.text:
Trust relationships also have a type.

Common Active Directory relationships include:

Parent-Child
Tree-Root
Shortcut
External
Forest
Realm

The type affects:

Transitivity
Scope
Authentication
Security Boundary
SID Filtering

docs.title: Parent-Child Relationships
docs.text:
A child domain automatically establishes a trust with its parent.

Example:

corp.example
     |
     v
emea.corp.example

The relationship is normally:

Two-Way
Transitive
Intra-Forest

docs.title: Parent-Child Authentication
docs.text:
Conceptually:

emea.corp.example
        |
        v
corp.example

and:

corp.example
        |
        v
emea.corp.example

can use the forest's trust infrastructure for authentication referrals.

docs.title: Tree-Root Relationships
docs.text:
A forest can contain multiple domain trees.

Example:

             Forest
               |
       +-------+-------+
       |               |
corp.example      services.example

The root domains of separate trees within the same forest have a:

Tree-Root Trust

which is normally:

Two-Way
Transitive

docs.title: Shortcut Trusts
docs.text:
Large forests may contain long authentication paths.

Example:

Domain A
   |
   v
Domain B
   |
   v
Domain C
   |
   v
Domain D

A shortcut trust may be created:

Domain A
   |
   +------------------+
                      |
                      v
                   Domain D

This can reduce the Kerberos referral path.

docs.title: External Trusts
docs.text:
An external trust connects specific domains without establishing a forest-wide relationship.

Example:

CORP.EXAMPLE
      |
      | External Trust
      |
      v
LEGACY.EXAMPLE

External trusts are generally:

Non-Transitive

docs.title: Forest Trusts
docs.text:
A forest trust connects two Active Directory forests.

Forest A
   |
   | Forest Trust
   |
   v
Forest B

Forest trusts can be:

One-Way
Two-Way

and are important because they connect separate Active Directory security boundaries.

docs.title: Realm Trusts
docs.text:
Realm trusts connect Active Directory to a non-Windows Kerberos realm.

Active Directory
       |
       v
Realm Trust
       |
       v
Kerberos Realm

Realm trusts may be:

One-Way
Two-Way
Transitive
Non-Transitive

depending on configuration.

docs.title: Transitivity
docs.text:
Transitivity determines whether the trust relationship can extend through additional domains.

Consider:

Domain A
   |
   v
Domain B
   |
   v
Domain C

If the relevant relationships are transitive, authentication relationships may extend beyond the directly connected pair.

docs.title: Transitive Trust
docs.text:
Conceptually:

A trusts B
B trusts C

may allow a trust path involving:

A
|
B
|
C

depending on the trust types and forest topology.

docs.title: Non-Transitive Trust
docs.text:
With a non-transitive relationship:

A trusts B

does not automatically mean:

A trusts domains trusted by B

This can significantly reduce the trust scope.

docs.title: Intra-Forest Relationships
docs.text:
Domains within the same forest have particularly strong relationships.

Common intra-forest trusts include:

Parent-Child
Tree-Root
Shortcut

docs.title: Forest Security Boundary
docs.text:
A critical Active Directory principle is:

Forest
=
Primary Security Boundary

Domains within a forest should not normally be treated as independent security boundaries against a sufficiently privileged compromise elsewhere in that forest.

docs.title: Domain Boundary vs Forest Boundary
docs.text:
A domain provides important:

Administrative
Policy
Replication
Naming

boundaries.

However:

Domain
!=
Strong Isolation Boundary

within the same forest.

docs.title: Cross-Forest Relationship
docs.text:
A trust between forests is different:

Forest A
   |
   v
Trust Boundary
   |
   v
Forest B

Security controls such as:

SID Filtering
Selective Authentication
Network Segmentation
Separate Administration

become particularly important.

docs.title: Trust Relationship Enumeration
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Current Domain
      |
      v
Current Forest
      |
      v
Known Domains
      |
      v
Trust Objects
      |
      v
Direction
      |
      v
Type
      |
      v
Transitivity
      |
      v
Security Attributes
      |
      v
Foreign Principals
      |
      v
Actual Access

docs.title: Current Domain
docs.text:
Using the ActiveDirectory PowerShell module:

Get-ADDomain

Useful properties include:

DNSRoot
NetBIOSName
DomainSID
Forest
ParentDomain
ChildDomains
DomainMode

docs.title: Current Forest
docs.text:
Get-ADForest

Useful properties include:

Name
RootDomain
Domains
GlobalCatalogs
ForestMode
DomainNamingMaster
SchemaMaster

docs.title: Enumerate Forest Domains
docs.text: Get-ADForest | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Domains

docs.title: Native Windows Trust Enumeration
docs.text:
nltest.exe provides native trust enumeration.

nltest /domain_trusts

For broader trust information:

nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts

docs.title: ActiveDirectory Module
docs.text:
Enumerate trusts:

Get-ADTrust -Filter *

Focused output:

Get-ADTrust -Filter * |
    Select-Object Name,Source,Target,Direction,TrustType,ForestTransitive,IntraForest,SelectiveAuthentication

docs.title: Query a Specific Relationship
docs.text:
Get-ADTrust -Identity 'partner.example'

This is useful when investigating one known relationship.

docs.title: Trust Object Properties
docs.text:
Important properties can include:

Source
Target
Direction
TrustType
ForestTransitive
IntraForest
SelectiveAuthentication
SIDFilteringForestAware
SIDFilteringQuarantined

The exact properties available depend on the environment and tooling.

docs.title: PowerView Trust Enumeration
docs.text:
PowerView versions commonly provide functions such as:

Get-DomainTrust

Check first:

Get-Command Get-DomainTrust -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If available:

Get-DomainTrust

docs.title: Trust Mapping with PowerView
docs.text:
Some PowerView versions provide:

Get-DomainTrustMapping

Verify before use:

Get-Command Get-DomainTrustMapping -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Then:

Get-DomainTrustMapping

Do not allow automated mapping to extend testing into out-of-scope domains.

docs.title: LDAP Trust Enumeration
docs.text:
Trusts are represented by:

trustedDomain

objects.

They are commonly stored under:

CN=System

in the domain naming context.

docs.title: LDAP Example
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
  -D 'audituser@corp.example' -W \
  -b 'CN=System,DC=corp,DC=example' \
  '(objectClass=trustedDomain)' \
  cn flatName trustPartner trustDirection trustType trustAttributes securityIdentifier

docs.title: Trusted Domain Object
docs.text:
A trustedDomain object may contain:

cn
flatName
trustPartner
trustDirection
trustType
trustAttributes
securityIdentifier

These values can be used to reconstruct the relationship.

docs.title: trustPartner
docs.text:
trustPartner identifies the DNS name associated with the trusted domain.

Example:

partner.example

docs.title: flatName
docs.text:
flatName commonly represents the NetBIOS-style name.

Example:

PARTNER

docs.title: securityIdentifier
docs.text:
The:

securityIdentifier

attribute can identify the SID associated with the trusted domain.

This can be useful when interpreting:

Foreign Security Principals
SIDHistory
Cross-Domain ACLs

docs.title: trustDirection
docs.text:
Common numeric values are:

0 = Disabled
1 = Inbound
2 = Outbound
3 = Bidirectional

Always interpret them relative to the domain containing the trustedDomain object.

docs.title: trustType
docs.text:
Common values include:

1 = Downlevel / legacy Windows trust
2 = Active Directory trust
3 = MIT Kerberos realm

Trust type should be interpreted together with:

trustAttributes

rather than in isolation.

docs.title: trustAttributes
docs.text:
trustAttributes is a bit field.

Depending on configuration, flags can represent characteristics such as:

Non-Transitive
Uplevel
Quarantined Domain
Forest Transitive
Cross Organisation
Within Forest
Treat As External
Uses RC4 Encryption
Cross Organisation No TGT Delegation
PIM Trust

Multiple flags may be present simultaneously.

docs.title: Do Not Guess Trust Attributes
docs.text:
Instead of manually interpreting an unfamiliar decimal value during an assessment:

Record Raw Value
      |
      v
Decode Flags
      |
      v
Confirm with Additional Tooling

Use multiple data sources where practical.

docs.title: LDAP and PowerShell Correlation
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Get-ADTrust
     |
     v
High-Level Relationship
     |
     v
LDAP trustedDomain
     |
     v
Underlying Attributes

This provides both:

Readable Interpretation

and:

Raw Directory Data

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec can help establish:

Domain
Hostname
Authentication Context

during broader Active Directory enumeration.

Check current options:

nxc ldap -h

A basic LDAP authentication check against an authorised DC may look like:

nxc ldap dc01.corp.example -u 'audituser' -p 'PASSWORD'

Use password prompting or other protected credential handling where practical.

docs.title: BloodHound Trust Mapping
docs.text:
BloodHound is particularly useful because a trust should rarely be analysed by itself.

See:

BloodHound

The more useful graph is often:

Trust
  +
Group Membership
  +
ACL
  +
Session
  +
Administrative Rights

docs.title: BloodHound Relationship Model
docs.text:
Example:

PARTNER\User
      |
      v
PARTNER\Helpdesk
      |
      v
CORP\Server-Support
      |
      v
AdminTo
      |
      v
CORP\APP01

The important finding is not simply:

PARTNER trusts CORP

but the resulting privilege path.

docs.title: Foreign Security Principals
docs.text:
Foreign identities referenced in another domain can be represented by:

ForeignSecurityPrincipal

objects.

These commonly exist under:

CN=ForeignSecurityPrincipals

docs.title: Foreign Principal Model
docs.text:
Foreign Domain
      |
      v
Foreign SID
      |
      v
ForeignSecurityPrincipal
      |
      v
Local Domain Group
      |
      v
Permission

docs.title: Enumerate Foreign Security Principals
docs.text:
Example:

Get-ADObject `
    -SearchBase 'CN=ForeignSecurityPrincipals,DC=corp,DC=example' `
    -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=foreignSecurityPrincipal)' `
    -Properties objectSid

This is read-only enumeration.

docs.title: Resolve Foreign SIDs
docs.text:
A foreign principal may initially appear as:

S-1-5-21-...

Resolution may require communication with the domain responsible for that SID.

Do not query an out-of-scope trusted domain merely to resolve the identity.

docs.title: Cross-Domain Group Membership
docs.text:
One of the highest-value trust checks is:

Foreign Principal
      |
      v
Local Group
      |
      v
Privilege

docs.title: Domain Local Groups
docs.text:
Domain Local groups are particularly important because they can grant permissions to resources in the local domain while containing identities from trusted domains.

Example:

PARTNER\App-Team
        |
        v
CORP\App-Server-Admins
        |
        v
APP01

docs.title: Enumerate Group Membership
docs.text:
For an authorised group:

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'App-Server-Admins'

Recursive:

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'App-Server-Admins' -Recursive

Investigate unexpected foreign identities.

docs.title: Universal Groups
docs.text:
Universal groups can span domains within a forest.

This creates paths such as:

Domain A Global Group
        |
        v
Universal Group
        |
        v
Domain B Domain Local Group
        |
        v
Permission

docs.title: AGDLP
docs.text:
A common permissions model is:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

or:

A -> G -> DL -> P

docs.title: AGUDLP
docs.text:
Multi-domain environments may use:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Universal Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

or:

A -> G -> U -> DL -> P

Trust assessment should therefore follow nested group relationships rather than looking only for direct assignments.

docs.title: Cross-Domain ACLs
docs.text:
Foreign principals can also appear directly in Active Directory ACLs.

Example:

PARTNER\Helpdesk
       |
       v
GenericWrite
       |
       v
CORP\ServiceAccount

See:

ACL and ACE

docs.title: Cross-Domain ACL Model
docs.text:
Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Trust
      |
      v
Directory ACL
      |
      v
Object Control

This can create a privilege path without any obvious foreign membership in a privileged group.

docs.title: Local Group Relationships
docs.text:
Foreign groups can also be members of local Windows groups.

Example:

PARTNER\ServerAdmins
          |
          v
APP01\Administrators

This can provide direct administrative access to the target.

docs.title: Enumerate Local Administrators
docs.text:
Where authorised on the target:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'

Look for:

Foreign Domain Users
Foreign Domain Groups
Unexpected Domain Groups

docs.title: Trust Authentication
docs.text:
A trust primarily enables authentication.

Authorisation remains separate.

Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Trust
      |
      v
Authenticated
      |
      v
ACL / Group
      |
      v
Authorised?

docs.title: Kerberos Referrals
docs.text:
Kerberos commonly handles cross-domain authentication using referrals.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Source KDC
 |
 v
Referral TGT
 |
 v
Target KDC
 |
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Service

docs.title: Example Referral Path
docs.text:
Suppose:

alice@EMEA.CORP.EXAMPLE

requests access to:

cifs/files01.corp.example

The source KDC may provide a referral toward:

CORP.EXAMPLE

The destination KDC can then issue the required service ticket if authentication and trust requirements are satisfied.

docs.title: Inspect Tickets
docs.text:
Windows:

klist

Linux:

klist

Cross-domain authentication may result in referral-related tickets appearing in the cache.

See:

Kerberos Tickets

docs.title: DNS Requirements
docs.text:
Trust relationships depend heavily on working name resolution.

Cross-domain DNS may use:

Conditional Forwarders
Stub Zones
Delegation
Forest-Wide DNS
Other Enterprise DNS Integration

docs.title: Query Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Linux:

dig _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.partner.example SRV

Kerberos:

dig _kerberos._tcp.partner.example SRV

Windows:

Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV '_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.partner.example'

Only perform remote-domain queries when within scope.

docs.title: Network Requirements
docs.text:
A correctly configured trust can still be unusable if network communication is blocked.

The complete model is:

Trust
  +
DNS
  +
Network Reachability
  +
Authentication
  +
Authorisation
  =
Resource Access

docs.title: Trust Without Network Reachability
docs.text:
Example:

Forest A
   |
   | Trust
   |
Forest B

Workstation A
     |
     X
     |
Server B

The trust exists, but the workstation cannot reach the remote service.

This can be an effective security control.

docs.title: Selective Authentication
docs.text:
Selective authentication adds another security decision to cross-boundary authentication.

Without selective authentication:

Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Trust
      |
      v
Resource Authentication

With selective authentication:

Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Trust
      |
      v
Allowed to Authenticate?
      |
      +--> No
      |
      +--> Yes
             |
             v
      Resource Authentication

docs.title: Enumerate Selective Authentication
docs.text:
Get-ADTrust -Filter * |
    Select-Object Name,Direction,SelectiveAuthentication

docs.title: Allowed to Authenticate
docs.text:
When selective authentication is enabled, foreign identities require appropriate:

Allowed to authenticate

rights on the relevant computer or service security principal.

This limits where foreign users may authenticate.

docs.title: Selective Authentication Benefit
docs.text:
Instead of:

Partner Forest
      |
      v
Authenticate to Entire Corporate Forest

the environment can move toward:

Partner Forest
      |
      v
Approved Application Servers Only

docs.title: SID Filtering
docs.text:
SID filtering protects trust boundaries from inappropriate SID information crossing the relationship.

Conceptually:

Incoming Token
     |
     v
SID Filtering
     |
     +--> Permitted SID
     |
     X
     |
     +--> Filtered SID

docs.title: Why SID Filtering Matters
docs.text:
An access token can contain multiple SIDs.

These may include:

Primary SID
Group SIDs
SIDHistory

The receiving environment must determine which SID information is valid across the trust boundary.

docs.title: SIDHistory
docs.text:
SIDHistory supports migrations by allowing a new account to retain an old SID.

Example:

New Account
SID: NEW-SID

SIDHistory:
OLD-SID

An existing ACL referencing:

OLD-SID

can continue to authorise the migrated account.

docs.title: SIDHistory and Trust Relationships
docs.text:
Trust analysis should therefore ask:

Is SIDHistory Present?

Why Is It Present?

Is It Migration Related?

Is It Still Required?

How Does SID Filtering Treat It?

The dedicated page covers this in more detail:

Active Directory SID History

docs.title: Trust Relationships and SID Filtering
docs.text:
Different trust types can have different SID-filtering behaviour.

Do not make assumptions based only on:

External

or:

Forest

labels.

Inspect the actual:

Trust Attributes
SID Filtering State
Migration Requirements

docs.title: Trust Attributes and Security
docs.text:
Trust attributes can materially alter security behaviour.

Examples include characteristics related to:

Forest Transitivity
SID Filtering
Treat-As-External
TGT Delegation
PIM Trust
Encryption Compatibility

These settings should be documented during high-value trust assessments.

docs.title: Treat-As-External
docs.text:
A forest trust can have behaviour altered so that it is treated more like an external trust for certain SID-filtering decisions.

This is security-sensitive configuration and should not be modified during testing.

docs.title: TGT Delegation Across Trusts
docs.text:
Kerberos delegation across trust boundaries requires careful security consideration.

Trust configuration can affect whether:

Ticket Granting Tickets

may be delegated across an organisation boundary.

This becomes especially important for:

Unconstrained Delegation
Cross-Forest Authentication
Privileged Accounts

See:

Unconstrained Delegation

docs.title: Cross-Organisation Trusts
docs.text:
Trust relationships connecting separate organisations should receive additional scrutiny.

Example:

Company A
   |
   | Trust
   |
Company B

This creates a technical security dependency between organisations.

docs.title: Mergers and Acquisitions
docs.text:
Trusts are frequently created during:

Acquisition
Migration
Consolidation

A common lifecycle is:

Separate Forests
      |
      v
Temporary Trust
      |
      v
Migration
      |
      v
Migration Completed
      |
      v
Trust Should Be Reviewed

Temporary relationships sometimes become permanent through operational inertia.

docs.title: Legacy Trust Risk
docs.text:
A legacy forest may have:

Older Operating Systems
Weak Password Policies
Legacy NTLM
Unsupported Applications
Reduced Monitoring
Broader Administrator Access

If that forest is trusted by production infrastructure, its compromise may affect the stronger environment.

docs.title: Security Dependency
docs.text:
Trust analysis should therefore measure:

Security Dependency

not merely:

Connectivity

Example:

Production Forest
      |
      | trusts
      v
Legacy Forest

If legacy identities have privileged production access:

Legacy Forest Security
        |
        v
Production Forest Security

becomes an important dependency.

docs.title: Cross-Forest Administrative Access
docs.text:
Particularly dangerous relationships include:

Forest A Administrator
        |
        v
Forest B Domain Controller

or:

Forest A Group
        |
        v
Forest B Tier 0 System

Separate forests provide limited security value if their privileged administration is tightly interconnected.

docs.title: Tier 0 Relationships
docs.text:
Pay particular attention to foreign identities with access to:

Domain Controllers
AD CS
ADFS
Privileged Access Systems
Identity Synchronisation
Backup Infrastructure
Virtualisation Platforms Hosting DCs

These can effectively provide control over the identity plane.

docs.title: Enterprise Admins
docs.text:
Within a forest:

Enterprise Admins

is a forest-wide privileged group located in the forest root domain.

Compromise of Enterprise Admin-level control should generally be considered:

Forest Compromise

docs.title: Schema Admins
docs.text:
Schema Admins

can modify the forest-wide Active Directory schema.

Membership should be tightly controlled.

docs.title: Trusts and AD CS
docs.text:
Trust relationships can affect certificate-based authentication and resource access.

Review:

CA Location
Forest Membership
Enrollment Permissions
Certificate Mapping
Authentication Trust
Cross-Forest Access

See:

Active Directory Certificate Services

docs.title: Trusts and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
A trust can create a path:

Compromised Identity
       |
       v
Trusted Domain
       |
       v
Cross-Domain Group
       |
       v
Remote Administration
       |
       v
Target System

See:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Trusts and SMB
docs.text:
Example:

PARTNER\User
      |
      v
CORP\File-Access
      |
      v
FILE01

See:

SMB

docs.title: Trusts and WinRM
docs.text:
A foreign identity may have:

Remote Management Users

or administrative rights on a system in another domain.

See:

WinRM

docs.title: Trusts and WMI
docs.text:
Administrative cross-domain relationships may permit remote WMI.

See:

WMI

docs.title: Trusts and DCOM
docs.text:
The same excessive administrative relationship may permit DCOM.

See:

DCOM

docs.title: Trusts and Pivoting
docs.text:
A trust relationship does not guarantee a network path.

A pivot may be required to reach resources in the remote domain.

See:

Pivoting

docs.title: Trusts and BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can combine:

Trust
Group Membership
ACL
Session
Local Administrator
Remote Management

relationships into a single graph.

This is usually more valuable than viewing the trust in isolation.

docs.title: Trusts and Group Policy
docs.text:
Cross-domain administrative relationships may be delivered through:

Group Policy
Restricted Groups
Group Policy Preferences
Local Group Policy Configuration

See:

Group Policy

docs.title: Trusts and Service Accounts
docs.text:
Cross-domain service dependencies should also be reviewed.

Examples:

Backup Service
Monitoring Service
SQL Service
Application Service
Scheduled Task
Deployment Service

A highly privileged service account crossing a forest boundary can create a significant security dependency.

docs.title: Trust Relationships and Authentication Protocols
docs.text:
Do not assume all cross-domain access uses Kerberos.

Depending on the environment, authentication may involve:

Kerberos
NTLM

The actual protocol should be determined from:

Ticket Cache
Authentication Logs
Network Context
Application Behaviour

docs.title: Kerberos Preferred
docs.text:
For normal modern Active Directory environments:

Kerberos

should generally be preferred over NTLM where supported.

Cross-domain Kerberos relies on:

DNS
KDC Discovery
Trust
SPNs
Time

docs.title: NTLM Fallback
docs.text:
NTLM may appear when:

Kerberos Cannot Be Used
Legacy Application
IP Address Used
SPN Problem
DNS Problem
Application Limitation

See:

NTLM

docs.title: Trust Validation
docs.text:
A safe trust validation does not require administrative compromise.

A simple authorised test might validate:

Foreign User
      |
      v
Trust Authentication
      |
      v
Approved Test Resource

Examples include:

LDAP Read
Test File Share
Approved Application

docs.title: Minimal Validation Principle
docs.text:
Prefer:

Can the approved account read the approved resource?

over:

Can the approved account execute commands remotely?

unless command execution is specifically required to demonstrate the risk.

docs.title: Safe Trust Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
Identify Domain
      |
      v
Identify Forest
      |
      v
Enumerate Trust
      |
      v
Interpret Direction
      |
      v
Interpret Type
      |
      v
Interpret Transitivity
      |
      v
Review Security Attributes
      |
      v
Confirm Scope
      |
      v

      |
      v
Map Group Membership
      |
      v
Map ACLs
      |
      v
Map Network Reachability
      |
      v
Validate Minimum Access
      |
      v
Report Security Dependency

docs.text: Get-ADDomain

docs.title: Step 2 - Forest
docs.text: Get-ADForest

docs.title: Step 3 - Trusts
docs.text: Get-ADTrust -Filter *

docs.title: Step 4 - Native Verification
docs.text: nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts

docs.title: Step 5 - LDAP Verification
docs.text:
Query:

(objectClass=trustedDomain)

under:

CN=System

docs.title: Step 6 - Scope Check
docs.text:
Before contacting a newly discovered environment:

Is Target Domain In Scope?
        |
        +--> No --> Record and Stop
        |
        +--> Yes --> Continue

docs.title: Step 7 - Foreign Principals
docs.text:
Review:

ForeignSecurityPrincipals
Domain Local Groups
Universal Groups
Local Administrators
ACLs

docs.title: Step 8 - Security Controls
docs.text:
Review:

Selective Authentication
SID Filtering
Network Segmentation
Administrative Separation

docs.title: Step 9 - Minimal Access Test
docs.text: Validate only the access necessary to demonstrate the relationship.

docs.title: Step 10 - Evidence
docs.text:
Record:

Source Domain
Target Domain
Source Forest
Target Forest
Trust Direction
Trust Type
Transitivity
Trust Attributes
Authentication Scope
SID Filtering
Foreign Principal
Group
Resource
Access Level

docs.text:

Current Forest
