docs.title: Sensitive Information
docs.text:
Do not unnecessarily store:

Passwords
NTLM Hashes
Kerberos Tickets
Trust Secrets
Private Keys

in reports or screenshots.

docs.title: Trust Relationship Detection
docs.text:
Monitoring should focus on:

Trust Creation
Trust Removal
Trust Modification
Foreign Privileged Membership
Cross-Domain Authentication
SIDHistory Changes
Unexpected Privileged Logons

docs.title: Event 4706
docs.text:
Security event:

4706

indicates:

A new trust was created to a domain

Trust creation should be rare in stable environments.

docs.title: Event 4707
docs.text:
Security event:

4707

indicates:

A trust to a domain was removed

docs.title: Event 4716
docs.text:
Security event:

4716

indicates:

Trusted domain information was modified

Unexpected changes should be investigated.

docs.title: Directory Changes
docs.text:
Where appropriate auditing is enabled:

5136

may provide visibility into Active Directory object modifications.

Correlate with:

Administrator
Source System
Change Window
Ticket

docs.title: Cross-Domain Logons
docs.text:
Authentication telemetry may include:

4624
4625
4648
4672
4768
4769
4771
4776

depending on authentication protocol and operation.

docs.title: Monitoring Foreign Administrators
docs.text:
High-value monitoring includes:

Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Privileged Group

and:

Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Tier 0 System

docs.title: Monitoring SIDHistory
docs.text:
Unexpected modification of:

sIDHistory

should receive particular attention.

Legitimate migration operations should be:

Planned
Documented
Time-Bounded
Monitored

docs.title: Trust Relationship Hardening
docs.text:
A mature model includes:

Minimum Number of Trusts
Minimum Direction
Minimum Transitivity
Selective Authentication
SID Filtering
Minimum Foreign Privilege
Separate Administrators
Network Segmentation
Trust Monitoring
Periodic Review

docs.title: Minimise Trust Count
docs.text:
Every trust creates:

Operational Dependency

and:

Security Dependency

Maintain only relationships that have a documented business requirement.

docs.title: Minimise Direction
docs.text:
If access is required in only one direction:

One-Way

may be preferable to:

Two-Way

where operationally appropriate.

docs.title: Minimise Authentication Scope
docs.text:
Where appropriate, use:

Selective Authentication

instead of unnecessarily broad cross-forest authentication.

docs.title: Maintain SID Filtering
docs.text:
Do not disable SID filtering without understanding the full security consequences.

Migration exceptions should be temporary and documented.

docs.title: Minimise Foreign Privilege
docs.text:
Avoid:

Foreign Domain
      |
      v
Broad Administrative Group
      |
      v
Entire Server Estate

Prefer narrowly scoped role-based access.

docs.title: Separate Forest Administrators
docs.text:
A stronger model is:

Forest A Admin
      |
      v
Forest A

Forest B Admin
      |
      v
Forest B

rather than:

Shared Admin
    |
    +--> Forest A
    |
    +--> Forest B

docs.title: Restrict Network Connectivity
docs.text:
A trust should not imply:

Any Host in Forest A
        |
        v
Any Host in Forest B

Restrict communication to required:

Systems
Protocols
Ports
Directions

docs.title: Protect Tier 0
docs.text:
Foreign identities should not have Tier 0 access unless there is a strong documented requirement.

Review access to:

Domain Controllers
AD CS
ADFS
Identity Synchronisation
Privileged Access Systems
Backup Systems
Virtualisation Control Planes

docs.title: Periodic Review
docs.text:
Trust relationships should be reviewed periodically.

Ask:

Who Owns This Trust?

Why Does It Exist?

Is the Direction Still Required?

Is Two-Way Still Required?

Is Transitivity Required?

Is Selective Authentication Appropriate?

Are Foreign Privileged Groups Still Required?

Is SIDHistory Still Required?

Is the Trusted Environment Still Maintained?

docs.title: Reporting Trust Relationship Findings
docs.text:
Do not report:

A trust exists

as a vulnerability.

Report the actual weakness.

Examples:

Unnecessary Bidirectional Forest Trust

Foreign Domain Group Has Excessive Administrative Rights

Legacy Domain Remains Trusted After Migration

Selective Authentication Not Used Across High-Risk Trust

Excessive Cross-Forest Administrative Dependency

Unnecessary Cross-Forest Network Reachability

docs.title: Example Finding - Foreign Administrative Group
docs.text:
Finding:
Foreign Domain Group Has Administrative Access to Corporate Servers

Description:
A group originating from the trusted PARTNER.EXAMPLE domain was a
member of an administrative group used across multiple systems in the
CORP.EXAMPLE domain.

The trust itself was required for application access, but the
administrative relationship was broader than the documented business
requirement.

Impact:
Compromise of an account with membership in the foreign group could
provide administrative access to systems in the corporate domain.

This increases the security dependency on the trusted environment.

Recommendation:
Remove unnecessary foreign identities from administrative groups.

Use narrowly scoped role-based groups and separate privileged
identities for administration across security boundaries.

docs.title: Example Finding - Unnecessary Bidirectional Trust
docs.text:
Finding:
Forest Trust Is Bidirectional Without Business Requirement

Description:
The trust between the corporate and partner forests was configured as
bidirectional.

The documented requirement only required partner identities to access
specific corporate resources.

No requirement for corporate identities to authenticate to partner
resources was identified.

Impact:
The additional trust direction unnecessarily expands the
authentication relationship between two separate forest security
boundaries.

Recommendation:
Determine whether the trust can be converted to a one-way relationship
that matches the documented access requirement.

Test application compatibility through the organisation's normal
change-management process before modifying the production trust.

docs.title: Example Finding - Broad Authentication
docs.text:
Finding:
Cross-Forest Authentication Scope Is Broader Than Required

Description:
Trusted-forest identities were permitted to authenticate broadly
across the corporate forest even though only a small number of
application systems required cross-forest access.

Impact:
Compromise of an identity in the trusted forest could expose a larger
authentication surface in the corporate environment than required.

Normal resource authorisation remains necessary, but the broad
authentication scope increases opportunities for configuration errors
and lateral movement.

Recommendation:
Evaluate selective authentication and permit foreign identities to
authenticate only to systems requiring cross-forest access.

Review existing cross-forest groups and ACLs before implementing the
change.

docs.title: Example Finding - Legacy Trust
docs.text:
Finding:
Unused Legacy Forest Trust Remains Configured

Description:
A trust relationship remained between the production forest and a
legacy forest used during a previous migration.

No active application, user or administrative dependency requiring the
trust was identified.

Impact:
The trust preserves an unnecessary authentication relationship with a
legacy environment.

If the legacy forest is compromised, the trust and any remaining
cross-forest permissions may provide additional opportunities to
access production resources.

Recommendation:
Confirm the absence of business dependencies with the relevant
technical and business owners.

Remove the trust through the normal change-management process if it is
no longer required.

docs.title: Example Finding - Cross-Forest Tier 0 Dependency
docs.text:
Finding:
Foreign Forest Administrators Have Access to Tier 0 Infrastructure

Description:
Administrative identities originating from another forest were
permitted to administer systems forming part of the corporate identity
control plane.

Affected systems included Tier 0 or equivalent identity
infrastructure.

Impact:
Compromise of privileged identities in the trusted forest could
directly affect the security of the corporate forest.

The two forests therefore do not operate as independent security
boundaries in practice.

Recommendation:
Use separate privileged identities for each forest.

Remove unnecessary foreign administrative access to Tier 0 systems and
restrict privileged management to dedicated administrative
workstations and approved management networks.

docs.title: Trust Relationship Testing Model
docs.text:
The basic model is:

Domain A
   |
   v
Trust
   |
   v
Domain B

The direction model is:

DOMAIN-A trusts DOMAIN-B

DOMAIN-B Identity
        |
        v
DOMAIN-A Resource

The two-way model is:

DOMAIN-A
   <---->
DOMAIN-B

The authentication model is:

Identity
   |
   v
Source KDC
   |
   v
Trust
   |
   v
Target KDC
   |
   v
Service

The authorisation model is:

Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Trust
      |
      v
Authentication
      |
      v
Group / ACL
      |
      v
Resource

The group model is:

Foreign Account
      |
      v
Global Group
      |
      v
Domain Local Group
      |
      v
Permission

The multi-domain model is:

Account
   |
   v
Global Group
   |
   v
Universal Group
   |
   v
Domain Local Group
   |
   v
Permission

The selective-authentication model is:

Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Trust
      |
      v
Allowed to Authenticate?
      |
      +--> No
      |
      +--> Yes
             |
             v
      Resource Authorisation

The SID model is:

Identity
   |
   v
Security Token
   |
   +--> User SID
   +--> Group SIDs
   +--> SIDHistory
   |
   v
Trust Boundary
   |
   v
SID Filtering
   |
   v
Authorisation

The cross-forest model is:

Forest A
   |
   v
Trust
   |
   v
Forest B

The privilege model is:

Forest A Identity
       |
       v
Forest B Group
       |
       v
Forest B Privilege
       |
       v
Cross-Boundary Dependency

The network model is:

Trust
  +
DNS
  +
Network Reachability
  +
Authentication
  +
Authorisation
  =
Access

The defensive model is:

Minimum Trust
     +
Minimum Direction
     +
Minimum Transitivity
     +
Selective Authentication
     +
SID Filtering
     +
Minimum Foreign Privilege
     +
Network Segmentation
     +
Administrative Separation
     =
Reduced Trust Risk

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Can I attack the trusted forest?"

Ask:
"Is the trusted forest in scope,
and what security dependency does
the trust create?"

For defenders:

Do Not Ask:
"Is this trust working?"

Ask:
"Does this trust provide only the
minimum authentication relationship
required by the business?"

The complete model is:

Business Requirement
       |
       v
Trust Relationship
       |
       v
Authentication Scope
       |
       v
Security Controls
       |
       v
Foreign Identity
       |
       v
Authorisation
       |
       v
Resource Access
       |
       v
Security Dependency

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK - Domain Trust Discovery
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK - T1482 Domain Trust Discovery

sequenceDiagram
      participant S as Source identity
      participant T as Trust boundary
      participant H as Target service
      participant R as Resource
      S->>T: Cross-domain authentication
      T->>H: Identity and policy evaluation
      H->>R: Authorization check
      R-->>S: Access, denial, or bounded result

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Trust relationships should be analysed as:

Security Dependencies

rather than merely:

Active Directory Configuration

The correct assessment path is:

Discover Trust
     |
     v
Understand Direction
     |
     v
Understand Type
     |
     v
Understand Transitivity
     |
     v
Confirm Scope
     |
     v
Review Security Controls
     |
     v
Identify Foreign Principals
     |
     v
Map Groups and ACLs
     |
     v
Validate Minimum Access
     |
     v
Determine Security Impact

The trust itself is rarely the vulnerability.

More important weaknesses include:

Unnecessary Trust Direction
Excessive Transitivity
Broad Authentication
Disabled or Weakened SID Filtering
Excessive Foreign Group Membership
Cross-Forest Administrative Access
Legacy Trusts
Unnecessary Network Connectivity

A trust should provide only:

The Minimum Authentication Relationship
Required by the Business

and should be reinforced with:

Selective Authentication
SID Filtering
Least Privilege
Network Segmentation
Administrative Separation
Monitoring

The most important distinction remains:

Authentication
!=
Authorisation

A trust may allow an identity to be recognised without granting access to any useful resource.

The assessment therefore should not stop at:

Trust Found

It should continue to:

Trust Found
    |
    v
Foreign Identity Identified
    |
    v
Permission Identified
    |
    v
Resource Identified
    |
    v
Security Impact Established

The next page focuses on one of the most important SID-related mechanisms affecting domain migrations and trust security:

SID History

docs.title: Active Directory Trust Tickets
docs.text:
Active Directory uses Kerberos trust relationships to allow authentication to cross domain boundaries.

When a user in one domain needs to access a service in another domain, the user's Key Distribution Center (KDC) does not normally issue the final service ticket directly.

Instead, Kerberos uses a referral process.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Source Domain KDC
 |
 v
Referral TGT
 |
 v
Target Domain KDC
 |
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Target Service

These cross-domain Kerberos tickets are commonly referred to during offensive security discussions as:

Inter-Realm Tickets
Referral Tickets
Trust Tickets

The underlying mechanism is legitimate Kerberos functionality.

From a security perspective, trust tickets become particularly important when an attacker obtains cryptographic material associated with an Active Directory trust.

Compromise of trust-related secrets can potentially allow forged cross-domain authentication material to be created.

Authorised testing only

Trust-ticket testing can affect multiple Active Directory domains or forests. A trust relationship does not automatically place the remote domain or forest within scope. Do not extract trust secrets, forge tickets or authenticate to another security boundary unless this activity is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Trust Tickets at a Glance
docs.text:
Normal authentication inside one domain:

User
 |
 v
AS-REQ
 |
 v
KDC
 |
 v
TGT
 |
 v
TGS-REQ
 |
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Service

Cross-domain authentication introduces a referral:

User
 |
 v
Source KDC
 |
 v
Source TGT
 |
 v
Referral Request
 |
 v
Inter-Domain Referral TGT
 |
 v
Target KDC
 |
 v
Target Service Ticket
 |
 v
Target Service

The trust allows the target domain to validate authentication information originating through the source domain.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Understanding trust tickets requires familiarity with:

Kerberos
TGTs
Service Tickets
KDCs
SPNs
Domains
Forests
Trust Relationships

See:

Kerberos

Kerberos Tickets

Domain and Forest Trusts

Trust Relationships

docs.title: Kerberos Components
docs.text:
The main components are:

Client
KDC
Authentication Service
Ticket Granting Service
Service Principal

The KDC normally runs on a domain controller.

docs.title: Ticket Granting Ticket
docs.text:
A user initially obtains a:

Ticket Granting Ticket

or:

TGT

The TGT allows the user to request tickets for services without repeatedly supplying credentials.

docs.title: Service Ticket
docs.text:
When accessing a service such as:

CIFS
HTTP
LDAP
MSSQLSvc
HOST

the client requests a:

Service Ticket

from the KDC.

docs.title: Single-Domain Kerberos
docs.text:
Suppose:

alice@CORP.EXAMPLE

wants to access:

cifs/files01.corp.example

The simplified process is:

Alice
 |
 v
CORP KDC
 |
 v
TGT
 |
 v
CORP KDC
 |
 v
CIFS Service Ticket
 |
 v
FILE01

The KDC responsible for Alice is also capable of issuing the required ticket for the service in the same domain.

docs.title: Cross-Domain Kerberos
docs.text:
Now suppose:

alice@EMEA.CORP.EXAMPLE

wants to access:

cifs/files01.corp.example

The source KDC belongs to:

EMEA.CORP.EXAMPLE

while the service belongs to:

CORP.EXAMPLE

The source KDC therefore provides a referral toward the destination domain.

docs.title: Referral Model
docs.text:
Alice
 |
 v
EMEA.CORP.EXAMPLE KDC
 |
 v
Referral TGT
 |
 v
CORP.EXAMPLE KDC
 |
 v
CIFS/files01.corp.example
 |
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
FILE01

This allows Kerberos authentication to traverse the trust relationship.

docs.title: Inter-Realm TGT
docs.text:
A referral ticket is effectively an inter-realm Ticket Granting Ticket.

It identifies another Kerberos realm as the next destination.

Example conceptual service principal:

krbtgt/CORP.EXAMPLE

when moving from:

EMEA.CORP.EXAMPLE

toward:

CORP.EXAMPLE

docs.title: Trust Account Concept
docs.text:
Active Directory maintains secret material associated with domain trust relationships.

This cryptographic material allows the participating domains to validate trust-related Kerberos information.

Conceptually:

Domain A
   |
   | Shared Trust Relationship
   |
   v
Domain B

The trust relationship has associated secret material known to the relevant domain controllers.

docs.title: Trust Password
docs.text:
Trust relationships use automatically managed passwords.

These secrets are not intended to be manually used by administrators during normal operations.

Windows manages trust password changes as part of the relationship.

docs.title: Trust Secret
docs.text:
From an offensive security perspective, trust-related cryptographic material may sometimes be described as:

Trust Key
Trust Secret
Trust Password Hash
Inter-Realm Key

The exact terminology depends on the tool and context.

docs.title: Trust Secret Security
docs.text:
Trust secrets should be considered highly sensitive.

Conceptually:

Trust Secret
     |
     v
Validate Inter-Realm Authentication
     |
     v
Cross-Domain Security

Compromise can therefore affect more than one domain.

docs.title: Trust Direction and Tickets
docs.text:
Trust direction remains important.

Suppose:

DOMAIN-A trusts DOMAIN-B

The potential access direction is:

DOMAIN-B User
      |
      v
DOMAIN-A Resource

Kerberos referral behaviour must be interpreted together with:

Trust Direction
Trust Type
Transitivity
Authentication Scope

docs.title: Trust Ticket Flow
docs.text:
A simplified cross-domain flow is:

User in Domain A
       |
       v
Domain A KDC
       |
       v
TGT for Domain A
       |
       v
Request Service in Domain B
       |
       v
Domain A KDC
       |
       v
Referral TGT for Domain B
       |
       v
Domain B KDC
       |
       v
Service Ticket
       |
       v
Domain B Service

docs.title: Kerberos Referral Discovery
docs.text:
The client does not necessarily need to know the entire trust path in advance.

Kerberos referrals can direct the client toward the appropriate realm.

In complex forests:

Domain A
   |
   v
Domain B
   |
   v
Domain C

the client may receive multiple referrals before reaching the domain responsible for the target service.

docs.title: Parent-Child Referral
docs.text:
Example:

corp.example
      |
      v
emea.corp.example

A user in:

emea.corp.example

accessing a service in:

corp.example

can use the automatically established parent-child trust.

docs.title: Forest Referral
docs.text:
Inside a forest:

Domain A
    |
    v
Forest Trust Topology
    |
    v
Domain B

Kerberos can navigate the domain hierarchy using referrals.

docs.title: Cross-Forest Referral
docs.text:
For separate forests:

Forest A
   |
   | Forest Trust
   |
   v
Forest B

Kerberos referrals can cross the forest trust when:

Trust Direction Allows It
Authentication Requirements Are Met
Name Resolution Works
Network Connectivity Exists

docs.title: DNS Requirements
docs.text:
Kerberos referrals depend heavily on DNS.

The client must be able to locate:

Domain Controllers
KDCs
Services

in the appropriate domains.

docs.title: Kerberos SRV Records
docs.text:
Useful DNS records include:

_kerberos._tcp.DOMAIN

and:

_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.DOMAIN

Example:

dig _kerberos._tcp.corp.example SRV

Windows:

Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV '_kerberos._tcp.corp.example'

Only query remote domains when they are within scope.

docs.title: Inspect Current Kerberos Tickets
docs.text:
Windows:

klist

This displays tickets in the current logon session.

docs.title: Purging Tickets
docs.text:
Windows also supports:

klist purge

However, this changes the current Kerberos session state.

Do not purge tickets on production systems merely for enumeration.

Use a dedicated test session if ticket lifecycle testing is required.

docs.title: Linux Ticket Cache
docs.text:
On Linux:

klist

The current cache location may be shown through:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

docs.title: Referral Tickets in the Cache
docs.text:
After accessing a cross-domain service, the ticket cache may contain entries conceptually resembling:

krbtgt/CORP.EXAMPLE@EMEA.CORP.EXAMPLE

along with the final service ticket.

Exact ticket presentation varies by platform and tooling.

docs.title: Kerberos Ticket Analysis
docs.text:
Important fields include:

Client
Server
Realm
Start Time
End Time
Renew Time
Encryption Type
Ticket Flags

These help establish:

Who Authenticated?
To Which Realm?
For Which Service?
When?

docs.title: Windows Ticket Inspection
docs.text:
Basic:

klist

Specific sessions can also be inspected by administrators using appropriate klist functionality.

Avoid interacting with unrelated user sessions during routine assessment.

docs.title: Linux Ticket Inspection
docs.text:
klist -e

can display encryption information where supported.

Example output may include:

AES-256
AES-128
RC4

depending on environment and ticket.

docs.title: Trust Enumeration Before Ticket Analysis
docs.text:
Always understand the trust first.

PowerShell:

Get-ADTrust -Filter * |
    Select-Object Name,Source,Target,Direction,TrustType,ForestTransitive,IntraForest,SelectiveAuthentication

Native Windows:

nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts

docs.title: Identify Domain SIDs
docs.text:
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot,DomainSID

If the trusted domain is in scope and querying it is authorised:

Get-ADDomain -Identity 'partner.example' |
    Select-Object DNSRoot,DomainSID

docs.title: Why Domain SIDs Matter
docs.text:
Kerberos authorisation information ultimately interacts with Windows SIDs.

Trust-ticket analysis therefore often intersects with:

Domain SID
Group SID
SIDHistory
SID Filtering

See:

SID History

docs.title: SID Filtering
docs.text:
SID filtering protects trust boundaries by controlling which SID information is accepted across the trust.

Conceptually:

Kerberos Authentication Data
          |
          v
Trust Boundary
          |
          v
SID Filtering
          |
          +--> Permitted SID Information
          |
          X
          |
          +--> Filtered SID Information

docs.title: Trust Ticket Does Not Bypass Authorisation
docs.text:
A valid cross-domain ticket does not automatically provide administrative access.

The complete model remains:

Valid Ticket
    |
    v
Authentication
    |
    v
Security Token
    |
    v
ACL / Group Membership
    |
    v
Authorisation

docs.title: Privilege Still Matters
docs.text:
A normal user from a trusted domain may authenticate successfully but have:

No Access

to a particular resource.

The trust provides:

Authentication Relationship

not:

Automatic Privilege

docs.title: Selective Authentication
docs.text:
Selective authentication can further restrict where trusted-domain identities are permitted to authenticate.

Conceptually:

Foreign Identity
      |
      v
Kerberos Trust
      |
      v
Allowed to Authenticate?
      |
      +--> No --> Stop
      |
      +--> Yes
             |
             v
      Resource Authorisation

docs.title: Forest-Wide Authentication
docs.text:
A forest trust may instead allow broader authentication.

This does not eliminate resource ACL checks, but it increases the number of systems to which trusted identities may potentially authenticate.

docs.title: Trust Ticket Abuse
docs.text:
The offensive security significance of trust tickets arises when an attacker obtains cryptographic material used by the trust.

The conceptual chain is:

High Privilege in Domain
       |
       v
Trust Secret Compromised
       |
       v
Inter-Realm Ticket Material
       |
       v
Cross-Domain Authentication Attempt

This is fundamentally different from simply requesting a legitimate referral ticket as a normal user.

docs.title: Legitimate Referral vs Forged Trust Ticket
docs.text:
Legitimate:

Normal User
   |
   v
Source KDC
   |
   v
Legitimate Referral
   |
   v
Target KDC

Forged:

Compromised Trust Secret
        |
        v
Offline Ticket Construction
        |
        v
Target Trust Boundary

The second scenario represents a major security incident.

docs.title: Trust Ticket vs Golden Ticket
docs.text:
A Golden Ticket normally involves compromise of:

krbtgt

key material for a domain.

Conceptually:

krbtgt Key
    |
    v
Forge Domain TGT
    |
    v
Domain Persistence / Authentication

A trust-ticket scenario instead concerns:

Trust Key
    |
    v
Inter-Realm Authentication
    |
    v
Trusted Domain

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Technique Key Material Primary Scope Golden Ticket Domain krbtgt key Domain Kerberos authentication Trust Ticket Trust relationship key Cross-domain trust authentication Silver Ticket Service account key Specific service Pass-the-Ticket Existing ticket Rights represented by captured ticket

docs.title: Trust Ticket vs Pass-the-Ticket
docs.text:
Pass-the-Ticket uses:

Existing Kerberos Ticket

whereas trust-ticket forgery involves constructing authentication material using compromised trust cryptographic material.

See:

Pass-the-Ticket

docs.title: Trust Ticket vs Golden Certificate
docs.text:
Golden Certificate abuse involves:

CA Private Key

and certificate-based authentication.

Trust tickets involve:

Kerberos Trust Cryptographic Material

These compromise different parts of the identity infrastructure.

See:

Golden Certificate

docs.title: Trust Ticket Security Boundary
docs.text:
Trust-ticket abuse can cross:

Domain Boundaries

and potentially:

Forest Boundaries

depending on the trust.

Therefore the first question before testing is:

Is the Destination Security Boundary Explicitly In Scope?

docs.title: Trust Secret Exposure
docs.text:
Trust secrets normally require significant privilege to obtain.

Their exposure should therefore be treated as evidence of substantial compromise in the source environment.

Possible sources of exposure can include:

Domain Controller Compromise
Directory Database Compromise
Credential Dumping
Highly Privileged Replication Access
Backup Exposure

docs.title: NTDS Context
docs.text:
Trust-related secrets may exist within the broader Active Directory credential material protected by domain controllers.

See:

NTDS

Access to this material should already be considered a critical security event.

docs.title: DCSync Context
docs.text:
An identity capable of replicating sensitive directory secrets may have highly privileged control.

Trust-secret extraction through replication should therefore not be treated as a low-impact enumeration technique.

docs.title: Trust Ticket Testing Philosophy
docs.text:
For normal penetration testing:

Trust Found
    |
    v
Enumerate Direction
    |
    v
Identify Foreign Permissions
    |
    v
Validate Legitimate Authentication

is usually sufficient.

You generally do not need:

Trust Secret Extraction
      |
      v
Ticket Forgery

to demonstrate that an excessive trust relationship creates risk.

docs.title: When Forgery Testing May Be Appropriate
docs.text:
Trust-ticket forgery may be appropriate in:

Dedicated AD Lab
Red-Team Exercise
Adversary Simulation
Explicit Trust Compromise Scenario

where:

Both Security Boundaries Are In Scope

and destructive or persistence-related restrictions are understood.

docs.title: Lab Architecture
docs.text:
A safe laboratory might contain:

FORESTA.LOCAL
      |
      | Two-Way Forest Trust
      |
      v
FORESTB.LOCAL

with:

DC-A
DC-B
CLIENT-A
SERVER-B

All systems should be disposable and controlled.

docs.title: Lab Testing Stages
docs.text:
A structured laboratory workflow is:

Enumerate Trust
      |
      v
Observe Legitimate Referral
      |
      v
Inspect Ticket Cache
      |
      v
Study Trust Cryptography
      |
      v
Perform Controlled Forgery
      |
      v
Observe Target Logs
      |
      v
Destroy Lab State

The production assessment normally stops much earlier.

docs.title: Impacket Kerberos Tooling
docs.text:
Impacket provides several Kerberos-related utilities useful for authorised laboratories and troubleshooting.

See:

Impacket

Available commands depend on the installed version.

Always verify:

impacket-ticketConverter -h

or the relevant tool's help output before relying on remembered syntax.

docs.title: Ticket Cache Interoperability
docs.text:
Kerberos tickets may appear in formats such as:

ccache
kirbi

Tooling exists to convert between formats.

This is useful for:

Lab Analysis
Ticket Inspection
Interoperability

but does not itself create privilege.

docs.title: Rubeus Context
docs.text:
Rubeus is commonly encountered in Windows Kerberos research and red-team environments.

It can inspect and interact with Kerberos tickets.

Because functionality and command-line options vary across releases and forks, verify syntax against the specific version being used.

Do not execute ticket manipulation against production identity infrastructure without explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Mimikatz Context
docs.text:
Mimikatz historically demonstrated many Kerberos ticket and trust techniques.

It is useful for understanding:

Kerberos Internals
Ticket Structure
Trust Authentication

but credential extraction and ticket-forgery functionality is highly intrusive.

Use such functionality only in explicitly authorised environments.

docs.title: Cross-Domain Access Validation
docs.text:
A safer production validation is to use legitimate credentials.

Example conceptual workflow:

Approved User in Domain A
       |
       v
Authenticate Normally
       |
       v
Access Approved Resource in Domain B
       |
       v
Observe Referral Tickets
       |
       v
Stop

This proves the trust path without manipulating trust secrets.

docs.title: SMB Validation
docs.text:
If an approved foreign user has access to a test share:

Domain A User
      |
      v
Kerberos Referral
      |
      v
Domain B CIFS Ticket
      |
      v
Approved Share

See:

SMB

docs.title: WinRM Validation
docs.text:
Where remote management is explicitly part of the test:

Foreign User
     |
     v
Kerberos Referral
     |
     v
HTTP Service Ticket
     |
     v
WinRM

See:

WinRM

docs.title: LDAP Validation
docs.text:
Read-only LDAP is often sufficient to demonstrate cross-domain authentication.

Conceptually:

Foreign User
     |
     v
Kerberos
     |
     v
LDAP
     |
     v
Read Approved Directory Data

docs.title: SPNs Across Trusts
docs.text:
Kerberos relies on Service Principal Names.

Examples include:

cifs/files01.partner.example
HTTP/web01.partner.example
ldap/dc01.partner.example
MSSQLSvc/sql01.partner.example

Correct:

DNS
SPN
Realm

information is essential.

docs.title: Hostname vs IP Address
docs.text:
Kerberos normally depends on service names.

Using:

Hostname

is therefore preferable to using:

IP Address

for Kerberos validation.

Using an IP address can cause Kerberos to fail or another authentication mechanism to be attempted depending on the client and application.

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Kerberos is time sensitive.

Cross-domain authentication therefore depends on acceptable clock synchronisation.

Windows:

w32tm /query /status

Linux:

timedatectl

docs.title: Cross-Forest DNS
docs.text:
Separate forests may use:

Conditional Forwarders
Stub Zones
Delegations
DNS Forwarding

to allow domain discovery.

A broken trust may actually be:

DNS Failure

rather than:

Kerberos Failure

docs.title: Troubleshooting Model
docs.text:
Cross-Domain Authentication Fails
            |
            v
          DNS?
            |
            v
      KDC Reachable?
            |
            v
      Correct Hostname?
            |
            v
       Correct SPN?
            |
            v
      Clock Correct?
            |
            v
    Trust Direction?
            |
            v
      Trust Healthy?
            |
            v
Selective Authentication?
            |
            v
     Authorisation?

docs.title: Verify Trust Health
docs.text:
Administrators can use native tooling to investigate trust relationships.

Example:

nltest /domain_trusts

Domain controller discovery:

nltest /dsgetdc:partner.example

Avoid repair or reset operations during assessment.

docs.title: Do Not Reset Trusts
docs.text:
Native administrative tools can modify or reset trust relationships.

Do not perform operations such as:

Trust Reset
Trust Password Reset
Trust Recreation

during normal penetration testing.

These can disrupt authentication between domains.

docs.title: Do Not Change Trust Direction
docs.text:
Changing:

One-Way

to:

Two-Way

or otherwise modifying trust direction is a production configuration change.

It is not required to validate trust security.

docs.title: Do Not Disable SID Filtering
docs.text:
SID filtering is a defensive control.

Do not weaken it to demonstrate a theoretical attack.

The correct assessment is:

Observe Configuration
      |
      v
Determine Exposure
      |
      v
Report

docs.title: Trust Ticket Detection
docs.text:
Defenders should monitor both:

Normal Cross-Domain Kerberos

and:

Abnormal Trust-Related Authentication

The challenge is that legitimate trust authentication is common in some environments.

docs.title: Kerberos Event 4768
docs.text:
Event:

4768

records Kerberos Authentication Service activity for TGT requests on domain controllers.

It can help establish:

Account
Client Address
Encryption Type
Pre-Authentication

context.

docs.title: Kerberos Event 4769
docs.text:
Event:

4769

records Kerberos service-ticket requests on domain controllers.

This is particularly useful for analysing:

Service
Account
Client Address
Ticket Encryption

docs.title: Cross-Domain Kerberos Visibility
docs.text:
Monitoring should understand expected relationships such as:

Domain A Users
      |
      v
Specific Services in Domain B

Unexpected relationships are more useful than raw ticket volume.

docs.title: Authentication Baseline
docs.text:
Example expected pattern:

PARTNER\AppUsers
       |
       v
CORP\APP01

Unexpected:

PARTNER\AppUsers
       |
       v
CORP\Domain Controller

The second deserves significantly more attention.

docs.title: Event 4624
docs.text:
Successful logons can produce:

4624

on the target system.

Correlate:

Account Domain
Account Name
Source Address
Logon Type
Authentication Package
Target Host

docs.title: Event 4625
docs.text:
Failed logons:

4625

can reveal repeated or unexpected cross-domain authentication attempts.

docs.title: Event 4672
docs.text:
Event:

4672

indicates special privileges assigned to a new logon.

Cross-domain identities receiving privileged logons should be reviewed carefully.

docs.title: Trust Changes
docs.text:
Trust-related administrative events include:

4706
4707
4716

These cover trust creation, removal and modification.

See:

Trust Relationships

docs.title: Directory Changes
docs.text:
Where appropriate auditing is enabled:

5136

may provide additional visibility into Active Directory object modifications.

docs.title: Detecting Forged Tickets
docs.text:
Forged-ticket detection is difficult because:

Cryptographically Valid

does not necessarily mean:

Legitimately Issued

Detection therefore benefits from correlation.

docs.title: Correlation Model
docs.text:
Kerberos Ticket Activity
        |
        v
Expected Account?
        |
        v
Expected Source?
        |
        v
Expected Domain?
        |
        v
Expected Service?
        |
        v
Expected Privilege?
        |
        v
Expected Trust Path?

docs.title: KDC vs Resource Correlation
docs.text:
Where telemetry permits, compare:

KDC Events

with:

Target Logon Events

and:

Endpoint Process Activity

Unexpected inconsistencies can warrant investigation.

docs.title: Privileged Cross-Domain Authentication
docs.text:
High-value alerts include:

Foreign User -> Domain Controller
Foreign User -> AD CS Server
Foreign User -> ADFS
Foreign User -> Privileged Management Host
Foreign User -> Backup Infrastructure

unless explicitly expected.

docs.title: Encryption Types
docs.text:
Kerberos encryption types may provide useful context.

Modern environments should generally prefer strong supported encryption such as:

AES

Legacy environments may still expose:

RC4

dependencies.

Do not infer compromise solely from RC4 use, but investigate why it remains necessary.

docs.title: Trust Encryption Compatibility
docs.text:
Some trust configurations and legacy environments can influence which encryption types are available.

Review:

Domain Functional Level
Trust Configuration
Account Encryption Support
Legacy Dependencies

before making remediation recommendations.

docs.title: Trust Ticket Hardening
docs.text:
A strong trust-security model includes:

Minimum Trusts
Minimum Trust Direction
Selective Authentication
SID Filtering
Strong Kerberos Configuration
Separate Privileged Accounts
Network Segmentation
Tier 0 Isolation
Trust Monitoring
Rapid Secret Rotation After Compromise

docs.title: Minimise Trust Relationships
docs.text:
Every trust creates an additional authentication relationship.

Maintain only trusts with:

Documented Business Purpose
Owner
Required Direction
Required Scope
Review Date

docs.title: Prefer One-Way Trusts
docs.text:
Where only one direction is required:

One-Way

may reduce exposure compared with:

Two-Way

depending on the architecture.

docs.title: Use Selective Authentication
docs.text:
For high-risk forest relationships:

Selective Authentication

can reduce the systems to which foreign identities may authenticate.

docs.title: Maintain SID Filtering
docs.text:
SID filtering should remain appropriately configured across trust boundaries.

See:

SID History

docs.title: Separate Privileged Accounts
docs.text:
Avoid using one privileged identity across multiple forest security boundaries.

Prefer:

Forest A Admin
Forest B Admin

rather than:

Shared Cross-Forest Admin

docs.title: Protect Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Trust secrets are protected by the domain's identity infrastructure.

Domain controllers should therefore receive:

Tier 0 Protection
Dedicated Administration
Credential Isolation
Network Restrictions
EDR
Security Monitoring
Secure Backups

docs.title: Protect Directory Backups
docs.text:
Backups containing Active Directory data may expose highly sensitive credential material.

Protect them using:

Encryption
Access Control
Separation
Monitoring
Offline Protection
Retention Controls

docs.title: Protect Replication Rights
docs.text:
Accounts with directory replication privileges can represent substantial risk.

Review rights associated with:

Replicating Directory Changes
Replicating Directory Changes All

and other sensitive replication capabilities.

docs.title: Trust Secret Compromise Response
docs.text:
If trust cryptographic material is believed compromised:

Contain Source Domain
      |
      v
Assess Target Domain
      |
      v
Identify Trust
      |
      v
Rotate / Reset Trust Secret
      |
      v
Investigate Cross-Domain Authentication
      |
      v
Review Privileged Access

Trust reset procedures should be performed by qualified administrators following Microsoft guidance.

docs.title: Golden Ticket Relationship
docs.text:
If an attacker has obtained enough control to extract:

krbtgt

and:

Trust Secrets

the incident should be treated as:

Major Identity Infrastructure Compromise

Rotating only normal user passwords is insufficient.

docs.title: Trust Secret Rotation
docs.text:
Trust passwords are normally rotated automatically by Windows.

After compromise, incident responders may need to deliberately reset trust credentials using supported administrative procedures.

Do not improvise trust-secret rotation.

Incorrect trust changes can disrupt cross-domain authentication.

docs.title: Incident Response Scope
docs.text:
A compromised trust should expand investigation to:

Both Sides of the Trust

when organisational ownership and authority permit.

Example:

Domain A Compromised
       |
       v
Trust Secret Exposed
       |
       v
Investigate Domain B Authentication

docs.title: Cross-Organisation Trusts
docs.text:
For a trust connecting separate organisations:

Company A
   |
   v
Trust
   |
   v
Company B

incident response may require:

Joint Coordination
Legal Review
Contractual Notification
Shared Timeline
Cross-Organisation IOC Exchange

docs.title: Reporting Trust Ticket Risk
docs.text:
Do not report:

Kerberos Referrals Exist

as a vulnerability.

Referrals are normal Kerberos behaviour.

Likewise:

Trust Tickets Exist

is not a finding.

Report the actual weakness.

docs.title: Potential Findings
docs.text:
Examples include:

Excessive Cross-Domain Administrative Access

Trust Secret Exposed Through Domain Controller Compromise

Bidirectional Trust Unnecessarily Expands Authentication Scope

Foreign Privileged Accounts Can Access Tier 0 Systems

Legacy Trust Permits Unnecessary Cross-Domain Authentication

Weak Trust Governance Allows Excessive Security Dependency

docs.title: Example Finding - Trust Secret Exposure
docs.text:
Finding:
Active Directory Trust Secret Exposed Following Domain Controller Compromise

Description:
The assessment demonstrated access to highly sensitive Active
Directory credential material on a domain controller.

The affected material included cryptographic information associated
with an Active Directory trust relationship.

No forged trust ticket was created because sufficient evidence of the
cross-domain risk had already been established.

Impact:
Compromise of trust cryptographic material may allow an attacker with
the required knowledge and access to construct authentication material
associated with the affected trust.

Because the relationship crosses Active Directory security
boundaries, the impact may extend beyond the initially compromised
domain.

Recommendation:
Treat the affected domain as a major identity compromise.

Investigate authentication activity on both sides of the trust,
contain privileged access, rotate affected trust secrets using
supported administrative procedures and review whether the trust is
still required.

Protect domain controllers, directory backups and replication rights
as Tier 0 assets.

docs.title: Example Finding - Excessive Trust Direction
docs.text:
Finding:
Bidirectional Trust Creates Unnecessary Cross-Domain Authentication Path

Description:
A bidirectional trust existed between two Active Directory
environments.

The documented business requirement required authentication in only
one direction.

Impact:
The additional trust direction unnecessarily increases the
authentication relationship between the environments.

Compromise or privilege misconfiguration in either environment may
therefore have broader consequences than required.

Recommendation:
Review whether the relationship can be converted to a one-way trust.

Where appropriate, combine the reduced trust direction with selective
authentication, SID filtering and network segmentation.

docs.title: Example Finding - Cross-Domain Tier 0 Access
docs.text:
Finding:
Trusted-Domain Administrators Can Access Tier 0 Infrastructure

Description:
Administrative identities from a trusted domain were permitted to
authenticate to and administer identity infrastructure in the target
domain.

Affected systems included Tier 0 or equivalent assets.

Impact:
Compromise of privileged identities in the trusted domain could
directly affect the security of the target domain.

The target environment therefore depends on the security of the
trusted administrative environment.

Recommendation:
Separate privileged identities between security boundaries.

Remove unnecessary foreign administrative access to Tier 0 systems
and restrict identity-infrastructure administration to dedicated
management paths and privileged workstations.

docs.title: Example Finding - Legacy Trust
docs.text:
Finding:
Legacy Trust Preserves Unnecessary Kerberos Authentication Relationship

Description:
A trust remained configured with a legacy Active Directory
environment after the associated migration had been completed.

No current application dependency requiring the trust was identified.

Impact:
The legacy environment remains part of the authentication topology.

Compromise of the legacy domain may therefore create additional
opportunities to interact with production resources through the
remaining trust.

Recommendation:
Confirm that the trust is no longer required and remove it through the
normal change-management process.

Review remaining foreign group memberships, ACLs and SID History
dependencies before removing the relationship.

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Trust tickets are a normal part of Kerberos authentication across Active Directory trust relationships.

The legitimate model is:

User
 |
 v
Source KDC
 |
 v
Referral
 |
 v
Target KDC
 |
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Resource

Their existence is not a vulnerability.

The security significance appears when:

Trust Relationship
       |
       v
Trust Secret
       |
       v
Secret Compromise
       |
       v
Cross-Domain Authentication Risk

A penetration test should therefore not begin with ticket forgery.

The preferred workflow is:

Enumerate Trust
      |
      v
Understand Direction
      |
      v
Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Observe Legitimate Referral
      |
      v
Identify Foreign Permissions
      |
      v
Validate Minimum Access
      |
      v
Report Actual Security Impact

Only explicitly authorised adversary simulations or dedicated laboratories should normally progress toward:

Trust Secret Extraction
      |
      v
Ticket Forgery

The most important defensive controls remain:

Minimum Trust Relationships
Selective Authentication
SID Filtering
Least Privilege
Separate Forest Administration
Tier 0 Protection
Network Segmentation
Kerberos Monitoring

The final question should always be:

If one side of this trust is compromised,
what security impact can that compromise
have on the other side?

That question captures the real security significance of Active Directory trust tickets.

docs.title: Active Directory Domain and Forest Trusts
docs.text:
Active Directory trusts allow authentication and resource access to cross domain or forest boundaries.

Trusts are fundamental to many enterprise Active Directory environments because organisations may operate:

Multiple Domains
Child Domains
Multiple Forests
Legacy Domains
Acquired Companies
Partner Environments
Resource Forests
Administrative Forests

A trust creates a relationship in which one domain or forest may accept authentication originating from another.

Conceptually:

Domain A
   |
   | Trust
   v
Domain B

However, a trust does not automatically mean:

Every User in Domain A
        |
        v
Full Access to Domain B

Authentication and authorisation remain separate concepts.

The important security question is:

Which identities from one security boundary
can authenticate to and access resources
inside another security boundary?

During an authorised Active Directory assessment, trust analysis should determine:

Which Trusts Exist?
What Type Are They?
Which Direction Do They Operate?
Are They Transitive?
What Authentication Model Is Used?
What SID Filtering Is Applied?
What Resources Are Accessible?
Are Privileged Relationships Crossing the Trust?

Authorised testing only

Trust enumeration can reveal relationships with domains, forests, subsidiaries or partner organisations that are outside the assessment scope. The existence of a trust does not automatically authorise testing of the trusted or trusting environment. Treat every domain and forest as a separate scope boundary unless explicitly stated otherwise.

docs.title: Trusts at a Glance
docs.text:
A trust relationship can be represented as:

Domain A
   |
   v
Trust Relationship
   |
   v
Domain B

The practical security path is:

Identity
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Trust
   |
   v
Remote Domain / Forest
   |
   v
Authorisation
   |
   v
Resource

The existence of a trust establishes an authentication relationship.

Actual access still depends on:

Groups
ACLs
Local Permissions
Share Permissions
Application Permissions
Authentication Policies
SID Filtering
Selective Authentication

docs.title: Why Trusts Exist
docs.text:
Organisations use trusts to provide controlled access between administrative boundaries.

Examples include:

Parent and Child Domains
Corporate Forests
Resource Forests
Mergers and Acquisitions
Legacy Environments
Partner Organisations
Migration Environments

Without a trust, identities from one domain normally cannot automatically authenticate to resources in another independent domain.

docs.title: Trust Terminology
docs.text:
Several terms must be understood before analysing trust relationships:

Trusting Domain
Trusted Domain
Trust Direction
Transitivity
Trust Type
Forest Trust
External Trust
Realm Trust
Parent-Child Trust
Tree-Root Trust
SID Filtering
Selective Authentication

docs.title: Trusted Domain
docs.text:
The:

Trusted Domain

contains the identities that are trusted.

Conceptually:

Domain A trusts Domain B

means:

Users from Domain B
may be accepted by Domain A

Therefore:

Domain B
=
Trusted Domain

docs.title: Trusting Domain
docs.text:
The:

Trusting Domain

contains resources that may accept identities from the trusted domain.

If:

Domain A trusts Domain B

then:

Domain A
=
Trusting Domain

and:

Domain B
=
Trusted Domain

docs.title: Trust Direction
docs.text:
Trust direction is one of the most commonly misunderstood Active Directory concepts.

Suppose:

CORP.LOCAL
trusts
PARTNER.LOCAL

The authentication relationship is:

PARTNER.LOCAL users
        |
        v
CORP.LOCAL resources

because CORP trusts identities from PARTNER.

docs.title: One-Way Trust
docs.text:
A one-way trust operates in one direction.

Example:

CORP.LOCAL
    |
    | trusts
    v
PARTNER.LOCAL

Authentication flows conceptually in the opposite direction:

PARTNER users
      |
      v
CORP resources

This distinction is essential during trust analysis.

docs.title: Two-Way Trust
docs.text:
A two-way trust allows both domains to trust identities from the other.

Domain A
   <---->
Domain B

Conceptually:

Domain A Users
      |
      v
Domain B Resources

and:

Domain B Users
      |
      v
Domain A Resources

subject to authorisation.

docs.title: Trust Direction Values
docs.text:
Active Directory tools may display trust direction using values such as:

Inbound
Outbound
Bidirectional

Always interpret the value from the perspective of the domain being queried.

Do not rely solely on visual arrows without understanding the querying context.

docs.title: Transitive Trusts
docs.text:
A transitive trust can extend beyond the two directly connected domains.

Example:

Domain A
   |
   v
Domain B
   |
   v
Domain C

A transitive trust relationship may allow authentication relationships to extend across the chain.

docs.title: Non-Transitive Trusts
docs.text:
A non-transitive trust applies only between the directly configured domains.

Domain A
   |
   v
Domain B

does not automatically extend to:

Domain C

docs.title: Trust Types
docs.text:
Important Active Directory trust types include:

Parent-Child Trust
Tree-Root Trust
External Trust
Forest Trust
Shortcut Trust
Realm Trust

Each has different security implications.

docs.title: Parent-Child Trust
docs.text:
When a child domain is created inside an existing forest, Active Directory automatically creates a:

Two-Way
Transitive
Parent-Child Trust

Example:

corp.example
     |
     v
emea.corp.example

The domains belong to the same forest.

docs.title: Parent-Child Trust Model
docs.text:
corp.example
      ^
      |
Two-Way Transitive Trust
      |
      v
emea.corp.example

This supports authentication across the forest.

docs.title: Tree-Root Trust
docs.text:
When a new domain tree is created inside an existing forest, Active Directory creates a:

Two-Way
Transitive
Tree-Root Trust

Example:

corp.example
      |
      | Forest
      |
      +------ example-services.net

The DNS namespaces differ, but both domain trees belong to the same forest.

docs.title: Forest Trust
docs.text:
A forest trust connects:

Forest A

and:

Forest B

Example:

corp.example
     |
     | Forest Trust
     |
partner.example

Forest trusts can be:

One-Way
Two-Way

and can provide transitive authentication relationships between domains in the participating forests according to the trust configuration.

docs.title: Forest Trust Security Boundary
docs.text:
A forest is generally the primary Active Directory security boundary.

Therefore:

Domain Boundary

and:

Forest Boundary

should not be treated as equivalent.

Within a single forest, domains have strong trust relationships and share forest-wide infrastructure.

docs.title: External Trust
docs.text:
An external trust is commonly used between:

Domains in Different Forests

without establishing a forest-wide trust.

External trusts are generally:

Non-Transitive

and apply to the specific domains involved.

docs.title: External Trust Model
docs.text:
corp.example
      |
      | External Trust
      |
legacy.example

The relationship does not automatically extend to every domain in either forest.

docs.title: Shortcut Trust
docs.text:
Shortcut trusts can be created between domains in the same forest to shorten authentication paths.

Example:

child-a.corp.example
          |
          | Shortcut Trust
          |
child-b.corp.example

This may improve authentication efficiency in complex domain trees.

docs.title: Realm Trust
docs.text:
Realm trusts allow Active Directory to establish trust relationships with non-Windows Kerberos realms.

Conceptually:

Active Directory
      |
      | Realm Trust
      |
      v
Kerberos Realm

Realm trusts can have different:

Direction
Transitivity
Authentication

properties.

docs.title: Trust Enumeration Strategy
docs.text:
A structured trust assessment should follow:

Identify Current Domain
        |
        v
Identify Current Forest
        |
        v
Enumerate Domain Trusts
        |
        v
Enumerate Forest Trusts
        |
        v
Determine Direction
        |
        v
Determine Transitivity
        |
        v
Review Trust Attributes
        |
        v
Identify Cross-Domain Groups
        |
        v
Identify Cross-Domain ACLs
        |
        v
Identify Accessible Resources
        |
        v
Assess Security Controls

docs.text:
Native Windows:

$env:USERDNSDOMAIN

Alternative:

whoami /fqdn

Domain controller discovery:

nltest /dsgetdc:corp.example

docs.text:
With the ActiveDirectory PowerShell module:

Get-ADForest

Useful properties include:

Name

docs.text:
Get-ADForest | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Domains

Example:

docs.text:
Get-ADDomain
