docs.text: Get-ADDomain | Select-Object -ExpandProperty ChildDomains

docs.title: Native Trust Enumeration
docs.text:
Windows provides:

nltest.exe

which can help inspect trust relationships.

Example:

nltest /domain_trusts

This can display known trust relationships for the current domain.

docs.title: Detailed NLTest Output
docs.text:
nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts

Review the returned trust information carefully.

Do not assume every displayed domain is within assessment scope.

docs.title: Domain Controller Discovery
docs.text:
For a known trusted domain:

nltest /dsgetdc:partner.example

This performs domain controller discovery.

Use only where querying the domain is within the approved scope.

docs.title: ActiveDirectory PowerShell Trust Enumeration
docs.text:
The ActiveDirectory module provides:

Get-ADTrust -Filter *

Useful properties include:

Name
Source
Target
Direction
ForestTransitive
IntraForest
SelectiveAuthentication
SIDFilteringForestAware
SIDFilteringQuarantined
TrustType

docs.title: Focused Trust Output
docs.text:
Get-ADTrust -Filter * |
    Select-Object Name,Source,Target,Direction,TrustType,ForestTransitive,IntraForest,SelectiveAuthentication

This provides a useful high-level trust inventory.

docs.title: Query a Specific Trust
docs.text:
Get-ADTrust -Identity 'partner.example'

Use this when reviewing a known relationship rather than repeatedly enumerating every trust.

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView can enumerate domain trust relationships.

Depending on the PowerView version, commonly used functions include:

Get-DomainTrust

and:

Get-DomainTrustMapping

Always verify the available functions in the version being used.

Example:

Get-Command Get-DomainTrust -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: PowerView Domain Trusts
docs.text:
Where available:

Get-DomainTrust

can provide information about trust relationships known to the current domain.

docs.title: Trust Mapping
docs.text:
Where supported:

Get-DomainTrustMapping

can help visualise relationships across domains.

Do not automatically query domains outside the authorised scope.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound is particularly useful for understanding how trust relationships interact with:

Group Membership
ACLs
Sessions
Administrative Rights
Cross-Domain Principals

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: Trusts in BloodHound
docs.text:
Trust relationships can provide context for paths such as:

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
Foreign Group Membership
 |
 v
Trusted Domain
 |
 v
Administrative Relationship

The trust itself is only part of the path.

docs.title: BloodHound Trust Analysis
docs.text:
Useful questions include:

Which Domains Exist?

Which Forests Exist?

Which Trusts Connect Them?

Are Foreign Principals Members of Privileged Groups?

Do Cross-Domain ACLs Exist?

Can One Domain Administer Systems in Another?

docs.title: Linux Trust Enumeration
docs.text:
Trust information can also be queried from Linux using LDAP and Active Directory tooling.

Useful tools include:

ldapsearch
NetExec
Impacket
BloodHound Collectors

docs.title: LDAP Trusted Domain Objects
docs.text:
Active Directory stores trust relationships as:

trustedDomain

objects.

These are normally located beneath:

CN=System

in the domain naming context.

docs.title: LDAP Trust Search
docs.text:
Example:

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
  -D 'audituser@corp.example' -W \
  -b 'CN=System,DC=corp,DC=example' \
  '(objectClass=trustedDomain)' \
  cn trustDirection trustType trustAttributes securityIdentifier

This is enumeration only.

docs.title: Important Trust Attributes
docs.text:
Useful LDAP attributes include:

trustDirection
trustType
trustAttributes
securityIdentifier
flatName
trustPartner

These values help determine the nature of the trust.

docs.title: Trust Direction Values in LDAP
docs.text:
The trustDirection attribute is represented numerically.

Common values are:

0 = Disabled
1 = Inbound
2 = Outbound
3 = Bidirectional

Interpret direction from the perspective of the domain containing the trust object.

docs.title: Trust Type Values
docs.text:
The trustType attribute identifies the trust mechanism.

Common values include:

1 = Windows non-Active Directory
2 = Active Directory
3 = MIT Kerberos realm

Do not rely on the numeric value alone.

Also evaluate:

trustAttributes

and the environment.

docs.title: Trust Attributes
docs.text:
trustAttributes is a bit field describing trust characteristics.

Possible characteristics can include:

Non-Transitive
Uplevel
Quarantined Domain
Forest Transitive
Cross-Organisation
Within Forest
Treat-As-External
Uses RC4 Encryption
Cross-Organisation No TGT Delegation
PIM Trust

Interpret these carefully because multiple flags can exist simultaneously.

docs.title: Trust Analysis
docs.text:
Trust enumeration should produce a table similar to:

Source Target Direction Type Transitive Selective Authentication corp.example emea.corp.example Bidirectional Parent-Child Yes No corp.example partner.example Bidirectional Forest Yes Yes corp.example legacy.example Outbound External No No

The values above are illustrative only.

docs.title: Authentication vs Authorisation
docs.text:
A trust answers:

Can this identity be recognised?

It does not automatically answer:

What can this identity access?

The full model is:

Identity
   |
   v
Trust
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Authorisation
   |
   v
Resource

docs.title: Cross-Domain Group Membership
docs.text:
One of the most important trust assessment areas is:

Foreign Principal
      |
      v
Local Domain Group
      |
      v
Privilege

For example:

PARTNER\User
      |
      v
CORP\Server-Admins
      |
      v
Administrative Access

This may be more important than the trust configuration itself.

docs.title: Foreign Security Principals
docs.text:
Active Directory can represent security principals from trusted domains using:

Foreign Security Principals

typically beneath:

CN=ForeignSecurityPrincipals

docs.title: ForeignSecurityPrincipals Container
docs.text:
Conceptually:

CN=ForeignSecurityPrincipals
        |
        +--> Foreign SID
        |
        +--> Foreign SID
        |
        +--> Foreign SID

These objects can represent users or groups from trusted domains that have been referenced in the local domain.

docs.title: Enumerate Foreign Security Principals
docs.text:
With the ActiveDirectory module:

Get-ADObject -SearchBase 'CN=ForeignSecurityPrincipals,DC=corp,DC=example' -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=foreignSecurityPrincipal)' -Properties *

Review:

Name
ObjectSID
MemberOf

where available.

docs.title: Foreign Group Membership
docs.text:
A foreign identity may be added to a local domain group.

Example:

PARTNER\Domain Admins
         |
         v
CORP\Application-Admins
         |
         v
Server Administration

This can create a significant cross-boundary privilege path.

docs.title: Enumerate Group Members
docs.text:
Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Application-Admins'

Investigate unexpected:

ForeignSecurityPrincipal

entries.

docs.title: Recursive Membership
docs.text:
Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Application-Admins' -Recursive

Recursive membership can help reveal nested cross-domain relationships.

docs.title: Domain Local Groups
docs.text:
Domain Local groups are particularly relevant to cross-domain access because they can contain principals from trusted domains and grant access to resources in the local domain.

Conceptually:

Trusted Domain User
        |
        v
Domain Local Group
        |
        v
Local Resource

docs.title: AGDLP
docs.text:
A common Active Directory permissions model is:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

or:

A
|
G
|
DL
|
P

Trust analysis should therefore include:

Domain Local Group Membership

rather than looking only for direct ACL assignments.

docs.title: AGUDLP
docs.text:
Multi-domain environments may use:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Universal Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

or:

A
|
G
|
U
|
DL
|
P

This can make privilege relationships span several domains.

docs.title: Universal Groups
docs.text:
Universal groups can contain principals from multiple domains within the forest.

They are therefore important when reviewing forest-wide privilege relationships.

docs.title: Enterprise Admins
docs.text:
The:

Enterprise Admins

group exists in the forest root domain.

It has highly privileged capabilities across the forest.

A compromise involving Enterprise Admin-level control should therefore be treated as:

Forest-Wide Security Impact

rather than merely a compromise of one domain.

docs.title: Schema Admins
docs.text:
The:

Schema Admins

group also exists in the forest root domain.

Schema modifications affect the forest-wide Active Directory schema.

Membership should be extremely limited.

docs.title: Forest Is the Security Boundary
docs.text:
A critical principle is:

Forest
=
Primary Active Directory Security Boundary

Domains within a forest provide:

Administrative Organisation
Policy Boundaries
Replication Boundaries
Naming Boundaries

but should not normally be treated as strong isolation boundaries against a fully compromised domain with sufficiently privileged control.

docs.title: Intra-Forest Trusts
docs.text:
Within a forest:

Parent-Child
Tree-Root

trusts are automatically:

Two-Way
Transitive

This allows authentication throughout the forest.

docs.title: Cross-Forest Trusts
docs.text:
Between separate forests, security controls become especially important.

Relevant controls include:

SID Filtering
Selective Authentication
Authentication Policies
Network Segmentation
Group Membership
ACL Review

docs.title: SID Filtering
docs.text:
SID filtering is designed to prevent inappropriate SIDs from one trust boundary being accepted across another.

Conceptually:

Authentication Token
       |
       v
SID Filtering
       |
       +--> Expected SIDs
       |
       X
       |
       +--> Disallowed SIDs

docs.title: Why SID Filtering Matters
docs.text:
Windows access tokens can contain multiple SIDs.

Without appropriate filtering, manipulated or inappropriate SID information crossing a trust could potentially affect authorisation decisions.

SID filtering therefore protects trust boundaries.

docs.title: SIDHistory
docs.text:
Active Directory supports:

sIDHistory

to assist migration scenarios.

A migrated account can retain SIDs associated with previous identities so that existing permissions continue to work.

Conceptually:

New Account SID
      +
Old SID in SIDHistory
      |
      v
Existing Resource ACL

docs.title: SIDHistory Security Relevance
docs.text:
SIDHistory is legitimate functionality.

However, excessive or inappropriate SIDHistory values can create unexpected privilege relationships.

Trust analysis should therefore consider:

SID Filtering
SIDHistory
Migration Configuration
Cross-Domain Permissions

A dedicated SIDHistory page will cover this topic in more depth.

docs.title: Enumerate SIDHistory
docs.text:
Where authorised:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties SIDHistory |
    Where-Object { $_.SIDHistory } |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,SID,SIDHistory

For groups:

Get-ADGroup -Filter * -Properties SIDHistory |
    Where-Object { $_.SIDHistory } |
    Select-Object Name,SID,SIDHistory

Large environments should use appropriately scoped LDAP filters rather than unnecessarily retrieving every account.

docs.title: Selective Authentication
docs.text:
Forest and external trusts can use:

Selective Authentication

to restrict which trusted identities are permitted to authenticate to specific systems.

Without selective authentication, the trust may permit broader authentication across the trusting environment, subject to resource authorisation.

docs.title: Selective Authentication Model
docs.text:
Without selective authentication:

Trusted Domain
      |
      v
Broad Authentication Relationship
      |
      v
Resource Authorisation

With selective authentication:

Trusted Domain
      |
      v
Allowed to Authenticate?
      |
      +--> No --> Stop
      |
      +--> Yes
             |
             v
      Resource Authorisation

docs.title: Allowed to Authenticate
docs.text:
Selective authentication uses the:

Allowed to authenticate

extended right on computer objects and other applicable security principals.

This provides an additional boundary before normal resource authorisation.

docs.title: Enumerate Selective Authentication
docs.text:
Using the ActiveDirectory module:

Get-ADTrust -Filter * |
    Select-Object Name,Direction,SelectiveAuthentication

A value indicating selective authentication is enabled should then be evaluated alongside actual delegated authentication rights.

docs.title: Trust Authentication Scope
docs.text:
During assessment, determine:

Can Foreign Users Authenticate Everywhere?

Or:

Can Foreign Users Authenticate Only to Approved Systems?

The latter generally provides stronger cross-boundary isolation.

docs.title: Forest-Wide Authentication
docs.text:
Forest trusts can be configured for broader forest-wide authentication.

This may be operationally convenient but increases the importance of:

Resource ACLs
Group Membership
Network Controls
Privilege Separation

docs.title: Trust Passwords
docs.text:
Active Directory trusts maintain secret material used to support authentication between domains.

These secrets should be treated as highly sensitive.

Trust account compromise can have serious security implications.

docs.title: Trusted Domain Objects
docs.text:
Trust relationships are represented by:

trustedDomain

objects in Active Directory.

Conceptually:

CN=System
   |
   v
Trusted Domain Object
   |
   +--> Trust Partner
   +--> Direction
   +--> Type
   +--> Attributes
   +--> Security Information

docs.title: Trust Accounts
docs.text:
Inter-domain trust relationships can involve special trust account representations.

These are not normal user accounts and should not be managed as ordinary identities.

docs.title: Trust Secret Rotation
docs.text:
Trust passwords are managed by Windows as part of the trust relationship.

Administrators should avoid manually manipulating trust secrets unless following documented Microsoft procedures.

docs.title: Trust Tickets
docs.text:
Kerberos trust relationships allow referral tickets to support authentication across domains.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Domain A KDC
 |
 v
Referral
 |
 v
Domain B KDC
 |
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Resource

docs.title: Cross-Domain Kerberos
docs.text:
Suppose:

user@CHILD.CORP.EXAMPLE

needs access to:

fileserver.corp.example

Kerberos can use trust referrals to move authentication toward the domain responsible for the destination service.

docs.title: Kerberos Referral Model
docs.text:
User
 |
 v
Source KDC
 |
 v
Inter-Domain Referral
 |
 v
Target KDC
 |
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Target Service

See:

Kerberos

and:

Kerberos Tickets

docs.title: Inspect Kerberos Tickets
docs.text:
Windows:

klist

Linux:

klist

Cross-domain activity may result in referral-related tickets appearing in the cache.

docs.title: Trust Tickets and Security Testing
docs.text:
Trust-ticket abuse can have significant cross-domain consequences when sufficiently privileged trust material is compromised.

This should be tested only in:

Dedicated Labs
Explicitly Approved Scenarios

because the impact can cross domain and forest boundaries.

A dedicated Trust Tickets page should contain the detailed methodology.

docs.title: Trusts and DNS
docs.text:
Cross-domain authentication often depends on DNS.

Important records can include:

Domain Controllers
Kerberos
LDAP
Global Catalog

docs.title: SRV Records
docs.text:
Example:

dig _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.partner.example SRV

Kerberos:

dig _kerberos._tcp.partner.example SRV

Only query trusted domains included in the authorised scope.

docs.title: Windows DNS Lookup
docs.text: Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV '_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.partner.example'

docs.title: Trusts and Network Connectivity
docs.text:
A trust may exist while network controls prevent direct access.

Example:

Forest A
   |
   | Trust
   |
Forest B

but:

Forest A Workstation
        |
        X
        |
Forest B Server

This can be an intentional and effective control.

docs.title: Trust Does Not Equal Network Reachability
docs.text:
The full relationship is:

Trust
  +
Network Path
  +
Authentication
  +
Authorisation
  =
Resource Access

Removing any required component can prevent access.

docs.title: Trusts and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
A trust can expand the potential lateral-movement graph.

Example:

Compromised User
      |
      v
Domain A Group
      |
      v
Foreign Group Membership
      |
      v
Domain B Server

See:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Trusts and Pivoting
docs.text:
Network segmentation may require a pivot before systems in another trusted domain are reachable.

Domain A
   |
   v
Pivot
   |
   v
Domain B Network

See:

Pivoting

The trust and network path should be assessed separately.

docs.title: Trusts and ACLs
docs.text:
Cross-domain principals may appear in Active Directory ACLs.

Example:

PARTNER\Security-Team
          |
          v
GenericAll
          |
          v
CORP\ServiceAccount

This could create an unexpected cross-domain privilege path.

See:

ACL and ACE

docs.title: Trusts and Group Policy
docs.text:
Foreign principals may receive administrative rights through:

Group Policy

For example:

Foreign Group
      |
      v
GPO
      |
      v
Local Administrators
      |
      v
Servers

See:

Group Policy

docs.title: Trusts and Local Administrators
docs.text:
Check whether trusted-domain groups have been added to local administrative groups.

Example:

PARTNER\IT-Support
       |
       v
Local Administrators
       |
       v
CORP Server

This may be legitimate, but it significantly expands the security dependency between environments.

docs.title: Trusts and Service Accounts
docs.text:
Service accounts from one domain may be granted access to resources in another.

Review:

Service Accounts
gMSAs
Application Pools
Scheduled Tasks
SQL Services
Backup Accounts
Monitoring Accounts

for cross-domain dependencies.

See:

gMSA

docs.title: Trusts and SQL Server
docs.text:
SQL Server deployments can introduce cross-domain access through:

Windows Authentication
Service Accounts
Linked Servers
Administrative Groups

These relationships should be included when analysing trust exposure.

docs.title: Trusts and File Servers
docs.text:
Cross-domain access frequently exists on file servers.

Review:

Share Permissions
NTFS Permissions
Domain Local Groups
Foreign Security Principals

Do not assume that trust access is limited to Active Directory objects.

docs.title: Trusts and RDP
docs.text:
Foreign users may have:

Remote Desktop Users

or local administrator rights on systems in another domain.

This can create direct cross-domain interactive access.

docs.title: Trusts and WinRM
docs.text:
Trusted-domain users may also have WinRM rights through:

Local Administrators
Remote Management Users
JEA Configuration
Custom Endpoint Permissions

See:

WinRM

docs.title: Trusts and SMB
docs.text:
Cross-domain SMB access may occur through:

Share ACL
NTFS ACL
Domain Local Group
Foreign Principal

See:

SMB

docs.title: Trusts and WMI / DCOM
docs.text:
Administrative identities from trusted domains may also have remote WMI or DCOM access.

See:

WMI

and:

DCOM

docs.title: Trusts and NTLM
docs.text:
Trust relationships are primarily associated with domain authentication mechanisms, but NTLM may still appear in cross-domain environments depending on:

Name Resolution
Application Behaviour
Legacy Systems
Trust Type
Authentication Configuration

See:

NTLM

docs.title: Trusts and Kerberos
docs.text:
Kerberos is central to normal Active Directory cross-domain authentication.

Trust analysis should therefore understand:

Referral TGTs
SPNs
KDC Discovery
DNS
Trust Direction

See:

Kerberos

docs.title: Cross-Forest Administrative Dependencies
docs.text:
A major security concern is:

Forest A
   |
   v
Privileged Account
   |
   v
Administration
   |
   v
Forest B

This means compromise of Forest A may have security consequences for Forest B even if the forests are technically separate security boundaries.

docs.title: Privileged Cross-Forest Groups
docs.text:
Review whether foreign principals are members of:

Administrators
Server Admin Groups
Backup Operators
Remote Management Groups
Application Admin Groups
Database Admin Groups
Virtualisation Admin Groups

in another forest.

docs.title: Shared Administrative Accounts
docs.text:
Avoid designs where the same privileged account is used across independent forests.

A stronger model is:

Forest A Admin
      |
      X
      |
Forest B

Forest B Admin
      |
      v
Forest B

with dedicated credentials for each boundary.

docs.title: Trust and Tier 0
docs.text:
Any trust relationship that provides access to:

Domain Controllers
AD CS
Identity Infrastructure
Federation Services
Privileged Access Systems

should receive particular scrutiny.

These systems may effectively belong to:

Tier 0

or an equivalent privileged control plane.

docs.title: AD CS Across Trusts
docs.text:
Certificate authentication can also interact with multi-domain and multi-forest environments.

Review:

Enterprise CAs
Certificate Templates
Enrollment Permissions
Certificate Mapping
Forest Membership
Trust Relationships

See:

Active Directory Certificate Services

docs.title: Forest Trust Authentication Controls
docs.text:
When separate forests require a trust, consider:

One-Way Trust Where Possible
Selective Authentication
SID Filtering
Minimal Group Membership
Network Segmentation
Dedicated Administrative Accounts
Monitoring

docs.title: Trust Direction Principle
docs.text:
If only:

Forest B users

need access to:

Forest A resources

do not automatically create:

Two-Way Trust

if a:

One-Way Trust

meets the business requirement.

docs.title: Minimise Transitivity
docs.text:
Where a trust does not need to extend beyond specific domains, avoid unnecessarily broad transitive relationships.

This reduces the authentication scope.

docs.title: Selective Authentication Principle
docs.text:
For higher-risk forest relationships, consider:

Selective Authentication

so that foreign identities cannot authenticate broadly across the trusting forest.

docs.title: SID Filtering Principle
docs.text:
SID filtering should remain enabled where appropriate.

Do not disable SID filtering merely to make a legacy application work without first understanding the security consequences.

docs.title: Migration Considerations
docs.text:
Some trust controls are weakened temporarily during:

Domain Migration
Forest Migration
Mergers
Acquisitions

For example, migration designs may rely on:

SIDHistory

These temporary configurations should have:

Documented Purpose
Defined Owner
Expiration Date
Post-Migration Review

docs.title: Legacy Trusts
docs.text:
Trusts frequently remain after the original business requirement has disappeared.

Examples:

Completed Migration
Old Subsidiary
Retired Application
Former Partner
Legacy Forest

Unused trusts should be reviewed and removed through controlled administrative procedures.

docs.title: Trust Enumeration Is Not Exploitation
docs.text:
Discovering:

partner.example

through a trust does not mean the tester should:

Enumerate Every Partner Host

The correct workflow is:

Discover Trust
      |
      v
Record Relationship
      |
      v
Check Scope
      |
      +--> Out of Scope --> Stop
      |
      +--> In Scope
             |
             v
      Continue Assessment

docs.title: Safe Trust Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
A controlled trust assessment should follow:

Identify Current Domain
        |
        v
Identify Forest
        |
        v
Enumerate Trust Objects
        |
        v
Map Direction
        |
        v
Map Transitivity
        |
        v
Identify Security Controls
        |
        v
Identify Foreign Principals
        |
        v
Identify Cross-Domain Groups
        |
        v
Identify Cross-Domain ACLs
        |
        v
Validate Minimum Access
        |
        v
Document Security Impact

docs.title: Step 1 - Identify Domain
docs.text: Get-ADDomain

docs.title: Step 2 - Identify Forest
docs.text: Get-ADForest

docs.title: Step 3 - Enumerate Trusts
docs.text: Get-ADTrust -Filter *

docs.title: Step 4 - Record Direction
docs.text:
For every trust, determine:

Inbound
Outbound
Bidirectional

from the perspective of the current domain.

docs.title: Step 5 - Record Type
docs.text:
Determine whether the relationship is:

Parent-Child
Tree-Root
Forest
External
Shortcut
Realm

docs.title: Step 6 - Record Transitivity
docs.text:
Determine:

Transitive

or:

Non-Transitive

docs.title: Step 7 - Review Controls
docs.text:
Review:

SID Filtering
Selective Authentication
Forest-Wide Authentication
Network Segmentation

docs.title: Step 8 - Review Foreign Principals
docs.text:
Identify foreign identities referenced by:

Groups
ACLs
Local Administrators
Applications
File Shares

docs.title: Step 9 - Validate Access
docs.text:
If validation is required, use the minimum safe action.

For example:

Read an Approved Test Share

or:

Query an Approved LDAP Object

may be sufficient.

Do not jump directly to remote command execution.

docs.title: Step 10 - Document Boundary
docs.text:
Record exactly which security boundary was crossed.

Example:

Source:
CORP.EXAMPLE

Target:
PARTNER.EXAMPLE

Trust:
One-Way Forest Trust

Authentication:
Selective Authentication Enabled

Authorisation:
CORP\App-Support granted access to PARTNER\APP01

docs.title: Trust Evidence Checklist
docs.text:
Record:

Source Domain
Source Forest
Target Domain
Target Forest
Trust Name
Trust Type
Trust Direction
Transitivity
Trust Attributes
Selective Authentication
SID Filtering
Forest-Wide Authentication
Source Domain SID
Target Domain SID
Foreign Security Principals
Cross-Domain Group Membership
Cross-Domain ACLs
Cross-Domain Local Admin Rights
Accessible Resources
Authentication Protocol
Network Path
Timestamp
Tool
Exact Validation

docs.title: Evidence Handling
docs.text:
Avoid including unnecessary:

Passwords
NTLM Hashes
Kerberos Tickets
Trust Secrets
Private Keys

in assessment evidence.

If sensitive material must be retained:

Encrypt
Restrict
Redact
Delete When No Longer Required

docs.title: Trust Detection
docs.text:
Trust-related security monitoring should focus on:

Trust Creation
Trust Modification
Cross-Domain Authentication
Foreign Privileged Membership
SIDHistory Changes
Unexpected Kerberos Referrals
Privileged Cross-Forest Logons

docs.title: Trust Modification Events
docs.text:
Security monitoring should detect administrative changes to trust relationships.

Relevant auditing can include:

Trusted Domain Object Changes
Directory Service Changes
Administrative Activity

Event availability depends on audit policy and the specific modification.

docs.title: Event 4706
docs.text:
Windows Security Event:

4706

indicates:

A new trust was created to a domain

This should be rare and reviewed.

docs.title: Event 4707
docs.text:
Event:

4707

indicates:

A trust to a domain was removed

Unexpected trust removal should be investigated.

docs.title: Event 4716
docs.text:
Event:

4716

indicates:

Trusted domain information was modified

This is particularly important for detecting trust configuration changes.

docs.title: Directory Service Changes
docs.text:
Where Directory Service Changes auditing is configured, events such as:

5136

may provide visibility into modifications of Active Directory objects, including relevant trust-related objects.

docs.title: Cross-Domain Authentication
docs.text:
Relevant authentication events may include:

4624
4625
4648
4768
4769
4771
4776

depending on:

Protocol
Authentication Type
Domain
Target

docs.title: Kerberos Service Tickets
docs.text:
Event:

4769

can provide useful context for cross-domain Kerberos activity.

Analyse:

Account
Service
Client Address
Ticket Encryption
Domain

in combination with trust information.

docs.title: Privileged Logons
docs.text:
Event:

4672

may indicate assignment of special privileges to a new logon.

Cross-domain privileged logons should be correlated with:

Source Domain
Source Host
Target Host
Group Membership
Business Purpose

docs.title: SIDHistory Monitoring
docs.text:
Changes involving:

sIDHistory

should be tightly controlled and monitored.

Unexpected SIDHistory values can create hidden or non-obvious access relationships.

docs.title: Group Membership Monitoring
docs.text:
Monitor changes to privileged groups that introduce:

Foreign Security Principals

or groups from trusted domains.

Important examples include:

Administrators
Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Server Administration Groups
Application Administration Groups

docs.title: Trust Detection Model
docs.text:
Trust Change
    |
    v
Cross-Domain Identity
    |
    v
Authentication
    |
    v
Privileged Group / ACL
    |
    v
Sensitive Resource

Detection should correlate these layers.

docs.title: Trust Hardening
docs.text:
A strong trust security model includes:

Minimise Trusts
Use One-Way Trusts Where Possible
Limit Transitivity
Use Selective Authentication
Maintain SID Filtering
Minimise Foreign Privileged Membership
Separate Administrative Accounts
Segment Networks
Monitor Trust Changes
Review SIDHistory
Review Trusts Regularly

docs.title: Remove Unnecessary Trusts
docs.text:
Every trust should have:

Business Owner
Technical Owner
Documented Purpose
Required Direction
Required Scope
Review Date

Trusts without a valid business requirement should be considered for controlled removal.

docs.title: Prefer One-Way Trusts
docs.text:
Do not create:

Two-Way

relationships merely for convenience when:

One-Way

access meets the requirement.

docs.title: Use Selective Authentication
docs.text: For security-sensitive forest relationships, selective authentication can reduce the number of systems to which trusted-domain users may authenticate.

docs.title: Maintain SID Filtering
docs.text:
SID filtering provides important protection across trust boundaries.

Disabling it can significantly alter the trust's security properties.

docs.title: Review Foreign Privileged Membership
docs.text:

docs.title: Reporting Trust Findings
docs.text:
Do not report:

Forest Trust Exists

as a vulnerability by itself.

Report the actual security weakness.

Examples include:

Unnecessary Bidirectional Forest Trust

Selective Authentication Not Enabled Across High-Risk Forest Trust

Foreign Domain Group Has Excessive Administrative Rights

Legacy Trust Remains After Migration

Excessive Cross-Forest Administrative Dependencies

SID Filtering Disabled Across External Trust

docs.title: Example Finding - Excessive Cross-Forest Privilege
docs.text:
Finding:
Foreign Domain Group Has Administrative Access to Internal Servers

Description:
A security group originating from the trusted partner forest was a
member of a local administrative group used across multiple internal
servers.

The trust itself is required for business operations, but the foreign
group's administrative access was broader than necessary.

Impact:
Compromise of a member account in the trusted forest could provide
administrative access to systems in the internal forest.

This increases the security dependency between otherwise separate
forest security boundaries.

Recommendation:
Remove unnecessary foreign principals from privileged groups and
replace broad administrative assignments with role-specific access.

Use dedicated administrative identities and restrict cross-forest
authentication to systems where it is explicitly required.

docs.title: Example Finding - Unnecessary Two-Way Trust
docs.text:
Finding:
Forest Trust Provides Unnecessary Bidirectional Authentication

Description:
A bidirectional forest trust was configured between the corporate and
partner forests.

The documented business requirement required partner users to access
specific corporate resources but did not require corporate identities
to access partner resources.

Impact:
The bidirectional relationship unnecessarily expands authentication
relationships between the two forest security boundaries.

A compromise or configuration error in either environment may
therefore have broader security implications than required by the
business use case.

Recommendation:
Review the trust design and determine whether a one-way trust can meet
the documented business requirement.

Apply selective authentication and network restrictions to further
limit cross-forest access.

docs.title: Example Finding - Selective Authentication
docs.text:
Finding:
Broad Forest-Wide Authentication Permitted Across External Security Boundary

Description:
The forest trust allowed trusted-forest identities to authenticate
broadly to systems in the corporate forest.

Only a limited number of application servers required access from the
trusted forest.

Impact:
A compromised trusted-forest identity may be able to authenticate to a
larger number of corporate systems than required.

Although resource authorisation remains necessary, broad
authentication increases the available attack surface.

Recommendation:
Consider enabling selective authentication and grant the Allowed to
authenticate right only on systems that require cross-forest access.

Validate application compatibility before making production changes.

docs.title: Example Finding - Legacy Trust
docs.text:
Finding:
Legacy Domain Trust Remains After Migration

Description:
An Active Directory trust remained configured with a legacy domain
that was originally used during a completed migration.

No current business application or documented operational process
required the trust.

Impact:
Unused trust relationships increase Active Directory complexity and
may preserve unnecessary authentication paths to legacy environments.

If the legacy environment is less securely maintained, compromise of
that environment may create additional risk to the production domain.

Recommendation:
Confirm the trust is no longer required with the relevant system and
business owners.

Remove the trust through the organisation's normal change-management
process and verify that no applications or identities depend on it.

docs.title: Example Finding - Cross-Domain Administrative Dependency
docs.text:
Finding:
Privileged Administration Crosses Forest Security Boundaries

Description:
Administrative identities from one forest were used to manage Tier 0
or equivalent infrastructure in another forest.

This creates a direct privileged dependency between otherwise separate
forest security boundaries.

Impact:
Compromise of the source forest or its privileged administrative
accounts could affect the security of the target forest.

Recommendation:
Use separate privileged identities for each forest and prevent
privileged credentials from crossing forest security boundaries where
possible.

Use dedicated privileged administrative workstations and tightly
controlled management paths for Tier 0 administration.

docs.title: Conceptual Scope and Trust Interpretation
docs.text: This page is the broad conceptual reference for Active Directory trust types, direction, transitivity, and domain or forest security boundaries. For operational enumeration, authentication-direction testing, cross-domain access checks, and controlled validation, continue to Trust Relationships.

docs.title: Direction From the Relevant Domain
docs.text:
Trust direction is described from the perspective of the domain or forest being trusted:

Domain A trusts Domain B
   -> Domain A accepts authentication from Domain B
   -> Domain B is the trusted domain
   -> Domain A is the trusting domain

An inbound trust from the perspective of a domain means authentication is accepted into that domain from the other side. An outbound trust means the domain can authenticate toward the other side. Always state the perspective used in notes and evidence; GUI labels and command output can describe the same relationship from opposite sides.

Trust existence establishes a configured relationship. It does not by itself establish that every identity can authenticate, that authentication is accepted by a particular service, that a resource is accessible, or that administrative rights or execution are available.

docs.title: Transitivity and Boundaries
docs.text:
Transitive trust can allow the relationship to extend through an additional trusted domain or forest according to the trust architecture. It does not automatically grant resource access across every hop. Non-transitive trust is limited to the directly related domains or realms and should not be interpreted as a route through unrelated domains.

Intra-forest relationships normally rely on the forest's internal trust model and shared directory assumptions. Inter-forest and external relationships cross a more explicit administrative boundary and require careful review of authentication, SID handling, selective authentication, and resource permissions. A parent-child or tree-root relationship is not equivalent to unrestricted administrative control of every forest resource.

docs.title: Boundary Controls and Interpretation
docs.text:
SID filtering can reduce the risk of untrusted SID history being presented across a trust. Selective authentication restricts which users from the trusted side may authenticate to computers on the trusting side. Neither control should be inferred solely from the trust type: verify the effective configuration and the target resource's authorization.

Use this interpretation chain:

Observed trust
   -> Candidate authentication relationship
   -> Confirm direction, transitivity, filtering, and selective authentication
   -> Test approved identity and service/resource boundary
   -> Evidence of actual access or denial
   -> Security conclusion

Record the querying domain, trust direction, trust type, source identity, target service or resource, authentication result, authorization result, and any administrative or execution consequence separately. Do not report a trust as a vulnerability because it exists or because a graph shows a cross-domain relationship.

docs.title: Evidence and Defensive Considerations
docs.text:
Useful evidence includes the trust object and attributes, source and target domains or forests, effective SID filtering and selective-authentication settings, approved authentication test, resource ACL or group context, and relevant success or denial events. Redact unrelated domain and identity information when it is outside scope.

Defensive review should minimise trust scope, prefer one-way relationships where appropriate, use selective authentication for sensitive resources, preserve SID filtering, restrict foreign group membership, limit network paths, separate privileged administration, and monitor trust, group, ACL, and authentication changes. Retest after changes from the relevant source identity and verify both legitimate cross-domain access and denied access.

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
Unconstrained Kerberos delegation is an Active Directory configuration that allows a trusted service to act on behalf of an authenticated user when accessing other Kerberos services.

It was designed to solve the Kerberos "double-hop" problem.

A simplified legitimate use case is:

User
 |
 v
Front-End Server
 |
 | Needs to access another resource
 | as the user
 v
Back-End Server

Without delegation:

User
 |
 v
Front-End Server
 |
 X
Cannot automatically reuse the
user's authentication context
for another Kerberos service

With delegation:

User
 |
 v
Delegation-Enabled Server
 |
 | Acts on behalf of user
 v
Back-End Service

Unconstrained delegation is the broadest and least restrictive form of Kerberos delegation.

Microsoft describes it as allowing the front-end service to access other services on the client's behalf without restricting the destination services, and recommends against using unconstrained delegation because of this broad trust model.

The security concern is therefore:

Unconstrained Delegation
        |
        v
Broad Delegation Capability
        |
        v
High-Value User Authenticates
        |
        v
Delegated Authentication Material
        |
        v
Compromise of Delegation Host
        |
        v
Potential Impersonation

Authorised testing only

Unconstrained delegation testing can expose reusable Kerberos authentication material belonging to other users. Only perform active validation against accounts and systems explicitly included in scope. Avoid coercing privileged production identities to authenticate unless this has been specifically approved. A configuration finding can often be demonstrated through enumeration and controlled test accounts without interacting with real administrator credentials.

docs.title: Delegation Types
docs.text:
Active Directory supports several Kerberos delegation models.

Kerberos Delegation
       |
       +--> Unconstrained Delegation
       |
       +--> Constrained Delegation
       |
       +--> Resource-Based
            Constrained Delegation

A useful comparison is:

Delegation Type Where Trust Is Defined Scope Unconstrained Delegation Front-end service account Broad Constrained Delegation Front-end service account Specific services RBCD Back-end resource Specific principals

Microsoft currently describes unconstrained delegation as the easiest model to implement but the least secure because the services to which the front-end can act on behalf of the user are not restricted.

docs.title: The Double-Hop Problem
docs.text:
The purpose of delegation is easiest to understand through the double-hop problem.

Consider:

User
 |
 | Hop 1
 v
Web Server
 |
 | Hop 2
 v
Database Server

The user authenticates to:

WEB01

The application on WEB01 then needs to access:

SQL01

as the user.

Without delegation:

User
 |
 v
WEB01
 |
 X
No suitable delegated user
authentication for SQL01

Delegation provides a mechanism for:

WEB01
 |
 v
Act on behalf of User
 |
 v
SQL01

docs.title: Why Unconstrained Delegation Exists
docs.text:
Legacy enterprise applications commonly required:

Client
 |
 v
Application Server
 |
 v
Database / File Server

while preserving the user's identity through the entire transaction.

Examples might include:

IIS
 |
 v
SQL Server

or:

Application Server
 |
 v
File Server

Unconstrained delegation provided a simple solution.

The problem is that its trust boundary is extremely broad.

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation Model
docs.text:
The core concept is:

User
 |
 | Kerberos Authentication
 v
Server Trusted for
Unconstrained Delegation
 |
 | Delegated user context
 v
Other Kerberos Services

Unlike constrained delegation:

Unconstrained
     |
     v
Any suitable Kerberos service

rather than:

Constrained
     |
     v
Explicitly configured services

docs.title: Security Impact
docs.text:
The main security risk appears when the delegation-enabled system itself is compromised.

Privileged User
      |
      v
Authenticates to
Delegation Server
      |
      v
Delegated Kerberos
Authentication Material
      |
      v
Attacker Controls Server
      |
      v
Authentication Material Exposed
      |
      v
Potential Impersonation

The problem is therefore not simply:

Delegation enabled

but:

Delegation enabled
       +
Sensitive identity authenticates
       +
Delegation host compromised

docs.title: Why It Is Dangerous
docs.text:
A server configured for unconstrained delegation becomes an important credential boundary.

Consider:

DC01
 |
 | Administrator authenticates
 v
APP01
 |
 | Unconstrained Delegation
 v
Reusable delegated context

If:

APP01

is compromised, the attacker may gain access to authentication material belonging to identities that authenticate to it.

The compromise can therefore expand from:

APP01

to:

Other resources accessible
by those identities

docs.title: Delegation Trust Flag
docs.text:
Unconstrained delegation is represented through the:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

flag.

The corresponding userAccountControl bit is:

0x00080000

or:

524288

Microsoft documents this as:

ADS_UF_TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

This flag indicates that the account is trusted for Kerberos delegation.

docs.title: Important Distinction
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

with:

TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

They represent different delegation configurations.

A useful model is:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
        |
        v
Unconstrained Delegation


TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION
        |
        v
Protocol Transition
within Constrained Delegation

The second flag will be covered in the constrained delegation notes.

docs.title: User and Computer Accounts
docs.text:
Delegation configuration exists on the account under which the service operates.

This may be:

Computer Account

or:

User / Service Account

Examples:

WEB01$
APP01$
svc_web
svc_app

Therefore, enumeration should inspect both:

Computers

and:

Users

docs.title: Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Domain controllers are normally trusted for delegation because of their role in Active Directory.

Therefore:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

on a domain controller is not automatically a security finding.

When enumerating unconstrained delegation, separate:

Domain Controllers

from:

Non-DC Systems

The latter are generally the systems of greatest interest.
