Determine Identity Mapping
   |
   v
Determine Resulting Privilege

The important distinction is:

Template Exists
      |
      X
Template Is Exploitable

and:

Template Published
      |
      X
Template Is Vulnerable

and:

Certipy Candidate
      |
      X
Confirmed Finding

The final determination requires:

Template Configuration
        +
Effective Permissions
        +
CA Publication
        +
CA Configuration
        +
Certificate Mapping
        +
Resulting Identity

For offensive security assessments, enumeration should therefore produce an:

Attack Path Map

rather than merely an:

ESC List

For defensive assessments, it should produce a:

PKI Trust Map

showing:

Who Can Request
Who Can Modify
Who Can Approve
Who Can Administer
Which Certificates Authenticate
Which CAs Establish Trust

That map becomes the foundation for assessing ESC1 through ESC15 and any certificate-related attack paths that do not fit neatly into the ESC taxonomy.

docs.title: AD CS ESC1 - Enrollee-Supplied Subject for Authentication Certificates
docs.text:
ESC1 is an Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) privilege escalation condition where a certificate template allows an authorised enrollee to supply identity information in the certificate request and the resulting certificate can be used for authentication.

The classic attack path is:

Low-Privileged Principal
        |
        v
Can Enroll
        |
        v
Certificate Template
        |
        +--> Enrollee Supplies Subject
        |
        +--> Authentication Capability
        |
        +--> No Effective Approval Barrier
        |
        v
Certificate Request
        |
        v
Certificate Representing Another Identity
        |
        v
Certificate-Based Authentication
        |
        v
Privilege Escalation

ESC1 is dangerous because the attacker does not necessarily need to:

Know Victim Password
Steal Victim NT Hash
Steal Victim Kerberos Ticket
Reset Victim Password

Instead, the certificate infrastructure may issue new authentication material that represents another Active Directory identity.

Authorised testing only

Requesting a certificate representing another account is an active identity-impersonation action. Begin with template, ACL, CA publication, issuance, and certificate-mapping analysis. Where proof is required, use an approved test identity wherever possible and request only the minimum certificate necessary to demonstrate the issue. Treat generated PFX files and private keys as credentials.

docs.title: ESC1 Concept
docs.text:
The fundamental problem is a dangerous combination of certificate-template properties.

Conceptually:

Template
   |
   +--> Attacker Can Enroll
   |
   +--> Attacker Controls Subject Information
   |
   +--> Certificate Supports Authentication
   |
   +--> Request Can Be Issued
   |
   v
Potential Identity Impersonation

No single setting should normally be analysed in isolation.

docs.title: The Normal Certificate Enrollment Model
docs.text:
A securely designed authentication template commonly derives identity information from Active Directory.

Conceptually:

CORP\alice
    |
    v
Certificate Request
    |
    v
CA Reads Alice's AD Identity
    |
    v
Certificate for Alice

The requester cannot simply decide:

I want to be Administrator

because the identity is derived from the requester's directory object.

docs.title: The ESC1 Model
docs.text:
With an unsafe enrollee-supplied subject configuration:

CORP\alice
    |
    v
Certificate Request
    |
    +--> Requester Supplies Identity Information
    |
    v
Certificate Authority
    |
    v
Certificate

If other conditions permit, the supplied identity may represent a different account.

Conceptually:

alice
  |
  v
Certificate Request
  |
  +--> Identity = privileged-user@corp.example
  |
  v
Authentication Certificate

This creates an identity issuance problem.

docs.title: Why ESC1 Matters
docs.text:
ESC1 can turn:

Certificate Enrollment Permission

into:

Account Impersonation

and potentially:

Privilege Escalation

The resulting severity depends heavily on which identity can be represented.

For example:

Domain User
   |
   v
ESC1 Template
   |
   v
Privileged User Certificate
   |
   v
Privileged Authentication

can represent a severe trust-boundary failure.

docs.title: ESC1 Preconditions
docs.text:
A classic ESC1 candidate generally involves several conditions.

A useful assessment model is:

1. Enterprise CA Exists
2. CA Publishes Template
3. Attacker Has Enrollment Rights
4. Enrollee Can Supply Subject Information
5. Certificate Can Be Used for Authentication
6. Issuance Requirements Do Not Block Request
7. Certificate Mapping Permits the Intended Identity

Every relevant condition should be validated.

docs.title: Condition 1 - Enterprise CA
docs.text:
The template must be usable through an issuing Enterprise CA.

Conceptually:

Template Exists
      |
      X
Automatically Exploitable

Instead:

Template Exists
      |
      v
CA Publishes Template
      |
      v
Certificate Can Be Requested

docs.title: Condition 2 - Enrollment Permission
docs.text:
The attacker's effective security context must be able to request the certificate.

Enrollment might be granted directly to:

User
Group
Computer
Service Account

or indirectly through nested groups.

Example:

alice
  |
  v
Domain Users
  |
  v
Enroll
  |
  v
ESC1 Template

docs.title: Broad Enrollment Groups
docs.text:
Common groups requiring attention include:

Domain Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Computers
Everyone
Large Department Groups
Large VPN Groups
Large Application Groups

Broad enrollment is not automatically a vulnerability.

The risk comes from its combination with security-sensitive template settings.

docs.title: Condition 3 - Enrollee Supplies Subject
docs.text:
The central ESC1 template setting is commonly represented by:

CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT

with value:

0x00000001

in:

msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag

In the Certificate Templates console this is associated with:

Subject Name
    |
    v
Supply in the request

This means identity information can originate from the certificate request rather than being entirely constructed from the requester's Active Directory object.

docs.title: Microsoft Processing Model
docs.text:
At a high level:

Enrollee Supplies Subject Disabled
        |
        v
CA Uses Directory-Derived Identity Rules

versus:

Enrollee Supplies Subject Enabled
        |
        v
Request Contains Subject Information
        |
        v
CA Processes Request-Supplied Identity

This distinction is central to ESC1.

docs.title: Subject Alternative Name
docs.text:
The:

Subject Alternative Name

or:

SAN

can contain identity information.

Examples include:

UPN
DNS Name
Email Address

depending on certificate type and request.

For Active Directory authentication, UPN and other mapping information can become security-sensitive.

docs.title: UPN SAN
docs.text:
A User Principal Name might look like:

alice@corp.example

A dangerous identity substitution could conceptually be:

Requesting User:
alice@corp.example

Requested Identity:
privileged-user@corp.example

Whether the resulting certificate authenticates as that account depends on the complete certificate mapping and security configuration.

docs.title: DNS SAN
docs.text:
Computer-oriented certificate paths may involve DNS identities.

Example:

dc01.corp.example

The exact authentication implications differ from user UPN mappings and must be analysed separately.

docs.title: Condition 4 - Authentication Capability
docs.text:
Supplying another identity is not enough.

The certificate must also be useful for authentication.

Important EKUs and application policies can include:

Client Authentication
Smart Card Logon
PKINIT Client Authentication
Any Purpose

Certificates with no restrictive EKU may also require careful analysis depending on the Windows PKI context.

docs.title: Client Authentication
docs.text:
The Client Authentication EKU is:

1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2

A template containing this EKU may issue certificates suitable for client authentication.

docs.title: Smart Card Logon
docs.text:
The Smart Card Logon EKU is:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.2

This is directly relevant to Windows certificate-based logon scenarios.

docs.title: PKINIT Client Authentication
docs.text:
The PKINIT Client Authentication EKU is:

1.3.6.1.5.2.3.4

PKINIT allows public-key credentials to participate in Kerberos authentication.

docs.title: Any Purpose
docs.text:
The Any Purpose EKU is:

2.5.29.37.0

A broadly usable certificate deserves careful review because its purposes are not narrowly constrained.

docs.title: No EKU
docs.text:
Do not assume:

No EKU
   =
Cannot Authenticate

Certificates without restrictive EKUs can have broad usage semantics in some Windows PKI contexts.

Always evaluate the complete certificate and authentication path.

docs.title: Condition 5 - Issuance Requirements
docs.text:
A dangerous subject configuration may still be protected by issuance controls.

Review:

CA Certificate Manager Approval
Authorized Signatures
Enrollment Agent Requirements
Other Issuance Policies

docs.title: Manager Approval
docs.text:
If the template requires:

CA Certificate Manager Approval

the workflow becomes:

Request
   |
   v
Pending
   |
   v
CA Manager
   |
   +--> Approve
   |
   +--> Deny

This can prevent immediate certificate issuance.

docs.title: Authorized Signatures
docs.text:
A template can require one or more authorised signatures before issuance.

Conceptually:

Attacker Request
      |
      v
Required Signature
      |
      X
No Appropriate Signer

This may prevent the straightforward ESC1 path.

docs.title: Condition 6 - Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Modern ESC1 assessment must account for certificate mapping.

The old simplified assumption was:

Certificate Contains Victim UPN
        |
        v
Authenticate as Victim

Modern Windows environments can enforce stronger certificate-to-account mapping.

Therefore the actual model is:

Certificate
    |
    v
Identity Information
    |
    v
Certificate Mapping Rules
    |
    v
Mapped AD Account
    |
    v
Authentication

docs.title: Strong Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Microsoft introduced stronger certificate-based authentication mapping requirements following security hardening associated with KB5014754.

Current assessments should consider:

Domain Controller Patch Level
Strong Certificate Mapping
SID Security Extension
Certificate Mapping Method
Certificate Issuance Date
Certificate Properties

Do not assume an old ESC1 proof of concept behaves identically on a current environment.

docs.title: Full Enforcement
docs.text:
Current Windows certificate-based authentication hardening means weak certificate mapping assumptions from older AD CS research may no longer apply unchanged.

The assessment should therefore distinguish:

Template Misconfiguration

from:

Successfully Mapped Authentication Certificate

A template may still represent a serious configuration weakness even where a particular historical authentication path has been mitigated by current mapping enforcement.

docs.title: SID Security Extension
docs.text:
Modern Enterprise CA-issued certificates may contain a security extension linking the certificate to the requester's Active Directory SID.

Conceptually:

Certificate
   |
   +--> Requested Identity Information
   |
   +--> SID Security Information

This additional identity binding affects modern certificate mapping behaviour.

docs.title: Do Not Ignore the SID Extension
docs.text:
A legacy assessment model might only inspect:

UPN SAN

A modern assessment should inspect:

UPN / SAN
SID Security Extension
Issuer
Template
Mapping Behaviour
KDC Behaviour

docs.title: ESC1 vs Certificate Mapping Hardening
docs.text:
Think of these as different layers:

Layer 1
Template permits dangerous identity input

Layer 2
CA issues certificate

Layer 3
Authentication service maps certificate

Layer 4
Identity receives access

A weakness at Layer 1 does not automatically prove successful Layer 4 compromise.

docs.title: Enumerating ESC1 with Certipy
docs.text:
Certipy can identify certificate templates that appear to satisfy ESC1-related conditions.

Start by checking the installed version:

certipy --help

Then:

certipy find -h

A typical authenticated enumeration pattern is:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

Use an approved assessment identity.

docs.title: Review Certipy Output
docs.text:
Look for fields relating to:

Certificate Authorities
Template Name
Enabled
Enrollment Rights
Enrollee Supplies Subject
Client Authentication
Extended Key Usage
Manager Approval
Authorized Signatures
Potential ESC1

Exact labels vary between Certipy versions.

docs.title: Certipy Candidate
docs.text:
A Certipy result should be treated as:

Potential ESC1

until manually confirmed.

The workflow is:

Certipy
   |
   v
ESC1 Candidate
   |
   v
Verify Template
   |
   v
Verify Enrollment
   |
   v
Verify CA Publication
   |
   v
Verify Issuance Requirements
   |
   v
Verify Mapping
   |
   v
Determine Impact

docs.title: Native PowerShell Enumeration
docs.text:
Start with the template container:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties * |
    Select-Object Name,DisplayName

docs.title: Enumerate Subject Name Flags
docs.text:
$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties 'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag' |
    Select-Object Name,'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag'

docs.title: Identify Enrollee-Supplied Subject Flag
docs.text:
The relevant bit is:

0x00000001

PowerShell can test it:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties 'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag' |
    Where-Object {
        ([int]$_.'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag' -band 0x00000001) -ne 0
    } |
    Select-Object Name,DisplayName,'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag'

This identifies templates where the relevant subject-supply bit is present.

It does not by itself prove ESC1.

docs.title: Enumerate EKUs
docs.text:
$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties pKIExtendedKeyUsage |
    Select-Object Name,pKIExtendedKeyUsage

docs.title: Find Client Authentication Templates
docs.text:
$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(pKIExtendedKeyUsage=1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2)' -Properties pKIExtendedKeyUsage |
    Select-Object Name,pKIExtendedKeyUsage

Remember that this is not the only potentially relevant authentication capability.

docs.title: Correlate Subject Flag and Client Authentication
docs.text:
A basic read-only triage query can combine both conditions:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties 'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag',pKIExtendedKeyUsage |
    Where-Object {
        (([int]$_.'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag' -band 0x00000001) -ne 0) -and
        ($_.pKIExtendedKeyUsage -contains '1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2')
    } |
    Select-Object Name,DisplayName,'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag',pKIExtendedKeyUsage

This is useful for candidate discovery.

It still does not evaluate:

Enrollment Rights
CA Publication
Approval
Signatures
Certificate Mapping

docs.title: Enumerate Issuance Requirements
docs.text:
Retrieve:

msPKI-Enrollment-Flag
msPKI-RA-Signature

with:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties 'msPKI-Enrollment-Flag','msPKI-RA-Signature' |
    Select-Object Name,'msPKI-Enrollment-Flag','msPKI-RA-Signature'

Interpret the flags against Microsoft protocol documentation or trusted tooling.

docs.title: Verify CA Publication
docs.text:
Find Enterprise CAs:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$enrollmentBase = "CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $enrollmentBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKIEnrollmentService)' -Properties certificateTemplates,dNSHostName |
    Select-Object Name,dNSHostName,certificateTemplates

Confirm the candidate template appears in:

certificateTemplates

for an issuing CA.

docs.title: Find Which CA Publishes a Template
docs.text:
Example:

$templateName = 'CorpUserAuth'

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$enrollmentBase = "CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $enrollmentBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKIEnrollmentService)' -Properties certificateTemplates,dNSHostName |
    Where-Object {
        $_.certificateTemplates -contains $templateName
    } |
    Select-Object Name,dNSHostName

docs.title: Enumerate Template ACL
docs.text:
$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateDN = "CN=CorpUserAuth,CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

(Get-Acl "AD:$templateDN").Access |
    Select-Object IdentityReference,ActiveDirectoryRights,AccessControlType,ObjectType,IsInherited

This provides raw ACL information.

docs.title: Effective Enrollment Rights
docs.text:
Do not stop at direct ACEs.

Consider:

Direct Group Membership
Nested Group Membership
Inherited Permissions
Extended Rights
Ownership

The actual question is:

Can the assessment identity effectively enroll?

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView can help inspect template ACLs.

Example:

Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity 'CN=CorpUserAuth,CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=example' -ResolveGUIDs

Look for relevant enrollment and object-control rights.

Exact output depends on PowerView version.

docs.title: LDAP Enumeration from Linux
docs.text:
Templates can be inspected directly over LDAP.

Example:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\audit-user' \
    -W \
    -b 'CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' \
    cn \
    displayName \
    pKIExtendedKeyUsage \
    msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag \
    msPKI-Enrollment-Flag \
    msPKI-RA-Signature

This is a low-impact way to collect the core configuration.

docs.title: Search for Enrollee-Supplied Subject
docs.text:
Raw LDAP values can be difficult to interpret because:

msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag

is a bit field.

Use tooling or locally decode the values rather than matching one decimal value exactly, because multiple flags can be combined.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can help connect:

Principal
   |
   v
Enrollment Rights
   |
   v
Certificate Template
   |
   v
Certificate Authority

and broader AD privilege relationships.

The useful question is:

Who can reach the template?

not simply:

Is the template unsafe?

docs.title: Indirect ESC1 Path
docs.text:
Consider:

alice
  |
  v
AddMember
  |
  v
PKI-Enrollment
  |
  v
Enroll
  |
  v
ESC1 Template

The attacker may not have direct enrollment permission but still have an effective path to it.

docs.title: Another Indirect Path
docs.text:
alice
  |
  v
GenericWrite
  |
  v
bob
  |
  v
PKI-Enrollment
  |
  v
ESC1 Template

This demonstrates why AD CS findings should be integrated with general Active Directory attack-path analysis.

docs.title: Template Control vs ESC1
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

ESC1

with:

ESC4

A simplified distinction is:

ESC1
Existing template configuration is dangerous

versus:

ESC4
Attacker can modify a template

ESC4 may potentially be used to create an ESC1-like configuration, but the initial weakness is different.

docs.title: ESC1 vs ESC2
docs.text:
ESC1 focuses on:

Enrollee-Supplied Identity
+
Authentication Capability

ESC2 focuses on overly broad certificate purposes such as:

Any Purpose

or similarly unconstrained usage.

The conditions and exploitation paths differ.

docs.title: ESC1 vs ESC3
docs.text:
ESC3 concerns:

Enrollment Agent

functionality.

The conceptual model is:

ESC1
Requester controls identity information

versus:

ESC3
Enrollment Agent requests on behalf of another identity

docs.title: ESC1 vs ESC6
docs.text:
ESC1 is primarily a:

Certificate Template

condition.

ESC6 historically concerns:

CA-Wide Configuration

affecting SAN processing.

Do not treat the two as interchangeable.

docs.title: ESC1 vs Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
ESC1:

Certificate Template
      |
      v
CA Issues Certificate

Shadow Credentials:

Write msDS-KeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
Add Key Credential

Both can involve certificate-based authentication, but the trust path is different.

See:

Active Directory Shadow Credentials

docs.title: ESC1 vs Password Reset
docs.text:
Password reset:

Attacker
   |
   v
Changes Victim Password
   |
   v
Victim Secret Replaced

ESC1:

Attacker
   |
   v
Obtains Alternate Authentication Credential
   |
   v
Victim Password Unchanged

This difference matters for both detection and incident response.

docs.title: Certificate Request Validation
docs.text:
When explicit validation is authorised, Certipy can request certificates.

Before doing so:

certipy req -h

Confirm syntax against the installed version.

A request requires information such as:

CA
Template
Authentication Identity
CA Target
Requested Certificate Identity

docs.title: Avoid Copying Old Certipy Syntax Blindly
docs.text:
Certipy has changed significantly across releases.

Always begin with:

certipy --help
certipy req -h
certipy auth -h

before following an older blog post.

docs.title: Controlled ESC1 Validation
docs.text:
The preferred validation hierarchy is:

Template Configuration
        |
        v
Enrollment Permission
        |
        v
CA Publication
        |
        v
Issuance Requirements
        |
        v
Mapping Analysis
        |
        v
Test Certificate
        |
        v
Authentication Proof

Stop as soon as sufficient evidence exists.

docs.title: Test Account Strategy
docs.text:
Where possible create or use:

adcs-test-user

and another approved:

adcs-test-target

Then demonstrate the identity boundary using test accounts rather than production privileged identities.

For example:

adcs-test-user
      |
      v
Requests Certificate
      |
      v
adcs-test-target

This proves cross-account certificate issuance without affecting a real administrator.

docs.title: Privileged Identity Validation
docs.text:
If the engagement specifically requires proving impact against a privileged identity:

Obtain Written Approval
Use One Certificate
Authenticate Once
Do Not Perform Additional Privileged Actions
Record Evidence
Revoke Certificate
Delete Private Key

Avoid unnecessary actions after authentication succeeds.

docs.title: Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
If an authorised test certificate has been issued, authentication can be validated using tooling that supports certificate-based Kerberos or Schannel authentication.

Certipy provides:

auth

functionality.

Check:

certipy auth -h

before use.

The conceptual path is:

PFX
 |
 v
Certificate + Private Key
 |
 v
PKINIT
 |
 v
KDC
 |
 v
TGT

docs.title: Authentication Is the Strongest Proof
docs.text:
The strongest technical validation is:

Certificate Issued
      |
      v
Certificate Maps to Target
      |
      v
Authentication Succeeds

However, it is not always necessary.

If the risk is already demonstrated by configuration and approved architectural evidence, avoid creating additional reusable credentials.

docs.title: Do Not Retrieve More Credentials Than Necessary
docs.text:
Some certificate authentication tooling can also derive or expose additional credential material under suitable conditions.

For a normal ESC1 validation, the assessment may only need to prove:

Certificate-Based Authentication

Do not retrieve:

NT Hashes
Additional Tickets
Service Credentials

unless required by the engagement objective.

docs.title: Protect PFX Files
docs.text:
A PFX generated during testing may contain:

Certificate
Private Key
Certificate Chain

Treat it as a credential.

Never:

Commit It to Git
Upload It to a Public Scanner
Attach It to the Report
Paste Its Private Key into Notes
Leave It in /tmp

docs.title: Certificate Evidence
docs.text:
Record non-secret evidence such as:

Certificate Subject
SAN
Issuer
Serial Number
Thumbprint
Template
Validity
Authentication Result

Avoid recording the private key.

docs.title: Certificate Lifetime
docs.text:
Record:

Not Before
Not After

because the lifetime affects persistence risk.

A certificate valid for:

2 Years

has a different exposure window than one valid for:

8 Hours

docs.title: Password Reset and ESC1 Certificates
docs.text:
An important consequence of certificate-based authentication is that changing the account password does not inherently remove an already issued certificate.

Conceptually:

Certificate
    |
    v
Issued Credential
    |
    +---------------------+
    |                     |
Password Changed      Certificate Exists
                          |
                          v
                    May Remain Usable

Incident response must address the certificate itself.

docs.title: Persistence Risk
docs.text:
If an attacker obtains a long-lived authentication certificate:

Authentication Certificate
          |
          v
Password Rotation
          |
          X
Certificate Automatically Removed

The certificate may remain usable until:

Expiration
Revocation
Trust Change
Other Authentication Control

depending on the environment.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
ESC1 detection should consider several stages:

Template Configuration
Certificate Request
Certificate Issuance
Certificate Authentication
Subsequent Privileged Activity

docs.title: Detect Dangerous Templates
docs.text:
Defenders should continuously inventory templates with combinations involving:

Enrollee Supplies Subject
+
Authentication EKU
+
Broad Enrollment

Then evaluate:

Approval
Signatures
Mapping
CA Publication

docs.title: Monitor Template Changes
docs.text:
Certificate templates are Active Directory objects.

Changes can be detected using Directory Service Changes auditing where configured.

Relevant events can include:

5136

for directory object modifications.

docs.title: Event 5136
docs.text:
Monitor changes to:

msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag
pKIExtendedKeyUsage
msPKI-Certificate-Application-Policy
msPKI-Enrollment-Flag
msPKI-RA-Signature
nTSecurityDescriptor

on certificate-template objects.

A change such as:

Build from Active Directory
        |
        v
Supply in the request

should receive particular attention.

docs.title: Monitor Template ACL Changes
docs.text:
A secure template may be converted into an unsafe one if an attacker obtains control over it.

Monitor changes involving:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteProperty
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
Enroll
Autoenroll

docs.title: Certificate Issuance Monitoring
docs.text:
Monitor certificates where:

Requester

does not logically correspond to:

Certificate Identity

especially for privileged identities.

For example:

Requester:
CORP\alice

Certificate Identity:
privileged-user@corp.example

should warrant investigation unless explicitly expected.

docs.title: Monitor Privileged Certificates
docs.text:
Pay particular attention to certificates representing:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Administrators
Domain Controllers
PKI Administrators
Tier 0 Service Accounts

Unexpected issuance should be investigated.

docs.title: Certificate Authentication Monitoring
docs.text:
Certificate-based Kerberos authentication can generate Kerberos authentication telemetry.

Correlate:

Account
Source
Certificate Information
Certificate Issuer
Serial Number
Thumbprint
Authentication Time

where available.

docs.title: Event 4768
docs.text:
Kerberos TGT requests can generate:

4768

on Domain Controllers.

Certificate-based pre-authentication may provide certificate-related information depending on Windows version and event configuration.

Use current Microsoft event documentation when building production detections.

docs.title: Correlate Issuance and Authentication
docs.text:
A powerful detection model is:

Certificate Issued
       |
       v
Privileged Identity
       |
       v
Short Time Window
       |
       v
Certificate Authentication
       |
       v
Unexpected Source

This provides stronger context than either event alone.

docs.title: Baseline Legitimate Enrollment
docs.text:
Some organisations legitimately issue authentication certificates to many users.

Therefore:

Authentication Certificate Issued

is not automatically malicious.

Baseline:

Normal Templates
Normal Requesters
Normal Subjects
Normal CAs
Normal Enrollment Hosts
Normal Authentication Sources

docs.title: Hardening ESC1
docs.text:
The best remediation is to remove the unsafe trust relationship.

Possible controls include:

Disable Enrollee-Supplied Subject
Restrict Enrollment
Remove Authentication EKUs
Require Manager Approval
Require Authorized Signatures
Fix Template ACLs
Unpublish Unnecessary Template
Use Strong Certificate Mapping
Monitor Certificate Issuance

The correct combination depends on the template's business purpose.

docs.title: Disable Supply in the Request
docs.text:
Where not required, configure the template to derive identity from Active Directory.

Conceptually:

Supply in the Request
        |
        v
Disable
        |
        v
Build from Active Directory

This removes the classic attacker-controlled identity input.

docs.title: Restrict Enrollment
docs.text:
Replace broad groups such as:

Domain Users
Authenticated Users

with narrowly scoped groups where possible.

Example:

Corp-VPN-Certificate-Users

The group should contain only identities that genuinely require the certificate.

docs.title: Remove Unnecessary Authentication EKUs
docs.text:
If a certificate exists only for:

Server TLS
Document Signing
Code Signing
Encryption

it should not also provide unnecessary:

Client Authentication

capability.

Apply least privilege to certificate purposes.

docs.title: Require Approval
docs.text:
For highly sensitive certificate workflows:

Manager Approval

may provide an additional control.

However, approval processes must themselves be secured.

docs.title: Require Authorized Signatures
docs.text:
Sensitive enrollment workflows may require:

Authorized Signatures

where appropriate.

This adds another trust requirement before certificate issuance.

docs.title: Protect Template ACLs
docs.text:
Restrict:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteProperty
WriteDACL
WriteOwner

on certificate templates.

A secure template is only secure while its configuration cannot be altered by inappropriate principals.

docs.title: Remove Unused Templates from CAs
docs.text:
If a template is no longer required:

Unpublish

it from issuing CAs.

After appropriate dependency analysis, retire the template if it is obsolete.

docs.title: Do Not Break Production PKI
docs.text:
Before modifying a template, determine whether it supports:

VPN
Wi-Fi
Smart Cards
LDAPS
Machine Authentication
Applications
Service Authentication

Changes to certificate templates can cause significant outages.

docs.title: Certificate Mapping Hardening
docs.text:
Maintain current Microsoft certificate-mapping protections.

Do not weaken strong certificate mapping simply to preserve compatibility with poorly configured legacy certificate workflows.

Instead:

Identify Legacy Dependency
Update Certificate Issuance
Fix Mapping
Test
Deploy

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
If ESC1 abuse is suspected:

Identify Template
      |
      v
Identify CA
      |
      v
Identify Requester
      |
      v
Identify Issued Certificates
      |
      v
Identify Represented Accounts
      |
      v
Identify Authentication Activity
      |
      v
Revoke Malicious Certificates
      |
      v
Fix Template

docs.title: Identify the Certificate
docs.text:
Collect:

Serial Number
Thumbprint
Subject
SAN
Issuer
Template
Requester
Issue Time
Expiration

docs.title: Identify All Certificates Issued During Exposure
docs.text:
If the template was unsafe for a long period:

Misconfiguration Start
       |
       v
Current Time

review certificates issued during that window.

Do not assume the certificate discovered during the incident is the only malicious one.

docs.title: Revoke Malicious Certificates
docs.text:
Where appropriate:

Revoke Certificate
      |
      v
Publish Updated Revocation Information

Ensure relying systems can obtain current revocation information.

docs.title: Fix the Template
docs.text:
Possible actions include:

Disable Enrollee-Supplied Subject
Restrict Enrollment
Change EKUs
Require Approval
Require Signatures
Fix ACL
Unpublish Template

docs.title: Password Reset Alone Is Insufficient
docs.text:
If an attacker possesses an issued certificate:

Reset Victim Password
      |
      X
Issued Certificate Automatically Removed

The malicious certificate must also be addressed.

docs.title: Investigate the Requesting Principal
docs.text:
Determine how the attacker obtained:

Enrollment Rights

The root cause might be:

Compromised User
Nested Group
Excessive Group Membership
Compromised Service Account
Template ACL Abuse

docs.title: Investigate Related AD CS Paths
docs.text:
An ESC1 incident should trigger review of:

Other Templates
Other CAs
Template ACLs
CA Permissions
Enrollment Services
Certificate Mapping
Other Issued Certificates

The discovered certificate may be only one part of a larger PKI compromise.

docs.title: Reporting ESC1
docs.text:
Avoid reporting only:

ESC1

A better title describes the actual trust failure.

Examples:

Low-Privileged Users Can Request Authentication Certificates for Arbitrary Domain Identities

Certificate Template Allows Requester-Controlled Identity in Authentication Certificates

Broad Enrollment Rights and Enrollee-Supplied Subject Enable Account Impersonation

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Certificate Template Allows Requester-Controlled Identity in
Authentication Certificates

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Affected Template:
CorpUserAuthentication

Affected Principal:
CORP\Domain Users

Description:
The CorpUserAuthentication certificate template is published by the
CORP-CA01 Enterprise Certification Authority.

Members of CORP\Domain Users have enrollment rights on the template.

The template permits the enrollee to supply certificate subject
information and is configured to issue certificates suitable for
authentication.

The template does not provide sufficient issuance restrictions to
prevent low-privileged users from requesting certificates containing
security-sensitive identity information.

The certificate mapping configuration and current Domain Controller
hardening were also reviewed when determining exploitability.

Impact:
A compromised low-privileged domain account may be able to obtain
certificate-based authentication material representing another
Active Directory identity.

If a privileged identity can be represented and successfully mapped,
this may result in privilege escalation and potentially compromise of
high-value Active Directory resources.

Certificate-based access may also survive a password change until the
certificate is revoked, expires, or is otherwise made unusable.

Recommendation:
Configure the template to derive identity information from Active
Directory unless requester-supplied subject information is explicitly
required.

Restrict enrollment rights to a dedicated group containing only
authorised principals.

Remove unnecessary authentication EKUs.

Where appropriate, require certificate manager approval or authorised
signatures.

Review the template ACL and remove unnecessary modification rights.

Review previously issued certificates from the affected template and
revoke any certificates issued inappropriately.

docs.title: Severity Assessment
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

Who Can Enroll?
      +
Which Identity Can Be Represented?
      +
Can the Certificate Authenticate?
      +
Does Mapping Succeed?
      +
What Privilege Does the Target Have?
      =
Severity

docs.title: Example High-Severity Path
docs.text:
Domain User
   |
   v
ESC1 Template
   |
   v
Privileged Identity Certificate
   |
   v
Successful Authentication
   |
   v
Tier 0 Access

This may warrant a critical severity depending on the environment and demonstrated impact.

docs.title: Example Reduced-Impact Path
docs.text:
Restricted Enrollment Group
      |
      v
Requester-Supplied Subject
      |
      v
Non-Authentication Certificate

This may represent a configuration concern but not the classic ESC1 privilege escalation path.

docs.title: ESC1 Testing Model
docs.text:
The normal enrollment model is:

User
 |
 v
Template
 |
 v
Identity Derived from AD
 |
 v
Certificate for User

The ESC1 model is:

User
 |
 v
Template
 |
 v
Requester Supplies Identity
 |
 v
Certificate

The dangerous combination is:

Enroll
  +
Enrollee Supplies Subject
  +
Authentication Capability
  +
Weak Issuance Restrictions
  +
Successful Certificate Mapping
  =
Potential Account Impersonation

The attack-path model is:

Low-Privileged User
        |
        v
Enroll
        |
        v
ESC1 Template
        |
        v
Requested Identity
        |
        v
Certificate
        |
        v
Certificate Mapping
        |
        v
Target Account

The PKINIT model is:

Certificate + Private Key
          |
          v
PKINIT
          |
          v
KDC
          |
          v
TGT

The persistence model is:

Issued Certificate
        |
        v
Password Changed
        |
        X
Certificate Automatically Removed

The modern assessment model is:

Template Configuration
        |
        v
Certificate Issuance
        |
        v
Certificate Mapping
        |
        v
Authentication

The safe-testing model is:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Confirm Template
   |
   v
Confirm Enrollment
   |
   v
Confirm CA Publication
   |
   v
Analyse Mapping
   |
   v
Use Test Identity
   |
   v
Request One Certificate
   |
   v
Authenticate if Required
   |
   v
Stop
   |
   v
Clean Up

The defensive model is:

Secure Subject Configuration
          +
Restricted Enrollment
          +
Restricted EKUs
          +
Strong Issuance Requirements
          +
Protected Template ACL
          +
Strong Certificate Mapping
          =
Reduced ESC1 Risk

The most important relationship is:

Who Can Request
      |
      v
Which Identity Can They Place in the Request
      |
      v
What Can the Certificate Do
      |
      v
Which Account Will Windows Map It To

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Does Certipy print ESC1?"

Ask:
"Can my effective security context obtain an
authentication certificate that Windows will
accept as another identity?"

For defenders:

Do Not Ask:
"Do we have Supply in the Request enabled?"

Ask:
"Who can use that capability, what certificates
can they obtain, which identities can those
certificates represent, and how will Windows
map them?"

The complete ESC1 trust relationship is:

Principal
   |
   v
Enrollment Permission
   |
   v
Certificate Template
   |
   v
Requester-Controlled Identity
   |
   v
Certificate Authority
   |
   v
Authentication Certificate
   |
   v
Certificate Mapping
   |
   v
Active Directory Account
   |
   v
Privilege

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
ESC1 is fundamentally an:

Identity Issuance Failure

The dangerous configuration allows the certificate requester to influence:

Who the Certificate Represents

while the certificate may also provide:

Authentication

The classic relationship is:

Low-Privileged User
      |
      v
Can Enroll
      |
      v
Supply in the Request
      |
      v
Authentication Certificate
      |
      v
Another Identity

However, modern Windows environments require another critical layer:

Certificate Mapping

Therefore the modern model is:

Enrollment
    +
Requester-Controlled Identity
    +
Authentication Capability
    +
Issuance
    +
Successful Mapping
    =
ESC1 Impact

Do not treat:

Supply in the Request

alone as proof of compromise.

Likewise, do not treat:

Certipy: ESC1

as the entire finding.

The assessment must determine:

Who Can Enroll?
Which CA Issues It?
What Identity Can Be Requested?
What EKUs Exist?
Is Approval Required?
Are Signatures Required?
What SID Information Is Present?
How Does Windows Map the Certificate?
What Privilege Does the Target Identity Have?

For defenders, the most effective strategy is to remove unnecessary flexibility from certificate issuance.

Directory-Derived Identity
        +
Restricted Enrollment
        +
Minimal EKUs
        +
Protected Template ACL
        +
Strong Certificate Mapping
        =
Safer Authentication Template

For penetration testers, the strongest finding is not:

ESC1 exists

but:

A low-privileged principal can cause the
enterprise PKI to issue authentication
material that the domain accepts as a
higher-privileged identity.

That is the actual trust failure represented by a successfully exploitable ESC1 condition.

docs.title: AD CS ESC10 - Weak Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
ESC10 describes Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) attack paths caused by weak certificate mapping on domain controllers.

Certificate mapping is the process Windows uses to determine:

Which Active Directory Account
        |
        v
Belongs to This Certificate?

A certificate may contain several identity-related values:

Subject
Subject Alternative Name
UPN
DNS Name
Issuer
Serial Number
SID Security Extension

The Key Distribution Center (KDC) must map the certificate presented during certificate-based authentication to an Active Directory security principal.

A secure model is:

Certificate
     |
     v
Strong Identity Binding
     |
     v
Active Directory Account

ESC10 becomes relevant when domain controllers permit weak mappings that rely on identity information which may be changed, duplicated, spoofed, or otherwise insufficiently bound to the original certificate requester.

Historically, ESC10 was strongly associated with registry settings such as:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

and:

CertificateMappingMethods

However, Microsoft's certificate-based authentication hardening introduced through KB5014754 significantly changed this area.

In a current, fully patched Active Directory environment, legacy ESC10 techniques must not be assumed to work.

The central assessment question is:

Can a certificate be mapped to a different
Active Directory account because the
environment accepts an insufficiently
strong certificate mapping?

Authorised testing only

Certificate mapping tests can affect authentication and identity relationships across the domain. Begin with read-only inspection of certificate templates, domain-controller configuration, IIS/Schannel configuration where relevant, and explicit mappings. Do not weaken certificate mapping, modify production identities, or change domain-controller registry settings merely to demonstrate ESC10. Use dedicated test accounts when active validation is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Certificate authentication requires Windows to answer:

Who owns this certificate?

Conceptually:

Certificate
     |
     v
Identity Information
     |
     v
Certificate Mapping
     |
     v
Active Directory Object

If the mapping mechanism is strong:

Certificate A
     |
     v
Account A

should not become:

Certificate A
     |
     v
Account B

simply because an attacker manipulates a weak name-based identifier.

docs.title: Why Certificate Mapping Exists
docs.text:
A certificate does not inherently contain an Active Directory object reference that every authentication service automatically understands.

The certificate may instead contain information such as:

UPN
DNS Name
Subject
Issuer
Serial Number
SID

Windows must determine how those values correspond to an account.

docs.title: Strong vs Weak Mapping
docs.text:
The most important ESC10 concept is:

Strong Mapping

versus:

Weak Mapping

A simplified model is:

Certificate Mapping
      |
      +--> Strong Mapping
      |
      +--> Weak Mapping

docs.title: Weak Mapping
docs.text:
Weak mappings historically included mappings based primarily on certificate names.

Examples include certificate identities derived from:

Subject
UPN
Email
DNS Name

depending on authentication mechanism and configuration.

The problem is that names may be:

Changed
Reused
Duplicated
Manipulated

more easily than cryptographically or administratively strong identifiers.

docs.title: Strong Mapping
docs.text:
Strong mappings provide a stronger relationship between:

Certificate

and:

Specific Security Principal

Examples include mappings involving security identifiers or strong explicit certificate mappings.

Conceptually:

Certificate
     |
     v
Strong Identifier
     |
     v
Specific AD Object

docs.title: ESC10 Historical Definition
docs.text:
ESC10 historically covered two important weak-mapping configurations.

These were commonly separated into:

ESC10 Case 1

and:

ESC10 Case 2

The two cases involve different Windows components.

docs.title: ESC10 Case 1
docs.text:
The first historical ESC10 condition involved:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

on domain controllers.

Historically, weak settings could permit certificate authentication using mappings that were not sufficiently bound to the original account.

Conceptually:

Certificate
     |
     v
KDC
     |
     v
Weak Mapping Accepted
     |
     v
Different Account

docs.title: StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement
docs.text:
The relevant historical registry location is:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Kdc

with the value:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

This setting was introduced as part of Microsoft's KB5014754 certificate-authentication hardening.

docs.title: Historical Modes
docs.text:
Historically the setting supported modes corresponding approximately to:

Disabled
Compatibility
Full Enforcement

Older ESC10 guidance frequently focused on environments where strong certificate binding was disabled or not fully enforced.

docs.title: Current 2026 Context
docs.text:
This historical configuration must be interpreted carefully today.

Microsoft's KB5014754 rollout moved domain controllers toward:

Full Enforcement

beginning with the February 2025 security update.

Microsoft also documented that the ability to return to Compatibility mode through the registry setting ended with the:

September 9, 2025

Windows security update.

Therefore, on a normally patched domain controller in 2026:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

should not be treated as a supported mechanism for returning to the historical weak-mapping state.

docs.title: Why Old ESC10 Guides Can Mislead
docs.text:
Older write-ups may instruct testers to check:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement = 0

and immediately classify the domain as vulnerable.

That historical interpretation should not be blindly applied to a current environment.

Instead determine:

Windows Patch State
        |
        v
Current Enforcement Behaviour
        |
        v
Available Certificate Mapping

docs.title: Do Not Change the Registry
docs.text:
Never change:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

on a production domain controller merely to recreate a historical ESC10 attack.

That would deliberately weaken domain authentication.

docs.title: ESC10 Case 2
docs.text:
The second historical ESC10 condition concerns Schannel certificate mapping.

The relevant configuration is commonly associated with:

CertificateMappingMethods

under:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL

docs.title: Schannel
docs.text:
Schannel is the Windows Secure Channel security package used for TLS.

Certificate authentication through Schannel can appear in services such as:

LDAPS
IIS
Remote Access
Other TLS Client-Certificate Services

depending on environment configuration.

docs.title: CertificateMappingMethods
docs.text:
Historically:

CertificateMappingMethods

controls which certificate mapping methods Schannel can use.

This is distinct from:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

used in the KDC certificate-authentication context.

Therefore:

KDC Mapping

and:

Schannel Mapping

must be assessed separately.

docs.title: ESC10 Mapping Surfaces
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Certificate Authentication
        |
        +--> Kerberos / PKINIT
        |       |
        |       v
        |      KDC
        |
        +--> TLS Client Authentication
                |
                v
             Schannel

ESC10 analysis should identify which authentication surface is actually involved.

docs.title: Kerberos PKINIT
docs.text:
Kerberos can use certificates during:

PKINIT

to obtain a Ticket Granting Ticket.

Conceptually:

Certificate
     |
     v
KDC
     |
     v
Certificate Mapping
     |
     v
Account
     |
     v
TGT

docs.title: Schannel Authentication
docs.text:
Schannel can authenticate a client certificate to a Windows service.

Conceptually:

Certificate
     |
     v
TLS
     |
     v
Schannel
     |
     v
Certificate Mapping
     |
     v
Windows Account

docs.title: ESC10 Is Not Only AD CS
docs.text:
This is an important distinction.

The vulnerable component in ESC10 is primarily:

Certificate Mapping Configuration

rather than necessarily:

Certificate Authority Configuration

AD CS provides the certificates, but the weakness occurs when Windows maps them insecurely.

docs.title: ESC10 and ESC9
docs.text:
ESC9 disables the SID security extension at the template level.

Conceptually:

ESC9
 |
 v
Certificate Without SID

ESC10 asks:

Can Windows Still Accept a Weak Mapping?

The combination historically created important attack paths.

docs.title: ESC9 + ESC10
docs.text:
A simplified relationship is:

ESC9 Template
      |
      v
Certificate Without SID
      |
      v
ESC10 Weak Mapping
      |
      v
Different AD Account

In a modern environment, verify whether Full Enforcement blocks the mapping.

docs.title: ESC10 and ESC16
docs.text:
ESC16 can suppress the SID security extension at the CA level.

Therefore:

ESC16
   |
   v
Certificate Without SID
   |
   v
ESC10 Analysis

may become relevant.

docs.title: ESC10 and ESC6
docs.text:
ESC6 concerns requester-controlled SAN information.

Historically:

Requester-Controlled SAN
        +
Weak Certificate Mapping

could produce dangerous identity-mapping scenarios.

Modern strong mapping must still be considered.

docs.title: ESC10 and ESC1
docs.text:
ESC1 allows an enrollee to supply identity information under vulnerable template conditions.

Conceptually:

ESC1
 |
 v
Attacker-Controlled Certificate Identity
 |
 v
Certificate Mapping

ESC10 may influence whether that certificate identity maps successfully.

docs.title: ESC10 and ESC14
docs.text:
ESC14 concerns weak explicit certificate mappings through:

altSecurityIdentities

ESC10 primarily concerns weak mapping behaviour configured at the authentication infrastructure level.

They should be assessed together but reported according to the actual root cause.

docs.title: ESC10 Preconditions
docs.text:
A meaningful ESC10 path generally requires:

Certificate
      +
Authentication Capability
      +
Weak Mapping Configuration
      +
Manipulable / Reusable Identity
      +
Reachable Target Account
      =
Potential ESC10

docs.title: Certificate Requirement
docs.text:
The attacker first needs a usable certificate.

That certificate might originate from:

Legitimate Enrollment
ESC1
ESC2
ESC3
ESC6
ESC8
ESC9
ESC16
Stolen Certificate

ESC10 determines how that certificate maps to an account.

docs.title: Authentication Capability
docs.text:
The certificate must be useful for the target authentication mechanism.

Relevant EKUs can include:

Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2

Smart Card Logon
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.2

PKINIT Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.2.3.4

The exact requirements depend on the authentication path.

docs.title: Enumerate Domain Controllers
docs.text:
From Windows:

Get-ADDomainController -Filter * |
    Select-Object HostName,IPv4Address,OperatingSystem,OperatingSystemVersion

This helps establish:

Domain Controllers
Windows Versions
Patch Context

docs.title: Patch State Matters
docs.text:
For modern ESC10 assessment, record:

Operating System
Build
Patch Level
Certificate Mapping Enforcement

Do not infer mapping behaviour solely from the OS marketing version.

docs.title: Check KDC Configuration
docs.text:
On an authorised domain controller:

Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Kdc' -Name StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Interpret the result in the context of:

Current Windows Patching

and Microsoft's current KB5014754 enforcement behaviour.

docs.title: Registry Value Missing
docs.text:
Do not automatically interpret:

Value Not Present

as:

Vulnerable

Default behaviour has changed during Microsoft's multi-year rollout.

The effective behaviour of the patched domain controller matters.

docs.title: Query with reg.exe
docs.text:
An alternative is:

reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Kdc /v StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

Again, absence of the value is not itself evidence of ESC10.

docs.title: Check Schannel Mapping
docs.text:
On an authorised target:

Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL' -Name CertificateMappingMethods -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

or:

reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL /v CertificateMappingMethods

docs.title: CertificateMappingMethods Is a Bitmask
docs.text:
The Schannel configuration is a bitmask.

Historically documented mapping methods include categories such as:

Subject / Issuer
Issuer
UPN
S4U-Based Mapping

Exact supported behaviour should be checked against the current Microsoft documentation for the Windows version being assessed.

Do not infer vulnerability from the decimal value without decoding the enabled methods.

docs.title: Inventory Schannel Services
docs.text:
Identify where certificate-based TLS authentication is actually used.

Potential examples include:

LDAPS
IIS
VPN
Remote Access
Custom Windows Services

A weak Schannel configuration has limited practical impact if no relevant service accepts client certificates.

docs.title: LDAPS
docs.text:
LDAP over TLS commonly uses:

636/tcp

Discover:

nmap -Pn -p636 dc01.corp.example

This establishes service availability, not certificate mapping vulnerability.

docs.title: Test TLS
docs.text:
For basic TLS inspection:

openssl s_client -connect dc01.corp.example:636 -showcerts

This inspects the server-side TLS service.

It does not prove that client certificate mapping is weak.

docs.title: Explicit Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Active Directory accounts can contain:

altSecurityIdentities

which can explicitly associate certificates with accounts.

Enumerate the attribute:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties altSecurityIdentities |
    Where-Object { $_.altSecurityIdentities } |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,altSecurityIdentities

docs.title: Computer Explicit Mappings
docs.text:
Also review computer objects:

Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties altSecurityIdentities |
    Where-Object { $_.altSecurityIdentities } |
    Select-Object Name,SamAccountName,altSecurityIdentities

docs.title: Why altSecurityIdentities Matters
docs.text:
An explicit mapping can override assumptions based solely on certificate names.

Conceptually:

Certificate
     |
     v
Explicit Mapping
     |
     v
Account

This may create either:

Strong Mapping

or:

Weak Mapping

depending on the mapping form.

ESC14 covers weak explicit mappings in more detail.

docs.title: Certipy Enumeration
docs.text:
Certipy can assist with AD CS and certificate mapping analysis.

Start with:

certipy --version

Then:

certipy find -h

A typical read-only enumeration command is:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

docs.title: Certipy and ESC10
docs.text:
Certipy may identify ESC10-related conditions when it can determine relevant registry or mapping information.

However, tool output should be treated as:

Lead

rather than:

Final Proof

because:

Patch State
Effective Enforcement
Certificate Type
Authentication Surface

all matter.

docs.title: Remote Registry Limitations
docs.text:
Remote registry enumeration may fail because:

Remote Registry Disabled
Firewall
Permissions
Service State
RPC Restrictions

Failure to read the setting does not imply that the system is secure or vulnerable.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify certificate attack paths around:

Certificate Templates
Enrollment Rights
Certificate Authorities
Account Control

See:

BloodHound

However, effective certificate mapping behaviour should still be validated directly.

docs.title: Identity Attribute Control
docs.text:
Historical ESC10 exploitation can depend on the ability to manipulate identity attributes.

Potentially relevant attributes include:

userPrincipalName
dNSHostName
altSecurityIdentities

depending on the specific mapping path.

docs.title: UPN
docs.text:
A user's:

userPrincipalName

is commonly represented as:

alice@corp.example

Historically, weak UPN mapping created opportunities where certificate identity could be redirected toward another user.

docs.title: dNSHostName
docs.text:
Computer certificate mapping may involve:

dNSHostName

in some certificate and authentication scenarios.

Treat changes to computer identity attributes as security-sensitive.

docs.title: Historical User Mapping Model
docs.text:
A historical weak-mapping model is:

Attacker Controls User A
        |
        v
Manipulates Identity Attribute
        |
        v
Requests Certificate
        |
        v
Certificate Contains Target Identity
        |
        v
Restores Attribute
        |
        v
Weak Mapping
        |
        v
User B

Current Full Enforcement may block this path.

docs.title: Historical Computer Mapping Model
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Controlled Computer A
        |
        v
Manipulated Computer Identity
        |
        v
Certificate
        |
        v
Weak Mapping
        |
        v
Computer B

Again, do not assume this works against current patched systems.

docs.title: Safe Validation
docs.text:
The preferred approach is:

Read Configuration
       |
       v
Determine Mapping Method
       |
       v
Assess Certificate Source
       |
       v
Assess Identity Control
       |
       v
Determine Whether Active Proof Is Needed

Often this is sufficient.

docs.title: Dedicated Test Accounts
docs.text:
If active validation is necessary, use:

ESC10-Requester
ESC10-Target

or equivalent dedicated accounts.

Avoid:

Administrator
Domain Admin
Enterprise Admin
krbtgt
Production Service Accounts
Domain Controllers

docs.title: Record Original Attributes
docs.text:
Before an approved identity modification:

Get-ADUser -Identity 'ESC10-Requester' -Properties userPrincipalName,altSecurityIdentities |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,userPrincipalName,altSecurityIdentities

Save the values as evidence.

docs.title: Do Not Weaken Mapping for Testing
docs.text:
Do not change:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement
CertificateMappingMethods

to create an exploitable condition.

The assessment should test:

Existing Security Posture

not manufacture a vulnerability.

docs.title: Certificate Inspection
docs.text:
For any test certificate record:

Subject
Issuer
Serial Number
Thumbprint
SAN
UPN
DNS Name
EKUs
SID Security Extension
Validity

docs.title: Windows Inspection
docs.text: certutil -dump esc10-test.cer

docs.title: OpenSSL
docs.text:
openssl x509 -in esc10-test.pem -text -noout

For DER:

openssl x509 -in esc10-test.cer -inform DER -text -noout

docs.title: Certipy Authentication
docs.text:
If certificate authentication is explicitly required:

certipy auth -h

Verify the installed syntax before testing.

Use only the approved test certificate and identity.

docs.title: Successful Authentication
docs.text:
If a certificate issued to:

ESC10-Requester

authenticates as:

ESC10-Target

under the environment's existing mapping configuration, the cross-account mapping impact has been demonstrated.

Stop there unless further validation is explicitly required.

docs.title: Failed Authentication
docs.text:
A failed authentication can be equally informative.

For example:

Certificate
     |
     v
No Acceptable Strong Mapping
     |
     v
KDC Rejects Authentication

This may demonstrate that current Full Enforcement mitigates the historical attack path.

docs.title: Do Not Bypass the Mitigation
docs.text:
If authentication fails because strong mapping is enforced:

Stop

Do not weaken the domain controller to continue the attack.

Document:

Historical ESC10 Condition Not Exploitable
Under Current Enforcement

where appropriate.

docs.title: Schannel Validation
docs.text:
If the issue concerns:

CertificateMappingMethods

test only the specific service that relies on Schannel client-certificate authentication.

Do not extrapolate a result from:

IIS

to:

LDAP

or vice versa without evidence.

docs.title: Mapping Method Matters
docs.text:
A complete finding should identify:

Authentication Service
Mapping Method
Certificate Identity
Mapped Account

For example:

Service:
LDAPS

Certificate:
ESC10-Test

Mapping:
UPN

Mapped Account:
ESC10-Target

This is much stronger evidence than simply reporting a registry value.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
ESC10 detection should cover:

Mapping Configuration Changes
Identity Attribute Changes
Certificate Enrollment
Explicit Mapping Changes
Certificate Authentication

docs.title: Monitor KDC Configuration
docs.text:
Monitor unexpected changes under:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Kdc

particularly historical certificate-binding configuration.

docs.title: Monitor Schannel Configuration
docs.text:
Monitor:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL

for changes to certificate mapping configuration.

docs.title: Registry Monitoring
docs.text:
EDR or configuration-management tooling can detect unexpected changes to:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement
CertificateMappingMethods

where those values are relevant to the Windows version.

docs.title: Monitor UPN Changes
docs.text:
Unexpected modifications to:

userPrincipalName

should be monitored.

A suspicious sequence can be:

UPN Changed
    |
    v
Certificate Requested
    |
    v
UPN Restored

docs.title: Monitor Computer Identity Changes
docs.text:
Monitor unusual changes to:

dNSHostName

and other computer identity attributes.

These attributes should not change frequently in most environments.

docs.title: Monitor Explicit Mappings
docs.text:
Monitor:

altSecurityIdentities

for:

Addition
Modification
Deletion

especially on privileged accounts.

docs.title: Event 5136
docs.text:
Where Directory Service Changes auditing is enabled:

5136

can provide visibility into modifications to Active Directory attributes.

Relevant attributes can include:

userPrincipalName
dNSHostName
altSecurityIdentities

docs.title: Event 4738
docs.text:
User account modifications may also produce:

4738

depending on the change and audit configuration.

Correlate with certificate issuance.

docs.title: Certificate Request Monitoring
docs.text:
Where Certificate Services auditing is configured:

4886

can indicate receipt of a certificate request.

docs.title: Certificate Issuance
docs.text:
4887

can indicate successful certificate issuance.

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication
docs.text:
Certificate-based Kerberos authentication can result in:

4768

TGT-request telemetry.

Correlate:

Identity Attribute Change
        |
        v
Certificate Request
        |
        v
Certificate Issuance
        |
        v
4768

docs.title: Suspicious Timing
docs.text:
One of the strongest detection patterns is:

Identity Changed
      |
      v
Certificate Issued
      |
      v
Identity Restored
      |
      v
Certificate Authentication

within a short period.

docs.title: Monitor Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Certificate mapping is an identity-control-plane function.

Changes to domain-controller certificate authentication configuration should therefore receive high-priority monitoring.

docs.title: Hardening ESC10
docs.text:
The primary objective is:

Use Strong Certificate Mapping

docs.title: Maintain Full Enforcement
docs.text:
Keep domain controllers:

Fully Patched

and operating with Microsoft's current strong certificate-binding enforcement.

Do not restore obsolete compatibility behaviour.

docs.title: Do Not Depend on Deprecated Compatibility Modes
docs.text: Legacy applications should be migrated to supported strong certificate mappings rather than weakening domain-wide authentication.

docs.title: Review Schannel Mapping
docs.text:
Identify services that use:

Schannel Client Certificate Authentication

and verify that weak mapping methods are not unnecessarily enabled.

docs.title: Review CertificateMappingMethods
docs.text:
Document the effective:

CertificateMappingMethods

configuration for systems that rely on Schannel certificate authentication.

Compare against current Microsoft guidance and application requirements.

docs.title: Use Strong Explicit Mappings
docs.text:
Where explicit mappings are required, prefer strong mapping forms supported by Microsoft.

Avoid weak mappings based only on mutable certificate names.

docs.title: Review altSecurityIdentities
docs.text:
Audit:

altSecurityIdentities

across:

Privileged Users
Service Accounts
Administrators
Computer Accounts
Certificate-Based Accounts

docs.title: Protect Mapping Attributes
docs.text:
Restrict who can modify:

userPrincipalName
dNSHostName
altSecurityIdentities

and other identity-related attributes.

docs.title: Review ACLs
docs.text:
A user may not directly control a privileged account but may have an ACL path allowing modification of a mapping-related attribute.

See:

Active Directory ACL and ACE Abuse

docs.title: Review Group Delegation
docs.text:
Helpdesk or identity-management systems may legitimately have permissions to modify:

UPN

or other identity attributes.

Determine whether those permissions can interact with certificate enrollment.

docs.title: Review Certificate Templates
docs.text:
Strong mapping does not replace secure template configuration.

Continue to review:

ESC1
ESC2
ESC3
ESC4
ESC6
ESC9
ESC15
ESC16

where relevant.

docs.title: Review ESC9
docs.text:
If an authentication template has:

NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

review it immediately.

See:

AD CS ESC9

docs.title: Review ESC16
docs.text: If certificates across multiple templates unexpectedly lack the SID security extension, investigate CA-wide configuration.

docs.title: Protect Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Domain controllers should have:

Current Security Updates
Restricted Administrative Access
Configuration Monitoring
EDR
Secure Registry ACLs
Administrative Tiering

docs.text:
Maintain a baseline containing:

Domain Controller
OS Build
Patch Level
Strong Mapping State

Certificate Authentication Services

If a malicious certificate exists:

docs.text:
If a malicious:

altSecurityIdentities

mapping was created:

Remove Mapping

and determine who had permission to create it.

docs.title: Correct Mapping Configuration
docs.text:
If weak mapping is still enabled on a supported system:

Move to Supported Strong Mapping

following current Microsoft guidance.

docs.title: Investigate Why Weak Mapping Existed
docs.text:
Common causes include:

Legacy Smart Card Deployment
Old PKI Configuration
Application Compatibility
Migration
Manual Registry Changes
Legacy IIS Authentication
Third-Party Certificate Integration

Fix the underlying dependency rather than simply changing a registry value without testing.

docs.title: Reporting ESC10
docs.text:
Avoid reporting only:

ESC10

Prefer a title describing the actual mapping weakness.

Examples:

Weak Certificate Mapping Permits Cross-Account Authentication

or:

Schannel Accepts Weak Certificate-to-Account Mapping

or:

Legacy Certificate Mapping Configuration Weakens Active Directory Authentication

docs.title: Example Finding - Historical Configuration Present
docs.text:
Finding:
Legacy Certificate Mapping Configuration Identified

Affected Systems:
dc01.corp.example
dc02.corp.example

Description:
Certificate-based authentication configuration associated with
historical weak certificate mapping was identified on the domain
controllers.

Microsoft has significantly changed certificate mapping behaviour
through the KB5014754 rollout, including Full Enforcement and the
removal of the supported Compatibility-mode fallback.

The registry configuration alone therefore does not establish that
cross-account certificate authentication is currently possible.

Impact:
If the effective domain-controller configuration still accepts weak
certificate mappings, a certificate containing manipulable identity
information may potentially map to an unintended Active Directory
security principal.

The practical impact depends on the current Windows patch state,
effective certificate mapping behaviour, available certificates, and
control over identity attributes.

Recommendation:
Confirm that all domain controllers are fully patched and operating
with Microsoft's current Full Enforcement behaviour.

Remove obsolete certificate-mapping compatibility configuration where
appropriate.

Review certificate templates that omit strong identity information
and audit explicit certificate mappings.

docs.title: Example Finding - Exploitable Mapping Demonstrated
docs.text:
Finding:
Weak Certificate Mapping Permits Cross-Account Authentication

Affected Service:
<service>

Affected System:
<hostname>

Requester:
CORP\ESC10-Requester

Mapped Identity:
CORP\ESC10-Target

Description:
The affected certificate-authentication service accepts a weak
certificate mapping that does not sufficiently bind the presented
certificate to the account for which it was issued.

During controlled validation, two dedicated test identities were
used.

A certificate associated with the requester test identity was
accepted as the separate target test identity because of the
effective certificate mapping configuration.

No privileged production identity was used during validation.

Impact:
An attacker who can obtain a suitable certificate and manipulate the
relevant identity or mapping information may be able to authenticate
as another Active Directory account.

The resulting impact depends on the privileges of the mapped account.

Recommendation:
Configure the affected authentication service to use Microsoft's
supported strong certificate mapping mechanisms.

Maintain current Windows security updates and Full Enforcement on
domain controllers.

Review explicit certificate mappings and restrict modification of
identity attributes that influence certificate mapping.
