docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
ESC14 demonstrates an important difference between:

Certificate Trust

and:

Certificate-to-Account Mapping

A certificate can be completely legitimate:

Valid Signature
Valid Trust Chain
Valid Private Key
Valid Authentication EKU

while still being mapped to the wrong Active Directory principal because of an unsafe explicit mapping.

The core object is:

altSecurityIdentities

and every Active Directory security assessment involving certificate authentication should answer two questions:

Which accounts have explicit
certificate mappings?

and:

Who can modify those mappings?

The first identifies:

Existing Mapping Risk

while the second identifies:

Account Takeover Risk

Microsoft's modern certificate-binding protections make the distinction between weak and strong explicit mappings particularly important.

Weak mappings are:

X509IssuerSubject
X509SubjectOnly
X509RFC822

Strong mappings are:

X509IssuerSerialNumber
X509SKI
X509SHA1PublicKey

However, the most important ESC14 lesson is that:

Strong Mapping

does not protect an account when:

Attacker Can Write the Mapping

An attacker who controls both:

Certificate

and:

Target altSecurityIdentities

may be able to deliberately create a strong mapping between them.

Therefore:

Strong Certificate Binding

must be combined with:

Strong Active Directory ACLs

The practical assessment model is:

Enumerate altSecurityIdentities
        |
        v
Classify Mapping
        |
        v
Review Target ACL
        |
        v
Review Certificate Enrollment
        |
        v
Review Current DC Mapping Behaviour
        |
        v
Determine Real Attack Path

For weak existing mappings, do not automatically report critical exploitation.

Determine whether:

Mapped Identifier
       |
       v
Can Actually Be Reproduced
       |
       v
Through Available Certificate Enrollment
       |
       v
Under Current DC Enforcement

For writable mappings, focus on the ACL root cause.

A read-only proof showing:

Attacker
   |
   v
Effective Write Access
   |
   v
altSecurityIdentities
   |
   v
Sensitive Target

combined with a legitimate attacker-controlled authentication certificate can often establish the risk without changing the production target.

Finally, ESC14 should be considered alongside:

Shadow Credentials
ACL Abuse
Certificate Template Abuse
Weak Certificate Mapping
Certificate Authentication

because all of these mechanisms can converge on the same security objective:

Control Authentication Mapping
          |
          v
Control Identity

docs.title: AD CS ESC15 - Arbitrary Application Policies (EKUwu)
docs.text:
ESC15 is an Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) privilege-escalation technique associated with:

CVE-2024-49019

The technique became widely known as:

EKUwu

ESC15 affects vulnerable AD CS environments where certificate requests based on certain certificate templates can influence the resulting certificate's:

Application Policies

in ways that were not intended by the template administrator.

The security significance is substantial because Application Policies determine what a certificate may be used for.

A certificate template intended for a limited purpose could potentially result in a certificate containing a more privileged application policy.

Conceptually:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Vulnerable Certificate Template
        |
        v
Certificate Request
        |
        v
Arbitrary Application Policy
        |
        v
Certificate with Additional Capability
        |
        v
Privilege Escalation

Microsoft tracks the underlying vulnerability as:

CVE-2024-49019

and Microsoft Defender for Identity identifies the corresponding AD CS configuration as:

ESC15

Microsoft describes vulnerable configurations as allowing an attacker to issue certificates containing arbitrary Application Policies and Subject Alternative Names, potentially leading to privilege escalation and domain compromise.

Patch state matters

ESC15 is not simply a certificate-template misconfiguration. Exploitability depends on the AD CS server being vulnerable to CVE-2024-49019. A template that historically met ESC15 prerequisites should not automatically be reported as exploitable when every issuing CA has received the relevant security update.

Authorised testing only

ESC15 can potentially transform low-privilege certificate enrollment into authentication or enrollment-agent capabilities. Begin with CA patch verification and read-only template enumeration. Do not request certificates containing privileged Application Policies for production administrative identities merely to prove impact.

docs.title: ESC15 at a Glance
docs.text:
The core ESC15 relationship is:

Schema Version 1 Template
        |
        v
Low-Privilege Enrollment
        |
        v
Supply Subject Information
        |
        v
Unpatched AD CS
        |
        v
Application Policy Injection
        |
        v
More Powerful Certificate

The vulnerability breaks an important assumption:

Template Defines Certificate Purpose

because under vulnerable conditions:

Requester Influences Certificate Purpose

docs.title: CVE-2024-49019
docs.text:
CVE-2024-49019 concerns Active Directory Certificate Services.

Microsoft addressed the vulnerability through security updates released in:

November 2024

The vulnerability relates to how AD CS processes certificate requests and Application Policies.

For modern assessments, the first question should therefore be:

Is the issuing CA patched?

before attempting to establish an ESC15 attack path.

docs.title: Why ESC15 Is Different
docs.text:
Many AD CS escalation techniques involve:

Identity

For example:

ESC1

can allow control over who a certificate represents.

ESC15 instead introduces another important dimension:

What is the certificate allowed to do?

Conceptually:

Identity
   +
Certificate Purpose
   =
Authentication Capability

ESC15 can affect the:

Certificate Purpose

part of this relationship.

docs.title: Extended Key Usage
docs.text:
X.509 certificates can contain an:

Extended Key Usage

extension.

Common EKUs include:

Client Authentication
Server Authentication
Code Signing
Smart Card Logon
Certificate Request Agent

An EKU describes the intended purposes for which a certificate can be used.

docs.title: Application Policies
docs.text:
Windows also uses:

Application Policies

to describe certificate purposes.

Application Policies can contain OIDs representing capabilities such as:

Client Authentication
Certificate Request Agent
Code Signing

In many normal certificate configurations, the effective Application Policies correspond closely to the EKUs defined by the certificate template.

docs.title: Why Application Policies Matter
docs.text:
Suppose a template is intended only for:

Server Authentication

The expected certificate should not suddenly provide:

Client Authentication

or:

Certificate Request Agent

capabilities.

The intended security boundary is:

Template
   |
   v
Approved Certificate Purpose

ESC15 can violate that boundary.

docs.title: EKU vs Application Policies
docs.text:
These concepts are related but should not be treated as identical.

Conceptually:

Certificate Purpose
      |
      +--> Extended Key Usage
      |
      +--> Application Policies

Windows certificate processing can use Application Policies when determining certificate capabilities.

ESC15 specifically focuses on the ability to influence:

Application Policies

during certificate issuance.

docs.title: Why "EKUwu"?
docs.text:
The research community nicknamed ESC15:

EKUwu

because the technique effectively enables manipulation of certificate-purpose semantics normally associated with EKUs and Application Policies.

For reporting, however, prefer descriptive terminology such as:

Arbitrary Application Policies in AD CS Certificate Requests

rather than relying only on the nickname.

docs.title: Certificate Template Schema Versions
docs.text:
Certificate templates have schema versions.

Common versions include:

Version 1
Version 2
Version 3
Version 4

ESC15 is particularly associated with:

Schema Version 1

certificate templates.

docs.title: Why Version 1 Matters
docs.text:
Version 1 certificate templates originate from older Active Directory certificate-template designs.

They have different configuration and request-processing semantics from later template versions.

The vulnerable interaction that became ESC15 involves how Application Policies can be supplied when using these templates on an unpatched CA.

docs.title: Template Schema Version Attribute
docs.text:
The template schema version can be identified through:

msPKI-Template-Schema-Version

For ESC15, pay particular attention to:

msPKI-Template-Schema-Version = 1

docs.title: Enumerate Schema Versions
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Import-Module ActiveDirectory

Determine the Configuration naming context:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext

Build the certificate-template container:

$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Enumerate templates and schema versions:

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties displayName,msPKI-Template-Schema-Version |
    Select-Object Name,displayName,msPKI-Template-Schema-Version

docs.title: Find Version 1 Templates
docs.text:
Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(&(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)(msPKI-Template-Schema-Version=1))' -Properties displayName,msPKI-Template-Schema-Version |
    Select-Object Name,displayName,msPKI-Template-Schema-Version,DistinguishedName

This is a useful first read-only ESC15 discovery step.

docs.title: Version 1 Alone Is Not ESC15
docs.text:
Do not report:

Schema Version 1
=
ESC15

A Version 1 template is only one part of the attack path.

Further conditions must be evaluated.

docs.title: ESC15 Core Preconditions
docs.text:
A useful assessment model is:

Schema Version 1 Template
        +
Template Published
        +
Low-Privilege Enrollment
        +
Supply in Request
        +
No Blocking Approval Controls
        +
Unpatched Issuing CA
        =
Potential ESC15

Additional certificate and authentication conditions determine the final impact.

docs.title: Condition 1 - Schema Version 1
docs.text:
Check:

msPKI-Template-Schema-Version

The classic ESC15 condition focuses on:

1

docs.title: Condition 2 - Template Is Published
docs.text:
The certificate template must normally be available through an Enterprise CA.

Conceptually:

Template
   |
   v
Published?
   |
   +--> No -> No Normal Enrollment Path
   |
   +--> Yes

docs.title: Enumerate Enterprise CAs
docs.text:
$enrollmentBase = "CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Then:

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $enrollmentBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKIEnrollmentService)' -Properties dNSHostName,certificateTemplates |
    Select-Object Name,dNSHostName,certificateTemplates

docs.title: Condition 3 - Low-Privilege Enrollment
docs.text:
Determine who can enroll.

Potentially broad principals include:

Authenticated Users
Domain Users
Domain Computers
Everyone
Large Departmental Groups

Broad enrollment does not automatically mean ESC15.

It becomes dangerous when combined with the remaining conditions.

docs.title: Template ACL Review
docs.text:
Retrieve a template:

$template = Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(cn=TargetTemplate)'

Inspect its ACL:

Get-Acl "AD:$($template.DistinguishedName)" |
    Format-List Owner,AccessToString

Review:

Enroll
Autoenroll
GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner

docs.title: Condition 4 - Supply in the Request
docs.text:
Microsoft specifically recommends disabling:

Supply in the request

when remediating vulnerable ESC15 templates.

The relevant template name flag is associated with:

CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT

This setting allows the requester to supply subject information in the certificate request.

docs.title: msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag
docs.text:
The relevant template attribute is:

msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag

Inspect it:

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(cn=TargetTemplate)' -Properties msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag |
    Select-Object Name,msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag

docs.title: Supply-in-Request Significance
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Requester
   |
   v
Controls Certificate Request
   |
   +--> Subject Information
   |
   +--> SAN Information
   |
   +--> Vulnerable Application Policy Processing

The exact behaviour depends on CA patch state.

docs.title: Condition 5 - No Manager Approval
docs.text:
A certificate template requiring:

CA Certificate Manager Approval

adds an administrative approval step.

This can disrupt a straightforward low-privilege ESC15 path.

Do not assume:

Manager Approval Enabled
=
Impossible Forever

but it materially changes exploitability.

docs.title: Condition 6 - No Required Authorised Signatures
docs.text:
Templates may require authorised signatures.

If:

Authorised Signatures > 0

the attacker needs additional prerequisites before enrollment succeeds.

Therefore this setting must be included in the assessment.

docs.title: Condition 7 - Vulnerable CA
docs.text:
This is the defining modern ESC15 condition.

The issuing CA must be vulnerable to:

CVE-2024-49019

A template that looks vulnerable from LDAP alone is not sufficient evidence.

You must correlate:

Template Configuration

with:

Issuing CA Patch State

docs.title: Modern Assessment Rule
docs.text:
In a current assessment:

Interesting Template
        |
        v
Which CA Publishes It?
        |
        v
Is That CA Patched?
        |
        +--> Yes -> Historical ESC15 Path Blocked
        |
        +--> No -> Investigate Further

This prevents false positives.

docs.title: Multiple CAs Matter
docs.text:
A template may be published by:

CA01
CA02
CA03

If:

CA01 = Patched
CA02 = Patched
CA03 = Unpatched

the template may still have an exploitable enrollment path through:

CA03

Therefore assess every CA publishing the template.

docs.title: Patch State Is Per CA
docs.text:
Do not evaluate CVE-2024-49019 only at the domain level.

The important asset is:

Certificate Authority Server

because that system processes the certificate request.

docs.title: Checking Windows Patch State
docs.text:
On an authorised CA host, basic patch inventory can be reviewed with:

Get-HotFix |
    Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 20 HotFixID,InstalledOn,Description

However, cumulative Windows servicing means:

Specific KB Missing

does not necessarily prove:

System Vulnerable

A later cumulative update may contain the fix.

docs.title: Better Patch Validation
docs.text:
Use:

Windows Version
Build Number
Installed Cumulative Update
Microsoft Security Update Guidance

together.

Record:

CA Operating System
Build
Patch Level
Assessment Date

docs.title: Do Not Remove Patches for Testing
docs.text:
Never:

Uninstall Security Update

or:

Roll Back CA

to prove ESC15.

If the CA is patched, report the template configuration as a hardening consideration only where appropriate.

Do not report CVE-2024-49019 exploitation as currently possible.

docs.title: Certipy Enumeration
docs.text:
Certipy can identify AD CS configuration and modern ESC conditions.

Check the version first:

certipy --version

Then:

certipy find -h

A typical authorised enumeration:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

Review:

Certificate Authorities
Certificate Templates
Schema Versions
Enrollment Rights
Subject Name Flags
Application Policies
ESC Findings

docs.title: Certipy ESC15
docs.text:
Modern Certipy versions can identify templates associated with ESC15 conditions.

Treat scanner output as:

Candidate

not:

Final Finding

Manually validate:

Template Version
Published CA
Enrollment Rights
Supply in Request
Approval Controls
CA Patch State

docs.title: Certipy Vulnerability Context
docs.text:
A tool may identify:

ESC15

because the directory configuration matches known prerequisites.

But LDAP enumeration alone cannot always prove the issuing Windows CA lacks the CVE-2024-49019 patch.

Therefore:

Certipy Finding
       |
       v
Verify CA Patch State
       |
       v
Determine Exploitability

docs.title: LDAP Enumeration from Linux
docs.text:
Enumerate Version 1 templates:

ldapsearch -LLL -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\audit-user' \
    -W \
    -b 'CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(&(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)(msPKI-Template-Schema-Version=1))' \
    cn \
    displayName \
    msPKI-Template-Schema-Version \
    msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag \
    pKIExtendedKeyUsage

docs.title: Enumerate Published Templates from Linux
docs.text:
Query Enrollment Services:

ldapsearch -LLL -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\audit-user' \
    -W \
    -b 'CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(objectClass=pKIEnrollmentService)' \
    cn \
    dNSHostName \
    certificateTemplates

docs.title: Certificate Application Policy OID
docs.text:
Application Policies are represented by OIDs.

One especially important example is:

Certificate Request Agent

OID:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1

This is associated with enrollment-agent functionality.

docs.title: Client Authentication
docs.text:
A commonly important authentication EKU is:

Client Authentication

OID:

1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2

docs.title: Smart Card Logon
docs.text:
Smart Card Logon

OID:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.2

docs.title: PKINIT Client Authentication
docs.text:
Another authentication-related OID is:

1.3.6.1.5.2.3.4

associated with PKINIT client authentication.

docs.title: ESC15 Application-Policy Injection
docs.text:
The important conceptual issue is that a vulnerable CA may accept requester-controlled Application Policies that are not authorised by the certificate template.

Conceptually:

Template Says:
Server Authentication
       |
       v
Request Adds:
Client Authentication
       |
       v
Vulnerable CA
       |
       v
Issued Certificate Contains
Unexpected Application Policy

docs.title: Why This Is Dangerous
docs.text:
The requester may transform:

Limited Certificate

into:

Authentication Certificate

or potentially:

Enrollment Agent Certificate

depending on the environment and request.

This can turn an otherwise low-risk template into a privilege-escalation primitive.

docs.title: ESC15 Path 1 - Authentication Capability
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Vulnerable V1 Template
       |
       v
Supply Request Data
       |
       v
Add Authentication Application Policy
       |
       v
Certificate
       |
       v
Certificate Authentication

Additional identity-mapping requirements still apply.

docs.title: ESC15 Path 2 - Enrollment Agent Capability
docs.text:
Another important conceptual chain is:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Vulnerable V1 Template
       |
       v
Add Certificate Request Agent Policy
       |
       v
Enrollment Agent Certificate
       |
       v
Request Certificate on Behalf of Another Principal

This creates a relationship between:

ESC15

and concepts normally associated with:

ESC3

docs.title: Enrollment Agent
docs.text:
An Enrollment Agent certificate allows a principal to participate in:

Enroll on Behalf Of

workflows.

Conceptually:

Enrollment Agent
       |
       v
Signs Request
       |
       v
Certificate for Another User

This is legitimate functionality when properly restricted.

docs.title: ESC15 to ESC3-Like Chain
docs.text:
A vulnerable environment can conceptually allow:

ESC15
   |
   v
Obtain Enrollment Agent Capability
   |
   v
Enrollment-on-Behalf-of Workflow
   |
   v
Authentication Certificate for Target

Whether this succeeds depends on the second template, enrollment-agent restrictions and CA configuration.

docs.title: Second Template Matters
docs.text:
Obtaining an Enrollment Agent certificate does not automatically grant:

Certificate for Any User

A second template must permit the relevant enrollment-on-behalf-of workflow.

Therefore assess:

Agent Template
      +
Target Template
      +
Enrollment Agent Restrictions
      +
CA Configuration

docs.title: Enrollment Agent Restrictions
docs.text:
Enterprise CAs can restrict:

Which Enrollment Agents

may request:

Which Templates

for:

Which Users

These restrictions can materially reduce impact.

docs.title: ESC15 and ESC1
docs.text:
ESC1 generally involves:

Requester-Controlled Subject/SAN
+
Authentication-Capable Template

ESC15 can involve:

Requester-Controlled Subject/SAN
+
Requester-Controlled Application Policy

on a vulnerable CA.

docs.title: Key Difference
docs.text:
ESC1:

Template Already Permits Authentication

ESC15:

Requester May Be Able to Add
Authentication Capability

This distinction is critical.

docs.title: ESC15 and ESC2
docs.text:
ESC2 involves:

Any Purpose

or:

No EKU

certificate templates.

ESC15 instead abuses request processing to introduce arbitrary Application Policies.

docs.title: ESC15 and ESC3
docs.text:
ESC3 involves legitimate Enrollment Agent capability exposed through insecure template configuration.

ESC15 may allow a requester to introduce:

Certificate Request Agent

as an Application Policy under vulnerable conditions.

docs.title: ESC15 and ESC4
docs.text:
ESC4 involves dangerous ACL permissions over a certificate template.

If an attacker can modify a template directly:

ESC4

may already provide a path to change its security properties.

ESC15 differs because the requester may not need template-write access.

docs.title: ESC15 and ESC6
docs.text:
ESC6 concerns CA-level SAN configuration through:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

ESC15 concerns:

Application Policies

and vulnerable request processing.

Do not merge them into one finding.

docs.title: ESC15 and ESC9
docs.text:
ESC9 concerns:

No SID Security Extension

on a template.

ESC15 concerns:

Arbitrary Application Policies

through CVE-2024-49019.

Both may interact with certificate authentication, but their root causes differ.

docs.title: ESC15 and ESC10
docs.text:
ESC10 concerns weak certificate mapping configuration.

ESC15 concerns certificate issuance and certificate purpose.

A certificate obtained through ESC15 still needs to be mapped to an account for authentication.

docs.title: ESC15 and ESC14
docs.text:
ESC14 concerns:

altSecurityIdentities

explicit certificate mappings.

ESC15 concerns:

Application Policy Injection

They can potentially form parts of the same larger certificate-authentication attack graph.

docs.title: ESC15 and ESC13
docs.text:
ESC13 involves:

Issuance Policies

linked to Active Directory groups.

ESC15 involves:

Application Policies

These are different certificate extensions and security concepts.

Do not confuse them.

docs.title: Application Policy vs Issuance Policy
docs.text:
A useful distinction:

Application Policy
       |
       v
What May This Certificate Do?

versus:

Issuance Policy
       |
       v
Under What Policy Was
This Certificate Issued?

ESC15 concerns:

Application Policy

ESC13 concerns:

Issuance Policy

docs.title: Safe Validation Strategy
docs.text:
For production assessments, prefer:

Template Enumeration
        |
        v
Identify ESC15 Candidate
        |
        v
Identify Publishing CA
        |
        v
Verify Patch State
        |
        v
Determine Exposure

This usually provides sufficient evidence.

docs.title: Read-Only Proof
docs.text:
A strong read-only proof can demonstrate:

Template = Version 1
Template = Published
Low-Privilege User = Enroll
Supply in Request = Enabled
Approval = Not Required
CA = Vulnerable / Unpatched

This is often enough to establish ESC15 exposure without requesting a malicious certificate.

docs.title: Do Not Inject Privileged Policies by Default
docs.text:
Avoid requesting production certificates containing arbitrary:

Client Authentication

or:

Certificate Request Agent

policies solely to prove the vulnerability.

This can create a real credential with unintended privileges.

docs.title: Controlled Laboratory Validation
docs.text:
If end-to-end proof is required:

Dedicated Test CA
       |
       v
Dedicated V1 Template
       |
       v
Dedicated Test User
       |
       v
Controlled Application Policy
       |
       v
Test Certificate

Do not use:

Administrator
Domain Admin
Enterprise Admin
Production Service Account

as the target.

docs.title: Certificate Inspection
docs.text:
If an authorised test certificate has been issued, inspect it.

Windows:

certutil -dump esc15-test.cer

Review:

Enhanced Key Usage
Application Policies
Subject
Subject Alternative Name
Certificate Template
Issuer

docs.title: OpenSSL Inspection
docs.text:
For PEM:

openssl x509 -in esc15-test.pem -text -noout

For DER:

openssl x509 -in esc15-test.cer -inform DER -text -noout

Remember that Microsoft-specific certificate extensions may be easier to interpret with Windows certificate tooling.

docs.title: Expected vs Actual Policy
docs.text:
The most useful evidence is:

Template Expected Policy
          |
          v
Compare
          |
          v
Issued Certificate Policy

If the issued certificate contains capabilities not authorised by the template, that is significant.

docs.title: Certificate Request Archive
docs.text:
Where available and authorised, CA request records can help determine:

What Was Requested?

and:

What Was Issued?

This is useful for both assessment and incident response.

docs.title: Detecting ESC15
docs.text:
Detection should combine:

CA Patch State
       +
Template Configuration
       +
Certificate Requests
       +
Issued Certificate Policies
       +
Authentication Activity

docs.title: Microsoft Defender for Identity
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender for Identity includes a security posture assessment named:

Prevent Certificate Enrollment with arbitrary Application Policies (ESC15)

The assessment identifies vulnerable templates associated with unpatched AD CS servers.

docs.title: MDI Remediation Guidance
docs.text:
Microsoft's current guidance includes:

Remove enrollment permission
for unprivileged users

and:

Disable "Supply in the request"

and:

Patch vulnerable AD CS servers

The CA patch is the critical CVE remediation.

docs.title: Certificate Services Auditing
docs.text:
Where Certificate Services auditing is enabled, monitor:

4886

for certificate requests and:

4887

for certificate issuance.

docs.title: Suspicious Request Pattern
docs.text:
A useful detection concept is:

Low-Privilege Requester
       |
       v
Version 1 Template
       |
       v
Unexpected Request Attributes
       |
       v
Certificate Issued
       |
       v
Authentication / Enrollment Agent Use

docs.title: Monitor Version 1 Templates
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory of:

Schema Version 1 Templates

especially those that are:

Published
Broadly Enrollable
Supply in Request

docs.title: Monitor Template Publication
docs.text:
A previously unused template can become dangerous if an administrator suddenly publishes it.

Monitor changes to:

certificateTemplates

on Enrollment Services objects.

docs.title: Monitor Template ACLs
docs.text:
A safe template today may become dangerous if:

Enrollment Rights

are broadened.

Monitor changes to:

nTSecurityDescriptor

on certificate templates.

docs.title: Monitor Name Flags
docs.text:
Changes to:

msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag

can affect whether requesters can supply identity information.

docs.title: Event 5136
docs.text:
With Directory Service Changes auditing enabled:

5136

may provide visibility into modifications to certificate-template objects and related PKI configuration stored in Active Directory.

docs.title: Monitor CA Patch Compliance
docs.text:
Because ESC15 includes a software vulnerability component, configuration monitoring alone is insufficient.

Maintain:

CA Asset Inventory
+
OS Version
+
Build
+
Security Update Compliance

docs.title: Hardening ESC15
docs.text:
The strongest mitigation is:

Patch Every AD CS Server

affected by CVE-2024-49019.

Do not rely only on certificate-template changes.

docs.title: Patch All Enterprise CAs
docs.text:
Inventory every issuing CA:

Root CA
Issuing CA
Enterprise CA
Online Subordinate CA

Determine whether the operating system requires the relevant security update.

docs.title: Offline Root CAs
docs.text:
An offline root CA may not process ordinary enterprise certificate requests, but it should still be maintained according to the organisation's patching and PKI lifecycle procedures.

Focus ESC15 exposure analysis on:

CAs Processing Attacker-Reachable Requests

docs.title: Restrict Enrollment
docs.text:
Remove unnecessary enrollment permissions from:

Authenticated Users
Domain Users
Domain Computers
Everyone

for sensitive templates.

docs.title: Disable Supply in the Request
docs.text:
Where not required:

Supply in the request

should be disabled.

Microsoft specifically recommends this for vulnerable ESC15 template configurations.

docs.title: Use Modern Templates
docs.text:
Where operationally feasible, migrate legacy:

Version 1

templates to modern template designs.

Do not simply duplicate a template and assume the resulting configuration is secure.

Review:

Enrollment Rights
Name Flags
EKUs
Application Policies
Approval
Signatures
Validity
Private-Key Settings

docs.title: Require Approval Where Appropriate
docs.text:
For sensitive certificate types, consider:

CA Certificate Manager Approval

where operationally appropriate.

This should complement patching and least-privilege enrollment.

docs.title: Authorised Signatures
docs.text:
Sensitive workflows may benefit from:

Authorised Signature Requirements

depending on the certificate use case.

docs.title: Review Enrollment Agent Templates
docs.text:
Because ESC15 can potentially introduce:

Certificate Request Agent

capability, review all templates and CA restrictions related to enrollment agents.

docs.title: Review Enrollment Agent Restrictions
docs.text:
Confirm that enrollment agents cannot indiscriminately request certificates:

For Any User

using:

Any Template

unless this is explicitly required and strongly controlled.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Certificate enrollment should follow:

Need to Enroll

rather than:

Convenient to Enroll

Broad enrollment increases the impact of future template or CA vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
If ESC15 exploitation is suspected:

Identify Vulnerable CA
       |
       v
Identify Vulnerable Templates
       |
       v
Identify Requests
       |
       v
Identify Issued Certificates
       |
       v
Inspect Application Policies
       |
       v
Identify Authentication / Agent Use
       |
       v
Revoke Malicious Certificates

docs.title: Determine Exposure Window
docs.text:
Establish:

When Was CA Vulnerable?

and:

When Was Patch Installed?

Then review certificate requests during that period.

docs.title: Identify Relevant Templates
docs.text:
Search for templates that were:

Version 1
Published
Broadly Enrollable
Supply in Request

during the vulnerable period.

docs.title: Search CA Database
docs.text:
Review requests for affected templates.

Capture:

Request ID
Requester
Template
Subject
SAN
Disposition
Serial Number
Request Time
Issue Time

docs.title: Inspect Suspicious Certificates
docs.text:
Review:

Application Policies
Extended Key Usage
Subject
SAN
Requester
Template

Look for policies inconsistent with the intended template purpose.

docs.title: Enrollment Agent Investigation
docs.text:
If a suspicious certificate contains:

Certificate Request Agent

determine whether it was subsequently used to request certificates on behalf of other principals.

docs.title: Authentication Investigation
docs.text:
If a suspicious certificate contains authentication capabilities, review:

4768

and related Kerberos activity where available.

Correlate:

Certificate Issuance
       |
       v
Certificate Authentication
       |
       v
Privileged Activity

docs.title: Revoke Suspicious Certificates
docs.text:
Where malicious certificates are identified:

Revoke
   |
   v
Publish Updated CRL
   |
   v
Verify Revocation Availability

docs.title: Patch the CA
docs.text:
Incident containment should include applying the appropriate Microsoft security updates to affected CA servers.

Do not only revoke certificates while leaving the issuance vulnerability available.

docs.title: Review Template Configuration
docs.text:
After patching, also remediate dangerous template configuration.

For example:

Remove Broad Enrollment
Disable Supply in Request
Review Legacy V1 Templates

This provides defence in depth.

docs.title: Reporting ESC15
docs.text:
Avoid a title containing only:

ESC15

Prefer:

Unpatched AD CS Allows Arbitrary Certificate Application Policies

or:

Low-Privilege Users Can Request Certificates with Arbitrary Application Policies

or:

AD CS Vulnerable to CVE-2024-49019 Through Legacy Certificate Template

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
AD CS Allows Low-Privilege Certificate Enrollment with Arbitrary
Application Policies

CVE:
CVE-2024-49019

AD CS Technique:
ESC15

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Affected Template:
LegacyWebServer

Template Schema:
Version 1

Description:
The LegacyWebServer certificate template is published by CORP-CA01
and permits enrollment by low-privileged domain users.

The template is a schema version 1 template and permits requesters
to supply subject information in the certificate request.

The issuing Certificate Authority has not received the security
update addressing CVE-2024-49019.

Under this configuration, a low-privileged requester may be able to
influence Application Policies in certificates issued from the
affected template.

This could allow a certificate intended for a limited purpose to
receive additional capabilities such as authentication or
Certificate Request Agent functionality.

Impact:
Successful exploitation could enable certificate-based privilege
escalation.

Depending on the available certificate templates, certificate
mapping configuration and Enrollment Agent restrictions, the
resulting certificate could potentially be used to impersonate
higher-privileged identities and compromise sensitive Active
Directory resources.

Testing:
The finding was validated through read-only template enumeration,
enrollment-permission analysis and CA patch-state verification.

No certificate containing unauthorised Application Policies was
requested from the production CA.

Recommendation:
Apply the Microsoft security update addressing CVE-2024-49019 to
all affected AD CS servers.

Remove unnecessary enrollment permissions for low-privileged
principals.

Disable "Supply in the request" on templates where requester-defined
subject information is not required.

Review legacy schema version 1 certificate templates and migrate
them to appropriately secured modern templates where possible.

Review Enrollment Agent templates and restrictions for additional
certificate-based escalation paths.

docs.title: Patched Environment Reporting
docs.text:
If:

Template Matches Historical ESC15 Conditions

but:

All Publishing CAs Are Patched

do not report:

Exploitable CVE-2024-49019

Instead consider whether the remaining template configuration warrants a separate hardening observation.

docs.title: False-Positive Avoidance
docs.text:
Do not determine ESC15 from:

Version 1 Template

alone.

Do not determine ESC15 from:

Supply in Request

alone.

Do not determine ESC15 from:

Broad Enrollment

alone.

Do not determine ESC15 from:

Certipy Label

alone.

Correlate the complete path.

docs.title: ESC15 Severity Model
docs.text:
Use:

Unpatched CA
      +
Vulnerable Template
      +
Low-Privilege Enrollment
      +
Attacker-Controlled Request
      +
Useful Application Policy
      +
Usable Identity Path
      =
Impact

docs.title: Lower-Risk Example
docs.text:
Version 1 Template
       |
       v
Administrators Only
       |
       v
Patched CA

This does not represent a practical low-privilege ESC15 path.

docs.title: High-Risk Example
docs.text:
Domain Users
     |
     v
Version 1 Template
     |
     v
Supply in Request
     |
     v
Unpatched CA
     |
     v
Authentication Capability

This requires serious investigation.

docs.title: Critical Example
docs.text:
Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Vulnerable Template
       |
       v
Unpatched Enterprise CA
       |
       v
Arbitrary Application Policy
       |
       v
Enrollment Agent / Authentication
       |
       v
Privileged Identity
       |
       v
Domain Compromise

This may represent critical impact.

  • [ ] Separate historical from current exploitability
  • [ ] Avoid unnecessary active exploitation
  • [ ] Provide patch and configuration remediation

docs.title: ESC15 Testing Model
docs.text:
The normal certificate model is:

Certificate Template
       |
       v
Defined Certificate Purpose
       |
       v
Certificate

The ESC15 model is:

Certificate Template
       |
       v
Vulnerable Request Processing
       |
       v
Requester-Controlled Application Policy
       |
       v
Certificate with Additional Capability

The authentication model is:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Version 1 Template
       |
       v
Unpatched CA
       |
       v
Authentication Application Policy
       |
       v
Authentication Certificate

The Enrollment Agent model is:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
ESC15
       |
       v
Certificate Request Agent Policy
       |
       v
Enrollment Agent Certificate
       |
       v
On-Behalf-Of Enrollment
       |
       v
Target Certificate

The patch model is:

Potential ESC15 Template
       |
       v
Publishing CA
       |
       v
CVE-2024-49019 Patched?
       |
       +--> Yes
       |     |
       |     v
       | Historical Exploit Path Blocked
       |
       +--> No
             |
             v
        Continue Analysis

The multi-CA model is:

Template
   |
   +--> CA01 -> Patched
   |
   +--> CA02 -> Patched
   |
   +--> CA03 -> Unpatched
                    |
                    v
              Exposure Remains

The safe-testing model is:

Enumerate Template
       |
       v
Identify Publishing CA
       |
       v
Verify Patch State
       |
       v
Validate Permissions
       |
       v
Evidence Sufficient?
       |
       +--> Yes -> Report
       |
       +--> No
               |
               v
         Dedicated Test CA
               |
               v
         Controlled Request
               |
               v
         Inspect Certificate

The detection model is:

Vulnerable CA
     +
Vulnerable Template
     |
     v
Certificate Request
     |
     v
Unexpected Application Policy
     |
     v
Certificate Issuance
     |
     v
Authentication / Agent Use

The defensive model is:

Patched CA
   +
Restricted Enrollment
   +
No Unnecessary Supply-in-Request
   +
Modern Templates
   +
Enrollment Agent Restrictions
   +
Monitoring
   =
Reduced ESC15 Risk

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Can I issue myself a Domain Admin
authentication certificate?"

Ask:
"Can I establish that an unpatched
CA processes a vulnerable Version 1
template available to my principal?"

For defenders:

Do Not Assume:
"The template only contains a harmless
EKU, so certificates from it are harmless."

Ask:
"Can the requester influence the
Application Policies that the CA places
into the resulting certificate?"

The complete ESC15 relationship is:

Low-Privilege Enrollment
        |
        v
Schema Version 1 Template
        |
        v
Supply in Request
        |
        v
Unpatched AD CS
        |
        v
CVE-2024-49019
        |
        v
Arbitrary Application Policies
        |
        v
Certificate Capability
        |
        v
Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Microsoft - ESC15 Security Posture Assessment
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender for Identity - Certificate Security Posture Assessments

Microsoft Defender for Identity includes the:

Prevent Certificate Enrollment with arbitrary Application Policies (ESC15)

assessment.

Microsoft states that the recommendation directly addresses:

CVE-2024-49019

and identifies vulnerable certificate templates associated with unpatched AD CS servers.

Microsoft's remediation guidance includes:

Remove enrollment permission for unprivileged users
Disable "Supply in the request"
Patch vulnerable AD CS servers

docs.title: Microsoft - CVE-2024-49019
docs.text:
Microsoft Security Response Center - CVE-2024-49019

Use the Microsoft Security Response Center information together with the CA operating-system version and current cumulative update to determine whether the issuing CA is vulnerable.

Certipy supports AD CS enumeration and modern ESC analysis.

Always verify the installed version:

certipy --version
certipy find -h

before relying on command syntax or vulnerability classification.

docs.text:
SpecterOps - Certified Pre-Owned

Certified Pre-Owned provides the foundational AD CS privilege-escalation model from which the ESC taxonomy developed.

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
ESC15 introduced another important question into AD CS assessments.

Historically, testers commonly asked:

Who Can Enroll?

Who Can the Certificate Represent?

and:

What EKUs Does the Template Have?

ESC15 adds:

Can the Requester Influence the
Application Policies of the
Issued Certificate?

The expected security model is:

Template
   |
   v
Defines Certificate Purpose
   |
   v
CA Enforces Purpose
   |
   v
Certificate

ESC15 breaks this model under vulnerable conditions:

Template
   |
   v
Requester Influences Purpose
   |
   v
Vulnerable CA
   |
   v
More Powerful Certificate

The technique is especially important because a template that initially appears harmless may become security-sensitive if the requester can introduce:

Client Authentication

or:

Certificate Request Agent

capabilities.

However, ESC15 assessment in modern environments must always include:

CA Patch State

CVE-2024-49019 is a patched software vulnerability.

Therefore:

Vulnerable-Looking Template

does not automatically mean:

Exploitable ESC15

The complete assessment should establish:

Schema Version
       |
       v
Enrollment Rights
       |
       v
Supply in Request
       |
       v
Publishing CA
       |
       v
Patch State
       |
       v
Application Policy Impact

Microsoft currently recommends three particularly important defensive actions:

Patch the AD CS server

Remove unnecessary enrollment
permissions for unprivileged users

Disable Supply in the request
where it is not required

For penetration testers, the safest evidence is normally:

Low-Privilege Enrollment
        +
Vulnerable Template Configuration
        +
Unpatched Publishing CA

rather than issuing a certificate containing a privileged Application Policy.

For defenders, ESC15 is another reason AD CS should be treated as:

Tier 0 Infrastructure

and managed through:

Patch Management
Template Governance
Least-Privilege Enrollment
Configuration Monitoring
Certificate Auditing

The next technique to assess is:

ESC16

which moves from a template-specific missing SID security extension to a CA-wide configuration that can suppress the SID security extension across certificates issued by the CA.

docs.title: AD CS ESC16 - CA-Wide SID Security Extension Disabled
docs.text:
ESC16 is an Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) security condition in which a Certification Authority is configured so that certificates it issues do not contain the Active Directory SID security extension:

szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT

OID:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

The SID security extension was introduced as part of Microsoft's certificate-based authentication hardening following:

CVE-2022-26923

and:

KB5014754

Its purpose is to provide a strong relationship between:

Certificate

and:

Active Directory SID

Conceptually:

Certificate
    |
    v
SID Security Extension
    |
    v
Active Directory SID
    |
    v
Specific User / Computer

ESC16 occurs when the CA suppresses this extension globally.

The important distinction is:

ESC9
=
Individual Template Omits SID Extension

whereas:

ESC16
=
CA Omits SID Extension Globally

This makes ESC16 particularly significant because the weakness can affect certificates issued from many templates rather than one specific template.

Authorised testing only

ESC16 can become part of certificate-based account-impersonation chains. During production assessments, begin with read-only CA configuration, template and certificate inspection. Do not modify user UPNs, enable ESC6, disable certificate extensions, weaken domain-controller certificate mapping, or request certificates for privileged production identities merely to demonstrate impact.

docs.title: ESC16 at a Glance
docs.text:
The expected certificate issuance model is:

Certificate Request
        |
        v
Enterprise CA
        |
        v
SID Security Extension Added
        |
        v
Issued Certificate
        |
        v
Strong Account Mapping

ESC16 changes this to:

Certificate Request
        |
        v
ESC16 CA
        |
        v
SID Security Extension Suppressed
        |
        v
Issued Certificate
        |
        v
No SID Security Extension

The practical security impact then depends on:

Certificate Identity
        +
Certificate Mapping
        +
Other AD CS Conditions
        +
Domain Controller Behaviour

docs.title: Why the SID Security Extension Exists
docs.text:
Historically, Windows certificate authentication could map certificates to Active Directory accounts using identity information such as:

UPN
DNS Name
Subject
Issuer

Some of these mappings were not cryptographically tied to one specific Active Directory object.

Conceptually:

Certificate
    |
    v
UPN = alice@corp.example
    |
    v
Find Alice

If an attacker could manipulate the identity information appearing in the certificate, this could create impersonation opportunities.

docs.title: Strong Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Microsoft introduced stronger certificate binding so that a certificate could contain information tied directly to the Active Directory principal.

The important extension is:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

Conceptually:

Certificate
    |
    v
SID Extension
    |
    v
S-1-5-21-...-1105
    |
    v
CORP\Alice

This provides substantially stronger identity binding than relying only on a UPN or DNS name.

docs.title: Security Extension Name
docs.text:
The Microsoft security extension is commonly referenced as:

szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT

OID:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

During assessment, remember both forms because tools and documentation may display either.

docs.title: ESC16 Root Cause
docs.text:
ESC16 is associated with the CA's:

DisableExtensionList

configuration.

If the SID security extension OID appears in this list:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

the CA can suppress the SID security extension from certificates it issues.

Conceptually:

CA Policy Module
      |
      v
DisableExtensionList
      |
      v
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2
      |
      v
SID Extension Disabled

docs.title: CA-Wide Scope
docs.text:
The word:

CA-Wide

is important.

With ESC9:

Template A -> No SID Extension
Template B -> SID Extension
Template C -> SID Extension

With ESC16:

                ESC16 CA
                   |
        +----------+----------+
        |          |          |
        v          v          v
    Template A Template B Template C
        |          |          |
        v          v          v
     No SID      No SID     No SID

The CA-level policy affects certificate issuance regardless of the normal template expectation.

docs.title: ESC9 vs ESC16
docs.text:
+----------------------+-----------------------------+
| Technique            | SID Extension Suppression   |
+----------------------+-----------------------------+
| ESC9                 | Certificate template        |
| ESC16                | Certification Authority     |
+----------------------+-----------------------------+

ESC9 is primarily a:

Template Configuration

issue.

ESC16 is primarily a:

CA Configuration

issue.

docs.title: ESC9 Configuration
docs.text:
ESC9 is associated with:

CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

in:

msPKI-Enrollment-Flag

on an individual certificate template.

docs.title: ESC16 Configuration
docs.text:
ESC16 instead involves:

DisableExtensionList

at the CA policy-module level.

The relevant value is:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

docs.title: Why ESC16 Matters More Broadly
docs.text:
Consider a CA publishing:

User
Computer
WebServer
VPNUser
WorkstationAuthentication
CustomAuthentication

If only:

VPNUser

has ESC9, only certificates from that template intentionally omit the SID security extension.

With ESC16:

All Certificates Issued by the CA

can be affected by the CA-wide suppression.

This dramatically increases the number of templates that must be reviewed.

docs.title: ESC16 Does Not Automatically Mean Domain Compromise
docs.text:
Finding:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

in:

DisableExtensionList

is an important security finding.

But it does not mean:

Any Domain User
Can Immediately Become
Domain Administrator

Additional conditions determine exploitability.

docs.title: ESC16 Attack Model
docs.text:
A better model is:

ESC16
   |
   v
Certificate Has No SID Extension
   |
   v
Can Attacker Influence Identity?
   |
   +--> No -> Limited Direct Exploitability
   |
   +--> Yes
           |
           v
    Mapping Path Available?
           |
           +--> No -> Blocked
           |
           +--> Yes
                   |
                   v
             Impersonation Path

docs.title: Important Prerequisites
docs.text:
Potential exploitation can depend on combinations involving:

Enrollment Rights
Authentication-Capable Template
Identity Manipulation
ESC6
Explicit Mapping
Domain Controller Patch State
Certificate Mapping Behaviour

Do not analyse ESC16 in isolation.

docs.title: Modern 2026 Context
docs.text:
ESC16 must be assessed using current certificate-binding behaviour.

Microsoft's KB5014754 rollout substantially changed certificate authentication.

By the current enforcement model, supported and fully patched domain controllers should be operating under Microsoft's strong certificate-binding requirements.

Historical guidance based on permanent compatibility-mode fallback should therefore not be assumed to describe a modern fully patched environment.

docs.title: Historical Compatibility Mode
docs.text:
Earlier deployments could use:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

to control Kerberos certificate-binding enforcement.

Historical values included behaviour corresponding to:

Disabled
Compatibility
Full Enforcement

Many older ESC9 and ESC16 attack descriptions rely on compatibility behaviour.

docs.title: Full Enforcement
docs.text:
Under Full Enforcement, domain controllers require strong certificate mapping rather than freely falling back to historical weak certificate mappings.

This substantially changes simple UPN-manipulation attack paths.

Therefore:

No SID Security Extension

does not automatically mean:

UPN Mapping Will Work

on a modern fully patched domain.

docs.title: September 2025 Change
docs.text:
Microsoft's KB5014754 deployment timeline is important for current assessments.

The historical registry-based compatibility mechanism was transitional.

By September 2025, Microsoft removed support for using the legacy registry configuration to return patched domain controllers to the previous compatibility behaviour.

Therefore, in 2026:

Old Lab Assumptions

should not be applied blindly to:

Fully Patched Production Domains

docs.title: ESC16 Still Matters
docs.text:
Strong certificate binding does not make ESC16 irrelevant.

The SID security extension exists for a reason.

Globally suppressing it:

Weakens Certificate Identity Binding

and can become exploitable when combined with other certificate identity mechanisms.

One particularly important relationship is:

ESC16 + ESC6

docs.title: ESC16 and ESC6
docs.text:
ESC6 occurs when a CA permits requester-supplied SAN information through the CA-wide:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

configuration.

Conceptually:

ESC6
 |
 v
Attacker Influences SAN

ESC16 provides:

ESC16
 |
 v
Normal SID Extension Missing

Together:

ESC6
   +
ESC16
   |
   v
Attacker-Controlled Certificate Identity
   |
   v
No Normal SID Security Extension

This combination requires careful investigation.

docs.title: SID in SAN URL
docs.text:
Modern certificate mapping introduced a special SAN URL representation that can contain a SID.

Conceptually:

URL=tag:microsoft.com,2022-09-14:sid:<SID>

This mechanism is important when analysing modern ESC6 combinations with ESC9 or ESC16.

Do not treat it as equivalent to the normal CA-generated SID security extension.

docs.title: Normal SID Extension vs SAN SID
docs.text:
Normal strong issuance:

CA
 |
 v
SID Security Extension
 |
 v
Requester SID

Potential abuse chain:

Requester
   |
   v
Attacker-Controlled SAN
   |
   v
SID URL

The trust boundary is therefore very different.

docs.title: ESC16 + ESC6 Conceptual Chain
docs.text:
Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Authentication Template
       |
       v
ESC6 CA
       |
       +--> Target UPN
       |
       +--> Target SID URL
       |
       v
ESC16
       |
       v
Normal SID Extension Suppressed
       |
       v
Certificate
       |
       v
Certificate Authentication

This is one reason ESC16 remains security-relevant even with modern certificate-binding protections.

docs.title: Do Not Enable ESC6 for Testing
docs.text:
If ESC16 exists but ESC6 does not:

Do Not Enable
EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

to create an attack chain.

That would introduce another CA-wide vulnerability.

Report the existing condition and explain the potential chaining risk.

docs.title: ESC16 and ESC9
docs.text:
The result of ESC9 and ESC16 can look similar in an issued certificate:

No SID Security Extension

But the cause differs.

ESC9:

Template Says:
Do Not Include Security Extension

ESC16:

CA Says:
Do Not Include Security Extension

docs.title: ESC16 Can Override Secure Templates
docs.text:
A template may be correctly configured to include the SID security extension.

But if the CA globally disables the extension:

Secure Template
      |
      v
ESC16 CA
      |
      v
Certificate Without SID Extension

Therefore template-only auditing can miss ESC16.

docs.title: ESC16 and ESC10
docs.text:
ESC10 concerns weak certificate mapping configuration.

ESC16 concerns certificate issuance without the normal SID security extension.

Historically:

ESC16
   +
Weak Mapping
   |
   v
Increased Impersonation Risk

In a modern environment, evaluate current Microsoft mapping enforcement before claiming the historical chain remains viable.

docs.title: ESC16 and ESC14
docs.text:
ESC14 concerns:

altSecurityIdentities

and explicit certificate mappings.

Explicit strong mappings can provide a valid mapping even when a certificate lacks the normal SID security extension.

Therefore:

ESC16

and:

ESC14

should be analysed as different security conditions.

docs.title: ESC16 and ESC1
docs.text:
ESC1 concerns insecure certificate templates where a requester can control certificate identity and obtain an authentication-capable certificate.

ESC16 concerns CA-wide suppression of the SID security extension.

A template vulnerable to ESC1 should be reported based on its own root cause.

ESC16 can increase the overall certificate-identity attack surface but should not replace the ESC1 analysis.

docs.title: ESC16 and ESC4
docs.text:
ESC4 concerns dangerous ACL permissions over certificate templates.

An attacker with template-control rights may be able to create or expose additional certificate abuse paths.

ESC16 increases the importance of reviewing all authentication-capable templates published by the affected CA.

docs.title: ESC16 and CA Permissions
docs.text:
ESC16 is usually an administrative CA configuration issue.

Therefore also review:

Who Can Administer the CA?

Relevant privilege paths may include:

CA Administrator
Local Administrator on CA
Enterprise PKI Administrators
Dangerous CA ACLs

A malicious actor who controls the CA may be able to alter far more than DisableExtensionList.

docs.title: ESC5 Relationship
docs.text:
Dangerous control over PKI infrastructure can fall into the broader:

ESC5

category.

If an attacker can modify CA policy-module registry configuration because they control the CA server, the root cause may be:

PKI Infrastructure Compromise

rather than merely a static ESC16 misconfiguration.

docs.title: Enumerating ESC16 with Certipy
docs.text:
Certipy can enumerate CA configuration and identify ESC16.

Check the installed version:

certipy --version

Then review:

certipy find -h

A typical authorised enumeration is:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

docs.title: Certipy ESC16 Indicator
docs.text:
Modern Certipy output can identify:

ESC16

when the CA's disabled-extension configuration contains the SID security extension.

A relevant result may conceptually show:

Disabled Extensions:
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

ESC16:
Security Extension is disabled

docs.title: Treat Tool Output as Evidence, Not the Entire Analysis
docs.text:
Do not stop at:

Certipy Says ESC16

Determine:

Which CA?
Which Templates?
Who Can Enroll?
Which Templates Authenticate?
Is ESC6 Present?
What Certificates Are Being Issued?
What Is the Current DC Mapping Behaviour?

docs.title: Native CA Enumeration
docs.text:
On the CA itself, an administrator can inspect the policy-module disabled extension configuration with:

certutil -getreg policy\DisableExtensionList

This is a read-only command.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
Search the output for:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

If present, investigate ESC16.

docs.title: Registry Location
docs.text:
The CA policy configuration is stored beneath:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration

with CA-specific policy-module configuration below the relevant CA.

Do not hard-code a policy-module subkey name without first enumerating the actual CA configuration because deployments can differ.

docs.title: Read CA Name
docs.text:
On the CA:

certutil -getreg CA\CAName

docs.title: PowerShell Registry Discovery
docs.text:
A read-only approach can begin with:

$base = 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration'
Get-ChildItem $base

Then inspect the relevant CA configuration.

docs.title: Search for DisableExtensionList
docs.text:
A controlled administrative audit can search beneath the CA configuration:

$base = 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration'

Get-ChildItem $base -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    ForEach-Object {
        $item = Get-ItemProperty $_.PSPath -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        if ($null -ne $item.DisableExtensionList) {
            [PSCustomObject]@{
                Path                 = $_.PSPath
                DisableExtensionList = $item.DisableExtensionList
            }
        }
    }

This avoids changing the CA configuration.

docs.title: CA Access Requirements
docs.text:
Local registry enumeration usually requires suitable administrative access to the CA.

A penetration tester without CA administrative access should not assume:

Cannot Read Registry
=
Cannot Assess ESC16

Remote AD CS tooling such as Certipy may provide the required configuration visibility depending on permissions and protocols available.

docs.title: Enumerate Published Templates
docs.text:
Once ESC16 is identified, determine which templates are published by the affected CA.

PowerShell:

Import-Module ActiveDirectory

Determine the Configuration naming context:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext

Query Enrollment Services:

$base = "CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $base -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKIEnrollmentService)' -Properties dNSHostName,certificateTemplates |
    Select-Object Name,dNSHostName,certificateTemplates

docs.title: Why Template Enumeration Matters
docs.text:
ESC16 affects the CA.

Impact depends heavily on what that CA can issue.

For example:

ESC16 CA
   |
   +--> Web Server Only
   |
   +--> Client Authentication
   |
   +--> Computer Authentication
   |
   +--> User Authentication

The second group is generally much more interesting for identity abuse.

docs.title: Authentication-Capable Templates
docs.text:
Prioritise templates containing purposes such as:

Client Authentication
Smart Card Logon
PKINIT Client Authentication
Any Purpose

or templates with no restrictive EKU where Windows semantics make them broadly usable.

docs.title: Any Purpose OID
docs.text: 2.5.29.37.0

docs.title: Enumerate Template EKUs
docs.text:
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties displayName,pKIExtendedKeyUsage |
    Select-Object Name,displayName,pKIExtendedKeyUsage

docs.title: Enrollment Rights Matter
docs.text:
An ESC16 CA may publish authentication-capable templates.

But the next question is:

Can the Attacker Enroll?

Review:

Authenticated Users
Domain Users
Domain Computers
Specific Department Groups
Service Accounts

and calculate effective enrollment permissions.

docs.title: Certificate Inspection
docs.text:
A useful defensive validation is to inspect a certificate legitimately issued to a dedicated test principal.

Windows:

certutil -dump test.cer

Search for:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

docs.title: OpenSSL Inspection
docs.text:
For PEM:

openssl x509 -in test.pem -text -noout

For DER:

openssl x509 -in test.cer -inform DER -text -noout

Microsoft-specific extension decoding may be clearer with Windows tooling.

docs.title: Compare Expected and Actual Certificates
docs.text:
A strong validation method is:

Template Expected to Include SID
           |
           v
Certificate Issued by CA
           |
           v
SID Extension Present?

If:

No

then investigate whether:

Template = ESC9

or:

CA = ESC16

docs.title: Distinguishing ESC9 from ESC16
docs.text:
Suppose:

Template A -> No SID

Check another normal authentication template.

If:

Template B -> SID Present

the issue may be template-specific.

If:

Template A -> No SID
Template B -> No SID
Template C -> No SID

then investigate the CA-wide configuration.

The authoritative answer should come from configuration review rather than certificate sampling alone.

docs.title: Legacy Unpatched CAs
docs.text:
An important edge case is a CA that never received the Microsoft updates introducing the SID security extension.

Such a CA may issue certificates without the extension even if:

DisableExtensionList

does not explicitly contain the OID.

Conceptually:

Old CA
  |
  v
Does Not Implement SID Extension
  |
  v
Certificates Lack SID Extension

Given the age of the relevant 2022 security updates, this should be treated as a serious patch-management concern in a current environment.

docs.title: Patch Verification
docs.text:
Record:

CA Operating System
Windows Build
Installed Cumulative Update
Assessment Date

Do not determine patch status only by searching for one historical KB number because cumulative updates supersede earlier fixes.

docs.title: ESC16 Candidate Classification
docs.text:
A useful classification is:

Confirmed ESC16 Configuration

when:

DisableExtensionList
contains
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

A separate condition is:

Legacy CA Missing SID Extension Support

when the CA is too old or unpatched to issue the extension correctly.

Document the actual root cause.

docs.title: Safe Validation
docs.text:
The preferred production workflow is:

Enumerate CA
     |
     v
Read DisableExtensionList
     |
     v
Confirm SID OID Disabled
     |
     v
Enumerate Published Templates
     |
     v
Identify Authentication Templates
     |
     v
Assess Enrollment Rights

This is usually sufficient to report the configuration weakness.

docs.title: Optional Certificate Validation
docs.text:
If certificate issuance is already approved:

Dedicated Test User
       |
       v
Normal Authentication Template
       |
       v
Affected CA
       |
       v
Test Certificate
       |
       v
Inspect Extensions

The purpose is only to verify:

SID Security Extension Missing

not to impersonate another account.

docs.title: Do Not Modify a Victim UPN by Default
docs.text:
Historical ESC9 and ESC16 attack demonstrations often involve changing:

userPrincipalName

on an account the attacker controls.

Do not perform such manipulation against production identities unless explicitly approved and necessary.

Read-only evidence is usually sufficient.

docs.title: Do Not Target Administrator
docs.text:
There is no need to request a certificate representing:

Administrator

or another Tier 0 principal merely to prove ESC16.

docs.title: Do Not Disable the Extension for Testing
docs.text:
Never run a configuration change whose purpose is:

Add SID OID to DisableExtensionList

on a secure production CA.

That would intentionally create ESC16.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
The core remediation is:

Remove
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2
from DisableExtensionList

so that the CA can include the SID security extension normally.

docs.title: Change Control Required
docs.text:
CA configuration changes can affect enterprise authentication.

Therefore remediation should use:

PKI Change Management
Testing
Backup
Rollback Planning
Maintenance Window
Validation

docs.title: Native Remediation
docs.text:
Microsoft CA registry settings can be managed using:

certutil

However, do not blindly copy a configuration-changing command into production.

First record the current value:

certutil -getreg policy\DisableExtensionList

Then follow current Microsoft PKI guidance to remove only:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

while preserving any legitimate disabled extensions.

docs.title: Do Not Clear the Entire List
docs.text:
Avoid:

Delete DisableExtensionList

without understanding its existing contents.

Other extensions may have been intentionally disabled for legitimate PKI reasons.

The objective is:

Remove the SID Security Extension OID
from the Disabled List

not:

Destroy Existing CA Policy Configuration

docs.title: Certificate Services Restart
docs.text:
Some CA policy configuration changes require the Certificate Services service to be restarted before they take effect.

Plan this operationally.

Do not restart a production CA during an assessment unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Patch the CA
docs.text:
If the CA lacks the security updates required to support the SID security extension:

Patch the CA

according to the supported Windows servicing path.

A registry fix cannot substitute for missing security functionality in an obsolete or unpatched operating system.

docs.title: Keep Domain Controllers Patched
docs.text:
ESC16 should not be remediated only at the CA.

Maintain current certificate-binding protections on domain controllers.

The defensive relationship is:

Secure CA Issuance
       +
Strong DC Mapping
       =
Strong Certificate Identity

docs.title: Review ESC6
docs.text:
If ESC16 exists, immediately determine whether the same CA also exposes:

ESC6

because the combination materially changes potential impact.

docs.title: Review ESC9
docs.text:
Check templates for:

CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

Even after fixing ESC16, individual templates may continue to omit the SID extension through ESC9.

docs.title: Review ESC10
docs.text:
Review certificate mapping configuration and legacy mapping dependencies.

ESC16 may have been introduced historically to resolve compatibility problems.

Those compatibility dependencies should be identified and fixed rather than preserving insecure global suppression.

docs.title: Review ESC14
docs.text:
Inventory explicit certificate mappings:

altSecurityIdentities

because some legacy applications may use explicit mapping rather than SID-based implicit mapping.

docs.title: Why Administrators May Have Created ESC16
docs.text:
A plausible historical cause is:

2022 Certificate Hardening Update
        |
        v
Legacy Authentication Breaks
        |
        v
Administrator Troubleshooting
        |
        v
Globally Disable SID Extension

This may have restored compatibility while weakening certificate identity security.

docs.title: Do Not Preserve Insecure Workarounds
docs.text:
The long-term fix should be:

Identify Legacy Dependency
       |
       v
Fix Certificate Mapping
       |
       v
Restore Strong Security Extension

not:

Keep Global Security Feature Disabled

docs.text:
ESC16 detection should include:

CA Configuration
Certificate Content
Template Configuration
Certificate Requests
Certificate Authentication

docs.title: Baseline DisableExtensionList
docs.text:
Defenders should periodically inventory:

DisableExtensionList

on every Enterprise CA.

Alert when:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

appears.

docs.title: Monitor CA Registry Changes
docs.text:
Changes beneath:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration

should be treated as sensitive.

Use:

Registry Auditing
Configuration Management
Change Management

to detect unexpected modification.

docs.title: Monitor CA Administrative Activity
docs.text:
Unexpected administrative activity on a CA is high risk.

Monitor:

Interactive Administrator Logons
Remote Management
PowerShell
Registry Modification
Service Control
Certificate Services Configuration

docs.text:
Where Certificate Services auditing is enabled, useful events include:

4887

for certificate requests and issuance.

These events do not directly mean ESC16 exploitation occurred.

They become useful when correlated with:

Affected CA
+

+
Suspicious Identity Information

docs.title: Directory Service Changes
docs.text:
Certificate-template and PKI object modifications in Active Directory can produce:

5136

where appropriate Directory Service Changes auditing is enabled.

ESC16 itself is primarily CA-local configuration, so do not rely on 5136 to detect the CA registry change.

docs.title: Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
Kerberos certificate authentication can contribute to:

telemetry.

Correlate suspicious certificate issuance with subsequent TGT requests.

Do not only monitor future changes.

If ESC6 was also enabled during the same period:

docs.title: Review UPN Changes
docs.text:

docs.text:
After evidence preservation and change approval, restore normal SID security extension issuance.

Then validate using a dedicated test certificate.

docs.text:
The remediation validation model is:

Apply Required Service Change
       |
       v
Request Test Certificate
       |
       v
Inspect Certificate
       |
       v
SID Security Extension Present

docs.title: Reassess All Templates
docs.text:
After fixing ESC16:

Do Not Stop

Individual templates may still expose:

ESC1
ESC2
ESC3
ESC4
ESC9
ESC15

or other AD CS weaknesses.

docs.title: Reporting ESC16
docs.text:
Avoid a title containing only:

ESC16

Prefer a descriptive title.

Examples:

Certification Authority Globally Disables the Active Directory SID Security Extension

AD CS Certificate Issuance Lacks Strong SID Binding

CA-Wide Configuration Suppresses the NTDS SID Security Extension

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Certification Authority Globally Disables the Active Directory SID
Security Extension

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Affected Host:
ca01.corp.example

AD CS Technique:
ESC16

Disabled Extension:
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

Description:
The Certification Authority is configured to suppress the Microsoft
NTDS CA security extension from certificates it issues.

The affected OID is:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

This extension contains the Active Directory SID information used
for strong certificate-to-account binding.

The OID is present in the CA policy module's DisableExtensionList,
causing the security extension to be omitted at the CA level rather
than only from a specific certificate template.

As a result, authentication-capable certificates issued by the CA
may lack the normal SID security extension regardless of whether
their certificate templates are individually configured to include
it.

Impact:
The configuration weakens certificate-to-account identity binding
across certificates issued by the affected CA.

The practical privilege-escalation impact depends on additional
conditions including certificate enrollment permissions, certificate
mapping behaviour, identity-control permissions and other AD CS
configuration such as ESC6.

Where additional certificate identity manipulation paths exist, the
condition can contribute to certificate-based account impersonation.

Recommendation:
Remove OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2 from the CA policy module's
DisableExtensionList using an approved PKI change process.

Ensure the CA and domain controllers are fully patched.

After remediation, issue a certificate to a dedicated test identity
and verify that the SID security extension is present.

Review authentication-capable templates published by the affected
CA and assess the environment for related ESC6, ESC9, ESC10 and
certificate-mapping weaknesses.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity should reflect the complete environment.

Do not assign:

Critical

solely because:

Certipy Reports ESC16

Consider:

Who Can Enroll?
What Templates Authenticate?
Is ESC6 Present?
Can Identity Attributes Be Modified?
What Mapping Paths Exist?
How Privileged Are the Reachable Targets?

docs.title: Lower-Risk Example
docs.text:
ESC16 CA
   |
   v
Only Restricted Non-Authentication Templates
   |
   v
Administrators Only

Still a security-hardening concern, but the immediate attack path may be limited.

docs.title: Higher-Risk Example
docs.text:
ESC16 CA
   |
   v
Domain Users Can Enroll
   |
   v
Authentication-Capable Template
   |
   v
Additional Identity Manipulation

This warrants deeper investigation.

docs.title: Critical Chain Example
docs.text:
Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Authentication Template
       |
       v
ESC6 + ESC16 CA
       |
       v
Attacker-Controlled Identity
       |
       v
Certificate Authentication
       |
       v
Privileged Principal

A demonstrated path to a Tier 0 identity can represent critical impact.

ESC9
