docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
ESC5 is broader than a vulnerable certificate template.

It concerns control over the infrastructure that defines:

Which CAs Are Trusted
Which PKI Objects Exist
How Enterprise CAs Are Registered
How Certificate Policies Are Represented
How Certificate Chains Are Built
How Revocation Information Is Distributed

The central security problem is:

Untrusted Principal
        |
        v
Trusted PKI Configuration

The most important assessment question is therefore not:

"Is ESC5 present?"

but:

"Which PKI control-plane object can this
principal modify, and what does that object
allow them to influence?"

A GenericWrite permission over one PKI object may have a very different impact from GenericWrite over another.

For example:

Write Access to Metadata

is not equivalent to:

Write Access to Authentication Trust

Similarly:

Control of an Enrollment Services AD Object

is not automatically equivalent to:

Control of the CA Private Key

The assessment must preserve those distinctions.

The complete security model is:

Principal
   |
   v
Effective Permission
   |
   v
PKI Object
   |
   v
Security Function
   |
   v
Possible Modification
   |
   v
Certificate / Trust Impact
   |
   v
Authentication Impact

ESC5 is especially important because many of the affected objects live in the:

Configuration Naming Context

and therefore belong to forest-wide PKI configuration.

For defenders, the entire:

CN=Public Key Services

hierarchy should be treated as privileged identity infrastructure.

For penetration testers, read-only ACL evidence will often demonstrate the risk without making dangerous changes to production PKI.

The strongest ESC5 finding identifies:

The Principal
        +
The Effective Permission
        +
The Exact PKI Object
        +
The Security Function
        +
The Resulting Trust Impact

rather than relying solely on the ESC5 label.

docs.title: AD CS ESC6 - CA Allows Requester-Supplied Subject Alternative Names
docs.text:
ESC6 is an Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) configuration weakness involving the Certification Authority setting:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

When this CA-wide flag is enabled, the Enterprise Certification Authority can accept Subject Alternative Name (SAN) information supplied through certificate request attributes.

Historically, this could allow a requester who could enroll in an authentication-capable certificate template to request a certificate containing another account's identity.

The classic ESC6 relationship is:

Low-Privileged User
        |
        v
Can Enroll in Authentication Template
        |
        v
Enterprise CA
        |
        v
EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 Enabled
        |
        v
Requester Supplies SAN
        |
        v
Certificate Contains Alternate Identity
        |
        v
Certificate Authentication
        |
        v
Potential Privilege Escalation

However, ESC6 must now be understood together with Microsoft's certificate-based authentication hardening.

Modern, fully patched Active Directory environments enforce stronger certificate mappings. Microsoft moved domain controllers to Full Enforcement beginning with the February 2025 security update and ended support for the StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement compatibility-mode registry fallback with the September 9, 2025 security update.

Therefore:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 Enabled

does not automatically mean:

Arbitrary Domain Authentication

in a current environment.

The certificate's SID security extension, certificate mapping behaviour, template configuration, CA configuration, and domain controller patch state must all be considered.

Authorised testing only

ESC6 testing can involve requesting authentication certificates containing alternative identities. Begin with read-only CA and template enumeration. Where active validation is explicitly authorised, use dedicated test accounts and the minimum privilege necessary. Do not request certificates representing production administrators or other privileged users merely to demonstrate the configuration weakness.

docs.title: ESC6 Concept
docs.text:
ESC1 and ESC6 are related but operate at different levels.

ESC1 concerns the:

Certificate Template

whereas ESC6 concerns the:

Certification Authority

The distinction is:

ESC1
 |
 v
Template Allows Requester-Supplied Subject

versus:

ESC6
 |
 v
CA Allows Requester-Supplied SAN Attributes

ESC6 is therefore primarily a:

CA-Wide Configuration Weakness

docs.title: The Important Flag
docs.text:
The key configuration flag is:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

It belongs to the CA's policy-module configuration.

Conceptually:

Certification Authority
        |
        v
Policy Module
        |
        v
EditFlags
        |
        v
EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

When enabled, SAN information supplied as request attributes may be included in issued certificates.

docs.title: Why ESC6 Is CA-Wide
docs.text:
This distinction is extremely important.

ESC1 is normally associated with:

One Certificate Template

ESC6 affects behaviour at the:

Certification Authority

level.

Conceptually:

CA
 |
 +--> Template A
 |
 +--> Template B
 |
 +--> Template C
 |
 +--> Template D

If the CA accepts requester-supplied SAN attributes, multiple templates may need to be evaluated.

Therefore an ESC6 assessment should not stop after finding one template.

docs.title: Subject Alternative Name
docs.text:
The Subject Alternative Name extension can contain several identity forms.

Examples include:

UPN
DNS Name
Email Address
IP Address
OtherName

For Active Directory certificate authentication, a UPN is particularly important.

Example:

administrator@corp.example

docs.title: SAN and Certificate Identity
docs.text:
A simplified certificate identity model is:

Certificate
    |
    +--> Subject
    |
    +--> SAN
           |
           +--> UPN
           |
           +--> DNS
           |
           +--> Other Identity Data

Windows certificate authentication may use certificate identity information when mapping the certificate to an Active Directory security principal.

Modern strong certificate mapping significantly changes how safely this information can be used.

docs.title: ESC6 vs ESC1
docs.text:
The classic ESC1 requirement includes a template configuration allowing requester-controlled subject information.

Conceptually:

Certificate Template
       |
       v
ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT

ESC6 instead relies on:

Certification Authority
       |
       v
EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

Therefore:

ESC1 = Template-Level
ESC6 = CA-Level

docs.title: Why ESC6 Was Historically Dangerous
docs.text:
Historically, an attacker could potentially combine:

Low-Privileged Enrollment
        +
Authentication-Capable Template
        +
ESC6 CA Configuration

and request a certificate containing a privileged user's UPN.

For example:

Attacker
   |
   v
Enroll
   |
   v
User Template
   |
   v
CA Accepts SAN Attribute
   |
   v
SAN UPN:
administrator@corp.example

If certificate mapping accepted the supplied identity:

Certificate
    |
    v
Administrator

the attacker could authenticate as the privileged account.

docs.title: Historical ESC6 Attack Model
docs.text:
The traditional chain was:

Low-Privileged User
       |
       v
Authentication Template
       |
       v
Certificate Request
       |
       v
Requester-Supplied SAN
       |
       v
Enterprise CA
       |
       v
EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2
       |
       v
Certificate with Privileged UPN
       |
       v
PKINIT
       |
       v
Privileged TGT

This historical model is no longer sufficient by itself when assessing a modern patched environment.

docs.title: Modern ESC6
docs.text:
Microsoft's certificate-based authentication hardening introduced stronger mappings between certificates and Active Directory accounts.

The important conceptual change is:

Certificate Identity
       |
       v
Must Strongly Map
       |
       v
Active Directory Account

rather than relying only on weaker identity information such as:

UPN
Subject
Issuer + Subject

docs.title: KB5014754
docs.text:
Microsoft introduced certificate-based authentication hardening through:

KB5014754

The changes were designed to address certificate spoofing and weak certificate-to-account mappings.

The deployment evolved through:

Compatibility
     |
     v
Enforcement
     |
     v
Full Enforcement

docs.title: Current Enforcement Timeline
docs.text:
For modern assessments, the timeline matters.

Microsoft states that domain controllers moved to Full Enforcement when the February 2025 Windows security update was installed unless administrators had explicitly configured a supported override.

Support for returning to Compatibility mode remained temporarily available.

That compatibility mechanism ended with the:

September 9, 2025

Windows security update.

After that point, Microsoft no longer supports the:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

registry key for returning domain controllers to the older compatibility behaviour.

Therefore, in a normally patched environment in 2026:

Strong Certificate Mapping

should be treated as the expected baseline.

docs.title: Why This Matters for ESC6
docs.text:
Historically:

Attacker Certificate
       |
       v
SAN = Administrator UPN
       |
       v
Administrator Authentication

Modern mapping can instead produce:

Attacker Certificate
       |
       +--> SAN = Administrator UPN
       |
       +--> SID Extension = Attacker SID
       |
       v
Strong Mapping
       |
       v
Mismatch
       |
       v
Authentication Fails

This is a critical difference.

docs.title: SID Security Extension
docs.text:
Modern Enterprise CA-issued certificates can contain a security extension identifying the requester's SID.

The extension is commonly referred to as the:

SID Security Extension

and is associated with:

szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT

The extension binds the certificate more strongly to the Active Directory security principal associated with the request.

Conceptually:

Certificate
    |
    +--> SAN UPN
    |
    +--> SID Security Extension
             |
             v
        Requester SID

docs.title: ESC6 and SID Binding
docs.text:
Suppose:

Requester:
CORP\alice

with SID:

S-1-5-21-...-1105

attempts to supply:

administrator@corp.example

as the SAN UPN.

The issued certificate may conceptually contain:

SAN:
administrator@corp.example

SID Security Extension:
S-1-5-21-...-1105

Strong certificate mapping can use the SID extension to prevent the certificate from being mapped to the administrator account.

docs.title: ESC6 Is Not Necessarily Gone
docs.text:
Do not conclude:

KB5014754
    =
ESC6 Can Never Matter

That is too broad.

ESC6 remains an important security configuration because its impact depends on factors such as:

Template Configuration
SID Security Extension
Certificate Mapping
CA Configuration
Domain Controller Patch State
Explicit Certificate Mappings
Other ESC Conditions

docs.title: ESC6 and ESC9
docs.text:
ESC9 involves certificate templates configured to omit the SID security extension.

Conceptually:

ESC6
 |
 v
Requester-Supplied SAN

combined with:

ESC9
 |
 v
No SID Security Extension

can materially change the certificate mapping analysis.

This is why modern AD CS testing must consider combinations of ESC conditions.

docs.title: ESC6 and ESC16
docs.text:
ESC16 concerns CA-wide suppression of the SID security extension.

Conceptually:

ESC6
 |
 +--> CA Accepts SAN
 |
ESC16
 |
 +--> CA Does Not Add SID Security Extension
 |
 v
Certificate Mapping Risk

This can make ESC6 significantly more relevant in modern environments.

ESC16 should therefore be evaluated whenever ESC6 is identified.

docs.title: ESC6 and ESC10
docs.text:
ESC10 concerns weak certificate mapping configurations.

Conceptually:

ESC6
 |
 v
Attacker-Controlled SAN
 |
 v
Weak Certificate Mapping
 |
 v
Potential Alternate Identity

Modern assessments should evaluate certificate mapping rather than assuming default legacy behaviour.

docs.title: ESC6 and ESC1
docs.text:
ESC6 can coexist with ESC1.

For example:

Template
 |
 +--> ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT
 |
CA
 |
 +--> EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

In this case, multiple mechanisms may permit requester-controlled certificate identity.

Report the actual configuration rather than treating the ESC labels as mutually exclusive.

docs.title: ESC6 and ESC7
docs.text:
ESC7 concerns dangerous CA permissions.

A principal with sufficient CA administrative rights may potentially change CA configuration.

Conceptually:

ESC7
 |
 v
CA Administrative Control
 |
 v
Change EditFlags
 |
 v
Enable ESC6

This creates an important relationship:

ESC7
    ->
ESC6

where authorised CA management rights are misdelegated.

docs.title: ESC6 Preconditions
docs.text:
A meaningful ESC6 assessment generally considers:

Enterprise CA
        +
EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 Enabled
        +
Attacker Can Enroll
        +
Suitable Certificate Template
        +
Certificate Can Be Issued
        +
Authentication / Trust Use
        +
Relevant Mapping Behaviour

Not every enabled flag results in privilege escalation.

docs.title: Enterprise CA
docs.text:
First identify Enterprise Certification Authorities.

Using Certipy:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

Review discovered:

Certificate Authorities
Certificate Templates
CA Configuration
Vulnerabilities

docs.title: Certipy Enumeration
docs.text:
Begin by checking the installed version:

certipy --version

and available discovery options:

certipy find -h

A common read-only enumeration pattern is:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

docs.title: Certipy ESC6 Output
docs.text:
Depending on the Certipy release, CA vulnerability analysis may identify:

ESC6

when the CA permits requester-supplied SAN attributes.

Review:

CA Name
DNS Name
Web Enrollment
User Specified SAN
Request Disposition
Permissions
Vulnerabilities

Exact field names vary between releases.

docs.title: Certipy JSON Output
docs.text:
Structured output can make larger assessments easier to analyse.

Review the installed version's options:

certipy find -h

and store results securely.

Certificate infrastructure enumeration may contain sensitive information about:

CA Names
Templates
Permissions
PKI Configuration

docs.title: Native CA Enumeration
docs.text:
From an authorised Windows system, CA configuration can be queried using:

certutil -config - -ping

This can assist with identifying available Certification Authorities.

docs.title: Query CA Policy Configuration
docs.text:
Where administrative access and scope permit, certutil can query CA policy configuration.

The relevant policy-module configuration contains:

EditFlags

and should be reviewed for:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

Do not modify the setting during enumeration.

docs.title: CA Registry Location
docs.text:
On the CA server, policy-module configuration is associated with the CA registry hierarchy under:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration

The exact CA instance appears beneath the configuration key.

Conceptually:

CertSvc
  |
  v
Configuration
  |
  v
<CA Name>
  |
  v
PolicyModules
  |
  v
CertificateAuthority_MicrosoftDefault.Policy
  |
  v
EditFlags

docs.title: Read EditFlags with PowerShell
docs.text:
On an authorised CA server, first identify the CA configuration:

Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration'

Then inspect the relevant policy-module key.

For example:

$caName = 'CORP-CA'

$policyPath = "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration\$caName\PolicyModules\CertificateAuthority_MicrosoftDefault.Policy"

Get-ItemProperty -Path $policyPath -Name EditFlags

This is read-only.

docs.title: Do Not Modify EditFlags During Enumeration
docs.text:
Avoid commands that change:

EditFlags

during normal testing.

Changing CA policy behaviour can affect certificate requests from multiple templates and applications.

docs.title: Certutil Policy Query
docs.text:
Where supported by the installed Windows version and administrative context, inspect CA configuration using certutil.

Start with:

certutil -?

and:

certutil -getreg

Then query the relevant policy-module configuration according to the installed version.

Prefer read-only queries.

docs.title: CA Configuration vs Active Directory Configuration
docs.text:
An important distinction is:

Certificate Template
       |
       v
Stored in Active Directory

while:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2
       |
       v
CA Policy Configuration

Therefore ordinary LDAP enumeration of certificate templates does not by itself establish ESC6.

docs.title: Enumerate Templates Published by the CA
docs.text:
Once an ESC6 CA is identified, enumerate the templates it publishes.

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$enrollmentBase = "CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $enrollmentBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKIEnrollmentService)' -Properties certificateTemplates,dNSHostName |
    Select-Object Name,dNSHostName,certificateTemplates

docs.title: Identify Authentication Templates
docs.text:
For each published template, determine whether certificates can be used for authentication.

Relevant EKUs can include:

Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2

Smart Card Logon
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.2

PKINIT Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.2.3.4

Other certificate-purpose configurations may also require analysis.

docs.title: Enumerate Template EKUs
docs.text:
$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties pKIExtendedKeyUsage,'msPKI-Certificate-Application-Policy' |
    Select-Object Name,pKIExtendedKeyUsage,'msPKI-Certificate-Application-Policy'

docs.title: Enrollment Rights
docs.text:
The attacker must normally be able to request a certificate from a relevant template.

Review:

Enroll
Autoenroll

permissions.

Enrollment rights may be assigned to:

Domain Users
Domain Computers
Authenticated Users
Specific Groups
Application Groups
Service Accounts

docs.title: Manager Approval
docs.text:
A template may require certificate manager approval.

Conceptually:

Request
   |
   v
Pending
   |
   v
Certificate Manager Approval
   |
   v
Issued

This can interrupt a straightforward ESC6 path.

docs.title: Authorized Signatures
docs.text:
Templates may also require authorised signatures.

Review:

msPKI-RA-Signature

A value requiring one or more authorised signatures can prevent direct issuance.

docs.title: Request Disposition
docs.text:
CA request disposition should also be considered.

If certificate requests are:

Pending

rather than automatically issued, the attack path changes.

Do not infer automatic issuance from template enrollment rights alone.

docs.title: ESC6 Enumeration Model
docs.text:
A good enumeration workflow is:

Identify Enterprise CAs
        |
        v
Check CA EditFlags
        |
        v
Is EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 Enabled?
        |
        +--> No -> ESC6 Not Identified
        |
        +--> Yes
                |
                v
        Enumerate Published Templates
                |
                v
        Identify Enrollable Templates
                |
                v
        Identify Authentication Capability
                |
                v
        Check Issuance Requirements
                |
                v
        Check SID Extension
                |
                v
        Check Certificate Mapping

docs.title: Modern Validation Strategy
docs.text:
Do not immediately attempt:

Administrator UPN

Instead use two controlled accounts.

For example:

CORP\esc6-requester
CORP\esc6-target

Both should be dedicated assessment accounts.

docs.title: Controlled Test Model
docs.text:
A safe validation model is:

esc6-requester
       |
       v
Certificate Request
       |
       v
SAN = esc6-target@corp.example
       |
       v
Certificate Issued
       |
       v
Inspect Certificate
       |
       v
Determine SID Extension
       |
       v
Test Mapping Only If Approved

This demonstrates the relevant behaviour without involving a privileged production account.

docs.title: Inspect the Certificate Before Authentication
docs.text:
After obtaining an approved test certificate, inspect:

Subject
SAN
UPN
Issuer
Serial Number
EKUs
SID Security Extension
Validity
Template

Do not jump directly from issuance to authentication.

docs.title: Windows Certificate Inspection
docs.text:
For an exported certificate:

certutil -dump test.cer

For a PFX:

certutil -dump test.pfx

Protect any private-key material.

docs.title: OpenSSL Inspection
docs.text:
Where appropriate:

openssl x509 -in test.cer -inform DER -text -noout

or for PEM:

openssl x509 -in test.pem -text -noout

Review:

X509v3 extensions
Subject Alternative Name
Extended Key Usage
Other Microsoft-specific extensions

docs.title: Check SID Extension
docs.text:
The important question is:

Which SID Is Bound to the Certificate?

For a modern CA-issued certificate, determine whether the SID corresponds to:

Requester

or whether the relevant security extension is absent.

docs.title: Expected Modern Behaviour
docs.text:
A common modern result is:

Requester:
alice

Requested SAN:
administrator@corp.example

Certificate SID:
alice SID

Strong mapping should prevent the certificate from simply becoming an Administrator certificate.

This should be documented as:

ESC6 Configuration Present
but
Classic Privilege Escalation Mitigated by Strong Mapping

if that is what testing establishes.

docs.title: Do Not Overstate ESC6
docs.text:
Avoid reporting:

Domain Admin Compromise

solely because:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

is enabled.

Instead determine:

Is Alternate SAN Accepted?
Is SID Extension Present?
Which SID Is Embedded?
Which Mapping Method Is Used?
Can Authentication Actually Map to Another Account?

docs.title: Strong Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Modern certificate mapping considers strong identifiers.

Microsoft distinguishes stronger mappings from legacy weaker name-based mappings.

The objective is to prevent:

Certificate Name
       |
       v
Arbitrary Account

without a cryptographically or administratively stronger relationship.

docs.title: Current 2026 Baseline
docs.text:
For a fully patched Active Directory environment in 2026:

Full Enforcement

should be expected.

Microsoft's compatibility fallback through:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

ceased to be supported after the September 9, 2025 security update.

Therefore legacy ESC6 write-ups should not be copied directly into modern findings.

docs.title: Legacy Systems
docs.text:
An assessment may still encounter:

Unpatched Domain Controllers
Unsupported Windows Server Versions
Delayed Security Updates
Isolated Legacy Domains
Special Compatibility Configurations

Document actual patch state rather than assuming modern behaviour.

docs.title: Check Domain Controller Versions
docs.text:
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * |
    Select-Object HostName,OperatingSystem,OperatingSystemVersion

Operating system version alone does not establish patch level.

docs.title: Check Installed Updates
docs.text:
On an authorised domain controller:

Get-HotFix |
    Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 20 HotFixID,InstalledOn,Description

For modern Windows versions, update inventory may also require the organisation's patch-management or servicing records.

docs.title: Registry Checks
docs.text:
Older ESC6 guidance frequently recommends checking:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

to determine certificate mapping behaviour.

In current patched environments, this registry setting should not be treated as a supported method for reverting to legacy compatibility behaviour after the September 2025 enforcement transition.

Use actual:

Patch State
Authentication Behaviour
Microsoft-Supported Configuration

when assessing current systems.

docs.title: ESC6 and Explicit Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Explicit certificate mappings may also influence authentication.

Active Directory supports certificate mappings through:

altSecurityIdentities

This becomes particularly relevant to:

ESC14

and weak explicit mapping configurations.

docs.title: ESC6 and UPN Mapping
docs.text:
Legacy certificate authentication often relied heavily on:

SAN UPN

mapping.

Modern environments should not be assessed as though UPN alone is always sufficient.

This is one of the largest differences between historical and current ESC6 testing.

docs.title: ESC6 and Computer Accounts
docs.text:
SAN manipulation is not limited conceptually to user UPNs.

Certificate identity may also involve:

DNS Names
Computer Accounts
Machine Authentication

depending on certificate type and authentication protocol.

Again, modern mapping must be evaluated.

docs.title: ESC6 and Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Do not request certificates representing:

Domain Controllers

during routine validation.

Domain controller certificates participate in critical services including:

Kerberos
LDAPS
Smart Card Authentication
PKINIT

Use dedicated test systems where proof is required.

docs.title: Certipy Request Syntax
docs.text:
Certipy changes over time.

Before requesting a certificate, inspect the installed version:

certipy req -h

and:

certipy auth -h

For an authorised ESC6 assessment, use the syntax documented by the installed release to:

Select CA
Select Template
Supply Approved Test SAN
Request Certificate
Inspect Result

Do not copy request syntax from old ESC6 write-ups without checking the installed Certipy version.

docs.title: Why We Verify Tool Syntax
docs.text:
AD CS tooling evolves alongside Microsoft's certificate hardening.

Commands from older research may assume:

Legacy Mapping
Legacy Certipy CLI
Legacy Windows Behaviour

A modern assessment should verify both:

Tool Version

and:

Target Behaviour

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can provide useful context around:

Enrollment Rights
CA Relationships
Template Relationships
PKI Privilege Paths

See:

BloodHound

Graph data should complement, not replace, direct CA configuration verification.

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView is useful for:

Template ACLs
Group Membership
Object Control

but ESC6 itself is a CA policy configuration.

Therefore:

PowerView Template Enumeration

alone cannot prove:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

is enabled.

docs.title: LDAP Enumeration
docs.text:
LDAP can enumerate:

Certificate Templates
Enrollment Services
Template Permissions
PKI Objects

but the ESC6 flag is associated with CA policy configuration.

Therefore:

LDAP

should be combined with:

CA Configuration Enumeration

docs.title: ESC6 and Web Enrollment
docs.text:
Web Enrollment is not required for ESC6.

Do not confuse:

ESC6

with:

ESC8

ESC8 concerns NTLM relay to AD CS HTTP enrollment endpoints.

ESC6 concerns:

Requester-Supplied SAN Attributes

at the CA policy level.

docs.title: ESC6 and RPC Enrollment
docs.text:
Certificate requests can reach a CA through mechanisms other than Web Enrollment.

Therefore:

No /certsrv/

does not mean:

ESC6 Cannot Exist

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
ESC6 detection has two major components:

Configuration Monitoring

and:

Certificate Request / Issuance Monitoring

docs.title: Detect CA Configuration Changes
docs.text:
Monitor changes to the CA policy-module configuration.

Particularly important:

EditFlags

Changes enabling:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

should be investigated.

docs.title: Registry Monitoring
docs.text:
On CA systems, monitor changes beneath:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration

especially policy-module configuration.

Use:

EDR
Registry Auditing
Configuration Management
Change Control

as appropriate.

docs.title: CA Service Restart
docs.text:
Some CA configuration changes may require:

Certificate Services Restart

to become effective.

Unexpected CA service restarts near policy configuration changes can therefore provide useful investigation context.

docs.title: Certificate Services Events
docs.text:
Where Certificate Services auditing is enabled, relevant events can include:

4886 - Certificate Services received a certificate request

4887 - Certificate Services approved a certificate request and issued a certificate

Event availability depends on auditing configuration.

docs.title: Monitor Request Attributes
docs.text:
Where telemetry permits, inspect certificate requests for unexpected:

SAN
UPN
DNS
Subject

values.

A particularly useful comparison is:

Requester Identity
        |
        v
Requested Certificate Identity

docs.title: Suspicious Identity Mismatch
docs.text:
For example:

Requester:
CORP\alice

Requested SAN:
administrator@corp.example

should receive investigation even if strong mapping ultimately prevents successful authentication.

The request itself indicates suspicious activity.

docs.title: Correlate Certificate Issuance
docs.text:
A useful detection chain is:

Certificate Request
       |
       v
Unexpected SAN
       |
       v
Certificate Issued
       |
       v
Certificate Authentication Attempt

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication
docs.text:
Certificate-based Kerberos authentication can generate:

4768

for a Ticket Granting Ticket request.

Certificate-related information in authentication telemetry can help correlate:

Certificate Issuance

with:

PKINIT Authentication

depending on logging and Windows version.

docs.title: Monitor CA Administrative Activity
docs.text:
Changes to ESC6 configuration should normally be performed only by authorised PKI administrators.

Correlate:

Administrative Logon
Registry Modification
CA Configuration Change
CertSvc Restart

docs.title: Detect ESC7 to ESC6
docs.text:
If a principal with inappropriate CA administrative permissions enables the ESC6 flag, the sequence may look like:

CA Administrative Access
       |
       v
EditFlags Modified
       |
       v
CA Service Restart
       |
       v
Certificate Request with SAN

This is a high-value detection chain.

docs.title: Hardening ESC6
docs.text:
The primary remediation is:

Disable EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

unless there is a documented and justified requirement for CA-wide requester-supplied SAN attributes.

docs.title: Prefer Template-Level Controls
docs.text:
If an application genuinely requires requester-supplied identity information, prefer tightly scoped template controls rather than enabling broad CA-wide behaviour.

Conceptually:

One Controlled Template

is preferable to:

Every Template Processed by the CA

where technically feasible.

docs.title: Review Business Requirement
docs.text:
Before retaining ESC6 configuration, establish:

Which Application Requires It?
Which Template Uses It?
Who Can Enroll?
Why Is CA-Wide Behaviour Necessary?
Can It Be Replaced?

Legacy requirements should not automatically remain enabled indefinitely.

docs.title: Review All Published Templates
docs.text:
If ESC6 is enabled, review every template published by that CA for:

Enrollment Rights
Authentication EKUs
Issuance Requirements
SID Extension Behaviour
Approval
Authorized Signatures

Do not evaluate ESC6 in isolation.

docs.title: Restrict Enrollment
docs.text:
Reduce unnecessary enrollment rights.

Avoid broad access such as:

Domain Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Computers

unless genuinely required.

docs.title: Restrict Authentication Templates
docs.text:
Authentication-capable templates deserve particular attention.

Examples include certificates used for:

Client Authentication
Smart Card Logon
PKINIT

docs.title: Require Approval Where Appropriate
docs.text:
Sensitive certificate workflows may use:

Certificate Manager Approval

to introduce an additional control.

This should not be treated as a substitute for correcting an unnecessary ESC6 configuration.

docs.title: Authorized Signatures
docs.text:
High-value templates may require:

Authorized Signatures

where organisational workflows support them.

Again, this is defence in depth rather than justification for unsafe CA-wide SAN behaviour.

docs.title: Maintain Current Windows Patching
docs.text:
Domain controllers and CA servers should remain fully patched.

Certificate authentication security depends on:

CA Behaviour
Domain Controller Behaviour
Certificate Mapping

not just template configuration.

docs.title: Strong Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Modern environments should maintain Microsoft's strong certificate mapping protections.

Do not weaken certificate mapping to preserve legacy workflows without a detailed security review.

docs.title: Review ESC9
docs.text:
If ESC6 exists, explicitly review templates for:

CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

because this can remove the SID security extension.

See the future ESC9 notes.

docs.title: Review ESC10
docs.text:
Review domain certificate mapping configuration for weak mappings.

This becomes especially important when requester-controlled certificate identity exists.

docs.title: Review ESC16
docs.text:
Review whether the CA itself is configured to suppress the SID security extension.

This is especially important because:

ESC6 + ESC16

may recreate a much more dangerous certificate identity manipulation path.

docs.title: Protect CA Administrative Permissions
docs.text:
Because CA administrators may be able to modify CA configuration, review:

ManageCA

and other CA administrative rights.

This is covered in detail under ESC7.

docs.title: Change Control
docs.text:
Changes to:

EditFlags

should require documented PKI change control.

Record:

Who
What
Why
When
Approved By
Previous Value
New Value
Rollback Plan

docs.title: Baseline CA Configuration
docs.text:
Maintain a baseline of:

CA Name
CA Host
Policy Module
EditFlags
Request Disposition
Published Templates
CA Permissions
Enrollment Endpoints

Compare periodically for drift.

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
If ESC6 abuse is suspected:

Identify CA
    |
    v
Confirm ESC6 Configuration
    |
    v
Determine When Enabled
    |
    v
Identify Requests with Supplied SANs
    |
    v
Identify Issued Certificates
    |
    v
Determine SID Extension
    |
    v
Identify Authentication
    |
    v
Revoke Malicious Certificates

docs.title: Determine When the Flag Was Enabled
docs.text:
Establish whether:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

was:

Long-Standing Configuration

or:

Recently Enabled

A recent unexpected change may indicate active compromise.

docs.title: Identify Certificate Requests
docs.text:
Review requests during the exposure period for unusual:

SAN UPN
SAN DNS
Subject
Requester
Template

combinations.

docs.title: Identify Requester and Certificate Identity
docs.text:
Compare:

Requester

with:

Certificate SAN

and:

SID Security Extension

This helps determine whether attempted identity substitution occurred.

docs.title: Identify Issued Certificates
docs.text:
For suspicious certificates record:

Serial Number
Thumbprint
Requester
Subject
SAN
Template
Issuer
Issue Time
Expiration
EKUs
SID Extension

docs.title: Identify Authentication
docs.text:
Correlate suspicious certificates with:

Kerberos TGT Requests
Smart Card Authentication
Client Certificate Authentication
Application Authentication

depending on certificate purpose.

docs.title: Revoke Malicious Certificates
docs.text:
Where malicious certificates were issued:

Revoke Certificate
       |
       v
Publish Updated CRL
       |
       v
Verify Revocation Distribution

docs.title: Password Reset Is Not Enough
docs.text:
As with other AD CS abuse:

Password Reset
      |
      X
Certificate Revocation

An issued certificate remains separate credential material until it expires or is revoked and revocation is enforced.

docs.title: Disable Unnecessary ESC6 Configuration
docs.text:
If the setting is not required:

Disable
EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

through the organisation's approved PKI change process.

Do not make emergency CA changes without understanding application dependencies.

docs.title: Review Other ESC Conditions
docs.text:
Following suspected ESC6 abuse, review:

ESC1
ESC4
ESC5
ESC7
ESC9
ESC10
ESC16

because attackers may combine multiple PKI weaknesses.

docs.title: Reporting ESC6
docs.text:
Avoid reporting only:

ESC6

A clearer finding title is:

Certification Authority Accepts Requester-Supplied Subject Alternative Names

or:

CA-Wide SAN Configuration Permits Requester-Controlled Certificate Identity

docs.title: Example Finding - Configuration Present, Modern Mapping Mitigates Exploitation
docs.text:
Finding:
Certification Authority Accepts Requester-Supplied Subject
Alternative Names

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Configuration:
EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 enabled

Description:
The Enterprise Certification Authority CORP-CA01 is configured to
accept Subject Alternative Name information supplied through
certificate request attributes.

This behaviour applies at the CA level rather than being limited to
a single certificate template.

Historically, this configuration could allow a requester with
enrollment rights over an authentication-capable template to request
a certificate containing another Active Directory account's UPN.

During controlled validation, a certificate request submitted by the
approved test account was able to include the UPN of a second test
account.

The issued certificate retained the requester's SID security
extension. Authentication as the alternate test identity was not
possible under the domain's enforced strong certificate mapping
configuration.

Impact:
The CA exposes unnecessary requester-controlled SAN functionality
across certificate templates processed by the CA.

The classic ESC6 arbitrary-identity authentication path was not
demonstrated because strong certificate mapping bound the issued
certificate to the requester's SID.

The configuration nevertheless increases PKI attack surface and may
become exploitable when combined with other weaknesses that remove
the SID security extension or weaken certificate mappings.

Recommendation:
Disable EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 unless there is a documented
business requirement for CA-wide requester-supplied SAN attributes.

Review all templates published by the affected CA and identify
whether any omit the SID security extension or otherwise permit weak
certificate mappings.

Maintain current Windows security updates and strong certificate
mapping enforcement.

Where requester-supplied SAN information is legitimately required,
use the most narrowly scoped certificate enrollment design supported
by the application.

docs.title: Example Finding - Exploitable Combination
docs.text:
Where testing demonstrates a real alternate-identity authentication path, document the complete chain.

Finding:
Requester-Supplied SAN Configuration Enables Certificate-Based
Privilege Escalation

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Affected Template:
CorpAuthentication

Description:
The Enterprise Certification Authority accepts requester-supplied
Subject Alternative Name attributes.

The CorpAuthentication certificate template is available to the
affected low-privileged principal and issues certificates suitable
for Active Directory authentication.

Additional certificate mapping controls in the environment do not
prevent the issued certificate from mapping to the alternate
identity supplied in the approved test request.

Impact:
A principal with enrollment rights may be able to obtain certificate
credentials representing another Active Directory identity.

Where a privileged identity is reachable, this may result in
privilege escalation without knowledge of the target account's
password.

Recommendation:
Disable the CA-wide requester-supplied SAN configuration.

Review certificate templates published by the CA, restrict enrollment
rights, ensure the SID security extension is present where required,
and maintain strong certificate mapping enforcement.

Revoke certificates issued through unauthorised identity substitution
and investigate certificate-based authentication during the exposure
period.

docs.title: Severity Assessment
docs.text:
ESC6 severity should consider:

CA Flag Enabled
      +
Enrollable Template
      +
Authentication Capability
      +
Issuance Requirements
      +
SID Extension Behaviour
      +
Certificate Mapping
      +
Reachable Identity
      =
Severity

docs.title: Do Not Rate on Flag Alone
docs.text:
For example:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2
       |
       v
Enabled

does not automatically establish:

Critical

The actual authentication path matters.

docs.title: High-Risk Combination
docs.text:
A significantly more dangerous combination may look like:

ESC6
 |
 +--> Requester-Controlled SAN
 |
ESC9 / ESC16
 |
 +--> SID Security Extension Missing
 |
Weak / Applicable Mapping
 |
 +--> Alternate Identity Accepted
 |
 v
Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Reduced Exploitability Example
docs.text:
ESC6 Enabled
      |
      v
Authentication Template
      |
      v
Certificate Issued
      |
      v
Requester SID Extension Present
      |
      v
Strong Mapping Enforced
      |
      v
Alternate Identity Rejected

The unsafe CA configuration still deserves review, but the demonstrated impact differs substantially.

docs.title: Evidence Checklist
docs.text:
For an ESC6 assessment record:

CA Host
CA Type
Policy Module

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 State

Enrollment Rights

Manager Approval

Request Disposition
Requester
Requested SAN
Issued Subject
Issued SAN

SID Value
Certificate Serial Number
Certificate Thumbprint
Domain Controller Patch State

Authentication Result
Validation Accounts
Cleanup Result

docs.title: ESC6 Testing Model
docs.text:
The ESC1 model is:

Template
   |
   v
Requester-Supplied Subject

The ESC6 model is:

CA
 |
 v
EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2
 |
 v
Requester-Supplied SAN Attribute

The historical attack model is:

Low-Privileged User
       |
       v
Enroll
       |
       v
Authentication Template
       |
       v
ESC6 CA
       |
       v
SAN = Administrator
       |
       v
Certificate
       |
       v
Administrator Authentication

The modern model is:

Requester
   |
   v
Certificate Request
   |
   +--> Alternate SAN
   |
   v
Enterprise CA
   |
   +--> SID Security Extension
   |
   v
Certificate
   |
   v
Strong Mapping
   |
   +--> Identity Matches -> Authentication
   |
   +--> Identity Mismatch -> Rejected

The ESC6 + ESC9 model is:

ESC6
 |
 +--> Requester-Supplied SAN
 |
ESC9
 |
 +--> Template Omits SID Extension
 |
 v
Certificate Mapping Analysis

The ESC6 + ESC16 model is:

ESC6
 |
 +--> Requester-Supplied SAN
 |
ESC16
 |
 +--> CA-Wide SID Extension Disabled
 |
 v
Alternate Identity Risk

The ESC7 relationship is:

ESC7
 |
 v
CA Administrative Control
 |
 v
Modify EditFlags
 |
 v
Enable ESC6

The safe validation model is:

Enumerate CA
    |
    v
Confirm ESC6 Flag
    |
    v
Enumerate Templates
    |
    v
Identify Candidate
    |
    v
Evaluate Modern Mapping
    |
    v
Need Active Proof?
    |
    +--> No -> Report
    |
    +--> Yes
           |
           v
       Test Requester
           |
           v
       Test Target
           |
           v
       Request Certificate
           |
           v
       Inspect SAN + SID
           |
           v
       Controlled Mapping Test
           |
           v
       Revoke / Cleanup

The detection model is:

EditFlags Change
      |
      v
CA Service Restart
      |
      v
Certificate Request
      |
      v
Unexpected SAN
      |
      v
Certificate Issuance
      |
      v
Authentication Attempt

The defensive model is:

ESC6 Disabled
      +
Restricted Enrollment
      +
Strong Mapping
      +
SID Security Extension
      +
Current Patching
      +
Restricted CA Administration
      +
Monitoring
      =
Reduced ESC6 Risk

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Is EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 enabled?"

Also Ask:
"Can an enrolled certificate actually map to
another security principal under the target's
current certificate mapping configuration?"

For defenders:

Do Not Assume:
"Strong mapping means ESC6 can be ignored."

Instead Ask:
"Why does the CA accept requester-controlled
SAN information at all, and could another PKI
weakness remove the protection we currently
depend on?"

That distinction is central to modern ESC6 testing.

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
ESC6 is one of the AD CS techniques where historical exploitation guidance must be interpreted in the context of modern Windows security changes.

The old mental model was:

ESC6
 |
 v
Supply Administrator UPN
 |
 v
Get Administrator Certificate

That is no longer an accurate universal model.

The modern model is:

Requester-Controlled SAN
        |
        v
Certificate Issuance
        |
        v
SID Security Extension
        |
        v
Strong Certificate Mapping
        |
        v
Actual Account Mapping

Microsoft's certificate-based authentication hardening materially changed the final stage of this chain.

In a fully patched 2026 environment, Full Enforcement should be expected, and the legacy StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement compatibility fallback is no longer supported after the September 9, 2025 security update.

Therefore:

ESC6 Flag Present

and:

ESC6 Privilege Escalation Demonstrated

are not the same statement.

A strong assessment determines:

Is the Flag Enabled?
        |
        v
Which Templates Are Published?
        |
        v
Who Can Enroll?
        |
        v
Can the Certificate Authenticate?
        |
        v
Is the SID Extension Present?
        |
        v
Which SID Is Embedded?
        |
        v
How Does the DC Map the Certificate?
        |
        v
Can Another Identity Actually Be Reached?

ESC6 becomes especially important when combined with other AD CS weaknesses.

In particular:

ESC6 + ESC9

or:

ESC6 + ESC16

may alter the strong-mapping protection provided by the SID security extension.

Similarly:

ESC7

may provide a route to enabling ESC6 through inappropriate CA administrative control.

For penetration testers, the correct approach is therefore to test the entire certificate identity chain rather than reproducing an old SAN impersonation command and assuming success.

For defenders, the safest configuration remains to disable unnecessary CA-wide requester-supplied SAN behaviour even when strong mapping currently prevents the classic exploitation path.

Defence in depth should ensure:

ESC6 Disabled
        +
SID Security Extension Present
        +
Strong Mapping Enforced
        +
Templates Hardened
        +
CA Permissions Restricted
        +
Current Windows Updates

rather than depending on a single mitigation to protect an unnecessarily permissive CA configuration.

docs.title: AD CS ESC7 - Vulnerable Certification Authority Permissions
docs.text:
ESC7 is an Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) privilege escalation condition involving excessive administrative permissions on a Certification Authority (CA).

The two permissions most commonly associated with ESC7 are:

ManageCA
ManageCertificates

These permissions are significantly different from ordinary certificate enrollment rights.

They provide administrative control over the CA or its certificate requests.

A simplified ESC7 relationship is:

Low-Privileged Principal
        |
        v
Dangerous CA Permission
        |
        +--> ManageCA
        |
        +--> ManageCertificates
        |
        v
Certification Authority
        |
        v
Administrative CA Actions
        |
        v
Certificate Abuse
        |
        v
Potential Privilege Escalation

The key assessment question is:

Can a principal that should not administer
the Certification Authority perform privileged
CA management operations?

Authorised testing only

CA administrative permissions can affect certificate issuance and authentication across an Active Directory environment. Begin with read-only enumeration. Do not change CA configuration, enable certificate templates, approve production certificate requests, alter CA security descriptors, or restart Certificate Services merely to demonstrate ESC7. Where active validation is required, use dedicated test identities and obtain explicit approval for the specific CA operation.

docs.title: ESC7 Concept
docs.text:
AD CS separates several types of access.

For example:

Certificate Enrollment
        |
        v
Request Certificate

is different from:

CA Administration
        |
        v
Manage CA

and:

Certificate Management
        |
        v
Manage Certificate Requests

ESC7 concerns the latter administrative capabilities.

docs.title: Certification Authority Permissions
docs.text:
Important CA permissions include:

Read
Issue and Manage Certificates
Manage CA
Request Certificates

The exact names shown by tools may vary.

For ESC7, the most important permissions are commonly represented as:

ManageCA
ManageCertificates

docs.title: ManageCA
docs.text:
ManageCA represents CA administrative control.

Conceptually:

Principal
   |
   v
ManageCA
   |
   v
CA Configuration

Depending on the CA configuration and the principal's effective rights, this can expose security-sensitive administrative operations.

docs.title: ManageCertificates
docs.text:
ManageCertificates is commonly associated with:

Issue and Manage Certificates

Conceptually:

Principal
   |
   v
ManageCertificates
   |
   v
Certificate Requests
   |
   v
Issue / Deny / Manage

This can become particularly dangerous when combined with other CA or template conditions.

docs.title: ESC7 Is About Effective Permissions
docs.text:
Do not assess only direct user permissions.

The effective path may be:

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
Nested Group
 |
 v
ManageCA

or:

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
ManageCertificates

Therefore always resolve:

Direct Permissions
Group Membership
Nested Groups
Inherited Administrative Roles

docs.title: ESC7 vs Enrollment Rights
docs.text:
A principal that can:

Enroll

does not necessarily have ESC7.

Enrollment means:

Request a Certificate

ESC7 concerns:

Administer the CA

or:

Manage Certificate Requests

These are different trust boundaries.

docs.title: ESC7 vs ESC4
docs.text:
ESC4 concerns:

Certificate Template ACL

For example:

User
 |
 v
GenericWrite
 |
 v
Certificate Template

ESC7 concerns:

CA Permission

For example:

User
 |
 v
ManageCA
 |
 v
Certification Authority

docs.title: ESC7 vs ESC5
docs.text:
ESC5 concerns control over broader PKI objects or infrastructure.

For example:

User
 |
 v
GenericWrite
 |
 v
PKI Object

ESC7 specifically focuses on:

Certification Authority Administrative Permissions

A finding should identify the actual permission rather than relying only on the ESC number.

docs.title: ESC7 vs ESC6
docs.text:
ESC6 concerns a CA configured with:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

ESC7 may provide a route to changing CA configuration.

Conceptually:

ESC7
 |
 v
ManageCA
 |
 v
CA Configuration Change
 |
 v
Enable Dangerous Behaviour

This creates an important relationship between:

ESC7

and:

ESC6

docs.title: CA Security Descriptor
docs.text:
Certification Authorities maintain a security descriptor controlling administrative access.

Conceptually:

Certification Authority
        |
        v
Security Descriptor
        |
        +--> CA Administrators
        |
        +--> Certificate Managers
        |
        +--> Certificate Requesters

ESC7 occurs when these permissions are assigned too broadly.

docs.title: Common Principals to Review
docs.text:
Look carefully for permissions assigned to:

Domain Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Computers
Helpdesk Groups
Application Teams
Service Accounts
Legacy PKI Groups
Deployment Accounts
Certificate Enrollment Groups
Non-PKI Administrators

Not every non-default principal represents a vulnerability.

The question is whether the administrative permission is appropriate for that principal's role.

docs.title: Discover Certification Authorities
docs.text:
Certipy provides convenient AD CS enumeration.

Begin with:

certipy --version

Then review discovery options:

certipy find -h

A typical authenticated read-only discovery command is:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

docs.title: Review CA Permissions with Certipy
docs.text:
Certipy output can include CA permissions such as:

Owner
Access Rights
ManageCa
ManageCertificates
Enroll

Field names can vary between releases.

Always record:

CA
Principal
Permission
Effective Group Path

docs.title: Example Enumeration Result
docs.text:
Conceptually, a problematic result might resemble:

Certificate Authority:
CORP-CA

Permissions:
  ManageCa:
    CORP\PKI-Operators

  ManageCertificates:
    CORP\Certificate-Managers

The next question is:

Who can become a member of these groups?

docs.title: Resolve Group Membership
docs.text:
From Windows:

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'PKI-Operators' -Recursive |
    Select-Object Name,SamAccountName,ObjectClass

Also inspect the group itself:

Get-ADGroup 'PKI-Operators' -Properties * |
    Select-Object Name,GroupScope,GroupCategory,DistinguishedName

docs.title: Determine Current User Membership
docs.text:
whoami /groups

This can help identify security groups represented in the current access token.

docs.title: Native CA Discovery
docs.text:
Windows provides native certificate utilities.

Discover available CA configurations with:

certutil -config - -ping

This can identify Enterprise CAs reachable from the current environment.

docs.title: Certification Authority Console
docs.text:
On authorised administrative systems, the Certification Authority management console can be opened with:

certsrv.msc

The console exposes administrative areas such as:

Revoked Certificates
Issued Certificates
Pending Requests
Failed Requests
Certificate Templates

Do not perform changes during routine enumeration.

docs.title: CA Properties
docs.text:
CA security settings can be reviewed through the Certification Authority management console.

Conceptually:

Certification Authority
       |
       v
Properties
       |
       v
Security

Review which principals possess:

Manage CA
Issue and Manage Certificates
Request Certificates

docs.title: Read-Only Validation
docs.text:
For most assessments, evidence such as:

Low-Privileged Principal
        |
        v
ManageCA

or:

Low-Privileged Principal
        |
        v
ManageCertificates

combined with documentation of the available administrative capability may be sufficient.

Do not modify CA configuration merely to prove that the permission works.

docs.title: CA Permissions vs Active Directory ACLs
docs.text:
This distinction is important.

Certificate templates are Active Directory objects.

CA permissions are associated with the Certification Authority itself.

Therefore:

Get-Acl AD:<template DN>

is useful for:

ESC4

but does not by itself establish:

ESC7

docs.title: CA Object in Active Directory
docs.text:
Enterprise CA registration information also exists under:

CN=Enrollment Services,
CN=Public Key Services,
CN=Services,
CN=Configuration,...

However:

Control of Enrollment Services AD Object

is not automatically equivalent to:

ManageCA

These are separate security boundaries.

docs.title: ManageCA Capabilities
docs.text:
The exact operations available through ManageCA depend on the CA configuration and Windows behaviour.

Security-sensitive examples may include management of:

CA Configuration
CA Security
Certificate Managers
Policy Module Settings
Exit Module Settings
Published Templates
Other CA Properties

Do not assume every administrative operation is available through every interface.

Verify the target configuration.

docs.title: Why ManageCA Is Dangerous
docs.text:
A CA is part of the identity trust infrastructure.

Conceptually:

ManageCA
    |
    v
CA Configuration
    |
    v
Certificate Issuance Behaviour
    |
    v
Authentication

Therefore inappropriate ManageCA assignment can expose a powerful control-plane path.

docs.title: ManageCA and CA Security
docs.text:
One particularly important question is whether a CA manager can change:

CA Security Permissions

If so, an existing administrative permission may be used to grant additional CA rights.

Conceptually:

ManageCA
    |
    v
Modify CA Security
    |
    v
Additional CA Permission

The exact operation should be verified against the target CA and current tooling before active testing.

docs.title: ManageCA and ManageCertificates
docs.text:
A historically important ESC7 chain involves combining:

ManageCA

with:

ManageCertificates

because CA administration may allow a principal to gain or assign certificate-management capability depending on the effective CA security configuration.

Conceptually:

ManageCA
    |
    v
CA Administrative Control
    |
    v
Certificate Management Capability

Do not perform this permission change in production merely to demonstrate the theoretical path.

docs.title: ManageCertificates
docs.text:
ManageCertificates gives a principal certificate-manager capabilities.

This commonly affects requests that are:

Pending

rather than automatically issued.

Conceptually:

Certificate Request
       |
       v
Pending
       |
       v
Certificate Manager
       |
       +--> Issue
       |
       +--> Deny

docs.title: Certificate Manager Approval
docs.text:
Some templates require:

Certificate Manager Approval

This is normally a security control.

The normal workflow is:

User Requests Certificate
        |
        v
Request Pending
        |
        v
Certificate Manager Reviews
        |
        v
Issue / Deny

docs.title: Why ManageCertificates Changes the Model
docs.text:
If an attacker is themselves a certificate manager:

Attacker Requests
      |
      v
Pending
      |
      v
Attacker Approves

the manager-approval control may no longer provide meaningful separation.

This is why inappropriate certificate-manager permissions are dangerous.

docs.title: SubCA Template
docs.text:
Historical ESC7 research often discusses the built-in:

SubCA

certificate template.

The SubCA template is important because it can provide powerful certificate capabilities.

However, several conditions matter:

Template Availability
Enrollment Rights
Request Disposition
Certificate Manager Rights
CA Configuration
Current Windows Behaviour

Do not assume the presence of the template automatically creates an exploitable path.

docs.title: Historical ESC7 Certificate Manager Path
docs.text:
A classic model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
ManageCertificates
   |
   v
Submit Certificate Request
   |
   v
Request Becomes Pending
   |
   v
Issue Pending Request
   |
   v
Certificate

This becomes dangerous if the resulting certificate can be used for unintended authentication or certificate issuance purposes.

docs.title: Certificate Manager Restrictions
docs.text:
AD CS can support restrictions on certificate managers.

Conceptually:

Certificate Manager
       |
       v
Restricted to
       |
       +--> Specific Templates
       |
       +--> Specific Subjects / Groups

Review whether certificate-manager permissions are broadly scoped.

docs.title: Do Not Assume All Certificate Managers Are Equal
docs.text:
A principal may have:

ManageCertificates

but still be restricted by certificate-manager restrictions.

Therefore assess:

Permission
     +
Manager Restrictions
     +
Template
     +
Request

before determining impact.

docs.title: Enumerate Published Templates
docs.text:
Use Active Directory to determine templates published by Enterprise CAs.

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$enrollmentBase = "CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $enrollmentBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKIEnrollmentService)' -Properties certificateTemplates,dNSHostName |
    Select-Object Name,dNSHostName,certificateTemplates

docs.title: Enumerate Certificate Templates
docs.text:
$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties displayName,pKIExtendedKeyUsage,'msPKI-Certificate-Application-Policy','msPKI-Enrollment-Flag' |
    Select-Object Name,displayName,pKIExtendedKeyUsage,'msPKI-Certificate-Application-Policy','msPKI-Enrollment-Flag'

docs.title: Evaluate Authentication Capability
docs.text:
If ESC7 could result in certificate issuance, determine what the certificate can actually do.

Relevant EKUs may include:

Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2

Smart Card Logon
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.2

PKINIT Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.2.3.4

Any Purpose
2.5.29.37.0

Do not infer authentication capability solely from the template name.

docs.title: Certificate Mapping Still Matters
docs.text:
As with other AD CS techniques, modern certificate authentication must be evaluated against Microsoft's strong certificate mapping protections.

Therefore:

Certificate Issued

does not automatically mean:

Privileged Account Compromised

Evaluate:

Certificate Identity
SID Security Extension
Certificate Mapping
Domain Controller Behaviour

docs.title: ESC7 and Strong Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Strong certificate mapping does not eliminate the underlying ESC7 permission problem.

ESC7 concerns:

Who Can Administer the CA?

Strong mapping concerns:

How Does a Certificate Map to an Account?

These are separate controls.

docs.title: ESC7 and ESC6
docs.text:
A CA administrator may have the ability to alter policy-module settings.

One historically dangerous setting is:

EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2

Conceptually:

ManageCA
    |
    v
Modify CA Policy
    |
    v
ESC6 Condition

Current strong mapping and SID-extension protections must still be considered before claiming alternate-identity authentication.

docs.title: ESC7 and ESC9
docs.text:
ESC9 is associated with certificate templates that omit the SID security extension.

An ESC7 path may become more dangerous when other template weaknesses already exist.

Conceptually:

ESC7
 |
 v
CA Administrative Control
 |
 +--> Existing ESC9 Template
 |
 v
Certificate Abuse Path

docs.title: ESC7 and ESC16
docs.text:
ESC16 concerns CA-wide suppression of the SID security extension.

Because ESC16 is CA-wide, inappropriate CA administrative access is particularly relevant.

Conceptually:

ESC7
 |
 v
CA Administrative Control
 |
 v
Security-Sensitive CA Configuration
 |
 v
Potential ESC16-Related Condition

Do not alter SID-extension configuration during routine validation.

docs.title: ESC7 and ESC8
docs.text:
ESC8 concerns NTLM relay to AD CS HTTP enrollment endpoints.

ESC7 concerns:

CA Administrative Permissions

These can coexist but are separate weaknesses.

docs.title: ESC7 and ESC11
docs.text:
ESC11 concerns NTLM relay to AD CS RPC enrollment under vulnerable conditions.

Again:

ESC7 = CA Administration
ESC11 = Enrollment Relay

The attack paths can interact but should be reported separately when they have different root causes.

docs.title: ESC7 and ESC4
docs.text:
Another possible relationship is:

ESC4
 |
 v
Template Control

combined with:

ESC7
 |
 v
CA Control

A principal controlling both certificate-template configuration and CA administration has significantly greater PKI influence.

docs.title: ESC7 and ESC5
docs.text:
ESC5 and ESC7 together can indicate broader PKI control-plane compromise.

For example:

PKI Object Control
        +
CA Administrative Control
        =
Broad PKI Administrative Capability

This should be treated as a major identity-security concern.

docs.title: Certipy ESC7 Enumeration
docs.text:
Certipy can identify dangerous CA permissions.

A typical discovery command is:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

Look for output identifying:

ESC7

and inspect the associated:

Principal
CA
Permission

docs.title: Verify Certipy Version
docs.text:
Before using operational commands:

certipy --version

Review:

certipy ca -h

and:

certipy req -h

Certipy syntax changes between releases.

Do not rely blindly on commands from older AD CS write-ups.

docs.title: Certipy CA Functionality
docs.text:
The ca command family can expose CA management functionality supported by the installed Certipy release.

Review:

certipy ca -h

before performing any operation.

Potential administrative functions can be security-sensitive.

Do not execute modification options unless they are explicitly within scope.

docs.title: Safe Certipy Use
docs.text:
For routine assessment:

find

should generally come before:

ca

or:

req

The workflow should be:

Discover
   |
   v
Analyse
   |
   v
Determine Whether Active Proof Is Needed

docs.title: Do Not Enable Templates Merely to Prove ESC7
docs.text:
Some historical ESC7 exploitation chains involve enabling a certificate template on the CA.

Do not do this in production merely to demonstrate:

ManageCA

Enabling a template can expose certificate enrollment to other users and systems.

docs.title: Do Not Change CA Security Merely to Prove ESC7
docs.text:
Likewise, avoid changing:

CA ACL

to grant yourself:

ManageCertificates

during routine validation.

The existing permission plus documented administrative capability may already provide sufficient evidence.

docs.title: Do Not Restart CertSvc Casually
docs.text:
Some CA configuration changes require restarting:

CertSvc

Restarting Certificate Services can affect production certificate enrollment.

Do not restart the CA service unless explicitly authorised and operational impact has been considered.

docs.title: Safe Validation Strategy
docs.text:
A preferred ESC7 workflow is:

Enumerate CA
    |
    v
Identify Dangerous Permission
    |
    v
Resolve Effective Principal
    |
    v
Determine Administrative Capability
    |
    v
Review Existing CA Configuration
    |
    v
Can Impact Be Demonstrated Read-Only?
    |
    +--> Yes -> Stop and Report
    |
    +--> No
           |
           v
       Obtain Explicit Approval
           |
           v
       Controlled Test

docs.title: Controlled Test Accounts
docs.text:
If certificate-manager functionality must be demonstrated, use:

Dedicated Requester Account
Dedicated Certificate Manager Account
Dedicated Test Template
Dedicated Test Certificate

where possible.

Avoid:

Administrator
Domain Admin
Enterprise Admin
Domain Controller
Production Service Account

as target identities.

docs.title: Minimum-Impact Validation
docs.text:
A controlled validation might demonstrate only that the authorised test principal can:

View Pending Request

or another non-destructive administrative action.

The exact validation should be agreed with the organisation before testing.

docs.title: Certificate Request Approval
docs.text:
If explicitly approved, certificate-manager capability can be validated against a dedicated test request.

Conceptually:

Test Account
    |
    v
Submit Test Request
    |
    v
Pending Request
    |
    v
Approved Test Certificate Manager
    |
    v
Controlled Administrative Action

Do not use production user requests for validation.

docs.title: Record Request IDs
docs.text:
Certificate requests have request identifiers.

For approved testing, record:

Request ID
Requester
Template
Subject
SAN
Submission Time
Disposition
Manager
Issue Time

This helps with evidence and cleanup.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
ESC7 detection should focus on:

CA Permission Changes
CA Administrative Actions
Certificate Manager Activity
CA Configuration Changes
Certificate Issuance

docs.title: CA Security Changes
docs.text:
Monitor changes to the CA security descriptor.

Unexpected additions of:

Manage CA
Issue and Manage Certificates

should be investigated.

docs.title: CA Administrative Groups
docs.text:
Maintain a baseline of principals authorised to administer the CA.

For example:

Approved PKI Administrators
Approved Certificate Managers
Approved Enrollment Groups

Alert on unexpected additions.

docs.title: Event 4880
docs.text:
Where Certificate Services auditing is configured, Windows can generate CA-related auditing events.

One important category includes changes to Certificate Services configuration.

Exact event availability depends on:

Windows Version
CA Role
Audit Configuration
Action Performed

Do not rely on a single event ID for ESC7 detection.

docs.title: Event 4886
docs.text:
Certificate Services can log:

4886

when it receives a certificate request.

This can provide useful context for certificate-manager abuse.

docs.title: Event 4887
docs.text:
Certificate Services can log:

4887

when a certificate request is approved and a certificate is issued.

Correlate:

Requester
Template
Request ID
Issue Time

docs.title: Event 4888
docs.text:
Certificate Services auditing can also record denial of a certificate request.

This can provide additional request-management context.

docs.title: Event 4889
docs.text:
Certificate Services auditing can record a certificate request being set to pending.

This is particularly relevant when analysing certificate-manager workflows.

docs.title: Pending to Issued Correlation
docs.text:
A useful detection model is:

Request Submitted
      |
      v
Pending
      |
      v
Certificate Manager Action
      |
      v
Issued

Investigate unexpected managers approving their own requests or requests associated with unusual identities.

docs.title: Monitor CA Configuration
docs.text:
Changes to:

EditFlags
Request Disposition
Policy Module
Exit Module
CA Security
Published Templates

should be monitored and subject to change control.

docs.title: Monitor Template Publication
docs.text:
Unexpected publication of a sensitive certificate template can indicate CA administrative abuse.

Conceptually:

CA Administrator
      |
      v
Enable Template
      |
      v
New Enrollment Path

docs.title: Monitor CA Service Restarts
docs.text:
Correlate unexpected:

CertSvc Restart

with:

CA Configuration Change
CA Permission Change
Template Publication

docs.title: Monitor Administrative Logons
docs.text:
CA servers should have a very small administrative population.

Monitor:

Interactive Logons
Remote Interactive Logons
Remote Administration
PowerShell Remoting
Service Creation
Scheduled Tasks

according to organisational monitoring capabilities.

docs.title: Monitor Certipy-Like Activity Carefully
docs.text:
Do not attempt to detect only a specific tool name.

Focus on behaviour:

CA Enumeration
CA Permission Change
Template Publication
Certificate Request
Request Approval
Certificate Authentication

Tools can change while the underlying activity remains the same.

docs.title: Correlate with Kerberos
docs.text:
Where issued certificates are used for PKINIT, correlate certificate issuance with:

4768

Ticket Granting Ticket requests.

This can help connect:

Certificate Administration

to:

Certificate Authentication

docs.title: Hardening ESC7
docs.text:
The primary mitigation is:

Restrict CA Administrative Permissions

Only dedicated PKI administrators should normally possess:

ManageCA

Only approved certificate managers should possess:

ManageCertificates

docs.title: Review ManageCA
docs.text:
Identify every principal with:

ManageCA

For each principal ask:

Why Is This Required?
Who Are the Members?
Can Membership Be Modified?
Is It Still Needed?
Is the Account Tiered?
Is It Monitored?

docs.title: Review ManageCertificates
docs.text:
Likewise review every principal with:

ManageCertificates

Certificate managers can participate directly in issuance decisions.

Treat this as privileged access.

docs.title: Avoid Broad Groups
docs.text:
Administrative CA permissions should not normally be assigned to broad principals such as:

Domain Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Computers
Everyone

Any such configuration requires immediate investigation.

docs.title: Review Nested Groups
docs.text:
A seemingly secure assignment may still be vulnerable.

For example:

PKI-Admins
    |
    v
Contains
    |
    v
Helpdesk

If Helpdesk membership is broad:

ManageCA

may effectively be broad as well.

docs.title: Review Group Management
docs.text:
Also ask:

Who Can Modify PKI-Admins?

A user may not directly possess ManageCA but may control a group that does.

Conceptually:

alice
 |
 v
GenericWrite
 |
 v
PKI-Admins
 |
 v
ManageCA
 |
 v
CA

docs.title: Use BloodHound for Indirect Paths
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify relationships such as:

User
 |
 v
Group Control
 |
 v
PKI Admin Group
 |
 v
CA Permission

Always verify graph-derived relationships directly.

docs.title: Separate CA Administration
docs.text:
Where operationally possible, separate:

CA Administrators
Certificate Managers
Template Administrators
Enrollment Operators
Server Administrators

This reduces the blast radius of a single compromised role.

docs.title: Protect CA Administrative Accounts
docs.text:

Privileged Access Workstations

docs.title: Treat Enterprise CA as Tier 0
docs.text:
Where the CA issues certificates used for Active Directory authentication, compromise of the CA can affect the identity control plane.

Therefore Enterprise PKI should generally receive protections comparable to other highly privileged identity infrastructure.

docs.text:

However, CA administrators may operate on systems containing extremely sensitive key material.

Strict Key ACLs
Secure Backup

where appropriate.

docs.title: Reporting ESC7
docs.text:
Avoid finding titles such as:

ESC7 Found

Prefer:

Low-Privileged Group Has Manage CA Permission

or:

Excessive Certification Authority Permissions Allow Certificate Management

or:

Non-PKI Administrators Can Manage Enterprise Certification Authority

docs.title: Example Finding - ManageCA
docs.text:
Finding:
Low-Privileged Group Has Manage CA Permission

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Affected Principal:
CORP\PKI-Operators

Permission:
ManageCA

Description:
The CORP\PKI-Operators group has Manage CA permission over the
Enterprise Certification Authority CORP-CA01.

Membership of CORP\PKI-Operators includes accounts that are not
designated PKI administrators.

Manage CA provides security-sensitive administrative capability over
the Certification Authority and can affect CA configuration and
certificate issuance behaviour.

Impact:
Compromise of a member of CORP\PKI-Operators may provide
administrative influence over the enterprise certificate authority.

Depending on the CA configuration and other certificate-service
controls, this may permit additional certificate-management
capabilities or changes that create certificate-based privilege
escalation paths.

No CA configuration was modified during the assessment because the
existing effective permission provides sufficient evidence of the
administrative control weakness.

Recommendation:
Remove Manage CA from CORP\PKI-Operators unless CA administration is
an explicitly required business function.

Restrict Manage CA to dedicated PKI administrators and review nested
group membership and control over all groups receiving CA
administrative permissions.

Monitor changes to CA permissions and maintain an approved baseline
of CA administrators.

docs.title: Example Finding - ManageCertificates
docs.text:
Finding:
Excessive Certificate Manager Permissions on Enterprise CA

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Affected Principal:
CORP\Helpdesk-Certificates

Permission:
Issue and Manage Certificates

Description:
The CORP\Helpdesk-Certificates group has certificate-manager
permissions on the Enterprise Certification Authority.

The affected group contains accounts that do not require unrestricted
certificate approval capabilities.

Certificate managers can participate in certificate request
disposition and may be able to approve pending certificate requests
depending on configured certificate-manager restrictions.

Impact:
Compromise of an affected account may allow unauthorised certificate
requests to be approved.

The resulting impact depends on the certificate template, certificate
purpose, request identity, SID security extension, certificate
mapping, and certificate-manager restrictions.

Recommendation:
Restrict certificate-manager permissions to dedicated PKI personnel.

Configure certificate-manager restrictions where supported and
maintain separation between certificate requesters and approvers.

Review historical certificate approvals performed by members of the
affected group.
