docs.title: Active Directory Cheatsheet
docs.text:
This cheatsheet is a practical reference for assessing Microsoft Active Directory environments during authorised penetration tests, red team exercises and security labs.

It is designed around a simple question:

I have access to an Active Directory environment. What should I check next, what does the result mean, and where should I investigate further?

For detailed explanations of individual techniques, use the Active Directory Notes.

Authorised Security Testing

Only use these techniques against systems and environments you are explicitly authorised to test. Credential attacks, authentication testing and remote administration can lock accounts, trigger security controls or affect production systems.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
A typical Active Directory assessment progresses through:

Identify Domain
      |
      v
Identify Domain Controllers
      |
      v
DNS
      |
      v
SMB / LDAP / Kerberos
      |
      v
Validate Credentials
      |
      v
Enumerate Users and Groups
      |
      v
Enumerate Computers
      |
      v
Enumerate Shares
      |
      v
BloodHound
      |
      v
Kerberos
      |
      +--> AS-REP Roasting
      |
      +--> Kerberoasting
      |
      +--> Delegation
      |
      v
AD CS
      |
      v
ACLs / Privilege Relationships
      |
      v
Credential Access
      |
      v
Lateral Movement
      |
      v
Privilege Paths
      |
      v
Validate
      |
      v
Evidence
      |
      v
Report

docs.title: Quick Reference Variables
docs.text:
Throughout this cheatsheet, examples use:

DOMAIN="corp.local"
DC="dc01.corp.local"
DC_IP="10.10.10.10"
USER="asif"
PASSWORD='Password123!'
TARGET="10.10.10.20"

For NTLM authentication examples:

NT_HASH="0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef"

Replace all values with the authorised test environment.

docs.title: Know Your Starting Position
docs.text:
Before running tools, determine what you already have.

Starting Position Useful First Actions Network access only DNS, DC discovery, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos Username only Validate username carefully, review Kerberos opportunities Domain credentials NetExec, LDAP, BloodHound, shares, Kerberos NTLM hash Determine which approved tools/protocols accept hash authentication Kerberos ticket Confirm ticket cache and service/domain context Local foothold Host enumeration, domain context, identity, routes Domain user shell BloodHound, Kerberos, shares, ACLs, privilege paths Local administrator Determine whether privilege is local only or reusable elsewhere Domain privilege Identify why the privilege exists and affected trust boundaries

docs.title: Current Windows Identity
docs.text:
whoami

More detail:

whoami /all

Domain information:

whoami /fqdn

Environment variables:

$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:USERDNSDOMAIN
$env:LOGONSERVER

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Example:

CORP\asif

This indicates the current security context is associated with the CORP domain.

whoami /all is particularly useful because it shows:

User SID

Group memberships

Privileges

Integrity level

Do not assume membership in a group automatically provides an exploitable privilege. Determine whether the membership actually grants access to a relevant resource.

docs.title: Discover the Domain
docs.text:
From Windows:

systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"Domain"

PowerShell:

[System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()

Using nltest:

nltest /dsgetdc:corp.local

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
DC: \\DC01.corp.local
Address: \\10.10.10.10
Dom Guid: ...
Dom Name: corp.local
Forest Name: corp.local
Dc Site Name: HQ

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This can identify:

Domain controller

Domain

Forest

AD site

The domain controller is often the starting point for DNS, LDAP and Kerberos enumeration.

docs.title: DNS SRV Records
docs.text:
dig _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local SRV

Alternative:

nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text: _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local. 600 IN SRV 0 100 389 dc01.corp.local.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This indicates that:

dc01.corp.local

advertises the LDAP domain-controller service for the domain.

docs.title: Resolve the Domain Controller
docs.text:
dig dc01.corp.local

or:

nslookup dc01.corp.local

Confirm:

ping -c 1 dc01.corp.local

Remember that ICMP may be blocked even when the host is reachable.

docs.title: Common Active Directory Ports
docs.text: Port Protocol Purpose 53 DNS Name resolution 88 Kerberos Authentication 135 RPC RPC endpoint mapper 139 NetBIOS Legacy SMB 389 LDAP Directory services 445 SMB File sharing and remote administration 464 Kerberos Password changes 636 LDAPS LDAP over TLS 3268 Global Catalog Forest-wide LDAP 3269 Global Catalog TLS Forest-wide LDAP over TLS 5985 WinRM HTTP 5986 WinRM HTTPS

docs.title: Initial Port Check
docs.text:
A focused scan against an authorised domain controller:

nmap -Pn -sT -p 53,88,135,139,389,445,464,636,3268,3269 "$DC_IP"

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A typical domain controller commonly exposes several of:

53
88
135
389
445
464
3268

Port exposure alone does not constitute a vulnerability. It identifies services available for subsequent assessment.

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Kerberos is sensitive to clock differences.

Check local time:

date

Check the DC's time information through SMB:

nxc smb "$DC_IP"

If Kerberos tools return clock-skew errors, compare your test system's time with the domain controller before troubleshooting credentials.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
Check the configured resolver:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Query the domain:

dig "$DOMAIN"

Query the DC:

dig "$DC"

Reverse lookup:

dig -x "$DC_IP"

docs.title: Why DNS Matters
docs.text:
Active Directory depends heavily on DNS.

Incorrect DNS can cause apparently unrelated failures involving:

Kerberos

LDAP

BloodHound

SMB hostnames

SPNs

Domain discovery

When a tool works by IP but fails by hostname, DNS should be one of the first things checked.

docs.title: /etc/hosts for Lab Environments
docs.text:
When appropriate for a controlled lab:

10.10.10.10 dc01.corp.local dc01 corp.local

Check:

getent hosts dc01.corp.local

Prefer functioning DNS in real environments rather than relying extensively on static host entries.

docs.title: Basic NetExec SMB Enumeration
docs.text: nxc smb "$DC_IP"

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text: SMB  10.10.10.10  445  DC01  [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC01) (domain:corp.local) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Useful fields include:

Hostname

Domain

Operating system

SMB signing

SMBv1

For example:

signing:True

means SMB signing is enabled/required according to the tool's reported state.

Do not treat every SMB configuration value as a vulnerability without understanding the exact server configuration and attack prerequisites.

docs.title: Validate Domain Credentials
docs.text: nxc smb "$DC_IP" -u "$USER" -p "$PASSWORD"

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text: SMB  10.10.10.10  445  DC01  [+] corp.local\asif:Password123!

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
[+] indicates authentication succeeded.

This proves that the supplied credential was accepted for the tested SMB authentication path.

It does not prove:

Domain administrator access

Local administrator access

Access to every domain host

Access to every SMB share

Those require separate validation.

docs.title: Administrative SMB Access
docs.text:
Against an authorised member server:

nxc smb "$TARGET" -u "$USER" -p "$PASSWORD"

You may see output similar to:

SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  [+] corp.local\asif:Password123! (Pwn3d!)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
(Pwn3d!) is NetExec's indication that the tested account has administrative-level access relevant to the SMB assessment on that host.

This should be investigated further:

Why does the account have administrative access?

Is the privilege expected?

Is it local or domain-derived?

Which group or policy grants it?

Is the same privilege present on other systems?

docs.title: Avoid Unnecessary Credential Spray
docs.text:
Do not immediately run credentials against an entire subnet.

Start narrowly:

nxc smb "$DC_IP" -u "$USER" -p "$PASSWORD"

Then expand only when the engagement scope and objective justify it.

This reduces:

Account lockout risk

Unnecessary authentication noise

Production impact

Scope mistakes

docs.title: Enumerate SMB Shares
docs.text: nxc smb "$TARGET" -u "$USER" -p "$PASSWORD" --shares

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  Share       Permissions
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  -----       -----------
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  ADMIN$      READ
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  Public      READ,WRITE

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A writable share such as:

Public READ,WRITE

is a candidate for further review.

It does not automatically constitute a vulnerability.

Determine:

What data is stored there?

Who should have access?

Can files be modified?

Are files consumed by privileged processes?

Does the share contain credentials or configuration?

Is write access operationally expected?

docs.title: SMBClient
docs.text:
List shares:

smbclient -L "//$TARGET" -U "$DOMAIN/$USER"

Connect:

smbclient "//$TARGET/Public" -U "$DOMAIN/$USER"

Useful interactive commands:

ls
cd
pwd
get
put
mkdir
help
exit

Only modify or upload files where authorised.

docs.title: Enumerate Domain Users with NetExec
docs.text:
Check the version-specific options first:

nxc ldap "$DC_IP" --help

NetExec syntax changes over time, so confirm the available LDAP enumeration options for the installed version rather than assuming an old flag remains valid.

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text:
LDAP provides structured access to Active Directory objects.

Useful object types include:

Users

Groups

Computers

Organisational Units

Group Policies

Service accounts

Trusts

Certificate-related objects

docs.title: LDAP RootDSE
docs.text:
A useful initial LDAP query:

ldapsearch -x -H "ldap://$DC_IP" -s base namingContexts

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
namingContexts: DC=corp,DC=local
namingContexts: CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=local
namingContexts: CN=Schema,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=local

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The domain naming context is:

DC=corp,DC=local

This becomes the base DN for many LDAP queries.

docs.title: Authenticated LDAP Query
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x \
  -H "ldap://$DC_IP" \
  -D "$USER@$DOMAIN" \
  -w "$PASSWORD" \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=user)" \
  sAMAccountName

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Look for:

sAMAccountName

which represents the traditional Active Directory logon name.

Large environments can return substantial output. Use narrow filters where possible.

docs.title: Query Computers
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x \
  -H "ldap://$DC_IP" \
  -D "$USER@$DOMAIN" \
  -w "$PASSWORD" \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=computer)" \
  dNSHostName

docs.title: Representative Result
docs.text:
dNSHostName: DC01.corp.local
dNSHostName: SRV01.corp.local
dNSHostName: WS01.corp.local

This helps build an authorised host inventory.

docs.title: Query Groups
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x \
  -H "ldap://$DC_IP" \
  -D "$USER@$DOMAIN" \
  -w "$PASSWORD" \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=group)" \
  cn

Prioritise groups such as:

Domain Admins

Enterprise Admins

Administrators

Server administration groups

Helpdesk groups

Application administration groups

Backup groups

Do not limit analysis to built-in privileged groups. Custom groups frequently provide important access.

docs.title: Native Windows Domain Enumeration
docs.text:
Current domain:

net user /domain

Domain groups:

net group /domain

Domain Admins:

net group "Domain Admins" /domain

Specific user:

net user asif /domain

docs.title: Why Native Commands Matter
docs.text:
They can provide useful context when:

Third-party tooling is unavailable

Application control restricts tooling

You need a quick local check

You want to compare tool results

docs.title: PowerShell AD Module
docs.text:
If the Active Directory PowerShell module is available:

Get-Module -ListAvailable ActiveDirectory

Import:

Import-Module ActiveDirectory

Domain:

Get-ADDomain

Forest:

Get-ADForest

Users:

Get-ADUser -Filter *

Computers:

Get-ADComputer -Filter *

Groups:

Get-ADGroup -Filter *

Group members:

Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins"

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound helps model relationships between:

Users

Groups

Computers

Sessions

ACLs

Delegation

Local administration

Remote access

Certificate Services

Its main value is not simply enumeration.

It helps answer:

How can the access I currently have lead to more privileged access?

docs.title: BloodHound Collection Strategy
docs.text:
Start with the least disruptive collection appropriate for the engagement.

Before collection, confirm the collector's supported options:

bloodhound-python --help

or for SharpHound:

.\SharpHound.exe --help

Collector syntax and available methods can change between versions.

docs.title: BloodHound Python
docs.text:
A common authenticated collection pattern is:

bloodhound-python \
  -u "$USER" \
  -p "$PASSWORD" \
  -d "$DOMAIN" \
  -ns "$DC_IP" \
  -c All

Caution

-c All can perform substantially more collection than a narrow query. Review the collection methods and engagement requirements before using broad collection in production environments.

docs.title: BloodHound Output
docs.text:
Typical collection produces JSON files representing objects such as:

users

groups

computers

domains

ous

gpos

Depending on collector and collection methods, additional relationship information may also be present.

docs.title: BloodHound Import
docs.text:
After collection:

Collector
   |
   v
JSON / ZIP
   |
   v
BloodHound
   |
   v
Import
   |
   v
Graph Analysis

Verify that the imported dataset actually contains expected objects.

docs.title: Incomplete BloodHound Data
docs.text:
If BloodHound contains:

Users: 0
Computers: 0
Groups: 0

or unexpectedly limited data, investigate:

DNS resolution

Domain name

Domain controller selection

Credentials

LDAP connectivity

Collector errors

Collection method

Import errors

Do not interpret an empty graph as proof that no attack paths exist.

docs.title: BloodHound Analysis Priorities
docs.text:
Useful questions include:

What can my current user control?

Which systems can my user administer?

Which groups can my user modify?

Which ACLs are interesting?

Which users have paths to privileged groups?

Which computers expose useful privilege relationships?

Which delegation relationships exist?

Which AD CS relationships exist?

docs.title: BloodHound Path Thinking
docs.text:
Avoid:

Find Domain Admin.

Think instead:

Current Principal
      |
      v
Relationship
      |
      v
Intermediate Principal
      |
      v
Computer / Group / ACL
      |
      v
Privilege Boundary
      |
      v
Target

docs.title: BloodHound Result Interpretation
docs.text:
A graph edge is a relationship, not automatically a confirmed exploit.

For every interesting edge ask:

What does the relationship mean?

Which permissions create it?

Does it still exist?

Can my current principal exercise it?

Would exercising it modify the environment?

Is the action authorised?

What evidence can prove the risk safely?

See the BloodHound Notes for deeper analysis.

docs.title: Kerberos
docs.text:
Kerberos commonly involves:

Client

KDC

TGT

TGS

SPN

Service

Simplified flow:

User
 |
 v
AS-REQ
 |
 v
Domain Controller
 |
 v
TGT
 |
 v
TGS-REQ
 |
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Target Service

docs.title: Check Kerberos Tickets on Windows
docs.text: klist

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
Cached Tickets: (2)

#0> Client: asif @ CORP.LOCAL
    Server: krbtgt/CORP.LOCAL @ CORP.LOCAL

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A krbtgt ticket indicates a Ticket Granting Ticket is present in the current cache.

Other tickets may identify services the current security context has accessed.

docs.title: Kerberos from Linux
docs.text:
Impacket tools commonly support Kerberos authentication with options such as:

-k

and ticket-cache usage.

Always inspect the specific tool:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

because authentication options differ between utilities.

docs.title: Kerberos Credential Cache
docs.text:
Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

List tickets:

klist

A cache path may resemble:

FILE:/tmp/krb5cc_1000

docs.title: Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Kerberoasting targets accounts associated with Service Principal Names.

The important prerequisite is:

Account has an SPN

Enumeration is therefore the first step.

docs.title: Enumerate SPNs
docs.text:
Using Impacket:

impacket-GetUserSPNs \
  "$DOMAIN/$USER:$PASSWORD" \
  -dc-ip "$DC_IP"

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
ServicePrincipalName          Name       MemberOf
----------------------------  ---------  ----------------
MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local     svc_sql
HTTP/web01.corp.local         svc_web

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This identifies accounts with SPNs.

An SPN does not itself mean:

Weak password

Compromised account

Privilege escalation

It means the account is a candidate for Kerberos service-ticket analysis.

docs.title: Request Service Tickets
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised, Impacket supports requesting service tickets for identified SPN accounts.

Check the installed syntax:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

The assessment should focus on:

Which accounts have SPNs?

What privileges do they hold?

Are they human or service identities?

Are strong managed credentials used?

Would compromise create a meaningful attack path?

See Kerberoasting.

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting
docs.text:
AS-REP roasting applies when an account does not require Kerberos preauthentication.

The important condition is:

DONT_REQ_PREAUTH

This is a specific account configuration, not a general property of Active Directory users.

docs.title: Identify AS-REP Candidates
docs.text:
With valid domain credentials, directory enumeration can identify accounts configured without Kerberos preauthentication.

For Impacket capabilities:

impacket-GetNPUsers -h

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A returned account should be investigated for:

Why preauthentication is disabled

Account privilege

Account usage

Credential policy

Whether the configuration is still required

See AS-REP Roasting.

docs.title: Password Spraying
docs.text:
Password spraying can cause:

Account lockouts

Security alerts

Operational impact

Incident-response escalation

Before any spraying activity, determine:

Is password spraying explicitly authorised?

What is the lockout threshold?

What is the observation window?

Which accounts are excluded?

What rate is approved?

Who must be notified?

See Password Spraying.

Do not begin spraying merely because usernames have been enumerated.

docs.title: Account Lockout Policy
docs.text:
From a domain-connected Windows system:

net accounts /domain

Review:

Lockout threshold

Lockout duration

Lockout observation window

Minimum password age

Maximum password age

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The policy helps determine whether authentication testing could lock accounts.

It does not automatically account for:

Fine-grained password policies

Identity-provider controls

Third-party authentication

Conditional access

Application-specific lockouts

docs.title: NTLM
docs.text:
NTLM remains relevant in many Active Directory environments.

During assessment, determine:

Where NTLM is still used

Which systems accept it

Whether SMB signing is enforced

Whether LDAP signing is required

Whether Extended Protection is configured where applicable

Whether legacy authentication remains necessary

See NTLM.

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
Check with NetExec:

nxc smb "$DC_IP"

Example:

(signing:True)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
SMB signing configuration affects the feasibility of some relay scenarios.

Do not conclude:

SMB signing disabled = domain compromised

Relay feasibility depends on multiple conditions, including:

Source authentication

Target protocol

Target signing requirements

Authentication method

Channel protections

Identity privilege

Network reachability

docs.title: NTLM Relay Assessment
docs.text:
Treat relay as a prerequisite chain:

Can Authentication Be Induced?
           |
           v
Is NTLM Used?
           |
           v
Can Attacker Receive It?
           |
           v
Does Target Accept Relay?
           |
           v
Are Required Protections Missing?
           |
           v
What Privilege Does the Identity Have?

See:

  • NTLM Relay
  • Authentication Coercion

docs.title: LDAP Signing and Channel Binding
docs.text:
These controls can materially affect LDAP relay opportunities.

Assessment should determine:

Is LDAP signing required?

Is LDAPS available?

Is channel binding enforced where relevant?

Which clients still depend on insecure compatibility settings?

Avoid reporting a generic relay vulnerability without validating the relevant protocol protections.

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
Important delegation categories include:

Unconstrained Delegation

Constrained Delegation

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
Look for computers or accounts configured for unconstrained delegation.

Questions:

Which principal is trusted for delegation?

Is it a workstation or server?

Which users authenticate to it?

Are privileged identities protected?

Is the configuration still required?

See Unconstrained Delegation.

docs.title: Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Constrained delegation restricts which services may be delegated to.

Review:

Principal

Allowed service

Target host

Protocol transition

Privilege of delegated identity

See Constrained Delegation.

docs.title: Resource-Based Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
RBCD places delegation configuration on the target resource.

The important relationship is:

Principal
    |
    v
Can Modify Relevant Target Attribute
    |
    v
Target Computer

A BloodHound relationship or writable attribute is a candidate requiring validation.

See Resource-Based Constrained Delegation.

docs.title: S4U
docs.text:
Service-for-User Kerberos extensions are relevant to several delegation scenarios.

Understand:

S4U2Self

S4U2Proxy

before interpreting delegation paths.

See S4U.

docs.title: ACLs and ACEs
docs.text:
Active Directory permissions can create indirect privilege paths.

Important rights may include:

GenericAll

GenericWrite

WriteDACL

WriteOwner

AddMember

ForceChangePassword

WriteProperty

The exact security impact depends on the target object.

docs.title: ACL Analysis Model
docs.text:
Principal
    |
    v
Permission
    |
    v
Target Object
    |
    v
Permitted Modification
    |
    v
Security Consequence

Example:

Helpdesk Group
      |
      v
Can Modify
      |
      v
Server Admin Group

This may represent a privilege path, but the actual ACE and effective permissions should be verified before reporting.

docs.title: GenericAll
docs.text:
GenericAll generally represents extensive control over the target object.

But interpretation depends on whether the target is:

User

Group

Computer

OU

GPO

Domain object

Do not describe all GenericAll relationships with the same impact.

docs.title: GenericWrite
docs.text:
GenericWrite permits writing a set of properties.

The practical impact depends on:

Target object

Writable attributes

Inheritance

Security-sensitive properties

docs.title: WriteDACL
docs.text:
WriteDACL allows modification of the target object's discretionary ACL.

This can be highly significant because it may allow the principal to grant additional rights.

Validation should establish:

Effective permission

Target importance

Inheritance

Safe proof

Potential privilege path

docs.title: WriteOwner
docs.text:
Ownership can affect the ability to modify an object's permissions.

Again:

Ownership Relationship
        !=
Immediate Domain Compromise

Follow the complete path.

docs.title: Group Membership
docs.text:
Enumerate important groups:

net group "Domain Admins" /domain

PowerShell:

Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins" -Recursive

docs.title: Why Recursive Membership Matters
docs.text:
Privilege may be inherited through nested groups.

Example:

asif
 |
 v
IT-Support
 |
 v
Server-Admins
 |
 v
Administrators

Looking only at direct membership may miss this relationship.

docs.title: Local Administrators
docs.text:
A domain user may have local administrative access without being a Domain Admin.

This distinction is critical:

Local Administrator
       !=
Domain Administrator

Local administrative access may still create a wider attack path if:

Credentials are reused

Privileged sessions exist

Management systems are reachable

Service accounts are present

Administrative tiers are weak

docs.title: LAPS
docs.text:
LAPS helps manage unique local administrator passwords.

Assessment questions include:

Is LAPS deployed?

Which systems are covered?

Who can read the managed password?

Who can modify LAPS-related permissions?

Are legacy and Windows LAPS configurations understood?

Are privileged readers appropriately restricted?

See LAPS.

docs.title: gMSA
docs.text:
Group Managed Service Accounts provide automatically managed service-account passwords.

Assessment should determine:

Which gMSAs exist?

Which systems use them?

Which principals can retrieve their managed passwords?

What privileges does the gMSA hold?

See gMSA.

docs.title: Machine Account Quota
docs.text:
Review the domain's machine-account creation policy.

The important question is not simply:

Is MachineAccountQuota non-zero?

but:

Can the current user create a computer?

Does that capability combine with another relationship?

Is the default behaviour required?

Does it enable a meaningful privilege path?

See Machine Account Quota.

docs.title: Active Directory Certificate Services
docs.text:
AD CS can introduce privilege paths through:

Certificate templates

Enrollment rights

Template permissions

CA configuration

Web enrollment

Certificate mapping

Authentication settings

docs.title: Find Certificate Services
docs.text:
With appropriate tooling, determine whether an enterprise CA exists.

Useful tools may include:

Certipy

Certify

Native certificate utilities

Confirm your installed Certipy version:

certipy -h

or, depending on packaging:

certipy-ad -h

docs.title: Certipy Enumeration
docs.text:
Review the installed syntax:

certipy find -h

A typical authenticated assessment collects information about:

Certificate authorities

Templates

Enrollment rights

Template settings

Potentially risky configurations

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not report an ESC classification solely because a tool labels something as vulnerable.

Manually validate:

Template settings

Enrollment rights

Effective permissions

CA configuration

Authentication capability

Current principal

Required prerequisites

docs.title: AD CS Review Model
docs.text:
Certificate Authority
        |
        v
Certificate Template
        |
        v
Who Can Enroll?
        |
        v
Template Configuration
        |
        v
Certificate Purpose
        |
        v
Authentication Capability
        |
        v
Privilege Consequence

docs.title: ESC1
docs.text:
At a high level, ESC1 involves a certificate template configuration where an enrollee can influence identity information under conditions that can make authentication as another principal possible.

Review:

Enrollment rights

Subject/SAN control

Authentication EKUs

Manager approval

Authorised signatures

Target identity

See ESC1.

docs.title: ESC2 - ESC17
docs.text:
The detailed AD CS section contains separate notes for each currently documented ESC category:

ESC1
ESC2
ESC3
ESC4
ESC5
ESC6
ESC7
ESC8
ESC9
ESC10
ESC11
ESC12
ESC13
ESC14
ESC15
ESC16
ESC17

Start with:

Active Directory Certificate Services

docs.title: AD CS Enumeration Results
docs.text:
When tooling reports something similar to:

Template: ExampleTemplate
Enabled: True
Client Authentication: True
Enrollment Rights: CORP\Domain Users

do not stop at the output.

Ask:

Can my principal actually enroll?

What identity can the certificate represent?

Can it be used for authentication?

Does the CA issue the template?

Are approvals required?

Are signatures required?

Which account would be affected?

docs.title: Certificate Evidence
docs.text:
Useful evidence includes:

CA name

Template name

Template configuration

Enrollment rights

Relevant permissions

Authentication EKUs

Approval requirements

Target principal

Observed result

Avoid including unnecessary private-key material in reports.

docs.title: Shares
docs.text:
Shares often expose valuable operational context.

Prioritise:

SYSVOL

NETLOGON

Application shares

Deployment shares

Backup shares

User shares

IT administration shares

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
Connect:

smbclient "//$DC/SYSVOL" -U "$DOMAIN/$USER"

Review:

Group Policy files

Scripts

Configuration files

Deployment information

Do not modify SYSVOL during routine enumeration.

docs.title: NETLOGON
docs.text:
smbclient "//$DC/NETLOGON" -U "$DOMAIN/$USER"

Look for:

Logon scripts

Configuration

Mapped-drive scripts

Legacy administrative scripts

docs.title: Search Downloaded Files
docs.text:
If files have been legitimately copied into an assessment workspace:

rg -n -i 'password|passwd|secret|token|apikey|api_key|connectionstring' .

Treat matches as candidates.

Example:

config.xml:18:<Password>Example123!</Password>

This may indicate a credential, but verify:

Is it active?

Which system uses it?

Is it a placeholder?

Is it encrypted?

What privilege does it provide?

Is validation authorised?

docs.title: Group Policy
docs.text:
Group Policy can affect:

Security configuration

Local groups

Scripts

Software deployment

Firewall

PowerShell

Application control

Scheduled tasks

Registry settings

See Group Policy.

docs.title: Group Policy Result Interpretation
docs.text:
A GPO linked to an OU does not automatically mean every setting applies to every object in that OU.

Consider:

Link status

Inheritance

Security filtering

WMI filtering

Enforced links

Block inheritance

Object type

Resultant policy

docs.title: Credential Access
docs.text:
Potential Active Directory credential sources include:

Service accounts

Configuration files

Scripts

Deployment systems

Shares

Scheduled tasks

Application pools

Backup systems

CI/CD

Management platforms

Privileged sessions

Credential discovery should be driven by the engagement objective and data-handling rules.

docs.title: Credential Validation
docs.text:
If a credential is discovered:

Credential
    |
    v
Identify Owner
    |
    v
Identify Intended Use
    |
    v
Determine Scope
    |
    v
Validate Minimally
    |
    v
Determine Privilege
    |
    v
Stop When Proven

Avoid unnecessary authentication attempts across the environment.

docs.title: Credential Reuse
docs.text:
A credential valid on one host should not automatically be tested against every system.

Instead determine:

Account type

Expected administrative scope

Target systems

Authorised test boundaries

Lockout implications

docs.title: Pass-the-Hash
docs.text:
NTLM hashes may be accepted by some tools and protocols in circumstances where NTLM authentication is supported.

The important assessment question is:

Does possession of this credential material permit authentication
to a security-relevant target?

See Pass-the-Hash.

docs.title: Pass-the-Ticket
docs.text:
Kerberos tickets can represent existing authenticated security contexts.

Before analysing a ticket, identify:

Client principal

Service principal

Ticket type

Validity

Domain

Encryption type

See Pass-the-Ticket.

docs.title: OverPass-the-Hash
docs.text:
OverPass-the-Hash concerns using credential material in a Kerberos authentication context rather than treating the technique as simply another SMB authentication method.

See OverPass-the-Hash.

docs.title: Pass-the-Key
docs.text:
Kerberos keys may also be relevant to authentication depending on the account and available key material.

See Pass-the-Key.

docs.title: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Common Active Directory remote-management surfaces include:

SMB

WinRM

WMI

DCOM

RDP

SSH

Management platforms

The presence of a protocol does not prove the current account can use it.

docs.title: WinRM Reachability
docs.text: nmap -Pn -sT -p 5985,5986 "$TARGET"

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Open 5985 or 5986 indicates WinRM may be available.

It does not prove:

Authentication succeeds

The current user has remote-management rights

The host is exploitable

docs.title: NetExec WinRM Validation
docs.text:
Check available syntax:

nxc winrm --help

A credential can be tested against a specifically authorised target using the installed version's authentication syntax.

Start with a single target rather than a large range.

docs.title: Evil-WinRM
docs.text:
For authorised remote administration:

evil-winrm -i "$TARGET" -u "$USER" -p "$PASSWORD"

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A successful session demonstrates that the account has sufficient access for the tested WinRM path.

Record:

Target

Account

Privilege level

Group-derived access

Why access exists

docs.title: SMB Remote Administration
docs.text:
Administrative SMB access can indicate a lateral movement path.

The important chain is:

Credential
    |
    v
Target Accepts Authentication
    |
    v
Administrative Rights
    |
    v
Remote Management Capability

Each step should be demonstrated separately.

docs.title: WMI
docs.text:
WMI may provide remote-management capabilities where:

RPC is reachable

Authentication succeeds

The account has sufficient permissions

See WMI.

docs.title: DCOM
docs.text:
DCOM is another Windows remote-management surface.

See DCOM.

Treat DCOM access as a protocol and permission question rather than assuming its availability automatically enables lateral movement.

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
Check:

nmap -Pn -sT -p 3389 "$TARGET"

An open port only demonstrates network reachability.

Determine separately:

Can the user authenticate?

Does the user have RDP logon rights?

Is NLA required?

Is MFA involved?

Would an interactive logon be appropriate for the engagement?

docs.title: Pivoting
docs.text:
When internal systems are not directly reachable:

Operator
    |
    v
Compromised / Test Host
    |
    v
Internal Network

Common authorised assessment options include:

Ligolo-ng

Chisel

SSH forwarding

SOCKS proxying

See Active Directory Pivoting and Red Team Lateral Movement.

docs.title: Trusts
docs.text:
Active Directory environments may contain:

Parent-child trusts

Forest trusts

External trusts

Shortcut trusts

See:

  • Trusts
  • Trust Relationships

docs.title: Trust Analysis
docs.text:
For every trust determine:

Source domain

Target domain

Direction

Transitivity

Trust type

SID filtering

Authentication scope

Privilege relationships

Do not assume:

Trust Exists
    =
Privilege Escalation

The trust establishes a relationship. Additional permissions determine practical security impact.

docs.title: SID History
docs.text:
SID History can preserve access during migrations.

Review:

Which accounts contain SIDHistory?

Which historical SID is present?

What access does that SID grant?

Is the configuration legitimate?

Is SID filtering relevant across the trust?

See SID History.

docs.title: Trust Tickets
docs.text:
Kerberos trust relationships involve inter-realm authentication material.

See Trust Tickets for the detailed trust-ticket model.

docs.title: Domain Infrastructure
docs.text:
Do not limit AD assessment to users and domain controllers.

Important infrastructure may include:

SCCM

WSUS

MDT

SCOM

ADFS

AD CS

DNS

Backup infrastructure

Virtualisation

Identity management

Privileged access systems

docs.title: SCCM
docs.text:
SCCM can represent an important administrative trust boundary because it manages large numbers of endpoints.

Questions:

Who administers SCCM?

Which systems are managed?

Which accounts are used?

Where are distribution points?

What privileges do site servers hold?

Can low-privileged users interact with sensitive components?

See SCCM.

docs.title: WSUS
docs.text:
Review:

WSUS topology

Administrative permissions

Update approval model

Transport protections

Managed systems

See WSUS.

docs.title: MDT
docs.text:
Deployment infrastructure may contain:

Deployment credentials

Scripts

Configuration

Images

Domain join information

See MDT.

docs.title: ADFS
docs.text:
Federation infrastructure can represent a critical identity boundary.

Review:

Federation servers

Service accounts

Certificates

Trust relationships

Authentication methods

Administrative access

See ADFS.

docs.title: Active Directory DNS
docs.text:
AD-integrated DNS can expose important infrastructure information.

See ADIDNS.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Decision Tree
docs.text:
Current Domain User
        |
        v
Any Interesting Group Membership?
        |
    +---+---+
    |       |
   Yes      No
    |       |
    v       v
Analyse   BloodHound
Rights       |
             v
        Interesting ACL?
             |
         +---+---+
         |       |
        Yes      No
         |       |
         v       v
      Validate  Kerberos
                  |
             +----+----+
             |         |
          SPNs?     No-Preauth?
             |         |
             v         v
          Review     Review
             |

docs.title: Candidate vs Confirmed
docs.text: This distinction is important throughout Active Directory testing.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
Examples:

SPN exists

Writable share exists

Interesting BloodHound edge exists

Template is flagged by tooling

Remote service is exposed

User belongs to an interesting group

These require further investigation.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
Examples:

Current principal has a relevant ACL

Writable location is consumed by a privileged service

Certificate enrollment rights and risky settings coexist

Account has administrative group-derived rights

Multiple prerequisites are present.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
A controlled validation demonstrates the security consequence.

For example:

Approved test account successfully performs the relevant
privileged action against the authorised test object.

Stop once sufficient evidence exists.

docs.title: Reporting an Attack Path
docs.text:
Avoid reporting every intermediate observation as an isolated high-severity finding.

Where appropriate, describe the complete path.

Example:

Standard Domain User
        |
        v
Writable Group Membership
        |
        v
Server Administration Group
        |
        v
Local Administrator on APP01
        |
        v
Privileged Service Credential
        |
        v
Sensitive Application Access

This explains why the individual relationships matter.

docs.title: Example Attack-Path Evidence Table
docs.text: Step Observation Evidence Result 1 User belongs to Helpdesk LDAP Confirmed 2 Helpdesk can modify Server-Admins ACL Confirmed 3 Server-Admins administer APP01 BloodHound + validation Confirmed 4 APP01 contains privileged application context Host review Confirmed

docs.title: Reporting Language
docs.text:
Prefer:

The CORP\Helpdesk group has effective permissions that allow modification of the Server-Admins group. The tested account is a member of Helpdesk. Controlled validation using an authorised test object confirmed that the delegated permission can be exercised.

Avoid:

BloodHound says GenericAll, therefore Domain Admin.

docs.title: KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW
docs.text:

and compare with the domain environment.

docs.title: KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED
docs.text:

Incorrect password

Incorrect key

Wrong principal

Domain mismatch

Authentication configuration

Do not assume the account does not exist.

docs.title: STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE
docs.text:

docs.title: STATUS_ACCOUNT_LOCKED_OUT
docs.text:

Do not continue retrying credentials.

docs.text:
Active Directory assessment should also identify the defensive controls protecting each attack path.

Important controls include:

Tiered administration

Privileged access workstations

Unique local administrator passwords

Windows LAPS

gMSA

Credential Guard

Protected Users

SMB signing

LDAP signing

docs.title: Detection Questions
docs.text:
For every validated technique ask:

Was authentication logged?

Was process execution visible?

Was directory modification logged?

Was an alert generated?

Could the SOC identify the account?

Could the SOC identify the source host?

Could the SOC identify the target?

Could analysts reconstruct the attack path?

docs.title: Remediation Themes
docs.text:
Common Active Directory remediation themes include:

Least privilege

Remove unnecessary group memberships

Remove stale accounts

Restrict delegated permissions

Protect privileged identities

Use managed service accounts

Deploy LAPS

Reduce credential reuse

Harden Kerberos configuration

Reduce NTLM dependency

Require protocol protections

Segment administrative access

Harden AD CS

Monitor directory changes

Improve authentication monitoring

Separate administrative tiers

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
A good retest verifies the underlying privilege relationship rather than simply checking whether a tool stops reporting it.

Example:

Original:

Helpdesk
   |
   v
Can Modify Server-Admins


Remediation:

Delegated permission removed


Retest:

1. Re-enumerate ACL.
2. Confirm permission no longer exists.
3. Confirm effective access is removed.
4. Confirm authorised test principal cannot perform the
   previously demonstrated modification.

Use the detailed notes when the cheatsheet stops being enough

The purpose of this page is to help you move quickly from an observation to the correct next question. The detailed Active Directory pages contain the deeper explanation for individual protocols, techniques and privilege relationships.

Re-enumerate after privilege changes

Active Directory assessment is iterative. New credentials, group membership, host access or delegated rights may reveal relationships that were not relevant from the previous security context.

A tool finding is not automatically a vulnerability

NetExec, BloodHound, Certipy, Impacket and other tools provide evidence and identify candidates. Confirm prerequisites, effective permissions, security context and practical impact before reporting a vulnerability.

Authentication answers:

Session management answers:

How does the application maintain that authenticated identity
across multiple requests?

Security testing should evaluate the complete lifecycle rather than testing only the login form.

Login

MFA
     |

Session Creation

     |

Privilege Change
     |

Password Change
     |

Logout
     |
     v
Session Invalidation
     |

Authorised Security Testing

Perform authentication and session testing only against systems and accounts explicitly included in the assessment scope. Password spraying, brute-force testing, MFA testing and account lockout testing can affect real users and availability. Use dedicated test accounts and agreed request rates whenever possible.

Known User
   |
   v
Password Hash Verification
   |
   v
Response

versus:

Unknown User
   |
   v
Immediate Reject

docs.title: Timing Test
docs.text:
Timing differences require careful statistical interpretation.

Do not conclude:

Username enumeration

from one slow request.

docs.title: Timing Noise
docs.text:
Consider:

Network latency

Load balancing

Caching

Database load

Rate limiting

WAF processing

Application load

docs.title: Registration Enumeration
docs.text:
Registration may reveal existing users.

Example:

An account already exists for this email.

docs.title: Password Reset Enumeration
docs.text:
Forgot-password functionality may reveal account existence.

Example:

Reset email sent.

versus:

No account exists.

docs.title: Preferred Response
docs.text:
If an account exists for that address,
password reset instructions will be sent.

docs.title: Enumeration Through Side Effects
docs.text:
Even when the response is generic, test whether observable side effects differ.

Examples:

Email received

SMS received

Different response timing

Different rate-limit behaviour

docs.title: Password Policy
docs.text:
Review:

Minimum length

Maximum length

Character requirements

Password reuse

Common password blocking

Breached password checks

Password history

Unicode handling

Whitespace handling

docs.title: Long Password Support
docs.text:
Applications should permit reasonably long passwords.

Test using a dedicated account.

Examples:

64 characters

100 characters

Do not submit extremely large passwords solely to consume resources.

docs.title: Password Truncation
docs.text:
Check whether:

Password123456789ABC

and:

Password123456789XYZ

behave unexpectedly as equivalent due to truncation.

docs.title: Important
docs.text: Only perform truncation tests on dedicated test accounts where changing passwords is safe.

docs.title: Password Normalisation
docs.text:
Potential differences include:

Leading spaces

Trailing spaces

Unicode normalisation

Case handling

docs.title: Password Change
docs.text:
Review the password-change workflow.

Ask:

Is current password required?

Is MFA required?

Is the new password validated?

Are existing sessions invalidated?

Are remembered devices invalidated?

Is the user notified?

docs.title: Password Change Request
docs.text:
Example:

POST /account/password HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=...
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "current_password": "CurrentPassword123!",
  "new_password": "NewPassword456!"
}

docs.title: Test Current Password Requirement
docs.text: Do not assume that being authenticated is sufficient for sensitive account changes.

docs.title: Sensitive Actions
docs.text:
Consider re-authentication for:

Password change

Email change

MFA disablement

Recovery configuration

Payment details

API key generation

Account deletion

docs.title: Password Reset Workflow
docs.text:
Typical flow:

Email Address
     |
     v
Reset Request
     |
     v
Random Token
     |
     v
Email
     |
     v
Reset Endpoint
     |
     v
New Password

docs.title: Password Reset Testing
docs.text:
Review:

Account enumeration

Token randomness

Token length

Token lifetime

Single use

User binding

Session invalidation

Host header handling

Rate limiting

Token leakage

Referer leakage

Password policy

docs.title: Reset Token Properties
docs.text:
A reset token should be:

Cryptographically random

Sufficiently long

Single-use

Time-limited

Bound to the correct account

docs.title: Reset Token Replay
docs.text:
After successfully using a reset token:

Use Token
   |
   v
Password Changed
   |
   v
Replay Same Token

Expected:

Rejected

docs.title: Reset Token Expiry
docs.text: Verify expired tokens cannot be reused.

docs.title: Reset Token Account Binding
docs.text:
A token generated for:

Account A

must not reset:

Account B

docs.title: Do Not Brute Force Reset Tokens
docs.text:
Token quality can often be assessed through:

Length

Format

Source review

Multiple generated samples

Randomness design

without brute-force attempts.

docs.title: Password Reset Host Handling
docs.text:
Applications sometimes construct reset links using request-derived host information.

Conceptually:

Host Header
    |
    v
Reset URL Generator
    |
    v
Email

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Determine whether reset links use:

Trusted configured origin

rather than blindly trusting request headers.

docs.title: Password Reset Token Leakage
docs.text:
Review whether reset tokens appear in:

Referer headers

Analytics requests

Third-party scripts

Logs

Browser history

Error messages

docs.title: Reset Page Resources
docs.text: A reset page loading third-party content may unintentionally expose sensitive URL data through browser behaviour depending on how the token is transported.

docs.title: Prefer
docs.text: Sensitive tokens should not remain unnecessarily in URLs after use.

docs.title: Email Change
docs.text:
Email addresses often participate in account recovery.

Review:

Current password required?

MFA required?

Old address notified?

New address verified?

Existing sessions affected?

docs.title: Email Change Risk
docs.text:
If an attacker with a stolen session can change:

Email

and then:

Reset password

the session compromise may become persistent account takeover.

docs.title: MFA Testing
docs.text: MFA should strengthen authentication rather than merely add another UI page.

docs.title: MFA Flow
docs.text:
Username + Password
        |
        v
Primary Authentication
        |
        v
Partial Session
        |
        v
MFA Verification
        |
        v
Fully Authenticated Session

docs.title: Critical Question
docs.text: Can the partially authenticated session access endpoints intended only for fully authenticated users?

docs.title: MFA Bypass Through Direct Navigation
docs.text:
After password validation but before MFA completion, request:

/account

/dashboard

/api/me

/admin

as appropriate to the account's expected authorization.

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
MFA required

until verification completes.

docs.title: MFA State
docs.text:
Avoid relying only on:

Browser page flow

Enforcement must occur server-side.

docs.title: MFA Code Reuse
docs.text:
After successful verification:

Code Used
   |
   v
Replay Code

Expected behaviour depends on the MFA mechanism, but one-time codes should not remain valid outside their intended window/use model.

docs.title: TOTP
docs.text:
Review:

Time window

Replay handling

Rate limiting

Recovery process

Secret storage

docs.title: Do Not Exhaustively Guess OTPs
docs.text: Use a dedicated account and a very small number of agreed requests to evaluate controls.

docs.title: MFA Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Test whether repeated incorrect codes trigger:

Delay

Temporary block

Challenge reset

Additional verification

docs.title: MFA Reset
docs.text:
Often more important than MFA itself.

Review:

Who can reset MFA?

What proof is required?

Can support bypass MFA?

Can email alone disable MFA?

Are users notified?

docs.title: Backup Codes
docs.text:
Review:

Randomness

One-time use

Storage

Regeneration

Invalidation

Display behaviour

docs.title: Backup Code Replay
docs.text:
After using a backup code:

Replay Same Code

Expected:

Rejected

docs.title: MFA Enrolment
docs.text:
Ask:

Does enrolment require current authentication?

Does it require re-authentication?

Can an attacker with a stolen session register their own MFA device?

Is the existing MFA factor required?

docs.title: MFA Disablement
docs.text:
Sensitive operation:

Disable MFA

should normally require strong verification.

docs.title: Remember Me
docs.text: Remember-me functionality often creates long-lived authentication tokens.

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
Capture:

Normal session cookie

Remember-me cookie

Expiry

Cookie attributes

Logout behaviour

Password-change behaviour

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
A remember-me token should not simply contain:

Username

User ID

Role

without strong protection.

docs.title: Remember-Me Lifecycle
docs.text:
Login
  |
  v
Long-Lived Token
  |
  v
Browser
  |
  v
Future Authentication

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Ask:

Is token random?

Is it revocable?

Does logout revoke it?

Does password change revoke it?

Can users view remembered devices?

Can users revoke all devices?

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
After authentication, the application typically issues a session identifier.

Example:

Set-Cookie: session=RANDOM_VALUE; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

docs.title: Session Identifier Properties
docs.text:
A good session identifier should be:

Unpredictable

Unique

Sufficiently random

Meaningless to the client

Server-side validated

docs.title: Session Token Analysis
docs.text:
Do not judge randomness from one token.

Collect several tokens from your own test accounts and compare:

Length

Character set

Structure

Static components

Timestamp patterns

User identifiers

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Tokens:

abc001-user42-1700000000

abc002-user42-1700000010

abc003-user42-1700000020

would deserve investigation because they appear structured and potentially predictable.

docs.title: Opaque Tokens
docs.text:
Prefer tokens that appear as random opaque identifiers.

However:

Looks random

does not prove:

Cryptographically secure

docs.title: Source Review Can Confirm Generation
docs.text: Search for session generation logic where source is available.

docs.title: Cookie Attributes
docs.text:
Review:

Secure

HttpOnly

SameSite

Path

Domain

Expires

Max-Age

docs.title: Secure
docs.text:
Example:

Set-Cookie: session=...; Secure

Meaning:

Browser should send cookie only over secure transport.

docs.title: HttpOnly
docs.text:
Example:

Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly

Meaning:

Client-side JavaScript cannot normally access the cookie.

docs.title: Important
docs.text: HttpOnly helps reduce some XSS consequences but does not prevent XSS from making authenticated requests in the victim's browser.

docs.title: SameSite
docs.text:
Common values:

Strict

Lax

None

docs.title: SameSite=None
docs.text:
Modern browsers require:

Secure

with:

SameSite=None

docs.title: SameSite Is Contextual
docs.text:
The correct value depends on application requirements such as:

SSO

Cross-site integrations

Embedded applications

docs.title: Cookie Domain
docs.text:
Review:

Domain=.example.com

Broad cookie scope can expose a session cookie to additional subdomains.

docs.title: Prefer Narrow Scope
docs.text:
Use the narrowest appropriate:

Domain

Path

docs.title: Cookie Path
docs.text:
Example:

Path=/

may be necessary, but unnecessary broad scope should be avoided.

docs.title: Cookie Expiration
docs.text:
Session cookies may be:

Browser-session cookies

Persistent cookies

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Compare:

Application sensitivity

Session lifetime

Idle timeout

Absolute timeout

Remember-me functionality

docs.title: Session Fixation
docs.text: Session fixation occurs when an attacker can establish or predict a session identifier that remains valid after the victim authenticates.

docs.title: Test Model
docs.text:
Pre-Login Session ID
        |
        v
User Logs In
        |
        v
Post-Login Session ID

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: The session identifier should normally rotate after successful authentication.

docs.title: Capture Before Login
docs.text: Cookie: session=PRE_AUTH_VALUE

docs.title: Capture After Login
docs.text: Cookie: session=POST_AUTH_VALUE

docs.title: Compare
docs.text:
Expected:

PRE_AUTH_VALUE != POST_AUTH_VALUE

docs.title: Session Rotation
docs.text:
Also consider rotation after:

MFA completion

Privilege elevation

Sensitive authentication events

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
A cookie value remaining the same does not automatically prove exploitable fixation.

Determine:

Can an attacker choose or obtain the pre-authentication value?

Does the server bind authentication to that same value?

docs.title: Session Upgrade
docs.text:
Some applications use:

Anonymous session

before authentication.

That is normal.

The security question is whether authentication creates a new secure session context.

docs.title: Session Invalidation
docs.text:
Test:

Logout

Password change

Password reset

MFA reset

Account disablement

Administrative session revocation

docs.title: Logout Testing
docs.text:
Workflow:

Login
  |
  v
Capture Authenticated Request
  |
  v
Logout
  |
  v
Replay Old Authenticated Request

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Unauthorized / Redirect to Login

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Deleting the cookie only in the browser is not sufficient.

Server-side session state should be invalidated where server-side sessions are used.

docs.title: Replay After Logout
docs.text:
In Burp Repeater, resend a request captured before logout with the old session identifier.

Expected:

Session rejected

docs.title: Browser vs Server Logout
docs.text:
Weak implementation:

Logout
  |
  v
Browser Deletes Cookie

but:

Server Session Remains Valid

docs.title: Stronger Model
docs.text:
Logout
  |
  +--> Browser Removes Token
  |
  +--> Server Revokes Session

docs.title: Password Change Session Behaviour
docs.text: After password change, determine whether existing sessions remain active.

docs.title: Security Decision
docs.text:
Applications may choose different policies based on risk.

High-risk applications often invalidate:

Other sessions

Remember-me tokens

Recovery sessions

docs.title: Password Reset Session Behaviour
docs.text: Password reset should generally trigger consideration of active-session invalidation because the reset may have occurred after suspected credential compromise.

docs.title: Session Timeout
docs.text:
Test:

Idle timeout

Absolute timeout

docs.title: Idle Timeout
docs.text:
Last Activity
     |
     v
Idle Period
     |
     v
Session Invalidated

docs.title: Absolute Timeout
docs.text:
Session Created
     |
     v
Maximum Lifetime
     |
     v
Session Invalidated

even if the user remains active.

docs.title: Do Not Wait Manually During Every Test
docs.text: Where source/configuration is available, verify configured timeout values and perform representative dynamic validation.

docs.title: Concurrent Sessions
docs.text:
Test whether multiple sessions can exist.

Example:

Browser A -> Session A

Browser B -> Session B

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Ask:

Are concurrent sessions intended?

Can users see active sessions?

Can users revoke individual sessions?

Can users revoke all sessions?

Are new-login notifications provided where appropriate?

docs.title: Session Management Page
docs.text:
Useful functionality may display:

Device

Browser

Approximate location

Created time

Last activity

Revoke button

docs.title: Session Revocation Test
docs.text:
Session A revokes Session B
        |
        v
Replay Session B

Expected:

Rejected

docs.title: CSRF and Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication endpoints can interact with CSRF.

Potential areas:

Login CSRF

Logout CSRF

Password change

Email change

MFA settings

docs.title: Login CSRF
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Victim
  |
  v
Forced Login
  |
  v
Attacker's Account

This can cause the victim to unknowingly interact with an attacker-controlled account.

docs.title: Login CSRF Impact
docs.text:
Potential examples:

Victim enters personal data into attacker's account

Search history saved to attacker's account

Payment information associated with wrong account

docs.title: Authentication and Caching
docs.text: Authenticated responses should not unintentionally leak through shared caches.

docs.title: Review Headers
docs.text:
Cache-Control:
Pragma:
Vary:

docs.title: Sensitive Pages
docs.text:
Consider whether pages containing:

Account data

Tokens

Personal information

Recovery information

can be cached inappropriately.

docs.title: Authentication Headers
docs.text:
APIs may use:

Authorization: Bearer TOKEN

or:

Authorization: Basic ...

docs.title: Basic Authentication
docs.text:
Basic authentication credentials are merely Base64 encoded.

They require HTTPS.

docs.title: Bearer Tokens
docs.text:
Anyone possessing a valid bearer token can generally use it within its scope.

Protect bearer tokens from:

Logs

URLs

Referer headers

Client-side storage exposure

Third-party scripts

docs.title: Tokens in URLs
docs.text:
Avoid:

https://target.example/account?token=SECRET

because URLs may appear in:

Browser history

Logs

Analytics

Referer headers

docs.title: Session Tokens in Local Storage
docs.text:
Applications sometimes store tokens in:

localStorage

sessionStorage

docs.title: Review Trade-Offs
docs.text:
JavaScript-accessible token storage increases exposure to:

XSS

docs.title: Cookie-Based Sessions
docs.text:
Properly configured HttpOnly cookies reduce direct JavaScript access to session tokens.

But cookie-based authentication requires appropriate consideration of:

CSRF

SameSite

Origin checks

docs.title: Authentication State in Front-End Code
docs.text:
Do not trust:

if (user.isAdmin) {
    showAdminPanel();
}

as an authorization control.

Client-side state can improve UX but security decisions must be enforced server-side.

docs.title: API Authentication
docs.text: Test API endpoints independently from the GUI.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
GUI:

/account

API:

/api/account

docs.title: Remove Authentication
docs.text:
Send:

GET /api/account HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

without the session or bearer token.

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
401 Unauthorized

or equivalent.

docs.title: Invalid Token
docs.text:
Test:

Authorization: Bearer INVALID_TOKEN_7f3a9

docs.title: Expired Token
docs.text: Where safely available, verify expired tokens are rejected.

docs.title: API Status Codes
docs.text:
Common semantics:

401 -> authentication missing/invalid

403 -> authenticated but not permitted

Applications may vary, so interpret behaviour rather than relying solely on status codes.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text: Authentication endpoints often require abuse controls.

docs.title: Candidate Endpoints
docs.text:
Login

Password reset

Registration

MFA verification

Magic links

Verification codes

Recovery codes

docs.title: Safe Rate-Limit Validation
docs.text:
Use:

Dedicated account

Small request count

Agreed test rate

Controlled window

docs.title: Observe
docs.text:
429 response

Retry-After

Increasing delay

Temporary account protection

IP throttling

Account throttling

docs.title: Rate Limit Scope
docs.text:
Determine whether controls apply by:

IP address

Account

Username

Session

Device

Combination

docs.title: Weak IP-Only Controls
docs.text:
Pure IP-based controls may be insufficient in distributed attack scenarios.

However, bypass testing should remain within the agreed assessment scope.

docs.title: Account Lockout
docs.text: Lockout can reduce guessing but can also create denial-of-service risk.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Threshold

Duration

Unlock mechanism

Notification

Scope

Administrative recovery

docs.title: Do Not Lock Real Users
docs.text: Use dedicated test accounts.

docs.title: Lockout Enumeration
docs.text:
Different behaviour for:

Existing account

Unknown account

may itself expose usernames.

docs.title: Credential Stuffing
docs.text:
Credential stuffing tests should use only credentials specifically authorised for the assessment.

Do not use leaked third-party credentials against real users.

docs.title: Password Spraying
docs.text:
Password spraying sends a small number of common passwords across multiple accounts.

This can trigger:

Lockouts

Alerts

Incident response

and must be explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Magic Links
docs.text: Passwordless authentication may use emailed links.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Randomness

Lifetime

Single use

Account binding

Session binding

Redirect handling

Token leakage

docs.title: Magic Link Replay
docs.text:
After successful authentication:

Replay Same Link

Expected:

Rejected

if designed as a one-time authentication token.

docs.title: Email Verification
docs.text:
Review:

Token randomness

Token lifetime

Account binding

Replay

Whether unverified users gain restricted functionality

docs.title: Registration Workflow
docs.text:
Review:

Duplicate accounts

Email verification

Username enumeration

Mass assignment

Default roles

Invitation controls

Tenant assignment

docs.title: Default Role
docs.text: New users should receive the intended least-privileged role.

docs.title: Invitation Systems
docs.text:
Test:

Invitation token randomness

Expiry

Single use

Recipient binding

Tenant binding

Role binding

docs.title: Account Activation
docs.text:
Activation tokens should not permit:

Activating another account

Changing identity

Escalating role

docs.title: SSO Authentication
docs.text:
SSO may use:

SAML

OAuth 2.0

OpenID Connect

These require protocol-specific testing beyond ordinary session testing.

docs.title: SSO Session Lifecycle
docs.text:
Still verify:

Local session creation

Session rotation

Logout

Local session invalidation

Role mapping

docs.title: Authentication Bypass Through Alternate Endpoints
docs.text:
An application may protect:

/login

correctly but expose alternate functionality.

docs.title: Search For
docs.text:
/api/login

/mobile/login

/v1/auth

/legacy/login

/admin/login

/sso/callback

/internal/auth

docs.title: Versioned APIs
docs.text:
Check:

/api/v1/

/api/v2/

because older authentication paths may remain reachable.

docs.title: HTTP Method Variations
docs.text:
If appropriate, compare:

GET

POST

PUT

PATCH

only where the endpoint or framework suggests alternate method handling.

docs.title: Do Not Interpret Every 405 as Security-Relevant
docs.text: Method testing should be driven by application behaviour.

docs.title: Authentication Bypass Through Parameters
docs.text:
Review parameters such as:

authenticated

isAdmin

role

userId

verified

mfaComplete

if they are supplied by the client.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "username": "testuser",
  "password": "password",
  "authenticated": true
}

The server must ignore client-supplied authentication state.

docs.title: Hidden Fields
docs.text:
HTML:

<input type="hidden" name="role" value="user">

Hidden does not mean trusted.

docs.title: Source Code Review
docs.text:
Authentication source review should trace:

Credential Input
      |
      v
Identity Lookup
      |
      v
Password Verification
      |
      v
MFA
      |
      v
Session Creation
      |
      v
Authorization Context

docs.title: Generic Authentication Searches
docs.text: rg -ni 'login|signin|authenticate|authentication|password|session|cookie|logout|mfa|totp|reset.*password' src/

docs.title: Password Verification
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'bcrypt|argon2|scrypt|pbkdf2|password.*verify|verify.*password|check_password' .

docs.title: Password Hashing
docs.text:
Preferred password storage should use dedicated password hashing algorithms such as:

Argon2id

bcrypt

scrypt

PBKDF2

with appropriate parameters.

docs.title: Avoid Fast General-Purpose Hashes
docs.text:
Do not store passwords using only:

MD5

SHA-1

SHA-256

SHA-512

without an appropriate password hashing construction.

docs.title: Be Careful With Search Results
docs.text:
This may find:

Tests

Examples

Documentation

Dummy credentials

Validate context before reporting.

docs.title: Session Source Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'session|Set-Cookie|cookie|HttpOnly|SameSite|Secure|Max-Age|Expires' src/

docs.title: Session Rotation Search
docs.text:
Framework-specific APIs vary.

Search conceptually for:

regenerate

rotate

invalidate

destroy session

docs.title: Generic
docs.text: rg -ni 'regenerate|rotate.*session|invalidate.*session|destroy.*session|session.*invalidate' src/

docs.title: Password Reset Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'forgot.*password|reset.*password|reset.*token|password.*token|recovery' src/

docs.title: Token Generation Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'random|SecureRandom|secrets\.|randomBytes|random_bytes|token_urlsafe|UUID' src/

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
A random-looking API name does not automatically mean the token is cryptographically secure.

Trace the actual generator.

docs.title: MFA Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'mfa|2fa|totp|otp|backup.*code|recovery.*code|authenticator' src/

docs.title: Authentication Middleware
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'middleware|auth_required|login_required|RequireAuthorization|Authorize|authenticated' src/

docs.title: Source Review Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

How are users identified?

How are passwords verified?

What password hashing algorithm is used?

Are authentication errors generic?

When is the session created?

Does the session ID rotate after login?

Does it rotate after MFA?

What state represents partial authentication?

Can partial sessions reach protected endpoints?

How are sessions invalidated?

How are reset tokens generated?

How are reset tokens stored?

Are reset tokens hashed at rest?

Are tokens single-use?

How is MFA reset?

How are backup codes generated?

How are remembered devices implemented?

How are authorization roles loaded?

Does any security decision trust client-controlled state?

docs.title: Framework Session Controls
docs.text: Use framework-provided session mechanisms where possible rather than designing custom session tokens.

docs.title: Custom Authentication
docs.text:
Custom authentication code deserves additional scrutiny.

Look for:

Custom crypto

Predictable tokens

Manual cookie construction

Client-side roles

Unsigned state

Home-grown password hashing

docs.title: Session Token Entropy
docs.text:
Do not estimate entropy solely by:

Token length

A 64-character token can still be predictable if generated from deterministic data.

docs.title: Better Evidence
docs.text:
Use:

Source review

Documented framework behaviour

Token generation implementation

docs.title: Session Binding
docs.text:
Some applications bind sessions to:

IP address

User-Agent

Device identifier

These controls can provide additional signals but can also cause usability issues and should not replace unpredictable session identifiers.

docs.title: IP Binding
docs.text: Be cautious with strict IP binding because legitimate users may change networks.

docs.title: Session Replay
docs.text:
Bearer-style sessions are inherently replayable while valid.

The security objective is usually:

Prevent token theft

Limit lifetime

Support revocation

Detect suspicious use

docs.title: Session Exposure
docs.text:
Search for session identifiers in:

URLs

HTML

JavaScript

Logs

Error messages

Analytics

Third-party requests

docs.title: Session ID in URL
docs.text:
Example:

/account?session=SECRET

is generally undesirable.

docs.title: URL Risks
docs.text:
URLs can appear in:

Browser history

Proxy logs

Server logs

Referer headers

Screenshots

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text: Authentication and session traffic should use HTTPS.

docs.title: HTTP Redirect
docs.text:
Check whether:

http://target.example

redirects to:

https://target.example

docs.title: HSTS
docs.text:
Review:

Strict-Transport-Security:

for HTTPS applications where HSTS is appropriate.

docs.title: Do Not Test TLS Only From Browser Icons
docs.text: Inspect actual protocol and headers.

docs.title: Error Messages
docs.text:
Authentication errors should avoid exposing:

Database errors

Stack traces

Internal usernames

LDAP details

Directory paths

Authentication backend details

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Applications should log security-relevant events such as:

Successful login

Failed login

docs.title: Reporting Username Enumeration
docs.text: The authentication endpoint responds differently depending on whether a supplied username exists. Requests containing a valid username and an incorrect password return a different response from requests containing a non-existent username. This allows unauthenticated users to determine valid account identifiers and may facilitate password spraying, credential stuffing or targeted social engineering.

docs.title: Reporting Session Fixation
docs.text: The application retains the same session identifier before and after successful authentication. Testing confirmed that a pre-authentication session identifier can become associated with an authenticated account rather than being replaced during authentication. The application should regenerate the session identifier when the authentication state changes.

docs.title: Reporting Logout Failure
docs.text: Logging out removes the session cookie from the browser but does not invalidate the corresponding server-side session. Replaying an authenticated request using the pre-logout session identifier after logout continued to return authenticated content. Logout should invalidate the server-side session in addition to removing the browser cookie.

docs.title: Reporting MFA Bypass
docs.text: After valid username and password authentication, the application creates a partially authenticated session and presents an MFA challenge. However, the same partial session can directly access an endpoint intended for fully authenticated users without completing MFA. MFA state must be enforced server-side for every protected request.

docs.title: Reporting Password Reset Replay
docs.text: Password reset tokens remain valid after successful use. A reset token that had already been used to change the account password could be replayed to perform another password change. Reset tokens should be invalidated atomically after their first successful use.

docs.title: Reporting Cookie Configuration
docs.text: The application's primary authentication cookie is transmitted without the HttpOnly attribute. Because the cookie represents the authenticated session, client-side scripts can access its value. The session cookie should be configured with HttpOnly unless the application has a documented requirement for JavaScript access.

docs.title: Reporting Client-Controlled Authentication State
docs.text: The application accepts security-relevant account state from a client-controlled request parameter and uses that value when constructing the authenticated session. Authentication and authorization state must be derived from trusted server-side identity information rather than values supplied by the client.

docs.title: Reporting Weak Session Revocation
docs.text: Changing the account password does not invalidate existing authenticated sessions. A session established before the password change remained fully usable afterwards. For this application's threat model, password changes should revoke other active sessions and long-lived authentication tokens.

Authentication testing is not only:

Does the session rotate after MFA?

Are session identifiers unpredictable?

Are authentication cookies properly scoped?

Are sensitive cookies Secure?

Are sensitive cookies HttpOnly?

Is SameSite appropriate?

Are old or alternate authentication endpoints still exposed?

Are secrets present in URLs or logs?

Are security events monitored?

Does account recovery provide weaker authentication than login?

Have the findings been demonstrated with dedicated test accounts?

Test the lifecycle

A strong authentication assessment follows the account from login through MFA, session creation, password changes, recovery, logout and revocation rather than treating each screen as an isolated feature.

Use two dedicated accounts

Separate test accounts make it much easier to distinguish authentication problems from authorization problems and reduce the risk of affecting real users.

Replay sessions after security events

Replaying an existing authenticated request after logout, password reset, password change or explicit session revocation is one of the simplest ways to validate whether server-side invalidation actually occurs.

Do not lock out real users

Brute-force, password-spraying, OTP and lockout testing can affect availability and trigger incident response. Use dedicated accounts, controlled request counts and the agreed assessment scope.

A cookie attribute is not the whole finding

Cookie attributes should be assessed according to the cookie's purpose, authentication model and actual attack path. Avoid reporting every cookie with a missing attribute as an exploitable session vulnerability without establishing relevance.

Perform authorization testing only against accounts, objects and tenants included in the assessment scope. Use dedicated test accounts and test data wherever possible. Avoid accessing, modifying or deleting real user information simply to demonstrate an authorization weakness.

docs.text:
For:

POST

PUT

PATCH

DELETE

use dedicated test objects.

docs.text: Deleting or modifying real user objects solely to prove an issue.

docs.text:
Treat automated authorization results as candidates.

Endpoint

Method

Role

docs.text: Endpoint User Object Expected Actual /api/profile/101 A A Allow Allow /api/profile/102 A B Deny Allow /api/admin/users A Admin Deny Deny

docs.text:
Example:

GET /api/messages/5001 HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=SESSION_A

docs.title: Test

docs.text:
Original:

Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: session=SESSION_A

  "display_name": "Account A"

docs.text:
Using a dedicated Account B:

Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: session=SESSION_A

  "display_name": "Authorization Test"

docs.title: Function-Level Authorization
docs.text:
Object access is only one part of authorization.

Test whether users can invoke functions they should not have.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Create user

Delete user

Approve payment

Generate API key

Export data

Change role

Disable MFA

Impersonate user

View audit logs

docs.title: UI Restriction Is Not Authorization
docs.text:
Example:

Normal user UI:
No "Delete User" button

But request:

DELETE /api/users/123 HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=NORMAL_USER

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Denied server-side
