docs.text:
Admin Account
    |
    v
Perform Admin Action
    |
    v
Capture Request
    |
    v
Replace Admin Session
    |
    v
Normal User Session
    |
    v
Replay

docs.title: Keep Request Identical
docs.text:
Change only:

Authentication context

when testing vertical access.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Admin request:

POST /api/users/1002/disable HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=ADMIN_SESSION

docs.title: Replay
docs.text:
POST /api/users/1002/disable HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=USER_SESSION

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
403 Forbidden

or equivalent.

docs.title: URL-Based Authorization
docs.text:
Applications sometimes protect only expected routes.

Example:

/admin

may be protected while:

/admin/

/ADMIN

/api/admin

/v1/admin

/internal/admin

behave differently.

docs.title: Test Only Plausible Variants
docs.text:
Do not blindly generate enormous path permutations.

Use:

Application routes

JavaScript

API documentation

Source code

Observed redirects

docs.title: HTTP Method Authorization
docs.text:
Authorization should apply consistently across methods.

Example:

GET /api/users/123

may be protected while:

PATCH /api/users/123

is not.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
GET

POST

PUT

PATCH

DELETE

where each method is legitimately supported or suggested by application behaviour.

docs.title: Method Override
docs.text:
Some frameworks support:

X-HTTP-Method-Override:

or request parameters that override methods.

docs.title: Test Only When Relevant
docs.text: Do not assume method override support exists.

docs.title: Property-Level Authorization
docs.text: An API may correctly restrict access to an object but fail to restrict individual properties.

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
{
  "id": 1001,
  "name": "Alice",
  "email": "alice@example.com",
  "internal_role": "administrator",
  "mfa_secret": "..."
}

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Should the current user receive every returned property?

docs.title: Excessive Data Exposure
docs.text:
Authorization review should consider:

Sensitive fields

Internal fields

Administrative metadata

Secrets

Tenant information

docs.title: Property-Level Update
docs.text:
Example:

{
  "display_name": "Alice",
  "role": "admin"
}

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Can a normal user modify:

role

even though they are allowed to modify:

display_name

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text: Mass assignment can become an authorization issue when user-controlled properties map directly to privileged object fields.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
PATCH /api/users/me HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "display_name": "Alice",
  "is_admin": true
}

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
The server should:

Ignore

Reject

or independently authorize

security-sensitive fields.

docs.title: Allowlist Fields
docs.text:
Prefer:

display_name

language

timezone

rather than automatically binding every supplied property.

docs.title: Hidden Fields
docs.text:
A field missing from the UI may still be accepted by the backend.

Inspect:

JavaScript

API schemas

Responses

Source code

for additional properties.

docs.title: Tenant Isolation
docs.text:
Multi-tenant applications require authorization at both:

User level

Tenant level

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Tenant A
  |
  +--> User A1
  +--> User A2

Tenant B
  |
  +--> User B1
  +--> User B2

docs.title: Cross-Tenant Test
docs.text:
User A1
  |
  v
Tenant B Object

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Denied

docs.title: Tenant Identifier Locations
docs.text:
Look for:

tenant_id

organisation_id

organization_id

account_id

workspace_id

company_id

team_id

docs.title: Example
docs.text: GET /api/tenants/10/projects/500 HTTP/1.1

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
Change:

tenant 10

to the ID of a dedicated test tenant:

GET /api/tenants/11/projects/500 HTTP/1.1

docs.title: Tenant ID in Header
docs.text:
Example:

X-Tenant-ID: 10

docs.title: Critical Question
docs.text: Does the server trust the supplied tenant header or derive tenant membership from the authenticated identity?

docs.title: Tenant ID in JWT
docs.text:
A token may contain:

{
  "sub": "123",
  "tenant": "10"
}

Even when the token is valid, the application must correctly enforce tenant authorization.

docs.title: Nested Resource Authorization
docs.text:
Example:

/projects/10/documents/500

docs.title: Potential Bug
docs.text:
The application verifies:

User can access project 10

but retrieves:

document 500

without checking whether the document actually belongs to project 10.

docs.title: Parent-Child Authorization
docs.text:
Verify:

Requested Child
      |
      v
Belongs to Requested Parent?
      |
      v
User Can Access Parent?

docs.title: Example Secure Query
docs.text:
Conceptually:

SELECT document
WHERE document_id = ?
AND project_id = ?
AND project_id IN user's_allowed_projects

docs.title: Do Not Trust Parent IDs Alone
docs.text:
If the backend performs:

load(document_id)

after separately checking only the supplied project ID, authorization may be bypassed.

docs.title: Indirect Object References
docs.text:
Some applications map public references to internal IDs.

Example:

Public Reference
      |
      v
Server Mapping
      |
      v
Internal Object

This can reduce identifier exposure but does not replace authorization.

docs.title: API Authorization
docs.text: APIs are especially susceptible to object-level authorization failures because identifiers frequently appear directly in requests.

docs.title: API Inventory
docs.text:
Review:

REST

GraphQL

WebSockets

Mobile APIs

Legacy APIs

Internal APIs exposed externally

docs.title: REST
docs.text:
Typical resources:

/api/users/{id}

/api/orders/{id}

/api/files/{id}

/api/projects/{id}

docs.text:
For each object:

Create

Read

Update

Delete

docs.text: Operation Example Create POST /api/projects Read GET /api/projects/123 Update PATCH /api/projects/123 Delete DELETE /api/projects/123

docs.text:
Check whether users can create resources under another:

Tenant

User

Project

Account

docs.text:
{
  "tenant_id": 11,
  "name": "Test Project"
}

docs.text:
Where appropriate:

Authenticated User
       |
       v
Tenant Membership
       |
       v
Allowed Tenant

rather than trusting arbitrary client-selected tenant identifiers.

docs.title: List Endpoints
docs.text:
Authorization bugs are not limited to direct object endpoints.

Example:

GET /api/orders

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Does the list contain:

Only current user's orders

or:

All users' orders

docs.title: Search Endpoints
docs.text:
Example:

GET /api/orders/search?q=test

docs.text: Search results must apply the same authorization filters as direct object retrieval.

docs.text:
High-value candidates:

/export

/download

/report

/csv

/pdf

docs.text: GET /api/reports/123/export

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Export authorization may differ from:

GET /api/reports/123

docs.title: File Downloads
docs.text:
Example:

GET /download?file_id=500

docs.title: Test
docs.text: Use a file created by Account B and request it as Account A.

docs.title: Signed URLs
docs.text:
Signed URLs may intentionally permit possession-based access.

Review:

Expiry

Scope

Object binding

Method binding

Leakage

Revocation requirements

docs.title: Do Not Report Intended Sharing
docs.text: Determine whether the application intentionally provides shareable links before classifying access as unauthorized.

docs.title: GraphQL Authorization
docs.text:
GraphQL often exposes object identifiers through:

Arguments

Variables

Nested queries

Mutations

docs.title: Query Example
docs.text:
query GetUser($id: ID!) {
  user(id: $id) {
    id
    name
    email
  }
}

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
{
  "id": "1001"
}

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
Change to Account B's controlled object:

{
  "id": "1002"
}

docs.title: Authorization Must Be Resolver-Side
docs.text: The GraphQL schema alone does not provide authorization.

docs.title: Nested GraphQL Authorization
docs.text:
Example:

query {
  project(id: "10") {
    documents {
      id
      name
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Authorization may be correct on:

project

but missing on:

documents

docs.title: GraphQL Mutations
docs.text:
Example:

mutation UpdateUser($id: ID!, $name: String!) {
  updateUser(id: $id, name: $name) {
    id
    name
  }
}

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
Use controlled Account B data and change:

id

docs.title: GraphQL Aliases
docs.text:
Aliases can send multiple object requests in one GraphQL operation.

For authorization testing, use them cautiously and keep request volume controlled.

docs.title: WebSocket Authorization
docs.text: Authentication during WebSocket connection establishment does not guarantee authorization for every message.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Authenticated WebSocket
        |
        v
Message
        |
        v
Object ID
        |
        v
Authorization Check

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "action": "subscribe",
  "channel_id": "123"
}

docs.title: Test
docs.text: Can Account A subscribe to a channel belonging only to Account B?

docs.title: Subscription Authorization
docs.text:
Review:

Chat rooms

Notifications

Projects

Tenant events

Administrative streams

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
Authorization should occur before scheduling privileged work.

Example:

POST /api/reports/export HTTP/1.1

{
  "account_id": 1002
}

docs.title: Potential Problem
docs.text: The API may accept the job and a worker later exports Account B's data without revalidating authorization.

docs.title: Second-Order Authorization
docs.text:
Flow:

User Request
    |
    v
Queue
    |
    v
Worker
    |
    v
Object Access

docs.title: Review
docs.text: Authorization context must survive safely across asynchronous boundaries.

docs.title: Business Workflow Authorization
docs.text:
Authorization may depend on workflow state.

Example:

Draft
  |
  v
Submitted
  |
  v
Approved

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
Can a user directly call:

/approve

without being an approver?

docs.title: State Transition Authorization
docs.text:
Review:

Who can transition?

From which state?

To which state?

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "status": "approved"
}

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text: Can the client directly set privileged workflow state?

docs.title: Role Manipulation
docs.text:
Review requests containing:

role

permissions

groups

is_admin

admin

privilege

access_level

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "name": "Test User",
  "role": "admin"
}

docs.title: Test Safely
docs.text: Use dedicated accounts and verify whether the server independently authorizes role changes.

docs.title: Invitation Authorization
docs.text:
Invitation workflows may permit role selection.

Review:

Who can invite?

Which roles can they assign?

Which tenant receives the invite?

Can invitation parameters be changed?

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "email": "test@example.com",
  "role": "administrator"
}

docs.title: Support and Impersonation
docs.text:
Administrative applications may contain:

Login as user

Impersonate

View as customer

docs.title: High-Impact Controls
docs.text:
Review:

Who can impersonate?

Which users can be impersonated?

Is re-authentication required?

Is the action logged?

Can impersonation cross tenants?

docs.title: Administrative APIs
docs.text:
Do not test only administrative web pages.

Look for:

/api/admin

/admin/api

/internal

/management

/support

docs.title: JavaScript Route Discovery
docs.text:
Search front-end files for:

/admin

/api/

role

permission

tenant

userId

docs.title: ripgrep
docs.text: rg -ni 'admin|permission|role|tenant|account_id|user_id|owner_id|is_admin' .

docs.title: JavaScript Files
docs.text: rg -ni '/api/|admin|role|permission|tenant' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' -g '*.tsx' -g '*.jsx' .

docs.title: Source Code Review
docs.text:
Authorization source review should trace:

Request
  |
  v
Authenticated Identity
  |
  v
Requested Object
  |
  v
Authorization Check
  |
  v
Database Query
  |
  v
Response / Action

docs.title: Strong Pattern
docs.text: Authorization should be applied close to the object query or business operation.

docs.title: Vulnerable Concept
docs.text:
document = Document.get(request.args["id"])
return document

docs.title: Better Concept
docs.text:
document = Document.query.filter_by(
    id=request.args["id"],
    owner_id=current_user.id
).first_or_404()

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Actual framework syntax varies.

The security principle is:

Object ID
    +
Authorized Scope

docs.title: Query Scoping
docs.text:
Prefer:

Current User
    |
    v
Authorized Objects
    |
    v
Requested Object

docs.title: Instead Of
docs.text:
Requested Object
    |
    v
Return Object

docs.title: Python Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'current_user|user_id|owner_id|tenant_id|permission|authorize|login_required' -g '*.py' .

docs.title: Django
docs.text:
Look for:

request.user

permission_required

user_passes_test

get_object_or_404

queryset filtering

docs.title: Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'request\.user|permission_required|user_passes_test|get_object_or_404|queryset' -g '*.py' .

docs.title: Django Object Query
docs.text:
Review whether objects are scoped to:

request.user

organization

tenant

docs.text:

@PreAuthorize

Method security

URL security

Repository query scope

docs.text: rg -ni '\[Authorize|ClaimsPrincipal|User\.Identity|IsInRole|AuthorizationService|userId|ownerId|tenantId' -g '*.cs' .

docs.text:

[Authorize]

Policies

Claims

Database query scoping

docs.text: rg -ni 'user_id|owner_id|tenant_id|role|permission|authorize|auth' -g '*.php' .

docs.text:

Policies

Gates

Middleware

Route authorization

Model queries

docs.text: rg -ni 'current_user|authorize|policy|role|permission|user_id|owner_id|tenant_id' -g '*.rb' .

docs.title: Rails
docs.text:
Review:

before_action

Pundit policies

CanCanCan abilities

Controller object queries

docs.title: Go
docs.text: rg -ni 'userID|ownerID|tenantID|permission|authorize|role|claims' -g '*.go' .

docs.title: SQL Review
docs.text: Authorization failures frequently originate in database queries.

docs.title: Dangerous Concept
docs.text:
SELECT *
FROM documents
WHERE id = ?;

docs.title: Safer Concept
docs.text:
SELECT *
FROM documents
WHERE id = ?
AND owner_id = ?;

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Concept
docs.text:
SELECT *
FROM documents
WHERE id = ?
AND tenant_id = ?;

docs.title: Stronger Context
docs.text: The tenant ID should come from trusted authenticated context, not merely another client-controlled parameter.

docs.title: Repository Pattern
docs.text:
Centralized data-access layers should provide functions such as:

getDocumentForUser()

getProjectForTenant()

getOrderForCustomer()

rather than unrestricted generic object retrieval where possible.

docs.title: Middleware Limitations
docs.text:
Middleware may establish:

User is authenticated

but cannot always determine:

User owns object 123

Object authorization often belongs closer to business logic.

docs.title: Client-Side Authorization
docs.text:
Examples:

if (user.role === "admin") {
    showDeleteButton();
}

docs.title: This Is UI Logic
docs.text:
Server must still enforce:

DELETE /api/users/123

docs.title: Disabled Buttons
docs.text:
<button disabled>Delete</button>

does not enforce authorization.

docs.title: Hidden Inputs
docs.text:
<input type="hidden" name="role" value="user">

are attacker-controlled.

docs.title: HTTP Status Codes
docs.text:
Common secure responses include:

401 Unauthorized

403 Forbidden

404 Not Found

docs.title: 404 for Unauthorized Objects
docs.text:
Applications sometimes return:

404

for objects the user is not allowed to know exist.

This can reduce object enumeration.

docs.title: Status Alone Is Not Enough
docs.text:
A response can return:

200

but still hide sensitive fields.

Or:

403

after already performing a state-changing action.

docs.title: Validate Side Effects
docs.text: For write operations, verify actual state.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Response:

403 Forbidden

but Account B's object was modified.

This is still vulnerable.

docs.title: Response vs State
docs.text:
Always distinguish:

HTTP Response

from:

Backend Effect

docs.title: Blind Authorization Issues
docs.text:
Some unauthorized actions may not return sensitive data.

Example:

Delete another user's notification

Trigger another user's workflow

Change another user's setting

docs.title: Verify Through Controlled Side Effects
docs.text: Use Account B to confirm the result.

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Authorization decisions may be vulnerable to state changes or timing issues.

These are separate from ordinary IDOR/BOLA testing and should be tested only when the application workflow suggests relevance.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Authorization-sensitive responses must not leak between users through caches.

docs.title: Potential Flow
docs.text:
User A Requests Object
        |
        v
Shared Cache
        |
        v
User B Receives Cached Response

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Cache-Control

Vary

CDN behaviour

Cache keys

Authorization headers

docs.title: Authorization and CORS
docs.text:
CORS does not provide authorization.

Even if browsers cannot read a cross-origin response:

Server-side authorization must still be correct.

docs.title: Authorization and CSRF
docs.text:
CSRF and authorization are different.

CSRF:
Can another site cause the victim to send an authorized request?

Authorization:
Should the victim be permitted to perform that action?

docs.title: Authorization and Authentication
docs.text:
Do not report:

Unauthenticated endpoint

as an authorization vulnerability if the endpoint is intentionally public.

docs.title: Establish Intended Policy
docs.text:
Before concluding, determine:

Who should have access?

What should they access?

Which actions should they perform?

docs.title: Sources of Intended Policy
docs.text:
Use:

Application behaviour

Role descriptions

Requirements

Documentation

API specifications

Stakeholder confirmation

Source code

Comparable endpoints

docs.title: Public Resources
docs.text:
Some objects are intentionally public.

Example:

Public profile

Published article

Shared document

docs.title: Do Not Assume Private
docs.text: Confirm intended access.

docs.title: Shared Resources
docs.text:
Objects may be intentionally shared between users.

Review:

Owner

Member

Viewer

Editor

Public

docs.title: Evidence Chain - Horizontal IDOR
docs.text:
Strong evidence:

1. Account A owns object A.

2. Account B owns object B.

3. Account A requests object A successfully.

4. Only the object identifier is changed.

5. Account A requests object B.

6. Object B data is returned.

7. Ownership is confirmed using Account B.

docs.title: Evidence Chain - Vertical Authorization
docs.text:
1. Admin performs privileged action.

2. Request is captured.

3. Authentication context is replaced with normal-user credentials.

4. Request is replayed.

5. Privileged action succeeds.

6. Side effect is verified.

docs.title: Evidence Chain - Property Authorization
docs.text:
1. Normal user can edit profile.

2. Legitimate request contains allowed fields.

3. Privileged field is added.

4. Server accepts the field.

5. Resulting privilege/state change is confirmed.

docs.title: Evidence Chain - Tenant Isolation
docs.text:
1. Tenant A and Tenant B are controlled test tenants.

2. Object B belongs to Tenant B.

3. User A belongs only to Tenant A.

4. User A requests Object B.

5. Tenant B data is returned or modified.

6. Cross-tenant ownership is confirmed.

docs.title: Reporting IDOR
docs.text: The application does not enforce object-level authorization when retrieving user documents. A user authenticated as Account A can modify the document identifier in the request and retrieve a document belonging to Account B. Testing was performed using two dedicated assessment accounts, confirming that the returned object was owned by a different user.

docs.title: Reporting BOLA
docs.text: The API accepts an object identifier from the request and retrieves the corresponding resource without verifying that the authenticated user is authorized to access that object. Changing the identifier from an object owned by Account A to an object owned by Account B returned Account B's data.

docs.title: Reporting Vertical Privilege Escalation
docs.text: A function intended for administrative users is accessible to a normal authenticated user. An administrative request was captured and replayed using a normal-user session without otherwise modifying the request. The server performed the privileged action despite the lower-privileged authentication context.

docs.title: Reporting Cross-Tenant Access
docs.text: Tenant isolation is not enforced when retrieving project resources. A user belonging exclusively to Tenant A was able to request a project owned by Tenant B by modifying the tenant and project identifiers. The application returned Tenant B data without verifying tenant membership.

docs.title: Reporting Mass Assignment Authorization
docs.text: The profile update endpoint accepts security-sensitive properties that are not exposed through the normal user interface. Adding the privileged role property to a legitimate profile update request caused the server to persist the supplied value. The endpoint should explicitly allow only user-editable properties and independently authorize security-sensitive changes.

docs.title: Reporting Object Existence Disclosure
docs.text: The endpoint returns distinguishable responses for existing but unauthorized objects and non-existent objects. This allows authenticated users to determine whether specific object identifiers exist. Testing did not demonstrate unauthorized access to the object contents.

docs.title: Reporting Function-Level Authorization
docs.text: The application hides the user-management function from normal users in the interface, but the underlying endpoint does not enforce the same role restriction. A normal-user session successfully invoked the administrative endpoint directly.

docs.text:

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
Authorization testing is not:

Change ID
   |
   v
Got 200
   |
   v
Report IDOR

It is:

KNOWN SUBJECT
     |
     v
KNOWN PERMISSION
     |
     v
KNOWN OBJECT OWNER
     |
     v
CONTROLLED CHANGE
     |
     v
SERVER AUTHORIZATION DECISION
     |
     v
VERIFIED RESULT

For every authorization-sensitive request ask:

Who is making the request?

What role do they have?

Which tenant do they belong to?

What object are they requesting?

Who owns that object?

Is the object intentionally shared?

What action is being performed?

Should this role perform that action?

Where does the object identifier originate?

Can the identifier be modified?

Does the server scope the query to the current user?

Does the server scope the query to the current tenant?

Are nested objects independently authorized?

Are write operations protected as strongly as reads?

Are delete operations protected?

Are export/download endpoints protected?

Are search/list endpoints filtered?

Can hidden properties be modified?

Can role or tenant properties be supplied by the client?

Are administrative endpoints protected server-side?

Does GraphQL enforce authorization in resolvers?

Do WebSocket messages enforce object authorization?

Do background workers preserve authorization context?

Does a 403 actually prevent the side effect?

Are predictable identifiers being confused with the actual vulnerability?

Have two controlled accounts been used?

Have controlled objects been used?

Has ownership been verified?

Has the exact demonstrated impact been documented?

Have equivalent endpoints been reviewed?

Has the fix been retested using the original authorization boundary?

The strongest evidence is:

CONTROLLED ACCOUNT A
        |
        v
KNOWN OBJECT B
        |
        v
OBJECT B BELONGS TO CONTROLLED ACCOUNT B
        |
        v
REQUEST MADE AS ACCOUNT A
        |
        v
ONLY AUTHORIZATION-RELEVANT VALUE CHANGED
        |
        v
SERVER ALLOWS UNAUTHORIZED ACCESS
        |
        v
RESULT VERIFIED

Use two accounts

Account A and Account B with known object ownership provide much stronger authorization evidence than changing random identifiers and guessing who owns the returned resource.

Change one dimension at a time

For horizontal testing, keep Account A's session and change only the object identifier. For vertical testing, keep the request identical and change only the authentication context. This makes the authorization failure much easier to demonstrate and defend.

Verify state, not only responses

A 403 Forbidden response does not prove that a write operation was prevented. Verify the underlying object using the second controlled account whenever testing updates, deletes or workflow actions.

Scope database queries

One of the strongest authorization patterns is to retrieve objects from the authenticated user's or tenant's authorized scope rather than loading arbitrary objects first and attempting to authorize them afterwards.

Predictable IDs are not IDOR

Sequential integers, UUIDs, encoded identifiers and hidden parameters are object references. The vulnerability exists when the server fails to enforce the required authorization when those references are used.

Stop after proving the boundary

Once unauthorized access to a controlled object has been demonstrated, there is usually no need to enumerate additional users, tenants or production records. Capture the evidence and move on to root-cause and equivalent-endpoint review.

docs.title: BloodHound Cheatsheet
docs.text:
BloodHound maps relationships between Active Directory identities, computers, groups, sessions, permissions and other security objects into a graph that can be analysed for privilege and attack paths.

Instead of looking at Active Directory as isolated objects:

User

Group

Computer

Session

ACL

GPO

Domain

OU

BloodHound focuses on the relationships between them:

User
 |
 v
MemberOf
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
AdminTo
 |
 v
Server
 |
 v
HasSession
 |
 v
Privileged User

This makes it particularly useful for understanding how apparently low-privileged access can connect to more privileged systems or identities.

The core methodology should be:

Collect
   |
   v
Import
   |
   v
Verify Dataset
   |
   v
Identify Relationship
   |
   v
Understand Edge
   |
   v
Validate Preconditions
   |
   v
Confirm Real-World Access
   |
   v
Determine Impact
   |
   v
Capture Evidence
   |
   v
Remediate
   |
   v
Retest

Authorised Security Testing

BloodHound and its collectors should only be used in environments you are authorised to assess. Collection can generate substantial LDAP, SMB and other Active Directory traffic depending on the selected methods. Session and local-group collection can be significantly more intrusive than basic directory enumeration.

docs.title: What BloodHound Answers
docs.text:
BloodHound is particularly useful for questions such as:

Which users can become administrators?

Which systems can this user administer?

Which groups indirectly grant privilege?

Where are privileged users logged on?

Which ACLs provide escalation opportunities?

Which computers expose paths to privileged identities?

Which accounts can modify sensitive groups?

Which objects have dangerous delegated permissions?

Which trust relationships create cross-domain paths?

Which principals can control another principal?

docs.title: What BloodHound Does Not Automatically Prove
docs.text:
A graph path does not automatically mean:

Compromise succeeded.

The entire path is currently exploitable.

Every edge is current.

Every session still exists.

The target is online.

Network connectivity exists.

Required protocols are reachable.

EDR controls can be bypassed.

Credentials are available.

The operator has satisfied every prerequisite.

BloodHound identifies relationships and potential paths.

Important paths should be independently validated.

and:

Edges

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
Common nodes include:

Users

Groups

Computers

Domains

Organisational Units

Group Policy Objects

Containers

Certificate Authorities

Certificate Templates

Available object types depend on BloodHound version, collector and imported dataset.

docs.title: Edges
docs.text:
Edges describe relationships.

Examples include:

MemberOf

AdminTo

HasSession

GenericAll

GenericWrite

WriteDacl

WriteOwner

AddMember

ForceChangePassword

CanRDP

CanPSRemote

ExecuteDCOM

AllowedToDelegate

AllowedToAct

Owns

The exact edge set depends on BloodHound version and available data.

docs.title: Edge Interpretation Model
docs.text:
For every interesting edge ask:

1. What does the edge represent?

2. What permission or observation created it?

3. Is the source object controlled?

4. Is the destination object reachable?

5. Are additional prerequisites required?

6. Is the relationship current?

7. Can it be independently verified?

8. What security boundary does it cross?

docs.title: Example Environment
docs.text:
Examples throughout this page use:

Domain:
corp.local

Domain Controller:
dc01.corp.local

DC IP:
10.10.10.10

User:
CORP\asif

Workstation:
WS01

Server:
SRV01

Privileged Group:
Domain Admins

These are placeholders for a controlled environment.

docs.title: BloodHound Components
docs.text:
A BloodHound deployment generally consists of:

Collector
   |
   v
Active Directory
   |
   v
Collection Data
   |
   v
BloodHound
   |
   v
Graph Database / Application
   |
   v
Queries and Analysis

Collection and analysis should be considered separate phases.

docs.title: BloodHound Community Edition
docs.text:
BloodHound Community Edition is the modern BloodHound platform maintained by SpecterOps.

Before following older installation guides, determine whether the guide refers to:

BloodHound Legacy

BloodHound Community Edition

Older Neo4j-based deployment

Current BloodHound deployment model

Do not mix installation instructions from different generations.

docs.title: Verify BloodHound Version
docs.text:
Use the version information exposed by the deployment or installation method.

Record the version in assessment evidence when graph behaviour or edge definitions matter.

docs.title: Collector Selection
docs.text:
Common collection approaches include:

SharpHound

BloodHound.py

NetExec BloodHound collection

Other compatible collectors

The correct collector depends on:

Operating system

Available credentials

Network position

Assessment restrictions

Required data

BloodHound version

docs.title: Collection Strategy
docs.text:
Do not immediately collect everything.

Use:

Assessment Objective
       |
       v
Required Relationships
       |
       v
Minimum Collection Methods
       |
       v
Collect
       |
       v
Analyse
       |
       v
Expand Collection If Required

docs.title: Collection Categories
docs.text:
Collection may include information about:

Directory objects

Group memberships

ACLs

Local administrators

Remote-management rights

Sessions

Trusts

Containers

GPO relationships

Object properties

Different collection methods have different network and operational footprints.

docs.title: Collection Safety
docs.text:
Before collecting ask:

How many domain objects exist?

How many computers exist?

Will hosts be contacted directly?

Will SMB be used?

Will session enumeration occur?

Will local groups be queried?

Could endpoint security alert?

Could unavailable systems cause delays?

Is the SOC aware where required?

Do I actually need every collection method?

docs.title: SharpHound
docs.text:
SharpHound is the official BloodHound data collector for Active Directory environments.

Before using it, review the options for the installed version:

.\SharpHound.exe --help

Do not rely solely on old blog posts because collection method names and behaviour can change.

docs.title: SharpHound Basic Methodology
docs.text:
SharpHound
    |
    v
Authenticate as Current User
    |
    v
Query Active Directory
    |
    v
Collect Selected Relationships
    |
    v
Create Output
    |
    v
Import into BloodHound

docs.title: Check Current Identity
docs.text:
Before collection:

whoami

Domain information:

$env:USERDOMAIN

Current DNS domain:

$env:USERDNSDOMAIN

This helps document which identity performed the collection.

docs.title: SharpHound Help
docs.text:
.\SharpHound.exe --help

Review available collection methods rather than assuming an old command remains valid.

docs.title: Collection Method Selection
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Need Basic Directory Relationships?
             |
             v
      Directory Collection
             |
             v
Need ACL Relationships?
             |
             v
        ACL Collection
             |
             v
Need Local Admin Information?
             |
             v
     Host-Based Collection
             |
             v
Need Session Information?
             |
             v
       Session Collection

Increase collection depth only when it supports the assessment objective.

docs.title: SharpHound Output
docs.text:
Collection commonly produces archive or JSON data suitable for import into BloodHound.

After collection, record:

Collector version

Collection methods

Domain

Identity

Timestamp

Output filename

Number of objects if available

docs.title: Do Not Modify Collection Data
docs.text:
Preserve the original collection archive where evidence requirements justify it.

Use a copy for:

Analysis

Processing

Testing

Screenshots

docs.title: Linux-Based Collection
docs.text:
When collecting from Linux, options may include:

BloodHound.py

NetExec-supported BloodHound collection

Linux collection can be particularly useful when the assessment workstation is Kali Linux and domain credentials are available.

docs.title: BloodHound.py
docs.text:
Check the installed tool:

bloodhound-python -h

Depending on installation, the command name may differ.

Review:

Domain

Username

Password

Nameserver

Domain controller

Collection methods

before execution.

docs.title: DNS Is Critical
docs.text:
Linux BloodHound collection frequently fails because of DNS configuration.

Check:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Resolve the domain controller:

getent hosts dc01.corp.local

Query:

dig dc01.corp.local

Query LDAP SRV records:

dig _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local SRV

Query Kerberos:

dig _kerberos._tcp.corp.local SRV

docs.title: Example DNS Model
docs.text:
Your assessment host should ideally be able to resolve:

corp.local

dc01.corp.local

srv01.corp.local

ws01.corp.local

Using only IP addresses can create problems for:

Kerberos

LDAP discovery

SPNs

Collector domain discovery

docs.title: BloodHound.py Collection
docs.text:
Because collection flags can change, start with:

bloodhound-python -h

A collection command generally needs to establish:

Domain

Credential

Domain controller / nameserver

Collection methods

Use the current tool help to build the exact command.

docs.title: NetExec BloodHound Collection
docs.text:
Some NetExec versions expose BloodHound collection through LDAP.

Check:

nxc ldap --help

Look for the installed version's BloodHound options.

Do not copy an old NetExec or CrackMapExec BloodHound command without verifying the available flags.

docs.title: NetExec Collection Workflow
docs.text:
Domain Credential
       |
       v
Validate LDAP
       |
       v
Check nxc ldap --help
       |
       v
Select BloodHound Collection
       |
       v
Specify Correct DNS / DC
       |
       v
Collect
       |
       v
Import
       |
       v
Verify Dataset

docs.title: Why --help Matters Here
docs.text:
BloodHound integration has changed across:

CrackMapExec

Early NetExec versions

Current NetExec releases

BloodHound Legacy

BloodHound CE

The stable lesson is therefore:

Understand required inputs
+
Verify current syntax locally
+
Record the exact command used

docs.title: Importing Data
docs.text:
After collection, import the resulting dataset into BloodHound.

The exact interface depends on the BloodHound deployment.

After import, do not immediately begin analysing paths.

First verify the dataset.

docs.title: Dataset Verification
docs.text:
Check that expected object categories exist.

For example:

Users

Groups

Computers

Domain

OUs

GPOs

Then check relationships such as:

MemberOf

AdminTo

ACL edges

Sessions

where those collection methods were expected.

docs.title: Why Dataset Verification Matters
docs.text:
Suppose BloodHound shows:

0 HasSession relationships

This could mean:

No sessions existed.

But it could also mean:

Session collection was not performed.

Hosts were unreachable.

SMB was blocked.

Collector lacked permissions.

Collection failed.

Endpoint controls interfered.

Data was not imported correctly.

Therefore:

No Edge

does not always mean:

No Relationship

docs.title: Dataset Completeness Model
docs.text:
Graph Result
    |
    v
Was Relevant Data Collected?
    |
   / \
 No   Yes
 |     |
 v     v
Cannot  Analyse
Conclude

docs.title: Record Collection Metadata
docs.text:
For every dataset record:

Collector:
SharpHound

Collector Version:
<version>

Collection Date:
<timestamp>

Collection Identity:
CORP\asif

Domain:
corp.local

Collection Methods:
<methods used>

Known Limitations:
<unreachable hosts / blocked protocols / permissions>

docs.title: Search for a User
docs.text:
In BloodHound, begin with a principal you actually control or are authorised to assess.

Example:

ASIF@CORP.LOCAL

Review:

Group memberships

Outbound control

Local administrative relationships

Remote-management rights

Sessions

Object permissions

docs.title: Marking Owned Principals
docs.text:
Where the interface supports ownership marking, mark only identities actually controlled during the assessment.

Do not mark:

Hypothetical users

Unverified credentials

Accounts you merely discovered

as owned.

docs.title: Owned vs Compromised
docs.text:
A useful assessment distinction:

Discovered

means:

Account exists.

Credential Found

means:

Potential authentication material exists.

Owned

should mean:

Control has been established within the authorised assessment.

docs.title: Search for Domain Admins
docs.text:
A useful high-value group is:

DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.LOCAL

But do not focus exclusively on Domain Admin.

Other sensitive groups may include:

Enterprise Admins

Administrators

Account Operators

Backup Operators

Server administration groups

Virtualisation administrators

Application administrators

PKI administrators

Custom delegated groups

docs.title: Shortest Paths
docs.text:
One of BloodHound's most useful concepts is:

Shortest Path

For example:

Owned User
    |
    v
Group
    |
    v
Computer
    |
    v
Privileged Session
    |
    v
Domain Admin

docs.title: Do Not Blindly Trust Shortest Path
docs.text:
The shortest graph path is not necessarily:

The easiest path

The safest path

The most reliable path

The least detectable path

The currently exploitable path

A longer path may be more realistic.

docs.title: Path Validation Model
docs.text:
For a path:

A -> B -> C -> D

validate:

A -> B

then:

B -> C

then:

C -> D

Do not jump directly from:

A

to:

D

in the report.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Assume BloodHound identifies:

ASIF@CORP.LOCAL
       |
       | MemberOf
       v
HELPDESK@CORP.LOCAL
       |
       | GenericAll
       v
SERVER-ADMINS@CORP.LOCAL
       |
       | AdminTo
       v
SRV01.CORP.LOCAL

This is an interesting path.

Now interpret each edge.

docs.title: Step 1 - MemberOf
docs.text:
ASIF
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
HELPDESK

This means the user is a member of the Helpdesk group.

Verify with directory tooling where necessary.

From Windows:

whoami /groups

or appropriate Active Directory queries.

The important question:

Is this membership current and expected?

docs.title: Step 2 - GenericAll
docs.text:
HELPDESK
   |
   | GenericAll
   v
SERVER-ADMINS

This is much more security relevant.

It indicates broad control over the destination object in the graph model.

Questions:

What object grants the permission?

Is it direct or inherited?

Which ACE provides it?

Is Helpdesk supposed to manage this group?

Can group membership actually be changed?

Are protected-object behaviours relevant?

docs.title: Step 3 - AdminTo
docs.text:
SERVER-ADMINS
      |
      | AdminTo
      v
SRV01

This indicates the group has administrative control over the computer according to collected data.

Validate:

Is SRV01 online?

Is the group still a local administrator?

Which mechanism grants access?

GPO?

Local group?

Manual assignment?

docs.title: Worked Example Conclusion
docs.text:
Do not report:

BloodHound says ASIF can become admin on SRV01.

Prefer:

BloodHound identified a path from CORP\asif to administrative control of SRV01 through membership of CORP\Helpdesk, delegated control over CORP\Server-Admins, and the administrative rights of Server-Admins on SRV01. Independent validation should confirm the delegated directory permission and the current local administrative assignment before the complete privilege path is treated as confirmed.

docs.title: Common Edge - MemberOf
docs.text:
USER
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
GROUP

Meaning:

The source principal is a member of the destination group.

Security significance depends on the group's privileges.

docs.title: Nested Group Membership
docs.text:
Example:

ASIF
 |
 v
HELPDESK
 |
 v
IT-USERS
 |
 v
SERVER-OPERATORS

Nested groups can make effective privileges difficult to identify manually.

BloodHound is particularly useful for exposing these chains.

docs.title: Common Edge - AdminTo
docs.text:
USER/GROUP
     |
     | AdminTo
     v
COMPUTER

Meaning:

The principal has administrative-level rights over the computer
according to the collected relationship.

Validate the current local group or policy configuration where the edge is important.

docs.title: AdminTo Does Not Mean Online
docs.text:
A computer object may be:

Offline

Decommissioned

Firewalled

Unreachable

Stale

BloodHound describes the relationship represented by the dataset, not necessarily current network reachability.

docs.title: Common Edge - HasSession
docs.text:
COMPUTER
   |
   | HasSession
   v
USER

This indicates the collector observed a session relationship.

Session data is especially time-sensitive.

docs.title: Session Data Can Become Stale Quickly
docs.text:
A session observed at:

09:00

may not exist at:

15:00

Always record:

Collection timestamp

Session collection method

Host

User

docs.title: Session Edge Interpretation
docs.text:
A session relationship can be security relevant when:

You control the computer
+
A privileged user has a session

But additional questions remain:

Can credential material actually be accessed?

What protections exist?

Is Credential Guard enabled?

Is the session still active?

What privilege does the user hold?

docs.title: Common Edge - GenericAll
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | GenericAll
    v
OBJECT

GenericAll generally represents broad control over the destination object.

The practical impact depends heavily on object type.

docs.title: GenericAll Over User
docs.text:
Potential implications may include account-control operations depending on effective permissions and environment configuration.

Validate the actual ACE and allowed operations before reporting a specific impact.

docs.title: GenericAll Over Group
docs.text:
Potentially relevant to group membership management.

Questions:

Can the controlled principal modify membership?

Is the target group privileged?

Is the permission inherited?

Is the object protected?

Would modification cross a security boundary?

docs.title: GenericAll Over Computer
docs.text:
Potential implications differ from user/group objects.

Do not apply a generic "GenericAll exploit" without understanding the destination object's semantics.

docs.title: Common Edge - GenericWrite
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | GenericWrite
    v
OBJECT

This indicates write access to certain attributes of the destination object.

The security consequence depends on:

Object type

Writable attributes

Existing configuration

Effective permissions

docs.title: Common Edge - WriteDacl
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | WriteDacl
    v
OBJECT

This indicates the principal can modify the object's discretionary access-control list.

This can be highly security relevant because permissions may potentially be delegated to another principal.

docs.title: WriteDacl Validation
docs.text:
Before reporting:

Confirm the ACE.

Confirm effective permission.

Identify target object.

Determine whether the permission is inherited.

Determine whether changing the DACL would create meaningful control.

docs.title: Common Edge - WriteOwner
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | WriteOwner
    v
OBJECT

Ownership can influence an object's security descriptor.

Again, the important issue is the resulting security control, not simply the edge label.

docs.title: Common Edge - Owns
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | Owns
    v
OBJECT

Ownership should be analysed together with:

DACL

Object type

Inheritance

Effective rights

docs.title: Common Edge - AddMember
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | AddMember
    v
GROUP

This can indicate the ability to add members to a group.

If the destination is privileged, this may create a direct privilege-escalation path.

docs.title: AddMember Validation
docs.text:
Confirm:

Exact group

Exact source principal

Permission source

Inheritance

Current membership-management controls

Privilege granted by the group

docs.title: Common Edge - ForceChangePassword
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | ForceChangePassword
    v
USER

This indicates a password-management relationship.

Security significance depends on:

Target account privilege

Whether the permission is expected

Operational consequences

Identity protections

docs.title: Common Edge - CanRDP
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | CanRDP
    v
COMPUTER

This indicates remote desktop rights represented in the graph.

It does not automatically mean:

RDP is reachable.

Interactive logon will succeed.

The user is administrator.

docs.title: Validate RDP Relationship
docs.text:
Check:

Network reachability

RDP service

Authentication

Logon rights

NLA

Firewall

Account restrictions

docs.title: Common Edge - CanPSRemote
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | CanPSRemote
    v
COMPUTER

This indicates PowerShell remoting/WinRM-related access.

Validate:

WinRM reachable?

Account authorised?

Which group grants access?

Administrative or non-administrative session?

docs.title: Common Edge - ExecuteDCOM
docs.text:
PRINCIPAL
    |
    | ExecuteDCOM
    v
COMPUTER

This indicates a DCOM-related remote execution relationship.

Validate:

RPC reachability

DCOM configuration

Account permission

Firewall

Target availability

See DCOM.

docs.title: Delegation Edges
docs.text:
BloodHound can identify delegation relationships including configurations related to:

Unconstrained Delegation

Constrained Delegation

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

These relationships require careful Kerberos interpretation.

See:

  • Unconstrained Delegation
  • Constrained Delegation
  • RBCD
  • S4U

docs.title: AllowedToDelegate
docs.text:
Conceptually:

ACCOUNT
   |
   | AllowedToDelegate
   v
SERVICE

Do not treat the edge as a complete exploitation path without understanding:

Delegation type

Controlled account

SPN

Target service

Kerberos requirements

Account flags

docs.title: AllowedToAct
docs.text:
This relationship is relevant to resource-based constrained delegation.

Again:

Graph Edge
   !=
Complete Exploit

Validate the actual directory configuration before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: ACL Analysis
docs.text:
ACL edges are among the most valuable BloodHound relationships.

Examples:

GenericAll

GenericWrite

WriteDacl

WriteOwner

AddMember

ForceChangePassword

Use BloodHound to locate them, then independently inspect the underlying directory permission for important findings.

docs.title: ACL Validation Workflow
docs.text:
BloodHound Edge
      |
      v
Identify Source
      |
      v
Identify Destination
      |
      v
Identify Permission
      |
      v
Determine Direct / Inherited
      |
      v
Inspect Actual ACE
      |
      v
Determine Effective Rights
      |
      v
Determine Security Consequence

docs.title: ACL False Positives
docs.text:
Potential reasons an apparent path may not produce the expected outcome:

Stale collection

Permission inherited differently than expected

Protected object behaviour

Permission removed after collection

Object disabled

Target group no longer privileged

Application-specific controls

Collector interpretation differs from current state

docs.title: Group Policy Relationships
docs.text:
BloodHound may expose relationships involving:

GPOs

OUs

Computers

Users

Groups

GPO-related paths can be highly significant because a single GPO may affect many systems.

docs.title: GPO Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Who can modify the GPO?

Where is it linked?

Which systems/users receive it?

Is inheritance blocked?

Are security filters present?

Is the GPO actually applied?

What privilege would modification provide?

docs.title: Do Not Assume Linked Means Applied
docs.text:
A GPO relationship may be affected by:

Security filtering

WMI filtering

Inheritance

Enforced links

Blocked inheritance

Object location

Validate effective application where it matters.

docs.title: Computer Analysis
docs.text:
For an interesting computer review:

Local administrators

Inbound administrative relationships

Outbound relationships

Sessions

Remote-management rights

Operating system

Group memberships

GPO relationships

docs.title: High-Value Computers
docs.text:
Do not limit analysis to domain controllers.

High-value systems may include:

Certificate authorities

SCCM infrastructure

Backup servers

Virtualisation hosts

Identity-management servers

Jump hosts

Management servers

Database servers

Deployment systems

Monitoring systems

docs.title: User Analysis
docs.text:
For an interesting user review:

Group memberships

Outbound object control

Inbound control

Sessions

SPNs

Delegation

Administrative relationships

Password-related properties

Certificate relationships

docs.title: Group Analysis
docs.text:
For an interesting group:

Direct members

Nested members

Object control

Systems administered

GPO rights

Delegated directory rights

Inbound control

docs.title: Domain Analysis
docs.text:
Review:

Domain trusts

High-value groups

Domain controllers

Privilege paths

ACL delegation

GPO relationships

Certificate services

Administrative tiers

docs.title: Trust Analysis
docs.text:
BloodHound can help visualise trust relationships between domains.

Trust alone does not automatically create a privilege path.

Analyse:

Trust direction

Trust type

Transitivity

SID filtering

Selective authentication

Cross-domain group memberships

Actual privileged relationships

docs.title: Path to Domain Admin
docs.text:
A common query objective is:

Owned Principal
      |
      v
Shortest Path
      |
      v
Domain Admin

This is useful, but not sufficient by itself.

docs.title: Better Question
docs.text:
Instead of only asking:

How do I get Domain Admin?

also ask:

Which security control failed?

Why can this low-privileged principal control this object?

Which delegation created the path?

Which group assignment is excessive?

Which system creates credential exposure?

How can the organisation break the path?

docs.title: Path Breaking
docs.text:
BloodHound is valuable defensively because an attack path can often be broken at several locations.

Example:

USER
 |
 v
HELPDESK
 |
 v
SERVER-ADMINS
 |
 v
SRV01
 |
 v
PRIVILEGED SESSION

Potential remediation points:

Remove unnecessary Helpdesk membership

Remove excessive ACL over Server-Admins

Remove unnecessary Server-Admins local admin

Prevent privileged sessions on SRV01

docs.title: Attack Path Choke Points
docs.text:
A choke point is a relationship that appears in many attack paths.

Examples:

Over-privileged group

Management server

Shared administrator account

Dangerous ACL

Tier-crossing system

GPO

Certificate template

These can be higher remediation priorities than fixing individual paths one by one.

docs.title: Cypher Queries
docs.text:
BloodHound uses graph queries for advanced analysis.

The exact query language and supported schema can differ between BloodHound generations.

Verify the current BloodHound documentation before relying on old query collections.

docs.title: Basic Cypher Concept
docs.text:
A conceptual graph query looks for:

Node
 |
 v
Relationship
 |
 v
Node

Example conceptual pattern:

MATCH (u:User)-[:MemberOf]->(g:Group)
RETURN u, g

docs.title: Find Users
docs.text:
MATCH (u:User)
RETURN u
LIMIT 25

Use this as a simple graph exploration example where supported by the deployment.

docs.title: Find Groups
docs.text:
MATCH (g:Group)
RETURN g
LIMIT 25

docs.title: Find Computers
docs.text:
MATCH (c:Computer)
RETURN c
LIMIT 25

docs.title: Membership Relationships
docs.text:
MATCH (u:User)-[r:MemberOf]->(g:Group)
RETURN u, r, g
LIMIT 50

This helps visualise direct membership relationships.

docs.title: GenericAll Relationships
docs.text:
MATCH (a)-[r:GenericAll]->(b)
RETURN a, r, b
LIMIT 50

Do not assume every returned relationship is exploitable without validating object type and current permissions.

docs.title: GenericWrite Relationships
docs.text:
MATCH (a)-[r:GenericWrite]->(b)
RETURN a, r, b
LIMIT 50

docs.title: WriteDacl Relationships
docs.text:
MATCH (a)-[r:WriteDacl]->(b)
RETURN a, r, b
LIMIT 50

docs.title: WriteOwner Relationships
docs.text:
MATCH (a)-[r:WriteOwner]->(b)
RETURN a, r, b
LIMIT 50

docs.title: Administrative Relationships
docs.text:
A conceptual query:

MATCH (a)-[r:AdminTo]->(c:Computer)
RETURN a, r, c
LIMIT 50

docs.title: Session Relationships
docs.text:
A conceptual query:

MATCH (c:Computer)-[r:HasSession]->(u:User)
RETURN c, r, u
LIMIT 50

Remember that session data is highly time-sensitive.

docs.title: Query Results Are Leads
docs.text:
The correct process is:

Cypher Result
    |
    v
Interesting Relationship
    |
    v
Inspect Object
    |
    v
Inspect Edge
    |
    v
Validate Outside BloodHound
    |
    v
Determine Impact

docs.title: Built-In Queries
docs.text:
Depending on BloodHound version, built-in analysis may provide queries for areas such as:

Shortest paths to high-value targets

Domain Admin relationships

Kerberoastable accounts

AS-REP roastable accounts

Local administrative rights

Sessions

Dangerous object control

Treat built-in queries as investigation starting points.

docs.title: BloodHound + NetExec Workflow
docs.text:
A strong combination is:

BloodHound
    |
    v
ASIF AdminTo SRV01
    |
    v
NetExec
    |
    v
Validate Authentication / Admin Context
    |
    v
Confirm Relationship

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
BloodHound suggests:

ASIF@CORP.LOCAL
      |
      | AdminTo
      v
SRV01.CORP.LOCAL

A narrow validation can then determine whether the tested account currently has administrative access to that host.

Do not test every host merely because the graph contains many relationships.

docs.title: BloodHound + Impacket Workflow
docs.text:
BloodHound
    |
    v
Specific Protocol Relationship
    |
    v
Understand Preconditions
    |
    v
Impacket
    |
    v
Focused Validation

For example, a Kerberos or remote-administration relationship may justify selecting one specialised Impacket utility.

See the Impacket Cheatsheet.

docs.title: BloodHound + PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView can be useful for independently validating directory relationships discovered in BloodHound.

Conceptually:

BloodHound
    |
    v
Interesting ACL
    |
    v
PowerView / Native AD Query
    |
    v
Actual ACE
    |
    v
Interpretation

docs.title: BloodHound + Native PowerShell
docs.text:
Native Windows tooling can also verify many relationships.

Current groups:

whoami /groups

Local administrators where authorised:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators

Domain information where AD tooling is available can provide additional validation.

docs.title: BloodHound + Active Directory Users and Computers
docs.text:
For some findings, graphical administrative tools can provide useful supporting evidence.

Examples:

Group membership

OU placement

Delegation

Object properties

Do not rely on a single interface if the finding depends on subtle ACL behaviour.

docs.title: Data Freshness
docs.text:
BloodHound data is a snapshot.

It should always be associated with:

Collection time

rather than interpreted as permanently current.

docs.title: Stale Users
docs.text:
Possible indicators:

Disabled accounts

Old logon timestamps

Legacy service accounts

Accounts no longer used

A stale object can still be security relevant, but its current operational role must be verified.

docs.title: Stale Computers
docs.text:
Computer objects may represent:

Decommissioned systems

Offline systems

Reimaged systems

Old test systems

Cloud-hosted systems no longer active

Validate reachability before using them in an attack-path conclusion.

docs.title: Stale Sessions
docs.text:
Session data should be treated as especially volatile.

Collection at 10:00

does not prove:

Session exists at 16:00

docs.title: Incomplete Collection
docs.text:
Common reasons include:

DNS failure

Firewall restrictions

SMB blocked

RPC blocked

Insufficient privileges

Collector errors

EDR interference

Offline systems

Collection method not selected

Timeouts

docs.title: Recognising Incomplete Data
docs.text:
Warning signs:

Very few computers

No local admin edges

No sessions

No ACL edges

Missing expected domain controllers

Missing expected groups

Collection errors

docs.title: Incomplete Dataset Example
docs.text:
Suppose the organisation has:

2,500 computers

but BloodHound contains:

183 computers

Do not conclude:

The remaining systems have no attack paths.

The dataset is likely incomplete.

docs.title: Collection Coverage
docs.text:
Track:

Expected Computers:
2500

Collected Computers:
183

Coverage:
7.3%

This changes the confidence level of the analysis.

docs.title: Confidence Levels
docs.text:
You can classify BloodHound conclusions as:

Observed

Validated

Incomplete

Stale

Unconfirmed

docs.title: Observed
docs.text:
Example:

BloodHound contains an AdminTo relationship between
CORP\asif and SRV01.

docs.title: Validated
docs.text:
Example:

The relationship was independently confirmed against the
current local administrator configuration.

docs.title: Incomplete
docs.text:
Example:

Session collection failed against a significant portion of
workstations.

docs.title: Stale
docs.text:
Example:

The session was collected several hours before validation and
could no longer be reproduced.

docs.title: Unconfirmed
docs.text:
Example:

The relationship could not be independently validated within
the assessment window.

docs.title: False Positive Example - AdminTo
docs.text:
BloodHound:

HELPDESK
   |
   | AdminTo
   v
WS01

Independent validation:

HELPDESK is no longer present in the local Administrators group.

Possible explanation:

Collection predates a policy change.

Conclusion:

Do not report current administrative access.

docs.title: False Positive Example - Session
docs.text:
BloodHound:

SRV01
 |
 | HasSession
 v
DOMAIN ADMIN

Later validation:

Session no longer exists.

Conclusion:

The session was observed during collection but was transient.

docs.title: Alternative Explanation Example - Missing Sessions
docs.text:
BloodHound:

No sessions found.

Collector log:

Host enumeration failed because SMB was blocked.

Correct conclusion:

Session state could not be determined.

Incorrect conclusion:

No privileged users have sessions.

docs.title: Attack Path Validation
docs.text:
For every significant path create a table.

Step BloodHound Edge Validation Result 1 ASIF -> MemberOf -> HELPDESK Directory membership Confirmed 2 HELPDESK -> GenericAll -> SERVER-ADMINS ACL review Confirmed 3 SERVER-ADMINS -> AdminTo -> SRV01 Local admin review Confirmed 4 SRV01 -> HasSession -> ADMIN1 Session recheck Not confirmed

This prevents a partially valid path from being reported as fully exploitable.

docs.title: Evidence Capture
docs.text:
For each important path record:

Collection timestamp

Collector

Collector version

Collection methods

BloodHound version

Source principal

Destination

Path

Edges

Independent validation

Limitations

docs.title: Screenshot Evidence
docs.text:
A useful BloodHound screenshot should show:

Source principal

Destination

Complete relevant path

Edge names

Avoid screenshots containing:

Unrelated user data

Large unreadable graphs

Sensitive usernames not relevant to the finding

docs.title: Evidence Example
docs.text:
Test ID:
AD-BH-004

Timestamp:
2026-09-06 16:00 UTC

Tool:
BloodHound

Collector:
SharpHound

Collection Identity:
CORP\asif

Domain:
corp.local

Source:
ASIF@CORP.LOCAL

Target:
SRV01.CORP.LOCAL

Observed Path:
ASIF
 -> MemberOf
HELPDESK
 -> GenericAll
SERVER-ADMINS
 -> AdminTo
SRV01

Validation:
Membership confirmed.
GenericAll ACE independently confirmed.
SERVER-ADMINS local administrative assignment confirmed.

Conclusion:
The tested user can influence a group that provides
administrative access to SRV01.

Limitations:
No modification was performed during validation.

docs.title: Reporting BloodHound Findings
docs.text:
Do not report:

BloodHound found an attack path.

BloodHound is evidence and analysis tooling, not the root cause.

docs.title: Better Finding Title
docs.text:
Instead of:

BloodHound Attack Path to Server

prefer:

Excessive Active Directory Delegation Enables Privilege Escalation

or:

Helpdesk Group Can Modify Privileged Server Administration Group

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
Members of the CORP\Helpdesk group have excessive directory
permissions over CORP\Server-Admins.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
BloodHound identified a GenericAll relationship from Helpdesk
to Server-Admins. Independent ACL review confirmed the
permission.

docs.title: Security Consequence
docs.text:
Server-Admins provides administrative access to SRV01.
Consequently, compromise of a Helpdesk account could permit
unauthorised administrative access to the server.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Remove unnecessary delegated control over Server-Admins and
review other privileged groups for similar permissions.

docs.title: Do Not Report the Tool
docs.text:
Avoid:

BloodHound vulnerability

Report:

Excessive ACL

Excessive group membership

Unnecessary local administrator rights

Unsafe delegation

Privileged session exposure

Insecure GPO permissions

BloodHound reveals the condition.

docs.title: Remediation - ACL Paths
docs.text:
Review:

GenericAll

GenericWrite

WriteDacl

WriteOwner

AddMember

ForceChangePassword

Remove permissions that are not required by the principal's operational role.

docs.title: Remediation - Group Membership
docs.text:
Apply:

Least privilege

Role-based administration

Separate privileged identities

Regular membership review

Remove nested privilege where unnecessary

docs.title: Remediation - Local Administrators
docs.text:
Review:

Domain groups in local Administrators

Legacy helpdesk access

Shared administrator groups

Application service accounts

Deployment accounts

Use appropriate privileged-access management.

docs.title: Remediation - Privileged Sessions
docs.text:
Reduce unnecessary privileged logons to lower-trust systems.

Consider:

Administrative tiering

Privileged Access Workstations

Dedicated administration hosts

Remote Credential Guard where appropriate

Credential Guard

Restricted administrative workflows

docs.title: Remediation - GPO Control
docs.text:
Restrict:

Who can modify GPOs

Who can modify GPO links

Who can modify related files

Who controls sensitive OUs

docs.title: Remediation - Delegation
docs.text:
Review:

Unconstrained delegation

Constrained delegation

RBCD

Legacy delegation

Service-account privilege

Remove delegation that is no longer required.

docs.title: Retesting BloodHound Findings
docs.text: A good retest verifies the root cause rather than merely importing a new graph.

docs.title: Example Retest - GenericAll
docs.text:
Before:

HELPDESK
   |
   | GenericAll
   v
SERVER-ADMINS

Remediation:

Excessive ACE removed.

Retest:

1. Inspect the target object's ACL.
2. Confirm the ACE is absent.
3. Recollect relevant BloodHound ACL data.
4. Import the new dataset.
5. Confirm the edge is absent.
6. Confirm no equivalent privilege path remains.

docs.title: Example Retest - Local Admin
docs.text:
Before:

HELPDESK
   |
   | AdminTo
   v
SRV01

Retest:

1. Confirm Helpdesk is no longer a local administrator.
2. Recollect local-group information.
3. Confirm BloodHound no longer produces the edge.
4. Validate that another nested group does not recreate access.

docs.title: Why Edge Disappearance Is Not Enough
docs.text:
Suppose an edge disappears because:

Collection failed.

That is not remediation.

Therefore:

No Edge
    |
    v
Was Data Successfully Collected?
    |
   / \
 No   Yes
 |     |
 v     v
Unknown Remediation
        Candidate

docs.title: Retest Dataset Comparison
docs.text:
Track:

Metric Before After Users 5,200 5,198 Groups 1,120 1,121 Computers 2,480 2,477 GenericAll edges 83 62 WriteDacl edges 41 29 High-value attack paths 17 5

Counts alone do not prove security improvement, but they can help measure changes when collection conditions are comparable.

docs.title: BloodHound for Purple Teaming
docs.text:
BloodHound can support purple-team exercises by helping select realistic privilege paths.

Example:

BloodHound Path
      |
      v
Select One Relationship
      |
      v
Define Expected Telemetry
      |
      v
Controlled Validation
      |
      v
Blue Team Observation
      |
      v
Detection Gap
      |
      v
Remediation

docs.title: Purple Team Example
docs.text:
Path:

Helpdesk User
     |
     v
Dangerous ACL
     |
     v
Server Admin Group

Exercise objective:

Can defenders detect and investigate unauthorised modification
of a privileged Active Directory group?

docs.title: Detection Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Was the directory modification logged?

Was the initiating account identified?

Was the target object identified?

Was an alert generated?

Did the SOC understand the privilege consequence?

Could analysts reconstruct the complete path?

docs.title: Defensive BloodHound Analysis
docs.text:
Blue teams can use BloodHound to identify:

Privilege concentration

Dangerous ACLs

Excessive administrative access

Tier violations

Privileged session exposure

Attack-path choke points

Overly broad delegation

High-value systems with excessive inbound control

docs.title: Continuous Analysis
docs.text:
A mature defensive workflow could be:

Scheduled Collection
       |
       v
Graph Analysis
       |
       v
Identify New Privilege Relationships
       |
       v
Validate Change
       |
       v
Remediate
       |
       v
Recollect

docs.title: Compare Snapshots
docs.text:
Useful questions:

Which new AdminTo edges appeared?

Which new ACL edges appeared?

Which accounts gained control over privileged groups?

Which new systems became high value?

Which attack paths disappeared?

Which privileged session patterns changed?

docs.title: Collect Everything Immediately
docs.text:
Problem:

Unnecessary traffic and noise.

Better:

Collect what is needed for the current objective.

docs.title: Assume No Edge Means No Risk
docs.text:
Problem:

Dataset may be incomplete.

Better:

Check collection coverage.

docs.title: Assume Every Path Is Exploitable
docs.text:
Problem:

Edges may be stale or have unmet prerequisites.

Better:

Validate important edges independently.

docs.title: Focus Only on Domain Admin
docs.text:
Problem:

Other identities and systems may be equally important.

Better:

Define organisational high-value assets.

docs.title: Report BloodHound Instead of Root Cause
docs.text:
Problem:

"BloodHound found..."

Better:

"Excessive delegated ACL..."

docs.title: Ignore Collection Time
docs.text:
Problem:

Sessions and relationships may change.

Better:

Record collection timestamps.

docs.title: Ignore Collector Errors
docs.text:
Problem:

Missing data can appear as missing relationships.

Better:

Review collector output and coverage.

docs.title: Use Giant Graph Screenshots
docs.text:
Problem:

Evidence becomes unreadable.

Better:

Capture the smallest graph that demonstrates the relationship.

docs.title: BloodHound Contains No Data
docs.text:
Check:

Was import successful?

Was the correct archive imported?

Did collection complete?

Did the collector produce objects?

Are filters hiding results?

docs.title: Users Exist but Computers Are Missing
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Collection method

LDAP query limitations

Domain selection

Collector failure

Import issue

docs.title: Computers Exist but No Sessions
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Session collection not selected

SMB blocked

Hosts unreachable

Permission restrictions

No sessions observed

Collection errors

Do not assume the last explanation without checking the others.

docs.title: No AdminTo Edges
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Local-group collection not performed

Hosts unreachable

Permissions insufficient

Firewall

Collector errors

No such relationships

docs.title: Linux Collector Cannot Find Domain
docs.text:
Check:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

dig corp.local

dig _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local SRV

getent hosts dc01.corp.local

docs.title: Kerberos Errors During Collection
docs.text:
Check:

date

klist

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

and verify DNS.

docs.title: Collection Is Very Slow
docs.text:
Possible reasons:

Large domain

Unreachable hosts

Timeouts

Session collection

Local-group enumeration

Network filtering

DNS delays

Reduce collection scope if appropriate rather than repeatedly restarting broad collection.

docs.title: Collector Produces Errors for Some Hosts
docs.text:
Record them.

Example:

Total Computers:
2000

Successfully Contacted:
1480

Failed:
520

This is important context for the confidence of host-level analysis.

docs.title: Graph Looks Different After New Collection
docs.text:
Possible reasons:

Environment changed

Sessions changed

Groups changed

Permissions changed

Different collection methods used

Different collector version

Different scope

Previous data remained in database

Make sure snapshot comparisons use comparable collection conditions.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
BloodHound should help answer:

Who controls what?

Why do they control it?

Through which relationship?

Is the relationship current?

What does the relationship permit?

What additional prerequisite exists?

Can the relationship be independently confirmed?

What security boundary can be crossed?

Which configuration created the path?

Where should the organisation break the path?

The graph is the beginning of the analysis, not the end.
