  • BloodHound.py GitHub
  • NetExec Documentation
  • Microsoft Learn - Active Directory Domain Services
  • Microsoft Learn - Active Directory Security Groups
  • Microsoft Learn - Group Policy
  • Microsoft Learn - Kerberos Authentication
  • MITRE ATT&CK - Enterprise

Validate the edge, not just the path

A BloodHound path is made of individual relationships. Validate the security-relevant edges independently before treating the complete path as confirmed.

Missing data is not negative evidence

If host collection failed, the absence of AdminTo or HasSession relationships does not prove those relationships do not exist. Record collection coverage and limitations alongside the graph analysis.

Report the root cause

BloodHound is the analysis tool. The finding is usually the excessive ACL, unnecessary group membership, administrative assignment, unsafe delegation, GPO permission or privileged-session exposure that created the path.

Session information is volatile

HasSession data represents an observation made during collection. Treat it as time-sensitive and revalidate important session relationships before relying on them in an attack-path conclusion.

Do not optimise for the shortest graph

The shortest path is mathematically interesting, but it is not automatically the most realistic security path. Prefer paths whose prerequisites, permissions, reachability and current state can be defensibly established.

docs.title: Burp Suite Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Burp Suite is an integrated platform for web application and API security testing.

Rather than treating Burp as a collection of individual tools, use it as an assessment workflow:

Browser / Client
       |
       v
     Proxy
       |
       v
  HTTP History
       |
       v
Identify Interesting Request
       |
       v
    Repeater
       |
       v
Controlled Modification
       |
       +--> Authentication
       +--> Authorisation
       +--> Input Validation
       +--> Business Logic
       +--> API Behaviour
       |
       v
Compare Responses
       |
       v
Further Validation
       |
       v
Evidence
       |
       v
Finding

Authorised Security Testing

Only use Burp Suite against applications, APIs and infrastructure that you are explicitly authorised to assess. Intruder, extensions, active scanning and automated testing can generate substantial traffic or change application state. Understand the assessment scope before using automated functionality.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Burp Tool Capture browser traffic Proxy Review requests HTTP history Modify and resend requests Repeater Automate controlled input variations Intruder Encode/decode data Decoder Compare responses Comparer Analyse session token randomness Sequencer Out-of-band interaction testing Collaborator Organise interesting requests Organizer Inspect WebSockets WebSockets history Extend Burp Extensions / BApp Store Automated vulnerability testing Scanner - Professional Browser testing Burp's browser

docs.title: Practical Testing Model
docs.text:
A strong Burp workflow is:

BASELINE
   |
   v
Understand Normal Request
   |
   v
Identify Security Boundary
   |
   v
Change One Variable
   |
   v
Observe Response
   |
   v
Compare With Baseline
   |
   v
Determine Alternative Explanations
   |
   v
Validate Again
   |
   v
Document Security Consequence

Avoid:

Intercept Request
      |
      v
Change Everything
      |
      v
Unexpected Response
      |
      v
Report Vulnerability

Controlled testing produces much stronger evidence.

docs.title: Starting Burp Suite
docs.text:
On Kali Linux:

burpsuite

Check the installed package:

apt policy burpsuite

For the latest supported release and installation options, use the official PortSwigger distribution appropriate to your environment.

docs.title: Burp's Browser
docs.text:
A convenient testing method is:

Proxy
    |
    v
Open Browser

Burp's embedded browser is already configured to proxy traffic through Burp.

This avoids manually configuring a separate browser for many assessment workflows.

docs.title: External Browser
docs.text:
Typical Burp proxy listener:

127.0.0.1:8080

Configure the assessment browser to use:

HTTP Proxy: 127.0.0.1
Port:       8080

HTTPS traffic also needs Burp's CA certificate trusted in the dedicated assessment browser if you want Burp to inspect TLS-protected application traffic.

docs.title: Dedicated Assessment Browser
docs.text:
Prefer a browser/profile used specifically for security testing.

This helps separate:

Personal sessions

Production credentials

Assessment accounts

Burp certificates

Proxy configuration

Testing extensions

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
The Proxy is the central point through which browser HTTP/S traffic passes.

Browser
   |
   v
Burp Proxy
   |
   v
Application

docs.title: Intercept
docs.text:
When interception is enabled:

Browser
   |
   v
Burp Holds Request
   |
   v
Tester Reviews / Modifies
   |
   v
Forward
   |
   v
Server

Use interception when you specifically need to modify a request before it reaches the server.

docs.title: Intercept Off Is Normal
docs.text:
You do not need to leave interception enabled constantly.

A common workflow is:

Intercept Off
     |
     v
Browse Application Normally
     |
     v
HTTP History
     |
     v
Find Interesting Request
     |
     v
Send to Repeater

This is often more efficient than manually forwarding every request.

docs.title: HTTP History
docs.text:
Proxy HTTP history records requests passing through Burp.

Review fields such as:

Host

Method

URL

Status

Length

MIME type

Extension

TLS

Notes

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
During normal application browsing, identify:

Authentication endpoints

Password reset

Account settings

Administrative endpoints

API requests

Object identifiers

File downloads

File uploads

Search parameters

Redirect parameters

Role-related functionality

Hidden application features

GraphQL endpoints

WebSocket connections

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Define the assessment target before spending significant time in HTTP history.

Conceptually:

Everything Browser Contacts
          |
          v
       Burp
          |
    +-----+-----+
    |           |
    v           v
In Scope     Out of Scope
    |
    v
Assessment

Scope helps reduce noise from:

Analytics

CDNs

Advertising

Browser services

Third-party APIs

External identity providers

Do not assume a third-party service becomes authorised merely because the application communicates with it.

docs.title: Target Scope
docs.text:
Add only authorised hosts and URLs.

Example:

https://app.example.com/
https://api.example.com/

Avoid accidentally including unrelated domains.

docs.title: Site Map
docs.text:
The Target site map helps visualise discovered application content.

Look for:

Directories

Endpoints

Parameters

API routes

Static resources

Different response codes

Unexpected functionality

docs.title: Repeater
docs.text:
Repeater is one of the most important Burp tools.

Use it to:

Replay requests

Modify parameters

Change headers

Change cookies

Change methods

Test object identifiers

Test authentication boundaries

Test API requests

Compare responses

Validate findings

docs.title: Send to Repeater
docs.text:
From HTTP history:

Right-click request
      |
      v
Send to Repeater

Common shortcut:

Ctrl+R

Then open Repeater and send the request.

docs.title: Repeater Testing Model
docs.text:
Original Request
      |
      v
Send
      |
      v
Baseline Response
      |
      v
Change One Input
      |
      v
Send Again
      |
      v
Modified Response
      |
      v
Compare

docs.title: Baseline First
docs.text:
Before modifying a request, send the original.

Record:

Status

Response length

Response body

Headers

Timing

Application state

This becomes the baseline.

docs.title: Example Baseline
docs.text:
GET /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Cookie: session=<account-a-session>
Accept: application/json

Representative response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "id": 1001,
  "username": "account-a"
}

Now modifications can be compared against known behaviour.

docs.title: Change One Variable
docs.text:
For example:

Baseline:
GET /api/orders/1001

Modified:
GET /api/orders/2001

Keep:

Method

Session

Headers

Body

constant.

This makes the effect of the object identifier easier to interpret.

docs.title: Repeater Tabs
docs.text:
Use descriptive names where possible:

Login Baseline

Account A Own Object

Account A -> Account B

Admin Endpoint

Upload Baseline

CORS Test

This reduces confusion during large assessments.

docs.title: Authentication Testing
docs.text:
Start by understanding:

Login

Logout

Session creation

Session invalidation

Password reset

MFA

Remember-me

Account recovery

Session expiration

docs.title: Login Baseline
docs.text:
Capture a valid login request.

Example:

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=testuser&password=<password>

Determine:

Success response

Failure response

Redirect behaviour

Session cookie changes

Authentication tokens

docs.title: Login Response
docs.text:
Possible:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /dashboard
Set-Cookie: session=<value>; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

This provides several observations:

Authentication appears successful.

A session cookie is issued.

The application redirects to /dashboard.

It does not prove the overall authentication implementation is secure.

docs.title: Session Testing
docs.text:
Review:

Session creation

Cookie attributes

Session rotation

Logout invalidation

Concurrent sessions

Idle timeout

Absolute timeout

Privilege changes

docs.title: Cookie Attributes
docs.text:
Inspect:

Secure

HttpOnly

SameSite

Domain

Path

Expires

Max-Age

Example:

Set-Cookie: session=<value>; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

docs.title: Session Rotation
docs.text:
A useful controlled test:

Before Login
    |
    v
Session A
    |
    v
Authenticate
    |
    v
Session B?

If the application uses session identifiers before and after authentication, determine whether they are appropriately rotated according to the application's design.

docs.title: Logout Testing
docs.text:
Authenticated Session
       |
       v
Logout
       |
       v
Reuse Old Session
       |
      / \
 Accepted Rejected

A rejected old session supports successful server-side invalidation.

Do not rely only on the browser deleting the cookie.

docs.title: Authorisation Testing
docs.text:
Authorisation is one of the strongest uses of Repeater.

A controlled approach uses at least two test identities:

Account A

Account B

Prefer accounts created specifically for the assessment.

docs.title: Two-Account Matrix
docs.text: Request Expected A -> A object Allowed A -> B object Denied B -> B object Allowed B -> A object Denied Unauthenticated -> protected object Denied

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA Example
docs.text:
Controlled environment:

Account A owns order 1001.

Account B owns order 2001.

Account A baseline:

GET /api/orders/1001 HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <account-a-token>

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

{
  "orderId": 1001,
  "owner": "account-a"
}

docs.title: Cross-Account Test
docs.text:
Change only:

1001

to:

2001

Request:

GET /api/orders/2001 HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <account-a-token>

Secure behaviour may be:

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

or:

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

depending on application design.

docs.title: Positive Authorisation Result
docs.text:
If Account A receives:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

{
  "orderId": 2001,
  "owner": "account-b",
  "deliveryAddress": "..."
}

validate:

Is 2001 definitely owned by Account B?

Is Account A definitely authenticated?

Should Account A be denied?

Is protected information returned?

Can the behaviour be reproduced?

docs.title: Defensible Conclusion
docs.text:
Do not report:

Changing the ID returned 200.

Prefer:

The API did not enforce object-level authorisation for order resources. A session authenticated as controlled Account A could request the identifier of an order belonging to controlled Account B and receive the protected order information.

docs.title: Horizontal Authorisation
docs.text:
User A
  |
  X
  |
User B Resource

Test whether one user can access another user's equivalent resources.

docs.title: Vertical Authorisation
docs.text:
Standard User
     |
     X
     |
Administrative Function

Test whether lower-privileged accounts can access functions reserved for privileged roles.

docs.title: Function-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Do not test only links visible in the UI.

Capture the actual administrative request with an authorised admin test account, then determine how the application responds when the same controlled function is requested under a lower-privileged test account.

docs.title: Unauthenticated Testing
docs.text:
Remove:

Cookie

Authorization header

Session token

and resend the protected request.

Determine whether the endpoint still exposes protected functionality or data.

docs.title: Method Testing
docs.text:
Suppose:

GET /api/profile/1001

is authorised correctly.

Where relevant and safe, determine whether other supported methods apply equivalent controls:

POST

PUT

PATCH

DELETE

Do not use destructive methods against real data without explicit authorisation.

docs.title: API Testing
docs.text:
Burp works especially well with:

REST

JSON

GraphQL

SOAP

Custom HTTP APIs

docs.title: JSON Request
docs.text:
POST /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "displayName": "Test User"
}

Review:

Input validation

Authorisation

Unexpected fields

Server-side validation

Error handling

Object ownership

docs.title: Hidden JSON Fields
docs.text:
Suppose the normal client sends:

{
  "displayName": "Test User"
}

Server response contains:

{
  "displayName": "Test User",
  "role": "user"
}

Do not automatically assume sending:

{
  "role": "admin"
}

will be accepted.

If testing mass assignment in an authorised environment, use controlled accounts and safe properties, and validate server-side behaviour rather than relying on the presence of a field name.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
Common endpoint patterns:

/graphql

/api/graphql

A GraphQL request may resemble:

POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "{ currentUser { id username } }"
}

Review:

Authentication

Object authorisation

Field-level authorisation

Error handling

Introspection policy

Query complexity controls

See the detailed GraphQL Notes.

docs.title: HTTP Headers
docs.text:
Useful headers to review:

Host

Origin

Referer

Authorization

Cookie

Content-Type

Accept

X-Forwarded-For

X-Forwarded-Host

Forwarded

X-Original-URL

X-Rewrite-URL

The presence of proxy-related headers does not itself imply a bypass.

docs.title: Host Header Testing
docs.text:
Baseline:

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com

Controlled modification:

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: test.example.invalid

Observe:

Status

Redirects

Absolute URLs

Password-reset links

Cache behaviour

Backend routing

A changed response alone does not prove a Host header vulnerability.

docs.title: CORS Testing
docs.text:
Baseline request:

GET /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Origin: https://app.example.com
Cookie: session=<value>

Controlled origin:

Origin: https://example.invalid

Review:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials

Vary

docs.title: CORS Interpretation
docs.text:
A reflected origin is not automatically exploitable.

Determine:

Can credentials be included?

Does the browser permit the response to be read?

Does the endpoint return sensitive information?

Is the origin actually trusted?

Does the behaviour apply to authenticated requests?

docs.title: Preflight
docs.text:
Example:

OPTIONS /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Origin: https://example.invalid
Access-Control-Request-Method: GET
Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization

Review the server response.

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
When testing state-changing requests, determine:

Does the request depend on cookies?

Is there a CSRF token?

Is the token validated?

Is SameSite relevant?

Does Origin/Referer validation exist?

Can a cross-site request produce the state change?

Do not conclude CSRF solely because a token is absent.

docs.title: Open Redirect
docs.text:
Example:

GET /redirect?next=/dashboard HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com

Controlled modification:

next=https://example.invalid/

Review:

Location header

Validation

Allowed destinations

URL parsing behaviour

See Open Redirect.

docs.title: File Upload
docs.text:
Capture a normal authorised upload.

Example:

POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=...

...
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="test.txt"
Content-Type: text/plain

Authorised assessment test file
...

Review:

Filename handling

Content-Type validation

Extension validation

Storage location

Download behaviour

Authorisation

Metadata handling

docs.title: Safe Upload Baseline
docs.text:
Start with a harmless file:

test.txt

Establish:

Upload succeeds?

Where is it stored?

Can it be downloaded?

Who can access it?

Is filename changed?

Is Content-Type changed?

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Example application request:

GET /download?file=report.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com

First determine how the application normally identifies files.

Testing should focus on controlled files and the authorised environment.

See Path Traversal.

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
Server-side request functionality may appear in:

URL previews

Webhook configuration

Import-by-URL

Image fetchers

PDF generators

Integrations

Callback configuration

A controlled test should answer:

Did the application server make the request?

Was only DNS resolution performed?

Was an HTTP request received?

Which source IP connected?

Which protocol was used?

docs.title: Collaborator
docs.text:
Burp Collaborator can support detection of out-of-band interactions in authorised assessments.

Typical workflow:

Collaborator Payload
       |
       v
Controlled Input
       |
       v
Application Processes Input
       |
       v
DNS / HTTP Interaction?
       |
       v
Collaborator

docs.title: Collaborator Interpretation
docs.text:
Suppose you observe:

DNS interaction only

This supports:

Some component attempted to resolve the supplied hostname.

It does not necessarily prove:

The application performed an HTTP request.

Internal resources are reachable.

Sensitive data can be retrieved.

docs.title: HTTP Interaction
docs.text:
If Collaborator records:

DNS
+
HTTP request

this is stronger evidence that an HTTP-capable component attempted a server-side request.

Still determine:

Which component made it?

What source IP was used?

What input triggered it?

Can the behaviour be reproduced?

What destinations/protocols are permitted?

What security consequence follows?

docs.title: Collaborator Evidence
docs.text:
Capture:

Payload

Request containing payload

Interaction timestamp

Interaction type

Source IP

DNS details

HTTP request where present

Correlation ID

docs.title: Intruder
docs.text:
Intruder automates repeated requests with controlled variations.

Useful legitimate assessment cases include:

Parameter enumeration

Identifier variation

Header comparison

Input boundary testing

Response comparison

Content discovery

Be cautious with:

Authentication attempts

Account recovery

MFA

Expensive API operations

State-changing endpoints

docs.title: Intruder Workflow
docs.text:
Baseline Request
      |
      v
Send to Intruder
      |
      v
Choose Positions
      |
      v
Define Payloads
      |
      v
Control Request Rate
      |
      v
Run
      |
      v
Sort Responses
      |
      v
Investigate Outliers

docs.title: Payload Positions
docs.text:
Intruder marks positions using:

§value§

Example:

GET /api/items/§1001§ HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com

Only mark the value that should vary.

docs.title: Response Analysis
docs.text:
Useful Intruder columns include:

Status

Length

Words

Lines

Time

Error

Custom grep results

Outliers can indicate interesting behaviour but require manual validation.

docs.title: Response Length
docs.text:
Example:

1001 -> 200 -> 842 bytes
1002 -> 403 -> 120 bytes
1003 -> 403 -> 120 bytes
1004 -> 200 -> 915 bytes

The 1004 response deserves investigation.

It does not automatically mean:

Authorisation bypass confirmed.

docs.title: Intruder Rate
docs.text:
Before automated testing consider:

Application capacity

Production impact

Rate limiting

Account lockout

Monitoring

Rules of engagement

Use the minimum request volume needed to answer the assessment question.

docs.title: Authentication and Intruder
docs.text:
Do not start credential attacks simply because Intruder supports repeated requests.

Before any authentication automation establish:

Explicit authorisation

Test accounts

Lockout policy

Allowed request rate

Monitoring expectations

Stop conditions

docs.title: Decoder
docs.text:
Decoder helps transform data between common encodings.

Common uses:

URL encoding

Base64

Hex

HTML encoding

docs.title: Example Base64
docs.text:
Input:

dGVzdA==

Decode:

test

Encoding is not encryption.

docs.title: URL Encoding
docs.text:
Example:

Test Value

may become:

Test%20Value

Understand where decoding occurs:

Browser

Proxy

Web server

Framework

Application

docs.title: Multiple Decoding Layers
docs.text:
A value may pass through several parsers:

Client
  |
  v
Proxy
  |
  v
Web Server
  |
  v
Framework
  |
  v
Application

Unexpected behaviour can result from different decoding stages.

docs.title: Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer helps identify differences between:

Responses

Requests

Tokens

Application output

Useful for:

Authorisation comparisons

Authentication responses

Error messages

Different user roles

Different backend responses

docs.title: Two-Account Comparer Workflow
docs.text:
Account A Response
       |
       v
Comparer
       ^
       |
Account B Response

This can highlight differences that are difficult to spot manually.

docs.title: Compare Baseline vs Modified
docs.text:
Baseline
   |
   v
Comparer
   ^
   |
Modified

Then determine whether the difference is security relevant.

docs.title: Sequencer
docs.text:
Sequencer analyses the quality of tokens whose unpredictability matters.

Potential candidates:

Session identifiers

CSRF tokens

Password reset tokens

Other security-sensitive values

Only test tokens generated for authorised assessment accounts.

docs.title: Sequencer Workflow
docs.text:
Identify Token
     |
     v
Determine Security Purpose
     |
     v
Collect Sufficient Samples
     |
     v
Sequencer Analysis
     |
     v
Interpret Carefully

Statistical output should not be translated directly into a vulnerability without considering how the token is generated and used.

docs.title: Organizer
docs.text:
Organizer can help preserve important requests during a large assessment.

Useful categories:

Potential Finding

Needs Validation

Interesting Endpoint

Authentication

Authorisation

API

Upload

Business Logic

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Add notes to important requests such as:

Account A baseline

Account B object

Admin-only endpoint

Potential IDOR - needs ownership confirmation

Interesting 500 response

This reduces rework later.

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
Modern applications may use WebSockets for:

Chat

Notifications

Live dashboards

Trading interfaces

Administrative consoles

Real-time APIs

docs.title: WebSocket History
docs.text:
Burp can display WebSocket messages passing through the proxy.

Review:

Connection establishment

Authentication

Message structure

Object identifiers

Authorisation

Server responses

docs.title: WebSocket Security Model
docs.text:
Do not assume:

Authenticated WebSocket
        |
        v
Every Message Authorised

Individual messages may still require server-side authorisation.

docs.title: WebSocket Testing
docs.text:
Controlled approach:

Account A Connection
       |
       v
Normal Message
       |
       v
Baseline Response
       |
       v
Modify Object Identifier
       |
       v
Observe Server Behaviour

docs.title: Scanner
docs.text:
Burp Scanner is available in Burp Suite Professional.

It can assist with detecting classes of web vulnerabilities.

Automated scanner output should be treated as:

Scanner Observation
       |
       v
Review Request
       |
       v
Review Response
       |
       v
Understand Detection Logic
       |
       v
Manual Validation
       |
       v
Security Conclusion

docs.title: Do Not Report Scanner Output Blindly
docs.text:
Automated findings may be:

True positive

False positive

Informational

Context-dependent

Duplicate

Not exploitable

Manual validation remains important.

docs.title: Passive vs Active Scanning
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Passive
   |
   v
Observe Existing Traffic

Active
   |
   v
Send Additional Test Requests

Active scanning may:

Generate substantial traffic

Modify application state

Trigger monitoring

Reach sensitive endpoints

Use it according to scope and rules of engagement.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
Burp can be extended through the BApp Store.

Useful categories include:

Authorisation testing

Request manipulation

API testing

HTTP request smuggling

JWT analysis

GraphQL

Logging

Response comparison

docs.title: Extension Safety
docs.text:
Extensions can:

Read traffic

Modify traffic

Generate requests

Store sensitive data

Connect to external services

Before installing an extension, understand:

What data it accesses

Whether it sends data externally

Whether it generates requests

Whether it is actively maintained

Whether the engagement permits it

docs.title: Useful Extension - Autorize
docs.text:
Autorize can assist with authorisation testing by comparing requests under different authentication contexts.

Conceptually:

Privileged Request
       |
       v
Repeat With Lower-Privilege Context
       |
       v
Compare

Manual confirmation is still required.

docs.title: Useful Extension - AuthMatrix
docs.text:
AuthMatrix can help model:

Users

Roles

Requests

Expected permissions

This is useful for complex role-based applications.

docs.title: Useful Extension - Logger++
docs.text:
Logger++ can provide enhanced HTTP logging and filtering.

Useful for:

Large assessments

Traffic review

Search

Filtering

Request history

docs.title: Useful Extension - JWT Editor
docs.text:
JWT Editor can assist with JWT inspection and controlled testing.

Review JWTs for:

Header

Claims

Signature

Key selection

Expiration

Issuer

Audience

Authorisation use

See JWT Notes.

docs.title: Useful Extension - HTTP Request Smuggler
docs.text:
PortSwigger's HTTP Request Smuggler extension can support authorised HTTP desynchronisation testing.

This is specialised testing that should only be performed when:

In scope

Operational impact understood

Testing method understood

Request volume controlled

See HTTP Request Smuggling.

docs.title: Useful Extension - Param Miner
docs.text:
Param Miner can help identify:

Hidden parameters

Headers

Cookies

Cache-related input

Automated discovery results still require validation.

docs.title: Useful Extension - Turbo Intruder
docs.text:
Turbo Intruder supports specialised high-performance request workflows.

It can generate substantial traffic.

Use it only when:

Necessary

Explicitly authorised

Rate understood

Impact understood

Stop conditions defined

docs.title: Extension Workflow
docs.text:
Install Extension
      |
      v
Understand Behaviour
      |
      v
Configure Scope
      |
      v
Use Against Controlled Target
      |
      v
Review Generated Requests
      |
      v
Manually Validate Results

docs.title: Content Discovery
docs.text:
Burp can assist with identifying application endpoints through:

Normal browsing

Site map

JavaScript requests

API traffic

Scanner observations

Extensions

Combine this with the Web Application Security Cheatsheet.

docs.title: JavaScript Analysis
docs.text:
Review JavaScript responses for:

API paths

Route names

Parameter names

Feature flags

Internal references

Source maps

Client-side validation

Do not automatically report every internal-looking string as sensitive information.

docs.title: Search HTTP History
docs.text:
Search for terms such as:

/admin

/api/

/graphql

token

Authorization

password

redirect

upload

download

debug

Use this as a discovery technique, not as proof of a vulnerability.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Interesting responses include:

400

401

403

404

405

409

415

429

500

502

503

Pay particular attention to differences between baseline and modified requests.

docs.title: 500 Responses
docs.text:
A server error may indicate:

Unhandled input

Application exception

Backend failure

Parsing error

Unexpected state

It does not automatically prove exploitable behaviour.

docs.title: Sensitive Error Information
docs.text:
Review error responses for unnecessary disclosure such as:

Stack traces

Filesystem paths

Internal hostnames

Database details

Framework information

Source code fragments

Determine whether the disclosed information creates meaningful security impact.

docs.title: Response Length
docs.text:
Length differences are useful signals.

Example:

Baseline: 403 / 120 bytes
Modified: 200 / 842 bytes

This is worth investigation.

But:

Different length

does not equal:

Vulnerability.

docs.title: Status Codes
docs.text: Code General Meaning Assessment Question 200 Success Was the requester authorised? 201 Created Was creation permitted? 204 Success, no body Did an authorised state change occur? 301 Permanent redirect Where is the client redirected? 302 Redirect Is the destination expected? 307 Redirect preserving method Is method/body preserved appropriately? 308 Permanent redirect preserving method Is destination expected? 400 Bad request Does the error disclose internals? 401 Authentication required/failed Is authentication consistently enforced? 403 Forbidden Is authorisation consistently enforced? 404 Not found Is existence intentionally hidden? 405 Method not allowed Are other methods handled differently? 415 Unsupported media type Which content types are accepted? 429 Rate limited How is the control scoped? 500 Server error Is sensitive diagnostic information exposed?

docs.title: Response Comparison
docs.text:
When testing security controls, compare:

Length

Headers

Body

Timing

Cookies

Redirects

Application state

Do not rely on only one indicator.

docs.title: Business Logic Testing
docs.text:
Burp is particularly valuable for business-logic testing because requests can be replayed outside the normal UI sequence.

Map:

Step 1
  |
  v
Step 2
  |
  v
Step 3
  |
  v
Final Action

Then ask:

Can a step be skipped?

Can a step be repeated?

Can requests be reordered?

Is server-side state validated?

Does one user control another user's workflow?

Are important values trusted from the client?

docs.title: Business Logic Baseline
docs.text:
Document the legitimate workflow before modifying it.

Example:

Add Item
   |
   v
Review Cart
   |
   v
Confirm Address
   |
   v
Confirm Order

Then test only safe, controlled deviations.

docs.title: Client-Side Controls
docs.text:
A browser may prevent:

Negative values

Unexpected characters

Disabled options

Hidden fields

Role selections

Burp allows the raw request to be examined.

The security question is:

Does the server enforce the same security rule?

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Controlled testing can compare repeated requests.

Possible response:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 60

This demonstrates some rate-limiting behaviour.

It does not prove the control is sufficient across:

Accounts

IPs

Sessions

Endpoints

Distributed sources

docs.title: Cache Behaviour
docs.text:
Review headers such as:

Cache-Control

Age

Vary

ETag

Via

X-Cache

Names vary across infrastructure.

Cache testing should use controlled requests because shared caches can affect other users.

docs.title: Request Smuggling
docs.text:
HTTP request smuggling/desynchronisation testing is specialised.

Before testing establish:

Reverse proxy architecture

Scope

Production impact

Request volume

Safe endpoint

Stop conditions

Do not blindly send copied desynchronisation payloads to production applications.

docs.title: Reporting Example - IDOR/BOLA
docs.text:
Weak:

Changing id=1001 to id=2001 worked.

Better:

The order API did not enforce object-level authorisation. A session authenticated as controlled Account A could request order 2001, which belonged to controlled Account B, and the API returned Account B's protected order information. The issue was reproduced using both controlled accounts.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Missing Cookie Attribute
docs.text:
Weak:

HttpOnly is missing.

Better:

The application's session cookie was issued without the HttpOnly attribute. This allows browser-side JavaScript to access the session identifier. The practical risk depends on whether script execution can occur in the application's origin and should therefore be considered together with the application's XSS exposure and session design.

docs.title: Reporting Example - CORS
docs.text:
Weak:

Origin is reflected.

Better:

The API reflected an untrusted Origin value and permitted credentialed cross-origin access to an authenticated endpoint returning protected account information. Browser-based validation confirmed that a page hosted on the controlled external origin could read the authenticated response.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: Retest the underlying security control rather than only checking whether the exact original request changed.

docs.title: IDOR Retest
docs.text:
Before:

After:

Account A -> Account B Object -> Denied

docs.text: Test Expected A -> A object Allowed A -> B object Denied B -> B object Allowed B -> A object Denied Unauthenticated -> protected object Denied

docs.text:

docs.text:
Avoid unsafe modifications to:

Financial records

Administrative configuration

Shared resources

Prefer dedicated assessment accounts and test data.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Not Recording Account Context
docs.text:
A request is much less useful as evidence if you cannot later determine:

Which account sent it?

Which role did it have?

Proxy port

VPN

DNS

docs.title: Troubleshooting - HTTPS Certificate Warning
docs.text:
When using a separate assessment browser, ensure the Burp CA certificate is correctly installed for that dedicated browser/profile.

Do not weaken certificate validation outside the assessment environment unnecessarily.

docs.text:

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Too Much HTTP History
docs.text:
Use:

Search

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Session Keeps Expiring
docs.text:
Check:

Cookie changed?

CSRF token changed?

Access token expired?

Refresh token required?

Application requires workflow state?

Content-Type

Origin

Referer

Repeater is your validation workspace

HTTP history helps you discover interesting requests. Repeater is where those requests should become controlled experiments with a baseline, one deliberate modification, a comparison and a defensible interpretation.

Use two controlled accounts for authorisation testing

A two-account model gives you known resource ownership and expected access boundaries. This produces much stronger IDOR/BOLA evidence than guessing whether an identifier belongs to another real user.

Use automation to find candidates

Scanner, Intruder and extensions can help locate interesting behaviour. Move important candidates into Repeater and manually establish the security consequence before reporting them.

Do not treat Collaborator DNS interactions as full SSRF

A DNS interaction demonstrates that hostname resolution occurred somewhere in the processing chain. An HTTP interaction provides stronger evidence of server-side HTTP behaviour, but the actual security impact still requires further validation.

Keep third-party systems out of scope

Burp will often display requests to analytics providers, identity platforms, payment services, CDNs and other external systems. Their presence in HTTP history does not make those systems part of the authorised assessment scope.

docs.title: Command Injection Cheatsheet
docs.text:
OS command injection occurs when attacker-controlled input reaches an operating-system command execution mechanism without being safely separated from the command itself.

A simplified vulnerable flow is:

User Input
    |
    v
Application
    |
    v
Command String
    |
    v
Shell
    |
    v
Operating System

Example concept:

User supplies:
example.com

Application builds:
ping -c 1 example.com

If the application constructs a shell command directly from user input, the security boundary becomes:

DATA
 |
 v
COMMAND STRING

The important question is:

Can attacker-controlled data change the structure or meaning
of the command executed by the operating system?

Authorised Security Testing

Perform command injection testing only against systems explicitly included in the assessment scope. Start with harmless commands that produce deterministic output or short timing changes. Do not use reverse shells, persistence, destructive commands, credential access or system modification simply to prove command execution.

docs.title: Command Injection vs Argument Injection
docs.text: These are related but different.

docs.title: Command Injection
docs.text:
Command injection changes the command structure.

Conceptually:

Expected:

tool USER_INPUT

becomes:

tool value ; second-command

docs.title: Argument Injection
docs.text:
Argument injection occurs when attacker-controlled data remains part of the intended process invocation but introduces unintended command-line options.

Conceptually:

tool USER_INPUT

becomes:

tool --unexpected-option

No second shell command is necessarily required.

docs.title: Shell vs Direct Process Execution
docs.text: This distinction is extremely important.

docs.title: Shell Execution
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
/bin/sh -c "command USER_INPUT"

The shell interprets metacharacters.

docs.title: Direct Process Execution
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
execve()
    |
    v
["command", "USER_INPUT"]

There may be no shell parsing.

This substantially reduces classic shell injection risk, although argument injection may still be relevant.

docs.title: First Question: Is an OS Command Used?
docs.text:
Do not assume a network diagnostic feature necessarily calls:

ping

The application may use:

Native networking library

Framework API

DNS library

HTTP client

Source review is especially valuable here.

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Suppose the application exposes:

POST /api/diagnostics HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "host": "127.0.0.1"
}

docs.title: Baseline Response
docs.text:
Representative result:

PING 127.0.0.1
64 bytes from 127.0.0.1

This suggests that a system utility may be involved.

It does not prove command injection.

docs.title: Do Not Guess OS From One String
docs.text:
A Linux-hosted application could call a Windows service and vice versa.

Use multiple pieces of evidence.

docs.title: Harmless Marker Commands
docs.text: Where command execution testing is authorised, use commands with minimal impact.

docs.title: Unix-Like Systems
docs.text:
Examples of low-impact commands include:

id

whoami

printf CMD_TEST_7f3a9

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Low-impact examples include:

whoami

or:

echo CMD_TEST_7f3a9

docs.text:
A marker such as:

CMD_TEST_7f3a9

makes response correlation easier.

docs.title: Basic Unix Shell Separators
docs.text:
A semicolon can separate commands in many Unix-like shells:

;

Conceptually:

expected-command input ; harmless-command

docs.title: Logical AND
docs.text:
&&

The second command normally executes only if the first succeeds.

docs.title: Logical OR
docs.text:
||

The second command normally executes if the first command fails.

docs.title: Pipe
docs.text:
|

The output of one command can become input to another.

docs.title: Background Operator
docs.text:
&

Shell behaviour varies depending on placement and environment.

docs.title: Newline
docs.text:
A newline can sometimes separate commands when the input reaches a shell.

Encoding may be relevant when the input travels through HTTP parameters.

docs.title: Controlled Testing Principle
docs.text:
Start with:

One operator

One harmless marker

One request

Do not spray dozens of command separators before understanding the application.

docs.title: Example Controlled Test
docs.text:
Baseline input:

127.0.0.1

Candidate concept:

127.0.0.1 ; printf CMD_TEST_7f3a9

docs.title: Representative Positive Response
docs.text:
PING 127.0.0.1
...

CMD_TEST_7f3a9

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: If the unique marker appears because the second command executed, this provides strong evidence that attacker-controlled input changed the shell command structure.

docs.title: Repeat the Test
docs.text:
Use another unique marker:

CMD_TEST_91bc2

A repeatable result reduces ambiguity.

docs.title: Command Substitution
docs.text:
Unix-like shells may support command substitution using:

$(...)

and, in some shells:

`...`

docs.title: Example Concept
docs.text: value$(printf CMD_TEST_7f3a9)

docs.title: Applicability
docs.text: Command substitution matters only if the user input reaches a shell that supports the syntax.

docs.title: Do Not Assume Bash
docs.text:
The application may invoke:

/bin/sh

dash

bash

zsh

busybox sh

another shell

docs.title: Quoting Context
docs.text:
Input may appear inside:

Unquoted argument

Single quotes

Double quotes

Command substitution

Environment variable

Understanding the surrounding command matters.

docs.title: Example Unquoted Context
docs.text:
Application:

ping -c 1 USER_INPUT

docs.title: Example Double-Quoted Context
docs.text:
Application:

ping -c 1 "USER_INPUT"

docs.title: Example Single-Quoted Context
docs.text:
Application:

ping -c 1 'USER_INPUT'

docs.title: Why Context Matters
docs.text: Different shell characters have different meaning depending on quoting.

docs.title: White-Box Review
docs.text: If source is available, determine the exact command construction rather than blindly trying payload variations.

docs.title: Blind Command Injection
docs.text:
Sometimes the command executes but its output is not returned.

Model:

Input
  |
  v
OS Command
  |
  v
Execution
  |
  X
No Output Returned

docs.title: Blind Validation Methods
docs.text:
Common low-impact methods include:

Timing

Controlled DNS callback

Controlled HTTP callback

Use only assessment-controlled infrastructure.

docs.title: Timing Validation
docs.text:
A short controlled delay can demonstrate execution when response content is unavailable.

Conceptually:

Baseline:
~200 ms

Candidate:
~3 seconds

docs.title: Timing Evidence Requires Repetition
docs.text:
Network latency varies.

Use:

Multiple baseline requests

Multiple candidate requests

Consistent timing difference

docs.title: Do Not Use Excessive Delays
docs.text:
A few seconds is usually sufficient.

Avoid long sleeps that consume application workers unnecessarily.

docs.title: Timing Test Model
docs.text:
Baseline
   |
   v
Measure
   |
   v
Short Delay Candidate
   |
   v
Measure
   |
   v
Repeat

docs.title: Timing Is Supporting Evidence
docs.text:
A single slow request does not prove command execution.

Possible alternatives include:

Network latency

Backend timeout

Rate limiting

Database delay

Application load

docs.title: Out-of-Band Validation
docs.text: Where authorised, a command may cause a harmless lookup or request to assessment-controlled infrastructure.

docs.title: OOB Model
docs.text:
Application
    |
    v
OS Command
    |
    v
Controlled Domain

docs.title: Use Unique Identifiers
docs.text:
Example:

cmd-7f3a9.assessment.example

Then repeat with:

cmd-91bc2.assessment.example

docs.title: DNS vs HTTP
docs.text:
DNS interaction supports:

Hostname resolution occurred.

HTTP interaction provides evidence that an HTTP client or command reached the controlled server.

Determine which process actually caused the interaction.

docs.title: Do Not Overclaim OOB Evidence
docs.text:
A DNS callback alone does not necessarily establish:

Interactive shell access

Arbitrary file read

Privilege escalation

docs.title: Windows Command Processing
docs.text:
Windows applications may invoke:

cmd.exe

PowerShell

Direct process APIs

docs.title: cmd.exe
docs.text:
Common command separators include:

&

&&

||

Exact behaviour depends on command context.

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
PowerShell has its own parsing and command semantics.

Do not assume that a payload designed for:

cmd.exe

will behave identically in:

powershell.exe

pwsh.exe

docs.title: Determine the Interpreter
docs.text:
Source or process information may reveal:

cmd.exe /c

powershell.exe -Command

/bin/sh -c

bash -c

docs.title: Command Injection vs PowerShell Injection
docs.text: If attacker-controlled input is inserted into a PowerShell script or command string, analyse the PowerShell parsing context specifically.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Shell commands may use environment variables.

Unix examples:

$PATH

$HOME

Windows examples:

%PATH%

%TEMP%

PowerShell:

$env:PATH

Do not use environment manipulation unless it is relevant to the actual source-to-sink flow.

docs.title: PATH Resolution
docs.text:
A process invocation using:

tool

rather than:

/usr/bin/tool

may depend on PATH.

This can create separate execution risks in certain local or privileged contexts.

It is not automatically remote command injection.

docs.title: Argument Injection
docs.text:
Consider:

Application executes:
tool USER_INPUT

If the process is launched safely without a shell, an input beginning with:

-

may still be interpreted as a command-line option by the called program.

docs.title: Example Concept
docs.text: tool --unexpected-option

docs.title: Argument Injection Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Does the program accept dangerous options?

Can options specify files?

Can options specify configuration?

Can options trigger network requests?

Can options execute helper programs?

docs.title: End-of-Options Marker
docs.text:
Many Unix utilities support:

--

to mark the end of command-line options.

Example concept:

tool -- USER_INPUT

This can help prevent attacker-controlled values from being interpreted as options when supported by the utility.

docs.title: Do Not Assume Every Tool Supports --
docs.text: Verify the called program's documentation.

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
If a parameter should contain an IP address, validate it as an IP address.

Do not merely remove:

;

|

&

docs.title: Example Business Constraint
docs.text:
Expected:

IPv4 or IPv6 address

Then the application should parse the input as an IP address rather than attempt to sanitise arbitrary shell syntax.

docs.title: Allowlist Model
docs.text:
User Input
    |
    v
Parse Expected Data Type
    |
    +--> Valid -> Continue
    |
    +--> Invalid -> Reject

docs.title: Shell Escaping
docs.text:
Shell escaping is difficult to implement correctly across:

Shells

Platforms

Quoting contexts

Encodings

The preferred remediation is usually:

Do not invoke a shell.

docs.title: Direct Process Invocation
docs.text:
Preferred:

Application
    |
    v
Executable + Argument Array
    |
    v
Operating System

rather than:

Application
    |
    v
String Concatenation
    |
    v
Shell

docs.title: Python Vulnerable Pattern
docs.text:
import os

host = request.args.get("host")

os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)

docs.title: Source-to-Sink
docs.text:
request.args["host"]
        |
        v
String Concatenation
        |
        v
os.system()

docs.title: Python Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'os\.system|os\.popen|subprocess\.|commands\.' -g '*.py' .

docs.title: Python shell=True
docs.text:
High-priority candidate:

subprocess.run(
    command,
    shell=True
)

docs.title: Search
docs.text: rg -n -C 5 'shell\s*=\s*True' -g '*.py' .

docs.title: Safer Python Pattern
docs.text:
Prefer an argument list:

subprocess.run(
    ["/usr/bin/ping", "-c", "1", host],
    check=True
)

with strict validation of host.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Using an argument array substantially reduces shell injection risk because the input is passed as an argument rather than interpreted by a shell.

Argument-specific risks should still be considered.

docs.title: Node.js Child Processes
docs.text:
Common APIs include:

exec()

execSync()

spawn()

spawnSync()

execFile()

execFileSync()

docs.title: Node.js Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'child_process|exec\(|execSync|spawn\(|spawnSync|execFile' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

docs.title: Node.js High-Risk Pattern
docs.text: exec("ping -c 1 " + req.query.host);

docs.title: Source-to-Sink
docs.text:
req.query.host
      |
      v
String Concatenation
      |
      v
exec()

docs.title: Node.js Safer Pattern
docs.text:
Conceptually:

spawn("/usr/bin/ping", ["-c", "1", host]);

with validation of host.

docs.title: exec vs spawn
docs.text:
The important question is not simply which API name appears.

Review whether:

A shell is invoked

A command string is built

Arguments are passed separately

docs.title: Java Command Execution
docs.text:
Common APIs:

Runtime.getRuntime().exec()

ProcessBuilder

docs.title: Java Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder' -g '*.java' .

docs.title: Java Candidate
docs.text:
Runtime.getRuntime().exec(
    "ping " + host
);

docs.title: ProcessBuilder
docs.text:
A safer structure generally passes arguments separately:

new ProcessBuilder(
    "ping",
    "-c",
    "1",
    host
);

The application must still validate the intended data type and consider argument injection.

docs.title: .NET Process Execution
docs.text:
Common APIs include:

Process.Start

ProcessStartInfo

docs.title: .NET Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'Process\.Start|ProcessStartInfo' -g '*.cs' .

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
var psi = new ProcessStartInfo();
psi.FileName = "/bin/sh";
psi.Arguments = "-c \"ping " + host + "\"";

docs.title: High-Risk Signal
docs.text:
Look for:

cmd.exe /c

powershell.exe

pwsh.exe

/bin/sh -c

bash -c

combined with attacker-controlled strings.

docs.title: PHP Command Execution
docs.text:
Potential sinks include:

system()

exec()

shell_exec()

passthru()

popen()

proc_open()

docs.title: PHP Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'system\(|exec\(|shell_exec|passthru|popen|proc_open' -g '*.php' .

docs.title: PHP Candidate
docs.text: system("ping -c 1 " . $_GET["host"]);

docs.title: PHP Source-to-Sink
docs.text:
$_GET["host"]
      |
      v
Concatenation
      |
      v
system()

docs.title: Ruby Command Execution
docs.text:
Potential sinks include:

system()

exec()

Open3

backticks

docs.title: Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'system\(|exec\(|Open3|IO\.popen' -g '*.rb' .

docs.title: Go Command Execution
docs.text:
Go commonly uses:

os/exec

docs.title: Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'os/exec|exec\.Command|exec\.CommandContext' -g '*.go' .

docs.title: Go Safer Pattern
docs.text:
exec.Command(
    "/usr/bin/ping",
    "-c",
    "1",
    host,
)

This passes arguments separately rather than using a shell command string.

docs.title: Dangerous Go Pattern
docs.text:
A high-risk design may explicitly invoke:

sh -c

with user-controlled command content.

docs.title: Search Shell Invocation
docs.text: rg -ni 'sh.*-c|bash.*-c|cmd\.exe|powershell' .

docs.title: Generic Source Review Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'exec|system|shell|spawn|ProcessBuilder|ProcessStartInfo|os\.system|subprocess|child_process' src/

docs.title: Search With Context
docs.text: rg -n -C 8 'os\.system|shell=True|child_process|ProcessBuilder|ProcessStartInfo|shell_exec|exec\.Command' src/

docs.title: Source Review Workflow
docs.text:
Find Command Sink
      |
      v
Identify Executable
      |
      v
Shell Involved?
      |
      v
Identify Arguments
      |
      v
Trace User Input
      |
      v
Validation?
      |
      v
Can Structure Change?
      |
      v
Can Arguments Change Meaning?

docs.title: High-Priority Source Pattern
docs.text:
HTTP Input
    |
    v
String Concatenation
    |
    v
Shell Command

docs.title: Lower-Risk Pattern
docs.text:
HTTP Input
    |
    v
Strict Data Validation
    |
    v
Argument Array
    |
    v
Direct Process API

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Proxy
  |
  v
Identify Candidate Parameter
  |
  v
Send to Repeater
  |
  v
Baseline
  |
  v
Harmless Marker
  |
  +--> Output?
  |
  +--> Timing?
  |
  +--> OOB?
  |
  v
Repeat
  |
  v
Evidence

docs.title: Repeater Baseline
docs.text:
POST /api/diagnostics HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "host": "127.0.0.1"
}

docs.title: Controlled Modification
docs.text:
Conceptually:

{
  "host": "127.0.0.1 ; printf CMD_TEST_7f3a9"
}

Use syntax appropriate to the confirmed environment.

docs.title: Compare Responses
docs.text:
Record:

Status

Length

Body

Timing

Errors

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text: Useful when candidate responses differ subtly from baseline.

docs.title: Burp Intruder
docs.text:
Intruder can test a small controlled set of separators or input positions.

Do not use a huge command injection payload list by default.

docs.title: Collaborator
docs.text: For blind command injection, Burp Collaborator can provide controlled OOB evidence where outbound interaction testing is authorised.

docs.title: OOB Correlation
docs.text:
Use a different identifier for every request.

Example concept:

cmd-001

cmd-002

cmd-003

docs.title: curl Baseline
docs.text:
curl -i \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"host":"127.0.0.1"}' \
  'https://target.example/api/diagnostics'

docs.title: Shell Quoting Warning
docs.text:
When testing command syntax through curl, your local shell may interpret characters before curl sends them.

Use appropriate quoting so the intended bytes reach the target.

docs.title: Inspect Exact Request
docs.text: Burp Suite is often easier for command injection testing because the request can be edited without local shell interpretation.

docs.title: URL Parameters
docs.text:
Example:

curl -i \
  --get \
  --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1' \
  'https://target.example/diagnostics'

docs.title: URL Encoding
docs.text:
When testing metacharacters in query parameters, using:

--data-urlencode

can help ensure they are transmitted as parameter data.

docs.title: Error Messages
docs.text:
Command-related errors can provide useful clues.

Examples:

command not found

unknown option

invalid argument

No such file or directory

The system cannot find the file specified

docs.title: Shell Error
docs.text:
An error mentioning:

sh

bash

cmd.exe

PowerShell

may help identify the execution context.

docs.title: Utility Error
docs.text:
Example:

ping: invalid option

may indicate that user input reached the command as an argument.

This can support argument-injection analysis.

docs.title: Error Does Not Equal Exploitability
docs.text:
An unexpected utility error proves only that input influenced program behaviour.

Determine whether the influence crosses a meaningful security boundary.

docs.title: Input Filtering
docs.text:
Applications may block specific characters.

Examples:

;

|

&

docs.title: Character Blocking Is Not Root-Cause Remediation
docs.text:
A blacklist may be bypassable through:

Different syntax

Different interpreter behaviour

Encoding

Alternative execution paths

The preferred control is to avoid shell interpretation.

docs.title: Whitespace
docs.text:
Shells support several ways of separating tokens.

Do not build a finding around bypass tricks unless the underlying unsafe command construction has been established.

docs.title: Encoding Layers
docs.text:
Input may pass through:

URL decoder

JSON parser

Framework

Application validation

Shell

Understand where transformations occur.

docs.title: Double Encoding
docs.text:
Do not automatically try double encoding.

Use it when architecture suggests multiple decoding stages.

docs.title: Command Injection in File Names
docs.text:
File-processing functions may invoke external utilities with uploaded filenames.

Example flow:

Uploaded Filename
       |
       v
Image Converter Command
       |
       v
Shell

docs.title: Review Uploaded Filenames
docs.text:
Source code may contain:

convert " + filename

ffmpeg ... " + filename

unzip " + filename

docs.title: Safer Design
docs.text:
Use:

Generated storage filename

Argument array

No shell

docs.title: Command Injection in Git Integrations
docs.text:
Applications may execute utilities such as:

git

for repository operations.

Review whether attacker-controlled:

Repository name

Branch

Path

URL

Commit reference

becomes command-line input.

docs.title: Command Injection in Backup Features
docs.text:
Potential commands include:

tar

zip

gzip

database dump utilities

Review all user-controlled arguments.

docs.title: Command Injection in Network Tools
docs.text:
Common utilities include:

ping

traceroute

nslookup

dig

curl

wget

A network diagnostics feature should ideally use native APIs rather than constructing shell commands.

docs.title: Command Injection in Media Processing
docs.text:
Potential utilities:

ffmpeg

ImageMagick

GraphicsMagick

Review both:

Command construction

Parser vulnerabilities

as separate attack surfaces.

docs.title: Command Injection in PDF Generation
docs.text:
Applications sometimes invoke external document converters.

Potential architecture:

User Input
   |
   v
Document Generator
   |
   v
Command-Line Converter

docs.title: Command Injection in Admin Interfaces
docs.text:
Administrative functionality may expose powerful system-management operations.

Authentication does not make unsafe command construction acceptable.

docs.title: Privilege Context
docs.text:
Determine which account executes the command.

Examples:

www-data

app

nginx

IIS application pool identity

container user

service account

docs.title: Do Not Assume Root
docs.text: Command injection typically executes with the privileges of the application process.

docs.title: Container Context
docs.text:
If the application runs in a container:

Command Injection
      |
      v
Container Process

This does not automatically mean:

Host Command Execution

docs.title: Container Impact
docs.text:
Still assess:

Mounted secrets

Mounted volumes

Network access

Service credentials

Container privileges

docs.title: Cloud Environment
docs.text:
Command execution inside a cloud workload may expose additional resources depending on:

Workload identity

Instance role

Managed identity

Network access

Mounted credentials

Do not access cloud credentials unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Is Separate
docs.text:
A command injection finding should normally establish:

Application-level OS command execution

You do not need to escalate privileges to prove it.

docs.title: Do Not Add Persistence
docs.text: Persistence is not required for command injection validation.

docs.title: Do Not Deploy Reverse Shells by Default
docs.text:
A reverse shell usually adds little evidentiary value once arbitrary command execution has been safely demonstrated.

Prefer:

Unique marker

Identity command

Controlled timing

Controlled callback

docs.title: False Positive - Reflection
docs.text:
Input:

; CMD_TEST_7f3a9

may simply be reflected in the response.

That does not prove command execution.

docs.title: False Positive - Validation Error
docs.text:
A response such as:

Invalid host: ; CMD_TEST_7f3a9

shows input handling, not execution.

docs.title: False Positive - Timing
docs.text: One slow request is not sufficient evidence.

docs.title: False Positive - OOB Callback
docs.text:
Ensure the callback originated from the command execution path rather than:

URL validation

Application HTTP client

Security scanner

Monitoring component

docs.title: False Positive - Scanner Alert
docs.text: Automated scanner findings require manual validation.

docs.title: False Positive - Source Sink Without Reachability
docs.text:
Source review may reveal:

os.system(command)

but the command may use only trusted constants.

Trace actual attacker control.

docs.title: False Positive - Shell-Looking Code
docs.text:
Example:

subprocess.run(
    ["/usr/bin/tool", trusted_value]
)

is not equivalent to:

subprocess.run(
    "/usr/bin/tool " + user_value,
    shell=True
)

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Capture:

Finding ID

Endpoint

Method

Parameter

Authentication context

Baseline input

Candidate input

Operating system evidence

Interpreter evidence

Unique marker

Response output

Response timing

OOB interaction

Timestamp

Application privilege context if known

docs.title: Strong Output-Based Evidence
docs.text:
1. Establish baseline.

2. Submit harmless second command.

3. Unique marker appears in response.

4. Repeat with different marker.

5. Stop.

docs.title: Strong Blind Evidence
docs.text:
1. Establish timing baseline.

2. Submit short-delay candidate.

3. Observe repeatable delay.

4. Repeat baseline.

5. Repeat candidate.

6. Optionally correlate controlled OOB interaction.

7. Stop.

docs.title: Evidence Should Demonstrate Causality
docs.text:
The goal is:

Specific Input
     |
     v
Specific Execution Effect
     |
     v
Repeatable Observation

docs.title: Reporting Example - Output-Based Command Injection
docs.text: The host parameter in the network diagnostics endpoint is incorporated into an operating-system command that is executed through a shell. During testing, a harmless command separator followed by a unique marker command caused the marker CMD_TEST_7f3a9 to appear in the application response. Repeating the test with a second unique marker produced the corresponding output, confirming OS command injection.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Blind Command Injection
docs.text: The diagnostics endpoint incorporates attacker-controlled input into an operating-system command. Command output is not returned directly; however, introducing a short controlled delay caused a repeatable increase in response time compared with baseline requests. The behaviour was reproduced across multiple requests, supporting blind OS command injection.

docs.title: Reporting Example - OOB Command Injection
docs.text: A unique command-injection test caused the application environment to initiate a correlated request to assessment-controlled infrastructure. The interaction used a unique per-request identifier and was reproduced with a second identifier, confirming that attacker-controlled input reaches an operating-system command execution path.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Argument Injection
docs.text: The application invokes the external utility using attacker-controlled input as a command-line argument without restricting option-like values. Although no shell command separator was required, user input could introduce unintended options to the invoked utility. The demonstrated impact is therefore command-line argument injection rather than classic shell command injection.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Source Review
docs.text: User-controlled input from the host request parameter is concatenated into a command string passed to os.system(). No strict host validation or argument separation is performed before execution. This creates an OS command injection path because the shell interprets attacker-controlled command syntax.

docs.title: Remediation - Avoid Shell Execution
docs.text:
The preferred remediation is:

Do not construct shell commands from user input.

docs.title: Use Native APIs
docs.text:
Instead of:

Application
    |
    v
ping command

consider:

Application
    |
    v
Networking library

docs.title: Use Argument Arrays
docs.text:
If an external executable is genuinely required:

Executable

Argument 1

Argument 2

User Value

should be passed separately through a direct process API.

docs.title: Avoid
docs.text: "command " + user_input

docs.title: Prefer
docs.text:
Conceptually:

["command", "fixed-argument", validated_user_value]

docs.title: Strict Data Validation
docs.text:
Validate according to business meaning.

Examples:

IP address -> parse as IP address

Port -> integer within allowed range

Filename -> server-side mapping

Hostname -> defined hostname grammar

docs.title: Avoid Shell Escaping as Primary Defence
docs.text:
Escaping is fragile and interpreter-specific.

Removing the shell is safer.

docs.title: Fixed Executable Paths
docs.text:
Where practical, use explicit executable paths:

/usr/bin/ping

instead of relying unnecessarily on environment search paths.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text: The application should run with minimal operating-system permissions.

docs.title: Network Restrictions
docs.text:
If application workers do not need arbitrary outbound access, restrict it.

This can reduce the impact of command execution but does not fix command injection.

docs.title: Container Isolation
docs.text:
Use:

Non-root container user

Read-only filesystem where practical

Minimal capabilities

Restricted mounts

Network restrictions

as defence in depth.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Log security-relevant failures without recording sensitive user data unnecessarily.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: Retest the exact original input path.

docs.title: Retest Baseline
docs.text: Confirm legitimate functionality still works.

docs.title: Retest Original Separator
docs.text: The original injection string should no longer alter command structure.

docs.title: Retest Alternative Shell Syntax
docs.text: Where a shell has been removed entirely, alternative separators should have no command interpretation.

docs.title: Retest Argument Injection
docs.text: If direct process execution replaced shell execution, verify attacker-controlled values cannot introduce unsafe options to the called utility.

docs.title: Retest Timing
docs.text: The original short-delay technique should no longer affect response time beyond normal variation.

docs.title: Retest OOB
docs.text: No controlled DNS or HTTP interaction should occur from command injection attempts.

docs.title: Retest Errors
docs.text: Input should be rejected with an application-level validation error rather than reaching shell or utility parsing.

docs.title: Retest Source
docs.text:
Verify:

No shell command concatenation

Arguments passed separately

Strict validation present

docs.title: Root Cause Review
docs.text:
After finding one command injection path, search the entire codebase for other command execution sinks.

Python:

rg -ni 'os\.system|os\.popen|subprocess\.|shell\s*=\s*True' -g '*.py' .

Node.js:

rg -ni 'child_process|exec\(|execSync|spawn\(|execFile' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

Java:

rg -ni 'Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder' -g '*.java' .

.NET:

rg -ni 'Process\.Start|ProcessStartInfo' -g '*.cs' .

PHP:

rg -ni 'system\(|exec\(|shell_exec|passthru|popen|proc_open' -g '*.php' .

Ruby:

rg -ni 'system\(|exec\(|Open3|IO\.popen' -g '*.rb' .

Go:

rg -ni 'os/exec|exec\.Command|exec\.CommandContext' -g '*.go' .

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
The key question is not:

Does the parameter accept a semicolon?

It is:

CAN ATTACKER-CONTROLLED DATA
           |
           v
REACH AN OPERATING-SYSTEM EXECUTION SINK
           |
           v
AND CHANGE THE MEANING OF THE EXECUTED COMMAND?

A strong workflow is:

Identify Candidate Function
        |
        v
Establish Baseline
        |
        v
Determine Execution Mechanism
        |
        v
Identify Shell / Direct Process
        |
        v
Use Harmless Marker
        |
        v
Observe Output / Timing / OOB
        |
        v
Repeat
        |
        v
Determine Actual Privilege Context
        |
        v
Capture Evidence
        |
        v
Remove Unsafe Command Construction
        |
        v
Retest

For every command injection candidate ask:

Does the application actually execute an OS command?

Could the functionality use a native API instead?

Which executable is invoked?

Is a shell involved?

Which shell?

Does user input reach the command string?

Where is the user input placed?

Is it quoted?

Can the input change command structure?

Can the input introduce command-line options?

Is output returned?

Is the issue blind?

Can a short timing test establish execution?

Can a controlled callback establish execution?

Did the application itself generate the callback?

Can the result be reproduced?

What user executes the process?

Is the application containerised?

What privileges were actually demonstrated?

Am I confusing reflection with execution?

Am I confusing argument injection with shell injection?

Did I use the minimum command required to prove the issue?

Does remediation remove the shell?

Are arguments passed separately?

Is the input validated according to its business type?

Have equivalent execution sinks been reviewed?

The strongest conclusion is not:

A command separator changed the response.

It is:

CONTROLLED INPUT
      |
      v
COMMAND STRUCTURE CHANGED
      |
      v
UNIQUE EXECUTION EFFECT
      |
      v
REPEATABLE OBSERVATION
      |
      v
CONFIRMED COMMAND INJECTION
