docs.title: Related Notes
docs.text:
The deeper notes relevant to this cheatsheet are expected under:

docs/web/command-injection.md
docs/source-code-review/

Use the corresponding notes page for longer explanations and keep this cheatsheet as the operational assessment reference.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• PortSwigger Web Security Academy - OS Command Injection
  • OWASP Web Security Testing Guide - Testing for Command Injection
  • OWASP Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • CWE-78 - Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command

Prove execution, not payload acceptance

A semicolon being accepted or an error changing does not establish command injection. Prefer a unique harmless marker, a repeatable short timing effect or a correlated assessment-controlled callback.

Find out whether a shell exists

The difference between shell command + user input and a direct process call with an argument array is fundamental. Source review can eliminate a large amount of unnecessary payload guessing.

Separate command injection from argument injection

An attacker-controlled value becoming an unintended option to the intended executable is not necessarily shell command injection. Report the mechanism you actually demonstrate.

A reverse shell is unnecessary

Once a unique harmless command can be executed reliably, arbitrary command execution has been demonstrated. A reverse shell adds operational risk without normally adding meaningful evidence.

Do not fix command injection with a character blacklist

Blocking ;, | or & does not address unsafe command construction. Remove unnecessary shell invocation, pass arguments separately and strictly validate input according to its intended business type.

docs.title: Content Discovery Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Content discovery attempts to identify web resources that are not immediately visible through normal application navigation.

Common targets include:

Directories

Files

API endpoints

Administrative interfaces

Backup files

Configuration files

Development endpoints

Documentation

Legacy applications

Hidden functionality

Virtual hosts

Three commonly used tools are:

ffuf

Gobuster

feroxbuster

They overlap, but each has strengths.

ffuf
 |
 +--> Flexible fuzzing
 +--> Directories and files
 +--> Virtual hosts
 +--> Parameters
 +--> Values
 +--> Request templates
 +--> Powerful filtering

Gobuster
 |
 +--> Directory discovery
 +--> DNS discovery
 +--> Virtual hosts
 +--> Simple predictable CLI

feroxbuster
 |
 +--> Recursive content discovery
 +--> Automatic link extraction
 +--> Large application trees
 +--> Fast recursive enumeration

Authorised Security Testing

Content discovery can generate substantial numbers of HTTP requests. Only enumerate systems that are explicitly within scope. Configure request rates, recursion depth, wordlists and concurrency according to the rules of engagement and the capacity of the target.

docs.title: ffuf Directory Discovery
docs.text: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ

docs.title: ffuf File Extensions
docs.text: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -e .php,.html,.txt

docs.title: Gobuster Directory Discovery
docs.text: gobuster dir -u https://example.com/ -w wordlist.txt

docs.title: Gobuster Extensions
docs.text: gobuster dir -u https://example.com/ -w wordlist.txt -x php,html,txt

docs.title: feroxbuster
docs.text: feroxbuster -u https://example.com/

docs.title: feroxbuster With Wordlist
docs.text: feroxbuster -u https://example.com/ -w wordlist.txt

docs.title: ffuf Virtual Hosts
docs.text: ffuf -w subdomains.txt -u https://example.com/ -H "Host: FUZZ.example.com"

docs.title: Gobuster Virtual Hosts
docs.text: gobuster vhost -u https://example.com/ -w subdomains.txt --append-domain

docs.title: ffuf POST Parameter Names
docs.text: ffuf -w parameters.txt -u https://example.com/api/search -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" -d "FUZZ=test"

docs.title: ffuf
docs.text:
On Kali Linux:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install ffuf

Verify:

ffuf -V

Help:

ffuf -h

docs.title: Gobuster
docs.text:
Install:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install gobuster

Verify:

gobuster version

Help:

gobuster --help

docs.title: feroxbuster
docs.text:
Install:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install feroxbuster

Verify:

feroxbuster --version

Help:

feroxbuster --help

docs.title: Wordlists
docs.text:
Wordlist selection strongly affects content discovery.

On Kali Linux, useful wordlists may be available under:

/usr/share/wordlists/

SecLists is commonly used for web discovery.

Typical location when installed:

/usr/share/seclists/

docs.title: Install SecLists
docs.text:
sudo apt install seclists

Explore:

ls /usr/share/seclists/

Web content lists:

ls /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/

docs.title: Useful SecLists Wordlists
docs.text:
Examples commonly useful for initial discovery include:

common.txt

directory-list-2.3-small.txt

directory-list-2.3-medium.txt

raft-small-words.txt

raft-medium-words.txt

raft-large-words.txt

raft-small-directories.txt

raft-medium-directories.txt

raft-small-files.txt

raft-medium-files.txt

docs.title: Wordlist Strategy
docs.text:
Do not immediately use the largest available wordlist.

Prefer:

Small Targeted List
        |
        v
Review Results
        |
        v
Technology-Specific List
        |
        v
Medium List
        |
        v
Larger List If Needed

This reduces unnecessary traffic.

docs.title: Start With Application Mapping
docs.text:
Before brute-force discovery:

Browse Application
      |
      v
Review robots.txt
      |
      v
Review sitemap.xml
      |
      v
Review JavaScript
      |
      v
Review Proxy History
      |
      v
Crawl
      |
      v
Content Discovery

Brute-force discovery should complement normal application mapping rather than replace it.

docs.title: Manual Checks First
docs.text:
Useful initial requests:

/robots.txt

/sitemap.xml

/.well-known/

/security.txt

For example:

curl -i https://example.com/robots.txt

curl -i https://example.com/sitemap.xml

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Before enumeration, request a path that almost certainly does not exist:

curl -i https://example.com/this-path-should-not-exist-938475

Observe:

Status code

Content length

Response body

Redirect

Headers

This is important because applications may return:

200 OK

for nonexistent resources.

docs.title: Standard 404
docs.text:
Example:

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 153

This makes filtering relatively straightforward.

docs.title: Soft 404
docs.text:
A soft 404 may look like:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 4217

<html>
...
Page not found
...
</html>

The HTTP status says:

200

but the application behaviour means:

Resource does not exist.

This must be accounted for during enumeration.

docs.title: Redirect-Based Not Found
docs.text:
Another application may respond:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /not-found

Every invalid path could therefore appear interesting unless the baseline is understood.

docs.title: Content Discovery Model
docs.text:
Wordlist Entry
      |
      v
HTTP Request
      |
      v
Response
      |
      v
Status + Size + Words + Lines
      |
      v
Filter Known Noise
      |
      v
Candidate Resource
      |
      v
Manual Validation

docs.title: ffuf
docs.text:
ffuf uses the keyword:

FUZZ

to identify the location where values from the wordlist should be inserted.

docs.title: Basic ffuf Directory Discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ

Possible output:

admin                   [Status: 302, Size: 0, Words: 1, Lines: 1]
api                     [Status: 200, Size: 812, Words: 93, Lines: 24]
assets                  [Status: 301, Size: 178, Words: 6, Lines: 8]
login                   [Status: 200, Size: 3481, Words: 421, Lines: 87]

docs.title: Interpret ffuf Output
docs.text:
Example:

api [Status: 200, Size: 812, Words: 93, Lines: 24]

This means the request using:

/api

returned:

Status: 200

Response size: 812 bytes

Words: 93

Lines: 24

It does not mean /api is vulnerable.

It means:

/api is a discovery candidate worth reviewing.

docs.title: ffuf File Discovery
docs.text: ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-files.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
If the application uses PHP:

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -e .php

Multiple extensions:

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -e .php,.html,.txt,.json

docs.title: Technology-Specific Extensions
docs.text:
Possible extensions depend on the application.

PHP

.php
.inc

ASP.NET

.aspx
.ashx
.asmx
.config

Java

.jsp
.do
.action

Static

.html
.htm
.js
.json
.xml
.txt

docs.title: Do Not Guess Extensions Blindly
docs.text:
Determine technology first using:

HTTP headers

Cookies

HTML

JavaScript

Wappalyzer

WhatWeb

Application behaviour

Then select relevant extensions.

docs.title: ffuf Status Filtering
docs.text:
Match specific status codes:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -mc 200,204,301,302,307,401,403

docs.title: Status Codes Worth Reviewing
docs.text:
Common interesting responses:

200

204

301

302

307

308

401

403

But context matters.

A:

403

can be highly interesting because it may confirm that a resource exists but access is restricted.

docs.title: 403 Interpretation
docs.text:
Example:

admin [Status: 403, Size: 287]

This supports:

The server handles /admin differently from a nonexistent path.

It does not automatically prove:

/admin exists as an accessible application interface.

Manually verify the behaviour.

docs.title: Filter Status
docs.text:
Exclude a status:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -fc 404

Multiple:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -fc 404,400

docs.title: Filter by Size
docs.text:
Suppose invalid paths always return:

Size: 4217

Filter:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -fs 4217

docs.title: Why Size Filtering Matters
docs.text:
Suppose:

random123     200 4217
doesnotexist  200 4217
fakepage      200 4217
admin         200 9281

The common:

4217

response is probably the application's soft 404.

Filtering it makes:

admin 200 9281

stand out.

docs.title: Filter Words
docs.text: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -fw 42

docs.title: Filter Lines
docs.text: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -fl 15

docs.title: Match Size
docs.text: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -ms 812

docs.title: Auto Calibration
docs.text:
ffuf provides automatic calibration functionality.

A common invocation is:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -ac

Automatic calibration can help reduce repetitive baseline responses.

Still manually understand the application's not-found behaviour rather than relying exclusively on automatic filtering.

docs.title: ffuf Recursion
docs.text:
Where appropriate:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -recursion

Control depth:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -recursion -recursion-depth 2

docs.title: Recursion Risk
docs.text:
Without careful controls:

/
 |
 +-- api/
 |    |
 |    +-- v1/
 |         |
 |         +-- users/
 |
 +-- assets/
 |    |
 |    +-- js/
 |
 +-- admin/

can rapidly produce a large request volume.

Set reasonable depth.

docs.title: ffuf Threads
docs.text:
ffuf supports concurrency configuration.

Before increasing concurrency, consider:

Target capacity

Rules of engagement

WAF

Rate limiting

Monitoring

Production impact

Faster is not automatically better.

docs.title: ffuf Delay
docs.text:
Where request pacing is needed, review the current ffuf help for the supported delay/rate controls:

ffuf -h

Use conservative rates on production systems.

docs.title: ffuf Headers
docs.text:
Add a header:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -H "X-Test: authorised-assessment"

docs.title: Authenticated Discovery
docs.text:
Cookie example:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -H "Cookie: session=<session>"

Bearer token:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Do not place real credentials in shell history unnecessarily.

docs.title: Authenticated vs Unauthenticated Discovery
docs.text:
Comparing both views can be useful:

Unauthenticated
      |
      v
Discovered Paths

Authenticated
      |
      v
Discovered Paths

      |
      v
Compare

This may reveal functionality exposed only after authentication.

docs.title: ffuf Output
docs.text:
Save JSON:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -o ffuf-results.json -of json

HTML output where supported:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -o ffuf-results.html -of html

CSV:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ -o ffuf-results.csv -of csv

docs.title: Preserve Assessment Results
docs.text:
Useful naming:

example.com-ffuf-root.json

example.com-ffuf-api.json

example.com-ffuf-authenticated.json

docs.title: ffuf Virtual Host Discovery
docs.text:
Some applications use multiple virtual hosts on the same IP.

Conceptually:

IP Address
   |
   +--> www.example.com
   |
   +--> api.example.com
   |
   +--> admin.example.com

docs.title: Host Header Fuzzing
docs.text: ffuf -w subdomains.txt -u https://example.com/ -H "Host: FUZZ.example.com"

docs.title: Virtual Host Baseline
docs.text:
Before trusting results, send a random hostname:

curl -k -i https://example.com/ -H "Host: random-does-not-exist.example.com"

Observe the default response.

docs.title: VHost False Positives
docs.text:
A web server may return the same default site for every Host header.

Example:

admin.example.com   -> 200 / 8124 bytes
fake.example.com    -> 200 / 8124 bytes
random.example.com  -> 200 / 8124 bytes

This does not demonstrate three valid virtual hosts.

Filter the default response.

docs.title: ffuf VHost Size Filter
docs.text:
If the default response is:

8124 bytes

use:

ffuf -w subdomains.txt -u https://example.com/ -H "Host: FUZZ.example.com" -fs 8124

docs.title: Validate VHost Candidate
docs.text:
Suppose:

admin [Status: 200, Size: 12831]

Manually test:

curl -k -i https://example.com/ -H "Host: admin.example.com"

Then compare against the baseline.

docs.title: DNS vs Virtual Host
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

DNS enumeration

with:

HTTP virtual-host discovery.

A hostname may:

exist in DNS but not host a unique web application

or:

be recognised by the web server without public DNS.

docs.title: ffuf Parameter Name Discovery
docs.text:
Suppose an endpoint is:

/search

A controlled parameter-name test could use:

ffuf -w parameters.txt -u 'https://example.com/search?FUZZ=test'

Compare responses against a random parameter.

docs.title: Parameter Baseline
docs.text:
curl -i 'https://example.com/search?randomparameter=test'

Then compare discovered candidates.

docs.title: POST Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -w parameters.txt \
  -u https://example.com/search \
  -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "FUZZ=test"

docs.title: JSON Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Example:

ffuf -w parameters.txt \
  -u https://example.com/api/search \
  -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"FUZZ":"test"}'

Use only where the request format and endpoint are already understood.

docs.title: Parameter Discovery Interpretation
docs.text:
Suppose:

randomparameter -> 400 / 91 bytes
debug           -> 200 / 812 bytes

This suggests:

debug

may be recognised differently.

It does not prove the parameter creates a security issue.

docs.title: Parameter Value Fuzzing
docs.text:
Suppose the parameter is known:

?format=json

Values can be tested:

ffuf -w values.txt -u 'https://example.com/export?format=FUZZ'

Use targeted value lists rather than arbitrary high-volume fuzzing.

docs.title: Multiple FUZZ Positions
docs.text:
ffuf can support more advanced workflows using multiple wordlists and keywords.

For complex testing, check:

ffuf -h

and use named input keywords deliberately rather than creating uncontrolled combinatorial request volumes.

docs.title: Request From File
docs.text:
For complex authenticated requests, saving the request from Burp can be useful.

A raw request might look like:

POST /api/search HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{"query":"FUZZ"}

ffuf supports raw request-based workflows. Confirm the exact options supported by your installed version:

ffuf -h

This is especially useful when:

Cookies

Custom headers

JSON bodies

Authentication

Complex request structure

are involved.

docs.title: Burp + ffuf Workflow
docs.text:
Browser
   |
   v
Burp Proxy
   |
   v
Interesting Request
   |
   v
Save Request
   |
   v
Replace Input With FUZZ
   |
   v
ffuf
   |
   v
Candidates
   |
   v
Burp Repeater
   |
   v
Manual Validation

docs.title: Proxy ffuf Through Burp
docs.text:
For selected controlled tests, proxying through Burp can make requests visible for analysis.

Check the current proxy option:

ffuf -h

This can be useful when debugging a small test, but sending a large fuzzing run through Burp may create enormous HTTP history.

docs.title: Gobuster
docs.text:
Gobuster provides several enumeration modes.

Display available commands:

gobuster --help

docs.title: Gobuster Directory Mode
docs.text:
Basic:

gobuster dir -u https://example.com/ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt

docs.title: Gobuster Extensions
docs.text:
gobuster dir \
  -u https://example.com/ \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt \
  -x php,html,txt

docs.title: Gobuster Status Codes
docs.text:
Review the installed version's directory-mode options:

gobuster dir --help

Use status filtering based on the target's baseline behaviour.

docs.title: Gobuster Cookies
docs.text:
For authenticated discovery, inspect:

gobuster dir --help

and use the supported cookie/header options for your installed version.

Avoid copying sensitive session tokens into shared terminal logs.

docs.title: Gobuster Headers
docs.text:
Custom headers are useful for:

Authentication

Assessment identifiers

Application-specific headers

Check:

gobuster dir --help

for exact syntax supported by the installed release.

docs.title: Gobuster Output
docs.text:
Save output:

gobuster dir \
  -u https://example.com/ \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt \
  -o gobuster-results.txt

docs.title: Gobuster VHost Mode
docs.text:
gobuster vhost \
  -u https://example.com/ \
  -w subdomains.txt \
  --append-domain

Again, establish the default Host response first.

docs.title: Gobuster VHost Validation
docs.text:
Candidate
   |
   v
Manual curl Request
   |
   v
Compare Against Random Host
   |
   v
Distinct Application?

docs.title: Gobuster DNS Mode
docs.text:
Gobuster also provides DNS enumeration functionality.

Check:

gobuster dns --help

Use DNS mode only for domains included within the authorised scope.

docs.title: Gobuster Strength
docs.text:
Gobuster is useful when you want:

Simple CLI

Predictable directory discovery

VHost discovery

DNS enumeration

Easy text output

docs.title: feroxbuster
docs.text:
feroxbuster focuses heavily on recursive web content discovery.

Basic:

feroxbuster -u https://example.com/

docs.title: Custom Wordlist
docs.text:
feroxbuster \
  -u https://example.com/ \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-words.txt

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
feroxbuster \
  -u https://example.com/ \
  -x php,html,txt,json

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
Recursive enumeration is a core feroxbuster feature.

Conceptually:

/
 |
 +-- admin/
 |     |
 |     +-- users/
 |     |
 |     +-- settings/
 |
 +-- api/
       |
       +-- v1/
             |
             +-- accounts/

This is useful for larger hierarchical applications.

docs.title: Depth
docs.text:
Limit recursion depth according to the assessment.

Check supported options:

feroxbuster --help

Avoid unnecessary deep recursion.

docs.title: feroxbuster Filters
docs.text:
Filtering may be based on characteristics such as:

Status

Size

Words

Lines

Use:

feroxbuster --help

to confirm exact options for the installed release.

docs.title: feroxbuster Headers
docs.text:
Authenticated or custom-header discovery is possible.

Check:

feroxbuster --help

and use only the options required for the assessment.

docs.title: feroxbuster Output
docs.text:
Save results according to the options supported by the installed version.

A useful naming pattern is:

example.com-ferox-root.txt

docs.title: feroxbuster Strength
docs.text:
feroxbuster is especially useful for:

Recursive discovery

Large site trees

Link extraction

Finding nested content

Automated traversal

docs.title: Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
A useful assessment sequence is:

Browser / Burp
      |
      v
Passive Discovery
      |
      v
robots.txt / sitemap.xml
      |
      v
JavaScript Analysis
      |
      v
Crawler
      |
      v

      |
      v
Review
      |
      v
Technology-Specific Discovery
      |
      v
Recursive Discovery
      |
      v
Manual Validation

docs.title: Root Discovery
docs.text:
Start:

ffuf \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt \
  -u https://example.com/FUZZ

docs.title: Then Target Interesting Directories
docs.text:
Suppose:

/api

is discovered.

Run targeted discovery:

ffuf \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-words.txt \
  -u https://example.com/api/FUZZ

This is usually better than blindly increasing the global wordlist size.

docs.title: Recursive Strategy
docs.text:
/
 |
 +--> api/
 |      |
 |      +--> Targeted discovery
 |
 +--> admin/
 |      |
 |      +--> Targeted discovery
 |
 +--> assets/
        |
        +--> Usually lower priority

Prioritise based on security relevance.

docs.title: Prioritising Results
docs.text:
Higher-priority candidates often include:

/admin

/api

/internal

/debug

/manage

/management

/swagger

/api-docs

/graphql

/upload

/download

/export

/import

/backup

/config

/health

/metrics

But the significance depends entirely on application context.

docs.title: API Documentation
docs.text:
Potentially useful discovery candidates:

/swagger

/swagger-ui

/api-docs

/openapi.json

/swagger.json

If found, review whether documentation exposure is intended and whether it reveals security-relevant functionality.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
Common paths:

/graphql

/api/graphql

Discovery alone does not establish insecure GraphQL configuration.

See GraphQL Notes.

docs.title: Health and Metrics
docs.text:
Possible paths:

/health

/healthz

/status

/metrics

These may be intentional operational endpoints.

Review:

Information disclosed

Authentication

Network exposure

Environment details

docs.title: Development and Debug Endpoints
docs.text:
Potential terms:

/debug

/dev

/test

/console

/internal

A name is only a clue.

Determine actual functionality and access control.

docs.title: Administrative Paths
docs.text:
Potential:

/admin

/administrator

/manage

/management

/control

A discovered login page is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: Backup Files
docs.text:
Backup files can sometimes expose source or configuration.

Possible naming patterns include:

file.bak

file.old

file.backup

file~

Use targeted discovery where justified rather than indiscriminately multiplying every path by many extensions.

docs.title: Source Maps
docs.text:
JavaScript source maps may use:

.js.map

Review JavaScript references and deployed static assets.

Source maps can improve source analysis but their presence alone is not necessarily a vulnerability.

docs.title: Response Interpretation
docs.text:
Do not classify only by status code.

Use:

Status

Size

Words

Lines

Title

Headers

Redirect

Body

Authentication state

docs.title: Example Results
docs.text:
admin       403  287
api         200  812
random123   200  4217
debug       302  0
backup      404  153

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
admin
 |
 +--> 403 differs from baseline
 |
 +--> Validate manually

api
 |
 +--> 200 and distinct size
 |
 +--> Review content

random123
 |
 +--> Matches known soft 404
 |
 +--> Ignore/filter

debug
 |
 +--> Redirect
 |
 +--> Follow redirect manually

backup
 |
 +--> Standard 404
 |
 +--> No evidence of resource

docs.title: 401 vs 403
docs.text:
Typical interpretation:

401
 |
 +--> Authentication required

403
 |
 +--> Request understood but access denied

Actual application behaviour may vary.

Both can identify interesting attack surface.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
Suppose:

/admin -> 302 /login

This may indicate:

/admin exists and requires authentication

or:

the application redirects all unknown paths to /login.

Test a random path:

curl -i https://example.com/random-does-not-exist-283746

Compare.

docs.title: Response Size Clustering
docs.text:
Suppose results contain:

200 4217
200 4217
200 4217
200 4217
200 9281
200 4217

The outlier:

9281

deserves attention.

docs.title: Size Is Not Everything
docs.text:
Dynamic pages may change response length because of:

CSRF tokens

Timestamps

Request IDs

Advertisements

User information

Random content

Use multiple response characteristics.

docs.title: Wildcard Responses
docs.text:
Some servers respond successfully for any path.

Example:

/a123      -> 200
/b456      -> 200
/random    -> 200
/admin     -> 200

Compare bodies and sizes before trusting results.

docs.title: Authentication Context
docs.text:
Content discovery results may change between:

Unauthenticated

Standard User

Privileged User

This can reveal role-specific application surfaces.

docs.title: Controlled Comparison
docs.text:
Unauthenticated Crawl
         |
         v
Paths A

Standard User Crawl
         |
         v
Paths B

Admin Crawl
         |
         v
Paths C

Compare these sets during an authorised role-based assessment.

docs.title: Discovered Does Not Mean Accessible
docs.text:
A resource may return:

401

403

302 -> login

and still be valuable for mapping.

The finding is not:

"Hidden endpoint exists."

The security question is:

Is the endpoint exposed inappropriately?

Does it disclose sensitive information?

Are authentication and authorisation correct?

Does it contain vulnerable functionality?

docs.title: Content Discovery and Authorisation
docs.text:
Suppose you discover:

/api/admin/users

Do not immediately attempt arbitrary modifications.

First:

Capture baseline

Determine expected role

Use controlled test account

Send GET where safe

Compare role behaviour

Validate authorisation

docs.title: Burp Repeater Validation
docs.text:
Every high-value candidate should usually be manually reviewed.

ffuf / Gobuster / feroxbuster
            |
            v
         Candidate
            |
            v
       Burp Repeater
            |
            v
         Baseline
            |
            v
       Controlled Test
            |
            v
       Interpretation

docs.title: Validate With curl
docs.text:
Example:

curl -k -i https://example.com/admin

Authenticated:

curl -k -i https://example.com/admin \
  -H "Cookie: session=<session>"

docs.title: Content Discovery and JavaScript
docs.text:
JavaScript often reveals endpoints more efficiently than brute force.

Search downloaded JavaScript:

rg -ni '/api/|/admin|/internal|graphql|upload|download' .

Then validate discovered routes.

docs.title: Crawler + Content Discovery
docs.text:
A strong workflow:

Crawler
   |
   v
Known URLs
   |
   v
Extract Directories
   |
   v
Targeted Wordlists
   |
   v
ffuf / feroxbuster

This is more efficient than treating every target identically.

docs.title: Wordlist Customisation
docs.text:
Build application-specific words from:

Company terminology

Feature names

JavaScript

API routes

Page titles

Technology

Product names

Documentation

Example:

invoice

billing

customer

employee

portal

reports

exports

Save:

custom.txt

docs.title: Combine Wordlists
docs.text:
cat common.txt custom.txt | sort -u > combined.txt

Then:

ffuf -w combined.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ

docs.title: Extract Candidate Words From URLs
docs.text:
If you already have URLs in:

urls.txt

manual processing can help build a targeted list.

For example:

cat urls.txt | sed 's/[?#].*$//' | tr '/' '\n' | sort -u

Review the output before using it as a wordlist.

docs.title: Avoid Blind Wordlist Expansion
docs.text:
Do not automatically combine:

100,000 words
x
20 extensions
x
multiple hosts
x
deep recursion

This can create millions of requests.

Estimate impact first.

docs.title: Request Estimate
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Requests =
Wordlist Entries
x
Extensions
x
Targets
x
Recursive Locations

Example:

20,000 words
x
5 extensions
x
4 discovered directories

= approximately 400,000 candidate requests

This matters during production assessments.

docs.title: Rate Control
docs.text:
Before large enumeration establish:

Maximum acceptable rate

Maximum concurrency

Testing window

Monitoring expectations

Stop conditions

If the application begins returning:

429

502

503

504

investigate whether your testing is contributing to instability.

docs.title: WAF Behaviour
docs.text:
Content discovery may trigger:

WAF

Rate limiting

Bot protection

IP blocking

Do not attempt to evade defensive controls unless that behaviour is explicitly part of the assessment scope.

docs.title: 429 Responses
docs.text:
Example:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 60

Reduce request rate.

Do not treat rate limiting as an obstacle that must automatically be bypassed.

docs.title: 503 Responses
docs.text:
Repeated:

503 Service Unavailable

during enumeration may indicate service stress or defensive throttling.

Stop or reduce activity according to the rules of engagement.

docs.title: TLS Errors
docs.text:
For a lab or authorised target using a self-signed certificate, tools may require configuration to handle certificate verification appropriately.

Do not globally disable certificate validation on your system merely to simplify testing.

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
If:

https://app.internal.example.com

does not resolve, first verify:

dig app.internal.example.com

or:

host app.internal.example.com

In lab environments, a hosts entry may be required:

192.0.2.10 app.internal.example.com

Only modify resolution for known authorised targets.

docs.title: Proxy and VPN
docs.text:
If discovery works in the browser but not the CLI, check:

VPN route

DNS

Proxy configuration

Host resolution

TLS

Authentication

docs.title: Content Discovery Through a VPN
docs.text:
Confirm target connectivity before fuzzing:

curl -I https://example.com/

Then run discovery.

docs.title: Common Mistake - No Baseline
docs.text:
Bad:

Run ffuf
 |
 v
Thousands of 200 responses
 |
 v
Assume thousands of files

Better:

Random Path
 |
 v
Understand 404 Behaviour
 |
 v
Configure Filters
 |
 v
Run Discovery

docs.title: Common Mistake - Filtering Every 403
docs.text:
Do not automatically discard:

403

A forbidden resource may reveal important application structure.

Keep useful 403 responses and investigate manually.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Treating Every 200 as Valid
docs.text:
Soft 404 pages frequently return:

200 OK

Compare:

Size

Words

Lines

Body

Title

docs.title: Common Mistake - Using Only One Wordlist
docs.text:
Different wordlists contain different naming styles.

Use wordlists based on:

Technology

Application type

Initial results

Target terminology

docs.title: Common Mistake - Starting With Huge Lists
docs.text:
Large wordlists increase:

Traffic

Time

Noise

Rate-limit risk

Operational impact

Start targeted.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Ignoring Extensions
docs.text:
A directory wordlist might test:

config

but the actual resource could be:

config.php

Use technology-appropriate extensions.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Too Much Recursion
docs.text:
Recursive enumeration can explode:

/
 |
 +-- a/
 |   +-- a/
 |   +-- b/
 |
 +-- b/
     +-- a/
     +-- b/

Limit depth.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Not Saving Results
docs.text:
Always save significant enumeration results.

Otherwise:

Interesting Resource
       |
       v
Terminal Scrollback Lost
       |
       v
Cannot Reproduce Evidence

docs.title: Common Mistake - Reporting Discovery Alone
docs.text:
Weak:

/admin exists.

Better assessment reasoning:

/admin discovered
       |
       v
Authentication required?
       |
       v
Authorisation correct?
       |
       v
Sensitive functionality?
       |
       v
Security consequence?

docs.title: Common Mistake - Ignoring Scope
docs.text:
A discovered redirect may lead to:

thirdparty.example.net

Do not continue testing it unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Fuzzing Destructive Endpoints
docs.text:
Be careful with:

/delete

/reset

/logout

/payment

/checkout

/admin/actions

Automated requests may change application state.

docs.title: Discovery Evidence
docs.text:
Record:

Target

Timestamp

Tool

Tool version

Command

Wordlist

Authentication context

Request rate

Filters

Result

Manual validation

docs.title: Example Evidence
docs.text:
Target:
https://example.com/

Tool:
ffuf

Wordlist:
common.txt

Authentication:
Unauthenticated

Candidate:
/api

Automated Result:
200 / 812 bytes

Manual Validation:
GET /api returned JSON API metadata.

Security Conclusion:
Attack-surface discovery only. No vulnerability established by discovery alone.

docs.title: Finding vs Observation
docs.text:
Content discovery often produces:

Assessment Observation

rather than:

Security Finding.

Example:

/swagger discovered

is an observation.

If it exposes sensitive internal API documentation without intended access controls, that may support a finding depending on context and impact.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Exposed Backup
docs.text:
Weak:

backup.zip found.

Better:

An unauthenticated request to /backup.zip returned an application backup archive. The archive contained server-side application source and configuration information. The file was accessible without authentication and was not linked through the normal application interface.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Admin Interface
docs.text:
Weak:

Hidden admin panel.

Better:

Content discovery identified the /admin/ application route. Manual validation confirmed that the route presents the administrative authentication interface. No authentication bypass was identified; therefore the route itself was treated as attack-surface information rather than a vulnerability.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Debug Endpoint
docs.text:
Weak:

/debug exists.

Better:

The /debug endpoint was accessible without authentication and returned application environment information including internal service names and runtime configuration. The exposure was manually reproduced independently of the discovery tool.

docs.title: Reporting Example - API Documentation
docs.text:
Weak:

Swagger exposed.

Better:

The application exposed its OpenAPI documentation without authentication at /openapi.json. The documentation enumerated internal administrative API operations not otherwise visible to unauthenticated users. The security significance depends on whether this documentation is intended to be public and whether the disclosed information materially assists unauthorised access.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation, repeat the exact original request first.

Example:

curl -i https://example.com/backup.zip

Expected:

404

or another intended secure response.

docs.title: Do Not Retest Only With ffuf
docs.text:
For a reported resource:

Original Exact Request
       |
       v
Manual Retest
       |
       v
Confirm Secure Behaviour

Then optionally rerun discovery to identify equivalent exposures.

docs.title: Equivalent Resources
docs.text:
If:

backup.zip

was exposed, consider safe searches for equivalent deployment artefacts according to scope.

The root cause may be:

Deployment process publishes backup files

rather than one specific filename.

docs.title: Discovery Comparison
docs.text:
Save results over time:

before.txt

after.txt

Compare:

diff -u before.txt after.txt

This can assist remediation validation.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
Content discovery is attack-surface discovery, not vulnerability confirmation.

Do not stop at:

Wordlist
   |
   v
Tool
   |
   v
/admin Found
   |
   v
Finding

Use:

Wordlist
   |
   v
Discovery Tool
   |
   v
Candidate
   |
   v
Compare With Baseline
   |
   v
Manual Request
   |
   v
Understand Function
   |
   v
Authentication?
   |
   v
Authorisation?
   |
   v
Sensitive Information?
   |
   v
Security Consequence?
   |
   +--> No  -> Attack-Surface Note
   |
   +--> Yes -> Validate -> Evidence -> Finding

For every interesting result ask:

Does the path actually exist?

How does it differ from a random path?

Is this a soft 404?

Is the response unique?

What does the resource do?

Is authentication required?

Is authorisation enforced?

Does the resource expose sensitive information?

Is the functionality intended to be public?

Is this host actually in scope?

Could the response be a wildcard?

Could the result be caused by a generic redirect?

Can I reproduce it manually?

What security consequence exists?

The tool should help answer:

WHAT EXISTS?

Manual testing should then answer:

DOES IT MATTER?

docs.text:
• Burp Suite Cheatsheet
  • Web Application Security Cheatsheet
  • curl Cheatsheet
  • Nmap Cheatsheet
  • Git and ripgrep Cheatsheet
  • Networking Cheatsheet

docs.text:
• Web Application Security
  • Web Testing Methodology
  • Reconnaissance
  • Content Discovery
  • Parameter Discovery
  • JavaScript Analysis
  • Technology Identification
  • Authentication
  • Authorisation
  • API Security
  • GraphQL

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• ffuf GitHub Repository
  • Gobuster GitHub Repository
  • feroxbuster Documentation
  • feroxbuster GitHub Repository
  • SecLists GitHub Repository
  • PortSwigger - Content Discovery
  • OWASP Web Security Testing Guide

Baseline before filtering

Request a random nonexistent resource before starting enumeration. Knowing how the application responds to nonexistent content makes status, size, word and line filters much more reliable.

Use discovery to build the attack surface

/admin, /api, /debug or /swagger are not vulnerabilities simply because a discovery tool finds them. Move interesting resources into Burp Repeater or curl and determine what they actually expose.

Targeted discovery beats blind volume

Information from JavaScript, application terminology, observed routes and technology identification can produce much better wordlists than immediately sending hundreds of thousands of generic requests.

Control recursion

Recursive discovery can increase request volume extremely quickly. Limit depth and prioritise security-relevant branches of the application rather than recursively enumerating every static directory.

Do not discard every 403

A 403 Forbidden response can be valuable attack-surface information because it may indicate that the server handles a path differently from a nonexistent resource. Validate it manually before deciding whether it is relevant.

docs.title: CORS and CSRF Security Testing Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) and Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) are closely related to browser security, but they address different problems.

CORS
 |
 v
Can JavaScript running on another origin
read or interact with this response?

CSRF
 |
 v
Can another site cause the victim browser
to perform an authenticated action?

Understanding this distinction is essential.

Authorised Security Testing

Test CORS and CSRF only against applications, APIs, accounts and actions included in the assessment scope. Use dedicated test accounts and reversible state changes where possible. Avoid destructive operations, mass requests or actions affecting unrelated users.

docs.title: Core Mental Model
docs.text:
Browser security begins with the same-origin policy.

Browser
   |
   v
Same-Origin Policy
   |
   +--> Same Origin
   |       |
   |       v
   |     Allowed
   |
   +--> Cross Origin
           |
           v
      Browser Restrictions
           |
           v
        CORS Policy

CSRF operates differently:

Attacker Site
     |
     v
Victim Browser
     |
     +--> Automatically Attached Credentials
     |
     v
Target Application
     |
     v
State-Changing Request

docs.title: Origin
docs.text:
An origin consists of:

Scheme
+
Host
+
Port

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
https://app.example.com:443

contains:

Scheme: https
Host: app.example.com
Port: 443

docs.title: Different Origins
docs.text:
These are different origins:

https://example.com

http://example.com

https://api.example.com

https://example.com:8443

docs.title: Same-Origin Examples
docs.text:
These URLs are normally the same origin:

https://example.com/account

https://example.com/api/profile

https://example.com/images/logo.png

docs.title: Path Does Not Define Origin
docs.text:
These remain the same origin:

https://example.com/a

https://example.com/b

docs.title: Subdomains Are Different Origins
docs.text:
https://app.example.com

and:

https://api.example.com

are different origins.

docs.title: Same-Origin Policy
docs.text: The same-origin policy restricts how documents and scripts from one origin interact with resources from another origin.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
The same-origin policy does not simply mean:

Cross-origin requests cannot be sent.

Browsers can send many cross-origin requests.

The restrictions often concern:

Reading responses

JavaScript access

Credential behaviour

Certain request types

docs.title: CORS
docs.text: CORS allows a server to relax browser same-origin restrictions for selected origins.

docs.title: Basic CORS Response
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text:
The server tells the browser:

JavaScript from https://app.example.com
may access this response.

docs.title: CORS Is Enforced by Browsers
docs.text:
CORS is primarily a browser security mechanism.

Tools such as:

curl

Burp Repeater

Postman

Server-side scripts

do not enforce browser CORS policy in the same way.

docs.title: Critical Testing Principle
docs.text:
Seeing a sensitive response in Burp after adding:

Origin: https://attacker.example

does not by itself prove exploitable CORS.

You must evaluate the returned CORS headers and browser behaviour.

docs.title: CORS Request
docs.text:
Example:

GET /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Origin: https://app.example.com
Cookie: session=SESSION_VALUE

docs.title: CORS Response
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "username": "testuser"
}

docs.title: Important CORS Headers
docs.text: Header Purpose Access-Control-Allow-Origin Allowed requesting origin Access-Control-Allow-Credentials Whether credentialed CORS requests are permitted Access-Control-Allow-Methods Methods permitted during preflight Access-Control-Allow-Headers Request headers permitted during preflight Access-Control-Expose-Headers Response headers exposed to JavaScript Access-Control-Max-Age Preflight cache lifetime

docs.title: Access-Control-Allow-Origin
docs.text:
Example:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com

docs.title: Wildcard
docs.text: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

docs.title: Wildcard Is Not Automatically Vulnerable
docs.text:
A wildcard can be appropriate for genuinely public resources.

Example:

Public documentation API

Public static data

Unauthenticated public content

docs.title: Ask
docs.text:
Is sensitive data returned?

Are credentials involved?

Should arbitrary origins be able to read it?

docs.title: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
docs.text:
Example:

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: The response permits credentialed cross-origin access when the rest of the browser's CORS and cookie requirements are satisfied.

docs.title: Credentials Can Include
docs.text:
Cookies

HTTP authentication

Client certificates

depending on the request and browser context.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
This combination is invalid for credentialed browser access:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

Browsers do not allow wildcard origin to authorize credentialed CORS response access.

docs.title: Dynamic Origin Reflection
docs.text:
A common CORS weakness occurs when the server reflects arbitrary origins.

Request:

Origin: https://attacker.example

docs.title: Vulnerable Response Pattern
docs.text:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker.example
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Does the application:

Trust arbitrary origins
+
Allow credentials
+
Return sensitive data

If yes, the issue may permit another origin to read authenticated responses in the victim's browser.

docs.title: Baseline CORS Workflow
docs.text:
Start with a normal request.

GET /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Cookie: session=SESSION_VALUE

docs.title: Add Trusted Origin
docs.text: Origin: https://app.example.com

docs.title: Record Response
docs.text:
Look for:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials

Vary: Origin

docs.title: Test Untrusted Origin
docs.text: Origin: https://attacker.example

docs.title: Compare
docs.text:
Trusted origin response

vs

Untrusted origin response

docs.title: Secure Behaviour
docs.text:
Possible secure results include:

No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header

or:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin only for an approved origin

docs.title: Origin Reflection Test
docs.text:
Request:

Origin: https://cors-test.invalid

docs.title: Potentially Interesting Response
docs.text: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://cors-test.invalid

docs.title: Do Not Stop Here
docs.text:
Determine:

Are credentials allowed?

Is sensitive information returned?

Can a real browser read it?

Are cookies actually sent cross-site?

docs.title: Origin Allowlist
docs.text:
Secure applications commonly maintain an explicit list.

Example:

https://app.example.com

https://admin.example.com

docs.title: Weak Validation Patterns
docs.text:
Dangerous conceptual checks include:

Origin contains "example.com"

Origin ends with "example.com"

Origin starts with "https://example.com"

docs.title: Why Substring Matching Fails
docs.text:
A check such as:

contains "example.com"

may incorrectly trust:

https://example.com.attacker.example

docs.title: Why Suffix Matching Can Fail
docs.text:
A naive suffix check for:

example.com

may trust:

https://notexample.com

depending on implementation.

docs.title: Better Validation
docs.text:
Parse the origin and compare against exact trusted origins.

Conceptually:

Parse Origin
    |
    v
Scheme + Host + Port
    |
    v
Exact Trusted Entry?
    |
 +--+--+
 |     |
Yes    No
 |     |
 v     v
Allow Reject

docs.title: Subdomain Trust
docs.text:
Some applications intentionally allow:

https://*.example.com

This creates a broader trust boundary.

docs.title: Review All Trusted Subdomains
docs.text:
Ask whether any trusted subdomain is:

User-controlled

Abandoned

Vulnerable to takeover

Hosting untrusted content

Weakly isolated

docs.title: CORS Trust Inherits Origin Security
docs.text:
If:

https://legacy.example.com

is trusted by CORS, compromise of that origin may affect the CORS security boundary.

docs.title: null Origin
docs.text:
Browsers can send:

Origin: null

in certain contexts.

docs.title: Possible Sources
docs.text:
Depending on browser behaviour and context:

Sandboxed documents

Local files

Opaque origins

Certain embedded documents

docs.title: Test
docs.text: Origin: null

docs.title: Interesting Response
docs.text:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Do not report this based solely on the header.

Determine whether an attacker can create a relevant browser context that:

Produces null origin

Sends required credentials

Reads sensitive response

docs.title: Multiple Origin Header Values
docs.text:
Malformed or duplicate Origin headers may reveal parser differences.

Example controlled testing:

Origin: https://trusted.example
Origin: https://untrusted.example

docs.title: Caution
docs.text:
Behaviour can vary between:

Reverse proxy

CDN

Application server

Framework

Test at low volume and interpret parser differences carefully.

docs.title: Preflight Requests
docs.text: Some cross-origin requests trigger a browser preflight request.

docs.title: Preflight
docs.text:
The browser sends:

OPTIONS /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

docs.title: Preflight Mental Model
docs.text:
Browser
   |
   v
OPTIONS Preflight
   |
   v
Server CORS Policy
   |
   +--> Allowed
   |       |
   |       v
   |   Actual Request
   |
   +--> Denied
           |
           v
      Browser Blocks

docs.title: Requests That May Trigger Preflight
docs.text:
Common reasons include:

Non-simple methods

Custom request headers

Certain Content-Type values

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Methods such as:

PUT

PATCH

DELETE

normally trigger preflight in cross-origin JavaScript requests.

docs.title: Authorization Header
docs.text:
A request containing:

Authorization: Bearer TOKEN

normally requires preflight for cross-origin browser requests.

docs.title: Content-Type
docs.text:
These content types are relevant to simple-request rules:

application/x-www-form-urlencoded

multipart/form-data

text/plain

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
application/json

normally causes a preflight in cross-origin JavaScript requests.

docs.title: Preflight Is Not Authentication
docs.text:
A successful:

OPTIONS

response does not mean the actual request will be authorized.

docs.title: Test Actual Request
docs.text:
Always verify:

Preflight policy

Actual response

Credentials

Authorization

docs.title: Access-Control-Allow-Methods
docs.text:
Example:

Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT

docs.title: Do Not Report Broad Methods Alone
docs.text:
A response advertising:

DELETE

does not prove an attacker can successfully perform a privileged DELETE operation.

Validate actual authorization.

docs.title: Access-Control-Allow-Headers
docs.text:
Example:

Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type

docs.title: Security Context
docs.text: Broad header allowance matters only when combined with an origin that should not be trusted and an exploitable browser interaction.

docs.title: Access-Control-Expose-Headers
docs.text:
Browsers expose only certain response headers to JavaScript by default.

Applications can expose additional headers:

Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Request-ID

docs.title: Sensitive Headers
docs.text:
Review whether the application exposes headers containing:

Tokens

Internal identifiers

Sensitive metadata

docs.title: Vary Origin
docs.text:
Dynamic CORS responses often need:

Vary: Origin

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Caches need to distinguish responses based on the request Origin.

docs.title: Missing Vary
docs.text:
Missing:

Vary: Origin

can create caching problems when responses dynamically vary CORS headers.

docs.title: Do Not Automatically Report
docs.text: Demonstrate actual cache behaviour before claiming cache poisoning or cross-user impact.

docs.title: CORS Testing Matrix
docs.text:
Test origins such as:

Expected trusted origin

Completely unrelated origin

Lookalike origin

Trusted-domain prefix

Trusted-domain suffix

Sibling subdomain

HTTPS vs HTTP

Different port

null

docs.title: Example Matrix
docs.text: Origin Question https://app.example.com Expected trusted origin https://attacker.example Arbitrary external origin https://example.com.attacker.example Prefix validation https://notexample.com Naive suffix validation https://dev.example.com Sibling subdomain trust http://app.example.com Scheme validation https://app.example.com:8443 Port validation null Null-origin trust

docs.title: Browser Proof
docs.text: When a CORS issue appears exploitable, validate with a controlled browser page.

docs.title: Read-Only CORS Test Page
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>CORS Test</title>
</head>
<body>
  <pre id="output">Testing...</pre>

  <script>
    fetch("https://target.example/api/profile", {
      credentials: "include"
    })
      .then(response => response.text())
      .then(data => {
        document.getElementById("output").textContent = data;
      })
      .catch(error => {
        document.getElementById("output").textContent = String(error);
      });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Use a Read-Only Endpoint First
docs.text:
Prefer:

Profile

Current-user information

Non-destructive account data

rather than state-changing actions.

docs.title: Expected Vulnerable Behaviour
docs.text:
The attacker-origin page can:

Send request

Include relevant victim credentials

Read sensitive response

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Capture:

Attacker origin

Request Origin header

Target response

Access-Control-Allow-Origin

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials

Browser-readable response

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text: Cross-Site Request Forgery causes a victim browser to submit an unwanted authenticated request.

docs.title: CSRF Model
docs.text:
Victim Authenticated to Target
          |
          v
      Session Cookie
          |
          v
Victim Visits Attacker Site
          |
          v
Cross-Site Request
          |
          v
Browser Sends Credentials
          |
          v
Target Accepts Action

docs.title: CSRF Requires Context
docs.text:
A useful CSRF assessment asks:

Does the browser send authentication automatically?

Can the attacker construct the request?

Does the server require unpredictable authorization data?

Does SameSite prevent the request?

Does Origin/Referer validation prevent it?

Does the action have meaningful impact?

docs.title: Common CSRF Targets
docs.text:
Examples:

Change email address

Change profile data

Add shipping address

Modify notification settings

Link external account

Create API key

Change application configuration

Invite user

Modify permissions

docs.title: High-Risk Actions
docs.text:
Actions such as:

Change password

Disable MFA

Add privileged user

Change payment destination

deserve careful testing but should only be exercised in controlled accounts and within scope.

docs.title: Baseline CSRF Workflow
docs.text:
Capture a legitimate state-changing request.

Example:

POST /account/email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=SESSION_VALUE
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=test2@example.com

docs.title: Identify Authentication
docs.text:
Ask whether authentication comes from:

Cookie

HTTP authentication

Client certificate

Bearer token manually added by JavaScript

docs.title: Automatically Attached Credentials
docs.text: CSRF is particularly relevant when browsers automatically attach authentication credentials.

docs.title: Cookie Authentication
docs.text:
Typical example:

Cookie: session=SESSION_VALUE

docs.title: Bearer Token Header
docs.text:
If the application requires JavaScript to add:

Authorization: Bearer TOKEN

an external site normally cannot simply force the victim browser to attach that header.

This can significantly change CSRF exposure.

docs.title: Do Not Assume
docs.text:
API endpoint

means:

Not vulnerable to CSRF

Check how authentication actually works.

docs.title: CSRF Tokens
docs.text: A common defense is an unpredictable token tied to the user session or transaction.

docs.title: Form Example
docs.text: <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="RANDOM_VALUE">

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
POST /account/email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=SESSION_VALUE
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=test2@example.com&csrf_token=RANDOM_VALUE

docs.title: CSRF Token Properties
docs.text:
A robust token should be:

Unpredictable

Validated server-side

Bound appropriately to the session

Unavailable to unrelated origins

Required on protected actions

docs.title: Test Missing Token
docs.text:
Remove:

csrf_token

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Request rejected

docs.title: Test Empty Token
docs.text: csrf_token=

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Rejected

docs.title: Test Invalid Token
docs.text: csrf_token=invalid-test-value

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Rejected

docs.title: Test Another Session's Token
docs.text:
With two controlled accounts:

Account A token

Account B session

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
If tokens are session-bound:

Rejected

docs.title: Why Two Accounts Help
docs.text:
This distinguishes:

Globally valid token

from:

Session-bound token

docs.title: Token Reuse
docs.text:
Some applications intentionally allow a CSRF token to remain valid for the session.

Therefore:

Token reusable

is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: Security Property
docs.text: The important question is whether an attacker can obtain or predict a valid token for the victim's request.

docs.title: Predictable CSRF Tokens
docs.text: If tokens follow a predictable pattern, assess whether that predictability allows unauthorized cross-site requests.

docs.title: Do Not Infer From Appearance
docs.text:
A short token is not automatically predictable.

A long token is not automatically secure.

Test actual entropy only when justified.

docs.title: Token in Cookie and Request
docs.text:
Some applications use a double-submit cookie pattern.

Example:

Cookie: csrf=ABC123

and:

csrf=ABC123

in the request.

docs.title: Double-Submit Model
docs.text:
CSRF Cookie
     |
     +--> Browser Cookie
     |
     +--> Request Parameter/Header
              |
              v
           Compare

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Review:

Can attacker set the cookie?

Is token cryptographically bound?

Are subdomains trusted?

Is cookie scope safe?

docs.title: Signed Double-Submit
docs.text: A stronger design can bind the CSRF token to session-specific information using a server-side secret.

docs.title: Custom Header Defense
docs.text:
APIs may require a custom header:

X-CSRF-Token: RANDOM_VALUE

docs.title: Why It Helps
docs.text: Cross-origin JavaScript cannot normally add arbitrary custom headers without passing CORS preflight.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
If CORS trusts an attacker-controlled origin, a custom-header CSRF defense may become ineffective.

This is why CORS and CSRF should sometimes be reviewed together.

docs.title: CORS + CSRF Interaction
docs.text:
Attacker Origin
      |
      v
CORS Allows Origin
      |
      v
Browser Permits Custom Header
      |
      v
CSRF Header Added
      |
      v
Authenticated Request

docs.title: Origin Validation
docs.text:
Servers can validate:

Origin: https://app.example.com

docs.title: State-Changing Request
docs.text:
Example:

POST /account/email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Origin: https://app.example.com

docs.title: Secure Policy
docs.text:
For protected state-changing requests:

Expected trusted origin
        |
        v
Allow

Unexpected origin
        |
        v
Reject

docs.title: Test Untrusted Origin
docs.text:
Using Repeater:

Origin: https://attacker.example

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
Rejected

when Origin validation is part of the CSRF defense.

docs.title: Missing Origin
docs.text:
Test:

No Origin header

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Some legitimate requests may omit Origin depending on browser/request context.

Applications using Origin validation should have a carefully designed fallback policy.

docs.title: Referer Validation
docs.text:
Applications may inspect:

Referer: https://app.example.com/account

docs.title: Secure Parsing
docs.text: Do not validate with naive substring matching.

docs.title: Dangerous Concept
docs.text: Referer contains "example.com"

docs.title: Better
docs.text:
Parse the URL and verify the expected:

Scheme

Host

Port

docs.title: Origin Preferred
docs.text: For CSRF origin checks, Origin is often easier to validate because it contains only the origin rather than a full URL.

docs.title: Referer Privacy
docs.text:
Referer may be omitted or reduced due to:

Referrer-Policy

Browser privacy behaviour

Navigation context

docs.title: SameSite Cookies
docs.text: SameSite controls when cookies are sent with cross-site requests.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
Strict

Lax

None

docs.title: Cookie Example
docs.text: Set-Cookie: session=VALUE; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

docs.title: SameSite Strict
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Cross-site request
      |
      v
Cookie generally withheld

docs.title: SameSite Lax
docs.text: Lax allows cookies in some top-level navigation scenarios while restricting many cross-site subrequests.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not reduce SameSite behaviour to:

Lax = no CSRF

Request method and navigation context matter.

docs.title: SameSite None
docs.text: SameSite=None; Secure

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: The cookie may be sent in cross-site contexts, subject to browser cookie rules.

docs.title: Secure Requirement
docs.text:
Modern browsers require:

Secure

with:

SameSite=None

docs.title: Same-Site vs Same-Origin
docs.text:
These concepts are different.

Same Origin

is stricter than:

Same Site

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Depending on scheme and registrable domain:

app.example.com

api.example.com

may be:

Cross-origin

while still:

Same-site

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
SameSite cookie protections are based on:

Site

not the exact same-origin definition used by CORS.

docs.title: Sibling Subdomains
docs.text: A compromised sibling subdomain can therefore matter in CSRF and SameSite threat modelling.

docs.title: SameSite Is Defense-in-Depth
docs.text:
Do not rely exclusively on SameSite for every sensitive application action.

Robust applications commonly combine appropriate controls such as:

CSRF token

Origin validation

SameSite cookies

Reauthentication

docs.title: GET Requests
docs.text: State-changing actions should not normally be implemented through GET.

docs.title: Dangerous Pattern
docs.text: GET /account/delete?id=123 HTTP/1.1

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
GET requests can be triggered through many browser mechanisms:

<img src="https://target.example/account/delete?id=123">

docs.title: Correct Design
docs.text:
Use appropriate state-changing methods such as:

POST

PUT

PATCH

DELETE

with suitable CSRF defenses.

docs.title: Important
docs.text: Using POST alone does not prevent CSRF.

docs.title: Simple POST
docs.text:
An attacker page can submit a normal HTML form.

Example:

<form action="https://target.example/account/email" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="email" value="controlled@example.com">
</form>

<script>
  document.forms[0].submit();
</script>

docs.title: Browser Request
docs.text:
This can produce:

POST /account/email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

docs.title: JSON CSRF
docs.text:
An endpoint requiring:

Content-Type: application/json

is harder to invoke using a traditional HTML form with that exact content type.

docs.title: Example Target
docs.text:
POST /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"name":"test"}

docs.title: Browser Constraint
docs.text:
Cross-origin JavaScript using:

application/json

normally triggers CORS preflight.

docs.title: Security Benefit
docs.text:
If the server:

Rejects simple content types

Requires application/json

Does not trust attacker origins through CORS

this can reduce CSRF exposure.

docs.title: But Test Parsing
docs.text:
Some APIs accept JSON-like bodies using:

text/plain

application/x-www-form-urlencoded

or ignore Content-Type.

docs.title: Example Test
docs.text:
Change:

Content-Type: application/json

to:

Content-Type: text/plain

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: If the server still processes the body, an attacker may be able to create a simple cross-site request.

docs.title: Content-Type Enforcement
docs.text: Review whether the API genuinely requires the intended content type.

docs.title: Multipart Forms
docs.text:
HTML forms can submit:

multipart/form-data

without CORS preflight.

docs.title: File Upload CSRF
docs.text: Upload or import functionality can therefore require CSRF review when authentication uses cookies.

docs.text:

POST

docs.title: CSRF and XSS

Read responses

docs.title: Reporting CORS Origin Reflection
docs.text: The API dynamically trusts arbitrary request origins and permits credentialed cross-origin access to authenticated responses. A page hosted on a controlled external origin was able to issue a request using the test user's browser credentials and read sensitive account data. The API should permit credentialed CORS access only from explicitly trusted origins.

docs.title: Reporting Weak Origin Validation
docs.text: The CORS allowlist uses insufficient origin matching and accepts origins that are not part of the intended trust boundary. A controlled lookalike origin was returned in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and could read the authenticated response in a browser. Origin values should be parsed and compared against explicit trusted scheme, host and port combinations.

docs.title: Reporting Null-Origin Trust
docs.text: The application permits credentialed cross-origin access from the null origin. A controlled browser context capable of generating a null origin successfully read authenticated response data. The application should remove null from the trusted origin policy unless it is explicitly required and supported by an equivalent security control.

docs.title: Reporting CSRF
docs.text: The account update endpoint accepts authenticated state-changing requests without verifying that they originated from the legitimate application. A controlled cross-site form caused the test user's browser to submit its existing session credentials and modify the account email address without a valid anti-CSRF token. State-changing browser requests should require robust CSRF protection such as a session-bound anti-CSRF token and appropriate origin validation.

docs.title: Reporting Missing CSRF Validation
docs.text: The application includes an anti-CSRF token in legitimate requests but does not enforce it server-side. Removing the token from a controlled state-changing request did not prevent the operation from completing. The server must reject protected requests when the expected CSRF token is missing, invalid or not associated with the appropriate session.

docs.title: Reporting Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking
docs.text: The WebSocket endpoint authenticates users through browser cookies but does not restrict connection establishment to trusted origins. A controlled external origin was able to establish an authenticated WebSocket connection using the test user's existing browser session and access protected functionality. The WebSocket handshake should validate the Origin header against an explicit trusted allowlist in addition to enforcing normal authentication and authorization.

docs.title: Reporting GET State Change
docs.text: The application performs a state-changing operation through an authenticated GET request. Because cross-site GET requests can be triggered through standard browser navigation and embedded resources, another origin can cause the victim browser to perform the operation. State changes should use an appropriate non-GET method and require effective CSRF protection.

docs.text:
Do not report:

docs.title: Do Not Report
docs.text:

Request requirements

docs.title: Do Not Report

docs.title: Do Not Report
docs.text:
Origin reflected

without establishing whether:

Browser can send credentials

Sensitive response is readable

Origin is truly untrusted

docs.text:

https://app.example.com

Scheme

Host

docs.text:

docs.text:
Enable:

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

docs.title: Minimize Trusted Origins
docs.text: Every trusted origin expands the browser trust boundary.

docs.title: Review Subdomains
docs.text: Remove obsolete or unnecessary origins from the allowlist.

docs.title: Preflight Policy
docs.text: Allow only methods and headers required by legitimate clients.

docs.title: Remediation - CSRF

Conceptually:

docs.text:

docs.title: Origin Validation
docs.text: Validate trusted origins for sensitive state-changing requests where appropriate.

docs.title: SameSite
docs.text: Use an appropriate SameSite policy for session cookies as defense-in-depth.

docs.title: Avoid State Changes Through GET
docs.text: Use methods appropriate to the operation.

docs.title: Reauthentication
docs.text: Require recent authentication for high-risk security changes where appropriate.

docs.title: Content-Type
docs.text: For APIs, strictly requiring intended content types can make simple cross-site request construction harder, but it should complement rather than replace the broader CSRF design.

docs.title: Custom Headers
docs.text: Requiring a custom anti-CSRF header can be effective for AJAX APIs when combined with a restrictive CORS policy.

docs.title: Protect XSS Boundary
docs.text: Because XSS can often bypass CSRF controls from within the trusted origin, XSS prevention remains essential.

docs.title: Retesting CORS

docs.title: CORS Header Matrix
docs.text: Header Security Question Access-Control-Allow-Origin Which origins can read the response? Access-Control-Allow-Credentials Can credentialed requests be exposed cross-origin? Access-Control-Allow-Methods Which methods are permitted by preflight? Access-Control-Allow-Headers Which request headers are permitted? Access-Control-Expose-Headers Which response headers can JavaScript read? Access-Control-Max-Age How long may preflight policy be cached? Vary: Origin Do caches distinguish origin-dependent responses?

docs.title: Final Questions
docs.text:
For every CORS implementation ask:

Which origins are supposed to be trusted?

Is the origin parsed correctly?

Is exact scheme, host and port validation used?

Are arbitrary origins reflected?

Are lookalike domains accepted?

Are sibling subdomains trusted?

Are abandoned subdomains trusted?

Is null origin trusted?

Are credentials enabled?

Are credentials actually required?

Does the endpoint return sensitive data?

Can an attacker-controlled browser origin read the response?

Does the browser actually send the relevant cookie?

Are wildcard origins used only for public resources?

Are preflight methods unnecessarily broad?

Are custom headers unnecessarily allowed?

Are sensitive response headers exposed?

Is Vary: Origin correct where caching matters?

Is CORS configured at multiple layers?

Can duplicate headers create inconsistent behaviour?

Does the API still enforce authentication?

Does the API enforce authorization?

Does the API enforce object ownership?

Does the API enforce tenant boundaries?

docs.title: For Every CSRF Implementation Ask
docs.text:
How is the user authenticated?

Does the browser attach credentials automatically?

Which requests change state?

Can those requests be created cross-site?

Are any state changes performed through GET?

Is a CSRF token present?

Is the token actually validated?

What happens when the token is removed?

What happens when the token is empty?

What happens when the token is invalid?

Is the token bound to the session?

Can another account's token be reused?

Is Origin validated?

Is Referer used as fallback?

Are origin URLs parsed safely?

What happens when Origin is missing?

What SameSite value does the session cookie use?

Are sibling subdomains part of the same-site trust boundary?

Does the endpoint accept simple content types?

Can application/json be changed to text/plain?

Can a form-encoded body reach the same handler?

Is multipart/form-data accepted?

Are method overrides supported?

Can a custom header defense be bypassed through CORS?

Does the application require reauthentication for high-risk actions?

Are account-linking operations protected?

Are MFA changes protected?

Are administrative operations protected?

Are file uploads protected?

Are WebSocket connections origin-validated?

Does GraphQL accept state-changing GET requests?

Does the application verify actual state change rather than only HTTP status?

Are framework CSRF exclusions justified?

Does XSS undermine the assumed CSRF protection?

Has the issue been demonstrated with controlled accounts?

Is the action reversible?

Has the exact impact been verified?

Have session cookies and tokens been redacted from evidence?
