Start with the authentication model

Before testing CSRF, determine exactly how the browser authenticates to the target. Cookie-based sessions and JavaScript-added bearer tokens have different cross-site request properties.

CORS needs a browser proof

Burp Repeater can reveal server-side CORS policy, but the strongest validation demonstrates that JavaScript running on a controlled untrusted origin can actually read the sensitive authenticated response in a browser.

Verify the state change

For CSRF testing, do not treat an HTTP 200 or redirect as proof. Confirm that the intended account or application state actually changed.

Review CORS and CSRF together

A custom anti-CSRF header can be an effective control because cross-origin JavaScript normally requires preflight to send it. If CORS also trusts an attacker-controlled origin, that security assumption may fail.

CORS is not authorization

CORS controls browser response access. It does not prevent curl, Burp, mobile applications or other non-browser clients from calling an API. Authentication and authorization must still be enforced independently.

SameSite is not the whole CSRF model

SameSite cookies provide important browser-level protection, but the effective security depends on request type, site relationships, cookie configuration and application architecture. Sensitive applications should use a layered CSRF defense appropriate to their threat model.

docs.title: curl Cheatsheet
docs.text:
curl is one of the most useful command-line tools for interacting with HTTP and HTTPS services during security assessments.

It is particularly useful when you need to quickly answer:

Does this endpoint respond?

Which HTTP status code is returned?

Which headers are present?

Where does this redirect?

Does the endpoint require authentication?

How does the server handle different HTTP methods?

What happens when I send JSON?

Which cookies are issued?

Does the behaviour change through a proxy?

Which TLS certificate is presented?

Can I reproduce the request outside the browser?

A practical workflow is:

Endpoint
   |
   v
Basic Request
   |
   v
Inspect Status and Headers
   |
   v
Understand Authentication
   |
   v
Reproduce Required Request
   |
   v
Modify One Input
   |
   v
Compare Response
   |
   v
Interpret Behaviour
   |
   v
Validate
   |
   v
Capture Evidence

Authorised Security Testing

Only send requests to applications, APIs and infrastructure that you are authorised to assess. Avoid destructive methods, excessive request rates, large uploads and state-changing operations unless they are explicitly permitted by the assessment scope.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Basic request:

curl https://example.com/

Headers only:

curl -I https://example.com/

Verbose request:

curl -v https://example.com/

Follow redirects:

curl -L https://example.com/

Save response:

curl https://example.com/ -o response.html

Ignore certificate validation for an authorised test environment:

curl -k https://example.com/

JSON request:

curl -X POST https://example.com/api/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"test","password":"test"}'

Proxy through Burp Suite:

curl -k -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 https://example.com/

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Kali/Debian:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install curl

Check:

curl --version

Locate:

which curl

Help:

curl --help

Full help:

curl --help all

Manual:

man curl

docs.title: curl Version
docs.text:
curl --version

Representative output:

curl 8.x.x ...
Protocols: ...
Features: ...

Record the locally installed version when behaviour depends on supported protocols or features.

docs.title: Basic GET Request
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/

The response body is written to standard output.

docs.title: Explicit GET
docs.text:
curl -X GET https://example.com/

Usually this is unnecessary because GET is already the default.

Prefer:

curl https://example.com/

unless explicitly setting the method improves clarity.

docs.title: Include Response Headers
docs.text:
curl -i https://example.com/

Representative output:

HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html
server: nginx
content-length: 1234

<html>
...

-i includes response headers with the response body.

docs.title: Headers Only
docs.text:
curl -I https://example.com/

This sends a HEAD request.

Do not assume HEAD behaves identically to GET.

Some applications:

Disable HEAD

Handle HEAD differently

Return different headers

Route HEAD differently

docs.title: Better Header Validation
docs.text:
When you specifically need headers from a normal GET request:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/

This performs a GET while displaying the response headers.

docs.title: Status Code Only
docs.text:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com/

Representative output:

200

docs.title: Status and Final URL
docs.text: curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'Status: %{http_code}\nURL: %{url_effective}\n' -L https://example.com/

docs.title: Useful Write-Out Fields
docs.text:
curl -s -o /dev/null \
  -w 'HTTP: %{http_code}\nRemote IP: %{remote_ip}\nContent Type: %{content_type}\nTotal: %{time_total}s\n' \
  https://example.com/

Useful variables include:

http_code

url_effective

remote_ip

remote_port

local_ip

content_type

size_download

time_connect

time_starttransfer

time_total

docs.title: Silent Mode
docs.text:
curl -s https://example.com/

This suppresses progress output.

docs.title: Silent but Show Errors
docs.text:
curl -sS https://example.com/

This is usually better for scripts because errors remain visible.

docs.title: Fail on HTTP Errors
docs.text:
curl -f https://example.com/

Useful in automation.

Remember that HTTP responses such as:

401

403

404

500

may themselves be valuable security-assessment evidence, so do not hide them when investigating application behaviour.

docs.title: Verbose Mode
docs.text:
curl -v https://example.com/

Verbose output shows information about:

DNS resolution

TCP connection

TLS negotiation

Request headers

Response headers

Redirect behaviour

docs.title: Verbose Output Symbols
docs.text:
Typical verbose output uses:

> request data

< response data

* curl diagnostic information

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
> GET / HTTP/1.1
> Host: example.com
> User-Agent: curl/...
> Accept: */*

< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Content-Type: text/html

This is useful for understanding exactly what curl sent and received.

docs.title: Trace
docs.text:
For deeper troubleshooting:

curl --trace-ascii trace.txt https://example.com/

Be careful:

Trace files may contain credentials.

Trace files may contain cookies.

Trace files may contain tokens.

Trace files may contain sensitive response data.

Handle them as assessment evidence.

docs.title: Save Response Body
docs.text: curl https://example.com/ -o response.html

docs.title: Preserve Remote Filename
docs.text:
curl -O https://example.com/file.txt

Only use this when you trust the intended output location and filename.

docs.title: Headers to File
docs.text:
curl -D headers.txt https://example.com/ -o response.html

This creates separate:

headers.txt

response.html

docs.title: Complete Evidence Capture
docs.text:
curl -sS -D headers.txt https://example.com/ -o response.html

Then record the exact command separately.

docs.title: HTTP Methods
docs.text:
Common methods:

GET

POST

PUT

PATCH

DELETE

HEAD

OPTIONS

docs.title: OPTIONS
docs.text:
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://example.com/api/users

Possible response:

Allow: GET, POST, OPTIONS

Do not assume the Allow header completely describes application authorisation.

docs.title: POST Form Data
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://example.com/login \
  -d 'username=test&password=test'

curl automatically uses:

application/x-www-form-urlencoded

for standard -d form data unless overridden.

docs.title: POST JSON
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/api/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"test","password":"test"}'

Using -d causes curl to use POST unless another method is explicitly specified.

docs.title: JSON with Accept Header
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/api/users \
  -H 'Accept: application/json'

docs.title: PUT
docs.text:
For a non-destructive authorised endpoint:

curl -X PUT https://example.com/api/profile \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"displayName":"Test User"}'

Only use state-changing methods where explicitly authorised.

docs.title: PATCH
docs.text:
curl -X PATCH https://example.com/api/profile \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"displayName":"Test User"}'

docs.title: DELETE
docs.text:
Syntax:

curl -X DELETE https://example.com/api/resource/123

State-Changing Request

Do not send DELETE requests to real application objects unless the assessment explicitly permits destructive testing and the target object is safe to remove.

docs.title: Custom Header
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/ \
  -H 'X-Test: authorised-assessment'

docs.title: Multiple Headers
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/api/users \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  -H 'X-Test: authorised-assessment'

docs.title: User-Agent
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/ \
  -A 'Authorised-Security-Assessment'

Equivalent:

curl https://example.com/ \
  -H 'User-Agent: Authorised-Security-Assessment'

docs.title: Referer
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/ \
  -e 'https://example.com/'

docs.title: Host Header
docs.text:
curl http://192.0.2.10/ \
  -H 'Host: app.example.com'

This is useful when testing:

Virtual hosting

Reverse proxies

Load balancers

Applications behind shared IP addresses

Do not automatically interpret a changed response as a Host-header vulnerability.

docs.title: Virtual Host Validation
docs.text:
Suppose:

curl http://192.0.2.10/

returns:

Default server

while:

curl http://192.0.2.10/ -H 'Host: portal.example.com'

returns:

Application login page

Interpretation:

The web server uses Host-based virtual hosting.

This is expected behaviour in many environments.

docs.title: Resolve Hostname to Specific IP
docs.text:
A better option for HTTPS virtual-host testing is often:

curl --resolve app.example.com:443:192.0.2.10 https://app.example.com/

This preserves:

URL hostname

Host header

TLS SNI hostname

while connecting to the specified IP.

docs.title: Why --resolve Is Useful
docs.text:
Compare:

curl https://192.0.2.10/ -H 'Host: app.example.com'

with:

curl --resolve app.example.com:443:192.0.2.10 https://app.example.com/

The second approach better represents a normal HTTPS request to:

app.example.com

because TLS SNI also uses the hostname.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
Without -L:

curl -i http://example.com/

Possible:

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://example.com/

Follow:

curl -L http://example.com/

docs.title: Show Redirect Chain
docs.text:
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null -L http://example.com/

This helps identify:

HTTP -> HTTPS

Login redirects

Canonical-host redirects

Application routing

docs.title: Do Not Hide Redirects Too Early
docs.text:
If investigating redirect behaviour, first inspect without:

-L

Otherwise the original:

301

302

303

307

308

may be less obvious.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Send cookie:

curl https://example.com/ \
  -b 'session=examplevalue'

docs.title: Multiple Cookies
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/ \
  -b 'session=examplevalue; preference=dark'

docs.title: Save Cookies
docs.text: curl -c cookies.txt https://example.com/login

docs.title: Load Cookies
docs.text: curl -b cookies.txt https://example.com/profile

docs.title: Save and Reuse Cookies
docs.text: curl -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt https://example.com/

docs.title: Cookie Workflow
docs.text:
Login
  |
  v
Receive Set-Cookie
  |
  v
Store Cookie Jar
  |
  v
Authenticated Request
  |
  v
Observe Authorisation

docs.title: Cookie Security Attributes
docs.text:
Look for:

Secure

HttpOnly

SameSite

Path

Domain

Expires

Max-Age

Example:

Set-Cookie: session=...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: curl supports several authentication mechanisms.

docs.title: Basic Authentication
docs.text:
curl -u 'testuser:testpassword' https://example.com/

Be careful:

Credentials may appear in shell history.

Credentials may appear in process information.

Credentials may be captured in evidence.

docs.title: Prompt for Password
docs.text:
Safer than embedding the password:

curl -u testuser https://example.com/

curl can prompt for the password.

docs.title: Bearer Token
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/api/profile \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'

docs.title: API Key Header
docs.text:
Example:

curl https://example.com/api/data \
  -H 'X-API-Key: <api-key>'

The exact header depends on the application.

docs.title: Avoid Publishing Real Tokens
docs.text:
Documentation and screenshots should use:

<token>

<api-key>

<session-cookie>

rather than real credentials.

docs.title: Proxy Through Burp Suite
docs.text:
HTTP:

curl -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 http://example.com/

HTTPS:

curl -k -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 https://example.com/

docs.title: Burp Workflow
docs.text:
curl
 |
 v
Burp Proxy
 |
 v
Target
 |
 v
Burp HTTP History

This is useful when:

Reproducing CLI requests

Comparing curl with browser behaviour

Modifying requests in Repeater

Capturing evidence

docs.title: Environment Proxy
docs.text:
export HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8080
export HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8080

Remove:

unset HTTP_PROXY
unset HTTPS_PROXY

docs.title: Check Proxy Variables
docs.text: env | grep -i proxy

docs.title: Ignore Proxy for Target
docs.text:
curl --noproxy '*' https://example.com/

Useful when environment proxy variables unexpectedly affect testing.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
HTTPS request:

curl https://example.com/

docs.title: Certificate Validation Failure
docs.text:
You may see:

SSL certificate problem

Possible reasons:

Self-signed certificate

Expired certificate

Hostname mismatch

Untrusted CA

Incomplete certificate chain

docs.title: Ignore TLS Validation
docs.text:
For an authorised test environment:

curl -k https://example.com/

or:

curl --insecure https://example.com/

Do Not Normalise -k

-k is useful in labs and assessment environments, but it disables certificate verification. A request succeeding with -k does not mean the certificate configuration is valid.

docs.title: Inspect TLS Verbosely
docs.text:
curl -v https://example.com/

This can expose useful TLS and certificate information.

docs.title: TLS Version
docs.text:
Where supported by the target and local curl build:

curl --tlsv1.2 https://example.com/

Minimum TLS 1.3:

curl --tlsv1.3 https://example.com/

Use dedicated TLS tooling for comprehensive cipher/protocol analysis.

docs.title: Client Certificate
docs.text:
Where the assessment provides an authorised client certificate:

curl --cert client.pem --key client.key https://example.com/

Protect private-key material carefully.

docs.title: Custom CA
docs.text:
curl --cacert assessment-ca.pem https://example.com/

This is preferable to -k when you have the appropriate CA certificate.

docs.title: HTTP Protocol Version
docs.text:
Force HTTP/1.1:

curl --http1.1 https://example.com/

Request HTTP/2:

curl --http2 https://example.com/

Availability depends on the local curl build and server capabilities.

docs.title: HTTP Version Comparison
docs.text:
Useful workflow:

HTTP/1.1
   |
   v
Observe Behaviour

HTTP/2
   |
   v
Observe Behaviour

Compare

Differences may result from:

Reverse proxy

CDN

Load balancer

Protocol-specific routing

Application gateway

Do not automatically interpret differences as vulnerabilities.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
Show resolution and connection details:

curl -v https://example.com/

Resolve manually:

getent hosts example.com

or:

dig example.com

docs.title: Force IPv4
docs.text: curl -4 https://example.com/

docs.title: Force IPv6
docs.text: curl -6 https://example.com/

docs.title: Test Different Backend IPs
docs.text:
Suppose:

app.example.com

192.0.2.10

192.0.2.11

Test first backend:

curl --resolve app.example.com:443:192.0.2.10 https://app.example.com/

Second:

curl --resolve app.example.com:443:192.0.2.11 https://app.example.com/

This can help identify backend inconsistencies where those IPs are within scope.

docs.title: API Testing
docs.text: curl is particularly useful for APIs because requests can be precisely reproduced.

docs.title: GET JSON
docs.text:
curl -sS https://example.com/api/users \
  -H 'Accept: application/json'

docs.title: Pretty Print JSON with jq
docs.text: curl -sS https://example.com/api/users | jq

docs.title: POST JSON
docs.text:
curl -sS https://example.com/api/users \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Test User"}'

docs.title: JSON from File
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/api/users \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @request.json

docs.title: Why File-Based Requests Help
docs.text:
For larger bodies:

request.json

is easier to:

Version

Review

Repeat

Modify

Preserve as evidence

than a large inline shell string.

docs.title: Form Submission
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/login \
  -d 'username=test&password=test'

docs.title: Multipart Form
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/profile \
  -F 'displayName=Test User'

docs.title: File Upload
docs.text:
For an authorised upload test:

curl https://example.com/upload \
  -F 'file=@test.txt'

Add another field:

curl https://example.com/upload \
  -F 'description=Assessment test file' \
  -F 'file=@test.txt'

Use harmless assessment files unless the scope specifically requires another controlled test case.

docs.title: Specify Multipart Content Type
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/upload \
  -F 'file=@test.txt;type=text/plain'

docs.title: Download File
docs.text:
curl https://example.com/files/test.pdf -o test.pdf

Check:

file test.pdf

Hash:

sha256sum test.pdf

docs.title: Resume Download
docs.text: curl -C - https://example.com/large-file.zip -o large-file.zip

docs.title: API Authorisation Testing
docs.text:
curl is useful for controlled two-account authorisation testing.

Example:

Account A owns object 1001

Account B owns object 2001

docs.title: Baseline - Account A Own Object
docs.text:
curl -i https://example.com/api/orders/1001 \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <account-a-token>'

Expected:

200 OK

docs.title: Cross-Account Test
docs.text:
curl -i https://example.com/api/orders/2001 \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <account-a-token>'

Secure behaviour might be:

403 Forbidden

or:

404 Not Found

depending on application design.

docs.title: Authorisation Interpretation
docs.text:
If Account A receives Account B's protected object:

Controlled Account A
        |
        v
Request Object B
        |
        v
Protected Data Returned
        |
        v
Confirm Object Ownership
        |
        v
Reproduce
        |
        v
Authorisation Failure

The important evidence is not simply:

HTTP 200

but:

User A was not authorised to access object B, yet the application returned B's protected data.

docs.title: Compare Responses
docs.text:
Save baseline:

curl -sS https://example.com/api/orders/1001 \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <account-a-token>' \
  -o account-a-own.json

Cross-account:

curl -sS https://example.com/api/orders/2001 \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <account-a-token>' \
  -o account-a-other.json

Compare:

diff -u account-a-own.json account-a-other.json

docs.title: Response Size
docs.text:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{size_download}\n' https://example.com/

Response-size differences can help identify behavioural changes, but size alone is not proof of a security issue.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}
' https://example.com/

More detailed:

curl -s -o /dev/null \
  -w 'DNS: %{time_namelookup}
Connect: %{time_connect}
TTFB: %{time_starttransfer}
Total: %{time_total}
' \
  https://example.com/

docs.title: Timing Interpretation
docs.text:
Response timing can be affected by:

Network latency

Application load

Caching

Database load

CDN

Rate limiting

Backend selection

TLS negotiation

Do not infer a vulnerability from a single slow request.

docs.title: Repeat Timing Tests
docs.text: Where timing matters, collect multiple controlled observations rather than comparing only one request against another.

docs.title: Security Headers
docs.text:
Quick check:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/

Review headers such as:

Content-Security-Policy

Strict-Transport-Security

X-Content-Type-Options

Referrer-Policy

Permissions-Policy

Set-Cookie

Cache-Control

docs.title: Header Absence Is Contextual
docs.text:
Do not automatically report every missing security header.

Consider:

Application type

Response content

Browser exposure

Existing equivalent controls

Threat model

docs.title: HSTS
docs.text:
Check:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/ | grep -i strict-transport-security

A missing HSTS header may be relevant for browser-facing HTTPS applications but must be assessed in context.

docs.title: CSP
docs.text:
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/ | grep -i content-security-policy

Presence of CSP does not mean the policy is strong.

The policy itself requires review.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Send an Origin header:

curl -i https://example.com/api/profile \
  -H 'Origin: https://example.invalid'

Review:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials

Vary

docs.title: CORS Preflight
docs.text:
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://example.com/api/profile \
  -H 'Origin: https://example.invalid' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: GET'

Do not conclude CORS exploitation solely from a reflected origin.

Consider:

Credentials

Browser behaviour

Sensitive response

Allowed methods

Allowed headers

docs.title: Cache Behaviour
docs.text:
Headers:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/

Review:

Cache-Control

Age

ETag

Expires

Vary

Via

X-Cache

Header names vary by infrastructure.

docs.title: Conditional Request
docs.text:
If an ETag is returned:

curl -i https://example.com/resource \
  -H 'If-None-Match: "<etag>"'

Possible:

304 Not Modified

docs.title: Content Types
docs.text:
Check:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/

Look for:

Content-Type

Do not rely only on file extensions to determine response type.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text:
Request compressed content:

curl --compressed https://example.com/

This tells curl to request supported compression and decompress the response.

docs.title: Range Requests
docs.text:
Request first 100 bytes:

curl -H 'Range: bytes=0-99' https://example.com/file.bin

Possible response:

206 Partial Content

Useful when validating download behaviour.

docs.title: Basic Reconnaissance
docs.text:
A quick web-service triage:

curl -k -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/

Then:

curl -k -v https://example.com/

Then inspect the body:

curl -k -sS https://example.com/

docs.title: Nmap to curl Workflow
docs.text:
Nmap
 |
 v
443/tcp open
 |
 v
curl
 |
 +--> Status
 +--> Headers
 +--> Redirect
 +--> TLS
 +--> Application Response
 |
 v
Browser / Burp

Example:

nmap -sV -p 443 192.0.2.10

Then:

curl -k -v https://192.0.2.10/

docs.title: Virtual Host Workflow
docs.text:
IP Address
    |
    v
Default Response
    |
    v
Known Hostname
    |
    v
--resolve
    |
    v
Application Response

Example:

curl --resolve portal.example.com:443:192.0.2.10 \
  https://portal.example.com/

docs.title: Burp to curl Workflow
docs.text:
A request identified in Burp can often be reproduced with curl.

Conceptually:

Burp Request
     |
     v
Method
     |
     v
URL
     |
     v
Headers
     |
     v
Cookies / Token
     |
     v
Body
     |
     v
curl

This is useful for:

Reproduction

Automation

Evidence

Response comparison

docs.title: curl to Burp Workflow
docs.text:
curl -k -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 \
  https://example.com/api/profile \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'

The request can then be examined and sent to Repeater.

docs.title: Request from File
docs.text:
Body:

curl https://example.com/api/test \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @request.json

Headers can also be managed carefully in scripts when repeated testing is required.

docs.title: Preserve Exact Body
docs.text:
--data-binary is useful when the exact body should be sent without -d style transformations:

curl https://example.com/api/test \
  --data-binary @request.bin

docs.title: URL Encoding
docs.text:
Encode form value:

curl https://example.com/search \
  --data-urlencode 'q=test value'

For GET query construction:

curl -G https://example.com/search \
  --data-urlencode 'q=test value'

This produces an encoded query parameter.

docs.title: Multiple Query Parameters
docs.text:
curl -G https://example.com/search \
  --data-urlencode 'q=test value' \
  --data-urlencode 'page=1'

docs.title: Why -G Is Useful
docs.text:
Without -G, -d normally creates a request body.

With:

-G

the data is appended to the URL query string.

docs.title: Request Timeout
docs.text:
Maximum total time:

curl --max-time 10 https://example.com/

Connection timeout:

curl --connect-timeout 5 https://example.com/

docs.title: Retry
docs.text:
curl --retry 3 https://example.com/

Use retries carefully during testing because repeated requests can alter:

Rate limiting

Lockout behaviour

Application state

Monitoring

docs.title: Rate Limiting Observation
docs.text:
Suppose repeated authorised requests produce:

200

200

200

429

This supports the observation that the application is applying some form of request-rate control.

It does not automatically prove:

The rate limit is secure.

The rate limit cannot be bypassed.

The limit applies across accounts/IPs/endpoints.

docs.title: HTTP 401
docs.text:
401 Unauthorized

typically indicates authentication is required or authentication failed.

Inspect:

WWW-Authenticate

where present.

docs.title: HTTP 403
docs.text:
403 Forbidden

typically means the server understood the request but refused it.

Do not assume:

Resource does not exist.

docs.title: HTTP 404
docs.text:
404 Not Found

may mean:

Resource absent

Routing rejected

Authorisation intentionally hidden

Application custom behaviour

Compare controlled requests before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: HTTP 405
docs.text:
405 Method Not Allowed

suggests the requested method is not supported for the resource.

Check:

Allow

where provided.

docs.title: HTTP 429
docs.text:
429 Too Many Requests

indicates rate limiting or request throttling.

Review:

Retry-After

where present.

docs.title: HTTP 500
docs.text:
500 Internal Server Error

does not automatically indicate exploitable behaviour.

It may reveal:

Unhandled exception

Application bug

Backend failure

Invalid input handling

Review the response carefully for unnecessary internal information.

docs.title: Response Comparison Model
docs.text:
When testing an input:

Baseline Request
      |
      v
Baseline Response
      |
      v
Change One Variable
      |
      v
Modified Response
      |
      v
Compare
      |
      v
Explain Difference

Avoid changing several parameters simultaneously because this makes causality harder to establish.

docs.title: Good Controlled Comparison
docs.text:
Baseline:

curl -i 'https://example.com/api/items/1001' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'

Modified:

curl -i 'https://example.com/api/items/1002' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'

Only the object identifier changes.

docs.title: Poor Comparison
docs.text:
Changing:

Object ID

Token

User-Agent

Method

Content-Type

Body

all at once makes the result difficult to interpret.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Always Using -k
docs.text:
Problem:

Certificate problems become invisible.

Better:

Try normal certificate validation first.

Use -k only when the assessment requires bypassing trust validation.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Always Using -L
docs.text:
Problem:

Important redirect behaviour may be hidden.

Better:

Inspect the original response first.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Using -I as GET Evidence
docs.text:
Problem:

-I performs HEAD.

Better for GET response headers:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/

docs.title: Common Mistake - Explicit -X POST with -d
docs.text:
This works:

curl -X POST https://example.com/api \
  -d 'a=b'

but -d already selects POST in ordinary usage.

Simpler:

curl https://example.com/api \
  -d 'a=b'

docs.title: Common Mistake - Reporting Server Header as Confirmed Version
docs.text:
Response:

Server: nginx

or a version-bearing banner may be:

Modified

Hidden

Proxied

Generated by an intermediary

Use it as supporting evidence rather than unquestionable product identification.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Exposing Secrets in Shell History
docs.text:
Avoid:

curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer REAL_SECRET_TOKEN' ...

when working with sensitive production credentials if safer alternatives are available.

Be conscious of:

Shell history

Terminal recordings

Screenshots

Process lists

Shared logs

docs.title: Environment Variables for Test Tokens
docs.text:
For temporary authorised testing:

export TEST_TOKEN='<token>'

Then:

curl https://example.com/api/profile \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_TOKEN"

Remove:

unset TEST_TOKEN

This reduces repeated token exposure in copied commands, although environment variables themselves are not a universal secret-storage solution.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Confusing Network and Application Errors
docs.text:
Example:

Connection refused

is different from:

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

The first is primarily a connection/service observation.

The second is an application/protocol response.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Could Not Resolve Host
docs.text:
Example:

curl: (6) Could not resolve host

Check:

getent hosts example.com

dig example.com

If testing a known in-scope backend:

curl --resolve example.com:443:192.0.2.10 https://example.com/

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Connection Refused
docs.text:
Check:

nmap -p 443 example.com

or:

nc -vz example.com 443

Possible causes:

Service not listening

Wrong port

Firewall rejection

Wrong IP

Service stopped

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Timeout
docs.text:
curl --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10 https://example.com/

Then investigate:

DNS

Routing

Firewall

Proxy

VPN

Service health

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Certificate Error
docs.text:
Use verbose mode:

curl -v https://example.com/

Inspect:

Hostname

Issuer

Trust

Validity

Certificate chain

Use -k only when bypassing certificate validation is appropriate for the test.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Wrong Application
docs.text:
If the IP hosts multiple sites:

curl --resolve app.example.com:443:192.0.2.10 https://app.example.com/

This often resolves virtual-host/SNI issues.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Proxy Unexpectedly Used
docs.text:
Check:

env | grep -i proxy

Bypass:

curl --noproxy '*' https://example.com/

docs.title: Troubleshooting - HTTP vs HTTPS
docs.text:
Test HTTP:

curl -v http://example.com/

HTTPS:

curl -v https://example.com/

The HTTP endpoint may simply redirect to HTTPS.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For an important HTTP test record:

Test ID

Timestamp

Source IP

Target hostname

Target IP where relevant

URL

Method

Authentication context

Request headers

Request body where relevant

Response status

Response headers

Relevant response body

curl version

Exact command

Interpretation

docs.title: Example Evidence Record
docs.text:
Test ID:
WEB-CURL-007

Timestamp:
2026-09-06 18:45 UTC

Tool:
curl

Target:
https://portal.example.com/api/orders/2001

Method:
GET

Authentication:
Controlled Account A

Objective:
Determine whether Account A can access an object belonging
to controlled Account B.

Baseline:
Account A successfully accessed its own object 1001.

Test:
Account A requested Account B object 2001.

Result:
HTTP 200 returned with Account B order details.

Interpretation:
The application did not enforce the expected object-level
authorisation boundary between the two controlled accounts.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Do not report:

curl returned HTTP 200.

Report the underlying security condition.

Example:

The API did not enforce object-level authorisation when accessing order resources. A session authenticated as controlled Account A could request the identifier of an order belonging to controlled Account B and receive the protected order details.

docs.title: Evidence Quality
docs.text:
Weak:

Screenshot of terminal showing 200.

Better:

Controlled account ownership documented.

Baseline request preserved.

Modified request preserved.

Response preserved.

Only object identifier changed.

Protected data identified.

Behaviour reproduced.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Use the same controlled test after remediation.

Before:

Account A -> Object B -> 200 + protected data

After:

Account A -> Object B -> 403

or another intentionally secure response.

docs.title: Retest Example
docs.text:
curl -i https://example.com/api/orders/2001 \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <account-a-token>'

Expected after remediation:

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

or an application-designed equivalent.

docs.title: Retest More Than Status
docs.text:
Do not validate only:

Status changed from 200 to 403.

Also confirm:

Protected data absent

Alternative methods denied

Equivalent endpoints protected

Account A still accesses own object

Account B still accesses own object

docs.title: API Retest Matrix
docs.text: Test Expected A -> A object Allowed A -> B object Denied B -> B object Allowed B -> A object Denied Unauthenticated -> A Denied

docs.title: curl and jq
docs.text:
Pretty print:

curl -sS https://example.com/api/data | jq

Specific field:

curl -sS https://example.com/api/data | jq '.id'

Array:

curl -sS https://example.com/api/users | jq '.[].username'

Use only when the response is valid JSON.

docs.title: curl and grep
docs.text:
Headers:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/ | grep -i server

Cookies:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/ | grep -i set-cookie

Security headers:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com/ | grep -Ei 'content-security-policy|strict-transport-security|x-content-type-options'

docs.title: curl and diff
docs.text:
Baseline:

curl -sS https://example.com/api/item/1001 -o baseline.txt

Modified:

curl -sS https://example.com/api/item/1002 -o modified.txt

Compare:

diff -u baseline.txt modified.txt

docs.title: curl and sha256sum
docs.text:
Download:

curl -sS https://example.com/file.bin -o file.bin

Hash:

sha256sum file.bin

docs.text:

Use curl for reproducibility

Browser testing is essential, but a concise curl command can make an HTTP observation much easier to reproduce, compare and preserve as assessment evidence.

Use --resolve for HTTPS virtual hosts

When an application hostname must be tested against a specific in-scope IP address, --resolve usually provides a cleaner test than connecting directly to the IP and changing only the Host header because it also preserves the hostname used for TLS SNI.

Change one variable at a time

Controlled comparisons are much easier to defend. Keep the method, identity, headers and body constant while changing only the parameter or object identifier being investigated.

HEAD is not GET

curl -I sends a HEAD request. If you need the headers produced by a normal GET request, use curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null <URL> instead.

HTTP success does not prove correct authorisation

A 200 OK response only establishes that the request succeeded at the HTTP/application level. For access-control testing, establish who owns the resource, which identity made the request and whether that identity was permitted to receive the returned data or perform the action.

docs.title: Insecure Deserialization Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Insecure deserialization occurs when an application deserializes attacker-controlled data in a way that allows the data to influence application objects, program behaviour or dangerous code paths.

A simplified flow is:

Attacker-Controlled Data
          |
          v
      Decoder
          |
          v
    Deserializer
          |
          v
     Object Graph
          |
          v
Application Behaviour

The fundamental security question is:

Can an attacker control serialized data that crosses
a trust boundary and is reconstructed into application objects?

Potential consequences depend heavily on the platform and implementation.

They may include:

Object manipulation

Authorization bypass

Application logic manipulation

Integrity violations

Sensitive data exposure

Unexpected method invocation

Denial of service

Code execution

Authorised Security Testing

Perform deserialization testing only against systems explicitly included in the assessment scope. Start by identifying formats, trust boundaries and integrity controls. Do not deploy destructive gadget chains, execute operating-system commands, establish shells or modify production data simply to demonstrate unsafe deserialization.

docs.title: JSON.parse Is Not Equivalent to Native Object Deserialization
docs.text:
Normal:

JSON.parse(userInput)

produces JSON-compatible values.

It does not inherently reconstruct arbitrary executable application classes.

docs.title: But Review Downstream Use
docs.text:
A parsed object may still become dangerous through:

Prototype pollution

Dynamic module loading

Unsafe property assignment

Dynamic function invocation

Command construction

docs.title: JSON Deserialization
docs.text:
JSON is generally preferable to native object serialization for untrusted data because it represents simpler data structures.

However:

JSON

docs.title: MAC vs Hash
docs.text:

docs.title: Preferred
docs.text:

docs.title: Strong Black-Box Evidence
docs.text:
A defensible chain might be:

1. Client receives serialized state.

2. Format is identified.

3. Controlled modification is made.

4. Modified object is accepted.

5. Server reconstructs attacker-controlled state.

6. Security-relevant application behaviour changes.

7. Result is repeatable.

docs.title: Strong White-Box Evidence
docs.text:
1. External request value identified.

2. Value is decoded.

3. Data flows directly to unsafe deserializer.

4. No prior integrity verification exists.

5. Deserializer permits dangerous object reconstruction.

6. Reachability is confirmed.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Unsafe Native Deserialization
docs.text: The application deserializes attacker-controlled data using a native object deserialization mechanism. The serialized value is accepted from the client and reaches the deserializer without an appropriate trusted-data boundary. Controlled mutations confirmed that client-supplied serialized state is processed by the server. Native object deserialization should not be used for untrusted input.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Client-Side Serialized State
docs.text: The application stores security-relevant state in a client-controlled serialized object. The object can be modified and re-submitted without effective integrity validation. A controlled change to the serialized state was accepted by the server and altered application behaviour. Security-sensitive state should not be trusted from the client without cryptographic integrity protection and server-side authorization.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Java
docs.text: The application passes attacker-controlled serialized data to ObjectInputStream.readObject(). The input reaches Java native deserialization before any effective trust validation. This exposes the application to unsafe object reconstruction and should be replaced with a constrained data format and explicit schema validation.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Python
docs.text: Attacker-controlled request data is passed to pickle.loads(). Python pickle is capable of reconstructing arbitrary Python objects and is not designed for untrusted input. The application should replace pickle at this trust boundary with a data-only format such as JSON and explicit schema validation.

docs.title: Reporting Example - PHP
docs.text: The application passes a client-controlled value to PHP unserialize(). The deserializer is therefore able to reconstruct values and potentially objects based on attacker-controlled serialized input. The application should avoid PHP object serialization across untrusted boundaries and use a constrained data representation instead.

docs.title: Reporting Example - .NET
docs.text: The application deserializes attacker-controlled input using BinaryFormatter. This API is unsuitable for untrusted data because object reconstruction can invoke unexpected runtime behaviour. The serialized interface should be redesigned using a constrained serializer and explicitly defined data types.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Polymorphic JSON
docs.text: The API accepts attacker-controlled type metadata during JSON deserialization. The configured deserializer can resolve runtime types based on values supplied in the request rather than restricting deserialization to an explicit set of application types. Polymorphic deserialization should be constrained to an allowlist of known types.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
The key question is not:

Is this value serialized?

It is:

CAN ATTACKER-CONTROLLED DATA
           |
           v
CROSS A TRUST BOUNDARY
           |
           v
REACH AN OBJECT DESERIALIZER
           |
           v
AND INFLUENCE SECURITY-RELEVANT BEHAVIOUR?

A strong workflow is:

Identify Candidate State
        |
        v
Preserve Original
        |
        v
Decode
        |
        v
Identify Format
        |
        v
Identify Deserializer
        |
        v
Determine Integrity Protection
        |
        v
Perform Controlled Mutation
        |
        v
Observe Server Behaviour
        |
        v
Trace Source to Sink
        |
        v
Determine Actual Impact
        |
        v
Capture Evidence
        |
        v
Replace Unsafe Object Deserialization
        |
        v
Retest

For every deserialization candidate ask:

Where did this value originate?

Can an attacker control it?

Is it merely encoded?

Is it encrypted?

Is it integrity-protected?

What serialization format is used?

Which runtime deserializes it?

Which API performs deserialization?

Does verification happen before deserialization?

Can the attacker influence object types?

Are types explicitly allowlisted?

Does the format reconstruct native objects?

Are dangerous magic methods or callbacks available?

Are third-party classes involved?

Is this a client-side state problem instead?

Is authorization based on values inside the object?

Could this be second-order?

Does a queue or worker deserialize it later?

Can I demonstrate the issue with a harmless mutation?

Is a gadget chain actually required to prove impact?

Am I claiming RCE without demonstrating it?

Could a simpler data-only format replace this mechanism?

Can authorization state be moved server-side?

Have equivalent deserialization sinks been reviewed?

The strongest conclusion is not:

The cookie contains serialized data.

It is:

ATTACKER-CONTROLLED DATA
          |
          v
CROSSES TRUST BOUNDARY
          |
          v
UNSAFE DESERIALIZATION
          |
          v
SECURITY-RELEVANT BEHAVIOUR
          |
          v
REPEATABLE RESULT

Identify the trust boundary first

A serialization format is not a vulnerability by itself. Determine whether attacker-controlled data actually crosses a trust boundary and reaches a deserializer.

Use controlled mutations

A one-field or one-byte change can reveal integrity protection, parsing behaviour and server trust without requiring dangerous gadget chains.

Separate the mechanism from the impact

Unsafe native deserialization, missing state integrity and broken authorization can appear together but are not identical vulnerabilities. Report the root cause and demonstrated impact accurately.

Prefer data, not objects

Untrusted interfaces should normally exchange explicitly defined data structures rather than serialized runtime object graphs.

Base64 is not a security control

Encoding serialized data does not provide confidentiality, integrity or authenticity.

Do not prove deserialization with command execution

If controlled mutations, type-resolution behaviour or source-to-sink analysis already establish unsafe deserialization, operating-system command execution usually adds unnecessary risk without improving the technical conclusion.

docs.title: File Upload Security Cheatsheet
docs.text:
File upload functionality introduces a boundary where attacker-controlled content enters application-controlled storage and processing.

The security question is not simply:

Can I upload a file?

The important questions are:

What files are accepted?

How is the file validated?

Where is it stored?

What filename is used?

Can the uploaded file be retrieved?

How is it served?

Is it processed?

Can processing reach dangerous parsers?

Can another user access it?

Can it overwrite another file?

Can uploaded content become executable?

A typical upload pipeline is:

Client
  |
  v
Upload Endpoint
  |
  v
Validation
  |
  v
Storage
  |
  v
Processing
  |
  v
Retrieval / Rendering

Every stage can introduce a different vulnerability.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform file upload testing only against systems explicitly included in the assessment scope. Prefer harmless marker files, non-executable test content and assessment-controlled filenames. Avoid uploading malware, executable payloads, destructive archives or files designed to exhaust server resources unless that testing is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Start With the Business Function
docs.text:
Determine why the application accepts files.

Examples:

Profile avatar

Support attachment

Invoice upload

Document management

Evidence upload

CSV import

XML import

Backup import

Theme upload

Media library

Report attachment

docs.title: Understand Expected Files
docs.text:
For each upload feature record:

Expected file type

Expected extension

Expected content

Maximum size

Maximum number of files

Expected processing

Expected storage duration

Who can retrieve the file

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Start with a valid expected file.

Example:

test.jpg

Record:

Request

Response

File identifier

Returned filename

Retrieval URL

Content-Type

Content-Disposition

Processing delay

docs.text:
POST /api/avatar HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----TestBoundary

------TestBoundary

docs.text:
Example:

{
  "id": "8a91f7",
  "filename": "avatar.jpg",

}

docs.title: Questions After Baseline
docs.text:
Ask:

Was the original filename retained?

Was a new identifier generated?

Was the extension changed?

Was the file processed?

Was the file resized?

Can it be downloaded?

Can another account retrieve it?

What headers are used when serving it?

docs.title: Multipart Anatomy
docs.text:
A multipart upload commonly contains:

Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="report.pdf"
Content-Type: application/pdf

There are several independent pieces of information:

Form field name

Client filename

Client MIME type

File bytes

docs.title: Do Not Trust Client MIME Type
docs.text:
This value:

Content-Type: image/jpeg

is supplied by the client.

It can be changed easily.

docs.title: Burp MIME Modification
docs.text:
Original:

Content-Type: text/plain

Modified:

Content-Type: image/jpeg

If changing only the MIME type bypasses validation, the application is relying too heavily on client-controlled metadata.

docs.title: File Extension Validation
docs.text:
An application may allow:

.jpg

.jpeg

.png

and reject:

.txt

This demonstrates extension validation.

It does not establish that file content is validated.

docs.title: Extension Allowlist
docs.text:
Prefer:

Known required extensions

over:

Block dangerous extensions

docs.title: Why Denylists Are Weak
docs.text:
A denylist must anticipate:

Languages

Web server handlers

Platform differences

Alternative extensions

Future configuration changes

docs.title: Extension Case
docs.text:
Applications should handle extension comparison consistently.

Examples:

image.JPG

image.Jpg

image.PnG

Case behaviour can vary by:

Application

Filesystem

Web server

Operating system

docs.title: Multiple Extensions
docs.text:
Example:

report.txt.jpg

Determine which component interprets:

First extension

Last extension

Full filename

docs.title: Do Not Assume Double Extensions Are Exploitable
docs.text:
A filename such as:

file.php.jpg

is only meaningful if some component interprets it in an unsafe way.

Validate actual behaviour rather than reporting the filename alone.

docs.title: Trailing Characters
docs.text:
Different platforms can treat trailing:

Spaces

Dots

differently.

These cases are relevant primarily when the application's target platform or normalisation behaviour makes them applicable.

docs.title: MIME Validation
docs.text:
Applications may inspect:

Multipart Content-Type

Detected content type

File signature

Parser result

docs.title: Client MIME vs Detected MIME
docs.text:
Client says:
image/jpeg

Actual bytes:
plain text

A secure design should not rely solely on the client claim.

docs.title: File Signatures
docs.text:
Many formats begin with characteristic bytes.

These are often called:

Magic bytes

File signatures

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
JPEG commonly begins with:

FF D8 FF

PNG begins with:

89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A

PDF begins with:

%PDF-

ZIP commonly begins with:

PK

docs.title: Signature Validation
docs.text:
File signatures can help identify obviously mismatched files.

However:

Valid signature != safe file

A valid file can still contain:

Malicious active content

Dangerous parser structures

Unexpected metadata

Embedded content

docs.title: File Command
docs.text:
On Linux:

file test.pdf

docs.title: Example
docs.text: test.pdf: PDF document, version 1.7

docs.text: file --mime-type test.pdf

docs.title: Example

docs.title: Hex Inspection
docs.text: xxd -l 32 test.pdf

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
00000000: 2550 4446 2d31 2e37

This corresponds to:

%PDF-1.7

docs.title: Filename Security
docs.text:
Client-supplied filenames are untrusted input.

Example:

filename="report.pdf"

docs.text:
Prefer:

Original filename:
Quarterly Report.pdf

Stored filename:
8f46c7f0-9c3a-4df1-b4d0.bin

docs.text:
This helps reduce:

Name collisions

File overwrite

Special-character issues

Predictable object names

A dangerous pattern is:

filename="../../outside.txt"

docs.text:
A harmless filename test might use:

and verify whether the application:

Changes

Normalises

Rejects

docs.title: Special Characters
docs.text:
Relevant filename characters can include:

Spaces

Unicode

Quotes

Parentheses

Ampersands

Angle brackets

Testing should focus on how the filename is:

Stored

Displayed

Encoded

Logged

Returned in headers

docs.title: Filename-Based Stored XSS
docs.text:
A filename may later appear in HTML.

Example filename:

report-7f3a9.txt

First determine whether it is rendered safely.

Do not jump directly to active JavaScript payloads if simple HTML encoding analysis is enough.

docs.title: Safe Rendering
docs.text:
If the filename:

report<test>.txt

appears as:

report<test>.txt

the application is HTML-encoding the value in that context.

docs.title: Context Matters
docs.text:
A filename may appear in:

HTML text

HTML attribute

JavaScript

JSON

HTTP header

Email

PDF report

Each context requires appropriate output encoding.

docs.title: Content-Disposition
docs.text:
A download response may use:

Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="report.pdf"

This usually encourages download rather than inline rendering.

docs.title: Inline Content
docs.text:
A response such as:

Content-Disposition: inline

may cause supported formats to render in the browser.

docs.title: Content-Type
docs.text:
The response should use an appropriate MIME type.

Example:

Content-Type: application/pdf

docs.title: X-Content-Type-Options
docs.text:
A useful response header is:

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

This reduces MIME-sniffing behaviour in browsers.

docs.title: Storage Location
docs.text:
Determine whether files are stored:

Inside web root

Outside web root

Object storage

Database

Separate file service

docs.title: Web Root Storage
docs.text:

Upload
  |
  v
/var/www/html/uploads/
  |
  v
Direct Public URL

If the server interprets certain file types, this can increase risk.

docs.title: Preferred Model
docs.text:
Upload
  |
  v
Non-Executable Storage
  |
  v
Application Download Handler
  |
  v
Authorisation

docs.title: Object Storage
docs.text:
Applications frequently use:

Amazon S3

Azure Blob Storage

Google Cloud Storage

S3-compatible storage

Security questions include:

Is the object public?

Is the URL predictable?

Are signed URLs used?

How long are signed URLs valid?

Is access tenant-isolated?

Can content type be controlled?

docs.title: Public Object Storage
docs.text:
An upload being stored in cloud object storage is not itself a vulnerability.

The important question is:

Who can retrieve the object?

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text: Test file ownership separately from file type validation.

docs.title: Two-Account Model
docs.text:
Account A
   |
   v
Uploads File A
   |
   v
File ID / URL
   |
   v
Account B Attempts Access

docs.title: Expected Secure Result
docs.text: Account B should not access Account A's private upload unless sharing is intentionally supported.

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
If another user can retrieve a private file by changing:

File ID

Object key

UUID

Path

the primary issue may be:

IDOR / BOLA

rather than unrestricted file upload.

docs.title: Predictable URLs
docs.text:
Example:

/files/1001

/files/1002

/files/1003

Predictability is not itself the vulnerability.

The important control is:

Authorisation on retrieval.

docs.title: File Replacement
docs.text:
Test whether uploading another file with the same name:

report.pdf

causes:

Overwrite

Rename

Versioning

Rejection

docs.title: Safe Test
docs.text:
Use only files belonging to the assessment account.

Do not attempt to overwrite another user's files unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Collision Handling
docs.text:
Secure systems commonly use:

Random identifiers

UUIDs

Database IDs

Versioned object keys

docs.title: Upload Size
docs.text:
Determine:

Maximum file size

Maximum request size

Maximum total storage

Maximum number of files

docs.title: Size Validation
docs.text:
A response may indicate:

File too large

Record the configured behaviour without attempting resource exhaustion.

docs.title: Do Not Perform Storage Exhaustion
docs.text:
Avoid repeatedly uploading large files simply to prove that storage limits might be weak.

Denial-of-service testing requires explicit authorisation.

docs.title: File Count Limits
docs.text:
A user may be restricted by:

Number of attachments

Daily upload quota

Total account storage

docs.title: Empty Files
docs.text:
A zero-byte file can reveal validation order.

Example:

touch empty.txt

docs.title: Validation Question
docs.text:
Does the application validate:

Extension first?

Size first?

Content first?

Parser first?

docs.title: Image Uploads
docs.text:
Image functionality often includes server-side processing.

Typical pipeline:

Upload
  |
  v
Image Decoder
  |
  v
Resize
  |
  v
Re-encode
  |
  v
Store

docs.title: Re-Encoding
docs.text:
Re-encoding uploaded images can remove some unnecessary embedded content.

It is not a universal security solution, but it can reduce attack surface.

docs.title: Image Processing Libraries
docs.text:
Potential components include:

ImageMagick

GraphicsMagick

libvips

Pillow

Sharp

GD

docs.title: Source Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'ImageMagick|GraphicsMagick|Pillow|PIL|sharp|libvips|imagecreate|Intervention' .

docs.title: Image Metadata
docs.text:
Images may contain:

EXIF

GPS information

Camera model

Timestamps

Comments

Applications handling privacy-sensitive images may need to remove unnecessary metadata.

docs.title: exiftool
docs.text:
Inspect metadata:

exiftool image.jpg

docs.title: Metadata Removal Test
docs.text:
Compare metadata before and after application processing.

Do not assume metadata retention is automatically a security vulnerability; evaluate the application's privacy requirements.

docs.title: SVG Uploads
docs.text: SVG deserves special attention because it is XML-based and can contain active or externally referenced content depending on how it is processed and served.

docs.title: Minimal SVG
docs.text:
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
     width="100"
     height="100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40"/>
</svg>

docs.title: SVG Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Is SVG allowed?

Is it sanitised?

Is it parsed server-side?

Is it re-rendered?

Is it served inline?

Is it served as an attachment?

What Content-Type is returned?

Does server-side processing resolve external resources?

docs.title: SVG Security Surfaces
docs.text:
SVG
 |
 +--> Stored active content
 |
 +--> XML parser
 |
 +--> External resource references
 |
 +--> Image conversion library

docs.title: SVG and XSS
docs.text:
If an uploaded SVG is rendered directly in a browser under the application's origin, active SVG content may create a stored client-side injection risk.

Validate actual browser behaviour and response headers.

docs.title: SVG and XXE
docs.text:
If the server parses SVG as XML, parser configuration should be reviewed for XXE.

See:

XXE Cheatsheet

docs.title: SVG and SSRF
docs.text:
Server-side SVG processing may retrieve external resources in some processing pipelines.

If this occurs, determine whether the root cause is:

XML processing

Image renderer behaviour

Generic URL retrieval

docs.title: PDF Uploads
docs.text:
PDF files are complex documents that can contain:

Metadata

Embedded objects

Links

Forms

JavaScript features

Attachments

depending on the document and viewer.

docs.title: PDF Acceptance Is Not a Vulnerability
docs.text:
The fact that an application accepts PDFs does not mean it must reject every PDF containing active features.

Risk depends on:

How the PDF is processed

How it is served

Which viewer opens it

Whether server-side parsers inspect it

docs.title: PDF Processing
docs.text:
Applications may:

Extract text

Generate thumbnails

Merge documents

Convert to images

Perform OCR

Scan for malware

docs.title: Parser Attack Surface
docs.text:
Each processing step introduces another parser or library.

Conceptually:

PDF
 |
 v
Parser
 |
 +--> Metadata
 |
 +--> Text extraction
 |
 +--> Thumbnail generation

docs.title: Office Documents
docs.text:
Formats such as:

DOCX

XLSX

PPTX

are ZIP-based document formats containing XML and other resources.

docs.title: Office Processing Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Is the document merely stored?

Is text extracted?

Is it converted?

Is XML parsed?

Are macros relevant to the workflow?

Are external references processed?

docs.title: Macro-Enabled Formats
docs.text:
Examples include:

.docm

.xlsm

.pptm

Whether these should be accepted depends on business requirements.

docs.title: Do Not Execute Uploaded Documents
docs.text:
File upload testing normally focuses on server/application handling.

Opening untrusted uploaded documents on analyst workstations introduces unnecessary risk.

docs.title: XML Uploads
docs.text:
An application accepting XML should be reviewed for parser configuration.

See:

XXE Cheatsheet

docs.title: CSV Uploads
docs.text:
CSV imports can introduce:

Parser errors

Formula injection downstream

Data validation issues

Mass assignment

Business logic issues

docs.title: CSV Formula Injection
docs.text:
If uploaded CSV content is later exported or opened in spreadsheet software, cells beginning with formula syntax may require special handling.

This is separate from the upload mechanism itself.

docs.title: Archive Uploads
docs.text:
Applications may accept:

.zip

../../outside.txt

docs.text:

Assessment-controlled extraction directory

docs.title: Archive Bombs
docs.text:
Highly compressed or recursively nested archives can consume substantial resources.

Do not use archive bombs during routine testing.

docs.title: Archive Limits
docs.text:
Secure systems should consider:

Compressed size

Uncompressed size

Number of entries

Nested archive depth

Extraction time

docs.title: Password-Protected Archives
docs.text:
Antivirus or content scanners may not be able to inspect encrypted archives.

Whether these files should be accepted depends on the application's business requirements.

docs.title: Malware Scanning
docs.text: Applications may use antivirus or malware scanning as one layer of upload security.

docs.title: EICAR
docs.text:
The EICAR anti-malware test file is a standard harmless test artifact designed to trigger antivirus products.

Use it only where antivirus validation is explicitly in scope and coordinate appropriately because it may generate security alerts.

docs.title: Antivirus Is Not File Validation
docs.text:
Even when malware scanning is present, the application still needs controls for:

File type

Filename

Storage

Access control

Parser security

Serving behaviour

docs.title: Scanner Failure Behaviour
docs.text:
Determine what happens when the malware scanner:

Times out

Is unavailable

Returns an error

docs.title: Fail Open vs Fail Closed
docs.text: Security-sensitive upload workflows should deliberately define behaviour when scanning cannot complete.

docs.title: Quarantine
docs.text:

Upload
  |
  v
Quarantine

  v

The upload may initially return:

Pending

docs.title: Race Condition
docs.text:

  v

Conversion errors

Worker failures

docs.title: Source Review Questions
docs.text:
For every upload path ask:

Who can upload?

What file types are expected?

How is extension validated?

How is MIME type validated?

Is content inspected?

Is the original filename trusted?

Is a server-side filename generated?

Where is the file stored?

Is storage executable?

Can the user control the storage path?

Can existing files be overwritten?

Is the file processed?

Which parsers process it?

Can processors access the network?

Can processors access sensitive files?

Is malware scanning performed?

Is scanning synchronous?

Can the file be accessed before scanning?

Who can retrieve it?

How is retrieval authorised?

What response headers are used?

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
A captured multipart request can be modified directly.

Baseline:

POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----Test

------Test
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="test.txt"
Content-Type: text/plain

UPLOAD_TEST_7f3a9
------Test--

docs.title: Change One Variable at a Time
docs.text:
For example:

Test 1:
Change extension only.

Test 2:
Change MIME type only.

Test 3:
Change filename only.

Test 4:
Change content only.

This makes the validation logic easier to understand.

docs.title: Burp Intruder

docs.title: Reporting Example - Weak Type Validation
docs.text: The document upload endpoint validates the file type using the client-controlled multipart Content-Type value. During testing, a file that would normally be rejected was accepted after changing only the multipart MIME type while leaving the file contents unchanged. This demonstrates that the upload policy can be bypassed because the application trusts client-supplied type metadata.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Filename Path Traversal
docs.text: The upload handler uses the client-supplied filename when constructing the destination filesystem path without adequately enforcing the upload directory boundary. A controlled filename containing a parent-directory reference caused a harmless assessment marker file to be written outside the intended upload directory.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Broken File Access Control
docs.text: Files uploaded by one authenticated user can be retrieved by another authenticated user by requesting the first user's file identifier. The download endpoint does not enforce ownership or equivalent authorisation before returning the stored object.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Unsafe Inline SVG
docs.text: The application accepts SVG uploads and serves the uploaded files inline from the primary application origin without sanitising active SVG content. A controlled SVG uploaded through the normal attachment workflow executed browser-side content when viewed, demonstrating stored active-content injection through the upload feature.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Quarantine Race
docs.text: Uploaded files become retrievable immediately after upload while malware scanning remains in the pending state. The application therefore exposes unscanned content before the security validation workflow has completed.

docs.title: Avoid Overclaiming
docs.text:
Do not write:

Arbitrary file upload leads to remote code execution.

unless execution was actually established.

Prefer:

The application accepts file types outside the documented upload policy.

Then describe separately what security consequence was demonstrated.

docs.text:

Example:

Avatar:
JPEG

Where appropriate validate:

Extension

Detected MIME

File signature

Successful parsing

docs.text: Do not use raw client filenames as storage paths.

docs.title: Store Original Name as Metadata

Quarterly Report.pdf

c07a6241-f42d-4fb0-9db5

docs.text: Uploaded data should not normally reside in directories where the web server or application runtime can execute it.

docs.title: Separate Origin
docs.text: Serve untrusted user content from a separate origin where appropriate.

docs.text:
Depending on the use case:

Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Content-Disposition: attachment
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

The correct Content-Type depends on whether safe inline rendering is intentionally required.

docs.text:

Unpredictable URL

docs.text:
Any component processing untrusted files should use:

docs.text:

If SVG is not required:

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: Retest the original vulnerable workflow rather than only checking the new validation code.

docs.title: Retest Baseline
docs.text: Confirm legitimate files still upload successfully.

docs.title: Retest Extension
docs.text: Verify disallowed extensions are rejected.

docs.title: Retest MIME
docs.text: Changing only client-controlled MIME metadata should not bypass the policy.

docs.title: Retest Content
docs.text: A file with a valid extension but invalid content should be handled according to the intended policy.

docs.title: Retest Filename
docs.text:
Verify client filenames cannot:

Escape directories

Overwrite arbitrary files

Create unexpected paths

docs.title: Retest Storage
docs.text: Confirm uploaded files are stored in the intended non-executable location.

docs.title: Retest Retrieval
docs.text:
Check:

Content-Type

Content-Disposition

nosniff

Authorisation

Caching

docs.title: Retest Two Accounts
docs.text:

Account A upload

Account B access

Expected:

Denied

docs.title: Retest Quarantine
docs.text: Confirm pending or rejected files are not retrievable.

docs.title: Retest SVG
docs.text:
If SVG remains supported, retest:

Sanitisation

Rendering

Response origin

Response headers

Server-side processing

docs.title: Retest Archives
docs.text: Verify extraction cannot escape the intended directory.

docs.title: Retest Processing Workers
docs.text: Confirm malformed or unsupported files fail safely without exposing verbose internal errors.

rg -ni 'multer|formidable|busboy|originalname|mimetype' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

Java:

rg -ni 'MultipartFile|Part|getOriginalFilename|transferTo' -g '*.java' .

.NET:

rg -ni 'IFormFile|CopyTo|CopyToAsync|FileName|ContentType' -g '*.cs' .

rg -ni '\$_FILES|move_uploaded_file|is_uploaded_file' -g '*.php' .

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
The key question is not:

Can I upload an unusual extension?

The real model is:

WHAT DOES THE APPLICATION TRUST
          |
          v
ABOUT THE FILE
          |
          v
AND WHAT HAPPENS TO THAT FILE
          |
          v
AFTER IT IS ACCEPTED?

A strong workflow is:

Understand Upload Function
        |
        v
Upload Valid Baseline
        |
        v
Determine Validation
        |
        v
Change One Property at a Time
        |
        v
Understand Filename Handling
        |
        v
Identify Storage
        |
        v
Identify Processing
        |
        v
Retrieve File
        |
        v
Test Authorisation
        |
        v
Assess Browser Behaviour
        |
        v
Capture Evidence
        |
        v
Remediate Root Cause
        |
        v
Retest Entire Lifecycle

For every file upload ask:

Why does the application need uploads?

Which file types are actually required?

Does it trust the extension?

Does it trust client MIME?

Does it inspect file content?

Does it parse the file?

Does it generate a storage filename?

Is the original filename used as a path?

Can the filename traverse directories?

Can a file overwrite another file?

Where is the file stored?

Can uploaded files execute there?

Is storage inside the web root?

Is the file processed?

Which parser processes it?

Does the processor have filesystem access?

Does the processor have network access?

Are archives extracted?

Are archive paths canonicalised?

Is malware scanning performed?

Can the file be accessed before scanning finishes?

Can another user retrieve it?

Can another tenant retrieve it?

How is the file served?

Is it rendered inline?

What Content-Type is returned?

Is `nosniff` present?

Is Content-Disposition appropriate?

Does the application use a separate content origin?

What impact was actually demonstrated?

Was the upload policy bypassed or merely changed?

Has the complete upload lifecycle been retested?

The strongest file upload finding is not:

The server accepted test.xyz.

It is:

UNTRUSTED FILE
      |
      v
SECURITY CONTROL FAILURE
      |
      v
UNSAFE STORAGE / PROCESSING / RETRIEVAL
      |
      v
REPEATABLE SECURITY IMPACT

  • OWASP Unrestricted File Upload
  • CWE-434 - Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type

Change one property at a time

If you simultaneously change the filename, extension, MIME type and file bytes, you cannot tell which validation control failed. Start with a valid upload and modify one property per request.

Follow the complete lifecycle

Upload acceptance is only the first stage. Storage, processing, malware scanning, retrieval, browser rendering and authorisation often reveal more important weaknesses than the initial extension filter.

Use harmless marker files

A unique value such as UPLOAD_TEST_7f3a9 provides clean evidence for storage, transformation and retrieval testing without introducing executable or malicious content.

Use two accounts

File upload testing should include retrieval authorisation. A perfectly validated PDF can still create a serious vulnerability if Account B can retrieve Account A's private document.

Do not equate upload with code execution

Accepting an unexpected extension does not demonstrate remote code execution. Establish how the file is stored and served, whether the environment can execute it, and what security consequence actually occurs.

Antivirus is only one layer

Malware scanning does not replace extension validation, content inspection, filename safety, storage isolation, parser hardening, authorisation or safe content delivery.

docs.title: Git and ripgrep Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Git and ripgrep (rg) are two of the most useful tools for manual source-code security review.

Git answers questions such as:

What changed?

Who changed it?

When was it changed?

What did the previous implementation look like?

Was sensitive information committed historically?

Which commit introduced this behaviour?

Which branches contain this code?

ripgrep answers questions such as:

Where is this function used?

Where does this parameter enter the application?

Where are commands executed?

Where are database queries constructed?

Where are files opened?

Where are HTTP requests made?

Where are authentication checks performed?

Where are authorisation decisions made?

Where are secrets referenced?

Used together:

Repository
    |
    v
Git Reconnaissance
    |
    v
Understand Structure and History
    |
    v
ripgrep Search
    |
    v
Security-Relevant Candidate
    |
    v
Read Surrounding Code
    |
    v
Trace Input to Sensitive Operation
    |
    v
Git History
    |
    v
Understand Why / When It Changed
    |
    v
Validate Security Assumptions
    |
    v
Evidence
    |
    v
Finding or Dismissal

Authorised Security Review

Review only source code and repositories that you are authorised to access. Repositories may contain credentials, API keys, customer information, proprietary code, internal infrastructure details and historical secrets. Treat cloned repositories and extracted evidence as sensitive assessment material.

docs.text:
Suppose:

rg -n 'password\s*=' .

returns:

config/example.py:7:password = "changeme"
app/settings.py:32:password = os.environ["DB_PASSWORD"]

Interpretation:

tests/test_login.py
    |
    +--> Test credential candidate
    |
    +--> Determine whether test-only

config/example.py
    |
    +--> Example/default value
    |
    +--> Determine whether deployed

docs.title: Command Execution Search
docs.text:
Command execution is a high-value review category.

Python:

rg -n 'os\.system|subprocess\.(run|Popen|call|check_output|check_call)' -g '*.py' .

Node.js:

rg -n 'exec\(|execSync\(|spawn\(|spawnSync\(' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

PHP:

rg -n '\b(system|exec|shell_exec|passthru|popen|proc_open)\s*\(' -g '*.php' .

Java:

rg -n 'Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder' -g '*.java' .

.NET:

docs.title: Command Execution Does Not Equal Command Injection
docs.text:
Example:

subprocess.run(["uptime"], check=True)

This executes a command.

It does not show user-controlled command construction.

docs.title: Worked Example - Command Injection Candidate
docs.text:
Assume the repository contains:

from flask import Flask, request
import subprocess

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.get("/diagnostics/ping")
def ping():
    host = request.args.get("host", "")
    result = subprocess.run(
        "ping -c 1 " + host,
        shell=True,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True
    )
    return result.stdout

docs.title: Step 1 - Find Command Execution
docs.text:
rg -n -g '*.py' 'subprocess\.(run|Popen)|os\.system' .

Representative output:

app/health.py:18:    subprocess.run(["uptime"], check=True)
app/diagnostics.py:9:    result = subprocess.run(

docs.title: Step 2 - Interpret Matches
docs.text:
First result:

subprocess.run(["uptime"], check=True)

Observation:

Fixed command.

No user input visible.

No shell invocation visible.

Initial classification:

Low-priority candidate.

Second result requires more context.
