docs.text:
Potential source:

request.args.get("host", "")

This indicates:

HTTP query parameter
       |
       v
host

docs.title: Step 5 - Identify Sink
docs.text:
Sensitive operation:

subprocess.run(...)

with:

shell=True

docs.title: Step 6 - Trace Data Flow
docs.text:
HTTP Request
    |
    v
?host=
    |
    v
request.args.get()
    |
    v
host
    |
    v
String Concatenation
    |
    v
subprocess.run()
    |
    v
shell=True

docs.title: Step 7 - Search for Validation
docs.text:
Search for the variable and related validation:

rg -n -C 5 '\bhost\b|validate|allowlist|regex|hostname' app/diagnostics.py

Questions:

Is host validated?

Is there an allowlist?

Is input canonicalised?

Is the route authenticated?

Is the route reachable?

Does another middleware restrict access?

docs.title: Step 8 - Security Interpretation
docs.text:
The source code provides evidence of a potentially dangerous data flow:

User-controlled input
        |
        v
Shell command string
        |
        v
Shell interpreter

However, before writing a final finding determine:

Is this code reachable?

Is the route deployed?

Does middleware restrict access?

Does upstream validation exist?

Does configuration disable the feature?

What account executes the process?

Can the behaviour be reproduced safely?

docs.title: Stronger Conclusion
docs.text:
A source review conclusion could state:

The /diagnostics/ping handler obtains the host query parameter and concatenates it directly into a command string executed through subprocess.run() with shell=True. No validation is present in the reviewed function. This creates a command-injection candidate that requires confirmation of route reachability, upstream controls and runtime behaviour before final severity is assigned.

docs.title: Safer Implementation Pattern
docs.text:
Where possible, avoid shell interpretation.

For example:

subprocess.run(
    ["ping", "-c", "1", host],
    shell=False,
    capture_output=True,
    text=True
)

Input should still be validated according to the application's intended hostname/IP requirements.

docs.title: SQL Search
docs.text:
Python:

rg -ni 'execute\(|executemany\(|raw\(' -g '*.py' .

Java:

rg -n 'createStatement|prepareStatement|executeQuery|executeUpdate' -g '*.java' .

PHP:

rg -n 'mysqli_query|->query\(|->prepare\(' -g '*.php' .

.NET:

rg -n 'SqlCommand|ExecuteReader|ExecuteNonQuery|FromSqlRaw' -g '*.cs' .

docs.title: SQL Candidate
docs.text:
Potentially interesting:

query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + user_id
cursor.execute(query)

Safer pattern:

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s",
    (user_id,)
)

Exact parameter syntax depends on the database library.

docs.title: SQL Interpretation
docs.text:
Do not search only for:

SELECT

Instead trace:

Request Input
      |
      v
Query Construction
      |
      v
Database API

Determine whether parameterisation occurs.

docs.title: File Operations
docs.text:
Python:

rg -n '\b(open|send_file|send_from_directory)\s*\(' -g '*.py' .

Node.js:

rg -n 'readFile|readFileSync|createReadStream|writeFile|writeFileSync' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

Java:

rg -n 'new File\(|Files\.(read|write|copy|move)' -g '*.java' .

.NET:

rg -n 'File\.(Read|Write|Open|Delete|Copy|Move)|FileStream' -g '*.cs' .

docs.title: File Review Model
docs.text:
User Input
    |
    v
Filename / Path
    |
    v
Normalisation?
    |
    v
Base Directory?
    |
    v
Access Control?
    |
    v
File Operation

docs.title: Path Construction
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'path\.join|os\.path\.join|Path\(|filepath|filename|upload|download' .

Determine whether user input controls filesystem paths.

docs.title: Upload Handling
docs.text:
rg -ni 'upload|multipart|filename|content-type|mimetype|extension' .

Review:

Extension checks

Content checks

Storage directory

Filename generation

Permissions

Serving behaviour

Authorisation

docs.title: Network Requests / SSRF Review
docs.text:
Python:

rg -n 'requests\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)|httpx\.|urllib\.request' -g '*.py' .

Node.js:

rg -n 'fetch\(|axios\.|http\.request|https\.request' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

Java:

rg -n 'HttpClient|HttpURLConnection|RestTemplate|WebClient' -g '*.java' .

.NET:

rg -n 'HttpClient|WebRequest|WebClient' -g '*.cs' .

docs.title: SSRF Review Model
docs.text:
User-Controlled URL?
       |
       v
URL Parser
       |
       v
Scheme Restrictions?
       |
       v
Hostname Validation?
       |
       v
DNS Resolution
       |
       v
IP Validation?
       |
       v
Redirect Handling?
       |
       v
Outbound Request

docs.title: SSRF Candidate Example
docs.text:
url = request.json["url"]
response = requests.get(url)

This is security relevant because request input directly influences an outbound request.

But determine:

Authentication required?

URL allowlist?

Network egress controls?

Redirect handling?

DNS rebinding protections?

Response returned to user?

Blind or non-blind behaviour?

docs.title: Deserialization Search
docs.text:
Python:

rg -n 'pickle\.loads?|yaml\.load|marshal\.loads?' -g '*.py' .

Java:

rg -n 'ObjectInputStream|readObject\(' -g '*.java' .

PHP:

rg -n '\bunserialize\s*\(' -g '*.php' .

.NET:

rg -n 'BinaryFormatter|LosFormatter|ObjectStateFormatter' -g '*.cs' .

A match requires analysis of:

Input trust

Serializer configuration

Object types

Reachability

Existing integrity controls

docs.title: Template Rendering
docs.text:
Python:

rg -n 'render_template_string|Template\(' -g '*.py' .

Node:

rg -ni 'render\(|ejs|handlebars|pug|nunjucks' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

PHP:

rg -ni 'twig|blade|smarty' -g '*.php' .

Review whether user-controlled input becomes:

Template data

or:

Template source

These are very different security situations.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'redirect|returnUrl|return_url|nextUrl|next_url|callbackUrl|callback_url' .

Trace:

User Input
    |
    v
Destination Validation
    |
    v
Redirect

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'cors|access-control-allow-origin|allowed_origins|allow_origins' .

Review:

Allowed origins

Credential support

Wildcard behaviour

Environment-specific configuration

docs.title: Cryptography
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'md5|sha1|aes|des|ecb|encrypt|decrypt|cipher|random|rand\(' .

Do not report every occurrence of:

MD5

SHA-1

Determine purpose.

For example:

File integrity identifier

is different from:

Password storage.

docs.title: Password Hashing
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'bcrypt|argon2|scrypt|pbkdf2|password_hash|hash_password' .

Trace where passwords are:

Received

Processed

Hashed

Stored

Compared

docs.title: Randomness
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'random|rand\(|Math\.random|Random\(' .

Determine whether the value protects:

Sessions

Password reset

CSRF

API credentials

Cryptographic keys

Non-security randomness has different requirements.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'logger\.|logging\.|console\.log|print\(' .

Look for sensitive values being logged:

Passwords

Tokens

Session identifiers

API keys

Personal data

docs.title: Debug Functionality
docs.text:
rg -ni 'debug|development|dev_mode|trace|verbose' .

Also inspect configuration files.

docs.title: Flask Debug
docs.text: rg -n 'debug\s*=\s*True|FLASK_DEBUG' -g '*.py' -g '*.env*' .

docs.title: Django Debug
docs.text: rg -n 'DEBUG\s*=\s*True' -g '*.py' .

docs.title: Environment-Specific Configuration
docs.text:
Find:

find . -type f \( \
  -name '*.env*' -o \
  -name '*prod*' -o \
  -name '*production*' -o \
  -name '*staging*' -o \
  -name '*development*' \
\) -print

Security behaviour may differ significantly between environments.

docs.title: Infrastructure as Code
docs.text:
Search repository files:

rg --files | rg '\.(tf|tfvars|ya?ml|json)$'

Look for:

Public exposure

IAM permissions

Secrets

Security groups

Storage permissions

Container privileges

Network configuration

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Find Dockerfiles:

find . -type f \( -name 'Dockerfile' -o -name 'Dockerfile.*' \) -print

Search:

rg -ni 'USER|EXPOSE|COPY|ADD|ENTRYPOINT|CMD' -g 'Dockerfile*' .

docs.title: Docker Security Questions
docs.text:
Does the container run as root?

Are secrets copied into the image?

Is unnecessary software installed?

Are sensitive files copied?

Are dangerous capabilities required?

What ports are exposed?

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'privileged:|runAsUser:|runAsNonRoot:|hostNetwork:|hostPID:|hostPath:' -g '*.yaml' -g '*.yml' .

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.text:
Inspect:

.github/workflows/

.gitlab-ci.yml

Jenkinsfile

azure-pipelines.yml

Search:

rg -ni 'secret|token|password|credential|curl|wget|docker|sudo' .github/ 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Git History
docs.text:
Current code is only part of the story.

Git history may reveal:

Removed credentials

Old endpoints

Security fixes

Temporary bypasses

Previous implementations

Deleted validation

Configuration changes

docs.title: Recent Commits
docs.text: git log --oneline -20

docs.title: Graph
docs.text: git log --oneline --all --decorate --graph -30

docs.title: Commit Details
docs.text: git show <commit>

docs.title: Specific File History
docs.text: git log --oneline -- path/to/file

docs.title: Show File Changes
docs.text: git log -p -- path/to/file

docs.title: Follow Renames
docs.text: git log --follow -- path/to/file

docs.title: Search Commit Messages
docs.text:
git log --oneline --all --grep='security'

Case insensitive:

git log --oneline --all --regexp-ignore-case --grep='auth'

docs.title: Useful Commit Terms
docs.text:
Search commit messages for:

security

auth

authentication

authorization

permission

fix

hotfix

password

secret

token

admin

validation

sanitize

escape

CVE

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
git log --oneline --all --regexp-ignore-case --grep='security\|auth\|permission\|validation'

Commit messages are hints, not proof.

docs.title: Search Historical Content
docs.text:
Git can search revisions for text.

Example:

git log -S'API_KEY' --oneline --all

This searches for commits where the number of occurrences of the specified string changed.

docs.title: Search Password History
docs.text: git log -S'password' --oneline --all

docs.title: Search Function History
docs.text: git log -S'authorize_user' --oneline --all

docs.title: Regex Diff Search
docs.text:
-G searches changed lines matching a regex.

Example:

git log -G'password|secret|token' --oneline --all

docs.title: -S vs -G
docs.text:
Conceptually:

-S
 |
 v
Did the number of occurrences of this string change?

-G
 |
 v
Did changed lines match this regex?

docs.title: Show Matching Historical Commit
docs.text: git show <commit>

docs.title: Git Blame
docs.text:
git blame path/to/file

Useful for identifying the commit responsible for specific lines.

docs.title: Blame Selected Lines
docs.text: git blame -L 40,60 app/auth.py

docs.title: Then Inspect Commit
docs.text: git show <commit>

docs.title: Security Use of Blame
docs.text:
Suppose you find:

if user:
    return admin_data()

Use:

git blame -L 120,125 app/admin.py

Then inspect the associated commit:

git show <commit>

This may reveal:

Why the check changed

Previous implementation

Related files

Tests

Developer intent

docs.title: Do Not Use Blame for Attribution
docs.text:
During security review, git blame is primarily a technical history tool.

The goal is:

Understand Code History

not:

Assign Personal Fault

docs.title: Compare Branches
docs.text: git diff main..develop

docs.title: Compare Specific File
docs.text: git diff main..develop -- app/auth.py

docs.title: Compare Commits
docs.text: git diff <old_commit> <new_commit>

docs.title: Changed Files
docs.text: git diff --name-only <old_commit> <new_commit>

docs.title: Security-Focused Diff Review
docs.text:
For a release or pull-request review:

Changed Files
     |
     v
Security-Relevant Changes?
     |
     +--> Authentication
     +--> Authorisation
     +--> Input Handling
     +--> Cryptography
     +--> Network Requests
     +--> File Handling
     +--> Configuration
     +--> Dependencies

docs.title: Review Current Changes
docs.text:
Unstaged:

git diff

Staged:

git diff --cached

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text: git diff --stat

docs.title: Word-Level Diff
docs.text: git diff --word-diff

docs.title: History of Deleted Secret
docs.text:
Suppose current search returns nothing:

rg -nF 'SECRET_KEY=' .

That does not prove the repository never contained it.

Search history:

git log -S'SECRET_KEY=' --oneline --all

Then:

git show <commit>

docs.title: Secret Removed From Current Branch
docs.text:
If a real credential was historically committed:

Deleting it from the latest file

does not necessarily invalidate it.

Security response may require:

Credential rotation

Repository history review

Access-log review

Secret-management migration

History rewriting alone is not equivalent to credential rotation.

docs.title: Branch Review
docs.text:
List:

git branch -a

Security-relevant code or secrets may exist in branches not currently checked out.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
git tag

Inspect:

git show <tag>

Tags may contain older release code.

docs.title: Git Objects and History
docs.text:
Avoid manually manipulating .git during routine review.

Prefer Git commands because they preserve context and reduce accidental repository corruption.

docs.title: Dependency Files
docs.text:
Search:

rg --files | rg '(^|/)(package-lock\.json|yarn\.lock|pnpm-lock\.yaml|requirements\.txt|poetry\.lock|Pipfile\.lock|pom\.xml|go\.sum|Cargo\.lock)$'

These files help identify dependencies for separate dependency-vulnerability analysis.

docs.title: Search Dependency Usage
docs.text:
Suppose a security-sensitive package appears in dependencies.

Search:

rg -n 'package_name' .

Determine whether it is actually used and where.

docs.title: Search Configuration Keys
docs.text:
Example:

rg -ni 'verify_ssl|verify_tls|certificate|tls|ssl' .

Potentially interesting:

requests.get(url, verify=False)

But determine:

Production code?

Test code?

Development environment?

Controlled internal endpoint?

Actual deployment configuration?

docs.title: Search Disabled TLS Verification
docs.text:
Python:

rg -n 'verify\s*=\s*False' -g '*.py' .

Node.js:

rg -n 'rejectUnauthorized\s*:\s*false' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

docs.title: Search Security Headers
docs.text:
rg -ni 'content-security-policy|strict-transport-security|x-frame-options|x-content-type-options' .

Absence in source code does not prove the deployed application lacks the header.

It may be added by:

Reverse proxy

Load balancer

CDN

Web server

Ingress controller

docs.title: Search Authentication Bypass Logic
docs.text:
Useful terms:

rg -ni 'skip_auth|disable_auth|bypass_auth|no_auth|anonymous|allow_anonymous' .

Interpret carefully because legitimate public routes may use similar terminology.

docs.title: Search Role Checks
docs.text:
rg -ni 'is_admin|role\s*==|roles\.contains|has_role|permission' .

Trace whether security decisions occur:

Only in UI

Client side

Server side

Middleware

Database layer

docs.title: Client-Side Authorisation
docs.text:
Search JavaScript/TypeScript:

rg -ni 'isAdmin|role|permission|canAccess|hasPermission' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' -g '*.tsx' .

Client-side checks can improve UX but should not be the sole enforcement mechanism for server-side resources.

docs.title: API Endpoint Inventory
docs.text:
Examples:

rg -n '@.*\.route\(' -g '*.py' .

rg -n '\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)\(' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

Export if useful:

rg -n '@.*\.route\(' -g '*.py' > flask-routes.txt

docs.title: Search Query Parameters
docs.text:
Python:

rg -n 'request\.(args|form|json|files|headers|cookies)' -g '*.py' .

Node:

rg -n 'req\.(query|body|params|headers|cookies)' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Review
docs.text:
This is one of the most important manual review techniques.

SOURCE
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATIONS
  |
  v
VALIDATION
  |
  v
SECURITY CONTROL
  |
  v
SINK

docs.title: Common Sources
docs.text:
HTTP query parameters

POST body

JSON body

Headers

Cookies

Uploaded files

Database content

Message queues

Environment variables

External APIs

docs.title: Common Sensitive Sinks
docs.text:
Shell execution

SQL queries

File operations

Template engines

Deserializers

Redirects

Outbound HTTP requests

LDAP queries

XML parsers

Logging

HTML output

docs.title: Trace a Variable
docs.text:
Suppose:

filename = request.args["file"]

Search:

rg -n '\bfilename\b' .

Then inspect each use.

docs.title: Search Exact Function
docs.text: rg -nF 'download_file(' .

docs.title: Search Definition and Calls
docs.text:
Python:

rg -n 'def download_file|download_file\(' -g '*.py' .

docs.title: Context Is Essential
docs.text:
Do not only collect:

app/files.py:77: open(filename)

Collect enough surrounding code to understand:

Where filename came from

Whether it was validated

Whether it was normalised

Whether a base directory was enforced

docs.title: Representative Output vs Proof
docs.text:
Suppose:

rg -n 'open\(' app/

returns:

app/config.py:20:with open("config.json") as f:
app/files.py:77:with open(filename, "rb") as f:

Interpretation:

config.py
    |
    +--> Fixed path
    |
    +--> Likely low priority

files.py
    |
    +--> Variable path
    |
    +--> Trace filename

This prioritisation is where manual review becomes valuable.

docs.title: Search Result Classification
docs.text:
A useful classification model:

Classification Meaning Informational Match exists but no immediate security relevance Review Candidate Security-sensitive API or control identified Strong Candidate User-controlled data appears to reach sensitive operation Validated Finding Security consequence has been established False Positive Match does not create the suspected condition

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Common reasons:

Test code

Documentation

Examples

Dead code

Vendored code

Generated code

Unreachable route

Safe API usage

Fixed values

Input validation elsewhere

Framework protection

Feature disabled in production

Environment-specific configuration

docs.title: Tests Can Be Valuable
docs.text:
Do not automatically ignore:

tests/

Tests can explain:

Expected security behaviour

Authorisation requirements

Edge cases

Security regressions

Developer assumptions

docs.title: Search Security Tests
docs.text: rg -ni 'unauthorized|forbidden|permission|authentication|csrf|xss|injection' tests/ 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Review Test Expectations
docs.text:
Example:

def test_other_user_cannot_read_order():
    response = client.get("/orders/2001")
    assert response.status_code == 403

This gives useful information about intended authorisation behaviour.

It does not prove production enforcement without reviewing the implementation and, where appropriate, runtime behaviour.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni 'security|authentication|authorization|permission|admin' README* docs/ 2>/dev/null

Documentation can clarify intended design.

docs.title: Security Assumption Mismatch
docs.text:
An important finding pattern is:

Documentation Says
       |
       v
Only Administrators
       |
       X
       |
Implementation Checks
       |
       v
Any Authenticated User

This can strengthen the interpretation of an access-control issue.

docs.title: Commit-Level Security Review
docs.text:
For a pull request or patch:

git diff <base>...<head>

Review:

New routes

Changed permissions

New external requests

New file operations

New dependencies

Configuration changes

Removed validation

Changed authentication

docs.title: Identify Security-Relevant Changed Files
docs.text:
git diff --name-only <base>...<head>

Then focus on relevant areas.

docs.title: Search Only Changed Files
docs.text:
One practical workflow:

git diff --name-only <base>...<head> > changed-files.txt

Review the list before processing it further.

docs.title: Security Fix Review
docs.text:
When reviewing a security fix:

Original Vulnerability
       |
       v
Root Cause
       |
       v
Patch
       |
       v
Does Patch Address Root Cause?
       |
       v
Alternative Paths?
       |
       v
Regression Tests?

docs.title: Patch Example
docs.text:
Before:

if user:
    return get_admin_report()

After:

if user and user.is_admin:
    return get_admin_report()

Review further:

Is user.is_admin trustworthy?

Is this the only route?

Are related endpoints protected?

Is role information server-controlled?

Are tests present?

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a source-code finding record:

Finding ID

Repository

Branch

Commit

File

Line number

Function/class

Relevant source

Input source

Sensitive sink

Existing controls

Missing/insufficient control

Reachability

Runtime validation

Security consequence

docs.title: Record Repository State
docs.text:
git remote -v

git branch --show-current

git rev-parse HEAD

docs.title: Save Search Results
docs.text:
Example:

rg -n -C 5 'subprocess\.(run|Popen)|os\.system' \
  -g '*.py' . > command-execution-review.txt

docs.title: Evidence Should Include Context
docs.text:
Avoid evidence containing only:

app/diagnostics.py:8:subprocess.run(...)

Prefer:

File:
app/diagnostics.py

Lines:
5-13

Source:
request.args.get("host")

Sink:
subprocess.run(..., shell=True)

Observed validation:
None in reviewed function.

Additional validation:
Middleware and route configuration reviewed separately.

docs.title: Record Search Command
docs.text:
Keeping the exact command makes review reproducible.

Example:

Search:
rg -n -C 8 'subprocess\.run' app/diagnostics.py

docs.title: Evidence and Sensitive Code
docs.text:
Do not unnecessarily copy entire proprietary source files into reports.

Capture only enough code to establish:

Source

Data flow

Control

Sink

Security consequence

docs.title: Reporting Example - Command Injection Candidate
docs.text:
Weak:

subprocess.run is insecure.

Better:

The diagnostics handler reads the host query parameter and concatenates it into a command string passed to subprocess.run() with shell=True. No input validation was identified in the reviewed function. Runtime validation should confirm route reachability and upstream controls before the issue is assigned final severity.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Hardcoded Credential
docs.text:
Weak:

Password found in Git.

Better:

A credential was committed directly to the repository in config/production.yml and remained present in the reviewed revision. The value was configured for the production database account. The credential should be rotated and migrated to the organisation's approved secret-management mechanism.

docs.title: Historical Credential Reporting
docs.text:
If only history contains it:

Repository history contains a previously committed credential that was removed from the current source tree. Removal from the latest revision does not invalidate the credential. Confirm whether the credential was rotated and whether historical repository access could have exposed it.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Missing Authorisation
docs.text:
Weak:

No role check.

Better:

The administrative export endpoint requires authentication but does not perform the role check applied to other administrative routes. As a result, any authenticated user reaching this handler enters the export workflow. Controlled runtime testing should confirm whether the endpoint returns administrative data to a standard user.

docs.title: Remediation Principles
docs.text:
Fix the underlying security boundary.

Examples:

Command injection
    -> Avoid shell interpretation and validate structured input.

SQL injection
    -> Use parameterised queries.

Path traversal
    -> Enforce server-controlled base paths and validate file identifiers.

SSRF
    -> Restrict destinations and protocols using robust server-side controls.

Authorisation
    -> Enforce access decisions server side for every protected operation.

Secrets
    -> Rotate exposed credentials and use approved secret management.

docs.title: Retesting Source Changes
docs.text:
After remediation:

Original Candidate
      |
      v
Review New Code
      |
      v
Repeat Original Search
      |
      v
Trace New Data Flow
      |
      v
Review Alternative Paths
      |
      v
Run Relevant Tests
      |
      v
Runtime Retest Where Appropriate

docs.title: Search Disappearance Is Not Proof
docs.text:
Suppose the original code contained:

os.system(command)

After remediation:

rg -n 'os\.system' .

returns nothing.

This only proves:

That exact pattern is no longer present.

The code might now use:

subprocess.run(command, shell=True)

Therefore retesting must verify the root cause.

docs.title: Retest the Root Cause
docs.text:
For command injection:

User Input
    |
    v
Can it still influence shell syntax?

For authorisation:

Unauthorised Identity
    |
    v
Can it still access protected object/function?

For SSRF:

User-Controlled Destination
    |
    v
Can server still reach prohibited destination?

docs.title: Potential Secrets
docs.text:
rg --hidden \
  -g '!.git/**' \
  -ni 'password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|access[_-]?token|private[_-]?key' .

docs.title: Authentication and Authorisation
docs.text: rg -ni 'authenticate|authorize|permission|role|session|jwt|login' .

docs.title: Python Command Execution
docs.text: rg -n -g '*.py' 'os\.system|subprocess\.(run|Popen|call|check_output|check_call)' .

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
The most important rule when using ripgrep for security review is:

A MATCH IS A LEAD.

Not:

A MATCH IS A VULNERABILITY.

For every interesting search result ask:

What exactly matched?

Is this application code?

Is it production code?

Is the code reachable?

What data enters this function?

Who controls that data?

How is the data transformed?

Is validation performed?

Is authentication required?

Is authorisation enforced?

What sensitive operation receives the data?

Does the framework provide protection?

Does configuration change the behaviour?

What does Git history reveal?

Can the security consequence be demonstrated?

What evidence supports the conclusion?

The strongest workflow is:

rg
 |
 v
Find Candidate
 |
 v
Read Context
 |
 v
Trace Source
 |
 v
Trace Sink
 |
 v
Identify Controls
 |
 v
Review Git History
 |
 v
Validate
 |
 v
Conclude

This prevents the common source-review mistake of converting security-sensitive API usage directly into findings.

Search broadly, validate narrowly

Broad searches are useful for identifying candidates. Once a security-sensitive match is found, narrow the review to the relevant function, data flow, security control and runtime context.

Record the commit hash

A file and line number can change after the assessment. Recording the repository commit makes source-code evidence reproducible.

Use Git history as context

Git history can explain why a security-sensitive implementation exists, identify earlier versions and reveal whether a credential or vulnerable pattern previously existed even after it disappears from the current tree.

Do not report regex matches as vulnerabilities

subprocess, open, requests.get, MD5, password and similar terms identify areas worth reviewing. The security conclusion depends on how the code is actually used.

Removed secrets may still matter

Deleting a credential from the latest source revision does not invalidate it. If a real secret was committed, credential rotation and exposure analysis are generally more important than simply removing the string from the current file.

docs.title: Impacket Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Impacket is a collection of Python classes and command-line tools for working with network protocols commonly encountered in Windows and Active Directory environments.

It includes specialised utilities for:

SMB

MSRPC

Kerberos

NTLM

LDAP-related workflows

MSSQL

WMI

Windows services

Remote administration

Credential and ticket analysis

This cheatsheet focuses on using Impacket as a focused protocol toolkit during authorised penetration tests, red team exercises and security labs.

The objective is not simply:

Find Impacket command
        |
        v
Run command

Instead:

Identify Objective
        |
        v
Choose Protocol
        |
        v
Choose Impacket Tool
        |
        v
Check Prerequisites
        |
        v
Run Focused Test
        |
        v
Interpret Result
        |
        v
Determine What It Proves
        |
        v
Validate Further If Required
        |
        v
Collect Evidence

For the broader workflow, see:

  • Active Directory Cheatsheet
  • NetExec Cheatsheet

Authorised Security Testing

Only use these techniques against systems, accounts and environments you are explicitly authorised to test. Some Impacket utilities can perform remote administration, request authentication material, access sensitive credential stores or make changes to systems. Use the least intrusive method necessary to prove the assessment objective.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
A useful way to think about Impacket is:

What do I have?
      |
      +--> Password
      |
      +--> NTLM Hash
      |
      +--> Kerberos Ticket
      |
      +--> Kerberos Key
      |
      +--> Administrative Access
      |
      +--> SQL Credentials
      |
      v
What am I trying to learn?
      |
      +--> Enumerate SPNs
      |
      +--> Check Preauthentication
      |
      +--> Access SMB
      |
      +--> Query MSSQL
      |
      +--> Validate Remote Administration
      |
      +--> Inspect Credential Stores
      |
      +--> Work with Kerberos Tickets
      |
      v
Select the smallest appropriate Impacket utility

docs.title: Common Impacket Tools
docs.text:
Tool Primary Purpose GetUserSPNs.py Enumerate accounts with SPNs and Kerberos service-ticket candidates GetNPUsers.py Identify/test accounts without Kerberos preauthentication getTGT.py Request a Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket getST.py Request Kerberos service tickets in supported scenarios ticketConverter.py Convert between Kerberos ticket-cache formats secretsdump.py Access credential material where sufficient privilege exists smbclient.py SMB share interaction lookupsid.py SID/RPC-based domain enumeration rpcdump.py Enumerate RPC endpoints samrdump.py Query SAMR information mssqlclient.py Microsoft SQL Server client wmiexec.py WMI-based remote administration psexec.py Service-based remote administration smbexec.py SMB/service-based remote administration atexec.py Scheduled-task-based remote administration dcomexec.py DCOM-based remote administration

Depending on the installation, command names may be prefixed with:

impacket-

For example:

impacket-GetUserSPNs

instead of:

GetUserSPNs.py

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
On Kali Linux, Impacket may already be installed.

Check:

python3 -m pip show impacket

Check installed command wrappers:

compgen -c | grep '^impacket-' | sort -u

Package version:

python3 -m pip show impacket | grep -E '^(Name|Version):'

Example:

Name: impacket
Version: <installed-version>

docs.title: Help Before Execution
docs.text:
For any utility:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

impacket-GetNPUsers -h

impacket-secretsdump -h

impacket-wmiexec -h

impacket-mssqlclient -h

This matters because syntax and supported authentication options can change between releases.

docs.title: Example Environment
docs.text:
Examples throughout this cheatsheet use:

Domain:     corp.local
DC:         dc01.corp.local
DC IP:      10.10.10.10

Server:     srv01.corp.local
Server IP:  10.10.10.20

SQL Server: sql01.corp.local
SQL IP:     10.10.10.30

Username:   asif
Password:   Password123!

Example NTLM hash:

0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef

These are placeholders only.

docs.title: Impacket Target Syntax
docs.text:
Many Impacket utilities use a target string resembling:

domain/username:password@target

Example:

corp.local/asif:Password123!@10.10.10.20

Some tools instead take:

domain/username:password

and a separate:

-dc-ip

option.

Always check:

impacket-<tool> -h

before assuming the target format.

docs.title: Passwords with Special Characters
docs.text:
Shell metacharacters can alter a command.

Prefer single quotes around target strings where possible:

impacket-smbclient 'corp.local/asif:Password123!@10.10.10.20'

For complex credentials, interactive prompting or other supported authentication options may be safer than placing the password directly on the command line.

docs.title: Command-Line Credential Exposure
docs.text:
Be aware that passwords supplied directly as command arguments may be exposed through:

Shell history

Process listings

Terminal recordings

Screenshots

Assessment logs

Where supported, prefer prompting for the password.

In reports, always redact real credentials.

docs.title: Domain Controller Discovery
docs.text:
Before Kerberos-focused testing, identify the domain controller.

From Linux:

dig _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local SRV

or:

nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local

Example:

_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local. 600 IN SRV 0 100 389 dc01.corp.local.

docs.title: DNS Check
docs.text:
dig dc01.corp.local

getent hosts dc01.corp.local

Kerberos problems are frequently caused by DNS rather than by Impacket itself.

docs.title: Time Check
docs.text:
Kerberos depends on reasonably synchronised clocks.

Check:

date

If Kerberos errors indicate clock skew, compare the assessment host's time with the domain environment before changing authentication options.

docs.title: SMBClient
docs.text:
Impacket provides an SMB client for interacting with SMB shares.

Check:

impacket-smbclient -h

Connect:

impacket-smbclient 'corp.local/asif:Password123!@10.10.10.20'

docs.title: Representative Session
docs.text:
Impacket v...

Type help for list of commands
# shares
ADMIN$
C$
IPC$
Public
Software

Useful interactive commands may include:

help

shares

use

ls

cd

pwd

get

put

mkdir

exit

Check help inside the client for the installed version.

docs.title: SMBClient Workflow
docs.text:
Credential
    |
    v
SMB Authentication
    |
    v
List Shares
    |
    v
Select Relevant Share
    |
    v
List Files
    |
    v
Review Business Purpose
    |
    v
Retrieve Only Relevant Evidence

docs.title: Interpreting Share Access
docs.text:
If you can list a share:

Authentication
      |
      v
Share Access

has been demonstrated.

This does not automatically prove:

Administrative access

Sensitive-data exposure

Remote code execution

Privilege escalation

The contents and intended permissions determine the security significance.

docs.title: Writable Share
docs.text:
A writable share should trigger questions such as:

Who is expected to write?

Which systems consume files?

Are files executed?

Are configuration files loaded?

Does a privileged service read the directory?

Can application behaviour be changed?

Do not automatically conclude:

WRITE = RCE

docs.title: LookUpSID
docs.text:
lookupsid uses Windows RPC mechanisms to enumerate SID information.

Help:

impacket-lookupsid -h

Authenticated example:

impacket-lookupsid 'corp.local/asif:Password123!@10.10.10.10'

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
[*] Brute forcing SIDs at 10.10.10.10
[*] StringBinding ncacn_np:10.10.10.10[\pipe\lsarpc]
[*] Domain SID is: S-1-5-21-...
...
500: CORP\Administrator
501: CORP\Guest
1104: CORP\asif

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Useful information may include:

Domain SID

Usernames

Group names

Relative identifiers

The existence of a user or group is inventory information, not a vulnerability.

docs.title: RPCDump
docs.text:
Enumerate RPC endpoints:

impacket-rpcdump 10.10.10.20

or use the authentication syntax supported by the installed version.

RPC endpoints can reveal:

Available RPC interfaces

Named pipes

Protocol sequences

Service exposure

docs.title: RPCDump Interpretation
docs.text:
RPC endpoint enumeration is mainly reconnaissance.

Do not report:

RPC endpoint exists

as a vulnerability without identifying an actual insecure configuration or exploitable security consequence.

docs.title: SAMRDump
docs.text:
Check:

impacket-samrdump -h

Against an authorised target:

impacket-samrdump 'corp.local/asif:Password123!@10.10.10.20'

Depending on permissions and target configuration, SAMR information may include account-related information.

Interpret returned data according to the account's expected directory visibility and the environment's security model.

docs.title: Kerberos Overview
docs.text:
A simplified Kerberos workflow is:

User
 |
 v
AS-REQ
 |
 v
KDC
 |
 v
TGT
 |
 v
TGS-REQ
 |
 v
Service Ticket

Service

Important concepts:

KDC

TGT

TGS

SPN

Realm

Service Ticket

Ticket Cache

docs.title: GetUserSPNs
docs.text:
GetUserSPNs is commonly used to enumerate accounts associated with Service Principal Names.

Help:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

Authenticated enumeration:

impacket-GetUserSPNs 'corp.local/asif:Password123!' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
ServicePrincipalName             Name       MemberOf
-------------------------------  ---------  ------------------------
MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433   svc_sql
HTTP/web01.corp.local            svc_web

docs.title: What This Proves
docs.text:
It identifies directory accounts associated with SPNs visible to the current principal.

It does not prove:

The account password is weak

The account is compromised

The account is privileged

Kerberoasting will recover a password

docs.title: Interpreting SPNs
docs.text:
Example:

MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433

This indicates a service principal associated with Microsoft SQL Server.

Investigate:

Which account owns the SPN?

What service uses it?

Is the identity a managed service account?

What privileges does it hold?

Is the service still active?

Where can the account log on?

docs.title: Kerberoasting Assessment Model
docs.text:
Domain Credential
      |
      v
Enumerate SPNs
      |
      v
Service Account Found
      |
      v
Determine Privilege
      |
      v
Determine Credential Management
      |
      v
Requesting Ticket Necessary?
      |
      v
Authorised Controlled Validation
      |
      v
Assess Password Resilience Offline
      |
      v
Document Impact

The most important security question is not simply whether a service ticket can be requested.

Service-ticket issuance is normal Kerberos behaviour.

The risk arises when a service account uses crackable credential material and that account provides meaningful access.

docs.title: Requesting Service Tickets
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised, GetUserSPNs supports requesting service tickets.

Review the installed options:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

Use only the minimum number of accounts required for the assessment objective.

Avoid requesting tickets for every SPN merely because the tool supports it.

docs.title: Kerberoasting Evidence
docs.text:
Useful evidence includes:

Service account

SPN

Associated service

Account privilege

Password-management model

Whether an authorised ticket request was performed

Whether offline password testing was in scope

Result of controlled validation

Avoid including reusable credential material in the final report.

docs.title: GetNPUsers
docs.text:
GetNPUsers is used when assessing Kerberos accounts configured without preauthentication.

Help:

impacket-GetNPUsers -h

Authenticated directory assessment example:

impacket-GetNPUsers 'corp.local/asif:Password123!' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

Exact options for user lists and ticket requests should be confirmed with:

impacket-GetNPUsers -h

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting Prerequisite
docs.text:
The relevant account configuration is:

Do not require Kerberos preauthentication

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Preauthentication Required?
   |
 +---+---+
 |       |
Yes      No
 |       |
 v       v
Normal   AS-REP Assessment Candidate

docs.title: What an AS-REP Candidate Means
docs.text:
It does not automatically mean:

Password recovered

Account compromised

Privilege escalation

It means the account has a security-relevant Kerberos configuration that may expose password-derived material to offline analysis.

docs.title: AS-REP Follow-Up
docs.text:
Determine:

Why is preauthentication disabled?

Is the account enabled?

What privilege does it have?

Is it a service account?

Is the password strong?

Is the configuration still required?

docs.title: GetTGT
docs.text:
getTGT can request a Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket when appropriate credential material is available.

Help:

impacket-getTGT -h

A password-based example in a controlled environment may resemble:

impacket-getTGT 'corp.local/asif:Password123!' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

Successful execution typically creates a Kerberos credential cache file.

docs.title: Inspect the Ticket Cache
docs.text:
Set the cache:

export KRB5CCNAME=/path/to/asif.ccache

Inspect:

klist

Representative output:

Ticket cache: FILE:/path/to/asif.ccache
Default principal: asif@CORP.LOCAL

Valid starting       Expires              Service principal
...
krbtgt/CORP.LOCAL@CORP.LOCAL

docs.title: What a TGT Proves
docs.text:
A valid TGT demonstrates that the represented principal has an authenticated Kerberos context.

It does not mean:

Administrator

Domain Admin

Access to every service

Authorisation still depends on the target service and the principal's permissions.

docs.title: Ticket Cache Environment Variable
docs.text:
Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

Set:

export KRB5CCNAME=/tmp/asif.ccache

Then:

klist

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication with Impacket
docs.text:
Many Impacket utilities support Kerberos options such as:

-k

and:

-no-pass

depending on the utility.

Always check the relevant help output.

Example pattern:

impacket-<tool> -k -no-pass <target>

The exact target syntax depends on the utility.

docs.title: Kerberos Name Resolution
docs.text:
Kerberos usually works best when:

DNS is correct

Hostnames match SPNs

Realm is correct

Clock is synchronised

If an IP-based command fails but a hostname-based command works, the difference may be Kerberos/SPN related rather than a network problem.

docs.title: GetST
docs.text:
getST handles Kerberos service-ticket operations used in several legitimate administration and delegation-related testing scenarios.

Help:

impacket-getST -h

Before using it, understand:

Which principal you control

Which service is involved

Which delegation configuration exists

Which SPN is required

What the resulting ticket represents

For delegation concepts see:

  • Constrained Delegation
  • RBCD
  • S4U

docs.title: Do Not Treat getST as a Generic Command
docs.text:
The correct model is:

Directory Relationship
        |
        v
Delegation Configuration
        |
        v
Controlled Principal
        |
        v
Target Service
        |
        v
Required Ticket
        |
        v
getST

not:

Run getST
    |
    v
See What Happens

docs.title: TicketConverter
docs.text:
Impacket can convert between Kerberos ticket formats.

Help:

impacket-ticketConverter -h

Conceptually:

Kirbi
  |
  v
ticketConverter
  |
  v
CCache

or the reverse where supported.

docs.title: Why Ticket Conversion Matters
docs.text:
Different tooling ecosystems may use different ticket formats.

For example:

Windows-oriented tooling

Linux Kerberos tooling

may expect different representations.

Conversion changes the file format. It does not grant additional privilege.

docs.text:
Credential / Existing Ticket
          |
          v
Identify Principal
          |
          v
Identify Realm
          |
          v
Identify Ticket Type
          |
          v
Check Validity
          |
          v
Set KRB5CCNAME If Needed
          |
          v
klist
          |
          v
Use Against Authorised Service
          |
          v
Interpret Authorisation

docs.title: NTLM Hash Authentication
docs.text:
Several Impacket utilities support NTLM hash authentication.

Check the specific utility:

impacket-wmiexec -h

Common options may include:

-hashes

A typical hash pair format is:

LMHASH:NTHASH

When the LM hash is unavailable, tools commonly accept an empty LM component:

:NTHASH

Example placeholder:

:0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef

docs.title: What Hash Authentication Proves
docs.text:
If the target accepts the NTLM credential material:

Credential Material
        |
        v
Authentication

has been demonstrated.

It does not prove:

Plaintext password known

Domain Admin

Credential works everywhere

docs.text:

    |
    v

    |

    |

    |
    v

docs.title: Remote Administration Tools
docs.text:
Impacket includes several utilities capable of remote administration when sufficient permissions exist.

Important examples:

wmiexec

psexec

smbexec

atexec

dcomexec

These tools use different Windows mechanisms.

Do not treat them as interchangeable.

docs.title: Remote Administration Comparison
docs.text:
Tool General Mechanism Important Consideration wmiexec WMI Requires appropriate WMI/DCOM permissions psexec SMB + service creation Creates/uses a service mechanism smbexec SMB/service-based execution Service-related artefacts may be created atexec Task Scheduler Scheduled-task artefacts and logs dcomexec DCOM DCOM/RPC connectivity and permissions

Operational footprint differs significantly between methods.

docs.title: Before Remote Execution
docs.text:
Confirm:

Is remote execution explicitly authorised?

Do I already have enough evidence?

Is the target production-critical?

What artefacts will be created?

What logs will be generated?

Will a service be created?

Will a scheduled task be created?

Is cleanup required?

Can the same conclusion be proven more safely?

docs.title: WMIExec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-wmiexec -h

Password-based authorised example:

impacket-wmiexec 'corp.local/asif:Password123!@10.10.10.20'

docs.title: What Success Proves
docs.text:
A successful remote administrative session demonstrates that:

The supplied credential authenticates
+
The account has sufficient permissions for the WMI-based path

This is stronger evidence than simple SMB authentication.

docs.title: WMIExec with Hash Authentication
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised, inspect:

impacket-wmiexec -h

for the current -hashes syntax.

Use a single authorised target first.

docs.title: WMIExec Interpretation
docs.text:
If WMI-based administration succeeds, investigate:

Why does the account have remote WMI rights?

Is it local administrator?

Is access inherited from a domain group?

Is the access expected?

Which other systems share the same administrative model?

docs.title: PSExec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-psexec -h

psexec uses a service-based remote administration mechanism.

Because this can create service-related artefacts, it generally has a different operational footprint from WMI-based approaches.

docs.title: PSExec Safety
docs.text:
Before using it, understand:

Service creation

File/service artefacts

Windows event logging

EDR visibility

Cleanup requirements

Do not use it merely to prove credentials are valid.

docs.title: SMBExec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-smbexec -h

This also uses SMB/service-related mechanisms.

The exact artefacts and behaviour should be understood before production use.

docs.title: ATExec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-atexec -h

This uses Task Scheduler-related functionality.

Potential telemetry includes:

Task creation

Task execution

Process creation

Authentication events

Use only where the engagement objective requires remote execution.

docs.title: DCOMExec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-dcomexec -h

DCOM-based remote administration depends on:

RPC connectivity

DCOM availability

Authentication

Relevant permissions

For deeper context see DCOM.

docs.title: Choosing a Remote Administration Method
docs.text:
Do not choose based on:

Which command is shortest?

Choose based on:

Assessment objective

Permissions

Protocol availability

Operational impact

Telemetry

Cleanup

Rules of engagement

docs.title: MSSQLClient
docs.text:
Impacket includes a Microsoft SQL Server client.

Help:

impacket-mssqlclient -h

A controlled Windows-authentication example may resemble:

impacket-mssqlclient 'corp.local/asif:Password123!@10.10.10.30' -windows-auth

Exact authentication options should be confirmed with:

impacket-mssqlclient -h

docs.title: Representative MSSQL Session
docs.text:
[*] Encryption required, switching to TLS
[*] ENVCHANGE(DATABASE): Old Value: master, New Value: master
SQL>

docs.title: Initial SQL Questions
docs.text:
After authentication, determine:

Who am I?

Which database am I using?

Which roles do I have?

Which databases are accessible?

Is the account sysadmin?

Are linked servers configured?

docs.title: Safe SQL Context Queries
docs.text:
Current login:

SELECT SYSTEM_USER;

Current database:

SELECT DB_NAME();

Server name:

SELECT @@SERVERNAME;

Version:

SELECT @@VERSION;

Check sysadmin membership:

SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin');

docs.title: Interpret IS_SRVROLEMEMBER
docs.text:
Example:

1

generally indicates membership in the requested server role.

Example:

0

indicates the current login is not a member.

This provides much stronger evidence than simply assuming that successful SQL authentication means administrative database access.

docs.title: SQL Linked Servers
docs.text:
Linked servers can create trust relationships between SQL systems.

List them using an appropriate SQL query or client functionality supported in the environment.

Then determine:

Which server is linked?

Which authentication context is used?

What permissions exist remotely?

Is the link bidirectional?

Does it cross a security boundary?

docs.title: MSSQL Attack-Path Thinking
docs.text:
Domain User
    |
    v
SQL Login
    |
    v
Database Role
    |
    v
Linked Server
    |
    v
Different Security Context
    |
    v
Sensitive Database / Server

Do not assume the path exists until each relationship is validated.

docs.title: SecretsDump
docs.text:
secretsdump is one of the most sensitive Impacket utilities.

It can access credential material from Windows systems and Active Directory where sufficient privileges and conditions exist.

Help:

impacket-secretsdump -h

Potential data can include:

Local SAM hashes

LSA secrets

Cached domain logons

Service-account secrets

Domain credential material

Sensitive Operation

Credential extraction should only be performed when it is explicitly authorised and necessary to meet the assessment objective. Domain-controller credential extraction can expose highly sensitive domain-wide authentication material.

docs.title: Before Using SecretsDump
docs.text:
Ask:

Do I need credential material to prove the finding?

Is credential extraction explicitly in scope?

Can I demonstrate the privilege without collecting secrets?

Is the target a domain controller?

How will evidence be protected?

What data-retention requirements apply?

Will the command create temporary artefacts?

docs.title: Local Administrative Context
docs.text:
Against a specifically authorised test host where administrative access is already established, secretsdump can be used to validate whether that level of access exposes local credential stores.

Do not run it simply because an account receives (Pwn3d!) in NetExec.

docs.title: SecretsDump Result Interpretation
docs.text:
If credential material is retrieved:

Administrative Access
        |
        v
Sensitive Credential Store Accessible
        |
        v
Credential Material Retrieved

has been demonstrated.

Next determine:

Which accounts are represented?

Are they local or domain accounts?

Are any credentials reusable?

What privilege do they provide?

Is further validation necessary?

docs.title: Do Not Over-Collect
docs.text:
If the objective is:

Determine whether local administrative compromise exposes reusable credentials.

you may only need enough evidence to demonstrate that sensitive credential material is accessible.

You do not necessarily need to validate every recovered credential against every system.

docs.title: Domain Controller Considerations
docs.text:
A domain controller represents a significantly different risk level.

Potential credential data may affect:

Entire domain

Privileged users

Service accounts

Machine accounts

Trust relationships

Kerberos infrastructure

Treat any DC credential-access activity as a high-impact assessment step requiring explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Credential Handling
docs.text:
Never place real credential material in public notes or final reports.

Prefer:

Administrator:500:<REDACTED>

instead of preserving a reusable hash.

docs.title: Credential Validation Workflow
docs.text:
Credential Material

docs.title: Impacket and NetExec
docs.text:
These tools complement each other.

A practical workflow is:

NetExec
   |
   v
Broad Access Mapping
   |
   v
Interesting Target
   |
   v
Impacket
   |
   v
Focused Protocol Validation

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
NetExec:

nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -d corp.local -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!'

Suppose the result shows administrative access.

Rather than running every Impacket remote-administration tool, determine what you need to prove.

If WMI access is specifically relevant, a focused WMI validation may be appropriate.

If SMB share access is the objective, use an SMB client instead.

Choose the tool according to the question.

docs.title: Impacket and BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound identifies relationships.

Impacket can help validate selected protocol-level paths.

BloodHound

    v
Interesting Relationship
    |
    v
Understand Preconditions
    |
    v
Choose Appropriate Impacket Tool
    |

Evidence

docs.title: Impacket and Kerberos
docs.text:
Impacket's Kerberos utilities are particularly useful for:

SPN enumeration

Preauthentication assessment

TGT handling

Service tickets

Delegation validation

Kerberos authentication

Use them after understanding the underlying Kerberos relationship.

docs.title: Impacket and AD CS
docs.text:
Impacket is not the primary toolkit for all AD CS assessment workflows.

For AD CS-specific enumeration and certificate analysis, specialised tools such as Certipy are often more appropriate.

See:

Active Directory Certificate Services

First:

klist

Then determine:

Who is the client?

When does it expire?

What target is relevant?

If required:

export KRB5CCNAME=/path/to/ticket.ccache

docs.title: Candidate vs Confirmed
docs.text: Impacket output should be interpreted in stages.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
Examples:

SPN identified

Account without preauthentication identified

RPC endpoint exposed

SQL server reachable

Administrative credential available

These indicate something worth investigating.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
Examples:

Account has SPN and weak credential policy

Administrative credential authenticates to target

SQL login has elevated server role

Sensitive credential store is accessible

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
A controlled test demonstrates the actual security consequence.

Examples:

Authorised account successfully performs the relevant
administrative action.

Controlled credential analysis demonstrates that a service
account uses weak password-derived material.

SQL role query confirms sysadmin membership.

docs.title: KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW
docs.text:
Meaning:

Clock difference between client and Kerberos infrastructure
is too large.

Check:

date

Then compare against the domain environment.

docs.title: KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Incorrect password

Incorrect key

Wrong principal

Wrong realm

Authentication mismatch

docs.title: KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Incorrect username

Incorrect realm

Principal does not exist

Naming issue

docs.title: KDC_ERR_S_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN
docs.text:
Often related to:

Incorrect SPN

Wrong hostname

DNS issue

Service principal not registered

docs.title: STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Incorrect username

Incorrect password/hash

Wrong domain

Authentication restriction

docs.title: STATUS_ACCOUNT_LOCKED_OUT
docs.text:
Stop testing that account.

Do not repeatedly retry credentials.

docs.title: STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED
docs.text:
This often means:

Authentication succeeded

but:

Requested action is not authorised

Separate authentication from authorisation.

docs.title: rpc_s_access_denied
docs.text:
The account does not have sufficient permission for the requested RPC operation.

This is not necessarily an authentication failure.

docs.title: Connection Refused
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Service not listening

Firewall

Wrong port

Wrong host

Service disabled

docs.title: Name or Service Not Known
docs.text:
Check:

getent hosts target.corp.local

dig target.corp.local

DNS problems are especially important with Kerberos.

docs.title: Kerberos Works by Hostname but Not IP
docs.text:
This can be expected.

Kerberos uses service principal names that are normally associated with hostnames.

Prefer correct DNS names for Kerberos workflows.

docs.title: Ticket Not Found
docs.text:
Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

Then:

ls -l "$KRB5CCNAME"

if the variable contains a direct file path.

Finally:

klist

docs.title: Expired Ticket
docs.text:
klist shows ticket validity.

Do not troubleshoot network connectivity when the actual problem is simply an expired credential cache.

docs.title: Special Characters Break Target String
docs.text:
Use quoting:

'impacket-target-string'

rather than leaving shell-sensitive characters unquoted.

docs.title: Old Impacket Writeup Does Not Work
docs.text:
Check:

python3 -m pip show impacket

Then:

impacket-<tool> -h

Old examples may use different:

Executable names

Arguments

Authentication flags

Target formats

docs.title: Tool Selection Guide
docs.text: Objective Consider List SMB shares smbclient Enumerate SPNs GetUserSPNs Assess no-preauth users GetNPUsers Request TGT getTGT Work with service tickets getST Convert ticket format ticketConverter Enumerate SIDs lookupsid Enumerate RPC endpoints rpcdump Query SAMR information samrdump Connect to MSSQL mssqlclient Validate WMI administration wmiexec Validate service-based administration psexec / smbexec Validate scheduled-task administration atexec Validate DCOM administration dcomexec Assess sensitive credential stores secretsdump

docs.title: Do Not Default to the Most Powerful Tool
docs.text:
Example:

Question:
Can this user read the Finance share?

Use:

SMB client

not:

secretsdump

Another example:

Question:
Does this account have SQL sysadmin?

Use:

mssqlclient
+
SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin');

not:

Remote OS execution

Match the validation to the question.

docs.text:
For each important Impacket test record:

Test ID

Timestamp

Tool

Target system

Domain

Account

Protocol

Command

Interpretation

Security consequence

docs.title: Example Evidence Record
docs.text:
Test ID:
AD-IMP-003

Timestamp:
2026-09-06 15:20 UTC

Tool:
Impacket GetUserSPNs

Version:
<installed version>

Source:
Assessment workstation

Target:
DC01 / 10.10.10.10

Domain:
corp.local

Identity:
CORP\asif

Objective:
Identify domain accounts associated with Service Principal Names.

Command:
impacket-GetUserSPNs 'corp.local/asif:<REDACTED>' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

Result:
svc_sql associated with MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433.

Interpretation:
The account is associated with an MSSQL service principal and
is therefore relevant to the Kerberos service-account review.

Security Conclusion:
No password weakness or account compromise is established by
SPN enumeration alone.

docs.title: Evidence for Remote Administration
docs.text:
Record:

Account

Target

Protocol/mechanism

Authentication result

Privilege demonstrated

Command used

Minimal output

Any artefacts created

Cleanup performed

docs.title: Evidence for Credential Access
docs.text:
Do not preserve unnecessary credential material.

Prefer:

Credential store access confirmed.
2 local account hashes were accessible.
Values redacted.

rather than including the reusable secrets.

docs.title: Evidence for Kerberos
docs.text:
Useful fields:

Principal

Realm

SPN

Ticket type

Target service

Timestamp

Relevant configuration

Result

Avoid publishing complete reusable tickets.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Service Account
docs.text:
Avoid:

GetUserSPNs found svc_sql, therefore the account is vulnerable to Kerberoasting.

Prefer:

The domain account CORP\svc_sql is associated with the MSSQL service principal MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433. This makes the account eligible for normal Kerberos service-ticket issuance. The security impact depends on the strength and management of the account credential and the privileges assigned to the service account. Further controlled validation should therefore focus on password resilience and account privilege rather than treating the SPN itself as a vulnerability.

docs.title: Reporting Example - No Preauthentication
docs.text:
Prefer:

The account CORP\legacy_service is configured so that Kerberos preauthentication is not required. This configuration permits an unauthenticated requester to obtain password-derived authentication material for offline analysis. Review whether the configuration remains necessary and ensure the account uses a sufficiently strong managed credential.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Administrative Access
docs.text:
Prefer:

The supplied domain credential successfully established a WMI-based administrative session on SRV01. This confirms that the account has sufficient remote-management privileges on the server. Review identified that the privilege is inherited through the Server-Admins domain group.

docs.title: Reporting Example - SQL Privilege
docs.text:
Prefer:

The tested domain account successfully authenticated to SQL01 using Windows authentication. A direct server-role query returned 1 for IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'), confirming that the account is a member of the SQL Server sysadmin role.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Credential Store Access
docs.text:
Prefer:

Controlled validation confirmed that local administrative access to SRV01 permits access to sensitive local credential material. Reusable credential values were not included in the report. This increases the impact of compromise of accounts with local administrative privileges and reinforces the need for unique managed local credentials and protection of privileged logon sessions.

docs.title: Remediation - Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Focus on:

Long, high-entropy service-account passwords

gMSA where appropriate

Least privilege

Remove unnecessary SPNs

Reduce service-account privileges

Monitor abnormal service-ticket activity

Review legacy service identities

docs.title: Remediation - AS-REP
docs.text:
Focus on:

Require Kerberos preauthentication

Use strong managed credentials

Review why the setting was disabled

Remove stale accounts

Restrict service-account privilege

docs.title: Remediation - Administrative Access
docs.text:
Focus on:

Least privilege

Separate administrative accounts

Tiered administration

Restrict remote administration

Review local administrator membership

Use Windows LAPS

Reduce credential reuse

docs.title: Remediation - Credential Exposure
docs.text:
Focus on:

Windows LAPS

gMSA

Credential Guard

Privileged access workstations

Administrative tiering

Limit privileged sessions

Reduce local administrator access

Monitor credential-access behaviour

docs.title: Remediation - SQL
docs.text:
Focus on:

Least privilege

Remove unnecessary sysadmin membership

Separate application and administrative identities

Review linked servers

Restrict remote SQL exposure

Use managed service identities where appropriate

Audit privileged SQL operations

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: A retest should verify the root cause.

docs.title: Kerberos Preauthentication
docs.text:
Original:

legacy_service
    |
    v
Preauthentication disabled

Retest:

1. Re-query account configuration.
2. Confirm preauthentication is required.
3. Confirm the previous AS-REP condition is no longer present.

docs.title: Service Account Password
docs.text:
Original:

Service Account
     |
     v
Weak Password

Retest:

1. Confirm credential rotation.
2. Confirm password-management mechanism.
3. Verify account privilege was reviewed.
4. Repeat only the minimum authorised password-resilience test if required.

docs.title: Administrative Access
docs.text:
Original:

CORP\asif
    |
    v
Admin on SRV01

After remediation:

1. Validate normal authentication if still expected.
2. Confirm administrative remote-management action is denied.
3. Confirm group/policy assignment has been removed.

docs.title: SQL Privilege
docs.text:
Original:

SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin');

Result:

1

After remediation, repeat the same query.

Expected:

0

assuming sysadmin membership was the issue being remediated.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
Impacket should not become:

Tool List
   |
   v
Copy Commands
   |
   v
Run Everything

The stronger methodology is:

Question
   |
   v
Protocol
   |
   v
Prerequisites
   |
   v
Specific Impacket Utility
   |
   v
Focused Command
   |
   v
Representative Result
   |
   v
Interpretation
   |
   v
Alternative Explanation
   |
   v
Minimal Additional Validation
   |
   v
Defensible Conclusion

For every Impacket result, be able to answer:

What exactly did I test?

Why did I use this tool?

What prerequisite did I already establish?

What did the result prove?

What did it not prove?

What is the security consequence?

What additional evidence is actually necessary?

Can I stop here?

Use the smallest tool that answers the question

If the objective is to determine whether an account can read a share, use an SMB client. If the objective is to determine whether a SQL login is sysadmin, query the SQL role. Do not use a more intrusive remote-administration or credential-access technique when a smaller test already provides sufficient evidence.

Read the output, not just the exit status

A successful Impacket connection may prove authentication while still showing that the requested operation is denied. Separate authentication, authorisation and security impact when interpreting results.

Credential access is not routine enumeration

Utilities capable of accessing password hashes, tickets, secrets or domain credential material should be treated as sensitive assessment actions. Establish the need, authorisation, evidence-handling requirements and stop condition before using them.

A successful technique is not the end of the analysis

After a technique succeeds, determine why it succeeded, which permission or configuration enabled it, what security boundary was crossed, whether the access was expected, how defenders could observe it, and what change would remove the root cause.

docs.title: JWT Security Testing Cheatsheet
docs.text:
JSON Web Tokens are commonly used to carry authenticated identity and authorization information between systems.

A typical JWT looks like:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9
.
eyJzdWIiOiIxMjMiLCJyb2xlIjoidXNlciJ9
.
SIGNATURE

The three components are:

HEADER
  |
  v
PAYLOAD
  |
  v
SIGNATURE

More precisely:

Base64URL(Header)
      .
Base64URL(Payload)
      .
Signature

Authorised Security Testing

Test JWT implementations only against applications and accounts included in the assessment scope. Use dedicated test accounts and controlled tokens where possible. Do not attempt to forge privileged production tokens or access unrelated user data simply to demonstrate a validation weakness.

docs.title: JWT Mental Model
docs.text:
JWT security depends on more than:

Is the token signed?

A stronger model is:

Token Received
     |
     v
Parse Token
     |
     v
Validate Algorithm
     |
     v
Select Trusted Key
     |
     v
Verify Signature
     |
     v
Validate Issuer
     |
     v
Validate Audience
     |
     v
Validate Time Claims
     |
     v
Interpret Claims
     |
     v
Authorization Decision

docs.title: JWT vs JWS vs JWE
docs.text:
JWT is a token format.

JWTs may be represented using:

JWS

for signed or MAC-protected content, or:

JWE

for encrypted content.

docs.title: JWS
docs.text:
A common signed JWT contains three segments:

HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

docs.title: JWE
docs.text:
A compact JWE contains five segments.

Conceptually:

HEADER
.
ENCRYPTED KEY
.
IV
.
CIPHERTEXT
.
AUTHENTICATION TAG

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Most JWTs encountered during ordinary web application testing are signed JWS tokens.

Do not assume:

JWT = encrypted

docs.title: Base64URL Is Not Encryption
docs.text: The header and payload of an ordinary signed JWT can usually be decoded without knowing the signing key.

docs.title: Example Payload
docs.text:
{
  "sub": "123",
  "name": "Test User",
  "role": "user"
}

docs.title: Security Property
docs.text:
The signature protects integrity and authenticity when implemented correctly.

It does not inherently provide confidentiality.

docs.title: Identify JWTs
docs.text:
JWTs commonly appear in:

Authorization headers

Cookies

API responses

localStorage

sessionStorage

OAuth/OIDC flows

WebSocket authentication

Mobile application traffic

docs.title: Authorization Header
docs.text: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

docs.title: Cookie
docs.text: Cookie: access_token=eyJhbGciOi...

docs.title: JSON Response
docs.text:
{
  "access_token": "eyJhbGciOi..."
}

docs.title: Browser Storage
docs.text:
Applications may store tokens in:

localStorage

sessionStorage

docs.title: Storage Is Security-Relevant
docs.text: JavaScript-accessible storage can increase token exposure if the application has an XSS vulnerability.

docs.title: Token Inventory
docs.text:
Record:

Token Location Purpose Lifetime Access token Authorization header API access Short ID token OIDC client Identity assertion Short Refresh token Cookie/storage Token renewal Longer

docs.title: Do Not Treat All Tokens the Same
docs.text:
An:

Access Token

is not necessarily interchangeable with:

ID Token

or:

Refresh Token

docs.title: Decode JWT Locally
docs.text:
JWT segments use Base64URL rather than ordinary Base64.

Python:

python3 - <<'PY'
import base64
import json

token = "PASTE_TOKEN_HERE"
parts = token.split(".")

for i, part in enumerate(parts[:2]):
    part += "=" * (-len(part) % 4)
    decoded = base64.urlsafe_b64decode(part)
    try:
        print(json.dumps(json.loads(decoded), indent=2))
    except Exception:
        print(decoded)
PY

docs.title: Do Not Paste Sensitive Tokens Into Public Websites
docs.text:
Production JWTs may grant direct access to:

Accounts

APIs

Personal data

Administrative functions

Prefer local tooling for sensitive tokens.

docs.title: JWT Header
docs.text:
Example:

{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "typ": "JWT",
  "kid": "key-2026-01"
}

docs.title: Common Header Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Meaning alg Cryptographic algorithm typ Token type kid Key identifier jku JWK Set URL jwk Embedded JSON Web Key x5u X.509 certificate URL x5c X.509 certificate chain crit Critical header parameters

docs.title: JWT Payload
docs.text:
Example:

{
  "iss": "https://auth.example.com",
  "sub": "123",
  "aud": "api.example.com",
  "exp": 1780000000,
  "iat": 1779996400,
  "role": "user"
}

docs.title: Registered Claims
docs.text:
Important registered claims include:

iss

sub

aud

exp

nbf

iat

jti

docs.title: Claim Reference
docs.text: Claim Meaning iss Issuer sub Subject aud Audience exp Expiration time nbf Not before iat Issued at jti JWT identifier

docs.title: Custom Claims
docs.text:
Applications may add:

role

roles

permissions

scope

tenant

tenant_id

email

username

is_admin

groups

docs.title: Claims Are Security-Sensitive
docs.text:
A token may contain:

{
  "role": "admin"
}

but the security question is:

Who created and signed this claim?

Was the signature validated?

Is the issuer trusted?

Is this claim appropriate for this application?

Does the server independently enforce authorization?

docs.title: JWT Testing Workflow
docs.text:

     |
     v
Identify Purpose
     |
     v
Decode Header
     |

Decode Payload

     v

     |
