docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Capture a legitimate authenticated request.

GET /api/me HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Authorization: Bearer VALID_TOKEN

docs.title: Record Baseline
docs.text:
Capture:

HTTP status

Response body

Token header

Token payload

Issuer

Audience

Subject

Expiration

Role

Scope

Key identifier

docs.title: Invalid Token Baseline
docs.text:
Modify one character in the signature.

Example concept:

VALID_SIGNATURE

becomes:

VALID_SIGNATURX

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Token rejected

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: Before testing complex JWT behaviour, establish that signature verification is actually being performed.

docs.title: Signature Validation
docs.text:
The most fundamental JWT security property is:

Modified signed content
        |
        v
Signature no longer valid
        |
        v
Token rejected

docs.title: Modify Payload Without Re-Signing
docs.text:
Original:

{
  "sub": "123",
  "role": "user"
}

docs.title: Controlled Modification
docs.text:
{
  "sub": "123",
  "role": "admin"
}

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
If the signature has not been recreated using a trusted signing key:

Rejected

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
A server returning:

401

or:

403

after payload modification supports the conclusion that the modified token was not accepted.

Do not infer the exact validation logic from the status code alone.

docs.title: The alg Header
docs.text:
The JWT header identifies the cryptographic algorithm.

Examples:

HS256

HS384

HS512

RS256

RS384

RS512

PS256

PS384

PS512

ES256

ES384

ES512

EdDSA

docs.title: Algorithm Families
docs.text:
Conceptually:

HS*
 |
 v
Shared secret MAC

RS* / PS*
 |
 v
RSA signatures

ES*
 |
 v
Elliptic curve signatures

docs.title: HMAC
docs.text:
With HMAC:

Signing Key = Verification Key

The same secret is shared by token issuer and verifier.

docs.title: RSA / ECDSA
docs.text:
With asymmetric signing:

Private Key
    |
    v
Sign Token

Public Key
    |
    v
Verify Token

docs.title: Security Benefit
docs.text: API services can verify tokens using a public key without possessing the private signing key.

docs.title: Algorithm Allowlisting
docs.text:
Applications should explicitly define which algorithms are acceptable.

Conceptually:

Expected:
RS256

Received:
HS256

Result:
Reject

docs.title: Do Not Trust Token-Selected Algorithms Blindly
docs.text:
The token is attacker-controlled input.

The application should know:

Which algorithm should be used

rather than trusting arbitrary algorithm choices from the token.

docs.title: Unsecured JWTs
docs.text:
JOSE defines an unsecured JWS representation using:

{
  "alg": "none"
}

docs.title: Security Expectation
docs.text: Applications requiring signed tokens must reject unsecured JWTs.

docs.title: Safe Validation
docs.text:
You can determine whether an application improperly accepts unsigned tokens using a dedicated low-privilege test account and controlled claims.

Do not use the issue to create or exercise unauthorized privileged production access.

docs.title: Algorithm Confusion
docs.text:
Algorithm confusion can occur when a verifier incorrectly allows a token to influence whether a key is interpreted as:

Asymmetric verification key

or:

HMAC secret

docs.title: Conceptual Risk
docs.text:
Application expects RS256
        |
        v
Public RSA Key
        |
        v
Attacker changes token algorithm
        |
        v
Verifier incorrectly treats public key
as HMAC material

docs.title: Secure Behaviour
docs.text:
The server should bind:

Algorithm

Key type

Issuer

Token purpose

to trusted server-side configuration.

docs.title: Do Not Test by Guessing Production Secrets
docs.text:
Algorithm-confusion testing should focus on validation behaviour and known public verification material where applicable.

Do not attempt unrelated key theft or secret harvesting.

docs.title: Weak HMAC Secrets
docs.text: HMAC JWT security depends on the strength of the shared secret.

docs.title: Weak Example
docs.text:
Conceptually weak values include:

secret

password

jwtsecret

companyname

docs.title: Source Review
docs.text:
Search configuration for JWT secrets:

rg -ni 'jwt.*secret|secret.*jwt|signing.*key|token.*secret|JWT_SECRET' .

docs.title: Environment Files
docs.text: rg -ni 'JWT|TOKEN|SIGNING|SECRET' -g '.env*' -g '*.yaml' -g '*.yml' -g '*.json' -g '*.toml' .

docs.title: Important
docs.text: Do not expose secrets discovered during source review in screenshots or public reports.

docs.title: Secret Rotation
docs.text:
If a signing secret is exposed:

Changing application code

is not enough.

The secret itself must be rotated.

docs.title: kid - Key Identifier
docs.text:
Example:

{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "kid": "key-2026-01"
}

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: kid helps the verifier select the correct key from a key set.

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
How does the server resolve:

kid

to:

verification key

docs.title: Dangerous Design
docs.text:
Avoid treating kid as an unrestricted:

File path

Database query fragment

Command argument

URL

docs.title: Safe Model
docs.text:
kid
 |
 v
Lookup in trusted key set
 |
 v
Known key

docs.title: Unknown kid
docs.text:
Test a controlled unknown identifier:

{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "kid": "does-not-exist"
}

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
Token rejected safely

without:

Stack trace

File path disclosure

Database error

Internal key material

docs.title: jku - JWK Set URL
docs.text:
Example:

{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "jku": "https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
  "kid": "key1"
}

docs.title: Risk
docs.text: If the application blindly trusts a token-controlled jku, the token may influence where verification keys are obtained.

docs.title: Secure Design
docs.text:
Trust:

Configured issuer

Configured JWKS endpoint

Approved key set

not arbitrary token-provided locations.

docs.title: SSRF Consideration
docs.text:
Remote key retrieval can also create SSRF risk if arbitrary URLs are accepted.

JWT key handling and SSRF should therefore be reviewed together where remote key retrieval exists.

docs.title: jwk - Embedded Key
docs.text:
A JWT header may contain an embedded JSON Web Key.

Example concept:

{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "jwk": {
    "kty": "RSA",
    "kid": "key1"
  }
}

docs.title: Security Expectation
docs.text: The application should not automatically trust an attacker-supplied embedded verification key unless the protocol and trust model explicitly require and validate it.

docs.title: x5u
docs.text: x5u can reference an X.509 certificate or certificate chain location depending on the JOSE design.

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text: Can an untrusted token control where the application retrieves certificate material?

docs.title: x5c
docs.text:
x5c carries certificate chain information directly in the JOSE header.

Certificate presence does not itself establish trust.

The verifier must validate the chain and expected trust relationship appropriately.

docs.title: JWKS
docs.text:
A JSON Web Key Set contains public verification keys.

Common endpoint:

/.well-known/jwks.json

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "keys": [
    {
      "kty": "RSA",
      "kid": "key-1",
      "use": "sig",
      "alg": "RS256",
      "n": "...",
      "e": "AQAB"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Public Keys Are Usually Not Secrets
docs.text:
Public verification keys are intended to be distributable.

Do not report:

Public JWKS accessible

as a vulnerability by itself.

docs.title: JWKS Review
docs.text:
Check:

Trusted origin

HTTPS

Key identifiers

Algorithm consistency

Key rotation

Caching

Unknown-key behaviour

docs.title: Key Rotation
docs.text:
Systems should support moving from:

Old Key

to:

New Key

without unsafe trust expansion.

docs.title: Rotation Model
docs.text:
Key A signs existing tokens

Key B introduced

New tokens signed with Key B

Key A retained during overlap

Key A eventually retired

docs.title: Retired Keys
docs.text: Determine whether tokens signed with a retired key remain accepted beyond the intended transition period.

docs.title: Issuer Validation
docs.text:
iss identifies the token issuer.

Example:

{
  "iss": "https://auth.example.com"
}

docs.title: Security Expectation
docs.text: The verifier should compare the issuer against a trusted expected value.

docs.title: Why Issuer Matters
docs.text: Without correct issuer validation, an application may accept tokens from another identity system that uses compatible keys or token structure.

docs.title: Audience Validation
docs.text:
aud identifies the intended recipient.

Example:

{
  "aud": "payments-api"
}

docs.title: Security Expectation
docs.text:
A service should reject a token intended only for:

different-api

docs.title: Cross-Service Token Confusion
docs.text:
Architecture:

Service A

Service B

If both trust the same issuer but fail to validate audience:

Token for Service A
        |
        v
Presented to Service B
        |
        v
Incorrectly accepted

docs.title: Subject
docs.text:
sub normally identifies the principal.

Example:

{
  "sub": "user-123"
}

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Determine whether the application uses:

sub

email

username

custom user ID

as its identity key.

docs.title: Avoid Mutable Identity Keys
docs.text:
Using mutable claims such as email addresses as permanent internal identity keys can create lifecycle complexity.

Prefer stable subject identifiers where appropriate.

docs.title: Expiration
docs.text:
Example:

{
  "exp": 1780000000
}

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
After expiration:

Token rejected

docs.title: Test Expiration
docs.text: Use a token from your own test account and verify behaviour after the configured expiration period.

docs.title: Clock Skew
docs.text:
Small clock-skew allowances may be legitimate.

Do not report a token being accepted a few seconds beyond the nominal timestamp without understanding configured tolerance.

docs.title: nbf
docs.text:
nbf means:

Not valid before this time

docs.title: Expected

docs.title: Reporting Missing Signature Validation
docs.text: The API accepts JWTs whose signed payload has been modified without a valid corresponding signature. A token issued to a dedicated test account was modified and replayed without possession of the trusted signing key, and the API continued to treat the request as authenticated. The application must cryptographically verify the token before processing any identity or authorization claims.

docs.title: Reporting Algorithm Validation Weakness
docs.text: The application does not restrict JWT verification to the algorithm expected by the authentication architecture. The verifier accepts an alternative token algorithm rather than binding the algorithm and key type to trusted server-side configuration. JWT verification should use an explicit algorithm allowlist and trusted key configuration.

docs.title: Reporting Missing Audience Validation
docs.text: The API accepts a valid JWT issued for a different service because the token audience is not validated against the current API. This allows tokens intended for one relying service to be reused against another service sharing the same trust environment.

docs.title: Reporting Missing Issuer Validation
docs.text: The application verifies the token signature but does not enforce the expected issuer. Tokens should be accepted only from the identity provider explicitly trusted by the application.

docs.title: Reporting Expired Token Acceptance
docs.text: The API continues to accept access tokens after their exp claim has passed. A token issued to a dedicated test account remained usable after expiration and successfully accessed an authenticated endpoint. Token lifetime validation should be enforced during every authenticated request.

docs.title: Reporting Untrusted JWKS Source
docs.text: JWT verification accepts key material from a location controlled through an untrusted token header rather than restricting verification to the application's configured trusted key set. The verification key source must be derived from trusted issuer configuration and must not be selected from arbitrary token-controlled URLs.

docs.title: Reporting Token Exposure
docs.text: The application transmits bearer JWTs in URL query parameters. Because URLs may be retained in browser history, server logs, proxy logs and analytics systems, this increases the likelihood of token disclosure. Bearer tokens should be transmitted using an appropriate authorization header or protected cookie according to the application's authentication architecture.

docs.title: Reporting Stale Privilege Claims
docs.text: Authorization privileges are embedded in long-lived JWTs and remain effective after the corresponding server-side role is removed. The application should reduce the lifetime of privilege-bearing tokens or introduce an appropriate revocation or authorization-state mechanism for security-sensitive privilege changes.

docs.title: Do Not Report

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
JWT testing is not:

Decode Token
    |
    v
Change role=user to role=admin
    |
    v
Done

It is:

TOKEN PURPOSE
     |
     v
CRYPTOGRAPHIC TRUST
     |
     v
KEY TRUST
     |
     v
CLAIM VALIDATION
     |
     v
TOKEN LIFECYCLE
     |
     v
AUTHORIZATION

For every JWT implementation ask:

What type of token is this?

Who issued it?

Which service should accept it?

Which algorithm is expected?

Is the algorithm fixed by trusted configuration?

Which key verifies the token?

How is that key selected?

Can the token influence the key source?

Is the signature always verified?

Are unsecured tokens rejected?

Are unexpected algorithms rejected?

Is the issuer validated?

Is the audience validated?

Is expiration enforced?

Is not-before enforced where relevant?

What clock skew is allowed?

How long does the token live?

What does the subject identify?

Which roles or permissions are present?

Are scopes enforced?

Are tenant boundaries independently enforced?

Can an ID token be misused as an access token?

Can a token for one API be reused against another?

How are refresh tokens protected?

Are refresh tokens rotated?

Can refresh-token replay be detected?

What happens after logout?

What happens after password change?

What happens after password reset?

What happens after account disablement?

What happens after a role change?

Can tokens be revoked when required?

Are tokens stored in URLs?

Are tokens logged?

Are browser tokens exposed to JavaScript?

Are unnecessary sensitive claims present?

Are public keys being confused with secrets?

Are private signing keys properly protected?

Are equivalent JWT verifiers configured consistently?

Does a valid JWT still receive proper object-level authorization?

Has every finding been demonstrated through actual server behaviour?

Have token values been redacted from evidence?

  • OWASP JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet for Java
  • PortSwigger Web Security Academy - JWT Attacks

Start with trust

Before modifying claims, determine which issuer, algorithm and verification keys the application is supposed to trust. Most meaningful JWT weaknesses occur when that trust model is implemented incorrectly.

A valid JWT is not authorization

Successful signature verification establishes token integrity according to the configured trust model. The application must still enforce roles, scopes, ownership and tenant boundaries for every protected resource.

Change one property at a time

Modify one JWT property per test whenever possible. This makes it clear whether acceptance resulted from missing signature validation, issuer handling, audience handling, key selection, lifetime validation or authorization.

Review every verifier

In microservice environments, the same token may be validated by an API gateway, multiple backend services, WebSocket infrastructure and legacy APIs. One correctly configured verifier does not prove that the others are equally secure.

JWT payloads are usually readable

Ordinary signed JWT payloads are encoded rather than encrypted. Being able to decode a payload is expected and is not itself a vulnerability.

Never expose live bearer tokens

JWTs frequently function as bearer credentials. Redact them from screenshots, reports, logs and public tooling, and avoid submitting production tokens to third-party token-decoding websites.

find / -user root -type f -perm -4000 -exec ls -ldb {} \; 2>/dev/null

docs.title: SGID
docs.text:
find / -type f -perm -2000 2>/dev/null

Alternative:

find / -type f -perm -g=s 2>/dev/null

docs.title: SUID and SGID Together
docs.text: find / -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -exec ls -la {} \; 2>/dev/null

docs.title: SUID Analysis
docs.text:
Use:

SUID Binary
    |
    v
Expected?
    |
    +--> No --> Investigate Origin
    |
    +--> Yes
           |
           v
      Safe Functionality?
           |
           v
      GTFOBins / Vendor Research

Check unusual binaries against:

GTFOBins

Do not assume every SUID binary is vulnerable.

docs.text:

cap_setuid
cap_setgid
cap_dac_override
cap_dac_read_search
cap_sys_admin
cap_sys_ptrace
cap_net_admin
cap_net_raw

Interpret the capability together with the executable.

docs.title: Capability Analysis
docs.text:
Executable
    |
    v
Linux Capability
    |
    v
What Kernel Privilege Is Granted?
    |
    v
Can Existing Program Functionality
Cross a Security Boundary?

Check relevant executables against GTFOBins.

docs.text: lsattr file

System crontab:

Directories:

ls -la /etc/cron.daily/
ls -la /etc/cron.weekly/
ls -la /etc/cron.monthly/

docs.text:
Review:

Schedule
   |
   v
Execution User
   |
   v
Command
   |
   v
Script
   |
   v
Dependencies
   |
   v
Permissions

Questions:

Can I modify the script?
Can I modify its directory?
Can I modify a dependency?
Does it use wildcards?
Does it rely on PATH?
Does it load writable configuration?

docs.text:

Timer:

docs.title: Shell Startup Files
docs.text:
Current user:

Common files:

~/.bashrc
~/.bash_profile
~/.profile
~/.zshrc

Inspect:

cat ~/.bashrc
cat ~/.profile

Writable startup files belonging to another security context may warrant investigation.

docs.title: MOTD
docs.text:
Dynamic MOTD configuration may exist under:

ls -la /etc/update-motd.d/ 2>/dev/null

Review permissions:

find /etc/update-motd.d -maxdepth 1 -type f -exec ls -l {} \; 2>/dev/null

Unexpected non-root write access to privileged login-time scripts can be security-sensitive.

Do not modify them during routine assessment.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Directory:

ls -la ~/.ssh/

Configuration:

cat ~/.ssh/config 2>/dev/null

Authorised keys:

Known hosts:

cat ~/.ssh/known_hosts 2>/dev/null

docs.text:

find ~/.ssh -maxdepth 1 -type f -ls 2>/dev/null

Common names:

id_rsa
id_ed25519
id_ecdsa

Treat private keys as credentials.

docs.text:

or:

systemctl status sshd

sshd -T

Review:

permitrootlogin
passwordauthentication
pubkeyauthentication
allowusers
allowgroups

docs.text:
ssh user@example.com

ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user@example.com

Port:

Verbose:

ssh -v user@example.com

docs.text:
Only establish tunnels when explicitly within scope.

Local forwarding:

ssh -L 8080:internal.example:80 user@jump.example

Dynamic SOCKS:

ssh -D 1080 user@jump.example

Remote forwarding:

ssh -R 8080:127.0.0.1:8000 user@remote.example

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Common locations:

/etc/
/opt/
/srv/
/var/www/
/usr/local/etc/
/home/<user>/

Search common formats:

find /etc -type f \( \
    -name '*.conf' -o \
    -name '*.ini' -o \
    -name '*.yaml' -o \
    -name '*.yml' \
\) 2>/dev/null

docs.text:
Use targeted locations:

grep -RniE 'password|passwd|secret|token|api[_-]?key' /opt /srv /var/www 2>/dev/null

Common interesting file types:

.env
.conf
.ini
.yml
.yaml
.json
.xml
.properties

docs.text:
find /var/www /opt /srv -type f -name '.env' 2>/dev/null

Do not expose discovered secrets in screenshots or reports.

docs.title: Shell History
docs.text:
history

Bash:

cat ~/.bash_history 2>/dev/null

Zsh:

cat ~/.zsh_history 2>/dev/null

Search:

grep -Ei 'password|passwd|token|secret|key' ~/.bash_history 2>/dev/null

History is not a complete audit trail.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Potential credential sources include:

Shell History
Environment Variables
Application Configuration
Database Configuration
SSH Keys
Cloud CLI Configuration
Backup Files
Service Configuration
Mounted Shares

The objective is to determine:

Does Sensitive Authentication Material
Exist Where the Current User Can Access It?

Do not collect more secret material than required to demonstrate the finding.

docs.title: Backup Files
docs.text:
Search common patterns:

find / -type f \( \
    -name '*.bak' -o \
    -name '*.backup' -o \
    -name '*.old' -o \
    -name '*.save' \
\) 2>/dev/null

Prefer targeted paths where possible.

docs.text:
Search:

find / -type f \( \
    -name '*.zip' -o \
    -name '*.tar' -o \
    -name '*.tar.gz' -o \
    -name '*.tgz' -o \
    -name '*.7z' \
\) 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Web Servers
docs.text:
Common application locations:

/var/www/
/srv/www/
/opt/
/srv/

docs.text:
Processes:

pgrep -a apache2

or:

pgrep -a httpd

Common configuration:

/etc/apache2/
/etc/httpd/

docs.text:
pgrep -a nginx

Configuration:

ls -la /etc/nginx/ 2>/dev/null

Where permitted:

docs.text:
Processes:

ps aux | grep -Ei 'mysql|mariadb|postgres|mongod|redis'

Listening:

Common ports:

3306   MySQL / MariaDB
5432   PostgreSQL
6379   Redis
27017  MongoDB

Port number alone does not prove the service.

docs.text:
Common locations:

/etc/mysql/
/etc/my.cnf
~/.my.cnf

Search:

find /etc -iname '*mysql*' -o -iname '*mariadb*' 2>/dev/null

docs.title: PostgreSQL Configuration
docs.text:
Common locations vary by distribution and version.

Find:

find /etc -iname 'postgresql.conf' -o -iname 'pg_hba.conf' 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Version:

docker --version

Information:

docker info

Containers:

docker ps

All:

docker ps -a

Images:

docker images

Networks:

docker network ls

Volumes:

docker volume ls

docs.title: Docker Group
docs.text:
getent group docker

Current membership:

id

Docker socket:

ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

Control of a privileged Docker daemon can imply extensive control over the host.

Do not start a privileged container merely to prove the security impact unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Podman
docs.text:
podman info

podman ps

Rootless Podman should not automatically be treated as equivalent to access to a root-controlled Docker daemon.

docs.title: LXD / LXC
docs.text:
Groups:

getent group lxd

getent group lxc

Current user:

id

If available:

lxc list

Administrative control of privileged container infrastructure can have host-security implications.

Validate the actual configuration before reporting.

docs.title: Container Detection
docs.text:
systemd-detect-virt

Docker indicator:

test -f /.dockerenv && echo 'Docker environment indicator present'

Cgroups:

cat /proc/1/cgroup

No single method detects every container environment.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Current context:

kubectl config current-context

Contexts:

kubectl config get-contexts

Authorisation:

kubectl auth can-i --list

Configuration:

ls -la ~/.kube/

Kubeconfig may contain sensitive authentication information.

docs.title: Cloud Credentials
docs.text:
Common user configuration locations include:

~/.aws/
~/.azure/
~/.config/gcloud/

List:

ls -la ~/.aws 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.azure 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.config/gcloud 2>/dev/null

Treat cloud tokens and credentials as sensitive and remain within the authorised cloud scope.

docs.title: NFS Privilege Analysis
docs.text:
Check mounts:

findmnt -t nfs,nfs4

Local exports:

cat /etc/exports 2>/dev/null

Review export options such as:

root_squash
no_root_squash
rw
ro

Do not modify remote files merely to prove an unsafe export.

docs.title: Shared Libraries
docs.text:
Loaded libraries:

ldd /path/to/binary

Dynamic loader information:

ldconfig -p

Environment:

env | grep '^LD_'

Potentially relevant variables include:

LD_LIBRARY_PATH
LD_PRELOAD

Privileged execution often applies additional loader restrictions, so evaluate the actual execution context.

docs.title: Writable Library Paths
docs.text:
For a specific privileged application:

ldd /path/to/binary

Then inspect relevant library and directory permissions:

ls -l /path/to/library.so
ls -ld /path/to/library-directory

Do not replace production libraries during routine testing.

docs.title: Kernel
docs.text:
uname -a

uname -r

cat /proc/version

Installed kernel packages on Debian-based systems:

dpkg -l 'linux-image*' 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Kernel Vulnerability Assessment
docs.text:
Do not assume:

Old Kernel Version
=
Exploitable

Distribution vendors frequently backport security patches without changing the upstream version in the way a simple version comparison expects.

Validate:

Distribution
Kernel Package
Vendor Patch Level
Architecture
Exploit Preconditions
Mitigations

before reporting a kernel vulnerability.

docs.title: Linux Privilege Escalation Automation
docs.text:
Common assessment tools include:

LinPEAS
Linux Exploit Suggester
Linux Smart Enumeration

These tools can accelerate enumeration but should not replace manual validation.

Use them only when tooling execution is authorised.

docs.title: LinPEAS
docs.text:
Project:

PEASS-ng

Use the current project documentation for installation and execution.

Review findings manually before reporting them.

docs.title: Linux Exploit Suggester
docs.text:
Project:

Linux Exploit Suggester

Treat suggestions as:

Candidates for Investigation

not confirmed vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Linux Smart Enumeration
docs.text:
Project:

Linux Smart Enumeration

Use according to the rules of engagement.

docs.title: Automated Enumeration Model
docs.text:
Enumeration Tool
       |
       v
Candidate Finding
       |
       v
Manual Verification
       |
       v
Context Analysis
       |
       v
Minimal Validation
       |
       v
Report

Never use:

Scanner Says Vulnerable

as the entire evidence chain.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Checklist
docs.text:
Start with:

id
sudo -l
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
env

Then:

find / -type f -perm -4000 2>/dev/null

getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

cat /etc/crontab

systemctl list-timers --all

systemctl --type=service --state=running

ps aux

ss -tulpn

mount

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Decision Tree
docs.text:
Current User
    |
    v
sudo -l
    |
    +--> Interesting Rule? --> Analyse Binary / GTFOBins
    |
    v
SUID / SGID
    |
    +--> Unusual Binary? --> GTFOBins / Vendor Research
    |
    v
Capabilities
    |
    +--> Sensitive Capability? --> Analyse Program
    |
    v
Cron / Timers
    |
    +--> Writable Dependency? --> Validate Path
    |
    v
Services
    |
    +--> Writable Component? --> Validate Path
    |
    v
Credentials
    |
    +--> Reusable Credential? --> Scope Check
    |
    v
Groups
    |
    +--> Docker / LXD / Other Privileged Group?
    |
    v
Kernel / Software
    |
    +--> Known Vulnerability? --> Verify Patch State

docs.title: GTFOBins Workflow
docs.text:
When you discover:

sudo
SUID
Capability

use:

GTFOBins

Search the binary.

Then determine:

Does the Required Context Match?
Does the Binary Have the Required Permission?
Does the Technique Modify State?
Can Impact Be Proven Read-Only?

GTFOBins itself notes that listed programs are not necessarily vulnerable; the issue is how legitimate functionality can interact with unsafe security configuration.

docs.title: Exploit Notes Workflow
docs.text:
Exploit Notes provides a broad Linux privilege-escalation reference covering areas such as:

OS / Kernel Information
Users
Shell Configuration
SUID / SGID
Writable Files
Capabilities
Sudo
Scheduled Execution
Containers
Software-Specific Privilege Escalation

Use it primarily as:

Enumeration Reference
       +
Research Starting Point

and independently validate findings before reporting.

Reference:

Exploit Notes - Linux Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful evidence model:

Command
   |
   v
Relevant Output
   |
   v
Security Context
   |
   v
Affected Component

   v
Impact

Hostname
Username
UID / Groups

Command
Relevant Output

docs.title: Sensitive Evidence
docs.text:
Avoid unnecessarily storing:

Passwords
Private Keys
Tokens
Cloud Credentials
Database Credentials
Session Cookies
API Keys
Hashes

Prefer evidence such as:

File Exists
+
Current User Can Read It
+
Secret Value Redacted

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Evidence
docs.text:
A strong finding should demonstrate:

Low-Privilege Principal
        |
        v
Misconfiguration
        |
        v
Privileged Resource
        |
        v
Security Impact

Example:

User
 |
 v
sudo Permission
 |
 v
Binary with Unsafe Functionality
 |
 v
Potential Root-Level Capability

The finding is the unsafe privilege relationship, not simply that a binary exists.

docs.title: Do Not Overreport
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

SUID Binary Exists
Docker Installed
Old Kernel String
Cron Exists
sudo Installed
Capability Exists
Writable /tmp
SSH Enabled

Instead determine:

Can the Current User Cross
a Security Boundary?

What Privilege Does It Provide?

       v
Is That Privilege Intended?
       |
       v
Can It Be Demonstrated Safely?

  • [ ] Review libraries
  • [ ] Review credentials
  • [ ] Review privileged groups
  • [ ] Review containers
  • [ ] Review NFS
  • [ ] Review kernel/software candidates
  • [ ] Manually validate automated findings

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Record hostname
  • [ ] Record current user
  • [ ] Record groups
  • [ ] Record command
  • [ ] Capture relevant output
  • [ ] Record affected object
  • [ ] Record permissions
  • [ ] Explain privilege boundary
  • [ ] Redact secrets
  • [ ] Document any state changes
  • [ ] Perform cleanup where required

docs.title: Testing Model
docs.text:
The Linux privilege model can be simplified as:

User
 |
 v
Permission
 |
 v
Resource
 |
 v
Privileged Execution

For sudo:

User
 |
 v
sudo Rule
 |
 v
Binary
 |
 v
Privileged Functionality

For SUID:

User
 |
 v
SUID Binary
 |
 v
Effective Owner
 |
 v
Privileged Functionality

For capabilities:

User
 |
 v
Executable
 |
 v
Linux Capability
 |
 v
Kernel Privilege

For scheduled tasks:

User-Writable Component
        |
        v
Scheduled Execution
        |
        v
Privileged User

For services:

Writable Component
       |
       v
Privileged Service
       |
       v
Higher Privilege

For credentials:

Readable Secret
     |
     v
More-Privileged Identity
     |
     v
Privilege Escalation

For containers:

Container Management
        |
        v
Host Resource Access
        |
        v
Potential Host Control

The overall assessment model is:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Identify Candidate
   |
   v
Research
   |
   +--> GTFOBins
   |
   +--> Exploit Notes
   |
   +--> Vendor Documentation
   |
   v
Validate Preconditions
   |
   v
Minimal Proof
   |
   v
Evidence
   |
   v
Remediation

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
# Identity
whoami
id
groups

# Host
hostname
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release

# Sudo
sudo -l

# Environment
env
echo "$PATH"

# Network
ip -br addr
ip route
ip neigh
cat /etc/resolv.conf
ss -tulpn

# Processes
ps aux
ps -U root -u root

# Services
systemctl --type=service --state=running
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --state=enabled

# Filesystems
mount
findmnt
df -h
lsblk -f

# SUID
find / -type f -perm -4000 2>/dev/null

# SGID
find / -type f -perm -2000 2>/dev/null

# Capabilities
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

# Cron
cat /etc/crontab
ls -la /etc/cron.d/
crontab -l

# Timers
systemctl list-timers --all

# Writable files
find /path -type f -writable 2>/dev/null

# Writable directories
find /path -type d -writable 2>/dev/null

# Shell history
history
cat ~/.bash_history 2>/dev/null

# SSH
ls -la ~/.ssh/
cat ~/.ssh/config 2>/dev/null

# Logs
journalctl -n 100

# Docker
docker info
docker ps
ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

# Security
getenforce
aa-status
cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space

docs.title: GTFOBins
docs.text:
GTFOBins

Use GTFOBins when assessing security-sensitive Unix executables exposed through contexts such as:

sudo
SUID
Capabilities

Remember that inclusion in GTFOBins does not mean the binary itself is vulnerable.

docs.title: Exploit Notes
docs.text:
Exploit Notes - Linux Privilege Escalation

Useful as a practical reference for Linux privilege-escalation enumeration and technique research.

docs.title: PEASS-ng
docs.text:
PEASS-ng

Includes LinPEAS for automated Linux privilege-escalation enumeration.

docs.title: Linux Exploit Suggester
docs.text:
Linux Exploit Suggester

Use suggestions as candidates requiring manual validation.

docs.title: Linux Smart Enumeration
docs.text: Linux Smart Enumeration

docs.title: Linux man-pages
docs.text: Linux man-pages Project

docs.title: systemd
docs.text: systemd Documentation

docs.title: OpenSSH
docs.text: OpenSSH Manual Pages

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: Docker Documentation

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
For Linux assessments, start simple:

Who Am I?
   |
   v
What System Is This?
   |
   v
What Can I Run?
   |
   v
What Runs as Root?
   |
   v
What Can I Modify?

The highest-value initial commands are often:

id
sudo -l
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
ps aux
ss -tulpn
find / -type f -perm -4000 2>/dev/null
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
systemctl list-timers --all

When you discover an unusual privileged binary:

Binary
   |
   v
Check Permission Context
   |
   v
GTFOBins
   |
   v
Exploit Notes
   |
   v
Vendor Documentation
   |
   v
Validate Preconditions

The important distinction is:

Interesting Configuration
        !=
Confirmed Privilege Escalation

For example:

SUID Binary

alone is not the finding.

The relevant question is:

Can the Current User Use
That Binary's Functionality
to Cross a Security Boundary?

Similarly:

Old Kernel

does not automatically mean:

Kernel Privilege Escalation

and:

Docker Installed

does not automatically mean:

Root Access

Always validate the complete path:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Specific Misconfiguration
        |
        v
Reachable Privileged Capability
        |
        v
Security Boundary Crossed

For authorised penetration testing, prefer:

Enumeration
    |
    v
Analysis
    |
    v
Minimal Validation
    |
    v
Evidence
    |
    v
Cleanup

over unnecessary system modification.

The Linux cheatsheet should therefore function as:

Command Reference
      +
Privilege Checklist
      +
Research Map

with GTFOBins and Exploit Notes used as supporting references when a potentially dangerous Unix executable or privilege-escalation condition is discovered.

docs.title: NetExec Cheatsheet
docs.text:
NetExec is a network service enumeration and assessment framework commonly used during authorised Windows and Active Directory security testing.

It provides a consistent interface for interacting with protocols such as:

SMB

LDAP

WinRM

MSSQL

SSH

FTP

RDP

This cheatsheet focuses on a practical workflow:

What protocol is available?
        |
        v
Can I authenticate?
        |
        v
What does that access provide?
        |
        v
What can I enumerate?
        |
        v
Is anything security relevant?
        |
        v
What should I verify next?

For broader Active Directory methodology, see the Active Directory Cheatsheet.

Authorised Security Testing

Only use NetExec against systems and accounts that are explicitly within the authorised scope. Authentication testing, enumeration and remote actions can create logs, trigger detections, lock accounts or affect production systems.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
A common NetExec workflow is:

Identify Targets
      |
      v
Identify Protocol
      |
      v
Collect Basic Host Information
      |
      v
Validate One Credential
      |
      v
Determine Privilege
      |
      v
Enumerate Relevant Resources
      |
      v
Investigate Interesting Results
      |
      v
Validate Minimally
      |
      v
Capture Evidence

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Follow the current NetExec installation documentation where possible.

Check whether NetExec is already available:

which nxc

Version:

nxc --version

General help:

nxc --help

docs.title: Why Version Matters
docs.text:
NetExec changes over time.

Options shown in:

Old blog posts

Archived CrackMapExec guides

CTF writeups

Older pentest notes

may no longer match the installed version.

Before using a protocol-specific option, check:

nxc <protocol> --help

For example:

nxc smb --help

or:

nxc ldap --help

docs.title: Supported Protocols
docs.text:
List the protocols supported by the installed version:

nxc --help

Depending on the version, protocols may include:

smb

ldap

winrm

mssql

ssh

ftp

rdp

wmi

Do not assume every installation exposes exactly the same protocol set.

docs.title: General Syntax
docs.text:
The basic structure is:

nxc <protocol> <target> [options]

Examples:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10

nxc ldap 10.10.10.10

nxc winrm 10.10.10.20

docs.title: Target Formats
docs.text: NetExec can work with several target formats.

docs.title: Single IP
docs.text: nxc smb 10.10.10.20

docs.title: Hostname
docs.text: nxc smb srv01.corp.local

docs.title: Network Range
docs.text: nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24

docs.title: Target File
docs.text:
Create:

10.10.10.10
10.10.10.20
10.10.10.30

Then:

nxc smb targets.txt

Caution

Do not move from a single-host test to an entire subnet merely because NetExec supports CIDR ranges. Confirm the engagement scope and authentication-testing constraints first.

docs.title: Example Environment
docs.text:
Examples throughout this page use:

Domain:   corp.local
DC:       dc01.corp.local
DC IP:    10.10.10.10
Server:   srv01.corp.local
Server IP:10.10.10.20
User:     asif

Example password:

Password123!

These are placeholders for a controlled environment.

docs.title: Protocol-First Methodology
docs.text:
Use NetExec as a protocol assessment tool rather than as a single "Active Directory attack command".

Target
  |
  +--> SMB
  |
  +--> LDAP
  |
  +--> WinRM
  |
  +--> MSSQL
  |
  +--> SSH
  |
  +--> Other Supported Protocols

Each protocol answers different questions.

docs.title: SMB
docs.text:
SMB is one of the most useful NetExec protocols for Windows and Active Directory assessment.

It can provide information about:

Hostname

Domain

Operating system

SMB signing

SMBv1

Authentication

Shares

Local access

Administrative access

docs.title: Basic SMB Enumeration
docs.text: nxc smb 10.10.10.20

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text: SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:SRV01) (domain:corp.local) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False)

docs.title: How to Read the Result
docs.text:
Important fields include:

10.10.10.20

SRV01

Windows Server 2022

corp.local

signing:True

SMBv1:False

This provides environmental context before authentication is attempted.

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
Example:

(signing:True)

SMB signing affects the integrity protection of SMB communications and is relevant when assessing certain authentication-relay scenarios.

Do not automatically report:

signing:False

as a complete vulnerability.

Instead determine:

Is signing optional or disabled?

Which system is affected?

Can authentication reach the target?

Is NTLM being used?

Are other relay prerequisites present?

What privilege would the relayed identity have?

docs.title: SMBv1
docs.text:
Example:

(SMBv1:False)

This indicates NetExec did not identify SMBv1 as enabled for the tested service.

If SMBv1 is reported as enabled, investigate why the legacy protocol is still required and validate the actual configuration before reporting.

docs.title: Validate a Password
docs.text: nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!'

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text: SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  [+] corp.local\asif:Password123!

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
[+] indicates that authentication succeeded for the tested SMB authentication path.

It demonstrates:

The account was accepted by the target.

It does not demonstrate:

Local administrator

Domain administrator

Remote code execution

Access to every share

Access to other systems

docs.title: Failed Authentication
docs.text:
Representative output may contain:

[-] corp.local\asif:Password123! STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE

Possible explanations include:

Incorrect password

Incorrect username

Wrong domain

Authentication restrictions

Account state

Authentication method mismatch

Do not immediately retry many passwords.

docs.title: Locked Account
docs.text:
If the result indicates:

STATUS_ACCOUNT_LOCKED_OUT

stop authentication attempts for that account.

Record:

Account

Target

Timestamp

Test performed

and follow the engagement's escalation procedure.

docs.title: Disabled or Restricted Accounts
docs.text:
Authentication errors can also reflect:

Disabled account

Expired account

Logon restrictions

Password expiration

Workstation restrictions

Policy restrictions

A failed SMB login is therefore not always proof that the password itself is incorrect.

docs.title: Local vs Domain Authentication
docs.text:
This distinction is important.

A username may represent:

CORP\asif

or:

SRV01\administrator

Those are different security principals.

docs.title: Domain Authentication
docs.text:
Typical domain credential test:

nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -d corp.local -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!'

Alternatively, depending on the installed version and environment:

nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!' -d corp.local

docs.title: Local Authentication
docs.text:
For a specifically authorised local account, review:

nxc smb --help

for the installed version's local-authentication option.

Do not accidentally interpret a local account as a domain account or vice versa.

docs.title: Administrative Access
docs.text:
A successful administrative result may resemble:

SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  [+] corp.local\asif:Password123! (Pwn3d!)

docs.title: What Pwn3d! Means
docs.text:
NetExec uses (Pwn3d!) to indicate administrative-level access relevant to the tested protocol/host.

This is substantially different from:

[+]

alone.

docs.title: Authentication Only
docs.text:
[+] corp.local\asif:Password123!

Interpretation:

Credential accepted.

docs.title: Administrative Access
docs.text:
[+] corp.local\asif:Password123! (Pwn3d!)

Interpretation:

Credential accepted and administrative-level access identified
for the tested SMB target.

docs.title: What to Do After Pwn3d!
docs.text:
Do not immediately execute commands.

First determine:

Why is the account an administrator?

Is it directly assigned?

Is access inherited through a group?

Is the account supposed to administer this server?

Does the same relationship exist elsewhere?

Does the host contain sensitive administrative sessions?

Does this create an attack path?

Useful next steps may include:

Review group membership

Review BloodHound relationships

Review local administrative design

Document affected host

Validate only the minimum required privilege

docs.title: Enumerate Shares
docs.text: nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!' --shares

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  Share       Permissions
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  -----       -----------
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  ADMIN$      READ
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  C$          READ
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  Public      READ,WRITE
SMB  10.10.10.20  445  SRV01  Software    READ

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Focus on:

Share name

Read access

Write access

Administrative shares

Business purpose

docs.title: Writable Shares
docs.text:
Example:

Public READ,WRITE

A writable share is a candidate, not automatically a vulnerability.

Investigate:

Who is expected to write?

What files are stored there?

Are files executed?

Are files imported by applications?

Does a privileged process consume files?

Can configuration be changed?

Could business data be altered?

docs.title: Readable Shares
docs.text:
Readable shares may expose:

Configuration

Scripts

Documentation

Deployment packages

Backups

Credentials

API keys

Connection strings

But ordinary read access to a public business share may be completely expected.

docs.title: Administrative Shares
docs.text:
Common administrative shares include:

ADMIN$

C$

IPC$

Access to these shares should be interpreted in the context of the account's administrative rights.

docs.title: Enumerating Multiple Targets
docs.text:
nxc smb targets.txt -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!' --shares

This can be useful after the scope and credential-testing plan have been confirmed.

For large environments, prefer targeted enumeration rather than unnecessarily querying every host.

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text:
Shell redirection:

nxc smb targets.txt -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!' --shares | tee nxc-shares.txt

This provides a local assessment artefact.

Be aware that output files may contain:

Usernames

Hostnames

Domains

Credential strings supplied on the command line

Store them according to the engagement's evidence-handling requirements.

docs.title: Target Inventory
docs.text:
Basic SMB enumeration across an authorised target list:

nxc smb targets.txt

This can quickly provide an inventory such as:

DC01    Windows Server
SRV01   Windows Server
WS01    Windows 11
WS02    Windows 11

docs.title: Parse Interesting Hosts
docs.text:
Instead of immediately launching additional actions, first identify categories:

Domain Controllers

Member Servers

Workstations

Legacy Hosts

Systems Without Expected Signing

Systems Accepting the Credential

Systems Where Administrative Access Exists

docs.title: SMB Workflow
docs.text:
SMB Target
    |
    v
Basic Enumeration
    |
    v
Hostname / Domain / OS
    |
    v
Signing / SMB Version
    |
    v
Credential Available?
   / \
 No   Yes
 |     |
 v     v
Stop  Validate
       |
       v
Authentication Successful?
       |
   +---+---+
   |       |
  No      Yes
   |       |
   v       v
Review   Shares
Error      |
           v
      Admin Access?
       /       \
     No         Yes
     |           |
     v           v
 Document    Determine Why

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text:
LDAP is particularly valuable against Active Directory domain controllers.

It can help enumerate:

Users

Groups

Computers

SPNs

Delegation

Directory relationships

Domain configuration

docs.title: Basic LDAP Connection
docs.text: nxc ldap 10.10.10.10

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
Depending on the environment/version, NetExec may identify information such as:

Domain controller

Domain

Hostname

LDAP availability

docs.title: LDAP Authentication
docs.text: nxc ldap 10.10.10.10 -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!'

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Successful LDAP authentication means the account can authenticate to the directory service through the tested path.

This commonly enables directory enumeration according to the permissions granted to that principal.

docs.title: LDAP Help First
docs.text:
Because LDAP enumeration flags can change between NetExec releases, check:

nxc ldap --help

Look for capabilities relevant to:

Users

Groups

Computers

SPNs

Delegation

LDAP queries

BloodHound

docs.title: Why LDAP Is Valuable
docs.text:
SMB may tell you:

Credential works.

LDAP can help answer:

Who is the account?

Which groups is it in?

Which users exist?

Which computers exist?

Which service accounts exist?

Which directory relationships exist?

docs.title: LDAP Enumeration Workflow
docs.text:
Domain Credentials
       |
       v
LDAP Authentication
       |
       v
Users
       |
       v
Groups
       |
       v
Computers
       |
       v
Service Accounts
       |
       v
Delegation
       |
       v
Interesting Relationships
       |
       v
BloodHound / Manual Validation

docs.title: LDAP Result Interpretation
docs.text:
Do not treat directory enumeration output as vulnerabilities by itself.

Examples:

User exists

is inventory.

User has SPN

is a Kerberos assessment candidate.

Account has delegated control over privileged group

may represent a privilege path.

Context determines significance.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Use:

nxc ldap --help

to identify the current version's user-enumeration functionality.

When user information is returned, prioritise attributes such as:

Username

Description

Enabled state

Group membership

Service-account indicators

Password-related configuration

Administrative purpose

docs.title: User Descriptions
docs.text:
Descriptions sometimes contain operational information.

Example:

svc_backup - Backup service account

This is useful context.

If a description contains what appears to be a password or secret, treat it as sensitive evidence and validate carefully rather than immediately using it across the environment.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Group enumeration helps identify:

Administrative groups

Helpdesk groups

Server-management groups

Application administrators

Backup operators

Custom delegated groups

Custom groups can be as security-sensitive as built-in groups.

docs.title: Computers
docs.text:
Computer enumeration helps build:

Domain controller inventory

Server inventory

Workstation inventory

Management infrastructure

Potential attack-path targets

Correlate directory data with actual network reachability rather than assuming every computer object is online.

docs.title: SPNs
docs.text:
Service Principal Names are important for identifying Kerberos service accounts.

Use the current LDAP help:

nxc ldap --help

to identify supported SPN enumeration capabilities.

Interpret SPN results as:

Potential service-account relationship

not:

Password compromised

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
NetExec LDAP capabilities may assist with identifying delegation configuration.

Relevant categories include:

Unconstrained Delegation

Constrained Delegation

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

For deeper analysis use:

  • Active Directory Cheatsheet
  • Unconstrained Delegation
  • Constrained Delegation
  • RBCD

docs.title: BloodHound Through NetExec
docs.text:
Some NetExec versions expose BloodHound-related LDAP functionality.

Check:

nxc ldap --help

before using it.

When available, consider:

Collection method

DNS configuration

Domain controller

Scope

Operational impact

Output location

For full collection and graph interpretation, see the BloodHound Cheatsheet.

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
WinRM provides remote Windows management.

Typical ports:

5985 - HTTP

5986 - HTTPS

docs.title: Basic WinRM Check
docs.text:
nxc winrm 10.10.10.20

This can determine whether the service is available to NetExec.

Network exposure alone does not demonstrate access.

docs.title: WinRM Credential Validation
docs.text: nxc winrm 10.10.10.20 -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!'

docs.title: Representative Outcome
docs.text:
A successful result indicates that the supplied account was accepted for the tested WinRM path.

Depending on version and permissions, NetExec may also identify elevated access.

docs.title: WinRM Interpretation
docs.text:
Separate:

Port Open

Service Recognised

Authentication Successful

Remote Management Authorised

Administrative Privilege

These are different conclusions.

docs.title: What to Check After WinRM Authentication
docs.text:
Determine:

Which group grants access?

Is the account a Remote Management Users member?

Is it an administrator?

Is access expected?

Which systems expose the same management path?

docs.title: WinRM Workflow
docs.text:
Port 5985/5986
      |
      v
WinRM Available
      |
      v
Credential
      |
      v
Authentication
      |
   +--+--+
   |     |
 Fail  Success
   |     |
   v     v
Review  Determine
Error   Privilege
          |
          v
      Is Access Expected?

docs.title: MSSQL
docs.text:
NetExec can also interact with Microsoft SQL Server where supported.

Check:

nxc mssql --help

Basic target:

nxc mssql 10.10.10.30

docs.title: MSSQL Authentication
docs.text:
For an authorised account:

nxc mssql 10.10.10.30 -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!'

Review the installed version's options for:

Windows authentication

Domain authentication

SQL authentication

Encryption

Port selection

docs.title: MSSQL Interpretation
docs.text:
Successful database authentication does not automatically mean:

Database administrator

Operating-system administrator

Remote command execution

Determine:

Database role

Server role

Database permissions

Linked servers

Authentication mode

Service-account context

docs.title: MSSQL Security Questions
docs.text:
After authentication, ask:

Which SQL roles does the account hold?

Which databases are accessible?

Is the account sysadmin?

Are linked servers configured?

What identity runs SQL Server?

Are dangerous server features enabled?

Is the privilege expected?

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Where the installed NetExec version supports SSH:

nxc ssh --help

Basic service check:

nxc ssh 10.10.10.40

Credential validation:

nxc ssh 10.10.10.40 -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!'

docs.title: SSH Interpretation
docs.text:
Successful SSH authentication demonstrates access to the target under the supplied identity.

It does not automatically imply:

root

sudo

administrator

privilege escalation

Follow with normal Linux privilege and configuration assessment.

docs.title: FTP
docs.text:
Where supported:

nxc ftp --help

Basic check:

nxc ftp 10.10.10.50

Authentication:

nxc ftp 10.10.10.50 -u 'asif' -p 'Password123!'

Assess:

Authentication

Readable directories

Writable directories

Data sensitivity

Application relationships

Do not upload or modify files unless required and authorised.

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
Where supported:

nxc rdp --help

Use RDP testing to distinguish:

RDP reachable

Authentication accepted

Interactive logon permitted

These are not equivalent.

docs.title: NTLM Hash Authentication
docs.text:
NetExec supports NTLM hash-based authentication for relevant protocols.

First inspect:

nxc smb --help

for the installed version's hash option.

A common form for authorised SMB testing is:

nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -u 'asif' -H '0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef'

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If authentication succeeds, the tested NTLM credential material was sufficient for authentication to that target through the selected protocol.

This does not mean:

The plaintext password is known.

The account is Domain Admin.

Every host accepts the hash.

docs.title: Hash Validation Strategy
docs.text:
Avoid:

Hash
 |
 v
Entire /16 Network

Prefer:

Hash
 |
 v
Identify Account
 |
 v
Identify Expected Administrative Scope
 |
 v
Choose One Authorised Target
 |
 v
Validate
 |
 v
Determine Privilege
 |
 v
Expand Only If Necessary

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication
docs.text:
NetExec supports Kerberos authentication for relevant protocols.

Check:

nxc smb --help

and:

nxc ldap --help

for the installed version's Kerberos options.

Before troubleshooting NetExec, verify the ticket cache:

klist

Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

docs.title: Kerberos Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Common causes of failure include:

DNS

Clock skew

Incorrect SPN

Incorrect hostname

Missing ticket

Expired ticket

Wrong realm

Ticket cache not exported

Kerberos frequently depends on correct hostnames, so avoid replacing hostnames with IP addresses without understanding the protocol consequences.

docs.title: Password Spraying
docs.text:
NetExec can authenticate many usernames and passwords efficiently.

That does not mean it should be used casually for password spraying.

Before any spray:

Explicitly authorised?

Lockout threshold known?

Observation window known?

Excluded accounts known?

Approved password count known?

Approved rate known?

SOC informed if required?

If any of these are unresolved, do not begin the spray.

docs.title: Account Lockout Policy
docs.text:
From a domain-connected Windows system:

net accounts /domain

Review:

Lockout threshold

Lockout duration

Observation window

Remember that fine-grained password policies may differ from the domain default.

docs.title: Authentication Matrix
docs.text:
Maintain a controlled matrix rather than repeatedly guessing.

Account Target Protocol Result Privilege CORP\asif DC01 SMB Success User CORP\asif SRV01 SMB Success Admin CORP\asif SRV01 WinRM Success Remote access CORP\asif SQL01 MSSQL Fail N/A

This makes the emerging access model much easier to understand.

docs.title: "I Found Lots of Hosts - What Next?"
docs.text:
Classify them.

Hosts
 |
 +--> Domain Controllers
 |
 +--> Servers
 |
 +--> Workstations
 |
 +--> Database Servers
 |
 +--> Management Systems
 |
 +--> Legacy Systems
 |
 +--> Unknown Systems

Then prioritise based on the assessment objective.

docs.title: "My Credential Works Everywhere"
docs.text:
Do not immediately interpret this as a vulnerability.

Determine:

Is the account expected to have broad access?

Is it an administrator?

Is it a service account?

Is it a management account?

Is the same password being reused?

Is access granted through domain groups?

Which systems represent sensitive boundaries?

docs.title: "My Credential Is Admin on Several Hosts"
docs.text:
Build the relationship:

CORP\asif
    |
    +--> Admin on WS01
    |
    +--> Admin on WS02
    |
    +--> Admin on SRV01

Then investigate why.

BloodHound can help model this relationship.

docs.title: Target Selection
docs.text:
Good target selection reduces unnecessary activity.

Prioritise:

Domain controllers

Management servers

Application servers

Database servers

Hosts related to the objective

Hosts indicated by BloodHound

Systems where current credentials have expected relevance

docs.title: Avoid Blind Network-Wide Execution
docs.text:
NetExec makes commands such as this technically easy:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 ...

But assessment quality improves when the operator first understands:

What am I trying to prove?

Why do I need every host?

What will the authentication traffic look like?

Could accounts lock?

Will the SOC interpret this as an incident?

Can I prove the same thing against fewer systems?

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
NetExec provides modules that extend protocol functionality.

List or inspect module functionality using the options provided by the installed version:

nxc smb --help

and the NetExec documentation.

Modules can vary between versions.

docs.title: Module Safety
docs.text:
Before running a module, determine:

What does it query?

Does it write anything?

Does it execute remotely?

Does it access credentials?

Does it modify configuration?

Does it create files?

Does it start services?

Does it generate significant authentication traffic?

Do not treat every enumeration module as passive.

docs.title: Remote Execution
docs.text:
Some NetExec functionality can perform remote command execution when sufficient administrative access exists.

During an assessment, remote execution should only be used when:

It is explicitly within scope.

Administrative access has already been established.

The command is necessary to prove the objective.

The command is low impact.

The expected artefacts are understood.

Cleanup is possible.

Do not execute commands merely because (Pwn3d!) appears.

docs.title: Safer Validation Principle
docs.text:
Prefer:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Establish Permission
   |
   v
Minimal Validation
   |
   v
Stop

over:

Admin Access
   |
   v
Run Many Commands
   |
   v
Dump Everything

docs.title: Credential Access
docs.text:
NetExec may expose functionality related to credential material on systems where administrative rights are available.

Credential extraction is sensitive because it may expose:

Password hashes

Cached credentials

Service secrets

LSA secrets

Domain credentials

Only perform credential-access actions when explicitly required by the assessment and covered by the rules of engagement.

Before doing so, determine whether the same security conclusion can be demonstrated with less sensitive evidence.

docs.title: Credential Evidence Handling
docs.text:
If sensitive credential material is collected:

Minimise collection.

Do not place secrets in screenshots unnecessarily.

Encrypt evidence at rest.

Restrict access.

Follow retention requirements.

Remove temporary artefacts.

Do not publish secrets in reports.

docs.title: Domain Controller Caution
docs.text:
Domain controllers contain highly sensitive directory information.

Do not treat a DC like an ordinary member server.

Before performing any privileged action against a DC, confirm:

Explicit scope

Business justification

Testing method

Potential impact

Data-handling requirements

Cleanup

Escalation contact

docs.title: NetExec and PrivEsc
docs.text:
NetExec can reveal:

Administrative access

Remote-management access

Interesting shares

Host relationships

For host-level privilege escalation candidates use the PrivEsc Explorer.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text: NetExec output is useful evidence, but it must be interpreted.

docs.title: Informational
docs.text:
Example:

Windows Server 2022

This identifies platform information.

It is not a vulnerability.

docs.title: Security Configuration
docs.text:
Example:

signing:False

This may affect a security scenario but requires prerequisite analysis.

docs.title: Authentication Evidence
docs.text:
Example:

[+] CORP\asif:Password123!

This demonstrates successful authentication.

docs.title: Privilege Evidence
docs.text:
Example:

(Pwn3d!)

This indicates administrative-level access identified by NetExec for the tested context.

docs.title: Resource Permission
docs.text:
Example:

Public READ,WRITE

This demonstrates the tested identity's access to the share.

Impact depends on how the share is used.

docs.title: Evidence Template
docs.text:
For an important NetExec result record:

Test ID:
AD-NXC-001

Timestamp:
2026-09-06 14:30 UTC

Tool:
NetExec

Version:
<record installed version>

Source:
Assessment workstation

Target:
SRV01 / 10.10.10.20

Protocol:
SMB

Identity:
CORP\asif

Objective:
Determine whether the standard domain account has administrative
access to SRV01.

Command:
nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -u asif -p <redacted>

Result:
Authentication successful.
Administrative access identified.

Interpretation:
The tested domain account has administrative-level access to the
target through the assessed SMB context.

Further Validation:
Determine which group or local assignment grants the privilege.

Evidence:
Relevant NetExec output captured.

Cleanup:
No modification performed.

docs.title: Report Passwords Safely
docs.text:
Do not include:

nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -u asif -p 'ActualProductionPassword'

in a report.

Prefer:

nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -u asif -p '<REDACTED>'

docs.title: Evidence Screenshot
docs.text:
A good screenshot should show:

Tool

Target

Protocol

Account

Relevant result

Crop or redact unrelated sensitive information.

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
The standard domain account CORP\asif successfully authenticated
to SRV01 over SMB. NetExec identified the account as having
administrative-level access on the server.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The access relationship was independently reviewed against the
account's group membership and the target's administrative
configuration.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
If the account is compromised, the assigned administrative
privilege could provide an attacker with elevated control over
SRV01.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Review the administrative assignment and remove access that is
not required for the account's business function.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Writable Share
docs.text:
Avoid:

The Public share is writable, therefore remote code execution is possible.

Prefer:

The tested domain account has write access to the Public SMB share on SRV01. Review confirmed that the share is intended for collaborative file storage. No evidence was identified that files written to the share are automatically executed by a privileged process. The observation should therefore be evaluated primarily as an access-control and data-integrity issue rather than assumed to provide code execution.

docs.title: [+] Means Domain Admin
docs.text:
Incorrect.

It means authentication succeeded.

docs.title: Pwn3d! Means Domain Admin
docs.text:
Incorrect.

It indicates administrative-level access to the tested host/protocol context.

The account may only be a local administrator on one machine.

docs.title: Writable Share Means RCE
docs.text:
Incorrect.

A writable share only proves write access.

Execution requires additional conditions.

docs.title: SMB Signing Disabled Means Immediate Compromise
docs.text:
Incorrect.

It may satisfy one prerequisite for certain relay scenarios.

Other prerequisites must still exist.

docs.title: Open WinRM Means Remote Shell
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Authentication and authorisation must also succeed.

docs.title: LDAP Access Means Elevated Directory Rights
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Standard domain users commonly have substantial read access to directory information.

docs.title: DNS Problems
docs.text:
Symptoms:

Hostname cannot be resolved

Kerberos fails

LDAP behaves unexpectedly

Domain name incorrect

Check:

getent hosts dc01.corp.local

dig dc01.corp.local

cat /etc/resolv.conf

docs.title: Kerberos Clock Skew
docs.text:
Check:

date

Kerberos authentication can fail when the client and KDC clocks differ significantly.

docs.title: Wrong Domain
docs.text:
Symptoms may include:

STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE

Unexpected local authentication

LDAP bind failure

Verify:

Domain name

Username format

Target hostname

Domain controller

docs.title: SMB Works but LDAP Fails
docs.text:
Investigate:

Are you targeting a domain controller?

Is LDAP reachable?

Are credentials supplied correctly?

Is the domain correct?

Does the environment require LDAP protections?

Is DNS correct?

docs.title: IP Works but Hostname Fails
docs.text:
Likely areas:

DNS

/etc/hosts

Search domain

Resolver configuration

Kerberos especially benefits from correct hostname resolution.

docs.title: Hostname Works but IP Fails with Kerberos
docs.text:
This can be expected because Kerberos service identities are tied to SPNs and hostnames.

Use the correct DNS names when performing Kerberos-based testing.

docs.title: Old NetExec Command Fails
docs.text:
First:

nxc --version

Then:

nxc <protocol> --help

Do not assume old CrackMapExec syntax remains valid.

docs.title: NetExec vs CrackMapExec
docs.text:
NetExec evolved from the CrackMapExec ecosystem.

As a result, older resources may use:

crackmapexec

or:

cme

where modern workflows use:

nxc

Do not mechanically replace the executable name in old commands. Flags and functionality may also have changed.

docs.title: STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Bad username

Bad password

Wrong domain

Authentication restriction

docs.title: STATUS_ACCOUNT_LOCKED_OUT
docs.text:
Meaning:

Account is locked.

Action:

Stop authentication attempts.

docs.title: STATUS_ACCOUNT_DISABLED
docs.text:
Meaning:

Account is disabled.

docs.title: STATUS_PASSWORD_EXPIRED
docs.text:
Meaning:

Password has expired.

Do not automatically attempt to change the password during an assessment.

docs.title: STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED
docs.text:
Authentication may have succeeded, but the requested operation is not permitted.

Separate:

Authentication

from:

Authorisation

docs.title: Authentication vs Authorisation
docs.text:
This distinction is central to NetExec.

Authentication

"Who are you?"
       |
       v
Credential accepted


Authorisation

"What are you allowed to do?"
       |
       v
Shares / Admin / WinRM / SQL / etc.

A successful login does not imply permission to perform every operation.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
Before running a NetExec command ask:

How many targets?

How many accounts?

How many authentication attempts?

Does this query modify anything?

Could it trigger lockout?

Could it trigger EDR?

Could it create a service?

Could it access sensitive credentials?

Could it affect production?

Do I actually need this action?

docs.title: Rate and Scope Discipline
docs.text:
Prefer:

One Account
    |
    v
One Target
    |
    v
One Protocol
    |
    v
Understand Result
    |
    v
Expand

rather than:

Many Accounts
     x
Many Passwords
     x
Entire Network

docs.title: Detection Perspective
docs.text:
NetExec activity can generate telemetry across:

Windows Security logs

Domain-controller authentication logs

SMB logs

PowerShell logs

WinRM logs

SQL logs

EDR

Network monitoring

SIEM

docs.title: Authentication Events
docs.text:
Useful Windows events may include:

Event ID General Meaning 4624 Successful logon 4625 Failed logon 4648 Explicit credentials 4672 Special privileges 4768 Kerberos TGT request 4769 Kerberos service ticket 4771 Kerberos preauthentication failure 4776 NTLM credential validation

Exact telemetry depends on:

Protocol

Authentication method

Audit configuration

Target role

Collection configuration

docs.title: Purple Team Validation
docs.text:
NetExec can also be useful in controlled purple team exercises.

Example objective:

Validate whether repeated SMB authentication attempts are visible
to the SOC.

Record:

Source

Target

Account

Protocol

Timestamp

Number of attempts

Expected telemetry

Observed telemetry

Detection

SOC response

docs.title: Detection Questions
docs.text:
After a controlled NetExec test ask:

Was authentication visible?

Was the source IP recorded?

Was the username recorded?

Was the target visible?

Was the authentication method visible?

Was administrative access visible?

Did an alert fire?

Could analysts reconstruct the activity?

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
If a privilege or access issue is remediated, repeat the same narrow validation.

Example:

Before:

CORP\asif
   |
   v
SRV01
   |
   v
(Pwn3d!)


Remediation:

Unnecessary local administrator assignment removed.


Retest:

nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -u asif -p '<REDACTED>'


Expected:

Authentication may still succeed.

Administrative indicator should no longer be present.

This is stronger than merely checking that a configuration change was made.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Scope confirmed
  • [ ] Target list confirmed
  • [ ] Accounts authorised for testing
  • [ ] Lockout policy understood
  • [ ] Tool version recorded
  • [ ] Protocol help reviewed
  • [ ] DNS configured
  • [ ] Time synchronisation checked where Kerberos is used

docs.title: SMB
docs.text:
• [ ] Basic SMB information collected
  • [ ] Hostname recorded
  • [ ] Domain recorded
  • [ ] OS information recorded
  • [ ] SMB signing reviewed
  • [ ] SMBv1 reviewed
  • [ ] Authentication validated narrowly
  • [ ] Shares enumerated where relevant
  • [ ] Read/write permissions interpreted
  • [ ] Administrative access distinguished from authentication

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text:
• [ ] Domain controller identified
  • [ ] LDAP authentication validated
  • [ ] Users reviewed
  • [ ] Groups reviewed
  • [ ] Computers reviewed
  • [ ] SPNs considered
  • [ ] Delegation considered
  • [ ] BloodHound considered
  • [ ] Results treated as relationships rather than automatic findings

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
• [ ] WinRM availability reviewed
  • [ ] Authentication tested where relevant
  • [ ] Remote-management privilege distinguished from port exposure
  • [ ] Group-derived access understood

docs.title: MSSQL
docs.text:
• [ ] SQL service identified
  • [ ] Authentication mode understood
  • [ ] Account privilege reviewed
  • [ ] SQL roles considered
  • [ ] Linked servers considered where relevant
  • [ ] OS privilege not assumed from database authentication

docs.title: Other Protocols
docs.text:
• [ ] SSH considered where applicable
  • [ ] FTP considered where applicable
  • [ ] RDP considered where applicable
  • [ ] Installed NetExec protocol support confirmed

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
• [ ] Password testing kept narrow
  • [ ] Hash testing kept narrow
  • [ ] Kerberos context understood
  • [ ] Password spraying separately authorised
  • [ ] Lockout errors acted on immediately
  • [ ] Sensitive credentials protected

docs.title: Privilege
docs.text:
• [ ] [+] interpreted as authentication only
  • [ ] (Pwn3d!) interpreted in host context
  • [ ] Administrative access independently understood
  • [ ] Group/policy source investigated
  • [ ] Attack-path relevance considered

docs.title: Shares
docs.text:
• [ ] Read access reviewed
  • [ ] Write access reviewed
  • [ ] Business purpose understood
  • [ ] Sensitive content reviewed appropriately
  • [ ] Writable share not automatically labelled RCE
  • [ ] Privileged consumers considered

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• [ ] No unnecessary subnet-wide authentication
  • [ ] No unnecessary remote execution
  • [ ] No unnecessary credential extraction
  • [ ] No unnecessary file modification
  • [ ] Domain-controller actions treated carefully
  • [ ] Stop conditions understood

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Timestamp recorded
  • [ ] Source recorded
  • [ ] Target recorded
  • [ ] Protocol recorded
  • [ ] Account recorded
  • [ ] NetExec version recorded
  • [ ] Command recorded
  • [ ] Passwords redacted
  • [ ] Relevant output captured
  • [ ] Interpretation documented

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• [ ] Authentication separated from authorisation
  • [ ] Candidate separated from confirmed finding
  • [ ] Root cause identified
  • [ ] Business/security impact established
  • [ ] Attack-path context included where relevant
  • [ ] Remediation addresses privilege/access source
  • [ ] Retest procedure documented

Use NetExec to answer a question

Start with a specific objective such as "Does this credential authenticate to SRV01?", "Which shares can this account access?" or "Does this user have administrative access?". This produces cleaner evidence than running every available option against every target.

Authentication is not authorisation

[+] proves that authentication succeeded for the tested protocol. It does not by itself demonstrate administrative privilege. Interpret the access available after authentication before drawing a security conclusion.

Do not let automation replace analysis

NetExec can query many systems quickly, but the important part of an assessment is understanding why access exists, whether it is expected, what security boundary it crosses and what the evidence actually proves.
