Flow:

localhost:8443
      |
      v
SSH Tunnel
      |
      v
10.10.20.10:443

Then:

curl https://127.0.0.1:8443/

Certificate hostname mismatches may occur because the connection uses localhost.

docs.title: SSH Remote Port Forward
docs.text:
General form:

ssh -R REMOTE_PORT:DESTINATION:DESTINATION_PORT user@ssh-server

Example for a controlled lab service:

ssh -R 8080:127.0.0.1:8000 user@jump.example.com

Review SSH server forwarding policy before use.

docs.title: SSH Dynamic SOCKS Proxy
docs.text:
ssh -D 1080 user@pivot.example.com

This creates a local SOCKS proxy.

Concept:

Application
    |
    v
127.0.0.1:1080
    |
    v
SSH
    |
    v
Pivot
    |
    v
Internal Destination

docs.title: ProxyChains
docs.text:
Configuration commonly resides at:

/etc/proxychains4.conf

Example SOCKS entry:

socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

Then, for tools that work correctly through the proxy:

proxychains4 curl http://10.10.20.10/

Not every protocol or scanning mode works reliably through SOCKS.

docs.title: Nmap Through Proxy
docs.text:
Full SYN scanning does not operate through a normal SOCKS proxy in the same way as direct raw-packet scanning.

For limited TCP connect testing:

proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -n -p 80,443 10.10.20.10

Expect limitations and slower performance.

docs.title: Chisel
docs.text:
Project:

Chisel

Chisel can transport connections over HTTP using an SSH-secured tunnel.

Typical assessment use cases include:

Port Forwarding
SOCKS Proxying
Traversing Restricted Network Paths

Use the current project documentation for exact client/server syntax because options can change between versions.

docs.title: Ligolo-ng
docs.text:
Project:

Ligolo-ng

Ligolo-ng provides network tunnelling using a TUN-based approach.

Conceptually:

Tester
  |
  v
Ligolo Proxy
  |
  v
Agent
  |
  v
Internal Network

A TUN approach can make many tools behave more naturally than application-level SOCKS proxying.

Use the project's current documentation for exact deployment and route configuration.

docs.title: socat
docs.text:
TCP listener forwarding to a controlled service:

socat TCP-LISTEN:8080,fork TCP:127.0.0.1:8000

Concept:

:8080
  |
  v
socat
  |
  v
127.0.0.1:8000

Be careful about listener binding.

A listener exposed on all interfaces can unintentionally expose an internal service to other networks.

docs.title: SSH Tunnels - Security Considerations
docs.text:
Before creating a tunnel determine:

Who Can Connect to the Listener?
Where Does It Forward?
Does It Cross a Segmentation Boundary?
Does It Expose an Internal Service?
Will It Persist?
How Will It Be Removed?

Prefer loopback listeners where remote access is unnecessary.

docs.title: Linux IP Forwarding
docs.text:
Check:

sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward

or:

cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward

Do not enable forwarding on production systems merely for testing without explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Windows IP Forwarding
docs.text:
Inspect routing-related configuration rather than enabling forwarding by default.

Routing behaviour may also be provided by:

RRAS
VPN Software
Hyper-V
Containers
Security Products
Third-Party Networking Software

docs.title: Network Namespaces - Linux
docs.text:
List:

ip netns list

Interfaces can also exist in:

Containers
Network Namespaces
Virtual Machines
VPNs

so the default namespace may not show every relevant network path.

docs.title: VPN Interfaces
docs.text:
Linux:

ip addr

Look for interfaces such as:

tun0
tap0
wg0
ppp0

Windows:

Get-NetAdapter

docs.title: WireGuard
docs.text:
Linux:

wg show

Routes still matter:

ip route

docs.title: Docker Networking
docs.text:
Networks:

docker network ls

Inspect:

docker network inspect bridge

Container interfaces and routes can expose additional network paths.

Only query Docker where authorised and accessible.

docs.title: Kubernetes Networking
docs.text:
Basic context:

kubectl cluster-info

Services:

kubectl get services -A

Pods:

kubectl get pods -A -o wide

Network assessment of Kubernetes should use dedicated container/Kubernetes methodology rather than relying solely on host networking commands.

docs.title: Cloud Metadata Addresses
docs.text:
A commonly used link-local address is:

169.254.169.254

Cloud providers use metadata services differently and modern deployments often require additional authentication or request controls.

Do not query metadata endpoints outside explicit scope.

docs.title: Loopback Services
docs.text:
Linux:

ss -ltnp

Look for:

127.0.0.1
::1

Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen |
    Where-Object {
        $_.LocalAddress -eq '127.0.0.1' -or
        $_.LocalAddress -eq '::1'
    }

A loopback-only service may still matter after obtaining authorised local access or through an approved tunnel.

docs.title: Binding Addresses
docs.text:
Important distinction:

127.0.0.1:8080

means IPv4 loopback only.

0.0.0.0:8080

generally means all IPv4 interfaces.

[::]:8080

generally means all IPv6 interfaces and can have platform-specific dual-stack behaviour.

docs.title: Network Exposure Model
docs.text:
Process
   |
   v
Socket
   |
   v
Bind Address
   |
   v
Firewall
   |
   v
Routing
   |
   v
Network ACL
   |
   v
Remote Client

An open local socket does not automatically mean it is remotely reachable.

docs.title: Proxy Awareness
docs.text:
When testing HTTP connectivity consider:

Application Proxy
System Proxy
Environment Proxy
Transparent Proxy
Security Gateway
Direct Route

The path observed by curl may differ from the path used by another application.

docs.title: HTTP Proxy with curl
docs.text:
curl -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 https://example.com/

SOCKS5:

curl --socks5 127.0.0.1:1080 https://example.com/

SOCKS with proxy-side DNS resolution:

curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 https://example.com/

The DNS distinction is important during pivoting.

docs.title: DNS Through a Proxy
docs.text:
A common mistake is:

Application traffic -> Proxy
DNS lookup -> Local machine

This can:

Fail to resolve internal names
Leak DNS queries
Produce misleading results

Use proxy-aware DNS resolution where supported.

docs.title: HTTPX
docs.text:
Project:

httpx

Probe hosts:

httpx -l hosts.txt

Useful information:

httpx -l hosts.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect

Save:

httpx -l hosts.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect -o alive.txt

Use only against authorised targets.

docs.title: Subdomain to Alive Host Workflow
docs.text:
Subdomain Enumeration
        |
        v
DNS Resolution
        |
        v
HTTP Probe
        |
        v
Alive Web Services

Example:

subfinder -d example.com -silent > subdomains.txt

Then:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -silent -status-code -title -tech-detect -o alive.txt

This confirms responsive HTTP/HTTPS services, not whether the host itself is "alive" for every protocol.

docs.title: Nmap vs httpx
docs.text:
Nmap
 |
 +--> Network ports
 +--> Service detection
 +--> TCP / UDP

httpx
 |
 +--> HTTP / HTTPS
 +--> Status
 +--> Titles
 +--> Web technologies

They complement rather than replace one another.

docs.title: Curl vs Test-NetConnection
docs.text:
Test-NetConnection
       |
       +--> Can TCP connection be established?

curl / Invoke-WebRequest
       |
       +--> Does the application protocol work?

For example:

Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443

may succeed while:

Invoke-WebRequest https://example.com/

fails because of:

TLS
Proxy
HTTP Authentication
Application Behaviour
Certificate Validation

docs.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Use layers:

Interface
   |
   v
Address
   |
   v
Route
   |
   v
DNS
   |
   v
TCP
   |
   v
TLS
   |
   v
Application

Example:

ip addr
ip route
dig example.com
nc -vz example.com 443
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com
curl -v https://example.com/

docs.title: Windows Connectivity Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute
Resolve-DnsName example.com
Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443
Invoke-WebRequest https://example.com/

docs.title: Linux Connectivity Troubleshooting
docs.text:
ip addr
ip route
ip neigh
cat /etc/resolv.conf
dig example.com
ping -c 4 example.com
traceroute example.com
nc -vz example.com 443
curl -v https://example.com/

docs.title: Network Segmentation Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Identify Source Zone
        |
        v
Identify Destination Zone
        |
        v
Define Expected Policy
        |
        v
Test Required Ports
        |
        v
Compare Expected vs Actual
        |
        v
Record Evidence

Avoid unnecessary full-port scans where the assessment objective can be answered with specific connectivity tests.

docs.title: Internal Network Enumeration
docs.text:
After obtaining authorised access to an internal host, start with local information:

Linux:

ip addr
ip route
ip neigh
ss -tulpn
cat /etc/resolv.conf

Windows:

Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute
Get-NetNeighbor
Get-NetTCPConnection
Get-DnsClientServerAddress

This often reveals:

Internal Subnets
Gateways
DNS Servers
Domain Controllers
Management Networks
VPN Networks
Local Services
Existing Connections

without immediately scanning the network.

docs.title: Existing Connections
docs.text:
Linux:

ss -tanp

Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established

Existing connections can reveal important infrastructure without generating new scan traffic.

docs.title: Network Shares
docs.text:
Windows:

net use

PowerShell:

Get-SmbMapping

Linux mounts:

mount

NFS:

mount -t nfs

Existing mounts can reveal trusted infrastructure.

docs.title: Hosts File
docs.text:
Linux:

cat /etc/hosts

Windows:

Get-Content "$env:WINDIR\System32\drivers\etc\hosts"

Hosts-file entries may reveal:

Internal Names
Development Systems
Legacy Infrastructure
Overrides

docs.title: Linux Network Configuration Files
docs.text:
Depending on distribution:

/etc/network/interfaces
/etc/netplan/
/etc/NetworkManager/
/etc/systemd/network/
/etc/resolv.conf

Do not modify network configuration during enumeration.

docs.title: Windows Network Configuration
docs.text:
Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetAdapter
Get-NetIPAddress
Get-NetRoute
Get-DnsClientServerAddress

docs.title: Active Directory Networking
docs.text:
Important protocols commonly include:

Port Protocol 53 DNS 88 Kerberos 135 RPC Endpoint Mapper 389 LDAP 445 SMB 464 Kerberos password change 636 LDAPS 3268 Global Catalog 3269 Global Catalog TLS 5985 WinRM HTTP 5986 WinRM HTTPS

RPC also uses dynamic ports.

Do not assume AD communication is limited to this table.

docs.title: Domain Controller Discovery
docs.text:
Windows:

nltest /dsgetdc:example.local

List:

nltest /dclist:example.local

DNS:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

Kerberos:

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.local

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
Nmap:

nmap -p 445 --script smb2-security-mode 10.10.10.10

Signing configuration is especially important when assessing NTLM relay exposure.

See the dedicated Active Directory and SMB notes for deeper analysis.

docs.title: LDAP TLS
docs.text:
Test LDAPS:

openssl s_client -connect dc01.example.local:636 -servername dc01.example.local

LDAP StartTLS can be assessed using appropriate LDAP tooling.

Certificate presence alone does not prove that all LDAP clients are protected.

docs.title: Proxy Protocol Limitations
docs.text:
Not all protocols work through all proxies.

SOCKS
 |
 +--> TCP applications generally work well
 |
 +--> UDP support depends on tool/proxy
 |
 +--> Raw packets generally do not work
 |
 +--> SYN scanning does not behave like direct scanning

Choose tooling based on the actual transport path.

docs.title: Network Performance
docs.text:
Linux interface statistics:

ip -s link

Socket summary:

ss -s

Windows adapter statistics:

Get-NetAdapterStatistics

docs.title: Listening Service Review
docs.text:
Linux:

ss -ltnp

Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

For every unexpected listener determine:

Process
   |
   v
Service
   |
   v
Bind Address
   |
   v
Firewall Exposure
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Business Requirement

docs.title: External Exposure vs Internal Exposure
docs.text:
Listening on 0.0.0.0
        |
        v
Host Firewall
        |
        v
Network Firewall
        |
        v
NAT / Load Balancer
        |
        v
Internet

A service bound to all interfaces is not necessarily Internet exposed.

Validate the complete path.

docs.title: NAT
docs.text:
Concept:

Private Host
    |
    v
NAT Gateway
    |
    v
Public Address

Common forms:

SNAT
DNAT
PAT

NAT is not itself a security control equivalent to a firewall.

docs.title: Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Concept:

Listener A
    |
    v
Forwarder
    |
    v
Destination B

Port forwarding can be legitimate:

Load Balancing
Reverse Proxy
SSH Administration
Containers
Development

or security-sensitive when it crosses intended network boundaries.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy
docs.text:
Concept:

Client
   |
   v
Reverse Proxy
   |
   +--> Application 1
   +--> Application 2
   +--> Application 3

Common technologies include:

Nginx
Apache
HAProxy
Traefik
IIS ARR
Cloud Load Balancers

When testing a reverse proxy, distinguish proxy behaviour from backend behaviour.

docs.title: Forward Proxy
docs.text:
Client
   |
   v
Forward Proxy
   |
   v
Internet / Destination

Forward proxies can enforce:

Authentication
URL Filtering
TLS Inspection
Logging
Network Egress Policy

docs.title: Egress Testing
docs.text:
Define exactly what should be allowed.

Example:

Endpoint
   |
   v
TCP 443
   |
   v
Approved Proxy
   |
   v
Internet

Testing should answer questions such as:

Can the host connect directly?
Must it use the proxy?
Which ports are allowed?
Which destinations are allowed?
Is DNS restricted?

Avoid unnecessary external callbacks when a simple controlled connectivity test answers the question.

docs.title: HTTP Connectivity Test
docs.text:
Linux:

curl -I https://example.com/

Windows:

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://example.com/' -Method Head

TCP-only:

Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443

These test different layers.

docs.title: Network Evidence
docs.text:
For every network finding record:

Source Host
Source IP
Destination Host
Destination IP
Protocol
Port
Timestamp
Command
Result
Expected Policy
Actual Policy

docs.title: Example Segmentation Finding
docs.text:
Weak:

Port 445 is open.

Better:

A standard-user workstation in the User VLAN was able to
establish an SMB connection to TCP/445 on a server in the
restricted management network, despite the documented
segmentation policy requiring SMB traffic between these
zones to be blocked.

docs.title: Example Listener Finding
docs.text:
Weak:

Port 8080 is listening.

Better:

The administrative web service listens on 0.0.0.0:8080
and is reachable from the standard user network without
an intermediate access-control boundary.

Then validate authentication and business requirements before assigning severity.

docs.title: Example DNS Finding
docs.text:
Weak:

DNS zone transfer works.

Better:

The authoritative DNS server permitted an unauthenticated
AXFR request for the assessed zone from the testing network,
disclosing the zone's host and service records.

docs.title: Example Firewall Finding
docs.text:
Weak:

Firewall allows traffic.

Better:

The assessed endpoint was able to establish direct outbound
TCP/443 connections to Internet destinations despite the
documented requirement that Internet traffic traverse the
organisation's authenticated web proxy.

docs.text:

  • [ ] Identify interfaces

  • [ ] HTTPS
  • [ ] Redirects
  • [ ] Headers

  • [ ] SNI
  • [ ] Proxy path
  • [ ] HTTP technology probing where authorised

docs.title: Windows / AD
docs.text:

  • [ ] Kerberos
  • [ ] LDAP
  • [ ] LDAPS
  • [ ] SMB
  • [ ] RPC
  • [ ] Global Catalog
  • [ ] WinRM
  • [ ] RDP where relevant
  • [ ] SMB signing where relevant

docs.title: Segmentation
docs.text:
• [ ] Define source zone
  • [ ] Define destination zone
  • [ ] Define expected policy
  • [ ] Test required protocols
  • [ ] Record actual result
  • [ ] Compare against architecture
  • [ ] Avoid unnecessary broad scanning

docs.title: Traffic Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Identify correct interface
  • [ ] Apply targeted capture filters
  • [ ] Store PCAP securely
  • [ ] Minimise sensitive-data collection
  • [ ] Use display filters
  • [ ] Remove captures when no longer required

docs.text:
• [ ] Explicitly confirm pivoting is in scope
  • [ ] Identify reachable subnet
  • [ ] Choose routing/proxying/forwarding model

  • [ ] Record tunnel configuration
  • [ ] Avoid persistence unless explicitly required

docs.text:
• [ ] Record timestamp
  • [ ] Record source
  • [ ] Record destination
  • [ ] Record protocol
  • [ ] Record port

  • [ ] Capture relevant output
  • [ ] Record expected behaviour
  • [ ] Record actual behaviour

docs.title: Quick Troubleshooting Checklist
docs.text:
When a service cannot be reached:

1. Is the local interface up?
2. Does the host have the expected IP?
3. Is there a route?
4. Does DNS resolve correctly?
5. Is the destination reachable?
6. Is the TCP/UDP port reachable?
7. Is TLS working?
8. Is the application responding?
9. Is a proxy required?
10. Is a firewall or ACL blocking the path?

Linux:

ip addr
ip route
dig example.com
ping -c 4 example.com
nc -vz example.com 443
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com
curl -v https://example.com/

Windows:

Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute
Resolve-DnsName example.com
Test-Connection example.com
Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443
Invoke-WebRequest https://example.com/

docs.title: Quick Pentest Workflow
docs.text:
Scope
  |
  v
Local Network Context
  |
  v
Passive Discovery
  |
  v
Host Discovery
  |
  v
Port Discovery
  |
  v
Service Identification
  |
  v
Protocol Enumeration
  |
  v
Segmentation Testing
  |
  v
Application Testing
  |
  v
Evidence

Useful initial Linux commands:

ip addr
ip route
ip neigh
cat /etc/resolv.conf
ss -tulpn

Then, for an authorised target:

nmap -Pn -p- 10.10.10.10 -oA all-ports

Follow with targeted service enumeration:

nmap -Pn -sC -sV -p 22,80,443,445 10.10.10.10 -oA services

docs.title: Do Not Overreport
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

Port 445 Open
Port 3389 Open
WinRM Enabled
IPv6 Enabled
ICMP Allowed
DNS Reachable
Internal Route Exists
HTTP Service Uses Port 8080
Service Bound to 0.0.0.0

Instead determine:

Is It Reachable?
      |
      v
From Where?
      |
      v
Should It Be Reachable?
      |
      v
What Authentication Exists?
      |
      v
What Security Boundary Is Affected?

docs.title: Safe Validation Model
docs.text:
Prefer:

Read Local Configuration
        |
        v
Review Existing Connections
        |
        v
Test Specific Connectivity
        |
        v
Enumerate Required Service
        |
        v
Document Result

before:

Broad Scanning
High-Rate Scanning
Intrusive NSE Scripts
Protocol Mutation
Service Exploitation
Network Reconfiguration

docs.title: Network Testing Model
docs.text:
A network finding generally involves more than an open port.

Source
  |
  v
Route
  |
  v
Firewall / ACL
  |
  v
Destination
  |
  v
Service
  |
  v
Authentication
  |
  v
Application

For segmentation:

Source Zone
    |
    v
Expected Restriction
    |
    v
Unexpected Reachability
    |
    v
Security Impact

For exposed services:

Service
   |
   v
Bind Address
   |
   v
Firewall
   |
   v
Reachability
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Impact

For pivoting:

Tester
   |
   v
Authorised Pivot
   |
   v
Previously Unreachable Network
   |
   v
Approved Target

The key distinction is:

Network Reachability
       !=
Vulnerability

Reachability becomes security-relevant when it violates the intended network or trust boundary.

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
For local network awareness:

ip addr
ip route
ip neigh
ss -tulpn
cat /etc/resolv.conf

On Windows:

Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute
Get-NetNeighbor
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen
Get-DnsClientServerAddress

For connectivity:

DNS
 |
 v
Route
 |
 v
TCP / UDP
 |
 v
TLS
 |
 v
Application

Test each layer independently.

For discovery:

Host
 |
 v
Port
 |
 v
Protocol
 |
 v
Service
 |
 v
Configuration
 |
 v
Security Boundary

For internal assessments, begin with information already available from the host before generating additional network traffic.

For segmentation assessments:

Expected
   |
   v
Test
   |
   v
Actual
   |
   v
Difference
   |
   v
Impact

For pivoting:

Reachability
    |
    v
Authorised Pivot
    |
    v
Controlled Tunnel
    |
    v
Approved Destination
    |
    v
Cleanup

The goal is not simply to discover as many open ports as possible.

The goal is to understand:

What can communicate?
Why can it communicate?
Should it communicate?
What security boundary exists?
Can that boundary be crossed?

That turns basic network enumeration into meaningful security assessment.

docs.title: Nmap Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Nmap is one of the primary tools used during network reconnaissance and security assessments.

It can help answer:

Which hosts are reachable?

Which TCP ports are exposed?

Which UDP services are available?

What services appear to be listening?

Which versions are reported?

Which network paths are filtered?

Which protocols require deeper investigation?

A good Nmap workflow is not:

nmap <target>

followed immediately by:

Start testing everything.

Instead:

Define Scope
    |
    v
Host Discovery
    |
    v
Port Discovery
    |
    v
Service Identification
    |
    v
Focused Enumeration
    |
    v
Manual Validation
    |
    v
Interpret Exposure
    |
    v
Capture Evidence

Authorised Security Testing

Only scan systems and networks that you are explicitly authorised to assess. Network scanning can generate significant traffic, trigger monitoring systems, affect fragile services, and violate assessment rules if performed outside the agreed scope.

docs.text:
A practical external or internal assessment often follows:

Target

  |

  |

Document Exposure

docs.text:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install nmap

nmap --version

docs.title: Help

Manual:

man nmap

Always check the locally installed version when relying on less common options or NSE behaviour.

docs.title: Target Formats
docs.text:
Single IP:

nmap 192.168.1.10

Hostname:

nmap server.example.com

Multiple targets:

nmap 192.168.1.10 192.168.1.20

CIDR:

nmap 192.168.1.0/24

Range:

nmap 192.168.1.10-50

Input file:

nmap -iL targets.txt

docs.title: Excluding Targets
docs.text:
Exclude one host:

nmap 192.168.1.0/24 --exclude 192.168.1.1

Exclude multiple:

nmap 192.168.1.0/24 --exclude 192.168.1.1,192.168.1.254

Exclude from file:

nmap 192.168.1.0/24 --excludefile exclude.txt

docs.title: Scope First
docs.text:
Before scanning:

[ ] IP range authorised
[ ] Hostnames authorised
[ ] Cloud assets included if relevant
[ ] Third-party systems excluded
[ ] Production restrictions understood
[ ] Scan windows understood
[ ] Rate restrictions understood
[ ] UDP testing permitted
[ ] NSE restrictions understood

docs.title: Host Discovery
docs.text:
Before performing large port scans, determine which systems appear reachable.

Basic discovery:

nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

This performs host discovery without a port scan.

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
Nmap scan report for 192.168.1.10
Host is up (0.0021s latency).

Nmap scan report for 192.168.1.20
Host is up (0.0034s latency).

Interpretation:

Nmap received sufficient responses to classify the hosts as up.

It does not prove:

Other hosts are definitely offline.

docs.title: Why Host Discovery Can Miss Systems
docs.text:
Discovery may be affected by:

Firewall rules

ICMP filtering

Network segmentation

Host firewall

Cloud security groups

Routing

Probe type

Network ACLs

A system that appears down may simply not respond to the discovery probes used.

docs.title: Skip Host Discovery
docs.text:
When you already know the target exists or discovery probes are blocked:

nmap -Pn 192.168.1.10

-Pn tells Nmap to treat the target as online and proceed with scanning.

Use this carefully across large ranges because every address will be treated as a scan target.

docs.title: ARP Discovery
docs.text:
On a local Ethernet network, Nmap can use ARP discovery.

A local-network scan may identify hosts even when ICMP is filtered.

This is one reason internal discovery behaviour can differ from remote scanning.

docs.title: TCP SYN Discovery
docs.text:
Host discovery can also use TCP probes.

For example:

nmap -PS80,443 192.168.1.0/24

This can be useful when ICMP-based discovery is restricted.

docs.title: TCP ACK Discovery
docs.text:
nmap -PA80,443 192.168.1.0/24

The usefulness depends on network architecture and filtering.

docs.title: ICMP Echo Discovery
docs.text:
nmap -PE 192.168.1.0/24

Do not assume lack of ICMP response means the system does not exist.

docs.title: Basic TCP Scan
docs.text:
nmap 192.168.1.10

By default, Nmap scans a selection of commonly used TCP ports.

docs.title: SYN Scan
docs.text:
With suitable privileges:

sudo nmap -sS 192.168.1.10

SYN scanning is commonly used for TCP port discovery.

docs.title: TCP Connect Scan
docs.text:
nmap -sT 192.168.1.10

A TCP connect scan completes the operating system's normal TCP connection process.

This is useful when raw packet privileges are unavailable.

docs.title: SYN vs Connect
docs.text:
Conceptually:

SYN Scan

SYN
 |
 v
Target
 |
 +--> SYN/ACK -> Open
 |
 +--> RST     -> Closed

A connect scan uses the host operating system's normal TCP connection mechanism.

docs.title: Specific Port
docs.text:
nmap -p 443 192.168.1.10

Multiple:

nmap -p 22,80,443,445,3389 192.168.1.10

Range:

nmap -p 1-1000 192.168.1.10

docs.title: All TCP Ports
docs.text:
nmap -p- 192.168.1.10

This scans TCP ports:

1-65535

docs.title: Why Full-Port Scanning Matters
docs.text:
A default Nmap scan does not test every TCP port.

Applications may listen on:

8080

8443

8888

9000

9443

10000

Custom high ports

A common mistake is:

Default Scan
     |
     v
No Interesting Ports
     |
     v
Assume No Services

A better workflow is:

Initial Scan
     |
     v
Full TCP Port Discovery
     |
     v
Focused Service Enumeration

docs.title: Fast Scan
docs.text:
nmap -F 192.168.1.10

This scans fewer ports than the default selection.

Useful for:

Quick triage

Large networks

Initial discovery

It is not a replacement for comprehensive port discovery where that is required.

docs.title: Top Ports
docs.text:
nmap --top-ports 100 192.168.1.10

or:

nmap --top-ports 1000 192.168.1.10

Useful when balancing:

Coverage

Time

Network impact

docs.title: Open Ports Only
docs.text:
nmap --open 192.168.1.10

This reduces output clutter by focusing on open or potentially open ports.

docs.title: Port States
docs.text:
Nmap can report states such as:

open

closed

filtered

unfiltered

open|filtered

closed|filtered

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
Example:

443/tcp open https

Generally means:

A service accepted or responded to the probe in a way consistent
with an open port.

docs.title: Closed
docs.text:
Example:

443/tcp closed https

Generally means:

The target is reachable, but no service is accepting connections
on that port.

docs.title: Filtered
docs.text:
Example:

445/tcp filtered microsoft-ds

This means Nmap cannot determine whether the port is open because packet filtering prevents a conclusive response.

Possible causes:

Firewall

ACL

Security group

Packet filter

Network device

docs.title: Filtered Does Not Mean Closed
docs.text:
This distinction matters:

closed

and:

filtered

represent different observations.

Do not report:

SMB is disabled.

solely because:

445/tcp filtered

The correct conclusion may simply be:

TCP/445 could not be directly assessed from the tested network position because traffic appeared to be filtered.

docs.title: Open or Filtered
docs.text:
Commonly seen with UDP:

53/udp open|filtered domain

This means Nmap cannot distinguish between:

An open service that did not respond

and:

Filtering that silently dropped the probe

docs.title: Service Detection
docs.text:
After finding ports:

nmap -sV -p 22,80,443 192.168.1.10

Example:

PORT    STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp  open  ssh     OpenSSH ...
80/tcp  open  http    nginx
443/tcp open  ssl/http nginx

docs.title: What -sV Does
docs.text:
Service detection sends additional probes to identify:

Protocol

Product

Version

Additional service information

It is more active than basic port discovery.

docs.title: Do Not Treat Version Detection as Absolute
docs.text:
Example:

Apache httpd 2.x

may be influenced by:

Banner configuration

Reverse proxy

Backported patches

Custom builds

Middleboxes

Incomplete fingerprints

Use the result as evidence for further validation, not automatic proof of vulnerability.

docs.title: Default Scripts and Version Detection
docs.text:
A commonly used focused scan is:

nmap -sC -sV -p 22,80,443 192.168.1.10

Where:

-sC

runs the default NSE script set.

And:

-sV

performs service/version detection.

docs.title: Understand -sC
docs.text:
Do not use -sC blindly against fragile or sensitive production systems.

Review the assessment rules and understand the scripts being invoked.

docs.title: Operating System Detection
docs.text:
sudo nmap -O 192.168.1.10

OS detection uses network-stack characteristics to estimate the operating system.

docs.title: OS Detection Interpretation
docs.text:
Example:

Running: Linux

should generally be interpreted as:

Network fingerprint appears consistent with Linux.

Not necessarily:

Operating system definitively confirmed.

docs.title: Aggressive Detection
docs.text:
nmap -A 192.168.1.10

-A enables several advanced detection features.

It is convenient but can be substantially noisier than a focused scan.

docs.title: Prefer Focused Enumeration
docs.text:
Instead of automatically:

nmap -A target

consider:

nmap -sV -p <identified-ports> target

followed by protocol-specific testing.

This gives better control over traffic and assessment scope.

docs.title: UDP Scanning
docs.text:
UDP is frequently overlooked.

Basic UDP scan:

sudo nmap -sU 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Common UDP Services
docs.text: Port Service 53 DNS 67/68 DHCP 69 TFTP 88 Kerberos 123 NTP 137 NetBIOS 161 SNMP 162 SNMP Trap 500 IKE 514 Syslog 1900 SSDP 4500 IPsec NAT-T

docs.title: UDP Is Different
docs.text:
UDP has no TCP-style handshake.

Conceptually:

Probe
 |
 v
UDP Service
 |
 +--> Application Response -> Open
 |
 +--> ICMP Unreachable     -> Closed
 |
 +--> No Response          -> Open or Filtered

docs.title: Faster UDP Triage
docs.text:
Instead of scanning every UDP port immediately:

sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 192.168.1.10

Then expand where justified.

docs.title: TCP and UDP Together
docs.text:
For selected ports:

sudo nmap -sS -sU -p T:22,80,443,U:53,161 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Protocol-Focused Enumeration
docs.text:
After discovery, switch from:

Which ports exist?

to:

What is this service?

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 80,443,8080,8443 192.168.1.10

Useful NSE discovery:

nmap --script http-title -p 80,443,8080,8443 192.168.1.10

Headers:

nmap --script http-headers -p 80,443 192.168.1.10

docs.title: HTTPS and TLS
docs.text:
Certificate information:

nmap --script ssl-cert -p 443 192.168.1.10

Cipher enumeration:

nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 192.168.1.10

Use TLS results as the starting point for configuration analysis.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 22 192.168.1.10

Algorithms:

nmap --script ssh2-enum-algos -p 22 192.168.1.10

Host keys:

nmap --script ssh-hostkey -p 22 192.168.1.10

docs.title: SMB
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 139,445 192.168.1.10

Protocol information:

nmap --script smb-protocols -p 445 192.168.1.10

Security mode:

nmap --script smb-security-mode -p 445 192.168.1.10

For detailed AD/SMB testing, continue with the Active Directory Cheatsheet and NetExec Cheatsheet.

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 389,636,3268,3269 192.168.1.10

LDAP exposure should be interpreted in the context of:

Authentication

TLS

Directory role

Network location

docs.title: Kerberos
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 88 192.168.1.10

In Active Directory environments, Kerberos exposure is normally expected on domain controllers.

The existence of port 88 is not a vulnerability.

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 3389 192.168.1.10

RDP-related NSE scripts available locally can be found with:

ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/rdp*

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 5985,5986 192.168.1.10

Common interpretation:

5985 -> HTTP WinRM

5986 -> HTTPS WinRM

Validate actual protocol behaviour rather than relying solely on port number.

docs.title: MSSQL
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 1433 192.168.1.10

SQL Server may also use:

Dynamic ports

Named instances

so do not assume:

1433 closed = no MSSQL

docs.title: MySQL
docs.text: nmap -sV -p 3306 192.168.1.10

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: nmap -sV -p 5432 192.168.1.10

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
TCP:

nmap -sV -p 53 192.168.1.10

UDP:

sudo nmap -sU -sV -p 53 192.168.1.10

docs.title: SNMP
docs.text:
sudo nmap -sU -sV -p 161 192.168.1.10

SNMP exposure can reveal substantial infrastructure information depending on configuration and access controls.

docs.title: NTP
docs.text: sudo nmap -sU -sV -p 123 192.168.1.10

docs.title: FTP
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 21 192.168.1.10

Identify:

Product

Version

TLS support

Authentication requirements

docs.title: Common Enterprise Ports
docs.text: Port Typical Service 21 FTP 22 SSH 25 SMTP 53 DNS 80 HTTP 88 Kerberos 110 POP3 111 RPC 123 NTP 135 MSRPC 139 NetBIOS 143 IMAP 389 LDAP 443 HTTPS 445 SMB 465 SMTPS 587 SMTP submission 636 LDAPS 1433 MSSQL 1521 Oracle 2049 NFS 3268 Global Catalog 3269 Global Catalog TLS 3306 MySQL 3389 RDP 5432 PostgreSQL 5985 WinRM HTTP 5986 WinRM HTTPS 6379 Redis 8080 Alternate HTTP 8443 Alternate HTTPS 9200 Elasticsearch

docs.title: NSE
docs.text:
Nmap Scripting Engine scripts extend Nmap beyond basic scanning.

Locate scripts:

ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/

Search:

ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ | grep http

or:

ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ | grep smb

docs.title: NSE Help
docs.text:
nmap --script-help http-title

This is particularly important before running unfamiliar scripts.

docs.title: Run One Script
docs.text: nmap --script http-title -p 80 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Multiple Scripts
docs.text: nmap --script http-title,http-headers -p 80,443 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Script Categories
docs.text:
NSE scripts can belong to categories such as:

auth

broadcast

brute

default

discovery

dos

exploit

external

fuzzer

intrusive

malware

safe

version

vuln

docs.title: Do Not Treat NSE Categories Equally
docs.text:
There is a major difference between:

safe

and:

dos

or:

intrusive

Do not run broad script categories against production environments without understanding their behaviour and having explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Review Script Before Running
docs.text:
Script files are commonly stored under:

/usr/share/nmap/scripts/

Inspect:

less /usr/share/nmap/scripts/<script>.nse

This is useful when operational impact is unclear.

docs.title: Default Scripts
docs.text:
nmap -sC 192.168.1.10

Equivalent to using the default NSE script category in typical Nmap usage.

Use deliberately rather than mechanically.

docs.title: Vulnerability Scripts
docs.text:
Nmap includes scripts associated with vulnerability detection.

List locally:

ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ | grep vuln

Or review script categories through Nmap's documentation.

Do not assume:

NSE says VULNERABLE

equals:

Confirmed exploitable vulnerability

Manual validation and version/configuration analysis may still be necessary.

docs.title: NSE Result Interpretation
docs.text:
Treat NSE output as:

Automated Observation
        |
        v
Check Script Logic
        |
        v
Understand Detection Method
        |
        v
Verify Target State
        |
        v
Manual Validation
        |
        v
Conclusion

docs.title: Scan Timing
docs.text:
Nmap supports timing templates:

-T0

-T1

-T2

-T3

-T4

-T5

docs.title: Typical Default
docs.text:
-T3

is the normal timing template.

docs.title: Faster Scanning
docs.text:
A common assessment command may use:

nmap -T4 192.168.1.10

But faster is not automatically better.

docs.title: Timing Trade-Off
docs.text:
Faster Scan
    |
    +--> Less Time
    |
    +--> More Traffic
    |
    +--> Potential Accuracy Impact
    |
    +--> More Monitoring Visibility
    |
    +--> Greater Risk to Fragile Systems

docs.title: Rate Control
docs.text:
Minimum packet rate:

nmap --min-rate 1000 192.168.1.10

Maximum rate:

nmap --max-rate 100 192.168.1.10

Do not use aggressive rate settings simply because a copied command contains them.

docs.title: Large Network Scanning
docs.text:
For large environments:

Start with discovery

Prioritise known subnets

Control scan rate

Separate discovery from enumeration

Save output

Avoid repeatedly rescanning everything

docs.title: Recommended Large-Network Model
docs.text:
CIDR
 |
 v
Host Discovery
 |
 v
Alive Targets
 |
 v
Port Discovery
 |
 v
Interesting Services
 |
 v
Focused Enumeration

docs.title: Output Formats
docs.text: Nmap supports several useful output formats.

docs.title: Normal Output
docs.text: nmap 192.168.1.10 -oN scan.txt

docs.title: XML
docs.text:
nmap 192.168.1.10 -oX scan.xml

Useful for:

Automation

Parsing

Import into other tools

Long-term evidence

docs.title: Grepable Output
docs.text:
nmap 192.168.1.10 -oG scan.gnmap

This format is useful for some legacy parsing workflows.

docs.title: All Major Formats
docs.text:
nmap 192.168.1.10 -oA scans/server01

This produces several output files with the same basename.

docs.title: Create Output Directory
docs.text:
mkdir -p scans

Then:

nmap -sV -p- 192.168.1.10 -oA scans/server01

docs.title: Why Save Raw Output
docs.text:
Raw scan output provides:

Evidence

Reproducibility

Comparison

Reporting support

Retest baseline

docs.title: Useful Naming Convention
docs.text:
YYYYMMDD_target_scan-type

Example:

20260906_192.168.1.10_tcp-full

docs.title: Verbose Output
docs.text:
nmap -v 192.168.1.10

More:

nmap -vv 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Show Reasons
docs.text:
nmap --reason 192.168.1.10

This helps explain why Nmap assigned a particular host or port state.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
PORT    STATE    SERVICE REASON
443/tcp filtered https   no-response

This provides useful context for interpretation.

docs.title: Packet Trace
docs.text:
For troubleshooting:

sudo nmap --packet-trace -p 443 192.168.1.10

This can generate substantial output but is useful for understanding probe/response behaviour.

docs.title: Scan Through a Specific Interface
docs.text:
List interfaces:

ip addr

Nmap interface information:

nmap --iflist

Specify interface:

sudo nmap -e eth0 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Source Port
docs.text:
Nmap supports selecting a source port where appropriate:

sudo nmap --source-port 53 -p 443 192.168.1.10

This should only be used when there is a legitimate assessment reason, such as validating firewall policy behaviour.

Do not assume changing the source port will bypass a firewall.

docs.title: IPv6
docs.text:
Scan IPv6:

nmap -6 <IPv6-address>

Example:

nmap -6 2001:db8::10

Do not forget IPv6 during internal assessments when the environment uses it.

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Disable DNS resolution:

nmap -n 192.168.1.10

This can improve speed and avoid unnecessary DNS queries.

docs.title: Force DNS Resolution
docs.text:
nmap -R 192.168.1.10

Use only when name resolution is useful to the assessment.

docs.title: Traceroute
docs.text:
nmap --traceroute 192.168.1.10

This may help understand network position and routing.

docs.title: Firewall Analysis
docs.text:
Nmap can provide evidence of filtering, but interpreting firewall policy requires care.

Example:

22/tcp  open
80/tcp  filtered
443/tcp open
445/tcp filtered

A reasonable observation:

The tested source could establish connectivity to TCP/22 and
TCP/443, while TCP/80 and TCP/445 appeared filtered.

Do not automatically claim:

Firewall correctly configured.

A firewall assessment requires comparison against intended policy.

docs.title: Same Host, Different Source
docs.text:
A valuable validation method is scanning from different authorised network positions.

Example:

Internet
   |
   v
443 only

Internal User VLAN
   |
   v
443,445,3389

Admin VLAN
   |
   v
22,443,445,5985

This can reveal segmentation behaviour.

docs.title: Segmentation Validation
docs.text:
Source Zone
    |
    v
Target Zone
    |
    v
Expected Policy
    |
    v
Nmap Observation
    |
    v
Compare

docs.title: Do Not Equate Reachability with Authorisation
docs.text:
If:

445/tcp open

that proves network reachability to SMB.

It does not prove:

Anonymous access

Authenticated access

Administrative access

Sensitive share access

docs.title: Manual Validation
docs.text:
Nmap should often be followed by protocol-specific tools.

Example:

Nmap
 |
 v
445/tcp open
 |
 v
NetExec / smbclient
 |
 v
Authentication and Share Validation

docs.title: HTTP Validation
docs.text:
Nmap:

443/tcp open https

Follow with:

curl -k -I https://192.168.1.10/

where appropriate.

Then continue with browser/Burp-based application analysis.

docs.title: TLS Validation
docs.text:
Nmap may identify TLS.

Continue with appropriate TLS analysis and certificate inspection rather than treating:

443 open

as sufficient security evidence.

docs.title: SMB Validation
docs.text:
Nmap:

445/tcp open microsoft-ds

Continue with:

nxc smb 192.168.1.10

or other authorised SMB tooling.

See NetExec Cheatsheet.

docs.title: RDP Validation
docs.text:
Nmap:

3389/tcp open ms-wbt-server

Next determine:

Is RDP actually reachable?

Is NLA enabled?

Who can log on?

Is exposure expected?

docs.title: WinRM Validation
docs.text:
Nmap:

5985/tcp open

Continue with appropriate Windows or Active Directory testing.

See:

  • Windows Cheatsheet
  • PowerShell Cheatsheet
  • NetExec Cheatsheet

docs.title: Phase 1 - Discovery
docs.text: nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 -oA scans/discovery

docs.title: Phase 2 - TCP Discovery
docs.text:
For a known authorised host:

nmap -p- --open 192.168.1.10 -oA scans/192.168.1.10_tcp

docs.title: Phase 3 - Service Enumeration
docs.text:
Suppose discovery returned:

22
80
443
445

Then:

nmap -sV -sC -p 22,80,443,445 192.168.1.10 -oA scans/192.168.1.10_services

docs.title: Phase 4 - UDP
docs.text: sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 192.168.1.10 -oA scans/192.168.1.10_udp

docs.title: Phase 5 - Focused Enumeration
docs.text:
Example:

nmap --script ssl-cert,ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 192.168.1.10

or:

nmap --script smb-protocols,smb-security-mode -p 445 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Phase 6 - Manual Validation
docs.text: Use the appropriate protocol-specific tooling rather than continuing to stack Nmap scripts indefinitely.

docs.title: Web Server Example
docs.text:
Initial:

nmap -p- 192.168.1.50

Representative result:

22/tcp   open ssh
8080/tcp open http-proxy
8443/tcp open https-alt

Focused:

nmap -sV -sC -p 22,8080,8443 192.168.1.50

Interpretation:

The host exposes SSH and two web-related TCP services.

Next:

Open web applications in browser/Burp.

Identify virtual hosts.

Review HTTP headers.

Identify application technology.

Perform content discovery.

Do not spend the entire web assessment inside Nmap.

docs.title: Active Directory Example
docs.text:
Initial:

nmap -sV -p 53,88,135,139,389,445,464,636,3268,3269,3389,5985,5986 10.10.10.10

Representative result:

53/tcp   open domain
88/tcp   open kerberos-sec
135/tcp  open msrpc
389/tcp  open ldap
445/tcp  open microsoft-ds
636/tcp  open ldaps
3268/tcp open globalcatLDAP

This pattern is consistent with Active Directory infrastructure.

It does not by itself prove:

Domain Controller definitively confirmed

Anonymous LDAP available

SMB misconfigured

Kerberos vulnerable

Continue with AD-specific enumeration.

docs.title: Database Example
docs.text:
Nmap:

nmap -sV -p 1433,3306,5432 192.168.1.30

Representative:

1433/tcp open ms-sql-s

Next determine:

Is remote database exposure expected?

Which authentication methods are supported?

Which network zones can reach it?

Does the service reveal unnecessary version information?

Are credentials available within scope?

docs.title: Scan Result Classification
docs.text:
A useful model:

OPEN PORT
   |
   v
SERVICE IDENTIFIED?
   |
  / \
 No   Yes
 |     |
 v     v
Manual  VERSION
Probe     |
          v
    EXPECTED SERVICE?
        /      \
      Yes       No
      |          |
      v          v
 Config       Investigate
 Review       Exposure

docs.title: Observation vs Finding
docs.text:
Example observation:

TCP/3389 is reachable from the user network.

This is not automatically a vulnerability.

A finding may exist if:

Policy requires RDP to be restricted to an admin network

but testing demonstrates:

User VLAN -> TCP/3389 -> Management Server

The vulnerability is then the segmentation/access-control weakness, not simply:

RDP open.

docs.title: Service Version vs Vulnerability
docs.text:
Nmap:

22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH <version>

Do not immediately:

Search CVE
    |
    v
Report Critical

Instead:

Reported Version
      |
      v
Verify Product
      |
      v
Verify Actual Version
      |
      v
Check Vendor Packaging
      |
      v
Check Backported Fixes
      |
      v
Confirm Vulnerable Configuration
      |
      v
Determine Reachability
      |
      v
Controlled Validation

docs.title: Backported Patches
docs.text:
Linux distributions frequently backport security fixes without changing the upstream version in the way vulnerability scanners expect.

Therefore banner-based version matching can produce false positives.

docs.title: Version Detection
docs.text:
Possible reasons:

Custom banner

Reverse proxy

Backported patch

Load balancer

Middlebox

Incomplete fingerprint

docs.title: Filtered Port
docs.text:
Possible reasons:

Firewall

Host firewall

Cloud ACL

Packet loss

Routing issue

docs.title: Host Down
docs.text:
Possible reasons:

Discovery probes blocked

ICMP filtered

Firewall

Network path

Host actually offline

docs.title: Open or Filtered UDP
docs.text:
Possible reasons:

Silent UDP service

Firewall silently dropping probes

Application does not respond to Nmap probe

docs.title: Only Running Default Scan
docs.text:
nmap target

and stopping.

Problem:

High ports may be missed.

docs.title: Ignoring UDP
docs.text:
Problem:

DNS, SNMP, NTP, IKE and other UDP services may be missed.

docs.title: Running -A Everywhere
docs.text:
Problem:

Unnecessary probes and noise.

docs.title: Running Every NSE Script
docs.text:
Problem:

Some scripts are intrusive, brute-force, exploit, fuzzing or DoS related.

docs.title: Treating filtered as closed
docs.text:
Problem:

Different network observations.

docs.title: Treating Version as Confirmed Vulnerability
docs.text:
Problem:

Version identification is not vulnerability confirmation.

docs.title: Not Saving Output
docs.text:
Problem:

Poor reproducibility and weak evidence.

docs.title: Scanning Out-of-Scope Addresses
docs.text:
Problem:

Authorisation violation.

docs.title: Host Appears Down
docs.text:
Try against a known authorised target:

nmap -Pn 192.168.1.10

Then verify routing:

ip route get 192.168.1.10

Check connectivity with appropriate protocol-specific tools.

docs.title: Everything Is Filtered
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Firewall

Wrong network

VPN issue

Routing

Cloud ACL

Source restrictions

Check:

ip addr

ip route

nmap --iflist

docs.title: Nmap Uses Wrong Interface
docs.text:
Check:

nmap --iflist

Then where justified:

sudo nmap -e <interface> <target>

docs.title: DNS Is Slow
docs.text:
Disable reverse DNS:

nmap -n 192.168.1.0/24

docs.title: Service Detection Takes Too Long
docs.text:
Limit it to identified ports:

nmap -sV -p 22,80,443 192.168.1.10

rather than performing service detection against every port unnecessarily.

docs.title: UDP Takes Too Long
docs.text:
Start with:

sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 192.168.1.10

Then expand based on the assessment objective.

docs.title: Nmap Needs Root
docs.text:
Some scan types require raw-packet privileges.

Use:

sudo nmap ...

when required and authorised.

Do not assume every Nmap feature behaves identically as an unprivileged user.

2026-09-06 18:30 UTC

Nmap

Source:
Assessment workstation

Result:

Interpretation:
HTTPS and SMB were directly reachable from the assessment
source. RDP could not be conclusively assessed because the

docs.title: Reporting Port Exposure
docs.text:
Avoid:

Port 445 is open and vulnerable.

Prefer:

TCP/445 was reachable from the tested user-network segment and responded as an SMB service. Whether this exposure represents a security weakness depends on the intended network-access policy and the authentication and authorisation controls protecting the service.

docs.title: Reporting Segmentation
docs.text:
Example:

Testing from the corporate user VLAN demonstrated direct TCP connectivity to the management interface on SRV01 over TCP/5985. According to the intended segmentation model, WinRM administration should only be accessible from the administrative network. The observed exposure therefore indicates insufficient network segmentation between the user and management zones.

docs.title: Reporting Unsupported Protocol
docs.text:
Example:

The server accepted SMB connections using an outdated protocol version. Protocol negotiation was independently validated after Nmap identified SMB exposure. Legacy SMB versions should be disabled where no operational dependency remains.

The finding should focus on:

Protocol configuration

rather than:

Nmap result

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Use the same source position whenever possible.

Example before remediation:

User VLAN
   |
   v
TCP/5985
   |
   v
SRV01
   |
   v
open

After remediation:

nmap -Pn -p 5985 --reason 10.10.10.20

Then compare against the expected network policy.

docs.title: Retest Interpretation
docs.text:
If the result becomes:

5985/tcp filtered

and filtering is the intended control, this supports successful remediation.

But also verify:

Same source network

Same target

Same route

Firewall change applied

No alternate management port remains exposed

docs.title: Compare Before and After
docs.text:
Before:

22/tcp   open
443/tcp  open
445/tcp  open
3389/tcp open
5985/tcp open

After:

443/tcp open

Then determine whether the reduced exposure matches the intended architecture.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
Nmap is best used as a discovery and validation tool, not as a substitute for understanding the service behind the port.

Do not stop at:

PORT
 |
 v
SERVICE

Continue:

PORT
 |
 v
SERVICE
 |
 v
PROTOCOL
 |
 v
CONFIGURATION
 |
 v
ACCESS CONTROL
 |
 v
APPLICATION
 |
 v
SECURITY CONSEQUENCE

For every important Nmap result ask:

Why is this port reachable?

From which network position?

Is the exposure intended?

What service actually responds?

How confident is the fingerprint?

What authentication protects it?

What protocol configuration is in use?

Does the result require manual validation?

What does this exposure enable?

What would remediation change?

How will I prove the change during retesting?

Discover broadly, enumerate narrowly

Port discovery and detailed service enumeration do not need to be the same scan. First identify the exposed attack surface, then run focused service detection and protocol-specific checks against the ports that actually matter.

Use --reason when the result is unclear

--reason can make open, closed, filtered and host-discovery results easier to understand because it exposes the response or lack of response that contributed to Nmap's classification.

Save the raw scan

Use -oA or another appropriate output option for important assessment scans. The raw result is far more useful during reporting and retesting than relying on terminal history or screenshots alone.

An open port is an observation, not automatically a vulnerability

The security significance depends on the exposed service, intended network architecture, authentication, protocol configuration and what the reachable service actually permits.

NSE scripts have different operational impacts

Before running unfamiliar scripts, inspect their documentation and category. Discovery and safe scripts are operationally different from brute-force, intrusive, exploit, fuzzing and denial-of-service scripts.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Security Testing Cheatsheet
docs.text:
OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect are widely used for delegated authorization, API access and federated authentication.

They solve related but different problems.

OAuth 2.0
    |
    v
Delegated Authorization

OpenID Connect
    |
    v
Authentication Layer Built on OAuth 2.0

A simplified OAuth question is:

Can this client access this resource
with this authorization?

A simplified OpenID Connect question is:

Who authenticated at the identity provider?

Authorised Security Testing

Test OAuth and OpenID Connect only against applications, clients, accounts and identity providers included in the assessment scope. Use dedicated test accounts and controlled authorization grants wherever possible. Avoid connecting unrelated third-party accounts, accessing real user data or changing production identity-provider configuration solely to demonstrate a weakness.

The system that:

Obtains authorization

docs.text:
For every OAuth flow ask:

Who initiated the flow?

Which client requested authorization?

Which redirect URI was used?

Was the request correlated to the browser session?

Was PKCE used?

Was the code bound to the correct client?

Which scopes were granted?

Which tokens were returned?

Where were tokens delivered?

How are tokens validated?

How is the external identity linked to the local account?

docs.title: state
docs.text:
state is commonly used to maintain request correlation and protect authorization flows against CSRF-like attacks.

Conceptually:

Client Generates State
       |
       v
Authorization Request
       |
       v
Authorization Server
       |
       v
Callback With State
       |
       v
Client Compares State

docs.title: Secure Behaviour
docs.text:
Sent state
    =
Returned state

and the value should be bound to the initiating user-agent session or transaction.

docs.title: Baseline State Test
docs.text:
Capture a legitimate authorization request:

state=abc123

docs.title: Callback
docs.text: /callback?code=CODE&state=abc123

docs.title: Controlled Modification
docs.text:
Change:

state=abc123

to:

state=invalid-test-value

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: The client should reject the callback or otherwise fail the authorization transaction safely.

docs.title: Missing State
docs.text:
If an application does not use state, determine whether another mechanism provides equivalent request correlation.

Do not report:

No state parameter

without understanding the actual flow and protections.

docs.title: State Quality
docs.text:
A state value should generally be:

Unpredictable

Bound to the browser session

Single-use or transaction-specific

Validated on callback

docs.title: Static State
docs.text:
Example:

state=12345

on every login may indicate ineffective request correlation.

docs.title: State Must Be Validated
docs.text:
Simply sending a state parameter is not enough.

Generate
   |
   v
Send
   |
   v
Receive
   |
   v
Compare

docs.title: PKCE
docs.text:
PKCE stands for:

Proof Key for Code Exchange

PKCE binds an authorization code to the client instance that initiated the authorization request.

docs.title: PKCE Model
docs.text:
Client Generates
code_verifier
     |
     v
Derives
code_challenge
     |
     v
Authorization Request
     |
     v
Authorization Code
     |
     v
Token Request + code_verifier
     |
     v
Server Verifies

docs.title: S256
docs.text:
The recommended challenge transformation is:

S256

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier))

produces the:

code_challenge

docs.title: Generate a Test Verifier
docs.text:
For a controlled lab or assessment client:

python3 - <<'PY'
import secrets
print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))
PY

docs.title: Generate S256 Challenge
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
import base64
import hashlib

verifier = "PASTE_CONTROLLED_VERIFIER"
digest = hashlib.sha256(verifier.encode()).digest()
challenge = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(digest).rstrip(b"=").decode()
print(challenge)
PY

docs.title: PKCE Validation Test
docs.text:
Use a code generated through your own controlled account.

Attempt the token exchange with an incorrect:

code_verifier

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Token exchange rejected

docs.title: Missing Verifier
docs.text: If the original authorization request included a PKCE challenge, test whether the token endpoint incorrectly accepts the code without the corresponding verifier.

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Rejected

docs.title: PKCE Downgrade
docs.text:
If the client normally uses:

S256

determine whether the authorization server unexpectedly permits the security property to be removed or downgraded for the same client where policy requires PKCE.

docs.title: Do Not Assume PKCE Replaces State
docs.text:
PKCE and state address overlapping but not identical concerns.

Think of:

state
  |
  v
Authorization request correlation

PKCE
  |
  v
Authorization code binding

docs.title: Authorization Code Security
docs.text:
Authorization codes should be:

Short-lived

Single-use

Bound to the client

Bound to the redirect URI where applicable

Bound to PKCE verifier when PKCE is used

docs.title: Code Reuse
docs.text:
Use a controlled authorization code.

Exchange it once successfully.

Then attempt the same exchange again.

docs.title: Expected
docs.text: Second exchange rejected

docs.title: Code Lifetime
docs.text:
Authorization codes should have a limited lifetime.

Do not assume a specific number of seconds is universally required.

Evaluate:

Provider design

Standards guidance

Application sensitivity

docs.title: Code Binding
docs.text:
A code issued to:

Client A

should not be redeemable by:

Client B

docs.title: Redirect URI Security
docs.text:
Redirect URI handling is one of the most important OAuth security boundaries.

After authorization, sensitive values may be delivered to the redirect URI.

Depending on the flow, this can include:

Authorization code

Error information

State

Legacy front-channel tokens

docs.title: Secure Principle
docs.text: Redirect URIs should be compared using strict matching according to the protocol and client registration model.

docs.title: Registered Redirect URI
docs.text:
Example:

https://app.example.com/oauth/callback

docs.title: Test Variations Carefully
docs.text:
Potentially relevant controlled variations include:

Different path

Different subdomain

Different scheme

Different port

Added query parameters

docs.title: Reporting Missing State Validation
docs.text: The OAuth callback does not adequately validate the authorization transaction against the browser session that initiated it. A callback containing a mismatched controlled state value was accepted and completed the authentication flow. The client should generate an unpredictable transaction-specific state value, bind it to the initiating session and verify it before processing the authorization response.

docs.title: Reporting PKCE Validation Failure
docs.text: The authorization server issues an authorization code with a PKCE challenge but the token endpoint does not enforce possession of the corresponding verifier. A code generated through a controlled test account was successfully exchanged using an incorrect verifier. The token endpoint must cryptographically bind the authorization code to the original PKCE verifier.

docs.title: Reporting Redirect URI Weakness
docs.text: The authorization server accepts a redirect URI outside the client's intended registered callback set. A modified authorization request caused the authorization response to be delivered to a controlled alternate destination. Redirect URIs should be registered explicitly and validated using strict matching appropriate to the client type.

docs.title: Reporting Code Reuse
docs.text: Authorization codes are not invalidated after successful redemption. The same controlled authorization code was exchanged more than once and each exchange returned valid token material. Authorization codes should be short-lived, single-use credentials and must be invalidated after successful redemption.

docs.title: Reporting Scope Enforcement Failure
docs.text: The resource server does not enforce the permissions represented by the access token scope. A token containing only the orders:read scope successfully performed an operation requiring write access. The API should validate the required scope or authorization policy for every protected operation.

docs.title: Reporting ID Token Confusion
docs.text: The API accepts an OpenID Connect ID token as an API authorization credential even though the token is intended for the client application rather than the resource server. Resource servers should accept only access tokens intended for that API and validate token audience, purpose and required authorization claims.

docs.title: Reporting Account Linking Weakness
docs.text: The application links a federated identity to an existing local account based solely on an email claim without adequately proving that the external identity is authorized to control the existing account. Federated account mapping should use a trusted issuer and stable subject identifier, with explicit proof of account ownership where identities are linked.

docs.title: Reporting Client Secret Exposure
docs.text: A confidential OAuth client secret is included in browser-delivered application code. Because browser clients cannot protect embedded secrets from users, the credential should be rotated and removed from client-side code. If the application is a public client, it should use an OAuth flow designed for public clients rather than relying on a client secret for confidentiality.

docs.title: Reporting Token Leakage
docs.text: OAuth bearer tokens are exposed through URL parameters during the application flow. URLs may be retained by browser history, reverse proxies, application logs and analytics systems. Sensitive bearer credentials should be transmitted using protocol-appropriate mechanisms that minimize unintended disclosure.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
OAuth testing is not:

Find /authorize
      |
      v
Change random parameters
      |
      v
Report OAuth issue

It is:

UNDERSTAND ACTORS
       |
       v
UNDERSTAND FLOW
       |
       v
IDENTIFY TRUST BOUNDARIES
       |
       v
CONTROL ONE VARIABLE
       |
       v
OBSERVE SECURITY DECISION
       |
       v
VERIFY IMPACT

For every OAuth or OIDC implementation ask:

Which authorization server is trusted?

Which client is involved?

Is the client public or confidential?

Which flow is being used?

Which redirect URIs are registered?

How strictly are redirect URIs validated?

Can an untrusted origin receive authorization material?

Is the authorization request bound to the browser session?

Is state used and actually validated?

Is PKCE used?

Is S256 used?

Is the verifier required?

Can PKCE be removed or downgraded?

Are authorization codes short-lived?

Are authorization codes single-use?

Are codes bound to the correct client?

Are codes bound to the redirect URI where required?

Which scopes are requested?

Which scopes are granted?

Are scopes actually enforced by APIs?

Does object-level authorization still occur?

Are tenant boundaries enforced?

Which token types are issued?

Can an ID token be used as an access token?

Can a token for one API be used against another?

Is issuer validation correct?

Is audience validation correct?

Are token lifetimes enforced?

Are refresh tokens protected?

Are refresh tokens rotated where appropriate?

Can refresh-token replay be detected?

Are tokens exposed in URLs?

Are tokens exposed in logs?

Are client secrets exposed?

Is a public client incorrectly expected to keep a secret?

Does OIDC use a stable issuer and subject for identity?

Is nonce validated where required?

How are external identities linked to local accounts?

Can an attacker influence account linking?

What happens after logout?

What happens after account disablement?

What happens after unlinking an identity provider?

Are callback errors handled safely?

Can forwarded headers influence callback URLs?

Are old development redirect URIs still registered?

Are abandoned callback domains registered?

Do mobile and SPA clients use appropriate public-client protections?

Do all resource servers validate the same token consistently?

Have findings been demonstrated using controlled accounts?

Has actual impact been verified rather than inferred?

Have access tokens, refresh tokens, codes and secrets been redacted from evidence?
