Map the flow before attacking it

OAuth and OIDC requests contain many interdependent values. Capture one complete successful authentication flow first and identify the client, authorization server, redirect URI, state, PKCE values, scopes and token types before changing anything.

Change one parameter at a time

Testing state, redirect_uri, PKCE, scopes and token handling independently makes it much easier to identify which security control failed and to produce defensible evidence.

Separate protocol layers

A secure OAuth authorization flow does not guarantee secure application authorization. After validating the token, the resource server must still enforce scopes, roles, object ownership and tenant boundaries.

Use controlled identities

Two dedicated test accounts are especially useful for login CSRF, federated account linking and identity-mapping tests because they allow the complete security consequence to be demonstrated without involving unrelated users.

Public metadata is not a vulnerability

Client IDs, OIDC discovery metadata and public JWKS documents are normally designed to be visible. Focus on whether the application establishes and enforces the correct trust relationships rather than treating public protocol metadata as sensitive information.

Protect OAuth credentials in evidence

Authorization codes, access tokens, refresh tokens, ID tokens and confidential-client secrets may all provide security-sensitive access. Redact them from reports, screenshots and shared logs.

docs.title: Path Traversal and File Inclusion Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Path traversal occurs when attacker-controlled input influences a filesystem path and allows access outside the directory intended by the application.

Related vulnerabilities include:

Path Traversal

Directory Traversal

Local File Inclusion (LFI)

Remote File Inclusion (RFI)

Arbitrary File Read

Unsafe File Download

Unsafe File Write

These issues are related but should not automatically be treated as equivalent.

A simplified path traversal flow is:

User Input
    |
    v
File Parameter
    |
    v
Application Path Construction
    |
    v
Filesystem
    |
    v
Unexpected File

Example:

GET /download?file=report.pdf

Application logic:

/var/www/files/ + report.pdf

Expected result:

/var/www/files/report.pdf

If traversal is possible:

/var/www/files/ + ../../etc/hostname

the resolved path may become:

/etc/hostname

Authorised Security Testing

Perform path traversal and file inclusion testing only against systems explicitly included in the assessment scope. Start with harmless known files and application-owned resources. Do not access credentials, private keys, tokens, personal data or other sensitive files unless that level of validation is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Common Parameters
docs.text:
file

filename

path

filepath

page

template

include

document

download

attachment

resource

folder

directory

dir

image

img

view

theme

lang

language

locale

content

docs.title: Basic Linux Traversal
docs.text: ../../../etc/hostname

docs.title: Basic Windows Traversal
docs.text: ..\..\..\Windows\win.ini

docs.title: URL-Encoded Traversal
docs.text:
..%2f..%2f..%2f

Windows-style:

..%5c..%5c..%5c

docs.title: Absolute Linux Path
docs.text: /etc/hostname

docs.title: Absolute Windows Path
docs.text: C:\Windows\win.ini

docs.title: Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use:

../ accepted
     |
     v
Vulnerable

Use:

Identify File Operation
        |
        v
Establish Baseline
        |
        v
Understand Expected Directory
        |
        v
Use Controlled Traversal
        |
        v
Observe Known File Content
        |
        v
Determine Normalisation
        |
        v
Determine Security Boundary
        |
        v
Evidence

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Path traversal allows a user to escape the intended filesystem directory.

Intended Directory
      |
      v
/var/www/files/
      |
      v
../../../
      |
      v
Outside Directory

docs.title: Arbitrary File Read
docs.text:
Arbitrary file read describes the resulting capability when an attacker can retrieve files from unintended locations.

Path traversal is one possible cause.

docs.title: Local File Inclusion
docs.text:
Local File Inclusion usually means attacker-controlled input causes the application to include or interpret a local file.

Conceptually:

User Input
    |
    v
include()
    |
    v
Local File
    |
    v
Application Processing

docs.title: Remote File Inclusion
docs.text:
Remote File Inclusion involves loading or including content from a remote location.

Whether RFI is possible depends heavily on:

Language

Runtime configuration

Application code

Network access

docs.title: Unsafe File Download
docs.text:
An endpoint may allow arbitrary local files to be downloaded without actually including or executing them.

Example:

/download?file=...

This may be better described as:

Path Traversal leading to Arbitrary File Read

rather than LFI.

docs.title: Path Traversal vs LFI
docs.text:
These terms are frequently used interchangeably, but they describe different aspects.

Path Traversal
      |
      v
Filesystem Path Escaped

versus:

Local File Inclusion
      |
      v
Application Includes Local File

docs.title: Example Path Traversal
docs.text:
Request:

GET /download?file=report.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Application:

path = "/var/www/files/" + request.args["file"]

return send_file(path)

docs.title: Expected Path
docs.text: /var/www/files/report.pdf

docs.title: Traversal Input
docs.text: ../../../etc/hostname

docs.title: Resulting Path
docs.text:
Conceptually:

/var/www/files/../../../etc/hostname

Normalised:

/etc/hostname

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Look for functionality involving:

Downloads

Attachments

Images

Templates

Language files

Themes

Reports

Exports

Documents

Static resources

Log viewers

File previews

Configuration files

Backup retrieval

docs.title: Candidate URLs
docs.text:
Examples:

/download?file=report.pdf

/view?page=home.html

/image?path=logo.png

/document?id=manual.pdf

/template?name=default

/lang?file=en.json

/export?filename=report.csv

docs.title: Candidate JSON
docs.text:
{
  "file": "report.pdf"
}

docs.title: Nested JSON
docs.text:
{
  "document": {
    "path": "reports/2026/report.pdf"
  }
}

docs.title: REST-Style Paths
docs.text:
Traversal input may also appear directly in a route.

Example:

/files/report.pdf

or:

/api/files/reports/2026/report.pdf

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Less commonly, file names may be influenced through:

Content-Disposition

X-Original-URL

X-Rewrite-URL

Custom application headers

Only test headers that are relevant to the application's behaviour.

docs.title: Step 1 - Establish Baseline
docs.text:
Start with a legitimate file.

GET /download?file=manual.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

docs.title: Record Baseline
docs.text:
Capture:

Status code

Content-Type

Content-Length

Content-Disposition

Response body

Response time

docs.title: Step 2 - Identify Expected Directory
docs.text:
Where possible, determine the intended storage location.

Source code might reveal:

DOWNLOAD_DIR = "/srv/app/downloads"

docs.title: White-Box Advantage
docs.text: Knowing the expected base directory lets you design a minimal traversal rather than guessing excessive directory depth.

docs.title: Step 3 - Use a Harmless Known File
docs.text:
For Linux, a low-impact system identification file may be appropriate when authorised.

A better white-box test is an assessment-created file such as:

/tmp/traversal-test.txt

containing:

TRAVERSAL_TEST_7f3a9

docs.title: Controlled Linux Example
docs.text:
Suppose the application base directory is:

/srv/app/downloads/

and the test file is:

/srv/app/traversal-test.txt

A minimal candidate might be:

../traversal-test.txt

docs.title: Controlled Evidence
docs.text:
Expected returned content:

TRAVERSAL_TEST_7f3a9

This provides clean evidence without retrieving sensitive operating-system files.

docs.title: Windows Controlled File
docs.text:
Example controlled file:

C:\Temp\traversal-test.txt

containing:

TRAVERSAL_TEST_7f3a9

docs.title: Windows Traversal Syntax
docs.text:
..\..\..\Temp\traversal-test.txt

The correct number of traversal segments depends on the application's base directory.

docs.title: Separator Differences
docs.text:
Linux normally uses:

/

Windows normally uses:

\

Many frameworks and libraries may accept more than one separator representation.

docs.title: Basic Linux Traversal
docs.text: ../

docs.title: Basic Windows Traversal
docs.text: ..\

docs.title: Multiple Levels
docs.text:
../../

../../../

../../../../

docs.title: Do Not Guess Excessive Depth Immediately
docs.text: Start with the minimum traversal necessary when architecture or source information is available.

docs.title: Absolute Paths
docs.text:
Some applications may accept absolute paths directly.

Linux:

/etc/hostname

Windows:

C:\Windows\win.ini

docs.title: Absolute Path Interpretation
docs.text:
If an application accepts an absolute path, the issue may not require ../ traversal at all.

The root cause is still:

User-controlled filesystem path without adequate restriction.

docs.title: URL Encoding
docs.text:
HTTP clients and frameworks may decode URL parameters before application processing.

Basic encoded slash:

%2f

Encoded backslash:

%5c

docs.title: Encoded Traversal
docs.text: ..%2f..%2f..%2f

docs.title: Fully Encoded Dots and Slash
docs.text: %2e%2e%2f

docs.title: Encoded Windows Traversal
docs.text: %2e%2e%5c

docs.title: Why Encoding Matters
docs.text:
A request may pass through several layers:

Browser / Client
      |
      v
Reverse Proxy
      |
      v
Web Server
      |
      v
Framework
      |
      v
Application

Each layer may:

Decode

Normalise

Reject

Rewrite

the path differently.

docs.title: Double Encoding
docs.text:
A double-encoded slash may appear as:

%252f

because:

%25

represents:

%

docs.title: Double-Decoding Model
docs.text:
..%252f
    |
    v
..%2f
    |
    v
../

docs.title: When Double Encoding Matters
docs.text:
Only test double encoding when there is evidence that:

Multiple decoding stages exist

A filter operates before a later decode

The architecture makes it relevant

docs.title: Do Not Blindly Spray Encodings
docs.text: Use controlled variations and compare responses.

docs.title: Normalisation
docs.text:
A secure implementation should reason about the canonical filesystem path rather than the raw user string.

Conceptually:

User Path
    |
    v
Join With Base Directory
    |
    v
Canonicalise
    |
    v
Verify Still Inside Base
    |
    v
Open File

docs.title: Weak Validation
docs.text:
Example:

if "../" in filename:
    reject()

This is fragile because it reasons about a string rather than the resolved filesystem path.

docs.title: Stronger Model
docs.text:
BASE DIRECTORY
      |
      v
Join User-Supplied Relative Name
      |
      v
Resolve Canonical Path
      |
      v
Is Result Inside BASE?
      |
    Yes / No

docs.title: Prefix Removal
docs.text:
Some applications attempt to remove traversal sequences.

Example concept:

Input:
../../test.txt

Filter removes:
../

Result:
../test.txt

A transformation-based filter can therefore behave unexpectedly.

docs.title: Filtering vs Canonicalisation
docs.text:
Prefer:

Canonicalise then enforce boundary

over:

Repeatedly replace suspicious strings.

docs.title: File Extensions
docs.text:
Applications may append an extension.

Example:

filename = request.args["page"] + ".html"

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Input:

help

becomes:

help.html

docs.title: Extension Restrictions
docs.text:
Determine whether the application:

Appends extension

Requires extension

Checks extension

Replaces extension

docs.title: Do Not Assume Extension Checks Are Security Boundaries
docs.text: An extension allowlist may be useful for business logic, but filesystem containment must still be enforced independently.

docs.title: Null Bytes
docs.text:
Historical applications and language/runtime combinations sometimes treated null bytes specially.

Modern runtimes generally handle this differently or reject them.

Do not treat null-byte techniques as universally applicable.

docs.title: Legacy Candidate
docs.text:
Historical notation:

%00

Use only when testing a relevant legacy stack and when there is a technical reason to do so.

docs.title: Path Prefix Requirements
docs.text:
An application may expect:

images/

before a file name.

Example:

images/logo.png

docs.title: Validation Question
docs.text:
Determine whether the application validates:

Raw input

or:

Canonical resolved path.

docs.title: File Download Example
docs.text:
Baseline:

GET /api/download?file=report.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

docs.title: Traversal Test
docs.text:
GET /api/download?file=../traversal-test.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

docs.title: Representative Positive Result
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="traversal-test.txt"

TRAVERSAL_TEST_7f3a9

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This demonstrates:

The user-controlled file parameter escaped the intended download directory and accessed a file outside that directory.

docs.title: Representative Negative Result
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

Invalid file path

docs.title: Negative Result Interpretation
docs.text:
This may indicate:

Traversal validation

Canonical path containment

Application-level block

Further testing may still be required to understand the control.

docs.title: File Not Found
docs.text:
Example:

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

This does not prove traversal was blocked.

Possible explanations:

File genuinely absent

Wrong traversal depth

Path normalised differently

Application rewrote input

Access denied translated to 404

docs.title: Permission Denied
docs.text:
Example:

Permission denied

This may indicate:

The path reached filesystem access but the application account could not read the target.

It does not demonstrate successful disclosure.

docs.title: Different Error Messages
docs.text:
Compare:

File does not exist

Invalid path

Permission denied

Directory not allowed

Path outside root

These can help understand where validation occurs.

docs.title: Response Length
docs.text:
Traversal responses may differ in:

Content length

Content type

Content disposition

Status

Use Burp Comparer or response comparison when differences are subtle.

docs.title: File Inclusion
docs.text: File inclusion is particularly associated with applications that dynamically load templates or scripts based on user input.

docs.title: Conceptual PHP Example
docs.text:
$page = $_GET['page'];

include($page);

docs.title: Input
docs.text: ?page=about.php

docs.title: Application Behaviour
docs.text: include("about.php")

docs.title: Unsafe Input
docs.text: If arbitrary local paths are accepted, the application may include unintended files.

docs.title: LFI vs Arbitrary File Read
docs.text:
An endpoint that performs:

readfile($path);

is different from:

include($path);

The first reads data.

The second may interpret the file according to the runtime's inclusion semantics.

docs.title: Report the Actual Sink
docs.text:
Prefer precise descriptions such as:

Path Traversal in File Download

Arbitrary Local File Read

Local File Inclusion

rather than using LFI for every filesystem issue.

docs.title: Remote File Inclusion
docs.text:
RFI requires a runtime or application that supports remote resources in the relevant inclusion operation.

Conceptually:

User URL
   |
   v
include()
   |
   v
Remote Resource

docs.title: Controlled RFI Validation
docs.text:
If remote inclusion is relevant and explicitly authorised, use only a harmless controlled resource.

Example conceptual content:

RFI_TEST_7f3a9

Do not use executable payloads simply to prove remote resource retrieval.

docs.title: RFI vs SSRF
docs.text:
If the application merely retrieves a remote resource:

User URL
   |
   v
HTTP Client

that is more likely SSRF.

If the runtime:

includes/interprets remote content

the classification may be RFI.

docs.title: Path Traversal in APIs
docs.text:
API request:

POST /api/document HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "path": "reports/annual.pdf"
}

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
{
  "path": "../traversal-test.txt"
}

docs.title: Nested Object
docs.text:
{
  "options": {
    "template": "../templates/test.html"
  }
}

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
A GraphQL argument can also become a filesystem path.

Example:

query {
  download(file: "report.pdf")
}

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
The transport mechanism does not matter.

The important flow is:

GraphQL Argument
      |
      v
Resolver
      |
      v
Filesystem Path

docs.title: Path Traversal in Archives
docs.text:
Archive extraction introduces a related vulnerability commonly called:

Zip Slip

Conceptually:

ZIP Entry
   |
   v
../../outside.txt
   |
   v
Extraction
   |
   v
File Written Outside Destination

docs.title: Zip Slip Is a Write Problem
docs.text:
Traditional path traversal often concerns reading files.

Zip Slip commonly concerns writing extracted files outside the intended extraction directory.

docs.title: Archive Entry Example
docs.text:
Conceptual malicious archive entry:

../../outside.txt

The secure extractor must ensure the canonical output path remains inside the extraction root.

docs.title: Do Not Test Destructive Archive Writes
docs.text: Use an assessment-controlled directory and harmless marker files where archive extraction testing is authorised.

docs.title: File Upload Path Manipulation
docs.text:
Applications may use the supplied filename when saving uploads.

Example:

filename="../../outside.txt"

docs.title: Upload Model
docs.text:
Multipart Filename
       |
       v
Application Save Path
       |
       v
Filesystem

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Does the application:

Discard client filename?

Generate its own filename?

Use basename only?

Canonicalise output path?

Enforce upload directory containment?

docs.title: Multipart Filename
docs.text:
Example:

Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="report.pdf"

docs.title: Filename Trust
docs.text: Client-supplied filenames should not determine arbitrary filesystem locations.

docs.title: Path Traversal in Log Viewers
docs.text:
Example:

/logs?file=application.log

These endpoints deserve attention because logs may exist in predictable filesystem directories.

docs.title: Path Traversal in Image Endpoints
docs.text:
Example:

/image?name=avatar.png

Check whether:

Image ID

or:

Raw filesystem path

is used internally.

docs.title: Path Traversal in Templates
docs.text:
Example:

/template?name=invoice

Source:

render_template(request.args["name"])

Review how the template engine resolves names and whether directory boundaries are enforced.

docs.title: Language Files
docs.text:
Example:

?lang=en

Application:

languages/en.json

If the user controls the full path rather than a known language identifier, traversal may become possible.

docs.title: Safer Language Design
docs.text:
Prefer:

en -> /app/languages/en.json

nl -> /app/languages/nl.json

using a server-side mapping.

docs.title: File IDs vs File Paths
docs.text:
Prefer:

GET /download?id=7812

where:

7812

maps server-side to an authorised file.

Avoid exposing raw filesystem paths when unnecessary.

docs.title: Indirect References
docs.text:
User
 |
 v
File ID
 |
 v
Database Lookup
 |
 v
Authorisation Check
 |
 v
Server-Controlled Path
 |
 v
File

docs.title: Path Traversal and Authorisation
docs.text:
Even when path containment is secure, file access may still have an authorisation problem.

Example:

/download?id=1001

may allow access to another user's document.

That is typically:

IDOR / BOLA

rather than path traversal.

docs.title: Keep Findings Separate
docs.text:
Filesystem Boundary
      |
      v
Path Traversal

versus:

Object Ownership Boundary
      |
      v
IDOR / BOLA

docs.title: Path Traversal and Symlinks
docs.text:
Symbolic links can complicate path validation.

Example:

/downloads/public-link
          |
          v
/etc/sensitive-directory

docs.title: Symlink Security Model
docs.text:
A path may appear to be inside the allowed directory before filesystem resolution.

Secure designs should account for filesystem semantics and symlink behaviour.

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
A check such as:

Validate Path
     |
     v
Open File

may be vulnerable to race conditions if filesystem state can change between those operations.

This is especially relevant in environments where attackers can create or modify files or symlinks.

docs.title: TOCTOU
docs.text:
Time of Check
     |
     v
Filesystem Changes
     |
     v
Time of Use

docs.title: Source Code Review
docs.text: Path traversal is particularly suitable for source-to-sink analysis.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Common attacker-controlled sources:

Query parameter

Path parameter

JSON property

Form field

Multipart filename

Cookie

Header

Database value derived from user input

docs.title: Sinks
docs.text:
Common filesystem sinks:

open()

readFile()

readFileSync()

sendFile()

File()

FileInputStream()

Files.readAllBytes()

File.ReadAllText()

File.Open()

include()

require()

readfile()

fopen()

docs.title: Python Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'open\(|send_file|send_from_directory|Path\(|read_text|read_bytes' -g '*.py' .

docs.title: Python Candidate
docs.text:
filename = request.args.get("file")

return send_file(
    "/srv/app/downloads/" + filename
)

docs.title: Source-to-Sink
docs.text:
request.args["file"]
        |
        v
String Concatenation
        |
        v
send_file()

docs.title: Python pathlib
docs.text:
Potential path construction:

path = Path(BASE_DIR) / user_input

This is not automatically vulnerable.

Review whether the resolved path is constrained to the intended base.

docs.title: JavaScript / Node.js Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'readFile|readFileSync|createReadStream|sendFile|path\.join|path\.resolve' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

docs.title: Node.js Candidate
docs.text:
const file = req.query.file;

res.sendFile(
    path.join("/srv/app/downloads", file)
);

docs.title: Important Node.js Review
docs.text:
Do not assume:

path.join()

provides a security boundary.

Review the final resolved path and containment check.

docs.title: Java Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'FileInputStream|Files\.read|Paths\.get|new File|Path\.of' -g '*.java' .

docs.title: Java Candidate
docs.text:
String file = request.getParameter("file");

Path path = Paths.get("/srv/app/downloads", file);

docs.title: .NET Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'File\.Read|File\.Open|FileStream|Path\.Combine|PhysicalFile' -g '*.cs' .

docs.title: .NET Candidate
docs.text:
var path = Path.Combine(
    downloadDirectory,
    userFile
);

return PhysicalFile(path, "application/octet-stream");

docs.title: PHP Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'include|require|readfile|file_get_contents|fopen' -g '*.php' .

docs.title: PHP Candidate
docs.text:
$file = $_GET['file'];

readfile("/srv/app/downloads/" . $file);

docs.title: Go Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'os\.Open|os\.ReadFile|filepath\.Join|filepath\.Clean|http\.ServeFile' -g '*.go' .

docs.title: Go Candidate
docs.text:
file := r.URL.Query().Get("file")

path := filepath.Join(baseDir, file)

http.ServeFile(w, r, path)

docs.title: Ruby Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'File\.read|File\.open|send_file|File\.join|Pathname' -g '*.rb' .

docs.title: Source Review Workflow
docs.text:
Find File Operations
       |
       v
Identify Path Argument
       |
       v
Trace Backwards
       |
       v
User Controlled?
       |
       v
Path Construction
       |
       v
Canonicalisation
       |
       v
Containment Check
       |
       v
Authorisation
       |
       v
Filesystem Operation

docs.title: Search Path Parameters
docs.text: rg -ni 'file|filename|filepath|path|directory|folder|template|document|download' src/

docs.title: Search Concatenation Near File Operations
docs.text: rg -n -C 5 'open\(|readFile|sendFile|FileInputStream|File\.Read|readfile|fopen' src/

docs.title: Search Path Helpers
docs.text: rg -ni 'path\.join|path\.resolve|Path\.Combine|filepath\.Join|Paths\.get|Path\(' src/

docs.title: Low Concern
docs.text:
Server-Controlled Constant Path
          |
          v
Filesystem

docs.title: Medium Candidate
docs.text:
User File ID
     |
     v
Database Mapping
     |
     v
Server-Controlled Path

Review authorisation and mapping integrity.

docs.title: High-Priority Candidate
docs.text:
User Filename
      |
      v
Base + Filename
      |
      v
Filesystem

docs.title: Very High-Priority Candidate
docs.text:
User Path
    |
    v
Filesystem API

with no visible containment check.

docs.title: Canonicalisation
docs.text:
A strong containment check should operate on canonical paths.

Conceptually:

BASE:
/srv/app/downloads

INPUT:
../traversal-test.txt

JOIN:
/srv/app/downloads/../traversal-test.txt

RESOLVE:
/srv/app/traversal-test.txt

CHECK:
Is resolved path inside /srv/app/downloads?

NO -> Reject

docs.title: Python Conceptual Defence
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

BASE = Path("/srv/app/downloads").resolve()

candidate = (BASE / user_filename).resolve()

if BASE not in candidate.parents:
    raise ValueError("Invalid file path")

docs.title: Important Edge Case
docs.text:
The base directory itself may also be a valid target depending on application behaviour.

Production code should implement containment carefully and account for:

Exact base path

Children

Symlinks

Platform semantics

docs.title: Java Conceptual Defence
docs.text:
Path base = Paths.get("/srv/app/downloads")
                 .toRealPath();

Path candidate = base.resolve(userInput)
                     .normalize();

if (!candidate.startsWith(base)) {
    throw new SecurityException("Invalid path");
}

docs.title: Important Java Note
docs.text:
normalize() resolves path syntax such as:

..

.

but filesystem-specific symlink behaviour may require additional consideration.

docs.title: .NET Conceptual Defence
docs.text:
var basePath = Path.GetFullPath(downloadDirectory);

var candidate = Path.GetFullPath(
    Path.Combine(basePath, userFile)
);

Then enforce that the canonical candidate belongs to the intended base directory using platform-appropriate path comparison.

docs.title: Node.js Conceptual Defence
docs.text:
const base = path.resolve("/srv/app/downloads");

const candidate = path.resolve(base, userFile);

Then verify that the final path is contained within the intended directory.

docs.title: Do Not Use Naive Prefix Checks
docs.text:
Example fragile logic:

candidate.startsWith("/srv/app/download")

could potentially confuse:

/srv/app/download

docs.title: curl Baseline

docs.title: curl Traversal
docs.text:
Use URL encoding carefully because curl may interpret or normalise URL components differently depending on how the request is constructed.

For query parameters:

curl -i 'https://target.example/download?file=..%2ftraversal-test.txt'

docs.title: Preserve Path Segments
docs.text:
When testing traversal directly inside a URL path, curl provides:

--path-as-is

to avoid normalising sequences such as ../ before sending them.

docs.title: curl Path Example
docs.text: curl --path-as-is -i 'https://target.example/files/../traversal-test.txt'

docs.title: Why --path-as-is Matters
docs.text:
Without it, the client may normalise:

before the request reaches the server.

docs.title: Browser Behaviour
docs.text:
Browsers can also normalise URL paths.

For precise traversal testing, Burp Repeater or curl with appropriate options is usually easier to reason about.

docs.text:

Reverse Proxy

Web Server

Framework

Application

docs.text:
A reverse proxy may:

Collapse dot segments

Reject encoded separators

docs.title: Application vs Proxy Finding
docs.text:
Determine which layer actually allows or blocks the traversal.

This matters for remediation.

docs.title: Web Server Static Files
docs.text:
Static file servers typically have built-in path handling.

Custom file-serving endpoints deserve particular attention because application code may bypass framework protections.

docs.title: Framework Helpers
docs.text:
Functions such as:

send_from_directory()

safe_join()

may provide security protections when used correctly.

Do not classify framework usage as vulnerable without tracing actual behaviour.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Filesystem permissions provide an important secondary control.

The application should not be able to read:

Private keys

Deployment secrets

Unrelated application data

System administration files

unless required.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
A containerised application's filesystem view may differ from the host.

Traversal may expose:

Container filesystem

Mounted configuration

Mounted secrets

Application files

docs.title: Do Not Assume Host Access
docs.text:
A path such as:

/etc/...

inside a container generally refers to the container's filesystem namespace unless host paths are mounted.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Application containers may have mounted:

Configuration

Secrets

Service account data

Volumes

The actual exposure depends on pod configuration and filesystem permissions.

Do not access sensitive mounted data unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Chroot / Sandbox
docs.text:
A process may operate inside a restricted filesystem environment.

Traversal may escape an application subdirectory while still remaining inside:

Container

chroot

sandbox

docs.title: Impact Should Reflect the Actual Boundary
docs.text:
Do not write:

Full server filesystem access

when testing only demonstrated:

Read access outside the application's intended download directory.

docs.title: Error-Based Discovery
docs.text:

docs.text:
This may reveal:

Framework

Filesystem structure

but an error alone is not proof that arbitrary files can be read.

docs.title: Directory Access
docs.text:
A file endpoint may behave differently when given a directory.

404

Application error

docs.title: File Existence Oracle
docs.text:
Different responses for:

Existing file

Non-existing file

may create a file existence oracle even if contents cannot be retrieved.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Existing:
403 Forbidden

Missing:
404 Not Found

This can disclose filesystem state.

docs.title: Report Separately When Appropriate
docs.text: A file existence oracle is generally weaker than arbitrary file read.

docs.title: Strong Evidence Chain
docs.text:
1. Retrieve legitimate file.

2. Show expected endpoint behaviour.

3. Submit minimal traversal.

4. Retrieve harmless known file outside intended directory.

5. Capture unique known marker.

6. Repeat if necessary.

7. Stop once the security boundary is demonstrated.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Path Traversal
docs.text: The file parameter used by the document download endpoint is incorporated into a filesystem path without adequately enforcing the intended download directory boundary. During testing, a relative path containing a parent-directory reference caused the application to retrieve an assessment-created file located outside the configured download directory. This demonstrates path traversal leading to unauthorised local file read.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Arbitrary File Read
docs.text: The download endpoint accepts an absolute filesystem path supplied by the authenticated user. A request referencing an assessment-created file outside the application's document directory returned the known file contents. The application therefore permits local file reads outside the intended storage location.

docs.title: Reporting Example - LFI
docs.text: The page parameter controls the local file passed to the application's inclusion mechanism. A relative traversal sequence caused the application to include a controlled local file outside the intended template directory, demonstrating local file inclusion.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Encoded Traversal
docs.text: Direct parent-directory sequences were rejected by the application; however, URL-encoded path separators were decoded after the validation step. Supplying the same traversal using encoded separators allowed the resulting canonical path to escape the intended directory and retrieve a controlled test file.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Write Traversal
docs.text: The application uses the client-supplied filename when constructing the output path for generated files. Parent-directory references in the filename caused a harmless assessment marker file to be written outside the intended output directory, demonstrating path traversal in a filesystem write operation.

docs.title: Avoid Overclaiming
docs.text:
Do not write:

The attacker can read every file on the server.

unless permissions and testing actually support that conclusion.

Prefer:

The application can read files outside the intended document directory that are accessible to the application process.

Accessible file sensitivity

docs.text: Use framework-provided secure file-serving helpers correctly where available.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: Retest the exact original endpoint and path.

docs.title: Retest Baseline
docs.text:
Confirm normal downloads still work:

manual.pdf

docs.title: Retest Original Traversal
docs.text:
Example:

Expected:

Rejected

or:

Not accessible

docs.title: Retest Encoded Variants

docs.title: Retest Windows Separators

docs.title: Retest Absolute Paths
docs.text: If the original application accepted absolute paths, confirm they are rejected unless explicitly required.

docs.title: Retest Normalisation
docs.text: Verify that canonical paths outside the base directory are rejected regardless of raw representation.

docs.title: Retest Symlinks
docs.text: Where symlink behaviour contributed to the original issue and the assessment permits it, verify the final filesystem resolution cannot escape the approved directory.

docs.title: Retest Write Operations
docs.text: If the original issue affected uploads or generated files, verify that output paths remain inside the approved directory.

docs.title: Retest Authorisation
docs.text:
Do not stop at traversal remediation.

Confirm legitimate file access still enforces ownership and role permissions.

docs.title: Root Cause Review
docs.text:
After finding one path traversal issue, search for equivalent file operations across the codebase.

Python:

rg -ni 'open\(|send_file|send_from_directory|Path\(' -g '*.py' .

Node.js:

rg -ni 'readFile|readFileSync|createReadStream|sendFile|path\.join|path\.resolve' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

Java:

rg -ni 'FileInputStream|Files\.read|Paths\.get|new File|Path\.of' -g '*.java' .

.NET:

rg -ni 'File\.Read|File\.Open|FileStream|Path\.Combine|PhysicalFile' -g '*.cs' .

PHP:

rg -ni 'include|require|readfile|file_get_contents|fopen' -g '*.php' .

Go:

rg -ni 'os\.Open|os\.ReadFile|filepath\.Join|filepath\.Clean|http\.ServeFile' -g '*.go' .

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
The key question is:

CAN USER-CONTROLLED INPUT
          |
          v
INFLUENCE A FILESYSTEM PATH
          |
          v
SO THAT THE FINAL RESOLVED PATH
          |
          v
ESCAPES THE INTENDED SECURITY BOUNDARY?

A strong path traversal workflow is:

Find File Function
       |
       v
Establish Baseline
       |
       v
Identify Intended Directory
       |
       v
Use Minimal Traversal
       |
       v
Retrieve Harmless Known File
       |
       v
Test Relevant Normalisation
       |
       v
Determine Actual Capability
       |
       v
Capture Evidence
       |
       v
Fix Path Handling
       |
       v
Retest

For every candidate ask:

What file operation occurs?

Does the user control a filename or a full path?

What is the intended base directory?

Is the path relative or absolute?

How is the path constructed?

Which component decodes the input?

Is URL decoding performed more than once?

Are path separators normalised?

Is the path canonicalised?

Is the canonical path checked against the intended root?

Are symbolic links relevant?

Does the application read, include or write the file?

Does the application use the client-supplied upload filename?

Does a file ID map to a server-controlled path?

Is authorisation checked independently?

What filesystem permissions does the application process have?

Is the application containerised?

Did I retrieve a known controlled file?

Did I demonstrate read access or only different errors?

Am I describing path traversal, LFI, RFI, SSRF or IDOR accurately?

What impact was actually demonstrated?

Was the root cause fixed or was one payload merely blocked?

The strongest evidence is not:

../ changed the response.

It is:

CONTROLLED FILE REFERENCE
          |
          v
PATH ESCAPES APPROVED DIRECTORY
          |
          v
KNOWN OUTSIDE FILE
          |
          v
KNOWN CONTENT RETURNED
          |
          v
REPEATABLE SECURITY BOUNDARY FAILURE

Use a controlled file when possible

If source access or a cooperative assessment allows it, create a harmless marker file outside the intended application directory and use that for validation. Retrieving TRAVERSAL_TEST_7f3a9 is cleaner evidence than unnecessarily reading operating-system or application secrets.

Canonical paths matter

A filter that searches for ../ is not equivalent to filesystem containment. Security decisions should be based on the final canonical path and whether that path remains inside the approved directory.

Classify the sink accurately

Reading a file, including a file, fetching a remote URL and accessing another user's document are different behaviours. Distinguishing path traversal, LFI, RFI, SSRF and IDOR makes both the technical analysis and remediation more precise.

Do not prove impact by collecting secrets

Once a harmless file outside the intended directory has been retrieved, the core security boundary failure is established. Access sensitive files only when additional impact validation is explicitly required by the assessment.

Do not fix individual payload strings

Blocking ../, %2f or one known system path does not address the root cause. Remove unnecessary user-controlled paths or canonicalise the final path and enforce that it remains within the approved filesystem root.

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process |
    ForEach-Object {
        $owner = Invoke-CimMethod -InputObject $_ -MethodName GetOwner -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

            PID     = $_.ProcessId
            Process = $_.Name
            User    = if ($owner.User) {
                "$($owner.Domain)\$($owner.User)"
            } else {

docs.title: PowerShell EncodedCommand
docs.text:
PowerShell's -EncodedCommand expects Base64 representing UTF-16LE command text.

Create an encoded command:

$command = 'Get-Date'

$bytes = [Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command)

$encoded = [Convert]::ToBase64String($bytes)

$encoded

Decode for analysis:

$bytes = [Convert]::FromBase64String($encoded)

[Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString($bytes)

Encoded commands are not encryption.

They are frequently used for legitimate automation as well as malicious activity.

InternalAllTheThings also highlights the UTF-16LE requirement for PowerShell encoded commands.

docs.title: FullLanguage
docs.text:
FullLanguage provides the normal PowerShell language capabilities.

It is common on ordinary Windows systems.

Do not automatically report:

LanguageMode = FullLanguage

as a vulnerability.

Instead determine whether the endpoint's intended security architecture requires application control and PowerShell restrictions for untrusted users.

docs.title: Constrained Language Mode
docs.text:
Constrained Language Mode restricts access to certain PowerShell language features and .NET capabilities.

Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

A result such as:

ConstrainedLanguage

should be evaluated together with:

AppLocker
WDAC / App Control
PowerShell Version
Security Product
Policy Scope

Do not attempt to bypass Constrained Language Mode merely to test whether it can be bypassed unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: InternalAllTheThings and Constrained Mode
docs.text:
InternalAllTheThings includes historical PowerShell constrained-mode techniques.

Treat historical techniques carefully.

For modern Windows environments, validate:

Windows Version
PowerShell Version
WDAC/AppLocker
Patch State
Current Microsoft Behaviour

before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: SecureString Security Note
docs.text:
SecureString should not be treated as a universal encrypted-secret storage solution.

Its behaviour and security properties depend on the platform and how it is persisted.

Do not convert protected secrets to plaintext merely for convenience during an assessment.

InternalAllTheThings includes SecureString-to-plaintext handling, but credential disclosure should only be performed where explicitly required and authorised.

docs.text:
InternalAllTheThings highlights PowerShell encoded-command handling.

For assessment and incident response, decoding an observed command is often more useful than executing it.

[Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString(

docs.text:

docs.text:

It is also one reason application-control and PowerShell security architecture should be assessed as a whole.

This cheatsheet intentionally does not include shellcode runners or memory-execution examples.

docs.title: SQL Injection Cheatsheet
docs.text:
SQL injection occurs when untrusted input influences the structure of a database query instead of being handled purely as data.

A simplified vulnerable flow is:

User Input
    |
    v
Application
    |
    v
SQL String Construction
    |
    v
Database

For example:

username = request.form["username"]

query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + username + "'"

cursor.execute(query)

Input is inserted directly into the SQL statement.

The intended query might be:

SELECT * FROM users
WHERE username = 'alice';

A security tester should determine whether supplied input can alter the SQL syntax or query logic.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform SQL injection testing only against applications and databases that are explicitly within scope. Start with low-impact detection and validation. Database extraction, file access, operating-system interaction, destructive queries and high-volume automation can materially affect systems and should only be performed when specifically authorised.

docs.title: Initial Character Tests
docs.text:
'

"

`

)

'))

These are probes, not proof of SQL injection.

docs.title: Boolean Comparison
docs.text:
AND 1=1

AND 1=2

String context may require different syntax.

docs.title: ORDER BY
docs.text:
ORDER BY 1

ORDER BY 2

ORDER BY 3

docs.title: UNION Shape
docs.text:
UNION SELECT NULL

UNION SELECT NULL,NULL

UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
Common SQL comment syntax includes:

--

#

/* */

Support depends on the DBMS and query context.

docs.text: sqlmap -u 'https://example.com/product?id=1'

   |
   v
Different Response
   |
   v
SQL Injection

Baseline
   |
   v
Controlled Input
   |
   v
Response Difference
   |
   v
Repeat
   |
   v
True / False Comparison
   |
   v
Understand Context
   |
   v
Confirm Database Influence
   |
   v
Determine Impact
   |
   v
Evidence

docs.title: Where to Test
docs.text:
Potential SQL-backed inputs include:

Query parameters

POST parameters

JSON properties

Path parameters

Cookies

HTTP headers

Search fields

Filters

Sorting parameters

Pagination

Login forms

Registration forms

Reporting functions

Export functions

Administrative interfaces

API parameters

docs.text:
?id=42

?user=alice

?category=books

?sort=name

?order=asc

?page=2

?filter=active

docs.title: Do Not Ignore Non-Numeric Inputs
docs.text:
SQL injection is not limited to:

?id=1

Inputs such as:

?username=alice

?category=laptops

?status=active

may also influence database queries.

docs.title: HTTP Headers
docs.text:
Applications may store or query values from:

User-Agent

Referer

X-Forwarded-For

X-Client-ID

Custom application headers

These are lower-probability inputs but can matter in logging, analytics and administrative workflows.

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Before modifying a parameter, capture the normal response.

Example:

GET /product?id=10 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

Record:

Status code

Response length

Response body

Response time

Redirects

Displayed records

Application errors

docs.title: Baseline Example
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 4821

Page:

Product: Security Handbook
Price: 49.99

docs.title: First Probe
docs.text:
A simple quote can test whether the input reaches a string-sensitive query:

GET /product?id=10' HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

Possible outcomes:

Same response

Different response

Application error

Database error

500 response

Empty result

Redirect

WAF response

docs.title: Quote Error Is Not Proof
docs.text:
Suppose:

?id=10'

returns:

500 Internal Server Error

This does not prove SQL injection.

The quote may cause:

Input validation failure

Framework parsing error

Application exception

WAF behaviour

Database syntax error

Further validation is required.

docs.title: Error-Based Clues
docs.text:
Database errors may expose strings such as:

SQL syntax

ODBC

JDBC

ORA-

PostgreSQL

SQLite

MySQL

SQL Server

Unclosed quotation mark

unterminated quoted string

These can indicate that database syntax was affected, but a controlled confirmation is still preferable.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
A practical manual workflow:

Proxy
  |
  v
Capture Request
  |
  v
Send to Repeater
  |
  v
Baseline
  |
  v
Modify One Input
  |
  v
Compare
  |
  v
Repeat
  |
  v
Document

docs.title: Send to Repeater
docs.text:
In Burp:

Proxy
  -> HTTP history
  -> Select request
  -> Send to Repeater

Then modify only the suspected input.

docs.title: Change One Variable at a Time
docs.text:
Bad methodology:

Change parameter

Change cookie

Change header

Change method

Change path

all in one request.

Better:

Baseline
   |
   v
Change One Parameter
   |
   v
Observe

docs.title: Numeric Context
docs.text:
Suppose the application constructs:

SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE id = 10;

Potential user input occupies:

10

without quotes.

This is a numeric context.

docs.title: String Context
docs.text:
Suppose:

SELECT id, username
FROM users
WHERE username = 'alice';

The input occupies:

'alice'

A successful test must account for the surrounding quote.

docs.title: Context Matters
docs.text:
The same payload will not work in every query.

Potential contexts include:

Numeric

Single-quoted string

Double-quoted identifier/string depending on DBMS

LIKE expression

ORDER BY

LIMIT/OFFSET

INSERT

UPDATE

Nested subquery

docs.title: Boolean-Based Validation
docs.text:
A useful low-impact approach is comparing logically true and false expressions.

Conceptually:

Original Request
      |
      v
True Condition
      |
      v
Response A

False Condition
      |
      v
Response B

If the application consistently behaves differently, investigate further.

docs.title: Numeric Boolean Example
docs.text:
Baseline:

?id=10

True condition:

?id=10 AND 1=1

False condition:

?id=10 AND 1=2

docs.title: Expected Pattern
docs.text:
Potentially vulnerable behaviour:

?id=10
        -> Product returned

?id=10 AND 1=1
        -> Same product returned

?id=10 AND 1=2
        -> Product not returned

This is much stronger evidence than a single error response.

docs.title: Repeatability
docs.text:
Repeat each request.

For example:

Baseline
True
False
True
False
Baseline

This helps distinguish deterministic database behaviour from:

Caching

Dynamic content

Load balancing

Random application errors

Rate limiting

docs.title: String Boolean Example
docs.text:
A string parameter may require closing the original string before adding a condition.

Conceptually:

WHERE category = '<INPUT>'

A test must preserve valid SQL syntax while producing controlled true and false conditions.

Exact syntax depends on the query and DBMS.

docs.title: Response Comparison
docs.text:
Compare:

Status

Length

Words

Lines

Specific text

Number of records

JSON properties

Redirects

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
True:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 5821

Contains:

12 products found

False:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 2910

Contains:

No products found

The status remains:

200

but the application state differs.

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Burp Comparer can help compare responses where differences are subtle.

Useful workflow:

True Response
     |
     v
Send to Comparer

False Response
     |
     v
Send to Comparer
     |
     v
Compare

docs.title: Dynamic Responses
docs.text:
Response length alone may be unreliable when pages contain:

CSRF tokens

Timestamps

Request IDs

Random recommendations

Advertisements

User-specific content

Look for stable semantic differences.

docs.title: Stable Response Markers
docs.text:
Examples:

"productFound": true

"count": 12

"No results"

"Welcome alice"

Specific table row

docs.title: ORDER BY Technique
docs.text:
ORDER BY can sometimes help determine the number of selected columns.

Example sequence:

ORDER BY 1

ORDER BY 2

ORDER BY 3

ORDER BY 4

Conceptually:

ORDER BY 1
    -> Valid

ORDER BY 2
    -> Valid

ORDER BY 3
    -> Valid

ORDER BY 4
    -> Error

This may suggest:

3 selected columns

provided the behaviour is caused by SQL ordering rather than application logic.

docs.title: ORDER BY Interpretation
docs.text:
Do not conclude column count from one failed request.

Confirm:

ORDER BY 3 consistently works

ORDER BY 4 consistently fails

docs.title: UNION-Based SQL Injection
docs.text:
UNION combines the result sets of compatible SELECT statements.

Conceptually:

SELECT a,b
FROM products

UNION

SELECT c,d
FROM another_table;

The result sets generally need compatible column counts and data types.

docs.title: Determine Column Count
docs.text:
A common controlled approach uses NULL:

UNION SELECT NULL

UNION SELECT NULL,NULL

UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL

Increase until the query shape is accepted.

docs.title: Why NULL?
docs.text:
NULL is often useful because it can be compatible with multiple data types.

It is not guaranteed to work in every context.

docs.title: UNION Example
docs.text:
Suppose:

UNION SELECT NULL,NULL

fails but:

UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL

succeeds.

This suggests a three-column result may be involved.

docs.title: Determine Reflected Column
docs.text:
After determining the query shape, a harmless marker can help determine which output column is rendered.

Conceptually:

UNION SELECT NULL,'TEST123',NULL

If:

TEST123

appears in the page, that column is reflected.

docs.title: Do Not Jump Directly to Data Extraction
docs.text:
For many assessments, proving:

Controlled UNION data can be returned

is enough to demonstrate the vulnerability.

Bulk database extraction may not be necessary and may exceed scope.

docs.title: UNION Validation Model
docs.text:
Determine Column Count
        |
        v
Determine Compatible Columns
        |
        v
Place Harmless Marker
        |
        v
Marker Appears
        |
        v
SQL Query Influence Confirmed

docs.title: Error-Based SQL Injection
docs.text:
Some DBMS operations can cause controlled database errors that include query-derived information.

The exact functions and behaviour differ substantially between:

MySQL

MariaDB

PostgreSQL

Microsoft SQL Server

Oracle

SQLite

For normal assessments, prefer the least invasive proof necessary.

docs.title: Error-Based Testing Principle
docs.text:
A useful error-based proof demonstrates:

Input
  |
  v
Database Expression
  |
  v
Controlled Database Error

rather than merely crashing the application.

docs.title: Boolean Blind SQL Injection
docs.text:
Blind SQL injection occurs when query results are not directly displayed.

Instead, the tester infers database behaviour from differences such as:

Content

Status

Redirect

Boolean state

docs.title: Boolean Blind Model
docs.text:
Condition True
     |
     v
Response A

Condition False
     |
     v
Response B

If this is repeatable, individual facts can theoretically be inferred through true/false questions.

docs.title: Keep Blind Validation Minimal
docs.text:
A formal assessment usually does not require extracting an entire database.

A minimal proof can demonstrate:

True expression produces state A.

False expression produces state B.

This is often sufficient to establish query control.

docs.title: Time-Based Blind SQL Injection
docs.text:
Time-based testing is useful when:

Response body does not change

Status does not change

No errors are shown

but database-controlled delay can influence response time.

docs.title: Time-Based Model
docs.text:
Normal Request
      |
      v
Baseline Timing

Conditional Delay Request
      |
      v
Longer Timing

Control Request
      |
      v
Normal Timing

docs.title: Timing Requires Repetition
docs.text:
Do not use:

One request took 5 seconds

as proof.

Network latency can vary.

docs.title: Better Timing Test
docs.text:
Collect multiple measurements:

Baseline:
0.31
0.28
0.34
0.30
0.29

Control:
0.33
0.30
0.31

Conditional delay:
5.31
5.29
5.34

A repeated, controlled delay is much stronger evidence.

docs.title: Timing Noise
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Network latency

Database load

Application load

Rate limiting

Queueing

CDN behaviour

WAF processing

Garbage collection

docs.title: Keep Delays Short
docs.text:
Do not use unnecessarily long delays.

A small repeatable difference is preferable to repeatedly holding database connections open for long periods.

docs.title: DBMS Identification
docs.text:
Identifying the DBMS can help select appropriate syntax.

Possible systems:

MySQL / MariaDB

PostgreSQL

Microsoft SQL Server

Oracle Database

SQLite

docs.title: Do Not Rely Only on Server Errors
docs.text:
DBMS identification can also come from:

Application stack

Dependency files

Connection strings

Source code

Database drivers

SQL syntax

SQLMap fingerprinting

docs.title: Common DBMS Characteristics
docs.text: DBMS Common Indicators MySQL/MariaDB MySQL drivers, backticks, LIMIT PostgreSQL PostgreSQL drivers, ::type, RETURNING SQL Server SqlClient, T-SQL, TOP, brackets Oracle Oracle drivers, PL/SQL, DUAL SQLite SQLite libraries, local .db files

docs.title: SQL Comments
docs.text: Common syntax:

docs.title: Standard SQL-Style
docs.text:
-- comment

Some DBMSs require whitespace after -- in particular contexts.

docs.title: MySQL-Style
docs.text: # comment

docs.title: Block Comment
docs.text: /* comment */

docs.title: Comment Syntax Matters
docs.text:
If the application appends SQL after user input, correctly terminating or balancing the remainder of the original query may be necessary for controlled testing.

Do not assume one comment form works everywhere.

docs.title: Authentication Forms
docs.text:
Login queries are a classic SQL injection location.

Conceptually vulnerable code:

SELECT id
FROM users
WHERE username = '<username>'
AND password = '<password>';

Modern applications should not construct authentication queries this way and should not store passwords in directly comparable plaintext form.

docs.title: Authentication Testing
docs.text:
During authorised testing, focus on whether:

Input alters authentication query logic

rather than attempting access to arbitrary real accounts.

docs.title: Search Functionality
docs.text:
Search functions commonly produce queries using:

LIKE

Example:

SELECT id, title
FROM articles
WHERE title LIKE '%<search>%';

The surrounding % and quotes affect injection context.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Filters may generate:

WHERE status = ?
AND category = ?

or dynamically concatenate conditions.

Dynamic query builders deserve careful review.

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
Sorting parameters can be interesting because identifiers often cannot be parameterised in the same way as normal values.

Example application logic:

?sort=name

may influence:

ORDER BY name

Safe implementations should map user choices to known server-side column identifiers.

docs.title: Safe Sort Mapping
docs.text:
Example:

allowed_sort = {
    "name": "name",
    "date": "created_at",
    "price": "price"
}

column = allowed_sort.get(request.args.get("sort"), "name")

The user selects a logical option rather than supplying arbitrary SQL.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Review:

page

limit

offset

size

These values may influence:

LIMIT

OFFSET

TOP

depending on DBMS.

docs.title: JSON APIs
docs.text:
Example:

POST /api/search HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "laptop",
  "sort": "price"
}

Test each field independently.

docs.title: Nested JSON
docs.text:
Do not overlook:

{
  "filter": {
    "category": "books",
    "owner": "alice"
  }
}

Nested properties can reach separate database operations.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL resolvers may ultimately construct database queries.

Test the application's GraphQL inputs and resolver behaviour rather than assuming GraphQL itself prevents SQL injection.

See:

GraphQL Notes

docs.title: REST APIs
docs.text:
Potential parameters exist in:

Path

Query

JSON body

Headers

Cookies

Example:

GET /api/users/42

The path value:

42

may become a database identifier.

docs.title: Stored / Second-Order SQL Injection
docs.text:
Second-order SQL injection occurs when malicious or malformed input is stored safely at one stage but later used unsafely in a different SQL query.

Conceptually:

Input
  |
  v
Stored in Database
  |
  v
Later Retrieved
  |
  v
Concatenated Into New SQL
  |
  v
Injection

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
Registration
     |
     v
Display Name Stored
     |
     v
Admin Reporting Function
     |
     v
Display Name Added to Dynamic SQL

The vulnerable behaviour occurs later, not during initial storage.

docs.title: Second-Order Testing
docs.text:
Track user-controlled values across workflows:

Create

Store

Read

Update

Search

Export

Admin view

Reporting

docs.title: Common Second-Order Locations
docs.text:
User profiles

Organisation names

Saved searches

Report names

Imported records

CSV data

Administrative dashboards

Audit/log viewers

docs.title: Out-of-Band Behaviour
docs.text:
Some database environments can perform external network interactions through database or extension functionality.

Out-of-band testing can have broader operational consequences and should only be used when specifically authorised.

For normal SQL injection validation, prefer:

Boolean

Error

UNION marker

Controlled timing

where possible.

docs.title: Stored Procedures
docs.text:
Stored procedures do not automatically prevent SQL injection.

Safe:

Stored procedure
    |
    v
Parameters
    |
    v
Static SQL

Potentially unsafe:

Stored procedure
    |
    v
Dynamic SQL String
    |
    v
EXECUTE

docs.title: ORM Does Not Automatically Prevent SQL Injection
docs.text:
ORMs reduce many SQL injection risks when their normal parameterised APIs are used.

Risk can return through:

Raw queries

String concatenation

Dynamic filters

Dynamic sorting

Unsafe query fragments

docs.title: Source-Code Review
docs.text:
Search for database operations using ripgrep.

Python:

rg -ni 'execute\(|executemany\(|raw\(' -g '*.py' .

Java:

rg -ni 'createStatement|prepareStatement|executeQuery|executeUpdate' -g '*.java' .

PHP:

rg -ni 'mysqli_query|->query\(|->prepare\(' -g '*.php' .

.NET:

rg -ni 'SqlCommand|ExecuteReader|ExecuteNonQuery|FromSqlRaw' -g '*.cs' .

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Review
docs.text:
HTTP Input
    |
    v
Variable
    |
    v
Transformation
    |
    v
Query Construction
    |
    v
Database API

docs.title: Vulnerable Source Example
docs.text:
user_id = request.args["id"]

query = "SELECT username FROM users WHERE id = " + user_id

cursor.execute(query)

docs.title: Safer Source Example
docs.text:
user_id = request.args["id"]

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT username FROM users WHERE id = %s",
    (user_id,)
)

Exact placeholder syntax depends on the database driver.

docs.title: Important Distinction
docs.text:
This:

query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + user_id
cursor.execute(query)

is different from:

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s",
    (user_id,)
)

The second separates:

SQL structure

from:

data.

docs.title: Search String Formatting
docs.text:
Python:

rg -n 'execute\(.*f"|execute\(.*format|execute\(.*\+' -g '*.py' .

This is heuristic only.

A match requires manual review.

docs.title: Search Raw SQL in ORMs
docs.text:
Examples:

rg -ni 'raw\(|execute\(|FromSqlRaw|createNativeQuery' .

Again:

Raw SQL

does not automatically mean:

SQL injection.

docs.title: Validation Questions
docs.text:
For every candidate ask:

Is user input involved?

Can the user control SQL structure?

Is parameterisation used?

Is an allowlist used for identifiers?

Does validation occur before the query?

Is the code reachable?

Which database driver is used?

Is the affected query read-only?

What privileges does the database account have?

docs.title: Database Privileges Matter
docs.text:
SQL injection impact depends partly on the application's database account.

Potential privileges:

SELECT

INSERT

UPDATE

DELETE

CREATE

DROP

EXECUTE

A least-privileged account can reduce impact.

docs.title: Do Not Assume DBA Privileges
docs.text:
A SQL injection vulnerability does not automatically imply:

Database administrator

Operating-system access

File-system access

Determine actual privileges only as far as authorised and necessary.

docs.title: SQLMap
docs.text:
SQLMap can automate SQL injection detection and validation.

Use it after understanding the request and obtaining a manual baseline where possible.

docs.title: Basic GET Request
docs.text: sqlmap -u 'https://example.com/product?id=10'

docs.title: Specific Parameter
docs.text: sqlmap -u 'https://example.com/product?id=10' -p id

docs.title: POST Data
docs.text: sqlmap -u 'https://example.com/search' --data='q=test'

docs.title: JSON Request
docs.text:
sqlmap -u 'https://example.com/api/search' \
  --method POST \
  --data='{"query":"test"}' \
  --headers='Content-Type: application/json'

docs.title: Burp Request File
docs.text:
Save the raw HTTP request as:

request.txt

Then:

sqlmap -r request.txt

docs.title: Why -r Is Useful
docs.text:
It preserves complex request details such as:

Method

Path

Cookies

Headers

POST body

JSON

Authentication

docs.title: Select Parameter With Request File
docs.text: sqlmap -r request.txt -p id

docs.title: Batch Mode
docs.text:
sqlmap -r request.txt -p id --batch

Use automation cautiously because automatic choices may increase test volume.

docs.title: SQLMap Level
docs.text:
SQLMap provides increasing test levels.

Check installed help:

sqlmap -hh

Higher levels can test additional inputs and send more requests.

docs.title: SQLMap Risk
docs.text:
SQLMap also has a risk setting.

Before increasing it, review:

sqlmap -hh

Higher-risk tests may include queries with greater operational impact.

Do not increase settings simply because the default did not find anything.

docs.title: Technique Selection
docs.text:
SQLMap supports technique selection.

Common technique letters include categories for:

Boolean-based blind

Error-based

UNION query

Stacked queries

Time-based blind

Inline queries

Check:

sqlmap -hh

for the exact syntax supported by your installed version.

docs.title: Restrict Automation
docs.text:
A better workflow is:

Understand Request
      |
      v
Identify Candidate Parameter
      |
      v
Manual Validation
      |
      v
SQLMap Against Specific Parameter

rather than:

Run SQLMap Everywhere

docs.title: SQLMap Through Proxy
docs.text:
When you need to observe a small controlled SQLMap test in Burp, review SQLMap's current proxy options:

sqlmap -hh

Large automated scans through Burp can create substantial proxy history.

docs.title: SQLMap Output Interpretation
docs.text:
Do not report:

SQLMap says parameter is injectable.

Capture:

Parameter

Injection type

DBMS

Representative request

Representative response

Manual confirmation

Security consequence

docs.title: SQLMap False Positives
docs.text:
Automation can be confused by:

Dynamic pages

Unstable responses

WAFs

Rate limiting

Caching

Random server errors

Authentication expiry

Manually validate important findings.

docs.title: WAF Behaviour
docs.text:
SQL injection probes may trigger:

403

406

429

Connection reset

Challenge page

This demonstrates defensive behaviour, not necessarily the presence or absence of SQL injection.

docs.title: Do Not Treat WAF Blocking as Proof of Safety
docs.text:
A WAF may block:

obvious test string

while the underlying application still constructs unsafe queries.

The appropriate conclusion is:

The tested request was blocked by a defensive control.

not:

The application is not vulnerable.

docs.title: Do Not Automatically Evade WAFs
docs.text:
If WAF bypass testing is not explicitly part of scope, do not escalate into obfuscation or bypass techniques simply to continue automated testing.

Document the control and coordinate where necessary.

docs.title: Authentication Expiry
docs.text:
Automated testing may fail because:

Session expires

CSRF token changes

JWT expires

Anti-automation token rotates

Reconfirm the request remains valid.

docs.title: CSRF Tokens
docs.text:
If a request requires a dynamic CSRF token, manual Repeater testing may be easier.

For automation, use tool-supported token handling only when necessary and within scope.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Authenticated request:

Cookie: session=<session>

Treat session values as credentials.

Do not expose them in screenshots or reports unnecessarily.

docs.title: HTTP Parameter Pollution
docs.text:
Applications may behave differently when a parameter is supplied more than once:

?id=1&id=2

This is not SQL injection itself but can affect which value reaches the query.

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
Burp normally helps URL-encode request parameters.

Remember:

URL syntax

Application decoding

Framework parsing

Database syntax

are separate processing stages.

docs.title: Prepared Statements
docs.text:
Prepared statements are the primary defence for data values.

Conceptually:

SQL Template
      +
Parameter Values
      |
      v
Database Driver

The values are not interpreted as query structure.

docs.title: Java Example
docs.text:
Safer:

PreparedStatement stmt =
    connection.prepareStatement(
        "SELECT id, username FROM users WHERE username = ?"
    );

stmt.setString(1, username);

docs.title: C# Example
docs.text:
Safer:

using var command = new SqlCommand(
    "SELECT Id, Username FROM Users WHERE Username = @username",
    connection
);

command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@username", username);

docs.title: PHP PDO Example
docs.text:
Safer:

$stmt = $pdo->prepare(
    "SELECT id, username FROM users WHERE username = ?"
);

$stmt->execute([$username]);

docs.title: Python Example
docs.text:
Driver syntax varies.

Conceptually:

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT id, username FROM users WHERE username = %s",
    (username,)
)

docs.title: Dynamic Identifiers
docs.text:
Parameters often cannot directly represent SQL identifiers such as:

Table names

Column names

ASC / DESC

Use allowlists.

docs.title: Sort Direction Example
docs.text:
direction = request.args.get("direction", "asc").lower()

if direction not in {"asc", "desc"}:
    direction = "asc"

Then map only known server-controlled values into the query.

docs.title: Input Validation Is Secondary
docs.text:
Validation is useful, but do not use it as the sole SQL injection defence.

Prefer:

Parameterised Query
        +
Input Validation
        +
Least Privilege

docs.title: Escaping Alone Is Fragile
docs.text:
Manually escaping:

'

or other SQL characters is error-prone because behaviour depends on:

DBMS

Encoding

Connection settings

Query context

Use the database driver's parameterisation facilities.

docs.title: Stored Procedures
docs.text:
Stored procedures should use parameters internally.

Avoid:

Stored Procedure
      |
      v
String Concatenation
      |
      v
Dynamic SQL

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Application database accounts should receive only required permissions.

For example:

Reporting Application

Needs:
SELECT

Does not need:
DROP
CREATE
ALTER

docs.title: Separate Accounts
docs.text:
Where appropriate:

Read-only component
      -> Read-only DB account

Write component
      -> Limited write account

Administration
      -> Separate privileged workflow

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Production applications should not expose raw database errors.

Bad:

SQLSTATE[42000] ...

ORA-00933 ...

Unclosed quotation mark ...

Prefer controlled application errors while retaining useful server-side logging.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Log enough to investigate suspicious behaviour without logging:

Passwords

Full authentication tokens

Sensitive query results

Unnecessary personal information

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Potential SQL injection indicators include:

Repeated syntax errors

Unusual SQL keywords in parameters

High request volume against one parameter

Repeated true/false patterns

Repeated delayed requests

Database errors

docs.title: Detection Limitations
docs.text:
Do not rely only on keyword matching such as:

UNION SELECT

because:

Legitimate requests may contain SQL terminology

Attack strings can vary

Application context matters

docs.title: Database Monitoring
docs.text:
Useful defensive telemetry can include:

Database errors

Query failures

Unusual query shapes

Unexpected database account activity

Slow queries

Privilege violations

docs.title: Application Telemetry
docs.text:
Capture:

Request ID

Route

User/account

Parameter names

Status

Response time

Application exception

Avoid storing sensitive parameter values unless necessary and approved.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a SQL injection finding record:

Finding ID

Target

Endpoint

Method

Parameter

Authentication context

Baseline request

Baseline response

True request

True response

False request

False response

Injection technique

DBMS if established

Security impact

Database privileges if relevant

Timestamp

docs.title: Minimal Evidence
docs.text:
A strong proof might contain:

1. Baseline request returns product.

2. True SQL condition returns same product.

3. False SQL condition returns no product.

4. Behaviour is repeatable.

5. Only the tested parameter changes.

docs.title: Avoid Sensitive Database Dumps
docs.text:
Do not place large extracted datasets in a report.

Prefer the minimum evidence necessary to prove impact.

docs.title: Sensitive Data
docs.text:
If limited data access must be demonstrated:

Use a controlled test record where possible.

Minimise rows.

Redact unnecessary values.

Stop once impact is established.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Boolean SQL Injection
docs.text:
Weak:

The id parameter is vulnerable to SQL injection.

Better:

The id parameter on GET /product influences the application's database query. A logically true condition produced the normal product response, while an equivalent false condition consistently produced the application's no-result state. Repeated control requests produced the original response, demonstrating that the parameter can alter database query logic.

docs.title: Reporting Example - UNION SQL Injection
docs.text: The category parameter was confirmed to influence a SQL query. After determining the result shape, a controlled UNION SELECT test caused a harmless marker supplied by the tester to be returned in the application response. This demonstrates that attacker-controlled SQL result data can be incorporated into the application's query output.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Time-Based SQL Injection
docs.text: The tested parameter produced a repeatable database-controlled timing difference. Baseline and false-condition requests consistently completed within the normal response range, while the conditional-delay expression introduced the expected additional delay across repeated trials. No bulk database extraction was performed.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Source Review
docs.text: The application constructs the product lookup query by concatenating the id request parameter directly into the SQL statement before passing the resulting string to the database driver. No parameterisation was identified in the reviewed data flow. Runtime validation confirmed that controlled boolean expressions alter the query result.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Primary recommendation:

Use parameterised queries / prepared statements.

Also:

Allowlist dynamic identifiers.

Validate input according to business requirements.

Use least-privileged database accounts.

Avoid exposing raw database errors.

Review similar query construction throughout the application.

Add regression tests.

docs.title: Root Cause Review
docs.text:
Do not remediate only:

/product?id=

Search for the coding pattern.

For example:

String concatenation
      |
      v
Database execution

may exist in multiple endpoints.

docs.title: Source Search During Remediation
docs.text:
Python:

rg -ni 'execute\(|executemany\(|raw\(' -g '*.py' .

.NET:

rg -ni 'SqlCommand|FromSqlRaw|ExecuteSqlRaw' -g '*.cs' .

Java:

rg -ni 'createStatement|prepareStatement|createNativeQuery' -g '*.java' .

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Retest the exact original endpoint and parameter first.

Original Request
      |
      v
Original True Condition
      |
      v
Original False Condition
      |
      v
No SQL-Controlled Difference
      |
      v
Normal Functionality Works

docs.title: Do Not Retest Only the Original String
docs.text:
A developer may block one test string without fixing the query.

For example:

Block "UNION"

does not fix:

String concatenation into SQL.

Retest the root cause.

docs.title: Source-Level Retest
docs.text:
Confirm the code now uses:

Parameterised query

rather than:

User input concatenated into SQL.

docs.title: Functional Retest
docs.text:
Also verify:

Valid product lookup works

Search works

Sorting works

Filtering works

Pagination works

Security remediation should not unnecessarily break intended functionality.

docs.title: Regression Testing
docs.text:
Add tests such as:

Normal input returns expected data.

Special characters are treated as data.

Boolean SQL syntax does not alter query logic.

Invalid identifiers are rejected.

Authorised functionality remains available.

docs.title: Generic 500 Error
docs.text:
'
   -> 500

Could be:

Application parser

Validation

WAF

Unhandled exception

Need controlled SQL-specific confirmation.

docs.title: Different Response Length
docs.text:
Could be:

Dynamic token

Timestamp

Random content

Cache

Personalisation

docs.title: Slow Response
docs.text:
Could be:

Network

Load

Rate limit

Database contention

Need repeated controlled timing.

docs.title: SQL Keyword Blocked
docs.text:
Could indicate:

WAF rule

not necessarily SQL injection.

docs.title: SQL Error in Page
docs.text:
A database error confirms database-related processing but does not always prove attacker-controlled query structure.

Validate further.

docs.title: Testing Only Quotes
docs.text:
'

is a probe, not a complete methodology.

docs.title: Testing Only Numeric IDs
docs.text: Search, sorting, filters and JSON APIs are also important.

docs.title: Trusting SQLMap Without Manual Validation
docs.text: Automation should support analysis, not replace it.

docs.title: Dumping the Database Immediately
docs.text: Usually unnecessary for proving SQL injection.

docs.title: Ignoring Authentication Context
docs.text:
A vulnerability available only to:

Administrator

has a different threat model from one available to:

Unauthenticated Internet User.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
The goal is not to send the largest number of SQL payloads.

The goal is to establish whether:

USER-CONTROLLED DATA
        |
        v
CAN ALTER
        |
        v
DATABASE QUERY STRUCTURE

A defensible workflow is:

Baseline
   |
   v
Identify Input
   |
   v
Controlled Probe
   |
   v
True / False Comparison
   |
   v
Repeat
   |
   v
Understand SQL Context
   |
   v
Minimal Confirmation
   |
   v
Determine Impact
   |
   v
Evidence
   |
   v
Remediation
   |
   v
Retest Root Cause

For every candidate ask:

What parameter is being tested?

What was the baseline?

What exactly changed?

Can the behaviour be reproduced?

Does a true condition behave differently from a false condition?

Could application validation explain the difference?

Could a WAF explain it?

Could dynamic content explain it?

What SQL context is likely involved?

Which DBMS is involved?

What is the minimum evidence needed?

What privileges does the database account have?

Is sensitive data actually exposed?

Does the issue require authentication?

Is there a second-order path?

Does source code confirm unsafe construction?

Has the root cause been fixed with parameterisation?

The strongest SQL injection finding is not:

SQLMap found SQLi.

It is:

Input
  |
  v
Controlled SQL Behaviour
  |
  v
Repeatable Evidence
  |
  v
Security Consequence
