docs.title: Capture With tshark
docs.text:
Basic:

sudo tshark -i eth0

Specific interface:

sudo tshark -i tun0

Write directly to file:

sudo tshark -i tun0 -w assessment.pcapng

docs.title: Capture a Limited Number of Packets
docs.text:
sudo tshark -i eth0 -c 100

Write 100 packets:

sudo tshark -i eth0 -c 100 -w capture.pcapng

docs.title: Capture for a Fixed Duration
docs.text:
Capture for 60 seconds:

sudo tshark -i eth0 -a duration:60 -w capture.pcapng

docs.title: Capture File Size Limit
docs.text:
Example:

sudo tshark -i eth0 -a filesize:100000 -w capture.pcapng

Review local tshark help for the units and behaviour supported by the installed version.

docs.title: Capture Filters vs Display Filters
docs.text:
This distinction is extremely important.

CAPTURE FILTER
     |
     v
Controls what is recorded

DISPLAY FILTER
     |
     v
Controls what recorded traffic is displayed

docs.title: Capture Filter
docs.text:
Capture filters use BPF-style syntax.

Example:

sudo tshark -i eth0 -f 'host 192.168.1.10'

Only matching traffic is captured.

docs.title: Display Filter
docs.text:
Display filters use Wireshark syntax.

Example:

tshark -r capture.pcapng -Y 'ip.addr == 192.168.1.10'

The entire capture remains intact, but only matching packets are displayed.

docs.title: Why the Difference Matters
docs.text:
If you use an overly restrictive capture filter:

Uncaptured traffic is gone.

If you use a display filter:

Other packets remain available in the PCAP.

For investigative work, a broader capture followed by focused display filtering is often safer when storage and privacy constraints permit.

docs.title: Common Capture Filters
docs.text:
Single host:

host 192.168.1.10

Source host:

src host 192.168.1.10

Destination host:

dst host 192.168.1.10

TCP:

tcp

UDP:

udp

Port:

port 443

TCP port:

tcp port 443

UDP port:

udp port 53

Network:

net 192.168.1.0/24

docs.title: Combine Capture Filters
docs.text:
Host and port:

host 192.168.1.10 and port 443

HTTP or HTTPS:

tcp port 80 or tcp port 443

Exclude SSH management traffic:

not port 22

Example:

sudo tshark -i eth0 -f 'host 192.168.1.10 and not port 22'

docs.title: Common Display Filters
docs.text:
IPv4:

ip

IPv6:

ipv6

TCP:

tcp

UDP:

udp

DNS:

dns

HTTP:

http

TLS:

tls

SMB:

smb

SMB2/3:

smb2

Kerberos:

kerberos

LDAP:

ldap

ICMP:

icmp

docs.title: Filter by IP
docs.text:
Either source or destination:

ip.addr == 192.168.1.10

Source:

ip.src == 192.168.1.10

Destination:

ip.dst == 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Filter by TCP Port
docs.text:
tcp.port == 443

Source:

tcp.srcport == 443

Destination:

tcp.dstport == 443

docs.title: Filter by UDP Port
docs.text: udp.port == 53

docs.title: Combine Display Filters
docs.text:
AND:

ip.addr == 192.168.1.10 && tcp.port == 443

OR:

tcp.port == 80 || tcp.port == 443

NOT:

!(tcp.port == 22)

docs.title: TCP Analysis
docs.text: TCP analysis is one of the most valuable uses of Wireshark.

docs.title: TCP Handshake
docs.text:
Normal handshake:

Client                         Server
  |                              |
  | -------- SYN -------------> |
  |                              |
  | <------ SYN/ACK ------------ |
  |                              |
  | -------- ACK -------------> |
  |                              |
  |       Connection Ready       |

docs.title: SYN Filter
docs.text: tcp.flags.syn == 1

docs.title: Initial SYN Without ACK
docs.text:
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0

Useful for identifying connection attempts.

docs.title: SYN/ACK
docs.text: tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 1

docs.title: Reset
docs.text:
tcp.flags.reset == 1

A reset may indicate:

Closed port

Application rejection

Connection termination

Firewall behaviour

Protocol mismatch

Context matters.

docs.title: FIN
docs.text: tcp.flags.fin == 1

docs.title: TCP Retransmissions
docs.text:
tcp.analysis.retransmission

Retransmissions can result from:

Packet loss

Congestion

Delayed responses

Network path problems

Capture artefacts

Do not automatically interpret retransmissions as a security issue.

docs.title: Duplicate ACK
docs.text: tcp.analysis.duplicate_ack

docs.title: Lost Segment
docs.text:
tcp.analysis.lost_segment

Remember that a capture taken at only one network position may itself miss packets.

docs.title: TCP Stream
docs.text:
A TCP stream represents a conversation.

Wireshark:

Right-click packet
    |
    v
Follow
    |
    v
TCP Stream

This can reconstruct application traffic where the protocol is not encrypted.

docs.title: Filter a TCP Stream
docs.text:
tcp.stream == 5

The stream number depends on the capture.

docs.title: tshark TCP Stream
docs.text:
List stream values:

tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -T fields \
  -e tcp.stream | sort -n | uniq

Follow a selected stream:

tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z follow,tcp,ascii,0

docs.title: Connection Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Suppose:

Client -> SYN -> Server

but no SYN/ACK returns.

Possible explanations:

Firewall silently dropping traffic

Target offline

Routing problem

Packet lost

Capture point cannot see return traffic

Do not conclude:

Port is closed.

A closed TCP port often produces a reset, while silent filtering may produce no response.

docs.title: DNS Analysis
docs.text:
Display DNS:

dns

docs.title: DNS Queries
docs.text: dns.flags.response == 0

docs.title: DNS Responses
docs.text: dns.flags.response == 1

docs.title: Query Name
docs.text:
dns.qry.name

Example filter:

dns.qry.name == "example.com"

docs.title: Query Contains Text
docs.text: dns.qry.name contains "example"

docs.title: A Record Queries
docs.text: dns.qry.type == 1

docs.title: AAAA Queries
docs.text: dns.qry.type == 28

docs.title: DNS Response Code
docs.text: dns.flags.rcode

docs.title: NXDOMAIN
docs.text:
dns.flags.rcode == 3

This can help identify failed hostname resolution.

docs.title: Extract DNS Queries With tshark
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0' \
  -T fields \
  -e frame.time \
  -e ip.src \
  -e dns.qry.name

docs.title: Unique DNS Queries
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0' \
  -T fields \
  -e dns.qry.name | sort -u

docs.title: DNS Troubleshooting Workflow
docs.text:
Application Request
       |
       v
DNS Query Generated?
      / \
    No   Yes
    |     |
    v     v
Client   DNS Response?
Issue      / \
         No   Yes
         |     |
         v     v
      Network  Correct IP?
      / DNS      / \
                No  Yes
                |    |
                v    v
              DNS   Continue
             Issue  Connection

docs.title: HTTP Analysis
docs.text:
Display:

http

Requests:

http.request

Responses:

http.response

docs.title: HTTP Request Method
docs.text:
http.request.method

GET:

http.request.method == "GET"

POST:

http.request.method == "POST"

docs.title: HTTP Host
docs.text:
http.host

Example:

http.host == "example.com"

docs.title: HTTP URI
docs.text:
http.request.uri

Contains:

http.request.uri contains "/api/"

docs.title: HTTP Status
docs.text:
http.response.code

Example:

http.response.code == 403

docs.title: HTTP Error Responses
docs.text:
http.response.code >= 400

This can quickly identify:

400

401

403

404

429

500

responses in unencrypted HTTP traffic.

docs.title: Extract HTTP Requests
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'http.request' \
  -T fields \
  -e frame.time \
  -e ip.src \
  -e http.request.method \
  -e http.host \
  -e http.request.uri

docs.title: HTTP Credentials
docs.text:
Unencrypted HTTP traffic may expose:

Cookies

Authorization headers

Form data

Tokens

Application data

Treat packet captures containing these values as highly sensitive.

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text:
For HTTPS:

Application Data
      |
      v
TLS Encryption
      |
      v
TCP
      |
      v
Network

Without decryption material, Wireshark normally cannot display the encrypted HTTP payload.

docs.title: TLS Filter
docs.text: tls

docs.title: TLS Handshake
docs.text: tls.handshake

docs.title: Client Hello
docs.text: tls.handshake.type == 1

docs.title: Server Hello
docs.text: tls.handshake.type == 2

docs.title: TLS Handshake Model
docs.text:
Client                         Server
  |                              |
  | ------ ClientHello --------> |
  |                              |
  | <------ ServerHello -------- |
  |                              |
  | <----- Certificate ---------- |
  |                              |
  |       Key Establishment       |
  |                              |
  | ===== Encrypted Data =======> |

docs.title: TLS Server Name
docs.text:
Depending on protocol version and capture conditions, SNI can be visible in the ClientHello.

Useful filter:

tls.handshake.extensions_server_name

Example:

tls.handshake.extensions_server_name == "example.com"

docs.title: Extract TLS SNI
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'tls.handshake.extensions_server_name' \
  -T fields \
  -e ip.dst \
  -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name

docs.title: TLS Certificate Information
docs.text:
Wireshark can dissect certificates exchanged during appropriate TLS handshakes.

For certificate-focused CLI validation, also use:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com

and the curl Cheatsheet.

docs.title: TLS Failure Analysis
docs.text:
A failed TLS connection may involve:

Protocol mismatch

Certificate problem

Cipher incompatibility

Client authentication requirement

Application gateway

Connection reset

TLS alert

docs.title: TLS Alerts
docs.text:
Filter:

tls.alert_message

An alert provides useful protocol evidence but must be interpreted in context.

docs.title: SMB Analysis
docs.text:
SMB2 and SMB3 traffic is commonly displayed using:

smb2

docs.title: SMB Ports
docs.text:
Common:

TCP/445

Legacy NetBIOS-based SMB may involve:

TCP/139

docs.title: Filter SMB to a Host
docs.text: smb2 && ip.addr == 192.168.1.10

docs.title: SMB Commands
docs.text:
Wireshark can display SMB command types and responses.

This can help investigate:

Session setup

Tree connections

File access

Authentication

Protocol negotiation

docs.title: SMB Negotiation
docs.text:
A typical sequence:

Client
  |
  v
SMB Negotiate Request
  |
  v
Server
  |
  v
SMB Negotiate Response
  |
  v
Session Setup

docs.title: SMB Interpretation
docs.text:
Seeing:

TCP/445

SMB negotiation

supports:

SMB communication occurred.

It does not automatically prove:

Anonymous access

Administrative access

Signing weakness

Credential compromise

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
Protocol negotiation may provide information relevant to SMB signing.

For focused security validation, combine packet analysis with tools such as:

NetExec

Nmap

smbclient

See the NetExec Cheatsheet.

docs.title: Kerberos Analysis
docs.text:
Display:

kerberos

Kerberos traffic commonly uses:

TCP/88

UDP/88

docs.title: Kerberos High-Level Flow
docs.text:
Client
  |
  | AS-REQ
  v
KDC
  |
  | AS-REP
  v
Client
  |
  | TGS-REQ
  v
KDC
  |
  | TGS-REP
  v
Client
  |
  v
Service

docs.title: Kerberos Message Types
docs.text:
Wireshark can distinguish messages such as:

AS-REQ

AS-REP

TGS-REQ

TGS-REP

KRB-ERROR

docs.title: Kerberos Errors
docs.text:
Filter:

kerberos.error_code

Errors can help investigate:

Authentication failures

Clock problems

Principal problems

Ticket issues

Encryption compatibility

Do not interpret an error code without understanding the Kerberos exchange around it.

docs.title: Active Directory Authentication Troubleshooting
docs.text:
A useful sequence:

DNS
 |
 v
Domain Controller Discovery
 |
 v
Kerberos
 |
 v
LDAP / SMB
 |
 v
Application Protocol

If domain authentication fails, packet capture can help identify where the process stopped.

docs.title: LDAP Analysis
docs.text:
Display:

ldap

Common ports:

389/tcp

636/tcp

3268/tcp

3269/tcp

docs.title: LDAP vs LDAPS
docs.text:
Conceptually:

LDAP
 |
 +--> TCP/389
 |
 +--> May use StartTLS

LDAPS
 |
 +--> TLS-protected LDAP
 |
 +--> Commonly TCP/636

Do not assume encryption solely from the port number. Validate the observed protocol.

docs.title: LDAP Operations
docs.text:
Wireshark may expose operations such as:

Bind

Search

Search Result

Modify

Unbind

when traffic is not protected by TLS or another mechanism that prevents payload inspection.

docs.title: NTLM
docs.text:
NTLM authentication may appear inside protocols such as:

SMB

HTTP

LDAP

RPC

Wireshark may dissect relevant NTLMSSP messages.

docs.title: NTLMSSP Filter
docs.text:
A commonly useful display filter is:

ntlmssp

docs.title: NTLM Authentication Flow
docs.text:
High level:

Client                     Server
  |                           |
  | ---- Negotiate ---------> |
  |                           |
  | <--- Challenge ---------- |
  |                           |
  | ---- Authenticate ------> |

docs.title: Security Interpretation
docs.text:
Seeing NTLM authentication establishes:

NTLM was involved in the observed authentication exchange.

It does not automatically establish:

NTLM relay is possible.

Credentials were compromised.

SMB signing is disabled.

The authentication is vulnerable.

Those require additional context and validation.

docs.title: ICMP
docs.text:
Filter:

icmp

Echo request:

icmp.type == 8

Echo reply:

icmp.type == 0

docs.title: ICMP Destination Unreachable
docs.text:
icmp.type == 3

This can provide useful information during UDP and routing troubleshooting.

docs.title: ARP
docs.text:
Filter:

arp

ARP is useful for understanding local-layer communication.

docs.title: ARP Request
docs.text:
Typical:

Who has 192.168.1.10?

Response:

192.168.1.10 is at <MAC>

docs.title: ARP Analysis
docs.text:
ARP can help answer:

Is the target local?

Is address resolution working?

Which MAC address responded?

Is there unexpected ARP behaviour?

docs.title: DHCP
docs.text:
Filter:

dhcp

Depending on Wireshark version/dissector naming, BOOTP-related fields may also appear.

Typical DHCP flow:

Discover
   |
   v
Offer
   |
   v
Request
   |
   v
ACK

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
SSH traffic:

tcp.port == 22

SSH payload is encrypted after protocol negotiation.

You can still inspect:

Connection establishment

Endpoints

Timing

Packet sizes

Connection termination

but not normal encrypted session content.

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
Common filter:

tcp.port == 3389

Packet analysis can help determine:

Was TCP established?

Did TLS negotiation begin?

Was the connection reset?

Did the target respond?

Application-level authentication may require additional tooling and logs.

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
HTTP WinRM commonly uses:

5985/tcp

HTTPS WinRM commonly uses:

5986/tcp

Filter:

tcp.port == 5985 || tcp.port == 5986

For unencrypted HTTP-level traffic where applicable:

http && tcp.port == 5985

docs.title: MSSQL
docs.text:
Common:

tcp.port == 1433

SQL Server may also use dynamic ports, so use actual observed traffic rather than relying only on standard port numbers.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: tcp.port == 5432

docs.title: MySQL
docs.text: tcp.port == 3306

docs.title: Redis
docs.text: tcp.port == 6379

docs.title: NFS
docs.text:
Commonly associated with:

2049/tcp

2049/udp

Filter:

tcp.port == 2049 || udp.port == 2049

docs.title: Follow Conversations
docs.text:
One of Wireshark's most useful features is reconstructing conversations.

Possible follow options include:

TCP Stream

UDP Stream

HTTP Stream

depending on the selected packet and protocol.

docs.title: Follow TCP Stream
docs.text:
Wireshark:

Right-click
    |
    v
Follow
    |
    v
TCP Stream

This isolates the conversation.

docs.title: Stream Filter
docs.text:
After selecting a stream, Wireshark applies a filter similar to:

tcp.stream eq 0

docs.title: Conversation Statistics
docs.text:
Wireshark:

Statistics
    |
    v
Conversations

Useful views include:

Ethernet

IPv4

IPv6

TCP

UDP

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Wireshark:

Statistics
    |
    v
Endpoints

This helps identify:

Active IP addresses

MAC addresses

Conversation volume

docs.title: Protocol Hierarchy
docs.text:
Wireshark:

Statistics
    |
    v
Protocol Hierarchy

Useful for quickly understanding the protocols present in a capture.

docs.title: Expert Information
docs.text:
Wireshark:

Analyze
    |
    v
Expert Information

This can highlight:

Warnings

Errors

Retransmissions

Protocol anomalies

Expert Information is a diagnostic aid, not an automatic vulnerability scanner.

docs.title: tshark Protocol Hierarchy
docs.text: tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z io,phs

docs.title: tshark Conversations
docs.text:
TCP:

tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z conv,tcp

UDP:

tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z conv,udp

IP:

tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z conv,ip

docs.title: tshark Endpoints
docs.text:
IPv4:

tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z endpoints,ip

TCP:

tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z endpoints,tcp

docs.title: Extract Fields
docs.text:
tshark becomes particularly powerful when extracting structured fields.

General model:

tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y '<filter>' \
  -T fields \
  -e <field1> \
  -e <field2>

docs.title: Extract Source and Destination
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -T fields \
  -e frame.number \
  -e ip.src \
  -e ip.dst

docs.title: Extract TCP Connections
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'tcp' \
  -T fields \
  -e frame.time \
  -e ip.src \
  -e tcp.srcport \
  -e ip.dst \
  -e tcp.dstport

docs.title: Extract HTTP Requests
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'http.request' \
  -T fields \
  -e ip.src \
  -e http.request.method \
  -e http.host \
  -e http.request.uri

docs.title: Extract DNS
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0' \
  -T fields \
  -e ip.src \
  -e dns.qry.name

docs.title: Extract TLS SNI
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'tls.handshake.extensions_server_name' \
  -T fields \
  -e ip.src \
  -e ip.dst \
  -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name

docs.title: CSV-Style Output
docs.text:
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0' \
  -T fields \
  -E separator=, \
  -E quote=d \
  -e frame.time \
  -e ip.src \
  -e dns.qry.name

Redirect:

tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0' \
  -T fields \
  -E separator=, \
  -E quote=d \
  -e frame.time \
  -e ip.src \
  -e dns.qry.name > dns.csv

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text:
For automation:

tshark -r capture.pcapng -T json > capture.json

Be aware that large captures can produce very large JSON files.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - No Packets
docs.text:
Check interfaces:

tshark -D

Check routes:

ip route

Check target route:

ip route get 192.168.1.10

You may simply be capturing on the wrong interface.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Only Outbound Packets
docs.text:
Possible causes:

No server response

Wrong capture point

Asymmetric routing

Firewall drop

Capture interface problem

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Traffic Is Encrypted
docs.text:
This is expected for protocols such as:

HTTPS

SSH

LDAPS

Encrypted SMB sessions

Many modern application protocols

Packet capture still provides metadata and protocol-handshake information.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Wireshark Shows TCP Instead of Protocol
docs.text:
Possible causes:

Non-standard port

Incomplete capture

Encrypted protocol

Dissector not selected

Protocol not recognised

Wireshark can sometimes manually decode traffic using:

Analyze
    |
    v
Decode As

Only do this when you have reason to believe the traffic is a specific protocol.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Checksum Errors
docs.text:
Packet captures taken on the sending host can show apparent checksum errors due to checksum offloading.

Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
Operating System
    |
    v
Packet Capture
    |
    v
NIC Adds Final Checksum
    |
    v
Network

The capture may occur before the NIC calculates the final checksum.

Therefore:

Bad checksum in local capture

does not automatically mean malformed traffic was transmitted.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Retransmissions Everywhere
docs.text:
Possible explanations:

Actual packet loss

Capture loss

Asymmetric visibility

High system load

Congestion

Incorrect capture point

Correlate with network and host telemetry.

docs.title: Capture Loss
docs.text:
Large or high-speed captures can drop packets.

This can create misleading analysis.

Consider:

Capture interface capacity

Disk speed

Capture filters

Buffer size

Host load

docs.title: Example Evidence Record
docs.text:
Test ID:
NET-PCAP-012

Objective:
Determine why HTTPS connectivity from the assessment
workstation to APP01 failed.

Capture Point:
Assessment workstation

Interface:
tun0

Source:
10.10.14.20

Destination:
10.10.10.25

Destination Port:
443/tcp

Display Filter:
ip.addr == 10.10.10.25 && tcp.port == 443

Observation:
Repeated TCP SYN packets were transmitted toward APP01.
No SYN/ACK or RST response was observed in the capture.

Interpretation:
The capture demonstrates that the assessment host attempted
the connection. The capture alone does not determine whether
the missing response resulted from filtering, routing,
packet loss, the target being unavailable, or incomplete
visibility of the return path.

docs.title: Strong vs Weak Conclusions
docs.text:
Weak:

No response, therefore firewall blocked it.

Better:

No response was observed at the assessment capture point.

Then investigate:

Firewall logs

Routing

Target availability

Capture location

docs.title: Another Example - DNS
docs.text:
Observed:

Client -> DNS Query -> DNS Server

DNS Server -> NXDOMAIN -> Client

Defensible conclusion:

The DNS server responded and indicated that the requested
name did not exist according to the queried DNS context.

Not:

The network is broken.

docs.title: Example - TCP Refused
docs.text:
Observed:

SYN
 |
 v
RST/ACK

This supports:

The target responded but did not accept the TCP connection
on the tested port at that time.

This is different from:

No response.

docs.title: Example - HTTP Redirect
docs.text:
Observed unencrypted HTTP:

GET / HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://example.com/

This supports:

The HTTP endpoint redirected the tested request to HTTPS.

Further testing should determine whether HTTPS is consistently enforced across relevant application paths.

docs.title: Example - TLS
docs.text:
Observed:

ClientHello
   |
   v
ServerHello
   |
   v
Certificate
   |
   v
Encrypted Application Data

This supports:

TLS negotiation occurred and encrypted application
communication followed.

It does not by itself prove:

TLS configuration is secure.

docs.title: Example - SMB
docs.text:
Observed:

TCP/445 connection

SMB2 negotiation

Session setup

This supports:

The client established SMB communication with the target.

Further security analysis may require:

Signing validation

Authentication context

Share permissions

Protocol versions

Authorisation

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Packet capture is usually supporting evidence rather than the vulnerability itself.

Avoid:

Wireshark showed TCP/445.

Prefer:

Network validation demonstrated that SMB over TCP/445 was directly reachable from the corporate user network to the management server. This exposure was confirmed at the packet level and did not align with the documented segmentation requirement restricting management protocols to the administrative network.

docs.title: Reporting Authentication Failure
docs.text:
Avoid:

Kerberos is broken.

Prefer:

During the controlled authentication attempt, the client reached the domain controller and received a Kerberos error response. Packet analysis confirms network connectivity to the KDC; further investigation is required at the identity and Kerberos configuration layers.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Packet captures are particularly useful for comparing before and after remediation.

Before:

User VLAN
   |
   | SYN
   v
Management Server
   |
   | SYN/ACK
   v
User VLAN

After segmentation change:

User VLAN
   |
   | SYN
   v
Firewall
   |
   X

The retest must still consider where the capture was taken.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
Packet capture provides visibility into what was observable at a specific point on the network.

That qualification matters.

Do not use:

Packet Not Visible
      |
      v
Event Did Not Happen

Use:

Packet Not Visible
      |
      v
Was Capture Point Correct?
      |
      v
Was Interface Correct?
      |
      v
Could Routing Be Asymmetric?
      |
      v
Could Capture Have Dropped Packets?
      |
      v
What Do Other Telemetry Sources Show?

Likewise, do not stop at:

Packet
  |
  v
Protocol

Continue:

Packet
  |
  v
Conversation
  |
  v
Protocol State
  |
  v
Application / Authentication Context
  |
  v
Expected Behaviour
  |
  v
Observed Behaviour
  |
  v
Security Meaning

For every important packet-analysis result ask:

Where was this captured?

Which interface was used?

Who sent the packet?

Who received it?

Did the other side respond?

Was the TCP handshake completed?

Which protocol was negotiated?

Was the traffic encrypted?

What can actually be observed?

What cannot be determined from this capture?

Does another telemetry source confirm the interpretation?

What evidence should be preserved?

How would I reproduce the test?

Start with a question

Do not open a large PCAP and randomly browse packets. Define the question first - for example, "Did the TCP handshake complete?" or "Which DNS response did the client receive?" - and build the analysis around that question.

Record the display filter

The filter used to isolate the relevant traffic is useful assessment evidence because another tester can reopen the PCAP and reproduce your analysis.

Correlate timestamps

Packet timestamps become substantially more useful when correlated with firewall, EDR, SIEM, authentication and application logs.

A PCAP only represents its capture point

Absence of a packet does not necessarily prove that the packet never existed elsewhere on the network. Capture location, asymmetric routing, dropped packets and interface selection must be considered.

PCAP files can contain secrets

Packet captures can contain authentication material, cookies, tokens, usernames, internal infrastructure details and application data. Store and share them according to the engagement's evidence-handling requirements.

docs.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Cross-site scripting (XSS) occurs when attacker-controlled data reaches a browser execution context without appropriate handling, allowing unintended client-side script execution.

A simplified model is:

Attacker-Controlled Input
          |
          v
      Application
          |
          v
      HTML / DOM
          |
          v
 Browser Interprets Input
          |
          v
 JavaScript Execution

The important question is not simply:

Is my input reflected?

It is:

Where does my input appear?

How is it encoded?

How does the browser parse it?

Can it reach an executable context?

Authorised Security Testing

Perform XSS testing only against applications that are explicitly within scope. Prefer harmless proof-of-concept execution and controlled test accounts. Avoid payloads that access real user sessions, sensitive information, browser storage or external systems unless that activity is specifically authorised.

docs.text: <script>alert(1)</script>

docs.text: <img src=x onerror=alert(1)>

docs.title: JavaScript String Context Probe
docs.text: ';alert(1);//

docs.title: Harmless Marker
docs.text: XSS_TEST_7f3a9

docs.title: HTML-Sensitive Characters
docs.text:
<
>
"
'
&

docs.title: URL-Encoding Examples
docs.text:
<  -> %3C
>  -> %3E
"  -> %22
'  -> %27

docs.title: XSS Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use:

Input Reflected
      |
      v
     XSS

Use:

Input
  |
  v
Reflection / Storage / DOM Flow
  |
  v
Identify Context
  |
  v
Determine Encoding
  |
  v
Determine Browser Parsing
  |
  v
Controlled Execution?
  |
  +--> No  -> Reflection / Candidate
  |
  +--> Yes -> XSS Confirmed

docs.title: Main XSS Types
docs.text:
The three major categories are:

Reflected XSS

Stored XSS

DOM-Based XSS

docs.title: Reflected XSS
docs.text:
Reflected XSS occurs when request data is included in the immediate HTTP response and reaches an executable browser context.

Request
   |
   v
Server
   |
   v
Response Contains Input
   |
   v
Browser Parses Response
   |
   v
Execution

docs.title: Reflected Example
docs.text:
Request:

GET /search?q=test HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

Response:

<h2>Search results for test</h2>

The value:

test

is reflected.

This alone is not XSS.

docs.title: Safe Reflection
docs.text:
If:

?q=<test>

becomes:

<h2>Search results for <test></h2>

the application is applying HTML encoding for that context.

The browser displays:

<test>

as text instead of interpreting it as markup.

docs.title: Potentially Unsafe Reflection
docs.text:
If:

?q=<b>test</b>

becomes:

<h2>Search results for <b>test</b></h2>

the browser interprets the supplied HTML.

This demonstrates HTML injection.

It does not yet necessarily demonstrate JavaScript execution.

docs.title: Reflected XSS Validation
docs.text:
If a harmless execution marker such as:

<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>

is inserted into an executable HTML context and the event handler runs, reflected XSS is established.

docs.title: Stored XSS
docs.text:
Stored XSS occurs when attacker-controlled data is persisted and later rendered to one or more users.

Attacker Input
      |
      v
   Database
      |
      v
Stored Value
      |
      v
Victim Loads Page
      |
      v
Browser Executes

docs.title: Common Stored XSS Locations
docs.text:
Profile names

Comments

Support tickets

Forum posts

Product reviews

File names

Organisation names

Chat messages

Administrative notes

Imported records

CMS content

Audit/log viewers

      v

      |
      v

      |
      v

docs.text:
Example:

Standard User

     v
Creates Support Ticket
     |
     v
Stored in Database
     |
     v
Administrator Opens Ticket
     |
     v
Payload Executes

This can materially increase impact because execution occurs in a more privileged user's browser context.

docs.text:
A profile name might appear in:

Administrative panel

Audit history

Emails

Each output context must be considered separately.

docs.title: DOM-Based XSS
docs.text:
DOM-based XSS occurs when client-side JavaScript reads attacker-controlled data and writes it into a dangerous DOM or JavaScript sink.

Source
  |
  v
JavaScript
  |
  v
Transformation
  |
  v
Sink
  |
  v
Browser Execution

docs.text:

docs.text:
Security-sensitive sinks can include:

docs.text:
This:

element.innerHTML = "<strong>Hello</strong>";

The relevant question is:

Can untrusted data reach the sink?

docs.text:
Source
  |
  v
Variable
  |
  v
Transformation
  |
  v
Validation / Sanitisation?
  |
  v
Sink

docs.title: DOM Example
docs.text:
Potentially unsafe:

const message = location.hash.substring(1);
document.getElementById("output").innerHTML = message;

Flow:

location.hash
     |
     v
message
     |
     v
innerHTML

docs.title: Safer Alternative
docs.text:
If the value should be text:

const message = location.hash.substring(1);
document.getElementById("output").textContent = message;

textContent treats the value as text rather than HTML.

docs.title: Start With a Marker
docs.text:
Before trying execution, use a unique marker:

XSS_TEST_7f3a9

Submit:

?q=XSS_TEST_7f3a9

Then search for it in:

HTTP response

Rendered DOM

JavaScript

HTML attributes

JSON

Stored pages

docs.title: Why Unique Markers Help
docs.text:
A unique marker makes it easier to distinguish your input from:

Existing application text

Other test traffic

Cached values

Unrelated reflections

docs.title: Identify the Output Context
docs.text:
This is one of the most important XSS testing steps.

Possible contexts:

HTML text

HTML attribute

JavaScript string

JavaScript expression

URL

CSS

JSON

DOM

docs.title: HTML Text Context
docs.text:
Example:

<div>
USER_INPUT
</div>

If the application outputs raw markup here, HTML tags may be interpreted.

docs.title: HTML Attribute Context
docs.text:
Example:

<input value="USER_INPUT">

The important surrounding syntax is:

value="
       ^

A test must account for the quote delimiting the attribute.

docs.title: Unquoted Attribute
docs.text:
Example:

<input value=USER_INPUT>

This has different parsing behaviour from a quoted attribute.

docs.title: Single-Quoted Attribute
docs.text:
Example:

<input value='USER_INPUT'>

The relevant delimiter is:

'

docs.title: JavaScript String Context
docs.text:
Example:

<script>
const search = 'USER_INPUT';
</script>

The value is inside:

JavaScript
    +
single-quoted string

HTML payloads designed for normal page markup may not work in this context.

docs.title: Double-Quoted JavaScript String
docs.text:
<script>
const search = "USER_INPUT";
</script>

The delimiter is:

"

docs.title: JavaScript Expression Context
docs.text:
Example:

<script>
const userId = USER_INPUT;
</script>

The input is not inside a quoted string.

This creates a different injection context.

docs.title: URL Context
docs.text:
Example:

<a href="USER_INPUT">Open</a>

The security question becomes:

Can attacker-controlled input create an unsafe navigation or executable URL?

docs.title: JSON Context
docs.text:
Example response:

{
  "query": "USER_INPUT"
}

JSON reflection by itself is generally not XSS.

Determine:

How is this JSON consumed?

Is it later inserted into HTML?

Is it embedded directly into a script block?

docs.title: HTML Encoding
docs.text:
Important characters include:

Character HTML Entity < < > > " " ' context dependent & &

docs.title: Encoding Must Match Context
docs.text:
There is no single universal:

XSS encoding

Different contexts require different handling.

HTML text
    -> HTML encoding

HTML attribute
    -> Attribute-safe encoding

JavaScript
    -> JavaScript-safe serialization/encoding

URL
    -> URL validation + appropriate encoding

docs.title: HTML Encoding vs URL Encoding
docs.text:
These are different.

HTML:

< -> <

URL:

< -> %3C

Do not treat URL encoding as a universal XSS defence.

docs.title: Browser Decoding Layers
docs.text:
Input can pass through multiple transformations:

URL Encoding
     |
     v
Server Decoding
     |
     v
Application Processing
     |
     v
HTML Encoding
     |
     v
Browser Parsing

docs.title: Test What the Browser Receives
docs.text:
Do not rely only on what appears in the address bar.

Inspect:

Raw HTTP response

Browser DOM

JavaScript execution context

docs.title: View Source vs DOM
docs.text:
The original response source and the live DOM may differ.

HTTP Response
     |
     v
Browser Parses
     |
     v
JavaScript Modifies Page
     |
     v
Final DOM

DOM-based XSS may exist even when the dangerous markup does not appear in the original server response.

docs.title: Browser Developer Tools
docs.text:
Useful tabs:

Elements

Console

Network

Sources

docs.title: Elements
docs.text:
Use Elements to inspect the live DOM and determine:

Where input appears

Whether attributes were created

Whether tags were created

Whether JavaScript modified the DOM

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
The console can help identify:

JavaScript errors

DOM behaviour

CSP violations

Source/sink behaviour

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Use Network to determine:

Which request produced the page

Redirects

JavaScript files loaded

CSP headers

API calls

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Browser
  |
  v
Burp Proxy
  |
  v
HTTP History
  |
  v
Identify Input
  |
  v
Repeater
  |
  v
Marker
  |
  v
Context Analysis
  |
  v
Controlled XSS Test

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Use Repeater to modify one input at a time.

Baseline:

GET /search?q=hello HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

Marker:

GET /search?q=XSS_TEST_7f3a9 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

docs.title: Inspect Raw Response
docs.text:
Search for:

XSS_TEST_7f3a9

Determine whether it appears as:

XSS_TEST_7f3a9

or:

XSS_TEST_7f3a9

inside an attribute, script, JSON object or other context.

docs.title: Burp Search
docs.text:
Search HTTP history for the marker.

This is particularly useful for stored input because the value may appear on a different endpoint.

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer can help when encoding transformations are subtle.

Compare:

Original Response

Modified Response

docs.title: Burp Decoder
docs.text:
Decoder can help inspect:

URL encoding

HTML encoding

Base64

Hex

Encoding and decoding are not automatically security bypasses; use them to understand how data is transformed.

docs.title: Burp DOM Invader
docs.text:
DOM Invader can assist with client-side security testing and source/sink analysis.

It can be useful for:

DOM XSS

postMessage testing

DOM clobbering analysis

Client-side sources and sinks

docs.title: DOM Invader Workflow
docs.text:
Open Target in Burp Browser
        |
        v
Enable DOM Invader
        |
        v
Inject Canary
        |
        v
Interact With Application
        |
        v
Review Sources / Sinks
        |
        v
Validate Manually

docs.title: Do Not Report Tool Output Alone
docs.text:
A scanner or DOM analysis tool finding:

source -> sink

should be manually validated.

Determine whether:

Input is attacker controlled

Sanitisation occurs

Execution is possible

The flow is reachable

docs.title: Reflected XSS Workflow
docs.text:
Parameter
   |
   v
Unique Marker
   |
   v
Marker Reflected?
   |
   +--> No -> Other Inputs
   |
   +--> Yes
          |
          v
      Find Context
          |
          v
      Check Encoding
          |
          v
    Harmless HTML Test
          |
          v
 Controlled Execution

docs.title: Stored XSS Workflow
docs.text:
Input Field
   |
   v
Unique Marker
   |
   v
Save
   |
   v
Locate Render Locations
   |
   v
Determine Context
   |
   v
Controlled Payload
   |
   v
View With Relevant Role
   |
   v
Execution?

docs.title: DOM XSS Workflow
docs.text:
Source
  |
  v
Can Attacker Control It?
  |
  v
Trace JavaScript
  |
  v
Sink
  |
  v
Sanitisation?
  |
  v
Browser Interpretation
  |
  v
Execution?

docs.title: Common HTML Proofs
docs.text:
A basic script element:

<script>alert(1)</script>

An event-handler example:

<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>

SVG:

<svg onload=alert(1)>

Use the smallest proof appropriate for the identified context.

docs.title: Prefer Unique Proof Markers
docs.text:
Instead of:

alert(1)

you can use:

alert('XSS-7f3a9')

This makes screenshots and evidence easier to associate with the assessment.

docs.title: Do Not Use Sensitive Proofs
docs.text:
Avoid proof-of-concept code that:

Reads real cookies

Reads localStorage tokens

Changes passwords

Performs transactions

Creates privileged users

Sends data externally

unless specifically authorised and required.

docs.title: Attribute Context
docs.text:
Suppose:

<input value="USER_INPUT">

A test input must first determine whether the application safely handles:

"

If quotes are encoded:

<input value=""">

breaking out of the attribute may not be possible through that value.

docs.title: Attribute Validation
docs.text:
Check characters individually:

"

'

<

>

Observe exactly how each is represented in the response and DOM.

docs.title: Event Handler Context
docs.text:
Suppose input controls:

<button onclick="USER_INPUT">

This is already a JavaScript-capable context.

The key questions are:

Can an attacker control the attribute?

Is the value safely encoded?

Can JavaScript syntax be influenced?

docs.title: URL Attribute Context
docs.text:
Examples:

<a href="USER_INPUT">

<iframe src="USER_INPUT">

<form action="USER_INPUT">

Review:

Allowed schemes

URL parsing

Navigation restrictions

CSP

Browser behaviour

docs.title: Do Not Assume Every href Reflection Is XSS
docs.text:
A value such as:

<a href="/profile?next=USER_INPUT">

may be safely URL encoded.

Context determines exploitability.

docs.title: Script Block Context
docs.text:
Example:

<script>
var username = 'USER_INPUT';
</script>

Inspect:

Quote handling

Backslash handling

Newline handling

HTML script termination

JavaScript encoding

docs.title: Safe JavaScript Data Embedding
docs.text:
Prefer framework-supported serialization.

For example, safely serialize structured data rather than concatenating untrusted strings into executable JavaScript.

docs.title: JavaScript Template Literals
docs.text:
Example:

const message = `USER_INPUT`;

Template literals have their own syntax and should not be treated as equivalent to single-quoted strings.

docs.title: Client-Side Templates
docs.text:
Review frameworks that render data client-side.

The relevant flow may be:

API Response
    |
    v
JavaScript Object
    |
    v
Template
    |
    v
DOM

docs.title: Framework Auto-Escaping
docs.text:
Modern frameworks commonly provide escaping by default.

Examples include:

React

Angular

Vue

Django templates

Jinja2

Twig

Razor

Risk often appears when developers bypass normal escaping.

docs.title: React
docs.text:
Normal JSX:

<div>{userInput}</div>

is generally rendered as text.

A high-risk API is:

dangerouslySetInnerHTML

docs.title: React Source Search
docs.text: rg -n 'dangerouslySetInnerHTML' -g '*.js' -g '*.jsx' -g '*.ts' -g '*.tsx' .

docs.title: Angular
docs.text:
Review APIs and patterns that intentionally bypass sanitisation.

Search:

rg -ni 'bypassSecurityTrust|innerHTML' -g '*.ts' -g '*.html' .

docs.title: Vue
docs.text:
Normal interpolation:

{{ userInput }}

is generally escaped.

Review:

v-html

because it intentionally renders HTML.

docs.title: Vue Source Search
docs.text: rg -n 'v-html' -g '*.vue' .

docs.title: Server-Side Templates
docs.text:
Search for explicit safe/raw rendering functionality.

Examples depend on the template engine.

The important pattern is:

Untrusted Data
      |
      v
Escaping Disabled
      |
      v
HTML Output

docs.title: innerHTML
docs.text:
Potentially dangerous:

element.innerHTML = userInput;

Safer for text:

element.textContent = userInput;

docs.title: outerHTML
docs.text:
Review:

element.outerHTML = userInput;

because supplied markup may replace the element.

docs.title: insertAdjacentHTML
docs.text:
Review:

element.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", userInput);

because it parses the supplied value as HTML.

docs.title: document.write
docs.text:
Review:

document.write(userInput);

because it writes markup into the document parser.

docs.title: eval
docs.text:
Review:

eval(userInput);

This is a JavaScript execution sink and should generally not receive untrusted data.

docs.title: Function
docs.text:
Review:

new Function(userInput)();

This similarly interprets strings as JavaScript.

docs.title: setTimeout
docs.text:
Potentially unsafe:

setTimeout(userInput, 1000);

Safer:

setTimeout(function () {
    doSomething();
}, 1000);

docs.title: setInterval
docs.text:
Potentially unsafe:

setInterval(userInput, 1000);

Avoid string-based execution.

docs.title: jQuery
docs.text:
Legacy applications may contain sinks such as:

.html()
.append()
.after()
.before()

Security depends on what data reaches them and how the API processes the value.

docs.title: Search JavaScript for Sinks
docs.text: rg -ni 'innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|eval\(|new Function|setTimeout\(|setInterval\(' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

docs.title: Search JavaScript for Sources
docs.text: rg -ni 'location\.href|location\.search|location\.hash|document\.referrer|window\.name|localStorage|sessionStorage|postMessage' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

docs.title: Search Source and Sink Together
docs.text:
First find sources:

rg -n 'location\.(search|hash|href)|document\.referrer' src/

Then find sinks:

rg -n 'innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write' src/

Trace candidate flows manually.

docs.title: Example Source Review
docs.text:
const params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const name = params.get("name");

document.querySelector("#welcome").innerHTML =
    "Welcome " + name;

Flow:

location.search
      |
      v
URLSearchParams
      |
      v
name
      |
      v
innerHTML

docs.title: Safer Version
docs.text:
const params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const name = params.get("name");

document.querySelector("#welcome").textContent =
    "Welcome " + name;

docs.title: Sanitisation
docs.text:
If HTML must intentionally be supported, use a well-maintained sanitisation library appropriate to the application.

Do not attempt to create a home-grown sanitizer using a few string replacements.

docs.title: Sanitisation Is Different From Encoding
docs.text:
Encoding
   |
   v
Treat Input as Text

versus:

Sanitisation
   |
   v
Allow Some Markup
   |
   v
Remove Unsafe Constructs

docs.title: Rich Text
docs.text:
Applications may intentionally permit:

<b>

<i>

<p>

<ul>

<li>

but need to reject dangerous markup and attributes.

This is a sanitisation problem rather than simple text encoding.

docs.title: DOMPurify
docs.text:
DOMPurify is a commonly used HTML sanitisation library for browser environments.

Use it according to the project's documented configuration and threat model.

Do not weaken sanitisation by subsequently modifying sanitized markup in unsafe ways.

docs.title: Sanitisation Foot-Guns
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Untrusted HTML
      |
      v
Sanitise
      |
      v
Safe HTML
      |
      v
Unsafe String Manipulation
      |
      v
Danger Reintroduced

docs.title: Content Security Policy
docs.text: Content Security Policy (CSP) can reduce the impact of XSS, but should normally be treated as defence in depth rather than a replacement for safe output handling.

docs.title: Check CSP Header
docs.text:
curl -I https://example.com/

Look for:

Content-Security-Policy:

docs.title: Example CSP
docs.text: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'

docs.title: CSP Report-Only
docs.text:
This header:

Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only:

does not enforce the policy.

It reports violations for monitoring/testing purposes.

docs.title: CSP Questions
docs.text:
Review:

Is CSP enforced?

What is script-src?

Are nonces used?

Are hashes used?

Is unsafe-inline allowed?

Is unsafe-eval allowed?

Are broad external script origins trusted?

Are wildcard sources used?

Are dangerous schemes allowed?

docs.title: unsafe-inline
docs.text:
A policy containing:

'unsafe-inline'

may permit inline JavaScript depending on the rest of the policy.

Its significance must be evaluated in the complete CSP.

docs.title: unsafe-eval
docs.text:
A policy containing:

'unsafe-eval'

permits certain string-to-code JavaScript operations.

It weakens CSP but is not, by itself, proof of XSS.

docs.title: Nonces
docs.text:
Example:

<script nonce="RANDOM_VALUE">

with:

Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-RANDOM_VALUE'

A nonce should be unpredictable and generated per response.

docs.title: Do Not Report CSP Alone as XSS
docs.text:
This:

CSP contains unsafe-inline

does not demonstrate:

XSS vulnerability

It is a hardening observation unless a meaningful security consequence is established.

docs.title: XSS With CSP
docs.text:
If XSS exists but CSP blocks a simple inline proof:

Input Injection Exists
       |
       v
Browser Creates Markup
       |
       v
CSP Blocks Script Execution

Document both facts accurately.

Do not claim successful JavaScript execution if CSP prevented it.

docs.title: CSP Console Errors
docs.text:
Browser console may show:

Refused to execute inline script...

This is useful evidence that CSP affected the test.

docs.title: Trusted Types
docs.text:
Trusted Types can reduce DOM XSS risk in supported applications by restricting assignment to dangerous DOM sinks.

Review:

Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script'

where applicable.

docs.title: HTTPOnly Cookies
docs.text:
HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from directly reading a cookie.

Example:

Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure

This reduces one common XSS impact but does not fix XSS.

docs.title: XSS Impact Is Not Only Cookie Theft
docs.text:
XSS can potentially perform actions available to the victim's browser context.

Depending on the application:

Read page data

Modify page content

Send same-origin requests

Interact with APIs

Access non-HttpOnly browser storage

Perform actions as the user

Therefore:

Session cookie is HttpOnly

does not mean:

XSS has no impact.

docs.title: SameSite Cookies
docs.text: SameSite is primarily a cross-site request control and does not prevent JavaScript already executing within the application's origin from interacting with same-origin application functionality.

docs.title: Secure Cookies
docs.text:
The Secure attribute ensures a cookie is sent only over secure transport.

It does not remediate XSS.

docs.title: Stored XSS in File Names
docs.text:
Applications may display uploaded file names.

Example:

report.pdf

Test whether filename values are:

Stored

Reflected

HTML encoded

Displayed to other users

docs.title: File Name Testing
docs.text:
Use a harmless marker first.

For example:

XSS_TEST_7f3a9.pdf

Upload normally and determine where the filename is rendered.

docs.title: File Name Context
docs.text:
Possible render locations:

Upload confirmation

File list

Administrative portal

Download page

Audit history

docs.title: Do Not Confuse File Content With Filename XSS
docs.text:
These are separate surfaces:

Filename handling

File content handling

Content-Type handling

Inline rendering

docs.title: Stored XSS in Logs
docs.text:
Some applications display request data in web-based administrative log viewers.

Potential stored values include:

User-Agent

Referer

URL

Search term

Username

Use harmless markers first and only test administrator-facing execution where authorised.

docs.title: Blind XSS Concept
docs.text:
Blind XSS occurs when supplied input executes in a location the tester cannot directly view, often in a different workflow or privileged interface.

Conceptually:

Input Submitted
      |
      v
Stored / Logged
      |
      v
Different User Opens Record
      |
      v
Execution

docs.title: Blind XSS Testing
docs.text:
Blind XSS often relies on an external callback service.

Because this causes an out-of-band interaction, use only infrastructure and domains approved for the assessment.

Do not send real application data in callbacks.

docs.title: Safe Blind XSS Design
docs.text:
A controlled callback should prove only what is necessary, such as:

Unique test ID

Target identifier

Execution timestamp

Avoid collecting:

Cookies

Tokens

Page contents

Personal data

docs.title: postMessage
docs.text:
postMessage is another important client-side input source.

Listener example:

window.addEventListener("message", function (event) {
    output.innerHTML = event.data;
});

Questions:

Is event.origin validated?

Is event.source validated where needed?

How is event.data used?

Does it reach a dangerous sink?

docs.title: postMessage Origin Validation
docs.text:
Weak:

if (event.origin.includes("example.com")) {

Prefer exact expected origins where appropriate.

The exact implementation depends on the application's architecture.

docs.title: URL Fragment
docs.text:
Example:

https://example.com/#hello

The fragment:

#hello

is normally not sent to the server.

Client-side JavaScript can still read:

location.hash

making it relevant for DOM XSS.

docs.title: Query String
docs.text:
https://example.com/?q=hello

JavaScript can read:

location.search

docs.title: Referrer
docs.text:
JavaScript may read:

document.referrer

Whether an attacker can meaningfully control it depends on navigation and browser behaviour.

docs.title: localStorage
docs.text:
Example:

const name = localStorage.getItem("name");
output.innerHTML = name;

The relevant question is:

Can an attacker cause malicious data to enter localStorage?

docs.title: sessionStorage
docs.text:
Same principle:

sessionStorage.getItem(...)

Storage is a source only if untrusted values can reach it.

docs.title: Mutation XSS
docs.text:
Browser parsing and HTML sanitisation can interact in complex ways.

Do not assume:

Sanitised string looked safe before DOM insertion

always means:

Resulting DOM is safe.

For rich HTML functionality, rely on mature sanitisation libraries and browser-aware testing.

docs.title: Multi-Context Reflection
docs.text:
The same input can appear multiple times:

<h1>USER_INPUT</h1>

<input value="USER_INPUT">

<script>
const q = "USER_INPUT";
</script>

Each reflection has a different security context.

docs.title: Test Every Reflection
docs.text:
Do not stop after determining that one reflection is safely encoded.

Another occurrence may be unsafe.

docs.title: Reflection in HTML Comment
docs.text:
Example:

<!-- USER_INPUT -->

This is a distinct parser context.

Determine whether input can alter comment structure before making any security conclusion.

docs.title: Reflection in CSS
docs.text:
Example:

<style>
.profile {
    background: USER_INPUT;
}
</style>

CSS injection and modern browser security behaviour differ from standard JavaScript XSS.

Analyse the actual impact rather than labeling every CSS-context injection as XSS.

docs.title: Meta Tags
docs.text:
Example:

<meta content="USER_INPUT">

Again, context and browser interpretation determine impact.

docs.title: Template Injection vs XSS
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

Server-Side Template Injection

with:

Cross-Site Scripting

An input such as:

{{7*7}}

may be relevant to template processing, while XSS concerns browser-side execution.

See:

SSTI Notes

docs.title: HTML Injection vs XSS
docs.text:
HTML injection:

<b>Injected</b>

demonstrates attacker-controlled markup.

XSS requires an executable browser context.

Relationship:

HTML Injection
      |
      +--> Markup Only
      |
      +--> Executable Context
              |
              v
             XSS

docs.title: Open Redirect vs XSS
docs.text:
If attacker input controls:

Location:

or a navigation URL, the issue may be open redirect rather than XSS.

See:

Open Redirect Notes

docs.title: XSS vs JavaScript URL
docs.text:
A controllable URL may require separate analysis of:

Allowed schemes

Browser behaviour

CSP

User interaction

Do not classify solely from the string value.

docs.title: XSS vs CRLF Injection
docs.text: If input affects HTTP headers rather than HTML/DOM output, investigate response splitting or header injection separately.

docs.title: XSS vs SQL Injection
docs.text:
A quote producing an error does not tell you which interpreter is involved.

Always determine the processing context:

Browser?

SQL?

Shell?

Template?

LDAP?

XML?

docs.title: Scanner Findings
docs.text:
Automated scanners may report:

Possible reflected XSS

Input reflected

Potential DOM sink

CSP weakness

These are candidates requiring validation.

docs.title: Scanner False Positives
docs.text:
Common reasons:

Input HTML encoded

Reflection occurs inside JSON

Reflection occurs in non-executable text

CSP blocks execution

Sanitiser removes dangerous attributes

Input never reaches browser DOM

docs.title: Scanner False Negatives
docs.text:
Automated scanning can miss:

Stored XSS

Multi-step workflows

Role-dependent rendering

DOM XSS

JavaScript-generated contexts

Blind XSS

Second-order rendering

docs.title: Application Workflow Matters
docs.text:
Example:

Create User
   |
   v
Set Display Name
   |
   v
No Execution on Profile
   |
   v
Admin Opens User Management
   |
   v
Execution

Testing only the submission response would miss the vulnerability.

docs.title: Multi-Role Testing
docs.text:
For stored input, consider:

Attacker role

Same user

Different standard user

Administrator

Support user

Only where these roles are available and authorised.

docs.title: XSS and Access Control
docs.text:
Impact depends on who can create the payload and who can trigger it.

Example:

Admin -> Admin

may have lower practical impact than:

Unauthenticated -> Administrator

docs.title: Impact Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Who can supply the input?

Who receives the output?

Does execution require interaction?

Which origin executes the script?

What functionality is available to the victim?

Does CSP restrict execution?

Are sensitive APIs accessible from the browser?

Does the application contain privileged administrative actions?

docs.title: Do Not Overstate Impact
docs.text:
Do not automatically claim:

Account takeover

Credential theft

Server compromise

from every XSS.

Explain the impact supported by the tested application.

docs.title: Source-Code Review
docs.text:
Search for output-related functions.

JavaScript:

rg -ni 'innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|eval\(|new Function' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

React:

rg -n 'dangerouslySetInnerHTML' -g '*.jsx' -g '*.tsx' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' .

Vue:

rg -n 'v-html' -g '*.vue' .

Angular:

rg -ni 'bypassSecurityTrust|innerHTML' -g '*.ts' -g '*.html' .

docs.title: Search for Template Raw Output
docs.text:
Framework syntax differs.

Look for mechanisms that mean:

Do not escape this value.

Then determine whether attacker-controlled input can reach them.

docs.title: Search for Sanitisation
docs.text:
rg -ni 'DOMPurify|sanitize|sanitise|escapeHtml|encodeForHTML' .

A sanitisation function name does not prove correct use.

Review configuration and data flow.

docs.title: Search Sources
docs.text: rg -ni 'location\.search|location\.hash|location\.href|document\.referrer|window\.name|localStorage|sessionStorage' .

docs.title: Trace Candidate
docs.text:
Suppose:

app.js:18: const value = location.hash.substring(1);
app.js:47: output.innerHTML = value;

Inspect context:

rg -n -C 6 'location\.hash|innerHTML' app.js

docs.text:
const value = location.hash.substring(1);

if (value.length < 100) {
    output.innerHTML = value;
}

The length check:

does not provide HTML sanitisation.

The important flow remains:

Attacker-Controlled Fragment

docs.text:

Generally lower risk for XSS.

Security-relevant candidate.

Not attacker-controlled.

docs.title: False Positive - Encoded Reflection
docs.text:
Input:

<script>alert(1)</script>

Response:

<script>alert(1)</script>

Browser renders it as text.

No execution is demonstrated.

docs.title: False Positive - JSON Response
docs.text:
Response:

  "query": "<script>alert(1)</script>"
}

This alone is not XSS.

Determine how the JSON is consumed.

docs.title: False Positive - Sanitised Flow

docs.title: False Positive - CSP

docs.title: Reporting Example - Reflected XSS
docs.text:
Weak:

The q parameter is vulnerable to XSS.

Better:

The q parameter on the search endpoint is reflected into the HTML response without context-appropriate output encoding. A controlled event-handler payload supplied through the parameter was inserted into the resulting DOM and executed in the application's origin when the response was rendered in the browser.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Stored XSS
docs.text: The profile display name is stored by the application and later rendered without context-appropriate encoding in the administrative user-management interface. A value submitted by a standard user executed JavaScript when the corresponding record was viewed using the authorised administrator test account.

docs.title: Reporting Example - DOM XSS
docs.text: Client-side code reads attacker-controlled data from location.hash and assigns the resulting value to innerHTML without sanitisation. A controlled fragment value therefore produced executable markup in the live DOM without requiring the value to be reflected by the server.

docs.title: Reporting Example - HTML Injection Only
docs.text: The tested parameter is rendered as raw HTML and allows attacker-controlled markup to alter page presentation. JavaScript execution was not demonstrated during testing, so the issue was classified as HTML injection rather than cross-site scripting.

docs.title: Reporting Example - CSP Prevented Execution
docs.text: The application reflects attacker-controlled markup into the response without HTML encoding. The supplied markup was created in the DOM; however, the tested inline JavaScript execution was blocked by the application's enforced Content Security Policy. No successful JavaScript execution was demonstrated using the tested technique.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Primary principle:

Apply context-appropriate output encoding.

docs.title: HTML Text
docs.text:
For values intended to be text:

Encode HTML-sensitive characters.

Prefer framework APIs that escape by default.

docs.title: DOM Text
docs.text:
Prefer:

textContent

instead of:

innerHTML

when HTML rendering is unnecessary.

docs.title: Rich HTML
docs.text:
If users are intentionally allowed to submit HTML:

Use a mature HTML sanitiser.

Define allowed elements.

Define allowed attributes.

Keep the sanitiser updated.

Test configuration.

docs.title: JavaScript Context
docs.text:
Avoid dynamically constructing executable JavaScript with untrusted data.

Prefer:

Structured data

DOM APIs

Safe serialization

Event listeners

docs.title: URL Context
docs.text:
Validate:

Allowed schemes

Allowed destinations

Expected URL structure

and apply appropriate URL handling.

docs.title: Framework Defaults
docs.text: Do not disable framework escaping unless there is a clear requirement and the data has been appropriately sanitised.

docs.title: CSP
docs.text:
Deploy a strong CSP as defence in depth.

Prefer policies based on:

Nonces

Hashes

Explicit script origins

rather than relying on broad inline-script allowances.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Use:

HttpOnly

Secure

Appropriate SameSite

for session cookies.

These reduce some impact but do not remediate XSS.

docs.title: Trusted Types
docs.text: Where appropriate for the application, consider Trusted Types to reduce dangerous DOM sink usage.

docs.text:
After finding one XSS issue, search for the underlying pattern.

For example:

Old malicious record

Newly created record

Administrator

Rich HTML is sanitised.

Unsafe attributes are removed.

Normal Unicode input still works.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
The key XSS question is:

Can attacker-controlled data reach an executable browser context?

A strong testing workflow is:

Input
  |
  v
Unique Marker
  |
  v
Find Reflection / Storage / Source
  |
  v
Identify Context
  |
  v
Understand Encoding
  |
  v
Understand Browser Parsing
  |
  v
Minimal Context-Specific PoC
  |
  v
Execution?
  |
  +--> No
  |     |
  |     v
  |  Document Candidate / HTML Injection / Safe Handling
  |
  +--> Yes
        |
        v
   Determine Victim
        |
        v
   Determine Impact
        |
        v
      Evidence
        |
        v
    Remediation
        |
        v
      Retest

For every candidate ask:

Where does the input originate?

Is the attacker able to control it?

Is it reflected immediately or stored?

Where does it appear?

What parser context is involved?

Which characters are encoded?

Is HTML actually created?

Is JavaScript execution possible?

Does the browser DOM differ from the server response?

Does JavaScript move the value into another sink?

Does CSP affect execution?

Who can submit the value?

Who views the value?

Does the issue cross privilege boundaries?

Could the observation only be HTML injection?

Could framework auto-escaping already make it safe?

Is sanitisation being used?

Can the behaviour be reproduced?

What is the minimum safe proof?

Has the root cause been fixed?

Do not stop at:

Payload reflected.

Move through:

REFLECTION
    |
    v
CONTEXT
    |
    v
PARSING
    |
    v
EXECUTION
    |
    v
IMPACT

That distinction turns a payload collection into a defensible XSS testing methodology.

Start with context, not payload lists

A unique marker and five minutes of context analysis are usually more valuable than blindly sending hundreds of XSS strings. Determine where the value appears and how the browser parses it before selecting a proof.

Inspect both response and DOM

The server response shows what the application returned. The live DOM shows what the browser ultimately constructed after parsing and JavaScript execution. DOM-based vulnerabilities may only become apparent in the latter.

Separate HTML injection from XSS

If attacker-controlled markup changes the page but JavaScript execution cannot be demonstrated, describe the observed behaviour accurately as HTML injection rather than automatically calling it XSS.

Trace source to sink

During client-side review, a dangerous sink such as innerHTML is only part of the story. Identify whether attacker-controlled data can actually reach that sink, what transformations occur and whether sanitisation is applied.

Keep the proof harmless

An alert or similarly harmless unique execution marker is normally sufficient to establish XSS. Avoid accessing real cookies, tokens, page data or privileged functionality simply to make the proof more dramatic.

CSP is defence in depth

A Content Security Policy can substantially reduce XSS impact, but it should not replace context-appropriate encoding, safe DOM APIs and sanitisation. Document separately whether unsafe injection exists and whether CSP prevents the tested execution path.

docs.title: XML External Entity (XXE) Cheatsheet
docs.text:
XML External Entity (XXE) vulnerabilities occur when an application processes attacker-controlled XML using a parser configured to resolve external entities or otherwise access external resources.

A simplified model is:

Attacker-Controlled XML
          |
          v
      XML Parser
          |
          v
External Entity Processing
          |
          +----> Local File
          |
          +----> Network Resource
          |
          +----> External DTD

The central question is not simply:

Does the application accept XML?

It is:

Which XML parser processes the input?

Are DTDs supported?

Are external entities resolved?

Can the parser access local or remote resources?

Is the resulting data returned or observable?

Authorised Security Testing

Perform XXE testing only against systems explicitly included in the assessment scope. Local file access, internal network requests, external DTD retrieval and out-of-band callbacks can access resources beyond the immediate application. Use harmless controlled resources wherever possible and avoid retrieving sensitive files unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Minimal XML
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<root>
    <value>test</value>
</root>

docs.title: Internal Entity Test
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE root [
    <!ENTITY test "XXE_TEST_7f3a9">
]>
<root>&test;</root>

docs.title: Controlled External Entity
docs.text:

<!DOCTYPE root [
    <!ENTITY test SYSTEM "https://xxe-test.example/xxe-7f3a9">
]>
<root>&test;</root>

docs.text:

    <!ENTITY test SYSTEM "file:///tmp/xxe-test.txt">
]>
<root>&test;</root>

    <xi:include href="file:///tmp/xxe-test.txt" parse="text"/>
</root>

docs.title: XML Basics
docs.text:
A normal XML document may look like:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<user>
    <name>alice</name>
    <role>user</role>
</user>

docs.title: Document Type Definition
docs.text:
A DTD can define the structure and entities used by an XML document.

Example:

<!DOCTYPE user [
    <!ENTITY company "Example Corporation">
]>

The entity can then be referenced:

<name>&company;</name>

docs.title: Internal Entity
docs.text:
Example:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE root [
    <!ENTITY marker "XXE_TEST_7f3a9">
]>
<root>▮</root>

If processed normally, the parser may produce:

<root>XXE_TEST_7f3a9</root>

This demonstrates entity processing.

It does not by itself demonstrate external entity access.

docs.title: External Entity
docs.text:
An external entity references a resource outside the XML document.

Example:

<!ENTITY test SYSTEM "https://xxe-test.example/resource">

Conceptually:

XML
 |
 v
Parser
 |
 v
External Entity
 |
 v
Remote Resource

docs.title: External File Entity
docs.text:
A parser that allows external entities may support a local file URI:

<!ENTITY test SYSTEM "file:///tmp/xxe-test.txt">

Whether this works depends on:

Parser

Configuration

Runtime

Operating system

File permissions

URI handler

docs.title: Do Not Start With Sensitive Files
docs.text:
Prefer a harmless known file created for the assessment.

For example:

/tmp/xxe-test.txt

containing:

XXE_TEST_7f3a9

This demonstrates local file access without unnecessarily accessing operating-system secrets.

but does not yet prove:
