docs.title: DNS vs HTTP
docs.text:
A DNS interaction means:

The supplied hostname was resolved.

An HTTP interaction provides stronger evidence that:

The parser attempted to retrieve the external resource over HTTP.

docs.title: Do Not Treat DNS as File Disclosure
docs.text:
A DNS callback demonstrates external interaction.

It does not demonstrate that the parser can read local files.

docs.title: Basic File Disclosure
docs.text:
In an authorised lab or against a known harmless test file:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE root [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///tmp/xxe-test.txt">
]>
<root>&xxe;</root>

docs.title: Representative Result
docs.text:
If /tmp/xxe-test.txt contains:

XXE_TEST_7f3a9

and the response becomes:

<root>XXE_TEST_7f3a9</root>

this supports local file disclosure through external entity resolution.

docs.title: Windows Lab File
docs.text:
A controlled Windows test file might be:

C:\Temp\xxe-test.txt

A corresponding file URI is typically represented as:

file:///C:/Temp/xxe-test.txt

Actual parser behaviour can vary.

docs.title: File Permissions Still Apply
docs.text:
XXE does not automatically bypass operating-system permissions.

The parser runs with the permissions of the application process.

Conceptually:

XXE
 |
 v
Application Process
 |
 v
OS File Permissions
 |
 v
Readable?

docs.title: Parser Errors
docs.text:
XXE testing frequently produces parser errors.

Examples:

DOCTYPE is disallowed

Entity not defined

External entity resolution disabled

Content is not allowed in prolog

Malformed XML

DTD processing prohibited

docs.title: DOCTYPE Blocked
docs.text:
If the parser returns:

DOCTYPE is disallowed

this is strong evidence that DTD processing is intentionally disabled for that parser path.

docs.title: Entity Not Defined
docs.text:
Example:

The entity "xxe" was referenced, but not declared.

This may indicate:

DTD ignored

DTD stripped

Entity declaration rejected

Malformed declaration

docs.title: External Resolution Disabled
docs.text:
The parser may allow internal entities but reject external entities.

Model:

Internal Entity
     |
     +--> Allowed

External Entity
     |
     X--> Blocked

docs.title: XXE Types
docs.text:
Useful categories include:

Classic XXE

Blind XXE

Out-of-Band XXE

Error-Based XXE

XInclude Injection

XXE through file processing

docs.title: Classic XXE
docs.text:
Classic XXE returns the external entity content directly in the application response.

External Resource
      |
      v
XML Parser
      |
      v
Application Response

docs.title: Blind XXE
docs.text:
Blind XXE occurs when external entity processing takes place but retrieved data is not directly returned.

XML
 |
 v
Parser
 |
 v
External Interaction
 |
 v
No Content Returned

docs.title: Blind XXE Example
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE root [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "https://UNIQUE-ID.oastify.com/xxe-test">
]>
<root>&xxe;</root>

docs.title: Blind XXE Evidence
docs.text:
A strong minimal proof can be:

1. Submit XML containing unique external entity URL.

2. Application processes the request.

3. OOB service receives DNS lookup.

4. OOB service receives HTTP request.

5. Unique token matches the submitted request.

6. Test is repeated with a second unique token.

docs.title: Burp Collaborator
docs.text:
Burp Collaborator is useful for blind XXE.

Conceptually:

<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "https://UNIQUE-ID.oastify.com/">

docs.title: Burp Collaborator Workflow
docs.text:
Generate Collaborator Payload
        |
        v
Create External Entity
        |
        v
Send XML Request
        |
        v
Poll Collaborator
        |
        v
DNS?
        |
        +--> Yes -> Resolution occurred
        |
        v
HTTP?
        |
        +--> Yes -> External retrieval attempted

docs.title: Interactsh
docs.text:
ProjectDiscovery Interactsh can also be used for approved OOB validation.

Use a unique generated hostname for each test case.

docs.title: External DTD
docs.text:
An XML document may reference an external DTD.

Example:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE root SYSTEM "https://xxe-test.example/test.dtd">
<root>test</root>

docs.title: External DTD Retrieval
docs.text:
If the controlled server records:

GET /test.dtd HTTP/1.1

the parser attempted to retrieve the external DTD.

docs.title: Why External DTDs Matter
docs.text:
External DTD support can provide additional entity-processing capabilities.

It also demonstrates that XML parsing can cause server-side network interactions.

docs.title: Parameter Entities
docs.text:
DTD syntax supports parameter entities.

Example syntax:

<!ENTITY % test "value">

and:

%test;

Parameter entities are primarily used within DTDs.

docs.title: Parameter Entity Example
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE root [
    <!ENTITY % marker "<!ENTITY test 'XXE_TEST_7f3a9'>">
    %marker;
]>
<root>&test;</root>

This is useful for understanding parser behaviour in a controlled environment.

docs.title: Out-of-Band XXE
docs.text:
An external DTD can be useful when direct response reflection is unavailable.

Conceptually:

Target XML
    |
    v
External DTD
    |
    v
Parser Processes DTD
    |
    v
Controlled Callback

docs.title: OOB Testing Principle
docs.text:
The goal of initial OOB testing should be:

Prove external entity retrieval

rather than immediately attempting to extract sensitive data.

docs.title: Error-Based XXE
docs.text:
Some parsers include external entity content inside error messages.

Conceptually:

External Resource
      |
      v
Parser Error
      |
      v
Application Error Response

docs.title: Error-Based Validation
docs.text:
Use only harmless test data.

Do not deliberately force sensitive local data into verbose error messages unless that level of testing is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: XXE and SSRF
docs.text:
XXE can sometimes cause the parser to make server-side network requests.

Example:

<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "https://xxe-test.example/">

This behaviour resembles SSRF.

However, the root cause is XML external entity processing.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
Use:

XXE

when the vulnerable component is:

XML external entity resolution

even when the security consequence includes server-side network requests.

docs.title: SSRF Relationship
docs.text:
Attacker XML
     |
     v
XML Parser
     |
     v
External Entity
     |
     v
HTTP Request

The final HTTP request is an SSRF-like effect of the XXE vulnerability.

docs.title: Internal Network Requests
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised, a controlled internal service can help determine whether the parser can reach internal network resources.

Prefer:

Known test service

over:

Broad internal scanning

docs.title: Do Not Use XXE for Broad Port Scanning
docs.text:
Large-scale internal host or port testing can create unnecessary traffic and risk.

Use the minimum internal validation required by the engagement.

docs.title: XInclude
docs.text:
Some applications accept XML data but do not allow control over the document's DOCTYPE.

XInclude may represent a separate XML processing surface.

docs.title: XInclude Example
docs.text:
<root xmlns:xi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XInclude">
    <xi:include href="file:///tmp/xxe-test.txt" parse="text"/>
</root>

docs.title: XInclude Model
docs.text:
XML Element
    |
    v
XInclude Processor
    |
    v
External Resource

docs.title: XInclude Is Not Identical to DTD XXE
docs.text:
The underlying XML processing feature differs.

Report the actual mechanism observed.

docs.title: XInclude Applicability
docs.text:
XInclude testing is relevant only when:

The parser or downstream XML processor supports XInclude

User-controlled XML elements reach that processor

docs.title: XML Content-Type Conversion
docs.text:
Some endpoints primarily expect:

application/json

but may also accept:

application/xml

Test content-type alternatives only when reasonable and within scope.

docs.title: JSON Baseline
docs.text:
POST /api/user HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "alice"
}

docs.title: XML Alternative
docs.text:
POST /api/user HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/xml

<user>
    <name>alice</name>
</user>

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If the XML request succeeds, this establishes an XML parsing surface.

It does not establish XXE.

docs.title: SOAP
docs.text:
SOAP applications commonly use XML.

Example:

POST /service HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: text/xml

<soap:Envelope xmlns:soap="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/">
    <soap:Body>
        <GetUser>
            <id>1</id>
        </GetUser>
    </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>

docs.title: SOAP XXE Review
docs.text:
Identify:

SOAP parser

DTD configuration

External entity configuration

Schema validation

Framework defaults

docs.title: SOAPAction
docs.text:
SOAP requests may contain:

SOAPAction:

This header is separate from XXE processing.

Do not confuse SOAP action manipulation with XML parser vulnerabilities.

docs.title: SVG
docs.text:
SVG is XML-based.

Example:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
     width="100"
     height="100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40"/>
</svg>

docs.title: SVG Upload Processing
docs.text:
Potential flow:

SVG Upload
   |
   v
Image Processor
   |
   v
XML Parser
   |
   v
External Resource Processing?

docs.title: SVG Testing Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Is SVG accepted?

Is it parsed server-side?

Is it merely stored?

Is it converted to another format?

Is it rendered directly in the browser?

Does server-side processing resolve external resources?

docs.title: SVG Can Have Multiple Security Surfaces
docs.text:
An SVG file may involve:

Server-side XML processing

Client-side active content

File upload handling

Content-Type handling

Keep these issues distinct.

docs.title: Office Documents
docs.text:
Modern Office formats such as:

DOCX

XLSX

PPTX

are ZIP archives containing XML files.

docs.title: Document Processing
docs.text:
An application that:

Uploads document
       |
       v
Extracts archive
       |
       v
Parses XML

may expose XML parsing surfaces.

docs.title: Do Not Assume Office Upload Means XXE
docs.text: The application must actually parse attacker-controlled XML using vulnerable settings.

docs.title: ZIP-Based Formats
docs.text:
Other formats can also contain XML.

Always understand the server-side processing chain.

docs.title: SAML
docs.text:
SAML messages are XML.

Example components include:

SAMLRequest

SAMLResponse

Assertions

Metadata

XML parser security remains relevant, but SAML has additional signature and trust requirements that must be analysed separately.

docs.title: SAML Metadata Import
docs.text: Functionality that imports metadata from XML may provide a useful XML parser review surface.

docs.title: XML Configuration Uploads
docs.text:
Applications may accept:

Configuration files

Workflow definitions

Integration definitions

Project files

Data imports

in XML format.

docs.title: XML-RPC
docs.text:
XML-RPC also uses XML request bodies.

Example:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<methodCall>
    <methodName>example.test</methodName>
    <params>
        <param>
            <value>test</value>
        </param>
    </params>
</methodCall>

docs.title: Parser Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Error messages can sometimes reveal parser technology.

Examples may reference:

libxml

SAX

DOM

DocumentBuilder

XMLReader

XmlReader

Xerces

Treat parser fingerprinting as supporting evidence, not proof of insecure configuration.

docs.title: Java XML Parsers
docs.text:
Common Java XML APIs include:

DocumentBuilderFactory

SAXParserFactory

XMLInputFactory

TransformerFactory

SchemaFactory

docs.title: Java Source Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'DocumentBuilderFactory|SAXParserFactory|XMLInputFactory|TransformerFactory|SchemaFactory' -g '*.java' .

docs.title: Java Candidate
docs.text:
DocumentBuilderFactory factory =
    DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();

DocumentBuilder builder =
    factory.newDocumentBuilder();

Document document =
    builder.parse(inputStream);

This should be reviewed for secure parser configuration.

docs.title: Java Review Questions
docs.text:
Look for settings related to:

DOCTYPE processing

External general entities

External parameter entities

External DTD loading

XInclude

Entity expansion

docs.title: Java Secure Configuration
docs.text:
Exact secure settings depend on:

Parser implementation

Java version

Framework

Application requirements

Follow current vendor and OWASP guidance rather than copying a single parser configuration across every Java XML API.

docs.title: .NET XML APIs
docs.text:
Common .NET APIs include:

XmlReader

XmlDocument

XDocument

XmlTextReader

XmlSerializer

docs.title: .NET Source Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'XmlReader|XmlDocument|XDocument|XmlTextReader|XmlSerializer' -g '*.cs' .

docs.title: .NET Review
docs.text:
Review:

DtdProcessing

XmlResolver

Reader settings

Framework version

docs.title: Python XML APIs
docs.text:
Python applications may use:

xml.etree.ElementTree

xml.dom.minidom

xml.sax

lxml

Security behaviour depends on library and configuration.

docs.title: Python Source Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'ElementTree|xml\.dom|minidom|xml\.sax|lxml|etree' -g '*.py' .

docs.title: Python defusedxml
docs.text:
Python applications processing untrusted XML may use:

defusedxml

which provides hardened alternatives for several XML processing APIs.

docs.title: Search for defusedxml
docs.text: rg -ni 'defusedxml' -g '*.py' .

docs.title: PHP XML APIs
docs.text:
Potential XML functionality includes:

DOMDocument

SimpleXML

XMLReader

libxml

docs.title: PHP Source Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'DOMDocument|simplexml|XMLReader|libxml' -g '*.php' .

docs.title: libxml
docs.text:
Parser behaviour depends on:

libxml version

PHP version

Parser flags

Application configuration

docs.title: Ruby XML Libraries
docs.text:
Potential libraries include:

REXML

Nokogiri

docs.title: Ruby Source Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'REXML|Nokogiri' -g '*.rb' .

docs.title: Node.js XML Libraries
docs.text:
Node.js applications may use third-party XML parsing packages.

Search dependencies and parser construction rather than assuming one standard XML parser.

docs.title: Node.js Source Search
docs.text: rg -ni 'xml2js|fast-xml-parser|libxml|xmldom|sax' -g '*.js' -g '*.ts' -g 'package.json' .

docs.title: Go XML
docs.text:
Go applications commonly use:

encoding/xml

Search:

rg -ni 'encoding/xml|xml\.NewDecoder|xml\.Unmarshal' -g '*.go' .

docs.title: Go Interpretation
docs.text:
Do not classify the presence of:

encoding/xml

as XXE.

Review the actual parser behaviour and application data flow.

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Model
docs.text:
HTTP Request
     |
     v
XML Body
     |
     v
Application Handler
     |
     v
XML Parser
     |
     v
DTD / Entity Settings
     |
     +--> External Access Disabled
     |
     +--> External Access Enabled

docs.title: Source Review Workflow
docs.text:
Find XML Input
      |
      v
Find Parser
      |
      v
Identify Configuration
      |
      v
Check DTD Handling
      |
      v
Check Entity Resolution
      |
      v
Check External Resource Access
      |
      v
Check Output Usage

docs.title: Search XML Endpoints
docs.text: rg -ni 'application/xml|text/xml|application/soap\+xml|image/svg\+xml' .

docs.title: Search DTD References
docs.text: rg -ni 'DOCTYPE|DTD|external entity|entity resolver|XmlResolver|DtdProcessing' .

docs.title: Search XML File Processing
docs.text: rg -ni '\.xml|\.svg|\.docx|\.xlsx|\.pptx' src/ config/

docs.title: Search Parser Construction
docs.text: rg -ni 'parse\(|parseString|loadXML|readXML|newDocumentBuilder|XmlReader|DOMDocument' src/

docs.title: Low Priority
docs.text:
Constant trusted XML
       |
       v
Parser

No attacker-controlled XML.

docs.title: Medium Priority
docs.text:
User Data
   |
   v
XML Builder
   |
   v
Safe Serializer

Review how XML is generated and parsed.

docs.title: High Priority
docs.text:
Raw User XML
      |
      v
XML Parser

especially when parser hardening cannot be identified.

docs.title: High-Priority Pattern
docs.text:
Upload
  |
  v
XML / SVG / Document
  |
  v
Server-Side Parser

This deserves focused review.

docs.title: Parser Configuration Matters
docs.text:
Two applications using the same XML library may have different risk:

Application A
     |
     v
External Entities Disabled

versus:

Application B
     |
     v
External Entities Enabled

docs.title: Library Presence Is Not a Finding
docs.text:
Do not report:

Application uses XML parser.

Report:

Untrusted XML is processed with external entity resolution enabled.

when supported by evidence.

docs.title: Entity Expansion
docs.text:
XML entities can also create resource-consumption concerns.

This is related to XML parser security but is distinct from external entity file/network access.

docs.title: Resource Exhaustion
docs.text:
Avoid high-expansion XML payloads during normal assessments because they can consume significant:

CPU

Memory

Parser resources

and may cause denial of service.

docs.title: Safe Parser Testing
docs.text:
Prefer:

Single internal entity

Single external callback

Small controlled file

over resource-intensive parser stress tests.

docs.title: XSLT
docs.text:
Some XML processing pipelines apply XSL transformations.

Flow:

XML
 |
 v
XSLT Processor
 |
 v
Output

XSLT processing introduces additional capabilities and should be reviewed separately.

docs.title: XML Schema
docs.text:
XML Schema validation does not automatically prevent XXE.

The relevant question remains:

How is external resource resolution configured?

docs.title: External Schema References
docs.text:
Some XML processing systems can retrieve remote schemas.

This creates another server-side external resource retrieval surface.

docs.title: Namespace URLs
docs.text:
An XML namespace declaration such as:

xmlns:x="https://example.org/schema"

does not necessarily cause the parser to retrieve that URL.

Do not assume every namespace URI creates an outbound request.

docs.title: Schema Location
docs.text:
Attributes related to schema location can have different processing behaviour depending on the parser and validation configuration.

Test only when relevant to the application's XML pipeline.

docs.title: XML Comments
docs.text:
<!-- test -->

have no special XXE significance by themselves.

docs.title: CDATA
docs.text:
CDATA:

<![CDATA[
    <test>
]]>

prevents contained text from being interpreted as normal markup.

It is not an XXE defence for the XML document as a whole.

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
XML may declare encodings:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>

Parser behaviour should be tested with normal valid documents first.

docs.title: Content-Type vs Body
docs.text:
A request may contain:

Content-Type: application/xml

while the body is not valid XML.

Always establish a valid baseline before interpreting parser errors.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Proxy
  |
  v
Find XML Request
  |
  v
Send to Repeater
  |
  v
Baseline XML
  |
  v
Internal Entity
  |
  v
Controlled External Entity
  |
  v
Collaborator
  |
  v
Interpret Result

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Baseline:

POST /api/import HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/xml

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<user>
    <name>alice</name>
</user>

docs.title: Internal Entity Test
docs.text:
POST /api/import HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/xml

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE user [
    <!ENTITY marker "XXE_TEST_7f3a9">
]>
<user>
    <name>▮</name>
</user>

docs.title: External Entity Test
docs.text:
POST /api/import HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/xml

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE user [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "https://UNIQUE-ID.oastify.com/xxe-7f3a9">
]>
<user>
    <name>&xxe;</name>
</user>

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer can help identify subtle differences between:

Baseline response

Internal entity response

External entity response

docs.title: Burp Decoder
docs.text:
Decoder can help inspect encoded XML values when XML is embedded inside:

Base64

URL parameters

JSON strings

docs.title: XML Embedded in JSON
docs.text:
Example:

{
  "document": "<user><name>alice</name></user>"
}

The XML parser may be downstream from the JSON handler.

docs.title: Base64-Encoded XML
docs.text:
Example flow:

Base64 Input
    |
    v
Decode
    |
    v
XML Parser

Do not assume encoded data is safe simply because XML is not directly visible in the HTTP request.

docs.title: Multipart XML Upload
docs.text:
Example:

POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----test

The uploaded file may later be parsed as XML.

docs.title: File Upload Workflow
docs.text:
Upload File
    |
    v
File Stored
    |
    v
Background Processor
    |
    v
XML Parser

This can create delayed or blind XXE.

docs.title: Asynchronous Processing
docs.text:
Allow sufficient time for callbacks when XML is processed by:

Queues

Workers

Import jobs

Document processors

Scheduled tasks

docs.title: Stored XML
docs.text:
An application may store XML and process it only later.

Example:

Upload
  |
  v
Database / Object Storage
  |
  v
Import Job
  |
  v
Parser

docs.title: Blind Processing
docs.text:
The initial upload may return:

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted

while XXE processing occurs later.

docs.title: OOB Correlation
docs.text:
Use unique identifiers:

xxe-7f3a9

xxe-91bc2

for separate requests.

docs.title: Repeatability
docs.text:
A good validation uses:

Test A -> callback A

Test B -> callback B

This reduces ambiguity.

docs.title: Callback Source
docs.text:
The observed callback may originate from:

Web server

Worker

Proxy

NAT gateway

Document conversion service

Do not assume the source IP is the frontend server.

docs.title: User-Agent
docs.text:
An OOB HTTP request may contain a User-Agent that hints at the underlying library.

Treat it as supporting evidence only.

docs.title: Response Differences
docs.text:
If external entity retrieval is blocked, responses may differ.

Example:

Baseline:
200 OK

Internal entity:
200 OK

External entity:
500 Internal Server Error

This may indicate external entity processing was attempted and failed.

Further validation is required.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
An external entity pointing to an unreachable destination may cause a delay.

However:

Timeout != confirmed XXE

because many application behaviours can produce timing differences.

docs.title: False Positive - XML Accepted
docs.text:
application/xml accepted

does not prove XXE.

docs.title: False Positive - Internal Entity
docs.text: Internal entity expansion alone does not prove external resource access.

docs.title: False Positive - Scanner Alert
docs.text:
A scanner reporting:

Possible XXE

is a candidate requiring validation.

docs.title: False Positive - DNS Interaction
docs.text:
Determine whether the interaction was triggered by:

XML parser

Security scanner

URL validator

Other application component

Use unique tokens and repeatability.

docs.title: False Positive - Reflected XML
docs.text: If the server merely reflects the XML body without parsing it, entity syntax may appear in the response unchanged.

docs.title: Example Unparsed Response
docs.text:
Input:

<root>&xxe;</root>

Response:

You submitted: <root>&xxe;</root>

This does not demonstrate entity expansion.

docs.title: False Positive - Client-Side Parsing
docs.text:
If JavaScript in the browser parses the XML, the issue is not server-side XXE in the tested application backend.

Determine where parsing occurs.

docs.title: False Positive - Namespace URL
docs.text: A namespace URI appearing in XML does not prove the parser retrieves it.

docs.title: Common Testing Mistake - /etc/passwd First
docs.text:
Do not start by accessing sensitive system files.

Use:

Controlled callback

Harmless test file

first.

docs.title: Common Testing Mistake - Ignoring Blind XXE
docs.text: A parser may resolve external entities even when nothing appears in the response.

docs.title: Common Testing Mistake - Ignoring File Uploads
docs.text:
XML parsing often occurs in:

SVG

Office documents

Configuration imports

Metadata files

rather than obvious XML API endpoints.

docs.title: Common Testing Mistake - Ignoring Background Jobs
docs.text: The parser may run asynchronously.

docs.title: Common Testing Mistake - Confusing XXE and SSRF
docs.text: If XML entity processing causes the request, identify XXE as the root cause.

docs.title: Common Testing Mistake - Assuming All Parsers Behave the Same
docs.text:
Parser security depends heavily on:

Library

Version

Configuration

Framework defaults

docs.title: Common Testing Mistake - Using DoS Payloads
docs.text:
Entity expansion attacks can destabilise the target.

Avoid resource-exhaustion testing unless specifically authorised.

docs.title: Common Testing Mistake - Testing Only DOCTYPE
docs.text: If the application constructs XML internally, other XML processing features such as XInclude may still matter.

docs.title: Common Testing Mistake - Overclaiming
docs.text:
Do not claim:

XXE gives full server compromise.

when you demonstrated only:

External DNS resolution.

docs.title: Impact Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Can external entities be resolved?

Can local files be read?

Which files are readable by the application account?

Can external HTTP requests be made?

Can internal resources be reached?

Is the response returned?

Is the issue blind?

Can external DTDs be loaded?

Does processing occur with elevated privileges?

Does the parser run in a separate worker?

Are cloud/internal services reachable?

docs.title: Severity Considerations
docs.text:
Consider:

Authentication required

Parser privileges

Local file access

Response visibility

Internal network access

Cloud environment

External network access

Stored/asynchronous processing

Data sensitivity

docs.text:
Record:

Finding ID

Endpoint

HTTP method

Content-Type

Authentication context

XML input location

Parser behaviour

Entity declaration

Controlled marker

OOB hostname

DNS interaction

HTTP interaction

Local test file if used

Returned content

Timestamp

Response

Parser error

docs.title: Basic XXE Evidence Chain
docs.text:
1. Valid baseline XML accepted.

2. Internal entity processed.

3. Controlled external entity submitted.

4. External callback observed.

5. Test repeated with unique identifier.

6. Local harmless file used if required and authorised.

7. File contents returned.

docs.title: Blind XXE Evidence Chain
docs.text:
Request
   |
   v
Unique External Entity
   |
   v
Application Response
   |
   v
OOB DNS / HTTP
   |
   v
Timestamp Correlation
   |
   v
Repeat

docs.title: Evidence for File Disclosure
docs.text:
Capture:

Controlled test file creation

Known file contents

XML payload

Application response

Exact returned marker

docs.title: Reporting Example - External Entity Resolution
docs.text: The XML import endpoint processes user-controlled XML with external entity resolution enabled. An XML document containing an external entity referencing assessment-controlled infrastructure caused the application environment to perform a correlated HTTP request to the supplied destination. This demonstrates that untrusted XML can trigger server-side external resource retrieval.

docs.title: Reporting Example - File Disclosure
docs.text: The XML parser used by the import functionality resolves external file entities. During controlled testing, an entity referencing a harmless assessment-created file on the application host was expanded and the known file contents were returned in the application response. This demonstrates that files readable by the application process can be disclosed through XML entity resolution.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Blind XXE
docs.text: The application processes external entities but does not return the retrieved resource in the HTTP response. A unique external entity referencing assessment-controlled infrastructure resulted in correlated DNS and HTTP interactions from the application environment. The behaviour was reproduced with a second unique identifier, confirming blind XXE.

docs.title: Reporting Example - DNS Only
docs.text: A unique external entity hostname resulted in a correlated DNS lookup from the application environment. No HTTP request or local file disclosure was observed during repeated testing. The result demonstrates external hostname resolution during XML processing but does not establish successful HTTP resource retrieval or file disclosure.

docs.title: Reporting Example - XInclude
docs.text: The application processes user-controlled XInclude elements. A controlled XInclude reference to an assessment-created local test file caused the known file contents to be included in the processed document. The issue results from unsafe XInclude processing rather than DTD-based external entity resolution.

docs.title: Reporting Example - Secure Parser
docs.text:
If testing shows:

DOCTYPE rejected

No OOB interaction

No XInclude processing

do not report XXE.

Record the secure behaviour in assessment notes if useful.

docs.title: Remediation Principle
docs.text:
The preferred approach is:

Do not process DTDs or external entities when they are not required.

docs.title: Disable DTD Processing
docs.text:
Where application functionality does not require DTDs:

Disable DTD processing.

docs.title: Disable External Entities
docs.text:
Disable:

External general entities

External parameter entities

External DTD retrieval

where supported by the parser.

docs.title: Disable External Resolution
docs.text:
Ensure the XML parser cannot automatically retrieve:

Local files

HTTP resources

Other external resources

docs.title: Disable XInclude
docs.text:
If XInclude is unnecessary:

Disable XInclude processing.

docs.title: Use Hardened Parser APIs
docs.text:
Use parser configurations recommended by:

Language vendor

Framework vendor

OWASP

for the exact library and runtime version.

docs.title: Avoid Generic Copy-Paste Parser Fixes
docs.text:
A secure configuration for:

Java DocumentBuilderFactory

does not automatically apply to:

SAXParserFactory

XMLInputFactory

TransformerFactory

Configure each XML processing API appropriately.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text: The application process should have access only to files and network destinations required for its function.

docs.title: File Permissions
docs.text:
Even with parser hardening:

Application account
      |
      v
Minimal filesystem access

reduces the impact of parser mistakes.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Prevent XML-processing workloads from reaching unnecessary:

Management networks

Metadata services

Database networks

Administrative interfaces

docs.title: Egress Filtering
docs.text:
If the parser does not need outbound Internet access:

Block unnecessary outbound access.

docs.title: Isolate Document Processing
docs.text:
Complex document conversion can be isolated.

Application
    |
    v
Restricted Processing Worker
    |
    X--> Sensitive Internal Networks

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
Schema validation can help ensure expected document structure.

However:

Schema validation alone != XXE protection

docs.title: Update Libraries
docs.text: Keep XML parsers and document-processing libraries supported and patched.

docs.title: Avoid Verbose Parser Errors
docs.text:
Detailed parser errors can reveal:

Filesystem paths

Library details

Internal configuration

Return generic errors to untrusted clients while retaining useful server-side logging.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: Retest the exact original XML processing path.

docs.title: Retest Baseline
docs.text:
Confirm valid legitimate XML still works:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<root>
    <value>normal</value>
</root>

docs.title: Retest Internal Entity
docs.text: Depending on the intended parser configuration, entity processing should be handled according to the security design.

docs.title: Retest External Entity
docs.text:
Submit a controlled external entity:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE root [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "https://UNIQUE-ID.oastify.com/retest">
]>
<root>&xxe;</root>

Expected secure result:

DOCTYPE rejected

or:

External entity not resolved

with no OOB interaction.

docs.title: Retest Collaborator
docs.text:
Poll the controlled OOB service.

Expected:

No DNS interaction

No HTTP interaction

docs.title: Retest Local File
docs.text: Where authorised and appropriate, confirm the harmless test file can no longer be retrieved.

docs.title: Retest XInclude
docs.text: If the original issue involved XInclude, test the original XInclude path separately.

docs.title: Retest File Upload
docs.text:
If the vulnerability occurred through:

SVG

Office document

XML import

retest the exact file-processing workflow.

docs.title: Retest Background Processing
docs.text: Allow the normal worker/job cycle to complete before concluding remediation is effective.

docs.title: Retest All XML Parsers
docs.text:
An application can contain multiple XML-processing paths:

API parser

Import parser

Document parser

SOAP parser

SAML parser

Fixing one does not automatically fix the others.

docs.title: Root Cause Search
docs.text:
After one XXE issue is found, search the codebase for other parser construction sites.

Java:

rg -ni 'DocumentBuilderFactory|SAXParserFactory|XMLInputFactory|TransformerFactory' -g '*.java' .

.NET:

rg -ni 'XmlReader|XmlDocument|XDocument|XmlTextReader' -g '*.cs' .

Python:

rg -ni 'ElementTree|xml\.dom|xml\.sax|lxml|etree' -g '*.py' .

PHP:

rg -ni 'DOMDocument|simplexml|XMLReader|libxml' -g '*.php' .

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
The key XXE question is:

CAN ATTACKER-CONTROLLED XML
             |
             v
CAUSE THE XML PARSER
             |
             v
TO RESOLVE AN EXTERNAL RESOURCE?

A strong XXE workflow is:

Identify XML Input
       |
       v
Establish Valid Baseline
       |
       v
Test Internal Entity
       |
       v
Determine Entity Processing
       |
       v
Use Controlled External Entity
       |
       v
Observe DNS / HTTP
       |
       v
Repeat With Unique Marker
       |
       v
Use Harmless Local Test File if Required
       |
       v
Determine Actual Impact
       |
       v
Capture Evidence
       |
       v
Remediate Parser Configuration
       |
       v
Retest

For every XXE candidate ask:

Does the application actually parse XML?

Where does parsing occur?

Which parser is used?

Does it support DTDs?

Are internal entities expanded?

Are external general entities enabled?

Are external parameter entities enabled?

Can external DTDs be retrieved?

Can XInclude be processed?

Can the parser make outbound requests?

Did I observe DNS only?

Did I observe HTTP?

Can a harmless local file be read?

Does the application return entity content?

Is processing synchronous or asynchronous?

Does a worker perform the parsing?

What operating-system privileges does the parser have?

Can the parser reach internal networks?

Is the observed network request an effect of XXE?

Could the XML merely be reflected rather than parsed?

Could a scanner be generating the callback?

Can the behaviour be reproduced?

What impact was actually demonstrated?

Has every relevant XML parser been hardened?

Do not stop at:

The endpoint accepts XML.

Move through:

XML INPUT
    |
    v
PARSER
    |
    v
ENTITY PROCESSING
    |
    v
EXTERNAL RESOLUTION
    |
    v
OBSERVABLE EVIDENCE
    |
    v
SECURITY IMPACT

That distinction separates a parser candidate from a defensible XXE finding.

Start with a harmless marker

First determine whether the application parses XML and expands entities. A controlled marker such as XXE_TEST_7f3a9 produces cleaner evidence than immediately requesting operating-system files.

Use OOB testing for blind parsers

When entity content is not returned in the response, a unique assessment-controlled hostname can establish whether the parser performs external DNS resolution or HTTP retrieval.

Separate DNS from HTTP

A DNS lookup demonstrates hostname resolution. An HTTP callback provides stronger evidence that the external resource was actually requested. Record the interaction type accurately.

Review every parser path

Applications often contain more than one XML parser. SOAP, SAML, document import, SVG processing and configuration import may each use different libraries or parser settings.

Avoid destructive entity expansion

XML entity expansion can consume substantial CPU and memory. Resource-exhaustion testing is unnecessary for routine XXE validation and should not be performed unless denial-of-service testing is explicitly authorised.

Fix the parser, not the payload

Blocking strings such as DOCTYPE, SYSTEM or file:// at the application-input layer is not a reliable XXE defence. Disable unnecessary DTD, external entity and external resource processing in the XML parser itself, and apply least privilege and network restrictions as additional controls.

docs.title: Azure Security
docs.text:
Microsoft Azure security testing combines cloud infrastructure, identity, permissions, applications, and Microsoft Entra ID.

Unlike a traditional Active Directory assessment, an Azure assessment is not limited to hosts and domain relationships. Identity and access decisions can span tenants, subscriptions, resource groups, applications, service principals, managed identities, Azure resources, and Microsoft 365 services.

These notes provide a foundation for Azure security testing and will be expanded as practical experience with Azure environments and labs grows.

Note

This section intentionally focuses on core concepts and repeatable assessment methodology rather than attempting to document every Azure attack technique.

docs.title: Azure Security Model
docs.text:
A useful starting point is to separate the major layers of an Azure environment.

flowchart TD
    A["Microsoft Entra ID"] --> B["Users and Groups"]
    A --> C["Applications and Service Principals"]
    A --> D["Managed Identities"]

    B --> E["Azure RBAC"]
    C --> E
    D --> E

    E --> F["Subscriptions"]
    F --> G["Resource Groups"]
    G --> H["Azure Resources"]

    H --> I["Storage"]
    H --> J["Virtual Machines"]
    H --> K["App Services"]
    H --> L["Key Vault"]
    H --> M["Other Azure Services"]

The important security question is not simply:

What resources exist?

It is:

Which identities can influence which resources, through which permissions, and what security boundary can that access cross?

docs.title: Core Terminology
docs.text:
Understanding Azure terminology is important before attempting enumeration or attack-path analysis.

Term Description Tenant An organisation's Microsoft Entra ID directory Entra ID Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service User Human identity within the tenant Group Collection of identities used for access and administration Application Application definition registered in Entra ID Service Principal Tenant-specific identity representing an application or service Managed Identity Azure-managed identity that allows a resource to authenticate to other services Subscription Administrative and billing boundary containing Azure resources Resource Group Logical container for Azure resources Resource Azure object such as a VM, Key Vault, Storage Account, or App Service Azure RBAC Role-based access control used to authorise access to Azure resources Role Assignment Association between an identity, role, and scope Scope Level at which permissions apply Access Token Token used to access a particular API or resource Refresh Token Token that may be used to obtain new access tokens

docs.title: Resource Hierarchy
docs.text:
Azure resources are organised hierarchically.

Tenant
└── Management Groups
    └── Subscriptions
        └── Resource Groups
            └── Resources

Permissions assigned at a higher scope may be inherited by objects below it.

For example:

Subscription
    |
    | Contributor
    v
User

may give the user significant control over resources throughout the subscription.

Always determine both:

Permission
+
Scope

A powerful role at a narrow scope may have limited impact, while the same role at subscription scope can have much greater consequences.

docs.title: Identity Is Central
docs.text:
Azure assessments are heavily identity-driven.

Important identity objects include:

  • users;
  • groups;
  • service principals;
  • applications;
  • managed identities;
  • devices;
  • administrative roles.

A useful mental model is:

Identity
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Token
   ↓
Permission
   ↓
Resource
   ↓
Security Impact

Possession of valid credentials does not automatically mean administrative access.

Similarly:

Authentication Success
!=
Authorisation
!=
Administrative Rights

The permissions associated with the authenticated identity still need to be established.

docs.title: Microsoft Entra ID
docs.text:
Microsoft Entra ID is the identity layer used by Azure and many Microsoft cloud services.

During an authorised assessment, relevant areas may include:

  • users and groups;
  • directory roles;
  • applications;
  • service principals;
  • enterprise applications;
  • OAuth permissions;
  • managed identities;
  • devices;
  • Conditional Access;
  • authentication methods;
  • tenant relationships.

Entra ID should not be treated as simply "Active Directory in the cloud".

Traditional Active Directory and Entra ID have different protocols, objects, trust models, authentication flows, and administrative boundaries.

docs.title: Azure RBAC
docs.text:
Azure Role-Based Access Control determines what identities can perform against Azure resources.

A role assignment can be viewed as:

Security Principal
        +
Role Definition
        +
Scope
        =
Effective Access

Common built-in roles include:

Role General Meaning Reader View resources Contributor Manage resources but generally cannot assign Azure RBAC roles Owner Full resource management including access delegation User Access Administrator Manage user access to Azure resources

Custom roles may also exist.

Do not infer impact from the role name alone. Review the actual permissions and scope.

docs.title: Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
A basic Azure assessment can follow:

flowchart LR
    A["Identify Tenant"] --> B["Authenticate"]
    B --> C["Enumerate Identity"]
    C --> D["Enumerate Azure Resources"]
    D --> E["Map Permissions"]
    E --> F["Identify Attack Paths"]
    F --> G["Validate Safely"]
    G --> H["Collect Evidence"]
    H --> I["Security Conclusion"]

The same reasoning model used throughout these notes applies:

Observation → Candidate → Validation → Evidence → Security Conclusion

docs.title: 1. Identify the Tenant
docs.text:
Start by understanding the Microsoft cloud environment being assessed.

Identify:

  • tenant ID;
  • tenant domain;
  • verified domains;
  • subscription IDs where available;
  • accessible Microsoft cloud services;
  • current identity;
  • assessment scope.

Avoid assuming that discovering a tenant automatically means the associated resources are within scope.

docs.title: 2. Establish the Current Identity
docs.text:
When authenticated, determine:

  • username or service identity;
  • tenant;
  • object ID;
  • groups;
  • directory roles;
  • Azure RBAC assignments;
  • accessible subscriptions;
  • token context.

The objective is to understand:

Who am I?
        ↓
What can I access?
        ↓
What can I modify?

docs.title: 3. Enumerate the Environment
docs.text:
Initial enumeration should build an inventory of:

Users
Groups
Applications
Service Principals
Managed Identities
Subscriptions
Resource Groups
Resources
Role Assignments

Enumeration should be treated as discovery.

Finding an interesting object or permission does not automatically demonstrate a vulnerability.

docs.title: 4. Map Relationships
docs.text:
The next step is understanding how identities and resources are connected.

For example:

User
  ↓
Group
  ↓
Role Assignment
  ↓
Subscription
  ↓
Resource

or:

User
  ↓
Application
  ↓
Service Principal
  ↓
Permission
  ↓
Azure Resource

Complex environments are easier to analyse when relationships are represented as attack paths rather than isolated objects.

docs.title: 5. Validate Effective Access
docs.text:
Permissions should be validated carefully.

Distinguish between:

Permission Exists

and:

Permission Produces Security Impact

Questions include:

  • What action does the permission allow?
  • At what scope?
  • Can the identity actually perform the action?
  • Is another control preventing it?
  • Can the action influence another identity or resource?
  • Does it cross a security boundary?

docs.title: 6. Collect Evidence
docs.text:
Useful evidence may include:

  • tenant information;
  • current identity;
  • role assignments;
  • resource scope;
  • relevant application permissions;
  • Azure CLI output;
  • Microsoft Graph output;
  • Azure Resource Manager output;
  • AzureHound relationships;
  • ROADtools enumeration;
  • screenshots;
  • controlled validation results.

Evidence should demonstrate the reasoning chain rather than simply contain large tool dumps.

docs.title: Basic Tooling
docs.text: Several tools are useful when learning and assessing Azure environments.

docs.title: Azure CLI
docs.text:
Azure CLI is Microsoft's command-line interface for Azure.

Check the current account:

az account show

List available subscriptions:

az account list -o table

Show the active subscription:

az account show --query "{name:name,id:id,tenantId:tenantId,user:user.name}" -o json

List resource groups:

az group list -o table

List resources:

az resource list -o table

Note

The resources returned depend on the permissions of the authenticated identity.

docs.title: AzureHound
docs.text:
AzureHound is the Azure data collector used with BloodHound.

It can help collect Azure and Entra-related information so relationships can be analysed as a graph.

The conceptual workflow is:

Azure / Entra ID
       ↓
AzureHound
       ↓
Collected Relationships
       ↓
BloodHound
       ↓
Attack Path Analysis

AzureHound is particularly useful when many identity and permission relationships make manual analysis difficult.

Typical questions include:

  • Which users have privileged relationships?
  • Which groups influence privileged resources?
  • Which service principals have interesting permissions?
  • Which identities can reach higher-privileged objects?
  • What attack paths exist between the current identity and sensitive resources?

Important

A BloodHound path is a candidate attack path. Validate whether the permissions and relationships are actually usable in the assessed environment before reporting impact.

docs.title: ROADtools
docs.text:
ROADtools is a framework for interacting with and exploring Microsoft Entra ID.

The project includes several components.

docs.title: ROADrecon
docs.text:
ROADrecon focuses on collecting and exploring Entra ID information.

A simplified workflow is:

Authenticate
    ↓
Gather
    ↓
Store
    ↓
Analyse

The collected data can be analysed locally, which is useful for understanding:

  • users;
  • groups;
  • applications;
  • service principals;
  • directory relationships;
  • policies;
  • tenant configuration.

docs.title: ROADlib
docs.text: ROADlib provides reusable authentication and Entra ID functionality used by the ROADtools ecosystem.

docs.title: roadtx
docs.text:
roadtx focuses on Microsoft identity authentication and token-related workflows.

Because tokens can provide access to different resources and APIs, always identify:

Identity
+
Client
+
Resource / Scope
+
Token

before drawing conclusions about what a token permits.

docs.title: AzureHound vs ROADtools
docs.text:
The tools overlap in the broader goal of understanding Microsoft cloud environments but serve different purposes.

Tool Primary Use Azure CLI Interacting with Azure resources and subscriptions AzureHound Collecting relationships for BloodHound attack-path analysis ROADrecon Detailed Entra ID enumeration and offline exploration ROADlib Authentication and reusable Entra ID functionality roadtx Authentication and token-oriented workflows

They should be treated as complementary rather than competing tools.

docs.title: Subdomain Takeover
docs.text:
Azure services can become part of a subdomain takeover condition when organisational DNS continues to reference a deleted or otherwise unavailable cloud resource.

The important distinction is:

Dangling DNS
!=
Confirmed Subdomain Takeover

Resource claimability must be validated before describing the issue as a confirmed takeover.

Azure Subdomain Takeover

PWNCLOUDOS is a cloud-focused security operating system containing tooling for Azure, AWS, and GCP.

It can provide a dedicated environment for cloud security labs instead of manually building a large cloud tooling environment.

It is useful as a technical reference while working through labs, but findings should always be validated against current Microsoft behaviour and the actual environment.

docs.text:

docs.text:

flowchart LR

Rather than documenting advanced techniques before using them, new Azure pages should be added after the underlying concept has been studied or validated in a lab.

This keeps the notes practical and experience-driven.

docs.title: Azure Subdomain Takeover
docs.text:
Azure subdomain takeover can occur when an organisation's DNS record continues to reference an Azure resource that no longer exists, while the referenced resource name or endpoint can still be registered or controlled by another party.

This creates a dangling DNS record.

A dangling DNS record is an important indicator, but it does not automatically mean that a subdomain takeover is possible. The referenced Azure resource must also be reclaimable or otherwise controllable by an unauthorised party.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
The key distinction during testing is between identifying a dangling dependency and demonstrating that the dependency can actually cross a security boundary.

flowchart TD
    A["Organisation Subdomain"] --> B["DNS Record"]
    B --> C["Azure Service Hostname"]
    C --> D{"Azure Resource Exists?"}

    D -->|Yes| E["No Dangling Resource"]
    D -->|No| F["Dangling DNS"]

    F --> G{"Resource or Name Reclaimable?"}

    G -->|No| H["Dangling DNS Only"]
    G -->|Yes| I["Takeover Candidate"]

    I --> J["Controlled Validation"]
    J --> K{"Control Demonstrated?"}

    K -->|No| L["Unconfirmed"]
    K -->|Yes| M["Confirmed Subdomain Takeover"]

Important

An NXDOMAIN response, Azure error page, or known service fingerprint identifies a candidate condition, not a confirmed vulnerability. Confirmation requires evidence that the referenced resource can actually be controlled by an unauthorised party.

The assessment should therefore follow:

Observation → Candidate → Validation → Evidence → Security Conclusion

docs.title: How Azure Subdomain Takeover Happens
docs.text:
A typical configuration looks like:

app.example.com
        |
        | CNAME
        v
example-app.azurewebsites.net

While the Azure resource exists, requests to:

app.example.com

are routed to:

example-app.azurewebsites.net

The risk appears when the Azure resource is deleted but the organisation leaves the DNS record in place.

The resulting state may look like:

app.example.com
        |
        | CNAME
        v
example-app.azurewebsites.net
        |
        v
Azure resource no longer exists

If another party can legitimately register or control the referenced Azure resource or equivalent namespace, traffic intended for the organisation's subdomain may be directed to infrastructure outside the organisation's control.

docs.title: Conditions Required
docs.text:
A potential Azure subdomain takeover generally requires several conditions:

  1. The organisation controls a DNS name.

  2. The DNS record references an Azure-managed hostname or service.

  3. The original Azure resource has been deleted, removed, or otherwise become unavailable.

  4. The DNS record remains configured.

  5. The referenced Azure resource name, endpoint, or equivalent namespace can be controlled by another party.

  6. Requests for the organisation's subdomain can subsequently reach that resource.

The presence of only the first four conditions generally indicates dangling DNS, not necessarily a confirmed takeover.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Subdomain takeover testing normally begins with the organisation's known subdomains.

Potential sources include:

  • passive DNS data;
  • certificate transparency logs;
  • DNS enumeration;
  • asset inventories;
  • historical DNS records;
  • search engines;
  • archived URLs;
  • application JavaScript;
  • source code and configuration;
  • cloud asset inventories.

For general subdomain discovery methodology, see:

Subdomain Enumeration

docs.title: Inspect DNS Records
docs.text: Start by resolving the candidate hostname.

docs.title: dig
docs.text:
dig app.example.com

Query the CNAME directly:

dig CNAME app.example.com

Short output:

dig +short app.example.com

Follow the complete resolution:

dig app.example.com +trace

docs.title: host
docs.text: host app.example.com

docs.title: nslookup
docs.text: nslookup app.example.com

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Resolve-DnsName app.example.com

Query specifically for CNAME records:

Resolve-DnsName app.example.com -Type CNAME

docs.title: Follow the Entire CNAME Chain
docs.text:
Do not stop after discovering the first alias.

For example:

app.example.com
        |
        v
service.example.net
        |
        v
example-app.azurewebsites.net

The Azure dependency may only become visible after following multiple aliases.

The complete DNS chain should therefore be documented.

docs.title: Azure Service Namespaces
docs.text:
Azure uses many service-specific DNS namespaces.

Examples that may appear during an assessment include:

Azure Service Example Namespace Azure App Service *.azurewebsites.net Azure Traffic Manager *.trafficmanager.net Azure Storage *.blob.core.windows.net Azure API Management *.azure-api.net Azure SQL Database *.database.windows.net Azure AI Search *.search.windows.net Azure Container Registry *.azurecr.io Azure Container Instances *.azurecontainer.io Azure Cache for Redis *.redis.cache.windows.net Azure Service Bus *.servicebus.windows.net Azure VM Public DNS Azure regional cloud hostnames Azure CDN / Front Door Azure-managed delivery hostnames

Warning

The presence of an Azure hostname does not mean that the associated subdomain is vulnerable to takeover.

Azure service behaviour changes over time. Microsoft may introduce custom-domain verification, resource-name reservation, ownership validation, namespace restrictions, or other protections.

Always validate the current behaviour of the specific Azure service.

docs.title: Candidate Identification
docs.text:
Suppose DNS shows:

portal.example.com. 300 IN CNAME example-portal.azurewebsites.net.

The next step is to determine whether:

example-portal.azurewebsites.net

still represents an active resource.

Query the Azure hostname directly:

dig example-portal.azurewebsites.net

or:

host example-portal.azurewebsites.net

A failure to resolve can indicate that the original Azure resource no longer exists.

However:

NXDOMAIN != confirmed takeover

It only establishes part of the required condition.

docs.title: HTTP and HTTPS Validation
docs.text:
Check the organisation-controlled hostname:

curl -I https://portal.example.com

Follow redirects:

curl -IL https://portal.example.com

Inspect the response:

curl -i https://portal.example.com

Then compare it with the referenced Azure hostname:

curl -i https://example-portal.azurewebsites.net

Look for:

  • Azure-specific error pages;
  • missing-site responses;
  • unresolved hostnames;
  • service-specific error messages;
  • TLS certificate behaviour;
  • redirects;
  • HTTP status codes;
  • evidence that the backend resource is absent.

These observations help identify a candidate but should not independently be treated as proof of takeover.

docs.title: Example: Azure App Service
docs.text:
Consider:

shop.example.com
        |
        | CNAME
        v
company-shop.azurewebsites.net

The original Azure App Service is later deleted.

The DNS record remains:

shop.example.com CNAME company-shop.azurewebsites.net

An assessment may show:

dig CNAME shop.example.com

with output similar to:

shop.example.com. 300 IN CNAME company-shop.azurewebsites.net.

But:

dig company-shop.azurewebsites.net

may return:

NXDOMAIN

At this point the correct conclusion is:

The organisation has a dangling DNS record referencing an unavailable Azure resource.

The next question is:

Can the referenced Azure resource or equivalent endpoint actually be controlled by another Azure tenant?

Only after that question has been safely validated should the issue be described as a confirmed subdomain takeover.

docs.title: Resource Claimability
docs.text:
Resource claimability is the critical validation stage.

Questions to investigate include:

  1. Does the Azure resource still exist?

  2. Is the resource name globally unique or scoped to a subscription, tenant, region, or service?

  3. Can the same resource name currently be created?

  4. Does Azure reserve deleted resource names?

  5. Does the service require custom-domain ownership verification?

  6. Does Azure prevent another tenant from binding the organisation's domain?

  7. Are there service-specific takeover protections?

  8. Has the behaviour changed since older takeover research was published?

A known historical fingerprint should therefore be treated as a research lead, not as permanent proof of exploitability.

docs.title: Azure Portal Validation
docs.text:
Where authorised, the Azure Portal can help determine whether a candidate resource name is currently available.

The objective is to determine whether the Azure dependency can be legitimately created or controlled.

Do not create resources against third-party domains unless the assessment scope explicitly permits controlled validation.

Warning

Avoid causing disruption, serving arbitrary content, intercepting user traffic, collecting credentials, or interacting with real users.

The objective is to establish the minimum evidence necessary to prove or disprove the security condition.

docs.title: Controlled Proof of Concept
docs.text:
Where explicit authorisation permits resource creation, use the least invasive validation possible.

A controlled proof may demonstrate only that:

  • the Azure resource name can be registered;
  • the resource is under tester control;
  • the organisation's DNS record references that resource;
  • the custom domain can be associated where required;
  • a harmless marker can be returned.

For example, a harmless validation response could contain:

Security validation - authorised assessment

Do not reproduce the legitimate application or impersonate the organisation unnecessarily.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Good evidence should demonstrate the complete chain.

For example:

Organisation Subdomain
        ↓
DNS CNAME
        ↓
Azure Resource
        ↓
Resource Absent
        ↓
Resource Reclaimable
        ↓
Controlled Validation
        ↓
Confirmed Security Impact

Capture:

  • affected subdomain;
  • DNS record type;
  • complete CNAME chain;
  • Azure service;
  • Azure resource hostname;
  • DNS response;
  • HTTP response;
  • resource availability;
  • custom-domain verification requirements;
  • controlled proof, if authorised;
  • timestamp;
  • remediation status.

docs.title: Evidence Strength
docs.text:
Not all observations provide the same level of confidence.

Observation Evidence Strength Azure hostname discovered Informational Azure-specific error response Weak Azure hostname returns NXDOMAIN Candidate Dangling CNAME confirmed Candidate Historical takeover fingerprint matches Candidate Azure resource name appears available Strong candidate Resource can be controlled Strong Organisation subdomain resolves to controlled resource Confirmed

This distinction is important when writing findings.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text: Common false positives include:

docs.title: Deleted but Protected Resource
docs.text: The original Azure resource is gone, but Azure prevents the resource name from being reused.

docs.title: Custom-Domain Verification
docs.text: The resource name can be registered, but Azure requires proof of domain ownership before the organisation's hostname can be attached.

docs.title: Reserved Names
docs.text: Azure may reserve or protect previously used names.

docs.title: Service Behaviour Changed
docs.text: A service that historically allowed takeover may no longer permit it.

docs.title: Temporary DNS Failure
docs.text: An Azure endpoint may temporarily fail to resolve without the underlying resource being permanently deleted.

docs.title: Incorrect Fingerprint
docs.text: An error page may resemble a known takeover fingerprint but represent a different condition.

docs.title: Tool-Assisted Discovery
docs.text:
Automated tools can help identify takeover candidates.

They should be used for discovery and prioritisation, not as the sole evidence for a finding.

docs.title: Nuclei
docs.text:
A list of subdomains can be scanned using takeover-related templates:

nuclei -l subdomains.txt -tags takeover

A positive result should be manually validated.

The correct workflow is:

Scanner Match
     ↓
Candidate
     ↓
Manual DNS Validation
     ↓
Service Validation
     ↓
Claimability Validation
     ↓
Evidence
     ↓
Security Conclusion

docs.title: can-i-take-over-xyz
docs.text:
The can-i-take-over-xyz project documents known service fingerprints and historical takeover behaviour.

It is useful for identifying:

  • service-specific fingerprints;
  • vulnerable service patterns;
  • known error messages;
  • historical takeover conditions;
  • provider-specific notes.

However, cloud providers continuously change their protections.

Always verify the current status of the relevant Azure service instead of assuming that an older fingerprint remains exploitable.

docs.title: Global and Regional Names
docs.text:
Some Azure resource names are globally unique while others may be scoped differently.

Determine the actual namespace rules before concluding that a resource can be reclaimed.

docs.title: Custom-Domain Verification
docs.text:
Some Azure services require domain ownership verification before accepting a custom hostname.

This can prevent a dangling DNS condition from becoming a practical takeover.

docs.title: Resource Name Reuse
docs.text:
Deleted Azure resources may not always become immediately available for reuse.

Resource-name protection can significantly change takeover feasibility.

docs.title: Legacy Services
docs.text:
Older Azure services may behave differently from newer services.

Documentation and takeover research should therefore be checked against current service behaviour.

docs.title: DNS Aliases
docs.text:
Complex DNS chains can hide the Azure dependency.

For example:

portal.example.com
        ↓
app.cdn.example.net
        ↓
service.azureedge.net

Follow the chain until the actual service dependency is understood.

docs.title: Potential Impact
docs.text:
A confirmed subdomain takeover may allow an attacker to serve attacker-controlled content from a hostname trusted by users and applications.

Potential impact can include:

  • phishing;
  • malicious content hosting;
  • reputation abuse;
  • trust abuse;
  • security-policy bypasses;
  • cookie exposure in certain configurations;
  • OAuth redirect abuse;
  • CORS trust abuse;
  • application integration abuse;
  • bypass of hostname-based allowlists.

The actual impact depends on how the affected subdomain is used.

docs.title: Cookie Considerations
docs.text:
Review cookies scoped broadly to the parent domain.

For example:

Domain=.example.com

A controlled subdomain may interact with application trust assumptions differently from a completely unrelated domain.

Cookie impact depends on:

  • Domain;
  • Path;
  • Secure;
  • HttpOnly;
  • SameSite;
  • browser behaviour;
  • application architecture.

Do not automatically claim session compromise simply because a subdomain takeover exists.

Validate the actual cookie configuration.

docs.title: OAuth and Trusted Redirects
docs.text:
Check whether the affected hostname appears in:

  • OAuth redirect URI allowlists;
  • OpenID Connect configuration;
  • SAML endpoints;
  • application callback URLs;
  • trusted origin lists;
  • CORS allowlists;
  • webhook destinations;
  • API allowlists.

A seemingly low-value abandoned hostname may have greater impact if another system continues to trust it.

See:

OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

and:

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Organisations should continuously compare DNS records with active cloud resources.

Useful detection approaches include:

  • DNS inventory monitoring;
  • Azure resource inventory;
  • certificate transparency monitoring;
  • cloud asset management;
  • DNS change monitoring;
  • external attack-surface management;
  • scheduled takeover scanning;
  • decommissioning reviews.

The objective is to detect:

DNS Reference Exists
        +
Cloud Resource Does Not Exist

before the abandoned dependency becomes externally controllable.

docs.title: Remove DNS Before Deleting Resources
docs.text:
Where operationally possible, remove the public DNS dependency before deleting the Azure resource.

Preferred sequence:

Identify Dependencies
        ↓
Remove DNS Reference
        ↓
Verify DNS Propagation
        ↓
Remove Azure Resource
        ↓
Verify External State

docs.title: Maintain Asset Ownership
docs.text:
Track:

  • DNS records;
  • Azure resources;
  • subscriptions;
  • resource groups;
  • service owners;
  • application owners;
  • business owners;
  • decommission dates.

docs.title: Monitor Dangling DNS
docs.text: Regularly identify records pointing to resources that no longer exist.

docs.title: Review Custom Domains
docs.text: Maintain an inventory of Azure services with custom domains attached.

docs.title: Include DNS in Decommissioning
docs.text:
Deleting a cloud resource should never be treated as an isolated task.

The decommissioning process should include:

Application
DNS
Certificates
CDN
Cloud Resources
OAuth Integrations
Monitoring
Secrets
External Dependencies

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
For a confirmed or suspected dangling Azure dependency:

  1. Identify the DNS record.

  2. Confirm whether the record is still required.

  3. Determine the associated Azure resource.

  4. If the service is no longer required, remove the DNS record.

  5. If the service is required, restore or correctly configure the Azure resource.

  6. Review other DNS records for the same service or application.

  7. Review certificates and application integrations.

  8. Verify that the hostname no longer references an unowned resource.

  9. Retest externally.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation:

dig CNAME app.example.com

Confirm that the vulnerable or obsolete alias has been removed or updated.

Then:

dig app.example.com

and:

curl -I https://app.example.com

Confirm that the hostname either:

  • resolves to an organisation-controlled service; or
  • no longer resolves if the service has been retired.

docs.title: Assessment Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Enumerate organisation subdomains
  • [ ] Resolve CNAME records
  • [ ] Follow complete CNAME chains
  • [ ] Identify Azure-managed hostnames
  • [ ] Determine whether the Azure resource exists
  • [ ] Inspect HTTP and HTTPS behaviour
  • [ ] Identify service-specific fingerprints
  • [ ] Determine current Azure service behaviour
  • [ ] Check resource-name availability
  • [ ] Check custom-domain verification requirements
  • [ ] Distinguish dangling DNS from confirmed takeover
  • [ ] Perform controlled validation only when authorised
  • [ ] Capture evidence
  • [ ] Review cookies and trusted integrations
  • [ ] Document actual impact
  • [ ] Retest after remediation

docs.title: Security Conclusion
docs.text: The conclusion should reflect what was actually demonstrated.

docs.title: Confirmed Takeover
docs.text:
Use wording such as:

The affected subdomain referenced an Azure resource that no longer existed. During controlled validation, the referenced resource could be brought under tester control and the organisation's subdomain resolved to the controlled resource. This confirms that the dangling DNS configuration resulted in a subdomain takeover condition.

docs.title: Dangling DNS Only
docs.text:
If claimability was not demonstrated:

The affected subdomain contains a dangling DNS record referencing an Azure resource that no longer appears to exist. Resource claimability was not demonstrated; therefore, the condition should be reported as dangling DNS or a potential subdomain takeover rather than a confirmed takeover.

This distinction prevents an observation from being overstated as proven impact.
