Use these techniques only on Linux systems you own or have explicit permission to assess. Prefer configuration, permission, and execution-chain evidence over modifying service resources. Restarting, stopping, crashing, or changing production services can affect availability and should only be performed when explicitly authorised and operationally safe.

docs.title: sudo Security
docs.text:
sudo allows authorised users to execute commands as another user according to configured policy.

It is commonly used to delegate administrative capabilities without giving users unrestricted access to the root account.

During an authorised Linux security assessment, sudo configuration is one of the most important privilege-related areas to review.

The objective is not simply to identify commands that can be executed with sudo.

The objective is to determine whether delegated functionality allows a lower-privileged user to cross an unintended security boundary.

Current User
     |
     v
sudo Policy
     |
     v
Permitted Command
     |
     v
Target User
     |
     v
Command Functionality
     |
     +---- Arguments
     +---- Environment
     +---- Referenced files
     +---- Child processes
     +---- Plugins / modules
     +---- External commands
     |
     v
Can Delegated Access Exceed Intended Boundary?

A sudo rule is not automatically a vulnerability.

The security question is:

Can the permitted command or something it trusts be influenced in a way that provides capabilities beyond those intentionally delegated?

Authorised Security Testing

Use these techniques only on systems you own or have explicit permission to assess. Prefer configuration inspection and non-destructive validation. Do not alter production sudoers files, privileged scripts, system binaries or application configuration merely to demonstrate impact.

docs.title: 1. What sudo Does
docs.text:
The basic syntax is:

sudo command

A command can also be executed as another user:

sudo -u username command

sudo policy determines whether the requesting user is permitted to perform the requested operation.

Important components include:

Requesting User

Host

Run-As User

Run-As Group

Command

Arguments

Authentication Requirement

Environment

sudo Options

These relationships are normally configured through:

/etc/sudoers

and commonly:

/etc/sudoers.d/

Configuration should normally be edited with visudo, not by directly modifying the files.

During an assessment, prefer read-only inspection.

docs.title: 2. Establish the Current Context
docs.text:
Start with:

whoami
id

Record:

Username

UID

Primary GID

Supplementary groups

Then determine whether the user belongs to an administrative group.

groups

Common administrative groups may include:

sudo
wheel

depending on the distribution.

Group membership alone does not prove what the user can execute.

The effective sudo policy is more important.

docs.title: 3. Enumerate sudo Permissions
docs.text:
The primary assessment command is:

sudo -l

This lists commands the current user is permitted to execute according to the applicable sudo policy.

Representative output may resemble:

User analyst may run the following commands on server01:
    (root) /usr/bin/systemctl status example.service

Interpretation:

Requesting user:
analyst

Run-as user:
root

Permitted command:
/usr/bin/systemctl status example.service

Do not stop at the command name.

Determine what the command can actually do.

docs.title: 4. sudo -l Without Prompting for a Password
docs.text:
In some assessment situations, you may want to avoid an unexpected interactive password prompt.

Use:

sudo -n -l

The -n option requests non-interactive behavior.

If authentication is required and no cached credentials are available, sudo should fail instead of prompting.

This can be useful during controlled enumeration or automated collection.

Do not interpret failure as proof that no sudo rights exist.

Authentication state and policy can affect the result.

docs.title: 5. Understanding sudo -l Output
docs.text:
A rule may resemble:

(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart example.service

Another might resemble:

(backup) /usr/local/bin/backup-status

The section in parentheses represents the permitted run-as context.

For example:

(root)

means the command can be executed as root according to that rule.

(backup)

means it can be executed as the backup user.

Do not assume that only root delegation is security relevant.

Access to another service or application account can expose:

Credentials

Configuration

Data

SSH keys

Application secrets

Additional sudo permissions

Group memberships

Files inaccessible to the original user

Privilege escalation can therefore be multi-stage.

docs.title: 6. Run-As Users
docs.text:
A useful model is:

analyst
   |
   | sudo
   v
backup
   |
   +---- Sensitive files
   +---- SSH keys
   +---- Application configuration
   +---- Additional privileges
   |
   v
Potential Additional Security Boundary

Always determine:

Which user can the command run as?

Which group can it run as?

What access does that identity have?

Does the target identity have additional sudo permissions?

If authorised and appropriate, the target user's effective privileges can be assessed separately after access has been legitimately established.

docs.title: 7. NOPASSWD
docs.text:
A rule may contain:

NOPASSWD:

Example:

(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart example.service

This means the applicable command can be executed without sudo requiring the user's password under that rule.

NOPASSWD is not automatically a vulnerability.

The relevant question remains:

What functionality has been delegated?

A narrowly restricted non-interactive operational command may be intentional.

A broadly capable command may represent significantly greater risk.

docs.title: 8. PASSWD Versus NOPASSWD
docs.text:
The difference affects authentication requirements:

PASSWD
   |
   +---- sudo may require authentication

NOPASSWD
   |
   +---- command can be authorised without that password prompt

However:

Password Required != Secure Rule

NOPASSWD != Vulnerable Rule

The capability exposed by the command remains the primary security consideration.

docs.title: 9. sudo Authentication Cache
docs.text:
sudo can cache successful authentication for a period determined by policy.

This means subsequent commands may not immediately prompt again.

The assessment should therefore distinguish:

Rule permits command

from:

Authentication currently cached

The two are not equivalent.

Do not infer NOPASSWD simply because no password prompt appeared.

docs.title: 10. List sudo Version
docs.text:
Version information can be obtained with:

sudo --version

The output can include:

sudo version

sudoers policy plugin version

sudoers file grammar version

I/O plugin information

Build options

Version information can help understand supported features.

Do not report a vulnerability based solely on a version string.

Confirm:

Distribution package

Vendor patches

Security backports

Configuration

Exploit prerequisites

Actual affected condition

before reaching a vulnerability conclusion.

docs.title: 11. sudoers Configuration
docs.text:
The primary policy file is commonly:

/etc/sudoers

Additional configuration may exist under:

/etc/sudoers.d/

Whether the current user can read these files depends on system configuration.

Where access is permitted:

ls -l /etc/sudoers
ls -ld /etc/sudoers.d
ls -l /etc/sudoers.d 2>/dev/null

If the files are readable within scope:

sudo cat /etc/sudoers

should not be used merely to circumvent normal read permissions unless the applicable sudo policy explicitly permits and the assessment requires it.

In most cases:

sudo -l

is the safer starting point for determining the current user's effective delegated commands.

docs.title: 12. Never Edit sudoers Directly During Testing
docs.text:
Administrators normally use:

visudo

because it validates syntax before committing changes.

A malformed sudoers configuration can affect administrative access.

During a penetration test:

Do not add yourself to sudoers.

Do not change NOPASSWD rules.

Do not weaken command restrictions.

Do not alter /etc/sudoers merely to prove write access.

If unexpected write access is identified, validate the filesystem permission safely and report the security relationship.

docs.title: 13. Check sudoers Permissions
docs.text:
Inspect:

stat /etc/sudoers

and where relevant:

getfacl /etc/sudoers

Inspect the directory:

stat /etc/sudoers.d

getfacl /etc/sudoers.d

The important questions are:

Can an unprivileged user modify sudo policy?

Can an unprivileged user create trusted policy files?

Are unexpected ACLs present?

Are parent directory permissions appropriate?

Unexpected write access to effective sudo policy is highly security sensitive.

Do not modify the policy to demonstrate the issue.

docs.title: 14. Command Paths
docs.text:
sudo rules should be analysed using the exact command specification.

For example:

(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart application.service

is very different from a broadly scoped rule.

Record the exact:

Executable path

Arguments

Wildcards

Run-as identity

Tags

Options

Do not simplify a rule during reporting in a way that changes its security meaning.

docs.title: 15. Verify the Binary
docs.text:
If a rule permits:

/usr/local/bin/backup-status

inspect the actual object:

ls -l /usr/local/bin/backup-status

stat /usr/local/bin/backup-status

getfacl /usr/local/bin/backup-status

Inspect the complete path:

namei -l /usr/local/bin/backup-status

Questions include:

Who owns the binary?

Who can modify it?

Can its parent directory be modified?

Is it a script?

Is it a symbolic link?

Does it load additional configuration?

A carefully restricted sudo rule can become unsafe if the permitted executable itself is modifiable by the requesting user.

docs.title: 16. Writable sudo Executable
docs.text:
Consider:

analyst ALL=(root) /usr/local/bin/backup-status

If:

stat /usr/local/bin/backup-status

shows that analyst can modify the file, the relationship is significant.

analyst
   |
   v
Write Access
   |
   v
/usr/local/bin/backup-status
   |
   v
sudo
   |
   v
root

Do not modify the executable during routine validation.

The combination of:

sudo rule
+
confirmed write permission
+
root run-as context

can provide sufficient evidence of the trust-boundary problem.

docs.title: 17. Parent Directory Permissions
docs.text:
The executable itself may appear protected:

-rwxr-xr-x root root /usr/local/bin/custom-backup

but its parent directory must also be inspected.

namei -l /usr/local/bin/custom-backup

A lower-privileged user may be unable to modify the existing file contents while still having meaningful control over the directory entry under certain permission configurations.

Therefore always review:

Executable

Parent directory

Complete path

ACLs

See Linux Filesystem Permissions.

docs.title: 18. Scripts Permitted Through sudo
docs.text:
A sudo rule may permit a script:

(root) /opt/application/maintenance.sh

Inspect:

stat /opt/application/maintenance.sh
getfacl /opt/application/maintenance.sh
namei -l /opt/application/maintenance.sh

Then inspect what the script depends on.

Possible dependencies include:

Configuration files

Helper scripts

Environment files

External commands

Libraries

Temporary files

Input files

Plugins

The top-level script can be root-owned and protected while still trusting another writable resource.

docs.title: 19. Script Dependency Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

sudo Rule
    |
    v
Root-Owned Script
    |
    +---- Helper script
    |
    +---- Configuration
    |
    +---- External command
    |
    +---- Input file
    |
    +---- Temporary resource
    |
    v
Can User Influence Any Dependency?

Do not evaluate only the first file in the execution chain.

docs.title: 20. External Commands
docs.text:
Suppose an authorised script invokes external programs.

Determine whether it uses:

Absolute paths

such as:

/usr/bin/logger

or relies on command lookup such as:

logger

Relative command resolution may require further assessment of the execution environment and sudo policy.

Do not assume that a command without an absolute path is exploitable.

You must determine the effective PATH and whether an attacker-controlled location can actually influence resolution.

docs.title: 21. PATH Handling
docs.text:
Display the current PATH:

printf '%s\n' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'

However, the current user's shell PATH may not be the PATH used by sudo.

sudo policy can define a controlled path using settings such as:

secure_path

Where visible through sudo -l, policy options may provide relevant context.

The assessment question is:

What PATH is effective for the privileged command?

not:

What PATH does my current shell have?

docs.title: 22. secure_path
docs.text:
A sudoers configuration can define a trusted executable search path.

Conceptually:

Defaults secure_path="..."

This can reduce risk from user-controlled PATH entries.

However, the presence of secure_path does not automatically make every sudo rule safe.

You must still assess:

Permitted binary

Arguments

Dependencies

Writable resources

Environment

Command functionality

docs.title: 23. Environment Variables
docs.text:
sudo normally applies environment-handling rules when executing commands.

Relevant policy concepts include:

env_reset

env_keep

env_check

env_delete

setenv

The effective configuration depends on sudoers policy and build configuration.

During assessment, determine whether environment variables relevant to the permitted program can be influenced.

Examples might include application-specific variables controlling:

Configuration paths

Plugin paths

Runtime behaviour

Temporary directories

Language runtimes

Do not assume arbitrary environment variables survive sudo execution.

Validate the actual policy.

docs.title: 24. SETENV
docs.text:
Some sudo rules can allow users greater control over environment variables.

If SETENV appears in applicable policy output, determine:

Which command does it apply to?

Which environment variables matter to that command?

Does the application trust those variables?

Can they influence privileged behaviour?

SETENV alone is not automatically a finding.

The privileged program's behavior determines impact.

docs.title: 25. Command Arguments
docs.text:
Argument restrictions are critical.

Compare:

/usr/bin/systemctl status example.service

with a rule that allows substantially broader argument selection.

When reviewing a sudo rule, capture the complete command specification exactly as shown.

Ask:

Are arguments fixed?

Are arguments optional?

Can additional arguments be supplied?

Are wildcards present?

Can arguments reference files?

Can arguments change configuration?

Can arguments launch another program?

Do not assume that a restricted-looking command remains restricted without understanding how sudo matches that rule.

docs.title: 26. Wildcards
docs.text:
sudoers command specifications can contain wildcard patterns.

Wildcards require careful analysis because command-line arguments are matched according to sudoers policy rules rather than according to an administrator's intuitive idea of a filesystem pattern.

A rule that appears to constrain access to:

/var/log/application/*

should therefore be reviewed carefully.

Questions include:

What portion of the command is wildcarded?

Can multiple arguments be supplied?

Can path traversal or alternate path forms affect the application?

How does the permitted program interpret the resulting arguments?

Do not assume that every wildcard creates an escape.

The exact rule and program behavior must be validated.

docs.title: 27. Broad Command Delegation
docs.text:
Some commands expose substantially more functionality than their names suggest.

Examples of command categories requiring careful review include:

Text editors

Pagers

Interpreters

Shells

Debuggers

Package managers

Service managers

Archive utilities

File-management tools

Build tools

Version-control tools

Network clients

The question is not whether a command appears administrative.

The question is:

Does the permitted functionality allow execution, file modification, subprocess creation or another action outside the intended delegated task?

docs.title: 28. Interpreters
docs.text:
Interpreters can expose broad program execution capabilities.

Examples include:

python
python3
perl
ruby
php
bash
sh

If an interpreter is delegated through sudo, determine whether:

The script is fixed

Arguments are fixed

Interactive execution is possible

Arbitrary code can be supplied

Additional modules can be loaded

Environment variables affect module resolution

Do not conclude from the interpreter name alone.

The exact sudo command specification matters.

docs.title: 29. Editors
docs.text:
Text editors may provide functionality beyond simply editing one file.

Potential capabilities can include:

Opening additional files

Writing additional files

Launching subprocesses

Using plugins

Using configuration files

If an editor is permitted through sudo, determine whether the policy genuinely restricts it to the intended operation.

Do not use editor subprocess functionality during production testing unless such impact validation is explicitly authorised and necessary.

docs.title: 30. Pagers
docs.text:
Programs used to display text can sometimes expose additional interactive features.

The security relevance depends on:

Program

Version

Invocation

Environment

sudo restrictions

Interactive context

Do not assume that every pager invocation permits arbitrary execution.

Assess the exact delegated command.

docs.title: 31. Service Management
docs.text:
sudo rules frequently delegate service operations.

Example:

(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart application.service

This may be entirely legitimate.

The assessment should correlate the rule with the service configuration.

Inspect:

systemctl cat application.service

Determine:

Who owns the unit?

Who owns the executable?

Can the current user modify configuration?

Can the current user modify EnvironmentFile resources?

Can the current user modify the service executable?

Can the current user modify scripts called by the service?

The rule becomes more significant when the user can control a resource the privileged service consumes.

See Linux Services.

docs.title: 32. Example Service Relationship
docs.text:
Suppose:

analyst ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart reports.service

The restart permission itself may be expected.

But:

systemctl cat reports.service

shows:

ExecStart=/opt/reports/start.sh

and:

stat /opt/reports/start.sh

shows the user can modify the script.

The relevant relationship is:

analyst
   |
   +---- Can modify start.sh
   |
   +---- Can restart reports.service through sudo
   |
   v
root executes start.sh

The vulnerability is not simply:

User can restart a service.

It is the combined trust relationship.

docs.title: 33. Scheduled Job Management
docs.text:
A delegated command may also interact with scheduled tasks or timers.

If a sudo rule permits management of a timer or scheduled service, determine whether the user can modify resources consumed by the resulting privileged execution.

Correlate with Scheduled Jobs.

docs.title: 34. File Operations
docs.text:
Commands that read, copy, move or otherwise manipulate files should be analysed based on their permitted scope.

Ask:

Can the user choose the source?

Can the user choose the destination?

Can protected files be read?

Can protected files be replaced?

Can ownership or mode be preserved or changed?

Can symbolic links affect behavior?

Do not perform destructive file replacement during routine validation.

docs.title: 35. Archive Utilities
docs.text:
Archive tools can interact with many files and directories.

When delegated through sudo, determine:

Can archive contents be chosen?

Can extraction paths be chosen?

Can options invoke external functionality?

Can protected files be read?

Can privileged paths be written?

The exact utility, arguments and sudo rule determine whether a meaningful security boundary exists.

docs.title: 36. Package Management
docs.text:
Package-management tools are highly privileged because software installation inherently changes system state.

Examples include distribution-specific tools such as:

apt
apt-get
dnf
yum
rpm
dpkg

If package management is delegated, determine whether the scope is intentionally equivalent to administrative software installation.

Do not install or remove packages merely to prove impact.

The delegated capability itself may already establish the level of access.

docs.title: 37. Shell Delegation
docs.text:
If policy explicitly allows a root shell, the security meaning is usually clear.

For example, a policy equivalent to unrestricted root command execution should not be reported as a privilege escalation vulnerability if the user is intentionally authorised as an administrator.

Always distinguish:

Intended Administrative Access

from:

Unintended Privilege Escalation

Context matters.

docs.title: 38. ALL Rules
docs.text:
An applicable sudo rule may grant broad command execution.

Conceptually:

ALL

can represent very broad permissions depending on where it appears in the sudoers rule.

Do not interpret ALL without understanding its position.

sudoers specifications can involve:

User

Host

Run-as user

Run-as group

Command

Record the complete rule rather than reporting only the word ALL.

docs.title: 39. Group-Based sudo Rules
docs.text:
sudo permissions can be assigned to groups.

A typical policy concept may resemble:

%administrators

where % denotes a Unix group in sudoers syntax.

Determine:

id

and:

groups

Then correlate group membership with effective output from:

sudo -l

The effective policy matters more than simply finding a group definition.

docs.title: 40. Included sudoers Files
docs.text:
sudo policy can be split across multiple files.

Commonly:

/etc/sudoers.d/

is used for modular policy.

Assess:

ls -ld /etc/sudoers.d

and, where permitted:

ls -l /etc/sudoers.d

Check:

Directory owner

Directory permissions

File owners

File permissions

ACLs

Unexpected unprivileged write access to a trusted policy location requires careful investigation.

docs.title: 41. Symbolic Links and sudo Resources
docs.text:
If a sudo-permitted script or configuration is a symbolic link, resolve it:

readlink -f /path/to/resource

Then inspect:

namei -l /path/to/resource

The security assessment should consider the actual target rather than only the visible link.

docs.title: 42. Configuration Dependencies
docs.text:
Suppose:

(root) /usr/local/bin/report-generator

is permitted.

The executable itself is protected.

However, it loads:

/etc/report-generator/config.yml

or:

/opt/reports/config.yml

Inspect:

stat /opt/reports/config.yml
getfacl /opt/reports/config.yml
namei -l /opt/reports/config.yml

If the current user can modify security-sensitive configuration consumed by the privileged command, the sudo rule requires deeper analysis.

docs.title: 43. Plugin and Extension Directories
docs.text:
Applications can support:

Plugins

Modules

Extensions

Hooks

Templates

If a sudo-permitted application loads code or behavior from such locations, determine:

Which directories are searched?

Who owns them?

Who can write to them?

Does the application load them during privileged execution?

Can configuration change the search location?

Do not create malicious plugins merely to validate the relationship unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: 44. Temporary Files
docs.text:
Privileged commands may create or consume temporary files.

Review whether they use:

/tmp

/var/tmp

Application-specific temporary directories

The existence of temporary files is not itself a weakness.

The security question is whether privileged software trusts attacker-controlled temporary resources unsafely.

Kernel protections, sticky-bit semantics and application behavior all affect the result.

docs.title: 45. sudoedit
docs.text:
sudoedit provides a controlled mechanism for editing authorised files.

It should be distinguished from simply running an editor as root.

Where sudoedit permissions are present, determine:

Which files can be edited?

Are paths fixed?

Are wildcards involved?

Which sudo version and vendor package are present?

What policy restrictions apply?

Do not infer a vulnerability solely because sudoedit is available.

docs.title: 46. Command Digests
docs.text:
sudoers can support command digests that tie an allowed command to cryptographic content.

Where such configuration is used, it can help ensure that the authorised command has not changed.

During assessment, document digest restrictions if they materially affect the command's trust model.

Do not assume every sudo deployment uses command digests.

docs.title: 47. NOEXEC
docs.text:
sudo can support a NOEXEC policy tag in applicable environments.

Its purpose is to restrict certain delegated programs from executing additional commands through supported mechanisms.

However, NOEXEC should be treated as defense-in-depth rather than a universal guarantee.

Its effectiveness depends on:

Operating system

Program behavior

How subprocesses are created

sudo build and configuration

Do not assume that NOEXEC makes an otherwise excessively powerful command safe.

docs.title: 48. INTERCEPT and Other Policy Features
docs.text:
Modern sudo versions can support additional policy and execution-control features depending on build and configuration.

Do not assume that every system supports or enables the same sudo features.

During assessment, use:

sudo --version

and effective policy output to understand the local environment.

Avoid designing findings around a feature that is not actually deployed.

docs.title: 49. GTFOBins
docs.text:
GTFOBins documents legitimate Unix binaries that can expose security-sensitive functionality when placed in particular privilege contexts.

GTFOBins

It can be useful when reviewing an unfamiliar sudo-permitted binary.

However:

Binary Listed on GTFOBins

does not mean:

System Vulnerable

The correct workflow is:

sudo -l
   |
   v
Identify Permitted Binary
   |
   v
Understand Exact Rule
   |
   v
Understand Binary Functionality
   |
   v
Check Version / Environment
   |
   v
Check Restrictions
   |
   v
Determine Actual Security Impact

docs.title: 50. Practical Validation Workflow
docs.text:
Use this workflow for each interesting sudo rule.

sudo -l
   |
   v
Identify Rule
   |
   v
Record Run-As User
   |
   v
Record Exact Command
   |
   v
Record Arguments
   |
   v
Record Tags / Options
   |
   v
Inspect Binary
   |
   v
Inspect Parent Directories
   |
   v
Inspect Dependencies
   |
   v
Inspect Environment
   |
   v
Understand Program Functionality
   |
   v
Determine Security Boundary
   |
   v
Safe Validation
   |
   v
Evidence
   |
   v
Conclusion

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
sudo -l returns:

(root) NOPASSWD: /opt/vendor/backup.sh

docs.title: Step 1 - Establish Identity
docs.text: id

docs.title: Step 2 - Record sudo Rule
docs.text: sudo -l

docs.title: Step 3 - Inspect Script
docs.text:
stat /opt/vendor/backup.sh

getfacl /opt/vendor/backup.sh

docs.title: Step 4 - Inspect Complete Path
docs.text: namei -l /opt/vendor/backup.sh

docs.title: Step 5 - Check Effective Write Access
docs.text:
if test -w /opt/vendor/backup.sh; then
    echo "[+] Current context reports write access"
else
    echo "[-] Current context does not report write access"
fi

Do not modify the script.

docs.title: 52. Representative Positive Result
docs.text:
Suppose the evidence shows:

User:
analyst

sudo rule:
(root) NOPASSWD: /opt/vendor/backup.sh

Script owner:
root

Script group:
developers

Permissions:
-rwxrwxr-x

Current user's groups:
developers

Relationship:

analyst
   |
   v
developers
   |
   v
Write Access
   |
   v
backup.sh
   |
   v
sudo as root

This provides strong evidence that the sudo trust boundary is incorrectly configured.

The production script does not need to be modified to demonstrate the underlying condition.

docs.title: 53. Representative Negative Result
docs.text:
Suppose:

(root) /usr/bin/systemctl status application.service

is permitted.

Further assessment determines:

Arguments are restricted.

Service resources are root-owned.

Application configuration is protected.

No writable dependencies are identified.

No additional privileged functionality is available through the permitted invocation.

The appropriate conclusion may be:

The delegated command was reviewed and no unintended privilege escalation
path was identified under the assessed configuration.

This is a valid assessment outcome.

docs.title: 54. Multi-Step Privilege Relationships
docs.text:
sudo does not always lead directly to root.

Example:

webuser
   |
   | sudo
   v
deploy
   |
   +---- Deployment credentials
   |
   +---- Application configuration
   |
   +---- Additional group membership
   |
   | sudo
   v
root

Assessment should consider the complete privilege graph.

A transition to another account can materially change the security context even when it does not immediately provide UID 0.

docs.title: 55. False Positives and Alternative Explanations
docs.text:
Common false positives include:

NOPASSWD rule for narrowly restricted operational command

sudo permission intentionally equivalent to administrator access

Read-only status command with no additional functionality

Service restart permission where all service resources are protected

GTFOBins-listed binary invoked with effective restrictions

Writable file unrelated to the sudo-permitted command

Current shell PATH mistaken for sudo's effective PATH

sudo authentication cache mistaken for NOPASSWD

Inactive or obsolete sudo configuration

Rule that does not actually apply to current host or user

Always validate the effective policy.

docs.title: 56. Automated Enumeration
docs.text:
Tools such as:

LinPEAS

LinEnum

linux-smart-enumeration

can highlight sudo permissions.

However:

Automated Tool
      |
      v
Interesting sudo Rule
      |
      v
Manual Review
      |
      v
Program Analysis
      |
      v
Dependency Analysis
      |
      v
Security Conclusion

Do not treat automated classification as proof of exploitability.

docs.title: 57. Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each significant sudo observation, capture:

Hostname

Current user

UID

GID

Groups

sudo version

sudo -l output

Run-as user

Run-as group

Authentication requirement

Exact permitted command

Arguments

Tags

Binary path

Binary owner

Binary group

Binary permissions

ACLs

Parent directory permissions

Relevant dependencies

Relevant environment behavior

Validation result

Useful commands include:

id
sudo --version
sudo -l
stat /path/to/command
getfacl /path/to/command
namei -l /path/to/command

docs.title: 58. Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

User has sudo access.

This provides insufficient context.

Prefer:

The analyst account is permitted to execute /opt/vendor/backup.sh as root through sudo without additional authentication. The script is writable by the developers group, of which analyst is a member. As a result, a lower-privileged user can modify code that sudo subsequently executes with UID 0.

This identifies:

Principal

sudo rule

Target identity

Controllable resource

Trust relationship

Security impact

docs.title: Observation
docs.text: The assessed user can execute a group-writable maintenance script as root through sudo.

docs.title: Current User
docs.text: analyst

docs.title: sudo Rule
docs.text: (root) NOPASSWD: /opt/vendor/maintenance.sh

docs.title: Affected Resource
docs.text: /opt/vendor/maintenance.sh

docs.title: Permission Relationship
docs.text:
Owner: root
Group: developers
Group permission: write
Current user: member of developers

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: A lower-privileged user can influence code that is explicitly authorised to execute as root.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text: Remove write access to the script and its trusted dependencies from non-administrative principals.

docs.title: 60. Reporting Intentional Administrative Access
docs.text:
Not every broad sudo rule is a vulnerability.

Suppose:

User:
sysadmin

Role:
Linux administrator

sudo:
Full root administration

If this access is intentionally required and consistent with the approved privilege model, reporting:

User can become root through sudo

as a vulnerability would be misleading.

Instead review:

Is the user expected to be an administrator?

Is the account appropriately protected?

Is access centrally managed?

Is privileged activity logged?

Is the access still required?

docs.title: 61. Remediation
docs.text:
sudo remediation should follow least privilege.

Prefer:

Specific commands

Specific target users

Specific arguments where practical

Protected executables

Protected configuration

Protected dependencies

Minimal environment exposure

Avoid unnecessarily broad delegation.

For example, administrators should consider whether users need:

Full shell

Full interpreter

Generic editor

Package manager

Broad service manager

Wildcard command

when a narrower administrative operation would satisfy the business requirement.

docs.title: 62. Protect sudo-Executed Resources
docs.text:
All resources trusted by privileged sudo commands should have appropriate ownership and permissions.

Review:

Executable

Script

Configuration

Environment file

Helper script

Plugin directory

Library path

Parent directories

The security model should resemble:

Privileged sudo Command
       |
       v
Trusted Resource
       |
       v
Writable Only by Trusted Administrators

docs.title: 63. Prefer Purpose-Built Administrative Interfaces
docs.text:
Instead of delegating a broadly capable command, consider purpose-built wrappers or service-management interfaces that expose only the required operation.

However, wrapper scripts must themselves be designed securely.

A wrapper should avoid:

User-controlled command execution

Unsafe wildcards

Untrusted PATH resolution

Writable dependencies

Unvalidated file paths

Unnecessary environment inheritance

A poorly designed wrapper can be more dangerous than the original command.

docs.title: 64. Logging
docs.text:
sudo can generate security-relevant logs depending on system configuration.

Common sources may include:

systemd journal

Authentication logs

sudo-specific logs

Central logging

On systemd systems:

journalctl _COMM=sudo --no-pager 2>/dev/null

Availability and permissions vary.

Possible traditional log locations include distribution-specific authentication logs.

Do not assume the same file exists on every Linux distribution.

docs.title: 65. I/O Logging
docs.text:
sudo can support command input/output logging depending on policy and configuration.

Where deployed, this can provide additional visibility into privileged administrative activity.

During a security review, determine whether privileged activity is:

Logged

Protected

Centralised

Monitored

Retained appropriately

Logging does not replace least privilege, but it improves accountability and detection.

docs.title: 66. Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation, repeat:

sudo -l

Confirm that:

Unnecessary rule removed

Command narrowed

Run-as context corrected

NOPASSWD removed where policy requires authentication

Wildcards restricted where practical

Unsafe environment handling removed

Writable dependencies protected

Then inspect affected resources:

stat /path/to/resource
getfacl /path/to/resource
namei -l /path/to/resource

If the original issue involved group write access, confirm the user no longer has effective modification rights.

docs.title: Practical Questions
docs.text:
For every sudo rule, answer:

1. Which user receives the delegated capability?

2. Which target user or group can the command run as?

3. What exact command is permitted?

4. Which arguments are permitted?

5. Is authentication required?

6. Which environment is used?

7. Can the executable be modified?

8. Can its parent directory be modified?

9. Is it a script?

10. What dependencies does it trust?

11. Are configuration files writable?

12. Are helper scripts writable?

13. Are external commands resolved safely?

14. Are wildcards present?

15. Does the command expose additional functionality?

16. Is this capability intentionally delegated?

17. Does the observed behavior cross an intended security boundary?

18. Can the issue be demonstrated without modifying production resources?

If these questions cannot be answered, the sudo assessment is incomplete.

flowchart LR
   A["Current user"] --> B["sudo policy"]
   B --> C["Permitted command"]
   C --> D["Arguments and environment"]
   D --> E["Target user"]
   E --> F["Validated capability"]

docs.title: sudo Security Mindset
docs.text:
Do not think:

sudo = Vulnerable

NOPASSWD = Vulnerable

GTFOBins Match = Root

Service Restart = Root

Wildcard = Exploitable

Editor = Automatically Vulnerable

Old sudo Version = Vulnerable

Instead think:

What Is Delegated?
        |
        v
To Which Principal?
        |
        v
As Which User / Group?
        |
        v
With Which Arguments?
        |
        v
Under Which Environment?
        |
        v
What Does the Program Actually Allow?
        |
        v
What Resources Does It Trust?
        |
        v
Can I Influence Those Resources?
        |
        v
Does This Exceed the Intended Delegation?
        |
        v
Can the Security Boundary Be Safely Validated?

This approach produces defensible sudo findings rather than simply reporting the existence of privileged commands.

Start with sudo -l

sudo -l is normally the most useful starting point because it shows the policy relevant to the current user. Record the complete command specification rather than extracting only the executable name.

Follow the dependencies

A protected sudo-permitted executable can still trust writable configuration files, helper scripts, environment files or other resources. Analyse the complete execution chain.

Distinguish delegation from escalation

sudo exists specifically to delegate privilege. A user having sudo rights is therefore not automatically a vulnerability. The important question is whether the effective capability exceeds the organisation's intended privilege model.

Do not modify privileged resources unnecessarily

When a sudo-permitted script or executable is writable, permission metadata and the applicable sudo rule can often establish the security problem without replacing or modifying the production resource.

docs.title: Linux SUID and SGID Security
docs.text:
Linux supports special permission bits that can change the effective identity associated with execution or affect group behavior on directories.

Two important mechanisms are:

SUID - Set User ID

SGID - Set Group ID

During an authorised security assessment, SUID and SGID executables deserve particular attention because they can intentionally provide functionality using privileges different from those of the invoking user.

The existence of an SUID or SGID binary is not automatically a vulnerability.

The important question is:

Does the executable expose functionality, trust relationships or dependencies that allow a lower-privileged user to exceed the intended security boundary?

A useful assessment model is:

Current User
     |
     v
SUID / SGID Executable
     |
     v
Effective Identity
     |
     +---- Program functionality
     +---- Arguments
     +---- Environment
     +---- PATH
     +---- Configuration
     +---- Helper programs
     +---- Libraries
     +---- Files
     |
     v
Can User Influence Privileged Behaviour?

Authorised Security Testing

Perform SUID and SGID testing only on systems you own or have explicit permission to assess. Prefer enumeration, metadata inspection and non-destructive validation. Do not replace privileged binaries, modify production dependencies or create persistence merely to prove impact.

docs.title: 1. Unix Identity During Execution
docs.text:
A Linux process can have several identity values.

Important concepts include:

Real UID
Effective UID
Saved Set-User-ID

Real GID
Effective GID
Saved Set-Group-ID

At a high level:

Real UID
    |
    +---- Identity of the user that started the process

Effective UID
    |
    +---- Identity commonly used for permission checks

SUID can cause the effective user ID associated with execution to be derived from the executable file's owner, subject to operating system rules.

SGID can similarly affect the effective group ID.

This is why a root-owned SUID executable requires careful review.

docs.title: 2. SUID
docs.text:
SUID means:

Set User ID

The numeric special permission value is:

4000

An SUID executable can appear as:

-rwsr-xr-x

Notice:

s

in the owner's execute position.

Example:

ls -l /usr/bin/passwd

A system may show something similar to:

-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ... /usr/bin/passwd

This is expected on many Linux systems because changing a password requires controlled access to privileged authentication resources.

The important point is:

SUID root != Vulnerability

docs.title: 3. SGID
docs.text:
SGID means:

Set Group ID

The numeric special permission value is:

2000

An SGID executable can appear as:

-rwxr-sr-x

The:

s

appears in the group execute position.

When applied to an executable, SGID can cause the process to operate with an effective group identity associated with the executable's group, subject to system semantics.

This can provide access to resources that the invoking user could not otherwise access.

docs.title: 4. SGID on Directories
docs.text:
SGID has a different and very common use on directories.

Example:

drwxrwsr-x root developers project/

For directories, SGID commonly causes newly created entries to inherit the directory's group rather than simply using the creator's primary group.

This is useful for shared working directories.

Therefore:

SGID Directory

does not mean:

Privilege Escalation

File and directory semantics must be distinguished.

docs.title: 5. SUID and SGID Numeric Modes
docs.text:
Special permission bits can be represented numerically.

SUID = 4000
SGID = 2000

Example:

4755

means:

4000 - SUID
0755 - rwxr-xr-x

Example:

2755

means:

2000 - SGID
0755 - rwxr-xr-x

Example:

6755

contains both:

SUID + SGID

Do not assess security solely from the numeric mode.

docs.title: 6. Establish the Current Context
docs.text:
Before assessing privileged executables, record the current identity.

whoami
id
groups

Example:

uid=1001(analyst) gid=1001(analyst) groups=1001(analyst),1002(developers)

Record:

Username

UID

Primary GID

Supplementary groups

sudo permissions

This allows you to determine whether the SUID or SGID execution context provides access beyond what the user already possesses.

docs.title: 7. Enumerate SUID Executables
docs.text:
A common enumeration command is:

find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 -print 2>/dev/null

This searches the current filesystem for regular files with the SUID bit set.

The:

-xdev

option prevents find from descending into other mounted filesystems during that search.

If other filesystems are relevant, inspect them separately.

docs.title: 8. Enumerate SGID Executables
docs.text:
Use:

find / -xdev -type f -perm -2000 -print 2>/dev/null

This identifies regular files with SGID set.

Again, results require manual analysis.

A long list of SUID or SGID executables does not mean the system contains multiple privilege escalation vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 9. Enumerate Both SUID and SGID
docs.text:
A combined search can be performed with:

find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -print 2>/dev/null

For each result, determine:

Path

Owner

Group

Mode

File type

Package

Purpose

Whether it is expected

Whether it is custom

Whether it is writable

Dependencies

Security-sensitive functionality

docs.title: 10. Display Useful Metadata
docs.text:
Instead of collecting only filenames:

find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) \
    -exec stat -c '%A %a %U %G %n' {} \; 2>/dev/null

Representative output:

-rwsr-xr-x 4755 root root /usr/bin/example
-rwxr-sr-x 2755 root shadow /usr/bin/example2

This immediately exposes:

Permissions

Numeric mode

Owner

Group

Path

docs.title: 11. Inspect an Individual Binary
docs.text:
For an interesting result:

ls -l /path/to/binary

stat /path/to/binary

getfacl /path/to/binary

namei -l /path/to/binary

Determine:

Who owns it?

Which group owns it?

Is SUID present?

Is SGID present?

Can the current user modify it?

Can the parent directory be modified?

Are ACLs present?

docs.title: 12. Identify the File Type
docs.text:
Use:

file /path/to/binary

Potential results include:

ELF executable

Shell script

Python script

Perl script

Symbolic link

Other data

For ELF files, architecture and linkage information may also be useful.

Example:

file /usr/local/bin/custom-helper

Understanding the file type determines which additional analysis techniques are appropriate.

docs.title: 13. SUID Scripts
docs.text:
Modern Linux systems generally do not treat the SUID bit on interpreted scripts in the same way as SUID native executables.

Therefore, finding:

-rwsr-xr-x root root script.sh

does not by itself mean the script executes with root privileges.

Do not infer behavior from the mode bits alone.

Validate the actual operating system behavior and execution mechanism.

docs.title: 14. Expected SUID Programs
docs.text:
Many legitimate Linux installations contain SUID programs.

Examples may include utilities related to:

Password changes

User identity transitions

Mounting

Authentication

Privilege delegation

The exact list depends on:

Distribution

Installed packages

System role

Configuration

Avoid creating a static rule such as:

Any SUID root binary is suspicious.

Instead establish a baseline for the host.

docs.title: 15. Custom SUID Binaries
docs.text:
Custom SUID binaries deserve additional attention.

Examples may appear under:

/usr/local/bin/

/opt/

/srv/

Application-specific directories

A useful targeted search is:

find /usr/local /opt /srv -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) \
    -print 2>/dev/null

A custom executable may have received less security review than a distribution-provided utility.

This does not automatically make it vulnerable, but it increases assessment priority.

docs.title: 16. Identify Package Ownership
docs.text:
For distribution-managed binaries, determine which package owns the file.

Debian-based systems:

dpkg -S /path/to/binary 2>/dev/null

RPM-based systems:

rpm -qf /path/to/binary 2>/dev/null

If no package owns a privileged binary, it may be:

Locally compiled

Vendor supplied

Manually installed

Application specific

That is useful context for prioritisation.

docs.title: 17. Compare Against Package Metadata
docs.text:
Where appropriate, package verification can help identify unexpected modification.

On RPM-based systems:

rpm -V package-name

On Debian-based systems, available verification mechanisms depend on installed tooling and package metadata.

Do not assume a locally modified privileged binary is malicious.

Administrators may legitimately deploy custom builds.

Investigate the reason for the difference.

docs.title: 18. Check Binary Ownership
docs.text:
A privileged executable should normally be controlled by an appropriately trusted principal.

Example:

stat -c '%A %a %U %G %n' /usr/local/bin/custom-helper

Suppose:

-rwsr-xr-x 4755 root root /usr/local/bin/custom-helper

The executable itself appears root-controlled.

Now inspect:

namei -l /usr/local/bin/custom-helper

because the parent directory also matters.

docs.title: 19. Writable SUID Binary
docs.text:
A root-owned SUID executable writable by a lower-privileged user is highly security sensitive.

Check effective write access:

if test -w /usr/local/bin/custom-helper; then
    echo "[+] Current context reports write access"
else
    echo "[-] Current context does not report write access"
fi

Also inspect:

getfacl /usr/local/bin/custom-helper

Do not modify the binary.

The evidence chain may already be sufficient:

Current User
      |
      v
Write Access
      |
      v
Root-Owned SUID Executable
      |
      v
Privileged Execution Context

docs.title: 20. Parent Directory Control
docs.text:
A binary itself may not be writable:

-rwsr-xr-x root root /opt/vendor/bin/helper

but inspect:

namei -l /opt/vendor/bin/helper

The complete path could reveal an unexpected writable directory.

Directory-entry manipulation and file-content modification are different permission relationships.

See Linux Filesystem Permissions.

docs.title: 21. POSIX ACLs
docs.text:
Do not rely only on:

ls -l

Inspect ACLs:

getfacl /path/to/binary

and relevant directories:

getfacl /path/to/directory

A named ACL can provide access not obvious from traditional mode bits.

docs.title: 22. Symbolic Links
docs.text:
Resolve the path:

readlink -f /path/to/binary

Then inspect:

namei -l /path/to/binary

Determine:

Is the path a symlink?

Who controls the link?

What is the actual target?

Who controls the target?

Can the target change?

Always assess the actual object being executed.

docs.title: 23. SUID Program Functionality
docs.text:
After permissions, the next question is:

What does the program actually do?

Potential security-sensitive functionality includes:

Execute external programs

Read arbitrary files

Write arbitrary files

Change file ownership

Change permissions

Load plugins

Load configuration

Use environment variables

Invoke interpreters

Process attacker-controlled filenames

Perform privileged network operations

A SUID program becomes dangerous when exposed functionality exceeds the intended privileged operation.

docs.title: 24. Strings as an Initial Clue
docs.text:
For a custom binary, strings can provide initial clues.

strings /usr/local/bin/custom-helper | less

Search for interesting references:

strings /usr/local/bin/custom-helper | grep -E \
'(/bin/|/usr/bin/|/usr/local/|/etc/|/tmp/|system|exec|popen|PATH|HOME|LD_)'

Potential discoveries include:

External command names

Configuration paths

Temporary paths

Error messages

Library names

Environment variables

strings output is not proof of execution behavior.

Use it to guide deeper analysis.

docs.title: 25. Dynamic Dependencies
docs.text:
For dynamically linked ELF binaries:

ldd /path/to/binary

This can show shared-library dependencies.

However, treat ldd carefully when analysing untrusted executables.

For an unknown or potentially hostile binary, prefer safer static inspection approaches rather than executing mechanisms that may cause code execution depending on the binary and platform behavior.

For normal trusted system binaries in an authorised environment, dependency inspection can still be useful.

docs.title: 26. readelf
docs.text:
readelf can inspect ELF metadata without executing the target.

Example:

readelf -h /path/to/binary

Dynamic section:

readelf -d /path/to/binary

Symbols:

readelf -s /path/to/binary

Potentially useful information includes:

Architecture

ELF type

Shared-library dependencies

RPATH

RUNPATH

Symbols

docs.title: 27. RPATH and RUNPATH
docs.text:
Inspect:

readelf -d /path/to/binary | grep -E 'RPATH|RUNPATH'

If an SUID or SGID binary searches for shared libraries in an unsafe location, additional analysis may be required.

Assessment model:

Privileged Binary
      |
      v
Library Search Path
      |
      v
Writable Directory?
      |
   +--+--+
   |     |
  No    Yes
   |     |
   v     v
Record   Determine Actual Loader Behaviour

Do not assume a writable directory automatically results in library hijacking.

Dynamic-loader behavior for privileged executables includes additional security restrictions.

docs.title: 28. Shared Libraries
docs.text:
For each relevant library dependency, determine:

Library path

Owner

Group

Permissions

ACLs

Parent directory permissions

Example:

stat /usr/local/lib/libvendor.so

getfacl /usr/local/lib/libvendor.so

namei -l /usr/local/lib/libvendor.so

A privileged executable should not normally depend on libraries modifiable by untrusted users.

docs.title: 29. Environment Variables
docs.text:
Privileged execution can change how environment variables are handled.

Do not assume that environment variables affecting ordinary executables will have the same effect on SUID or SGID programs.

The runtime loader and application may apply secure-execution restrictions.

Potential variables still worth understanding include application-specific settings controlling:

Configuration

Plugins

Data files

Temporary directories

External command behavior

Validate actual behavior rather than relying on a generic environment-hijacking assumption.

docs.title: 30. PATH Dependencies
docs.text:
A custom privileged executable may invoke another program.

For example, internal logic may conceptually perform:

backup

instead of:

/usr/local/sbin/backup

If command lookup uses PATH, determine:

Effective PATH

Search order

Writable directories

Execution identity

Whether environment sanitisation occurs

Whether an absolute path is actually used

A meaningful relationship requires more than simply finding a command name in strings.

docs.title: 31. External Command Execution
docs.text:
Common C library functions associated with external command execution include:

system()

popen()

execve()

execl()

execlp()

execvp()

Static analysis can help identify references.

Example:

readelf -Ws /path/to/binary | grep -E 'system|popen|exec'

The presence of one of these symbols is not itself a vulnerability.

You must determine:

How it is called

Which command is executed

Whether arguments are user controlled

Whether PATH is involved

Whether privileges are retained

docs.title: 32. Absolute Versus Relative Commands
docs.text:
Compare:

/usr/bin/logger

with:

logger

An absolute path removes PATH-based lookup for that executable.

However, even an absolute path does not prove the complete operation is secure.

The privileged program may still trust:

Arguments

Configuration

Files

Environment

Plugins

Libraries

Temporary resources

docs.title: 33. User-Controlled Arguments
docs.text:
A SUID program may accept command-line arguments.

Inspect usage:

/path/to/binary --help

only when it is safe and appropriate to execute the binary.

For unknown custom binaries, static inspection may be preferable first.

Questions include:

Can the user choose a filename?

Can the user choose a destination?

Can the user choose a command?

Can options change configuration?

Can arguments cause another program to run?

Can path traversal affect file access?

docs.title: 34. File Read Functionality
docs.text:
A privileged executable that reads files may expose unintended data.

Assessment questions:

Can the user choose the path?

Are paths restricted?

Are symbolic links followed?

Are ownership checks performed?

Can arbitrary privileged files be read?

This may create information disclosure without providing arbitrary code execution.

Do not reduce every SUID issue to "root shell".

docs.title: 35. File Write Functionality
docs.text:
Similarly, privileged file-writing functionality can be dangerous.

Determine:

Can destination path be chosen?

Can existing files be overwritten?

Are symlinks followed?

Are permissions preserved?

Is content attacker controlled?

Are directories restricted?

A privileged arbitrary-file-write primitive can have serious impact even if the binary never executes another command.

Avoid overwriting privileged files during routine validation.

docs.title: 36. Temporary Files
docs.text:
Privileged binaries may use temporary files.

Potential locations include:

/tmp

/var/tmp

Application-specific temporary directories

Assess:

Filename predictability

Creation flags

Ownership

Permissions

Symlink handling

Existing-file behavior

Sticky-bit protections

Do not assume use of /tmp alone is vulnerable.

docs.title: 37. Configuration Files
docs.text:
A SUID program may load configuration.

Example:

/etc/vendor/helper.conf

Inspect:

stat /etc/vendor/helper.conf
getfacl /etc/vendor/helper.conf
namei -l /etc/vendor/helper.conf

Determine what configuration controls.

A writable cosmetic configuration setting is different from a writable setting that controls:

Executable path

Plugin path

File destination

Command

Privilege behavior

docs.title: 38. User Configuration
docs.text:
Privileged programs should be reviewed carefully when they load configuration from user-controlled locations.

Examples might include:

Home directories

Current working directory

Environment-selected paths

Assessment questions:

Does the program load user configuration before dropping privileges?

Which settings can be controlled?

Can those settings influence privileged behavior?

Do not assume user configuration is loaded simply because the non-SUID version of an application supports it.

docs.title: 39. Working Directory
docs.text:
A privileged binary may use relative paths.

Determine the current working directory:

pwd

Then inspect whether the binary references resources such as:

./config

./helper

./plugins/

../data/

If a privileged executable trusts relative resources from a user-controlled working directory, further analysis may be required.

docs.title: 40. Privilege Dropping
docs.text:
Well-designed SUID applications may obtain required privilege and then drop it.

A simplified model is:

Start
  |
  v
Elevated Effective Identity
  |
  v
Perform Narrow Privileged Operation
  |
  v
Drop Privilege
  |
  v
Continue Unprivileged

Do not assume the process remains privileged for its entire lifetime.

Understanding when privileges are dropped can materially change exploitability.

docs.title: 41. Real and Effective UID Validation
docs.text:
For a custom application under controlled laboratory conditions, developers can inspect:

getuid()

geteuid()

getgid()

getegid()

These expose real and effective identities.

During a black-box assessment, system tracing or debugging may affect SUID behavior and should be used carefully.

Do not assume traced execution behaves identically to normal privileged execution.

docs.title: 42. Tracing Considerations
docs.text:
Tools such as:

strace

ltrace

gdb

can be useful for program analysis.

However, privileged execution introduces additional security restrictions.

Tracing an SUID program may:

Change privilege behavior

Be blocked

Cause privileges to be dropped

Produce behavior different from normal execution

Therefore, observations from a traced process must not automatically be treated as proof of normal SUID behavior.

docs.title: 43. Static Analysis First
docs.text:
For unfamiliar privileged binaries, a good workflow is:

file
 |
 v
stat
 |
 v
readelf
 |
 v
strings
 |
 v
Package Identification
 |
 v
Configuration Review
 |
 v
Controlled Dynamic Analysis if Needed

This reduces unnecessary execution of unknown privileged code.

docs.title: 44. GTFOBins
docs.text:
GTFOBins documents Unix binaries whose legitimate functionality can become security relevant when combined with privilege mechanisms such as:

sudo

SUID

capabilities

Use:

GTFOBins

The correct assessment model is:

SUID Binary Found
       |
       v
Is Binary Known?
       |
       v
Review GTFOBins / Documentation
       |
       v
Does Technique Apply to This Mode?
       |
       v
Does Version / Configuration Matter?
       |
       v
Does It Cross Intended Boundary?

A GTFOBins match is a lead, not automatic proof.

docs.title: 45. SUID and Shell Behavior
docs.text:
Some programs can legitimately invoke a shell or other subprocess.

Whether privileges are retained depends on:

Program

Shell

Invocation

UID handling

Operating system behavior

Privilege dropping

Do not assume:

SUID + shell-capable binary = guaranteed root shell

Validate the exact context.

docs.title: 46. Unexpected SUID Copies
docs.text:
An important assessment pattern is an unexpected copy of a normally non-SUID utility with SUID enabled.

Search results should therefore be reviewed for:

Unusual paths

Duplicate utilities

Files under /tmp

Files under home directories

Files under application directories

Recently modified privileged executables

Example metadata collection:

find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 \
    -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM %u %g %m %p\n' 2>/dev/null

Timestamps are clues, not proof of malicious activity.

docs.title: 47. Compare Against Known Baseline
docs.text:
If you have:

Golden image

Configuration-management baseline

Previous assessment output

Package inventory

compare the current SUID/SGID set.

This can reveal:

New privileged executables

Removed privileged executables

Permission changes

Unexpected vendor binaries

Local customisations

Baseline comparison is generally more useful than declaring every SUID binary suspicious.

docs.title: 48. Find Recently Modified SUID Files
docs.text:
A targeted example:

find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 -mtime -30 -print 2>/dev/null

This identifies SUID files whose modification time is within the specified range.

Interpret cautiously.

Legitimate causes include:

Package updates

System upgrades

Application deployment

Administrative maintenance

Do not report recent modification as compromise evidence without corroboration.

docs.title: 49. SGID Group Access
docs.text:
SGID executables may provide access associated with a privileged group.

Example relationship:

analyst
   |
   v
SGID Binary
   |
   v
Effective Group
   |
   v
Protected Resource

The target group may control:

Logs

Authentication data

Device files

Application data

Database resources

Determine what the group actually grants.

docs.title: 50. SGID and Sensitive Groups
docs.text:
Do not assume every privileged-looking group means root-equivalent access.

Determine:

Which files are group-owned?

Which devices are accessible?

Which sockets are accessible?

Which application resources are controlled?

Can group access be chained into another privilege boundary?

SGID findings may produce confidentiality or integrity impact without UID 0.

docs.title: 51. SUID and Linux Capabilities
docs.text:
Linux capabilities can provide selected privileged operations without full SUID root behavior.

Therefore, enumeration should consider both:

SUID / SGID

and:

File capabilities

A system may intentionally replace some SUID functionality with capabilities.

The next dedicated page covers this in depth:

Linux Capabilities Security

docs.title: 52. Mount Options
docs.text:
SUID behavior can be affected by mount configuration.

Inspect the filesystem containing a binary:

findmnt -T /path/to/binary

Relevant mount options can include:

nosuid

If a filesystem is mounted with nosuid, set-user-ID and set-group-ID behavior can be restricted according to the operating system and filesystem semantics.

Therefore:

SUID Bit Present

does not always mean:

SUID Behavior Effective

docs.title: 53. Check Mount Context
docs.text:
For an interesting binary:

findmnt -T /opt/vendor/bin/helper

Representative information can include:

TARGET

SOURCE

FSTYPE

OPTIONS

Record whether:

nosuid

is present.

Mount context is an important false-positive check.

docs.title: 54. Network Filesystems
docs.text:
SUID and SGID behavior on network filesystems can depend on:

Mount options

Server configuration

Filesystem semantics

UID mapping

Security model

Do not assume a privileged bit observed on a remote filesystem behaves identically to one on a local filesystem.

docs.title: 55. Containers
docs.text:
Container environments can complicate SUID analysis.

A root-owned SUID binary inside a container may provide:

Container root

without providing:

Host root

Determine:

Am I inside a container?

Which user namespace is used?

Is root mapped?

Which host resources are mounted?

Are privileged devices available?

What is the actual security boundary?

Do not report container UID 0 as host compromise without evidence.

docs.title: 56. User Namespaces
docs.text:
User namespaces can map container or namespace identities to different host identities.

Therefore:

UID 0

inside a namespace does not necessarily equal unrestricted host root.

Assessment must identify the actual privilege boundary.

docs.title: 57. SELinux
docs.text:
SELinux can impose mandatory access controls beyond Unix UID/GID permissions.

Check:

getenforce 2>/dev/null

Possible results include:

Enforcing
Permissive
Disabled

A SUID process may still be constrained by SELinux policy.

Do not ignore mandatory access controls when determining effective impact.

docs.title: 58. AppArmor
docs.text:
Check:

aa-status 2>/dev/null

An AppArmor profile can restrict a privileged program's:

File access

Execution

Network access

Capabilities

The presence of SUID does not bypass every other security mechanism.

docs.title: 59. Core Security Question
docs.text:
For every SUID or SGID binary, ask:

What privilege does it receive?

Why does it need that privilege?

What functionality does it expose?

Can the user control arguments?

Can the user control input files?

Can the user control output paths?

Can the user control configuration?

Can the user control dependencies?

Can the user influence PATH?

Can the user influence libraries?

Does it drop privilege?

Do mount options restrict it?

Do MAC controls restrict it?

Does the resulting capability exceed the intended design?

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Enumeration identifies:

/usr/local/bin/report-helper

with:

-rwsr-xr-x root root

docs.title: Step 1 - Establish Identity
docs.text: id

docs.title: Step 2 - Inspect Metadata
docs.text:
stat /usr/local/bin/report-helper

getfacl /usr/local/bin/report-helper

docs.title: Step 3 - Inspect Complete Path
docs.text: namei -l /usr/local/bin/report-helper

docs.title: Step 4 - Determine File Type
docs.text: file /usr/local/bin/report-helper

docs.title: Step 5 - Determine Package Ownership
docs.text:
Debian-based:

dpkg -S /usr/local/bin/report-helper 2>/dev/null

RPM-based:

rpm -qf /usr/local/bin/report-helper 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Step 6 - Inspect Static Metadata
docs.text:
readelf -h /usr/local/bin/report-helper

readelf -d /usr/local/bin/report-helper

strings /usr/local/bin/report-helper | less

docs.title: Step 7 - Check Mount Context
docs.text:
findmnt -T /usr/local/bin/report-helper

This creates a strong initial evidence set without modifying or exploiting the binary.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Static analysis suggests that a custom root-owned SUID binary invokes:

report-archive

without an obvious absolute path.

Do not immediately create a replacement command.

First determine:

Does the string correspond to actual execution?

Which API performs the execution?

What PATH is used?

Does the process retain privilege?

Can the current user write to any relevant PATH directory?

Inspect PATH directories where appropriate:

for d in /usr/local/sbin /usr/local/bin /usr/sbin /usr/bin; do
    stat -c '%A %a %U %G %n' "$d" 2>/dev/null
done

A defensible finding requires the complete relationship.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A root-owned SUID application loads:

/opt/vendor/helper.conf

Inspect:

stat /opt/vendor/helper.conf

getfacl /opt/vendor/helper.conf

namei -l /opt/vendor/helper.conf

Then determine which settings are consumed.

Do not modify the production configuration merely to prove write access.

A finding requires evidence that the writable setting can influence privileged behavior.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
An SGID executable is owned by:

root:reports

and executes with effective group:

reports

Determine which resources are accessible to that group.

Example:

find /var/lib/reports -maxdepth 2 -group reports -ls 2>/dev/null

Assess whether the executable exposes access beyond its intended function.

The issue may involve:

Unauthorised reading

Unauthorised modification

Credential exposure

Indirect privilege escalation

docs.title: 64. Representative Positive Result
docs.text:
Suppose:

Current user:
analyst

Binary:
/usr/local/bin/report-helper

Permissions:
-rwsr-xr-x root root

Behavior:
Executes an external helper using PATH lookup

Effective execution:
Privileged

Relevant PATH directory:
/usr/local/vendor/bin

Directory permissions:
Writable by developers

Current user:
Member of developers

The relationship is:

analyst
   |
   v
developers
   |
   v
Writable PATH Directory
   |
   v
External Command Resolution
   |
   v
SUID root Binary
   |
   v
Privileged Execution

If all components are validated, this can support a privilege escalation finding.

docs.title: 65. Representative Negative Result
docs.text:
Suppose:

/usr/bin/example

is SUID root.

Further assessment shows:

Distribution-managed binary

Expected SUID permission

Protected executable

Protected parent directories

No writable configuration

No unsafe command execution

No user-controlled privileged file operation

Privileges dropped appropriately

Relevant filesystem not unexpectedly writable

The correct conclusion may be:

The SUID executable was reviewed and no unintended privilege escalation
condition was identified under the assessed configuration.

Do not report it simply because the SUID bit exists.

docs.title: 66. False Positives
docs.text:
Common false positives include:

Expected distribution SUID binary

SGID shared directory

SUID script whose bit is not effective as assumed

SUID binary on a nosuid filesystem

GTFOBins entry that does not apply to the installed configuration

Binary that drops privilege before dangerous functionality

PATH reference where all search directories are protected

Library search assumption blocked by secure loader behavior

Container root mistaken for host root

SELinux or AppArmor restrictions ignored during analysis

Manual validation is essential.

docs.title: 67. Automated Enumeration
docs.text:
Common enumeration tools can identify SUID and SGID candidates.

Examples include:

LinPEAS

LinEnum

linux-smart-enumeration

Use them as candidate generators.

Automated Enumeration
        |
        v
SUID / SGID Candidate
        |
        v
Expected or Unusual?
        |
        v
Permission Review
        |
        v
Functionality Review
        |
        v
Dependency Review
        |
        v
Security Control Review
        |
        v
Manual Validation

docs.title: 68. Compare with GTFOBins
docs.text:
A simple workflow is:

Enumerate SUID
     |
     v
Extract Basenames
     |
     v
Check GTFOBins
     |
     v
Review SUID-Specific Technique
     |
     v
Confirm Local Preconditions

Do not blindly execute every technique found online.

Some techniques:

Change files

Spawn shells

Alter permissions

Create persistence

Access sensitive information

and may be inappropriate for production validation.

docs.title: 69. Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For an SUID or SGID finding, capture:

Hostname

Distribution

Kernel

Current user

UID

GID

Groups

Binary path

File type

Owner

Group

Mode

ACL

Parent directory permissions

Mount point

Mount options

Package ownership

Binary purpose

Arguments

Relevant environment

External commands

Configuration dependencies

Library dependencies

Privilege behavior

Security-control context

Validation method

Evidence should explain why the executable crosses an intended security boundary.

docs.title: 70. Evidence Commands
docs.text:
Useful commands include:

id

stat /path/to/binary

getfacl /path/to/binary

namei -l /path/to/binary

file /path/to/binary

readelf -h /path/to/binary

readelf -d /path/to/binary

findmnt -T /path/to/binary

Use only the commands required to support the conclusion.

docs.title: 71. Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

SUID binary found.

Avoid:

/usr/local/bin/helper runs as root.

Prefer:

The custom executable /usr/local/bin/report-helper is installed with the SUID bit and owned by root. The program performs a privileged operation while resolving an external helper through a search path containing a directory writable by the developers group. The assessed analyst account is a member of this group, allowing the user to influence code resolution within the privileged execution context.

This explains:

Principal

Privileged mechanism

Executable

Controllable dependency

Execution context

Security impact

docs.title: Observation
docs.text: A custom root-owned SUID executable trusts a lower-privileged writable dependency.

docs.title: Current User
docs.text: analyst

docs.title: Binary
docs.text: /usr/local/bin/report-helper

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: -rwsr-xr-x root root

docs.title: Controllable Resource
docs.text: /usr/local/vendor/bin/

docs.title: Security Relationship
docs.text:
analyst
   |
   v
developers
   |
   v
Writable Dependency Location
   |
   v
report-helper
   |
   v
SUID root Execution

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: A lower-privileged user can influence a resource consumed during a privileged execution path.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text: Use trusted absolute paths and ensure all privileged executable dependencies are writable only by trusted administrative principals.

docs.title: 73. Remediation
docs.text:
SUID and SGID remediation should address the underlying requirement.

Potential measures include:

Remove unnecessary SUID bits

Remove unnecessary SGID bits

Use Linux capabilities where narrower privilege is sufficient

Protect privileged executables

Protect parent directories

Protect configuration

Protect helper programs

Use absolute executable paths

Avoid user-controlled privileged input

Drop privileges as early as possible

Use dedicated service interfaces

Apply SELinux or AppArmor where appropriate

Do not remove special bits blindly.

Some system functionality legitimately requires them.

docs.title: 74. Remove Unnecessary SUID
docs.text:
Administrators can remove SUID with:

chmod u-s /path/to/binary

or numerically by setting an appropriate mode without the 4000 bit.

This should only be done after confirming that the application does not require SUID functionality.

During an assessment, recommend the change rather than altering production permissions yourself unless remediation activity is explicitly in scope.

docs.title: 75. Remove Unnecessary SGID
docs.text:
For executables:

chmod g-s /path/to/binary

Again, determine whether SGID is required before changing it.

For directories, remember that SGID may intentionally support group inheritance.

Do not recommend removing it without understanding the operational design.

docs.title: 76. Prefer Narrow Privileges
docs.text:
If an application needs only one privileged operation, full SUID root may provide more authority than necessary.

Depending on the requirement, alternatives may include:

Linux capabilities

Dedicated service

Privileged helper with narrow interface

sudo rule for a specific operation

File ACLs

Group-based access

Each alternative has its own security considerations.

The goal is:

Minimum Privilege Required

rather than:

No Privilege Mechanisms Anywhere

docs.title: 77. Protect Dependencies
docs.text:
A privileged binary should not trust resources modifiable by lower-privileged users.

Review:

Binary

Parent directories

Shared libraries

Configuration files

Helper programs

Plugin directories

Temporary paths

Data files that control behavior

The security chain is only as strong as the least-protected trusted component.

docs.title: 78. Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation, repeat enumeration:

find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -print 2>/dev/null

For the affected resource:

stat /path/to/binary
getfacl /path/to/binary
namei -l /path/to/binary
findmnt -T /path/to/binary

Confirm:

Unnecessary special bit removed

Required functionality still works

Writable dependency corrected

Unsafe path corrected

Configuration protected

Application still functions

Security boundary no longer exists

docs.title: Practical Testing Model
docs.text:
For an interesting privileged executable, use:

1. When does this apply?

   SUID or SGID is present and effective.

2. What should I inspect?

   Identity, permissions, executable, dependencies and security controls.

3. What result matters?

   A lower-privileged user can influence privileged behavior.

4. What does the result mean?

   Determine exactly which security boundary is crossed.

5. What else could explain it?

   Expected SUID behavior, privilege dropping, nosuid, MAC controls,
   containers or protected dependencies.

6. What should I capture?

   Identity, metadata, execution relationship and dependency evidence.

7. How should it be remediated?

   Remove unnecessary privilege or protect the complete trust chain.

8. How should it be retested?

   Repeat the original validation and confirm the trust relationship
   no longer exists.
