Cloud console access

Temporary access should not remain simply because it may be useful for future retesting.

docs.title: Tool Cleanup
docs.text:
Tools copied to customer systems should be inventoried.

Examples:

Enumeration tools

Network utilities

Test scripts

Framework agents

Portable binaries

Configuration files

Remove engagement copies unless the customer requests otherwise.

docs.title: Tool Hashes
docs.text:
Maintain SHA-256 hashes for deployed tooling.

This assists:

Cleanup

SOC deconfliction

Threat hunting

Reporting

docs.title: Temporary Web Servers
docs.text:
If temporary web servers were used:

Stop server

Verify port closed

Remove hosted files

Remove firewall rule

Remove service if created

docs.title: Listener Verification
docs.text:
Linux:

ss -lntup

Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

Compare against the engagement listener inventory.

docs.title: Network Cleanup
docs.text:
Review:

Routes

Firewall rules

Port forwards

Proxy settings

DNS changes

VPN configuration

Temporary listeners

docs.title: Proxy Settings
docs.text:
If system proxy settings were changed, restore the original values.

Do not assume that "no proxy" was the original configuration.

docs.title: DNS Changes
docs.text:
If local DNS configuration was modified:

Hosts file

Resolver configuration

DNS server

Search suffix

restore the recorded original state.

docs.title: Hosts Files
docs.text:
Common locations:

Windows:

C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts

Linux:

/etc/hosts

Remove only engagement-created entries.

docs.title: Evidence Is Not the Same as an Artifact
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Customer-System Artifact

from:

Red-Team Evidence

For example:

C:\Temp\rt-test.txt

may need removal.

A screenshot proving it existed may need retention.

docs.title: Evidence Retention
docs.text:
Retain only what is required by:

Statement of Work

Rules of Engagement

Customer policy

Legal requirements

Reporting requirements

docs.title: Evidence Classification
docs.text:
Classify evidence such as:

Public

Internal

Confidential

Restricted

according to the engagement's data-handling requirements.

docs.title: Evidence Storage
docs.text:
Protect evidence using:

Encryption

Access control

Dedicated storage

Backup policy

Retention schedule

docs.title: Evidence Minimisation
docs.text:
Avoid retaining unnecessary:

Passwords

Tokens

Private keys

Personal data

Large production datasets

Complete mailbox contents

docs.title: Evidence Sanitisation
docs.text:
Reports may use:

Redacted screenshots

Partial usernames

Masked tokens

Synthetic data

Hashes

instead of raw sensitive material.

docs.title: Retention Schedule
docs.text:
Example:

Data Retention Action Final report Contract defined Retain Screenshots Contract defined Retain/delete Raw tool output Short term Delete Production credentials None Rotate/delete Synthetic data Engagement only Delete

docs.title: Do Not Delete Defensive Telemetry
docs.text:
Red team cleanup should preserve evidence useful to defenders.

Do not delete:

SIEM events

EDR events

Firewall logs

Authentication logs

Cloud audit logs

Email security events

SOC tickets

unless the customer explicitly owns a separate retention decision.

docs.title: Detection Validation During Cleanup
docs.text:
Cleanup itself may generate useful telemetry.

Examples:

Account deletion

Privilege removal

Task deletion

Service removal

Token revocation

Cloud resource deletion

Defenders may use this to validate administrative monitoring.

docs.title: Cleanup Verification
docs.text:
Cleanup should be verified rather than assumed.

Cleanup Action
      |
      v
Artifact Query
      |
      v
Still Present?
   /        \
 Yes         No
 |            |
 v            v
Retry      Mark Verified

docs.title: Independent Verification
docs.text:
For high-risk artifacts, consider:

Operator A removes artifact

Operator B verifies removal

This reduces errors.

docs.title: Verification Methods
docs.text:
Use:

File existence check

Account query

Group membership query

Service query

Task query

Port scan

Route table review

Cloud inventory

DNS query

Authentication test

Token validation

docs.title: Authentication Verification
docs.text:
For a revoked test credential:

Credential Revoked
      |
      v
Controlled Authentication Test
      |
      v
Authentication Fails
      |
      v
Verified

Avoid repeated authentication attempts that could trigger lockouts.

docs.title: Network Verification
docs.text:
Confirm temporary services are no longer exposed.

Examples:

ss -lntup

and, from an authorised validation host:

nmap -sT -Pn -p 443,8000,8080 <approved-test-host>

Use only against approved engagement infrastructure or in-scope hosts.

docs.title: DNS Verification
docs.text:
Use:

dig example.test

or:

nslookup example.test

to confirm retired records behave as expected.

docs.title: Cloud Verification
docs.text:
After cleanup, review the engagement tag or naming convention.

The desired result is:

No unexpected temporary resources remain.

docs.title: Residual Artifact Hunt
docs.text:
Perform a final search using known engagement identifiers.

Examples:

Campaign ID

Test username

Payload filename

Tool hash

Domain

Service name

Task name

Directory name

This is more reliable than relying on memory.

docs.title: Engagement Naming Convention
docs.text:
Consistent names make cleanup easier.

Example:

RT-2026-04

RT-Test-User

RT-Test-Task

rt-2026-04-vm

Do not use predictable red team naming when it would invalidate an explicitly authorised detection objective, but still maintain an internal artifact inventory.

docs.title: Threat Hunting After Cleanup
docs.text:
Provide defenders with relevant engagement indicators where agreed.

Examples:

Domains

IPs

File hashes

Account names

Process names

Tool hashes

Certificate fingerprints

This allows the blue team to verify whether residual activity remains.

docs.text:
Example:

Type Value Purpose Domain test.example C2 SHA-256 <hash> Test binary Account RT-Test-01 Synthetic identity IP 192.0.2.10 Test infrastructure

docs.title: False Attribution Risk
docs.text:
After the engagement, defenders may later encounter a historical artifact.

Without documentation, they may interpret it as a real compromise.

Maintain sufficient records to answer:

Was this ours?

When was it deployed?

Where?

Why?

Was it removed?

docs.title: Unexpected Artifacts
docs.text:
During cleanup, you may find an artifact that was not created by the red team.

Examples:

Unknown account

Unknown scheduled task

Unknown SSH key

Unknown service

Unknown web shell

Unknown cloud identity

Do not remove it automatically.

docs.title: Real Compromise
docs.text:
If cleanup reveals indicators of a real compromise:

Stop normal cleanup where necessary

Preserve evidence

Notify authorised contacts

Separate red team activity from unknown activity

Support deconfliction

Follow incident-response procedures

docs.title: Do Not Contaminate Evidence
docs.text:
Avoid modifying unknown artifacts merely to investigate them.

The incident-response team may need:

Timestamps

Metadata

Logs

File hashes

Memory state

Cloud audit history

docs.title: Customer-Owned Artifacts
docs.text:
Some artifacts may intentionally remain.

Examples:

Detection rules

Synthetic test accounts

Dedicated lab systems

Test certificates

Automation

Purple team infrastructure

Mark these:

Customer Owned

rather than "not cleaned."

docs.title: Handover
docs.text:
If an artifact remains, document:

Artifact

Location

Owner

Reason retained

Credentials

Security considerations

Expiration

Required future action

docs.title: Cleanup Exceptions
docs.text:
Not every artifact can always be removed immediately.

Examples:

Customer requests retention

System unavailable

Change freeze

Production risk

Third-party dependency

Evidence preservation requirement

docs.title: Exception Record
docs.text:
Example:

Artifact:
RT-Test-Account

Location:
Active Directory

Status:
Retained by Agreement

Reason:
Customer detection engineering team requires account for
retesting.

Owner:
Security Engineering

Expiration:
2026-10-01

Required Action:
Disable and remove after validation programme.

docs.title: Cleanup Failure
docs.text:
If cleanup fails:

Do not silently mark complete.

Record:

What remains

Why it remains

Risk

Owner

Required action

Deadline

docs.title: High-Risk Residuals
docs.text:
Prioritise residual artifacts that provide continuing access.

Examples:

Privileged accounts

SSH keys

API keys

Cloud roles

OAuth applications

Certificates

C2 agents

Persistence

Open firewall rules

Exposed listeners

docs.title: Residual Risk
docs.text:
A cleanup exception should have a risk assessment.

Example:

Residual:
Temporary cloud API key remains active.

Risk:
Key retains read access to test subscription.

Immediate Action:
Customer cloud administrator to revoke key.

Compensating Control:
Associated identity disabled.

Status:
Open.

reviewed during cleanup.

cloud resources were removed and their removal was verified.

One synthetic Active Directory account was retained at the
customer's request for subsequent detection-engineering

docs.title: Avoid Absolute Claims
docs.text:
Avoid:

There are absolutely no red team artifacts anywhere.

Prefer:

All artifacts recorded in the engagement inventory were
reviewed and either removed, verified or documented as approved
exceptions.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Red team cleanup can be reduced to:

Plan cleanup before deployment.

Track every meaningful change.

Record the original state.

Assign every artifact an owner.

Stop active operations before cleanup.

Remove only confirmed engagement artifacts.

Restore configuration instead of blindly deleting it.

Remove persistence.

Remove temporary privileges.

Remove temporary accounts.

Revoke credentials and tokens.

Terminate sessions.

Remove tunnels and routes.

Remove payloads and tools.

Decommission C2 infrastructure.

Review cloud residuals.

Retire phishing infrastructure.

Remove unnecessary customer data.

Preserve defensive telemetry.

Do not clear logs.

Do not delete unknown artifacts.

Escalate possible real compromise.

Verify every high-risk cleanup action.

Document customer-owned artifacts.

Document every exception.

Retain only required evidence.

Verify residual access is gone.

Close the engagement only after cleanup is verified.

The artifact inventory is the cleanup plan

If every account, file, route, service, task, credential, cloud resource, payload and infrastructure change is recorded when it is created, cleanup becomes a controlled verification exercise instead of a memory exercise.

Cleanup is not anti-forensics

Never clear logs, destroy defensive telemetry or remove unknown suspicious artifacts under the label of cleanup. Red team artifacts should be removed, but evidence needed for detection validation, incident response and customer investigation should remain available according to the engagement agreement.

docs.title: Red Team Collection
docs.text:
Collection is the process of identifying and gathering information required to satisfy an authorised red team objective.

Collection normally occurs after discovery has identified systems, applications, repositories, shares or other locations containing potentially relevant information.

A useful distinction is:

Discovery:
Where might useful information exist?

Collection:
Which specific information should be gathered?

Exfiltration:
Can authorised test information leave the controlled environment?

Collection should not mean:

Copy everything that is accessible.

Instead:

Objective
   |
   v
Identify Required Evidence
   |
   v
Locate Data
   |
   v
Confirm Scope
   |
   v
Minimise Collection
   |
   v
Collect
   |
   v
Protect
   |
   v
Validate Detection
   |
   v
Cleanup

Authorised testing only

Collection can expose confidential, personal, regulated or otherwise sensitive information. Collect only information required by the Rules of Engagement and engagement objectives. Prefer synthetic data, customer-provided marker files, metadata, counts, hashes or screenshots over copying real sensitive datasets.

docs.title: Collection Objectives
docs.text:
Typical collection objectives include:

Demonstrate access to objective data

Validate access-control boundaries

Identify objective-relevant files

Demonstrate access to a business system

Validate access to selected records

Prepare synthetic data for exfiltration testing

Capture evidence of compromise

Validate DLP and monitoring controls

Measure defensive visibility

docs.text:
Initial Access

Discovery

Not every engagement requires exfiltration.

Sometimes demonstrating controlled access to the target information is sufficient to prove the objective.

docs.text:
Discovery might reveal:

Finance share exists

Database server exists

Source repository exists

Email platform exists

Backup system exists

Collection asks:

Which authorised information from that system is necessary to
prove the objective?

docs.text:
Credential Access focuses primarily on authentication material.

Examples:

Passwords

Hashes

Tokens

API keys

SSH keys

Certificates

Collection focuses primarily on objective-relevant information.

Examples:

Documents

Database records

Source code

Email

Application data

Business information

See:

Credential Access

docs.title: Collection Planning
docs.text:
Before collecting anything, answer:

What is the engagement objective?

What information would prove it?

Where is that information expected?

Is the source in scope?

Is the data itself in scope?

How sensitive is it?

Can synthetic data be used instead?

What is the minimum amount required?

Where will collected material be stored?

How will it be protected?

When will it be deleted?

docs.title: Data Minimisation
docs.text:
Data minimisation should be the default.

Prefer:

One file instead of a directory

One record instead of a table

Metadata instead of content

A count instead of records

A hash instead of a copy

A screenshot instead of a dataset

A synthetic marker instead of production information

docs.title: Minimum Necessary Evidence
docs.text:
Suppose the objective is:

Determine whether a compromised application server can access
the finance share.

You may not need:

All finance documents

A safer proof might be:

Share accessible

Target directory accessible

Customer-provided marker file readable

That may be sufficient to prove the attack path.

docs.title: Synthetic Data
docs.text:
Synthetic data is one of the safest approaches for collection testing.

Examples:

Customer-provided marker file

Dummy database record

Synthetic customer account

Test email

Non-sensitive document

Generated CSV

Random binary file

docs.title: Example Marker
docs.text:
A customer might create:

\\fileserver\finance\redteam-objective.txt

with:

RED TEAM OBJECTIVE - FINANCE SHARE ACCESS CONFIRMED

The engagement objective becomes:

Demonstrate authorised read access to the marker.

No real finance documents need to be copied.

docs.title: Data Classification
docs.text:
Understand the organisation's classification model where available.

Possible categories include:

Public

Internal

Confidential

Restricted

Highly Restricted

Collection handling should reflect the highest classification encountered.

docs.title: Sensitive Data
docs.text:
Potentially sensitive information includes:

Personal data

Health information

Financial records

Customer information

Employee information

Authentication material

Private keys

Source code

Legal documents

Security configurations

Incident records

Business strategy

Intellectual property

docs.title: Stop Conditions
docs.text:
Collection should stop if unexpected high-risk information appears.

Examples:

Large amounts of personal data

Medical records

Payment-card information

Production private keys

Unrelated customer information

Third-party confidential information

Out-of-scope tenant data

Unexpected regulated information

Record the minimum necessary evidence and follow the engagement escalation procedure.

docs.title: Collection Sources
docs.text:
Potential collection sources include:

Local filesystem

Cloud storage

docs.title: Windows Filesystem Discovery
docs.text:
Current directory:

Get-Location

Drives:

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Directory listing:

Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath "C:\Path"

Recursive enumeration should be limited to a known authorised location:

Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath "C:\Authorised\TestData" -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object FullName,Length,LastWriteTime

docs.text:
Metadata may be sufficient:

Get-Item -LiteralPath "C:\Authorised\TestData\objective.txt" |
    Select-Object FullName,Length,CreationTime,LastWriteTime

docs.title: Windows File Hash
docs.text:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath "C:\Authorised\TestData\objective.txt"

A hash can prove exactly which test artifact was accessed without repeatedly preserving duplicate copies.

docs.title: Windows Controlled Copy
docs.text:
When copying an explicitly approved test file:

Copy-Item -LiteralPath "C:\Authorised\TestData\objective.txt" -Destination "C:\RedTeamStaging\objective.txt"

Verify:

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath "C:\RedTeamStaging\objective.txt"

docs.title: Windows File Size
docs.text: (Get-Item -LiteralPath "C:\RedTeamStaging\objective.txt").Length

docs.title: Linux Filesystem Discovery
docs.text:
Current directory:

pwd

Directory listing:

ls -la

Known authorised location:

find /opt/redteam-testdata -maxdepth 2 -type f -printf '%p %s bytes\n' 2>/dev/null

Avoid broad filesystem searches for sensitive filenames unless required by the objective.

docs.title: Linux Metadata
docs.text: stat /opt/redteam-testdata/objective.txt

docs.title: Linux Hash
docs.text: sha256sum /opt/redteam-testdata/objective.txt

docs.title: Linux Controlled Copy
docs.text:
mkdir -p /tmp/redteam-staging
cp /opt/redteam-testdata/objective.txt /tmp/redteam-staging/objective.txt

Verify:

sha256sum /tmp/redteam-staging/objective.txt

docs.title: File Content Validation
docs.text:
Before displaying a file's contents, consider whether metadata is sufficient.

A good progression is:

File Exists
    |
    v
Metadata
    |
    v
Hash
    |
    v
Small Approved Content Sample
    |
    v
Full Copy Only If Necessary

docs.title: Network Share Collection
docs.text:
Network shares are common sources of business information.

Potential platforms include:

Windows SMB

NFS

NAS

Distributed file services

Cloud-backed enterprise shares

docs.title: Windows SMB Shares
docs.text:
Local shares:

Get-SmbShare

For a known authorised server:

For a known authorised path:

    Select-Object FullName,Length,LastWriteTime

If reading the marker is required:

Mounted NFS resources can be identified with:

Prefer targeted queries related to:

Objective groups

Objective computers

Relevant administrative relationships

Relevant certificate infrastructure

Orders

docs.text:
Prefer:

Schema information

Table names

Record counts

Customer-provided test records

over:

Database Access

docs.text:
A read-only query against an explicitly authorised test table might be:

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM redteam_test_records;

Or:

SELECT id, test_marker
FROM redteam_test_records
WHERE id = 1;

FROM customers;

when a synthetic or narrowly scoped record proves the same objective.

Examples:

Demonstrate mailbox access

docs.title: Synthetic Email

A customer can send:

RED TEAM OBJECTIVE 2026

docs.text:
Source repositories may be high-value engagement objectives.

GitHub

Internal Git servers

docs.title: Source Repository Validation
docs.text:
A red team objective may only require proving:

Repository readable

Specific project accessible

Protected branch visible

Customer-created marker file readable

A complete repository clone may not be necessary.

docs.title: Local Git Repository
docs.text:
Repository status:

git status

Remote configuration:

git remote -v

Recent commits:

git log --oneline -n 10

Do not expose repository credentials in evidence.

docs.title: Repository Evidence
docs.text:
Prefer:

Repository name

Access level

Relevant path

Commit identifier

Timestamp

docs.title: Application Data
docs.text:
Applications may expose information through:

Web interfaces

APIs

docs.title: Application Export Functions
docs.text:
Applications may provide:

CSV export

Report generation

Backup export

Administrative download

These features can create collection paths.

Test using:

Synthetic account

Synthetic records

Small result sets

where possible.

docs.title: API Collection
docs.text:
An API may expose objective-relevant information.

A safe approach is:

Authenticate

Identify approved endpoint

Request one known test object

Record response metadata

Avoid bulk pagination

docs.title: API Evidence
docs.text:
Capture:

Endpoint

Method

Identity

docs.title: Browser-Based Collection
docs.text:
Browsers can contain:

History

docs.text:
Screen capture may sometimes be sufficient to prove access.

For example:

Restricted application area

Test message

Test document

docs.text:
Clipboard contents may contain:

Text

Credentials

Commands

Business information

docs.title: Audio and Video
docs.text:
ATT&CK includes audio and video capture techniques.

These techniques carry significant privacy risk.

They should normally require explicit approval and a specific objective.

Prefer synthetic or controlled test environments.

docs.title: Keylogging and Input Capture
docs.text:
Input capture can expose:

Passwords

Personal messages

Financial information

Sensitive business data

Do not deploy keylogging or similar input-capture mechanisms as routine collection.

If the scenario specifically requires validation, establish:

Explicit approval

Test user

Test credentials

Limited duration

Defined application

Immediate cleanup

docs.title: Cloud Storage
docs.text:
Potential services include:

Amazon S3

Google Cloud Storage

Prefer:

Bucket/container metadata

Object names

Customer-provided test objects

Small synthetic files

over bulk downloads.

docs.title: Cloud Object Validation
docs.text:
A safe objective might be:

Demonstrate that the compromised identity can read
redteam-validation.txt from the authorised storage location.

docs.title: Cloud Database Collection
docs.text:

Potential SaaS platforms include:

Microsoft 365

docs.text:

docs.text:
Kubernetes workloads may expose:

docs.text:
Potential information repositories include:

OneDrive

Confluence

Teams

Internal wikis

Document-management systems

Use search terms only when objective-driven and authorised.

docs.text:
Backup infrastructure may contain copies of:

Servers

Databases

Documents

Configuration

Directory services

Cloud workloads

Demonstrating administrative access to the backup platform may be sufficient without restoring or downloading production backups.

docs.text:
Security platforms may contain:

Alerts

Vulnerability data

Investigation notes

Avoid altering or deleting security information.

docs.text:
Prefer existing authorised access paths.

For example:

Application UI

Existing share

Existing database session

Approved API

Current filesystem permissions

docs.text:
Automation can increase both efficiency and risk.

Excessive volume

Performance impact

Unexpected scope expansion

Collection Task

Small / Targeted?

docs.title: Collection Inventory
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory of collected artifacts.

Example:

ID Source Artifact Size Classification Purpose COL-001 APP01 objective.txt 128 B Test Objective proof COL-002 FILE01 Marker metadata N/A Test Share validation COL-003 DB01 Test record 1 row Test Database validation

docs.title: Collection Metadata
docs.text:
For each artifact record:

Collection ID

Source host/system

Source path/object

Source identity

Timestamp

Size

Hash

Classification

Reason collected

Storage location

Retention requirement

Cleanup status

docs.title: Staging
docs.text:
Staging is the temporary organisation of collected material before further validation.

Example:

Source
   |
   v
Collection
   |
   v
Controlled Staging
   |
   +--> Hash
   |
   +--> Inventory
   |
   +--> Evidence
   |
   v
Exfiltration Test or Cleanup

docs.title: Staging Principles
docs.text:
A staging location should be:

Authorised

Access controlled

Temporary

Documented

Encrypted where appropriate

Easy to clean up

docs.title: Windows Staging Example
docs.text:
Create a dedicated test directory:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "C:\RedTeamStaging" -Force

Inventory:

Get-ChildItem "C:\RedTeamStaging" -File |
    Select-Object Name,Length,LastWriteTime

Hash:

Get-ChildItem "C:\RedTeamStaging" -File |
    Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256

docs.title: Linux Staging Example
docs.text:
mkdir -p /tmp/redteam-staging
chmod 700 /tmp/redteam-staging

Inventory:

find /tmp/redteam-staging -maxdepth 1 -type f -printf '%f %s bytes\n'

Hashes:

sha256sum /tmp/redteam-staging/*

Use a more appropriate protected location if /tmp does not satisfy the engagement's data-handling requirements.

docs.title: Archive Collected Data
docs.text:
ATT&CK includes:

Archive Collected Data

as a technique because adversaries may combine data before moving it.

In an authorised assessment, archiving should only be used when required by the test plan.

For synthetic test data on Linux:

tar -czf redteam-testdata.tar.gz redteam-testdata/

On Windows:

Compress-Archive -Path "C:\RedTeamStaging\TestData\*" -DestinationPath "C:\RedTeamStaging\redteam-testdata.zip"

Use synthetic or explicitly approved test data.

docs.title: Archive Hashing
docs.text:
Windows:

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "C:\RedTeamStaging\redteam-testdata.zip"

Linux:

sha256sum redteam-testdata.tar.gz

docs.title: Compression Ratio and Size
docs.text:
Record archive size because it helps correlate later network telemetry.

Windows:

Get-Item "C:\RedTeamStaging\redteam-testdata.zip" |
    Select-Object Name,Length

Linux:

stat -c '%n %s bytes' redteam-testdata.tar.gz

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Collected sensitive data may require encryption at rest.

The exact encryption method should follow:

Customer policy

Engagement policy

Organisation standards

Approved tooling

Do not invent ad-hoc encryption procedures for customer-sensitive data.

docs.title: Evidence vs Collected Data
docs.text:
Keep these conceptually separate.

Collected Data:
Material obtained during objective validation.

Evidence:
Material required to demonstrate what happened.

The report usually needs much less information than was technically accessible.

docs.title: Evidence Minimisation
docs.text:
Instead of embedding a sensitive document:

Screenshot:
Full confidential document

prefer:

Filename

Path

Classification

Hash

Small redacted screenshot

Access context

docs.title: Hashing Evidence
docs.text:
Hashing helps establish integrity.

Windows:

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "C:\RedTeamStaging\objective.txt"

Linux:

sha256sum /tmp/redteam-staging/objective.txt

docs.title: Evidence Naming
docs.text:
Use predictable names.

Example:

COL-001-WS01-objective-file.png

COL-002-FILE01-share-access.txt

COL-003-DB01-test-record.png

Avoid putting customer secrets directly into filenames.

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text:
Use consistent timestamps.

Prefer:

UTC

Example:

2026-09-05T18:42:11Z

Consistent time improves correlation with:

EDR

SIEM

Firewall

Proxy

Cloud audit

SOC investigation

docs.title: Collection Timeline
docs.text:
Example:

14:02 - Objective share identified
14:05 - Scope confirmed
14:08 - Marker file metadata recorded
14:10 - Marker file read
14:12 - SHA-256 recorded
14:15 - Defender/SIEM telemetry reviewed
14:20 - Temporary local copy removed

docs.title: Collection Detection Hypothesis
docs.text:
Example:

Hypothesis:
A compromised workstation reading an unusual finance-share test
artifact should generate SMB and endpoint telemetry sufficient
for investigation.

Test:
Read a customer-provided marker from the authorised finance share.

Expected:
Share-access telemetry and endpoint activity are recorded.

Result:
Record whether telemetry, detection and analyst response occur.

docs.text:
Hypothesis:
Creation of an archive containing objective-relevant test files
should be observable through endpoint telemetry.

Test:
Archive a small synthetic dataset in the approved staging location.

Expected:
Process and file-creation telemetry are generated.

Result:
Record whether the behaviour is logged or alerted.

docs.text:

Prevented

Allowed and Detected

Allowed and Logged

Allowed without Alert

No Useful Visibility

docs.text:
Volume matters.

Total bytes

Files:
5

4.2 MB

Do not create large collection loads merely to make detection easier.

    v
Small Dataset
    |
    v
Controlled Batch
    |
    v
Larger Simulation Only If Required

docs.title: Objective-Based Collection
docs.text:
Every collected artifact should answer:

Why do we need this?

Good:

This marker proves access to the finance share.

Poor:

It looked interesting.

docs.title: Collection and OPSEC
docs.text:
Collection creates operational risk because collected data may become a second copy of sensitive customer information.

Controls include:

Dedicated staging

Restricted access

Encryption

Inventory

Hashes

Minimal retention

Controlled transfer

Verified deletion

See:

Red Team OPSEC

docs.title: Collection and Detection Validation
docs.text:
Collection should also answer:

Did endpoint telemetry record access?

Did file auditing record access?

Did DLP detect the activity?

Did the SIEM receive the event?

Was an alert generated?

Did the SOC investigate?

Could defenders identify the source identity?

See:

Detection Validation

docs.title: Collection and Reporting
docs.text:
A red team report should explain:

What was accessible

Why it mattered

What was actually collected

How much was collected

Whether synthetic data was used

How it was protected

Whether defenders detected it

Whether it was removed

See:

Red Team Reporting

docs.title: Candidate vs Confirmed
docs.text: Collection findings should use precise evidence states.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text: A finance share was discovered.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
The current identity appears to have read permission to the
finance objective directory.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
The assessment identity successfully read the customer-provided
finance objective marker.

docs.title: Do Not Overstate Access
docs.text:
Avoid:

All finance information was compromised.

when only:

One authorised test file was accessed.

Instead:

The assessment confirmed that the compromised identity had read
access to the tested finance share location. The assessment did
not perform bulk collection of production finance data.

docs.title: Example Finding - Sensitive Share Access
docs.text:
Title:
Standard User Context Provides Access to Restricted Finance Share

Observation:
Following compromise of a standard workstation account, the
assessment identified a network share used by the finance
department.

The assessment account successfully accessed the authorised
red team marker within the restricted finance directory.

No production finance documents were copied.

Impact:
An attacker who compromises the same class of user account may
be able to access information stored within the affected share,
potentially exposing confidential business information.

Recommendation:
Review share and NTFS permissions, remove unnecessary group
access, implement least privilege and monitor unusual access to
sensitive file repositories.

docs.title: Example Finding - Excessive Database Access
docs.text:
Title:
Application Identity Has Unnecessary Read Access to Restricted Database Data

Observation:
The compromised application identity could query a database
outside the data required for its normal application function.

Validation was limited to a customer-provided test record.

Impact:
Compromise of the application identity could provide an attacker
with access beyond the application's intended data boundary.

Recommendation:
Restrict database permissions to the schemas, tables and
operations required by the application. Use separate identities
for workloads with different privilege requirements.

docs.title: Example Finding - Source Repository Access
docs.text:
Title:
Compromised Service Account Can Access Restricted Source Repository

Observation:
The assessment demonstrated that the compromised service account
could access a restricted source-code repository.

Validation was limited to repository metadata and a
customer-provided marker file.

Impact:
Compromise of the service account could expose proprietary source
code and potentially provide additional information useful for
attacking internal applications.

Recommendation:
Review repository membership, service-account permissions and
token scope. Apply least privilege and monitor unusual repository
access by non-human identities.

docs.title: Example Positive Security Result
docs.text:
Not every collection test should produce a vulnerability.

Example:

Control:
Data Loss Prevention

Test:
A synthetic document containing customer-approved test data was
placed in the collection staging directory.

Result:
The endpoint DLP control generated an alert and the SOC correctly
identified the host, user and file involved.

Conclusion:
The tested collection activity was successfully detected.

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text:
Collection-related weaknesses commonly originate from:

Excessive file permissions

Excessive share permissions

Overprivileged service accounts

Weak database authorisation

Excessive API permissions

Overly broad cloud IAM

Weak repository access controls

Poor data segmentation

Insufficient DLP

Insufficient auditing

Credential reuse

docs.title: Remediation - Files and Shares
docs.text:
Consider:

Least-privilege ACLs

Role-based access

Separate sensitive shares

Remove broad groups

Review inherited permissions

Enable appropriate auditing

Classify sensitive information

Monitor unusual access

docs.title: Remediation - Databases
docs.text:
Consider:

Separate application identities

Least-privilege roles

Restrict schemas

Restrict tables

Restrict export functionality

Enable database auditing

Protect backups

Monitor unusual queries

docs.title: Remediation - Cloud
docs.text:
Consider:

Least-privilege IAM

Restrict object access

Separate workloads

Use managed identities

Use short-lived credentials

Enable data-access logging

Apply DLP/classification

Monitor unusual downloads

docs.title: Remediation - Repositories
docs.text:
Consider:

Least-privilege repository access

Short-lived tokens

Scoped automation credentials

Protected branches

Secret scanning

Audit logging

Regular membership reviews

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
All temporary collection artifacts should be tracked and removed according to the engagement plan.

Possible artifacts include:

Copied files

Archives

Temporary exports

Database exports

Screenshots

Temporary directories

Synthetic data

Cloud test objects

Temporary reports

docs.title: Windows Cleanup
docs.text:
Review:

Get-ChildItem "C:\RedTeamStaging" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Remove an approved temporary staging directory after evidence requirements are satisfied:

Remove-Item "C:\RedTeamStaging" -Recurse -Force

Verify:

Test-Path "C:\RedTeamStaging"

docs.title: Linux Cleanup
docs.text:
Review:

find /tmp/redteam-staging -maxdepth 2 -ls 2>/dev/null

Remove:

rm -rf /tmp/redteam-staging

Verify:

test ! -e /tmp/redteam-staging && echo "Staging directory removed"

docs.title: Cleanup Verification
docs.text:
Record:

Artifact

Original location

Staging location

Deletion performed

Deletion verified

Operator

Timestamp

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
Some evidence may need to remain after technical cleanup.

Define:

What evidence is retained?

Where is it stored?

Who can access it?

Is it encrypted?

When is it deleted?

Who approves deletion?

Follow contractual and organisational requirements.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Collection can be reduced to:

Know the objective.

Identify only the data required to prove it.

Confirm both the system and data are in scope.

Prefer synthetic data.

Prefer metadata before content.

Prefer one record before a dataset.

Avoid bulk collection.

Protect anything collected.

Inventory every artifact.

Hash important evidence.

Use consistent timestamps.

Validate endpoint, server, cloud and DLP visibility.

Do not confuse accessibility with permission to collect.

Stop when sufficient evidence exists.

Remove temporary artifacts.

Retain only the evidence required for reporting.

Proof is more important than volume

If one synthetic record, marker file, hash or screenshot proves that the security boundary has been crossed, collecting thousands of production records usually adds risk without materially improving the finding.

Access does not equal permission to collect

A compromised identity may technically be able to access large amounts of sensitive information. That does not mean the red team should copy it. Follow the Rules of Engagement, minimise collection and stop once sufficient evidence has been obtained.

docs.title: Command and Control
docs.text:
Command and Control (C2) is the communication layer used by an authorised red team to manage controlled agents, issue tasks, receive results, and coordinate activity during an assessment.

A basic C2 architecture can be represented as:

Operator
   |
   v
Team Server
   |
   v
Listener
   |
   v
Redirector
   |
   v
Internet
   |
   v
Authorised Test Host

C2 should not be considered only from the offensive perspective.

A mature assessment should also evaluate:

Endpoint visibility
Network visibility
DNS visibility
Proxy visibility
Firewall visibility
Authentication controls
Application control
EDR telemetry
SIEM correlation
Incident response

The objective is to determine whether authorised adversary-like communication can operate in the environment and how effectively defensive controls identify and respond to it.

docs.title: C2 Terminology
docs.text:
Common C2 terminology includes:

Term Description Team server Backend system coordinating C2 activity Operator Authorised tester interacting with the framework Listener Service waiting for agent communication Agent Controlled software component running on an authorised test system Beacon Common term for an agent that periodically checks in Implant Another term commonly used for an agent Session Active communication context with an agent Callback Communication initiated by an agent toward C2 infrastructure Check-in Periodic agent communication Tasking Instructions provided to an agent Redirector Internet-facing system forwarding permitted traffic to the backend Transport Communication mechanism used by the C2 channel Sleep Delay between periodic check-ins Jitter Variation applied to timing Profile Configuration controlling communication behaviour in frameworks that support it

docs.title: High-Level C2 Architecture
docs.text:
A simple architecture:

+----------------+
|    Operator    |
+-------+--------+
        |
        v
+----------------+
|  Team Server   |
+-------+--------+
        |
        v
+----------------+
|    Listener    |
+-------+--------+
        |
        v
+----------------+
|   Redirector   |
+-------+--------+
        |
        v
     Internet
        |
        v
+----------------+
| Authorised Host|
+----------------+

For a small lab, several components may exist on the same system.

For a larger engagement, separating them provides better security and operational control.

docs.title: C2 Communication Model
docs.text:
A common communication model is agent initiated.

Authorised Host
      |
      | 1. Check in
      v
Redirector
      |
      v
Team Server
      |
      | 2. Retrieve task
      v
Authorised Host
      |
      | 3. Execute authorised task
      |
      | 4. Return result
      v
Redirector
      |
      v
Team Server
      |
      v
Operator

This communication creates opportunities for defensive monitoring at multiple layers.

docs.title: C2 Components
docs.text:
A C2 environment commonly contains:

Operator Client
Team Server
Listener
Agent
Redirector
Domain
DNS
TLS Certificate
Firewall
Logging
Management Network

Each component should have a clearly defined purpose.

docs.title: Operator
docs.text:
The operator is the authorised tester interacting with the C2 platform.

Operators may:

Review active sessions
Issue approved tasks
Collect command results
Coordinate operations
Review logs
Manage listeners
Track objectives
Record evidence

Operator access should be tightly controlled.

docs.title: Operator Security
docs.text:
Protect operator systems using controls such as:

Strong authentication
Dedicated engagement accounts
Encrypted storage
Screen locking
Minimal local secrets
Separate engagement workspaces
Restricted administrative access
Logging
VPN access

Avoid sharing a single administrative account between operators where individual accounts are supported.

docs.title: Team Server
docs.text:
The team server is the backend of the C2 architecture.

It may contain:

Agent state
Operator accounts
Listener configuration
Task history
Results
Infrastructure configuration
Logs
Assessment metadata
Cryptographic material

Compromise of the team server can expose significant engagement information.

It should therefore normally receive stronger protection than an internet-facing redirector.

docs.title: Team Server Exposure
docs.text:
Prefer:

Internet
   |
   X
Team Server

with operational communication routed through controlled infrastructure:

Internet
   |
   v
Redirector
   |
   v
Team Server

Administrative access should preferably follow a separate path:

Operator
   |
   v
Management VPN
   |
   v
Team Server

docs.title: Management Plane vs C2 Plane
docs.text:
Separating management traffic from operational C2 traffic is useful.

MANAGEMENT PLANE

Operator
   |
   v
VPN
   |
   v
Team Server


C2 PLANE

Authorised Host
   |
   v
Internet
   |
   v
Redirector
   |
   v
Listener
   |
   v
Team Server

This reduces unnecessary exposure of administrative services.

docs.title: Listener
docs.text:
A listener receives communication associated with authorised agents.

Conceptually:

Agent
  |
  v
Transport
  |
  v
Listener
  |
  v
Team Server

Listeners may use different communication mechanisms depending on the framework and assessment design.

docs.title: Listener Inventory
docs.text:
Track active listeners.

Example:

Listener Purpose Transport Exposure Redirected web-01 Workstation testing HTTPS Public redirector Yes lab-01 Internal lab HTTPS Internal No

Do not create unnecessary listeners.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
An agent is the controlled component communicating with the C2 infrastructure.

Depending on the framework, agents may support:

Command execution
Process information
Filesystem operations
Network discovery
Task execution
Session management
Data collection
Framework-specific extensions

Agent capabilities vary significantly between frameworks.

Only functionality permitted by the Rules of Engagement should be used.

docs.title: Agent Lifecycle
docs.text:
A useful operational model is:

Generate
   |
   v
Record
   |
   v
Deploy
   |
   v
Execute
   |
   v
Operate
   |
   v
Collect Required Evidence
   |
   v
Terminate
   |
   v
Remove
   |
   v
Verify Cleanup

Every deployed assessment artifact should have a cleanup plan.

docs.title: C2 Transport
docs.text:
C2 communication requires a transport mechanism.

Common concepts include:

HTTP
HTTPS
DNS
TCP
Named pipes
Framework-specific peer-to-peer channels

Availability depends on the framework.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
A simplified HTTP C2 model:

Agent
   |
   | HTTP
   v
Redirector
   |
   v
Listener

HTTP communication can be observed by:

Endpoint telemetry
Network monitoring
Proxy logs
Firewall logs
Web server logs
DNS logs

Plain HTTP also exposes network content and should generally not be preferred for internet-facing assessment infrastructure.

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text:
HTTPS adds TLS protection around the HTTP communication.

Agent
   |
   | TLS
   v
Redirector
   |
   v
Listener

HTTPS does not make communication invisible.

Defenders can still observe metadata such as:

Destination domain
Destination IP
Connection timing
Connection frequency
TLS characteristics
DNS lookups
Proxy metadata
Certificate information
Process responsible for connection

docs.title: DNS-Based Communication
docs.text:
Some C2 frameworks can use DNS-related communication.

Conceptually:

Agent
   |
   v
DNS Query
   |
   v
Recursive Resolver
   |
   v
Authoritative Infrastructure
   |
   v
C2 Backend

DNS communication can produce distinctive telemetry.

Defensive monitoring can examine:

Query volume
Query length
Subdomain entropy
Unusual record types
Rare domains
Newly observed domains
Repeated periodic queries
Endpoint process relationships

DNS-based communication should only be used where explicitly permitted because it can generate substantial infrastructure and monitoring activity.

docs.title: Direct TCP Communication
docs.text:
Some tools support direct TCP-based communication.

Agent
   |
   v
TCP Connection
   |
   v
Listener

Direct connections can be simple operationally but may provide fewer infrastructure layers between the test host and backend.

docs.title: Peer-to-Peer Communication
docs.text:
Some frameworks support peer-to-peer communication between controlled systems.

Conceptually:

Agent A
   |
   v
Agent B
   |
   v
Agent C
   |
   v
External C2

This may reduce the number of systems communicating directly with external infrastructure.

However, it also introduces additional complexity and should only be used when relevant to the engagement.

docs.title: Redirectors
docs.text:
A redirector sits between the authorised target environment and the C2 backend.

Target
   |
   v
Redirector
   |
   v
Team Server

Potential benefits include:

Backend isolation
TLS termination
Traffic filtering
Logging
Service separation
Simpler backend firewalling
Replaceable internet-facing infrastructure

docs.title: Redirector Architecture
docs.text:
A recommended conceptual separation is:

                     Internet
                        |
                        v
                 +-------------+
                 | Redirector  |
                 +------+------+
                        |
                  Allowed Route
                        |
                        v
                 +-------------+
                 | Team Server |
                 +------+------+
                        |
                        v
                 Management VPN
                        |
                        v
                    Operator

The backend should preferably only accept the required operational traffic from known redirectors.

docs.title: Multiple Redirectors
docs.text:
Larger engagements may use multiple redirectors.

                 Internet
                    |
         +----------+----------+
         |                     |
         v                     v
   Redirector A          Redirector B
         |                     |
         +----------+----------+
                    |
                    v
               Team Server

Potential reasons include:

Separation of roles
Availability
Different engagement phases
Different network paths
Infrastructure replacement
Testing different control points

docs.title: Reverse Proxy
docs.text:
A reverse proxy is commonly used as part of redirector infrastructure.

Examples include:

Nginx
Apache
Caddy
HAProxy
Traefik
Cloud load balancers

A reverse proxy can provide:

TLS termination
Access logging
Backend routing
Request filtering
Rate limiting
Health checks

docs.title: Backend Firewalling
docs.text:
The backend should accept only necessary traffic.

Conceptually:

Internet ----------X----------> Team Server

Redirector --------ALLOW------> Team Server

Operator VPN ------ALLOW------> Management Interface

Verify firewall rules from both the host and provider layers.

docs.title: Domains
docs.text:
C2 infrastructure may use dedicated assessment domains.

Example structure:

assessment-example.net
        |
        +--> c2.assessment-example.net
        |
        +--> files.assessment-example.net
        |
        +--> vpn.assessment-example.net

Domains should be tracked as engagement resources.

docs.title: DNS Records
docs.text:
A typical HTTPS endpoint may use:

c2.assessment-example.net
            |
            v
         A Record
            |
            v
       Redirector IP

Verify:

dig +short c2.assessment-example.net

or:

nslookup c2.assessment-example.net

docs.title: TLS Certificates
docs.text:
HTTPS infrastructure should use appropriately configured TLS.

Check a certificate:

openssl s_client -connect c2.assessment-example.net:443 -servername c2.assessment-example.net

Review:

Subject
Issuer
Validity
SANs
Certificate chain

Certificate lifecycle should be included in infrastructure cleanup planning.

docs.title: Sleep
docs.text:
Periodic C2 agents commonly wait between check-ins.

Conceptually:

Check In
   |
   v
Wait
   |
   v
Check In
   |
   v
Wait

The configured interval influences:

Responsiveness
Network frequency
Infrastructure load
Operational tempo
Defensive visibility

docs.title: Jitter
docs.text:
Jitter introduces variation into a periodic interval.

Without variation:

60
60
60
60
60

With variation:

54
67
58
63
51

From a defensive perspective, periodic or near-periodic outbound communication remains an important behavioural signal.

The exact implementation varies by framework.

docs.title: C2 Timing
docs.text:
Timing should reflect the engagement objective.

Factors include:

Testing window
Operational responsiveness
Network monitoring objectives
Endpoint monitoring objectives
Infrastructure capacity
Engagement duration
Rules of Engagement

Do not optimise solely for stealth.

For purple-team-oriented work, predictable activity may actually make telemetry correlation easier.

docs.title: Communication Profiles
docs.text:
Some frameworks allow communication behaviour to be configured through profiles.

Profiles may influence concepts such as:

Request paths
Headers
Timing
Transport
Connection behaviour
Framework-specific metadata

Profiles should be treated as controlled engagement configuration.

Avoid attempting to impersonate unrelated organisations or abuse third-party infrastructure.

docs.title: C2 Framework Selection
docs.text:
Framework selection should be based on engagement requirements.

Consider:

Operating systems
Agent support
Transport support
Team collaboration
Authentication
Logging
Extensibility
Infrastructure requirements
Detection objectives
Maintenance
Community activity
Rules of Engagement

docs.title: MITRE CALDERA
docs.text:
MITRE CALDERA focuses on automated adversary emulation.

It can be useful when the objective is repeatable security-control validation rather than traditional operator-driven red teaming.

MITRE CALDERA

docs.title: Framework Comparison
docs.text:
A conceptual comparison:

Framework Model Typical Use Cobalt Strike Commercial C2 Red teaming Sliver Open-source C2 Red teaming and research Mythic Modular C2 platform Collaborative red teaming Havoc Open-source C2 Red teaming and research Metasploit Exploitation framework Penetration testing and controlled sessions CALDERA Adversary emulation Automated security validation

Capabilities evolve, so verify current framework documentation before relying on a particular feature.

docs.title: C2 Authentication
docs.text:
Operator authentication should be protected.

Consider:

Individual operator accounts
Strong passwords
MFA where supported
VPN restrictions
Source restrictions
Credential rotation
Account removal after engagement

Do not expose administrative interfaces unnecessarily.

docs.title: C2 Secrets
docs.text:
Potentially sensitive C2 material includes:

Operator credentials
TLS private keys
Framework secrets
Agent configuration
Listener secrets
API tokens
Infrastructure credentials
VPN keys
SSH keys

These should not be committed to public repositories.

docs.title: C2 Configuration Storage
docs.text:
A controlled directory structure may resemble:

redteam/
├── infrastructure/
├── c2/
├── redirectors/
├── logs/
└── inventory/

Secrets should be stored separately from normal configuration where practical.

docs.title: Git Exclusions
docs.text:
Example:

.env
*.key
*.pem
*.pfx
*.p12
secrets/
credentials/
logs/
engagement-data/

Always review staged files before committing:

git status

and:

git diff --cached

docs.title: Agent Tracking
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory of controlled agents.

Example:

Agent Host User First Seen Purpose Cleanup A01 TEST-WKS01 testuser 10:15 UTC Detection test Required A02 TEST-SRV01 svc-test 11:04 UTC Lateral movement validation Required

This is particularly important when multiple operators are active.

docs.title: Task Tracking
docs.text:
Important actions should be traceable.

Record:

Timestamp
Operator
Agent
Host
Identity
Task
Result
Objective
Evidence

Example:

2026-09-05 11:12 UTC
Operator: A
Agent: A01
Host: TEST-WKS01
Task: Identity enumeration
Result: Successful
Objective: Establish security context

docs.title: C2 Logging
docs.text:
Preserve enough C2 logs to reconstruct assessment activity.

Potential logs include:

Operator login
Listener creation
Agent registration
Task execution
Task results
Agent termination
Infrastructure errors
Framework events

Log retention should follow the engagement agreement.

docs.title: Network Logging
docs.text:
Infrastructure-side telemetry can include:

Reverse-proxy access logs
Firewall logs
DNS logs
VPN logs
TLS logs
Cloud flow logs
Provider firewall logs

These logs help reconstruct communication independently from the C2 framework.

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Synchronise infrastructure clocks.

Check:

timedatectl

Prefer a consistent timeline such as UTC.

Operator activity: UTC
C2 logs: UTC
Redirector logs: UTC
Evidence: UTC
Blue-team comparison: converted consistently

docs.title: Endpoint Detection
docs.text:
Endpoint telemetry may reveal:

Process creation
Parent-child relationships
Network connections
Module loads
Script execution
File creation
Service activity
Scheduled tasks
Authentication activity
Memory-related telemetry
Security-control alerts

Exact visibility depends on the endpoint security stack.

docs.title: Network Detection
docs.text:
Network monitoring may identify:

Unusual destinations
Rare domains
Periodic connections
Long-lived sessions
Unexpected ports
DNS anomalies
Proxy anomalies
TLS metadata
Unusual connection volume

Encrypted traffic still exposes useful metadata.

docs.title: DNS Detection
docs.text:
Useful DNS signals can include:

Newly observed domains
Rare domains
High-entropy labels
Repeated queries
Unusual record types
Long labels
Unexpected query volume
Endpoint-to-domain relationships

docs.title: Proxy Detection
docs.text:
Proxy telemetry can reveal:

Destination
HTTP method
Request frequency
Response size
User identity
Endpoint identity
TLS information
Category
Policy result

Where TLS inspection is used, additional visibility may exist depending on organisational policy and architecture.

docs.title: Firewall Detection
docs.text:
Firewall logs can provide:

Source IP
Destination IP
Destination port
Protocol
Connection duration
Bytes transferred
Allow or deny decision

docs.title: C2 Behaviour Analytics
docs.text:
One useful defensive concept is beaconing analysis.

Conceptually:

Connection
   |
   v
Wait
   |
   v
Connection
   |
   v
Wait
   |
   v
Connection

Analysts can examine:

Periodicity
Destination rarity
Connection duration
Byte patterns
Domain age
Endpoint process
Time of day
Peer population

No single signal should automatically be treated as proof of C2.

docs.title: Baseline vs Anomaly
docs.text:
Detection works better when behaviour is compared with a baseline.

Normal Endpoint
     |
     +--> Microsoft services
     +--> Corporate applications
     +--> Known SaaS

Test Endpoint
     |
     +--> Normal traffic
     +--> Rare assessment domain

The rare destination may provide useful investigative context.

docs.title: Detection Validation
docs.text:
During an authorised assessment, record whether each C2 stage is visible.

Example:

Stage Telemetry Alert Investigated DNS lookup Yes No No HTTPS connection Yes No No Agent execution Yes Yes Yes Task execution Yes Yes Yes

This makes the exercise useful beyond simply demonstrating connectivity.

docs.title: Purple Team C2 Testing
docs.text:
C2 behaviours are particularly suitable for purple teaming.

Red Team
   |
   v
Execute Controlled Behaviour
   |
   v
Blue Team
   |
   v
Observe Telemetry
   |
   v
Create / Tune Detection
   |
   v
Repeat

This allows individual behaviours to be tested without requiring a complete attack chain.

docs.title: C2 Infrastructure Hardening
docs.text:
Protect C2 infrastructure using multiple layers.

Provider Firewall
       |
       v
Host Firewall
       |
       v
Management VPN
       |
       v
Strong Authentication
       |
       v
Restricted Team Server
       |
       v
Redirector
       |
       v
TLS

docs.title: Server Baseline
docs.text:
Before deployment:

sudo apt update

sudo apt full-upgrade -y

Review listening services:

sudo ss -lntup

Review firewall:

sudo nft list ruleset

or, where UFW is used:

sudo ufw status numbered

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Prefer key-based administration.

Example connection:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/redteam-engagement operator@SERVER

Review effective SSH settings:

sudo sshd -T

Validate configuration before reload:

sudo sshd -t

docs.title: Provider Firewall
docs.text:
A layered architecture:

Internet
   |
   v
Cloud / Provider Firewall
   |
   v
Host Firewall
   |
   v
C2 Infrastructure

Management ports should normally be restricted to authorised source addresses or a management network.

docs.title: C2 Availability
docs.text:
Operational infrastructure may fail.

Possible causes include:

Server failure
Network failure
DNS failure
Certificate expiry
Firewall error
Provider issue
Configuration error
Disk exhaustion
Process crash

Monitor infrastructure during active engagements.

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
Examples:

uptime

df -h

free -h

ss -lntup

systemctl --failed

docs.title: Redirector Health
docs.text:
For HTTPS infrastructure:

curl -I https://c2.assessment-example.net/

TLS validation:

openssl s_client -connect c2.assessment-example.net:443 -servername c2.assessment-example.net

The expected HTTP response depends on the infrastructure design.

docs.title: Kill Switch
docs.text:
A C2 architecture should have a rapid shutdown mechanism.

Possible actions include:

Disable listener
Stop redirector
Block operational port
Remove DNS record
Revoke operator access
Terminate controlled agents
Disable infrastructure

The procedure should be known before testing begins.

docs.title: Emergency Model
docs.text:
Unexpected Event
       |
       v
Stop Tasking
       |
       v
Disable Listener
       |
       v
Restrict Infrastructure
       |
       v
Preserve Required Logs
       |
       v

       |
       v
Investigate

docs.title: Agent Cleanup
docs.text:
When an agent is no longer required:

Stop Tasking
    |
    v
Terminate Session
    |
    v
Remove Assessment Artifact
    |
    v
Remove Persistence if Used
    |
    v
Verify Process Stopped
    |
    v
Verify File Removed
    |
    v
Record Cleanup

Do not assume closing a session removes the deployed artifact.

docs.title: Infrastructure Cleanup
docs.text:
At engagement completion:

Stop listeners
       |
       v
Terminate agents
       |
       v
Collect required logs
       |
       v
Remove payloads
       |
       v
Revoke temporary credentials
       |
       v
Remove DNS
       |
       v
Remove firewall exceptions
       |
       v
Destroy temporary servers
       |
       v
Verify cleanup

docs.title: C2 Evidence
docs.text:
For each meaningful C2 event, record:

Timestamp
Operator
Agent
Host
Identity
Listener
Transport
Action
Result
Detection result
Evidence reference

This enables later correlation with defensive telemetry.

docs.title: C2 Reporting
docs.text:
The final report should not simply state:

C2 established successfully.

Instead explain:

How communication was established
Which system communicated externally
Which transport was used
Which controls observed it
Which controls alerted
How long detection took
Whether the activity was investigated
What defensive gaps were identified

docs.title: Example Detection Narrative
docs.text:
The authorised test workstation established HTTPS communication
with the assessment redirector.

Endpoint telemetry recorded the originating process and outbound
connection.

The DNS lookup and HTTPS connection were present in network telemetry.

No alert was generated for the initial communication.

Subsequent controlled task execution generated an endpoint alert,
which was investigated by the defensive team.

This provides substantially more value than merely documenting successful connectivity.

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK
docs.text:
Command and Control is represented by the MITRE ATT&CK Command and Control tactic.

Relevant technique families can include communication through:

Application-layer protocols
Non-application-layer protocols
Proxy infrastructure
Encrypted channels
Web services

Map only techniques actually demonstrated during the engagement.

MITRE ATT&CK - Command and Control
