Authorised testing only

Command-and-control infrastructure should only be deployed for explicitly authorised security assessments and controlled security research. Restrict C2 activity to approved systems, identities, networks, and objectives. Protect operator credentials and customer information, maintain an inventory of deployed agents, and verify that assessment artifacts and temporary infrastructure are removed when testing is complete.

docs.title: Credential Access
docs.text:
Credential access is the process of identifying and validating authentication material that may provide access to systems, applications, services, or identities during an authorised security assessment.

Credential material can include much more than passwords.

Credential Material
        |
        +--> Passwords
        |
        +--> Password Hashes
        |
        +--> Kerberos Tickets
        |
        +--> Access Tokens
        |
        +--> API Keys
        |
        +--> SSH Keys
        |
        +--> Cloud Credentials
        |
        +--> Application Secrets
        |
        +--> Service Credentials
        |
        +--> Certificates
        |
        +--> Session Material

Credential access is often one of the most sensitive phases of a red team assessment.

A credential obtained from one authorised system may provide technical access to systems outside the approved scope.

Technical access does not extend authorisation.

docs.title: Credential Access Objectives
docs.text:
Credential access testing should answer questions such as:

Where is authentication material exposed?
Which identities are affected?
Why was the material accessible?
What privilege was required to access it?
Can the material actually be used?
What systems trust the credential?
What defensive controls observed access?
How should the exposure be remediated?

The objective is not to collect the largest possible number of credentials.

Collect and validate only what is necessary to demonstrate the agreed security impact.

docs.title: Credential Access Model
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Current Access
      |
      v
Identify Credential Sources
      |
      v
Credential Candidate
      |
      v
Determine Owner
      |
      v
Determine Scope
      |
      v
Validation Authorised?
    /       \
  No         Yes
  |           |
  v           v
Document   Minimal Validation
              |
              v
         Determine Impact
              |
              v
         Protect Evidence
              |
              v
            Cleanup

docs.title: Credential Types
docs.text:
Credential material can be divided into several broad categories.

Type Examples Password User or service password Hash NTLM or application password hash Kerberos material TGT, TGS, key material Token OAuth, API, session or access token Private key SSH or application key Certificate Client or authentication certificate Cloud credential Access key, secret, service principal Application secret Database password, connection string Browser/session material Session token or stored credential Configuration secret Secret embedded in a file or deployment configuration

The security impact depends on what trusts the credential.

docs.title: Credential Sources
docs.text:
Potential credential sources include:

Files
Configuration
Environment variables
Shell history
PowerShell history
Credential stores
Browser storage
Process environment
Service configuration
Scheduled tasks
Deployment scripts
Repositories
CI/CD systems
Backups
Shares
Cloud configuration
Application databases
Memory
Directory services

Not every source should be accessed during every assessment.

docs.title: Credential Discovery Workflow
docs.text:
Host Access
    |
    v
Establish Current Privilege
    |
    v
Identify Applications and Services
    |
    v
Review Likely Credential Locations
    |
    v
Find Candidate Secret
    |
    v
Determine Identity
    |
    v
Determine Trust Boundary
    |
    v
Minimal Validation

docs.title: Credential Handling
docs.text:
Treat discovered credentials as sensitive information.

Do not:

Paste credentials into public tickets
Store credentials in public Git repositories
Send credentials through unapproved messaging systems
Reuse credentials outside scope
Keep unnecessary copies
Include plaintext passwords in reports unless required

Prefer evidence that proves the issue without unnecessarily exposing the complete secret.

docs.title: Credential Inventory
docs.text:
During a substantial engagement, maintain a controlled inventory.

Example:

ID Type Identity Source Validation Cleanup CRED-001 Password Test service account Configuration Validated Rotation required CRED-002 SSH key Test administrator Home directory Not validated Customer review CRED-003 API token Test application Environment Validated Revoke

Avoid storing plaintext secrets in the inventory itself.

docs.title: Credential Validation
docs.text:
A discovered secret is not automatically valid.

Secret Found
    |
    v
Identify Type
    |
    v
Identify Owner
    |
    v
Identify Intended Service
    |
    v
Check Scope
    |
    v
Minimal Authentication Test
    |
    +--> Fails
    |
    +--> Works

Record the result without performing unnecessary follow-on actions.

docs.title: Minimal Validation
docs.text:
If a credential is believed to provide access to an authorised service, minimal validation may be sufficient.

Examples include:

Successful authentication
Identity confirmation
Permission query
Access to an approved synthetic object

Avoid downloading data merely to prove that authentication succeeded.

docs.title: Windows Credential Sources
docs.text:
Windows systems may expose authentication material through several locations.

Common assessment areas include:

Credential Manager
PowerShell history
Environment variables
Configuration files
Unattended installation files
Service configuration
Scheduled tasks
Registry
Application configuration
Browser storage
Network shares
Backup files
Process context
LSA-managed secrets
Kerberos material
Local account material

docs.title: Windows Identity Context
docs.text:
Before investigating credentials, establish the current identity.

whoami

whoami /all

PowerShell:

whoami /all

Review current privileges:

whoami /priv

Review groups:

whoami /groups

Credential accessibility often depends heavily on the current security context.

docs.title: Windows Credential Manager
docs.text:
Windows Credential Manager can contain stored credentials used by applications and network resources.

Enumerate stored credential targets using:

cmdkey /list

The output may identify:

Target
Credential type
Username
Persistence

A listed credential should be treated as a credential-access candidate rather than automatic proof that the secret can be extracted or reused.

docs.title: PowerShell History
docs.text:
PowerShell command history can unintentionally contain:

Passwords
Tokens
Connection strings
Administrative commands
API keys
Remote hostnames
Credentials passed as arguments

The commonly used PSReadLine history path can be obtained with:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Review the configured path:

$historyPath = (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath
$historyPath

If authorised to inspect it:

Get-Content -LiteralPath (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Do not assume every password-like string remains valid.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Applications and deployment processes sometimes expose secrets through environment variables.

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Command Prompt:

set

Look for variables associated with:

API
TOKEN
SECRET
PASSWORD
PASS
KEY
DATABASE
AWS
AZURE
GITHUB
CI

Context is required because many values are identifiers rather than secrets.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Potential Windows configuration files include:

web.config
app.config
*.config
*.xml
*.json
*.ini
*.yml
*.yaml
.env
connectionStrings.config

Common locations include:

C:\inetpub\
C:\ProgramData\
C:\Program Files\
C:\Program Files (x86)\
Application-specific directories
User profile directories

Search should be targeted rather than recursively reading every file on the host.

docs.title: Unattended Installation Files
docs.text:
Windows deployment processes may leave configuration files containing historical credentials.

Potential filenames include:

Unattend.xml
Autounattend.xml
sysprep.xml
sysprep.inf

Possible locations can include:

C:\Windows\Panther\
C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend\
C:\Windows\System32\Sysprep\

The presence of a file does not mean it contains credentials.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Windows services can reveal useful identity information.

Enumerate:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, State, PathName

Service identities may include:

LocalSystem
LocalService
NetworkService
Domain service accounts
Managed service accounts
Custom local accounts

A service running as a privileged identity does not mean its password is retrievable.

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks can reveal:

Execution identity
Scripts
Arguments
Executable paths
Configuration references
Network paths

Enumerate:

schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

Focus on tasks relevant to the current attack path.

docs.title: Registry
docs.text:
The Windows Registry may contain application or deployment configuration.

Searches should be targeted to known applications or specific candidate locations.

Examples of useful contextual information include:

Service configuration
Application configuration
AutoLogon configuration
Software settings
Installed products

Registry access should not be treated as unrestricted credential discovery.

docs.title: AutoLogon
docs.text:
Windows can be configured for automatic logon.

Relevant configuration may exist under:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon

Inspect selected values:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon' |
    Select-Object AutoAdminLogon, DefaultUserName, DefaultDomainName

If sensitive values are exposed to the current user, document the access condition and impact.

Do not assume AutoLogon is enabled solely because a username value exists.

docs.title: Network Shares
docs.text:
Configuration and deployment shares can contain sensitive information.

Examples include:

Scripts
Configuration files
Backups
Deployment packages
Documentation
Legacy installers

Access should be limited to shares within scope and to material relevant to the assessment.

docs.title: Windows Credential Stores and Memory
docs.text:
Some Windows authentication material is protected by privileged operating-system components.

Examples can include:

LSASS-managed authentication material
Kerberos tickets
LSA secrets
Local account hashes
DPAPI-protected secrets

Accessing these areas can require elevated privileges and may trigger defensive controls.

Use such testing only when explicitly required by the engagement objective.

docs.title: LSASS
docs.text:
The Local Security Authority Subsystem Service is central to Windows authentication.

Defensive technologies may monitor or protect access using controls such as:

EDR
Microsoft Defender
Credential Guard
LSA protection
Attack Surface Reduction
Process access monitoring

From a red team perspective, the important questions are:

Is credential material adequately protected?
Can an inappropriate process access sensitive authentication state?
Was the attempt prevented?
Was it detected?

docs.title: Credential Guard
docs.text:
Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to help isolate certain authentication secrets.

Check relevant security configuration through approved system-management interfaces and defensive tooling.

Do not report the absence of Credential Guard as a vulnerability by itself.

Evaluate it as part of the overall credential protection model.

docs.title: LSA Protection
docs.text:
LSA protection can provide additional protection for LSASS.

It should be considered together with:

Credential Guard
EDR
Application control
Administrative privilege management
Attack Surface Reduction
Patch management

docs.title: Kerberos Credentials
docs.text:
In Active Directory environments, authentication material may include:

Ticket Granting Tickets
Service Tickets
Session keys
Long-term account keys

Kerberos material can have substantial security impact.

Use the dedicated Active Directory notes for detailed Kerberos assessment.

Kerberos

Kerberos Tickets

docs.title: NTLM
docs.text:
NTLM-related authentication material may include password-derived hashes or challenge-response material.

The impact depends on:

Protocol
Credential type
Target
Signing requirements
Authentication policy
Account privilege
Network controls

Use:

NTLM

docs.title: Linux Credential Sources
docs.text:
Linux systems may expose credentials through:

Shell history
Environment variables
Configuration files
SSH keys
Service configuration
Application configuration
Cron jobs
systemd units
Backup files
Git repositories
Cloud configuration
Container configuration
Mounted filesystems
Process environments

docs.title: Linux Identity Context
docs.text:
Start with:

whoami

id

Review groups:

groups

Determine the home directory:

echo "$HOME"

Understand the current user's permissions before inspecting credential sources.

docs.title: Shell History
docs.text:
Shell history may contain security-sensitive commands.

Potential files include:

~/.bash_history
~/.zsh_history
~/.python_history

Review your authorised user's Bash history:

cat ~/.bash_history

History may reveal:

Passwords passed on command lines
SSH destinations
Database commands
API tokens
Administrative commands
Internal hostnames

Historical entries should be validated carefully because they may be obsolete.

docs.title: Linux Environment Variables
docs.text:
Inspect:

env

or:

printenv

Potentially sensitive variable names can include:

PASSWORD
TOKEN
SECRET
KEY
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
DATABASE_URL
GITHUB_TOKEN

Do not assume a variable is sensitive based solely on its name.

docs.title: Linux Configuration Files
docs.text:
Common locations include:

/etc/
/opt/
/srv/
/var/www/
/home/
/usr/local/

Application configuration may use:

.env
config.php
settings.py
application.yml
application.yaml
config.json
database.yml
*.ini
*.conf

Search should remain targeted.

docs.title: SSH Keys
docs.text:
SSH credentials may exist under:

~/.ssh/

Common files include:

id_rsa
id_ed25519
id_ecdsa
authorized_keys
known_hosts
config

List:

ls -la ~/.ssh/

Private keys are sensitive authentication material.

Do not attempt to use a discovered key until its ownership, target, and scope are understood.

docs.title: SSH Configuration
docs.text:
SSH configuration can identify infrastructure relationships.

Review:

cat ~/.ssh/config

Potentially useful information includes:

Host aliases
Usernames
Jump hosts
Identity files
Internal systems
Ports

This information may be valuable even when no private key is exposed.

docs.title: Service Configuration
docs.text:
Linux services frequently obtain credentials from:

Environment files
Configuration files
systemd unit variables
Secret stores
Container configuration

Inspect service metadata where authorised:

systemctl list-units --type=service

For a specific service:

systemctl cat SERVICE

Look for references to configuration rather than assuming secrets are embedded directly in the unit.

docs.title: systemd Environment Files
docs.text:
A service unit may reference an environment file.

Conceptually:

Service Unit
     |
     v
EnvironmentFile
     |
     v
Application Secret

If the current user can read a privileged service's environment file, evaluate whether sensitive information is actually exposed.

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Cron jobs may reference:

Scripts
Configuration
Backup credentials
Database credentials
Remote systems

Review:

cat /etc/crontab

and relevant files under:

/etc/cron.d/

The focus should be on relevant credential paths rather than broad data collection.

docs.title: Git Repositories
docs.text:
Git repositories can expose secrets in:

Current files
Previous commits
Deleted files
Branches
Configuration
Remote URLs

Check repository status:

git status

Review remotes:

git remote -v

Secret exposure can remain in repository history even after deletion from the latest version.

docs.title: Application Credentials
docs.text:
Applications often require credentials for:

Databases
Message queues
APIs
Cloud services
SMTP
Storage
Directory services
Third-party integrations

A common trust chain is:

Application
    |
    v
Configuration
    |
    v
Credential
    |
    v
Backend Service

The security impact depends on the privileges of the backend identity.

docs.title: Database Credentials
docs.text:
Database credentials may appear in:

Connection strings
Environment variables
Application configuration
Deployment scripts
Secret stores

When discovered:

Identify Database
      |
      v
Identify Account
      |
      v
Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Minimal Authentication
      |
      v
Determine Privilege

Avoid enumerating or exporting production datasets unnecessarily.

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text:
API keys can provide access to:

Cloud services
SaaS platforms
Internal APIs
CI/CD systems
Monitoring systems
Developer platforms
Third-party services

Determine:

Provider
Owner
Scope
Permissions
Expiry
Environment

A production third-party API key may cross an engagement boundary.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
Tokens may represent:

Application sessions
OAuth access
API authentication
CI/CD authentication
Cloud sessions
Service-to-service authentication

Unlike passwords, some tokens may be:

Short lived
Scoped
Device bound
Audience restricted
Revocable

Understand the token before attempting validation.

docs.title: OAuth Tokens
docs.text:
OAuth environments may involve:

Access token
Refresh token
ID token
Client secret
Authorization code

These objects have different purposes.

An ID token, for example, should not automatically be treated as equivalent to an API access token.

docs.title: JWTs
docs.text:
JSON Web Tokens can contain useful claims such as:

Issuer
Audience
Subject
Roles
Scopes
Expiry

Decode for inspection using approved tooling without assuming that decoding implies compromise.

The security impact depends on signature validation, claims handling, token scope, and application behaviour.

Use:

JWT

docs.title: Cloud Credentials
docs.text:
Cloud authentication material can include:

Access keys
Secret keys
Session tokens
Service principals
Application secrets
Certificates
Managed identity tokens
CLI credentials
Federated tokens

Cloud credentials can have a very large blast radius.

Always identify the account or tenant before validation.

docs.title: AWS Credential Locations
docs.text:
Potential developer-side AWS configuration can exist under:

~/.aws/credentials
~/.aws/config

Inspect only where authorised:

ls -la ~/.aws/

Environment variables may also contain temporary AWS authentication material.

docs.title: Azure and Entra ID Credentials
docs.text:
Potential credential material can include:

User tokens
Service principal secrets
Application certificates
CLI authentication state
Managed identity tokens
Automation credentials

Cloud identity testing should remain restricted to the explicitly authorised tenant.

docs.title: CI/CD Credentials
docs.text:
CI/CD systems frequently require powerful credentials.

Potential examples include:

Repository tokens
Cloud deployment credentials
Container registry credentials
Package registry tokens
SSH deployment keys
Signing credentials
API tokens

These credentials can bridge development and production environments.

docs.title: CI/CD Trust Chain
docs.text:
Developer
    |
    v
Repository
    |
    v
CI/CD
    |
    v
Deployment Credential
    |
    v
Production

A credential exposed at the CI/CD layer can therefore have significantly greater impact than a normal developer credential.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
Containers may expose secrets through:

Environment variables
Mounted files
Configuration
Orchestration secrets
Image layers
Build arguments
Application files

Inspect only resources accessible from the authorised container context.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Useful contextual information includes:

docker ps

where the current user is authorised to access Docker.

Container inspection may reveal environment configuration:

docker inspect CONTAINER

Docker access itself can be highly privileged on many systems, so use the dedicated Linux privilege escalation notes when assessing that condition.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Kubernetes environments can involve:

Service account tokens
Kubeconfig
Secrets
Cloud identities
Registry credentials
Certificates

Credential access in Kubernetes should be assessed within the authorised cluster and namespace scope.

Do not assume cluster-wide access is authorised simply because a token technically permits it.

docs.title: Browser Credentials and Sessions
docs.text:
Browsers may store:

Saved passwords
Cookies
Session tokens
Client certificates
Autofill information
Application state

Browser credential testing is highly sensitive.

It should only be performed when directly relevant to the engagement objective and explicitly permitted.

docs.title: Password Managers
docs.text:
Enterprise password managers can significantly reduce insecure credential storage.

However, their security depends on:

Authentication
MFA
Vault policy
Session controls
Device trust
Sharing configuration
Administrative roles
Recovery process

The presence of a password manager is generally a positive control and should not itself be treated as an attack target unless included in scope.

docs.title: Password Reuse
docs.text:
Password reuse can turn one exposed credential into a broader attack path.

Credential Exposure
       |
       v
Account A
       |
       +--> Service 1
       |
       +--> Service 2
       |
       +--> Service 3

Reuse testing should be carefully scoped because the same credential may work against unrelated or third-party services.

docs.title: Service Accounts
docs.text:
Service accounts often deserve additional attention because they may have:

Long-lived credentials
Non-interactive use
Broad access
Weak rotation
Legacy configurations
Elevated privileges
Multiple dependent systems

Prefer managed identities or managed service-account technologies where available.

docs.title: gMSA
docs.text:
Group Managed Service Accounts can reduce risks associated with manually managed service-account passwords in Active Directory.

Benefits include:

Automatic password management
Long random passwords
Reduced manual handling
Controlled password retrieval

Use the dedicated notes:

gMSA

docs.title: LAPS
docs.text:
Windows LAPS helps manage unique local administrator passwords.

A strong LAPS deployment reduces the blast radius of local administrator credential reuse.

Use:

LAPS

docs.title: Credential Reuse and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Credential access frequently connects directly to lateral movement.

Credential
    |
    v
Identify Trust
    |
    v
Scope Check
    |
    v
Remote Authentication
    |
    v
Lateral Movement

Use:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Credential Access and Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Credentials can also provide privilege escalation.

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Exposed Credential
       |
       v
Privileged Local Account
       |
       v
Elevated Access

Use:

  • Windows PrivEsc Explorer
  • Linux PrivEsc Explorer

docs.title: Credential Access and Active Directory
docs.text:
Active Directory introduces additional credential and authentication concepts:

NTLM
Kerberos
Service accounts
Machine accounts
Delegation
gMSA
LAPS
Certificates
Directory ACLs
Trust relationships

Use:

Active Directory

docs.title: Credential Access and AD CS
docs.text:
Certificates and private keys may themselves function as authentication material.

In Active Directory Certificate Services environments:

Certificate
     +
Private Key
     |
     v
Authentication

Use:

Active Directory Certificate Services

docs.title: Credential Access and C2
docs.text:
C2 agents can sometimes operate in security contexts where credential material becomes accessible.

The relevant question is not:

Can the framework dump everything?

Instead:

What credential material should this security context be able to access?

Can inappropriate credential access occur?

Was it prevented?

Was it detected?

Use:

Command and Control

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Credential access can produce telemetry across:

Endpoint
   |
   v
Identity
   |
   v
Application
   |
   v
Network
   |
   v
Cloud
   |
   v
SIEM

docs.title: Windows Detection
docs.text:
Potential signals include:

Sensitive process access
Registry access
Credential-store access
PowerShell activity
File access
Authentication events
Security-control alerts
Unusual process relationships
Access to protected authentication components

The available telemetry depends on the endpoint security configuration.

docs.title: Linux Detection
docs.text:
Potential signals include:

Sensitive file access
Unexpected shell commands
Audit events
Authentication logs
sudo activity
SSH authentication
Process execution
Access to application secrets

Linux audit frameworks can provide additional visibility where configured.

docs.title: Cloud Detection
docs.text:
Cloud platforms can provide telemetry such as:

Authentication
Token issuance
API activity
Secret access
Role assumption
Service principal activity
New device
New location
Permission changes
Key creation
Credential use

Cloud audit logging should be centralised and monitored.

docs.title: Credential Honeytokens
docs.text:
Defenders may deploy synthetic credentials or honeytokens that should never be used legitimately.

Any attempted use can provide a high-value alert.

Conceptually:

Synthetic Secret
      |
      v
Unexpected Use
      |
      v
High-Confidence Alert

Honeytokens should be carefully managed so they do not create unintended access.

docs.title: Detection Validation
docs.text:
For each controlled credential-access action, record:

Activity Logged Alerted Prevented Investigated Configuration secret read Yes No No No Sensitive credential-store access Yes Yes Yes Yes Test credential authentication Yes Yes No Yes

This provides useful defensive measurement.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Credential-access evidence should minimise exposure of the secret itself.

Prefer:

Credential type
Identity
Source location
Access permissions
Redacted value
Successful validation result
Privilege demonstrated
Relevant telemetry

Instead of:

Full plaintext password copied into every screenshot and report section

docs.title: Redaction
docs.text:
Example:

Username:
CORP\svc-app

Password:
Sup**************

Source:
Application configuration

Validation:
Successful authentication to approved test service

Where possible, retain the full secret only in the controlled evidence location if it is genuinely required.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots can accidentally capture:

Passwords
Tokens
Customer information
Browser sessions
Internal hostnames
Personal information
Unrelated credentials

Review and redact screenshots before including them in reports.

docs.title: Reporting Credential Exposure
docs.text:
A credential finding should explain the root cause.

Weak:

Password found.

Better:

A domain service-account credential was stored in a configuration
file readable by standard users.

The credential was minimally validated against the authorised
service and provided access as the service identity.

docs.title: Finding Structure
docs.text:
A credential-access finding can use:

Title
Severity
Affected System
Affected Identity
Credential Type
Source
Required Access
Description
Validation
Impact
Attack Path
Detection
Remediation
Evidence
References

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Credential exposure severity depends on:

Credential privilege
Credential scope
Required access
Ease of discovery
Credential lifetime
MFA
Network restrictions
Affected systems
Data access
Attack chaining
Detection

A plaintext password is not automatically critical.

A low-privilege test credential limited to one isolated service may have substantially less impact than a broadly privileged service credential.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
Potential authentication material is identified.

Examples:

Credential Manager entry
Private-key file
Password-like configuration value
Token-like environment variable

Validity has not been established.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
Context strongly indicates usable authentication material.

Examples:

Credential format valid
Associated account identified
Target service identified
Credential appears current

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text: Minimal authorised testing demonstrates successful authentication or equivalent security impact.

docs.title: Remediation Model
docs.text:
Credential Exposure
       |
       v
Remove Exposure
       |
       v
Rotate / Revoke Secret
       |
       v
Identify Where Else It Was Used
       |
       v
Reduce Privilege
       |
       v
Improve Secret Storage
       |
       v
Improve Authentication
       |
       v
Improve Monitoring
       |
       v
Validate Again

docs.title: Secret Rotation
docs.text:
When a credential is exposed:

Identify Credential
      |
      v
Identify Dependencies
      |
      v
Create Replacement
      |
      v
Update Applications
      |
      v
Revoke Old Credential
      |
      v
Verify

Blindly rotating a service credential without understanding dependencies can cause outages.

docs.title: Secret Management
docs.text:
Prefer managed secret-storage solutions over plaintext configuration where appropriate.

Potential approaches include:

Cloud secret managers
Enterprise vaults
Managed identities
gMSA
Short-lived tokens
Workload identities
Protected configuration
CI/CD secret stores

The correct approach depends on the platform and application architecture.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Credentials should have only the permissions required.

Application
    |
    v
Service Identity
    |
    +--> Required Database
    |
    X--> Domain Administration
    |
    X--> Unrelated Servers

Excessive privilege increases the blast radius of credential exposure.

docs.title: Short-Lived Credentials
docs.text:
Where possible, prefer:

Short-lived tokens
Temporary cloud sessions
Automatic certificate rotation
Managed service identities
Dynamic secrets

over:

Static passwords
Permanent API keys
Long-lived shared secrets

Authorised testing only

Credential access testing can expose passwords, hashes, authentication tokens, private keys, certificates, cloud credentials, application secrets, and other highly sensitive material. Only access and validate credentials when explicitly permitted by the Rules of Engagement. Confirm the identity, target, tenant, account, and scope before using discovered authentication material. Minimise collection, redact evidence where possible, protect retained secrets, and never use credentials against unrelated or third-party systems.

docs.title: Defence Evasion
docs.text:
Defence evasion describes techniques used to avoid, disable, bypass, or otherwise interfere with security controls.

During an authorised red team assessment, the objective should be to determine whether defensive controls:

Prevent
Detect
Alert
Contain
Record
Respond

to relevant attacker behaviour.

A useful assessment model is:

Security Control
      |
      v
Safe Validation
      |
      +--> Prevented
      |
      +--> Detected
      |
      +--> Allowed + Logged
      |
      +--> Allowed + Not Detected

The most important result is not whether a particular tool "bypasses Defender."

The important questions are:

Which control was expected to stop the behaviour?
Was the control enabled?
Was the behaviour prevented?
Was telemetry generated?
Was an alert generated?
Did the SOC investigate?
What security boundary failed?

Defence evasion testing can affect endpoint protection, logging, application control, and other critical security controls.

Only perform testing explicitly permitted by the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Defence Evasion Objectives
docs.text:
Common assessment objectives include:

Validate antivirus protection
Validate EDR prevention
Validate EDR detection
Validate Microsoft Defender
Validate AMSI integration
Validate PowerShell restrictions
Validate Constrained Language Mode
Validate application control
Validate AppLocker
Validate WDAC
Validate Attack Surface Reduction
Validate script controls
Validate LOLBin restrictions
Validate security logging
Validate tamper protection
Validate network protection
Validate cloud-delivered protection
Validate SOC visibility

docs.title: Defence Evasion Testing Model
docs.text:
Identify Control
      |
      v
Determine Expected Behaviour
      |
      v
Select Safe Test
      |
      v
Execute
      |
      +------------------+
      |                  |
      v                  v
  Prevented            Allowed
      |                  |
      v                  v
 Was Alerted?        Was Logged?
      |                  |
      v                  v
Record Result       Was Alerted?
                         |
                         v
                    Record Result

docs.title: Test Controls Individually
docs.text:
Avoid immediately combining multiple techniques.

For example:

PowerShell
   +
Obfuscation
   +
AMSI modification
   +
Application-control bypass
   +
Security-product tampering

may produce an interesting result but provides poor diagnostic information.

Prefer:

Test 1 -> Antivirus

Test 2 -> AMSI

Test 3 -> PowerShell Language Mode

Test 4 -> AppLocker / WDAC

Test 5 -> ASR

Test 6 -> LOLBin policy

Test 7 -> Logging

Test 8 -> EDR visibility

This makes the root cause much easier to identify.

docs.title: Defence Evasion Control Stack
docs.text:
A Windows endpoint may contain several independent security layers.

                     User Activity
                          |
                          v
                    PowerShell
                          |
                +---------+---------+
                |                   |
                v                   v
               AMSI            Language Mode
                |                   |
                +---------+---------+
                          |
                          v
                 Application Control
                          |
                  +-------+-------+
                  |               |
                  v               v
              AppLocker          WDAC
                  |
                  v
                ASR
                  |
                  v
        Microsoft Defender / EDR
                  |
                  v
               Logging
                  |
                  v
                 SIEM
                  |
                  v
                  SOC

One control allowing an action does not mean all other controls failed.

Hostname

Privilege

Relevant EDR product

Windows context:

whoami /all

$PSVersionTable

docs.title: Microsoft Defender
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender Antivirus provides:

Real-time protection
Signature-based detection
Behaviour monitoring
Cloud-delivered protection
AMSI integration
Network protection
Attack Surface Reduction
Tamper protection
EDR integration where licensed/configured

docs.title: Defender Status
docs.text:
Query:

Get-MpComputerStatus

Useful fields:

Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,
                  RealTimeProtectionEnabled,
                  BehaviorMonitorEnabled,
                  IoavProtectionEnabled,
                  NISEnabled,
                  AntivirusSignatureVersion,
                  AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated

The output should be recorded before testing.

docs.title: Defender Version
docs.text:
Useful version information:

Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object AMEngineVersion,
                  AMProductVersion,
                  AntivirusSignatureVersion,
                  AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated

Version information can help reproduce results and determine whether signatures were current.

docs.title: Defender Preferences
docs.text:
Where permissions permit:

Get-MpPreference

Relevant configuration may include:

Exclusions
Cloud protection
Sample submission
Attack Surface Reduction
Network protection
Controlled folder access
PUA protection

docs.title: EICAR Antivirus Test
docs.text:
The EICAR Anti-Malware Test File is a standard harmless test file designed to verify antivirus detection.

It is not malware.

The canonical EICAR test string is:

X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*

The complete test file should contain only that string.

docs.title: EICAR Test Purpose
docs.text:
EICAR can answer:

Is antivirus active?
Does real-time protection inspect the file?
Is the file quarantined?
Is an alert generated?
Does the EDR record the event?
Does the SOC receive the alert?

docs.title: Create EICAR Test File with PowerShell
docs.text:
Use an authorised temporary directory.

$eicar = 'X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*'
Set-Content -Path "$env:TEMP\eicar.com.txt" -Value $eicar -NoNewline

If real-time protection is functioning, creation or subsequent access may be blocked or quarantined.

docs.title: Create EICAR with cmd.exe
docs.text:
The special characters in the EICAR string make shell quoting awkward.

PowerShell is generally easier for creating the test file accurately.

Verify only if the file remains present:

Test-Path "$env:TEMP\eicar.com.txt"

If Defender immediately removes it, that is an expected successful prevention result.

docs.title: EICAR Expected Result
docs.text:
Typical successful control behaviour:

EICAR Created
     |
     v
Antivirus Inspects File
     |
     v
Detection
     |
     v
Block / Quarantine
     |
     v
Security Alert

docs.title: EICAR Evidence
docs.text:
Record:

Timestamp
Host
User
Defender state
Signature version
File path
Whether creation succeeded
Whether file remained present
Detection name
Defender alert
EDR alert
SOC response

docs.title: Defender Threat History
docs.text:
Where available:

Get-MpThreatDetection

Useful fields:

Get-MpThreatDetection |
    Select-Object InitialDetectionTime,
                  ThreatName,
                  Resources,
                  ActionSuccess

Depending on permissions and platform version, some information may not be available to a standard user.

docs.title: Defender Event Logs
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender Antivirus events can be reviewed under:

Applications and Services Logs
  |
  Microsoft
    |
    Windows
      |
      Windows Defender
        |
        Operational

PowerShell:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational' -MaxEvents 50

Filter around the assessment timestamp rather than exporting excessive logs.

docs.title: EICAR Is Not an EDR Test
docs.text:
EICAR primarily validates antivirus handling.

It does not demonstrate whether an EDR can detect:

Credential access
Lateral movement
Persistence
PowerShell abuse
Process injection
C2
Identity attacks
Cloud attacks

Use behaviour-specific tests for those controls.

docs.title: AMSI
docs.text:
The Antimalware Scan Interface allows applications and scripting engines to submit content to registered antimalware products for inspection.

A simplified PowerShell model is:

PowerShell Content
       |
       v
      AMSI
       |
       v
Antimalware Provider
       |
       v
Allow / Detect / Block

AMSI is an interface rather than an antivirus engine itself.

docs.title: AMSI Coverage
docs.text:
AMSI can be integrated into technologies including:

PowerShell
Windows Script Host
JavaScript
VBScript
Office VBA
Applications implementing AMSI

Actual coverage depends on platform and application configuration.

docs.title: AMSI Validation
docs.text:
AMSI should be tested independently from an actual bypass.

A safe validation can use a known security-product test string designed for AMSI testing rather than deploying malicious code.

The goal is:

Submit Known Test Content
        |
        v
Does AMSI Inspect It?
        |
        v
Does Defender Detect It?

docs.title: Microsoft AMSI Test String
docs.text:
Microsoft documents an AMSI sample test string for validating integration:

AMSI Test Sample

Because vendor test strings and behaviour can change, use the test sample documented for the security product and platform being assessed rather than relying on copied offensive payloads.

The validation result should record:

Content blocked
Content allowed
Defender event
EDR event
PowerShell event
SOC alert

docs.title: AMSI Bypass Assessment
docs.text:
AMSI bypass research evaluates whether a process can prevent or interfere with AMSI inspection.

Potential bypass categories historically include:

Runtime state manipulation
Memory modification
Reflection-based manipulation
Provider interference
Content transformation
Host-specific weaknesses
Implementation weaknesses

A production assessment normally does not require deploying a working AMSI patch to demonstrate that AMSI is an important security boundary.

Prefer:

AMSI test sample
        |
        v
Confirm Detection
        |
        v
Review Tamper / EDR Controls
        |
        v
Controlled Bypass Simulation if Explicitly Approved

Do not treat AMSI as the only defensive layer.

docs.title: AMSI Bypass Test Result Model
docs.text:
If bypass testing is explicitly authorised, record the control outcome rather than only stating "AMSI bypassed."

AMSI Initially Detects Test
          |
          v
Controlled Bypass Attempt
          |
       +--+--+
       |     |
       v     v
    Blocked  Allowed
       |       |
       v       v
 EDR Alert?  AMSI Still
             Effective?

Useful findings include:

AMSI bypass attempt prevented by EDR

AMSI modification allowed but generated high-confidence alert

AMSI inspection became ineffective without alert

AMSI bypass ineffective against current endpoint configuration

docs.title: AMSI Logging
docs.text:
Correlate AMSI-related tests with:

PowerShell logs
Defender logs
EDR telemetry
Process creation
Script content
Security alerts
SOC investigation

Do not infer AMSI failure solely because a PowerShell command executed.

docs.title: PowerShell Security Controls
docs.text:
PowerShell security should be assessed as a collection of controls:

Language Mode
AMSI
Script Block Logging
Module Logging
Transcription
Application Control
Execution Policy
Defender / EDR
ASR
Identity privilege

docs.title: PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Common results include:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

docs.title: FullLanguage
docs.text:
FullLanguage provides normal PowerShell language capabilities.

Seeing:

FullLanguage

is not automatically a vulnerability.

The security significance depends on:

User privilege
Endpoint role
Application control
EDR
AMSI
Administrative model
Security requirements

docs.title: Constrained Language Mode
docs.text:
Constrained Language Mode restricts access to various PowerShell capabilities.

Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Expected hardened endpoint result may be:

ConstrainedLanguage

depending on the organisation's design.

docs.title: CLM Purpose
docs.text:
CLM is intended to reduce access to powerful PowerShell language capabilities in constrained environments.

Examples of affected capabilities can include:

Arbitrary .NET type usage
COM access
Some reflection capabilities
Native API interaction through PowerShell
Custom type creation

Exact behaviour depends on PowerShell and platform version.

docs.title: CLM Validation
docs.text:
Test expected restrictions using harmless operations.

For example:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Then test whether creation of a harmless custom type is restricted:

Add-Type -TypeDefinition 'public class CLMTest { public static string Value() { return "test"; } }'

Under an appropriately constrained environment, this type of operation may be restricted.

Record the actual result.

docs.title: CLM Bypass Assessment
docs.text:
CLM bypass testing asks whether a user constrained in one PowerShell environment can obtain an execution environment that provides capabilities outside the intended policy.

The assessment should distinguish:

PowerShell process
        |
        v
ConstrainedLanguage

from

Different trusted execution path
        |
        v
Unexpected FullLanguage capability

The finding is not simply:

PowerShell became FullLanguage.

The finding should explain which security boundary allowed that transition.

docs.title: CLM Bypass Categories
docs.text:
Historically relevant categories include:

Alternative PowerShell hosts
Trusted binaries
Application-control policy gaps
Legacy PowerShell environments
Incorrect WDAC/AppLocker integration
Custom hosts
Misconfigured trusted paths

Do not assume a technique described in older research remains effective on a modern patched endpoint.

docs.title: Safe CLM Bypass Testing
docs.text:
A safe test methodology is:

1. Confirm ConstrainedLanguage.

2. Confirm a harmless restricted operation fails.

3. Review application-control policy.

4. Identify approved execution hosts.

5. Test whether an approved host unexpectedly provides
   FullLanguage capabilities.

6. Repeat the harmless restricted operation.

7. Record EDR and PowerShell telemetry.

8. Stop when the control boundary is demonstrated.

There is no need to deploy a payload to prove a CLM control failure.

docs.title: CLM Finding Example
docs.text:
Weak:

CLM bypass possible.

Better:

PowerShell operated in ConstrainedLanguage mode for the standard
user. However, an application permitted by the endpoint
application-control policy launched a PowerShell runspace that
operated with FullLanguage capabilities.

A harmless custom-type test that was rejected in the constrained
session succeeded through the alternate execution path.

docs.title: CLM Remediation
docs.text:
Consider:

WDAC
AppLocker
Removal of unnecessary script hosts
Removal of legacy PowerShell versions
Application allowlisting
EDR
Least privilege
PowerShell logging
Administrative tiering

docs.title: Execution Policy
docs.text:
PowerShell execution policy can be queried with:

Get-ExecutionPolicy -List

Execution Policy is primarily a safety feature and should not be treated as a strong security boundary.

Do not report:

ExecutionPolicy is Bypass

as a critical vulnerability without relevant context.

docs.title: PowerShell Script Block Logging
docs.text:
Check policy configuration where readable:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

PowerShell Operational log:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational' -MaxEvents 50

Script Block Logging can provide visibility into PowerShell activity.

docs.title: PowerShell Module Logging
docs.text:
Potential policy location:

HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging

Check:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: PowerShell Transcription
docs.text:
Potential policy location:

HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription

Check:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Transcription can capture sensitive content, so storage permissions and retention should also be reviewed.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Application control restricts which software can execute.

Common Windows technologies include:

AppLocker
Windows Defender Application Control
Software Restriction Policies
EDR application-control features

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
AppLocker supports rule collections for:

Executables
Windows Installer
Scripts
Packaged applications
DLLs

Retrieve the effective policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Summarise collections:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Select-Object CollectionType, EnforcementMode

docs.title: AppLocker Rule Collections
docs.text:
Possible results include:

Exe
Msi
Script
Appx
Dll

Each collection can have its own enforcement state.

Do not assume DLL enforcement exists because EXE enforcement is enabled.

docs.title: AppLocker Test
docs.text:
AppLocker provides Test-AppLockerPolicy.

Example:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\wscript.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

The result can indicate whether the executable is expected to be allowed by policy.

docs.title: Test a File
docs.text:
For an existing harmless file:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path 'C:\Path\To\Test.exe' -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Possible policy decisions can include:

Allowed
Denied
DeniedByDefault
AllowedByDefault

Exact output depends on policy and platform.

docs.title: AppLocker Path Rules
docs.text:
Path rules deserve careful review.

Example:

Allow:
%WINDIR%\*

The security question is not simply whether the wildcard exists.

Determine:

Can a standard user write to a location covered by the allow rule?

The risky combination is:

User-Writable Directory
        +
Allowed Path Rule
        =
Potential Application-Control Gap

docs.title: Writable Path Validation
docs.text:
Test directory permissions without placing an operational payload.

PowerShell:

Get-Acl 'C:\Path\To\Directory' |
    Format-List Owner,AccessToString

A temporary write test can establish whether the current user can write there.

Use a unique temporary filename and remove it immediately after testing.

docs.title: AppLocker Policy Model
docs.text:
Executable
    |
    v
Rule Collection Enabled?
    |
   / \
 No   Yes
 |     |
 v     v
No    Matching Rule?
Rule     |
       /   \
     No     Yes
     |       |
     v       v
 Default   Allow / Deny
 Action

docs.title: WDAC
docs.text:
Windows Defender Application Control provides stronger application-control capabilities based on Code Integrity policy.

Depending on configuration, WDAC can control:

Executables
DLLs
Drivers
Scripts
Installers
Packaged applications
Managed code

docs.title: WDAC Assessment
docs.text:
Useful questions include:

Is WDAC deployed?
Is policy enforced or audit-only?
Which signing policies are trusted?
Are user-writable paths trusted?
Are scripts covered?
Are DLLs covered?
Are managed applications covered?
Are supplemental policies present?
Is policy telemetry monitored?

docs.title: WDAC and CLM
docs.text:
PowerShell can integrate with application-control policy.

Conceptually:

Application Control
       |
       v
PowerShell Trust Decision
       |
       v
Language Restrictions

This is why CLM should not be evaluated in isolation.

docs.title: Code Integrity Logs
docs.text:
Useful Windows logs include:

Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational

Query:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational' -MaxEvents 50

These events can help explain why execution was allowed or denied.

docs.title: AppLocker Logs
docs.text:
Relevant logs can include:

Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL
Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script

Query:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL' -MaxEvents 50

and:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script' -MaxEvents 50

docs.title: LOLBins
docs.text:
Living-off-the-land binaries are legitimate operating-system or signed applications that can expose functionality useful to attackers.

Examples often assessed include:

PowerShell
cmd.exe
rundll32.exe
regsvr32.exe
mshta.exe
wscript.exe
cscript.exe
msbuild.exe
InstallUtil.exe
certutil.exe
bitsadmin.exe
curl.exe
schtasks.exe
sc.exe
wmic.exe

Availability varies by Windows version and installed components.

docs.title: LOLBin Testing
docs.text:
Do not treat:

Binary Exists

as equivalent to:

Security Control Bypass

A useful workflow is:

Binary Exists
      |
      v
Can User Execute It?
      |
      v
Can It Perform Relevant Function?
      |
      v
Was Behaviour Allowed?
      |
      v
Was Behaviour Detected?

docs.title: Check Binary Presence
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-Command rundll32.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-Command mshta.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-Command wscript.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-Command cscript.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Test AppLocker Decision for LOLBins
docs.text:
Example:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\rundll32.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

For wscript.exe:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\wscript.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

For mshta.exe:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\mshta.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

docs.title: rundll32 Validation
docs.text:
rundll32.exe is a legitimate Windows component used to invoke exported functions from DLLs.

A harmless built-in validation can open a Control Panel component.

For example:

& "$env:WINDIR\System32\rundll32.exe" "shell32.dll,Control_RunDLL" "main.cpl"

This demonstrates that rundll32.exe is executable without loading an assessment DLL.

Record:

AppLocker decision
Process execution
EDR telemetry
Command-line telemetry
User context

docs.title: Windows Script Host
docs.text:
Windows Script Host includes:

wscript.exe
cscript.exe

Application-control testing should distinguish:

Executable allowed

from

Untrusted script allowed

For example, wscript.exe may be permitted while scripts from user-writable directories are denied.

docs.title: Harmless VBS Test
docs.text:
Create:

'WScript.Echo "Assessment test"' | Set-Content "$env:TEMP\wscript-test.vbs"

Test policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:TEMP\wscript-test.vbs" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Cleanup:

Remove-Item "$env:TEMP\wscript-test.vbs" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

This provides better evidence than assuming executable policy determines script policy.

docs.title: MSHTA
docs.text:
mshta.exe hosts HTML Applications.

Check:

Get-Command mshta.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\mshta.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

For defence-evasion assessment, determine whether unnecessary script hosts are restricted and monitored.

There is no need to execute remote script content merely to establish the control state.

docs.title: MSBuild
docs.text:
MSBuild is a legitimate Microsoft build engine.

It may exist with Visual Studio, Build Tools, or .NET tooling.

Locate:

Get-Command msbuild.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If it exists, evaluate:

Who can execute it?
Does application control permit it?
Is it required on the endpoint?
Is execution monitored?

Developer systems and build servers may legitimately require MSBuild.

docs.title: InstallUtil
docs.text:
InstallUtil.exe is associated with .NET Framework installer components.

Locate possible copies:

Get-ChildItem "$env:WINDIR\Microsoft.NET\Framework*" -Filter InstallUtil.exe -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object FullName

The existence of InstallUtil is not itself a vulnerability.

Evaluate policy and business requirement.

docs.title: certutil
docs.text:
certutil.exe is a legitimate certificate-management utility.

Check:

Get-Command certutil.exe

It may be required for normal certificate administration.

Defensive monitoring should focus on unusual usage rather than simply blocking all execution without context.

docs.title: BITS
docs.text:
Background Intelligent Transfer Service supports asynchronous file transfers used by Windows and applications.

PowerShell exposes BITS functionality through commands such as:

Get-Command *BitsTransfer*

BITS usage should be monitored in context.

Do not classify all BITS traffic as malicious.

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
Modern Windows systems may provide:

curl.exe

Check:

Get-Command curl.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

A download utility existing on a system does not itself constitute defence evasion.

docs.title: LOLBin Assessment Table
docs.text:
Maintain results such as:

Binary Present Policy Safe Test Logged Alerted PowerShell Yes Allowed Completed Yes No rundll32 Yes Allowed Completed Yes Yes mshta Yes Denied Not run Yes Yes wscript Yes Allowed Script denied Yes No msbuild No N/A N/A N/A N/A

docs.title: Attack Surface Reduction
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender Attack Surface Reduction rules can restrict behaviours frequently associated with attacks.

Query configured rules:

Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids,
                  AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

The two arrays correspond by position.

docs.title: ASR Actions
docs.text:
Depending on configuration, ASR rules can operate in modes such as:

Disabled
Block
Audit
Warn

Interpret results according to the current Microsoft documentation and endpoint configuration.

docs.title: ASR Validation
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Enumerate Rules
      |
      v
Map Rule IDs to Names
      |
      v
Determine Mode
      |
      v
Select Safe Validation
      |
      v
Execute
      |
      v
Review Defender / EDR

docs.title: ASR Testing Principles
docs.text:
Do not test every ASR rule simply because it exists.

Focus on rules relevant to the endpoint role.

Examples:

Office workstation
    |
    +--> Office child-process controls
    +--> Script controls
    +--> Credential protection

Developer workstation
    |
    +--> Script controls
    +--> Executable-content controls

Server
    |
    +--> Credential controls
    +--> Remote-management behaviour

docs.title: Network Protection
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender Network Protection can help restrict access to malicious or untrusted network destinations.

Query relevant Defender configuration through:

Get-MpPreference

Network protection should be evaluated separately from host antivirus.

docs.title: Controlled Folder Access
docs.text:
Controlled Folder Access can protect designated directories against unauthorised modification by untrusted applications.

Relevant questions include:

Is it enabled?
Which folders are protected?
Which applications are allowed?
Are block events visible?
Is it appropriate for the endpoint role?

docs.title: Tamper Protection
docs.text:
Tamper Protection helps protect security settings against unauthorised modification.

During a red team assessment, do not disable security products simply because the current account technically allows it.

Instead test:

Can the current identity modify the security control?

Is the modification blocked?

Is an alert generated?

A safe validation should avoid leaving protection disabled.

docs.title: Defender Exclusions
docs.text:
Exclusions can significantly reduce antivirus visibility.

Where readable:

(Get-MpPreference).ExclusionPath

Also review:

(Get-MpPreference).ExclusionProcess

and:

(Get-MpPreference).ExclusionExtension

Do not create an exclusion merely to demonstrate that administrators can configure Defender.

docs.title: Security Product Tampering
docs.text:
Potential tampering categories include:

Stopping services
Changing configuration
Adding exclusions
Disabling protection
Modifying security components
Interfering with telemetry
Changing logging

These are high-impact actions.

Prefer testing whether the action is prevented or authorised without actually disabling protection.

docs.title: Safe Tamper Testing Model
docs.text:
Security Setting
      |
      v
Current User Has Modification Permission?
      |
      +--> No
      |
      +--> Yes
              |
              v
        Tamper Protection?
              |
              v
        Modification Blocked?

Where possible, use policy inspection rather than changing the setting.

docs.title: Security Logging
docs.text:
Defence evasion is not only about prevention.

An action may be allowed but fully visible.

Technique
   |
   +--> Prevented
   |
   +--> Detected
   |
   +--> Logged
   |
   +--> Invisible

The last case is generally the most concerning.

docs.title: Windows Process Creation
docs.text:
Security Event ID:

4688

can record process creation when the relevant audit policy is enabled.

Useful fields can include:

New process
Parent process
User
Command line
Timestamp

docs.title: Sysmon
docs.text:
Where deployed, Sysmon can provide telemetry such as:

Process creation
Network connections
File creation
Registry changes
Process access
Image loading
DNS queries

Configuration quality is critical.

Installing Sysmon is not equivalent to monitoring all attacker behaviour.

docs.title: Event Log Validation
docs.text:
Review relevant logs around the assessment timestamp.

Example:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName='Security'
    StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)
} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Access to the Security log may require elevated privileges.

docs.title: EDR Validation
docs.text:
EDR testing should evaluate the complete detection lifecycle.

Activity
   |
   v
Endpoint Sensor
   |
   v
Telemetry
   |
   v
Detection Logic
   |
   v
Alert
   |
   v
SOC
   |
   v
Investigation
   |
   v
Response

An endpoint alert that nobody investigates is not the same as an effective detection-and-response process.

docs.title: EDR Test Categories
docs.text:
Useful safe categories include:

EICAR antivirus test
Known vendor simulation tests
PowerShell test activity
Scheduled-task test
Service-creation test
Harmless remote administration
Known test process trees
Controlled authentication activity
Atomic simulation tests approved by the organisation

docs.title: Atomic Red Team
docs.text:
Atomic Red Team provides small tests mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.

It can be useful for controlled detection validation.

Before running an atomic test:

Read the test
Understand prerequisites
Understand commands
Understand cleanup
Confirm scope
Confirm expected impact
Run one test
Review telemetry
Run cleanup
Verify cleanup

Never bulk-run a large set of tests against production endpoints without review.

docs.title: Obfuscation
docs.text:
Attackers may transform commands or scripts to make static analysis more difficult.

Examples conceptually include:

Encoding
String construction
Variable substitution
Whitespace changes
Command aliases
Dynamic resolution
Nested interpreters

For defence validation, start with transparent test content.

Only introduce controlled transformations when the objective specifically requires testing detection resilience.

docs.title: Obfuscation Testing Model
docs.text:
Plain Test
    |
    v
Detected?
    |
   Yes
    |
    v
Controlled Transformation
    |
    v
Still Detected?

This isolates whether detection relies only on a simple static signature.

docs.title: Behaviour vs Signature
docs.text:
A resilient defensive strategy should not depend entirely on one exact string.

Signature Detection
       +
Behaviour Detection
       +
Identity Analytics
       +
Network Telemetry
       +
Application Control
       =
Layered Defence

docs.title: File Reputation
docs.text:
Some security products use:

File hash
Digital signature
Prevalence
Cloud reputation
Download origin
Mark of the Web
Behaviour

A newly compiled harmless executable may therefore be treated differently from a common signed application.

docs.title: Mark of the Web
docs.text:
Files downloaded from external locations may receive zone information.

This can influence:

SmartScreen
Office behaviour
Script execution
Security warnings
Application behaviour

Assessment results should record how the file reached the endpoint because delivery context can change security behaviour.

docs.title: SmartScreen
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender SmartScreen provides reputation-based protection for certain downloaded content and web activity.

Do not confuse:

SmartScreen
Defender Antivirus
EDR
AMSI
ASR
Application Control

They are separate defensive components.

docs.title: Application Allowlisting Gap
docs.text:
A useful application-control assessment model is:

Allowed Binary
      |
      v
Expected Business Use?
    /       \
  Yes        No
  |           |
  v           v
Required    Consider Restriction
  |
  v
Can It Execute
Untrusted Content?
  |
  v
Is Behaviour Controlled?

The presence of a dual-use binary alone is insufficient evidence.

docs.title: Trusted Path Assessment
docs.text:
A potentially dangerous configuration is:

Trusted Path
    +
Standard User Write Access

Assessment:

Trusted Directory
      |
      v
Check ACL
      |
      v
User Writable?
   /       \
 No         Yes
 |           |
 v           v
Good      Safe Write Test
              |
              v
       Application Control
       Allows Content?

docs.title: Safe Writable Directory Test
docs.text:
PowerShell:

$folder = 'C:\Path\To\Candidate'
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID.tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Host '[+] Write succeeded'
}
catch {
    Write-Host '[-] Write failed'
}
finally {
    Remove-Item $file -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}

This demonstrates write access without leaving an executable.

docs.title: DLL Application Control
docs.text:
DLL rule enforcement should be reviewed separately from executable enforcement.

AppLocker may have:

EXE: Enabled

DLL: NotConfigured

This is a policy observation.

Whether it represents a material security weakness depends on the intended application-control design and other controls such as WDAC and EDR.

docs.title: Script Application Control
docs.text:
Script controls should be tested independently.

Potential script types include:

PowerShell
VBScript
JScript
Batch
Command files

A policy that blocks executables from a directory may not necessarily provide identical coverage for scripts.

docs.title: Office Security Controls
docs.text:
On endpoints with Microsoft Office, defence-evasion testing may include validation of:

Macro policy
Mark of the Web
Protected View
ASR
Child-process restrictions
Application control
AMSI integration
EDR

Use harmless documents and vendor-supported simulations.

docs.title: Credential Protection
docs.text:
Defence evasion intersects with credential access when an attacker attempts to interfere with controls protecting authentication material.

Relevant defensive technologies include:

Credential Guard
LSA protection
Defender
EDR
ASR
Application control
Administrative tiering

docs.title: Credential Guard
docs.text:
Credential Guard should be evaluated as part of a layered credential-protection strategy.

Do not report its absence as a vulnerability by itself.

The important question is whether sensitive credentials are sufficiently protected against the assessed threat model.

docs.title: LSA Protection
docs.text:
LSA protection can make unauthorised access to LSASS more difficult.

Assessment should focus on:

Is protection configured?
Can inappropriate processes access LSASS?
Was access blocked?
Was access detected?

docs.title: Firewall Evasion vs Network Validation
docs.text:
Avoid treating every permitted outbound connection as "firewall bypass."

A more accurate model is:

Destination
    |
    v
Protocol
    |
    v
Firewall Policy
    |
    +--> Explicitly Allowed
    |
    +--> Explicitly Blocked
    |
    +--> Unrestricted

If outbound HTTP is intentionally allowed, successfully reaching an HTTP server does not constitute bypassing the firewall.

docs.title: Connectivity Test
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Test-NetConnection HOST -Port 443

This confirms TCP reachability only.

docs.title: HTTP Test
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://example.com/' -UseBasicParsing

Use an assessment-controlled or otherwise approved destination when validating egress controls.

docs.title: DNS Controls
docs.text:
DNS can provide useful defensive telemetry.

Review:

DNS query logs
Resolver policy
Filtering

Newly registered domains
Dynamic DNS
Internal DNS activity

docs.title: Proxy Controls
docs.text:
Corporate proxies may provide:

URL filtering
Authentication
TLS inspection
Category filtering
Logging
Malware scanning
DLP

Defence-evasion testing should determine whether alternative network paths undermine the intended proxy policy.

docs.title: Security Control Bypass Terminology
docs.text:
Use precise language.

Instead of:

Defender bypassed

consider:

The test file was not detected by Microsoft Defender Antivirus.

Instead of:

AppLocker bypassed

consider:

A standard user could execute the test application from a
user-writable path covered by an AppLocker allow rule.

Instead of:

CLM bypassed

consider:

An AppLocker-permitted execution path provided FullLanguage
PowerShell capabilities to a user whose interactive PowerShell
session was restricted to ConstrainedLanguage.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
A potential defensive gap is identified.

Examples:

LOLBin allowed
DLL collection not configured
FullLanguage available
Writable allowed directory
Security logging appears incomplete

docs.title: Likely
docs.text: The configuration appears capable of enabling behaviour outside the intended defensive model.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text: A controlled, non-destructive test demonstrates that the intended security control can be circumvented or does not provide the expected protection.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

User privilege
Control bypassed
Endpoint role
Attack path
Security layers remaining
Required prerequisites
Detection
Repeatability
Business impact
Ability to chain techniques

For example:

FullLanguage PowerShell

on a developer workstation may be expected.

The same capability on a tightly controlled kiosk or privileged access workstation may be much more significant.

Authorised testing only

Defence-evasion testing interacts directly with endpoint security controls. Start with configuration review, harmless built-in actions, EICAR, vendor-provided test artifacts, and controlled simulations. Do not disable antivirus, EDR, logging, application control, AMSI, or other security controls unless the Rules of Engagement explicitly require and permit that action. CLM and AMSI bypass testing should demonstrate the control boundary with the minimum necessary action rather than deploying an operational payload. Record the original security state, correlate every test with defensive telemetry, stop when the objective is proven, and verify that all security controls remain enabled after testing.

docs.title: Detection Validation
docs.text:
Detection validation determines whether security controls can observe, identify, alert on, and support investigation of attacker behaviour.

A successful red team assessment should not only answer:

Could the attacker perform the action?

It should also answer:

Was the action prevented?

Was telemetry generated?

Was the activity detected?

Was an alert created?

Did the SIEM receive it?

Did the SOC investigate it?

Could the organisation respond?

A useful model is:

Red Team Activity
       |
       v
Endpoint / Network / Identity
       |
       v
Telemetry
       |
       v
Detection Logic
       |
       v
Alert
       |
       v
SIEM / Security Platform
       |
       v
SOC Analyst
       |
       v
Investigation
       |
       v
Response

A failure anywhere in this chain can create a detection gap.

Authorised testing only

Detection validation should be performed only against systems and identities included in the assessment scope. Use harmless vendor test artifacts and controlled simulations before progressing to more intrusive techniques. Coordinate disruptive tests through the Rules of Engagement and stop once the required security objective has been demonstrated.

docs.text:

Validate antivirus

Validate ASR
Validate Sysmon
Validate Windows auditing
Validate identity detections
Validate network detections
Validate SIEM ingestion
Validate correlation rules
Validate SOC triage
Validate incident investigation
Validate containment procedures
Validate ATT&CK coverage
Identify detection gaps
Measure time to detect
Measure time to respond
Retest detection improvements

docs.title: Detection Is a Pipeline
docs.text:
A detection should not be considered only as an alert rule.

Activity
   |
   v
Sensor
   |
   v
Telemetry
   |
   v
Collection
   |
   v
Normalisation
   |
   v
Detection Rule
   |
   v
Alert
   |
   v
Triage
   |
   v
Investigation
   |
   v
Response

For example, an excellent SIEM rule cannot detect an event that never reaches the SIEM.

docs.title: Prevention, Detection, and Response
docs.text:
These should be measured separately.

                    Technique
                       |
          +------------+------------+
          |            |            |
          v            v            v
      Prevention    Detection     Response
          |            |            |
          v            v            v
        Block        Alert       Contain

Possible outcomes include:

Prevention Detection Interpretation Blocked Alerted Strong control Blocked No alert Prevention works, visibility may be weak Allowed Alerted Detective control worked Allowed Logged only Telemetry exists but detection may be missing Allowed No telemetry Major visibility gap

docs.text:
Process creation is one of the most useful telemetry sources.

When configured appropriately, Event ID:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{

    Id=4688
    StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)
} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Access may require appropriate permissions.

       |

Context matters.
