docs.title: EICAR Validation
docs.text:
EICAR is a standard harmless antivirus test artifact.

Canonical test string:

X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*

Create an authorised temporary test file:

$eicar = 'X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*'
Set-Content -Path "$env:TEMP\eicar.com.txt" -Value $eicar -NoNewline

Expected flow:

Create File
    |
    v
Antivirus Inspection
    |
    v
Detection
    |
    v
Block / Quarantine
    |
    v
Endpoint Alert
    |
    v
Central Security Platform

docs.title: EICAR Validation Questions
docs.text:
Record:

Was creation prevented?

Was the file immediately removed?

Was it quarantined?

Was a local notification generated?

Was a Defender event generated?

Did the EDR receive the event?

Was a central alert generated?

Did the SOC see the alert?

How long did this take?

docs.title: EICAR Is Only a Baseline
docs.text:
EICAR demonstrates basic antivirus handling.

It does not validate detection of:

Credential access
Persistence
Lateral movement
PowerShell abuse
Identity attacks
C2
Privilege escalation
Cloud attacks

Use behaviour-specific simulations for these.

docs.title: AMSI
docs.text:
The Antimalware Scan Interface allows compatible applications to submit content to antimalware providers.

Simplified model:

Script Content
      |
      v
     AMSI
      |
      v
Antimalware Provider
      |
      v
Allow / Detect / Block

AMSI should be evaluated together with:

PowerShell
Defender
EDR
Application Control
Logging

docs.title: AMSI Detection Validation
docs.text:
The objective is not automatically to bypass AMSI.

First establish:

Does the application use AMSI?

Does the security provider inspect the content?

Is suspicious content detected?

Does the endpoint generate telemetry?

Does the central platform receive the result?

Use vendor-provided test content where available.

docs.title: AMSI Bypass Detection
docs.text:
If bypass simulation is explicitly part of the assessment, defenders should look for behaviour associated with interference with security interfaces rather than relying solely on one known bypass implementation.

Potential detection dimensions include:

Suspicious memory modification
Unexpected reflection behaviour
Security-interface tampering
Unusual PowerShell host behaviour
Process ancestry
Script telemetry
EDR behavioural detections

A red team assessment should stop once the security boundary and detection outcome are sufficiently demonstrated.

docs.title: PowerShell Telemetry
docs.text:
PowerShell can provide several useful logging sources:

Script Block Logging
Module Logging
Transcription
PowerShell Operational events
Process creation
AMSI
EDR telemetry

docs.title: PowerShell Operational Log
docs.text:
Query:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational' -MaxEvents 100

docs.title: Script Block Logging
docs.text:
Potential policy location:

HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging

Query:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Event ID 4104
docs.text:
PowerShell Script Block Logging commonly uses:

4104

Query:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName='Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational'
    Id=4104
    StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)
} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: PowerShell Module Logging
docs.text:
Potential policy location:

HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging

Query:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: PowerShell Transcription
docs.text:
Potential policy location:

HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription

Query:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Transcripts may contain sensitive information.

Protect their storage appropriately.

docs.title: PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Detection validation should distinguish:

Control prevented activity

from

Control allowed activity but EDR detected it

For example, Constrained Language Mode is primarily a restriction mechanism, while PowerShell logging provides visibility.

docs.title: AppLocker Telemetry
docs.text:
AppLocker logs can provide useful application-control events.

Relevant logs include:

Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL
Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script

docs.title: AppLocker EXE and DLL
docs.text:
Query:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL' -MaxEvents 100

docs.title: AppLocker MSI and Script
docs.text:
Query:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script' -MaxEvents 100

docs.title: AppLocker Effective Policy
docs.text:
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Summarise collections:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Select-Object CollectionType,EnforcementMode

docs.title: AppLocker Detection Test
docs.text:
For a harmless existing binary:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\rundll32.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

The result helps establish expected policy behaviour before execution.

docs.title: Application Control Validation
docs.text:
Policy Says Deny
      |
      v
Safe Execution Attempt
      |
      +--> Blocked
      |       |
      |       v
      |    Event Generated?
      |
      +--> Allowed
              |
              v
          Policy Gap?

docs.title: WDAC and Code Integrity
docs.text:
Windows Defender Application Control is closely associated with Code Integrity telemetry.

Useful log:

Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational

Query:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational' -MaxEvents 100

docs.title: WDAC Validation Questions
docs.text:
Determine:

Is policy present?

Is it enforced?

Is it audit-only?

Was execution allowed?

Was execution blocked?

Was a Code Integrity event generated?

Did the EDR receive the event?

Did the SIEM receive the event?

docs.title: Attack Surface Reduction
docs.text:
Attack Surface Reduction rules can operate as both prevention and detection controls.

Query:

Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids,
                  AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

docs.title: ASR Validation Model
docs.text:
ASR Rule
   |
   v
Configured?
   |
   v
Mode?
   |
   +--> Block
   |
   +--> Audit
   |
   +--> Warn
   |
   +--> Disabled

Then perform an approved safe test appropriate to that specific rule.

docs.title: ASR Detection Questions
docs.text:
Record:

Rule ID
Rule name
Configured action
Test
Expected result
Observed result
Defender event
EDR event
SIEM alert
SOC response

docs.title: Sysmon
docs.text:
Sysmon provides detailed Windows telemetry when installed and configured.

Check whether the service exists:

Get-Service Sysmon* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Common log:

Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational

docs.title: Query Sysmon
docs.text: Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' -MaxEvents 100

docs.title: Common Sysmon Event IDs
docs.text:
Exact visibility depends heavily on the deployed Sysmon configuration.

Event ID Common Meaning 1 Process creation 2 File creation time changed 3 Network connection 5 Process terminated 6 Driver loaded 7 Image loaded 8 CreateRemoteThread 10 Process access 11 File created 12 Registry object create/delete 13 Registry value set 14 Registry object renamed 15 FileCreateStreamHash 17 Pipe created 18 Pipe connected 22 DNS query 23 File delete 25 Process tampering 26 File delete detected

docs.title: Sysmon Event ID 1
docs.text:
Process creation:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'
    Id=1
    StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)
} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Sysmon Event ID 3
docs.text:
Network connections:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'
    Id=3
    StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)
} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Network connection logging depends on the Sysmon configuration.

docs.title: Sysmon Event ID 22
docs.text:
DNS queries:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'
    Id=22
    StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)
} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Sysmon Configuration Matters
docs.text:
Do not write:

Sysmon installed, therefore detection coverage is good.

A weak configuration may exclude the exact behaviour defenders need.

Validate:

Which event types are enabled?

Which processes are excluded?

Which paths are excluded?

Which network connections are captured?

Are events forwarded?

Are they used by detection rules?

docs.title: Windows Event Forwarding
docs.text:
Windows Event Forwarding can centralise Windows events.

Conceptually:

Windows Endpoint
      |
      v
Event Log
      |
      v
Windows Event Forwarding
      |
      v
Collector
      |
      v
SIEM

Validation should confirm the event reaches the final security platform, not merely the local endpoint.

docs.title: EDR Validation
docs.text:
An EDR platform typically provides more than antivirus.

Capabilities may include:

Process telemetry
File telemetry
Network telemetry
Identity context
Behavioural detection
Threat intelligence
Alerting
Investigation
Response
Isolation
Live response

docs.title: EDR Detection Lifecycle
docs.text:
Technique
   |
   v
Sensor Observes
   |
   v
Telemetry Uploaded
   |
   v
Analytics
   |
   v
Detection
   |
   v
Alert
   |
   v
Analyst

docs.title: EDR Test Questions
docs.text:
For every significant test:

Did the EDR record the process?

Did it record the command line?

Did it record the parent process?

Did it record the user?

Did it record network activity?

Did it identify the technique?

Did it generate an alert?

Was the alert severity appropriate?

Did it correlate related activity?

Did the SOC investigate it?

docs.title: Antivirus vs EDR
docs.text:
Do not treat them as identical.

Antivirus
   |
   +--> File/content detection
   +--> Malware prevention
   +--> Behaviour protection

EDR
   |
   +--> Endpoint telemetry
   +--> Behaviour analytics
   +--> Investigation
   +--> Detection
   +--> Response

Products may integrate both capabilities, but the assessment questions remain different.

docs.title: Network Telemetry
docs.text:
Host telemetry should be correlated with network visibility.

Sources may include:

Firewall
Proxy
DNS
IDS
IPS
NDR
VPN
Load balancer
Web proxy
Secure web gateway
Cloud firewall

docs.title: Network Detection Model
docs.text:
Process
   |
   v
Connection
   |
   v
Endpoint Telemetry
   |
   +----------------+
   |                |
   v                v
Firewall          Proxy
   |                |
   +-------+--------+
           |
           v
          SIEM

docs.title: DNS Detection
docs.text:
DNS can reveal activity that process-only monitoring misses.

Useful context includes:

Host
User
Query
Timestamp
Resolver
Domain age
Frequency
Response
Associated process

docs.title: DNS Test
docs.text:
Resolve an assessment-controlled domain:

Resolve-DnsName test.example.com

or:

nslookup test.example.com

Use a domain that is authorised for the assessment.

docs.title: Network Connectivity
docs.text:
Test TCP reachability:

Test-NetConnection HOST -Port 443

Record:

Source host
Destination
Port
Timestamp
Result
Firewall event
EDR event
SIEM event

docs.title: HTTP Visibility
docs.text:
A controlled HTTP request can validate:

Proxy telemetry
Firewall telemetry
Endpoint network telemetry
DNS
TLS inspection
URL filtering

Example:

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://example.com/' -UseBasicParsing

Use an approved destination for actual validation.

docs.title: Command and Control Detection
docs.text:
C2 validation should focus on observable behaviour rather than only specific framework signatures.

Relevant dimensions include:

Process initiating connection
Destination
Port
Protocol
Connection frequency
DNS
TLS
Proxy metadata
User context
Host role
Connection duration

docs.title: C2 Detection Model
docs.text:
Assessment Process
       |
       v
Outbound Connection
       |
       +--> Endpoint Telemetry
       |
       +--> DNS
       |
       +--> Firewall
       |
       +--> Proxy
       |
       +--> NDR
       |
       v
      SIEM
       |
       v
Detection / Correlation

See:

Command and Control

docs.title: Lateral Movement Detection
docs.text:
Lateral movement may produce telemetry across multiple systems.

Source Host
    |
    | Authentication
    v
Target Host
    |
    v
Remote Activity

Potential evidence includes:

Source endpoint process
Authentication event
Target logon
Network connection
Remote service activity
EDR event
SIEM correlation

docs.title: Windows Authentication Events
docs.text:
Useful events can include:

4624 - Successful logon
4625 - Failed logon
4648 - Explicit credentials
4768 - Kerberos TGT
4769 - Kerberos service ticket
4771 - Kerberos pre-authentication failure
4776 - NTLM validation

docs.title: Logon Types
docs.text:
Windows logon events include a logon type.

Common examples include:

2  - Interactive
3  - Network
4  - Batch
5  - Service
7  - Unlock
8  - NetworkCleartext
9  - NewCredentials
10 - RemoteInteractive
11 - CachedInteractive

The logon type can help explain how authentication occurred.

docs.title: Lateral Movement Correlation
docs.text:
Example:

WS01
 |
 | Remote authentication
 v
SRV01

Detection should attempt to correlate:

WS01 process
      +
WS01 network connection
      +
SRV01 logon
      +
SRV01 process creation

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Detection
docs.text:
Privilege escalation tests may generate:

Process creation
Service events
Scheduled-task events
File modifications
Registry changes
Privilege assignment
Application-control events
EDR alerts

docs.title: Service Detection
docs.text:
Relevant Windows telemetry may include:

Service installation
Service start
Service configuration change
Process creation

Security Event ID:

4697

may record service installation when appropriate auditing is enabled.

System logs may also provide service-control events.

docs.title: Scheduled Task Detection
docs.text:
Relevant Security events can include:

4698 - Scheduled task created
4702 - Scheduled task updated

Task Scheduler also maintains operational telemetry.

docs.title: Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Persistence detection should focus on changes that survive normal process termination or logon cycles.

Potential areas include:

Services
Scheduled tasks
Startup locations
Registry
Accounts
SSH keys
Cloud identities
Certificates
Application configuration

docs.title: Credential Access Detection
docs.text:
Credential-access testing can be high impact.

Use controlled simulations and explicit authorisation.

Detection dimensions may include:

Sensitive process access
Credential store access
Suspicious authentication
Directory replication behaviour
Browser credential access
Security-account database access
Unusual ticket activity
EDR behavioural alerts

docs.title: Credential Access Correlation
docs.text:
Process
   |
   v
Sensitive Resource Access
   |
   v
Credential Material
   |
   v
Subsequent Authentication

A mature detection strategy should attempt to correlate credential access with later use.

docs.title: Identity Detection
docs.text:
Identity telemetry is increasingly important.

Potential sources include:

Active Directory
Microsoft Entra ID
VPN
SSO
MFA
PAM
Cloud IAM
Application authentication

docs.title: Identity Detection Questions
docs.text:
Consider:

Was the login expected?

Was the source expected?

Was MFA used?

Was the device trusted?

Was privilege unusual?

Was authentication followed by unusual activity?

Was the identity recently compromised?

Was there impossible or abnormal access?

docs.title: Active Directory Detection
docs.text:
Potential AD detection areas include:

Password spraying
Kerberos abuse
NTLM activity
Privilege-group changes
ACL changes
Account creation
Delegation changes
AD CS activity
Directory replication
Trust changes
GPO changes

docs.title: Password Spray Validation
docs.text:
If explicitly authorised, detection validation should focus on controlled authentication patterns and avoid unnecessary account lockouts.

Measure:

Authentication failures
Source
Target accounts
Lockout behaviour
Identity alerts
SIEM correlation
SOC response

Do not exceed agreed authentication thresholds.

docs.title: Kerberos Visibility
docs.text:
Useful events include:

4768
4769
4771

Detection should consider:

Account
Service
Encryption type
Source address
Failure code
Volume
Timing

docs.title: NTLM Visibility
docs.text:
Event:

4776

can provide NTLM credential validation information in relevant circumstances.

NTLM should be evaluated alongside:

Source
Target
Account
Protocol
Host role
Expected authentication behaviour

docs.title: Cloud Detection
docs.text:
Modern attack paths may move between endpoint and cloud environments.

Potential telemetry includes:

Interactive sign-ins
Non-interactive sign-ins
Service principals
Role changes
Application consent
Token activity
Mailbox activity
Cloud audit logs
Conditional Access
Resource changes

docs.title: SIEM Validation
docs.text:
The SIEM should receive the telemetry required for detection.

Validate:

Source generates event
        |
        v
Collector receives event
        |
        v
SIEM ingests event
        |
        v
Fields parsed
        |
        v
Detection rule evaluates
        |
        v
Alert generated

docs.title: SIEM Ingestion Gap
docs.text:
A common problem is:

Endpoint Event Exists
       |
       v
SIEM Event Missing

Potential causes include:

Forwarder failure
Collector failure
Filtering
Licensing
Retention policy
Parsing issue
Connector issue
Network problem
Misconfiguration

docs.title: Parsing Validation
docs.text:
An event reaching the SIEM is not enough.

Important fields should be usable.

Examples:

Hostname
Username
Process
Parent process
Command line
Source IP
Destination IP
Destination port
Event ID
Timestamp
Hash
Domain

docs.title: Detection Rule Validation
docs.text:
A rule should be tested against known expected behaviour.

Known Test
    |
    v
Expected Telemetry
    |
    v
Detection Query
    |
    v
Expected Match
    |
   / \
 No   Yes
 |     |
 v     v
Fix   Alert

docs.title: Detection Rule Quality
docs.text:
Review:

Coverage
Precision
False positives
False negatives
Context
Severity
Suppression
Thresholds
Dependencies
Data sources
Response guidance

docs.title: Detection Rule Documentation
docs.text:
A useful rule record contains:

Rule name
Description
ATT&CK technique
Data source
Required fields
Detection logic
Known false positives
Severity
Triage guidance
Response guidance
Test procedure
Last validation date

docs.title: Atomic Red Team
docs.text:
Atomic Red Team provides small tests mapped to ATT&CK techniques.

It is useful for controlled detection validation when each test is reviewed before execution.

Workflow:

Select ATT&CK Technique
        |
        v
Select Atomic Test
        |
        v
Read Test
        |
        v
Review Prerequisites
        |
        v
Review Impact
        |
        v
Review Cleanup
        |
        v
Approve
        |
        v
Run One Test
        |
        v
Collect Telemetry
        |
        v
Cleanup
        |
        v
Verify

docs.title: Atomic Test Selection
docs.text:
Do not select tests only because they are easy to execute.

Select tests based on:

Threat model
Attack path
Missing detection
Business risk
Security-control objective
Previous incident
Known ATT&CK gap

docs.title: Atomic Test Record
docs.text:
Example:

Test ID:
RT-DV-014

ATT&CK:
T1059.001

Atomic:
Reviewed and approved test

Host:
WS01

Expected telemetry:
Process creation
PowerShell Operational
EDR process event

Expected alert:
Suspicious PowerShell activity

Cleanup:
Reviewed before execution

docs.title: Do Not Bulk Execute Tests
docs.text:
Avoid:

Run every atomic
        |
        v
Generate thousands of events
        |
        v
Unknown system impact
        |
        v
Poor diagnostic value

Prefer:

One hypothesis
      |
      v
One controlled test
      |
      v
Review
      |
      v
Improve
      |
      v
Retest

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK Coverage
docs.text:
ATT&CK can help structure detection validation.

Example:

ATT&CK Tactic Technique Test Telemetry Detection Status Execution PowerShell RT-DV-001 Yes Yes Covered Persistence Scheduled Task RT-DV-002 Yes No Gap Credential Access Test simulation RT-DV-003 Yes Yes Covered Lateral Movement Remote service RT-DV-004 Yes No Gap C2 Controlled HTTPS RT-DV-005 Partial No Gap

docs.title: ATT&CK Coverage Is Not Binary
docs.text:
Do not simply write:

T1059.001 = Covered

Coverage depends on:

Technique variation
Operating system
User context
Execution method
Data source
Detection rule
Security product
Environment

docs.title: Coverage Levels
docs.text:
A useful model is:

0 - No telemetry

1 - Telemetry available

2 - Detection exists

3 - Alert enriched

4 - Analyst can investigate

5 - Response procedure validated

docs.title: Detection Coverage Matrix
docs.text:
Example:

Technique Telemetry Detection Alert Investigation Response PowerShell Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Scheduled Task Yes No No No No Service Creation Yes Yes Yes Yes No C2 HTTPS Partial No No No No Lateral Movement Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes

docs.title: ATT&CK Heatmap Interpretation
docs.text:
A heatmap should represent tested coverage, not assumed coverage.

Avoid marking a technique green simply because:

EDR vendor says it supports the technique.

Prefer:

Technique actually tested
        |
        v
Telemetry confirmed
        |
        v
Detection confirmed
        |
        v
SOC response confirmed

docs.title: Detection Hypothesis
docs.text:
Detection engineering works well when expressed as a hypothesis.

Example:

If a standard workstation launches an unusual script interpreter
that subsequently establishes an outbound connection, the endpoint
and network telemetry should allow the SOC to identify and
investigate the behaviour.

Then design a safe test around that hypothesis.

docs.title: Behaviour-Based Detection
docs.text:
Avoid relying entirely on:

Tool name
File name
Known hash
Exact command
Exact string

Consider behaviour:

Process ancestry
Identity
Privilege
Destination
Authentication
Resource access
Sequence
Timing
Host role

docs.title: Detection Chain
docs.text:
Individual low-confidence events can become meaningful when correlated.

Unusual Process
      |
      v
Credential Access
      |
      v
Remote Authentication
      |
      v
New Host Process
      |
      v
Outbound Connection

Each event alone may be ambiguous.

Together they describe an attack path.

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
Useful correlation dimensions include:

Same user
Same source host
Same destination
Same process tree
Short time window
Credential use
Network connection
Privilege change

docs.title: Detection Timing
docs.text:
Record at least:

T0 - Test begins

T1 - Endpoint event generated

T2 - Event reaches SIEM

T3 - Alert generated

T4 - Analyst acknowledges

T5 - Investigation begins

T6 - Containment begins

docs.title: Time to Detect
docs.text: TTD = Alert Time - Activity Start Time

docs.title: Mean Time to Detect
docs.text:
Across multiple tests:

MTTD = Sum of Detection Times / Number of Detected Tests

Be careful with small sample sizes.

A few controlled tests should not be presented as statistically representative of all incidents.

docs.title: Time to Triage
docs.text: TTT = Analyst Triage Time - Alert Time

docs.title: Time to Respond
docs.text:
A practical measurement may be:

TTR = Response Action Time - Detection Time

Define the organisation's metric before comparing results.

docs.title: Example Timeline
docs.text:
10:00:00 - Test starts

10:00:04 - Endpoint telemetry generated

10:00:19 - SIEM receives event

10:00:31 - Detection rule triggers

10:02:10 - Analyst acknowledges alert

10:05:22 - Investigation begins

10:09:40 - Host containment initiated

docs.title: Detection Gap Categories
docs.text:
Not all failures are the same.

Useful categories include:

Telemetry Gap
Collection Gap
Parsing Gap
Detection Gap
Correlation Gap
Alerting Gap
Triage Gap
Investigation Gap
Response Gap

docs.title: Telemetry Gap
docs.text:
Activity occurred
      |
      v
No relevant event generated

Potential remediation:

Enable audit source
Deploy endpoint telemetry
Improve Sysmon configuration
Enable PowerShell logging
Enable identity auditing
Add network visibility

docs.title: Collection Gap
docs.text:
Local Event Exists
      |
      v
Central Platform Missing Event

Potential remediation:

Fix forwarding
Fix connector
Review filters
Review ingestion
Review licensing
Review network path

docs.title: Parsing Gap
docs.text:
Event Ingested
      |
      v
Important Fields Missing

Potential remediation:

Fix parser
Fix normalisation
Preserve raw event
Map identity fields
Map process fields
Map network fields

docs.title: Detection Gap
docs.text:
Telemetry Exists
      |
      v
No Rule Detects Behaviour

Potential remediation:

Create detection
Improve analytics
Add correlation
Tune threshold
Add context

docs.title: Alerting Gap
docs.text:
Rule Matches
    |
    v
Alert Not Reaching Analyst

Review:

Routing
Severity
Suppression
Notification
Queue
Case creation
Integration

docs.title: Triage Gap
docs.text:
Alert Exists
    |
    v
Incorrectly Closed

Potential causes:

Insufficient context
Weak playbook
Analyst training
Alert fatigue
Poor enrichment
Incorrect severity

docs.title: Response Gap
docs.text:
Attack Detected
      |
      v
Organisation Cannot Contain

Review:

Authority
Processes
EDR response capability
Identity suspension
Network isolation
Communication
Escalation

docs.title: Detection Gap Severity
docs.text:
Severity should consider:

Technique impact
Attack-path position
Privilege
Asset criticality
Telemetry availability
Ease of detection engineering
Existing compensating controls
Repeatability
Threat relevance

docs.title: Title
docs.text: PowerShell Script Execution Was Logged but Did Not Generate an Alert

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
PowerShell Script Block Logging recorded the controlled assessment
activity on the workstation.

The corresponding events were successfully forwarded to the SIEM.

No detection rule generated an alert for the tested behaviour.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
An attacker may be able to perform similar script-based activity
without generating an actionable SOC alert, despite the required
telemetry being available.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Telemetry was present but detection logic did not identify the
tested behaviour.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Develop and validate behaviour-focused PowerShell analytics using
process ancestry, script telemetry, user context, and related
network activity rather than relying solely on static strings.

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Endpoint Security Events Were Not Forwarded to the SIEM

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
The controlled test generated the expected event locally.

The event could not be located in the central SIEM during the
assessment window.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Investigate:

Forwarder
Collector
Filtering
Connector
Network
Ingestion

docs.title: Positive Detection Finding
docs.text:
Not every result should describe a weakness.

Example:

The controlled lateral-movement simulation generated endpoint,
authentication, and network telemetry.

The SIEM correlated the events and generated a high-confidence
alert within 42 seconds.

The SOC acknowledged the alert within three minutes and correctly
identified both the source and target systems.

This is valuable evidence of effective security controls.

docs.title: SOC Validation
docs.text:
Detection engineering is incomplete without analyst validation.

Questions include:

Did the analyst receive the alert?

Did they understand it?

Did they identify the user?

Did they identify the source?

Did they identify the target?

Did they reconstruct the attack path?

Did they escalate appropriately?

Did they contain the activity?

Did they preserve evidence?

docs.title: Blind Red Team
docs.text:
In a blind assessment, the SOC may not know the exact timing or techniques.

This can measure realistic detection and response.

However, the assessment still requires:

Authorisation
Emergency communication
Stop conditions
Safety monitoring

docs.title: Purple Team Validation
docs.text:
Purple teaming enables direct collaboration.

Red Team Executes
       |
       v
Blue Team Observes
       |
       v
Compare Telemetry
       |
       v
Identify Gap
       |
       v
Improve Detection
       |
       v
Red Team Repeats
       |
       v
Confirm Improvement

This is especially useful for detection engineering.

docs.title: Purple Team Test Cycle
docs.text:
A practical cycle:

1. Select technique

2. Define expected telemetry

3. Execute controlled test

4. Blue team searches telemetry

5. Compare expected vs observed

6. Identify missing data

7. Create or improve detection

8. Repeat test

9. Validate alert

10. Document result

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Every detection improvement should be retested.

Original Test
      |
      v
Detection Failed
      |
      v
Rule Improved
      |
      v
Same Test Repeated
      |
      v
Detection Succeeds

docs.title: Use the Same Test
docs.text:
Changing the test during retesting makes comparison harder.

Record:

Same host class
Same user privilege
Same technique
Same test parameters
Same expected telemetry

where practical.

docs.title: Regression Testing
docs.text:
A detection that works today may stop working after:

EDR update
SIEM migration
Parser change
Operating-system update
Logging change
Rule modification
Infrastructure change
Agent failure

Important detections should therefore be validated periodically.

docs.title: Detection-as-Code
docs.text:
Where supported, detection rules should be version controlled.

Benefits include:

Change history
Peer review
Testing
Rollback
Documentation
Automation
Consistency

docs.title: Sigma
docs.text:
Sigma provides a generic format for expressing log-based detection logic.

Conceptually:

title: Example Detection
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows

detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\example.exe'

  condition: selection

This is only an illustrative structure.

Production detections require environment-specific context, exclusions, validation, and tuning.

docs.title: Sigma Workflow
docs.text:
Detection Hypothesis
      |
      v
Sigma / Native Rule
      |
      v
Test Dataset
      |
      v
Controlled Validation
      |
      v
Tune
      |
      v
Deploy
      |
      v
Monitor
      |
      v
Retest

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
A detection that alerts constantly may become operationally ineffective.

During testing record:

Expected legitimate behaviour
Alert frequency
Affected user groups
Affected systems
Known administrative tools
Developer workflows
Automation
Service accounts

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
A false negative occurs when behaviour that should have been detected is missed.

Potential causes include:

Missing telemetry
Incorrect query
Overly strict conditions
Unexpected technique variation
Parser failure
Suppression
Incorrect field mapping
Sensor failure

docs.title: Detection Tuning
docs.text:
Avoid tuning exclusively around the exact red team command.

Weak:

Alert when command line contains exact-test-string.

Better:

Detect unusual behaviour based on process relationships,
identity, execution context, and related activity.

docs.title: Detection Resilience
docs.text:
A resilient detection should survive minor variations.

Consider whether the detection still works when:

Filename changes
Path changes
Whitespace changes
Parent process changes
User changes
Destination changes
Command syntax changes

Testing such variations should remain controlled and aligned with the threat model.

docs.title: Detection Enrichment
docs.text:
Useful alert enrichment includes:

Hostname
User
Department
Asset criticality
Process
Parent process
Command line
Hash
Signature
Source IP
Destination IP
Domain
Threat intelligence
Recent authentication
Related alerts

docs.title: Asset Context
docs.text:
The same activity may have different importance on:

Developer workstation
Standard workstation
Domain controller
Certificate authority
Jump server
Backup server
Privileged workstation
Production database

Detection severity should consider host role.

docs.title: Identity Context
docs.text:
Likewise:

Standard user
Service account
Administrator
Domain administrator
Break-glass account
Application identity

should influence detection priority.

docs.title: Detection Evidence
docs.text:
For each validation collect:

Test ID
Technique
ATT&CK mapping
Timestamp
Host
User
Privilege
Command or action
Expected telemetry
Observed telemetry
Endpoint event
SIEM event
Detection rule
Alert
SOC response
Result
Cleanup

docs.title: Screenshot Evidence
docs.text:
Useful screenshots may include:

Local event
EDR process tree
SIEM query
Detection alert
SOC case
Timeline
Response action

Use a consistent naming convention:

YYYYMMDD-HHMM-testid-host-description.png

docs.title: Detection Validation Table
docs.text:
Example:

Test ID Technique Prevented Telemetry Alert SOC Result DV-001 EICAR Yes Yes Yes Yes Pass DV-002 PowerShell No Yes Yes Yes Pass DV-003 Scheduled Task No Yes No No Gap DV-004 Lateral Movement No Yes Yes Yes Pass DV-005 HTTPS C2 simulation No Partial No No Gap

docs.title: Result Classification
docs.text:
A useful classification:

PASS
Expected prevention/detection/response occurred.

PARTIAL
Some expected controls worked but important gaps remain.

FAIL
Expected control did not function.

NOT TESTED
Technique was not executed.

NOT APPLICABLE
Technique does not apply to the environment.

docs.title: Detection Maturity Model
docs.text:
Level 0
No telemetry

Level 1
Telemetry available locally

Level 2
Telemetry centralised

Level 3
Detection exists

Level 4
Alert enriched and actionable

Level 5
SOC response validated

Level 6
Detection continuously tested

docs.title: Detection Validation Dashboard
docs.text:
Useful summary metrics:

Tests executed
Tests prevented
Tests detected
Tests logged only
Tests invisible
Alerts generated
Alerts investigated
Mean time to detect
Mean time to triage
ATT&CK techniques tested
Detection gaps
Retests passed

docs.title: Example Metrics
docs.text:
Tests executed:              24

Prevented:                    6

Allowed but detected:        11

Logged but not detected:      5

No useful visibility:         2

SOC investigated:            13

Retests passed:               7 / 8

docs.title: Prevention Rate
docs.text:
Prevention Rate =
Prevented Tests / Total Applicable Tests

docs.title: Detection Rate
docs.text:
For tests that were actually observable and expected to generate detection:

Detection Rate =
Detected Tests / Detection-Expected Tests

Define the denominator clearly in reports.

docs.title: Visibility Rate
docs.text:
Visibility Rate =
Tests with Useful Telemetry / Tests Executed

docs.title: Investigation Rate
docs.text:
Investigation Rate =
Alerts Investigated / Alerts Generated

docs.title: Metrics Need Context
docs.text:
Do not write:

EDR detected 80 percent of attacks.

when only five selected tests were performed.

Prefer:

Eight of the ten controlled techniques selected for this
assessment generated the expected EDR alert.

This accurately describes the tested sample.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Detection validation can be reduced to:

Do not ask only:

"Did the EDR alert?"

Ask:

Did the activity happen?

Was it prevented?

What telemetry was generated?

Did the telemetry reach the security platform?

Could defenders find it?

Did a detection identify it?

Was the alert actionable?

Did the SOC investigate it?

Could the organisation respond?

Did the improvement survive retesting?

What good detection validation looks like

The strongest result is not a screenshot showing that an EDR generated an alert. A mature validation demonstrates the complete path from controlled attacker behaviour to endpoint or identity telemetry, central collection, detection, analyst investigation, and response. When a gap is identified, improve the relevant layer and repeat the same test to demonstrate that the gap has actually been closed.

Authorised testing only

Detection validation may intentionally generate security alerts and can involve authentication, endpoint execution, network connections, application-control events, and other behaviours normally associated with attacks. Coordinate tests through the Rules of Engagement, avoid uncontrolled bulk execution, protect any credentials or customer data encountered, use vendor test artifacts and controlled simulations where possible, and remove all introduced artifacts after testing.

docs.title: Red Team Discovery
docs.text:
Discovery is the process of understanding the environment after obtaining an authorised foothold.

Reconnaissance primarily asks:

What can be learned before access?

Discovery asks:

Where am I?

Who am I?

What can I access?

What systems surround me?

Which security boundaries exist?

Which identities and privileges are present?

Which services and applications are important?

Which defensive controls are operating?

What should I investigate next?

A practical model is:

Foothold
   |
   v
Current Context
   |
   v
Host Discovery
   |
   v
Network Discovery
   |
   v
Identity Discovery
   |
   v
Domain Discovery
   |
   v
Security-Control Discovery
   |
   v
Attack-Path Decisions

Discovery should be deliberate rather than an uncontrolled collection of system information.

Authorised testing only

Discovery can expose sensitive infrastructure, identities, network architecture and business systems. Remain within the authorised scope, minimise unnecessary collection, avoid disruptive scanning, and do not automatically interact with every system discovered from a compromised host.

docs.text:
Typical objectives include:

Identify the current host

Identify the current user

Determine current privileges

Determine domain membership

Identify operating-system details

Identify running processes

Identify installed software

Identify services

Identify network configuration

Identify local routes

Identify DNS configuration

Identify neighbouring systems

Identify remote services

Identify Active Directory relationships

Identify security controls

Identify cloud context

Identify container context

Identify candidate privilege paths

Identify candidate lateral-movement paths

Identify objective-relevant systems

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Get-ScheduledTask |
    Select-Object TaskName,TaskPath,State

Scheduled tasks may reveal:

Administrative automation

Maintenance scripts

Backup processes

Custom applications

Service accounts

Potential privilege relationships

docs.title: Installed Software
docs.text:
Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher,InstallLocation

Also inspect 32-bit applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher,InstallLocation

docs.title: Software Discovery Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

What applications are installed?

Which are business-critical?

Which run privileged services?

Which provide remote administration?

Which security products are installed?

Which appear outdated?

Which contain interesting configuration?

docs.title: Windows Users
docs.text:
Get-LocalUser

Groups:

Get-LocalGroup

Membership of a specific group:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators

docs.title: Current Sessions
docs.text:
query user

This may reveal interactive sessions on the current host.

Do not assume every visible session should be targeted.

docs.title: Windows Drives
docs.text:
Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Alternative:

Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk |
    Select-Object DeviceID,DriveType,FileSystem,Size,FreeSpace

docs.title: Linux Processes
docs.text:
ps aux

Process tree:

ps -ef --forest

docs.title: Linux Services
docs.text:
systemctl --type=service --state=running

Service files:

systemctl list-unit-files --type=service

docs.title: Linux Timers
docs.text: systemctl list-timers --all

docs.title: Linux Cron
docs.text:
cat /etc/crontab

ls -la /etc/cron.d/

User cron:

crontab -l

docs.title: Linux Users
docs.text:
cat /etc/passwd

Current groups:

groups

All groups:

getent group

docs.title: Interactive Linux Users
docs.text:
A simple filter for common interactive shells:

awk -F: '$7 ~ /(bash|zsh|sh|fish)$/ {print $1 ":" $7}' /etc/passwd

This is only an indicator because shell configuration varies.

docs.title: Linux Installed Packages
docs.text:
Debian-based systems:

dpkg -l

RPM-based systems:

rpm -qa

Use the package manager appropriate to the target.

docs.title: Linux Filesystems
docs.text:
df -h

Mounts:

findmnt

Block devices:

lsblk

docs.title: Mount Options
docs.text:
Review:

noexec

nosuid

nodev

rw

ro

These can affect later privilege-escalation and execution decisions.

docs.title: Phase 3 - Network Discovery
docs.text:
Network discovery should answer:

Which interfaces exist?

Which networks are directly connected?

Which routes exist?

Which DNS servers are configured?

Which services are listening locally?

Which systems are already known?

Which internal networks are reachable?

docs.title: Windows Network Configuration
docs.text:
Get-NetIPConfiguration

Addresses:

Get-NetIPAddress

Interfaces:

Get-NetAdapter

docs.title: Windows Routes
docs.text:
Get-NetRoute |
    Sort-Object DestinationPrefix

Traditional:

route print

docs.title: Windows DNS
docs.text:
Get-DnsClientServerAddress

DNS suffixes:

Get-DnsClient |
    Select-Object InterfaceAlias,ConnectionSpecificSuffix

docs.title: Windows Listening Ports
docs.text:
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen |
    Select-Object LocalAddress,LocalPort,OwningProcess

docs.title: Map Port to Process
docs.text:
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen |
    ForEach-Object {
        $process = Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

        [PSCustomObject]@{
            Address = $_.LocalAddress
            Port    = $_.LocalPort
            PID     = $_.OwningProcess
            Process = $process.ProcessName
        }
    }

docs.title: Windows Connections
docs.text:
Get-NetTCPConnection |
    Select-Object LocalAddress,LocalPort,RemoteAddress,RemotePort,State,OwningProcess

Existing connections can reveal systems the host normally communicates with.

docs.title: ARP / Neighbour Cache
docs.text:
Get-NetNeighbor

Traditional:

arp -a

This may reveal recently observed local network neighbours.

docs.title: Linux Interfaces
docs.text:
ip addr

Compact:

ip -br addr

docs.title: Linux Routes
docs.text: ip route

docs.title: Linux DNS
docs.text:
Depending on the environment:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

On systems using systemd-resolved:

resolvectl status

docs.title: Linux Listening Services
docs.text: ss -lntup

docs.title: Linux Connections
docs.text:
ss -ntup

Existing connections may reveal:

Database servers

Management servers

Proxies

Application backends

Monitoring systems

Directory services

docs.title: Linux Neighbours
docs.text: ip neigh

docs.title: Network Discovery Model
docs.text:
Current Host
    |
    +--> Interfaces
    |
    +--> Routes
    |
    +--> DNS
    |
    +--> Listening Services
    |
    +--> Existing Connections
    |
    +--> Neighbours
    |
    v
Reachable Networks

docs.title: Routes Are High-Value
docs.text:
Routes may reveal internal networks unavailable from the original operator system.

Example:

10.10.10.0/24

172.16.20.0/24

192.168.50.0/24

This can indicate that the compromised host may later function as a pivot.

See:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Do Not Scan Every Route Automatically
docs.text:
Finding a route does not mean:

Every host on that network is in scope.

Before scanning:

Check scope

Check ROE

Check segmentation objectives

Select appropriate targets

Use conservative discovery

docs.title: Connectivity Validation
docs.text:
Windows:

Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 443

Linux:

nc -vz TARGET 443

Use known authorised hosts and ports when possible.

docs.title: Important Internal Ports
docs.text:
Common services include:

Port Typical Service 22 SSH 53 DNS 80 HTTP 88 Kerberos 135 RPC 389 LDAP 443 HTTPS 445 SMB 464 Kerberos password change 636 LDAPS 1433 Microsoft SQL Server 3306 MySQL 3389 RDP 5432 PostgreSQL 5985 WinRM HTTP 5986 WinRM HTTPS

Port numbers are indicators rather than proof of protocol.

docs.title: Targeted Internal Validation
docs.text:
When authorised, a targeted Nmap scan can validate selected systems:

nmap -sT -Pn -sV -p 22,80,443,445,3389,5985,5986 192.0.2.10

Avoid unnecessary broad scanning when existing host information already answers the question.

docs.title: Phase 4 - Identity Discovery
docs.text:
Identity discovery determines:

Who is the current user?

Which local groups exist?

Which domain groups apply?

Which sessions exist?

Which service identities exist?

Which administrative identities interact with this host?

docs.title: Windows Current Identity
docs.text: whoami /all

docs.title: Windows Local Groups
docs.text:
Get-LocalGroup

Administrators:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators

docs.title: Domain Membership
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem |
    Select-Object Name,Domain,PartOfDomain

docs.title: Domain User Context
docs.text:
whoami /fqdn

whoami /user

whoami /groups

docs.title: Kerberos Tickets
docs.text:
Windows includes:

klist

This can show Kerberos tickets associated with the current logon session.

Useful information can include:

Client identity

Service principal

Ticket validity

Kerberos realm

Treat authentication material carefully.

docs.title: Linux Identity
docs.text:
id

Logged-in users:

who

Recent login information where authorised:

last

docs.title: Identity Discovery Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Is this a normal user?

Is this a service account?

Is this an administrator?

Is the identity domain joined?

What groups apply?

Are privileged sessions present?

What systems does this identity normally access?

docs.title: Phase 5 - Active Directory Discovery
docs.text:
If the host is domain joined, Active Directory becomes a major discovery source.

Determine:

Domain name

Domain controllers

DNS domain

Current user

Current computer

Groups

Trusts

Organisational structure

Privileged groups

Service accounts

Delegation

AD CS

GPO

docs.title: Domain Name
docs.text:
$env:USERDNSDOMAIN

Or:

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem |
    Select-Object Domain

docs.title: Domain Controller Discovery
docs.text:
Built-in Windows tooling:

nltest /dsgetdc:%USERDNSDOMAIN%

List domain controllers:

nltest /dclist:%USERDNSDOMAIN%

docs.title: DNS SRV Records
docs.text:
Domain controllers can also be discovered through DNS.

Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV "_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.$env:USERDNSDOMAIN"

docs.title: LDAP and Kerberos
docs.text:
Typical domain services include:

53   DNS

88   Kerberos

389  LDAP

445  SMB

464  Kerberos password services

636  LDAPS

docs.title: Built-In Domain Enumeration
docs.text:
Current domain information:

net user /domain

Domain groups:

net group /domain

Domain administrators:

net group "Domain Admins" /domain

Use targeted queries rather than collecting unnecessary directory information.

docs.title: PowerShell AD Module
docs.text:
If the ActiveDirectory module is legitimately installed:

Get-Module -ListAvailable ActiveDirectory

Domain:

Get-ADDomain

Domain controllers:

Get-ADDomainController -Filter *

Groups:

Get-ADGroup -Filter * |
    Select-Object Name

Large directory queries should be performed only when justified.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can help analyse Active Directory relationships.

Examples include:

Group membership

Administrative rights

Sessions

ACLs

Delegation

Trusts

Certificate relationships

Use collection modes appropriate to the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: BloodHound Model
docs.text:
Current User
     |
     v
Group Membership
     |
     v
Permissions
     |
     v
Computers
     |
     v
Sessions
     |
     v
Privileged Identity

docs.title: BloodHound Is Analysis, Not Proof
docs.text:
A path such as:

User -> Group -> Computer -> Session -> Admin

represents relationships.

Validate:

Current permissions

Reachability

Authentication

Host state

Security controls

Scope

before treating the path as confirmed.

docs.title: Domain Trust Discovery
docs.text:
Trusts can influence attack paths.

Built-in query:

nltest /domain_trusts

See:

Active Directory Trusts

docs.title: Group Discovery
docs.text:
Important groups may include:

Domain Admins

Enterprise Admins

Administrators

Server Operators

Backup Operators

Account Operators

DNSAdmins

Custom administrative groups

Custom groups often matter as much as built-in groups.

docs.title: Service Accounts
docs.text:
Service accounts may be visible through:

Windows services

Scheduled tasks

IIS application pools

SQL services

Domain objects

Application configuration

Service accounts can connect:

Host Discovery
      |
      v
Credential Access
      |
      v
Lateral Movement
      |
      v
Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Group Managed Service Accounts
docs.text:
gMSAs may exist in modern Active Directory environments.

See:

gMSA

docs.title: LAPS
docs.text:
Windows LAPS may manage local administrator passwords.

See:

LAPS

Its presence generally represents a security improvement when correctly configured.

docs.title: Group Policy
docs.text:
GPOs can reveal:

Security configuration

Scripts

Software deployment

Application control

Firewall policy

Administrative settings

See:

Group Policy

docs.title: AD CS Discovery
docs.text:
Determine whether Active Directory Certificate Services exists.

Possible indicators include:

Enterprise CA

Certificate templates

Certificate enrolment infrastructure

Certificate-related Active Directory objects

See:

Active Directory Certificate Services

docs.title: Phase 6 - Security-Control Discovery
docs.text:
Understanding defensive controls is a normal part of red team situational awareness.

The objective should be:

Understand the defensive environment

rather than:

Immediately disable the defensive environment

docs.title: Security-Control Categories
docs.text:
Look for:

Antivirus

EDR

Application control

Host firewall

PowerShell restrictions

AMSI

ASR

Credential protection

Disk encryption

Logging

SIEM agents

Network security agents

docs.title: Microsoft Defender
docs.text:
Get-MpComputerStatus

Useful fields:

Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,
                  RealTimeProtectionEnabled,
                  BehaviorMonitorEnabled,
                  IoavProtectionEnabled

docs.title: Defender Preferences
docs.text:
Get-MpPreference

Do not alter configuration merely because it can be queried.

docs.title: ASR
docs.text:
Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids,
                  AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

docs.title: PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text: $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Select-Object CollectionType,EnforcementMode

docs.title: AppLocker Detailed Policy
docs.text: Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

docs.title: Code Integrity
docs.text: Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational" -MaxEvents 20

docs.title: Windows Firewall
docs.text:
Profiles:

Get-NetFirewallProfile |
    Select-Object Name,Enabled,DefaultInboundAction,DefaultOutboundAction

This helps understand host network boundaries.

docs.title: BitLocker
docs.text:
Get-BitLockerVolume -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Disk encryption is generally relevant to physical/offline access rather than ordinary live-session privilege.

docs.title: Credential Guard
docs.text:
Credential Guard and LSA protections may materially affect credential-access paths.

Record their presence where relevant rather than assuming credential extraction techniques will work.

See:

Credential Access

docs.title: Linux Security Controls
docs.text:
Possible controls include:

SELinux

AppArmor

auditd

EDR

Host firewall

Container security

sudo policy

docs.title: SELinux
docs.text:
getenforce 2>/dev/null

Possible results:

Enforcing

Permissive

Disabled

docs.title: AppArmor
docs.text:
aa-status 2>/dev/null

If the command exists and permissions allow it.

docs.title: Linux Firewall
docs.text:
nftables:

sudo -n nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null

iptables where relevant:

sudo -n iptables -L -n 2>/dev/null

If the current account lacks permission, record that rather than forcing access.

docs.title: auditd
docs.text:
systemctl status auditd

Rules where authorised:

auditctl -l

docs.title: Security-Control Discovery Model
docs.text:
Host
 |
 +--> Antivirus
 |
 +--> EDR
 |
 +--> Application Control
 |
 +--> Firewall
 |
 +--> Logging
 |
 +--> Identity Protection
 |
 +--> Script Controls
 |
 v
Defensive Posture

docs.title: Do Not Infer Too Much from Process Names
docs.text:
A security-agent process may be:

Running

Partially functional

Disconnected

Misconfigured

Healthy

Likewise, absence of an obvious process does not prove the host lacks EDR.

Correlate multiple sources.

docs.title: Phase 7 - Application Discovery
docs.text:
Applications can reveal important business systems.

Look for:

Web applications

Databases

Management software

Backup systems

File-transfer applications

Development tools

Administrative consoles

Custom business applications

docs.title: Windows Application Indicators
docs.text:
Sources include:

Installed software

Services

Processes

Scheduled tasks

Listening ports

Configuration files

Browser bookmarks

Avoid collecting unrelated personal browser information.

docs.title: Linux Application Indicators
docs.text:
Sources include:

Processes

systemd services

Listening sockets

Packages

Configuration directories

Web server configuration

Container configuration

docs.title: Web Server Discovery
docs.text:
Possible software includes:

IIS

Apache

nginx

Tomcat

Node.js

Python application servers

The presence of a web server may indicate an internal application worth mapping.

docs.title: IIS
docs.text:
On Windows:

Get-Service W3SVC -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If IIS administration modules are installed and access is authorised, additional site configuration may be available.

docs.title: Apache and nginx
docs.text:
Linux processes:

ps aux | grep -E '[a]pache2|[h]ttpd|[n]ginx'

Listening ports:

ss -lntp

docs.title: Database Discovery
docs.text:
Common databases include:

Microsoft SQL Server

PostgreSQL

MySQL

MariaDB

Oracle

MongoDB

Processes and listening services can identify candidate database systems.

docs.title: Database Ports
docs.text:
Typical defaults include:

Port Service 1433 Microsoft SQL Server 1521 Oracle 3306 MySQL/MariaDB 5432 PostgreSQL 27017 MongoDB

Applications may use non-default ports.

docs.title: Configuration Discovery
docs.text:
Configuration files can contain:

Server names

Database endpoints

API URLs

Authentication providers

Service accounts

Cloud resource names

Handle secrets separately under the credential-access methodology.

docs.title: Phase 8 - Share Discovery
docs.text:
File shares can reveal:

Department data

Deployment files

Scripts

Software

Configuration

Administrative resources

Discovery should not become bulk collection.

docs.title: Windows Shares
docs.text:
Local shares:

Get-SmbShare

Traditional:

net share

docs.title: Remote Share Discovery
docs.text:
For a known authorised server:

net view \\SERVER

Do not enumerate arbitrary servers simply because their names were discovered.

docs.title: Share Access Model
docs.text:
Share Discovered
      |
      v
In Scope?
      |
      v
Current User Has Access?
      |
      v
Objective-Relevant?
      |
      v
Minimal Review

docs.title: Active Directory Shares
docs.text:
See:

Active Directory Shares

Shares may become relevant to:

Credential exposure

Deployment scripts

Lateral movement

Objective data

docs.title: Phase 9 - Virtualisation Discovery
docs.text:
Determine whether the system is:

Physical

Virtual machine

Cloud VM

Container

VDI

docs.title: Windows Virtualisation Indicators
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem |
    Select-Object Manufacturer,Model

Possible indicators may reference:

VMware

VirtualBox

Hyper-V

Cloud vendors

Treat these as architecture information.

docs.title: Linux Virtualisation
docs.text:
Where available:

systemd-detect-virt

Possible results include:

kvm

vmware

microsoft

docker

none

docs.title: Why Virtualisation Matters
docs.text:
It can help explain:

Network architecture

Management interfaces

Cloud identity

Snapshot behaviour

Container boundaries

Host/guest relationships

docs.title: Phase 10 - Container Discovery
docs.text:
Containers introduce another security boundary.

Determine:

Am I in a container?

Which runtime exists?

What permissions exist?

Which volumes are mounted?

Which networks exist?

Is host-management access available?

docs.title: Docker Indicator
docs.text: test -f /.dockerenv && echo "Docker indicator present"

docs.title: cgroup Information
docs.text: cat /proc/1/cgroup

docs.title: Docker CLI
docs.text:
If legitimately available:

docker version

Containers:

docker ps

Only use the daemon if the current identity is authorised to do so.

docs.title: Docker Socket
docs.text:
ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

Access to the Docker daemon can represent a major security boundary.

See:

Linux Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Container Networks
docs.text:
If authorised:

docker network ls

Container network architecture may reveal internal application relationships.

docs.title: Kubernetes Discovery
docs.text:
Possible indicators include:

KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST

Service-account paths

kubectl configuration

Container environment variables

Check:

env | grep -i kubernetes

Do not access cluster resources beyond authorised scope.

docs.title: Phase 11 - Cloud Discovery
docs.text:
Cloud-connected hosts may expose context about:

Cloud provider

Subscription/account/project

Managed identity

Instance role

Storage

Secrets

Management agents

Cloud networking

docs.title: Cloud Discovery Principles
docs.text:
Do not automatically query metadata endpoints simply because a cloud provider is suspected.

First determine:

Cloud testing is in scope?

Metadata interaction is permitted?

Current host belongs to customer?

Identity testing is permitted?

docs.title: Cloud Environment Indicators
docs.text:
Environment variables:

Windows:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Linux:

env

Look for application and platform indicators without assuming exposed variables are credentials.

docs.title: Cloud CLI Discovery
docs.text:
Possible clients:

aws

az

gcloud

Linux:

command -v aws
command -v az
command -v gcloud

PowerShell:

Get-Command aws -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-Command az -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-Command gcloud -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Cloud Configuration
docs.text:
User profiles may contain legitimate CLI configuration.

Examples include:

AWS configuration

Azure CLI context

Google Cloud configuration

Treat tokens and credentials as sensitive material.

docs.title: Phase 12 - Security Boundary Discovery
docs.text:
At this stage, transform raw observations into security boundaries.

Examples:

Standard User -> Administrator

Workstation -> Server

User VLAN -> Management VLAN

Domain User -> Privileged Group

Container -> Host

Application User -> Administrator

On-Premises -> Cloud

Normal Account -> Service Account

docs.title: Boundary Model
docs.text:
Current Context
      |
      v
Observed Relationship
      |
      v
Security Boundary
      |
      v
Required Preconditions
      |
      v
Candidate Attack Path

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Discovery identifies:

Current host:
WS01

Current user:
CORP\user1

Domain:
corp.example

Route:
10.20.0.0/16

Existing connection:
APP01:443

Local group:
No administrative membership

PowerShell:
FullLanguage

Application control:
Enabled

Domain:
AD environment present

This does not yet prove compromise of another system.

It provides the context needed to choose the next tests.

docs.title: Phase 13 - Attack-Path Prioritisation
docs.text:
Prioritise discovered information based on engagement objectives.

High-value categories often include:

Privileged identities

Administrative systems

Domain controllers

Certificate authorities

Management servers

Backup infrastructure

Identity providers

Cloud management

Database systems

Deployment infrastructure

Security tooling

Objective systems

docs.title: Crown Jewels
docs.text:
The Rules of Engagement may identify systems such as:

Domain controllers

Payment systems

Customer databases

Source-code repositories

Identity infrastructure

Cloud control plane

Backup infrastructure

Discovery should help determine a path toward these objectives without unnecessarily compromising unrelated systems.

docs.title: Prioritisation Model
docs.text:
Discovered Asset
      |
      v
In Scope?
   /      \
 No        Yes
 |          |
Stop        v
       Objective Relevant?
         /         \
       No           Yes
       |             |
       v             v
   Low Priority   Reachable?
                  /      \
                No        Yes
                |          |
                v          v
              Record    Privilege /
                        Credential
                         Relationship?
                          /       \
                        No         Yes
                        |           |
                        v           v
                     Review     High Priority

docs.title: Discovery and Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Discovery may reveal:

Writable service resources

Interesting privileges

Sudo rules

SUID binaries

Capabilities

Scheduled tasks

Container-management access

See:

Privilege Escalation

PrivEsc Explorer

docs.title: Discovery and Credential Access
docs.text:
Discovery may identify potential credential locations without accessing them.

Examples:

Service accounts

Configuration files

Credential Manager

SSH directories

Environment variables

Cloud CLI configuration

See:

Credential Access

docs.title: Discovery and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Discovery may identify:

Remote hosts

Administrative protocols

Existing connections

Routes

Domain computers

Shares

Remote-management services

See:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Discovery and C2
docs.text:
Network discovery helps determine:

Outbound connectivity

DNS configuration

Proxy configuration

Segmentation

Reachable management infrastructure

See:

Command and Control

docs.title: Discovery and Persistence
docs.text:
Discovery may identify legitimate mechanisms such as:

Scheduled tasks

Services

Startup locations

Cron

systemd

Cloud automation

See:

Persistence

docs.title: Discovery and Defence Evasion
docs.text:
Security-control discovery provides context for defence-evasion validation.

See:

Defence Evasion

The objective is to understand:

Which controls exist?

Which controls apply?

Which events are generated?

Which behaviours are prevented?

Which behaviours are detected?

docs.title: Discovery and Collection
docs.text:
Discovery identifies where objective-relevant information may exist.

Collection should remain a separate decision.

Discovery
    |
    v
Interesting Data Location
    |
    v
Objective Relevant?
    |
    v
Collection Decision

Do not automatically collect data merely because it was discovered.

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Discovery activity can generate significant telemetry.

Potential sources include:

Process creation

PowerShell

Command-line auditing

LDAP

SMB

DNS

Network connections

EDR

Active Directory logs

Cloud audit logs

SIEM

docs.title: Windows Process Telemetry
docs.text:
Commands such as:

whoami

nltest

net

ipconfig

route

systeminfo

PowerShell CIM queries

may be visible through process telemetry.

Detection should normally consider behaviour and sequence rather than treating every administrative command as malicious.

docs.title: PowerShell Telemetry
docs.text:
Potential sources:

Process creation

Script Block Logging

Module Logging

AMSI

Transcription

EDR

Review:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" -MaxEvents 50

docs.title: LDAP Discovery Telemetry
docs.text:
Large directory queries may produce:

LDAP traffic

Directory-service query patterns

EDR telemetry

Network telemetry

Identity analytics

This is one reason targeted directory discovery is preferable to unnecessary bulk enumeration.

docs.title: Network Discovery Telemetry
docs.text:
Defenders may observe:

Sequential connections

Port sweeps

DNS queries

SMB enumeration

LDAP queries

Authentication attempts

Use the least amount of activity required to answer the engagement question.

docs.title: Discovery Detection Hypothesis
docs.text:
Example:

Hypothesis:
A compromised workstation performing unusual domain and network
discovery should generate sufficient telemetry for the SOC to
identify suspicious situational-awareness activity.

Test:
Perform a small approved sequence of host, identity and domain
discovery actions.

Expected:
Endpoint telemetry and relevant network activity are collected.

Result:
Record whether telemetry, detection and analyst response occur.

docs.title: Detection Outcome
docs.text:
Classify:

Prevented

Detected

Logged

No Alert

No Useful Visibility

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Discovery evidence should remain concise.

Capture:

Test ID

Host

User

Timestamp

Command/query

Relevant result

Security significance

Scope status

docs.title: Example Evidence Record
docs.text:
Evidence ID:
DISC-011

Host:
WS01

User:
CORP\test-user

Observation:
The workstation is joined to corp.example.

Domain Controller:
DC01.corp.example

Source:
DNS SRV lookup and nltest

Security Significance:
Confirms Active Directory environment and identifies the
authoritative domain infrastructure.

Scope:
Domain infrastructure confirmed in scope.

docs.title: Network Evidence Example
docs.text:
Evidence ID:
DISC-019

Host:
APP01

Observation:
The host contains a route to 10.20.30.0/24 that was not directly
reachable from the operator network.

Security Significance:
The host provides network reachability into an additional internal
segment.

Validation:
No broad scanning was performed until scope was confirmed.

docs.title: Security-Control Evidence Example
docs.text:
Evidence ID:
DISC-024

Host:
WS01

Observation:
Microsoft Defender real-time protection was enabled.

AppLocker:
Executable and script collections enabled.

PowerShell:
FullLanguage.

Security Significance:
Provides context for later execution and defence-evasion
validation.

docs.title: Candidate vs Finding
docs.text:
Most discovery observations are not findings.

Examples:

Domain controller discovered

is architecture information.

Microsoft Defender present

is architecture information.

Internal route discovered

is architecture information.

A finding requires a security-relevant weakness.

docs.title: Example Finding - Excessive Network Reachability
docs.text:
Title:
User Workstations Can Directly Reach Administrative Server Network

Observation:
During post-compromise discovery, the assessment workstation was
found to have direct network reachability to the administrative
server segment.

Selected management services on authorised systems were reachable
from the standard workstation network.

Impact:
An attacker who compromises a normal user workstation may be able
to directly interact with higher-value server infrastructure,
increasing opportunities for credential-based lateral movement
and further compromise.

Recommendation:
Review network segmentation between workstation and administrative
server networks. Permit only explicitly required flows and monitor
administrative protocols crossing security zones.

docs.title: Example Finding - Excessive Information Exposure
docs.text:
Title:
Application Configuration Exposes Internal Infrastructure Details

Observation:
A configuration file accessible to the standard assessment user
contained internal server names, service endpoints and environment
information.

No credential material was required to demonstrate the issue.

Impact:
The information significantly reduces the discovery effort
required after initial compromise and provides an attacker with
direct knowledge of internal application dependencies.

Recommendation:
Restrict access to sensitive configuration information and remove
unnecessary infrastructure details from files accessible to
standard users.

docs.title: Running Everything Immediately
docs.text:
Avoid:

Run every enumeration tool

Scan every subnet

Query every AD object

Enumerate every share

Start with context and expand only when justified.

docs.title: Treating Information as Vulnerability
docs.text:
Example:

Domain Admins group exists

is not a vulnerability.

docs.title: Ignoring Existing Connections
docs.text:
Existing connections can be more useful than scanning.

They reveal systems the host already communicates with.

docs.title: Ignoring Routes
docs.text: Routes often explain where the host can reach and whether pivoting may be possible.

docs.title: Ignoring DNS
docs.text:
Internal DNS can reveal:

Domains

Domain controllers

Application servers

Management systems

Service records

docs.title: Ignoring Security Controls
docs.text: Knowing which controls are active is necessary to correctly interpret later execution and detection results.

docs.title: Over-Collecting
docs.text:
Do not collect:

Entire user profiles

All documents

All shares

All browser data

Every domain object

unless specifically required and authorised.

docs.title: Trusting Automated Enumeration Blindly
docs.text:
Automated tools produce candidates.

Always validate important observations manually.

docs.title: Automated Discovery Tools
docs.text:
Tools commonly used in authorised assessments include:

Seatbelt

WinPEAS

SharpHound

BloodHound

LinPEAS

LinEnum

NetExec

Nmap

Each can generate substantial telemetry and output.

docs.title: Built-In First
docs.text:
Built-in commands are often sufficient for initial discovery.

Advantages:

Less deployment

Lower operational complexity

Easier cleanup

Clearer evidence

Reduced tooling dependency

Specialist tools remain useful when they provide justified additional value.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Discovery can be reduced to:

Understand where you are.

Understand who you are.

Understand what privilege you have.

Understand the host.

Understand the network.

Understand identity.

Understand the domain.

Understand applications.

Understand defensive controls.

Identify security boundaries.

Identify candidate attack paths.

Validate scope before expanding.

Prefer existing context over unnecessary scanning.

Collect only what supports the objective.

Record important observations.

Use discovery to decide what to test next.

Discovery should answer a question

Before running a discovery command or tool, know what question it is intended to answer. If the result will not change the attack-path decision, the activity may not be necessary.

Discovery is not permission expansion

An internal hostname, subnet, domain, cloud resource, share, or administrative system becoming visible from a compromised host does not automatically bring that resource into scope. Revalidate the Rules of Engagement before expanding active testing.

docs.title: Red Team Execution
docs.text:
Execution is the stage where an attacker causes code, commands, scripts, or applications to run on a target system.

Within an authorised red team assessment, execution testing should answer:

What can execute?

Under which identity?

With which privileges?

From which locations?

Which interpreters are available?

Which application-control policies apply?

Which endpoint controls inspect execution?

What telemetry is generated?

Is suspicious execution detected?

Can defenders reconstruct what happened?

Execution should not be treated as:

Payload runs = security control bypassed

Instead, evaluate the complete control path:

Execution Attempt
      |
      v
Application Control
      |
      v
Endpoint Prevention
      |
      v
Execution
      |
      v
Telemetry
      |
      v
Detection
      |
      v
Response

Authorised testing only

Execute commands, scripts, binaries, and remote administration activity only on explicitly authorised systems. Prefer harmless validation artifacts and minimal-impact techniques when determining whether an execution boundary exists.

docs.title: Execution Objectives
docs.text:
Common objectives include:

Determine available execution mechanisms

Determine execution context

Identify interpreters

Identify application-control boundaries

Identify writable execution locations

Validate script-control policies

Validate endpoint prevention

Validate execution telemetry

Validate detection logic

Understand remote execution boundaries

Determine whether execution enables the next attack phase

docs.title: Execution Is a Security Boundary
docs.text:
The important question is not merely:

Can I run a command?

Ask:

What should this identity be allowed to execute?

What should be blocked?

Which locations are trusted?

Which binaries are permitted?

Which scripts are permitted?

Which interpreters are available?

Which controls enforce those decisions?

docs.title: Constrained Language Mode
docs.text:
PowerShell Constrained Language Mode, or CLM, restricts certain PowerShell capabilities.

Typical restrictions affect:

Arbitrary .NET type access

COM interaction

Type creation

Some method invocation

Advanced scripting functionality

CLM is most useful when enforced as part of a broader application-control architecture.

docs.title: Safe CLM Validation
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

A harmless restricted-operation test can help determine whether language restrictions are actually enforced.

For example:

Add-Type -TypeDefinition 'public class ExecutionControlTest { public static string Value = "test"; }'

Under a restricted language environment, this may be prevented.

The goal is to validate the boundary, not to bypass it.

docs.title: Execution Policy
docs.text:

docs.title: Execution Policy Is Not Application Control
docs.text:
PowerShell Execution Policy should not be treated as a strong security boundary by itself.

It primarily helps control script execution behaviour.

Stronger controls include:

AppLocker

Windows Defender Application Control

Endpoint security

Privilege management

Script logging

AMSI

Binary Launches

docs.title: EICAR Validation
docs.text:
The EICAR test file is designed to validate antivirus detection without using real malware.

Canonical EICAR test string:

X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*

Create the test artifact:

$eicar = 'X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*'
Set-Content -Path "$env:TEMP\eicar.com.txt" -Value $eicar -NoNewline

Expected behaviour depends on endpoint configuration.

Possible outcomes:

Creation blocked

File quarantined

Detection generated

Alert generated

File remains but detection recorded

docs.title: EICAR Interpretation
docs.text:
If EICAR is blocked:

Antivirus signature validation succeeded.

It does not prove:

Every malicious technique will be blocked.

Likewise, if a behavioural simulation executes, that does not automatically prove the endpoint product has been bypassed.

docs.text:
The Antimalware Scan Interface provides an interface through which applications can submit content to antimalware products for inspection.

AMSI commonly applies to environments such as:

JavaScript

VBScript

Other integrated applications

docs.title: AMSI Validation
docs.text:
The objective should be to determine:

Is AMSI-integrated inspection present?

Does suspicious test content generate telemetry?

Does endpoint security respond?

Are detections forwarded centrally?

A red team report should distinguish an AMSI control observation from a claim that AMSI itself was defeated.

docs.title: AMSI Bypass Assessment
docs.text:
During an authorised assessment, bypass resistance may be evaluated conceptually across areas such as:

AMSI integration

Script content inspection

Runtime protections

Application control

Behaviour monitoring

EDR telemetry

Detection engineering

Avoid treating one execution result as proof of a universal AMSI bypass.

A useful safe validation mechanism is:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\wscript.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Possible result:

Allowed

or:

Denied

docs.title: Test a Specific File
docs.text:
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "C:\Path\To\Test.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

This checks the effective policy decision without requiring execution.

docs.title: AppLocker Path Rules
docs.text:
A rule such as:

%WINDIR%\*

allows files matching that path according to the rule's scope and collection.

The security question becomes:

Can a lower-privileged user modify locations covered by an
allow rule?

docs.title: Writable Trusted Locations
docs.text:
A potentially important control condition is:

Writable by Standard User
          +
Allowed by Application Control
          =
Potential Execution-Control Weakness

Both conditions should be validated.

docs.title: Test Directory Permissions
docs.text:
Example:

Get-Acl -LiteralPath "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder" |
    Format-List Owner,AccessToString

Do not assume a directory is writable solely because of its location.

docs.title: Safe Write Test
docs.text:
$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID.tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Output "Write succeeded"
}
finally {
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}

This validates write access without introducing an executable payload.

docs.text:

      v

docs.title: WDAC
docs.text:
Windows Defender Application Control is now generally described by Microsoft as App Control for Business.

It can control which:

Executables

DLLs

Scripts

Installers

Applications

docs.text:
Important logs include:

Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational" -MaxEvents 50

docs.text:

Policy exists in audit mode

Policy exists and allowed the file

Policy exists and blocked the file
