Authorised testing only

Red team infrastructure should only be used to support explicitly authorised security assessments. Restrict infrastructure to approved targets and activities, protect customer information and credentials, maintain appropriate logging, and remove temporary infrastructure when the engagement ends.

docs.title: Initial Access
docs.text:
Initial access is the stage of a red team assessment where an authorised tester establishes the first controlled foothold in the target environment.

The objective is not simply to obtain execution.

Initial access should answer questions such as:

Which external security boundary was crossed?
What weakness or trust relationship enabled access?
Which identity or system was affected?
What privilege level was obtained?
Which defensive controls observed the activity?
Was the activity detected?
What business systems became reachable?

A simplified model is:

Reconnaissance
      |
      v
Attack Surface
      |
      v
Candidate Entry Point
      |
      v
Validate
      |
      v
Initial Access
      |
      v
Establish Context
      |
      v
Controlled Foothold

Initial access techniques must remain within the approved scope and Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Initial Access Objectives
docs.text:
The purpose of initial access depends on the engagement.

Potential objectives include:

Obtain access to a test workstation
Authenticate to an exposed service
Establish access to a web application
Access an approved cloud identity
Reach a controlled internal system
Evaluate phishing controls
Evaluate remote-access controls
Evaluate external application security
Measure detection and response

Initial access should normally stop once sufficient access has been obtained to continue the agreed attack path.

docs.title: Initial Access Model
docs.text:
A useful methodology is:

External Attack Surface
         |
         v
Identify Entry Points
         |
         +--> Web Applications
         |
         +--> Remote Services
         |
         +--> Identity
         |
         +--> Cloud
         |
         +--> Email
         |
         +--> VPN
         |
         +--> Third Parties
         |
         v
Prioritise
         |
         v
Validate
         |
         v
Initial Foothold
         |
         v
Document

docs.title: Before Testing
docs.text:
Before attempting initial access, confirm:

Written authorisation
Target scope
Permitted techniques
Testing window
Source infrastructure
Credential-use rules
Social-engineering permissions
Payload restrictions
Data-access restrictions
Third-party exclusions
Availability restrictions
Emergency contacts
Stop conditions

Do not infer authorisation from a system being internet accessible.

docs.title: Attack Surface Mapping
docs.text:
Initial access begins with understanding the external attack surface.

Potential assets include:

Domains
Subdomains
IP addresses
Web applications
APIs
VPN gateways
Remote desktop gateways
SSH services
Email infrastructure
Identity providers
Cloud services
Administrative portals
File-transfer services
Developer portals
CI/CD systems
Third-party integrations

The objective is to transform raw reconnaissance into candidate entry points.

docs.title: Attack Surface Workflow
docs.text:
Domains
   |
   v
Subdomains
   |
   v
Resolve DNS
   |
   v
Identify Live Services
   |
   v
Fingerprint Technology
   |
   v
Identify Authentication
   |
   v
Prioritise Entry Points

docs.title: Domain Discovery
docs.text:
Start with the authorised root domains.

Examples:

example.com
example.nl
example.org

Potential sources for subdomain discovery include:

Certificate transparency
DNS records
Search engines
Public repositories
Passive DNS
Internet datasets
Cloud references
Organisation documentation

Subdomain enumeration should be covered in the dedicated reconnaissance notes where applicable.

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Resolve discovered names before deeper testing.

Examples:

dig +short portal.example.com

host portal.example.com

nslookup portal.example.com

Record the relationship:

Hostname
   |
   v
IP Address
   |
   v
Hosting Provider / ASN
   |
   v
Observed Service

docs.title: HTTP Probing
docs.text:
For an authorised list of discovered hosts, HTTP probing can identify reachable web services.

Useful information includes:

URL
Status code
Page title
Technology
Web server
Redirect
TLS
IP address

A typical ProjectDiscovery workflow can use httpx.

Example:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -title -tech-detect -status-code

Save results where required:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -title -tech-detect -status-code -o httpx-results.txt

Review results rather than treating every responsive host equally.

docs.title: Technology Identification
docs.text:
Technology identification helps prioritise testing.

Potential technologies include:

IIS
Nginx
Apache
Tomcat
Next.js
WordPress
SharePoint
Exchange
Citrix
Fortinet
Palo Alto
VMware
Jenkins
GitLab
Grafana
Kibana
Custom applications

Useful tools can include:

httpx
WhatWeb
Wappalyzer
Nmap
Manual inspection

Example:

whatweb https://portal.example.com

Technology detection is a starting point, not proof of vulnerability.

docs.title: Authentication Surface
docs.text:
Identify which external services require authentication.

Examples:

VPN
SSO
Microsoft 365
Citrix
RDP gateway
Webmail
Administrative portals
Developer portals
Cloud consoles
Git services
File-transfer services

For each authentication surface, record:

Authentication method
MFA
SSO provider
Username format
Password policy observations
Rate limiting
Lockout behaviour
Federation
External identity support

docs.title: Initial Access Categories
docs.text:
Initial access can broadly originate from:

Application Weakness
Credential Access
Remote Service
Cloud Identity
Misconfiguration
Approved Social Engineering
Approved Physical Access
Third-Party Trust
Supply-Chain Scenario

The exact categories tested depend on the engagement.

docs.title: External Web Applications
docs.text:
Internet-facing applications are common initial access surfaces.

Testing may identify weaknesses involving:

Authentication
Authorisation
File upload
Command injection
Deserialization
Server-side request forgery
SQL injection
Path traversal
File inclusion
Business logic
API security
Known vulnerable components
Administrative functionality

Use the dedicated web application security notes for detailed testing.

Web Application Security

docs.title: Application Initial Access Model
docs.text:
External Application
        |
        v
Identify Weakness
        |
        v
Validate Impact
        |
        v
Does It Cross a Security Boundary?
        |
       Yes
        |
        v
Controlled Access
        |
        v
Establish Context

Do not unnecessarily escalate a web vulnerability into operating-system access when the engagement objective has already been met.

docs.title: Known Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Exposed software should be checked against known security issues where relevant.

A responsible workflow is:

Identify Product
      |
      v
Identify Version
      |
      v
Verify Configuration
      |
      v
Research Advisory
      |
      v
Check Preconditions
      |
      v
Validate Safely

Do not rely solely on version banners.

Backported patches and vendor-specific builds can invalidate simple version comparisons.

docs.title: Vulnerability Research Sources
docs.text:
Useful sources include:

Vendor advisories
NVD
CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog
GitHub Security Advisories
Project repositories
Security research publications

Prefer primary vendor information when determining whether a particular version or configuration is affected.

docs.title: Remote Services
docs.text:
Externally exposed remote services can provide initial access where valid credentials or an authorised vulnerability are available.

Examples include:

VPN
SSH
RDP
Remote Desktop Gateway
Citrix
WinRM
SMB
VNC
Administrative web interfaces
File-transfer services

Exposure alone is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: Remote Service Assessment
docs.text:
For each service:

Identify Service
      |
      v
Identify Version
      |
      v
Identify Authentication
      |
      v
Identify MFA
      |
      v
Check Configuration
      |
      v
Check Known Vulnerabilities
      |
      v
Assess Credential Risk

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
SSH may be externally exposed for legitimate administration.

Identify:

Version
Authentication methods
Password authentication
Public-key authentication
Source restrictions
MFA
Rate limiting
Administrative accounts

Basic service identification:

nmap -sV -p 22 TARGET

Do not perform password guessing unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
RDP exposure should be evaluated in context.

Potential considerations include:

Internet exposure
Network Level Authentication
MFA
RD Gateway
Account lockout
Administrative access
Source restrictions
Version and patching

Basic service identification:

nmap -sV -p 3389 TARGET

Direct internet exposure can increase attack surface, but the final finding should reflect the actual controls present.

docs.title: VPN
docs.text:
VPN gateways are important initial access surfaces because successful authentication may provide internal network access.

Assess:

Product
Version
Authentication
MFA
Certificate requirements
Account lockout
Conditional access
Device compliance
Split tunnelling
Accessible networks

A valid credential without MFA can have significantly different impact from the same credential protected by strong MFA and device controls.

docs.title: File Transfer Services
docs.text:
Externally accessible file-transfer infrastructure may include:

SFTP
FTPS
Managed File Transfer
Web-based upload portals
Vendor file-transfer products

Assess:

Authentication
Anonymous access
Version
Administrative interfaces
Upload controls
Access boundaries
Known vulnerabilities

docs.title: Credential-Based Initial Access
docs.text:
Valid credentials may provide initial access without exploiting a software vulnerability.

Potential sources during an authorised assessment include:

Customer-provided test credentials
Credentials discovered during approved testing
Approved password-spray results
Previously compromised test identities
Configuration exposure
Approved credential reuse scenarios

Credential handling should follow the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Password Spraying
docs.text:
Password spraying tests whether a small number of candidate passwords work across multiple accounts.

It differs from traditional brute force:

Brute Force

One Account
    |
    +--> Password 1
    +--> Password 2
    +--> Password 3
    +--> Password 4


Password Spray

Password 1
    |
    +--> User A
    +--> User B
    +--> User C
    +--> User D

Password spraying can lock accounts or trigger defensive controls.

It should only be performed when explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Password Spray Planning
docs.text:
Before an approved spray, understand:

Account lockout threshold
Lockout duration
Authentication provider
MFA
Conditional access
Excluded accounts
Testing window
Maximum attempts
Monitoring requirements
Emergency stop procedure

Do not guess safe spray rates without understanding the target policy.

docs.title: Username Enumeration
docs.text:
Authentication systems may expose whether an account exists through differences in:

Error messages
HTTP status
Response size
Response timing
Password-reset workflow
Registration workflow
SSO behaviour

Where observed, determine whether the difference provides meaningful security impact.

docs.title: Multi-Factor Authentication
docs.text:
MFA significantly changes the initial access model.

Password
   |
   v
Correct
   |
   v
MFA
   |
   +--> Failed --> Access Denied
   |
   +--> Passed --> Access Granted

Assess the actual MFA implementation rather than simply recording that MFA exists.

docs.title: MFA Considerations
docs.text:
Potential areas include:

Coverage
Enrolment
Recovery
Legacy authentication
Trusted devices
Conditional access
Session lifetime
Remembered sessions
Administrative accounts
Break-glass accounts

MFA testing should remain within explicitly authorised scenarios.

docs.title: Identity Provider
docs.text:
Common identity platforms can include:

Microsoft Entra ID
Active Directory Federation Services
Okta
Ping Identity
Google Workspace
Custom SAML providers
OIDC providers

Identity architecture can become a central initial access boundary.

docs.title: SSO
docs.text:
Single sign-on can connect one authentication event to many applications.

Identity Provider
       |
       +--> Application A
       |
       +--> Application B
       |
       +--> Application C
       |
       +--> VPN

Compromise of one identity may therefore have broader impact than compromise of a standalone application account.

docs.title: Cloud Initial Access
docs.text:
Cloud environments introduce additional initial access surfaces.

Potential examples include:

Cloud console
Cloud API
Access keys
Service principals
Application registrations
Federated identities
CI/CD secrets
Storage credentials
Managed identities
Developer credentials

Cloud access should be tested against the explicitly authorised tenant and subscriptions/accounts.

docs.title: Cloud Credential Exposure
docs.text:
Potential credential locations may include:

Public repositories
CI/CD configuration
Environment files
Application configuration
Developer workstations
Shell history
Deployment scripts
Infrastructure-as-code files

If credentials are discovered, first determine:

Which tenant/account do they belong to?
Are they still valid?
What permissions do they have?
Is validation authorised?

Do not use discovered credentials against unrelated environments.

docs.title: Public Repositories
docs.text:
Public repositories can unintentionally expose security-sensitive information.

Review authorised organisational repositories for:

API keys
Tokens
Passwords
Connection strings
Internal hostnames
Cloud identifiers
Deployment scripts
Private endpoints
Configuration files
Historical secrets

Secret scanning should include repository history where appropriate.

docs.title: Secret Validation
docs.text:
A discovered secret should not automatically be used.

Use:

Secret Found
    |
    v
Identify Owner
    |
    v
Identify Scope
    |
    v
Confirm Validation Is Authorised
    |
   Yes
    |
    v
Minimal Validation
    |
    v
Document

Avoid accessing unnecessary data after proving the credential is valid.

docs.title: Email as an Initial Access Surface
docs.text:
Email infrastructure may be relevant when social engineering is explicitly authorised.

Potential assessment areas include:

Phishing resilience
Attachment controls
URL filtering
Authentication
MFA
Email gateway detection
User reporting
Security awareness
Incident response

Social engineering requires explicit Rules of Engagement because it involves human participants.

docs.title: Phishing
docs.text:
A phishing simulation should have a defined objective.

Examples:

Measure delivery
Measure link interaction
Measure credential submission to a synthetic portal
Measure attachment blocking
Measure user reporting
Measure SOC response

Avoid collecting real passwords where synthetic validation can achieve the same objective.

docs.title: Phishing Safety
docs.text:
A controlled phishing exercise should define:

Target population
Excluded users
Approved pretext
Approved sender infrastructure
Permitted attachment types
Permitted links
Credential-handling policy
Testing window
Emergency contact
Data retention
Success criteria

Sensitive groups may require exclusion depending on the engagement.

docs.title: Synthetic Credential Collection
docs.text:
Where credential-entry behaviour is being measured, prefer synthetic collection models.

For example:

User Opens Test Page
       |
       v
User Submits Form
       |
       v
Record Event
       |
       v
Discard Password Value

Often it is sufficient to record that submission occurred rather than storing the entered secret.

docs.title: Payload Delivery
docs.text:
Some authorised assessments may involve delivery of a controlled assessment artifact.

Delivery mechanisms can include:

Approved web download
Approved email attachment
Customer-provided transfer mechanism
Existing authorised foothold
Controlled shared location

Every delivered file should be tracked.

docs.title: Payload Inventory
docs.text:
Example:

Artifact Purpose SHA-256 Target Cleanup assessment.bin Controlled execution test <hash> Test workstation Required enum.ps1 Enumeration <hash> Test workstation Required

Calculate a hash on Linux:

sha256sum assessment.bin

PowerShell:

Get-FileHash .\assessment.bin -Algorithm SHA256

docs.title: Payload Hosting
docs.text:
Payload infrastructure should be controlled.

A typical architecture is:

Operator Repository
       |
       v
Controlled HTTPS Server
       |
       v
Authorised Target

Do not expose:

Customer evidence
Operator SSH keys
C2 credentials
Infrastructure secrets
Unrelated tooling
Internal reports

docs.title: Initial Execution
docs.text:
Once an approved artifact reaches a target, execution itself may cross an important defensive boundary.

Relevant controls can include:

Application control
Antivirus
EDR
Attack Surface Reduction
Script controls
AMSI
Browser protections
Email security
Mark-of-the-Web
User privilege

Record which controls permit, block, or alert on the action.

docs.title: Windows Initial Context
docs.text:
After obtaining authorised Windows access, establish the security context before further action.

whoami

whoami /all

hostname

ipconfig /all

PowerShell:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Do not immediately begin broad internal enumeration before understanding the host.

docs.title: Linux Initial Context
docs.text:
For Linux:

whoami

id

hostname

uname -a

cat /etc/os-release

ip addr

Determine:

Current user
Groups
Host
Operating system
Network interfaces
Privilege level

docs.title: Establishing the Foothold
docs.text:
A useful post-access workflow is:

Initial Access
      |
      v
Identify User
      |
      v
Identify Host
      |
      v
Identify Privilege
      |
      v
Identify Security Controls
      |
      v
Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Record Evidence
      |
      v
Continue Only as Required

docs.title: Scope Revalidation
docs.text:
Initial access can reveal systems that were not visible during external reconnaissance.

For example:

External Application
        |
        v
Initial Access
        |
        v
Internal Network
        |
        +--> Server A
        +--> Server B
        +--> Third Party
        +--> Management Network

Do not assume every newly reachable system is in scope.

Revalidate the scope before interacting with uncertain assets.

docs.title: Third-Party Boundaries
docs.text:
Modern organisations depend heavily on third parties.

Examples include:

SaaS
Cloud providers
Managed service providers
Payment providers
CDNs
Email providers
Identity providers
External developers
Suppliers

Technical connectivity does not establish testing authorisation.

Third-party systems require appropriate permission.

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Initial access can generate telemetry across several layers.

Internet
   |
   v
Firewall
   |
   v
WAF / Proxy
   |
   v
Application
   |
   v
Identity
   |
   v
Endpoint
   |
   v
EDR
   |
   v
SIEM

docs.title: Web Detection
docs.text:
Potential web telemetry includes:

HTTP requests
Authentication failures
Application errors
WAF events
Suspicious parameters
File uploads
Administrative access
New sessions
Unusual user agents
Source addresses

Application telemetry should be correlated with infrastructure and identity logs where possible.

docs.title: Identity Detection
docs.text:
Potential identity signals include:

Failed authentication
Successful authentication
New device
New location
Impossible travel
MFA challenge
MFA failure
Password spray
Account lockout
Risky sign-in
Legacy authentication
Token issuance

Cloud identity providers can provide particularly rich authentication telemetry.

docs.title: Endpoint Detection
docs.text:
Where initial access results in endpoint execution, telemetry can include:

Process creation
File creation
Network connections
Script execution
Module loads
Security-control events
User logon
Child processes
Application-control events

The exact data depends on the defensive stack.

docs.title: Network Detection
docs.text:
Network controls may observe:

External source
Destination
Port
DNS query
TLS metadata
Proxy request
Connection duration
Bytes transferred
Connection frequency

docs.title: Detection Validation
docs.text:
Track the defensive outcome of important actions.

Example:

Activity Logged Alerted Investigated Prevented External authentication Yes No No No Test artifact download Yes Yes Yes No Controlled execution Yes Yes Yes Yes

This turns initial access testing into measurable security-control validation.

docs.title: Initial Access Evidence
docs.text:
Evidence should establish:

Timestamp
Source
Target
Technique
Affected identity
Affected system
Result
Privilege obtained
Security control response
Objective relationship

For example:

Timestamp:
2026-09-05 10:14 UTC

Source:
Authorised assessment infrastructure

Target:
TEST-WKS01

Identity:
CORP\testuser

Result:
Controlled access established

Privilege:
Standard user

Detection:
Endpoint alert generated

docs.title: Minimal Evidence
docs.text:
After proving initial access, avoid unnecessary actions.

Access Established
       |
       v
Objective Proven?
    /       \
  Yes        No
   |          |
   v          v
 Stop      Continue
           Minimally

The ability to access additional information does not mean it must be collected.

docs.title: Candidate vs Confirmed
docs.text: Use clear confidence levels.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
Evidence suggests a possible initial access path.

Exposed service
Potential credential
Interesting configuration
Potential vulnerability

Further validation is required.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
Multiple conditions support practical initial access.

Affected version confirmed
Required configuration confirmed
Authentication weakness confirmed

Minimal validation may still be required.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
Controlled testing demonstrates the security boundary can actually be crossed.

Authentication succeeded
Controlled execution occurred
Approved account accessed
Approved objective reached

docs.title: Initial Access Does Not Mean Domain Compromise
docs.text:
A foothold should be reported accurately.

For example:

Internet
   |
   v
Web Application
   |
   v
Low-Privilege Service Account

does not automatically mean:

Domain Compromise

The report should reflect the actual privilege and reachability demonstrated.

docs.title: Initial Access Does Not Mean Administrator
docs.text:
Likewise:

Standard User Access

should not be described as:

Administrative Access

unless that privilege boundary was actually crossed.

docs.title: Common Assessment Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid:

Testing hosts outside scope
Assuming every exposed service is vulnerable
Using discovered credentials without checking scope
Running uncontrolled password attacks
Ignoring MFA
Collecting unnecessary sensitive data
Deploying untracked artifacts
Ignoring third-party boundaries
Continuing after the objective is proven
Failing to record defensive response

docs.title: Remediation Model
docs.text:
Initial access remediation depends on the entry path.

A general model is:

Reduce Attack Surface
        |
        v
Patch External Services
        |
        v
Harden Authentication
        |
        v
Enforce MFA
        |
        v
Apply Conditional Access
        |
        v
Restrict Administrative Interfaces
        |
        v
Remove Exposed Secrets
        |
        v
Improve Application Security
        |
        v
Improve Endpoint Controls
        |
        v
Improve Detection
        |
        v
Test Again

docs.title: External Service Hardening
docs.text:
Potential controls include:

Remove unnecessary internet exposure
Restrict source networks
Use VPN or zero-trust access
Patch promptly
Disable legacy protocols
Enforce MFA
Use strong authentication
Monitor authentication
Rate limit where appropriate
Use account lockout carefully

docs.title: Credential Hardening
docs.text:
Potential improvements include:

MFA
Unique passwords
Password managers
Credential rotation
Secret scanning
Conditional access
Risk-based authentication
Removal of legacy authentication
Privileged access management
Short-lived credentials

docs.title: Application Hardening
docs.text:
Potential improvements include:

Secure development lifecycle
Dependency management
Authentication hardening
Authorisation testing
Input validation
Secure file handling
Secret management
Security headers
Logging
WAF where appropriate
Regular penetration testing

docs.title: Phishing Resilience
docs.text:
Where phishing is part of the threat model:

Email filtering
URL analysis
Attachment controls
MFA
Phishing-resistant authentication
User reporting
Security awareness
Browser protections
Endpoint controls
SOC monitoring

User awareness should complement technical controls rather than replace them.

docs.title: Initial Access and C2
docs.text:
Initial access and C2 are separate concepts.

Initial Access

Execution / Authentication

      v

      |

C2 if Required

An engagement may successfully establish initial access without deploying a C2 agent.

Where C2 is required, use the dedicated notes:

Command and Control

  • Windows PrivEsc Explorer

Authorised testing only

Initial access testing can affect internet-facing applications, identities, remote-access services, cloud environments, endpoints, email systems, and human participants. Perform only techniques explicitly permitted by the Rules of Engagement. Password attacks, social engineering, payload delivery, credential use, and access to third-party systems require particularly clear authorisation. Collect only the evidence required to demonstrate the agreed security impact.

docs.title: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Lateral movement is the process of using an existing authorised foothold to access another system, identity, application, or network segment during a security assessment.

A typical attack path can be represented as:

Initial Access
      |
      v
Workstation A
      |
      v
Credential / Trust
      |
      v
Server B
      |
      v
Additional Network Access
      |
      v
Server C

Lateral movement should answer more than:

Can I reach another machine?

A useful assessment should determine:

Why was the movement possible?
Which identity enabled it?
Which protocol was used?
Which trust boundary was crossed?
What privilege was obtained?
Which segmentation controls were bypassed or correctly enforced?
Was the activity logged?
Was it detected?
How far could the attack path reasonably continue?

Lateral movement should always remain within the approved scope and Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Lateral Movement Objectives
docs.text:
Potential objectives include:

Validate credential reuse
Validate administrative access
Test network segmentation
Evaluate remote-management controls
Evaluate identity boundaries
Test east-west monitoring
Validate privileged access design
Evaluate detection and response
Reach an approved assessment objective

The objective should not be to access every reachable host.

Stop once sufficient evidence exists to demonstrate the relevant attack path.

docs.title: Lateral Movement Model
docs.text:
Current Foothold
      |
      v
Identify Identity
      |
      v
Identify Reachable Systems
      |
      v
Identify Trust
      |
      v
Identify Authentication Material
      |
      v
Select Remote Access Method
      |
      v
Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Minimal Validation
      |
      v
New Security Context
      |
      v
Record Detection

docs.title: Lateral Movement vs Pivoting
docs.text: These concepts are related but different.

docs.title: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Lateral movement establishes access to another system or security context.

Host A
  |
  | Authentication / Remote Administration
  v
Host B

Examples:

SMB
WinRM
RDP
SSH
WMI
DCOM
Remote service administration
Application administration

docs.title: Pivoting
docs.text:
Pivoting uses one system as a network path to reach another network or host.

Operator
   |
   v
Host A
   |
   v
Internal Network
   |
   v
Host B

Tools such as:

Ligolo-ng
Chisel
SSH
SOCKS proxies
proxychains
Framework-specific pivots

primarily provide network reachability.

They do not by themselves provide authentication to the destination system.

A common attack path therefore combines both concepts:

Pivot
  +
Credential
  +
Remote Protocol
  =
Lateral Movement

docs.title: Before Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Before moving to another system, verify:

Destination is in scope
Identity use is authorised
Credential use is authorised
Protocol is permitted
Testing window permits the activity
Availability requirements are understood
Third-party boundaries are understood
Expected security controls are known

Technical reachability does not establish authorisation.

docs.title: Establish Current Context
docs.text:
Before lateral movement, understand the existing foothold.

On Windows:

whoami

whoami /all

hostname

ipconfig /all

route print

PowerShell:

Get-NetIPConfiguration

Get-NetRoute

On Linux:

whoami

id

hostname

ip addr

ip route

Determine:

Current identity
Privilege
Network interfaces
Routes
DNS configuration
Domain membership
Reachable networks
Security controls

docs.title: Network Reachability
docs.text:
Lateral movement requires a usable network path.

Conceptually:

Source Host
    |
    v
Network Control
    |
    +--> Allowed
    |
    +--> Blocked

Useful questions include:

Can the source reach the destination?
Which ports are reachable?
Does a firewall restrict east-west traffic?
Does the destination accept remote administration?
Does authentication work from this source?

docs.title: Windows Connectivity Testing
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Test-NetConnection SERVER -Port 445

WinRM:

Test-NetConnection SERVER -Port 5985

RDP:

Test-NetConnection SERVER -Port 3389

SSH:

Test-NetConnection SERVER -Port 22

A successful TCP connection only confirms network reachability.

It does not confirm authentication or authorisation.

docs.title: Linux Connectivity Testing
docs.text:
Useful options include:

nc -vz SERVER 22

nc -vz SERVER 445

nc -vz SERVER 3389

nc -vz SERVER 5985

Nmap can be useful where scanning the internal segment is permitted:

nmap -Pn -p 22,135,139,445,3389,5985,5986 SERVER

Keep internal scanning proportional to the assessment objective.

docs.title: Common Lateral Movement Protocols
docs.text:
Common remote-access mechanisms include:

Method Common Port Typical Platform SMB TCP 445 Windows WinRM HTTP TCP 5985 Windows WinRM HTTPS TCP 5986 Windows RDP TCP 3389 Windows WMI/DCOM TCP 135 + dynamic RPC Windows SSH TCP 22 Windows/Linux VNC TCP 5900+ Windows/Linux Application administration Varies Both

Ports can differ from defaults.

docs.title: Credential Reuse
docs.text:
Credential reuse is one of the most important lateral movement conditions.

Host A
   |
   v
Credential
   |
   +--> Host B
   |
   +--> Host C
   |
   +--> Host D

Examples include:

Reused local administrator password
Reused service-account credential
Domain account with access to multiple hosts
Shared SSH key
Shared application credential
Cloud identity with access to multiple systems

Credential reuse increases the blast radius of a single compromise.

docs.title: Local Administrator Password Reuse
docs.text:
Consider:

HOST-A
Administrator : Password-A

HOST-B
Administrator : Password-A

HOST-C
Administrator : Password-A

Compromise of one local administrator credential can potentially affect multiple systems.

Controls such as Windows LAPS are designed to reduce this risk.

See:

LAPS

docs.title: Windows Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Windows environments commonly expose several remote-management mechanisms.

SMB
WinRM
RDP
WMI
DCOM
Remote services
Scheduled administration
PowerShell remoting
SSH

docs.title: SMB
docs.text:
Server Message Block is used for:

File sharing
Administrative shares
Named pipes
Remote administration
Authentication

Common port:

TCP 445

Basic reachability:

Test-NetConnection SERVER -Port 445

docs.title: SMB Shares
docs.text:
From Windows:

net view \\SERVER

Access an authorised share:

dir \\SERVER\SHARE

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem \\SERVER\SHARE

Access to a share does not automatically imply administrative access.

docs.title: Administrative Shares
docs.text:
Windows commonly provides administrative shares such as:

ADMIN$
C$
IPC$

Their accessibility can indicate elevated remote privileges.

Example validation:

dir \\SERVER\C$

Use only where the supplied identity is authorised for the target.

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec can help validate authorised authentication across Windows services.

General SMB syntax:

nxc smb TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD'

For a domain account:

nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD'

Against an approved host list:

nxc smb targets.txt -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD'

Avoid broad credential testing unless the engagement explicitly permits it.

See:

NetExec Cheatsheet

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
Windows Remote Management provides remote management using WS-Management.

Common ports:

5985 - HTTP
5986 - HTTPS

Check reachability:

Test-NetConnection SERVER -Port 5985

PowerShell can test whether WinRM responds:

Test-WSMan SERVER

docs.title: PowerShell Remoting
docs.text:
Where authorised and configured:

Enter-PSSession -ComputerName SERVER

With an approved credential object:

$cred = Get-Credential
Enter-PSSession -ComputerName SERVER -Credential $cred

For remote command execution:

Invoke-Command -ComputerName SERVER -ScriptBlock { hostname }

This provides a clean validation of remote administrative access.

docs.title: Evil-WinRM
docs.text:
Evil-WinRM is commonly used during authorised Windows assessments where WinRM access is available.

Typical syntax:

evil-winrm -i SERVER -u USER -p 'PASSWORD'

It should be treated as a remote administration client rather than proof of a vulnerability.

The finding should explain why the identity had inappropriate remote access if that is the actual issue.

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
Remote Desktop Protocol provides interactive graphical access to Windows systems.

Default port:

TCP 3389

Check:

Test-NetConnection SERVER -Port 3389

RDP access can be constrained by:

Firewall
Network Level Authentication
User rights
Remote Desktop Users group
MFA
RD Gateway
Conditional access
Network segmentation

docs.title: Linux RDP Client
docs.text:
FreeRDP can connect to an authorised Windows host:

xfreerdp /v:SERVER /u:USER

Domain identity:

xfreerdp /v:SERVER /d:DOMAIN /u:USER

Prefer interactive password entry rather than placing passwords directly in shell history.

docs.title: WMI
docs.text:
Windows Management Instrumentation supports remote management.

Conceptually:

Source
  |
  v
RPC Endpoint Mapper
  |
  v
WMI
  |
  v
Target

WMI commonly involves:

TCP 135
Dynamic RPC ports

PowerShell can query a remote authorised system using CIM where the environment permits it:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem -ComputerName SERVER

A successful remote query can be sufficient to demonstrate that the identity has remote-management access.

docs.title: Impacket WMIExec
docs.text:
Impacket includes remote administration utilities frequently used in authorised assessments.

A common WMI authentication form is:

impacket-wmiexec DOMAIN/USER@SERVER

The tool will request the password interactively when needed.

See:

Impacket Cheatsheet

docs.title: DCOM
docs.text:
Distributed Component Object Model is another Windows remote-management technology.

It relies heavily on RPC and Windows permissions.

Conceptually:

Source Host
     |
     v
RPC / DCOM
     |
     v
Remote COM Object
     |
     v
Destination

DCOM availability does not automatically indicate a vulnerability.

Evaluate:

Which identity can activate remote objects?
Why is that permission required?
Which network segments can access RPC?
Is the activity monitored?

docs.title: Remote Services
docs.text:
Windows service management can provide remote administrative functionality when an identity has appropriate rights.

Conceptually:

Administrator
     |
     v
Service Control Manager
     |
     v
Remote Host

From a defensive perspective, remote service creation or modification is highly relevant telemetry.

docs.title: PsExec Model
docs.text:
PsExec-style administration commonly involves:

Administrative Authentication
        |
        v
SMB
        |
        v
Service Control Manager
        |
        v
Temporary / Remote Service

Sysinternals PsExec is a legitimate administrative tool and should not automatically be treated as malicious.

The context determines whether its use is expected.

docs.title: Impacket PsExec
docs.text:
Impacket provides a PsExec-style remote administration utility:

impacket-psexec DOMAIN/USER@SERVER

Use interactive password entry where possible.

Remote service-based execution is generally noisy and can produce useful defensive telemetry.

docs.title: SMBExec
docs.text:
Impacket also provides SMB-based remote execution:

impacket-smbexec DOMAIN/USER@SERVER

Different remote administration methods can produce different telemetry.

Choose the method appropriate to the assessment objective rather than attempting every available technique.

docs.title: Kerberos-Based Lateral Movement
docs.text:
In Active Directory environments, Kerberos can provide authentication to remote services.

Relevant material can include:

Password
NT hash
Kerberos key
TGT
Service ticket
Certificate-derived authentication

Kerberos authentication should be understood separately from the remote protocol itself.

For example:

Kerberos Credential
       |
       v
SMB

or:

Kerberos Credential
       |
       v
WinRM

Use the dedicated notes:

Kerberos

Kerberos Tickets

docs.title: Pass-the-Ticket
docs.text:
Where an authorised Kerberos ticket is available, it may be possible to authenticate without using the account password.

Conceptually:

Kerberos Ticket
      |
      v
Target Service
      |
      v
Authenticated Session

Use:

Pass-the-Ticket

docs.title: Pass-the-Hash
docs.text:
NTLM authentication may permit authentication using password-derived NT hash material in environments where the protocol and service support it.

Conceptually:

NT Hash
   |
   v
NTLM Authentication
   |
   v
Remote Service

Use:

Pass-the-Hash

The defensive objective should include reducing NTLM usage, protecting privileged credentials, and limiting where privileged identities can authenticate.

docs.title: Overpass-the-Hash
docs.text:
Another Active Directory concept involves using password-derived key material to obtain Kerberos authentication material.

Use:

Overpass-the-Hash

docs.title: Linux Lateral Movement
docs.text:
SSH is the primary remote-administration protocol on many Linux systems.

Potential access material includes:

Password
SSH private key
SSH certificate
Agent-forwarded identity
Kerberos authentication
Application credential

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Basic connection:

ssh user@SERVER

Specific private key:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user@SERVER

Specific port:

ssh -p 2222 user@SERVER

Verbose troubleshooting:

ssh -v user@SERVER

Avoid copying private keys unnecessarily between assessment systems.

docs.title: SSH Key Reuse
docs.text:
A private key may be trusted by multiple systems.

Private Key
    |
    +--> Server A
    |
    +--> Server B
    |
    +--> Server C

This can create a lateral movement path if the same identity and key are trusted broadly.

The finding should focus on the actual trust and key-management weakness.

docs.title: SSH Configuration
docs.text:
SSH configuration can reveal intended relationships:

cat ~/.ssh/config

Potential information includes:

Host aliases
Usernames
Identity files
Jump hosts
Ports
Internal systems

This can help identify legitimate administration paths that may also become attack paths after credential compromise.

docs.title: SSH Agent Forwarding
docs.text:
SSH agent forwarding allows authentication through an intermediate system without placing the private key on that system.

Conceptually:

Operator
   |
   | SSH Agent
   v
Jump Host
   |
   v
Destination

It is operationally useful but creates security considerations if the intermediate system is compromised.

Prefer safer architecture such as explicit jump-host configuration where possible and avoid unnecessary agent forwarding.

docs.title: Pivoting
docs.text:
A foothold may have access to networks that the operator cannot reach directly.

Example:

Operator
   |
   X
10.20.30.0/24


Operator
   |
   v
Compromised / Test Host
   |
   v
10.20.30.0/24

A pivot creates a controlled route through the authorised foothold.

Common options include:

Ligolo-ng
Chisel
SSH port forwarding
SOCKS proxying
proxychains
Framework-native pivots

docs.title: Pivoting Decision Model
docs.text:
Destination
    |
    v
Directly Reachable?
   /        \
 Yes         No
  |           |
  |           v
  |       Foothold Has
  |        Route?
  |       /     \
  |     No       Yes
  |     |         |
  |    STOP       v
  |          Pivot Permitted?
  |            /       \
  |          No         Yes
  |          |           |
  |         STOP         v
  |                  Create Pivot
  |                       |
  +-----------------------+
                          |
                          v
                    Validate Route

docs.title: Ligolo-ng
docs.text:
Ligolo-ng is a tunnelling and pivoting tool that can create network access through an authorised agent.

Its major advantage is that it can expose a routed network interface to the operator rather than requiring every application to support a SOCKS proxy.

Conceptually:

Kali / Operator
      |
      v
Ligolo Proxy
      |
      v
Encrypted Tunnel
      |
      v
Ligolo Agent
      |
      v
Internal Network

docs.title: Ligolo-ng Architecture
docs.text:
Operator System
                         |
                         v
                  +--------------+
                  | Ligolo Proxy |
                  +------+-------+
                         |
                         | Tunnel
                         |
                  +------+-------+
                  | Ligolo Agent |
                  +------+-------+
                         |
                         v
                  Internal Network
                         |
              +----------+----------+
              |                     |
              v                     v
           Server A              Server B

docs.title: Ligolo-ng Use Case
docs.text:
Suppose:

Operator:
192.0.2.10

Foothold:
10.10.10.25

Internal network reachable by foothold:
172.16.20.0/24

The operator cannot directly reach:

172.16.20.0/24

but the foothold can.

Ligolo-ng can provide a controlled network path:

Operator
   |
   v
Foothold
   |
   v
172.16.20.0/24

docs.title: Ligolo-ng Proxy
docs.text:
The proxy component runs on the operator-controlled infrastructure.

Exact command-line options can change between releases, so verify the installed version:

./proxy -h

The proxy waits for an authorised Ligolo agent to connect.

docs.title: Ligolo-ng Agent
docs.text:
The agent runs on the authorised pivot system.

Check available options:

agent -h

After the agent establishes a connection to the operator-controlled proxy, the session can be selected from the proxy interface.

docs.title: Ligolo Interface
docs.text:
Ligolo-ng commonly uses a TUN interface on Linux.

A typical Linux preparation model is:

sudo ip tuntap add user "$(whoami)" mode tun ligolo

Bring it up:

sudo ip link set ligolo up

Verify:

ip addr show ligolo

docs.title: Ligolo Route
docs.text:
After establishing the authorised session, add only the required internal route.

Example:

sudo ip route add 172.16.20.0/24 dev ligolo

Verify:

ip route

Conceptually:

172.16.20.0/24
      |
      v
ligolo
      |
      v
Pivot Agent

Do not add broad routes when only a small authorised network is required.

docs.title: Ligolo Validation
docs.text:
Once the tunnel is active, normal applications can use the route.

For example:

nc -vz 172.16.20.10 445

or, where internal scanning is permitted:

nmap -Pn -p 22,445,3389 172.16.20.10

The important distinction is:

Ligolo provides network reachability.

It does not provide authentication.

docs.title: Ligolo Double Pivot Concept
docs.text:
Multiple network layers can exist:

Operator
   |
   v
Pivot A
   |
   v
Network B
   |
   v
Pivot B
   |
   v
Network C

Multi-hop pivoting increases complexity and should only be used when necessary for the authorised objective.

Record every route and pivot host.

docs.title: Ligolo Detection
docs.text:
Potential defensive indicators include:

Unexpected outbound connection from pivot host
Long-lived connection
New process
Unusual executable
Unexpected internal connections originating from pivot host
Connection patterns inconsistent with host role
Endpoint security alerts

Network routing through a host can make that host appear to initiate connections to systems it does not normally access.

docs.title: Ligolo Cleanup
docs.text:
After testing:

Stop Ligolo session
Remove temporary agent
Remove TUN route
Remove TUN interface if created for assessment
Verify no process remains
Record cleanup

Example route removal:

sudo ip route del 172.16.20.0/24 dev ligolo

Interface removal:

sudo ip link delete ligolo

docs.title: Chisel
docs.text:
Chisel is a TCP tunnelling tool that operates over HTTP and uses SSH for tunnel security.

It is useful when a SOCKS or specific TCP forwarding model is more appropriate than routed TUN access.

Conceptually:

Operator
   |
   v
Chisel Server
   |
   v
HTTP Transport
   |
   v
Chisel Client
   |
   v
Internal Network

docs.title: Chisel Architecture
docs.text:
Operator System
                       |
                       v
                +-------------+
                | Chisel      |
                | Server      |
                +------+------+
                       |
                       | Tunnel
                       |
                +------+------+
                | Chisel      |
                | Client      |
                +------+------+
                       |
                       v
                Internal Network

docs.title: Chisel Reverse SOCKS Concept
docs.text:
A useful authorised pivot model is:

Operator
   |
   v
SOCKS Proxy
   |
   v
Chisel Tunnel
   |
   v
Pivot Host
   |
   v
Internal Network

The SOCKS proxy can then be used by proxy-aware applications.

docs.title: Chisel Server
docs.text:
Review the installed options:

chisel server --help

A reverse-capable server can be configured on operator-controlled infrastructure.

For example, when appropriate for the lab or engagement:

chisel server --reverse --port 8000

Ensure the listening port is permitted by the infrastructure firewall.

docs.title: Chisel Client
docs.text:
The authorised pivot host connects back to the controlled Chisel server.

Review:

chisel client --help

A reverse SOCKS tunnel can be established using the syntax supported by the installed Chisel release.

A commonly used model is:

Pivot Host
    |
    v
Operator Chisel Server
    |
    v
SOCKS Listener

Verify the exact release syntax before use rather than assuming options remain unchanged.

docs.title: Chisel and proxychains
docs.text:
Once a SOCKS listener is available, tools that support SOCKS can use it directly.

Other TCP clients can sometimes be routed using proxychains.

Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
proxychains
    |
    v
SOCKS
    |
    v
Chisel
    |
    v
Pivot
    |
    v
Target

docs.title: proxychains
docs.text:
ProxyChains can force many TCP applications through a configured proxy.

Configuration is commonly stored under:

/etc/proxychains4.conf

or:

/etc/proxychains.conf

A SOCKS entry conceptually looks like:

socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

Check the local configuration before use.

docs.title: proxychains Example
docs.text:
After the approved SOCKS pivot is active:

proxychains4 nc -vz 172.16.20.10 445

For a single authorised host:

proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -p 445 172.16.20.10

When using Nmap through a SOCKS proxy, TCP connect scanning is generally more appropriate than raw-packet scan types because proxychains operates at the socket API layer.

docs.title: proxychains Limitations
docs.text:
Not every application or protocol works cleanly through proxychains.

Potential limitations include:

UDP support
ICMP
Raw sockets
DNS behaviour
High-volume scanning
Application-specific networking
Performance

A routed TUN approach such as Ligolo-ng can be more convenient when broad TCP reachability is required.

docs.title: Ligolo-ng vs Chisel
docs.text:
Feature Ligolo-ng Chisel Primary model Routed/TUN pivot TCP/SOCKS tunnelling Application changes Usually none after route Proxy-aware or proxychains Routing experience Similar to normal network route Proxy based Specific port forwarding Possible depending on design Strong fit SOCKS workflow Not primary requirement Common Multi-network testing Convenient Possible but more proxy-oriented

Both can be useful.

Select the tool based on the network architecture and assessment objective.

docs.title: SSH Local Port Forwarding
docs.text:
SSH can provide simple port forwarding without additional tunnelling software.

Local forwarding:

ssh -L LOCAL_PORT:DESTINATION:DESTINATION_PORT user@PIVOT

Conceptually:

Operator:8443
     |
     v
SSH Tunnel
     |
     v
Pivot
     |
     v
Internal:443

Example:

ssh -L 8443:172.16.20.10:443 user@PIVOT

The operator can then connect to:

127.0.0.1:8443

and SSH forwards the connection to the authorised internal destination.

docs.title: SSH Dynamic Port Forwarding
docs.text:
SSH can also create a local SOCKS proxy.

Syntax:

ssh -D 1080 user@PIVOT

Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
127.0.0.1:1080
    |
    v
SSH
    |
    v
Pivot
    |
    v
Internal Network

Configure proxy-aware tools or proxychains to use the local SOCKS listener.

docs.title: SSH Remote Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Remote forwarding exposes a port on the remote SSH side and forwards it toward a destination reachable from the local side.

General syntax:

ssh -R REMOTE_PORT:DESTINATION:DESTINATION_PORT user@SERVER

Use remote forwarding carefully because it can create a new listening service on the remote side depending on SSH configuration.

docs.title: SSH Jump Hosts
docs.text:
OpenSSH supports jump hosts using ProxyJump.

Example:

ssh -J user@PIVOT user@DESTINATION

Conceptually:

Operator
   |
   v
Jump Host
   |
   v
Destination

This is often preferable to unnecessary agent forwarding.

docs.title: SOCKS Proxying
docs.text:
SOCKS provides an application-level proxy model.

Tool
 |
 v
SOCKS Proxy
 |
 v
Pivot
 |
 v
Destination

Common SOCKS versions include:

SOCKS4
SOCKS5

SOCKS5 supports additional capabilities, but actual behaviour depends on the proxy implementation.

docs.title: DNS Through Proxies
docs.text:
DNS deserves particular attention during proxy-based pivoting.

A common mistake is:

Application traffic -> Proxy

DNS query -> Local network

This can cause:

Failed hostname resolution
Information leakage
Incorrect routing
Unexpected DNS telemetry

Where hostname resolution must occur through the pivot, configure the selected proxy tooling appropriately.

docs.title: Framework-Native Pivoting
docs.text:
Some C2 frameworks provide their own pivoting capabilities.

Depending on the framework, concepts can include:

SOCKS proxies
Port forwarding
Peer-to-peer agents
Internal listeners
Route management

Use the framework's current documentation because implementations and syntax change over time.

Do not deploy a second tunnelling tool when the existing authorised framework already provides the required functionality without unnecessary complexity.

docs.title: Choosing a Pivot Method
docs.text:
A simple decision model:

Need One Internal TCP Service?
          |
         Yes
          |
          v
   SSH Local Forward
       or Chisel


Need Multiple Proxy-Aware Tools?
          |
         Yes
          |
          v
    SOCKS / Chisel
          |
          v
     proxychains


Need Broad Routed Access?
          |
         Yes
          |
          v
      Ligolo-ng


Already Have C2 Pivot Support?
          |
         Yes
          |
          v
 Consider Framework-Native Pivot

docs.title: Pivot Route Inventory
docs.text:
Record pivot routes during an engagement.

Example:

Pivot Source Reachable Network Tool Cleanup PIVOT-01 TEST-WKS01 172.16.20.0/24 Ligolo-ng Required PIVOT-02 LINUX-JUMP01 10.30.5.0/24 SSH SOCKS Required

This becomes especially important when multiple operators are active.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Lateral movement frequently reveals segmentation weaknesses.

A strong model might look like:

User Workstations
       |
       X
Domain Controllers


User Workstations
       |
       X
Management Network


Admin Workstations
       |
       v
Management Network

Segmentation should follow business and administrative requirements.

docs.title: Flat Network
docs.text:
A flat network may permit unnecessary east-west connectivity:

Workstation A
     |
     +--> Workstation B
     |
     +--> Server A
     |
     +--> Database
     |
     +--> Management Server

Reachability alone is not necessarily a vulnerability.

The assessment should determine whether the access violates the intended security architecture.

docs.title: Administrative Tiering
docs.text:
Privileged identities should not routinely authenticate to lower-trust systems.

Conceptually:

Tier 0
Domain Controllers
Identity Infrastructure
        |
        X
        |
Tier 2 Workstations

If highly privileged credentials are exposed on a normal workstation, the problem may originate from administrative workflow rather than the workstation itself.

docs.title: Privileged Access Workstations
docs.text:
Dedicated administrative workstations can reduce credential exposure.

Normal Workstation
       |
       X
Tier 0 Administration


Privileged Workstation
       |
       v
Tier 0 Administration

The goal is to reduce where privileged credentials and sessions appear.

docs.title: Windows Firewall
docs.text:
Host firewalls can significantly restrict lateral movement.

For example:

Workstation
   |
   X--> SMB from peer workstations
   |
   X--> WinRM from user networks
   |
   X--> RDP from arbitrary sources
   |
   v
Management traffic from approved admin network

Host-based segmentation remains valuable even inside trusted networks.

docs.title: Authentication Restrictions
docs.text:
Remote access can also be restricted through:

User rights
Local group membership
Authentication policy
MFA
Network Level Authentication
SSH AllowUsers
SSH AllowGroups
Sudo policy
Conditional access
Privileged access management

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Lateral movement can produce telemetry at several layers.

Source Endpoint
      |
      v
Network
      |
      v
Authentication
      |
      v
Destination Endpoint
      |
      v
EDR
      |
      v
SIEM

docs.title: Windows Authentication Telemetry
docs.text:
Relevant Windows events can include successful and failed logons.

Commonly investigated event IDs include:

4624 - Successful logon
4625 - Failed logon
4648 - Logon using explicit credentials
4672 - Special privileges assigned

The usefulness of an event depends on logon type, source, identity, destination, and surrounding activity.

docs.title: Logon Types
docs.text:
Windows logon types provide useful context.

Examples include:

Logon Type Meaning 2 Interactive 3 Network 10 RemoteInteractive

Do not interpret the event ID without considering the logon type.

docs.title: RDP Detection
docs.text:
Potential telemetry includes:

Authentication events
RemoteInteractive logon
Terminal Services logs
Network connection
Source IP
User identity
Session creation
EDR telemetry

docs.title: WinRM Detection
docs.text:
WinRM activity can produce:

Authentication events
WinRM operational logs
PowerShell logs
Process creation
Network connections
EDR telemetry

PowerShell remoting can also produce useful script and process telemetry depending on logging configuration.

docs.title: SMB Detection
docs.text:
Potential SMB lateral movement indicators include:

Network logons
Administrative share access
Remote service activity
Named pipe access
Unusual workstation-to-workstation SMB
Authentication failures
EDR telemetry

docs.title: WMI Detection
docs.text:
WMI-based remote administration can produce:

WMI operational logs
Authentication events
RPC connections
Process creation
EDR alerts
Source-to-destination relationships

docs.title: SSH Detection
docs.text:
Linux SSH telemetry can include:

Successful authentication
Failed authentication
Source address
Username
Public-key fingerprint
Session creation
sudo activity
Command history where applicable
Audit events

Logs may be available through:

journalctl -u ssh

or:

journalctl -u sshd

depending on the distribution.

docs.title: Pivot Detection
docs.text:
Pivoting can alter normal network relationships.

Example:

Normal:

Workstation A ---> Application Server


During Pivot:

Workstation A ---> Database Server
Workstation A ---> Management Server
Workstation A ---> Internal Web Server

Useful indicators include:

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
A possible lateral movement path exists.

Examples:

Port reachable
Credential discovered
User belongs to remote-access group
SSH key discovered
Administrative share visible

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
Multiple conditions support practical movement.

Examples:

Credential appears valid
Destination is reachable
Remote service is available
Identity has relevant permissions

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text: Controlled testing demonstrates successful access to the authorised destination.

docs.title: Lateral Movement Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

Source privilege
Destination privilege
Identity privilege
Credential reuse
Number of reachable systems
Network segmentation
Administrative tier crossed
Detection
Business impact
Attack chaining

A single permitted SSH connection between two expected administration systems should not automatically be considered a vulnerability.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
A useful finding should identify the root cause.

Weak:

WinRM allowed lateral movement.

Better:

A domain service account held local administrator privileges on
multiple servers and was permitted to authenticate remotely using
WinRM.

After the account credential became available from the authorised
source host, it was minimally validated against a second in-scope
server, where it provided local administrative access.

docs.title: Reporting Pivoting
docs.text:
Avoid reporting:

Ligolo bypassed the network.

unless the evidence actually supports that conclusion.

Better:

The compromised workstation had network connectivity to the
restricted server segment that was not directly reachable from
the assessment infrastructure.

A controlled tunnel through the workstation demonstrated that
this existing network path could be used to reach the approved
server segment.

The underlying issue is usually:

Segmentation
Trust
Host access
Firewall policy

not the tunnelling tool itself.

Authorised testing only

Lateral movement and pivoting can provide access to systems and network segments that were not visible from the original assessment infrastructure. Confirm that every destination system, identity, subnet, protocol, and credential remains within the approved scope before interacting with it. Keep tunnels and routes as narrow as practical, minimise authentication attempts, avoid unnecessary data access, record deployed pivot infrastructure, and remove temporary agents, routes, proxies, tunnels, and assessment artifacts when testing is complete.

docs.title: Red Team Methodology
docs.text:
A red team assessment evaluates how an organisation withstands a realistic attack against defined objectives.

Unlike isolated vulnerability testing, red teaming focuses on complete attack paths.

Reconnaissance
      |
      v
Initial Access
      |
      v
Foothold
      |
      v
Situational Awareness
      |
      v
Privilege Escalation
      |
      v
Credential Access
      |
      v
Internal Discovery
      |
      v
Lateral Movement
      |
      v
Objective

Supporting activities may include:

Infrastructure
Command and Control
Persistence
Defence Evasion
Pivoting
Detection Validation
Evidence Collection

The objective is not to execute every possible technique.

The objective is to determine whether realistic attacker behaviour can achieve the agreed goals and whether the organisation can prevent, detect, investigate, and respond to that behaviour.

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Red team activity must operate within explicit written authorisation.

Before testing begins, establish:

Customer
Authorising authority
Assessment dates
In-scope organisations
In-scope systems
In-scope identities
In-scope networks
Permitted techniques
Prohibited techniques
Testing windows
Emergency contacts
Stop conditions
Data-handling requirements
Cleanup requirements

When an action falls outside the Rules of Engagement, do not perform it simply because it is technically possible.

docs.text:
The two disciplines overlap but normally have different emphasis.

Area Penetration Testing Red Teaming Primary focus Vulnerabilities Attack paths Scope Systems/applications Organisational objective Techniques Broad testing Selected realistic techniques Detection Useful Core measurement Stealth Usually secondary Scenario dependent Duration Often shorter Often longer Findings Individual weaknesses Attack chains and control gaps SOC evaluation Optional Frequently important Threat model Useful Usually central

docs.title: Phase 0 - Engagement Preparation
docs.text:
Do not begin technical activity until the engagement is operationally ready.

Confirm:

  • [ ] Rules of Engagement approved
  • [ ] Scope approved
  • [ ] Testing window approved
  • [ ] Emergency contacts confirmed
  • [ ] Stop conditions defined
  • [ ] Infrastructure prepared
  • [ ] Evidence handling agreed
  • [ ] Data restrictions understood
  • [ ] Cleanup responsibilities agreed
  • [ ] Detection coordination model agreed

docs.title: Rules of Engagement
docs.text:
The Rules of Engagement should define what is allowed.

Typical categories include:

External reconnaissance
Active scanning
Password spraying
Social engineering
Payload execution
C2
Privilege escalation
Credential access
Lateral movement
Persistence
Defence evasion
Cloud testing
Physical testing
Data access
Exfiltration simulation
Denial of service
Production modifications

Never assume permission for a high-impact activity because another activity was authorised.

docs.title: Stop Conditions
docs.text:
Examples include:

Production instability
Unexpected customer impact
Access to excluded systems
Access to highly sensitive excluded data
Unexpected privileged access
Security incident unrelated to testing
Loss of control over assessment infrastructure
Customer request
Safety concern

Operators should know exactly who can stop the engagement.

docs.title: Phase 1 - Define Objectives
docs.text:
Red team objectives should describe outcomes rather than tools.

Weak objective:

Get Domain Admin.

Better objective:

Determine whether an external attacker can obtain administrative
control over systems supporting the defined business service.

Another example:

Determine whether a compromised standard-user workstation can be
used to access the defined sensitive application and whether the
SOC detects the attack path.

docs.text:
Initial access establishes the first authorised foothold.

An assumed-breach engagement may intentionally skip external compromise.

docs.text:
Once initial access succeeds, avoid immediately executing large amounts of tooling.

First determine:

What privilege do I have?
What security controls exist?
What network am I connected to?
What is the assessment objective?

Application configuration
Stored credentials
Installer policy
Application control
Local groups

docs.text:
Review:

sudo
SUID
SGID
Capabilities
Cron
systemd
Writable scripts
PATH
Credentials
Containers
NFS
Kernel context

docs.title: Minimum Necessary Validation
docs.text:
Do not execute every possible escalation.

Prefer:

Candidate
   |
   v
Validate Permissions
   |
   v
Confirm Execution Context
   |
   v
Objective Proven
   |
   v
STOP

This reduces unnecessary system modification.

docs.title: Phase 10 - Credential Access
docs.text:
Credentials can enable movement across systems and security boundaries.

Potential credential material includes:

Passwords
NTLM hashes
Kerberos tickets
SSH keys
API keys
Tokens
Certificates
Browser credentials
Cloud credentials
Service-account secrets
Configuration secrets

docs.title: Credential Access Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Which credentials are available?
Why are they available?
Which identity owns them?
Where can they be used?
Are they privileged?
Are they reusable?
Are they protected?
Was access detected?

docs.title: Credential Handling
docs.text:
Treat obtained credentials as sensitive assessment data.

Never place credentials in:

Public repositories
Screenshots unnecessarily
Chat systems
Unencrypted notes
Shared terminals
Shell scripts committed to Git

docs.title: Credential Chain
docs.text:
Compromised Host
      |
      v
Credential Material
      |
      v
Identity
      |
      v
Accessible Systems
      |
      v
Higher-Value Asset

Use:

Credential Access

docs.title: Phase 11 - Active Directory Discovery
docs.text:
When the environment uses Active Directory, build an understanding of:

Domain
Forest
Users
Groups
Computers
Sessions
SPNs
Delegation
ACLs
GPOs
Trusts
Certificate Services
Privileged identities

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
Use the dedicated section:

Active Directory

docs.text:
BloodHound can help model relationships between:

Users
Groups
Computers

docs.text:
Do not simply search for Domain Admin.

Analyse paths such as:

Current User

docs.title: Phase 12 - Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Lateral movement uses existing access or credentials to reach another authorised system.

Use:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Common Windows Remote Management Paths
docs.text:
Depending on configuration:

SMB
WinRM
WMI
RDP
DCOM
Remote services
Scheduled tasks

These are legitimate administration mechanisms.

Their existence alone is not a vulnerability.

docs.title: Linux Remote Administration
docs.text:
Common mechanisms include:

SSH
Configuration-management systems
Administrative APIs
Container management
Orchestration platforms

docs.title: Credential Reuse
docs.text:
A common movement path is:

Host A
  |
  v
Credential
  |
  v
Host B
  |
  v
Additional Credential
  |
  v
Host C

This demonstrates why credential isolation is important.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Before moving to another host, determine whether the connection should be permitted.

Source
   |
   v
Network Control
   |
   +--> Allowed
   |
   +--> Blocked

A blocked path is useful assessment evidence.

docs.title: Pivoting
docs.text:
Sometimes an operator cannot directly reach the next target.

Operator
    |
    v
Foothold
    |
    v
Internal Network
    |
    v
Target

A controlled tunnel or proxy may be used when authorised.

docs.title: Ligolo-ng
docs.text:
Ligolo-ng can provide a tunnel between an operator and an authorised pivot host.

Conceptually:

Operator
    |
    v
Ligolo Proxy
    |
    v
Ligolo Agent
    |
    v
Internal Network

Use it only for networks explicitly included in the assessment scope.

docs.title: Chisel
docs.text:
Chisel provides TCP tunnelling over HTTP/WebSocket transport.

Conceptually:

Operator
    |
    v
Chisel Server
    |
    v
Chisel Client
    |
    v
Internal Service

Tunnelling should be documented because it changes the apparent network source of subsequent assessment activity.

docs.title: SSH Tunnelling
docs.text:
SSH can provide native forwarding where SSH access already exists.

Types include:

Local forwarding
Remote forwarding
Dynamic SOCKS forwarding

SSH tunnelling may be preferable when it uses an existing approved administrative channel.

docs.title: SOCKS Proxy
docs.text:
A SOCKS proxy can allow compatible assessment tools to reach systems through a pivot.

Assessment Tool
      |
      v
SOCKS
      |
      v
Pivot
      |
      v
Internal Target

Ensure tools do not accidentally reach excluded networks through the proxy.

docs.title: Phase 13 - Command and Control
docs.text:
C2 provides an operator communication channel to an authorised assessment component.

Use:

Command and Control

docs.title: C2 Questions
docs.text:
Record:

Which host?
Which user?
Which protocol?
Which destination?
Which port?
Which process?
Which security controls observed it?
Was the connection blocked?
Was it detected?

docs.text:
Operator
   |
   v
Management Plane
   |
   v
Team Server
   |
   v
Edge / Redirector
   |

Administrative interfaces should not be unnecessarily exposed to target networks or the public Internet.

docs.text:

Possible categories include:

Services

Is it necessary?

   No   Yes

docs.title: Phase 16 - Objective Execution
docs.text:
The assessment should eventually answer the business objective.

Example:

Can an external attacker access the finance reporting system?

Attack chain:

External Exposure
      |
      v
Initial Access
      |
      v
Workstation
      |
      v
Credential Access
      |
      v
Server Access
      |
      v
Application Access
      |
      v

docs.title: Proof of Access
docs.text:
Use the least invasive proof possible.

Examples:

Directory listing
Hostname
Database name
Synthetic record
Application role
File metadata
Screenshot
Authorised marker file

Avoid unnecessary access to real sensitive data.

docs.title: Synthetic Data
docs.text:
Where data access or exfiltration must be demonstrated, use synthetic test data whenever possible.

Example:

red-team-proof.txt

containing:

Authorised red team assessment test file.
No production data.

This can prove the path without exposing customer information.

docs.title: Phase 17 - Detection Validation
docs.text:
A red team engagement should evaluate the defensive chain.

Activity
   |
   v
Telemetry
   |
   v

docs.title: Prevention vs Detection
docs.text:
Track both.

Technique Prevented Logged Alerted Investigated Initial access test No Yes Yes Yes PrivEsc test Yes Yes Yes Yes Credential access No Yes No No Lateral movement No Yes Yes Yes Persistence test No Yes No No

docs.title: Detection Gap
docs.text:
A useful detection finding describes:

Activity
Expected Telemetry
Observed Telemetry
Alert
SOC Visibility
Investigation
Response

Avoid simply writing:

EDR bypassed.

docs.title: Detection Quality
docs.text:
A detection may exist but still be ineffective.

Consider:

Was the alert timely?
Was severity appropriate?
Was context useful?
Was the correct host identified?
Was the correct user identified?
Was the attack chain visible?
Was it investigated?
Was containment possible?

docs.title: Phase 18 - Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Evidence should be collected continuously.

For every important action record:

Timestamp
Operator
Source
Target
Identity
Command or technique
Result
Security control
Detection result
Evidence location
Cleanup requirement

docs.title: Timestamp Standard
docs.text:
Prefer a consistent timezone such as UTC.

Example:

2026-09-05 18:42:11 UTC

Infrastructure and target clocks should be synchronised where possible.

docs.title: Operator Log
docs.text:
Example:

Time Operator Source Target Action Result 10:12 OP01 RT01 WS01 Initial access validation Success 10:24 OP01 WS01 WS01 PrivEsc validation Blocked 10:41 OP02 WS01 SRV01 WinRM authentication Success

docs.title: Evidence Quality
docs.text:
Good evidence demonstrates:

Who
What
Where
When
How
Impact

Avoid screenshots without context.

docs.title: Screenshot Naming
docs.text:
A useful convention:

YYYYMMDD-HHMM-host-technique-description.png

Example:

20260905-1420-WS01-applocker-policy.png

docs.title: Command Logging
docs.text:
Record commands that materially support findings.

Do not flood reports with every enumeration command.

Keep detailed operator logs separately from the executive report.

docs.title: Phase 19 - Attack Path Documentation
docs.text:
Individual findings often make more sense when combined into an attack path.

Example:

External Application
       |
       | Initial Access
       v
Standard User
       |
       | Writable Service
       v
Local Administrator
       |
       | Credential Exposure
       v
Server Administrator
       |
       | Credential Reuse
       v
Critical Server

docs.text: Step Technique Security Weakness Result 1 Initial access Application weakness User foothold 2 PrivEsc Writable privileged component Local admin 3 Credential access Credential exposure Server credential 4 Lateral movement Credential reuse Server access 5 Objective Excessive application privilege Sensitive system access

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Do not report only the final technique.

For example:

Domain Admin compromised

is an outcome.

The useful analysis is:

Why could the attack path reach Domain Admin?

Potential root causes include:

Credential reuse
Excessive delegation
Weak segmentation
Misconfigured ACL
Legacy authentication
Excessive local administration
Insufficient application control
Missing detection

docs.title: Phase 21 - Reporting
docs.text:
A red team report should explain the attack story.

Typical structure:

Executive Summary

Objectives

Scope

Rules of Engagement

Methodology

Attack Narrative

Attack Paths

Technical Findings

Detection Analysis

Positive Security Controls

Recommendations

Cleanup Confirmation

Appendices

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
The executive summary should answer:

Did the red team achieve the objective?

How?

What were the major control failures?

What worked well?

What is the business impact?

What should be fixed first?

docs.title: Attack Narrative
docs.text:
A useful attack narrative follows chronology.

The assessment began from an external attacker position.

An exposed application provided the initial foothold.

The compromised identity had standard-user privileges.

A local configuration weakness enabled privilege escalation.

Credential material recovered from the system enabled access to
an internal server.

The internal connection was permitted by network segmentation.

The resulting access provided a path to the defined assessment
objective.

The narrative should connect individual technical findings.

docs.title: Finding Structure
docs.text:
A technical finding should contain:

Title
Severity
Affected Assets
Description
Prerequisites
Attack Path
Validation
Evidence
Impact
Detection
Remediation
References

docs.title: Positive Findings
docs.text:
Red team reports should also identify controls that worked.

Examples:

MFA prevented account compromise

ASR blocked the test technique

AppLocker denied execution

Network segmentation prevented lateral movement

EDR generated a high-confidence alert

SOC investigated within five minutes

Credential Guard prevented expected credential exposure

This helps organisations understand which investments are effective.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
Recommendations should address root causes.

Weak:

Block attacker tool.

Better:

Reduce administrative credential exposure by separating
administrative identities from workstation logons and enforcing
privileged-access workstations for tier-0 administration.

Tool-specific blocking alone rarely resolves the underlying attack path.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Retesting should reproduce the original attack path.

Original Technique
       |
       v
Original Control Gap
       |
       v
Remediation
       |
       v
Repeat Same Validation
       |
       v
Prevented / Detected?

docs.title: Red Team Metrics
docs.text:
Useful measurements include:

Time to initial access
Time to detection
Time to triage
Time to investigation
Time to containment
Number of attack steps detected
Number of attack steps prevented
Number of attack steps invisible
Objective achieved
Privilege obtained
Systems reached
Credential exposure

docs.title: Detection Coverage
docs.text:
Example:

Total meaningful attack actions: 20

Prevented:       4
Detected:        8
Logged only:     5
No visibility:   3

This is often more informative than simply counting vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
The methodology can ultimately be reduced to:

Know the objective.

Understand the current access.

Identify the shortest meaningful attack path.

Validate one security boundary at a time.

Collect evidence.

Measure defensive visibility.

Stop when the objective is proven.

Remove everything introduced during testing.

Explain the attack path and its root causes.

flowchart TD
      A["Objective and starting access"] --> B["Scope and ROE"]
      B --> C["Candidate attack path"]
      C --> D["Controlled execution"]
      D --> E["Observed outcome and detection"]
      E --> F["Cleanup, evidence and retest"]
