Authorised testing only

This methodology is intended for authorised red team, penetration testing, purple team, and security validation engagements. Every action must remain within the agreed scope and Rules of Engagement. Use the minimum-impact technique necessary to demonstrate each security boundary, protect credentials and customer data, stop when an objective has been sufficiently demonstrated, maintain an artifact inventory throughout the engagement, and verify complete cleanup before closing the assessment.

docs.title: Red Team OPSEC
docs.text:
Operational security, or OPSEC, is the discipline of preventing information about an assessment from being accidentally exposed, mixed between engagements, lost, or disclosed to unauthorised parties.

In an authorised red team engagement, OPSEC is primarily about protecting:

Customer information
Assessment credentials
Operator identities
Assessment infrastructure
Payloads and test artifacts
Evidence
Reports
Attack-path information
Internal network information
Cloud resources
Communication channels

A useful model is:

                 RED TEAM OPSEC
                       |
        +--------------+--------------+
        |              |              |
        v              v              v
     PEOPLE         SYSTEMS          DATA
        |              |              |
        +--------------+--------------+
                       |
                       v
                   PROCESS
                       |
                       v
                  ENGAGEMENT
                    SAFETY

Good OPSEC should make the engagement easier to control, investigate, reproduce, and clean up.

Authorised testing only

OPSEC does not expand the authorised scope of an assessment. It should protect customer information and assessment operations, not be used to conceal unauthorised activity. Rules of Engagement, legal authorisation, customer safety, and stop conditions always take priority.

docs.title: OPSEC Objectives
docs.text:
The primary objectives are:

Prevent cross-client data exposure

Prevent credential leakage

Protect assessment infrastructure

Protect evidence

Separate operator identities

Prevent accidental out-of-scope activity

Maintain reliable attribution of assessment actions

Prevent uncontrolled payload distribution

Maintain an accurate infrastructure inventory

Support incident investigation

Support complete cleanup

docs.title: OPSEC Threat Model
docs.text:
Before an engagement, consider what could go wrong.

                     Engagement
                         |
       +-----------------+-----------------+
       |                 |                 |
       v                 v                 v
  Data Leakage     Infrastructure      Human Error
                       Exposure
       |                 |                 |
       v                 v                 v
Credentials        Admin Interface     Wrong Target
Evidence           Public Storage      Wrong Client
Reports            Weak Access         Wrong Account
Client Data        Stale Services      Wrong Payload

docs.title: OPSEC Is More Than Stealth
docs.text:
Red team OPSEC should not be reduced to:

Avoid detection.

A broader model is:

Operational Security
        |
        +--> Customer confidentiality
        |
        +--> Engagement isolation
        |
        +--> Infrastructure security
        |
        +--> Credential protection
        |
        +--> Evidence integrity
        |
        +--> Operator accountability
        |
        +--> Scope enforcement
        |
        +--> Cleanup

Detection by the customer's security team may actually be a desired assessment outcome.

docs.title: OPSEC Lifecycle
docs.text:
Preparation
    |
    v
Environment Isolation
    |
    v
Infrastructure Deployment
    |
    v
Operational Testing
    |
    v
Continuous Logging
    |
    v
Evidence Handling
    |
    v
Cleanup
    |
    v
Infrastructure Destruction
    |
    v
Credential Revocation
    |
    v
Archive / Retention

docs.title: Engagement Separation
docs.text:
One of the most important OPSEC controls is strict separation between engagements.

Avoid:

Client A files
      +
Client B credentials
      +
Client C infrastructure
      +
Personal projects

inside the same uncontrolled environment.

Prefer:

Operator Device
     |
     +--> Engagement A Workspace
     |
     +--> Engagement B Workspace
     |
     +--> Training / Lab Workspace

Each workspace should have clearly separated:

Credentials
Notes
Evidence
Infrastructure
Browser state
SSH configuration
VPN configuration
Payloads
Reports
Cloud resources

docs.title: Engagement Identifier
docs.text:
Assign each engagement a unique identifier.

Example:

RT-2026-001
RT-2026-002
PT-2026-001

Use the identifier consistently for:

Directories
Infrastructure
Evidence
Screenshots
Cloud tags
Operator logs
DNS records
Reports
Tickets
Cleanup records

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
Example:

engagements/
└── RT-2026-001/
    ├── scope/
    ├── notes/
    ├── recon/
    ├── evidence/
    ├── screenshots/
    ├── hashes/
    ├── infrastructure/
    ├── payloads/
    ├── logs/
    ├── reports/
    └── cleanup/

Do not store unnecessary customer data simply because a directory exists for it.

docs.title: File Naming
docs.text:
Use predictable names.

Example:

YYYYMMDD-HHMM-host-technique-description.ext

Example:

20260905-1430-WS01-applocker-policy.txt

Screenshot:

20260905-1435-WS01-defender-status.png

Network evidence:

20260905-1440-WS01-SRV01-connectivity.txt

docs.title: Operator Workstation
docs.text:
The operator workstation should be treated as security-sensitive infrastructure.

Protect it with:

Full-disk encryption
Strong authentication
Automatic screen locking
Current security updates
Minimal unnecessary software
Secure browser configuration
Protected SSH keys
Protected VPN credentials
Encrypted evidence
Backups where appropriate
Endpoint security

docs.title: Dedicated Assessment Environment
docs.text:
Where practical, use a dedicated environment for assessment work.

Options include:

Dedicated workstation
Virtual machine
Cloud workstation
Disposable VM
Separate user profile
Container for selected tooling

The choice depends on:

Engagement sensitivity
Customer requirements
Tool compatibility
Data-handling policy
Isolation requirements

docs.title: Virtual Machine Separation
docs.text:
A simple model:

Host Workstation
      |
      +--> Client-A VM
      |
      +--> Client-B VM
      |
      +--> Lab VM

Avoid sharing unnecessary:

Clipboard
Folders
Browser profiles
SSH agents
Credentials
Cloud sessions
VPN connections

between environments.

docs.title: VM Snapshots
docs.text:
Snapshots can provide useful rollback points.

Example:

Clean OS
   |
   v
Tools Installed
   |
   v
Pre-Engagement Snapshot
   |
   v
Assessment
   |
   v
Archive Required Evidence
   |
   v
Destroy / Revert

Be careful: snapshots can contain credentials and customer information.

docs.title: Operator Identity
docs.text:
Separate:

Personal identity
Corporate identity
Customer-provided identity
Assessment identity
Infrastructure identity

Do not use personal accounts for customer assessment infrastructure unless specifically required and approved.

docs.title: Customer-Provided Accounts
docs.text:
Customer-provided identities should be documented.

Example:

Account Purpose Privilege Owner Expiry rt-user01 Assumed breach Standard user Customer Engagement end rt-admin01 Recovery only Admin Customer Engagement end

Track:

Account
Purpose
Privilege
Systems
Credential owner
MFA
Creation time
Expiration
Revocation

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Assessment infrastructure should also follow least privilege.

Do not give every operator:

Root
Cloud Owner
DNS Administrator
Repository Administrator
Billing Administrator

unless required.

Prefer:

Operator
    |
    v
Required Role
    |
    v
Required Resource

docs.title: Privileged Infrastructure Access
docs.text:
Administrative interfaces should be reachable only through controlled management paths.

Example:

Operator
   |
   v
VPN / Bastion
   |
   v
Management Network
   |
   v
Team Server

Avoid:

Internet
   |
   v
Public Administrative Interface

docs.title: Infrastructure Inventory
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory from the beginning.

Example:

ID Type Address Provider Purpose Owner Status RT01 VPS 203.0.113.10 Provider Edge OP01 Active RT02 VPS Private Provider Management OP01 Active RTDNS01 Domain example.test Registrar Assessment OP02 Active

docs.title: Infrastructure Lifecycle
docs.text:
Every resource should move through a lifecycle.

Requested
    |
    v
Created
    |
    v
Configured
    |
    v
Validated
    |
    v
Active
    |
    v
Retired
    |
    v
Destroyed
    |
    v
Verified

docs.title: Cloud Resource Tags
docs.text:
Use provider tagging where supported.

Example:

Engagement=RT-2026-001
Owner=RedTeam
Purpose=Assessment
Expiry=2026-09-30

This helps identify forgotten resources.

docs.title: Resource Expiration
docs.text:
Every temporary resource should have an expected expiration.

Track:

VPS
Domains
Certificates
API tokens
Storage
DNS
VPN users
Temporary accounts
Cloud roles

An engagement should not leave forgotten infrastructure running indefinitely.

docs.title: Infrastructure Hardening
docs.text:
Assessment servers should be hardened like other Internet-facing systems.

Typical controls:

Patch operating system
Restrict administrative access
Use SSH keys
Disable unnecessary services
Use host firewall
Use MFA at provider
Protect API tokens
Monitor authentication
Enable logging
Synchronise time
Back up required configuration

docs.title: Linux Baseline
docs.text:
For Debian/Ubuntu-based infrastructure:

sudo apt update

Apply approved updates according to the engagement environment:

sudo apt upgrade

Review listening services:

sudo ss -lntup

Review firewall:

sudo ufw status verbose

Review failed services:

systemctl --failed

docs.title: Remote Administration Safety
docs.text:
Before modifying a remote firewall:

1. Confirm the current SSH connection.

2. Confirm the management source address.

3. Permit the required administrative path.

4. Validate the rule.

5. Only then enable restrictive firewall policy.

6. Keep a second administrative session available during validation.

This reduces the chance of locking yourself out.

docs.title: SSH Key Generation
docs.text:
Generate a dedicated key where appropriate:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 100

Use meaningful filenames:

~/.ssh/rt-2026-001-management

Never share the private key.

docs.title: SSH Key Permissions
docs.text:
Linux:

chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/rt-2026-001-management

Public key:

chmod 644 ~/.ssh/rt-2026-001-management.pub

docs.title: SSH Configuration
docs.text:
A local SSH configuration can help prevent using the wrong identity.

Example:

Host rt-2026-001-edge
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User operator
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/rt-2026-001-management
    IdentitiesOnly yes

This reduces accidental key selection.

docs.title: Verify SSH Server Configuration
docs.text:
Before reloading configuration:

sudo sshd -t

If validation succeeds, reload the appropriate service for the distribution.

On many Debian/Ubuntu systems:

sudo systemctl reload ssh

Maintain an existing session until the new connection has been tested.

docs.title: SSH Hardening
docs.text:
Typical settings may include:

PermitRootLogin no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
PasswordAuthentication no

Do not disable password authentication until key-based access has been successfully tested.

docs.title: Firewall Principles
docs.text:
Expose only required services.

Example:

Internet
   |
   +--> HTTPS
   |
   X--> SSH
   |
   X--> Administrative UI

Management traffic:

Approved Operator IP / VPN
           |
           +--> SSH
           |
           +--> Administrative UI

docs.title: UFW Baseline
docs.text:
Example:

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing

Allow SSH before enabling the firewall:

sudo ufw allow OpenSSH

Then:

sudo ufw enable

Review:

sudo ufw status verbose

Use more restrictive source-based rules where practical.

docs.title: Management Plane Separation
docs.text:
Separate operator management traffic from assessment traffic.

                   Operator
                      |
                      v
               Management Plane
                      |
                      v
                  Backend
                      |
                      v
                Assessment Edge
                      |
                      v
                    Target

This improves:

Access control
Logging
Troubleshooting
Cleanup
Infrastructure security

docs.title: DNS OPSEC
docs.text:
Domains used for assessments should be managed carefully.

Track:

Registrar
Account
MFA
Nameservers
DNS provider
Records
Purpose
Expiration
Engagement

docs.title: DNS Inventory
docs.text:
Example:

Name Type Value Purpose edge.example.test A 203.0.113.10 Assessment edge files.example.test A 203.0.113.20 Controlled hosting www.example.test CNAME edge.example.test Web endpoint

docs.title: DNS Record Types
docs.text:
Common records:

Record Purpose A IPv4 address AAAA IPv6 address CNAME Alias MX Mail TXT Text/policy data NS Nameserver

docs.title: DNS Validation
docs.text:
dig example.test

Specific record:

dig A example.test

Nameservers:

dig NS example.test

TXT:

dig TXT example.test

docs.title: DNS Cleanup
docs.text:
At engagement completion:

Remove temporary records
Remove stale subdomains
Remove mail records if temporary
Remove verification records
Remove unused nameserver delegations
Document retained records
Verify resolution

docs.title: Domain Safety
docs.text:
Avoid unnecessary brand impersonation.

Domain naming and social-engineering infrastructure should follow explicit customer approval.

Consider:

Customer trademark
Third-party trademark
Registrar policy
Provider terms
Engagement scope
Social-engineering authorisation

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Use TLS for administrative and assessment services where appropriate.

Benefits include:

Transport confidentiality
Server authentication
Integrity
Reduced accidental credential exposure

docs.title: TLS Validation
docs.text:
Inspect:

openssl s_client -connect example.test:443 -servername example.test

Basic HTTPS validation:

curl -I https://example.test/

docs.title: Certificate Inventory
docs.text:
Track:

Certificate
Hostname
Issuer
Private-key location
Creation
Expiration
Renewal
Revocation

docs.title: Private Keys
docs.text:
Private keys should never be stored in:

Public Git repositories
Shared chat
Public storage
Unencrypted evidence
Screenshots
Issue trackers
Documentation repositories

Protect file permissions and access.

docs.title: Secrets Management
docs.text:
Assessment secrets may include:

SSH keys
VPN credentials
API tokens
Cloud credentials
DNS tokens
C2 credentials
Customer accounts
Certificates
Repository tokens
Passwords

docs.title: Secret Storage
docs.text:
Prefer:

Password manager
Secret vault
Protected environment
Encrypted credential store

Avoid:

notes.txt
passwords.txt
Desktop files
Public repositories
Shell scripts
Chat history
Screenshots

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables may be useful for temporary automation but are not automatically secure.

They may be exposed through:

Process inspection
Debug output
Shell history
Crash information
CI/CD logs
Child processes

Do not treat environment variables as a replacement for proper secret management.

docs.title: Shell History
docs.text:
Be aware that commands may be stored in shell history.

Linux:

history

PowerShell:

Get-History

PSReadLine history may also persist separately.

Do not type sensitive credentials directly into commands where avoidable.

docs.title: Git Repository OPSEC
docs.text:
Repositories can accidentally expose:

Credentials
API keys
Internal domains
Customer IP addresses
Screenshots
Payloads
Reports
Private keys
Environment files

docs.title: Repository Separation
docs.text:
Prefer:

Public Notes Repository
        |
        X
        |
Customer Engagement Repository

Never use the public notes repository as an engagement evidence store.

docs.title: .gitignore
docs.text:
Common exclusions may include:

.env
.env.*
*.key
*.pem
*.pfx
*.p12
credentials/
secrets/
evidence/
screenshots/
customer-data/

A .gitignore prevents new accidental additions but does not remove secrets already committed.

docs.title: Check Git Status
docs.text:
Before committing:

git status

Review the actual diff:

git diff

Review staged content:

git diff --cached

docs.title: Secret Scanning
docs.text:
Where available, use repository secret-scanning capabilities.

The goal is to detect:

API tokens
Cloud keys
Private keys
Passwords
Authentication tokens

before they leave the controlled environment.

docs.title: Committed Secret Response
docs.text:
If a secret is committed:

Do not assume deleting the file fixes the issue.

Treat the secret as potentially compromised.

Response:

Revoke
    |
    v
Rotate
    |
    v
Remove from active repository
    |
    v
Assess history exposure
    |
    v
Clean history where required
    |
    v
Verify

docs.title: Browser OPSEC
docs.text:
Browsers can mix identities through:

Cookies
Saved passwords
Autofill
History
Extensions
Cloud sync
SSO sessions
Downloads
Certificates

docs.title: Browser Profiles
docs.text:
Use separate browser profiles where appropriate.

Example:

Browser
   |
   +--> Corporate
   |
   +--> Engagement RT-2026-001
   |
   +--> Engagement RT-2026-002
   |
   +--> Research

Do not enable personal browser synchronisation inside an assessment profile.

docs.title: Browser Extensions
docs.text:
Review extensions before using a browser for sensitive assessment work.

Extensions may have permission to read:

Page content
URLs
Clipboard
Downloads
Authentication data

Use the minimum required set.

docs.title: Cookies and Sessions
docs.text:
Customer authentication sessions are sensitive.

After an engagement:

Log out
Revoke test sessions where possible
Clear engagement browser data
Remove customer certificates
Remove saved credentials
Destroy disposable profiles

docs.title: VPN Separation
docs.text:
Before connecting to a customer VPN, understand:

Routes
DNS changes
Split tunnelling
Default gateway
Accessible networks
Excluded networks
Local network behaviour

A VPN may alter the operator's routing unexpectedly.

docs.title: Route Validation
docs.text:
Linux:

ip route

Windows:

route print

Record routes before and after connecting to a customer network if network isolation is important.

docs.title: DNS After VPN Connection
docs.text:
Linux:

resolvectl status

Windows:

ipconfig /all

This helps identify DNS changes introduced by the VPN.

docs.title: Scope Enforcement
docs.text:
Do not rely on memory to determine which targets are authorised.

Maintain machine-readable scope where possible.

Example:

scope/
├── domains.txt
├── ips.txt
├── excluded-ips.txt
├── urls.txt
└── notes.md

docs.title: Scope Before Action
docs.text:
Use the mental model:

Target
  |
  v
In Scope?
 /     \
No     Yes
|       |
STOP    v
     Technique
       Allowed?
      /      \
     No      Yes
     |        |
    STOP      v
           Execute

docs.title: Out-of-Scope Discovery
docs.text:
If an apparently related system is discovered but is not explicitly in scope:

Discover
   |
   v
Record
   |
   v
Do Not Test
   |
   v
Request Clarification

Do not infer authorisation from ownership or naming.

docs.title: Third-Party Services
docs.text:
Modern organisations rely heavily on third parties.

Examples:

CDN
SaaS
Cloud provider
Email provider
Payment processor
Identity provider
Managed service
Hosting provider

Customer authorisation does not automatically provide permission to test third-party infrastructure.

docs.title: Payload Management
docs.text:
Assessment payloads and binaries should be controlled.

Track:

Filename
Purpose
Hash
Source
Build date
Target
Deployment location
Cleanup status

docs.title: Payload Hashing
docs.text:
Linux:

sha256sum file

Windows:

Get-FileHash .\file.exe -Algorithm SHA256

Record the hash in operator notes.

docs.title: Payload Inventory
docs.text:
Example:

File SHA-256 Purpose Host Status assessment-test.exe ... Controlled validation WS01 Removed test-script.ps1 ... Detection test WS02 Removed

docs.title: Controlled File Hosting
docs.text:
Assessment file hosting should avoid accidental public exposure.

Prefer:

Authentication
Source restrictions
Non-indexed locations
Minimal retention
Logging
Explicit file inventory

Avoid open directory listing unless there is a specific reason.

docs.title: Temporary Hosting
docs.text:
Concept:

Operator
    |
    v
Controlled File Server
    |
    v
Authorised Target

After the test:

Remove artifact
Stop server if unnecessary
Archive required logs
Verify no unrelated downloads occurred

docs.title: Cloud Storage
docs.text:
Do not use public storage buckets for sensitive assessment artifacts.

Prefer:

Private storage
Restricted identities
Encryption
Short retention
Access logging
Lifecycle rules

docs.title: Signed URLs
docs.text:
Temporary signed URLs may reduce the need for permanently public files.

However:

Signed URL = Temporary Credential

Protect it accordingly.

docs.title: Payload Cleanup
docs.text:
After a test:

Target file
Assessment server copy
Temporary web copy
Cloud storage copy
Operator working copy

should each have an intentional retention or deletion decision.

docs.title: C2 OPSEC
docs.text:
Command-and-control infrastructure is security-sensitive.

Administrative access should be separated from target-facing communication.

Operator
   |
   v
Management Channel
   |
   v
C2 Server
   |
   v
Assessment Channel
   |
   v
Authorised Endpoint

See:

Command and Control

docs.title: C2 Administrative Interfaces
docs.text:
Do not expose administrative interfaces unnecessarily.

Protect with:

VPN
IP allowlisting
Strong authentication
TLS
Firewall
Separate management interface

docs.title: C2 Credentials
docs.text:
Treat C2 credentials as privileged infrastructure secrets.

Use:

Unique credentials
Strong authentication
Per-engagement access
Credential rotation
Access removal after engagement

docs.title: C2 Logging
docs.text:
Where supported, retain useful operational records such as:

Operator
Session
Host
Timestamp
Action
Result

This helps answer:

Who performed the action?

When?

Against which system?

Why?

docs.title: Pivoting OPSEC
docs.text:
Pivoting changes network reachability.

Examples include:

Ligolo-ng
Chisel
SSH forwarding
SOCKS
VPN

Every pivot should have:

Purpose
Operator
Pivot host
Reachable network
Routes
Start time
Stop time
Cleanup

docs.title: Pivot Scope Risk
docs.text:
A pivot may expose networks that were not previously reachable.

Operator
    |
    v
Pivot
    |
    +--> In-Scope Network
    |
    +--> Out-of-Scope Network

Do not assume every network reachable through a compromised host is authorised.

docs.title: Route Inventory
docs.text:
Before pivoting:

Known Scope
    |
    v
Required Network
    |
    v
Route Added
    |
    v
Validation

After testing:

Remove Route
    |
    v
Stop Tunnel
    |
    v
Remove Agent
    |
    v
Verify

docs.title: Ligolo-ng Cleanup
docs.text:
When Ligolo-ng has been used, verify:

Agent process terminated
Proxy stopped
Tunnel interface removed
Routes removed
Temporary files removed
Firewall changes restored

docs.title: Chisel Cleanup
docs.text:
Verify:

Client stopped
Server stopped
Listeners removed
Temporary binaries removed
Service definitions removed if created
Logs handled according to policy

docs.title: SSH Tunnel Cleanup
docs.text:
Confirm no unexpected forwarding remains.

Linux:

ps aux | grep '[s]sh'

Review listening sockets:

ss -lntp

docs.title: Evidence OPSEC
docs.text:
Evidence can be more sensitive than the tools used to collect it.

Evidence may contain:

Credentials
Hostnames
IP addresses
Usernames
Internal URLs
Source code
Configuration
Customer data
Screenshots
Attack paths
Security-control details

docs.title: Evidence Minimisation
docs.text:
Collect only what is necessary to demonstrate the finding.

Prefer:

Relevant lines
       |
       v
Context
       |
       v
Proof

instead of:

Entire database
Entire mailbox
Entire filesystem

docs.title: Screenshot Review
docs.text:
Before including a screenshot, check for:

Passwords
Tokens
Personal data
Other customer tabs
Personal bookmarks
Notifications
Chat windows
Internal URLs
Unrelated terminals
Browser account details

docs.title: Screenshot Cropping
docs.text:
Cropping can reduce unnecessary disclosure, but preserve enough context to make the evidence meaningful.

Do not manipulate evidence in a way that changes its meaning.

docs.title: Evidence Integrity
docs.text:
For important files, calculate a hash.

Linux:

sha256sum evidence.bin

Windows:

Get-FileHash .\evidence.bin -Algorithm SHA256

docs.title: Evidence Manifest
docs.text:
Example:

evidence/
├── 001-defender-status.txt
├── 002-applocker-policy.txt
├── 003-network-test.txt
└── SHA256SUMS

Generate on Linux:

sha256sum evidence/* > SHA256SUMS

Ensure the output file itself is not unintentionally included in a recursive hashing workflow.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Sensitive evidence should be encrypted at rest and in transit according to customer and organisational requirements.

Protect:

Operator laptop
External storage
Cloud storage
Backups
Report drafts
Evidence archives

docs.title: Data Classification
docs.text:
A useful assessment classification may include:

Public
Internal
Confidential
Highly Sensitive
Credential Material

Follow the customer's classification requirements when provided.

docs.title: Personal Data
docs.text:
Avoid collecting personal data unless required for the assessment.

If encountered:

Minimise access
Do not copy unnecessarily
Do not include unnecessarily in screenshots
Follow retention policy
Follow legal requirements

docs.title: Credential Evidence
docs.text:
A finding normally does not require publishing the full credential.

Instead of:

Password: SuperSecretPassword123!

use:

A valid credential for the affected account was obtained during
the authorised assessment. The credential has been omitted from
the report.

docs.title: Hash Evidence
docs.text:
Similarly, avoid placing reusable authentication material directly in reports.

Use:

Credential material was successfully accessed and validated
against the authorised target.

Store the sensitive artifact separately only when required.

docs.title: Report OPSEC
docs.text:
Reports often contain:

Attack paths
Credentials
Network architecture
Security weaknesses
Screenshots
Internal hostnames
Sensitive recommendations

Treat draft reports as confidential assessment data.

docs.title: Report Distribution
docs.text:
Maintain an approved recipient list.

Example:

Customer Engagement Lead
Security Lead
Authorised Technical Contacts

Avoid forwarding reports through uncontrolled channels.

docs.title: Communications
docs.text:
Define approved communication channels before testing.

Examples:

Corporate email
Customer ticketing system
Approved secure chat
Emergency telephone
Project platform

Do not use personal messaging accounts for sensitive engagement data unless explicitly approved.

docs.title: Emergency Communication
docs.text:
Operators should know:

Who to contact

How to contact them

When to stop

How to identify the engagement

How to describe the affected system

How to preserve evidence

docs.title: Emergency Message Structure
docs.text:
Engagement:
RT-2026-001

Time:
2026-09-05 18:42 UTC

System:
WS01

Observation:
Unexpected production instability following authorised test.

Action:
Testing stopped.

Current State:
No further activity being performed.

Contact:
OP01

docs.title: Operational Logging
docs.text:
Maintain an operator timeline.

Example:

Time Operator Source Target Action Result 10:00 OP01 RT01 WS01 Connectivity test Success 10:12 OP01 WS01 WS01 Enumeration Success 10:31 OP02 WS01 SRV01 Authentication validation Blocked

docs.title: Operator Accountability
docs.text:
Shared accounts make investigation difficult.

Prefer:

OP01
OP02
OP03

over:

redteam

for management access where practical.

docs.title: Command Logging
docs.text:
Important assessment commands should be recorded.

The objective is:

Reproducibility
Accountability
Evidence
Cleanup
Troubleshooting

not indiscriminate collection of every terminal keystroke.

docs.title: Terminal Separation
docs.text:
A common source of mistakes is using the wrong terminal.

Use obvious visual or naming separation.

Example:

[CLIENT-A]
[CLIENT-B]
[LAB]
[INFRA]

Terminal titles, tmux sessions, or dedicated workspaces can help.

docs.title: tmux Sessions
docs.text:
Example:

tmux new -s rt-2026-001

List:

tmux ls

Attach:

tmux attach -t rt-2026-001

Avoid placing secrets in session names.

docs.title: Working Directory Check
docs.text:
Before running an engagement command:

pwd

Repository:

git status

VPN:

ip route

These simple checks can prevent mistakes.

docs.title: Clipboard Risk
docs.text:
The clipboard may contain:

Passwords
Hashes
Tokens
Commands
Customer data
Internal URLs

Be careful when switching between:

Customer environment
Personal browser
Chat
Documentation
Other engagement

docs.title: Copy/Paste Verification
docs.text:
Before pressing Enter:

Correct terminal?

Correct host?

Correct client?

Correct command?

Correct target?

Correct scope?

This is one of the simplest OPSEC controls.

docs.title: Command History Review
docs.text:
At the end of an engagement, review whether local histories contain sensitive material.

Do not automatically destroy logs that are required for evidence or accountability.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Red team OPSEC can be reduced to:

Know which engagement you are working on.

Know which identity you are using.

Know which infrastructure belongs to the engagement.

Know exactly which targets are authorised.

Protect credentials and customer data.

Keep assessment resources isolated.

Record important actions.

Track everything introduced into the environment.

Treat unexpected activity seriously.

Remove everything that should not remain.

Verify cleanup rather than assuming it succeeded.

OPSEC should make testing safer

Good red team OPSEC is not measured by how difficult the assessment is to attribute to the authorised testers. It is measured by whether customer data, credentials, infrastructure, evidence, and operator activity remain controlled throughout the engagement and whether every introduced artifact can be accounted for and removed.

Authorised testing only

Operational security does not override scope, customer safety, provider terms, or the Rules of Engagement. Do not use OPSEC practices to conceal unauthorised activity. Maintain sufficient logs for deconfliction and accountability, immediately escalate unexpected production impact or suspected third-party activity, and verify complete cleanup at the end of every assessment.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Persistence is the process of maintaining authorised access to a system, identity, application, or environment across events that might otherwise remove the original foothold.

Examples include:

User logoff
Process termination
System reboot
Credential rotation
Service restart
Application restart
Temporary session expiry

A simplified model is:

Initial Access
      |
      v
Foothold
      |
      v
Persistence Required?
    /       \
  No         Yes
  |           |
  v           v
Continue    Select
Without     Controlled
Persistence Mechanism
              |
              v
          Validate
              |
              v
          Document
              |
              v
           Cleanup

Persistence can create long-lived security impact and should only be tested when explicitly permitted by the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Persistence Objectives
docs.text:
Persistence testing should answer questions such as:

Can an attacker maintain access?
Which security boundary enables persistence?
What privilege is required?
Does persistence survive reboot or logon?
Which identity or component is affected?
Was the modification detected?
Would defenders identify the persistence?
Can the change be reliably removed?

The objective is not to install every possible persistence mechanism.

Use the minimum persistence required to demonstrate the security control or attack path being assessed.

docs.title: Persistence vs Initial Access
docs.text:
Initial access establishes the first foothold.

Persistence attempts to retain access.

Initial Access

External
   |
   v
Target


Persistence

Target
  |
  v
Access Survives
Security State Change

An engagement can successfully achieve its objectives without persistence.

docs.title: Persistence vs Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Persistence and privilege escalation are also separate concepts.

Persistence:
Keep existing access


Privilege Escalation:
Obtain greater privilege

A persistence mechanism may run with higher privileges if installed from an already privileged context, but the persistence mechanism itself does not necessarily create that privilege.

docs.title: Persistence vs C2
docs.text:
Persistence and command and control are different layers.

Persistence
    |
    v
Starts Assessment Component
    |
    v
Command and Control

Persistence determines how access is re-established.

C2 determines how the controlled component communicates with the operator.

docs.title: Persistence Lifecycle
docs.text:
A useful persistence lifecycle is:

Requirement
    |
    v
Select Mechanism
    |
    v
Record Original State
    |
    v
Deploy
    |
    v
Validate
    |
    v
Measure Detection
    |
    v
Use Only as Required
    |
    v
Remove
    |
    v
Verify Original State

docs.title: Before Testing Persistence
docs.text:

Target is in scope
Current privilege is understood
Mechanism is permitted
Reboot testing is permitted
Account creation is permitted
Credential modification is permitted
Cloud modification is permitted
Directory modification is permitted
Cleanup procedure is known
Emergency contact is available

Persistence testing should always have a cleanup plan before deployment.

docs.title: Persistence Inventory
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory of every persistence change.

Example:

ID Host Mechanism Location Created Cleanup PERS-001 TEST-WKS01 Scheduled task Task Scheduler Yes Required PERS-002 TEST-LNX01 systemd unit /etc/systemd/system/ Yes Required PERS-003 Test account SSH key authorized_keys Yes Required

Do not rely on memory for cleanup.

docs.title: Record Original State
docs.text:
Before changing a persistence location, record its existing state.

For example:

Original file
Original permissions
Original registry value
Original task configuration
Original service configuration
Original account membership
Original SSH authorized_keys
Original cloud role assignment

This makes reliable restoration possible.

docs.title: Windows Persistence
docs.text:
Windows provides many legitimate mechanisms that can start software or maintain access.

Common categories include:

Scheduled tasks
Services
Run keys
Startup folders
User accounts
Group membership
PowerShell profiles
WMI event subscriptions
Application-specific startup
Logon scripts
Authentication material
Remote-management configuration

docs.title: Windows Persistence Model
docs.text:
Windows Persistence
       |
       +--> Scheduled Tasks
       |
       +--> Services
       |
       +--> Registry
       |
       +--> Startup
       |
       +--> Accounts
       |
       +--> PowerShell
       |
       +--> WMI
       |
       +--> Application
       |
       +--> Active Directory

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Windows Task Scheduler can execute programs:

At startup
At logon
At a specific time
On an event
On a repeating schedule

Enumerate:

schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

A scheduled task can be legitimate administration or a persistence mechanism depending on context.

docs.title: Inspect a Scheduled Task
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'TASKNAME'

Review actions:

(Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'TASKNAME').Actions

Review:

Task name
Execution identity
Trigger
Action
Arguments
Executable
Working directory
Privilege level

docs.title: Scheduled Task Persistence Assessment
docs.text:
A persistence path can be represented as:

Trigger
   |
   v
Scheduled Task
   |
   v
Configured Action
   |
   v
Assessment Component

Important questions include:

Who can create the task?
Who can modify it?
Which identity executes it?
Does it survive reboot?
Is task creation monitored?
Is the action protected from modification?

docs.title: Safe Scheduled Task Validation
docs.text:
Where task creation is explicitly authorised, prefer a harmless proof such as writing a marker file rather than launching a remote-access component.

Example PowerShell:

$action = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute 'cmd.exe' -Argument '/c echo PersistenceTest > C:\Windows\Temp\persistence-test.txt'
$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Once -At (Get-Date).AddMinutes(2)
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'Assessment-Persistence-Test' -Action $action -Trigger $trigger -Description 'Authorised security assessment persistence validation'

Verify:

Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'Assessment-Persistence-Test'

After the test:

Unregister-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'Assessment-Persistence-Test' -Confirm:$false

Remove the marker:

Remove-Item 'C:\Windows\Temp\persistence-test.txt' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Windows Services
docs.text:
Services can provide persistence because they can start:

Automatically at boot
On demand
Through service dependencies
Through administrative action

Enumerate:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, State, StartMode, PathName

Services should be assessed together with:

Service permissions
Executable permissions
Directory permissions
Service identity
Startup mode
Configuration protection

docs.title: Service Persistence Model
docs.text:
System Boot
    |
    v
Service Control Manager
    |
    v
Service
    |
    v
Configured Executable

A service running as LocalSystem represents a particularly sensitive persistence location.

docs.title: Service Creation
docs.text:
Service creation is a significant system modification.

Where explicitly authorised, a benign test service can validate whether the current security context can create a persistent service without deploying an operational payload.

Example:

sc.exe create AssessmentPersistenceTest binPath= "C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /c exit 0" start= demand

Inspect:

sc.exe qc AssessmentPersistenceTest

Remove:

sc.exe delete AssessmentPersistenceTest

Use unique assessment names to make cleanup and detection correlation easier.

docs.title: Registry Run Keys
docs.text:
Windows supports programs that run when users log on.

Common locations include:

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

Enumerate:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'

System-wide:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'

The current-user location generally affects that user, while machine-level locations can have broader impact depending on configuration.

docs.title: Run Key Validation
docs.text:
Where modification is authorised, a harmless marker command can demonstrate persistence.

Example current-user test:

New-ItemProperty -Path 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' -Name 'AssessmentPersistenceTest' -Value 'cmd.exe /c echo PersistenceTest > %TEMP%\persistence-test.txt' -PropertyType String

Verify:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'

Cleanup:

Remove-ItemProperty -Path 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' -Name 'AssessmentPersistenceTest'

docs.title: Startup Folder
docs.text:
Windows also supports startup folders.

Current-user startup folder:

[Environment]::GetFolderPath('Startup')

Common startup folder:

[Environment]::GetFolderPath('CommonStartup')

Assess:

Who can write to the directory?
Which users are affected?
What files already exist?
Are changes monitored?

docs.title: Startup Folder Model
docs.text:
User Logon
    |
    v
Startup Folder
    |
    v
Configured File
    |
    v
Execution

Writable startup locations can become persistence opportunities when an attacker has sufficient access.

docs.title: User Accounts
docs.text:
Account creation can provide persistent access.

Review local users:

Get-LocalUser

Review local groups:

Get-LocalGroup

Administrators:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'

Account creation should only be tested when explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Test Accounts
docs.text:
If a temporary assessment account is approved:

Use a recognisable name
Use a unique strong password
Record creation time
Record group membership
Do not reuse the password
Remove the account after testing
Verify removal

Prefer customer-provided test identities where possible.

docs.title: Local Group Persistence
docs.text:
An existing account may gain persistent administrative access through group membership.

Conceptually:

User
  |
  v
Local Administrators
  |
  v
Persistent Administrative Access

Monitor changes to sensitive groups such as:

Administrators
Remote Desktop Users
Remote Management Users
Backup Operators

docs.title: PowerShell Profiles
docs.text:
PowerShell profiles can execute PowerShell content when certain PowerShell hosts start.

List profile paths:

$PROFILE | Format-List *

Current profile:

$PROFILE

Check whether it exists:

Test-Path $PROFILE

PowerShell profiles are legitimate customisation mechanisms but can also become persistence locations if writable by an inappropriate user.

docs.title: PowerShell Profile Assessment
docs.text:
Review:

Profile path
Owner
ACL
Affected user
Affected PowerShell host
Existing content
Application-control policy
PowerShell language mode

Do not overwrite an existing profile during testing.

docs.title: WMI Event Subscription
docs.text:
WMI supports permanent event subscriptions that can react to system events.

The conceptual structure is:

Event Filter
     |
     v
Consumer
     |
     v
Binding

Permanent WMI subscriptions are sensitive because they can survive reboots.

Assessment should normally focus on whether such persistence is detectable and whether inappropriate identities can create it.

docs.title: WMI Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Useful defensive areas include:

WMI-Activity logs
WMI repository changes
Process creation
PowerShell telemetry
EDR telemetry
Unusual permanent event consumers

docs.title: Logon Scripts
docs.text:
Windows and Active Directory can execute scripts during user logon.

Potential locations include:

Local policy
Group Policy
Domain logon scripts
SYSVOL
Application-specific login processes

Changes to domain-managed logon scripts can affect many users and should not be performed unless specifically approved.

docs.title: Application Persistence
docs.text:
Applications may provide their own startup or extension mechanisms.

Examples include:

Plugins
Modules
Startup scripts
Scheduled jobs
Hooks
Extensions
Application services
Administrative automation

An application-specific persistence path should be assessed against the application's intended security model.

docs.title: Linux Persistence
docs.text:
Common Linux persistence mechanisms include:

Cron
systemd
Shell startup files
SSH authorized_keys
User accounts
Sudo configuration
Application startup
Init scripts
Timers
Container configuration

docs.title: Linux Persistence Model
docs.text:
Linux Persistence
      |
      +--> Cron
      |
      +--> systemd
      |
      +--> SSH
      |
      +--> Shell Startup
      |
      +--> Accounts
      |
      +--> Sudo
      |
      +--> Applications
      |
      +--> Containers

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Cron executes commands on schedules.

Review system crontab:

cat /etc/crontab

List cron directories:

ls -la /etc/cron.d/

ls -la /etc/cron.daily/

Current user:

crontab -l

Cron persistence depends on:

Who owns the cron entry?
Which identity executes it?
Which command is executed?
Can the command or script be modified?

docs.title: Cron Persistence Model
docs.text:
Cron Scheduler
      |
      v
Cron Entry
      |
      v
Script / Command
      |
      v
Execution

A privileged cron entry that references a writable script is also a privilege escalation concern.

docs.title: Safe Cron Validation
docs.text:
For a dedicated authorised test account, a harmless marker can validate persistence.

Example user crontab entry:

*/5 * * * * /usr/bin/touch /tmp/assessment-persistence-test

After validation, remove the entry and marker.

Do not modify production cron jobs merely to prove persistence.

docs.title: systemd
docs.text:
systemd manages services on many Linux distributions.

List services:

systemctl list-unit-files --type=service

Inspect a specific unit:

systemctl cat SERVICE

Review:

Unit path
ExecStart
User
Group
EnvironmentFile
Restart policy
Enablement
File permissions

docs.title: systemd Persistence Model
docs.text:
Boot
 |
 v
systemd
 |
 v
Unit
 |
 v
ExecStart
 |
 v
Application

A service enabled at boot can provide persistent execution.

docs.title: systemd Timers
docs.text:
systemd timers provide scheduled execution similar to cron.

List:

systemctl list-timers --all

Conceptually:

Timer
  |
  v
Service Unit
  |
  v
Command

Review timers together with the service units they trigger.

docs.title: Shell Startup Files
docs.text:
Shells can execute user configuration during login or interactive startup.

Examples include:

~/.bashrc
~/.bash_profile
~/.profile
~/.zshrc

These are normally user-level persistence locations.

Review:

ls -la ~

Inspect only files relevant to the authorised identity.

docs.title: Shell Startup Persistence Model
docs.text:
User Starts Shell
      |
      v
Startup File
      |
      v
Configured Command

The exact startup files depend on the shell and invocation mode.

docs.title: SSH authorized_keys
docs.text:
SSH public-key authentication commonly uses:

~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Review:

ls -la ~/.ssh/

Where authorised:

cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Adding a public key can provide persistent SSH access to that identity.

This is a significant account modification and should only be performed where explicitly permitted.

docs.title: SSH Key Persistence Model
docs.text:
Operator Public Key
       |
       v
authorized_keys
       |
       v
SSH Authentication
       |
       v
User Account

The private key remains with the operator.

Only the public key should be added to the authorised account.

docs.title: SSH authorized_keys Options
docs.text:
Entries can include restrictions such as:

from=
command=
no-agent-forwarding
no-port-forwarding
no-pty

Restricting keys can reduce the impact of specialised automation or service keys.

docs.title: SSH Persistence Cleanup
docs.text:
If an assessment key is added:

Record exact public key
Record file before modification
Add only one unique line
Validate access
Remove exact line
Verify file
Verify permissions

Do not replace the complete authorized_keys file.

docs.title: Linux User Accounts
docs.text:
Review:

cat /etc/passwd

Current identity:

id

Privileged group membership:

getent group sudo

or on some distributions:

getent group wheel

Account creation or privilege modification should only occur when specifically authorised.

docs.title: Sudo Persistence
docs.text:
Changes to sudo configuration can create long-lived privileged access.

Relevant locations include:

/etc/sudoers
/etc/sudoers.d/

Review safely:

sudo -l

Do not modify production sudo policy merely to demonstrate that a privileged user could modify it.

docs.title: Sudoers Safety
docs.text:
When legitimate sudo configuration must be changed, administrators should use:

visudo

For assessment purposes, prefer configuration review and permission validation rather than changing security-critical policy.

docs.title: Application Persistence on Linux
docs.text:
Applications may provide:

Plugins
Modules
Startup hooks
Worker services
Scheduled jobs
Configuration callbacks
Custom scripts

Assess whether lower-privilege users can modify components executed by more privileged application identities.

docs.title: Container Persistence
docs.text:
Containers introduce additional persistence considerations.

Examples include:

Restart policies
Mounted host directories
Container images
Orchestrator configuration
Startup commands
Volumes
Secrets
Kubernetes workloads

Persistence at the container layer may disappear when the container is replaced.

Persistence at the orchestration layer may survive replacement.

docs.title: Docker Restart Policies
docs.text:
Docker containers can use restart policies.

Inspect:

docker inspect CONTAINER

A container configured to restart automatically may survive host or daemon restarts depending on configuration.

Do not create persistent containers on production infrastructure unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Kubernetes Persistence
docs.text:
Kubernetes persistence may involve objects such as:

Deployment
DaemonSet
StatefulSet
CronJob
ServiceAccount
RoleBinding
ClusterRoleBinding
Admission configuration

These objects can affect many systems.

Kubernetes persistence testing should be restricted to the authorised cluster and namespaces.

docs.title: Active Directory Persistence
docs.text:
Active Directory persistence can have a significantly larger blast radius than local host persistence.

Potential categories include:

Privileged group membership
Directory ACLs
Kerberos keys
Delegation
Certificates
Authentication configuration
Group Policy
SIDHistory
Service accounts
Machine accounts
Trust relationships

docs.title: Active Directory Persistence Model
docs.text:
Domain Identity
      |
      v
Directory Modification
      |
      v
Persistent Trust / Permission
      |
      v
Future Authentication

Directory persistence should only be tested where specifically included in the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Privileged Group Membership
docs.text:
Sensitive groups can include:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Administrators
Account Operators
Backup Operators
Server Operators
DNSAdmins

Membership changes can create straightforward persistent privilege.

Review:

Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins'

where the Active Directory PowerShell module is available and the query is authorised.

docs.title: Nested Group Persistence
docs.text:
Privilege may also be inherited through nested groups.

User
 |
 v
Group A
 |
 v
Group B
 |
 v
Privileged Group

Reviewing only direct membership can therefore miss persistence paths.

BloodHound can help visualise these relationships.

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: ACL-Based Persistence
docs.text:
Active Directory objects have access control lists.

Persistent control can result from rights over objects such as:

Users
Groups
Computers
Organisational Units
Group Policy Objects
Certificate infrastructure
Domain objects

Examples of sensitive permissions include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
Specific attribute write permissions

Use:

ACL and ACE

docs.title: Group Policy Persistence
docs.text:
Group Policy can affect large numbers of systems and users.

GPO
 |
 +--> Workstations
 |
 +--> Servers
 |
 +--> Users

Changes to GPOs can therefore create broad persistence.

During normal assessments, avoid modifying production GPOs unless the scenario explicitly requires it.

docs.title: SIDHistory
docs.text:
SIDHistory can influence access because Windows authorization can consider historical SIDs associated with an account.

Unexpected privileged SIDHistory values can represent a serious security concern.

Use:

SIDHistory

docs.title: Kerberos Persistence
docs.text:
Kerberos persistence can involve long-term domain authentication material.

High-impact examples can involve compromise of:

KRBTGT key material
Service account keys
Machine account keys
Trust keys

Such testing can have domain-wide implications.

docs.title: Golden Ticket Concept
docs.text:
A Golden Ticket scenario relates to compromise of the Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket account key material.

Conceptually:

KRBTGT Key Material
       |
       v
Forged TGT Capability
       |
       v
Domain Authentication Impact

This represents extremely sensitive domain-level access.

Do not perform Golden Ticket persistence testing unless explicitly required and approved.

docs.title: Trust Tickets
docs.text:
Inter-domain trust relationships introduce additional Kerberos trust material.

Use:

Trust Tickets

and:

Trust Relationships

docs.title: Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Active Directory authentication can involve key-based credential attributes.

Improper control of these attributes can provide persistent authentication to an account.

Use:

Shadow Credentials

docs.title: Resource-Based Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation can alter which identities may act to services associated with a computer object.

Misconfigured object permissions can sometimes create durable attack paths.

Use:

RBCD

docs.title: Machine Accounts
docs.text:
Computer objects are security principals.

Machine account manipulation can sometimes become part of a persistence chain.

Use:

Machine Account Quota

docs.title: AD CS Persistence
docs.text:
Active Directory Certificate Services can create powerful authentication paths.

A certificate and corresponding private key may continue to authenticate independently of the account password.

Certificate
     +
Private Key
     |
     v
Authentication

This makes certificate lifecycle management important during incident response.

docs.title: Certificate Persistence
docs.text:
A simplified model is:

Privileged Certificate
       |
       v
Password Rotated
       |
       v
Certificate Still Valid?
       |
      Yes
       |
       v
Authentication May Remain Possible

This is one reason password rotation alone may be insufficient after certificate-based compromise.

docs.title: Golden Certificate
docs.text:
Compromise of a certificate authority's signing key can have severe consequences.

Use:

Golden Certificate

Testing CA key compromise should be considered exceptionally sensitive and is rarely necessary in production assessments.

docs.title: AD CS
docs.text:
Use the dedicated AD CS section for certificate-service attack paths:

Active Directory Certificate Services

docs.title: Cloud Persistence
docs.text:
Cloud persistence can involve:

User accounts
API keys
Application registrations
Service principals
Certificates
Role assignments
Federated identities
Automation accounts
Access policies
CI/CD credentials
OAuth applications
Long-lived tokens

docs.title: Cloud Persistence Model
docs.text:
Cloud Identity
      |
      v
Persistent Credential
      |
      v
Role / Permission
      |
      v
Cloud Resource Access

Cloud modifications can affect multiple subscriptions, projects, accounts, or tenants.

docs.title: Cloud Access Keys
docs.text:
Long-lived access keys can provide persistent programmatic authentication.

Assess:

Owner
Creation date
Last use
Permissions
Expiry
Rotation
Source restrictions

Prefer short-lived or managed credentials where possible.

docs.title: Service Principals
docs.text:
Application identities can provide persistent cloud access.

Potential credential types include:

Client secrets
Certificates
Federated credentials
Managed identities

Service principals should have narrowly scoped permissions and controlled credential lifecycle.

docs.title: OAuth Applications
docs.text:
OAuth applications may receive delegated or application permissions.

Persistence risk depends on:

Consent
Scopes
Application permissions
Refresh tokens
Administrative consent
Publisher trust
Credential lifetime

Unexpected high-privilege applications should be investigated.

docs.title: Cloud Role Assignments
docs.text:
Persistent privilege can also result from assigning an identity a role.

Conceptually:

Identity
   |
   v
Role Assignment
   |
   v
Resource Access

Monitor creation and modification of privileged role assignments.

docs.title: CI/CD Persistence
docs.text:
CI/CD environments can provide durable access through:

Pipeline modifications
Deployment credentials
Repository hooks
Runner configuration
Build agents
Service connections
Automation identities

Changes can propagate into production environments.

Treat CI/CD persistence as high impact.

docs.title: Web Application Persistence
docs.text:
Applications may contain mechanisms such as:

Administrative accounts
API tokens
OAuth clients
Plugins
Scheduled jobs
Webhooks
Extensions
Service integrations

If an attacker gains application administration, these legitimate features may provide persistent access.

The root cause should be reported accurately.

docs.title: Database Persistence
docs.text:
Database environments can contain:

Database users
Roles
Scheduled jobs
Stored procedures
External integrations
Credentials

Do not create persistent database objects merely to demonstrate administrative access unless the engagement specifically requires it.

docs.title: Persistence Through Credentials
docs.text:
Sometimes no startup mechanism is required.

A long-lived credential can itself provide persistence.

Initial Access
      |
      v
Create / Obtain Credential
      |
      v
Original Foothold Removed
      |
      v
Credential Still Valid
      |
      v
Access Restored

Examples include:

SSH key
API key
Cloud access key
Certificate
Service-account password
Refresh token

docs.title: Persistence Through Remote Access
docs.text:
Remote access configuration can also provide continued access.

Examples include:

SSH authorization
VPN account
RDP permission
WinRM permission
Remote-management group membership
Cloud administrative role

The persistence mechanism is the retained trust or permission rather than the remote protocol itself.

docs.title: Persistence and Credential Rotation
docs.text:
Credential rotation can remove some persistence mechanisms but not others.

Password Changed
      |
      +--> Old Password Invalid
      |
      +--> Existing Certificate May Still Work
      |
      +--> SSH Key May Still Work
      |
      +--> OAuth Grant May Still Work
      |
      +--> API Key May Still Work

Incident response should consider all authentication mechanisms associated with the compromised identity.

docs.title: Persistence and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Persistence may be established on a system reached through lateral movement.

Initial Host
     |
     v
Lateral Movement
     |
     v
Server
     |
     v
Persistence

Use:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Persistence and Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
A common attack chain is:

Initial Access
      |
      v
Low Privilege
      |
      v
Privilege Escalation
      |
      v
Administrator / root
      |
      v
Privileged Persistence

Use:

  • Windows PrivEsc Explorer
  • Linux PrivEsc Explorer

docs.title: Persistence and C2
docs.text:
A persistence mechanism may restart an authorised C2 component after a reboot or user logon.

System Boot
     |
     v
Persistence Mechanism
     |
     v
Assessment Component
     |
     v
C2

Use:

Command and Control

docs.title: Persistence and Defence Evasion
docs.text:
Persistence can overlap with defence evasion, but they have different objectives.

Persistence:
Maintain access

Defence Evasion:
Avoid or reduce defensive interference

A persistence mechanism should not automatically be made stealthier merely because stealth is technically possible.

Use:

Defence Evasion

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Persistence can produce telemetry across:

Endpoint
   |
   +--> Process
   |
   +--> File
   |
   +--> Registry
   |
   +--> Services
   |
   +--> Scheduled Tasks
   |
   +--> Accounts
   |
   v
Identity
   |
   v
Cloud
   |
   v
SIEM

docs.title: Windows Scheduled Task Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

New task creation
Task modification
Unexpected execution identity
Unusual action path
Execution from writable directories
Task started shortly after creation
EDR alerts

Useful Windows security telemetry can include event ID:

4698 - Scheduled task created
4699 - Scheduled task deleted
4702 - Scheduled task updated

Availability depends on auditing configuration.

docs.title: Windows Service Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

New service
Changed service executable
Changed service account
Changed startup type
Unexpected service binary
Service creation followed by execution

A commonly investigated System event is:

7045 - A service was installed in the system

docs.title: Registry Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Monitor security-sensitive autostart locations.

Examples include:

Run keys
RunOnce keys
Winlogon-related configuration
Service registry configuration

Useful telemetry can come from:

EDR
Sysmon
Registry auditing
Configuration monitoring

docs.title: Account Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

Account creation
Account enablement
Password reset
Group membership changes
Privilege assignment
Remote-access group changes

Sensitive group changes should receive additional scrutiny.

docs.title: PowerShell Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Potential telemetry includes:

PowerShell process execution
Script block logging
Module logging
Profile modifications
File monitoring
EDR alerts

Monitor unusual modifications to PowerShell profile locations.

docs.title: WMI Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

Permanent event filters
Event consumers
Filter-to-consumer bindings
WMI repository activity
WMI operational logs
Unexpected child processes

docs.title: Linux Cron Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

Crontab modification
New files under /etc/cron.d/
Unexpected root cron entries
Unexpected scripts
File integrity changes
Audit events

docs.title: Linux systemd Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

New unit files
Changed unit files
daemon-reload activity
New enabled services
Unexpected ExecStart
Unexpected service users
New timers

docs.title: Linux SSH Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

authorized_keys modifications
New SSH keys
SSH login from unusual source
Unexpected key fingerprint
File permission changes
Account changes

docs.title: Linux Account Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

/etc/passwd changes
/etc/shadow changes
Group membership changes
sudoers changes
New home directories
SSH key creation

docs.title: Active Directory Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Potential high-value events include:

Privileged group membership changes
Directory ACL changes
GPO changes
Certificate changes
Delegation changes
Account modifications
SIDHistory changes
New machine accounts
Authentication policy changes

docs.title: Cloud Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Cloud monitoring should include:

New user
New access key
New service principal credential
New application
New OAuth consent
New role assignment
New federation configuration
New certificate
New API token
Policy modification

docs.title: Persistence Baselines
docs.text:
Defenders should know what normal persistence looks like.

Examples:

Approved scheduled tasks
Approved services
Approved startup applications
Approved systemd units
Approved cron jobs
Approved SSH keys
Approved privileged groups
Approved cloud applications
Approved service principals

Baselines make unexpected changes easier to identify.

docs.title: Persistence Detection Model
docs.text:
Configuration Change
       |
       v
Telemetry
       |
       v
Baseline Comparison
       |
       v
Expected?
   /       \

docs.text:

docs.title: Confirmed

docs.title: What Not to Report Automatically
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

Task Scheduler exists
systemd exists
Cron exists
SSH supports authorized_keys
Windows has Run keys
Administrators can create services
Domain Admins can modify the directory
Cloud administrators can create identities

These are expected platform capabilities.

A security finding requires an inappropriate permission, trust relationship, control failure, or demonstrated attack path.

docs.title: Reporting Persistence
docs.text:
Weak:

Scheduled tasks can be used for persistence.

Better:

The compromised standard-user account had write access to the
action script executed by a scheduled task running as a privileged
service identity.

A non-destructive marker-file test confirmed that modifying the
script caused code to execute in the privileged task context.

docs.title: Reporting Directory Persistence
docs.text:
Weak:

Active Directory allows persistence.

Better:

The delegated support group had WriteDACL permission over a
privileged administrative group.

This permission could allow members of the support group to grant
themselves durable control over the privileged group without
requiring membership at the time of modification.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Persistence cleanup is mandatory unless the customer explicitly requests otherwise.

A cleanup workflow is:

       |
       v

       v

Remove Artifact
       |
       v
Restore Original State

Verify

docs.title: Cleanup Verification
docs.text:
Do not assume a deletion command succeeded.

Verify:

Task no longer exists
Service no longer exists
Registry value removed
Startup file removed
SSH key removed
Cron entry removed
systemd unit removed
Account removed
Group membership restored
Cloud role removed
Certificate revoked where required

docs.title: Reboot Validation
docs.text:
Persistence is often defined by surviving reboot, but rebooting production systems can cause disruption.

Only perform reboot validation when explicitly permitted.

Otherwise, document:

Mechanism configured for startup
Configuration verified
Reboot not performed due to availability constraints

Do not create operational risk merely to prove an already established configuration property.

Authorised testing only

Persistence testing creates deliberate changes that may survive logoff, restart, credential changes, or other lifecycle events. Only create accounts, scheduled tasks, services, startup entries, SSH keys, directory permissions, certificates, cloud identities, role assignments, or other persistent changes when explicitly permitted by the Rules of Engagement. Record every modification before deployment, use recognisable assessment identifiers, minimise the blast radius, avoid modifying production-wide controls unless specifically required, and verify complete cleanup at the end of testing.

docs.title: Red Team Phishing
docs.text:
Phishing is a social engineering technique that uses electronic communication to influence a target into performing an action.

Typical attacker objectives include:

Open a link

Open an attachment

Submit credentials

Approve authentication

Execute content

Provide information

Initiate a business process

In an authorised red team assessment, phishing should instead be treated as a controlled test of:

Email Security

User Awareness

Identity Controls

Endpoint Controls

Reporting

SOC Detection

Incident Response

A safe phishing model is:

Authorised Objective
        |
        v
Approved Target Group
        |
        v
Controlled Message
        |
        v
Safe Landing Page / Test Artifact
        |
        v
User Action
        |
        v
Security Controls
        |
        v
Detection / Reporting
        |
        v
Evidence
        |
        v
Debrief / Cleanup

Explicit authorisation required

Phishing directly targets people and may interact with production email, identity and endpoint controls. Campaign scope, recipients, sending infrastructure, domains, landing pages, credential handling, attachments, QR codes, MFA interactions, data retention and stop conditions should be explicitly approved before testing.

docs.title: Phishing Objectives
docs.text:
Typical objectives include:

Validate secure email gateway controls

Validate anti-phishing controls

Validate domain authentication

Validate malicious-link protection

Validate attachment controls

Validate browser protections

Validate endpoint protections

Validate identity controls

Validate user reporting

Validate SOC visibility

Measure incident-response performance

docs.title: Phishing Is More Than Click Rate
docs.text:
A phishing assessment should not be reduced to:

How many people clicked?

A better model is:

Message Delivery
      |
      v
Email Security
      |
      v
User Decision
      |
      v
Identity / Endpoint Control
      |
      v
User Reporting
      |
      v
SOC Detection
      |
      v
Response

A user clicking a test link does not automatically mean the organisation has suffered a serious control failure.

For example:

User Clicks
    |
    v
Browser Blocks
    |
    v
Security Alert
    |
    v
SOC Responds

may demonstrate successful defence in depth.

SPF allows a domain to define which mail systems are authorised to send mail on its behalf.

docs.title: MFA
docs.text:
Modern identity environments often use MFA.

Phishing assessments should evaluate:

Does MFA prevent account compromise?

Is phishing-resistant MFA deployed?

Are risky sign-ins detected?

Are users trained not to approve unexpected prompts?

Are recovery processes secure?

docs.title: MFA Safety Boundary
docs.text:
Do not attempt to capture or relay live MFA sessions unless that specific high-risk scenario has been explicitly approved.

Safer validation can use:

Test tenant

Test authenticator

Controlled login environment

docs.title: Phishing-Resistant MFA
docs.text:
Examples of stronger authentication approaches include:

FIDO2 security keys

Passkeys

Certificate-based authentication

Device-bound authentication

These can significantly reduce traditional credential-phishing risk.

docs.title: MFA Push Fatigue
docs.text:
Repeatedly generating MFA prompts can disrupt users and may cause account or security incidents.

Do not conduct MFA fatigue testing unless explicitly approved.

A tabletop or synthetic-account exercise is usually safer.

docs.title: EICAR
docs.text:
When antivirus validation is specifically part of the exercise, the EICAR test file can provide a standard non-malicious antivirus test.

Canonical EICAR string:

X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*

Coordinate EICAR testing

EICAR is intentionally detected by security products. Sending it through production email can trigger gateways, antivirus, EDR and SOC workflows. Use it only when the defensive team has approved that test.

docs.title: Detection Hypothesis - Link
docs.text:
Hypothesis:
A user visiting the approved phishing simulation domain should
generate email, proxy, DNS and endpoint telemetry sufficient for
the security team to identify the event.

Test:
Send the approved link-based scenario to the pilot group.

Expected:
The email platform records delivery, web controls record the
click and the SIEM receives relevant telemetry.

Result:
Record prevention, telemetry, alerting and user reporting.

docs.title: Detection Hypothesis - Attachment
docs.text:
Hypothesis:
Opening the approved test attachment should generate endpoint
telemetry and allow the SOC to correlate the activity with the
original phishing message.

Test:
Deliver the benign attachment scenario to approved test users.

Expected:
Email and endpoint telemetry are available for investigation.

Result:
Record visibility and response.

docs.title: Detection Hypothesis - Identity
docs.text:
Hypothesis:

identity should be visible through identity monitoring.

Test:

page.

Expected:
Relevant identity telemetry is generated without exposing
production credentials.

Result:
Record detection and response.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
The test message reached the secure email gateway without being

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
The approved phishing simulation message was delivered to 41 of
50 targeted mailboxes.

docs.title: Accurate Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

Eight employees were compromised.

when:

Eight users clicked a safe test link.

Prefer:

Eight of 41 recipients who received the simulation visited the
approved landing page. No production credentials were collected,
and subsequent identity controls were not bypassed.

docs.title: Example Finding - Email Impersonation
docs.text:
Title:
External Email Impersonation Controls Do Not Reliably Identify Synthetic Executive Display Names

Observation:
The authorised campaign used a customer-approved external test
domain and a synthetic executive-style display name.

The test messages were delivered without a prominent
impersonation warning to the tested recipients.

No production executive mailbox or domain was spoofed.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to create messages that appear familiar
to recipients and increase the likelihood of successful social
engineering.

Recommendation:
Review anti-phishing and impersonation-protection policies,
particularly for high-risk identities. Combine technical
controls with clear external-sender indicators and user
reporting mechanisms.

docs.title: Example Finding - Weak User Reporting
docs.text:
Title:
Phishing Reporting Mechanism Is Not Consistently Used

Observation:
The campaign delivered 41 authorised simulation messages.

Eight recipients visited the controlled landing page, while only
three messages were reported through the organisation's
designated phishing-report mechanism during the agreed
observation period.

Impact:
Low reporting rates may delay security-team awareness of
phishing campaigns and reduce the organisation's ability to
protect other recipients.

Recommendation:
Reinforce the phishing-reporting process, ensure the reporting
mechanism is easily accessible and provide periodic scenario-
based awareness exercises.

docs.title: Example Finding - Missing SOC Correlation
docs.text:
Title:
Phishing Link Interaction Is Logged but Does Not Generate Actionable SOC Detection

Observation:
The approved campaign generated email delivery, DNS and proxy
telemetry when users visited the controlled phishing simulation
domain.

The events were successfully ingested by the SIEM, but no
correlated alert was generated.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to interact with users through phishing
infrastructure without producing an actionable alert despite
relevant telemetry being available.

Recommendation:
Develop correlation logic combining email delivery, web
navigation, domain reputation and endpoint or identity events.
Validate the resulting detection using repeatable phishing
simulation scenarios.

docs.title: Example Positive Security Result
docs.text:
Control:
Secure Email Gateway

Scenario:
Approved link-based phishing simulation

Result:
The gateway quarantined the message before delivery.

Telemetry:
The event was forwarded to the SIEM.

SOC:
An analyst reviewed the event and correctly identified the
campaign domain.

Conclusion:
The tested phishing message was successfully prevented and
detected.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Phishing testing can be reduced to:

Define the objective.

Obtain explicit authorisation.

Target only the approved population.

Use controlled infrastructure.

Use safe scenarios.

Avoid harmful pretexts.

Prefer synthetic identities.

Prefer synthetic credentials.

Do not store production passwords.

Do not capture live sessions unless explicitly approved.

Use harmless attachments where possible.

Treat user reporting as success.

Measure the entire defensive chain.

Validate email security.

Validate browser and endpoint controls.

Validate identity controls.

Validate SIEM visibility.

Measure SOC response.

Report aggregate control behaviour.

Do not shame employees.

Debrief appropriately.

Remove campaign infrastructure and sensitive data.

Retest after improvements.

A useful phishing exercise evaluates message delivery, gateway controls, user reporting, browser protection, identity controls, endpoint visibility, SIEM correlation and SOC response. Click rate is only one small part of that picture.

Never make real credentials the objective

If the campaign can prove that a user attempted to submit credentials, that is normally sufficient. Production passwords, session tokens and live authentication sessions introduce unnecessary risk and should not be collected unless an exceptional scenario has been explicitly authorised and controlled.

docs.title: Red Team Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Privilege escalation is the process of moving from the current security context to one with additional permissions or authority.

In a red team assessment, privilege escalation is not limited to:

User -> Administrator

or:

User -> root

Privilege boundaries can exist across:

Operating systems

Applications

Active Directory

Cloud platforms

Containers

Databases

Service accounts

Administrative tiers

Security tooling

A useful model is:

Current Context
      |
      v
Enumerate Privilege Boundaries
      |
      v
Identify Candidate Paths
      |
      v
Validate Preconditions
      |
      v
Minimal Safe Validation
      |
      v
Higher Privilege
      |
      v
Reassess Attack Path

The objective is to determine whether an attacker who already has an authorised foothold can cross a security boundary that should prevent access to more privileged resources.

Authorised testing only

Privilege escalation can affect highly sensitive operating-system and identity controls. Validate only the minimum conditions required to demonstrate the security boundary. Avoid destructive changes, production disruption, unnecessary credential access, or persistent privileged modifications.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Objectives
docs.text:
Common objectives include:

Determine current privilege

Identify local privilege boundaries

Identify misconfigured services

Identify scheduled execution paths

Identify writable privileged resources

Identify excessive user rights

Identify credential-based escalation paths

Identify identity and group escalation paths

Identify Active Directory privilege paths

Identify cloud privilege paths

Validate application-control assumptions

Determine defensive visibility

Reach an engagement objective

docs.title: Candidate vs Confirmed
docs.text:

Candidate

Confirmed

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
A potentially interesting configuration exists.

Example:

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
Required preconditions appear to exist.

Example:

The service executes as SYSTEM and a referenced directory appears
writable by the assessment user.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
Minimal authorised validation demonstrates the boundary.

Example:

The assessment confirmed that the standard user could modify the
privileged service resource and that the service executes the
resource under a higher-privileged context.

docs.title: Safe Write Validation
docs.text:
When write access is uncertain:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID-$(Get-Random).tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Output "Write succeeded: $file"
}
catch {
    Write-Output "Write failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}
finally {
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}

This validates write access without replacing privileged files.

            [PSCustomObject]@{
                TaskName  = $task.TaskName
                TaskPath  = $task.TaskPath
                Execute   = $action.Execute
                Arguments = $action.Arguments

The goal is proof, not maximum exploitation complexity.
