docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Privilege escalation testing can be reduced to:

Understand the current identity.

Understand the current privilege.

Enumerate before exploiting.

Identify the exact security boundary.

Validate every prerequisite.

Separate candidates from confirmed findings.

Prefer the lowest-risk path.

Use harmless validation where possible.

Do not access sensitive data unnecessarily.

Confirm the resulting privilege.

Determine what defenders observed.

Preserve sufficient evidence.

Remove introduced artifacts.

Explain the root cause.

Connect the escalation to the wider attack path.

docs.title: Campaign-Level Scope
docs.text:
This page describes privilege escalation as a Red Teaming campaign activity: reassessing the foothold, prioritising attack paths, coordinating safe validation, considering detection and operational impact, and recording the resulting security boundary. It is not a replacement for platform-specific enumeration or exploit-validation notes.

Use the dedicated technical pages for implementation detail:

  • Windows Privilege Escalation for Windows services, tasks, tokens, permissions, registry, UAC, and application control.
  • Linux Privilege Escalation for sudo, SUID/SGID, capabilities, services, scheduled jobs, filesystem permissions, and Linux-specific boundaries.
  • PrivEsc Explorer, Windows PrivEsc Explorer, and Linux PrivEsc Explorer for observed conditions and candidate privilege mechanisms.
  • Active Directory Privilege Escalation, BloodHound, and ACL/ACE Abuse for directory relationships and validation.

The campaign model remains:

Current foothold
      -> Candidate privilege path
      -> Platform-specific prerequisite validation
      -> Minimum authorised operation
      -> Demonstrated boundary and detection evidence
      -> Reassess, clean up, and report

Do not treat an enumeration result, graph edge, writable resource, or tool alert as a confirmed escalation. Keep the campaign decision separate from the technical mechanism and record the identity, boundary, trigger, consequence, and cleanup requirements.

Privilege escalation is a relationship

A writable file, SUID binary, Windows privilege, sudo rule, Active Directory ACL, or cloud role is not automatically a vulnerability. The important question is whether the current identity can use that condition to cross a security boundary and obtain authority it should not possess.

Stop when the boundary is proven

Obtaining SYSTEM, root, a privileged domain identity, or an equivalent cloud or application privilege is usually sufficient evidence that the escalation path exists. Do not perform additional destructive actions or access unrelated sensitive information simply because the elevated context makes it possible.

docs.title: Red Team Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Reconnaissance is the process of collecting and analysing information about a target before and during an authorised red team assessment.

The objective is not simply to collect as much information as possible.

The objective is to transform external and internal observations into an accurate attack-surface model that supports the engagement objectives.

Authorised Scope
      |
      v
Passive Reconnaissance
      |
      v
Asset Discovery
      |
      v
Active Validation
      |
      v
Technology Mapping
      |
      v
Identity Mapping
      |
      v
Attack Surface
      |
      v
Candidate Entry Points
      |
      v
Initial Access

Reconnaissance should answer:

What does the organisation expose?

Which assets actually belong to the organisation?

Which systems are alive?

Which technologies are present?

Where are authentication boundaries?

Which identities are externally visible?

Which cloud and SaaS services are used?

Which assets are likely to be security-relevant?

Which observations justify further testing?

Authorised testing only

Passive discovery may reveal systems belonging to subsidiaries, suppliers, cloud providers, CDNs, SaaS platforms, or unrelated third parties. Discovery does not establish authorisation. Validate ownership and scope before performing active testing.

docs.title: Reconnaissance Objectives
docs.text:
Typical objectives include:

Identify Internet-facing assets

Discover domains and subdomains

Identify IP ranges and network ownership

Map DNS infrastructure

Identify web applications

Identify remote-access services

Identify authentication portals

Identify externally exposed technologies

Identify cloud infrastructure

Identify public code repositories

Identify exposed documents and metadata

Identify publicly exposed identities

Identify email infrastructure

Identify candidate initial-access paths

Validate scope boundaries

docs.text:
Reconnaissance can broadly be divided into:

Passive Reconnaissance

Active Reconnaissance

docs.title: Passive Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Passive reconnaissance uses information available without directly interacting with the target application or system where practical.

Examples:

Search engines

Certificate Transparency

Public DNS information

WHOIS/RDAP

Public code repositories

Public documents

Job advertisements

Company websites

Public cloud references

Internet archives

Public vulnerability information

Search-engine indexes

docs.title: Active Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Active reconnaissance directly interacts with target infrastructure.

Examples:

DNS queries

HTTP requests

Port scanning

Service identification

TLS inspection

Content discovery

Technology fingerprinting

Application mapping

Active reconnaissance should only be performed against authorised targets.

docs.text:

docs.text:

docs.title: Certificate Discovery Limitations
docs.text:
A certificate hostname does not guarantee:

The host is reachable

The organisation still owns it

The system is in scope

Treat certificate results as candidates.

docs.title: Subdomain Enumeration
docs.text:
Subdomain enumeration combines multiple data sources.

Useful tools include:

Subfinder

Amass

Certificate Transparency

DNS data

Historical sources

docs.title: Subfinder
docs.text:
Subfinder performs passive subdomain discovery.

Basic usage:

subfinder -d example.com

Save results:

subfinder -d example.com -silent -o subfinder.txt

docs.title: Amass
docs.text:
OWASP Amass can be used for attack-surface discovery.

Passive enumeration:

amass enum -passive -d example.com

Save:

amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt

docs.title: Combine Enumeration Results
docs.text:
Example:

cat subfinder.txt amass.txt | sort -u > subdomains.txt

Count:

wc -l subdomains.txt

docs.title: Normalise Results
docs.text:
Remove empty lines:

sed '/^[[:space:]]*$/d' subdomains.txt | sort -u > subdomains-clean.txt

This produces a clean candidate list.

docs.title: Candidate vs Resolved vs Alive
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

Discovered Subdomain
        |
        v
DNS Resolved
        |
        v
Network Reachable
        |
        v
HTTP Reachable

These represent different states.

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Use dnsx to validate DNS candidates.

Example:

dnsx -l subdomains-clean.txt -silent

Save resolved names:

dnsx -l subdomains-clean.txt -silent -o resolved.txt

docs.title: Resolve with IP Information
docs.text:
dnsx -l subdomains-clean.txt -silent -a -resp

This can help map hostnames to addresses.

docs.title: HTTP Validation
docs.text:
Use httpx to identify HTTP/HTTPS services.

Basic:

httpx -l resolved.txt -silent

Save:

httpx -l resolved.txt -silent -o alive-http.txt

docs.title: HTTP Metadata
docs.text:
A useful reconnaissance probe:

httpx -l resolved.txt -silent -status-code -title -tech-detect -ip

This may provide:

URL

Status code

Page title

Technology

IP address

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
https://portal.example.com [200] [Customer Portal] [nginx] [203.0.113.10]
https://vpn.example.com [302] [Login] [203.0.113.20]
https://old.example.com [404] [Not Found] [203.0.113.30]

A 404 host can still be relevant because the web service itself is alive.

docs.text:
Redirects can reveal:

Canonical hostnames

Inspect:

docs.title: HTTP Headers
docs.text:
Headers may reveal:

Reverse proxies

CDNs

Frameworks

Security controls

Inspect:

curl -I https://example.com/

Do not assume a disclosed Server header is perfectly accurate.

docs.title: Technology Identification
docs.text:
Technology identification helps determine which testing methodology is relevant.

Useful tools:

httpx

WhatWeb

Wappalyzer

Nuclei technology templates

Manual inspection

docs.title: WhatWeb
docs.text:
WhatWeb:

whatweb https://example.com

docs.title: Technology Mapping
docs.text:
Record technologies by asset.

Example:

Asset Technology Confidence www.example.com nginx High portal.example.com ASP.NET High api.example.com Unknown API Medium auth.example.com SSO portal High

docs.title: Technology Confidence
docs.text:
Useful levels:

Low

Medium

High

Confirmed

Do not report technology fingerprinting as confirmed merely because one scanner guessed it.

docs.title: HTTP Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots can make large HTTP attack surfaces easier to review.

Useful tools include:

EyeWitness

gowitness

Screenshots help identify:

Login pages

Administrative interfaces

Default pages

Legacy applications

Error pages

Development environments

Duplicate applications

docs.title: gowitness
docs.text:
gowitness can capture web screenshots.

Review the project's current command syntax before using it because CLI options can change between releases.

docs.title: HTTP Attack Surface Categories
docs.text:
Classify discovered web assets.

Example:

Corporate Website

Customer Portal

Employee Portal

VPN

SSO

API

Administrative Interface

Development

Testing

Staging

Legacy

File Transfer

Monitoring

Unknown

docs.title: Authentication Surface
docs.text:
Authentication endpoints deserve specific attention.

Look for:

/login

/signin

/auth

/oauth

/saml

/oidc

/admin

/vpn

/remote

/password-reset

Do not assume these exact paths exist; identify them through normal application discovery.

docs.title: Authentication Inventory
docs.text:
Example:

Asset Authentication MFA Identity Provider VPN Username/password Yes Entra ID Portal SSO Yes Entra ID Legacy App Local account Unknown Local API Token N/A Application

docs.title: Identity Provider Discovery
docs.text:
Common identity systems include:

Microsoft Entra ID

Active Directory Federation Services

Okta

Ping Identity

Auth0

Google Workspace

Custom SAML/OIDC

Identity architecture often determines the most important attack surface.

docs.title: Microsoft Tenant Information
docs.text:
Public authentication behaviour may reveal whether an organisation uses Microsoft cloud identity.

Do not treat the existence of a Microsoft tenant as a vulnerability.

Record it as architecture information.

docs.title: Remote Access Surface
docs.text:
Look for externally exposed services such as:

VPN

Remote Desktop gateways

VDI

Citrix

SSH

File transfer

Remote support

Web administration

These may represent important initial-access boundaries.

docs.title: Port Discovery
docs.text:
Port scanning is active reconnaissance and should only target authorised addresses.

A basic Nmap scan:

nmap -sT -Pn -T3 192.0.2.10

A targeted service scan:

nmap -sT -Pn -sV -p 22,80,443,445,3389 192.0.2.10

Use conservative timing appropriate to the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Why TCP Connect Scanning?
docs.text:
-sT

uses the operating system's TCP connect mechanism.

It is useful when:

Raw socket privileges are unavailable

Traffic is being routed through certain proxy mechanisms

A simple validation scan is sufficient

docs.title: Nmap Output
docs.text:
Save normal output:

nmap -sT -Pn -sV 192.0.2.10 -oN nmap.txt

XML:

nmap -sT -Pn -sV 192.0.2.10 -oX nmap.xml

docs.title: Port State Interpretation
docs.text:
Common states:

open

closed

filtered

filtered does not necessarily mean the host is offline.

A firewall may be preventing a definitive response.

docs.title: Service Identification
docs.text:
Common Internet-facing services:

Port Typical Service 22 SSH 25 SMTP 53 DNS 80 HTTP 443 HTTPS 445 SMB 587 SMTP Submission 993 IMAPS 3389 RDP

Ports are indicators, not proof of the application protocol.

docs.title: IP Address Reconnaissance
docs.text:
IP addresses can help identify:

Hosting providers

Cloud infrastructure

CDNs

Dedicated infrastructure

Network ownership

Related assets

docs.title: ASN
docs.text:
An Autonomous System Number identifies a network participating in Internet routing.

ASN information may help determine whether an organisation operates its own address space.

Do not assume all addresses announced by an organisation's ASN are automatically authorised for testing.

docs.title: ASN Model
docs.text:
Organisation
     |
     v
    ASN
     |
     v
IP Prefixes
     |
     v
Candidate Infrastructure

docs.title: IP Ownership
docs.text:
Differentiate:

Organisation-owned IP

Cloud-hosted IP

CDN IP

SaaS IP

Third-party IP

This distinction is important for scope.

docs.title: CDN and Reverse Proxy
docs.text:
An application's DNS may point to:

Cloudflare

Akamai

Fastly

CloudFront

Azure Front Door

Other reverse proxies

The visible edge address may not be the origin server.

Do not attempt to bypass a third-party edge service unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: TLS Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Inspect a certificate:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com

Useful certificate fields include:

Subject

Issuer

Validity

Subject Alternative Names

docs.title: TLS Certificate Information
docs.text:
A simpler certificate extraction:

echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates

docs.title: Subject Alternative Names
docs.text:
SANs may reveal additional names associated with the certificate.

Example:

DNS:example.com
DNS:www.example.com
DNS:portal.example.com

Again, these are candidates rather than automatically authorised targets.

docs.title: Cloud Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Modern attack surfaces frequently extend into cloud environments.

Look for evidence of:

AWS

Microsoft Azure

Google Cloud

Cloud storage

Cloud-hosted applications

Serverless services

Container registries

Cloud identity

CI/CD platforms

docs.title: Cloud Asset Classification
docs.text:
Cloud Asset
    |
    +--> Compute
    |
    +--> Storage
    |
    +--> Identity
    |
    +--> Application
    |
    +--> API
    |

docs.title: Cloud Storage
docs.text:
Public references may identify storage services.

Examples:

Amazon S3

Azure Blob Storage

Google Cloud Storage

Discovery does not justify accessing data outside the authorised scope.

docs.title: Cloud Metadata in Applications
docs.text:
Application code may reference:

Storage names

API endpoints

Tenant IDs

Region names

Cloud resource names

CDN hostnames

These are useful for architecture mapping.

docs.title: Public Code Repositories
docs.text:
Search authorised public sources for repositories associated with the organisation.

Potential sources:

GitHub

GitLab

Bitbucket

Public package registries

docs.title: Repository Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Look for:

Domain references

API endpoints

Infrastructure configuration

Documentation

Cloud resource names

Email formats

Technology information

Accidentally committed secrets

Do not use discovered credentials against systems unless credential validation is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: GitHub Search
docs.text:
Useful search concepts include:

"example.com"

org:example

"@example.com"

Search should focus on publicly available information.

docs.title: Repository Secret Exposure
docs.text:
Potential secret types include:

API keys

Cloud credentials

Passwords

Private keys

Tokens

Database connection strings

If discovered during an authorised engagement:

Preserve minimal evidence

Do not unnecessarily expose the secret

Do not commit it into notes

Follow the Rules of Engagement

Coordinate rotation where required

docs.title: Git History
docs.text:
A secret removed from the current branch may remain in repository history.

The security issue is therefore:

Secret exposed in repository history

rather than merely:

Secret in current file

docs.title: Public Documents
docs.text:
Publicly available documents can reveal useful architecture information.

Examples:

PDF

DOCX

XLSX

PPTX

Potential information:

Author names

Usernames

Software versions

Internal hostnames

File paths

Organisation names

Document templates

docs.title: Metadata Extraction
docs.text:
ExifTool can inspect metadata.

Example:

exiftool document.pdf

For multiple files:

exiftool documents/

docs.title: Metadata Interpretation
docs.text:
Metadata should be treated carefully.

A username in a document may be:

Current employee

Former employee

External contractor

Template author

Generic build account

Validate before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: Identity Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Public information may reveal:

Employee names

Job titles

Departments

Email formats

Technology teams

Administrators

Developers

Security personnel

Identity information can be sensitive even when publicly available.

docs.title: Identity Sources
docs.text:
Possible sources:

Company website

Public professional profiles

Conference presentations

Public repositories

Public documents

Press releases

Job advertisements

docs.title: Email Format
docs.text:
Public addresses may reveal a naming convention.

Examples:

firstname.lastname@example.com

firstinitiallastname@example.com

firstname@example.com

Do not automatically generate or test large account lists merely because a pattern is known.

docs.title: Username Validation
docs.text:
Username enumeration against authentication systems can trigger:

Account lockouts

Security alerts

Rate limits

Privacy concerns

Only perform active account validation when explicitly permitted.

docs.title: Job Advertisements
docs.text:
Job advertisements can provide architecture clues.

Examples:

Microsoft 365

Active Directory

AWS

Azure

Kubernetes

Citrix

VMware

CrowdStrike

Microsoft Defender

Splunk

Sentinel

This information helps build hypotheses but does not confirm deployment.

docs.text:

            v
Possible Kubernetes Environment

Additional Evidence?

docs.title: Search Engines
docs.text:
Search engines can reveal indexed content such as:

Subdomains

Documents

Login pages

Old applications

Public directories

Error messages

Use normal public search functionality within the engagement rules.

docs.title: Search Examples
docs.text:
Examples of search syntax:

site:example.com

site:example.com filetype:pdf

site:example.com filetype:xlsx

site:example.com login

These queries search publicly indexed content.

docs.title: Internet Archive
docs.text:
Historical web data can reveal:

Old endpoints

Previous applications

Historical paths

Retired technologies

Old documentation

Historical existence does not mean the system still exists.

docs.title: robots.txt
docs.text:
Review:

curl https://example.com/robots.txt

It may identify:

Crawler exclusions

Application paths

Administrative paths

Legacy content

robots.txt is not an access-control mechanism.

docs.title: sitemap.xml
docs.text:
Review:

curl https://example.com/sitemap.xml

Sitemaps may reveal application structure.

docs.title: security.txt
docs.text:
Check:

curl https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt

This may provide:

Security contact

Disclosure policy

Acknowledgement information

docs.title: Content Discovery
docs.text:
Once a web application is confirmed in scope, content discovery may identify:

Directories

Files

APIs

Administrative interfaces

Backup files

Documentation

Hidden application paths

See:

Content Discovery

docs.title: Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Parameters may reveal additional application functionality.

Sources include:

HTML forms

JavaScript

Historical URLs

Application links

API documentation

See:

Parameter Discovery

docs.title: JavaScript Reconnaissance
docs.text:
JavaScript files can reveal:

API routes

Internal application paths

Feature flags

Service names

Cloud endpoints

Authentication logic

Client-side configuration

See:

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: API Discovery
docs.text:
Look for:

/api/

/v1/

/v2/

/graphql

/swagger

/openapi

These are common conventions, not guaranteed paths.

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
An exposed OpenAPI specification can provide:

Endpoints

Methods

Parameters

Authentication schemes

Schemas

The existence of API documentation is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL endpoints may provide a distinct application attack surface.

Common architecture:

Client
  |
  v
GraphQL Endpoint
  |
  v
Resolvers
  |
  v
Backend Services

See:

GraphQL

docs.title: Virtual Hosts
docs.text:
Multiple applications may share one address.

Concept:

203.0.113.10
     |
     +--> www.example.com
     |
     +--> portal.example.com
     |
     +--> api.example.com

Hostname-based discovery can therefore reveal more than IP-only scanning.

docs.title: Development and Staging Systems
docs.text:
Look for naming patterns such as:

dev

test

qa

uat

stage

staging

preprod

demo

old

legacy

Do not assume such systems have weaker security.

Validate configuration independently.

docs.title: Environment Classification
docs.text:
Example:

Host Environment Confidence www.example.com Production High dev.example.com Development Medium uat.example.com UAT High old.example.com Unknown/legacy Medium

docs.title: Forgotten Assets
docs.text:
Potential forgotten assets include:

Old portals

Temporary applications

Legacy VPNs

Development systems

Deprecated APIs

Old DNS records

Unused cloud resources

These can be valuable reconnaissance findings because asset management is itself a security control.

docs.title: Dangling DNS
docs.text:
A DNS record may reference a resource that no longer exists.

Concept:

sub.example.com
       |
       v
External Service
       |
       v
Resource Removed

This may represent a subdomain takeover candidate depending on the provider and exact configuration.

Do not claim takeover until safely confirmed according to scope.

docs.title: DNS Wildcards
docs.text:
Wildcard DNS can make every tested hostname appear to resolve.

Test random names:

dig +short random-name-that-should-not-exist.example.com

If arbitrary names resolve, account for wildcard behaviour when processing subdomain results.

docs.title: HTTP Wildcards
docs.text:
Applications may also respond identically to unknown hostnames or paths.

Compare:

Status

Content length

Title

Response body

Redirect destination

before treating every response as a unique asset.

docs.title: Catch-All Authentication
docs.text:
Some identity providers deliberately return similar responses for valid and invalid accounts.

Do not infer account existence solely from one response difference.

docs.title: Vulnerability Intelligence
docs.text:
Once technologies are identified, research relevant vulnerabilities.

Sources include:

NIST National Vulnerability Database

CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog

GitHub Security Advisories

docs.title: Version Matching
docs.text:
A version banner is not sufficient to confirm vulnerability.

Use:

Observed Version
      |
      v
Affected Version?
      |
      v
Required Configuration?
      |
      v
Reachable Attack Surface?
      |
      v
Safe Validation

docs.title: Do Not Report CVEs from Version Strings Alone
docs.text:
Weak:

nginx version X is vulnerable to CVE-XXXX-XXXX.

Better:

The service disclosed a version potentially associated with
CVE-XXXX-XXXX. Exploitability was not confirmed during the
assessment.

docs.title: Automated Template Scanning
docs.text:
Tools such as Nuclei can assist with authorised attack-surface validation.

Example against one authorised target:

nuclei -u https://example.com

For a target list:

nuclei -l alive-http.txt

Use appropriate rate limits and template selection for the environment.

docs.title: Nuclei Results
docs.text:
Treat automated results as:

Candidate Finding
       |
       v
Manual Review
       |
       v
Safe Validation
       |
       v
Confirmed / Rejected

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Reconnaissance tools can generate substantial traffic.

Consider:

Application capacity

WAF thresholds

IDS/IPS

Rate limits

Customer monitoring

Testing window

Rules of Engagement

Start conservatively.

docs.title: OPSEC
docs.text:
Reconnaissance itself generates observable activity.

Defenders may observe:

DNS queries

Sequential connections

HTTP requests

TLS handshakes

Port scans

Directory discovery

Repeated user agents

Do not attempt to conceal activity outside the engagement requirements.

Maintain enough logging for deconfliction.

docs.title: Source Infrastructure
docs.text:
Track which infrastructure performs active reconnaissance.

Example:

Source Purpose RT01 HTTP reconnaissance RT02 Approved scanning Operator VPN Manual validation

docs.title: Deconfliction
docs.text:
Provide assessment indicators when required:

Source IP addresses

Domains

Testing windows

Operator identifiers

Known payload hashes

This helps distinguish authorised reconnaissance from unrelated malicious activity.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Reconnaissance evidence may include:

DNS results

Certificate data

HTTP headers

Screenshots

Service banners

Technology fingerprints

Port results

Public repository references

Public document metadata

docs.title: Evidence Record
docs.text:
Example:

Evidence ID:
RECON-014

portal.example.com

HTTPS 200

Title:
Customer Portal

Technology:
ASP.NET

docs.text:
Maintain a central inventory.

Example:

Asset Type IP Status Scope Notes www.example.com Web 203.0.113.10 Alive Yes Corporate portal.example.com Web 203.0.113.20 Alive Yes Login legacy.example.com Web 203.0.113.30 Alive Pending Ownership review cdn.example.com CDN Third party Alive No Provider

Low

docs.text:
Multiple sources may identify the same asset.

Subfinder ----+
              |
Amass --------+--> portal.example.com
              |

docs.title: Example Pipeline
docs.text:
For an authorised domain:

subfinder -d example.com -silent -o subfinder.txt

amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt

Combine:

cat subfinder.txt amass.txt | sort -u > subdomains.txt

Resolve:

dnsx -l subdomains.txt -silent -o resolved.txt

Probe HTTP:

httpx -l resolved.txt -silent -status-code -title -tech-detect -ip -o http.txt

This produces a useful first-pass HTTP attack-surface inventory.

docs.text:
Primary Domain
                    |
          +---------+---------+
          |                   |
          v                   v
      Subfinder             Amass
          |                   |
          +---------+---------+
                    |
                    v
                  sort -u
                    |
                    v
                   dnsx
                    |
                    v
                  httpx
                    |
                    v
            Alive HTTP Assets
                    |
                    v
             Manual Validation

docs.title: Keep Raw Data
docs.text:
Do not overwrite raw discovery results.

Prefer:

raw/
processed/
validated/

Example:

recon/
├── raw/
├── processed/
└── validated/

docs.text:
Raw data helps with:

Troubleshooting

Reproducibility

Automation is useful for:

Collection

False positives

Attack-path decisions

Not every asset deserves equal attention.

Prioritise based on:

docs.text:
Reconnaissance may identify candidates such as:

Infrastructure

Source IPs

DNS

docs.text:
Reconnaissance findings should support later attack-path analysis.

Red Team Reporting

docs.title: Reporting Reconnaissance Findings
docs.text:
Potential reportable issues include:

Unknown Internet-facing assets

Legacy systems

Exposed administrative interfaces

Sensitive metadata

Public credential exposure

Dangling DNS

Unexpected cloud resources

Excessive technology disclosure

Not every reconnaissance observation is a vulnerability.

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Title:
Unmanaged Internet-Facing Application Identified

Observation:
An externally reachable application was discovered through
Certificate Transparency and confirmed through DNS and HTTPS.

The asset was not present in the customer-provided Internet asset
inventory.

Impact:
Unknown or unmanaged Internet-facing systems may fall outside
normal vulnerability management, monitoring, and patching
processes.

Recommendation:
Validate ownership, assign an asset owner, include the system in
the central asset inventory, and ensure vulnerability management
and monitoring controls apply.

docs.title: Candidate vs Confirmed
docs.text:
Use clear states.

Candidate

Validated Asset

Confirmed Finding

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Certificate Transparency hostname
          |
          v
       Candidate
          |
          v
    DNS Resolution
          |
          v
    Validated Asset
          |
          v
Configuration Review
          |
          v
    Confirmed Finding

docs.title: Assuming Every Subdomain Is Alive
docs.text:
Discovery does not equal reachability.

Validate DNS and service state.

docs.title: Assuming Every IP Is Owned by the Customer
docs.text: Cloud and CDN addresses may be shared or third-party controlled.

docs.title: Treating Technology Detection as Proof
docs.text: Fingerprinting tools can be wrong.

docs.title: Treating Version Detection as Vulnerability Confirmation
docs.text: Version matching is only one prerequisite.

docs.title: Ignoring Redirects
docs.text: A redirect may reveal the real authentication or application endpoint.

docs.title: Ignoring Non-200 Responses
docs.text:
Interesting systems may return:

301

302

401

403

404

500

A non-200 response does not mean the service is irrelevant.

docs.title: Ignoring DNS
docs.text: DNS frequently provides some of the most valuable attack-surface context.

docs.title: Ignoring Authentication
docs.text: Authentication surfaces often matter more than static corporate websites.

docs.title: Ignoring Third Parties
docs.text: Testing a discovered third-party asset without authorisation creates unnecessary risk.

docs.title: Collecting Without Analysing
docs.text:
Thousands of subdomains are not useful unless they are:

Resolved

Classified

Scoped

Prioritised

Analysed

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Reconnaissance can be reduced to:

Start with known authorised assets.

Collect passive information.

Discover candidate assets.

Resolve and validate them.

Identify live services.

Map technologies.

Map authentication.

Understand identity and cloud dependencies.

Separate customer assets from third parties.

Record confidence.

Prioritise security-relevant systems.

Preserve evidence.

Turn observations into attack hypotheses.

Revalidate scope before active testing.

Reconnaissance should produce decisions

A list containing thousands of hostnames is not yet useful reconnaissance. The value comes from resolving, validating, classifying, scoping, enriching, and prioritising those assets until they form an understandable attack surface that can guide the next phase of the assessment.

Discovery does not equal permission

Certificate Transparency, DNS, search engines, repositories, ASN information, and cloud metadata can reveal infrastructure beyond the authorised target. Treat newly discovered assets as candidates until ownership and scope have been confirmed. Do not actively test third-party or uncertain infrastructure merely because it appears related to the organisation.

docs.title: Red Team Reporting
docs.text:
Red team reporting converts assessment activity into information that an organisation can use to reduce risk.

A useful red team report should explain:

What happened?

How did access begin?

Which security boundaries were crossed?

Which systems and identities were affected?

What attack paths were demonstrated?

Which controls prevented activity?

Which controls detected activity?

Which activity remained undetected?

How did the SOC respond?

What was the realistic impact?

What should be fixed first?

How can the organisation verify the improvements?

The objective is not to produce the largest possible collection of screenshots or commands.

The objective is to communicate the security story clearly.

Authorised assessments only

Reports should contain only information obtained during the authorised assessment. Protect credentials, customer data, internal architecture, screenshots, payload information, and other sensitive evidence according to the Rules of Engagement and applicable data-handling requirements.

docs.title: Reporting Model
docs.text:
A red team report normally serves several audiences.

                    RED TEAM REPORT
                           |
          +----------------+----------------+
          |                |                |
          v                v                v
      MANAGEMENT       SECURITY TEAM     TECHNICAL TEAM
          |                |                |
          v                v                v
     Business Risk     Attack Paths       Evidence
     Key Outcomes      Detection Gaps     Technical Detail
     Priorities        SOC Response       Remediation

Each audience needs different information.

docs.title: Core Reporting Principle
docs.text:
Do not make the reader reconstruct the engagement from raw evidence.

Instead:

Evidence
   |
   v
Observation
   |
   v
Attack Path
   |
   v
Security Impact
   |
   v
Root Cause
   |
   v
Recommendation

docs.title: Suggested Report Structure
docs.text:
A practical structure is:

1. Executive Summary

2. Engagement Overview

3. Scope

4. Objectives

5. Rules of Engagement

6. Assessment Methodology

7. Attack Narrative

8. Attack Path Summary

9. Key Findings

10. Detection and Response Assessment

11. MITRE ATT&CK Mapping

12. Recommendations

13. Strategic Improvement Roadmap

14. Retest Results

15. Cleanup Confirmation

16. Technical Findings

17. Evidence Appendix

18. Technical Appendix

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
The executive summary should be understandable without requiring deep technical knowledge.

Focus on:

Overall security outcome
Business impact
Attack path
Critical weaknesses
Detection effectiveness
Response effectiveness
Priority improvements

Avoid filling the executive summary with:

Tool names
Long commands
Payload details
Raw logs
Excessive ATT&CK identifiers
Low-level technical terminology

docs.title: Executive Summary Example
docs.text:
The assessment demonstrated that an attacker with access to a
standard user account could progress through multiple security
boundaries and obtain access to systems containing elevated
administrative privileges.

The attack path was primarily enabled by excessive credential
reuse, insufficient network segmentation, and weaknesses in
administrative access controls.

Endpoint security controls detected several stages of the
assessment, including suspicious process execution and remote
administration activity. However, some authentication and lateral
movement activity did not generate actionable alerts.

The highest-priority improvements are to reduce privileged
credential exposure, strengthen administrative tiering, restrict
east-west administrative protocols, and improve correlation of
authentication and endpoint telemetry.

docs.title: Management Summary
docs.text:
A shorter management summary can follow:

Initial Access
     |
     v
Standard User
     |
     v
Credential Exposure
     |
     v
Internal Movement
     |
     v
Privileged System
     |
     v
Business Impact

Management should understand the security boundaries that failed, not every command used to cross them.

docs.title: Engagement Overview
docs.text:
Document:

Customer
Engagement type
Assessment dates
Testing team
Primary contact
Assessment model
Scope
Objectives
Assumptions
Limitations

docs.title: Engagement Type
docs.text:
Clearly identify whether the work was:

Red Team Assessment
Purple Team Assessment
Assumed Breach
Internal Red Team
External Red Team
Adversary Simulation
Detection Validation
Penetration Test

Do not use these terms interchangeably.

docs.title: Assessment Dates
docs.text:
Record:

Testing start
Testing end
Reporting period
Retest date

Use a consistent timezone.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
Examples:

Determine whether an external attacker could obtain internal access.

Determine whether a compromised standard user could reach
privileged systems.

Evaluate whether security controls detect credential access and
lateral movement.

Evaluate whether the SOC can reconstruct the attack path.

Identify opportunities to improve prevention, detection, and
response.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Document the authorised scope.

Examples:

Domains
IP ranges
Applications
Cloud tenants
User accounts
Workstations
Servers
Active Directory
Email
Physical locations
Wireless networks

docs.title: Exclusions
docs.text:
Also document exclusions.

Example:

Production denial-of-service testing

Third-party infrastructure

Destructive testing

Unapproved social engineering

Unapproved credential collection

Data modification

Persistence beyond the agreed period

docs.title: Rules of Engagement
docs.text:
Summarise relevant operational restrictions.

Examples:

Testing window
Permitted techniques
Prohibited techniques
Authentication limits
Social-engineering rules
Data-access limits
Persistence limits
Stop conditions
Emergency contacts

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Be explicit about limitations.

Examples:

Certain production systems were excluded.

Testing was limited to standard-user privileges.

Password spraying was not performed.

Social engineering was excluded.

No destructive actions were performed.

Some detection validation was performed collaboratively with the
SOC and therefore should not be interpreted as blind-response
testing.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
Examples:

Customer-provided credentials were assumed to represent a
compromised standard user.

Assessment infrastructure was assumed to be external to the
customer network.

Customer-provided asset lists were assumed to be accurate.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
Explain the assessment process.

Example:

Planning
   |
   v
Reconnaissance
   |
   v
Initial Access
   |
   v
Foothold
   |
   v
Discovery
   |
   v
Privilege Escalation
   |
   v
Credential Access
   |
   v
Lateral Movement
   |
   v
Objective
   |
   v
Detection Validation
   |
   v
Cleanup

docs.title: Methodology Should Match the Engagement
docs.text:
Do not claim:

Full red team simulation

if the engagement actually consisted of:

Known credentials
Limited internal testing
Predefined systems
Collaborative detection validation

Describe what was actually tested.

docs.title: Attack Narrative
docs.text:
The attack narrative is one of the most important parts of a red team report.

It explains the assessment as a connected sequence.

Example:

External Exposure
       |
       v
Initial Access
       |
       v
Standard User
       |
       v
Credential Discovery
       |
       v
Internal Server
       |
       v
Administrative Context
       |
       v
Sensitive Resource

docs.title: Narrative vs Findings
docs.text:
Individual findings may look like:

F01 - Credential Exposure

F02 - Weak Network Segmentation

F03 - Excessive Administrative Rights

F04 - Missing Lateral Movement Detection

But the attack narrative explains:

F01
 |
 v
enabled
 |
 v
F02
 |
 v
enabled
 |
 v
F03
 |
 v
resulting in
 |
 v
Objective

This relationship is critical.

docs.title: Security Boundary Model
docs.text:
A useful report should identify the boundaries crossed.

Examples:

Internet -> Internal Network

Standard User -> Local Administrator

Workstation -> Server

User Network -> Management Network

Application User -> Database

On-Premises -> Cloud

Standard Account -> Privileged Account

docs.title: Why Security Boundaries Matter
docs.text:
A remote service being reachable is not necessarily a vulnerability.

The meaningful question is:

Did the attacker cross a security boundary that should have
prevented or restricted the attack path?

docs.title: Attack Path Evidence
docs.text:
For each major transition record:

Source
Target
Identity
Privilege
Technique
Timestamp
Evidence
Security control
Result

docs.title: Attack Path Record
docs.text:
Example:

Transition:
WS01 -> SRV01

Identity:
CORP\test-user

Technique:
Approved remote administration

Expected Control:
Network segmentation and access control

Observed:
TCP/445 reachable and authentication accepted.

Result:
Security boundary crossed.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Each finding should describe a specific weakness or control gap.

Recommended structure:

Title

Severity

Description

Observation

Evidence

Attack Path

Impact

Likelihood

Root Cause

MITRE ATT&CK

Detection

Recommendation

Validation

References

docs.title: Finding Title
docs.text:
A title should describe the weakness.

Good:

Privileged Credentials Accessible to Standard Users

Better than:

Mimikatz

Good:

Workstation-to-Server Administrative Traffic Is Insufficiently Restricted

Better than:

SMB Lateral Movement

docs.title: Avoid Tool-Based Finding Titles
docs.text:
Avoid titles such as:

BloodHound Finding

NetExec Vulnerability

PowerShell Issue

Impacket Exploit

The tool is not the vulnerability.

docs.title: Finding Description
docs.text:
Explain the security condition.

Example:

Standard-user systems were able to initiate administrative
protocol connections directly to server systems.

This increases the ability of an attacker who compromises a
workstation to attempt credential reuse and lateral movement
against internal servers.

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
Describe what happened during the assessment.

Example:

From workstation WS01, the assessment team confirmed TCP
connectivity to the SMB service on SRV01.

The customer-provided assessment identity was accepted by the
remote system and provided access beyond the original workstation.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Evidence should demonstrate the observation.

Possible evidence:

Command output
Screenshot
Event log
SIEM event
EDR process tree
Authentication record
HTTP request/response
Configuration
Network capture
Cloud audit event

docs.title: Evidence Should Be Minimal
docs.text:
Do not include ten screenshots when one demonstrates the issue.

Prefer:

Evidence
   |
   v
Clear Proof

instead of:

Evidence
   |
   v
Large Raw Data Dump

docs.title: Evidence Identifier
docs.text:
Use identifiers:

EVID-001
EVID-002
EVID-003

Example:

EVID-014 - Successful authentication from WS01 to SRV01

docs.title: Evidence Metadata
docs.text:
Record:

Evidence ID
Finding ID
Timestamp
Host
User
Operator
Source
Target
Description
File
Hash where required

docs.title: Evidence Naming
docs.text:
Example:

20260905-1042-F03-WS01-SRV01-authentication.png

docs.title: Screenshot Caption
docs.text:
Example:

Figure 4 - Successful authorised authentication from WS01 to SRV01
using the assessment identity.

Captions should explain what the reader should notice.

docs.title: Sensitive Evidence
docs.text:
Do not expose reusable secrets in the report.

Redact:

Passwords
API tokens
Session cookies
Private keys
Reusable hashes
Authentication tokens
Personal data

Retain original evidence securely if required.

docs.title: Command Evidence
docs.text:
Commands can be useful when they explain reproducibility.

Example:

Test-NetConnection SRV01 -Port 445

Do not turn the main report into a command transcript.

docs.title: Output Evidence
docs.text:
Show only relevant output.

Example:

ComputerName     : SRV01
RemotePort       : 445
TcpTestSucceeded : True

This demonstrates reachability without unnecessary output.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Explain what the weakness enables.

Weak:

An attacker could use this.

Better:

An attacker who compromises a standard workstation may be able to
reuse valid credentials against internal server systems, increasing
the likelihood that a single endpoint compromise progresses into a
broader internal compromise.

docs.title: Impact Categories
docs.text:
Consider:

Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Privilege
Identity
Network reach
Business process
Detection capability
Recovery capability

docs.title: Do Not Overstate Impact
docs.text:
If testing demonstrated:

Remote service reachable

do not automatically report:

Full domain compromise possible.

Use evidence-based language.

docs.title: Evidence Strength
docs.text:
Useful classifications:

Candidate

Likely

Confirmed

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
Example:

A potentially exploitable configuration was identified but was not
validated.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
Example:

The prerequisite conditions appear to be present, but exploitation
was not performed because of engagement restrictions.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
Example:

The assessment team successfully crossed the security boundary
using the authorised validation procedure.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Root cause describes why the weakness exists.

Examples:

Credential reuse

Excessive privilege

Missing segmentation

Weak application control

Inadequate secret management

Insufficient authentication policy

Legacy protocol dependency

Missing logging

Missing detection logic

Configuration drift

Inadequate administrative tiering

docs.title: Root Cause vs Symptom
docs.text:
Example symptom:

Remote administration succeeded.

Potential root cause:

Administrative access from user workstations is not restricted.

Fixing the root cause is more valuable.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity should represent demonstrated risk.

Consider:

Impact

Likelihood

Privilege obtained

Asset criticality

Attack complexity

Prerequisites

User interaction

Security boundary crossed

Detection capability

Compensating controls

docs.title: Example Severity Model
docs.text:
Critical
Direct path to highly privileged or business-critical compromise
with limited prerequisites.

High
Significant security boundary can be crossed and meaningful
privilege or sensitive access obtained.

Medium
Useful attacker capability exists but meaningful prerequisites,
limitations, or compensating controls apply.

Low
Limited security impact or significant constraints.

Informational
Observation or improvement opportunity without demonstrated
security impact.

docs.title: Severity Is Not Technique Severity
docs.text:
Do not assign severity because:

Pass-the-Hash = High

or:

PowerShell = Medium

Severity depends on the actual environment and impact.

docs.title: Attack Path Severity
docs.text:
An individual weakness may be moderate alone but important in a chain.

Example:

Weakness A - Medium
       |
       v
Weakness B - Medium
       |
       v
Weakness C - Medium
       |
       v
Domain-Level Impact

The report should highlight this chain.

docs.title: Likelihood
docs.text:
Consider:

Required access
Required privilege
Required credentials
Network reachability
User interaction
Exploit reliability
Existing security controls
Attacker knowledge
Repeatability

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Recommendations should address the root cause.

Weak:

Block PowerShell.

Better:

Restrict unnecessary PowerShell capabilities for standard users,
enforce application-control policy, enable appropriate PowerShell
logging, and ensure endpoint detections cover suspicious
interpreter behaviour.

docs.title: Recommendation Layers
docs.text:
Useful structure:

Immediate
   |
   v
Tactical
   |
   v
Strategic

docs.title: Immediate Recommendation
docs.text:
Example:

Rotate the exposed credential and terminate active sessions.

docs.title: Tactical Recommendation
docs.text:
Example:

Remove the credential from the affected configuration and migrate
the application to an approved secret-management mechanism.

docs.title: Strategic Recommendation
docs.text:
Example:

Implement centralised secret management and automated secret
scanning across repositories and deployment pipelines.

docs.title: Recommendation Ownership
docs.text:
Where practical, associate recommendations with responsible teams.

Example:

Recommendation Owner Restrict SMB between workstation and server networks Network Security Deploy LAPS Endpoint Engineering Improve 4624/4648 correlation Detection Engineering Rotate service account Identity Team

docs.title: Recommendation Priority
docs.text:
Example:

P0 - Emergency

P1 - Immediate

P2 - Near Term

P3 - Planned Improvement

docs.title: Remediation Roadmap
docs.text:
Example:

Priority Improvement Target P1 Rotate exposed credentials Immediate P1 Restrict workstation-to-server admin protocols 30 days P2 Deploy LAPS broadly 60 days P2 Improve lateral movement detections 60 days P3 Implement privileged access workstations Strategic

docs.title: Prevention, Detection, Response
docs.text:
For each important attack path, consider all three.

                     Attack Technique
                           |
          +----------------+----------------+
          |                |                |
          v                v                v
      Prevention       Detection         Response

docs.title: Prevention Reporting
docs.text:
Document:

Control expected
Control observed
Whether activity was prevented
Control weakness
Recommendation

docs.title: Detection Reporting
docs.text:
Document:

Telemetry expected
Telemetry observed
EDR event
SIEM event
Detection rule
Alert
Severity
Time to detect

docs.title: Response Reporting
docs.text:
Document:

Alert received
Analyst acknowledgement
Investigation
Escalation
Containment
Recovery

docs.title: Detection Result Table
docs.text: Technique Prevented Telemetry Alert SOC Response Result Controlled PowerShell No Yes Yes Yes Effective Scheduled Task No Yes No No Detection gap Lateral Movement No Yes Yes Yes Effective HTTPS C2 Simulation No Partial No No Visibility gap

docs.title: Positive Security Results
docs.text:
A red team report should also document controls that worked.

Examples:

Microsoft Defender blocked the EICAR test artifact.

AppLocker prevented execution from the tested user-writable path.

The SOC detected remote authentication within two minutes.

Network segmentation prevented direct RDP access.

MFA prevented authentication using the compromised password.

This gives a balanced assessment.

docs.title: Detection Gap Categories
docs.text:
Useful categories:

Telemetry Gap

Collection Gap

Parsing Gap

Detection Gap

Correlation Gap

Alerting Gap

Triage Gap

Response Gap

docs.title: Detection Gap Example
docs.text:
The endpoint generated the expected process telemetry and the event
was successfully forwarded to the SIEM.

No detection rule generated an alert.

This represents a detection-logic gap rather than a telemetry gap.

docs.title: Telemetry Gap Example
docs.text:
The controlled activity was successfully executed, but the
required endpoint telemetry was not available locally or in the
central security platform.

docs.title: Collection Gap Example
docs.text:
The expected event was present on the endpoint but was not present
in the SIEM during the assessment window.

docs.title: SOC Response
docs.text:
Record:

Detection time
Acknowledgement time
Triage time
Investigation time
Containment time
Escalation path
Correctness of conclusion

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
Maintain a timeline of important events.

Example:

Time Stage Source Target Result 09:05 Initial Access External WS01 Access 09:32 Discovery WS01 AD Successful 10:04 Credential Access WS01 Local Credential identified 10:42 Lateral Movement WS01 SRV01 Successful 10:44 Detection EDR SOC Alert 10:47 SOC Analyst Alert Investigating 11:02 Objective SRV01 Resource Demonstrated

docs.title: Attack Timeline Diagram
docs.text:
09:05              10:04              10:42              11:02
  |                   |                  |                  |
  v                   v                  v                  v
Initial            Credential          Lateral          Objective
Access              Access             Movement
  |                   |                  |
  +-------------------+------------------+
                      |
                      v
                 SOC Detection
                    10:44

docs.title: Time to Detect
docs.text: TTD = Detection Time - Activity Time

docs.title: Time to Respond
docs.text:
Define the response point clearly.

Example:

TTR = Containment Time - Detection Time

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Useful metrics may include:

Objectives achieved
Security boundaries crossed
Critical attack paths
Findings by severity
Techniques tested
Techniques prevented
Techniques detected
Techniques not detected
SOC investigations
Mean time to detect
Mean time to respond
Retests passed

docs.title: Example Metrics
docs.text:
Assessment objectives:        5

Objectives achieved:          4

Security boundaries crossed:  3

Techniques validated:         18

Prevented:                    5

Detected:                    11

Logged but not alerted:       4

No useful visibility:         3

SOC investigations:           9

docs.title: Metrics Need Context
docs.text:
Avoid:

EDR detected 75 percent of attacks.

unless the methodology supports that conclusion.

Prefer:

Nine of the twelve selected techniques for which an EDR alert was
expected generated the anticipated alert during the assessment.

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK Mapping
docs.text:
Map observed behaviour to ATT&CK where useful.

Example:

Stage ATT&CK Tactic Technique Execution Execution PowerShell Credential Access Credential Access Unsecured Credentials Lateral Movement Lateral Movement Remote Services Persistence Persistence Scheduled Task/Job C2 Command and Control Application Layer Protocol

docs.title: ATT&CK Mapping Purpose
docs.text:
ATT&CK can help:

Standardise terminology

Map attack paths

Map detections

Identify coverage gaps

Compare exercises

Plan retesting

ATT&CK should support the report, not dominate it.

docs.title: Do Not Over-Map
docs.text:
One command may theoretically map to several techniques.

Only include mappings that meaningfully describe the tested behaviour.

docs.title: ATT&CK Coverage
docs.text:
A useful model:

Technique Tested
      |
      v
Telemetry?
 /        \
No         Yes
|           |
Gap         v
        Detection?
         /      \
       No        Yes

docs.text: Technique Tested Telemetry Detection Response T1059.001 Yes Yes Yes Yes T1021.002 Yes Yes No No T1053 Yes Yes Yes No

docs.title: ATT&CK Heatmaps
docs.text:
If an ATT&CK heatmap is included, explain what the colours represent.

Example:

Green  = Tested and detected

Yellow = Tested with partial visibility

Red    = Tested without expected detection

Grey   = Not tested

Do not present untested techniques as validated coverage.

docs.title: Technical Findings
docs.text:
Technical findings should contain enough detail for remediation and retesting.

Recommended format:

Finding ID

Title

Severity

Affected Systems

Description

Prerequisites

Observation

Evidence

Impact

Attack Path

Detection

Root Cause

Recommendation

Validation Procedure

References

docs.title: Finding ID
docs.text:
Use consistent identifiers.

Example:

RT-01
RT-02
RT-03

or:

FIND-001
FIND-002

docs.title: Affected Systems
docs.text:
List:

Hostname
IP
Application
Domain
Cloud resource
Identity

Do not write:

All systems

unless that was actually established.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Document what an attacker needs.

Examples:

Internal network access

Standard domain account

Local workstation access

Compromised service account

Access to specific subnet

docs.title: Reproduction
docs.text:
For findings where reproduction is useful, document a minimal validation procedure.

Prefer:

1. Authenticate using an authorised test identity.

2. Confirm the target service is reachable.

3. Perform the minimum action required to demonstrate the boundary.

4. Record the result.

5. Stop.

6. Cleanup.

Avoid unnecessary destructive or intrusive reproduction steps.

docs.title: Validation Procedure
docs.text:
The recommendation should be testable.

Example:

After implementing network restrictions, repeat the TCP
connectivity test from a standard workstation.

Administrative SMB and WinRM access to server networks should no
longer be available unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
A retest should answer:

Was the original weakness fixed?

Can the original attack path still be completed?

Did the remediation introduce another path?

Does detection now work?

Is the control consistently enforced?

docs.title: Retest Status
docs.text:
Use:

Resolved

Partially Resolved

Not Resolved

Not Retested

Risk Accepted

docs.title: Retest Table
docs.text: Finding Original Retest Status RT-01 High Blocked Resolved RT-02 High Partial restriction Partially Resolved RT-03 Medium Alert generated Resolved

docs.title: Retest Evidence
docs.text:
Preserve:

Original evidence

Remediation description

Retest date

Retest action

Retest evidence

Final result

docs.title: Attack Path Retesting
docs.text:
Do not only retest individual findings.

Retest the complete path where appropriate.

Original:

A -> B -> C -> D


After remediation:

A -> B -> X

This demonstrates whether the attack chain was actually broken.

docs.title: Strategic Recommendations
docs.text:
Individual findings often share root causes.

Group them into themes.

Examples:

Identity Security

Privileged Access

Network Segmentation

Endpoint Hardening

Application Control

Credential Management

Detection Engineering

Security Monitoring

SOC Response

Cloud Security

docs.title: Strategic Roadmap
docs.text:
Example:

0-30 Days
    |
    +--> Rotate exposed credentials
    +--> Restrict high-risk remote administration
    +--> Fix critical detection gaps

30-90 Days
    |
    +--> Deploy LAPS
    +--> Improve segmentation
    +--> Improve central logging
    +--> Expand identity detections

90+ Days
    |
    +--> Administrative tiering
    +--> Privileged access workstations
    +--> Continuous ATT&CK validation
    +--> Purple team programme

docs.title: Prioritise Attack-Path Breakers
docs.text:
A useful question is:

Which remediation breaks the largest number of demonstrated
attack paths?

Example:

                 Credential Reuse
                       |
          +------------+------------+
          |            |            |
          v            v            v
        SRV01        SRV02        SRV03

Eliminating credential reuse may remove multiple paths at once.

docs.title: Compensating Controls
docs.text:
If immediate remediation is difficult, document compensating controls.

Examples:

Network restriction
Additional monitoring
MFA
Temporary account restrictions
Increased alerting
Manual review
EDR policy
Firewall rule

docs.title: Risk Acceptance
docs.text:
If a risk is accepted, record:

Finding
Risk owner
Reason
Compensating controls
Review date
Approval

docs.title: Cleanup Reporting
docs.text:
The report should confirm introduced artifacts were addressed.

Possible artifacts:

Certificates
Routes
Tunnels

Cloud resources
DNS records

Temporary files

docs.title: Cleanup Statement
docs.text:
Example:

All known assessment artifacts introduced by the red team were
removed at the conclusion of testing.

Temporary infrastructure and assessment credentials were revoked
or decommissioned according to the engagement cleanup inventory.

docs.title: Cleanup Exceptions
docs.text:
If something remains:

Artifact:
RT monitoring account

Reason:
Customer requested retention for retesting.

Owner:
Customer Security Team

Action:

A vulnerability is version-specific

Reproduction requires the same environment

docs.text:
At the end of an engagement, defenders may benefit from receiving:

This makes it easier to connect:

Finding

Attack Path

docs.title: Attack Path Record
docs.text:
Example:

AP-01

Objective:
Reach privileged server environment.

Entry:
Compromised standard user workstation.

Path:
WS01 -> Credential -> SRV01 -> Administrative Context

Findings:
RT-01

docs.title: Objective Status
docs.text:
Use clear statuses.

Achieved

Partially Achieved

Not Achieved

Not Tested

docs.title: Objective Table
docs.text: Objective Result Detection Notes Obtain internal foothold Achieved Yes Detected after execution Reach server environment Achieved Partial Authentication detected Obtain privileged access Achieved No Detection gap Access critical data Not Tested N/A Proof stopped before data access

docs.title: Proof Without Data Collection
docs.text:
Sometimes the objective can be demonstrated without accessing real sensitive data.

Example:

Instead of downloading sensitive records:

Demonstrate access to the containing system or directory.

Record permissions.

Use a customer-provided synthetic marker.

Stop.

This reduces customer risk.

docs.title: Synthetic Proof
docs.text:
Example:

C:\RedTeamValidation\objective.txt

or:

/opt/redteam-validation/objective.txt

The customer can pre-position a harmless marker specifically for the assessment.

docs.title: Report Language
docs.text:
Use evidence-based language.

Prefer:

The assessment demonstrated...

The tested configuration allowed...

The assessment team confirmed...

The available evidence indicates...

The technique was not validated because...

docs.title: Avoid Absolute Claims
docs.text:
Avoid:

This can never be detected.

The organisation has no security.

All servers are vulnerable.

EDR can be bypassed.

unless the evidence genuinely supports the precise claim, which is uncommon.

docs.title: Accurate Control Language
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Allowed

Blocked

Logged

Detected

Alerted

Investigated

Contained

These are not equivalent.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Do not write:

Defender failed.

when the evidence shows:

The activity was allowed, but Defender generated a behavioural
alert that was visible in the security platform.

That is a detection success, not a complete failure.

docs.title: Another Example
docs.text:
Do not write:

AppLocker bypassed.

when:

The tested binary was allowed because the applicable AppLocker
collection did not contain an enforced rule restricting that path.

Report the actual policy condition.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots should:

Show relevant evidence

Be readable

Have captions

Avoid unnecessary customer data

Avoid exposed credentials

Show sufficient context

Match the narrative

docs.title: Screenshot Naming
docs.text:
Example:

Figure 1 - Initial access validation

Figure 2 - Credential exposure

Figure 3 - Lateral movement to SRV01

Figure 4 - EDR detection

Figure 5 - SOC investigation

docs.title: Figure References
docs.text:
Reference figures from the text.

Example:

As shown in Figure 3, the assessment identity successfully
authenticated to SRV01 from WS01.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Tables are useful for:

Findings
Attack paths
Objectives
Detection results
ATT&CK coverage
Affected assets
Recommendations
Retests
Timelines

docs.title: Avoid Giant Raw Tables
docs.text:
A table with hundreds of rows rarely helps management.

Put large technical inventories in an appendix or separate evidence package.

docs.title: Redaction
docs.text:
When redacting:

Preserve enough information to understand the evidence.

Remove only information that does not need to be distributed.

Examples:

Password: [REDACTED]

Token: [REDACTED]

User: CORP\test-user

Internal IP: 10.10.x.x

Whether IP addresses or hostnames require redaction depends on report handling requirements.

docs.title: Report Versioning
docs.text:
Example:

v0.1 - Internal Draft

v0.2 - Technical Review

v0.9 - Customer Draft

v1.0 - Final

v1.1 - Retest

docs.title: Peer Review
docs.text:
Before delivery, another reviewer should verify:

docs.title: Technical Quality Review
docs.text:
Check:

Can another tester understand what happened?

Can the customer reproduce the finding safely?

Can the customer verify remediation?

Are prerequisites clear?

Are limitations documented?

docs.title: Management Quality Review
docs.text:
Check:

Can a non-technical reader understand the risk?

Are priorities clear?

Is the attack path understandable?

Is business impact explained?

Are strategic improvements clear?

docs.title: Security Review
docs.text:
Before sending:

Search report for passwords

Search for API tokens

Search for private keys

Review screenshots

Review document metadata

Review hidden comments

Review revision history

Verify recipient list

docs.title: Report Delivery
docs.text:
Use the approved delivery mechanism.

Examples:

Customer secure portal

Encrypted file transfer

Approved document platform

Encrypted email where authorised

Avoid uncontrolled public file-sharing services.

docs.title: Report Retention
docs.text:
Document:

Storage location

Access permissions

Retention period

Deletion date

Backup policy

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
A red team report can be reduced to:

Do not report only what commands worked.

Explain the attack path.

Explain which security boundaries were crossed.

Explain why those boundaries could be crossed.

Show enough evidence to prove the result.

Separate prevention from detection.

Explain what defenders saw.

Explain what defenders missed.

Describe the realistic business impact.

Recommend controls that break the attack path.

Provide a way to validate those controls.

Retest the complete path where appropriate.

Report attack paths, not just vulnerabilities

The most useful red team report explains how multiple weaknesses interacted. A credential exposure issue, permissive network path, excessive privilege, and missing detection may each appear manageable in isolation but together form a path to a critical objective. Prioritising controls that break these paths usually provides more value than treating every observation as an independent vulnerability.

Protect the report

A red team report may provide a detailed map of an organisation's security weaknesses, identities, internal architecture, detection gaps, and attack paths. Treat the report and its evidence as sensitive security information, distribute it only through approved channels, remove reusable credentials from distributed copies, and apply the agreed retention and deletion requirements.

docs.title: Red Team Social Engineering
docs.text:
Social engineering tests whether an attacker can influence people or abuse organisational processes to gain access, obtain information or advance an attack path.

Technical security controls may be strong while human and procedural controls remain vulnerable.

Examples include:

Help desk verification

Telephone requests

Impersonation scenarios

Physical access requests

Information elicitation

Account recovery

Password reset processes

MFA recovery

Visitor procedures

Third-party verification

Business process manipulation

Social engineering should be treated as a controlled security exercise rather than an unrestricted attempt to deceive employees.

Authorised Scenario
       |
       v
Defined Target Group
       |
       v
Approved Pretext
       |
       v
Controlled Interaction
       |
       v
Security Decision
       |
       v
Detection / Escalation
       |
       v
Evidence
       |
       v
Debrief / Cleanup

Explicit authorisation required

Social engineering directly involves people and may expose personal information, cause distress or disrupt business processes. The exact techniques, target groups, communication channels, prohibited actions, escalation procedures and stop conditions should be explicitly defined in the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Social Engineering Objectives
docs.text:
Typical objectives include:

Validate employee security awareness

Validate help desk identity verification

Validate password reset procedures

Validate MFA recovery procedures

Validate visitor management

Validate physical security processes

Validate sensitive-information handling

Validate escalation procedures

Validate reporting mechanisms

Measure SOC or security-team visibility

docs.title: Social Engineering Is a Process Test
docs.text:
A successful social engineering interaction does not necessarily mean:

Employee failed.

The underlying problem may instead involve:

Weak verification procedures

Ambiguous policy

Insufficient training

Poor escalation paths

Excessive help desk authority

Weak visitor controls

Missing technical enforcement

Unsafe recovery procedures

Focus reporting on the security process rather than blaming individuals.

docs.title: Human Layer of Security
docs.text:
Security controls can be represented as:

Technology
    |
    v
Process
    |
    v
People

An attacker may target whichever layer provides the easiest path.

For example:

Strong MFA
   |
   v
Account Recovery
   |
   v
Help Desk
   |
   v
Weak Verification
   |
   v
Account Access

The technical control may be strong while the recovery process undermines it.

docs.title: Approved Pretext Design
docs.text:
A pretext is the scenario used to explain the tester's request.

A good authorised pretext should be:

Plausible

Limited in scope

Non-threatening

Easy to terminate

Easy to explain during debrief
