docs.text:
After authentication, identify how identity moves through the application.

Examples:

HttpContext.User
SecurityContext
Principal
Authentication
request.user
current_user
req.user
session.user
JWT claims

Trace:

Authentication
      |
      v
Identity Object
      |
      v
Controller
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
Authorisation Decision

docs.title: Authentication Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text:
Authentication can itself be analysed as a source-to-sink flow.

Credentials / Token
        |
        v
Parser
        |
        v
Verification
        |
        v
Identity Mapping
        |
        v
Session / Security Context

Ask:

What proves identity?

What values are trusted?

What verification occurs?

How is identity mapped?

What security context is created?

docs.title: Password Authentication
docs.text:
Typical flow:

Username
   +
Password
   |
   v
Account Lookup
   |
   v
Password Verification
   |
   v
Account State Check
   |
   v
MFA
   |
   v
Session Creation

Review each stage.

docs.title: Password Storage
docs.text:
Search for:

bcrypt
argon2
scrypt
PBKDF2
PasswordHasher
BCryptPasswordEncoder
hashpw
checkpw

Also search potentially dangerous primitives:

rg -n -i \
'md5|sha1|sha256|sha512|MessageDigest|CreateHash|hashlib' \
.

The presence of a general hash function does not prove insecure password storage.

Determine what the hash is used for.

docs.title: Password Verification
docs.text:
Identify:

Password lookup
Hash verification
Account lock status
Disabled account status
Password expiration
MFA requirement

Example:

Password Correct
      |
      v
Account Disabled?
      |
      v
MFA Required?
      |
      v
Session

Do not inspect password comparison in isolation.

docs.title: Login Failure Behaviour
docs.text:
Review:

Error messages
Timing differences
Account lockout
Rate limiting
Audit logging
Failed attempt tracking

Potential issues may include:

Username enumeration
Missing rate limiting
Lockout weaknesses
Information disclosure

These require runtime validation where appropriate.

docs.title: Session Authentication
docs.text:
Typical flow:

Session Cookie
      |
      v
Session Lookup
      |
      v
Session Validation
      |
      v
User Identity

Review:

Session generation
Session rotation
Expiration
Logout invalidation
Concurrent sessions
Privilege-change handling
Cookie configuration

docs.title: Session Fixation
docs.text:
Trace session creation around authentication.

Potentially safer model:

Anonymous Session
       |
       v
Login
       |
       v
Rotate Session Identifier
       |
       v
Authenticated Session

Look for whether session identifiers are regenerated after authentication or major privilege changes.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:
Trace:

Logout Request
      |
      v
Server Session Invalidated?
      |
      v
Cookie Removed?
      |
      v
Tokens Revoked?

Deleting a browser cookie alone may not invalidate a server-side session.

docs.title: JWT Authentication
docs.text:
Typical flow:

JWT
 |
 v
Parse
 |
 v
Signature Verification
 |
 v
Claims Validation
 |
 v
Identity Mapping
 |
 v
Authorisation

Search:

rg -n -i \
'jwt|jsonwebtoken|JwtSecurityToken|JwtDecoder|JwtEncoder|decode\(|verify\(' \
.

docs.title: JWT Verification
docs.text:
Review:

Signature verification
Allowed algorithms
Signing key
Issuer
Audience
Expiration
Not-before
Subject
Key selection
Claims mapping

Do not assume:

Token parsed

means:

Token securely verified

docs.title: JWT Claims
docs.text:
Sensitive claims may include:

sub
role
roles
permissions
tenant
scope
groups
admin

Trace how claims influence authorisation.

JWT Claim
    |
    v
Identity
    |
    v
Role / Permission
    |
    v
Sensitive Operation

docs.title: JWT Authorisation Mistakes
docs.text:
Review for patterns such as:

Role accepted directly from untrusted data
Missing issuer validation
Missing audience validation
Incorrect key selection
Claims trusted before verification
Sensitive custom claims mapped incorrectly

A suspicious configuration is a candidate for further analysis, not automatic proof of exploitability.

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'api.?key|x-api-key|apikey' \
.

Trace:

Header
  |
  v
API Key Lookup
  |
  v
Identity / Service
  |
  v
Permissions

Review:

Storage
Comparison
Rotation
Scopes
Logging
Revocation

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect
docs.text:
Typical authentication flow:

User
 |
 v
Authorization Request
 |
 v
Identity Provider
 |
 v
Callback
 |
 v
Authorization Code
 |
 v
Token Exchange
 |
 v
Token Validation
 |
 v
Identity Mapping
 |
 v
Session

Search:

rg -n -i \
'oauth|openid|oidc|authorization.?code|redirect_uri|state|nonce|pkce|code_verifier|code_challenge' \
.

docs.title: OAuth / OIDC Review
docs.text:
Review:

state validation
nonce validation
PKCE
redirect URI handling
token validation
issuer
audience
identity mapping
account linking
session creation

docs.title: Account Linking
docs.text:
Pay special attention to:

External identity
      |
      v
Email / Subject
      |
      v
Existing Local Account

Ask:

What uniquely identifies the external user?

Is email trusted?

Is email verified?

Can identities from different providers collide?

Can an attacker link themselves to another account?

docs.title: SAML
docs.text:
Typical flow:

SAMLResponse
     |
     v
XML Parsing
     |
     v
Signature Validation
     |
     v
Assertion Validation
     |
     v
Identity Mapping
     |
     v
Session

Search:

rg -n -i \
'saml|SAMLResponse|assertion|acs|metadata|single.?sign.?on|single.?logout' \
.

Review:

Signature validation
Assertion conditions
Audience
Recipient
Destination
Issuer
Time conditions
Identity mapping
Session creation

docs.title: MFA
docs.text:
Typical flow:

Primary Authentication
        |
        v
MFA Required?
        |
        v
Challenge
        |
        v
Verification
        |
        v
Authenticated Session

Search:

rg -n -i \
'mfa|2fa|totp|otp|authenticator|recovery.?code|backup.?code' \
.

docs.title: MFA State
docs.text:
Identify how the application remembers:

MFA pending
MFA completed
MFA enrolled
Trusted device
Recovery authentication

The state may exist in:

Session
JWT claim
Database
Cookie
Temporary token

docs.title: MFA Bypass Review
docs.text:
Map every route capable of creating a fully authenticated session.

Password Login
OAuth Login
SAML Login
Password Reset
Recovery Code
Magic Link
Administrative Impersonation
Remember Device

Then determine whether MFA is consistently enforced.

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text:
Typical flow:

Reset Request
     |
     v
Account Lookup
     |
     v
Token Generation
     |
     v
Token Delivery
     |
     v
Token Verification
     |
     v
Password Change
     |
     v
Token Invalidation

Search:

rg -n -i \
'forgot.?password|reset.?password|password.?reset|reset.?token' \
.

docs.title: Password Reset Review
docs.text:
Review:

Token entropy
Token expiration
Single use
Account binding
Invalidation
Host/header handling
Rate limiting
Session invalidation
MFA interaction

docs.title: Magic Links
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'magic.?link|passwordless|login.?link' \
.

Trace:

Email
  |
  v
Token
  |
  v
Callback
  |
  v
Identity
  |
  v
Session

Review the token similarly to password-reset tokens.

docs.title: Authorisation Architecture
docs.text:
After authentication is understood, identify the authorisation model.

Common models include:

RBAC
ABAC
ACL
Ownership
Tenant isolation
Scopes
Claims
Policies
Permissions
Relationship-based access

Applications frequently combine several.

docs.title: RBAC
docs.text:
Role-Based Access Control:

User
 |
 v
Role
 |
 v
Permissions

Example:

Alice
 |
 v
Administrator
 |
 v
user:delete

Review:

Role assignment
Role hierarchy
Role checks
Default roles
Role modification

docs.title: ABAC
docs.text:
Attribute-Based Access Control may consider:

User department
Resource classification
Tenant
Location
Time
Account status
Ownership

Conceptually:

Subject Attributes
       +
Resource Attributes
       +
Environment
       |
       v
Policy Decision

docs.title: ACL
docs.text:
Access Control Lists may associate permissions directly with resources.

Document
 |
 +-- Alice -> Read
 +-- Bob   -> Read/Write
 +-- Admin -> Full Control

Review both:

ACL creation
ACL enforcement

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
A common pattern:

Resource.ownerId == currentUser.id

Search:

rg -n -i \
'owner|ownerId|userId|createdBy|belongsTo|tenantId|organisationId|organizationId' \
.

These are discovery indicators only.

docs.title: ASP.NET Core Authentication
docs.text:
Common security components include:

AddAuthentication
AddAuthorization
UseAuthentication
UseAuthorization
[Authorize]
[AllowAnonymous]
RequireAuthorization
Policies
Claims
Roles

Search:

rg -n \
'AddAuthentication|AddAuthorization|UseAuthentication|UseAuthorization|\[Authorize|\[AllowAnonymous|RequireAuthorization|RequireClaim|RequireRole' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: ASP.NET Identity
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'UserManager|SignInManager|RoleManager|PasswordHasher|IdentityUser|IdentityRole' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

Trace:

Login
 |
 v
SignInManager
 |
 v
Identity
 |
 v
ClaimsPrincipal
 |
 v
HttpContext.User

docs.title: ASP.NET Authorisation
docs.text:
Example:

[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
[HttpDelete("{id}")]
public IActionResult DeleteUser(
    int id
)
{
    ...
}

This provides function-level authorisation.

Still review object-level or business-level checks where relevant.

docs.title: ASP.NET Policies
docs.text:
Example:

[Authorize(
    Policy = "CanManageUsers"
)]

Follow:

CanManageUsers

to its policy definition.

Search:

rg -n \
'AddPolicy|RequireClaim|RequireRole|IAuthorizationRequirement|AuthorizationHandler' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: ASP.NET Object Authorisation
docs.text:
Example:

var document =
    repository.Get(id);

if (
    document.OwnerId !=
    currentUserId
)
{
    return Forbid();
}

Trace where:

currentUserId

originates and whether the comparison applies to every sensitive action.

docs.title: ASP.NET Resource-Based Authorisation
docs.text:
Look for:

IAuthorizationService
AuthorizeAsync
AuthorizationHandler

Example:

await authorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(
    User,
    document,
    "CanEditDocument"
);

Review the corresponding handler.

docs.title: Java / Spring Security
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'SecurityFilterChain|HttpSecurity|authorizeHttpRequests|requestMatchers|permitAll|authenticated|hasRole|hasAuthority|@PreAuthorize|@PostAuthorize|@Secured|@RolesAllowed' \
-g '*.java' \
-g '*.kt' \
.

docs.title: Spring Route Security
docs.text:
Example:

http
    .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/admin/**")
        .hasRole("ADMIN")
        .requestMatchers("/api/**")
        .authenticated()
    );

Create a security map:

/admin/** -> ADMIN
/api/**   -> Authenticated

Compare it with the route inventory.

docs.title: Spring Method Security
docs.text:
Example:

@PreAuthorize(
    "hasRole('ADMIN')"
)
public void deleteUser(
    Long id
) {
    ...
}

Search:

rg -n \
'@PreAuthorize|@PostAuthorize|@PreFilter|@PostFilter|@Secured|@RolesAllowed' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: Spring Expression Authorisation
docs.text:
Example:

@PreAuthorize(
    "#userId == authentication.principal.id"
)

Review:

Expression
Principal
Object ID
Service behaviour

Complex expressions deserve manual inspection.

docs.title: Spring Security Context
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'SecurityContextHolder|getAuthentication\(|Principal|Authentication' \
-g '*.java' \
.

Trace how identity is obtained.

docs.title: PHP / Laravel Authentication
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Auth::|auth\(\)|middleware\(["'\'']auth|->middleware\(["'\'']auth|Gate::|authorize\(|can\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Laravel Middleware
docs.text:
Example:

Route::middleware(
    'auth'
)->group(function () {
    ...
});

Map which routes inherit the middleware.

docs.title: Laravel Gates
docs.text:
Example:

Gate::authorize(
    'update-post',
    $post
);

Follow the gate definition.

Search:

rg -n \
'Gate::define|Gate::authorize|Gate::allows|Gate::denies' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Laravel Policies
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Policy|authorize\(|can\(|cannot\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Review methods such as:

view
create
update
delete
restore
forceDelete

docs.title: PHP Direct Authorisation
docs.text:
Legacy PHP may implement checks manually.

Example:

if ($_SESSION['role'] !== 'admin') {
    http_response_code(403);
    exit;
}

Search:

rg -n -i \
'\$_SESSION|role|permission|admin|user_id|owner' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Django Authentication
docs.text:
Django commonly exposes:

request.user
login_required
permission_required
LoginRequiredMixin
PermissionRequiredMixin

Search:

rg -n \
'request\.user|login_required|permission_required|LoginRequiredMixin|PermissionRequiredMixin|authenticate\(|login\(|logout\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Django Authorisation
docs.text:
Example:

@login_required
def document(request, id):

    document =
        Document.objects.get(
            id=id,
            owner=request.user
        )

    return ...

The query itself constrains ownership.

docs.title: Django Dangerous Lookup Pattern
docs.text:
Candidate:

document =
    Document.objects.get(
        id=id
    )

Then:

Where is ownership checked?

Do not report IDOR solely from the lookup.

Search the surrounding execution path.

docs.title: Django Permissions
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'has_perm|has_perms|permission_required|user_passes_test|is_staff|is_superuser' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Django REST Framework
docs.text:
Authentication and authorisation frequently use:

authentication_classes
permission_classes
get_permissions
has_permission
has_object_permission

Search:

rg -n \
'authentication_classes|permission_classes|get_permissions|has_permission|has_object_permission|IsAuthenticated|AllowAny|IsAdminUser' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: DRF Object-Level Permissions
docs.text:
Pay particular attention to:

def has_object_permission(
    self,
    request,
    view,
    obj
):
    ...

But also verify that the framework path actually invokes object permission checks for the relevant operation.

docs.title: DRF Queryset Filtering
docs.text:
Object isolation may occur through:

def get_queryset(self):

    return Document.objects.filter(
        owner=self.request.user
    )

This may be a meaningful object-level security control.

Review all alternate access paths.

docs.title: Flask Authentication
docs.text:
Flask security is frequently implemented through extensions or custom decorators.

Search:

rg -n \
'login_required|current_user|before_request|jwt_required|roles_required|permission|session\[' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Flask-Login
docs.text:
Common identity:

current_user

Example:

@login_required
def profile():
    return ...

This proves authentication enforcement at the decorator level, not necessarily object-level authorisation.

docs.title: Flask Object Authorisation
docs.text:
Example:

document =
    Document.query.get(id)

if (
    document.user_id !=
    current_user.id
):
    abort(403)

Trace all routes using the same document service.

docs.title: Node.js / Express Authentication
docs.text:
Common patterns:

req.user
req.session
authenticate middleware
JWT middleware
Passport
Custom middleware

Search:

rg -n \
'req\.user|req\.session|passport|authenticate|isAuthenticated|requireAuth|verifyToken|jwt\.verify' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Express Middleware Chain
docs.text:
Example:

router.delete(
    "/users/:id",
    authenticate,
    requireAdmin,
    deleteUser
);

Map:

Route
  |
  v
authenticate
  |
  v
requireAdmin
  |
  v
deleteUser

docs.title: Express Middleware Ordering
docs.text:
Compare:

app.use(
    authenticate
);

app.use(
    "/api",
    router
);

with:

app.use(
    "/api",
    router
);

app.use(
    authenticate
);

Ordering may affect security behaviour.

Confirm framework/runtime semantics before reporting.

docs.title: Express Object Authorisation
docs.text:
Candidate:

const document =
    await Document.findById(
        req.params.id
    );

return res.json(document);

Ask:

Where is ownership or tenant access checked?

docs.title: NestJS Authentication
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'@UseGuards|AuthGuard|RolesGuard|@Roles|CanActivate|ExecutionContext' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: NestJS Guards
docs.text:
Example:

@UseGuards(
    JwtAuthGuard,
    RolesGuard
)
@Roles("admin")
@Delete(":id")
deleteUser() {
    ...
}

Trace guard implementation.

docs.title: Client-Side Authorisation
docs.text:
Client-side checks are not server-side security boundaries.

Example:

if (
    currentUser.role === "admin"
) {
    showDeleteButton();
}

This controls UI behaviour.

It does not prove:

DELETE /api/users/{id}

is protected.

Always find the server-side check.

docs.title: Hidden Buttons
docs.text:
A hidden administrator button is not authorisation.

Frontend
   |
   v
Hide Button

must be backed by:

Server
  |
  v
Permission Check

docs.title: GraphQL Authentication
docs.text:
GraphQL may authenticate:

At HTTP middleware
In GraphQL context
At resolver level
Through directives

Search:

rg -n -i \
'context|currentUser|user|auth|permission|guard|directive' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
-g '*.py' \
-g '*.java' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

Manual triage is required.

docs.title: GraphQL Authorisation
docs.text:
Map each sensitive resolver:

Mutation
   |
   v
Resolver
   |
   v
Identity
   |
   v
Permission
   |
   v
Object

Example:

deleteDocument(id)
       |
       v
documentResolver
       |
       v
findById(id)
       |
       v
ownership?
       |
       v
delete()

docs.title: GraphQL Field-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Sensitive fields may include:

email
phone
salary
internalNotes
permissions
tokens
billing
personal data

An object may be accessible while specific fields should not be.

docs.title: GraphQL Mutations
docs.text:
Prioritise:

create
update
delete
invite
approve
transfer
reset
changeRole
changePassword
disableMFA

These are only review priorities.

docs.title: gRPC Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication may be implemented through:

Metadata
Interceptors
mTLS
JWT
API keys
Service identity

Typical model:

gRPC Request
     |
     v
Interceptor
     |
     v
Identity
     |
     v
RPC Handler

docs.title: gRPC Authorisation
docs.text:
Do not stop at the interceptor.

Review:

Service-level authorisation
RPC-level authorisation
Object-level authorisation
Tenant isolation

Example:

DeleteDocumentRequest.id
          |
          v
DeleteDocument()
          |
          v
Document Lookup
          |
          v
Ownership?
          |
          v
Delete

docs.title: WebSocket Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication may occur:

During HTTP upgrade
Through cookie
Through query token
Through first message
Through protocol-specific authentication

Trace how the authenticated identity is stored for later messages.

docs.title: WebSocket Authorisation
docs.text:
Every sensitive message handler should be reviewed.

Example:

socket.on(
    "delete-document",
    async id => {
        await documents.delete(id);
    }
);

Ask:

Who owns the socket?

Where is the user identity?

Where is document ownership checked?

docs.title: Webhook Authentication
docs.text:
Webhooks usually authenticate the sender rather than a human user.

Typical controls:

HMAC signature
Asymmetric signature
Shared secret
mTLS
Source authentication

Model:

Webhook Request
      |
      v
Signature Verification
      |
      v
Event Processing

Review whether verification occurs before sensitive processing.

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
Authorisation may occur earlier than the worker.

Example:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Authorisation
     |
     v
Queue Job
     |
     v
Worker

But ask:

Can another producer create jobs?

Does the job contain trusted user IDs?

Does the worker independently validate tenant boundaries?

Can stored data change between authorisation and execution?

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
The core pattern is:

Attacker-Controlled Identifier
            |
            v
Object Lookup
            |
            v
Authorisation?
            |
            v
Sensitive Operation

docs.title: IDOR Review Strategy
docs.text:
Search for identifiers:

rg -n -i \
'user.?id|account.?id|document.?id|order.?id|invoice.?id|tenant.?id|organisation.?id|organization.?id|owner.?id' \
.

Then identify lookups.

docs.title: Database Lookup Patterns
docs.text:
Potential examples:

findById
getById
FindAsync
Single
First
get()
filter()
findOne
findByPk

Do not report these methods themselves.

Trace what happens after the lookup.

docs.title: Secure Ownership Query Pattern
docs.text:
Example:

SELECT *
FROM documents
WHERE id = ?
AND owner_id = ?

Conceptually:

Attacker Object ID
       +
Authenticated User ID
       |
       v
Constrained Lookup

This can provide strong object-level isolation.

docs.title: Post-Lookup Authorisation
docs.text:
Another valid model:

Object Lookup
     |
     v
Ownership Check
     |
     v
Return Object

Both models may be secure if correctly implemented.

docs.title: Missing Ownership Check
docs.text:
Candidate:

Route ID
   |
   v
Repository.findById(id)
   |
   v
Return

Compare against the application's normal pattern:

Route ID
   |
   v
Repository.findById(id)
   |
   v
checkOwnership()
   |
   v
Return

This comparison is powerful during variant analysis.

docs.title: Horizontal Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
User A
  |
  v
Object ID belonging to User B
  |
  v
Sensitive Operation

Examples:

Read another user's profile
Download another user's document
Modify another user's order
Delete another user's resource

docs.title: Vertical Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Normal User
    |
    v
Administrator Function

Examples:

Change role
Disable user
View audit logs
Modify system settings
Generate API keys

docs.title: Tenant Escape
docs.text:
Tenant A User
      |
      v
Tenant B Object ID
      |
      v
Object Lookup
      |
      v
Sensitive Operation

Search for whether database queries include:

tenantId
organisationId
organizationId
customerId
accountId

where required.

docs.title: Role Assignment
docs.text:
Role-management code deserves high priority.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'role|roles|permission|permissions|isAdmin|admin|grant|revoke' \
.

Review:

Who can assign roles?

Can users assign their own role?

Can mass assignment modify role fields?

Can tenant administrators assign global roles?

docs.title: Mass Assignment and Authorisation
docs.text:
Example:

await User.update(
    req.body,
    {
        where: {
            id: req.user.id
        }
    }
);

Potential sensitive fields:

role
isAdmin
permissions
tenantId
verified

Review DTOs, allowlists, serializers, and ORM behaviour before concluding exploitability.

docs.title: Administrative Impersonation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'impersonat|login.?as|switch.?user|assume.?user' \
.

Review:

Who can impersonate?

Is the action audited?

Can privileged identities be impersonated?

How is impersonation ended?

Can the impersonation state be forged?

docs.title: Security Context Switching
docs.text:
Applications may support:

Switch tenant
Switch organisation
Assume role
Act on behalf of
Delegation

These are important authorisation boundaries.

docs.title: Sensitive Operations
docs.text:
Prioritise operations such as:

Create administrator
Change role
Change email
Change password
Disable MFA
Generate recovery codes
Create API key
Delete user
Delete tenant
Transfer funds
Issue refund
Approve request
Change ownership
Export sensitive data

Use Find All References to identify every path to these operations.

docs.title: Reverse Authorisation Analysis
docs.text:
Instead of starting from routes, begin at sensitive operations.

Sensitive Operation
        |
        v
Who calls it?
        |
        v
Find All References
        |
        v
Controllers / Resolvers / Workers
        |
        v
Where is authorisation?

This is one of the strongest techniques for finding alternate-entry-point vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose:

userService.deleteUser(id);

is security-sensitive.

Find every caller:

REST AdminController
GraphQL UserMutation
gRPC UserService
Background CleanupJob

Then compare controls.

REST
 |
 +--> @PreAuthorize ADMIN
 |
 v
deleteUser()


GraphQL
 |
 +--> authenticated
 |
 v
deleteUser()


gRPC
 |
 +--> AdminInterceptor
 |
 v
deleteUser()

The GraphQL path deserves further investigation.

docs.title: Alternate Entry Points
docs.text:
The same operation may be reachable through:

REST
GraphQL
gRPC
WebSocket
Admin panel
Internal API
Background worker
CLI

Compare security controls across all paths.

docs.title: Security Control Consistency Matrix
docs.text:
Operation REST GraphQL gRPC WebSocket Read document Auth + owner Auth + ? Auth + owner N/A Delete document Auth + owner Auth + ? Admin Auth + owner Change role Admin Admin Admin N/A

Question marks become review targets.

docs.title: Missing Authorisation Search
docs.text:
Once a common security control is identified:

checkPermission()

search for its usage:

rg -n \
'checkPermission\(' \
.

Then search sensitive operations that do not call it.

docs.title: Custom Security Helpers
docs.text:
Common names:

authorize
authorise
checkPermission
checkAccess
canAccess
canEdit
canDelete
requireRole
requirePermission
verifyOwnership
validateTenant

Search:

rg -n -i \
'authori[sz]e|check.?permission|check.?access|can.?access|can.?edit|can.?delete|require.?role|require.?permission|verify.?owner|validate.?tenant' \
.

docs.title: Negative Security Pattern Analysis
docs.text:
Sometimes the safest code has a consistent structure.

Example:

getDocument()
checkOwnership()
updateDocument()

Search for:

getDocument()
updateDocument()

without:

checkOwnership()

This is a powerful candidate-discovery technique.

docs.title: Security Control Bypass Through Direct Service Calls
docs.text:
Controllers may be protected while services are callable from alternate entry points.

Example:

AdminController
      |
      v
Role Check
      |
      v
UserService.changeRole()

but:

GraphQL Resolver
      |
      v
UserService.changeRole()

with no equivalent role check.

docs.title: Security in Controllers vs Services
docs.text:
If security exists only in controllers:

Controller
   |
   v
Authorisation
   |
   v
Service

then every alternate caller must reproduce the same security check.

Security enforced closer to the sensitive operation may reduce this risk, depending on architecture.

docs.title: Default-Allow vs Default-Deny
docs.text:
Determine the application's security model.

Default deny:

Everything protected
       |
       v
Explicit anonymous exceptions

Default allow:

Everything accessible
       |
       v
Explicit protected routes

Default-deny models are generally easier to reason about securely.

Verify actual framework behaviour.

docs.title: Anonymous Exceptions
docs.text:
Search:

AllowAnonymous
permitAll
AllowAny
public
anonymous
skipAuth

Examples:

rg -n -i \
'AllowAnonymous|permitAll|AllowAny|anonymous|skip.?auth|publicRoute' \
.

Review every exception.

But:

Anonymous route
    !=
Vulnerability

Many routes legitimately require public access.

docs.title: Authentication Bypass Through Route Matching
docs.text:
Review security configuration against route definitions.

Example:

Security:
/api/admin/** -> ADMIN

Actual route:

/admin/api/users

The rule may not apply.

Do not infer bypass from visual similarity alone.

Confirm framework route matching semantics.

docs.title: HTTP Method Differences
docs.text:
Security may differ by method.

Example:

GET /api/users/{id}
POST /api/users/{id}
DELETE /api/users/{id}

Review each separately.

A GET route may be public while DELETE should require stronger privileges.

docs.title: Method-Level Security
docs.text:
Map:

Path
+
HTTP Method

rather than path alone.

docs.title: Case and Normalisation
docs.text:
Security components and routers may interpret paths differently.

Potential areas for careful review:

Trailing slashes
Case sensitivity
URL decoding
Encoded separators
Path normalisation
Proxy rewrites

Do not claim bypassability without confirming actual routing behaviour.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Authorisation
docs.text:
Some applications rely partly on:

NGINX
API gateway
Ingress
Service mesh
Identity-aware proxy

Map:

Internet
   |
   v
Gateway Authentication
   |
   v
Application

Then determine whether the application is reachable through another path that bypasses the gateway.

docs.title: Trusting Identity Headers
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'x-user|x-username|x-role|x-groups|x-auth|remote-user|remote_user' \
.

Applications behind trusted proxies sometimes consume identity headers.

Review:

Who sets the header?

Can clients supply it directly?

Does the proxy overwrite it?

Can the application be reached without the proxy?

docs.title: Tenant Headers
docs.text:
Similarly search:

X-Tenant-ID
X-Organisation-ID
X-Account-ID

Trace whether tenant context is securely bound to the authenticated identity.

docs.title: Client-Controlled Role Headers
docs.text:
A pattern such as:

X-Role: admin

deserves investigation if the application trusts it.

But determine whether trusted infrastructure injects or overwrites the value before reporting.

docs.title: CSRF and Authorisation
docs.text:
CSRF does not replace authorisation.

A request can be:

Properly authorised

but vulnerable to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

Similarly, CSRF protection does not prove the user is authorised for the underlying action.

Treat the controls separately.

docs.title: CORS and Authorisation
docs.text:
CORS is not an authorisation mechanism.

CORS

controls browser cross-origin response access.

It does not replace:

Authentication
Authorisation

Server endpoints must enforce access independently.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Authentication-related endpoints often require rate limiting.

Prioritise:

Login
Password reset
MFA verification
OTP verification
Account recovery
Magic links
API key validation

Search:

rg -n -i \
'rate.?limit|throttle|attempt|lockout|failed.?login' \
.

docs.title: Authentication State Machines
docs.text:
Complex authentication should be modelled as states.

Example:

Unauthenticated
      |
      v
Password Verified
      |
      v
MFA Pending
      |
      v
MFA Verified
      |
      v
Authenticated

Then identify routes allowed in each state.

docs.title: MFA State Machine Example
docs.text:
LOGIN
  |
  v
Password Correct
  |
  +--> MFA Disabled -> Full Session
  |
  +--> MFA Enabled
            |
            v
       MFA Pending
            |
            v
       OTP Verified
            |
            v
       Full Session

Search for any path:

MFA Pending
     |
     v
Sensitive Application

without completion of MFA.

docs.title: Password Reset State Machine
docs.text:
Reset Requested
      |
      v
Token Issued
      |
      v
Token Presented
      |
      v
Token Validated
      |
      v
Password Changed
      |
      v
Token Invalidated

Look for transitions that skip expected checks.

docs.title: Business Authorisation State Machines
docs.text:
Example:

Draft
  |
  v
Submitted
  |
  v
Approved
  |
  v
Paid

Review whether users can call later-stage operations directly.

docs.title: TOCTOU and Authorisation
docs.text:
A potential pattern:

Check Permission
      |
      v
Delay / Async Boundary
      |
      v
Resource Changes
      |
      v
Sensitive Operation

This can matter where ownership or state can change between check and use.

docs.title: Cached Authorisation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'permission.*cache|role.*cache|authorization.*cache|authorisation.*cache' \
.

Review whether permission changes invalidate cached decisions appropriately.

docs.title: Revocation
docs.text:
Ask:

What happens when:

User is disabled?
Role is removed?
Password changes?
MFA is reset?
API key is revoked?
Session is terminated?

Determine whether existing credentials remain valid.

docs.title: Privilege Changes
docs.text:
A session created as:

Normal User

may later become:

Administrator

or vice versa.

Review whether:

Sessions
JWTs
Cached permissions
Refresh tokens

reflect changes appropriately.

docs.title: Implicit Trust
docs.text:
Watch for assumptions such as:

Internal user = trusted

Authenticated user = trusted

Administrator = unrestricted

Database value = trusted

Service request = trusted

Each assumption should be justified by the architecture.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Authorisation failures should not accidentally expose protected data.

Example:

Load object
     |
     v
Render object
     |
     v
Check permission

is dangerous if rendering or logging already exposes sensitive information.

Prefer conceptual ordering:

Load minimal object
     |
     v
Authorise
     |
     v
Return sensitive data

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Authentication logs may contain:

Usernames
Session IDs
JWTs
Reset tokens
OTP values
Passwords
API keys

Search:

rg -n -i \
'log.*password|log.*token|log.*session|logger.*password|logger.*token|console\.log.*token' \
.

Manual inspection is required.

docs.title: Secrets in Authentication Code
docs.text:
Search for:

JWT secrets
OAuth client secrets
SAML keys
API keys
Cookie secrets
Session secrets

Use dedicated secrets scanning as well.

Do not treat every string matching secret as a credential.

docs.title: Static Analysis
docs.text:
Static analysis can help discover:

Anonymous endpoints
Missing authorisation
Direct object lookups
Security annotations
Role checks
Permission helpers
Authentication configuration

But:

Static Analysis Finding
        !=
Confirmed Access Control Vulnerability

docs.title: ripgrep Workflow
docs.text:
Start broad:

rg -n -i \
'auth|authori[sz]|permission|role|owner|tenant|session|jwt|oauth|saml|mfa' \
.

Then narrow to framework-specific controls.

docs.title: Semgrep / OpenGrep
docs.text:
Structural rules can identify patterns such as:

Sensitive route without expected decorator

Object lookup without common ownership helper

AllowAnonymous on sensitive controller

Direct role assignment from request body

These should produce review candidates.

docs.title: Conceptual Missing Authorisation Rule
docs.text:
Suppose the application normally uses:

check_permission(
    current_user,
    document
)

A project-specific rule can search document update handlers where this expected pattern is absent.

Project-specific rules are often more valuable than generic rules for business authorisation.

docs.title: CodeQL
docs.text:
CodeQL can help trace:

Request ID
    |
    v
Controller
    |
    v
Service
    |
    v
Repository Lookup

and identify whether common security helpers appear along related paths.

It can also help perform variant analysis across complex codebases.

docs.title: Static Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
ripgrep
   |
   v
Discover Security Architecture
   |
   v
Semgrep / OpenGrep
   |
   v
Find Structural Candidates
   |
   v
CodeQL
   |
   v
Trace Complex Data Flow
   |
   v
VS Code
   |
   v
Manual Authorisation Analysis
   |
   v
Burp Suite
   |
   v
Runtime Validation

docs.title: Dynamic Validation
docs.text:
Once source review identifies a candidate:

Source
  |
  v
Potential Missing Control
  |
  v
Burp Suite
  |
  v
Controlled Runtime Test

For access control, compare requests using authorised test identities with different privileges.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Conceptually:

1. Capture a legitimate request.

2. Identify the source-code handler.

3. Determine the expected authentication.

4. Determine the expected authorisation.

5. Identify the object or sensitive operation.

6. Reproduce the request with an authorised test account.

7. Compare behaviour across permitted test roles/users.

8. Change only the relevant object or operation where allowed.

9. Confirm whether the source-code control behaves as expected.

10. Record evidence.

docs.title: IDOR Runtime Validation Model
docs.text:
Test User A
   |
   v
Access Object A
   |
   v
Expected Success

Test User A
   |
   v
Access Object B
   |
   v
Expected Denial

If the second operation succeeds contrary to the intended policy, investigate the source path and impact.

docs.title: Role Validation Model
docs.text:
Administrator
   |
   v
Sensitive Function
   |
   v
Expected Success

Normal User
   |
   v
Same Function
   |
   v
Expected Denial

docs.title: Do Not Test Destructive Actions Blindly
docs.text:
Sensitive operations may include:

Delete account
Transfer money
Change production configuration
Revoke credentials
Disable MFA
Delete tenant

Understand the code path and use safe test data appropriate to the engagement.

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
After confirming one access-control flaw:

Confirmed Finding
       |
       v
Identify Missing Control
       |
       v
Find Normal Secure Pattern
       |
       v
Search Similar Routes
       |
       v
Search Same Service
       |
       v
Search Same Object Type
       |
       v
Search Alternate Protocols

docs.title: IDOR Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Known finding:

GET /documents/{id}
        |
        v
findById(id)
        |
        v
No Ownership Check

Search for:

updateDocument
deleteDocument
downloadDocument
shareDocument
exportDocument

and other calls to the same repository.

docs.title: Function-Level Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Known finding:

GraphQL changeRole()

missing administrator authorisation.

Search:

REST changeRole
gRPC ChangeRole
Admin controller
Internal API
UserService.changeRole()

docs.title: Find All References
docs.text:
If the sensitive sink is:

changeRole()

use Visual Studio Code:

Shift + F12

to identify all callers.

This can quickly reveal inconsistent security controls.

docs.title: Git History
docs.text:
Security regressions can be investigated through Git history.

Useful commands:

git log --all --oneline

Search changes:

git log -S 'Authorize' --all

or:

git log -S 'checkPermission' --all

Review why security controls were added or removed.

Do not assume an old vulnerable implementation is still reachable.

docs.title: Security Tests
docs.text:
Search for tests such as:

shouldReturnForbidden
shouldRejectUnauthorised
shouldRejectUnauthorized
requiresAdmin
cannotAccessOtherUser
cannotAccessOtherTenant

Using:

rg -n -i \
'forbidden|unauthori[sz]ed|requires.?admin|permission|other.?user|other.?tenant' \
.

Tests can document expected policy.

docs.title: Missing Security Tests
docs.text:
Compare sensitive functionality against test coverage.

For example:

deleteDocument

may have:

success test
not-found test

but no:

unauthorised-user test

This is useful review context, but missing tests alone are not a vulnerability.

docs.title: Authorisation Matrix
docs.text:
For complex applications, build a matrix.

Operation Anonymous User Manager Admin View own profile No Yes Yes Yes View other profile No No Limited Yes Update role No No No Yes Delete user No No No Yes Export tenant No No Yes Yes

Then compare source code against intended policy.

docs.title: Object Matrix
docs.text:
Example:

Actor Own Object Same Tenant Other Tenant User Read/Write No No Manager Read Read No Admin Read/Write Read/Write Depends

This makes BOLA and tenant-isolation review more systematic.

AUTHZ-001

Entry Point:
GET /api/documents/{id}

Handler:
DocumentController.get()

Identity:
current_user

Object Identifier:
id

Object Lookup:
Document.findById(id)

Required Policy:
User must own document

Authorisation Check:
...

Return document

docs.title: Access-Control Finding Evidence
docs.text:
Strong evidence includes:

Entry point
Required privilege
Actual privilege
Identity source
Object identifier
Authorisation path
Missing or ineffective control
Sensitive operation
Runtime behaviour
Impact

docs.title: Weak Finding Description
docs.text:
Avoid:

The endpoint may be vulnerable to IDOR because it accepts an ID.

An identifier alone does not prove broken access control.

docs.title: Stronger Finding Description
docs.text:
Prefer:

The document identifier supplied through GET /api/documents/{id}
is passed to DocumentRepository.findById() and the returned document
is sent to the authenticated user without an ownership or tenant
authorisation check along this execution path.

Runtime testing with authorised test accounts confirmed that a user
could retrieve a document belonging to another user by supplying the
other document identifier.

This connects:

Source
+
Missing Control
+
Sink
+
Runtime Evidence
+
Impact

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Authorisation remediation should enforce the intended security policy at a reliable security boundary.

Potential patterns include:

Centralised policies
Resource-based authorisation
Object-level permissions
Tenant-constrained queries
Explicit field allowlists
Service-layer permission checks
Default-deny routing

The appropriate design depends on the application architecture.

docs.title: Object-Level Remediation
docs.text:
Instead of:

findById(objectId)

consider an architecture that enforces:

findByIdAndOwner(
    objectId,
    currentUser
)

or:

findByIdAndTenant(
    objectId,
    authorisedTenant
)

where appropriate.

This reduces the chance that a retrieved object escapes the intended security boundary.

docs.title: Centralise Repeated Security Logic
docs.text:
If every controller manually implements:

if object.owner != current_user:
    deny

security inconsistencies become easier to introduce.

Where appropriate, centralise through:

Policies
Permission services
Repository constraints
Framework authorisation
Resource-based authorisation

docs.title: Defence in Depth
docs.text:
Strong access control may include:

Authentication
       +
Function-Level Authorisation
       +
Object-Level Authorisation
       +
Tenant Isolation
       +
Business Rules
       +
Audit Logging

No single layer should be assumed to replace all others.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:

Review Code Change

Verify Security Control
      |
      v
Test Expected Allowed Action
      |
      v
Test Expected Denied Action
      |
      v
Test Alternate Entry Points
      |
      v

docs.title: Practical Testing Model
docs.text:
For every sensitive operation answer:

1. What is the entry point?

2. What authentication mechanism applies?

3. How is identity established?

4. What function-level permission is required?

5. Where is that permission enforced?

6. Does the operation reference an object?

7. Who controls the object identifier?

8. Where is the object retrieved?

9. Where is ownership checked?

10. Where is tenant membership checked?

11. Are sensitive properties separately protected?

12. Are business rules enforced?

13. Are there alternate entry points?

14. Do those entry points use equivalent controls?

15. Can the operation be reached asynchronously?

16. Can the control be bypassed through another service?

17. Does runtime behaviour match the source?

18. Are similar variants present elsewhere?

If these questions can be answered, the authentication and authorisation path is understood.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Authentication establishes identity.

Authorisation determines what that identity may do.

The source-review workflow is:

Map Authentication
       |
       v
Trace Identity
       |
       v
Map Routes
       |
       v
Find Sensitive Operations
       |
       v
Map Function-Level Controls
       |
       v
Map Object-Level Controls
       |
       v
Map Tenant Boundaries
       |
       v
Map Business Rules
       |
       v
Find Alternate Entry Points
       |
       v
Compare Security Controls
       |
       v
Runtime Validation
       |
       v
Variant Analysis

The final rule is:

Authenticated
    !=
Authorised

and:

Role Check
    !=
Object-Level Authorisation

and:

One Protected Entry Point
    !=
Every Entry Point Protected

A complete review therefore determines:

WHO
can perform
WHAT ACTION
on
WHICH OBJECT
inside
WHICH TENANT / SECURITY CONTEXT
through
WHICH ENTRY POINTS
under
WHICH BUSINESS RULES

That model should be applied to every security-sensitive operation in the application.

docs.title: Django Source Code Review
docs.text:
Django is a Python web framework that provides many security controls by default, including template escaping, CSRF protection, authentication, session management, ORM query parameterisation and host validation.

These protections significantly reduce common vulnerabilities when used correctly.

However, Django applications can still introduce vulnerabilities when developers:

Bypass framework protections
Use raw SQL
Disable CSRF protection
Mark attacker-controlled HTML as safe
Perform missing object-level authorisation
Trust user-controlled object IDs
Use unsafe redirects
Construct paths from user input
Make outbound requests using attacker-controlled URLs
Perform unsafe deserialization
Expose sensitive settings
Use weak permission logic
Trust Host or proxy headers incorrectly
Mass assign model fields
Expose dangerous administrative functionality

The objective of Django source-code review is therefore not simply:

Find dangerous functions

but:

Understand how the application uses Django's security model
and identify where application code bypasses or weakens it.

The fundamental model remains:

SOURCE
  |
  v
ATTACKER-CONTROLLED DATA
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATIONS
  |
  +-- forms
  +-- serializers
  +-- validation
  +-- parsing
  +-- business logic
  |
  v
SECURITY CONTROLS
  |
  +-- authentication
  +-- permissions
  +-- CSRF
  +-- ORM
  +-- template escaping
  |
  v
SINK
  |
  v
SECURITY-SENSITIVE OPERATION

Remember:

Django application
    !=
Automatically secure

and:

grep match
    !=
vulnerability

A source-code match identifies a location that requires investigation.

Exploitability requires understanding the complete data flow.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform source-code review and dynamic validation only against Django applications, repositories and environments for which you have explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Review Strategy
docs.text:
A practical Django review can follow:

1. Identify Django version

2. Identify project structure

3. Review settings.py

4. Map URL configurations

5. Map views and API endpoints

6. Identify authentication controls

7. Identify authorisation controls

8. Review object-level access

9. Review forms and serializers

10. Review ORM usage

11. Search raw SQL

12. Review templates

13. Search escaping bypasses

14. Review CSRF protection

15. Review redirects

16. Review file uploads

17. Review file-system access

18. Review outbound requests

19. Review session configuration

20. Review host/proxy handling

21. Review Django REST Framework

22. Review business logic

23. Review background workers

24. Search secrets

25. Review dependencies

26. Run static analysis

27. Perform variant analysis

28. Validate findings dynamically where authorised

docs.title: Identify Django
docs.text:
Search dependency files:

rg -n -i \
'django|djangorestframework|django-rest-framework' \
requirements*.txt pyproject.toml Pipfile setup.py setup.cfg 2>/dev/null

Typical dependency:

Django==5.x.x

or:

dependencies = [
    "Django>=5.2",
]

Determine the exact deployed version rather than relying only on development dependency files.

docs.title: Identify Django Version
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Django[=<>~!]|django[=<>~!]' \
requirements*.txt pyproject.toml Pipfile* poetry.lock uv.lock 2>/dev/null

If the environment is available:

python3 -m django --version

or:

python3 -c "import django; print(django.get_version())"

Version identification matters because:

Security behaviour changes
Deprecated APIs change
Supported versions change
Security fixes are version-specific
Middleware behaviour evolves

Do not report an outdated Django version without confirming the actual runtime or deployed dependency.
