docs.title: Client-Side JavaScript Source Code Review
docs.text:
Client-side JavaScript is one of the most important areas of web application source-code review because security-sensitive behaviour increasingly occurs inside the browser.

Modern applications may use JavaScript for:

  • DOM manipulation
  • Routing
  • Authentication state
  • API communication
  • OAuth and OIDC flows
  • WebSockets
  • Cross-window communication
  • Browser storage
  • File processing
  • URL handling
  • Dynamic HTML generation
  • Third-party integrations
  • Feature flags
  • Client-side validation
  • Single-page applications
  • Service workers
  • Web workers
  • WebAssembly integration

Client-side JavaScript review differs from server-side review because the browser itself becomes part of the trust boundary.

The fundamental rule is:

Anything controlled by the browser
must ultimately be considered attacker-controlled
by the server.

Client-side controls can improve usability and provide defence in depth, but they cannot replace server-side:

Authentication
Authorisation
Validation
Business rules
Tenant isolation
Access control

The primary review methodology remains:

SOURCE
  |
  v
Attacker-Controlled Data
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATIONS
  |
  +-- parsing
  +-- decoding
  +-- sanitisation
  +-- filtering
  +-- validation
  +-- object merging
  |
  v
SINK
  |
  v
Security-Sensitive Browser Operation

Examples:

location.search
      |
      v
URLSearchParams
      |
      v
innerHTML

or:

postMessage
    |
    v
message event
    |
    v
eval()

or:

location.hash
     |
     v
redirect logic
     |
     v
location.href

The key question is:

Can attacker-controlled data reach a dangerous browser sink
without an effective security control?

Remember:

Source found
    !=
Vulnerability

and:

Sink found
    !=
Vulnerability

A vulnerability normally requires:

Attacker-controlled source
        +
Reachable data flow
        +
Dangerous sink
        +
Missing or ineffective protection
        +
Security impact

Authorised Security Testing

Perform source-code review and dynamic validation only against applications, repositories and environments for which you have explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Review Strategy
docs.text:
A practical client-side JavaScript review can follow:

1. Identify JavaScript files

2. Identify JavaScript frameworks

3. Identify application bundles

4. Identify source maps

5. Identify third-party scripts

6. Identify URL-derived sources

7. Identify DOM-derived sources

8. Identify postMessage handlers

9. Identify browser storage usage

10. Identify API requests

11. Identify WebSocket connections

12. Identify dangerous DOM sinks

13. Identify dynamic JavaScript execution

14. Identify redirect sinks

15. Identify dynamic script loading

16. Review HTML sanitisation

17. Review prototype pollution

18. Review DOM clobbering

19. Review client-side authentication logic

20. Review client-side authorisation assumptions

21. Review OAuth/OIDC handling

22. Review secrets and configuration

23. Review CSP and Trusted Types

24. Review third-party JavaScript

25. Review service workers

26. Review Web Workers

27. Review WebAssembly integration

28. Perform source-to-sink tracing

29. Run static analysis

30. Perform variant analysis

31. Validate candidates dynamically where authorised

docs.title: Identify JavaScript Files
docs.text:
Search:

find . -type f \( \
-name '*.js' \
-o -name '*.mjs' \
-o -name '*.cjs' \
-o -name '*.jsx' \
-o -name '*.ts' \
-o -name '*.tsx' \
\) -print

For a downloaded website:

find . -type f -name '*.js' -print

Count:

find . -type f -name '*.js' | wc -l

docs.title: Identify Source Maps
docs.text:
Search:

find . -type f -name '*.map' -print

Search JavaScript references:

rg -n \
'sourceMappingURL' \
--glob '*.js' \
.

Example:

//# sourceMappingURL=app.js.map

Source maps may expose:

Original source files
Framework structure
Comments
Internal endpoints
Function names
API calls
Configuration
Development code
Potential secrets

Source maps are not automatically vulnerabilities.

Determine whether exposed information has meaningful security impact.

docs.title: Identify Frameworks
docs.text:
Search package manifests:

cat package.json

Common frameworks and libraries include:

React
Angular
Vue
Svelte
Next.js
Nuxt
jQuery
Alpine.js
Backbone
Ember
Lit
Axios
Lodash
DOMPurify

Search:

rg -n -i \
'react|angular|vue|svelte|next|nuxt|jquery|lodash|dompurify|axios' \
package.json package-lock.json yarn.lock pnpm-lock.yaml 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Bundled Applications
docs.text:
Production JavaScript may be bundled using:

Webpack
Vite
Rollup
Parcel
esbuild
Turbopack

Search:

find . -maxdepth 3 -type f \( \
-name 'webpack.config.*' \
-o -name 'vite.config.*' \
-o -name 'rollup.config.*' \
-o -name 'next.config.*' \
-o -name 'nuxt.config.*' \
\) -print

Bundling can obscure source relationships.

Source maps can greatly improve review quality.

docs.title: Beautifying JavaScript
docs.text:
Minified JavaScript is difficult to review.

Common tools include:

npx prettier app.js > app.pretty.js

or:

js-beautify app.js > app.pretty.js

Do not modify the original evidence file.

docs.title: Client-Side Sources
docs.text:
High-value attacker-controlled sources include:

location
location.href
location.search
location.hash
location.pathname
document.URL
document.documentURI
document.referrer
window.name

Other sources include:

postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage
IndexedDB
Cookies
WebSocket messages
API responses
DOM attributes
Form values
URL parameters

docs.title: URL Sources
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'location\.(href|search|hash|pathname|host|hostname)|document\.(URL|documentURI|referrer)|window\.name' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: location.search
docs.text:
Example:

const params =
    new URLSearchParams(
        location.search
    );

const name =
    params.get("name");

This creates an attacker-controlled source when the URL can be influenced.

docs.title: location.hash
docs.text:
Example:

const section =
    location.hash.substring(1);

Fragments are not normally sent to the server.

They are nevertheless attacker-controlled browser input.

docs.title: document.referrer
docs.text:
Example:

const previousPage =
    document.referrer;

Do not treat the referrer as trusted security data.

docs.title: window.name
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'window\.name' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

window.name can persist across navigations and should be treated as untrusted input.

docs.title: DOM Sources
docs.text:
Form elements:

element.value

Search:

rg -n \
'\.value\b|FormData\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
Example:

const id =
    element.dataset.id;

Search:

rg -n \
'\.dataset\b|getAttribute\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

DOM attributes may originate from attacker-controlled HTML or server responses.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'document\.cookie' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Client-side JavaScript cannot read cookies marked:

HttpOnly

Do not assume every cookie is available to JavaScript.

docs.title: Web Storage
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'localStorage|sessionStorage' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Common operations:

localStorage.getItem()
localStorage.setItem()

sessionStorage.getItem()
sessionStorage.setItem()

Data in browser storage should generally be considered attacker-controllable from the application's trust perspective.

docs.title: IndexedDB
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'indexedDB|IDBDatabase|IDBObjectStore' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review whether data retrieved from IndexedDB reaches dangerous sinks.

docs.title: API Responses as Sources
docs.text:
Example:

const response =
    await fetch("/api/profile");

const data =
    await response.json();

element.innerHTML =
    data.biography;

Flow:

Server-Stored Data
      |
      v
API Response
      |
      v
response.json()
      |
      v
data.biography
      |
      v
innerHTML

This can create stored DOM XSS.

docs.title: Fetch
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\bfetch\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Axios
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'axios\.(get|post|put|patch|delete|request)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: XMLHttpRequest
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'XMLHttpRequest|\.open\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Dangerous DOM Sinks
docs.text:
High-value sinks include:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML()
document.write()
document.writeln()

Search:

rg -n \
'innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write\(|document\.writeln\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: innerHTML
docs.text:
Candidate:

const name =
    new URLSearchParams(
        location.search
    ).get("name");

document.querySelector(
    "#welcome"
).innerHTML =
    name;

Flow:

location.search
      |
      v
URLSearchParams
      |
      v
name
      |
      v
innerHTML

This is a high-value DOM XSS candidate.

docs.title: outerHTML
docs.text:
Candidate:

element.outerHTML =
    userInput;

Search:

rg -n \
'outerHTML\s*=' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: insertAdjacentHTML
docs.text:
Candidate:

element.insertAdjacentHTML(
    "beforeend",
    content
);

Search:

rg -n \
'insertAdjacentHTML\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: document.write
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'document\.write\(|document\.writeln\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Trace attacker-controlled values carefully.

docs.title: Safer Text Output
docs.text:
When HTML interpretation is unnecessary:

element.textContent =
    value;

or:

element.innerText =
    value;

Search:

rg -n \
'textContent|innerText' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

These are generally preferable to HTML-parsing sinks when only text output is required.

docs.title: DOM XSS
docs.text:
The core DOM XSS pattern is:

ATTACKER SOURCE
      |
      v
JavaScript Processing
      |
      v
HTML / JS SINK

Example:

location.hash
     |
     v
decodeURIComponent()
     |
     v
innerHTML

docs.title: DOM XSS Sources
docs.text:
Common sources:

location.href
location.search
location.hash
document.URL
document.referrer
window.name
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage
API responses

docs.title: DOM XSS Sinks
docs.text:
Common sinks:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write
document.writeln
eval
Function
setTimeout with string
setInterval with string
script.src
iframe.src
location

The security context differs between sinks.

Do not treat every sink identically.

Refer to:

DOM-Based Vulnerabilities

Cross-Site Scripting

docs.title: Dynamic JavaScript Execution
docs.text:
High-value sinks:

eval()
Function()
new Function()
setTimeout()
setInterval()

Search:

rg -n \
'\beval\(|new Function\(|\bFunction\(|setTimeout\(|setInterval\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: eval()
docs.text:
Candidate:

const expression =
    new URLSearchParams(
        location.search
    ).get("expr");

eval(expression);

Flow:

location.search
      |
      v
expr
      |
      v
eval()

docs.title: Function Constructor
docs.text:
Candidate:

const fn =
    new Function(
        userInput
    );

Search:

rg -n \
'new Function\(|Function\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: setTimeout
docs.text:
This is not inherently dangerous:

setTimeout(
    updateUI,
    1000
);

A string-based call deserves additional attention:

setTimeout(
    userInput,
    1000
);

Trace whether strings are evaluated as code.

docs.title: setInterval
docs.text:
The same distinction applies:

setInterval(
    callback,
    1000
);

versus attacker-controlled string input.

docs.title: URL-Based Sinks
docs.text:
High-value URL sinks include:

location
location.href
location.assign()
location.replace()
window.open()

Search:

rg -n \
'location\s*=|location\.href\s*=|location\.assign\(|location\.replace\(|window\.open\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Client-Side Open Redirect
docs.text:
Candidate:

const next =
    new URLSearchParams(
        location.search
    ).get("next");

location.href =
    next;

Flow:

location.search
      |
      v
next
      |
      v
location.href

Determine whether arbitrary external destinations are accepted.

Refer to:

Open Redirect

docs.title: URL Validation
docs.text:
A stronger pattern may use the URL parser:

const target =
    new URL(
        userInput,
        location.origin
    );

if (
    target.origin ===
    location.origin
) {
    location.assign(
        target.href
    );
}

The correct policy depends on the application.

Avoid fragile checks such as:

url.startsWith(
    "https://trusted.example"
);

without understanding URL parsing and origin boundaries.

docs.title: javascript: URLs
docs.text:
Review URL assignment where attacker-controlled values can reach navigation or executable URL contexts.

Search:

rg -n \
'\.href\s*=|setAttribute\(["'\'']href|window\.open\(|location\.' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

The browser context and applicable platform protections must be validated dynamically.

docs.title: Dynamic Script Loading
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'createElement\(["'\'']script["'\'']\)|script\.src|appendChild\(.*script|import\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Candidate:

const script =
    document.createElement(
        "script"
    );

script.src =
    userInput;

document.head.appendChild(
    script
);

Review whether attackers can influence script origins.

docs.title: Dynamic import()
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'import\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Dynamic imports are not automatically vulnerable.

Determine whether untrusted input influences module selection or URL resolution.

docs.title: iframe Sources
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'iframe|\.src\s*=|srcdoc' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,html}' \
.

High-value sinks include:

iframe.src
iframe.srcdoc

docs.title: srcdoc
docs.text:
Candidate:

iframe.srcdoc =
    userInput;

This creates an HTML parsing context.

Review attacker control and sandboxing.

docs.title: postMessage
docs.text:
Cross-window messaging is a major source of client-side vulnerabilities.

Search:

rg -n \
'postMessage\(|addEventListener\(["'\'']message|onmessage\s*=' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Sending Messages
docs.text:
Example:

targetWindow.postMessage(
    data,
    targetOrigin
);

Review the target origin.

docs.title: Wildcard Target Origin
docs.text:
Candidate:

targetWindow.postMessage(
    sensitiveData,
    "*"
);

This may expose information to unintended origins depending on window relationships and application flow.

Do not report every wildcard message without establishing impact.

docs.title: Receiving Messages
docs.text:
Example:

window.addEventListener(
    "message",
    event => {
        ...
    }
);

The primary questions are:

Is event.origin validated?
Is event.source validated where necessary?
What data is trusted?
Which sinks receive event.data?

docs.title: Missing Origin Validation
docs.text:
Candidate:

window.addEventListener(
    "message",
    event => {
        document.querySelector(
            "#result"
        ).innerHTML =
            event.data;
    }
);

Flow:

postMessage
    |
    v
event.data
    |
    v
innerHTML

docs.title: Origin Validation
docs.text:
A strict comparison is usually preferable:

if (
    event.origin !==
    "https://trusted.example"
) {
    return;
}

Avoid fragile patterns such as:

event.origin.includes(
    "trusted.example"
);

or:

event.origin.endsWith(
    "trusted.example"
);

unless the exact domain policy has been carefully implemented.

docs.title: Regex Origin Checks
docs.text:
Candidate:

if (
    /trusted\.example/.test(
        event.origin
    )
) {
    ...
}

Review regex boundaries carefully.

docs.title: event.source
docs.text:
For some communication flows, validating only the origin may not be sufficient.

Review whether the application expects a particular:

Window
iframe
popup
parent
opener

and whether event.source should also be checked.

docs.title: postMessage Source-to-Sink
docs.text:
Untrusted Window
      |
      v
postMessage()
      |
      v
message event
      |
      v
event.data
      |
      v
innerHTML

or:

event.data
    |
    v
location.href

or:

event.data
    |
    v
eval()

Prioritise these flows.

docs.title: DOM Clobbering
docs.text:
DOM clobbering occurs when HTML elements alter how JavaScript resolves expected properties or global variables.

This is particularly relevant when JavaScript relies on named DOM elements.

Example HTML:

<form id="config">
</form>

JavaScript may reference:

window.config

because named elements can interact with browser property resolution.

docs.title: DOM Clobbering Search
docs.text:
Look for implicit globals:

rg -n \
'window\[[^]]+\]|window\.[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_$]*|document\.[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_$]*' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Manual review is required because most matches are normal.

docs.title: Named Elements
docs.text:
Search HTML:

rg -n \
'(id|name)=["'\''][^"'\'']+' \
--glob '*.{html,htm}' \
.

Review JavaScript that assumes global variables correspond to application objects.

docs.title: Defensive Pattern
docs.text:
Prefer explicit lookups:

const config =
    document.getElementById(
        "config"
    );

over relying on named properties appearing on window.

docs.title: DOM Clobbering Impact
docs.text:
Clobbering becomes security-relevant when the modified value reaches sinks such as:

script.src
location
iframe.src
innerHTML
dynamic imports
URL construction
security decisions

Do not report DOM clobbering without establishing an attacker-controlled HTML primitive and meaningful impact.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Prototype pollution is important in both server-side and client-side JavaScript.

Potential sources:

URL parameters
JSON
postMessage
API responses
localStorage

Potential operations:

Object.assign()
deep merge
recursive setters
dynamic properties

Search:

rg -n \
'Object\.assign\(|merge\(|mergeWith\(|defaultsDeep\(|set\(|setWith\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Dynamic Property Assignment
docs.text:
Candidate:

object[
    key
] =
    value;

Search:

rg -n \
'\[[A-Za-z0-9_.$]+\]\s*=' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review whether attacker-controlled keys can include:

__proto__
constructor
prototype

docs.title: Recursive Property Assignment
docs.text:
Candidate:

function setValue(
    object,
    path,
    value
) {
    ...
}

Search for utility functions that recursively create object properties.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution Impact
docs.text:
Pollution itself is only part of the analysis.

Trace polluted properties into gadgets such as:

innerHTML
script.src
iframe.src
fetch options
jQuery configuration
authorisation-like client logic
sanitiser configuration

Refer to:

Prototype Pollution

docs.title: Object Spread
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\.\.\.[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_.$]*' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Object spread is not automatically prototype pollution.

Understand the exact language semantics and data flow before reporting.

docs.title: jQuery
docs.text:
Legacy and modern applications may use jQuery.

Search:

rg -n \
'\$\(|jQuery\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: jQuery HTML Sinks
docs.text:
High-value operations include:

.html()
.append()
.prepend()
.before()
.after()
.replaceWith()

Search:

rg -n \
'\.(html|append|prepend|before|after|replaceWith)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Context and jQuery version matter.

docs.title: jQuery Selector Inputs
docs.text:
Review attacker-controlled input entering $().

The behaviour depends on:

Input format
jQuery version
Browser behaviour
Context

Do not classify every dynamic selector as XSS.

docs.title: React
docs.text:
React applications generally escape values inserted through JSX expressions.

Example:

<div>
    {username}
</div>

This is different from inserting raw HTML.

docs.title: dangerouslySetInnerHTML
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'dangerouslySetInnerHTML' \
--glob '*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Example:

<div
    dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{
        __html:
            userContent
    }}
/>

Trace the source of userContent.

docs.title: React URL Handling
docs.text:
Review attacker-controlled values used in:

href
src
formAction
redirects
window.location

Do not assume React's text escaping makes every URL context safe.

docs.title: React Client-Side Authorisation
docs.text:
Candidate:

{
    user.role === "admin" &&
        <AdminPanel />
}

This may correctly control the UI.

It must not be the only control protecting server-side administrative functionality.

docs.title: Angular
docs.text:
Angular templates provide contextual output encoding and sanitisation mechanisms.

Review explicit bypasses.

Search:

rg -n \
'bypassSecurityTrust|DomSanitizer|innerHTML' \
--glob '*.{js,ts,html}' \
.

docs.title: Angular DomSanitizer
docs.text:
High-value methods include:

bypassSecurityTrustHtml
bypassSecurityTrustScript
bypassSecurityTrustUrl
bypassSecurityTrustResourceUrl
bypassSecurityTrustStyle

Search:

rg -n \
'bypassSecurityTrust(Html|Script|Url|ResourceUrl|Style)' \
--glob '*.{js,ts}' \
.

These APIs do not automatically create vulnerabilities.

Determine whether attacker-controlled values are being explicitly marked trusted.

docs.title: Angular innerHTML
docs.text:
Example:

<div
    [innerHTML]="content">
</div>

Angular may sanitise HTML depending on the context.

Review:

Framework version
Sanitisation
DomSanitizer bypasses
Data source

docs.title: Vue
docs.text:
Vue normally escapes interpolation:

<div>
    {{ username }}
</div>

Review:

v-html
dynamic URLs
runtime templates

Search:

rg -n \
'v-html|innerHTML' \
--glob '*.{vue,js,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Vue v-html
docs.text:
Candidate:

<div
    v-html="userContent">
</div>

Trace the source of userContent.

docs.title: Svelte
docs.text:
Review Svelte raw HTML:

{@html ...}

Search:

rg -n \
'\{@html' \
--glob '*.{svelte,js,ts}' \
.

Example:

{@html content}

Trace whether content is attacker-controlled and appropriately sanitised.

docs.title: Sanitisation
docs.text:
One of the most common HTML sanitisation libraries is DOMPurify.

Search:

rg -n \
'DOMPurify|sanitize\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: DOMPurify
docs.text:
Example:

const clean =
    DOMPurify.sanitize(
        dirty
    );

element.innerHTML =
    clean;

This can be an appropriate pattern for applications that intentionally permit limited HTML.

Review:

DOMPurify version
Configuration
Allowed tags
Allowed attributes
Hooks
Subsequent transformations

docs.title: Sanitisation Mutation
docs.text:
A dangerous design may be:

Untrusted HTML
     |
     v
DOMPurify
     |
     v
Further String Manipulation
     |
     v
innerHTML

Post-sanitisation transformations can potentially invalidate assumptions made by the sanitiser.

Review the complete flow.

docs.title: Custom HTML Sanitisation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'sanitize|escapeHtml|stripTags|allowedTags|allowedAttributes' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Custom sanitisation implementations deserve careful review.

Regex-based HTML sanitisation should receive additional scrutiny.

docs.title: Trusted Types
docs.text:
Trusted Types can reduce DOM XSS exposure by restricting assignments to certain injection sinks.

Search:

rg -n \
'trustedTypes|TrustedHTML|TrustedScript|TrustedScriptURL|require-trusted-types-for|trusted-types' \
.

docs.title: Trusted Types Policy
docs.text:
Example:

const policy =
    trustedTypes.createPolicy(
        "default",
        {
            createHTML:
                input =>
                    DOMPurify.sanitize(
                        input
                    )
        }
    );

Review policy implementations carefully.

A permissive policy can undermine the protection.

docs.title: Permissive Trusted Types
docs.text:
Candidate:

trustedTypes.createPolicy(
    "default",
    {
        createHTML:
            input =>
                input
    }
);

This may effectively convert untrusted strings into trusted HTML without meaningful validation.

docs.title: CSP
docs.text:
Search HTML and configuration:

rg -n -i \
'content-security-policy|script-src|default-src|nonce-|unsafe-inline|unsafe-eval|strict-dynamic|require-trusted-types-for' \
.

CSP is defence in depth.

It should not replace safe source-to-sink handling.

Refer to:

HTTP Security Headers

docs.title: Nonces
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'nonce=' \
--glob '*.{html,htm,js,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review whether nonces are:

Random
Per response
Correctly applied
Not attacker-controlled

docs.title: unsafe-eval
docs.text:
If CSP allows:

'unsafe-eval'

then some CSP restrictions on string-to-code APIs are weakened.

Do not automatically report this as a standalone exploitable vulnerability.

Determine whether dangerous code paths exist.

docs.title: Third-Party JavaScript
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'<script[^>]+src=' \
--glob '*.{html,htm}' \
.

Identify:

CDNs
Analytics
Tag managers
Chat widgets
Payment scripts
Advertising
Monitoring
Support widgets
A/B testing

docs.title: External Script Trust
docs.text:
A third-party script executes with the privileges of the page.

It may access:

DOM
Non-HttpOnly cookies
localStorage
sessionStorage
Page content
JavaScript variables

This makes third-party JavaScript part of the application's browser-side trust boundary.

docs.title: Subresource Integrity
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'integrity=' \
--glob '*.{html,htm}' \
.

Example:

<script
    src="https://cdn.example/library.js"
    integrity="sha384-..."
    crossorigin="anonymous">
</script>

SRI can protect eligible externally hosted static resources against unexpected modification.

It is not appropriate for every dynamically changing third-party script.

Refer to:

Third-Party JavaScript Security

docs.title: Dynamic Third-Party Scripts
docs.text:
Tag managers may dynamically load additional scripts.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'googletagmanager|gtm|analytics|segment|hotjar|intercom|zendesk|script\.src' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,html}' \
.

Map the actual script dependency chain.

docs.title: Client-Side Secrets
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'api[_-]?key|secret|client[_-]?secret|access[_-]?token|private[_-]?key|password|bearer' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,json,map}' \
.

docs.title: Public API Keys
docs.text:
Not every API key found in JavaScript is a secret.

Some services intentionally use public browser-side identifiers.

Determine:

What service uses the key?
What permissions does it grant?
Is it intended to be public?
Is it restricted by origin?
Can it perform privileged operations?
Can it incur cost?

docs.title: Build-Time Environment Variables
docs.text:
Frameworks may intentionally expose selected environment variables to browser bundles.

Examples include framework-specific public variable prefixes.

Search:

rg -n \
'process\.env|import\.meta\.env' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review what values actually reach the browser bundle.

docs.title: Client-Side Authentication
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'login|logout|authenticated|isAuthenticated|currentUser|accessToken|refreshToken|jwt|bearer|session' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Client-Side Authentication State
docs.text:
Example:

if (
    localStorage.getItem(
        "isAdmin"
    ) === "true"
) {
    showAdminPanel();
}

This may be acceptable for UI rendering.

It must not be relied upon by the server as proof of authorisation.

docs.title: Hidden UI Is Not Access Control
docs.text:
Example:

if (
    !user.isAdmin
) {
    adminButton.remove();
}

This hides the interface.

It does not protect:

/admin
/api/admin
GraphQL mutations
WebSocket events

The server must enforce access control.

docs.title: Discover Hidden Endpoints
docs.text:
Client-side JavaScript frequently reveals endpoints that are not visible through normal navigation.

Search:

rg -n \
'["'\'']/api/|["'\'']/admin|["'\'']/internal|["'\'']/debug|["'\'']/graphql|["'\'']/auth' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: URL Extraction
docs.text:
Simple candidate search:

rg -o \
'https?://[^"'\'') ]+' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Also search relative API paths:

rg -o \
'["'\'']/[A-Za-z0-9_./?&=%:{}-]+' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Expect false positives.

Manual review is required.

docs.title: API Method Discovery
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'fetch\(|axios\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)|method\s*:\s*["'\''](GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE)' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Build an endpoint inventory.

docs.title: Client-Side Route Discovery
docs.text:
Single-page applications often define routes.

Search React Router:

rg -n \
'<Route|createBrowserRouter|createHashRouter|useRoutes|path\s*:' \
--glob '*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Angular:

rg -n \
'Routes\s*=|RouterModule\.forRoot|RouterModule\.forChild|path\s*:' \
--glob '*.{ts,js}' \
.

Vue:

rg -n \
'createRouter|routes\s*:|path\s*:' \
--glob '*.{js,ts,vue}' \
.

Client-side routes can reveal hidden functionality but do not prove server-side endpoints are accessible.

docs.title: Client-Side Authorisation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'isAdmin|role|roles|permission|permissions|canAccess|hasPermission|authoriz|authoris|featureFlag' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Use these findings to identify security-sensitive functionality for server-side testing.

docs.title: JWT Handling
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'jwt|decodeJwt|jwtDecode|accessToken|refreshToken|Authorization|Bearer' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: JWT Decode
docs.text:
Client applications often decode JWTs to display user information.

Example:

const claims =
    jwtDecode(token);

This is not necessarily a vulnerability.

The problem occurs when decoded but unverified claims are treated as authoritative by a security boundary that trusts the browser.

docs.title: Token Storage
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'localStorage.*token|sessionStorage.*token|setItem\([^)]*token|getItem\([^)]*token' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review token storage in the application's overall threat model.

Consider:

XSS exposure
Token lifetime
Refresh tokens
Session design
Cookie alternatives
Application architecture

Do not automatically classify localStorage token usage as a vulnerability without context.

docs.title: OAuth and OIDC
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'oauth|oidc|openid|authorization_endpoint|token_endpoint|client_id|redirect_uri|code_verifier|code_challenge|state|nonce' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: OAuth Callback Handling
docs.text:
Review:

Authorization code
State
Nonce
PKCE
Redirect URI
Token storage
Error handling
Account linking

docs.title: State
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\bstate\b' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Do not assume any variable named state is OAuth state.

Trace the OAuth flow.

docs.title: PKCE
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'code_verifier|code_challenge|S256' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Refer to:

OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Security

docs.title: CORS Misconceptions
docs.text:
Client-side JavaScript cannot make an insecure server-side CORS policy safe.

Review JavaScript to understand:

Origins
Credentials
API locations
Authentication mechanisms

but validate CORS primarily through server response behaviour.

Search:

rg -n \
'credentials\s*:|withCredentials|mode\s*:\s*["'\'']cors' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Refer to:

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

docs.title: fetch Credentials
docs.text:
Example:

fetch(
    "/api/profile",
    {
        credentials:
            "include"
    }
);

This indicates cookie credentials may be sent.

Review:

CSRF
CORS
SameSite
Authentication

docs.title: CSRF Tokens
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'csrf|xsrf|x-csrf-token|x-xsrf-token' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Client-side code can reveal how anti-CSRF tokens are obtained and transmitted.

Do not conclude CSRF is absent merely because no token is visible in JavaScript.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'new WebSocket\(|socket\.io|io\(|socket\.emit\(|socket\.on\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: WebSocket URL
docs.text:
Example:

const socket =
    new WebSocket(
        "wss://example.com/socket"
    );

Map:

Endpoint
Authentication
Messages
Event types
Identifiers

docs.title: WebSocket Messages
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\.send\(|\.emit\(|\.on\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Expect many false positives.

Focus on WebSocket objects and Socket.IO instances.

docs.title: Client-Side Message Inventory
docs.text:
Example:

connect
authenticate
join-room
send-message
delete-message
update-profile
admin-action

These can reveal server-side attack surface.

Refer to:

WebSocket Security

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'graphql|gql`|query\s+[A-Za-z]|mutation\s+[A-Za-z]|subscription\s+[A-Za-z]' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,graphql,gql}' \
.

Client bundles frequently contain:

Queries
Mutations
Fragments
Field names
Object types
Endpoints

docs.title: GraphQL Endpoint
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'/graphql|graphqlEndpoint|uri\s*:' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: GraphQL Mutations
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\bmutation\b' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,graphql,gql}' \
.

Mutations reveal high-value operations.

Refer to:

GraphQL API Security

docs.title: gRPC-Web
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'grpc-web|protobuf|proto3|grpc' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Client code may expose:

Service names
RPC methods
Message structures
Endpoints

Refer to:

gRPC Security

docs.title: Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'EventSource\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Example:

const stream =
    new EventSource(
        "/api/events"
    );

Review:

Endpoint
Authentication
Sensitive data
Cross-origin behaviour
DOM sinks receiving event data

docs.title: Service Workers
docs.text:
Find:

find . -type f \( \
-name '*service-worker*.js' \
-o -name 'sw.js' \
-o -name 'serviceWorker.js' \
\) -print

Search:

rg -n \
'serviceWorker\.register|self\.addEventListener\(["'\'']fetch|caches\.open|CacheStorage' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Service Worker Scope
docs.text:
Example:

navigator.serviceWorker.register(
    "/sw.js"
);

Review:

Worker location
Scope
Caching
Fetch interception
Sensitive responses
Update behaviour

docs.title: Service Worker Cache
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'caches\.open|cache\.put|cache\.add|cache\.addAll|caches\.match' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Review whether sensitive authenticated responses are cached inappropriately.

docs.title: Service Worker Fetch Handler
docs.text:
Example:

self.addEventListener(
    "fetch",
    event => {
        ...
    }
);

Trace:

Request
  |
  v
Service Worker
  |
  +-- Network
  |
  +-- Cache

Review cache key and user-context assumptions.

docs.title: Web Workers
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'new Worker\(|new SharedWorker\(|importScripts\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review worker message handling similarly to postMessage.

docs.title: Worker postMessage
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'onmessage|postMessage\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Trace worker-controlled or attacker-influenced messages into sensitive operations.

docs.title: WebAssembly
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'WebAssembly\.|\.wasm' \
.

Client applications may load WebAssembly modules for:

Cryptography
Media processing
Parsing
Games
Security functions
Business logic

Do not assume code moved into WebAssembly becomes a security boundary.

docs.title: Client-Side Cryptography
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'crypto\.subtle|window\.crypto|getRandomValues|randomUUID' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Web Crypto
docs.text:
Example:

crypto.getRandomValues(
    buffer
);

This provides cryptographically strong random values through the browser's cryptographic API.

docs.title: Math.random
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Math\.random\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Do not report every use.

Prioritise uses involving:

Security tokens
Password reset values
MFA values
Session identifiers
Cryptographic nonces

Client-generated security tokens also require broader architectural review because the client itself is attacker-controlled.

docs.title: Client-Side Encryption
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'encrypt|decrypt|crypto\.subtle|AES|RSA|PBKDF2|deriveKey|importKey' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review:

Key source
Key storage
Threat model
Nonce / IV
Algorithm
Authentication
Server trust

Do not assume client-side encryption protects data from a server that controls the JavaScript delivered to the browser.

docs.title: File Handling
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'FileReader|Blob\(|URL\.createObjectURL|showOpenFilePicker|showSaveFilePicker' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review:

File content
Filename
MIME type
Preview rendering
Uploads
Downloads
DOM insertion

docs.title: FileReader
docs.text:
Example:

const reader =
    new FileReader();

reader.onload =
    () => {
        preview.innerHTML =
            reader.result;
    };

The security significance depends on file type and rendering context.

docs.title: Blob URLs
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'URL\.createObjectURL|URL\.revokeObjectURL' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Blob URLs are not automatically dangerous.

Review how their content is generated and where they are used.

docs.title: Dynamic Downloads
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'createElement\(["'\'']a["'\'']\)|\.download\s*=|URL\.createObjectURL' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review whether attacker-controlled content or filenames create security or social-engineering risks.

docs.title: HTML Parsing APIs
docs.text:
Additional APIs deserve review:

DOMParser()
Range.createContextualFragment()

Search:

rg -n \
'DOMParser\(|createContextualFragment\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: DOMParser
docs.text:
Candidate:

const parser =
    new DOMParser();

const doc =
    parser.parseFromString(
        userInput,
        "text/html"
    );

Parsing attacker-controlled HTML is not automatically XSS.

Review what happens to the resulting DOM.

docs.title: createContextualFragment
docs.text:
Candidate:

const fragment =
    range.createContextualFragment(
        userInput
    );

element.appendChild(
    fragment
);

Trace attacker control and browser execution behaviour.

docs.title: setAttribute
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'setAttribute\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

High-value attributes include:

href
src
srcdoc
action
formaction
style

Context matters.

docs.title: Event Handler Attributes
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'setAttribute\(["'\'']on[a-z]+' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Dynamic event-handler creation deserves careful review.

docs.title: Dynamic Event Handlers
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\.onclick\s*=|\.onload\s*=|\.onerror\s*=|addEventListener\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Normal callback registration is not dangerous by itself.

Trace dynamic code or attacker-controlled behaviour.

docs.title: Client-Side Template Systems
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'template|compile|render|handlebars|mustache|nunjucks|lodash\.template' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review whether attacker-controlled input becomes:

Template data

or:

Template source

These have very different security implications.

docs.title: Lodash Templates
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'_\.template\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Trace whether attackers control the template string.

docs.title: Client-Side HTML Injection
docs.text:
Not every unsafe HTML insertion produces JavaScript execution.

A flow may still permit HTML injection:

location.search
      |
      v
innerHTML

with execution constrained by context or browser behaviour.

Determine the actual impact.

Refer to:

HTML Injection

docs.title: CSS Injection
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\.style\.|style\.cssText|setAttribute\(["'\'']style' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Modern browser behaviour limits many historical CSS attack techniques, but attacker-controlled CSS can still have security or UI impact depending on context.

Avoid overclaiming.

docs.title: Client-Side Host Handling
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'location\.(host|hostname|origin)|document\.domain' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review whether host-derived values influence:

API URLs
OAuth redirects
WebSocket endpoints
Security decisions

docs.title: document.domain
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'document\.domain' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Legacy applications may use document.domain to relax same-origin restrictions between related subdomains.

Modern application designs should generally prefer explicit cross-origin communication mechanisms rather than relying on this legacy behaviour.

docs.title: Origin Checks
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'location\.origin|event\.origin|new URL\(.*\)\.origin|\.origin\s*===' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review exact comparisons and parsing.

docs.title: XS-Leaks
docs.text:
Client-side source review can identify features relevant to XS-Leaks, such as:

Cross-origin windows
iframes
window.open
postMessage
resource loading
navigation
timing

Search:

rg -n \
'window\.open\(|iframe|postMessage|performance\.now|PerformanceObserver|onload|onerror' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,html}' \
.

Source review alone usually does not prove an XS-Leak.

Browser behaviour and cross-origin response differences must be tested.

Refer to:

XS-Leaks

docs.title: Client-Side Cache
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'localStorage|sessionStorage|caches\.|CacheStorage|indexedDB' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review whether sensitive data remains after:

Logout
Account switching
Tenant switching
Shared-device use

docs.title: Logout Cleanup
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'localStorage\.clear|sessionStorage\.clear|removeItem\(|logout' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Do not assume all storage must be cleared.

Identify sensitive state specifically.

docs.title: Feature Flags
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'featureFlag|feature_flag|features|isEnabled|enabledFeatures' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Client-side feature flags can reveal hidden functionality.

They should not be treated as access-control mechanisms.

docs.title: Debug Functionality
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'debug|development|devMode|localhost|staging|testMode|console\.log' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review for:

Hidden endpoints
Debug panels
Verbose errors
Test credentials
Internal URLs
Feature switches

docs.title: Environment Detection
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'NODE_ENV|import\.meta\.env|process\.env|location\.hostname' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Client-side environment checks can expose production/development assumptions.

docs.title: Hard-Coded Endpoints
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'https?://|wss?://' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,json}' \
.

Look for:

Internal APIs
Staging systems
Development systems
Cloud storage
GraphQL
WebSockets
Admin APIs
Monitoring

docs.title: Internal IP Addresses
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\b(10\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}|192\.168\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3})\b' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,json,map}' \
.

Internal addresses may constitute information disclosure depending on context and impact.

docs.title: Cloud Storage URLs
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
's3\.amazonaws|blob\.core\.windows|storage\.googleapis|cloudfront|firebaseio|supabase' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,json,map}' \
.

Review access controls separately.

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text: The most valuable part of JavaScript review is connecting sources to sinks.

docs.title: Example - DOM XSS
docs.text:
location.search
      |
      v
URLSearchParams
      |
      v
name
      |
      v
innerHTML

Code:

const params =
    new URLSearchParams(
        location.search
    );

const name =
    params.get("name");

output.innerHTML =
    name;

docs.title: Example - postMessage DOM XSS
docs.text:
Attacker Window
      |
      v
postMessage()
      |
      v
event.data
      |
      v
innerHTML

Code:

window.addEventListener(
    "message",
    event => {
        output.innerHTML =
            event.data;
    }
);

Review origin validation.

docs.title: Example - Client-Side Open Redirect
docs.text:
location.search
      |
      v
next
      |
      v
location.href

Code:

const next =
    new URLSearchParams(
        location.search
    ).get("next");

location.href =
    next;

docs.title: Example - Dynamic Script Loading
docs.text:
location.search
      |
      v
scriptUrl
      |
      v
script.src
      |
      v
Browser Script Execution

docs.title: Example - Stored DOM XSS
docs.text:
Attacker Input
      |
      v
Server Database
      |
      v
API Response
      |
      v
response.json()
      |
      v
innerHTML

docs.title: Example - localStorage DOM XSS
docs.text:
localStorage
      |
      v
getItem()
      |
      v
innerHTML

The key question becomes:

Can an attacker influence the stored value?

docs.title: Example - Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
location.search
      |
      v
Query Parser
      |
      v
Deep Merge
      |
      v
Object.prototype
      |
      v
Security-Relevant Gadget

docs.title: Example - postMessage Redirect
docs.text:
Attacker Window
      |
      v
postMessage()
      |
      v
event.data.url
      |
      v
location.href

docs.title: Example - Client-Side Authorisation Discovery
docs.text:
JavaScript Bundle
      |
      v
isAdmin Check
      |
      v
Hidden Admin Function
      |
      v
/api/admin/users

The client-side check is not necessarily the vulnerability.

The discovered server endpoint should be tested for server-side authorisation.

docs.title: Reverse Sink Analysis
docs.text:
For large JavaScript bundles, start with high-value sinks.

Example:

innerHTML
    ^
    |
renderMessage()
    ^
    |
handleMessage()
    ^
    |
event.data

Search sinks first and trace backwards.

docs.title: Forward Source Analysis
docs.text:
Start from attacker-controlled sources:

location.search
location.hash
postMessage
localStorage
API response

Then trace forward.

Example:

location.hash
     |
     v
parseRoute()
     |
     v
renderContent()
     |
     v
innerHTML

docs.title: High-Value Sink Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write\(|document\.writeln\(|\beval\(|new Function\(|\bFunction\(|setTimeout\(|setInterval\(|location\.href\s*=|location\.assign\(|location\.replace\(|window\.open\(|script\.src|srcdoc|dangerouslySetInnerHTML|v-html|\{@html' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,vue,svelte}' \
.

docs.title: High-Value Source Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'location\.(href|search|hash|pathname)|document\.(URL|documentURI|referrer|cookie)|window\.name|event\.data|localStorage|sessionStorage|postMessage|URLSearchParams' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: DOM XSS Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|document\.writeln|dangerouslySetInnerHTML|v-html|\{@html' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,vue,svelte}' \
.

docs.title: JavaScript Execution Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\beval\(|new Function\(|\bFunction\(|setTimeout\(|setInterval\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Redirect Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'location\s*=|location\.href\s*=|location\.assign\(|location\.replace\(|window\.open\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: postMessage Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'postMessage\(|addEventListener\(["'\'']message|onmessage\s*=|event\.origin|event\.source|event\.data' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Storage Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'localStorage|sessionStorage|indexedDB' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: API Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\bfetch\(|axios\.(get|post|put|patch|delete|request)\(|XMLHttpRequest|/api/' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: WebSocket Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'new WebSocket\(|socket\.emit\(|socket\.on\(|io\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: GraphQL Search
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'/graphql|\bquery\b|\bmutation\b|\bsubscription\b|gql`' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,graphql,gql}' \
.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Object\.assign\(|merge\(|mergeWith\(|defaultsDeep\(|set\(|setWith\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Sanitisation Search
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'DOMPurify|sanitize|escapeHtml|trustedTypes|TrustedHTML|bypassSecurityTrust' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Secret Search
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'api[_-]?key|secret|client[_-]?secret|access[_-]?token|refresh[_-]?token|private[_-]?key|password|bearer' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,json,map}' \
.

docs.title: Endpoint Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'https?://|wss?://|/api/|/graphql|/admin|/internal|/debug' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,json,map}' \
.

docs.title: Broad JavaScript Review Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'location\.(href|search|hash|pathname)|document\.(URL|documentURI|referrer|cookie)|window\.name|event\.data|localStorage|sessionStorage|innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write\(|document\.writeln\(|\beval\(|new Function\(|setTimeout\(|setInterval\(|location\.href\s*=|location\.assign\(|location\.replace\(|window\.open\(|postMessage\(|addEventListener\(["'\'']message|script\.src|srcdoc|dangerouslySetInnerHTML|Object\.assign\(|merge\(|DOMPurify|trustedTypes|\bfetch\(|axios\.|new WebSocket\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Treat this as candidate discovery.

Not vulnerability confirmation.

docs.title: Static Analysis
docs.text:
Useful tools include:

Semgrep
CodeQL
ESLint
Retire.js
Dependency scanners
Custom grep/ripgrep

docs.title: Semgrep
docs.text:
Run:

semgrep scan \
--config auto \
.

Semgrep can help identify:

DOM XSS
Dynamic code execution
Unsafe framework APIs
Potential prototype pollution
Hard-coded secrets
Dangerous URL handling

Manual validation remains necessary.

docs.title: CodeQL
docs.text:
CodeQL supports JavaScript and TypeScript analysis including:

Data flow
Taint tracking
Control flow
Call graphs
Security queries

A useful conceptual query is:

SOURCE
location.search
      |
      v
TAINT FLOW
      |
      v
SINK
innerHTML

or:

SOURCE
event.data
      |
      v
TAINT FLOW
      |
      v
SINK
eval()

CodeQL is especially useful when source and sink are separated across multiple functions or modules.

docs.title: ESLint
docs.text:
Run where appropriate:

npx eslint .

Security-relevant lint rules may identify dangerous patterns, but lint results are not vulnerability proof.

docs.title: Retire.js
docs.text:
Retire.js can identify known vulnerable client-side JavaScript libraries.

Example:

retire

or:

retire --path .

Verify current tool syntax before integrating it into automation.

Dependency findings still require contextual validation.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Client-side source review works well alongside Burp Suite.

A practical workflow is:

Browser
   |
   v
Burp Proxy
   |
   v
Application
   |
   v
JavaScript Files
   |
   v
Source Review
   |
   v
Candidate Source-to-Sink Flow
   |
   v
Burp Repeater / Browser Validation

docs.title: Burp Target
docs.text:
Use:

Target
  -> Site map

Identify:

.js
.map
.json
GraphQL
WebSocket
API

docs.title: Burp Search
docs.text:
Useful search terms include:

innerHTML

docs.title: Burp DOM Invader
docs.text:
Burp's DOM Invader can assist with browser-side testing of DOM-based vulnerabilities.

It is especially useful for investigating:

DOM XSS
postMessage
DOM clobbering
Prototype pollution
Client-side sources and sinks

Use DOM Invader as a testing aid rather than treating every reported source/sink as a confirmed vulnerability.

docs.title: Burp JavaScript Analysis
docs.text:
Burp's JavaScript analysis and site map can help identify:

Endpoints
Parameters
Secrets
WebSockets
API calls
Client-side routes

Correlate dynamic observations with source review.

docs.title: Browser DevTools Workflow
docs.text:
DevTools is extremely useful for client-side source review.

Use:

Sources
Network
Application
Console
Debugger
DOM Inspector

docs.title: Sources Panel
docs.text:
Use the Sources panel to:

Pretty-print JavaScript
Set breakpoints
Inspect call stacks
Trace variables
Inspect event handlers
Review loaded scripts

docs.title: Breakpoint at Sink
docs.text:
For a candidate:

element.innerHTML =
    value;

set a breakpoint and inspect:

value
Call stack
Originating event
URL
Storage
API response

This can help confirm source-to-sink relationships.

docs.title: Event Listener Breakpoints
docs.text:
Browser DevTools can pause on:

Mouse events
Keyboard events
Message events
DOM mutations
XHR/fetch

This can be valuable when tracing complex applications.

docs.title: Network Panel
docs.text:
Use the Network panel to map:

REST APIs
GraphQL
WebSockets
JavaScript
Source maps
Third-party scripts
OAuth redirects

docs.title: Application Panel
docs.text:
Review:

Cookies
localStorage
sessionStorage
IndexedDB
Service Workers
Cache Storage

Correlate stored values with source-code usage.

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text: Once a vulnerability is confirmed, search for other occurrences of the same pattern.

docs.title: DOM XSS Variants
docs.text:
rg -n \
'innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|dangerouslySetInnerHTML|v-html|\{@html' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx,vue,svelte}' \
.

docs.title: postMessage Variants
docs.text:
rg -n \
'addEventListener\(["'\'']message|onmessage\s*=' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

Review every receiver.

docs.title: Redirect Variants
docs.text:
rg -n \
'location\.href\s*=|location\.assign\(|location\.replace\(|window\.open\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution Variants
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Object\.assign\(|merge\(|mergeWith\(|defaultsDeep\(|set\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Dynamic Code Variants
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\beval\(|new Function\(|setTimeout\(|setInterval\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Dynamic Script Variants
docs.text:
rg -n \
'createElement\(["'\'']script["'\'']\)|script\.src|import\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,jsx,ts,tsx}' \
.

docs.title: Compare Similar Components
docs.text:
Example:

SearchResults
    -> textContent

ProfileBiography
    -> DOMPurify + innerHTML

AdminAnnouncement
    -> innerHTML directly

The inconsistent output handling is a strong review signal.

docs.title: Compare Input Channels
docs.text:
The same dangerous sink may receive data from:

URL
postMessage
API
localStorage
WebSocket

Example:

             +-- location.search
             |
             +-- API response
             |
innerHTML <--+-- postMessage
             |
             +-- localStorage

Search every route into the sink.

docs.title: Finding Validation Model
docs.text:
Before reporting:

STATIC MATCH
     |
     v
ATTACKER-CONTROLLED SOURCE?
     |
     +-- No --> Usually informational
     |
     v
REACHABLE DATA FLOW?
     |
     +-- No --> Discard / investigate
     |
     v
DANGEROUS SINK?
     |
     +-- No --> Contextual review
     |
     v
SANITISATION / VALIDATION?
     |
     +-- Effective --> Protected
     |
     v
BROWSER / FRAMEWORK PROTECTION?
     |
     +-- Effective --> Protected
     |
     v
EXPLOITABLE?
     |
     +-- No --> Defence-in-depth / contextual
     |
     v
SECURITY IMPACT?
     |
     v
CONFIRMED FINDING

docs.title: Example Finding - DOM XSS
docs.text:
Title:
DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting Through URL Parameter

Source:
location.search

Parameter:
name

Data Flow:

location.search
      |
      v
URLSearchParams
      |
      v
name
      |
      v
innerHTML

Security Control:
No effective HTML sanitisation or safe text sink was identified.

Impact:
An attacker able to influence the URL may be able to cause attacker-controlled content to be interpreted as HTML in the victim's browser.

Recommendation:
Use textContent when HTML rendering is unnecessary. If limited HTML is required, apply a well-maintained allowlist-based HTML sanitiser before insertion into an HTML parsing sink.

docs.title: Example Finding - postMessage Origin Validation
docs.text:
Title:
Cross-Origin Message Handler Does Not Validate Message Origin

Source:
window message event

Data Flow:

External Window
      |
      v
postMessage()
      |
      v
event.data
      |
      v
Sensitive Browser Action

Security Control:
The message handler does not verify event.origin before trusting the message.

Recommendation:
Validate event.origin using an exact allowlist of expected origins and validate event.source where the communication flow expects a specific window.

docs.title: Example Finding - Client-Side Open Redirect
docs.text:
Title:
Client-Side Open Redirect Through next Parameter

Source:
location.search

Data Flow:

location.search
      |
      v
next
      |
      v
location.href

Security Control:
No effective destination restriction was identified.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to construct a trusted application URL that redirects victims to an external destination.

Recommendation:
Use server-controlled redirect identifiers or validate the parsed destination against an explicit allowlist of permitted origins or paths.

docs.title: Example Finding - Dynamic Script Loading
docs.text:
Title:
Attacker-Controlled URL Used for Dynamic Script Loading

Source:
location.search

Data Flow:

location.search
      |
      v
scriptUrl
      |
      v
script.src
      |
      v
document.head.appendChild()
      |
      v
Browser Script Execution

Security Control:
No effective restriction was identified on the script origin.

Impact:
If an attacker can control the script URL, arbitrary JavaScript may execute in the application's origin.

Recommendation:
Do not construct script locations from attacker-controlled input. Use server-controlled script identifiers mapped to explicitly trusted resources.

docs.title: Example Finding - Stored DOM XSS
docs.text:
Title:
Stored DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting in Profile Biography

Source:
API response containing stored biography

Data Flow:

Stored Biography
      |
      v
GET /api/profile
      |
      v
response.json()
      |
      v
data.biography
      |
      v
innerHTML

Security Control:
The stored value is inserted into an HTML parsing sink without effective sanitisation.

Recommendation:
Use textContent for plain-text biographies. If HTML is a required feature, sanitise the content using a well-maintained allowlist-based HTML sanitiser.

docs.title: Example Finding - Client-Side Authorisation Is Not Server Enforcement
docs.text:
Title:
Administrative Functionality Identified Through Client-Side Role Check

Observation:

if (user.role === "admin") {
    showAdminPanel();
}

The JavaScript bundle references:

POST /api/admin/users/create

Security Assessment:
The client-side role check controls interface visibility but does not establish whether the API itself enforces authorisation.

Required Validation:
Test the server-side endpoint using an authenticated non-administrative account within the authorised test environment.

Reporting:
Do not report broken access control unless the server-side operation can actually be performed without the required permission.

docs.title: Example Finding - Prototype Pollution Candidate
docs.text:
Title:
Potential Prototype Pollution Through Recursive Object Merge

Source:
URL query parameters

Data Flow:

location.search
      |
      v
Query Parser
      |
      v
Recursive Merge
      |
      v
Application Configuration

Review:
Determine whether special property names can modify object prototypes.

Impact Validation:
Identify whether polluted properties influence a security-sensitive gadget.

Reporting:
Do not report a confirmed prototype pollution vulnerability solely from the presence of a recursive merge function.

docs.title: Every innerHTML Is XSS
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Determine:

Data source
Attacker control
Sanitisation
Framework behaviour
HTML context
Reachability

docs.title: Every location.href Assignment Is Open Redirect
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Determine whether the attacker controls the destination and whether external navigation is permitted.

docs.title: Every postMessage Handler Is Vulnerable
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Review:

event.origin
event.source
event.data
Sink
Impact

docs.title: Every postMessage("*") Is a Vulnerability
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Determine whether sensitive information can reach an unintended recipient.

docs.title: Every localStorage Value Is a Vulnerability
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Determine:

What is stored?
Who can influence it?
Where is it used?
What is the threat model?

docs.title: JWT in localStorage Automatically Means Vulnerability
docs.text:
Incorrect.

It can increase exposure to successful XSS, but the overall security assessment depends on architecture, token lifetime, refresh-token handling and other controls.

docs.title: Every API Key in JavaScript Is a Secret
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Some browser-side API identifiers are intentionally public.

Determine privileges and intended exposure.

docs.title: Every Source Map Is a Vulnerability
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Assess whether the map exposes security-sensitive information that materially changes the attack surface.

docs.title: Every Object.assign Is Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Trace attacker-controlled keys and actual prototype mutation behaviour.

docs.title: Every React JSX Value Is XSS
docs.text:
Incorrect.

React normally escapes values rendered through JSX expressions.

Review explicit raw HTML mechanisms such as:

dangerouslySetInnerHTML

docs.title: Every Angular innerHTML Is XSS
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Angular applies framework sanitisation in relevant contexts.

Review bypass APIs and actual data flow.

docs.title: Every Vue Interpolation Is XSS
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Normal Vue interpolation is escaped.

Review:

v-html

and other raw HTML paths.

docs.title: Every Svelte Variable Is XSS
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Review explicit raw HTML:

{@html ...}

docs.title: CSP Means XSS Is Impossible
docs.text:
Incorrect.

CSP is defence in depth.

Safe source-to-sink handling remains necessary.

docs.title: DOMPurify Means XSS Is Impossible
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Review:

Version
Configuration
Hooks
Post-sanitisation mutation
Destination context

docs.title: Client-Side Validation Means Input Is Safe
docs.text:
Incorrect.

The browser is controlled by the user.

Server-side validation remains necessary.

docs.title: Hidden Button Means Protected Function
docs.text:
Incorrect.

UI visibility is not server-side authorisation.

docs.title: Final Client-Side JavaScript Review Model
docs.text:
CLIENT-SIDE JAVASCRIPT
                              |
                              v
                            SOURCE
                              |
        +---------------------+----------------------+
        |                     |                      |
        v                     v                      v
      URL                postMessage              Storage
        |                     |                      |
        |                     |                      |
        +----------+----------+----------+-----------+
                   |                     |
                   v                     v
               API Data             DOM Data
                   |                     |
                   +----------+----------+
                              |
                              v
                       TRANSFORMATIONS
                              |
            +-----------------+------------------+
            |                 |                  |
            v                 v                  v
         Parsing          Validation         Sanitisation
            |                 |                  |
            +-----------------+------------------+
                              |
                              v
                             SINK
                              |
      +-------------+---------+---------+--------------+
      |             |                   |              |
      v             v                   v              v
     HTML         JavaScript          Navigation      Script
      |             |                   |              |
      v             v                   v              v
 innerHTML        eval()          location.href     script.src
      |             |                   |              |
      +-------------+---------+---------+--------------+
                              |
                              v
                        SECURITY IMPACT

A second useful model is:

URL / Storage / Message / API
             |
             v
        JavaScript
             |
     +-------+-------+
     |               |
     v               v
Sanitisation     No Sanitisation
     |               |
     v               v
   Sink            Sink
     |               |
     v               v
Browser Behaviour / Framework Protection
             |
             v
       Exploitability
             |
             v
           Impact

The core question remains:

Can attacker-controlled browser data reach a security-sensitive
sink without an effective protection?

Evaluate:

Source
+
Transformations
+
Framework behaviour
+
Sanitisation
+
Sink
+
Browser behaviour
+
Reachability
+
Exploitability
+
Impact

Only then classify the candidate as a confirmed vulnerability.

docs.title: Source Code Review Methodology
docs.text:
Source code review is the systematic examination of an application's source code to identify security weaknesses that may not be visible through black-box testing alone.

Unlike traditional penetration testing, where the application is primarily analysed from the outside, source code review allows the reviewer to examine how the application actually processes data internally.

This makes it possible to answer questions such as:

Where are the application entry points?

Where does user-controlled input enter the application?

Where is authentication implemented?

Where is authorisation enforced?

Where is input validated?

Where are database queries constructed?

Where are operating system commands executed?

Where are files accessed?

Where are outbound HTTP requests made?

Where are templates rendered?

Where are objects deserialised?

Where are secrets stored?

Where are security-sensitive operations performed?

Can attacker-controlled data reach those operations?

The fundamental methodology is:

SOURCE
  |
  v
USER-CONTROLLED INPUT
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATIONS
  |
  +-- validation
  +-- parsing
  +-- decoding
  +-- normalisation
  +-- sanitisation
  +-- business logic
  +-- authorisation
  |
  v
SINK
  |
  v
SECURITY-SENSITIVE OPERATION

Examples:

HTTP Parameter
     |
     v
Controller
     |
     v
Service
     |
     v
Repository
     |
     v
SQL Query

or:

JSON Body
    |
    v
API Controller
    |
    v
URL Builder
    |
    v
HTTP Client
    |
    v
External Request

or:

Path Parameter
     |
     v
Controller
     |
     v
Database Lookup
     |
     v
Object Returned

The final example may represent an IDOR / BOLA vulnerability if ownership or authorisation is not verified.

The core principle is:

grep match
    !=
vulnerability

Similarly:

Sink found
    !=
Vulnerability found

A candidate normally becomes a confirmed vulnerability only when the reviewer establishes:

Attacker-controlled source
        +
Reachable data flow
        +
Security-sensitive sink
        +
Missing or ineffective security control
        +
Meaningful security impact

Authorised Security Testing

Perform source code review only against applications, repositories and environments for which you have explicit authorisation. Dynamic validation should be performed only within the agreed scope and rules of engagement.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
A security-focused source code review should attempt to understand:

Application architecture
Attack surface
Entry points
Trust boundaries
Authentication
Authorisation
Session management
Input validation
Data flows
Dangerous sinks
Business logic
External integrations
Secrets
Dependencies
Security configuration
Logging
Error handling
Cryptography
Concurrency
Background processing

The objective is not simply to search for dangerous functions.

The objective is to understand:

How does attacker-controlled data move through the application?

docs.title: Source Code Review Workflow
docs.text:
A practical review can follow this process:

1. Prepare the review environment

2. Identify the technology stack

3. Understand the project structure

4. Build the application where possible

5. Identify configuration

6. Identify routes and entry points

7. Identify authentication

8. Identify authorisation

9. Identify user-controlled input

10. Identify validation and sanitisation

11. Identify dangerous sinks

12. Trace sources to sinks

13. Trace sinks back to sources

14. Identify trust boundaries

15. Review business logic

16. Review security controls

17. Review secrets and configuration

18. Review dependencies

19. Review background processing

20. Review external integrations

21. Run static-analysis tools

22. Perform variant analysis

23. Dynamically validate candidates

24. Document evidence

25. Report confirmed findings

This can be visualised as:

Repository
    |
    v
Technology Identification
    |
    v
Architecture Mapping
    |
    v
Attack Surface Mapping
    |
    v
Entry Point Discovery
    |
    v
Source Discovery
    |
    v
Sink Discovery
    |
    v
Data Flow Analysis
    |
    v
Security Control Analysis
    |
    v
Exploitability Validation
    |
    v
Variant Analysis
    |
    v
Reporting

docs.title: Review Types
docs.text: Source code review can generally be performed in two ways.

docs.title: Baseline Review
docs.text:
A baseline review examines the application broadly.

Useful when:

Reviewing a new application
Performing a full security assessment
Reviewing a legacy application
Reviewing an unfamiliar codebase
Establishing an initial security baseline

The reviewer attempts to understand the entire application architecture and attack surface.

docs.title: Diff-Based Review
docs.text:
A diff-based review focuses on changes.

Examples:

Pull request
Commit
Feature branch
Release
Security patch
Hotfix

Useful commands:

git diff

Compare branches:

git diff main..feature

Changed files:

git diff --name-only main..feature

Security review then concentrates on:

New entry points
Changed authentication
Changed authorisation
New sinks
Changed validation
New dependencies
New external integrations
Changed configuration

docs.title: Hybrid Review
docs.text:
A hybrid approach combines:

Baseline understanding
        +
Diff-focused investigation

This is often useful during continuous security review.

docs.title: Visual Studio Code as the Review IDE
docs.text:
Visual Studio Code is a useful IDE for source code review because it provides:

Repository-wide search
Regex search
Go to Definition
Go to References
Call hierarchy
Symbol navigation
Integrated terminal
Git integration
Debugging
Extensions
Multi-language support

The IDE does not replace manual analysis.

It makes navigation and data-flow tracing significantly easier.

docs.title: Open the Repository in Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
From a terminal:

code .

Or:

code /path/to/project

Before reviewing individual files, inspect the repository structure.

docs.title: Initial Repository View
docs.text:
The first objective is not finding vulnerabilities.

The first objective is answering:

What am I looking at?

Look for:

src/
app/
server/
client/
backend/
frontend/
controllers/
routes/
services/
repositories/
models/
entities/
templates/
static/
config/
middleware/
filters/

Also identify build and dependency files.

docs.title: VS Code Explorer
docs.text:
Use the Explorer panel to understand application organisation.

Do not immediately open random files.

Build a mental model:

Application
│
├── Controllers
│
├── Services
│
├── Repositories
│
├── Models
│
├── Security
│
├── Configuration
│
├── Templates
│
└── Static Content

For example:

src/
└── main/
    ├── java/
    │   └── com/example/app/
    │       ├── controller/
    │       ├── service/
    │       ├── repository/
    │       ├── security/
    │       └── model/
    │
    └── resources/
        ├── application.yml
        ├── templates/
        └── static/

This immediately tells the reviewer where different security controls are likely to exist.

docs.text:
One of the most useful source review features is repository-wide search.

Use:

Ctrl + Shift + F

on Windows/Linux.

This searches across the repository.

Examples:

login
password
executeQuery
Process.Start
Runtime.exec
innerHTML
HttpClient
eval(

docs.title: Enable Regex Search
docs.text:
VS Code search supports regular expressions.

Enable the:

.*

button in the Search panel.

Example:

exec\(|system\(|shell_exec\(

Another example:

innerHTML|outerHTML|document\.write

Another:

SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE

Regex searching is extremely useful for sink discovery.

docs.title: Search File Types
docs.text:

Example:

*.java

or:

*.cs

or:

*.php

or:

*.py

or:

*.js

docs.text:
Example:

src/**/*.java

This limits the search scope.

docs.title: Exclude Patterns
docs.text:
Exclude directories such as:

node_modules
vendor
dist
build
target
bin
obj

Example VS Code exclude pattern:

**/node_modules/**,**/vendor/**,**/dist/**,**/build/**,**/target/**

This reduces noise.

docs.title: VS Code Go to Definition
docs.text:
When a function is called:

userService.getUser(id);

use:

F12

or:

Right-click
    ->
Go to Definition

This allows the reviewer to follow the implementation.

Example:

Controller
    |
    v
userService.getUser()
    |
    v
UserService.getUser()

docs.text:

Alt + F12

to inspect a function without leaving the current file.

This is useful during data-flow analysis.

docs.title: Go to References
docs.text:
Place the cursor on a function or variable and use:

Shift + F12

This identifies where the symbol is used.

Example:

findUser()
    |
    +-- UserController
    |
    +-- AdminController
    |
    +-- PasswordResetService
    |
    +-- ExportService

This is extremely useful for variant analysis.

docs.title: Find All References
docs.text:
Suppose a security-sensitive method exists:

Finding all references may reveal:

Admin endpoint
Background job
API endpoint
Debug endpoint
Internal service

One vulnerable call site may indicate additional variants.

docs.title: Call Hierarchy
docs.text:
For supported languages and language servers, VS Code can display call relationships.

Use:

Right-click
    ->
Show Call Hierarchy

Then inspect:

Incoming Calls
Outgoing Calls

Conceptually:

HTTP Controller
      |
      v
processRequest()
      |
      v
generateReport()
      |
      v
runConverter()
      |
      v
ProcessBuilder

Call hierarchy can make source-to-sink tracing significantly faster.

docs.title: Outline and Symbols
docs.text:
VS Code can display symbols such as:

Classes
Methods
Functions
Properties
Interfaces

Use:

Ctrl + Shift + O

to navigate symbols within the current file.

Use:

Ctrl + T

to search workspace symbols.

This can quickly locate:

LoginController
SecurityConfig
AuthService
UserRepository

docs.text:
Open the VS Code terminal:

Ctrl + `

This allows commands such as:

rg
git
semgrep
codeql
mvn

dotnet
npm
python

to be run without leaving the review environment.

docs.title: Recommended Review Layout
docs.text:
A useful VS Code layout is:

+-------------------+-----------------------------+
|                   |                             |
| Explorer          | Source Code                 |
|                   |                             |
| Search            | Controller / Service        |
|                   |                             |
+-------------------+-----------------------------+
|                                                 |
| Integrated Terminal                             |
|                                                 |
+-------------------------------------------------+

During tracing:

Left editor:
Controller

Right editor:
Service / Repository

Bottom:
ripgrep / Git / static analysis

Split editors can make multi-file data flow easier to understand.

docs.title: Stage 1 - Understand the Architecture
docs.text:
Before searching for vulnerabilities, identify:

Application components
Framework
Database
Authentication mechanism
Session mechanism
External services
Message queues
Caches
File storage
Background jobs
APIs

Create a simple architecture model.

Example:

Browser
   |
   v
Reverse Proxy
   |
   v
Web Application
   |
   +-----------> Database
   |
   +-----------> Redis
   |
   +-----------> File Storage
   |
   +-----------> External API
   |
   +-----------> Message Queue

docs.title: Identify Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
A trust boundary exists whenever data moves between components with different trust levels.

Example:

Internet
   |
   | Trust Boundary
   v
Web Application
   |
   | Trust Boundary
   v
Database

Another:

Web Application
      |
      | Trust Boundary
      v
Third-Party API

Another:

User
  |
  v
Uploaded File
  |
  v
Background Processor

Trust boundaries are important because validation assumptions frequently fail at these transitions.

docs.title: Stage 2 - Build the Attack Surface
docs.text:
Create an inventory of externally reachable functionality.

Look for:

HTTP routes
API endpoints
GraphQL
gRPC
WebSockets
File uploads
Webhooks
OAuth callbacks
SAML endpoints
Password reset
Authentication
Admin interfaces
Debug endpoints
Background job triggers
Message consumers
