@RequestMapping
@GetMapping
@PostMapping
@PutMapping
@PatchMapping
@DeleteMapping

docs.title: Django
docs.text:
path(
re_path(

docs.title: Flask
docs.text:
@app.route
@blueprint.route

docs.title: Express
docs.text:
app.get(
app.post(
app.put(
app.patch(
app.delete(

router.get(
router.post(

docs.title: Route Inventory
docs.text:
Create a table during the review:

Method Route Handler Authentication Authorisation Input GET /api/users/{id} getUser() Yes Review Path POST /api/users createUser() Yes Admin JSON POST /upload upload() Yes User File GET /redirect redirect() No N/A Query

This immediately exposes suspicious areas.

docs.title: Stage 3 - Identify Sources
docs.text:
A source is where potentially attacker-controlled data enters the program.

Common sources include:

HTTP query parameters
Path parameters
POST bodies
JSON
XML
Headers
Cookies
File uploads
WebSocket messages
GraphQL arguments
gRPC messages
Message queues
Webhooks
Database data
Environment variables
Configuration

Not every source is directly attacker-controlled.

The reviewer must determine the trust boundary.

docs.title: HTTP Sources
docs.text:
Conceptually:

GET /users?id=123
             |
             v
            id

The parameter:

id

becomes a source.

docs.title: Headers as Sources
docs.text:
Examples:

Host
X-Forwarded-Host
X-Forwarded-For
User-Agent
Referer
Origin
Custom headers

Headers should not automatically be considered trusted.

docs.title: Cookies as Sources
docs.text: Cookies are also client-controlled from the server's perspective unless integrity protection or another security mechanism changes the trust model.

docs.title: File Upload Sources
docs.text:
Uploaded files contain multiple attacker-controlled properties:

Filename
Content
MIME type
Size
Extension
Metadata
Archive contents

docs.title: Database Data as a Source
docs.text:
A common mistake is assuming:

Database data = trusted

This is not always true.

Example:

Attacker Input
     |
     v
Database
     |
     v
Background Job
     |
     v
Command Execution

This is a second-order data flow.

docs.title: Stage 4 - Identify Sinks
docs.text:
A sink is a security-sensitive operation.

High-value categories include:

Database queries
Operating system commands
HTML output
Template rendering
File operations
Network requests
Deserialisation
XML parsing
Dynamic code execution
Redirects
Logging
Cryptographic operations
Authentication decisions
Authorisation decisions

docs.title: SQL Sinks
docs.text:
Examples:

executeQuery
executeUpdate
SqlCommand
FromSqlRaw
createNativeQuery
mysqli_query
PDO::query
cursor.execute

The existence of one of these functions does not prove SQL injection.

The query construction must be examined.

docs.title: Command Execution Sinks
docs.text:
Examples:

Runtime.exec
ProcessBuilder
Process.Start
system
exec
shell_exec
subprocess
os.system
child_process.exec

docs.title: File Sinks
docs.text:
Examples:

File.Open
File.ReadAllText
Files.readString
open()
fopen()
fs.readFile

Potential vulnerabilities include:

Path traversal
Arbitrary file read
Arbitrary file write
Unsafe archive extraction
File inclusion

docs.title: Network Sinks
docs.text:
Examples:

HttpClient
WebClient
RestClient
WebClient
requests
urllib
curl
axios
fetch

Potential issue:

SSRF

docs.title: HTML Sinks
docs.text:
Examples:

innerHTML
outerHTML
document.write
th:utext
Raw
Html.Raw

Potential issue:

XSS
HTML Injection

docs.title: Deserialisation Sinks
docs.text:
Examples:

ObjectInputStream
BinaryFormatter
pickle.loads
unserialize

The exact risk depends on:

Format
Library
Configuration
Trust boundary
Available types
Application version

docs.title: Stage 5 - Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text:
Source-to-sink analysis follows attacker-controlled data forward through the application.

Example:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
request.getParameter("name")
     |
     v
name
     |
     v
buildQuery(name)
     |
     v
executeQuery()

The reviewer should ask at every step:

Is the value still attacker-controlled?

Was it validated?

Was it normalised?

Was it encoded?

Was it parameterised?

Was authorisation performed?

Did the data change context?

docs.title: Example - SQL Injection Analysis
docs.text:
Candidate:

String id =
    request.getParameter("id");

String sql =
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = "
    + id;

statement.executeQuery(sql);

Trace:

request.getParameter("id")
          |
          v
         id
          |
          v
String Concatenation
          |
          v
         sql
          |
          v
executeQuery()

Candidate vulnerability:

SQL Injection

docs.title: Safe SQL Comparison
docs.text:
Example:

PreparedStatement statement =
    connection.prepareStatement(
        "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"
    );

statement.setString(
    1,
    id
);

The same source exists:

id

and the same database operation exists.

But the security control changes the analysis:

Attacker Input
      |
      v
Prepared Statement Parameter
      |
      v
SQL Engine

docs.title: Stage 6 - Reverse Sink Analysis
docs.text:
For large applications, starting from every source may be inefficient.

Instead:

Find dangerous sink
        |
        v
Trace backwards
        |
        v
Determine data origin

Example:

ProcessBuilder
      ^
      |
executeCommand()
      ^
      |
generateReport()
      ^
      |
ReportController
      ^
      |
HTTP Parameter

This is called reverse sink analysis.

docs.title: Why Reverse Sink Analysis Works
docs.text:
Applications may contain:

Thousands of inputs

but only:

A small number of command execution functions
A small number of raw SQL functions
A small number of deserialisation functions
A small number of outbound HTTP clients

Searching sinks first can therefore be very efficient.

docs.title: Recommended Combination
docs.text:
Use both:

SOURCE -> SINK

and:

SINK -> SOURCE

The combination provides better coverage.

docs.title: Stage 7 - Follow Transformations
docs.text:
Data rarely moves directly from source to sink.

Example:

Request
  |
  v
Controller
  |
  v
DTO
  |
  v
Service
  |
  v
Utility
  |
  v
Repository
  |
  v
Database

Each transformation must be reviewed.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
@GetMapping("/search")
public ResponseEntity<?> search(
    @RequestParam String q
) {
    return service.search(q);
}

Then:

public List<User> search(
    String q
) {
    String filter =
        prepareFilter(q);

    return repository.search(
        filter
    );
}

Then:

private String prepareFilter(
    String input
) {
    return input.trim();
}

Then:

entityManager
    .createNativeQuery(
        "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '"
        + filter
        + "'"
    );

trim() does not remove attacker control.

Flow:

q
 |
 v
trim()
 |
 v
filter
 |
 v
SQL concatenation

docs.title: Sanitisation Must Match the Sink
docs.text:
A critical principle:

Sanitisation is context-specific.

Examples:

HTML escaping
    !=
SQL parameterisation

URL validation
    !=
Command argument safety

SQL escaping
    !=
LDAP escaping

A transformation that is safe for one sink may be irrelevant for another.

docs.title: Stage 8 - Authentication Review
docs.text:
Locate:

Login
Logout
Session creation
Token creation
Password validation
Identity providers
JWT validation
OAuth
OIDC
SAML
MFA

Search:

rg -n -i \
'login|logout|authenticate|authentication|password|jwt|oauth|oidc|saml|mfa|totp' \
.

docs.title: Authentication Flow
docs.text:
Map:

Credentials
    |
    v
Login Endpoint
    |
    v
Credential Validation
    |
    v
Session / Token Creation
    |
    v
Authenticated Request

Questions:

How are credentials validated?

How are passwords stored?

How are sessions created?

How are tokens signed?

How are tokens validated?

How does logout work?

Is MFA enforced?

Are alternate login flows protected?

docs.title: Stage 9 - Authorisation Review
docs.text:
Authentication asks:

Who are you?

Authorisation asks:

Are you allowed to perform this action?

These must be reviewed separately.

docs.title: Authorisation Mapping
docs.text:
For every sensitive route, identify:

Authentication required?
Role required?
Permission required?
Object ownership checked?
Tenant checked?

Example:

GET /api/users/123
       |
       v
Authenticated User
       |
       v
findById(123)
       |
       v
Return User

Missing step:

Does authenticated user have permission
to access user 123?

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA Review
docs.text:
Search object lookups:

findById
getById
findOne
getUser
getAccount
getOrder
getDocument

Then inspect whether the application checks:

Ownership
Tenant
Organisation
Role
Permission
Relationship

docs.title: Secure Pattern
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Object Requested
      |
      v
Object Loaded
      |
      v
Ownership / Permission Check
      |
      +-- Denied
      |
      +-- Allowed
             |
             v
          Response

docs.title: Stage 10 - Input Validation
docs.text:
Locate:

Validators
Schemas
DTO constraints
Regex checks
Type validation
Length limits
Allowlist validation

Remember:

Validation
    !=
Authorisation

and:

Validation
    !=
Output Encoding

and:

Validation
    !=
SQL Parameterisation

Each solves a different problem.

docs.title: Validation Location
docs.text:
Review whether validation occurs:

Client side
Server side
Controller
Service
Domain layer
Database

Client-side validation must not be treated as a server-side security boundary.

docs.title: Stage 11 - Business Logic
docs.text:
Automated tools are particularly weak at identifying business logic vulnerabilities.

Examples:

Negative quantities
Repeated refunds
Coupon reuse
Workflow bypass
Order state manipulation
Privilege transitions
Account linking
Approval bypass
Payment race conditions
Invitation abuse
Tenant switching

docs.title: Model the State Machine
docs.text:
Example:

Created
   |
   v
Approved
   |
   v
Paid
   |
   v
Shipped

Ask:

Can Created become Shipped directly?

Can Paid become Created?

Can Approved be skipped?

Can an action be repeated?

docs.title: Business Invariants
docs.text:
Identify rules such as:

Balance cannot become negative

A refund cannot exceed payment

Only an owner can delete a resource

An invitation can only be used once

An MFA challenge must precede sensitive action

An order can only be shipped after payment

Then find where these rules are enforced.

docs.title: Stage 12 - Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Look for:

Request Body
      |
      v
Automatic Object Binding
      |
      v
Database Entity

Example attacker-controlled fields:

role
isAdmin
balance
ownerId
tenantId
verified
status

Prefer explicit DTOs and explicit mapping for security-sensitive models.

docs.title: Stage 13 - SSRF
docs.text:
Find outbound network clients.

Search examples:

rg -n \
'HttpClient|WebClient|RestTemplate|RestClient|requests\.|urllib|axios|fetch\(' \
.

Then trace:

User Input
    |
    v
URL Construction
    |
    v
HTTP Client

Review:

Scheme
Hostname
Port
Redirects
DNS resolution
Internal addresses
Cloud metadata
Egress controls

docs.title: Stage 14 - Command Injection
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Process\.Start|ProcessBuilder|Runtime\.getRuntime|os\.system|subprocess|child_process|shell_exec|system\(' \
.

Then determine whether attacker-controlled input reaches:

Command
Executable
Arguments
Shell
Working directory
Environment

docs.title: Shell Boundary
docs.text:
A useful distinction is:

Program + argument array

versus:

Shell command string

Example:

/bin/sh -c
cmd.exe /c
powershell -Command
bash -c

Shell invocation substantially changes parsing behaviour and should receive additional scrutiny.

docs.title: Stage 15 - File Operations
docs.text:
Search for:

File reads
File writes
Path construction
Archive extraction
Uploads
Downloads
Temporary files

Data flow:

User Filename
     |
     v
Path Construction
     |
     v
File Read

Potential:

Path Traversal

docs.title: Path Normalisation
docs.text:
Do not assume:

Path.Combine
Path.resolve
Paths.get

automatically prevents traversal.

Review whether the final canonical or normalised path is constrained to the intended base directory.

Conceptually:

Requested Path
      |
      v
Resolve
      |
      v
Normalise
      |
      v
Check Base Boundary
      |
      +-- Outside -> Reject
      |
      +-- Inside -> Continue

docs.title: Stage 16 - File Upload Review
docs.text:
Trace:

Multipart Request
      |
      v
Uploaded File
      |
      +-- Filename
      +-- Content
      +-- MIME Type
      +-- Size
      |
      v
Validation
      |
      v
Storage

Review:

Extension
Content
MIME type
Filename
Storage location
Generated filenames
Permissions
Web accessibility
Archive extraction
Downstream processing

docs.title: Stage 17 - Deserialisation
docs.text:
Search for deserialisation APIs.

Then determine:

What data format is used?

Who controls the data?

Which types can be created?

Is polymorphism enabled?

Are dangerous classes available?

Are integrity controls present?

Do not report:

ObjectMapper.readValue()

or similar generic parsing APIs as inherently insecure.

Configuration and trust boundaries matter.

docs.title: Stage 18 - XML Parsing
docs.text:
Search for:

XML parsers
Document builders
SAX
DOM
XMLReader
XMLInputFactory
lxml
XMLDecoder

Review:

External entities
DTD processing
Network access
Parser configuration
Library version

Do not assume parser defaults without verifying the exact runtime and configuration.

docs.title: Stage 19 - Template Rendering
docs.text:
Find:

Template engines
Dynamic template names
Template strings
Expression engines

Distinguish:

Attacker-controlled template data

from:

Attacker-controlled template source

The latter is much more likely to create SSTI.

docs.title: Stage 20 - XSS and Output Handling
docs.text:
Trace:

User Input
    |
    v
Stored / Processed
    |
    v
Output
    |
    v
HTML Context

Review context:

HTML
Attribute
JavaScript
CSS
URL

Encoding must match the output context.

docs.title: Stage 21 - Redirects
docs.text:
Search:

redirect
RedirectView
sendRedirect
Response.Redirect
location.href

Trace whether attacker-controlled data determines the destination.

Prefer:

Internal identifiers
Relative paths
Explicit allowlists
Parsed origin checks

rather than fragile string matching.

docs.title: Stage 22 - Host Header and Proxy Trust
docs.text:
Search:

Host
X-Forwarded-Host
X-Forwarded-Proto
X-Forwarded-For
Forwarded

Determine whether these values influence:

Password reset URLs
OAuth URLs
Absolute links
Security decisions
Redirects

Also review proxy trust configuration.

docs.title: Stage 23 - Secrets
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|access[_-]?token|private[_-]?key|client[_-]?secret' \
.

Also inspect:

.env
appsettings.json
application.yml
application.properties
config files
Docker files
CI/CD files
Kubernetes manifests
Terraform
Source maps
Tests
Example configuration

A string called:

password

does not prove credential exposure.

Determine whether the value is real, sensitive and usable.

docs.title: Git History
docs.text:
Deleted secrets may remain in Git history.

Useful commands:

git log --all --oneline

Search historical changes:

git log -p

Search commits affecting a file:

git log -p -- path/to/file

Search commits that added or removed a string:

git log -S 'password' -p

Use Git history review only where repository history is within scope.

docs.title: Stage 24 - Dependencies
docs.text:
Identify manifests:

pom.xml
build.gradle
*.csproj
packages.lock.json
composer.json
composer.lock
requirements.txt
pyproject.toml
package.json
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml

Review:

Direct dependencies
Transitive dependencies
Versions
Unsupported packages
Known vulnerabilities
Dependency sources
Build scripts
Install hooks

docs.title: Dependency Finding Validation
docs.text:
Do not report:

Library X appears in manifest

as a vulnerability without considering:

Installed version
Reachability
Affected component
Vulnerable functionality
Mitigations
Deployment context

docs.title: Stage 25 - Logging
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'log\.|logger\.|Console\.Write|console\.log|print\(' \
.

Review whether logs contain:

Passwords
Tokens
Session IDs
API keys
Personal data
Sensitive business data

Also consider log forging when attacker-controlled data is written to structured or security-sensitive logs.

docs.title: Stage 26 - Error Handling
docs.text:
Search:

catch
except
Exception
stack trace
error
debug

Review whether errors expose:

Stack traces
Filesystem paths
SQL
Secrets
Internal hosts
Source code
Configuration

docs.title: Stage 27 - Cryptography
docs.text:
Search for:

Cipher
MessageDigest
Hash
AES
DES
RSA
Random
SecureRandom
PBKDF
bcrypt
scrypt
Argon

Review:

Algorithm
Mode
Key length
Key generation
Key storage
Nonce / IV
Authentication
Password hashing
Randomness

Avoid simple pattern-based conclusions.

For example:

MD5 found

does not automatically mean a vulnerability.

Determine what it is used for.

docs.title: Stage 28 - Race Conditions
docs.text:
Identify operations involving:

Balances
Inventory
Coupons
Tokens
Invitations
Password resets
MFA
Payments
Reservations
Counters
State transitions

Look for:

Read
 |
 v
Check
 |
 v
Modify
 |
 v
Write

without atomic enforcement.

docs.title: TOCTOU Pattern
docs.text:
Check
  |
  | Time Gap
  v
Use

Another request may change the state between the two operations.

Review:

Transactions
Locks
Atomic operations
Unique constraints
Optimistic locking
Pessimistic locking
Idempotency

Absence of an obvious lock does not automatically prove a race condition.

docs.title: Stage 29 - Background Processing
docs.text:
Security review should not stop at HTTP controllers.

Search:

Scheduled jobs
Workers
Queues
Consumers
Event handlers
Cron jobs
Async jobs

Potential data flow:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Database
     |
     v
Queue
     |
     v
Worker
     |
     v
Dangerous Sink

This is a common second-order flow.

docs.title: Stage 30 - Message Queues
docs.text:
Identify:

Kafka
RabbitMQ
JMS
SQS
Azure Service Bus
Redis queues
Celery
Bull

Questions:

Who can produce messages?

Are messages trusted?

Are fields validated?

Can messages trigger privileged actions?

Can messages reach dangerous sinks?

docs.title: Stage 31 - Webhooks
docs.text:
Search:

webhook
callback
signature
HMAC
event

Review:

Authentication
Signature verification
Replay protection
Event type validation
Authorisation
Destination URLs

docs.title: Stage 32 - Caching
docs.text:
Search:

Cache
Redis
MemoryCache
@Cacheable
cache.get
cache.set

Review cache keys.

Example:

cache["profile:" + userId]

Ask whether the key includes all required security context:

User
Tenant
Organisation
Permission
Locale

Missing identity dimensions can cause cross-user or cross-tenant data exposure.

docs.title: Stage 33 - API Review
docs.text:
For APIs identify:

Routes
Methods
Authentication
Authorisation
Object identifiers
Schemas
Rate limiting
Mass assignment
Error handling
Versioning

Create:

Endpoint Auth Authz Object Input Sink /api/users/{id} Yes Review User ID DB /api/import Yes Admin File Upload Parser /api/fetch Yes User URL JSON HTTP Client

docs.title: Stage 34 - GraphQL
docs.text:
Search:

Query
Mutation
Subscription
Resolver
DataFetcher
@QueryMapping
@MutationMapping

Map:

GraphQL Operation
       |
       v
Resolver
       |
       v
Service
       |
       v
Repository

Review authorisation at resolver and service boundaries.

docs.title: Stage 35 - gRPC
docs.text:
Search:

.proto
service
rpc
BindableService

Map:

RPC
 |
 v
Handler
 |
 v
Service
 |
 v
Sink

Do not assume an RPC is internal merely because it uses gRPC.

docs.title: Stage 36 - WebSockets
docs.text:
Identify:

Connection authentication
Message handlers
Channel subscriptions
Object identifiers
Server-side authorisation

Map:

WebSocket Message
       |
       v
Message Handler
       |
       v
Business Logic
       |
       v
Sensitive Operation

docs.title: Stage 37 - Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Look for controls around:

Login
Password reset
MFA
OTP
Registration
Invitation
Search
Expensive APIs
Messaging
Payments

Rate limiting may exist outside application source code.

For example:

Reverse proxy
API gateway
WAF
Cloud service
Load balancer

Therefore:

No rate-limit code found

does not prove:

No rate limiting exists

docs.title: Stage 38 - Static Analysis
docs.text:
Manual review should be complemented with automated analysis.

Useful tools include:

ripgrep
Semgrep
CodeQL
Language-specific SAST
Dependency scanners
Secret scanners

Automated results are candidate generators.

They are not automatically confirmed vulnerabilities.

docs.title: ripgrep
docs.text:
ripgrep is extremely useful during manual review.

Basic search:

rg -n 'pattern' .

Case-insensitive:

rg -ni 'password' .

File type:

rg -n 'executeQuery' -g '*.java' .

Multiple patterns:

rg -n \
'executeQuery|executeUpdate|ProcessBuilder|Runtime\.getRuntime' \
.

docs.title: Excluding Noise
docs.text:
Example:

rg -n \
'password|secret|token' \
. \
-g '!node_modules/**' \
-g '!vendor/**' \
-g '!dist/**' \
-g '!build/**'

docs.title: Search Routes
docs.text:
rg -n \
'HttpGet|HttpPost|HttpPut|HttpDelete|RequestMapping|GetMapping|PostMapping|app\.get|app\.post|router\.get|router\.post|@app\.route|path\(' \
.

docs.title: Search Authentication
docs.text:
rg -ni \
'authorize|authorise|authenticate|authentication|login|required|permission|role|jwt|oauth|oidc|saml' \
.

docs.title: Search SQL
docs.text:
rg -n \
'executeQuery|executeUpdate|SqlCommand|FromSqlRaw|ExecuteSqlRaw|createNativeQuery|mysqli_query|PDO|cursor\.execute|\.query\(' \
.

docs.title: Search Commands
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Runtime\.getRuntime|ProcessBuilder|Process\.Start|os\.system|subprocess|child_process|shell_exec|system\(' \
.

docs.title: Search Files
docs.text:
rg -n \
'File\.Read|File\.Open|Files\.read|FileInputStream|FileOutputStream|fopen|file_get_contents|open\(|fs\.readFile|fs\.writeFile' \
.

docs.title: Search SSRF Candidates
docs.text:
rg -n \
'HttpClient|WebClient|RestTemplate|RestClient|requests\.|urllib|urlopen|axios|fetch\(' \
.

docs.title: Search Deserialisation
docs.text:
rg -n \
'ObjectInputStream|readObject|BinaryFormatter|pickle\.loads|unserialize|XMLDecoder|yaml\.load' \
.

docs.title: Search XSS Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'innerHTML|outerHTML|document\.write|Html\.Raw|th:utext|dangerouslySetInnerHTML|v-html' \
.

docs.title: Search Redirects
docs.text:
rg -n \
'redirect|RedirectView|sendRedirect|Response\.Redirect|location\.href' \
.

docs.title: Search Secrets
docs.text:
rg -ni \
'password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|access[_-]?token|refresh[_-]?token|private[_-]?key|client[_-]?secret' \
.

docs.title: Semgrep
docs.text:
Semgrep can quickly identify security-relevant code patterns.

Basic scan:

semgrep --config=auto .

Depending on the installed Semgrep version, the equivalent command may also be exposed through the newer semgrep scan interface.

Always verify the current CLI syntax before incorporating it into automation.

Semgrep is useful for:

Dangerous APIs
Injection candidates
Hard-coded secrets
Framework-specific patterns
Security anti-patterns

docs.title: Semgrep Review Workflow
docs.text:
Semgrep Result
      |
      v
Open File in VS Code
      |
      v
Identify Source
      |
      v
Trace Data Flow
      |
      v
Inspect Security Controls
      |
      v
Determine Exploitability

docs.title: CodeQL
docs.text:
CodeQL is particularly useful for deeper:

Data-flow analysis
Taint tracking
Variant analysis
Cross-function analysis
Security query development

Conceptually:

SOURCE
   |
   v
Data Flow Graph
   |
   v
SINK

A CodeQL result should still be manually validated.

docs.title: CodeQL and VS Code
docs.text:
The CodeQL extension for Visual Studio Code can be useful for:

Writing queries
Running queries
Viewing results
Exploring data-flow paths
Variant analysis

This is especially valuable after a vulnerability pattern has already been identified.

docs.title: Example Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose manual review discovers:

request parameter
      |
      v
buildCommand()
      |
      v
ProcessBuilder

Instead of stopping after one finding, search for:

Every ProcessBuilder call

and:

Every buildCommand() reference

Then identify similar flows.

docs.title: Variant Analysis Model
docs.text:
Confirmed Vulnerability
        |
        v
Identify Root Pattern
        |
        v
Search Similar Sinks
        |
        v
Search Similar Sources
        |
        v
Search Similar Data Flows
        |
        v
Validate Variants

docs.title: VS Code Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Useful features:

Find All References
Call Hierarchy
Global Search
Regex Search
Workspace Symbols
Git History

Example:

Confirmed:
UserController -> UserService -> unsafeQuery()

Find All References:
unsafeQuery()
    |
    +-- UserController
    +-- AdminController
    +-- SearchController
    +-- ExportService

Each call site becomes a candidate.

docs.title: Stage 39 - Dynamic Validation
docs.text:
Static analysis should be combined with runtime validation where appropriate and authorised.

Example:

Source Review
     |
     v
Potential SQL Injection
     |
     v
Identify Endpoint
     |
     v
Burp Repeater
     |
     v
Controlled Validation

Dynamic testing confirms assumptions that static review may not reveal.

docs.title: Static + Dynamic Testing
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

Source Code
    |
    v
Find Candidate
    |
    v
Understand Data Flow
    |
    v
Identify Endpoint
    |
    v
Burp Suite
    |
    v
Validate Behaviour
    |
    v
Return to Source
    |
    v
Identify Root Cause

docs.title: Burp Suite and VS Code Together
docs.text:
A practical setup:

Browser
   |
   v
Burp Suite
   |
   v
Running Application

        +

Visual Studio Code
   |
   v
Source Repository

Use Burp to observe:

Requests
Responses
Cookies
Headers
Parameters
Tokens
WebSockets

Use VS Code to determine:

Where is this parameter handled?

Where is this token validated?

Where is this object loaded?

Where is this header trusted?

Where does this value reach?

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
Burp request:

GET /api/users/123 HTTP/1.1
Host: application.example
Authorization: Bearer ...

VS Code search:

/api/users

Find:

@GetMapping("/api/users/{id}")

Follow:

Controller
   |
   v
UserService
   |
   v
UserRepository.findById(id)

Then ask:

Where is ownership checked?

If nowhere:

Potential IDOR / BOLA

Then validate dynamically with authorised test accounts.

docs.title: Stage 40 - Debugging
docs.text:
When source and an authorised test environment are available, debugging can provide excellent visibility into data flows.

Useful breakpoint locations:

Controller entry
Validation function
Authorisation function
Dangerous sink
Database query
HTTP client
File operation

docs.title: VS Code Breakpoints
docs.text:
Set a breakpoint by clicking next to the line number.

Then inspect:

Variables
Call stack
Arguments
Return values
Object state

Example:

HTTP Parameter
      |
      v
Breakpoint: Controller
      |
      v
Breakpoint: Service
      |
      v
Breakpoint: SQL Sink

This can confirm the exact runtime flow.

docs.title: Do Not Modify Evidence Accidentally
docs.text:
During a review, avoid unnecessary source modifications.

If testing requires modifications:

Create a separate branch

or:

Create a copy

Use:

git status

frequently.

This helps distinguish reviewer changes from original application code.

docs.title: Git Review
docs.text:
Useful commands:

git status

git log --oneline --all --decorate

git branch -a

git diff

git blame path/to/file

Git history can provide context for:

Why a security control exists
When vulnerable code was introduced
Previous implementation
Removed secrets
Security patches

docs.title: Review Tests
docs.text:
Do not ignore:

tests/
test/
spec/
integration-tests/

Tests can reveal:

Expected security behaviour
Hidden routes
Test credentials
Role models
Object relationships
Business rules
Authentication assumptions

docs.title: Search TODO Comments
docs.text:
rg -ni \
'TODO|FIXME|HACK|XXX|temporary|remove before production|bypass' \
.

These are not vulnerabilities.

They can identify interesting review areas.

docs.title: Search Security Comments
docs.text:
rg -ni \
'security|auth|permission|role|admin|validate|sanitize|escape|trusted' \
.

Developer comments can reveal intended security assumptions.

Always verify the implementation rather than trusting the comment.

docs.title: Identify Security Boundaries
docs.text:
During review, mark important boundaries.

Example:

[UNTRUSTED]
HTTP Request
     |
     v
Controller
     |
     v
[VALIDATION]
DTO Validator
     |
     v
Service
     |
     v
[AUTHORISATION]
Permission Check
     |
     v
Repository
     |
     v
[TRUSTED DATA STORE]
Database

This makes missing controls easier to identify.

docs.title: Review Data Context Changes
docs.text:
A value may be safe in one context and dangerous in another.

Example:

Username
   |
   v
Database
   |
   v
HTML

Another:

Filename
   |
   v
Database
   |
   v
Shell Command

Another:

URL
 |
 v
Database
 |
 v
HTTP Client

Always ask:

What security context is this value entering now?

docs.title: Second-Order Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Second-order vulnerabilities occur when attacker-controlled data is stored and used later.

Example:

Attacker
   |
   v
Profile Name
   |
   v
Database
   |
   v
Admin Dashboard
   |
   v
HTML Sink

Potential:

Stored XSS

Another:

Attacker Filename
      |
      v
Database
      |
      v
Nightly Job
      |
      v
Shell Command

Potential:

Second-order command injection

docs.title: Security Control Inventory
docs.text:
Create a list of controls:

Authentication middleware
Authorisation middleware
Input validators
Output encoding
CSRF protection
CORS configuration
Rate limiting
Security headers
Session configuration
Cryptographic helpers
Logging filters
File validators
URL validators

Then identify whether the controls are consistently applied.

docs.title: Inconsistent Security Controls
docs.text:
Example:

Controller A
    |
    v
@Authorize
    |
    v
Sensitive Action

Controller B
    |
    v
No Authorisation
    |
    v
Same Sensitive Action

This is a common source of vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Security Control Bypass Paths
docs.text:
Look for alternate entry points.

Example:

                   +--> Web Controller
                   |
Sensitive Service -+--> GraphQL Resolver
                   |
                   +--> Background Job
                   |
                   +--> WebSocket Handler

One path may have stronger controls than another.

docs.title: Entry Point Comparison
docs.text:
Example:

REST API
    |
    +-- Authentication
    +-- Authorisation
    +-- Validation

GraphQL
    |
    +-- Authentication
    +-- ???
    +-- Validation

The missing control becomes a high-value review target.

docs.title: Review by Vulnerability Class
docs.text:
After architecture mapping, perform dedicated passes.

Recommended order:

1. Authentication

2. Authorisation

3. IDOR / BOLA

4. Session Management

5. Input Validation

6. SQL Injection

7. NoSQL Injection

8. LDAP Injection

9. Command Injection

10. SSTI

11. SSRF

12. Path Traversal

13. File Upload

14. XXE

15. Deserialisation

16. XSS

17. HTML Injection

18. CSRF

19. CORS

20. Open Redirect

21. Host Header

22. Mass Assignment

23. Business Logic

24. Race Conditions

25. Rate Limiting

26. Secrets

27. Dependencies

28. Logging

29. Cryptography

30. APIs

docs.title: Prioritisation
docs.text:
Not every file deserves equal review time.

Prioritise code containing:

Authentication
Authorisation
Admin functionality
Payments
File handling
Database queries
Command execution
Network requests
Deserialisation
Template rendering
Password reset
MFA
OAuth
SAML
JWT
Cryptography
Secrets
Background processing

docs.title: High-Risk File Names
docs.text:
Search:

find . -type f | grep -Ei \
'auth|security|admin|login|password|reset|upload|file|command|exec|payment|token|jwt|oauth|saml|webhook|crypto'

This is prioritisation only.

Do not assume file names determine vulnerability.

docs.title: Create a Review Notebook
docs.text:
Maintain notes during review.

Example:

Application:
ExampleApp

Framework:
Spring Boot

Authentication:
JWT

Database:
PostgreSQL

External Services:
Payment API
Email API

High-Risk Areas:
File upload
Report generation
Admin API
Password reset

Potential Findings:
SRC-001
SRC-002
SRC-003

docs.title: Candidate Tracking
docs.text:
Use a table:

ID Candidate Source Sink Status C-001 SQLi q createNativeQuery Investigating C-002 SSRF url HttpClient Protected C-003 IDOR userId findById Confirmed C-004 Command Injection filename ProcessBuilder False Positive

This prevents duplicate work.

docs.title: Candidate States
docs.text:
Useful states:

Candidate
Investigating
Protected
Not Reachable
False Positive
Confirmed
Needs Dynamic Validation

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For confirmed findings record:

File
Line
Function
Route
Source
Transformations
Sink
Security control
Why control fails
Impact
Dynamic evidence
Remediation

docs.title: Source Code Evidence
docs.text:
Example:

File:
src/main/java/com/example/UserController.java

Method:
search()

Source:
@RequestParam String q

Sink:
EntityManager.createNativeQuery()

Flow:
q -> UserService.search() -> Repository.search() -> createNativeQuery()

Security Control:
No parameterisation identified.

Impact:
Potential SQL injection.

docs.title: Evidence Should Explain the Flow
docs.text:
Weak evidence:

createNativeQuery found.

Better:

The q HTTP parameter is passed from SearchController.search()
to SearchService.search(), concatenated into a native SQL query in
SearchRepository.search(), and executed through createNativeQuery().
No parameter binding is applied to q before execution.

The second explanation demonstrates exploitability much more clearly.

docs.title: Finding Template
docs.text:
Title:

Affected Component:

Affected Route:

Source:

Transformations:

Sink:

Security Control:

Security Control Weakness:

Data Flow:

Exploitability:

Impact:

Evidence:

Recommendation:

docs.title: Data Flow Template
docs.text:
SOURCE
  |
  v
Controller
  |
  v
Service
  |
  v
Transformation
  |
  v
Security Control
  |
  v
Sink

docs.title: Example Finding Model
docs.text:
Title:
Server-Side Request Forgery in URL Import Functionality

Source:
POST /api/import
JSON field: url

Data Flow:

request.url
    |
    v
ImportController
    |
    v
ImportService
    |
    v
HttpClient
    |
    v
Outbound Request

Security Control:
The application verifies that the URL begins with HTTP or HTTPS.

Weakness:
The validation does not restrict destination hosts or resolved IP addresses.

Impact:
An authenticated user may be able to cause the server to send requests to unintended network destinations.

docs.title: Avoid Overclaiming
docs.text:
Source review frequently produces suspicious code that is not exploitable.

Examples:

Raw SQL function

does not automatically mean:

SQL Injection

HttpClient

does not automatically mean:

SSRF

ProcessBuilder

does not automatically mean:

Command Injection

innerHTML

does not automatically mean:

XSS

ObjectInputStream

does not automatically mean:

Exploitable Deserialisation

Context determines security impact.

docs.title: False Positive Reduction
docs.text:
For every candidate ask:

1. Can an attacker control the source?

2. Can the attacker reach the code?

3. Does the data actually reach the sink?

4. Is there validation?

5. Is there sanitisation?

6. Is there parameterisation?

7. Is there encoding?

8. Is there authorisation?

9. Does framework behaviour provide protection?

10. Is the sink used in a dangerous context?

11. Is exploitation realistic?

12. What is the actual impact?

docs.title: Security Review Decision Tree
docs.text:
Interesting Code Pattern
        |
        v
Security-Sensitive Sink?
        |
   +----+----+
   |         |
  No        Yes
   |         |
   v         v
Lower     Trace Input
Priority      |
              v
      Attacker Controlled?
              |

      Lower     Security
      Priority   Control?

              +----+----+
              |         |

              |         |
              v         v

              |

         |         |
        Yes        No
         |         |
         v         v
     Protected   Candidate
                   |
                   v
             Dynamically
              Validate
                   |
                   v
                 Impact

docs.title: Manual Review and SAST
docs.text:
The strongest methodology combines:

Manual Review
     +
Pattern Searching
     +
SAST
     +
Dependency Analysis
     +
Dynamic Testing

No single technique provides complete coverage.

docs.title: What Automated Tools Are Good At
docs.text:
Automated tools are useful for:

Pattern detection
Known dangerous APIs
Known vulnerability classes
Repeated patterns
Dependency vulnerabilities
Secret patterns
Data-flow candidates

docs.title: What Humans Are Better At
docs.text:
Manual review is particularly important for:

Authorisation
Tenant isolation
Workflow vulnerabilities
Security assumptions
Context-specific validation
Race conditions
Trust boundaries
Chained vulnerabilities
Architecture

docs.title: Searching Only for Dangerous Functions
docs.text:
Finding:

exec()

is only the beginning.

The real question is:

Can attacker-controlled input reach exec()?

docs.title: Reviewing Only Controllers
docs.text:
Vulnerabilities frequently exist deeper in:

Services
Repositories
Utilities
Workers
Background jobs
Message handlers

Follow the complete call chain.

docs.title: Trusting Database Data
docs.text:
Stored data may originally have come from an attacker.

Always consider second-order flows.

docs.title: Ignoring Alternate Entry Points
docs.text:
The same service may be reachable through:

REST
GraphQL
WebSocket
gRPC
Background job
Admin interface

Security controls may differ.

docs.title: Treating Validation as Authorisation
docs.text:
Example:

userId must be numeric

does not answer:

Is the current user allowed to access userId?

docs.title: Treating Authentication as Authorisation
docs.text: Being logged in does not mean a user may access every object.

docs.title: Ignoring Framework Security
docs.text:
Frameworks may provide:

Output encoding
CSRF protection
Parameterisation
Security headers
Authentication middleware

Understand the framework before reporting.

docs.title: Assuming Framework Defaults
docs.text:
The opposite mistake is also dangerous.

Do not assume protections are enabled simply because the framework supports them.

Review:

Version
Configuration
Overrides
Custom code
Deployment

docs.title: Trusting Function Names
docs.text:
A function named:

sanitize()

is not automatically secure.

Open the implementation.

docs.title: Trusting Comments
docs.text:
A comment such as:

// validate URL

does not prove that URL validation is correct.

Review the implementation.

docs.title: Ignoring Configuration
docs.text:
Security behaviour may depend heavily on:

Environment variables
Production profiles
Reverse proxies
Feature flags
Cloud configuration
Deployment settings

Source code alone may not provide the complete answer.

docs.title: Ignoring Build Output
docs.text:
Generated or bundled code may differ from source.

Where relevant compare:

Source
Build configuration
Production artifact

docs.title: Stopping After the First Finding
docs.text:
A confirmed vulnerability often indicates a reusable vulnerable pattern.

Always perform:

Variant Analysis

flowchart LR
    A["Architecture and entry points"] --> B["Sources"]
    B --> C["Validation and authorization"]
    C --> D["Transformations"]
    D --> E["Sensitive sink"]
    E --> F["Runtime/impact validation"]

docs.title: Final Source Code Review Model
docs.text:
REPOSITORY
                               |
                               v
                     TECHNOLOGY IDENTIFICATION
                               |
                               v
                       ARCHITECTURE MAPPING
                               |
                               v
                     ATTACK SURFACE MAPPING
                               |
                               v
                          ENTRY POINTS
                               |
                               v
                            SOURCES
                               |
            +------------------+------------------+
            |                  |                  |
            v                  v                  v
         HTTP Input         Stored Data       Messages
            |                  |                  |
            +------------------+------------------+
                               |
                               v
                        TRANSFORMATIONS
                               |
       +-----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+
       |           |           |           |           |
       v           v           v           v           v
   Validation   Parsing    Normalisation  AuthZ    Business Logic
       |           |           |           |           |
       +-----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+
                               |
                               v
                             SINK
                               |
       +-----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+
       |           |           |           |           |
       v           v           v           v           v
      SQL       Command       File        HTTP       Output
       |           |           |           |           |
       +-----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+
                               |
                               v
                       SECURITY CONTROL
                               |
                         +-----+-----+
                         |           |
                         v           v
                     Effective   Ineffective
                         |           |
                         v           v
                     Protected    Candidate
                                     |
                                     v
                              Dynamic Validation
                                     |
                                     v
                                   Impact
                                     |
                                     v
                             Confirmed Finding
                                     |
                                     v
                              Variant Analysis

The review can therefore be reduced to five fundamental questions:

1. Where does data enter?

2. Where does the data go?

3. What security-sensitive operation does it reach?

4. What security controls exist between source and sink?

5. Can those controls be bypassed or are they ineffective?

Or even more simply:

SOURCE
   |
   v
DATA FLOW
   |
   v
SECURITY CONTROL
   |
   v
SINK
   |
   v
IMPACT

The tools help locate these components.

Visual Studio Code helps navigate them.

Static analysis helps identify candidates.

Dynamic testing helps validate behaviour.

The security reviewer determines whether the complete flow represents a real vulnerability.

docs.title: Node.js and Express Source Code Review
docs.text:
Node.js is widely used for REST APIs, web applications, GraphQL services, WebSocket applications, microservices, background workers and server-side rendering.

Express is one of the most common Node.js web frameworks, but the same review methodology applies to many JavaScript and TypeScript server applications.

Node.js applications are particularly interesting during source-code review because JavaScript applications commonly combine:

  • Dynamic typing
  • Object merging
  • JSON processing
  • Asynchronous execution
  • Large dependency trees
  • Middleware-based security controls
  • Multiple data stores
  • Server-side template engines
  • Client-side and server-side JavaScript
  • Background jobs
  • WebSockets
  • GraphQL
  • External APIs

The objective of source-code review is not simply to search for dangerous functions.

The objective is to identify:

Routes
Input sources
Authentication
Authorisation
Validation
Trust boundaries
Data transformations
Dangerous sinks
Security configuration

and determine whether attacker-controlled data can reach security-sensitive operations.

The core methodology is:

SOURCE
  |
  v
User-Controlled Input
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATIONS
  |
  +-- parsing
  +-- decoding
  +-- validation
  +-- sanitisation
  +-- object merging
  +-- business logic
  |
  v
SECURITY CONTROLS
  |
  +-- authentication
  +-- authorisation
  +-- tenant isolation
  +-- CSRF
  +-- rate limiting
  |
  v
SINK
  |
  v
Security-Sensitive Operation

Remember:

grep match
    !=
vulnerability

and:

Dangerous sink found
        !=
Confirmed vulnerability

A finding normally requires:

Attacker-controlled source
        +
Reachable code path
        +
Dangerous operation
        +
Missing or ineffective control
        +
Security impact

Authorised Security Testing

Perform source-code review and dynamic validation only against applications, repositories and environments for which you have explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Review Strategy
docs.text:
A practical Node.js review can follow:

1. Identify Node.js version

2. Identify package manager

3. Identify dependencies

4. Identify application entry points

5. Identify framework

6. Map middleware

7. Map routers

8. Map routes

9. Identify input sources

10. Map authentication

11. Map authorisation

12. Review object-level access

13. Review validation

14. Review database access

15. Review command execution

16. Review filesystem access

17. Review outbound HTTP requests

18. Review template engines

19. Review redirects

20. Review sessions and cookies

21. Review JWT handling

22. Review CORS

23. Review CSRF

24. Review proxy trust

25. Review file uploads

26. Review object merging and prototype pollution

27. Review GraphQL

28. Review WebSockets

29. Review business logic

30. Review asynchronous workflows

31. Review background jobs

32. Search secrets

33. Review dependencies

34. Run static analysis

35. Perform variant analysis

36. Validate candidates dynamically where authorised

docs.title: Identify the Project
docs.text:
Start with:

find . -maxdepth 3 -type f \( \
-name 'package.json' \
-o -name 'package-lock.json' \
-o -name 'yarn.lock' \
-o -name 'pnpm-lock.yaml' \
-o -name 'bun.lock' \
-o -name 'bun.lockb' \
-o -name 'tsconfig.json' \
-o -name '.npmrc' \
-o -name '.yarnrc*' \
\) -print

High-value files include:

package.json
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml
tsconfig.json

app.js
server.js
index.js
main.js

app.ts
server.ts
index.ts
main.ts

routes/
controllers/
middleware/
services/
models/
repositories/
graphql/
websocket/
workers/
jobs/
config/

docs.title: package.json
docs.text:
Inspect:

cat package.json

Important sections:

{
  "scripts": {},
  "dependencies": {},
  "devDependencies": {},
  "engines": {}
}

Look for:

express
fastify
koa
hapi
nestjs
mongoose
mongodb
sequelize
typeorm
prisma
knex
pg
mysql
mysql2
sqlite
jsonwebtoken
jose
passport
express-session
cookie-session
helmet
cors
csurf
express-rate-limit
multer
axios
got
node-fetch
undici
ejs
pug
handlebars
mustache
socket.io
ws
graphql
apollo

Dependencies reveal much of the attack surface.

docs.title: Node.js Version
docs.text:
Check:

node --version

Project requirements may appear in:

{
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=..."
  }
}

Search:

rg -n \
'"node"\s*:|node-version|NODE_VERSION' \
package.json .nvmrc .node-version Dockerfile* .github 2>/dev/null

Also inspect:

Docker images
CI workflows
Deployment manifests
Runtime configuration

Do not assume the developer's local Node.js version equals the production version.

docs.title: JavaScript vs TypeScript
docs.text:
Find:

find . -type f \( \
-name '*.js' \
-o -name '*.mjs' \
-o -name '*.cjs' \
-o -name '*.ts' \
-o -name '*.tsx' \
\) | head -100

TypeScript configuration:

cat tsconfig.json

TypeScript improves type safety but does not automatically prevent security vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Common Application Structure
docs.text:
A typical Express project may resemble:

src/
├── app.ts
├── server.ts
├── routes/
│   ├── auth.ts
│   ├── users.ts
│   └── admin.ts
├── controllers/
│   ├── authController.ts
│   └── userController.ts
├── middleware/
│   ├── auth.ts
│   └── permissions.ts
├── services/
│   ├── userService.ts
│   └── webhookService.ts
├── models/
│   └── User.ts
├── repositories/
├── jobs/
├── config/
└── views/

Trace:

Route
  |
  v
Middleware
  |
  v
Controller
  |
  v
Service
  |
  v
Repository
  |
  v
Database / External System

docs.title: Identify Express
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'require\(["'\'']express["'\'']\)|from ["'\'']express["'\'']|express\(\)' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Typical:

const express = require("express");
const app = express();

or:

import express from "express";

const app = express();

docs.title: Application Entry Points
docs.text:
Inspect package scripts:

rg -n \
'"(start|dev|serve)"\s*:' \
package.json

Example:

{
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node dist/server.js",
    "dev": "tsx src/server.ts"
  }
}

Trace the actual startup file.

docs.title: Middleware Order
docs.text:
Express security often depends heavily on middleware ordering.

Example:

app.use(express.json());

app.use(authenticate);

app.use("/api", apiRouter);

app.use(errorHandler);

Middleware order matters.

A route registered before authentication middleware may not receive the expected protection.

Search:

rg -n \
'app\.use\(|router\.use\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Map middleware sequentially.

docs.title: Route Discovery
docs.text:
Common Express routes:

app.get()
app.post()
app.put()
app.patch()
app.delete()

router.get()
router.post()
router.put()
router.patch()
router.delete()

Search:

rg -n \
'\b(app|router)\.(get|post|put|patch|delete|options|head|all)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Route Example
docs.text:
router.get(
    "/users/:id",
    authenticate,
    getUser
);

Map:

GET /users/:id
      |
      v
authenticate
      |
      v
getUser

docs.title: Router Mounting
docs.text:
Routes may be split across files.

Example:

app.use(
    "/api/users",
    userRouter
);

and:

router.get(
    "/:id",
    getUser
);

Final route:

GET /api/users/:id

Search:

rg -n \
'app\.use\(|router\.use\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Always combine:

Mount path
    +
Router path
    =
Final endpoint

docs.title: Express Router
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'express\.Router\(\)|Router\(\)' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Typical:

const router = express.Router();

docs.title: Dynamic Routes
docs.text:
Route parameters:

router.get(
    "/users/:userId",
    handler
);

Attacker-controlled source:

req.params.userId

docs.title: Route Inventory
docs.text:
Build:

Method Route Handler Authentication Authorisation GET /users/:id getUser JWT ? POST /users createUser JWT Admin? PATCH /users/:id updateUser JWT Owner? DELETE /users/:id deleteUser JWT Admin?

This makes inconsistent security controls easier to identify.

docs.title: User-Controlled Input Sources
docs.text:
The primary Express sources are:

req.query
req.params
req.body
req.headers
req.cookies
req.signedCookies
req.file
req.files

Other sources include:

req.get()
req.header()
req.hostname
req.ip
req.ips
req.protocol
req.originalUrl
req.url

docs.title: Input Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'req\.(query|params|body|headers|cookies|signedCookies|file|files|hostname|ip|ips|protocol|originalUrl|url)|req\.(get|header)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
Example:

const search = req.query.q;

Search:

rg -n \
'req\.query' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Route Parameters
docs.text:
const id = req.params.id;

Search:

rg -n \
'req\.params' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Request Body
docs.text:
const data = req.body;

Search:

rg -n \
'req\.body' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Treat nested fields individually.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
const token =
    req.headers.authorization;

Search:

rg -n \
'req\.headers|req\.get\(|req\.header\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Potentially attacker-controlled headers include:

Host
Origin
Referer
User-Agent
Authorization
X-Forwarded-For
X-Forwarded-Host
X-Forwarded-Proto
Custom headers

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'req\.cookies|req\.signedCookies' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Signed cookies provide integrity when implemented correctly.

They are not automatically secret.

docs.title: Body Parsers
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'express\.json\(|express\.urlencoded\(|bodyParser\.' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Review:

Body size
Accepted content types
Nested object behaviour
Raw body requirements
Signature verification

docs.title: Raw Bodies
docs.text:
Webhooks may require raw request bodies.

Search:

rg -n \
'express\.raw\(|express\.text\(|req\.rawBody' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

This is particularly important for:

Webhook signatures
Payment providers
Custom protocols

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
Common validation libraries include:

Joi
Zod
Ajv
express-validator
Yup
class-validator
Valibot

Search:

rg -n -i \
'joi|zod|ajv|express-validator|class-validator|yup|valibot|validate|schema' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Validation Example
docs.text:
const schema = z.object({
    email: z.string().email(),
    name: z.string().max(100)
});

const input =
    schema.parse(req.body);

Validation establishes constraints.

It does not automatically provide:

Authorisation
Safe SQL construction
Safe command construction
Safe HTML output
Object ownership

docs.title: Unknown Fields
docs.text:
Review whether schemas:

Reject unknown fields
Strip unknown fields
Preserve unknown fields

This matters for mass assignment.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Search broadly:

rg -n -i \
'authenticate|authentication|authorize|authorization|passport|jwt|bearer|session|login|logout|api.?key|currentUser|req\.user' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Authentication Middleware
docs.text:
Typical:

function authenticate(
    req,
    res,
    next
) {
    ...
}

Routes:

router.get(
    "/profile",
    authenticate,
    profile
);

Search:

rg -n \
'authenticate|authMiddleware|requireAuth|isAuthenticated|req\.user' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Read middleware implementations.

Do not trust names alone.

docs.title: Middleware Coverage
docs.text:
Compare:

router.get(
    "/account",
    authenticate,
    account
);

with:

router.post(
    "/account/delete",
    deleteAccount
);

The second route deserves investigation.

docs.title: Router-Level Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication may be applied globally:

router.use(authenticate);

Therefore:

No route-level middleware
    !=
Unauthenticated

Trace parent routers and application middleware.

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'role|permission|authorize|authorise|admin|owner|tenant|organization|organisation|workspace|req\.user' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Role Middleware
docs.text:
Example:

function requireAdmin(
    req,
    res,
    next
) {
    if (!req.user.isAdmin) {
        return res.sendStatus(403);
    }

    next();
}

Determine where req.user originates.

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
Candidate:

router.get(
    "/documents/:id",
    authenticate,
    async (req, res) => {
        const document =
            await Document.findById(
                req.params.id
            );

        res.json(document);
    }
);

Data flow:

req.params.id
      |
      v
Document.findById()
      |
      v
Document
      |
      v
Response

Question:

Where is ownership or tenant authorisation?

docs.title: Scoped Lookup
docs.text:
A stronger pattern may resemble:

const document =
    await Document.findOne({
        _id: req.params.id,
        ownerId: req.user.id
    });

For multi-tenant applications:

const document =
    await Document.findOne({
        _id: req.params.id,
        tenantId: req.user.tenantId
    });

The correct scope depends on application policy.

docs.title: Object Lookup Search
docs.text:
MongoDB/Mongoose:

rg -n \
'\.(findById|findOne|find|findOneAndUpdate|findByIdAndUpdate|findOneAndDelete|findByIdAndDelete)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

SQL ORMs:

rg -n \
'(findOne|findUnique|findFirst|findByPk|findAll|select|where)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Prioritise attacker-controlled identifiers.

Refer to:

IDOR and BOLA

Authorisation Testing

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Security
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'tenantId|tenant_id|organizationId|organisationId|workspaceId|accountId|ownerId' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Map:

Authenticated User
       |
       v
Tenant Membership
       |
       v
Tenant Identifier
       |
       v
Database Query
       |
       v
Object

Look for queries that omit tenant scope.

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
Node.js applications may use:

pg
mysql
mysql2
sqlite
Knex
Sequelize
TypeORM
Prisma
Raw SQL

Search:

rg -n \
'\.(query|execute|raw|queryRaw|executeRaw)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Raw SQL
docs.text:
Candidate:

const username =
    req.query.username;

const sql =
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" +
    username +
    "'";

db.query(sql);

Trace:

req.query.username
        |
        v
SQL String
        |
        v
db.query()

docs.title: Template Literal SQL
docs.text:
Candidate:

const sql =
    `SELECT * FROM users
     WHERE username = '${username}'`;

Search candidates:

rg -n \
'`[^`]*(SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE)[^`]*\$\{' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: PostgreSQL Parameterisation
docs.text:
Safer style:

await pool.query(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1",
    [userId]
);

Review dynamic structural elements separately:

Column names
Table names
ORDER BY
Operators
Directions

These usually require server-controlled mappings or allowlists.

docs.title: MySQL Parameterisation
docs.text:
Example:

connection.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?",
    [userId]
);

Review the actual driver and API semantics.

docs.title: Sequelize
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'sequelize\.query|Sequelize\.literal|literal\(|replacements|bind' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Raw query functionality deserves particular attention.

docs.title: Knex
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'knex\.raw|\.whereRaw|\.orderByRaw|\.havingRaw|\.joinRaw' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Prisma
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\$queryRaw|\$executeRaw|\$queryRawUnsafe|\$executeRawUnsafe' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Raw and explicitly unsafe query APIs deserve investigation.

Do not report normal ORM queries as SQL injection merely because attacker-controlled values are used as query values.

Refer to:

SQL Injection

docs.title: NoSQL Injection
docs.text:
NoSQL injection is especially relevant to Node.js applications using MongoDB.

Sources such as:

req.body
req.query

may contain nested objects rather than only strings.

Candidate:

const user =
    await User.findOne({
        username: req.body.username,
        password: req.body.password
    });

The security significance depends on:

Parser behaviour
ODM behaviour
Input validation
Object sanitisation
MongoDB operator handling
Library versions

Do not assume every object passed to Mongoose is injectable.

docs.title: Raw Query Object
docs.text:
Higher-risk pattern:

const query =
    req.body;

const user =
    await User.findOne(query);

Data flow:

req.body
   |
   v
Mongo Query Object
   |
   v
findOne()

docs.title: MongoDB Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\.(find|findOne|findById|aggregate|updateOne|updateMany|deleteOne|deleteMany|findOneAndUpdate)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: MongoDB Operators
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\$(where|regex|expr|ne|gt|gte|lt|lte|in|nin|or|and|lookup|function)' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Operator use is not automatically vulnerable.

Trace whether attackers control:

Operator names
Query structure
Expressions
Regular expressions
Aggregation stages

Refer to:

NoSQL Injection

docs.title: LDAP Injection
docs.text:
Node.js applications may use:

ldapjs
ldapts
Active Directory libraries
Custom LDAP clients

Search:

rg -n -i \
'ldap|ldapjs|ldapts|searchFilter|filter:' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

const filter =
    `(uid=${req.body.username})`;

Trace attacker-controlled values into LDAP filter syntax.

Refer to:

LDAP Injection

docs.title: Command Injection
docs.text:
Node.js exposes process execution through:

child_process.exec()
child_process.execSync()
child_process.spawn()
child_process.spawnSync()
execFile()
execFileSync()

Search:

rg -n \
'child_process|execSync\(|execFileSync\(|execFile\(|spawnSync\(|spawn\(|\bexec\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: exec()
docs.text:
High-risk candidate:

const host =
    req.body.host;

exec(
    `ping -c 1 ${host}`,
    callback
);

Flow:

req.body.host
      |
      v
Shell Command
      |
      v
exec()
      |
      v
Shell

Node.js documentation explicitly warns against passing unsanitised user input to shell-backed child-process execution.

docs.title: execSync()
docs.text:
Candidate:

const output =
    execSync(
        `nslookup ${domain}`
    );

Search:

rg -n \
'execSync\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: spawn()
docs.text:
Prefer argument arrays where possible:

spawn(
    "ping",
    [
        "-c",
        "1",
        host
    ]
);

This avoids shell parsing by default.

However:

spawn() with argument array
        !=
Automatically secure

Review:

Executable control
Argument semantics
Option injection
Working directory
Environment

docs.title: shell: true
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'shell\s*:\s*true|shell\s*=\s*true' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Example:

spawn(
    command,
    {
        shell: true
    }
);

Treat attacker-controlled input reaching shell-enabled execution as high priority.

Refer to:

OS Command Injection

docs.title: Dynamic JavaScript Execution
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\beval\(|new Function\(|Function\(|vm\.runIn(New|This)Context|vm\.runInContext|vm\.runInThisContext' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

const expression =
    req.body.expression;

const result =
    eval(expression);

Trace attacker control carefully.

docs.title: vm Module
docs.text:
The Node.js vm module is not a general security boundary for executing hostile code.

Search:

rg -n \
'node:vm|require\(["'\'']vm["'\'']\)|from ["'\'']node:vm["'\'']|runInNewContext|runInContext' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Review any attempt to use it as an untrusted-code sandbox.

docs.title: Server-Side Template Injection
docs.text:
Common Node.js template engines include:

EJS
Pug
Handlebars
Mustache
Nunjucks
Liquid

Search dependencies:

rg -n -i \
'ejs|pug|handlebars|mustache|nunjucks|liquid' \
package.json package-lock.json yarn.lock pnpm-lock.yaml 2>/dev/null

docs.title: res.render()
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.render\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Normal:

res.render(
    "profile",
    {
        username
    }
);

Passing attacker-controlled values as template data is not the same as allowing the attacker to control template source.

docs.title: Dynamic Template Names
docs.text:
Candidate:

res.render(
    req.query.template,
    data
);

Review whether users can select unintended templates or influence template resolution.

docs.title: EJS
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'ejs\.render|ejs\.renderFile|<%-' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts,ejs}' \
.

In EJS:

<%= value %>

and:

<%- value %>

have different escaping behaviour.

Review unescaped output carefully.

docs.title: Handlebars
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Handlebars\.compile|handlebars\.compile|{{{' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts,hbs,handlebars}' \
.

Triple braces can produce unescaped output.

docs.title: Pug
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'!=|!{' \
--glob '*.pug' \
.

Review unescaped output contexts.

docs.title: Template Source
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\.compile\(|\.render\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Determine whether attacker-controlled data becomes:

Template data

or:

Template source

This distinction is essential.

Refer to:

Server-Side Template Injection

docs.title: XSS
docs.text:
Server-side Node.js applications can introduce XSS through:

Unescaped templates
HTML string construction
Unsafe redirects into script contexts
Stored data rendered without encoding
Client-side JavaScript

docs.title: res.send()
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.send\(|res\.end\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

const name =
    req.query.name;

res.send(
    `<h1>Hello ${name}</h1>`
);

Trace:

req.query.name
      |
      v
HTML String
      |
      v
res.send()
      |
      v
Browser

docs.title: HTML Construction
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.send\(`|res\.send\(".*<|res\.send\('\''.*<' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Manual review is required.

docs.title: JSON Is Not Automatically XSS
docs.text:
Example:

res.json({
    username
});

This is not automatically XSS simply because username contains HTML characters.

The downstream browser context matters.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Scripting

HTML Injection

docs.title: Open Redirect
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.redirect\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

res.redirect(
    req.query.next
);

Trace whether attacker-controlled external destinations are accepted.

docs.title: Common Redirect Parameters
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'next|redirect|returnUrl|return_url|returnTo|continue|callbackUrl' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Validate destinations using an explicit policy.

Refer to:

Open Redirect

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
Common HTTP clients include:

fetch
axios
got
undici
node-fetch
http
https
superagent

Search:

rg -n \
'\bfetch\(|axios\.|got\(|got\.|request\(|http\.request\(|https\.request\(|undici|superagent\.' \

fs.createWriteStream()

docs.title: Deserialization
docs.text:
JSON parsing itself is not equivalent to unsafe native-code deserialization.

However, applications may use dangerous serialization packages or convert untrusted objects into executable structures.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'serialize|deserialize|node-serialize|unserialize|yaml\.load|js-yaml|JSON\.parse' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Do not flag every:

JSON.parse()

as insecure deserialization.

Review:

Library
Object type
Revivers
Prototype handling
Dynamic execution
Trust boundary

Refer to:

Insecure Deserialization

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Prototype pollution is especially important in JavaScript source review.

Potential sources:

req.body
req.query
JSON.parse()

Potential dangerous operations include:

Object.assign()
deep merge libraries
recursive setters
dynamic property assignment
lodash merge functions

Search:

rg -n \
'Object\.assign\(|merge\(|mergeWith\(|defaultsDeep\(|set\(|setWith\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Dynamic Property Assignment
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\[[A-Za-z0-9_.$]+\]\s*=' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

object[
    req.body.key
] = req.body.value;

Review whether keys such as:

__proto__
constructor
prototype

can affect object prototypes.

docs.title: Recursive Merge
docs.text:
Candidate:

function merge(
    target,
    source
) {
    for (
        const key in source
    ) {
        ...
    }
}

Custom recursive merge implementations deserve careful review.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution Impact
docs.text:
Pollution alone may not establish meaningful impact.

Trace polluted properties into:

Authorisation
Command execution
Template engines
Configuration
HTTP options
Filesystem operations
Privilege checks

Refer to:

Prototype Pollution

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Candidate:

const user =
    await User.create(
        req.body
    );

Potential attacker-controlled fields:

role
isAdmin
permissions
verified
status
tenantId
ownerId
balance
credits

rg -n \
'(create|update|findOneAndUpdate|findByIdAndUpdate)\(\s*req\.body|Object\.assign\(.*req\.body|\.\.\.req\.body' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Object Spread
docs.text:
Candidate:

const user = {
    ...req.body
};

Search:

rg -n \
'\.\.\.req\.(body|query|params)' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Safer Field Selection
docs.text:
Example:

const {
    name,
    email
} = req.body;

await User.updateOne(
    {
        _id: req.user.id
    },
    {
        name,
        email
    }
);

Explicit field selection makes the writable model clearer.

Refer to:

Mass Assignment

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:

Cookie-authenticated state-changing routes deserve particular attention.

Bearer tokens supplied explicitly in an Authorization header have a different CSRF threat model.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'csrf|csurf|csrfToken|sameSite' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: State-Changing Routes
docs.text:
Map:

POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

against:

Authentication mechanism
Cookie behaviour
SameSite
CSRF controls
Origin validation

Do not report missing CSRF middleware without understanding authentication.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

cors({

docs.text:

rg -n \
'jwt\.decode\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \

Decoding a JWT is not equivalent to verifying it.

A high-value pattern is:

const claims =
    jwt.decode(token);

if (
    claims.role === "admin"
) {
    ...
}

when security decisions occur before cryptographic verification.

docs.text:

req.ip
req.ips
req.hostname
req.protocol
Secure-cookie behaviour
IP-based access controls
Rate limiting
Logging
Absolute URL generation

docs.text:

app.use(

docs.text:

docs.text:

    productId,
    price

    productId,

Should price come from trusted server-side product data?

Business Logic Vulnerabilities

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Node.js being event-driven does not eliminate race conditions.

Example:

const account =
    await Account.findById(id);

if (
    account.balance >= amount
) {
    account.balance -= amount;

    await account.save();
}

Concurrent requests may interact with the same logical state.

docs.title: Race Review
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'transaction|startSession|withTransaction|lock|mutex|version|optimistic|increment|decrement|\$inc' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Review:

Read-check-write sequences
One-time tokens
Credits
Coupons
Inventory
Balances
Approvals

docs.title: Database Atomic Operations
docs.text:
Look for atomic operations such as:

$inc
findOneAndUpdate
transactions
conditional UPDATE
optimistic locking

Their presence does not automatically prove the workflow is race-safe.

Refer to:

Race Conditions

docs.title: Promise and Async Control Flow
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'async |await |Promise\.all|Promise\.race|forEach\(async|map\(async' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Security bugs can occur through incorrect asynchronous assumptions.

docs.title: forEach(async)
docs.text:
Candidate:

items.forEach(
    async item => {
        await authorise(item);
    }
);

performAction();

The surrounding code may continue before asynchronous callbacks finish.

Review security-sensitive async flows carefully.

docs.title: Missing await
docs.text:
Source review should inspect security functions that return promises.

Candidate:

if (
    checkPermission(user)
) {
    performSensitiveAction();
}

If checkPermission() returns a Promise, this logic may not behave as intended.

TypeScript and linting can help identify these mistakes.

docs.title: HTTP Request Smuggling
docs.text:
Application source alone is usually insufficient to prove HTTP request smuggling.

Review the complete chain:

Client
  |
  v
CDN / WAF
  |
  v
Reverse Proxy
  |
  v
Load Balancer
  |
  v
Node.js / Express

Relevant files include:

Nginx configuration
HAProxy configuration
Ingress configuration
Cloud load balancer settings
Node.js version
Express version
Proxy middleware

docs.text:

     |

docs.title: Example Finding - IDOR
docs.text:
Title:
Missing Object-Level Authorisation on Document Endpoint

Route:
GET /api/documents/:id

Source:
req.params.id

Data Flow:

req.params.id
      |
      v
Document.findById()
      |
      v
Document
      |
      v
res.json()

Authentication:
Authentication middleware is present.

Authorisation:
No ownership or tenant restriction was identified before returning the document.

Impact:
An authenticated user may be able to access another user's document by supplying its identifier.

Recommendation:
Scope the lookup to objects the authenticated user is authorised to access or perform an equivalent object-level permission check.

docs.title: Example Finding - Command Injection
docs.text:
Title:
OS Command Injection in Diagnostics Endpoint

Route:
POST /api/diagnostics

Source:
req.body.host

Data Flow:

req.body.host
      |
      v
Template Literal
      |
      v
child_process.exec()
      |
      v
Shell

Security Control:
No effective validation prevents attacker-controlled input from altering shell syntax.

Recommendation:
Avoid shell command construction. Invoke the required executable directly with controlled arguments and validate attacker-controlled values according to the expected input format.

docs.title: Example Finding - SSRF
docs.text:
Title:
Server-Side Request Forgery in URL Preview Endpoint

Route:
POST /api/preview

Source:
req.body.url

Data Flow:

req.body.url
      |
      v
fetch()
      |
      v
Network

Security Control:
No effective destination restriction was identified.

Impact:
The application may make server-side requests to destinations selected by the user, potentially including internal services depending on network access.

Recommendation:
Prefer server-controlled destinations. Where arbitrary external URLs are required, implement strict destination validation and network-level egress restrictions.

docs.title: Example Finding - NoSQL Injection
docs.text:
Title:
User-Controlled MongoDB Query Structure

Route:
POST /api/users/search

Source:
req.body

Data Flow:

req.body
      |
      v
User.find(req.body)
      |
      v
MongoDB

Security Concern:
The complete query object is supplied by the client rather than being constructed from server-controlled query structure.

Recommendation:
Define the permitted query structure server-side and copy only explicitly supported fields and operators from validated client input.

docs.title: Example Finding - Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Title:
Mass Assignment in User Profile Update

Route:
PATCH /api/users/me

Source:
req.body

Data Flow:

req.body
      |
      v
User.findByIdAndUpdate(
    req.user.id,
    req.body
)
      |
      v
User Model

Security Concern:
The client may be able to modify fields that were not intended to be user-controlled.

Recommendation:
Define an explicit allowlist of writable profile fields and construct the update object from those validated fields.

docs.title: Example Finding - Stored XSS
docs.text:
Title:
Stored Cross-Site Scripting Through Unescaped EJS Output

Source:
req.body.biography

Data Flow:

POST /profile
      |
      v
req.body.biography
      |
      v
Database
      |
      v
<%- biography %>
      |
      v
Browser

Security Control:
Template output escaping is explicitly bypassed for the stored value.

Recommendation:
Use escaped template output for attacker-controlled values. If rich HTML is required, use an appropriate allowlist-based HTML sanitisation strategy.

docs.text:
Incorrect.

Authentication may exist at:

app.use()
router.use()
Parent router
Reverse proxy
API gateway

Trace the complete request path.

docs.text:

It usually establishes identity.

Role
