docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Secrets and configuration review should answer:

What security-sensitive configuration exists?

Which configuration is effective in production?

Where are secrets stored?

How are secrets loaded?

Where are secrets used?

Can secrets reach logs, responses, bundles, or diagnostics?

Are production security settings safe?

Can environment overrides weaken them?

Do containers or deployment manifests introduce additional risk?

Does CI/CD expose credentials?

Does runtime behaviour match the source configuration?

The workflow is:

Discover Configuration
        |
        v
Identify Environments
        |
        v
Understand Precedence
        |
        v
Discover Secrets
        |
        v
Search Git History
        |
        v
Review Security Settings
        |
        v
Review Deployment
        |
        v
Review CI/CD
        |
        v
Trace Configuration Into Code
        |
        v
Runtime Validation
        |
        v
Variant Analysis

The final rule is:

Do not review configuration as isolated text.

Trace it into the security behaviour it controls.

and:

Do not report a secret-looking value solely because it
looks sensitive.

Determine what it represents, where it is used, and what
security impact its exposure creates.

and:

Do not assume the default configuration is the deployed
configuration.

Determine the effective configuration.

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text:
Source-to-sink analysis is one of the most important techniques in security source code review.

The objective is to determine whether attacker-controlled data can travel from an application entry point to a security-sensitive operation without sufficient validation, sanitisation, encoding, authorisation, or other security controls.

The fundamental model is:

SOURCE
  |
  v
ATTACKER-CONTROLLED DATA
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATIONS
  |
  +-- parsing
  +-- decoding
  +-- validation
  +-- normalisation
  +-- sanitisation
  +-- encoding
  +-- business logic
  +-- persistence
  |
  v
SINK
  |
  v
SECURITY-SENSITIVE OPERATION

Examples include:

HTTP Parameter
      |
      v
String Concatenation
      |
      v
SQL Execution

HTTP Parameter
      |
      v
Command Builder
      |
      v
Process Execution

User-Supplied URL
      |
      v
URL Parser
      |
      v
HTTP Client

Uploaded Filename
      |
      v
Path Construction
      |
      v
Filesystem Write

The presence of a source and sink alone does not prove a vulnerability.

Source
  +
Sink
  !=
Vulnerability

The complete question is:

Can attacker-controlled data
reach a security-sensitive sink
through a feasible execution path
without an effective security control?

docs.title: Authorised Testing
docs.text:
Use these techniques only when reviewing applications, repositories, and environments that you are authorised to assess.

Source code analysis can reveal sensitive information including:

Credentials
API keys
Internal endpoints
Database structure
Authentication logic
Authorisation logic
Cryptographic material
Infrastructure information
Business logic

Handle source code and findings according to the assessment rules of engagement.

docs.title: Why Source-to-Sink Analysis Matters
docs.text:
Searching for dangerous functions is useful.

For example:

rg -n 'Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder' .

may reveal command-execution functionality.

But:

Dangerous Sink Found
        |
        v
Vulnerability?

cannot be answered yet.

The sink may receive:

Hardcoded data
Trusted configuration
Administrator-controlled data
Validated input
Allowlisted values
Attacker-controlled data

Only the last case, or another attacker-influenced path, may create a vulnerability.

Therefore:

Sink Discovery
      |
      v
Data-Flow Analysis
      |
      v
Control Analysis
      |
      v
Reachability Analysis
      |
      v
Exploitability Analysis

docs.title: The Core Security Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

ENTRY POINT
     |
     v
SOURCE
     |
     v
PROPAGATION
     |
     v
TRANSFORMATION
     |
     v
SECURITY CONTROL
     |
     v
SINK
     |
     v
IMPACT

Each stage should be investigated separately.

docs.title: Entry Point
docs.text:
An entry point is where execution enters application-controlled code.

Examples:

HTTP route
REST endpoint
GraphQL resolver
gRPC method
WebSocket handler
Message queue consumer
Webhook handler
Background job
Scheduled task
CLI interface
File import
Event handler
Serverless function

An entry point is not necessarily a source.

For example:

@GetMapping("/health")
public String health() {
    return "OK";
}

This is an entry point but does not contain attacker-controlled input.

docs.title: Source
docs.text:
A source is where potentially attacker-controlled data enters the data flow.

Typical sources include:

Query parameters
Route parameters
Request bodies
HTTP headers
Cookies
Uploaded files
Uploaded filenames
GraphQL arguments
gRPC request fields
WebSocket messages
Webhook payloads
Queue messages
Environment-dependent external data
Database values originally supplied by users

docs.title: Sink
docs.text:
A sink is a security-sensitive operation.

Typical sink categories include:

Database execution
OS command execution
Dynamic code execution
Template evaluation
HTML rendering
HTTP requests
Filesystem operations
XML parsing
Deserialisation
LDAP queries
Redirects
Authentication decisions
Authorisation decisions
Cryptographic operations
Sensitive logging

A sink can be dangerous without being vulnerable.

docs.title: Transformations
docs.text:
Between source and sink, data may be transformed.

Example:

Request Parameter
       |
       v
URL Decode
       |
       v
Trim
       |
       v
Lowercase
       |
       v
Regex Validation
       |
       v
Database Lookup
       |
       v
Command Builder
       |
       v
Process Execution

Every transformation matters.

docs.title: Security Controls
docs.text:
Potential controls include:

Allowlisting
Type validation
Range validation
Canonicalisation
Path containment
Parameterised queries
Context-aware output encoding
URL validation
Authentication
Authorisation
CSRF validation
Cryptographic verification
Safe API usage
Sandboxing

The reviewer must determine whether the control is effective for the specific sink.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
A technically interesting flow is not necessarily a meaningful security vulnerability.

Determine what the sink allows.

Examples:

Database Read
Database Write
Command Execution
Internal HTTP Request
Arbitrary File Read
Arbitrary File Write
Cross-User Data Access
Privilege Change
Session Creation
HTML/JavaScript Execution
Sensitive Information Disclosure

docs.title: Forward Analysis
docs.text:
Forward analysis begins at a source.

SOURCE
  |
  v
Where does the data go?

Example:

@GetMapping("/search")
public String search(
    @RequestParam String q
) {
    return searchService.search(q);
}

Start with:

q

Then trace:

q
 |
 v
searchService.search()
 |
 v
repository.search()
 |
 v
SQL query

docs.title: Forward Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
Source
  |
  v
Find References
  |
  v
Assignments
  |
  v
Function Arguments
  |
  v
Return Values
  |
  v
Object Properties
  |
  v
Transformations
  |
  v
Sink

Forward analysis is useful when:

A suspicious parameter exists
A new endpoint is being reviewed
An uploaded file is processed
A webhook payload is consumed
A GraphQL argument is interesting
A security-sensitive request field exists

docs.title: Reverse Analysis
docs.text:
Reverse analysis begins at a sink.

SINK
  |
  v
Where does its data come from?

Example:

Runtime
    .getRuntime()
    .exec(command);

Start with:

command

Then trace backwards:

Runtime.exec()
      ^
      |
command
      ^
      |
buildCommand()
      ^
      |
host
      ^
      |
@RequestParam

docs.title: Reverse Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
Dangerous Sink
      |
      v
Inspect Arguments
      |
      v
Find Assignments
      |
      v
Trace Return Values
      |
      v
Trace Callers
      |
      v
Trace Controllers
      |
      v
Identify Source

Reverse analysis is often highly efficient because dangerous sinks are usually less numerous than application inputs.

docs.title: Bidirectional Analysis
docs.text:
The strongest approach combines both directions.

SOURCE
  |
  v
Forward Trace
  |
  v
Potential Sink

AND

SINK
  |
  v
Reverse Trace
  |
  v
Potential Source

If both analyses meet:

SOURCE
  |
  v
FLOW
  |
  v
SINK

the candidate deserves closer review.

docs.title: Recommended Review Strategy
docs.text:
Use:

1. Map entry points

2. Identify sources

3. Identify dangerous sinks

4. Trace important sources forward

5. Trace dangerous sinks backwards

6. Identify where the traces meet

7. Review transformations

8. Review security controls

9. Establish reachability

10. Establish attacker control

11. Establish impact

12. Validate dynamically where appropriate

13. Search for variants

docs.title: Visual Studio Code Workflow
docs.text:
Visual Studio Code is particularly useful for manual source-to-sink tracing.

Open the repository:

code .

Useful features include:

Global Search
Go to Definition
Peek Definition
Find All References
Call Hierarchy
Workspace Symbols
Integrated Terminal
Git History
Breakpoints
Debugger

docs.title: Global Search
docs.text:
Use:

Ctrl + Shift + F

to search across the repository.

Useful searches include:

exec(
Process.Start
Runtime.getRuntime
HttpClient
requests.get
fetch(
innerHTML
executeQuery
FromSqlRaw
pickle.loads
ObjectInputStream
redirect(

docs.title: Go to Definition
docs.text:
Use:

F12

to follow:

Controller
   |
   v
Service
   |
   v
Repository

docs.title: Find All References
docs.text:
Use:

Shift + F12

This is extremely useful for reverse sink analysis.

Example:

Dangerous Helper

executeCommand()
      |
      +--> Controller A
      +--> Controller B
      +--> Worker
      +--> Admin API

One helper may expose several attack paths.

docs.title: Call Hierarchy
docs.text:
Call Hierarchy can help understand:

Who calls this method?

and:

What does this method call?

This is especially useful in:

Java
C#
TypeScript
JavaScript
Python

when language-server support is available.

docs.title: Workspace Symbols
docs.text:
Use:

Ctrl + T

to search symbols across the project.

Useful when searching for:

Controllers
Services
Repositories
Security classes
Validators
Upload handlers
HTTP clients
Command wrappers

docs.title: Split Editor Workflow
docs.text:
A useful layout is:

+---------------------------------------------+
| Controller              | Sink              |
|                         |                   |
| UserController          | CommandService    |
|                         |                   |
+-------------------------+-------------------+
| Service                 | Notes             |
|                         |                   |
| UserService             | Source -> Sink    |
+-------------------------+-------------------+

Keep:

Source
Intermediate Function
Sink

visible simultaneously where possible.

docs.title: Trace Variables, Not Just Function Names
docs.text:
Consider:

String host =
    request.getParameter("host");

String target =
    host.trim();

String command =
    "ping " + target;

execute(command);

Trace:

request.getParameter("host")
          |
          v
        host
          |
          v
      host.trim()
          |
          v
        target
          |
          v
   "ping " + target
          |
          v
       command
          |
          v
      execute()

Do not lose track of attacker influence merely because the variable name changes.

docs.title: Assignment Propagation
docs.text:
Simple propagation:

user_input = request.args.get("url")
target = user_input
value = target
requests.get(value)

Flow:

request.args
     |
     v
user_input
     |
     v
target
     |
     v
value
     |
     v
requests.get

docs.title: Function Argument Propagation
docs.text:
Example:

def handler():
    value = request.args.get("url")
    fetch(value)

def fetch(target):
    requests.get(target)

Flow:

request.args
     |
     v
value
     |
     v
fetch(value)
     |
     v
target
     |
     v
requests.get(target)

docs.title: Return Value Propagation
docs.text:
Example:

def get_target():
    return request.args.get("url")

def handler():
    target = get_target()
    requests.get(target)

Flow:

request.args
     |
     v
get_target()
     |
     v
return value
     |
     v
target
     |
     v
requests.get()

docs.title: Object Property Propagation
docs.text:
Example:

const requestData = {
    target: req.query.url
};

service.fetch(requestData);

Later:

function fetch(data) {
    return axios.get(data.target);
}

Flow:

req.query.url
     |
     v
requestData.target
     |
     v
data.target
     |
     v
axios.get()

docs.title: DTO Propagation
docs.text:
Enterprise applications frequently move data through DTOs.

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Request DTO
     |
     v
Service DTO
     |
     v
Domain Object
     |
     v
Repository

Do not stop tracing because input has been converted into an object.

docs.title: Collection Propagation
docs.text:
Attacker-controlled data may pass through:

Lists
Arrays
Maps
Dictionaries
Sets
Queues

Example:

targets = []

targets.append(
    request.args.get("url")
)

for target in targets:
    requests.get(target)

The source remains attacker-controlled.

docs.title: String Transformation
docs.text:
Common transformations include:

Concatenation
Interpolation
Formatting
Replacement
Trimming
Case conversion
Substring
Encoding
Decoding
Escaping

Example:

host = request.args.get("host")

command = f"ping -c 1 {host}"

os.system(command)

The string transformation does not remove attacker control.

docs.title: Encoding Is Not Automatically Sanitisation
docs.text:
Example:

Base64 Encode
URL Encode
JSON Encode
HTML Encode

Encoding changes representation.

It does not necessarily make input safe for another context.

URL Encoding
    !=
Command Injection Protection

Base64
    !=
SQL Injection Protection

docs.title: Decoding Can Reintroduce Dangerous Input
docs.text:
Example:

Request
   |
   v
Validation
   |
   v
URL Decode
   |
   v
Sink

Ask:

Was validation performed before or after decoding?

Canonicalisation order matters.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Validation attempts to determine whether input is acceptable.

Examples:

Type checks
Length checks
Regex
Allowlist
Range checks
Enum validation
Schema validation

Example:

if host not in allowed_hosts:
    abort(400)

requests.get(host)

This may provide meaningful protection depending on how allowed_hosts is defined and how the HTTP request is constructed.

docs.title: Allowlisting
docs.text:
Allowlisting is often stronger than denylisting.

Example:

allowed = {
    "api.example.com",
    "images.example.com"
}

if hostname not in allowed:
    raise ValueError()

fetch(url)

But review:

URL parsing
DNS resolution
Redirects
Port handling
Scheme handling
Userinfo
Case normalisation
Trailing dots
Internationalised domain names

A conceptually correct allowlist can still be implemented incorrectly.

docs.title: Denylisting
docs.text:
Example:

if "127.0.0.1" in url:
    reject()

This may be insufficient because alternative representations or other internal destinations may exist.

Do not automatically report bypassability.

Determine whether the complete validation logic can actually be bypassed.

docs.title: Sanitisation
docs.text:
Sanitisation modifies data to make it safe for a particular sink.

Example:

Attacker HTML
     |
     v
HTML Sanitizer
     |
     v
innerHTML

The security question becomes:

Is the sanitizer appropriate?

Is it configured correctly?

Is sanitisation applied after the final transformation?

Can later operations undo the protection?

Is the output used in the expected context?

docs.title: Context Matters
docs.text:
Protection effective for one sink may be irrelevant for another.

HTML Encoding
    protects
HTML Text Context

but does not necessarily protect
    |
    +--> JavaScript
    +--> SQL
    +--> Shell
    +--> LDAP
    +--> Filesystem

Similarly:

SQL parameterisation

does not protect:

OS command execution

docs.title: Safe API Usage
docs.text:
Sometimes the strongest protection is using a safer API.

For SQL:

String Concatenation
      |
      v
Raw Query

versus:

Parameterized Query

For process execution:

Shell Command String

versus:

Executable + Argument Array

Even safer APIs still require review for context-specific risks.

docs.title: Reachability
docs.text:
A source-to-sink flow matters only if the code can execute.

Ask:

Is the route registered?

Is the feature enabled?

Is the code dead?

Is the function called?

Is the configuration active?

Is the endpoint exposed?

Is the branch reachable?

Is the environment relevant?

docs.title: Dead Code
docs.text:
Example:

if False:
    os.system(request.args.get("cmd"))

A scanner may find:

os.system

but the path is not normally reachable.

Do not report solely from textual evidence.

docs.title: Feature Flags
docs.text:
Example:

if FEATURE_DIAGNOSTICS:
    execute_command()

Determine:

Is the feature enabled in production?

Can users influence the feature flag?

Does another environment expose it?

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
A vulnerable sink may require authentication.

That affects:

Attack prerequisites
Severity
Exploitability

but does not automatically eliminate the vulnerability.

Document:

Unauthenticated
Authenticated user
Privileged user
Administrator
Service account

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Authorisation answers:

Are you allowed to do this?

Source-to-sink analysis must include both where relevant.

Example:

User-Controlled Document ID
          |
          v
Database Lookup
          |
          v
Document Returned

The missing security control may not be input validation.

It may be:

Ownership Check

docs.title: Security Controls Are Part of the Flow
docs.text:
For access control:

Request
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Object ID
   |
   v
Object Lookup
   |
   v
Authorisation
   |
   v
Sensitive Operation

The reviewer should verify:

Authorisation occurs
at the correct point
for the correct object
using the correct identity

docs.title: Source-to-Sink for SQL Injection
docs.text:
Model:

HTTP Input
    |
    v
SQL Construction
    |
    v
SQL Execution

Potential sources:

Query parameter
Route parameter
JSON field
Header
Cookie
Stored user data

Potential sinks:

execute()
executeQuery()
raw()
query()
FromSqlRaw()
createNativeQuery()

docs.title: Vulnerable SQL Pattern
docs.text:
username = request.args.get("username")

query = (
    "SELECT * FROM users "
    "WHERE username = '" +
    username +
    "'"
)

cursor.execute(query)

Flow:

request.args
     |
     v
username
     |
     v
SQL concatenation
     |
     v
cursor.execute()

docs.title: Safer SQL Pattern
docs.text:
username = request.args.get("username")

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s",
    (username,)
)

Here:

User Input
    |
    v
SQL Parameter

rather than:

User Input
    |
    v
SQL Syntax

docs.title: Stored / Second-Order SQL Injection
docs.text:
Do not only trace direct request flows.

HTTP Input
    |
    v
Database
    |
    v
Later Retrieval
    |
    v
SQL Construction
    |
    v
SQL Execution

The source may be temporally separated from the sink.

docs.title: Command Injection
docs.text:
Model:

HTTP Input
    |
    v
Command Construction
    |
    v
Process Execution

Potential sinks:

Runtime.exec
ProcessBuilder
Process.Start
os.system
subprocess
child_process.exec
shell_exec
system
exec

docs.title: Java Example
docs.text:
String host =
    request.getParameter("host");

Runtime
    .getRuntime()
    .exec(
        "ping " + host
    );

Flow:

request.getParameter
        |
        v
      host
        |
        v
concatenation
        |
        v
Runtime.exec

docs.title: .NET Example
docs.text:
var host =
    Request.Query["host"];

Process.Start(
    "cmd.exe",
    "/c ping " + host
);

Trace:

Request.Query
     |
     v
host
     |
     v
Process.Start

docs.title: Node.js Example
docs.text:
const host =
    req.query.host;

exec(
    `ping ${host}`
);

Trace:

req.query.host
     |
     v
template literal
     |
     v
exec()

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker-Controlled URL
          |
          v
URL Processing
          |
          v
HTTP Client

Potential sinks include:

HttpClient
requests
httpx
urllib
fetch
axios
RestTemplate
WebClient

docs.title: Python SSRF Example
docs.text:
url =
    request.args.get("url")

response =
    requests.get(url)

Flow:

request.args
     |
     v
url
     |
     v
requests.get()

Then review controls:

Scheme validation
Hostname validation
IP validation
DNS behaviour
Redirect handling
Port restrictions
Private address restrictions
Cloud metadata restrictions

docs.title: SSRF Through Helper
docs.text:
def preview(url):
    return requests.get(url)

def endpoint():
    target =
        request.args.get("url")

    return preview(target)

Trace:

request.args
     |
     v
target
     |
     v
preview()
     |
     v
url
     |
     v
requests.get()

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker-Controlled Path
          |
          v
Path Construction
          |
          v
Filesystem Operation

Potential sinks:

open()
File.ReadAllText
File.WriteAllText
Files.readString
send_file
fs.readFile
fs.writeFile

docs.title: Python Example
docs.text:
filename =
    request.args.get("file")

path =
    "/var/data/" + filename

return open(path).read()

Trace:

request.args
     |
     v
filename
     |
     v
path
     |
     v
open()

docs.title: Path Normalisation
docs.text:
A common pattern:

Input
  |
  v
Normalize
  |
  v
Filesystem

Normalisation alone may not ensure that the final path remains inside the intended directory.

Review:

Canonical path
Base directory
Containment check
Symlinks
Absolute paths
Platform path semantics

docs.title: File Upload
docs.text:
File upload contains several independent sources:

Uploaded File
     |
     +--> Filename
     +--> Extension
     +--> MIME type
     +--> Content
     +--> Size
     +--> Metadata

Each can flow to different sinks.

docs.title: Filename Flow
docs.text:
Original Filename
       |
       v
Path Construction
       |
       v
File Write

Potential issue:

Path Traversal

docs.title: File Content Flow
docs.text:
Uploaded Content
       |
       v
Parser
       |
       v
Image / PDF / XML / Archive Processor

Potential issues:

Parser vulnerabilities
XXE
Archive extraction issues
Unsafe deserialisation
Command execution
Resource exhaustion

docs.title: Archive Extraction
docs.text:
Trace:

Archive Entry Name
       |
       v
Destination Path
       |
       v
Filesystem Write

Review path containment after extraction path resolution.

docs.title: XXE
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker XML
     |
     v
XML Parser
     |
     v
External Entity Resolution

The sink is not merely:

XML parser exists

The important configuration includes:

DTD handling
External entities
External resources
Resolver configuration
Parser defaults

docs.title: Deserialisation
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker-Controlled Serialized Data
               |
               v
           Deserializer

Potential sinks include:

ObjectInputStream
pickle.loads
BinaryFormatter
YAML unsafe loaders
Language-specific object serializers

A deserializer is not automatically vulnerable.

Establish attacker control.

docs.title: SSTI
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker Input
     |
     v
Template Source
     |
     v
Template Engine

Important distinction:

Template Data

versus:

Template Source

Example:

render_template(
    "profile.html",
    username=user_input
)

is different from:

render_template_string(
    user_input
)

docs.title: Server-Side XSS Analysis
docs.text:
Model:

HTTP Input
    |
    v
Application
    |
    v
HTML Generation
    |
    v
Browser

Review:

Template autoescaping
Manual raw output
Context
Encoding
Sanitisation

docs.title: DOM XSS
docs.text:
Model:

Browser Source
      |
      v
JavaScript
      |
      v
DOM Sink

Sources include:

location.search
location.hash
location.href
document.URL
document.referrer
window.name
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage

Sinks include:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write
eval
Function
srcdoc

docs.title: DOM XSS Example
docs.text:
const value =
    new URLSearchParams(
        location.search
    ).get("message");

output.innerHTML =
    value;

Flow:

location.search
      |
      v
URLSearchParams
      |
      v
value
      |
      v
innerHTML

docs.title: HTML Injection
docs.text:
Not every HTML sink results in JavaScript execution.

Trace:

Attacker Input
     |
     v
HTML Interpretation

Then determine actual impact:

Markup injection
UI manipulation
Phishing
Form injection
Potential XSS

Do not automatically classify HTML injection as XSS.

docs.title: Open Redirect
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker-Controlled URL
          |
          v
Redirect Sink

Potential sinks:

redirect()
Response.Redirect()
sendRedirect()
location.href
location.assign()
location.replace()

Review validation of:

Scheme
Host
Path
Relative URLs
Protocol-relative URLs
Parsing
Normalisation

docs.title: LDAP Injection
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker Input
     |
     v
LDAP Filter Construction
     |
     v
LDAP Search

Review:

LDAP filter escaping
DN escaping
Filter construction
Framework API

LDAP DN and LDAP filter contexts require different handling.

docs.title: NoSQL Injection
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker Input
     |
     v
Query Object
     |
     v
NoSQL Database

Especially review cases where structured input is passed directly into query objects.

Example:

const filter =
    req.body.filter;

const result =
    await users.find(filter);

Trace whether attackers can control:

Operators
Nested objects
Query structure
Regular expressions

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Model:

Request Body
     |
     v
Automatic Object Binding
     |
     v
Domain Object
     |
     v
Database

Sensitive properties may include:

isAdmin
role
permissions
ownerId
tenantId
balance
status
verified

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
IDOR/BOLA is a source-to-security-decision problem.

Attacker-Controlled Object ID
           |
           v
Object Retrieval
           |
           v
Authorisation?
           |
           v
Sensitive Operation

The sink may be:

Read object
Modify object
Delete object
Download object
Execute action

docs.title: IDOR Example
docs.text:
@app.get("/documents/<id>")
def document(id):

    return Document.query.get(id)

Trace:

Route Parameter
      |
      v
id
      |
      v
Database Lookup
      |
      v
Document

Then ask:

Where is ownership checked?

docs.title: Business Logic
docs.text:
Not all source-to-sink flows end in classic dangerous APIs.

Example:

User-Controlled Quantity
        |
        v
Price Calculation
        |
        v
Payment

or:

User-Controlled Role
        |
        v
Account Update

or:

Coupon
   |
   v
Discount
   |
   v
Order Total

The sink may be a security-sensitive business action.

docs.title: Security-Sensitive Business Sinks
docs.text:
Examples:

Transfer money
Approve payment
Change email
Change password
Assign role
Reset MFA
Delete account
Invite administrator
Change ownership
Generate refund
Redeem voucher
Create API key

docs.title: Authentication Flow Analysis
docs.text:
Model:

Credentials
    |
    v
Authentication Logic
    |
    v
Identity
    |
    v
Session / Token

Trace:

Password verification
MFA verification
Session creation
JWT creation
OAuth callback
SAML assertion
Recovery flow

docs.title: JWT Flow
docs.text:
Token
  |
  v
Parse
  |
  v
Signature Verification
  |
  v
Claims Validation
  |
  v
Identity
  |
  v
Authorisation

Do not stop at:

JWT successfully verifies

Review:

Issuer
Audience
Expiration
Algorithm
Key selection
Claims
Role mapping
Authorisation

docs.title: OAuth / OIDC Flow
docs.text:
Authorization Response
         |
         v
Callback
         |
         v
state / nonce / PKCE
         |
         v
Token Exchange
         |
         v
Token Validation
         |
         v
Identity Mapping
         |
         v
Session

docs.title: SAML Flow
docs.text:
SAMLResponse
     |
     v
XML Parser
     |
     v
Signature Validation
     |
     v
Assertion Validation
     |
     v
Identity Mapping
     |
     v
Session

docs.title: Password Reset Flow
docs.text:
Reset Request
     |
     v
Token Generation
     |
     v
URL Generation
     |
     v
Delivery
     |
     v
Token Validation
     |
     v
Password Change

Trace all attacker-influenced values including:

Host headers
Email address
Reset token
User identifier
Redirect URL

docs.title: WebSocket Flow
docs.text:
WebSocket Message
       |
       v
Message Parser
       |
       v
Message Handler
       |
       v
Authorisation
       |
       v
Sensitive Operation

Authentication at connection time does not necessarily provide per-message authorisation.

docs.title: GraphQL Flow
docs.text:
GraphQL Argument
      |
      v
Resolver
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
Authorisation
      |
      v
Database / Sink

Review:

Resolver-level authorisation
Object-level authorisation
Field-level authorisation
Mutations
Subscriptions
Nested resolvers

docs.title: gRPC Flow
docs.text:
gRPC Request
     |
     v
RPC Handler
     |
     v
Interceptor
     |
     v
Service
     |
     v
Security-Sensitive Operation

Trace:

Request fields
Metadata
Identity
Object IDs
Authorisation
Streaming messages

docs.title: Webhook Flow
docs.text:
External Request
      |
      v
Webhook Endpoint
      |
      v
Signature Verification
      |
      v
Payload Processing
      |
      v
Sensitive Operation

The critical security control may be cryptographic authenticity rather than ordinary authentication.

docs.title: Queue Consumer Flow
docs.text:
Queue Message
     |
     v
Consumer
     |
     v
Parser
     |
     v
Business Logic
     |
     v
Sink

Do not automatically trust internal queue messages.

Ask:

Who can publish messages?

Can external input reach the queue?

Is message authenticity enforced?

Can another compromised service influence it?

docs.title: Background Job Flow
docs.text:
HTTP Input
     |
     v
Database
     |
     v
Scheduled Job
     |
     v
Dangerous Sink

This is a common second-order flow.

docs.title: Persistence Boundaries
docs.text:
A source-to-sink path may cross:

Database
Cache
File
Queue
Object storage
Session
Message broker

Example:

Attacker Input
      |
      v
Database
      |
      v
Later Worker
      |
      v
Template Engine

Do not assume the database makes input trusted.

docs.title: Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
Mark transitions such as:

Internet
   |
   v
Reverse Proxy
   |
   v
Web Application
   |
   v
Internal API
   |
   v
Database

and:

Browser
   |
   v
API
   |
   v
Queue
   |
   v
Worker

Data crossing an internal boundary may still be attacker-controlled.

docs.title: Trust Is Not Sanitisation
docs.text:
A common mistake:

Data came from our database
        =
Trusted

Incorrect.

The database may contain attacker-controlled values.

Likewise:

Internal API
Queue
Cache
Configuration service

can propagate attacker-controlled data.

docs.title: Multi-Stage Data Flow
docs.text:
Example:

POST /profile
      |
      v
display_name
      |
      v
Database
      |
      v
GET /admin/users
      |
      v
Admin Template
      |
      v
Raw HTML Output

This may create:

Stored XSS

The source and sink occur in different requests.

docs.title: Cross-Service Data Flow
docs.text:
Modern applications may involve:

Service A
    |
    v
API
    |
    v
Service B
    |
    v
Queue
    |
    v
Service C

A single repository may show only part of the flow.

Document:

Known Flow
Unknown Boundary
Expected Downstream Processing

Do not invent behaviour not supported by the available source.

docs.title: Source Classification
docs.text:
Classify sources.

Source Typical Trust Query parameter Untrusted Request body Untrusted Route parameter Untrusted Header Untrusted Cookie Untrusted Uploaded file Untrusted Database field Depends on origin Environment variable Configuration-dependent Internal API Depends on trust boundary Queue message Depends on producer Hardcoded constant Usually trusted

docs.title: Sink Classification
docs.text:
Classify sinks by security impact.

Sink Potential Impact SQL execution SQL injection Process execution Command injection HTTP client SSRF Filesystem read Path traversal / file disclosure Filesystem write Arbitrary file write Template evaluation SSTI HTML sink XSS / HTML injection Deserializer Unsafe deserialisation XML parser XXE LDAP query LDAP injection Redirect Open redirect Object lookup IDOR / BOLA Role update Privilege escalation

docs.title: Prioritising Sinks
docs.text:
A useful priority model:

Critical Review Priority
    |
    +--> OS command execution
    +--> Dynamic code execution
    +--> Unsafe deserialisation
    +--> Raw SQL
    +--> Arbitrary file write
    +--> Template evaluation

Then:

High Review Priority
    |
    +--> HTTP clients
    +--> Filesystem reads
    +--> XML parsers
    +--> LDAP queries
    +--> Sensitive object access
    +--> Role / permission changes

Priority is for review efficiency, not automatic severity.

docs.title: ripgrep Workflow
docs.text:
Use ripgrep for fast discovery.

General pattern:

rg -n -i 'pattern' .

docs.title: Find Command Execution Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder|Process\.Start|os\.system|subprocess|child_process|exec\(|shell_exec|system\(' \
.

docs.title: Find HTTP Client Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'HttpClient|RestTemplate|WebClient|requests\.(get|post|put|delete)|httpx\.|urllib|axios\.|fetch\(' \
.

docs.title: Find File Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'File\.Read|File\.Write|Files\.read|Files\.write|open\(|readFile|writeFile|send_file|sendFile' \
.

docs.title: Find SQL Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'executeQuery|executeUpdate|cursor\.execute|FromSqlRaw|ExecuteSqlRaw|createNativeQuery|raw\(|query\(' \
.

docs.title: Find Dynamic Execution
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'eval\(|exec\(|Function\(|compile\(' \
.

docs.title: Find Deserialisation
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'ObjectInputStream|pickle\.loads|pickle\.load|BinaryFormatter|yaml\.load|deserialize|unserialize' \
.

docs.title: Find Sources
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'request\.args|request\.form|request\.json|request\.files|req\.query|req\.params|req\.body|Request\.Query|Request\.Form|Request\.Headers|@RequestParam|@PathVariable|@RequestBody' \
.

docs.title: ripgrep Is Discovery, Not Proof
docs.text:
rg match
   |
   v
Candidate
   |
   v
Manual Trace

Never:

rg match
   =
Vulnerability

docs.title: Semgrep / OpenGrep
docs.text:
Semgrep and OpenGrep can identify structural patterns.

Instead of:

Find text containing exec

they can reason about code patterns.

Example conceptual rule:

rules:
  - id: python-command-execution
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review process execution
    severity: WARNING
    patterns:
      - pattern-either:
          - pattern: os.system(...)
          - pattern: subprocess.$FUNC(...)

This still identifies a candidate sink rather than proving command injection.

docs.title: Taint Analysis
docs.text:
A stronger static-analysis rule can model:

Source
   |
   v
Propagation
   |
   v
Sink

Conceptually:

mode: taint

pattern-sources:
  - ...

pattern-sinks:
  - ...

This is closer to manual source-to-sink reasoning.

docs.title: CodeQL
docs.text:
CodeQL is useful when flows become more complex.

Source
   |
   v
Function
   |
   v
Object
   |
   v
Service
   |
   v
Sink

CodeQL can perform:

Local data flow
Global data flow
Taint tracking
Path queries
Semantic queries
Variant analysis

Use CodeQL when simple structural matching does not provide enough context.

docs.title: Static Analysis Tool Model
docs.text:
ripgrep
   |
   v
Fast Pattern Discovery
   |
   v
Semgrep / OpenGrep
   |
   v
Structural / Taint Analysis
   |
   v
CodeQL
   |
   v
Deeper Semantic/Data-Flow Analysis
   |
   v
VS Code
   |
   v
Manual Validation

docs.title: Scanner Result Triage
docs.text:
For every static-analysis result ask:

1. What is the source?

2. Is it attacker-controlled?

3. What is the sink?

4. Is the sink security-sensitive?

5. What transformations occur?

6. What validation occurs?

7. What sanitisation occurs?

8. What authentication is required?

9. What authorisation is required?

10. Is the path reachable?

11. Is the flow feasible?

12. What is the impact?

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Worksheet
docs.text:
Use a repeatable worksheet.

Candidate:
STS-001

Entry Point:
POST /api/diagnostics

Source:
JSON field "host"

Source Location:
DiagnosticsController.java:42

Attacker Controlled:
Yes / No / Unknown

Transformations:
1.
2.
3.

Validation:
...

Sanitisation:
...

Authentication:
...

Authorisation:
...

Sink:
Runtime.exec()

Sink Location:
DiagnosticService.java:81

Flow:
DiagnosticsController
    -> DiagnosticService
    -> CommandBuilder
    -> Runtime.exec

Reachable:
Yes / No / Unknown

Runtime Preconditions:
...

Potential Impact:
...

Dynamic Validation:
...

Status:
Investigating / Confirmed / Rejected

docs.title: Draw the Flow
docs.text:
For complex findings, draw the complete flow.

Example:

POST /api/diagnostics
          |
          v
DiagnosticsRequest.host
          |
          v
DiagnosticsController.run()
          |
          v
DiagnosticsService.ping()
          |
          v
CommandBuilder.build()
          |
          v
"ping " + host
          |
          v
Runtime.exec()

Then add controls:

POST /api/diagnostics
          |
          v
Authentication
          |
          v
DiagnosticsRequest.host
          |
          v
Regex Validation
          |
          v
CommandBuilder
          |
          v
Runtime.exec()

This makes it easier to determine whether the validation actually breaks the dangerous flow.

docs.title: Security Control Inventory
docs.text:
During review, identify reusable controls.

Examples:

InputValidator
UrlValidator
PathValidator
HtmlSanitizer
AuthorizationService
PermissionChecker
SafeCommandRunner
RepositoryBase
SecurityMiddleware

Then search for:

Where is the control used?

Where is it not used?

docs.title: Missing-Control Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose the safe pattern is:

Controller
    |
    v
checkOwnership()
    |
    v
repository.get()

Search for variants:

Controller
    |
    v
repository.get()

without the expected ownership check.

This is especially powerful for:

IDOR
BOLA
Privilege escalation
Tenant isolation
Administrative actions

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Once one vulnerability is confirmed:

Confirmed Finding
      |
      v
Identify Root Cause
      |
      +--> Source
      +--> Sink
      +--> Missing Control
      +--> Unsafe Helper
      |
      v
Search Entire Repository

docs.title: Variant Analysis Example
docs.text:
Known vulnerable path:

req.query.url
     |
     v
previewService.fetch()
     |
     v
axios.get()

Search for:

previewService.fetch(

Then inspect every caller.

Also search for:

axios.get
axios.post
fetch
HTTP wrappers

to find equivalent sinks.

docs.title: Wrapper Functions
docs.text:
Dangerous APIs are often wrapped.

Example:

def run_process(command):
    return subprocess.run(
        command,
        shell=True
    )

Searching only:

subprocess

finds the wrapper.

After that, the important sink becomes:

run_process()

Search:

rg -n 'run_process\(' .

This can be more valuable than repeatedly searching the low-level API.

docs.title: HTTP Client Wrappers
docs.text:
Example:

async function fetchRemote(url) {
    return axios.get(url);
}

After identifying this:

axios.get

becomes:

fetchRemote

for application-specific SSRF analysis.

docs.title: Database Wrappers
docs.text:
Example:

public Result runQuery(
    String query
) {
    return jdbcTemplate.queryForList(query);
}

Now search:

runQuery()

and trace its callers.

docs.title: File Wrappers
docs.text:
Example:

public string ReadDocument(
    string path
) {
    return File.ReadAllText(path);
}

The application-specific sink becomes:

ReadDocument()

docs.title: Source Wrappers
docs.text:
Sources can also be wrapped.

Example:

def get_parameter(name):
    return request.args.get(name)

Searching only:

request.args

finds the wrapper but may miss most real sources.

After discovering it, search:

get_parameter(

docs.title: Framework Abstractions
docs.text:
Sources may be hidden behind:

DTO binding
Dependency injection
Framework decorators
Annotations
Resolvers
Middleware
Base controllers
Request contexts

Example:

public void update(
    @Valid UpdateUserRequest request
)

The request object itself contains attacker-controlled fields.

Trace individual properties:

request.email
request.role
request.ownerId

docs.title: Validation Annotations
docs.text:
Annotations such as:

@NotNull
@Size
@Pattern
[Required]
[StringLength]
RegularExpression
Pydantic constraints
Django validators

may provide useful validation.

But verify whether the validation addresses the sink.

Example:

@Size(max=200)

does not automatically prevent:

SQL injection
SSRF
Command injection

docs.title: Validation Placement
docs.text:
Correct validation should occur before dangerous interpretation.

Good conceptual flow:

Source
  |
  v
Decode
  |
  v
Canonicalise
  |
  v
Validate
  |
  v
Sink

Potentially problematic:

Source
  |
  v
Validate
  |
  v
Decode
  |
  v
Sink

because decoding may change the value after validation.

docs.title: Multiple Decoding
docs.text:
Review applications that perform:

URL Decode
HTML Decode
Base64 Decode
Unicode Normalisation
JSON Decode

multiple times.

Flow:

Encoded Input
     |
     v
Validation
     |
     v
Decode
     |
     v
Decode Again
     |
     v
Sink

This can invalidate earlier assumptions.

docs.title: Type Conversion
docs.text:
Type conversion can provide meaningful constraints.

Example:

user_id =
    int(request.args["id"])

This strongly limits the input to an integer if conversion succeeds.

For SQL injection through that value, this may break the relevant dangerous flow.

But it does not automatically solve:

IDOR
BOLA
Business logic

because an attacker can still choose another valid integer.

docs.title: Security Is Sink-Specific
docs.text:
The same validation can have different security meaning.

Integer Conversion

may be strong protection against:

SQL syntax injection

but irrelevant to:

IDOR

This is why source-to-sink analysis must consider the intended sink and security property.

docs.title: Data-Flow Labels
docs.text:
When taking notes, label data.

Example:

[A] attacker-controlled
[T] trusted
[V] validated
[S] sanitised
[E] encoded
[U] unknown

Then:

[A] request.url
        |
        v
[A] target
        |
        v
[V] validateUrl(target)
        |
        v
[?] normalizedTarget
        |
        v
[?] httpClient.get()

This makes uncertain assumptions visible.

docs.title: Do Not Upgrade Unknown to Trusted
docs.text:
If you cannot determine the origin of a value:

UNKNOWN

is the correct classification.

Do not silently assume:

Trusted

or:

Attacker-Controlled

without evidence.

docs.title: Dynamic Validation
docs.text:
Static analysis should guide controlled runtime testing.

Source Code
    |
    v
Candidate Flow
    |
    v
Route Mapping
    |
    v
Burp Suite
    |
    v
Controlled Input
    |
    v
Observe Runtime Behaviour

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify route from source

2. Capture legitimate request

3. Send to Repeater

4. Identify mapped source parameter

5. Modify only the relevant input

6. Observe application behaviour

7. Compare with source expectations

8. Confirm or reject candidate

docs.title: Runtime Validation Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Does the request reach this route?

Does this code path execute?

Does the validation run?

Does the sink execute?

Is the source transformed differently at runtime?

Does middleware modify the input?

Does infrastructure block the request?

Does the framework provide hidden protection?

docs.title: Debugger-Assisted Validation
docs.text:
Where authorised and practical:

Breakpoint at Source
       |
       v
Inspect Input
       |
       v
Step Through Transformations
       |
       v
Breakpoint at Sink
       |
       v
Inspect Final Value

This can provide extremely strong evidence.

docs.title: Example Debug Flow
docs.text:
Request
  |
  v
Breakpoint:
Controller
  |
  v
host = "example"
  |
  v
Step Into:
CommandBuilder
  |
  v
command = "ping example"
  |
  v
Breakpoint:
Runtime.exec

This confirms actual runtime propagation.

docs.title: Unit Tests
docs.text:
Security-focused unit tests can validate assumptions.

Example:

Given:
Untrusted URL

When:
validateUrl()

Then:
Internal destinations rejected

Tests are useful for understanding expected security behaviour.

But:

Passing test
    !=
Complete security

The test may not cover bypass cases.

docs.title: Reporting Source-to-Sink Findings
docs.text:
A strong finding should describe the complete flow.

Avoid:

The application uses Runtime.exec().

Prefer:

The host parameter supplied to POST /api/diagnostics
is passed through DiagnosticsService and concatenated into
a command string that is subsequently supplied to Runtime.exec().
No effective validation preventing command interpretation was
identified along this execution path.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Include:

Entry point
Source
Intermediate functions
Sink
Security controls
Relevant code locations
Runtime evidence
Impact

docs.title: Source Evidence
docs.text:
Example:

File:
src/controllers/DiagnosticsController.java

Line:
42

Source:
@RequestParam String host

docs.title: Sink Evidence
docs.text:
File:
src/services/DiagnosticService.java

Line:
81

Sink:
Runtime.getRuntime().exec(command)

docs.title: Flow Evidence
docs.text:
DiagnosticsController.run()
        |
        v
DiagnosticsService.ping()
        |
        v
CommandBuilder.build()
        |
        v
Runtime.exec()

docs.title: Remediation Should Break the Dangerous Flow
docs.text:
A remediation should address the root cause.

For example:

Attacker Input
     |
     v
Shell Command

could be redesigned to:

Validated Host/IP
     |
     v
Non-Shell Network API

rather than attempting to blacklist shell metacharacters.

docs.title: Defence in Depth
docs.text:
Strong remediation may include:

Safer API
        +
Strict Validation
        +
Least Privilege
        +
Authorisation
        +
Monitoring

Do not rely on one weak control where a safer design exists.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation:

Original Flow
     |
     v
Review Code Change
     |
     v
Verify Control
     |
     v
Runtime Retest
     |
     v
Variant Search

Also determine whether similar vulnerable paths remain elsewhere.

                               |

                                          |

The core rule is:

SOURCE
   +
FLOW
   +
SINK

is still not enough.

A meaningful vulnerability normally requires:

          +
Feasible Data Flow
          +
Reachable Security-Sensitive Sink
          +
Absent or Ineffective Security Control
          +
Security Impact

docs.title: Practical Testing Model
docs.text:
When reviewing any potential source-to-sink vulnerability, answer these questions:

1. Where does the data enter?

2. Who controls it?

3. What transformations occur?

4. Where is it validated?

5. Where is it sanitised?

6. Where is it encoded?

7. Which functions receive it?

8. Which objects store it?

9. Does it cross a persistence boundary?

10. Does it cross a trust boundary?

11. Which security-sensitive sink receives it?

12. Is the sink reachable?

13. What authentication is required?

14. What authorisation is required?

15. Are the controls appropriate for this sink?

16. Can runtime behaviour confirm the flow?

17. What security impact results?

18. Are there similar variants elsewhere?

If those questions can be answered, the source-to-sink path is understood.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Source-to-sink analysis can be reduced to one question:

Can attacker-controlled data reach a security-sensitive operation
through a feasible path without an effective security control?

The practical workflow is:

Map Entry Points
      |
      v
Identify Sources
      |
      v
Identify Sinks
      |
      v
Trace Forward
      |
      v
Trace Backwards
      |
      v
Map Transformations
      |
      v
Review Security Controls
      |
      v
Establish Reachability
      |
      v
Establish Attacker Control
      |
      v
Validate Runtime Behaviour
      |
      v
Determine Impact
      |
      v
Confirm Finding
      |
      v
Search for Variants

The final rule remains:

Sink found
    !=
Vulnerability found

Source reaches sink
    !=
Vulnerability automatically confirmed

Attacker-controlled source
    +
feasible flow
    +
security-sensitive sink
    +
ineffective controls
    +
security impact
    =
meaningful security finding

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Variant analysis is the process of using a known vulnerability, security weakness, or suspicious code pattern to systematically search for similar instances elsewhere in a codebase.

Instead of treating a confirmed vulnerability as an isolated finding:

Confirmed Vulnerability
        |
        v
Fix This Location

variant analysis asks:

Confirmed Vulnerability
        |
        v
What caused it?
        |
        v
What code pattern created it?
        |
        v
Where else does this pattern exist?
        |
        v
Find Related Variants

This is one of the most powerful techniques in source code security review.

A single vulnerability can reveal:

A repeated coding pattern
A missing security control
A dangerous helper
A vulnerable abstraction
A framework misuse
A repeated sink
A missing ownership check
A missing validation function
A dangerous API wrapper
A vulnerable architectural pattern

The objective is therefore not merely:

Find another copy of the vulnerable line

but:

Find every semantically similar path that may produce
the same security weakness.

docs.title: Authorised Testing
docs.text:
Use variant analysis only against source code, applications, and environments that you are authorised to assess.

Variant analysis can reveal large numbers of security-sensitive locations, including:

Administrative functionality
Internal APIs
Authentication logic
Authorisation controls
Database queries
File operations
Network requests
Command execution
Secrets
Debug functionality

Handle discovered information according to the rules of engagement.

docs.title: Why Variant Analysis Matters
docs.text:
Applications rarely contain security bugs in complete isolation.

Developers frequently reuse:

Functions
Libraries
Patterns
Frameworks
Helpers
Services
Controllers
Repository methods
Security controls

Therefore:

One Vulnerability
      |
      v
Underlying Pattern
      |
      v
Potentially Many Variants

For example, if this endpoint contains an IDOR:

GET /documents/{id}

the same object access pattern may exist in:

PUT /documents/{id}
DELETE /documents/{id}
GET /documents/{id}/download
POST /documents/{id}/share

GraphQL:
document(id)
updateDocument(id)
deleteDocument(id)

gRPC:
GetDocument
UpdateDocument
DeleteDocument

WebSocket:
delete-document
share-document

The original finding becomes the starting point for broader analysis.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Variant analysis should begin with understanding the root cause.

Do not search only for the vulnerable string.

Instead determine:

SOURCE
  |
  v
DATA FLOW
  |
  v
MISSING / WEAK CONTROL
  |
  v
SINK
  |
  v
IMPACT

Then search for variations of that pattern.

docs.title: Variant Analysis Model
docs.text:
CONFIRMED FINDING
       |
       v
UNDERSTAND ROOT CAUSE
       |
       v
IDENTIFY SOURCE
       |
       v
IDENTIFY SINK
       |
       v
IDENTIFY MISSING CONTROL
       |
       v
IDENTIFY CODE PATTERN
       |
       v
SEARCH EXACT VARIANTS
       |
       v
SEARCH STRUCTURAL VARIANTS
       |
       v
SEARCH SEMANTIC VARIANTS
       |
       v
TRACE CANDIDATES
       |
       v
VALIDATE
       |
       v
REPEAT

docs.title: A Variant Is Not Necessarily a Duplicate
docs.text:
A duplicate may be almost identical:

repository.findById(id);

appearing in several controllers.

A variant may be structurally different while creating the same security weakness.

Example:

repository.findById(id);

versus:

repository.findOne(
    specification
);

versus:

entityManager.find(
    Document.class,
    id
);

All may ultimately represent:

Attacker-Controlled ID
        |
        v
Object Lookup
        |
        v
Missing Ownership Check

docs.title: Three Levels of Variant Analysis
docs.text:
A practical model is:

Level 1 - Textual Variants

Level 2 - Structural Variants

Level 3 - Semantic Variants

docs.title: Level 1 - Textual Variants
docs.text:
Search for the same:

Function
Method
Class
String
Route
Helper
API
Sink

Tools:

ripgrep
VS Code Search
grep

Example:

rg -n \
'findById\(' \
.

This is fast but can miss semantically equivalent code.

docs.title: Level 2 - Structural Variants
docs.text:
Search for code with the same syntactic structure.

Tools:

Semgrep
OpenGrep
AST-based analysis

Example concept:

Request Parameter
      |
      v
Database Lookup

regardless of exact variable names.

docs.title: Level 3 - Semantic Variants
docs.text:
Search for equivalent data-flow or security behaviour.

Tools:

CodeQL
Taint analysis
Manual source-to-sink tracing
Call graph analysis

Example:

HTTP Request
      |
      v
Controller
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
Repository
      |
      v
Sensitive Sink

even if multiple functions separate source and sink.

docs.title: Start With a Confirmed Finding
docs.text:
Variant analysis is strongest when based on a confirmed vulnerability.

Record:

Finding
Entry point
Source
Transformations
Security controls
Missing security control
Sink
Impact

Example:

Finding:
IDOR

Route:
GET /api/documents/{id}

Source:
id

Lookup:
DocumentRepository.findById(id)

Expected Control:
Ownership validation

Actual Control:
None

Sink:
Document returned to user

Impact:
Another user's document can be retrieved

Now the variant search has a precise target.

docs.title: Root Cause Analysis
docs.text:
Before searching, answer:

Why is this vulnerable?

For example:

Because attacker-controlled object identifiers are used
to retrieve documents without constraining the lookup
to the authenticated user's authorised objects.

This is more useful than:

findById() is vulnerable.

findById() itself is not inherently vulnerable.

docs.title: Extract the Security Pattern
docs.text:
Convert the vulnerability into a reusable model.

ATTACKER-CONTROLLED OBJECT ID
            |
            v
       OBJECT LOOKUP
            |
            v
   NO OWNERSHIP / TENANT CHECK
            |
            v
     SENSITIVE OPERATION

Then search for every implementation of this model.

docs.title: Build a Variant Hypothesis
docs.text:
Before searching, define what variants might look like.

For IDOR:

Same object
Different HTTP method

Same object
Different controller

Same repository
Different route

Same service
Different API

Same object
GraphQL

Same object
gRPC

Same object
WebSocket

Different object
Same vulnerable lookup pattern

docs.text:

REST API     GraphQL
    |

F12

to follow:

    |

docs.title: ripgrep
docs.text:
ripgrep is usually the fastest first step.

If the vulnerability uses:

documentRepository.findById(

search:

rg -n \
'documentRepository\.findById\(' \
.

Then broaden:

rg -n \
'\.findById\(' \
.

Then search related methods:

rg -n \
'\.(findById|findOne|getById|getReferenceById)\(' \
.

docs.title: Search the Object Name
docs.text:
For a vulnerable Document object:

rg -n -i \
'document' \
.

Then narrow:

rg -n \
'DocumentRepository|DocumentService|DocumentController' \
.

docs.title: Search the Sensitive Operation
docs.text:
If the confirmed finding involves:

deleteDocument()

search:

rg -n \
'deleteDocument\(' \
.

and related sinks:

rg -n \
'\.(delete|deleteById|remove|destroy)\(' \
.

Manual triage is required.

docs.title: Search the Missing Security Control
docs.text:
Suppose secure routes normally use:

checkDocumentAccess()

Search:

rg -n \
'checkDocumentAccess\(' \
.

Now compare:

Where is the helper used?

Where is the same sensitive service called without it?

docs.title: Negative Pattern Analysis
docs.text:
This is particularly powerful.

Secure pattern:

loadDocument()
checkDocumentAccess()
returnDocument()

Potential vulnerable pattern:

loadDocument()
returnDocument()

Variant analysis asks:

Where is loadDocument() used without checkDocumentAccess()?

docs.title: Security Helper Inventory
docs.text:
Search for common security helpers:

rg -n -i \
'authori[sz]e|check.?access|check.?permission|verify.?owner|validate.?tenant|can.?access|can.?edit|can.?delete' \
.

Build a list.

Example:

authorizeDocument()
authorizeProject()
checkOwnership()
validateTenant()
requirePermission()

These become useful anchors for variant searches.

docs.title: Search the Sink, Not Only the Source
docs.text:
If a vulnerability ends in:

Runtime.exec()

search every use:

rg -n \
'Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder' \
-g '*.java' \
.

Then trace each sink backwards.

SINK
  ^
  |
INPUT

This is reverse source-to-sink analysis.

docs.title: Forward and Reverse Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Use both directions.

Forward:

Source
  |
  v
Find every path to dangerous sinks

Reverse:

Sink
  |
  v
Find every attacker-controlled path reaching it

Combined:

SOURCE ---> SINK
   \         ^
    \       /
     VARIANTS
