  • supported protocols change.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful evidence may include:

  • exact command;
  • tool version;
  • affected target;
  • timestamp;
  • request and response;
  • selected terminal output;
  • packet capture;
  • screenshot;
  • authentication context;
  • relevant configuration;
  • manual reproduction;
  • file hash;
  • session identifier;
  • certificate request identifier;
  • relevant endpoint telemetry;
  • relevant network telemetry.

Do not attach enormous raw tool outputs without interpretation.

Extract the evidence that supports the security conclusion.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
False positives may be caused by:

  • wildcard DNS;
  • generic responses;
  • catch-all routes;
  • authentication redirects;
  • reverse proxies;
  • WAF behaviour;
  • CDNs;
  • stale signatures;
  • misleading banners;
  • scanner assumptions;
  • incomplete directory context;
  • outdated attack-path assumptions;
  • certificate mapping changes;
  • tool-version differences.

A useful process is:

Tool Match
    |
    v
Inspect Raw Evidence
    |
    v
Establish Baseline
    |
    v
Reproduce Independently
    |
    v
Compare Results
    |
    v
Confirm or Reject

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Security tools can also miss real issues because of:

  • authentication;
  • unusual workflows;
  • JavaScript-heavy applications;
  • WAF interference;
  • missing routes;
  • custom protocols;
  • business logic;
  • state-dependent behaviour;
  • environment-specific conditions;
  • network segmentation;
  • tool-version limitations;
  • modern platform mitigations;
  • incomplete privileges.

A clean scan does not prove that the target is secure.

docs.title: Reporting Tool-Assisted Findings
docs.text:
Avoid:

Nuclei found a vulnerability.

Prefer:

Automated testing identified behaviour consistent with the suspected
condition. Manual validation subsequently reproduced the behaviour and
confirmed the security impact.

Avoid:

WinPEAS found privilege escalation.

Prefer:

Enumeration identified a security-relevant configuration. Manual
validation confirmed that the current user could influence the affected
resource and that it participated in a privileged execution path.

Avoid:

Certipy found ESC1.

Prefer describing:

Who can enrol
        +
Which certificate identity can be controlled
        +
Whether the certificate supports authentication
        +
How the environment maps that certificate
        =
Supported security impact

Avoid:

Cobalt Strike worked.

Prefer describing the actual boundary demonstrated, such as:

Code execution was possible in the tested user context and the process
established an outbound command-and-control connection to authorised
assessment infrastructure.

The report should describe the security condition rather than the tool.

docs.title: Tool Documentation Model
docs.text:
Detailed tool pages in this knowledge base generally follow:

Purpose
   |
   v
When to Use It
   |
   v
Installation / Verification
   |
   v
Core Workflow
   |
   v
Practical Examples
   |
   v
Representative Result
   |
   v
Interpretation
   |
   v
Common Mistakes
   |
   v
Manual Validation
   |
   v
Evidence
   |
   v
Detection / Defence
   |
   v
Cleanup
   |
   v
Related Security Topics

This keeps tooling connected to methodology.

docs.title: External References
docs.text:
External resources are used where they add specialist depth rather than duplicating local notes.

Priority is generally given to:

  1. official documentation;
  2. official repositories;
  3. vendor documentation;
  4. PortSwigger for web application security;
  5. Microsoft Learn for Windows and Active Directory;
  6. ProjectDiscovery documentation;
  7. strong specialist references such as 0xdf;
  8. HackTricks where broader offensive-security context is useful.

Useful references:

PortSwigger Web Security Academy

Burp Suite Documentation

ProjectDiscovery Documentation

Microsoft Learn

0xdf - Default 404 Pages

HackTricks

docs.title: Related Knowledge Base Sections
docs.text:
Web Application Security

Source Code Review

Active Directory

Windows

Linux

Privilege Escalation Explorer

Red Teaming

Purple Teaming

Vulnerability Research

Cheatsheets

docs.title: Final Tooling Model
docs.text:
Do not use security tools like this:

Run Tool
   |
   v
Read Highlight
   |
   v
Report Finding

Use them like this:

Security Question
       |
       v
Understand Methodology
       |
       v
Choose Appropriate Tool
       |
       v
Collect Observation
       |
       v
Interpret Context
       |
       v
Validate Manually
       |
       v
Correlate Evidence
       |
       v
Determine Supported Impact
       |
       v
Report
       |
       v
Remediate
       |
       v
Retest

The most valuable skill is not knowing the largest number of security tools.

It is knowing:

  • what question to ask;
  • which tool can help answer it;
  • what the output actually means;
  • when that output may be misleading;
  • how to validate it;
  • how it connects to the underlying security concept;
  • and when enough evidence exists to support a defensible conclusion.

docs.title: Certify
docs.text:
Certify is a C# Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) assessment tool from GhostPack. It is designed to enumerate enterprise certificate authorities, certificate templates, enrollment services, permissions, and certificate-related configurations that may create unintended privilege paths in Active Directory.

Certify is particularly useful during authorised Active Directory assessments because AD CS can introduce trust relationships that are not immediately visible through traditional user, group, ACL, or Kerberos enumeration.

Authorised Testing Only

Certificate enrollment can result in authentication material that may provide access as another identity. Use certificate-request functionality only when AD CS exploitation and the affected identities are explicitly within scope.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Certify can help answer questions such as:

Is AD CS deployed?
        |
        v
Which Enterprise CAs exist?
        |
        v
Which certificate templates exist?
        |
        v
Who can enroll?
        |
        v
What identities can certificates represent?
        |
        v
Which security controls apply?
        |
        v
Can the configuration create an unintended trust path?

Typical assessment areas include:

Area Purpose CA discovery Identify Enterprise Certificate Authorities Template enumeration Identify published certificate templates Enrollment permissions Determine who can request certificates Template permissions Review who can modify templates Subject configuration Determine how certificate identities are constructed EKUs Determine permitted certificate purposes Enrollment agents Identify certificate request agent configurations CA permissions Review CA-level administrative permissions Web enrollment Identify HTTP-based enrollment services Certificate requests Validate selected AD CS findings Authentication Determine whether issued certificates can support authentication

The important assessment model is:

AD CS Observation
        |
        v
Candidate Misconfiguration
        |
        v
Required Preconditions
        |
        v
Certificate Trust Relationship
        |
        v
Controlled Validation
        |
        v
Evidence
        |
        v
Security Conclusion

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
Certify is part of GhostPack.

  • Certify - Official GhostPack Repository
  • Certify README

Use the upstream project as the primary reference.

Certify is source-oriented, so assessment teams commonly compile it from source.

Record the exact source revision used during testing.

docs.title: Certify and AD CS
docs.text:
Active Directory Certificate Services provides Public Key Infrastructure functionality for Windows environments.

A simplified architecture is:

flowchart LR
    A[Active Directory] --> B[Enterprise CA]
    B --> C[Certificate Templates]
    D[Domain Principal] --> C
    C --> E[Certificate Request]
    E --> B
    B --> F[Issued Certificate]
    F --> G[Authentication or Other Purpose]

The certificate authority trusts Active Directory identities and policies when processing certificate requests.

This creates an important security boundary:

Active Directory Identity
        +
Certificate Template
        +
Enrollment Permission
        +
CA Policy
        =
Certificate Identity

If these components are configured incorrectly, certificate issuance may create an unintended privilege path.

docs.title: Certify vs Certipy
docs.text:
Certify and Certipy overlap significantly but target different operator environments.

Certify Certipy C# / .NET Python Primarily Windows Commonly Linux-based GhostPack Certipy project Native domain context convenient Remote assessment workflows convenient AD CS enumeration AD CS enumeration Certificate requests Certificate requests Template analysis Template analysis Windows-centric operation Broad AD CS workflow automation

A useful rule of thumb is:

Operating from Windows domain context
        |
        +--> Certify

Operating primarily from Linux
        |
        +--> Certipy

This is not absolute.

Using both tools can be useful for validating results independently.

docs.title: Build from Source
docs.text:
Clone the official repository in an authorised development environment:

git clone https://github.com/GhostPack/Certify.git

Enter the repository:

cd Certify

Record the source revision:

git rev-parse HEAD

Compile using a compatible Visual Studio/.NET development environment.

The resulting executable is typically:

Certify.exe

Record:

Source Repository
Commit
Build Environment
SHA256
Assessment Date

docs.title: Record the Executable
docs.text:
Before use:

Get-FileHash .\Certify.exe -Algorithm SHA256

Example evidence:

Tool: Certify
Source: GhostPack
Revision: <COMMIT>
SHA256: <HASH>
Timestamp: <TIME>

This provides reproducibility when the executable was compiled internally.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Display available commands:

.\Certify.exe

or:

.\Certify.exe --help

The exact command syntax depends on the Certify revision.

Always check the build being used rather than relying exclusively on commands from older write-ups.

docs.title: Establish the Current Context
docs.text:
Before running Certify, record the Windows and Active Directory context.

Identity:

whoami

Domain:

$env:USERDNSDOMAIN

Logon server:

$env:LOGONSERVER

Groups:

whoami /groups

Privileges:

whoami /priv

Domain Controller discovery:

nltest /dsgetdc:<DOMAIN>

This establishes the identity from which AD CS enumeration occurs.

docs.title: Discover Active Directory Certificate Services
docs.text:
The first question is:

Does the domain use AD CS?

Certify can enumerate Enterprise Certificate Authorities.

A commonly used discovery action is:

.\Certify.exe cas

Review the output for information such as:

CA Name
DNS Hostname
Certificate Subject
Certificate Serial Number
Validity
Enrollment Services
Permissions
Web Enrollment

The exact fields depend on the Certify build.

docs.title: Enterprise Certificate Authorities
docs.text:
An Enterprise CA is integrated with Active Directory.

Conceptually:

Active Directory
        |
        v
Enterprise CA
        |
        v
Certificate Templates
        |
        v
Domain Enrollment

Important assessment questions include:

Which CA hosts exist?

Which templates are published?

Who administers the CA?

Who can enroll?

Which authentication-capable templates exist?

Are HTTP enrollment interfaces enabled?

Do not assume that the existence of an Enterprise CA is itself a vulnerability.

docs.title: Enumerate Certificate Templates
docs.text:
Certify can enumerate certificate templates.

A broad template search can be performed using the relevant template enumeration functionality supported by the installed build.

A commonly used action is:

.\Certify.exe find

This can return information about:

Certificate Authorities
Certificate Templates
Enrollment Rights
Extended Key Usage
Subject Name Configuration
Manager Approval
Authorized Signatures
Validity
Renewal Period
Template Permissions

The objective is not merely to identify templates.

The objective is to understand their trust relationships.

docs.title: Find Potentially Vulnerable Templates
docs.text:
Certify includes filtering intended to identify templates with potentially dangerous configurations.

A commonly encountered workflow is:

.\Certify.exe find /vulnerable

Treat this as:

Candidate Discovery

not:

Confirmed Vulnerability

Every result must be validated.

The tool may identify conditions that are exploitable only when additional prerequisites exist.

docs.title: Current User Perspective
docs.text:
Where supported by the Certify build, vulnerable-template enumeration can be evaluated from the current user's security context.

This is important because:

Template Misconfiguration
        +
No Enrollment Rights
        =
Potentially Not Exploitable by Current User

while:

Template Misconfiguration
        +
Current User Can Enroll
        =
Candidate Attack Path

Always review both configuration and effective enrollment permissions.

docs.title: Certificate Template Security Model
docs.text:
A certificate template combines several security properties.

Certificate Template
├── Enrollment Permissions
├── Template ACL
├── Subject Name Rules
├── Extended Key Usage
├── Issuance Requirements
├── Authorized Signatures
├── Manager Approval
├── Validity Period
└── Cryptographic Settings

A meaningful finding often depends on several of these properties interacting.

docs.title: Enrollment Rights
docs.text:
Enrollment permissions determine which principals may request certificates from a template.

Relevant permissions can include concepts such as:

Enroll
Autoenroll

Principals may include:

Domain Users
Domain Computers
Authenticated Users
Specific Groups
Specific Users
Service Accounts

The existence of enrollment rights is not inherently insecure.

The risk depends on what identity and purpose the resulting certificate can represent.

docs.title: Template ACLs
docs.text:
Certificate templates are Active Directory objects and therefore have ACLs.

Important permissions may include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
WriteProperty

A principal capable of modifying a certificate template may be able to change security-sensitive properties.

The reasoning chain becomes:

Principal
    |
    v
Template Modification Rights
    |
    v
Security-Sensitive Property Change
    |
    v
Certificate Enrollment
    |
    v
Potential Authentication Path

Template ACL findings should therefore be correlated with Active Directory ACL analysis.

docs.title: Extended Key Usage
docs.text:
Extended Key Usage defines purposes for which a certificate may be used.

Common authentication-related EKUs include concepts such as:

Client Authentication
Smart Card Logon
PKINIT Client Authentication
Any Purpose

The security question is:

Can this certificate be used for authentication?

not merely:

Does the template issue certificates?

Templates used only for narrow non-authentication purposes may have very different security implications.

docs.title: Subject Alternative Name
docs.text:
Certificate identity may be influenced through the certificate subject or Subject Alternative Name.

Potential identity forms include:

DNS Name
User Principal Name
Email
Distinguished Name

The security-sensitive question is:

Who controls the identity placed into the certificate?

If an unprivileged requester can influence an authentication identity beyond their own account, the trust relationship requires careful review.

docs.title: Manager Approval
docs.text:
Some templates require certificate manager approval before issuance.

Conceptually:

Certificate Request
        |
        v
Pending
        |
        v
Manager Approval
        |
        v
Certificate Issued

This can significantly change exploitability.

Therefore:

Potentially Dangerous Template
        +
Manager Approval Required
        !=
Immediately Exploitable

Validate the actual issuance requirements.

docs.title: Authorized Signatures
docs.text:
Templates may require one or more authorised signatures before a certificate can be issued.

This creates an additional security boundary.

Record:

Authorized Signature Count
Required Application Policy
Enrollment Agent Requirements

when evaluating a candidate template.

docs.title: Enrollment Agents
docs.text:
Enrollment agents can request certificates on behalf of other users under specific configurations.

Conceptually:

Enrollment Agent
        |
        v
Certificate Request
        |
        v
On Behalf of User
        |
        v
CA

This is legitimate enterprise functionality.

The security risk depends on:

  • Who can become an enrollment agent
  • Which templates permit enrollment-agent use
  • Which users can be represented
  • Whether restrictions are correctly configured

docs.title: CA Permissions
docs.text:
Certificate Authority permissions are separate from certificate-template permissions.

Important CA-level roles and permissions may include:

Manage CA
Manage Certificates
Request Certificates

A principal with excessive CA-level permissions may have capabilities beyond ordinary certificate enrollment.

Keep these boundaries separate:

Template ACL
        !=
CA ACL
        !=
Enrollment Rights

docs.title: Certificate Enrollment Flow
docs.text:
A simplified enrollment process is:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Domain User
    participant AD as Active Directory
    participant CA as Certificate Authority

    U->>AD: Discover CA and Template
    AD-->>U: Template Configuration
    U->>CA: Certificate Request
    CA->>AD: Evaluate Identity and Policy
    AD-->>CA: Directory Information
    CA-->>U: Certificate or Denial

A successful certificate request means:

CA Accepted Request

It does not automatically mean:

Certificate Can Authenticate

The certificate's EKUs, identity, chain, and target authentication mechanism must also be considered.

docs.title: Certificate Requests
docs.text:
Certify can submit certificate requests using templates available to the current context.

Before requesting a certificate, establish:

Template
CA
Requester
Requested Identity
Purpose
Scope Approval

Use the current Certify help to review request syntax:

.\Certify.exe request /?

Certificate requests can create authentication material.

Do not submit requests against arbitrary privileged identities merely to see whether they work.

docs.title: Request Validation Model
docs.text:
Use:

Candidate Template
        |
        v
Confirm Enrollment Permission
        |
        v
Confirm Identity Control
        |
        v
Confirm Authentication EKU
        |
        v
Confirm Issuance Requirements
        |
        v
Request Approved Test Certificate
        |
        v
Validate Intended Security Property

This produces a controlled proof rather than indiscriminate certificate issuance.

docs.title: Certificate Output
docs.text:
Certificate enrollment may result in material such as:

Certificate
Private Key
PEM
PFX / PKCS#12

Treat this material as credentials.

Never:

  • Commit certificates containing private keys to Git
  • Store them in documentation repositories
  • Include private keys in screenshots
  • Upload them to shared services
  • Leave them on assessment hosts unnecessarily

docs.title: PEM and PFX
docs.text:
A certificate and private key may be represented in different formats.

PEM commonly resembles:

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

and:

-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
...
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----

PKCS#12 containers commonly use:

.pfx
.p12

and may contain:

Certificate
+
Private Key
+
Certificate Chain

Treat PFX files as sensitive authentication material.

docs.title: Convert Certificate Material
docs.text:
OpenSSL can be used in an authorised assessment environment to convert certificate formats.

For example, when converting approved test material into a PFX container:

openssl pkcs12 -export \
  -in certificate.pem \
  -inkey private-key.pem \
  -out certificate.pfx

Use a strong temporary export password.

Remove temporary certificate material after testing.

docs.title: Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
Active Directory can support certificate-based Kerberos authentication through PKINIT when the environment and certificate satisfy the required conditions.

Conceptually:

Certificate + Private Key
        |
        v
PKINIT
        |
        v
KDC
        |
        v
Kerberos Authentication

Therefore an authentication-capable certificate can become equivalent to powerful credential material.

The complete path must still be validated.

docs.title: AD CS Attack Paths
docs.text:
AD CS security research commonly categorises certificate-related privilege paths using ESC identifiers.

Examples include:

ESC1
ESC2
ESC3
ESC4
...

These identifiers describe different classes of AD CS configuration weakness.

Certify can assist with identifying some of the underlying conditions.

The dedicated AD CS notes should contain the full ESC taxonomy and exploitation prerequisites.

Certify should remain focused on:

Discovery
Enumeration
Validation
Tool Operation

docs.title: ESC1 Concept
docs.text:
A classic certificate-template risk can occur when several conditions combine.

For example:

Low-Privilege Enrollment
        +
Requester Controls Subject Identity
        +
Authentication-Capable EKU
        +
No Additional Approval Barrier
        =
Potential Identity Impersonation Path

The important point is that no single property proves the issue.

The complete combination must be validated.

docs.title: ESC2 Concept
docs.text:
Templates with overly broad certificate purposes can create security concerns.

For example:

Any Purpose

or configurations without sufficiently constrained application policies may expand how the resulting certificate can be used.

Exploitability depends on additional environmental conditions.

docs.title: ESC3 Concept
docs.text:
Enrollment-agent certificate functionality can create an impersonation path when enrollment-agent restrictions are insufficient.

The trust relationship becomes:

Principal
    |
    v
Enrollment Agent Certificate
    |
    v
Request on Behalf of Another Principal
    |
    v
Authentication Certificate

Validate all issuance and enrollment-agent restrictions.

docs.title: ESC4 Concept
docs.text:
Certificate-template ACL weaknesses can allow an attacker-controlled principal to modify template properties.

Conceptually:

Template ACL Control
        |
        v
Modify Template
        |
        v
Create Dangerous Configuration
        |
        v
Enroll
        |
        v
Restore Configuration

During production assessments, modifying certificate templates can affect legitimate enrollment and should not be performed casually.

Prefer configuration evidence where it sufficiently demonstrates the risk.

docs.title: CA-Level Misconfigurations
docs.text:
Not all AD CS issues exist at the template level.

Other security-sensitive areas can include:

CA Permissions
CA Policy
Enrollment Services
HTTP Enrollment
Certificate Mapping
NTLM Authentication
CA Security Extensions

Certify output should therefore be correlated with broader AD CS assessment tooling and manual validation.

docs.title: Web Enrollment
docs.text:
AD CS environments may expose web enrollment interfaces.

Common paths historically include services under:

/certsrv/

Do not assume the path exists merely because AD CS is deployed.

Identify the actual service first.

Where web enrollment exists, assess:

Authentication Method
HTTPS Enforcement
Extended Protection for Authentication
NTLM Exposure
Relay Protections
Network Accessibility

These conditions are particularly relevant to NTLM relay-related AD CS risks.

docs.title: Discover HTTP Enrollment
docs.text:
Certify output may provide information about CA enrollment endpoints depending on the build and environment.

Manual validation can also inspect known CA hosts for authorised HTTP/HTTPS services.

From Windows:

Test-NetConnection <CA_HOST> -Port 80

Test-NetConnection <CA_HOST> -Port 443

Network reachability alone does not prove web enrollment is enabled.

docs.title: Certify and LDAP
docs.text:
Much of AD CS discovery depends on Active Directory information stored in LDAP.

Relevant configuration exists under the Configuration naming context.

Conceptually:

Active Directory
        |
        v
Configuration
        |
        v
Public Key Services
        |
        +--> Certificate Templates
        |
        +--> Enrollment Services
        |
        +--> OIDs

This is why Certify generally benefits from normal domain connectivity and directory access.

docs.title: Required Connectivity
docs.text:
Relevant services may include:

Port Service 53 DNS 88 Kerberos 135 RPC 389 LDAP 445 SMB 636 LDAPS 3268 Global Catalog 3269 Global Catalog over TLS

Certificate enrollment itself may involve additional RPC/DCOM or HTTP-based services depending on the enrollment method.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
Correct DNS is important.

Check:

Resolve-DnsName <DOMAIN>

Domain Controller discovery:

Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<DOMAIN>

CA hostname:

Resolve-DnsName <CA_HOST>

Do not interpret a Certify connection error as an AD CS configuration issue until DNS and network connectivity have been validated.

docs.title: Certify Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Certify is typically run from Windows.

If the Windows host itself can reach the domain and CA, no external pivot may be necessary.

When operating from another network, validate:

DNS
LDAP
Kerberos
CA Enrollment Protocol

individually.

A tunnel providing only:

TCP/445

is not automatically sufficient for AD CS enumeration and enrollment.

docs.title: Current User vs Alternate Credentials
docs.text:
Whenever possible, begin enumeration using the current authorised domain context.

This provides an accurate answer to:

What can this principal discover and enroll in?

Using higher-privileged credentials can obscure the security boundary being tested.

Maintain the distinction:

Current User Can Enroll

versus:

Administrator Can Enroll

These have very different security implications.

docs.title: Template Permissions vs Enrollment Permissions
docs.text:
This distinction is important.

Enrollment Permission
        |
        +--> Can request a certificate

Template Modification Permission
        |
        +--> Can alter how certificates are issued

A principal may have:

Enroll

without:

Write

or:

Write

without currently having:

Enroll

Both can be security-relevant for different reasons.

docs.title: Effective Permissions
docs.text:
Group membership can make certificate permissions less obvious.

For example:

User
 |
 v
Group A
 |
 v
Group B
 |
 v
Certificate Template Permission

Therefore:

No Direct ACE

does not necessarily mean:

No Permission

Review nested group membership and effective access.

docs.title: Machine Certificates
docs.text:
AD CS is not limited to user certificates.

Computer templates can issue certificates representing machine identities.

Potential uses include:

Machine Authentication
TLS
IPsec
Network Authentication
Service Authentication

Computer certificate findings should therefore be assessed separately from user certificate findings.

docs.title: Certificate Validity
docs.text:
Record:

Validity Period
Renewal Period

Long-lived authentication certificates can increase the impact of certificate compromise.

The security significance depends on:

  • Certificate purpose
  • Revocation capability
  • Private-key protection
  • Identity represented
  • Lifetime
  • Renewal behaviour

docs.title: Private Key Protection
docs.text:
Certificate security does not stop at issuance.

Consider:

Where is the private key stored?

Is it exportable?

Which principal can access it?

Is hardware protection used?

Can another process access it?

How long does it remain valid?

Certificate-template assessment and endpoint private-key protection are related but separate security boundaries.

docs.title: Requester Supplied Subject
docs.text:
One security-sensitive template property is whether the requester can supply subject information.

The assessment question is:

Can the requester control the identity?

Then:

Can that identity be used for authentication?

Then:

Can the requester enroll?

Only the complete chain establishes a meaningful privilege path.

docs.title: Strong Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Modern Windows environments may enforce stronger certificate mapping behaviour.

This can affect whether a certificate that appears structurally suitable can actually authenticate as the intended Active Directory principal.

Therefore:

Certificate Issued
        !=
Identity Mapping Accepted
        !=
Authentication Successful

Always validate the effective environment.

docs.title: Certify Output Review
docs.text:
Do not read Certify output only for:

Vulnerable

Review:

CA Name
Template Name
Enabled State
Enrollment Rights
Template Permissions
Subject Configuration
EKUs
Manager Approval
Authorized Signatures
Validity
Private Key Flags
CA Configuration

The most useful output is often the combination of several properties.

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text:
For evidence collection:

.\Certify.exe find | Tee-Object -FilePath .\certify-find.txt

For candidate vulnerable configurations:

.\Certify.exe find /vulnerable |
    Tee-Object -FilePath .\certify-vulnerable.txt

Review files for sensitive information before including them in assessment evidence.

docs.title: Compare with Certipy
docs.text:
When possible, validate important findings using a second implementation.

For example:

Certify
    |
    v
Candidate Template
    |
    v
Certipy
    |
    v
Independent Enumeration
    |
    v
Manual Validation

Agreement between tools increases confidence, but manual interpretation remains necessary.

See:

docs/tools/certipy.md

docs.title: Certify Does Not Start
docs.text:
Check:

Get-Item .\Certify.exe

Hash:

Get-FileHash .\Certify.exe -Algorithm SHA256

Potential causes include:

  • Defender
  • EDR
  • WDAC
  • AppLocker
  • Missing .NET runtime
  • Build incompatibility
  • File corruption

docs.title: Domain Cannot Be Found
docs.text:
Check:

$env:USERDNSDOMAIN

Then:

Resolve-DnsName $env:USERDNSDOMAIN

Domain Controller:

nltest /dsgetdc:<DOMAIN>

LDAP:

Test-NetConnection <DC> -Port 389

Kerberos:

Test-NetConnection <DC> -Port 88

docs.title: CA Cannot Be Reached
docs.text:
Resolve the CA:

Resolve-DnsName <CA_HOST>

Then test the enrollment protocol relevant to the environment.

For HTTP:

Test-NetConnection <CA_HOST> -Port 80

HTTPS:

Test-NetConnection <CA_HOST> -Port 443

RPC endpoint mapper:

Test-NetConnection <CA_HOST> -Port 135

Do not assume one failed port means the CA itself is unavailable.

docs.title: No Vulnerable Templates Found
docs.text:
This can mean:

No Candidate Configuration Found

but it can also mean:

  • Current user lacks visibility
  • No Enterprise CA is available
  • Templates are not published
  • Tool version differs
  • Permissions differ
  • Network access is incomplete
  • Modern mitigations affect classification

Validate the environment before concluding:

AD CS Secure

docs.title: Template Appears Vulnerable but Request Fails
docs.text:
Check:

Template Published?
Enrollment Permission?
Manager Approval?
Authorized Signatures?
CA Accepting Template?
Subject Requirements?
Certificate Mapping?
Network Connectivity?

A candidate configuration and successful enrollment are separate stages.

docs.title: Certificate Issued but Authentication Fails
docs.text:
Check:

EKU
Certificate Identity
UPN / SID Mapping
Certificate Chain
KDC Support
PKINIT
Domain Controller Certificate
Certificate Validity
Strong Mapping Enforcement
Clock

Do not conclude that certificate authentication is possible solely because enrollment succeeded.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Certify execution may be affected by:

Defender
EDR
WDAC
AppLocker

If execution fails:

Observed Failure
        |
        v
Identify Enforcement Source
        |
        v
Validate Effective Policy
        |
        v
Security Conclusion

Do not label a failure as:

WDAC Block

unless WDAC was actually confirmed as the enforcing control.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful evidence may include:

  • Current user
  • Domain
  • Domain Controller
  • CA hostname
  • CA name
  • Template name
  • Template enabled state
  • Enrollment permissions
  • Template ACL
  • EKUs
  • Subject configuration
  • Manager approval
  • Authorized signatures
  • Certificate validity
  • Certify revision
  • Certify SHA256
  • Controlled certificate request result
  • Authentication validation result
  • Timestamp
  • Detection telemetry
  • Cleanup confirmation

A strong evidence chain is:

Principal
    |
    v
Enrollment / Modification Rights
    |
    v
Template Configuration
    |
    v
CA Issuance Behaviour
    |
    v
Certificate Capability
    |
    v
Authentication / Privilege Impact

docs.title: Security Interpretation
docs.text:
Do not report:

Certify says vulnerable.

Instead explain the actual security relationship.

For example:

Authenticated Users
        |
        v
Enroll Permission
        |
        v
Template Allows Requester-Controlled Identity
        |
        v
Authentication EKU
        |
        v
No Approval Requirement
        |
        v
Potential Certificate-Based Impersonation

This explains why the configuration matters.

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text: Defenders can monitor AD CS activity at several layers.

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
Monitor changes to:

Certificate Templates
Template ACLs
Enrollment Services
CA-related objects
Delegation around CA services

docs.title: Certificate Authority
docs.text:
CA auditing can provide visibility into:

Certificate Requests
Certificate Issuance
Certificate Denials
CA Configuration Changes
Certificate Revocation

Enable appropriate CA auditing based on organisational requirements.

docs.title: Windows Security Events
docs.text:
Relevant certificate-service events can include:

4886
4887
4888
4890
4891

The exact events generated depend on auditing configuration and the operation performed.

Correlate certificate events with:

Requester
Template
Certificate Subject
Certificate Serial Number
Timestamp
Source Host

docs.title: Monitor Template Changes
docs.text:
Template modification is particularly important.

A dangerous sequence can resemble:

Template Modified
        |
        v
Certificate Requested
        |
        v
Template Restored

A point-in-time configuration review may miss this.

Historical directory-change telemetry can therefore be valuable.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text:
Relevant controls include:

  • Restrict certificate enrollment permissions
  • Restrict certificate-template modification rights
  • Remove unnecessary requester-supplied subject configuration
  • Restrict authentication-capable EKUs
  • Require approval where appropriate
  • Configure enrollment-agent restrictions
  • Review CA administrative permissions
  • Protect CA hosts as privileged infrastructure
  • Require HTTPS for web enrollment
  • Configure Extended Protection for Authentication where supported
  • Reduce NTLM exposure
  • Monitor certificate issuance
  • Monitor certificate-template changes
  • Use strong certificate mapping
  • Maintain certificate revocation processes
  • Review long-lived authentication certificates
  • Use managed service identities where appropriate

The defensive objective is:

Controlled Enrollment
        +
Controlled Identity
        +
Restricted Certificate Purpose
        +
Protected CA
        +
Strong Mapping
        +
Monitoring
        =
Reduced AD CS Risk

docs.title: CA Security Tier
docs.text:
Enterprise Certificate Authorities should be treated as high-value infrastructure.

Compromise of a trusted CA can undermine identity controls far beyond one endpoint.

Protect CA systems using controls appropriate to privileged infrastructure:

Restricted Administration
Network Segmentation
Application Control
Privileged Monitoring
Secure Backup
Key Protection
Patch Management
Audit Logging

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
During production assessments:

  • Enumerate before requesting certificates
  • Limit requests to approved templates
  • Use designated test identities where possible
  • Avoid arbitrary privileged-user impersonation
  • Avoid modifying production templates unless explicitly authorised
  • Avoid CA configuration changes
  • Avoid certificate revocation unless authorised
  • Protect generated private keys
  • Remove test certificates and keys after use where appropriate
  • Record certificate serial numbers
  • Record every certificate request made during testing

AD CS is identity infrastructure.

Treat changes with the same caution as changes to privileged Active Directory objects.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Remove temporary output:

Remove-Item .\certify-find.txt -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Remove temporary test certificate files where required:

Remove-Item .\certificate.pem -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Remove-Item .\private-key.pem -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Remove-Item .\certificate.pfx -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If a certificate was installed into a certificate store during testing, identify it by thumbprint before removal.

Example inspection:

Get-ChildItem Cert:\CurrentUser\My

Do not remove certificates based only on a display name.

Record:

Subject
Thumbprint
Serial Number
Issuer

before making changes.

.\Certify.exe

docs.title: Certipy
docs.text:
Certipy is a Python toolkit for enumerating and assessing Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS). It supports discovery of certificate authorities and templates, certificate requests, certificate-based authentication, certificate and private-key handling, CA and template analysis, Shadow Credentials, relay assessment, and validation of AD CS privilege paths.

Certipy is particularly useful when conducting Active Directory assessments from Linux because it provides a broad AD CS workflow without requiring execution directly on a domain-joined Windows host.

Authorised Testing Only

Certipy can request authentication certificates, interact with certificate authorities, modify certificate-related Active Directory objects, and perform other security-sensitive operations. Use active functionality only when the affected domain, CA, accounts, templates, and authentication paths are explicitly within scope.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Certipy can help answer:

Is AD CS deployed?
        |
        v
Which CAs exist?
        |
        v
Which templates are published?
        |
        v
Who can enroll?
        |
        v
Who can modify templates or CA configuration?
        |
        v
Which identities can certificates represent?
        |
        v
Can certificates authenticate?
        |
        v
Does the configuration create a privilege path?

Major Certipy functionality includes:

Certipy
├── find
├── req
├── auth
├── cert
├── ca
├── template
├── account
├── shadow
├── relay
└── Certificate / AD CS analysis

The exact command set depends on the installed Certipy version.

Always confirm with:

certipy --help

and:

certipy <COMMAND> -h

before relying on syntax from older write-ups.

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
The AD CS assessment toolkit covered by this page is:

Certipy - Official GitHub Repository

Do not confuse it with other unrelated Python packages named Certipy.

The package name commonly used for installation is:

certipy-ad

Verify the installed tool after installation.

docs.title: Certipy vs Certify
docs.text:
Certipy and Certify overlap but have different operator workflows.

Certipy Certify Python C# / .NET Commonly Linux-based Commonly Windows-based Remote AD CS workflows Native Windows/domain workflows CA discovery CA discovery Template enumeration Template enumeration Certificate requests Certificate requests Certificate authentication Certificate enrollment workflows Shadow Credentials Primarily AD CS-focused Relay functionality Primarily direct AD CS enumeration Certificate manipulation Certificate enumeration/request workflows

A useful model is:

Linux Operator
    |
    +--> Certipy

Windows Domain Context
    |
    +--> Certify

This is not absolute.

Using both can provide independent validation of important findings.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
A common installation method is:

pipx install certipy-ad

Alternatively, use a dedicated Python virtual environment:

python3 -m venv .venv

Activate it:

source .venv/bin/activate

Install:

python3 -m pip install certipy-ad

Verify:

certipy --help

Check the version:

certipy -v

Depending on the packaging and operating system, the command may also appear as:

certipy

or historically:

certipy-ad

Use:

which certipy

to verify which executable is being used.

docs.title: Install from Source
docs.text:
For development or when testing a specific upstream revision:

git clone https://github.com/ly4k/Certipy.git

Enter the repository:

cd Certipy

Record the source revision:

git rev-parse HEAD

Create a virtual environment:

python3 -m venv .venv

Activate:

source .venv/bin/activate

Install the project:

python3 -m pip install .

Verify:

certipy --help

Recording the Git commit improves reproducibility during assessments.

docs.title: Establish the Assessment Context
docs.text:
Before using Certipy, record:

Domain
Username
Source Host
Domain Controller
DNS Server
Certificate Authority
Assessment Scope

Useful variables might conceptually be:

DOMAIN=corp.local
USER=analyst
DC=dc01.corp.local
DC_IP=10.10.10.10
CA=CORP-CA
CA_HOST=ca01.corp.local

Use placeholders in documentation.

Do not place real credentials in:

  • Git repositories
  • Shell history where avoidable
  • Screenshots
  • Reports
  • Shared notes

docs.title: Required Connectivity
docs.text:
AD CS assessment may depend on several Active Directory services.

Common ports include:

Port Protocol Service 53 TCP/UDP DNS 88 TCP/UDP Kerberos 135 TCP RPC Endpoint Mapper 389 TCP/UDP LDAP 445 TCP SMB 464 TCP/UDP Kerberos password operations 636 TCP LDAPS 3268 TCP Global Catalog 3269 TCP Global Catalog over TLS

CA enrollment may additionally use:

RPC
DCOM
HTTP
HTTPS

depending on the environment and enrollment mechanism.

docs.title: Validate DNS
docs.text:
Correct DNS is critical.

Query the domain:

dig @<DNS_SERVER> <DOMAIN>

Find LDAP Domain Controllers:

dig @<DNS_SERVER> _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<DOMAIN> SRV

Find Kerberos services:

dig @<DNS_SERVER> _kerberos._tcp.dc._msdcs.<DOMAIN> SRV

Resolve the CA:

dig @<DNS_SERVER> <CA_HOST>

Do not treat a Certipy error as an AD CS problem until DNS and routing have been validated.

docs.title: Validate Connectivity
docs.text:
LDAP:

nc -vz <DC_IP> 389

Kerberos:

nc -vz <DC_IP> 88

SMB:

nc -vz <DC_IP> 445

CA HTTP:

nc -vz <CA_IP> 80

CA HTTPS:

nc -vz <CA_IP> 443

RPC:

nc -vz <CA_IP> 135

Network reachability is only the first layer.

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
A good Certipy workflow is:

flowchart TD
    A[Validate Domain Connectivity] --> B[Enumerate AD CS]
    B --> C[Identify CAs]
    C --> D[Identify Published Templates]
    D --> E[Review Permissions and Configuration]
    E --> F[Identify Candidate ESC Paths]
    F --> G[Validate Preconditions]
    G --> H[Perform Minimum Required Proof]
    H --> I[Collect Evidence]
    I --> J[Cleanup]

Do not begin with exploitation.

Begin with enumeration.

docs.title: Find
docs.text:
The find action is the primary Certipy discovery workflow.

Review current options:

certipy find -h

A typical authenticated enumeration structure is:

certipy find \
  -u '<USER>@<DOMAIN>' \
  -p '<PASSWORD>' \
  -dc-ip <DC_IP>

Certipy can enumerate:

Certificate Authorities
Certificate Templates
Published Templates
Enrollment Rights
Template Permissions
CA Permissions
Extended Key Usage
Subject Configuration
Issuance Requirements
AD CS Security Settings

docs.title: Vulnerable-Only Enumeration
docs.text:
Certipy can filter results to candidate vulnerable configurations.

Typical structure:

certipy find \
  -u '<USER>@<DOMAIN>' \
  -p '<PASSWORD>' \
  -dc-ip <DC_IP> \
  -vulnerable

Treat this output as:

Candidate Findings

not:

Confirmed Exploitation

Each result must be reviewed manually.

docs.title: Enabled Templates
docs.text:
Where supported by the installed version, enumeration can focus on enabled/published templates.

Check:

certipy find -h

The distinction matters:

Template Exists
        !=
Template Published
        !=
Template Enrollable

A dangerous template that is not currently published may have different immediate risk.

docs.title: Output Formats
docs.text:
Certipy can generate structured output useful for analysis.

Depending on the version, output may include:

Text
JSON
BloodHound-compatible data

Keep the original output for evidence, but review it for sensitive information before attaching it to a report.

A useful evidence directory structure is:

certipy/
├── raw/
├── json/
├── screenshots/
└── notes/

Do not store private keys or authentication certificates in normal evidence repositories.

docs.title: BloodHound Integration
docs.text:
Certipy can generate information suitable for visualising certificate-related privilege paths.

Conceptually:

Certipy
    |
    v
AD CS Enumeration
    |
    v
Structured Data
    |
    v
BloodHound
    |
    v
Privilege Path Analysis

This is useful because certificate misconfigurations often interact with:

Group Membership
ACLs
Delegation
Account Control
CA Permissions
Template Permissions

Do not rely solely on graph edges.

Validate the underlying permissions and configuration.

docs.title: Authentication Methods
docs.text:
Depending on the installed version and command, Certipy may support authentication using:

Username + Password
NTLM Hash
Kerberos
SSPI
Certificate

Check the relevant action:

certipy <ACTION> -h

Use the least sensitive authentication material available for the assessment.

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication
docs.text:
When using Kerberos, Certipy can work with existing Kerberos credential-cache material where supported.

Check:

certipy find -h

for Kerberos-related options.

Before using Kerberos:

klist

or on Linux:

klist

Confirm:

Realm
Principal
Ticket Validity
KDC Reachability
DNS
Clock

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Kerberos is time-sensitive.

Check:

date

If necessary, compare with the Domain Controller using an approved method.

Kerberos failures may be caused by:

Clock Skew
DNS
Wrong Realm
KDC Reachability
Expired Ticket

rather than Certipy.

docs.title: Certificate Authorities
docs.text:
A Certificate Authority is a trust anchor.

A simplified model is:

Active Directory
        |
        v
Enterprise CA
        |
        v
Certificate Templates
        |
        v
Certificate Requests
        |
        v
Certificates

Certipy enumeration should identify:

CA Name
CA Host
CA Certificate
Published Templates
Enrollment Services
CA Permissions
Security Configuration
Web Enrollment

docs.title: Certificate Templates
docs.text:
Certificate templates define how Enterprise CAs issue certificates.

Important properties include:

Enrollment Permissions
Template ACL
Subject Name Configuration
Extended Key Usage
Issuance Requirements
Authorized Signatures
Manager Approval
Validity
Renewal
Private Key Options
Security Extensions

A vulnerability usually depends on a combination of properties.

docs.title: Enrollment Rights
docs.text:
Common enrollment-related permissions include:

Enroll
Autoenroll

Potential principals include:

Domain Users
Domain Computers
Authenticated Users
Specific Groups
Specific Users
Service Accounts

Enrollment itself is not a vulnerability.

The security question is:

What certificate can this principal obtain?

docs.title: Template ACLs
docs.text:
Templates are Active Directory objects.

Security-sensitive permissions may include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
WriteProperty

The reasoning model is:

Principal
    |
    v
Template Modification Rights
    |
    v
Security-Sensitive Configuration
    |
    v
Certificate Enrollment
    |
    v
Authentication Path

This is especially relevant to ESC4-style conditions.

docs.title: Extended Key Usage
docs.text:
Extended Key Usage determines what a certificate is intended to do.

Authentication-related purposes may include:

Client Authentication
Smart Card Logon
PKINIT Client Authentication
Any Purpose

Always ask:

Can this certificate authenticate?

rather than simply:

Can this template issue a certificate?

docs.title: Subject and SAN
docs.text:
Certificate identity may be represented through:

Subject
Subject Alternative Name
User Principal Name
DNS Name
SID-related extensions

The security-sensitive question is:

Who controls the certificate identity?

If the requester can influence an identity other than their own, investigate the complete mapping and issuance chain.

docs.title: Issuance Requirements
docs.text:
Templates can impose additional requirements.

Examples include:

Manager Approval
Authorized Signatures
Enrollment Agent Requirements

These controls can significantly affect exploitability.

Therefore:

Dangerous-Looking Template
        +
Approval Required
        !=
Immediately Exploitable

docs.title: Request Certificates
docs.text:
Certipy uses the req action for certificate enrollment.

Review:

certipy req -h

A normal approved certificate request conceptually requires:

Authenticated Principal
        +
CA
        +
Published Template
        +
Enrollment Permission
        =
Certificate Request

A typical request structure is:

certipy req \
  -u '<USER>@<DOMAIN>' \
  -p '<PASSWORD>' \
  -dc-ip <DC_IP> \
  -ca '<CA_NAME>' \
  -template '<TEMPLATE>'

Use only approved test identities and templates.

docs.title: Certificate Request Result
docs.text:
A successful request can result in:

Certificate
+
Private Key

commonly stored as:

.pfx

Treat this file as authentication material.

Do not:

  • Commit it to Git
  • Upload it to shared documentation
  • Include its private key in screenshots
  • Leave it on shared systems
  • Retain it unnecessarily

docs.title: PFX
docs.text:
PFX is a PKCS#12 container.

It may contain:

Certificate
Private Key
Certificate Chain

Inspect a test PFX without printing sensitive key material:

openssl pkcs12 \
  -in certificate.pfx \
  -info \
  -noout

Do not use:

-nodes

casually because it may expose unencrypted private-key material.

docs.title: cert Action
docs.text:
Certipy provides certificate-management functionality.

Review:

certipy cert -h

This can be useful for working with certificate and private-key formats.

Use it for:

Certificate Inspection
Certificate Conversion
Private-Key Handling
PFX Management

Treat all resulting private-key material as sensitive.

docs.title: Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
Certipy's:

auth

action can validate whether an approved certificate supports authentication.

Review:

certipy auth -h

Conceptually:

Certificate + Private Key
        |
        v
PKINIT / Certificate Authentication
        |
        v
KDC or Directory Service
        |
        v
Authenticated Identity

A successful certificate request does not prove successful authentication.

docs.title: PKINIT
docs.text:
PKINIT extends Kerberos with public-key authentication.

Simplified:

Certificate
    |
    v
AS-REQ with PKINIT
    |
    v
KDC
    |
    v
Identity Mapping
    |
    v
TGT

Several conditions can affect this process:

Certificate EKU
Certificate Identity
Certificate Mapping
KDC Certificate
Trust Chain
Strong Mapping Enforcement
Clock

docs.title: Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Modern Active Directory environments may enforce stronger certificate-to-account mapping.

Therefore:

Certificate Contains UPN
        !=
KDC Maps Certificate to that User

Certificate mapping can depend on:

SID Security Extension
Strong Mapping
Explicit Mapping
UPN
Issuer
Subject
Serial Number
Certificate Policy

Always validate the actual environment.

docs.title: Authentication Validation Model
docs.text:
Use:

Certificate Issued
        |
        v
Private Key Available
        |
        v
Certificate Supports Authentication
        |
        v
Identity Mapping Accepted
        |
        v
Authentication Successful
        |
        v
Authorisation Evaluated Separately

Do not collapse these stages.

docs.title: CA Action
docs.text:
Certipy provides a:

ca

action for CA-related operations.

Review:

certipy ca -h

This area can include security-sensitive CA administration functionality.

Begin with read-oriented analysis.

Do not modify:

CA Configuration
Certificate Requests
CA Permissions
Security Extensions

unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Template Action
docs.text:
Certipy provides:

template

functionality for interacting with certificate templates.

Review:

certipy template -h

Template modification is highly security-sensitive.

A production template may be used by:

Users
Computers
VPN
Wi-Fi
Web Servers
Domain Controllers
Applications

Changing it can have organisation-wide consequences.

Prefer read-only evidence whenever it sufficiently demonstrates the issue.

docs.title: Account Action
docs.text:
Certipy may expose account-management functionality relevant to certificate attack paths.

Review:

certipy account -h

Account modifications can affect Active Directory identity state.

Do not create or modify accounts unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Certipy includes:

shadow

functionality.

Shadow Credentials relate to the Active Directory attribute:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

At a high level:

Write Access to Account
        |
        v
Key Credential Added
        |
        v
Certificate-Based Authentication Material
        |
        v
Authentication as Account

This is not primarily an AD CS template vulnerability.

It uses certificate-based authentication mechanisms and Active Directory key credentials.

docs.title: Shadow Credential Preconditions
docs.text:
The key question is:

Can the current principal modify msDS-KeyCredentialLink
for the target account?

Possible permission paths may arise from:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
Specific WriteProperty
Other ACL relationships

Validate the ACL before performing any modification.

docs.title: Inspect Shadow Functionality
docs.text:
Review:

certipy shadow -h

Supported sub-actions depend on the installed version.

Potential operations can include:

list
add
remove
clear
info
auto

Some of these modify Active Directory.

Use read-only operations first.

docs.title: Shadow Credential Safety
docs.text:
Never use:

clear

casually.

Removing legitimate Key Credentials can break:

Windows Hello for Business
Certificate Authentication
Other Key Trust Relationships

A safe assessment workflow is:

Record Existing State
        |
        v
Add Controlled Test Entry if Authorised
        |
        v
Validate
        |
        v
Remove Only the Test Entry
        |
        v
Verify Original State

Do not delete unrelated entries.

docs.title: NTLM Relay and AD CS
docs.text:
Certipy includes:

relay

functionality for evaluating AD CS enrollment endpoints.

Review:

certipy relay -h

AD CS relay risk commonly depends on combinations such as:

NTLM Authentication
        +
Reachable Enrollment Endpoint
        +
Insufficient Relay Protection
        +
Enrollable Authentication Template
        =
Potential Certificate Relay Path

Relay testing should be explicitly authorised because it involves handling authentication from another security principal.

docs.title: ESC8 Concept
docs.text:
ESC8 is associated with NTLM relay to AD CS HTTP enrollment interfaces under vulnerable conditions.

A simplified model is:

Victim Authentication
        |
        v
NTLM
        |
        v
AD CS Web Enrollment
        |
        v
Certificate Request
        |
        v
Certificate for Victim Identity

Relevant protections include:

HTTPS
Extended Protection for Authentication
NTLM Restrictions
Network Segmentation
Enrollment Permissions

The presence of:

/certsrv/

alone does not prove ESC8.

docs.title: RPC Enrollment
docs.text:
Modern AD CS assessments should also consider certificate enrollment over RPC.

This is distinct from HTTP-based web enrollment.

The important point is:

AD CS Enrollment
    |
    +--> HTTP / HTTPS
    |
    +--> RPC

Different relay protections and exposure conditions may apply.

Review the current Certipy release and upstream documentation for supported relay/enrollment mechanisms.

docs.title: ESC Taxonomy
docs.text:
AD CS privilege paths are commonly categorised using:

ESC1
ESC2
ESC3
...
ESC17

Certipy can identify and assist with validation of many of these conditions.

The ESC identifier is a shorthand classification.

It is not the finding itself.

The report should explain:

Misconfiguration
        |
        v
Attacker-Controlled Property
        |
        v
Certificate Trust Decision
        |
        v
Authentication / Privilege Impact

docs.title: ESC1
docs.text:
ESC1 classically involves a certificate template where a low-privileged enrollee can influence certificate identity while the certificate supports authentication.

Conceptually:

Low-Privilege Enrollment
        +
Requester-Controlled Identity
        +
Authentication-Capable Certificate
        +
No Blocking Issuance Requirement
        =
Potential Impersonation Path

Modern certificate mapping behaviour must also be considered.

docs.title: ESC2
docs.text:
ESC2 concerns templates whose certificate purpose is overly broad under the relevant conditions.

Examples may involve:

Any Purpose

or insufficiently constrained certificate application policies.

Exploitability depends on the surrounding environment.

docs.title: ESC3
docs.text:
ESC3 involves Enrollment Agent functionality.

Conceptually:

Enrollment Agent Certificate
        |
        v
Request Certificate on Behalf of Another Principal
        |
        v
Authentication Certificate

Review:

Enrollment Agent EKU
Agent Enrollment Rights
Target Template
Enrollment Agent Restrictions

docs.title: ESC4
docs.text:
ESC4 concerns dangerous permissions over certificate-template objects.

Conceptually:

Template Write Access
        |
        v
Security-Sensitive Template Modification
        |
        v
Certificate Enrollment
        |
        v
Potential Privilege Path

Template modification should be avoided in production unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: ESC5
docs.text:
ESC5 covers broader PKI object-control issues where permissions over AD CS-related Active Directory objects create security impact.

The exact object and permission path matter.

Do not classify generic Active Directory write access as ESC5 without validating the PKI trust relationship.

docs.title: ESC6
docs.text:
ESC6 relates to CA configuration that can affect how requester-supplied certificate identity information is handled.

Modern Windows certificate security changes have altered the practical conditions for this class.

Always consider:

CA Configuration
Certificate Security Extension
Strong Certificate Mapping
Template Configuration

together.

docs.title: ESC7
docs.text:
ESC7 involves dangerous Certificate Authority permissions.

Examples of security-sensitive CA permissions include:

Manage CA
Manage Certificates

The complete privilege path depends on what the principal can actually change or approve.

docs.title: ESC8
docs.text:
ESC8 involves relay to HTTP-based AD CS enrollment under vulnerable conditions.

Review:

NTLM
HTTP Enrollment
EPA
HTTPS
Template
Victim Identity

docs.title: ESC9 and ESC10
docs.text:
These classes involve weak certificate mapping conditions.

Modern certificate mapping protections are especially important here.

The core question is:

How does Active Directory map the presented certificate
to an account?

Do not assess these solely from template properties.

docs.title: ESC11
docs.text:
ESC11 concerns certificate enrollment over RPC under relay-relevant conditions.

Evaluate:

RPC Enrollment
Authentication
Relay Protections
CA Configuration
Template Permissions

This is separate from HTTP web enrollment.

docs.title: ESC12 and Later Classes
docs.text:
Modern AD CS research has expanded the ESC taxonomy beyond the original Certified Pre-Owned classes.

Current Certipy releases support detection and assessment of newer classes through ESC17.

Because the taxonomy continues to evolve, use:

certipy --help

the current Certipy documentation, and the current SpecterOps AD CS research when interpreting these findings.

Do not copy an old ESC1-ESC8 checklist and assume it represents the complete modern AD CS attack surface.

docs.title: CA Permissions
docs.text:
CA permissions should be reviewed separately from template permissions.

Template ACL
        !=
CA ACL
        !=
Enrollment Rights

Important CA permissions can include:

Manage CA
Manage Certificates

A principal with excessive CA control may be able to influence certificate issuance beyond normal enrollment.

docs.title: Web Enrollment Discovery
docs.text:
If Certipy identifies web enrollment, validate the actual endpoint.

Potential paths historically include:

/certsrv/

Check HTTP:

curl -I http://<CA_HOST>/certsrv/

Check HTTPS:

curl -kI https://<CA_HOST>/certsrv/

A response only confirms the endpoint.

It does not prove relay vulnerability.

docs.title: Web Enrollment Security
docs.text:
Review:

HTTP vs HTTPS
Windows Authentication
NTLM
Extended Protection for Authentication
Channel Binding
Network Exposure
Template Availability

A secure configuration may expose web enrollment while still resisting known relay paths.

docs.title: Certificate Security Extensions
docs.text:
Modern Windows certificate issuance can include security extensions linking certificates to Active Directory security identifiers.

This changes how some historical AD CS techniques behave.

The assessment model should therefore be:

Template Configuration
        +
CA Configuration
        +
Certificate Contents
        +
Domain Controller Mapping Behaviour
        =
Effective Security

Do not assess only the template.

docs.title: Strong Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Strong certificate mapping is increasingly important in modern Active Directory environments.

A certificate that contains an arbitrary:

UPN

does not necessarily authenticate as that user.

The Domain Controller may require stronger binding between:

Certificate

and:

Active Directory Object

Always validate the effective runtime behaviour.

docs.title: Golden Certificates
docs.text:
Certipy has functionality associated with certificate forging when CA key material is already compromised.

This is fundamentally different from template misconfiguration.

The security condition is:

CA Private Key Compromised
        |
        v
CA Trust Compromised
        |
        v
Certificates Can Potentially Be Forged

Possession of a CA private key represents a severe PKI compromise.

Do not perform certificate forging in production unless explicitly required and authorised.

docs.title: CA Private Keys
docs.text:
Protect CA private keys as high-value authentication infrastructure.

Potential protection mechanisms include:

Hardware Security Module
TPM
Strong File Permissions
CA Host Isolation
Privileged Administration
Backup Protection

An Enterprise CA should be treated as privileged infrastructure.

docs.title: Certificate Revocation
docs.text:
Certificate-based access is affected by revocation.

Relevant concepts include:

Certificate Revocation List
CRL Distribution Point
Online Certificate Status Protocol
Certificate Validity

When demonstrating certificate-related findings, consider whether the organisation can effectively revoke compromised certificates.

docs.title: Machine Certificates
docs.text:
Certificates may represent computers as well as users.

Machine authentication can affect:

Kerberos
TLS
Network Authentication
IPsec
Device Authentication
Services

Therefore:

Machine Certificate

should be treated as credential material for the associated computer identity.

docs.title: Domain Controller Certificates
docs.text:
Domain Controllers commonly require certificates for functions such as:

LDAPS
Smart Card Authentication
PKINIT

Certificate configuration on Domain Controllers can therefore influence whether certificate-based Kerberos authentication is available.

docs.title: Certificate Lifetime
docs.text:
Review:

Validity Period
Renewal Period

Long-lived authentication certificates can increase the duration of credential exposure.

Consider:

Identity Privilege
Certificate Lifetime
Revocation Capability
Private-Key Protection

together.

docs.title: Private-Key Exportability
docs.text:
A certificate may be securely issued but poorly protected on the endpoint.

Ask:

Is the private key exportable?

Who can read it?

Where is it stored?

Is hardware protection used?

Can another process access it?

This is an endpoint-security question separate from certificate-template security.

docs.title: Certipy Through Ligolo-ng
docs.text:
Because Ligolo-ng provides routed access, Certipy can often operate normally once the relevant Active Directory networks are routed.

Validate:

ip route get <DC_IP>

Then:

nc -vz <DC_IP> 389

nc -vz <DC_IP> 88

and the required CA enrollment protocol.

See:

Ligolo-ng

docs.title: Certipy Through Chisel
docs.text:
SOCKS-based operation can be more complicated because Certipy may interact with several protocols.

Validate individual dependencies before assuming the complete workflow will operate correctly through ProxyChains.

A useful sequence is:

DNS
        |
        v
LDAP
        |
        v
Kerberos
        |
        v
CA Enrollment Protocol

For broad AD CS assessment, routed access through Ligolo-ng may be simpler than application-layer SOCKS forwarding.

See:

Chisel

docs.title: Compare Certipy and Certify Results
docs.text:
Important findings can be validated using both tools.

Example workflow:

Certipy
    |
    v
Candidate ESC Finding
    |
    v
Certify
    |
    v
Windows-Side Enumeration
    |
    v
Manual Permission Review
    |
    v
Confirmed Security Condition

Tool disagreement should trigger investigation.

Do not simply choose the result that appears more severe.

docs.title: BloodHound Correlation
docs.text:
Certificate findings often interact with broader Active Directory relationships.

Examples include:

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
Template ACL
 |
 v
Certificate Template
 |
 v
Authentication
 |
 v
Privileged Account

BloodHound can help identify these relationships.

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: Certipy Command Not Found
docs.text:
Check:

which certipy

Then:

python3 -m pip show certipy-ad

For pipx:

pipx list

Ensure the correct package is installed.

Remember that another unrelated package also uses the name Certipy.

docs.title: Wrong Certipy Installed
docs.text:
Check:

certipy --help

The AD CS tool should identify itself as the Active Directory Certificate Services toolkit by Oliver Lyak.

If the output describes generic certificate generation or local PKI management, the wrong Certipy package may be installed.

Install:

pipx install certipy-ad

rather than an unrelated package.

docs.title: DNS Resolution Fails
docs.text:
Test:

dig @<DNS_SERVER> <DC_HOST>

Then:

dig @<DNS_SERVER> <CA_HOST>

Check /etc/resolv.conf where appropriate.

A common failure pattern is:

IP Connectivity Works
        +
Hostname Resolution Fails
        =
DNS Problem

not a Certipy problem.

docs.title: LDAP Fails
docs.text:
Check:

nc -vz <DC_IP> 389

Then validate:

Credentials
Domain
Target
DNS
LDAP Signing
Channel Binding
TLS

depending on the operation being performed.

docs.title: Kerberos Fails
docs.text:
Check:

nc -vz <DC_IP> 88

Then review:

DNS
Realm
KDC
Clock
Credentials
Ticket Cache
SPN

Kerberos is sensitive to hostname and realm correctness.

docs.title: CA Enumeration Works but Request Fails
docs.text:
Check:

Template Published?
Enrollment Permission?
CA Accepting Template?
Manager Approval?
Authorized Signatures?
Subject Requirements?
Enrollment Protocol Reachable?

Enumeration and enrollment are different security boundaries.

docs.title: Certificate Request Succeeds but Authentication Fails
docs.text:
Check:

Certificate EKU
Certificate Identity
SID Security Extension
Certificate Mapping
PKINIT Support
KDC Certificate
Trust Chain
Clock
Certificate Validity

A successful request alone is not proof of identity impersonation.

docs.title: RPC Errors
docs.text:
Validate:

nc -vz <CA_IP> 135

Remember that RPC may negotiate dynamic ports after contacting the endpoint mapper.

Network filtering can therefore allow:

TCP/135

while still preventing the complete RPC workflow.

docs.title: Web Enrollment Not Found
docs.text:
Do not assume:

No /certsrv/

means:

No AD CS

The environment may use:

RPC Enrollment
Other Enrollment Services
No Web Enrollment

Enumerate the CA independently.

docs.title: Vulnerable Output but No Exploit Path
docs.text:
Review the complete preconditions.

For example:

Template Configuration
        +
Enrollment Rights
        +
Published State
        +
CA Configuration
        +
Certificate Mapping
        +
Authentication Support

All may affect the result.

Certipy's classification is the beginning of analysis, not the end.

docs.title: Security Interpretation
docs.text:
Avoid report statements such as:

Certipy identified ESC1.

Prefer:

Authenticated Users can enroll in an enabled certificate
template that permits requester-controlled identity information
and supports client authentication. The effective certificate
mapping configuration allows the issued certificate to represent
another directory identity.

The report should explain the security mechanism.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful Certipy evidence can include:

  • Certipy version
  • Certipy source revision where relevant
  • Current principal
  • Domain
  • Domain Controller
  • CA name
  • CA hostname
  • Template name
  • Template enabled state
  • Enrollment permissions
  • Template ACL
  • CA ACL
  • EKUs
  • Subject/SAN configuration
  • Issuance requirements
  • Certificate mapping state
  • Certificate request ID
  • Certificate serial number
  • Authentication result
  • Timestamp
  • Detection telemetry
  • Cleanup verification

A strong evidence chain is:

Principal
    |
    v
Permission
    |
    v
AD CS Configuration
    |
    v
Certificate Issuance
    |
    v
Certificate Mapping
    |
    v
Authentication
    |
    v
Authorisation Impact

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text: AD CS activity can be monitored across several layers.

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
Monitor:

Certificate Template Changes
Template ACL Changes
CA Object Changes
msDS-KeyCredentialLink Changes
Group Membership Changes Affecting Enrollment

docs.title: Certificate Authority
docs.text:
Monitor:

Certificate Requests
Certificate Issuance
Certificate Denials
Request Approval
CA Configuration Changes
Certificate Revocation

docs.title: Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Monitor:

Kerberos Authentication
Certificate-Based Authentication
LDAP Changes
Account Changes

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text:
Monitor:

Certipy Execution
Python Processes
Unusual Certificate Files
PFX Creation
Private-Key Access
Authentication Changes

Do not rely only on process names.

docs.title: Certificate Services Events
docs.text:
Depending on audit configuration, useful Windows events can include certificate-service events such as:

4886
4887
4888
4890
4891

Correlate:

Requester
Template
Certificate Subject
Serial Number
CA
Timestamp
Source

docs.title: Directory Change Monitoring
docs.text:
Certificate attack paths can involve modifications to:

Certificate Templates
Template ACLs
CA Objects
msDS-KeyCredentialLink

Directory Service Changes auditing can provide valuable evidence when configured.

A dangerous pattern may be:

Object Modified
        |
        v
Authentication Performed
        |
        v
Object Restored

Point-in-time configuration scanning may miss temporary modifications.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text:
Relevant controls include:

  • Restrict certificate enrollment
  • Restrict template modification permissions
  • Restrict CA administrative permissions
  • Remove unnecessary requester-controlled identity settings
  • Restrict authentication-capable EKUs
  • Require approval where appropriate
  • Configure Enrollment Agent restrictions
  • Harden certificate mapping
  • Keep Domain Controllers patched
  • Protect CA private keys
  • Use HSMs where appropriate
  • Require HTTPS for web enrollment
  • Configure Extended Protection for Authentication
  • Reduce NTLM usage
  • Restrict relay opportunities
  • Monitor certificate issuance
  • Monitor template changes
  • Monitor msDS-KeyCredentialLink
  • Protect privileged certificate templates
  • Review certificate validity periods
  • Maintain effective revocation

The goal is:

Controlled Enrollment
        +
Strong Identity Mapping
        +
Protected CA
        +
Restricted Administration
        +
Relay Protection
        +
Monitoring
        =
Reduced AD CS Attack Surface

docs.title: CA Infrastructure Protection
docs.text:
Treat Enterprise CAs as privileged infrastructure.

Relevant protections include:

Administrative Tiering
Network Segmentation
Restricted Interactive Logon
Application Control
EDR
Secure Backup
Private-Key Protection
Patch Management
Audit Logging
HSM

Compromise of a CA private key can undermine authentication trust beyond a single endpoint.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
During production assessments:

  • Enumerate before modifying
  • Prefer read-only validation
  • Use designated test identities
  • Limit certificate requests
  • Record every request
  • Record certificate serial numbers
  • Protect generated private keys
  • Avoid template modification unless explicitly authorised
  • Avoid CA configuration modification unless explicitly authorised
  • Avoid clearing Shadow Credentials
  • Avoid broad relay activity
  • Avoid certificate forging unless explicitly required
  • Remove temporary certificates and keys
  • Restore only objects you intentionally changed
  • Verify cleanup

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Review generated files:

find . -maxdepth 1 -type f \( \
  -name "*.pfx" -o \
  -name "*.pem" -o \
  -name "*.key" -o \
  -name "*.ccache" \
\) -print

Remove only files created during the assessment.

Example:

rm -f ./test-user.pfx

Do not use broad destructive cleanup commands in shared assessment directories.

Review Certipy enumeration output separately.

Preserve non-sensitive evidence according to the assessment evidence policy.

docs.title: Discovery

  • [ ] Templates enumerated

  • [ ] Enrollment permissions reviewed
  • [ ] Template ACLs reviewed

  • [ ] Required preconditions confirmed

  • [ ] Authentication separately validated

docs.title: Shadow Credentials

  • [ ] Existing Key Credentials recorded

  • [ ] Test entry removed
  • [ ] Original state verified

docs.title: Evidence

  • [ ] Temporary private keys removed

  • [ ] CA changes restored if authorised testing required them

docs.title: Installing the Wrong Certipy
docs.text:
The AD CS assessment tool is distributed as:

certipy-ad

Verify:

certipy --help

docs.title: Treating -vulnerable as Proof
docs.text:
Certipy identifies candidate configurations.

Manual validation remains necessary.

docs.title: Ignoring Certificate Mapping
docs.text: Modern Active Directory certificate mapping can substantially change exploitability.

docs.title: Ignoring CA Configuration
docs.text:
Template analysis alone is insufficient.

Review:

Template
+
CA
+
Domain Controller Mapping

docs.title: Ignoring Enrollment Protocol
docs.text: HTTP and RPC enrollment have different exposure and protection considerations.

docs.title: Treating Certificate Issuance as Authentication
docs.text:
Keep separate:

Certificate Issued
        !=
Authentication Successful
        !=
Privilege Obtained

docs.title: Leaving PFX Files Behind
docs.text:
A PFX containing a private key is credential material.

Protect and remove it appropriately.

docs.title: Clearing Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Never remove legitimate Key Credentials merely to simplify testing.

Remove only the test entry you created.

docs.title: Modifying Templates Unnecessarily
docs.text:
Template modification can affect production authentication and enrollment.

Prefer configuration evidence when sufficient.

docs.title: Using Old ESC Checklists
docs.text:
The AD CS research landscape has expanded considerably.

Use current Certipy and current AD CS research rather than assuming the original ESC classes are exhaustive.
