docs.title: Chisel
docs.text:
Chisel is a fast TCP/UDP tunnelling tool transported over HTTP and secured using SSH. It is commonly used during authorised security assessments to create port forwards, SOCKS proxies, reverse tunnels, and pivot paths through systems that can reach networks unavailable to the operator.

Where Ligolo-ng provides a TUN-based routed networking model, Chisel primarily provides explicit port forwarding and SOCKS-based access.

Authorised Testing Only

Use Chisel only on systems and networks for which you have explicit authorisation. Tunnelling can expose services and network segments that are outside the approved assessment scope.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A basic Chisel deployment consists of:

Component Typical Location Purpose Server Operator-controlled system Accepts Chisel client connections Client Pivot host Connects to the server and creates requested tunnels Remote Client configuration Defines the forwarding relationship SOCKS proxy Operator or pivot side Provides dynamic access to multiple destinations Reverse remote Server side Creates a listener whose traffic exits through the client

A common assessment architecture is:

flowchart LR
    A[Operator System] -->|HTTP / WebSocket| B[Chisel Client on Pivot]
    B --> C[Internal Network]
    C --> D[Internal Host]
    C --> E[Internal Service]

For a reverse SOCKS tunnel:

Operator
    |
    | 127.0.0.1:1080
    v
SOCKS5 Proxy
    |
    v
Chisel Server
    |
    | HTTP / WebSocket tunnel
    v
Chisel Client
    |
    v
Internal Network

Tools that support SOCKS directly, or tools used through ProxyChains, can then communicate with internal systems.

docs.title: When to Use Chisel
docs.text:
Chisel is useful when:

  • A pivot host can reach an internal network
  • The pivot can establish an outbound connection to the operator
  • A specific internal service must be forwarded
  • A SOCKS proxy is preferred over network-level routing
  • A reverse tunnel is required
  • HTTP/WebSocket transport is useful
  • Several forwards need to share one Chisel connection
  • Installing or configuring a TUN interface is undesirable
  • A lightweight single-binary tunnelling solution is preferred

Example:

Operator
10.10.14.10
     |
     v
Pivot Host
10.10.10.25
172.16.20.10
     |
     v
Internal Network
172.16.20.0/24

The operator cannot directly reach:

172.16.20.0/24

but the pivot can.

Chisel can provide either:

Specific Port Forward

or:

SOCKS Proxy

through that pivot.

docs.title: Chisel vs Ligolo-ng
docs.text:
Chisel and Ligolo-ng solve overlapping problems using different networking models.

Chisel Ligolo-ng Port-forward/SOCKS model TUN/routing model Often used with ProxyChains Applications generally use normal routing Excellent for explicit forwards Excellent for broad subnet access Reverse SOCKS support Routed pivoting No operator TUN required for basic use TUN interface normally involved HTTP/WebSocket transport Ligolo-ng-specific TLS transport Multiple remotes per connection Multiple tunnels/interfaces TCP and UDP forwarding TCP, UDP and ICMP echo support

A useful rule of thumb is:

Need one or several explicit forwards?
        |
        +--> Chisel

Need broad routed access to an internal subnet?
        |
        +--> Ligolo-ng

This is not absolute.

Choose the tool based on:

  • Network topology
  • Protocol requirements
  • Operating system
  • Available privileges
  • Egress restrictions
  • Tool compatibility
  • Assessment scope

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Before using Chisel, understand four concepts:

Server
Client
Remote
Reverse Remote

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
The Chisel server accepts incoming Chisel client connections.

Typical syntax:

./chisel server -p 8080

The server can additionally enable:

  • Reverse forwarding
  • SOCKS5
  • Authentication
  • TLS
  • Backend HTTP proxying

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
The client connects to the Chisel server.

Basic syntax:

./chisel client <SERVER> <REMOTE>

Example:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 8000:172.16.20.15:80

docs.title: Remote
docs.text:
A Chisel remote describes how traffic should be forwarded.

The general structure is:

<local-host>:<local-port>:<remote-host>:<remote-port>/<protocol>

The protocol defaults to TCP.

Example:

127.0.0.1:8445:172.16.20.15:445

Conceptually:

Operator
127.0.0.1:8445
        |
        v
Chisel
        |
        v
172.16.20.15:445

docs.title: Reverse Remote
docs.text:
A remote prefixed with:

R:

reverses the forwarding direction.

Conceptually:

Listener on Chisel Server
        |
        v
Chisel Tunnel
        |
        v
Chisel Client
        |
        v
Client-Reachable Destination

Reverse remotes require the server to enable:

--reverse

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Use the official Chisel project.

  • Chisel - Official GitHub Repository
  • Chisel Releases

Download the appropriate binary for the operator and pivot operating systems.

Check the version:

./chisel --version

or inspect:

./chisel --help

Windows:

.\chisel.exe --help

docs.title: Build from Source
docs.text:
If Go is installed:

go install github.com/jpillora/chisel@latest

Verify:

chisel --help

The official project also publishes packaged releases and container images.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Display help using the official container:

docker run --rm -it jpillora/chisel --help

For assessment infrastructure, prefer a deployment method that is easy to identify and remove after testing.

docs.title: Basic Port Forwarding
docs.text:
A simple forward exposes a remote service locally.

Assume:

Operator:     10.10.14.10
Pivot:        10.10.10.25
Internal:     172.16.20.15
Service:      172.16.20.15:80

Start the Chisel server on the operator:

./chisel server -p 8080

From the pivot:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 8000:172.16.20.15:80

The operator can then access:

127.0.0.1:8000

which Chisel forwards to:

172.16.20.15:80

Test:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000

The path is:

Operator:8000
     |
     v
Chisel Server
     |
     v
Chisel Client
     |
     v
172.16.20.15:80

docs.title: Bind the Local Forward Explicitly
docs.text:
To avoid exposing the local forwarding port unnecessarily, bind it to loopback:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 127.0.0.1:8000:172.16.20.15:80

This produces:

127.0.0.1:8000
        |
        v
172.16.20.15:80

Prefer loopback bindings unless other systems genuinely need to access the forwarding port.

docs.title: Forward SMB
docs.text:
Assume the internal host is:

172.16.20.15

and SMB is available on:

445/tcp

Create a local forward:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 8445:172.16.20.15:445

Then test from the operator:

nc -vz 127.0.0.1 8445

Remember:

Successful TCP Connection
        !=
Successful SMB Authentication
        !=
Administrative Access

Chisel establishes network reachability only.

docs.title: Forward RDP
docs.text:
For an internal RDP service:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 13389:172.16.20.15:3389

The operator can then connect to:

127.0.0.1:13389

The remote destination remains:

172.16.20.15:3389

Use valid authorised credentials and maintain normal assessment scope.

docs.title: Multiple Port Forwards
docs.text:
Chisel supports multiple remotes over a single connection.

Example:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 \
  8080:172.16.20.15:80 \
  8443:172.16.20.15:443 \
  8445:172.16.20.15:445

Conceptually:

Operator:8080 ---> Internal:80
Operator:8443 ---> Internal:443
Operator:8445 ---> Internal:445

This can be cleaner than running a separate Chisel process for each service.

docs.title: SOCKS5 Pivoting
docs.text:
A SOCKS proxy is useful when access to multiple hosts and ports is required.

The general architecture becomes:

Application
    |
    v
SOCKS5
    |
    v
Chisel
    |
    v
Pivot
    |
    v
Internal Network

Chisel can provide SOCKS in both normal and reverse configurations.

docs.title: Standard SOCKS5
docs.text:
Start the server with SOCKS support:

./chisel server -p 8080 --socks5

Connect the client:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 socks

By default, the local SOCKS listener is commonly:

127.0.0.1:1080

Applications can then use:

SOCKS5 127.0.0.1:1080

docs.title: Reverse SOCKS5
docs.text:
Reverse SOCKS is particularly useful during assessments where the pivot host can make an outbound connection to the operator.

Start the server:

./chisel server -p 8080 --reverse

From the pivot:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 R:socks

The result is typically a SOCKS5 listener on the server:

127.0.0.1:1080

Traffic sent to this SOCKS proxy exits through the Chisel client.

Architecture:

flowchart LR
    A[Operator Tool] --> B[SOCKS5 127.0.0.1:1080]
    B --> C[Chisel Server]
    C --> D[Chisel Client on Pivot]
    D --> E[Internal Network]

This is one of the most useful Chisel configurations during internal assessments.

docs.title: Custom Reverse SOCKS Port
docs.text:
A different server-side SOCKS port can be specified.

Example:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 R:1081:socks

The operator can then configure:

SOCKS5 127.0.0.1 1081

This is useful when:

  • Port 1080 is already occupied
  • Multiple pivots are active
  • Separate SOCKS proxies are required for different networks

For example:

Pivot A -> SOCKS 1080
Pivot B -> SOCKS 1081
Pivot C -> SOCKS 1082

docs.title: ProxyChains
docs.text:
Many command-line tools do not natively support SOCKS.

ProxyChains can redirect compatible TCP connections through the Chisel SOCKS proxy.

Edit:

/etc/proxychains4.conf

or:

/etc/proxychains.conf

Add:

socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

Then run:

proxychains4 curl http://172.16.20.15

or:

proxychains4 nc -vz 172.16.20.15 445

docs.title: ProxyChains DNS
docs.text:
DNS can become an important issue when pivoting.

If the tool resolves a hostname locally before connecting through SOCKS, internal hostnames may fail.

Review the ProxyChains configuration for:

proxy_dns

where appropriate.

Alternatively, query an internal DNS server explicitly.

Example:

proxychains4 dig @172.16.20.10 dc01.corp.local

Do not assume a working SOCKS proxy automatically solves internal DNS resolution.

docs.title: Nmap Through Chisel
docs.text:
Nmap requires special consideration when used through ProxyChains.

Use a TCP connect scan:

proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -p 80,443,445,3389 172.16.20.15

For a specific port:

proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -p 445 172.16.20.15

Avoid relying on SYN scanning through ProxyChains:

-sS

because ProxyChains operates at the application/connect layer rather than forwarding arbitrary raw packets.

A practical model is:

ProxyChains
     |
     v
TCP connect()
     |
     v
SOCKS5
     |
     v
Chisel

Prefer:

-sT

for SOCKS-based scanning.

docs.title: Reverse Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Chisel can expose a port on the server and send traffic through the client.

Start the server with reverse forwarding enabled:

./chisel server -p 8080 --reverse

Assume the pivot can reach:

172.16.20.15:80

Create:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 R:8000:172.16.20.15:80

The Chisel server now exposes:

8000

and traffic is forwarded through the client to:

172.16.20.15:80

Conceptually:

Operator:8000
     |
     v
Chisel Server
     |
     v
Chisel Client
     |
     v
172.16.20.15:80

docs.title: Explicit Reverse Binding
docs.text:
A reverse listener can specify the server-side interface.

For example:

R:127.0.0.1:8000:172.16.20.15:80

This limits the server-side listener to loopback.

Prefer:

127.0.0.1

where only the operator needs access.

Avoid exposing forwarded ports on:

0.0.0.0

unless the assessment specifically requires other systems to connect.

docs.title: UDP Forwarding
docs.text:
Chisel supports UDP forwarding.

The remote syntax can specify:

/udp

For example:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 1053:172.16.20.10:53/udp

This maps:

Operator:1053/UDP
        |
        v
172.16.20.10:53/UDP

UDP behaviour differs from TCP because it is connectionless.

Validate the actual protocol rather than relying only on port-state assumptions.

docs.title: DNS Through a UDP Forward
docs.text:
For an authorised internal DNS server:

172.16.20.10:53

create:

./chisel client 10.10.14.10:8080 1053:172.16.20.10:53/udp

Then query the local forwarded port using a DNS client that supports specifying the destination port.

For example:

dig @127.0.0.1 -p 1053 dc01.corp.local

This can be useful when a full SOCKS workflow is unnecessary.

docs.title: Client Through an Upstream Proxy
docs.text:
Chisel clients can connect through supported HTTP CONNECT or SOCKS proxies.

This can be useful in environments where direct outbound connectivity is unavailable but an authorised proxy is required.

Inspect:

./chisel client --help

for the installed version's proxy options.

The architecture becomes:

Chisel Client
      |
      v
Corporate / Assessment Proxy
      |
      v
Chisel Server

Do not attempt to bypass organisational proxy controls unless that behaviour is explicitly within scope.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Chisel supports authentication between clients and the server.

A simple server configuration can use:

./chisel server -p 8080 --reverse --auth user:password

The client then provides matching credentials.

Check:

./chisel client --help

for the exact current argument placement.

Authentication is strongly preferable when the Chisel server is reachable by systems other than the intended pivot.

docs.title: Authentication File
docs.text:
For multiple users or restricted forwarding destinations, Chisel supports an authentication file.

Example structure:

{
  "operator1:StrongPasswordHere": [
    "^172\\.16\\.20\\..*:.*$"
  ]
}

Start the server:

./chisel server -p 8080 --reverse --authfile users.json

The address patterns can restrict which destinations a particular authenticated user is allowed to request.

Warning

Chisel authentication-file entries use regular expressions. Anchor and escape patterns correctly. Overly broad expressions can unintentionally permit more destinations than intended.

docs.title: Restrict SOCKS Access
docs.text:
When an authentication file is used, SOCKS access should be explicitly considered.

A user requiring normal SOCKS access needs an allowed pattern matching:

socks

Reverse SOCKS permissions should likewise be restricted to the intended reverse listener.

Avoid using unrestricted:

""

unless full forwarding access is genuinely required.

docs.title: Server Fingerprint
docs.text:
Chisel generates an SSH server key and displays a fingerprint.

Clients can validate the expected server using:

--fingerprint

Example structure:

./chisel client --fingerprint '<EXPECTED_FINGERPRINT>' 10.10.14.10:8080 R:socks

Fingerprint verification helps protect against connecting to an unintended or intercepted Chisel server.

For repeatable infrastructure, use a persistent server key rather than generating a different identity every time.

docs.title: Persistent Server Key
docs.text:
Modern Chisel versions support key-file management.

Inspect:

./chisel server --help

for:

--keygen
--keyfile

Generate or configure a persistent server identity where appropriate.

This allows clients to validate a stable fingerprint.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Chisel can run with TLS.

Server options include certificate and key configuration.

Inspect:

./chisel server --help

for current options such as:

--tls-key
--tls-cert
--tls-domain

Using TLS can be useful where the server is exposed over HTTPS.

However:

Encrypted Tunnel
        !=
Authorised Tunnel

Authentication, network restrictions and scope controls remain important.

docs.title: Backend HTTP Proxying
docs.text:
The Chisel server can forward ordinary HTTP requests to another HTTP server.

This can make the listening endpoint behave like a normal web endpoint when the request is not a Chisel WebSocket connection.

Inspect:

--backend

or the supported alias:

--proxy

Example structure:

./chisel server -p 8080 --backend http://127.0.0.1:8000

This capability should not be treated as a substitute for proper network restrictions or authentication.

docs.title: Keepalive
docs.text:
Long-lived tunnels may pass through HTTP proxies, firewalls or load balancers that terminate idle connections.

Chisel supports keepalive configuration.

Inspect:

./chisel client --help

and:

./chisel server --help

for the current:

--keepalive

behaviour.

A tunnel repeatedly disconnecting after a predictable idle period may indicate an intermediate timeout rather than a Chisel failure.

docs.title: Automatic Reconnection
docs.text:
Chisel clients automatically attempt to reconnect when the connection is interrupted.

This can be useful for unstable assessment links.

However, it also means that terminating only the server-side connection may not permanently stop the client.

During cleanup:

Stop Client
        +
Stop Server
        +
Verify Listeners
        =
Confirmed Cleanup

docs.title: stdio Forwarding
docs.text:
Chisel supports forwarding through standard input/output.

One use is integrating Chisel with SSH ProxyCommand.

Conceptually:

ssh -o ProxyCommand='chisel client <SERVER> stdio:%h:%p' user@target

This allows SSH traffic to traverse the Chisel connection without creating a conventional local listener.

Use this only where the SSH destination is within the authorised scope.

docs.title: Active Directory Through Chisel
docs.text:
Reverse SOCKS is particularly useful for Active Directory assessments.

Example:

Operator
    |
    v
127.0.0.1:1080
    |
    v
Chisel Server
    |
    v
Pivot
    |
    v
172.16.20.0/24

Relevant services may include:

Port Service 53 DNS 88 Kerberos 135 RPC 389 LDAP 445 SMB 464 Kerberos password operations 636 LDAPS 3268 Global Catalog 3269 Global Catalog over TLS 3389 RDP

Test individual services first.

proxychains4 nc -vz 172.16.20.10 445

proxychains4 nc -vz 172.16.20.10 389

proxychains4 nc -vz 172.16.20.10 88

Do not interpret network reachability as proof of authentication or privilege.

docs.title: NetExec Through Chisel
docs.text:
With reverse SOCKS configured:

proxychains4 nxc smb 172.16.20.15

For a narrow authorised range:

proxychains4 nxc smb 172.16.20.0/24

SOCKS compatibility can vary by protocol and tool behaviour.

If a tool behaves unexpectedly, test the underlying service first with:

proxychains4 nc -vz <TARGET> <PORT>

See:

NetExec

docs.title: Impacket Through Chisel
docs.text:
Many Impacket tools use TCP-based protocols and can operate through ProxyChains where the relevant network and name-resolution requirements are satisfied.

The conceptual relationship is:

Impacket
    |
    v
ProxyChains
    |
    v
SOCKS5
    |
    v
Chisel
    |
    v
Internal Service

If an Impacket tool fails, validate:

  1. Network reachability
  2. SOCKS operation
  3. DNS/name resolution
  4. Required protocol ports
  5. Authentication
  6. Tool-specific requirements

See:

Impacket

docs.title: BloodHound Through Chisel
docs.text:
BloodHound collection can require several services and correct DNS resolution.

Depending on the collector and collection method, requirements may include:

  • DNS
  • LDAP
  • Kerberos
  • SMB
  • RPC

Do not troubleshoot BloodHound as a single black box.

Validate each dependency through the pivot.

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: Browser Through Chisel
docs.text:
A browser can use the Chisel SOCKS proxy directly.

Configure:

SOCKS5 Host: 127.0.0.1
Port: 1080

This is useful for internal web applications.

Where possible, ensure hostname resolution also occurs through the SOCKS path if internal DNS names are required.

docs.title: curl Through Chisel
docs.text:
curl supports SOCKS directly.

Example:

curl --socks5 127.0.0.1:1080 http://172.16.20.15

For proxy-side hostname resolution:

curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://internal.corp.local

The distinction is useful:

--socks5
    |
    +--> hostname may be resolved locally

--socks5-hostname
    |
    +--> hostname resolution occurs through SOCKS

For internal DNS names, the second behaviour may be preferable.

docs.title: Multi-Hop Pivoting
docs.text:
Chisel can be chained for multi-hop environments.

Example:

Operator
    |
    v
Pivot 1
172.16.20.10
    |
    v
Pivot 2
192.168.50.10
    |
    v
Internal Network
192.168.50.0/24

Each additional hop introduces:

  • Another Chisel process
  • Another forwarding relationship
  • Another potential SOCKS endpoint
  • Additional port-management complexity
  • Additional troubleshooting complexity

Before creating a multi-hop chain, document the network.

docs.title: Multi-Hop Network Map
docs.text:
Example:

[Operator]
    |
    | 10.10.10.0/24
    v
[WEB01]
    |
    | 172.16.20.0/24
    v
[APP01]
    |
    | 192.168.50.0/24
    v
[DC01]

Record:

Host Network Role Operator 10.10.10.0/24 Assessment system WEB01 172.16.20.0/24 Pivot 1 APP01 192.168.50.0/24 Pivot 2 DC01 192.168.50.0/24 Internal target

Avoid creating tunnel chains without first understanding which system can reach which network.

docs.title: Choosing Between Port Forwarding and SOCKS
docs.text:
Use an explicit port forward when:

One Service
or
Small Number of Services

For example:

Internal web application
Internal RDP service
Internal SSH service

Use SOCKS when:

Multiple Hosts
+
Multiple Ports
+
Multiple Tools

For example:

Active Directory assessment
Internal network enumeration
Several internal web applications

This keeps the tunnel configuration as simple as possible.

docs.title: Client Cannot Connect to Server
docs.text:
Verify the Chisel server:

ss -lntp | grep 8080

From Linux:

nc -vz <SERVER_IP> 8080

From Windows:

Test-NetConnection <SERVER_IP> -Port 8080

Possible causes include:

  • Incorrect server address
  • Incorrect port
  • Local firewall
  • Network firewall
  • Outbound filtering
  • Proxy requirement
  • TLS configuration
  • Authentication failure
  • Server not listening

docs.title: Chisel Connects but Internal Service Fails
docs.text:
Test the internal service from the pivot first.

Linux:

nc -vz 172.16.20.15 445

Windows:

Test-NetConnection 172.16.20.15 -Port 445

If the pivot cannot reach the service, Chisel cannot create reachability that the pivot itself does not have.

The correct troubleshooting sequence is:

Can Pivot Reach Target?
        |
        v
Can Client Reach Chisel Server?
        |
        v
Is Tunnel Established?
        |
        v
Is SOCKS / Forward Listening?
        |
        v
Can Operator Reach Through Tunnel?
        |
        v
Does Application Protocol Work?

docs.title: SOCKS Listener Is Missing
docs.text:
Check whether the server was started with the required mode.

For normal SOCKS:

--socks5

For reverse SOCKS:

--reverse

Then verify the client remote:

socks

or:

R:socks

Check listening ports:

ss -lntp

docs.title: ProxyChains Fails
docs.text:
First test the SOCKS proxy without the target application.

For example:

curl --socks5 127.0.0.1:1080 http://172.16.20.15

If this works but ProxyChains does not, investigate:

  • ProxyChains configuration
  • SOCKS4 vs SOCKS5
  • DNS handling
  • Application compatibility
  • Static binaries
  • Raw socket use

docs.title: IP Works but Hostname Fails
docs.text:
This usually indicates name-resolution problems.

Test the internal DNS server:

proxychains4 dig @172.16.20.10 dc01.corp.local

Or use a SOCKS-aware application that resolves hostnames through the proxy.

For curl:

curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://internal.corp.local

docs.title: Nmap Shows Everything Closed or Times Out
docs.text:
Use:

proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -p 445 172.16.20.15

Do not use a raw SYN scan through ProxyChains and expect normal SOCKS behaviour.

Compare with:

proxychains4 nc -vz 172.16.20.15 445

docs.title: Reverse Tunnel Does Not Work
docs.text:
Verify the server was started with:

--reverse

Then verify the remote begins with:

R:

Check server-side listeners:

ss -lntp

Also verify that the Chisel client itself can reach the requested destination.

docs.title: Authentication Fails
docs.text:
Check:

  • Username
  • Password
  • Argument placement
  • Server authentication configuration
  • Authfile regular expressions
  • Destination permissions
  • SOCKS permissions

Use:

./chisel client --help

and:

./chisel server --help

for the exact syntax supported by the installed release.

docs.title: Validation Model
docs.text: Validate Chisel in layers.

docs.title: Layer 1 - Pivot Reachability
docs.text: Can the pivot reach the internal target?

docs.title: Layer 2 - Chisel Transport
docs.text: Can the Chisel client connect to the server?

docs.title: Layer 3 - Tunnel
docs.text: Was the requested remote successfully created?

docs.title: Layer 4 - Listener
docs.text: Is the expected local or reverse port listening?

docs.title: Layer 5 - Network
docs.text: Can traffic traverse the tunnel?

docs.title: Layer 6 - Protocol
docs.text: Does the expected application protocol work?

docs.title: Layer 7 - Authentication
docs.text:
If required, does authentication succeed?

Keep these states separate.

Tunnel Established
        !=
Service Reachable
        !=
Authentication Successful
        !=
Authorised Resource Access
        !=
Administrative Rights

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful assessment evidence may include:

  • Pivot hostname
  • Pivot network interfaces
  • Pivot route table
  • Chisel server configuration
  • Chisel client connection
  • Remote configuration
  • SOCKS listener
  • Port-forward listener
  • Successful connection through the tunnel
  • Internal destination reached
  • Timestamp
  • Cleanup verification

A useful evidence chain is:

Pivot Can Reach Internal Service
        |
        v
Chisel Connection Established
        |
        v
SOCKS / Forward Created
        |
        v
Operator Reaches Service
        |
        v
Evidence Captured

Do not claim broader network access than was actually demonstrated.

docs.title: Security Interpretation
docs.text:
Chisel demonstrates a network pivot capability.

For example:

Low-Privilege Host
        |
        +--> Outbound HTTP/WebSocket Connectivity
        |
        +--> Internal Network Access
        |
        v
Potential Pivot Path

This may demonstrate weaknesses in:

  • Network segmentation
  • Egress filtering
  • Host application control
  • Network monitoring
  • Trust assumptions

It does not automatically prove:

  • Credential compromise
  • Privilege escalation
  • Administrative access
  • Domain compromise

Those require separate evidence.

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Defenders may investigate:

  • Long-lived HTTP/WebSocket connections
  • Unexpected outbound connections from servers
  • Chisel process execution
  • Unknown binaries in user-writable directories
  • Unexpected SOCKS listeners
  • Unexpected local forwarding ports
  • Unusual east-west traffic
  • New outbound connections followed by internal scanning
  • Connections to uncommon external ports
  • Process/network relationships inconsistent with the host role

Detection should not rely only on:

chisel.exe

or a known file hash.

The underlying behaviour is more important.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text:
Relevant controls include:

  • Restrict unnecessary outbound connectivity
  • Apply egress filtering
  • Restrict unnecessary east-west traffic
  • Use host-based firewalls
  • Implement application control
  • Monitor unusual binaries
  • Monitor long-lived WebSocket connections
  • Monitor unexpected local listeners
  • Correlate endpoint and network telemetry
  • Segment sensitive networks
  • Restrict administrative execution
  • Review proxy access controls

The underlying risk can be represented as:

Executable Capability
        +
Outbound Connectivity
        +
Internal Network Reachability
        =
Potential Pivot

Blocking one Chisel hash does not remove the underlying pivot opportunity.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminate the Chisel client.

Terminate the Chisel server when it is no longer required.

Verify local listeners:

ss -lntp

Verify UDP listeners where applicable:

ss -lnup

Remove:

  • Chisel binaries where required
  • Temporary configuration
  • Authentication files
  • Temporary TLS material
  • ProxyChains changes no longer required
  • Temporary browser proxy settings

Document cleanup.

docs.title: Start Server
docs.text: ./chisel server -p 8080

docs.title: Reverse-Enabled Server
docs.text: ./chisel server -p 8080 --reverse

docs.title: SOCKS-Enabled Server
docs.text: ./chisel server -p 8080 --socks5

docs.title: Reverse + Authentication
docs.text: ./chisel server -p 8080 --reverse --auth user:password

docs.title: Basic Port Forward
docs.text: ./chisel client <SERVER>:8080 8000:<TARGET>:80

docs.title: Explicit Loopback Forward
docs.text: ./chisel client <SERVER>:8080 127.0.0.1:8000:<TARGET>:80

docs.title: Multiple Forwards
docs.text:
./chisel client <SERVER>:8080 \
  8080:<TARGET>:80 \
  8443:<TARGET>:443 \
  8445:<TARGET>:445

docs.title: Normal SOCKS
docs.text:
Server:

./chisel server -p 8080 --socks5

Client:

./chisel client <SERVER>:8080 socks

docs.title: Reverse SOCKS
docs.text:
Server:

./chisel server -p 8080 --reverse

Client:

./chisel client <SERVER>:8080 R:socks

docs.title: Custom Reverse SOCKS Port
docs.text: ./chisel client <SERVER>:8080 R:1081:socks

docs.title: Reverse Port Forward
docs.text: ./chisel client <SERVER>:8080 R:8000:<TARGET>:80

docs.title: UDP Forward
docs.text: ./chisel client <SERVER>:8080 1053:<DNS_SERVER>:53/udp

docs.title: ProxyChains
docs.text: socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

docs.title: curl Through SOCKS
docs.text: curl --socks5 127.0.0.1:1080 http://<TARGET>

docs.title: curl with Proxy-Side Hostname Resolution
docs.text: curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://<HOSTNAME>

docs.title: Nmap Through SOCKS
docs.text: proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -p 80,443,445,3389 <TARGET>

docs.title: Test Port Through SOCKS
docs.text: proxychains4 nc -vz <TARGET> <PORT>

docs.title: Using SYN Scans Through ProxyChains
docs.text:
Prefer:

-sT

rather than expecting raw SYN forwarding.

docs.title: Forgetting DNS
docs.text: A working SOCKS proxy does not guarantee internal hostname resolution.

docs.title: Exposing Forwarded Ports Unnecessarily
docs.text:
Prefer:

127.0.0.1

over:

0.0.0.0

unless remote access to the forwarded port is intentionally required.

docs.title: Forgetting --reverse
docs.text: Reverse remotes require the server to permit reverse forwarding.

docs.title: Confusing Normal SOCKS and Reverse SOCKS
docs.text:
Normal:

socks

Reverse:

R:socks

They create the SOCKS listener on different sides of the Chisel relationship.

docs.title: Using an Unauthenticated Public Server
docs.text: If the Chisel server is reachable by untrusted systems, authentication and network restrictions should be considered.

docs.title: Treating the Tunnel as Proof of Privilege
docs.text:
A tunnel proves network connectivity.

It does not prove privileged access.

docs.title: Forgetting Cleanup
docs.text:
Stop:

  • Clients
  • Servers
  • SOCKS proxies
  • Port forwards

and restore temporary proxy configuration.

docs.title: Cobalt Strike
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike is a commercial adversary-simulation and red-team operations platform developed by Fortra. It provides collaborative command-and-control infrastructure, the Beacon post-exploitation agent, multiple communication channels, pivoting, Malleable C2, extensibility through Aggressor Script and Beacon Object Files (BOFs), reporting, automation, and other capabilities used during authorised security assessments.

Cobalt Strike is designed for threat-representative security testing rather than conventional vulnerability scanning.

Authorised Testing Only

Cobalt Strike provides command-and-control and post-exploitation capabilities. Use it only against systems explicitly included in an authorised security assessment. Define permitted hosts, networks, payload types, communication channels, privilege boundaries, lateral-movement actions, and cleanup requirements before deployment.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A typical Cobalt Strike architecture is:

Operator
    |
    v
Cobalt Strike Client
    |
    v
Team Server
    |
    v
Listener
    |
    v
Beacon
    |
    v
Authorised Test Host

Multiple operators can collaborate through the same Team Server:

flowchart TD
    O1[Operator 1] --> TS[Team Server]
    O2[Operator 2] --> TS
    O3[Operator 3] --> TS

    TS --> H[HTTP/HTTPS Beacon]
    TS --> D[DNS/DoH Beacon]
    TS --> S[SMB Beacon]
    TS --> T[TCP Beacon]

    H --> W1[Test Host 1]
    D --> W2[Test Host 2]
    S --> W3[Test Host 3]
    T --> W4[Test Host 4]

The main operational layers are:

Infrastructure
        |
        v
Team Server
        |
        v
Listener
        |
        v
Beacon
        |
        v
Session Context
        |
        v
Assessment Action

Keep these layers separate when troubleshooting.

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
Use official Cobalt Strike documentation as the primary reference.

  • Cobalt Strike
  • Cobalt Strike User Manuals
  • Cobalt Strike Support
  • Cobalt Strike Releases
  • Cobalt Strike Training

Cobalt Strike is commercial software.

Use only legitimate licensed copies obtained through authorised channels.

Avoid cracked or unofficial versions.

docs.title: Current Cobalt Strike
docs.text:
Modern Cobalt Strike includes considerably more functionality than older tutorials may describe.

Current capabilities include concepts such as:

Beacon
Malleable C2
HTTP/HTTPS C2
DNS
DNS over HTTPS
SMB Beacon
TCP Beacon
External C2
User Defined Command and Control
Beacon Object Files
BOF-PE
Beacon Interpreter
LLVM Beacon
Payload Store
Aggressor Script
REST API
SOCKS
Port Forwarding
Pivoting
Reporting
Multiplayer

Always verify the installed version before relying on old command syntax or tradecraft.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The primary components are:

Component Purpose Client Operator graphical interface Team Server Central collaboration and C2 server Listener Defines Beacon communication Beacon Post-exploitation agent Malleable C2 Customises communication behaviour Aggressor Script Extends the client and workflows BOF Executes compact native functionality through Beacon Payload Store Central payload management REST API Automation and integration SOCKS Proxies traffic through Beacon Port Forward Forwards selected traffic Reporting Generates assessment activity reports

docs.title: Team Server
docs.text:
The Team Server provides the central infrastructure for an engagement.

Conceptually:

Team Server
├── Operator Connections
├── Listeners
├── Beacon Metadata
├── Tasks
├── Results
├── Downloads
├── Logs
└── Collaboration

Treat the Team Server as sensitive assessment infrastructure.

It may contain information about:

Targets
Credentials
Beacon Sessions
Operator Activity
Downloaded Files
Assessment Infrastructure

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Follow the installation documentation supplied with the licensed Cobalt Strike distribution.

Before deployment, record:

Version
Build
License
Server Host
Assessment
Installation Date

Do not place licensed installation files in public repositories.

docs.title: Version
docs.text:
Record the exact version used during an assessment.

This matters because Cobalt Strike changes frequently.

For example, functionality relating to:

Beacon
BOFs
REST API
Malleable C2
Memory behaviour
Pivoting
Payload Generation

can differ between releases.

docs.title: Start the Team Server
docs.text:
The licensed Cobalt Strike distribution provides the Team Server launcher.

The general architecture is:

Linux Server
    |
    v
Team Server
    |
    v
TCP/50050
    |
    v
Cobalt Strike Clients

Use the official installation manual for the exact syntax for the installed release.

Do not expose Team Server administration directly to untrusted networks when avoidable.

docs.title: Team Server Connectivity
docs.text:
Before connecting a client, validate:

Team Server Running?
        |
        v
Management Port Listening?
        |
        v
Firewall Allows Operator?
        |
        v
TLS Fingerprint Verified?
        |
        v
Authentication Successful?

On Linux:

ss -lntp

Test connectivity:

nc -vz <TEAM_SERVER> 50050

where appropriate for the deployed configuration.

docs.title: Team Server Security
docs.text:
Protect the Team Server using:

Restricted Source IPs
Host Firewall
SSH Keys
Strong Authentication
Patch Management
Minimal Services
Disk Encryption
Secure Backups
Central Logging

The Team Server should not be treated as a disposable anonymous VPS.

It is part of the assessment evidence chain.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
The Cobalt Strike client provides the operator interface.

The client connects to the Team Server and allows authorised operators to:

Manage Listeners
Manage Beacons
Task Beacons
View Downloads
Review Credentials
Manage Pivots
Generate Reports
Load Extensions
Collaborate

Operators should use individual identities where possible.

docs.title: Collaboration
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike is designed for multi-operator engagements.

Conceptually:

Operator A ----+
               |
Operator B ----+--> Team Server --> Beacons
               |
Operator C ----+

This is useful for:

Red Teams
Purple Teams
Adversary Simulations
Large Penetration Tests
Training Exercises

Coordinate operators carefully to avoid conflicting tasks.

docs.title: Listeners
docs.text:
Listeners define how Beacon communicates.

Listener configuration can include:

Protocol
Host
Port
Profile
Domains
Proxy Behaviour
Communication Method

The exact options depend on the listener type and installed version.

docs.title: Listener Management
docs.text:
Before generating any test payload, create and validate the required listener.

The workflow should be:

Assessment Requirement
        |
        v
Choose Transport
        |
        v
Configure Listener
        |
        v
Validate Infrastructure
        |
        v
Generate Test Payload

Do not generate multiple payloads simply because the first one cannot connect.

Validate the listener first.

docs.title: Beacon
docs.text:
Beacon is Cobalt Strike's primary post-exploitation agent.

Conceptually:

Beacon
    |
    +--> C2 Communication
    |
    +--> Host Enumeration
    |
    +--> Task Execution
    |
    +--> File Transfer
    |
    +--> Pivoting
    |
    +--> Extensibility

Beacon should be viewed as:

Remote Assessment Agent

not:

Automatic Administrative Access

Its privileges are determined by the process and security context in which it executes.

docs.title: Beacon Context
docs.text:
When a Beacon is established, identify:

Hostname
Username
Process
PID
Architecture
Integrity
Network
Transport

before performing additional actions.

The reasoning should be:

Beacon Established
        |
        v
Host Confirmed
        |
        v
Identity Confirmed
        |
        v
Privilege Confirmed
        |
        v
Scope Confirmed
        |
        v
Action

docs.title: Beacon Commands
docs.text:
Beacon provides a command console.

Use:

help

to display commands available in the installed release.

For command-specific help:

help <COMMAND>

Do not assume commands from old Cobalt Strike tutorials still behave identically.

docs.title: Sleep
docs.text:
Beacon commonly operates asynchronously.

The:

sleep

setting controls check-in behaviour.

Conceptually:

Beacon
    |
    v
Sleep
    |
    v
Check In
    |
    v
Receive Task
    |
    v
Execute
    |
    v
Return Result

This affects both operational responsiveness and network behaviour.

docs.title: Interactive Mode
docs.text:
For tasks requiring responsive communication, Beacon can operate interactively.

Historically:

sleep 0

places Beacon into interactive behaviour.

Use this only when necessary.

Interactive communication can generate substantially more network traffic.

docs.title: Sleep and Jitter
docs.text:
Beacon timing can include:

Sleep
Jitter

Conceptually:

Base Interval
        +
Timing Variation
        =
Beacon Check-In Pattern

Do not choose timing solely for stealth.

Consider:

Assessment Objective
Network Load
Purple-Team Visibility
Operator Requirements
Test Duration

docs.title: Beacon Types
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike supports multiple Beacon communication methods.

Common examples include:

HTTP
HTTPS
DNS
DNS over HTTPS
SMB
TCP

Modern versions additionally support extensible communication models such as:

External C2
User Defined Command and Control

Different channels serve different network situations.

docs.title: HTTP Beacon
docs.text:
HTTP Beacon communicates using web requests.

Conceptually:

Beacon
    |
    v
HTTP
    |
    v
Team Server

This can be useful where ordinary outbound web connectivity exists.

HTTP traffic remains observable to:

Proxy
Firewall
IDS/IPS
EDR
Network Monitoring

docs.title: HTTPS Beacon
docs.text:
HTTPS adds TLS to the communication path.

Conceptually:

Beacon
    |
    v
TLS
    |
    v
HTTPS
    |
    v
Team Server

Encryption does not make traffic invisible.

Defenders can still analyse:

Destination
Certificate
TLS Behaviour
Connection Timing
Process
DNS
Traffic Volume

docs.title: DNS Beacon
docs.text:
DNS Beacon communicates through DNS.

Conceptually:

Beacon
    |
    v
DNS Query
    |
    v
Resolver
    |
    v
Authoritative Infrastructure
    |
    v
Team Server

DNS C2 requires correctly configured DNS infrastructure.

Relevant considerations include:

Domain Ownership
Delegation
Authoritative DNS
Resolvers
Query Types
Logging
Latency

docs.title: DNS over HTTPS
docs.text:
Modern Cobalt Strike supports DNS over HTTPS communication.

The architecture becomes:

Beacon
    |
    v
HTTPS
    |
    v
DoH Resolver / Infrastructure
    |
    v
DNS C2

DoH changes the network visibility model but does not eliminate endpoint telemetry.

docs.title: SMB Beacon
docs.text:
SMB Beacon supports peer-to-peer communication.

Conceptually:

Team Server
      |
      v
Beacon A
      |
      | SMB
      v
Beacon B

This can reduce the number of systems requiring direct outbound C2 connectivity.

It also introduces additional internal communication that defenders can monitor.

docs.title: TCP Beacon
docs.text:
TCP Beacon provides peer-to-peer communication over TCP.

Conceptually:

Beacon A
    |
    v
TCP
    |
    v
Beacon B

This can be useful when direct Team Server connectivity is unavailable but internal network connectivity exists.

Use only within authorised networks.

docs.title: Peer-to-Peer C2
docs.text:
SMB and TCP Beacons allow chained communication.

For example:

Team Server
    |
    v
HTTPS Beacon
    |
    v
SMB Beacon
    |
    v
TCP Beacon

The operational benefit is:

Only Selected Systems Need Direct External C2

However, troubleshooting becomes more complex because every link matters.

docs.title: Peer-to-Peer Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Use:

Parent Beacon Alive?
        |
        v
Internal Route Available?
        |
        v
Required Port Reachable?
        |
        v
Child Beacon Running?
        |
        v
Link Established?

If the parent disappears, dependent communication may also be affected.

docs.title: External C2
docs.text:
External C2 allows Cobalt Strike communication to be integrated with custom external communication channels.

Conceptually:

Beacon
    |
    v
External C2 Interface
    |
    v
Custom Transport
    |
    v
Team Server

This is an advanced capability.

Use the official documentation and a controlled lab before deploying custom communication mechanisms in an assessment.

docs.title: User Defined Command and Control
docs.text:
Modern Cobalt Strike supports User Defined Command and Control concepts.

This allows custom C2 channels to integrate more directly with Beacon.

Keep custom transport development in dedicated red-team tooling notes.

The Cobalt Strike tool page should focus on the architecture:

Beacon
    |
    v
Custom C2 Implementation
    |
    v
Cobalt Strike Infrastructure

docs.title: Malleable C2
docs.text:
Malleable C2 allows operators to define aspects of C2 communication behaviour.

A profile can influence properties associated with:

HTTP
HTTPS
Headers
URIs
Data Transformation
Beacon Behaviour
Process Behaviour
Post-Exploitation Behaviour

The objective during an authorised assessment should be to model an agreed threat profile, not merely to create arbitrary obfuscation.

docs.title: Malleable C2 Model
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Beacon Data
    |
    v
Malleable Transformation
    |
    v
Network Request
    |
    v
Team Server
    |
    v
Reverse Transformation

This makes communication behaviour configurable.

docs.title: Profile Validation
docs.text:
Before using a Malleable C2 profile in production, validate it.

Use the profile validation tools provided with the licensed distribution.

The workflow should be:

Write Profile
        |
        v
Validate Syntax
        |
        v
Test in Lab
        |
        v
Capture Traffic
        |
        v
Confirm Behaviour
        |
        v
Deploy

Never deploy an untested profile directly into a production engagement.

docs.title: Malleable C2 and Detection
docs.text:
Malleable C2 does not make C2 traffic automatically invisible.

Defenders can correlate:

Endpoint Process
DNS
Destination
TLS
Proxy Logs
Traffic Timing
Network Volume
Host Role

A realistic assessment should test whether the organisation detects the complete behaviour rather than one static signature.

docs.title: Payloads
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike can generate Beacon payloads in multiple forms.

Exact formats depend on the installed version.

Payload design should begin with:

Assessment Objective
        |
        v
Target Platform
        |
        v
Architecture
        |
        v
Listener
        |
        v
Delivery Method
        |
        v
Payload Format

Do not select a format simply because it is available.

docs.title: Staged vs Stageless
docs.text: Cobalt Strike supports staged and stageless payload concepts.

docs.title: Staged
docs.text:
Initial Component
        |
        v
Retrieve Additional Component
        |
        v
Beacon

docs.title: Stageless
docs.text:
Complete Beacon
        |
        v
Execution

Each has different:

Size
Network Behaviour
Reliability
Operational Requirements

Detailed staged-payload design belongs in the Red Teaming notes.

docs.title: Payload Store
docs.text:
Modern Cobalt Strike provides centralised payload-management functionality through the Payload Store.

Conceptually:

Generated Payload
        |
        v
Payload Store
        |
        +--> Metadata
        +--> Management
        +--> Reuse
        +--> Operator Workflow

This can improve consistency during multi-operator engagements.

Still maintain an independent assessment inventory of deployed files.

docs.title: Payload Tracking
docs.text:
For every deployed test artifact, record:

Payload Name
Format
Architecture
Listener
Generation Time
SHA256
Target
Deployment Time
Removal Time

Linux hash:

sha256sum <FILE>

Windows:

Get-FileHash .\<FILE> -Algorithm SHA256

This is important for detection validation and cleanup.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
Where available, payload guardrails can help constrain authorised test payloads to intended environments.

The defensive operational idea is:

Payload
    |
    v
Environment Check
    |
    +--> Approved Environment -> Continue
    |
    +--> Unexpected Environment -> Stop

Guardrails should complement, not replace:

Scope Control
Operator Discipline
Infrastructure Restrictions
Cleanup

docs.title: Post-Exploitation
docs.text:
Once Beacon is established, post-exploitation should follow an explicit objective.

A good workflow is:

Beacon
    |
    v
Establish Context
    |
    v
Define Test Objective
    |
    v
Minimum Required Action
    |
    v
Evidence
    |
    v
Cleanup

Avoid running large numbers of commands simply because they are available.

docs.title: File System
docs.text:
Beacon provides file-system interaction capabilities.

Common concepts include:

pwd
cd
ls
download
upload

Check:

help

for the current release.

Treat remote file access according to assessment data-handling requirements.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
Downloaded files may contain sensitive organisational information.

For each download, record:

Source
Reason
Operator
Timestamp
Storage Location
Retention
Deletion

Do not download entire directories when a single proof file is sufficient.

docs.title: Uploads
docs.text:
Before uploading a test file, record its hash:

sha256sum <FILE>

After transfer:

Get-FileHash C:\Path\To\<FILE> -Algorithm SHA256

Matching hashes provide evidence that the expected assessment file was transferred.

docs.title: Process Information
docs.text:
Process information can help determine:

Current Context
Architecture
Security Products
Applications
Potential Assessment Targets

Do not terminate or manipulate security processes merely because they are visible.

Detection and prevention may be the intended assessment result.

docs.title: Native Commands
docs.text:
Beacon can invoke operating-system functionality through several mechanisms depending on the task.

Always understand the telemetry generated by a command.

The reasoning should be:

Operator Command
        |
        v
Beacon Implementation
        |
        v
Windows API / Process / Shell
        |
        v
Endpoint Telemetry

Two commands producing the same visible output may generate very different telemetry.

docs.title: Beacon Object Files
docs.text:
Beacon Object Files provide a mechanism for running compact native functionality within Beacon.

Conceptually:

Operator
    |
    v
BOF
    |
    v
Beacon
    |
    v
Native Functionality

BOFs are useful because they extend Beacon without requiring every capability to exist permanently in the core agent.

docs.title: BOF Operational Model
docs.text:
The important distinction is:

Traditional External Tool
        |
        v
New Process / Separate Executable

versus

BOF
        |
        v
Beacon-Integrated Execution

This changes telemetry but does not remove telemetry.

Memory, API, network and behavioural monitoring can still detect activity.

docs.title: BOF-PE
docs.text:
Modern Cobalt Strike includes BOF-PE support.

This extends Beacon's BOF ecosystem to support additional PE-oriented development workflows.

Treat BOF-PE code as executable assessment tooling.

Apply the same review process as any other extension:

Source
        |
        v
Code Review
        |
        v
Compile
        |
        v
Lab Test
        |
        v
Authorised Deployment

docs.title: Beacon Interpreter
docs.text:
Modern Cobalt Strike includes Beacon Interpreter functionality.

This provides a mechanism for executing supported scriptable C functionality through Beacon.

Treat interpreted functionality as code execution.

Review and test any custom code before use against production systems.

docs.title: LLVM Beacon
docs.text:
Modern releases include an LLVM-based Beacon implementation.

This provides an alternative Beacon build architecture.

Do not assume different compilation automatically means:

Undetectable

Defenders can detect:

Behaviour
Memory
Network
Process Activity
C2

independent of compiler choice.

docs.title: Aggressor Script
docs.text:
Aggressor Script extends the Cobalt Strike client.

It can be used for:

Custom Commands
Automation
Menus
Event Handling
Workflow Integration
Data Processing

Treat Aggressor scripts as executable code.

docs.title: Aggressor Script Safety
docs.text:
Before loading a third-party script:

Identify Source
        |
        v
Review Code
        |
        v
Understand Commands
        |
        v
Test in Lab
        |
        v
Load

Do not automatically load large public script collections into assessment infrastructure.

docs.title: Community Kit
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike maintains a Community Kit containing community-developed resources.

Use community content as:

Reference
Extension
Research

not as automatically trusted production tooling.

Review every third-party component before use.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
Modern Cobalt Strike provides REST API functionality for automation and integration.

Conceptually:

Automation
    |
    v
REST API
    |
    v
Team Server
    |
    v
Cobalt Strike Operations

Potential uses include:

Automation
Task Tracking
Artifact Management
Custom Clients
Integration
Reporting

Protect API credentials as privileged assessment credentials.

docs.title: API Security
docs.text:
Apply:

Restricted Network Access
Strong Authentication
TLS
Credential Rotation
Audit Logging
Least Privilege

where supported.

Do not expose the Cobalt Strike REST API broadly to the Internet.

docs.title: Task Tracking
docs.text:
Modern releases associate task identifiers with operator tasks and responses.

This is useful for:

Automation
Evidence
Troubleshooting
Auditability

Where possible, preserve task IDs alongside significant assessment evidence.

docs.title: Pivoting
docs.text:
Beacon can act as a pivot point for authorised internal network access.

Before pivoting:

Identify Internal Network
        |
        v
Confirm Scope
        |
        v
Confirm Beacon Reachability
        |
        v
Choose Pivot Method
        |
        v
Validate One Service
        |
        v
Expand Only if Required

docs.title: SOCKS Proxy
docs.text:
Beacon supports SOCKS pivoting.

Use:

help socks

for the exact syntax of the installed release.

A common conceptual workflow is:

Operator Tool
    |
    v
SOCKS Proxy on Team Server
    |
    v
Beacon
    |
    v
Internal Target

Modern Cobalt Strike supports SOCKS4/SOCKS5 functionality.

docs.title: SOCKS Example
docs.text:
A common lab-style command is:

socks 8080

Use the installed version's:

help socks

before relying on additional arguments.

Review configured pivots through the Cobalt Strike proxy/pivot view.

docs.title: SOCKS5
docs.text:
Modern versions support SOCKS5 functionality, including authentication and logging options depending on release.

Always inspect:

help socks

because syntax has evolved.

Do not expose an unauthenticated SOCKS service to an untrusted network.

docs.title: Stop SOCKS
docs.text:
Use the current command help to stop the SOCKS server.

Historically:

socks stop

is used to terminate the associated proxy.

Verify that the listener is actually removed after cleanup.

docs.title: ProxyChains
docs.text:
A Cobalt Strike SOCKS listener can be used with ProxyChains.

Example /etc/proxychains4.conf entry:

socks5 127.0.0.1 8080

Test a specific service:

proxychains4 nc -vz <TARGET> <PORT>

Do not start with broad scanning.

docs.title: Nmap Through Beacon SOCKS
docs.text:
Use TCP connect scanning when operating Nmap through an application-layer SOCKS proxy.

Example:

proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -p 80,443,445,3389 <TARGET>

Avoid raw SYN assumptions through SOCKS.

The path is:

Nmap
    |
    v
connect()
    |
    v
ProxyChains
    |
    v
SOCKS
    |
    v
Beacon
    |
    v
Target

docs.title: Pivot Performance
docs.text:
SOCKS traffic becomes Beacon tasks.

Therefore Beacon timing affects pivot responsiveness.

Conceptually:

Application Request
        |
        v
SOCKS
        |
        v
Beacon Task
        |
        v
Beacon Check-In
        |
        v
Internal Connection

A long sleep interval can make interactive pivoting impractical.

docs.title: Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike supports port-forwarding capabilities.

Use:

help portfwd

and related command help for the installed version.

Port forwarding is useful when:

One Service
+
One Target

needs to be exposed.

docs.title: SOCKS vs Port Forward
docs.text:
Use:

Single Service
        |
        +--> Port Forward

Multiple TCP Services
        |
        +--> SOCKS

Broad Routed Network
        |
        +--> Ligolo-ng

Do not use a complex pivot when a simple forward is sufficient.

docs.title: Reverse Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Reverse port forwarding allows a listening service on the Beacon side of the network path to forward connections elsewhere.

This can be useful for controlled testing where inbound internal connectivity must reach authorised assessment infrastructure.

Use the installed command help before configuring it.

Always record:

Listening Host
Listening Port
Destination Host
Destination Port
Purpose
Cleanup

docs.title: Ligolo-ng vs Cobalt Strike Pivoting
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike pivoting is integrated into Beacon.

Ligolo-ng is purpose-built for routed tunnelling.

Use Cobalt Strike when:

Beacon Already Exists
+
Limited Internal Access Required

Use Ligolo-ng when:

Broad Routed Network Access
+
Many Tools
+
Many Services

is required.

See:

Ligolo-ng

docs.title: Chisel vs Cobalt Strike
docs.text:
Chisel provides lightweight HTTP/WebSocket tunnelling.

Cobalt Strike provides pivoting as part of a larger C2 framework.

Use the simplest tool appropriate to the objective.

See:

Chisel

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike can provide the operator channel during an Active Directory assessment.

However, AD-specific methodology should remain in the dedicated AD notes.

Conceptually:

Beacon
    |
    v
Domain Context
    |
    v
Dedicated AD Assessment Tool
    |
    v
Security Finding

Examples include:

BloodHound
NetExec
Impacket
Rubeus
Certify
Certipy

docs.title: Rubeus
docs.text:
Rubeus specialises in Kerberos assessment.

Cobalt Strike provides the remote operational channel.

Keep the security reasoning separate:

Beacon
    |
    v
Rubeus Test
    |
    v
Kerberos Behaviour
    |
    v
Security Conclusion

See:

Rubeus

docs.title: Mimikatz
docs.text:
Mimikatz focuses on Windows authentication and credential security.

Cobalt Strike is the C2 framework.

The relationship is:

Cobalt Strike
        |
        +--> Remote Operator Channel

Mimikatz
        |
        +--> Authentication Security Testing

See:

Mimikatz

docs.title: AD CS
docs.text:
Use Certify and Certipy for dedicated AD CS assessment.

See:

Certify

and:

Certipy

Do not duplicate their complete workflows inside the Cobalt Strike page.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound is better suited to relationship and attack-path analysis.

Cobalt Strike can provide host access during the assessment, but the graph analysis remains a separate stage.

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
A Beacon running as a normal user does not imply privilege escalation.

Always distinguish:

Beacon Running
        |
        v
Current User
        |
        v
Current Token
        |
        v
Current Integrity

from:

Administrator / SYSTEM

Use the dedicated Windows privilege-escalation methodology for analysing elevation candidates.

docs.title: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike supports workflows associated with lateral movement, but a successful remote connection does not by itself explain why lateral movement was possible.

The finding should identify:

Credential / Trust
        |
        v
Remote Access Permission
        |
        v
Reachable Service
        |
        v
Execution
        |
        v
New Security Context

Detailed lateral-movement techniques belong in the Active Directory and Windows notes.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike can maintain credential information discovered during an assessment.

Treat this data as highly sensitive.

Credential material should not be:

Committed to Git
Included in screenshots unnecessarily
Copied into normal notes
Retained after the engagement without need

Follow the assessment data-retention policy.

docs.title: BOFs and Tool Integration
docs.text:
Modern Cobalt Strike ecosystems commonly use BOFs for focused functionality.

The operational model should remain:

Need Identified
        |
        v
Tool / BOF Selected
        |
        v
Source Reviewed
        |
        v
Lab Tested
        |
        v
Authorised Execution
        |
        v
Evidence

Avoid turning Beacon into a collection of unreviewed third-party code.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike should be evaluated across multiple telemetry layers.

Endpoint
+
Network
+
DNS
+
Identity
+
Application Control
+
SIEM

Detection based solely on:

cobaltstrike.exe

or one static Beacon signature is insufficient.

docs.title: Endpoint Detection
docs.text:
Potential telemetry includes:

Process Creation
Process Access
Memory Allocation
Thread Creation
Module Loads
File Creation
Registry Activity
Network Connections
Named Pipes
Token Activity

Relevant sources may include:

EDR
Microsoft Defender
Sysmon
Windows Security Logs
ETW
Application Control

docs.title: Network Detection
docs.text:
Potential signals include:

Periodic Beaconing
Unexpected Destinations
Unusual TLS
DNS Patterns
Long-Lived Connections
Peer-to-Peer Internal C2
SOCKS Traffic
Port Forwarding

Always consider the expected network behaviour of the affected host.

docs.title: DNS Detection
docs.text:
DNS-based Beacon communication can produce behavioural signals involving:

Query Frequency
Subdomain Structure
Record Types
Authoritative Domain
Response Patterns
Query Volume

Do not use one simplistic DNS pattern as the only detection mechanism.

docs.title: SMB Beacon Detection
docs.text:
Potential telemetry includes:

Named Pipes
SMB Connections
Internal Host-to-Host Traffic
Process Activity
Authentication Events

Correlating endpoint and network telemetry provides stronger detection than either source alone.

docs.title: TCP Beacon Detection
docs.text:
TCP peer-to-peer C2 may create unusual internal listeners and connections.

Review:

Listening Ports
Process Owning Listener
Source Host
Destination Host
Connection Duration
Host Role

docs.title: Malleable C2 Detection
docs.text:
Malleable C2 changes network characteristics but does not eliminate behaviour.

Correlate:

Process
        +
Destination
        +
DNS
        +
TLS
        +
Timing
        +
Host Role

rather than relying only on HTTP strings.

docs.title: Memory Detection
docs.text:
Beacon operates in memory and can therefore be visible to:

EDR
Memory Scanners
ETW
API Monitoring
Call-Stack Analysis
Behavioural Analytics

Do not assume:

In Memory

means:

Invisible

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Controls may include:

WDAC
AppLocker
Defender
EDR
ASR

If a test artifact is blocked:

Execution Attempt
        |
        v
Observed Failure
        |
        v
Collect Telemetry
        |
        v
Identify Enforcing Control
        |
        v
Validate Effective Policy

Do not automatically move to evasion.

The block may be the desired assessment result.

docs.title: Purple-Team Use
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike is particularly useful for controlled purple-team exercises.

For each action, record:

Action
Host
User
Timestamp
Expected Telemetry
Observed Telemetry
Detection
Alert
Response

The workflow becomes:

flowchart LR
    R[Red Team Action] --> T[Timestamp]
    T --> E[Endpoint Telemetry]
    T --> N[Network Telemetry]
    T --> I[Identity Telemetry]
    E --> S[SIEM]
    N --> S
    I --> S
    S --> D[Detection]
    D --> B[Blue Team Response]
    B --> L[Lessons Learned]

This produces far more value than simply asking whether Beacon executed.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Use a layered approach.

flowchart TD
    A[Team Server Running?] --> B[Client Connected?]
    B --> C[Listener Active?]
    C --> D[Listener Reachable?]
    D --> E[Beacon Executed?]
    E --> F[Beacon Connected?]

Correct Host?
Correct Port?
DNS?
Firewall?
Proxy?
TLS?
Malleable C2?

nc -vz <C2_HOST> <PORT>

Validate infrastructure before regenerating payloads.

Redirector

Transport

docs.text:

        v

        v

        |
        v

The correct model is:

        |
        v
SOCKS / Forwarding
        |
        v
Operator Tool

A pivot cannot create network reachability that the Beacon does not possess.

docs.title: Peer-to-Peer Beacon Missing
docs.text:
Check:

Parent Alive?
Child Running?
Port Reachable?
Named Pipe / TCP Listener Available?
Correct Link?
Firewall?

Troubleshoot the immediate parent-child relationship.

docs.title: Security Interpretation
docs.text:
Avoid reporting:

Cobalt Strike worked.

Instead explain the control boundary.

For example:

A test executable launched successfully from a user-writable
directory under a standard-user context and established outbound
HTTPS command-and-control to external assessment infrastructure.
No endpoint prevention control blocked execution or the outbound
connection during the test window.

Then separately establish whether:

EDR Alerted
SOC Detected
Firewall Logged
Proxy Logged
Incident Response Triggered

docs.title: Detection vs Prevention
docs.text:
Keep these separate:

Execution Prevented

Execution Allowed but Detected

Execution Allowed and Not Detected

C2 Blocked

C2 Allowed but Alerted

These represent different control outcomes.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
During production assessments:

  • Use licensed Cobalt Strike
  • Confirm scope before deployment
  • Use identifiable test artifacts where practical

  • Track every Beacon
  • Avoid unnecessary persistence
  • Avoid unrelated data collection
  • Avoid uncontrolled credential access
  • Avoid uncontrolled lateral movement

  • Coordinate operators
  • Record timestamps
  • Protect downloaded data
  • Stop unused listeners
