docs.title: Rubeus
docs.text:
Rubeus is a Windows Kerberos assessment toolkit from GhostPack. It provides functionality for interacting with Kerberos authentication, tickets, ticket caches, delegation, service tickets, pre-authentication, and other Active Directory Kerberos mechanisms.

Rubeus is particularly useful during authorised Active Directory assessments because it exposes Kerberos behaviour that is otherwise difficult to inspect using standard Windows tooling alone.

Authorised Testing Only

Rubeus can request, inspect, import, export, and manipulate Kerberos authentication material. Use it only in environments where Kerberos and credential-access testing are explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Rubeus focuses primarily on:

Kerberos
├── Ticket inspection
├── Ticket requests
├── Ticket cache interaction
├── TGT operations
├── TGS operations
├── Kerberoasting assessment
├── AS-REP roasting assessment
├── Delegation analysis
├── Ticket renewal
├── Ticket import/export
├── Ticket description
├── Encryption types
├── KDC interaction
└── Kerberos security research

Typical assessment areas include:

Area Purpose Ticket enumeration Inspect Kerberos tickets associated with logon sessions TGT analysis Examine Ticket Granting Tickets TGS analysis Examine service tickets Kerberoasting Identify service accounts whose service tickets may expose password-strength risk AS-REP roasting Identify accounts configured without Kerberos pre-authentication Delegation Analyse Kerberos delegation configurations Ticket cache Inspect and manage Kerberos tickets Encryption Review Kerberos encryption types KDC interaction Test authentication behaviour against domain controllers

The key assessment principle is:

Kerberos Observation
        |
        v
Security Condition
        |
        v
Validation
        |
        v
Evidence
        |
        v
Security Conclusion

Do not treat every Rubeus result as a vulnerability.

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
Use the GhostPack repository as the primary source for Rubeus.

  • Rubeus - Official GitHub Repository
  • Rubeus README

Rubeus is source-oriented and the upstream repository may not always provide a precompiled executable for every current revision.

For repeatable assessments, record exactly which source revision or binary build was used.

docs.title: Execution Models
docs.text:
Rubeus is commonly encountered in two forms:

Native .NET Executable
        |
        +--> Rubeus.exe

PowerShell Wrapper
        |
        +--> Invoke-Rubeus.ps1

These are related but not identical execution models.

The official GhostPack project provides the Rubeus C# source.

Invoke-Rubeus.ps1 from PowerSharpPack is a third-party PowerShell wrapper around a compiled Rubeus assembly.

docs.title: Native Rubeus.exe
docs.text:
The conventional workflow uses:

Rubeus.exe

General syntax:

.\Rubeus.exe <action> [arguments]

Display help:

.\Rubeus.exe

or:

.\Rubeus.exe help

The exact actions available depend on the Rubeus revision being used.

Always check the installed build rather than assuming syntax from an older write-up still applies.

docs.title: Record the Binary
docs.text:
Before testing:

Get-FileHash .\Rubeus.exe -Algorithm SHA256

Record:

Tool: Rubeus
Source: GhostPack
Revision: <COMMIT_OR_VERSION>
Architecture: <ARCHITECTURE>
SHA256: <HASH>
Timestamp: <TIME>

This is especially useful when Rubeus has been compiled from source.

docs.title: Build from Source
docs.text:
Clone the official repository in an authorised development environment:

git clone https://github.com/GhostPack/Rubeus.git

The repository contains the Visual Studio solution and C# source.

Compile using a compatible Visual Studio/.NET build environment.

The resulting executable is typically:

Rubeus.exe

Record the source revision:

git rev-parse HEAD

This allows assessment evidence to identify the exact code revision used.

docs.title: Determine Current Windows Context
docs.text:
Before using Rubeus, establish the current security context.

Identity:

whoami

Groups:

whoami /groups

Privileges:

whoami /priv

Domain information:

whoami /fqdn

Logon server:

$env:LOGONSERVER

Domain:

$env:USERDNSDOMAIN

This helps explain which Kerberos context Rubeus is operating within.

docs.title: Native Kerberos Baseline
docs.text:
Before introducing Rubeus, inspect Kerberos using native Windows tooling.

The most important command is:

klist

This displays Kerberos tickets associated with the current logon session.

Typical information includes:

Client
Server
Kerberos Encryption Type
Ticket Flags
Start Time
End Time
Renew Time

This provides a useful baseline for comparison with Rubeus.

docs.title: Kerberos Fundamentals
docs.text:
A simplified Kerberos authentication flow is:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant K as KDC
    participant S as Service

    U->>K: AS-REQ
    K-->>U: AS-REP + TGT
    U->>K: TGS-REQ + TGT
    K-->>U: TGS-REP + Service Ticket
    U->>S: AP-REQ + Service Ticket
    S-->>U: Service Access

The Key Distribution Center normally consists logically of:

KDC
├── Authentication Service
└── Ticket Granting Service

The Domain Controller performs these roles in Active Directory.

docs.title: TGT
docs.text:
A Ticket Granting Ticket is issued after successful Kerberos authentication.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 | AS-REQ
 v
KDC
 |
 | AS-REP
 v
TGT

The TGT can then be used to request service tickets.

A TGT is not itself proof of administrative access.

It proves a Kerberos authentication context exists for the associated principal.

docs.title: TGS
docs.text:
A Ticket Granting Service ticket is issued for a specific service.

Conceptually:

TGT
 |
 | TGS-REQ
 v
KDC
 |
 | TGS-REP
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Service

The service is identified through a Service Principal Name.

Examples include:

cifs/server.domain.local
http/server.domain.local
ldap/dc.domain.local
host/server.domain.local

docs.title: Service Principal Names
docs.text:
Service Principal Names identify Kerberos-enabled services.

Native enumeration can start with:

setspn -Q */*

For a specific account:

setspn -L <ACCOUNT>

This helps establish the Kerberos environment before using Rubeus.

docs.title: Ticket Enumeration
docs.text:
Rubeus can inspect Kerberos ticket state.

A common read-oriented action is:

.\Rubeus.exe triage

This can provide a summary of Kerberos tickets visible to the current execution context.

Another inspection action is:

.\Rubeus.exe klist

Compare the result with:

klist

from Windows.

The assessment objective is to understand:

Which tickets exist?
For which principals?
For which services?
Which encryption types are used?
When do they expire?

docs.title: Ticket Description
docs.text:
Rubeus can parse and describe Kerberos ticket structures.

General concept:

.kirbi
   |
   v
Rubeus
   |
   v
Kerberos Ticket Metadata

This is useful for offline analysis of authorised ticket material.

Record:

  • Client principal
  • Service principal
  • Realm
  • Encryption type
  • Ticket flags
  • Start time
  • End time
  • Renewal time

Avoid retaining ticket material longer than required.

docs.title: Kerberos Encryption Types
docs.text:
Common Kerberos encryption types include:

AES256
AES128
RC4

Modern Active Directory environments should generally prefer AES where supported.

Older systems or accounts may still support RC4.

The security assessment should distinguish:

Encryption Type Supported
        !=
Encryption Type Negotiated
        !=
Encryption Type Required

Inspect actual ticket behaviour rather than relying only on account configuration.

docs.title: Kerberoasting Assessment
docs.text:
Kerberoasting evaluates service accounts associated with SPNs.

The high-level mechanism is:

Authenticated Domain User
        |
        v
Request Service Ticket
        |
        v
KDC Returns TGS
        |
        v
Ticket Protected with Service Account Key
        |
        v
Offline Password-Strength Assessment

The underlying security issue is generally not:

Kerberoasting Exists

because requesting service tickets is normal Kerberos functionality.

The risk depends on factors such as:

Weak Service Account Password
        +
Crackable Encryption
        +
Valuable Service Account Privileges
        =
Meaningful Risk

docs.title: Identify SPN Accounts
docs.text:
Native Windows tooling can provide initial context.

Example:

setspn -Q */*

In larger environments, use authorised directory enumeration tooling to identify user accounts with SPNs.

Record:

Account
SPN
Encryption Support
Password Age
Privilege
Service Purpose

before assessing risk.

docs.title: Rubeus Kerberoast Mode
docs.text:
Rubeus contains:

kerberoast

functionality.

Review the syntax supported by the current build:

.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /?

or consult the upstream documentation/source for the installed revision.

During production testing, limit requests to the accounts required for the assessment rather than automatically targeting every service account.

The result should be interpreted as:

Service Ticket Obtained
        !=
Password Recovered
        !=
Privilege Obtained

These are separate states.

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting Assessment
docs.text:
Kerberos normally requires pre-authentication.

Simplified normal flow:

AS-REQ + Pre-Authentication
        |
        v
KDC
        |
        v
AS-REP

Some accounts may be configured with:

Do not require Kerberos preauthentication

In that case:

AS-REQ
   |
   v
KDC
   |
   v
AS-REP

may occur without normal pre-authentication.

This configuration can expose material suitable for offline password-strength assessment.

docs.title: Rubeus AS-REP Assessment
docs.text:
Rubeus includes:

asreproast

functionality.

Review the current syntax:

.\Rubeus.exe asreproast /?

The security conclusion should distinguish:

Account Does Not Require Pre-Authentication
        |
        v
AS-REP Material Obtainable
        |
        v
Password Strength Determines Practical Risk

A strong password can substantially change the practical impact.

docs.title: Ticket Requests
docs.text:
Rubeus can perform raw Kerberos ticket requests.

Relevant actions include concepts such as:

asktgt
asktgs

These interact with the Kerberos Authentication Service and Ticket Granting Service.

Use them only where explicit ticket-request testing is required.

The important distinction is:

Credential Material Available
        |
        v
Kerberos Request Constructed
        |
        v
KDC Accepts Request
        |
        v
Ticket Issued

Each stage provides different evidence.

docs.title: Requesting a TGT
docs.text:
The asktgt functionality constructs an AS request.

Review:

.\Rubeus.exe asktgt /?

Rubeus supports several authentication inputs depending on the current build.

These may include:

Password
Kerberos key material
Certificate
Existing Kerberos context

Do not place real credentials in screenshots, command histories, documentation, or assessment reports.

Use placeholders in notes:

/user:<USER>
/domain:<DOMAIN>
/dc:<DOMAIN_CONTROLLER>

docs.title: Requesting a Service Ticket
docs.text:
The asktgs functionality can request a service ticket using appropriate authorised Kerberos material.

Review:

.\Rubeus.exe asktgs /?

The conceptual flow is:

Existing Kerberos Context
        |
        v
TGS-REQ
        |
        v
KDC
        |
        v
TGS-REP
        |
        v
Service Ticket

Again:

Ticket Issued
        !=
Service Access Granted

The service performs its own authorisation checks.

docs.title: Ticket Cache
docs.text:
Windows maintains Kerberos tickets associated with logon sessions.

Native inspection:

klist

Rubeus provides additional ticket-cache functionality.

The current execution context determines which sessions and tickets are visible.

Higher privileges may expose additional logon sessions.

Keep the distinction:

Current User Tickets
        !=
All Host Tickets

docs.title: Logon Sessions
docs.text:
Windows authentication sessions are identified internally using Logon IDs or LUIDs.

Conceptually:

Windows Host
├── Logon Session A
│   └── Kerberos Tickets
├── Logon Session B
│   └── Kerberos Tickets
└── Logon Session C
    └── Kerberos Tickets

Rubeus can expose ticket information associated with these sessions when the current security context permits it.

docs.title: Ticket Import and Export
docs.text:
Kerberos tickets may be represented in formats such as:

.kirbi

Rubeus can work with ticket files and encoded ticket representations.

Treat ticket material as sensitive authentication material.

Do not:

  • Commit tickets to Git
  • Upload them to shared notes
  • Include them in screenshots
  • Leave them on shared assessment systems
  • Retain them longer than necessary

docs.title: Ticket Injection Concept
docs.text:
Windows can associate Kerberos tickets with logon sessions.

Rubeus contains functionality for importing authorised ticket material into an appropriate Kerberos session.

This is commonly referred to as:

Pass-the-Ticket

The conceptual model is:

Kerberos Ticket
        |
        v
Windows Logon Session
        |
        v
Kerberos Authentication Context

Importing a ticket does not modify the permissions encoded in the associated account.

The service still performs authorisation.

docs.title: Ticket Purging
docs.text:
Windows provides native functionality to remove Kerberos tickets:

klist purge

Warning

Purging tickets can interrupt the current user's authentication to domain resources. Do not run this casually on production systems.

Use ticket cleanup only where necessary and authorised.

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
Rubeus contains functionality relevant to Kerberos delegation.

Important delegation models include:

Unconstrained Delegation
Constrained Delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

Delegation is primarily an Active Directory configuration topic.

The dedicated Active Directory notes should explain:

Configuration
Preconditions
Trust Boundary
Abuse Conditions
Detection
Remediation

Rubeus should remain the tool-operation reference.

docs.title: S4U
docs.text:
Kerberos includes Service-for-User extensions:

S4U2Self
S4U2Proxy

Simplified:

S4U2Self
Service requests a ticket representing a user to itself.

S4U2Proxy
Service requests a ticket to another service on behalf of that user.

These mechanisms are legitimate Kerberos functionality used by delegation.

Security problems occur when delegation is configured in a way that permits unintended privilege paths.

Rubeus contains:

s4u

functionality for assessing these conditions.

Review the exact syntax:

.\Rubeus.exe s4u /?

before testing.

docs.title: Monitor
docs.text:
Rubeus includes Kerberos monitoring functionality.

The purpose is to observe Kerberos ticket activity visible to the current execution context.

Review:

.\Rubeus.exe monitor /?

Monitoring authentication material can expose sensitive information.

Use narrow monitoring periods and stop collection as soon as the required evidence has been obtained.

docs.title: Harvest
docs.text:
Rubeus also contains ticket-harvesting functionality.

This should be treated as credential-access testing.

Do not run broad or long-duration harvesting in production merely because the tool supports it.

Use the minimum functionality required to demonstrate the security condition.

docs.title: Renew
docs.text:
Kerberos tickets may contain renewal information.

Rubeus can interact with ticket renewal behaviour.

Native ticket information can first be reviewed with:

klist

Look for:

Start Time
End Time
Renew Time

Ticket renewal should be interpreted within the account's Kerberos policy and current authentication context.

docs.title: Rubeus and Mimikatz
docs.text:
Rubeus and Mimikatz overlap in some Kerberos functionality but have different focuses.

Rubeus Mimikatz Kerberos-focused toolkit Broader Windows security toolkit Raw Kerberos interaction LSASS and authentication package interaction Ticket requests Credential and ticket inspection Delegation workflows Broad authentication research Kerberoasting Credential-access functionality AS-REP roasting DPAPI, LSA, tokens and more .NET/C# Native C/C++

Use Rubeus when the assessment question is primarily:

How is Kerberos behaving?

Use Mimikatz when the question involves broader Windows authentication internals.

See:

Mimikatz

docs.title: PowerSharpPack Invoke-Rubeus
docs.text:
A PowerShell wrapper for Rubeus is available in:

PowerSharpPack

The relevant file is:

PowerSharpBinaries/Invoke-Rubeus.ps1

Reference:

PowerSharpPack - Invoke-Rubeus.ps1

This is not the official GhostPack Rubeus distribution.

Treat it as a separate third-party execution wrapper.

docs.title: Invoke-Rubeus Execution Model
docs.text:
The PowerSharpPack wrapper embeds a compressed .NET Rubeus assembly inside PowerShell.

At a high level:

Invoke-Rubeus.ps1
        |
        v
Embedded Encoded Data
        |
        v
Decode
        |
        v
GZip Decompression
        |
        v
Byte Array
        |
        v
System.Reflection.Assembly.Load()
        |
        v
Rubeus Assembly in PowerShell Process

The wrapper then invokes the Rubeus program entry point and captures its console output.

This means:

Rubeus.exe on Disk

is not required for this execution model.

docs.title: Native EXE vs Invoke-Rubeus.ps1
docs.text:
Native Rubeus Invoke-Rubeus.ps1 Executes Rubeus.exe PowerShell hosts Rubeus Separate Rubeus process Rubeus assembly loaded into PowerShell PE normally present on disk Embedded assembly loaded from script Native process telemetry PowerShell and .NET telemetry File-based application controls relevant Script/.NET controls also relevant Official GhostPack code can be compiled Third-party PowerSharpPack wrapper

The underlying Kerberos functionality is based on Rubeus, but the execution and detection surfaces differ.

docs.title: Inspect Invoke-Rubeus.ps1
docs.text:
Before using a third-party wrapper:

Get-FileHash .\Invoke-Rubeus.ps1 -Algorithm SHA256

Review the file:

Get-Content .\Invoke-Rubeus.ps1 -TotalCount 50

Confirm its origin.

Do not blindly execute PowerShell wrappers downloaded from arbitrary mirrors.

docs.title: Load a Trusted Local Copy
docs.text:
For a trusted, authorised local copy, standard PowerShell loading mechanisms can make the function available to the current session.

After loading the script, verify:

Get-Command Invoke-Rubeus

Inspect syntax:

Get-Command Invoke-Rubeus -Syntax

or:

Get-Help Invoke-Rubeus

The PowerSharpPack wrapper exposes a:

-Command

parameter used to pass a Rubeus command string to the embedded assembly.

Use the wrapper only for the specific authorised Kerberos test being performed.

docs.title: In-Memory Does Not Mean Invisible
docs.text:
A common mistake is to assume:

Assembly Loaded in Memory
        =
No Detection

This is incorrect.

Potential telemetry includes:

PowerShell
├── Script Block Logging
├── Module Logging
├── AMSI
└── Transcription

.NET
├── Assembly loading
└── Runtime behaviour

Endpoint
├── Process behaviour
├── Memory behaviour
├── Kerberos API usage
└── EDR telemetry

Network
├── AS-REQ
├── TGS-REQ
└── Kerberos authentication patterns

Defenders can detect behaviour without relying on the filename Rubeus.exe.

docs.title: PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible values include:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

PowerSharpPack wrappers depend on PowerShell and .NET functionality.

Constrained Language Mode or application control may prevent some functionality.

A failure does not automatically prove which control caused it.

docs.title: AMSI
docs.text:
PowerShell content may be inspected through the Antimalware Scan Interface.

Conceptually:

PowerShell Content
        |
        v
AMSI
        |
        v
Registered Security Product
        |
        v
Inspection

The fact that Rubeus is embedded in a PowerShell wrapper does not automatically bypass AMSI or endpoint protection.

AMSI testing belongs in the dedicated Windows application-control material.

docs.title: WDAC and AppLocker
docs.text:
Native and PowerShell execution can encounter different policy paths.

For example:

Rubeus.exe
    |
    +--> EXE policy
    +--> WDAC
    +--> Defender / EDR

Invoke-Rubeus.ps1
    |
    +--> Script policy
    +--> PowerShell controls
    +--> WDAC
    +--> AMSI
    +--> Defender / EDR

Therefore:

EXE Blocked
+
PowerShell Wrapper Executes

does not automatically prove a WDAC or AppLocker bypass.

Identify the actual effective policy and enforcement path.

docs.title: Rubeus Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Kerberos commonly requires connectivity to a Domain Controller.

Relevant ports can include:

Port Protocol Purpose 53 TCP/UDP DNS 88 TCP/UDP Kerberos 389 TCP/UDP LDAP 445 TCP SMB 464 TCP/UDP Kerberos password operations 636 TCP LDAPS 3268 TCP Global Catalog 3269 TCP Global Catalog over TLS

When working through a pivot, validate the required services individually.

For example:

Test-NetConnection <DC> -Port 88

From Linux through an appropriate tunnel:

nc -vz <DC> 88

docs.title: DNS Matters
docs.text:
Kerberos depends heavily on correct naming.

Validate DNS:

Resolve-DnsName <DOMAIN>

Domain Controller discovery:

Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _kerberos._tcp.dc._msdcs.<DOMAIN>

Example structure:

_kerberos._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local

Kerberos failures during pivoting are frequently caused by:

  • Incorrect DNS
  • Wrong realm/domain
  • Inaccessible KDC
  • Clock skew

rather than Rubeus itself.

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Kerberos is time-sensitive.

Check local time:

Get-Date

Windows time status:

w32tm /query /status

Compare with the Domain Controller where authorised.

Significant clock skew can cause Kerberos authentication failures.

The troubleshooting model should therefore include:

DNS
+
KDC Reachability
+
Time
+
Credentials
+
Ticket State

docs.title: Rubeus Does Not Start
docs.text:
Check:

Get-Item .\Rubeus.exe

Hash:

Get-FileHash .\Rubeus.exe -Algorithm SHA256

Potential causes include:

  • Defender
  • EDR
  • WDAC
  • AppLocker
  • Missing .NET requirements
  • Corrupt build
  • Architecture/environment issue

docs.title: Rubeus Command Is Unknown
docs.text:
Run:

.\Rubeus.exe

and inspect the actions supported by that build.

Rubeus evolves over time.

Do not rely exclusively on syntax from old blog posts.

docs.title: Domain Cannot Be Found
docs.text:
Check:

$env:USERDNSDOMAIN

Then:

Resolve-DnsName $env:USERDNSDOMAIN

Check Domain Controller discovery:

nltest /dsgetdc:<DOMAIN>

Verify Kerberos:

Test-NetConnection <DC> -Port 88

docs.title: Kerberos Request Fails
docs.text:
Check:

Domain
User
KDC
DNS
Time
Encryption Type
Pre-Authentication
Credential Material

Do not assume the tool is malfunctioning.

Kerberos errors often provide useful information about which stage failed.

docs.title: Invoke-Rubeus Is Not Recognised
docs.text:
Check:

Get-Command Invoke-Rubeus -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If no function is returned, the PowerShell wrapper has not loaded successfully.

Review:

  • Script path
  • PowerShell errors
  • Script integrity
  • Language mode
  • Application control
  • Endpoint security telemetry

docs.title: Invoke-Rubeus Loads but Command Fails
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Then investigate:

  • Wrapper version
  • Embedded Rubeus version
  • PowerShell/.NET compatibility
  • Required Kerberos connectivity
  • Command syntax
  • Endpoint security
  • Current execution context

Remember that the embedded Rubeus version may differ from the latest GhostPack source.

docs.title: Kerberos Error Interpretation
docs.text:
Kerberos errors should be recorded rather than discarded.

Examples of useful categories include:

Principal Unknown
Pre-Authentication Required
Pre-Authentication Failed
Clock Skew
Ticket Expired
Policy Restriction
Encryption Type Not Supported

A Kerberos error often tells you more about the environment than a generic application failure.

Record:

Operation
KDC
Principal
Error Code
Error Name
Context

without exposing sensitive credential material.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful Rubeus assessment evidence can include:

  • Hostname
  • Current identity
  • Domain
  • Domain Controller
  • Rubeus source revision
  • Binary SHA256
  • PowerShell wrapper SHA256
  • Execution model
  • Kerberos ticket metadata
  • Encryption type
  • Ticket flags
  • SPN
  • Relevant account configuration
  • KDC response
  • Timestamp
  • Detection event
  • Cleanup verification

A useful evidence chain is:

Observed Kerberos Condition
        |
        v
Rubeus Validation
        |
        v
KDC Response
        |
        v
Ticket / Configuration Evidence
        |
        v
Security Impact

docs.title: Security Interpretation
docs.text:
Rubeus often demonstrates authentication conditions rather than vulnerabilities by itself.

For example:

Service Ticket Obtained

is normal Kerberos behaviour.

Risk emerges when additional conditions exist:

Service Account
        +
Weak Password
        +
Crackable Ticket Encryption
        +
High Privilege
        =
Kerberoasting Risk

Similarly:

Delegation Configured

does not automatically mean:

Privilege Escalation

The complete trust path must be validated.

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text: Defenders can monitor Rubeus-related activity through multiple telemetry sources.

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

  • Rubeus.exe execution
  • PowerShell hosting embedded .NET assemblies
  • Unusual .NET assembly loading
  • Ticket cache interaction
  • Security-process access
  • Unusual command-line arguments

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
For Invoke-Rubeus-style execution:

PowerShell Script Block Logging
PowerShell Module Logging
AMSI
PowerShell Transcription
EDR PowerShell Telemetry

Relevant PowerShell event IDs may include:

Event ID Description 4103 Module logging 4104 Script block logging

Logging depends on system configuration.

docs.title: Domain Controller
docs.text:
Kerberos activity is also visible from the KDC side.

Relevant events can include:

Event ID Description 4768 Kerberos authentication ticket requested 4769 Kerberos service ticket requested 4770 Kerberos service ticket renewed 4771 Kerberos pre-authentication failed

These events provide valuable context for Kerberos assessment activity.

docs.title: Kerberoasting Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

Large Number of TGS Requests
        |
        +
Many Different SPNs
        |
        +
Unusual Client
        |
        +
Legacy Encryption Requests

Detection should account for legitimate applications that also request many service tickets.

Behavioural baselining is preferable to simplistic thresholds.

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include authentication requests involving accounts configured without Kerberos pre-authentication.

The strongest remediation is usually to correct the account configuration and enforce strong credentials rather than relying solely on detection.

docs.title: Delegation Detection
docs.text:
Defenders should monitor changes to delegation-related Active Directory attributes and privileged delegation configurations.

Important concepts include:

TrustedForDelegation
TrustedToAuthForDelegation
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity

These belong primarily in the Active Directory delegation notes.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text:
Relevant controls include:

  • Require Kerberos pre-authentication
  • Use strong service-account passwords
  • Prefer group Managed Service Accounts where appropriate
  • Prefer AES Kerberos encryption
  • Reduce RC4 dependencies
  • Review SPNs regularly
  • Review delegation configuration
  • Minimise privileged service accounts
  • Protect privileged logon sessions
  • Monitor Kerberos events
  • Monitor abnormal ticket requests
  • Use Defender/EDR
  • Use WDAC/AppLocker where appropriate
  • Enable PowerShell logging
  • Monitor unusual .NET assembly loading
  • Maintain accurate time synchronisation

The defensive objective is not simply:

Block Rubeus.exe

Instead:

Strong Kerberos Configuration
        +
Strong Service Credentials
        +
Safe Delegation
        +
Protected Privileged Sessions
        +
Authentication Monitoring
        =
Reduced Kerberos Attack Surface

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
During production assessments:

  • Limit Kerberos requests
  • Avoid broad ticket collection
  • Avoid unnecessary ticket injection
  • Do not purge production tickets without need
  • Avoid collecting unrelated user tickets
  • Avoid password changes unless explicitly authorised
  • Avoid persistent authentication modifications
  • Record exact actions performed
  • Remove exported ticket material after use
  • Treat .kirbi files as credentials
  • Minimise offline password testing to approved accounts

The goal is to demonstrate the security condition with minimum operational impact.

docs.title: Native Rubeus
docs.text:
Help:

.\Rubeus.exe

Hash:

Get-FileHash .\Rubeus.exe -Algorithm SHA256

Ticket baseline:

klist

Rubeus ticket triage:

.\Rubeus.exe triage

Rubeus ticket list:

.\Rubeus.exe klist

Review Kerberoast syntax:

.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /?

Review AS-REP syntax:

.\Rubeus.exe asreproast /?

Review TGT request syntax:

.\Rubeus.exe asktgt /?

Review TGS request syntax:

.\Rubeus.exe asktgs /?

Review delegation/S4U syntax:

.\Rubeus.exe s4u /?

docs.title: PowerSharpPack Invoke-Rubeus
docs.text:
Hash:

Get-FileHash .\Invoke-Rubeus.ps1 -Algorithm SHA256

Confirm function after loading:

Get-Command Invoke-Rubeus

Syntax:

Get-Command Invoke-Rubeus -Syntax

Help:

Get-Help Invoke-Rubeus

The wrapper accepts Rubeus arguments through:

-Command

Conceptually:

Invoke-Rubeus
    |
    +--> -Command "<RUBEUS_ACTION_AND_ARGUMENTS>"

Use the same Kerberos safety principles as with the native executable.

docs.title: Native Windows Baseline
docs.text:
Identity:

whoami

Domain:

$env:USERDNSDOMAIN

Logon server:

$env:LOGONSERVER

Kerberos tickets:

klist

SPNs:

setspn -Q */*

Domain Controller:

nltest /dsgetdc:<DOMAIN>

Kerberos port:

Test-NetConnection <DC> -Port 88

DNS:

Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _kerberos._tcp.dc._msdcs.<DOMAIN>

Time:

w32tm /query /status

PowerShell language mode:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

docs.text:
• [ ] Kerberos testing explicitly authorised
  • [ ] Domain is within scope
  • [ ] Accounts are within scope
  • [ ] Domain Controllers are within scope
  • [ ] Rubeus source identified

  • [ ] Binary/script hash recorded
  • [ ] Test objective defined

docs.title: Baseline
docs.text:
• [ ] Current identity recorded
  • [ ] Domain recorded
  • [ ] Domain Controller identified
  • [ ] DNS validated
  • [ ] Kerberos port validated
  • [ ] Time synchronisation checked
  • [ ] Existing ticket state recorded

docs.title: Execution

  • [ ] Rubeus build identified

docs.title: Sliver
docs.text:
Sliver is an open-source command-and-control (C2) framework developed by Bishop Fox for authorised adversary simulation, red teaming, penetration testing, and security research.

Sliver provides a central server, operator clients, generated implants, session and beacon management, multiple communication protocols, pivoting, SOCKS proxies, port forwarding, multiplayer operation, and an extension ecosystem through the Armory.

Authorised Testing Only

Sliver provides remote command-and-control capabilities. Use it only against systems explicitly included in an authorised security assessment. Define the permitted hosts, networks, execution methods, communication channels, and post-exploitation actions before deployment.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A typical Sliver deployment consists of:

Operator
    |
    v
Sliver Client
    |
    v
Sliver Server
    |
    v
C2 Listener
    |
    v
Authorised Test Implant
    |
    v
Assessment Host

Multiple operators can connect to the same Sliver server:

flowchart TD
    A[Operator 1] --> S[Sliver Server]
    B[Operator 2] --> S
    C[Operator 3] --> S

    S --> L1[mTLS Listener]
    S --> L2[HTTP/HTTPS Listener]
    S --> L3[DNS Listener]

    L1 --> I1[Test Implant 1]
    L2 --> I2[Test Implant 2]
    L3 --> I3[Test Implant 3]

Sliver separates:

C2 Infrastructure
        |
        v
Operator Access
        |
        v
Communication Listener
        |
        v
Implant
        |
        v
Session / Beacon

Understanding these layers makes troubleshooting significantly easier.

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
Use the official Bishop Fox project as the primary source.

  • Sliver - Official GitHub Repository
  • Sliver Documentation
  • Sliver Releases
  • Bishop Fox

Avoid downloading Sliver binaries from unknown mirrors.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The main components are:

Component Purpose Sliver Server Central C2 infrastructure Sliver Client Operator console Listener Accepts implant communications Implant Authorised test agent Session Interactive implant connection Beacon Asynchronous implant connection Multiplayer Multiple operators using one server Armory Extension and package ecosystem SOCKS Proxy access through a controlled implant Port Forward Explicit forwarding through a controlled implant

Conceptually:

                    +----------------+
                    | Sliver Server  |
                    +-------+--------+
                            |
             +--------------+--------------+
             |              |              |
            mTLS          HTTPS           DNS
             |              |              |
             v              v              v
         Implant A      Implant B      Implant C

docs.title: Server and Client
docs.text:
Sliver commonly uses separate:

sliver-server

and:

sliver-client

components.

The server maintains the C2 infrastructure.

The client provides the operator console.

This separation is important for team environments because operators do not need direct administrative access to the underlying C2 server.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Use an official Sliver release appropriate for the operator platform.

After obtaining the authorised release, verify it before use.

Example:

sha256sum sliver-server

and:

sha256sum sliver-client

Record:

Tool
Version
Source
SHA256
Assessment
Date

Check the installed version:

./sliver-server version

or use the version/help functionality provided by the installed release.

Because Sliver evolves regularly, always review:

help

inside the console before relying on commands from older write-ups.

docs.title: Start the Server
docs.text:
A local lab server can be started with:

./sliver-server

The Sliver console should appear.

Use:

help

to display available commands.

The server console is used to manage:

Listeners
Implants
Sessions
Beacons
Operators
Jobs
Profiles
Extensions

depending on the installed version.

docs.title: Help System
docs.text:
Sliver has extensive built-in help.

Start with:

help

Then inspect individual commands:

help sessions

help beacons

help generate

help jobs

help socks5

Use the installed release's help as the authoritative syntax reference.

docs.title: Listener Concepts
docs.text:
Sliver supports several communication mechanisms.

Common C2 transports include:

mTLS
HTTP
HTTPS
DNS

Different transports have different:

Network Requirements
Performance
Reliability
Visibility
Operational Complexity

Choose the simplest transport that satisfies the authorised assessment objective.

docs.title: mTLS
docs.text:
Mutual TLS is one of Sliver's core communication options.

Conceptually:

Implant
   |
   | mTLS
   v
Sliver Server

A lab listener can be started using the mTLS functionality provided by the server console.

Review:

help mtls

before starting it.

mTLS is useful when:

  • Direct TCP connectivity exists
  • Reliable interactive communication is required
  • DNS-based communication is unnecessary
  • The assessment infrastructure permits the selected listener port

docs.title: HTTP and HTTPS
docs.text:
Sliver supports HTTP and HTTPS communication.

Conceptually:

Implant
    |
    v
HTTP / HTTPS
    |
    v
Sliver Server

Review:

help http

and:

help https

HTTP-based communication may fit environments where web traffic is permitted, but an assessment should not assume that:

TCP/443

automatically means:

Traffic Is Indistinguishable from Normal HTTPS

Network and endpoint controls can still identify abnormal behaviour.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
Sliver supports DNS-based C2.

Conceptually:

Implant
    |
    v
DNS Queries
    |
    v
Authoritative DNS Infrastructure
    |
    v
Sliver Server

DNS-based C2 requires additional infrastructure planning.

Relevant considerations include:

Domain Ownership
Authoritative DNS
Delegation
Resolver Behaviour
Query Volume
Latency
Logging
Scope

Use DNS C2 only when it is required by the assessment plan.

Do not introduce unnecessary DNS infrastructure for a test that can be completed safely using a simpler transport.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
Listeners and other server-side tasks may appear as jobs.

Inspect:

jobs

Use:

help jobs

for the installed release.

A useful troubleshooting sequence is:

Listener Command Issued
        |
        v
Job Created?
        |
        v
Port Listening?
        |
        v
Network Reachable?
        |
        v
Implant Connects?

Do not troubleshoot the implant first if the listener itself is not active.

docs.title: Listener Validation
docs.text:
After starting an authorised listener, verify the operating system is actually listening.

Linux:

ss -lntup

For a specific TCP port:

ss -lntp | grep '<PORT>'

Also verify firewall policy.

The correct sequence is:

Sliver Listener
        |
        v
Operating System Listener
        |
        v
Host Firewall
        |
        v
Network Firewall
        |
        v
Target Connectivity

docs.title: Implant Generation
docs.text:
Sliver can generate implants for authorised assessment systems.

Review:

help generate

before generating an implant.

Generation options vary between releases and may include choices relating to:

Operating System
Architecture
C2 Endpoint
Transport
Connection Mode
Output Format

The assessment should define these parameters before generation.

docs.title: Implant Naming
docs.text:
Use identifiable test names.

For example:

LAB-WIN11-01
VDI-TEST-01
ADLAB-WS01

Avoid intentionally misleading names during ordinary penetration tests unless masquerading is explicitly part of the authorised adversary-simulation objective.

Clear names improve:

  • Evidence collection
  • Operator coordination
  • Cleanup
  • Incident-response deconfliction

docs.title: Implant Tracking
docs.text:
For each generated test implant, record:

Name
Sliver Version
Generation Time
Operating System
Architecture
Transport
C2 Endpoint
SHA256
Target Host
Deployment Time
Removal Time

Hash a generated file:

Linux:

sha256sum <FILE>

Windows:

Get-FileHash .\<FILE> -Algorithm SHA256

This creates a reliable chain between generated test tooling and endpoint telemetry.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
A Sliver session represents an interactive connection.

List sessions:

sessions

A session may expose information such as:

Session ID
Name
Transport
Remote Address
Hostname
Username
Operating System
Architecture
Last Activity

Select a session using the syntax shown by:

help use

or:

help sessions

depending on the installed version.

docs.title: Session Model
docs.text:
An interactive session can be represented as:

Operator
    |
    v
Sliver Server
    |
    v
Live Connection
    |
    v
Test Implant

Interactive sessions generally provide faster command execution but require a more continuously available communication path.

docs.title: Beacons
docs.text:
Sliver also supports asynchronous beaconing.

List beacons:

beacons

A beacon periodically checks in with the server.

Conceptually:

Implant
    |
    | wait
    |
    v
Check In
    |
    v
Receive Task
    |
    v
Execute
    |
    v
Return Result
    |
    v
Wait

This differs from an interactive session.

docs.title: Session vs Beacon
docs.text:
Session Beacon Interactive Asynchronous Live connection Periodic check-in Fast command response Delayed task execution Continuous communication Intermittent communication Useful for interactive testing Useful for controlled asynchronous testing

The correct mode depends on the assessment.

Do not select beacon mode solely because it may produce less continuous traffic.

docs.title: Beacon Timing
docs.text:
Beacon behaviour may involve concepts such as:

Interval
Jitter

These control when an authorised test implant checks in.

Before changing timing, consider:

Assessment Objective
Network Load
Detection Exercise Requirements
Operator Coordination
Test Duration

Very aggressive beacon timing can generate unnecessary traffic.

docs.title: Current Context
docs.text:
Once an authorised session or beacon exists, establish the host context before doing anything else.

Relevant questions include:

Which host?
Which user?
Which operating system?
Which architecture?
Which network interfaces?
Which privileges?

Do not assume the session landed in the context expected by the operator.

docs.title: Basic Host Validation
docs.text:
Sliver provides commands for basic host context.

Use:

help

inside the selected session to inspect the available functionality.

Typical assessment information includes:

Hostname
Username
Process ID
Working Directory
Network Interfaces
Operating System
Architecture

Where possible, correlate this information with native operating-system commands.

docs.title: Process Information
docs.text:
Process enumeration can be useful for:

Host Context
Security Product Identification
Application Discovery
Evidence
Troubleshooting

Use the minimum required enumeration.

Do not terminate or manipulate processes merely because they appear security-relevant.

docs.title: File-System Operations
docs.text:
Sliver provides remote file-system functionality.

Common concepts include:

pwd
ls
cd
cat
download
upload

Exact command names and options should be checked with:

help

Treat remote file access as normal assessment access:

  • Stay within scope
  • Minimise sensitive-data collection
  • Avoid unrelated user files
  • Record transferred files
  • Remove temporary files

docs.title: File Transfer
docs.text:
When transferring an authorised test file, record:

Source
Destination
SHA256
Purpose
Timestamp
Cleanup

Before transfer:

sha256sum <FILE>

After transfer on Windows:

Get-FileHash C:\Path\To\<FILE> -Algorithm SHA256

Matching hashes demonstrate that the intended test file was transferred unchanged.

docs.title: Remote Command Execution
docs.text:
Sliver provides remote execution functionality through an established authorised session.

The security significance is:

Established Test Agent
        |
        v
Command Execution
        |
        v
Current User Context

This does not automatically mean:

Administrative Access

Always establish the current token and privileges separately.

docs.title: Privilege Context
docs.text:
On Windows, useful native validation includes:

whoami

whoami /groups

whoami /priv

On Linux:

id

and:

sudo -l

where authorised.

Keep the distinction:

C2 Session
        !=
Privileged Session

docs.title: Network Interfaces
docs.text:
Before using a compromised test host as a pivot, identify its network interfaces.

Conceptually:

Host
├── External / User Network
├── Internal Network
└── Management Network

A dual-homed system may expose a potential network pivot path.

The correct reasoning is:

Additional Interface Observed
        |
        v
Network Identified
        |
        v
Route / Reachability Validated
        |
        v
Scope Confirmed
        |
        v
Pivot Candidate

docs.title: Pivoting
docs.text:
Sliver can provide network pivoting capabilities through an authorised implant.

Before enabling any pivot:

  1. Identify the reachable network.
  2. Confirm that network is in scope.
  3. Determine which services need to be reached.
  4. Select the simplest forwarding mechanism.
  5. Record the configuration.
  6. Remove it after testing.

Do not expose an entire internal network merely because the implant can reach it.

docs.title: SOCKS5
docs.text:
Sliver provides SOCKS5 functionality through an established implant.

Review:

help socks5

The conceptual architecture is:

Operator Tool
    |
    v
SOCKS5 Listener
    |
    v
Sliver Server
    |
    v
Authorised Implant
    |
    v
Internal Service

This is useful for applications that support SOCKS directly or can operate through ProxyChains.

docs.title: SOCKS Validation
docs.text:
After starting an authorised SOCKS proxy, confirm the local listener.

Linux:

ss -lntp

Then test a specific in-scope service.

For example:

curl --socks5 127.0.0.1:<SOCKS_PORT> http://<INTERNAL_HOST>

For proxy-side hostname resolution:

curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:<SOCKS_PORT> http://<INTERNAL_HOSTNAME>

docs.title: ProxyChains
docs.text:
Configure the local SOCKS endpoint in:

/etc/proxychains4.conf

Example structure:

socks5 127.0.0.1 <SOCKS_PORT>

Then validate a specific TCP service:

proxychains4 nc -vz <TARGET> <PORT>

Do not begin with broad network scanning.

Confirm the forwarding path first.

docs.title: Nmap Through SOCKS
docs.text:
When Nmap is used through ProxyChains, prefer TCP connect scanning.

Example:

proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -p 80,443,445,3389 <TARGET>

The reasoning is:

Nmap
    |
    v
TCP connect()
    |
    v
ProxyChains
    |
    v
SOCKS

Raw SYN scanning does not map cleanly to application-layer SOCKS proxying.

docs.title: Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Sliver also provides port-forwarding functionality.

Use:

help portfwd

or the equivalent help command available in the installed release.

Explicit port forwarding is useful when:

One Host
+
One Service

needs to be reached.

SOCKS is often preferable when:

Multiple Hosts
+
Multiple Services

are required.

docs.title: Pivot Choice
docs.text:
A useful decision model is:

Need One Internal Service?
        |
        +--> Port Forward

Need Several TCP Services?
        |
        +--> SOCKS

Need Broad Routed Network Access?
        |
        +--> Consider Ligolo-ng

Do not add complexity without a reason.

See:

Chisel

and:

Ligolo-ng

docs.title: Multiple Sessions
docs.text:
A Sliver server may manage several authorised test systems simultaneously.

Example:

Sliver Server
├── WS01
├── WS02
├── APP01
└── WEB01

Always verify the selected session before issuing a command.

A useful operational habit is:

Session
    |
    v
Hostname
    |
    v
Username
    |
    v
Scope
    |
    v
Action

This reduces accidental execution on the wrong host.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text:
Sliver supports multiplayer operation.

This allows multiple operators to connect to a shared server.

Conceptually:

Operator A ----+
               |
Operator B ----+--> Sliver Server --> Test Systems
               |
Operator C ----+

Multiplayer is useful for:

  • Red-team exercises
  • Purple-team exercises
  • Collaborative assessments
  • Operator handover
  • Separate infrastructure and testing roles

docs.title: Operator Configuration
docs.text:
Sliver can generate operator configuration for remote clients.

Review the server's current multiplayer/operator help before creating a configuration.

Treat operator configuration files as credentials.

They may grant access to:

C2 Server
Sessions
Beacons
Assessment Data

Do not commit them to Git or distribute them through insecure channels.

docs.title: Operator Security
docs.text:
For each operator:

Unique Identity
        |
        v
Individual Configuration
        |
        v
Controlled Server Access

Avoid sharing one operator configuration among an entire team.

Individual access improves:

  • Accountability
  • Revocation
  • Auditability
  • Incident response

docs.title: Armory
docs.text:
Sliver provides an extension ecosystem called the:

Armory

Use:

armory

and:

help armory

to inspect functionality supported by the installed version.

Armory packages can extend Sliver with additional commands and capabilities.

docs.title: Armory Trust Model
docs.text:
Treat extensions as code.

Before installing an extension:

Identify Source
        |
        v
Review Purpose
        |
        v
Review Code / Package
        |
        v
Check Compatibility
        |
        v
Install

Do not install every available package into production C2 infrastructure.

Third-party extensions expand both capability and attack surface.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
Sliver extensions may integrate external tooling or custom functionality.

For each extension, record:

Name
Version
Source
Purpose
Assessment
Removal

Remove extensions that are no longer required.

This keeps assessment infrastructure reproducible.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Sliver supports reusable generation configuration through profiles in relevant releases.

The purpose is to avoid repeatedly specifying the same implant configuration.

Conceptually:

Profile
├── Operating System
├── Architecture
├── C2 Transport
├── C2 Endpoint
└── Generation Options

Use:

help profiles

or the appropriate installed-version help.

Profiles improve consistency but should not cause operators to reuse inappropriate configurations across unrelated assessments.

docs.title: Stagers
docs.text:
Sliver includes functionality associated with staged delivery.

Staging separates:

Initial Component
        |
        v
Secondary Component
        |
        v
Operational Agent

This is a delivery architecture rather than a requirement for Sliver operation.

For ordinary assessments, use the simplest deployment model that satisfies the test objective.

Detailed staged-payload design belongs in the dedicated Red Teaming notes rather than this tool page.

docs.title: Sliver and Windows
docs.text:
On Windows, Sliver testing may interact with security controls including:

Microsoft Defender
EDR
WDAC
AppLocker
AMSI
PowerShell Controls
Network Firewall
ASR Rules

A blocked implant does not automatically prove which control caused the block.

The correct workflow is:

Execution Attempt
        |
        v
Observed Result
        |
        v
Collect Endpoint Telemetry
        |
        v
Identify Enforcement Source
        |
        v
Confirm Effective Control

docs.title: Sliver and Application Control
docs.text:
If a generated test binary cannot execute, investigate:

WDAC
AppLocker
Defender
EDR
File Reputation
Path Rules
Publisher Rules
Hash Rules

Do not immediately modify the payload to evade the control.

For an application-control assessment, a block may be the expected and valuable result.

docs.title: Sliver and Linux
docs.text:
On Linux, establish:

id

Current directory:

pwd

Interfaces:

ip addr

Routes:

ip route

Listeners:

ss -lntup

Again:

Agent Running
        !=
Root Access

docs.title: Sliver and Active Directory
docs.text:
Sliver can provide a remote execution and pivoting platform during an authorised Active Directory assessment.

However, Active Directory-specific reasoning should remain in the AD notes.

A useful workflow is:

Sliver Session
        |
        v
Host / User Context
        |
        v
Domain Context
        |
        v
Network Reachability
        |
        v
Dedicated AD Tool

Examples of dedicated tools include:

  • BloodHound
  • NetExec
  • Impacket
  • Rubeus
  • Certify
  • Certipy

Do not duplicate their complete functionality inside the Sliver page.

docs.title: Sliver and Mimikatz
docs.text:
Mimikatz is a dedicated Windows authentication-security tool.

Sliver is a C2 framework.

The distinction is:

Sliver
    |
    +--> Command and Control

Mimikatz
    |
    +--> Windows Authentication Research

If credential-access testing is authorised, use the dedicated Mimikatz methodology and record the security boundary separately.

See:

Mimikatz

docs.title: Sliver and Rubeus
docs.text:
Rubeus focuses on Kerberos.

Sliver provides the remote operator channel.

Keep the reasoning separate:

Sliver Session Established
        |
        v
Rubeus Kerberos Test
        |
        v
KDC Response
        |
        v
Kerberos Security Conclusion

See:

Rubeus

docs.title: Sliver and AD CS
docs.text:
Certify and Certipy should remain the primary AD CS references.

See:

Certify

and:

Certipy

Sliver may provide access to the assessment host, but it does not replace AD CS-specific analysis.

docs.title: DNS Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a Sliver-controlled system can reach an IP address but not an internal hostname, investigate DNS separately.

Windows:

Resolve-DnsName <HOSTNAME>

Linux:

dig <HOSTNAME>

The correct distinction is:

C2 Connectivity
        !=
Internal DNS Resolution

docs.title: Network Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Use a layered model:

flowchart TD
    A[Sliver Server Running?] --> B[Listener Running?]
    B --> C[Listener Port Reachable?]
    C --> D[Implant Running?]
    D --> E[Session or Beacon Established?]
    E --> F[Pivot Started?]
    F --> G[Internal Target Reachable from Implant?]
    G --> H[Operator Traffic Reaches Target?]
    H --> I[Application Protocol Works?]

Test one layer at a time.

docs.title: Implant Does Not Connect
docs.text:
Check:

Correct C2 Endpoint?
Correct Port?
Listener Active?
Host Firewall?
Network Firewall?
DNS?
Proxy?
TLS?
Server Reachable?

From Windows:

Test-NetConnection <SERVER> -Port <PORT>

From Linux:

nc -vz <SERVER> <PORT>

Do not regenerate the implant repeatedly before validating basic connectivity.

docs.title: Session Disappears
docs.text:
Possible causes include:

Process Exited
Network Interrupted
Endpoint Security Terminated Process
Listener Stopped
Host Rebooted
Firewall Changed

Check:

sessions

and:

beacons

Then correlate with endpoint and server telemetry.

docs.title: Beacon Does Not Return Quickly
docs.text:
Remember:

Beacon
        !=
Interactive Session

The task may not execute until the next check-in.

Review:

Beacon Interval
Jitter
Last Check-In
Task Queue

before assuming failure.

docs.title: SOCKS Starts but Target Is Unreachable
docs.text:
First determine whether the implant can reach the target.

The correct sequence is:

Can Implant Reach Target?
        |
        v
Is SOCKS Running?
        |
        v
Can Operator Reach SOCKS?
        |
        v
Can Application Use SOCKS?
        |
        v
Does Target Protocol Work?

If the implant cannot reach the destination, the SOCKS proxy cannot create that reachability.

docs.title: ProxyChains Fails
docs.text:
Test SOCKS directly first.

For HTTP:

curl --socks5 127.0.0.1:<PORT> http://<TARGET>

If that works but ProxyChains fails, review:

ProxyChains Configuration
SOCKS Version
DNS
Application Compatibility
Raw Socket Requirements

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful Sliver evidence can include:

  • Sliver version
  • Server hostname
  • Listener type
  • Listener port
  • Operator identity
  • Implant identifier
  • Implant SHA256
  • Target hostname
  • Target username
  • Target architecture
  • Session or beacon ID
  • Transport
  • Connection time
  • Pivot configuration
  • SOCKS listener
  • Specific authorised validation
  • Endpoint detection result
  • Network detection result
  • Cleanup time

A strong evidence chain is:

Authorised Test Implant
        |
        v
Execution Observed
        |
        v
C2 Connection Established
        |
        v
Session Context Confirmed
        |
        v
Approved Capability Tested
        |
        v
Detection / Security Control Evaluated
        |
        v
Cleanup Confirmed

docs.title: Security Interpretation
docs.text:
The existence of a Sliver session demonstrates:

Code Execution
        +
Network Communication
        =
C2 Capability

It does not automatically demonstrate:

Privilege Escalation
Credential Access
Lateral Movement
Domain Compromise
Data Exfiltration

Each of those requires separate evidence.

For example:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Sliver Agent Executes
        |
        v
Outbound C2 Established

may demonstrate weaknesses in:

Application Control
Endpoint Detection
Egress Filtering
Network Monitoring

without demonstrating administrative compromise.

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Defenders can detect Sliver activity across several layers.

Endpoint
+
Network
+
DNS
+
Identity
+
Application Control

Detection should not rely on one indicator.

docs.title: Endpoint Detection
docs.text:
Potential telemetry includes:

Process Creation
Executable Creation
File Hash
Parent / Child Relationships
Memory Behaviour
Network Connections
File Transfers
Command Execution

Relevant sources may include:

  • Microsoft Defender
  • EDR
  • Sysmon
  • Windows Security auditing
  • Linux audit frameworks
  • Process accounting

docs.title: Network Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

Unexpected Outbound Connections
Long-Lived Connections
Periodic Beaconing
Unusual TLS Behaviour
Unexpected DNS Patterns
Connections to New Infrastructure
Internal SOCKS / Pivot Traffic

Network behaviour should be correlated with the expected role of the host.

A workstation and a production server may have very different normal communication patterns.

docs.title: DNS Detection
docs.text:
DNS-based C2 may create unusual:

Query Frequency
Subdomain Length
Record Patterns
Authoritative Domains
Query Types
Response Patterns

However, defenders should avoid simplistic detection based only on:

Long DNS Name

because legitimate applications can also produce complex DNS traffic.

Use behavioural context.

docs.title: Beacon Detection
docs.text:
Periodic traffic can produce timing patterns.

Conceptually:

Connection
    |
    v
Wait
    |
    v
Connection
    |
    v
Wait

Jitter can change timing but does not remove other behavioural signals.

Correlate:

Timing
Destination
Process
Protocol
Host Role

docs.title: File Detection
docs.text:
Generated test files may be detected through:

Hash
Static Signature
Metadata
Structure
Reputation
Behaviour

A successful detection is valuable evidence.

Do not automatically attempt to bypass it unless evasion testing is explicitly part of the assessment.

docs.title: Application-Control Detection
docs.text:
Relevant controls can include:

WDAC
AppLocker
Defender
EDR
ASR

Record:

File
Path
Hash
User
Rule
Control
Result
Timestamp

This provides significantly stronger evidence than simply stating:

Sliver was blocked.

docs.title: Purple-Team Validation
docs.text:
Sliver is useful for controlled purple-team exercises because a specific action can be correlated with defensive telemetry.

A useful workflow is:

flowchart LR
    R[Red Team Action] --> T[Timestamp]
    T --> N[Network Telemetry]
    T --> E[Endpoint Telemetry]
    T --> S[SIEM]
    N --> A[Analysis]
    E --> A
    S --> A
    A --> D[Detection Improvement]

For every test:

Action
Timestamp
Host
User
Expected Telemetry
Observed Telemetry
Detection
Response

should be recorded.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text:
Relevant controls include:

  • Application control
  • Endpoint detection and response
  • Microsoft Defender
  • Attack Surface Reduction rules
  • Egress filtering
  • Network segmentation
  • DNS monitoring
  • TLS/network analytics
  • Host-based firewalls
  • Least privilege
  • Privileged access management
  • PowerShell security controls
  • Centralised logging
  • Process telemetry
  • Network telemetry
  • Incident-response playbooks

The defensive objective should not be:

Block sliver.exe

Instead:

Prevent Unauthorised Execution
        +
Restrict Outbound Communication
        +
Detect C2 Behaviour
        +
Limit Privilege
        +
Segment Networks
        +
Respond Quickly

docs.title: C2 Infrastructure Security
docs.text:
The Sliver server itself is sensitive infrastructure.

It may contain:

Operator Credentials
Assessment Metadata
Implant Information
Session Information
Generated Files
Target Information

Protect it using:

Restricted Administrative Access
Host Firewall
SSH Key Authentication
Strong Authentication
Patch Management
Disk Encryption
Backups Where Appropriate
Central Logging

Do not expose unnecessary Sliver management interfaces directly to the Internet.

docs.title: Assessment Separation
docs.text:
Where possible, separate:

Operator Workstation
        |
        v
Management Channel
        |
        v
Sliver Server
        |
        v
C2 Listener

This reduces the need for operators to administer the C2 server directly during every test.

docs.title: Infrastructure Inventory
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory such as:

Item Value Server <C2_SERVER> Sliver version <VERSION> Operator <OPERATOR> Listener <TRANSPORT> Port <PORT> Assessment <ASSESSMENT> Start <TIME> End <TIME>

This becomes particularly important when multiple assessments share infrastructure.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
During production assessments:

  • Use only authorised hosts
  • Use clear test identifiers
  • Generate only required implants
  • Avoid unnecessary persistence
  • Avoid destructive commands
  • Avoid broad credential collection
  • Avoid unrelated file access
  • Avoid uncontrolled lateral movement
  • Limit pivot networks to scope
  • Coordinate multi-operator activity
  • Record timestamps
  • Record file hashes
  • Track every deployed implant
  • Remove test tooling after use
  • Confirm all listeners are stopped

A C2 framework increases operational capability and therefore also increases the need for disciplined change control.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Cleanup should cover both:

Target Infrastructure

and:

C2 Infrastructure

docs.title: Target Cleanup
docs.text:
Verify:

  • Test process terminated
  • Test binary removed where required
  • Temporary files removed
  • Port forwards stopped
  • SOCKS proxies stopped
  • No persistence remains
  • No unintended configuration changes remain

docs.title: Server Cleanup
docs.text:
Review:

sessions

beacons

jobs

and any active SOCKS or forwarding functionality.

Stop no-longer-required listeners and jobs using the installed release's help.

Do not blindly terminate infrastructure used by another authorised operator.

docs.title: File Cleanup
docs.text:
On Linux, identify assessment files before removal:

find <ASSESSMENT_DIRECTORY> -maxdepth 2 -type f -print

On Windows:

Get-ChildItem C:\Path\To\Assessment -Recurse -File

Remove only files known to belong to the assessment.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Checklist
docs.text:
When Sliver does not behave as expected, work through:

Server
    |
    v
Listener
    |
    v
Network
    |
    v
Implant
    |
    v
Session / Beacon
    |
    v
Current Context
    |
    v
Requested Capability

Do not skip directly to payload modification.

docs.title: Treating a Session as Administrator Access
docs.text:
Always verify:

User
Groups
Privileges
Integrity

separately.

docs.title: Generating Before Starting a Listener
docs.text: Validate the C2 infrastructure first.

docs.title: Regenerating When Connectivity Is Broken
docs.text:
Test:

Server
Port
Firewall
DNS
Route

before rebuilding the implant.

docs.title: Confusing Sessions and Beacons
docs.text:
Sessions are interactive.

Beacons are asynchronous.

Expect different response behaviour.

docs.title: Starting Broad Pivots Without Scope Validation
docs.text: Confirm the destination network is authorised before forwarding traffic.

docs.title: Treating SOCKS as Routed Networking
docs.text:
SOCKS is an application-layer proxy.

If broad subnet routing is required, Ligolo-ng may be a better fit.

docs.title: Using SYN Scans Through SOCKS
docs.text:
Prefer:

-sT

for Nmap through ProxyChains.

docs.title: Ignoring DNS
docs.text: A working pivot does not guarantee internal hostname resolution.

docs.title: Installing Unreviewed Armory Packages
docs.text:
Extensions execute code and expand the C2 trust boundary.

Review them first.

docs.title: Sharing Operator Credentials
docs.text: Use individual operator configurations.

docs.title: Treating In-Memory as Invisible
docs.text:
Memory-resident activity can still be visible through:

EDR
AMSI
ETW
Process Telemetry
Network Telemetry
Memory Analysis

docs.title: Bypassing a Successful Security Control Automatically
docs.text:
If Defender, EDR, WDAC, AppLocker, or another control blocks the test, record and investigate the control first.

Evasion is a separate assessment objective.

docs.title: Forgetting Cleanup
docs.text:
Track every:

Implant
Listener
Session
Beacon
SOCKS Proxy
Port Forward
Temporary File
Extension

created during the assessment.
