docs.text:
A useful Linux workflow is:

Current User
    |
    v
id
    |
    v
Groups / sudo / environment
    |
    v
Manual Enumeration
    |
    v
LinPEAS / LSE
    |
    v
Candidate Condition
    |
    v
Manual Permission Validation
    |
    v
Privileged Execution Path

Related notes:

Linux Enumeration

Linux Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Start with Identity
docs.text:
Before interpreting any privilege escalation output, understand the current context.

On Windows:

whoami

whoami /groups

whoami /priv

On Linux:

id

groups

This establishes:

Who am I?

Which groups do I belong to?

Which privileges do I have?

What should I already be able to access?

Without this context, enumeration results are harder to interpret correctly.

docs.title: Windows Services
docs.text:
Windows services are a common privilege escalation review area.

Relevant questions include:

Which account runs the service?

What executable does it start?

Can the current user modify that executable?

Can the current user modify the service configuration?

Can the current user restart the service?

Does the service start automatically?

The relationship matters:

Writable File
      +
Privileged Service
      +
Reachable Execution Path
      =
Potential Privilege Escalation

Related note:

Windows Services

docs.title: Service Binary Permissions
docs.text:
A tool may highlight a service executable.

Validate manually.

Questions:

Is the executable writable?

Is the parent directory writable?

Who owns the file?

Which ACL grants access?

Does the service actually execute this file?

A writable file that is never executed by a privileged context may have little security impact.

docs.title: Service Configuration Permissions
docs.text:
The binary itself may be protected while the service configuration is modifiable.

Relevant settings include:

  • executable path;
  • service account;
  • startup configuration;
  • dependencies.

Always assess effective permissions rather than relying only on directory location.

docs.title: Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
An unquoted service path is often highlighted by Windows enumeration tools.

Example concept:

C:\Program Files\Example App\service.exe

If the path contains spaces and is unquoted, investigate how Windows resolves it.

However:

An unquoted service path is not automatically exploitable.

Also determine:

  • whether an earlier path location is writable;
  • whether the service runs privileged;
  • whether the service can restart;
  • whether an appropriate executable path could actually be influenced.

docs.title: Windows Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks can represent privileged execution paths.

Questions include:

Which account executes the task?

What program or script is launched?

Can the current user modify it?

Can the user modify its working directory?

Can the user influence referenced files?

When does the task execute?

Related note:

Windows Scheduled Tasks

docs.title: Windows Registry
docs.text:
The registry can influence privileged execution.

Interesting areas may include:

  • service configuration;
  • application configuration;
  • installer policy;
  • startup behaviour;
  • execution paths.

A registry key is only security relevant if:

Current User Can Modify
        +
Privileged Component Reads It
        +
Meaningful Execution Influence

Related note:

Windows Registry

docs.title: Windows Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Filesystem permissions are central to privilege escalation analysis.

Review:

Files
Directories
Executable paths
Scripts
Configuration
DLL search locations
Scheduled-task resources
Service resources

Related note:

Windows Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Writable Directories
docs.text:
A writable directory may be interesting, but context matters.

Ask:

Who writes there?

Who executes from there?

Is the location searched automatically?

Does a privileged application load resources from it?

A generic writable directory does not automatically create privilege escalation.

docs.title: Windows Credentials
docs.text:
Enumeration tools may identify potential credential material.

Possible locations include:

  • configuration files;
  • scripts;
  • deployment artefacts;
  • saved credentials;
  • environment variables;
  • application files.

Treat any discovered credentials as sensitive evidence.

Related note:

Windows Credentials

docs.title: Windows UAC
docs.text:
User Account Control affects how administrative users receive elevated tokens.

UAC should not be confused with a normal privilege boundary between unrelated users.

Review UAC in the context of:

  • current account;
  • group membership;
  • integrity level;
  • elevation configuration.

Related note:

Windows User Account Control

docs.title: Windows Application Control
docs.text:
Privilege escalation analysis should also consider security controls that may prevent a discovered path from being practically usable.

These may include:

  • AppLocker;
  • Windows Defender Application Control;
  • Defender;
  • script controls;
  • endpoint-security policy.

Related notes:

Windows Application Control

Microsoft Defender

A tool may identify an execution path that is technically writable but blocked by another control.

docs.title: Linux sudo
docs.text:
sudo configuration is one of the most important Linux privilege escalation areas.

Start with:

sudo -l

Review:

  • allowed commands;
  • target user;
  • password requirement;
  • environment handling;
  • wildcards;
  • command arguments.

Related note:

Linux sudo

docs.title: sudo Tool Output
docs.text:
LinPEAS or LSE may highlight sudo rules.

Do not stop at the highlight.

Determine:

Exact sudo rule
    |
    v
Exact command
    |
    v
Allowed arguments
    |
    v
Execution context
    |
    v
Whether privilege can actually be increased

docs.title: SUID and SGID
docs.text:
SUID and SGID binaries can execute with an effective identity different from the invoking user.

Enumerate manually:

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

SGID:

find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Tools such as LinPEAS and LSE can highlight interesting entries.

Related note:

Linux SUID and SGID

docs.title: Linux Capabilities
docs.text:
Linux capabilities split traditional root privileges into smaller units.

Enumerate:

getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

Potentially interesting capabilities depend on:

  • executable;
  • capability;
  • configuration;
  • available arguments.

Related note:

Linux Capabilities

docs.title: Linux Scheduled Jobs
docs.text:
Linux scheduled execution can include:

  • cron;
  • systemd timers;
  • application schedulers.

Questions include:

Who executes the job?

Which command is called?

Can the current user modify the script?

Can the user modify a parent directory?

Can PATH influence command resolution?

Related note:

Linux Scheduled Jobs

docs.title: Linux Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Filesystem review should consider:

  • file owner;
  • group;
  • mode;
  • ACLs;
  • parent directories;
  • mounts.

Useful commands include:

ls -la

namei -l /path/to/file

getfacl /path/to/file

Related note:

Linux Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Linux Credentials
docs.text:
Enumeration tools may identify:

  • shell history;
  • configuration files;
  • environment variables;
  • SSH keys;
  • database configuration;
  • application secrets.

Handle such data carefully.

Related note:

Linux Credentials

docs.title: PATH Analysis
docs.text:
PATH-based privilege escalation depends on command resolution.

Example:

Privileged Script
      |
      v
Calls:
backup
      |
      v
Shell Searches PATH

Questions include:

Is an absolute path used?

Which PATH is active?

Can the current user write to an earlier PATH directory?

Does the privileged process inherit that PATH?

A writable PATH directory alone is not sufficient without a privileged execution path.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables can influence:

  • executable resolution;
  • libraries;
  • interpreters;
  • application configuration.

Their relevance depends on whether privileged processes inherit or trust them.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
Running processes provide useful context.

On Linux:

ps aux

On Windows:

Get-Process

Questions include:

  • Which services are running?
  • Which accounts own them?
  • Which applications are installed?
  • Are privileged processes loading resources from modifiable locations?

docs.title: Installed Software
docs.text:
Enumeration tools often list installed applications.

This can help identify:

  • locally privileged services;
  • management software;
  • outdated products;
  • custom applications.

Do not equate:

Old version installed

with:

Exploitable vulnerability

Validate configuration and patch context.

docs.title: Security Products
docs.text:
Enumeration tools may report:

  • antivirus;
  • EDR;
  • AppLocker;
  • WDAC;
  • SELinux;
  • AppArmor.

These observations help explain what privilege escalation paths may or may not be practical.

Do not disable security controls unless explicitly permitted.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
Linux enumeration may reveal containerisation.

Possible indicators include:

  • Docker;
  • containerd;
  • Kubernetes;
  • LXC.

Container privilege boundaries require separate analysis.

A container context may affect:

  • filesystem visibility;
  • capabilities;
  • mounts;
  • device access;
  • namespaces.

Do not assume root inside a container equals root on the host.

docs.title: Mounts
docs.text:
Linux mount configuration can influence privilege escalation.

Review:

mount

and:

findmnt

Potentially interesting properties include:

  • writable network shares;
  • unusual local mounts;
  • container mounts;
  • privileged files exposed through mounts.

docs.title: Network Shares
docs.text:
Windows and Linux systems may expose mounted or accessible network shares.

Shared locations can contain:

  • deployment scripts;
  • configuration;
  • credentials;
  • binaries;
  • administrative tooling.

Ensure remote systems are within scope before interacting with them.

docs.title: Effective Permissions
docs.text:
Tooling often interprets permissions heuristically.

Manual validation should determine effective permissions.

On Windows, consider:

  • user SID;
  • group SIDs;
  • inherited ACEs;
  • deny ACEs;
  • allow ACEs;
  • ownership;
  • integrity level.

On Linux, consider:

  • UID;
  • GID;
  • supplementary groups;
  • mode bits;
  • ACLs;
  • mount options.

docs.title: Writable Does Not Mean Exploitable
docs.text:
This principle should remain central:

Writable
   !=
Executed

and:

Executed
   !=
Privileged

and:

Privileged
   !=
Current user can trigger

A meaningful chain may require all of them:

Writable
   +
Privileged Execution
   +
Reachability
   =
Candidate PrivEsc

docs.title: Reachability
docs.text:
A condition can exist but be unreachable.

Example:

Writable executable

but:

Service disabled
No restart rights
Never executed

The security impact may therefore be limited.

Always verify the full execution path.

docs.title: Trigger Conditions
docs.text:
Privilege escalation may depend on:

  • reboot;
  • service restart;
  • scheduled execution;
  • user login;
  • application launch;
  • administrator action.

Document the trigger clearly.

docs.title: Current User Can Restart Service?
docs.text:
On Windows, the ability to modify a service-related file does not automatically imply the current user can cause immediate execution.

Possible triggers include:

  • service restart;
  • host reboot;
  • scheduled service recovery.

Do not assume trigger capability.

docs.title: Root-Owned Cron Is Not Enough
docs.text:
On Linux:

root cron job

is not automatically vulnerable.

The interesting question is:

Can the current user influence anything the root cron job executes?

This may include:

  • script;
  • directory;
  • executable;
  • configuration;
  • PATH-resolved binary.

docs.title: Tool Colour Coding
docs.text:
Tools such as PEASS may use colours to prioritise output.

Treat colours as triage aids.

Do not interpret:

red

as:

confirmed vulnerability

Colour usually means:

worth investigating

docs.title: Running Multiple Tools
docs.text:
Running multiple enumeration tools can provide additional coverage.

Example:

WinPEAS
   |
   +--> candidate service

PowerUp
   |
   +--> same service

PrivescCheck
   |
   +--> confirms permissions

This increases confidence that the configuration deserves attention.

It still does not replace manual validation.

docs.title: Tool Correlation
docs.text:
A strong Windows workflow might be:

WinPEAS --------+
                |
PowerUp --------+
                |
PrivescCheck ---+----> Candidate Service
                |
Manual ACL -----+
                |
                v
Validated Condition

Linux:

LinPEAS --------+
                |
LSE ------------+
                |
Manual sudo ----+
                |
Manual ACL -----+----> Validated Condition

docs.title: Avoid Duplicate Noise
docs.text:
Multiple tools often report the same issue.

Do not create several findings for:

Same writable service

because three tools identified it.

Consolidate the evidence around the underlying condition.

docs.title: Tool Version
docs.text:
Record tool versions where possible.

For example:

WinPEAS release:
LinPEAS release:
PrivescCheck version:
PowerUp source revision:
LSE version/revision:

This matters because checks evolve.

docs.title: Integrity of Downloaded Tools
docs.text:
Security tools are high-trust code.

Prefer:

  • official repositories;
  • official releases;
  • cryptographic hashes where provided;
  • controlled internal mirrors.

Avoid downloading modified copies from unknown sources.

docs.title: Endpoint Security Detection
docs.text:
Privilege escalation scripts are commonly detected by endpoint-security products.

This does not mean the tool is malicious in an authorised assessment.

However, it can affect:

  • execution;
  • logging;
  • telemetry;
  • alerting;
  • assessment coordination.

Coordinate intrusive tool use where required.

docs.title: Script Execution Restrictions
docs.text:
On Windows, PowerShell tooling may be affected by:

  • execution policy;
  • AppLocker;
  • WDAC;
  • Constrained Language Mode;
  • Defender;
  • EDR.

A tool failing to run does not mean the system is free of privilege escalation conditions.

Switch to manual enumeration where necessary.

docs.title: Living-off-the-Land Enumeration
docs.text:
When third-party tooling is unavailable, native operating-system tools can still provide strong enumeration coverage.

Windows examples:

whoami
sc.exe
schtasks.exe
icacls.exe
reg.exe
PowerShell cmdlets

Linux examples:

id
sudo
find
ls
getfacl
getcap
ps
systemctl
findmnt

Automated tools accelerate this process; they do not replace the underlying knowledge.

docs.title: Manual Windows Validation
docs.text:
For any Windows candidate, investigate:

Identity
    |
    v
Object
    |
    v
ACL
    |
    v
Privileged Consumer
    |
    v
Trigger
    |
    v
Impact

Example categories:

Service executable
Scheduled task script
Registry value
DLL location
Application configuration

docs.title: Manual Linux Validation
docs.text:
For Linux:

Identity
    |
    v
File / Command / Configuration
    |
    v
Owner / Group / ACL
    |
    v
Privileged Process
    |
    v
Execution Trigger
    |
    v
Impact

docs.title: Representative Windows Scenario
docs.text:
An enumeration tool reports:

Potentially writable service executable:
C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe

Service account:
LocalSystem

Do not immediately conclude privilege escalation.

Validate:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe"

Then determine:

Does current user have write/modify rights?

Is the service actually configured to use this binary?

Can the service be restarted?

Does the service run as SYSTEM?

Are application-control controls relevant?

Possible outcome:

Current user cannot modify file

Conclusion:

Tool-generated candidate not confirmed.

Alternative outcome:

Current user can modify file
Service runs as SYSTEM
Service restarts automatically

This is a much stronger security condition.

docs.title: Representative Linux Scenario
docs.text:
LinPEAS reports:

Interesting SUID binary

Validate:

ls -l /path/to/binary

Then determine:

Owner
Permissions
Binary behaviour
Arguments
Configuration
Whether effective UID is retained

The presence of SUID alone is not necessarily a vulnerability.

Many legitimate system binaries use it intentionally.

docs.title: Representative sudo Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose:

sudo -l

shows an allowed command.

The analysis should determine:

Exact executable
Allowed arguments
Wildcard use
Environment
Whether command offers shell/file/process influence

Do not report sudo configuration simply because an entry exists.

docs.title: Representative Scheduled Task Scenario
docs.text:
A Windows tool reports:

Task runs as SYSTEM
Script path is C:\ProgramData\Scripts\backup.ps1

Validate:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Scripts\backup.ps1"

Then:

Can current user modify it?

When does the task run?

Can execution be triggered?

Is PowerShell allowed by application control?

The complete chain determines risk.

docs.title: Representative Cron Scenario
docs.text:
A Linux tool reports:

root executes /opt/scripts/backup.sh every minute

Check:

ls -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

and:

namei -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

A protected script may still reside in a writable parent directory.

Evaluate the full path.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Common reasons automated tools produce misleading privilege escalation candidates include:

  • writable directory unrelated to privileged execution;
  • inherited ACL interpretation;
  • disabled service;
  • inactive scheduled task;
  • root-owned file that is not executed;
  • package version without vulnerable configuration;
  • protected resource misidentified as writable;
  • effective permissions differing from simple mode bits.

Manual validation resolves these uncertainties.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Enumeration tools can miss real privilege escalation paths.

Possible reasons include:

  • custom application logic;
  • non-standard directories;
  • unusual service configuration;
  • transient files;
  • application-specific IPC;
  • undocumented privileged workflows;
  • security-control interference;
  • custom scripts.

A clean WinPEAS or LinPEAS run does not prove that no escalation path exists.

docs.title: Evidence to Capture
docs.text:
For each validated condition, retain:

Current user:
Current groups:
Relevant privilege:
Affected object:
Owner:
Permissions:
Privileged execution context:
Trigger:
Manual validation:
Observed result:
Security impact:

For Windows:

Service/task name
Executable/script path
Service account
ACL output
Startup/trigger condition

For Linux:

File path
Owner/group
Mode/ACL
sudo/SUID/capability context
Privileged consumer
Trigger

docs.title: Evidence Should Show the Chain
docs.text:
Weak evidence:

Screenshot of WinPEAS red text

Strong evidence:

WinPEAS candidate
      |
      v
icacls output
      |
      v
service configuration
      |
      v
service account
      |
      v
trigger condition

The evidence should explain why the condition matters.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
The finding should describe the underlying security weakness rather than the enumeration tool.

Avoid:

WinPEAS found a vulnerable service.

Prefer:

A service running as LocalSystem used an executable that was modifiable
by the tested standard user. The service represented a privileged
execution path, allowing the low-privileged user to influence code
executed in the LocalSystem context.

Similarly, avoid:

LinPEAS found a cron vulnerability.

Prefer:

A root-owned scheduled job executed a script located in a path that was
modifiable by the tested user, allowing the user to influence commands
executed by the privileged scheduled process.

docs.title: Negative Results
docs.text:
Negative results are also useful.

Example:

Tool:
WinPEAS

Candidate:
Writable service executable

Manual validation:
Effective ACL did not grant write or modify rights to the current user.

Conclusion:
The suspected privilege escalation path was not confirmed.

This is useful assessment evidence.

docs.title: Severity Depends on the Chain
docs.text:
A privilege escalation condition may be severe where:

Normal user
    |
    v
Immediate SYSTEM/root

But severity may be lower if:

  • privileged trigger requires an administrator;
  • execution occurs rarely;
  • additional conditions are required;
  • strong controls limit practical exploitation.

Assess the actual environment.

docs.title: Remediation Principles
docs.text:
Remediation commonly involves removing the user's ability to influence privileged execution.

Examples:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
• correct service binary ACLs;
  • correct service configuration ACLs;
  • secure scheduled-task scripts;
  • restrict writable directories;
  • quote service paths where relevant;
  • protect registry values;
  • remove unnecessary privileges.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
• correct file ownership;
  • remove unsafe write permissions;
  • correct sudo rules;
  • remove unnecessary SUID/SGID;
  • remove unnecessary capabilities;
  • secure cron scripts;
  • use absolute paths;
  • protect privileged configuration.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
A good retest confirms the root cause was removed.

Example:

Before:
Standard user -> Modify service executable

After:
Standard user -> Read/Execute only

Then verify:

Service still functions
Privileged execution path remains protected

Do not retest only by rerunning the enumeration tool.

Manually confirm the relevant permission or configuration.

docs.title: Recommended Testing Order - Windows
docs.text:
A practical sequence is:

1. Identity
2. Groups
3. Token privileges
4. System information
5. Services
6. Scheduled tasks
7. Filesystem permissions
8. Registry
9. Credentials
10. Installed applications
11. Security controls
12. Automated enumeration
13. Manual validation

Automated tooling can be used earlier, but understanding the underlying areas first improves interpretation.

docs.title: Recommended Testing Order - Linux
docs.text:
1. Identity
2. Groups
3. sudo
4. SUID/SGID
5. capabilities
6. cron/systemd
7. filesystem permissions
8. processes
9. credentials
10. mounts
11. environment/PATH
12. automated enumeration
13. manual validation

docs.text:

A useful workflow is:

WinPEAS

Candidate

Native Validation

docs.title: Choosing a Tool
docs.text:
Ask:

What platform am I on?

What execution restrictions exist?

How much telemetry is acceptable?

Do I need broad coverage or a focused check?

Can I transfer third-party tools?

Would native commands be more appropriate?

Then choose accordingly.

docs.title: Tool Transfer Considerations
docs.text:
If a tool must be transferred to a target, consider:

  • engagement rules;
  • endpoint security;
  • file provenance;
  • cleanup;
  • logging;
  • integrity verification.

Do not leave unnecessary assessment artefacts behind.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Where tooling creates files or logs on the target, remove them when the engagement requires cleanup.

Document:

What was uploaded?

Where?

When?

Was it removed?

Avoid deleting legitimate system or security logs.

docs.title: Logging and Telemetry
docs.text:
Privilege escalation enumeration can generate telemetry through:

  • PowerShell;
  • process creation;
  • registry access;
  • filesystem enumeration;
  • security product alerts.

In purple-team exercises, this can be useful.

In sensitive production assessments, coordinate the expected activity.

Related section:

Purple Teaming

docs.title: Tool-Assisted Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Privilege escalation tools can also be used to validate defensive visibility.

Example:

WinPEAS / LinPEAS
      |
      v
Enumeration Activity
      |
      v
Endpoint Telemetry
      |
      v
Detection Engineering

The objective may be both:

Identify exposure

and:

Measure detection visibility

Related note:

Detection Engineering

docs.text:
The tool pages should connect directly to the existing Privilege Escalation Explorer.

Tool Output
    |
    v
Candidate Category
    |
    +--> Windows Service
    +--> Scheduled Task
    +--> Registry
    +--> sudo
    +--> SUID
    +--> Capability
    |
    v
Privilege Escalation Explorer

docs.title: Practical Validation Model
docs.text:
For each candidate, answer:

1. What did the tool identify?
2. Why could this matter?
3. Does the current user actually have the required access?
4. Which privileged component consumes the resource?
5. Can the execution path be triggered?
6. Which security controls apply?
7. What privilege would be gained?
8. Can the condition be reproduced safely?
9. What evidence supports the conclusion?

If these questions cannot be answered, the candidate may not yet be a finding.

docs.title: Reporting Tool Colour
docs.text:
Bad:

WinPEAS marked this red.

Better:

The effective ACL grants the standard user Modify rights over a binary
executed by a LocalSystem service.

docs.title: Ignoring Effective Permissions
docs.text:
Do not infer permissions solely from location.

Example:

C:\Program Files\

is commonly protected, but individual subdirectories may have different ACLs.

Similarly:

/opt/

does not imply a particular Linux permission model.

Check the actual object.

docs.title: Ignoring Parent Directories
docs.text:
A protected file can still be affected through a writable parent directory depending on platform and operation.

Review the complete path.

docs.title: Ignoring Trigger Conditions
docs.text:
A candidate may require:

restart
reboot
scheduled execution
administrator action

Document this.

docs.title: Ignoring Security Controls
docs.text:
A technically writable execution path may still be constrained by:

  • AppLocker;
  • WDAC;
  • SELinux;
  • AppArmor;
  • endpoint security.

This does not necessarily eliminate the configuration weakness, but it affects practical risk.

docs.title: Running Tools Without Understanding Output
docs.text:
The objective is not:

Run WinPEAS
Scroll for red lines

The objective is:

Run WinPEAS
Understand candidate
Validate manually

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• [ ] Current user identified.
  • [ ] Current groups identified.
  • [ ] Current privileges identified.
  • [ ] Host/platform understood.
  • [ ] Assessment scope confirmed.

docs.title: Automated Enumeration
docs.text:

  • [ ] Tool obtained from trusted source.
  • [ ] Tool version/revision recorded where useful.
  • [ ] Endpoint-security impact considered.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:

  • [ ] Filesystem ACLs reviewed.
  • [ ] Registry permissions reviewed.
  • [ ] Credentials reviewed.
  • [ ] Application control considered.
  • [ ] UAC context understood.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
• [ ] sudo reviewed.
  • [ ] SUID/SGID reviewed.
  • [ ] capabilities reviewed.
  • [ ] cron/systemd reviewed.
  • [ ] filesystem permissions reviewed.
  • [ ] credentials reviewed.
  • [ ] PATH/environment reviewed.
  • [ ] mounts reviewed.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Candidate object identified.
  • [ ] Effective permissions confirmed.
  • [ ] Privileged consumer identified.
  • [ ] Execution context confirmed.
  • [ ] Trigger condition confirmed.
  • [ ] Security controls considered.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:

  • [ ] Relevant permission output retained.
  • [ ] Relevant configuration retained.
  • [ ] Privileged execution context documented.
  • [ ] Trigger documented.
  • [ ] Conclusion based on technical evidence.
  • [ ] Sensitive credentials redacted where necessary.

docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use privilege escalation tools like this:

Run Tool
   |
   v
Find Highlighted Line
   |
   v
Report PrivEsc

Use them like this:

Understand Current Identity
        |
        v
Run Focused Enumeration
        |
        v
Identify Candidate Condition
        |
        v
Understand Why It Matters
        |
        v
Check Effective Permissions
        |

Identify Privileged Consumer
        |
        v
Confirm Trigger / Reachability
        |
        v
Consider Security Controls
        |
        v
Validate Impact
        |
        v
Capture Evidence
        |
        v
Report the Underlying Weakness

Privilege escalation tools are most valuable when they accelerate discovery without replacing technical understanding.

The tool identifies where to look.

The tester determines whether a real privilege escalation path exists.

docs.title: LinPEAS
docs.text:
LinPEAS is part of the PEASS-ng project and is designed to enumerate Linux systems for conditions that may be relevant to local privilege escalation.

It can inspect a broad range of areas, including:

  • users and groups;
  • sudo configuration;
  • SUID and SGID binaries;
  • Linux capabilities;
  • cron jobs;
  • systemd services and timers;
  • filesystem permissions;
  • writable directories;
  • environment variables;
  • PATH configuration;
  • credentials;
  • processes;
  • network configuration;
  • mounted filesystems;
  • containers;
  • installed software;
  • security controls;
  • interesting files.

LinPEAS is most useful as an enumeration accelerator.

It does not automatically determine whether every highlighted condition is exploitable.

Linux Host
   |
   v
LinPEAS
   |
   +-- Identity
   +-- sudo
   +-- SUID / SGID
   +-- Capabilities
   +-- Cron / systemd
   +-- Filesystem
   +-- Credentials
   +-- Processes
   +-- Mounts
   +-- Containers
   +-- Security Controls
   |
   v
Candidate Conditions
   |
   v
Manual Validation
   |
   v
Privilege Escalation Conclusion

Authorised testing only

Run LinPEAS only on Linux systems where local security enumeration is explicitly authorised. It performs many checks across the host and may generate security telemetry or access sensitive configuration locations. Review the rules of engagement before transferring or executing third-party enumeration tooling.

docs.title: Where LinPEAS Fits
docs.text:
LinPEAS normally follows initial access to a Linux system.

A useful workflow is:

Initial Local Access
        |
        v
Identify Current User
        |
        v
Manual Baseline
        |
        v
Run LinPEAS
        |
        v
Review Interesting Results
        |
        v
Validate With Native Tools
        |
        v
Confirm or Reject Candidate

Related notes:

Privilege Escalation Tools

Linux Privilege Escalation

Linux Enumeration

Linux Privilege Escalation Explorer

docs.title: What LinPEAS Does
docs.text:
LinPEAS automates many checks that would otherwise need to be performed manually.

Conceptually:

System State
    |
    +-- Users
    +-- Groups
    +-- sudo
    +-- SUID / SGID
    +-- Capabilities
    +-- Cron
    +-- systemd
    +-- Files
    +-- Credentials
    +-- Processes
    +-- Mounts
    +-- Containers
    |
    v
LinPEAS Checks
    |
    v
Prioritised Output

The tool attempts to highlight items that may deserve additional investigation.

The key principle is:

Highlighted
    !=
Exploitable

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
LinPEAS is maintained as part of PEASS-ng.

Official project:

PEASS-ng - GitHub

Official releases:

PEASS-ng Releases

Use the official project or trusted internal mirrors.

Avoid unknown modified copies.

docs.title: Before Running LinPEAS
docs.text:
Understand the current user context first.

Run:

whoami

Then:

id

And:

groups

Useful questions include:

Which user am I?

Which groups do I belong to?

Am I already privileged?

Do I belong to sudo-related groups?

Do I belong to Docker, LXD, disk, or similar sensitive groups?

Without this baseline, tool output is harder to interpret.

docs.title: Record System Context
docs.text:
Capture basic host information.

Useful commands include:

hostname

uname -a

cat /etc/os-release

id

This provides context for:

  • operating system;
  • kernel;
  • distribution;
  • current identity;
  • later evidence.

docs.title: Obtaining LinPEAS
docs.text:
Prefer the official PEASS-ng release or repository.

Verify:

  • source;
  • release provenance;
  • file integrity where appropriate;
  • engagement approval;
  • internal malware-handling procedures.

Security products may identify offensive-security tooling even when it is being used legitimately.

docs.title: Common LinPEAS Form
docs.text:
LinPEAS is commonly distributed as a shell script:

linpeas.sh

The exact content and checks evolve over time.

Do not assume an old copy provides complete coverage.

docs.title: Basic Execution
docs.text:
A common authorised workflow is:

chmod +x linpeas.sh

Then:

./linpeas.sh

It can also be invoked through a shell:

bash linpeas.sh

Use the method permitted by the environment.

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text:
Large LinPEAS runs can produce substantial output.

Saving the results makes later review easier.

Example:

./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas-output.txt

This allows:

  • later searching;
  • comparison;
  • evidence extraction;
  • review outside the terminal.

Protect the resulting file because it may contain sensitive information.

docs.title: Output May Contain Secrets
docs.text:
LinPEAS can expose:

  • passwords;
  • API keys;
  • tokens;
  • database credentials;
  • private keys;
  • configuration secrets;
  • shell history;
  • environment variables;
  • usernames;
  • internal paths.

Do not:

  • commit raw output to Git;
  • upload it to public services;
  • include full output in reports;
  • share it outside the authorised assessment team.

Retain only what is necessary.

docs.title: Colour Coding
docs.text:
LinPEAS uses colour and formatting to draw attention to interesting results.

Do not interpret colour as certainty.

Bad model:

Red
 |
 v
Confirmed vulnerability

Better:

Highlighted
   |
   v
Investigate

Colour is a triage mechanism.

docs.title: Major Enumeration Areas
docs.text:
LinPEAS may inspect categories such as:

Users
Groups
sudo
SUID / SGID
Capabilities
Cron
systemd
Filesystem
Processes
Credentials
Network
Mounts
Containers
Environment
Security Controls

Each area requires different manual validation.

docs.title: Current User
docs.text:
Start with:

id

Representative result:

uid=1001tester gid=1001tester groups=1001tester,27sudo

The result immediately provides context.

If the user is already a member of a highly privileged group, that may be more relevant than later enumeration findings.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Group membership can significantly change privilege.

Inspect:

groups

and:

id

Potentially sensitive groups depend on the environment but may include groups controlling:

  • sudo;
  • containers;
  • storage devices;
  • logs;
  • privileged services;
  • virtualisation.

Do not assume group membership alone is exploitable.

Understand what that group can actually control.

docs.title: sudo
docs.text:
sudo is one of the most important Linux privilege escalation areas.

Always inspect manually:

sudo -l

Questions include:

Which commands are allowed?

Which target user?

Is a password required?

Are wildcards present?

Are arguments restricted?

Are environment variables preserved?

Related note:

Linux sudo

docs.title: Interpreting sudo Output
docs.text:
Suppose LinPEAS highlights:

User may run /usr/bin/example as root

Do not stop there.

Determine:

What exactly can the binary do?

Are arguments unrestricted?

Does it load configuration?

Can it write files?

Can it spawn another process?

Does it invoke external commands?

The privilege escalation condition depends on the actual behaviour.

docs.title: sudo NOPASSWD
docs.text:
A rule containing:

NOPASSWD

means the command can be executed without entering the user's password.

This may increase practical reachability.

It does not automatically mean privilege escalation is possible.

The allowed command still needs analysis.

docs.title: sudo Wildcards
docs.text:
Wildcard-based sudo rules deserve careful review.

Example concept:

/usr/bin/example *

Questions include:

What arguments can be supplied?

Are paths controlled?

Does the command interpret options?

Can additional files be referenced?

A wildcard itself is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: sudo Environment
docs.text:
Environment handling may matter for certain privileged commands.

Review sudo configuration rather than assuming inherited variables are trusted.

Useful command:

sudo -V

and configuration review where authorised.

The relevant question is whether an environment-controlled value influences privileged execution.

docs.title: SUID
docs.text:
SUID binaries execute with the effective user identity of the file owner.

Find them manually:

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Typical output might include:

/usr/bin/passwd
/usr/bin/sudo
/usr/bin/su

Many legitimate Linux utilities require SUID.

Therefore:

SUID
  !=
Vulnerable

Related note:

Linux SUID and SGID

docs.title: Validate SUID Permissions
docs.text:
Inspect a candidate:

ls -l /path/to/binary

Representative:

-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 123456 Jan 1 12:00 /path/to/binary

The s in the owner's execute position indicates SUID.

Next investigate:

  • owner;
  • binary purpose;
  • supported arguments;
  • configuration;
  • external commands;
  • environment handling;
  • version;
  • whether privileges are dropped.

docs.title: SGID
docs.text:
SGID binaries execute with the effective group identity associated with the file.

Enumerate:

find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null

SGID is often legitimate.

Assess whether the group privilege creates meaningful access.

docs.title: GTFOBins as a Research Aid
docs.text:
For known Linux utilities, GTFOBins can help identify security-sensitive functionality such as:

  • sudo abuse;
  • SUID behaviour;
  • file read;
  • file write;
  • command execution.

Use it as a reference, not proof that a path is exploitable.

GTFOBins

The actual binary, permissions, arguments, and environment must still be validated.

docs.title: Linux Capabilities
docs.text:
Linux capabilities divide traditional root privileges into smaller units.

Enumerate:

getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

Representative output:

/usr/bin/example cap_net_raw=ep

Potential security impact depends on:

  • capability;
  • executable;
  • effective/permitted state;
  • command functionality;
  • configuration.

Related note:

Linux Capabilities

docs.title: Capability Validation
docs.text:
Inspect the exact capability:

getcap /path/to/binary

Then determine what the binary can do with it.

For example:

Capability
    |
    v
Binary Functionality
    |
    v
Current User Control
    |
    v
Security Impact

The capability name alone is not enough.

docs.title: Scheduled Jobs
docs.text:
LinPEAS can identify scheduled execution.

Relevant mechanisms include:

  • cron;
  • system cron directories;
  • user crontabs;
  • systemd timers;
  • custom schedulers.

Related note:

Linux Scheduled Jobs

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Inspect cron configuration manually.

Examples:

cat /etc/crontab

ls -la /etc/cron.d/

ls -la /etc/cron.daily/

where access is permitted.

The important questions are:

Who executes the command?

What is executed?

Can the current user modify it?

Can the current user modify a parent directory?

Can PATH influence command resolution?

docs.title: Root Cron Jobs
docs.text:
A root cron job is not automatically a vulnerability.

Example:

root executes /opt/scripts/backup.sh

Validate:

ls -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

and:

namei -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

If the current user cannot influence the script or execution path, the condition may be secure.

docs.title: User Crontabs
docs.text:
Inspect authorised user crontabs with:

crontab -l

System-level cron jobs may be visible through:

/etc/crontab
/etc/cron.d/

Do not modify scheduled jobs during validation unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: systemd Services
docs.text:
systemd services may provide privileged execution paths.

List relevant units:

systemctl list-units --type=service

Inspect a specific unit:

systemctl cat example.service

Review:

User=
Group=
ExecStart=
Environment=
WorkingDirectory=

The question is whether the current user can influence something consumed by the privileged service.

docs.title: systemd Timers
docs.text:
Timers provide scheduled systemd execution.

List timers:

systemctl list-timers --all

Inspect the timer and corresponding service.

A timer itself is not vulnerable.

The security question is whether a low-privileged user can influence the privileged execution chain.

docs.title: Service Files
docs.text:
Typical systemd unit locations include:

/etc/systemd/system/
/usr/lib/systemd/system/
/lib/systemd/system/

Actual locations vary by distribution.

Check permissions rather than assuming.

docs.title: Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Weak filesystem permissions are central to Linux privilege escalation.

Review:

  • files;
  • directories;
  • scripts;
  • configuration;
  • service resources;
  • cron resources;
  • binaries;
  • application data.

Related note:

Linux Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Basic Permission Inspection
docs.text:
Use:

ls -l /path/to/file

Example:

-rwxrwxr-x 1 root developers 1024 Jan 1 12:00 /opt/app/start.sh

Interpret:

Owner
Group
Mode bits

Then compare those permissions with the current user's identity and groups.

docs.title: namei
docs.text:
namei -l is very useful for analysing complete path permissions.

Example:

namei -l /opt/app/scripts/backup.sh

This helps reveal whether a parent directory is writable even if the final file is protected.

docs.title: ACLs
docs.text:
Traditional mode bits may not show the entire permission picture.

Inspect ACLs:

getfacl /path/to/file

ACLs can grant additional permissions to specific users or groups.

Always consider effective permissions.

docs.title: Writable Directories
docs.text:
Findings such as:

World-writable directory

must be interpreted carefully.

Ask:

Does a privileged process use this directory?

Does it load executables from here?

Does it source scripts?

Does it load configuration?

Can files be replaced?

A writable directory without a privileged consumer may not create escalation.

docs.title: World-Writable Files
docs.text:
A world-writable file may be highly relevant if consumed by root.

It may be irrelevant if it is only user data.

The security significance depends on:

Who can modify it?
+
Who trusts it?
+
How is it used?

docs.title: Parent Directories
docs.text:
Always inspect parent directories.

Example:

/opt/app/config/settings.conf

The file itself might be protected while:

/opt/app/config/

is writable.

Depending on filesystem permissions, the user may be able to replace the file.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Inspect:

stat /path/to/file

Useful properties include:

  • owner;
  • group;
  • mode;
  • timestamps.

Ownership helps explain expected trust boundaries.

docs.title: PATH
docs.text:
PATH-based issues occur when privileged scripts or programs execute commands without absolute paths.

Inspect:

echo "$PATH"

Then:

printf '%s\n' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'

Questions include:

Which directory is searched first?

Is it writable?

Does a privileged process inherit this PATH?

Does the privileged script call a command without an absolute path?

A writable PATH directory is only one part of the chain.

docs.title: PATH Hijacking Model
docs.text:
Privileged Script
      |
      v
Calls:
backup
      |
      v
PATH Search
      |
      v
Writable Directory First
      |
      v
Attacker-Controlled Binary

Every step must be validated.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Inspect:

env

or:

printenv

Environment variables may contain:

  • tokens;
  • credentials;
  • application paths;
  • configuration;
  • runtime settings.

Security relevance depends on who can read them and whether privileged processes trust them.

docs.title: Shell History
docs.text:
LinPEAS may inspect shell history files.

Examples include:

~/.bash_history
~/.zsh_history

History may contain:

  • commands;
  • passwords accidentally supplied inline;
  • URLs;
  • administrative actions;
  • database commands.

Treat shell history as sensitive data.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
LinPEAS may identify possible credentials in:

  • configuration files;
  • shell history;
  • environment variables;
  • scripts;
  • application directories;
  • backup files;
  • SSH material.

Related note:

Linux Credentials

docs.title: Credential Validation
docs.text:
A string that resembles a password may be:

  • example data;
  • expired;
  • fake;
  • encrypted;
  • unused;
  • a hash rather than plaintext.

Do not automatically attempt to authenticate with every discovered secret.

First determine whether validation is necessary and authorised.

docs.title: SSH Keys
docs.text:
Interesting files may include:

id_rsa
id_ed25519
authorized_keys
known_hosts

The presence of a private key does not automatically mean it can be used elsewhere.

Consider:

  • ownership;
  • permissions;
  • passphrase;
  • authorised scope;
  • associated account;
  • destination systems.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Application configuration may expose:

  • database credentials;
  • service accounts;
  • API keys;
  • internal endpoints.

Common locations vary by application.

The relevant security issue may be:

Low-privileged user can read sensitive configuration

rather than:

LinPEAS found password

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
Running processes reveal valuable context.

Use:

ps aux

or:

ps -ef

Review:

  • privileged services;
  • custom applications;
  • root processes;
  • service commands;
  • interpreters;
  • unusual working directories.

docs.title: Process Command Lines
docs.text:
Process arguments may expose:

  • passwords;
  • tokens;
  • configuration paths;
  • scripts.

Example:

root  /usr/bin/example --config /opt/app/config.yml

This may identify a privileged configuration path worth reviewing.

docs.title: Process Ownership
docs.text:
A root-owned process is only interesting if the current user can influence something it uses.

Possible influence points include:

  • configuration;
  • executable;
  • script;
  • socket;
  • writable working directory;
  • plugin directory.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
List services:

systemctl --type=service

or inspect running processes.

Custom root-owned services deserve particular attention.

The objective is to trace:

Service
  |
  v
Executable
  |
  v
Configuration
  |
  v
Files / Environment

and identify user-controlled components.

docs.title: Network Services
docs.text:
Local services can be security relevant.

Inspect:

ss -lntup

where permissions allow.

Potentially interesting services include:

  • local-only administration APIs;
  • databases;
  • development interfaces;
  • management sockets.

Do not assume access to a local port creates privilege escalation.

Validate authentication and privilege context.

docs.title: Unix Sockets
docs.text:
Privileged services may expose Unix-domain sockets.

Find them with appropriate filesystem and process inspection.

A socket may be relevant if the current user has permission to interact with a privileged service that exposes sensitive functionality.

docs.title: Mounts
docs.text:
Mount configuration can expose security-relevant conditions.

Inspect:

mount

and:

findmnt

Potential areas include:

  • NFS;
  • CIFS;
  • bind mounts;
  • container mounts;
  • removable storage;
  • shared filesystems.

Related privilege depends on the mount and its options.

docs.title: /etc/fstab
docs.text:
Review where authorised:

cat /etc/fstab

This may reveal:

  • network shares;
  • mount credentials;
  • filesystem options;
  • custom mount points.

Treat embedded credentials as sensitive.

docs.title: NFS
docs.text:
NFS configuration can have security implications.

The local client view alone may not reveal server-side export configuration.

Do not infer a server-side weakness purely from the fact that an NFS mount exists.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
LinPEAS may identify whether the host or current process is running inside a container.

Useful clues include:

  • Docker;
  • containerd;
  • Kubernetes;
  • LXC;
  • cgroups;
  • namespaces.

Root inside a container is not automatically root on the host.

docs.title: Docker Group
docs.text:
Membership in the Docker group can be highly privileged because Docker can control host resources.

First validate:

id

and:

groups

Then determine whether the Docker daemon is accessible:

docker info

where authorised.

The security conclusion should describe the excessive privilege associated with daemon access, not simply group membership.

docs.title: Docker Socket
docs.text:
A common local resource is:

/var/run/docker.sock

Inspect:

ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

Questions include:

Which group owns it?

Can the current user access it?

Does it control the host Docker daemon?

Avoid modifying containers during validation unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: LXD / LXC
docs.text:
Container-management groups can also provide substantial privileges.

As with Docker:

Group Membership
       |
       v
Management Access
       |
       v
Host Resource Control

Manual validation is required.

docs.title: Kubernetes Context
docs.text:
On containerised systems, LinPEAS may surface:

  • service-account tokens;
  • mounted secrets;
  • Kubernetes environment variables;
  • container metadata.

These may belong to a different security domain and must be assessed against engagement scope.

docs.title: Kernel Information
docs.text:
LinPEAS may identify kernel version information.

Check manually:

uname -r

Do not immediately map a kernel version to a local exploit.

Instead determine:

Kernel version
    |
    v
Distribution package
    |
    v
Vendor patch status
    |
    v
Configuration
    |
    v
Applicability

Linux distributions frequently backport security fixes.

docs.title: Kernel Exploit Candidates
docs.text:
Treat automated kernel exploit suggestions as research leads.

A version match is insufficient.

Validate:

  • architecture;
  • exact kernel;
  • distribution;
  • patch level;
  • configuration;
  • required namespace or capability;
  • stability risk.

Kernel exploitation can destabilise a system and should only be attempted where explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Installed Packages
docs.text:
Enumerate package information with distribution-appropriate tools.

Examples:

dpkg -l

or:

rpm -qa

depending on the platform.

Old-looking versions may still contain backported fixes.

docs.title: Custom Applications
docs.text:
Custom root-run applications can be more important than standard packages.

Review:

  • binary location;
  • scripts;
  • configuration;
  • working directories;
  • update mechanisms;
  • plugin directories.

LinPEAS may provide clues, but custom logic usually requires manual analysis.

docs.title: Sensitive Groups
docs.text:
Some groups deserve closer review because membership may grant control over privileged resources.

Examples can include groups related to:

sudo
docker
lxd
disk
adm
backup

Exact impact is environment-specific.

Do not report group membership without understanding the permissions it grants.

docs.title: Disk Access
docs.text:
Membership in a group with raw block-device access can represent substantial privilege.

Validate:

  • actual device permissions;
  • current group membership;
  • mounted resources;
  • assessment rules.

Raw-disk operations can damage systems and should not be used casually for validation.

docs.title: Log Access
docs.text:
Groups that grant access to logs may expose:

  • tokens;
  • credentials;
  • sensitive application data.

This may be an information-disclosure issue even if it does not directly provide root access.

docs.title: Backup Files
docs.text:
LinPEAS may locate files such as:

*.bak
*.old
*.backup
~

Backup files can expose:

  • configuration;
  • credentials;
  • previous permissions;
  • source code.

Validate relevance before reporting.

docs.title: Temporary Directories
docs.text:
Common writable locations include:

/tmp
/var/tmp
/dev/shm

These are intentionally writable on many systems.

A writable temporary directory is not itself a vulnerability.

It becomes relevant only when a privileged component trusts or executes user-controlled content from it.

docs.title: /tmp Misinterpretation
docs.text:
Bad:

/tmp is writable
    |
    v
Privilege escalation

Correct:

/tmp is writable
    |
    v
Expected behaviour

Need additional condition:
Privileged process consumes predictable/user-controlled file

docs.title: File Race Conditions
docs.text:
Some privileged programs may create or access files in unsafe shared locations.

This can create race-condition or symlink-related risks.

Such conditions require careful, low-impact validation.

Do not perform destructive race testing on production systems unless explicitly approved.

docs.title: Home Directories
docs.text:
Review whether one user can improperly access another user's home directory.

Potentially sensitive data includes:

  • SSH keys;
  • shell history;
  • configuration;
  • application credentials.

The finding may be excessive local file access rather than privilege escalation.

docs.title: Root-Owned Files
docs.text:
Root ownership does not imply security by itself.

Check:

Owner
Group
Mode
ACL
Parent Directory

A root-owned file can still be modifiable by another group or ACL entry.

docs.title: World-Readable Files
docs.text:
World-readable files are common.

The important question is what the file contains.

For example:

/etc/passwd

is normally world-readable.

That is not a vulnerability.

Context matters.

docs.title: /etc/passwd
docs.text:
Normal permissions generally allow users to read:

/etc/passwd

Sensitive password hashes should normally be stored in:

/etc/shadow

A tool highlighting /etc/passwd simply because it is readable should not be interpreted as a security issue.

docs.title: /etc/shadow
docs.text:
Access to:

/etc/shadow

is much more security sensitive.

Check permissions:

ls -l /etc/shadow

Do not collect or crack password hashes unless explicitly authorised and necessary for the assessment.

docs.title: Shells
docs.text:
Inspect:

cat /etc/shells

and user account entries where relevant.

This provides context about interactive users and available shells.

docs.title: Current Shell
docs.text:
Check:

echo "$SHELL"

and:

ps -p $$ -o comm=

This can help explain script behaviour and environment differences.

docs.title: SELinux
docs.text:
Security controls may constrain a technically interesting path.

Check:

getenforce

where SELinux is installed.

Possible states include:

Enforcing
Permissive
Disabled

Do not assume Enforcing means all privilege escalation paths are prevented.

It is one security layer.

Related note:

Linux Security Controls

docs.title: AppArmor
docs.text:
AppArmor may restrict application behaviour.

Check where available:

aa-status

The exact command may require additional privileges.

As with SELinux, application confinement affects exploitability but does not automatically remove an underlying permission weakness.

docs.title: no_new_privs
docs.text:
Linux processes can use the no_new_privs security attribute to prevent gaining additional privileges through certain execution mechanisms.

Where relevant, inspect process security context.

This can affect the practical behaviour of SUID or file-capability execution.

Related note:

Linux Security Controls

docs.title: Seccomp
docs.text:
Containers and sandboxed processes may use seccomp filters.

This can restrict system calls.

Its presence can affect exploitability.

Do not assume an automated candidate remains fully usable within a heavily constrained execution environment.

docs.title: Read-Only Filesystems
docs.text:
A filesystem or mount may be read-only even when traditional permissions appear writable.

Check:

findmnt

and mount options.

Effective write capability depends on both permissions and mount state.

docs.title: ACL vs Mode Bits
docs.text:
A file might show:

-rw-r-----

but ACLs may grant additional access.

Check:

getfacl /path/to/file

Effective permission analysis should include both.

docs.title: Capabilities vs SUID
docs.text:
Capabilities and SUID are different privilege mechanisms.

SUID
  |
  v
Effective user identity changes

Capabilities:

Capability
  |
  v
Specific privilege granted

Review both independently.

docs.title: LinPEAS and LSE
docs.text:
LinPEAS and linux-smart-enumeration overlap in several areas.

A useful workflow is:

LinPEAS
   |
   v
Broad Candidate Set
   |
   v
LSE / Manual Review
   |
   v
Confirm Important Conditions

Related tool:

linux-smart-enumeration

docs.title: LinPEAS and Manual Enumeration
docs.text:
Automated and manual approaches complement each other.

LinPEAS
   |
   +-- breadth
   +-- fast triage

Manual Tools
   |
   +-- precision
   +-- context
   +-- evidence

Native Linux commands should validate important findings.

docs.title: Native Validation Tools
docs.text:
Useful commands include:

id
sudo
find
ls
stat
namei
getfacl
getcap
ps
systemctl
findmnt
ss

LinPEAS should guide which manual checks matter.

docs.title: Searching Saved Output
docs.text:
If results were saved:

linpeas-output.txt

search them:

grep -i "sudo" linpeas-output.txt

grep -i "capabil" linpeas-output.txt

grep -i "writable" linpeas-output.txt

Retain surrounding context when interpreting matches.

docs.title: Review by Category
docs.text:
A practical result-review sequence is:

1. User and groups
2. sudo
3. SUID / SGID
4. Capabilities
5. Cron / systemd
6. Filesystem
7. Processes
8. Credentials
9. Containers
10. Mounts
11. Kernel / software
12. Security controls

This is easier than scrolling randomly through the entire output.

docs.title: Prioritising Findings
docs.text:
High-value candidates usually combine:

User Influence
      +
Privileged Consumer
      +
Reachable Trigger

For example:

Writable script
      +
Executed by root cron
      +
Runs every minute

This deserves closer review.

docs.title: Candidate Evaluation Table
docs.text:
For each candidate, ask:

Question Answer Can current user influence the object? Which privileged user/process consumes it? Is the path active? Can execution be triggered? Are additional conditions required? Do SELinux/AppArmor/no_new_privs affect it? What privilege would be obtained?

This prevents overreporting.

docs.title: Representative sudo Scenario
docs.text:
LinPEAS highlights:

User can run /usr/local/bin/backup with sudo

Validate:

sudo -l

Then inspect:

ls -l /usr/local/bin/backup

If readable and permitted:

file /usr/local/bin/backup

Determine:

  • arguments;
  • configuration;
  • files accessed;
  • external commands;
  • whether the program intentionally drops privileges.

Only then determine security impact.

docs.title: Representative SUID Scenario
docs.text:
LinPEAS highlights:

/opt/custom/helper

Validate:

ls -l /opt/custom/helper

Suppose:

-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ...

Next determine:

What does the binary do?

Does it retain elevated EUID?

Does it process user-controlled files?

Does it invoke external commands?

Does it validate arguments?

Do not report merely because it is SUID.

docs.title: Representative Capability Scenario
docs.text:
LinPEAS reports:

/usr/local/bin/example cap_dac_read_search=ep

Validate:

getcap /usr/local/bin/example

Then determine whether the executable exposes functionality that permits the current user to misuse that capability.

The security condition depends on the binary, not just the capability label.

docs.title: Representative Cron Scenario
docs.text:
LinPEAS identifies:

root cron:
* * * * * /opt/scripts/backup.sh

Check:

ls -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

Then:

namei -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

Suppose the script is:

root:root
-rwxr-xr-x

but the parent directory is writable by the current user.

That parent-directory permission may be the relevant condition.

docs.title: Representative systemd Scenario
docs.text:
LinPEAS identifies:

example.service

running as root.

Inspect:

systemctl cat example.service

Suppose:

ExecStart=/opt/example/start.sh

Then:

ls -l /opt/example/start.sh

and:

namei -l /opt/example/start.sh

Again, validate the whole execution chain.

docs.title: Representative Credential Scenario
docs.text:
LinPEAS finds:

DB_PASSWORD=examplevalue

in an application configuration file.

The next questions are:

Is this an actual secret?

Which service uses it?

Does the current user already have legitimate access?

Is validation necessary?

Does the credential provide additional privilege?

The finding may be:

Sensitive credential accessible to local low-privileged users

rather than:

Privilege escalation via LinPEAS

docs.title: Representative Docker Scenario
docs.text:
LinPEAS highlights Docker-related access.

Validate:

id

and:

ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

If the current user can control the host Docker daemon, document the trust implication.

Avoid making state-changing container modifications solely for proof unless required and authorised.

docs.title: Representative Kernel Scenario
docs.text:
LinPEAS suggests a possible kernel-related issue.

Do not immediately run a kernel exploit.

First establish:

uname -a

cat /etc/os-release

Then verify:

  • distribution advisory;
  • installed package version;
  • required kernel configuration;
  • applicability;
  • stability impact.

Kernel exploitation should be considered a high-risk validation step.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
LinPEAS can highlight conditions that are not exploitable.

Common examples include:

  • legitimate SUID programs;
  • harmless world-writable temporary directories;
  • inactive cron entries;
  • writable files not used by root;
  • capabilities with no useful interface;
  • stale credentials;
  • kernel-version heuristics;
  • expected container configuration.

Manual validation is mandatory.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
LinPEAS can miss real privilege escalation paths.

Possible reasons include:

  • custom applications;
  • unusual directories;
  • proprietary services;
  • transient files;
  • uncommon ACLs;
  • custom IPC;
  • dynamically created resources;
  • application-specific logic.

A clean LinPEAS run does not prove that no local privilege escalation path exists.

docs.title: Security Controls Can Change Exploitability
docs.text:
A candidate may appear strong but be constrained by:

  • SELinux;
  • AppArmor;
  • seccomp;
  • no_new_privs;
  • read-only mounts;
  • container namespaces.

Separate:

Underlying Weak Configuration

from:

Practical Exploitability

Both matter.

docs.title: Do Not Disable Security Controls
docs.text:
During ordinary privilege escalation testing, do not disable:

SELinux
AppArmor
seccomp
security agents

merely to make a candidate path easier to exploit.

Their presence is part of the environment being assessed.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each validated candidate, retain:

Current user:
Groups:
Relevant LinPEAS section:
Affected object:
Owner:
Group:
Permissions:
ACL:
Privileged consumer:
Trigger:
Security controls:
Manual validation:
Observed impact:

For example:

Current user:
tester

Candidate:
Writable root cron script

File:
 /opt/scripts/backup.sh

Owner:
root

Consumer:
root cron

Trigger:
Every minute

Validation:
Current user had write access through group permission.

docs.title: Evidence Should Show the Chain
docs.text:
Weak:

Screenshot of red LinPEAS output

Strong:

LinPEAS candidate
      |
      v
ls/stat/getfacl evidence
      |
      v
cron/systemd configuration
      |
      v
root execution context
      |
      v
trigger
      |
      v
impact

The reader should understand why the condition matters.

docs.title: Reporting a Cron Weakness
docs.text:
Avoid:

LinPEAS found an insecure cron job.

Prefer:

A scheduled task executed by root referenced a script located in a
directory that was modifiable by the tested standard user. This allowed
the low-privileged user to influence content consumed by a privileged
scheduled process.

The finding describes the security weakness.

docs.title: Reporting a sudo Weakness
docs.text:
Avoid:

LinPEAS found sudo privilege escalation.

Prefer:

The tested user was permitted to execute the specified application as
root through sudo. The application exposed functionality that allowed
the user to perform operations outside the intended administrative
task, resulting in an effective privilege boundary bypass.

docs.title: Reporting a Negative Result
docs.text:
Example:

LinPEAS highlighted a root-owned scheduled script as potentially
interesting. Manual validation showed that neither the script nor its
parent directories were writable by the tested user. The suspected
privilege escalation path was therefore not confirmed.

Negative validation is useful evidence.

docs.title: Remediation Principles
docs.text:
The general principle is:

Low-privileged users should not be able to modify resources that are trusted or executed by higher-privileged processes.

Common remediation areas include:

  • sudo;
  • file permissions;
  • cron;
  • systemd;
  • SUID/SGID;
  • capabilities;
  • credentials;
  • container-management permissions.

docs.title: sudo Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • minimise allowed commands;
  • avoid unnecessary wildcards;
  • restrict arguments;
  • avoid unnecessarily broad NOPASSWD;
  • use least privilege;
  • remove shell-capable or overly flexible binaries where inappropriate.

docs.title: SUID / SGID Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove unnecessary SUID/SGID bits;
  • replace privileged helper logic with safer designs;
  • validate user-controlled input;
  • use least privilege.

docs.title: Capability Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove unnecessary file capabilities;
  • assign the minimum required capability;
  • restrict execution permissions.

docs.title: Cron Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • protect scripts;
  • protect parent directories;
  • use absolute paths;
  • set safe ownership;
  • avoid executing user-controlled content;
  • minimise privileged scheduled jobs.

docs.title: systemd Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • protect unit files;
  • protect referenced scripts/binaries;
  • use dedicated low-privileged service accounts;
  • protect environment files;
  • avoid writable working directories where they influence execution.

docs.title: Credential Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove plaintext secrets;
  • rotate exposed credentials;
  • use appropriate secret storage;
  • tighten filesystem permissions;
  • remove obsolete backup/configuration files.

docs.title: Container Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • restrict Docker/LXD group membership;
  • protect management sockets;
  • avoid unnecessary privileged containers;
  • minimise host filesystem mounts;
  • apply least privilege.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Do not retest only by rerunning LinPEAS.

For a corrected file permission:

ls -l /path/to/file

and:

getfacl /path/to/file

For a corrected cron path:

namei -l /path/to/script

For corrected sudo configuration:

sudo -l

Confirm that the underlying weakness has been removed.

Then optionally rerun LinPEAS as a secondary regression check.

docs.title: Tool Transfer Considerations
docs.text:
If LinPEAS must be transferred to the target, document:

Source
Destination
Hash where relevant
Execution time
Output location
Cleanup status

Use approved temporary locations.

Do not leave unnecessary tooling behind.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Where required, remove:

linpeas.sh
linpeas-output.txt
temporary test files

Do not remove legitimate system logs.

Assessment evidence should be retained according to policy.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Running LinPEAS can generate activity such as:

  • filesystem enumeration;
  • process inspection;
  • permission checks;
  • package queries;
  • configuration reads;
  • system calls.

In a purple-team exercise, this may be intentionally useful for validating defensive visibility.

Related notes:

Purple Teaming

Detection Engineering

docs.title: LinPEAS in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
A controlled exercise might use:

LinPEAS
   |
   v
Host Enumeration
   |
   v
Linux Audit / EDR Telemetry
   |
   v
Detection Review
   |
   v
Detection Improvement

The expected activity should be coordinated in advance.

docs.title: LinPEAS Review Workflow
docs.text:
A strong review process is:

1. Confirm scope
      |
      v
2. Record current identity
      |
      v
3. Record host context
      |
      v
4. Perform basic manual checks
      |
      v
5. Obtain official LinPEAS
      |
      v
6. Run approved enumeration
      |
      v
7. Save output securely
      |
      v
8. Review by category
      |
      v
9. Prioritise real execution paths
      |
      v
10. Validate with native commands
      |
      v
11. Consider security controls
      |
      v
12. Confirm or reject candidates
      |
      v
13. Capture evidence
      |
      v
14. Clean up assessment artefacts

docs.title: Current User
docs.text: whoami

docs.title: Identity and Groups
docs.text: id

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: groups

docs.title: OS Information
docs.text: cat /etc/os-release

docs.title: Kernel
docs.text: uname -a

docs.title: Run LinPEAS
docs.text: ./linpeas.sh

docs.title: Run Through Bash
docs.text: bash linpeas.sh

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text: ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas-output.txt

docs.title: sudo
docs.text: sudo -l

docs.title: SUID
docs.text: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

docs.title: SGID
docs.text: find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

docs.title: File Permissions
docs.text: ls -l /path/to/file

docs.title: Full Path Permissions
docs.text: namei -l /path/to/file

docs.title: ACL
docs.text: getfacl /path/to/file

docs.title: File Metadata
docs.text: stat /path/to/file

docs.title: Processes
docs.text: ps aux

docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use LinPEAS like this:

Run LinPEAS
    |
    v
Look for Red Text
    |
    v
Assume Root

Use it like this:

Understand Current Identity
        |
        v
Run LinPEAS
        |
        v
Identify Candidate
        |
        v
Understand Why It Was Flagged
        |
        v
Validate With Native Tools
        |
        +-- sudo
        +-- ls
        +-- namei
        +-- getfacl
        +-- getcap
        +-- systemctl
        +-- findmnt
        |
        v
Confirm User Influence
        |
        v
Identify Privileged Consumer
        |
        v
Confirm Trigger
        |
        v
Consider Security Controls
        |
        v
Determine Actual Impact
        |
        v
Capture Evidence
        |
        v
Report the Underlying Weakness

LinPEAS is valuable because it quickly surveys a large number of Linux privilege escalation areas.

It identifies where to investigate.

The tester determines whether those observations form a real path to additional privilege.

docs.title: linux-smart-enumeration
docs.text:
linux-smart-enumeration, commonly abbreviated as LSE, is a Linux enumeration script designed to identify local system conditions that may be relevant to privilege escalation.

It provides a focused way to review areas such as:

  • users and groups;
  • sudo configuration;
  • SUID and SGID binaries;
  • Linux capabilities;
  • cron and scheduled execution;
  • services and processes;
  • filesystem permissions;
  • writable files and directories;
  • environment configuration;
  • credentials;
  • mounts;
  • networking;
  • containers;
  • security-relevant local configuration.

LSE is best treated as a triage and enumeration tool.

It helps answer:

Which parts of this Linux host deserve closer privilege escalation analysis?

It does not automatically prove exploitability.

Linux Host
   |
   v
LSE
   |
   +-- Identity
   +-- sudo
   +-- SUID / SGID
   +-- Capabilities
   +-- Cron
   +-- Services
   +-- Filesystem
   +-- Credentials
   +-- Mounts
   +-- Environment
   |
   v
Candidate Conditions
   |
   v
Manual Validation
   |
   v
Privilege Escalation Conclusion

Authorised testing only

Use linux-smart-enumeration only on systems where local security testing is explicitly authorised. Enumeration scripts may access sensitive configuration and generate security telemetry. Review the rules of engagement before transferring or executing third-party tooling.

docs.title: Where LSE Fits
docs.text:
LSE normally follows initial local access and a basic manual review of the current Linux context.

Initial Access
      |
      v
Current User
      |
      v
Manual Baseline
      |
      v
LSE
      |
      v
Candidate Conditions
      |
      v
Native Linux Validation
      |
      v
Confirm or Reject
