docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
linux-smart-enumeration is maintained in the following repository:

linux-smart-enumeration - GitHub

Use the official project or a trusted internal mirror.

Avoid random modified copies from unknown repositories.

docs.title: What LSE Does
docs.text:
LSE performs a series of checks intended to highlight potentially interesting local conditions.

Conceptually:

System State
    |
    +-- Users
    +-- Groups
    +-- sudo
    +-- Files
    +-- Permissions
    +-- SUID
    +-- Capabilities
    +-- Cron
    +-- Services
    +-- Environment
    +-- Credentials
    |
    v
LSE Checks
    |
    v
Prioritised Output

The output is intended to reduce the amount of manual searching required.

docs.title: LSE vs LinPEAS
docs.text:
LSE and LinPEAS overlap but have different styles.

LinPEAS
   |
   +-- very broad enumeration
   +-- large output
   +-- extensive heuristics

LSE
   |
   +-- focused enumeration
   +-- structured levels
   +-- easier targeted review

A useful workflow is:

LSE
   |
   v
Focused Candidate Set
   |
   v
LinPEAS
   |
   v
Additional Coverage
   |
   v
Manual Validation

or the reverse:

LinPEAS
   |
   v
Broad Candidate Set
   |
   v
LSE
   |
   v
Focused Cross-Check

Related note:

LinPEAS

docs.title: Before Running LSE
docs.text:
Always record the current user context first.

Run:

whoami

Then:

id

And:

groups

Useful questions include:

Which user am I?

Which groups do I belong to?

Do I have sudo rights?

Am I inside a container?

Do I belong to a privileged management group?

This baseline is essential when interpreting tool output.

docs.title: Record Host Context
docs.text:
Useful commands include:

hostname

uname -a

cat /etc/os-release

This records:

  • hostname;
  • kernel;
  • operating system;
  • distribution;
  • architecture context.

docs.title: Obtaining LSE
docs.text:
Prefer the official repository.

If downloaded to a controlled workstation, preserve:

Source
Revision
Hash where relevant
Transfer path
Execution time

Tool provenance improves reproducibility.

docs.title: Common Script Name
docs.text:
The project is commonly used through:

lse.sh

The exact script behaviour can change between revisions.

Always review the version being used.

docs.title: Basic Execution
docs.text:
If the script is executable:

./lse.sh

Alternatively:

bash lse.sh

If required:

chmod +x lse.sh

Then:

./lse.sh

Use the least intrusive execution approach permitted by the environment.

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
Inspect the script help:

./lse.sh -h

or:

bash lse.sh -h

Use the tool's built-in help for the exact options supported by the current version.

docs.title: Level-Based Enumeration
docs.text:
One of LSE's useful concepts is adjusting how much detail is displayed.

Depending on the version, LSE supports levels intended to control the amount or depth of output.

Conceptually:

Lower Level
   |
   +-- more important findings
   +-- less noise

Higher Level
   |
   +-- more detail
   +-- broader context

Always verify exact supported values with:

./lse.sh -h

This makes LSE particularly useful when a quick triage pass is preferred before deeper enumeration.

docs.title: Start Focused
docs.text:
A good workflow is:

Start with focused output
        |
        v
Review high-value candidates
        |
        v
Increase detail if needed

rather than immediately generating the maximum possible output.

This reduces analysis noise.

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text:
For later review:

./lse.sh | tee lse-output.txt

If using options:

./lse.sh <options> | tee lse-output.txt

The output may contain sensitive system information.

Protect it appropriately.

docs.title: Sensitive Output
docs.text:
LSE may expose:

  • usernames;
  • group memberships;
  • credentials;
  • configuration;
  • file paths;
  • network information;
  • sensitive local files.

Do not:

  • commit raw output to Git;
  • upload it to public services;
  • attach full output to reports;
  • share it beyond the authorised team.

Extract relevant evidence only.

docs.title: Identity Checks
docs.text:
LSE can help highlight current user context.

Validate manually:

id

Representative output:

uid=1001(tester) gid=1001(tester) groups=1001(tester),27(sudo)

This result may immediately show important group membership.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Group membership can significantly affect local privilege.

Potentially sensitive group categories may include:

sudo
docker
lxd
disk
backup
adm

Exact impact depends on the operating system and environment.

Do not report group membership alone.

Determine what the group can actually control.

docs.title: sudo
docs.text:
sudo is one of the highest-value Linux privilege escalation areas.

Always validate:

sudo -l

Questions include:

Which commands are allowed?

As which user?

Is a password required?

Are arguments restricted?

Are wildcards used?

Are environment variables preserved?

Related note:

Linux sudo

docs.title: sudo Candidate Model
docs.text:
sudo Rule
   |
   v
Allowed Binary
   |
   v
Allowed Arguments
   |
   v
Binary Behaviour
   |
   v
Can Privilege Boundary Be Crossed?

The sudo entry itself is not always vulnerable.

docs.title: NOPASSWD
docs.text:
LSE may highlight sudo commands that use:

NOPASSWD

This means the user can execute the permitted sudo command without entering a password.

The impact still depends on what that command permits.

docs.title: sudo Wildcards
docs.text:
Wildcard rules deserve careful analysis.

Example concept:

/usr/local/bin/backup *

Investigate:

  • argument parsing;
  • file path control;
  • option injection;
  • command behaviour.

A wildcard is only part of the potential chain.

docs.title: GTFOBins
docs.text:
GTFOBins can help research security-sensitive functionality in Linux binaries.

Examples include:

  • sudo behaviour;
  • SUID behaviour;
  • command execution;
  • file read;
  • file write.

Reference:

GTFOBins

Use it as a research aid.

Do not treat a GTFOBins entry as proof that the local configuration is exploitable.

docs.title: SUID
docs.text:
LSE may highlight SUID binaries.

Enumerate manually:

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Typical legitimate examples may include:

/usr/bin/passwd
/usr/bin/su
/usr/bin/sudo

The presence of SUID alone is not a vulnerability.

Related note:

Linux SUID and SGID

docs.title: Validate SUID
docs.text:
Inspect the binary:

ls -l /path/to/binary

Example:

-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 123456 Jan 1 12:00 /path/to/binary

Then determine:

Who owns it?

What does it do?

Does it retain effective UID?

Does it invoke external commands?

Does it process user-controlled input?

docs.title: Custom SUID Binaries
docs.text:
Custom SUID programs often deserve higher priority than standard distribution binaries.

Examples:

/opt/vendor/helper
/usr/local/bin/custom-tool

Review:

  • ownership;
  • permissions;
  • file type;
  • strings or source where authorised;
  • arguments;
  • privileged operations.

docs.title: SGID
docs.text:
Enumerate SGID binaries:

find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null

SGID changes effective group context.

The security impact depends on what access that group provides.

docs.title: Linux Capabilities
docs.text:
LSE may highlight binaries with file capabilities.

Validate:

getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

For one binary:

getcap /path/to/binary

Related note:

Linux Capabilities

docs.title: Capability Analysis
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Binary
   |
   v
Capability
   |
   v
Available Functionality
   |
   v
User-Controlled Input
   |
   v
Potential Impact

A capability name alone does not prove escalation.

docs.title: Scheduled Jobs
docs.text:
LSE can help identify scheduled execution.

Potential mechanisms include:

cron
anacron
systemd timers
custom application schedulers

Related note:

Linux Scheduled Jobs

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Inspect:

cat /etc/crontab

and where authorised:

ls -la /etc/cron.d/

Also:

crontab -l

The key questions are:

Who executes it?

What executes?

Can the current user influence it?

How often does it run?

docs.title: Root Cron Jobs
docs.text:
A root cron job is not automatically vulnerable.

Example:

* * * * * root /opt/scripts/backup.sh

Validate:

ls -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

Then:

namei -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

Review the entire path.

docs.title: Parent Directory Analysis
docs.text:
namei -l is especially useful.

Example:

namei -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

This can reveal:

/
opt
scripts
backup.sh

with permissions at each level.

A protected file may still be replaceable if the parent directory grants sufficient rights.

docs.title: systemd Services
docs.text:
LSE may highlight service-related configuration.

List services:

systemctl list-units --type=service

Inspect a specific service:

systemctl cat example.service

Review:

User=
Group=
ExecStart=
Environment=
WorkingDirectory=

The key security question is:

Can the current user influence something that a privileged service consumes?

docs.title: systemd Timers
docs.text:
List:

systemctl list-timers --all

Inspect the corresponding timer and service units.

A timer alone is not a vulnerability.

Focus on the privileged execution chain.

docs.title: Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
LSE can highlight potentially interesting local permissions.

Relevant categories include:

  • writable files;
  • writable directories;
  • executable scripts;
  • service resources;
  • cron resources;
  • configuration.

Related note:

Linux Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Basic File Review
docs.text:
Use:

ls -l /path/to/file

and:

stat /path/to/file

This reveals:

  • owner;
  • group;
  • permissions;
  • timestamps;
  • metadata.

docs.title: ACLs
docs.text:
POSIX ACLs can grant permissions beyond traditional mode bits.

Inspect:

getfacl /path/to/file

Effective permission analysis should consider ACLs when present.

docs.title: Writable Files
docs.text:
A writable file is only significant if a privileged process trusts or executes it.

Writable File
    |
    v
Privileged Consumer?
    |
    +-- No -> may be irrelevant
    |
    +-- Yes -> investigate

docs.title: Writable Directories
docs.text:
Common writable directories include:

/tmp
/var/tmp
/dev/shm

These are intentionally writable on many Linux systems.

Their presence is not a vulnerability.

The relevant question is whether a privileged component trusts user-controlled content stored there.

docs.title: Temporary Directory Risks
docs.text:
Potential issues can arise when privileged processes use predictable or insecure temporary files.

Relevant questions include:

Does privileged software create predictable files?

Does it follow symlinks?

Are permissions checked?

Can another user replace the file?

Do not perform destructive race-condition testing without explicit approval.

docs.title: PATH
docs.text:
Inspect:

echo "$PATH"

A clearer view:

printf '%s\n' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'

LSE may highlight writable PATH locations.

This is only relevant when a privileged process resolves a command through that PATH.

docs.title: PATH Hijacking Model
docs.text:
Privileged Script
      |
      v
Calls:
backup
      |
      v
PATH Search
      |
      v
Writable Directory
      |
      v
User-Controlled Executable

The entire chain must be demonstrated.

docs.title: Absolute Paths
docs.text:
Privileged scripts should generally use explicit executable paths where practical.

Compare:

tar

with:

/usr/bin/tar

The latter does not depend on PATH lookup.

This can reduce PATH-based ambiguity.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Inspect:

env

or:

printenv

Potentially relevant variables include:

  • PATH;
  • application configuration;
  • credentials;
  • runtime options.

Security relevance depends on whether privileged processes inherit or trust them.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
LSE may identify potential secrets in:

  • configuration files;
  • shell history;
  • environment variables;
  • scripts;
  • backup files;
  • application directories.

Related note:

Linux Credentials

docs.title: Shell History
docs.text:
Common locations include:

~/.bash_history
~/.zsh_history

History can contain:

  • administrative commands;
  • credentials supplied inline;
  • internal paths;
  • connection information.

Treat it as sensitive evidence.

docs.title: SSH Material
docs.text:
Potentially sensitive files include:

~/.ssh/id_rsa
~/.ssh/id_ed25519
~/.ssh/config
~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Do not assume a private key is reusable.

Consider:

  • passphrase;
  • owner;
  • destination;
  • scope.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Potential secrets may appear in:

.env
config files
application YAML/JSON
database configuration
service files

The finding may be insecure local access to secrets rather than privilege escalation itself.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
Inspect:

ps aux

or:

ps -ef

Look for:

  • root-owned custom processes;
  • command-line secrets;
  • scripts;
  • application paths;
  • interpreters;
  • unusual service commands.

docs.title: Process Command Lines
docs.text:
A root process may expose an interesting path.

Example:

root /usr/bin/python3 /opt/app/service.py

Next inspect:

ls -l /opt/app/service.py

and its parent directories.

The process identifies the privileged consumer.

docs.title: Listening Services
docs.text:
Inspect:

ss -lntup

where permitted.

Interesting services may include:

  • local administration interfaces;
  • databases;
  • management daemons;
  • custom local APIs.

A listening service is not automatically a privilege escalation route.

docs.title: Unix Domain Sockets
docs.text:
Privileged local services may expose Unix sockets.

Relevant questions include:

Who owns the socket?

Which group can access it?

What functionality does the service expose?

A writable or accessible management socket can be more important than a network port.

docs.title: Mounts
docs.text:
Inspect:

findmnt

or:

mount

Mounts can reveal:

  • NFS;
  • CIFS;
  • bind mounts;
  • removable media;
  • containers;
  • unusual filesystem options.

docs.title: Mount Options
docs.text:
Relevant options may affect:

  • execution;
  • device access;
  • SUID behaviour;
  • write capability.

Examples include:

ro
rw
nosuid
noexec
nodev

Do not judge file permissions without considering mount options.

docs.title: /etc/fstab
docs.text:
Where authorised:

cat /etc/fstab

This can reveal:

  • persistent mounts;
  • network shares;
  • mount options;
  • credential references.

Treat credential material carefully.

docs.title: NFS
docs.text:
NFS mounts may create privilege-related conditions depending on server export configuration and local mount behaviour.

Do not infer server-side configuration from the client mount alone.

Assess the actual trust relationship.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
LSE may identify container-related context.

Potential technologies include:

  • Docker;
  • LXC;
  • LXD;
  • containerd;
  • Kubernetes.

Root inside a container is not automatically root on the host.

docs.title: Docker Group
docs.text:
Check:

id

If the current user belongs to:

docker

determine whether the Docker daemon is accessible.

Check socket permissions:

ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

Do not modify containers merely to prove access unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Docker Socket
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Current User
     |
     v
Docker Socket
     |
     v
Docker Daemon
     |
     v
Host Resources

Access to the Docker daemon can represent a major trust boundary.

The finding should describe that control relationship.

docs.title: LXD / LXC
docs.text:
Membership in container-management groups may grant powerful host-level capabilities.

Validate actual access before reporting.

Do not assume group membership alone is sufficient.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Container environments may expose:

  • service-account tokens;
  • mounted secrets;
  • namespace information;
  • API endpoints.

Ensure cloud/Kubernetes resources are within assessment scope before further interaction.

docs.title: Kernel Information
docs.text:
LSE may provide kernel-related clues.

Validate:

uname -r

and:

cat /etc/os-release

Do not map a kernel version directly to exploitability.

Linux distributions often backport security patches.

docs.title: Kernel Research Workflow
docs.text:
Kernel Version
    |
    v
Distribution
    |
    v
Package Version
    |
    v
Vendor Advisory
    |
    v
Configuration
    |
    v
Applicability

Kernel exploitation can destabilise systems and should only be performed when specifically authorised.

docs.title: Installed Software
docs.text:
LSE may help identify installed software or unusual applications.

Custom privileged applications are often worth prioritising.

Review:

  • binary path;
  • owner;
  • configuration;
  • service identity;
  • writable resources.

docs.title: Old Version Does Not Equal Vulnerable
docs.text:
Avoid:

Package version looks old
       |
       v
Report CVE

Use:

Installed package
       |
       v
Distribution package revision
       |
       v
Vendor security advisory
       |
       v
Applicability

docs.title: Security Controls
docs.text:
Linux security controls can significantly affect exploitability.

Potential controls include:

  • SELinux;
  • AppArmor;
  • seccomp;
  • no_new_privs;
  • mount restrictions.

Related note:

Linux Security Controls

docs.title: SELinux
docs.text:
Check where installed:

getenforce

Possible results include:

Enforcing
Permissive
Disabled

SELinux can restrict privileged process behaviour.

Its presence should be included in the analysis.

docs.title: AppArmor
docs.text:
Where available:

aa-status

Some systems may require elevated access for complete output.

Do not assume AppArmor blocks every candidate.

Review the actual profile applied to the privileged process.

docs.title: no_new_privs
docs.text:
no_new_privs can prevent certain privilege transitions.

Its presence may affect:

  • SUID;
  • capabilities;
  • sandboxed applications.

Consider this when a privilege transition does not behave as expected.

docs.title: seccomp
docs.text:
seccomp may restrict available system calls.

This is common in containers and sandboxed services.

It can change practical exploitability without fixing the underlying permission weakness.

docs.title: Read-Only Mounts
docs.text:
A path may appear writable according to mode bits but reside on a read-only mount.

Check:

findmnt

Actual write capability is what matters.

docs.title: LSE Output Levels
docs.text:
LSE's focused output can be useful when triaging a host under time pressure.

A practical approach is:

Low-noise pass
      |
      v
Review strongest candidates
      |
      v
Increase detail
      |
      v
Manual validation

Check exact supported options:

./lse.sh -h

docs.title: Review by Category
docs.text:
A useful review order is:

1. Identity and groups
2. sudo
3. SUID / SGID
4. Capabilities
5. Cron / systemd
6. Filesystem
7. Processes
8. Credentials
9. Containers
10. Mounts
11. Kernel / software
12. Security controls

This keeps the analysis structured.

docs.title: Searching Saved Output
docs.text:
If results are stored in:

lse-output.txt

search:

grep -i "sudo" lse-output.txt

grep -i "suid" lse-output.txt

grep -i "writ" lse-output.txt

grep -i "capab" lse-output.txt

Do not remove the surrounding context from interesting matches.

docs.title: Candidate Evaluation Model
docs.text:
For each LSE result, answer:

Question Answer What did LSE identify? Can the current user influence it? Which permission proves this? Which privileged process consumes it? Which user executes that process? Can the process be triggered? Which security controls apply? What privilege would result?

This turns tool output into security analysis.

docs.title: User Influence
docs.text:
The first major question is:

Can the current user actually control the candidate resource?

Possible control can include:

  • write;
  • modify;
  • replace;
  • delete;
  • execute with elevated context;
  • interact through socket or daemon;
  • change configuration.

Without user influence, the candidate usually does not represent privilege escalation.

docs.title: Privileged Consumer
docs.text:
The next question is:

Which higher-privileged component trusts or executes the resource?

Examples include:

root cron
root systemd service
sudo
SUID binary
container daemon

A writable file without a privileged consumer may be irrelevant.

docs.title: Trigger
docs.text:
Determine how the privileged action occurs.

Possible triggers include:

scheduled execution
service restart
system reboot
administrator action
user login
manual sudo execution

This affects practical risk.

docs.title: Security Control Context
docs.text:
Ask:

Does SELinux restrict the process?

Does AppArmor restrict it?

Does no_new_privs apply?

Is filesystem mounted noexec/nosuid/read-only?

These controls may affect practical exploitation.

docs.title: Representative sudo Scenario
docs.text:
LSE highlights:

sudo permission:
(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/backup

Validate:

sudo -l

Then inspect:

ls -l /usr/local/bin/backup

Determine:

What does the command do?

Can arguments be controlled?

Does it invoke another program?

Does it access user-controlled files?

Does it provide functionality beyond the intended task?

Only then determine whether privilege escalation exists.

docs.title: Representative SUID Scenario
docs.text:
LSE highlights:

/usr/local/bin/helper

Validate:

ls -l /usr/local/bin/helper

Suppose:

-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ...

Next determine:

What operations does the helper expose?

Does it retain EUID 0?

Does it trust environment variables?

Does it invoke commands without full paths?

Do not report based on SUID alone.

docs.title: Representative Cron Scenario
docs.text:
LSE identifies:

root cron:
* * * * * /opt/backup/backup.sh

Check:

ls -l /opt/backup/backup.sh

Then:

namei -l /opt/backup/backup.sh

If a parent directory is writable by the tested user, that may create a security-relevant execution path.

docs.title: Representative Capability Scenario
docs.text:
LSE reports:

/usr/local/bin/example cap_dac_override=ep

Validate:

getcap /usr/local/bin/example

Then determine whether the executable's functionality allows the current user to misuse that capability.

Do not treat the capability string as a complete finding.

docs.title: Representative Docker Scenario
docs.text:
LSE highlights Docker access.

Validate:

id

and:

ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

If the current user has access to the host Docker daemon, the risk may be significant.

Document the control relationship rather than merely saying:

User is in docker group.

docs.title: Representative Credential Scenario
docs.text:
LSE identifies:

password=example

inside an application configuration file.

Validate:

Who owns the file?

Why can current user read it?

Is the credential active?

Does it provide additional privilege?

Is authentication testing needed?

The underlying weakness may be insecure local secret storage.

docs.title: Representative Negative Scenario
docs.text:
LSE highlights a root-owned script as potentially interesting.

Manual validation:

ls -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

and:

namei -l /opt/scripts/backup.sh

show that neither the file nor any relevant parent directory is writable.

Conclusion:

The candidate was reviewed, but the tested user could not influence the
resource or its execution path. The suspected privilege escalation
condition was not confirmed.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
LSE can highlight benign or non-exploitable conditions.

Common examples include:

  • legitimate SUID binaries;
  • intentionally writable temporary directories;
  • harmless group membership;
  • inactive cron jobs;
  • writable files with no privileged consumer;
  • capabilities that expose no useful operation;
  • stale credentials;
  • inaccessible container-management services.

Manual validation is required.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
LSE can also miss real privilege escalation paths.

Possible reasons include:

  • proprietary applications;
  • custom scripts;
  • unusual service directories;
  • transient resources;
  • custom IPC;
  • uncommon ACLs;
  • application-specific logic.

A clean LSE result does not prove the host is secure.

docs.title: LSE Does Not Replace Manual Enumeration
docs.text:
Do not stop at:

LSE completed

Continue reviewing:

Identity
sudo
SUID
Capabilities
Cron
systemd
Filesystem
Processes
Credentials
Containers
Mounts
Security Controls

Manual knowledge remains essential.

docs.title: LSE and LinPEAS Correlation
docs.text:
Example:

LSE:
Writable cron script

LinPEAS:
Same cron script highlighted

Manual:
Permissions confirm write access

Cron:
Runs as root

This provides strong supporting evidence.

The actual finding remains the insecure privileged scheduled execution path.

docs.title: LSE and Native Tools
docs.text:
A strong model is:

LSE
  |
  v
Candidate
  |
  v
Native Validation
  |
  +-- sudo
  +-- ls
  +-- stat
  +-- namei
  +-- getfacl
  +-- getcap
  +-- systemctl
  +-- findmnt
  |
  v
Conclusion

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a validated candidate, retain:

Current user:
Groups:
LSE result:
Affected path/object:
Owner:
Group:
Permissions:
ACL:
Privileged consumer:
Execution user:
Trigger:
Security controls:
Observed impact:

Example:

Current user:
tester

Candidate:
Writable cron script

Path:
/opt/scripts/backup.sh

Consumer:
root cron

Trigger:
Every minute

Validation:
Current user had group write permission over the script.

docs.title: Evidence Should Explain the Chain
docs.text:
Weak:

Screenshot of LSE warning

Strong:

LSE candidate
      |
      v
ls/stat/getfacl
      |
      v
cron/systemd configuration
      |
      v
root execution identity
      |
      v
trigger
      |
      v
impact

The evidence should independently support the conclusion.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

LSE found a privilege escalation vulnerability.

Prefer:

A script executed by a root-owned scheduled task was writable by the
tested standard user. Native filesystem permission checks confirmed
that the low-privileged user could influence content subsequently
executed in the root context.

The finding describes the actual security condition.

docs.title: Reporting an Unconfirmed Candidate
docs.text:
Example:

linux-smart-enumeration highlighted a custom SUID binary. Manual review
confirmed the SUID bit was present, but testing did not identify any
user-controlled functionality that could be used to cross the intended
privilege boundary. A privilege escalation condition was therefore not
confirmed.

docs.title: Remediation Principles
docs.text:
The central remediation principle is:

Low-privileged users should not be able to influence resources or interfaces trusted by higher-privileged processes.

Typical areas include:

  • sudo;
  • SUID/SGID;
  • capabilities;
  • cron;
  • systemd;
  • filesystem permissions;
  • credentials;
  • container management.

docs.title: sudo Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • minimise allowed commands;
  • restrict arguments;
  • avoid unnecessary wildcards;
  • avoid broad NOPASSWD;
  • use least privilege.

docs.title: SUID / SGID Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove unnecessary SUID/SGID bits;
  • restrict execution;
  • redesign privileged helpers;
  • validate untrusted input;
  • drop privileges as early as possible.

docs.title: Capability Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove unnecessary capabilities;
  • assign minimum capabilities;
  • restrict binary execution;
  • review custom privileged binaries.

docs.title: Cron Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • protect scripts;
  • protect parent directories;
  • use absolute executable paths;
  • restrict ownership;
  • avoid root execution where unnecessary.

docs.title: systemd Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • secure unit files;
  • secure referenced scripts;
  • use dedicated service identities;
  • protect environment files;
  • minimise privilege.

docs.title: Filesystem Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove unnecessary group/world write;
  • correct owner/group;
  • review ACLs;
  • protect parent directories;
  • avoid privileged trust in shared writable locations.

docs.title: Credential Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove plaintext credentials;
  • rotate exposed secrets;
  • restrict local read access;
  • use secret-management mechanisms;
  • remove stale backups.

docs.title: Container Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • restrict Docker/LXD group membership;
  • protect daemon sockets;
  • remove unnecessary privileged container access;
  • minimise host mounts;
  • follow least privilege.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Do not retest only by rerunning LSE.

For a corrected file:

ls -l /path/to/file

getfacl /path/to/file

For a corrected cron path:

namei -l /path/to/script

For sudo:

sudo -l

For capabilities:

getcap /path/to/binary

Then optionally rerun LSE as a secondary regression check.

docs.title: LSE in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
LSE can be useful during purple-team exercises where local enumeration visibility is being evaluated.

LSE
 |
 v
Local Enumeration
 |
 v
Audit / EDR Telemetry
 |
 v
Detection Review

Related notes:

Purple Teaming

Detection Engineering

The activity should be coordinated before execution.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
LSE may generate observable activity through:

  • filesystem enumeration;
  • process enumeration;
  • privilege checks;
  • configuration reads;
  • package queries.

This may be useful defensive telemetry during controlled exercises.

Do not attempt to suppress security logging unless that is specifically part of the authorised test objective.

docs.title: Tool Transfer
docs.text:
Where the script must be transferred, document:

Tool:
lse.sh

Source:
Official repository

Destination:
Approved temporary directory

Execution:
Authorised

Output:
Stored securely

Cleanup:
Completed

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Where required, remove:

lse.sh
lse-output.txt
temporary assessment files

Do not remove legitimate operating-system or security logs.

docs.title: Practical LSE Workflow
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

1. Confirm scope
      |
      v
2. Record current identity
      |
      v
3. Record groups
      |
      v
4. Record OS/kernel context
      |
      v
5. Perform manual baseline
      |
      v
6. Obtain official LSE
      |
      v
7. Review help/options
      |
      v
8. Run focused enumeration
      |
      v
9. Increase detail if needed
      |
      v
10. Save output securely
      |
      v
11. Review high-value categories
      |
      v
12. Validate with native Linux tools
      |
      v
13. Confirm user influence
      |
      v
14. Identify privileged consumer
      |
      v
15. Confirm trigger
      |
      v
16. Consider security controls
      |
      v
17. Confirm or reject candidate
      |
      v
18. Capture evidence
      |
      v
19. Clean up assessment artefacts

It helps identify where to look.

docs.title: PowerUp
docs.text:
PowerUp is a PowerShell-based collection of Windows privilege escalation checks from the PowerSploit project.

It is designed to identify local Windows configuration conditions that may deserve further investigation during an authorised security assessment.

Typical areas include:

  • Windows services;
  • service executable permissions;
  • service configuration permissions;
  • unquoted service paths;
  • registry configuration;
  • installer-related policy;
  • writable application locations;
  • potentially exposed credentials;
  • autologon configuration;
  • DLL-related conditions;
  • other local privilege escalation candidates.

PowerUp should be treated as an enumeration and triage tool.

It does not automatically prove that a highlighted configuration can be used to gain additional privilege.

Windows Host
    |
    v
PowerUp
    |
    +-- Services
    +-- Permissions
    +-- Registry
    +-- Installer Policy
    +-- Credentials
    +-- Execution Paths
    |
    v
Candidate Conditions
    |
    v
Manual Validation
    |
    v
Privilege Escalation Conclusion

Authorised testing only

Use PowerUp only on Windows systems where local security testing is explicitly authorised. PowerShell-based security tooling can generate endpoint-security telemetry and may be blocked by application control or endpoint protection. Review the rules of engagement before loading or executing third-party scripts.

docs.title: Where PowerUp Fits
docs.text:
PowerUp normally sits between initial local enumeration and focused manual validation.

Initial Access
    |
    v
Current User Context
    |
    v
Manual Baseline
    |
    v
PowerUp
    |
    v
Candidate Condition
    |
    v
Native Windows Validation
    |
    v
Confirm or Reject

Related notes:

Privilege Escalation Tools

Windows Privilege Escalation

Windows Enumeration

Windows Privilege Escalation Explorer

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
PowerUp is part of PowerSploit.

Project reference:

PowerUp - PowerSploit

The PowerSploit repository should be treated as the canonical historical source for the original PowerUp implementation.

Because PowerSploit is an older project, always review:

  • repository state;
  • script provenance;
  • last update;
  • PowerShell compatibility;
  • endpoint-security impact;
  • environment restrictions;

before relying on a copy during an assessment.

docs.title: What PowerUp Does
docs.text:
PowerUp automates checks for local Windows configurations that may allow a lower-privileged user to influence privileged execution.

A useful model is:

System Configuration
        |
        +-- Services
        +-- Registry
        +-- Files
        +-- Directories
        +-- Installer Policy
        +-- Credentials
        |
        v
PowerUp Checks
        |
        v
Potential PrivEsc Candidates

The tool tries to answer:

Where should I investigate further?

It does not answer:

Which findings are definitely exploitable?

docs.title: Before Running PowerUp
docs.text:
Start with the current security context.

Run:

whoami

Then:

whoami /groups

And:

whoami /priv

Useful questions include:

Who am I?

Am I already a local administrator?

Which groups do I belong to?

Which token privileges are available?

Is the shell elevated?

This context is essential when interpreting PowerUp output.

docs.title: PowerShell Environment
docs.text:
PowerUp depends on PowerShell.

Check the PowerShell version:

$PSVersionTable

Check the current language mode:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible language modes include:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

PowerUp may not function fully in restricted environments.

docs.title: Execution Policy
docs.text:
Execution policy can affect script loading.

Check:

Get-ExecutionPolicy -List

Execution policy is not intended to be a hard security boundary.

However, it may affect how PowerUp can be loaded in a particular environment.

Do not change enterprise execution policy merely to run the script unless that change is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
PowerUp may be affected by:

  • AppLocker;
  • Windows Defender Application Control;
  • PowerShell Constrained Language Mode;
  • Defender;
  • EDR controls.

Related notes:

Windows Application Control

Microsoft Defender

If PowerUp cannot run, use native Windows commands to perform the underlying checks manually.

docs.title: Obtaining PowerUp
docs.text:
Prefer the official PowerSploit repository.

Review the script before use.

Do not use random modified copies from paste sites or unknown repositories.

Record where the script came from when evidence provenance matters.

docs.title: Importing PowerUp
docs.text:
If an authorised local copy exists:

Import-Module .\PowerUp.ps1

Another common approach is dot-sourcing:

. .\PowerUp.ps1

The exact method depends on the script copy and PowerShell environment.

After loading, inspect available functions rather than assuming a particular function set.

For example:

Get-Command -Module PowerUp

if imported as a module.

If dot-sourced, use:

Get-Command *Service* | Where-Object Source -eq ''

or inspect the script help directly.

docs.title: Script Help
docs.text:
Use built-in PowerShell help where available.

For example:

Get-Help Invoke-AllChecks

Detailed help:

Get-Help Invoke-AllChecks -Full

The installed or downloaded script is the best source for exact function syntax.

docs.title: Invoke-AllChecks
docs.text:
A commonly used PowerUp entry point is:

Invoke-AllChecks

This runs multiple local privilege escalation checks.

Conceptually:

Invoke-AllChecks
      |
      +-- Service Checks
      +-- Permission Checks
      +-- Registry Checks
      +-- Installer Policy
      +-- Credential Checks
      |
      v
Candidate Findings

Do not treat the output as confirmed exploitation.

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text:
For assessment work, save output for later review.

Example:

Invoke-AllChecks | Tee-Object -FilePath .\powerup-output.txt

PowerUp output may contain:

  • usernames;
  • service paths;
  • permissions;
  • registry values;
  • potential credentials.

Protect the output appropriately.

docs.title: PowerUp and Services
docs.text:
Services are one of PowerUp's most important areas.

Potential findings may involve:

  • writable service executable;
  • writable service directory;
  • weak service permissions;
  • unquoted service path;
  • modifiable service configuration.

A good service analysis model is:

Service
  |
  +-- Runs privileged?
  |
  +-- User can influence binary?
  |
  +-- User can influence configuration?
  |
  +-- Execution can be triggered?
  |
  v
Potential PrivEsc

Related note:

Windows Services

docs.title: Service Configuration
docs.text:
If PowerUp reports a service-related candidate, first confirm the service configuration.

Use:

sc.exe qc ExampleService

Review:

SERVICE_NAME
START_TYPE
BINARY_PATH_NAME
SERVICE_START_NAME

PowerShell can also help:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object Name -eq 'ExampleService'

This confirms what the service actually executes and which account it uses.

docs.title: Service Identity
docs.text:
A service may run as:

LocalSystem
LocalService
NetworkService
Domain service account
Custom local account

Impact depends strongly on the execution identity.

A service running as LocalSystem generally represents a more privileged execution context than a low-privileged service account.

docs.title: Writable Service Executable
docs.text:
Suppose PowerUp reports:

Service binary may be writable

Validate with:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe"

Review:

  • current user;
  • group memberships;
  • explicit permissions;
  • inherited permissions;
  • deny entries.

Do not rely solely on PowerUp's interpretation.

docs.title: Writable Service Directory
docs.text:
The executable itself may be protected while its parent directory is modifiable.

Check:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example"

The relevant question is:

Can the current user replace, rename, delete, or otherwise influence the service binary through directory permissions?

The exact answer depends on effective ACLs.

docs.title: Weak Service Permissions
docs.text:
Service objects themselves have security descriptors.

A user may lack file write access but still have permissions to modify the service configuration.

Possible security-relevant rights include the ability to alter:

  • binary path;
  • service configuration;
  • service identity;
  • startup configuration.

Do not infer these permissions from filesystem ACLs.

They are separate security objects.

docs.title: Service Permission Model
docs.text:
A service privilege escalation condition can arise through:

Weak File ACL

or:

Weak Directory ACL

or:

Weak Service Object ACL

These are distinct.

A complete review should identify which trust boundary is weak.

docs.title: Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
PowerUp commonly checks for unquoted service paths.

Example:

C:\Program Files\Example Application\Service.exe

The important distinction is:

Unquoted Path
   !=
Exploitable Path

Also verify:

  • service runs privileged;
  • earlier path locations exist;
  • user can write to a relevant location;
  • service can be triggered;
  • application-control policy.

docs.title: Unquoted Path Validation Model
docs.text:
Unquoted Service Path
        |
        v
Contains Spaces?
        |
        v
Potential Earlier Executable Resolution
        |
        v
Relevant Directory Writable?
        |
        v
Privileged Service?
        |
        v
Reachable Trigger?

Only the full chain determines risk.

docs.title: Example Unquoted Service Path
docs.text:
Suppose:

C:\Program Files\Example App\Service.exe

Potential path interpretation may involve earlier components depending on Windows executable resolution behaviour.

Do not create proof files on production systems without explicit authorisation.

First validate permissions and service configuration safely.

docs.title: Service Restart Conditions
docs.text:
Even when a service path can be influenced, execution may require a trigger.

Determine whether:

  • current user can restart the service;
  • service restarts automatically on failure;
  • service starts at boot;
  • an administrator action is required.

Check state:

sc.exe query ExampleService

Document the actual trigger.

docs.title: PowerUp Service Findings and Native Validation
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

PowerUp
   |
   v
Candidate Service
   |
   v
sc.exe qc
   |
   v
icacls
   |
   v
Service Permission Review
   |
   v
Trigger Review
   |
   v
Conclusion

docs.title: Registry Checks
docs.text:
PowerUp may inspect registry configuration related to privilege escalation.

Potential areas can include:

  • service configuration;
  • installer settings;
  • autologon;
  • application settings;
  • execution paths.

Related note:

Windows Registry

docs.title: AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
PowerUp may check the Windows Installer policy commonly associated with AlwaysInstallElevated.

The condition is only security relevant when the required policy configuration is present in the relevant machine and user contexts.

Do not report based on one registry value alone.

A validation process should determine:

Machine policy set?
User policy set?
Current user context?
Actual installer behaviour?

The underlying issue is an unsafe elevated installer policy.

docs.title: AlwaysInstallElevated Validation
docs.text:
Inspect the relevant policy configuration using native registry tools.

For example, query the configured Windows Installer policy locations rather than trusting tool output alone.

Document:

Registry path
Value
Current user context
Machine context

Avoid creating or executing installer payloads merely to prove the policy unless explicit exploitation validation is required and authorised.

docs.title: Autologon Information
docs.text:
PowerUp may identify autologon-related registry information.

Possible values may include:

DefaultUserName
DefaultDomainName
DefaultPassword

where configured.

If sensitive credentials are present, treat them carefully.

Related note:

Windows Credentials

docs.title: Autologon Does Not Always Mean Plaintext Password
docs.text:
Do not assume every autologon configuration exposes a usable plaintext password.

Validate what values actually exist.

Possible outcomes include:

Username only

or:

Domain information only

or:

Credential material present

Report only what the evidence supports.

docs.title: Credential Findings
docs.text:
PowerUp may identify possible credential material in local configuration.

A candidate credential could be:

  • active;
  • expired;
  • unused;
  • placeholder;
  • test data.

Do not automatically attempt authentication with every discovered value.

First determine whether validation is necessary and authorised.

docs.title: Filesystem Checks
docs.text:
PowerUp may identify writable files or directories associated with privileged applications.

Validate with:

icacls "C:\Path\To\File"

and:

icacls "C:\Path\To\Directory"

Related note:

Windows Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Effective Permissions
docs.text:
The security question is not:

Does an ACL contain "Users"?

It is:

Does the current user, through their effective security token,
actually have the permission required to influence the object?

Consider:

  • direct user ACEs;
  • group ACEs;
  • inherited ACEs;
  • deny ACEs;
  • owner;
  • integrity level.

docs.title: Parent Directory Permissions
docs.text:
Always consider the full path.

Example:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\App\Service.exe

Review:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\App\Service.exe"

and, where relevant:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\App"

The parent directory may allow operations that affect the child object.

docs.title: DLL-Related Conditions
docs.text:
PowerUp may identify potential DLL-related privilege escalation conditions.

DLL loading issues require careful validation.

Relevant factors include:

Which process loads the DLL?

Which DLL name is requested?

Which search order applies?

Which directories are writable?

What account executes the process?

Do application-control policies apply?

A writable directory alone does not prove a DLL hijacking condition.

docs.title: DLL Search Order
docs.text:
Windows searches for DLLs according to a specific loading process influenced by:

  • application path;
  • system directories;
  • current directory;
  • PATH;
  • SafeDllSearchMode;
  • application-specific loading behaviour.

The exact mechanism depends on how the program loads the library.

Do not make broad conclusions from a generic writable PATH directory.

docs.title: PATH Checks
docs.text:
PowerUp may flag writable directories in PATH.

Inspect:

$env:Path -split ';'

Then check individual paths with:

icacls "C:\Path"

The key question is:

Does a privileged process search this directory for a binary or DLL?

If not, the writable PATH entry may not create a privilege escalation path.

docs.title: Startup Locations
docs.text:
PowerUp may identify autostart-related configuration.

Potential areas include:

  • Run keys;
  • Startup folders;
  • services;
  • scheduled tasks.

The important questions are:

What executes?

Who can modify it?

Who executes it?

When is it triggered?

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
PowerUp historically focuses strongly on services and local configuration, but scheduled tasks should still be reviewed manually as part of the overall privilege escalation methodology.

Use:

schtasks.exe /query /fo LIST /v

or:

Get-ScheduledTask

Related note:

Windows Scheduled Tasks

Do not assume PowerUp provides complete coverage of every scheduled execution path.

docs.title: PowerUp vs WinPEAS
docs.text:
PowerUp and WinPEAS overlap, but they are not identical.

WinPEAS
   |
   +-- very broad host enumeration

PowerUp
   |
   +-- focused Windows privilege escalation checks
   +-- PowerShell-based

A useful workflow is:

WinPEAS
   |
   v
Broad Candidates
   |
   v
PowerUp
   |
   v
Focused Cross-Check
   |
   v
Native Validation

Related note:

WinPEAS

docs.title: PowerUp vs PrivescCheck
docs.text:
PrivescCheck provides another PowerShell-based approach to local Windows privilege escalation enumeration.

PowerUp
    |
    +--> Candidate

PrivescCheck
    |
    +--> Related candidate

Native Tools
    |
    v
Validation

Related note:

PrivescCheck

docs.title: PowerUp and Manual Enumeration
docs.text:
PowerUp should supplement native Windows analysis.

Useful native tools include:

whoami.exe
sc.exe
icacls.exe
schtasks.exe
reg.exe
PowerShell cmdlets

The tool helps identify where to focus those checks.

docs.title: PowerUp and AppLocker
docs.text:
PowerUp may identify a technically interesting writable execution path.

AppLocker may restrict executable or script execution from that location.

This changes practical exploitability.

It does not automatically correct the weak ACL.

Separate:

Underlying permission issue

from:

Defence-in-depth control

Related note:

Windows Application Control

docs.title: PowerUp and WDAC
docs.text:
WDAC may enforce code integrity beyond normal filesystem permissions.

A candidate path could be:

Writable

but:

Unapproved binary cannot execute

This may substantially reduce practical risk.

However, the configuration should still be evaluated according to the intended security boundary.

docs.title: PowerUp and Constrained Language Mode
docs.text:
Constrained Language Mode may limit PowerShell functionality.

Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

If PowerUp cannot execute fully:

PowerUp failure
    !=
No privilege escalation issues

Switch to native/manual enumeration.

docs.title: PowerUp and Defender
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender or EDR may detect or block PowerUp.

Do not disable endpoint protection simply to run the tool unless the engagement explicitly authorises such action.

Instead:

  • coordinate testing;
  • use allowed tooling;
  • perform equivalent native checks.

Related note:

Microsoft Defender

docs.title: Script Provenance
docs.text:
Because PowerUp is frequently copied between repositories, preserve provenance.

Useful record:

Tool:
PowerUp.ps1

Source:
PowerSploit repository

Commit/release:
Recorded where relevant

Hash:
Recorded where required

This makes results more reproducible.

docs.title: PowerUp Function Names
docs.text:
PowerUp contains multiple functions targeting different Windows privilege escalation conditions.

Function names can vary across forks and versions.

Do not build a permanent knowledge base around an assumed function list without checking the actual script.

Use:

Get-Command

and:

Get-Help

against the version being used.

docs.title: Reviewing PowerUp Source
docs.text:
PowerShell source is readable.

Before using a function:

  1. locate it in PowerUp.ps1;
  2. understand what it checks;
  3. understand what constitutes a positive result;
  4. determine whether the function performs only enumeration or also modifies state.

This is especially important for functions that include exploitation or write functionality.

docs.title: Enumeration vs Modification
docs.text:
A security tool may contain both:

Check functions

and:

Abuse / write functions

These should be treated differently.

For normal validation:

Prefer read-only enumeration first

Then use separate controlled validation only where necessary and authorised.

docs.title: Do Not Automatically Run Exploitation Functions
docs.text:
PowerUp has historically included functionality beyond passive enumeration.

Do not automatically use functions that:

  • modify services;
  • create users;
  • alter files;
  • change registry values;
  • modify system configuration.

A finding can often be validated through permissions and configuration evidence without modifying the host.

docs.title: Safe Validation Principle
docs.text:
Prefer:

Read configuration
      |
      v
Check ACL
      |
      v
Confirm privileged consumer
      |
      v
Confirm trigger

before:

Modify privileged resource

This reduces operational impact.

docs.title: Representative Service Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose:

Invoke-AllChecks

reports a potentially writable service executable.

PowerUp output identifies:

ServiceName:
ExampleService

Path:
C:\ProgramData\Example\Service.exe

Validate service configuration:

sc.exe qc ExampleService

Then file permissions:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Example\Service.exe"

Then directory permissions:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Example"

Determine:

Which account runs service?

Can current user modify file?

Can current user replace file?

Can current user trigger service?

Does application control restrict execution?

Only then reach a conclusion.

docs.title: Representative Weak Service Configuration Scenario
docs.text:
PowerUp identifies that the current user may have service configuration rights.

Validate the service's security permissions using an appropriate native or administrative inspection method available in the environment.

The relevant security question is:

Can the low-privileged user alter how a higher-privileged service executes?

If yes, the weak service object permission is the finding.

docs.title: Representative Unquoted Service Path Scenario
docs.text:
PowerUp reports:

C:\Program Files\Example App\Service.exe

Validate:

  1. service account;
  2. exact service path;
  3. write permissions on candidate directories;
  4. service trigger;
  5. application-control restrictions.

If all candidate locations are protected:

Unquoted path present

may represent hardening debt without a practical local privilege escalation path for the tested user.

Do not overstate it.

docs.title: Representative AlwaysInstallElevated Scenario
docs.text:
PowerUp reports that installer policy may allow elevated MSI installation.

Validate both policy contexts.

If only one required policy value is configured, the full privilege escalation condition may not exist.

The conclusion should state exactly what was verified.

docs.title: Representative Autologon Scenario
docs.text:
PowerUp identifies:

DefaultUserName
DefaultPassword

If a plaintext password is exposed to the low-privileged user, assess:

  • account privilege;
  • password reuse scope where authorised;
  • whether the account provides higher local privilege.

The primary finding may be insecure local credential storage.

docs.title: Representative Writable PATH Scenario
docs.text:
PowerUp highlights:

C:\Tools

because the directory is writable and appears in PATH.

Do not conclude privilege escalation immediately.

Determine whether a privileged service or scheduled process executes an unqualified command that could resolve through this path.

Without a privileged consumer, there may be no escalation path.

docs.title: Representative DLL Scenario
docs.text:
PowerUp reports a possible DLL hijacking condition.

Validate:

Target process
Requested DLL
Load method
Search order
Writable directory
Execution identity
Trigger

If no privileged process loads the DLL from the writable location, the candidate is not confirmed.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
PowerUp can produce misleading candidates because of:

  • broad ACL heuristics;
  • inherited permissions;
  • disabled services;
  • protected candidate directories;
  • incomplete service-trigger context;
  • application-control restrictions;
  • registry values without full policy conditions;
  • stale credential configuration.

Manual validation is essential.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
PowerUp can also miss privilege escalation paths.

Possible reasons include:

  • custom applications;
  • scheduled-task logic;
  • proprietary services;
  • unusual registry usage;
  • non-standard directories;
  • application-specific IPC;
  • newer Windows features;
  • configurations added after the script's development.

Do not treat a clean PowerUp result as proof that the host has no local privilege escalation weaknesses.

docs.title: Why PowerUp Age Matters
docs.text:
PowerUp remains useful because many Windows privilege escalation fundamentals have not changed.

However, Windows platforms and defensive controls have evolved.

Modern environments may include:

  • WDAC;
  • AppLocker;
  • stronger Defender protections;
  • EDR;
  • newer service and application configurations.

Therefore combine PowerUp with:

  • WinPEAS;
  • PrivescCheck;
  • native commands;
  • manual reasoning.

docs.title: Candidate Evaluation Model
docs.text:
For each PowerUp result, ask:

Question Answer What exactly was identified? Can the current user influence it? What effective permission proves this? Which privileged process consumes it? What identity runs that process? Can execution be triggered? Which security controls apply? What additional privilege results?

If these questions cannot be answered, the result may not yet be a finding.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a PowerUp-supported finding, retain:

Current user:
Current groups:
PowerUp function/check:
PowerUp result:
Affected object:
Native validation:
Effective ACL:
Privileged consumer:
Execution identity:
Trigger:
Security controls:
Impact:

For example:

Current user:
CORP\tester

Candidate:
Service executable permission

Affected path:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Service.exe

Service:
VendorService

Service account:
LocalSystem

Validation:
icacls confirmed Modify permission through an assigned local group.

docs.title: Evidence Should Be Native Where Possible
docs.text:
PowerUp output is useful supporting evidence.

The strongest primary evidence is often:

  • sc.exe output;
  • icacls.exe output;
  • registry configuration;
  • scheduled-task configuration;
  • effective user/group context.

This makes the finding independently understandable without requiring the reader to know PowerUp.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

PowerUp found privilege escalation.

Prefer:

The tested standard user had Modify permission over an executable
configured to run as part of a LocalSystem service. Native service and
filesystem permission checks confirmed that the low-privileged user
could influence a privileged execution path.

PowerUp may have identified the candidate, but the finding describes the underlying condition.

docs.title: Reporting an Unconfirmed Candidate
docs.text:
Example:

PowerUp identified an unquoted service path. Manual validation showed
that the service ran as LocalSystem, but all candidate path locations
were protected from modification by the tested user. A practical local
privilege escalation path was therefore not confirmed.

This is more accurate than reporting every PowerUp warning.

docs.title: Reporting a Defence-in-Depth Condition
docs.text:
Example:

A privileged service referenced a file located in a directory with weak
write permissions. However, execution from the affected location was
restricted by application-control policy during testing. The underlying
filesystem permission should still be corrected because application
control represents a separate defence-in-depth layer.

This preserves both facts.

docs.title: Remediation Principles
docs.text:
PowerUp findings commonly map to a simple principle:

Standard users should not be able to modify resources that determine how privileged processes execute.

Remediation areas include:

  • service ACLs;
  • service executable ACLs;
  • directory ACLs;
  • service paths;
  • registry policy;
  • autologon credentials;
  • PATH;
  • DLL loading locations.

docs.title: Service Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove unnecessary Modify/Write access;
  • restrict service configuration rights;
  • use least-privileged service identities;
  • protect service directories;
  • quote executable paths where applicable.

docs.title: AlwaysInstallElevated Remediation
docs.text:
Disable unsafe installer policy where it is not specifically required.

Enterprise policy should be managed centrally through appropriate administrative controls.

docs.title: Autologon Remediation
docs.text:
Where plaintext credentials are exposed:

  • remove unnecessary autologon;
  • avoid storing reusable plaintext secrets;
  • rotate exposed credentials;
  • apply least privilege to the account.

docs.title: PATH Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove insecure writable directories from privileged PATH contexts;
  • use absolute executable paths in privileged automation;
  • correct directory permissions.

docs.title: DLL Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • use explicit library paths;
  • secure application directories;
  • remove writable search locations;
  • use appropriate application-control and code-integrity protections.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Do not retest only by running:

Invoke-AllChecks

again.

For a service ACL fix, confirm:

icacls "C:\Path\To\Service.exe"

and:

sc.exe qc ExampleService

For installer policy, confirm the relevant registry values.

For a PATH issue, confirm:

$env:Path -split ';'

and directory ACLs.

Then optionally rerun PowerUp as a secondary regression check.

docs.title: PowerUp in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
PowerUp execution can also generate useful telemetry during purple-team exercises.

Conceptually:

PowerUp
   |
   v
Privilege Escalation Enumeration
   |
   v
PowerShell / Process / EDR Telemetry
   |
   v
Detection Review

Related notes:

Purple Teaming

Detection Engineering

The exercise objective should be agreed before execution.

docs.title: Logging and Telemetry
docs.text:
PowerUp may generate observable activity through:

  • PowerShell script loading;
  • registry queries;
  • service enumeration;
  • filesystem ACL inspection;
  • process activity.

This may be expected in an authorised assessment.

Do not attempt to evade logging merely to make the tool execute unless that is explicitly part of the engagement objective.

docs.title: Tool Transfer
docs.text:
Document transferred security tooling where appropriate.

Example:

Tool:
PowerUp.ps1

Source:
Official PowerSploit repository

Destination:
Approved temporary working directory

Execution:
Authorised

Cleanup:
Completed after testing

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Where required, remove:

PowerUp.ps1
powerup-output.txt
temporary assessment artefacts

Do not delete legitimate Windows event logs or security telemetry.

Retain assessment evidence according to policy.

docs.title: Practical PowerUp Workflow
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

1. Confirm scope
      |
      v
2. Record current user
      |
      v
3. Record groups and privileges
      |
      v
4. Check PowerShell environment
      |
      v
5. Obtain official PowerUp
      |
      v
6. Review script/version
      |
      v
7. Load PowerUp
      |
      v
8. Run enumeration checks
      |
      v
9. Save output securely
      |
      v
10. Prioritise service and permission findings
      |
      v
11. Validate with native Windows tools
      |
      v
12. Identify privileged consumer
      |
      v
13. Confirm trigger
      |
      v
14. Consider AppLocker/WDAC/EDR
      |
      v
15. Confirm or reject candidate
      |
      v
16. Capture evidence
      |
      v
17. Clean up assessment artefacts

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Target system explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Current user recorded.
  • [ ] Groups recorded.
  • [ ] Privileges recorded.
  • [ ] PowerShell version known.
  • [ ] Language mode checked.
  • [ ] Execution policy understood.
  • [ ] AppLocker/WDAC context considered.
  • [ ] Official PowerSploit source used.
  • [ ] Script provenance recorded where useful.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
• [ ] Script reviewed before loading.
  • [ ] Enumeration functions preferred first.
  • [ ] State-changing functions not used automatically.
  • [ ] Output retained securely.
  • [ ] Sensitive data protected.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
• [ ] Service account confirmed.
  • [ ] Binary path confirmed.
  • [ ] File ACL confirmed.
  • [ ] Parent directory ACL confirmed.
  • [ ] Service object permissions considered.
  • [ ] Restart/trigger condition reviewed.
  • [ ] Unquoted path candidates manually validated.

docs.title: Registry
docs.text:
• [ ] Interesting registry values confirmed manually.
  • [ ] Installer policy evaluated in full context.
  • [ ] Autologon findings validated.
  • [ ] Sensitive registry data protected.

docs.title: Filesystem
docs.text:
• [ ] Writable files manually checked.
  • [ ] Writable directories manually checked.
  • [ ] Effective permissions understood.
  • [ ] Privileged consumer identified.

docs.title: PATH / DLL
docs.text:
• [ ] Writable PATH entries treated as candidates only.
  • [ ] Privileged PATH consumer confirmed.
  • [ ] DLL loading behaviour understood.
  • [ ] Search path and writable locations validated.
  • [ ] Application-control restrictions considered.

docs.title: Security Controls
docs.text:
• [ ] Defender considered.
  • [ ] EDR considered.
  • [ ] AppLocker considered.
  • [ ] WDAC considered.
  • [ ] Constrained Language Mode considered.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] PowerUp result treated as candidate evidence.
  • [ ] Native commands used for confirmation.
  • [ ] Effective user influence confirmed.
  • [ ] Privileged execution context confirmed.
  • [ ] Trigger confirmed.
  • [ ] False positives considered.
  • [ ] Security impact established.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Current identity retained.
  • [ ] Relevant PowerUp output retained.
  • [ ] Native ACL/configuration evidence retained.
  • [ ] Privileged consumer documented.
  • [ ] Trigger documented.
  • [ ] Security-control context documented.
  • [ ] Sensitive values redacted where required.
  • [ ] Finding describes underlying security weakness.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
• [ ] PowerUp script removed where required.
  • [ ] Temporary output removed where required.
  • [ ] Evidence retained according to policy.
  • [ ] Legitimate Windows/security logs preserved.
