        +-- icacls.exe
        +-- reg.exe
        +-- schtasks.exe
        |
        v
Confirm Effective User Influence
        |
        v
Identify Privileged Consumer
        |
        v
Confirm Trigger
        |
        v
Consider AppLocker / WDAC / EDR
        |
        v
Determine Actual Impact
        |
        v
Capture Evidence
        |
        v
Report the Underlying Weakness

PowerUp remains useful because it automates a number of important Windows local privilege escalation checks in a readable PowerShell implementation.

Its greatest value is not automatically exploiting the host.

Its value is identifying configurations that deserve careful, native Windows validation.

docs.title: PrivescCheck
docs.text:
PrivescCheck is a PowerShell-based Windows privilege escalation enumeration tool designed to identify local security conditions that may allow a lower-privileged user to influence privileged execution or access sensitive local resources.

It can help review areas such as:

  • users and groups;
  • token privileges;
  • Windows services;
  • scheduled tasks;
  • filesystem permissions;
  • registry permissions;
  • installed applications;
  • credentials;
  • environment configuration;
  • startup locations;
  • security controls;
  • potentially sensitive files.

PrivescCheck should be treated as an enumeration and triage tool.

Its output identifies conditions that deserve investigation.

It does not automatically prove that a privilege escalation path exists.

Windows Host
    |
    v
PrivescCheck
    |
    +-- Identity
    +-- Privileges
    +-- Services
    +-- Tasks
    +-- Files
    +-- Registry
    +-- Credentials
    +-- Applications
    +-- Security Controls
    |
    v
Candidate Conditions
    |
    v
Native Validation
    |
    v
Privilege Escalation Conclusion

Authorised testing only

Run PrivescCheck only on Windows systems where local security assessment is explicitly authorised. PowerShell-based enumeration can generate endpoint-security telemetry and may inspect sensitive local configuration. Review the rules of engagement before execution.

docs.title: Where PrivescCheck Fits
docs.text:
PrivescCheck normally follows initial local access and a basic understanding of the current security context.

Initial Access
      |
      v
Current User
      |
      v
Manual Baseline
      |
      v
PrivescCheck
      |
      v
Candidate Conditions
      |
      v
Native Validation
      |
      v
Confirm or Reject

Related notes:

Privilege Escalation Tools

Windows Privilege Escalation

Windows Enumeration

Windows Privilege Escalation Explorer

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
PrivescCheck is maintained by itm4n.

Official project:

PrivescCheck - GitHub

Use the official repository or a trusted internal mirror.

Avoid modified copies from unknown sources.

docs.title: What PrivescCheck Does
docs.text:
PrivescCheck automates local Windows checks that would otherwise require many individual commands.

Conceptually:

Windows Configuration
       |
       +-- Services
       +-- Scheduled Tasks
       +-- Registry
       +-- Filesystem
       +-- Credentials
       +-- Users
       +-- Privileges
       +-- Applications
       |
       v
PrivescCheck
       |
       v
Potential Security Conditions

The purpose is to answer:

Which areas should I investigate further?

not:

Which findings are definitely exploitable?

docs.title: Before Running PrivescCheck
docs.text:
Start by recording the current security context.

whoami

whoami /groups

whoami /priv

Also consider:

whoami /all

This helps answer:

Who am I?

Which groups apply?

Which token privileges exist?

Am I already an administrator?

Which security identifiers influence ACL evaluation?

docs.title: Record Host Context
docs.text:
Useful commands include:

hostname

systeminfo

and, where available:

Get-ComputerInfo

This establishes:

  • hostname;
  • Windows version;
  • architecture;
  • domain context;
  • patch context.

docs.title: PowerShell Environment
docs.text:
Check the PowerShell version:

$PSVersionTable

Check the current language mode:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

This matters because PowerShell restrictions can affect tool execution.

docs.title: Execution Policy
docs.text:
Review:

Get-ExecutionPolicy -List

Execution policy can affect script loading but should not be confused with a strong security boundary.

Do not change enterprise policy merely to run the tool unless that change is specifically authorised.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
PrivescCheck may be affected by:

  • AppLocker;
  • Windows Defender Application Control;
  • Constrained Language Mode;
  • Microsoft Defender;
  • EDR controls.

Related notes:

Windows Application Control

Microsoft Defender

If the script cannot execute, the underlying checks can still be performed manually.

docs.title: Obtaining PrivescCheck
docs.text:
Prefer the official repository.

Useful information to retain includes:

Tool:
PrivescCheck

Source:
Official GitHub repository

Revision:
Recorded where useful

Hash:
Recorded where required

This improves reproducibility.

docs.title: Basic Execution
docs.text:
The exact invocation should always be confirmed against the version being used.

A typical workflow is:

. .\PrivescCheck.ps1

Then invoke the main PrivescCheck function exposed by that version.

Before running:

Get-Content .\PrivescCheck.ps1 -Head 40

and inspect the documentation in the repository.

Do not assume all historical versions expose identical function names or parameters.

docs.title: Inspect Available Functions
docs.text:
After loading the script, inspect functions related to the tool.

For example:

Get-Command | Where-Object Name -like '*Privesc*'

or use:

Get-Help

for the main function exposed by the installed version.

The exact script remains the best reference for exact syntax.

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text:
For longer assessments, save results.

A common PowerShell pattern is:

<PrivescCheckCommand> | Tee-Object -FilePath .\privesccheck-output.txt

Replace:

<PrivescCheckCommand>

with the main command from the version being used.

The output may contain sensitive information.

Protect it accordingly.

docs.title: Output Can Be Sensitive
docs.text:
PrivescCheck may surface:

  • usernames;
  • service accounts;
  • filesystem paths;
  • weak permissions;
  • credentials;
  • registry values;
  • potentially sensitive configuration.

Do not:

  • commit raw output to Git;
  • paste full output into public tickets;
  • upload it to third-party services;
  • attach unnecessary sensitive data to reports.

Extract only relevant evidence.

docs.title: Result Interpretation
docs.text:
A useful model is:

PrivescCheck Result
        |
        v
Candidate
        |
        v
Native Validation
        |
        v
Execution Context
        |
        v
Reachability
        |
        v
Impact

The tool result alone is not enough.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Windows services are one of the most important local privilege escalation areas.

PrivescCheck may identify conditions involving:

  • weak service permissions;
  • weak executable permissions;
  • weak directory permissions;
  • unquoted service paths;
  • privileged service identities.

Related note:

Windows Services

docs.title: Service Configuration
docs.text:
Validate a service with:

sc.exe qc ExampleService

Review:

BINARY_PATH_NAME
SERVICE_START_NAME
START_TYPE

You can also use:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object Name -eq 'ExampleService'

This confirms the actual service configuration.

docs.title: Service Identity
docs.text:
Common service identities include:

LocalSystem
LocalService
NetworkService
Domain service account
Custom local account

A service running as LocalSystem generally represents a highly privileged execution context.

The service identity is critical to impact assessment.

docs.title: Service Executable Permissions
docs.text:
If PrivescCheck identifies a potentially writable service binary, validate:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe"

Review:

Current user
Current groups
Explicit ACEs
Inherited ACEs
Allow permissions
Deny permissions

The security question is:

Can the current user actually modify or replace this executable?

docs.title: Service Directory Permissions
docs.text:
The executable may be protected while the parent directory is writable.

Check:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example"

This may reveal rights allowing:

  • file creation;
  • deletion;
  • replacement;
  • rename operations.

Parent directory permissions can matter as much as the file ACL.

docs.title: Weak Service Object Permissions
docs.text:
Filesystem ACLs and service-object ACLs are different.

A user may have no write access to the binary but still have permission to modify the service itself.

Possible security-relevant controls include the ability to change:

  • service binary path;
  • startup configuration;
  • service identity.

The underlying weakness in that case is the service object security descriptor.

docs.title: Restartability
docs.text:
A service-related condition may require execution to be triggered.

Questions include:

Can the current user stop the service?

Can the current user start it?

Does it restart automatically?

Will it execute at reboot?

Does an administrator action trigger it?

Check state:

sc.exe query ExampleService

Do not assume immediate exploitability without a reachable trigger.

docs.title: Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
PrivescCheck may identify unquoted service paths.

Example:

C:\Program Files\Vendor Application\Service.exe

The presence of spaces alone is not sufficient.

Also determine:

Is the path unquoted?

Which candidate path components are evaluated?

Can current user write to one?

Does the service run privileged?

Can the service be triggered?

An unquoted path with protected directories may not provide a practical escalation path.

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks can execute in privileged contexts.

PrivescCheck may identify:

  • task name;
  • action;
  • execution identity;
  • potentially writable referenced files.

Related note:

Windows Scheduled Tasks

docs.title: Scheduled Task Enumeration
docs.text:
Use native tooling:

schtasks.exe /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

For a specific task:

Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "ExampleTask"

Inspect actions:

(Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "ExampleTask").Actions

docs.title: Task Execution Identity
docs.text:
Determine whether the task runs as:

SYSTEM
Administrator
Service account
Normal user

The privilege of the task determines the importance of writable resources it consumes.

docs.title: Task Actions
docs.text:
Suppose the task runs:

C:\ProgramData\Scripts\backup.ps1

Validate:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Scripts\backup.ps1"

and:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Scripts"

The complete execution chain matters.

docs.title: Task Trigger
docs.text:
Determine whether the task runs:

At startup
At logon
On schedule
On event
Manually

Document the actual trigger.

A condition that executes every few minutes is different from one requiring an administrator reboot.

docs.title: Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Filesystem permissions are one of the most important areas in local privilege escalation.

PrivescCheck may identify:

  • writable files;
  • writable directories;
  • privileged executables;
  • configuration files;
  • scripts.

Related note:

Windows Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Validate Files with icacls
docs.text:
Use:

icacls "C:\Path\To\File"

For a directory:

icacls "C:\Path\To\Directory"

Common permission abbreviations include:

F  -> Full control
M  -> Modify
RX -> Read and execute
R  -> Read
W  -> Write

Always interpret permissions in combination with current group membership.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
Windows ACLs often contain inherited permissions.

A child object may inherit rights from a parent.

Therefore review:

Explicit ACE
Inherited ACE
Parent ACL

Do not assume the permission originates directly on the file.

docs.title: Deny ACEs
docs.text:
Explicit deny entries can affect effective permission evaluation.

A simple match for:

Users:(M)

is not always sufficient to determine effective access.

Review the complete ACL and security token.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Ownership may grant the ability to modify an object's security descriptor depending on the current security context.

Therefore:

Owner

can be relevant even when direct write permission is absent.

Do not assume ownership automatically results in exploitability.

docs.title: Registry Permissions
docs.text:
The Windows registry can influence privileged execution.

PrivescCheck may identify writable registry locations associated with:

  • services;
  • applications;
  • startup;
  • policy;
  • installer behaviour.

Related note:

Windows Registry

docs.title: Registry Query
docs.text:
Read configuration with:

reg.exe query "HKLM\Software\Example"

The interesting condition is not simply that a key exists.

It is whether:

Current user can modify it
        +
Privileged process trusts it

docs.title: Service Registry Keys
docs.text:
Windows services are represented in the registry under system service configuration.

However, do not infer service configuration permissions solely from registry visibility.

Use appropriate service and ACL inspection methods to determine effective rights.

docs.title: Installer Policy
docs.text:
PrivescCheck may inspect Windows Installer policy related to elevated installations.

If an elevated installer policy is identified, verify the complete configuration rather than relying on one registry value.

The underlying security issue is an unsafe installer policy allowing lower-privileged influence over elevated installation.

docs.title: Startup Locations
docs.text:
Windows startup mechanisms may include:

Run keys
Startup folders
Services
Scheduled tasks
Application-specific autostart

The relevant questions are:

What runs?

Who can modify it?

Who runs it?

When is it executed?

docs.title: PATH
docs.text:
PrivescCheck may identify writable PATH directories.

Inspect:

$env:Path -split ';'

Then validate relevant paths:

icacls "C:\Path"

A writable PATH directory is only relevant if a privileged process performs unqualified executable resolution through it.

docs.title: PATH Privilege Escalation Model
docs.text:
Privileged Process
      |
      v
Calls Binary Without Full Path
      |
      v
Searches PATH
      |
      v
Writable Directory Appears First
      |
      v
User Can Influence Resolution

Every step must be demonstrated.

docs.title: DLL Search Conditions
docs.text:
PrivescCheck may identify conditions relevant to DLL loading.

A real DLL hijacking path requires understanding:

Which process loads the DLL?

Which name is requested?

Which search order applies?

Which locations are writable?

What privilege runs the process?

Can the process be triggered?

A writable directory by itself is not enough.

docs.title: Installed Applications
docs.text:
PrivescCheck can identify software and configuration relevant to local privilege escalation.

Custom or third-party applications deserve particular attention because they may introduce:

  • services;
  • scheduled jobs;
  • writable configuration;
  • weak installation directories;
  • insecure update mechanisms.

Do not report old-looking versions without validating patch status and actual applicability.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
PrivescCheck may identify possible credential exposure.

Potential sources include:

  • configuration files;
  • unattended deployment files;
  • registry values;
  • scripts;
  • application files;
  • environment variables.

Related note:

Windows Credentials

Treat any credential-like material as sensitive.

docs.title: Credential Validation
docs.text:
A candidate credential may be:

Current
Expired
Unused
Placeholder
Example data
Encrypted

Do not automatically authenticate with it.

Determine whether validation is:

  • necessary;
  • within scope;
  • low risk.

The exposure itself may already be the relevant finding.

docs.title: Autologon
docs.text:
Windows autologon configuration can expose sensitive credential-related information in some configurations.

If PrivescCheck highlights autologon data, verify what is actually present.

Do not assume a password exists simply because autologon-related keys are configured.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables may expose:

  • secrets;
  • application settings;
  • PATH;
  • internal locations.

Inspect:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Security relevance depends on content and privilege context.

docs.title: Token Privileges
docs.text:
PrivescCheck may highlight token privileges.

Confirm manually:

whoami /priv

Potentially interesting privileges must be interpreted according to:

  • current state;
  • process context;
  • Windows protections;
  • privilege preconditions.

The presence of a privilege is not the same as successful privilege escalation.

docs.title: User and Group Membership
docs.text:
PrivescCheck output should always be interpreted alongside:

whoami /groups

Group membership may explain:

  • filesystem access;
  • registry access;
  • service rights;
  • local administrative rights.

Without group context, ACL findings can be misleading.

docs.title: UAC Context
docs.text:
If the current user belongs to the local Administrators group, User Account Control may affect the current token.

Check the broader context before describing the situation as ordinary privilege escalation.

Related note:

Windows User Account Control

UAC should not be confused with a normal privilege boundary between unrelated users.

docs.title: Security Controls
docs.text:
PrivescCheck output should be interpreted in the context of security controls such as:

  • AppLocker;
  • WDAC;
  • Microsoft Defender;
  • EDR;
  • PowerShell controls.

A candidate may be technically present but practically constrained.

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
A writable privileged resource may not allow arbitrary executable or script execution if AppLocker blocks the relevant file type or path.

This changes practical exploitability.

It does not necessarily correct the underlying permission issue.

Related note:

Windows Application Control

docs.title: WDAC
docs.text:
WDAC can enforce stronger code-integrity restrictions.

The assessment should distinguish:

Weak ACL

from:

Ability to execute modified code under current policy

These are separate security questions.

docs.title: Constrained Language Mode
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

If the result is:

ConstrainedLanguage

some PowerShell functionality may be unavailable.

A failed PrivescCheck execution does not mean the endpoint has no local privilege escalation weaknesses.

Use native tools where necessary.

docs.title: Microsoft Defender
docs.text:
PowerShell privilege escalation enumeration tools may be inspected or blocked by Defender or another endpoint product.

Do not disable security controls merely to make the tool run unless specifically authorised.

Related note:

Microsoft Defender

docs.title: Native Validation
docs.text:
PrivescCheck should lead to native validation.

Useful native tools include:

whoami.exe
sc.exe
schtasks.exe
icacls.exe
reg.exe
net.exe
PowerShell cmdlets

The goal is to make each conclusion understandable without depending on PrivescCheck output alone.

docs.title: PrivescCheck vs WinPEAS
docs.text:
WinPEAS provides broad Windows enumeration.

PrivescCheck provides another structured Windows privilege escalation perspective.

WinPEAS
   |
   +-- broad local enumeration

PrivescCheck
   |
   +-- structured PowerShell-based checks

A useful workflow is:

WinPEAS
    |
    v
Candidate
    |
    v
PrivescCheck
    |
    v
Native Validation

Related note:

WinPEAS

docs.title: PrivescCheck vs PowerUp
docs.text:
PowerUp and PrivescCheck overlap in several areas.

PowerUp is historically associated with PowerSploit.

PrivescCheck is a separate project with its own implementation and checks.

PowerUp
    |
    +--> Candidate A

PrivescCheck
    |
    +--> Candidate A

Native Windows Tools
    |
    v
Confirm Actual Condition

Related note:

PowerUp

docs.title: Running Multiple Tools
docs.text:
Multiple tools can improve coverage.

However:

Three tools report same service

does not mean:

Three vulnerabilities

Consolidate duplicate results around the actual underlying weakness.

docs.title: Candidate Correlation
docs.text:
Example:

WinPEAS:
Writable service candidate

PowerUp:
Service permission candidate

PrivescCheck:
Same service highlighted

icacls:
Modify confirmed

sc.exe:
Runs as LocalSystem

This provides strong evidence that the service deserves further investigation.

docs.title: Representative Service Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose PrivescCheck reports:

Service:
ExampleService

Binary:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Service.exe

Potential issue:
Writable executable

Validate:

sc.exe qc ExampleService

Then:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Service.exe"

And:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

Questions:

Does current user have Modify or Write?

Which group grants access?

Does the service run as LocalSystem?

Can execution be triggered?

Does AppLocker or WDAC affect execution?

Only the complete chain determines risk.

docs.title: Representative Negative Service Scenario
docs.text:
PrivescCheck highlights:

C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe

Manual validation:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe"

shows only:

SYSTEM
Administrators
TrustedInstaller

with modification rights.

Conclusion:

The service executable was highlighted during automated enumeration,
but manual ACL validation did not show write or modify permissions for
the tested low-privileged user or its groups. The suspected privilege
escalation path was not confirmed.

docs.title: Representative Scheduled Task Scenario
docs.text:
PrivescCheck identifies:

Task:
BackupTask

Runs as:
SYSTEM

Action:
C:\ProgramData\Backup\backup.ps1

Validate:

schtasks.exe /query /tn "\BackupTask" /fo LIST /v

Then:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Backup\backup.ps1"

and:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Backup"

The key question is:

Can the current user influence a resource executed by the SYSTEM task?

docs.title: Representative PATH Scenario
docs.text:
PrivescCheck identifies:

C:\Tools

as writable and present in PATH.

Validate:

icacls "C:\Tools"

Then investigate whether any privileged service or scheduled task invokes a command without a fully qualified path.

Without that privileged consumer:

Writable PATH

may remain only a hardening observation.

docs.title: Representative Registry Scenario
docs.text:
PrivescCheck highlights a writable registry value.

Do not immediately call it privilege escalation.

Determine:

Which process reads this value?

What privilege does that process run with?

Can the current user modify it?

Can the change affect execution?

The privileged consumer is essential.

docs.title: Representative Credential Scenario
docs.text:
PrivescCheck reports a potential password in a configuration file.

Validate:

Is it plaintext?

Is the current user allowed to read the file?

Which account is referenced?

Does the credential provide more privilege?

Is testing the credential necessary?

Do not over-validate sensitive secrets.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
PrivescCheck results can be misleading because of:

  • inherited ACL interpretation;
  • disabled services;
  • inactive scheduled tasks;
  • writable resources without privileged consumers;
  • stale credentials;
  • security-control restrictions;
  • assumptions about execution triggers;
  • generic weak-permission heuristics.

Manual validation is essential.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
PrivescCheck can miss real privilege escalation paths.

Possible reasons include:

  • proprietary applications;
  • non-standard directories;
  • custom IPC;
  • transient resources;
  • newer Windows features;
  • unusual service architectures;
  • application-specific logic.

A clean result does not prove the host is free of local privilege escalation weaknesses.

docs.title: Tool Coverage Is Not Complete Coverage
docs.text:
A good assessment does not end with:

PrivescCheck:
No findings

Continue with manual analysis of:

Identity
Privileges
Services
Scheduled Tasks
Filesystem
Registry
Credentials
Applications
Security Controls

Automation improves coverage but cannot guarantee completeness.

docs.title: Review Output by Category
docs.text:
For large output, review systematically:

1. Identity
2. Privileges
3. Services
4. Scheduled tasks
5. Filesystem permissions
6. Registry
7. Credentials
8. Applications
9. Security controls
10. Miscellaneous findings

This is more effective than looking only for highlighted strings.

docs.title: Search Saved Output
docs.text:
If output was saved:

privesccheck-output.txt

search with:

Select-String -Path .\privesccheck-output.txt -Pattern "service"

or:

Select-String -Path .\privesccheck-output.txt -Pattern "writ"

or:

Select-String -Path .\privesccheck-output.txt -Pattern "credential"

Preserve surrounding context.

docs.title: Candidate Evaluation Model
docs.text:
For each candidate, answer:

Question Answer What did PrivescCheck identify? Can the current user influence it? Which ACL or permission proves this? Which privileged process consumes it? Which identity runs that process? Can it be triggered? Which security controls apply? What privilege would result?

This turns automated output into structured analysis.

docs.title: User Influence
docs.text:
The first major question is:

Can the current user actually influence the resource?

This may mean:

  • write;
  • modify;
  • delete;
  • replace;
  • reconfigure;
  • control service object;
  • change registry value.

A result without user influence is rarely a privilege escalation condition.

docs.title: Privileged Consumer
docs.text:
The second major question is:

What privileged process trusts or executes the resource?

Examples include:

LocalSystem service
SYSTEM scheduled task
Administrator-started application
Privileged installer

Without a privileged consumer, a writable resource may have little privilege escalation relevance.

docs.title: Reachable Trigger
docs.text:
The third question is:

Can execution occur?

Possible triggers include:

  • service restart;
  • reboot;
  • scheduled execution;
  • logon;
  • administrator action;
  • application launch.

Document this clearly.

docs.title: Security Control Context
docs.text:
The fourth question is:

Will another security control constrain the path?

Examples include:

  • AppLocker;
  • WDAC;
  • Defender;
  • EDR.

Do not ignore defence-in-depth controls when assessing practical exploitability.

docs.title: Evidence Model
docs.text:
Weak evidence:

Screenshot of PrivescCheck output

Better:

PrivescCheck candidate
      |
      v
Native configuration query
      |
      v
ACL evidence
      |
      v
Privileged identity
      |
      v
Trigger
      |
      v
Impact

The evidence should tell the story without requiring the reader to trust the tool.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a validated condition, retain:

Current user:
Current groups:
PrivescCheck result:
Affected object:
Native configuration:
ACL:
Privileged consumer:
Execution identity:
Trigger:
Security controls:
Observed impact:

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

PrivescCheck found privilege escalation.

Prefer:

The tested standard user had Modify rights over a script executed by a
scheduled task running as SYSTEM. Native ACL and task configuration
checks confirmed that the low-privileged user could influence content
executed by a privileged process.

The finding is the weak privilege boundary, not the tool result.

docs.title: Reporting an Unconfirmed Candidate
docs.text:
Example:

PrivescCheck identified a potentially writable service resource.
Manual validation showed that the tested user did not have effective
write or modify rights over the file or its parent directory. The
suspected privilege escalation path was therefore not confirmed.

This avoids false-positive reporting.

docs.title: Reporting Security Control Impact
docs.text:
Example:

The tested user had write access to a file referenced by a privileged
service. However, application-control policy prevented execution of
unapproved code from the affected path during testing. The filesystem
permission remains weaker than necessary and should be corrected, while
the application-control policy currently provides an additional
defence-in-depth layer.

This describes both conditions accurately.

docs.title: Remediation Principles
docs.text:
The general remediation principle is:

A low-privileged user should not be able to modify configuration or resources that determine how a higher-privileged process executes.

Typical remediation areas include:

  • service permissions;
  • service executable ACLs;
  • scheduled-task resources;
  • filesystem permissions;
  • registry permissions;
  • PATH;
  • installer policy;
  • credentials.

docs.title: Service Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove unnecessary Modify/Write access;
  • restrict service-object permissions;
  • protect executable directories;
  • use least-privileged service accounts;
  • quote service executable paths where relevant.

docs.title: Scheduled Task Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • protect task scripts and binaries;
  • protect parent directories;
  • restrict task modification;
  • use least privilege;
  • remove obsolete privileged tasks.

docs.title: Filesystem Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove unnecessary writable ACLs;
  • avoid broad permissions such as excessive Users or Everyone access;
  • secure parent directories;
  • use inheritance carefully.

docs.title: Registry Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • restrict write access;
  • protect privileged application configuration;
  • remove insecure installer policies;
  • review startup-related keys.

docs.title: Credential Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove plaintext credentials;
  • rotate exposed secrets;
  • use secure credential storage;
  • restrict file access;
  • remove obsolete configuration.

docs.title: PATH Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove writable directories from privileged PATH contexts;
  • use explicit executable paths;
  • correct directory ACLs.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Do not retest only by rerunning PrivescCheck.

For a file ACL fix:

icacls "C:\Path\To\File"

For service configuration:

sc.exe qc ExampleService

For a scheduled task:

schtasks.exe /query /tn "\ExampleTask" /fo LIST /v

For registry configuration:

reg.exe query "HKLM\Software\Example"

Then optionally rerun PrivescCheck as a secondary regression check.

docs.title: PrivescCheck in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
PrivescCheck can also be useful in purple-team exercises where the objective includes understanding defensive visibility.

PrivescCheck
     |
     v
Local Enumeration
     |
     v
PowerShell / EDR Telemetry
     |
     v
Detection Review

Related notes:

Purple Teaming

Detection Engineering

The activity should be coordinated in advance.

docs.title: Detection Considerations
docs.text:
Potential telemetry may include:

  • PowerShell script execution;
  • service queries;
  • registry access;
  • filesystem enumeration;
  • process creation.

Do not attempt to bypass defensive monitoring unless that activity is explicitly part of the approved test objective.

Tool:
PrivescCheck.ps1

Official repository

Approved temporary assessment folder

Authorised

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Where required, remove:

PrivescCheck.ps1
privesccheck-output.txt
temporary assessment files

Do not remove legitimate event logs or security telemetry.

docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

1. Confirm scope
      |
      v
2. Record current identity

      v
3. Record groups and privileges

      v
4. Record host context
      |
      v
5. Check PowerShell restrictions

6. Obtain trusted PrivescCheck copy

      v
7. Review tool documentation
      |
      v
8. Run approved enumeration
      |
      v
9. Save output securely
      |
      v
10. Review by category
      |
      v
11. Prioritise privileged execution paths
      |
      v
12. Validate with native Windows tools
      |
      v
13. Confirm effective permissions

      v
14. Identify privileged consumer

19. Clean up assessment artefacts

docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use PrivescCheck like this:

Run PrivescCheck
      |
      v
Find Warning
      |
      v
Report PrivEsc

Use it like this:

Understand Current Identity
        |
        v
Run PrivescCheck
        |
        v
Identify Candidate
        |
        v
Understand Why It Was Flagged
        |
        v
Validate With Native Tools
        |
        +-- icacls
        +-- sc.exe
        +-- schtasks.exe
        +-- reg.exe
        |
        v
Confirm Effective User Influence
        |
        v
Identify Privileged Consumer
        |
        v
Confirm Trigger
        |
        v
Consider AppLocker / WDAC / Defender
        |
        v
Determine Actual Impact
        |
        v
Capture Evidence
        |
        v
Report the Underlying Weakness

PrivescCheck is valuable because it provides structured Windows privilege escalation enumeration without replacing the need to understand Windows security boundaries.

The tool highlights where to investigate.

The tester determines whether the condition can actually cross a privilege boundary.

docs.title: WinPEAS
docs.text:
WinPEAS is part of the PEASS-ng project and is designed to enumerate Windows systems for conditions that may be relevant to local privilege escalation.

It can inspect a broad range of areas, including:

  • users and groups;
  • token privileges;
  • services;
  • scheduled tasks;
  • registry configuration;
  • filesystem permissions;
  • installed applications;
  • credentials;
  • environment variables;
  • network configuration;
  • security products;
  • potentially sensitive files;
  • interesting execution paths.

WinPEAS is most useful as an enumeration accelerator.

It is not a vulnerability scanner that can automatically determine whether every highlighted condition is exploitable.

Windows Host
    |
    v
WinPEAS
    |
    +-- Identity
    +-- Privileges
    +-- Services
    +-- Scheduled Tasks
    +-- Registry
    +-- Filesystem
    +-- Credentials
    +-- Applications
    +-- Security Controls
    |
    v
Candidate Conditions
    |
    v
Manual Validation
    |
    v
Privilege Escalation Conclusion

Authorised testing only

Run WinPEAS only on Windows systems where local security enumeration is explicitly authorised. It performs a large number of checks and may generate endpoint-security telemetry. Review the rules of engagement before transferring or executing third-party enumeration tooling.

docs.title: Where WinPEAS Fits
docs.text:
WinPEAS normally follows initial access to a Windows system.

A useful workflow is:

Initial Local Access
        |
        v
Identify Current User
        |
        v
Manual Baseline
        |
        v
Run WinPEAS
        |
        v
Review Interesting Results
        |
        v
Validate With Native Tools
        |
        v
Confirm or Reject Candidate

Related notes:

Privilege Escalation Tools

Windows Privilege Escalation

Windows Enumeration

Privilege Escalation Explorer

docs.title: What WinPEAS Does
docs.text:
WinPEAS automates many checks that could otherwise be performed manually.

Conceptually:

System State
    |
    +-- Users
    +-- Groups
    +-- Privileges
    +-- Services
    +-- Tasks
    +-- ACLs
    +-- Registry
    +-- Credentials
    +-- Software
    +-- Security Controls
    |
    v
WinPEAS Checks
    |
    v
Prioritised Output

The tool attempts to highlight items that may deserve further investigation.

The important word is:

may

A highlighted result is a lead, not a confirmed finding.

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
WinPEAS is maintained as part of PEASS-ng.

Official project:

PEASS-ng - GitHub

Use official releases or the official repository when obtaining the tool.

Avoid modified copies from untrusted sources.

docs.title: Before Running WinPEAS
docs.text:
First understand the current user context.

Run:

whoami

Then:

whoami /groups

And:

whoami /priv

Useful questions include:

Which user am I?

Am I a local administrator?

Which groups do I belong to?

Which token privileges are available?

What integrity level am I running at?

Without this context, tool output is harder to interpret.

docs.title: Record System Context
docs.text:
Before running a large enumeration tool, record basic host information.

Useful native commands include:

hostname

whoami

systeminfo

PowerShell:

Get-ComputerInfo

where available and permitted.

This creates a baseline for later evidence.

docs.title: Obtaining WinPEAS
docs.text:
Prefer the official PEASS-ng releases or repository.

Verify:

  • repository source;
  • release provenance;
  • filename;
  • hash where appropriate;
  • internal malware-scanning requirements;
  • engagement approval.

Third-party security tools may be detected by endpoint protection even when they are being used legitimately during an authorised assessment.

docs.title: Common WinPEAS Formats
docs.text:
PEASS-ng may provide different WinPEAS builds or forms depending on the release.

Examples can include:

winPEAS.exe
winPEASx64.exe
winPEASx86.exe
winPEAS.bat

The exact filenames available can change between releases.

Always inspect the official release being used rather than assuming a specific filename exists.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Determine whether the host is 32-bit or 64-bit where this matters.

Useful command:

$env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE

Another option:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object OSArchitecture

Choose the appropriate binary for the environment.

docs.title: Basic Execution
docs.text:
A common usage pattern is:

.\winPEAS.exe

The exact binary name depends on the downloaded release.

If using another official build:

.\winPEASx64.exe

Do not assume all PEASS-ng releases use the same naming convention.

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text:
For assessment work, saving output is often more useful than relying entirely on the terminal.

For example:

.\winPEAS.exe | Tee-Object -FilePath .\winpeas-output.txt

This allows the tester to:

  • search results later;
  • compare findings;
  • retain evidence;
  • avoid losing information during long runs.

Be aware that output may contain sensitive information.

Protect the file appropriately.

docs.title: Output May Contain Secrets
docs.text:
WinPEAS can surface information such as:

  • passwords;
  • API keys;
  • connection strings;
  • tokens;
  • usernames;
  • application secrets;
  • sensitive paths.

Do not casually:

  • upload raw output;
  • paste it into public tickets;
  • attach it to reports;
  • commit it to Git;
  • share it outside the authorised assessment team.

Sanitise evidence where necessary.

docs.title: Colour Coding
docs.text:
WinPEAS uses colour to draw attention to potentially interesting items.

A common mistake is:

Red output
    |
    v
Confirmed vulnerability

This is wrong.

The correct interpretation is:

Highlighted output
    |
    v
Worth investigating

Then validate the result manually.

docs.title: WinPEAS Is a Triage Tool
docs.text:
A useful mental model is:

WinPEAS
   |
   v
Triage
   |
   v
Investigation
   |
   v
Validation

Not:

WinPEAS
   |
   v
Automatic Finding Generator

docs.title: Major Enumeration Areas
docs.text:
WinPEAS may inspect areas such as:

System Information
Users and Groups
Token Privileges
Services
Scheduled Tasks
Registry
Filesystem
Installed Software
Credentials
Network
Security Products
Interesting Files
Environment

Each category requires a different validation approach.

docs.title: System Information
docs.text:
System information provides context.

Useful details may include:

  • Windows edition;
  • build;
  • architecture;
  • hostname;
  • domain membership;
  • current user;
  • patch information.

The purpose is to understand the environment, not simply collect version numbers.

docs.title: Patch Information
docs.text:
Operating system version and patch information can provide useful context.

Do not automatically conclude:

Old-looking build
    =
Vulnerable

Instead determine:

  • current patch state;
  • vendor advisory applicability;
  • configuration;
  • exploit preconditions;
  • whether the relevant component is present.

Version-based conclusions require care.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
WinPEAS can enumerate local or domain-related user information visible from the system.

Manual validation may include:

Get-LocalUser

where available.

Or:

net user

Useful questions:

Which users exist?

Which accounts are administrative?

Are service accounts present?

Are disabled accounts still relevant?

Are unusual local accounts configured?

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Review local group membership.

For example:

Get-LocalGroup

and:

Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators

where available.

Or:

net localgroup

Group membership can significantly change the interpretation of a privilege escalation condition.

docs.title: Token Privileges
docs.text:
Check:

whoami /priv

WinPEAS may highlight potentially interesting privileges.

Do not assume a privilege is exploitable simply because it appears in the token.

Consider:

Privilege present?
Privilege enabled?
Current process context?
Operating-system restrictions?
Required preconditions?

Related note:

Windows Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Windows services are one of the most important areas to review.

WinPEAS may identify:

  • service names;
  • service accounts;
  • executable paths;
  • startup modes;
  • unquoted paths;
  • writable service binaries;
  • potentially writable service directories;
  • modifiable service configurations.

The validation model is:

Service
  |
  +-- Runs privileged?
  |
  +-- Binary/path modifiable?
  |
  +-- Configuration modifiable?
  |
  +-- Trigger available?
  |
  v
Potential PrivEsc

Related note:

Windows Services

docs.title: Validate Service Configuration
docs.text:
Use native tooling.

For example:

sc.exe qc ExampleService

This can show information such as:

SERVICE_START_NAME
BINARY_PATH_NAME
START_TYPE

PowerShell can also be useful:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object Name -eq 'ExampleService'

The objective is to confirm what the service actually executes and under which identity.

docs.title: Service Accounts
docs.text:
A service may run as:

LocalSystem
LocalService
NetworkService
Domain account
Custom local account

The potential security impact depends heavily on this execution identity.

A writable binary used by a low-privileged service is not equivalent to one used by LocalSystem.

docs.title: Service Binary Permissions
docs.text:
If WinPEAS highlights a service executable, validate the ACL.

Example:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe"

Review whether the current user or one of their groups has rights such as:

F
M
W

which may correspond to:

Full control
Modify
Write

Do not infer permissions from the directory name alone.

docs.title: Directory Permissions
docs.text:
Even when a binary itself is protected, the containing directory may matter.

Check:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example"

Review:

  • inherited permissions;
  • group permissions;
  • write/modify rights;
  • creator-owner behaviour.

The complete path may matter.

docs.title: Effective Permissions Matter
docs.text:
A tool may flag a path because one ACL entry appears writable.

You still need to understand:

  • inherited ACEs;
  • group membership;
  • deny ACEs;
  • owner;
  • integrity level;
  • application control.

The real question is:

Can the current security context actually modify the object?

docs.title: Service Restartability
docs.text:
A service-related condition may require a restart before changed content executes.

Check whether the current user can control the service.

Example information gathering:

sc.exe query ExampleService

Do not assume the user can stop or start the service.

Possible execution triggers include:

Immediate restart
Automatic recovery
Scheduled restart
System reboot
Administrator action

Document the actual trigger.

docs.title: Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
WinPEAS may highlight unquoted service paths.

Example:

C:\Program Files\Example App\Service.exe

An unquoted path alone is not enough for exploitation.

Also determine whether:

  • an earlier path component can be influenced;
  • relevant directories are writable;
  • the service runs privileged;
  • the service can be triggered.

Related note:

Windows Services

docs.title: Service Configuration Permissions
docs.text:
The service executable might be protected while the service object itself is modifiable.

Relevant properties include:

  • executable path;
  • service identity;
  • startup configuration.

A service configuration weakness can be more significant than a file-permission weakness.

Manual validation is required.

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks can create privileged execution paths.

WinPEAS may identify:

  • task name;
  • user context;
  • trigger;
  • executable;
  • script;
  • argument;
  • potentially writable referenced files.

Related note:

Windows Scheduled Tasks

docs.title: Validate Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Native command:

schtasks.exe /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

For a specific task:

Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "ExampleTask"

Then inspect the action:

(Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "ExampleTask").Actions

docs.title: Task Execution Identity
docs.text:
Important questions include:

Who runs the task?

SYSTEM?

Administrator?

Service account?

Current user?

A writable task script has much greater impact if executed in a privileged context.

docs.title: Task Trigger
docs.text:
Also determine:

When does it execute?

At startup?

At logon?

On a schedule?

On an event?

A condition that executes every minute has different practical characteristics from one requiring a reboot or administrator logon.

docs.title: Task File Permissions
docs.text:
If a task invokes:

C:\ProgramData\Scripts\backup.ps1

validate:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Scripts\backup.ps1"

Also check its parent directory:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Scripts"

docs.title: Registry
docs.text:
WinPEAS can highlight registry locations relevant to privilege escalation.

Potentially important categories include:

  • service configuration;
  • application startup;
  • installer settings;
  • application configuration;
  • credentials;
  • execution-related registry values.

Related note:

Windows Registry

docs.title: Registry Permissions
docs.text:
Validate potentially writable keys.

PowerShell can inspect registry objects, while native tools can query values.

Example:

reg.exe query "HKLM\Software\Example"

For permissions, use an appropriate ACL inspection method.

The key question is:

Can the current user modify a value that a privileged process trusts?

docs.title: AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
Some enumeration tools check Windows Installer policy related to elevated MSI installation.

If such a condition is reported, validate both relevant policy locations and the actual environment before drawing a conclusion.

The security significance depends on whether the configuration permits a lower-privileged user to influence elevated installer execution.

Do not report merely because one registry value exists.

docs.title: Filesystem Enumeration
docs.text:
WinPEAS inspects many filesystem locations.

Potentially interesting findings include:

  • writable privileged executables;
  • writable scripts;
  • configuration files;
  • credential files;
  • weakly protected directories;
  • startup resources.

Related note:

Windows Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Validate Files with icacls
docs.text:
Use:

icacls "C:\Path\To\File"

and:

icacls "C:\Path\To\Directory"

Interpret:

  • explicit ACEs;
  • inherited ACEs;
  • user/group rights;
  • deny entries.

The result should support a specific conclusion.

docs.title: Parent Directory Analysis
docs.text:
A protected file may still be replaceable depending on parent-directory permissions.

Example structure:

C:\
  ProgramData\
    Example\
      service.exe

Check each relevant level where needed.

The question is not only:

Can I write the file?

but also:

Can I rename/delete/replace it through directory permissions?

docs.title: Installed Applications
docs.text:
WinPEAS may identify installed software.

This can help find:

  • privileged services;
  • custom applications;
  • management tools;
  • legacy products;
  • local agents.

Do not convert every old version into a vulnerability.

Validate:

  • exact build;
  • vendor patch status;
  • exposed functionality;
  • configuration;
  • exploit preconditions.

docs.title: Application Directories
docs.text:
Third-party applications are often installed under:

C:\Program Files\
C:\Program Files (x86)\
C:\ProgramData\

Review whether application-specific subdirectories have unusual permissions.

Do not assume the whole top-level directory is writable simply because one application directory is.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
WinPEAS may identify potentially sensitive credential material.

Examples can include:

  • configuration files;
  • scripts;
  • saved credentials;
  • environment variables;
  • deployment artefacts;
  • connection strings;
  • unattended installation files.

Related note:

Windows Credentials

Treat discovered credentials as high-sensitivity assessment data.

docs.title: Credential Findings Require Validation
docs.text:
A string that looks like a password may be:

  • example data;
  • expired;
  • unused;
  • encrypted;
  • placeholder content;
  • test data.

Before describing credential exposure as exploitable, determine whether it is genuine and relevant.

Avoid unnecessary authentication attempts.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables can expose:

  • application paths;
  • credentials;
  • tokens;
  • configuration;
  • execution paths.

Inspect manually:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Security relevance depends on whether sensitive information is actually exposed or whether a privileged process trusts modifiable environment data.

docs.title: PATH
docs.text:
Windows PATH configuration can sometimes matter when privileged software resolves commands without explicit paths.

Inspect:

$env:Path -split ';'

Then assess:

Which directories appear first?

Are any writable?

Does a privileged application actually resolve a command through PATH?

A writable PATH directory without a privileged consumer is not automatically exploitable.

docs.title: DLL Search Paths
docs.text:
WinPEAS may highlight DLL-related conditions.

DLL loading security depends on:

  • application load behaviour;
  • DLL search order;
  • writable locations;
  • application-control policy;
  • execution context.

A writable directory alone does not prove a DLL hijacking path.

Related note:

Windows Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Autoruns and Startup Locations
docs.text:
Startup mechanisms may include:

  • Run keys;
  • Startup directories;
  • services;
  • scheduled tasks;
  • application-specific autostart mechanisms.

The key questions are:

What executes?

Who can modify it?

Who executes it?

When does it execute?

docs.title: Network Information
docs.text:
WinPEAS can provide network context.

This may include:

  • interfaces;
  • listening services;
  • connections;
  • domain information;
  • DNS.

Network data can help identify local services or management components relevant to privilege escalation analysis.

docs.title: Listening Services
docs.text:
A locally bound administrative service may be relevant.

Check:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

where available.

Or:

netstat -ano

Then map the process ID to an application.

Do not interact with services outside assessment scope.

docs.title: Security Products
docs.text:
WinPEAS may identify endpoint-security products and security controls.

Examples can include:

  • Microsoft Defender;
  • EDR;
  • AppLocker;
  • WDAC;
  • PowerShell restrictions.

These controls influence how practical a privilege escalation path may be.

Related notes:

Microsoft Defender

Windows Application Control

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
An execution path may be writable but restricted by AppLocker.

This can affect practical execution.

However, application control does not automatically remove the underlying weak permission.

Separate:

Configuration weakness

from:

Exploitability under current controls

Related note:

Windows Application Control

docs.title: WDAC
docs.text:
Windows Defender Application Control can also restrict execution.

Where applicable, review whether:

  • executable;
  • script;
  • DLL;

execution is constrained.

Again, document the distinction between:

weak permission

and:

execution prevented by defence-in-depth

docs.title: PowerShell Restrictions
docs.text:
WinPEAS execution or PowerShell-based follow-up tooling can be affected by:

  • execution policy;
  • AppLocker;
  • WDAC;
  • language mode;
  • endpoint security.

A blocked script does not mean no privilege escalation condition exists.

Use native commands for validation where necessary.

docs.title: Native Validation Is Important
docs.text:
Useful native Windows tools include:

whoami.exe
sc.exe
schtasks.exe
icacls.exe
reg.exe
net.exe
wmic.exe where available
PowerShell cmdlets

WinPEAS should guide you toward which native checks matter.

docs.title: WinPEAS and PowerUp
docs.text:
WinPEAS and PowerUp overlap in several areas.

A useful workflow is:

WinPEAS
   |
   v
Candidate Service
   |
   v
PowerUp
   |
   v
Second Perspective
   |
   v
Native Validation

Related tool:

PowerUp

docs.title: WinPEAS and PrivescCheck
docs.text:
PrivescCheck can provide another structured perspective on Windows privilege escalation conditions.

WinPEAS
     |
     +--> Candidate

PrivescCheck
     |
     +--> Related candidate

Native tools
     |
     +--> Confirm effective configuration

Related tool:

PrivescCheck

docs.title: WinPEAS and Manual Enumeration
docs.text:
Automated and manual enumeration should complement each other.

WinPEAS
   |
   +-- breadth

Manual Checks
   |
   +-- precision
   +-- context
   +-- interpretation

This combination produces stronger assessment conclusions.

docs.title: Searching WinPEAS Output
docs.text:
Large output can be difficult to review.

If saved:

winpeas-output.txt

search for relevant areas with PowerShell:

Select-String -Path .\winpeas-output.txt -Pattern "service"

or:

Select-String -Path .\winpeas-output.txt -Pattern "writable"

Do not rely only on keyword searching; preserve enough surrounding context to interpret the result.

docs.title: Review by Category
docs.text:
A practical review order is:

1. Current user and groups
2. Privileges
3. Services
4. Scheduled tasks
5. Filesystem permissions
6. Registry
7. Credentials
8. Installed applications
9. Security controls
10. Miscellaneous findings

This helps prevent long output from becoming unmanageable.

docs.title: Prioritising WinPEAS Findings
docs.text:
High-value candidates often share three characteristics:

Current user can influence something
        |
        +
Privileged component trusts it
        |
        +
Execution can be triggered

This is more useful than prioritising based solely on colour.

docs.title: Candidate Scoring Model
docs.text:
A simple mental model can be:

Question Yes/No Can current user modify the resource? Is the resource consumed by a privileged process? Can execution be triggered? Is the path currently active? Are security controls likely to block it? Is additional user interaction required?

More "yes" answers generally mean the candidate deserves deeper investigation.

docs.title: Representative Service Scenario
docs.text:
WinPEAS reports:

Service:
ExampleService

Runs as:
LocalSystem

Binary:
C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe

Potential issue:
Writable binary

Manual validation:

sc.exe qc ExampleService

Then:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe"

Suppose the ACL shows no write or modify rights for the current user.

Conclusion:

The WinPEAS candidate was reviewed, but effective filesystem
permissions did not allow the tested user to modify the service
executable. The suspected privilege escalation path was therefore not
confirmed.

docs.title: Representative Confirmed Permission Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose:

Service:
ExampleService

Account:
LocalSystem

Binary:
C:\ProgramData\Example\Service.exe

Manual validation confirms:

Current standard user:
Modify

The next steps are to determine:

Is the service active?

Can it restart?

Will it execute this exact file?

Do application-control policies affect execution?

Only after the full path is validated should the security condition be reported.

docs.title: Representative Scheduled Task Scenario
docs.text:
WinPEAS reports:

Task:
ExampleBackup

Runs as:
SYSTEM

Action:
C:\ProgramData\Scripts\backup.ps1

Check:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Scripts\backup.ps1"

Then check the directory:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Scripts"

Inspect task details:

schtasks.exe /query /tn "\ExampleBackup" /fo LIST /v

The security question is:

Can the tested user influence content that the SYSTEM task executes?

docs.title: Representative Credential Scenario
docs.text:
WinPEAS identifies:

Potential password in configuration file

Validate carefully:

Is it an actual credential?

Is it still valid?

Which account does it belong to?

Is use of that account in scope?

Is validation necessary?

Do not perform unnecessary authentication tests merely to prove a credential exists.

The exposure itself may already be the relevant issue depending on the engagement.

docs.title: Representative Application Control Scenario
docs.text:
WinPEAS identifies a writable privileged execution path.

AppLocker analysis shows execution from that location is denied.

The correct conclusion may be:

A weak filesystem permission exists, but the tested execution path is
currently constrained by application-control policy. The underlying
permission weakness should still be corrected because the application
control acts as a separate defence-in-depth layer.

This is more accurate than either:

No issue because AppLocker exists

or:

Immediate SYSTEM compromise

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
WinPEAS results can be misleading because of:

  • heuristic assumptions;
  • inherited ACLs;
  • group membership interpretation;
  • disabled services;
  • inactive tasks;
  • stale files;
  • false credential patterns;
  • protected execution paths;
  • security-control interference.

Manual verification is mandatory for high-confidence conclusions.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
WinPEAS can also miss real issues.

Possible reasons include:

  • custom applications;
  • unusual service logic;
  • non-standard directories;
  • transient files;
  • proprietary software;
  • custom IPC;
  • unusual ACL arrangements;
  • application-specific privileged workflows.

A clean WinPEAS output does not prove the system has no privilege escalation path.

docs.title: Do Not Rely on One Tool
docs.text:
Strong local review might combine:

WinPEAS
    |
    +--> broad enumeration

PowerUp
    |
    +--> Windows-specific checks

PrivescCheck
    |
    +--> additional structured checks

Manual Native Tools
    |
    +--> actual validation

The objective is not tool quantity.

The objective is evidence quality.

docs.title: Endpoint Security and Telemetry
docs.text:
Running WinPEAS can produce observable behaviour through:

  • process execution;
  • registry enumeration;
  • WMI/CIM access;
  • filesystem access;
  • security-product interaction.

In purple-team exercises, this can be useful for measuring detection coverage.

Related notes:

Purple Teaming

Detection Engineering

docs.title: WinPEAS in Purple Team Exercises
docs.text:
A purple-team use case may look like:

WinPEAS Execution
      |
      v
Host Enumeration
      |
      v
EDR / Windows Telemetry
      |
      v
Detection Review
      |
      v
Rule Improvement

The exercise objective should be agreed in advance.

docs.title: Tool Transfer
docs.text:
Where transfer is authorised, retain records such as:

Tool:
WinPEAS

Source:
Official PEASS-ng release

Destination:
Approved temporary test directory

Timestamp:
Recorded

Cleanup:
Completed after testing

Do not leave unnecessary assessment tools behind.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
After the assessment, remove transferred tool artefacts where required.

For example:

winPEAS executable
output files
temporary working files

Do not remove legitimate operating-system or security logs.

Evidence retention should follow the engagement's rules.

docs.title: Logging the Run
docs.text:
A useful record is:

Host:
User:
WinPEAS release:
Binary:
Command:
Start time:
End time:
Output file:
Relevant findings:
Manual validation:

This improves reproducibility.

docs.title: Evidence Quality
docs.text:
Weak evidence:

Screenshot of highlighted WinPEAS line

Better evidence:

WinPEAS output
      |
      v
Native configuration query
      |
      v
ACL output
      |
      v
Execution identity
      |
      v
Trigger
      |
      v
Conclusion

The report should explain the chain.

docs.title: Reporting a Validated Service Weakness
docs.text:
Avoid:

WinPEAS identified an insecure service.

Prefer:

The tested standard user had Modify permissions over an executable
configured to run as part of a LocalSystem service. This allowed the
user to influence a privileged execution path. The condition was
validated through the effective filesystem permissions and service
configuration.

docs.title: Reporting a Negative Result
docs.text:
Example:

WinPEAS highlighted a service executable as potentially writable.
Manual validation with icacls showed that the current user and its
groups did not have write or modify permissions. The suspected
privilege escalation path was therefore not confirmed.

Negative validation prevents scanner-style overreporting.

docs.title: Severity Assessment
docs.text:
Privilege escalation severity depends on:

  • starting privilege;
  • resulting privilege;
  • interaction required;
  • trigger requirements;
  • reliability;
  • security controls;
  • environment importance.

Example:

Standard user
    |
    v
SYSTEM

with an immediate and reliable trigger may represent a high-impact issue.

A path requiring rare administrator action may have different practical risk.

docs.title: Remediation Principles
docs.text:
WinPEAS findings commonly lead to remediation in areas such as:

  • ACLs;
  • service configuration;
  • scheduled tasks;
  • registry permissions;
  • credentials;
  • startup paths;
  • installer policy.

The general principle is:

Low-privileged users should not be able to influence resources that are executed or trusted by higher-privileged processes.

docs.title: Service Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove unnecessary write permissions;
  • restrict service configuration rights;
  • protect service executable directories;
  • quote service paths where relevant;
  • use least-privileged service identities.

docs.title: Scheduled Task Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • protect scripts and binaries;
  • protect parent directories;
  • restrict task modification;
  • use least privilege;
  • review unnecessary tasks.

docs.title: Credential Remediation
docs.text:
Typical measures include:

  • remove plaintext secrets;
  • rotate exposed credentials;
  • use secure secret storage;
  • limit file permissions;
  • remove obsolete deployment artefacts.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Do not retest only by rerunning WinPEAS.

For example, after fixing an ACL:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Example\Service.exe"

Verify that the tested low-privileged identity no longer has inappropriate modification rights.

Then confirm the application or service still operates correctly.

Optionally rerun WinPEAS as a secondary regression check.

docs.title: WinPEAS Review Workflow
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

1. Confirm scope
      |
      v
2. Record current identity
      |
      v
3. Record host context
      |
      v
4. Obtain official WinPEAS build
      |
      v
5. Run approved enumeration
      |
      v
6. Save output securely
      |
      v
7. Prioritise interesting findings
      |
      v
8. Validate with native tools
      |
      v
9. Identify privileged consumer
      |
      v
10. Confirm trigger
      |
      v
11. Consider application controls
      |
      v
12. Confirm or reject candidate
      |
      v
13. Capture evidence
      |
      v
14. Clean up assessment artefacts

docs.title: Current User
docs.text: whoami

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: whoami /groups

docs.title: Privileges
docs.text: whoami /priv

docs.title: Basic Execution
docs.text:
.\winPEAS.exe

Use the actual filename from the official release.

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text: .\winPEAS.exe | Tee-Object -FilePath .\winpeas-output.txt

docs.title: Service Configuration
docs.text: sc.exe qc ExampleService

docs.title: Service Status
docs.text: sc.exe query ExampleService

docs.title: File ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\Path\To\File"

docs.title: Directory ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\Path\To\Directory"

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text: schtasks.exe /query /fo LIST /v

docs.title: Specific Scheduled Task
docs.text: schtasks.exe /query /tn "\ExampleTask" /fo LIST /v

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Get-ChildItem Env:

docs.title: PATH
docs.text: $env:Path -split ';'

docs.title: Listening Ports
docs.text:
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

Fallback:

netstat -ano

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Host explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Current identity recorded.
  • [ ] Current groups recorded.
  • [ ] Current privileges recorded.
  • [ ] System architecture known.
  • [ ] Official PEASS-ng source used.
  • [ ] Tool transfer approved where necessary.
  • [ ] Endpoint-security implications understood.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
• [ ] Correct WinPEAS build selected.
  • [ ] Output retained securely.
  • [ ] Sensitive output protected.
  • [ ] Excessive or unnecessary execution avoided.
  • [ ] Tool version or release recorded where useful.

docs.title: Service Review
docs.text:
• [ ] Privileged services identified.
  • [ ] Service account confirmed.
  • [ ] Binary path confirmed.
  • [ ] Binary ACL checked.
  • [ ] Parent directory ACL checked.
  • [ ] Service configuration permissions considered.
  • [ ] Restart/trigger conditions confirmed.
  • [ ] Unquoted paths validated rather than assumed exploitable.

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
• [ ] Privileged tasks identified.
  • [ ] Task identity confirmed.
  • [ ] Action path confirmed.
  • [ ] Script/binary permissions checked.
  • [ ] Parent directories checked.
  • [ ] Trigger confirmed.

docs.title: Registry
docs.text:
• [ ] Interesting keys reviewed.
  • [ ] Effective permissions validated.
  • [ ] Privileged consumer identified.
  • [ ] Installer-related policy interpreted carefully.

docs.title: Filesystem
docs.text:
• [ ] Interesting writable files validated.
  • [ ] Interesting writable directories validated.
  • [ ] Parent directories reviewed.
  • [ ] Actual privileged consumer confirmed.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
• [ ] Potential secrets reviewed carefully.
  • [ ] Sensitive values protected.
  • [ ] Stale/example credentials distinguished from active secrets.
  • [ ] Unnecessary authentication attempts avoided.

docs.title: Security Controls
docs.text:
• [ ] Defender considered.
  • [ ] AppLocker considered.
  • [ ] WDAC considered.
  • [ ] PowerShell restrictions considered.
  • [ ] EDR impact considered.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] WinPEAS result treated as candidate.
  • [ ] Native validation performed.
  • [ ] Effective permissions confirmed.
  • [ ] Privileged execution context confirmed.
  • [ ] Trigger confirmed.
  • [ ] False-positive explanations considered.
  • [ ] Security impact demonstrated appropriately.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Current identity retained.
  • [ ] Relevant WinPEAS excerpt retained.
  • [ ] Native ACL/configuration evidence retained.
  • [ ] Execution context documented.
  • [ ] Trigger documented.
  • [ ] Sensitive values redacted where appropriate.
  • [ ] Finding describes underlying weakness, not WinPEAS output.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
• [ ] WinPEAS binary removed if required.
  • [ ] Temporary output removed if required.
  • [ ] Evidence retained according to engagement policy.
  • [ ] Legitimate logs left intact.
