docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use WinPEAS like this:

Run WinPEAS
    |
    v
Find Red Text
    |
    v
Call It PrivEsc

Use it like this:

Understand Current Identity
        |
        v
Run WinPEAS
        |
        v
Identify Candidate
        |
        v
Understand Why It Was Flagged
        |
        v
Validate With Native Tools
        |
        +-- icacls
        +-- sc.exe
        +-- schtasks.exe
        +-- registry inspection
        |
        v
Confirm Effective Permissions
        |
        v
Identify Privileged Consumer
        |
        v
Confirm Trigger
        |
        v
Consider Security Controls
        |
        v
Determine Actual Impact
        |
        v
Capture Evidence
        |
        v
Report the Underlying Weakness

WinPEAS is most valuable when it reduces the amount of Windows configuration that must be inspected manually.

It identifies where to look.

The tester still has to determine whether the highlighted condition forms a genuine privilege escalation path.

docs.title: Red Teaming Tools
docs.text:
Red teaming tools support authorised adversary simulation by helping operators reproduce realistic attacker behaviours across an environment.

They may be used for:

  • command and control;
  • payload delivery;
  • operator tasking;
  • credential access;
  • lateral movement;
  • persistence;
  • collection;
  • exfiltration simulation;
  • infrastructure management;
  • detection validation;
  • reporting and replay.

A red team tool should never be treated as the objective itself.

The objective is to emulate a defined adversary behaviour safely and measure whether the organisation can prevent, detect, investigate, and respond to it.

Red Team Objective
      |
      v
Adversary Behaviour
      |
      v
Choose Appropriate Tool
      |
      v
Controlled Execution
      |
      v
Telemetry
      |
      v
Detection / Response
      |
      v
Evidence
      |
      v
Assessment Conclusion

Authorised testing only

Use red team tooling only inside explicitly authorised engagements. Command-and-control frameworks and post-exploitation tools can provide powerful remote capabilities and may trigger or bypass security controls depending on configuration. Scope, target systems, persistence, credential access, and network communication must be agreed before use.

docs.title: Where Red Teaming Tools Fit
docs.text:
Red team tooling usually appears after objectives and rules of engagement have been defined.

Threat / Objective
      |
      v
Rules of Engagement
      |
      v
Initial Access Simulation
      |
      v
Command and Control
      |
      v
Post-Exploitation
      |
      +-- Discovery
      +-- Credential Access
      +-- Lateral Movement
      +-- Persistence
      +-- Collection
      |
      v
Detection and Response Measurement
      |
      v
Cleanup
      |
      v
Reporting

Related methodology:

Red Teaming

Purple Teaming

Detection Engineering

docs.title: Core Tool Categories
docs.text:
A practical red team toolkit may include:

Category Example Tools / Technologies Command and control Sliver, Mythic, Havoc, commercial platforms where authorised Payload hosting / delivery HTTP servers, controlled staging infrastructure Remote administration / movement Native Windows tools, WinRM, SMB, RDP, SSH AD analysis NetExec, Impacket, BloodHound, Certipy, Rubeus Credential access support Platform-specific approved tooling Network tunnelling / proxying SOCKS, SSH, controlled tunnelling tools Reconnaissance Nmap, httpx, DNS tooling Detection validation Atomic-style controlled tests, custom test artefacts Evidence Operator logs, timestamps, screenshots, packet captures where needed

The exact tools depend on:

  • objective;
  • scope;
  • platform;
  • detection goals;
  • engagement restrictions.

docs.title: Command and Control
docs.text:
Command-and-control, commonly abbreviated C2, provides a way for an authorised operator to communicate with an implant or agent on a target system.

Conceptually:

Operator
   |
   v
C2 Server
   |
   v
Network Channel
   |
   v
Agent / Implant
   |
   v
Target Host

A C2 framework may provide features such as:

  • tasking;
  • file transfer;
  • process execution;
  • tunnelling;
  • session management;
  • operator collaboration;
  • logging;
  • payload generation.

Detailed note:

C2 Frameworks

docs.title: C2 Is Not the Assessment
docs.text:
A common mistake is to think:

C2 Session Established
      |
      v
Red Team Success

A better model is:

C2 Session
      |
      v
Controlled Capability
      |
      v
Execute Agreed Technique
      |
      v
Observe Defensive Response
      |
      v
Measure Objective

A session is merely the mechanism used to conduct the authorised activity.

docs.title: C2 Framework Selection
docs.text:
Choose a framework based on the engagement.

Useful questions include:

Which operating systems are in scope?

Which transports are permitted?

Which security controls are present?

Is multi-operator support needed?

Is payload generation required?

Is detailed task logging required?

Will the exercise include detection engineering?

Do not choose a framework solely because it is popular.

docs.title: Open-Source and Commercial C2
docs.text:
Red teams may use:

Open-source frameworks
Commercial frameworks
Organisation-specific tooling

Each has different implications for:

  • support;
  • payload behaviour;
  • observability;
  • operator workflow;
  • detection coverage;
  • licensing.

The engagement should define which toolsets are acceptable.

docs.title: Sliver
docs.text:
Sliver is an open-source adversary emulation and red team framework maintained by Bishop Fox.

It supports multi-platform operations and provides capabilities associated with:

  • session management;
  • payload generation;
  • command execution;
  • network interaction;
  • operator workflows.

Official project:

Sliver - GitHub

Official documentation:

Sliver Documentation

docs.title: Mythic
docs.text:
Mythic is a collaborative command-and-control platform designed around modular agents and operator workflows.

It is useful where teams need:

  • multi-user operation;
  • task tracking;
  • agent modularity;
  • browser-based management;
  • collaborative adversary emulation.

Official project:

Mythic - GitHub

docs.title: Havoc
docs.text:
Havoc is another command-and-control framework used in adversary simulation and research.

As with any C2 framework, use it only within a controlled and authorised environment.

Official project:

Havoc - GitHub

docs.title: Framework Features vs Security Objective
docs.text:
The fact that a framework supports a capability does not mean it should be used.

For example:

Framework supports persistence

does not mean:

Persistence is automatically authorised

Similarly:

Framework supports credential dumping

does not mean:

Credential access is automatically in scope

The rules of engagement determine what is allowed.

docs.title: Rules of Engagement
docs.text:
Before red team tooling is deployed, document:

  • target systems;
  • excluded systems;
  • permitted hours;
  • permitted techniques;
  • prohibited techniques;
  • credential handling;
  • persistence rules;
  • data handling;
  • payload storage;
  • cleanup requirements;
  • emergency stop procedure.

The tool should operate inside those constraints.

docs.title: Kill Switch
docs.text:
A red team engagement should define how activity can be stopped quickly.

A practical process may include:

Authorised Contact
      |
      v
Stop Request
      |
      v
Operator Halts Tasks
      |
      v
Disable / Remove C2 Access
      |
      v
Confirm Cleanup

The exact mechanism depends on the engagement.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Red team infrastructure can include:

  • C2 servers;
  • redirectors;
  • domain names;
  • TLS certificates;
  • cloud servers;
  • DNS;
  • payload hosting;
  • logging infrastructure.

Infrastructure should be built specifically for the engagement or reused under a controlled internal process.

docs.title: Infrastructure Segmentation
docs.text:
Separate red team infrastructure from unrelated environments.

A practical model is:

Operator Workstation
      |
      v
Red Team Infrastructure
      |
      v
Authorised Target Environment

Avoid routing unrelated personal or corporate traffic through engagement infrastructure.

docs.title: VPS Use
docs.text:
A VPS can provide:

  • C2 hosting;
  • payload hosting;
  • redirectors;
  • testing infrastructure.

Use:

  • firewall restrictions;
  • strong SSH authentication;
  • minimal exposed services;
  • logging;
  • timely patching.

The VPS itself becomes part of the assessment infrastructure and must be secured.

docs.title: Firewalling Red Team Infrastructure
docs.text:
Restrict unnecessary inbound access.

Conceptually:

Internet
   |
   v
Firewall
   |
   +-- Required management
   +-- Required C2 listener
   +-- Required web listener
   |
   X
Everything else

Avoid exposing management services to broad networks when not required.

docs.title: SSH Management
docs.text:
Prefer key-based authentication for management infrastructure.

Protect:

  • private keys;
  • operator accounts;
  • sudo access;
  • SSH configuration.

Do not place private keys in assessment reports or public repositories.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Where HTTPS is used, TLS should provide normal transport protection.

Certificates may come from:

  • public certificate authorities;
  • controlled internal PKI;
  • engagement-specific certificates.

TLS is not a substitute for authorisation or C2 operational security.

docs.title: Redirectors
docs.text:
A redirector can separate exposed infrastructure from the primary C2 server.

Conceptually:

Agent
  |
  v
Redirector
  |
  v
C2 Server

Redirectors may also help:

  • isolate infrastructure;
  • enforce routing;
  • collect network telemetry.

Use them only where the engagement architecture requires them.

docs.title: Payload Hosting
docs.text:
Red teams may need to deliver test artefacts.

Potential methods include:

  • HTTP;
  • HTTPS;
  • SMB;
  • approved software deployment mechanisms;
  • removable media in physical exercises.

Hosting should be limited to authorised artefacts.

docs.title: Simple HTTP Hosting
docs.text:
For controlled lab or engagement delivery, a temporary web server may be appropriate.

Example:

python3 -m http.server 8000

This serves files from the current directory.

Before use:

  • ensure only intended files are present;
  • restrict network access where possible;
  • stop the service after testing.

Do not expose sensitive assessment directories accidentally.

docs.title: Payload Inventory
docs.text:
Keep an inventory of delivered artefacts.

Example:

Artifact:
test-agent.exe

Hash:
SHA256 recorded

Source:
Red team build

Target:
Authorised workstation

Purpose:
C2 connectivity validation

Cleanup:
Required

This makes cleanup and reporting easier.

docs.title: Hashing Artefacts
docs.text:
On Linux:

sha256sum test-agent.exe

On Windows:

Get-FileHash .\test-agent.exe -Algorithm SHA256

Recording hashes helps prove exactly which artefact was used.

docs.title: Initial Access Simulation
docs.text:
Initial access should reproduce an agreed behaviour rather than attempt every available method.

Examples may include:

  • controlled phishing simulation;
  • approved file delivery;
  • exposed application testing;
  • assumed breach;
  • pre-positioned agent;
  • physical access exercise.

The chosen method should match the assessment objective.

docs.title: Assumed Breach
docs.text:
An assumed-breach engagement starts with a pre-defined foothold.

Example:

Standard Domain User
      |
      +
Controlled Workstation Access
      |
      v
Internal Adversary Simulation

This avoids spending exercise time on initial-access techniques when internal detection and lateral movement are the real objectives.

docs.title: Pre-Positioned Agent
docs.text:
A controlled agent may be installed by administrators before the exercise.

This can reduce operational risk.

Blue Team / Admin
      |
      v
Approved Test Agent
      |
      v
Red Team Begins From Agreed Position

This can be especially useful in purple-team exercises.

docs.title: Native Tools
docs.text:
Red team operations often benefit from native operating-system utilities.

Examples on Windows may include:

whoami
hostname
ipconfig
net
nltest
sc.exe
schtasks.exe
PowerShell

Linux examples include:

id
hostname
ip
ss
ps
systemctl

Native tooling can reduce the need for unnecessary third-party binaries.

docs.title: Native Does Not Mean Invisible
docs.text:
A common misconception is:

Native Windows tool
      =
Undetectable

This is incorrect.

Native utilities can generate:

  • process telemetry;
  • command-line telemetry;
  • network activity;
  • authentication events;
  • security logs.

Use them because they are appropriate, not because they are assumed to be invisible.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Discovery techniques help understand the compromised environment.

Potential areas include:

  • hostname;
  • current user;
  • groups;
  • network interfaces;
  • processes;
  • services;
  • domain information;
  • nearby systems.

The exercise should define how much discovery is necessary.

docs.title: Discovery Should Be Purposeful
docs.text:
Avoid:

Run every discovery command

Prefer:

What information do I need for the next objective?

For example:

Need domain context
    |
    v
Query domain context only

This reduces unnecessary telemetry and operational impact.

docs.title: Active Directory Tooling
docs.text:
Active Directory-focused tooling may include:

  • NetExec;
  • Impacket;
  • BloodHound;
  • Certipy;
  • Rubeus;
  • PowerView.

Related section:

Active Directory Tools

Use these tools according to a specific AD objective.

docs.title: BloodHound in Red Teaming
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify potential privilege paths.

Example:

Current User
     |
     v
Group Relationship
     |
     v
Computer Control
     |
     v
Higher-Value Identity

A graph path should still be validated before operational use.

docs.title: NetExec in Red Teaming
docs.text:
NetExec can assist with:

  • SMB enumeration;
  • authentication validation;
  • remote access mapping;
  • LDAP analysis.

Avoid broad authentication attempts that could lock accounts.

docs.title: Impacket in Red Teaming
docs.text:
Impacket provides protocol tooling for authorised Windows and AD workflows.

Because many utilities can perform remote actions, use only the specific utility required for the exercise.

docs.title: Credential Access
docs.text:
Credential access is a high-impact part of red teaming.

It may involve:

  • credential files;
  • tokens;
  • cached authentication;
  • password stores;
  • Kerberos material;
  • application credentials.

Credential access should be explicitly covered by the rules of engagement.

docs.title: Use Test Credentials Where Possible
docs.text:
Where the exercise objective can be met without collecting real user credentials, prefer:

  • synthetic accounts;
  • pre-created test secrets;
  • controlled canary credentials.

This reduces data-handling risk.

docs.title: Credential Minimisation
docs.text:
Do not collect more credential material than necessary.

For example:

Objective:
Validate EDR detection of credential access

Required:
One controlled test identity

Not required:
Bulk collection of employee credentials

Align collection with the objective.

docs.title: Credential Storage
docs.text:
Any collected authentication material should be protected.

Do not place:

  • passwords;
  • hashes;
  • tickets;
  • tokens;
  • private keys;

in public notes or screenshots.

docs.title: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Lateral movement tests whether an adversary can move from one authorised host to another.

Potential mechanisms include legitimate remote administration technologies such as:

  • WinRM;
  • SMB;
  • RDP;
  • SSH;
  • remote management systems.

The security question is:

Why is this identity allowed to access the destination?

not:

Which tool connected?

docs.title: Lateral Movement Scope
docs.text:
Every destination must be in scope.

A broad domain credential does not grant permission to access every system it can technically reach.

Maintain an explicit target list.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Lateral movement testing can validate segmentation.

Example:

Workstation Segment
      |
      X
Server Management Segment

If an authorised test identity unexpectedly reaches the protected segment, investigate the control failure.

docs.title: Remote Administration
docs.text:
Legitimate administration protocols may be used by attackers and administrators alike.

Defensive conclusions should therefore consider:

  • user identity;
  • source host;
  • destination;
  • timing;
  • process lineage;
  • command context.

Tool name alone is weak detection logic.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Persistence techniques cause access to survive:

  • process termination;
  • logout;
  • reboot;
  • service restart.

Persistence is often more operationally sensitive than normal execution.

Use persistence only where explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Persistence Validation
docs.text:
A lower-impact approach may be:

Create controlled persistence artefact
      |
      v
Confirm detection
      |
      v
Remove immediately

rather than leaving it active for the remainder of the engagement.

docs.title: Persistence Inventory
docs.text:
If persistence is used, record:

Host
Technique
File / registry / task / service
Creation time
Expected trigger
Cleanup time

No persistence mechanism should be forgotten during cleanup.

docs.title: Collection
docs.text:
Collection simulates an adversary identifying information of interest.

Prefer:

  • synthetic documents;
  • canary data;
  • pre-approved datasets.

Avoid collecting real sensitive business information when the same objective can be demonstrated safely.

docs.title: Exfiltration Simulation
docs.text:
Exfiltration does not always require sending actual sensitive data externally.

A safer model may use:

Synthetic Data
      |
      v
Controlled Transfer
      |
      v
Detection Validation

This proves the control objective without unnecessary data exposure.

docs.title: Network Tunnelling
docs.text:
Some operations require controlled tunnelling or proxying.

Examples include:

  • SOCKS proxying;
  • SSH tunnels;
  • C2-supported proxying.

Tunnelling can change network reachability and should be specifically authorised.

docs.title: SOCKS
docs.text:
A SOCKS proxy can allow operator tools to reach services through an established session.

Conceptually:

Operator Tool
     |
     v
SOCKS Proxy
     |
     v
Compromised Host
     |
     v
Internal Service

This can be useful for controlled internal testing.

docs.title: SSH Tunnelling
docs.text:
SSH can provide controlled port forwarding in Linux or mixed environments.

Use it only through authorised systems and accounts.

Document temporary forwarding so it can be removed after use.

docs.title: ProxyChains
docs.text:
ProxyChains can route compatible Linux tools through supported proxy services.

Its use should be deliberate because it can cause tools to interact with internal systems through a pivot.

Maintain scope discipline.

docs.title: Network Scanning Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Do not automatically run broad port scans through C2 or SOCKS infrastructure.

Consider:

  • bandwidth;
  • latency;
  • target scope;
  • IDS impact;
  • stability.

Use focused discovery where possible.

docs.title: C2 Transport
docs.text:
C2 communications may use different transports depending on the framework.

Examples can include:

  • HTTPS;
  • DNS;
  • other framework-supported channels.

The transport should match the exercise objective and rules.

docs.title: HTTPS C2
docs.text:
HTTPS may resemble normal encrypted web traffic at the network layer.

Detection can still use:

  • destination reputation;
  • process behaviour;
  • TLS metadata;
  • timing;
  • endpoint telemetry.

Encryption does not make activity invisible.

docs.title: DNS-Based C2
docs.text:
DNS-based communication can generate distinctive query patterns.

It can also create operational load and dependencies on DNS infrastructure.

Use it only where specifically required for the exercise.

docs.title: Beaconing
docs.text:
Periodic agent check-ins may create regular network patterns.

Conceptually:

Agent
 |
 +---- wait ----> callback
 |
 +---- wait ----> callback

Regularity can become a detection signal.

Some frameworks support configurable intervals.

Changes should remain within the exercise design.

docs.title: Jitter
docs.text:
Jitter changes timing between agent callbacks.

Its purpose in adversary simulation may be to reproduce less predictable timing.

Do not use traffic shaping solely to avoid detection unless evasion testing is specifically authorised.

docs.title: Detection Evasion
docs.text:
Red teaming may include testing whether security controls resist evasion.

This must be explicitly authorised.

There is an important distinction:

Test Detection Robustness

versus:

Disable or Destroy Security Controls

The latter carries substantially greater operational risk.

docs.title: Security Control Tampering
docs.text:
Avoid:

  • disabling EDR;
  • stopping antivirus;
  • deleting logs;
  • changing central security policy;

unless this is an explicit, approved objective.

Many detection objectives can be measured without tampering with defensive controls.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Windows environments may use:

  • AppLocker;
  • WDAC;
  • Defender;
  • Constrained Language Mode.

Related notes:

Windows Application Control

Microsoft Defender

These controls are part of the environment being assessed.

docs.title: Red Team Response to Blocked Execution
docs.text:
If an artefact is blocked:

Attempt
  |
  v
Control Blocks
  |
  v
Record Evidence

Do not automatically attempt every possible bypass.

Whether further evasion is appropriate depends on the exercise objective.

docs.title: Endpoint Telemetry
docs.text:
Red team activity may generate:

  • process creation;
  • parent-child process relationships;
  • file writes;
  • registry modification;
  • module loading;
  • script execution;
  • network connections;
  • authentication events.

This telemetry is often more valuable than whether one antivirus signature fired.

docs.title: Network Telemetry
docs.text:
Network controls may observe:

  • DNS;
  • proxy traffic;
  • TLS connections;
  • SMB;
  • Kerberos;
  • LDAP;
  • RDP;
  • SSH.

The exercise should map techniques to expected telemetry sources.

docs.title: Purple Team Integration
docs.text:
Red team tools can become controlled inputs to purple-team validation.

Technique
   |
   v
Red Team Action
   |
   v
Telemetry
   |
   v
Blue Team Investigation
   |
   v
Feedback
   |
   v
Detection Improvement

Related section:

Purple Teaming

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK provides a useful common language for describing adversary behaviours.

A red team test may map:

Tool Action
      |
      v
Technique
      |
      v
ATT&CK ID

The tool itself should not be the primary mapping.

For example:

PowerShell

can be used for many different techniques.

Map the behaviour, not merely the executable.

Official resource:

MITRE ATT&CK

docs.title: Technique Mapping
docs.text:
A useful test record might contain:

Technique:
Service Discovery

ATT&CK:
Relevant technique identifier

Action:
Enumerated local services

Tool:
Native Windows command

Expected telemetry:
Process creation
Service enumeration

This is more useful than simply recording the tool name.

docs.title: Atomic Testing
docs.text:
Small, controlled tests can be useful for validating one technique at a time.

This is particularly effective for:

  • purple teaming;
  • detection engineering;
  • regression testing.

A small test is often easier to measure than a long multi-stage C2 workflow.

docs.title: Operator Logs
docs.text:
Maintain operator logs.

Useful fields include:

Timestamp
Operator
Host
User context
Technique
Command / action
Tool
Expected result
Observed result
Cleanup

These logs become essential during incident-response validation.

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Operator, infrastructure, endpoint, SIEM, and EDR timestamps should be as aligned as practical.

Otherwise:

Red Team:
14:02

EDR:
14:07

SIEM:
13:59

can make event correlation unnecessarily difficult.

docs.title: Timestamp Discipline
docs.text:
Use a consistent timezone for reporting.

For example:

UTC

or the engagement's agreed local timezone.

Document the timezone explicitly.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each relevant red team activity, retain:

Objective:
Technique:
ATT&CK mapping:
Target:
User context:
Tool:
Tool version:
Timestamp:
Command / task:
Observed target result:
Observed defensive response:
Cleanup status:

This supports both offensive and defensive conclusions.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots can be useful for:

  • C2 session evidence;
  • defensive alerts;
  • command execution;
  • blocked actions.

However, screenshots alone are weak evidence.

Prefer combining them with:

  • operator logs;
  • raw command output;
  • EDR event details;
  • SIEM events.

docs.title: Tool Logs
docs.text:
Many C2 frameworks retain:

  • operator activity;
  • session metadata;
  • task history.

Preserve relevant logs according to engagement requirements.

Do not retain them longer than necessary if they contain sensitive information.

docs.title: Red Team Data Sensitivity
docs.text:
Operational data may contain:

  • usernames;
  • hostnames;
  • internal IPs;
  • credentials;
  • hashes;
  • file contents;
  • business information.

Treat red team project directories as sensitive.

docs.title: Separate Engagement Workspaces
docs.text:
Use separate directories per engagement.

Example:

engagements/
└── example-client/
    ├── infrastructure/
    ├── payloads/
    ├── logs/
    ├── evidence/
    └── cleanup/

Avoid mixing client artefacts.

docs.title: Artefact Naming
docs.text:
Use descriptive filenames.

Example:

2026-09-10_ws01_process-discovery.txt

rather than:

output1.txt

This makes evidence easier to correlate.

docs.title: Payload Versioning
docs.text:
If multiple payload builds are used, record:

Build
Hash
Configuration
Target
Date

This avoids uncertainty about which binary generated which telemetry.

docs.title: C2 Server Security
docs.text:
A C2 server may contain:

  • active sessions;
  • credentials;
  • payloads;
  • operational logs.

Protect it like sensitive security infrastructure.

Recommended principles include:

  • restrict management access;
  • strong authentication;
  • patch operating system;
  • minimal services;
  • firewalling;
  • encrypted storage where appropriate;
  • backups only where necessary.

docs.title: Multi-Operator Access
docs.text:
If several operators share a framework:

  • use individual accounts where supported;
  • avoid credential sharing;
  • maintain audit logs;
  • coordinate tasking.

This improves accountability.

docs.title: Operator Coordination
docs.text:
Without coordination, two operators may:

  • duplicate actions;
  • interfere with application state;
  • create unnecessary noise;
  • damage cleanup accuracy.

Use an agreed operation log or team channel.

docs.title: Tool Provenance
docs.text:
Use official project sources.

Record:

Repository
Version / commit
Build method
Hash

where practical.

Avoid unknown precompiled binaries.

docs.title: Build Integrity
docs.text:
If a framework is built from source, retain:

Source revision
Build environment
Build date
Output hash

This improves reproducibility.

docs.title: Supply-Chain Risk
docs.text:
Red team tools themselves can be compromised.

Security tooling often receives broad access to:

  • credentials;
  • networks;
  • endpoint sessions.

Therefore verify the source before execution.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Cleanup is part of the assessment.

Potential artefacts include:

  • agents;
  • binaries;
  • scripts;
  • scheduled tasks;
  • services;
  • registry entries;
  • user accounts;
  • certificates;
  • tunnels;
  • temporary files;
  • payload hosting.

Every state-changing action should have a cleanup plan.

docs.title: Cleanup Ledger
docs.text:
Maintain a table such as:

Host Artefact Created Removal Required Removed WS01 Test agent 14:05 Yes Yes SRV01 Temporary file 14:27 Yes Yes LAB01 Test scheduled task 15:01 Yes Yes

This reduces the chance of leaving artefacts behind.

docs.title: Do Not Delete Defensive Evidence
docs.text:
Cleanup does not mean erasing security logs.

Do not delete:

  • Windows event logs;
  • EDR telemetry;
  • SIEM data;
  • firewall logs;

unless log-tampering itself is a specifically authorised technique.

Normal cleanup removes red team artefacts, not defensive evidence.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Red team findings should describe control outcomes.

Avoid:

Sliver obtained SYSTEM.

Prefer:

The tested standard-user context could influence a privileged service
execution path, resulting in code execution as LocalSystem. The
resulting activity did not generate a timely defensive alert during the
exercise.

This explains:

  • initial privilege;
  • weakness;
  • impact;
  • detection outcome.

docs.title: Detection Findings
docs.text:
A red team exercise may produce findings even when prevention works.

Example:

Execution prevented by WDAC

This may be a positive control result.

But if the organisation did not detect the attempt despite expecting detection, there may still be a visibility gap.

docs.title: Prevention and Detection Are Separate
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Technique
   |
   +--> Prevention?
   |
   +--> Detection?
   |
   +--> Investigation?
   |
   +--> Response?

A blocked technique can still generate valuable detection evidence.

docs.title: Measuring Outcome
docs.text:
For each test, record:

Prevented?
Detected?
Alerted?
Investigated?
Escalated?
Contained?

This provides a richer result than simply:

Success / Failure

docs.title: Red Team Tool Success Does Not Equal Control Failure
docs.text:
If a C2 agent connects successfully, that does not automatically mean the organisation failed.

The assessment may be testing:

  • post-compromise detection;
  • lateral movement;
  • identity security;
  • response speed.

Interpret results against the agreed objective.

docs.title: Failed Tool Execution Does Not Equal Strong Security
docs.text:
Similarly:

Payload blocked

does not prove:

Environment is secure

Another allowed execution path may still exist.

The test proves only the specific observed condition.

docs.title: False Conclusions
docs.text:
Avoid:

EDR did not alert in five minutes
    =
Undetectable

Possible alternative explanations include:

  • delayed ingestion;
  • alert routing;
  • suppression;
  • analyst backlog;
  • missing test correlation;
  • wrong telemetry source.

Validate with the defensive team.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
Before any red team action ask:

Could this disrupt production?

Could this lock an account?

Could this restart a service?

Could this corrupt data?

Could this generate large traffic?

Could this affect a third party?

If the answer is yes, use a lower-impact validation approach where possible.

docs.title: High-Risk Actions
docs.text:
Examples that normally deserve explicit approval include:

  • password spraying;
  • persistence;
  • security-control tampering;
  • credential dumping;
  • broad lateral movement;
  • production service restart;
  • destructive file modification;
  • kernel exploitation;
  • mass scanning;
  • data exfiltration.

docs.title: Read-Only First
docs.text:
A good operating principle is:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Understand
   |
   v
Validate Read-Only
   |
   v
Escalate Test Intensity Only If Needed

This reduces avoidable risk.

docs.title: Stop Conditions
docs.text:
Define stop conditions such as:

  • production instability;
  • unexpected outage;
  • real malware discovery;
  • unintended third-party impact;
  • account lockout;
  • sensitive data exposure beyond agreed limits.

Operators should know who to contact immediately.

docs.title: Need Command and Control
docs.text:
Use an approved C2 framework.

Examples:

Sliver
Mythic
Havoc
Approved commercial framework

docs.title: Need Active Directory Analysis
docs.text:
Use:

NetExec
Impacket
BloodHound
Certipy
Rubeus

as appropriate.

docs.title: Need Web Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Use:

httpx
WhatWeb
Wappalyzer
Nmap

Related section:

Web Enumeration Tools

docs.title: Need Web Application Testing
docs.text:
Use:

Burp Suite
ffuf
Nuclei
Katana

Related section:

Web Application Testing Tools

docs.title: Need Windows Privilege Escalation Enumeration
docs.text:
Use:

WinPEAS
PowerUp
PrivescCheck

Related section:

Privilege Escalation Tools

docs.title: Need Linux Privilege Escalation Enumeration
docs.text:
Use:

LinPEAS
linux-smart-enumeration

docs.title: Engagement Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Objectives documented.
  • [ ] Rules of engagement approved.
  • [ ] In-scope systems defined.
  • [ ] Excluded systems defined.
  • [ ] Approved techniques defined.
  • [ ] Prohibited techniques defined.
  • [ ] Emergency contacts defined.
  • [ ] Stop conditions defined.
  • [ ] Cleanup requirements defined.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• [ ] C2 infrastructure secured.
  • [ ] Management access restricted.
  • [ ] SSH keys protected.
  • [ ] Firewall configured.
  • [ ] Unnecessary services disabled.
  • [ ] TLS configured where required.
  • [ ] Infrastructure logging enabled.
  • [ ] Infrastructure ownership documented.

docs.title: Payloads
docs.text:
• [ ] Payload source trusted.
  • [ ] Build/revision recorded.
  • [ ] SHA256 recorded.
  • [ ] Intended target recorded.
  • [ ] Delivery method authorised.
  • [ ] Cleanup plan documented.

docs.title: C2
docs.text:
• [ ] Framework approved.
  • [ ] Version recorded.
  • [ ] Listener configuration documented.
  • [ ] Operator accounts controlled.
  • [ ] Session scope monitored.
  • [ ] Tasking logged.
  • [ ] Unnecessary capabilities avoided.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• [ ] Commands aligned with objective.
  • [ ] Broad enumeration avoided where unnecessary.
  • [ ] Sensitive systems excluded.
  • [ ] Output protected.

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
• [ ] Domain scope confirmed.
  • [ ] Credentials handled securely.
  • [ ] Account lockout risk reviewed.
  • [ ] NetExec/Impacket modules selected carefully.
  • [ ] BloodHound collection scoped.
  • [ ] Certipy actions reviewed.
  • [ ] Kerberos actions controlled.

docs.title: Credential Access
docs.text:
• [ ] Explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Real credentials minimised.
  • [ ] Synthetic credentials used where possible.
  • [ ] Credential artefacts protected.
  • [ ] Validation limited to objective.

docs.title: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
• [ ] Destination in scope.
  • [ ] Protocol approved.
  • [ ] Identity understood.
  • [ ] Segmentation objectives documented.
  • [ ] State-changing actions minimised.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
• [ ] Explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Technique documented.
  • [ ] Trigger understood.
  • [ ] Artefact recorded.
  • [ ] Removal procedure tested.
  • [ ] Persistence removed after objective where appropriate.

docs.title: Collection / Exfiltration
docs.text:
• [ ] Synthetic data used where possible.
  • [ ] Data volume minimised.
  • [ ] Destination controlled.
  • [ ] Sensitive information protected.
  • [ ] Cleanup confirmed.

docs.title: Detection Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] ATT&CK technique mapped.
  • [ ] Expected telemetry documented.
  • [ ] Action timestamp recorded.
  • [ ] EDR/SIEM evidence correlated.
  • [ ] Prevention measured separately from detection.
  • [ ] Analyst response measured where applicable.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Operator logs retained.
  • [ ] Tool versions retained.
  • [ ] Commands/actions retained.
  • [ ] Target/user context retained.
  • [ ] Relevant screenshots retained.
  • [ ] Sensitive secrets redacted.
  • [ ] Timezone documented.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
• [ ] Agents removed.
  • [ ] Payloads removed.
  • [ ] Scripts removed.
  • [ ] Temporary services removed.
  • [ ] Scheduled tasks removed.
  • [ ] Persistence removed.
  • [ ] Tunnels closed.
  • [ ] Certificates handled appropriately.
  • [ ] Test accounts handled according to plan.
  • [ ] Defensive logs preserved.
  • [ ] Cleanup independently confirmed.

Deploy C2
   |
   v
Run Techniques
   |
   v
Try to Avoid Detection
   |
   v
Declare Success

Use them like this:

Define Objective
      |
      v
Define Rules of Engagement
      |
      v
Choose Adversary Behaviour
      |
      v
Choose Appropriate Tool
      |
      v
Execute Controlled Technique
      |
      v
Record Exact Timestamp
      |
      v
Observe Target Result
      |
      v
Observe Defensive Telemetry
      |
      +-- Prevention
      +-- Detection
      +-- Investigation
      +-- Response
      |
      v
Validate Security Conclusion
      |
      v
Clean Up
      |
      v
Feed Lessons Back Into Defences

Red team tools provide the technical capability to reproduce attacker behaviour.

Their value comes from using that capability in a controlled way to answer a defined security question, measure the effectiveness of defensive controls, and produce evidence that the organisation can act on.

docs.title: C2 Frameworks
docs.text:
Command-and-control frameworks, commonly abbreviated as C2 frameworks, provide authorised red team operators with a structured way to manage remote test agents, issue tasks, maintain operator workflows, and collect evidence during adversary simulation.

A C2 framework may provide capabilities such as:

  • agent or implant management;
  • operator tasking;
  • remote command execution;
  • file transfer;
  • session management;
  • transport configuration;
  • operator collaboration;
  • SOCKS or pivot support;
  • task logging;
  • payload generation;
  • infrastructure management;
  • post-exploitation modules.

The framework itself is not the objective.

A better model is:

Assessment Objective
      |
      v
Adversary Behaviour
      |
      v
C2 Framework
      |
      v
Controlled Action
      |
      v
Endpoint / Network Telemetry
      |
      v
Detection and Response
      |
      v
Evidence

Authorised testing only

C2 frameworks provide powerful remote administration and post-exploitation capabilities. Use them only in explicitly authorised engagements and only within agreed rules of engagement. Payload deployment, persistence, credential access, lateral movement, tunnelling, and security-control testing should be separately authorised where relevant.

docs.title: Where C2 Fits
docs.text:
C2 typically appears after a controlled foothold or as part of an assumed-breach exercise.

Rules of Engagement
      |
      v
Initial Access / Assumed Breach
      |
      v
Agent Execution
      |
      v
C2 Session
      |
      v
Approved Technique
      |
      v
Telemetry
      |
      v
Detection / Response Measurement

Related notes:

Red Teaming Tools

Red Teaming

Purple Teaming

Detection Engineering

docs.title: Basic C2 Architecture
docs.text:
A simplified C2 architecture contains:

Operator
   |
   v
Team Server
   |
   v
Listener
   |
   v
Network
   |
   v
Agent
   |
   v
Target Host

Depending on the framework, there may also be:

Redirector
Proxy
Database
Web UI
Multiple Operators
Payload Server

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
Most modern C2 platforms contain some variation of the following components.

Component Purpose Team server Coordinates sessions, listeners, tasks, and operators Operator client Interface used by the red team operator Listener Receives agent communications Agent / implant Runs on the authorised endpoint Transport Defines how communication occurs Payload builder Produces agent artefacts Tasking system Sends operator actions to an agent Logging Records operator and agent activity Collaboration layer Supports multiple operators Pivot / proxy layer Provides access through an established foothold

Framework terminology varies.

docs.title: C2 Is Remote Tasking
docs.text:
At the most basic level:

Operator
   |
   | Task
   v
Agent
   |
   | Result
   v
Operator

Examples of legitimate red-team tasks may include:

  • identity discovery;
  • host information collection;
  • controlled process execution;
  • checking network configuration;
  • testing visibility of approved techniques.

The task should always exist because it supports an agreed objective.

docs.title: C2 Is Not Automatically Persistence
docs.text:
A C2 agent may run only for the lifetime of a process.

Agent Starts
     |
     v
C2 Session
     |
     v
Process Ends
     |
     v
Session Ends

Persistence is a separate technique.

Do not automatically configure persistence merely because the C2 framework supports it.

docs.title: C2 Is Not Automatically Evasion
docs.text:
C2 tools often provide features associated with stealth, obfuscation, or transport customisation.

The existence of those capabilities does not mean they should be used.

A red team should distinguish:

Normal authorised C2 operation

from:

Explicit evasion testing

Evasion activity should only be performed when specifically permitted.

docs.title: Rules of Engagement First
docs.text:
Before deploying a C2 framework, confirm:

Which systems are in scope?

Which users are in scope?

Which payload types are allowed?

Which transports are allowed?

Can agents persist?

Can credentials be accessed?

Can tunnelling occur?

Can security controls be tested?

Which actions are prohibited?

The answers determine framework configuration.

docs.title: Framework Selection
docs.text:
A framework should be chosen based on the engagement rather than popularity.

Useful selection questions include:

Which operating systems are in scope?

Do multiple operators need access?

Which network transports are permitted?

Is browser-based management preferred?

Is cross-platform support required?

How important are audit logs?

Will detection engineering be part of the exercise?

Is commercial support required?

docs.title: Common C2 Frameworks
docs.text:
Commonly encountered frameworks include:

  • Sliver;
  • Mythic;
  • Havoc;
  • commercial red team platforms;
  • organisation-developed internal C2.

Each has different architecture and operational characteristics.

docs.title: Sliver
docs.text:
Sliver is an open-source adversary emulation and red team framework maintained by Bishop Fox.

It supports multi-platform red team operations and provides capabilities associated with:

  • agent management;
  • listener management;
  • operator tasking;
  • remote execution;
  • networking;
  • session management;
  • multi-operator workflows.

Official resources:

Sliver - GitHub

Sliver Documentation

docs.title: Sliver Architecture
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Operator
   |
   v
Sliver Server
   |
   v
Listener
   |
   v
Agent

The server coordinates:

  • listeners;
  • sessions;
  • operators;
  • tasking;
  • results.

Use the official Sliver documentation for current installation and operational syntax.

docs.title: Sliver Use Cases
docs.text:
Sliver may be suitable when:

  • cross-platform support is required;
  • an open-source C2 is desired;
  • multiple operators need access;
  • structured red team workflows are required;
  • adversary emulation is being performed in a controlled lab or engagement.

docs.title: Mythic
docs.text:
Mythic is a modular collaborative C2 platform.

It provides a framework into which different agents and communication components can be integrated.

Official project:

Mythic - GitHub

Official documentation:

Mythic Documentation

docs.title: Mythic Architecture
docs.text:
A simplified model is:

Operators
    |
    v
Mythic Platform
    |
    +-- Agents
    +-- C2 Profiles
    +-- Tasks
    +-- Results
    +-- Web Interface

Its modular approach can be useful where an engagement requires different agents or communication patterns.

docs.title: Mythic Use Cases
docs.text:
Mythic may be useful where:

  • operator collaboration is important;
  • a web-based interface is preferred;
  • modular agent development is useful;
  • multiple communication profiles are needed;
  • detailed task tracking is valuable.

docs.title: Havoc
docs.text:
Havoc is another command-and-control framework used in red team and adversary simulation environments.

Official project:

Havoc - GitHub

Its use should follow the same operational controls applied to other C2 frameworks.

docs.title: Havoc Use Cases
docs.text:
Havoc may be encountered in:

  • red team labs;
  • adversary emulation;
  • training environments;
  • controlled security assessments.

Framework capability should never be interpreted as permission to use every available feature.

docs.title: Commercial C2 Platforms
docs.text:
Commercial red team platforms may provide:

  • vendor support;
  • enterprise collaboration;
  • documentation;
  • maintained payloads;
  • reporting;
  • team management.

The organisation may select a commercial platform because of:

  • support requirements;
  • procurement policy;
  • assurance;
  • operational maturity;
  • established internal procedures.

The same rules of engagement apply regardless of licensing model.

docs.title: Internal C2 Platforms
docs.text:
Some organisations build or maintain their own C2 tooling.

Advantages can include:

  • predictable behaviour;
  • controlled source code;
  • custom telemetry;
  • reduced dependency on public frameworks;
  • tailored workflows.

Disadvantages can include:

  • maintenance burden;
  • security risk;
  • incomplete testing;
  • operator training requirements.

Internal tooling should be treated like production security software.

docs.title: C2 Server
docs.text:
The team server is the central component.

It may store:

  • session information;
  • task history;
  • payload configuration;
  • credentials;
  • operator activity;
  • target metadata.

Compromise of the team server could expose the entire exercise.

Therefore, it should be strongly protected.

docs.title: C2 Server Security
docs.text:
Recommended principles include:

Dedicated Infrastructure
Restricted Management Access
Strong Authentication
Minimal Services
Firewalling
Patch Management
Operator Logging
Secure Backups Where Needed

Do not expose C2 management interfaces broadly to the internet.

docs.title: Dedicated Infrastructure
docs.text:
Prefer separate infrastructure for red team operations.

For example:

Operator Workstation
      |
      v
Dedicated C2 Server
      |
      v
Authorised Target Network

Avoid mixing:

  • personal workloads;
  • unrelated client data;
  • production corporate services;
  • C2 infrastructure.

docs.title: VPS-Based C2
docs.text:
A VPS is commonly used for red team infrastructure.

Typical security considerations include:

  • SSH hardening;
  • firewall rules;
  • key-based authentication;
  • minimal exposed services;
  • timely updates;
  • logging.

The VPS itself becomes part of the trusted assessment environment.

docs.title: Firewalling
docs.text:
A C2 server should expose only the services required for the engagement.

Conceptually:

Internet
   |
   v
Firewall
   |
   +-- Operator Management
   +-- Approved Listener
   |
   X
Unnecessary Services

Management access should be more restrictive than agent communication where possible.

docs.title: Management Interface
docs.text:
The operator interface may be:

  • command line;
  • desktop GUI;
  • web interface.

Protect management access separately from C2 listener traffic.

Do not expose administrative interfaces unnecessarily.

docs.title: Operator Authentication
docs.text:
Where supported, use:

  • individual operator accounts;
  • unique credentials;
  • strong authentication;
  • audit logging.

Avoid shared operator accounts when multi-user support exists.

docs.title: Multi-Operator Environments
docs.text:
Multiple operators require coordination.

Without coordination:

Operator A
    |
    +--> changes system

Operator B
    |
    +--> tests same system

may lead to:

  • confusing results;
  • duplicated actions;
  • broken application state;
  • inaccurate evidence.

Use shared operation logs or the framework's collaboration features.

docs.title: Listener
docs.text:
A listener accepts incoming agent communication.

Listener configuration may define:

  • network interface;
  • transport;
  • port;
  • certificates;
  • communication profile.

Only listeners required for the exercise should be active.

docs.title: Listener Inventory
docs.text:
Record active listeners.

Example:

Listener Purpose Exposure Required HTTPS test listener Endpoint C2 Internet-facing Yes Internal listener Lab-only testing Internal Yes Legacy listener None Disabled No

Remove or disable listeners that are no longer required.

docs.title: C2 Transport
docs.text:
The transport determines how an agent communicates with the server.

Possible categories include:

HTTPS
DNS
Other framework-supported transports

The transport chosen should support the exercise objective.

docs.title: HTTPS Transport
docs.text:
HTTPS is frequently used because it provides normal TLS-protected network communication.

From a defensive perspective, HTTPS traffic can still be analysed through:

  • endpoint process telemetry;
  • destination;
  • DNS;
  • TLS characteristics;
  • connection timing;
  • proxy logs.

Encrypted does not mean invisible.

docs.title: DNS Transport
docs.text:
Some C2 systems support DNS-based communication.

DNS transport can create:

  • unusual query patterns;
  • encoded subdomains;
  • high query volume;
  • distinctive timing.

It should be used only where DNS-based command and control is part of the approved simulation.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
The agent is the target-side component.

It may receive tasks and return results.

A red team should know:

Where is it running?

Which user context?

Which process?

Which architecture?

When did it start?

When should it stop?

This information is essential for evidence and cleanup.

docs.title: Session Context
docs.text:
When a session appears, first establish:

Hostname
Current user
Integrity / privilege
Operating system
Process identity
Time

Do not assume a session has administrative privilege.

docs.title: Example Session Baseline
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Host:
WS01

User:
EXAMPLE\tester

Privilege:
Standard user

Objective:
Validate local discovery telemetry

This baseline makes later privilege changes measurable.

docs.title: Agent Lifecycle
docs.text:
A well-managed agent has a clear lifecycle.

Create
  |
  v
Deploy
  |
  v
Execute
  |
  v
Use
  |
  v
Terminate
  |
  v
Remove

Do not leave unused agents running.

docs.title: Payload Generation
docs.text:
Many C2 frameworks can generate target-specific agents.

Payload generation should be controlled because different builds may have different:

  • hashes;
  • transports;
  • configuration;
  • architectures;
  • telemetry.

Every assessment artefact should be traceable.

docs.title: Payload Inventory
docs.text:
Record:

Filename
Framework
Framework version
Architecture
Configuration
Hash
Target
Purpose
Creation date
Cleanup status

Example:

Framework:
Approved C2

Artifact:
agent-ws01.exe

Architecture:
x64

Purpose:
Controlled C2 validation

SHA256:
Recorded internally

docs.title: Hashing Payloads
docs.text:
On Windows:

Get-FileHash .\agent.exe -Algorithm SHA256

On Linux:

sha256sum agent.exe

Hashes help correlate:

  • endpoint detections;
  • EDR telemetry;
  • operator logs;
  • evidence.

docs.title: Payload Storage
docs.text:
Store payloads in dedicated assessment directories.

For example:

engagement/
└── payloads/
    ├── windows/
    ├── linux/
    └── hashes.txt

Do not leave offensive artefacts mixed with unrelated files.

docs.title: Payload Delivery
docs.text:
Delivery is a separate assessment stage.

Possible approved mechanisms may include:

  • administrative pre-placement;
  • controlled web hosting;
  • approved file transfer;
  • exercise-specific delivery workflows.

The choice should match the engagement objective.

docs.title: Administrative Pre-Placement
docs.text:
In many purple-team exercises, administrators can place the agent on the endpoint before testing.

This reduces unnecessary complexity.

Administrator
     |
     v
Approved Agent Placement
     |
     v
Red Team Executes Agreed Technique

This is often preferable when the exercise is focused on post-compromise visibility rather than initial access.

docs.title: Assumed Breach
docs.text:
An assumed-breach exercise may begin with:

Valid Domain User
       +
Controlled Endpoint
       +
Pre-Positioned Agent

This allows the assessment to focus on:

  • discovery;
  • identity controls;
  • lateral movement;
  • privilege escalation;
  • detection;
  • response.

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
A C2 server may manage many sessions.

Useful metadata includes:

Hostname
User
Operating system
Agent
Last seen
Privilege
IP

Avoid tasking a session unless the target has been confirmed as in scope.

docs.title: Session Naming
docs.text:
Where supported, use meaningful labels.

Example:

WS01-standard-user
SRV02-test-account
LAB-DC01

This reduces accidental tasking of the wrong endpoint.

docs.title: Session Scope
docs.text:
A newly connected endpoint must still be checked against the engagement scope.

New Session
    |
    v
Confirm Host
    |
    v
Check Scope
    |
    +-- In scope -> continue
    |
    +-- Unknown -> stop and verify

docs.title: Operator Tasking
docs.text:
Every task should support an objective.

Bad workflow:

Session Connected
      |
      v
Run Every Available Command

Better:

Objective:
Validate process discovery detection

Task:
Perform approved process discovery

Evidence:
Record operator and EDR timestamps

docs.title: Discovery Tasks
docs.text:
Common low-impact discovery categories include:

  • current user;
  • hostname;
  • network configuration;
  • processes;
  • services;
  • domain context.

These often provide useful starting telemetry.

docs.title: Privilege Awareness
docs.text:
Before using privileged functionality, confirm the current context.

Standard User
      |
      v
Different capabilities

versus:

Administrator / SYSTEM / root
      |
      v
Much broader capabilities

Do not infer privilege from the existence of a C2 session.

docs.title: Native Command Execution
docs.text:
Many C2 platforms can launch operating-system commands.

Native utilities may be appropriate for:

  • identity checks;
  • process review;
  • network review;
  • service inspection.

Use commands aligned with the objective.

docs.title: C2 File Transfer
docs.text:
Frameworks may support uploading and downloading files.

File transfer can create operational risks.

Before downloading:

Is the file needed?

Does it contain sensitive data?

Can synthetic data be used instead?

Where will it be stored?

When will it be deleted?

docs.title: Data Minimisation
docs.text:
A red team should collect the minimum data necessary to demonstrate the objective.

Avoid:

Download entire file share

when:

Proof of access to controlled file

is sufficient.

docs.title: SOCKS and Pivoting
docs.text:
Some C2 frameworks provide SOCKS or proxy functionality.

Conceptually:

Operator Tool
      |
      v
SOCKS
      |
      v
Agent
      |
      v
Internal Network

This can alter network reachability significantly.

Use pivoting only where explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Pivot Scope
docs.text:
Before using a pivot:

  • identify reachable network ranges;
  • confirm authorised subnets;
  • define target list;
  • limit tooling to those targets.

Do not assume that every reachable system is in scope.

docs.title: Tunnelling Risk
docs.text:
Tunnels can:

  • bypass normal network paths;
  • increase bandwidth;
  • create unexpected routing;
  • affect monitoring.

Document active tunnels and terminate them during cleanup.

docs.title: Beaconing
docs.text:
Many agents periodically contact the server.

A simplified pattern is:

Agent
  |
  +---- callback
  |
  +---- callback
  |
  +---- callback

This periodic behaviour may create a detectable pattern.

docs.title: Sleep Interval
docs.text:
A callback interval affects:

  • responsiveness;
  • network traffic;
  • detectability;
  • server load.

Short intervals generate more traffic.

Long intervals make operator actions slower.

Choose values according to the exercise.

docs.title: Jitter
docs.text:
Jitter introduces variation in callback timing.

Conceptually:

10 seconds
13 seconds
8 seconds
12 seconds

instead of:

10
10
10
10

Changing timing characteristics should support an authorised simulation objective.

docs.title: Network Telemetry
docs.text:
Defensive teams may observe:

  • destination IP;
  • destination domain;
  • port;
  • TLS;
  • DNS;
  • periodic connections;
  • unusual processes initiating traffic.

A C2 exercise can therefore validate several detection layers simultaneously.

docs.title: Endpoint Telemetry
docs.text:
Endpoint telemetry may include:

  • agent process creation;
  • parent process;
  • child processes;
  • file writes;
  • network connections;
  • modules;
  • command lines;
  • PowerShell activity.

This is often more useful than signature-based detection alone.

docs.title: Parent-Child Relationships
docs.text:
An EDR may observe:

Parent Process
      |
      v
Agent
      |
      v
Child Process

Detection logic should consider whether the process chain is expected in the environment.

docs.title: Operator Logs
docs.text:
Operator logs should include:

Timestamp
Operator
Target
Current user
Task
Framework
Result

These are essential when correlating with defensive telemetry.

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Ensure that:

Operator
C2 server
Endpoints
EDR
SIEM

use sufficiently aligned time.

Otherwise correlation becomes difficult.

docs.title: Timezone
docs.text:
Use one agreed timezone for evidence.

Example:

UTC

or:

Europe/Amsterdam

Document it in the report.

docs.title: C2 and MITRE ATT&CK
docs.text:
C2 tasks should be mapped to behaviour, not merely framework features.

Example:

Framework:
Sliver

Task:
Process discovery

ATT&CK mapping:
Process Discovery

The technique is the behaviour.

The framework is the delivery mechanism.

Official reference:

MITRE ATT&CK

docs.title: Technique-Level Logging
docs.text:
A useful record might contain:

Technique:
Process Discovery

Target:
WS01

User:
EXAMPLE\tester

Framework:
Approved C2

Timestamp:
20:15:42

Expected telemetry:
Process query and agent child activity

This makes purple-team analysis easier.

docs.title: Detection Validation
docs.text:
C2 frameworks can reproduce attacker behaviours while blue teams observe.

Red Team
   |
   v
C2 Task
   |
   v
Endpoint Behaviour
   |
   v
Telemetry
   |
   v
SIEM / EDR
   |
   v
Analyst

Measure each stage separately.

docs.title: Prevention vs Detection
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Technique Attempted
       |
       +--> Prevented?
       |
       +--> Telemetry generated?
       |
       +--> Detection generated?
       |
       +--> Alert investigated?
       |
       +--> Response performed?

A blocked technique may still reveal a monitoring gap.

docs.title: C2 Detection Does Not Equal Agent Detection
docs.text:
A defensive control might detect:

Known agent signature

without detecting:

Underlying behaviour

For mature detection engineering, measure both:

Tool-Specific Detection

and:

Technique-Level Detection

docs.title: Tool-Specific Detection
docs.text:
Tool-specific detection may include:

  • executable hashes;
  • known strings;
  • known network indicators;
  • framework-specific metadata.

These can be useful but fragile.

docs.title: Behavioural Detection
docs.text:
Behavioural detection focuses on:

  • unusual process relationships;
  • suspicious network behaviour;
  • identity context;
  • discovery patterns;
  • privilege changes;
  • unusual remote administration.

Behavioural coverage is generally more resilient to tooling changes.

docs.title: Framework Switching
docs.text:
If the blue team detects one C2 family, switching frameworks solely to obtain an undetected payload should not automatically become the next objective.

Instead ask:

Are we testing signature resistance?

or:

Are we testing behavioural detection?

The answer determines whether framework variation is justified.

docs.title: Security Control Interaction
docs.text:
C2 execution may be affected by:

  • Defender;
  • EDR;
  • AppLocker;
  • WDAC;
  • firewall;
  • proxy;
  • DNS filtering;
  • network segmentation.

These controls are part of the assessment environment.

docs.title: Blocked Payload
docs.text:
If an approved payload is blocked:

Attempt
  |
  v
Security Control Blocks
  |
  v
Record Exact Result

This can be a successful control outcome.

Do not immediately try to bypass the control unless evasion testing is explicitly in scope.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Windows application control may restrict:

  • executables;
  • DLLs;
  • scripts;
  • installers;
  • packaged applications.

Related note:

Windows Application Control

A blocked C2 artefact may provide valuable evidence about application-control effectiveness.

docs.title: Defender and EDR
docs.text:
Endpoint products may:

  • quarantine payloads;
  • block processes;
  • alert on child process behaviour;
  • detect network activity;
  • terminate sessions.

Record what happened rather than focusing only on whether the agent survived.

docs.title: Firewall Controls
docs.text:
Network controls may prevent C2 callbacks.

Potential control points include:

Host firewall
Network firewall
Proxy
DNS filtering
Egress filtering

A failed callback can therefore be a useful network-control result.

docs.title: Proxy Environments
docs.text:
Some enterprise environments require HTTP traffic through a proxy.

This may affect C2 connectivity.

Do not reconfigure enterprise proxy policy without authorisation.

Record the environmental restriction.

docs.title: Egress Filtering
docs.text:
C2 testing is a useful way to evaluate outbound network controls.

For example:

Endpoint
   |
   v
Unknown external destination
   |
   X
Egress filter

A blocked connection may demonstrate effective control.

docs.title: DNS Controls
docs.text:
DNS filtering may:

  • block newly created domains;
  • log suspicious requests;
  • prevent certain resolutions.

Include DNS telemetry when evaluating C2 behaviour.

docs.title: Redirectors
docs.text:
Some red team architectures place a redirector between the target and primary C2 server.

Agent
  |
  v
Redirector
  |
  v
Team Server

Possible reasons include:

  • architecture separation;
  • routing;
  • traffic control;
  • telemetry.

Redirectors introduce additional infrastructure that must be secured and monitored.

docs.title: Redirector Logging
docs.text:
A redirector can provide useful evidence such as:

Source
Timestamp
Request
Destination

Do not store unnecessary target data.

docs.title: C2 Infrastructure Domains
docs.text:
If dedicated domains are used for authorised exercises:

  • document ownership;
  • restrict use to the assessment;
  • secure DNS administration;
  • remove records when no longer required.

Infrastructure should not remain active indefinitely.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
TLS certificates used by C2 infrastructure should be tracked.

Record:

Domain
Certificate source
Validity
Listener
Cleanup / expiry

Do not reuse unrelated production private keys.

docs.title: Framework Updates
docs.text:
C2 frameworks evolve quickly.

Before an engagement:

Review release
Test in lab
Validate payload generation
Validate listener
Validate logging

Do not upgrade the production assessment infrastructure mid-engagement without reason.

docs.title: Lab Validation
docs.text:
Before deployment, test the framework in a controlled lab.

Validate:

  • server stability;
  • listener connectivity;
  • logging;
  • payload lifecycle;
  • cleanup;
  • operator access.

A lab is the correct place to discover configuration problems.

docs.title: Framework Version
docs.text:
Record the version.

For example:

Framework:
Sliver

Version:
Recorded from installed build

Do not rely on memory or external documentation alone.

docs.title: Build Provenance
docs.text:
If built from source, record:

Repository
Commit
Build date
Build environment
Hash

This helps correlate detections.

docs.title: Supply-Chain Risk
docs.text:
A C2 framework has access to extremely sensitive information.

Potential compromise of the framework itself could expose:

  • operator credentials;
  • target sessions;
  • payloads;
  • collected data;
  • infrastructure credentials.

Use trusted sources.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
C2 servers may depend on:

  • databases;
  • containers;
  • language runtimes;
  • web components.

Secure the entire platform rather than only the main executable.

docs.title: Containerised Deployment
docs.text:
Some frameworks use Docker or container orchestration.

Security considerations include:

  • exposed ports;
  • mounted secrets;
  • container privileges;
  • volumes;
  • update lifecycle.

Do not expose management containers publicly without need.

docs.title: Backup Strategy
docs.text:
C2 backups may contain highly sensitive information.

Ask whether backup is actually required.

If so:

  • encrypt appropriately;
  • restrict access;
  • define retention;
  • delete according to policy.

docs.title: Session Data Retention
docs.text:
Do not retain operational session data indefinitely.

Define:

Retention period
Evidence requirements
Deletion process

This should align with engagement policy.

docs.title: Credentials in C2
docs.text:
A C2 framework may encounter:

  • passwords;
  • tokens;
  • hashes;
  • tickets;
  • private keys.

These should be treated as high-sensitivity secrets.

Do not store them in normal notes.

docs.title: Do Not Paste Secrets into Reports
docs.text:
Instead of:

Password:
P@ssw0rd123

write:

A reusable credential was exposed. The value has been redacted.

Store the actual evidence separately if retention is required.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots can show:

  • agent connection;
  • task execution;
  • session context;
  • defensive alert.

However, screenshots should not be the only evidence.

Combine with:

  • operator logs;
  • endpoint logs;
  • SIEM/EDR events;
  • timestamped outputs.

docs.title: C2 Evidence Model
docs.text:
A useful evidence chain is:

Operator Task
     |
     v
C2 Timestamp
     |
     v
Endpoint Result
     |
     v
EDR Event
     |
     v
SIEM Alert
     |
     v
Analyst Action

This is particularly useful for purple-team exercises.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Cleanup should be planned before deployment.

Potential C2 artefacts include:

  • agent binary;
  • script;
  • service;
  • task;
  • startup entry;
  • configuration file;
  • tunnel;
  • certificate;
  • temporary download;
  • listener;
  • DNS record.

docs.title: Cleanup Ledger
docs.text:
Maintain a table such as:

Target Artefact Purpose Removal Required Removed WS01 Test agent C2 validation Yes Yes VPS01 HTTPS listener Engagement C2 Yes Yes DNS Test record Listener routing Yes Yes

This reduces cleanup mistakes.

docs.title: Terminate Sessions
docs.text:
Before dismantling infrastructure:

Stop Tasking
      |
      v
Terminate Agents
      |
      v
Remove Target Artefacts
      |
      v
Disable Listeners
      |
      v
Retire Infrastructure

Follow the engagement cleanup procedure.

docs.title: Do Not Delete Security Logs
docs.text:
Normal cleanup should not delete:

  • event logs;
  • EDR telemetry;
  • SIEM events;
  • firewall logs;
  • DNS logs.

These are defensive evidence.

Log deletion is a separate adversary technique and should only be tested if explicitly approved.

docs.title: Persistence Cleanup
docs.text:
If persistence was separately authorised, every persistence artefact should be tracked.

Examples include:

Scheduled task
Service
Registry startup value
Systemd unit
Cron entry

Verify removal independently.

docs.title: Validate Cleanup
docs.text:
Do not assume cleanup succeeded.

Check:

File absent?
Process terminated?
Task absent?
Service removed?
Listener disabled?
DNS record removed?

Document completion.

docs.title: Incident Handling
docs.text:
If unexpected behaviour occurs:

Unexpected Production Impact
      |
      v
Stop Activity
      |
      v
Contact Engagement Lead
      |
      v
Preserve Evidence
      |
      v
Support Recovery

Do not continue testing while an unplanned incident is unresolved.

docs.title: Stop Conditions
docs.text:
Potential stop conditions include:

  • production outage;
  • unstable endpoint;
  • unexpected sensitive data access;
  • third-party impact;
  • real compromise discovered;
  • account lockout;
  • defensive team emergency request.

Operators should know these before starting.

docs.title: Purple Team Workflow
docs.text:
A C2 framework is especially useful when the goal is repeatable behaviour.

Technique Selected
      |
      v
Task Executed
      |
      v
Timestamp Recorded
      |
      v
Blue Team Searches
      |
      v
Detection Result
      |
      v
Rule Improved
      |
      v
Technique Replayed

This supports continuous validation.

Related note:

Continuous Validation

docs.title: After-Action Review
docs.text:
C2 logs can help reconstruct:

What happened?

When?

On which host?

Under which identity?

What did security controls observe?

What was missed?

Related note:

After-Action Review

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Potential C2-related purple-team metrics include:

Time to telemetry
Time to alert
Time to analyst triage
Time to containment
Technique detection rate
Technique prevention rate

Related note:

Metrics and Measurement

docs.title: Framework Comparison
docs.text:
A high-level comparison can help with selection.

Area Sliver Mythic Havoc Open source Yes Yes Yes Multi-operator Yes Yes Yes Modular architecture Yes Strong focus Yes Cross-platform focus Strong Depends on agent Framework-dependent Web interface Not primary operator model Strong GUI-focused Suitable for lab/adversary simulation Yes Yes Yes

Capabilities change over time.

Verify current official documentation before making deployment decisions.

docs.title: Choosing Sliver
docs.text:
Sliver may fit when:

  • cross-platform operations matter;
  • open-source infrastructure is preferred;
  • CLI workflows are comfortable;
  • multi-operator support is needed.

docs.title: Choosing Mythic
docs.text:
Mythic may fit when:

  • collaborative web workflows matter;
  • modular agents are desirable;
  • several operators need structured task visibility;
  • extensibility is important.

docs.title: Choosing Havoc
docs.text:
Havoc may fit where:

  • the team is already trained on it;
  • the engagement has approved it;
  • its operational model matches the objective.

Tool familiarity matters because operator error can be more dangerous than framework limitations.

docs.title: Do Not Constantly Switch Frameworks
docs.text:
Every additional framework increases:

  • infrastructure complexity;
  • training burden;
  • artefact management;
  • cleanup requirements;
  • evidence complexity.

Use the minimum tooling needed to meet the objective.

docs.title: C2 and Native Tools
docs.text:
C2 can act as transport for normal operating-system actions.

Example:

C2
 |
 v
Native Host Command
 |
 v
Endpoint Telemetry

The detection should focus on meaningful behaviour.

docs.title: C2 and Active Directory
docs.text:
C2 sessions may provide a foothold from which authorised AD analysis is performed.

Related section:

Active Directory Tools

Tools such as BloodHound, NetExec, Certipy, Impacket, or native utilities may then support specific directory objectives.

docs.title: C2 and Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
After establishing a standard-user foothold, privilege escalation enumeration may be performed using approved techniques.

Related section:

Privilege Escalation Tools

The C2 framework does not itself establish that privilege escalation is possible.

docs.title: C2 and Web Testing
docs.text:
A red team may identify internal web applications reachable only from an established position.

The same scope rules still apply.

Related section:

Web Application Testing Tools

Do not test internal applications merely because a pivot makes them reachable.

docs.title: Operational Workflow
docs.text:
A mature C2 workflow can be:

1. Define objective
      |
      v
2. Confirm rules of engagement
      |
      v
3. Select approved framework
      |
      v
4. Build isolated infrastructure
      |
      v
5. Secure management access
      |
      v
6. Configure only required listeners
      |
      v
7. Create controlled artefact
      |
      v
8. Record hash and configuration
      |
      v
9. Deploy to approved target
      |
      v
10. Confirm session identity
      |
      v
11. Execute agreed technique
      |
      v
12. Record timestamps and results
      |
      v
13. Correlate defensive telemetry
      |
      v
14. Stop unnecessary sessions
      |
      v
15. Remove artefacts
      |
      v
16. Disable infrastructure
      |
      v
17. Complete after-action review

docs.title: Engagement
docs.text:
• [ ] Engagement authorised.
  • [ ] Targets defined.
  • [ ] Exclusions defined.
  • [ ] Techniques agreed.
  • [ ] Prohibited actions documented.
  • [ ] Stop conditions documented.
  • [ ] Emergency contact identified.
  • [ ] Cleanup requirements documented.

docs.title: Framework
docs.text:
• [ ] Framework approved.
  • [ ] Official source used.
  • [ ] Version recorded.
  • [ ] Lab tested.
  • [ ] Operator team trained.
  • [ ] Only required functionality enabled.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• [ ] Dedicated server used.
  • [ ] Management access restricted.
  • [ ] Firewall configured.
  • [ ] Unnecessary ports closed.
  • [ ] Operator authentication configured.
  • [ ] TLS configured where required.
  • [ ] Logging enabled.
  • [ ] Time synchronised.

docs.title: Listener
docs.text:
• [ ] Listener purpose documented.
  • [ ] Exposure understood.
  • [ ] Network port approved.
  • [ ] Transport approved.
  • [ ] Unused listeners disabled.

docs.title: Payload
docs.text:
• [ ] Target architecture known.
  • [ ] Payload configuration recorded.
  • [ ] SHA256 recorded.
  • [ ] Delivery method approved.
  • [ ] Target identified.
  • [ ] Cleanup procedure defined.

docs.title: Session Checklist
docs.text:
When a new agent connects:

  • [ ] Hostname confirmed.
  • [ ] IP confirmed.
  • [ ] Current user confirmed.
  • [ ] Privilege level confirmed.
  • [ ] Operating system confirmed.
  • [ ] Target checked against scope.
  • [ ] Session labelled clearly.
  • [ ] Objective confirmed before tasking.

docs.title: Tasking Checklist
docs.text:
Before issuing a task:

  • [ ] Security objective known.
  • [ ] Technique approved.
  • [ ] Expected target impact understood.
  • [ ] State-changing effect understood.
  • [ ] Expected telemetry identified.
  • [ ] Exact timestamp recorded.
  • [ ] Sensitive data collection minimised.

docs.title: Detection Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Endpoint telemetry checked.
  • [ ] Network telemetry checked.
  • [ ] DNS telemetry checked.
  • [ ] Proxy telemetry checked where relevant.
  • [ ] SIEM ingestion checked.
  • [ ] Alert generation checked.
  • [ ] Analyst visibility checked.
  • [ ] Response measured separately from prevention.

docs.title: Evidence Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Framework recorded.
  • [ ] Framework version recorded.
  • [ ] Agent hash recorded.
  • [ ] Target recorded.
  • [ ] User context recorded.
  • [ ] Task timestamp recorded.
  • [ ] Result recorded.
  • [ ] Defensive event IDs or alert references retained.
  • [ ] Screenshots contain no unnecessary secrets.
  • [ ] Operator log retained.

docs.title: Cleanup Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Agent terminated.
  • [ ] Payload removed.
  • [ ] Temporary files removed.
  • [ ] Tunnels closed.
  • [ ] Persistence removed if used.
  • [ ] Listeners disabled.
  • [ ] Temporary DNS removed.
  • [ ] Certificates handled appropriately.
  • [ ] VPS/infrastructure retired where required.
  • [ ] Cleanup independently confirmed.
  • [ ] Defensive logs preserved.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Do not write:

Sliver bypassed the environment.

unless the evidence actually supports a specific defensive-control failure.

Prefer:

The approved red team agent successfully established outbound
communication from the tested workstation to the assessment
infrastructure. The connection generated endpoint network telemetry but
did not result in an alert during the agreed observation window.

This states:

  • what happened;
  • where;
  • what telemetry existed;
  • what detection outcome occurred.

docs.title: Reporting a Blocked Agent
docs.text:
Example:

Execution of the approved red team agent was prevented by application
control on the tested workstation. The attempt generated corresponding
endpoint telemetry and was visible to the defensive team.

This is a positive control result.

docs.title: Reporting a Network Block
docs.text:
Example:

The test agent executed locally but was unable to establish outbound
communication to the authorised assessment server. Network telemetry
showed the connection attempt was blocked by the organisation's egress
controls.

This separates execution from communication.

docs.title: Reporting a Detection Gap
docs.text:
Example:

The test agent successfully established the authorised C2 channel and
performed the agreed host-discovery action. Endpoint telemetry was
available, but no alert was generated during the exercise. This
indicates a detection-logic gap rather than a telemetry-collection gap.

This makes the conclusion actionable.

docs.title: Reporting a Telemetry Gap
docs.text:
Example:

The agreed technique executed successfully, but the expected endpoint
event was not present in the available telemetry. The result should be
investigated as a collection or logging coverage gap before additional
detection logic is developed.

docs.title: Prevention, Telemetry, Detection, Response
docs.text:
A useful final result model is:

Stage Result Execution Allowed / blocked Communication Allowed / blocked Telemetry Present / absent Detection Alert / no alert Triage Correct / missed Response Effective / ineffective

This prevents overly simplistic conclusions.
