docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use source code review tooling like this:

Run Semgrep
Run CodeQL
Run Secret Scanner
      |
      v
Export Alerts
      |
      v
Report Everything

Use it like this:

Understand Repository
        |
        v
Map Entry Points and Trust Boundaries
        |
        v
Identify Security Questions
        |
        v
Choose Appropriate Tool
        |
        +-- ripgrep
        +-- Semgrep
        +-- OpenGrep
        +-- CodeQL
        +-- secret scanner
        |
        v
Identify Candidate Code
        |
        v
Read Surrounding Implementation
        |
        v
Trace Source to Sink
        |
        v
Understand Validation and Sanitisation
        |
        v
Confirm Reachability
        |
        v
Validate Runtime Behaviour Where Needed
        |
        v
Perform Variant Analysis
        |
        v
Capture Evidence
        |
        v
Report the Underlying Code Weakness

Source code review tools are most valuable when they reduce the amount of code that must be searched manually and reveal relationships that deserve deeper investigation.

The tools identify patterns.

The tester determines whether those patterns form a real security vulnerability.

docs.title: Vulnerability Research Tools
docs.text:
Vulnerability research requires different tools depending on the stage of investigation.

Typical activities include:

  • understanding application behaviour;
  • reverse engineering;
  • debugging;
  • dynamic analysis;
  • fuzzing;
  • crash reproduction;
  • root-cause analysis;
  • patch diffing;
  • variant analysis;
  • proof-of-concept development;
  • exploitability assessment;
  • regression testing;
  • responsible disclosure.

No single tool covers all of these activities.

A mature workflow combines several categories:

Target
  |
  v
Understand Attack Surface
  |
  v
Static / Dynamic Analysis
  |
  +-- Disassembler
  +-- Debugger
  +-- Tracing
  |
  v
Fuzzing
  |
  v
Crash
  |
  v
Root Cause
  |
  v
Variant Analysis
  |
  v
Controlled PoC
  |
  v
Remediation / Disclosure

Authorised research only

Perform vulnerability research only against software, systems, products, binaries, source code, and environments that you are authorised to analyse. Fuzzing, debugging, malformed-input testing, and proof-of-concept development can crash software or alter state. Prefer dedicated research environments rather than production systems.

docs.title: Where Vulnerability Research Tools Fit
docs.text:
The toolchain should follow the research question.

A useful model is:

What am I trying to learn?
        |
        v
Choose Research Technique
        |
        v
Choose Tool
        |
        v
Collect Evidence
        |
        v
Interpret Behaviour
        |
        v
Form Security Hypothesis
        |
        v
Validate

Related methodology:

Vulnerability Research

Vulnerability Research Methodology

Attack Surface Analysis

docs.title: Tool Categories
docs.text:
A practical vulnerability research toolkit may include:

Category Example Tools Windows debugging WinDbg, x64dbg Linux debugging GDB, GEF, pwndbg Static reverse engineering Ghidra, IDA Free/Pro, Binary Ninja Dynamic instrumentation Frida Linux tracing strace, ltrace Windows tracing Process Monitor, Process Explorer Fuzzing AFL++, libFuzzer, honggfuzz Coverage analysis compiler sanitizers, debugger coverage, fuzzing instrumentation Crash analysis GDB, WinDbg, sanitizers Patch diffing BinDiff-style tools, Diaphora, Git diff, binary comparison Source analysis ripgrep, Semgrep, OpenGrep, CodeQL Network/protocol analysis Wireshark, tcpdump File-format inspection strings, file, readelf, objdump, PE utilities Scripting Python Version control Git

The best tool is the one that answers the current research question with the least unnecessary complexity.

docs.title: Tool Output Is Not a Vulnerability
docs.text:
A debugger exception, fuzzer crash, static-analysis match, or unusual binary instruction does not automatically mean a security vulnerability exists.

Crash
  !=
Vulnerability

Static Match
  !=
Vulnerability

Debugger Exception
  !=
Exploitable Condition

Patch Difference
  !=
Root Cause

The research process must establish:

Reachability
Controllability
Root cause
Security boundary
Impact
Reproducibility

docs.title: Research Environment
docs.text:
Vulnerability research should normally take place in a controlled environment.

Typical components include:

Research Workstation
      |
      +-- Debugger
      +-- Disassembler
      +-- Fuzzer
      +-- Scripts
      |
      v
Isolated Target
      |
      +-- VM
      +-- Container
      +-- Test build

Isolation helps contain:

  • crashes;
  • malformed files;
  • unstable builds;
  • experimental instrumentation;
  • temporary modifications.

docs.title: Virtual Machines
docs.text:
Virtual machines are useful because they allow:

  • snapshots;
  • repeatable state;
  • operating-system isolation;
  • version comparison;
  • debugger installation.

A useful workflow is:

Clean Snapshot
    |
    v
Install Target
    |
    v
Run Research
    |
    v
Crash / Modify State
    |
    v
Revert Snapshot

Snapshots improve reproducibility.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
Containers can be useful for:

  • Linux targets;
  • fuzzing;
  • build environments;
  • dependency isolation.

They are less suitable when research depends heavily on:

  • kernel behaviour;
  • GUI software;
  • full system services;
  • low-level Windows behaviour.

Choose the environment based on the target.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
For every research environment, record:

Operating system
Architecture
Application version
Build number
Compiler where known
Libraries
Configuration
Research tool versions
Input file / request

Without this information, reproducing a crash later can become difficult.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
Debuggers provide visibility into program execution.

Typical questions include:

Where did the program crash?

Which instruction failed?

Which register contains attacker-controlled data?

Which function processes the input?

What code path led to the fault?

Which security mitigations are active?

Related methodology:

Debugging and Dynamic Analysis

docs.title: Windows Debuggers
docs.text:
Common Windows debugging tools include:

  • WinDbg;
  • x64dbg;
  • Visual Studio Debugger.

Each has different strengths.

docs.title: WinDbg
docs.text:
WinDbg is Microsoft's debugger for Windows.

It is useful for:

  • user-mode debugging;
  • crash-dump analysis;
  • kernel debugging;
  • exception inspection;
  • stack analysis;
  • symbol-aware debugging.

Official resource:

WinDbg - Microsoft Learn

docs.title: WinDbg Mental Model
docs.text:
Target Process
     |
     v
Exception
     |
     v
WinDbg
     |
     +-- Registers
     +-- Stack
     +-- Memory
     +-- Modules
     +-- Symbols
     |
     v
Root-Cause Analysis

docs.title: WinDbg Basic Context
docs.text:
Common research questions include:

Which exception occurred?

Where is the instruction pointer?

Which module contains the fault?

What does the stack look like?

What input caused the condition?

Do not jump directly from:

Access violation

to:

Remote code execution

The crash still requires analysis.

docs.title: Symbols
docs.text:
Symbols make debugging substantially easier.

They can provide:

  • function names;
  • variable context;
  • module information;
  • stack readability.

Use vendor or locally generated symbols where authorised and available.

A missing symbol does not prevent debugging but usually makes analysis slower.

docs.title: Crash Dumps
docs.text:
Windows crash dumps can preserve state at the moment of failure.

Useful evidence includes:

Exception code
Faulting address
Module
Stack
Registers
Process architecture
Input

Protect crash dumps because they may contain sensitive process memory.

docs.title: x64dbg
docs.text:
x64dbg is a popular Windows user-mode debugger and reverse-engineering tool.

It provides:

  • disassembly;
  • breakpoints;
  • registers;
  • memory views;
  • call stack;
  • module inspection;
  • patching in controlled research environments.

Official project:

x64dbg

GitHub:

x64dbg - GitHub

docs.title: When x64dbg Is Useful
docs.text:
x64dbg is particularly convenient for:

  • interactive user-mode debugging;
  • following control flow;
  • setting breakpoints;
  • examining memory;
  • inspecting function calls.

It can be easier than WinDbg for some interactive reverse-engineering tasks.

docs.title: GDB
docs.text:
GNU Debugger, commonly called GDB, is one of the main debugging tools for Linux and Unix-like systems.

It can inspect:

  • registers;
  • memory;
  • stack;
  • functions;
  • breakpoints;
  • signals;
  • shared libraries.

Official resource:

GDB

docs.title: GDB Basic Workflow
docs.text:
Program
  |
  v
Run Under GDB
  |
  v
Provide Test Input
  |
  v
Crash / Breakpoint
  |
  v
Inspect
  |
  +-- Registers
  +-- Backtrace
  +-- Memory
  +-- Instructions

docs.title: GDB Basic Commands
docs.text:
Start:

gdb ./target

Run:

run

Backtrace:

bt

Registers:

info registers

Disassemble a function:

disassemble main

Inspect instructions around the current program counter:

x/10i $pc

These are foundational debugging commands.

docs.title: GEF
docs.text:
GEF is an extension for GDB aimed at exploit development and reverse engineering.

It improves debugger usability through enhanced:

  • context views;
  • register display;
  • memory inspection;
  • architecture information;
  • security property inspection.

Official project:

GEF - GitHub

docs.title: pwndbg
docs.text:
pwndbg is another GDB extension commonly used in low-level vulnerability research.

It provides enhanced support for:

  • memory analysis;
  • heap research;
  • register context;
  • disassembly;
  • binary security analysis.

Official project:

pwndbg - GitHub

docs.title: GEF vs pwndbg
docs.text:
Both extend GDB.

Choose based on:

  • preference;
  • target architecture;
  • workflow;
  • plugin compatibility.

Avoid loading multiple large debugger frameworks simultaneously unless you know they are compatible.

docs.title: Reverse Engineering
docs.text:
Reverse engineering helps understand software when source code is unavailable or incomplete.

Typical questions include:

Which parser handles this file?

Which function validates the input?

Where is memory allocated?

Where is authentication checked?

Which protocol messages are supported?

Which function changed between versions?

docs.title: Ghidra
docs.text:
Ghidra is a reverse-engineering framework developed by the National Security Agency and released as open source.

It provides:

  • disassembly;
  • decompilation;
  • function analysis;
  • cross-references;
  • scripting;
  • data-type analysis.

Official project:

Ghidra - GitHub

docs.title: Ghidra Workflow
docs.text:
Binary
  |
  v
Import
  |
  v
Auto Analysis
  |
  v
Identify Interesting Functions
  |
  v
Cross-References
  |
  v
Decompiler
  |
  v
Security Hypothesis

docs.title: Decompiler Output Is Approximate
docs.text:
Decompiler output is reconstructed from machine code.

It may contain:

  • incorrect variable names;
  • imperfect types;
  • confusing control flow;
  • compiler artefacts.

Never assume decompiled code is identical to original source.

Use it as an analysis aid.

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:
Cross-references are one of the most useful reverse-engineering features.

For example:

Dangerous Function
      |
      v
Find Xrefs
      |
      v
Identify Callers
      |
      v
Trace Input

This is similar to source-to-sink analysis.

docs.title: IDA
docs.text:
IDA is a mature disassembler and reverse-engineering platform.

Free and commercial editions provide different capabilities.

Official resource:

IDA

Use current vendor documentation for edition-specific capabilities.

docs.title: Binary Ninja
docs.text:
Binary Ninja is another reverse-engineering platform with strong analysis and scripting capabilities.

Official resource:

Binary Ninja

Tool choice is largely determined by workflow and analyst preference.

docs.title: Static vs Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Static analysis:

Binary / Source
      |
      v
Inspect Without Running

Dynamic analysis:

Run Target
    |
    v
Observe Runtime Behaviour

Both are valuable.

docs.title: Static Analysis Advantages
docs.text:
Static analysis can reveal:

  • hidden code paths;
  • functions not reached during testing;
  • constant values;
  • parser structure;
  • dangerous APIs.

docs.title: Dynamic Analysis Advantages
docs.text:
Dynamic analysis can reveal:

  • actual runtime paths;
  • real variable values;
  • loaded libraries;
  • timing;
  • environment-dependent behaviour.

The strongest research often combines both.

docs.title: Frida
docs.text:
Frida is a dynamic instrumentation toolkit that allows runtime observation and modification of applications in controlled research environments.

It can help researchers inspect:

  • function calls;
  • arguments;
  • return values;
  • runtime libraries;
  • application behaviour.

Official project:

Frida

docs.title: Dynamic Instrumentation
docs.text:
A simplified model:

Running Application
       |
       v
Instrumentation
       |
       +-- Observe Function
       +-- Inspect Arguments
       +-- Inspect Return
       |
       v
Understand Runtime Behaviour

Instrumentation is particularly useful where debugger attachment is inconvenient or where many repeated calls need observation.

docs.title: Linux Tracing
docs.text: Linux provides several useful native tracing tools.

docs.title: strace
docs.text:
strace records system calls made by a process.

Example:

strace ./target

It can help answer:

Which files are opened?

Which network calls occur?

Which processes are created?

Which system calls fail?

docs.title: Trace One Process
docs.text:
Example:

strace -f ./target

The -f option follows child processes.

Use:

strace -h

for current options.

docs.title: ltrace
docs.text:
ltrace can trace dynamic library calls on supported systems.

Example:

ltrace ./target

It can be useful when investigating:

  • libc calls;
  • string handling;
  • file operations;
  • library function usage.

docs.title: Windows Process Monitor
docs.text:
Process Monitor from Microsoft Sysinternals records real-time Windows activity such as:

  • filesystem operations;
  • registry operations;
  • process activity.

Official resource:

Process Monitor

docs.title: Process Monitor Use
docs.text:
Procmon is especially useful when asking:

Which DLL did the application try to load?

Which registry key controls this behaviour?

Which file does this parser open?

Where does the application store configuration?

Filters are essential because raw Procmon output can be extremely noisy.

docs.title: Process Explorer
docs.text:
Process Explorer provides detailed process information.

It can help inspect:

  • parent-child relationships;
  • loaded DLLs;
  • process users;
  • handles;
  • process properties.

Official resource:

Process Explorer

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text:
Fuzzing repeatedly provides generated or mutated input to a target in order to discover unexpected behaviour.

A simplified workflow is:

Seed Inputs
    |
    v
Fuzzer
    |
    v
Target
    |
    +-- Normal
    |
    +-- Hang
    |
    +-- Crash

Related methodology:

Fuzzing

docs.title: Fuzzing Is More Than Random Data
docs.text:
Modern fuzzers often use:

  • mutation;
  • code coverage;
  • instrumentation;
  • corpus evolution;
  • dictionaries;
  • feedback.

The aim is to explore new program states efficiently.

docs.title: AFL++
docs.text:
AFL++ is a widely used coverage-guided fuzzer.

Official project:

AFL++ - GitHub

Documentation:

AFL++ Documentation

docs.title: AFL++ Model
docs.text:
Seed Corpus
    |
    v
Mutation
    |
    v
Target Execution
    |
    v
Coverage Feedback
    |
    v
Interesting Input
    |
    v
Corpus Update

docs.title: Good Seed Corpus
docs.text:
A seed corpus should ideally contain:

  • valid examples;
  • different file structures;
  • different protocol messages;
  • edge cases.

The goal is diversity, not simply volume.

docs.title: Corpus Minimisation
docs.text:
Too many redundant seeds can slow fuzzing.

Corpus minimisation attempts to preserve useful coverage while reducing duplicate input.

The exact mechanism depends on the fuzzer.

docs.title: Dictionaries
docs.text:
Protocol- or format-specific dictionaries can help fuzzers discover important syntax.

Examples may include:

keywords
magic values
field names
protocol tokens

A dictionary should reflect the target format.

docs.title: libFuzzer
docs.text:
libFuzzer is an in-process coverage-guided fuzzer integrated with LLVM.

It works especially well where a fuzz harness can directly call the target function.

Official documentation:

libFuzzer

docs.title: Harness-Based Fuzzing
docs.text:
A fuzz harness provides a small entry point around the function being tested.

Conceptually:

Fuzzer Input
     |
     v
Harness
     |
     v
Target Parser / Function

Good harnesses:

  • isolate the interesting function;
  • avoid unnecessary setup;
  • execute quickly;
  • clean state between inputs.

docs.title: Fuzzing Speed Matters
docs.text:
A fuzzer running:

20 executions / second

will explore much less than one running:

20,000 executions / second

Optimise:

  • target startup;
  • harness;
  • I/O;
  • instrumentation;
  • logging.

Performance affects coverage.

docs.title: Persistent Execution
docs.text:
Some fuzzing models keep the target process alive across many inputs.

This reduces process startup overhead.

Persistent operation must ensure state from one input does not incorrectly affect later inputs.

docs.title: Sanitizers
docs.text:
Compiler sanitizers are extremely useful during fuzzing and crash analysis.

Common examples include:

  • AddressSanitizer;
  • UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer;
  • MemorySanitizer where appropriate.

docs.title: AddressSanitizer
docs.text:
AddressSanitizer, commonly ASan, detects memory errors such as:

  • out-of-bounds access;
  • use-after-free;
  • some double-free conditions.

Official documentation:

AddressSanitizer

docs.title: Why ASan Helps
docs.text:
A normal crash may only show:

Segmentation fault

ASan may provide:

Type of memory error
Faulting location
Allocation context
Stack trace

This can substantially accelerate root-cause analysis.

docs.title: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer
docs.text:
UBSan detects several categories of undefined behaviour.

Official documentation:

UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer

It is useful for identifying conditions that may not immediately crash.

docs.title: Fuzzer Crash Is Only the Start
docs.text:
When a fuzzer reports a crash:

Crash Input
    |
    v
Reproduce Manually
    |
    v
Minimise
    |
    v
Debug
    |
    v
Root Cause
    |
    v
Assess Impact

Related methodology:

Crash Analysis

docs.title: Reproduce First
docs.text:
A crash should be reproducible outside the fuzzer.

For example:

target crashing-input

If the crash cannot be reproduced, investigate:

  • timing;
  • nondeterminism;
  • environment;
  • resource exhaustion;
  • state.

docs.title: Minimise Crash Input
docs.text:
A large crashing file may contain thousands of irrelevant bytes.

Input minimisation helps identify the smallest structure necessary to trigger the bug.

Benefits include:

  • easier root-cause analysis;
  • clearer PoC;
  • easier reporting;
  • faster regression testing.

docs.title: Crash Bucketing
docs.text:
Large fuzzing campaigns may discover the same bug many times.

Crashes can be grouped using information such as:

Exception
Faulting instruction
Stack trace
Top stack frames
Sanitizer report

Do not count each crashing file as a separate vulnerability.

docs.title: Crash Deduplication
docs.text:
A simplified process:

1000 Crashes
     |
     v
Stack / Fault Analysis
     |
     v
20 Buckets
     |
     v
Manual Root Cause
     |
     v
3 Unique Bugs

Deduplication prevents wasted effort.

docs.title: Crash Severity
docs.text:
Not every crash is security relevant.

Possible categories include:

Null dereference
Assertion failure
Stack exhaustion
Out-of-bounds read
Out-of-bounds write
Use-after-free
Integer issue
Logic error

Security impact depends on:

  • attacker control;
  • process privilege;
  • reachable interface;
  • mitigation;
  • reliability.

docs.title: Denial of Service
docs.text:
A reliably reachable crash may represent a denial-of-service issue even when code execution is not feasible.

Assess:

  • service restart;
  • availability impact;
  • authentication requirement;
  • crash frequency;
  • affected users.

docs.title: Root-Cause Analysis
docs.text:
The goal of crash analysis is to determine why the software entered an unsafe state.

Input
  |
  v
Parser
  |
  v
Validation Error
  |
  v
Unsafe State
  |
  v
Crash

The crash location is not always the root cause.

docs.title: Root Cause vs Crash Site
docs.text:
Example:

Length field incorrectly trusted
        |
        v
Memory allocation too small
        |
        v
Later copy
        |
        v
Crash

The crash occurs during the copy.

The root cause may be the earlier length validation.

docs.title: Taint / Data-Flow Reasoning
docs.text:
Track attacker-controlled data.

Input Byte
    |
    v
Parser Field
    |
    v
Length Calculation
    |
    v
Memory Access

The research question is:

How much control does the attacker have over the value that causes the unsafe operation?

docs.title: Exploitability Assessment
docs.text:
Once root cause is understood, assess potential impact.

Questions include:

Can attacker control written data?

Can attacker control write location?

Can attacker control instruction pointer?

Is only a read possible?

Is memory disclosure possible?

Which mitigations are enabled?

Does process sandboxing reduce impact?

Avoid overclaiming.

docs.title: Binary Security Properties
docs.text:
Relevant mitigations may include:

  • ASLR;
  • DEP/NX;
  • stack canaries;
  • CFG;
  • CET;
  • PIE;
  • RELRO;
  • sandboxing.

The mitigation set depends on platform.

docs.title: Linux Binary Properties
docs.text:
Tools such as readelf and appropriate analysis utilities can reveal ELF properties.

Example:

readelf -h ./target

Sections:

readelf -S ./target

Dynamic dependencies:

ldd ./target

Use caution with ldd against untrusted binaries.

docs.title: file
docs.text:
The Unix file utility quickly identifies binary type.

file ./target

Example information may include:

ELF
Architecture
Dynamically linked
Stripped

docs.title: strings
docs.text:
strings can reveal embedded text.

strings ./target

Useful discoveries may include:

  • file paths;
  • error messages;
  • URLs;
  • function names;
  • protocol strings;
  • format names.

Strings are hints, not definitive program behaviour.

docs.title: objdump
docs.text:
objdump can inspect object files and binaries.

Example:

objdump -d ./target

Use tool help:

objdump --help

for available analysis options.

docs.title: readelf
docs.text:
readelf is useful for ELF structures.

Examples:

readelf -h ./target

readelf -l ./target

readelf -s ./target

docs.title: Windows PE Inspection
docs.text:
Windows Portable Executable files can be inspected using:

  • debugger module views;
  • Ghidra;
  • PE analysis utilities;
  • Sysinternals tools;
  • compiler/linker tooling.

Useful properties include:

Architecture
Imports
Exports
Sections
Debug information
Mitigations

docs.title: Imports
docs.text:
Imported functions can reveal likely application behaviour.

Examples:

Networking APIs
File APIs
Cryptographic APIs
Memory functions
Process APIs

Imports are useful starting points for reverse engineering.

docs.title: Exports
docs.text:
DLL exports can reveal externally callable functionality.

On Windows, exported functions may be inspected with appropriate PE tools or development utilities.

Exports can help identify:

  • plugin interfaces;
  • callable functions;
  • COM-style entry points;
  • library interfaces.

docs.title: Patch Diffing
docs.text:
Patch diffing compares vulnerable and fixed versions to identify what changed.

Related methodology:

Patch Diffing

docs.title: Patch Diffing Workflow
docs.text:
Old Version
    |
    +----+
         |
         v
      Compare
         ^
         |
    +----+
    |
Fixed Version
      |
      v
Changed Functions
      |
      v
Security-Relevant Difference
      |
      v
Root Cause

docs.title: Source-Level Diffing
docs.text:
If source is available:

git diff <old> <new>

or:

git show <commit>

This is usually easier than binary diffing.

docs.title: Git History
docs.text:
Useful Git commands include:

git log

git show <commit>

git blame path/to/file

Git history can reveal:

  • when code changed;
  • why it changed;
  • related commits;
  • previous implementations.

docs.title: Security Fix Commit
docs.text:
A security patch may not explicitly say:

security fix

Look for changes involving:

  • bounds validation;
  • authentication;
  • authorisation;
  • parser hardening;
  • memory allocation;
  • input validation.

Do not assume every suspicious change is security related.

docs.title: Binary Diffing
docs.text:
When source is unavailable, compare binaries.

Potential approaches include:

  • disassembly comparison;
  • function similarity;
  • changed constants;
  • changed branches;
  • imported API changes.

Tools such as Ghidra scripts and binary diffing platforms can help.

docs.title: Diaphora
docs.text:
Diaphora is a program-diffing tool commonly used with IDA.

Official project:

Diaphora - GitHub

It can assist with identifying changed functions between binary versions.

docs.title: Patch Diffing Is Not Automatic Vulnerability Discovery
docs.text:
A changed function may represent:

  • refactoring;
  • performance work;
  • feature change;
  • compatibility change;
  • bug fix.

The researcher still needs to identify:

What changed?

Why?

Does old behaviour cross a security boundary?

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Once one bug is understood, search for similar patterns.

Related methodology:

Variant Analysis

docs.title: Variant Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
Known Vulnerability
      |
      v
Root Cause
      |
      v
Generalise Pattern
      |
      v
Search Other Functions
      |
      v
Search Other Components
      |
      v
Validate Candidates

docs.title: Source-Level Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Useful tools include:

  • ripgrep;
  • Semgrep;
  • OpenGrep;
  • CodeQL.

Canonical references:

ripgrep

Semgrep

OpenGrep

CodeQL

docs.title: Binary Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Without source code, variant analysis may use:

  • similar call patterns;
  • cross-references;
  • repeated parser structures;
  • shared libraries;
  • related binaries;
  • patch differences.

This is slower but can still identify sibling issues.

docs.title: Fuzzer-Guided Variant Analysis
docs.text:
After identifying one parser weakness:

Fix / Block Original Crash
       |
       v
Continue Fuzzing
       |
       v
Explore Nearby State Space
       |
       v
Find Related Bugs

Do not stop a fuzzing campaign after the first crash.

docs.title: Proof-of-Concept Development
docs.text:
A proof of concept should demonstrate the security condition with the minimum necessary complexity.

Related methodology:

Proof-of-Concept Development

docs.title: PoC Principle
docs.text:
Prefer:

Minimal
Deterministic
Reproducible
Safe
Understandable

Avoid:

Large exploit framework
Unnecessary persistence
Unrelated payloads
Complex environmental dependencies

docs.title: Crash PoC
docs.text:
For a memory-corruption issue, an initial PoC may simply:

Trigger deterministic crash

This can be enough to demonstrate the root cause while exploitability is still under investigation.

docs.title: Security Impact PoC
docs.text:
Where necessary, a PoC may demonstrate:

  • controlled read;
  • controlled write;
  • authentication bypass;
  • privilege boundary bypass;
  • server-side request;
  • information disclosure.

Use the minimum impact required to validate the issue.

docs.title: Avoid Unnecessary Weaponisation
docs.text:
A disclosure-quality PoC rarely needs:

  • persistence;
  • stealth;
  • unrelated lateral movement;
  • destructive payloads.

The objective is to prove the vulnerability.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Python is extremely useful for vulnerability research.

Common uses include:

  • generating test files;
  • mutating input;
  • interacting with protocols;
  • parsing logs;
  • crash deduplication;
  • automation;
  • PoC development.

docs.title: Binary Data in Python
docs.text:
Python is convenient for byte-level input manipulation.

Example:

data = b"A" * 100

Write a test file:

with open("test.bin", "wb") as f:
    f.write(data)

Keep research scripts clear and reproducible.

docs.title: struct
docs.text:
Python's struct module helps encode binary values.

Example:

import struct

value = struct.pack("<I", 100)

This is useful for file-format and protocol research.

docs.title: Logging Test Cases
docs.text:
A useful script should record:

Input
Target
Timestamp
Result

rather than silently sending large numbers of tests.

docs.title: Network Protocol Research
docs.text:
Protocol vulnerabilities often require packet-level visibility.

Useful tools include:

  • Wireshark;
  • tcpdump;
  • protocol-specific clients;
  • Python.

docs.title: Wireshark
docs.text:
Wireshark can inspect network traffic in detail.

Official resource:

Wireshark

It can help analyse:

  • protocol structure;
  • malformed requests;
  • connection resets;
  • TLS negotiation;
  • retransmission;
  • server responses.

docs.title: tcpdump
docs.text:
tcpdump provides command-line packet capture.

Example:

tcpdump -i eth0

Use filters to minimise unnecessary captured data.

Packet captures may contain credentials or sensitive application traffic.

Protect them appropriately.

docs.title: HTTP Research
docs.text:
For HTTP-facing vulnerabilities, useful tools may include:

  • Burp Suite;
  • curl;
  • browser developer tools;
  • Python.

Related tool:

Burp Suite

docs.title: Burp in Vulnerability Research
docs.text:
Burp Suite is useful where a vulnerability involves:

  • HTTP parsing;
  • APIs;
  • session behaviour;
  • request manipulation;
  • protocol differences;
  • application state.

Repeater is especially useful for controlled experimentation.

docs.title: Binary vs Web Research
docs.text:
Tool choice depends on target type.

Web Application
    |
    +-- Burp
    +-- browser
    +-- static source tools

Native Binary
    |
    +-- debugger
    +-- disassembler
    +-- fuzzer

Network Service
    |
    +-- protocol client
    +-- Wireshark
    +-- debugger
    +-- fuzzer

docs.title: Attack Surface Analysis
docs.text:
Before fuzzing or debugging everything, identify likely attack surfaces.

Related methodology:

Attack Surface Analysis

Potential surfaces include:

Network listeners
File parsers
IPC
RPC
Browser handlers
Plugins
Import/export
Update mechanisms
Authentication interfaces
APIs

docs.title: Parser Research
docs.text:
Parsers are common vulnerability research targets because they process complex, attacker-controlled structures.

Examples include:

  • images;
  • archives;
  • documents;
  • protocol messages;
  • configuration formats.

A strong parser workflow is:

Valid Sample
    |
    v
Understand Structure
    |
    v
Identify Parser
    |
    v
Instrument
    |
    v
Fuzz

docs.title: File Format Research
docs.text:
Useful tools include:

  • hex editors;
  • Python;
  • file-format specifications;
  • Ghidra;
  • debugger;
  • fuzzer.

A file-format model may look like:

Header
Length
Metadata
Data
Footer

Fields controlling lengths, offsets, counts, and types often deserve careful review.

docs.title: Hex Editors
docs.text:
Hex editors allow direct inspection and modification of binary files.

Useful features include:

  • offsets;
  • byte editing;
  • comparisons;
  • templates.

The exact editor is a matter of preference.

docs.title: Magic Bytes
docs.text:
Many file formats begin with distinctive bytes.

Use:

xxd sample.bin | head

or:

hexdump -C sample.bin | head

This can help map the file structure.

docs.title: xxd
docs.text:
xxd converts binary data to a hexadecimal view.

Example:

xxd sample.bin

Reverse a hex dump where appropriate:

xxd -r

Check:

xxd -h

for exact syntax.

docs.title: Diffing Test Inputs
docs.text:
Compare files:

cmp file1.bin file2.bin

or use:

xxd file1.bin > file1.hex
xxd file2.bin > file2.hex
diff -u file1.hex file2.hex

This can help identify fields changed by an application.

docs.title: Process Monitoring
docs.text:
Dynamic application behaviour can reveal attack surface.

For example:

Open File
   |
   v
Application loads DLL
   |
   v
Application opens temp file
   |
   v
Application creates child process

Tools such as Procmon, strace, and debugger tracing make these relationships visible.

docs.title: API Monitoring
docs.text:
A debugger breakpoint on a sensitive function can reveal when and how it is called.

Useful target APIs may relate to:

  • memory operations;
  • file access;
  • process creation;
  • network access;
  • cryptography;
  • parsing.

Choose breakpoints based on the research hypothesis.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Coverage answers:

Which code did my tests actually execute?

This is crucial for fuzzing.

Input A -> Paths 1,2,3
Input B -> Paths 1,2,4
Input C -> Paths 1,5,6

A fuzzer can use this feedback to preserve inputs that reach new code.

docs.title: Coverage Is Not Security Coverage
docs.text:
High code coverage does not prove all security-relevant states were tested.

A program may require:

  • specific values;
  • long state sequences;
  • authentication;
  • environmental conditions.

Coverage is one measurement, not proof of completeness.

docs.title: Fuzzing Hangs
docs.text:
A fuzzer may classify input as a hang if the target exceeds a timeout.

Potential causes include:

  • infinite loop;
  • deadlock;
  • expensive computation;
  • slow valid behaviour.

Reproduce hangs separately before reporting.

docs.title: Resource Exhaustion
docs.text:
Malformed input may cause:

  • excessive memory use;
  • CPU exhaustion;
  • disk growth;
  • recursion.

These can represent denial-of-service conditions.

Measure carefully to avoid destabilising shared systems.

docs.title: Memory Leaks
docs.text:
Long-running fuzzing or repeated requests may expose memory leaks.

Useful evidence includes:

Memory before
Memory after repeated input
Rate of growth
Recovery behaviour

A one-time allocation increase is not automatically a leak.

docs.title: Integer Issues
docs.text:
Integer overflow, truncation, or signedness problems may lead to unsafe sizes or bounds checks.

A common reasoning pattern is:

Input Length
    |
    v
Integer Conversion
    |
    v
Unexpected Value
    |
    v
Allocation / Copy Mismatch

Debuggers and sanitizers can help identify this chain.

docs.title: Use-After-Free
docs.text:
A use-after-free occurs when memory is accessed after its lifetime has ended.

ASan can often identify:

  • allocation location;
  • free location;
  • invalid later use.

Exploitability depends on control and memory reuse.

docs.title: Out-of-Bounds Read
docs.text:
An out-of-bounds read may lead to:

  • crash;
  • memory disclosure;
  • unexpected application behaviour.

Determine whether sensitive adjacent memory can be exposed.

docs.title: Out-of-Bounds Write
docs.text:
An out-of-bounds write can be more severe because memory state is modified.

Still assess:

  • data control;
  • destination control;
  • process mitigations;
  • reachable interface.

Do not automatically label all writes as code execution.

docs.title: Stack Overflow
docs.text:
A stack buffer overflow may corrupt:

  • local variables;
  • saved control data;
  • adjacent stack state.

Modern mitigations can affect exploitability.

The vulnerability is the unsafe memory operation, not the eventual exploit technique.

docs.title: Heap Corruption
docs.text:
Heap corruption can manifest far from the original unsafe operation.

Debuggers and sanitizers are particularly important for finding the earlier root cause.

docs.title: Assertions
docs.text:
Assertion failures can expose logic assumptions.

An assertion crash may be:

  • non-security bug;
  • denial of service;
  • indication of deeper state corruption.

Investigate what attacker-controlled condition violates the assumption.

docs.title: Exception Handling
docs.text:
Programs may catch malformed input safely.

Example:

Invalid Input
    |
    v
Parser Error
    |
    v
Graceful Rejection

This is different from:

Invalid Input
    |
    v
Unhandled Exception
    |
    v
Service Crash

docs.title: Crash Reproduction Template
docs.text:
Record:

Target:
Version:
OS:
Architecture:
Input:
Command:
Expected:
Observed:
Exception:
Faulting module:
Reproducibility:

This makes crash triage systematic.

docs.title: Crash Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
Crash Found
   |
   v
Reproduce
   |
   v
Minimise
   |
   v
Debugger
   |
   v
Identify Fault
   |
   v
Trace Back to Root Cause
   |
   v
Assess Attacker Control
   |
   v
Determine Impact

docs.title: Patch Validation
docs.text:
After a vendor fix:

Original PoC
     |
     v
Fixed Version
     |
     +-- Still triggers -> investigate
     |
     +-- Rejected safely -> continue

Then inspect whether the patch addresses the root cause.

docs.title: Regression Testing
docs.text:
A good regression test preserves the smallest safe input that reproduces the original issue.

After remediation:

Run Original Regression Input
      |
      v
Expected Safe Behaviour

The same test can help prevent reintroduction.

docs.title: CVE Research
docs.text:
When researching a known CVE, establish:

Affected component
Affected versions
Attack vector
Prerequisites
Vendor advisory
Patch
Root cause
Public technical analysis

Related methodology:

CVE Research

docs.title: Vendor Advisory First
docs.text:
For known vulnerabilities, start with the vendor where possible.

Then compare:

  • CVE record;
  • vendor advisory;
  • patch;
  • independent research.

Do not rely only on exploit repositories or copied blog posts.

docs.title: Version Validation
docs.text:
A service banner may not reveal exact patch state.

Consider:

  • backports;
  • vendor build numbers;
  • custom patches;
  • distribution packages.

Version identification should be supported by reliable evidence.

docs.title: Proof-of-Concept Authenticity
docs.text:
Public PoCs vary significantly in quality.

Before running third-party code:

  • read the source;
  • inspect network destinations;
  • inspect file operations;
  • run in an isolated environment;
  • verify author/repository;
  • remove unnecessary functionality.

Never blindly execute exploit code.

docs.title: Malicious PoCs
docs.text:
Fake or modified PoCs have historically been used to compromise researchers.

Treat exploit code as untrusted.

A safe workflow is:

Download
  |
  v
Read Source
  |
  v
Static Inspection
  |
  v
Isolated Execution

docs.title: Responsible Disclosure
docs.text:
Once a new vulnerability is confirmed, research should transition into controlled disclosure.

Related methodology:

Responsible Disclosure

Typical evidence includes:

  • affected version;
  • reproduction instructions;
  • minimal PoC;
  • root cause;
  • impact;
  • suggested mitigation.

docs.title: Do Not Overstate Impact
docs.text:
A crash does not automatically justify:

Remote Code Execution

Likewise:

Memory corruption

does not always mean:

Arbitrary code execution

Use the strongest impact supported by evidence.

docs.title: Evidence Preservation
docs.text:
Preserve:

Original binary
Hash
Crashing input
Minimised input
Debugger output
Stack trace
Patch version
PoC
Research notes

These artefacts are invaluable during disclosure.

docs.title: Hash Target Binaries
docs.text:
Windows:

Get-FileHash .\target.exe -Algorithm SHA256

Linux:

sha256sum ./target

This confirms exactly which binary was analysed.

docs.title: Hash Crash Inputs
docs.text:
Also hash important inputs:

sha256sum crash.bin

This prevents confusion when several similar crash files exist.

docs.title: Naming Crash Files
docs.text:
Prefer descriptive names such as:

crash-oob-read-parser-field17.bin

rather than:

id_000013

Keep the original fuzzer filename as metadata where useful.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
Maintain a timeline.

Example:

14:10 - Fuzzer found crash
14:18 - Reproduced manually
14:31 - ASan reports heap-buffer-overflow
15:05 - Reduced input to 92 bytes
16:10 - Root cause identified in parse_record()

This makes research easier to resume.

docs.title: Git for Research Scripts
docs.text:
Keep custom scripts under version control where appropriate.

Do not commit:

  • proprietary binaries;
  • customer data;
  • credentials;
  • embargoed vulnerability details;

to public repositories.

docs.title: Debug Symbols and Proprietary Data
docs.text:
Vendor symbols or proprietary binaries may be subject to licensing and confidentiality restrictions.

Respect those terms.

docs.title: Tool Version Recording
docs.text:
Record versions for:

GDB
GEF/pwndbg
WinDbg
Ghidra
AFL++
Compiler
Sanitizers
Python

Research behaviour can change between versions.

docs.title: Automate Repetitive Work
docs.text:
Good research automation includes:

  • starting target;
  • sending input;
  • detecting crash;
  • restarting target;
  • collecting logs;
  • deduplicating crashes.

Automation should make the experiment more reproducible.

docs.title: Do Not Automate Interpretation
docs.text:
A script can classify:

Crash at address X

but the researcher still determines:

Is this unique?

Is it attacker controlled?

What is the root cause?

What is the impact?

docs.title: Tool Chaining
docs.text:
A common native-binary workflow may be:

Ghidra
  |
  v
Identify Parser
  |
  v
AFL++ / libFuzzer
  |
  v
Crash
  |
  v
GDB / WinDbg
  |
  v
Root Cause
  |
  v
Python PoC

docs.title: Web-Application Research Workflow
docs.text:
Source / Application
       |
       v
Burp Suite
       |
       v
Interesting Behaviour
       |
       v
Source Review
       |
       v
Root Cause
       |
       v
Variant Search

docs.title: Patch-Diff Workflow
docs.text:
Vendor Patch
    |
    v
Git / Binary Diff
    |
    v
Changed Function
    |
    v
Debugger
    |
    v
Understand Old Behaviour
    |
    v
PoC

docs.title: Fuzzing Workflow
docs.text:
Attack Surface
      |
      v
Harness
      |
      v
Seed Corpus
      |
      v
Fuzzer
      |
      v
Crash Corpus
      |
      v
Deduplicate
      |
      v
Minimise
      |
      v
Debug

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Research
docs.text:
Source-code tools can also support vulnerability research.

User Input
    |
    v
Source
    |
    v
Program Logic
    |
    v
Sink

Canonical tools:

Source Code Review Tools

docs.title: LLM-Assisted Vulnerability Research
docs.text:
LLMs can help with:

  • explaining unfamiliar code;
  • drafting harnesses;
  • suggesting debugger questions;
  • summarising patches;
  • generating search patterns;
  • comparing functions;
  • helping reason about parser structures.

However:

LLM Suggestion
     |
     v
Research Hypothesis
     |
     v
Independent Validation
     |
     v
Evidence
     |
     v
Conclusion

Never treat an LLM statement as proof of a vulnerability.

docs.title: LLM Limitations
docs.text:
LLMs may:

  • invent APIs;
  • misunderstand assembly;
  • miss compiler transformations;
  • misread decompiler output;
  • hallucinate CVEs;
  • overstate exploitability;
  • ignore mitigations.

Use them as assistants, not authorities.

docs.title: Sensitive Research and AI
docs.text:
Do not upload:

  • proprietary source;
  • unreleased binaries;
  • customer data;
  • private symbols;
  • embargoed vulnerability information;

to external AI services unless organisational policy explicitly permits it.

docs.title: Practical Vulnerability Research Workflow
docs.text:
A mature workflow can be:

1. Confirm authorisation
      |
      v
2. Record target/version
      |
      v
3. Build isolated environment
      |
      v
4. Map attack surface
      |
      v
5. Perform static analysis
      |
      v
6. Perform dynamic analysis
      |
      v
7. Build targeted harness/test
      |
      v
8. Fuzz or mutate inputs
      |
      v
9. Capture crashes/anomalies
      |
      v
10. Reproduce
      |
      v
11. Minimise
      |
      v
12. Debug
      |
      v
13. Identify root cause
      |
      v
14. Assess attacker control
      |
      v
15. Determine security impact
      |
      v
16. Search for variants
      |
      v
17. Develop minimal PoC
      |
      v
18. Validate patch/remediation
      |
      v
19. Preserve evidence
      |
      v
20. Disclose responsibly

docs.text:
Use:

WinDbg
x64dbg

docs.title: Need Linux Crash Analysis
docs.text:
Use:

GDB

docs.text:
Use:

docs.text:
Use:

docs.title: Need Linux Runtime Tracing
docs.text:
Use:

docs.title: Need Windows Runtime Tracing
docs.text:
Use:

docs.title: Need Coverage-Guided Fuzzing
docs.text:
Use:

AFL++

depending on target and build access.

docs.title: Need Memory Error Diagnostics
docs.text:
Use:

AddressSanitizer

where compilation/instrumentation is available.

docs.text:
Use:

Use:

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Research explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Exact target identified.
  • [ ] Version/build recorded.
  • [ ] Binary hash recorded.
  • [ ] Architecture recorded.
  • [ ] Research environment isolated.
  • [ ] Snapshot available where useful.
  • [ ] Tool versions recorded.

docs.title: Attack Surface
docs.text:
• [ ] External interfaces identified.
  • [ ] File parsers identified.
  • [ ] Network listeners identified.
  • [ ] IPC/RPC interfaces considered.
  • [ ] Plugins/extensions considered.
  • [ ] Privileged components identified.
  • [ ] Trust boundaries understood.

docs.title: Static Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Strings reviewed.
  • [ ] Imports reviewed.
  • [ ] Exports reviewed.
  • [ ] Interesting functions identified.
  • [ ] Cross-references reviewed.
  • [ ] Parser structures mapped.
  • [ ] Security checks identified.

docs.title: Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Target run under debugger where useful.
  • [ ] Breakpoints placed according to hypothesis.
  • [ ] Runtime file/network behaviour inspected.
  • [ ] Relevant function arguments observed.
  • [ ] Exceptions captured.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text:
• [ ] Target/harness selected.
  • [ ] Valid seed corpus created.
  • [ ] Corpus diversity considered.
  • [ ] Timeout appropriate.
  • [ ] Instrumentation configured.
  • [ ] Sanitizers enabled where possible.
  • [ ] Crashes saved.
  • [ ] Hangs saved separately.

docs.title: Crash Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Crash reproduced outside fuzzer.
  • [ ] Crash input preserved.
  • [ ] Crash input hash recorded.
  • [ ] Crash minimised.
  • [ ] Exception identified.
  • [ ] Faulting instruction identified.
  • [ ] Stack trace captured.
  • [ ] Root cause traced.
  • [ ] Duplicate crashes removed.

docs.title: Security Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Attacker-controlled data identified.
  • [ ] Reachability established.
  • [ ] Preconditions established.
  • [ ] Security boundary identified.
  • [ ] Mitigations reviewed.
  • [ ] Impact not overstated.
  • [ ] Denial-of-service distinguished from code execution.

docs.title: Patch Diffing
docs.text:
• [ ] Vulnerable version retained.
  • [ ] Fixed version retained.
  • [ ] Changed functions identified.
  • [ ] Security-relevant change understood.
  • [ ] Root cause compared with patch.
  • [ ] Original test run against fixed version.

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Root cause generalised.
  • [ ] Similar code searched.
  • [ ] Related components reviewed.
  • [ ] Shared library usage reviewed.
  • [ ] New candidates manually validated.

docs.title: PoC
docs.text:
• [ ] Minimal.
  • [ ] Deterministic.
  • [ ] Reproducible.
  • [ ] Safe.
  • [ ] Target version checked.
  • [ ] Unnecessary weaponisation avoided.
  • [ ] Output clearly demonstrates condition.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Target hash retained.
  • [ ] Crash input retained.
  • [ ] Crash input hash retained.
  • [ ] Debugger output retained.
  • [ ] Stack trace retained.
  • [ ] Research notes retained.
  • [ ] PoC retained.
  • [ ] Patch comparison retained.
  • [ ] Sensitive data protected.

docs.title: Final Research Model
docs.text:
Do not use vulnerability research tools like this:

Run Fuzzer
   |
   v
Find Crash
   |
   v
Call It RCE

Use them like this:

Understand Target
      |
      v
Map Attack Surface
      |
      v
Form Research Hypothesis
      |
      v
Choose Appropriate Tool
      |
      +-- Debugger
      +-- Disassembler
      +-- Fuzzer
      +-- Tracer
      +-- Static Analysis
      |
      v
Observe Behaviour
      |
      v
Capture Interesting Input
      |
      v
Reproduce
      |
      v
Minimise
      |
      v
Identify Root Cause
      |
      v
Trace Attacker Control
      |
      v
Assess Security Boundary
      |
      v
Evaluate Mitigations
      |
      v
Determine Supported Impact
      |
      v
Search for Variants
      |
      v
Build Minimal PoC
      |
      v
Validate Remediation
      |
      v
Preserve Evidence
      |
      v
Disclose Responsibly

Vulnerability research tools provide visibility into how software behaves internally.

The tools help reveal crashes, code paths, state changes, and implementation details.

The researcher determines whether those observations represent a real security vulnerability, what the root cause is, and what impact the available evidence actually supports.

docs.title: Web Enumeration Tools
docs.text:
Web enumeration is the process of collecting and validating information about web applications before deeper testing begins.

The objective is not simply to run several fingerprinting tools.

The objective is to answer questions such as:

  • Which hosts actually expose HTTP or HTTPS?
  • Which applications are reachable?
  • Which technologies appear to be in use?
  • Which frameworks, CMS platforms, or libraries may be present?
  • Which ports expose web services?
  • Which redirects occur?
  • Which TLS endpoints exist?
  • Which application titles and response patterns are interesting?
  • Are there default error pages or framework-specific responses?
  • Are multiple applications hosted behind the same IP address?
  • Which targets deserve deeper manual testing?
  • Which observations can be independently validated?

A useful web enumeration workflow is:

Domains / IP Addresses
        |
        v
Identify Web Services
        |
        v
Collect HTTP Metadata
        |
        +-- Status Codes
        +-- Titles
        +-- Headers
        +-- Redirects
        +-- TLS
        |
        v
Technology Fingerprinting
        |
        +-- WhatWeb
        +-- Wappalyzer
        +-- httpx
        |
        v
Manual Validation
        |
        +-- HTML
        +-- Headers
        +-- Cookies
        +-- Asset Paths
        +-- Error Pages
        |
        v
Prioritised Web Targets
        |
        v
Deeper Web Testing

Authorised testing only

Perform web enumeration only against systems and applications that are explicitly within the authorised assessment scope. Enumeration tools can generate large numbers of requests, follow redirects, probe multiple ports, or interact with third-party infrastructure. Review the rules of engagement before increasing concurrency, recursion, or scan coverage.

docs.title: Primary Tools
docs.text:
The core tools in this section are:

Tool Primary Purpose WhatWeb Fingerprint web technologies Wappalyzer Identify technologies during browser-based inspection httpx Probe HTTP services and collect structured metadata Nmap Identify open ports and web services curl Manually inspect HTTP behaviour Burp Suite Interactively inspect and validate application responses

The first three are the primary web enumeration tools documented in this section.

docs.title: WhatWeb
docs.text:
WhatWeb is designed specifically for website fingerprinting.

It identifies indicators associated with technologies such as:

  • web servers;
  • frameworks;
  • CMS platforms;
  • JavaScript libraries;
  • analytics platforms;
  • application components;
  • HTTP headers;
  • cookies;
  • HTML patterns;
  • page metadata.

Basic usage:

whatweb https://example.test

Typical workflow:

Target
  |
  v
WhatWeb
  |
  +-- Headers
  +-- HTML
  +-- Cookies
  +-- Metadata
  +-- Known Patterns
  |
  v
Technology Candidates
  |
  v
Manual Validation

A WhatWeb result is generally a fingerprinting indicator rather than definitive proof.

For example:

WhatWeb:
Apache

Response header:
Server: Apache

Default error page:
Apache-style response

Asset structure:
Consistent with candidate stack

Result:
Higher-confidence fingerprint

Detailed note:

WhatWeb

Official project:

WhatWeb - GitHub

docs.title: Wappalyzer
docs.text:
Wappalyzer identifies technologies associated with websites and web applications.

It is especially useful during interactive browser-based reconnaissance.

Depending on the interface being used, Wappalyzer may identify:

  • web frameworks;
  • CMS platforms;
  • JavaScript frameworks;
  • analytics systems;
  • CDN providers;
  • server technologies;
  • e-commerce platforms;
  • tag managers;
  • development frameworks;
  • security-related infrastructure.

A typical workflow is:

Browser
  |
  v
Application
  |
  v
Wappalyzer
  |
  +-- Framework
  +-- CMS
  +-- Libraries
  +-- Infrastructure
  |
  v
Candidate Technologies
  |
  v
Manual Validation

Wappalyzer findings should be correlated with other observations.

Useful supporting evidence includes:

  • response headers;
  • cookies;
  • HTML source;
  • JavaScript bundles;
  • asset paths;
  • application behaviour;
  • error pages;
  • WhatWeb results;
  • httpx results.

Detailed note:

Wappalyzer

Official resource:

Wappalyzer

docs.title: httpx
docs.text:
ProjectDiscovery httpx is designed for HTTP probing and enrichment.

It is particularly useful when reconnaissance produces a large set of domains or subdomains.

A simple workflow is:

subdomains.txt
      |
      v
    httpx
      |
      +-- Reachable hosts
      +-- HTTP status
      +-- Title
      +-- Technology
      +-- Redirect
      +-- TLS
      |
      v
alive-web.txt

This allows a large discovery set to be reduced into a more useful collection of reachable web services.

Useful output may include:

  • URL;
  • HTTP status code;
  • page title;
  • content length;
  • content type;
  • redirect location;
  • server information;
  • technology indicators;
  • IP address;
  • TLS information;
  • response hashes;
  • favicon information.

Detailed note:

httpx

Official documentation:

ProjectDiscovery httpx

httpx Usage

docs.title: Supporting Tools
docs.text:
Web enumeration frequently involves additional tools.

These may not be dedicated fingerprinting tools, but they can provide important supporting evidence.

docs.title: Nmap
docs.text:
Nmap can identify open ports and services before HTTP-specific probing begins.

For example:

nmap -sV -p 80,443,8000,8080,8443 example.test

Potential observations include:

80/tcp    open  http
443/tcp   open  https
8080/tcp  open  http-proxy
8443/tcp  open  https-alt

These results indicate where additional HTTP enumeration may be useful.

A useful workflow is:

Host
 |
 v
Nmap
 |
 +-- 80
 +-- 443
 +-- 8080
 +-- 8443
 |
 v
HTTP Probing

Nmap service detection should not automatically be treated as definitive technology identification.

Banners can be:

  • removed;
  • modified;
  • proxied;
  • misleading;
  • affected by backported software.

Official documentation:

Nmap Reference Guide

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
curl is extremely useful for validating individual HTTP observations manually.

Examples:

curl -i https://example.test/

curl -I https://example.test/

curl -v https://example.test/

curl can help inspect:

  • HTTP headers;
  • redirects;
  • cookies;
  • TLS behaviour;
  • server headers;
  • response content;
  • virtual host behaviour;
  • API responses.

For reconnaissance, curl is particularly useful for confirming whether an automated fingerprint corresponds to the actual HTTP response.

Example:

WhatWeb
   |
   v
Candidate technology
   |
   v
curl
   |
   +-- inspect headers
   +-- inspect response
   +-- inspect redirect
   |
   v
Manual confirmation

Quick reference:

curl Cheatsheet

docs.title: Burp Suite
docs.text:
Burp Suite is useful when web enumeration becomes interactive.

For example, after initial fingerprinting, Burp can help inspect:

  • complete HTTP history;
  • unusual redirects;
  • cookies;
  • authentication flows;
  • API calls;
  • JavaScript requests;
  • hidden endpoints;
  • headers;
  • error behaviour.

Related tool section:

Web Application Testing Tools

docs.title: Passive and Active Enumeration
docs.text: Web enumeration can be broadly divided into passive and active activities.

docs.title: Passive Enumeration
docs.text:
Passive techniques attempt to collect information without directly interacting with the target application or by minimising direct interaction.

Examples include:

  • examining previously collected asset information;
  • reviewing DNS data;
  • reviewing certificate transparency information;
  • reviewing publicly indexed resources;
  • analysing known technology information;
  • examining historical URLs.

Passive techniques can provide useful context but may contain stale data.

docs.title: Active Enumeration
docs.text:
Active techniques interact directly with the target.

Examples include:

  • HTTP probing;
  • requesting application pages;
  • examining headers;
  • fingerprinting technologies;
  • requesting non-existing resources;
  • following redirects;
  • probing known web ports.

Examples:

whatweb https://example.test

curl -I https://example.test

httpx -u https://example.test

Active enumeration generally produces more current information but must remain within the agreed scope and testing constraints.

docs.title: HTTP Status Codes
docs.text:
HTTP status codes are useful enumeration signals.

Common examples include:

Status General Meaning 200 Request succeeded 201 Resource created 204 Successful response without body 301 Permanent redirect 302 Temporary redirect 307 Temporary redirect preserving request method 308 Permanent redirect preserving request method 400 Bad request 401 Authentication required 403 Request understood but access denied 404 Resource not found 405 HTTP method not allowed 429 Rate limit or request throttling 500 Internal server error 502 Gateway or upstream error 503 Service unavailable

A status code is useful context, but it should not be interpreted in isolation.

For example:

403

may represent:

  • genuine authorisation denial;
  • WAF blocking;
  • IP restrictions;
  • missing authentication;
  • reverse proxy behaviour;
  • virtual host mismatch;
  • application routing.

Similarly:

404

may be:

  • genuine resource absence;
  • custom application response;
  • soft 404;
  • wildcard routing;
  • intentional security behaviour.

docs.title: Response Titles
docs.text:
HTML page titles are useful for quickly understanding a large set of HTTP targets.

For example:

200  Admin Portal
200  Grafana
302  Login
403  Forbidden
200  Jenkins

Titles may reveal:

  • administrative interfaces;
  • development systems;
  • monitoring platforms;
  • application names;
  • product names;
  • login interfaces;
  • default applications.

Titles should be combined with other evidence because custom applications can use arbitrary titles.

docs.title: HTTP Headers
docs.text:
HTTP headers can provide valuable fingerprinting indicators.

Examples include:

Server:
X-Powered-By:
Via:
X-AspNet-Version:
X-Generator:
X-Drupal-Cache:
X-Runtime:
X-Request-ID:

Example:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
Content-Type: text/html

Another example:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Powered-By: Express
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Headers may indicate a candidate technology, but they may also be:

  • disabled;
  • rewritten;
  • inserted by proxies;
  • removed by CDNs;
  • intentionally misleading.

The absence of a technology header does not prove the technology is absent.

docs.title: Cookie Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Cookie names can sometimes provide useful application or framework indicators.

Examples may include session cookies, CSRF cookies, or framework-specific defaults.

A useful methodology is:

Observe Cookie
      |
      v
Identify Possible Framework Association
      |
      v
Check Other Indicators
      |
      +-- Headers
      +-- HTML
      +-- JavaScript
      +-- Paths
      |
      v
Determine Confidence

Do not rely solely on cookie names.

Applications frequently rename default cookies.

docs.title: HTML Source
docs.text:
HTML can contain useful fingerprinting information.

Review:

  • comments;
  • generator tags;
  • asset paths;
  • script names;
  • framework markers;
  • template structure;
  • application names;
  • build identifiers;
  • JavaScript framework artefacts.

Example:

<meta name="generator" content="WordPress">

Another possible indicator might be characteristic asset paths.

Automated tools often perform this analysis internally, but manual inspection is valuable for confirming their results.

docs.title: JavaScript Fingerprinting
docs.text:
JavaScript files can reveal:

  • frameworks;
  • libraries;
  • build systems;
  • application routes;
  • API endpoints;
  • versions;
  • source maps;
  • package names;
  • internal paths.

Related note:

JavaScript Analysis

Useful questions include:

Which bundles are loaded?

Which framework generated them?

Are source maps exposed?

Which API endpoints are referenced?

Are version strings visible?

Which third-party libraries are used?

JavaScript fingerprinting should be part of broader application analysis rather than a standalone conclusion.

docs.title: Default Error Pages
docs.text:
Default error pages are often useful technology indicators.

Useful responses include:

  • 404 Not Found;
  • 403 Forbidden;
  • 500 Internal Server Error;
  • framework routing errors;
  • application exception pages;
  • default container error pages.

A simple testing pattern is:

Request random resource
      |
      v
/nonexistent-8472631
      |
      v
Observe response
      |
      +-- Status
      +-- HTML
      +-- Headers
      +-- Cookies
      +-- Error wording
      |
      v
Compare with known fingerprints

Example request:

curl -i https://example.test/nonexistent-8472631

A useful external comparison reference is:

0xdf - Default 404 Pages

Default error pages can suggest a technology but should not be treated as definitive identification.

docs.title: Custom Error Pages
docs.text:
Applications frequently replace default framework error pages.

For example:

Default framework response
        |
        v
Custom application template
        |
        v
Fingerprint hidden

This means failure to recognise a default 404 page does not mean the application cannot be fingerprinted.

Other indicators may still reveal the stack:

  • cookies;
  • headers;
  • HTML structure;
  • asset names;
  • JavaScript bundles;
  • application routes;
  • TLS;
  • response behaviour.

docs.title: Soft 404 Responses
docs.text:
Some applications return a 200 OK response even when a requested resource does not exist.

Example:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

with body:

Sorry, the page you requested does not exist.

This is commonly called a soft 404.

Soft 404 behaviour matters because it can affect:

  • content discovery;
  • automated scanners;
  • response filtering;
  • endpoint discovery;
  • crawler output.

Always establish a baseline for non-existing resources.

Example:

curl -i https://example.test/random-not-found-918273

Record:

Status:
Content length:
Word count:
Line count:
Title:
Body pattern:

This baseline becomes useful when interpreting tools such as ffuf.

docs.title: Redirect Analysis
docs.text:
Redirects frequently reveal application structure.

Examples include:

http://example.test
        |
        v
https://example.test

or:

/
 |
 v
/login

or:

/app
 |
 v
/auth/signin

Useful observations include:

  • destination;
  • status code;
  • hostname changes;
  • scheme changes;
  • path changes;
  • authentication redirects;
  • external redirects.

Example:

curl -I https://example.test

Example response:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /login

Following redirects can reveal the final application, but the intermediate redirect chain can also contain useful information.

docs.title: Virtual Hosts
docs.text:
Several websites may share the same IP address.

             +--> app.example.test
IP Address --+--> admin.example.test
             +--> api.example.test

This is often implemented through HTTP virtual hosting.

Therefore:

IP address

and:

hostname

may return completely different applications.

When validating a web service, preserve the hostname where possible.

docs.title: TLS Information
docs.text:
TLS can provide additional reconnaissance information.

Useful observations include:

  • certificate subject;
  • Subject Alternative Names;
  • issuer;
  • validity period;
  • protocol support;
  • hostname relationships.

Certificate information may reveal additional hostnames.

However, certificate names must still be validated against scope before further testing.

Certificate
    |
    v
Additional Hostname
    |
    v
Scope Check
    |
    +-- In scope -> investigate
    |
    +-- Out of scope -> record only

docs.title: Favicon Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Favicons can provide additional technology fingerprints.

A favicon can be:

  • downloaded;
  • hashed;
  • compared with known fingerprints;
  • correlated with product-specific behaviour.

This can sometimes assist in identifying:

  • administrative products;
  • monitoring tools;
  • dashboards;
  • frameworks;
  • appliances.

Favicon matches should be treated as supporting evidence rather than definitive proof.

docs.title: Framework Asset Paths
docs.text:
Frameworks and applications often expose characteristic asset paths.

Examples of useful categories include:

Static resources
Build assets
Framework bundles
Generated JavaScript
CSS
Image directories
Application-specific paths

These patterns can assist technology identification.

However, applications may:

  • proxy assets;
  • rename paths;
  • bundle multiple technologies;
  • retain legacy files;
  • serve static resources through a CDN.

Therefore, path-based fingerprinting should be correlated with behavioural evidence.

docs.title: API Fingerprinting
docs.text:
APIs often reveal technology information differently from traditional web pages.

Useful indicators include:

  • JSON error formats;
  • response headers;
  • default documentation endpoints;
  • structured validation errors;
  • route behaviour;
  • authentication headers.

Example:

{
  "detail": "Not Found"
}

This may resemble the default behaviour of particular frameworks, but additional evidence is required.

Related notes:

API Security

GraphQL API Security

gRPC Security

docs.title: Administrative Interfaces
docs.text:
Enumeration may reveal administrative or management interfaces.

Examples include:

/admin
/login
/dashboard
/console
/manager
/manage

The existence of an administrative interface is not automatically a vulnerability.

It may still be useful attack-surface information.

Assess:

  • authentication;
  • exposure;
  • network restrictions;
  • MFA;
  • authorisation;
  • version information;
  • default configuration.

Do not perform credential guessing unless specifically authorised.

docs.title: Technology Identification Confidence
docs.text:
Technology identification should be treated as a confidence problem.

A single indicator might provide low confidence:

Server: nginx

Multiple independent indicators provide stronger confidence:

WhatWeb
   |
   +-- nginx

HTTP Headers
   |
   +-- Server: nginx

404 Response
   |
   +-- nginx-style error page

TLS / Behaviour
   |
   +-- consistent architecture

Result
   |
   v
Higher Confidence

A useful confidence model is:

Confidence Evidence Low Single weak indicator Moderate Several related indicators High Multiple independent indicators Confirmed Direct technical evidence establishes the technology

Avoid presenting low-confidence fingerprints as confirmed facts.

docs.title: Version Detection
docs.text:
Version identification requires additional caution.

For example:

Server: Apache/2.4.x

does not automatically mean that every vulnerability associated with the upstream Apache version is exploitable.

Reasons include:

  • vendor backports;
  • distribution-specific patches;
  • reverse proxies;
  • modified banners;
  • custom builds;
  • security patches without version changes.

The correct workflow is:

Version Indicator
       |
       v
Candidate Version
       |
       v
Vendor / Distribution Context
       |
       v
Security Advisory Review
       |
       v
Behavioural Validation

Do not report vulnerabilities solely because a banner appears to match an affected version.

docs.title: Establishing a Baseline
docs.text:
Before fuzzing or content discovery, establish normal application behaviour.

Request:

/

then request a deliberately non-existing resource:

/random-resource-482719

Compare:

Property Normal Page Non-Existing Page Status ? ? Length ? ? Words ? ? Lines ? ? Title ? ? Redirect ? ?

This helps distinguish real discoveries from generic application responses.

docs.title: Wildcard Behaviour
docs.text:
Some applications or infrastructure respond similarly for every requested path or hostname.

For example:

/random-one
/random-two
/admin
/test

may all return:

200 OK
Content-Length: 5234

This can create false positives during automated discovery.

Similarly, wildcard DNS may cause every hostname to resolve.

random-123.example.test
random-456.example.test
admin.example.test

If they all resolve to the same infrastructure, subdomain discovery results require additional validation.

docs.title: Reverse Proxies and CDNs
docs.text:
Web enumeration may identify the technology directly exposed to the internet rather than the underlying application.

Example:

Internet
   |
   v
CDN
   |
   v
Reverse Proxy
   |
   v
Application

A header might reveal:

Server: cloud proxy

while the backend application uses a completely different technology.

Therefore, distinguish:

  • edge technology;
  • reverse proxy;
  • application server;
  • application framework.

docs.title: WAF Influence
docs.text:
A Web Application Firewall can influence enumeration output.

Possible effects include:

  • blocked requests;
  • altered status codes;
  • generic error pages;
  • connection termination;
  • CAPTCHA responses;
  • rate limiting;
  • response replacement.

Example:

Enumeration Request
       |
       v
      WAF
       |
       +-- Blocked
       +-- Modified
       +-- Allowed
       |
       v
Application

Unexpected behaviour should therefore be interpreted carefully.

docs.title: Authentication State
docs.text:
Fingerprinting results can differ before and after authentication.

Unauthenticated:

/login

Authenticated:

/dashboard
/api/
/admin/
/account/

Authentication can reveal a much larger attack surface.

Where authorised credentials are available, repeat relevant enumeration after authentication.

Do not assume anonymous reconnaissance represents the entire application.

docs.title: Multiple User Roles
docs.text:
Different application roles may expose different features.

Example:

User
 |
 +-- Standard User
 |
 +-- Manager
 |
 +-- Administrator

Technology fingerprinting may remain the same, but:

  • routes;
  • APIs;
  • JavaScript bundles;
  • administrative functionality;
  • integrations;

may differ.

Enumeration should therefore support later role-based testing.

docs.title: Output Normalisation
docs.text:
When working with many tools, consistent output becomes important.

Useful fields include:

hostname
url
scheme
port
status
title
server
technology
redirect
ip
tls
notes

Example:

https://portal.example.test
443
200
Customer Portal
nginx
React
-
192.0.2.10
TLS enabled

Structured output is especially useful when combining reconnaissance tools.

docs.title: Example Enumeration Pipeline
docs.text:
A common authorised reconnaissance workflow might look like:

Known Domain
    |
    v
Subdomain Discovery
    |
    v
Resolved Hosts
    |
    v
httpx
    |
    +-- status
    +-- title
    +-- technology
    |
    v
Interesting Web Targets
    |
    +--> WhatWeb
    |
    +--> Wappalyzer
    |
    +--> curl
    |
    v
Manual Validation
    |
    v
Attack Surface Analysis

The important part is that each step reduces uncertainty.

docs.title: Manual Validation Workflow
docs.text:
For an interesting target:

1. Record URL
2. Record HTTP status
3. Record redirect behaviour
4. Inspect headers
5. Inspect cookies
6. Inspect HTML source
7. Inspect JavaScript assets
8. Request a non-existing page
9. Compare default/error behaviour
10. Review WhatWeb/Wappalyzer/httpx results
11. Correlate the indicators
12. Record likely technologies and confidence

This produces more reliable reconnaissance than depending on a single tool.

docs.title: Example Evidence Record
docs.text:
A useful enumeration record may look like:

Target:
https://portal.example.test

Observed:
HTTP 200

Title:
Customer Portal

Headers:
Server: nginx

WhatWeb:
nginx
JavaScript

Wappalyzer:
React
nginx

404 Behaviour:
Custom application error page

Additional Evidence:
React-style application bundle structure

Assessment:
nginx is strongly indicated.
React is likely used by the client-side application.

Confidence:
High for nginx.
Moderate to high for React.

Notice that this does not claim more than the evidence supports.

docs.title: Trusting One Fingerprint
docs.text:
Bad approach:

Wappalyzer says React
        |
        v
Technology confirmed

Better:

Wappalyzer
    |
    v
Candidate
    |
    +--> JavaScript inspection
    +--> asset analysis
    +--> application behaviour
    |
    v
Higher confidence

docs.title: Treating Version Detection as Vulnerability Proof
docs.text:
Bad:

Apache version found
        |
        v
CVE reported

Better:

Version indicator
      |
      v
Candidate exposure
      |
      v
Vendor patch status
      |
      v
Technical validation
      |
      v
Finding if supported

docs.title: Ignoring Redirects
docs.text:
A redirect may reveal:

  • canonical hostname;
  • authentication boundary;
  • application base path;
  • HTTPS enforcement;
  • another application.

Always inspect redirect chains.

docs.title: Ignoring Error Pages
docs.text:
Error responses may reveal:

  • server;
  • framework;
  • backend behaviour;
  • proxy layers;
  • application routing.

Do not inspect only successful 200 responses.

docs.title: Ignoring Non-Standard Ports
docs.text:
Web services may exist on ports such as:

8000
8080
8081
8443
8888
9000
9443

Port numbers alone do not prove a service type, so validate the protocol.

docs.title: Ignoring Scope Boundaries
docs.text:
Reconnaissance frequently discovers additional hostnames.

Discovery does not automatically grant permission to test them.

New Hostname
    |
    v
Check Scope
    |
    +-- Authorised -> continue
    |
    +-- Not authorised -> record only

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Fingerprinting tools may produce false positives because of:

  • generic HTML patterns;
  • shared JavaScript libraries;
  • reused templates;
  • reverse proxies;
  • stale assets;
  • copied error pages;
  • custom headers;
  • CDN behaviour;
  • intentionally misleading banners.

Always inspect the evidence behind a fingerprint where the conclusion matters.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Technologies may remain undetected because:

  • headers are removed;
  • error pages are customised;
  • JavaScript is bundled;
  • frameworks are hidden behind proxies;
  • CDN behaviour masks the origin;
  • fingerprint signatures are incomplete;
  • applications use custom builds.

Absence from WhatWeb or Wappalyzer output does not prove absence from the application.

docs.title: Evidence to Capture
docs.text:
For important enumeration results, capture:

  • target;
  • date and time;
  • tool;
  • tool version where relevant;
  • exact command;
  • HTTP status;
  • title;
  • relevant headers;
  • relevant cookies;
  • redirect chain;
  • technology indicators;
  • screenshots where useful;
  • raw response where useful;
  • confidence;
  • manual validation notes.

Do not retain unnecessary sensitive information.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Web enumeration results normally support later findings rather than becoming findings themselves.

For example:

Technology fingerprinting indicated that the application was served
through nginx and used a client-side JavaScript framework. These
observations were used to guide subsequent testing.

Avoid statements such as:

Wappalyzer proved the site uses framework X.

unless stronger evidence confirms the claim.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• [ ] Target is explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Hostnames are within scope.
  • [ ] IP ranges are within scope.
  • [ ] Third-party services are identified.
  • [ ] Testing restrictions are understood.

docs.title: HTTP Services
docs.text:
• [ ] HTTP services identified.
  • [ ] HTTPS services identified.
  • [ ] Non-standard web ports reviewed.
  • [ ] Redirect chains reviewed.
  • [ ] Virtual hosting considered.

docs.title: Technology Fingerprinting
docs.text:
• [ ] WhatWeb used where appropriate.
  • [ ] Wappalyzer used where appropriate.
  • [ ] httpx metadata reviewed.
  • [ ] Headers inspected.
  • [ ] Cookies inspected.
  • [ ] HTML inspected.
  • [ ] JavaScript assets reviewed.
  • [ ] Error pages reviewed.
  • [ ] Version claims validated carefully.

docs.title: Application Behaviour
docs.text:
• [ ] Normal page baseline collected.
  • [ ] Non-existing resource tested.
  • [ ] Soft 404 behaviour considered.
  • [ ] Authentication redirects reviewed.
  • [ ] WAF behaviour considered.
  • [ ] CDN/proxy behaviour considered.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Important fingerprints corroborated.
  • [ ] Automated output manually reviewed.
  • [ ] False-positive explanations considered.
  • [ ] Confidence recorded appropriately.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Relevant requests retained.
  • [ ] Relevant responses retained.
  • [ ] Commands recorded.
  • [ ] Tool versions recorded where useful.
  • [ ] Findings are based on technical evidence rather than tool labels.
