docs.title: Final Model
docs.text:
Web enumeration is not:

Run WhatWeb
Run Wappalyzer
Run httpx
Copy output

It is:

Define Scope
    |
    v
Identify Web Services
    |
    v
Collect HTTP Information
    |
    v
Fingerprint Technologies
    |
    v
Inspect Application Behaviour
    |
    v
Correlate Indicators
    |
    v
Validate Manually
    |
    v
Assign Confidence
    |
    v
Prioritise Testing

The strongest enumeration result is not the one produced by the largest number of tools.

It is the one where the available evidence has been interpreted correctly and can be used to make the next stage of testing more focused.

docs.title: httpx
docs.text:
ProjectDiscovery httpx is an HTTP toolkit commonly used during reconnaissance to identify reachable web services and enrich them with useful metadata.

It is particularly valuable after asset discovery because raw domain and subdomain lists often contain:

  • hosts that do not resolve;
  • hosts with no reachable HTTP service;
  • HTTP-only services;
  • HTTPS-only services;
  • redirects;
  • administrative interfaces;
  • APIs;
  • development systems;
  • services on non-standard ports.

httpx helps turn those raw assets into a more useful web-target inventory.

Discovered Assets
       |
       v
      httpx
       |
       +-- Reachable HTTP Services
       +-- Status Codes
       +-- Titles
       +-- Technologies
       +-- Redirects
       +-- TLS Information
       +-- IP Addresses
       +-- Server Metadata
       |
       v
Prioritised Web Targets

Authorised testing only

Run httpx only against assets that are explicitly within the authorised assessment scope. Some options increase concurrency, probe additional ports, perform additional requests, or enrich results using further network interaction. Review the rules of engagement before increasing scan breadth or request rate.

docs.title: Where httpx Fits
docs.text:
httpx normally sits between asset discovery and deeper application testing.

Known Domain
    |
    v
Subdomain Discovery
    |
    v
Resolved / Candidate Hosts
    |
    v
httpx
    |
    v
Reachable Web Services
    |
    v
Technology Enrichment
    |
    v
Prioritisation
    |
    v
Manual Web Testing

Related methodology:

Web Enumeration Tools

Subdomain Enumeration

Technology Identification

Attack Surface Analysis

docs.title: What httpx Does
docs.text:
httpx performs HTTP probing and can collect information about reachable web services.

Depending on the options and installed version, useful output may include:

  • URL;
  • scheme;
  • hostname;
  • port;
  • HTTP status code;
  • page title;
  • content length;
  • content type;
  • redirect location;
  • server header;
  • technology fingerprints;
  • IP address;
  • CNAME;
  • CDN information;
  • TLS information;
  • certificate data;
  • favicon data;
  • response hashes;
  • JSON output.

The important distinction is:

Asset Discovery
      |
      v
Hostname Exists

versus:

httpx
      |
      v
HTTP Service Responds

These are different stages of reconnaissance.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
httpx is maintained by ProjectDiscovery.

Check whether it is installed:

which httpx

Check the version:

httpx -version

Display help:

httpx -h

Official installation and usage documentation:

ProjectDiscovery httpx

httpx Usage

Official repository:

ProjectDiscovery httpx - GitHub

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Probe a single URL:

httpx -u https://example.test

Probe a hostname:

httpx -u example.test

A common file-based workflow is:

httpx -l targets.txt

A quieter form that is useful in pipelines is:

httpx -l targets.txt -silent

Representative output may look like:

https://portal.example.test
https://api.example.test
http://legacy.example.test

The exact behaviour depends on the version and supplied flags.

docs.title: Input from Standard Input
docs.text:
httpx works particularly well in Unix-style pipelines.

Example:

cat targets.txt | httpx -silent

Another common pattern is:

subfinder -d example.test -silent | httpx -silent

This allows one tool's output to become another tool's input.

docs.title: Input Files
docs.text:
A repeatable workflow is usually easier to manage with files.

Example:

subdomains.txt

containing:

app.example.test
portal.example.test
api.example.test
admin.example.test

Probe them with:

httpx -l subdomains.txt

Save reachable endpoints:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -silent > alive-web.txt

This creates a useful transition from subdomain discovery to web testing.

docs.title: Basic Reconnaissance Pipeline
docs.text:
A common workflow is:

Domain
  |
  v
Subfinder
  |
  v
subdomains.txt
  |
  v
httpx
  |
  v
alive-web.txt
  |
  v
WhatWeb / Browser / Burp

Example:

subfinder -d example.test -silent > subdomains.txt

Then:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -silent > alive-web.txt

Then:

whatweb -i alive-web.txt

The purpose of httpx here is to reduce the asset list to services that appear to respond over HTTP or HTTPS.

docs.title: Status Codes
docs.text:
HTTP status codes are among the most useful enrichment fields.

Example:

httpx -l targets.txt -status-code

Representative output:

https://portal.example.test [200]
https://admin.example.test [403]
https://old.example.test [301]
https://api.example.test [401]

These status codes provide useful prioritisation information.

However:

403

does not automatically mean:

Interesting hidden application

and:

404

does not automatically mean:

Nothing exists

Interpret status codes with the application context.

docs.title: Page Titles
docs.text:
Page titles can quickly reveal what a web service appears to be.

Example:

httpx -l targets.txt -title

Representative output:

https://portal.example.test [Customer Portal]
https://grafana.example.test [Grafana]
https://admin.example.test [Admin Login]

Titles may reveal:

  • product names;
  • application names;
  • administrative portals;
  • dashboards;
  • monitoring systems;
  • default applications;
  • authentication portals.

Titles are useful for prioritisation but can be arbitrary or misleading.

docs.title: Status Code and Title Together
docs.text:
A common reconnaissance combination is:

httpx -l targets.txt -status-code -title

Representative output:

https://portal.example.test [200] [Customer Portal]
https://admin.example.test [302] [Sign In]
https://grafana.example.test [200] [Grafana]

This is much more useful than a simple list of URLs.

docs.title: Technology Detection
docs.text:
httpx can perform technology detection.

A common option is:

httpx -l targets.txt -tech-detect

Representative output may resemble:

https://portal.example.test [nginx,React]
https://blog.example.test [Apache,WordPress,jQuery]

Technology detection should be treated as fingerprinting evidence rather than absolute proof.

Use it to generate hypotheses.

docs.title: Correlating Technology Detection
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

httpx
  |
  +-- React
  +-- nginx
  |
  v
WhatWeb
  |
  +-- React
  +-- nginx
  |
  v
Wappalyzer
  |
  +-- React
  |
  v
Manual HTTP / JS Review
  |
  v
Higher Confidence

Related notes:

WhatWeb

Wappalyzer

docs.title: Web Server Information
docs.text:
Server information can sometimes be displayed as part of httpx enrichment.

For example:

Server: nginx

or:

Server: Apache

This can help identify edge technologies.

However, server headers may be:

  • removed;
  • rewritten;
  • inserted by reverse proxies;
  • provided by CDNs;
  • intentionally changed.

Treat them as indicators.

docs.title: Content Length
docs.text:
Content length is useful for grouping and filtering responses.

For example:

httpx -l targets.txt -content-length

Representative output:

https://portal.example.test [200] [4812]
https://admin.example.test [403] [153]

Content length becomes particularly useful when many endpoints return the same generic response.

Example:

/admin        403  153 bytes
/internal     403  153 bytes
/management   403  153 bytes

This may indicate a shared block page rather than three unique applications.

docs.title: Content Type
docs.text:
Content type helps distinguish different kinds of applications.

Examples include:

text/html
application/json
application/xml
text/plain

An API endpoint returning:

application/json

may deserve different follow-up testing than a normal HTML page.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
Redirect behaviour is important reconnaissance information.

For example:

http://example.test
       |
       v
https://example.test

or:

https://example.test
       |
       v
https://login.example.test/

Redirects can reveal:

  • canonical hostnames;
  • HTTPS enforcement;
  • authentication portals;
  • application base paths;
  • external services.

Use redirect information as part of attack-surface analysis.

docs.title: Following Redirects
docs.text:
Following redirects can be useful when the final application is more relevant than the initial endpoint.

However, preserve the original redirect information.

Example:

Initial:
http://portal.example.test

Redirect:
https://portal.example.test/

Final:
200 OK

The redirect itself is useful evidence.

Be cautious when redirects lead to third-party infrastructure that may be outside scope.

docs.title: HTTP and HTTPS Discovery
docs.text:
A hostname may support:

HTTP only
HTTPS only
Both

httpx can help determine the reachable scheme.

For example:

portal.example.test
      |
      +--> https://portal.example.test

This makes later tooling more reliable because the correct scheme is already known.

docs.title: Non-Standard Ports
docs.text:
Web applications are frequently exposed on non-standard ports.

Examples include:

8000
8008
8080
8081
8443
8888
9000
9443

When the assessment scope includes them, httpx can be combined with port discovery.

Conceptually:

Nmap / Port Discovery
       |
       v
Host:Port Pairs
       |
       v
httpx
       |
       v
HTTP Services

Do not assume a service is HTTP simply because its port number commonly hosts web traffic.

docs.title: Probe Common Web Ports
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised, it may be useful to probe selected web ports.

Always check the installed version's port-related flags:

httpx -h

before building automation around them.

The workflow should be:

Known Hosts
    |
    v
Known / Approved Ports
    |
    v
httpx
    |
    v
Validated HTTP Services

Avoid indiscriminately probing large port ranges without assessment justification.

docs.title: IP Addresses
docs.text:
httpx can enrich HTTP endpoints with IP-address information.

This can help identify:

  • several hostnames sharing the same infrastructure;
  • separate application clusters;
  • CDN-backed hosts;
  • unexpected infrastructure differences.

Example:

app.example.test       -> 192.0.2.10
portal.example.test    -> 192.0.2.10
api.example.test       -> 192.0.2.20

This can guide architecture analysis.

docs.title: CNAME Information
docs.text:
CNAME information can reveal:

  • cloud platforms;
  • SaaS services;
  • CDN providers;
  • delegated infrastructure;
  • third-party hosting.

A hostname such as:

portal.example.test

may point to:

provider.example.net

This is useful reconnaissance information, but the external provider is not automatically authorised for testing.

docs.title: CDN Detection
docs.text:
httpx can help identify when an endpoint appears to use a CDN or similar edge service.

This matters because the architecture may be:

Client
  |
  v
CDN
  |
  v
Reverse Proxy
  |
  v
Application

The IP address or server behaviour observed externally may therefore belong to the CDN rather than the origin application.

docs.title: TLS Information
docs.text:
TLS metadata can provide additional reconnaissance information.

Useful details may include:

  • certificate subject;
  • issuer;
  • Subject Alternative Names;
  • validity;
  • hostname information.

Certificate data may reveal additional hostnames.

Always apply a scope check before investigating newly discovered certificate names.

Certificate SAN
      |
      v
New Hostname
      |
      v
Scope Check
      |
      +-- In scope -> investigate
      |
      +-- Out of scope -> record only

docs.title: TLS Certificate Names
docs.text:
Certificate SAN entries can sometimes expose:

  • legacy hostnames;
  • administrative hostnames;
  • alternate application names;
  • development systems.

These are discovery leads, not automatic authorisation.

docs.title: Favicon Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Favicons can be useful for identifying web products and application families.

A typical fingerprinting model is:

Target
  |
  v
/favicon.ico
  |
  v
Hash
  |
  v
Known Fingerprint

httpx can assist with favicon-related metadata depending on the installed version.

A favicon match should be treated as supporting evidence.

docs.title: Response Hashing
docs.text:
Response hashes can help group similar applications.

For example:

Host A -> same response hash
Host B -> same response hash
Host C -> different hash

This may suggest that Host A and Host B serve the same application or template.

Hash equality does not always prove identical backend systems.

Dynamic content can also alter hashes between requests.

docs.title: Duplicate Applications
docs.text:
Large organisations often expose many hostnames that lead to the same application.

Example:

app.example.test
portal.example.test
customer.example.test

all redirecting to:

login.example.test

httpx metadata can help identify and deduplicate these patterns.

This can reduce unnecessary repetitive testing.

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text:
Structured output is extremely useful for automation and analysis.

Depending on the installed version, JSON line output can be enabled.

Check:

httpx -h

for the exact JSON output option supported by that version.

A typical pipeline concept is:

httpx
  |
  v
JSONL
  |
  +--> jq
  |
  +--> Python
  |
  +--> spreadsheet/report pipeline

Structured output is generally preferable to parsing coloured terminal output.

docs.title: Working with jq
docs.text:
When httpx produces JSONL, jq can be used to extract specific fields.

Conceptually:

cat httpx.jsonl | jq

For example, one might extract:

URL
Status
Title
Technologies
IP

The exact JSON field names should be checked against output produced by the installed version rather than assumed.

docs.title: Saving Output
docs.text:
Basic output can be saved using shell redirection:

httpx -l targets.txt -silent > alive-web.txt

For richer assessments, preserve structured output where possible.

A useful evidence directory might contain:

recon/
|
+-- subdomains.txt
+-- resolved.txt
+-- alive-web.txt
+-- httpx.jsonl
+-- whatweb.txt

This makes the reconnaissance process reproducible.

docs.title: Filtering Status Codes
docs.text:
For some workflows, specific response categories may be more relevant.

Examples:

200
301
302
401
403
500

Before applying filters, think about what might be lost.

For example, keeping only 200 responses can discard:

401 -> authenticated API
403 -> restricted administration portal
302 -> login redirect
500 -> unusual application behaviour

Therefore:

Filter

should follow:

Objective

not convenience.

docs.title: Interesting Status Codes
docs.text:
A useful triage model is:

Status Why It May Be Interesting 200 Reachable content 301/302 Redirect destination may reveal application structure 401 Authentication boundary 403 Restricted resource or edge control 404 Error-page fingerprinting or routing behaviour 405 Endpoint exists but method may differ 429 Rate limiting 500 Server-side error or unexpected input handling

No status code is automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: Filtering by Content Length
docs.text:
Generic block or error pages often have identical lengths.

Example:

host1 -> 403 -> 153
host2 -> 403 -> 153
host3 -> 403 -> 153

This may indicate:

Shared WAF / proxy response

Grouping by response size can therefore reduce noise.

docs.title: Silent Output
docs.text:
The -silent option is useful for pipelines:

httpx -l targets.txt -silent

It avoids unnecessary banners and status information when the output is being passed into another tool.

For manual analysis, additional metadata flags are often more useful.

docs.title: Combining Useful Fields
docs.text:
A typical enrichment command may include several fields.

For example:

httpx -l targets.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect

This produces a compact view of:

URL
Status
Title
Technology

For larger assessments, structured output is usually preferable.

docs.title: httpx and Subfinder
docs.text:
A very common combination is:

subfinder -d example.test -silent | httpx -silent

Conceptually:

Domain
  |
  v
Subfinder
  |
  v
Candidate Subdomains
  |
  v
httpx
  |
  v
Reachable Web Applications

This is useful because passive subdomain discovery alone does not tell you whether a hostname currently hosts an accessible web application.

docs.title: httpx and WhatWeb
docs.text:
After identifying live web applications:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -silent > alive-web.txt

feed them into WhatWeb:

whatweb -i alive-web.txt

Workflow:

httpx
   |
   v
Live Web Services
   |
   v
WhatWeb
   |
   v
Detailed Fingerprints

Related note:

WhatWeb

docs.title: httpx and Wappalyzer
docs.text:
For large scopes:

Thousands of Hosts
      |
      v
httpx
      |
      v
Interesting Web Targets
      |
      v
Browser + Wappalyzer

This is generally more practical than manually browsing every hostname discovered during reconnaissance.

Related note:

Wappalyzer

docs.title: httpx and Nuclei
docs.text:
httpx output is frequently suitable as input for further automated checks.

Conceptually:

Subdomains
    |
    v
httpx
    |
    v
Reachable Web Services
    |
    v
Nuclei

However:

Reachable

does not mean:

Safe to scan aggressively

Confirm that the rules of engagement allow the intended Nuclei templates and scan intensity.

docs.title: httpx and Katana
docs.text:
httpx can identify reachable applications.

Katana can then crawl selected applications.

Candidate Hosts
      |
      v
httpx
      |
      v
Reachable URLs
      |
      v
Katana
      |
      v
Discovered Endpoints

This is a natural transition from broad reconnaissance to endpoint discovery.

docs.title: httpx and Burp Suite
docs.text:
httpx is useful for breadth.

Burp Suite is useful for depth.

httpx
   |
   v
Interesting Target
   |
   v
Browser through Burp
   |
   +-- Requests
   +-- Responses
   +-- Authentication
   +-- APIs
   +-- Sessions

Do not attempt to replace manual application understanding with httpx metadata.

docs.title: httpx and curl
docs.text:
curl is useful for verifying individual httpx results.

Example:

httpx:
https://admin.example.test [403]

Check manually:

curl -i https://admin.example.test

Review:

  • response body;
  • headers;
  • cookies;
  • WAF behaviour;
  • server details.

Quick reference:

curl Cheatsheet

docs.title: httpx and Nmap
docs.text:
Nmap can identify network services.

httpx can determine whether discovered services behave as HTTP.

Example:

Nmap
 |
 +-- 80
 +-- 443
 +-- 8080
 +-- 8443
 |
 v
httpx
 |
 v
Validated Web Services

This is particularly useful for non-standard ports.

docs.title: Establishing a Web Inventory
docs.text:
A mature reconnaissance workflow should produce more than alive.txt.

Useful inventory fields include:

Hostname
URL
Scheme
Port
Status
Title
Technology
Server
IP
CNAME
CDN
Redirect
TLS
Notes

Example:

URL Status Title Technology IP Notes https://portal.example.test 200 Customer Portal nginx, React 192.0.2.10 Main application https://api.example.test 401 - nginx 192.0.2.20 API https://admin.example.test 403 Forbidden CDN 192.0.2.30 Restricted

This is more useful than an unstructured URL list.

docs.title: Prioritising Targets
docs.text:
httpx metadata can help prioritise web applications.

Potentially interesting characteristics include:

  • administrative titles;
  • development systems;
  • login portals;
  • unusual status codes;
  • management products;
  • uncommon technologies;
  • legacy servers;
  • exposed APIs;
  • uncommon ports;
  • detailed version information.

Prioritisation means:

Investigate earlier

not:

Assume vulnerable

docs.title: Authentication Boundaries
docs.text:
A 401 or authentication redirect can be valuable attack-surface information.

Example:

https://api.example.test [401]

This tells us:

HTTP service exists
Authentication is required

It does not tell us:

Authentication is secure

That requires deeper application testing.

Related note:

Authentication Testing

docs.title: 403 Responses
docs.text:
A 403 Forbidden response may come from:

  • application authorisation;
  • WAF;
  • CDN;
  • reverse proxy;
  • IP restriction;
  • access-control policy;
  • virtual host behaviour.

Example:

httpx:
https://admin.example.test [403]

Manual validation:

curl -i https://admin.example.test

Inspect the actual response before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: 404 Responses
docs.text:
A 404 response can still provide useful information.

It may expose:

  • server fingerprint;
  • framework error format;
  • routing behaviour;
  • default error page.

A useful external reference for comparison is:

0xdf - Default 404 Pages

A 404 should not automatically be discarded from reconnaissance.

docs.title: Soft 404 Behaviour
docs.text:
A host may return 200 OK for unknown resources.

This can make automated enumeration misleading.

Example:

/random-a -> 200 5234 bytes
/random-b -> 200 5234 bytes
/admin    -> 200 5234 bytes

This may represent one generic soft-404 page.

Before using httpx results to drive content discovery, establish the target's unknown-resource baseline manually.

docs.title: 500 Responses
docs.text:
A 500 Internal Server Error may represent:

  • temporary backend failure;
  • unexpected routing;
  • application error;
  • proxy failure;
  • target instability.

Do not assume it is a vulnerability.

It may still be worth prioritising for manual investigation.

docs.title: Redirect Chains
docs.text:
A service may pass through several redirects.

Example:

http://example.test
        |
        v
https://example.test
        |
        v
https://login.example.test/

Each stage may provide useful architecture information.

Preserve the original endpoint even if the final destination is the most relevant application.

docs.title: Virtual Hosting
docs.text:
Different hostnames sharing one IP address may serve different applications.

192.0.2.10
   |
   +-- app.example.test
   +-- admin.example.test
   +-- api.example.test

Therefore, probe hostnames rather than relying only on IP addresses when virtual hosts are known.

docs.title: Wildcard DNS
docs.text:
Wildcard DNS can cause nonexistent subdomains to resolve.

Example:

random-123.example.test
random-456.example.test
anything.example.test

all resolving to the same IP.

httpx may then show them all as reachable if the web server uses a catch-all virtual host.

This can create false-positive asset lists.

Validate random hostname behaviour when results look suspicious.

docs.title: Catch-All Virtual Hosts
docs.text:
A reverse proxy or web server may return the same application for every hostname.

Example:

a.example.test -> same title
b.example.test -> same title
c.example.test -> same title
random.example.test -> same title

Compare:

  • status;
  • title;
  • length;
  • response hash;
  • redirect;
  • IP.

This can help distinguish genuine applications from catch-all routing.

docs.title: WAF Influence
docs.text:
A WAF can affect httpx results.

Possible behaviours include:

  • 403;
  • 429;
  • CAPTCHA;
  • JavaScript challenge;
  • connection reset;
  • generic body;
  • altered headers.

Therefore:

httpx result

may represent:

WAF behaviour

rather than:

Application behaviour

docs.title: CDN Influence
docs.text:
A CDN may also change:

  • IP address;
  • headers;
  • TLS certificate;
  • error pages;
  • caching;
  • status behaviour.

When interpreting results, separate:

Edge Layer

from:

Origin Application

docs.title: DNS Resolution Problems
docs.text:
If httpx produces no result for an expected host, verify DNS.

getent hosts example.test

or:

dig example.test

Then test directly:

curl -I https://example.test

A missing httpx result should be investigated before assuming the service is offline.

docs.title: TLS Problems
docs.text:
HTTPS services may fail because of:

  • certificate problems;
  • hostname mismatch;
  • unsupported protocols;
  • interception;
  • network controls.

Use curl for detailed investigation:

curl -v https://example.test

Do not disable TLS verification casually.

For legitimate internal PKI or interception environments, prefer adding the appropriate trusted CA where feasible.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
Large reconnaissance runs can encounter:

  • slow hosts;
  • dead hosts;
  • filtered ports;
  • unstable services.

httpx provides timeout and retry controls depending on version.

Check:

httpx -h

before adjusting them.

A shorter timeout increases speed but may increase false negatives.

A longer timeout improves patience but may make large scans much slower.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Concurrency and request rate matter operationally.

High request rates may:

  • trigger WAF controls;
  • overload fragile systems;
  • produce unreliable responses;
  • trigger monitoring alerts;
  • violate engagement restrictions.

Always tune scans to the target and rules of engagement.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Parallel requests make httpx efficient.

They also increase load.

A suitable value depends on:

  • number of targets;
  • network conditions;
  • application sensitivity;
  • target infrastructure;
  • testing restrictions.

Do not treat maximum concurrency as the correct default.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
Retries can help compensate for unstable networks.

Too many retries can also:

  • increase load;
  • lengthen scans;
  • duplicate evidence;
  • trigger rate controls.

Use them intentionally.

docs.title: Proxying httpx Traffic
docs.text:
In some assessment workflows, HTTP traffic may need to pass through a proxy for inspection or network requirements.

Check the installed version:

httpx -h

for proxy-related options.

For individual request validation, curl or Burp Suite may provide easier inspection.

docs.title: Custom Headers
docs.text:
Some applications require specific headers.

Examples might include:

Authorization
Accept
User-Agent
Host
Custom organisation headers

When adding headers during authorised testing, document them so that results remain reproducible.

Do not accidentally expose authentication tokens in:

  • shell history;
  • logs;
  • screenshots;
  • shared output files.

docs.title: User-Agent Differences
docs.text:
Applications may return different results based on User-Agent.

Possible reasons include:

  • bot detection;
  • CDN logic;
  • device-specific rendering;
  • security controls.

If httpx output differs significantly from browser behaviour, compare the requests.

docs.title: Authentication and httpx
docs.text:
httpx is primarily useful for broad probing rather than full authenticated application testing.

Authenticated application mapping is usually better handled with:

  • browser;
  • Burp Suite;
  • application-specific scripts;
  • API clients.

A 401, login redirect, or unauthenticated landing page does not represent the full authenticated attack surface.

docs.title: API Endpoints
docs.text:
httpx can help identify API services through clues such as:

  • JSON content type;
  • 401 status;
  • API-specific titles or headers;
  • unusual routes.

After discovery, move to appropriate API testing.

Related note:

API Security

docs.title: JSON Responses
docs.text:
A web endpoint that returns:

Content-Type: application/json

may be:

  • API;
  • authentication service;
  • backend endpoint;
  • framework-generated error response.

Inspect the body manually.

docs.title: JavaScript Applications
docs.text:
httpx may identify the page title and technology but cannot replace browser-based analysis of JavaScript-heavy applications.

Continue with:

JavaScript Analysis

and interactive testing through Burp Suite.

docs.title: Fingerprinting Confidence
docs.text:
A single httpx technology match should usually be treated as:

Indicator

not:

Confirmed fact

Confidence increases when independent evidence agrees.

httpx:
nginx

WhatWeb:
nginx

HTTP Header:
Server: nginx

Result:
High confidence

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Possible causes include:

  • generic fingerprint strings;
  • shared assets;
  • CDN pages;
  • catch-all hosts;
  • reverse proxies;
  • misleading headers;
  • wildcard DNS.

Always manually validate important observations.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Possible causes include:

  • timeouts;
  • DNS problems;
  • blocked probes;
  • unusual ports;
  • TLS errors;
  • authentication requirements;
  • WAF behaviour;
  • non-standard HTTP implementations.

A host missing from httpx output should not automatically be considered dead.

docs.title: Representative Reconnaissance Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose subdomain enumeration produces:

portal.example.test
api.example.test
admin.example.test
legacy.example.test

Run:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect

Representative result:

https://portal.example.test [200] [Customer Portal] [nginx,React]
https://api.example.test [401] [] [nginx]
https://admin.example.test [403] [Forbidden] [Cloudflare]
http://legacy.example.test [301] [] [Apache]

Interpretation:

portal
  -> reachable main application
  -> likely React frontend
  -> good manual-testing target

api
  -> reachable API
  -> authentication boundary exists

admin
  -> reachable restricted service
  -> edge/WAF behaviour needs interpretation

legacy
  -> redirects
  -> inspect destination and server behaviour

This is much more useful than treating every hostname equally.

docs.title: Prioritised Follow-Up
docs.text:
Based on the example above:

portal
  |
  +--> Browser + Burp
  +--> Wappalyzer
  +--> WhatWeb
  +--> JavaScript Analysis

api
  |
  +--> API mapping
  +--> Authentication review

admin
  |
  +--> Manual 403 inspection
  +--> Scope validation

legacy
  |
  +--> Redirect analysis
  +--> Technology validation

httpx helps decide where to spend deeper testing effort.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For useful httpx observations, retain:

Target list
Tool version
Exact command
Date/time
Output format
Relevant URLs
Status codes
Titles
Technology indicators
Redirects
IP information
TLS information
Manual validation

Example:

Tool:
httpx

Target:
portal.example.test

Result:
https://portal.example.test
200
Customer Portal
nginx
React

Manual validation:
Browser confirmed application availability.
HTTP response contained nginx Server header.
JavaScript assets supported React identification.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
httpx output is normally reconnaissance evidence rather than a finding.

Example wording:

HTTP probing identified the externally reachable web applications and
was used to prioritise endpoints for further manual testing. Relevant
services were subsequently validated through direct HTTP requests and
interactive application review.

Avoid:

httpx found vulnerabilities on these hosts.

unless separate security validation actually supports that conclusion.

docs.title: Keeping Only HTTP 200
docs.text:
This can discard:

401 APIs
403 management interfaces
302 authentication portals
500 unusual services

Keep enough data to understand the attack surface.

docs.title: Treating Every Resolving Host as Unique
docs.text: Wildcard DNS and catch-all virtual hosts can produce large amounts of duplicate noise.

docs.title: Treating Technology Detection as Proof
docs.text: Use WhatWeb, Wappalyzer, headers, assets, and manual inspection to corroborate important fingerprints.

docs.title: Ignoring Redirects
docs.text: A redirect can reveal the canonical application or authentication architecture.

docs.title: Ignoring Non-Standard Ports
docs.text: Relevant web applications may not use 80 or 443.

docs.title: Scanning Too Aggressively
docs.text: High concurrency can affect reliability and target stability.

docs.title: Ignoring Structured Output
docs.text: For large assessments, JSONL is usually more useful than parsing human-readable terminal output.

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text:
A mature httpx workflow can be:

1. Define scope
      |
      v
2. Collect candidate domains/subdomains
      |
      v
3. Resolve and deduplicate
      |
      v
4. Probe with httpx
      |
      v
5. Collect metadata
      |
      +-- status
      +-- title
      +-- technology
      +-- IP
      +-- TLS
      +-- redirects
      |
      v
6. Identify wildcard/catch-all behaviour
      |
      v
7. Prioritise interesting applications
      |
      v
8. Validate manually
      |
      +-- curl
      +-- WhatWeb
      +-- Wappalyzer
      +-- Browser/Burp
      |
      v
9. Feed selected targets into deeper workflows

Because ProjectDiscovery tools evolve, verify advanced options against:

httpx -h

before using them in reusable scripts.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Scope confirmed.
  • [ ] Target input deduplicated.
  • [ ] Newly discovered third-party infrastructure treated separately.
  • [ ] Rules of engagement reviewed.
  • [ ] httpx version recorded where useful.

docs.title: Probing
docs.text:
• [ ] Reachable HTTP services identified.
  • [ ] HTTPS considered.
  • [ ] Relevant non-standard ports considered.
  • [ ] Status codes retained.
  • [ ] Redirects retained.
  • [ ] Titles collected where useful.
  • [ ] Technology detection used where useful.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• [ ] IP information reviewed.
  • [ ] CNAME information reviewed where relevant.
  • [ ] CDN/proxy behaviour considered.
  • [ ] TLS information reviewed where relevant.
  • [ ] Wildcard DNS considered.
  • [ ] Catch-all virtual hosts considered.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• [ ] 401 responses not discarded.
  • [ ] 403 responses manually reviewed where useful.
  • [ ] 404 responses considered for fingerprinting.
  • [ ] 500 responses investigated where relevant.
  • [ ] Technology matches treated as indicators.
  • [ ] Duplicate applications identified where possible.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
• [ ] Request rate appropriate.
  • [ ] Concurrency appropriate.
  • [ ] Timeouts appropriate.
  • [ ] Retries appropriate.
  • [ ] Sensitive authentication headers protected.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Input list retained.
  • [ ] Exact command retained.
  • [ ] Output retained.
  • [ ] Structured output used for large assessments where useful.
  • [ ] Manual validation recorded.
  • [ ] Tool output not confused with vulnerability confirmation.

docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use httpx like this:

Subdomains
    |
    v
httpx
    |
    v
Discard Everything Except 200

Use it like this:

Candidate Assets
      |
      v
httpx
      |
      +-- Reachability
      +-- Status
      +-- Title
      +-- Technology
      +-- Redirect
      +-- IP
      +-- TLS
      |
      v
Interpret Results
      |
      +-- 200 application?
      +-- 401 API?
      +-- 403 restricted service?
      +-- 302 authentication flow?
      +-- duplicate application?
      +-- wildcard host?
      |
      v
Prioritise
      |
      v
Validate Manually
      |
      +-- curl
      +-- WhatWeb
      +-- Wappalyzer
      +-- Browser/Burp
      |
      v
Deeper Testing

The value of httpx is not simply identifying which hosts respond.

Its value is turning a large, noisy asset list into a structured and prioritised inventory of web services that can be investigated more intelligently.

docs.title: Wappalyzer
docs.text:
Wappalyzer is a technology profiling platform used to identify technologies associated with websites and web applications.

It can help identify categories such as:

  • web frameworks;
  • content management systems;
  • JavaScript libraries;
  • analytics platforms;
  • tag managers;
  • CDN providers;
  • web servers;
  • e-commerce platforms;
  • development technologies;
  • advertising platforms;
  • customer-support platforms;
  • infrastructure technologies;
  • security technologies.

Wappalyzer is especially useful during interactive web reconnaissance because it can provide technology context while the tester is browsing the application.

Browser
   |
   v
Target Application
   |
   v
Wappalyzer
   |
   +-- Framework
   +-- CMS
   +-- JavaScript
   +-- Server
   +-- CDN
   +-- Analytics
   +-- Other Technologies
   |
   v
Technology Hypotheses
   |
   v
Manual Validation
   |
   v
Focused Testing

Authorised testing only

Use Wappalyzer only while assessing systems and applications that are explicitly authorised. Technology discovery may reveal third-party services, external domains, or infrastructure that is not automatically part of the assessment scope.

docs.title: Where Wappalyzer Fits
docs.text:
Wappalyzer normally fits into the technology-identification stage of web reconnaissance.

Scope
  |
  v
Identify Reachable Web Application
  |
  v
Browse Application
  |
  v
Wappalyzer
  |
  +-- Technologies
  +-- Libraries
  +-- Infrastructure
  |
  v
Validate Indicators
  |
  v
Attack Surface Analysis
  |
  v
Focused Testing

Related methodology:

Web Enumeration Tools

Technology Identification

Web Reconnaissance

Attack Surface Analysis

docs.title: What Wappalyzer Actually Does
docs.text:
Wappalyzer identifies technologies by looking for recognisable patterns in publicly observable web content.

Potential indicators can include:

HTML
HTTP Headers
Cookies
JavaScript
Script URLs
Meta Tags
DOM Elements
CSS
Asset Paths
Response Behaviour

Conceptually:

HTTP Response
      |
      +-- HTML
      +-- Headers
      +-- Cookies
      +-- Scripts
      +-- Metadata
      |
      v
Technology Detection Rules
      |
      v
Technology Matches

The important point is:

Wappalyzer Match
      !=
Absolute Proof

Instead:

Wappalyzer Match
      |
      v
Technology Indicator
      |
      v
Corroborate

docs.title: Browser-Based Use
docs.text:
A common way to use Wappalyzer is through browser-based technology detection.

The general workflow is:

Open Application
      |
      v
Browse Important Pages
      |
      v
Review Wappalyzer Results
      |
      +-- Frontend Framework
      +-- CMS
      +-- Libraries
      +-- Infrastructure
      |
      v
Investigate Interesting Indicators

This is useful because technologies may only become visible after navigating specific parts of the application.

For example:

/
    -> public frontend technologies

/login
    -> authentication technologies

/dashboard
    -> authenticated frontend

/admin
    -> separate administration application

Do not assume the technology profile from the homepage represents the entire application.

docs.title: Installation and Access
docs.text:
Wappalyzer is available through several interfaces and services.

Depending on the workflow, this may include:

  • browser integration;
  • hosted technology lookup;
  • APIs;
  • other Wappalyzer-supported products or interfaces.

Because available products and browser integrations can change over time, refer to the current official documentation for installation and usage options.

Official resource:

Wappalyzer

docs.title: Basic Reconnaissance Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

1. Open target in browser
       |
       v
2. Browse relevant pages
       |
       v
3. Review Wappalyzer
       |
       v
4. Record candidate technologies
       |
       v
5. Validate important matches
       |
       v
6. Use results to guide testing

For example:

Wappalyzer:
React
nginx
Google Analytics

The next question is not:

Which vulnerabilities affect React and nginx?

The next question is:

Which of these technologies are actually present, where are they used, and what evidence supports the identification?

docs.title: Reading Technology Categories
docs.text:
Wappalyzer commonly groups detected technologies by category.

Examples may include:

Category Examples of What It Can Represent JavaScript frameworks Client-side application technologies CMS Content management platforms Web servers HTTP-serving technologies CDN Edge or content delivery infrastructure Analytics Tracking and analytics services Tag managers Client-side tag management E-commerce Shopping and payment-related platforms Programming languages Server-side or client-side language indicators UI frameworks Frontend presentation frameworks

These categories help organise observations but do not necessarily reveal the full application architecture.

docs.title: Architecture Matters
docs.text:
A target may expose several technology layers at once.

For example:

Cloudflare
    |
    v
nginx
    |
    v
Node.js
    |
    v
Express
    |
    v
React

These technologies may represent:

Edge
 |
 v
Reverse Proxy
 |
 v
Runtime
 |
 v
Server Framework
 |
 v
Client Framework

Do not treat all detections as if they perform the same role.

docs.title: Wappalyzer vs WhatWeb
docs.text:
Wappalyzer and WhatWeb complement each other.

WhatWeb is particularly useful for command-line-driven fingerprinting.

Wappalyzer is particularly useful during interactive browser reconnaissance.

WhatWeb
   |
   +-- CLI
   +-- automation-friendly
   +-- plugin-based fingerprinting

Wappalyzer
   |
   +-- interactive
   +-- browser context
   +-- broad technology categories

When both agree:

WhatWeb:
React

Wappalyzer:
React

JavaScript assets:
React-related bundles

confidence increases.

When they disagree:

WhatWeb:
Technology A

Wappalyzer:
Technology B

investigate the evidence rather than arbitrarily choosing one result.

Related note:

WhatWeb

docs.title: Wappalyzer vs httpx
docs.text:
httpx is useful for large-scale HTTP discovery and enrichment.

Wappalyzer is useful for deeper interactive inspection.

A typical workflow is:

Subdomains
    |
    v
httpx
    |
    v
Reachable Web Applications
    |
    v
Prioritised Targets
    |
    v
Browser + Wappalyzer
    |
    v
Technology Validation

This is usually more practical than manually browsing every discovered hostname.

Related note:

httpx

docs.title: Wappalyzer and Burp Suite
docs.text:
Wappalyzer can help identify technologies while Burp Suite provides request-level evidence.

Browser
   |
   +--> Wappalyzer
   |
   +--> Burp Proxy

Wappalyzer may indicate:

React
Express
nginx

Burp may then reveal:

HTTP Headers
Cookies
API Calls
JavaScript Assets
Redirects
Authentication Flow

Combined analysis provides better context.

Related tool section:

Web Application Testing Tools

docs.title: Wappalyzer and curl
docs.text:
curl is useful for manually verifying HTTP-level indicators.

For example, Wappalyzer may identify nginx.

Check:

curl -I https://example.test

Representative output:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
Content-Type: text/html

This provides an additional independent indicator.

Another useful request is:

curl -i https://example.test

which shows both headers and response body.

Quick reference:

curl Cheatsheet

docs.title: Web Server Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Wappalyzer may identify web-server technologies.

Possible examples include:

nginx
Apache HTTP Server
Microsoft IIS
LiteSpeed

A web-server fingerprint may come from:

  • HTTP headers;
  • error pages;
  • characteristic response behaviour;
  • other observable indicators.

Validate manually where the exact technology matters.

Example:

curl -I https://example.test

Possible output:

Server: nginx

This increases confidence in the detection.

docs.title: Framework Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Framework detection may be based on several clues.

Potential indicators include:

  • JavaScript globals;
  • generated HTML;
  • asset paths;
  • cookies;
  • response headers;
  • DOM structures;
  • framework-specific metadata.

Example workflow:

Wappalyzer
     |
     v
Candidate Framework
     |
     +-- JavaScript
     +-- HTML
     +-- Assets
     +-- Cookies
     |
     v
Manual Confirmation

Framework identification should guide testing, not replace it.

docs.title: Client-Side Frameworks
docs.text:
Wappalyzer is particularly useful for identifying client-side frameworks.

Potential categories include:

React
Vue
Angular
Svelte
other JavaScript frameworks

After detecting a frontend framework, review:

  • JavaScript bundles;
  • source maps;
  • frontend routes;
  • API calls;
  • client-side state;
  • third-party dependencies.

Related notes:

JavaScript Analysis

DOM-Based Vulnerabilities

Third-Party JavaScript Security

docs.title: CMS Detection
docs.text:
Wappalyzer may identify Content Management Systems.

Possible indicators include:

  • HTML metadata;
  • known resource paths;
  • page structures;
  • asset names;
  • JavaScript;
  • cookies.

A detected CMS should be validated.

For example:

Wappalyzer
   |
   v
WordPress candidate
   |
   +-- HTML generator metadata
   +-- /wp-content/
   +-- /wp-includes/
   |
   v
Higher confidence

Do not immediately infer vulnerability from the CMS name.

docs.title: JavaScript Library Detection
docs.text:
Wappalyzer may identify JavaScript libraries.

Examples include:

jQuery
React
Vue
Angular
Bootstrap
other libraries

Important questions include:

  • Is the library actually used?
  • Is a version detectable?
  • Is it first-party or third-party?
  • Is the identified version reliable?
  • Are multiple versions present?
  • Is the library loaded only on certain routes?

Related note:

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: Version Detection
docs.text:
Version information should be treated carefully.

If Wappalyzer reports:

Technology X
Version 1.2.3

treat it as:

Candidate Version

until independently validated.

Potential validation sources include:

  • JavaScript filenames;
  • package metadata;
  • source maps;
  • headers;
  • HTML;
  • documented application assets;
  • direct behavioural evidence.

Do not report a vulnerability solely because a detected version appears in a CVE advisory.

docs.title: Why Version Detection Can Be Wrong
docs.text:
Version fingerprinting can be affected by:

  • stale assets;
  • cached JavaScript;
  • copied libraries;
  • customised builds;
  • vendor backports;
  • altered banners;
  • reverse proxies;
  • bundled dependencies.

Therefore:

Detected Version
      |
      v
Candidate
      |
      v
Independent Validation

docs.title: HTTP Headers
docs.text:
Wappalyzer can use response headers as detection indicators.

Useful headers may include:

Server
X-Powered-By
Via
X-AspNet-Version
X-Generator

Example:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
X-Powered-By: Express

This may indicate multiple layers:

nginx
  |
  v
Reverse Proxy
  |
  v
Express

Do not assume these represent conflicting results.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Cookie names can provide technology clues.

Examples of useful questions include:

Does the cookie name match a framework default?

Is the cookie used for authentication?

Is it related to CSRF?

Is the name application-specific?

Could the application have renamed the default?

Cookie-based fingerprints should be considered supporting evidence.

docs.title: HTML Metadata
docs.text:
Some technologies expose metadata in HTML.

For example:

<meta name="generator" content="Example CMS">

This can provide strong evidence, but still consider whether it may be:

  • stale;
  • manually added;
  • copied from another template;
  • intentionally misleading.

Manual inspection is valuable.

docs.title: JavaScript Globals
docs.text:
Some frontend technologies expose characteristic JavaScript objects or runtime behaviour.

Wappalyzer may use such indicators for detection.

Manual investigation may include:

  • browser developer tools;
  • loaded JavaScript;
  • DOM inspection;
  • network requests;
  • framework-specific properties.

The exact indicator depends on the technology.

docs.title: Asset Paths
docs.text:
Asset paths may reveal framework or CMS information.

Useful categories include:

Static JavaScript
CSS
Images
Framework bundles
CMS resource directories
Generated build artefacts

For example:

/assets/
/static/
/_next/
/wp-content/

may contribute to technology identification depending on the broader context.

A path alone should not always be considered conclusive.

docs.title: Default Error Pages
docs.text:
Error pages provide an additional fingerprinting source.

Request a random path:

curl -i https://example.test/not-real-819273

Review:

Status
Headers
HTML
Error wording
Footer
Cookies

The response may reveal:

  • web server;
  • framework;
  • application server;
  • routing behaviour.

A useful external reference is:

0xdf - Default 404 Pages

Use it as a comparison aid rather than definitive proof.

docs.title: Combining Wappalyzer with 404 Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Example:

Wappalyzer
    |
    v
Candidate Technology
    |
    v
Random 404 Request
    |
    v
Default Error Page
    |
    v
Compare Known Behaviour
    |
    v
Additional Evidence

Suppose:

Wappalyzer:
Express

404 response:
Cannot GET /random-path

Headers:
X-Powered-By: Express

The combined evidence provides a stronger fingerprint than any one indicator alone.

docs.title: Custom Error Pages
docs.text:
A production application may hide default framework error pages.

Framework
   |
   v
Custom Error Handler
   |
   v
Branded 404

In this case, error-page fingerprinting may provide little useful information.

Other indicators may still identify the technology.

docs.title: Response Behaviour
docs.text:
Technology identification can also come from behaviour rather than static strings.

Examples include:

  • redirect patterns;
  • routing behaviour;
  • API error structures;
  • authentication responses;
  • default methods;
  • content types;
  • status-code behaviour.

For example:

GET /nonexistent
        |
        v
JSON response
        |
        v
Characteristic API error format

This may help identify a framework family when combined with other evidence.

docs.title: API Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Traditional Wappalyzer detections may be less useful when an endpoint exposes only an API.

In that case, inspect:

  • response headers;
  • JSON error structures;
  • OpenAPI endpoints;
  • GraphQL endpoints;
  • authentication headers;
  • cookies;
  • routing patterns.

Related notes:

API Security

GraphQL API Security

gRPC Security

docs.title: Authentication Changes Technology Visibility
docs.text:
Some technologies may only be visible after login.

For example:

Unauthenticated
     |
     +-- generic login page

Authenticated
     |
     +-- React dashboard
     +-- API requests
     +-- analytics
     +-- administration modules

If authorised credentials are available, repeat technology review after authentication.

docs.title: Different Routes May Use Different Stacks
docs.text:
Modern applications are often composed of several components.

Example:

/
   -> frontend application

/api/
   -> API service

/admin/
   -> administration interface

/legacy/
   -> older application

Wappalyzer results may vary between these routes.

Do not assume the root page represents the entire target.

docs.title: Microservices and Reverse Proxies
docs.text:
A single public hostname may route to multiple backend systems.

Internet
   |
   v
Reverse Proxy
   |
   +--> Frontend
   |
   +--> API
   |
   +--> Authentication
   |
   +--> Legacy Application

Wappalyzer may identify technologies from several layers or only from the visible frontend.

This is why fingerprinting should be interpreted in architectural context.

docs.title: CDN Influence
docs.text:
CDNs can affect observable technology information.

They may:

  • rewrite headers;
  • terminate TLS;
  • cache responses;
  • serve error pages;
  • hide backend addresses;
  • inject their own indicators.

Therefore distinguish:

Edge Technology

from:

Application Technology

docs.title: WAF Influence
docs.text:
A Web Application Firewall may also affect what Wappalyzer observes.

Possible effects include:

  • altered headers;
  • generic block pages;
  • CAPTCHA;
  • denied resources;
  • JavaScript challenges;
  • bot-detection responses.

If the browser receives a WAF page rather than the application, Wappalyzer may profile the intermediary instead.

docs.title: Third-Party Technologies
docs.text:
Wappalyzer often identifies third-party technologies loaded by the application.

Examples include:

Analytics
Tag Managers
Chat Widgets
Advertising
CDNs
Customer Support
Payment Providers

These detections may be useful for architecture understanding.

However:

A third-party domain referenced by an in-scope application is not automatically in scope.

Do not test external providers without explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Tracking and Analytics Technologies
docs.text:
Analytics detections can reveal:

  • tracking providers;
  • tag managers;
  • marketing platforms;
  • monitoring scripts.

These are normally architecture observations rather than vulnerabilities.

They can, however, help identify third-party JavaScript dependencies that may deserve security review.

Related note:

Third-Party JavaScript Security

docs.title: Security Technologies
docs.text:
Wappalyzer may identify technologies related to:

  • CDN protection;
  • WAFs;
  • bot management;
  • security headers;
  • identity providers.

Such detections can help explain application behaviour.

For example:

Unexpected 403
      |
      v
WAF technology detected
      |
      v
Possible security-control response

The detection itself does not prove exactly how the control is configured.

docs.title: Login Page Profiling
docs.text:
Login pages often reveal technologies not visible elsewhere.

Review:

  • identity-provider branding;
  • cookies;
  • JavaScript;
  • authentication redirects;
  • OAuth/OIDC endpoints;
  • SAML endpoints;
  • third-party identity services.

Related notes:

Authentication Testing

OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Security

SAML Security

docs.title: Administrative Interfaces
docs.text:
An administrative interface may use a different technology stack from the main application.

For example:

Main Site:
React

Admin:
Angular

API:
Java

Browse authorised administration interfaces separately when they are in scope.

Do not assume a detected administration technology represents a security issue by itself.

docs.title: Technology Inventory
docs.text:
Wappalyzer results can contribute to a technology inventory.

Example:

Target Category Technology Supporting Evidence Confidence portal.example.test Web server nginx Header + Wappalyzer High portal.example.test Frontend React Wappalyzer + JS assets High api.example.test API framework Candidate Error behaviour Moderate blog.example.test CMS WordPress Wappalyzer + asset paths High

This is more useful than storing screenshots of technology names without context.

docs.title: Technology Confidence
docs.text:
A useful confidence model is:

Confidence Meaning Low One weak indicator Moderate Several related indicators High Multiple independent indicators Confirmed Direct evidence establishes the technology

Example:

Wappalyzer:
nginx

Confidence:
Low to Moderate

Then:

HTTP header:
Server: nginx

404:
nginx default response

Now:

Confidence:
High

docs.title: Correlation Workflow
docs.text:
Use several complementary data sources.

Wappalyzer --------+
                   |
WhatWeb -----------+
                   |
HTTP Headers ------+----> Technology Hypothesis
                   |
JavaScript --------+
                   |
Error Page --------+
                   |
Manual Analysis ---+

The objective is not to maximise the number of tools.

The objective is to reduce uncertainty.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
A Wappalyzer detection can be wrong.

Possible causes include:

  • generic JavaScript;
  • reused templates;
  • copied HTML;
  • stale resources;
  • old framework assets;
  • third-party libraries;
  • proxy-generated content;
  • shared page components;
  • misleading headers.

Example:

Wappalyzer:
WordPress

Manual review:
Only an old WordPress image path remains

Current application:
Custom application

Correct interpretation:

A WordPress-related fingerprint was observed, but current use of
WordPress was not confirmed.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Wappalyzer can also miss technologies.

Possible reasons include:

  • headers removed;
  • JavaScript bundled;
  • framework identifiers stripped;
  • custom application builds;
  • authentication required;
  • server-side technology hidden behind a proxy;
  • technology not covered by current fingerprints.

Therefore:

Not detected

does not mean:

Not present

docs.title: Conflicting Results
docs.text:
Suppose:

WhatWeb:
Apache

Wappalyzer:
nginx

Possible explanations include:

  • reverse proxy in front of Apache;
  • stale fingerprint;
  • inconsistent responses;
  • load-balanced backend systems;
  • WAF or CDN behaviour;
  • one tool producing a false positive.

Investigate:

curl -I https://example.test

Then compare multiple responses and routes.

The correct architecture may be:

nginx
   |
   v
Apache
   |
   v
Application

Both tools could therefore have observed valid but different layers.

docs.title: JavaScript-Heavy Applications
docs.text:
Single-page applications may expose technology indicators primarily through JavaScript.

A useful workflow is:

Wappalyzer
    |
    v
Frontend Framework Candidate
    |
    v
Browser DevTools
    |
    +-- Network
    +-- Sources
    +-- JavaScript
    +-- Source Maps
    |
    v
Manual Validation

Related note:

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: Source Maps
docs.text:
Source maps can reveal:

  • original source filenames;
  • framework structure;
  • development code;
  • package information;
  • application routes.

A framework detected by Wappalyzer may sometimes be corroborated through exposed source maps.

Source-map exposure should be evaluated separately for information-disclosure impact.

Related note:

Information Disclosure

docs.title: Dependency Identification
docs.text:
A technology detection may reveal a library or framework that should be reviewed for dependency risk.

But:

Library Detected
       |
       X
Do not immediately report CVEs

Instead:

Library Detected
       |
       v
Version Validation
       |
       v
Deployment Context
       |
       v
Vendor Advisory
       |
       v
Technical Validation

Related note:

Dependency Security

docs.title: Browser Developer Tools
docs.text:
Browser developer tools complement Wappalyzer well.

Useful areas include:

Network
Sources
Application
Storage
Console
Elements

Review:

  • loaded scripts;
  • API requests;
  • cookies;
  • local storage;
  • application bundles;
  • source maps;
  • response headers.

Wappalyzer can indicate what to investigate, while developer tools show the underlying evidence.

docs.title: Wappalyzer and Source Code Review
docs.text:
Technology identification can also guide source code review.

For example:

Wappalyzer:
Django

may suggest prioritising Django-specific source review when source access exists.

Related note:

Django Source Code Review

Similarly:

Wappalyzer:
Flask

Related note:

Flask Source Code Review

Technology fingerprinting can therefore connect black-box reconnaissance with white-box analysis.

docs.title: Wappalyzer and Attack Surface Analysis
docs.text:
A detected technology can guide the next phase.

Example:

Wappalyzer
    |
    +-- React
    |
    +-- nginx
    |
    +-- identity provider
    |
    v
Attack Surface Questions
    |
    +-- JavaScript/API surface?
    +-- Reverse proxy behaviour?
    +-- OAuth/OIDC?

Related note:

Attack Surface Analysis

The tool should help generate better questions.

docs.title: Practical Validation Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose Wappalyzer reports:

React
nginx
Google Analytics

docs.title: Step 1 - Inspect HTTP Headers
docs.text:
curl -I https://example.test

Representative output:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
Content-Type: text/html

This supports the nginx detection.

docs.title: Step 2 - Inspect HTML
docs.text:
Review the page source.

Representative example:

<script src="/static/js/main.js"></script>

docs.title: Step 3 - Inspect JavaScript
docs.text: Review the loaded bundle and browser developer tools for React-related runtime or build indicators.

docs.title: Step 4 - Review Third Parties
docs.text: Confirm whether the analytics technology is loaded from an external service.

docs.title: Step 5 - Assign Confidence
docs.text:
nginx:
High

React:
Moderate to High

Analytics:
High if script source is directly observed

This produces a more defensible technology profile than copying the Wappalyzer display alone.

docs.title: Example of a Misleading Detection
docs.text:
Suppose Wappalyzer reports a CMS.

Manual investigation finds:

/legacy-assets/cms-logo.png

but no other evidence of the CMS.

The correct conclusion is:

A fingerprint associated with the CMS was observed, but manual
validation did not establish that the current application is running
that CMS.

Do not overstate the result.

docs.title: Manual Validation Checklist for a Technology
docs.text:
When a technology matters to later testing, check several sources.

Technology Candidate
        |
        +-- Headers?
        +-- Cookies?
        +-- HTML?
        +-- JavaScript?
        +-- Static Assets?
        +-- Error Pages?
        +-- Routing Behaviour?
        +-- Independent Tool?
        |
        v
Confidence

Not every technology requires exhaustive validation.

Focus effort where the identification affects:

  • vulnerability research;
  • testing strategy;
  • attack surface;
  • report conclusions;
  • remediation.

docs.title: Larger Assessments
docs.text:
For large environments, Wappalyzer is usually better used selectively.

Example:

2,000 hostnames
     |
     v
Subdomain Resolution
     |
     v
httpx
     |
     v
150 interesting HTTP endpoints
     |
     v
Prioritisation
     |
     v
Interactive Wappalyzer Review

This avoids spending manual browsing time on low-value or duplicate hosts.

docs.title: Prioritisation
docs.text:
Technology findings can help prioritise:

  • legacy platforms;
  • administrative systems;
  • uncommon frameworks;
  • development applications;
  • externally exposed management tools;
  • applications disclosing detailed versions.

Prioritisation is not the same as vulnerability confirmation.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For relevant Wappalyzer results, capture:

Target:
Date/time:
Page:
Detected technology:
Technology category:
Supporting header:
Supporting HTML:
Supporting JavaScript:
Supporting asset:
Additional tool result:
Confidence:

Example:

Target:
https://portal.example.test

Page:
/

Wappalyzer:
React
nginx

Supporting evidence:
HTTP Server header indicated nginx.
JavaScript application bundles were consistent with a React frontend.

Confidence:
High for nginx.
Moderate to high for React.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots can be useful when showing:

  • the detected technology list;
  • a corresponding application page;
  • a relevant header or browser view.

However, a screenshot of the Wappalyzer interface alone is weak technical evidence.

Where a fingerprint matters, retain the underlying response or other supporting evidence.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Technology identification normally belongs in:

  • reconnaissance notes;
  • architecture observations;
  • assessment methodology;
  • supporting evidence.

Example wording:

Technology fingerprinting indicated that the application used a
React-based client and was served through nginx. These observations
were corroborated through JavaScript asset analysis and HTTP response
headers.

Avoid:

Wappalyzer proved that the application uses React and nginx.

The first statement explains the evidence.

docs.title: Technology Disclosure as a Finding
docs.text:
Technology information itself is not automatically a vulnerability.

Potentially security-relevant disclosure may include:

  • exact vulnerable version information;
  • internal infrastructure names;
  • development error pages;
  • stack traces;
  • internal paths;
  • sensitive framework configuration.

Evaluate actual impact.

Related note:

Information Disclosure

docs.title: Treating Wappalyzer as Proof
docs.text:
Bad:

Wappalyzer -> Technology X
             |
             v
Technology X confirmed

Better:

Wappalyzer
    |
    v
Candidate
    |
    v
Supporting Evidence
    |
    v
Confidence

docs.title: Looking Only at the Homepage
docs.text:
A homepage may expose only part of the application.

Review important routes where authorised.

docs.title: Ignoring Authenticated Areas
docs.text: Authenticated functionality may expose different technologies.

docs.title: Ignoring Third Parties
docs.text: Not every detected technology belongs to the organisation being assessed.

docs.title: Reporting CVEs from a Technology Name
docs.text:
A technology name alone does not establish:

  • version;
  • patch level;
  • vulnerable configuration;
  • exploitability.

docs.title: Ignoring Architectural Layers
docs.text:
A CDN, proxy, application server, framework, and frontend library may all appear in the same result.

Interpret them according to their role.

docs.title: Wappalyzer Detects Nothing
docs.text:
Possible causes include:

  • limited fingerprint exposure;
  • unusual application stack;
  • custom frontend;
  • minimal HTML;
  • bundled JavaScript;
  • authentication boundary.

Use:

  • WhatWeb;
  • curl;
  • browser developer tools;
  • JavaScript analysis;
  • manual response inspection.

docs.title: Detection Changes Between Pages
docs.text:
This may be normal.

Different routes may use different components.

Map the technologies to the routes where they appear.

docs.title: Browser Result Differs from CLI Tooling
docs.text:
Possible causes include:

  • JavaScript execution;
  • cookies;
  • browser-specific responses;
  • authentication;
  • user-agent differences;
  • dynamic content.

Compare equivalent requests.

docs.title: Technology Appears Only After Login
docs.text: Repeat browser-based profiling after authentication if that activity is authorised.

docs.title: Third-Party Technology Dominates Results
docs.text:
Separate:

Application Technology

from:

Embedded Third-Party Technology

This avoids misrepresenting the target architecture.

docs.title: Wappalyzer Workflow
docs.text:
A strong workflow can be summarised as:

1. Confirm authorised target
       |
       v
2. Open application
       |
       v
3. Browse representative routes
       |
       v
4. Review Wappalyzer technologies
       |
       v
5. Group by architectural role
       |
       v
6. Validate important matches
       |
       +-- HTTP headers
       +-- HTML
       +-- JavaScript
       +-- assets
       +-- cookies
       +-- error pages
       |
       v
7. Correlate with WhatWeb/httpx
       |
       v
8. Assign confidence
       |
       v
9. Use technology knowledge to guide testing

docs.title: Quick Validation Commands
docs.text: Wappalyzer itself is commonly used interactively, but supporting validation can be performed with other tools.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text: curl -I https://example.test

docs.title: Full Response
docs.text: curl -i https://example.test

docs.title: Verbose HTTP/TLS Interaction
docs.text: curl -v https://example.test

docs.title: Random 404
docs.text: curl -i https://example.test/not-real-928173

docs.title: WhatWeb Comparison
docs.text: whatweb https://example.test

docs.title: Nmap Service Identification
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 80,443,8080,8443 example.test

Use supporting tools to investigate specific questions rather than automatically running every command.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• [ ] Target is authorised.
  • [ ] Related third-party domains are recognised.
  • [ ] Newly discovered domains are checked against scope before testing.

docs.title: Initial Review
docs.text:
• [ ] Homepage reviewed.
  • [ ] Important application routes reviewed.
  • [ ] Authenticated areas reviewed where authorised.
  • [ ] Detected technologies recorded.
  • [ ] Categories understood.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] HTTP headers inspected where relevant.
  • [ ] Cookies reviewed.
  • [ ] HTML inspected.
  • [ ] JavaScript assets inspected.
  • [ ] Error pages reviewed.
  • [ ] WhatWeb compared where useful.
  • [ ] httpx information compared where useful.
  • [ ] Conflicting results investigated.

docs.title: Version Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Version information treated as a candidate.
  • [ ] Version evidence independently validated.
  • [ ] Vendor patching/backports considered.
  • [ ] CVEs not inferred solely from a detected product/version.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• [ ] Edge/CDN distinguished from backend.
  • [ ] Reverse proxy distinguished from application server.
  • [ ] Server-side and client-side technologies separated.
  • [ ] Third-party technologies separated from target-owned components.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Relevant page recorded.
  • [ ] Relevant fingerprint recorded.
  • [ ] Supporting technical evidence retained.
  • [ ] Confidence documented.
  • [ ] Tool output not presented as proof without validation.

docs.text:
