docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use web-testing tools like this:

Burp
ffuf
Nuclei
sqlmap
Katana
Interactsh
      |
      v
Run everything
      |
      v
Copy results

Use them like this:

Understand Application
        |
        v
Choose Testing Question
        |
        v
Choose Appropriate Tool
        |
        v
Perform Focused Test
        |
        v
Observe Behaviour
        |
        v
Interpret Evidence
        |
        v
Validate Independently
        |
        v
Demonstrate Security Impact
        |
        v
Report Defensible Finding

The value of these tools is not the amount of output they produce.

Their value is how effectively they help answer a specific security question and support a technically defensible conclusion.

docs.title: Burp Suite
docs.text:
Burp Suite is one of the most widely used platforms for manual and semi-automated web application security testing.

Its main strength is that it sits directly between the tester and the application, allowing HTTP and WebSocket traffic to be inspected, modified, replayed, compared, automated, and extended.

Browser
   |
   v
Burp Suite
   |
   +-- Proxy
   +-- HTTP History
   +-- Repeater
   +-- Intruder
   +-- Decoder
   +-- Comparer
   +-- Sequencer
   +-- Extensions
   +-- Scanner            [Professional]
   +-- Collaborator       [Professional workflows]
   |
   v
Target Application

Burp Suite should not be treated as a scanner that replaces methodology.

The strongest workflow is:

Understand Application
        |
        v
Capture Request
        |
        v
Establish Baseline
        |
        v
Modify One Variable
        |
        v
Observe Difference
        |
        v
Interpret Behaviour
        |
        v
Validate Security Impact
        |
        v
Capture Evidence

Authorised testing only

Use Burp Suite only against applications and APIs that are explicitly authorised for testing. Automated scanning, Intruder attacks, out-of-band testing, and repeated authenticated requests can create significant traffic or alter application state. Confirm the rules of engagement before using high-volume or intrusive functionality.

docs.title: Where Burp Suite Fits
docs.text:
Burp Suite is useful throughout most phases of a web assessment.

Reconnaissance
      |
      v
Application Mapping
      |
      v
Proxy Traffic
      |
      v
Identify Interesting Requests
      |
      v
Manual Testing
      |
      +-- Repeater
      +-- Comparer
      +-- Decoder
      +-- Intruder
      |
      v
Automated Assistance
      |
      +-- Scanner
      +-- Extensions
      |
      v
Manual Validation
      |
      v
Evidence

Related methodology:

Web Application Testing Tools

Web Application Security

Web Application Testing Methodology

Web Application Pentesting Checklist

docs.title: Community vs Professional
docs.text:
Burp Suite is available in multiple editions.

For practical security work, the most important distinction is usually between Community Edition and Professional.

docs.title: Community Edition
docs.text:
Community Edition is suitable for many manual testing activities.

Useful capabilities include:

  • Proxy;
  • HTTP history;
  • Repeater;
  • Decoder;
  • Comparer;
  • Sequencer;
  • extensions;
  • manual WebSocket inspection;
  • manual request manipulation.

It is entirely possible to perform serious manual testing with Community Edition.

docs.title: Professional Edition
docs.text:
Professional adds functionality intended for larger, faster, and more automated assessment workflows.

Important examples include:

  • Burp Scanner;
  • crawling and auditing;
  • enhanced Intruder capability;
  • Burp Collaborator integration;
  • additional automated discovery and testing workflows.

Exact edition differences can change over time.

Always verify current product capabilities against:

Burp Suite Editions

docs.title: A Better Way to Think About Editions
docs.text:
Do not think:

Community
   =
Weak

Professional
   =
Powerful

A better model is:

Community
   |
   +-- strong manual testing
   +-- learning workflows
   +-- request manipulation
   +-- protocol understanding

Professional
   |
   +-- everything above
   +-- automation
   +-- scanner
   +-- faster repeated testing
   +-- Collaborator integration

The core testing skill remains understanding application behaviour.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
A normal setup places Burp between the browser and target application.

Browser
   |
   v
Burp Proxy
   |
   v
Application

The browser sends requests through Burp.

Burp can then:

  • intercept them;
  • inspect them;
  • modify them;
  • forward them;
  • store them in HTTP history.

docs.title: Burp Browser
docs.text:
Burp provides an embedded browser configured to work with Burp's proxy.

This is often the easiest way to begin testing because:

  • proxy settings are already configured;
  • HTTPS interception is handled;
  • requests immediately appear in Proxy history.

For many assessments:

Burp
   |
   v
Proxy
   |
   v
Open Browser

is enough to begin application mapping.

docs.title: External Browser Setup
docs.text:
A separate browser can also be configured to use Burp as an HTTP proxy.

A common local proxy configuration is:

127.0.0.1:8080

The exact listener should be confirmed in:

Proxy
  -> Proxy settings
  -> Proxy listeners

The browser must trust Burp's CA certificate if HTTPS interception is required.

docs.title: Burp CA Certificate
docs.text:
HTTPS interception works because Burp acts as a local TLS interception proxy.

Conceptually:

Browser
   |
 TLS
   |
   v
Burp
   |
 TLS
   |
   v
Application

The browser sees certificates generated by Burp.

For a dedicated testing browser, install the Burp CA according to the official documentation.

Do not install testing CA certificates broadly across production workstations unless there is a justified need.

Official documentation:

Installing Burp's CA Certificate

docs.title: Proxy Intercept
docs.text:
Intercept allows requests to be paused before they are forwarded.

This provides an opportunity to modify:

  • parameters;
  • headers;
  • cookies;
  • HTTP methods;
  • request bodies;
  • content types;
  • tokens.

Example conceptual flow:

Browser Request
      |
      v
Intercept
      |
      +-- modify
      +-- forward
      +-- drop
      |
      v
Application

Intercept is useful for focused testing.

For normal browsing, leaving interception off while reviewing HTTP history is often more convenient.

docs.title: HTTP History
docs.text:
HTTP history records proxied HTTP traffic.

It is one of the most useful areas for mapping an application.

Review:

Host
Method
URL
Status
MIME type
Extension
Length
Comment
Highlight

Typical interesting requests include:

  • login;
  • logout;
  • password reset;
  • user profile;
  • admin endpoints;
  • file uploads;
  • API calls;
  • role changes;
  • object access;
  • search;
  • export functions;
  • state-changing actions.

docs.title: Application Mapping
docs.text:
A practical mapping workflow is:

Browse Application
       |
       v
HTTP History
       |
       +-- Pages
       +-- APIs
       +-- Static Assets
       +-- Authentication
       +-- Background Requests
       |
       v
Identify Security-Sensitive Endpoints

Map the application before deeply testing individual parameters.

docs.title: Site Map
docs.text:
Burp can build a hierarchical view of observed application content.

This can help identify:

  • paths;
  • endpoints;
  • parameters;
  • APIs;
  • hostnames;
  • files;
  • application structure.

Use the site map together with HTTP history rather than relying on one view alone.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Burp scope configuration is important.

Without scope control, HTTP history can become noisy with:

  • analytics domains;
  • CDNs;
  • browser background traffic;
  • third-party APIs;
  • advertising;
  • update services.

Define the assessment target appropriately.

Conceptually:

All Browser Traffic
      |
      v
Burp Scope
      |
      +-- In Scope
      |
      +-- Out of Scope

This also helps avoid accidental interaction with third-party systems.

docs.title: Scope Is Not Authorisation
docs.text:
An important distinction:

Burp Scope
     !=
Legal / Contractual Scope

Adding a hostname to Burp scope does not grant authorisation to test it.

The rules of engagement remain authoritative.

docs.title: Repeater
docs.text:
Repeater is one of the most important Burp tools.

It allows the tester to manually replay HTTP requests repeatedly.

A strong testing pattern is:

Capture Valid Request
        |
        v
Send to Repeater
        |
        v
Send Baseline
        |
        v
Change One Variable
        |
        v
Send Again
        |
        v
Compare Result

This isolates cause and effect.

docs.title: Sending Requests to Repeater
docs.text:
From HTTP history or Proxy:

Right-click request
    |
    v
Send to Repeater

The request can then be modified and resent.

Commonly modified values include:

URL
Path
Method
Query parameters
POST parameters
JSON properties
Headers
Cookies
Tokens
Object IDs
Host
Content-Type

docs.title: Establishing a Baseline in Repeater
docs.text:
Before testing an input, send the original request unchanged.

Record:

Status
Response length
Response body
Headers
Timing
Application state

Then modify a single input.

Example:

Original:
user_id=100

Modified:
user_id=101

Compare the result.

docs.title: One Variable at a Time
docs.text:
Changing too many things at once makes interpretation difficult.

Bad:

Change:
ID
Role
Method
Cookie
Header

Then observe a different response.

You may not know what caused the difference.

Better:

Baseline
   |
   v
Change ID only
   |
   v
Observe
   |
   v
Change role only
   |
   v
Observe

docs.title: Authorisation Testing
docs.text:
Repeater is especially useful for authorisation testing.

Example model:

User A
  |
  v
GET /api/account/100

Capture the request.

Then use another authorised test account:

User B
  |
  v
GET /api/account/100

Compare behaviour.

Questions include:

  • Can another user's object be accessed?
  • Does changing the object identifier matter?
  • Is the server checking ownership?
  • Is access enforced server-side?

Related notes:

Authorisation Testing

IDOR and BOLA

docs.title: Authentication Testing
docs.text:
Burp helps inspect:

  • login requests;
  • session creation;
  • authentication cookies;
  • tokens;
  • logout behaviour;
  • password reset;
  • MFA flows;
  • remember-me functionality.

Related notes:

Authentication Testing

Password Reset Security

Multi-Factor Authentication Security

docs.title: Session Testing
docs.text:
Burp makes session behaviour visible.

Review:

Set-Cookie
Cookie
Authorization
JWT
CSRF tokens
Refresh tokens
Session identifiers

Questions include:

  • Does the token rotate after login?
  • Does logout invalidate the session?
  • Does privilege change rotate session state?
  • Are sessions scoped correctly?
  • Are cookies protected appropriately?

Related note:

Session Management

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Cookies can be inspected in both requests and responses.

Example response:

Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

Useful properties include:

Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
Domain
Path
Expires
Max-Age

Cookie configuration must be interpreted according to application context.

docs.title: JSON Requests
docs.text:
Many modern applications send JSON.

Example:

POST /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "Alice",
  "email": "alice@example.test"
}

Repeater allows individual JSON properties to be changed and tested.

This is useful for:

  • APIs;
  • mass assignment;
  • authorisation;
  • business logic;
  • injection testing.

Related notes:

API Security

Mass Assignment

docs.title: HTTP Methods
docs.text:
Burp makes it easy to experiment with HTTP methods when relevant.

Examples include:

GET
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE
OPTIONS
HEAD

Changing a method may reveal:

  • alternate endpoint behaviour;
  • API functionality;
  • authorisation differences;
  • method restrictions.

Do not assume changing a method alone creates a vulnerability.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Security-relevant headers may include:

Host
Origin
Referer
Authorization
Cookie
X-Forwarded-For
X-Forwarded-Host
Content-Type
Accept

Burp Repeater is useful because these values can be modified precisely.

Related notes:

HTTP Host Header Attacks

CORS

HTTP Security Headers

docs.title: Content-Type Testing
docs.text:
Applications sometimes parse input differently depending on Content-Type.

Examples:

application/json
application/x-www-form-urlencoded
multipart/form-data
application/xml

A request may behave differently when the content type changes.

The test should be based on a specific hypothesis rather than random format changes.

docs.title: Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer highlights differences between two pieces of data.

This can be useful for:

  • role comparison;
  • authenticated vs unauthenticated responses;
  • injection response differences;
  • session comparison;
  • cache behaviour;
  • access-control testing.

Conceptually:

Response A
    |
    v
Comparer
    ^
    |
Response B

docs.title: Word Comparison
docs.text:
Comparer can compare content by words.

This is useful where responses contain the same general structure with subtle textual differences.

docs.title: Byte Comparison
docs.text:
Byte-level comparison can identify very small differences.

This is useful when:

  • token values change;
  • binary data differs;
  • whitespace or encoding differences matter.

docs.title: Decoder
docs.text:
Decoder can transform data between common formats.

Useful operations include:

  • URL encoding;
  • URL decoding;
  • HTML encoding;
  • HTML decoding;
  • Base64 encoding;
  • Base64 decoding;
  • hexadecimal conversions.

Example:

admin%40example.test

decode to:

admin@example.test

Encoding does not imply encryption.

docs.title: Sequencer
docs.text:
Sequencer helps analyse the randomness of tokens.

Potential candidates include:

  • session identifiers;
  • CSRF tokens;
  • password-reset tokens;
  • anti-automation values.

A token that looks random should not automatically be assumed secure.

Sequencer can assist statistical analysis, but the security conclusion should also consider:

  • token length;
  • entropy;
  • predictability;
  • generation method;
  • lifecycle;
  • binding.

docs.title: Intruder
docs.text:
Intruder automates repeated requests with varying payload positions.

Conceptually:

Request Template
      |
      v
Payload Positions
      |
      v
Payload List
      |
      v
Repeated Requests
      |
      v
Compare Responses

Use Intruder where repeated controlled testing is justified.

docs.title: Intruder Attack Types
docs.text:
Burp Intruder supports different payload-placement strategies.

The exact available options and terminology should be checked in current PortSwigger documentation.

Typical concepts include:

  • one payload position at a time;
  • multiple positions with coordinated payloads;
  • combinations across positions.

The right mode depends on the test objective.

docs.title: Intruder for Enumeration
docs.text:
Intruder can assist with controlled enumeration of:

  • IDs;
  • parameters;
  • values;
  • endpoints;
  • roles.

For large content-discovery tasks, dedicated tools such as ffuf may be faster.

Use the tool best suited to the problem.

docs.title: Intruder and Authentication
docs.text:
Be careful when using Intruder against authentication workflows.

Potential consequences include:

  • account lockout;
  • MFA triggering;
  • rate limiting;
  • security alerts;
  • password-reset email generation.

Do not perform password attacks unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Intruder Grep and Response Analysis
docs.text:
Repeated requests are only useful when the results can be interpreted.

Compare:

Status
Length
Words
Headers
Redirect
Response body
Timing

A small response difference can indicate meaningful application behaviour.

docs.title: Burp Scanner
docs.text:
Burp Scanner is available in Burp Suite Professional.

It can automate portions of:

  • crawling;
  • passive analysis;
  • active security testing;
  • issue identification.

Scanner results should be treated as:

Candidates

until manually validated.

docs.title: Passive Scanning
docs.text:
Passive scanning analyses traffic without sending additional attack requests for that analysis.

It may identify issues such as:

  • missing headers;
  • information disclosure;
  • insecure cookies;
  • suspicious application behaviour.

Passive findings still require context.

docs.title: Active Scanning
docs.text:
Active scanning sends additional requests designed to test application behaviour.

This can be more intrusive.

Before active scanning, confirm:

Scope
Authentication
Request rate
Application stability
State-changing risk
Testing window

docs.title: Scanner Validation Workflow
docs.text:
Do not do this:

Burp Scanner
     |
     v
Issue
     |
     v
Report

Do this:

Burp Scanner
     |
     v
Candidate
     |
     v
Read Issue Detail
     |
     v
Inspect Request/Response
     |
     v
Reproduce in Repeater
     |
     v
Validate Impact
     |
     v
Report

docs.title: Crawl and Audit
docs.text:
Burp Professional supports automated crawl and audit workflows.

Crawling helps discover:

  • pages;
  • routes;
  • forms;
  • APIs;
  • application states.

Auditing tests discovered attack surface.

Automated crawling may miss:

  • complex workflows;
  • multi-role functionality;
  • unusual JavaScript;
  • stateful business logic.

Manual mapping remains valuable.

docs.title: Burp Collaborator
docs.text:
Burp Collaborator supports out-of-band interaction testing.

It can help identify behaviour where the application communicates externally rather than returning direct evidence.

Examples may include:

  • blind SSRF;
  • blind XXE;
  • asynchronous interactions;
  • backend callbacks.

Conceptually:

Burp Request
    |
    v
Application
    |
    v
Outbound DNS / HTTP
    |
    v
Collaborator

Related notes:

Server Side Request Forgery

XML External Entity Injection

docs.title: Collaborator Correlation
docs.text:
An out-of-band event is useful only when it can be correlated with the request that caused it.

Retain:

Triggering request
Unique Collaborator address
Timestamp
Interaction protocol
Observed callback

This helps demonstrate causality.

docs.title: Interactsh as an Alternative
docs.text:
ProjectDiscovery Interactsh can provide similar out-of-band interaction functionality in appropriate workflows.

Related tool note:

Interactsh

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
Burp extensions expand functionality.

Extensions can be installed from:

Burp Suite BApp Store

Use extensions selectively.

Too many extensions can:

  • slow Burp;
  • generate noise;
  • modify traffic;
  • create duplicated findings;
  • complicate troubleshooting.

docs.text:

docs.text:

  • public reports.

docs.text:
Burp's search functionality is valuable on larger applications.

token
admin
password

api

docs.title: Highlighting and Comments
docs.text:
Burp allows requests to be highlighted and commented.

Example scheme:

Yellow -> needs review
Red    -> confirmed issue
Green  -> tested / no issue

Use any consistent system that works for the assessment.

docs.title: Organising Repeater Tabs
docs.text:
Large assessments can create many Repeater tabs.

Use meaningful tab names such as:

Login

Admin API
Password Reset
Upload
GraphQL
CORS

This makes workflows easier to resume and review.

docs.title: Request Naming
docs.text:
Good request organisation improves evidence quality.

Instead of:

Repeater 19
Repeater 20
Repeater 21

prefer:

IDOR - Baseline
IDOR - User B
IDOR - Modified Object

docs.title: Match and Replace
docs.text:
Burp supports Match and Replace rules for modifying traffic automatically.

Possible legitimate uses include:

  • adding a testing header;
  • modifying a User-Agent;
  • replacing a hostname;
  • adding custom environment markers.

Use these carefully because they affect many requests automatically.

docs.title: Proxy Rules
docs.text:
Proxy rules can control which traffic is intercepted or modified.

This can help reduce noise and avoid accidental third-party interaction.

docs.title: Upstream Proxies
docs.text:
Burp can be configured to send traffic through an upstream proxy when required by the environment.

This may be relevant for:

  • corporate proxy networks;
  • assessment jump hosts;
  • controlled network paths.

Document proxy configuration if it affects reproducibility.

docs.title: SOCKS Proxy
docs.text:
Burp can also be used with SOCKS proxying in applicable environments.

This can be useful when web applications are accessible through a controlled pivot or test network.

Ensure the network path itself is authorised.

docs.title: TLS Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If HTTPS traffic fails through Burp, check:

Browser trusts Burp CA?
Correct proxy listener?
Correct hostname?
TLS interception permitted?
Client certificate required?
Certificate pinning involved?

For normal web applications, the embedded Burp browser often avoids most setup problems.

docs.title: Client Certificates
docs.text:
Some applications require mutual TLS.

Burp supports client certificate configuration.

Where mTLS is in scope, ensure:

  • certificate is authorised;
  • private key is handled securely;
  • test identity is documented.

docs.title: Certificate Pinning
docs.text:
Mobile or thick-client applications may use certificate pinning.

This is a different testing problem from normal browser-based web applications.

Do not weaken production client security outside an authorised test environment.

docs.title: Logging Sensitive Data
docs.text:
Burp may capture:

  • passwords;
  • session tokens;
  • API keys;
  • personal information;
  • application secrets.

Assessment workspaces should therefore be protected appropriately.

Avoid unnecessary retention.

docs.title: Project Files
docs.text:
Burp Professional can use project files to retain assessment state.

Depending on workflow, retained state may include:

  • HTTP history;
  • site map;
  • Scanner data;
  • configuration.

Project files may contain sensitive information and should be protected accordingly.

docs.title: Temporary vs Project-Based Work
docs.text:
For quick labs:

Temporary project

may be sufficient.

For longer engagements:

Saved project

can help preserve testing state.

Consider organisational retention requirements.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Burp configuration can be exported and reused.

This can help standardise:

  • proxy settings;
  • extension configuration;
  • scope behaviour;
  • Scanner configuration.

Do not distribute configurations containing secrets.

docs.title: Testing Workflow
docs.text:
A mature Burp workflow may look like:

1. Confirm scope
       |
       v
2. Configure Burp project
       |
       v
3. Configure browser
       |
       v
4. Browse application normally
       |
       v
5. Build site map
       |
       v
6. Review HTTP history
       |
       v
7. Identify security-sensitive requests
       |
       v
8. Send candidates to Repeater
       |
       v
9. Establish baselines
       |
       v
10. Test one variable at a time
       |
       v
11. Use extensions/automation where appropriate
       |
       v
12. Validate findings manually
       |
       v
13. Capture reproducible evidence

docs.title: Representative Authorisation Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose a user requests:

GET /api/orders/1001 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
Cookie: session=user-a-session

The response returns User A's order.

Send the request to Repeater.

Change:

1001

to another authorised test object's identifier:

1002

Observe:

Status
Response body
Object owner
Sensitive fields

Then repeat using another authorised test account if needed.

The conclusion should be based on actual server-side authorisation behaviour.

docs.title: Representative CORS Scenario
docs.text:
Original request:

GET /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test

Test with:

Origin: https://example-attacker.test

Inspect the response headers.

Questions include:

Is the Origin reflected?

Are credentials permitted?

Is sensitive data returned?

Can a browser exploit the combination?

Do not report CORS merely because one permissive header exists.

docs.title: Representative Scanner Scenario
docs.text:
Burp Scanner reports a candidate issue.

Workflow:

Scanner Issue
     |
     v
Open Request
     |
     v
Send to Repeater
     |
     v
Reproduce
     |
     v
Determine Preconditions
     |
     v
Determine Impact
     |
     v
Capture Evidence

If manual reproduction fails, investigate:

  • authentication;
  • application state;
  • scanner assumption;
  • intermittent behaviour;
  • WAF;
  • false positive.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Burp-generated findings can be false positives because of:

  • generic error messages;
  • reflection without execution;
  • WAF responses;
  • soft 404s;
  • misleading headers;
  • ambiguous timing;
  • application state;
  • Scanner heuristics.

Manual validation is required.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Burp can also miss issues.

Possible causes include:

  • hidden functionality;
  • incomplete crawling;
  • business logic;
  • multiple user roles;
  • complex state;
  • WebSocket-only functionality;
  • unusual protocols;
  • client-side-only behaviour;
  • authentication barriers.

A clean Scanner result does not prove the application is secure.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Strong Burp evidence should usually include:

Target
Test account / role
Request
Response
Timestamp
Modified value
Expected behaviour
Observed behaviour
Manual validation
Impact

For screenshots, include only what helps the reader understand the issue.

Raw requests and responses are generally more useful than screenshots alone.

docs.title: Exporting Requests
docs.text:
Requests can be copied in several useful formats.

One common workflow is copying a request as a curl command for external reproduction.

Always review copied commands before sharing them because they may contain:

  • cookies;
  • bearer tokens;
  • API keys;
  • passwords.

Redact secrets where necessary.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
The finding should describe the vulnerability, not the Burp feature that discovered it.

Avoid:

Burp Scanner found an IDOR.

Prefer:

The application did not enforce server-side ownership checks when
accessing order objects. Changing the order identifier in an
authenticated request allowed one test account to retrieve an object
belonging to another authorised test account.

Burp is the testing mechanism.

The security condition is the finding.

docs.title: Burp Evidence Example
docs.text:
A useful evidence structure might be:

Request A:
User A requests /api/orders/1001

Result:
200 OK
User A object returned

Request B:
User A requests /api/orders/1002

Result:
200 OK
User B object returned

Control:
User A should not have access to User B object

Conclusion:
Server-side object-level authorisation was not enforced.

This is much stronger than:

Burp showed 200 OK.

docs.title: No Browser Traffic Appears
docs.text:
Check:

Proxy configured?
Correct listener?
Browser using Burp?
Scope filter hiding traffic?

Try the embedded Burp browser first.

docs.title: HTTPS Errors
docs.text:
Check:

Burp CA trusted?
Hostname correct?
TLS interception permitted?
Client certificate required?

docs.title: Repeater Request Behaves Differently
docs.text:
Possible causes include:

  • expired session;
  • CSRF token;
  • one-time token;
  • changing state;
  • missing browser-generated header;
  • anti-automation controls.

Compare the Repeater request with the original browser request.

docs.title: Authentication Keeps Expiring
docs.text:
Review:

  • session lifetime;
  • refresh tokens;
  • CSRF state;
  • authentication cookies;
  • token rotation.

For complicated workflows, Burp session-handling features may help.

docs.title: Scanner Produces Too Much Noise
docs.text:
Reduce scope.

Review:

  • crawl configuration;
  • audit configuration;
  • insertion points;
  • issue definitions.

Do not scan everything indiscriminately.

docs.title: Burp Becomes Slow
docs.text:
Possible causes include:

  • very large HTTP history;
  • too many extensions;
  • large responses;
  • Scanner activity;
  • insufficient system resources.

Disable unnecessary extensions and restrict scope.

docs.title: ffuf
docs.text:
ffuf is a fast web fuzzer commonly used for authorised web application discovery and content enumeration.

It is especially useful for:

  • directory discovery;
  • file discovery;
  • endpoint discovery;
  • virtual host discovery;
  • parameter-name discovery;
  • parameter-value testing;
  • extension discovery;
  • API path discovery;
  • replaying customised HTTP requests.

ffuf works by replacing a marker, usually:

FUZZ

with values from a wordlist.

A basic model is:

Target
  |
  v
Request Template
  |
  v
FUZZ Position
  |
  v
Wordlist
  |
  v
Requests
  |
  v
Response Analysis
  |
  v
Interesting Candidates

Authorised testing only

Use ffuf only against applications and infrastructure that are explicitly authorised for testing. High request rates can affect production systems, trigger rate limiting, create large log volumes, or cause service instability. Start conservatively and increase speed only where appropriate.

docs.title: Where ffuf Fits
docs.text:
ffuf usually sits after initial reconnaissance and before deeper manual validation.

Target Identified
      |
      v
Baseline Request
      |
      v
ffuf Discovery
      |
      v
Interesting Endpoint
      |
      v
Manual Validation
      |
      v
Burp / Browser Testing

Related notes:

Web Application Testing Tools

Web Enumeration Tools

Burp Suite

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
Official project:

ffuf - GitHub

Use the current official documentation and:

ffuf -h

to confirm exact options supported by the installed version.

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Check:

ffuf -V

or:

ffuf -h

depending on the installed release.

On Kali Linux, ffuf is commonly available through the package manager or may already be installed.

docs.title: Basic Concept
docs.text:
Suppose the target is:

https://example.test/FUZZ

and the wordlist contains:

admin
login
api
uploads

ffuf sends requests conceptually like:

https://example.test/admin
https://example.test/login
https://example.test/api
https://example.test/uploads

The task is then to distinguish meaningful responses from noise.

docs.title: Basic Directory Discovery
docs.text:
A common starting point is:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/FUZZ

This replaces:

FUZZ

with each word from the wordlist.

docs.title: Wordlists
docs.text:
Wordlist quality strongly affects discovery quality.

Useful categories include:

Common directories
Technology-specific paths
API endpoints
Administrative names
Backup filenames
Framework-specific locations

Do not rely on one giant wordlist for every application.

Targeted wordlists are often more effective.

docs.title: SecLists
docs.text:
SecLists is a widely used collection of security testing wordlists.

Official project:

SecLists - GitHub

Common categories include:

Discovery/Web-Content/
Fuzzing/
Usernames/
Passwords/

Use only wordlists appropriate to the authorised task.

docs.title: Start with a Baseline
docs.text:
Before fuzzing, understand how the application responds to:

Valid path
Invalid path
Trailing slash
Random filename

For example:

curl -i https://example.test/this-should-not-exist-834729

This helps identify:

  • normal 404 behaviour;
  • soft 404s;
  • redirects;
  • custom error pages;
  • wildcard routing.

Without a baseline, ffuf results can be misleading.

docs.title: Default 404 Pages
docs.text:
Default server error pages can sometimes help identify technology.

For visual comparison, see:

0xdf - Default 404 Pages

Do not rely on appearance alone.

Validate with headers, content, and other fingerprints.

docs.title: Soft 404s
docs.text:
A soft 404 occurs when a nonexistent resource returns something like:

200 OK

instead of:

404 Not Found

Example:

GET /totally-random-12345

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 4210

If every missing resource produces the same body, ffuf may report many false positives.

docs.title: Establish Random Baseline
docs.text:
Use a random path:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download}\n' https://example.test/random-834723984

Then compare ffuf results against that baseline.

docs.title: Status Code Filtering
docs.text:
ffuf can filter or match responses by HTTP status.

Because exact flags evolve, confirm current syntax using:

ffuf -h

Typical analysis categories include:

200
204
301
302
307
401
403
405
500

Interesting status does not automatically mean vulnerability.

docs.title: Response Size
docs.text:
Response size is one of the most useful ways to remove false positives.

If nonexistent paths consistently return:

Content-Length: 4242

then responses with that size may represent the custom error page.

Use ffuf response-size filtering according to the current help output.

docs.title: Word Count
docs.text:
Applications may return pages of similar byte length but different word counts.

Word count can therefore be useful when filtering repeated error templates.

docs.title: Line Count
docs.text:
Line count may also help distinguish:

Real page

from:

Standard error response

Use multiple response characteristics rather than relying on one field.

docs.title: Auto-Calibration
docs.text:
ffuf supports calibration features intended to help identify repetitive false-positive responses.

Consult:

ffuf -h

for the exact options supported by the installed version.

Calibration can be useful against:

  • wildcard routes;
  • virtual host defaults;
  • soft 404s.

Always inspect a sample manually.

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
ffuf can perform recursive discovery depending on configuration.

Conceptually:

/
 |
 +-- admin/
 |     |
 |     +-- users/
 |
 +-- api/
       |
       +-- v1/

Recursion can create significant request volume.

Use it carefully.

docs.title: Directory Discovery Workflow
docs.text:
A strong process is:

Baseline
   |
   v
Small Wordlist
   |
   v
Review Results
   |
   v
Technology-Specific Wordlist
   |
   v
Manual Validation

Avoid immediately using the largest possible list.

docs.title: File Discovery
docs.text:
ffuf can also discover filenames.

Example concept:

https://example.test/FUZZ

Wordlist:

config.php
backup.zip
robots.txt
sitemap.xml

Any discovered file should be reviewed according to scope and sensitivity.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
Applications may expose files under technology-specific extensions.

Examples:

.php
.aspx
.jsp
.json
.xml
.txt
.bak

Extension fuzzing should be based on observed technology.

Do not blindly test every extension.

docs.title: Extension Discovery Strategy
docs.text:
A useful process is:

Technology Fingerprint
       |
       v
Likely File Types
       |
       v
Targeted Extension Testing

For example, an ASP.NET application deserves different guesses from a PHP application.

docs.title: Multiple Extensions
docs.text:
Depending on the installed version, ffuf supports extension expansion.

Check exact syntax using:

ffuf -h

Keep the extension list focused.

docs.title: Trailing Slash Differences
docs.text:
These may behave differently:

/admin

and:

/admin/

Framework routing and reverse proxies may treat them differently.

Test both when results are ambiguous.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
A discovered path may return:

301
302
307
308

Follow-up questions include:

Where does it redirect?

Is destination in scope?

Does redirect reveal canonical path?

Is authentication involved?

Do not automatically follow redirects to third-party domains during automated testing.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Many interesting endpoints require authentication.

ffuf can send custom headers.

Example:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/FUZZ -H "Cookie: session=<REDACTED>"

Protect authentication material.

Do not save live session values in public notes or shell history unnecessarily.

docs.title: Authorization Header
docs.text:
For API testing:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/api/FUZZ -H "Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED>"

Ensure the token belongs to an approved test identity.

docs.title: Custom Headers
docs.text:
Custom headers may be necessary for:

  • authentication;
  • API versioning;
  • content negotiation;
  • virtual hosts;
  • application routing.

Example:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/FUZZ -H "Accept: application/json"

docs.title: User-Agent
docs.text:
Some environments behave differently based on User-Agent.

If necessary:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/FUZZ -H "User-Agent: authorised-security-test"

Only add custom identification if this aligns with the engagement.

docs.title: POST Requests
docs.text:
ffuf can fuzz request bodies.

Example:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/api/search -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query":"FUZZ"}'

This sends each wordlist value in the JSON field.

Use controlled values.

docs.title: Form Data
docs.text:
Example:

ffuf -w values.txt -u https://example.test/search -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" -d "q=FUZZ"

This can help test application behaviour around known input locations.

docs.title: Parameter Name Discovery
docs.text:
ffuf can be used to identify hidden parameter names.

Conceptually:

GET /endpoint?FUZZ=test

Wordlist:

debug
admin
redirect
callback
format

A discovered parameter is not automatically security relevant.

The next step is to understand what it controls.

docs.title: GET Parameter Example
docs.text:
ffuf -w parameters.txt -u 'https://example.test/page?FUZZ=test'

Compare responses for:

  • status;
  • size;
  • content;
  • headers;
  • timing.

docs.title: Parameter Value Testing
docs.text:
If a known parameter accepts a set of possible values:

ffuf -w values.txt -u 'https://example.test/page?mode=FUZZ'

This can reveal:

  • hidden modes;
  • alternate formats;
  • undocumented states.

Do not confuse functionality discovery with vulnerability confirmation.

docs.title: API Endpoint Discovery
docs.text:
ffuf is useful against API route structures.

Example:

ffuf -w api-endpoints.txt -u https://api.example.test/FUZZ

Potential findings may include:

/api/v1/users
/api/v1/admin
/api/v2
/swagger
/openapi.json

Manually validate all interesting responses.

docs.title: API Baseline
docs.text:
APIs may return identical JSON for unknown routes.

Example:

{
  "error": "Not found"
}

with:

HTTP 200

This is another soft-404 pattern.

Filter based on body characteristics.

docs.title: JSON Responses
docs.text:
Do not rely only on byte length.

Inspect:

  • response fields;
  • status;
  • error codes;
  • headers;
  • semantic differences.

A one-field difference may be important even when total size remains similar.

docs.title: Swagger and OpenAPI
docs.text:
Discovery may identify documentation paths such as:

/swagger
/swagger-ui
/openapi.json
/api-docs

These can help map the application attack surface.

API documentation exposure is not automatically a vulnerability.

Assess whether it exposes sensitive internal information or simply documents intended public APIs.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
A GraphQL application may expose endpoints such as:

/graphql
/api/graphql

ffuf can help discover likely locations.

GraphQL security assessment then requires GraphQL-specific methodology.

Related note:

GraphQL

docs.title: Virtual Host Discovery
docs.text:
Virtual host fuzzing attempts to identify additional hostnames served by the same IP or reverse proxy.

Conceptually:

Host: FUZZ.example.test

while sending requests to the same server.

docs.title: VHost Example
docs.text:
A typical pattern is:

ffuf -w subdomains.txt -u https://example.test/ -H "Host: FUZZ.example.test"

This assumes the target server and domain are authorised.

Use an appropriate baseline because wildcard virtual hosts can create false positives.

docs.title: VHost Baseline
docs.text:
First test a random hostname:

curl -k -i https://example.test/ -H "Host: random-does-not-exist.example.test"

Record:

  • status;
  • length;
  • title;
  • body;
  • redirect.

Then compare ffuf output.

docs.title: TLS and Virtual Hosts
docs.text:
HTTPS virtual host discovery can be complicated by:

  • SNI;
  • certificates;
  • reverse proxies;
  • load balancers.

The HTTP Host header and TLS SNI are related but separate concepts.

A request may reach one TLS virtual host and then supply a different HTTP host value.

Interpret results carefully.

docs.title: Wildcard Virtual Hosts
docs.text:
Some servers respond successfully for any hostname.

Example:

foo.example.test -> same page
bar.example.test -> same page
random123.example.test -> same page

This creates false positives.

Compare:

  • body size;
  • title;
  • headers;
  • TLS;
  • application behaviour.

docs.title: Host Header Testing
docs.text:
Virtual host discovery should not be confused with Host header vulnerability testing.

Discovery asks:

Which virtual hosts exist?

Host header security testing asks:

Does the application trust an attacker-controlled Host value in a
security-sensitive operation?

Related note:

Host Header Attacks

docs.title: Request Files
docs.text:
For complex requests, ffuf can work with request templates depending on the installed version and selected options.

This can be useful when reproducing requests from:

  • Burp Suite;
  • API clients;
  • browser traffic.

Check:

ffuf -h

for the exact request-file functionality available.

docs.title: Burp Suite Integration
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

Burp
  |
  v
Capture Valid Request
  |
  v
Identify Fuzz Position
  |
  v
ffuf
  |
  v
Interesting Responses
  |
  v
Burp Repeater

ffuf provides scale.

Burp provides manual validation.

docs.title: Proxying Through Burp
docs.text:
For selected debugging workflows, ffuf traffic can be routed through an HTTP proxy if the current version supports the relevant proxy option.

Use:

ffuf -h

to confirm exact syntax.

This can help inspect unusual requests manually.

Do not send large fuzzing campaigns through Burp unless necessary.

docs.title: Match vs Filter
docs.text:
ffuf generally provides two conceptual approaches:

Match interesting responses

or:

Filter known noise

Filtering known baseline responses is often more effective against custom error pages.

docs.title: Filtering Philosophy
docs.text:
Suppose all invalid pages return:

200
Size: 5301
Words: 842
Lines: 97

A useful approach is to filter that known response fingerprint.

Interesting results then stand out.

docs.title: Do Not Filter Too Aggressively
docs.text:
If you filter:

Size 5301

but a real endpoint happens to have the same size, it may disappear from results.

Use multiple observations and spot-check manually.

docs.title: Response Timing
docs.text:
Timing differences can sometimes indicate:

  • backend processing;
  • database interaction;
  • authentication logic;
  • rate limiting.

However, network timing is noisy.

Do not treat timing differences alone as proof of functionality or vulnerability.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
ffuf can generate requests very quickly.

This may trigger:

  • WAF;
  • rate limiting;
  • application throttling;
  • account controls;
  • infrastructure load.

Start conservatively.

docs.title: Threads / Concurrency
docs.text:
Higher concurrency means more simultaneous requests.

The correct setting depends on:

  • target stability;
  • network latency;
  • engagement rules;
  • WAF;
  • production sensitivity.

Do not maximise concurrency by default.

docs.title: Delay
docs.text:
Some versions support request delays or rate controls.

Use:

ffuf -h

for current syntax.

A lower request rate may be necessary against fragile systems.

docs.title: WAF Interaction
docs.text:
A WAF may begin blocking ffuf traffic after repeated requests.

Symptoms may include:

403 responses
429 responses
connection resets
challenge pages
same block page for every request

If this occurs, stop and understand the control.

Do not automatically attempt evasion.

docs.title: 429 Too Many Requests
docs.text:
A 429 response usually indicates rate limiting.

Treat this as an operational signal.

Reduce the request rate according to scope and engagement requirements.

Do not try to overwhelm the limit.

docs.title: 403 Responses
docs.text:
A 403 Forbidden result can still be interesting.

It may indicate:

Real endpoint exists
but
access denied

However, some WAFs also return 403 for generic invalid requests.

Compare against baseline.

docs.title: 401 Responses
docs.text:
A 401 Unauthorized response often indicates an authentication-protected resource.

Useful follow-up:

Which authentication mechanism?

Is the path expected?

Does current test account have access?

docs.title: 405 Responses
docs.text:
405 Method Not Allowed may indicate that the endpoint exists but does not accept the current HTTP method.

Manual testing with allowed methods may be appropriate.

Do not randomly submit state-changing methods.

docs.title: 500 Responses
docs.text:
A 500 Internal Server Error deserves review.

But:

500

does not automatically mean:

vulnerability

It may indicate:

  • invalid application input;
  • backend error;
  • WAF behaviour;
  • temporary instability.

Reproduce carefully.

docs.title: Wordlist Selection
docs.text:
Wordlists should reflect context.

For example:

Apache / PHP app

might justify different candidate paths from:

ASP.NET application

or:

REST API

Use reconnaissance to inform discovery.

docs.title: Technology-Guided Discovery
docs.text:
A good chain is:

WhatWeb / Wappalyzer
       |
       v
Technology Identified
       |
       v
Technology-Specific Wordlist
       |
       v
ffuf

Related tools:

WhatWeb

Wappalyzer

docs.title: JavaScript-Guided Discovery
docs.text:
JavaScript may reveal:

  • route names;
  • API versions;
  • endpoint fragments;
  • feature names.

These can be converted into a focused wordlist.

Related note:

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: robots.txt
docs.text:
Always review:

/robots.txt

before brute-force discovery.

It may disclose:

  • administrative paths;
  • staging content;
  • crawler exclusions.

A listed path is not automatically sensitive.

docs.title: sitemap.xml
docs.text:
Review:

/sitemap.xml

and related sitemap files.

These can provide intended application routes without fuzzing.

Use deterministic discovery before brute force where possible.

docs.title: Historical URLs
docs.text:
Historical application URLs can also provide valuable candidate paths.

Sources may include:

  • documentation;
  • archived application versions;
  • known route naming;
  • previous reconnaissance.

Only test the current authorised target.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Potential backup filenames may include variations such as:

config.bak
index.php.old
backup.zip
site.tar.gz

Discovery of backup files can expose sensitive data.

Do not download large archives unnecessarily.

First validate:

  • file exists;
  • size;
  • sensitivity;
  • scope.

docs.title: Source Control Files
docs.text:
Interesting locations may include:

.git/
.svn/

If exposed, they may disclose source or metadata.

Do not recursively download repository contents unless needed and authorised.

The exposure itself may already be demonstrable with minimal evidence.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Potentially sensitive files can include:

.env
web.config
application.properties
config.yml

Handle carefully.

If a response contains secrets:

  • stop unnecessary collection;
  • redact evidence;
  • follow disclosure procedures.

docs.title: Wordlist Mutation
docs.text:
Application-specific terms can improve discovery.

For example:

invoice
invoices
invoice-api
invoice_admin
invoice-v2

Generate focused mutations based on known naming conventions rather than massive blind lists.

docs.title: Case Sensitivity
docs.text:
Some servers treat:

/admin

and:

/Admin

differently.

This depends on:

  • operating system;
  • web server;
  • framework;
  • routing.

Only test variants where justified.

docs.title: URL Encoding
docs.text:
Applications may normalise encoded paths differently.

Do not broadly fuzz encoding tricks unless that is part of the specific testing objective.

For ordinary content discovery, use canonical paths first.

docs.title: Duplicate Routes
docs.text:
Different paths may map to the same application handler.

Example:

/login
/signin
/auth/login

Treat them as separate attack-surface entries initially, then consolidate if behaviour is identical.

docs.title: Endpoint Inventory
docs.text:
A useful ffuf result inventory may contain:

Path Status Size Notes /admin/ 403 1250 Review manually /api/ 200 431 JSON response /old/ 301 0 Redirect /health 200 82 Health endpoint

The table is only a triage view.

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text:
ffuf supports output files and several formats depending on the version.

Check:

ffuf -h

for current options.

Structured output is useful for:

  • automation;
  • deduplication;
  • reporting;
  • later analysis.

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text:
Where supported, JSON output is useful for scripting.

A processing workflow might be:

ffuf
  |
  v
JSON
  |
  v
jq / Python
  |
  v
Interesting Endpoint List

docs.title: jq
docs.text:
jq is useful for processing JSON results.

Example concept:

jq '.results[]' ffuf-results.json

The exact JSON structure should be inspected first.

docs.title: Python Processing
docs.text:
For larger assessments, Python can help:

  • merge results;
  • remove duplicates;
  • normalise URLs;
  • classify status codes;
  • produce reports.

Automation should not silently convert all results into findings.

docs.title: Deduplication
docs.text:
If ffuf discovers:

/admin
/admin/
/admin/index

they may represent the same underlying application area.

Keep raw discovery data, then consolidate during analysis.

docs.title: Multiple Hosts
docs.text:
For multiple targets, avoid blindly running the same aggressive wordlist against every system.

A better workflow is:

httpx inventory
      |
      v
Group by technology
      |
      v
Select wordlist
      |
      v
ffuf each target

Related tool:

httpx

docs.title: Per-Host Baselines
docs.text:
Each host may have different error behaviour.

Do not assume:

404 size on host A

matches:

404 size on host B

Calibrate each application separately.

docs.title: Virtual Hosting and CDN
docs.text:
A CDN or reverse proxy may cause many hostnames to return the same response.

This is particularly common during virtual host discovery.

Validate with:

  • body;
  • title;
  • cookies;
  • backend-specific headers;
  • TLS;
  • application behaviour.

docs.title: Reverse Proxies
docs.text:
Reverse proxies may rewrite:

  • paths;
  • status codes;
  • redirects;
  • Host headers.

This can make content discovery results look inconsistent.

Understand architecture where possible.

docs.title: Authentication State
docs.text:
Discovery results can differ significantly between:

Unauthenticated user
Normal user
Administrator

Run separate discovery only where authorised and useful.

Label the session context in evidence.

docs.title: Role-Aware Discovery
docs.text:
Example:

Normal User
     |
     v
/admin -> 403

Administrator
     |
     v
/admin -> 200

This may simply reflect correct access control.

It is useful attack-surface information, not necessarily a vulnerability.

docs.title: Session Expiry
docs.text:
Long ffuf runs may outlive an authenticated session.

Symptoms include many sudden:

302 -> /login

or:

401

responses.

Confirm the session is still valid before interpreting results.

docs.title: CSRF-Protected Requests
docs.text:
Some POST endpoints require dynamic CSRF tokens.

ffuf is less convenient when every request requires a fresh token.

In such cases:

  • Burp extensions;
  • custom scripts;
  • application-specific tooling;

may be more appropriate.

Choose the right tool.

docs.title: Stateful Workflows
docs.text:
ffuf works best when requests are relatively independent.

Complex workflows such as:

Create object
Get token
Submit step 2
Approve step 3

usually require custom automation or manual testing.

Do not force ffuf into workflows it does not fit well.

docs.title: Content Discovery vs Vulnerability Testing
docs.text:
Keep these stages separate.

ffuf discovers:
 /admin

This means:

Interesting endpoint identified

not:

Access control vulnerability

The next stage determines whether security controls work correctly.

docs.title: Practical Directory Discovery Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose the baseline invalid response is:

Status:
200

Size:
4137

Title:
Page Not Found

Run discovery:

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/FUZZ

Then filter the known baseline response using the appropriate current ffuf option.

Interesting result:

admin
Status: 403
Size: 729

Now manually validate:

curl -i https://example.test/admin

Interpretation:

The /admin path appears to exist but access is forbidden to the current
request context.

Do not report a vulnerability yet.

docs.title: Practical API Scenario
docs.text:
Target:

https://example.test/api/FUZZ

Run:

ffuf -w api.txt -u https://example.test/api/FUZZ -H "Accept: application/json"

Possible result:

users     [Status: 401]
health    [Status: 200]
v1        [Status: 200]
internal  [Status: 403]

Next steps:

  • inspect each response manually;
  • understand authentication;
  • determine whether endpoint exposure is intended.

docs.title: Practical Parameter Scenario
docs.text:
Known endpoint:

https://example.test/report

Test parameter names:

ffuf -w parameters.txt -u 'https://example.test/report?FUZZ=test'

Suppose:

format

changes the response.

Next:

Determine accepted values
Understand server-side behaviour
Validate whether it creates a security-relevant path

docs.title: Practical Virtual Host Scenario
docs.text:
Known server:

10.20.30.40

Known domain:

example.test

Before fuzzing, establish wildcard behaviour using a random host value.

Then use an authorised vhost wordlist against the same target.

If:

admin.example.test

returns a clearly different application response, validate it manually and add it to the authorised inventory if the scope definition includes such subdomains.

docs.title: Practical Authenticated Scenario
docs.text:
Capture a test-account session.

Run a focused endpoint list using the approved authentication header.

Then repeat only where necessary under another approved role.

Compare:

Path
Status
Response
Role

This can identify role-specific attack surface.

Do not use ffuf as a substitute for detailed authorisation testing.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Common causes include:

  • soft 404s;
  • wildcard routes;
  • WAF block pages;
  • CDN defaults;
  • redirects;
  • authentication expiry;
  • application catch-all routing;
  • wildcard virtual hosts.

Always establish baseline behaviour.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
ffuf may miss resources because of:

  • poor wordlists;
  • case sensitivity;
  • alternate extensions;
  • authenticated-only routes;
  • dynamic routing;
  • JavaScript-generated paths;
  • required headers;
  • required HTTP methods;
  • stateful workflows.

A clean ffuf result does not prove no hidden content exists.

docs.title: Troubleshooting No Results
docs.text:
Check:

Correct URL?
FUZZ marker present?
DNS works?
TLS issue?
Proxy issue?
Wordlist valid?
Application reachable?
Filtering too aggressive?

Test one known value manually.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Too Many Results
docs.text:
Common causes:

Soft 404
Wildcard routing
Generic 200 response
WAF block page

Use random baseline requests and compare:

  • status;
  • size;
  • words;
  • lines;
  • body.

docs.title: TLS Errors
docs.text:
In authorised lab environments, certificate issues may arise from:

  • self-signed certificates;
  • internal PKI;
  • test domains.

Use ffuf's current TLS-related options only when appropriate and verify syntax via:

ffuf -h

Do not disable certificate verification by default without understanding why.

docs.title: DNS Problems
docs.text:
Confirm:

dig example.test

or:

nslookup example.test

If using a lab-only domain, ensure the host resolves through:

  • DNS;
  • authorised hosts-file configuration.

docs.title: Proxy Problems
docs.text:
If using a proxy:

  • confirm proxy address;
  • confirm TLS handling;
  • confirm target reachability;
  • verify the proxy is not changing responses.

Compare one request directly and through the proxy.

docs.title: Request Reproducibility
docs.text:
For an interesting result, preserve a simple reproducible request.

Example:

curl -i https://example.test/admin

This is easier to include in evidence than relying solely on ffuf output.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For significant discoveries, retain:

Target:
Wordlist:
ffuf version:
Command:
Authentication context:
Baseline response:
Interesting path:
Status:
Response characteristics:
Timestamp:
Manual validation:

Do not retain unnecessary live credentials.

docs.title: Evidence Example
docs.text:
Target:
https://example.test/

Current context:
Unauthenticated

Discovery:
ffuf content enumeration

Candidate:
/internal/

Response:
HTTP 403

Manual validation:
Direct GET reproduced the 403 response.

Conclusion:
The path appears to exist but access was denied to the unauthenticated
request context.

This is defensible and does not overstate the result.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
ffuf is usually a discovery tool rather than the root cause of a finding.

Avoid:

ffuf found a vulnerability.

Prefer:

Content discovery identified an unauthenticated administrative endpoint
that exposed sensitive application configuration without requiring
authentication.

The vulnerability is the exposed behaviour.

docs.title: Reporting Hidden Endpoint Exposure
docs.text:
If an undocumented endpoint is discovered but securely protected:

No vulnerability may exist.

Hidden is not equivalent to secure or insecure.

Evaluate actual access controls and information exposure.

docs.title: Reporting Sensitive File Exposure
docs.text:
If ffuf discovers a readable configuration backup:

The application exposed a backup configuration file beneath the public
web root. The file was retrievable without authentication and contained
sensitive deployment information.

The issue is the exposed file.

docs.title: Reporting Directory Listing
docs.text:
If a discovered directory exposes file indexes:

Directory indexing was enabled on the affected path, allowing
unauthenticated users to enumerate files stored within the directory.

Again, the finding describes server behaviour.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Remediation depends on the actual discovered condition.

Potential controls include:

  • remove obsolete files;
  • move sensitive files outside web root;
  • disable directory listing;
  • enforce authentication;
  • enforce authorisation;
  • remove backup artefacts;
  • disable unused endpoints;
  • configure reverse proxy routing correctly.

Do not recommend:

Block ffuf

as the primary remediation.

docs.title: Detection Considerations
docs.text:
High-volume content discovery may be visible through:

  • web server logs;
  • WAF;
  • reverse proxy;
  • IDS;
  • SIEM.

Patterns may include:

Large number of unique paths
Short time window
Same source IP
Repeated 404/403 responses

This can be useful during purple-team exercises.

docs.title: Purple Teaming
docs.text:
A controlled ffuf exercise can validate web discovery detection.

Approved ffuf Run
      |
      v
Web / WAF Logs
      |
      v
SIEM
      |
      v
Detection Review

Use a controlled wordlist and agreed request rate.

Related note:

Purple Teaming

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
Before starting a larger run ask:

Is this production?

What rate is acceptable?

Could requests trigger expensive backend operations?

Could authentication attempts lock accounts?

Does the wordlist contain destructive route names?

Discovery should minimise application state changes.

docs.title: Avoid State-Changing Paths
docs.text:
A GET request should ideally be safe, but poorly designed applications may expose state-changing behaviour over GET.

If unusual effects are observed:

Stop
Document
Validate manually

Do not continue brute forcing blindly.

docs.title: Destructive Endpoint Risk
docs.text:
Avoid automatically sending methods such as:

DELETE
PUT
PATCH

across unknown paths.

Use passive or read-only discovery first.

docs.title: Large Wordlists
docs.text:
Very large wordlists can:

  • consume hours;
  • create excessive traffic;
  • increase log noise;
  • provide diminishing returns.

Use staged discovery.

docs.title: Staged Discovery
docs.text:
A strong model is:

Small Common List
      |
      v
Interesting Results
      |
      v
Technology-Specific List
      |
      v
Application-Specific Mutations

This usually produces better value than blindly using millions of entries.

docs.title: Tool Chaining
docs.text:
ffuf works well with other web tools.

Example:

httpx
  |
  v
Alive Host
  |
  v
WhatWeb / Wappalyzer
  |
  v
Technology
  |
  v
ffuf
  |
  v
Endpoint
  |
  v
Burp Suite

docs.title: ffuf and Katana
docs.text:
Katana discovers links through crawling.

ffuf discovers candidate paths through wordlists.

Katana
  |
  +-- linked/discovered routes

ffuf
  |
  +-- guessed/unlinked routes

Together they improve attack-surface coverage.

Related tool:

Katana

docs.title: ffuf and Nuclei
docs.text:
A useful order is:

ffuf
  |
  v
Interesting Endpoint
  |
  v
Manual Validation
  |
  v
Nuclei where appropriate

Do not automatically send broad template sets to every discovered path.

Related tool:

Nuclei

docs.title: ffuf and sqlmap
docs.text:
If manual testing identifies a plausible SQL injection candidate:

ffuf discovers endpoint
      |
      v
Burp identifies parameter
      |
      v
Manual SQLi validation
      |
      v
sqlmap where authorised

Related tool:

sqlmap

docs.title: ffuf and Interactsh
docs.text:
ffuf itself does not require out-of-band testing for normal discovery.

However, endpoints found by ffuf may later expose functionality involving:

  • callbacks;
  • webhooks;
  • URL fetchers.

Interactsh can then support controlled OOB validation.

Related tool:

Interactsh

docs.title: Basic Discovery
docs.text: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/FUZZ

docs.title: API Discovery
docs.text: ffuf -w api.txt -u https://example.test/api/FUZZ -H "Accept: application/json"

docs.title: Authenticated Discovery
docs.text: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/FUZZ -H "Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED>"

docs.title: Cookie-Based Session
docs.text: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.test/FUZZ -H "Cookie: session=<REDACTED>"

docs.title: Parameter Name Discovery
docs.text: ffuf -w parameters.txt -u 'https://example.test/page?FUZZ=test'

docs.title: Parameter Value Testing
docs.text: ffuf -w values.txt -u 'https://example.test/page?mode=FUZZ'

docs.title: POST JSON
docs.text: ffuf -w values.txt -u https://example.test/api/search -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query":"FUZZ"}'

docs.title: VHost Discovery
docs.text: ffuf -w subdomains.txt -u https://example.test/ -H "Host: FUZZ.example.test"

docs.title: Version / Help
docs.text: ffuf -h

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Target explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Scope confirmed.
  • [ ] Wordlist appropriate.
  • [ ] Baseline response understood.
  • [ ] Random nonexistent path tested.
  • [ ] Authentication context documented.
  • [ ] Rate appropriate for environment.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• [ ] Directory paths reviewed.
  • [ ] Files reviewed where relevant.
  • [ ] Extensions selected based on technology.
  • [ ] API routes considered.
  • [ ] robots.txt reviewed.
  • [ ] sitemap.xml reviewed.
  • [ ] JavaScript-derived routes considered.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
• [ ] Soft 404 checked.
  • [ ] Status baseline checked.
  • [ ] Response size baseline checked.
  • [ ] Word/line differences considered.
  • [ ] WAF block response identified.
  • [ ] Filtering not overly aggressive.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• [ ] Approved test account used.
  • [ ] Session still valid.
  • [ ] Secrets redacted.
  • [ ] Different roles kept separate.
  • [ ] Account lockout risk avoided.

docs.title: Virtual Hosts
docs.text:
• [ ] Base domain authorised.
  • [ ] Random vhost baseline tested.
  • [ ] Wildcard behaviour checked.
  • [ ] TLS/SNI context considered.
  • [ ] New host manually validated.
  • [ ] Scope confirmed before deeper testing.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
• [ ] Concurrency appropriate.
  • [ ] Rate limits respected.
  • [ ] No destructive methods sprayed.
  • [ ] Unexpected state changes trigger stop.
  • [ ] Large downloads avoided.
  • [ ] Third-party redirects not automatically tested.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Interesting endpoints reproduced manually.
  • [ ] Burp/curl used for validation.
  • [ ] Hidden endpoint not automatically called vulnerable.
  • [ ] 403/401 interpreted correctly.
  • [ ] 500 errors investigated carefully.
  • [ ] Actual security impact established separately.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] ffuf version retained.
  • [ ] Command retained.
  • [ ] Wordlist recorded.
  • [ ] Baseline recorded.
  • [ ] Candidate path recorded.
  • [ ] Authentication context recorded.
  • [ ] Manual validation retained.
  • [ ] Sensitive information redacted.
