docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use ffuf like this:

Run Huge Wordlist
      |
      v
See 200 / 403 / 500
      |
      v
Call Everything Interesting a Finding

Use it like this:

Understand Target
      |
      v
Establish Invalid-Path Baseline
      |
      v
Choose Focused Wordlist
      |
      v
Run Controlled ffuf Discovery
      |
      v
Filter Known Noise
      |
      v
Identify Interesting Difference
      |
      v
Reproduce Manually
      |
      v
Understand Endpoint Purpose
      |
      v
Test Authentication / Authorisation Where Relevant
      |
      v
Determine Actual Security Impact
      |
      v
Capture Evidence

ffuf is most valuable when it helps discover attack surface that normal navigation, crawling, or documentation did not reveal.

The tool identifies candidate resources.

The tester determines whether those resources create a real security issue.

docs.title: Interactsh
docs.text:
Interactsh is an out-of-band interaction service from ProjectDiscovery that helps detect server-side activity which does not produce a visible response in the application.

It is especially useful for testing conditions where a target may cause an external interaction such as:

  • DNS resolution;
  • HTTP callback;
  • blind SSRF;
  • blind XXE;
  • blind command execution indicators;
  • callback-based template behavior;
  • asynchronous backend requests;
  • external fetch behavior.

Interactsh gives the tester a unique callback domain and records interactions that reach the service.

A simplified model is:

Tester
  |
  v
Unique Interactsh Domain
  |
  v
Target Receives Input
  |
  v
Target Makes External Request
  |
  v
Interactsh Records Interaction

Authorised testing only

Use Interactsh only for explicitly authorised testing. Out-of-band payloads cause target systems or backend services to initiate external network activity. Confirm that external callbacks are permitted by the engagement and that the destination is approved before use.

docs.title: Where Interactsh Fits
docs.text:
Interactsh is most useful when direct response-based validation is difficult.

A common workflow is:

Security Hypothesis
      |
      v
Inject Unique Callback Value
      |
      v
Target Processes Input
      |
      v
External Interaction
      |
      v
Interactsh
      |
      v
Correlate
      |
      v
Manual Validation

Related tools:

Web Application Testing Tools

Burp Suite

Nuclei

Katana

ffuf

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
Official project:

Interactsh - GitHub

Official documentation:

Interactsh Documentation

Because Interactsh evolves over time, confirm current syntax with the installed client:

interactsh-client -h

docs.title: What Out-of-Band Means
docs.text:
An out-of-band, or OOB, test relies on an interaction that occurs outside the original HTTP response.

For example:

Original Request
      |
      v
Application
      |
      v
No Visible Difference

but internally:

Application
      |
      v
Backend Server
      |
      v
DNS / HTTP Request
      |
      v
Interactsh

The callback becomes supporting evidence that some component processed the supplied external destination.

docs.title: Why OOB Testing Is Useful
docs.text:
Some vulnerabilities are difficult to verify through the normal application response.

Examples include:

  • blind SSRF;
  • blind XXE;
  • asynchronous URL fetchers;
  • background processing;
  • server-side callbacks.

In these cases:

No application response difference

does not necessarily mean:

No server-side behavior

docs.title: Basic Interactsh Client Workflow
docs.text:
Start the client:

interactsh-client

The client typically generates a unique interaction domain.

Conceptually:

abc123.example-interact-domain

Use the generated value only within authorised tests.

docs.title: Unique Correlation Values
docs.text:
Each test should ideally use a unique identifier.

For example:

ssrf-profile-01.<interactsh-domain>

or:

import-test-02.<interactsh-domain>

This improves correlation when several tests are running.

docs.title: Why Unique Values Matter
docs.text:
Suppose you test:

/avatar
/webhook
/import

with the same callback hostname.

One interaction appears.

You may not know which feature caused it.

Instead:

avatar-01.<domain>
webhook-01.<domain>
import-01.<domain>

provides clearer evidence.

docs.title: DNS Interactions
docs.text:
A DNS interaction means that some system attempted to resolve the supplied hostname.

Conceptually:

Application Input
      |
      v
Backend
      |
      v
DNS Resolver
      |
      v
Interactsh

This proves name resolution occurred.

It does not automatically prove that an HTTP request followed.

docs.title: HTTP Interactions
docs.text:
An HTTP interaction provides stronger evidence that a component made a web request to the supplied destination.

Potential evidence may include:

  • timestamp;
  • source IP;
  • method;
  • path;
  • headers.

Interpret this carefully because the observed source may be a proxy, NAT gateway, or security product rather than the application host itself.

docs.title: DNS vs HTTP Evidence
docs.text:
A useful distinction is:

DNS callback
  ->
Name was resolved

HTTP callback
  ->
Web request reached interaction server

Do not report them as equivalent.

docs.title: SMTP and Other Protocols
docs.text:
Interactsh may support additional protocol interaction types depending on its current capabilities and deployment.

Use:

interactsh-client -h

and current ProjectDiscovery documentation for exact protocol support.

docs.title: Blind SSRF
docs.text:
Interactsh is commonly used to validate blind server-side request forgery.

Related note:

Server Side Request Forgery

A simplified flow is:

User-Controlled URL
      |
      v
Server-Side Fetcher
      |
      v
Interactsh URL
      |
      v
Observed Callback

docs.title: Blind SSRF Example
docs.text:
Suppose the application accepts:

POST /api/avatar

with:

{
  "url": "https://example.test/image.png"
}

A controlled OOB test may replace the URL with a unique Interactsh value.

If an external callback appears, that indicates the backend attempted to interact with the supplied destination.

The next question is:

Which component caused the interaction, and what control does the user have over it?

docs.title: SSRF Is More Than a Callback
docs.text:
A callback alone does not establish the full impact.

Consider:

Can host be controlled?

Can scheme be controlled?

Can port be controlled?

Are redirects followed?

Can internal destinations be reached?

Does DNS rebinding matter?

Are private ranges blocked?

Is response content returned?

OOB interaction confirms server-side behavior.

It does not automatically confirm internal-network access.

docs.title: Blind XXE
docs.text:
Out-of-band interaction can also support XML external entity testing where the XML parser causes an external lookup.

Related note:

XML External Entity Injection

The conceptual flow is:

XML Input
   |
   v
Parser
   |
   v
External Entity Resolution
   |
   v
Interactsh

docs.title: XXE Callback Interpretation
docs.text:
A DNS or HTTP interaction may indicate that external entity resolution occurred.

However, verify:

  • parser behavior;
  • XML location;
  • timing;
  • unique correlation value.

Do not attribute a callback to XXE unless the test input and timing support that conclusion.

docs.title: Blind Command Execution Indicators
docs.text:
In some authorised research scenarios, a callback may be used as a minimal indicator that command execution or template evaluation occurred.

The same caution applies:

Callback
  !=
Automatic proof of arbitrary command execution

The exact source of the interaction must be established.

docs.title: Template Injection
docs.text:
Some server-side template injection scenarios may allow external network interaction.

Related note:

Server-Side Template Injection

A callback can support a hypothesis, but the template engine and execution context should still be validated.

docs.title: Asynchronous Processing
docs.text:
Applications may process input later.

Examples include:

  • background queues;
  • scheduled jobs;
  • document processors;
  • email workers;
  • import pipelines.

A callback may arrive:

seconds
minutes
or longer

after the original request.

Keep timestamps.

docs.title: Timing Correlation
docs.text:
A useful evidence table is:

Event Timestamp Test request sent 14:05:10 DNS callback received 14:05:11 HTTP callback received 14:05:11

This creates a strong temporal correlation.

docs.title: Delayed Interaction
docs.text:
If a callback appears much later, do not automatically assume it belongs to the most recent request.

Use unique identifiers.

docs.title: Security Scanners
docs.text:
A callback may be generated by:

  • email scanner;
  • URL reputation scanner;
  • proxy;
  • WAF;
  • security sandbox;
  • link preview service.

This is a major source of false attribution.

docs.title: Scanner-Induced Callbacks
docs.text:
Suppose you submit:

https://unique-id.<interactsh-domain>

to an application.

An organisation's security gateway may inspect the URL and request it before the application ever processes it.

Therefore:

Callback

does not always mean:

Target application fetched the URL

docs.title: How to Distinguish Security Scanners
docs.text:
Look at:

  • source IP;
  • User-Agent;
  • headers;
  • timing;
  • repeated access;
  • protocol.

A corporate security scanner may have very different characteristics from the application backend.

docs.title: Source IP Is Not Always Backend IP
docs.text:
Outbound traffic may pass through:

  • NAT;
  • egress proxy;
  • cloud gateway;
  • service mesh.

Therefore the observed IP may represent infrastructure rather than the exact application server.

docs.title: Header Analysis
docs.text:
HTTP callbacks may reveal headers such as:

User-Agent
Accept
Host
Custom application headers

These can help identify the requesting component.

Do not rely on one header alone.

docs.title: Custom Paths
docs.text:
Use unique paths where possible.

Example:

https://<interactsh-domain>/avatar-test-01

This can improve correlation.

docs.title: Unique Query Values
docs.text:
Another option is:

https://<interactsh-domain>/?case=avatar-01

The exact callback format should match the tested application's accepted URL syntax.

docs.title: Multiple Variables
docs.text:
If a request contains several URL-like parameters, test them one at a time.

Example:

{
  "avatar": "URL1",
  "callback": "URL2"
}

Do not modify both simultaneously if you want clear attribution.

docs.title: One Variable at a Time
docs.text:
A good testing principle is:

Baseline
  |
  v
Change One Input
  |
  v
Observe

This improves evidence quality.

docs.title: Burp Suite Integration
docs.text:
Burp Repeater is ideal for controlled OOB testing.

Workflow:

Burp Proxy
   |
   v
Capture Valid Request
   |
   v
Repeater
   |
   v
Replace One Value with Unique Interactsh URL
   |
   v
Send
   |
   v
Observe Callback

Related tool:

Burp Suite

docs.title: Burp Collaborator vs Interactsh
docs.text:
Burp Suite Professional includes Burp Collaborator functionality for OOB testing.

Interactsh provides a separate OOB interaction platform.

Conceptually:

Burp Collaborator
        |
        +-- integrated with Burp Pro

Interactsh
        |
        +-- independent ProjectDiscovery workflow

Use whichever platform is approved and fits the workflow.

docs.title: Burp Community
docs.text:
Burp Community Edition does not provide the same integrated Collaborator workflow as Burp Professional.

Interactsh can therefore be useful in environments where a standalone OOB service is preferred.

docs.title: Nuclei Integration
docs.text:
Nuclei can use OOB interactions in relevant templates.

A simplified workflow is:

Nuclei
  |
  v
OOB Template
  |
  v
Target
  |
  v
Interactsh
  |
  v
Matched Interaction

Related tool:

Nuclei

docs.title: Nuclei OOB Results
docs.text:
A Nuclei match may combine:

  • request logic;
  • Interactsh callback;
  • template matchers.

Always inspect the template.

Do not report the template ID without understanding the underlying behavior.

docs.title: Manual Reproduction After Nuclei
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

Nuclei OOB Match
      |
      v
Read Template
      |
      v
Reproduce in Burp
      |
      v
Use New Unique Interactsh Value
      |
      v
Observe Callback

This produces better evidence.

docs.title: ffuf Integration
docs.text:
ffuf may discover functionality such as:

/webhook
/import
/fetch
/preview
/callback

These endpoints may later deserve OOB testing.

Related tool:

ffuf

docs.title: Katana Integration
docs.text:
Katana may discover parameters or routes through JavaScript.

Example:

POST /api/import
parameter: sourceUrl

That creates a potential OOB testing hypothesis.

Related tool:

Katana

docs.title: Webhook Features
docs.text:
Webhooks intentionally make outbound requests.

Therefore:

Webhook causes callback

is not a vulnerability.

The security questions may instead include:

Can destination be arbitrary?

Are private network destinations blocked?

Is authentication applied?

Can headers be controlled?

Can sensitive responses be exposed?

docs.title: URL Preview Features
docs.text:
Applications may fetch URLs to generate:

  • previews;
  • screenshots;
  • metadata;
  • thumbnails.

A callback may simply confirm intended fetch behavior.

The vulnerability depends on missing destination restrictions or other impact.

docs.title: Image Fetchers
docs.text:
Features that accept:

image URL

may intentionally retrieve external content.

The security question is whether the fetcher can be abused beyond the intended trust boundary.

docs.title: PDF Generators
docs.text:
Some PDF or document generation systems fetch:

  • images;
  • CSS;
  • external assets.

OOB testing may reveal these network interactions.

Do not assume the behavior is vulnerable.

docs.title: Import-From-URL Features
docs.text:
An import feature may legitimately retrieve external content.

Test:

Allowed schemes
Allowed hosts
Internal ranges
Redirect handling
Authentication

The callback only confirms outbound behavior.

docs.title: Callback Parameters
docs.text:
Applications may accept explicit callback URLs.

This may be intended.

Assess:

  • authorization;
  • validation;
  • destination restrictions;
  • sensitive data included in callbacks.

docs.title: Open Redirect vs SSRF
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

Browser redirect

with:

Server-side request

If the user's browser navigates to Interactsh, that is not SSRF.

The request must originate from a server-side component.

docs.title: Distinguishing Client-Side Requests
docs.text:
A callback might come from:

  • browser;
  • mobile application;
  • server.

Use:

  • source IP;
  • headers;
  • timing;
  • browser network logs.

to determine the likely origin.

docs.title: Browser Callback
docs.text:
If you click a supplied Interactsh URL manually:

your browser

will generate an interaction.

This is expected and should not be confused with application behavior.

docs.title: DNS Prefetch
docs.text:
Browsers and security tools may perform DNS prefetching.

A DNS lookup alone therefore needs careful interpretation in browser-driven workflows.

docs.title: Email Workflows
docs.text:
Links embedded in:

  • support requests;
  • email notifications;
  • password-reset messages;

may be visited by email-security scanners.

This can create OOB interactions unrelated to the target application's backend logic.

docs.title: Metadata Scanners
docs.text:
Some systems automatically inspect URLs to generate:

  • previews;
  • reputation;
  • anti-malware verdicts.

These can produce false attribution.

docs.title: Interaction Correlation
docs.text:
For every callback retain:

Unique payload ID
Original request timestamp
Interaction timestamp
Protocol
Source IP
Headers where available
Application endpoint
Parameter

This allows later analysis.

docs.title: Correlation Example
docs.text:
Test:
avatar-04

Application endpoint:
/api/avatar

Parameter:
url

Request time:
14:10:05

Interaction:
HTTP

Interaction time:
14:10:06

Path:
/avatar-04

This is stronger than:

Interactsh got a hit.

docs.title: Use Separate Identifiers Per Attempt
docs.text:
If retrying a test:

avatar-01
avatar-02
avatar-03

is better than reusing:

avatar

This prevents stale callbacks from creating confusion.

docs.title: DNS Caching
docs.text:
DNS caching can affect repeated tests.

A previously resolved hostname may not generate another DNS request immediately.

Unique hostnames reduce this problem.

docs.title: HTTP Caching
docs.text:
Proxies or application caches may also suppress repeated HTTP fetches.

Unique paths and hostnames can improve repeatability.

docs.title: Redirect Testing
docs.text:
A target may:

fetch initial URL

and then follow redirects.

A controlled test can distinguish:

direct fetch

from:

redirect-following behavior

Do not involve unauthorized internal or third-party targets.

docs.title: Redirects and SSRF
docs.text:
Redirect behavior matters because an application may validate:

initial URL

but not:

redirect destination

This can create a security issue.

Use only controlled authorised destinations during validation.

docs.title: Scheme Handling
docs.text:
Applications may support:

http
https

and potentially other URL schemes.

Do not spray unusual schemes without a specific testing objective.

Focus on the behavior relevant to the feature.

docs.title: Port Handling
docs.text:
A URL fetcher may allow custom ports.

A callback to a controlled external service can help determine whether the port is honored.

Do not use OOB testing to probe third-party or internal ports unless that scope is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Internal Network Access
docs.text:
One of the major SSRF impact questions is whether the server can reach private resources.

However, Interactsh is generally an external service.

It proves:

outbound interaction

not necessarily:

private network reachability

Additional internal validation must remain within scope.

docs.title: Cloud Metadata
docs.text:
Do not automatically test cloud metadata endpoints merely because SSRF is suspected.

Cloud metadata access can expose sensitive credentials.

Use lower-impact validation first and only test metadata services when explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Response Disclosure
docs.text:
Blind SSRF:

server makes request
but
response not returned

Non-blind SSRF may return:

fetched response

The security impact can differ significantly.

docs.title: Egress Filtering
docs.text:
An absent callback may mean:

No vulnerability

or:

Egress blocked

or:

DNS blocked

or:

Application did not process request

Do not interpret silence as definitive proof.

docs.title: Proxy Requirements
docs.text:
A backend service may require an outbound proxy.

If the application cannot reach Interactsh directly, a callback may not occur even though server-side URL handling exists.

docs.title: DNS Restrictions
docs.text:
Enterprise DNS controls may block interaction domains.

Again:

No callback

does not automatically equal:

No SSRF

docs.title: Asynchronous Queues
docs.text:
A backend job might process the URL later.

Wait long enough to match the application's known processing behavior.

Use unique IDs to avoid ambiguity.

docs.title: Repeated Callbacks
docs.text:
A single injected URL may produce multiple interactions because of:

  • DNS lookup;
  • HTTP request;
  • redirect;
  • retries;
  • scanners.

Do not count each callback as a separate vulnerability.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
An application may retry failed outbound requests.

Example:

14:10:01 HTTP
14:10:06 HTTP
14:10:16 HTTP

This may represent one application action with retry behavior.

docs.title: Resolver Behavior
docs.text:
A DNS callback may originate from a recursive resolver rather than the target host.

This is normal.

The resolver proves that some system attempted to resolve the name.

docs.title: Public Interactsh Infrastructure
docs.text:
Public interaction infrastructure is convenient, but organisational policy may prohibit sending target callbacks to public third-party services.

In that case, use an approved self-hosted or internal OOB service.

docs.title: Self-Hosting
docs.text:
Interactsh can be self-hosted.

This may be useful when:

  • data sensitivity is high;
  • public OOB services are not approved;
  • internal network testing requires controlled infrastructure;
  • callback logs must remain under organisational control.

Use current official documentation for deployment details.

docs.title: Self-Hosted Architecture
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Authorised Target
      |
      v
Controlled DNS / HTTP OOB Infrastructure
      |
      v
Researcher

The infrastructure becomes part of the engagement and must be secured.

docs.title: Domain Control
docs.text:
Self-hosted OOB infrastructure normally requires control over:

  • DNS;
  • domain records;
  • server;
  • listener ports.

Protect these assets like other red team infrastructure.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
HTTPS callbacks may require valid TLS depending on the target client.

Use controlled certificates where required.

The exact TLS deployment depends on the OOB infrastructure.

docs.title: Interaction Data Sensitivity
docs.text:
Callback data may contain:

  • source IPs;
  • internal proxy details;
  • User-Agent;
  • authentication headers;
  • query values.

Treat interaction logs as assessment evidence.

docs.title: Do Not Embed Secrets in Callback URLs
docs.text:
Avoid placing:

passwords
tokens
customer data

inside Interactsh hostnames or paths.

Use synthetic correlation identifiers.

docs.title: Subdomain Length
docs.text:
When embedding test identifiers in DNS labels, keep values reasonably short and compatible with DNS naming rules.

Use simple identifiers such as:

ssrf01
avatar02
import03

docs.title: Request Headers
docs.text:
Some server-side fetchers may forward:

  • User-Agent;
  • Referer;
  • custom headers.

These can provide useful evidence.

Do not assume forwarded headers are secrets unless they actually contain sensitive values.

docs.title: Host Header
docs.text:
The OOB request's Host value normally corresponds to the supplied Interactsh domain.

This is expected.

Do not confuse it with Host header injection in the original application.

docs.title: User-Agent
docs.text:
A callback User-Agent can help identify:

  • language runtime;
  • HTTP library;
  • security scanner;
  • browser.

It is supporting evidence, not absolute attribution.

docs.title: Source Port
docs.text:
Network source ports are usually ephemeral and have limited security significance.

Do not overinterpret them.

docs.title: Unique Interaction IDs
docs.text:
Interactsh-generated identifiers should be retained for the lifetime of the test.

They help connect:

request

to:

callback

docs.title: Blind Vulnerability Model
docs.text:
A useful generic OOB model is:

Input Controlled by Tester
      |
      v
Server-Side Processing
      |
      v
Outbound Interaction
      |
      v
Unique Callback
      |
      v
Correlation
      |
      v
Root-Cause Validation

docs.title: OOB Interaction Is Supporting Evidence
docs.text:
The strongest conclusion is usually not:

Interactsh received DNS.

It is:

The application caused server-side resolution of an attacker-controlled
hostname when processing the supplied input.

This explains the security behavior.

docs.title: Manual Validation
docs.text:
After an automated OOB result:

  1. create a fresh unique callback value;
  2. replay only the relevant request;
  3. capture the exact timestamp;
  4. observe the interaction;
  5. confirm the protocol;
  6. inspect headers/source;
  7. repeat if necessary.

This creates stronger evidence.

docs.title: Reproduce One Candidate at a Time
docs.text:
Avoid sending many different OOB candidates before checking results.

A better workflow is:

Candidate 1
    |
    v
Observe
    |
    v
Candidate 2
    |
    v
Observe

This makes attribution easier.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Common false-positive or false-attribution causes include:

  • security scanners;
  • browser prefetch;
  • email link scanners;
  • WAF inspection;
  • reverse proxy processing;
  • stale asynchronous jobs;
  • reused correlation values.

Always correlate carefully.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Possible reasons for no callback include:

  • egress filtering;
  • DNS filtering;
  • proxy requirements;
  • unsupported URL scheme;
  • application validation;
  • asynchronous delay;
  • network outage;
  • OOB infrastructure unavailable.

A clean OOB test does not prove absence of server-side URL processing.

docs.title: Baseline Testing
docs.text:
Before testing a suspected URL field, determine normal behavior.

For example:

Valid public image URL
      |
      v
Does application fetch it?

If the feature does not fetch normal URLs, an OOB failure may be expected.

docs.title: Known-Good External URL
docs.text:
Where permitted, use a controlled known-good external resource to understand intended behavior before testing security boundaries.

This can answer:

Does this feature actually perform server-side retrieval?

docs.title: Error Messages
docs.text:
Application errors can help interpret OOB behavior.

Examples:

Unable to fetch URL
Invalid hostname
Connection timed out
Unsupported scheme

Combine these with OOB observations.

docs.title: Timeout Behavior
docs.text:
If the application response becomes slower when using an unreachable destination, this may indicate backend fetching.

Timing alone is weak evidence.

Use OOB correlation where possible.

docs.title: Redirect Chain Evidence
docs.text:
When testing redirect behavior, preserve:

initial URL
redirect destination
callback observed

This can help explain how validation is performed.

docs.title: Nuclei Result Validation
docs.text:
If Nuclei reports an OOB finding:

Nuclei
  |
  v
Template ID
  |
  v
Interactsh Callback

inspect the exact template logic before reporting.

Related tool:

Nuclei

docs.title: Burp Reproduction
docs.text:
A clean manual reproduction might contain:

Request:
POST /api/import

Parameter:
url

Value:
https://import-01.<interactsh-domain>/

Result:
HTTP 202

OOB:
HTTP GET received 1 second later

This is much stronger than a scanner screenshot.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each important OOB test, retain:

Target:
Endpoint:
Parameter:
Authentication context:
Original request:
Unique OOB identifier:
Request timestamp:
Interaction timestamp:
Interaction protocol:
Source IP:
Headers:
Response:
Manual reproduction:
Conclusion:

docs.title: Evidence Example
docs.text:
Target:
https://portal.example.test

Endpoint:
/api/avatar

Parameter:
url

Context:
Authenticated standard user

Payload:
https://avatar-07.<interactsh-domain>/

Request time:
14:24:11

Interaction:
HTTP GET

Interaction time:
14:24:12

Conclusion:
The backend performed an outbound HTTP request to the user-supplied
destination while processing the avatar URL.

Further SSRF impact assessment would still be required.

docs.title: Reporting Blind SSRF
docs.text:
Avoid:

Interactsh got a DNS hit, therefore critical SSRF.

Prefer:

The avatar URL parameter caused the application backend to resolve and
request an attacker-controlled external hostname. This confirms
server-side outbound request capability. Additional testing was
required to determine whether internal or otherwise restricted
destinations were reachable.

docs.title: Reporting DNS-Only Behavior
docs.text:
Example:

The supplied hostname triggered an outbound DNS resolution from the
application environment. No corresponding HTTP interaction was
observed during testing. The evidence therefore confirms server-side
name resolution but does not establish successful HTTP retrieval.

docs.title: Reporting Scanner-Induced Interaction
docs.text:
Example:

The submitted URL generated an external request, but the callback
headers and source infrastructure were consistent with the
organisation's URL inspection service rather than the application
backend. The result was therefore not treated as evidence of SSRF.

docs.title: Reporting Intended Webhook Behavior
docs.text:
Example:

The application intentionally delivered HTTP requests to user-configured
webhook destinations. The outbound interaction itself was expected.
Security testing therefore focused on destination restrictions,
authorisation, and whether private network addresses could be targeted.

docs.title: Reporting an Unconfirmed Candidate
docs.text:
Example:

No unique DNS or HTTP interaction was observed for the supplied callback
value. Because the environment uses restricted outbound networking, the
result was considered inconclusive rather than proof that server-side
URL processing was absent.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
For SSRF-style issues, remediation may include:

  • strict destination allowlists;
  • blocking private and link-local address ranges where appropriate;
  • validating resolved addresses;
  • revalidating after redirects;
  • restricting supported URL schemes;
  • egress controls;
  • dedicated fetch proxies;
  • network segmentation.

The correct controls depend on the application's legitimate requirements.

docs.title: Allowlist Over Blocklist
docs.text:
Where possible, a strong design is:

Application needs to fetch:
images.example-cdn.com

Then allow only:

images.example-cdn.com

rather than trying to block every dangerous network range.

docs.title: DNS Validation
docs.text:
Hostname validation alone can be insufficient because DNS resolution can change.

Robust designs should consider the resolved destination.

The exact implementation depends on architecture and language.

docs.title: Redirect Validation
docs.text:
If redirects are followed:

Initial URL allowed
      |
      v
Redirect
      |
      v
New Destination

the new destination should also satisfy security policy.

docs.title: Network Egress Controls
docs.text:
Network-level controls can reduce SSRF impact.

Examples include:

  • outbound firewall rules;
  • application proxies;
  • segmentation;
  • cloud network policies.

These are defence-in-depth controls.

They do not replace secure application validation.

docs.title: Metadata Services
docs.text:
Cloud metadata endpoints deserve specific protection in cloud environments.

Use platform-recommended metadata protections and least-privileged identity design.

Do not rely solely on application-level URL filtering.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation:

  1. repeat the original public callback test;
  2. confirm expected legitimate behavior;
  3. test blocked destinations safely;
  4. test redirect validation where relevant;
  5. verify OOB interactions match intended policy.

The objective is to confirm the trust boundary, not merely make Interactsh stop receiving requests.

docs.title: Purple Teaming
docs.text:
OOB testing can also validate detection of suspicious server-side outbound communication.

Controlled OOB Request
      |
      v
Backend Callback
      |
      v
DNS / Proxy / Firewall Logs
      |
      v
SIEM
      |
      v
Detection Review

Related section:

Purple Teaming

docs.title: Detection Engineering
docs.text:
Potential telemetry includes:

  • DNS logs;
  • proxy logs;
  • firewall connections;
  • cloud egress logs;
  • application logs;
  • WAF logs.

Detection should consider application context.

A legitimate webhook service will naturally make outbound requests.

docs.title: OOB Detection Context
docs.text:
A useful detection question is:

Which application processes should make outbound connections?

Unexpected egress from normally isolated backend components may be more useful than detecting a specific Interactsh domain.

docs.title: Tool-Specific Indicators
docs.text:
Interactsh domains may appear in logs during testing.

These can support exercise correlation.

Long-term defensive logic should not depend only on one known OOB service domain.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
Before OOB testing ask:

Are external callbacks permitted?

Is public Interactsh permitted?

Could the feature trigger repeated background jobs?

Could the callback contain sensitive data?

Could third-party scanners interfere?

docs.title: Do Not Exfiltrate Real Data
docs.text:
An OOB test generally needs only:

unique identifier

Do not include real credentials, file content, or personal data in the callback.

docs.title: Minimise OOB Content
docs.text:
Prefer:

ssrf-test-01

over embedding:

database contents

or other sensitive information.

docs.title: Out-of-Scope Network Targets
docs.text:
Do not test internal IPs, cloud metadata, partner systems, or unrelated infrastructure simply because the application may be able to reach them.

Reachability is not authorisation.

docs.title: Public Service Availability
docs.text:
Public OOB services can occasionally be unavailable or delayed.

Before interpreting a negative result, confirm the interaction service itself is working using a harmless local test where appropriate.

docs.title: Local Verification
docs.text:
For example, if using a generated Interactsh domain, resolving or requesting it from your own authorised workstation can confirm that the interaction channel is functioning.

Clearly distinguish these self-generated callbacks from target-generated callbacks.

docs.title: Self-Test Labeling
docs.text:
Use a unique self-test identifier such as:

operator-selftest-01

so it cannot be confused with application callbacks.

docs.title: Interaction Log Hygiene
docs.text:
Keep only the interactions relevant to the assessment.

Public/shared OOB environments may generate unrelated noise.

Use unique identifiers and timestamps to avoid confusion.

docs.title: Workflow with Nuclei
docs.text:
A useful sequence is:

Target Inventory
      |
      v
Nuclei OOB Template
      |
      v
Interaction
      |
      v
Inspect Template
      |
      v
Manual Burp Reproduction
      |
      v
Root-Cause Validation

docs.title: Workflow with Katana
docs.text:
Katana
  |
  v
Discover /api/import?url=
  |
  v
Burp
  |
  v
Interactsh Test
  |
  v
Server-Side Callback

docs.title: Workflow with ffuf
docs.text:
ffuf
 |
 v
Discover /webhook
 |
 v
Manual Feature Review
 |
 v
Interactsh
 |
 v
OOB Validation

docs.title: Workflow with Source Review
docs.text:
White-box testing can make OOB validation substantially stronger.

Source Review
      |
      v
HTTP Client Sink
      |
      v
User-Controlled URL
      |
      v
Interactsh
      |
      v
Runtime Confirmation

Related section:

Source Code Review Tools

docs.title: Source-to-Sink SSRF Analysis
docs.text:
A code-level flow may look like:

request.json["url"]
      |
      v
validation()
      |
      v
http_client.get(url)

OOB testing can confirm the runtime behavior.

docs.title: Logs and Application Evidence
docs.text:
Where available, correlate OOB interactions with application logs.

Example:

14:24:11 request received
14:24:11 fetch job queued
14:24:12 outbound HTTP request
14:24:12 Interactsh callback

This creates very strong evidence.

docs.title: Start Client
docs.text: interactsh-client

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
interactsh-client -h

For server selection, output formats, authentication, polling, and self-hosted configuration, use the exact options documented by:

interactsh-client -h

and current ProjectDiscovery documentation.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Target explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] External callbacks permitted.
  • [ ] OOB provider approved.
  • [ ] Public vs self-hosted decision made.
  • [ ] Sensitive data handling understood.
  • [ ] Application feature understood.
  • [ ] Baseline behavior tested.

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
• [ ] Unique identifier used.
  • [ ] One identifier per test.
  • [ ] Original request timestamp retained.
  • [ ] Interaction timestamp retained.
  • [ ] Interaction protocol retained.
  • [ ] Source information retained.
  • [ ] Callback path/hostname retained.

docs.title: Attribution
docs.text:
• [ ] Browser callback ruled out.
  • [ ] Security scanner callback considered.
  • [ ] Email scanner considered where relevant.
  • [ ] Proxy/NAT considered.
  • [ ] Resolver source interpreted carefully.
  • [ ] Application backend attribution supported.

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
• [ ] User control over destination understood.
  • [ ] Scheme control understood.
  • [ ] Host control understood.
  • [ ] Port control understood where relevant.
  • [ ] Redirect behavior reviewed.
  • [ ] External callback not confused with internal reachability.
  • [ ] Cloud metadata not tested without explicit authorisation.

docs.title: XXE / Other OOB
docs.text:
• [ ] Exact parser/input path known.
  • [ ] Interaction tied to unique input.
  • [ ] Protocol understood.
  • [ ] Alternative callback causes considered.
  • [ ] Root cause manually validated.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
• [ ] No real secrets embedded in OOB values.
  • [ ] No customer data exfiltrated.
  • [ ] Out-of-scope systems not targeted.
  • [ ] Background retry behavior monitored.
  • [ ] Unexpected high callback volume investigated.
  • [ ] Testing stopped if production impact appears.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Target retained.
  • [ ] Endpoint retained.
  • [ ] Parameter retained.
  • [ ] Authentication context retained.
  • [ ] Original request retained.
  • [ ] Unique callback ID retained.
  • [ ] Interaction details retained.
  • [ ] Manual reproduction retained.
  • [ ] Sensitive values redacted.
  • [ ] Final conclusion states actual behavior.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• [ ] DNS interaction not overstated as HTTP.
  • [ ] External callback not automatically labeled SSRF.
  • [ ] Intended webhook behavior distinguished from vulnerability.
  • [ ] Security scanner callbacks excluded.
  • [ ] Internal reachability reported only if actually validated.
  • [ ] Remediation addresses destination trust.
  • [ ] Retest criteria explicit.

docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use Interactsh like this:

Insert Callback URL
      |
      v
Receive DNS Hit
      |
      v
Report Critical SSRF

Use it like this:

Understand Application Feature
      |
      v
Establish Baseline Behavior
      |
      v
Create Unique OOB Identifier
      |
      v
Modify One Controlled Input
      |
      v
Send Request
      |
      v
Record Exact Timestamp
      |
      v
Observe DNS / HTTP Interaction
      |
      v
Correlate Unique Identifier
      |
      v
Rule Out Browser / Scanner / Proxy Effects
      |
      v
Identify Server-Side Component
      |
      v
Determine Actual Destination Control
      |
      v
Assess Reachability and Security Boundary
      |
      v
Reproduce Manually
      |
      v
Capture Evidence
      |
      v
Report the Underlying Behavior

Interactsh is most valuable when an application performs security-relevant server-side activity that cannot be observed directly in the normal response.

The callback proves an interaction occurred.

The tester still needs to establish who caused it, why it occurred, what control the user has over it, and whether that behavior crosses a meaningful security boundary.

docs.title: Katana
docs.text:
Katana is a web crawler from ProjectDiscovery designed for fast attack-surface discovery across web applications.

It is especially useful for identifying:

  • reachable URLs;
  • linked endpoints;
  • parameters;
  • JavaScript-referenced paths;
  • API routes;
  • forms;
  • application resources;
  • client-side navigation;
  • deeper application structure.

Katana is most valuable when used after initial host discovery and before deeper manual testing.

Alive Web Host
    |
    v
Katana Crawl
    |
    +-- Links
    +-- JavaScript
    +-- Parameters
    +-- Forms
    +-- Resources
    |
    v
Endpoint Inventory
    |
    v
Manual Validation
    |
    v
Burp / Focused Testing

Authorised testing only

Use Katana only against web applications and infrastructure that are explicitly authorised for testing. Crawling can generate significant request volume and may traverse state-changing or sensitive application functionality. Start conservatively, define scope carefully, and review discovered destinations before expanding the crawl.

docs.title: Where Katana Fits
docs.text:
A common workflow is:

Subdomain Enumeration
      |
      v
httpx
      |
      v
Alive Web Hosts
      |
      v
Katana
      |
      v
Discovered URLs
      |
      v
Filtering / Deduplication
      |
      v
Manual Testing

Related tools:

Web Enumeration Tools

httpx

Web Application Testing Tools

Burp Suite

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
Official project:

Katana - GitHub

Official documentation:

Katana Documentation

Because Katana evolves quickly, verify exact current flags using:

katana -h

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Check:

katana -version

If the installed build uses different version syntax, use:

katana -h

The help output is the most reliable source for the current installed version.

docs.title: Basic Crawl
docs.text:
A simple starting point is:

katana -u https://example.test

This crawls the target and outputs discovered URLs.

Conceptually:

https://example.test
      |
      +-- /login
      +-- /account
      +-- /api/users
      +-- /assets/app.js
      +-- /admin

The discovered URLs become candidates for later testing.

docs.title: Crawl from a List
docs.text:
Katana can also process multiple targets.

A common pattern is:

katana -list urls.txt

or the equivalent supported by the installed version.

Always confirm exact syntax with:

katana -h

docs.title: Pipeline with httpx
docs.text:
A useful reconnaissance pipeline is:

cat subdomains.txt | httpx -silent | katana

Conceptually:

Subdomains
   |
   v
httpx
   |
   v
Alive URLs
   |
   v
Katana
   |
   v
Endpoint Inventory

For production assessments, consider saving each stage separately for reproducibility.

docs.title: Prefer Reproducible Pipelines
docs.text:
Instead of:

subfinder -d example.test | httpx -silent | katana

for all cases, consider:

subdomains.txt
alive.txt
katana.txt

This allows each stage to be reviewed independently.

docs.title: Save Alive Hosts First
docs.text:
Example:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -silent > alive.txt

Then:

katana -list alive.txt > katana.txt

Use the exact current input option supported by the installed version.

This provides a clear evidence chain.

docs.title: Crawling vs Fuzzing
docs.text:
Katana and ffuf perform different jobs.

Katana
  |
  +-- follows discovered links

ffuf
  |
  +-- guesses candidate paths

Katana discovers:

linked attack surface

ffuf discovers:

potentially unlinked attack surface

Related tool:

ffuf

docs.title: Why Use Both
docs.text:
Suppose the application exposes:

/
/login
/api/profile

through navigation.

Katana may discover all three.

But:

/admin-old

may not be linked anywhere.

ffuf may discover it.

A combined workflow improves coverage.

docs.title: Crawl Depth
docs.text:
Crawl depth controls how far Katana follows discovered relationships.

Conceptually:

Depth 0:
/

Depth 1:
 /login
 /products

Depth 2:
 /products/123
 /account/settings

Deeper crawling can improve coverage but also increases traffic.

Use the smallest depth that supports the objective.

docs.title: Depth Selection
docs.text:
Start with a moderate depth.

Increase only when:

  • the application is heavily nested;
  • important sections are missed;
  • the target can tolerate additional requests;
  • the engagement allows it.

Do not use deep crawling automatically against fragile production applications.

docs.title: Scope Control
docs.text:
Scope control is critical.

A crawler may encounter:

example.test
      |
      +-- api.example.test
      +-- auth.thirdparty.com
      +-- payments.example-payments.com

Do not automatically crawl all discovered domains.

Reachability does not equal authorisation.

docs.title: In-Scope vs Out-of-Scope Destinations
docs.text:
A useful mental model is:

Discovered URL
      |
      v
Scope Check
      |
      +-- In Scope -> crawl
      |
      +-- Out of Scope -> record only / ignore

Scope should be explicit.

docs.title: Third-Party Services
docs.text:
Modern applications often link to:

  • identity providers;
  • CDNs;
  • payment providers;
  • analytics;
  • support platforms;
  • SaaS services.

These should normally be excluded unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Scope Regex / Filters
docs.text:
Katana supports scope and filtering functionality.

Because exact flags may evolve, inspect:

katana -h

for the current options.

Use allowlists rather than relying only on broad exclusions where practical.

docs.title: Host Scope
docs.text:
If testing:

example.test

and scope explicitly includes:

*.example.test

then crawling multiple subdomains may be appropriate.

If scope contains only:

www.example.test

do not assume:

admin.example.test

is authorised.

docs.title: Redirect Scope
docs.text:
A crawler may follow:

https://example.test/login

to:

https://login.identity-provider.com/

The second host may be out of scope.

Review redirect behaviour carefully.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
Katana may discover URLs containing parameters.

Example:

https://example.test/search?q=test

Parameters can help identify:

  • search features;
  • object identifiers;
  • filters;
  • redirects;
  • API inputs.

Do not treat every parameter as security sensitive.

docs.title: Parameter Inventory
docs.text:
A useful endpoint record might look like:

URL Parameters Source /search q HTML form /user id JavaScript /redirect url anchor /api/report format JS request

This provides a useful starting point for manual review.

docs.title: Parameter Names Matter
docs.text:
Interesting parameter names may include:

id
user
account
file
path
url
redirect
callback
template
query
search
format
lang

Names are only hints.

The security relevance depends on server-side behaviour.

docs.title: JavaScript Discovery
docs.text:
JavaScript is a major source of hidden attack surface.

Scripts may reveal:

  • API routes;
  • feature flags;
  • internal endpoints;
  • parameter names;
  • versioned routes;
  • WebSocket URLs;
  • GraphQL endpoints.

Katana can help surface these references.

docs.title: JavaScript Example
docs.text:
A script may contain:

fetch("/api/v2/users/" + userId)

This may reveal:

/api/v2/users/

even when no visible link exists.

The endpoint still requires manual validation.

docs.title: JavaScript-Aware Crawling
docs.text:
ProjectDiscovery has added JavaScript-aware crawling capabilities over time.

Use:

katana -h

to verify the exact options supported by the installed version.

Do not rely on old examples for current headless/JavaScript flags.

docs.title: Static JavaScript vs Runtime Navigation
docs.text:
There is an important distinction between:

Static JS endpoint extraction

and:

Executing JavaScript in a browser context

Some application routes only become visible after runtime execution.

docs.title: Headless Crawling
docs.text:
Katana can support headless-style crawling in supported configurations.

This can be useful for:

  • single-page applications;
  • JavaScript routing;
  • runtime DOM generation;
  • client-side navigation.

Headless crawling is generally heavier than normal HTTP crawling.

Use it selectively.

docs.title: When Headless Crawling Helps
docs.text:
Consider headless crawling when:

Normal crawl finds almost nothing

but the browser shows:

large client-side application

Examples include:

  • React;
  • Angular;
  • Vue;
  • complex SPA frameworks.

docs.title: Headless Crawling Risks
docs.text:
A real browser context may:

  • execute JavaScript;
  • submit background requests;
  • interact with application logic;
  • load third-party services.

Scope and operational impact should therefore be reviewed carefully.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
Forms can reveal:

  • endpoints;
  • methods;
  • parameter names;
  • workflows.

Example:

<form action="/login" method="POST">

This exposes:

POST /login

and potentially fields such as:

username
password

docs.title: Form Discovery Is Not Form Submission
docs.text:
There is a major distinction between:

Identify form

and:

Submit form

A crawler should not blindly execute state-changing application actions.

docs.title: State-Changing Routes
docs.text:
Potentially dangerous operations include:

/delete
/logout
/reset
/purchase
/submit
/approve
/upload

Path names alone do not prove they change state, but they deserve caution.

docs.title: Safe Crawling Principle
docs.text:
Prefer:

GET-oriented discovery

before:

state-changing interaction

especially on production systems.

docs.title: HTTP Methods
docs.text:
Katana may identify methods through forms or application references.

Examples include:

GET
POST
PUT
DELETE
PATCH

Do not automatically replay state-changing methods.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Authenticated applications require session context for complete crawling.

Potential approaches include supplying:

  • cookies;
  • authorization headers;
  • other approved headers.

The exact Katana options should be checked using:

katana -h

docs.title: Cookie-Based Crawling
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Katana
  |
  +-- Cookie: approved test session
  |
  v
Authenticated Application

This can reveal:

  • account pages;
  • private APIs;
  • role-specific routes.

Protect live session values.

docs.title: Bearer Tokens
docs.text:
For APIs:

Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED>

may be required.

Use only test-account tokens and avoid committing them to shell history or repositories.

docs.title: Role-Aware Crawling
docs.text:
The same application may expose different routes to different roles.

Example:

User
  |
  +-- /profile
  +-- /orders

Admin
  |
  +-- /profile
  +-- /orders
  +-- /admin
  +-- /audit

Run role-specific crawls only where needed and authorised.

docs.title: Session Expiry
docs.text:
Long crawls may outlive the session.

Symptoms include:

302 -> /login
401
403

appearing suddenly across many routes.

Check authentication before interpreting later results.

docs.title: CSRF and Stateful Workflows
docs.text:
Applications with dynamic CSRF tokens or multi-step workflows may not crawl cleanly.

Examples include:

Step 1 -> get token
Step 2 -> submit form
Step 3 -> receive next token

Manual Burp testing or custom automation may be more appropriate.

docs.title: API Discovery
docs.text:
Katana is useful for finding API endpoints referenced by:

  • JavaScript;
  • HTML;
  • documentation;
  • linked resources.

Example:

/api/v1/profile
/api/v1/orders
/api/v2/admin

Each endpoint should be classified by:

  • authentication;
  • method;
  • parameters;
  • content type.

docs.title: API Versions
docs.text:
Versioned routes may include:

/api/v1/
/api/v2/
/api/internal/

Older versions deserve attention because they may have weaker controls.

Do not assume an older version is vulnerable solely because it exists.

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
Katana may discover:

/openapi.json
/swagger.json
/api-docs

These can reveal significant API structure.

Treat documentation exposure according to intended design.

docs.title: GraphQL Discovery
docs.text:
Katana may identify:

/graphql
/api/graphql

through JavaScript or application links.

Related note:

GraphQL

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
JavaScript may reveal:

ws://
wss://

endpoints.

These represent a different protocol surface.

Manual testing may require Burp or another WebSocket-capable client.

docs.title: Static Assets
docs.text:
Katana may enumerate:

  • CSS;
  • JavaScript;
  • images;
  • fonts;
  • source maps.

Not every static file needs deeper review.

Prioritise files that can reveal:

  • application logic;
  • routes;
  • configuration;
  • secrets;
  • debugging data.

docs.title: Source Maps
docs.text:
Source map files may expose original client-side source.

Common pattern:

app.js.map

If accessible, determine whether they reveal sensitive source or internal information.

Source maps are not automatically vulnerabilities.

docs.title: JavaScript Secrets
docs.text:
Client-side JavaScript may contain:

  • API keys;
  • environment values;
  • internal URLs.

Many API keys embedded in frontend code are intentionally public identifiers.

Do not report every key-looking string as a secret.

Determine its actual privilege and intended exposure.

docs.title: Endpoint Sources
docs.text:
When possible, retain where each endpoint came from.

Example:

Endpoint:
/api/export

Source:
app.js

Reference:
fetch("/api/export")

This improves reproducibility.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Large crawls often produce significant noise.

Common low-value resources include:

images
fonts
CSS
static media
tracking URLs
logout routes
third-party assets

Filtering can make results easier to review.

docs.title: Extension Filtering
docs.text:
Katana supports filtering functionality for extensions and other patterns.

Use:

katana -h

for exact current syntax.

Potential low-priority extensions include:

.png
.jpg
.gif
.svg
.woff
.woff2
.ico

Do not exclude JavaScript if endpoint discovery is important.

docs.title: Avoid Over-Filtering
docs.text:
Filtering:

.json

could hide:

/openapi.json

Filtering:

.js

could hide valuable JavaScript.

Choose filters according to the goal.

docs.title: Deduplication
docs.text:
Crawlers may discover equivalent URLs repeatedly.

Examples:

/page?id=1
/page?id=2
/page?id=3

Depending on the objective, these may represent:

same endpoint, different values

rather than three independent attack-surface items.

docs.title: Normalisation
docs.text:
Useful URL normalisation may include:

  • lowercasing hostnames;
  • removing fragments;
  • sorting parameters where appropriate;
  • removing duplicates;
  • separating path from value variants.

Do not alter URLs in a way that changes application semantics.

docs.title: Fragments
docs.text:
Browser fragments such as:

/page#section

are not normally sent to the server.

For server-side endpoint inventory, fragments can often be ignored.

Client-side SPA routing may still use them.

docs.title: Duplicate Query Values
docs.text:
These:

/item?id=1
/item?id=2

may map to the same route.

For attack-surface inventory, record:

/item?id=

while preserving example values separately.

docs.title: Crawling Loops
docs.text:
Applications may create infinite navigation patterns.

Examples:

/calendar/2026/01
/calendar/2026/02
/calendar/2026/03
...

or:

?page=1
?page=2
?page=3
...

Use depth and filtering controls to prevent runaway crawling.

docs.title: Calendar and Pagination Traps
docs.text:
Common crawler traps include:

  • calendars;
  • pagination;
  • session IDs in URLs;
  • search results;
  • faceted filtering.

Watch for rapidly growing URL counts.

docs.title: Stop Unexpected Expansion
docs.text:
If a target begins generating thousands of low-value paths:

Stop
Review
Refine scope/filtering
Resume

Do not let the crawler run indefinitely.

docs.title: Request Rate
docs.text:
Katana can generate substantial traffic.

Control:

  • concurrency;
  • rate;
  • depth;
  • target count.

Check current rate-related options:

katana -h

Start conservatively.

docs.title: Production Systems
docs.text:
For production applications:

  • keep depth moderate;
  • avoid excessive concurrency;
  • exclude state-changing paths;
  • monitor error rates;
  • stop if instability appears.

Crawling should not become load testing.

docs.title: 429 Responses
docs.text:
If the server returns:

429 Too Many Requests

the crawler is being rate limited.

Reduce request volume.

Do not attempt to bypass rate controls unless specifically authorised.

docs.title: WAF Behaviour
docs.text:
A WAF may respond with:

  • 403;
  • challenge pages;
  • connection resets;
  • CAPTCHA;
  • rate limiting.

This can distort crawler results.

Record the control instead of automatically attempting evasion.

docs.title: Robots.txt
docs.text:
Review:

/robots.txt

before large-scale crawling.

It may identify interesting paths.

Remember:

robots.txt

is crawler guidance, not an access control mechanism.

docs.title: sitemap.xml
docs.text:
Sitemaps can provide high-quality deterministic endpoint discovery.

Use:

/sitemap.xml

before relying solely on crawler exploration.

docs.title: Default 404 Behaviour
docs.text:
Before interpreting discovered unusual routes, understand missing-page behaviour.

Reference:

0xdf - Default 404 Pages

Validate technology with multiple signals.

docs.title: Soft 404s
docs.text:
A crawler may encounter catch-all routes returning:

200 OK

for any path.

Example:

/random-test-123 -> SPA index page

This does not mean every path is a real endpoint.

docs.title: SPA Catch-All
docs.text:
Single-page applications often serve the same frontend HTML for:

/
/users
/admin
/nonexistent

The client-side router then decides what to display.

Separate:

server route

from:

client route

docs.title: Manual Validation
docs.text:
For an interesting URL:

curl -i https://example.test/api/internal

or use Burp Repeater.

Check:

  • method;
  • response;
  • authentication;
  • content type;
  • redirects;
  • actual functionality.

docs.title: Burp Integration
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

Katana
  |
  v
Interesting URL
  |
  v
Burp Repeater
  |
  v
Understand Behaviour
  |
  v
Security Testing

Katana finds the route.

Burp helps understand it.

docs.title: Katana and ffuf
docs.text:
A practical order is:

Katana
  |
  v
Linked Attack Surface
  |
  v
ffuf
  |
  v
Unlinked Candidate Paths

or run both independently and merge the results.

docs.title: Katana and Nuclei
docs.text:
Nuclei can consume known URLs for template-based checks.

A controlled chain may be:

Katana
  |
  v
Deduplicated URLs
  |
  v
Select Relevant Targets
  |
  v
Nuclei

Do not automatically run every template against every discovered URL.

Related tool:

Nuclei

docs.title: Katana and sqlmap
docs.text:
Katana may reveal parameterized URLs.

Example:

/report?id=123

This does not justify immediately running sqlmap.

Use:

Katana
  |
  v
Parameterized Endpoint
  |
  v
Manual Review
  |
  v
SQLi Hypothesis
  |
  v
sqlmap if appropriate

Related tool:

sqlmap

docs.title: Katana and Interactsh
docs.text:
Katana may discover features such as:

  • webhooks;
  • callback URLs;
  • import-from-URL;
  • image fetchers.

Those features may later be appropriate for controlled OOB testing.

Related tool:

Interactsh

docs.title: JavaScript Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
A useful chain is:

Katana
  |
  v
JavaScript URLs
  |
  v
Download / Inspect Relevant Scripts
  |
  v
Extract Endpoints
  |
  v
Manual Validation

Related note:

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: Parameter Discovery Workflow
docs.text:
Katana can provide existing parameter names.

For additional unknown parameters, use tools such as:

ffuf
ParamSpider-style workflows
manual analysis

depending on the task.

docs.title: URL Inventory
docs.text:
A useful final crawl inventory might contain:

URL Method Parameters Source Auth /login GET/POST username, password form No /api/profile GET none JS Yes /report GET id link Yes /graphql POST GraphQL JS Yes

This is far more useful than a raw URL dump.

docs.title: Classify Endpoints
docs.text:
Useful categories include:

Authentication
Account
Administration
API
Upload
Download
Search
Reporting
Webhook
Redirect
Internal
Debug
Health

Classification helps prioritise testing.

docs.title: High-Value Endpoint Types
docs.text:
Prioritise routes involving:

  • authentication;
  • authorisation;
  • administration;
  • file handling;
  • URL fetching;
  • exports;
  • imports;
  • secrets;
  • account recovery;
  • identity changes.

docs.title: Health Endpoints
docs.text:
Crawlers may discover:

/health
/status
/metrics

These can be intended operational endpoints.

Assess:

  • information exposed;
  • authentication;
  • environment.

Do not automatically report them.

docs.title: Debug Endpoints
docs.text:
Potentially interesting routes include:

/debug
/trace
/dev
/internal

Again, validate actual behaviour.

A route name alone is not evidence.

docs.title: Error Endpoints
docs.text:
Some frameworks expose internal error handlers.

These may reveal:

  • stack traces;
  • framework versions;
  • file paths.

Test safely and avoid intentionally causing large numbers of server errors.

docs.title: Authentication Paths
docs.text:
Crawling may identify:

/login
/logout
/register
/reset-password
/mfa
/oauth/callback

These should be mapped as one authentication surface.

Related note:

Authentication Testing

docs.title: Authorisation Paths
docs.text:
Look for routes containing:

/admin
/manage
/users
/accounts
/roles
/permissions

But route names are only hints.

The actual security control must be tested.

Related note:

Authorisation Testing

docs.title: File Operations
docs.text:
Interesting endpoints may include:

/upload
/download
/export
/import
/attachment

These can map to:

  • file upload;
  • traversal;
  • insecure direct object reference;
  • SSRF;
  • parser attack surface.

docs.title: URL Fetching Features
docs.text:
Potential endpoint names include:

/webhook
/callback
/fetch
/import-url
/preview
/image

These deserve further SSRF-oriented analysis where appropriate.

Related note:

Server Side Request Forgery

docs.title: Output Handling
docs.text:
Katana supports multiple output modes depending on version.

Check:

katana -h

Structured output is preferable for larger assessments.

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text:
Where supported, JSON output can preserve richer metadata than plain URLs.

Possible useful fields include:

  • URL;
  • source;
  • method;
  • request;
  • response metadata.

Inspect the actual version's output structure before writing parsers.

docs.title: Plain URL Output
docs.text:
Plain output is useful for simple pipelines.

Example concept:

katana -u https://example.test -silent > urls.txt

Confirm the exact -silent behaviour using the installed version.

docs.title: Sort and Deduplicate
docs.text:
A basic Unix pattern is:

sort -u katana.txt > katana-unique.txt

This is appropriate for plain URL output.

Do not use it on JSON output.

docs.title: Extract Hosts
docs.text:
For authorised analysis, URL-processing tools or Python can help extract:

scheme
host
path
query parameters

This can help identify accidental out-of-scope discoveries.

docs.title: Scope QA
docs.text:
After a crawl, check whether output includes unexpected domains.

Conceptually:

cat katana.txt
      |
      v
Extract Hostnames
      |
      v
Compare with Scope

Remove out-of-scope targets from downstream automation.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a significant discovered endpoint, retain:

Target:
Katana version:
Crawl command:
Scope:
Authentication context:
Depth:
Endpoint:
Discovery source:
Timestamp:
Manual validation:

This makes the result reproducible.

docs.title: Evidence Example
docs.text:
Target:
https://portal.example.test

Context:
Authenticated standard user

Discovery:
Katana

Endpoint:
/api/export

Source:
Referenced by application JavaScript

Manual validation:
GET returned JSON metadata and required the standard user's active
session.

Conclusion:
Endpoint added to the authorised API attack-surface inventory.

No vulnerability is claimed unless later testing demonstrates one.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Katana itself usually does not produce findings.

Avoid:

Katana found a vulnerability.

Prefer:

Application crawling identified an undocumented administrative API
endpoint that was subsequently confirmed to expose sensitive
functionality without the expected authorisation control.

The finding comes from the endpoint behaviour.

docs.title: Hidden Endpoint Is Not a Vulnerability
docs.text:
An endpoint may be:

not linked in UI

but still intentionally available.

Security depends on:

  • authentication;
  • authorisation;
  • data exposure;
  • functionality.

Do not rely on obscurity as the finding.

docs.title: Sensitive JavaScript Exposure
docs.text:
If JavaScript exposes internal details, describe what was actually disclosed.

For example:

Client-side JavaScript disclosed an internal administrative API base
URL that was not otherwise referenced by the public user interface.

Then determine whether the endpoint itself is accessible.

docs.title: Source Map Reporting
docs.text:
If a source map exposes proprietary source:

A production JavaScript source map was publicly accessible and contained
the original client-side source code and internal file structure.

The security significance depends on the disclosed information.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
Before crawling ask:

Is the target production?

What depth is necessary?

Does the application contain destructive GET routes?

Will JavaScript execution trigger actions?

Are third-party domains present?

What request rate is acceptable?

docs.title: Start Small
docs.text:
A good approach is:

Single Target
     |
     v
Moderate Depth
     |
     v
Review Output
     |
     v
Expand If Needed

rather than immediately crawling every host deeply.

docs.title: Monitor Errors
docs.text:
During the crawl, watch for:

  • 500 errors;
  • timeouts;
  • connection resets;
  • rate limits;
  • service degradation.

If instability appears, stop and reassess.

docs.title: Crawling Is Not Load Testing
docs.text:
The objective is:

discover attack surface

not:

maximize request throughput

Use appropriate limits.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Common crawler interpretation mistakes include:

  • SPA catch-all routes;
  • duplicate query values;
  • third-party URLs;
  • stale JavaScript references;
  • inactive features;
  • tracking endpoints;
  • resources that redirect to login.

Manual validation resolves these.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Katana may miss endpoints because of:

  • authentication;
  • complex JavaScript;
  • WebSockets;
  • unlinked routes;
  • dynamic state;
  • required user interaction;
  • nonstandard protocols;
  • depth limits.

A clean crawl does not prove the attack surface is complete.

docs.title: Combine Discovery Methods
docs.text:
A strong web attack-surface workflow uses multiple sources.

Browser
   |
   +-- visible routes

Katana
   |
   +-- crawled routes

ffuf
   |
   +-- guessed paths

JavaScript analysis
   |
   +-- hidden API references

Documentation
   |
   +-- intended endpoints

Merge and deduplicate these.

docs.title: Practical Crawl Workflow
docs.text:
1. Confirm scope
      |
      v
2. Confirm target responds
      |
      v
3. Understand baseline application
      |
      v
4. Run moderate Katana crawl
      |
      v
5. Save output
      |
      v
6. Check for out-of-scope URLs
      |
      v
7. Deduplicate
      |
      v
8. Review JavaScript/API paths
      |
      v
9. Classify high-value endpoints
      |
      v
10. Validate manually
      |
      v
11. Run authenticated crawl if required
      |
      v
12. Merge with ffuf/browser discovery
      |
      v
13. Feed validated inventory into testing

docs.title: Basic Crawl
docs.text: katana -u https://example.test

docs.title: Help
docs.text: katana -h

docs.title: Version
docs.text: katana -version

docs.title: Crawl from Alive Hosts
docs.text:
katana -list alive.txt

Verify exact list-input syntax with the installed version.

docs.title: Pipeline from httpx
docs.text: cat subdomains.txt | httpx -silent | katana

docs.title: Save Plain Output
docs.text: katana -u https://example.test > katana.txt

docs.title: Deduplicate Plain URLs
docs.text: sort -u katana.txt > katana-unique.txt

docs.title: Validate One URL
docs.text: curl -i https://example.test/api/example

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Target explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Scope documented.
  • [ ] Third-party domains understood.
  • [ ] Authentication requirements known.
  • [ ] Katana version recorded.
  • [ ] Request rate appropriate.
  • [ ] Crawl depth selected deliberately.

docs.title: Crawl
docs.text:
• [ ] Basic crawl performed.
  • [ ] Output saved.
  • [ ] JavaScript endpoints considered.
  • [ ] Forms reviewed.
  • [ ] Query parameters retained.
  • [ ] API routes reviewed.
  • [ ] Redirects reviewed.
  • [ ] Third-party destinations excluded.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• [ ] Approved test account used where required.
  • [ ] Authentication data protected.
  • [ ] Session expiry monitored.
  • [ ] Role-specific crawls separated.
  • [ ] Admin context used only when authorised.

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text:
• [ ] Relevant JS files reviewed.
  • [ ] Hidden API routes extracted.
  • [ ] Source maps considered.
  • [ ] Client-side secrets interpreted carefully.
  • [ ] Stale references manually validated.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• [ ] Output hostnames reviewed.
  • [ ] Wildcard scope interpreted correctly.
  • [ ] Redirect targets checked.
  • [ ] Third-party SaaS excluded unless authorised.
  • [ ] Downstream automation receives in-scope URLs only.

docs.title: Noise Reduction
docs.text:
• [ ] Static assets filtered only where appropriate.
  • [ ] Duplicate URLs removed.
  • [ ] SPA catch-all behaviour understood.
  • [ ] Calendar/pagination traps checked.
  • [ ] Filtering did not remove valuable .js or .json resources.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
• [ ] Crawl is not excessive.
  • [ ] State-changing routes treated cautiously.
  • [ ] 429 responses respected.
  • [ ] 500 spikes investigated.
  • [ ] Application stability monitored.
  • [ ] Crawl stopped if unexpected impact occurs.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] High-value endpoints manually requested.
  • [ ] Burp used where appropriate.
  • [ ] Authentication checked.
  • [ ] Authorisation checked separately.
  • [ ] Hidden routes not automatically treated as vulnerabilities.
  • [ ] Endpoint purpose understood.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Target retained.
  • [ ] Version retained.
  • [ ] Command retained.
  • [ ] Scope retained.
  • [ ] Authentication context retained.
  • [ ] Discovery source retained.
  • [ ] Timestamp retained.
  • [ ] Manual validation retained.
