docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use Katana like this:

Run Deep Crawl
      |
      v
Collect Thousands of URLs
      |
      v
Treat Every URL as Interesting

Use it like this:

Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Identify Alive Web Target
      |
      v
Select Appropriate Crawl Depth
      |
      v
Run Controlled Katana Crawl
      |
      v
Check Scope of Discovered URLs
      |
      v
Extract Useful Paths / Parameters / JS
      |
      v
Deduplicate and Classify
      |
      v
Identify High-Value Endpoints
      |
      v
Validate Manually
      |
      v
Combine With ffuf / Browser Discovery
      |
      v
Feed Confirmed Attack Surface Into Testing

Katana is most valuable as an attack-surface discovery tool.

It helps show what the application links to, references, and exposes through normal or JavaScript-driven navigation.

The crawler discovers the routes.

The tester determines which routes matter, whether they are in scope, and whether any of them contain an actual security weakness.

docs.title: Nuclei
docs.text:
Nuclei is a template-driven security scanner from ProjectDiscovery.

It is designed to automate checks for known or repeatable security conditions across authorised targets.

Typical uses include:

  • known vulnerability checks;
  • exposed panels;
  • default configurations;
  • sensitive file exposure;
  • technology-specific checks;
  • misconfiguration detection;
  • CVE-oriented testing;
  • DNS, HTTP, TCP, SSL, file, and other supported template workflows depending on version.

Nuclei is most useful when it is treated as a candidate discovery tool.

It can rapidly answer:

Does this target exhibit behaviour matching this template?

It cannot automatically answer:

Is this a confirmed, exploitable vulnerability in this environment?

Target
  |
  v
Nuclei Template
  |
  v
Matcher / Extractor
  |
  v
Template Match
  |
  v
Manual Validation
  |
  v
Security Conclusion

Authorised testing only

Use Nuclei only against systems that are explicitly authorised for testing. Template collections can include high-volume, intrusive, or state-changing checks depending on the selected templates. Review template behaviour, scope, rate, and target sensitivity before execution.

docs.title: Where Nuclei Fits
docs.text:
Nuclei usually follows asset discovery and technology identification.

Subdomains
    |
    v
httpx
    |
    v
Alive Hosts
    |
    v
Technology / Endpoint Discovery
    |
    v
Nuclei
    |
    v
Candidate Matches
    |
    v
Manual Validation

Related tools:

Web Enumeration Tools

httpx

Katana

ffuf

Burp Suite

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
Official project:

Nuclei - GitHub

Official documentation:

Nuclei Documentation

Official template repository:

Nuclei Templates - GitHub

Because Nuclei changes frequently, always verify the exact syntax supported by the installed version:

nuclei -h

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Check the installed version:

nuclei -version

If syntax differs:

nuclei -h

The local help output should be preferred over old examples.

docs.title: Template Version Matters
docs.text:
Nuclei behaviour depends on both:

Nuclei engine version

and:

Template repository version

Record both where reproducibility matters.

docs.title: Update Templates
docs.text:
Nuclei provides mechanisms for maintaining its template collection.

Because exact update syntax may evolve, check:

nuclei -h

and current official documentation.

Do not assume a template set is current simply because the Nuclei binary is current.

docs.title: Basic Scan
docs.text:
A basic target pattern is:

nuclei -u https://example.test

Depending on configuration and version, Nuclei applies templates available to the engine.

For assessment work, explicit template selection is usually preferable to uncontrolled broad scanning.

docs.title: Scan from a List
docs.text:
A common workflow is:

nuclei -l urls.txt

Use:

nuclei -h

to confirm exact list-input syntax for the installed version.

docs.title: Why Target Preparation Matters
docs.text:
Nuclei performs best when input targets are already:

  • alive;
  • in scope;
  • normalized;
  • deduplicated.

A useful workflow is:

Subdomain Enumeration
      |
      v
DNS Validation
      |
      v
httpx
      |
      v
alive.txt
      |
      v
Nuclei

docs.title: Example Pipeline
docs.text:
A common reconnaissance chain is conceptually:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -silent > alive.txt
nuclei -l alive.txt

Saving the intermediate host list improves reproducibility.

docs.title: Do Not Feed Raw Subdomains Blindly
docs.text:
A raw subdomain list may contain:

  • dead hosts;
  • stale DNS;
  • duplicates;
  • non-HTTP systems.

Use reachability validation first where the template workflow expects HTTP.

docs.title: Nuclei Templates
docs.text:
Templates describe the security condition to test.

A template may define:

  • protocol;
  • request;
  • path;
  • headers;
  • payloads;
  • matchers;
  • extractors;
  • metadata;
  • severity;
  • tags.

Conceptually:

Template
   |
   +-- Metadata
   +-- Request
   +-- Matchers
   +-- Extractors
   |
   v
Target
   |
   v
Result

docs.title: Template Matchers
docs.text:
Matchers determine whether a response satisfies expected conditions.

Potential matcher concepts include:

  • status;
  • words;
  • regex;
  • binary values;
  • DSL conditions.

A template match depends heavily on matcher quality.

docs.title: Extractors
docs.text:
Extractors retrieve interesting data from responses.

Examples may include:

  • version strings;
  • tokens;
  • identifiers;
  • response values.

An extracted value is not automatically sensitive.

Interpret it in context.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Templates commonly use severity labels such as:

info
low
medium
high
critical

These labels come from template metadata.

They are not automatically the final risk rating for the target environment.

docs.title: Template Severity Is Not Final Severity
docs.text:
For example:

Template:
high

does not automatically mean:

Pentest finding:
High

Final severity should consider:

  • exploitability;
  • prerequisites;
  • target sensitivity;
  • available controls;
  • actual impact.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags help select template families.

Conceptually:

cve
exposure
misconfig
panel
tech

The exact available tags depend on the installed template repository.

Inspect templates rather than assuming a tag exists.

docs.title: Template Selection
docs.text:
Prefer focused template selection.

A useful model is:

Technology Identified
      |
      v
Relevant Template Family
      |
      v
Focused Nuclei Scan

rather than:

Run every template everywhere

docs.title: Technology-Aware Scanning
docs.text:
Suppose reconnaissance identifies:

WordPress

A targeted scan against relevant WordPress templates may be more useful than a large unrelated template set.

Similarly:

Exchange
Jenkins
Grafana
Kubernetes

should lead to context-specific template selection.

docs.title: Discovery Before Scanning
docs.text:
A mature workflow is:

WhatWeb / Wappalyzer / httpx
       |
       v
Technology Inventory
       |
       v
Choose Relevant Nuclei Templates

Related tools:

WhatWeb

Wappalyzer

httpx

docs.title: Template Categories
docs.text:
Common conceptual template categories include:

Known CVEs
Misconfigurations
Exposures
Panels
Default Credentials
Technology Detection
Network Services
SSL / TLS
DNS

Some categories can be more intrusive than others.

Review them before use.

docs.title: Informational Templates
docs.text:
Informational templates can identify:

  • technologies;
  • services;
  • panels;
  • metadata.

These are useful for attack-surface enrichment but are not vulnerabilities by default.

docs.title: Exposure Templates
docs.text:
Exposure-oriented templates may identify:

  • configuration files;
  • debug endpoints;
  • backups;
  • source maps;
  • internal metadata.

A template match still requires manual confirmation.

docs.title: CVE Templates
docs.text:
CVE templates aim to test behaviour associated with known vulnerabilities.

Do not report a CVE solely because a template matched.

Confirm:

Product
Version
Affected condition
Response behaviour
Patch status
Exploit prerequisites

docs.title: CVE Match Example
docs.text:
Suppose Nuclei returns:

CVE-20XX-XXXX

The next process should be:

Verify target product
      |
      v
Verify affected version / condition
      |
      v
Understand template logic
      |
      v
Reproduce manually
      |
      v
Consult vendor advisory
      |
      v
Confirm finding

docs.title: Vendor Advisories
docs.text:
For known vulnerabilities, prefer the vendor advisory where available.

Use Nuclei as:

Detection mechanism

not:

Primary source of vulnerability truth

docs.title: False Positive Risk
docs.text:
Nuclei may produce false positives because of:

  • generic matchers;
  • custom error pages;
  • reverse proxies;
  • WAFs;
  • version banners;
  • shared hosting;
  • redirects;
  • application rewrites;
  • stale templates.

Manual validation is required.

docs.title: False Negative Risk
docs.text:
Nuclei can also miss vulnerabilities because of:

  • custom paths;
  • authentication requirements;
  • WAF interference;
  • altered responses;
  • non-default configuration;
  • unsupported versions;
  • incomplete template coverage.

A clean Nuclei run does not prove the target is secure.

docs.title: Baseline Behaviour
docs.text:
Before trusting a match, understand the target's normal response.

For HTTP templates inspect:

Status
Headers
Body
Redirects
Content length
Application behaviour

This helps distinguish genuine matches from generic responses.

docs.title: Custom 404 Pages
docs.text:
A custom 404 page may contain words that accidentally satisfy weak template matchers.

Reference:

0xdf - Default 404 Pages

Compare the matched path against a random nonexistent path.

docs.title: Soft 404s
docs.text:
If every random path returns:

HTTP 200

with the same application body, exposure templates may produce misleading results.

Use manual validation.

docs.title: WAF Block Pages
docs.text:
A WAF may return the same block page for many requests.

Example:

403
Access denied

A matcher looking only for status or a common phrase may produce false positives.

Compare with normal blocked traffic.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Effects
docs.text:
A reverse proxy may:

  • rewrite status codes;
  • rewrite headers;
  • normalize paths;
  • serve generic errors.

Understand which layer generated the response.

docs.title: Authenticated Targets
docs.text:
Some findings only exist after login.

Nuclei supports custom headers and other input mechanisms depending on version.

For authenticated testing, use approved test accounts and protect secrets.

docs.title: Authorization Header
docs.text:
Conceptual example:

Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED>

Use exact current header-input options from:

nuclei -h

Avoid exposing tokens in shell history.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Authenticated web applications may require session cookies.

Use:

Cookie: session=<REDACTED>

only with approved test sessions.

Session state may expire during long scans.

docs.title: Role-Specific Testing
docs.text:
Different roles may expose different vulnerabilities.

Example:

Unauthenticated
Normal user
Administrator

Keep each scan context separate.

Label evidence clearly.

docs.title: Template Intrusiveness
docs.text:
Not all templates are equivalent.

Potential behaviour may include:

Simple GET
POST
Special headers
Payload generation
OOB interaction
State-changing request

Review high-impact templates before running them.

docs.title: Read Template Source
docs.text:
Before using a sensitive template:

  1. open the YAML;
  2. inspect the request;
  3. inspect matchers;
  4. inspect payloads;
  5. identify whether state changes are possible.

Templates are readable security logic.

docs.title: Safe Default Principle
docs.text:
Prefer:

Read-only or low-impact templates

before:

intrusive templates

Increase test intensity only when necessary.

docs.title: Request Volume
docs.text:
Nuclei can generate large volumes of traffic.

Request count depends on:

  • number of targets;
  • number of templates;
  • number of requests per template;
  • payload combinations.

Estimate scale before starting.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Control request rate according to:

  • rules of engagement;
  • production sensitivity;
  • WAF;
  • target capacity.

Consult:

nuclei -h

for current rate-control options.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Higher concurrency improves speed but increases target load.

Do not maximize concurrency by default.

Start conservatively.

docs.title: 429 Responses
docs.text:
If the target begins returning:

429 Too Many Requests

reduce the scanning rate.

Do not try to overwhelm rate controls.

docs.title: 500 Errors
docs.text:
If scanning causes increasing:

500 Internal Server Error

responses:

Stop
Review
Reduce intensity

Nuclei scanning is not load testing.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
Slow targets may create false negatives if request timeouts are too short.

However, increasing timeouts significantly can make broad scans very slow.

Tune based on target behaviour.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
Retries can improve reliability against unstable connections but increase request volume.

Use them carefully.

docs.title: Template Workflows
docs.text:
Nuclei supports workflow and chaining concepts depending on version.

These can conditionally run relevant templates based on prior results.

Conceptually:

Detect Technology
      |
      v
Run Relevant Checks

This can reduce unnecessary scanning.

Use current official documentation for exact workflow support.

docs.title: Custom Templates
docs.text:
One of Nuclei's strongest features is custom templates.

Custom templates can encode repeatable checks discovered during an assessment.

Example use cases:

  • organisation-specific exposures;
  • regression testing;
  • known internal misconfiguration;
  • recurring response patterns.

docs.title: Custom Template Workflow
docs.text:
Manual Finding
      |
      v
Understand Exact Behaviour
      |
      v
Write Template
      |
      v
Test Against Known Positive
      |
      v
Test Against Known Negative
      |
      v
Use for Regression

docs.title: Known Positive
docs.text:
A custom template should first be tested against a target known to exhibit the condition.

Confirm:

Expected match occurs

docs.title: Known Negative
docs.text:
Then test against a target known not to exhibit the condition.

Confirm:

No match

This helps reduce false positives.

docs.title: Matcher Quality
docs.text:
Weak matcher:

status == 200

Stronger matcher concept:

status == expected
AND
unique response marker exists
AND
known error marker absent

Template quality determines scanner quality.

docs.title: Multiple Match Conditions
docs.text:
When possible, require multiple independent indicators.

For example:

Specific status
+
Unique response string
+
Header

This is stronger than one generic word match.

docs.title: Template Metadata
docs.text:
Useful metadata may include:

name
author
severity
description
reference
tags

Keep custom templates well documented.

docs.title: References in Templates
docs.text:
For known vulnerabilities, include authoritative references such as:

  • vendor advisory;
  • CVE record;
  • original research.

Avoid relying solely on copied blogs.

docs.title: Template Naming
docs.text:
Use descriptive template names.

Example:

internal-backup-config-exposure

instead of:

test123

This improves maintenance.

docs.title: Custom Template Repository
docs.text:
For organisation-specific testing, store approved templates in a controlled repository.

Example:

templates/
├── exposures/
├── misconfigurations/
├── regression/
└── internal/

Use version control.

docs.title: Template Review
docs.text:
Treat Nuclei templates like executable test logic.

Review changes before merging them into shared repositories.

docs.title: Third-Party Templates
docs.text:
Community templates can be useful but should be trusted carefully.

Before running third-party templates:

  • inspect source;
  • inspect payloads;
  • inspect OOB actions;
  • confirm target impact.

Do not blindly run unknown template packs.

docs.title: Signed Templates
docs.text:
Nuclei has introduced template integrity and signing-related capabilities over time.

Use current official documentation to understand the exact behaviour of the installed version.

Template trust matters when scanning sensitive environments.

docs.title: Out-of-Band Testing
docs.text:
Some templates may rely on external interaction.

This can support testing for vulnerabilities where the application causes:

  • DNS lookup;
  • HTTP callback;
  • other supported interaction.

Interactsh is commonly used in this context.

Related tool:

Interactsh

docs.title: OOB Template Model
docs.text:
Nuclei Request
      |
      v
Target
      |
      v
Target Makes Callback
      |
      v
Interactsh
      |
      v
Correlation

This can help identify blind server-side behaviour.

docs.title: OOB Does Not Automatically Mean SSRF
docs.text:
A callback may result from:

  • URL fetch;
  • XML parser;
  • template processing;
  • email security scanner;
  • asynchronous backend job.

Determine which application component caused it.

docs.title: DNS Interaction
docs.text:
A DNS lookup proves:

Some component resolved the supplied domain

It does not automatically prove:

HTTP access

or:

internal network access

Interpret the observed interaction accurately.

docs.title: HTTP Interaction
docs.text:
An HTTP callback provides stronger evidence that a component made an outbound web request.

Still determine:

  • source;
  • headers;
  • timing;
  • application function.

docs.title: Nuclei and Interactsh
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Focused Nuclei Template
      |
      v
OOB Payload
      |
      v
Interactsh Interaction
      |
      v
Manual Reproduction

Never rely solely on the scanner label.

docs.title: Nuclei and Katana
docs.text:
Katana can generate a richer URL inventory.

Katana
  |
  v
Discovered URLs
  |
  v
Filter High-Value Targets
  |
  v
Nuclei

Related tool:

Katana

docs.title: Nuclei and ffuf
docs.text:
ffuf may discover hidden resources.

Then:

ffuf
  |
  v
Hidden Endpoint
  |
  v
Manual Validation
  |
  v
Relevant Nuclei Check

Related tool:

ffuf

docs.title: Nuclei and Burp Suite
docs.text:
Burp is useful for validating Nuclei results manually.

Nuclei Match
      |
      v
Capture Request
      |
      v
Burp Repeater
      |
      v
Modify One Variable
      |
      v
Confirm Behaviour

Related tool:

Burp Suite

docs.title: Nuclei and sqlmap
docs.text:
Nuclei may identify a candidate SQL-related issue through a template.

Do not automatically hand every parameter to sqlmap.

Instead:

Nuclei candidate
      |
      v
Manual SQLi validation
      |
      v
sqlmap where justified

Related tool:

sqlmap

docs.title: Nuclei and httpx
docs.text:
A strong broad workflow is:

Subdomains
   |
   v
httpx
   |
   v
Alive Web Hosts
   |
   v
Nuclei

httpx helps reduce dead-target noise.

docs.title: Nuclei and WhatWeb/Wappalyzer
docs.text:
Technology discovery can improve template selection.

Technology
   |
   v
Relevant Templates
   |
   v
Lower Noise

This is more efficient than indiscriminate scanning.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Nuclei supports several output formats depending on version.

For reproducible work, structured output is useful.

Check:

nuclei -h

for exact current options.

docs.title: Plain Output
docs.text:
Plain output is convenient for quick review.

A result may conceptually contain:

template-id
protocol
severity
target

Exact formatting varies by version.

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text:
Structured JSON output can support:

  • ingestion;
  • deduplication;
  • reporting;
  • correlation;
  • automation.

Inspect the actual schema produced by your installed version.

docs.title: Save Results
docs.text:
A practical approach is to preserve:

raw Nuclei output

and separately maintain:

validated findings

Do not overwrite raw evidence with a manually edited result file.

docs.title: Result Deduplication
docs.text:
The same underlying issue may match several templates.

Example:

exposed-config
sensitive-file
framework-config-exposure

all point to the same file.

Do not report three vulnerabilities.

Consolidate around the root cause.

docs.title: Duplicate CVE Templates
docs.text:
Different template variants may identify the same CVE.

Use:

one confirmed vulnerability

not:

one finding per template match

docs.title: Severity Deduplication
docs.text:
If duplicate templates use different severities, do not select the highest one automatically.

Assess actual risk independently.

docs.title: Result Prioritisation
docs.text:
A useful triage order may be:

Potential authentication bypass
Remote code execution candidate
Sensitive credential exposure
High-impact misconfiguration
Known CVE
Interesting exposure
Technology information

But environment and scope may change priorities.

docs.title: Informational Noise
docs.text:
Informational results can be valuable during reconnaissance but should not automatically appear in the findings section.

Examples include:

  • technology detection;
  • server banner;
  • panel identification.

Keep them in the attack-surface inventory.

docs.title: Practical CVE Validation Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose Nuclei returns:

CVE-20XX-YYYY
Target: https://example.test
Severity: high

Validation process:

  1. open the template;
  2. identify the exact request;
  3. identify matchers;
  4. review vendor advisory;
  5. confirm target product;
  6. reproduce request manually;
  7. compare response against unaffected behaviour;
  8. determine actual impact.

Only then report the CVE if supported.

docs.title: Practical Exposure Scenario
docs.text:
Nuclei reports:

configuration-file

on:

https://example.test/.env

Validate manually:

curl -i https://example.test/.env

If the response contains actual application configuration, stop unnecessary collection.

Redact secrets.

The finding is:

public exposure of sensitive configuration

not:

Nuclei matched a template.

docs.title: Practical Panel Scenario
docs.text:
Nuclei identifies:

administration panel

This may simply mean:

/admin

exists.

Next determine:

  • authentication required;
  • intended exposure;
  • version disclosure;
  • security controls.

An admin panel is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: Practical Misconfiguration Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose a template reports:

directory listing enabled

Validate manually.

If confirmed, determine:

Which files are exposed?

Are they sensitive?

Is indexing intended?

The impact depends on exposed content.

docs.title: Practical OOB Scenario
docs.text:
A template sends a unique external interaction value.

An interaction is observed.

Do not stop at:

callback received

Correlate:

request timestamp
callback timestamp
interaction protocol
unique correlation value
application action

Then reproduce manually where appropriate.

docs.title: Result Validation Questions
docs.text:
For every Nuclei result ask:

What exact request caused the match?

Which matcher succeeded?

Could a generic page produce the same result?

Is the product/version correct?

Is authentication required?

Does a WAF or proxy affect the response?

What actual security boundary is crossed?

docs.title: False Positive Example
docs.text:
Template expects:

200
+
"dashboard"

The target's generic 404 page contains:

Return to dashboard

Result:

Template matches nonexistent path

Manual baseline testing reveals the false positive.

docs.title: False Negative Example
docs.text:
A vulnerable admin endpoint exists at:

/custom-admin/

but the template tests only:

/admin/

No match occurs.

The application may still be vulnerable.

docs.title: Authentication False Negative
docs.text:
A template checks only unauthenticated behaviour.

The vulnerable feature exists only for a normal authenticated user.

Nuclei may miss it unless the correct session context is supplied.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

Nuclei found CVE-20XX-YYYY.

Prefer:

The application exhibited the vulnerable behaviour described in
CVE-20XX-YYYY. Manual reproduction confirmed that the affected endpoint
accepted the crafted request and produced the expected vulnerable
response on the tested product version.

docs.title: Reporting an Unconfirmed Match
docs.text:
Example:

Nuclei initially identified a possible exposed configuration file.
Manual validation showed that the matched response was the
application's generic soft-404 page and did not contain configuration
data. The candidate was therefore rejected as a false positive.

docs.title: Reporting a Version-Only Match
docs.text:
Avoid:

Vulnerable because version banner is X.

Prefer:

The application disclosed version X. The version may fall within a
published affected range, but vulnerability applicability was not
confirmed through behavioural testing.

If version disclosure alone is not a finding, keep it as reconnaissance context.

docs.title: Reporting a Known Vulnerability
docs.text:
A strong report includes:

Product
Affected version/build
CVE
Vendor advisory
Affected endpoint/component
Prerequisites
Manual reproduction
Observed impact
Remediation

Nuclei should be listed as supporting detection evidence if useful.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Remediation depends on the underlying issue.

Examples include:

  • apply vendor patch;
  • upgrade affected software;
  • remove exposed configuration;
  • disable unused service;
  • restrict administration interfaces;
  • correct TLS configuration;
  • add authentication;
  • fix access control.

Do not recommend:

Block Nuclei

as the root remediation.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation:

Original Manual Test
      |
      v
Expected Safe Behaviour

Then optionally:

Nuclei Regression Template

Use the manual test as primary validation.

docs.title: Nuclei for Regression Testing
docs.text:
Nuclei is particularly useful after a confirmed issue has been converted into a reliable custom template.

Finding
   |
   v
Custom Template
   |
   v
Fix
   |
   v
Retest
   |
   v
Future Regression Scan

This can support continuous validation.

docs.title: CI/CD Use
docs.text:
Nuclei can be incorporated into controlled CI/CD or security automation workflows.

Potential use cases include:

  • staging checks;
  • regression testing;
  • known exposure detection.

Avoid automatically launching intrusive template collections against production on every pipeline run.

docs.title: Template Governance
docs.text:
For organisation-wide automation, define:

Approved template sources
Approved severity/tags
Excluded intrusive templates
Rate limits
Target environment
Exception process

This improves predictability.

docs.title: Production vs Staging
docs.text:
Staging may tolerate:

  • broader scans;
  • experimental templates;
  • more verbose diagnostics.

Production should generally use more conservative, reviewed checks.

docs.title: Detection and Telemetry
docs.text:
Nuclei activity may be visible through:

  • web server logs;
  • WAF;
  • reverse proxy logs;
  • network IDS;
  • DNS logs;
  • SIEM.

Large template collections can create recognisable request patterns.

docs.title: Purple Teaming
docs.text:
A controlled Nuclei scan can test:

  • vulnerability-scanner detection;
  • suspicious path enumeration;
  • exploit-attempt visibility;
  • WAF response.
Nuclei
  |
  v
HTTP Requests
  |
  v
WAF / Web Logs
  |
  v
SIEM
  |
  v
Detection Review

Related section:

Purple Teaming

docs.title: Detection Should Focus on Behaviour
docs.text:
Blocking the string:

Nuclei

or a particular User-Agent may be fragile.

More useful detection may consider:

  • unusual path combinations;
  • known exploit request structures;
  • high request rates;
  • suspicious protocol behaviour.

Tool-specific detection can still supplement behavioural coverage.

docs.title: Operational Safety
docs.text:
Before scanning ask:

How many targets?

How many templates?

How many requests per template?

Are templates state-changing?

Could OOB callbacks leave artefacts?

Can target handle this rate?

Estimate scan impact.

docs.title: High-Risk Templates
docs.text:
Templates involving:

  • authentication attempts;
  • uploads;
  • write operations;
  • destructive requests;
  • heavy payload sets;

deserve additional review.

Do not assume every community template is safe for production.

docs.title: Read-Only First
docs.text:
Use:

Technology / Exposure / Low-Impact Checks

before:

Intrusive Behavioural Templates

unless the engagement specifically requires deeper validation.

docs.title: Stop Conditions
docs.text:
Stop or reduce scanning if:

  • service instability appears;
  • 429 responses increase;
  • 500 responses increase significantly;
  • unexpected data is exposed;
  • third-party targets appear;
  • security team requests a stop.

docs.title: Third-Party Scope
docs.text:
Templates may follow or interact with external services.

Always enforce scope.

A discovered SaaS URL is not automatically authorised.

docs.title: DNS Scope
docs.text:
DNS templates can affect a different set of targets than HTTP templates.

Confirm which domains are authorised for DNS testing.

docs.title: Network Templates
docs.text:
Nuclei supports non-HTTP protocols through relevant template types.

These can interact directly with:

  • TCP services;
  • TLS endpoints;
  • DNS;
  • other supported protocols.

Use only against explicitly authorised hosts and ports.

docs.title: Host and Port Scope
docs.text:
If scope is defined as:

https://example.test

do not automatically assume every network port on the resolved IP is authorised.

Scope definition matters.

docs.title: Cloud and Shared Infrastructure
docs.text:
A hostname may resolve to:

  • CDN;
  • shared cloud;
  • reverse proxy.

Do not scan unrelated infrastructure based solely on IP ownership or reachability.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each validated Nuclei result, retain:

Target:
Nuclei version:
Template ID:
Template revision/source:
Command:
Timestamp:
Authentication context:
Raw match:
Template request:
Matcher logic:
Manual reproduction:
Vendor reference:
Conclusion:

docs.title: Evidence Example
docs.text:
Target:
https://example.test

Template:
example-config-exposure

Nuclei result:
Template matched /config.json

Manual validation:
Direct GET reproduced the response and confirmed that internal
configuration values were publicly accessible.

Conclusion:
Public exposure of sensitive configuration confirmed.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Record:

Nuclei version
Template version
Target list
Template selection
Rate settings
Authentication context

Without these, repeating a scan later may produce different results.

docs.title: Raw vs Validated Output
docs.text:
Maintain separation:

results/
├── nuclei-raw.json
└── validated-findings.md

Raw scanner results are evidence candidates.

Validated findings contain conclusions.

docs.text: nuclei -h

docs.text: nuclei -version

docs.title: Single Target
docs.text: nuclei -u https://example.test

docs.text: nuclei -l alive.txt

docs.title: Pipeline Preparation
docs.text:

Then:

nuclei -l alive.txt

For exact template, severity, tag, rate, output, and authentication options, always confirm the current syntax with:

nuclei -h

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Targets explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Target list validated.
  • [ ] Dead targets removed where practical.
  • [ ] Nuclei version recorded.
  • [ ] Template collection version recorded.
  • [ ] Scope documented.
  • [ ] Authentication context documented.
  • [ ] Production sensitivity understood.

docs.title: Template Selection
docs.text:
• [ ] Relevant technology known where possible.
  • [ ] Templates selected deliberately.
  • [ ] Intrusive templates reviewed.
  • [ ] Third-party templates inspected.
  • [ ] Custom templates tested against known positives.
  • [ ] Custom templates tested against known negatives.

docs.title: Rate and Stability
docs.text:
• [ ] Rate selected conservatively.
  • [ ] Concurrency appropriate.
  • [ ] 429 responses monitored.
  • [ ] 500 response spikes monitored.
  • [ ] Timeouts appropriate.
  • [ ] Scan stopped if instability occurs.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• [ ] Approved test identity used.
  • [ ] Tokens/cookies protected.
  • [ ] Session expiry monitored.
  • [ ] Role-specific scans separated.
  • [ ] Secrets excluded from public logs.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• [ ] HTTP scope confirmed.
  • [ ] DNS scope confirmed where relevant.
  • [ ] Host/port scope confirmed.
  • [ ] Third-party systems excluded.
  • [ ] CDN/shared infrastructure handled carefully.
  • [ ] Redirect destinations reviewed.

docs.title: Result Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Exact template reviewed.
  • [ ] Request understood.
  • [ ] Matcher understood.
  • [ ] Extracted values understood.
  • [ ] Generic error page ruled out.
  • [ ] Soft 404 ruled out.
  • [ ] WAF block page ruled out.
  • [ ] Product/version confirmed where relevant.
  • [ ] Vendor advisory checked for CVEs.
  • [ ] Manual reproduction performed.

docs.title: OOB
docs.text:
• [ ] Interaction mechanism understood.
  • [ ] Unique correlation value used.
  • [ ] Timestamp retained.
  • [ ] Protocol identified.
  • [ ] Callback source interpreted carefully.
  • [ ] OOB callback not automatically labelled SSRF.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Target retained.
  • [ ] Nuclei version retained.
  • [ ] Template ID retained.
  • [ ] Template source/revision retained.
  • [ ] Command retained.
  • [ ] Raw output retained.
  • [ ] Manual validation retained.
  • [ ] Sensitive values redacted.
  • [ ] Final conclusion separated from scanner result.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• [ ] Scanner match not treated as root cause.
  • [ ] CVE not reported from banner alone.
  • [ ] Severity independently assessed.
  • [ ] Finding describes actual behaviour.
  • [ ] Remediation addresses root cause.
  • [ ] Retest criteria explicit.

docs.title: Select and Review Templates
docs.text:
Choose templates based on confirmed scope, technology, endpoint behavior, assessment objective, and risk. Record the template source, version or commit, author, tags, severity, variables, request method, matcher, extractor, and whether the template can alter state or generate external interactions. Prefer the official ProjectDiscovery collection or an approved reviewed repository; read the template before using an unfamiliar or intrusive check.

Severity is a prioritisation signal from the template, not the final severity of the finding. A template may match a version, banner, header, default page, or generic response without proving exposure or exploitability in the target context.

docs.title: Controlled Scanning
docs.text:
Confirm target scope before every run, exclude third-party infrastructure unless explicitly included, and use conservative rate, concurrency, timeout, retry, and host-error settings. Authenticated scanning should use dedicated least-privilege accounts and approved test data; protect cookies, tokens, and output files.

Interpret matcher and extractor behavior:

Template request
      -> Matcher condition
      -> Extracted value or evidence
      -> Candidate result
      -> Manual reproduction
      -> Security conclusion

A matcher may depend on status, word, regex, DSL, headers, body, or a combination. An extractor may only display a value; it does not prove that the value is sensitive or usable. Check generic pages, soft 404s, WAF/CDN responses, redirects, cached content, authentication state, version backports, and template assumptions before accepting a result.

docs.title: Manual Validation and Evidence
docs.text:
Read the template and reproduce the request with Burp Suite, curl, the relevant client, or another approved tool. Establish a baseline, change one condition where appropriate, and validate the smallest non-destructive proof. Confirm product/version, configuration, authorization, reachability, and impact with a safe read-back or owner-approved test.

Capture target and scope, template path and hash or commit, Nuclei version, command options, timestamp, request and response with secrets redacted, matcher or extractor that fired, baseline comparison, manual validation, and evidence of the actual security consequence. A Nuclei match is a candidate, not an automatic vulnerability.

docs.title: Troubleshooting, Remediation, and Retesting
docs.text:
For inconsistent results, check template version, target normalization, redirects, virtual hosts, TLS verification, rate limits, authentication headers, cookies, WAF behavior, concurrency, retries, and whether the response came from a shared cache or intermediary. Run the template alone at low rate and compare the raw response with a manual request.

Use the vendor advisory, product configuration, or application owner to remediate the underlying weakness. Retest with the same template version and options, then manually confirm the old response is absent or the vulnerable behavior is no longer reachable. Run a relevant neighboring template or manual check to detect a narrow fix without treating unrelated matches as proof.

docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use Nuclei like this:

Run All Templates
      |
      v
Receive Match
      |
      v
Copy Severity
      |
      v
Report Vulnerability

Use it like this:

Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Prepare Valid Targets
      |
      v
Understand Technology
      |
      v
Select Relevant Templates
      |
      v
Review Intrusive Behaviour
      |
      v
Run Controlled Nuclei Scan
      |
      v
Identify Template Match
      |
      v
Read Template
      |
      v
Understand Request and Matcher
      |
      v
Rule Out Generic / WAF / Soft-404 Behaviour
      |
      v
Validate Product and Version
      |
      v
Consult Vendor Advisory Where Relevant
      |
      v
Reproduce Manually
      |
      v
Determine Actual Security Impact
      |
      v
Capture Evidence
      |
      v
Report Underlying Weakness

Nuclei is most valuable as a fast and repeatable way to identify security conditions that deserve deeper validation.

The template provides the hypothesis.

The target behaviour and manual evidence determine whether a real vulnerability exists.

docs.title: sqlmap
docs.text:
sqlmap is an automated SQL injection testing tool.

It can help identify and validate SQL injection conditions in authorised web applications and APIs.

Typical uses include:

  • testing query-string parameters;
  • testing form data;
  • testing JSON bodies;
  • testing cookies;
  • testing selected HTTP headers;
  • fingerprinting a database management system;
  • confirming injectable parameters;
  • automating repetitive SQL injection checks.

sqlmap should be used after a plausible SQL injection candidate has been identified.

A strong workflow is:

Interesting Parameter
      |
      v
Manual SQLi Hypothesis
      |
      v
Controlled sqlmap Validation
      |
      v
Manual Confirmation
      |
      v
Evidence
      |
      v
Security Conclusion

Authorised testing only

Use sqlmap only against applications and databases that are explicitly authorised for testing. Some sqlmap capabilities can generate large request volumes, enumerate sensitive database information, modify data, write files, or perform operating-system interaction depending on the database and permissions. Start with low-impact validation and use intrusive functionality only when explicitly required and authorised.

docs.title: Where sqlmap Fits
docs.text:
sqlmap is not usually the first tool in a web application assessment.

A better sequence is:

Application Mapping
      |
      v
Parameter Discovery
      |
      v
Manual Testing
      |
      v
SQL Injection Candidate
      |
      v
sqlmap
      |
      v
Controlled Validation

Related tools:

Web Application Testing Tools

Burp Suite

ffuf

Katana

docs.title: Official Project
docs.text:
Official project:

sqlmap - GitHub

Official site:

sqlmap

Because sqlmap evolves over time, verify exact current syntax using:

sqlmap -h

For extended options:

sqlmap -hh

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Check:

sqlmap --version

and:

sqlmap -h

On Kali Linux, sqlmap is commonly available through package management or may already be installed.

docs.title: What sqlmap Does
docs.text:
sqlmap automates SQL injection testing by sending modified requests and analysing response behaviour.

Conceptually:

HTTP Request
    |
    v
Parameter
    |
    v
sqlmap Payloads
    |
    v
Application
    |
    v
Database
    |
    v
Response Differences

It attempts to determine whether user-controlled input can influence SQL execution.

docs.title: What sqlmap Does Not Prove Automatically
docs.text:
A positive-looking response does not automatically prove:

Critical database compromise

The actual impact depends on:

  • injectable context;
  • database privileges;
  • affected query;
  • authentication;
  • available controls;
  • reachable data.

Do not overstate findings.

docs.title: Manual Testing First
docs.text:
Before using sqlmap, understand the parameter manually.

For example:

GET /product?id=10

Questions include:

Does changing id affect database-backed content?

Does a quote produce an application error?

Are there timing differences?

Is input numeric or string-based?

Does the application use an ORM?

Use Burp Repeater or curl to establish baseline behaviour.

docs.title: Baseline Request
docs.text:
A baseline request might be:

GET /product?id=10 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
Cookie: session=<REDACTED>

Record the normal response before automated testing.

docs.title: Basic GET Parameter Testing
docs.text:
A simple sqlmap pattern is:

sqlmap -u "https://example.test/product?id=10"

sqlmap will identify parameters in the URL and test according to its selected options and defaults.

For production assessments, use deliberate scope and intensity settings rather than blindly accepting aggressive defaults.

docs.title: Specify a Parameter
docs.text:
If multiple parameters exist, focus on one.

Example:

sqlmap -u "https://example.test/product?id=10&lang=en" -p id

This reduces unnecessary testing.

docs.title: Why Parameter Selection Matters
docs.text:
Suppose the request contains:

id
lang
sort
page

Testing all four may create unnecessary traffic.

If manual testing points to:

id

start there.

docs.title: POST Form Testing
docs.text:
Example request body:

username=test&search=book

A common pattern is:

sqlmap -u "https://example.test/search" --data="username=test&search=book" -p search

Use exact current syntax from:

sqlmap -h

docs.title: JSON Requests
docs.text:
APIs often use JSON.

Example:

{
  "id": 10,
  "filter": "active"
}

For complex JSON, a raw request file from Burp is often clearer than manually reconstructing the request on the command line.

docs.title: Raw Request Files
docs.text:
One of the most useful sqlmap workflows is testing a raw HTTP request captured from Burp Suite.

Conceptually:

Burp
 |
 v
Capture Valid Request
 |
 v
Save Request
 |
 v
sqlmap

This preserves:

  • method;
  • headers;
  • cookies;
  • body;
  • content type.

docs.title: Request File Workflow
docs.text:
Save a valid request as:

request.txt

Then use the current sqlmap request-file option documented by:

sqlmap -h

This is especially useful for:

  • JSON;
  • custom headers;
  • authenticated requests;
  • complex POST bodies.

docs.title: Burp Suite Integration
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

Burp Proxy
    |
    v
Capture Valid Request
    |
    v
Repeater
    |
    v
Manual SQLi Candidate
    |
    v
Save Raw Request
    |
    v
sqlmap
    |
    v
Manual Confirmation

Related tool:

Burp Suite

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Authenticated endpoints require valid session context.

sqlmap may need:

  • cookies;
  • Authorization headers;
  • custom headers.

Use only approved test accounts.

Protect live credentials and session values.

docs.title: Cookie-Based Sessions
docs.text:
A session might be represented as:

Cookie: session=<REDACTED>

If the session expires during testing, results may become unreliable.

Symptoms can include:

302 to login
401
403
generic login page

docs.title: Bearer Tokens
docs.text:
API requests may require:

Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED>

Avoid storing live bearer tokens in public notes or shell history.

Prefer raw request files or controlled environment variables where appropriate.

docs.title: Role Context
docs.text:
A parameter may behave differently for:

Unauthenticated user
Normal user
Administrator

Always record the current role.

A SQL injection reachable only by an administrator has a different risk profile than an unauthenticated one.

docs.title: CSRF Tokens
docs.text:
Some applications require changing CSRF values.

Static request replay may fail when:

token expires

or:

token must match session

If sqlmap cannot maintain the required workflow, manual testing or custom scripting may be more appropriate.

docs.title: Stateful Applications
docs.text:
sqlmap works best when a request can be replayed independently.

Complex workflows such as:

Login
Get token
Create object
Submit query
Confirm operation

may require custom automation.

Do not force sqlmap into a workflow it cannot model reliably.

docs.title: Parameter Locations
docs.text:
Potential injectable input locations include:

Query parameters
POST form fields
JSON values
Cookies
Selected headers
URI path segments

The input source must eventually influence SQL syntax for SQL injection to exist.

docs.title: SQL Injection Model
docs.text:
A simplified vulnerable flow is:

User Input
   |
   v
String Concatenation
   |
   v
SQL Query
   |
   v
Database Execution

A safer flow is:

User Input
   |
   v
Bound Parameter
   |
   v
Prepared Query
   |
   v
Database Execution

docs.title: ORM Does Not Automatically Prevent SQL Injection
docs.text:
Object-relational mapping libraries often provide safe parameterisation.

However, SQL injection can still occur through:

  • raw query APIs;
  • string-built filters;
  • unsafe query fragments;
  • dynamic order clauses;
  • framework escape hatches.

Manual source review can help confirm the root cause.

docs.title: Error-Based Behaviour
docs.text:
One SQL injection indicator is database error behaviour.

Example concept:

Normal input
      |
      v
Normal response

Quote / malformed input
      |
      v
Database-related error

A database-looking error is suggestive, not definitive.

docs.title: Generic Error Pages
docs.text:
Applications may return:

500 Internal Server Error

for many malformed inputs.

Do not assume:

500
=
SQL injection

Identify database-specific evidence or differential behaviour.

docs.title: Boolean-Based Behaviour
docs.text:
Boolean-based SQL injection may produce response differences based on a condition.

Conceptually:

Condition TRUE
      |
      v
Response A

Condition FALSE
      |
      v
Response B

Differences may involve:

  • page content;
  • row count;
  • status;
  • response length.

sqlmap automates this analysis.

docs.title: Time-Based Behaviour
docs.text:
Time-based SQL injection relies on consistent delay differences.

Conceptually:

Normal request:
~200 ms

Conditional delay request:
~5000 ms

Timing is noisy.

Confirm repeated behaviour before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: Network Noise
docs.text:
Timing can be affected by:

  • latency;
  • load balancer;
  • WAF;
  • backend load;
  • database load;
  • caching.

A single slow response proves nothing.

docs.title: UNION-Based Behaviour
docs.text:
UNION-based techniques may be possible where a query result is reflected in the application response.

The application context and database query structure determine whether this technique applies.

Do not use aggressive enumeration merely because UNION-based behaviour is possible.

docs.title: Stacked Queries
docs.text:
Some database/application combinations may allow multiple statements.

Support depends on:

  • DBMS;
  • driver;
  • API;
  • query context.

The existence of SQL injection does not mean stacked queries are supported.

docs.title: DBMS Fingerprinting
docs.text:
sqlmap may attempt to identify the backend DBMS.

Possible database platforms include:

Microsoft SQL Server
MySQL / MariaDB
PostgreSQL
Oracle
SQLite

Confirm the result where important.

docs.title: Why DBMS Matters
docs.text:
Different DBMS platforms have different:

  • syntax;
  • functions;
  • permissions;
  • metadata;
  • error messages;
  • exploitation possibilities.

The backend database affects both testing and remediation.

docs.title: Version Detection
docs.text:
Database version detection may rely on behavioural or response characteristics.

Do not report an exact database version unless the evidence is sufficiently reliable.

docs.title: Database Privileges
docs.text:
An injectable query executes with the privileges of the database account used by the application.

This may be:

read-only application account

or:

highly privileged database account

These create very different impact.

docs.title: Least Privilege Matters
docs.text:
SQL injection impact is substantially reduced when the application account has only the permissions it requires.

The application should normally not use:

database administrator

or equivalent broad privileges for routine operations.

docs.title: Database Enumeration
docs.text:
sqlmap can support database enumeration.

This is more intrusive than simply confirming injection.

Before enumerating:

Do I need database names to prove the issue?

Do I need table names?

Do I need actual records?

Usually the minimum evidence is preferable.

docs.title: Minimal Proof Principle
docs.text:
Prefer:

Confirm injection
Identify DBMS
Demonstrate controlled database response

over:

Dump entire database

unless broader impact validation is explicitly required.

docs.title: Sensitive Data
docs.text:
Database enumeration may expose:

  • personal data;
  • credentials;
  • financial records;
  • health information;
  • application secrets.

Stop unnecessary collection once the security impact is clear.

docs.title: Do Not Dump Everything
docs.text:
A vulnerability can often be demonstrated without exporting data.

For example:

Controlled Boolean Difference
+
DBMS Identification

may be sufficient to confirm SQL injection.

docs.title: Metadata Before Data
docs.text:
Where additional validation is required, prefer metadata over real business data.

Conceptually:

Database Version
Schema Name
Table Name

before:

Customer Records

This reduces exposure.

docs.title: Row Limiting
docs.text:
If limited data retrieval is explicitly necessary, retrieve the minimum amount needed.

Do not collect thousands of records to demonstrate read access.

docs.title: Credential Tables
docs.text:
Avoid automatically dumping:

users
credentials
passwords

simply because sqlmap can identify them.

The assessment objective should determine whether this is required.

docs.title: Password Hashes
docs.text:
Database password hashes are sensitive credential material.

Do not export or crack them unless explicitly authorised.

The SQL injection itself may already demonstrate sufficient impact.

docs.title: File Read Capabilities
docs.text:
Some database platforms and configurations may allow database users to read local files.

This depends on:

  • DBMS;
  • account permissions;
  • database configuration;
  • operating-system access.

Do not test filesystem access unless needed and authorised.

docs.title: File Write Capabilities
docs.text:
Writing files through the database is significantly more intrusive.

Do not use file-write features as routine SQL injection validation.

docs.title: Operating-System Interaction
docs.text:
Some SQL injection scenarios can potentially lead to operating-system interaction depending on:

  • DBMS;
  • privileges;
  • configuration.

This crosses into a higher-impact test category.

Use only where explicitly authorised and necessary.

docs.title: SQL Injection vs RCE
docs.text:
Do not automatically write:

SQL injection
=
Remote code execution

A more accurate model is:

SQL Injection
      |
      v
Database Context
      |
      v
Database Privileges
      |
      v
Available Features
      |
      v
Possible Additional Impact

docs.title: Test Intensity
docs.text:
sqlmap exposes parameters commonly associated with how broadly and aggressively it tests.

Because exact behaviour and ranges can change, inspect:

sqlmap -hh

before using more aggressive settings.

Start with the lowest level needed to answer the question.

docs.title: Risk Settings
docs.text:
Some sqlmap options can increase the intrusiveness of payloads.

Do not raise them automatically.

Review what changes before using them against production.

docs.title: Level Settings
docs.text:
Higher testing levels can include more parameter locations and payload variations.

More is not always better.

If the suspected parameter is already known:

focus on it

instead of testing the entire request.

docs.title: Request Count
docs.text:
sqlmap may send many requests while testing:

  • techniques;
  • DBMS possibilities;
  • encodings;
  • payload variations.

Monitor application stability and WAF response.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Applications may return:

429 Too Many Requests

Reduce test intensity.

Do not attempt to overwhelm defensive controls.

docs.title: WAF Detection
docs.text:
A WAF may:

  • block quotes;
  • block keywords;
  • return generic 403 pages;
  • reset connections;
  • challenge requests.

This can produce false negatives or confusing behaviour.

Record the security control.

Do not automatically move into bypass testing.

docs.title: WAF vs Application Response
docs.text:
Compare:

normal application response

with:

blocked request response

If all candidate payloads receive the same WAF page, sqlmap may have insufficient visibility to determine the backend behaviour.

docs.title: Tamper Scripts
docs.text:
sqlmap includes mechanisms historically associated with transforming payloads.

These may be used to alter syntax or encoding.

Do not use them automatically to bypass WAF or filtering controls.

If evasion is specifically authorised, review the exact transformation before use.

docs.title: Evasion Is Separate From Validation
docs.text:
A useful distinction is:

Can we confirm SQL injection?

versus:

Can we evade this WAF?

These are different assessment objectives.

docs.title: Proxies
docs.text:
sqlmap can operate through proxy configurations.

This can be useful for:

  • Burp inspection;
  • controlled network routing.

Check current proxy syntax with:

sqlmap -h

Do not route high-volume sqlmap traffic through Burp unless there is a clear reason.

docs.title: Burp Proxying
docs.text:
A useful debugging workflow is:

sqlmap
  |
  v
Burp Proxy
  |
  v
Target

This allows selected requests to be inspected.

However, it can create a very large Burp history.

docs.title: Request Comparison
docs.text:
When sqlmap identifies an injection point, manually compare:

baseline

with:

positive condition

and:

negative condition

This provides understandable evidence.

docs.title: Manual Reproduction
docs.text:
A strong final finding should ideally be reproducible without depending on sqlmap.

Example:

Normal request
      |
      v
Response A

Modified request
      |
      v
Consistent database-driven difference

Use Burp Repeater to demonstrate the smallest reliable difference.

docs.title: Evidence Quality
docs.text:
Weak:

Screenshot:
sqlmap says injectable

Stronger:

Baseline request
Modified request
Observed response difference
DBMS-related behaviour
sqlmap supporting output

The finding should remain understandable without the scanner.

docs.title: sqlmap Session Data
docs.text:
sqlmap may retain local state for tested targets.

This can improve repeated testing but may also cause confusion if:

  • target changed;
  • application was patched;
  • authentication changed.

Be aware of cached session data during retesting.

docs.title: Fresh Retesting
docs.text:
When confirming remediation, ensure previous sqlmap state does not cause stale conclusions.

Use the tool's current documented mechanisms for fresh testing where necessary.

Also perform manual validation.

docs.title: Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Do not use sqlmap as your primary hidden-parameter discovery tool.

Use:

  • application analysis;
  • Burp;
  • ffuf;
  • Katana;
  • JavaScript analysis.

Then apply sqlmap to plausible SQL-backed parameters.

docs.title: ffuf Integration
docs.text:
A useful chain is:

ffuf
  |
  v
Hidden Endpoint / Parameter
  |
  v
Manual Validation
  |
  v
SQLi Candidate
  |
  v
sqlmap

Related tool:

ffuf

docs.title: Katana Integration
docs.text:
Katana may reveal:

/report?id=123
/search?q=test
/api/user?uid=15

These are parameterized endpoints.

Do not automatically send all of them to sqlmap.

Prioritise based on:

  • application behaviour;
  • technology;
  • manual response differences.

Related tool:

Katana

docs.title: Nuclei Integration
docs.text:
Nuclei may flag a SQL injection candidate through a template.

A mature workflow is:

Nuclei Candidate
      |
      v
Manual Review
      |
      v
sqlmap
      |
      v
Manual Confirmation

Related tool:

Nuclei

docs.title: Source Code Review Integration
docs.text:
White-box access can substantially improve SQL injection testing.

Search for:

raw SQL
string concatenation
query builders
unsafe ORM methods

Then identify the corresponding HTTP request.

Related section:

Source Code Review Tools

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Model
docs.text:
A code-level SQL injection path might be:

request.query["id"]
      |
      v
controller
      |
      v
service
      |
      v
"SELECT ... " + id
      |
      v
database execute

Dynamic sqlmap testing can then validate the code-level hypothesis.

docs.title: Prepared Statements
docs.text:
Prepared statements or parameter binding generally prevent data from altering SQL syntax when correctly used.

Example concept:

SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?

with:

id passed separately

is different from:

"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + id

docs.title: Dynamic Identifiers
docs.text:
Prepared statements may not directly parameterize certain SQL structural elements such as:

  • table names;
  • column names;
  • sort direction.

Applications should use strict allowlists for such values.

sqlmap results should be interpreted in the actual query context.

docs.title: ORDER BY
docs.text:
User-controlled sorting can be security sensitive.

Example:

sort=name
sort=date

If values are inserted directly into SQL syntax, parameter binding may not be sufficient.

Use strict server-side allowlists.

docs.title: LIMIT / OFFSET
docs.text:
Pagination parameters may also interact with SQL query construction.

Do not assume numeric-looking inputs are automatically safe.

docs.title: Search Fields
docs.text:
Search features frequently interact with database queries.

Potential parameters include:

q
search
filter
keyword
name

Manual response analysis should precede automation.

docs.title: Login Forms
docs.text:
SQL injection in authentication logic can have different impact from SQL injection in a search function.

Possible impact may involve:

  • authentication bypass;
  • data access;
  • database manipulation.

Test the exact behaviour.

docs.title: Authentication Bypass
docs.text:
Do not claim authentication bypass simply because the login parameter is injectable.

You must demonstrate that the query logic actually allows bypass of the intended authentication decision.

docs.title: API SQL Injection
docs.text:
APIs may return:

JSON

rather than HTML.

Response differences may involve:

  • status;
  • field values;
  • record count;
  • error object;
  • timing.

sqlmap can assist, but manual JSON comparison remains useful.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL variables may eventually reach SQL-backed resolvers.

However, GraphQL introduces an additional abstraction layer.

Test the underlying resolver behaviour rather than blindly scanning every GraphQL request.

Related note:

GraphQL

docs.title: Second-Order SQL Injection
docs.text:
Some SQL injection conditions occur when data is stored first and used unsafely later.

Conceptually:

User Input
   |
   v
Stored Safely
   |
   v
Later Retrieved
   |
   v
Unsafe SQL Construction

These workflows are harder for automated scanners.

Manual application understanding is important.

docs.title: Blind SQL Injection
docs.text:
Blind SQL injection may not return database errors or records directly.

Potential indicators include:

boolean response differences

or:

time differences

Automation can help, but reproducibility is critical.

docs.title: Out-of-Band SQL Injection
docs.text:
Some environments may support database-driven external interactions.

This is platform- and privilege-dependent.

Out-of-band testing is more intrusive and should only be used when explicitly required.

Related tool:

Interactsh

docs.title: DNS / Network Interaction
docs.text:
If a database causes an external callback, determine:

Which database feature caused it?

Which DB account privilege enabled it?

Which protocol was observed?

Was the interaction unique to the request?

Do not overstate the result.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Applications should avoid exposing raw database errors.

However, hiding errors does not fix SQL injection.

Error suppression may turn an error-based injection into blind SQL injection.

The root control is safe query construction.

docs.title: Database Error Disclosure
docs.text:
Example exposed information may include:

DBMS type
table name
column name
query fragment
filesystem path

This may be reportable as information disclosure separately from SQL injection if appropriate.

docs.title: Logging and Telemetry
docs.text:
sqlmap activity may generate:

  • WAF logs;
  • web-server logs;
  • reverse-proxy logs;
  • database errors;
  • SIEM alerts.

Large automated runs can be very visible.

docs.title: Purple Teaming
docs.text:
sqlmap can support controlled detection validation for SQL injection attempts.

Controlled SQLi Test
      |
      v
WAF / Web Logs
      |
      v
Application Logs
      |
      v
SIEM
      |
      v
Detection Review

Use a minimal, agreed test case rather than an unrestricted scan.

Related section:

Purple Teaming

docs.title: Detection Considerations
docs.text:
Useful detection opportunities may include:

  • unusual SQL metacharacters;
  • repeated parameter mutations;
  • error bursts;
  • characteristic request patterns;
  • high request rates.

Detection should not rely solely on a tool-specific User-Agent.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Potential causes include:

  • unstable responses;
  • dynamic content;
  • WAF pages;
  • caching;
  • random timing variation;
  • application errors unrelated to SQL;
  • load balancer behaviour.

Manual reproduction is essential.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
sqlmap may miss SQL injection because of:

  • authentication;
  • complex workflows;
  • unusual encoding;
  • custom protocols;
  • second-order behaviour;
  • WAF blocking;
  • custom query construction;
  • uncommon DBMS behaviour.

A clean sqlmap result does not prove a parameter is safe.

docs.title: Dynamic Content
docs.text:
Pages containing:

timestamps
random IDs
advertisements
personalised content

can make response comparison difficult.

Understand which parts of the page are stable.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Caching can hide request differences.

Possible layers include:

  • browser;
  • CDN;
  • reverse proxy;
  • application cache.

Use unique requests or controlled cache behaviour where appropriate.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation, test:

  1. original manual proof;
  2. modified values;
  3. sqlmap where useful;
  4. source change if white-box access exists.

The expected result is:

User-controlled data can no longer influence SQL syntax.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Primary remediation usually involves:

  • parameterized queries;
  • prepared statements;
  • safe ORM APIs;
  • strict allowlists for SQL structural values;
  • least-privileged database accounts.

Input validation can support these controls but should not replace safe query construction.

docs.title: Do Not Recommend Escaping Alone
docs.text:
Generic escaping can be fragile because SQL syntax differs across:

  • DBMS;
  • encoding;
  • query context.

Use parameter binding wherever possible.

docs.title: Database Least Privilege
docs.text:
Application database accounts should receive only required permissions.

This reduces impact if SQL injection occurs.

For example:

Read-only application

should not normally have:

DROP
ALTER
CREATE USER
filesystem access

unless required.

docs.title: Stored Procedures
docs.text:
Stored procedures are not automatically safe.

They can still construct dynamic SQL unsafely.

Review how parameters are used inside them.

docs.title: WAF Is Defence in Depth
docs.text:
A WAF may block SQL injection payloads.

It should not be the primary remediation.

Correct the vulnerable query construction.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a confirmed finding, retain:

Target:
Endpoint:
Parameter:
Method:
Authentication context:
Baseline request:
Modified request:
Observed difference:
sqlmap version:
sqlmap command:
DBMS:
Technique:
Timestamp:
Manual validation:

Protect sensitive database data.

docs.title: Evidence Example
docs.text:
Target:
https://example.test

Endpoint:
/product

Parameter:
id

Authentication:
None

Manual validation:
Boolean conditions produced consistent differences in database-backed
content.

sqlmap:
Confirmed the same parameter as injectable.

DBMS:
PostgreSQL

Conclusion:
The id parameter influences SQL query structure without adequate
parameterisation.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

sqlmap found SQL injection.

Prefer:

The `id` parameter was incorporated into a database query without
adequate parameterisation. Controlled boolean conditions produced
repeatable differences in the returned database-backed content,
confirming SQL injection.

docs.title: Reporting Limited Impact
docs.text:
If the vulnerable query uses a restricted account:

SQL injection was confirmed, but the application database account was
restricted to read access within the affected schema during testing.
This reduced the demonstrated impact but did not remove the underlying
injection vulnerability.

docs.title: Reporting an Unconfirmed Candidate
docs.text:
Example:

Automated testing initially suggested possible time-based SQL
injection. Repeated manual testing showed similar latency variation for
normal requests, and no deterministic database-controlled timing
difference could be established. The candidate was therefore not
confirmed.

docs.title: Reporting WAF Blocking
docs.text:
Example:

SQL injection-style test inputs were blocked by the web application
firewall before reaching the application during the observed tests.
The result demonstrates current filtering behaviour but does not by
itself establish whether the underlying application query is safely
parameterised.

docs.title: Help
docs.text: sqlmap -h

docs.title: Extended Help
docs.text: sqlmap -hh

docs.title: Version
docs.text: sqlmap --version

docs.title: Basic GET
docs.text: sqlmap -u "https://example.test/product?id=10"

docs.title: Specific Parameter
docs.text: sqlmap -u "https://example.test/product?id=10&lang=en" -p id

docs.title: POST Form
docs.text:
sqlmap -u "https://example.test/search" --data="search=book" -p search

For complex authenticated or JSON requests, prefer a valid raw HTTP request captured from Burp and use the request-file functionality documented by:

sqlmap -h

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Target explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Endpoint understood.
  • [ ] Parameter identified.
  • [ ] Authentication context recorded.
  • [ ] Baseline response captured.
  • [ ] Manual SQLi hypothesis exists.
  • [ ] sqlmap version recorded.
  • [ ] Production sensitivity considered.

docs.title: Parameter Testing
docs.text:
• [ ] Specific parameter selected where possible.
  • [ ] Query/form/JSON context understood.
  • [ ] Data type understood.
  • [ ] Dynamic response content considered.
  • [ ] Manual baseline retained.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• [ ] Approved test account used.
  • [ ] Cookie/token protected.
  • [ ] Session expiry monitored.
  • [ ] Role context documented.
  • [ ] CSRF requirements understood.

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text:
• [ ] Lowest necessary test intensity used.
  • [ ] Request volume monitored.
  • [ ] Rate limiting respected.
  • [ ] WAF behaviour observed.
  • [ ] 500 spikes monitored.
  • [ ] Testing stopped if instability appears.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] sqlmap result manually reproduced.
  • [ ] Generic error behaviour ruled out.
  • [ ] Timing differences repeated.
  • [ ] DBMS identification reviewed.
  • [ ] Parameter influence established.
  • [ ] Underlying SQL behaviour understood where possible.

docs.title: Data Access
docs.text:
• [ ] Database enumeration minimised.
  • [ ] Sensitive rows not dumped unnecessarily.
  • [ ] Credential tables avoided unless explicitly needed.
  • [ ] File read/write avoided unless explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] OS interaction avoided unless explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Collected data protected.

docs.title: WAF
docs.text:
• [ ] WAF blocking distinguished from application behaviour.
  • [ ] Evasion not attempted automatically.
  • [ ] Tamper functionality reviewed before use.
  • [ ] Underlying vulnerability not assumed fixed by WAF.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Endpoint retained.
  • [ ] Parameter retained.
  • [ ] Baseline request retained.
  • [ ] Modified request retained.
  • [ ] Response difference retained.
  • [ ] sqlmap version retained.
  • [ ] Command retained.
  • [ ] DBMS retained where confirmed.
  • [ ] Sensitive values redacted.
  • [ ] Manual validation retained.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• [ ] Finding describes unsafe query behaviour.
  • [ ] sqlmap output used only as supporting evidence.
  • [ ] Impact not overstated.
  • [ ] Database privileges considered.
  • [ ] WAF treated as defence in depth.
  • [ ] Remediation specifies parameterisation.
  • [ ] Retest criteria explicit.
