docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Do not use sqlmap like this:

Find Parameter
      |
      v
Run Aggressive sqlmap
      |
      v
Dump Database
      |
      v
Report SQL Injection

Use it like this:

Understand Endpoint
      |
      v
Identify Database-Backed Parameter
      |
      v
Capture Baseline Request
      |
      v
Perform Manual SQLi Checks
      |
      v
Form Injection Hypothesis
      |
      v
Run Focused sqlmap Validation
      |
      v
Understand Technique / DBMS
      |
      v
Reproduce Manually
      |
      v
Determine Database Privilege and Impact
      |
      v
Minimise Sensitive Data Access
      |
      v
Capture Evidence
      |
      v
Report Unsafe Query Construction

sqlmap is most valuable when it automates repetitive SQL injection testing after the tester already understands the request and suspected data flow.

The tool can help confirm and characterise the injection.

The final finding should be based on the underlying unsafe database interaction and reproducible evidence.

docs.title: Vulnerability Research
docs.text:
Vulnerability research is the systematic process of identifying, understanding, validating and responsibly communicating security weaknesses in software and systems.

The objective is to turn an interesting observation into a reproducible, technically defensible security conclusion.

A useful investigation establishes:

  • Where untrusted input enters and what the attacker controls.
  • How the input reaches a security-relevant operation.
  • Which assumption or security check fails.
  • Whether the behaviour can be reproduced and explained.
  • What access, capability or impact is demonstrated.
  • Which versions, configurations and related implementations are affected.
  • Whether remediation addresses the underlying cause.

Observation -> Candidate -> Validation -> Evidence -> Security Conclusion

Use this page as the research overview and navigation map. The ten dedicated pages provide detailed procedures for each part of the investigation.

Authorised research

Test only software, systems and environments where the activity is authorised. Use controlled installations and synthetic data wherever possible. Public source code, an accessible service or a published CVE does not authorise testing someone else's deployment. Review testing, disclosure and publication conditions separately.

docs.title: Start Here
docs.text:
• Research Methodology

    Define the target, scope, environment, research questions and evidence needed to support a conclusion.

    Vulnerability Research Methodology

  • Attack Surface Analysis

    Identify entry points, attacker-controlled inputs, trust boundaries and sensitive operations.

    Attack Surface Analysis

  • Debugging and Dynamic Analysis

    Observe reachable code, runtime values, security checks, process activity and failures.

    Debugging and Dynamic Analysis

  • Fuzzing

    Explore input space using appropriate harnesses, seed corpora, instrumentation and result classification.

    Fuzzing

  • Crash Analysis

    Reproduce and minimise failures, inspect runtime state and determine their security relevance.

    Crash Analysis

  • Patch Diffing

    Compare implementations to understand the security condition a change attempts to restore.

    Patch Diffing

  • Variant Analysis

    Search related functions, interfaces and implementations for the same underlying security mistake.

    Variant Analysis

  • Proof of Concept Development

    Build a minimal, controlled reproducer with explicit prerequisites, expected results and limitations.

    Proof of Concept Development

  • CVE Research

    Connect advisories, affected versions, patches and local reproduction to technical understanding.

    CVE Research

  • Responsible Disclosure

    Prepare evidence that maintainers can use to reproduce, investigate, remediate and retest the issue.

    Responsible Disclosure

docs.title: Choose a Research Route
docs.text:
The starting point determines which page is most useful.

Starting point Begin with Expected output A new product or unfamiliar component Methodology and Attack Surface Analysis Target model and prioritised research questions Suspicious source code Source Code Review and Debugging A candidate data flow with reachability evidence A parser or structured input format Fuzzing A suitable harness, corpus and triage process A crash, hang or sanitizer report Crash Analysis Reproducer, failure classification and security assessment A security patch or advisory CVE Research and Patch Diffing A hypothesis about the fixed condition A confirmed root cause Variant Analysis Independently validated related candidates A reproducible security failure PoC Development Minimal evidence supporting a specific claim A finding ready for coordination Responsible Disclosure A complete technical report and disclosure record

Not every investigation needs fuzzing, binary analysis or a CVE assignment. Select methods that resolve the current question.

docs.title: Research Lifecycle
docs.text:
The workflow is iterative. Patch analysis may start an investigation, dynamic evidence may contradict the source-review hypothesis, and a variant may require a different reproduction environment.

flowchart TD
    A["Authorised target and exact build"] --> B["Map inputs and security boundaries"]
    B --> C["Form a testable hypothesis"]
    C --> D["Analyse and test"]
    D --> E{"Result reproducible?"}
    E -->|No| F["Investigate state and prerequisites"]
    F --> C
    E -->|Yes| G["Minimise and investigate cause"]
    G --> H{"Security failure supported?"}
    H -->|No or uncertain| I["Record evidence and limitations"]
    I --> C
    H -->|Yes| J["Assess impact, versions and variants"]
    J --> K["Prepare reproducer and report"]
    K --> L["Coordinate remediation"]
    L --> M["Validate fix and preserve regression tests"]
Phase What to do What to expect What follows Prepare Record authorisation, target, build and configuration A controlled baseline Map relevant functionality Observe Identify inputs, transformations and sensitive operations Candidate security assumptions Define a testable hypothesis Test Combine appropriate static and dynamic methods Supported, unsupported or inconclusive behaviour Reproduce and investigate Explain Minimise the case and identify the failing condition Root-cause evidence and a bounded capability Assess security consequences Extend Review versions, patches and related implementations A supported scope of affected behaviour Prepare a report Remediate Coordinate a fix and repeat relevant tests Evidence that the intended security condition holds Preserve regression coverage

A complete explanation is desirable, but evidence may remain incomplete. Report confirmed behaviour and uncertainty separately rather than inventing a root cause.

docs.title: Scope and Environment
docs.text:
Record:

  • Product, component and deployment being tested.
  • Exact version, build, commit or package revision.
  • Operating system, architecture and runtime.
  • Dependencies, compiler settings and relevant mitigations.
  • Enabled features and configuration.
  • Test accounts, roles and representative application data.
  • Allowed techniques, excluded activity and stopping conditions.
  • Evidence handling, disclosure and publication requirements.

Where practical, use a resettable VM, container or dedicated lab with appropriate network isolation. Treat the isolation boundary itself as part of the environment, especially when investigating privileged components.

Prepare the observations needed for the question: source code, debugger, application logs, system monitoring, proxy, network capture, instrumentation or sanitizers.

Snapshots help restore state, but record what they contain and verify that each attempt starts from the intended baseline.

docs.title: Exact Version Record
docs.text:
An example record for a fictional target:

Product: Example Server
Component: Archive import service
Version: 4.2.1
Commit or build identifier: Record exact value
Platform: Linux x86_64
Runtime and dependencies: Record exact versions
Deployment: Isolated local installation
Configuration: Authentication enabled; archive import enabled
Test identity: Dedicated low-privileged research account
Instrumentation: Record debugger, sanitizer or tracing settings
Baseline: Record snapshot or reset procedure

Distinguish an instrumented research build from the distributed release. Instrumentation can help expose a defect, but deployment-specific conclusions still require evidence about the relevant product configuration.

docs.title: Research Workspace
docs.text:
Keep inputs, results and interpretation organised.

Directory Purpose notes/ Hypotheses, observations, decisions and negative results source/ Source snapshots and repository references builds/ Build records and version-specific outputs samples/ Known-good examples and controlled test inputs corpus/ Fuzzing seeds and retained coverage inputs crashes/ Original failures and triage records poc/ Minimal reproducers patches/ Relevant changes and patch analysis variants/ Related candidates and their validation evidence/ Logs, traces, captures and artefact identifiers reports/ Technical reports and disclosure material

Keep real credentials, sensitive data and restricted disclosure material out of public repositories.

docs.title: Model Inputs, Data Flow and Trust
Attack Surface and Entry Points
docs.text:
Potential surfaces include HTTP and API endpoints, network protocols, file parsers, uploads, import functions, authentication flows, IPC, command-line interfaces, plugins, update mechanisms, deserialisation, archive extraction and local services.

Identify the specific input rather than stopping at the feature name:

  • Parameter, header, JSON field or protocol field.
  • Uploaded file or archive entry.
  • Configuration value or environment variable.
  • IPC message or command-line argument.
  • Token, session value or object identifier.

Then determine who can control it, under which privileges and through which supported interface.

Continue with Attack Surface Analysis.

docs.title: Sources, Transformations and Sinks
docs.text:
Trace the input through decoding, parsing, normalisation, validation and use.

Sensitive operations may include:

  • Command execution and dynamic evaluation.
  • Database queries.
  • File access and modification.
  • Template rendering and deserialisation.
  • Memory allocation, indexing and copying.
  • Outbound network requests.
  • Authentication and authorisation decisions.

A function name is only a starting point. Determine whether the input reaches that operation under security-relevant conditions and whether an effective check constrains it.

Review the original representation, intermediate values and final value used. Validation of one representation may not constrain a later transformation.

Use Source Code Review and the existing Static Analysis section for detailed source-review methods.

docs.title: Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
Identify transitions such as:

Boundary Question Unauthenticated to authenticated Where is identity established and verified? Standard user to privileged operation Which permission permits the operation? User A to User B Is access authorised for the requested resource? Tenant A to Tenant B Is tenant context enforced throughout the operation? Application to operating system What authority does the process exercise? Untrusted file to parser What assumptions does processing make about structure and size? Container or sandbox to host Which resources and privileges are actually shared? Downloaded update to trusted code What establishes authenticity before use?

Network access or data movement alone does not establish a security violation. Explain the intended policy and how observed behaviour violates it.

docs.title: Define the Security Invariant
docs.text:
A security invariant is a condition that must hold for an operation to remain safe.

Area Example invariant Memory copy The source contains the requested bytes and the destination has sufficient capacity Array indexing The index is within the valid range, including any relevant lower bound Allocation arithmetic Size calculations do not overflow or produce an undersized allocation File extraction The write remains confined to the permitted destination under actual filesystem resolution Object access The authenticated principal is authorised for the requested operation on the object Update handling Authenticity is verified before the artefact is trusted or executed Object lifetime An object remains valid while it is accessed Privileged operation The caller has the required authority at the point of use

Common assumptions worth investigating include:

  • This value cannot be controlled by a user.
  • Another layer already validated the field.
  • This endpoint always requires authentication.
  • This object belongs to the current user.
  • This path remains within the intended directory.
  • This length cannot exceed the available buffer.
  • This pointer still refers to a live object.
  • This request can only originate internally.

Ask what evidence supports the assumption and what input or state could make it false.

An invariant provides a stronger basis for root-cause analysis, variant searches and remediation than the exact bytes of one successful input.

docs.title: Form and Test a Hypothesis
docs.text:
For example:

Observation:
The application accepts archive uploads.

Question:
How does it constrain extraction destinations?

Hypothesis:
The extraction helper may use entry paths without enforcing
containment within the permitted output directory.

Controlled test:
Use an isolated installation and a dedicated marker destination
inside the research workspace.

Expected secure behaviour:
Entries that would escape the extraction root are rejected
before an out-of-root write occurs.

Evidence required:
Exact archive, version, configuration, execution identity,
filesystem observations and relevant processing logic.

The test should distinguish the hypothesis from alternative explanations. A rejected archive may mean the control worked, the format was unsupported or the relevant path was never reached.

docs.title: Authentication and Authorisation
docs.text:
For authentication, inspect session creation, session validation, token handling, password reset, administrative routes and alternative flows.

For authorisation, inspect object access, operations, HTTP methods, nested resources, tenant context and privileged actions.

The user interface does not establish where security is enforced. Trace enforcement to the server-side operation.

An authenticated user may legitimately access shared resources. Establish the intended access policy before interpreting another user's object as evidence of a vulnerability.

docs.title: Static and Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Method Helps establish Limitation to resolve Source search Relevant functions, fields and checks Text matches do not prove reachability Static analysis Candidate data flows and missing checks Model assumptions may differ from runtime behaviour Debugging Executed paths, values and program state The observed run may not represent every configuration System tracing File, process and system-call behaviour A recorded operation still needs identity and policy context Network observation Requests, responses and protocol behaviour Intermediaries or cached state may affect interpretation Instrumentation and sanitizers Runtime defects and diagnostic evidence Product reachability and impact need separate assessment

Use static evidence to guide runtime tests, then return to the implementation when observations differ from expectations.

Continue with Debugging and Dynamic Analysis.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text:
Fuzzing generates or mutates inputs and observes target behaviour. Coverage feedback, assertions, sanitizers and other test oracles help identify cases worth investigating.

Define:

  • The component and entry point under test.
  • Harness assumptions and reset behaviour.
  • Representative seed inputs.
  • Input structure and relevant state transitions.
  • Time, memory and execution limits.
  • What counts as an interesting result.
  • How inputs, logs and coverage are preserved.
  • How suspected duplicates are grouped and reviewed.

Crashes, hangs, resource exhaustion, parser inconsistencies and unexpected states are investigation inputs. Neither the number of crashes nor the amount of coverage alone measures confirmed vulnerabilities.

A harness that invokes an internal function in an impossible state may reveal a real coding defect without demonstrating a reachable product vulnerability.

Continue with Fuzzing.

docs.title: Crash Analysis
docs.text:
For a failure, establish:

  1. Whether the original input reproduces under the recorded conditions.
  2. Whether the failure belongs to the target or the harness.
  3. The exception, signal, failing instruction and relevant stack.
  4. The allocation, lifetime and access details where memory is involved.
  5. Which input or state influences the operation.
  6. The earliest supported cause, rather than only the final symptom.
  7. The product entry point and security consequences.

Possible classifications include assertions, unhandled exceptions, resource exhaustion, out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, double free and integer-related memory defects.

AddressSanitizer can expose memory errors such as out-of-bounds accesses and use-after-free. Preserve its report with the triggering input and build information.

A crash does not automatically establish service-wide denial of service. An out-of-bounds write does not automatically establish code execution.

Continue with Crash Analysis.

docs.title: Reproduce, Minimise and Challenge the Result
Reproducibility
docs.text:
Record the exact version, configuration, input, sequence, expected behaviour and observed behaviour.

Reset the environment and repeat. If state or timing matters, document it. For intermittent behaviour, record attempts, successes and relevant conditions instead of describing the issue as either perfectly reliable or nonexistent.

The practical question is:

Can another researcher reproduce or meaningfully investigate the same security-relevant behaviour from these records?

docs.title: Minimal Reproduction
docs.text:
Reduce unnecessary requests, fields, files, dependencies and setup while preserving the same underlying failure.

After each reduction, confirm that the reproducer still exercises the same condition. A smaller input that produces a different crash may no longer demonstrate the original issue.

Preserve the original input as well as the minimised case.

Minimal reproductions help with diagnosis, vendor triage, patch validation and regression testing.

docs.title: Controls and Alternative Explanations
docs.text:
Check for:

  • Cached responses or stale files.
  • Existing privileged sessions.
  • Incorrect test identities.
  • Intentionally shared resources.
  • Debug-only configuration.
  • Unsupported builds or changed dependencies.
  • Proxy modifications.
  • Artefacts left by earlier attempts.
  • Harness defects or unrealistic invocation.
  • Environmental failures unrelated to the hypothesis.

For object-level authorisation testing, use dedicated accounts and known ownership:

Test Expected result Account A accesses its own permitted object Allowed Account A accesses Account B's private object Denied An unauthenticated session accesses a protected object Rejected Account A requests a nonexistent object Handled without disclosing protected data

The exact status code depends on the application's design. Judge the access and data returned, not the code alone.

Negative results remain useful. Record which hypothesis they weaken and what remains untested.

docs.title: Separate Root Cause, Capability and Impact
docs.text:
These are related but distinct conclusions.

Layer Example Observation A file appears outside the intended extraction directory Root cause The extraction operation does not enforce destination containment for the relevant entry type Capability The tested input controls a write to a demonstrated out-of-root location Preconditions Archive import is available and the service identity can write to that location Security boundary Untrusted archive data influences files outside the intended extraction area Demonstrated impact Creation or modification of the approved marker file Unproven extension Access to arbitrary system paths or code execution

Avoid describing a constrained read or write as arbitrary unless the evidence supports that degree of control.

Other capabilities may include unauthorised object access, request forgery, authentication-state manipulation, out-of-bounds access or command execution. Each needs its own reachability and impact analysis.

docs.title: Exploitability and Preconditions
docs.text:
Assess:

  • Authentication and privileges.
  • User interaction.
  • Network position and exposed interfaces.
  • Required features or configuration.
  • Knowledge of identifiers or application state.
  • Timing, races or multiple-stage dependencies.
  • Process authority and relevant mitigations.
  • Reliability and environmental differences.

These conditions belong in the finding, not only in private research notes.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Assess confidentiality, integrity and availability consequences alongside prerequisites, exposure and the boundary crossed.

FIRST CVSS provides a structured severity-scoring method. When using it, record the version, vector and justification. Keep severity distinct from the organisation's wider risk and remediation priority.

Clearly label observed impact and reasoned potential consequences. Do not perform unnecessary damaging actions merely to support a higher severity.

docs.title: Understand the Patch
docs.text:
Look for changed validation, bounds checks, authorisation, parsing, defaults, sanitisation and memory handling.

Ask:

  • What condition does the change enforce?
  • Is the relevant code reachable?
  • Does the check apply before the sensitive operation?
  • Do later transformations invalidate the check?
  • Is the change consistently applied across callers and branches?
  • Could unrelated refactoring explain part of the diff?

A security-relevant change supports a hypothesis. Controlled testing and implementation analysis establish what it actually fixes.

Continue with Patch Diffing.

docs.title: Search for Variants
docs.text:
After understanding the cause, inspect:

  • Shared helpers and their callers.
  • Sibling functions.
  • Related parsers and file formats.
  • Alternate endpoints and API versions.
  • Legacy implementations.
  • Platform-specific code.
  • Maintained branches.
  • Inconsistent application of the fix.

Each similar implementation is a candidate requiring its own reachability, control and impact analysis.

Group related manifestations by cause where appropriate, while retaining their distinct affected interfaces and conditions. Do not assume every matching line is a separate vulnerability.

Continue with Variant Analysis.

docs.title: Establish Affected Versions
docs.text:
Separate direct tests, source-history evidence and vendor statements.

Classification Meaning Confirmed affected The relevant failure was validated on the recorded build and configuration Fix validated The relevant reproduction and security checks were tested successfully Potentially affected Code or other evidence suggests applicability, but validation is incomplete Vendor-reported The range comes from an attributed advisory Not tested No direct conclusion is available

Do not infer that every version between two affected releases is vulnerable without supporting evidence.

Record maintained branches, platform differences, distribution patches and backports where relevant.

Continue with CVE Research.

docs.title: Useful Git History Commands
docs.text:
Run these in the target's research checkout. Replace placeholder revisions and paths before use.

git log --oneline --all
git log -p -- path/to/file
git blame -- path/to/file
git diff OLD_COMMIT NEW_COMMIT -- path/to/file

Expect commit history and implementation differences. Use them to identify candidates for testing, not to infer vulnerability solely from authorship or changed lines.

When a reproducible regression has known good and bad revisions, Git bisect can narrow the introduction point:

git bisect start
git bisect bad KNOWN_BAD_COMMIT
git bisect good KNOWN_GOOD_COMMIT

Build and test each selected revision, then classify that revision with one appropriate command:

git bisect good

git bisect bad

If the revision cannot be meaningfully tested:

git bisect skip

Finish with:

git bisect reset

Use a research checkout without uncommitted work. The result depends on a consistent test; skipped or unbuildable revisions can leave ambiguity.

docs.title: Develop a Minimal Proof of Concept
docs.text:
Define the smallest claim the PoC must establish.

A useful PoC includes:

  • Exact product, build and configuration.
  • Required access and preconditions.
  • Known-good baseline.
  • Minimal trigger or procedure.
  • Expected secure behaviour.
  • Observed security-relevant result.
  • Evidence collection and repeatability instructions.
  • Limitations and cleanup.
  • Fixed-version comparison where available.

Use synthetic data, dedicated accounts and controlled destinations.

A PoC should not require unrelated persistence, bulk collection, destructive changes or additional compromise when a smaller demonstration establishes the issue.

Examples of bounded claims include:

  • A specified unauthorised object was returned.
  • A controlled file was written outside the intended directory.
  • A documented input caused an out-of-bounds read in the tested parser.
  • A particular privileged action occurred without the required check.

Continue with Proof of Concept Development.

docs.title: Preserve Evidence and Research Notes
docs.text:
Capture evidence that directly supports the conclusion:

  • Requests and responses.
  • Application and system logs.
  • Source references and exact revisions.
  • Debugger state and stack traces.
  • Sanitizer reports.
  • Network captures.
  • Version and configuration records.
  • Reproducers, input files and output.
  • Screenshots where they add useful context.

Record timestamps and timezone. Retain the relationship between each input, attempt, build and result.

docs.title: Artefact Identification
docs.text:
For an existing input named poc.bin, calculate its hash.

Linux:

sha256sum poc.bin

PowerShell:

Get-FileHash .\poc.bin -Algorithm SHA256

The hash identifies the tested bytes. It does not independently prove when, where or how the input was executed.

Before sharing evidence, remove unnecessary passwords, session cookies, tokens, API keys, personal data, private URLs and internal identifiers. Preserve a controlled original and a sanitised sharing copy where required.

docs.title: Research Log Template
docs.text:
Research ID:
Date and timezone:
Target and component:
Version / build / commit:
Platform and configuration:
Test identity:
Baseline / reset procedure:

Observation:
Hypothesis:
Security invariant:
Attacker-controlled input:
Relevant source or runtime location:

Procedure:
Input identifier and hash:
Expected secure result:
Observed result:
Controls and alternative explanations:
Reproduction attempts:
Evidence references:

Root cause status:
Demonstrated capability:
Preconditions:
Security impact:
Remaining uncertainty:

Files or configuration changed:
Cleanup:
Next step:

Do not discard unsupported hypotheses. A documented negative result prevents duplicated work and improves the model of the target.

docs.title: Reporting and Coordinated Disclosure
docs.text:
A report should let maintainers understand, reproduce, investigate, patch and retest the issue.

Include:

  • Descriptive title and concise technical summary.
  • Product, component, tested versions and environment.
  • Vulnerability class and affected security condition.
  • Required access, configuration and user interaction.
  • Reproduction steps and minimal PoC.
  • Expected and observed behaviour.
  • Root cause, or a clear statement of what remains unknown.
  • Demonstrated impact and separately labelled potential consequences.
  • Evidence references.
  • Remediation and retest guidance.
  • Affected-version evidence and limitations.

Prefer a title such as:

Missing Object-Level Authorisation Allows Cross-User Access

A useful conclusion explains the underlying relationship:

The tested endpoint retrieves records using a caller-supplied identifier without enforcing the required object-level authorisation. With two dedicated accounts and verified private-object ownership, Account A retrieved Account B's object. This demonstrates an authorisation failure for the tested endpoint, version and configuration.

Avoid turning a specific result into a claim about every endpoint, tenant or release.

Follow the applicable disclosure policy, identify the appropriate security contact, protect sensitive evidence and coordinate remediation and publication. Testing permission and publication conditions are separate questions.

The CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure provides background on coordination. Use Responsible Disclosure for the detailed workflow.

docs.title: Validate Remediation
docs.text:
A fix should enforce the intended security condition rather than merely reject the original input.

For an object-access failure, remediation should enforce the appropriate server-side authorisation for the requested operation and resource. Blocking one identifier does not address the class of failure.

Retesting should verify both the security restriction and continued legitimate functionality.

flowchart TD
    A["Repeat original case on fixed build"] --> B{"Security failure still occurs?"}
    B -->|Yes| C["Record unresolved finding"]
    B -->|No| D["Verify intended path and blocking reason"]
    D --> E{"Relevant control caused the result?"}
    E -->|No or uncertain| F["Investigate or mark inconclusive"]
    E -->|Yes| G["Test legitimate use and relevant variants"]
    G --> H{"Expected outcomes supported?"}
    H -->|No| I["Investigate incomplete fix or regression"]
    H -->|Yes| J["Record bounded validation"]
    J --> K["Preserve regression tests"]

Check:

  • The same feature and relevant configuration remain enabled.
  • The test reaches the intended code path.
  • The security check, rather than an unrelated error, explains rejection.
  • Approved legitimate operations still work.
  • Relevant alternate inputs and entry points are covered.
  • Maintained branches and platforms are assessed where in scope.

A blocked PoC supports only the conclusion justified by these checks. State the tested scope rather than claiming the entire vulnerability class has been eliminated.

docs.title: Tools and Automation
docs.text:
Category Research purpose Internal route Source search and static analysis Locate candidate functions, checks and data flows Static Analysis Debuggers and runtime tracing Establish executed paths and program state Debugging and Dynamic Analysis Disassemblers and decompilers Investigate compiled implementations Vulnerability Research Tools Proxies and network analysis Inspect application and protocol behaviour Tools Fuzzers and coverage tools Explore input space and preserve useful cases Fuzzing Sanitizers and crash diagnostics Identify and explain runtime failures Crash Analysis Version control and comparison Investigate history and fixes Patch Diffing

Simple source searches remain useful:

rg -n 'exec|system|spawn|ProcessBuilder' .
rg -n 'deserialize|unserialize|pickle|ObjectInputStream' .
rg -n 'open|read|write|unlink|rename' .
rg -n 'memcpy|memmove|malloc|calloc|realloc' .

These broad expressions return candidates, including comments, tests and unrelated names. Narrow the search to relevant code and inspect callers, arguments, guards and runtime reachability.

Automation can build versions, generate inputs, run reproductions, preserve failures, search variants, capture output and hash artefacts.

Keep the expected result and failure conditions explicit. A script reporting success is not a substitute for evidence of the claimed security outcome.

docs.title: Research Status and Confidence
docs.text:
Track dimensions separately rather than treating every investigation as a mandatory progression.

Status What it establishes Hypothesis A testable explanation has been proposed Behaviour reproduced The observation occurs under recorded conditions Root cause supported Evidence identifies the defective logic or missing control Security impact confirmed The relevant security consequence has been validated Version scope assessed Affected and unaffected claims have stated evidence Variants assessed Related candidates have documented outcomes and search limits Remediation validated Retesting supports the intended fix within the recorded scope

A finding can have confirmed impact while its exact implementation cause remains uncertain. Variant analysis may continue after disclosure. Neither situation should be hidden by a single confidence label.

docs.title: Scope and Environment
docs.text:
• [ ] Confirm authorisation, target and permitted testing.
  • [ ] Review disclosure and publication conditions.
  • [ ] Record exact version, build, platform and configuration.
  • [ ] Prepare a controlled environment and baseline.
  • [ ] Configure relevant logging and diagnostic tools.
  • [ ] Define evidence handling, reset and cleanup procedures.

docs.title: Attack Surface
docs.text:
• [ ] Identify entry points, services, APIs and parsers.
  • [ ] Review uploads, imports, file handling and local interfaces.
  • [ ] Identify authentication and authorisation enforcement.
  • [ ] Identify privileged components and trust boundaries.
  • [ ] Establish who controls each relevant input.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Trace transformations and sensitive operations.
  • [ ] Identify checks and security assumptions.
  • [ ] Define the relevant security invariant.
  • [ ] Form hypotheses with expected outcomes.
  • [ ] Correlate static candidates with runtime evidence.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Establish a known-good baseline.
  • [ ] Execute the controlled test.
  • [ ] Reset and reproduce the behaviour.
  • [ ] Record reliability and state dependencies.
  • [ ] Minimise while preserving the same underlying failure.
  • [ ] Use controls and investigate alternative explanations.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
• [ ] Identify the affected component and defective condition.
  • [ ] Confirm input influence and product reachability.
  • [ ] Explain the missing or incorrect security check.
  • [ ] Identify the violated invariant and policy boundary.
  • [ ] Separate confirmed causes from hypotheses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• [ ] Record access, configuration and interaction prerequisites.
  • [ ] Describe the demonstrated capability precisely.
  • [ ] Assess confidentiality, integrity and availability consequences.
  • [ ] Distinguish observed impact from potential extensions.
  • [ ] Avoid unsupported arbitrary-access or code-execution claims.

docs.title: Patch Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Identify relevant vulnerable and fixed implementations.
  • [ ] Separate security changes from unrelated differences.
  • [ ] Explain what condition the patch enforces.
  • [ ] Check ordering, callers and later transformations.
  • [ ] Validate behaviour on the fixed build.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• [ ] Extract the underlying vulnerable pattern.
  • [ ] Review shared helpers, sibling functions and related endpoints.
  • [ ] Review legacy, branch and platform differences.
  • [ ] Check consistent application of the patch.
  • [ ] Validate each candidate and group related root causes.
  • [ ] Record the limits of the search.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
• [ ] Record directly tested affected builds.
  • [ ] Record fix-validation results.
  • [ ] Review relevant source and package history.
  • [ ] Assess maintained branches where applicable.
  • [ ] Distinguish tested, inferred and vendor-reported ranges.
  • [ ] Avoid guessing untested versions.

docs.title: Proof of Concept
docs.text:
• [ ] Define the minimum technical claim.
  • [ ] Keep the reproducer controlled and documented.
  • [ ] Include exact prerequisites, inputs and sequence.
  • [ ] Include expected and observed results.
  • [ ] Preserve input identifiers and relevant hashes.
  • [ ] Include limitations, reset and cleanup instructions.
  • [ ] Compare with a fixed build where available.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Preserve relevant requests, responses and logs.
  • [ ] Capture traces, sanitizer or debugger evidence where useful.
  • [ ] Record versions, code references and configurations.
  • [ ] Associate each result with the correct attempt and input.
  • [ ] Protect originals and sanitise sharing copies.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• [ ] Use a descriptive title.
  • [ ] Explain the condition, reproduction and preconditions.
  • [ ] State root-cause confidence and demonstrated impact.
  • [ ] Provide evidence and affected-version support.
  • [ ] Recommend remediation of the underlying cause.
  • [ ] Define retest criteria and remaining limitations.

docs.title: Disclosure
docs.text:
• [ ] Identify the appropriate security contact.
  • [ ] Follow the applicable programme policy.
  • [ ] Provide sufficient reproduction detail.
  • [ ] Protect sensitive information.
  • [ ] Maintain a coordination record.
  • [ ] Coordinate remediation and publication as applicable.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
• [ ] Repeat the original case.
  • [ ] Verify why the observed result changed.
  • [ ] Confirm intended secure behaviour.
  • [ ] Confirm legitimate functionality.
  • [ ] Test relevant variants and configurations.
  • [ ] Record the supported scope of remediation.
  • [ ] Preserve suitable regression tests.

docs.title: Vulnerability Research Attack Surface Analysis
docs.text:
Attack surface analysis is the process of systematically identifying the interfaces, components, inputs and trust boundaries through which software can be influenced.

For vulnerability research, the objective is not simply to enumerate endpoints.

The objective is to understand:

What can an attacker influence?

Where does attacker-controlled data enter?

Which component processes it?

Which privileges does that component have?

Which security boundaries are crossed?

Which sensitive operations can eventually be reached?

Where are security assumptions being made?

A good attack surface map helps transform vulnerability research from random testing into structured investigation.

docs.title: 1. The Vulnerability Research Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
Entry Point
   |
   v
Input
   |
   v
Parser / Handler
   |
   v
Transformation
   |
   v
Validation
   |
   v
Application Logic
   |
   v
Sensitive Operation
   |
   v
Security Boundary

The researcher attempts to understand every important transition.

The central question is:

Can attacker-controlled data reach a security-sensitive operation under conditions that violate an intended security boundary?

docs.title: 2. What Is an Attack Surface?
docs.text:
The attack surface consists of functionality that can receive or process data influenced by an attacker or lower-trust component.

Examples include:

Network services

HTTP endpoints

API endpoints

File parsers

Upload handlers

Import functionality

Authentication interfaces

IPC interfaces

RPC services

Command-line interfaces

Environment variables

Configuration files

Plugins

Browser handlers

URI schemes

Update mechanisms

Package managers

Deserializers

Database interfaces

Cloud APIs

Not every exposed interface is vulnerable.

The attack surface identifies where research should begin.

docs.title: 3. Attack Surface Versus Vulnerability
docs.text:
Do not confuse exposure with vulnerability.

For example:

Application exposes file upload

means:

Attack Surface Identified

It does not mean:

File Upload Vulnerability Confirmed

The next questions are:

Which files are accepted?

Where are they stored?

Who processes them?

Are they parsed?

Are filenames trusted?

Can paths be controlled?

Are uploaded files executed?

Are permissions enforced?

Which component opens them?

The attack surface generates hypotheses.

Testing validates or rejects them.

docs.title: 4. Start With the Architecture
docs.text:
Before testing individual inputs, understand the system architecture.

Example:

                    Internet
                       |
                       v
                  Reverse Proxy
                       |
                       v
                 Web Application
                    /       \
                   /         \
                  v           v
               API         File Service
                |               |
                v               v
             Database       Parser Worker
                                |
                                v
                         Privileged Service
                                |
                                v
                         Operating System

This immediately exposes several potential trust transitions.

docs.title: 5. Architecture Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Which components exist?

Which components communicate?

Which components accept external input?

Which components are privileged?

Which components access sensitive data?

Which components cross network boundaries?

Which components parse complex data?

Which components trust other components?

Which components execute commands?

Which components access the filesystem?

Architecture documentation can help, but verify assumptions against the running system or source code where possible.

docs.title: 6. Identify Trust Zones
docs.text:
Divide the architecture into trust zones.

Example:

+----------------------------+
|        Untrusted           |
|                            |
| Internet / External User   |
+-------------+--------------+
              |
              v
+----------------------------+
|       Application Zone     |
|                            |
| Web / API / Workers        |
+-------------+--------------+
              |
              v
+----------------------------+
|        Data Zone           |
|                            |
| Database / Storage         |
+-------------+--------------+
              |
              v
+----------------------------+
|      Privileged Zone       |
|                            |
| OS / Admin / Management    |
+----------------------------+

Transitions between zones deserve additional attention.

docs.title: 7. Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
A trust boundary exists when data or control moves between components with different security assumptions or privilege levels.

Examples:

Unauthenticated -> Authenticated

User -> Administrator

Client -> Server

Application -> Operating System

Web Process -> Privileged Service

Container -> Host

Tenant A -> Tenant B

External Network -> Internal Network

Plugin -> Main Application

Guest VM -> Hypervisor

Security vulnerabilities frequently appear where these transitions are incorrectly enforced.

docs.title: 8. Map Components
docs.text:
Create an inventory of major components.

Example:

Component Interface Privilege Input Trust Web Frontend HTTPS Low HTTP Untrusted API HTTPS Application JSON Untrusted Parser Worker Queue Application Files Partially trusted Database TCP Database service SQL Application Admin Service Local RPC High IPC Internal Updater HTTPS High Packages External source

This table helps prioritise research.

docs.title: 9. Enumerate External Interfaces
docs.text:
Start with interfaces accessible from outside the application.

Examples:

TCP services

UDP services

HTTP

HTTPS

WebSocket

gRPC

GraphQL

REST

SOAP

Custom protocols

File upload

Email processing

Webhook receivers

For each interface record:

Protocol

Port

Authentication

Encryption

Input format

Handler

Privilege

Exposure

docs.title: 10. Network Surface
docs.text:
For a controlled research environment, identify listening services.

Linux:

ss -lntup

Alternative:

sudo lsof -i -P -n

Windows PowerShell:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

The objective is to understand the exposed interfaces of the software being researched.

docs.title: 11. Interpret Listening Services
docs.text:
Example:

LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:8080
LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:9000

This suggests two different surfaces.

0.0.0.0:8080

may be remotely reachable depending on network controls.

127.0.0.1:9000

is bound to the local loopback interface.

The local service should not automatically be ignored.

Ask:

Can another application reach it?

Can untrusted local users reach it?

Can SSRF reach it?

Does the public application proxy requests to it?

Does it expose privileged functionality?

docs.title: 12. Local Interfaces Matter
docs.text:
A service does not need to be Internet-facing to be security-relevant.

Example:

External User
      |
      v
Web Application
      |
      v
Internal HTTP Client
      |
      v
127.0.0.1:9000
      |
      v
Management Service

A server-side request vulnerability could expose an otherwise local-only interface.

Attack surfaces should therefore be mapped in context.

docs.title: 13. HTTP Attack Surface
docs.text:
For web applications, enumerate:

Routes

Methods

Parameters

Headers

Cookies

Request bodies

File uploads

WebSockets

API versions

Administrative routes

Debug routes

Static resources

Redirect handlers

Do not focus only on pages visible in the browser.

docs.title: 14. Route Inventory
docs.text:
A route inventory might look like:

Method Route Authentication Input Function POST /login No Form Authentication GET /api/users/{id} Yes Path User lookup POST /api/import Yes File Import POST /api/webhook Token JSON Integration GET /admin/status Admin Query Diagnostics

Routes involving:

Files

URLs

Commands

Templates

Identifiers

Authentication

Administrative functionality

deserve additional attention.

docs.title: 15. HTTP Methods
docs.text:
Check which methods are implemented.

Typical methods include:

GET

POST

PUT

PATCH

DELETE

OPTIONS

HEAD

Security enforcement may differ between handlers.

Example:

GET /api/object/123

may correctly enforce authorisation while:

DELETE /api/object/123

uses a different code path.

docs.title: 16. API Surface
docs.text:
For APIs, map:

Endpoints

Versions

Methods

Parameters

Object identifiers

Authentication

Roles

Permissions

Relationships

State changes

Rate limits

Example:

/api/v1/users
/api/v1/users/{id}
/api/v1/projects
/api/v1/projects/{id}
/api/v1/projects/{id}/members

Object relationships are particularly important when investigating access-control vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 17. GraphQL Surface
docs.text:
GraphQL changes the shape of the attack surface.

Investigate:

Queries

Mutations

Subscriptions

Object types

Arguments

Resolvers

Custom scalars

Authorisation boundaries

The security boundary often exists inside resolvers rather than at a traditional URL endpoint.

docs.title: 18. gRPC Surface
docs.text:
For gRPC applications, identify:

Services

Methods

Messages

Metadata

Authentication

Streaming interfaces

Reflection availability

Then map:

Client Input
     |
     v
RPC Method
     |
     v
Handler
     |
     v
Business Logic

docs.title: 19. WebSocket Surface
docs.text:
WebSockets may expose long-lived application functionality.

Map:

Connection establishment

Authentication

Message types

Message format

State transitions

Authorisation

Server responses

Do not assume controls applied to normal HTTP routes automatically apply to WebSocket messages.

docs.title: 20. File-Based Attack Surface
docs.text:
Applications frequently process attacker-influenced files.

Examples:

Images

PDF documents

Office documents

Archives

Configuration files

Backups

Database files

Certificates

Media files

Templates

Firmware

Import files

Files can reach complex parsers that are otherwise inaccessible.

docs.title: 21. File Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
Map the complete lifecycle.

Upload
  |
  v
Temporary Storage
  |
  v
Validation
  |
  v
Parser
  |
  v
Transformation
  |
  v
Permanent Storage
  |
  v
Later Processing

Ask what happens at every stage.

docs.title: 22. File Questions
docs.text:
For each supported file type:

How is the type determined?

Extension?

MIME type?

Magic bytes?

Parser detection?

Where is the file stored?

Is the original filename preserved?

Is the file decompressed?

Is metadata parsed?

Is the file converted?

Does another service process it?

Does processing happen immediately or asynchronously?

The final parser may run with different privileges from the upload service.

docs.title: 23. Archive Attack Surface
docs.text:
Archive processing deserves special attention because archives contain internal paths and metadata.

Examples:

ZIP

TAR

7z

RAR

Package formats

Map:

Archive
   |
   v
Parser
   |
   v
Entry Name
   |
   v
Path Construction
   |
   v
Destination

Questions include:

Are paths canonicalised?

Are absolute paths rejected?

Are parent-directory references rejected?

Are symbolic links handled?

Are nested archives processed?

Are extraction limits enforced?

docs.title: 24. Parser Attack Surface
docs.text:
Complex parsers are attractive research targets.

A generic parser may contain:

Header
   |
   v
Length
   |
   v
Type
   |
   v
Payload
   |
   v
Nested Objects
   |
   v
Output Structure

Research each stage independently.

docs.title: 25. Parser Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

What happens with truncated input?

What happens with extra data?

What happens with duplicate fields?

What happens with unknown types?

What happens with invalid lengths?

What happens with deeply nested structures?

What happens with zero-length objects?

What happens with integer boundaries?

These questions can become fuzzing hypotheses later.

docs.title: 26. Command-Line Attack Surface
docs.text:
Command-line applications accept input through:

Arguments

Files

Environment variables

Standard input

Configuration

Working directory

Inherited handles

Example:

program --config config.yml input.dat

Potential research surfaces include:

Argument parsing

Path handling

Configuration parsing

File parsing

Environment expansion

docs.title: 27. Environment Variables
docs.text:
Applications may trust environment variables controlling:

Paths

Configuration

Proxies

Libraries

Runtime behavior

Temporary directories

Credentials

Debugging

Ask:

Who can control the environment?

Which process consumes the value?

Does the value cross a privilege boundary?

Environment-variable influence is only security-relevant when an attacker can control it under meaningful conditions.

docs.title: 28. Configuration Surface
docs.text:
Configuration may originate from:

Local files

Environment variables

Registry

Remote configuration

Database

Cloud metadata

Command-line arguments

Configuration can affect security-critical behavior.

Examples:

Authentication disabled

Debugging enabled

Unsafe parser mode

External command path

Plugin directory

Trusted host list

docs.title: 29. IPC Attack Surface
docs.text:
Inter-process communication may include:

Named pipes

Unix sockets

Shared memory

RPC

COM

DCOM

D-Bus

Local HTTP

Custom protocols

Map:

Client
   |
   v
IPC Endpoint
   |
   v
Privileged Service

Then determine who can access the endpoint.

docs.title: 30. Privileged Services
docs.text:
Privileged services are high-value research targets because they may cross a privilege boundary.

Example:

Unprivileged Application
        |
        v
IPC Message
        |
        v
SYSTEM / root Service
        |
        v
Sensitive Operation

Important questions include:

Who can connect?

How is the caller identified?

What operations are exposed?

Which parameters are trusted?

Are paths attacker-controlled?

Can commands be influenced?

Are object permissions checked?

docs.title: 31. Plugin Architecture
docs.text:
Applications supporting plugins introduce another trust relationship.

Map:

Application
    |
    v
Plugin Discovery
    |
    v
Plugin Selection
    |
    v
Plugin Loading
    |
    v
Execution

Investigate:

Search paths

Signature validation

File permissions

Plugin configuration

Load order

Update mechanism

docs.title: 32. Update Mechanisms
docs.text:
Software updaters often operate with elevated privileges.

Map:

Update Server
     |
     v
Metadata
     |
     v
Package Download
     |
     v
Verification
     |
     v
Installation

Questions include:

Is transport authenticated?

Are packages signed?

Are signatures verified?

Is metadata authenticated?

Can downgrade occur?

Can the update location be influenced?

Which privilege performs installation?

docs.title: 33. Dependency Surface
docs.text:
Applications depend on external components.

Examples:

Libraries

Packages

Plugins

Containers

Runtime modules

Operating-system libraries

Record important dependencies and their trust relationships.

Do not assume that the application code itself represents the complete attack surface.

docs.title: 34. Authentication Surface
docs.text:
Map every location where authentication state is created, accepted or changed.

Examples:

Login

Password reset

MFA

Remember-me

API tokens

OAuth

SAML

Session refresh

Account recovery

Device trust

Authentication flows frequently contain multiple transitions.

docs.title: 35. Authentication State Machine
docs.text:
Example:

Unauthenticated
      |
      v
Credentials Accepted
      |
      v
MFA Required
      |
      v
MFA Verified
      |
      v
Authenticated

Ask whether any transition can be skipped.

docs.title: 36. Authorisation Surface
docs.text:
Identify operations involving:

Object access

Administrative actions

Role changes

Tenant boundaries

Ownership

Resource creation

Resource deletion

Sensitive data

For each operation determine:

Who is the caller?

What object is requested?

Who owns the object?

Which role is required?

Where is the decision enforced?

docs.title: 37. Object Relationships
docs.text:
Object-level access control becomes easier to analyse when relationships are mapped.

Example:

User
 |
 +---- Project A
 |       |
 |       +---- Document 1
 |
 +---- Project B
         |
         +---- Document 2

Test whether identifiers alone determine access or whether ownership is independently validated.

docs.title: 38. Role Matrix
docs.text:
Build a role matrix.

Function Anonymous User Manager Admin View own profile No Yes Yes Yes View other profile No Limited Yes Yes Delete user No No No Yes Export data No No Yes Yes

Then compare expected behavior with actual enforcement.

docs.title: 39. State-Dependent Surface
docs.text:
Some functionality becomes reachable only after specific actions.

Example:

Create Account
     |
     v
Verify Email
     |
     v
Create Project
     |
     v
Invite User
     |
     v
Transfer Ownership

Business logic vulnerabilities often appear in unexpected state transitions.

docs.title: 40. State Machine Analysis
docs.text:
Represent important workflows explicitly.

CREATED
   |
   v
PENDING
   |
   v
APPROVED
   |
   v
COMPLETED

Then ask:

Can CREATED become COMPLETED?

Can COMPLETED return to PENDING?

Can the same transition occur twice?

Can two requests race?

Can state be modified directly?

docs.title: 41. Data Flow Mapping
docs.text:
For important inputs, trace data through the system.

Example:

HTTP Parameter
      |
      v
Controller
      |
      v
Decoder
      |
      v
Validation
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
Database Query

Record transformations and checks.

docs.title: 42. Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text:
Identify:

Source

where attacker-controlled data enters.

Then identify:

Sink

where a security-sensitive operation occurs.

Example:

HTTP parameter
      |
      v
String manipulation
      |
      v
Validation
      |
      v
Process execution

The research question becomes:

Can the source influence the sink?

docs.title: 43. High-Value Sinks
docs.text:
Common security-sensitive operations include:

Process creation

Shell execution

Dynamic evaluation

SQL execution

Filesystem access

Network requests

Template rendering

Deserialization

Memory operations

Authentication decisions

Authorisation decisions

Cryptographic operations

Finding a sink is not enough.

Determine whether attacker-controlled input can reach it.

docs.title: 44. Validation Boundaries
docs.text:
Identify where validation occurs.

Example:

Input
  |
  v
Validation
  |
  v
Decode
  |
  v
Sensitive Operation

This may be interesting because validation happens before transformation.

Compare with:

Input
  |
  v
Decode
  |
  v
Canonicalise
  |
  v
Validate
  |
  v
Sensitive Operation

The order of operations matters.

docs.title: 45. Sanitisation Versus Validation
docs.text:
These concepts are different.

Validation asks:

Is this input acceptable?

Sanitisation attempts:

Can this input be transformed into an acceptable form?

Security problems can arise when developers assume sanitisation handles every dangerous representation.

docs.title: 46. Normalisation
docs.text:
Look for transformations such as:

URL decoding

HTML decoding

Unicode normalisation

Case conversion

Path normalisation

Whitespace removal

JSON parsing

XML parsing

Archive extraction

Repeated transformations can create inconsistencies between security checks and final interpretation.

docs.title: 47. Privilege Mapping
docs.text:
Record the privilege of each component.

Example:

Component Identity Web Server www-data Worker app-worker Database postgres Management Agent root

This helps identify meaningful escalation boundaries.

docs.title: 48. Filesystem Access
docs.text:
Identify:

Files read

Files written

Temporary directories

Configuration files

Log files

Upload directories

Plugin directories

Executable paths

Then review permissions.

Linux:

namei -l /path/to/file

stat /path/to/file

Windows PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Path\To\File" | Format-List

The security significance depends on the process identity and attacker capabilities.

docs.title: 49. Temporary Files
docs.text:
Temporary file handling can introduce:

Predictable filenames

Race conditions

Unsafe permissions

Symlink problems

Cross-user access

Information disclosure

Map:

Creation

Permissions

Naming

Location

Use

Deletion

docs.title: 50. Database Surface
docs.text:
Map how applications interact with databases.

Identify:

Database type

Connection identity

Query construction

ORM

Stored procedures

Raw queries

Administrative functions

Questions include:

Which queries contain user input?

Which account executes them?

What permissions does the database account have?

Are multiple tenants stored together?

docs.title: 51. Outbound Network Surface
docs.text:
Applications frequently make outbound requests.

Potential sources include:

URL parameters

Webhooks

Import URLs

Image URLs

Feed readers

PDF generators

Cloud integrations

Update checks

Map:

User Input
    |
    v
URL Construction
    |
    v
Validation
    |
    v
HTTP Client
    |
    v
Destination

This can expose trust boundaries between external input and internal network access.

docs.title: 52. Cloud Metadata and Internal Services
docs.text:
When researching cloud-hosted applications, consider whether server-side network functionality can reach:

Metadata services

Internal APIs

Management interfaces

Private services

Do not probe infrastructure outside the authorised research scope.

docs.title: 53. Secrets Surface
docs.text:
Identify where secrets may exist:

Configuration files

Environment variables

Source code

Logs

Database

Process arguments

Temporary files

Backups

CI/CD configuration

Then determine which components and users can access them.

docs.title: 54. Cryptographic Surface
docs.text:
Security-sensitive cryptographic functionality may include:

Token signing

Password hashing

Encryption

Certificate validation

Random-number generation

Key storage

Signature verification

Focus on security assumptions rather than merely identifying algorithms.

docs.title: 55. Deserialization Surface
docs.text:
Locate functionality that reconstructs objects from external data.

Examples:

Session data

Message queues

Cache entries

API objects

Import files

RPC messages

Map:

Input
  |
  v
Deserializer
  |
  v
Object Construction
  |
  v
Application Behavior

Determine whether untrusted data reaches dangerous deserialization mechanisms.

docs.title: 56. Template Surface
docs.text:
Identify template engines used for:

Web pages

Emails

Reports

Documents

Notifications

Configuration generation

Then determine:

Who controls template content?

Who controls variables?

Are templates treated as code?

Where are templates rendered?

docs.title: 57. Logging Surface
docs.text:
Logs can become a security boundary when attacker-controlled values are recorded.

Consider:

Log injection

Sensitive-data exposure

Parser confusion

Terminal control characters

Downstream log processing

Map where logs are consumed after creation.

docs.title: 58. Administrative Interfaces
docs.text:
Administrative functionality deserves special attention.

Examples:

Management APIs

Debug endpoints

Health endpoints

Metrics

Configuration interfaces

Maintenance functions

Backup and restore

Import and export

Determine whether administrative functionality is exposed through alternate interfaces.

docs.title: 59. Debug Functionality
docs.text:
Search for:

debug

test

internal

development

diagnostic

trace

admin

Debug functionality may expose:

Configuration

Stack traces

Environment variables

Internal paths

Management operations

Presence alone does not prove vulnerability.

Verify exposure and access control.

docs.title: 60. Hidden and Legacy Functionality
docs.text:
Applications evolve.

Old functionality may remain accessible.

Look for:

Deprecated API versions

Legacy routes

Unused handlers

Old protocols

Migration endpoints

Compatibility modes

Backup files

Security controls may differ between new and legacy implementations.

docs.title: 61. Source Tree Reconnaissance
docs.text:
When source is available, begin by understanding the repository.

Useful commands:

find . -maxdepth 2 -type f | sort

For a cleaner overview:

tree -L 2

Identify:

Application entry points

Controllers

Routes

Services

Models

Parsers

Authentication

Authorisation

Configuration

Dependencies

Tests

docs.title: 62. Search for Routes
docs.text:
Examples vary by framework.

General search:

rg -n "route|router|endpoint|controller" .

For annotations:

rg -n "@(Get|Post|Put|Delete|Patch|Request)Mapping" .

For common JavaScript routing:

rg -n "\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)\(" .

Interpret results according to the framework.

docs.title: 63. Search for Network Listeners
docs.text:
Search for:

rg -n "listen|bind|accept|TcpListener|HttpListener" .

This can reveal services that are not obvious from application documentation.

docs.title: 64. Search for File Handling
docs.text:
rg -n "open|read|write|upload|extract|archive|temp" .

Then review candidate functions in context.

A keyword match is only a lead.

docs.title: 65. Search for Process Execution
docs.text:
rg -n "exec|system|spawn|ProcessBuilder|CreateProcess" .

For each result determine:

Can attacker-controlled data reach it?

Is a shell involved?

Are arguments separated?

What privilege executes the process?

docs.title: 66. Search for Network Requests
docs.text:
rg -n "http|request|url|fetch|client" .

Look for server-side functionality that accepts user-influenced destinations.

docs.title: 67. Search for Deserialization
docs.text:
rg -n "deserialize|unserialize|pickle|ObjectInputStream" .

Review:

Input origin

Deserializer

Allowed types

Validation

Object behavior

docs.title: 68. Search for Authentication
docs.text:
rg -n "login|authenticate|authentication|session|token" .

Map authentication entry points before reviewing individual implementations.

docs.title: 69. Search for Authorisation
docs.text:
rg -n "authorize|authorise|permission|role|ownership|access" .

Then determine whether security checks are:

Centralised

Distributed

Route-specific

Object-specific

Inconsistent authorisation is particularly interesting.

docs.title: 70. Search for Dangerous Assumptions
docs.text:
Comments can expose developer assumptions.

rg -n "TODO|FIXME|HACK|temporary|trusted|safe|internal" .

These strings do not imply vulnerabilities.

They can identify code requiring closer review.

docs.title: 71. Dependency Inventory
docs.text:
Depending on the ecosystem, inspect files such as:

package.json

package-lock.json

requirements.txt

pyproject.toml

pom.xml

build.gradle

go.mod

Cargo.toml

*.csproj

Understand which components perform security-sensitive operations.

docs.title: 72. Binary-Only Targets
docs.text:
When source is unavailable, the same methodology still applies.

Use:

Runtime observation

Strings

Imports

Exports

Network behavior

Filesystem behavior

Configuration

Disassembly

Decompilation

The objective remains:

Input -> Processing -> Sensitive Operation

docs.title: 73. Identify Binary Metadata
docs.text:
Linux:

file ./target

readelf -h ./target

Windows binaries can be inspected using appropriate PE-analysis tools.

Record:

Architecture

Binary format

Runtime

Dependencies

Security properties

docs.title: 74. Strings
docs.text:
Strings can reveal:

URLs

File paths

Error messages

Protocol commands

Configuration names

Debug functionality

API routes

Example:

strings ./target | less

Use strings as reconnaissance, not as proof of behavior.

docs.title: 75. Imported Functions
docs.text:
Imported APIs can reveal capabilities.

Examples:

Networking

Process creation

Filesystem access

Cryptography

Memory management

The presence of a function only indicates capability.

Reachability and attacker influence still need validation.

docs.title: 76. Runtime Observation
docs.text:
Observe what the application does.

Linux examples:

strace -f ./target

For filesystem-related activity:

strace -f -e trace=file ./target

Use controlled input and compare behavior.

docs.title: 77. Network Observation
docs.text:
Capture application traffic in a controlled environment.

Useful questions:

Which hosts are contacted?

Which protocols are used?

Is traffic encrypted?

Are certificates validated?

What data is transmitted?

Which actions trigger outbound requests?

docs.title: 78. Process Relationships
docs.text:
Understand the process tree.

Linux:

ps -ef --forest

The application may contain:

Parent process

Worker

Parser process

Updater

Privileged helper

Different processes may operate under different privileges.

docs.title: 79. Child Processes
docs.text:
If user input causes another process to start:

Input
  |
  v
Application
  |
  v
Child Process

investigate:

Executable selection

Arguments

Environment

Working directory

Privileges

This can reveal important trust boundaries.

docs.title: 80. Prioritising the Attack Surface
docs.text:
Not every component deserves equal research time.

A useful prioritisation model considers:

Attacker Control

Exposure

Privilege

Complexity

Security Boundary

Input Complexity

Historical Vulnerability Patterns

docs.title: 81. High-Priority Characteristics
docs.text:
A component becomes particularly interesting when several factors combine.

Example:

Remote Input
     +
Complex Parser
     +
Native Code
     +
High Privilege

or:

Low-Privilege User
     +
IPC
     +
SYSTEM Service
     +
File Operation

These combinations can guide research priorities.

docs.title: 82. Attack Surface Matrix
docs.text:
Example:

Surface Attacker Control Privilege Complexity Boundary Priority HTTP API High Medium Medium Auth High Image Parser High Medium High Process High Local Config Low High Low Local Medium Admin API Medium High Medium Role High Static Files Low Low Low None Low

The values are contextual, not universal.

docs.title: 83. Prioritise Security Boundaries
docs.text:
A useful rule is:

More Important Boundary
        +
More Attacker Control
        +
More Complex Processing
        =
Higher Research Priority

This is a prioritisation heuristic, not a vulnerability score.

docs.title: 84. Build Hypotheses
docs.text:
Once the surface is mapped, convert observations into testable hypotheses.

Weak:

Test file upload.

Better:

The archive extraction worker accepts attacker-controlled
archive entry names. If canonical destination paths are not
validated after extraction-path construction, an archive entry
may reference a location outside the intended extraction
directory.

The second hypothesis identifies:

Input

Processing

Missing control

Potential boundary

docs.title: 85. Hypothesis Template
docs.text:
Use:

Observation:

Attacker-Controlled Input:

Processing Component:

Security Assumption:

Sensitive Operation:

Hypothesis:

Expected Secure Behavior:

Test:

Evidence Required:

docs.title: 86. Example Hypothesis
docs.text:
Observation:
The application imports configuration from a user-supplied URL.

Attacker-Controlled Input:
Import URL.

Processing Component:
Backend import service.

Security Assumption:
The supplied URL resolves only to approved external resources.

Sensitive Operation:
Server-side HTTP request.

Hypothesis:
Destination validation may not correctly restrict internal
addresses after URL parsing or resolution.

Expected Secure Behavior:
Requests to prohibited destinations should be rejected.

Evidence Required:
Request behavior, server logs and destination validation logic.

Testing must remain within authorised infrastructure.

docs.title: 87. Rank Hypotheses
docs.text:
Possible fields:

Hypothesis Reachability Impact Confidence Cost Priority H-001 High High Medium Low High H-002 Medium High Low High Medium H-003 High Low High Low Medium

This prevents research from becoming an unstructured collection of experiments.

docs.title: 88. Record Negative Results
docs.text:
If a hypothesis is not supported:

Hypothesis:
Path validation occurs before canonicalisation.

Test:
Multiple controlled path representations.

Result:
All tested paths canonicalised before validation.

Conclusion:
Hypothesis not supported for tested version.

Next:
Review symbolic-link handling.

Negative results refine the attack surface.

docs.title: 89. Attack Surface Changes Over Time
docs.text:
Attack surfaces change when:

Features are added

APIs are introduced

Dependencies change

Plugins are installed

Cloud services are integrated

Authentication changes

Legacy functionality remains

Repeat attack surface analysis after major software changes.

docs.title: 90. Compare Versions
docs.text:
Version comparison can reveal newly introduced surfaces.

Version 1
   |
   v
Attack Surface A

Version 2
   |
   +---- New API
   |
   +---- New Parser
   |
   +---- New Plugin System

New functionality often creates new trust assumptions.

docs.title: 91. Compare Configurations
docs.text:
The same software may expose different surfaces depending on configuration.

Example:

Default Installation
        |
        +---- Public API
        |
        +---- Local Admin Interface

Enterprise Configuration
        |
        +---- SSO
        |
        +---- Plugin Service
        |
        +---- Remote Management

Document the configuration under test.

docs.title: 92. Default Versus Optional Features
docs.text:
Classify surfaces as:

Default

Optional

Deprecated

Experimental

Administrative

Development-only

This matters when assessing affected deployments.

docs.title: 93. Evidence to Capture
docs.text:
For attack surface analysis, retain:

Application version

Architecture diagram

Listening services

Routes

API documentation

Component identities

Trust boundaries

File formats

Process tree

Configuration

Relevant source locations

Hypotheses

Negative results

This evidence supports later research.

docs.title: 94. Attack Surface Record
docs.text:
A reusable record can look like:

Surface ID:
AS-001

Component:
Import Service

Interface:
POST /api/import

Authentication:
User

Input:
Uploaded archive

Processing:
Background parser worker

Worker Identity:
app-worker

Sensitive Operations:
Archive extraction and filesystem writes

Trust Boundary:
User -> Application filesystem

Hypotheses:
H-001 Path validation
H-002 Symbolic-link handling
H-003 Extraction resource limits

Priority:
High

docs.title: 95. Attack Surface Graph
docs.text:
For complex applications, model relationships.

                    [Internet]
                        |
                        v
                    [Web API]
                   /    |    \
                  /     |     \
                 v      v      v
             [Auth] [Upload] [Webhook]
                       |         |
                       v         v
                   [Queue]   [HTTP Client]
                       |
                       v
                  [Parser Worker]
                    /       \
                   v         v
              [Filesystem] [Database]
                   |
                   v
            [Privileged Helper]

The graph can expose attack chains that are difficult to see from endpoint lists.

docs.title: 96. Attack Chains
docs.text:
A vulnerability may require multiple surfaces.

Example:

Upload
  |
  v
Parser
  |
  v
Controlled File
  |
  v
Privileged Import

or:

Public API
   |
   v
Server-Side Request
   |
   v
Internal Management API

Attack surface analysis should therefore include relationships between components.

docs.title: 97. Do Not Overlook Error Paths
docs.text:
Error handling may invoke different functionality.

Example:

Input
  |
  v
Parser
  |
  +---- Success -> Normal Handler
  |
  +---- Failure -> Recovery Handler

Research:

Recovery

Rollback

Cleanup

Temporary files

Logging

Retry behavior

Security assumptions can differ on error paths.

docs.title: 98. Cleanup Paths
docs.text:
Cleanup code may perform:

File deletion

Directory removal

Rollback

Process termination

Resource release

If cleanup uses attacker-influenced paths or identifiers, it can become a security-sensitive surface.

docs.title: 99. Asynchronous Processing
docs.text:
Background jobs can hide important attack surfaces.

Example:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Queue
     |
     v
Worker
     |
     v
Parser

The initial HTTP response may reveal little about what happens later.

Inspect:

Queue message

Worker identity

Worker logs

Delayed actions

Retries

docs.title: 100. Cross-Component Validation
docs.text:
Different components may interpret the same data differently.

Example:

Frontend Validation
       |
       v
Queue Serialization
       |
       v
Worker Parsing
       |
       v
Filesystem

If each component performs different normalisation, security inconsistencies may appear.
