Preserve before investigating

The original crashing input, exact binary, environment and diagnostic output are evidence. Preserve them before minimising the input or changing the research build.

Separate the crash site from the root cause

Memory corruption may occur long before the application finally terminates. Trace attacker-controlled data backward from the observed failure until the incorrect security assumption or memory operation is understood.

Use multiple evidence sources

A minimised reproducer, sanitizer report, debugger state, source-code path and negative control together provide a substantially stronger conclusion than any one of them alone.

Keep the minimised reproducer

Once the root cause is fixed, the minimised input can become a regression test that verifies future versions continue to handle the condition safely.

Do not equate memory corruption with code execution

Confirm the memory primitive, attacker control, reachability, process context and relevant mitigations before making exploitability claims.

Crash severity depends on context

A local utility terminating on malformed input and an unauthenticated network service experiencing attacker-controlled memory corruption may contain similar implementation errors but present very different security risks.

docs.title: CVE Research
docs.text:
CVE research is the process of understanding whether a published vulnerability applies to a specific product, version, deployment, or environment.

A CVE identifier is only a reference.

It does not automatically prove that a target is vulnerable.

A mature CVE research process should answer:

What product is affected?

Which versions are affected?

Which versions are fixed?

What is the vulnerable component?

What is the root cause?

What prerequisites are required?

What is the attack vector?

What changed in the patch?

Does the tested environment actually satisfy the vulnerable condition?

Can the issue be reproduced safely?

What impact is supported by evidence?

The key distinction is:

Known CVE
   !=
Confirmed Vulnerability on Target

Authorised research only

Perform CVE validation only against software and systems that you are explicitly authorised to test. Public exploit availability does not create permission to use it. Prefer low-impact validation and avoid unnecessary data access, persistence, lateral movement, or destructive actions.

docs.title: Where CVE Research Fits
docs.text:
CVE research often begins after:

  • technology discovery;
  • product fingerprinting;
  • version identification;
  • vulnerability scanning;
  • vendor advisory review;
  • patch diffing;
  • source or binary analysis.

A useful model is:

Technology Identified
      |
      v
Possible CVE
      |
      v
Authoritative Research
      |
      v
Affected-Version Validation
      |
      v
Configuration / Prerequisite Validation
      |
      v
Safe Reproduction
      |
      v
Confirmed / Rejected / Inconclusive

Related methodology:

Vulnerability Research Methodology

Patch Diffing

Proof-of-Concept Development

docs.title: Start With the Product
docs.text:
Before researching a CVE, establish the exact product.

Record:

Vendor
Product
Component
Edition
Platform
Architecture

Avoid broad assumptions such as:

Apache detected

therefore:

Apache CVE applies

The exact affected component matters.

docs.title: Product Identity
docs.text:
Useful sources include:

  • product banners;
  • application UI;
  • package metadata;
  • vendor files;
  • API responses;
  • installation directories;
  • package manager output;
  • software inventory.

Use multiple signals where possible.

docs.title: Version Identification
docs.text:
Version identification is one of the most important steps.

Potential sources include:

HTTP headers
Application footer
Binary metadata
Package manager
File properties
CLI version output
Registry
Package manifest
Build information

The strongest source depends on the product.

docs.title: Banner Version Is Not Always Enough
docs.text:
A banner may be:

  • hidden;
  • modified;
  • generic;
  • stale;
  • reverse-proxy generated.

Do not rely on one header when stronger local or authenticated evidence exists.

docs.title: Backported Fixes
docs.text:
Some vendors patch vulnerabilities without changing the upstream version number.

This is common in:

  • Linux distributions;
  • enterprise software;
  • long-term-support packages.

Therefore:

Version appears affected

does not always mean:

Package is vulnerable

Check vendor-specific patch status.

docs.title: Distribution Packages
docs.text:
For Linux systems, check:

Package version
Distribution release
Security advisory
Backport status

A distribution package may contain a security fix that is not obvious from the upstream version.

docs.title: Build Numbers
docs.text:
Some products use:

major.minor.patch

while others rely heavily on:

build numbers

or:

revision numbers

Use the vendor's actual affected-version format.

docs.title: CVE Identifier
docs.text:
A CVE identifier looks like:

CVE-YYYY-NNNN

or a longer numeric sequence.

The identifier itself usually does not contain enough technical detail to determine applicability.

docs.title: Start With Authoritative Sources
docs.text:
Preferred sources include:

  1. vendor advisory;
  2. vendor release notes;
  3. CVE record;
  4. NVD;
  5. official project repository;
  6. original researcher publication;
  7. high-quality independent analysis.

Avoid beginning with random exploit repositories.

docs.title: Vendor Advisory
docs.text:
The vendor advisory should usually be the primary source for:

Affected versions
Fixed versions
Affected component
Mitigation
Patch
Configuration prerequisites

When vendor and third-party summaries disagree, investigate the vendor-specific details carefully.

docs.title: CVE Program
docs.text:
Official CVE resource:

CVE Program

Useful information may include:

  • identifier;
  • description;
  • references;
  • assigning authority.

docs.title: NVD
docs.text:
NIST National Vulnerability Database:

NVD

NVD may provide:

  • CVSS;
  • CPE information;
  • references;
  • affected-product metadata.

Treat this as supporting information rather than the sole source of truth.

docs.title: Vendor Security Pages
docs.text:
Many vendors maintain dedicated security portals.

Prefer those for:

  • patch status;
  • fixed builds;
  • mitigations;
  • configuration guidance.

docs.title: Original Research
docs.text:
Original researcher write-ups may provide:

  • root cause;
  • technical detail;
  • proof of concept;
  • attack chain;
  • edge cases.

Where possible, distinguish:

Vendor-confirmed facts

from:

Researcher interpretation

docs.title: Exploit Repositories
docs.text:
Exploit repositories can be useful for:

  • understanding public PoCs;
  • comparing trigger conditions;
  • reproducing known behavior.

But they are not authoritative vulnerability databases.

docs.title: Treat Public PoCs as Untrusted
docs.text:
Before executing a public PoC:

Read source
Inspect dependencies
Inspect network destinations
Inspect file operations
Inspect shell commands
Run in isolated environment

Never blindly execute code because it claims to exploit a CVE.

docs.title: Malicious PoCs
docs.text:
Fake exploit repositories have historically been used to target security researchers.

Possible malicious behavior may include:

  • credential theft;
  • reverse shells;
  • cryptominers;
  • destructive commands;
  • hidden network callbacks.

Always review the code.

docs.title: Research Folder Structure
docs.text:
A useful structure is:

research/
└── CVE-YYYY-NNNN/
    ├── notes.md
    ├── advisory/
    ├── vulnerable/
    ├── patched/
    ├── poc/
    ├── captures/
    └── hashes/

This keeps evidence organised.

docs.title: Initial CVE Record
docs.text:
Create a basic research record:

CVE:
Vendor:
Product:
Component:
Affected versions:
Fixed versions:
Attack vector:
Authentication:
User interaction:
Root cause:
Vendor advisory:
Patch:
Public PoC:
Status:

Update it as evidence improves.

docs.title: Validate Affected Versions
docs.text:
Do not trust a single copied affected-range statement.

Compare:

Vendor advisory
CVE record
Release notes
Patch commit
Package advisory

Resolve discrepancies before testing.

docs.title: Version Range Example
docs.text:
Suppose an advisory states:

Affected:
3.0.0 - 3.4.5

Fixed:
3.4.6

A target running:

3.4.4

is potentially affected.

But still verify:

  • configuration;
  • component availability;
  • backports;
  • mitigation.

docs.title: Exact Version Matters
docs.text:
These may not be equivalent:

Product 3.4.4

Product 3.4.4-enterprise-7

Distribution package 3.4.4-2ubuntu1.6

Vendor packaging can change patch status.

docs.title: Configuration Prerequisites
docs.text:
Many CVEs require specific configuration.

Examples include:

  • feature enabled;
  • endpoint exposed;
  • plugin installed;
  • authentication disabled;
  • unsafe option enabled;
  • specific protocol active.

A version match alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Feature Availability
docs.text:
Ask:

Is the affected feature enabled?

Is the vulnerable route reachable?

Is the vulnerable module installed?

Is the component exposed remotely?

If the feature is disabled, the vulnerability may not be reachable.

docs.title: Authentication Requirements
docs.text:
Determine whether exploitation requires:

No authentication
Low-privileged account
Administrative account
Local access

This affects practical risk.

docs.title: User Interaction
docs.text:
Some vulnerabilities require:

  • opening a file;
  • visiting a page;
  • clicking a link;
  • importing a document.

Record this clearly.

docs.title: Attack Vector
docs.text:
Common conceptual attack vectors include:

Network
Adjacent
Local
Physical

Use the actual CVSS specification when assigning formal scoring.

docs.title: Privilege Requirement
docs.text:
Determine whether the attacker needs:

None
Low privileges
High privileges

This is an important severity factor.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Do not stop at:

CVE causes RCE

Try to understand:

Why?

Possible root causes include:

  • missing authentication;
  • unsafe deserialization;
  • path traversal;
  • command injection;
  • memory corruption;
  • improper input validation;
  • authorization failure;
  • unsafe file handling;
  • protocol parsing error.

docs.title: Root-Cause Model
docs.text:
Attacker-Controlled Input
      |
      v
Missing / Incorrect Validation
      |
      v
Unsafe Operation
      |
      v
Security Impact

The CVE identifier sits above this technical reality.

docs.title: Patch Analysis
docs.text:
A patch is often one of the strongest sources for understanding root cause.

Related note:

Patch Diffing

A useful process is:

Vulnerable Version
      |
      +----+
           |
           v
         Diff
           ^
           |
      +----+
      |
Patched Version
      |
      v
Changed Security Condition

docs.title: Source Patch
docs.text:
If source is available:

git diff <old> <new>

or:

git show <commit>

Look for changes involving:

  • validation;
  • bounds checks;
  • authentication;
  • authorization;
  • sanitisation;
  • parsing;
  • memory allocation;
  • command execution.

docs.title: Patch Commit
docs.text:
Record:

Repository:
Commit:
Author:
Date:
Changed files:
Relevant function:

This makes research reproducible.

docs.title: Binary Patch
docs.text:
If source is unavailable, compare binaries using:

  • Ghidra;
  • IDA;
  • Binary Ninja;
  • Diaphora;
  • other binary diffing tools.

The objective is to identify:

what behavior changed

not merely:

which bytes changed

docs.title: Patch Does Not Always Fully Explain the CVE
docs.text:
A security release may contain:

  • multiple fixes;
  • refactoring;
  • hardening;
  • unrelated changes.

Trace the change that actually relates to the vulnerable behavior.

docs.title: Mitigation vs Fix
docs.text:
A mitigation reduces exposure.

A fix removes the root cause.

Example:

Disable vulnerable endpoint

may be a mitigation.

Correct unsafe parser logic

may be the actual fix.

Do not confuse the two.

docs.title: Workaround Validation
docs.text:
If a vendor recommends a workaround, test whether it:

  • blocks the vulnerable path;
  • changes the configuration;
  • disables the affected feature.

Document the residual risk.

docs.title: Reproduction Strategy
docs.text:
Prefer the minimum test needed to confirm applicability.

A good hierarchy is:

Version / configuration validation
      |
      v
Low-impact behavioral test
      |
      v
Controlled PoC
      |
      v
Higher-impact validation only if required

docs.title: Safe Validation First
docs.text:
Examples of low-impact evidence include:

  • vulnerable response difference;
  • controlled error;
  • benign callback;
  • deterministic crash;
  • unauthorized access to test data;
  • version-specific behavior.

Do not begin with maximum impact.

docs.title: Proof-of-Concept Review
docs.text:
Related note:

Proof-of-Concept Development

Before using a PoC, determine:

What exactly does it send?

What does it change?

Does it create files?

Does it execute commands?

Does it retrieve data?

Does it contact external infrastructure?

docs.title: PoC Minimisation
docs.text:
If a public exploit performs:

full remote shell

but the vulnerability can be confirmed with:

benign deterministic response

prefer the benign proof.

docs.title: Reproduce Independently
docs.text:
Do not rely solely on tool output.

A strong process is:

Scanner Match
      |
      v
Manual Reproduction
      |
      v
Root-Cause Understanding
      |
      v
Confirmed Finding

docs.title: Scanner Matches
docs.text:
Tools such as Nuclei may report CVE candidates.

Related tool:

Nuclei

Treat the result as:

candidate

until manually validated.

docs.title: CVE Template Validation
docs.text:
For a Nuclei CVE template:

  1. read the template;
  2. inspect request;
  3. inspect matcher;
  4. verify affected versions;
  5. reproduce manually;
  6. consult vendor advisory.

Do not report directly from the template output.

docs.title: Banner-Only Findings
docs.text:
A scanner may report:

Product X 1.2.3
CVE-YYYY-NNNN

based only on a banner.

This is not sufficient confirmation.

docs.title: Manual Validation
docs.text:
A manually validated CVE should establish:

Target satisfies affected condition
+
Vulnerable behavior reproduced

where safe and practical.

docs.title: Confirm the Target Path
docs.text:
Some CVEs affect only:

specific endpoint

or:

specific service

Confirm that the affected component is actually reachable.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Considerations
docs.text:
A target may expose a vulnerable backend through:

  • reverse proxy;
  • load balancer;
  • API gateway.

The visible product may not be the component handling the vulnerable request.

Understand the architecture.

docs.title: WAF Considerations
docs.text:
A WAF may block known exploit patterns.

This can create:

vulnerable backend
+
effective current filtering

The root vulnerability may still exist.

Do not assume the WAF represents remediation.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
A vulnerable service may be reachable only from:

internal network

This affects exploitation prerequisites and risk.

The vulnerability still exists if the affected condition is present.

docs.title: Authentication Controls
docs.text:
An affected endpoint may be protected by authentication even if the original CVE assumes anonymous access.

Validate the deployed context.

docs.title: Product Forks
docs.text:
Forked software may:

  • inherit a vulnerability;
  • patch it independently;
  • modify the vulnerable code.

Version mapping may not be straightforward.

Patch analysis can help.

docs.title: Embedded Components
docs.text:
A product may bundle vulnerable libraries.

Questions include:

Is vulnerable library present?

Is vulnerable function used?

Is attacker-controlled input reachable?

Is vulnerable feature compiled in?

Library presence alone may not prove exploitability.

docs.title: Dependency CVEs
docs.text:
Dependency scanners may report vulnerable package versions.

A strong process is:

Dependency Present
      |
      v
Affected Version?
      |
      v
Vulnerable API Used?
      |
      v
Attacker Reachable?
      |
      v
Impact?

docs.title: Reachability Analysis
docs.text:
This is especially important for library vulnerabilities.

A vulnerable function may exist but never be called.

Source review or runtime tracing can help.

docs.title: Container Images
docs.text:
Container scanners may identify CVEs in installed packages that are:

  • unused;
  • inaccessible;
  • build-only;
  • not reachable.

Prioritise based on actual runtime exposure.

docs.title: Operating-System Packages
docs.text:
A system package CVE may affect:

  • kernel;
  • library;
  • daemon;
  • userland tool.

Determine whether the vulnerable component is actually active.

docs.title: Kernel CVEs
docs.text:
Kernel vulnerabilities often require:

  • local access;
  • specific configuration;
  • affected driver/module;
  • hardware condition.

Do not validate them casually on production systems.

docs.title: Privilege-Escalation CVEs
docs.text:
For local privilege escalation, record:

Initial user
Required privileges
Kernel/OS build
Configuration
Resulting privilege

Avoid unnecessary exploitation when patch/version validation is sufficient.

docs.title: Client-Side CVEs
docs.text:
For browser, office, or document-processing vulnerabilities, determine:

  • vulnerable file format;
  • user interaction;
  • sandbox;
  • protected-view controls;
  • application version.

Do not expose real users to test payloads.

docs.title: Server-Side CVEs
docs.text:
For network-reachable server vulnerabilities, establish:

Service exposed?
Authentication required?
Affected feature enabled?
Input reachable?

docs.title: Memory-Corruption CVEs
docs.text:
For memory corruption, distinguish:

Crash

from:

Reliable code execution

Review:

  • attacker control;
  • memory protections;
  • sandbox;
  • process privilege.

docs.title: Denial-of-Service CVEs
docs.text:
A CVE may only support:

service crash

or:

resource exhaustion

Do not inflate the impact.

docs.title: Authentication-Bypass CVEs
docs.text:
Confirm that the test actually bypasses the intended authentication boundary.

For example:

Unauthenticated request
      |
      v
Protected resource accessible

The exact security decision should be clear.

docs.title: Authorization CVEs
docs.text:
Authorization flaws often depend on:

  • role;
  • object ownership;
  • tenant;
  • privilege.

Test with controlled identities.

docs.title: Injection CVEs
docs.text:
Injection vulnerabilities may involve:

  • SQL;
  • OS command;
  • LDAP;
  • template;
  • expression languages.

The root issue is unsafe interpretation of attacker-controlled input.

docs.title: Path Traversal CVEs
docs.text:
Determine:

Can the attacker control path components?

Is canonicalisation missing?

Can data escape the intended directory?

What files are reachable?

Use harmless files for validation where possible.

docs.title: File Upload CVEs
docs.text:
For upload-related CVEs, distinguish:

  • extension bypass;
  • content-type bypass;
  • storage path issue;
  • execution issue;
  • parser issue.

Do not automatically upload executable content unless required and authorised.

docs.title: SSRF CVEs
docs.text:
For SSRF CVEs:

External callback

may prove server-side request behavior.

It does not automatically prove:

cloud metadata access

or:

internal network compromise

Related tool:

Interactsh

docs.title: CVSS
docs.text:
CVSS can help communicate severity.

Use the current specification and base the metrics on the actual vulnerability.

Do not copy a score blindly from a third-party source.

docs.title: Vendor vs Environmental Severity
docs.text:
A vendor's CVSS score describes the vulnerability generally.

Your organisation may have different environmental risk because of:

  • exposure;
  • authentication;
  • segmentation;
  • compensating controls;
  • asset criticality.

docs.title: EPSS
docs.text:
EPSS estimates the probability of exploitation activity in the wild.

It can support prioritisation but does not replace technical validation.

Official resource:

FIRST EPSS

docs.title: CISA KEV
docs.text:
CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities can help identify vulnerabilities known to have been exploited.

Official resource:

CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog

Presence in KEV affects prioritisation.

It does not prove your specific target is vulnerable.

docs.title: Exploitation in the Wild
docs.text:
If reliable sources report active exploitation, record:

Source
Date
Observed campaign
Affected product

Keep this separate from your technical validation.

docs.title: Threat Intelligence
docs.text:
Threat intelligence can help prioritise CVEs based on:

  • exploitation;
  • threat actors;
  • malware use;
  • target sectors.

It should not replace patch applicability analysis.

docs.title: Exploit Availability
docs.text:
Public exploit availability may increase practical risk.

But distinguish:

PoC exists

from:

Reliable exploit exists

and:

Active exploitation exists

These are different.

docs.title: Metasploit Modules
docs.text:
A CVE may have a Metasploit module.

This means someone encoded an exploitation workflow.

It does not automatically mean the module applies to:

  • your version;
  • your configuration;
  • your target.

Review module conditions before use.

docs.title: Searchsploit
docs.text:
Exploit-DB references can help locate historical PoCs.

Example:

searchsploit CVE-YYYY-NNNN

Treat returned code as untrusted third-party material.

docs.title: GitHub Search
docs.text:
GitHub may contain:

  • PoCs;
  • patch analyses;
  • reproductions;
  • fake exploits.

Validate repository authenticity.

docs.title: Researcher Reputation
docs.text:
Signals of higher confidence include:

  • original discoverer;
  • vendor acknowledgement;
  • coordinated disclosure;
  • established security team;
  • reproducible technical detail.

Still inspect the evidence.

docs.title: Reproduction Environment
docs.text:
Record:

Target version
OS
Architecture
Configuration
PoC revision
Tool version
Network topology

A PoC may fail because environmental assumptions differ.

docs.title: Failed PoC
docs.text:
A failed public PoC does not automatically mean the target is patched.

Possible reasons include:

  • wrong path;
  • authentication;
  • configuration;
  • WAF;
  • version mismatch;
  • broken PoC;
  • wrong architecture.

Investigate.

docs.title: Successful PoC
docs.text:
Likewise:

PoC says success

does not guarantee exploitation actually occurred.

Validate observable behavior.

docs.title: Success Markers
docs.text:
A PoC may look for:

HTTP 200
specific word
response size

These can produce false positives.

Inspect exact success logic.

docs.title: Network Captures
docs.text:
Packet captures can help understand:

  • protocol;
  • request sequence;
  • callbacks;
  • retries.

Protect captures because they may contain sensitive values.

docs.title: HTTP Evidence
docs.text:
For web CVEs, preserve:

Baseline request
Exploit/validation request
Baseline response
Modified response

This often provides stronger evidence than scanner screenshots.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots can support the finding but should not be the only evidence.

Retain textual requests and responses where possible.

docs.title: Target Hash
docs.text:
For binaries:

sha256sum target

or on Windows:

Get-FileHash .\target.exe -Algorithm SHA256

This confirms exactly which build was tested.

docs.title: PoC Hash
docs.text:
Also hash the PoC or test input where relevant.

This helps identify which revision was used during research.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
Maintain a timeline.

Example:

09:10 - CVE identified
09:30 - vendor advisory reviewed
10:00 - affected version confirmed
10:45 - patch commit located
11:20 - root cause identified
12:00 - PoC reviewed
13:15 - safe reproduction successful

docs.title: Status Classification
docs.text:
A useful CVE status model is:

Candidate
Potentially affected
Confirmed affected
Not affected
Mitigated
Patched
Inconclusive

Avoid reducing everything to:

vulnerable / not vulnerable

too early.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
Use when:

Product/version may match

but no validation has been completed.

docs.title: Potentially Affected
docs.text:
Use when:

Affected version appears present

but configuration or behavioral validation is incomplete.

docs.title: Confirmed Affected
docs.text:
Use when:

Affected conditions confirmed
+
Vulnerable behavior reproduced

docs.title: Mitigated
docs.text:
Use when:

Underlying vulnerable version remains

but a compensating control currently prevents the tested path.

Document that distinction.

docs.title: Patched
docs.text:
Use when:

Vendor fix or equivalent root-cause remediation is present

and the vulnerable behavior no longer reproduces.

docs.title: Not Affected
docs.text:
Use only when evidence supports it.

Examples:

  • version outside affected range;
  • vulnerable component absent;
  • vendor backport confirmed;
  • feature not compiled into product.

docs.title: Inconclusive
docs.text:
Use when:

  • testing blocked;
  • version unknown;
  • environment inaccessible;
  • WAF obscures behavior;
  • PoC unreliable.

An inconclusive result is better than an unsupported conclusion.

docs.title: Patch Validation
docs.text:
After applying a fix:

Original PoC
      |
      v
Patched Target
      |
      v
Expected Safe Behavior

Then inspect whether the root cause changed.

docs.title: Regression Testing
docs.text:
A minimal PoC can become a regression test.

Example:

Known vulnerable input

should produce:

safe rejection

on the fixed build.

docs.title: Variant Research
docs.text:
Once the root cause is known, ask:

Does the same bug exist elsewhere?

Related note:

Variant Analysis

Search:

  • sibling functions;
  • alternate endpoints;
  • older versions;
  • shared libraries;
  • related products.

docs.title: 1-Day Research
docs.text:
A newly disclosed vulnerability with a patch but limited public detail may be researched through patch analysis.

A common workflow is:

Patch Released
      |
      v
Diff Vulnerable vs Fixed
      |
      v
Identify Security Change
      |
      v
Understand Root Cause
      |
      v
Create Safe Reproduction

This is often referred to as 1-day vulnerability research.

docs.title: 0-Day Research
docs.text:
An issue without a public fix or identifier is significantly more sensitive.

Do not publish or broadly share details before responsible disclosure.

Related note:

Responsible Disclosure

docs.title: Responsible Disclosure
docs.text:
If your research identifies a previously unknown vulnerability:

Stop broad publication
      |
      v
Preserve Evidence
      |
      v
Contact Vendor
      |
      v
Coordinate Remediation
      |
      v
Disclosure

Follow vendor and organisational disclosure policies.

docs.title: CVE Assignment
docs.text:
CVE identifiers may be assigned through a CVE Numbering Authority, depending on product/vendor arrangements.

Official resource:

CVE Numbering Authorities

docs.title: Report Writing
docs.text:
A CVE finding should explain the actual applicability.

Avoid:

Nuclei detected CVE-202X-XXXX.

Prefer:

The tested application was running an affected version of the product,
and manual validation reproduced the vulnerable behavior described in
CVE-202X-XXXX on the exposed endpoint.

docs.title: Report Affected Version
docs.text:
Include:

Detected version
Affected range
Fixed version
Evidence source

docs.title: Report Configuration
docs.text:
If exploitation requires a specific feature:

The vulnerable component was enabled and reachable without
authentication.

This is much stronger than version evidence alone.

docs.title: Report Mitigated Condition
docs.text:
Example:

The installed product version falls within the published affected range.
However, the vulnerable administrative endpoint was not reachable from
the tested network due to access-control restrictions. The underlying
software should still be updated because the vulnerable code remains
present.

docs.title: Report Patched Condition
docs.text:
Example:

The target reported a historically affected base version, but the
distribution's security package included the vendor backported fix.
Manual testing did not reproduce the vulnerable behavior.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Primary remediation normally includes:

  • upgrade to fixed release;
  • install vendor patch;
  • apply supported hotfix;
  • disable vulnerable component where necessary;
  • apply vendor mitigation temporarily.

Prefer vendor-supported remediation.

docs.title: Do Not Use WAF as Primary Fix
docs.text:
A WAF rule may reduce exploitability.

It does not remove the vulnerable code.

Use it as defence in depth while patching.

docs.title: Patch Prioritisation
docs.text:
Prioritisation may consider:

Internet exposure
Authentication requirement
Exploit availability
Active exploitation
CISA KEV
EPSS
Asset criticality
Compensating controls

docs.title: Emergency Mitigation
docs.text:
When a patch cannot be immediately applied:

Disable feature
Restrict access
Apply firewall/WAF rule
Segment service
Monitor exploitation attempts

Then plan permanent remediation.

docs.title: Retest
docs.text:
After remediation, confirm:

  • fixed version;
  • configuration;
  • original PoC;
  • root-cause behavior;
  • compensating controls if relevant.

docs.title: Identification
docs.text:
• [ ] CVE identifier confirmed.
  • [ ] Vendor confirmed.
  • [ ] Product confirmed.
  • [ ] Component confirmed.
  • [ ] Target version identified.
  • [ ] Build/package revision identified.

docs.title: Research Sources
docs.text:
• [ ] Vendor advisory reviewed.
  • [ ] CVE record reviewed.
  • [ ] NVD reviewed where useful.
  • [ ] Release notes reviewed.
  • [ ] Original researcher publication reviewed where available.
  • [ ] Patch/commit identified where available.

docs.title: Affected Versions
docs.text:
• [ ] Affected range confirmed.
  • [ ] Fixed versions confirmed.
  • [ ] Vendor backports considered.
  • [ ] Distribution package status checked.
  • [ ] Product fork status considered.

docs.title: Preconditions
docs.text:
• [ ] Feature enabled.
  • [ ] Component installed.
  • [ ] Endpoint reachable.
  • [ ] Authentication requirement known.
  • [ ] User interaction requirement known.
  • [ ] Required privileges known.
  • [ ] Network position understood.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
• [ ] Vulnerable function/component identified.
  • [ ] Input path understood.
  • [ ] Missing/incorrect control understood.
  • [ ] Patch behavior reviewed.
  • [ ] Root cause distinguished from symptom.

docs.title: PoC
docs.text:
• [ ] Public PoC source reviewed.
  • [ ] Code manually inspected.
  • [ ] Unexpected network calls ruled out.
  • [ ] Destructive behavior ruled out.
  • [ ] Dependencies reviewed.
  • [ ] PoC tested in isolated environment first.
  • [ ] Minimum-impact validation chosen.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Baseline behavior recorded.
  • [ ] Candidate behavior reproduced.
  • [ ] Manual validation performed.
  • [ ] Scanner match not used as sole evidence.
  • [ ] Success condition independently confirmed.
  • [ ] WAF/proxy effects considered.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• [ ] Actual privilege context known.
  • [ ] Reachability established.
  • [ ] Data exposure minimised.
  • [ ] RCE not inferred from crash alone.
  • [ ] Availability impact considered separately.
  • [ ] Compensating controls documented.
  • [ ] Severity independently assessed.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Product/version evidence retained.
  • [ ] Target hash retained where relevant.
  • [ ] Vendor advisory retained.
  • [ ] Patch/commit retained.
  • [ ] PoC revision retained.
  • [ ] Requests/responses retained.
  • [ ] Screenshots retained where useful.
  • [ ] Research timeline retained.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• [ ] Fixed version identified.
  • [ ] Vendor patch recommended.
  • [ ] Temporary mitigation documented where required.
  • [ ] WAF described only as defence in depth.
  • [ ] Retest criteria defined.

docs.title: Disclosure
docs.text:
• [ ] Previously unknown issue handled privately.
  • [ ] Vendor contact identified.
  • [ ] CVE assignment path considered.
  • [ ] Sensitive details protected.
  • [ ] Disclosure timeline recorded.

docs.title: Final CVE Research Model
docs.text:
Do not research a CVE like this:

Scanner
   |
   v
CVE Match
   |
   v
Affected Version String
   |
   v
Report Critical

Use this model:

Identify Product
      |
      v
Identify Exact Version / Build
      |
      v
Read Vendor Advisory
      |
      v
Confirm Affected Range
      |
      v
Check Backports / Packaging
      |
      v
Validate Configuration Prerequisites
      |
      v
Understand Root Cause
      |
      v
Review Patch
      |

      |

      |

      |

Confirm Target Applicability
      |

      |
      v
Document Evidence
      |
      v
Apply Vendor Fix
      |
      v
Retest

A CVE tells you that a vulnerability has been publicly identified.

CVE research determines whether the affected condition exists in the system you are actually testing, what the root cause is, and what impact the available evidence supports.

docs.title: Debugging and Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Dynamic analysis examines software while it is running.

Instead of only asking what the source code appears capable of doing, dynamic analysis helps determine what actually happens when a specific input reaches the application.

For vulnerability research, dynamic analysis can answer questions such as:

Which code path executed?

Which function received attacker-controlled data?

How was the input transformed?

Which security checks executed?

Which files were accessed?

Which processes were created?

Which network connections occurred?

Where did the application crash?

What values existed at the point of failure?

A useful model is:

Research Hypothesis
       |
       v
Controlled Input
       |
       v
Running Target
       |
       v
Runtime Observation
       |
       v
Evidence
       |
       v
Interpretation
       |
       v
Refined Hypothesis

Dynamic analysis should support technical reasoning rather than become a collection of debugger screenshots.

docs.title: 1. Static and Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Static analysis examines software without relying on execution.

Dynamic analysis observes the software while it executes.

Static Analysis                     Dynamic Analysis

Source / Binary                     Running Process
      |                                   |
      v                                   v
Potential Code Path                  Actual Code Path
      |                                   |
      v                                   v
Security Hypothesis                  Runtime Evidence
      |                                   |
      +---------------+-------------------+
                      |
                      v
                 Root Cause

The techniques complement each other.

Static analysis may reveal:

Interesting functions

Sources and sinks

Missing validation

Security-sensitive APIs

Potential vulnerable paths

Dynamic analysis can then determine whether those paths are reachable under attacker-controlled conditions.

docs.title: 2. When Dynamic Analysis Is Useful
docs.text:
Dynamic analysis is particularly useful when:

The source code is complex

Source code is unavailable

A code path is difficult to understand

Input undergoes multiple transformations

The application uses many processes

The issue depends on runtime state

The vulnerability involves a parser

The application crashes

A security check behaves unexpectedly

The application communicates with external components

It is also useful for confirming assumptions discovered during static analysis.

docs.title: 3. Research Environment
docs.text:
Perform debugging and instrumentation in an authorised research environment.

Prefer:

Local virtual machine

Disposable container

Dedicated test host

Vendor-provided research environment

Authorised laboratory

Avoid debugging production services unless this is explicitly authorised and operationally appropriate.

docs.title: 4. Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Before attaching a debugger or changing the environment, record:

Product

Version

Build

Commit

Operating system

Architecture

Runtime

Configuration

Process identity

Dependencies

Example:

Product:
Example Server

Version:
3.4.2

Platform:
Ubuntu Linux x86_64

Runtime:
Native ELF

Configuration:
Default laboratory configuration

Process Identity:
example-service

This makes observations reproducible.

docs.title: 5. Preserve the Environment
docs.text:
Where possible:

Create Snapshot
      |
      v
Run Experiment
      |
      v
Collect Evidence
      |
      v
Reset Snapshot
      |
      v
Repeat

Resetting the environment reduces contamination from previous tests.

This is particularly important when research modifies:

Files

Databases

Caches

Application state

Configuration

Temporary directories

docs.title: 6. Record the Experiment
docs.text:
Each dynamic experiment should answer a specific question.

Use a structure such as:

Experiment ID:

Hypothesis:

Target Version:

Input:

Preconditions:

Instrumentation:

Expected Result:

Observed Result:

Interpretation:

Next Step:

Example:

Experiment ID:
DYN-004

Hypothesis:
The import worker passes the archive entry name directly
to the extraction routine.

Instrumentation:
Breakpoint on the extraction helper.

Input:
Controlled test archive.

Expected:
Breakpoint receives the archive-controlled path.

Observed:
Archive entry name visible in function argument.

Interpretation:
Attacker-controlled data reaches the extraction helper.

Next:
Trace path canonicalisation and destination validation.

docs.title: 7. Start With the Process Model
docs.text:
Before debugging individual functions, understand how the application runs.

Linux:

ps -ef --forest

Alternative:

pstree -ap

This can reveal:

Main application

Worker processes

Parser processes

Helper processes

Update services

Privileged services

docs.title: 8. Process Relationships
docs.text:
An application may appear to be one service but actually contain several security boundaries.

Example:

Web Server
    |
    v
Queue
    |
    v
Worker
    |
    v
Parser
    |
    v
Privileged Helper

If the HTTP request is processed by the web server but the security-sensitive action occurs inside another process, debugging only the web server may miss the important behavior.

docs.title: 9. Record Process Identity
docs.text:
Linux:

ps -o pid,ppid,user,group,comm,args -p <PID>

Inspect the process directly:

cat /proc/<PID>/status

Useful fields include:

Name

Pid

PPid

Uid

Gid

The privilege of the process helps determine the significance of a vulnerability.

docs.title: 10. Executable Location
docs.text:
Linux:

readlink -f /proc/<PID>/exe

Working directory:

readlink -f /proc/<PID>/cwd

Command line:

tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/<PID>/cmdline

These help establish exactly which binary and configuration are running.

docs.title: 11. Loaded Libraries
docs.text:
Linux:

cat /proc/<PID>/maps

A more focused view:

grep '\.so' /proc/<PID>/maps

This can reveal:

Runtime libraries

Parser libraries

Cryptographic libraries

Application modules

Do not infer vulnerability from library presence alone.

docs.title: 12. Environment Variables
docs.text:
In an authorised local research environment:

tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/<PID>/environ

Environment variables may explain:

Configuration

Runtime paths

Feature flags

Proxy settings

Temporary directories

They may also contain secrets, so handle captured output appropriately.

docs.title: 13. Choose the Right Observation Layer
docs.text:
Different questions require different instrumentation.

Question Useful Technique Which function executed? Debugger Which file was opened? System-call tracing Which child process started? Process tracing Which host was contacted? Network monitoring Which library was loaded? Process inspection Why did the process crash? Debugger / core dump What HTTP request occurred? Proxy / packet capture Which application event occurred? Application logging

Start with the least invasive technique that answers the question.

docs.title: 14. Application Logging
docs.text:
Application logs are often the easiest dynamic-analysis source.

Look for:

Request processing

Parser errors

Authentication decisions

Authorisation decisions

File paths

External requests

Exceptions

Worker activity

Logs are useful but should not be assumed to represent the complete internal behavior.

docs.title: 15. Add Debug Logging When Source Is Available
docs.text:
For software you can modify in a research build, targeted logging can clarify data flow.

Conceptually:

Input Received
      |
      v
Log Relevant State
      |
      v
Transformation
      |
      v
Log Result
      |
      v
Validation

Avoid logging unnecessary secrets.

Instrumentation should answer a specific research question.

docs.title: 16. System-Call Tracing
docs.text:
System-call tracing can expose interaction between an application and the operating system.

On Linux, strace is commonly useful.

Run a program:

strace ./target

Follow child processes:

strace -f ./target

Attach to a running process:

sudo strace -f -p <PID>

Use this only on processes within the authorised research environment.

docs.title: 17. Reduce Trace Noise
docs.text:
A complete system-call trace can be large.

Filter according to the research question.

For file operations:

strace -f -e trace=file ./target

For process creation:

strace -f -e trace=process ./target

For network operations:

strace -f -e trace=network ./target

Focused tracing makes interpretation easier.

docs.title: 18. Trace to a File
docs.text:
Save output:

strace -f -o trace.log ./target

Then search:

rg -n "openat|execve|connect" trace.log

This preserves evidence and avoids losing information from the terminal.

docs.title: 19. Filesystem Observation
docs.text:
Suppose the research question is:

Which file does the application access after receiving this input?

A focused experiment could be:

Baseline
   |
   v
Start File Trace
   |
   v
Submit One Controlled Input
   |
   v
Stop Trace
   |
   v
Compare Observed Paths

This is preferable to generating unrelated application activity during the test.

docs.title: 20. Representative File Trace
docs.text:
Illustrative output:

openat(AT_FDCWD, "/tmp/import/test.zip", O_RDONLY) = 7
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/srv/app/import/config.json", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT, 0644) = 8

Interpretation:

The process opened the uploaded archive and subsequently
created config.json beneath the application import directory.

This does not by itself establish whether path validation is secure.

It confirms runtime filesystem behavior.

docs.title: 21. Process Creation Observation
docs.text:
To investigate child-process behavior:

strace -f -e trace=process ./target

Potential output:

execve("/usr/bin/example-helper", ["example-helper", "--parse", "input.dat"], ...) = 0

This demonstrates that a helper process was executed with the observed arguments.

The next research questions might be:

Where did the argument originate?

Can the user influence it?

Is a shell involved?

Which privilege executes the helper?

How are errors handled?

docs.title: 22. Network Observation
docs.text:
For network behavior, determine:

Destination

Protocol

Port

Trigger

Input influence

Authentication

Encryption

Useful tools may include:

tcpdump

Wireshark

tshark

Application proxy

System-call tracing

docs.title: 23. tcpdump
docs.text:
Capture traffic in a laboratory:

sudo tcpdump -i any -nn

Capture to a file:

sudo tcpdump -i any -nn -w research.pcap

Restricting the capture to the relevant host or port usually produces cleaner evidence.

docs.title: 24. Network Experiment
docs.text:
Example:

Hypothesis:
The application performs a backend HTTP request when an import
URL is submitted.

Procedure:
Capture network activity while submitting one controlled URL.

Observed:
Application establishes a TCP connection to the controlled
research server.

Interpretation:
The URL functionality causes a server-side network connection.

Further testing would be required to understand destination restrictions and security impact.

docs.title: 25. Proxy-Based Observation
docs.text:
HTTP proxies can help inspect:

Requests

Responses

Headers

Cookies

Redirects

API calls

WebSocket messages

For vulnerability research, a proxy can be used both as:

Input Controller

and:

Observation Point

Keep application-side observations as well because the proxy does not reveal everything happening after the request reaches the server.

docs.title: 26. Debuggers
docs.text:
A debugger allows researchers to:

Pause execution

Inspect variables

Inspect memory

Inspect registers

Follow control flow

Set breakpoints

Step through instructions

Analyse exceptions

Analyse crashes

Debugger choice depends on the target platform and software type.

docs.title: 27. Common Debugging Environments
docs.text:
Examples include:

GDB

LLDB

WinDbg

Visual Studio Debugger

Java debuggers

Python debuggers

Browser developer tools

Different targets require different techniques.

docs.title: 28. GDB Basics
docs.text:
For a native Linux research binary:

gdb ./target

Start execution:

run

Display a backtrace:

bt

Inspect registers:

info registers

List threads:

info threads

These commands are useful starting points during crash analysis and runtime tracing.

docs.title: 29. Breakpoints
docs.text:
Set a breakpoint by function:

break function_name

Run:

run

Continue:

continue

Step into:

step

Step over:

next

The exact usefulness depends on available symbols and target architecture.

docs.title: 30. Breakpoint Strategy
docs.text:
Do not set breakpoints everywhere.

Begin with a hypothesis.

Example:

Hypothesis:
User-controlled filename reaches create_output_file().

Then:

Breakpoint:
create_output_file()

Input:
Controlled filename

Question:
What argument reaches the function?

This produces targeted evidence.

docs.title: 31. Function Arguments
docs.text:
When a breakpoint is reached, inspect relevant function arguments according to:

Programming language

Architecture

Calling convention

Compiler

Debug information

If source-level debugging is available, inspecting variables is usually simpler than manually decoding registers.

docs.title: 32. Source-Level Debugging
docs.text:
When debug symbols and source are available:

Input
  |
  v
Breakpoint at Handler
  |
  v
Inspect Variable
  |
  v
Step Through Validation
  |
  v
Inspect Transformed Value
  |
  v
Observe Sensitive Operation

This can directly demonstrate how attacker-controlled data changes through the application.

docs.title: 33. Binary-Level Debugging
docs.text:
Without source code, the process becomes:

Input
  |
  v
Known Function / Import
  |
  v
Breakpoint
  |
  v
Disassembly
  |
  v
Registers / Memory
  |
  v
Control Flow

Combine debugger evidence with decompilation or disassembly where useful.

docs.title: 34. Symbols
docs.text:
Check whether a Linux binary contains useful symbols:

nm ./target

For dynamic symbols:

nm -D ./target

A stripped binary may expose fewer names.

That does not prevent analysis, but it changes the workflow.

docs.title: 35. Disassembly
docs.text:
Useful tools include:

objdump

GDB

Ghidra

IDA

Binary Ninja

radare2 / Cutter

For a quick Linux disassembly:

objdump -d ./target | less

The objective is to understand relevant code paths rather than inspect every instruction.

docs.title: 36. Break on Security-Sensitive Operations
docs.text:
Depending on the hypothesis, useful observation points may include functions related to:

File access

Memory allocation

Memory copying

Process creation

Network connections

Authentication

Cryptography

Parsing

A breakpoint on a sensitive function is useful only if it helps answer where its arguments came from and why the call is security-relevant.

docs.title: 37. Conditional Breakpoints
docs.text:
When a function executes frequently, a conditional breakpoint can reduce noise.

Conceptually:

Break only when:
length > expected_limit

or:

Break only when:
identifier == test_value

The syntax depends on the debugger and available symbols.

docs.title: 38. Watchpoints
docs.text:
Watchpoints can identify where a value changes.

Conceptually:

Input Buffer
    |
    v
Watch Memory
    |
    v
Execution Continues
    |
    v
Debugger Stops on Modification

This can help trace transformations of security-relevant data.

docs.title: 39. Threads
docs.text:
Modern applications may use many threads.

GDB:

info threads

Switch thread:

thread <number>

A crash may occur on a worker thread rather than the main thread.

Always inspect the faulting thread and relevant surrounding threads.

docs.title: 40. Backtraces
docs.text:
After a crash:

bt

A backtrace can show:

Faulting function

Caller

Previous processing stages

Parser path

Application handler

Example:

#0 parse_record()
#1 process_document()
#2 import_file()
#3 worker_loop()

This suggests where to begin root cause analysis.

docs.title: 41. Backtrace Interpretation
docs.text:
Do not conclude:

parse_record crashed

therefore:

parse_record contains the root cause.

Memory corruption may occur earlier and only become visible later.

Investigate the complete data flow.

docs.title: 42. Core Dumps
docs.text:
A core dump captures process state around a crash.

On supported Linux environments, configuration may be required before core dumps are generated.

Check:

ulimit -c

If core dumps are enabled and a dump is available:

gdb ./target core

Then inspect:

bt
info registers
info threads

Core-dump handling differs across Linux distributions.

docs.title: 43. Preserve Crash Evidence
docs.text:
For every interesting crash, record:

Target version

Input

Input hash

Command line

Environment

Exception or signal

Faulting instruction

Backtrace

Registers where relevant

Logs

Reproducibility

Do this before modifying the crashing input.

docs.title: 44. Hash the Input
docs.text:
Example:

sha256sum crash-input.bin

Store the hash with the crash record.

This helps ensure that later analysis refers to the exact same sample.

docs.title: 45. Crash Reproduction
docs.text:
A crash should first be reproduced.

Crash
  |
  v
Reset Environment
  |
  v
Run Same Input
  |
  v
Crash Again?
 /       \
No       Yes
|         |
v         v
Investigate   Begin Triage
Environment

Intermittent crashes may indicate:

Race condition

Uninitialised state

Concurrency

Resource dependency

Environmental differences

docs.title: 46. Crash Does Not Equal Exploitability
docs.text:
A crash can result from:

Null pointer dereference

Assertion

Unhandled exception

Stack exhaustion

Resource exhaustion

Memory corruption

Only further analysis determines the security implications.

Avoid immediately describing a crash as:

Remote Code Execution

unless evidence supports that conclusion.

docs.title: 47. Signals on Linux
docs.text:
Common crash signals include:

SIGSEGV

SIGABRT

SIGBUS

SIGILL

SIGFPE

The signal provides context but does not determine exploitability by itself.

docs.title: 48. Exceptions on Windows
docs.text:
Windows debugging may expose exceptions such as:

Access violation

Stack overflow

Breakpoint exception

Illegal instruction

Heap corruption

Again, the exception is a starting point for analysis.

docs.title: 49. WinDbg
docs.text:
For Windows-native research, WinDbg can inspect:

Exceptions

Threads

Registers

Memory

Modules

Stacks

Crash dumps

Microsoft provides current WinDbg documentation through Microsoft Learn.

Typical crash investigation focuses on:

Exception

Faulting instruction

Stack

Module

Attacker-controlled state

docs.title: 50. Windows Process Observation
docs.text:
Useful built-in PowerShell commands include:

Get-Process

Detailed process information:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process |
    Select-Object ProcessId, ParentProcessId, Name, ExecutablePath, CommandLine

This helps map process relationships.

docs.title: 51. Windows Network Observation
docs.text:
Listening connections:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

Connections for a process can be correlated using the owning process identifier.

Use this to understand application behavior, not to infer vulnerability from network exposure alone.

docs.title: 52. Windows Filesystem Observation
docs.text:
Useful tools for authorised research environments can include:

Process Monitor

Process Explorer

Windows Event Logs

ETW-based tooling

Application logs

Process Monitor is particularly useful for understanding:

File access

Registry access

Process creation

Image loading

docs.title: 53. Process Monitor Workflow
docs.text:
A focused workflow is:

Start Process Monitor
       |
       v
Filter to Target Process
       |
       v
Clear Existing Events
       |
       v
Perform One Test
       |
       v
Stop Capture
       |
       v
Review Relevant Events

Without filters, event volume can become difficult to interpret.

docs.title: 54. Windows Registry Observation
docs.text:
If the application reads configuration from the registry, monitor:

Registry key

Value

Process

Operation

Result

This can reveal configuration paths that are not obvious from application documentation.

docs.title: 55. Child Process Monitoring
docs.text:
On both Linux and Windows, process creation can reveal important security boundaries.

Record:

Parent

Child

Executable

Arguments

User

Working directory

Environment

Then trace attacker influence.

docs.title: 56. Dynamic Data-Flow Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose the application receives:

filename=test-marker-4821.txt

Track the unique marker through:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Controller
     |
     v
Worker Queue
     |
     v
Parser
     |
     v
Filesystem

Unique markers make runtime correlation easier.

docs.title: 57. Use Unique Test Markers
docs.text:
Prefer distinctive values such as:

VRTEST-20260909-001

rather than:

test

Unique markers help locate data in:

Logs

Memory

Network captures

Debugger variables

Files

Database records

docs.title: 58. Timestamp Correlation
docs.text:
Record timestamps for:

Input submission

Application processing

Worker activity

Network request

Crash

Alert or log event

Ensure clocks are sufficiently synchronised when comparing multiple systems.

docs.title: 59. Compare Baseline and Test Runs
docs.text:
Run:

Baseline Input

vs

Research Input

Then compare:

Processes

Files

Network connections

Logs

Functions

Return values

This helps isolate behavior caused by the research input.

docs.title: 60. Controlled Experiments
docs.text:
Change one important variable at a time.

Poor experiment:

Change filename

Change encoding

Change authentication

Change file format

Change server configuration

all at once.

Better:

Experiment 1:
Change filename only.

Experiment 2:
Change encoding only.

Experiment 3:
Change privilege only.

This makes causality easier to establish.

docs.title: 61. Positive and Negative Controls
docs.text:
Use both.

Example:

Positive Test:
Known valid file.

Negative Test:
Malformed file.

Research Test:
Boundary-condition file.

Controls help determine whether observed behavior is actually caused by the suspected condition.

docs.title: 62. Repeatability
docs.text:
For important observations:

Run 1

Run 2

Run 3

Record whether the result is:

Consistent

Intermittent

Environment-dependent

Intermittent behavior requires additional investigation.

docs.title: 63. Dynamic Authentication Analysis
docs.text:
Authentication flows can be observed at runtime.

Trace:

Credential Input
      |
      v
Authentication Handler
      |
      v
Credential Validation
      |
      v
MFA / Additional Checks
      |
      v
Session Creation

The objective is to identify where security decisions are actually made.

docs.title: 64. Dynamic Authorisation Analysis
docs.text:
For access-control research:

Request
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Object Lookup
   |
   v
Authorisation Decision
   |
   v
Response

Use controlled test accounts to determine:

Which object is loaded?

Which identity is checked?

Which role is evaluated?

Where is ownership enforced?

docs.title: 65. Dynamic File Analysis
docs.text:
For file-processing research:

Controlled File
      |
      v
Upload
      |
      v
Temporary Storage
      |
      v
Parser
      |
      v
Transformation
      |
      v
Output

Observe:

Temporary paths

Parser process

Files opened

Files created

Worker privilege

Cleanup

docs.title: 66. Dynamic Parser Analysis
docs.text:
For a parser:

Input
  |
  v
Header Parser
  |
  v
Length Parser
  |
  v
Object Parser
  |
  v
Memory Operation

Breakpoints around these stages can help identify where malformed input changes program state.

docs.title: 67. Length Fields
docs.text:
Length fields deserve particular attention in native parsers.

Conceptually:

Input Length
     |
     v
Parse Integer
     |
     v
Validate?
     |
     v
Allocate
     |
     v
Copy

Questions include:

Is the length signed or unsigned?

Can arithmetic overflow?

Is allocation based on the same value as copying?

Are nested lengths validated?

docs.title: 68. Integer Boundaries
docs.text:
During controlled parser research, examine values around relevant boundaries.

Examples:

0

1

Maximum expected

Maximum expected + 1

Maximum type value

The exact test values depend on the field type and parser specification.

docs.title: 69. Memory Observation
docs.text:
A debugger can inspect memory when a hypothesis requires it.

GDB example:

x/32bx <address>

Strings:

x/s <address>

Memory inspection should be guided by the relevant program state rather than arbitrary addresses.

docs.title: 70. Register Observation
docs.text:
For native crash analysis:

info registers

Registers can help determine:

Fault address

Function arguments

Control-flow state

Attacker influence

Interpretation depends heavily on architecture and calling convention.

docs.title: 71. Source Code and Runtime Correlation
docs.text:
When source is available, record:

Source File

Function

Line

Input

Runtime Value

Observed Branch

Example:

Source:
archive.cpp

Function:
extractEntry()

Observed:
entryName contains the controlled marker.

Branch:
canonical path validation executed.

This provides stronger evidence than source review alone.

docs.title: 72. Decompiled Code and Runtime Correlation
docs.text:
When only a binary is available:

Decompiler
     |
     v
Candidate Function
     |
     v
Debugger Address
     |
     v
Runtime Breakpoint
     |
     v
Observed Behavior

Rename functions and variables in the decompiler as understanding improves.

This creates a progressively clearer model of the target.

docs.title: 73. Address Space Layout Randomisation
docs.text:
Runtime addresses may change because of ASLR.

Therefore:

Absolute address from one run

may not equal:

Absolute address from another run

Prefer module-relative reasoning where appropriate.

docs.title: 74. Debug Builds
docs.text:
If source is available, a debug build can improve analysis through:

Symbols

Source lines

Variable names

Assertions

Sanitizers

However, verify important behavior against the relevant production-style build when necessary because compiler options can affect runtime behavior.

docs.title: 75. Compiler Optimisation
docs.text:
Optimised binaries can make debugging harder.

Effects may include:

Inlined functions

Reordered instructions

Removed variables

Merged code paths

Do not assume debugger behavior directly mirrors source-code layout.

docs.title: 76. Sanitizers
docs.text:
When supported by the target and build environment, sanitizers can make certain bugs easier to identify.

Common examples include:

AddressSanitizer

UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer

MemorySanitizer

Sanitizers are especially useful during parser and native-code research.

docs.title: 77. AddressSanitizer
docs.text:
AddressSanitizer can identify classes of memory errors such as:

Heap buffer overflow

Stack buffer overflow

Use-after-free

Double free

Representative output may contain:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow

This provides evidence of memory-safety failure.

It does not automatically prove practical code execution.

docs.title: 78. Preserve Sanitizer Reports
docs.text:
Record:

Input

Input hash

Target build

Compiler options

Sanitizer

Stack trace

Error type

Allocation context

Sanitizer reports can substantially improve root cause analysis.

docs.title: 79. Runtime Assertions
docs.text:
Assertions may terminate the application when an expected invariant fails.

Example:

assert(length <= buffer_size)

An assertion failure may indicate:

Invalid state

Unexpected input

Programming error

It still requires security analysis.

docs.title: 80. Exceptions
docs.text:
For managed applications, inspect:

Exception type

Message

Stack trace

Inner exception

Input

Application state

An unhandled exception may produce denial of service but does not automatically imply a more severe vulnerability.

docs.title: 81. Java Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Useful sources may include:

Application logs

JVM debugging

Stack traces

JFR

Process monitoring

HTTP proxying

When source is available, IDE debugging can make controller-to-service-to-sink analysis straightforward.

docs.title: 82. .NET Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Useful techniques may include:

Visual Studio Debugger

WinDbg

Application logs

ETW

Process Monitor

Decompiler-assisted debugging

For managed targets, decompiled code can often be correlated closely with runtime behavior.

docs.title: 83. Python Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Python applications can often be observed using:

Application logging

Debugger

Tracebacks

Monkey-patched research instrumentation

HTTP proxy

System-call tracing

When source is available, focus on data flow and security decisions rather than low-level instruction analysis.

docs.title: 84. Browser-Side Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
For client-side research, browser developer tools provide:

Network activity

JavaScript debugging

DOM inspection

Storage

Cookies

Source maps

WebSocket messages

Remember that client-side checks are not substitutes for server-side security enforcement.

docs.title: 85. Race Conditions
docs.text:
Dynamic analysis can help investigate concurrency problems.

A conceptual race:

Thread A                 Thread B

Check State
   |
   |                     Change State
   |                         |
   v                         v
Use Old Assumption       Complete

Race-condition research requires repeatable timing experiments and careful interpretation.

docs.title: 86. Timing Evidence
docs.text:
Record:

Request A timestamp

Request B timestamp

Thread activity

State before

State after

Result

Do not claim a race condition solely because two requests happened close together.

docs.title: 87. Resource Monitoring
docs.text:
Unexpected behavior may result from resource exhaustion rather than memory corruption.

Observe:

CPU

Memory

File descriptors

Threads

Disk usage

Network connections

Linux examples:

top

ps -o pid,%cpu,%mem,rss,vsz,comm -p <PID>

docs.title: 88. File Descriptor Analysis
docs.text:
Linux:

ls -l /proc/<PID>/fd

Count descriptors:

ls /proc/<PID>/fd | wc -l

Repeated growth may indicate a resource leak.

Whether that becomes a security issue depends on attacker control and impact.

docs.title: 89. Memory Usage
docs.text:
Observe process memory:

ps -o pid,rss,vsz,comm -p <PID>

Compare:

Baseline

After One Input

After Repeated Inputs

This can help identify resource-exhaustion behavior.

docs.title: 90. Network Connection Growth
docs.text:
If a test appears to leak connections, inspect:

ss -tanp

Determine whether connections:

Close normally

Remain established

Remain in unusual states

Increase without bound

Again, controlled reproduction is required.

docs.title: 91. Dynamic Analysis of Security Controls
docs.text:
Runtime analysis can also verify:

Authentication enforcement

Authorisation enforcement

Signature verification

Certificate validation

Input validation

Sandboxing

Privilege separation

Observe the actual control path rather than assuming configuration equals enforcement.

docs.title: 92. Security Check Reachability
docs.text:
Suppose source review finds:

validate_path()

Do not assume every file operation uses it.

Set an observation point and test multiple paths:

Upload

Import

Restore

Backup

Plugin Installation

Variant code paths may bypass a shared security assumption.

docs.title: 93. Error Paths
docs.text:
Instrument failure conditions as well as success conditions.

Example:

Parser
  |
  +---- Success -> Normal Processing
  |
  +---- Failure -> Cleanup
                    |
                    v
                 File Delete

Security-sensitive operations may occur during cleanup or recovery.

docs.title: 94. Retry Logic
docs.text:
Applications may retry failed operations.

Observe:

Retry count

Delay

Modified parameters

Alternate destination

Fallback authentication

Fallback protocol

Fallback paths may implement different security controls.

docs.title: 95. Cache Effects
docs.text:
Caching can distort dynamic experiments.

Potential caches include:

HTTP cache

DNS cache

Application cache

Database cache

Authentication cache

If two identical inputs produce different behavior, investigate state before concluding that the vulnerability is unreliable.

docs.title: 96. Reproduce From a Clean State
docs.text:
For high-confidence results:

Reset

Start Target

Verify Baseline

Submit Input

Observe

Collect Evidence

Reset

Repeat

This removes many alternative explanations.

docs.title: 97. False Positives
docs.text:
Dynamic observations can be misleading.

Example:

Observed:
A file appeared after the test.

Alternative explanations:

Previous test artifact

Background job

Different process

Scheduled task

Application startup behavior

Correlate:

Timestamp

Process

Input marker

Trace

Logs

before attributing the behavior to the test.

docs.title: 98. Instrumentation Side Effects
docs.text:
Instrumentation itself can alter behavior.

Debuggers may affect:

Timing

Thread scheduling

Memory layout

Exception handling

Performance

Tracing can also change timing-sensitive behavior.

For important findings, reproduce with reduced instrumentation where practical.

docs.title: 99. Debugger Detection
docs.text:
Some applications detect debugging or behave differently when instrumented.

This may occur for legitimate reasons such as:

Anti-tamper mechanisms

Licensing

Security software

Protected applications

Record this behavior rather than automatically attempting to defeat it.

docs.title: 100. Evidence Hierarchy
docs.text:
A strong conclusion may combine:

Controlled Input

Runtime Trace

Debugger State

Application Log

Source / Decompiled Code

Reproduction

No single evidence source is always sufficient.

docs.title: 101. Practical Scenario
docs.text:
Assume an authorised research target contains a document parser.

The research question is:

Does an attacker-controlled length field reach a memory-copy operation without appropriate validation?

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Target:
Example Document Parser

Version:
2.4.1

Platform:
Linux x86_64

Input:
Research document format

Environment:
Local disposable VM

docs.title: Static Observation
docs.text:
Source or decompiled analysis suggests:

parse_record()
     |
     v
read_length()
     |
     v
allocate_buffer()
     |
     v
copy_record()

A validation check is not immediately obvious.

This is a hypothesis, not yet a confirmed vulnerability.

docs.title: Baseline Test
docs.text:
Use a valid document.

Observed:

Record Length:
64

Allocation:
64 bytes

Copy:
64 bytes

Result:
Successful parse

This establishes expected behavior.

docs.title: Boundary Test
docs.text:
Use a controlled malformed document with a length value outside the normal range.

The target terminates.

docs.title: Debugger Observation
docs.text:
Representative illustrative output:

Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.

#0  copy_record()
#1  parse_record()
#2  parse_document()
#3  main()

At this stage the researcher knows:

The malformed input produces a reproducible crash.

The crash occurs while processing a record.

The copy routine is involved.

That is not yet sufficient to claim memory corruption caused by the length field.

docs.title: Trace the Input
docs.text:
Set breakpoints around:

read_length()

allocate_buffer()

copy_record()

Record the relevant values.

Representative observation:

Parsed length:
4096

Allocated destination:
256 bytes

Copy length:
4096

If confirmed, this provides much stronger evidence of an incorrect length relationship.

docs.title: Root Cause Question
docs.text:
Now investigate:

Why was 256 bytes allocated?

Why was 4096 bytes copied?

Which field controls each value?

Was validation expected?

Can arithmetic change the allocation size?

Is the copy length attacker-controlled?

docs.title: Sanitizer Validation
docs.text:
If source and an appropriate research build are available, reproduce under AddressSanitizer.

Representative output:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size ...

The exact output depends on the target.

This can confirm the memory-safety condition and provide additional stack information.

docs.title: Negative Control
docs.text:
Use:

Length:
255

and:

Length:
256

if those values are meaningful for the specific format.

Compare behavior.

The purpose is to identify the actual boundary rather than assume one from the initial crash.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Repeat the crashing input from a clean state.

Record:

Run 1:
Crash

Run 2:
Crash

Run 3:
Crash

Then hash the sample:

sha256sum research-crash.bin

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A defensible intermediate conclusion could be:

The malformed research file reproducibly causes the tested parser to perform a memory copy whose observed length exceeds the destination allocation in the instrumented build. AddressSanitizer reports a heap-buffer-overflow during the same parsing path. Further analysis is required to determine the complete attacker control, affected versions and practical exploitability.

This distinguishes:

Confirmed memory-safety failure

from:

Assumed remote code execution

docs.title: 102. Dynamic Analysis Record
docs.text:
Use a reusable format:

Experiment ID:

Target:

Version:

Build:

Environment:

Hypothesis:

Input:

Input Hash:

Instrumentation:

Breakpoint / Trace:

Expected Behavior:

Observed Behavior:

Relevant Values:

Process:

Privilege:

Stack:

Logs:

Reproducible:

Interpretation:

Alternative Explanations:

Next Step:

docs.title: 103. Evidence to Capture
docs.text:
For important runtime findings:

  • [ ] Exact product version
  • [ ] Build information
  • [ ] Operating system
  • [ ] Architecture
  • [ ] Configuration
  • [ ] Process identity
  • [ ] Input
  • [ ] Input hash
  • [ ] Timestamp
  • [ ] Relevant trace
  • [ ] Debugger output
  • [ ] Stack trace
  • [ ] Logs
  • [ ] Source or binary location
  • [ ] Reproduction count
  • [ ] Negative controls

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• [ ] Confirm authorisation
  • [ ] Use controlled environment
  • [ ] Record target version
  • [ ] Record architecture
  • [ ] Record configuration
  • [ ] Preserve baseline
  • [ ] Create experiment identifier

docs.title: Process Mapping
docs.text:
• [ ] Identify parent process
  • [ ] Identify child processes
  • [ ] Identify workers
  • [ ] Identify process identities
  • [ ] Identify executable paths
  • [ ] Identify relevant libraries

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
• [ ] Review application logs
  • [ ] Observe filesystem activity where relevant
  • [ ] Observe process creation where relevant
  • [ ] Observe network activity where relevant
  • [ ] Correlate timestamps
  • [ ] Use unique markers

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
• [ ] Define hypothesis
  • [ ] Select relevant breakpoint
  • [ ] Record function
  • [ ] Record arguments
  • [ ] Record important variables
  • [ ] Record control-flow decisions
  • [ ] Record thread
  • [ ] Record stack

docs.title: Crash Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Preserve crashing input
  • [ ] Hash input
  • [ ] Reproduce crash
  • [ ] Record signal or exception
  • [ ] Record faulting location
  • [ ] Record stack
  • [ ] Record relevant registers where appropriate
  • [ ] Determine attacker-controlled state
  • [ ] Avoid unsupported exploitability claims

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Compare baseline
  • [ ] Use negative control
  • [ ] Repeat test
  • [ ] Reset environment
  • [ ] Consider instrumentation side effects
  • [ ] Eliminate alternative explanations

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• [ ] Record expected behavior
  • [ ] Record observed behavior
  • [ ] Explain interpretation
  • [ ] Identify limitations
  • [ ] Define next experiment

docs.title: 105. Quick Dynamic Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
HYPOTHESIS
    |
    v
SELECT OBSERVATION POINT
    |
    v
ESTABLISH BASELINE
    |
    v
START INSTRUMENTATION
    |
    v
SUBMIT CONTROLLED INPUT
    |
    v
OBSERVE
    |
    v
CAPTURE EVIDENCE
    |
    v
COMPARE WITH BASELINE
    |
    v
REPEAT
    |
    v
INTERPRET
    |
    v
REFINE HYPOTHESIS
    |
    v
ROOT CAUSE

docs.title: 106. Choosing the Next Technique
docs.text:
Use the observation to determine what happens next.

Runtime Observation
        |
        +---- Unexpected File Access
        |          |
        |          v
        |     Trace Path Handling
        |
        +---- Unexpected Process
        |          |
        |          v
        |     Trace Arguments
        |
        +---- Unexpected Network Request
        |          |
        |          v
        |     Trace Destination Logic
        |
        +---- Crash
        |          |
        |          v
        |     Crash Analysis
        |
        +---- Memory Error
        |          |
        |          v
        |     Root Cause / Sanitizer
        |
        +---- Security Check Missing
                   |
                   v
              Variant Analysis

Dynamic analysis should continuously narrow the research question.

docs.title: 107. Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid:

Attaching a debugger without a hypothesis

Collecting enormous traces without filters

Assuming a crash is exploitable

Ignoring child processes

Ignoring process privileges

Changing many variables simultaneously

Failing to preserve the original input

Testing only once

Ignoring negative controls

Treating debugger output as the entire root cause

Ignoring instrumentation side effects

Failing to correlate runtime evidence with code

docs.title: 108. Dynamic Analysis Mindset
docs.text:
Do not think:

The Debugger Crashed = Vulnerability

SIGSEGV = RCE

A Process Started = Command Injection

A Connection Occurred = SSRF

A File Was Written = Arbitrary File Write

Instead think:

What Input Did I Control?
          |
          v
What Runtime Behavior Occurred?
          |
          v
Can I Reproduce It?
          |
          v
Which Component Performed It?
          |
          v
Under Which Privilege?
          |
          v
Which Code Path Caused It?
          |
          v
Which Security Check Applied?
          |
          v
What Boundary Was Crossed?
          |
          v
What Does the Evidence Actually Prove?

Dynamic analysis is strongest when every observation answers a specific research question.
