Begin with a question

Choose instrumentation because it answers a specific research question. A focused trace or breakpoint is usually more useful than collecting every possible runtime event.

Correlate runtime evidence

Unique markers, timestamps, process identifiers and controlled inputs make it easier to connect an external request to internal application behavior.

Combine static and dynamic analysis

Static analysis can identify a suspicious path while dynamic analysis confirms whether the path is reachable and what values actually reach it.

Preserve the first crash

Keep the original input, hash it and record the environment before minimising or modifying it. The original sample is valuable evidence if later experiments behave differently.

A crash is not automatically code execution

A reproducible crash establishes abnormal behavior. Determine the root cause, attacker control and security impact before assigning a vulnerability class or exploitability claim.

Instrumentation can change behavior

Debuggers, tracing and sanitizers can affect timing, memory layout and thread scheduling. Reproduce important findings with appropriate controls and, where practical, reduced instrumentation.

docs.title: Fuzzing for Vulnerability Research
docs.text:
Fuzzing is an automated testing technique that repeatedly provides a target with generated or mutated inputs and monitors the target for interesting behavior.

For vulnerability research, fuzzing can help discover:

Crashes

Memory-safety violations

Unhandled exceptions

Assertions

Parser inconsistencies

Resource exhaustion

Unexpected state transitions

Previously unexplored code paths

The basic model is:

Seed Corpus
    |
    v
Fuzzer
    |
    +---- Mutation / Generation
    |
    v
Target
    |
    v
Runtime Feedback
    |
    +---- Normal Execution -> Continue
    |
    +---- New Coverage -> Preserve Input
    |
    +---- Crash -> Preserve Input
    |
    +---- Timeout -> Investigate
    |
    +---- Sanitizer Finding -> Preserve Input

Fuzzing finds interesting behavior.

It does not automatically determine whether that behavior is a security vulnerability.

The researcher still needs to perform:

Reproduction

Minimisation

Crash triage

Root cause analysis

Exploitability analysis

Affected-version analysis

Variant analysis

docs.title: 1. When Fuzzing Is Useful
docs.text:
Fuzzing is particularly useful for software that processes structured or semi-structured attacker-controlled data.

Examples include:

File parsers

Image parsers

Archive parsers

Document parsers

Media codecs

Network protocols

RPC interfaces

Serialization formats

API parsers

Command-line parsers

Configuration parsers

Compilers

Interpreters

Libraries

Fuzzing becomes especially valuable when the target contains:

Complex parsing

Native memory operations

Large state spaces

Many input combinations

Historical memory-safety vulnerabilities

Numerous boundary conditions

docs.title: 2. Start With the Attack Surface
docs.text:
Do not fuzz an application simply because it exists.

First identify a meaningful attack surface.

See Attack Surface Analysis.

A useful sequence is:

Attack Surface
      |
      v
Attacker-Controlled Input
      |
      v
Parser / Handler
      |
      v
Security-Sensitive Processing
      |
      v
Fuzzing Candidate

Ask:

Can an attacker reach this parser?

What input format does it accept?

Which component processes the input?

What privilege does that component have?

Is the input processed before authentication?

Does processing cross a trust boundary?

This determines whether fuzzing the component is security-relevant.

docs.title: 3. Fuzzing Is an Experiment
docs.text:
A fuzzing campaign should have an objective.

Weak objective:

Fuzz the application.

Better:

Exercise the image decoder with malformed PNG chunk
structures and monitor the parser for memory-safety violations.

Another example:

Exercise the archive metadata parser with mutated entry headers
and lengths while preserving enough archive structure to reach
deep extraction logic.

The more specific the objective, the easier the results are to interpret.

docs.title: 4. Fuzzing Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

Select Target
      |
      v
Understand Input
      |
      v
Identify Parser Entry Point
      |
      v
Build Harness
      |
      v
Create Seed Corpus
      |
      v
Instrument Target
      |
      v
Validate Harness
      |
      v
Start Fuzzing
      |
      v
Monitor Coverage / Stability
      |
      v
Collect Interesting Inputs
      |
      v
Reproduce
      |
      v
Deduplicate
      |
      v
Minimise
      |
      v
Crash Analysis
      |
      v
Root Cause
      |
      v
Security Impact

docs.title: 5. Fuzzing Strategies
docs.text:
Common fuzzing strategies include:

Mutation-based fuzzing

Generation-based fuzzing

Coverage-guided fuzzing

Grammar-based fuzzing

Protocol-aware fuzzing

Stateful fuzzing

Differential fuzzing

These approaches can overlap.

docs.title: 6. Mutation-Based Fuzzing
docs.text:
Mutation-based fuzzing begins with existing inputs and modifies them.

Conceptually:

Valid Seed
   |
   v
Mutation
   |
   +---- Bit Flip
   +---- Byte Change
   +---- Insert Data
   +---- Delete Data
   +---- Duplicate Data
   +---- Change Integer
   |
   v
Mutated Input

Mutation-based fuzzing is useful when valid sample files are readily available.

docs.title: 7. Generation-Based Fuzzing
docs.text:
Generation-based fuzzing constructs inputs from knowledge of the input format.

Example:

Format Definition
      |
      +---- Header
      +---- Length
      +---- Type
      +---- Payload
      |
      v
Generated Input

Generation-based approaches can reach structured states that random mutation may struggle to preserve.

They require more understanding of the format.

docs.title: 8. Coverage-Guided Fuzzing
docs.text:
Coverage-guided fuzzers use runtime feedback to determine whether an input reaches previously unexplored program behavior.

Conceptually:

Input
  |
  v
Target
  |
  v
Coverage Feedback
  |
  +---- Existing Coverage -> Lower Interest
  |
  +---- New Coverage -> Preserve Input

This allows the fuzzer to progressively explore the target.

Popular coverage-guided fuzzers include:

  • AFL++
  • libFuzzer

docs.title: 9. Coverage Is Guidance
docs.text:
Coverage can indicate that more code has been explored.

It does not directly measure:

Security

Vulnerability coverage

Exploitability

Attack-path coverage

A fuzzer can achieve high code coverage while missing an important security condition.

Treat coverage as navigation feedback rather than proof of security.

docs.title: 10. Grammar-Based Fuzzing
docs.text:
Some formats are too structured for simple mutations to remain useful.

Example:

Document
├── Header
├── Object Table
├── Metadata
├── Payload
└── Checksum

If random mutation destroys the header immediately, the parser may reject the input before reaching deeper functionality.

A grammar-aware approach can preserve important structure while varying specific fields.

docs.title: 11. Stateful Fuzzing
docs.text:
Some targets depend on sequences rather than individual inputs.

Example:

CONNECT
   |
   v
AUTHENTICATE
   |
   v
CREATE
   |
   v
UPDATE
   |
   v
DELETE

A stateful fuzzer attempts to explore combinations of valid and invalid transitions.

This is useful for:

Network protocols

APIs

Authentication systems

Database protocols

Custom services

docs.title: 12. Differential Fuzzing
docs.text:
Differential fuzzing compares multiple implementations or versions.

Example:

Same Input
   |
   +------------+
   |            |
   v            v
Version A    Version B
   |            |
   v            v
Result A     Result B
   |
   +------ Compare

Differences may reveal:

Parser inconsistencies

Regression

Security fix

Unexpected behavior

A difference is a research lead, not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: 13. Understand the Input Format
docs.text:
Before fuzzing, determine the basic structure of the input.

Example:

Offset    Field

0x00      Magic
0x04      Version
0x08      Record Count
0x0C      Record Length
0x10      Payload

Useful questions include:

Which fields are mandatory?

Which fields contain lengths?

Which fields contain offsets?

Which fields select types?

Are checksums used?

Are fields nested?

Can records reference each other?

Is compression involved?

This knowledge helps design better seeds and dictionaries.

docs.title: 14. Length Fields
docs.text:
Length fields are important because they may influence:

Allocation

Copy size

Loop count

Offset calculation

Buffer access

A generic flow is:

Length Field
     |
     v
Parse Integer
     |
     v
Validate
     |
     v
Allocate
     |
     v
Copy / Process

Fuzzing can explore unusual relationships between these stages.

docs.title: 15. Offset Fields
docs.text:
Offsets may control where the parser reads.

Conceptually:

Base Address
     +
Attacker-Controlled Offset
     |
     v
Target Location

Interesting cases include:

Zero

Before expected region

End of input

Beyond input

Overlapping structures

Integer boundaries

The exact test strategy depends on the format and implementation.

docs.title: 16. Count Fields
docs.text:
Count values may influence loops:

Record Count
      |
      v
for each record
      |
      v
Parse

Investigate relationships between:

Declared count

Actual records

Input length

Allocation size

docs.title: 17. Nested Structures
docs.text:
Nested formats can expose:

Recursion depth

Stack exhaustion

Resource exhaustion

Parser state bugs

Example:

Object
  |
  +---- Object
          |
          +---- Object
                  |
                  +---- Object

Fuzzing can explore unusual nesting depth while monitoring resource behavior.

docs.title: 18. Seed Corpus
docs.text:
The seed corpus is the initial set of inputs supplied to the fuzzer.

A useful corpus should contain small examples representing different valid features.

Example:

corpus/
├── minimal.dat
├── metadata.dat
├── multi-record.dat
├── compressed.dat
└── optional-fields.dat

Quality is often more important than quantity.

docs.title: 19. Good Seeds
docs.text:
Good seeds are:

Valid

Small

Structurally diverse

Representative

Fast to process

Avoid starting with thousands of nearly identical large files.

They may increase fuzzing overhead without significantly increasing reachable behavior.

docs.title: 20. Minimal Seed
docs.text:
Where possible, create the smallest valid input.

Example:

Header

One record

Minimal payload

Small seeds generally make mutation faster and resulting crashes easier to analyse.

docs.title: 21. Corpus Diversity
docs.text:
Seeds should exercise different features.

Example:

Seed Feature minimal.dat Basic parser metadata.dat Metadata handling compressed.dat Decompression multi.dat Multiple records nested.dat Nested structure

The objective is behavioral diversity.

docs.title: 22. Corpus Collection
docs.text:
Potential sources include:

Application test cases

Project examples

Format specifications

Existing unit tests

Generated valid files

Your own controlled samples

Use samples you are permitted to use and avoid unnecessary sensitive data.

docs.title: 23. Corpus Minimisation
docs.text:
A large corpus can contain redundant inputs.

Corpus minimisation attempts to retain a smaller set that preserves useful coverage.

Conceptually:

Large Corpus
     |
     v
Coverage Analysis
     |
     v
Remove Redundant Inputs
     |
     v
Smaller Corpus

This can improve fuzzing efficiency.

docs.title: 24. Fuzzing Harness
docs.text:
A harness is a small program that exposes the target functionality to the fuzzer.

Instead of starting an entire application:

Fuzzer
   |
   v
Full Application
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Configuration
   |
   v
Parser

a harness may call the parser directly:

Fuzzer
   |
   v
Harness
   |
   v
Parser

This can dramatically increase execution speed.

docs.title: 25. Harness Objectives
docs.text:
A good harness should:

Reach the target function

Accept fuzzer-controlled input

Avoid unnecessary initialization

Avoid external dependencies where practical

Clean up between executions

Return predictably

Preserve realistic parser behavior

The harness should not accidentally remove the vulnerable condition.

docs.title: 26. Harness Boundary
docs.text:
Be careful when simplifying the application.

Suppose the real flow is:

Input
  |
  v
Decoder
  |
  v
Normaliser
  |
  v
Parser

A harness that calls only:

Parser

may miss vulnerabilities in:

Decoder

Normaliser

Interaction between stages

Choose the harness boundary according to the research objective.

docs.title: 27. Harness Validation
docs.text:
Before fuzzing:

Valid Input
     |
     v
Harness
     |
     v
Expected Parser Behavior?

Test several known-good samples.

If the harness cannot correctly process valid files, fuzzing results may not represent the real application.

docs.title: 28. Harness Stability
docs.text:
Run the same valid input repeatedly.

Expected:

Same Input
   |
   v
Same Behavior

Unstable behavior can produce noisy fuzzing results.

Potential causes include:

Global state

Threads

Randomness

Time dependencies

Network dependencies

Temporary files

docs.title: 29. Harness Performance
docs.text:
Execution speed matters because fuzzing may perform millions of iterations.

Avoid unnecessary:

Network connections

Disk writes

Logging

Application startup

Database operations

where they are not part of the behavior under investigation.

docs.title: 30. Persistent Execution
docs.text:
Some fuzzers support designs where the target remains alive across multiple inputs.

Conceptually:

Start Target Once
      |
      v
Input 1
      |
      v
Reset State
      |
      v
Input 2
      |
      v
Reset State

This can substantially improve speed.

State must be correctly reset between iterations.

docs.title: 31. In-Process Fuzzing
docs.text:
libFuzzer commonly operates in-process.

The target exposes a function that receives arbitrary bytes.

A common C/C++ interface is:

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>

extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(
    const uint8_t* data,
    size_t size
) {
    // Pass data and size to the parser being tested.
    return 0;
}

This is only the harness entry point.

The actual target parser must be called from inside the function.

docs.title: 32. Example Harness Structure
docs.text:
Conceptually:

extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(
    const uint8_t* data,
    size_t size
) {
    if (data == nullptr || size == 0) {
        return 0;
    }

    Parser parser;
    parser.parse(data, size);

    return 0;
}

The exact implementation depends on the target API.

Do not add artificial validation that prevents the parser from receiving malformed input unless the real application performs the same validation.

docs.title: 33. File-Based Harness
docs.text:
If the parser only accepts files:

Fuzzer Input
     |
     v
Temporary File
     |
     v
Parser API

This may be necessary but is generally slower than an in-memory interface.

Where possible, use an existing memory-based parsing API.

docs.title: 34. AFL++
docs.text:
AFL++ is a coverage-guided fuzzing framework commonly used for native software.

Official project:

https://github.com/AFLplusplus/AFLplusplus

AFL++ supports multiple instrumentation and fuzzing strategies.

docs.title: 35. AFL++ Installation
docs.text:
On systems where the distribution provides it, package installation may be available.

For current installation and build guidance, use the official AFL++ documentation rather than relying on an old command copied from another environment.

Confirm installation:

afl-fuzz -h

docs.title: 36. AFL++ Instrumented Build
docs.text:
For source-based research, AFL++ compiler wrappers can instrument the target.

A common pattern is:

CC=afl-clang-fast CXX=afl-clang-fast++ ./configure
make

The actual build process depends on the project.

For CMake-based projects, environment variables can similarly be provided during configuration.

Always confirm the resulting target executes normally before starting fuzzing.

docs.title: 37. AFL++ Input and Output
docs.text:
A typical directory structure is:

fuzzing/
├── input/
│   ├── seed1
│   └── seed2
└── output/

The input directory contains seed files.

The output directory stores:

Queue

Crashes

Hangs

Fuzzer state

docs.title: 38. Basic AFL++ Pattern
docs.text:
For a target that accepts a filename:

afl-fuzz -i input -o output -- ./target @@

@@ is replaced by the generated input filename.

This assumes:

./target <filename>

is the correct target interface.

docs.title: 39. Validate Before Fuzzing
docs.text:
Before launching the campaign:

./target input/seed1

Confirm that:

The seed is valid

The target reaches the intended parser

Execution terminates normally

The harness does not wait for user interaction

docs.title: 40. AFL++ Output
docs.text:
AFL++ provides runtime statistics that may include:

Executions

Execution speed

Corpus size

Coverage-related information

Crashes

Hangs

Use these statistics to evaluate whether the campaign is healthy.

Do not treat the raw number of executions as a security metric.

docs.title: 41. Slow Targets
docs.text:
If execution speed is unexpectedly low, investigate:

Application startup

Filesystem operations

Logging

Network operations

Large seeds

Expensive initialization

Timeouts

The solution may be a better harness rather than more hardware.

docs.title: 42. libFuzzer
docs.text:
libFuzzer is an in-process coverage-guided fuzzing engine commonly used with Clang.

Documentation:

LLVM libFuzzer

It works especially well when a target exposes a function that can directly process an in-memory byte buffer.

docs.title: 43. Building a libFuzzer Target
docs.text:
A common Clang pattern is:

clang++ \
  -g \
  -O1 \
  -fsanitize=fuzzer,address \
  fuzz_target.cpp \
  target.cpp \
  -o fuzz_target

This combines:

libFuzzer

AddressSanitizer

The exact build command depends on the project and build system.

docs.title: 44. Run libFuzzer
docs.text:
Create a corpus directory:

mkdir -p corpus

Run:

./fuzz_target corpus

The fuzzer will use and expand the corpus as it discovers interesting behavior.

docs.title: 45. Artifact Prefix
docs.text:
When useful, configure a directory for generated crash artifacts.

Example:

mkdir -p artifacts

./fuzz_target \
  -artifact_prefix=artifacts/ \
  corpus

This keeps interesting inputs organised.

docs.title: 46. Sanitizers
docs.text:
Sanitizers are extremely valuable when fuzzing native software.

Common examples include:

AddressSanitizer

UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer

MemorySanitizer

They can expose problems that do not immediately cause a normal process crash.

docs.title: 47. AddressSanitizer
docs.text:
AddressSanitizer can detect memory errors such as:

Heap buffer overflow

Stack buffer overflow

Use-after-free

Double free

Invalid memory access

A typical research build may use:

-fsanitize=address

The exact build configuration depends on the project.

docs.title: 48. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer
docs.text:
UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer can detect classes of undefined behavior.

A typical compiler option is:

-fsanitize=undefined

It may identify issues involving:

Invalid shifts

Signed integer overflow

Misaligned access

Invalid conversions

Not every UBSan finding is necessarily security-relevant.

docs.title: 49. Combine Sanitizers Carefully
docs.text:
A research build may use:

-fsanitize=address,undefined

where supported.

Validate that the target still behaves sufficiently like the intended application.

Instrumentation can alter:

Performance

Memory layout

Timing

docs.title: 50. Compiler Settings
docs.text:
For useful sanitizer reports, debug information is helpful:

-g

A common fuzzing optimisation level is:

-O1

However, use settings appropriate for the target and toolchain.

docs.title: 51. Dictionaries
docs.text:
A fuzzing dictionary contains tokens meaningful to the input format.

Example:

"HEADER"
"VERSION"
"TYPE"
"LENGTH"
"DATA"

For textual formats:

"true"
"false"
"null"
"admin"
"content-type"

A dictionary can help the fuzzer construct inputs that pass syntax checks.

docs.title: 52. Dictionary Design
docs.text:
Useful dictionary entries may come from:

Format specification

Protocol keywords

Magic values

Source code

Parser constants

Error messages

Existing samples

Avoid filling dictionaries with irrelevant strings.

docs.title: 53. Magic Values
docs.text:
Parsers often check constants before processing deeper structures.

Example:

Magic
  |
  v
Version
  |
  v
Parser

If random mutations constantly destroy the magic value, deeper code may become difficult to reach.

A dictionary or structured harness can help preserve important values.

docs.title: 54. Checksums
docs.text:
Checksums can block mutation-based exploration.

Possible research strategies include:

Recalculate checksum in harness

Patch checksum validation in a dedicated fuzz build

Use structure-aware mutation

Any modification must be documented.

If the real vulnerability depends on checksum handling itself, bypassing that logic would be inappropriate.

docs.title: 55. Encryption and Compression
docs.text:
Encrypted or compressed formats may also prevent useful mutation.

A research harness may target:

Post-decryption parser

Post-decompression parser

when the research question concerns that specific parser.

But this changes the tested attack surface.

Document the harness boundary clearly.

docs.title: 56. Coverage Bottlenecks
docs.text:
If fuzzing stops discovering new behavior, investigate:

Magic checks

Checksums

Deep state

Authentication

Global state

Large comparisons

Complex grammar

Encryption

Compression

Do not immediately assume the target has been sufficiently tested.

docs.title: 57. Compare Coverage Between Corpora
docs.text:
A useful experiment is:

Corpus A
   |
   v
Coverage

Corpus B
   |
   v
Coverage

If Corpus B reaches additional behavior, inspect which structural features are responsible.

This can guide seed design.

docs.title: 58. Fuzzing Campaign Monitoring
docs.text:
Monitor:

Execution speed

Corpus growth

Coverage growth

Crash count

Unique crashes

Timeouts

Target stability

System resources

A campaign running for days without meaningful exploration may require redesign.

docs.title: 59. Crashes
docs.text:
A fuzzer may report many crashing inputs.

Do not assume:

100 crash files = 100 vulnerabilities

Many may share the same root cause.

The next stage is triage.

docs.title: 60. Preserve Original Crashes
docs.text:
Do not immediately modify crash files.

Copy them into a research archive.

Example:

crashes/
├── originals/
├── minimized/
├── triage/
└── notes/

Preserve the original artifact for later comparison.

docs.title: 61. Hash Crash Inputs
docs.text:
Example:

sha256sum crash-input

Record:

Filename

SHA-256

Target version

Fuzzer

Date

Campaign

This helps track artifacts reliably.

docs.title: 62. Reproduce the Crash
docs.text:
Run the crashing input directly against the target.

Example:

./target crash-input

For a harness:

./fuzz_target crash-input

Confirm:

Does it still crash?

Is the failure deterministic?

Does the same sanitizer report appear?

docs.title: 63. Reproduction Matrix
docs.text:
Use:

Run Result 1 Crash 2 Crash 3 Crash 4 Crash 5 Crash

If results differ, investigate:

Race condition

Uninitialised memory

Environmental state

Randomness

Resource dependency

docs.title: 64. Crash Classification
docs.text:
Initial categories might include:

Heap buffer overflow

Stack buffer overflow

Use-after-free

Null dereference

Assertion

Integer issue

Stack exhaustion

Resource exhaustion

Unhandled exception

Unknown

Classification is provisional until root cause analysis is complete.

docs.title: 65. Deduplication
docs.text:
Multiple inputs may produce the same crash.

Useful deduplication signals include:

Faulting function

Stack trace

Sanitizer report

Exception type

Fault address

Allocation stack

Code path

Do not deduplicate solely by filename.

docs.title: 66. Stack-Based Deduplication
docs.text:
Example:

Crash A

parse_length()
process_record()
parse_document()

and:

Crash B

parse_length()
process_record()
parse_document()

may share a root cause.

But identical stacks can occasionally hide different underlying conditions.

Verify important cases manually.

docs.title: 67. Crash Minimisation
docs.text:
Minimisation reduces a crashing input while preserving the failure.

Original Crash
      |
      v
Remove Data
      |
      v
Still Crashes?
   /       \
 Yes       No
  |         |
  v         v
Continue   Restore

The result should ideally contain only data necessary to trigger the bug.

docs.title: 68. Why Minimise?
docs.text:
A smaller input makes it easier to understand:

Trigger field

Required structure

Boundary condition

Root cause

Affected code path

It also improves reporting and regression testing.

docs.title: 69. libFuzzer Minimisation
docs.text:
libFuzzer can minimise a crashing input.

A common pattern is:

./fuzz_target \
  -minimize_crash=1 \
  crash-input \
  -exact_artifact_path=minimized-crash

Verify the current libFuzzer documentation if behavior differs with the installed toolchain.

After minimisation, reproduce the result independently.

docs.title: 70. AFL++ Minimisation
docs.text:
AFL++ includes afl-tmin for test-case minimisation.

Typical pattern:

afl-tmin \
  -i crash-input \
  -o minimized-input \
  -- ./target @@

The exact command depends on how the target receives input.

Always verify that the minimised sample still reproduces the same underlying failure.

docs.title: 71. Corpus Minimisation With AFL++
docs.text:
AFL++ also provides tools for reducing redundant corpus inputs.

The objective is:

Preserve Useful Behavior

while

Reduce Corpus Size

Consult current AFL++ documentation for the appropriate workflow for the installed version.

docs.title: 72. Timeouts and Hangs
docs.text:
Fuzzers may classify inputs as hangs when execution exceeds a timeout.

Potential causes include:

Infinite loop

Extremely expensive computation

Deadlock

Resource exhaustion

Blocking I/O

Slow valid operation

A timeout is not automatically a denial-of-service vulnerability.

docs.title: 73. Reproduce Hangs
docs.text:
Test the input independently.

Measure:

CPU

Memory

Runtime

Threads

System calls

Determine whether the behavior is:

Deterministic

Input-dependent

Unbounded

Remotely reachable

docs.title: 74. Resource Exhaustion
docs.text:
Potential fuzzing discoveries include:

Memory growth

CPU exhaustion

Stack exhaustion

File descriptor exhaustion

Thread exhaustion

Disk growth

Security relevance depends on whether an attacker can trigger the behavior under realistic conditions.

docs.title: 75. Crash Triage Workflow
docs.text:
Fuzzer Finding
      |
      v
Preserve Input
      |
      v
Hash Input
      |
      v
Reproduce
      |
      v
Same Failure?
   /       \
 No       Yes
 |         |
 v         v
Investigate   Deduplicate
Environment       |
                  v
               Minimise
                  |
                  v
             Debug / Trace
                  |
                  v
              Root Cause
                  |
                  v
          Security Relevance

docs.title: 76. Debugging a Fuzzer Crash
docs.text:
Use the techniques from Debugging and Dynamic Analysis.

For a native Linux target:

gdb --args ./target crash-input

Then:

run

After the crash:

bt

Inspect the faulting context.

docs.title: 77. Sanitizer-Based Triage
docs.text:
Sanitizer output can often provide:

Error class

Fault location

Access type

Stack trace

Allocation context

Deallocation context

Preserve the complete report.

Do not keep only the first line.

docs.title: 78. Example Sanitizer Finding
docs.text:
Illustrative:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow

READ of size 4

#0 parse_record
#1 parse_document
#2 LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput

This supports the existence of an out-of-bounds memory access in the instrumented build.

It does not by itself establish exploitability.

docs.title: 79. Root Cause Analysis
docs.text:
After reproducing the finding, trace:

Fuzzer Input
     |
     v
Parsed Field
     |
     v
Transformation
     |
     v
Missing / Incorrect Validation
     |
     v
Memory / Logic Operation
     |
     v
Failure

The objective is to explain why the crash occurs.

docs.title: 80. Attacker Control
docs.text:
Determine exactly which values are influenced by the input.

For example:

Input controls:
record_length

Input does not control:
destination_buffer_size

Then determine how the relationship produces the failure.

This is stronger than simply stating that the file causes a crash.

docs.title: 81. Security Boundary
docs.text:
Ask:

Can an untrusted user provide the input?

Is authentication required?

Does a server process the input automatically?

What privilege processes it?

Is user interaction required?

Is the parser sandboxed?

Does the crash affect only the user's own process?

This determines security significance.

docs.title: 82. Exploitability
docs.text:
Do not assume that memory corruption automatically means arbitrary code execution.

Investigate:

Read or write?

Size?

Attacker-controlled data?

Attacker-controlled address?

Object lifetime?

Memory protections?

Process privilege?

Sandbox?

Reliability?

The final report should distinguish confirmed facts from theoretical possibilities.

docs.title: 83. False Positives
docs.text:
Potential false or misleading findings include:

Harness bug

Intentional abort

Invalid test environment

Instrumentation issue

Known assertion

Unsupported input

Out-of-memory caused by laboratory limits

Always determine whether the finding exists in the target rather than only in the harness.

docs.title: 84. Validate Against the Real Target
docs.text:
If fuzzing uses a simplified harness:

Harness Crash
      |
      v
Reproduce Through Real Interface

where practical.

This helps establish reachability.

If reproduction through the full application is not possible, document that limitation.

docs.title: 85. Harness Bugs
docs.text:
The harness itself can introduce errors.

Example:

char buffer[64];
memcpy(buffer, data, size);

If size is unbounded, the harness is vulnerable regardless of the target parser.

Do not report harness bugs as product vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 86. Differential Validation
docs.text:
Compare:

Vulnerable Version

Fixed Version

with the same crash input.

Example:

Version 2.4.1:
AddressSanitizer finding

Version 2.4.2:
Input rejected

This can support affected-version analysis.

docs.title: 87. Regression Testing
docs.text:
After a vulnerability is fixed, preserve the minimised input as a regression test where appropriate.

Crash Input
     |
     v
Patch
     |
     v
Regression Test
     |
     v
Future Builds

The expected result becomes:

No memory violation

Input safely rejected or handled

docs.title: 88. Variant Analysis
docs.text:
A fuzzing discovery may reveal a reusable bug pattern.

Example:

Root Cause:
Missing validation of record length

Search for:

Other record parsers

Other format versions

Related decoder functions

Shared helper functions

See the later Variant Analysis page for a complete methodology.

docs.title: 89. Improve the Fuzzer After a Discovery
docs.text:
A crash often teaches you something about the target.

Example:

Crash reveals:
TYPE=7 reaches previously unknown parser.

Add:

TYPE=7

to:

Corpus

Dictionary

Structured generator

Then continue exploring nearby behavior.

docs.title: 90. Multiple Fuzzing Campaigns
docs.text:
Instead of one enormous campaign, split targets logically.

Example:

Parser
├── Header Fuzzer
├── Metadata Fuzzer
├── Record Fuzzer
├── Compression Fuzzer
└── Import Fuzzer

Smaller focused harnesses can improve both speed and interpretation.

docs.title: 91. Parallel Fuzzing
docs.text:
Fuzzing can often be parallelised across CPU cores.

A general model is:

Worker 1 ----\
Worker 2 -----\
Worker 3 ------> Shared Research Campaign
Worker 4 -----/

The exact parallelisation mechanism depends on the fuzzer.

Follow the current tool documentation rather than assuming workers can simply write to the same arbitrary directory.

docs.title: 92. Reproducibility Across Builds
docs.text:
A finding should ideally be tested against:

Original fuzzing build

Clean debug build

Relevant release build

This helps identify instrumentation-specific behavior.

docs.title: 93. Fuzzing Third-Party Libraries
docs.text:
Applications frequently expose third-party parsers.

Determine:

Library

Version

Application integration

Input reachability

Configuration

Patch level

If a crash occurs inside a dependency, determine whether:

The application exposes the vulnerable functionality

The dependency version is affected

The application adds mitigating validation

docs.title: 94. Fuzzing APIs
docs.text:
API fuzzing can explore:

Parameter types

Missing fields

Duplicate fields

Nested objects

Unexpected arrays

Integer boundaries

State transitions

But preserve:

Authentication

Authorisation

Business context

when these are necessary to reach the target behavior.

docs.title: 95. Structured JSON Mutation
docs.text:
For JSON:

{
  "name": "example",
  "count": 1,
  "enabled": true
}

interesting transformations may include:

Missing field

Null

Wrong type

Negative integer

Large integer

Empty string

Large string

Nested object

Array instead of scalar

Duplicate semantic values

The purpose is to explore parser and application assumptions.

docs.title: 96. Protocol Fuzzing
docs.text:
A network protocol may have:

Handshake

Authentication

Command

Payload

Response

A useful fuzzer must often preserve enough state to reach the intended command parser.

Blindly sending random bytes to the first packet may exercise only the connection rejection path.

docs.title: 97. Stateful Protocol Harness
docs.text:
Where appropriate:

Initialize Session
      |
      v
Reach Target State
      |
      v
Inject Fuzzer Input
      |
      v
Observe
      |
      v
Reset Session

Keep the setup deterministic.

docs.title: 98. File Format Fuzzing
docs.text:
For file formats, identify:

Magic bytes

Version

Lengths

Offsets

Types

Checksums

Compression

Nested structures

Then determine which fields should be:

Preserved

Mutated

Generated

docs.title: 99. Fuzzing Parsers Behind Applications
docs.text:
Suppose:

HTTP Upload
      |
      v
Storage
      |
      v
Queue
      |
      v
Parser Library

Fuzzing through HTTP may be extremely slow.

If the research objective is the parser library, a direct harness may be more efficient.

Later reproduce important findings through the full application path.

docs.title: 100. Fuzzing Security Checks
docs.text:
Not all fuzzing needs to target memory corruption.

Fuzzing can also explore:

Validation inconsistencies

Canonicalisation

Parser differences

State-machine errors

Authentication parsing

Protocol confusion

These campaigns require meaningful oracles.

docs.title: 101. What Is an Oracle?
docs.text:
An oracle determines whether an input produced an interesting result.

For memory-safety fuzzing:

Crash

Sanitizer finding

can act as oracles.

For logic fuzzing, the oracle may be:

Unexpected success

Different parser result

Security invariant violation

Mismatch between implementations

Without a useful oracle, the fuzzer may generate behavior that cannot be automatically classified.

docs.title: 102. Security Invariants
docs.text:
Define properties that should always remain true.

Examples:

Unauthenticated users cannot access protected objects.

Archive entries remain inside the extraction directory.

Parsed offsets never reference outside the input buffer.

Tenant A cannot access Tenant B objects.

Invalid signatures are never accepted.

Fuzzing can then attempt to violate these invariants.

docs.title: 103. Differential Oracle
docs.text:
Suppose two parsers should interpret input identically.

Input
  |
  +---- Parser A -> Result A
  |
  +---- Parser B -> Result B

If:

Result A != Result B

preserve the input for investigation.

This can expose parsing discrepancies with security implications.

docs.title: 104. Fuzzing Time Budget
docs.text:
There is no universal number of hours that proves a target has been adequately fuzzed.

Campaign duration depends on:

Execution speed

Target complexity

Coverage growth

Corpus quality

Available resources

Research objective

Focus on whether the campaign continues to explore meaningful behavior.

docs.title: 105. When to Stop or Redesign
docs.text:
Consider redesigning the campaign when:

Coverage has plateaued

The same shallow paths dominate

Execution is too slow

Most inputs fail at the same validation

Harness instability is high

No useful states are reached

Possible responses include:

Improve corpus

Add dictionary

Change harness boundary

Split target

Model grammar

Remove irrelevant initialization

Investigate blocking validation

docs.title: 106. Fuzzing Metrics
docs.text:
Useful operational metrics include:

Executions per second

Corpus size

Coverage growth

Unique crash groups

Timeout rate

Harness stability

These describe the campaign.

They do not directly measure the security of the target.

docs.title: 107. Research Notes
docs.text:
Maintain a campaign record.

Example:

Campaign:
FUZZ-2026-001

Target:
Example Parser

Version:
2.4.1

Harness:
parse_document()

Fuzzer:
libFuzzer

Sanitizers:
AddressSanitizer

Corpus:
12 minimised valid samples

Start:
2026-09-09

Objective:
Explore record parsing and length handling.

docs.title: 108. Finding Record
docs.text:
For each interesting result:

Finding ID:

Campaign:

Target Version:

Input:

SHA-256:

Failure Type:

Reproducible:

Stack:

Sanitizer:

Minimised:

Root Cause:

Security Boundary:

Affected Versions:

Status:

docs.title: 109. Evidence to Preserve
docs.text:
Keep:

Original seed corpus

Harness source

Build configuration

Compiler version

Target commit

Fuzzer configuration

Dictionary

Original crash

Minimised crash

Crash hash

Sanitizer report

Debugger output

Research notes

Without the environment information, reproducing an old fuzzing result can become difficult.

docs.title: 110. Practical Fuzzing Scenario
docs.text:
Assume an authorised local research target contains a native parser for a fictional .vrd document format.

The parser accepts:

Header

Version

Record Count

Records

Each record contains:

Type

Length

Payload

docs.title: Research Objective
docs.text: Determine whether malformed record structures can trigger memory-safety failures in the parser.

docs.title: Attack Surface
docs.text:
User-Supplied Document
        |
        v
Document Import
        |
        v
VRD Parser
        |
        v
Record Parser

The parser therefore processes attacker-controlled file content.

docs.title: Initial Corpus
docs.text:
Create several valid documents:

corpus/
├── minimal.vrd
├── two-records.vrd
├── metadata.vrd
└── optional-record.vrd

Verify each file parses successfully before fuzzing.

docs.title: Harness
docs.text:
The harness should call the same parser used by the application.

Conceptually:

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>

#include "vrd_parser.h"

extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(
    const uint8_t* data,
    size_t size
) {
    if (data == nullptr || size == 0) {
        return 0;
    }

    VrdParser parser;
    parser.parse(data, size);

    return 0;
}

The actual API will depend on the software being researched.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
A representative Clang fuzzing build might use:

clang++ \
  -g \
  -O1 \
  -fsanitize=fuzzer,address \
  fuzz_vrd.cpp \
  vrd_parser.cpp \
  -o fuzz_vrd

Validate:

./fuzz_vrd corpus/minimal.vrd

before starting the campaign.

docs.title: Start Fuzzing
docs.text:
mkdir -p artifacts

./fuzz_vrd \
  -artifact_prefix=artifacts/ \
  corpus

Monitor:

Execution rate

Corpus growth

Coverage growth

Crashes

docs.title: Interesting Result
docs.text:
Suppose libFuzzer produces:

artifacts/crash-...

and AddressSanitizer reports:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow

This is a research lead.

docs.title: Preserve the Input
docs.text:
Copy the original artifact and hash it:

sha256sum artifacts/crash-*

Record:

Target version

Commit

Build options

Sanitizer

Input hash

Campaign

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
Run the artifact independently:

./fuzz_vrd artifacts/crash-...

Suppose the same AddressSanitizer finding occurs repeatedly.

The issue is now reproducible in the fuzzing build.

docs.title: Minimise
docs.text:
Use libFuzzer crash minimisation:

./fuzz_vrd \
  -minimize_crash=1 \
  artifacts/crash-... \
  -exact_artifact_path=minimized.vrd

Then verify:

./fuzz_vrd minimized.vrd

docs.title: Debug
docs.text:
Run:

gdb --args ./fuzz_vrd minimized.vrd

Inside GDB:

run

After the failure:

bt

Representative stack:

parse_record()
parse_document()
LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput()

docs.title: Root Cause Investigation
docs.text:
Inspection reveals the relevant conceptual path:

Record Header
     |
     v
Declared Length
     |
     v
Destination Allocation
     |
     v
Payload Copy

Suppose runtime analysis shows:

Declared payload length:
1024

Destination allocation:
128

Copy operation:
1024

The researcher should determine exactly why the allocation and copy lengths differ.

docs.title: Negative Control
docs.text:
Modify only the relevant length field to a known-safe value.

Example observation:

Length 128:
No sanitizer finding

Length 1024:
Heap-buffer-overflow

This helps isolate the triggering condition.

docs.title: Full Application Validation
docs.text:
If appropriate and authorised, test the minimised document through the real document-import functionality.

Determine whether:

The application accepts the document

The same parser is reached

The same memory-safety failure occurs

This establishes practical reachability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A defensible intermediate conclusion could be:

Coverage-guided fuzzing of the VRD record parser identified a reproducible heap-buffer-overflow in the AddressSanitizer-instrumented research build. The minimised input demonstrates that a record length derived from attacker-controlled file content can cause the parser to copy more data than the observed destination allocation. The same parser path should be validated through the full application interface, and additional analysis is required to determine affected versions and practical exploitability.

This states what the evidence supports.

It does not automatically claim:

Remote Code Execution

docs.title: 113. Fuzzing Mindset
docs.text:
Do not think:

More Executions = Secure

More Crashes = More Vulnerabilities

Crash = RCE

Coverage = Security Coverage

Long Campaign = Complete Testing

Sanitizer Finding = Maximum Severity

Instead think:

Is the Right Attack Surface Being Tested?
                |
                v
Does the Harness Reach the Right Code?
                |
                v
Does the Corpus Represent Useful Structure?
                |
                v
Is the Fuzzer Exploring New Behavior?
                |
                v
Is the Finding Reproducible?
                |
                v
What Is the Root Cause?
                |
                v
What Does the Attacker Control?
                |
                v
Which Security Boundary Is Affected?
                |
                v
What Impact Does the Evidence Support?

Fuzzing is a discovery mechanism.

Vulnerability research begins when an interesting result is investigated and explained.

flowchart LR
      A["Harness and target"] --> B["Generated input"]
      B --> C["Execution and telemetry"]
      C --> D["Crash or anomaly"]
      D --> E["Deduplicate and minimize"]
      E --> F["Root-cause validation"]

docs.text:

Fuzz the smallest meaningful target

A focused harness that directly exercises the security-relevant parser can execute substantially faster than repeatedly starting the complete application. Important findings should still be checked against the real application path where appropriate.

Corpus quality matters

A small collection of structurally diverse valid inputs is often more useful than thousands of nearly identical files.

Preserve every original finding

Keep the original crash before minimisation, record its hash and preserve the exact build and campaign configuration. This makes later reproduction substantially easier.

Let findings improve the campaign

When a crash or new code path reveals previously unknown structure, feed that knowledge back into the corpus, dictionary, harness or generator.

A fuzzer finds behavior, not conclusions

Crashes, hangs and sanitizer findings require reproduction, root cause analysis and security-context analysis before they should be reported as vulnerabilities.

Keep fuzzing controlled

Resource exhaustion and unstable targets can affect the research host. Run fuzzing in isolated, authorised environments with appropriate resource controls and recovery mechanisms.

docs.title: Vulnerability Research Methodology
docs.text:
Vulnerability research is the structured process of identifying, understanding, validating, and documenting software security weaknesses.

A mature methodology should answer:

What is the target?

What is the attack surface?

Where does untrusted input enter?

How is that input processed?

Which trust boundaries exist?

What happens when assumptions fail?

Can the behaviour be reproduced?

What is the root cause?

What security impact is actually supported?

Are related variants present?

How should the issue be validated after remediation?

The goal is not simply to produce a crash or unusual behaviour.

The goal is to determine whether a reproducible software condition crosses a meaningful security boundary.

Authorised research only

Perform vulnerability research only against software, source code, binaries, systems, products, services, or environments that you are authorised to analyse. Fuzzing, debugging, malformed input testing, and proof-of-concept development can crash applications or alter system state. Prefer isolated test environments rather than production systems.

docs.title: Methodology Overview
docs.text:
A useful vulnerability research lifecycle is:

Define Target
      |
      v
Establish Environment
      |
      v
Map Attack Surface
      |
      v
Understand Data Flow
      |
      v
Static Analysis
      |
      v
Dynamic Analysis
      |
      v
Targeted Testing / Fuzzing
      |
      v
Crash or Security Anomaly
      |
      v
Reproduce
      |
      v
Minimise
      |
      v
Root-Cause Analysis
      |
      v
Exploitability Assessment
      |
      v
Variant Analysis
      |
      v
Minimal Proof of Concept
      |
      v
Remediation Validation
      |
      v
Responsible Disclosure

Each stage should produce evidence that supports the next.

docs.title: Research Starts With a Question
docs.text:
Do not begin with:

Run every tool.

Begin with a research question.

Examples:

How does this parser process attacker-controlled length fields?

Can this service reach the vulnerable function without authentication?

What changed between the vulnerable and patched versions?

Which code path produces this crash?

Does user-controlled data reach an unsafe memory operation?

A focused question helps select the correct tools and reduces unnecessary testing.

docs.title: Define the Target
docs.text:
Record the exact target before analysis.

Useful information includes:

Product
Version
Build
Architecture
Operating system
Configuration
Installation source
Binary hash
Dependencies

For source review:

Repository
Branch
Commit
Build configuration

This creates a reproducible research baseline.

docs.title: Hash the Target
docs.text:
For a Windows binary:

Get-FileHash .\target.exe -Algorithm SHA256

For Linux:

sha256sum ./target

Record the result in the research notes.

docs.title: Build a Controlled Environment
docs.text:
Prefer:

  • virtual machines;
  • containers;
  • snapshots;
  • dedicated test systems;
  • disposable test data.

A useful structure is:

Research Workstation
      |
      +-- Debugger
      +-- Disassembler
      +-- Scripts
      +-- Fuzzer
      |
      v
Isolated Target

The target environment should be easy to restore.

docs.title: Record the Environment
docs.text:
Capture:

OS version
Architecture
Installed dependencies
Target configuration
Compiler if known
Security mitigations
Research tool versions

Environment differences can change behaviour.

docs.title: Snapshot Before Testing
docs.text:
Where practical:

Clean State
   |
   v
Snapshot
   |
   v
Research
   |
   v
Crash / State Change
   |
   v
Restore

This makes repeated experiments much easier.

docs.title: Map the Attack Surface
docs.text:
Before fuzzing, understand how data reaches the program.

Related note:

Attack Surface Analysis

Potential attack surfaces include:

  • network listeners;
  • file parsers;
  • APIs;
  • IPC;
  • RPC;
  • plugins;
  • import/export features;
  • command-line arguments;
  • environment variables;
  • configuration files;
  • browser handlers;
  • update mechanisms;
  • privileged services.

docs.title: Attack Surface Inventory
docs.text:
A useful table is:

Interface Input Auth Required Privilege Notes HTTP API JSON No Service user Remote File parser Document User action Desktop user Local Named pipe Binary protocol Local SYSTEM service IPC CLI Arguments Local Current user Local

This helps prioritise reachable and security-relevant paths.

docs.title: Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
Identify where data crosses between:

Untrusted

and:

Trusted

Examples:

Network -> parser
User -> privileged service
Document -> renderer
Plugin -> host application
Low privilege -> high privilege component

A bug is more security relevant when it crosses a meaningful boundary.

docs.title: Reachability
docs.text:
A vulnerable function that cannot be reached by an attacker may not represent a practical vulnerability.

Ask:

Can attacker-controlled input reach this function?

Is authentication required?

Is local access required?

Is user interaction required?

Is a privileged position required?

Reachability should be established early.

docs.title: Data-Flow Mapping
docs.text:
Track how attacker-controlled values move.

Input
  |
  v
Parser
  |
  v
Validation
  |
  v
Transformation
  |
  v
Sensitive Operation

Important questions include:

Where is the input validated?

Can integer conversion alter the value?

Can length and buffer size diverge?

Is canonicalisation performed?

Is ownership or authorisation checked?

docs.title: Source and Sink
docs.text:
A useful reasoning model is:

Source
  |
  v
Data Flow
  |
  v
Sink

Source examples:

Network packet
HTTP parameter
File field
IPC message
User-controlled string

Sink examples:

Memory copy
Allocation
File access
Command execution
Database query
Privilege decision

docs.title: Static Analysis
docs.text:
Static analysis studies software without executing the target.

Potential tools include:

  • source review;
  • ripgrep;
  • Semgrep;
  • OpenGrep;
  • CodeQL;
  • Ghidra;
  • IDA;
  • Binary Ninja;
  • strings;
  • objdump;
  • readelf.

Related tools:

Vulnerability Research Tools

docs.title: Static Analysis Goals
docs.text:
Useful static analysis questions include:

Where is input parsed?

Which functions perform allocation?

Where are bounds checked?

Where are authentication decisions made?

Which dangerous APIs are used?

Which functions changed after a patch?

Static analysis should support a hypothesis.

docs.title: Source Review
docs.text:
If source code exists, prefer understanding the original implementation before relying on decompiler output.

Search for:

parser functions
memory copies
raw pointer operations
dynamic SQL
filesystem access
authentication logic
privilege checks

docs.title: Binary Analysis
docs.text:
If source is unavailable:

Binary
  |
  v
Disassembler
  |
  v
Interesting Function
  |
  v
Cross References
  |
  v
Data-Flow Reasoning

Decompiler output should be treated as an approximation.

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:
Cross-references can reveal:

Who calls this function?

Where is this string used?

Which functions reach this parser?

Where is this dangerous API called?

This is one of the strongest techniques in binary analysis.

docs.title: Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Dynamic analysis observes the program while it runs.

Related note:

Debugging and Dynamic Analysis

Useful tools include:

GDB
GEF
pwndbg
WinDbg
x64dbg
Frida
strace
ltrace
Process Monitor

docs.title: Dynamic Analysis Goals
docs.text:
Use runtime analysis to answer:

What code path actually executes?

What values are present?

Which functions are called?

What memory is accessed?

Which file or registry operations occur?

Which network requests happen?

Dynamic analysis validates static assumptions.

docs.title: Breakpoints
docs.text:
Place breakpoints according to a research hypothesis.

For example:

Input parser
Memory allocation
Copy function
Authentication check
Exception handler

Do not set hundreds of arbitrary breakpoints without a reason.

docs.title: Runtime Observation
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Known Input
   |
   v
Run Under Debugger
   |
   v
Break at Interesting Function
   |
   v
Inspect Arguments
   |
   v
Trace State Change

docs.title: Differential Testing
docs.text:
Compare:

Valid input

with:

Slightly modified input

Observe:

  • branches;
  • allocation sizes;
  • error paths;
  • output;
  • timing.

Small controlled differences are easier to understand.

docs.title: Build a Valid Corpus
docs.text:
For parsers and protocols, begin with valid samples.

A corpus may include:

Small file
Large file
Different metadata
Different compression
Different record count
Different encoding

Valid input helps reach deeper application states.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text:
Fuzzing systematically mutates or generates input to discover abnormal behaviour.

Related note:

Fuzzing

A simplified workflow is:

Seed Corpus
    |
    v
Mutation
    |
    v
Target
    |
    +-- Normal
    +-- Hang
    +-- Crash

docs.title: Choose the Fuzz Target
docs.text:
Do not fuzz an entire application if a smaller function can be isolated.

Prefer:

Parser Function

over:

Full GUI Application Startup

when possible.

This improves:

  • speed;
  • reproducibility;
  • coverage.

docs.title: Harness Design
docs.text:
A good fuzz harness should:

  • call the target function directly;
  • initialise only required state;
  • avoid unnecessary disk/network activity;
  • clean up state;
  • execute quickly;
  • handle expected errors.

docs.title: Fuzzing Coverage
docs.text:
Coverage helps determine whether new code paths are being reached.

But:

100% code coverage

does not mean:

100% security-state coverage

Specific values and state transitions still matter.

docs.title: Sanitizers
docs.text:
Where source/build access exists, enable sanitizers.

Useful examples include:

  • AddressSanitizer;
  • UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.

They can provide much richer failure information than a generic crash.

docs.title: Monitor Stability
docs.text:
During fuzzing, monitor:

  • memory;
  • CPU;
  • disk;
  • process restarts;
  • crash rate;
  • timeout rate.

Resource exhaustion can distort results.

docs.title: Crash Discovery
docs.text:
When a crash appears:

Do not immediately classify it.

First preserve:

Input
Target version
Timestamp
Exception
Stack trace

docs.title: Crash Triage
docs.text:
Related note:

Crash Analysis

A crash triage process is:

Crash
  |
  v
Reproduce
  |
  v
Classify
  |
  v
Minimise
  |
  v
Debug
  |
  v
Root Cause

docs.title: Reproduce the Crash
docs.text:
A crash should ideally reproduce independently from the fuzzer.

Record the exact invocation.

If it does not reproduce, investigate:

  • timing;
  • process state;
  • race conditions;
  • resource exhaustion;
  • nondeterminism.

docs.title: Crash Minimisation
docs.text:
Reduce the triggering input to the smallest form that preserves the issue.

Benefits include:

  • easier analysis;
  • clearer PoC;
  • better disclosure;
  • easier regression testing.

docs.title: Crash Deduplication
docs.text:
Many inputs may trigger one root cause.

Group crashes by:

  • faulting instruction;
  • stack trace;
  • sanitizer location;
  • exception type;
  • top stack frames.

Do not report one vulnerability per crashing input.

docs.title: Root-Cause Analysis
docs.text:
The crash location is not necessarily the root cause.

Example:

Invalid length accepted
      |
      v
Allocation too small
      |
      v
Later copy
      |
      v
Crash

The copy is where the crash occurs.

The root cause is the earlier validation failure.

docs.title: Trace Backwards
docs.text:
From the crash:

Fault
  |
  v
Unsafe Operation
  |
  v
Bad State
  |
  v
Incorrect Validation
  |
  v
Attacker-Controlled Input

This reasoning is central to vulnerability research.

docs.title: Root-Cause Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

What condition became unsafe?

Where should it have been validated?

Which value is attacker controlled?

Which invariant was violated?

Could the same root cause exist elsewhere?

docs.title: Memory Corruption
docs.text:
Memory corruption can include:

  • out-of-bounds read;
  • out-of-bounds write;
  • use-after-free;
  • double free;
  • integer-related allocation error;
  • stack overflow.

The security impact must be assessed separately.

docs.title: Out-of-Bounds Read
docs.text:
Determine whether the condition can expose:

  • adjacent memory;
  • secrets;
  • pointers;
  • application data.

A crash-only read may have different impact from a reliable disclosure primitive.

docs.title: Out-of-Bounds Write
docs.text:
Determine:

What bytes can be controlled?

Where can they be written?

How far can the write extend?

What mitigations exist?

Do not automatically call it RCE.

docs.title: Use-After-Free
docs.text:
Investigate:

Where was object allocated?

Where was it freed?

Why is it used later?

Can memory be replaced by attacker-controlled data?

Sanitizers are particularly useful here.

docs.title: Integer Bugs
docs.text:
Common patterns include:

Integer overflow
Signed/unsigned conversion
Truncation
Multiplication overflow
Length mismatch

These can lead to incorrect allocations or bounds calculations.

docs.title: Logic Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Not all security bugs are memory corruption.

Other categories include:

  • authentication bypass;
  • authorisation bypass;
  • path traversal;
  • unsafe file handling;
  • injection;
  • insecure state transitions;
  • cryptographic mistakes.

Use the same root-cause methodology.

docs.title: Exploitability Assessment
docs.text:
After root cause is understood, determine what security impact is actually supported.

A useful model is:

Root Cause
    |
    v
Attacker Control
    |
    v
Reachability
    |
    v
Security Context
    |
    v
Mitigations
    |
    v
Impact

docs.title: Attacker Control
docs.text:
Determine whether the attacker controls:

Data
Length
Offset
Pointer
Destination
Index
Object lifetime
Branch condition

Greater control may increase exploitability.

docs.title: Security Context
docs.text:
Record:

Process privilege
Sandbox
Service identity
Integrity level
Container
User context

A bug inside a sandboxed process may still be serious, but impact differs.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
Relevant mitigations may include:

ASLR
DEP/NX
Stack canaries
CFG
CET
PIE
RELRO
Sandbox
Privilege separation

Mitigations affect exploitability, not whether the underlying bug exists.

docs.title: Exploitability Is Not Binary
docs.text:
Possible conclusions include:

Crash only
Denial of service
Information disclosure
Memory corruption with limited control
Potential code execution
Confirmed code execution
Privilege escalation
Authentication bypass

Use the strongest conclusion supported by evidence.

docs.title: Avoid Overclaiming
docs.text:
Do not write:

Memory corruption = RCE

or:

Crash = exploitable

without evidence.

docs.title: Patch Diffing
docs.text:
Patch diffing helps understand what changed between vulnerable and fixed versions.

Related note:

Patch Diffing

A useful process is:

Old Version
     |
     +----+
          |
          v
        Diff
          ^
          |
     +----+
     |
Fixed Version
      |
      v
Changed Function
      |
      v
Security-Relevant Change

docs.title: Source-Level Patch Diffing
docs.text:
If source is available:

git diff <old> <new>

or:

git show <commit>

Look for:

  • new checks;
  • changed bounds;
  • authentication conditions;
  • memory-allocation changes;
  • parser hardening.

docs.title: Binary Patch Diffing
docs.text:
Without source:

  • compare functions;
  • identify changed blocks;
  • compare control flow;
  • inspect new constants;
  • inspect validation branches.

Use the diff as a guide.

Still determine the root cause independently.

docs.title: Patch Does Not Explain Everything
docs.text:
A changed function may include:

  • refactoring;
  • unrelated fixes;
  • performance changes.

Do not assume every change is security related.

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
After identifying the root cause, search for similar patterns.

Related note:

Variant Analysis

A useful process is:

Known Bug
  |
  v
Generalise Root Cause
  |
  v
Search Related Code
  |
  v
Candidate Variants
  |
  v
Validate

docs.title: Generalise the Pattern
docs.text:
Instead of searching only for:

vulnerable_function()

search for the underlying pattern:

attacker-controlled length
+
allocation
+
unchecked copy

or:

object lookup
without
ownership validation

docs.title: Variant Sources
docs.text:
Search:

  • same module;
  • sibling parser;
  • alternate protocol;
  • older version;
  • shared library;
  • related product;
  • copied code.

docs.title: Static Tools for Variants
docs.text:
Where source exists, useful tools include:

  • ripgrep;
  • Semgrep;
  • OpenGrep;
  • CodeQL.

Related section:

Source Code Review Tools

docs.title: Fuzzing for Variants
docs.text:
After fixing or suppressing one crash path, continue fuzzing.

The first discovered bug may hide deeper paths.

docs.title: Proof-of-Concept Development
docs.text:
Related note:

Proof-of-Concept Development

A good PoC should be:

Minimal
Reproducible
Deterministic
Safe
Understandable

docs.title: PoC Purpose
docs.text:
The PoC should answer:

Can the issue be reliably reproduced?

not:

How much extra functionality can be added?

docs.title: Minimal Demonstration
docs.text:
For a memory bug, a deterministic crash may initially be enough.

For an authentication issue, a controlled access-control bypass may be enough.

For an information disclosure bug, retrieve the minimum data needed to demonstrate impact.

docs.title: Avoid Unnecessary Weaponisation
docs.text:
A disclosure PoC rarely needs:

  • persistence;
  • unrelated payloads;
  • lateral movement;
  • destructive actions.

Keep it focused on the vulnerability.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
The PoC should specify:

Target
Version
Environment
Input
Execution
Observed Result

Another authorised researcher should be able to reproduce it.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Maintain evidence throughout the research process.

Useful artefacts include:

Target binary
Hash
Source commit
Crash input
Minimised crash
Stack trace
Debugger output
Sanitizer report
Patch comparison
PoC
Research timeline

docs.title: Research Timeline
docs.text:
Example:

10:30 - target installed
11:10 - parser identified
12:45 - fuzzer started
14:32 - crash discovered
14:40 - crash reproduced
15:20 - input minimised
16:15 - root cause identified
17:00 - variant search started

This improves traceability.

docs.title: Screenshot Use
docs.text:
Screenshots can support:

  • debugger crash;
  • sanitizer output;
  • PoC result.

But preserve textual evidence where possible.

Text is easier to:

  • search;
  • compare;
  • reproduce.

docs.title: Store Raw Evidence
docs.text:
Do not modify the only copy of:

original crashing input

or:

original vulnerable binary

Store working copies separately.

docs.title: Naming Convention
docs.text:
Use descriptive names:

crash-heap-oob-parser-record.bin

instead of:

crash1.bin

Keep original fuzzer identifiers as metadata where useful.

docs.title: Responsible Disclosure
docs.text:
Once a new vulnerability is confirmed, transition from research to disclosure.

Related note:

Responsible Disclosure

A disclosure package should usually contain:

Product/version
Affected component
Root cause
Impact
Minimal reproduction
PoC
Suggested remediation

docs.title: Disclosure Scope
docs.text:
Do not disclose:

  • customer information;
  • unrelated credentials;
  • unrelated vulnerabilities;
  • sensitive infrastructure details;

unless necessary and authorised.

docs.title: Vendor Communication
docs.text:
Be precise and reproducible.

Avoid statements such as:

Your software is remotely exploitable.

unless the evidence supports that exact conclusion.

docs.title: CVE Research
docs.text:
For known or newly assigned vulnerabilities, maintain a consistent CVE research process.

Related note:

CVE Research

Useful information includes:

CVE identifier
Vendor advisory
Affected versions
Fixed versions
Root cause
Attack vector
Prerequisites
Patch

docs.title: Validate Vendor Versions
docs.text:
Product versions may be:

  • backported;
  • vendor-patched;
  • distribution-specific.

Do not rely only on a banner string.

docs.title: CVSS and Severity
docs.text:
Severity should be based on demonstrated and credible impact.

Do not assign a high score merely because:

memory corruption

or:

CVE exists

Consider:

  • attack vector;
  • authentication;
  • privileges;
  • user interaction;
  • impact;
  • environmental context.

docs.title: Remediation Validation
docs.text:
Research does not end when a patch is published.

Retest:

Original PoC
      |
      v
Patched Build

Then determine whether:

Root cause was fixed

or merely:

Specific input was blocked

docs.title: Patch Bypass vs Variant
docs.text:
If the original input no longer works, investigate whether:

  • the root cause is fixed;
  • an alternate path remains;
  • a related parser remains vulnerable.

This distinguishes effective remediation from input-specific blocking.

docs.title: Regression Test
docs.text:
Convert the minimised PoC into a safe regression case where possible.

Known Bad Input
      |
      v
Patched Build
      |
      v
Safe Rejection

This helps prevent reintroduction.

docs.title: Tool Selection
docs.text: Choose tools according to the question.

docs.title: Need Static Binary Understanding
docs.text:
Use:

Ghidra
IDA
Binary Ninja

docs.title: Need Linux Runtime Debugging
docs.text:
Use:

GDB
GEF
pwndbg

docs.title: Need Windows Runtime Debugging
docs.text:
Use:

WinDbg
x64dbg

docs.title: Need Fuzzing
docs.text:
Use:

AFL++
libFuzzer

docs.title: Need Runtime Tracing
docs.text:
Use:

strace
ltrace
Process Monitor
Frida

docs.title: Need Variant Search
docs.text:
Use:

ripgrep
Semgrep
OpenGrep
CodeQL

Related tool section:

Vulnerability Research Tools

docs.title: False Conclusions
docs.text: Avoid these common mistakes.

docs.title: Crash Equals Vulnerability
docs.text:
False.

A crash may be:

  • invalid input handling;
  • assertion;
  • resource exhaustion;
  • non-security bug.

Investigate root cause and security context.

docs.title: Memory Corruption Equals RCE
docs.text:
False.

Memory corruption must be assessed for:

  • control;
  • mitigations;
  • reachability;
  • reliability.

docs.title: Patch Difference Equals Root Cause
docs.text:
False.

Patch changes may be unrelated or broader than the vulnerability.

docs.title: Scanner Match Equals Vulnerability
docs.text:
False.

Static-analysis and scanning tools produce candidates.

Manual validation is required.

docs.title: CVE Version Match Equals Vulnerability
docs.text:
False.

Backports and configuration differences matter.

docs.title: Practical Research Workflow
docs.text:
A complete research process can be:

1. Confirm authorisation
      |
      v
2. Record exact target
      |
      v
3. Hash binary/source state
      |
      v
4. Build isolated environment
      |
      v
5. Map attack surface
      |
      v
6. Identify trust boundaries
      |
      v
7. Perform static analysis
      |
      v
8. Perform dynamic analysis
      |
      v
9. Build focused tests/harness
      |
      v
10. Fuzz or mutate input
      |
      v
11. Capture crash/anomaly
      |
      v
12. Reproduce independently
      |
      v
13. Minimise input
      |
      v
14. Deduplicate
      |
      v
15. Identify root cause
      |
      v
16. Trace attacker control
      |
      v
17. Assess exploitability
      |
      v
18. Search for variants
      |
      v
19. Build minimal PoC
      |
      v
20. Test patched version
      |
      v
21. Preserve evidence
      |
      v
22. Disclose responsibly

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
• [ ] Research explicitly authorised.
  • [ ] Target defined.
  • [ ] Environment defined.
  • [ ] Prohibited actions understood.
  • [ ] Production impact avoided where possible.

docs.title: Target Baseline
docs.text:
• [ ] Product recorded.
  • [ ] Version recorded.
  • [ ] Architecture recorded.
  • [ ] OS recorded.
  • [ ] Binary/source hash recorded.
  • [ ] Configuration recorded.
  • [ ] Tool versions recorded.

docs.title: Attack Surface
docs.text:
• [ ] Network interfaces reviewed.
  • [ ] File parsers reviewed.
  • [ ] IPC/RPC reviewed.
  • [ ] APIs reviewed.
  • [ ] Privileged services reviewed.
  • [ ] Plugins reviewed.
  • [ ] Trust boundaries identified.
  • [ ] Reachability established.

docs.title: Static Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Strings reviewed.
  • [ ] Imports reviewed.
  • [ ] Exports reviewed.
  • [ ] Interesting functions identified.
  • [ ] Cross-references reviewed.
  • [ ] Validation logic reviewed.
  • [ ] Sensitive operations identified.

docs.title: Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
• [ ] Known-good input tested.
  • [ ] Interesting functions traced.
  • [ ] Relevant breakpoints used.
  • [ ] Runtime values inspected.
  • [ ] File/network behaviour observed.
  • [ ] Exceptions recorded.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text:
• [ ] Target selected.
  • [ ] Harness appropriate.
  • [ ] Seed corpus valid.
  • [ ] Coverage considered.
  • [ ] Sanitizers enabled where possible.
  • [ ] Resource usage monitored.
  • [ ] Crashes retained.
  • [ ] Hangs retained separately.

docs.title: Crash Triage
docs.text:
• [ ] Crash reproduced.
  • [ ] Input preserved.
  • [ ] Input hash recorded.
  • [ ] Input minimised.
  • [ ] Exception classified.
  • [ ] Stack trace retained.
  • [ ] Duplicate crashes grouped.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
• [ ] Unsafe condition identified.
  • [ ] Crash site distinguished from root cause.
  • [ ] Attacker-controlled value identified.
  • [ ] Failed invariant identified.
  • [ ] Missing/incorrect validation identified.

docs.title: Exploitability
docs.text:
• [ ] Reachability confirmed.
  • [ ] Privilege context recorded.
  • [ ] Attacker control assessed.
  • [ ] Mitigations reviewed.
  • [ ] Impact not overstated.
  • [ ] Denial of service distinguished from code execution.
  • [ ] Information disclosure assessed separately.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• [ ] Root cause generalised.
  • [ ] Related code searched.
  • [ ] Shared components reviewed.
  • [ ] Sibling parsers reviewed.
  • [ ] Alternate versions reviewed.
  • [ ] Candidates manually validated.

docs.title: PoC
docs.text:
• [ ] Minimal.
  • [ ] Deterministic.
  • [ ] Reproducible.
  • [ ] Safe.
  • [ ] Environment documented.
  • [ ] Unnecessary weaponisation excluded.

docs.title: Patch Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Fixed version obtained.
  • [ ] Original PoC replayed.
  • [ ] Root-cause change reviewed.
  • [ ] Related variants considered.
  • [ ] Regression case retained.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Original target retained.
  • [ ] Hash retained.
  • [ ] Original crash retained.
  • [ ] Minimised crash retained.
  • [ ] Debugger output retained.
  • [ ] Patch diff retained.
  • [ ] PoC retained.
  • [ ] Timeline retained.
  • [ ] Sensitive data protected.

docs.title: Disclosure
docs.text:
• [ ] Affected versions identified.
  • [ ] Fixed versions identified where known.
  • [ ] Root cause documented.
  • [ ] Reproduction clear.
  • [ ] Impact supported by evidence.
  • [ ] Vendor process followed.
  • [ ] Disclosure timeline recorded.
  • [ ] Embargo respected where relevant.
