docs.title: Final Research Model
docs.text:
Do not research like this:

Run Fuzzer
   |
   v
Crash
   |
   v
Call It Critical

Use this model:

Define Target
      |
      v
Map Attack Surface
      |
      v
Understand Trust Boundary
      |
      v
Trace Attacker-Controlled Input
      |
      v
Static Analysis
      |
      v
Dynamic Analysis
      |
      v
Focused Testing / Fuzzing
      |
      v
Reproduce Anomaly
      |
      v
Minimise
      |
      v
Identify Root Cause
      |
      v
Assess Attacker Control
      |
      v
Evaluate Security Context
      |
      v
Determine Supported Impact
      |
      v
Search for Variants
      |
      v
Build Minimal PoC
      |
      v
Validate Patch
      |
      v
Preserve Evidence
      |
      v
Disclose Responsibly

The purpose of vulnerability research is not merely to make software fail.

It is to understand exactly why the failure occurs, whether an attacker can reach and control it, what security boundary is affected, and what evidence supports the resulting security impact.

docs.title: Patch Diffing for Vulnerability Research
docs.text:
Patch diffing is the process of comparing two versions of software to understand what changed.

In vulnerability research, the comparison is commonly:

Vulnerable Version
        |
        v
      Diff
        |
        v
Patched Version

The objective is not simply to find changed lines.

The objective is to determine:

What changed?

Why did it change?

Which security assumption changed?

What was the original root cause?

How does the patch prevent the condition?

Which input reaches the changed code?

Are equivalent vulnerable patterns present elsewhere?

Which versions are likely affected?

Patch diffing is particularly useful when a vendor has released a security update but the vulnerability description contains limited technical detail.

A practical workflow is:

Advisory / Update
       |
       v
Identify Versions
       |
       v
Acquire Artifacts
       |
       v
Verify Versions
       |
       v
Normalise Environment
       |
       v
Compare
       |
       v
Reduce Noise
       |
       v
Identify Security-Relevant Changes
       |
       v
Understand Changed Logic
       |
       v
Form Vulnerability Hypothesis
       |
       v
Validate Safely
       |
       v
Determine Root Cause
       |
       v
Variant Analysis

Patch diffing should only be performed on software and environments you are authorised to analyse.

docs.title: 1. Why Patch Diffing Matters
docs.text:
Security advisories frequently provide high-level descriptions such as:

Improper input validation

Memory corruption

Authentication bypass

Path traversal

Privilege escalation

Information disclosure

The patch may reveal the implementation detail behind that description.

For example:

Before:
User-controlled length
        |
        v
Memory copy

After:
User-controlled length
        |
        v
Bounds validation
        |
        v
Memory copy

The new validation is a strong clue about the original vulnerability.

docs.title: 2. Patch Diffing Is Evidence Gathering
docs.text:
A code difference does not automatically mean:

This is the vulnerability.

A release can contain:

Security fixes

Bug fixes

Refactoring

Formatting changes

Dependency updates

Compiler changes

Logging changes

Performance improvements

Feature changes

The researcher must connect the change to:

Security advisory

Affected component

Attack surface

Input path

Root cause

Observed behavior

docs.title: 3. Define the Research Question
docs.text:
Before comparing versions, define what you want to understand.

Examples:

Which code change fixed CVE-YYYY-NNNN?

What validation was added?

Which parser was modified?

What authentication check changed?

Which function contains the root cause?

Does the patch cover all equivalent code paths?

This prevents the analysis from becoming an unfocused comparison of every changed file.

docs.title: 4. Gather Public Context
docs.text:
Before examining code or binaries, collect available public information.

Useful sources include:

Vendor advisory

Release notes

CVE record

NVD entry

Security bulletin

Repository commit history

Issue tracker

Package changelog

Record:

CVE

Product

Affected versions

Fixed version

Component

Vulnerability class

Published date

Vendor description

References

Do not assume third-party affected-version ranges are authoritative when the vendor provides more precise information.

docs.title: 5. Establish the Version Pair
docs.text:
The ideal comparison is:

Last Known Vulnerable Version

versus

First Known Fixed Version

For example:

2.4.1
  |
  v
2.4.2

A large version gap creates unnecessary noise.

Avoid comparing:

1.0
  |
  v
5.0

when a smaller security-relevant transition is available.

docs.title: 6. Verify the Versions
docs.text:
Before diffing, confirm the actual versions.

Possible sources include:

Version output

Package metadata

Build information

Git tags

Commit IDs

File properties

Binary metadata

Checksums

Record the exact identifiers.

Example:

Vulnerable:

Version:
2.4.1

Commit:
abc123

SHA-256:
...

Fixed:

Version:
2.4.2

Commit:
def456

SHA-256:
...

docs.title: 7. Preserve Original Artifacts
docs.text:
Keep untouched copies.

Example:

patch-analysis/
├── originals/
│   ├── vulnerable/
│   └── fixed/
├── working/
├── diffs/
├── notes/
└── evidence/

Do not perform analysis only against files that have already been modified by tooling.

docs.title: 8. Hash the Artifacts
docs.text:
Linux:

sha256sum vulnerable-package
sha256sum fixed-package

PowerShell:

Get-FileHash .\vulnerable-package -Algorithm SHA256
Get-FileHash .\fixed-package -Algorithm SHA256

Record the hashes in the research notes.

docs.title: 9. Source Diffing Versus Binary Diffing
docs.text:
Patch analysis generally falls into two categories.

Source Available?
    |
    +---- Yes -> Source Diffing
    |
    +---- No -> Binary Diffing

Source diffing is usually easier because:

Function names

Variable names

Comments

Types

Control flow

are directly visible.

Binary diffing may be required for closed-source products.

docs.title: 10. Source Code Diffing
docs.text:
When source is available, useful tools include:

git diff

git log

git show

git blame

diff

Meld

Visual Studio Code

The version-control history may reveal exactly which commit introduced the fix.

docs.title: 11. Git Diff
docs.text:
Compare two commits:

git diff <old-commit> <new-commit>

Compare specific files:

git diff <old-commit> <new-commit> -- path/to/file

Summary:

git diff --stat <old-commit> <new-commit>

Changed filenames:

git diff --name-only <old-commit> <new-commit>

These commands help reduce a large repository to a smaller investigation set.

docs.title: 12. Git Show
docs.text:
Inspect a specific commit:

git show <commit>

Include statistics:

git show --stat <commit>

Inspect a file at a specific revision:

git show <commit>:path/to/file

docs.title: 13. Git Log
docs.text:
Search commit history:

git log --oneline

For a specific file:

git log --oneline -- path/to/file

Search commit messages:

git log --oneline --grep="security"

Also consider terms such as:

validation

bounds

sanitize

overflow

permission

authentication

authorization

parser

crash

CVE

Do not rely solely on commit messages.

Security fixes are not always labelled as security fixes.

docs.title: 14. Git Blame
docs.text:
When a relevant line is identified:

git blame path/to/file

This may reveal:

When the code was introduced

Which commit added it

Related historical changes

This can help determine the vulnerability's introduction point.

docs.title: 15. Repository Tags
docs.text:
List tags:

git tag

Sort version-like tags:

git tag --sort=-version:refname

Inspect a tag:

git show <tag>

Tags can help map:

Commit

Release

Affected Version

docs.title: 16. Worktrees for Side-by-Side Analysis
docs.text:
Git worktrees can provide two checked-out versions simultaneously.

Example structure:

research/
├── vulnerable/
└── fixed/

This can simplify:

Search

Build

Runtime testing

File comparison

Use the repository's supported workflow and avoid modifying original evidence.

docs.title: 17. Basic Directory Diff
docs.text:
For source trees:

diff -ru vulnerable/ fixed/

This can work well for small projects.

For large applications it may generate substantial noise.

docs.title: 18. Reduce Diff Noise
docs.text:
Common sources of noise include:

Whitespace

Formatting

Generated files

Build artifacts

Version strings

Dependencies

Lock files

Documentation

Translations

Separate these from security-relevant logic changes.

A useful classification is:

Changed File
    |
    +---- Build / Metadata
    |
    +---- Documentation
    |
    +---- Dependency
    |
    +---- Refactoring
    |
    +---- Runtime Logic
             |
             v
      Security Relevant?

docs.title: 19. Prioritise Runtime Logic
docs.text:
Prioritise changes involving:

Input parsing

Memory allocation

Memory copying

Length calculations

Path handling

Authentication

Authorisation

Cryptographic validation

Deserialization

Object ownership

File operations

Command execution

Privilege boundaries

Network parsing

These are often more relevant than cosmetic changes.

docs.title: 20. Search the Diff
docs.text:
Use git diff with grep or rg where appropriate.

Example:

git diff <old> <new> | rg -n "length|size|auth|permission|path|copy|validate"

This is a navigation technique.

It is not a substitute for understanding the changed code.

docs.title: 21. Added Validation
docs.text:
One common patch pattern is a new validation condition.

Before:

process_record(record);

After:

if (!validate_record(record)) {
    return ERROR_INVALID_RECORD;
}

process_record(record);

Questions:

What does validate_record() check?

Which input controls those fields?

Why was the check absent previously?

What operation follows the check?

docs.title: 22. Bounds Check Pattern
docs.text:
Before:

memcpy(destination, source, length);

After:

if (length > destination_size) {
    return ERROR_INVALID_LENGTH;
}

memcpy(destination, source, length);

This suggests investigation of:

length

destination_size

source size

allocation

attacker control

The patch strongly suggests a missing bounds validation, but runtime or source analysis should confirm the actual root cause.

docs.title: 23. Integer Validation Pattern
docs.text:
Before:

size = count * element_size;
buffer = malloc(size);

After:

if (count > MAX_COUNT) {
    return ERROR_INVALID_COUNT;
}

size = count * element_size;
buffer = malloc(size);

Investigate:

Integer width

Overflow behavior

Allocation size

Subsequent copy or loop

Attacker control

docs.title: 24. Authentication Check Pattern
docs.text:
Before:

Request
   |
   v
Sensitive Handler

After:

Request
   |
   v
Authentication Check
   |
   v
Sensitive Handler

Questions:

Which requests previously bypassed the check?

Is the check centralized?

Are alternate routes protected?

Does normalization occur before or after the check?

docs.title: 25. Authorisation Check Pattern
docs.text:
Before:

Load Object
    |
    v
Return Object

After:

Load Object
    |
    v
Verify Ownership / Permission
    |
    v
Return Object

This suggests an access-control issue.

Search for equivalent object retrieval functions elsewhere.

docs.title: 26. Path Validation Pattern
docs.text:
Before:

User Path
   |
   v
Base Directory + User Path
   |
   v
Open File

After:

User Path
   |
   v
Normalize
   |
   v
Verify Allowed Location
   |
   v
Open File

Investigate:

Canonicalisation

Traversal sequences

Absolute paths

Symlinks

Encoding

Platform-specific separators

docs.title: 27. Command Execution Pattern
docs.text:
Before:

User Input
   |
   v
Command String
   |
   v
Shell

After:

User Input
   |
   v
Strict Validation / Structured API
   |
   v
Process

Determine whether the original implementation allowed user-controlled data to alter command semantics.

docs.title: 28. Deserialization Pattern
docs.text:
Before:

Untrusted Data
    |
    v
Generic Deserializer

After:

Untrusted Data
    |
    v
Schema / Type Restriction
    |
    v
Deserializer

Investigate:

Allowed types

Object construction

Callbacks

Custom converters

Post-deserialization behavior

docs.title: 29. Memory Initialisation Pattern
docs.text:
Before:

object = malloc(sizeof(*object));

After:

object = calloc(1, sizeof(*object));

or:

memset(object, 0, sizeof(*object));

This may suggest:

Uninitialised state

Information disclosure

Invalid pointer

Logic inconsistency

Do not assume the security consequence without further analysis.

docs.title: 30. Lifetime Management Pattern
docs.text:
Before:

Create
  |
  v
Reference
  |
  v
Free
  |
  v
Use

After:

Create
  |
  v
Reference
  |
  v
Use
  |
  v
Release Safely

Changes involving:

Reference counts

Ownership

Cleanup

Object lifetime

may indicate a use-after-free or double-free issue.

docs.title: 31. Error Handling Changes
docs.text:
Before:

parse(data);
continue_processing();

After:

if (parse(data) != SUCCESS) {
    return ERROR_PARSE;
}

continue_processing();

The patch may be preventing later code from operating on invalid state.

Trace the old error path.

docs.title: 32. Order-of-Operations Changes
docs.text:
Security fixes sometimes reorder operations.

Before:

Use Data
   |
   v
Validate Data

After:

Validate Data
   |
   v
Use Data

This can reveal the root cause immediately.

docs.title: 33. Normalisation Changes
docs.text:
Before:

Security Check
     |
     v
Decode / Normalize
     |
     v
Use

After:

Decode / Normalize
     |
     v
Security Check
     |
     v
Use

This pattern is particularly relevant to:

Paths

URLs

Hostnames

Unicode

Encoded input

File names

docs.title: 34. Allowlist Changes
docs.text:
A patch may replace:

Block Known-Bad Values

with:

Allow Known-Good Values

This may indicate that the original denylist was incomplete.

Search for alternate representations that the old implementation handled differently.

docs.title: 35. Default-Deny Changes
docs.text:
Before:

Unknown State
     |
     v
Continue

After:

Unknown State
     |
     v
Reject

This can indicate a fail-open condition.

docs.title: 36. Privilege Boundary Changes
docs.text:
A patch may move an operation from:

High-Privilege Process

to:

Restricted Worker

or add explicit privilege checks.

Investigate:

Process identity

IPC boundary

Caller validation

Impersonation

Token handling

docs.title: 37. Binary Diffing
docs.text:
When source is unavailable, compare binaries.

Common tools include:

Ghidra

IDA

Binary Ninja

Diaphora

BinDiff

The workflow becomes:

Old Binary
     |
     v
Disassemble / Decompile
     |
     +-------------------+
                         |
New Binary               |
     |                   |
     v                   |
Disassemble / Decompile  |
     |                   |
     +---------+---------+
               |
               v
         Function Matching
               |
               v
        Changed Functions

docs.title: 38. Binary Diffing Challenges
docs.text:
Compiled binaries can differ because of:

Compiler version

Optimisation

Linker changes

Library changes

Build flags

Function layout

Inlining

Security mitigations

A binary diff can therefore contain far more changes than the source patch.

docs.title: 39. Match the Build Environment
docs.text:
Where possible, compare binaries produced using similar:

Compiler

Architecture

Optimisation

Dependencies

Build configuration

This reduces irrelevant differences.

docs.title: 40. File Metadata
docs.text:
Start with basic metadata.

Linux:

file vulnerable.bin
file fixed.bin

Hashes:

sha256sum vulnerable.bin fixed.bin

Strings:

strings vulnerable.bin > vulnerable.strings
strings fixed.bin > fixed.strings

Then compare:

diff -u vulnerable.strings fixed.strings

Strings alone rarely reveal the full vulnerability but can provide useful clues.

docs.title: 41. Symbol Comparison
docs.text:
If symbols are available:

nm vulnerable.bin > vulnerable.symbols
nm fixed.bin > fixed.symbols

Then:

diff -u vulnerable.symbols fixed.symbols

Look for:

New validation functions

Removed functions

Changed interfaces

Security-related helpers

docs.title: 42. Imported Functions
docs.text:
Changes in imported functions may provide clues.

Examples:

New cryptographic API

New validation routine

Different memory function

New privilege API

Treat these as leads rather than proof.

docs.title: 43. Ghidra Comparison
docs.text:
A practical manual workflow is:

Import vulnerable binary

Import fixed binary

Run analysis

Identify corresponding functions

Compare decompiled logic

Compare control flow

Record changed conditions

Focus on the smallest set of meaningful changed functions.

docs.title: 44. Function Matching
docs.text:
Binary diffing tools attempt to match functions using characteristics such as:

Control-flow structure

Instruction sequences

Call relationships

Constants

Strings

Function size

Prioritise functions that are:

Modified

Security-sensitive

Reachable from external input

docs.title: 45. Changed Basic Blocks
docs.text:
A patch may add only a few instructions.

Conceptually:

Old:

parse_length
    |
    v
copy

New:

parse_length
    |
    v
compare
    |
    +---- invalid -> return
    |
    v
copy

The new comparison may identify the missing security condition.

docs.title: 46. Control-Flow Graph Comparison
docs.text:
A control-flow graph can reveal:

New branches

Removed branches

New error paths

Changed validation order

New cleanup logic

A small structural change can be more significant than hundreds of changed instructions elsewhere.

docs.title: 47. Constants
docs.text:
New constants may be clues.

Examples:

Maximum size

Minimum size

Allowed type

Permission mask

Protocol version

Buffer limit

If a patch introduces:

0x1000

determine what that value represents before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: 48. Strings as Anchors
docs.text:
Useful strings include:

Error messages

Protocol names

File format names

Log messages

Function names

Configuration keys

If the fixed binary introduces:

"Invalid record length"

search for references to that string.

It may lead directly to the new validation path.

docs.title: 49. Cross-References
docs.text:
Once a relevant function is found, inspect:

Callers

Callees

Data references

String references

Global variables

This helps reconstruct:

External Input
      |
      v
Parser
      |
      v
Changed Function
      |
      v
Sensitive Operation

docs.title: 50. Compare Call Graphs
docs.text:
A new function call can be significant.

Before:

handler()
   |
   v
process()

After:

handler()
   |
   v
validate()
   |
   v
process()

Investigate the new call first.

docs.title: 51. Build a Patch Hypothesis
docs.text:
After identifying a suspicious change, write a hypothesis.

Example:

The vulnerable version appears to trust the record length from the input when copying data into a fixed-size destination. The fixed version adds a comparison between the declared length and destination capacity before the copy.

This is a hypothesis until validated.

docs.title: 52. Hypothesis Template
docs.text:
Input:

Changed Function:

Old Behavior:

New Behavior:

Security-Relevant Difference:

Suspected Root Cause:

Expected Vulnerable Result:

Expected Fixed Result:

This keeps the research focused.

docs.title: 53. Validate the Hypothesis
docs.text:
Create a controlled experiment.

Same Input
   |
   +----------------+
   |                |
   v                v
Old Version      New Version
   |                |
   v                v
Behavior A       Behavior B

The input should isolate the changed condition where possible.

docs.title: 54. Use the Same Input
docs.text:
For strong comparison, keep the test input identical.

Example:

Input SHA-256:
abc...

Test against:

Version 2.4.1

Version 2.4.2

This reduces ambiguity.

docs.title: 55. Representative Validation Matrix
docs.text:
Test Vulnerable Fixed Valid input Accepted Accepted Boundary input Accepted Accepted Invalid length Crash Rejected Oversized value Crash Rejected

This demonstrates the behavioral effect of the patch.

The exact tests depend on the vulnerability.

docs.title: 56. Use Negative Controls
docs.text:
Suppose:

Length 255 -> no crash
Length 256 -> no crash
Length 257 -> crash

and the fixed version rejects:

Length > 256

This strongly connects the patch to the observed boundary.

docs.title: 57. Runtime Tracing
docs.text:
Static analysis may show:

if (length > 256)

Runtime analysis can confirm:

Input:
257

Parsed:
257

Comparison:
257 > 256

Fixed:
Reject

Old:
Continue

Combining static and dynamic evidence strengthens the conclusion.

docs.title: 58. Debugger Comparison
docs.text:
Set equivalent breakpoints in both versions.

Compare:

Input values

Branch decisions

Allocation sizes

Copy lengths

Return values

Error paths

This can reveal the exact point where behavior diverges.

docs.title: 59. Vulnerable Execution
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Input Length
     |
     v
Parse
     |
     v
No Capacity Check
     |
     v
Copy
     |
     v
Memory Violation

docs.title: 60. Fixed Execution
docs.text:
Input Length
     |
     v
Parse
     |
     v
Capacity Check
     |
     +---- Too Large -> Reject
     |
     v
Copy

The security fix becomes a testable behavioral difference.

docs.title: 61. Determine the Root Cause
docs.text:
The patch itself is not the root cause.

For example:

Patch:
Add bounds check

Root cause:

Attacker-controlled record length was used as a copy size
without verifying that the destination buffer could hold
the declared amount of data.

Always express the root cause in terms of the unsafe assumption or missing security condition.

docs.title: 62. Root Cause Model
docs.text:
Attacker Input
      |
      v
Trusted Without Sufficient Validation
      |
      v
Sensitive Operation
      |
      v
Security Failure

The patch normally inserts or corrects a control somewhere in this chain.

docs.title: 63. Patch Completeness
docs.text:
Once the fix is understood, ask:

Was every equivalent path fixed?

Example:

parse_record_v1()
parse_record_v2()
parse_metadata()
parse_extension()

If only one receives the new validation, investigate the others.

This is the beginning of variant analysis.

docs.title: 64. Search for the Old Pattern
docs.text:
If source is available, search for equivalent code.

Example:

rg -n "memcpy\(" src/

This alone may produce too many results.

Combine it with contextual searches:

rg -n "record_length|payload_length|buffer_size" src/

The goal is semantic similarity, not merely textual similarity.

docs.title: 65. Search for the New Validation
docs.text:
Suppose the patch adds:

validate_record_length()

Search:

rg -n "validate_record_length" .

Determine:

Where is it used?

Where is it not used?

Are there alternate parsers?

Do older protocol versions bypass it?

docs.title: 66. Search Callers
docs.text:
If the fixed function is:

parse_record()

find all callers.

Questions:

Do all callers provide equivalent validation?

Can some call paths bypass the new check?

Are there alternate entry points?

docs.title: 67. Search Callees
docs.text:
Sometimes the vulnerability exists in a shared helper.

Example:

Parser A ----\
Parser B -----+--> unsafe_helper()
Parser C ----/

A patch in only Parser A may leave Parser B and Parser C exposed.

docs.title: 68. Search Related Data Structures
docs.text:
If the patch changes:

RecordHeader.length

search for all uses of:

RecordHeader

length

related record structures

Similar structures often contain similar mistakes.

docs.title: 69. Search Similar Formats
docs.text:
A product may support:

Format v1

Format v2

Legacy format

Import format

Export format

A vulnerability in one parser may have equivalents in another.

docs.title: 70. Search Platform Implementations
docs.text:
A project may contain separate:

Windows implementation

Linux implementation

macOS implementation

Check whether the security fix was applied consistently.

docs.title: 71. Search Language Bindings
docs.text:
The same native library may be exposed through:

Python binding

Java binding

Node.js binding

CLI

Server API

The underlying vulnerability may be reachable through several interfaces.

docs.title: 72. Search Forks and Embedded Copies
docs.text:
Applications sometimes embed copies of libraries.

A fixed upstream project does not automatically mean all downstream products are fixed.

Investigate:

Vendored source

Static linking

Forks

Backports

Embedded components

docs.title: 73. Determine Affected Versions
docs.text:
Combine:

Advisory

Tags

Commit history

Patch introduction

Runtime testing

Package history

A version matrix may look like:

Version Code Pattern Runtime Result 2.3.8 Safe No failure 2.3.9 Vulnerable pattern Failure 2.4.0 Vulnerable pattern Failure 2.4.1 Vulnerable pattern Failure 2.4.2 Fixed pattern Rejected

This supports a more defensible affected-version range.

docs.title: 74. Find the Introducing Commit
docs.text:
Once the vulnerable code is identified:

git blame path/to/file

or inspect history:

git log -p -- path/to/file

This may reveal the commit that introduced the unsafe behavior.

docs.title: 75. Git Bisect
docs.text:
When a reliable reproducer exists, git bisect can help locate the transition between good and bad commits.

Start with:

git bisect start

Mark a known bad revision:

git bisect bad <bad-commit>

Mark a known good revision:

git bisect good <good-commit>

Git selects intermediate commits for testing.

After completing the investigation:

git bisect reset

Use this only when the project can be built and the test result can be classified reliably.

docs.title: 76. Automated Bisect
docs.text:
When a deterministic test exists, git bisect run can automate classification.

The test script should return appropriate success/failure exit codes for the condition being measured.

Before automation, manually verify:

Known-good commit -> good result

Known-bad commit -> bad result

A broken test script can produce incorrect history conclusions.

docs.title: 77. Patch Introduction Versus Vulnerability Introduction
docs.text:
These are different questions.

Vulnerability Introduction:
When unsafe code first appeared.

Patch Introduction:
When corrective code appeared.

Both can be useful for affected-version analysis.

docs.title: 78. Backported Fixes
docs.text:
Vendors may patch multiple supported branches.

Example:

Main:
5.2.1 -> 5.2.2

LTS:
4.8.7 -> 4.8.8

The exact patch may differ between branches.

Analyse each relevant branch rather than assuming identical code.

docs.title: 79. Partial Backports
docs.text:
A backport may implement the same security objective differently.

Example:

Main Branch:
New validation helper

LTS:
Inline bounds check

Compare behavior and security invariant rather than only matching source text.

docs.title: 80. Dependency Updates
docs.text:
Sometimes the security fix is simply:

Dependency 1.4.2
       |
       v
Dependency 1.4.3

Then the research moves to the dependency.

Determine:

Which dependency changed?

What changed upstream?

Does the application expose the affected functionality?

Is the vulnerable code actually included?

docs.title: 81. Patch Diffing Dependency Updates
docs.text:
A useful flow is:

Application Update
       |
       v
Dependency Version Changed
       |
       v
Identify Upstream Commits
       |
       v
Diff Dependency
       |
       v
Identify Security Change
       |
       v
Validate Application Reachability

Do not report a dependency CVE against an application merely because the package is present.

Reachability and configuration matter.

docs.title: 82. Configuration Changes
docs.text:
Some fixes occur in configuration rather than code.

Examples:

Disable vulnerable feature

Restrict allowed algorithms

Change file permissions

Disable unsafe parser

Require authentication

Enable sandboxing

Compare:

Default configuration

Upgrade behavior

Fresh installation behavior

docs.title: 83. Schema Changes
docs.text:
Database or configuration schema changes may reveal security fixes.

Example:

Before:
owner_id optional

After:
owner_id required

or:

Before:
permission defaults to allow

After:
permission defaults to deny

Investigate how the schema affects runtime authorization.

docs.title: 84. API Changes
docs.text:
A patch may replace an unsafe API.

Before:

unsafe_copy(dst, src);

After:

bounded_copy(dst, dst_size, src);

Determine whether:

All call sites changed

Return values are checked

Truncation is handled safely

Destination size is correct

Changing API names does not guarantee a complete fix.

docs.title: 85. Added Logging
docs.text:
A patch may add logs such as:

Invalid signature

Unauthorized request

Path outside allowed root

Invalid length

These messages can reveal the new security invariant.

Trace the code that produces them.

docs.title: 86. New Tests
docs.text:
Security patches often add regression tests.

Inspect:

Unit tests

Integration tests

Fuzzing tests

Security tests

A new test may contain the smallest public description of the vulnerability trigger.

Do not assume test coverage proves complete remediation.

docs.title: 87. Test Diffing
docs.text:
Compare test directories:

git diff <old> <new> -- tests/

Look for:

New malformed inputs

Boundary values

Permission tests

Authentication tests

Parser regression tests

Tests can provide valuable clues about expected behavior.

docs.title: 88. New Fuzz Targets
docs.text:
A security fix may introduce:

New fuzz harness

New seed corpus

New sanitizer configuration

This can indicate which component maintainers considered security-sensitive.

docs.title: 89. Commit Messages
docs.text:
A commit message may say:

Fix crash when parsing malformed records

while the advisory says:

Memory corruption vulnerability

Combine both sources.

Do not assume the less severe wording means the security issue is unimportant.

docs.title: 90. Silent Security Fixes
docs.text:
Not every security patch mentions:

Security

CVE

Vulnerability

Potentially interesting messages include:

Improve validation

Fix malformed input handling

Prevent crash

Harden parser

Correct permission check

Normalize path before use

These should be investigated when relevant.

docs.title: 91. Patch Diffing and Crash Analysis
docs.text:
If a crash reproducer already exists:

Crash Input
     |
     +------------------+
     |                  |
     v                  v
Vulnerable Version   Fixed Version
     |                  |
     v                  v
Crash              Safe Handling

Then compare execution around the changed function.

See Crash Analysis.

docs.title: 92. Patch Diffing and Fuzzing
docs.text:
A patch can guide new fuzzing.

Suppose the fix adds:

Maximum record count = 1024

Useful fuzzing targets include values around the boundary:

1022

1023

1024

1025

1026

as well as structurally related fields.

This tests the corrected invariant without assuming the exact old bug is the only possible issue.

docs.title: 93. Patch-Guided Variant Fuzzing
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Understand Patch
      |
      v
Extract Security Invariant
      |
      v
Identify Similar Parsers
      |
      v
Build Targeted Corpus
      |
      v
Fuzz Similar Paths
      |
      v
Investigate Findings

This can discover variants that the original patch did not address.

docs.title: 94. Security Invariant
docs.text:
Try to express the patch as an invariant.

Examples:

Record length must not exceed destination capacity.

Object access requires ownership or explicit permission.

Resolved path must remain inside the configured root.

Unsigned data must not be accepted as trusted.

A freed object must not remain reachable.

The invariant is often more useful for variant analysis than the exact patch syntax.

docs.title: 95. Invariant-Based Search
docs.text:
Once the invariant is known, ask:

Where else does the software rely on this same assumption?

For example:

Security Invariant:
Destination capacity >= copy length

Search:
All parsers that copy attacker-controlled records.

This moves the research from one patch to an entire bug class.

docs.title: 96. Avoid Patch Overfitting
docs.text:
Do not test only the exact value fixed by the patch.

Example:

Patch rejects length > 256

Do not test only:

257

Also consider:

Zero

Boundary values

Integer maximums

Alternative record types

Nested structures

Related length fields

The objective is to understand the invariant, not merely replay the known trigger.

docs.title: 97. Patch Bypass Versus Variant
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Patch Bypass

from:

Variant

A patch bypass means the same protected condition can still be reached despite the intended fix.

A variant means another code path contains a similar root cause.

Both are valuable findings, but they should be described accurately.

docs.title: 98. Patch Bypass Model
docs.text:
Original Vulnerability
        |
        v
Patch
        |
        v
Expected Block
        |
        v
Alternative Representation / Path
        |
        v
Same Vulnerable Operation

The alternative may involve:

Encoding

Normalization

Protocol variant

Alternate endpoint

Alternate parser

State transition

docs.title: 99. Variant Model
docs.text:
Root Cause
   |
   +---- Function A -> Fixed
   |
   +---- Function B -> Vulnerable?
   |
   +---- Function C -> Vulnerable?

This is why understanding root cause is more powerful than memorising a proof of concept.

docs.title: 100. False Leads
docs.text:
Not every interesting diff is security-relevant.

Examples:

Version bump

Error message change

Refactoring

Compiler-generated difference

Dead code removal

Performance optimisation

Validate whether the change affects:

Input handling

Security decision

Memory safety

Trust boundary

Privilege boundary

docs.title: 101. Avoid Confirmation Bias
docs.text:
If an advisory says:

Buffer overflow

it is easy to interpret every new length check as the fix.

Instead test competing explanations.

For example:

Hypothesis A:
Destination bounds issue.

Hypothesis B:
Source bounds issue.

Hypothesis C:
Integer overflow.

Hypothesis D:
Parser-state issue.

Use evidence to eliminate alternatives.

docs.title: 102. Practical Patch Diffing Scenario
docs.text:
Assume a fictional parser has:

Version 3.2.0 - affected

Version 3.2.1 - fixed

A vendor advisory describes:

Improper validation of malformed document records.

The research objective is to understand the technical root cause.

docs.title: Step 1 - Record Versions
docs.text:
Vulnerable:
3.2.0

Fixed:
3.2.1

Record package hashes and source tags.

docs.title: Step 2 - Compare Changed Files
docs.text:
git diff --name-only v3.2.0 v3.2.1

Representative result:

src/parser/record.c
tests/parser/test_record.c
CHANGELOG.md

This significantly reduces the search area.

docs.title: Step 3 - Inspect the Parser Diff
docs.text:
git diff v3.2.0 v3.2.1 -- src/parser/record.c

Illustrative conceptual change:

 record_length = read_u32(input);

+if (record_length > destination_capacity) {
+    return PARSE_INVALID_LENGTH;
+}

 copy_record(destination, input, record_length);

The patch adds a destination-capacity check.

docs.title: Step 4 - Inspect Tests
docs.text:
git diff v3.2.0 v3.2.1 -- tests/parser/test_record.c

Suppose a new regression test contains:

Record length:
513

Destination capacity:
512

Expected:
PARSE_INVALID_LENGTH

This suggests a boundary condition.

docs.title: Step 5 - Form the Hypothesis
docs.text:
Input:
Record length field.

Old Behavior:
Length is used by copy_record() without checking destination capacity.

New Behavior:
Length greater than destination capacity is rejected.

Suspected Root Cause:
Missing destination bounds validation.

Expected Vulnerable Result:
Memory boundary violation.

Expected Fixed Result:
Input rejected.

docs.title: Step 6 - Create Controlled Inputs
docs.text:
Prepare:

record-511.dat
record-512.dat
record-513.dat

Keep other fields identical.

docs.title: Step 7 - Test Vulnerable Version
docs.text:
Representative observations:

511 -> accepted

512 -> accepted

513 -> AddressSanitizer heap-buffer-overflow

docs.title: Step 8 - Test Fixed Version
docs.text:
Representative observations:

511 -> accepted

512 -> accepted

513 -> rejected with PARSE_INVALID_LENGTH

The behavioral difference corresponds to the new check.

docs.title: Step 9 - Trace Runtime Values
docs.text:
Debugger analysis confirms:

Input Field:
513

Parsed record_length:
513

Destination capacity:
512

Vulnerable version:

copy_record(..., 513)

Fixed version:

513 > 512
      |
      v
Reject

docs.title: Step 10 - Root Cause
docs.text:
A defensible root cause is:

The affected parser trusts a record length derived from attacker-controlled document content when determining the number of bytes copied into a fixed-capacity destination. The affected code path does not verify that the declared record length is less than or equal to the destination capacity before performing the copy.

This explains the vulnerability rather than merely describing the patch.

docs.title: Step 11 - Search for Variants
docs.text:
Search related parser code:

rg -n "copy_record|record_length|destination_capacity" src/

Suppose this identifies:

parse_record_v1()

parse_record_v2()

parse_extension_record()

Check whether each path enforces the same invariant.

docs.title: Step 12 - Version History
docs.text:
Use:

git blame src/parser/record.c

and:

git log -p -- src/parser/record.c

Suppose the vulnerable copy logic first appeared in:

Version 3.0.0

That becomes evidence for affected-version investigation.

It is not enough by itself to declare every later release affected; confirm relevant code and configuration.

docs.title: Step 13 - Defensible Conclusion
docs.text:
A suitable conclusion could be:

Comparison of versions 3.2.0 and 3.2.1 identified a new destination-capacity validation in the document record parser. Controlled testing showed that a record length one byte above the destination capacity triggers an AddressSanitizer-detected heap-buffer-overflow in the tested 3.2.0 build, while 3.2.1 rejects the same input before the copy operation. Runtime analysis confirms that the record length originates from attacker-controlled document content. Related parser functions should be reviewed for equivalent missing validation.

This connects:

Patch

Runtime Behavior

Attacker Input

Root Cause

Follow-Up

docs.title: 103. Binary-Only Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose only:

product-5.1.0.exe

product-5.1.1.exe

are available.

A practical workflow is:

Hash Both Files
      |
      v
Inspect Metadata
      |
      v
Import Into Disassembler
      |
      v
Match Functions
      |
      v
Prioritise Changed Functions
      |
      v
Find New Branches / Calls
      |
      v
Identify Input Path
      |
      v
Form Hypothesis
      |
      v
Runtime Validation

Do not rely solely on decompiler output.

Validate important conclusions dynamically where possible.

docs.title: 104. Binary Diff Evidence Record
docs.text:
For a changed function, record:

Old Binary:

Old Function Address:

Old Module Offset:

New Binary:

New Function Address:

New Module Offset:

Matched Function Confidence:

Changed Basic Blocks:

New Calls:

Removed Calls:

New Constants:

Relevant Strings:

Security Hypothesis:

Runtime Validation:

This makes binary analysis reproducible.

docs.title: 105. Source Diff Evidence Record
docs.text:
For source-based analysis:

Repository:

Vulnerable Tag:

Fixed Tag:

Vulnerable Commit:

Fixed Commit:

Changed File:

Changed Function:

Old Logic:

New Logic:

Security Invariant:

Attacker-Controlled Input:

Sensitive Operation:

Runtime Validation:

Affected Versions:

Variant Candidates:

docs.title: 106. Evidence Quality
docs.text:
Strong patch-diff evidence combines:

Vendor Advisory
       +
Source / Binary Diff
       +
Runtime Validation
       +
Debugger / Sanitizer Evidence
       +
Version Testing
       =
Defensible Technical Conclusion

A diff alone is weaker than several independent sources agreeing.

docs.title: 107. Reporting a Patch-Diff Finding
docs.text:
A technical report should clearly distinguish:

Vendor-stated facts

Observed code changes

Observed runtime behavior

Researcher inference

Confirmed root cause

Unconfirmed exploitability

Example:

The vendor describes the issue as improper input validation. Independent comparison of the tested affected and fixed releases identified a newly introduced bounds check in the record parser. Dynamic testing confirmed that the affected release performs the copy with an oversized attacker-controlled record length, while the fixed release rejects the same input before the copy.

This makes the evidence chain explicit.

docs.title: 108. Do Not Overstate Version Ranges
docs.text:
Avoid:

All versions before 3.2.1 are vulnerable.

unless the evidence supports that statement.

Prefer:

The issue was reproduced in version 3.2.0 and was not reproduced in 3.2.1. Source history indicates that the relevant code was introduced earlier, but additional version testing is required to establish the complete affected range.

docs.title: 110. Quick Patch Diff Workflow
docs.text:
ADVISORY
   |
   v
VERSION PAIR
   |
   v
VERIFY + HASH
   |
   v
SOURCE OR BINARY?
   |
   +---- Source
   |       |
   |       v
   |    Git Diff
   |
   +---- Binary
           |
           v
      Function Diff
           |
           v
     CHANGED LOGIC
           |
           v
    REDUCE NOISE
           |
           v
  SECURITY-RELEVANT CHANGE
           |
           v
   SECURITY INVARIANT
           |
           v
      HYPOTHESIS
           |
           v
   CONTROLLED INPUT
           |
      +----+----+
      |         |
      v         v
    OLD        NEW
      |         |
      v         v
   FAILURE   SAFE HANDLING

           |

docs.title: 111. Patch Diffing Mindset
docs.text:
Do not think:

Changed Code = Vulnerability

New Check = Confirmed Root Cause

Vendor Version Range = Automatically Verified

No Crash After Patch = Complete Fix

Same Function = Same Bug

Different Function = Different Bug

Instead think:

What Security Assumption Changed?
             |
             v
What Input Reaches This Code?
             |
             v
What Did the Old Version Trust?
             |
             v
What Does the New Version Validate?
             |
             v
Which Sensitive Operation Is Protected?
             |
             v
Can I Reproduce the Difference?
             |
             v
Does Runtime Evidence Support the Hypothesis?
             |
             v
What Is the Actual Root Cause?
             |
             v
Where Else Does the Same Assumption Exist?

Patch diffing is most valuable when the patch becomes the beginning of the investigation rather than the end.
