Start with the smallest useful version gap

Comparing the last affected release with the first fixed release usually produces much less noise than comparing releases separated by many development cycles.

Extract the security invariant

The most useful result of a patch diff is often not the changed line itself but the rule the new code enforces. That invariant can guide testing of related functions and variants.

Read the tests

New regression tests can reveal the boundary condition, input structure or expected safe behavior more clearly than the production-code diff.

Combine static and dynamic evidence

A source or binary diff explains what changed. Runtime testing demonstrates what that change means for the same input. Together they provide a stronger technical conclusion.

A patch is not automatically the root cause

A new validation check may mitigate the vulnerability without fully explaining why the original code was unsafe. Trace attacker-controlled data through the old implementation to the sensitive operation.

Do not assume the patch is complete

Once the security invariant is understood, inspect related functions, alternate parsers, legacy paths and shared helpers for equivalent missing checks.

docs.title: Proof of Concept Development
docs.text:
A proof of concept, or PoC, demonstrates that a suspected vulnerability can be reproduced under controlled conditions.

The purpose of a vulnerability research PoC is not to maximise impact.

Its purpose is to provide sufficient technical evidence to demonstrate:

Input
  |
  v
Reachable Vulnerable Code
  |
  v
Security Invariant Violated
  |
  v
Observable Security Failure

A strong PoC should be:

Minimal

Reproducible

Controlled

Documented

Version-specific

Evidence-driven

Safe by default

A practical workflow is:

Research Finding
       |
       v
Confirm Root Cause
       |
       v
Define Minimum Claim
       |
       v
Build Test Environment
       |
       v
Create Minimal Input
       |
       v
Establish Baseline
       |
       v
Trigger Condition
       |
       v
Capture Evidence
       |
       v
Repeat
       |
       v
Test Fixed Version
       |
       v
Reduce PoC
       |
       v
Document

Only develop and execute PoCs against software, systems and environments you are authorised to test.

docs.title: 1. What a PoC Should Prove
docs.text:
Before writing code, define the exact claim.

Examples:

A malformed file causes an out-of-bounds read.

An oversized record causes an out-of-bounds write.

A request reaches a protected operation without the expected authorization check.

A path is resolved outside the intended directory.

A malformed object causes a reproducible application crash.

A fixed version rejects the same input accepted by the affected version.

Avoid beginning with a broad claim such as:

This gives remote code execution.

unless that impact has actually been demonstrated.

A PoC should prove the smallest defensible technical statement first.

docs.title: 2. PoC Versus Exploit
docs.text:
A PoC and an exploit are not necessarily the same thing.

PoC
 |
 v
Demonstrates Security Failure

An exploit may go further:

Security Failure
      |
      v
Controlled Exploitation
      |
      v
Security Impact

For vulnerability research, a crash, sanitizer finding, incorrect authorization result or controlled boundary violation may already provide sufficient evidence.

Do not add unnecessary weaponization.

docs.title: 3. Define the Research Claim
docs.text:
Create a short statement before developing the PoC.

Example:

The PoC should demonstrate that an attacker-controlled record length greater than the destination capacity reaches the memory-copy operation in the affected parser and produces an AddressSanitizer-detected out-of-bounds write.

This defines what evidence is required.

It also defines what is not required.

For this example, proving arbitrary code execution would not be necessary to establish the memory-safety vulnerability.

docs.title: 4. PoC Evidence Chain
docs.text:
A strong PoC should establish:

Controlled Input
      |
      v
Expected Entry Point
      |
      v
Attacker-Controlled Value
      |
      v
Relevant Code Path
      |
      v
Missing / Incorrect Control
      |
      v
Sensitive Operation
      |
      v
Observable Failure

If possible, also demonstrate:

Affected Version -> Failure

Fixed Version    -> Safe Handling

docs.title: 5. Start From Root Cause
docs.text:
PoC development should follow root cause analysis.

Suppose the root cause is:

Attacker-controlled length is used as a copy size without
checking destination capacity.

Then the PoC should focus on controlling:

Length

and observing:

Copy size

Destination capacity

Failure

Do not add unrelated complexity.

docs.title: 6. Extract the Security Invariant
docs.text:
Express the condition that should always hold.

Example:

copy_length <= destination_capacity

A vulnerable input should violate that invariant:

copy_length = 513

destination_capacity = 512

The PoC then becomes a controlled test of that condition.

docs.title: 7. Define the Minimum Trigger
docs.text:
Determine the smallest condition necessary to reproduce the issue.

Example:

Valid File
   |
   v
One Modified Length Field
   |
   v
Trigger

This is preferable to a large malformed file containing many unrelated mutations.

docs.title: 8. Establish a Known-Good Baseline
docs.text:
Before testing the vulnerable condition, confirm that a normal input works.

Example:

Input:
record_length = 512

Destination:
512 bytes

Expected:
Processed normally

Then test:

Input:
record_length = 513

Destination:
512 bytes

Expected:
Rejected safely

If the affected version instead produces a memory violation, the difference is meaningful.

docs.title: 9. Change One Variable
docs.text:
A useful PoC changes as little as possible.

For example:

baseline.bin

record_length:
512

and:

poc.bin

record_length:
513

Everything else should remain identical where possible.

This makes the causal relationship easier to demonstrate.

docs.title: 10. Record the Environment
docs.text:
Every PoC should document the test environment.

Example:

Product:
ExampleParser

Affected Version:
3.2.0

Fixed Version:
3.2.1

Operating System:
Ubuntu Linux

Architecture:
x86_64

Build:
Debug + AddressSanitizer

Input:
poc-record.bin

Input SHA-256:
<hash>

Environment details matter because behavior can differ across:

Operating systems

Architectures

Compilers

Build flags

Dependencies

Configurations

docs.title: 11. Preserve the Original Artifact
docs.text:
Keep the original affected software package or build separate from the working copy.

Example:

research/
├── originals/
│   ├── affected/
│   └── fixed/
├── builds/
├── poc/
├── evidence/
└── notes/

Do not overwrite original evidence.

docs.title: 12. Hash Test Artifacts
docs.text:
Linux:

sha256sum poc.bin

PowerShell:

Get-FileHash .\poc.bin -Algorithm SHA256

Also hash relevant software artifacts where useful.

This helps prove exactly which input and version were tested.

docs.title: 13. Create a PoC Workspace
docs.text:
A useful structure is:

poc/
├── README.md
├── generate.py
├── samples/
│   ├── baseline.bin
│   └── trigger.bin
├── evidence/
│   ├── affected.txt
│   ├── fixed.txt
│   └── debugger.txt
└── hashes.txt

The exact structure is less important than reproducibility.

docs.title: 14. PoC Input Strategies
docs.text:
Depending on the vulnerability, a PoC may be:

File

HTTP request

Protocol message

API request

Configuration file

Serialized object

Database record

Command-line argument

Environment variable

IPC message

Choose the smallest representation that reaches the vulnerable code.

docs.title: 15. File-Based PoCs
docs.text:
For a file parser, start from a valid sample when possible.

Known-Good File
      |
      v
Identify Relevant Field
      |
      v
Modify Field
      |
      v
Preserve Remaining Structure

This reduces parser rejection before the vulnerable code is reached.

docs.title: 16. Binary Input Modification
docs.text:
For simple binary formats, Python can modify specific bytes.

Example:

from pathlib import Path
import struct

source = Path("baseline.bin")
output = Path("trigger.bin")

data = bytearray(source.read_bytes())

record_length_offset = 0x20
record_length = 513

struct.pack_into("<I", data, record_length_offset, record_length)

output.write_bytes(data)

print(f"Wrote {output}")

This is preferable to manually editing the same field repeatedly.

Document what the offset represents.

docs.title: 17. Verify the Generated Input
docs.text:
Do not assume the generator produced the intended file.

Check:

sha256sum baseline.bin trigger.bin

Compare:

cmp -l baseline.bin trigger.bin

For a small controlled change, only the intended bytes should differ.

docs.title: 18. Hex Inspection
docs.text:
Useful tools include:

xxd

hexdump

hex editors

format-specific parsers

Example:

xxd -g 1 trigger.bin | head

For a known offset:

xxd -g 1 -s 0x20 -l 16 trigger.bin

Confirm that the encoded value matches expectations.

docs.title: 19. HTTP PoCs
docs.text:
For web vulnerabilities, preserve the complete request needed to reproduce the condition.

Example structure:

POST /api/example HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <redacted>

{
  "example": "value"
}

Remove:

Live credentials

Session tokens

Personal data

Unrelated headers

before sharing the PoC.

docs.title: 20. Minimise HTTP Requests
docs.text:
A captured browser request may contain many unnecessary headers.

Reduce it to the minimum required:

Method

Path

Host

Authentication where necessary

Required content type

Required body

Then verify that the reduced request still reproduces the behavior.

docs.title: 21. Baseline and Trigger Requests
docs.text:
Keep both.

Example:

baseline-request.txt

trigger-request.txt

The difference should clearly demonstrate the security condition.

docs.title: 22. Protocol PoCs
docs.text:
For a network protocol, document:

Connection requirements

Protocol state

Message sequence

Relevant field

Expected response

Observed response

A vulnerability may require a valid state transition before the malformed message is accepted.

docs.title: 23. Protocol State Matters
docs.text:
A PoC may fail if it sends the trigger before the application reaches the expected state.

Example:

Connect
   |
   v
Handshake
   |
   v
Authenticate
   |
   v
Negotiate Feature
   |
   v
Trigger Message

Document required preconditions.

docs.title: 24. Prefer Deterministic Inputs
docs.text:
A PoC should produce the same result repeatedly.

Avoid unnecessary:

Random values

Race conditions

Timing assumptions

Environment dependencies

External services

unless these are part of the vulnerability.

docs.title: 25. Deterministic Generation
docs.text:
If randomness is required, record or fix the seed.

Example:

import random

random.seed(1337)

This makes generated inputs reproducible.

docs.title: 26. Boundary-Oriented PoCs
docs.text:
For numeric conditions, use meaningful boundary values.

Suppose:

Maximum Safe Value:
512

Test:

511

512

513

This produces much stronger evidence than testing only:

999999

docs.title: 27. Boundary Matrix
docs.text:
Value Purpose 511 Below boundary 512 Exact boundary 513 First invalid value

If the behavior changes precisely at the security boundary, the relationship becomes easier to defend.

docs.title: 28. Zero and Empty Values
docs.text:
Also consider:

0

Empty string

Empty object

Empty array

Null value

when relevant to the data type.

These often exercise different code paths.

docs.title: 29. Integer Extremes
docs.text:
Where appropriate, test values related to the actual integer type.

Examples:

Maximum signed value

Maximum unsigned value

Sign boundary

Conversion boundary

The purpose is to understand the arithmetic behavior, not to generate arbitrary extreme values.

docs.title: 30. Controlled Crash PoCs
docs.text:
For memory-safety research, a controlled crash may be sufficient.

Useful evidence includes:

Signal / exception

Faulting instruction

Stack trace

Sanitizer report

Attacker-controlled value

Allocation size

Access size

A crash alone does not establish exploitability.

docs.title: 31. AddressSanitizer
docs.text:
When source is available, AddressSanitizer can provide high-quality memory-corruption evidence.

Typical findings include:

heap-buffer-overflow

stack-buffer-overflow

use-after-free

double-free

Preserve the complete sanitizer report.

docs.title: 32. Representative Sanitizer Evidence
docs.text:
Illustrative output:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow

WRITE of size 513

#0 copy_record
#1 parse_record
#2 parse_document
#3 main

The important questions are:

What memory operation failed?

Which value controlled the operation?

Can the input control that value?

Is the vulnerable path reachable?

docs.title: 33. Debugger Evidence
docs.text:
A debugger can connect the PoC to the root cause.

Capture values such as:

Parsed length

Buffer address

Buffer capacity

Copy length

Object state

Faulting instruction

Example:

record_length:
513

destination_capacity:
512

copy_length:
513

This directly demonstrates the violated invariant.

docs.title: 34. GDB Workflow
docs.text:
Start the affected program:

gdb --args ./target trigger.bin

Inside GDB:

run

After a crash:

bt

Inspect relevant variables where symbols are available:

frame 1

info locals

The exact debugging workflow depends on the target and build.

docs.title: 35. Core Dumps
docs.text:
When appropriate, preserve a core dump for later analysis.

Check the environment's core-dump policy before testing.

A core dump may contain sensitive memory, so store it securely.

docs.title: 36. Application Logs
docs.text:
Collect relevant logs:

Parser errors

Application exceptions

Security events

Service logs

System logs

Logs should support the PoC, not replace direct technical evidence where stronger evidence is available.

docs.title: 37. Web PoC Evidence
docs.text:
For a web vulnerability, useful evidence may include:

Baseline request

Baseline response

Trigger request

Trigger response

User identities

Object ownership

Relevant server-side logs

Authorization decision

Redact secrets before publication.

docs.title: 38. Authorization PoCs
docs.text:
For an authorization issue, use clearly separated test identities.

Example:

User A
Owns Object A

User B
Owns Object B

Test:

User A -> Object A
Expected: Allowed

User A -> Object B
Expected: Denied

If the second operation succeeds, capture evidence showing:

Authenticated identity

Requested object

Actual ownership

Observed authorization result

docs.title: 39. Avoid Real User Data
docs.text:
Use:

Test accounts

Synthetic records

Lab tenants

Dedicated test objects

where possible.

A PoC should not require unnecessary access to real user information.

docs.title: 40. Path Handling PoCs
docs.text:
For path-related issues, define the expected security boundary.

Example:

Allowed Root:
/srv/application/uploads/

The PoC should demonstrate whether the resolved path remains inside that root.

Capture:

Input path

Normalized path

Resolved path

Result

docs.title: 41. Command-Handling PoCs
docs.text:
When researching unsafe command construction, demonstrate the boundary failure with a harmless marker where possible.

The research objective is to establish:

Untrusted Input
      |
      v
Command Interpretation
      |
      v
Unexpected Controlled Behavior

Avoid unnecessary destructive actions.

docs.title: 42. Harmless Markers
docs.text:
Where a controlled execution indicator is needed, prefer effects such as:

Creating a uniquely named temporary file

Writing a fixed marker to a dedicated test location

Returning a deterministic value

The marker should be:

Non-destructive

Easy to verify

Easy to clean up

Unique to the test

docs.title: 43. Unique Test Identifiers
docs.text:
Use a unique identifier:

VR-PoC-2026-001

This can appear in:

Temporary filenames

Requests

Logs

Test records

It helps correlate evidence.

docs.title: 44. Avoid Persistent Changes
docs.text:
A PoC should generally avoid:

Persistence

Account creation

Privilege modification

Security-control disabling

Long-lived configuration changes

unless the vulnerability specifically requires such behavior and the activity is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: 45. Cleanup
docs.text:
Document cleanup requirements.

Example:

Temporary file:
Delete after validation.

Test account:
Remove after engagement.

Test object:
Delete after evidence collection.

Application state:
Restore snapshot.

A reproducible PoC should include a reproducible cleanup procedure.

docs.title: 46. Use Snapshots
docs.text:
Virtual machine or container snapshots are valuable for PoC development.

Clean Snapshot
      |
      v
Run PoC
      |
      v
Collect Evidence
      |
      v
Restore Snapshot

This reduces environmental drift.

docs.title: 47. Isolate the Environment
docs.text:
For risky parser or memory-corruption testing, prefer:

Dedicated VM

Container

Disposable test environment

Lab network

Avoid unnecessary exposure to production systems.

docs.title: 48. Network Isolation
docs.text:
If the PoC does not require Internet access, consider an isolated environment.

This reduces accidental:

Outbound communication

External dependency changes

Unexpected interaction

while improving reproducibility.

docs.title: 49. Record Preconditions
docs.text:
Every PoC should document preconditions.

Example:

Affected version installed

Feature X enabled

Test user authenticated

Sample project created

Parser accepts Format Y

Debug build available

Without preconditions, another researcher may incorrectly conclude the PoC does not work.

docs.title: 50. Record Exact Invocation
docs.text:
Example:

./example-parser ./samples/trigger.bin

Do not rely on prose such as:

Open the file with the application.

when a precise invocation is available.

docs.title: 51. Capture Exit Status
docs.text:
Linux:

./example-parser ./samples/trigger.bin
echo $?

This can help distinguish:

Normal exit

Handled rejection

Crash

Test harness failure

docs.title: 52. Capture Standard Output and Error
docs.text:
Example:

./example-parser ./samples/trigger.bin >stdout.txt 2>stderr.txt

This preserves evidence.

docs.title: 53. Use tee Where Useful
docs.text:
Example:

./example-parser ./samples/trigger.bin 2>&1 | tee run.txt

Be aware that pipeline behavior can affect exit-status handling.

If exit status matters, capture it carefully.

docs.title: 54. Timestamp Evidence
docs.text:
Record:

Date

Time

Timezone

when evidence is collected.

This is particularly useful when correlating:

Application logs

System logs

Network captures

SIEM events

docs.title: 55. Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
If multiple systems are involved, ensure their clocks are sufficiently synchronized.

Otherwise:

Client request:
14:02:10

Server event:
14:06:43

may create unnecessary ambiguity.

docs.title: 56. PoC Reduction
docs.text:
Once a vulnerability reproduces, reduce the PoC.

Working PoC
    |
    v
Remove Unnecessary Data
    |
    v
Retest
    |
    v
Still Reproduces?
   /       \
 No         Yes
 |           |
 v           v
Restore     Continue

Repeat until the smallest useful trigger remains.

docs.title: 57. Why Reduce a PoC
docs.text:
Reduction improves:

Understanding

Reproducibility

Root cause analysis

Vendor triage

Regression testing

Documentation

A 20-byte reproducer is often easier to understand than a 20 MB crashing sample.

docs.title: 58. Delta Debugging Concept
docs.text:
Reduction can be systematic.

Original Input
     |
     v
Remove Portion
     |
     v
Retest
     |
     +---- Still Fails -> Keep Reduction
     |
     +---- No Failure  -> Restore Portion

Repeat until further reduction destroys the trigger.

docs.title: 59. Preserve Structural Validity
docs.text:
For structured formats, aggressive reduction may cause rejection before the vulnerable path.

Maintain required:

Headers

Checksums

Lengths

Object relationships

Protocol state

as needed.

docs.title: 60. Generator Versus Static Sample
docs.text:
A PoC can be distributed as:

Static trigger file

or:

Generator script

A generator is often preferable because it documents how the malformed input is constructed.

docs.title: 61. Generator Advantages
docs.text:
A generator can make explicit:

Relevant offset

Field encoding

Boundary value

Structure

Mutation

This improves technical understanding.

docs.title: 62. Keep Generators Simple
docs.text:
Prefer:

data[offset:offset + 4] = value

over a large framework when only one field must change.

The PoC should make the vulnerability easier to understand.

docs.title: 63. Comment Security-Relevant Fields
docs.text:
Example:

# Offset 0x20 contains the 32-bit record length.
# 512 bytes is the destination capacity.
# 513 is the first value above the expected boundary.
record_length = 513

This connects implementation to root cause.

docs.title: 64. Avoid Hidden Dependencies
docs.text:
A PoC should not silently require:

Custom libraries

Specific environment variables

Unpublished files

Private services

Hard-coded local paths

If dependencies are required, document them.

docs.title: 65. Dependency File
docs.text:
For Python PoCs, use a dependency file when external packages are genuinely required.

Prefer the standard library when it is sufficient.

Fewer dependencies generally improve reproducibility.

docs.title: 66. Validate on a Clean Environment
docs.text:
After the PoC works on the research machine, test it from a clean environment.

This identifies hidden dependencies.

Research Environment
       |
       v
PoC Works
       |
       v
Clean Environment
       |
       v
PoC Works?

If not, determine what was missing.

docs.title: 67. Reproduce Multiple Times
docs.text:
A deterministic vulnerability should reproduce consistently.

Record:

Run 1

Run 2

Run 3

If behavior differs, investigate why.

docs.title: 68. Flaky PoCs
docs.text:
Possible causes include:

Race condition

Uninitialized memory

ASLR

Timing

Network latency

Application state

Background threads

Resource exhaustion

Do not hide instability.

Document it.

docs.title: 69. Race Conditions
docs.text:
For race-condition PoCs, record:

Number of attempts

Success count

Timing method

Concurrency

Environment

Example:

Attempts:
100

Observed condition:
7

Rate:
7%

This is more useful than saying:

Sometimes it works.

docs.title: 70. Do Not Artificially Inflate Reliability
docs.text:
Avoid changing the environment purely to make a PoC appear more reliable unless the change is part of a documented research technique.

If a vulnerability requires unusual conditions, report those conditions.

docs.title: 71. Differential Validation
docs.text:
Testing affected and fixed versions is particularly strong evidence.

Same PoC
   |
   +-------------------+
   |                   |
   v                   v
Affected             Fixed
   |                   |
   v                   v
Failure             Rejected

Keep:

Input

Invocation

Environment

as consistent as possible.

docs.title: 72. Version Comparison Table
docs.text:
Version Input Result 3.2.0 baseline.bin Accepted 3.2.0 trigger.bin Memory violation 3.2.1 baseline.bin Accepted 3.2.1 trigger.bin Rejected safely

This provides a concise evidence summary.

docs.title: 73. Fixed Version Testing
docs.text:
Do not merely observe:

No crash.

Determine what happened.

Possible results:

Input rejected by new validation

Input accepted but vulnerable operation changed

Feature disabled

Parser no longer reached

Application silently ignores record

Test failed for unrelated reason

Only the first few may actually demonstrate remediation.

docs.title: 74. Verify the Patch Path
docs.text:
If source is available, confirm that the fixed input reaches the expected new validation.

Example:

record_length:
513

destination_capacity:
512

comparison:
513 > 512

result:
PARSE_INVALID_LENGTH

This directly connects the PoC to the patch.

docs.title: 75. Negative Results
docs.text:
A PoC that does not reproduce can still provide useful information.

Record:

Version

Configuration

Input hash

Observed behavior

Logs

Debugger state

Do not silently discard negative results.

docs.title: 76. Distinguish Test Failure From Security Result
docs.text:
A failed PoC may mean:

Vulnerability not present

or:

Wrong version

Wrong configuration

Wrong input

Feature disabled

Incorrect build

Harness failure

Earlier parser rejection

Investigate before concluding the software is not affected.

docs.title: 77. PoC Assertions
docs.text:
Where possible, make the PoC check expected behavior.

Conceptually:

if observed_condition:
    print("[+] Expected vulnerable behavior observed")
else:
    print("[-] Expected condition was not observed")

Avoid ambiguous output.

docs.title: 78. Do Not Infer Impact From a Crash Alone
docs.text:
A crash demonstrates:

Availability impact

and potentially:

Memory-safety violation

depending on evidence.

It does not automatically demonstrate:

Arbitrary code execution

Keep impact claims aligned with evidence.

docs.title: 79. Do Not Infer Authentication Bypass From Status Code Alone
docs.text:
For web research:

HTTP 200

does not necessarily mean:

Authentication bypass.

Inspect:

Response content

Application state

Identity

Data access

Action result

docs.title: 80. Do Not Infer Authorization Failure From Object ID Change Alone
docs.text:
Changing:

/object/100

to:

/object/101

and receiving a response is not sufficient.

Verify:

Object 101 belongs to another test identity

The response contains unauthorized data or performs an unauthorized action

No legitimate permission grants access

docs.title: 81. False Positives
docs.text:
A PoC may appear successful because of unrelated behavior.

Examples:

Generic application crash

Existing test file

Cached response

Administrator privileges

Shared object permissions

Previous application state

Incorrect user identity

Design controls that eliminate alternative explanations.

docs.title: 82. Control Groups
docs.text:
Where appropriate, test:

Known Safe Input

Known Vulnerable Input

Candidate Input

Fixed Version

This provides context for interpreting the result.

docs.title: 83. Independent Reproduction
docs.text:
If possible, reproduce the PoC:

On another machine

From a clean build

By another researcher

Using documented instructions

Independent reproduction significantly improves confidence.

docs.title: 84. PoC Documentation
docs.text:
A PoC README should answer:

What is being demonstrated?

Which version is affected?

Which version was tested?

What environment is required?

What are the prerequisites?

How is the PoC generated?

How is it executed?

What result is expected?

What evidence confirms the issue?

How is cleanup performed?

docs.title: 85. Example PoC README Structure
docs.text:
# ExampleParser Record Length PoC

## Summary

## Tested Versions

## Environment

## Root Cause

## Security Invariant

## Files

## Prerequisites

## Generate Input

## Run

## Expected Affected Result

## Expected Fixed Result

## Evidence

## Cleanup

## Limitations

docs.title: 86. PoC Metadata
docs.text:
Maintain metadata such as:

PoC ID:

Researcher:

Date:

Product:

Affected Version:

Fixed Version:

Platform:

Architecture:

CVE:

Root Cause:

Security Invariant:

Input SHA-256:

Status:

This is especially useful when researching multiple vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 87. Evidence to Capture
docs.text:
Depending on the vulnerability:

PoC source

Generated input

Input hash

Software hash

Version output

Invocation

Terminal output

Stack trace

Debugger output

Sanitizer report

HTTP request

HTTP response

Network capture

Application logs

Screenshots where useful

Capture only what materially supports the finding.

docs.title: 88. Evidence Naming
docs.text:
Use consistent names.

Example:

01-version.txt

02-baseline.txt

03-trigger.txt

04-asan.txt

05-gdb.txt

06-fixed-version.txt

07-hashes.txt

This simplifies reporting and disclosure.

docs.title: 89. Preserve Raw Evidence
docs.text:
Keep raw output separately from notes.

evidence/raw/

evidence/processed/

Do not modify the only copy of original evidence for presentation.

docs.title: 90. Secrets and Sensitive Data
docs.text:
Before sharing a PoC, remove:

Passwords

API keys

Session cookies

Access tokens

Private URLs

Customer data

Internal hostnames where sensitive

Use placeholders:

<TEST_TOKEN>

<TEST_USER>

<TARGET>

docs.title: 91. Credentials
docs.text:
If authentication is required, document the role rather than publishing credentials.

Example:

Required:
Authenticated low-privilege test user.

Do not hard-code secrets into PoC source.

docs.title: 92. Logging Sensitive Inputs
docs.text:
Be aware that PoC execution may cause test data to appear in:

Application logs

Proxy logs

SIEM

EDR

Crash dumps

Audit logs

Use synthetic data.

docs.title: 93. Safe Failure Conditions
docs.text:
Define when to stop testing.

Examples:

Unexpected production impact

Unexpected data access

Service instability

Test leaves intended scope

Unexpected privilege change

Uncontrolled resource consumption

A PoC should not continue blindly after an unexpected effect.

docs.title: 94. Resource Limits
docs.text:
For tests involving:

Memory

CPU

Files

Threads

Connections

use reasonable limits in the research environment.

A vulnerability can often be demonstrated without exhausting the host.

docs.title: 95. Denial-of-Service PoCs
docs.text:
When the issue causes service failure, prefer the smallest controlled demonstration.

Document:

Single trigger

Observed process failure

Recovery behavior

Required restart

Affected service

Avoid repeated disruption unless specifically required and authorised.

docs.title: 96. Network Capture
docs.text:
For protocol vulnerabilities, a packet capture may help demonstrate:

Exact trigger message

Server response

Connection state

Protocol sequence

Store captures securely because they may contain credentials or sensitive traffic.

docs.title: 97. Reproducible Requests
docs.text:
For HTTP or API issues, raw requests can often be more reproducible than screenshots.

Keep:

request.txt

response.txt

Screenshots may supplement the evidence but should not be the only technical artifact.

docs.title: 98. PoC Script Output
docs.text:
A useful PoC should clearly report what it is doing.

Example:

[*] Reading baseline.bin
[*] Setting record length to 513
[*] Writing trigger.bin
[+] Generated trigger.bin
[+] SHA-256: ...

Avoid output that claims vulnerability before the target has actually been tested.

docs.title: 99. Separate Generator and Validator
docs.text:
Where useful:

generate.py

validate.sh

The generator creates the controlled input.

The validator runs the target and captures the result.

This separation can make the research easier to reproduce.

docs.title: 100. Avoid Hard-Coded Target Paths
docs.text:
Instead of:

target = "/home/researcher/build/example"

prefer command-line arguments.

Example:

python3 generate.py baseline.bin trigger.bin

This makes the PoC portable.

docs.title: 101. Validate Arguments
docs.text:
A PoC should fail clearly when required files are missing.

Conceptually:

Input exists?

Output writable?

Correct number of arguments?

Expected format?

A broken harness should not be mistaken for a security result.

docs.title: 102. PoC Error Handling
docs.text:
Distinguish:

PoC generation error

Connection error

Target error

Expected vulnerable behavior

Unexpected behavior

Clear error handling improves research quality.

docs.title: 103. Exit Codes
docs.text:
For automated validation, define meaningful exit codes.

Example:

0 = expected condition observed

1 = expected condition not observed

2 = test harness error

Document the convention.

docs.title: 104. Regression Testing
docs.text:
Once the vulnerability is fixed, the PoC can often become a regression test.

PoC
 |
 v
Minimal Reproducer
 |
 v
Expected Safe Behavior
 |
 v
Regression Test

For example:

Input:
length = capacity + 1

Expected:
PARSE_INVALID_LENGTH

This helps prevent reintroduction.

docs.title: 105. Regression Test Quality
docs.text:
A regression test should verify the security invariant.

Avoid a test that merely checks:

Application did not crash.

Prefer:

Invalid length was rejected before the memory operation.

where the test framework can verify that behavior.

docs.title: 106. PoC and Patch Diffing
docs.text:
Patch diffing can identify the condition a PoC should exercise.

Patch
  |
  v
New Validation
  |
  v
Security Invariant
  |
  v
Boundary Input
  |
  v
PoC

See Patch Diffing.

docs.title: 107. PoC and Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Once a minimal PoC exists, modify only the component necessary to test variants.

Example:

Original:
record_type = STANDARD

Variant:
record_type = LEGACY

Keep the vulnerable condition equivalent.

See Variant Analysis.

docs.title: 108. PoC and Fuzzing
docs.text:
Fuzzing often produces a large crashing input.

A useful workflow is:

Fuzzer Crash
    |
    v
Reproduce
    |
    v
Minimize
    |
    v
Root Cause
    |
    v
Controlled PoC

The final PoC should normally be easier to understand than the original fuzzer artifact.

docs.title: 109. PoC and Crash Analysis
docs.text:
A crash PoC should connect:

Input

Fault

Instruction

Data

Root Cause

rather than simply demonstrating application termination.

See Crash Analysis.

docs.title: 110. PoC and Responsible Disclosure
docs.text:
A vendor should be able to use the PoC to:

Reproduce

Understand

Patch

Retest

A useful disclosure package may contain:

Technical description

Affected version

Test environment

Minimal PoC

Reproduction steps

Observed result

Expected result

Root cause

Security impact

Suggested remediation direction

Supporting evidence

See Responsible Disclosure.

docs.title: 111. Public PoC Considerations
docs.text:
A PoC suitable for private vendor disclosure is not automatically suitable for immediate public release.

Consider:

Patch availability

Affected user population

Exploitability

Ease of abuse

Vendor coordination

Disclosure timeline

Downstream dependencies

The technical ability to publish something does not necessarily mean it should be published immediately.

docs.title: 112. Minimise Abuse Potential
docs.text:
When a vulnerability can be demonstrated without operational exploitation, prefer the safer demonstration.

Examples:

Crash rather than control-flow hijacking

Synthetic object access rather than real data access

Temporary marker rather than persistent execution

Controlled local lab rather than Internet scanning

The PoC should provide enough evidence for verification without adding unnecessary operational capability.

docs.title: 113. Reporting the PoC Result
docs.text:
A strong technical conclusion might be:

The supplied PoC modifies only the 32-bit record length at offset 0x20 of an otherwise valid test document. With the length set to 513 bytes, the tested affected build attempts to copy 513 bytes into a 512-byte destination and AddressSanitizer reports a heap-buffer-overflow. The baseline value of 512 bytes is processed normally. The tested fixed version rejects the same 513-byte input before the copy operation.

This clearly connects:

Input

Boundary

Behavior

Evidence

Fixed Version

docs.title: 114. Avoid Overstated Conclusions
docs.text:
Avoid:

This PoC gives full system compromise.

when the evidence demonstrates only:

Heap-buffer-overflow.

Prefer:

The PoC demonstrates an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds write in the tested configuration. Exploitability beyond the demonstrated memory corruption was not assessed.

This is technically stronger because the statement matches the evidence.

docs.title: 115. Negative Conclusion Example
docs.text:
If the candidate does not reproduce:

The tested input reached the candidate parser, but the length was rejected by an existing bounds check before the memory-copy operation. The security invariant was therefore not violated in the tested version and configuration.

This is more useful than:

Not vulnerable.

docs.title: 116. Inconclusive Result
docs.text:
Sometimes evidence is incomplete.

Example:

The candidate input reaches the relevant parser and controls the length field, but the exact destination capacity could not be established from the available build. The result should therefore be treated as inconclusive pending additional runtime analysis.

Use:

Inconclusive

when appropriate.

docs.title: 117. PoC Status Model
docs.text:
Useful states include:

DRAFT

REPRODUCES

MINIMIZED

ROOT_CAUSE_CONFIRMED

FIXED_VERSION_VALIDATED

INCONCLUSIVE

NOT_REPRODUCIBLE

READY_FOR_DISCLOSURE

RETIRED

docs.title: 118. Practical PoC Development Scenario
docs.text:
Assume a fictional parser contains a suspected memory-safety issue.

Environment:

Product:
ExampleParser

Affected:
3.2.0

Fixed:
3.2.1

Destination Capacity:
512 bytes

Input Field:
32-bit little-endian record length

The suspected root cause is:

record_length is used as the copy length without validating
that it does not exceed destination capacity.

docs.title: Step 1 - Establish the Baseline
docs.text:
Create:

baseline.bin

with:

record_length = 512

Run:

./example-parser baseline.bin

Representative result:

Document parsed successfully.

docs.title: Step 2 - Create the Trigger
docs.text:
Use a minimal generator:

from pathlib import Path
import struct

source = Path("baseline.bin")
output = Path("trigger.bin")

data = bytearray(source.read_bytes())

record_length_offset = 0x20
record_length = 513

struct.pack_into("<I", data, record_length_offset, record_length)

output.write_bytes(data)

print(f"[+] Wrote {output}")

The only intended semantic change is:

512 -> 513

docs.title: Step 3 - Verify the Difference
docs.text:
cmp -l baseline.bin trigger.bin

Then:

sha256sum baseline.bin trigger.bin

Record both hashes.

docs.title: Step 4 - Run the Affected Version
docs.text:
./example-parser trigger.bin

Representative AddressSanitizer result:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 513

The stack includes:

copy_record
parse_record
parse_document

docs.title: Step 5 - Inspect the Runtime Values
docs.text:
Run under GDB:

gdb --args ./example-parser trigger.bin

Inspect the relevant frame after the failure.

Representative values:

record_length = 513

destination_capacity = 512

copy_length = 513

The invariant:

copy_length <= destination_capacity

is violated.

docs.title: Step 6 - Test the Fixed Version
docs.text:
Run the identical file:

./example-parser-fixed trigger.bin

Representative result:

Invalid record length.

No memory copy is performed.

docs.title: Step 7 - Confirm the Fixed Path
docs.text:
Runtime analysis shows:

record_length:
513

destination_capacity:
512

check:
513 > 512

result:
PARSE_INVALID_LENGTH

docs.title: Step 8 - Repeat
docs.text:
Run both baseline and trigger several times.

Example matrix:

Version Input Run 1 Run 2 Run 3 3.2.0 baseline Pass Pass Pass 3.2.0 trigger Overflow Overflow Overflow 3.2.1 baseline Pass Pass Pass 3.2.1 trigger Reject Reject Reject

This demonstrates deterministic behavior in the tested environment.

docs.title: Step 9 - Final Technical Claim
docs.text:
The evidence supports:

An attacker-controlled record length of 513 bytes reaches a memory-copy operation using a destination capacity of 512 bytes in the tested affected version. The condition results in an AddressSanitizer-detected heap-buffer-overflow. The fixed version rejects the same input before the copy operation.

The evidence does not automatically support:

Remote code execution

Privilege escalation

Sandbox escape

Those require separate analysis.

docs.text:
• [ ] Testing is authorised
  • [ ] Target version is known
  • [ ] Environment is controlled
  • [ ] Safety conditions are defined
  • [ ] Cleanup requirements are known

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
• [ ] Attacker-controlled input identified
  • [ ] Entry point identified
  • [ ] Relevant transformation identified
  • [ ] Missing or incorrect control identified
  • [ ] Sensitive operation identified
  • [ ] Security invariant documented

docs.title: Baseline
docs.text:
• [ ] Known-good input available
  • [ ] Known-good behavior confirmed
  • [ ] Boundary identified
  • [ ] Baseline evidence captured

docs.title: PoC
docs.text:
• [ ] Minimum trigger identified
  • [ ] One variable changed where possible
  • [ ] Input generation documented
  • [ ] Dependencies documented
  • [ ] Input hash recorded
  • [ ] Exact invocation recorded

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Vulnerable path reached
  • [ ] Attacker-controlled value confirmed
  • [ ] Security invariant violated
  • [ ] Observable failure captured
  • [ ] Debugger evidence captured where useful
  • [ ] Sanitizer evidence captured where useful
  • [ ] Alternative explanations considered

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
• [ ] PoC repeated
  • [ ] Results consistent
  • [ ] Clean environment tested where practical
  • [ ] Hidden dependencies removed
  • [ ] Environment documented

docs.title: Differential Testing
docs.text:
• [ ] Affected version tested
  • [ ] Fixed version tested
  • [ ] Same input used
  • [ ] Fixed behavior understood
  • [ ] Patch path confirmed where possible

docs.title: Reduction
docs.text:
• [ ] Unnecessary input removed
  • [ ] Reduced PoC retested
  • [ ] Required structure preserved
  • [ ] Final trigger is understandable

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] PoC source preserved
  • [ ] Trigger preserved
  • [ ] Hashes preserved
  • [ ] Terminal output preserved
  • [ ] Logs preserved where relevant
  • [ ] Debugger output preserved
  • [ ] Sensitive data removed before sharing

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• [ ] Claim matches evidence
  • [ ] Exploitability is not overstated
  • [ ] Preconditions documented
  • [ ] Limitations documented
  • [ ] Cleanup documented
  • [ ] Vendor reproduction steps prepared

docs.title: 121. Quick PoC Workflow
docs.text:
SUSPECTED VULNERABILITY
          |
          v
     ROOT CAUSE
          |
          v
  SECURITY INVARIANT
          |
          v
    MINIMUM CLAIM
          |
          v
      BASELINE
          |
          v
    MINIMAL INPUT
          |
          v
      EXECUTE
          |
          v
   PATH REACHED?
      /       \
    No         Yes
    |           |

Investigate   INVARIANT
Environment   VIOLATED?
              /       \
            No         Yes
            |           |
            v           v
         Refine       CAPTURE

docs.title: 122. PoC Development Mindset
docs.text:
Do not think:

Make the PoC as powerful as possible.

A crash automatically means RCE.

More code makes the PoC better.

One successful run is sufficient.

No crash means fixed.

A screenshot is enough evidence.

Instead think:

What Is the Smallest Claim?
          |
          v
What Input Controls It?
          |
          v
What Security Invariant Fails?
          |
          v
What Is the Smallest Trigger?
          |
          v
Can I Reproduce It Reliably?
          |
          v
Can I Explain the Result?
          |
          v
Does the Fixed Version Behave Differently?
          |
          v
Can Another Researcher Reproduce It?

The best vulnerability research PoCs are often simple.

Their strength comes from the quality of the evidence, not from unnecessary complexity.

docs.title: 123. Final Testing Model
docs.text:
A defensible PoC should connect:

AUTHORISED ENVIRONMENT
          |
          v
KNOWN VERSION
          |
          v
CONTROLLED INPUT
          |
          v
REACHABLE CODE PATH
          |
          v
ATTACKER-CONTROLLED VALUE
          |
          v
SECURITY INVARIANT
          |
          v
VIOLATION
          |
          v
OBSERVABLE FAILURE
          |
          v
ROOT CAUSE
          |
          v
REPEATABLE RESULT
          |
          v
FIXED VERSION COMPARISON
          |
          v
DEFENSIBLE CONCLUSION

If one of these links cannot be established, document the limitation rather than overstating the result.

Prove the smallest claim first

If a controlled crash, sanitizer finding or authorization failure proves the vulnerability, establish that result before investigating more complex impact.

Keep a baseline

A known-good input makes the trigger easier to interpret. Boundary comparisons such as 511, 512 and 513 can provide much stronger evidence than one extreme malformed value.

Use the same PoC against the fixed version

Differential testing helps connect the observed behavior to the security fix and reduces alternative explanations.

Turn the PoC into a regression test

Once remediation is available, preserve the minimal reproducer and expected safe behavior so the security invariant can be tested in future releases.

A crash is not automatically code execution

Report the impact demonstrated by the evidence. Exploitability beyond the confirmed security failure requires separate analysis.

Remove sensitive material before sharing

Review PoC source, requests, logs, crash dumps and captures for credentials, tokens, personal data and internal information before disclosure or publication.

docs.title: Responsible Disclosure
docs.text:
Responsible disclosure is the process of communicating a newly discovered security vulnerability to the affected vendor or maintainer in a way that supports remediation while reducing unnecessary risk to users.

The objective is not simply to publish a vulnerability.

The objective is to:

  • notify the right party;
  • provide reproducible evidence;
  • minimise exposure;
  • coordinate remediation;
  • verify the fix;
  • support safe publication where appropriate.

A useful model is:

Vulnerability Confirmed
      |
      v
Preserve Evidence
      |
      v
Identify Vendor / Maintainer
      |
      v
Secure Initial Contact
      |
      v
Provide Reproduction
      |
      v
Coordinate Remediation
      |
      v
Validate Fix
      |
      v
Coordinate CVE / Advisory
      |
      v
Responsible Publication

Authorised and ethical research

Responsible disclosure does not create permission to test systems without authorisation. Research activity should remain within applicable law, contractual scope, vulnerability disclosure policy, bug bounty rules, or other explicit permission.

docs.title: Where Responsible Disclosure Fits
docs.text:
Responsible disclosure normally begins after the researcher has:

  • confirmed the security issue;
  • reproduced it;
  • identified the affected product or component;
  • established the root cause;
  • collected sufficient evidence;
  • assessed the supported impact.

Related pages:

Vulnerability Research Methodology

CVE Research

Proof-of-Concept Development

docs.title: Disclosure Is Part of the Research Lifecycle
docs.text:
The research process should not end at:

Bug Found

A stronger lifecycle is:

Bug Found
   |
   v
Root Cause
   |
   v
Impact
   |
   v
Evidence
   |
   v
Vendor Notification
   |
   v
Patch
   |
   v
Retest
   |
   v
Disclosure

docs.title: Confirm the Finding Before Disclosure
docs.text:
Before contacting a vendor, confirm that the issue is real.

Check:

Can it be reproduced?

Is the affected version known?

Is the behavior security relevant?

Is there a meaningful security boundary?

Is it already documented?

Is the issue caused by intended behavior?

Do not submit speculative findings as confirmed vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Reproduce Independently
docs.text:
A finding should ideally reproduce:

more than once

and preferably:

in a clean environment

This reduces confusion caused by:

  • local state;
  • stale data;
  • temporary errors;
  • unrelated configuration.

docs.title: Minimise the PoC
docs.text:
The disclosure PoC should be the minimum needed to demonstrate the issue.

Prefer:

Deterministic
Small
Safe
Reproducible

Avoid unnecessary:

persistence
data extraction
destructive actions
lateral movement

docs.title: Preserve Original Evidence
docs.text:
Before changing the environment, retain:

Affected version
Target hash
PoC
Crash input
Request/response
Debugger output
Screenshots
Research notes
Timeline

This supports later retesting and coordination.

docs.title: Evidence Integrity
docs.text:
Where useful, hash important artefacts.

Linux:

sha256sum poc.py

Windows:

Get-FileHash .\poc.py -Algorithm SHA256

This helps demonstrate exactly which file was used during validation.

docs.text:

Affected component
Vulnerability type
Impact

Reproduction steps
Minimal PoC

Observed result

Researcher contact

docs.title: Vulnerability Title
docs.text:
Use a concise technical title.

Good:

Unauthenticated Path Traversal in ExampleServer File Download Handler

Less useful:

Critical Vulnerability

The title should communicate:

what
where

docs.title: Product Identification
docs.text:
Include:

Vendor:
Product:
Edition:
Version:
Build:
Platform:

Avoid ambiguity.

docs.title: Affected Component
docs.text:
Be specific.

For example:

/api/export endpoint

or:

DocumentParser.dll

or:

authentication middleware

This helps the vendor route the report internally.

docs.title: Vulnerability Type
docs.text:
Use a clear category where possible.

Examples include:

  • SQL injection;
  • command injection;
  • path traversal;
  • SSRF;
  • authentication bypass;
  • authorization bypass;
  • memory corruption;
  • information disclosure;
  • insecure deserialization.

Where appropriate, include a CWE reference.

Official reference:

MITRE CWE

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
A strong disclosure explains the underlying control failure.

Weak:

The server crashes.

Better:

The parser trusts an attacker-controlled 32-bit length value when
allocating a destination buffer, but copies data using the original
unvalidated record length.

Root cause helps developers fix the issue correctly.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Describe only the impact supported by evidence.

Possible impacts include:

Information disclosure
Denial of service
Authentication bypass
Authorization bypass
Arbitrary file read
Privilege escalation
Code execution

Do not inflate severity.

docs.title: Preconditions
docs.text:
Include relevant requirements such as:

Authentication required
Specific role required
User interaction required
Feature must be enabled
Local access required
Network access required

These materially affect risk.

docs.title: Reproduction Steps
docs.text:
Reproduction should be:

  • concise;
  • deterministic;
  • complete;
  • safe.

Example structure:

1. Install affected version.
2. Enable the affected feature.
3. Authenticate as a standard user.
4. Send the supplied request.
5. Observe the response.

Avoid unnecessary exploitation steps.

docs.title: Expected vs Observed Behavior
docs.text:
Clearly separate:

Expected:
Request should be rejected because the user does not own the object.

Observed:
Application returns the object to the unauthorized user.

This makes the security boundary obvious.

docs.title: Proof of Concept
docs.text:
The PoC should demonstrate the issue without unnecessary complexity.

Related page:

Proof-of-Concept Development

A PoC may be:

  • HTTP request;
  • test file;
  • Python script;
  • crash input;
  • short source snippet;
  • debugger reproduction.

docs.title: PoC Safety
docs.text:
Avoid PoCs that:

  • delete data;
  • disable security controls;
  • establish persistence;
  • collect large datasets;
  • affect unrelated systems.

A vendor needs reproducibility, not weaponisation.

docs.title: Test Accounts
docs.text:
If account credentials are required, use dedicated test accounts where possible.

Do not include:

real employee passwords

or:

production credentials

in the disclosure.

docs.title: Sensitive Data
docs.text:
If the vulnerability exposes sensitive data, demonstrate the issue with the minimum amount necessary.

Prefer:

one controlled test record

over:

bulk extraction

docs.title: Redact Secrets
docs.text:
In screenshots and evidence, redact:

Passwords
Tokens
Session cookies
Private keys
Personal data

unless they are essential to the security claim.

docs.title: Do Not Over-Collect
docs.text:
Once impact is demonstrated:

Stop unnecessary access.

This is especially important for:

  • personal data;
  • credentials;
  • customer records;
  • production systems.

docs.title: Identify the Correct Vendor
docs.text:
The affected party may be:

  • software vendor;
  • open-source maintainer;
  • SaaS provider;
  • hardware vendor;
  • cloud provider;
  • customer organisation.

Confirm who actually owns the vulnerable component.

docs.title: Third-Party Components
docs.text:
A vulnerability discovered inside a product may actually exist in a bundled dependency.

Determine whether the issue belongs to:

Product vendor

or:

Dependency maintainer

or both.

docs.title: Vendor Security Contact
docs.text:
Preferred contact mechanisms may include:

  • security email;
  • vulnerability disclosure portal;
  • bug bounty platform;
  • PSIRT portal;
  • security.txt;
  • vendor support process.

docs.title: security.txt
docs.text:
Many organisations publish:

/.well-known/security.txt

This may provide:

  • contact address;
  • policy;
  • encryption key;
  • acknowledgement expectations.

Official standard:

security.txt - RFC 9116

docs.title: Vulnerability Disclosure Policy
docs.text:
Before contacting a vendor, review its vulnerability disclosure policy where available.

Look for:

Scope
Prohibited testing
Safe harbour
Submission method
Encryption
Disclosure timeline

docs.title: Bug Bounty Program
docs.text:
If the vendor operates a bug bounty program, follow its rules.

A bug bounty program may define:

  • in-scope assets;
  • out-of-scope vulnerabilities;
  • reward conditions;
  • disclosure restrictions.

Do not bypass the program's process unnecessarily.

docs.title: Initial Contact
docs.text:
The initial report should be concise enough to triage quickly.

Include:

Product
Affected version
Issue type
Impact
Reproduction
Contact details

Avoid sending an unstructured wall of text.

docs.title: Initial Disclosure Template
docs.text:
A basic structure is:

Subject:
Security vulnerability in <product/component>

Hello,

I identified a security vulnerability affecting <product> <version>.

Issue:
<short description>

Impact:
<supported impact>

Affected component:
<component/endpoint>

Reproduction:
<concise steps>

I can provide additional technical details and supporting evidence as
required.

Regards,
<researcher>

docs.title: Secure Communication
docs.text:
For sensitive vulnerabilities, use a secure communication method if the vendor supports one.

Potential methods include:

  • vendor portal;
  • encrypted email;
  • PGP;
  • authenticated ticketing system.

Avoid posting zero-day details publicly during initial coordination.

docs.title: PGP
docs.text:
Some vendors publish a PGP key for security reports.

Verify the key fingerprint through an authoritative source before use.

docs.title: Researcher Identity
docs.text:
A researcher may disclose:

  • real name;
  • organisation;
  • preferred contact;
  • vulnerability disclosure profile.

Follow the engagement or organisational policy.

docs.title: Anonymous Disclosure
docs.text:
Anonymous disclosure may be possible, but it can make:

  • coordination;
  • clarification;
  • CVE assignment;
  • acknowledgement;

more difficult.

Choose based on the situation.

docs.title: Disclosure Timeline
docs.text:
A disclosure timeline helps track coordination.

Example:

Day 0:
Initial vendor notification

Day 3:
Vendor acknowledges

Day 12:
Vendor confirms

Day 30:
Patch available for testing

Day 37:
Researcher verifies fix

Day 45:
Coordinated publication

The actual timeline varies.

docs.title: No Universal Disclosure Deadline
docs.text:
There is no single disclosure period that fits every vulnerability.

Consider:

  • severity;
  • exploitation status;
  • patch complexity;
  • user risk;
  • vendor responsiveness;
  • industry norms.

docs.title: Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure
docs.text:
Coordinated vulnerability disclosure means the researcher and affected party work together toward remediation and publication.

Researcher
   |
   v
Vendor
   |
   v
Fix
   |
   v
Users

docs.title: Vendor Acknowledgement
docs.text:
Record:

Date
Ticket number
Contact
Vendor status

This creates an audit trail.

docs.title: Vendor Triage
docs.text:
The vendor may initially request:

  • logs;
  • crash dump;
  • exact version;
  • PoC;
  • environment;
  • timestamps.

Provide the minimum necessary evidence.

docs.title: Reproduction Problems
docs.text:
If the vendor cannot reproduce the issue, compare:

OS
Architecture
Version
Build
Configuration
Feature state
Input
PoC revision

Small environment differences matter.

docs.title: Clarify Expected Behavior
docs.text:
Sometimes the vendor may believe the behavior is intended.

Explain the violated security boundary.

For example:

A standard user can access another tenant's report despite ownership
checks elsewhere in the application.

This is clearer than:

IDOR exists.

docs.title: Vendor Disagreement
docs.text:
A vendor may disagree about:

  • severity;
  • exploitability;
  • affected versions;
  • whether the behavior is intended.

Return to reproducible evidence.

Avoid argumentative language.

docs.title: Severity Discussion
docs.text:
Severity should be based on:

  • reachability;
  • attacker prerequisites;
  • affected data;
  • privileges;
  • user interaction;
  • integrity impact;
  • availability impact.

Avoid using severity as leverage.

docs.title: CVSS
docs.text:
Where CVSS is appropriate, document the reasoning for each metric.

Use the current official specification.

Do not simply copy a scanner score.

docs.title: CWE
docs.text:
A CWE classification can help describe the weakness type.

Official resource:

MITRE CWE

docs.title: CVE Assignment
docs.text:
A confirmed vulnerability may qualify for a CVE identifier.

Related page:

CVE Research

CVE assignment depends on the affected product and CNA structure.

docs.title: CVE Numbering Authority
docs.text:
A CNA can assign CVE identifiers for products within its scope.

Official directory:

CVE Numbering Authorities

docs.title: Vendor as CNA
docs.text:
Some vendors are CNAs and may assign the CVE directly.

Ask whether the vendor intends to coordinate assignment.

docs.title: Researcher CNA Request
docs.text:
If the vendor is not a CNA, another relevant CNA or CVE program route may be available.

Follow current CVE guidance.

docs.title: CVE Before Publication
docs.text:
Where possible, coordinate CVE assignment before public disclosure so:

  • vendor advisory;
  • researcher publication;
  • vulnerability databases;

can reference the same identifier.

docs.title: CVE Description
docs.text:
A good CVE description usually communicates:

Product
Affected versions
Weakness
Attack prerequisites
Impact

Avoid promotional language.

docs.title: Embargo
docs.text:
An embargo is a period during which vulnerability details are shared only with the parties necessary to coordinate remediation.

Potential participants include:

  • vendor;
  • researcher;
  • CNA;
  • affected downstream vendors;
  • security response teams.

docs.title: Respect the Embargo
docs.text:
Do not publish:

  • PoC;
  • screenshots;
  • patch analysis;
  • exploit details;

before the agreed date unless circumstances require a change.

docs.title: Embargo Data Handling
docs.text:
Treat embargoed vulnerability details as highly sensitive.

Do not place them in:

  • public repositories;
  • public issue trackers;
  • public AI services;
  • public paste sites.

docs.title: Downstream Vendors
docs.text:
A vulnerability may affect multiple products using the same component.

Coordinated disclosure may require notifying downstream maintainers.

Avoid disclosing the issue publicly to one party while others remain unprepared.

docs.title: Open-Source Projects
docs.text:
Open-source maintainers may use:

  • private security advisories;
  • private mailing lists;
  • repository security features.

Do not open a public GitHub issue for an unpatched vulnerability unless the project explicitly requests it.

docs.title: GitHub Security Advisories
docs.text:
GitHub supports private vulnerability reporting and security advisories for participating repositories.

Use the project's preferred workflow.

Official reference:

GitHub - Privately reporting a security vulnerability

docs.title: Vendor Patch
docs.text:
When the vendor provides a patch, validate it against the original root cause.

Do not only check whether:

original PoC no longer works

Ask whether:

underlying control failure is fixed

docs.title: Patch Validation Workflow
docs.text:
Original Vulnerable Build
      |
      v
Original PoC
      |
      v
Confirmed Vulnerability
      |
      v
Patched Build
      |
      v
Original PoC
      |
      v
Safe Behaviour

Then review the patch where possible.

docs.title: Root-Cause Fix vs Input Block
docs.text:
Weak remediation:

Block one exact payload

Stronger remediation:

Fix the unsafe validation or processing logic

Test alternate valid variants where appropriate.

docs.title: Regression Testing
docs.text:
Convert the minimal PoC into a regression test where possible.

The regression test should verify:

previously vulnerable condition is safely rejected

docs.title: Variant Analysis After Patch
docs.text:
Related page:

Variant Analysis

Once the root cause is understood, consider whether related paths share the same issue.

Do not assume the first patch covers every variant.

docs.title: Retest Evidence
docs.text:
Record:

Patched version
Build
Patch identifier
Retest date
Original PoC result
Variant result
Remaining limitations

docs.title: Vendor Says Fixed
docs.text:
Do not mark a vulnerability resolved solely because the vendor says:

fixed

Where possible, independently retest.

docs.title: Unable to Retest
docs.text:
If retesting is not possible, report:

Vendor reports fixed
Retest not independently performed

This is more accurate than:

Verified fixed

docs.title: Patch Release
docs.text:
Once the patch is publicly available, confirm:

  • version number;
  • release notes;
  • advisory;
  • download/update path.

docs.title: Advisory Review
docs.text:
Check that the vendor advisory accurately reflects:

  • affected versions;
  • fixed versions;
  • impact;
  • CVE.

If material errors exist, raise them privately before publication where possible.

docs.title: Coordinated Publication
docs.text:
A publication may include:

Summary
Timeline
Affected versions
Root cause
Technical analysis
PoC
Patch
Credits
References

The level of technical detail should consider current user risk.

docs.title: Publication Timing
docs.text:
A useful publication point is usually after:

Patch Available
+
Users Can Remediate

Exceptions may exist for:

  • abandoned products;
  • active exploitation;
  • vendor non-response.

docs.title: Active Exploitation
docs.text:
If active exploitation is discovered, disclosure urgency may increase.

Coordinate with:

  • vendor;
  • CERT/CSIRT;
  • CNA;
  • relevant security response organisations.

User protection should take priority.

docs.title: CISA KEV
docs.text:
If a vulnerability becomes known to be actively exploited, CISA KEV may be relevant.

Official reference:

CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog

docs.title: Vendor Non-Response
docs.text:
If the vendor does not respond:

  1. verify contact method;
  2. retry through another official channel;
  3. document attempts;
  4. consider relevant CERT/CNA escalation;
  5. reassess disclosure timeline.

Do not immediately publish sensitive details after one unanswered email.

docs.title: CERT Coordination
docs.text:
National or sector CERT/CSIRT organisations may help with difficult coordination cases.

Their role and process vary by region.

docs.title: Multi-Vendor Coordination
docs.text:
Shared dependencies can require coordination across multiple vendors.

A simplified model is:

Researcher
   |
   v
Upstream Maintainer
   |
   +-- Vendor A
   +-- Vendor B
   +-- Vendor C

This may require a longer embargo.

docs.title: End-of-Life Products
docs.text:
A vendor may confirm that the affected product is no longer supported.

Possible outcomes include:

  • upgrade to supported version;
  • compensating controls;
  • retirement;
  • public advisory.

Clearly communicate that no vendor patch may be available.

docs.title: Abandoned Open-Source Projects
docs.text:
For abandoned software:

  • verify the project is actually inactive;
  • attempt maintainer contact;
  • consider ecosystem impact;
  • coordinate with relevant CNA/CERT if appropriate.

Avoid premature publication of high-risk exploitation details.

docs.title: Cloud Services
docs.text:
For SaaS or cloud vulnerabilities:

Version numbers may not be visible

The vendor may patch server-side without a customer update.

Retest behavior rather than relying only on version.

docs.title: Managed Services
docs.text:
A managed service vulnerability may affect:

  • one tenant;
  • all tenants;
  • specific regions;
  • optional features.

Provide accurate scope.

docs.title: Tenant Isolation
docs.text:
For cross-tenant issues, use controlled accounts.

Never access another real customer's data to prove impact if controlled test tenants can demonstrate the boundary failure.

docs.title: Personal Data
docs.text:
If personal information is accidentally encountered:

  • stop unnecessary collection;
  • preserve minimum evidence;
  • notify according to engagement policy;
  • protect the data.

Do not include unnecessary personal details in the report.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
If credentials are exposed:

Do not test unrelated systems with them

unless explicitly authorised.

Report the credential exposure.

docs.title: Secrets in Reports
docs.text:
Redact:

API keys
Passwords
Tokens
Private keys
Cookies

Use:

<REDACTED>

where the actual value is not necessary.

docs.title: Crash Dumps
docs.text:
Crash dumps may contain:

  • credentials;
  • documents;
  • keys;
  • private application data.

Treat them as sensitive evidence.

docs.title: Vulnerability Databases
docs.text:
Once published, a vulnerability may appear in:

  • CVE;
  • NVD;
  • vendor advisories;
  • distribution advisories;
  • security databases.

Verify records for accuracy where practical.

docs.title: Researcher Advisory
docs.text:
A researcher publication can provide technical depth beyond the CVE record.

Useful content includes:

Root cause
Affected component
Patch analysis
Safe reproduction
Timeline
References

docs.title: Avoid Oversharing
docs.text:
A publication does not need to include every offensive capability discovered during research.

Focus on what users need to:

  • understand;
  • detect;
  • patch;
  • validate.

docs.title: Exploit Publication
docs.text:
Publishing full exploit code deserves additional consideration.

Questions include:

Is a patch widely available?

Are users able to update?

Is exploitation already public?

Does the exploit significantly lower the barrier to abuse?

A minimal PoC may be sufficient.

docs.title: PoC vs Weaponised Exploit
docs.text:
A PoC demonstrates:

vulnerability exists

A weaponised exploit may add:

automation
persistence
stealth
payload delivery

Responsible disclosure usually needs the first, not the second.

docs.title: Publication Credits
docs.text:
Agree on credit where appropriate.

Examples:

Researcher name
Organisation
Security team
CVE credit
Advisory acknowledgement

docs.title: Hall of Fame
docs.text:
Some vendors maintain security acknowledgements or Hall of Fame pages.

This is separate from the technical disclosure process.

Do not let recognition requirements interfere with safe remediation.

docs.title: Bug Bounty Rewards
docs.text:
Reward discussions should remain separate from the technical validity of the vulnerability.

Follow program rules.

docs.title: Duplicate Reports
docs.text:
A vendor may respond that the issue was already known.

Ask, where possible:

Was the report a duplicate?

Is a fix planned?

Is a CVE already assigned?

Respect confidential prior reports.

docs.title: Previously Public Issue
docs.text:
If the vulnerability is already public, disclosure handling changes.

Determine:

  • patch status;
  • CVE status;
  • vendor advisory;
  • public exploit status.

Do not claim original discovery if it was previously documented.

docs.title: Research Timeline
docs.text:
Maintain a disclosure timeline.

Example:

2026-01-10 - Vulnerability discovered
2026-01-12 - Root cause confirmed
2026-01-13 - Vendor notified
2026-01-15 - Vendor acknowledgement
2026-01-23 - Vendor confirms vulnerability
2026-02-05 - Patch received
2026-02-06 - Patch verified
2026-02-10 - CVE assigned
2026-02-15 - Coordinated disclosure

docs.title: Why the Timeline Matters
docs.text:
A timeline shows:

  • responsible handling;
  • vendor responsiveness;
  • remediation duration;
  • coordination history.

It should remain factual.

docs.title: Communication Log
docs.text:
Record important interactions:

Date
Sender
Recipient
Topic
Action required
Status

This is particularly useful for long-running cases.

docs.title: Avoid Emotional Language
docs.text:
Vendor coordination can be frustrating.

Keep communication:

  • factual;
  • concise;
  • technical;
  • professional.

Focus on the vulnerability and remediation.

docs.title: Reporting a Confirmed Vulnerability
docs.text:
A strong disclosure statement might be:

The affected endpoint accepts a user-controlled filesystem path and
resolves it without enforcing that the canonical path remains within the
intended export directory. An authenticated standard user can therefore
retrieve files outside the permitted directory.

This describes the actual control failure.

docs.title: Reporting Memory Corruption
docs.text:
Prefer:

A crafted record containing an oversized length value causes an
out-of-bounds write in the parser. The condition is remotely reachable
through the document import interface and reliably reproduces on the
tested build.

If RCE was not demonstrated, do not claim it.

docs.title: Reporting Denial of Service
docs.text:
Example:

A malformed request causes the service process to terminate. The
process is automatically restarted after approximately five seconds.
Testing demonstrated a repeatable availability impact but did not
establish code execution.

docs.title: Reporting Authentication Bypass
docs.text:
Example:

A request sent directly to the administrative API endpoint was processed
without the authentication middleware applied to the corresponding UI
route, allowing unauthenticated access to the protected operation.

docs.title: Reporting Authorization Bypass
docs.text:
Example:

The API retrieves the requested object by identifier but does not verify
that the object belongs to the authenticated user before returning it.

docs.title: Reporting SSRF
docs.text:
Example:

The server-side URL fetcher accepts an arbitrary user-controlled host
and performs outbound HTTP requests without applying the intended
destination restrictions.

docs.title: Remediation Guidance
docs.text:
Recommendations should address the root cause.

Avoid vague advice such as:

Improve security.

Provide actionable guidance.

docs.title: Vendor Patch Review
docs.text:
Where appropriate and permitted, inspect the fix.

Questions include:

Was validation added?

Was authorization centralized?

Was bounds checking corrected?

Was unsafe API usage removed?

Was the vulnerable feature disabled?

docs.title: Partial Fixes
docs.text:
If a patch only handles one input form, report the remaining variant privately.

Do not publish bypass details before the vendor has an opportunity to respond.

docs.title: Regression Risk
docs.text:
Once a vulnerability is fixed, maintain a regression test where possible.

This is especially valuable for:

  • parser bugs;
  • auth bugs;
  • access-control bugs;
  • input-validation bugs.

docs.title: Disclosure Status Model
docs.text:
Useful states include:

Discovered
Confirmed
Vendor notified
Acknowledged
Triaged
Fix in progress
Patch received
Fix verified
CVE assigned
Published
Closed

docs.title: Research Record Example
docs.text:
Status:
Fix verified

Vendor:
Example Corp

Product:
Example Server

Affected:
4.1.0 - 4.1.6

Fixed:
4.1.7

Reported:
2026-01-13

Acknowledged:
2026-01-15

CVE:
CVE-YYYY-NNNN

Publication:
2026-02-15

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
• [ ] Vulnerability reproduced.
  • [ ] Root cause identified.
  • [ ] Affected product confirmed.
  • [ ] Affected version/build confirmed.
  • [ ] Security boundary identified.
  • [ ] Impact supported by evidence.
  • [ ] False-positive explanations considered.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Original evidence preserved.
  • [ ] Target hash recorded where relevant.
  • [ ] Minimal PoC created.
  • [ ] Request/response retained.
  • [ ] Crash input retained where relevant.
  • [ ] Debugger evidence retained where relevant.
  • [ ] Research timeline maintained.
  • [ ] Sensitive evidence protected.

docs.title: PoC Safety
docs.text:
• [ ] PoC is minimal.
  • [ ] PoC is reproducible.
  • [ ] Destructive behavior excluded.
  • [ ] Unnecessary data extraction excluded.
  • [ ] Persistence excluded.
  • [ ] Unrelated systems not contacted.

docs.title: Vendor Identification
docs.text:
• [ ] Correct vendor identified.
  • [ ] Affected component owner identified.
  • [ ] security.txt checked.
  • [ ] Disclosure policy checked.
  • [ ] Bug bounty program checked where relevant.
  • [ ] Official security contact identified.

docs.title: Initial Report
docs.text:
• [ ] Clear title.
  • [ ] Product/version included.
  • [ ] Vulnerability type included.
  • [ ] Component included.
  • [ ] Preconditions included.
  • [ ] Reproduction included.
  • [ ] Supported impact included.
  • [ ] Root cause included where known.
  • [ ] Researcher contact included.

docs.title: Data Handling
docs.text:
• [ ] Credentials redacted.
  • [ ] Tokens redacted.
  • [ ] Personal data minimised.
  • [ ] Customer data minimised.
  • [ ] Crash dumps protected.
  • [ ] Embargoed material stored securely.

docs.title: Coordination
docs.text:
• [ ] Initial report date recorded.
  • [ ] Vendor acknowledgement recorded.
  • [ ] Ticket/reference recorded.
  • [ ] Follow-up dates recorded.
  • [ ] Vendor questions answered.
  • [ ] Disclosure timeline agreed where possible.

docs.title: CVE
docs.text:
• [ ] Existing CVE checked.
  • [ ] Vendor CNA status checked.
  • [ ] CVE assignment coordinated where appropriate.
  • [ ] CVE description reviewed where possible.
  • [ ] Affected/fixed versions aligned.

docs.title: Patch Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Patch obtained.
  • [ ] Patched version recorded.
  • [ ] Original PoC retested.
  • [ ] Root-cause fix reviewed where possible.
  • [ ] Variant analysis considered.
  • [ ] Regression test retained.

docs.title: Publication
docs.text:
• [ ] Patch available where possible.
  • [ ] Publication date coordinated.
  • [ ] Sensitive details reviewed.
  • [ ] Weaponisation minimised.
  • [ ] Timeline factual.
  • [ ] Credits confirmed.
  • [ ] Vendor advisory linked.
  • [ ] CVE linked.

docs.title: Follow-Up Template
docs.text:
Hello,

I am following up on the vulnerability report submitted on <date>
regarding <product/component>.

Reference:
<ticket/reference>

Could you confirm the current triage or remediation status?

I am available to provide additional reproduction information or to

Regards,

<Researcher>

docs.title: Fix Validation Response Template
docs.text:
Hello,

I tested the supplied fixed build against the original reproduction
case.

Tested version:
<version/build>

Original issue:
<short description>

Result:
The original vulnerable behavior no longer reproduces.

Additional validation:
<variant/regression tests>

Based on the testing performed, the supplied build appears to remediate
the reported issue.

Regards,

<Researcher>

Use more cautious wording if root-cause validation was incomplete.
