docs.title: Final Disclosure Model
docs.text:
Do not disclose like this:

Find Vulnerability
      |
      v
Publish PoC Immediately
      |
      v
Notify Vendor Afterwards

Use this model:

Confirm Vulnerability
      |
      v
Understand Root Cause
      |
      v
Minimise PoC
      |
      v
Preserve Evidence
      |
      v
Identify Correct Vendor
      |
      v
Use Official Security Contact
      |
      v
Provide Reproducible Technical Report
      |
      v
Coordinate Triage
      |
      v
Support Remediation
      |
      v
Validate Patch
      |
      v
Coordinate CVE
      |
      v
Publish Responsibly

Responsible disclosure is successful when the vulnerability is clearly understood, the affected party has enough information to fix it, users have an opportunity to remediate, and the technical record remains accurate and reproducible.

docs.title: Variant Analysis for Vulnerability Research
docs.text:
Variant analysis is the process of taking a confirmed vulnerability and systematically searching for other vulnerabilities that share the same or a closely related root cause.

A single confirmed vulnerability can reveal a broader bug class.

Confirmed Vulnerability
          |
          v
Understand Root Cause
          |
          v
Extract Security Invariant
          |
          v
Identify Similar Code
          |
          v
Identify Similar Data Flows
          |
          v
Identify Alternate Entry Points
          |
          v
Test Candidates
          |
          +-------------------+
          |                   |
          v                   v
      Not Affected         Variant
                              |
                              v
                       Root Cause Analysis
                              |
                              v
                       Expand Search Again

Variant analysis is especially useful after:

Crash analysis

Patch diffing

Source code review

Fuzzing

CVE research

Regression analysis

The objective is not to search randomly for more bugs.

The objective is to transform one confirmed root cause into a structured research hypothesis and test where else the same security assumption exists.

Only perform testing against software and environments you are authorised to analyse.

docs.title: 1. Why Variant Analysis Matters
docs.text:
Software frequently repeats:

Design patterns

Validation functions

Parser structures

Authentication logic

Authorisation logic

Memory operations

Serialization code

Protocol handlers

Helper functions

Framework conventions

If one implementation contains a security mistake, related implementations may contain the same mistake.

For example:

Image Parser
    |
    +---- JPEG Parser
    |
    +---- PNG Parser
    |
    +---- GIF Parser

If the PNG parser fails to validate an attacker-controlled length before copying data, similar logic may exist in the JPEG or GIF parser.

docs.title: 2. One Vulnerability May Represent a Bug Class
docs.text:
Consider a confirmed vulnerability:

Attacker-Controlled Length
          |
          v
Missing Bounds Check
          |
          v
Memory Copy
          |
          v
Heap Buffer Overflow

The useful question is not only:

Where else is this exact function called?

It is:

Where else does attacker-controlled length influence
a memory operation without equivalent validation?

That broader question drives effective variant analysis.

docs.title: 3. Start With a Confirmed Root Cause
docs.text:
Variant analysis works best when the original vulnerability is well understood.

Before beginning, establish:

Attacker-controlled input

Entry point

Data flow

Transformation

Missing or incorrect validation

Sensitive operation

Security consequence

If these are unclear, return to root cause analysis first.

docs.title: 4. Root Cause Template
docs.text:
Document the original finding:

Vulnerability:

Affected Component:

Entry Point:

Attacker-Controlled Input:

Input Transformation:

Security Check:

Missing / Incorrect Condition:

Sensitive Operation:

Failure:

Security Impact:

Patch:

Security Invariant:

Example:

Vulnerability:
Heap-buffer-overflow.

Affected Component:
Document record parser.

Entry Point:
Document import.

Attacker-Controlled Input:
Record length.

Transformation:
32-bit little-endian integer.

Missing Condition:
Declared length is not compared with destination capacity.

Sensitive Operation:
Memory copy.

Failure:
Out-of-bounds write.

Security Invariant:
Copy length must never exceed destination capacity.

The final line is especially important.

docs.title: 5. Extract the Security Invariant
docs.text:
A security invariant describes the condition that must remain true for the operation to be safe.

Examples:

Copy length <= destination capacity

Array index < element count

Resolved path remains inside allowed root

Object access requires ownership

Request requires authenticated identity

Signature must be verified before trust

Object must remain alive while referenced

Integer arithmetic must not overflow allocation size

Untrusted input must not become shell syntax

The invariant can often be searched more effectively than the original vulnerability syntax.

docs.title: 6. Root Cause Versus Symptom
docs.text:
Do not search only for:

SIGSEGV

when the root cause is:

Unchecked attacker-controlled length.

Do not search only for:

403 bypass

when the root cause is:

Authorization is applied to one route representation but
not an equivalent normalized route.

Do not search only for:

Path traversal

when the root cause is:

Security validation occurs before canonicalisation.

Variant analysis should follow the root cause.

docs.title: 7. Build a Variant Hypothesis
docs.text:
Convert the root cause into a testable hypothesis.

Example:

Other record parsers may use attacker-controlled length fields in memory operations without enforcing destination-capacity validation.

Another:

Other object retrieval endpoints may load objects by identifier without applying the ownership check introduced by the patch.

Another:

Other path-handling functions may validate the path before decoding or canonicalisation.

The hypothesis determines what you search for.

docs.title: 8. Variant Analysis Dimensions
docs.text:
Search across several dimensions.

                 Original Vulnerability
                          |
          +---------------+---------------+
          |               |               |
          v               v               v
      Same Code       Same Pattern     Same Interface
          |               |               |
          v               v               v
       Callers        Similar Code     Alternate Routes
          |
          +---------------+---------------+
                          |
                          v
                    Same Component
                          |
                          v
                   Related Components
                          |
                          v
                     Other Platforms

Useful dimensions include:

Same function

Same helper

Same data structure

Same parser family

Same endpoint family

Same protocol

Same authentication mechanism

Same authorization mechanism

Same library

Same framework

Same platform abstraction

Same developer pattern

Same patch pattern

docs.title: 9. Search the Exact Function
docs.text:
Start with the narrowest search.

Suppose the vulnerable function is:

copy_record()

Search:

rg -n "copy_record" .

Determine:

Where is it defined?

Who calls it?

What inputs reach it?

Do all callers perform validation?

docs.title: 10. Search Callers
docs.text:
A shared helper may be safe only when callers enforce preconditions.

Example:

parse_type_a()
       |
       v
validate_length()
       |
       v
copy_record()

parse_type_b()
       |
       v
copy_record()

The second caller may represent a variant.

docs.title: 11. Search Callees
docs.text:
Sometimes the vulnerability exists below the patched function.

Parser A ----\
Parser B -----+--> shared_helper()
Parser C ----/

If the patch protects only Parser A, determine whether the shared helper remains unsafe when reached through Parser B or Parser C.

docs.title: 12. Search the Same Data Structure
docs.text:
Suppose the vulnerability involves:

record->length

Search:

rg -n "record.*length|length.*record" src/

Then inspect how the field is used.

Potential sinks include:

Allocation

Copy

Loop bound

Pointer arithmetic

Array access

File read

Network read

docs.title: 13. Search Struct Fields
docs.text:
For C or C++:

rg -n "\.length|->length" src/

This may produce many results.

Reduce the scope:

rg -n "\.length|->length" src/parser/

Then classify each use.

docs.title: 14. Search Sensitive Operations
docs.text:
For memory-safety research, useful operations may include:

memcpy

memmove

strcpy

strncpy

read

recv

malloc

calloc

realloc

new

Example:

rg -n "memcpy|memmove|malloc|calloc|realloc" src/parser/

Do not treat every result as vulnerable.

Trace the sizes and validation.

docs.title: 15. Search the Validation Pattern
docs.text:
Suppose the patch introduces:

if (length > destination_capacity)
    return ERROR;

Search for related variables:

rg -n "destination_capacity|record_length|payload_length" src/

Look for functions that perform the same sensitive operation without an equivalent condition.

docs.title: 16. Search the New Helper
docs.text:
Suppose the patch introduces:

validate_record_length()

Search:

rg -n "validate_record_length" .

Ask:

Which parsers call it?

Which parsers do not?

Are legacy formats excluded?

Are alternate APIs excluded?

docs.title: 17. Search Similar Function Names
docs.text:
Suppose the patched function is:

parse_record_v2()

Search:

rg -n "parse_record" src/

Possible candidates:

parse_record_v1()

parse_record_v2()

parse_record_legacy()

parse_record_extension()

Naming conventions can expose related implementations quickly.

docs.title: 18. Search Similar Files
docs.text:
Example:

src/parsers/png.c

src/parsers/jpeg.c

src/parsers/gif.c

src/parsers/webp.c

If one parser contains a vulnerability, inspect the others for the same security invariant.

docs.title: 19. Search Sibling Components
docs.text:
A useful mental model is:

Confirmed:
src/import/document_parser.c

Potential Siblings:
src/import/archive_parser.c
src/import/template_parser.c
src/import/image_parser.c
src/export/document_parser.c

Shared design history may produce shared mistakes.

docs.title: 20. Search Legacy Implementations
docs.text:
Legacy code is particularly important.

Look for names such as:

legacy

old

compat

v1

deprecated

fallback

classic

A patch may protect the modern implementation while leaving an older compatibility path unchanged.

docs.title: 21. Search Alternate Protocol Versions
docs.text:
Example:

Protocol v1

Protocol v2

Protocol v3

If the fix is applied only to:

v3

inspect equivalent handlers in:

v1

v2

docs.title: 22. Search Alternate Content Types
docs.text:
A web service may expose similar processing through:

application/json

application/xml

multipart/form-data

application/x-www-form-urlencoded

Security controls may differ between parsers.

Do not assume one validated representation means all representations are safe.

docs.title: 23. Search Alternate Endpoints
docs.text:
Suppose the confirmed vulnerability is:

GET /api/v1/documents/{id}

Related interfaces might include:

GET /api/v2/documents/{id}

POST /api/documents/search

GET /mobile/documents/{id}

GET /admin/documents/{id}

Search for the same underlying object access and authorization invariant.

docs.title: 24. Search CRUD Operations
docs.text:
If an access-control issue exists in:

Read

also review:

Create

Update

Delete

Export

Share

Download

Example:

GET    /documents/{id}
PUT    /documents/{id}
DELETE /documents/{id}
GET    /documents/{id}/download

Authorization may be implemented independently.

docs.title: 25. Search Object Relationships
docs.text:
An object authorization issue may have variants through nested resources.

Example:

/projects/{project_id}

/projects/{project_id}/files/{file_id}

/projects/{project_id}/members/{user_id}

Check whether each nested object is validated against the correct parent and user context.

docs.title: 26. Search Authentication Paths
docs.text:
If an authentication issue exists in one login flow, related flows may include:

Password login

SSO

OAuth

OIDC

API token

Mobile login

Password reset

Remember-me token

Device authentication

Extract the underlying authentication invariant before testing related flows.

docs.title: 27. Search Authorization Middleware
docs.text:
A patch may add:

requirePermission()

to one route.

Search:

rg -n "requirePermission|authorize|permission" .

Compare route registration.

Conceptually:

Route A -> Auth -> Authorization -> Handler

Route B -> Auth -> Handler

Route B may deserve investigation.

docs.title: 28. Search Route Definitions
docs.text:
Depending on the framework, route definitions may reveal missing middleware.

Conceptually:

/admin/users/:id -> auth, adminOnly, handler

/admin/export    -> auth, handler

The difference does not automatically prove a vulnerability.

Determine what the handler itself enforces.

docs.title: 29. Search Path Handling
docs.text:
If the original vulnerability involves traversal or canonicalisation, search for:

join

resolve

normalize

canonicalize

realpath

filepath

basename

dirname

The exact function names depend on language and platform.

docs.title: 30. Search Validation Order
docs.text:
A particularly useful variant pattern is:

Validate
   |
   v
Transform
   |
   v
Use

when the safe order should be:

Transform
   |
   v
Validate
   |
   v
Use

Search for equivalent flows involving:

URL decoding

Unicode normalization

Path canonicalisation

Case normalization

Archive extraction

docs.title: 31. Search Command Construction
docs.text:
If a command-injection issue is confirmed, search for:

system

exec

shell

ProcessBuilder

Runtime.exec

subprocess

cmd.exe

powershell

Then determine whether untrusted input becomes part of shell or process arguments.

Prefer semantic analysis over simple keyword matching.

docs.title: 32. Search SQL Construction
docs.text:
If the root cause involves unsafe query construction, search for:

String concatenation

Formatting

Interpolation

Raw query APIs

Compare against:

Prepared statements

Parameter binding

ORM-safe query methods

Do not classify a query as vulnerable until untrusted input reaches an unsafe query context.

docs.title: 33. Search Deserialization Paths
docs.text:
If a deserialization vulnerability exists, search for:

Deserialize

Unmarshal

Decode

Load

ObjectInputStream

pickle

yaml.load

Then identify:

Input trust

Type restrictions

Callbacks

Object construction

Post-deserialization operations

docs.title: 34. Search File Operations
docs.text:
If the original vulnerability involves unsafe file handling, search for:

open

read

write

create

rename

delete

extract

upload

download

Then trace:

Attacker Path
      |
      v
Transformation
      |
      v
Validation
      |
      v
Filesystem Operation

docs.title: 35. Search Memory Allocation Patterns
docs.text:
Suppose the root cause is:

Allocation size derived differently from copy size.

Search for patterns where:

malloc(A)

memcpy(..., B)

and determine whether:

A >= B

is guaranteed.

docs.title: 36. Search Integer Conversions
docs.text:
Potentially relevant conversions include:

64-bit -> 32-bit

unsigned -> signed

signed -> unsigned

size_t -> int

string -> integer

A safe value in one representation may become unsafe after conversion.

docs.title: 37. Search Loop Bounds
docs.text:
Example:

for (i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    process(items[i]);
}

Investigate:

Who controls count?

How many items were allocated?

Is count validated?

Can arithmetic wrap?

Similar loops elsewhere may contain variants.

docs.title: 38. Search Index Validation
docs.text:
Security invariant:

index < element_count

Search array or vector accesses that use attacker-derived indexes.

Conceptually:

Input Index
    |
    v
Parse
    |
    v
Array Access

Check whether every path validates the index.

docs.title: 39. Search Ownership Patterns
docs.text:
For object lifetime vulnerabilities, identify:

Allocation

Reference creation

Reference transfer

Free

Reuse

Then search for similar ownership models.

A use-after-free variant often results from the same incorrect lifetime assumption repeated across object types.

docs.title: 40. Search Error Paths
docs.text:
Security bugs frequently hide in error handling.

Example:

Allocate
   |
   v
Operation Fails
   |
   v
Free
   |
   v
Caller Continues Using Pointer

Search:

goto cleanup

error labels

exception handlers

early returns

cleanup functions

docs.title: 41. Search Cleanup Functions
docs.text:
If the original issue involves double free or stale state, inspect:

destroy()

cleanup()

release()

free_*()

close()

Determine whether multiple execution paths can invoke cleanup on the same object.

docs.title: 42. Search State Machines
docs.text:
Logic vulnerabilities may depend on invalid state transitions.

Example:

Created
   |
   v
Approved
   |
   v
Executed

Potential variant:

Created
   |
   +------------> Executed

Search other actions that depend on the same state model.

docs.title: 43. Search Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
Map trust transitions:

Network -> Parser

User -> API

Plugin -> Host

Worker -> Privileged Service

Container -> Host Service

Client -> Authentication Service

Then search other functions crossing the same boundary.

docs.title: 44. Search Shared Libraries
docs.text:
A vulnerable function may be reused across multiple products or components.

Shared Library
   |
   +---- Product A
   |
   +---- Product B
   |
   +---- Product C

Determine:

Which products include the affected code?

Which versions?

Which expose the vulnerable function?

Which configurations enable it?

Presence alone does not prove reachability.

docs.title: 45. Search Vendored Dependencies
docs.text:
Look for:

vendor/

third_party/

external/

deps/

libraries/

An application may contain an embedded copy of vulnerable code that does not follow the upstream release schedule.

docs.title: 46. Search Forks
docs.text:
A project may fork another project and modify it independently.

Questions:

Was the upstream patch merged?

Was the vulnerable code modified?

Does the fork expose the same interface?

Did the fork introduce a different fix?

docs.title: 47. Search Platform-Specific Implementations
docs.text:
Example:

file_windows.cpp

file_linux.cpp

file_macos.cpp

A security fix may exist on only one platform.

Compare security invariants across implementations.

docs.title: 48. Search Client and Server Implementations
docs.text:
Protocols may have separate:

Client parser

Server parser

Both may process related attacker-controlled structures.

A bug in one direction may have a counterpart in the other.

docs.title: 49. Search Import and Export Paths
docs.text:
Example:

Import Parser

Export Parser

Although export normally processes trusted internal state, some applications import data before exporting it.

Determine actual data provenance before dismissing a path.

docs.title: 50. Search Mobile and Desktop Clients
docs.text:
Shared backend logic may have separate client-side implementations.

Example:

Web

Desktop

Android

iOS

Do not assume the same validation exists everywhere.

docs.title: 51. Search API Versions
docs.text:
APIs commonly retain:

/v1/

/v2/

/v3/

A security fix in the newest API may not automatically protect legacy versions.

docs.title: 52. Search Internal APIs
docs.text:
External routes may call internal services.

External API
     |
     v
Gateway
     |
     v
Internal Service

The external layer may contain the new validation while internal callers bypass it.

Determine whether internal interfaces are reachable from lower-trust components.

docs.title: 53. Search Alternative Encodings
docs.text:
When the root cause relates to representation, consider:

URL encoding

Double encoding

Unicode

Case differences

Path separators

Null bytes where relevant

Alternate serialization

The goal is not arbitrary bypass experimentation.

The goal is to test whether equivalent representations violate the same security invariant.

docs.title: 54. Search Parser Disagreement
docs.text:
Different components may interpret the same input differently.

Security Layer
     |
     v
Interpretation A

Backend
     |
     v
Interpretation B

This pattern is relevant to vulnerabilities involving:

HTTP parsing

Paths

URLs

Hostnames

Content length

Encoding

File formats

Variant analysis should identify where interpretation boundaries differ.

docs.title: 55. Search Default Configurations
docs.text:
A vulnerability may depend on:

Feature enabled

Legacy mode

Optional parser

Plugin

Compatibility setting

Check:

Default installation

Upgrade installation

Enterprise configuration

Legacy configuration

Do not generalize from one configuration.

docs.title: 56. Search Feature Flags
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n "feature|experimental|legacy|compat" .

A security fix may apply only when one feature path is active.

docs.title: 57. Search Conditional Compilation
docs.text:
C and C++ projects may contain:

#ifdef WINDOWS

#ifdef LEGACY_SUPPORT

#ifdef FEATURE_X

A patch may modify one compiled configuration but not another.

Review relevant build combinations.

docs.title: 58. Search Build Variants
docs.text:
Potential differences include:

Debug

Release

32-bit

64-bit

ARM

x86

Server

Client

A vulnerability may behave differently because of:

Integer width

Structure layout

Compiler optimization

Assertions

Memory protections

docs.title: 59. Search the Patch Itself
docs.text:
Patch diffing is one of the strongest inputs for variant analysis.

Suppose the patch changes:

Function A

and adds:

validate_size()

Search:

Functions structurally similar to A

Functions using the same data type

Functions calling the same sink

Functions lacking validate_size()

See Patch Diffing.

docs.title: 60. Patch Pattern Extraction
docs.text:
Transform:

+ if (size > buffer_capacity)
+     return ERROR;

into:

Invariant:
size <= buffer_capacity

Then search for:

Other attacker-controlled sizes

Other fixed-capacity buffers

Other copy operations

This is much more powerful than searching for the exact added code.

docs.title: 61. Search Regression Tests
docs.text:
A patch may introduce:

test_invalid_length()

test_unauthorized_object()

test_path_escape()

test_expired_token()

Search related tests.

Missing sibling tests may identify untested behavior.

docs.title: 62. Test Names as Clues
docs.text:
Example:

test_reject_oversized_header

Related candidates might be:

payload

metadata

footer

extension

legacy header

Test structure often mirrors implementation structure.

docs.title: 63. Search Documentation
docs.text:
Documentation can reveal parallel functionality.

For example:

Supported Import Formats:
A
B
C
D

If the vulnerability affects format A, the documentation immediately provides candidates for related parser analysis.

docs.title: 64. Search API Documentation
docs.text:
API documentation can reveal:

Legacy endpoints

Alternative object operations

Administrative APIs

Mobile APIs

Bulk operations

Export functions

These may not be obvious from the original vulnerability.

docs.title: 65. Search Error Messages
docs.text:
A fixed path may introduce:

"Invalid object owner"

Search:

rg -n "Invalid object owner|owner" .

Related error messages can lead to equivalent security decisions.

docs.title: 66. Search Constants
docs.text:
Suppose a patch introduces:

MAX_RECORD_SIZE

Search:

rg -n "MAX_.*SIZE|RECORD_SIZE|BUFFER_SIZE" .

Inspect how similar limits are enforced.

docs.title: 67. Search Security Helpers
docs.text:
Identify functions such as:

authorize()

validate_path()

check_bounds()

verify_signature()

sanitize_input()

check_owner()

Then ask:

Where should this helper logically be used but is not?

This is often a productive variant-analysis technique.

docs.title: 68. Missing Security Control Analysis
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Expected Pattern:

Input
  |
  v
Security Helper
  |
  v
Sensitive Operation

Search for:

Input
  |
  v
Sensitive Operation

without the helper.

The absence must still be validated because another layer may enforce the same condition.

docs.title: 69. Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text:
Model the original vulnerability:

Source:
request.parameter

Transform:
parseInteger()

Sink:
allocate/copy

Then search for equivalent flows:

Source -> Transform -> Sink

This can be performed manually or with static-analysis tooling.

docs.title: 70. Manual Data-Flow Search
docs.text:
Start with the source:

rg -n "record_length" src/

Follow:

Definition

Assignment

Transformation

Function arguments

Sensitive operation

Document the chain.

docs.title: 71. Static Analysis Tools
docs.text:
Depending on language and project, tools may include:

CodeQL

Semgrep

Compiler analyzers

Language-specific linters

These can help scale variant searches after the root cause is understood.

The query must model the vulnerability accurately enough to avoid overwhelming false positives.

docs.title: 72. CodeQL Variant Analysis
docs.text:
CodeQL is particularly suited to queries based on:

Sources

Sinks

Data flow

Control flow

Guards

Types

A useful workflow is:

Confirmed Root Cause
       |
       v
Model Source
       |
       v
Model Sink
       |
       v
Model Required Guard
       |
       v
Query Repository
       |
       v
Review Candidates

A static-analysis result is a candidate until validated.

docs.title: 73. Semgrep Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Semgrep can be useful when the vulnerable pattern is syntactically recognizable.

For example:

Unsafe function call

Missing wrapper

Specific API misuse

Repeated framework pattern

Avoid overly broad rules that simply search for dangerous function names.

docs.title: 74. Structural Search Versus Text Search
docs.text:
Text search:

Find "memcpy"

Structural search:

Find memory copies where the length is derived from untrusted
input and is not constrained by the destination capacity.

The second describes the actual vulnerability class.

docs.title: 75. Candidate Triage
docs.text:
Maintain a candidate table.

Candidate Similarity Reachable Validation Status Parser A High Yes Missing Investigate Parser B High Yes Present Closed Parser C Medium Unknown Unknown Review Legacy parser High Yes Missing Variant

This prevents repeated work.

docs.title: 76. Candidate States
docs.text:
Useful states include:

NEW

REVIEWING

NOT_REACHABLE

CONTROL_PRESENT

FALSE_POSITIVE

VARIANT_CONFIRMED

DUPLICATE_ROOT_CAUSE

NEEDS_MORE_EVIDENCE

docs.title: 77. Similarity Is Not Vulnerability
docs.text:
Suppose two functions both contain:

memcpy()

One may safely enforce:

length <= destination capacity

through a caller.

The other may not.

Therefore:

Same Sink != Same Vulnerability

Trace the complete security condition.

docs.title: 78. Reachability
docs.text:
Every candidate requires reachability analysis.

Attacker
   |
   v
External Interface
   |
   v
Candidate Function

Ask:

Can attacker-controlled input reach it?

Is authentication required?

Is a feature disabled?

Is the code dead?

Is the function used only by tests?

Does another layer validate first?

docs.title: 79. Precondition Analysis
docs.text:
Record:

Required Role

Required Feature

Required File Type

Required Protocol

Required Configuration

Required User Interaction

Required Platform

These conditions influence both reproducibility and severity.

docs.title: 80. Validation Layer Analysis
docs.text:
A candidate may appear unsafe locally but be protected by a caller.

Example:

Caller
   |
   v
Bounds Check
   |
   v
Unsafe-Looking Helper

If every reachable caller enforces the invariant, the helper may not be exploitable through the tested interfaces.

Do not report it without establishing a violating path.

docs.title: 81. Defense-in-Depth Versus Required Validation
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Primary security control

Defense-in-depth control

If removing one check still leaves another reliable check, the missing check may represent hardening rather than an exploitable vulnerability.

docs.title: 82. Reproduce the Original First
docs.text:
Before testing variants, confirm that your methodology reproduces the original vulnerability.

Known Vulnerable Case
        |
        v
Expected Failure

If the known case does not behave as expected, investigate:

Build

Configuration

Input

Environment

Patch level

Harness

before trusting variant results.

docs.title: 83. Create a Baseline
docs.text:
For each candidate:

Known Valid Input

Boundary Input

Variant Candidate Input

Compare behavior.

This reduces false conclusions.

docs.title: 84. Change One Variable
docs.text:
Suppose the original bug uses:

record_type = 1

and the candidate is:

record_type = 2

Keep other input fields as consistent as possible.

This makes behavioral differences easier to interpret.

docs.title: 85. Boundary Testing
docs.text:
For length-related variants, test meaningful boundaries.

Example:

capacity - 1

capacity

capacity + 1

Then consider wider values based on the data type and parser design.

Do not rely only on one crashing value.

docs.title: 86. Negative Controls
docs.text:
A good candidate test should include an input expected not to trigger the condition.

Example:

Length:
128

Capacity:
128

Expected:
Safe

Then:

Length:
129

Capacity:
128

Expected:
Reject safely

If the second instead causes memory corruption, the candidate deserves deeper analysis.

docs.title: 87. Debugger Validation
docs.text:
For a candidate memory-safety variant, verify:

Parsed value

Allocation size

Destination capacity

Copy size

Faulting instruction

This demonstrates whether the same invariant is actually violated.

docs.title: 88. Sanitizer Validation
docs.text:
When source builds are available, sanitizers can help distinguish:

Normal rejection

Crash

Out-of-bounds access

Use-after-free

Double free

See Crash Analysis.

docs.title: 89. Compare Original and Variant
docs.text:
Build a table:

Property Original Candidate Input source Record length Extension length Parser Record parser Extension parser Missing check Capacity Capacity Sink Memory copy Memory copy Failure Heap overflow Heap overflow Reachable Yes Yes

This supports classification as a true variant.

docs.title: 90. Same Root Cause
docs.text:
A strong variant often looks like:

Original:

Input A
  |
  v
Missing Check X
  |
  v
Sensitive Operation Y

Variant:

Input B
  |
  v
Missing Check X
  |
  v
Sensitive Operation Y

The source may differ while the security failure remains structurally equivalent.

docs.title: 91. Related Root Cause
docs.text:
Some variants are not identical.

Example:

Original:
Length not checked against destination capacity.

Variant:
Count multiplication overflows before destination capacity
is calculated.

Both may belong to a broader:

Unsafe size calculation

bug family.

Document the relationship accurately.

docs.title: 92. Variant Versus Duplicate
docs.text:
Two crashes may represent the same underlying bug.

Example:

Input A -> parse_record() -> overflow

Input B -> parse_record() -> same overflow

These may be different triggers for one vulnerability rather than separate variants.

Use root cause analysis and crash deduplication.

docs.title: 93. Variant Versus Patch Bypass
docs.text:
A patch bypass means:

Original vulnerable operation
        |
        v
Patch intends to protect it
        |
        v
Alternative input avoids protection
        |
        v
Same vulnerable operation

A variant means:

Original operation -> fixed

Different operation -> same root cause remains

Keep these categories separate.

docs.title: 94. Variant Versus Incomplete Fix
docs.text:
An incomplete fix may protect:

length > capacity

but miss:

integer overflow during capacity calculation

Whether this is described as a bypass, incomplete fix or related variant depends on the technical relationship and disclosure context.

Document the facts first.

docs.title: 95. Variant Analysis After Patch Diffing
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

Patch Diff
    |
    v
Identify New Check
    |
    v
Extract Invariant
    |
    v
Search Similar Code
    |
    v
Test Missing Checks

Example:

Patch:
check_owner(document)

Search:
All document retrieval handlers

Candidate:
export_document() lacks check_owner()

Then validate whether another authorization layer protects the export path.

docs.title: 96. Variant Analysis After Fuzzing
docs.text:
A fuzzer may discover:

Parser Type 4 -> crash

After root cause analysis:

Unchecked element count

Create targeted seeds for:

Parser Type 1

Parser Type 2

Parser Type 3

Parser Type 5

This is more focused than restarting completely unguided fuzzing.

docs.title: 97. Variant Analysis After Source Review
docs.text:
During source review, a confirmed pattern can become a repository-wide search rule.

Example:

Untrusted path
     |
     v
Filesystem API

Search for all equivalent file operations and determine whether each path is canonicalized and constrained appropriately.

docs.title: 98. Variant Analysis After CVE Research
docs.text:
A public CVE can reveal:

Component

Bug class

Patch

Affected function

Security invariant

Use this information to examine related functionality in an authorised research environment.

Do not assume a public CVE automatically proves related products are vulnerable.

docs.title: 99. Cross-Version Variant Analysis
docs.text:
A vulnerability may be fixed in:

Main branch

but remain in:

LTS branch

Legacy release

Enterprise branch

Fork

Compare each maintained code line.

docs.title: 100. Backport Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose:

Main Patch:
Introduces validate_length()

LTS Patch:
Adds inline check to Parser A

Search whether the LTS branch contains:

Parser B

Parser C

without equivalent protection.

Backports may unintentionally create variant opportunities because the implementation differs.

docs.title: 101. Cross-Product Variant Analysis
docs.text:
A vendor may reuse a library across:

Product A

Product B

Product C

If the root cause exists in the shared library, determine:

Which products include the affected version?

Which expose the affected feature?

Which configuration enables it?

Do not equate dependency presence with vulnerability.

docs.title: 102. Variant Analysis and Reachability
docs.text:
A candidate may contain vulnerable code but be unreachable.

Classify carefully:

Code Pattern Present:
Yes

Attacker Reachability:
Not demonstrated

Runtime Trigger:
Not demonstrated

A defensible conclusion might be:

The candidate component contains code structurally similar to the confirmed vulnerable implementation, but reachability from an attacker-controlled interface has not been established.

docs.title: 103. Variant Analysis and Exploitability
docs.text:
A confirmed memory-corruption variant does not automatically imply the same exploitability as the original vulnerability.

Differences may include:

Process privilege

Sandbox

Memory layout

Input restrictions

Architecture

Compiler protections

Reachability

Authentication

Assess each variant independently.

docs.title: 104. Variant Prioritisation
docs.text:
Not every candidate deserves equal research time.

Prioritise based on:

Similarity to confirmed root cause

External reachability

Privilege

Authentication requirement

Component exposure

Security boundary

Code reuse

Patch coverage

docs.title: 105. Prioritisation Matrix
docs.text:
Example:

Candidate Similarity Reachability Exposure Priority Network parser High Remote High High Legacy importer High Local file Medium Medium Test utility High Development only Low Low Dead function High None None Close

This keeps the investigation efficient.

docs.title: 106. Automating Candidate Discovery
docs.text:
Once the invariant is understood, automate repetitive searching where useful.

Possible approaches:

ripgrep queries

AST queries

Semgrep

CodeQL

Custom scripts

Compiler instrumentation

Automation should produce:

Candidates

not automatic vulnerability conclusions.

docs.title: 107. Simple Search Automation
docs.text:
Suppose the investigation concerns length-related memory operations.

A simple discovery workflow might search:

rg -n "memcpy|memmove" src/ > memory-copy-candidates.txt

Then:

rg -n "length|size|count|capacity" src/ > size-candidates.txt

Use these lists to navigate the code.

A semantic static-analysis query is preferable when the repository is large.

docs.title: 108. Candidate Tracking File
docs.text:
Example:

VAR-001
Function:
parse_extension()

Similarity:
High

Source:
extension_length

Sink:
memcpy()

Capacity Validation:
Unknown

Reachability:
Confirmed

Status:
Review

This scales better than keeping all findings in terminal history.

docs.title: 109. Evidence Directory
docs.text:
Example:

variant-analysis/
├── original/
│   ├── reproducer/
│   ├── debugger/
│   └── root-cause.md
├── candidates/
│   ├── VAR-001/
│   ├── VAR-002/
│   └── VAR-003/
├── queries/
├── diffs/
└── notes/

Keep evidence for each candidate separate.

docs.title: 110. Variant Record Template
docs.text:
Variant ID:

Original Vulnerability:

Candidate Component:

Candidate Function:

Candidate Entry Point:

Similarity:

Attacker-Controlled Source:

Transformations:

Security Invariant:

Observed Validation:

Sensitive Sink:

Reachability:

Authentication Required:

User Interaction:

Configuration:

Platform:

Runtime Result:

Debugger Result:

Sanitizer Result:

Root Cause:

Relationship to Original:

Security Impact:

Affected Versions:

Status:

Evidence:

docs.title: 111. Practical Variant Analysis Scenario
docs.text:
Assume a confirmed vulnerability exists in a fictional document parser.

Root cause:

Record length from attacker-controlled input is used as the
copy length without validating destination capacity.

The patch protects:

parse_standard_record()

The researcher now wants to determine whether equivalent parsers remain vulnerable.

docs.title: Step 1 - Extract the Invariant
docs.text: Copy length must not exceed destination capacity.

docs.title: Step 2 - Identify the Patched Pattern
docs.text:
Conceptually:

if (record_length > destination_capacity) {
    return PARSE_INVALID_LENGTH;
}

copy_record(destination, input, record_length);

docs.title: Step 3 - Search Related Functions
docs.text:
rg -n "parse_.*record|copy_record" src/

Representative results:

parse_standard_record()
parse_extended_record()
parse_legacy_record()
parse_metadata_record()

docs.title: Step 4 - Classify Candidates
docs.text:
parse_standard_record()
Patched.

parse_extended_record()
Uses same validation helper.

parse_legacy_record()
No obvious capacity validation.

parse_metadata_record()
Different destination model.

The strongest initial candidate is:

parse_legacy_record()

docs.title: Step 5 - Trace the Candidate
docs.text:
Data flow:

Legacy Record Length
        |
        v
read_u32()
        |
        v
legacy_length
        |
        v
copy_record(..., legacy_length)

No local capacity check is visible.

docs.title: Step 6 - Check Callers
docs.text:
Before concluding vulnerability:

Who calls parse_legacy_record()?

Suppose:

parse_document()
       |
       v
record_type == LEGACY
       |
       v
parse_legacy_record()

Check whether parse_document() validates the legacy length.

Suppose it does not.

The candidate remains viable.

docs.title: Step 7 - Establish Reachability
docs.text:
Create a valid document using:

Record Type:
LEGACY

Confirm:

Application
   |
   v
Document Import
   |
   v
parse_document()
   |
   v
parse_legacy_record()

Reachability is established in the authorised test environment.

docs.title: Step 8 - Establish a Safe Baseline
docs.text:
Suppose the destination capacity is:

256 bytes

Test:

Length 255

Length 256

Both process normally.

docs.title: Step 9 - Test the Boundary
docs.text:
Test:

Length 257

Suppose AddressSanitizer reports:

heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 257

with a stack containing:

copy_record
parse_legacy_record
parse_document

This is strong evidence.

docs.title: Step 10 - Confirm Attacker Control
docs.text:
Debugger inspection shows:

Input field:
257

legacy_length:
257

Destination capacity:
256

Copy length:
257

The attacker-controlled value reaches the sensitive operation.

docs.title: Step 11 - Compare With Original
docs.text:
Property Original Variant Parser Standard Legacy Source Record length Legacy record length Validation Missing before patch Missing Destination Fixed capacity Fixed capacity Sink copy_record copy_record Failure Heap overflow Heap overflow Reachable Yes Yes

This supports classification as a variant.

docs.title: Step 12 - Search Again
docs.text:
Do not stop immediately.

The confirmed variant expands the search:

Standard Parser -> Fixed

Legacy Parser -> Variant

Metadata Parser -> Review

Extension Parser -> Review

The same invariant should now be checked across the entire parser family.

docs.title: Step 13 - Defensible Conclusion
docs.text:
A suitable conclusion could be:

Variant analysis of the patched record parser identified an equivalent missing destination-capacity validation in the legacy record processing path. A record length controlled by document content reaches the same memory-copy helper without an equivalent bounds check. Controlled testing demonstrated an AddressSanitizer-detected heap-buffer-overflow when the declared legacy record length exceeds the destination capacity. The condition was reproduced through the authorised application import path.

This conclusion connects:

Original Root Cause

Variant Search

Attacker Control

Runtime Evidence

Application Reachability

docs.title: 112. Web Authorization Variant Scenario
docs.text:
Variant analysis is not limited to memory corruption.

Assume a patch adds ownership validation to:

GET /api/documents/{id}

The security invariant is:

A user may access a document only when authorized for that object.

Search related handlers:

GET    /api/documents/{id}
PUT    /api/documents/{id}
DELETE /api/documents/{id}
GET    /api/documents/{id}/download
POST   /api/documents/{id}/share

For each route determine:

Authentication

Object lookup

Ownership validation

Role validation

Tenant validation

Do not assume the absence of the exact patched helper proves a vulnerability; authorization may be enforced elsewhere.

docs.title: 113. Path Handling Variant Scenario
docs.text:
Assume a patch changes:

Validate Path
    |
    v
Canonicalize

to:

Canonicalize
    |
    v
Validate Path

Extract the invariant:

Security validation must operate on the canonical path representation.

Search:

Upload destination

Archive extraction

Template loading

Log download

Backup restore

Plugin loading

for equivalent validation-order problems.

docs.title: 114. Variant Analysis Decision Tree
docs.text:
CONFIRMED VULNERABILITY
                       |
                       v
                ROOT CAUSE KNOWN?
                  /          \
                No            Yes
                |              |
                v              v
          Analyse Further    Extract
                            Invariant
                               |
                               v
                       Build Hypothesis
                               |
                               v
                       Search Candidates
                               |
                               v
                        Similar Pattern?
                         /          \
                       No            Yes
                       |              |
                       v              v
                     Close        Reachable?
                                  /       \
                                No         Yes
                                |           |
                                v           v
                             Record      Control
                            Limitation    Present?
                                        /       \
                                      Yes        No
                                      |           |
                                      v           v
                                    Close       Test
                                                 |
                                                 v
                                         Invariant Violated?
                                           /          \
                                         No            Yes
                                         |              |
                                         v              v
                                       Close        Confirm
                                                   Root Cause
                                                       |
                                                       v
                                                  VARIANT
                                                       |
                                                       v
                                                Expand Search

docs.title: Searching Only for Function Names
docs.text:
Problem:

Search:
memcpy

Result:

Thousands of candidates.

Improvement:

Search the actual data-flow condition.

docs.title: Treating Similar Code as Vulnerable
docs.text:
Problem:

Same API call -> same vulnerability

Improvement:

Verify:

Source

Validation

Reachability

Sink

Runtime behavior

docs.title: Ignoring Callers
docs.text:
Problem:

A helper appears unsafe locally.

Reality:

Every reachable caller validates the input.

Improvement:

Analyse interprocedural context.

docs.title: Ignoring Alternate Entry Points
docs.text:
Problem:

Only the patched route is reviewed.

Improvement:

Map the complete feature surface.

docs.title: Ignoring Legacy Code
docs.text:
Problem:

Only the newest parser or API version is reviewed.

Improvement:

Inspect compatibility and fallback implementations.

docs.title: Ignoring Configuration
docs.text:
Problem:

Candidate code exists but is disabled.

Improvement:

Document configuration and default state.

docs.title: Confusing Variant With Duplicate
docs.text:
Problem:

Multiple inputs trigger the same root cause and are reported as separate vulnerabilities.

Improvement:

Deduplicate by root cause.

docs.title: Overstating Exploitability
docs.text:
Problem:

Variant produces memory corruption and is immediately described as RCE.

Improvement:

Perform separate exploitability analysis.

docs.title: 119. Variant Analysis Mindset
docs.text:
Do not think:

Find Same Function Name

Find Same Dangerous API

Find Same Crash

Find Same Payload

Instead think:

Why Was the Original Code Unsafe?
              |
              v
Which Security Invariant Was Violated?
              |
              v
Where Else Is the Same Assumption Made?
              |
              v
Can Attacker-Controlled Data Reach It?
              |
              v
Is Equivalent Validation Present?
              |
              v
Can the Invariant Be Violated?
              |
              v
Does Runtime Evidence Confirm It?

The most effective variant analysis is based on security reasoning rather than string matching.

docs.title: 120. Final Testing Model
docs.text:
A strong variant investigation should be able to demonstrate:

Original Vulnerability
        |
        v
Confirmed Root Cause
        |
        v
Security Invariant

        v
Candidate Selection
        |
        v
Attacker-Controlled Source
        |
        v
Reachable Candidate
        |
        v
Missing / Incorrect Control
        |
        v
Sensitive Operation
        |
        v
Observed Security Failure
        |
        v
Independent Reproduction
        |
        v
Variant Classification

If the chain breaks, document where it breaks rather than forcing a vulnerability conclusion.

flowchart TD

   B --> C["Search variants"]
   C --> D["Candidate triage"]

Search the invariant, not the payload

A proof of concept normally demonstrates one path to a vulnerability. The security invariant explains why that path is unsafe and provides a much stronger basis for finding related vulnerabilities.

Start narrow and expand

Begin with callers, callees, sibling functions and related data structures. Expand to related components, legacy implementations, alternate interfaces and platforms after understanding the immediate code family.

Treat static-analysis results as candidates

CodeQL, Semgrep and search tools can scale discovery, but a match is not automatically a vulnerability. Confirm attacker control, reachability, missing validation and security impact.

Search again after confirming a variant

A newly confirmed variant can reveal additional functions, data structures or implementation patterns that were not obvious from the original vulnerability.

Similar code is not sufficient evidence

Equivalent-looking code may be protected by callers, middleware, configuration or another validation layer. Establish a complete violating path before reporting a vulnerability.

Do not duplicate one root cause

Multiple inputs, crashes or endpoints may expose the same underlying vulnerability. Deduplicate findings based on root cause and affected security boundary rather than the number of triggering inputs.

docs.title: Web Application Security
docs.text:
Web application security testing focuses on identifying weaknesses in applications, APIs, authentication mechanisms, access controls, client-side behaviour, server-side processing and the infrastructure supporting them.

This section combines:

  • methodology;
  • reconnaissance;
  • manual testing;
  • tooling;
  • vulnerability-specific techniques;
  • evidence collection;
  • interpretation;
  • remediation;
  • retesting.

The objective is not simply to identify unusual behaviour.

It is to determine whether a meaningful security boundary can be crossed and whether the available evidence supports a defensible finding.

Authorised Security Testing

The techniques documented in these notes are intended for authorised security assessments, lab environments, security research and responsible vulnerability disclosure. Confirm scope, testing restrictions, rate limits, account requirements and operational risk before testing.

docs.title: Start Here
docs.text:
• :material-map-search-outline:{ .lg .middle } Reconnaissance

    Map the exposed application surface, technologies, endpoints, parameters, JavaScript, APIs and supporting infrastructure.

    :octicons-arrow-right-24: Web Reconnaissance

  • :material-account-key:{ .lg .middle } Authentication and Access Control

    Test login flows, sessions, MFA, password reset, authorisation, IDOR/BOLA, role boundaries and protected functionality.

    :octicons-arrow-right-24: Authentication

  • :material-code-braces:{ .lg .middle } Injection

    Investigate SQL, NoSQL, LDAP, command, template and XML parser injection paths.

    :octicons-arrow-right-24: SQL Injection

  • :material-server-security:{ .lg .middle } Server-Side Security

    Test SSRF, path traversal, file inclusion, file upload, deserialization, input validation and backend processing behaviour.

    :octicons-arrow-right-24: SSRF

  • :material-monitor-dashboard:{ .lg .middle } Client-Side Security

    Investigate XSS, DOM-based vulnerabilities, CSRF, CORS, clickjacking, browser storage, redirects and prototype pollution.

    :octicons-arrow-right-24: XSS

  • :material-api:{ .lg .middle } API Security

    Test REST APIs, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets, mass assignment, authentication and object-level authorisation.

    :octicons-arrow-right-24: API Security

  • :material-briefcase-search-outline:{ .lg .middle } Business Logic

    Assess workflows, trust boundaries, race conditions, rate limits, multi-step processes and application-specific abuse cases.

  • :material-tools:{ .lg .middle } Web Testing Tools

    Use Burp Suite, ffuf, Katana, Nuclei, sqlmap, Interactsh, WhatWeb, Wappalyzer and httpx as part of structured testing workflows.

      v
Evidence Collection
      |
      v
Reporting
      |
      v
Remediation
      |
      v
Retest

The methodology should remain flexible.

Different applications may require different emphasis depending on:

  • architecture;
  • authentication model;
  • API design;
  • application state;
  • technology;
  • role structure;
  • business logic;
  • deployment model.

View the Web Application Testing Methodology

Open the Web Application Pentesting Checklist

docs.title: Reconnaissance and Attack Surface
docs.text:
Reconnaissance focuses on understanding what is exposed before deeper testing begins.

Typical activities include:

  • subdomain enumeration;
  • DNS enumeration;
  • HTTP probing;
  • technology identification;
  • content discovery;
  • parameter discovery;
  • JavaScript analysis;
  • API discovery;
  • virtual host discovery;
  • historical URL analysis;
  • default error-page fingerprinting.

A useful flow is:

Domain / Application
      |
      v
Subdomains and Hosts
      |
      v
HTTP Services
      |
      v
Technology Indicators
      |
      v
Content and Endpoints
      |
      v
Parameters
      |
      v
Prioritised Attack Surface

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication testing focuses on how the application verifies identity.

Areas include:

  • login functionality;
  • username enumeration;
  • password policy;
  • account lockout;
  • password reset;
  • MFA;
  • remember-me functionality;
  • authentication state;
  • session creation;
  • authentication bypass;
  • SSO;
  • OAuth;
  • SAML.

Authentication should be tested as a complete workflow rather than only as a login form.

A useful model is:

Identity Claim
      |
      v
Authentication Mechanism
      |
      v
Session / Token
      |
      v
Authenticated State

Related notes:

Authentication

Password Reset

Multi-Factor Authentication

SAML Security

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Authorisation determines what an authenticated identity is allowed to access or perform.

Important areas include:

  • horizontal privilege escalation;
  • vertical privilege escalation;
  • IDOR;
  • BOLA;
  • missing function-level access control;
  • role manipulation;
  • forced browsing;
  • administrative functions;
  • API access control;
  • multi-tenant isolation.

A useful model is:

Authenticated Identity
      |
      v
Requested Resource / Function
      |
      v
Authorisation Decision
      |
      +-- Allow
      |
      +-- Deny

Testing should use multiple controlled roles where scope permits.

Related notes:

Authorisation

IDOR / BOLA

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
Session management controls how authenticated state is maintained.

Important areas include:

  • cookie security;
  • session fixation;
  • expiration;
  • logout;
  • token invalidation;
  • concurrent sessions;
  • replay;
  • remember-me tokens;
  • JWT handling.

A strong authentication mechanism can still be undermined by weak session handling.

Related notes:

Session Management

JSON Web Tokens

docs.title: Injection
docs.text:
Injection vulnerabilities occur when untrusted input is interpreted as part of a command, query or executable expression.

Important classes include:

  • SQL injection;
  • NoSQL injection;
  • LDAP injection;
  • OS command injection;
  • server-side template injection;
  • XML external entity injection.

The core model is:

User-Controlled Input
      |
      v
Insufficient Separation / Validation
      |
      v
Interpreter / Parser / Query Engine
      |
      v
Unexpected Execution

Related notes:

SQL Injection

NoSQL Injection

LDAP Injection

OS Command Injection

Server-Side Template Injection

XML External Entity Injection

docs.title: SQL Injection and sqlmap
docs.text:
Manual testing should generally come first.

A useful flow is:

Interesting Parameter
      |
      v
Manual SQLi Hypothesis
      |
      v
Burp Repeater
      |
      v
Focused sqlmap Validation
      |
      v
Manual Confirmation

sqlmap

docs.title: Client-Side Security
docs.text:
Client-side testing focuses on behaviour within the browser.

Important areas include:

  • cross-site scripting;
  • DOM-based vulnerabilities;
  • HTML injection;
  • CSRF;
  • CORS;
  • clickjacking;
  • open redirects;
  • XS-Leaks;
  • third-party JavaScript;
  • prototype pollution.

Modern applications often move significant logic into JavaScript, making client-side analysis a central part of testing.

Related notes:

docs.title: Server-Side Security
docs.text:
Server-side testing focuses on backend processing and server-side trust boundaries.

Important areas include:

  • SSRF;
  • XXE;
  • path traversal;
  • file inclusion;
  • file upload;
  • insecure deserialization;
  • command injection;
  • template injection;
  • input validation.

Potential consequences can include:

  • sensitive data access;
  • backend service interaction;
  • internal network access;
  • file access;
  • code execution;
  • privilege boundary violations.

Actual impact must be demonstrated rather than assumed.

Related notes:

docs.title: Out-of-Band Testing
docs.text:
Some server-side vulnerabilities do not create a visible response.

In these cases:

Application Request
      |
      v
Backend Processing
      |
      v
External DNS / HTTP Interaction
      |
      v
OOB Service

Interactsh can support controlled validation of such behaviour.

Related tool:

Interactsh

A callback proves that an interaction occurred.

It does not automatically prove the full vulnerability impact.

docs.title: HTTP and Infrastructure
docs.text:
Web application security also depends on HTTP behaviour and supporting infrastructure.

Areas include:

  • HTTP security headers;
  • request smuggling;
  • Host header attacks;
  • cache poisoning;
  • cache deception;
  • information disclosure.

Related notes:

docs.title: Business Logic
docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities occur when legitimate functionality can be used in unintended ways.

Examples include:

  • workflow bypass;
  • price manipulation;
  • quantity manipulation;
  • race conditions;
  • coupon abuse;
  • account state manipulation;
  • multi-step process bypass;
  • trust-boundary violations.

Business logic testing requires understanding:

How should this process work?

then asking:

What happens if the expected sequence changes?

Related notes:

Business Logic Vulnerabilities

Race Conditions

Rate Limiting and Anti-Automation

docs.title: API Security
docs.text:
Modern web applications frequently expose APIs.

Testing should include:

  • REST APIs;
  • GraphQL;
  • gRPC;
  • WebSockets;
  • authentication;
  • object-level authorisation;
  • function-level authorisation;
  • mass assignment;
  • rate limiting;
  • undocumented endpoints.

A useful model is:

API Endpoint
    |
    v
Authentication
    |
    v
Authorisation
    |
    v
Input Processing
    |
    v
Business Logic
    |
    v
Response

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
WebSockets create persistent two-way communication between client and server.

Testing areas include:

  • authentication;
  • Origin validation;
  • message manipulation;
  • authorisation;
  • session handling;
  • Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking;
  • input validation.

Burp Suite can be used to inspect and modify WebSocket traffic.

WebSockets

docs.title: Identity and Tokens
docs.text:
Modern web applications often rely on token-based or federated identity systems.

Important areas include:

  • OAuth 2.0;
  • OpenID Connect;
  • JWT;
  • SAML.

Related notes:

OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

docs.title: Software Supply Chain and Secrets
docs.text:
Application security also depends on:

  • third-party packages;
  • dependencies;
  • secrets;
  • build systems;
  • configuration.

Dependency Security

docs.text:
Modern attack surfaces increasingly include:

  • prototype pollution;

docs.title: Automated Discovery vs Manual Validation
docs.text:
Automation provides breadth.

Manual testing provides context.

Automation
    |
    +-- Discovery
    +-- Repetition
    +-- Coverage

Manual Testing
    |
    +-- Context
    +-- Business Logic
    +-- Reproduction
    +-- Impact

Together
    |
    v
Stronger Assessment

Do not rely on one alone.

docs.title: Tool Output Is Not a Finding
docs.text:
This principle applies throughout the web section.

Nuclei Match
      !=
Confirmed Vulnerability

Wappalyzer Detection
      !=
Certain Technology Identification

sqlmap Candidate
      !=
Final Security Conclusion

HTTP 500
      !=
Confirmed Injection

A tool result is an observation that requires interpretation.

docs.title: Evidence Before Conclusions
docs.text:
A useful confidence model is:

State Meaning Observation Something potentially relevant was observed Indicator Evidence suggests a specific condition Candidate The condition warrants testing Validated Behaviour was reproduced Confirmed Evidence demonstrates the security condition and impact

For example:

Scanner reports possible SSRF
      |
      v
Candidate
      |
      v
Controlled OOB callback
      |
      v
Validated server-side interaction
      |
      v
Destination control confirmed
      |
      v
Confirmed security condition

docs.title: Baseline First
docs.text:
Many web-testing mistakes happen because the tester does not understand the normal response.

Before fuzzing or modifying a request, record:

Status
Length
Body
Headers
Redirect
Timing
Authentication state

Then compare modified behaviour against the baseline.

docs.title: One Variable at a Time
docs.text:
Where practical:

Baseline
   |
   v
Change One Input
   |
   v
Observe

Changing too many values at once makes interpretation difficult.

docs.title: Authentication Context Matters
docs.text:
The same request may behave differently as:

Unauthenticated user
Standard user
Privileged user
Administrator

Always record the role used during testing.

docs.title: State Matters
docs.text:
Web applications can be stateful.

Testing may depend on:

  • session;
  • CSRF tokens;
  • previous workflow steps;
  • object ownership;
  • transaction state;
  • tenant;
  • account status.

A request should be interpreted within that state.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
False positives may result from:

  • generic 500 responses;
  • authentication redirects;
  • wildcard routing;
  • WAF behaviour;
  • CDN responses;
  • dynamic content;
  • caching;
  • scanner assumptions;
  • soft 404 responses.

A useful process is:

Tool Match
    |
    v
Inspect Raw Request / Response
    |
    v
Establish Baseline
    |
    v
Reproduce Manually
    |
    v
Compare Behaviour
    |
    v
Confirm or Reject

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Automated testing may miss vulnerabilities because of:

  • authentication;
  • stateful workflows;
  • JavaScript;
  • custom APIs;
  • business logic;
  • WAF interference;
  • unusual parameter formats;
  • multi-step attacks;
  • role requirements.

A clean scan does not prove that the application is secure.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful evidence includes:

Target
Endpoint
Method
Parameter
Authentication context
Baseline request
Modified request
Baseline response
Modified response
Timestamp
Tool version
Manual reproduction
Observed impact

Protect:

  • session cookies;
  • bearer tokens;
  • passwords;
  • personal data;
  • API keys.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
A strong finding should describe the underlying security condition.

Avoid:

Burp found an issue.

or:

Nuclei reported a vulnerability.

Prefer:

The application accepts an object identifier controlled by the user and
returns the requested object without verifying that it belongs to the
authenticated account.

The tool supports the evidence.

It is not the finding.

docs.title: Impact Assessment
docs.text:
The demonstrated behaviour should be translated into actual security impact.

Consider:

Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authentication
Authorisation
Privilege
Tenant isolation
Backend reachability
User interaction

Do not assume maximum impact.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Remediation should address the root cause.

Examples include:

  • parameterised database queries;
  • centralised authorisation checks;
  • secure session handling;
  • strict destination validation;
  • safe file handling;
  • output encoding;
  • CSRF protection;
  • secure parser configuration;
  • least privilege;
  • secure framework APIs.

WAF rules and signatures should usually be treated as defence in depth rather than the root fix.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation:

Original Test
      |
      v
Patched Application
      |
      v
Expected Safe Behaviour

Retesting should confirm:

  • the original issue no longer reproduces;
  • the root cause has been addressed;
  • alternative variants are not still present;
  • legitimate functionality still works.

docs.title: Web Testing Checklist
docs.text:
Use the full checklist for detailed assessment coverage:

Web Application Pentesting Checklist

A high-level review should include:

  • [ ] Scope confirmed.
  • [ ] Attack surface mapped.
  • [ ] Technologies identified.
  • [ ] Content discovered.
  • [ ] Parameters discovered.
  • [ ] Authentication tested.
  • [ ] Authorisation tested.
  • [ ] Sessions tested.
  • [ ] Injection tested.
  • [ ] Server-side behaviour tested.
  • [ ] Client-side behaviour tested.
  • [ ] API security tested.
  • [ ] Business logic tested.
  • [ ] Rate limiting reviewed.
  • [ ] HTTP behaviour reviewed.
  • [ ] Information disclosure reviewed.
  • [ ] Automated candidates manually validated.
  • [ ] Evidence captured.
  • [ ] Impact assessed.
  • [ ] Remediation provided.
  • [ ] Retest criteria defined.
