docs.title: Clickjacking
docs.text:
Clickjacking is a client-side attack in which a user is tricked into interacting with an application element that is hidden, transparent or visually disguised beneath attacker-controlled content.

The victim believes they are clicking one element:

Visible Attacker-Controlled Page
             ↓
        "Click Here"

but their click is actually delivered to another application:

Visible Attacker-Controlled Page
             ↓
Transparent / Hidden iframe
             ↓
Target Application
             ↓
Sensitive Action

Clickjacking is sometimes referred to as:

UI redressing
User interface redressing
Frame-based UI manipulation

The vulnerability normally exists when a sensitive application can be embedded inside another website without sufficient framing protections.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform Clickjacking testing only against applications included in the authorised assessment scope. Use controlled accounts and harmless actions for proof-of-concept testing. Do not cause actions on behalf of real users.

docs.title: How Clickjacking Works
docs.text:
Consider an application containing:

<button>Delete Account</button>

The application may require the user to be authenticated before this button is available.

An attacker cannot necessarily submit the action directly because protections such as:

Authentication
Session cookies
CSRF tokens

may prevent direct request forgery.

However, if the application can be loaded inside an iframe, an attacker may attempt to place the legitimate interface underneath another element.

Conceptually:

Attacker Page
      ↓
Loads Target in iframe
      ↓
iframe Positioned Over Decoy Content
      ↓
Victim Clicks Decoy
      ↓
Click Reaches Target Application
      ↓
Authenticated Action Occurs

The browser performs the action using the victim's existing authenticated session where cookie and browser policies permit it.

docs.title: Basic Clickjacking Architecture
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Attacker-Controlled Page             │
│                                      │
│       Click to continue              │
│              ↓                       │
│ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ Transparent iframe              │ │
│ │                                  │ │
│ │ Target Application               │ │
│ │                                  │ │
│ │       Sensitive Button           │ │
│ └──────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘

The iframe may be:

Transparent
Nearly transparent
Positioned absolutely
Resized
Layered using z-index
Aligned with another element

The attacker attempts to make the user interact with the underlying application without understanding what they are actually clicking.

docs.title: Clickjacking Preconditions
docs.text:
Several conditions usually need to be present.

Target can be framed
        ↓
Victim can authenticate to target
        ↓
Sensitive UI exists
        ↓
UI can be positioned predictably
        ↓
Victim interaction performs action

Important questions include:

Can the target page be loaded in an iframe?

Does authentication remain available inside the iframe?

Does the browser send the required cookies?

Can a meaningful action be triggered with a click?

Does the application require additional confirmation?

Are framing protections present?

docs.title: Initial Testing
docs.text:
The first test is simple:

Can the page be framed?

Create a minimal local HTML page:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Clickjacking Test</title>
</head>
<body>

<h1>Clickjacking Test</h1>

<iframe
    src="https://target.example/"
    width="1200"
    height="800">
</iframe>

</body>
</html>

Open the page in a browser.

Possible results:

Target loads normally
Target refuses to load
Browser displays framing error
Target redirects elsewhere
Authentication disappears
Target loads but session is unavailable

docs.title: Minimal Proof of Concept
docs.text:
For an authorised assessment, begin with a visible iframe.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Clickjacking PoC</title>
</head>
<body>

<h1>Authorised Clickjacking Test</h1>

<iframe
    src="https://target.example/account"
    width="1200"
    height="800"
    style="border: 3px solid;">
</iframe>

</body>
</html>

Do not immediately make the iframe transparent.

First establish:

Can it be framed?
Does authentication work?
Does the target render correctly?

docs.title: Transparent iframe Test
docs.text:
Once framing has been confirmed, transparency can demonstrate the underlying Clickjacking condition.

Example:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Clickjacking PoC</title>

    <style>
        iframe {
            position: absolute;
            width: 1000px;
            height: 700px;
            opacity: 0.2;
            z-index: 2;
        }

        .decoy {
            position: absolute;
            top: 200px;
            left: 300px;
            z-index: 1;
        }
    </style>
</head>

<body>

<div class="decoy">
    <button>Click Here</button>
</div>

<iframe src="https://target.example/account"></iframe>

</body>
</html>

During development, keep the iframe partially visible:

opacity: 0.2;

This makes alignment easier to verify.

For a controlled proof of concept, the purpose is to demonstrate that an authenticated interface can be overlaid and interacted with.

docs.title: CSS Positioning
docs.text:
Typical Clickjacking demonstrations rely on CSS properties such as:

position
top
left
width
height
opacity
z-index

Example:

iframe {
    position: absolute;
    top: 0;
    left: 0;
    width: 1000px;
    height: 700px;
    opacity: 0.1;
    z-index: 2;
}

The important security issue is not the CSS itself.

The issue is:

Can an untrusted origin embed the sensitive application?

docs.title: Frameability Test
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Interesting Page
      ↓
Inspect Response Headers
      ↓
Check X-Frame-Options
      ↓
Check CSP frame-ancestors
      ↓
Attempt iframe
      ↓
Observe Browser Behaviour
      ↓
Test Authenticated State
      ↓
Identify Sensitive UI

docs.title: X-Frame-Options
docs.text:
X-Frame-Options is a response header designed to restrict framing.

Common values are:

X-Frame-Options: DENY

and:

X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

docs.title: DENY
docs.text:
X-Frame-Options: DENY

means the page should not be displayed in a frame.

Conceptually:

Any Parent Origin
       ↓
Attempt to Frame
       ↓
Browser Blocks

docs.title: SAMEORIGIN
docs.text:
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

allows framing only when the relevant origin requirements are satisfied.

Conceptually:

Same Origin
    ↓
Allowed

Different Origin
    ↓
Blocked

docs.title: Content Security Policy
docs.text:
Modern applications can control framing using CSP:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';

or:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

docs.title: frame-ancestors 'none'
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';

prevents the resource from being embedded in framing contexts.

This is conceptually similar to:

X-Frame-Options: DENY

docs.title: frame-ancestors 'self'
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

restricts framing to the same origin.

docs.title: Allowing Specific Origins
docs.text:
Applications that legitimately require framing can define explicit trusted origins.

Conceptually:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted.example;

The policy should be as restrictive as the application's business requirements allow.

docs.title: CSP frame-src vs frame-ancestors
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

frame-src

with:

frame-ancestors

They solve different problems.

frame-src controls:

What this page may load inside frames

while frame-ancestors controls:

Which pages may embed this page

For Clickjacking protection, the relevant directive is:

frame-ancestors

docs.title: Checking Headers with Burp Suite
docs.text:
Browse to the target page through Burp Proxy.

Inspect the response.

Look for:

X-Frame-Options:

and:

Content-Security-Policy:

For CSP, specifically inspect:

frame-ancestors

Example:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

This indicates explicit framing protection.

docs.title: Missing Framing Headers
docs.text:
A response such as:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

with neither:

X-Frame-Options

nor:

CSP frame-ancestors

is worth investigating.

However:

Missing headers alone do not automatically demonstrate an exploitable Clickjacking vulnerability.

You should verify actual browser behaviour.

docs.title: curl Header Check
docs.text:
You can inspect headers using:

curl -I https://target.example/

or:

curl -s -D - -o /dev/null https://target.example/

Look for:

X-Frame-Options
Content-Security-Policy

docs.title: Testing Multiple Pages
docs.text:
Do not test only:

/

Framing policies may differ between endpoints.

Test security-sensitive pages such as:

/account
/profile
/settings
/preferences
/security
/admin
/dashboard
/payment
/checkout
/delete
/oauth

For example:

/                  → Protected
/account           → Protected
/profile/edit      → Missing protection
/settings/security → Missing protection

A single sensitive endpoint without framing protection may still be important.

docs.title: Authentication and Clickjacking
docs.text:
A Clickjacking vulnerability becomes more interesting when the target remains authenticated inside the iframe.

Test with a controlled account:

Login Normally
      ↓
Open Clickjacking PoC
      ↓
Target Loads in iframe
      ↓
Check Authentication State

Possible outcomes:

Authenticated
Unauthenticated
Redirected to login
Blocked by browser
Cookies unavailable

docs.title: SameSite Cookies
docs.text:
Modern cookie behaviour can influence Clickjacking.

A session cookie may use:

SameSite=Strict

SameSite=Lax

or:

SameSite=None; Secure

Whether the cookie is available in a cross-site iframe depends on browser cookie policies and the deployment context.

Therefore:

Do not determine Clickjacking exploitability solely from framing headers.

Test the real browser behaviour.

docs.title: Third-Party Cookie Restrictions
docs.text:
Modern browsers increasingly restrict third-party cookies.

This can affect traditional Clickjacking scenarios because the framed target may not receive the victim's authenticated session.

However:

Browser behaviour
Cookie attributes
Same-site relationships
Deployment architecture
Storage partitioning

can all influence the result.

Always test with the browsers relevant to the assessment.

docs.title: Clickjacking and CSRF
docs.text:
Clickjacking and Cross-Site Request Forgery are different vulnerabilities.

CSRF:

Attacker Causes Request
        ↓
Victim Browser Sends Request
        ↓
Application Processes Action

Clickjacking:

Attacker Frames Application
        ↓
Victim Physically Clicks
        ↓
Click Reaches Legitimate Interface
        ↓
Application Processes Action

A CSRF token may prevent traditional CSRF while Clickjacking remains possible.

Why?

Because the user is interacting with the legitimate application itself.

The legitimate page already contains the required token.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: Clickjacking With CSRF Protection
docs.text:
Consider:

<form action="/account/delete" method="POST">

<input
    type="hidden"
    name="csrf"
    value="RANDOM-TOKEN">

<button>Delete Account</button>

</form>

An attacker may not know:

RANDOM-TOKEN

Therefore direct CSRF could fail.

But if the legitimate page can be framed:

Target Page
    ↓
Contains Valid CSRF Token
    ↓
Victim Clicks Legitimate Button
    ↓
Valid Request Submitted

This demonstrates why CSRF protection does not replace anti-framing controls.

docs.title: Sensitive Actions
docs.text:
Prioritise pages containing actions such as:

Change email
Change profile information
Modify privacy settings
Enable features
Disable features
Delete content
Create resources
Submit forms
Approve requests
Confirm operations
Modify subscriptions
Change notification settings

For proof-of-concept testing, use the least destructive action available.

docs.title: Clickjacking Testing by Business Logic
docs.text:
Do not test Clickjacking as simply:

Does iframe work?

Instead ask:

What business actions become possible if framing works?

Examples follow.

docs.title: Account Settings
docs.text:
Suppose the application allows:

Change display name
Change email
Modify profile visibility

If the settings page can be framed:

Attacker Page
      ↓
Victim Click
      ↓
Settings Button
      ↓
Account State Changes

Use a harmless profile modification with a controlled account to demonstrate the condition.

docs.title: Administrative Interfaces
docs.text:
If an administrative interface can be framed, the impact may be greater.

Possible actions include:

Approve user
Disable user
Change configuration
Modify permissions
Publish content
Approve request

Do not perform destructive administrative actions.

Use a safe test action or stop once sufficient evidence exists.

docs.title: Financial Applications
docs.text:
Potential actions include:

Add beneficiary
Modify payment preference
Select subscription
Confirm purchase
Change billing setting

Financial actions can have real consequences.

Testing should use:

Test environments
Controlled accounts
Sandbox transactions
Explicitly authorised actions

docs.title: SaaS Applications
docs.text:
Interesting actions include:

Invite user
Create project
Change workspace settings
Enable integration
Generate API configuration
Modify notifications

Again, the objective is to demonstrate UI redressing, not to cause operational impact.

docs.title: Multi-Step Clickjacking
docs.text:
Some actions require multiple clicks.

Example:

Open Settings
      ↓
Click Security
      ↓
Click Disable
      ↓
Click Confirm

An attacker may theoretically attempt to guide a victim through multiple interactions.

This is known as:

Multi-step Clickjacking

For assessment purposes, demonstrate only as much interaction as is required to prove impact.

docs.title: Clickjacking With Form Input
docs.text:
Some actions require text input before submission.

A basic Clickjacking attack becomes more difficult when the victim must provide unpredictable data.

However, browser UI manipulation may sometimes combine:

Typing
Focus changes
Clicks
Keyboard navigation

Do not assume every form is exploitable simply because it can be framed.

Evaluate the complete interaction.

docs.title: Prepopulated Forms
docs.text:
Applications may prepopulate sensitive forms.

Example:

Email: user@example.com
Privacy: Public

If only a single click is required to submit a state change, Clickjacking may be more practical.

docs.title: Clickjacking and Confirmation Dialogues
docs.text:
A confirmation step can reduce exploitability.

Example:

Delete Account
      ↓
Are you sure?
      ↓
Confirm

But it does not necessarily eliminate Clickjacking if both interactions can be manipulated.

Evaluate:

Number of interactions
Predictability of UI
Placement
Timing
Additional authentication

docs.title: Reauthentication
docs.text:
Sensitive operations may require:

Password
MFA
Passkey
Security key
One-time code

Reauthentication significantly changes the practical impact of Clickjacking.

Document this clearly.

For example:

Page can be framed
but
sensitive action requires password re-entry

This should influence severity.

docs.title: Frame Busting
docs.text:
Some applications use JavaScript to attempt to prevent framing.

Historical examples include logic conceptually similar to:

if (top !== self) {
    top.location = self.location;
}

This is often called:

Frame busting

JavaScript-based frame busting should not be considered a strong replacement for browser-enforced policies such as:

CSP frame-ancestors
X-Frame-Options

docs.title: Why Frame-Busting JavaScript Is Weaker
docs.text:
Client-side scripts depend on:

JavaScript execution
Browser behaviour
Page loading order
Framing conditions
Implementation correctness

Browser-enforced response headers are more appropriate security controls.

docs.title: Nested Frames
docs.text:
Applications may use legitimate framing internally.

Example:

Parent Application
      ↓
Trusted iframe
      ↓
Embedded Component

Before recommending:

frame-ancestors 'none'

understand whether framing is part of the application's architecture.

The correct policy may instead allow explicitly trusted origins.

docs.title: Cross-Origin Framing
docs.text:
The central Clickjacking trust boundary is often:

Trusted Application
        ↓
Embedded by
        ↓
Untrusted Origin

For example:

target.example

should generally not be frameable by:

attacker.example

unless this is intentionally supported.

docs.title: Same-Origin Framing
docs.text:
Some applications intentionally frame their own content.

A policy such as:

X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

or:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

can permit this design while preventing arbitrary third-party framing.

docs.title: Subdomain Considerations
docs.text:
Suppose an organisation uses:

app.example.com
portal.example.com
support.example.com

Do not automatically assume all subdomains should be allowed to frame each other.

Different subdomains may have different trust levels.

Consider:

User-generated content
Third-party hosted subdomains
Legacy applications
Marketing systems
Support platforms

The framing policy should reflect actual trust boundaries.

docs.title: CSP Policy Review
docs.text:
When reviewing:

Content-Security-Policy:

identify:

frame-ancestors

Example:

Content-Security-Policy:
    default-src 'self';
    frame-ancestors 'self';

For Clickjacking, the important portion is:

frame-ancestors 'self'

docs.title: Multiple CSP Policies
docs.text:
Applications may return multiple CSP headers.

Do not inspect only one line and assume the effective policy.

Use browser Developer Tools and actual framing tests to confirm behaviour.

docs.title: Report-Only CSP
docs.text:
Be careful with:

Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only:

A report-only policy does not enforce the restriction.

For example:

Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: frame-ancestors 'none';

should not be treated as equivalent to:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';

Verify the enforcing policy.

docs.title: X-Frame-Options and CSP Together
docs.text:
Applications may return both:

X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

and:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

This can provide compatibility across different browser environments.

Modern browsers support CSP frame-ancestors, while X-Frame-Options remains common as an additional defence.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

Burp Proxy
     ↓
Browse Application
     ↓
HTTP History
     ↓
Identify Sensitive Pages
     ↓
Inspect Response Headers
     ↓
Check X-Frame-Options
     ↓
Check CSP frame-ancestors
     ↓
Build Visible iframe Test
     ↓
Open in Browser
     ↓
Test Authenticated Session
     ↓
Identify Safe Action
     ↓
Build Controlled PoC
     ↓
Document Result

docs.title: Burp Response Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose Burp shows:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Set-Cookie: session=...

but no:

X-Frame-Options:

and no:

frame-ancestors

This should trigger a framing test.

Do not report based solely on the headers.

docs.title: Browser Developer Tools
docs.text:
Developer Tools can help identify why a frame does not load.

Inspect:

Console
Network
Application
Elements

The Console may show browser messages relating to:

X-Frame-Options
CSP
frame-ancestors
Cookie restrictions
Cross-origin behaviour

docs.title: Console Example
docs.text:
When framing is blocked, the browser may report that the page refused to display because of:

X-Frame-Options

or:

Content Security Policy

The exact message varies by browser.

docs.title: Clickjacking PoC Development
docs.text:
A good development process is:

1. Start with visible iframe

2. Confirm target loads

3. Confirm authenticated state

4. Resize iframe

5. Identify target element coordinates

6. Position decoy content

7. Reduce opacity gradually

8. Verify alignment

9. Use harmless action

10. Capture evidence

This is much more reliable than immediately creating an invisible frame.

docs.title: Example Controlled PoC
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">

<head>

<meta charset="UTF-8">

<title>Authorised Clickjacking Test</title>

<style>

body {
    font-family: sans-serif;
}

.target-frame {
    position: absolute;
    top: 100px;
    left: 100px;
    width: 1000px;
    height: 700px;
    opacity: 0.25;
    z-index: 2;
}

.decoy {
    position: absolute;
    top: 250px;
    left: 300px;
    z-index: 1;
}

</style>

</head>

<body>

<h1>Authorised Clickjacking Test</h1>

<div class="decoy">
    <button>Test Button</button>
</div>

<iframe
    class="target-frame"
    src="https://target.example/account">
</iframe>

</body>

</html>

During an authorised test, adjust:

top
left
width
height

to match the controlled target page.

docs.title: Serving the PoC Locally
docs.text:
You can save the proof of concept as:

clickjacking-poc.html

and open it directly in the browser.

If browser behaviour requires an HTTP origin, you can serve the directory locally:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Then browse to:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/clickjacking-poc.html

This is useful for controlled local testing.

docs.title: Testing Different Viewports
docs.text:
Clickjacking alignment can depend on:

Screen resolution
Browser window size
Zoom level
Responsive layout
Mobile layout
Application state

This affects practical exploitability.

A PoC that works only at one exact resolution may be less reliable than one targeting a stable interface element.

docs.title: Responsive Applications
docs.text:
Modern applications may reposition buttons based on:

Viewport width
Viewport height
Device type
Navigation state

Test whether the sensitive control has a predictable position.

docs.title: Scroll Position
docs.text:
The target element may not initially be visible.

Clickjacking scenarios can be affected by:

iframe scroll position
Page scrolling
Sticky navigation
Responsive components
Dynamic content

Document any interaction required before the sensitive control becomes reachable.

docs.title: Dynamic Interfaces
docs.text:
Single-page applications may load elements asynchronously.

Example:

iframe loads
    ↓
API request
    ↓
UI renders
    ↓
Button appears

Timing can affect alignment.

Do not assume a static HTML proof of concept accurately represents every interaction.

docs.title: Clickjacking and SPA Applications
docs.text:
Applications built using:

React
Angular
Vue
Next.js
Single-page application frameworks

are still subject to framing protections.

The framework itself does not prevent Clickjacking.

Check the HTTP response headers delivered by:

Application
Reverse proxy
CDN
Web server

docs.title: Clickjacking and APIs
docs.text:
Pure JSON APIs generally do not provide clickable user interfaces.

Therefore traditional Clickjacking is primarily relevant to browser-rendered pages.

However, an API-backed web interface may still be vulnerable through its frontend.

docs.title: Clickjacking and CORS
docs.text:
CORS and Clickjacking address different browser security mechanisms.

CORS controls whether scripts from another origin can read certain cross-origin responses.

Clickjacking concerns whether an application can be visually embedded and interacted with.

Therefore:

Strict CORS

does not automatically prevent:

Clickjacking

Refer to:

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

once that page is added.

docs.title: Clickjacking and SOP
docs.text:
The Same-Origin Policy can prevent an attacker from reading the contents of a cross-origin iframe.

However, Clickjacking does not necessarily require reading the frame.

Conceptually:

Cannot Read iframe
        ≠
Cannot Overlay iframe

This distinction is fundamental to understanding Clickjacking.

docs.title: Testing Administrative Actions Safely
docs.text:
If the application contains administrative functionality, avoid destructive tests.

Prefer actions such as:

Open tab
Change harmless preference
Toggle test setting
Select non-destructive option
Modify controlled test object

If simply demonstrating that the sensitive page is frameable is sufficient under the assessment methodology, stop there.

docs.title: Business Impact Analysis
docs.text:
The severity should be based on what an attacker can realistically cause.

Consider:

Is authentication required?

Does the session work inside the frame?

What action can be triggered?

How many clicks are required?

Is reauthentication required?

Is MFA required?

Does the action have material impact?

Is the UI predictable?

Does browser cookie policy interfere?

Can a realistic victim reach the vulnerable state?

docs.title: Weak Clickjacking Finding
docs.text:
Example:

Public informational page can be framed

with no sensitive actions.

This may have little or no security impact.

docs.title: Stronger Clickjacking Finding
docs.text:
Example:

Authenticated account settings page can be framed
        ↓
Session remains authenticated
        ↓
Sensitive state-changing control is predictable
        ↓
No reauthentication required
        ↓
Controlled action succeeds

This provides much stronger evidence.

docs.title: Do Not Report Headers Alone
docs.text:
Avoid findings such as:

Missing X-Frame-Options

without analysing impact.

A better approach is:

1. Identify missing anti-framing controls

2. Verify target can actually be framed

3. Determine whether authentication survives

4. Identify sensitive interaction

5. Demonstrate controlled impact

6. Report the resulting Clickjacking condition

docs.title: Testing Matrix
docs.text:
Create a matrix:

Endpoint X-Frame-Options frame-ancestors Frames? Authenticated? Sensitive Action / Missing Missing Yes N/A No /login Missing Missing Yes N/A No /account Missing Missing Yes Yes Yes /security SAMEORIGIN 'self' No N/A Yes /admin DENY 'none' No N/A Yes

This provides much better assessment coverage than checking only the home page.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
[ ] Identify sensitive pages
[ ] Identify sensitive buttons
[ ] Identify state-changing actions
[ ] Check authentication requirements
[ ] Check confirmation requirements
[ ] Check reauthentication requirements

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
[ ] Check X-Frame-Options
[ ] Check CSP
[ ] Check frame-ancestors
[ ] Check Report-Only CSP
[ ] Check policies on individual endpoints

docs.title: Browser Testing
docs.text:
[ ] Create visible iframe
[ ] Verify page loads
[ ] Verify authenticated state
[ ] Check browser Console
[ ] Check cookie behaviour
[ ] Check multiple relevant browsers where required

docs.title: Proof of Concept
docs.text:
[ ] Use controlled account
[ ] Use harmless action
[ ] Keep iframe visible during development
[ ] Align target control
[ ] Reduce opacity
[ ] Verify click reaches target
[ ] Stop after sufficient evidence

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
[ ] Identify affected user role
[ ] Determine required interaction
[ ] Determine number of clicks
[ ] Check additional confirmation
[ ] Check MFA or reauthentication
[ ] Assess business impact

docs.title: Clickjacking Decision Tree
docs.text:
Sensitive Page
      ↓
Can It Be Framed?
      ↓
     NO
      ↓
Not Clickjacking Through This Path

      OR

     YES
      ↓
Does Authentication Work in Frame?
      ↓
     NO
      ↓
Impact Likely Reduced

      OR

     YES
      ↓
Sensitive UI Available?
      ↓
     NO
      ↓
Limited Impact

      OR

     YES
      ↓
Can Controlled User Interaction Trigger Action?
      ↓
     YES
      ↓
Additional Confirmation?
      ↓
Reauthentication?
      ↓
Assess Practical Exploitability
      ↓
Document
      ↓
Report

docs.title: Clickjacking Quick Reference
docs.text:
CHECK HEADERS

X-Frame-Options
Content-Security-Policy

X-FRAME-OPTIONS

DENY
SAMEORIGIN

CSP

frame-ancestors 'none'
frame-ancestors 'self'

BASIC TEST

<iframe src="https://target.example/"></iframe>

CSS

position: absolute;
opacity: 0.2;
z-index: 2;

TEST FLOW

Frame
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Sensitive UI
 ↓
Controlled Click
 ↓
State Change

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a confirmed finding, record:

Affected endpoint
Affected functionality
Required authentication
Affected user role
X-Frame-Options value
CSP frame-ancestors value
Browser tested
Cookie behaviour
Sensitive action
Number of interactions
Reauthentication requirements
Proof-of-concept HTML
Screenshots
Before state
After state

docs.title: Screenshot Evidence
docs.text:
Useful screenshots include:

Target application loaded inside iframe
PoC showing target and decoy alignment
Browser Developer Tools showing relevant headers
State before controlled interaction
State after controlled interaction

Avoid capturing unnecessary personal or sensitive information.

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Clickjacking on Authenticated Account Settings

Affected Endpoint:
/account/settings

Expected:
Sensitive authenticated pages should prevent framing by untrusted origins.

Observed:
The account settings page could be embedded in a cross-origin iframe. The controlled user's authenticated session remained available within the frame, and a harmless account preference could be changed through an overlaid interface.

Anti-Framing Controls:
X-Frame-Options: Missing
CSP frame-ancestors: Missing

Impact:
An attacker could potentially construct a page that visually disguises the framed account settings interface and induces an authenticated user to perform unintended actions.

docs.title: Example Lower-Impact Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Application Pages Can Be Framed by Arbitrary Origins

Observed:
Several application pages could be embedded within a third-party iframe because no effective X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors policy was present.

Impact:
The tested public pages did not expose sensitive state-changing functionality. The issue therefore presents limited direct security impact in the tested workflow.

Recommendation:
Implement an appropriate anti-framing policy to prevent future functionality from becoming exposed to UI-redressing attacks.

This is more accurate than exaggerating the finding.

docs.title: Interpret the Security Boundary
docs.text:
Use this sequence:

Page can be framed
      -> Sensitive interaction can be positioned or influenced
      -> Authenticated user can reach the page in the test context
      -> Meaningful state-changing action can be demonstrated
      -> Security conclusion

Missing X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors establishes a frameability observation, not automatically a significant vulnerability. Consider the page's authentication requirements, action sensitivity, CSRF protections, SameSite cookie behavior, browser policy, user interaction, and whether a framing ancestor is actually permitted.

frame-ancestors controls who may embed the protected page; frame-src controls what a page may embed and is not a substitute. Modern browsers generally give CSP frame-ancestors precedence where supported, while legacy or unsupported clients may interpret X-Frame-Options. Record multiple policies, report-only policy, nested frames, and browser differences rather than assuming one header determines every client.

docs.title: Controlled Validation and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Use a local or approved test origin and a dedicated account. Begin with a non-sensitive page, then test an authenticated page and a reversible state-changing action only when explicitly authorised. Do not use deceptive links or real users. Confirm that cookies are sent in the framing context, the page renders, the overlay can influence the intended interaction, and the resulting action is accepted by the server.

If the page appears frameable but the proof does not work, check CSP and X-Frame-Options on the final response, redirects, nested ancestors, response-specific headers, SameSite cookie mode, authentication state, browser version, sandboxing, cross-origin restrictions, UI scaling, and whether CSRF or reauthentication prevents the action. A blocked action is useful evidence that the control chain limits impact.

docs.title: Evidence, Remediation, and Retesting
docs.text:
Capture response headers, final URL, browser and account context, framing origin, screenshot or video of the controlled interaction, action result, CSRF and cookie conditions, and the expected-versus-observed behavior. Report the demonstrated action and affected users, not merely the missing header.

Remediation should use an appropriate CSP frame-ancestors policy, retain compatible X-Frame-Options where required, protect state-changing actions with robust CSRF and reauthentication controls, and review legitimate embedding requirements. Retest unauthenticated and authenticated pages, sensitive actions, redirects, nested framing, supported browsers, and the final response after deployment. See HTTP Security Headers, CSRF, Authentication, and Authorisation.

docs.title: Reporting Titles
docs.text:
Prefer specific titles:

Clickjacking on Authenticated Account Settings

Clickjacking Allows UI Redressing of Profile Controls

Sensitive Administrative Page Can Be Framed by Arbitrary Origins

Missing Anti-Framing Protection Allows Clickjacking

Clickjacking on Account Preference Functionality

Avoid vague titles such as:

X-Frame-Options Missing

when actual Clickjacking has been demonstrated.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Modern applications should control which origins may frame sensitive pages.

The preferred control is:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';

when framing is never required.

docs.title: Same-Origin Framing
docs.text:
If the application legitimately frames itself:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

may be appropriate.

docs.title: Explicit Trusted Origins
docs.text:
Where specific external applications must frame the page:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted.example;

Use the smallest possible allowlist.

docs.title: X-Frame-Options
docs.text:
For additional compatibility, applications may also return:

X-Frame-Options: DENY

or:

X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

depending on the required architecture.

docs.title: Sensitive Actions
docs.text:
Anti-framing controls should be combined with security measures appropriate to the action, such as:

CSRF protection
Reauthentication
MFA
Confirmation steps
Secure session management
Authorisation checks

Defence in depth is important.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Configuration
docs.text:
Anti-framing headers may be added at:

Application
Web server
Reverse proxy
Load balancer
CDN
API gateway

Ensure the policy applies consistently to all sensitive HTML responses.

docs.title: Nginx Example
docs.text:
Conceptually:

add_header Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'self'" always;
add_header X-Frame-Options "SAMEORIGIN" always;

The exact configuration should be tested against the application's legitimate framing requirements.

docs.title: Apache Example
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Header always set X-Frame-Options "SAMEORIGIN"
Header always set Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'self'"

Again, validate against the actual deployment architecture.

docs.title: Application-Level Example
docs.text:
Frameworks may also set security headers directly.

The important outcome is that the final HTTP response contains the intended policy consistently.

Test the response after:

Application
Proxy
CDN
Load balancer

have all processed it.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid relying solely on:

JavaScript frame busting
Hidden form fields
CSRF tokens
CORS
Same-Origin Policy
Referer checks

None of these is a direct replacement for a proper anti-framing policy.

docs.title: Clickjacking vs Related Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Clickjacking
    ↓
UI interaction is disguised

CSRF
    ↓
Cross-site request is induced

XSS
    ↓
Attacker-controlled script executes

HTML Injection
    ↓
Attacker-controlled markup is rendered

Open Redirect
    ↓
Trusted application redirects to external destination

These vulnerabilities can sometimes interact, but they should be tested and reported based on the behaviour actually demonstrated.

docs.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Clickjacking
docs.text:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/clickjacking

PortSwigger provides detailed material covering Clickjacking fundamentals, frame-based attacks and practical testing techniques.

docs.title: PortSwigger Clickjacking Labs
docs.text:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/all-labs#clickjacking

Useful practical labs for understanding Clickjacking behaviour.

docs.title: OWASP Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Clickjacking_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html

Useful defensive guidance covering CSP frame-ancestors, X-Frame-Options, SameSite cookies and related protections.

docs.title: MDN: X-Frame-Options
docs.text:
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/X-Frame-Options

Reference documentation for the X-Frame-Options response header.

docs.title: MDN: CSP frame-ancestors
docs.text:
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/frame-ancestors

Reference documentation for the CSP frame-ancestors directive.

docs.title: Final Clickjacking Testing Model
docs.text:
APPLICATION
                         ↓
                 IDENTIFY SENSITIVE UI
                         ↓
                  INSPECT RESPONSE
                         ↓
        ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
        ↓                                 ↓
 X-Frame-Options                   CSP frame-ancestors
        ↓                                 ↓
        └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                         ↓
                 ATTEMPT FRAMING
                         ↓
                  DOES PAGE LOAD?
                         ↓
                        YES
                         ↓
                AUTHENTICATED STATE?
                         ↓
                        YES
                         ↓
                 SENSITIVE ACTION?
                         ↓
                        YES
                         ↓
                 CONTROLLED ACCOUNT
                         ↓
                  VISIBLE iframe
                         ↓
                  ALIGN INTERFACE
                         ↓
                HARMLESS INTERACTION
                         ↓
                DOES ACTION SUCCEED?
                         ↓
                        YES
                         ↓
              PRACTICAL CLICKJACKING
                         ↓
                ASSESS BUSINESS IMPACT
                         ↓
                      REPORT

The key principle is:

Do not report Clickjacking simply because an anti-framing header is missing. Determine whether an untrusted origin can actually frame the application, whether the victim's authenticated state remains usable, and whether a meaningful action can be triggered through disguised user interaction.

docs.title: OS Command Injection
docs.text:
OS Command Injection occurs when attacker-controlled input is incorporated into an operating system command in an unsafe manner.

If an application passes user-controlled data to a shell or operating system command interpreter without appropriate controls, an attacker may be able to alter the intended command.

Command injection testing should not begin with large payload lists or automated tools. First determine where user input enters the application, what functionality may invoke operating system commands, how the input is transformed, and whether application behaviour indicates command execution.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform command injection testing only against applications and systems for which you have explicit authorisation. These notes are intended for authorised penetration testing, lab environments, security research and responsible vulnerability disclosure.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
The primary objectives are to determine:

  • whether user-controlled input reaches an operating system command
  • whether a shell is involved
  • whether command structure can be influenced
  • which operating system is likely involved
  • which shell or command interpreter may be used
  • whether command output is returned
  • whether execution can be inferred through timing
  • whether execution can be confirmed through an authorised callback
  • whether argument injection is possible
  • whether input validation can be bypassed
  • what privileges the affected process has
  • what security impact can be demonstrated safely

A useful mental model is:

User Input
    ↓
Application
    ↓
Validation / Transformation
    ↓
Command Construction
    ↓
Shell / Process API
    ↓
Operating System
    ↓
Command Execution

The most important question is:

Can attacker-controlled input alter the command that the application intended to execute?

docs.title: Command Injection Testing Workflow
docs.text:
A structured workflow can look like:

Discover Input
      ↓
Understand Functionality
      ↓
Establish Baseline
      ↓
Identify Possible OS Interaction
      ↓
Test Command Metacharacters
      ↓
Observe Response
      ↓
Determine OS / Shell
      ↓
Confirm Execution
      ↓
Targeted Automation
      ↓
Determine Execution Context
      ↓
Assess Impact
      ↓
Collect Minimal Evidence
      ↓
Report

Start with the application's intended functionality.

For example:

Ping utility
DNS lookup
File conversion
Image processing
Archive creation
PDF generation
Video processing
Backup functionality
Network diagnostics
System administration
Git operations
Build systems
Import / export
Monitoring functionality

These features are often more interesting than arbitrary text fields.

docs.title: Common Command Injection Locations
docs.text:
Potential locations include:

GET parameters
POST parameters
JSON properties
HTTP headers
Cookies
File names
File paths
Host names
IP addresses
URLs
Email addresses
Export parameters
Import parameters
Search parameters
Diagnostic tools
Administrative functionality
API parameters

Examples:

?host=127.0.0.1

?domain=example.com

?file=report.pdf

?url=https://example.com

?format=pdf

The parameter name alone does not prove that an operating system command is involved.

docs.title: High Value Functionality
docs.text:
Pay particular attention to functionality performing tasks such as:

Ping
Traceroute
DNS lookup
WHOIS
Network diagnostics
File conversion
Image resizing
Archive extraction
Archive creation
PDF generation
Video conversion
Backup creation
Log processing
Git operations
Package management
System monitoring
Printer interaction
External program execution

A useful thought process is:

Application Feature
       ↓
Could this require an external program?
       ↓
Could user input become an argument?
       ↓
How is that process started?

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Before modifying the parameter, send the normal request.

Example:

POST /api/ping HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "host": "127.0.0.1"
}

Record:

Status code
Response length
Response body
Response time
Application message
Returned command output

Example:

Status: 200
Time: 230 ms
Result: Host reachable

The baseline gives you something to compare subsequent tests against.

docs.title: Identify the Operating System
docs.text:
Technology identification can help determine whether the backend is likely running:

Linux
Unix
Windows
macOS
Containerised Linux

Potential indicators include:

Server headers
Error messages
File paths
Framework behaviour
Technology stack
Source code
Application documentation
Command output

Examples:

/var/www/
/home/
/tmp/

suggest a Unix-like environment.

Paths such as:

C:\Windows\
C:\Users\
C:\Program Files\

suggest Windows.

Do not rely on a single indicator.

docs.title: Shell Metacharacters
docs.text:
Shells interpret certain characters as having special meaning.

On Unix-like systems, interesting characters and constructs may include:

;
|
||
&&
&
`
$()
>
>>
<

On Windows command interpreters, interesting characters may include:

&
&&
|
||
>
>>
<

Support and behaviour depend on:

Operating system
Shell
Execution API
Quoting
Application framework
Input validation

Test characters individually to understand how they are handled.

docs.title: Character Testing
docs.text:
Start with controlled syntax changes.

Determine how the application handles:

;

then:

|

then:

&

then:

'

then:

"

Observe:

HTTP status
Response length
Application errors
Validation errors
Timing
Output changes

This can reveal whether characters are:

Accepted
Rejected
Encoded
Removed
Escaped
Normalised
Interpreted

docs.title: Linux Command Injection
docs.text:
Suppose an application performs functionality conceptually similar to:

ping -c 1 USER_INPUT

If USER_INPUT is concatenated directly into a shell command, shell metacharacters may alter the intended command.

A harmless authorised validation might conceptually test:

127.0.0.1; id

If command output is returned, you might observe:

uid=...
gid=...
groups=...

For authorised testing, prefer commands that demonstrate execution without modifying the system.

Examples:

id

whoami

hostname

uname -a

Avoid destructive commands.

docs.title: Windows Command Injection
docs.text:
A Windows application might conceptually execute:

ping USER_INPUT

If user-controlled input reaches cmd.exe unsafely, command separators may alter execution.

A benign validation might use:

whoami

or:

hostname

The objective is to demonstrate execution, not to modify the host.

docs.title: Output Based Command Injection
docs.text:
Output based command injection occurs when output from the injected command is returned through the application.

Example:

Input
 ↓
Command Construction
 ↓
Operating System
 ↓
Command Output
 ↓
Application Response

This is usually easier to validate than blind command injection.

Look for:

Username
Hostname
Operating system information
Command errors
Unexpected output

docs.title: Blind Command Injection
docs.text:
Blind command injection occurs when commands execute but their output is not returned in the HTTP response.

The application might simply return:

Operation completed successfully

regardless of what occurred on the backend.

Potential confirmation techniques include:

Timing differences
Controlled DNS interaction
Controlled HTTP interaction
Application state changes

Avoid unnecessary state changes where timing or controlled callbacks are sufficient.

docs.title: Time Based Blind Command Injection
docs.text:
Timing can be used to infer command execution when output is not visible.

The general concept is:

Normal Input
     ↓
Normal Response Time

Controlled Delay
     ↓
Delayed Response

For a Unix-like environment, a controlled test may use a short delay:

sleep 5

For Windows:

timeout /t 5

The exact syntax depends on how input reaches the command interpreter.

docs.title: Timing Workflow
docs.text:
Send Baseline
      ↓
Measure Response
      ↓
Repeat Baseline
      ↓
Determine Normal Variation
      ↓
Introduce Controlled Delay
      ↓
Repeat Test
      ↓
Compare Timing
      ↓
Confirm Correlation

Do not treat a single slow request as proof.

docs.title: Timing Evidence
docs.text:
Record several measurements.

Request Baseline Controlled Test 1 210 ms 5.2 s 2 195 ms 5.1 s 3 224 ms 5.2 s 4 203 ms 5.1 s

A predictable delay that repeatedly correlates with the test is significantly stronger evidence than one slow request.

docs.title: Out of Band Command Injection
docs.text:
When command output is unavailable, an authorised callback service can sometimes confirm execution.

Conceptually:

Application
     ↓
Command Injection
     ↓
Operating System
     ↓
DNS / HTTP Request
     ↓
Controlled Callback Infrastructure

This can be useful when:

Output is hidden
Timing is unreliable
Commands execute asynchronously
Background jobs process the input

docs.title: Burp Collaborator
docs.text:
Burp Collaborator can be useful for detecting out of band interactions during authorised testing.

Workflow:

Burp Repeater
      ↓
Generate Collaborator Domain
      ↓
Use Controlled Callback
      ↓
Send Request
      ↓
Poll Collaborator
      ↓
Interaction?
      ↓
Correlate With Request

Potential interaction types include:

DNS
HTTP
HTTPS
SMTP

A callback should be correlated with the exact request that triggered it.

docs.title: Interactsh
docs.text:
Interactsh is another useful out of band interaction service.

Project:

https://github.com/projectdiscovery/interactsh

A typical authorised workflow is:

Start interactsh-client
        ↓
Receive Unique Domain
        ↓
Use Domain in Controlled Test
        ↓
Send Request
        ↓
Monitor Interactions
        ↓
Correlate Callback

Start the client:

interactsh-client

The client provides a unique interaction domain that can be used for controlled testing.

docs.title: DNS Based Verification
docs.text:
DNS callbacks can be useful because outbound DNS resolution is sometimes available even when outbound HTTP is restricted.

Conceptually:

Command Execution
      ↓
DNS Resolution
      ↓
Controlled Domain
      ↓
Callback Logged

When using callbacks, assign unique identifiers to each injection location.

For example:

CMD-001 → host parameter
CMD-002 → filename parameter
CMD-003 → User-Agent
CMD-004 → JSON url property

This makes callback correlation significantly easier.

docs.title: HTTP Based Verification
docs.text:
HTTP interactions can provide another confirmation mechanism.

Conceptually:

Command Injection
      ↓
Operating System Utility
      ↓
HTTP Request
      ↓
Controlled Server

Use infrastructure that is explicitly authorised for the assessment.

Do not collect unnecessary information from the target.

docs.title: Asynchronous Command Execution
docs.text:
Some application functionality runs asynchronously.

Examples include:

Background workers
Job queues
File processing
Image conversion
PDF generation
Email processing
Scheduled tasks
Import jobs
CI/CD pipelines

The flow may be:

HTTP Request
     ↓
Queue
     ↓
HTTP Response
     ↓
Worker Processes Job Later
     ↓
Command Execution

Therefore, an immediate HTTP response may not reveal whether command execution occurred.

Out of band callbacks can be particularly useful in these situations.

docs.title: Argument Injection
docs.text:
Command injection and argument injection are related but not identical.

Consider:

program USER_INPUT

Even when shell metacharacters are not interpreted, attacker-controlled input may influence the arguments passed to the program.

For example:

Application
    ↓
External Utility
    ↓
Attacker Controls Argument
    ↓
Unexpected Program Behaviour

This is often called:

Argument Injection
Option Injection
Parameter Injection

docs.title: Option Injection
docs.text:
Many command-line programs treat values beginning with:

-

or:

--

as options.

If attacker-controlled input becomes a command-line argument, it may be possible to influence the external utility even without shell command separators.

The security question is:

Can user-controlled data become an option rather than ordinary data?

docs.title: End of Options Marker
docs.text:
Many Unix command-line utilities support:

--

to indicate the end of command options.

For example:

some-command -- USER_INPUT

This can help prevent user-controlled values beginning with - from being interpreted as options.

Support depends on the specific utility.

docs.title: Command Substitution
docs.text:
Unix shells may support command substitution using constructs such as:

$(...)

or:

`...`

Whether these are interpreted depends on whether the application invokes a shell.

For example:

Process API
   ↓
Direct Executable Invocation

behaves differently from:

Application
   ↓
Shell
   ↓
Command String

This distinction is important when determining exploitability.

docs.title: Direct Process Execution vs Shell Execution
docs.text:
Consider two conceptual designs.

Direct process execution:

Application
     ↓
Process API
     ↓
Executable + Separate Arguments

versus shell execution:

Application
     ↓
/bin/sh -c
     ↓
Constructed Command String

The second design introduces shell parsing.

Avoid invoking a shell when it is not necessary.

docs.title: Quoting
docs.text:
Applications sometimes attempt to make command execution safe by surrounding user input with quotes.

Example:

command "USER_INPUT"

Quoting alone should not be considered a complete defence.

Questions include:

Which quote is used?
Can the quote be terminated?
Are backslashes handled?
Does another decoding layer exist?
Does the shell perform expansion?

The safest approach is generally to avoid shell command construction entirely.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Shell environments may expand variables.

Unix-like examples include:

$HOME
$PATH
$USER

Windows examples include:

%PATH%
%USERNAME%
%TEMP%

Environment variable expansion can affect how input is interpreted.

docs.title: Whitespace
docs.text:
Input validation sometimes blocks normal spaces.

Rather than immediately attempting bypasses, determine:

Is whitespace blocked?
Is it encoded?
Is it normalised?
Does the application split arguments itself?
Is a shell involved?

Understanding the parser is more useful than blindly trying alternative syntax.

docs.title: URL Encoding
docs.text:
Characters may be transformed by URL encoding.

Examples:

;       → %3B
&       → %26
|       → %7C
space   → %20

Applications may decode input at different layers:

Browser
 ↓
Reverse Proxy
 ↓
Web Server
 ↓
Framework
 ↓
Application
 ↓
Shell

Determine which layer performs decoding.

docs.title: Double Encoding
docs.text:
Multiple decoding layers may introduce unexpected behaviour.

Conceptually:

%3B

represents:

;

while:

%253B

may become %3B after one decoding stage and ; after another.

Do not assume that the value observed in Burp is exactly what reaches the eventual sink.

docs.title: Command Injection Through File Names
docs.text:
File names are frequently passed to external utilities.

Examples:

Image conversion
PDF conversion
Archive creation
Archive extraction
Antivirus scanning
Media processing
Document processing
Backup operations

A flow might look like:

Upload
  ↓
File Name Stored
  ↓
Processing Worker
  ↓
External Program
  ↓
File Name Used as Argument

This can introduce:

Command injection
Argument injection
Option injection

Start with harmless file names that reveal how special characters are processed.

docs.title: Command Injection Through URLs
docs.text:
Applications may pass URLs to utilities such as:

curl
wget
ffmpeg
git
custom downloaders

Example functionality:

Import from URL
Webhook validation
Image fetch
Repository clone
Remote document processing

These locations may overlap with SSRF testing.

The underlying issue depends on where the user-controlled URL ultimately goes.

docs.title: HTTP Headers
docs.text:
HTTP headers can occasionally reach operating system commands through:

Logging utilities
Monitoring scripts
Administrative tools
Automation
Custom shell scripts
CI/CD pipelines

Interesting headers can include:

User-Agent
Referer
X-Forwarded-For
X-Forwarded-Host
X-Real-IP
Custom application headers

Start with a harmless marker:

User-Agent: AM-CMD-987654

Determine where it travels before performing further testing.

docs.title: JSON Command Injection
docs.text:
Modern APIs commonly receive JSON.

Example:

POST /api/diagnostics HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "host": "127.0.0.1"
}

Test each controllable property independently.

For example:

host
url
file
path
format
command
repository
destination

Do not assume JSON prevents command injection.

docs.title: Command Injection in APIs
docs.text:
Potentially interesting API functionality includes:

Diagnostics
File conversion
PDF generation
Export
Import
Repository operations
Backup
System health checks
Image processing
Network utilities

Map:

Endpoint
 ↓
Parameter
 ↓
Application Function
 ↓
Potential External Process

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Burp Suite is ideal for controlled command injection testing.

Proxy
  ↓
HTTP History
  ↓
Identify Interesting Function
  ↓
Send to Repeater
  ↓
Establish Baseline
  ↓
Test One Character
  ↓
Compare Response
  ↓
Test Execution Hypothesis
  ↓
Confirm Safely

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
For each interesting parameter:

1. Send the original request

2. Record baseline behaviour

3. Insert a unique marker

4. Test individual metacharacters

5. Observe validation and errors

6. Determine likely execution context

7. Perform minimal command execution validation

8. Repeat to confirm

Avoid changing several variables simultaneously.

docs.title: Burp Intruder
docs.text:
Intruder can help determine how the application handles command-related characters.

Example payload position:

POST /api/ping HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

host=127.0.0.1§PAYLOAD§

A small payload set might contain:

;
|
&
'
"
`
$
(
)

Compare:

Status
Length
Words
Lines
Response time

Interesting outliers can then be investigated manually in Repeater.

docs.title: Burp Collaborator Workflow
docs.text:
For suspected blind command injection:

Repeater
   ↓
Create Collaborator Payload
   ↓
Insert Controlled Interaction
   ↓
Send Request
   ↓
Poll Collaborator
   ↓
Interaction Received?
   ↓
Correlate
   ↓
Reproduce

Use unique callback identifiers for each test location.

docs.title: Commix
docs.text:
Commix, short for Command Injection Exploiter, is an automated tool for detecting and testing command injection vulnerabilities.

Project:

https://github.com/commixproject/commix

Commix can complement manual Burp Suite testing when a parameter appears likely to reach an operating system command.

The preferred workflow is:

Manual Discovery
       ↓
Burp Repeater
       ↓
Suspicious Parameter
       ↓
Commix
       ↓
Review Detection
       ↓
Manual Verification
       ↓
Minimal Evidence
       ↓
Report

Do not use automation as a substitute for understanding the affected request.

docs.title: Install Commix
docs.text:
Clone the official repository:

git clone https://github.com/commixproject/commix.git

Enter the directory:

cd commix

Check the available options:

python3 commix.py --help

The repository can later be updated with:

git pull

docs.title: Basic Commix Testing
docs.text:
For an authorised target with a query parameter:

python3 commix.py \
  --url="https://target.example/ping?host=127.0.0.1"

Commix can then analyse the request for command injection behaviour.

When multiple parameters exist, focus testing on the parameter that has already been identified as interesting during manual analysis.

docs.title: Commix With POST Data
docs.text:
For an authorised POST endpoint:

python3 commix.py \
  --url="https://target.example/api/ping" \
  --data="host=127.0.0.1"

This can be useful for:

Forms
API requests
Diagnostic functions
Administrative functions
File-processing requests

docs.title: Commix With Cookies
docs.text:
Authenticated functionality may require session cookies.

Conceptually:

python3 commix.py \
  --url="https://target.example/ping?host=127.0.0.1" \
  --cookie="session=YOUR_SESSION_COOKIE"

Use your authorised assessment session.

Avoid placing real credentials or session values in documentation, screenshots, or repositories.

docs.title: Commix With Headers
docs.text:
Applications may require custom headers.

For example, APIs may require:

Authorization
Content-Type
X-CSRF-Token
Custom application headers

Review Commix's current help output for the supported header options:

python3 commix.py --help

This is preferable to assuming command-line options remain unchanged between releases.

docs.title: Commix and Burp Suite
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Browser
   ↓
Burp Proxy
   ↓
HTTP History
   ↓
Interesting Request
   ↓
Burp Repeater
   ↓
Manual Analysis
   ↓
Commix
   ↓
Manual Verification

Burp should generally be used first to understand:

Endpoint
Method
Parameter
Authentication
Headers
Cookies
Request body
Normal response

Automation becomes significantly more useful after this context is known.

docs.title: Commix and Blind Command Injection
docs.text:
Automated tooling can also help investigate suspected blind command injection.

The overall methodology remains:

Baseline
   ↓
Manual Timing Test
   ↓
Possible Command Execution
   ↓
Commix
   ↓
Compare Detection
   ↓
Manual Confirmation

If the application has unstable response times, do not rely solely on automated timing detection.

docs.title: Commix Results
docs.text:
Do not report a command injection finding solely because Commix reports a potentially injectable parameter.

Verify:

Which endpoint?
Which parameter?
Which technique?
Which operating system?
What behaviour changed?
Can execution be reproduced manually?
What is the actual security impact?

The strongest evidence remains a manually reproducible source-to-execution path.

docs.title: Manual Testing vs Commix
docs.text:
Commix should complement rather than replace manual testing.

Use manual testing for:

Understanding application behaviour
Identifying interesting functionality
Determining parameter context
Character filtering
WAF behaviour
Argument injection
Complex authentication
Second-stage processing
False-positive elimination
Impact validation

Use Commix for:

Targeted automated command injection testing
Testing a suspicious parameter
Technique discovery
Confirming manually observed behaviour
Reducing repetitive testing

A good combination is:

Manual Understanding
        +
Targeted Commix Testing
        +
Manual Verification
        =
Reliable Finding

docs.title: Recommended Command Injection Tool Workflow
docs.text:
Application
                        ↓
                   Burp Proxy
                        ↓
                 HTTP History
                        ↓
             Interesting Function
                        ↓
                  Burp Repeater
                        ↓
               Establish Baseline
                        ↓
               Character Testing
                        ↓
                Suspicious Input?
                        ↓
                 ┌──────┴──────┐
                 │             │
                 ▼             ▼
              Commix      Manual Testing
                 │             │
                 └──────┬──────┘
                        ↓
                 Blind Behaviour?
                        ↓
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              │                   │
              ▼                   ▼
     Burp Collaborator        Interactsh
              │                   │
              └─────────┬─────────┘
                        ↓
                Manual Verification
                        ↓
                Minimal Evidence
                        ↓
                      Report

docs.title: Source Code Review
docs.text:
When source code is available, look for operating system execution APIs.

The general pattern is:

User Input
   ↓
Controller / Route
   ↓
Application Logic
   ↓
Process Execution API
   ↓
Operating System

The objective is to trace attacker-controlled data from source to sink.

docs.title: Python Command Execution Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Python APIs include:

os.system()
os.popen()
subprocess.run()
subprocess.call()
subprocess.Popen()
subprocess.check_output()

Pay particular attention to:

shell=True

Example unsafe pattern:

os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)

A safer pattern is to avoid the shell:

subprocess.run(
    ["ping", "-c", "1", host],
    shell=False
)

Validation should still be applied to host.

docs.title: PHP Command Execution Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting PHP functions include:

system()
exec()
shell_exec()
passthru()
popen()
proc_open()

Example unsafe pattern:

system("ping -c 1 " . $_GET["host"]);

Trace user-controlled input reaching these functions.

docs.title: Java Command Execution Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Java APIs include:

Runtime.getRuntime().exec()
ProcessBuilder

Example:

Runtime.getRuntime().exec(command);

Determine:

Where does command originate?
Is user input concatenated?
Is a shell explicitly invoked?
Are arguments passed separately?

ProcessBuilder is not automatically vulnerable. How it is used matters.

docs.title: .NET Command Execution Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting .NET APIs include:

System.Diagnostics.Process
Process.Start
ProcessStartInfo

Review properties such as:

FileName
Arguments
ArgumentList
UseShellExecute

Trace attacker-controlled values into process execution.

docs.title: Node.js Command Execution Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Node.js APIs include:

child_process.exec()
child_process.execSync()
child_process.spawn()
child_process.spawnSync()
child_process.execFile()

exec() is particularly interesting because it executes a command through a shell.

Example:

exec("ping -c 1 " + req.query.host);

Prefer APIs that execute a known executable with separately supplied arguments where possible.

docs.title: Ruby Command Execution Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Ruby functionality includes:

system
exec
spawn
IO.popen
Backticks
%x{}

Trace user-controlled input reaching these operations.

docs.title: Go Command Execution Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Go functionality includes:

os/exec
exec.Command()

For example:

exec.Command("sh", "-c", userInput)

is significantly more dangerous than executing a fixed program with separate controlled arguments.

docs.title: Search Source Code for Command Execution
docs.text:
A quick first pass can use grep or ripgrep.

Example:

grep -RniE \
'os\.system|os\.popen|subprocess|shell=True|Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder|Process\.Start|child_process|execSync|shell_exec|passthru|proc_open|exec\.Command' \
.

With ripgrep:

rg -n \
'os\.system|os\.popen|subprocess|shell=True|Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder|Process\.Start|child_process|execSync|shell_exec|passthru|proc_open|exec\.Command'

Search results are only potential sinks.

Trace whether user-controlled input reaches them.

docs.title: Source to Sink Analysis
docs.text:
A useful model is:

SOURCE
  ↓
Request Parameter
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Transformation
  ↓
Command Construction
  ↓
SINK
  ↓
Process Execution

For example:

req.query.host
      ↓
Controller
      ↓
Utility Function
      ↓
String Concatenation
      ↓
child_process.exec()

This provides much stronger evidence than merely finding exec() somewhere in the source code.

docs.title: Safe Validation Commands
docs.text:
During authorised testing, use minimal commands that demonstrate execution without changing the system.

Linux examples:

id

whoami

hostname

Windows examples:

whoami

hostname

The goal is:

Proof of execution

not:

Persistence
Privilege escalation
Data destruction

Stop when sufficient evidence exists.

docs.title: Determine Execution Context
docs.text:
If command execution is confirmed, determine the security context only to the extent required to understand impact.

Potential information includes:

Operating system
Process user
Hostname
Container environment
Application directory

For example:

whoami

or:

id

may be sufficient.

Avoid unnecessary enumeration once the vulnerability has been demonstrated.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
Modern applications frequently run inside containers.

Command execution might therefore initially occur inside:

Docker
Kubernetes workload
Container runtime
Application sandbox

Command injection inside a container is still a serious vulnerability.

Do not assume:

Container = no impact

Impact depends on:

Container privileges
Mounted volumes
Secrets
Network access
Service accounts
Runtime configuration
Host exposure

Do not attempt container escape unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: WAF Behaviour
docs.text:
A WAF may block common command injection syntax.

Indicators include:

403
406
Connection reset
Generic security page
Different response length
Parameter-specific blocking

Separate:

WAF Behaviour

from:

Application Behaviour

A blocked semicolon does not prove that the underlying command construction is safe.

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
Applications may allow only specific input formats.

For example, a host parameter might be intended to accept:

IPv4
IPv6
DNS hostnames

Strong allowlist validation can substantially reduce risk.

For an IPv4-only field, input should be parsed and validated as an actual IP address rather than treated as an arbitrary string.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Potential causes of false positives include:

Normal application latency
Backend timeouts
DNS resolution delays
Input validation
WAF behaviour
Application errors
Rate limiting
Asynchronous processing
Network instability

A reliable finding should demonstrate repeatable command-dependent behaviour.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A strong command injection finding should establish:

SOURCE
  ↓
Affected Input
  ↓
Command Construction
  ↓
Operating System Execution
  ↓
Observable Evidence
  ↓
Security Impact

For example:

host parameter
      ↓
Diagnostic endpoint
      ↓
Unsafely constructed ping command
      ↓
Shell execution
      ↓
Controlled timing difference

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful evidence includes:

Affected endpoint
HTTP method
Affected parameter
Authentication requirement
Original request
Modified request
Baseline response
Modified response
Response timing
Command output if visible
Callback evidence if used
Commix output if used
Operating system if known
Execution user if necessary
Required privileges
Relevant screenshot

Keep evidence minimal.

docs.title: Command Injection Reporting
docs.text:
A report should explain:

Which input is affected
How the input reaches an operating system command
Whether a shell is involved
How execution was confirmed
What privileges the application process has
What an attacker could achieve
What evidence was collected
How the issue should be remediated

docs.title: Example Finding Structure
docs.text:
Title
OS Command Injection in Network Diagnostic Function

Affected Endpoint
POST /api/diagnostics/ping

Affected Parameter
host

Authentication Required
Yes

Description
The application incorporates the host parameter into an operating
system command without safely separating user-controlled data from
the command structure.

Controlled testing demonstrated that additional operating system
commands could be executed in the context of the application process.

Impact
An attacker with access to the affected functionality may be able
to execute operating system commands with the privileges of the
application service account.

Recommendation
Avoid constructing operating system commands using user-controlled
strings. Invoke the required executable directly with separately
supplied arguments and apply strict allowlist validation to the
host parameter.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
The preferred remediation is:

Do not invoke a shell unless absolutely necessary.

Prefer:

Known Executable
      +
Separate Arguments

instead of:

Constructed Shell Command String

Additional controls include:

Strict allowlist validation
Safe process execution APIs
Argument separation
Least privilege
Container isolation
Application sandboxing
Restricted network access
Secure error handling
Monitoring

docs.title: Avoid Shell Execution
docs.text:
Unsafe conceptual pattern:

os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)

Better:

subprocess.run(
    ["ping", "-c", "1", host],
    shell=False
)

The input should also be validated as the expected type.

For example, if only IP addresses are expected:

Input
 ↓
IP Address Parser
 ↓
Valid?
 ↓
Pass as Separate Argument

docs.title: Allowlist Validation
docs.text:
If the application expects a particular format, enforce that format.

Examples:

IP address
Hostname
File extension
Known output format
Known command option

Avoid relying solely on blocklists such as:

Remove ;
Remove &
Remove |

Shell syntax is complex and platform-dependent.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
The application process should run with the minimum permissions required.

Avoid unnecessary:

root
Administrator
SYSTEM
Privileged containers
Writable system directories
Sensitive mounted volumes
Cloud administrative credentials

Least privilege does not fix command injection, but it can significantly reduce impact.

docs.title: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
docs.text:
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a browser security mechanism that allows a web application to selectively permit other origins to access its resources.

CORS is not a vulnerability by itself.

A vulnerability occurs when an application's CORS policy incorrectly trusts an attacker-controlled or otherwise untrusted origin, potentially allowing that origin to read sensitive responses from the victim's browser.

A simplified model is:

Attacker-Controlled Origin
          ↓
Victim Browser
          ↓
Cross-Origin Request
          ↓
Target Application
          ↓
CORS Policy Evaluated
          ↓
Browser Allows Response?
          ↓
Sensitive Data Read

The central testing question is:

Can an untrusted origin cause a victim's browser to make an authenticated or otherwise sensitive request and then read the response?

Authorised Security Testing

Perform CORS testing only against applications included in the authorised assessment scope. Use controlled accounts and controlled origins when demonstrating cross-origin access to sensitive information.

docs.title: Same-Origin Policy
docs.text:
Understanding CORS requires understanding the Same-Origin Policy.

The Same-Origin Policy restricts how content from one origin can interact with resources from another origin.

An origin consists primarily of:

Scheme
Host
Port

For example:

https://app.example.com:443

contains:

Scheme → https
Host   → app.example.com
Port   → 443

Changing one of these components can create a different origin.

docs.title: Origin Examples
docs.text:
Consider:

https://example.com

The following are different origins:

http://example.com
https://sub.example.com
https://example.com:8443
https://another.example

Even though some may belong to the same organisation, they are not necessarily the same browser origin.

docs.title: Same-Origin Policy Model
docs.text:
Without CORS:

Origin A
   ↓
JavaScript Request
   ↓
Origin B
   ↓
Response
   ↓
Browser Blocks Origin A
from Reading Response

The request may still reach the server.

The Same-Origin Policy primarily controls whether the requesting JavaScript can access the response.

docs.title: What CORS Changes
docs.text:
CORS allows the server to tell the browser:

This origin is permitted to read this response.

For example:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://trusted.example

The browser compares the requesting origin with the value returned by the server.

If the policy permits the origin, JavaScript may be allowed to access the response.

docs.title: Basic CORS Request
docs.text:
Suppose JavaScript running on:

https://client.example

requests:

https://api.example/account

The browser may send:

GET /account HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example
Origin: https://client.example

The server may respond:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://client.example

The browser then determines whether the response can be exposed to the calling JavaScript.

docs.title: Origin Header
docs.text:
The primary request header during CORS testing is:

Origin:

Example:

Origin: https://example.com

When testing manually with Burp Suite, changing the Origin header is one of the easiest ways to understand the server's CORS policy.

docs.title: Access-Control-Allow-Origin
docs.text:
The most important response header is:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin:

Examples include:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://trusted.example

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null

The security implications depend on the complete policy and the type of resource being accessed.

docs.title: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
docs.text:
Another important response header is:

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

This indicates that the response may be exposed to credentialed cross-origin requests when the rest of the CORS requirements are satisfied.

Credentials may include browser-managed authentication information such as cookies.

A particularly important combination to investigate is:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker-controlled.example
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

if the origin is not legitimately trusted.

docs.title: Important CORS Headers
docs.text:
During testing, look for:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Access-Control-Allow-Methods
Access-Control-Allow-Headers
Access-Control-Expose-Headers
Access-Control-Max-Age
Vary

Each reveals part of the application's CORS behaviour.

docs.title: Access-Control-Allow-Methods
docs.text:
Example:

Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE

This tells the browser which methods may be permitted for relevant cross-origin requests.

This header alone does not establish a vulnerability.

docs.title: Access-Control-Allow-Headers
docs.text:
Example:

Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type

This can permit requests containing headers that are not automatically allowed in simple cross-origin requests.

docs.title: Access-Control-Expose-Headers
docs.text:
Browsers expose only certain response headers to cross-origin JavaScript by default.

An application can expose additional headers:

Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Request-ID

or:

Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Custom-Header

Review whether sensitive information is placed in exposed response headers.

docs.title: Access-Control-Max-Age
docs.text:
Example:

Access-Control-Max-Age: 600

This allows the browser to cache the result of a preflight request for a period of time.

It is generally not a vulnerability by itself.

docs.title: Vary: Origin
docs.text:
When a server dynamically returns different CORS responses depending on the request origin, responses should generally account for the Origin header in caching behaviour.

For example:

Vary: Origin

This can be important when responses pass through:

CDNs
Reverse proxies
Shared caches

Incorrect caching can create unexpected cross-origin behaviour.

docs.title: Simple Requests
docs.text:
Some cross-origin requests can be sent without a preflight.

These are often referred to as:

Simple requests

A simplified example:

GET /profile HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Origin: https://client.example

The server responds normally.

The browser then decides whether JavaScript is allowed to read the response.

docs.title: Preflight Requests
docs.text:
Certain cross-origin requests cause the browser to send an OPTIONS request first.

This is called a:

Preflight request

A simplified flow is:

JavaScript
    ↓
Browser
    ↓
OPTIONS Request
    ↓
Server CORS Policy
    ↓
Browser Evaluates Policy
    ↓
Actual Request

docs.title: Example Preflight
docs.text:
Request:

OPTIONS /api/account HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Origin: https://client.example
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type

Possible response:

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://client.example
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT
