Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type

The browser evaluates this response before deciding whether to make the actual request.

docs.title: Access-Control-Request-Method
docs.text:
During a preflight, the browser may send:

Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT

This tells the server which method the subsequent request intends to use.

docs.title: Access-Control-Request-Headers
docs.text:
The browser may also send:

Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, content-type

The server then determines whether those headers are allowed.

docs.title: CORS Testing Methodology
docs.text:
A structured workflow looks like:

Identify Endpoint
      ↓
Determine Whether Response Is Sensitive
      ↓
Add Origin Header
      ↓
Observe CORS Response
      ↓
Test Trusted Origin
      ↓
Test Untrusted Origin
      ↓
Test Origin Validation
      ↓
Check Credentials
      ↓
Check null Origin
      ↓
Check Subdomains
      ↓
Check Preflight Behaviour
      ↓
Verify in Browser
      ↓
Assess Impact

docs.title: Start With Sensitive Endpoints
docs.text:
CORS matters most when the affected response contains information that should not be readable by an untrusted origin.

Prioritise endpoints such as:

/api/account
/api/profile
/api/user
/api/me
/api/settings
/api/orders
/api/payments
/api/messages
/api/admin
/api/notifications
/api/documents

The exact endpoints depend on the application.

docs.title: Baseline Request
docs.text:
Start with the normal request.

Example:

GET /api/account HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=CONTROLLED_SESSION

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "username": "test-user",
    "email": "test@example.com"
}

Establish that the endpoint contains information worth protecting.

docs.title: Add an Origin Header
docs.text:
Now add:

Origin: https://example.com

Request:

GET /api/account HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Origin: https://example.com
Cookie: session=CONTROLLED_SESSION

Inspect the response.

docs.title: Secure Example
docs.text:
The application may return:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

without:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin:

The server still returns the response to Burp because Burp is not enforcing browser CORS restrictions.

A browser, however, would not expose that response to JavaScript from the untrusted origin.

This distinction is critical.

docs.title: Potentially Vulnerable Example
docs.text:
Request:

GET /api/account HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Origin: https://example.com
Cookie: session=CONTROLLED_SESSION

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

If:

https://example.com

represents an untrusted or attacker-controlled origin, investigate further.

docs.title: Origin Reflection
docs.text:
One common implementation pattern is reflecting the supplied Origin value.

For example:

Request:

Origin: https://random.example

Response:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://random.example

Then:

Origin: https://another.example

Response:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://another.example

This suggests the server may be dynamically reflecting arbitrary origins.

docs.title: Origin Reflection Workflow
docs.text:
Test several clearly distinct origins:

https://example.com
https://test.example
https://untrusted.invalid

Observe whether:

No origins are reflected
Only trusted origins are reflected
All origins are reflected
Some pattern is reflected

Do not infer arbitrary reflection from a single request.

docs.title: Arbitrary Origin Reflection
docs.text:
A dangerous policy may conceptually behave like:

Request Origin
      ↓
Copy Value
      ↓
Access-Control-Allow-Origin

without validating whether the origin belongs to a trusted allowlist.

Example:

Origin: https://untrusted.example

Response:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://untrusted.example
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

If sensitive authenticated data is accessible, this may allow cross-origin data theft.

docs.title: Credentialed CORS
docs.text:
Credentialed CORS is particularly important.

A browser request may conceptually look like:

fetch("https://target.example/api/account", {
    credentials: "include"
});

The target must return an appropriate CORS policy before the browser exposes the response to the calling origin.

If an attacker-controlled origin is trusted and credentials are included, sensitive authenticated responses may become readable.

docs.title: Browser Proof of Concept
docs.text:
For an authorised controlled test, a simple page can demonstrate whether a target response is readable cross-origin.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">

<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>CORS Test</title>
</head>

<body>

<h1>Authorised CORS Test</h1>

<pre id="output">Waiting...</pre>

<script>

fetch("https://target.example/api/account", {
    credentials: "include"
})
.then(response => response.text())
.then(data => {
    document.getElementById("output").textContent = data;
})
.catch(error => {
    document.getElementById("output").textContent = error;
});

</script>

</body>

</html>

Use this only with controlled accounts and controlled origins.

The objective is to demonstrate whether the browser exposes the response, not to collect information belonging to other users.

docs.title: Why Browser Verification Matters
docs.text:
Burp Suite does not enforce the Same-Origin Policy.

Therefore:

Burp receives response

does not mean:

Cross-origin JavaScript can read response

The browser is the security enforcement point.

A good workflow is:

Burp
 ↓
Understand Policy
 ↓
Browser
 ↓
Verify Exploitability

docs.title: Wildcard Origin
docs.text:
An application may return:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

This allows any origin to access certain cross-origin responses.

However, the security impact depends on the resource and credential requirements.

docs.title: Wildcard and Credentials
docs.text:
Browsers do not permit the combination:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

to provide credentialed access in the same way as an explicitly allowed origin.

Therefore, do not automatically report:

ACAO: *

as a critical CORS vulnerability.

Determine:

Is the endpoint public?

Does it contain sensitive information?

Does it require credentials?

Are bearer tokens used separately?

Can an attacker access anything they should not?

docs.title: Public APIs
docs.text:
A public endpoint may intentionally return:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

Example:

Public product catalogue
Public documentation
Public status data
Public search API

This is not necessarily a vulnerability.

Always evaluate the sensitivity of the response.

docs.title: Bearer Tokens
docs.text:
Some applications authenticate using:

Authorization: Bearer TOKEN

instead of cookies.

Cross-origin exploitation may then depend on whether an attacker can cause the browser to include the required token.

If the token is only accessible to trusted JavaScript and not automatically attached cross-origin, a permissive CORS response may have different practical impact.

Analyse the complete authentication model.

docs.title: Testing Trusted Origins
docs.text:
Determine which origins are intentionally trusted.

Examples:

https://app.example.com
https://portal.example.com
https://admin.example.com

Then test how the application validates them.

The goal is not simply to enumerate accepted strings.

The goal is to understand the trust model.

docs.title: Weak Origin Validation
docs.text:
A weak implementation may use string operations such as:

startsWith()
endsWith()
contains()
regular expressions

instead of properly parsing the origin.

This can create trust-boundary mistakes.

docs.title: Prefix Matching
docs.text:
Suppose the intended trusted origin is:

https://trusted.example

A weak policy might conceptually accept anything beginning with:

https://trusted.example

The tester should determine whether the implementation validates the complete parsed origin or only a string prefix.

docs.title: Suffix Matching
docs.text:
Similarly, an implementation may attempt to trust:

example.com

using a suffix check.

The important question is whether hostname boundaries are correctly enforced.

Do not assume:

contains example.com

means:

is a subdomain of example.com

docs.title: Origin Parsing
docs.text:
An origin should be interpreted using proper URL parsing.

Security decisions should consider:

Scheme
Hostname
Port

rather than arbitrary string fragments.

docs.title: Subdomain Trust
docs.text:
Some applications intentionally trust:

*.example.com

This should immediately raise another question:

Are all subdomains equally trusted?

Potential subdomains may include:

Production applications
Development environments
Legacy systems
Marketing sites
User-generated content
Third-party services
Abandoned DNS records

A broad subdomain trust policy can become dangerous if one trusted subdomain is compromised or attacker-controlled.

docs.title: CORS and Subdomain Takeover
docs.text:
Consider:

Target API trusts *.example.com

and:

old.example.com

is vulnerable to subdomain takeover.

Conceptually:

Attacker Controls old.example.com
          ↓
Origin Is Still Trusted
          ↓
Victim Visits Attacker-Controlled Subdomain
          ↓
Cross-Origin Request to API
          ↓
API Trusts Origin
          ↓
Sensitive Response Exposed

This demonstrates why CORS trust should not automatically extend to every organisational subdomain.

docs.title: CORS and XSS on Trusted Origins
docs.text:
A similar issue can occur if:

API trusts portal.example.com

and:

portal.example.com

contains an exploitable XSS vulnerability.

Conceptually:

XSS on Trusted Origin
       ↓
JavaScript Executes
       ↓
Trusted Origin Makes API Request
       ↓
CORS Allows Response
       ↓
Sensitive Data Accessible

The CORS policy may be functioning as configured, but the overall trust model may still create a vulnerability chain.

docs.title: null Origin
docs.text:
Browsers can sometimes send:

Origin: null

in certain contexts.

Therefore test:

Origin: null

Request:

GET /api/account HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Origin: null
Cookie: session=CONTROLLED_SESSION

Potentially interesting response:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

This deserves further investigation.

docs.title: What Can Produce a null Origin?
docs.text:
Depending on browser behaviour and context, a null origin may be associated with situations such as:

Sandboxed documents
Certain local files
Opaque origins
Data URLs
Some isolated browser contexts

Because of these possibilities, blindly trusting:

null

can be dangerous.

docs.title: Testing null Origin
docs.text:
Do not report:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null

alone.

Determine whether a practical browser context can generate the required origin and read the sensitive response.

Again:

Header observation
        ↓
Browser verification
        ↓
Impact

docs.title: CORS and HTTPS
docs.text:
Suppose:

https://api.example.com

trusts:

http://trusted.example.com

The HTTP origin lacks transport security.

This can weaken the overall trust model because an attacker capable of interfering with the HTTP connection may potentially influence content loaded from that origin.

Avoid trusting insecure origins for sensitive credentialed CORS access.

docs.title: CORS and Mixed Trust
docs.text:
A policy may trust:

https://example.com
http://example.com

These are different origins.

The security properties are also different.

Treat scheme as part of the trust boundary.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
These are different origins:

https://example.com
https://example.com:8443

An application that dynamically trusts arbitrary ports on a hostname should be reviewed carefully.

Different ports may expose completely different services.

docs.title: Preflight Testing
docs.text:
Do not stop after testing simple GET requests.

If the application uses:

PUT
PATCH
DELETE
Custom headers
Authorization headers
JSON content types

test preflight behaviour.

docs.title: Example Preflight Test
docs.text:
OPTIONS /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Origin: https://example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type

Inspect:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Methods
Access-Control-Allow-Headers
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials

docs.title: Preflight Does Not Equal Authorisation
docs.text:
A permissive preflight response is not a replacement for server-side authorisation.

For example:

Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE

does not mean every user is authorised to use those methods.

CORS controls browser cross-origin access.

Authorisation controls whether the user may perform the action.

Refer to:

Authorisation Testing

docs.title: CORS and CSRF
docs.text:
CORS and CSRF are frequently confused.

CORS controls:

Can cross-origin JavaScript read the response?

CSRF concerns:

Can another site cause the victim's browser to perform an unwanted authenticated action?

A request can sometimes be sent cross-site even when its response cannot be read.

Therefore:

No CORS vulnerability

does not automatically mean:

No CSRF vulnerability

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: CORS and SameSite
docs.text:
SameSite cookie attributes can influence whether cookies are included in cross-site requests.

Possible values include:

Strict
Lax
None

However, CORS and SameSite solve different problems.

A proper assessment should examine:

Cookie policy
CORS policy
CSRF controls
Origin relationships
Browser behaviour

together.

docs.title: CORS and Clickjacking
docs.text:
CORS does not prevent Clickjacking.

CORS:

Controls JavaScript access to cross-origin responses

Clickjacking:

Controls whether a user can be tricked into interacting with a framed interface

A site can have strict CORS and still be vulnerable to Clickjacking.

Refer to:

Clickjacking

docs.title: CORS and SOP
docs.text:
CORS relaxes parts of the Same-Origin Policy.

It should therefore be considered a:

Trust declaration

rather than merely a collection of HTTP headers.

When an application returns:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://portal.example

it is effectively saying:

I trust JavaScript executing at portal.example
to access this response.

That trust should be justified.

docs.title: CORS and APIs
docs.text:
CORS is particularly common with APIs.

Architecture:

Frontend
   ↓
https://app.example.com

API
   ↓
https://api.example.com

Because these are different origins, the API may need to permit the frontend using CORS.

A secure configuration might be:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

provided:

app.example.com

is the intended trusted application.

docs.title: Multiple Frontends
docs.text:
Some APIs legitimately support several origins:

https://app.example.com
https://portal.example.com
https://admin.example.com

The server should validate the request origin against an explicit trusted list.

Conceptually:

Request Origin
      ↓
Exact Allowlist
      ↓
Trusted?
  ↓         ↓
Yes        No
 ↓          ↓
Return      Do Not Return
ACAO        ACAO

docs.title: Development Origins
docs.text:
Look for development origins such as:

http://localhost
http://127.0.0.1
https://dev.example.com
https://test.example.com
https://staging.example.com

These may have been left in production CORS allowlists.

Their risk depends on whether an attacker can actually control or meaningfully use the trusted origin.

docs.title: Localhost Trust
docs.text:
Applications sometimes allow:

http://localhost

for development purposes.

Whether this is exploitable depends on:

Exact origin matching
Port restrictions
Victim environment
Local services
Browser behaviour

Treat it as a trust-boundary question rather than automatically reporting it.

docs.title: Regex-Based CORS Policies
docs.text:
Some applications use regular expressions.

Conceptually:

if origin matches regex:
    allow origin

Review:

Anchoring
Escaping
Hostname boundaries
Scheme validation
Port validation
Case handling

Regex-based origin validation can easily become broader than intended.

docs.title: Case Sensitivity
docs.text:
Hostnames are case-insensitive, while other URL components may have different parsing rules.

Security checks should rely on proper URL/origin parsing rather than assumptions about raw string casing.

docs.title: Trailing Dots
docs.text:
DNS names can sometimes be represented with a trailing dot.

Example:

example.com.

Different components may canonicalise hostnames differently.

This can matter where:

Validation component

and:

Browser/server interpretation

do not agree.

The broader lesson is:

Validate canonical parsed origins, not hand-written string variations.

docs.title: Redirects and CORS
docs.text:
Cross-origin requests may encounter redirects.

Conceptually:

Attacker Origin
      ↓
Request
      ↓
Endpoint A
      ↓
Redirect
      ↓
Endpoint B

Browser CORS behaviour around redirects can affect whether the final response is exposed.

Test the actual browser flow instead of reasoning only from individual HTTP responses.

docs.title: CORS and Open Redirect
docs.text:
An Open Redirect on a trusted origin may become relevant in broader trust chains, but it does not automatically bypass CORS.

CORS decisions are based on origins and browser behaviour.

Do not assume:

Trusted redirect

means:

Trusted CORS destination

Verify the complete flow.

Refer to:

Open Redirect

docs.title: CORS and Web Cache Poisoning
docs.text:
Dynamic CORS responses may interact with shared caching.

Example:

Request Origin
      ↓
Server Reflects Trusted Origin
      ↓
Response Cached
      ↓
Another Request Receives Cached Headers

The presence or absence of:

Vary: Origin

can be relevant.

This should be investigated as part of cache behaviour rather than assuming a vulnerability from the header alone.

Refer to:

Web Cache Poisoning

once that page is added.

docs.title: CORS and CDN Configuration
docs.text:
CORS may be implemented at multiple layers:

Application
Reverse proxy
API gateway
CDN
Load balancer
Web server

This can create inconsistencies.

For example:

Application rejects origin
       ↓
CDN adds ACAO header

or:

Application returns ACAO
       ↓
Proxy overwrites it

Always inspect the final response received by the browser.

docs.title: Endpoint-Specific CORS
docs.text:
Do not assume one CORS policy applies to the entire application.

For example:

/                     → No CORS
/api/public            → ACAO: *
/api/account           → Trusted origins
/api/admin             → Misconfigured reflection

Test endpoints individually.

docs.title: Method-Specific CORS
docs.text:
Policies may also differ by method.

Example:

GET     → Allowed
POST    → Allowed
PUT     → Restricted
DELETE  → Restricted

Preflight testing can reveal these differences.

docs.title: Error Responses
docs.text:
Test CORS behaviour on:

200
201
204
400
401
403
404
500

Error responses may expose:

Stack traces
Internal identifiers
Validation details
Debug information

and may use different CORS middleware.

docs.title: Unauthenticated vs Authenticated
docs.text:
Test both states.

Example matrix:

Endpoint Unauthenticated Authenticated /api/public Public Public /api/profile 401 Sensitive data /api/settings 401 Sensitive data /api/admin 403 Role-dependent

CORS impact is often much greater for authenticated responses.

docs.title: Role-Based Testing
docs.text:
Use controlled accounts representing different roles where authorised:

Normal user
Privileged user
Administrator
Support user

The same endpoint may expose different data depending on role.

A CORS issue affecting an administrative response may have greater impact.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
A practical Burp workflow:

Proxy
  ↓
Browse Application
  ↓
HTTP History
  ↓
Identify API Requests
  ↓
Send to Repeater
  ↓
Add Origin
  ↓
Observe ACAO
  ↓
Change Origin
  ↓
Check Credentials
  ↓
Test null
  ↓
Test Trusted-Origin Boundaries
  ↓
Check Preflight
  ↓
Verify in Browser

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Suppose the baseline request is:

GET /api/me HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=CONTROLLED_SESSION

Add:

Origin: https://example.com

Then inspect:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Vary

Repeat with multiple origins.

docs.title: Suggested Origin Test Set
docs.text:
A useful controlled set is:

https://example.com
https://untrusted.invalid
null
https://subdomain.target.example
http://target.example
https://target.example:8443

The objective is to understand:

Exact match?
Subdomain match?
Scheme validation?
Port validation?
null trusted?
Arbitrary reflection?

Do not treat this as a blind payload list.

Each test should answer a specific policy question.

docs.title: Burp Intruder
docs.text:
For applications with many endpoints, Burp Intruder can help compare CORS behaviour.

Potential payload positions include:

Origin: §https://example.com§

A controlled list can contain different origin classes.

Review:

Status code
Response length
ACAO value
ACAC value
Vary header

Avoid high-volume testing when a small number of targeted requests is sufficient.

docs.title: Burp Extensions
docs.text:
Burp extensions can assist with identifying CORS misconfigurations.

However:

Automated extension output should be treated as a lead, not proof of exploitability.

Always verify:

Sensitive endpoint
Trusted origin behaviour
Credential requirements
Browser exploitability
Impact

manually.

docs.title: Browser Developer Tools
docs.text:
Use browser Developer Tools to inspect:

Console
Network
Application
Storage
Cookies

CORS failures often appear clearly in the Console.

The browser may indicate that a response was blocked because the required CORS header was missing or invalid.

docs.title: Browser Console vs Network
docs.text:
A useful distinction:

Network tab

may show that the HTTP request occurred.

But:

JavaScript

may still be unable to read the response.

This demonstrates the difference between:

Request transmission

and:

Response exposure

docs.title: JavaScript Fetch Test
docs.text:
A simple controlled test:

fetch("https://target.example/api/me", {
    credentials: "include"
})
.then(r => r.text())
.then(data => console.log(data))
.catch(error => console.error(error));

The browser determines whether the calling origin may access the returned data.

docs.title: XMLHttpRequest
docs.text:
Legacy applications may use XMLHttpRequest.

Conceptually:

var xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();

xhr.open(
    "GET",
    "https://target.example/api/me",
    true
);

xhr.withCredentials = true;

xhr.onreadystatechange = function () {
    if (xhr.readyState === 4) {
        console.log(xhr.responseText);
    }
};

xhr.send();

The same CORS principles apply.

docs.title: Controlled CORS PoC
docs.text:
For a controlled account:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">

<head>
<meta charset="UTF-8">
<title>CORS PoC</title>
</head>

<body>

<h1>Authorised CORS Test</h1>

<button id="test">Test CORS</button>

<pre id="result"></pre>

<script>

document.getElementById("test").addEventListener("click", async () => {

    const output = document.getElementById("result");

    try {

        const response = await fetch(
            "https://target.example/api/me",
            {
                credentials: "include"
            }
        );

        const data = await response.text();

        output.textContent = data;

    } catch (error) {

        output.textContent = String(error);

    }

});

</script>

</body>

</html>

This demonstrates whether the response is actually accessible from the test origin.

docs.title: Serving the PoC
docs.text:
Save as:

cors-poc.html

Serve it from a controlled origin.

For a basic local test:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Then browse to:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/cors-poc.html

Remember that:

http://127.0.0.1:8000

becomes the test origin.

The target must trust that exact origin for the browser to expose the response.

docs.title: Credentials in Fetch
docs.text:
The important option for cookie-based authenticated testing is:

credentials: "include"

Without it, cross-origin requests may not include credentials in the manner required by the test.

Browser cookie policies still apply.

docs.title: Third-Party Cookie Restrictions
docs.text:
Modern browsers increasingly restrict third-party cookies and cross-site tracking.

Therefore a CORS configuration that appears theoretically vulnerable may behave differently depending on:

Browser
Cookie attributes
SameSite
Storage partitioning
Third-party cookie settings
Site relationships

Always test the actual browser environment relevant to the application.

docs.title: CORS Testing Matrix
docs.text:
Create a matrix such as:

Endpoint Origin ACAO ACAC Sensitive Data Browser Readable /api/public https://example.com * No No Yes /api/me https://example.com Reflected Yes Yes Yes /api/me null Missing No Yes No /api/admin https://example.com Missing No Yes No

This makes the actual risk much easier to understand.

docs.title: Origin Validation Matrix
docs.text:
You can also map the policy:

Origin Type Example Allowed Exact trusted https://app.target.example Yes Random external https://example.com No Target subdomain https://test.target.example ? HTTP version http://app.target.example ? Alternate port https://app.target.example:8443 ? null null ?

This is more useful than randomly modifying origins.

docs.title: Common Misconfiguration: Arbitrary Reflection
docs.text:
Pattern:

Origin supplied
      ↓
Server reflects it
      ↓
Credentials allowed

Example:

Origin: https://example.com

Response:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

If the endpoint contains sensitive authenticated information, this can be serious.

docs.title: Common Misconfiguration: Broad Subdomain Trust
docs.text:
Pattern:

*.target.example

is trusted.

Potential problem:

Attacker gains control of one subdomain
          ↓
Subdomain is trusted by API
          ↓
CORS trust compromised

Review whether every allowed subdomain has an equivalent security posture.

docs.title: Common Misconfiguration: null Trusted
docs.text:
Pattern:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

Investigate whether a browser context under attacker influence can generate a null origin and access the response.

docs.title: Common Misconfiguration: Insecure Trusted Origin
docs.text:
Pattern:

HTTPS API
   ↓
Trusts
   ↓
HTTP Origin

An insecure trusted origin can undermine the security assumptions of the CORS policy.

docs.title: Common Misconfiguration: Development Origin
docs.text:
Pattern:

Production API
     ↓
Trusts
     ↓
Development / Staging Origin

Investigate whether that environment is:

Still active
Less protected
Externally accessible
Attacker-controllable

docs.title: Common Misconfiguration: Incorrect Regex
docs.text:
Pattern:

Origin
 ↓
Weak regex
 ↓
Unexpected origin accepted

Review regex boundaries and URL parsing.

docs.title: Common Misconfiguration: Trusting Every Origin
docs.text:
Some applications effectively implement:

Origin received?
      ↓
Yes
      ↓
Return same Origin

This defeats the purpose of restricting cross-origin access.

docs.title: CORS Is Not an Access Control Mechanism
docs.text:
CORS should never be used as server-side authorisation.

A server must still enforce:

Authentication
Authorisation
Object-level permissions
Function-level permissions

An API endpoint should not reason:

Request came from trusted Origin
therefore user is authorised

The Origin header is not an authentication credential.

docs.title: Origin Header Trust
docs.text:
Applications may use:

Origin:

as one signal in CSRF protection.

That is different from treating it as an identity mechanism.

Security decisions should clearly distinguish:

Browser origin validation

from:

User authentication and authorisation

docs.title: CORS and Mobile Applications
docs.text:
Native mobile applications are not governed by browser CORS in the same way as ordinary browser JavaScript.

Therefore:

CORS

should not be relied upon to prevent direct API access from arbitrary clients.

Server-side security controls remain essential.

docs.title: CORS and curl
docs.text:
Tools such as:

curl
Burp Suite
Postman
Python requests

do not enforce browser CORS restrictions.

For example:

curl \
  -H "Origin: https://example.com" \
  -i \
  https://target.example/api/me

is useful for inspecting headers.

But it does not demonstrate that a browser can exploit the policy.

docs.title: curl Example
docs.text:
curl -s -D - \
  -H "Origin: https://example.com" \
  -o /dev/null \
  https://target.example/api/me

Look for:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Vary

docs.title: OPTIONS with curl
docs.text:
A preflight can be inspected using:

curl -i \
  -X OPTIONS \
  -H "Origin: https://example.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type" \
  https://target.example/api/profile

This is useful for understanding the policy before browser verification.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
[ ] Identify API endpoints
[ ] Identify sensitive responses
[ ] Identify authenticated endpoints
[ ] Identify privileged endpoints
[ ] Identify CORS headers
[ ] Identify frontend/API origin relationships

docs.title: Origin Testing
docs.text:
[ ] Test intended trusted origin
[ ] Test unrelated external origin
[ ] Test null origin
[ ] Test trusted subdomains
[ ] Test HTTP vs HTTPS
[ ] Test alternate ports
[ ] Review origin parsing

docs.title: Response Headers
docs.text:
[ ] Access-Control-Allow-Origin
[ ] Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
[ ] Access-Control-Allow-Methods
[ ] Access-Control-Allow-Headers
[ ] Access-Control-Expose-Headers
[ ] Access-Control-Max-Age
[ ] Vary: Origin

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
[ ] Test unauthenticated response
[ ] Test authenticated response
[ ] Check cookie authentication
[ ] Check bearer-token authentication
[ ] Review SameSite cookies
[ ] Review third-party cookie behaviour

docs.title: Preflight
docs.text:
[ ] Test OPTIONS
[ ] Test allowed methods
[ ] Test allowed headers
[ ] Test custom headers
[ ] Test JSON requests
[ ] Test privileged methods

docs.title: Trust Relationships
docs.text:
[ ] Review all trusted origins
[ ] Review development origins
[ ] Review staging origins
[ ] Review subdomain trust
[ ] Review third-party origins
[ ] Review HTTP origins
[ ] Consider takeover risk
[ ] Consider XSS on trusted origins

docs.title: Browser Verification
docs.text:
[ ] Create controlled PoC
[ ] Use controlled account
[ ] Use controlled origin
[ ] Verify browser sends request
[ ] Verify credentials
[ ] Verify JavaScript can read response
[ ] Record Console output
[ ] Record Network behaviour

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
[ ] Identify exposed information
[ ] Identify affected role
[ ] Determine whether credentials are required
[ ] Determine attacker origin requirements
[ ] Determine user interaction
[ ] Determine realistic exploitation
[ ] Avoid hypothetical severity inflation

docs.title: CORS Decision Tree
docs.text:
Sensitive Endpoint
       ↓
Send Origin Header
       ↓
ACAO Returned?
       ↓
      NO
       ↓
No CORS Access Through Tested Origin

       OR

      YES
       ↓
Is Origin Trusted?
       ↓
      YES
       ↓
Expected Policy?
       ↓
Review Trust Boundary

       OR

      NO
       ↓
Untrusted Origin Allowed
       ↓
Credentials Required?
       ↓
      YES
       ↓
ACAC true?
       ↓
      YES
       ↓
Will Browser Send Credentials?
       ↓
      YES
       ↓
Can JavaScript Read Response?
       ↓
      YES
       ↓
Sensitive Data Exposed?
       ↓
      YES
       ↓
CORS Vulnerability Confirmed
       ↓
Assess Impact
       ↓
Report

docs.title: CORS Quick Reference
docs.text:
REQUEST

Origin: https://example.com

IMPORTANT RESPONSE HEADERS

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Access-Control-Allow-Methods
Access-Control-Allow-Headers
Access-Control-Expose-Headers
Vary

HIGH-VALUE CONDITION

Untrusted Origin
       +
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
       +
Sensitive Authenticated Response
       +
Browser Can Read Response

TEST ORIGINS

https://example.com
https://untrusted.invalid
null
https://subdomain.target.example
http://target.example
https://target.example:8443

PREFLIGHT

OPTIONS
Origin
Access-Control-Request-Method
Access-Control-Request-Headers

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a confirmed CORS vulnerability, record:

Affected endpoint
Affected method
Authentication state
Affected user role
Test origin
Access-Control-Allow-Origin value
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials value
Relevant preflight response
Sensitive information exposed
Browser tested
Proof-of-concept page
Request
Response
Screenshot

The strongest evidence demonstrates that the browser actually exposes sensitive information to the controlled untrusted origin.

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Arbitrary Origin Reflection Allows Credentialed Cross-Origin Access

Affected Endpoint:
/api/account

Authentication:
Authenticated user session

Expected:
Only explicitly trusted application origins should be permitted to read authenticated account information cross-origin.

Observed:
The API reflected an arbitrary Origin value into the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and returned Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

A browser-based proof of concept hosted on a controlled origin successfully read the authenticated test user's account response.

Impact:
An attacker who can cause an authenticated user to visit an attacker-controlled origin may be able to read information returned by the affected API using the victim's authenticated browser session, subject to the browser's applicable cookie policies.

docs.title: Example Broad Subdomain Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Overly Broad CORS Trust Extends to Untrusted Subdomains

Affected Endpoint:
/api/profile

Observed:
The API permits credentialed cross-origin access from a broad set of organisational subdomains.

One of the permitted origins is not maintained to the same security standard as the primary application.

Impact:
Compromise or attacker control of a trusted subdomain may allow that origin to access authenticated API responses that would otherwise be protected by the Same-Origin Policy.

Only use this impact statement when the weaker trusted origin has actually been demonstrated.

docs.title: Example Informational Observation
docs.text:
Observation:
Wildcard CORS Policy on Public API

Affected Endpoint:
/api/public/products

Observed:
The endpoint returns:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

The endpoint is accessible without authentication and returns information already intended for public consumption.

Impact:
No sensitive cross-origin data exposure was identified.

Recommendation:
Confirm that the endpoint is intentionally public and ensure that authenticated or sensitive API endpoints use a more restrictive CORS policy.

This prevents harmless public CORS configurations from being exaggerated.

docs.title: Reporting Titles
docs.text:
Prefer precise titles:

Credentialed CORS Misconfiguration Allows Arbitrary Origins

Arbitrary Origin Reflection on Authenticated API

CORS Policy Trusts Attacker-Controlled Subdomain

Sensitive API Permits Credentialed null Origin

Overly Broad CORS Allowlist Exposes Account Data

Insecure HTTP Origin Trusted by Sensitive API

Avoid titles such as:

CORS Header Missing

or:

CORS Enabled

Neither describes a vulnerability.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

Data sensitivity
Authentication
Victim requirements
Browser behaviour
Attacker origin requirements
Affected user role
Trusted-origin requirements
Available actions
Exploit reliability

For example:

ACAO: *

on a public API may have no security impact.

While:

Arbitrary Origin Reflection
+
Credentials
+
Sensitive Account Data
+
Browser-Verified Access

may represent a significant vulnerability.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
CORS should be configured around an explicit trust model.

A good design is:

Request Origin
      ↓
Parse Origin
      ↓
Compare Against Explicit Allowlist
      ↓
Trusted?
   ↓       ↓
 Yes      No
 ↓         ↓
Return    Do Not Return
ACAO      ACAO

docs.title: Explicit Allowlist
docs.text:
For example:

https://app.example.com
https://admin.example.com

Only origins with a legitimate requirement should be trusted.

Avoid broad wildcard subdomain policies where possible.

docs.title: Exact Origin Validation
docs.text:
Validation should account for:

Scheme
Hostname
Port

For example:

https://app.example.com

should not automatically imply trust for:

http://app.example.com
https://app.example.com:8443
https://anything.app.example.com

unless those origins are explicitly required.

docs.title: Do Not Reflect Arbitrary Origins
docs.text:
Avoid logic conceptually equivalent to:

Read Origin
    ↓
Return Same Origin

without validation.

This effectively allows arbitrary origins.

docs.title: Avoid null Unless Required
docs.text:
Do not trust:

Origin: null

unless the application has a clearly understood and justified requirement.

docs.title: Restrict Credentials
docs.text:
Only use:

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

where cross-origin credentialed requests are genuinely necessary.

Avoid exposing authenticated resources to origins that do not require access.

docs.title: Restrict Methods
docs.text:
Allow only required methods.

For example:

Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST

rather than unnecessarily exposing:

PUT
PATCH
DELETE

to cross-origin browser workflows.

This is defence in depth and does not replace authorisation.

docs.title: Restrict Headers
docs.text:
Allow only headers required by legitimate clients.

Avoid overly broad configurations without a clear business need.

docs.title: Protect Every Endpoint
docs.text:
CORS middleware should be applied consistently.

Do not configure:

Public API → correct policy
Account API → correct policy
Admin API → accidental arbitrary reflection

Centralised and well-tested CORS handling reduces configuration drift.

docs.title: Review Trusted Origins
docs.text:
Trusted origins should be periodically reviewed.

Remove:

Retired applications
Development environments
Old staging environments
Unused third-party integrations
Abandoned subdomains
HTTP origins

that no longer require access.

docs.title: CORS Is Defence in Depth
docs.text:
Even with a correct CORS policy, sensitive APIs still require:

Authentication
Authorisation
Secure session management
CSRF protection where applicable
Input validation
Output handling
Secure transport

CORS is not a substitute for any of these controls.

docs.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: CORS
docs.text:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/cors

PortSwigger provides detailed material covering CORS fundamentals, origin reflection, credentialed requests, null origins and trust relationships.

docs.title: PortSwigger CORS Labs
docs.text:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/all-labs#cross-origin-resource-sharing-cors

Useful practical labs for understanding common CORS misconfigurations.

docs.title: OWASP WSTG: Testing Cross Origin Resource Sharing
docs.text:
https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/11-Client-side_Testing/07-Testing_Cross_Origin_Resource_Sharing

Provides a structured testing methodology for reviewing CORS policies.

docs.title: MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
docs.text:
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

Useful reference documentation for browser CORS behaviour.

docs.title: MDN: Access-Control-Allow-Origin
docs.text:
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Access-Control-Allow-Origin

Reference for the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header.

docs.title: MDN: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
docs.text:
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Access-Control-Allow-Credentials

Reference for credentialed cross-origin requests.

docs.title: OWASP HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTML5_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html

Contains additional browser and cross-origin security guidance.

docs.title: Final CORS Testing Model
docs.text:
ENDPOINT
                           ↓
                  IS DATA SENSITIVE?
                           ↓
                          YES
                           ↓
                    ADD ORIGIN
                           ↓
                INSPECT CORS POLICY
                           ↓
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ↓                   ↓                   ↓
      ACAO                ACAC              PREFLIGHT
       ↓                   ↓                   ↓
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ↓
                  TEST TRUST MODEL
                           ↓
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ↓                   ↓                   ↓
    EXTERNAL           SUBDOMAIN             NULL
     ORIGIN              ORIGIN             ORIGIN
       ↓                   ↓                   ↓
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ↓
                  ORIGIN ACCEPTED?
                           ↓
                          YES
                           ↓
                  CREDENTIALS REQUIRED?
                           ↓
                          YES
                           ↓
                 WILL BROWSER SEND THEM?
                           ↓
                          YES
                           ↓
                  BROWSER-BASED PoC
                           ↓
                CAN JAVASCRIPT READ DATA?
                           ↓
                          YES
                           ↓
                  SENSITIVE DATA EXPOSED?
                           ↓
                          YES
                           ↓
               CORS VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED
                           ↓
                    ASSESS IMPACT
                           ↓
                        REPORT

The key principle is:

CORS testing is not about finding Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. Map the application's cross-origin trust relationships, determine whether an untrusted origin is accepted, establish whether credentials are available, and verify in a real browser whether sensitive information can actually cross the intended origin boundary.

docs.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery
docs.text:
Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) occurs when an attacker causes a victim's browser to perform an unwanted action against an application where the victim is already authenticated.

The vulnerability relies on the browser automatically including authentication information such as:

Session cookies
Authentication cookies
Client certificates
HTTP authentication credentials

A basic CSRF flow looks like:

Victim Authenticates
        ↓
Application Sets Session Cookie
        ↓
Victim Visits Attacker-Controlled Page
        ↓
Browser Sends Forged Request
        ↓
Session Cookie Automatically Included
        ↓
Application Accepts Request
        ↓
Victim's Account Performs Action

The attacker does not necessarily need to know the victim's session cookie.

The browser supplies it automatically when the request satisfies the relevant cookie rules.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform CSRF testing only against applications for which you have explicit authorisation. Use accounts and data you control. Avoid sending proof-of-concept requests to real users. For state-changing actions, use reversible changes wherever possible.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Suppose an authenticated user changes their email address using:

POST /account/email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=REDACTED
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=user@example.com

If the application relies only on the session cookie to authorise the action, another website may be able to cause the victim's browser to submit the same request.

Conceptually:

Attacker Website
      ↓
Victim Browser
      ↓
POST /account/email
      ↓
Browser Adds Session Cookie
      ↓
Target Application
      ↓
Email Address Changed

The core security question is:

Can another origin cause the victim's browser to perform an authenticated state-changing action?

docs.title: CSRF Requirements
docs.text:
Traditional CSRF normally requires several conditions.

1. A relevant state-changing action exists

2. Authentication is automatically attached by the browser

3. The attacker can reproduce the required request

4. The request lacks effective anti-CSRF protection

Potentially interesting actions include:

Change email address
Change password
Change phone number
Update profile
Add payment details
Change shipping address
Create API key
Delete API key
Enable integration
Disable security control
Add user
Remove user
Change role
Create administrator
Delete account
Submit transaction
Change notification settings
Connect external account
Change MFA settings

docs.title: CSRF vs XSS
docs.text:
CSRF and XSS are different vulnerability classes.

CSRF:

Attacker Site
     ↓
Victim Browser
     ↓
Authenticated Request
     ↓
Target Application

XSS:

Attacker Input
     ↓
Target Application
     ↓
Victim Browser
     ↓
Attacker-Controlled Script Executes

The important distinction is:

CSRF
Abuses authenticated browser requests

XSS
Executes attacker-controlled browser-side code

docs.title: XSS Can Defeat CSRF Protections
docs.text:
If an attacker has JavaScript execution within the target application's origin, many CSRF protections can potentially be bypassed because the malicious script operates from the trusted origin.

For example, same-origin JavaScript may be able to:

Read CSRF tokens
Submit authenticated requests
Read application responses
Interact with protected APIs

Therefore:

XSS can frequently undermine CSRF protections.

Fix XSS independently even when strong CSRF protection exists.

docs.title: CSRF vs CORS
docs.text:
CSRF and CORS are frequently confused.

They solve different problems.

CSRF asks:

Can another site cause the browser to send
an authenticated request?

CORS asks:

Can JavaScript from another origin read
or interact with a cross-origin response?

A browser may send a cross-origin request even when JavaScript cannot read the response.

Therefore:

CORS blocking response access
≠
CSRF protection

docs.title: Same-Origin Policy
docs.text:
The Same-Origin Policy primarily restricts how one origin can interact with resources from another origin.

An origin consists of:

Scheme
Host
Port

For example:

https://example.com

and:

https://example.com:8443

are different origins.

However, the Same-Origin Policy does not prevent every type of cross-origin request.

Browsers historically allow actions such as:

Form submissions
Image loading
Navigation
Script loading
Stylesheet loading

under various circumstances.

This is why CSRF is possible.

docs.title: CSRF Testing Workflow
docs.text:
A structured workflow can look like:

Identify State-Changing Functionality
              ↓
Capture Legitimate Request
              ↓
Identify Authentication Mechanism
              ↓
Identify CSRF Protection
              ↓
Remove CSRF Token
              ↓
Modify CSRF Token
              ↓
Test Token Binding
              ↓
Review SameSite Cookies
              ↓
Review Origin / Referer Validation
              ↓
Determine Cross-Origin Request Format
              ↓
Generate Controlled PoC
              ↓
Test With Controlled Victim Session
              ↓
Confirm State Change
              ↓
Assess Impact
              ↓
Report

docs.title: Start With State-Changing Requests
docs.text:
CSRF testing should focus primarily on requests that modify application state.

Examples:

POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

However, HTTP method alone does not determine whether an action changes state.

Applications sometimes incorrectly perform state-changing actions using:

GET

For example:

GET /account/delete?id=123 HTTP/1.1

This can be particularly easy to exploit through CSRF.

docs.title: Build a State-Changing Request Inventory
docs.text:
While browsing the application, keep track of interesting actions.

For example:

Action Method Endpoint Change email POST /account/email Change password POST /account/password Add user POST /admin/users Delete API key DELETE /api/keys/123 Update profile PATCH /api/profile Logout POST /logout

Then assess each request's CSRF protection.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Burp Suite is one of the best tools for manual CSRF testing.

A practical workflow:

Browser
  ↓
Burp Proxy
  ↓
HTTP History
  ↓
Find State-Changing Request
  ↓
Send to Repeater
  ↓
Analyse Cookies
  ↓
Analyse CSRF Token
  ↓
Modify / Remove Protection
  ↓
Generate CSRF PoC
  ↓
Test in Controlled Browser

docs.title: Burp Proxy
docs.text:
Use Proxy to capture legitimate application requests.

Look for:

POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

and state-changing GET requests.

Pay attention to:

Cookie
Authorization
Origin
Referer
Content-Type
CSRF token
Custom headers

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Send interesting requests to Repeater.

For example:

POST /account/email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=REDACTED
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Origin: https://target.example

email=test1@example.com

Confirm the request works normally.

Then systematically modify the request.

docs.title: First Test: Remove the CSRF Token
docs.text:
Suppose the legitimate request contains:

POST /account/email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=REDACTED
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=test@example.com&csrf=abc123

Remove:

csrf=abc123

and resend.

If the request still succeeds:

Token may not be required.

This is one of the first CSRF tests to perform.

docs.title: Second Test: Change the Token
docs.text:
Replace the token:

csrf=abc123

with:

csrf=invalid

or another clearly invalid controlled value.

If the request still succeeds:

The token may not be validated correctly.

docs.title: Third Test: Empty Token
docs.text:
Try:

csrf=

Some applications validate only whether the parameter exists rather than whether it contains a valid token.

Compare:

Missing
Empty
Invalid
Valid

docs.title: Token Validation Matrix
docs.text:
A simple matrix is useful:

Test Result Valid token Accepted Missing token ? Empty token ? Invalid token ? Token from another session ? Token from another user ? Reused token ?

This quickly shows how the protection behaves.

docs.title: CSRF Token Binding
docs.text:
A CSRF token should generally be associated with the user's authenticated session or otherwise cryptographically bound to the relevant security context.

Test:

User A Token
    ↓
User B Request

If User A's token works in User B's session:

Token may not be correctly bound.

Use only test accounts you control.

docs.title: Cross-Account Token Test
docs.text:
With two authorised accounts:

Account A
Account B

capture a valid CSRF token from Account A.

Then use:

Account B session cookie
+
Account A CSRF token

If the request succeeds, investigate whether the token is globally valid rather than session-bound.

docs.title: Static Tokens
docs.text:
A token may appear to be:

Same across requests
Same across sessions
Same across users

A static token is suspicious.

However, do not assume vulnerability solely because the token remains unchanged.

Determine whether:

Token is unpredictable
Token is secret
Token is session-bound
Token is validated

docs.title: Token Reuse
docs.text:
A CSRF token does not necessarily need to be single-use.

Reusable session-bound tokens are common.

Therefore:

Token works twice

does not automatically mean:

CSRF vulnerability

The important properties are usually:

Unpredictability
Validation
Correct binding

docs.title: Synchronizer Token Pattern
docs.text:
A common CSRF defence uses a server-generated token associated with the user's session.

Conceptually:

User Session
     ↓
Server Generates Token
     ↓
Token Embedded in Page
     ↓
Form Submission
     ↓
Server Compares Token

The attacker cannot normally know the token because another origin cannot read the protected page due to the Same-Origin Policy.

docs.title: Double-Submit Cookie Pattern
docs.text:
Another design uses a token in both:

Cookie
+
Request Parameter / Header

Conceptually:

CSRF Cookie
    +
CSRF Request Value
    ↓
Server Compares Values

A robust implementation should cryptographically bind the token to the authenticated session where appropriate.

Simply comparing attacker-influenceable values can be unsafe.

docs.title: Signed Double-Submit Cookie
docs.text:
A stronger double-submit design can bind the token to session-specific information using a keyed cryptographic construction.

Conceptually:

Session Information
      +
Server Secret
      ↓
HMAC
      ↓
CSRF Token

This prevents an attacker from simply creating arbitrary matching token values.

docs.title: CSRF Tokens in Headers
docs.text:
Modern applications often send tokens through headers such as:

X-CSRF-Token
X-CSRFToken
X-XSRF-TOKEN
XSRF-TOKEN
RequestVerificationToken

Example:

X-CSRF-Token: abc123

Custom headers can provide useful protection because ordinary HTML forms cannot arbitrarily add them.

However, CORS configuration becomes relevant.

docs.title: Angular XSRF Pattern
docs.text:
Angular commonly supports an XSRF pattern using:

XSRF-TOKEN

cookie and:

X-XSRF-TOKEN

request header.

Conceptually:

Cookie
 ↓
Angular Reads Token
 ↓
Adds Header
 ↓
Server Validates Header

The server still needs to validate the token correctly.

docs.title: Anti-Forgery Tokens in ASP.NET
docs.text:
ASP.NET applications may use anti-forgery functionality involving values such as:

__RequestVerificationToken

These may appear in:

Cookies
Form parameters
Headers

Do not remove only one component and conclude the protection is absent.

Determine the complete validation mechanism.

docs.title: Django CSRF
docs.text:
Django commonly uses:

csrftoken

and may expect:

csrfmiddlewaretoken

or:

X-CSRFToken

Django also performs origin-related checks for relevant requests.

When testing Django applications, determine whether the application uses the framework's protection correctly or disables it for specific endpoints.

docs.title: Laravel CSRF
docs.text:
Laravel applications commonly use:

_token

or headers such as:

X-CSRF-TOKEN
X-XSRF-TOKEN

Endpoints excluded from CSRF middleware should receive particular attention.

docs.title: Rails CSRF
docs.text:
Ruby on Rails commonly embeds authenticity tokens in forms and metadata.

Look for:

authenticity_token

The important question remains:

Is the token required and correctly validated?

docs.title: CSRF Token in JSON
docs.text:
Some applications include a token within JSON:

{
  "email": "test@example.com",
  "csrfToken": "abc123"
}

Test:

Remove token
Invalid token
Empty token
Other-session token

just as with form parameters.

docs.title: SameSite Cookies
docs.text:
Modern browsers support the SameSite cookie attribute.

Possible values include:

Strict
Lax
None

This attribute can significantly affect CSRF exploitability.

Example:

Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

docs.title: SameSite Strict
docs.text:
SameSite=Strict

provides the strongest cross-site cookie restriction.

The browser generally does not include the cookie in cross-site requests.

Conceptually:

Attacker Site
    ↓
Cross-Site Request
    ↓
Session Cookie Not Included

This can strongly reduce traditional CSRF risk.

However, application design and same-site relationships still matter.

docs.title: SameSite Lax
docs.text:
SameSite=Lax

allows cookies in certain top-level cross-site navigations, particularly safe-method navigation scenarios.

This means state-changing GET requests remain particularly dangerous.

For example:

<a href="https://target.example/account/delete">

could potentially trigger a state-changing GET action if the application incorrectly uses GET for sensitive operations.

docs.title: SameSite None
docs.text:
SameSite=None

allows cookies to be sent in cross-site contexts.

Modern browsers require:

Secure

alongside SameSite=None.

Example:

Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; SameSite=None

Applications using SameSite=None should not rely on SameSite as their primary CSRF defence.

docs.title: SameSite Default Behaviour
docs.text:
Modern browsers may apply default SameSite behaviour when the attribute is omitted.

Do not assume all browsers and application environments behave identically.

Explicitly configure the intended SameSite policy.

docs.title: Site vs Origin
docs.text:
SameSite and Same-Origin Policy do not use exactly the same security boundary.

This distinction is important.

Conceptually:

Origin
=
Scheme + Host + Port

while site calculations are based around the registrable domain and scheme.

Therefore, two applications can be:

Same-site

but:

Cross-origin

This matters when assessing sibling subdomains.

docs.title: Sibling Subdomains
docs.text:
Consider:

app.example.com
blog.example.com

These are different origins but may be considered same-site.

A vulnerable or attacker-controlled sibling subdomain can therefore change the threat model for SameSite-based protection.

Do not assume:

SameSite=Strict

solves every trust issue involving sibling subdomains.

docs.title: Cookie Domain
docs.text:
Review:

Domain=.example.com

versus a host-only cookie.

A broadly scoped cookie may be sent to multiple subdomains.

This can increase risk if another subdomain is:

Compromised
Untrusted
User-controlled
Vulnerable to subdomain takeover

docs.title: Origin Header
docs.text:
Browsers may send:

Origin: https://target.example

for relevant requests.

Applications can validate the Origin header to ensure the request originates from an approved origin.

For a cross-origin request:

Origin: https://attacker.example

The server can reject it.

docs.title: Origin Validation Testing
docs.text:
Capture a legitimate request:

Origin: https://target.example

Then test:

Remove Origin
Change Origin
Use unrelated origin
Use malformed origin where appropriate

Observe whether the request is accepted.

docs.title: Weak Origin Validation
docs.text:
Weak validation might conceptually check:

Origin contains "target.example"

rather than parsing and comparing the actual origin.

Secure validation should compare against explicit trusted origins.

Do not use substring matching.

docs.title: Referer Validation
docs.text:
Applications may also validate:

Referer: https://target.example/account

A cross-site request may contain:

Referer: https://attacker.example/

Referer checking can provide additional defence but should be implemented carefully.

docs.title: Missing Referer
docs.text:
Some clients or privacy controls may suppress Referer.

Applications therefore sometimes allow requests when:

Referer is missing

This can weaken the defence.

Test:

Valid Referer
Invalid Referer
Missing Referer

docs.title: Origin vs Referer
docs.text:
Prefer:

Origin

when available because it contains less path information and is specifically useful for origin validation.

A robust application may use:

Origin validation

with carefully designed fallback behaviour.

docs.title: Burp CSRF PoC Generator
docs.text:
Burp Suite can generate a CSRF proof of concept for suitable requests.

Typical workflow:

Proxy / Repeater
      ↓
Right-Click Request
      ↓
Engagement Tools
      ↓
Generate CSRF PoC

Depending on the Burp version and interface, the exact menu placement may differ.

The generated HTML can then be reviewed and tested in a controlled environment.

docs.title: Basic HTML Form PoC
docs.text:
Suppose the vulnerable request is:

POST /account/email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=csrf-test@example.com

A basic controlled PoC may look like:

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <body>
    <form action="https://target.example/account/email" method="POST">
      <input type="hidden" name="email" value="csrf-test@example.com">
      <input type="submit" value="Submit test">
    </form>
  </body>
</html>

Use only an account and state change you control.

docs.title: Automatic Form Submission
docs.text:
For controlled testing, the form can be automatically submitted:

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <body>
    <form id="csrf-test"
          action="https://target.example/account/email"
          method="POST">

      <input type="hidden"
             name="email"
             value="csrf-test@example.com">

    </form>

    <script>
      document.getElementById("csrf-test").submit();
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

This models how a victim visiting another page could trigger the action.

docs.title: GET-Based CSRF
docs.text:
State-changing GET requests are particularly problematic.

Suppose:

GET /account/email?email=csrf-test@example.com HTTP/1.1

A cross-site resource or navigation may be enough to trigger it.

For example:

<img src="https://target.example/account/email?email=csrf-test@example.com">

or:

<a href="https://target.example/account/email?email=csrf-test@example.com">
  Open
</a>

Sensitive state changes should not use GET.

docs.title: Why GET Should Be Safe
docs.text:
HTTP semantics expect GET to be:

Safe

meaning it should retrieve information rather than perform significant state changes.

Sensitive actions should use appropriate methods such as:

POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

together with CSRF protection where browser-managed authentication is used.

docs.title: Form Content Types
docs.text:
HTML forms normally support:

application/x-www-form-urlencoded
multipart/form-data
text/plain

This is important when determining whether a request can be reproduced cross-origin without JavaScript access to the target origin.

docs.title: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
docs.text:
This is the standard form encoding.

Example:

Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=test@example.com&name=Asif

It is straightforward to reproduce using an HTML form.

docs.title: multipart/form-data
docs.text:
HTML forms can also send:

multipart/form-data

This is commonly used for:

File uploads
Complex forms

Do not assume multipart requests are automatically protected from CSRF.

docs.title: text/plain
docs.text:
HTML forms can submit:

text/plain

This occasionally becomes relevant when APIs parse request bodies loosely.

Applications should validate expected content types strictly.

docs.title: JSON and CSRF
docs.text:
Developers sometimes assume:

JSON API = No CSRF

This is not always safe.

The actual questions are:

Can the browser create a request the endpoint accepts?

Are credentials automatically attached?

Does the server strictly require application/json?

Does CORS permit attacker-controlled JavaScript?

Does the server accept alternative content types?

Can method or format overrides be used?

docs.title: JSON Endpoint Example
docs.text:
Suppose:

POST /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=REDACTED
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "displayName": "Asif"
}

If the server strictly requires:

Content-Type: application/json

then a normal cross-origin HTML form cannot directly reproduce the same request body and content type.

However, continue testing the surrounding behaviour.

docs.title: Content-Type Confusion
docs.text:
Some APIs accept the same data using multiple content types.

For example:

application/json
application/x-www-form-urlencoded
text/plain

If an endpoint accepts a simple form-compatible content type, CSRF may become possible.

Test whether content-type validation is strict.

docs.title: JSON Parsing With text/plain
docs.text:
Some frameworks or custom middleware may attempt to parse a JSON-looking body even when:

Content-Type: text/plain

This can weaken assumptions that JSON endpoints are inherently protected.

Test the server's actual behaviour rather than relying on the documented API format.

docs.title: CORS and JSON CSRF
docs.text:
A cross-origin JavaScript request using:

application/json

typically triggers a CORS preflight.

Conceptually:

Attacker JavaScript
      ↓
OPTIONS Preflight
      ↓
Server
      ↓
CORS Decision
      ↓
Actual Request

If CORS is securely configured, arbitrary attacker origins should not be allowed to send credentialed requests requiring non-simple characteristics.

docs.title: Credentialed CORS
docs.text:
A dangerous configuration may involve:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker.example
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

If an attacker-controlled origin is trusted, the impact may extend beyond traditional CSRF because attacker JavaScript may also be able to read responses.

Report the CORS weakness separately where appropriate.

docs.title: Custom Headers
docs.text:
Requiring a custom header can help protect APIs because ordinary cross-origin forms cannot add arbitrary headers.

For example:

X-CSRF-Token: abc123

or even an application-specific header:

X-Requested-By: WebApp

However:

Custom Header
+
Overly Permissive CORS

can undermine the protection.

docs.title: Method Override
docs.text:
Some frameworks support method overrides such as:

_method=DELETE
_method=PUT

or headers such as:

X-HTTP-Method-Override

An endpoint that appears to require DELETE may still be reachable through a form-compatible POST.

Review method-override functionality.

docs.title: CSRF in REST APIs
docs.text:
For REST APIs, determine the authentication mechanism.

If authentication uses:

Cookie-based session

CSRF may be relevant.

If authentication requires:

Authorization: Bearer TOKEN

and the browser does not automatically attach the token cross-origin, traditional CSRF is usually much less applicable.

docs.title: Cookie Authentication vs Bearer Authentication
docs.text:
Cookie authentication:

Browser
 ↓
Automatically Adds Cookie
 ↓
CSRF Relevant

Bearer token stored and explicitly attached by JavaScript:

JavaScript
 ↓
Adds Authorization Header
 ↓
Attacker Site Does Not Know Token

Traditional CSRF generally relies on credentials being automatically attached.

However, token storage introduces separate risks such as XSS.

docs.title: HTTP Basic Authentication
docs.text:
Browsers can automatically reuse HTTP authentication credentials in some contexts.

Therefore applications relying on:

Basic Authentication
Digest Authentication

may still require CSRF consideration depending on browser and application behaviour.

docs.title: Client Certificates
docs.text:
Applications using client certificates can also have CSRF concerns because authentication occurs at the transport/browser level rather than through an attacker-known secret.

Again, determine whether cross-site requests are accepted.

docs.title: Login CSRF
docs.text:
CSRF is not limited to actions performed after login.

Login CSRF occurs when an attacker causes a victim to log into an application using an account controlled by the attacker.

Conceptually:

Attacker Creates Account
        ↓
Attacker Knows Credentials
        ↓
Victim Visits Malicious Page
        ↓
Login Request Submitted
        ↓
Victim Browser Logged Into Attacker Account

This can create confusing and potentially dangerous account interactions.

docs.title: Login CSRF Impact
docs.text:
Imagine an application where users later enter:

Search history
Personal information
Payment information
Uploaded documents
Messages

If the victim unknowingly uses an attacker-controlled account, that information may become visible to the attacker through that account.

Therefore login endpoints may also require CSRF protection.

docs.title: Logout CSRF
docs.text:
An attacker may be able to force a user to log out.

For example:

Attacker Site
    ↓
/logout
    ↓
Victim Session Destroyed

Logout CSRF is usually lower impact than account modification CSRF, but can still affect:

Availability
Workflow
User experience
Security-sensitive processes

Logout should ideally use an appropriate state-changing request rather than an unprotected GET.

docs.title: Password Change CSRF
docs.text:
Password changes are high-value CSRF targets.

A secure password change flow may require:

Current password
CSRF token
Reauthentication

If the application allows:

New password only

and lacks CSRF protection, an attacker may potentially change the victim's password.

Use controlled test accounts only.

docs.title: Email Change CSRF
docs.text:
Changing an email address can be particularly serious because email may be used for:

Password reset
Account recovery
Security notifications
MFA recovery

A vulnerable flow may enable account takeover.

Applications should consider:

CSRF protection
Reauthentication
Email confirmation
Notification to old address

docs.title: MFA Configuration CSRF
docs.text:
Security-sensitive actions include:

Enable MFA
Disable MFA
Change MFA device
Regenerate recovery codes
Change recovery phone

These should generally require stronger controls than ordinary profile updates.

Consider:

CSRF token
Reauthentication
Current MFA confirmation

docs.title: API Key CSRF
docs.text:
Actions involving API credentials are high value.

Examples:

Create API key
Delete API key
Rotate API key
Change API permissions

CSRF against an API-key creation endpoint could potentially cause credentials to be created under the victim's account.

Whether the attacker can obtain the resulting secret is a separate question.

docs.title: Administrative CSRF
docs.text:
Administrative interfaces can have particularly high-impact CSRF.

Interesting actions include:

Create user
Create administrator
Change role
Reset password
Disable account
Change security policy
Configure integration
Change callback URL
Modify SSO
Upload configuration
Change access control

Test only with authorised administrative test accounts.

docs.title: CSRF in Multi-Step Actions
docs.text:
Some actions involve several steps.

For example:

Step 1
Enter new email

Step 2
Review

Step 3
Confirm

Do not assume multi-step workflows prevent CSRF.

Determine whether:

Every state-changing step is protected

and whether an attacker can directly invoke the final step.

docs.title: Step Skipping
docs.text:
Capture the final request.

Then determine whether it requires server-side state created during previous steps.

For example:

Step 1
Generate transaction context

Step 2
Confirm transaction

If Step 2 accepts arbitrary values without validating the prior workflow, the intermediate step may provide little protection.

docs.title: Confirmation Pages
docs.text:
A confirmation page is not itself CSRF protection.

For example:

POST /change-email
        ↓
Confirmation Page
        ↓
POST /confirm-email

If both requests can be forged, the additional page does not prevent CSRF.

docs.title: Reauthentication
docs.text:
For particularly sensitive actions, requiring the user's password or MFA again provides additional protection.

Examples:

Change password
Disable MFA
Change recovery email
Delete account
Transfer funds
Create privileged administrator

Reauthentication complements CSRF protection.

It should not necessarily replace it.

docs.title: CSRF in File Uploads
docs.text:
File uploads can potentially be CSRF targets when:

Victim's browser can submit the form cross-site

However, browsers intentionally restrict programmatic selection of arbitrary local files.

An attacker cannot normally cause a victim's browser to upload an arbitrary local file without user interaction.

Still, upload forms may contain other state-changing fields worth testing.

docs.title: CSRF in Profile Changes
docs.text:
Profile functionality commonly contains good CSRF test cases:

Display name
Email
Phone
Address
Company
Website
Preferences
Notification settings

These are useful for controlled proof-of-concept testing because they are usually reversible.

docs.title: CSRF in Support Systems
docs.text:
Potential actions include:

Create ticket
Close ticket
Change ticket email
Add note
Change notification settings
Upload attachment

Assess impact rather than reporting every state-changing request equally.

docs.title: CSRF in CMS Platforms
docs.text:
High-value CMS actions include:

Create page
Publish page
Delete page
Change administrator
Install plugin
Change theme
Modify settings
Change integration

Administrative CSRF can have severe impact.

docs.title: CSRF in OAuth Flows
docs.text:
OAuth-related CSRF requires careful analysis.

A common security mechanism is:

state

The OAuth client generates a value and verifies that the callback contains the expected value.

Conceptually:

Client Starts OAuth
      ↓
Generate state
      ↓
Authorization Server
      ↓
Callback with state
      ↓
Client Verifies state

This helps protect the OAuth flow against CSRF and flow confusion.

docs.title: OAuth State Testing
docs.text:
When reviewing OAuth:

Is state present?

Is state unpredictable?

Is state validated?

Is state bound to the initiating browser session?

Can state be omitted?

Can another session's state be reused?

OAuth deserves its own detailed testing methodology, but these checks are directly relevant to CSRF.

docs.title: CSRF and Open Redirect
docs.text:
Open redirects can sometimes interact with:

OAuth
SSO
Origin trust
Referer-based logic

Do not automatically combine vulnerabilities.

Trace the actual request and trust decisions.

docs.title: CSRF in SSO
docs.text:
SSO flows may involve:

SAML
OAuth
OpenID Connect
Custom federation

Potential CSRF-like issues can occur around:

Login initiation
Account linking
Identity binding
Logout
Callback processing

Account-linking endpoints deserve particular attention because an attacker may attempt to bind their identity to the victim's authenticated account.

docs.title: Account Linking CSRF
docs.text:
Consider:

Victim logged into target.example
        ↓
Attacker controls external identity
        ↓
Victim receives forged account-link request
        ↓
External identity becomes linked

If successful, the attacker may later authenticate using the linked identity.

This can have account takeover impact.

docs.title: CSRF and WebSockets
docs.text:
WebSocket handshakes begin as HTTP requests and browsers can initiate cross-origin WebSocket connections.

Applications should validate:

Origin
Authentication
Authorisation

Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking is related to CSRF concepts but is generally treated as a separate vulnerability class.

docs.title: CSRF and GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL does not inherently prevent CSRF.

Suppose the application uses:

Cookie authentication

and accepts GraphQL mutations through form-compatible requests.

Then mutations may still be CSRF-relevant.

Interesting operations include:

updateProfile
changeEmail
changePassword
createUser
deleteUser
updateSettings

docs.title: GraphQL GET Requests
docs.text:
Some GraphQL implementations allow queries through GET.

Mutations should generally not be accepted through GET.

If state-changing GraphQL operations can be triggered through a top-level navigation, SameSite protections may behave differently.

docs.title: CSRF and Content-Type
docs.text:
For GraphQL and JSON APIs, determine whether the endpoint accepts:

application/json
application/graphql
application/x-www-form-urlencoded
text/plain

Strict content-type validation can reduce the set of browser-generated cross-origin requests that reach the application.

docs.title: CSRF and Fetch Metadata
docs.text:
Modern browsers can send Fetch Metadata headers such as:

Sec-Fetch-Site
Sec-Fetch-Mode
Sec-Fetch-Dest

For example:

Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site

Applications can use these headers as an additional defence.

docs.title: Sec-Fetch-Site
docs.text:
Possible values include:

same-origin
same-site
cross-site
none

A sensitive endpoint can potentially reject inappropriate:

cross-site

requests.

This should be considered defence in depth rather than the only security mechanism.

docs.title: Fetch Metadata Policy
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Request
   ↓
Sec-Fetch-Site
   ↓
Cross-Site?
   ↓
Sensitive Endpoint?
   ↓
Reject

This can significantly reduce cross-site request abuse when implemented carefully.

docs.title: Testing Fetch Metadata
docs.text:
Capture a legitimate browser request.

Look for:

Sec-Fetch-Site
Sec-Fetch-Mode
Sec-Fetch-Dest

Then test the actual browser-based cross-site PoC.

Do not simply modify these headers manually and assume a browser attacker can do the same.

Browsers control Fetch Metadata headers.

docs.title: Browser-Accurate Testing
docs.text:
This is an important principle for CSRF.

Repeater tells you:

What the server accepts

but the browser tells you:

What an attacker can actually cause

Therefore final CSRF validation should use a browser-based proof of concept.

docs.title: Repeater vs Browser
docs.text:
Use Repeater for:

Token validation
Origin validation
Referer validation
Parameter behaviour
Content-type behaviour

Use a browser for:

SameSite behaviour
Automatic cookies
Form restrictions
Cross-origin behaviour
Redirect behaviour
Actual exploitability

Both are necessary.

docs.title: Testing With Two Browser Sessions
docs.text:
A useful setup is:

Browser Profile A
Victim Test Account

Browser Profile B
Attacker / Secondary Test Account

This helps with:

Token binding
Login CSRF
Account linking
Cross-account testing

Use isolated profiles to avoid session confusion.

docs.title: Incognito / Private Windows
docs.text:
Private browsing can help isolate sessions, but be aware that browsers may share some state differently depending on configuration.

Separate browser profiles provide clearer isolation when testing multiple identities.

docs.title: Hosting the PoC Locally
docs.text:
A CSRF proof of concept can be hosted from a local test server.

For example:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Then open:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/

with the victim test browser.

The target application should remain the authorised system being assessed.

docs.title: Burp's Built-In PoC
docs.text:
Burp's CSRF PoC generator can save time for form-compatible requests.

However, always review the generated HTML.

Check:

Target URL
Method
Parameter names
Parameter values
Encoding
Automatic submission

Do not treat generated output as proof until it works in a real browser.

docs.title: CSRF Token Leakage
docs.text:
Even a correctly implemented CSRF token may fail if the token leaks to an attacker.

Potential leakage locations include:

URLs
Referer headers
Logs
Third-party resources
Analytics
Error messages
Browser history
External links

Tokens should not normally be placed in URLs.

docs.title: Token in URL
docs.text:
Avoid:

https://target.example/action?csrf=SECRET

URLs may appear in:

Browser history
Server logs
Proxy logs
Referer headers
Monitoring
Analytics

Prefer request bodies or custom headers.

docs.title: CSRF Token Entropy
docs.text:
Tokens should be:

Unpredictable
Generated using cryptographically secure randomness
Sufficiently long

Predictable values such as:

Username
Timestamp
Sequential ID
User ID
MD5(user ID)

should not be used as standalone CSRF tokens.

docs.title: Token Comparison
docs.text:
Token validation should use appropriate secure comparison logic.

The primary issue in most CSRF testing is whether the token is:

Required
Valid
Bound correctly
Unpredictable

Do not over-focus on theoretical comparison timing unless the application context makes it realistically relevant.

docs.title: CSRF Token Rotation
docs.text:
