Tokens may be:

Per session
Per request
Per form

All can potentially be valid designs.

Per-request rotation is not mandatory for effective CSRF protection.

Correct validation and binding matter more.

docs.title: Token Expiration
docs.text:
CSRF tokens should generally not remain valid indefinitely beyond the relevant session or security context.

When the session ends:

Associated CSRF protection should no longer remain useful.

docs.title: Session Rotation
docs.text:
After:

Login
Privilege elevation
Password change
Security-sensitive authentication event

the application may rotate the session.

Review whether CSRF tokens remain correctly associated with the new session.

docs.title: SameSite Is Defence in Depth
docs.text:
Do not rely exclusively on:

SameSite

for high-value state-changing operations.

Browser behaviour evolves and application architecture may include:

Sibling subdomains
SSO
Cross-site integrations
Legacy clients
Embedded content

A robust design combines:

CSRF token
Origin validation
SameSite cookies
Correct HTTP methods
Reauthentication where appropriate

docs.title: CSRF Protection Matrix
docs.text:
Document protections clearly.

Protection Present Effective CSRF token Yes / No Yes / No Token required Yes / No Yes / No Token validated Yes / No Yes / No Session-bound Yes / No Yes / No SameSite cookie Strict / Lax / None / Missing Origin validation Yes / No Yes / No Referer validation Yes / No Yes / No Custom header Yes / No Yes / No Reauthentication Yes / No Yes / No Fetch Metadata Yes / No Yes / No

docs.title: Common CSRF Testing Mistakes
docs.text:
Do not assume:

POST = protected

Do not assume:

JSON = protected

Do not assume:

CORS = CSRF protection

Do not assume:

SameSite = impossible to exploit

Do not assume:

Token present = token validated

Do not assume:

Confirmation page = CSRF protection

Test the actual browser behaviour.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
A request that succeeds in Repeater after removing the CSRF token does not automatically prove exploitable CSRF.

Why?

Because the browser may not send the required authentication cookie cross-site due to:

SameSite

or the attacker may not be able to reproduce the required request format.

Therefore:

Server accepts tokenless request

is evidence of weak token validation.

But final exploitability should account for:

Browser behaviour
Cookie behaviour
Request format
Origin restrictions

docs.title: Browser Validation Checklist
docs.text:
Before reporting exploitable CSRF, determine:

Can the PoC be loaded from another origin?

Does the browser submit the request?

Is the authentication cookie included?

Does the server accept the request?

Does the application state actually change?

This produces much stronger evidence.

docs.title: CSRF Through GET Example
docs.text:
Request:

GET /profile/set-email?email=csrf-test@example.com HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=REDACTED

Controlled PoC:

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <body>
    <img
      src="https://target.example/profile/set-email?email=csrf-test@example.com"
      alt="">
  </body>
</html>

If the victim's authenticated browser loads the image and the application changes the email address, the action is CSRF-vulnerable.

docs.title: CSRF Through POST Example
docs.text:
Request:

POST /profile/set-email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=csrf-test@example.com

Controlled PoC:

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <body>

    <form id="csrf"
          action="https://target.example/profile/set-email"
          method="POST">

      <input type="hidden"
             name="email"
             value="csrf-test@example.com">

    </form>

    <script>
      document.getElementById("csrf").submit();
    </script>

  </body>
</html>

docs.title: Multi-Parameter Requests
docs.text:
Suppose:

POST /profile HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

firstName=Asif&lastName=Minhas&email=csrf-test@example.com

The PoC must reproduce all parameters required by the server.

For example:

<form action="https://target.example/profile" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="firstName" value="Asif">
  <input type="hidden" name="lastName" value="Minhas">
  <input type="hidden" name="email" value="csrf-test@example.com">
</form>

Determine which parameters are actually required.

docs.title: Duplicate Parameters
docs.text:
Applications may behave unexpectedly with duplicate parameters:

csrf=valid&csrf=invalid

Different layers may select:

First value
Last value
All values

This can create validation inconsistencies.

Test duplicate parameters only when there is evidence that different components may parse the request differently.

docs.title: CSRF and Parameter Pollution
docs.text:
HTTP Parameter Pollution can interact with CSRF validation when:

Security middleware

and:

Application logic

interpret duplicate parameters differently.

Conceptually:

Request
 ↓
CSRF Middleware reads first csrf
 ↓
Application reads second csrf

This is implementation-specific.

docs.title: Method Validation
docs.text:
Ensure the server correctly restricts HTTP methods.

If:

POST /account/email

is expected, test whether:

GET

unexpectedly performs the same action.

Likewise, test whether alternate form-compatible methods or method overrides reach the same functionality.

docs.title: CSRF in Mobile APIs
docs.text:
Native mobile applications often use bearer tokens rather than browser-managed cookies.

Traditional CSRF may therefore be less applicable.

However, if the same API is also consumed by a browser using cookies, assess the browser threat model separately.

docs.title: CSRF in SPAs
docs.text:
Single Page Applications often use:

Cookie-based sessions
+
JSON APIs

Do not assume an SPA is immune to CSRF.

Review:

SameSite
CSRF headers
CORS
Content-Type
Origin validation
Authentication model

docs.title: CSRF in Microservices
docs.text:
A browser may interact with several backend services through:

API gateway
Reverse proxy
BFF

CSRF protection may exist at one layer but not another.

Trace:

Browser
  ↓
Gateway
  ↓
Application
  ↓
Internal Service

Determine where validation occurs.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Considerations
docs.text:
Applications behind reverse proxies may incorrectly reconstruct their origin using:

Host
X-Forwarded-Host
Forwarded
X-Forwarded-Proto

This can affect Origin or Referer validation.

Origin validation should use trusted proxy configuration rather than blindly trusting attacker-controlled forwarding headers.

docs.title: Host Header and CSRF
docs.text:
If CSRF protection constructs an expected origin using an attacker-controlled:

Host

or:

X-Forwarded-Host

header, the protection may be weakened.

Conceptually:

Expected Origin
=
"https://" + Host

If Host is not trustworthy, origin comparison may become unreliable.

docs.title: CSRF and Subdomain Takeover
docs.text:
Suppose session cookies are broadly scoped to:

.example.com

and a sibling subdomain can be taken over.

The attacker may gain a same-site position that changes:

SameSite behaviour
Cookie interactions
Origin assumptions

This demonstrates why subdomain security can affect CSRF threat models.

docs.title: CSRF and Cookie Injection
docs.text:
Some CSRF defence patterns can become weaker if an attacker can set cookies for the target application's domain.

Potential causes include:

Vulnerable sibling subdomain
HTTP response splitting
Cookie injection
Subdomain compromise

This is especially relevant to naive double-submit cookie implementations.

docs.title: CSRF and Clickjacking
docs.text:
CSRF and clickjacking can both cause unintended user actions, but the mechanisms differ.

CSRF:

Forged request

Clickjacking:

Victim is tricked into clicking hidden or disguised UI

An action protected from CSRF may still be vulnerable to clickjacking if it relies only on user interaction.

docs.title: CSRF and User Interaction
docs.text:
Some actions require:

Button click
Confirmation
Password
MFA code
CAPTCHA

This may make automated CSRF more difficult.

Determine whether the interaction genuinely requires information unavailable to the attacker.

A simple confirmation button alone may not be sufficient if the entire flow can still be forged.

docs.title: CAPTCHA
docs.text:
CAPTCHA can make some CSRF attacks more difficult, but it is not designed as a primary CSRF defence.

Use dedicated CSRF controls.

docs.title: Password Confirmation
docs.text:
Requiring:

Current password

can effectively prevent many sensitive CSRF actions because the attacker does not know the victim's password.

This is particularly useful for:

Password change
Email change
MFA changes
Account deletion

It should be combined with appropriate CSRF controls.

docs.title: Source Code Review
docs.text:
When source code is available, identify:

State-changing routes
CSRF middleware
Middleware exclusions
Token generation
Token validation
Origin checks
SameSite configuration
Authentication mechanism

docs.title: Python / Django Source Review
docs.text:
Search for:

csrf_exempt
CsrfViewMiddleware
csrf_protect

Example:

rg -n \
'csrf_exempt|CsrfViewMiddleware|csrf_protect|CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS'

Pay particular attention to:

@csrf_exempt

on state-changing endpoints.

docs.title: Flask Source Review
docs.text:
Flask applications may use extensions such as:

Flask-WTF
CSRFProtect

Search:

rg -n \
'CSRFProtect|Flask-WTF|csrf|WTF_CSRF'

Review:

Global protection
Blueprint exclusions
Route exclusions
Token validation

docs.title: Spring Security Source Review
docs.text:
Spring Security provides CSRF protection for browser applications.

Search:

rg -n \
'csrf\(|csrf\.disable|CsrfToken|CookieCsrfTokenRepository'

Pay particular attention to patterns conceptually equivalent to:

csrf disabled

Determine why it was disabled and whether cookie-authenticated browser endpoints remain exposed.

docs.title: ASP.NET Source Review
docs.text:
Search for:

ValidateAntiForgeryToken
AutoValidateAntiforgeryToken
Antiforgery
IgnoreAntiforgeryToken

Example:

rg -n \
'ValidateAntiForgeryToken|AutoValidateAntiforgeryToken|Antiforgery|IgnoreAntiforgeryToken'

Review exclusions carefully.

docs.title: Laravel Source Review
docs.text:
Search for:

VerifyCsrfToken
csrf_token
@csrf

Example:

rg -n \
'VerifyCsrfToken|csrf_token|@csrf|X-CSRF-TOKEN'

Review the middleware's excluded routes.

docs.title: Rails Source Review
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'protect_from_forgery|authenticity_token|skip_forgery_protection'

Interesting patterns include:

skip_forgery_protection

or controller-specific exclusions.

docs.title: Express / Node.js Source Review
docs.text:
Node.js applications may use packages or custom middleware for CSRF protection.

Search:

rg -ni \
'csrf|xsrf|csurf|sameSite|origin|referer'

Also review session cookie configuration.

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Model
docs.text:
CSRF is different from injection vulnerabilities because the primary flow is not simply source-to-sink.

A useful model is:

ATTACKER ORIGIN
      ↓
VICTIM BROWSER
      ↓
AUTOMATIC AUTHENTICATION
      ↓
STATE-CHANGING ENDPOINT
      ↓
MISSING / WEAK REQUEST AUTHENTICITY CHECK
      ↓
ACTION EXECUTED

docs.title: Source Review Questions
docs.text:
For every state-changing route, ask:

How is the user authenticated?

Are credentials browser-managed?

Is a CSRF token required?

Where is the token generated?

How is it validated?

Is it session-bound?

Is Origin validated?

Is Referer used?

What SameSite policy applies?

Can the action use GET?

Which content types are accepted?

Are custom headers required?

Are any routes excluded from middleware?

Does CORS affect the protection?

Does the action require reauthentication?

docs.title: Automated Testing
docs.text:
Automated scanners can help identify missing CSRF protections, but CSRF is highly dependent on browser behaviour and application logic.

Tools may identify:

State-changing form
No visible CSRF token
Missing SameSite
Token inconsistencies

However:

No token

does not automatically equal exploitable CSRF.

Manual browser validation remains important.

docs.title: Burp Scanner
docs.text:
Burp Scanner may identify potential CSRF weaknesses.

Use scanner findings as:

Candidate

then manually validate:

Authentication
SameSite
Token behaviour
Origin checks
Browser exploitability
State change

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
curl is useful for reproducing requests and checking server-side validation.

For example:

curl -i \
  -X POST \
  -H 'Cookie: session=REDACTED' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data 'email=csrf-test@example.com' \
  https://target.example/account/email

However, curl does not reproduce browser SameSite behaviour.

Use it for server testing, not final browser exploitability.

docs.text:

Name

docs.title: Testing Matrix
docs.text:
A practical CSRF testing matrix:

Test Purpose Remove token Determine whether token required Empty token Identify presence-only validation Invalid token Test actual validation Other-session token Test binding Other-user token Test binding Remove Origin Test fallback behaviour Change Origin Test origin validation Remove Referer Test fallback behaviour Cross-site form Confirm browser exploitability GET version Detect unsafe method handling Alternate content type Test form compatibility Method override Test alternate request path Real browser PoC Confirm actual state change

docs.text:
Useful CSRF evidence includes:

Affected action
Affected endpoint
HTTP method
Authentication mechanism
Session cookie SameSite value
Original request
CSRF token behaviour
Origin validation behaviour
Referer validation behaviour
PoC HTML
Victim test account
State before test
State after test

docs.title: Strong CSRF Evidence
docs.text:
Strong evidence demonstrates:

1. Victim is authenticated

2. Victim loads attacker-controlled page

3. Browser automatically submits forged request

4. Browser includes required authentication

5. Application accepts request

6. Application state changes

That is much stronger than simply showing:

CSRF token missing

docs.title: Minimal Proof
docs.text:
Use a reversible state change.

Good examples include:

Change display name
Change test email
Change notification preference
Change profile field

Avoid using destructive actions when a harmless state change proves the vulnerability.

docs.title: Example CSRF Finding
docs.text:
Title
Cross-Site Request Forgery in Email Address Change Functionality

Affected Endpoint
POST /account/email

Authentication Required
Yes

Description
The application allows authenticated users to change their account
email address through the /account/email endpoint.

The request relies on the user's session cookie for authentication
but does not require a valid anti-CSRF token or otherwise verify that
the request originated from the legitimate application.

A controlled HTML proof of concept hosted on a separate origin caused
the authenticated test browser to submit the email-change request.
The browser automatically included the victim test account's session
cookie and the application accepted the request.

The email address of the controlled test account was successfully
changed.

Impact
An attacker who can cause an authenticated user to visit an
attacker-controlled page could potentially perform the affected
action using the victim's authenticated session.

For email-change functionality, the impact may be particularly
significant when the email address is used for password recovery or
other account-security processes.

Recommendation
Implement robust anti-CSRF protection for all state-changing
browser-authenticated functionality.

Use framework-provided CSRF protection where available.

CSRF tokens should be unpredictable, validated server-side and
appropriately bound to the user's authenticated session.

Configure authentication cookies with an appropriate SameSite
attribute and validate request Origin information as defence in
depth.

Sensitive account-security changes should additionally require
reauthentication where appropriate.

docs.title: Example Weak Token Finding
docs.text:
Title
Anti-CSRF Token Is Not Validated

Description
The affected state-changing request contains a parameter named csrf.

Testing demonstrated that the request succeeds when the token is:

Missing
Empty
Invalid

The application therefore appears to include an anti-CSRF token in
the request but does not enforce it server-side.

A browser-based proof of concept confirmed that the affected action
can be triggered from another origin using the authenticated test
user's session.

Recommendation
Validate the anti-CSRF token server-side for every protected
state-changing request.

Requests containing missing, malformed or incorrect tokens should be
rejected before the requested action is processed.

docs.title: Example Token Binding Finding
docs.text:
Title
Anti-CSRF Tokens Are Not Bound to User Sessions

Description
The application requires a CSRF token for the affected request.

However, a valid token obtained from controlled test account A was
accepted when submitted together with the authenticated session of
controlled test account B.

This demonstrates that CSRF tokens are not correctly bound to the
user's security context.

Impact
Weak token binding may reduce the effectiveness of the application's
CSRF protection if an attacker can obtain a valid token through
another permitted context.

Recommendation
Cryptographically bind CSRF tokens to the authenticated session or
use the framework's established synchronizer-token implementation.

docs.title: Example GET-Based CSRF Finding
docs.text:
Title
State-Changing Account Action Can Be Triggered Through GET Request

Description
The affected endpoint performs a state-changing account operation
using an HTTP GET request.

Because GET requests can be initiated through ordinary cross-site
navigation and resource loading, the action can be triggered from
another origin when the victim's authentication cookie is included.

A controlled proof of concept demonstrated the issue against a test
account.

Recommendation
Do not perform state-changing operations using GET requests.

Use an appropriate state-changing HTTP method and require robust
anti-CSRF protection.

docs.title: Example Login CSRF Finding
docs.text:
Title
Login Endpoint Is Vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery

Description
The application's login endpoint accepts authentication requests
without validating request authenticity.

A controlled proof of concept caused the victim test browser to log
into an account controlled by the tester.

Impact
A victim may unknowingly interact with the application while logged
into an account controlled by an attacker.

Depending on the application, information subsequently entered by the
victim may become associated with and accessible through the
attacker-controlled account.

Recommendation
Apply CSRF protection to the login flow.

Bind login attempts to a browser-initiated authentication flow and
validate appropriate request authenticity controls.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
CSRF mitigation should use defence in depth.

A robust browser-authenticated application might use:

State-Changing Request
        ↓
Correct HTTP Method
        ↓
CSRF Token
        ↓
Token Validation
        ↓
Session Binding
        ↓
Origin Validation
        ↓
SameSite Cookie
        ↓
Authorisation
        ↓
Sensitive Action?
        ↓
Reauthentication
        ↓
Execute

docs.title: Use Framework Protection
docs.text:
Prefer established framework mechanisms.

Examples include:

Django CSRF middleware
Spring Security CSRF
ASP.NET Anti-Forgery
Laravel CSRF middleware
Rails request forgery protection
Flask-WTF CSRFProtect

Avoid creating custom CSRF systems unless necessary.

docs.title: Protect Every State-Changing Endpoint
docs.text:
Protection should apply consistently to:

POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

and any legacy state-changing GET requests should be redesigned.

Do not protect only:

HTML forms

while leaving:

API endpoints
Administrative routes
Legacy endpoints

unprotected.

docs.title: Use Strong Tokens
docs.text:
Tokens should be:

Cryptographically random
Unpredictable
Validated server-side
Bound to the relevant security context

Reject:

Missing
Invalid
Malformed
Unexpected

tokens.

docs.title: Configure SameSite
docs.text:
Use an appropriate SameSite policy for authentication cookies.

Prefer:

SameSite=Lax

or:

SameSite=Strict

where application requirements permit.

Use:

SameSite=None

only where cross-site cookie behaviour is genuinely required and pair it with strong CSRF controls.

docs.title: Use Secure Cookie Attributes
docs.text:
Authentication cookies should generally use:

Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite

and should have the narrowest appropriate:

Domain
Path

scope.

docs.title: Validate Origin
docs.text:
For sensitive state-changing requests, validate:

Origin

against an explicit list of trusted origins.

Do not use:

Substring matching
Suffix matching without domain boundaries
Attacker-controlled Host values

to make security decisions.

docs.title: Referer Fallback
docs.text:
Where Origin is unavailable, carefully designed Referer validation may provide additional defence.

Do not automatically trust:

Missing Referer

without understanding the resulting security implications.

docs.title: Fetch Metadata
docs.text:
Consider using:

Sec-Fetch-Site

and related Fetch Metadata headers as additional protection.

For example:

Reject inappropriate cross-site requests

to sensitive endpoints.

Do not treat this as the sole CSRF control.

docs.title: Reauthentication
docs.text:
Require additional authentication for highly sensitive operations.

Examples:

Change password
Change email
Disable MFA
Delete account
Change recovery settings
Create privileged credentials

docs.title: Avoid State Changes Through GET
docs.text:
GET should not perform actions such as:

Delete
Update
Enable
Disable
Transfer
Change
Create

Use state-changing HTTP methods.

docs.title: Strict Content-Type Validation
docs.text:
API endpoints should accept only the content types they actually require.

For example, if the API requires:

application/json

reject:

text/plain
application/x-www-form-urlencoded

unless explicitly supported.

This can reduce cross-origin form compatibility.

docs.title: CORS Configuration
docs.text:
Do not use permissive CORS configuration with cookie-authenticated sensitive APIs.

Review:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Allowed methods
Allowed headers

CORS should complement rather than replace CSRF protection.

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
Do not reduce CSRF testing to:

There is no CSRF token.

A missing token is only one part of the analysis.

Instead ask:

What action changes state?
        ↓
How is the victim authenticated?
        ↓
Does the browser attach those credentials automatically?
        ↓
Is a CSRF token present?
        ↓
Is the token actually required?
        ↓
Is it validated?
        ↓
Is it bound to the correct session?
        ↓
What SameSite policy applies?
        ↓
Is Origin validated?
        ↓
Is Referer validated?
        ↓
Can an ordinary cross-origin form reproduce the request?
        ↓
Does the endpoint accept alternative content types?
        ↓
Can GET or method overrides trigger the action?
        ↓
Does CORS change the threat model?
        ↓
Can a real browser PoC send the authenticated request?
        ↓
Does the application state actually change?
        ↓
What is the minimum reversible proof required?

The complete CSRF chain is:

ATTACKER-CONTROLLED ORIGIN
          ↓
VICTIM VISITS PAGE
          ↓
BROWSER GENERATES REQUEST
          ↓
AUTHENTICATION AUTOMATICALLY ATTACHED
          ↓
TARGET APPLICATION
          ↓
MISSING / INEFFECTIVE REQUEST
AUTHENTICITY VALIDATION
          ↓
AUTHORISED USER ACTION EXECUTED
          ↓
SECURITY IMPACT

The secure model is:

CROSS-SITE REQUEST
        ↓
SAMESITE / BROWSER CONTROLS
        ↓
CSRF TOKEN
        ↓
ORIGIN VALIDATION
        ↓
AUTHORISATION
        ↓
REAUTHENTICATION
WHEN REQUIRED
        ↓
STATE CHANGE

The key question throughout the assessment is:

Can an attacker-controlled origin cause an authenticated victim's browser to perform a state-changing action that the victim did not intend?

That is the model to use when assessing Cross-Site Request Forgery.

docs.title: Dependency Security
docs.text:
Dependency security is the process of identifying, assessing, maintaining, and securely consuming third-party software components used by an application.

Modern applications rarely consist entirely of code written by the organisation developing them.

Instead, applications commonly depend on:

Open-source libraries
Frameworks
Package-manager modules
SDKs
Runtime libraries
Operating-system packages
Container base images
Build plugins
CI/CD actions
Third-party components
Transitive dependencies

A typical application may therefore look like:

Application
    |
    +-- Application Code
    |
    +-- Framework
    |
    +-- Direct Dependency A
    |       |
    |       +-- Transitive Dependency A1
    |       +-- Transitive Dependency A2
    |
    +-- Direct Dependency B
    |       |
    |       +-- Transitive Dependency B1
    |
    +-- Runtime
    |
    +-- Operating-System Packages

A security weakness anywhere in this dependency graph can potentially affect the application.

Authorised Security Testing

Only scan repositories, package registries, container images, build systems, CI/CD environments, and infrastructure that are explicitly within the authorised assessment scope. Dependency analysis itself is generally passive, but package installation, build execution, dependency resolution, or running project scripts may execute third-party code.

docs.title: Why Dependency Security Matters
docs.text:
Third-party components can introduce vulnerabilities even when the application's own code is secure.

Examples include:

Remote code execution
Cross-site scripting
Prototype pollution
Path traversal
Authentication bypass
Deserialization vulnerabilities
SQL injection
Server-side request forgery
Denial of service
Information disclosure
Cryptographic weaknesses
Privilege escalation

The basic problem is:

Application
     |
     v
Uses Dependency
     |
     v
Dependency Contains Vulnerability
     |
     v
Application Uses Affected Functionality
     |
     v
Vulnerability May Become Reachable

However:

Vulnerable dependency detected

does not always mean:

Application is exploitable

The dependency must be assessed in context.

docs.title: Dependency Security vs Software Supply Chain Security
docs.text:
Dependency security is part of the larger software supply chain security problem.

Dependency security primarily focuses on:

What components does the application use?

Are they vulnerable?

Are they maintained?

Are they trustworthy?

Are versions controlled?

Can they be safely updated?

Software supply chain security is broader:

Source Code
    |
    v
Version Control
    |
    v
Dependencies
    |
    v
Build System
    |
    v
CI/CD
    |
    v
Artifact Repository
    |
    v
Container Registry
    |
    v
Deployment
    |
    v
Production

Threats can occur at every stage.

docs.title: Dependency Threat Model
docs.text:
Dependency-related security issues can be divided into several broad categories:

Known Vulnerabilities
        |
        +-- CVEs
        +-- Security advisories
        +-- Vulnerable versions

Outdated Components
        |
        +-- Unsupported versions
        +-- End-of-life software
        +-- Abandoned packages

Dependency Resolution Attacks
        |
        +-- Dependency confusion
        +-- Typosquatting
        +-- Namespace confusion

Compromised Dependencies
        |
        +-- Maintainer compromise
        +-- Malicious package update
        +-- Registry compromise

Build-Time Risks
        |
        +-- Installation scripts
        +-- Build scripts
        +-- Plugins
        +-- CI/CD dependencies

Integrity Risks
        |
        +-- Modified packages
        +-- Missing integrity verification
        +-- Untrusted registries

docs.title: Direct Dependencies
docs.text:
A direct dependency is explicitly declared by the application.

Example:

{
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "5.1.0"
  }
}

Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
Express

The application developer intentionally selected the dependency.

docs.title: Transitive Dependencies
docs.text:
Dependencies frequently depend on other dependencies.

Example:

Application
    |
    v
Package A
    |
    v
Package B
    |
    v
Package C

The application may never explicitly declare:

Package B
Package C

but they are still part of the application's dependency graph.

This is important because vulnerabilities frequently exist in transitive dependencies.

docs.title: Dependency Graph
docs.text:
A dependency graph shows the relationships between software components.

Example:

                     Application
                         |
             +-----------+-----------+
             |                       |
             v                       v
         Framework                 SDK
             |                       |
       +-----+-----+                 |
       |           |                 |
       v           v                 v
   Library A   Library B         Library C
       |                             |
       v                             v
   Library D                     Library E

Security testing should therefore consider:

Direct dependencies
+
Transitive dependencies

Manifest

Dependency Resolution

package 1.4.7

Lockfile

Lockfiles improve reproducibility by recording resolved versions.

docs.title: Why Lockfiles Matter
docs.text:
Without reliable dependency locking:

Build Today
    |
    v
Dependency 1.2.1

may differ from:

Build Next Month
    |
    v
Dependency 1.3.0

even when application source code has not changed.

This can introduce:

Unexpected behaviour
New vulnerabilities
Compatibility issues
Supply-chain risk

Lockfiles help make builds more deterministic.

docs.title: Pinning Dependencies
docs.text:
Dependency pinning controls which versions may be installed.

Examples:

Exact:

1.2.3

versus ranges such as:

>=1.2

or ecosystem-specific range syntax.

Pinning can improve reproducibility, but it creates an important responsibility:

Pinned dependencies must still be updated.

Otherwise:

Version pinning
      |
      v
Never updated
      |
      v
Known vulnerabilities accumulate

Therefore:

Pinning
+
Automated monitoring
+
Controlled updates

is stronger than pinning alone.

docs.title: Known Vulnerable Components
docs.text:
A dependency may have publicly known vulnerabilities.

Example:

Application
    |
    v
Library 2.4.1
    |
    v
Security Advisory
    |
    v
Versions < 2.4.5 affected

The first question is:

Is the installed version affected?

The second is:

Does the application expose the vulnerable functionality?

docs.title: Vulnerability Databases
docs.text:
Dependency scanners may use vulnerability information from sources such as:

OSV
NVD
GitHub Security Advisories
Vendor advisories
Language-specific advisory databases
CISA KEV

Different scanners may produce different results because they may use:

Different databases
Different package identification
Different version matching
Different severity information
Different update schedules

For important findings, review the original advisory.

docs.title: CVE
docs.text:
CVE stands for:

Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures

A CVE identifier resembles:

CVE-2025-12345

A CVE identifies a vulnerability.

It does not by itself tell you:

Whether your application is affected

Whether the vulnerable code is reachable

Whether exploitation is possible

Whether compensating controls exist

docs.title: CVSS
docs.text:
CVSS can provide a standardised vulnerability severity score.

For example:

CVSS 9.8 Critical

However:

CVSS score of upstream vulnerability

is not automatically:

Risk to this application

Application context still matters.

docs.title: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue identifies vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in the wild.

Conceptually:

Known vulnerability
      |
      v
Known exploitation?
      |
   +--+--+
   |     |
  NO    YES
   |     |
   v     v
Normal   Increased
triage   priority

Presence in a known-exploited catalogue can significantly influence remediation priority.

docs.title: Reachability
docs.text:
A vulnerable dependency may contain vulnerable functionality that the application never calls.

Example:

Application
    |
    v
Dependency
    |
    +-- safe_function()
    |
    +-- vulnerable_function()

If the application only uses:

safe_function()

the vulnerability may not currently be reachable.

However, this does not necessarily mean the dependency should remain unpatched.

Future code changes could make the vulnerable path reachable.

docs.title: Reachability Analysis
docs.text:
A stronger assessment asks:

Is dependency installed?

        |
        v

Is affected version installed?

        |
        v

Is vulnerable component loaded?

        |
        v

Is vulnerable function reachable?

        |
        v

Can attacker-controlled data reach it?

        |
        v

Are exploitation conditions satisfied?

This provides more useful information than simply reporting every CVE discovered by a scanner.

docs.title: Runtime vs Development Dependencies
docs.text:
Some ecosystems distinguish:

Runtime dependencies

from:

Development dependencies

Development dependencies may include:

Test frameworks
Linters
Build tools
Bundlers
Documentation generators
Developer utilities

A vulnerable development dependency may not be shipped into production.

However, it can still matter because it may execute inside:

Developer workstations
Build environments
CI/CD pipelines

Therefore:

Not present in production

does not automatically mean:

No security impact

docs.title: Build-Time Dependencies
docs.text:
Build systems may execute dependency code.

Examples:

npm lifecycle scripts
Maven plugins
Gradle plugins
Python build backends
GitHub Actions
CI plugins
Container build tools

This creates a separate attack surface:

Malicious Dependency
        |
        v
Package Installation
        |
        v
Build Script Executes
        |
        v
CI Runner Compromised

This is a software supply chain risk rather than simply a runtime application vulnerability.

docs.title: Outdated Dependencies
docs.text:
A dependency can be risky even when no currently known CVE applies.

Reasons include:

No longer maintained
Unsupported
End-of-life
No security patches
Abandoned repository
Deprecated

Conceptually:

Old Dependency
      |
      v
No Maintainer
      |
      v
New Vulnerability Found
      |
      v
No Patch Available

This creates long-term security risk.

docs.title: End-of-Life Components
docs.text:
An end-of-life component is no longer supported by its vendor or maintainers.

Examples may include:

Old frameworks
Old runtimes
Old operating systems
Deprecated libraries

Security testing should identify:

Component
Version
Support status
Upgrade path

docs.title: Dependency Confusion
docs.text:
Dependency confusion is a dependency-resolution attack.

Consider an organisation using an internal package:

company-auth

The build system searches:

Internal Registry
+
Public Registry

If resolution is unsafe:

Attacker publishes:

company-auth

to public registry

The package manager may select the attacker-controlled package.

Conceptually:

Build System
      |
      +----------------+
      |                |
      v                v
Internal Registry   Public Registry
company-auth        company-auth
1.0.0               99.0.0
      |                |
      +-------+--------+
              |
              v
      Unsafe Resolution
              |
              v
      Malicious Package

docs.title: Dependency Confusion Preconditions
docs.text:
Typical conditions include:

Private package namespace

Public registry also queried

Package name discoverable

Resolution rules prefer or allow public package

Attacker can publish matching name

Modern package managers and repository configurations differ considerably.

Always determine the actual resolution behaviour before concluding that dependency confusion is possible.

docs.title: Testing Dependency Confusion Safely
docs.text:
Do not publish packages matching an organisation's internal dependencies to a public registry unless this is explicitly authorised.

A safer assessment approach is:

Identify private package names
        |
        v
Inspect registry configuration
        |
        v
Understand package resolution
        |
        v
Check namespace protections
        |
        v
Use controlled internal test package
        |
        v
Verify resolution safely

Avoid creating packages that could accidentally be installed by production systems.

docs.title: Typosquatting
docs.text:
Typosquatting involves malicious packages with names resembling legitimate packages.

Example concept:

legitimate-package

versus:

legitmate-package

or:

legitimate_packagе

where visually similar characters may be involved.

The goal is to cause developers or automated systems to install the wrong package.

docs.title: Package Namespace Security
docs.text:
Package ecosystems use different namespace models.

Examples include:

Scoped packages
Organisation namespaces
Package ownership
Registry-level namespaces

Where available, organisations should reserve and protect package namespaces.

docs.title: Malicious Packages
docs.text:
Not all package risk comes from accidental vulnerabilities.

A package may intentionally contain malicious behaviour.

Examples:

Credential theft
Environment-variable collection
SSH key collection
Backdoors
Cryptocurrency mining
CI token theft
Network callbacks
Malicious install scripts

Traditional CVE scanning may not detect this.

docs.title: Maintainer Compromise
docs.text:
A legitimate package can become malicious if a maintainer account is compromised.

Conceptually:

Trusted Package
      |
      v
Maintainer Account Compromised
      |
      v
Malicious Version Published
      |
      v
Automatic Dependency Update
      |
      v
Consumers Install It

This is why dependency security requires more than vulnerability scanning.

docs.title: Package Ownership Changes
docs.text:
Security review should consider significant project changes such as:

New maintainers
Repository transfer
Namespace transfer
Package ownership changes
Sudden release activity
Unexpected dependency additions

These are not automatically malicious.

They are signals that may justify additional review.

docs.title: Package Installation Scripts
docs.text:
Some package ecosystems allow code execution during installation.

Examples include:

preinstall
install
postinstall
build hooks
setup hooks
plugins

This means:

Installing an untrusted package

can itself be dangerous.

Do Not Install Unknown Packages Casually

When investigating suspicious packages, avoid installing or building them directly on your normal workstation. Use an isolated analysis environment and understand whether installation or build operations execute package-controlled code.

docs.title: JavaScript and Node.js
docs.text:
Common dependency files:

package.json
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml

Inspect:

cat package.json

Look for:

dependencies
devDependencies
optionalDependencies
scripts

docs.title: npm audit
docs.text:
For npm projects:

npm audit

This audits dependencies described by the npm project and lockfile against vulnerability information available through the configured registry.

JSON output:

npm audit --json

A CI-oriented threshold can be specified:

npm audit --audit-level=high

This affects the exit behaviour based on vulnerability severity.

docs.title: Be Careful With npm audit fix
docs.text:
npm can attempt remediation:

npm audit fix

However, during a penetration test or code review, do not immediately modify the client's project.

Instead:

Scan
  |
  v
Understand vulnerability
  |
  v
Identify fixed version
  |
  v
Document recommendation

If remediation testing is authorised, changes should be performed in a controlled branch or test environment.

docs.title: npm audit --force
docs.text:
Be especially cautious with:

npm audit fix --force

This may install updates outside the normal dependency range and can introduce breaking changes.

Do not run it casually against client code.

docs.title: npm Dependency Tree
docs.text:
List installed packages:

npm list

A specific dependency:

npm list lodash

This can help identify:

Why is this package installed?

Is it direct?

Which package depends on it?

docs.title: npm Outdated
docs.text:
Check for outdated packages:

npm outdated

Remember:

Outdated

does not automatically mean:

Vulnerable

and:

Current

does not automatically mean:

Secure

These are different properties.

docs.title: Python Dependencies
docs.text:
Common Python dependency files include:

requirements.txt
pyproject.toml
Pipfile
Pipfile.lock
poetry.lock

A simple requirements file might contain:

Django==5.2.1
requests==2.32.3

docs.title: pip-audit
docs.text:
pip-audit is maintained under the Python Packaging Authority and audits Python environments and requirements-style dependency files for known vulnerabilities.

Install:

python3 -m pip install pip-audit

Audit the current Python environment:

pip-audit

Audit a requirements file:

pip-audit -r requirements.txt

docs.title: pip-audit JSON Output
docs.text:
For machine-readable results:

pip-audit -r requirements.txt -f json

Save:

pip-audit -r requirements.txt \
  -f json > pip-audit-results.json

docs.title: pip-audit Fixing
docs.text:
pip-audit supports automatic fixes:

pip-audit --fix

During assessment work, avoid modifying the target project unless remediation testing is explicitly intended.

Prefer:

Identify
Assess
Recommend
Retest

docs.title: Java Dependencies
docs.text:
Common Java dependency systems include:

Maven
Gradle

Maven:

pom.xml

Gradle:

build.gradle
build.gradle.kts

docs.title: Maven Dependency Tree
docs.text:
For Maven:

mvn dependency:tree

This helps identify transitive dependencies.

Example concept:

application
  |
  +-- framework
       |
       +-- vulnerable-library

The vulnerable library may not appear directly in:

pom.xml

docs.title: Gradle Dependencies
docs.text:
For Gradle:

./gradlew dependencies

This can show dependency relationships and resolved versions.

Warning

Running Maven or Gradle tasks can invoke build logic, plugins, or other project-controlled behaviour. Treat untrusted repositories as potentially executable code and use an isolated environment where appropriate.

docs.title: PHP Dependencies
docs.text:
Composer projects commonly contain:

composer.json
composer.lock

Composer provides:

composer audit

for checking installed packages against security advisories.

Inspect the dependency tree with:

composer show --tree

docs.title: Ruby Dependencies
docs.text:
Ruby projects commonly use:

Gemfile
Gemfile.lock

Dependency security tools in the Ruby ecosystem can inspect gems and advisories.

The important principle remains:

Manifest
+
Resolved versions
+
Advisories
+
Reachability/context

docs.title: Go Dependencies
docs.text:
Go modules commonly use:

go.mod
go.sum

List dependencies:

go list -m all

Go vulnerability analysis can also be performed using ecosystem tooling such as:

govulncheck
OSV-Scanner

docs.title: Rust Dependencies
docs.text:
Rust projects commonly use:

Cargo.toml
Cargo.lock

The lockfile records resolved crate versions.

Dependency analysis should include:

Direct crates
Transitive crates
Build dependencies
Features
Target-specific dependencies

docs.title: .NET Dependencies
docs.text:
.NET projects may use:

.csproj
packages.config
packages.lock.json

The .NET CLI can identify vulnerable packages in supported SDK versions.

Consult the installed SDK's current package-list command help because command naming and output can differ between SDK generations.

docs.title: OSV
docs.text:
OSV provides vulnerability information designed around open-source package ecosystems.

OSV advisories can precisely represent affected package versions and ecosystems.

Examples include:

npm
PyPI
Maven
Go
crates.io
RubyGems
NuGet
Packagist

Official service:

https://osv.dev/

docs.title: OSV-Scanner
docs.text:
OSV-Scanner is Google's open-source scanner for identifying known vulnerabilities in project dependencies.

Official repository:

https://github.com/google/osv-scanner

Modern OSV-Scanner uses commands such as:

osv-scanner scan source .

The shorter default form can also be used:

osv-scanner .

docs.title: Recursive OSV Scan
docs.text:
Scan a project recursively:

osv-scanner scan source -r .

This searches supported dependency information such as:

Lockfiles
SBOMs
Project dependency metadata

docs.title: Scan Specific Lockfiles
docs.text:
Example:

osv-scanner scan source \
  --lockfile=package-lock.json

Multiple lockfiles can be supplied.

This is useful for repositories containing multiple applications.

docs.title: OSV-Scanner Output
docs.text:
OSV-Scanner can produce machine-readable output.

For example:

osv-scanner scan source \
  --format=json \
  -r .

Save it:

osv-scanner scan source \
  --format=json \
  -r . > osv-results.json

docs.title: OSV Reachability and Call Analysis
docs.text:
OSV-Scanner supports call analysis for some ecosystems.

This can help distinguish:

Dependency contains vulnerable function

from:

Application actually calls vulnerable function

Support differs by language and can evolve.

Warning

Some call-analysis modes may compile project or dependency code. In particular, build systems can execute project-controlled scripts. Review the current OSV-Scanner documentation and use an isolated environment before enabling compilation-based analysis on untrusted code.

docs.title: OWASP Dependency-Check
docs.text:
OWASP Dependency-Check is a Software Composition Analysis tool designed to identify publicly disclosed vulnerabilities in project dependencies.

Official project:

https://owasp.org/www-project-dependency-check/

Documentation:

https://dependency-check.github.io/DependencyCheck/

It is especially established in ecosystems such as:

Java
.NET

with varying support for other package ecosystems.

docs.title: Dependency-Check Concept
docs.text:
Project
   |
   v
Dependency-Check
   |
   v
Identify Components
   |
   v
Match Vulnerability Data
   |
   v
Potential Vulnerabilities
   |
   v
Manual Review

Dependency matching is not infallible.

False positives and false negatives are possible.

docs.title: Dependency-Check CLI
docs.text:
After installing the Dependency-Check CLI, a typical scan resembles:

dependency-check.sh \
  --scan /path/to/project \
  --out ./dependency-check-report

Depending on installation method, the executable name and location may differ.

Always verify:

dependency-check.sh --help

against the installed version.

docs.title: Dependency-Check Reports
docs.text:
Dependency-Check can produce reports containing information such as:

Dependency
Version
Identifiers
CVE
Severity
Evidence
Vulnerability details

Treat automated component identification as evidence to review, not unquestionable proof.

docs.title: Trivy
docs.text:
Trivy is a security scanner maintained by Aqua Security.

It can scan several target types, including:

Filesystems
Repositories
Container images
SBOMs

It can detect areas such as:

Known vulnerabilities
Secrets
Misconfigurations
Licensing information

Official documentation:

https://trivy.dev/

docs.title: Trivy Filesystem Scan
docs.text:
Scan a local project:

trivy fs /path/to/project

For example:

trivy fs .

Trivy can identify vulnerable packages from supported lockfiles and package metadata.

docs.title: Trivy Vulnerability-Only Scan
docs.text:
Where explicit scanner selection is useful:

trivy fs \
  --scanners vuln \
  .

This focuses the filesystem scan on known vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Trivy Severity Filtering
docs.text:
For prioritisation:

trivy fs \
  --scanners vuln \
  --severity HIGH,CRITICAL \
  .

Do not ignore lower-severity vulnerabilities automatically.

Severity should be interpreted in application context.

docs.title: Trivy JSON Output
docs.text:
trivy fs \
  --scanners vuln \
  --format json \
  --output trivy-results.json \
  .

Scanner output may contain sensitive project information and should be protected as assessment evidence.

docs.title: Container Dependency Security
docs.text:
Containers combine multiple dependency layers:

Container Image
      |
      +-- Base OS
      |
      +-- OS Packages
      |
      +-- Language Runtime
      |
      +-- Application Dependencies
      |
      +-- Application Code

A vulnerability may exist in any of these layers.

docs.title: Trivy Container Scan
docs.text:
A common container scan is:

trivy image example/application:latest

This can identify known vulnerabilities in supported operating-system and language packages contained in the image.

docs.title: Base Images
docs.text:
Consider:

FROM node:20

The application inherits:

Operating system
Runtime
System libraries
Certificates
Package-manager components

from the base image.

Therefore base-image maintenance is part of dependency security.

docs.title: Floating Container Tags
docs.text:
A tag such as:

latest

does not provide strong build reproducibility.

For higher assurance, organisations may use:

Specific version tags
Image digests
Controlled internal registries

depending on their deployment model.

docs.title: Image Digests
docs.text:
Container images can be referenced using immutable digests.

Conceptually:

Image Tag
    |
    v
May point to different image later

versus:

Image Digest
    |
    v
Specific image content

Digest pinning improves reproducibility but still requires a process to update images when vulnerabilities are fixed.

docs.title: Software Bill of Materials
docs.text:
SBOM stands for:

Software Bill of Materials

An SBOM provides an inventory of software components.

Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
SBOM
    |
    +-- Component A
    +-- Component B
    +-- Component C
    +-- Component D

This helps answer:

What software are we actually using?

docs.title: Why SBOMs Matter
docs.text:
Without an inventory:

New vulnerability announced
        |
        v
Are we affected?
        |
        v
Unknown

With an accurate SBOM:

New vulnerability announced
        |
        v
Search component inventory
        |
        v
Affected projects identified
        |
        v
Prioritise remediation

docs.title: SBOM Formats
docs.text:
Common SBOM formats include:

CycloneDX
SPDX

Both are widely used standards.

docs.title: CycloneDX
docs.text:
CycloneDX is an OWASP standard for bill-of-materials and software supply chain information.

Common CycloneDX filenames include:

bom.json
bom.xml
*.cdx.json
*.cdx.xml

Official project:

https://cyclonedx.org/

docs.title: Example SBOM Concept
docs.text:
An SBOM may contain:

{
  "components": [
    {
      "type": "library",
      "name": "example-library",
      "version": "1.2.3"
    }
  ]
}

Actual CycloneDX and SPDX documents contain additional metadata and structure.

docs.title: SBOM Is Not a Vulnerability Report
docs.text:
An SBOM primarily answers:

What components exist?

A vulnerability scanner answers:

Are known vulnerabilities associated with them?

Conceptually:

SBOM
  |
  v
Component Inventory
  |
  v
Vulnerability Intelligence
  |
  v
Risk Findings

docs.title: SBOM Accuracy
docs.text:
An incomplete SBOM can create false confidence.

Verify whether the SBOM includes:

Direct dependencies
Transitive dependencies
Runtime dependencies
Container packages
Vendored components
Generated components

depending on the intended scope.

docs.title: OWASP Dependency-Track
docs.text:
OWASP Dependency-Track is an open-source component analysis platform designed around software supply chain and SBOM analysis.

Official project:

https://dependencytrack.org/

It can ingest SBOMs and continuously track components against vulnerability and policy information.

Conceptually:

Projects
   |
   v
SBOMs
   |
   v
Dependency-Track
   |
   +-- Component Inventory
   +-- Vulnerabilities
   +-- Policies
   +-- Portfolio Risk
   |
   v
Continuous Monitoring

docs.title: Dependency-Track vs Dependency-Check
docs.text:
These tools solve related but different problems.

Dependency-Check
        |
        v
Scan project dependencies
        |
        v
Find known vulnerabilities

versus:

Dependency-Track
        |
        v
Consume SBOMs
        |
        v
Maintain portfolio inventory
        |
        v
Continuously monitor risk

They can complement each other.

docs.title: Continuous Monitoring
docs.text:
Dependency security is not a one-time scan.

Consider:

Monday:

Dependency 1.2.3
No known vulnerability

Then:

Friday:

New CVE published
Dependency 1.2.3 affected

The application did not change.

Its known risk did.

Therefore:

Continuous monitoring

is necessary.

docs.title: SCA
docs.text:
SCA stands for:

Software Composition Analysis

SCA tools identify third-party software and correlate components with security or licensing information.

Examples include:

OWASP Dependency-Check
OWASP Dependency-Track
OSV-Scanner
Trivy
Snyk
GitHub dependency scanning
Other commercial SCA platforms

Different tools have different strengths and coverage.

docs.title: Scanner Comparison
docs.text:
A useful conceptual comparison:

npm audit
    |
    +-- npm ecosystem

pip-audit
    |
    +-- Python ecosystem

OSV-Scanner
    |
    +-- Multiple ecosystems
    +-- OSV data
    +-- Lockfiles / SBOMs

Dependency-Check
    |
    +-- SCA
    +-- Strong Java/.NET use cases

Trivy
    |
    +-- Application dependencies
    +-- Containers
    +-- Filesystems
    +-- OS packages

Dependency-Track
    |
    +-- SBOM ingestion
    +-- Portfolio monitoring

Using more than one source may reveal differences in coverage.

docs.title: Burp Suite and Dependency Security
docs.text:
Burp is not a full source-code SCA platform.

However, it is useful for detecting dependencies exposed through the running web application.

Conceptually:

Browser
   |
   v
Application
   |
   v
HTTP Responses
   |
   +-- JavaScript libraries
   +-- Framework versions
   +-- Server headers
   +-- Component fingerprints
   |
   v
Burp

Burp can therefore complement source-based dependency analysis.

docs.title: Burp Proxy Workflow
docs.text:
Browse the application normally.

Use Proxy HTTP history to identify:

JavaScript files
CSS
Framework resources
Versioned assets
Headers
Error messages
API responses

Examples:

/jquery-3.4.1.min.js

/bootstrap-4.3.1.min.js

/angular-1.6.0.js

Version information can then be investigated.

docs.title: Do Not Trust Filenames Alone
docs.text:
A filename such as:

jquery-3.4.1.min.js

suggests a version.

It does not prove the file actually contains that version.

Likewise:

jquery-latest.js

provides little reliable version information.

Use multiple indicators where possible.

docs.title: JavaScript Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Possible version indicators include:

Filename
Banner comment
Library metadata
Source content
Known hashes
Source map
Global version property
Build metadata

The reliability of each technique varies.

docs.title: Retire.js Burp Extension
docs.text:
The Burp BApp Store currently contains:

Retire.js

The extension passively analyses JavaScript resources and uses Retire.js signatures to identify vulnerable JavaScript libraries.

BApp Store:

https://portswigger.net/bappstore/36238b534a78494db9bf2d03f112265c

It can identify libraries using indicators such as:

URL
Filename
File content
Hash

Note

The Retire.js BApp is still available in the BApp Store, but the BApp Store entry shows that this Burp extension itself was last updated in December 2021. Treat its results as leads and verify findings against current vulnerability information.

docs.title: Retire.js Workflow
docs.text:
Burp Proxy
    |
    v
Application JavaScript
    |
    v
Retire.js Extension
    |
    v
Library Fingerprint
    |
    v
Known Vulnerability Match
    |
    v
Manual Verification

For every result verify:

Library identity

Version

Vulnerability advisory

Affected version range

Application use

Exploitability

docs.title: Software Vulnerability Scanner Burp Extension
docs.text:
A more recent BApp Store extension relevant to component fingerprinting is:

Software Vulnerability Scanner

BApp Store:

https://portswigger.net/bappstore/c9fb79369b56407792a7104e3c4352fb

The extension fingerprints software from HTTP responses and correlates detected versions with vulnerability information from Vulners.

It can provide:

Detected software
Versions
CVEs
Security advisories
Potentially relevant paths

Note

This is a third-party Burp extension and uses Vulners data. Findings should be independently verified before reporting.

docs.title: Burp Extension Safety
docs.text:
Burp extensions can access sensitive assessment traffic.

Before installing:

Review publisher
Review source where possible
Review permissions and behaviour
Understand external API communication
Avoid unnecessary extensions

PortSwigger explicitly notes that BApp Store extensions are third-party software and recommends reviewing extension code.

docs.title: Burp Scanner
docs.text:
Burp Scanner can identify some vulnerable JavaScript dependencies during application scanning.

However:

Burp Scanner

should not replace:

Repository SCA
SBOM analysis
Lockfile analysis
Container scanning

because Burp only observes what is exposed through the web application.

docs.title: Browser DevTools
docs.text:
Browser DevTools can complement Burp.

Inspect:

Network
Sources
Loaded JavaScript
Source maps
Runtime objects
Response headers

This can help identify client-side libraries and frameworks.

docs.title: Client-Side Dependency Security
docs.text:
JavaScript dependencies execute in the user's browser.

Potential impact includes:

DOM XSS
Prototype pollution
Client-side injection
Unsafe URL handling
Object manipulation
Data leakage

Refer to:

Cross-Site Scripting

DOM-Based Vulnerabilities

Prototype Pollution

docs.title: Third-Party JavaScript
docs.text:
Third-party JavaScript introduces a particularly important trust relationship.

Example:

<script src="https://cdn.example.net/library.js"></script>

Conceptually:

Application
     |
     v
Third-Party Script
     |
     v
Executes in Application Origin
     |
     v
Can interact with page

This topic deserves separate treatment and is covered in:

Third-Party JavaScript Security

docs.title: Subresource Integrity
docs.text:
Subresource Integrity, or SRI, can allow browsers to verify that certain externally loaded resources match an expected cryptographic hash.

Example:

<script
  src="https://cdn.example.net/library.js"
  integrity="sha384-BASE64_HASH"
  crossorigin="anonymous">
</script>

Conceptually:

Browser downloads resource
        |
        v
Calculate hash
        |
        v
Compare with integrity value
        |
     +--+--+
     |     |
   Match  Different
     |     |
     v     v
 Execute  Reject

SRI is particularly relevant for static third-party scripts and styles loaded from external origins.

docs.title: SRI Limitations
docs.text:
SRI is not a universal dependency-security solution.

It does not replace:

Dependency updates
Vulnerability scanning
Package integrity
Secure build systems
Registry security
SBOMs

It protects a specific browser resource-loading scenario.

docs.title: Integrity Files
docs.text:
Package managers may maintain integrity information in lockfiles.

For example, npm lockfiles can contain package integrity metadata.

This helps detect unexpected package-content changes under supported workflows.

Integrity controls are valuable, but they do not prove:

Package is non-malicious

A malicious package published legitimately can still have a valid integrity hash.

docs.title: Package Provenance
docs.text:
Software provenance provides information about:

Where software came from

How it was built

Which source produced it

Which build process created it

This can improve supply-chain assurance.

Conceptually:

Source
  |
  v
Trusted Build
  |
  v
Artifact
  |
  v
Provenance
  |
  v
Verification

docs.title: Signed Artifacts
docs.text:
Cryptographic signatures can help verify:

Publisher identity
Artifact integrity

depending on the ecosystem.

However:

Valid signature

does not guarantee:

No vulnerabilities
No malicious code

It primarily helps answer whether the artifact came from the expected signer and remained unchanged.

docs.title: Package Registries
docs.text:
Applications may use:

npm registry
PyPI
Maven Central
NuGet
RubyGems
crates.io
Packagist
Internal registries
Artifact repositories

Security review should determine:

Which registries are trusted?

Are public registries allowed?

Are internal packages isolated?

Are credentials protected?

Is TLS enforced?

Are packages cached internally?

Are package sources explicitly configured?

docs.title: Internal Artifact Repositories
docs.text:
Organisations often use internal repositories such as:

Artifact proxies
Package registries
Container registries

Benefits can include:

Centralised policy
Package allowlisting
Caching
Malware scanning
Audit logging
Controlled external access

The repository itself becomes security-critical infrastructure.

docs.title: Dependency Allowlisting
docs.text:
High-assurance environments may restrict which dependencies can be introduced.

Possible controls:

Approved package list
Approved versions
License policy
Maintainer review
Security review
Package-age policy
Source repository review
Integrity requirements

This reduces uncontrolled dependency growth.

docs.title: Dependency Minimisation
docs.text:
Every dependency increases:

Attack surface
Maintenance burden
Supply-chain exposure
Update requirements

Before adding a package ask:

Do we actually need it?

A package imported for a trivial function may not justify its dependency tree.

docs.title: Remove Unused Dependencies
docs.text:
Unused dependencies should generally be removed.

Benefits include:

Smaller attack surface
Fewer vulnerabilities
Smaller builds
Simpler SBOM
Reduced maintenance
Reduced supply-chain exposure

docs.title: Vendored Dependencies
docs.text:
Some applications copy third-party source code directly into the repository.

Example:

vendor/
third_party/
lib/

These dependencies may not appear in normal package-manager manifests.

Therefore SCA based solely on lockfiles may miss them.

docs.title: Forked Dependencies
docs.text:
Organisations may maintain internal forks.

Example:

upstream-library
       |
       v
Internal Fork
       |
       v
Application

Security teams must track:

Upstream vulnerabilities
Internal modifications
Patch divergence
Update process

Otherwise security fixes from upstream may never reach the fork.

docs.title: Monorepos
docs.text:
A monorepo may contain many dependency ecosystems.

Example:

repository/
|
+-- frontend/
|   +-- package.json
|
+-- backend/
|   +-- pom.xml
|
+-- worker/
|   +-- requirements.txt
|
+-- tooling/
    +-- go.mod

Recursive scanners such as OSV-Scanner or Trivy can be useful, but verify that every relevant project and lockfile was discovered.

docs.title: Generated Code
docs.text:
Generated code may introduce dependencies that are not obvious from manually written source.

Examples:

Generated SDKs
Protocol clients
ORM code
Build output
Vendor bundles

Determine whether generated artifacts are:

Built internally
Downloaded
Committed
Vendored
Generated during CI

docs.title: CI/CD Dependency Scanning
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

Developer
    |
    v
Commit
    |
    v
Pull Request
    |
    v
Dependency Scan
    |
    +-- Vulnerability?
    +-- Policy violation?
    +-- New dependency?
    |
    v
Review
    |
    v
Build

This catches issues before deployment.

docs.title: CI Security Gate
docs.text:
Example policy:

Critical vulnerability
        |
        v
Fail build

But simplistic severity-only gates can cause problems.

A better policy may consider:

Severity
Exploitability
Reachability
Known exploitation
Internet exposure
Fix availability
Business criticality
Accepted risk

docs.title: Dependency Update Automation
docs.text:
Automated dependency-update tools can reduce patch latency.

Examples include:

Dependabot
Renovate
Platform-specific update automation

Conceptually:

New Dependency Version
        |
        v
Automation Detects Update
        |
        v
Pull Request
        |
        v
Tests + Security Checks
        |
        v
Review
        |
        v
Merge

Automation should not mean:

Automatically deploy every update without testing

docs.title: Vulnerability Prioritisation
docs.text:
When a scanner reports a vulnerability, consider:

Severity
Exploitability
Reachability
Internet exposure
Authentication requirements
Privileges required
Known exploitation
Fix availability
Application criticality
Data sensitivity
Compensating controls

docs.title: Example Prioritisation
docs.text:
CVE A
CVSS: 9.8
Vulnerable function not reachable
Internal test tool only

CVE B
CVSS: 7.5
Internet-facing
Unauthenticated
Known exploitation
Reachable code path

CVE B may deserve faster remediation despite the lower base score.

docs.title: Exploitability
docs.text:
Do not automatically download or execute public exploits.

Start with:

Vendor advisory
CVE description
Affected versions
Patch commit
Technical analysis
Reachability
Application behaviour

If exploitation is required to confirm impact:

Use authorised target
Use controlled payload
Avoid destructive actions
Collect minimum evidence

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Dependency scanners can produce false positives.

Common causes include:

Incorrect package identification
Wrong version detection
Vendored patched copy
Backported security patch
Different package with same name
Unreachable vulnerable code
Incorrect CPE mapping
Platform-specific differences

Always verify important findings.

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Scanners can also miss vulnerabilities.

Possible causes:

Unknown vulnerability
Missing advisory
Unsupported ecosystem
Vendored dependency
Custom fork
Incorrect SBOM
Dynamically downloaded dependency
Runtime plugin
Manually copied library

Therefore:

No scanner findings

does not prove:

No dependency risk

docs.title: Backported Patches
docs.text:
Some vendors patch vulnerabilities without changing to the upstream version normally associated with the fix.

This is common in some operating-system distributions.

Example concept:

Upstream:

1.2.3 vulnerable
1.2.4 fixed

but distributor may provide:

1.2.3-distribution5

with the security patch backported.

Do not report based solely on the upstream version string without considering vendor security advisories.

docs.title: Version Detection
docs.text:
When testing a deployed web application, possible version sources include:

JavaScript banners
HTTP headers
Error messages
Static filenames
Package metadata
Source maps
API responses
Debug pages
SBOMs
Lockfiles
Container metadata

Rank evidence by reliability.

docs.title: Version Disclosure vs Vulnerable Dependency
docs.text:
These are different findings.

Server reveals:

Framework 5.2.1

may be:

Information disclosure

But if:

Framework 5.2.1

has an applicable known vulnerability, that may support:

Vulnerable dependency/component

Do not combine them automatically.

docs.title: Pentesting Workflow
docs.text:
A practical dependency-security assessment can follow:

1. Identify technology stack
        |
        v
2. Obtain dependency manifests
        |
        v
3. Obtain lockfiles
        |
        v
4. Build dependency inventory
        |
        v
5. Identify transitive dependencies
        |
        v
6. Run ecosystem scanners
        |
        v
7. Run general SCA scanner
        |
        v
8. Scan container if available
        |
        v
9. Review SBOM if available
        |
        v
10. Correlate vulnerabilities
        |
        v
11. Check reachability
        |
        v
12. Check known exploitation
        |
        v
13. Assess application exposure
        |
        v
14. Validate safely
        |
        v
15. Report

docs.title: Black-Box Workflow
docs.text:
When source code is unavailable:

Target
  |
  v
Technology Fingerprinting
  |
  +-- HTTP headers
  +-- JavaScript
  +-- Static assets
  +-- Errors
  +-- Source maps
  |
  v
Identify Components
  |
  v
Identify Versions
  |
  v
Research Advisories
  |
  v
Verify Version Evidence
  |
  v
Assess Applicability

Useful tools include:

Burp Suite
Retire.js BApp
Software Vulnerability Scanner BApp
Browser DevTools
Technology fingerprinting tools

docs.title: White-Box Workflow
docs.text:
With source access:

Repository
    |
    +-- Manifest files
    +-- Lockfiles
    +-- Vendored code
    +-- Containers
    +-- CI/CD
    +-- IaC
    |
    v
Dependency Inventory
    |
    +-- npm audit
    +-- pip-audit
    +-- OSV-Scanner
    +-- Dependency-Check
    +-- Trivy
    |
    v
Manual Validation

docs.title: Quick Scanner Workflow
docs.text:
For a repository containing multiple technologies:

osv-scanner scan source -r .

Then:

trivy fs --scanners vuln .

For Node.js projects:

npm audit

For Python:

pip-audit -r requirements.txt

For Maven:

mvn dependency:tree

These tools overlap.

That is useful because they can provide different visibility.

docs.title: Do Not Blindly Run Build Commands
docs.text:
Commands such as:

npm install
pip install
mvn package
gradle build
cargo build

may execute code or scripts from:

Dependencies
Build plugins
Project configuration
Install hooks

When assessing an untrusted repository:

Prefer static analysis first.

If execution is necessary:

Use an isolated environment.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each dependency finding record:

Application
Component
Installed version
Affected version range
Fixed version
Dependency type
Direct / transitive
Manifest
Lockfile
Dependency path
Advisory
CVE
Severity
Known exploitation
Reachability
Runtime exposure
Evidence
Remediation

docs.title: Dependency Path Evidence
docs.text:
For a transitive dependency, document why it exists.

Example:

application
  -> framework 4.2.0
      -> parser 2.1.3
          -> vulnerable-library 1.0.2

This makes remediation easier.

docs.title: Example Finding: Vulnerable JavaScript Library
docs.text:
Finding:
Vulnerable JavaScript Dependency

Affected resource:
https://example.com/assets/jquery-3.4.1.min.js

Observed:
The application loads a JavaScript library version associated with publicly documented security vulnerabilities.

The library identity and version were confirmed using multiple indicators rather than relying solely on the filename.

Applicability:
The relevant advisory was reviewed to determine whether the affected functionality is present in the deployed application.

Impact:
Depending on how the affected library functionality is used, exploitation may allow client-side security impact such as cross-site scripting.

Recommendation:
Upgrade the dependency to a currently supported version containing the relevant security fixes. Regression-test functionality affected by the upgrade and remove unused libraries.

docs.title: Example Finding: Vulnerable Transitive Dependency
docs.text:
Finding:
Known Vulnerability in Transitive Application Dependency

Observed:
Software composition analysis identified a vulnerable component that is not declared directly by the application.

Dependency path:

application
 -> framework
 -> parser
 -> vulnerable-component

The installed version falls within the affected range documented by the upstream security advisory.

Impact:
The vulnerable component is included in the application dependency graph and may expose the application to the documented vulnerability where the affected functionality is reachable.

Recommendation:
Upgrade the direct dependency to a version that resolves the vulnerable transitive component, apply an appropriate dependency override where supported, or follow the vendor's recommended remediation.

docs.title: Example Finding: End-of-Life Framework
docs.text:
Finding:
Unsupported Application Framework in Use

Observed:
The application uses a framework version that is no longer supported by the upstream project.

Impact:
Security vulnerabilities discovered in the unsupported branch may not receive patches, increasing long-term security and maintenance risk.

Recommendation:
Migrate the application to a currently supported framework release and establish lifecycle monitoring for major application dependencies.

docs.title: Example Finding: Vulnerable Container Base Image
docs.text:
Finding:
Known Vulnerabilities in Container Base Image

Observed:
Container analysis identified multiple known vulnerabilities in operating-system packages inherited from the configured base image.

Impact:
The application inherits the affected packages from its base image. Exploitability depends on whether affected functionality is present and reachable in the deployed container.

Recommendation:
Rebuild the application using a currently maintained base image containing the relevant security updates. Implement regular container rebuilds and continuous image vulnerability monitoring.

docs.title: Example Finding: Dependency Confusion Risk
docs.text:
Finding:
Unsafe Dependency Resolution Allows Potential Public Package Substitution

Observed:
The build configuration references private package names while also permitting resolution from a public package registry.

Testing in the authorised isolated environment demonstrated that the configured resolution policy could select an externally sourced package matching an internal dependency name.

Impact:
An attacker capable of publishing a matching package under applicable registry conditions may be able to introduce attacker-controlled code into the build process.

Recommendation:
Use protected namespaces, explicitly configure trusted registries for private packages, prevent unintended public fallback, and enforce package-source policies within CI/CD.

docs.title: Finding Titles
docs.text:
Useful report titles include:

Vulnerable Third-Party Dependency

Vulnerable JavaScript Dependency

Known Vulnerability in Transitive Dependency

Unsupported Third-Party Component

End-of-Life Application Framework

Vulnerable Container Base Image

Known Vulnerabilities in Container Packages

Outdated Security-Critical Dependency

Unsafe Dependency Resolution

Potential Dependency Confusion

Unpinned Build Dependency

Missing Dependency Integrity Controls

Unmaintained Third-Party Component

Incomplete Software Bill of Materials

Vulnerable Build-Time Dependency

Known Exploited Vulnerability in Application Dependency

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on context.

Possible factors:

Upstream severity
Reachability
Internet exposure
Authentication
Privileges required
Known exploitation
Exploit maturity
Data sensitivity
Application criticality
Fix availability
Compensating controls

Example:

Vulnerable package exists
but affected code not used

-> Lower practical risk

versus:

Internet-facing application
+
Unauthenticated vulnerable endpoint
+
Known exploited CVE
+
Reliable exploit path

-> High / Critical

docs.title: Upgrade Vulnerable Dependencies
docs.text:
Preferred remediation is usually:

Upgrade to fixed supported version

rather than attempting to patch around the dependency indefinitely.

docs.title: Remove Unused Dependencies
docs.text:
If a dependency is not required:

Remove it.

This eliminates:

Vulnerability exposure
Supply-chain exposure
Maintenance burden

docs.title: Replace Abandoned Dependencies
docs.text:
If a dependency is no longer maintained:

Identify supported alternative
        |
        v
Evaluate compatibility
        |
        v
Migrate
        |
        v
Remove abandoned component

docs.title: Maintain Lockfiles
docs.text:
Use lockfiles where appropriate and commit them according to the package ecosystem's recommended workflow.

Then:

Review
Update
Test
Regenerate
Monitor

them as dependencies change.

docs.title: Automate Vulnerability Monitoring
docs.text:
Integrate dependency scanning into:

Pull requests
CI/CD
Scheduled scans
Repository monitoring
Container pipelines
SBOM platforms

docs.title: Maintain an SBOM
docs.text:
Generate and maintain an accurate SBOM.

The SBOM should evolve with the application.

Build
  |
  v
Generate SBOM
  |
  v
Store SBOM
  |
  v
Monitor Components
  |
  v
New Advisory
  |
  v
Identify Affected Builds

docs.title: Protect Package Sources
docs.text:
Use:

Trusted registries
Namespace controls
TLS
Authentication
Repository policies
Integrity validation
Controlled mirrors

where appropriate.

docs.title: Restrict Build Environments
docs.text:
Build systems frequently contain valuable credentials.

Apply:

Least privilege
Ephemeral runners
Network restrictions
Secret isolation
Minimal credentials
Branch protection
Dependency controls

docs.title: Review New Dependencies
docs.text:
Before adopting a new dependency consider:

Is it maintained?

Is the repository active?

Who maintains it?

How many transitive dependencies does it introduce?

Does it execute installation scripts?

Is the licence acceptable?

Are releases signed or otherwise verifiable?

Are vulnerabilities handled responsibly?

Could existing platform functionality replace it?

docs.title: Patch Management
docs.text:
Dependency patching should have defined expectations.

Example:

Critical
    |
    v
Immediate prioritisation

High
    |
    v
Accelerated remediation

Medium / Low
    |
    v
Risk-based remediation

Exact SLAs should reflect organisational risk and should not rely on severity alone.

The most important principle is:

A scanner finding is a starting point for dependency analysis, not automatic proof that the application is exploitable.

For each vulnerable component ask:

What is the component?

What version is actually installed?

Is it direct or transitive?

What introduces it?

Which advisory applies?

Is this exact version affected?

Is a vendor patch backported?

Is the vulnerable functionality present?

Does the application call it?

Can attacker-controlled input reach it?

Is exploitation known in the wild?

Is the component present in production?

What privileges would exploitation provide?

What version fixes it?

Can the dependency be removed entirely?
