Reject / Quarantine

Always establish:

FILE
 ↓
VALIDATION
 ↓
STORAGE
 ↓
PROCESSING
 ↓
RETRIEVAL
 ↓
SECURITY IMPACT

docs.title: Example Finding: Insufficient File Type Validation
docs.text:
Title
Insufficient Server-Side File Type Validation

Affected Function
Document Upload

Description
The application does not sufficiently validate uploaded files.

Testing demonstrated that validation relied on attacker-controlled
file metadata rather than independently validating the actual file
format.

Impact
An authenticated attacker may be able to store files outside the
intended set of permitted document types.

The resulting impact depends on how uploaded files are stored,
processed and subsequently delivered to users.

Recommendation
Implement defence-in-depth upload validation.

Validate the final extension against an explicit allowlist, verify
the expected file signature and structure, generate server-side
filenames and store uploaded objects in non-executable storage.

Complex document formats should additionally be scanned for
malicious content before becoming available to users.

docs.title: Example Finding: Malware Detection Missing
docs.text:
Title
Uploaded Files Are Not Scanned for Malicious Content

Affected Function
Document Upload

Description
The application accepts user-controlled documents that can
subsequently be downloaded by other users.

Testing using the standard EICAR antivirus test file demonstrated
that recognised malicious test content was accepted, stored and
remained available for retrieval.

Impact
The application may be used as a distribution mechanism for
malicious files.

Users who trust documents delivered through the application could
be exposed to malicious content.

Recommendation
Integrate malware scanning into the upload pipeline.

Uploaded files should remain quarantined until scanning completes
successfully.

If the scanner is unavailable or returns an error, the file should
remain unavailable rather than being automatically treated as safe.

docs.title: Example Finding: Unsafe Filename Rendering
docs.text:
Title
Uploaded Filenames Are Rendered Without Sufficient Output Encoding

Affected Function
Document Management

Description
User-controlled filenames are stored and subsequently displayed in
the application.

The application does not consistently encode the filename for the
HTML context in which it is rendered.

Impact
Depending on the affected rendering context, attacker-controlled
filenames may alter application content or potentially create a
stored cross-site scripting condition.

Recommendation
Treat original filenames as untrusted data.

Generate separate server-side storage names and apply
context-appropriate output encoding whenever original filenames are
displayed.

docs.title: Example Finding: Upload Published Before Scan
docs.text:
Title
Uploaded Files Become Accessible Before Malware Scanning Completes

Description
Uploaded documents become retrievable immediately after upload,
while malware scanning occurs asynchronously.

This creates a period during which an unscanned document can be
downloaded by another user.

Recommendation
Store newly uploaded files in a quarantine state.

Only publish or expose the file after all required validation and
malware scanning stages complete successfully.

docs.title: Reporting File Upload Findings
docs.text:
Avoid reporting:

The application allows PDF uploads.

That is expected functionality.

Instead establish the failed security control:

Extension validation bypass

Content-Type trusted without verification

File signature not validated

File structure not validated

Malware scanning absent

EICAR accepted and retrievable

Unsafe filename rendering

Path traversal through filename

Upload stored in executable location

File accessible without authorisation

SVG rendered unsafely

Archive extraction traversal

Scanner failure causes fail-open behaviour

A useful reporting model is:

INPUT
  ↓
FAILED CONTROL
  ↓
PROCESSING / STORAGE
  ↓
EXPOSURE
  ↓
SECURITY IMPACT

docs.title: OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html

This should be the primary defensive reference for this page.

OWASP recommends a defence-in-depth upload strategy including extension allowlisting, not trusting Content-Type alone, filename controls, file size restrictions, storage outside the web root where possible, antivirus or sandbox analysis where appropriate, CDR for applicable document types and appropriate access controls.

docs.title: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide
docs.text:
https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/

Useful for the wider web application testing methodology surrounding upload functionality.

docs.title: File Upload Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/file-upload

PortSwigger provides practical material covering file upload validation, content types, extensions and server-side file handling.

docs.title: Anti-Malware Test File
docs.text:
https://www.eicar.org/download-anti-malware-testfile/

EICAR provides the standard harmless antivirus test file used to verify malware detection systems without using real malicious software.

docs.title: Client Side Exploits
docs.text:
https://www.offsec.com/metasploit-unleashed/client-side-exploits/

The OffSec documentation demonstrates client-side exploitation using Metasploit file-format modules, including the historical Adobe util.printf() PDF example.

The documented target is:

Adobe Reader v8.1.2
Windows XP SP3 English

This example is useful for understanding why:

Valid File Format

does not automatically mean:

Safe File

It should be reproduced only in an isolated authorised lab containing the intentionally vulnerable client.

docs.title: Upload Insecure Files
docs.text:
https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/tree/master/Upload%20Insecure%20Files

Useful reference for file upload validation and application-specific behaviours.

docs.title: File Upload
docs.text:
https://book.hacktricks.wiki/en/pentesting-web/file-upload/index.html

Additional practical reference covering file upload security testing.

docs.title: ProjectDiscovery Nuclei
docs.text:
https://github.com/projectdiscovery/nuclei

Useful for targeted automated checks with manual validation.

docs.title: Interactsh
docs.text:
https://github.com/projectdiscovery/interactsh

Useful when authorised backend file processing tests require controlled out-of-band interaction detection.

docs.title: Related Notes
docs.text:
Web Application Security
├── Methodology
├── Pentesting Checklist
├── Reconnaissance
│   ├── Subdomain Enumeration
│   ├── Technology Identification
│   ├── Content Discovery
│   ├── Parameter Discovery
│   └── JavaScript Analysis
├── Authentication
├── Authorisation
├── Session Management
├── Burp Suite
│   ├── Extensions
│   └── Testing Workflows
├── Cross-Site Scripting
├── SQL Injection
├── OS Command Injection
├── Server Side Request Forgery
├── XML External Entity Injection
├── Path Traversal
├── File Inclusion
└── File Upload

File Upload connects particularly strongly with:

File Upload
    │
    ├── Filename
    │      ↓
    │   Stored / Blind XSS
    │
    ├── Storage Path
    │      ↓
    │   Path Traversal
    │
    ├── SVG / XML
    │      ↓
    │   XXE / XSS
    │
    ├── Backend URL Fetching
    │      ↓
    │   SSRF
    │
    ├── File Inclusion
    │      ↓
    │   Uploaded File + LFI
    │
    ├── ZIP Extraction
    │      ↓
    │   Zip Slip
    │
    ├── Document Processing
    │      ↓
    │   Parser Attack Surface
    │
    └── Retrieval
           ↓
        Authorisation / IDOR

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
Do not reduce file upload testing to:

Can I upload a forbidden extension?

Instead ask:

What can I upload?
        ↓
How is the extension validated?
        ↓
How is the actual format validated?
        ↓
Is the content scanned?
        ↓
How is the filename handled?
        ↓
Where is the file stored?
        ↓
What processes the file?
        ↓
When does it become available?
        ↓
Who can retrieve it?
        ↓
How does the browser handle it?
        ↓
What happens when it is deleted?
        ↓
What is the actual security impact?

The complete security boundary is:

UNTRUSTED FILE
      ↓
VALIDATION
      ↓
QUARANTINE
      ↓
SCANNING
      ↓
PROCESSING
      ↓
STORAGE
      ↓
RETRIEVAL
      ↓
CONSUMER

That is the model to use when assessing file upload functionality.

docs.title: GraphQL API Security
docs.text:
GraphQL is a query language and API runtime that allows clients to request exactly the data they require.

Unlike traditional REST APIs, where functionality is commonly distributed across many endpoints, GraphQL applications frequently expose a single endpoint through which queries and mutations are performed.

Typical endpoints include:

/graphql
/api/graphql
/api
/graphql/api
/graphql/graphql
/v1/graphql
/v2/graphql
/query

A simplified architecture is:

Client
  ↓
GraphQL Endpoint
  ↓
GraphQL Parser
  ↓
Schema
  ↓
Resolvers
  ↓
Application Logic
  ↓
Database / Services

GraphQL itself is not inherently insecure.

Security issues generally arise from:

Weak authorisation
Missing object-level access controls
Exposed introspection
Excessive data exposure
Unsafe resolver logic
Injection vulnerabilities
Weak rate limiting
Query batching
Alias abuse
Excessive query complexity
CSRF
Information disclosure
Business logic vulnerabilities

Potential impact includes:

Sensitive data exposure
IDOR / BOLA
Privilege escalation
Authentication bypass
Authorisation bypass
Account compromise
Mass assignment
Brute-force amplification
Denial of service
Injection
Business logic abuse

Authorised Security Testing

GraphQL testing should only be performed against systems included in the authorised assessment scope. Query complexity, batching and alias testing can create significant server load, so begin with small controlled requests.

docs.title: GraphQL vs REST
docs.text:
A REST API may expose:

GET /api/users/123
GET /api/users/123/orders
GET /api/products
POST /api/users
DELETE /api/users/123

GraphQL may expose:

POST /graphql

and place the requested operation inside the request body.

For example:

query {
    user(id: 123) {
        id
        username
        email
    }
}

The same endpoint may also perform updates:

mutation {
    updateUser(
        id: 123
        name: "Alice"
    ) {
        id
        name
    }
}

Therefore:

REST
 ↓
Endpoint-focused testing

GraphQL
 ↓
Schema + resolver + object-focused testing

docs.title: GraphQL Terminology
docs.text:
Important terms include:

Schema
Type
Field
Argument
Query
Mutation
Subscription
Resolver
Variable
Fragment
Alias
Directive
Introspection

Understanding these concepts makes GraphQL security testing significantly easier.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
The GraphQL schema defines:

Available objects
Available fields
Queries
Mutations
Subscriptions
Arguments
Relationships
Input types
Enums

Conceptually:

Schema
 ├── Query
 │    ├── user
 │    ├── users
 │    └── products
 │
 ├── Mutation
 │    ├── createUser
 │    ├── updateUser
 │    └── deleteUser
 │
 └── Types
      ├── User
      ├── Product
      └── Order

From a penetration-testing perspective, the schema can become an extremely useful map of the application's attack surface.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
Queries normally retrieve information.

Example:

query {
    user(id: 123) {
        id
        username
        email
    }
}

Possible response:

{
  "data": {
    "user": {
      "id": "123",
      "username": "alice",
      "email": "alice@example.com"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Mutations
docs.text:
Mutations modify application state.

Examples may include:

createUser
updateUser
deleteUser
changePassword
createOrder
cancelOrder
updateRole
resetPassword

Example:

mutation {
    updateProfile(name: "Alice") {
        id
        name
    }
}

Mutations deserve particular attention because they often expose:

Authorisation flaws
Mass assignment
Business logic vulnerabilities
Privilege changes
Account modification

docs.title: Subscriptions
docs.text:
GraphQL subscriptions provide real-time updates.

They commonly use:

WebSockets

Conceptually:

Client
  ↓
GraphQL Subscription
  ↓
WebSocket
  ↓
Server Event
  ↓
Real-Time Response

If subscriptions are present, also review:

WebSocket Security

docs.title: Resolvers
docs.text:
Resolvers contain the server-side logic responsible for retrieving or modifying data.

Conceptually:

GraphQL Query
      ↓
Field
      ↓
Resolver
      ↓
Database / Service

For example:

user(id: 123)
      ↓
userResolver()
      ↓
Database
      ↓
User 123

Security controls often need to be enforced inside or before resolvers.

A schema may expose:

user(id: ID!): User

but whether the current user is actually allowed to access that object depends on resolver and application logic.

docs.title: GraphQL Request Structure
docs.text:
A common request looks like:

POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "query { user(id: 123) { id username email } }"
}

GraphQL requests may also use variables.

Example:

POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "query GetUser($id: ID!) { user(id: $id) { id username email } }",
  "variables": {
    "id": "123"
  }
}

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variables separate arguments from the GraphQL query.

Example:

query GetUser($id: ID!) {
    user(id: $id) {
        id
        username
        email
    }
}

Variables:

{
  "id": "123"
}

During testing, both should be reviewed:

GraphQL query
+
Variables

docs.title: GraphQL Testing Methodology
docs.text:
A structured workflow is:

Identify GraphQL Endpoint
          ↓
Confirm GraphQL
          ↓
Capture Legitimate Queries
          ↓
Identify Schema
          ↓
Test Introspection
          ↓
Enumerate Queries
          ↓
Enumerate Mutations
          ↓
Enumerate Types
          ↓
Map Arguments
          ↓
Test Authentication
          ↓
Test Object-Level Authorisation
          ↓
Test Field-Level Authorisation
          ↓
Test Mutations
          ↓
Test Input Validation
          ↓
Test Aliases / Batching
          ↓
Test Rate Limiting
          ↓
Test CSRF
          ↓
Test Query Complexity
          ↓
Test Business Logic
          ↓
Report

docs.title: Finding GraphQL Endpoints
docs.text:
The first step is identifying the GraphQL endpoint.

Common locations include:

/graphql
/api
/api/graphql
/graphql/api
/graphql/graphql
/v1/graphql
/v2/graphql
/query

Also inspect:

JavaScript
API documentation
Network traffic
Mobile API traffic
Source maps
Swagger/OpenAPI references
Error messages

docs.title: Universal GraphQL Query
docs.text:
A useful GraphQL probe is:

query {
    __typename
}

Compact form:

query{__typename}

Example request:

POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "query{__typename}"
}

A GraphQL service may respond with something similar to:

{
  "data": {
    "__typename": "Query"
  }
}

This is useful because __typename is available on GraphQL object types.

docs.title: GET Requests
docs.text:
Some GraphQL endpoints accept queries through GET requests.

Example:

/graphql?query=query{__typename}

During endpoint discovery, test both:

POST
GET

where appropriate.

docs.title: Content Types
docs.text:
GraphQL APIs may accept:

application/json
application/graphql
application/x-www-form-urlencoded

For security-sensitive operations, accepting alternative content types can become relevant to CSRF testing.

Record which combinations are accepted.

docs.title: Burp Suite GraphQL Detection
docs.text:
Burp Suite can recognise GraphQL traffic.

A practical workflow is:

Burp Browser
     ↓
Proxy
     ↓
HTTP History
     ↓
GraphQL Request
     ↓
GraphQL Editor
     ↓
Repeater

When Burp recognises GraphQL traffic, GraphQL-specific editing support can make requests easier to analyse.

docs.title: Initial Burp Workflow
docs.text:
Browse the application normally first.

Proxy
  ↓
HTTP History
  ↓
Filter Interesting Requests
  ↓
Locate GraphQL
  ↓
Send to Repeater

Do not begin by blindly generating large queries.

First understand what the normal application does.

docs.title: GraphQL Introspection
docs.text:
GraphQL introspection allows clients to query information about the schema itself.

This may reveal:

Queries
Mutations
Types
Fields
Arguments
Enums
Input types
Subscriptions

Conceptually:

Attacker
   ↓
Introspection
   ↓
Schema
   ↓
API Attack Surface

docs.title: Introspection Probe
docs.text:
A small introspection probe is:

{
    __schema {
        queryType {
            name
        }
    }
}

JSON request:

{
  "query": "{__schema{queryType{name}}}"
}

If introspection is enabled, the server may return schema information.

docs.title: Enumerating Query Types
docs.text:
Example:

{
    __schema {
        queryType {
            fields {
                name
            }
        }
    }
}

This may reveal queries such as:

user
users
product
products
order
orders
search
admin

docs.title: Enumerating Mutations
docs.text:
Mutations are often particularly valuable.

Example:

{
    __schema {
        mutationType {
            fields {
                name
            }
        }
    }
}

Potential results:

createUser
updateUser
deleteUser
changePassword
resetPassword
createOrder
cancelOrder
updateRole

docs.title: Full Introspection
docs.text:
A full introspection query can reveal the complete GraphQL schema.

Rather than manually maintaining a large introspection query, use tooling such as:

Burp Suite
InQL
GraphiQL
GraphQL Voyager
GraphQL IDEs

where authorised.

The resulting schema can then be analysed systematically.

docs.title: Introspection Disabled
docs.text:
If introspection is disabled, do not assume the API cannot be mapped.

Other sources include:

Application requests
JavaScript
Error messages
Field suggestions
Mobile applications
Documentation
Source maps
Historic endpoints
Known operation names

docs.title: GraphQL Suggestions
docs.text:
GraphQL implementations sometimes return suggestions when an invalid field name is supplied.

For example, requesting:

query {
    usre {
        id
    }
}

may produce an error similar to:

Cannot query field "usre".
Did you mean "user"?

These suggestions may assist schema reconstruction.

docs.title: Error-Based Schema Discovery
docs.text:
GraphQL error messages can reveal:

Field names
Type names
Expected argument types
Required arguments
Enum values
Mutation names
Validation rules

For example:

Field "user" argument "id" of type "ID!" is required

reveals:

Field: user
Argument: id
Type: ID!
Required: yes

docs.title: GraphQL Schema Mapping
docs.text:
Create a map such as:

Query
 ├── user(id)
 ├── users
 ├── product(id)
 ├── order(id)
 └── search(term)

Mutation
 ├── updateProfile
 ├── changePassword
 ├── createOrder
 ├── cancelOrder
 └── updateUser

Then prioritise:

Authentication
Users
Roles
Permissions
Orders
Payments
Files
Administrative functions
Password operations
API keys
Tokens

docs.title: GraphQL and IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
GraphQL APIs are highly relevant to object-level authorisation testing.

Consider:

query {
    user(id: 1001) {
        id
        username
        email
    }
}

Change:

1001

to:

1002

Then ask:

Is the authenticated user authorised to access user 1002?

This is fundamentally the same security question as REST API IDOR testing.

docs.title: Object-Level Authorisation Workflow
docs.text:
Authenticated User A
       ↓
Query Own Object
       ↓
Capture Object ID
       ↓
Identify User B Object
       ↓
Change ID
       ↓
Send Request
       ↓
Authorisation Enforced?

Use controlled test accounts whenever possible.

docs.title: Nested Object Authorisation
docs.text:
GraphQL allows nested relationships.

Example:

query {
    user(id: 123) {
        id
        username
        orders {
            id
            total
        }
    }
}

The API must enforce authorisation not only on:

user

but potentially also:

orders

A parent object being accessible does not automatically mean all nested objects should be accessible.

docs.title: Field-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Different fields may require different privileges.

Example:

query {
    user(id: 123) {
        id
        username
        email
        role
        passwordResetToken
        apiKey
    }
}

The user may legitimately access:

username
email

but not:

role
passwordResetToken
apiKey

Test fields individually.

docs.title: Excessive Data Exposure
docs.text:
GraphQL makes it easy for clients to request additional fields.

The UI may request:

user {
    id
    username
}

while the schema may expose:

user {
    id
    username
    email
    phone
    role
    internalId
    apiKey
}

Do not assume that fields absent from the normal frontend request are inaccessible.

docs.title: Hidden Fields
docs.text:
When schema information is available, compare:

Fields used by frontend

against:

Fields exposed by schema

The difference is particularly interesting.

For example:

Frontend uses:
id
username
avatar

Schema also exposes:
email
phone
role
internalNotes
apiToken

Investigate authorisation for those fields.

docs.title: Mutation Authorisation
docs.text:
Mutations should receive the same scrutiny as sensitive REST methods.

Example:

mutation {
    updateUser(
        id: 123
        name: "Alice"
    ) {
        id
        name
    }
}

Questions include:

Can another user's ID be supplied?
Can privileged fields be changed?
Can role be modified?
Can ownership be changed?
Can account state be changed?

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Consider an input type:

input UpdateUserInput {
    name: String
    email: String
    role: String
}

If a normal user should only modify:

name
email

but the API also accepts:

role

there may be a mass-assignment or authorisation issue.

Test schema-exposed input fields carefully.

docs.title: Input Object Enumeration
docs.text:
Introspection may reveal input types.

Conceptually:

Mutation
   ↓
Argument
   ↓
Input Type
   ↓
Fields

For example:

UpdateUserInput
 ├── username
 ├── email
 ├── role
 ├── verified
 └── status

Fields such as:

role
verified
status
owner
permissions

deserve particular attention.

docs.title: GraphQL Aliases
docs.text:
GraphQL aliases allow multiple fields or operations to be requested under different names.

Example:

query {
    first: user(id: 1) {
        username
    }

    second: user(id: 2) {
        username
    }
}

Response:

{
  "data": {
    "first": {
      "username": "alice"
    },
    "second": {
      "username": "bob"
    }
  }
}

Aliases are a legitimate GraphQL feature.

However, they can interact with security controls.

docs.title: Alias Abuse
docs.text:
Suppose an application rate-limits:

HTTP requests

rather than:

GraphQL operations

One HTTP request may contain many aliases.

Conceptually:

1 HTTP Request
      ↓
Alias 1
Alias 2
Alias 3
Alias 4
Alias 5
      ↓
5 Resolver Executions

This can potentially weaken naive request-based rate limiting.

docs.title: Safe Alias Testing
docs.text:
Begin with a very small number of operations.

For example:

query {
    one: user(id: 1) {
        id
    }

    two: user(id: 2) {
        id
    }
}

Do not generate hundreds or thousands of aliases against production systems.

The objective is to determine whether controls operate per:

HTTP request

or:

GraphQL operation / resolver

docs.title: Aliases and Authentication Testing
docs.text:
Alias behaviour may also matter for operations such as:

Login
OTP verification
Password reset
Username lookup
Coupon validation

The important question is:

Does one HTTP request permit multiple security-sensitive attempts?

docs.title: GraphQL Batching
docs.text:
Some implementations allow multiple GraphQL operations in one HTTP request.

Conceptually:

[
  {
    "query": "..."
  },
  {
    "query": "..."
  }
]

Batching can potentially interact with:

Rate limiting
Brute-force protection
Monitoring
Logging
Resource consumption

Test only with small controlled batches.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Rate limiting should consider:

Requests
Operations
Aliases
Resolvers
User identity
Target object
Authentication action

A control that only counts HTTP requests may not adequately protect GraphQL operations.

docs.title: GraphQL CSRF
docs.text:
GraphQL endpoints may be vulnerable to CSRF when they accept requests that browsers can send cross-origin without requiring a CORS preflight.

Pay attention when mutations accept:

GET
application/x-www-form-urlencoded
text/plain

or other browser-compatible request formats.

docs.title: CSRF Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Identify State-Changing Mutation
        ↓
Determine Accepted HTTP Methods
        ↓
Determine Accepted Content Types
        ↓
Check Cookie Authentication
        ↓
Check CSRF Token
        ↓
Check SameSite
        ↓
Determine Whether Browser Can Submit Request
        ↓
Validate With Controlled Account

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: JSON and CSRF
docs.text:
A GraphQL API that only accepts:

POST
Content-Type: application/json

is more resistant to traditional form-based CSRF because browsers cannot normally submit arbitrary cross-origin JSON requests without triggering CORS preflight behaviour.

However, do not rely on content type alone.

Use:

CSRF tokens
SameSite cookies
Origin validation
Appropriate CORS policy

where applicable.

docs.title: Content-Type Validation
docs.text:
Test whether:

Content-Type: application/json

can be changed to:

Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

or:

Content-Type: text/plain

while the mutation still executes.

If so, investigate CSRF implications.

docs.title: GET Mutations
docs.text:
State-changing operations should not normally be executable through GET requests.

Test whether the endpoint permits something equivalent to:

GET /graphql?query=mutation{...}

If state-changing operations can be performed through GET, investigate:

CSRF
Caching
Logging
URL leakage

docs.title: Injection Testing
docs.text:
GraphQL does not automatically eliminate injection vulnerabilities.

Resolver code may pass arguments into:

SQL
NoSQL
Operating system commands
Templates
LDAP
Search engines
File paths
URLs

Example:

query {
    search(term: "test") {
        id
        name
    }
}

The security question is:

How does the resolver process term?

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
If a GraphQL resolver builds unsafe SQL queries:

GraphQL Argument
      ↓
Resolver
      ↓
SQL Query

SQL injection may still occur.

Refer to:

SQL Injection

docs.title: NoSQL Injection
docs.text:
GraphQL is frequently used with applications backed by:

MongoDB
Document databases
NoSQL stores

GraphQL input should not be assumed safe merely because the schema specifies types.

Resolver and database logic still require review.

A dedicated page should cover:

NoSQL Injection

docs.title: Command Injection
docs.text:
If GraphQL input reaches system commands:

GraphQL Argument
      ↓
Resolver
      ↓
Shell / Process

command injection may be possible.

Refer to:

OS Command Injection

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
Resolvers may fetch remote resources.

Example conceptual query:

query {
    preview(url: "https://example.com") {
        title
    }
}

Flow:

GraphQL Argument
      ↓
Resolver
      ↓
Server-Side HTTP Request

This may create SSRF attack surface.

Refer to:

Server Side Request Forgery

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
GraphQL operations involving:

Files
Exports
Downloads
Templates
Reports
Images

may expose path-related arguments.

Example:

query {
    downloadFile(name: "report.pdf") {
        url
    }
}

Trace how the resolver handles the file identifier.

Refer to:

Path Traversal

docs.title: File Uploads
docs.text:
GraphQL APIs can support file uploads through implementation-specific mechanisms such as multipart requests.

Review:

File extension validation
MIME validation
Magic bytes
File size
Storage location
Authorisation
Metadata
Filename handling
Processing libraries

Refer to:

File Upload Security

docs.title: Business Logic
docs.text:
GraphQL exposes application functionality differently, but the underlying business rules remain critical.

For example:

mutation {
    applyDiscount(code: "TEST") {
        total
    }
}

Questions include:

Can the operation be repeated?
Can the same discount be reused?
Can negative quantities be supplied?
Can price fields be influenced?
Can workflow steps be skipped?

Refer to:

Business Logic Vulnerabilities

docs.title: GraphQL Business Logic Mapping
docs.text:
Map important mutations to business actions.

For example:

createOrder
      ↓
Creates Purchase

applyDiscount
      ↓
Changes Price

cancelOrder
      ↓
Changes Order State

approvePayment
      ↓
Changes Payment State

updateRole
      ↓
Changes Privilege

Then build security tests around the actual business rule.

docs.title: Query Depth
docs.text:
GraphQL allows nested queries.

Example:

query {
    user {
        orders {
            items {
                product {
                    supplier {
                        products {
                            id
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Deep nesting may require significant backend processing.

docs.title: Query Complexity
docs.text:
The actual cost of a GraphQL query may depend on:

Depth
Number of fields
Number of objects
Resolver complexity
Database queries
Recursive relationships
Aliases
Fragments

Therefore:

Small HTTP Request

can potentially trigger:

Large Server Workload

docs.title: Denial-of-Service Considerations
docs.text:
GraphQL resource exhaustion may involve:

Deep queries
Wide queries
Aliases
Recursive relationships
Large pagination values
Expensive resolvers
Batching

During authorised testing, avoid intentionally creating extreme resource consumption.

Start with small increases and observe:

Response time
CPU impact where observable
Error behaviour
Complexity limits
Depth limits

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Inspect pagination arguments such as:

first
last
limit
offset
page
pageSize

Example:

query {
    users(first: 20) {
        id
        username
    }
}

Questions include:

Is there a maximum?
Can negative values be supplied?
Can extremely large values be supplied?
Does pagination bypass authorisation?

Use modest values when testing production systems.

docs.title: Fragments
docs.text:
Fragments allow reusable field selections.

Example:

fragment UserFields on User {
    id
    username
    email
}

query {
    user(id: 123) {
        ...UserFields
    }
}

Fragments themselves are legitimate.

However, they can contribute to query complexity and should be included when understanding what the server actually executes.

docs.title: Directives
docs.text:
GraphQL supports directives such as:

@include
@skip

Custom schemas may expose additional directives.

Introspection can reveal available directives.

Review custom directives because they may influence:

Authentication
Authorisation
Caching
Data transformation
Resolver behaviour

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
GraphQL errors may expose significant information.

Look for:

Stack traces
Database errors
Internal paths
Framework names
Resolver names
Source files
SQL errors
NoSQL errors
Internal service URLs
Debug information

Example:

{
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "Database connection failed...",
      "extensions": {
        "stacktrace": []
      }
    }
  ]
}

Production responses should not expose unnecessary internal details.

docs.title: Partial Responses
docs.text:
GraphQL can return both:

data

and:

errors

in the same response.

Always inspect the entire response.

An error in one field does not necessarily mean the entire operation failed.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Test GraphQL authentication exactly as you would other application APIs.

Questions include:

Can queries execute without a token?
Can mutations execute without a token?
Are expired tokens accepted?
Are different authentication mechanisms handled consistently?
Are subscriptions authenticated?

Refer to:

Authentication Testing

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
GraphQL authorisation should be tested at several levels:

Operation
Object
Field
Nested object
Mutation
Subscription

Conceptually:

Can User Access Query?
        ↓
Can User Access Object?
        ↓
Can User Access Field?
        ↓
Can User Modify Object?

Refer to:

Authorisation Testing

docs.title: Multi-Tenant GraphQL
docs.text:
For multi-tenant applications, test whether tenant isolation is enforced inside resolvers.

Example:

query {
    organisation(id: 123) {
        users {
            id
            email
        }
    }
}

Questions include:

Can Tenant A query Tenant B?
Can nested objects cross tenants?
Can mutations modify another tenant?
Can IDs be enumerated?

docs.title: GraphQL and JWT
docs.text:
GraphQL APIs frequently use bearer tokens:

Authorization: Bearer eyJ...

JWT security should be tested independently from GraphQL security.

Refer to:

JSON Web Token Security

docs.text:

docs.text:
Modern Burp Suite versions understand GraphQL requests and provide GraphQL-specific request editing functionality.

This makes it easier to separate and modify:

docs.text:
Burp Scanner can assist with identifying GraphQL functionality and selected GraphQL security issues.

Useful automated checks can provide leads for:

Introspection
Schema-related information exposure
Content-type behaviour

Scanner findings should still be manually verified.

docs.text:

docs.text:

{

Controlled fuzzing

docs.text:

User B response

Unauthenticated response

This is useful when responses contain large JSON structures.

docs.title: Burp Logger
docs.text:
GraphQL applications can generate many similar requests.

Burp logging functionality can help identify:

Operation names
Endpoints
Repeated mutations
Authentication changes
Interesting responses

docs.text:
One of the most useful Burp extensions for GraphQL security testing is:

Introspection

Subscription generation

docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

InQL

        ↓

Generate Queries
        ↓

docs.title: Why InQL Is Useful
docs.text:
A large schema may contain:

Hundreds of types
Hundreds of fields
Dozens of mutations
Complex nested objects

Manually constructing every operation becomes inefficient.

InQL can help turn:

Schema

into:

Testable Requests

docs.title: InQL Schema Analysis
docs.text:
Once the schema is loaded, prioritise operations containing words such as:

admin
user
account
role
permission
password
reset
token
secret
key
payment
order
delete
update
upload
export
internal
debug

Do not assume names alone indicate vulnerabilities.

Use them to prioritise manual testing.

One of the most useful workflows is:

For example:

can be tested with controlled account identifiers.

Always remain within assessment scope and rate limits.

docs.text:
Another Burp extension is:

GraphQL Raider is designed specifically for testing GraphQL endpoints.

It provides GraphQL-aware request handling inside Burp.

docs.title: GraphQL Raider Features
docs.text:
Useful functionality includes:

GraphQL query editor
Variables editor
Readable GraphQL requests

GraphQL-aware request manipulation

This can be useful when GraphQL requests are embedded inside JSON and are otherwise inconvenient to edit manually.

docs.title: GraphQL Security Tester
docs.text:
The Burp BApp Store may also contain additional GraphQL-focused extensions.

Such extensions can provide additional automation around GraphQL testing.

Treat extension-generated findings as leads and manually validate anything security-sensitive.

docs.title: Burp Extension Security
docs.text:
Burp extensions execute within your testing environment.

Before installing third-party extensions:

Check maintainer
Check source
Check update history
Review permissions
Review network behaviour
Use trusted sources

Prefer installing through:

Burp Suite
 ↓
Extensions
 ↓
BApp Store

where possible.

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
GraphQL can also be tested using curl.

Example:

curl -k \
  -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"query":"query{__typename}"}' \
  https://target.example/graphql

docs.title: Authenticated curl Request
docs.text:
curl -k \
  -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"query":"query{me{id username email}}"}' \
  https://target.example/graphql

docs.title: jq
docs.text:
jq is extremely useful for GraphQL responses.

Example:

curl -sk \
  -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"query":"query{__typename}"}' \
  https://target.example/graphql | jq

This makes large JSON responses significantly easier to inspect.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For confirmed GraphQL vulnerabilities, record:

GraphQL endpoint
HTTP method
Authentication state
Operation name
Query / mutation
Variables
Affected object
Affected field
User role
Expected behaviour
Observed behaviour
Burp request
Burp response
Relevant schema information

Reproduction steps

docs.title: Example Finding: GraphQL IDOR
docs.text:
Finding:
GraphQL API Allows Unauthorised Access to Other Users' Data

Affected Endpoint:
/graphql

Affected Query:
user(id)

Observed:
A normal authenticated user was able to modify the user identifier supplied to the GraphQL user query and retrieve information associated with another controlled test account.

The API authenticated the request but did not enforce object-level authorisation for the requested user object.

Impact:
An authenticated user may access information belonging to other users.

Recommendation:
Implement object-level authorisation inside the relevant GraphQL resolver and verify that the authenticated user is authorised to access the requested object before returning data.

docs.title: Example Finding: Sensitive GraphQL Fields
docs.text:
Finding:
GraphQL API Exposes Sensitive User Fields to Unprivileged Users

Observed:
The GraphQL User type exposed additional security-sensitive fields that were not used by the normal application interface.

An unprivileged authenticated account was able to request these fields directly.

Impact:
Sensitive user information may be disclosed to users who should not have access to it.

Recommendation:
Implement field-level authorisation and remove unnecessary sensitive fields from the externally accessible GraphQL schema.

docs.title: Example Finding: Introspection
docs.text:
Finding:
GraphQL Introspection Enabled in Production

Observed:
The production GraphQL endpoint permitted schema introspection.

The schema disclosed available queries, mutations, types, arguments and input structures.

Impact:
An attacker can more easily map the GraphQL attack surface and identify sensitive or undocumented functionality.

Recommendation:
Where operationally appropriate, disable unrestricted introspection in production and ensure that security does not depend solely on hiding the schema. All operations must remain protected by appropriate authentication and authorisation controls.

docs.title: Example Finding: Alias Rate Limit Bypass
docs.text:
Finding:
GraphQL Aliases Allow Multiple Security-Sensitive Operations Within a Single Rate-Limited Request

Observed:
The application applied rate limiting at the HTTP request level.

Multiple GraphQL aliases within a single request caused the security-sensitive resolver to execute multiple times while consuming only one HTTP request from the configured rate limit.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to increase the number of attempts against the affected operation beyond the intended rate limit.

Recommendation:
Apply rate limiting to the underlying security-sensitive operation rather than only to HTTP requests. Consider GraphQL operation counts, aliases and resolver execution when enforcing limits.

docs.title: Example Finding: GraphQL CSRF
docs.text:
Finding:
GraphQL Mutation Vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery

Observed:
The GraphQL endpoint authenticated users through cookies and accepted state-changing mutations using a browser-compatible request format without requiring a valid CSRF token.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to cause an authenticated user's browser to perform unintended state-changing operations.

Recommendation:
Require JSON POST requests, validate the Content-Type header, implement robust CSRF protection and configure authentication cookies with appropriate SameSite attributes.

docs.title: Example Finding: Excessive Data Exposure
docs.text:
Finding:
GraphQL Schema Exposes Unnecessary Sensitive Account Data

Observed:
The GraphQL Account type exposed fields containing information not required by the normal client application.

These fields could be queried directly by a standard authenticated user.

Impact:
Users may obtain sensitive account information that should not be available to their role.

Recommendation:
Apply field-level authorisation and minimise the fields exposed through the GraphQL schema.

docs.title: Reporting Titles
docs.text:
Useful titles include:

GraphQL API Allows Unauthorised Access to Other Users' Data

GraphQL Mutation Missing Object-Level Authorisation

GraphQL API Exposes Sensitive Fields to Unprivileged Users

GraphQL Introspection Enabled in Production

GraphQL Aliases Bypass Application Rate Limiting

GraphQL Mutation Vulnerable to CSRF

GraphQL API Exposes Administrative Mutation to Standard Users

GraphQL API Allows Cross-Tenant Data Access

GraphQL Error Responses Disclose Internal Application Information

GraphQL Query Complexity Allows Excessive Resource Consumption

Avoid vague titles such as:

GraphQL Issue

Describe the actual security problem.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on demonstrated impact.

For example:

Introspection Enabled

may primarily increase attack-surface visibility.

While:

GraphQL IDOR
      ↓
Sensitive User Data

may have significant confidentiality impact.

And:

Unauthorised Administrative Mutation
        ↓
Privilege Escalation

may be critical.

Report the actual impact rather than assigning severity simply because GraphQL is involved.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
GraphQL security should be implemented in layers.

Authentication
      ↓
Operation Authorisation
      ↓
Object Authorisation
      ↓
Field Authorisation
      ↓
Input Validation
      ↓
Rate Limiting
      ↓
Complexity Controls
      ↓
Secure Error Handling

docs.title: Enforce Object-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Every resolver accessing an object should determine whether the authenticated user is authorised to access that object.

Do not rely solely on:

Object IDs
Frontend restrictions
Hidden queries
Schema obscurity

docs.title: Enforce Field-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Sensitive fields should be protected independently.

For example:

User
 ├── username       Standard User
 ├── avatar         Standard User
 ├── email          Restricted
 ├── role           Restricted
 ├── apiKey         Highly Restricted
 └── internalNotes  Administrative

docs.title: Protect Mutations
docs.text:
Mutations should validate:

Authentication
Object ownership
Role
Permission
Current state
Allowed transition
Allowed fields

before changing data.

docs.title: Restrict Introspection
docs.text:
Where appropriate for production deployments:

Disable unrestricted introspection

or limit it to authorised administrative/development contexts.

However:

Disabling introspection is not an authorisation control.

The API must remain secure even if the complete schema is known.

docs.title: Limit Query Depth
docs.text:
Configure a maximum acceptable query depth.

Conceptually:

Query
 ↓
Depth Calculation
 ↓
Within Limit?
 ↓
YES → Execute
NO  → Reject

docs.title: Query Complexity Analysis
docs.text:
More advanced GraphQL implementations can calculate query cost.

For example:

Simple scalar field = low cost

Large nested relationship = higher cost

Expensive resolver = high cost

Reject queries exceeding acceptable resource limits.

docs.title: Limit Aliases
docs.text:
Apply appropriate limits to:

Aliases
Root fields
Operations

especially around security-sensitive resolvers.

docs.title: Rate Limit Resolvers
docs.text:
Do not rely exclusively on:

Requests per IP

For sensitive functionality, rate limit based on:

Account
Operation
Target object
Resolver
Authentication identity

docs.title: Pagination Limits
docs.text:
Set sensible maximum values for:

first
last
limit
pageSize

Avoid allowing arbitrary result sizes.

docs.title: CSRF Protection
docs.text:
For state-changing GraphQL operations:

Use POST
Require application/json
Validate Content-Type
Use CSRF protection
Configure SameSite cookies
Validate Origin where appropriate

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
Validate GraphQL arguments according to their semantic purpose.

For example:

ID
Email
URL
Filename
Quantity
Price
Role
Date

GraphQL type validation does not replace application-level validation.

docs.title: Secure Error Handling
docs.text:
Production GraphQL responses should avoid exposing:

Stack traces
Source paths
Database queries
Internal service URLs
Secrets
Framework debugging data

Return useful but minimal error information.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Security monitoring should capture:

Operation name
Authenticated identity
Mutation
Target object
Failure
Rate-limit event
Complexity rejection
Authorisation rejection

Avoid unnecessarily logging:

Passwords
Tokens
Secrets
Sensitive personal information

docs.title: Test After Remediation
docs.text:
After fixes, repeat:

Original query
Changed object ID
Sensitive field query
Restricted mutation
Alias test
CSRF test
Introspection test

Confirm that controls operate at the correct GraphQL layer.

docs.title: OWASP GraphQL Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/GraphQL_Cheat_Sheet.html

Security guidance covering:

Input validation
Query limiting
Access control
Resource management
Server-side considerations

flowchart TD
  A["Schema and operation"] --> B["Authentication metadata"]
  B --> C["Resolver authorization"]
  C --> D["Object/field/tenant checks"]
  D --> E["Query or mutation execution"]
  E --> F["Safe read-back and evidence"]

docs.title: Final GraphQL Testing Model
docs.text:
APPLICATION
                              ↓
                     GRAPHQL ENDPOINT?
                              ↓
                             YES
                              ↓
                       query{__typename}
                              ↓
                      GRAPHQL CONFIRMED
                              ↓
               ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
               ↓              ↓              ↓
             BURP            InQL       GRAPHQL RAIDER
               ↓              ↓              ↓
               └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                              ↓
                         MAP SCHEMA
                              ↓
               ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
               ↓              ↓              ↓
            QUERIES        MUTATIONS        TYPES
               ↓              ↓              ↓
               └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                              ↓
                     IDENTIFY OBJECTS
                              ↓
                 TEST AUTHENTICATION
                              ↓
                  TEST AUTHORISATION
                              ↓
               ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
               ↓              ↓              ↓
             OBJECT          FIELD         MUTATION
               ↓              ↓              ↓
               └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                              ↓
                       TEST INPUTS
                              ↓
               ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
               ↓              ↓              ↓
             SQLi           NoSQLi          SSRF
               ↓              ↓              ↓
               └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                              ↓
                      TEST RATE LIMITS
                              ↓
                         ALIASES
                              ↓
                         BATCHING
                              ↓
                         TEST CSRF
                              ↓
                    TEST QUERY COMPLEXITY
                              ↓
                    TEST BUSINESS LOGIC
                              ↓
                     VALIDATE MANUALLY
                              ↓
                         DOCUMENT
                              ↓
                           REPORT

The key principle is:

Do not treat GraphQL as a single endpoint that only needs conventional parameter fuzzing. Treat the schema as a map of the application's objects, relationships and operations. Enumerate the available attack surface, then test authentication, object-level authorisation, field-level authorisation, mutations, aliases, rate limiting, input handling and business rules systematically. Burp Suite, InQL and GraphQL Raider can make the schema and requests significantly easier to work with, but manual validation remains essential.

docs.title: Schema and Operation Discovery
docs.text:
Identify the GraphQL endpoint, transport, authentication, content types, persisted-query mechanism, and WebSocket or subscription endpoints. Review approved introspection responses, client bundles, API documentation, error messages, persisted operation identifiers, and captured traffic. Record queries, mutations, subscriptions, arguments, input objects, interfaces, fragments, directives, and fields that differ by role.

Introspection being disabled does not prove that the schema is undiscoverable, and an exposed schema does not prove a vulnerability. InQL or Burp's GraphQL support can help format and explore operations; use the result to build a test inventory rather than sending every operation indiscriminately.

docs.title: Resolver-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Test each security boundary separately:

Boundary Controlled comparison Authentication Unauthenticated versus authenticated request Object access User A object versus User B object Field access Same object with sensitive and ordinary fields Function access Same mutation as ordinary and privileged roles Tenant isolation Tenant A identity and identifiers versus Tenant B Execution or side effect Read-only query versus approved test mutation

Change one object identifier, argument, variable, fragment, or field at a time. A resolver returning null, an error, or partial data must be interpreted with the schema's nullability and error policy in mind. Confirm whether data was actually disclosed and whether a mutation changed state.

docs.title: Aliases, Batching, and Complexity
docs.text:
Test whether aliases or batched operations bypass per-object checks, rate limits, or audit assumptions. Use a small number of approved test objects and unique markers. Review query depth, breadth, recursion, pagination, field cost, alias count, and persisted-query enforcement. Measure server behaviour rather than relying on a timeout alone; network conditions, proxy limits, and resolver latency can create false positives.

Do not perform denial-of-service testing against production. If complexity impact must be assessed, use a staging environment or an explicitly approved low-volume test and stop at the minimum evidence.

docs.title: Burp Workflow and Validation
docs.text:
Capture a normal query and mutation in Burp, save the variables and response as a baseline, then send controlled variants to Repeater. Use Comparer for response changes and InQL or GraphQL Raider for request construction where useful. Keep authentication headers, CSRF state, persisted-query identifiers, and operation names consistent unless they are the test variable.

An error message, successful HTTP status, or schema field visible in a tool is a candidate. Validate with a second account, an object created for testing, a safe read-back, and the smallest permitted mutation. Record whether the result establishes authentication, object access, field access, administrative authority, tenant crossing, or actual state change.

docs.title: Evidence, Troubleshooting, and Retesting
docs.text:
Capture endpoint, operation name, redacted query, variables, actor and tenant, baseline and modified responses, relevant errors, timestamps, and state before and after. Redact tokens and sensitive fields. Troubleshoot inconsistent results by checking persisted queries, schema version, subscriptions, caching, resolver authorization, batching limits, CSRF, session freshness, and gateway versus application errors.

After remediation, retest equivalent queries, mutations, aliases, batches, fragments, alternate API versions, and WebSocket operations. Confirm both denial and legitimate access, and verify that complexity limits and audit records behave as intended. See API Security, Authorisation, Burp Suite Testing Workflows, and Burp Suite Extensions.
