docs.title: gRPC Security
docs.text:
gRPC is a high-performance Remote Procedure Call framework commonly used for communication between microservices, backend systems, mobile applications, and distributed services.

Unlike a traditional REST API where you might interact with endpoints such as:

GET /api/users/123
POST /api/orders
DELETE /api/files/456

gRPC exposes services containing callable methods.

Conceptually:

REST

Client
  |
  | GET /api/users/123
  v
HTTP API
  |
  v
JSON Response

gRPC instead looks more like:

gRPC

Client
  |
  | UserService/GetUser
  v
gRPC Server
  |
  | Protocol Buffer message
  v
Response

A simplified gRPC architecture is:

Client
  |
  | RPC call
  v
gRPC Service
  |
  +-- HTTP/2 transport
  |
  +-- Metadata
  |     |
  |     +-- Authentication
  |     +-- Tracing
  |     +-- Custom metadata
  |
  +-- Protocol Buffer message
  |
  v
Service Method
  |
  +-- Authentication
  +-- Authorisation
  +-- Input validation
  +-- Business logic
  |
  v
gRPC Response
  |
  +-- Protobuf message
  +-- Metadata / trailers
  +-- gRPC status
  |
  v
Client

Authorised Security Testing

Perform gRPC security testing only against systems you are explicitly authorised to assess. gRPC services are frequently internal production services, and unsafe testing of streaming methods, large messages, concurrency, deadlines, or resource limits can affect service availability. Use controlled accounts, controlled objects and conservative request rates.

docs.title: Why gRPC Matters to Pentesters
docs.text:
gRPC is common in:

Microservices
Internal APIs
Cloud-native applications
Kubernetes environments
Mobile backends
Service-to-service communication
Distributed systems
High-performance APIs

A web application may look like:

Browser
   |
   v
Frontend
   |
   v
REST / GraphQL Gateway
   |
   v
Internal gRPC Services
   |
   +-- UserService
   +-- PaymentService
   +-- FileService
   +-- AdminService
   +-- NotificationService

A vulnerability in an internal gRPC service can therefore affect the security of the entire application.

docs.title: gRPC Is Not Simply REST With Binary Data
docs.text:
A common mistake is to approach gRPC exactly like a REST API.

There are similarities:

Authentication
Authorisation
Input validation
Business logic
Rate limiting
Transport security

but there are important architectural differences.

REST often uses:

HTTP methods
URLs
JSON
HTTP status codes

gRPC commonly uses:

Service definitions
RPC methods
Protocol Buffers
HTTP/2
gRPC metadata
gRPC status codes
Streaming

docs.title: Remote Procedure Calls
docs.text:
RPC stands for:

Remote Procedure Call

The basic idea is that a client invokes a function implemented on another system.

Conceptually:

Local programming:

getUser(123)

With RPC:

Client
   |
   | GetUser(123)
   v
Remote Server
   |
   v
GetUser()
   |
   v
Response

The network interaction is abstracted into something resembling a normal method call.

docs.title: gRPC Service Definitions
docs.text:
gRPC services are commonly defined using Protocol Buffers.

A .proto file might contain:

syntax = "proto3";

package users;

service UserService {

    rpc GetUser (
        GetUserRequest
    ) returns (
        GetUserResponse
    );

}

message GetUserRequest {

    int64 id = 1;

}

message GetUserResponse {

    int64 id = 1;
    string username = 2;
    string email = 3;

}

This describes:

Package:
users

Service:
UserService

Method:
GetUser

Request:
GetUserRequest

Response:
GetUserResponse

docs.title: RPC Method Naming
docs.text:
A gRPC method can conceptually be represented as:

package.Service/Method

For example:

users.UserService/GetUser

Another example:

payments.PaymentService/CreatePayment

or:

admin.AdminService/DeleteUser

This is one of the first major differences from REST.

Instead of looking only for:

/api/users
/api/orders
/api/admin

you should also think in terms of:

Services
Methods
Messages
Fields

docs.title: Protocol Buffers
docs.text:
Protocol Buffers, commonly called:

protobuf

are Google's language-neutral structured data serialization mechanism and are the default Interface Definition Language and message format used by gRPC.

A protobuf message might be:

message User {

    int64 id = 1;

    string username = 2;

    string email = 3;

    bool admin = 4;

}

The numbers:

1
2
3
4

are field numbers.

They are part of the protobuf wire format.

docs.title: Protobuf Is Binary on the Wire
docs.text:
Unlike a typical JSON REST request:

{
    "id": 123,
    "username": "alice"
}

native gRPC commonly transmits protobuf messages in binary form.

Conceptually:

Human-readable object
        |
        v
Protobuf serialization
        |
        v
Binary message
        |
        v
HTTP/2
        |
        v
gRPC server

This is why ordinary curl is generally not convenient for interacting with native gRPC services.

Tools such as:

grpcurl

understand gRPC and protobuf.

docs.title: grpcurl
docs.text:
grpcurl is one of the most useful command-line tools for testing gRPC services.

Conceptually:

curl
   |
   +-- HTTP APIs

grpcurl
   |
   +-- gRPC APIs

Official project:

https://github.com/fullstorydev/grpcurl

docs.title: Installing grpcurl
docs.text:
Check your package manager first.

On systems with Go installed:

go install github.com/fullstorydev/grpcurl/cmd/grpcurl@latest

Then verify:

grpcurl -help

If Go installs binaries into:

~/go/bin

ensure that directory is in your PATH.

docs.title: Four Types of gRPC RPCs
docs.text:
Understanding the four RPC models is essential.

They are:

1. Unary RPC
2. Server-streaming RPC
3. Client-streaming RPC
4. Bidirectional-streaming RPC

docs.title: Unary RPC
docs.text:
Unary RPC is the simplest model.

One request
     |
     v
Server
     |
     v
One response

Conceptually:

Client                    Server

  |                          |
  |------ Request ---------->|
  |                          |
  |<----- Response ----------|
  |                          |

Example:

rpc GetUser (
    GetUserRequest
) returns (
    GetUserResponse
);

This resembles a traditional request/response API.

docs.title: Server Streaming
docs.text:
The client sends one request and receives multiple responses.

Client                    Server

  |                          |
  |------ Request ---------->|
  |                          |
  |<----- Response 1 --------|
  |<----- Response 2 --------|
  |<----- Response 3 --------|
  |<----- Response 4 --------|
  |                          |

Example:

rpc ListEvents (
    EventRequest
) returns (
    stream Event
);

Potential use cases include:

Event feeds
Logs
Notifications
Large result sets
Monitoring

docs.title: Client Streaming
docs.text:
The client sends multiple messages and receives one response.

Client                    Server

  |                          |
  |------ Message 1 -------->|
  |------ Message 2 -------->|
  |------ Message 3 -------->|
  |                          |
  |<----- Response ----------|

Example:

rpc Upload (
    stream UploadChunk
) returns (
    UploadResult
);

Potential use cases include:

File uploads
Telemetry
Bulk data
Aggregations

docs.title: Bidirectional Streaming
docs.text:
Both sides send streams of messages.

Client                    Server

  |------ Message 1 -------->|
  |<----- Message A ---------|
  |------ Message 2 -------->|
  |<----- Message B ---------|
  |------ Message 3 -------->|
  |<----- Message C ---------|

Example:

rpc Chat (
    stream ChatMessage
) returns (
    stream ChatMessage
);

Potential uses:

Chat
Realtime events
Interactive applications
Long-lived service communication

docs.title: Why Streaming Matters for Security
docs.text:
Streaming introduces additional questions:

Is authentication checked when stream starts?

Is authorisation checked for every relevant message?

Can permissions change while a stream remains open?

Are message counts limited?

Are message sizes limited?

Are idle streams terminated?

Are deadlines enforced?

Can a client hold large numbers of streams open?

Can the stream consume excessive memory or CPU?

Do not treat a long-lived stream exactly like a single REST request.

docs.title: HTTP/2
docs.text:
Native gRPC uses HTTP/2.

HTTP/2 supports:

Multiplexing
Streams
Binary framing
Header compression
Long-lived connections

Multiple RPCs can therefore operate over the same underlying connection.

Conceptually:

TCP/TLS Connection
       |
       +-- HTTP/2 Stream 1
       |       |
       |       +-- RPC A
       |
       +-- HTTP/2 Stream 3
       |       |
       |       +-- RPC B
       |
       +-- HTTP/2 Stream 5
               |
               +-- RPC C

docs.title: gRPC Content Type
docs.text:
Native gRPC commonly uses:

Content-Type: application/grpc

You may therefore identify potential gRPC traffic by looking for:

HTTP/2
application/grpc
grpc-status
grpc-message

among other gRPC-specific characteristics.

docs.title: gRPC-Web Is Different
docs.text:
Browsers historically cannot use native gRPC in exactly the same manner as normal backend gRPC clients.

gRPC-Web provides a browser-compatible protocol for communicating with gRPC services, commonly through a proxy or compatible server.

Conceptually:

Browser
   |
   | gRPC-Web
   v
Proxy / Gateway
   |
   | Native gRPC
   v
Backend gRPC Service

Do not assume:

gRPC-Web
=
native gRPC

They are related but distinct protocols.

docs.title: Identifying gRPC-Web
docs.text:
Potential content types include:

application/grpc-web
application/grpc-web+proto
application/grpc-web-text
application/grpc-web-text+proto

Exact implementation behaviour can vary.

docs.title: gRPC-Web Security
docs.text:
When testing gRPC-Web consider:

Browser authentication
CORS
CSRF where applicable
Gateway behaviour
Protobuf messages
Authorisation
Service exposure
Method exposure
Error disclosure

The browser-facing layer may introduce vulnerabilities that do not exist in the underlying native gRPC service.

docs.title: .proto Files
docs.text:
.proto files are extremely valuable during security assessments because they describe the API schema.

For example:

service AccountService {

    rpc GetAccount(
        GetAccountRequest
    ) returns (
        Account
    );

    rpc UpdateAccount(
        UpdateAccountRequest
    ) returns (
        Account
    );

    rpc DeleteAccount(
        DeleteAccountRequest
    ) returns (
        Empty
    );

}

This immediately reveals:

Service names
Method names
Request types
Response types
Fields
Data types
Streaming behaviour

docs.title: Finding .proto Files
docs.text:
During an authorised assessment look for .proto files in:

Source repositories
Mobile applications
JavaScript bundles
Developer packages
SDKs
Documentation
Docker images
Build artefacts
CI/CD artefacts
API documentation
Public repositories

Also search source code for:

.proto
grpc
protobuf
protoc
grpc-js
grpcio
Google.Protobuf
io.grpc

docs.title: Protocol Descriptor Sets
docs.text:
Instead of .proto source files, you may encounter:

protoset

or:

FileDescriptorSet

data.

grpcurl can use descriptor sets to understand the service schema.

Example:

grpcurl \
  -protoset service.protoset \
  target.example:443 \
  list

docs.title: gRPC Server Reflection
docs.text:
gRPC reflection allows a client to discover service definitions at runtime.

Conceptually:

Client
   |
   | What services exist?
   v
Reflection Service
   |
   v
Service descriptors

This can make development and debugging considerably easier.

It also makes reconnaissance easier during a security assessment.

docs.title: Testing Reflection
docs.text:
For an authorised target:

grpcurl target.example:443 list

If reflection is enabled, this may return services such as:

grpc.reflection.v1.ServerReflection
users.UserService
payments.PaymentService
admin.AdminService

docs.title: Reflection and Plaintext
docs.text:
If the service intentionally uses unencrypted HTTP/2:

grpcurl \
  -plaintext \
  target.example:50051 \
  list

Important:

-plaintext

means:

Use plaintext HTTP/2 without TLS

It does not mean:

Ignore certificate validation

docs.title: TLS Certificate Verification
docs.text:
For TLS endpoints, normal usage is:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  list

If testing an authorised development environment with a self-signed certificate, grpcurl supports:

grpcurl \
  -insecure \
  target.example:443 \
  list

Warning

-insecure disables server certificate and hostname verification. It is useful for controlled testing but should not be treated as a secure production configuration.

docs.title: Reflection Is Not Automatically a Vulnerability
docs.text:
Do not report:

gRPC reflection enabled

automatically as:

Critical vulnerability

Reflection exposes information about:

Services
Methods
Messages
Schemas

which increases attack-surface visibility.

Whether this is reportable depends on:

Environment
Threat model
Exposure
Sensitivity
Production policy
Additional vulnerabilities

For production services, reducing unnecessary reflection exposure is generally good hardening.

docs.title: Enumerating Services
docs.text:
When reflection is available:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  list

Example:

grpc.health.v1.Health
grpc.reflection.v1.ServerReflection
users.UserService
payments.PaymentService

Record all services.

docs.title: Enumerating Methods
docs.text:
To list methods in a service:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  list users.UserService

Possible result:

users.UserService.CreateUser
users.UserService.DeleteUser
users.UserService.GetUser
users.UserService.ListUsers
users.UserService.UpdateUser

This creates an initial attack surface.

docs.title: Describing a Service
docs.text:
Use:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  describe users.UserService

This may show an equivalent protobuf definition.

docs.title: Describing a Method
docs.text:
Example:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  describe users.UserService.GetUser

This helps identify:

Request type
Response type
Streaming direction

docs.title: Describing a Message
docs.text:
Example:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  describe users.GetUserRequest

Potential output:

message GetUserRequest {

    int64 id = 1;

}

This tells you what input the method expects.

docs.title: Reflection Requires Authentication Sometimes
docs.text:
Some services may protect reflection.

If authorised credentials are required, metadata can be supplied.

For example:

grpcurl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" \
  target.example:443 \
  list

Do not assume reflection is globally accessible simply because authenticated users can use it.

docs.title: Using .proto Files Without Reflection
docs.text:
If reflection is disabled but you have an authorised .proto file:

grpcurl \
  -import-path ./proto \
  -proto users.proto \
  target.example:443 \
  list

Invoke a method:

grpcurl \
  -import-path ./proto \
  -proto users.proto \
  -d '{"id":123}' \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/GetUser

docs.title: Basic grpcurl Invocation
docs.text:
Suppose:

message GetUserRequest {

    int64 id = 1;

}

Then:

grpcurl \
  -d '{"id":123}' \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/GetUser

grpcurl accepts JSON input and converts it into the protobuf message expected by the service.

docs.title: Empty Request
docs.text:
If the RPC accepts an empty message:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/ListUsers

or, where required:

grpcurl \
  -d '{}' \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/ListUsers

docs.title: Pretty JSON Input
docs.text:
For more complex requests:

grpcurl \
  -d '{
    "username": "test-user",
    "email": "test@example.com"
  }' \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/CreateUser

docs.title: Reading Input From stdin
docs.text:
grpcurl supports:

-d @

Example:

cat request.json | \
grpcurl \
  -d @ \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/CreateUser

This is useful for repeatable testing.

docs.title: gRPC Metadata
docs.text:
Metadata is extremely important in gRPC security.

Metadata consists of key-value information associated with an RPC.

It can contain:

Authentication credentials
JWTs
Tracing information
Request identifiers
Tenant identifiers
Application-specific values

Metadata is transported using HTTP/2 headers and trailers.

docs.title: Authentication Metadata
docs.text:
A service may use:

Authorization

metadata.

For example:

authorization: Bearer eyJ...

With grpcurl:

grpcurl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" \
  -d '{"id":123}' \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/GetUser

docs.title: Custom Metadata
docs.text:
Applications may use custom values such as:

x-user-id
x-tenant-id
x-role
x-request-id
x-client-id

Example:

grpcurl \
  -H "x-tenant-id: 100" \
  target.example:443 \
  tenant.TenantService/GetSettings

Treat security-sensitive client-controlled metadata with suspicion.

docs.title: Metadata Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
A dangerous architecture might accept:

x-user-id: 100
x-role: admin
x-tenant-id: 5

directly from an untrusted client and trust those values for authorisation.

Conceptually:

Client
   |
   | x-role: admin
   v
Service
   |
   | blindly trusts metadata
   v
Admin privileges

Security-sensitive identity should be derived from trusted authentication context, not arbitrary user-controlled metadata.

docs.title: Metadata Testing Checklist
docs.text:
Look for:

authorization
x-user-id
x-role
x-admin
x-tenant-id
x-account-id
x-client-id
x-forwarded-user
x-authenticated-user

Test whether modifying them affects:

Identity
Role
Tenant
Authorisation
Object ownership
Business logic

using controlled accounts.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
gRPC does not remove the need for authentication.

Authentication may use:

OAuth 2.0 access tokens
JWTs
API keys
mTLS client certificates
Custom credentials
Service identities

A typical authenticated RPC:

Client
   |
   | Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
   v
gRPC Server
   |
   v
Authentication Interceptor
   |
   +-- valid
   |
   v
RPC Handler

docs.title: Authentication Interceptors
docs.text:
Many gRPC implementations use interceptors or middleware to perform cross-cutting security checks.

Conceptually:

RPC
 |
 v
Authentication Interceptor
 |
 v
Authorisation Interceptor
 |
 v
Logging / Rate Limiting
 |
 v
Service Method

A security issue may occur when:

Some services use interceptor
Some services do not

or:

Some methods are excluded accidentally

docs.title: Authentication Testing
docs.text:
Create a method matrix:

Method No Token Valid Token Invalid Token Expired Token GetUser Test Test Test Test UpdateUser Test Test Test Test DeleteUser Test Test Test Test AdminList Test Test Test Test

Look for inconsistent enforcement.

docs.title: Unauthenticated Request
docs.text:
For a safe read-only method:

grpcurl \
  -d '{"id":123}' \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/GetUser

Compare with:

grpcurl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer VALID_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"id":123}' \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/GetUser

If sensitive information is returned without authentication:

Potential missing authentication

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Authorisation answers:

What are you allowed to do?

gRPC services require both.

docs.title: Object-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Suppose:

rpc GetInvoice(
    GetInvoiceRequest
) returns (
    Invoice
);

message GetInvoiceRequest {

    int64 invoice_id = 1;

}

Account A owns:

invoice_id = 1001

Account B owns:

invoice_id = 2001

Test:

Account A token
+
invoice_id 1001

then:

Account A token
+
invoice_id 2001

If Account A receives Account B's invoice:

BOLA / IDOR

Refer to:

IDOR and BOLA

docs.title: grpcurl BOLA Example
docs.text:
Controlled Account A:

grpcurl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCOUNT_A_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"invoiceId":"1001"}' \
  target.example:443 \
  billing.InvoiceService/GetInvoice

Then:

grpcurl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCOUNT_A_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"invoiceId":"2001"}' \
  target.example:443 \
  billing.InvoiceService/GetInvoice

Use only controlled objects.

docs.title: Function-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
A normal user may discover:

admin.AdminService/ListUsers
admin.AdminService/DeleteUser
admin.AdminService/ChangeRole

The presence of these methods is not itself a vulnerability.

Test whether the server enforces role restrictions.

Conceptually:

Standard User
     |
     | ChangeRole()
     v
Authorisation Check
     |
     +---- DENY

If it instead reaches:

Role changed

there may be broken function-level authorisation.

docs.title: Authorisation Matrix
docs.text:
Build a matrix:

Method Anonymous User A User B Admin GetProfile Deny Own Own Any UpdateProfile Deny Own Own Any GetInvoice Deny Own Own Any DeleteUser Deny Deny Deny Allow ChangeRole Deny Deny Deny Allow

Then compare observed behaviour with expected behaviour.

docs.title: Tenant Isolation
docs.text:
gRPC is commonly used in multi-tenant systems.

Look for fields such as:

tenant_id
organisation_id
organization_id
workspace_id
account_id
customer_id
project_id

and metadata such as:

x-tenant-id

Test:

Tenant A credentials
+
Tenant B controlled identifier

The service must derive and validate tenant boundaries server-side.

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Protobuf messages may contain fields that should not be user-controlled.

Example:

message UpdateUserRequest {

    int64 id = 1;

    string display_name = 2;

    string email = 3;

    bool admin = 4;

    string role = 5;

}

If the application directly maps this message into an internal user object:

admin
role

might become security-sensitive mass-assignment candidates.

Refer to:

Mass Assignment

docs.title: Mass Assignment Test
docs.text:
Expected legitimate request:

{
    "id": "123",
    "displayName": "Test User"
}

Controlled test:

{
    "id": "123",
    "displayName": "Test User",
    "admin": true
}

The important step is:

Verify server-side state

Do not assume success because the field is accepted syntactically.

docs.title: Protobuf Unknown Fields
docs.text:
Modern protobuf implementations generally preserve or ignore unknown fields depending on language/runtime and processing path.

Do not assume:

Unknown field accepted by JSON parser
=
server state changed

Always verify the resulting state.

docs.title: Field Presence
docs.text:
Protobuf field presence has nuances that differ from ordinary JSON.

Depending on protobuf version and field definition, there can be important differences between:

Field absent

and:

Field present with default value

For security testing, test where relevant:

Missing value
Default value
Explicit zero
Explicit false
Empty string
Empty message

and verify how the application interprets them.

docs.title: Default Values
docs.text:
Examples of protobuf scalar defaults include concepts such as:

Numeric -> 0
Boolean -> false
String -> empty string

Application logic must not confuse:

default value

with:

authorised or valid value

docs.title: Enumeration Fields
docs.text:
A protobuf enum might be:

enum Role {

    ROLE_UNSPECIFIED = 0;

    ROLE_USER = 1;

    ROLE_ADMIN = 2;

}

Security testing should determine whether clients can improperly select privileged enum values.

Example candidate:

{
    "role": "ROLE_ADMIN"
}

The server must enforce authorisation independently of protobuf type validity.

docs.title: Nested Messages
docs.text:
Messages may contain nested structures:

message UpdateAccountRequest {

    int64 account_id = 1;

    Settings settings = 2;

}

message Settings {

    bool public_profile = 1;

    string role = 2;

}

Inspect nested fields carefully.

Security-sensitive properties can be hidden several levels deep.

docs.title: Repeated Fields
docs.text:
Protobuf supports repeated values:

message AddMembersRequest {

    int64 group_id = 1;

    repeated int64 user_ids = 2;

}

Test authorisation for:

Every supplied object

not merely the first.

A service must not validate:

user_ids[0]

and then trust the rest.

docs.title: Maps
docs.text:
Protobuf supports maps:

map<string, string> metadata = 1;

Review map-based fields for:

Unexpected keys
Security-sensitive configuration
Internal metadata
Privilege-related values

docs.title: Oneof Fields
docs.text:
Protobuf supports:

oneof

where one of several fields may be selected.

Example:

oneof identifier {

    int64 user_id = 1;

    string email = 2;

}

Test each supported variant.

Different code paths may have different security checks.

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
Protobuf provides:

Structure
Types
Field definitions

but protobuf schema validation is not the same as application security validation.

For example:

string filename = 1;

only means:

This field contains a string

It does not mean the value is safe for:

Filesystem access
SQL
LDAP
Shell commands
Templates
URLs
HTML

docs.title: Injection Testing
docs.text:
gRPC services can still be vulnerable to:

SQL injection
NoSQL injection
Command injection
LDAP injection
SSTI
Path traversal
SSRF

if protobuf fields reach unsafe sinks.

The binary transport does not prevent injection.

docs.title: SQL Injection Concept
docs.text:
Protobuf string
     |
     v
gRPC Handler
     |
     v
SQL Query Construction
     |
     v
Database

If the handler performs unsafe query construction:

SQL injection remains possible

Refer to:

SQL Injection

docs.title: Command Injection Concept
docs.text:
RPC field
   |
   v
Service handler
   |
   v
Shell command

Example risky application logic:

filename
   |
   v
"convert " + filename

The gRPC transport provides no protection against unsafe command construction.

Refer to:

OS Command Injection

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
A protobuf field might contain:

string url = 1;

Example service:

PreviewURL()
FetchRemoteImage()
ImportDocument()
SendWebhook()

These are potential SSRF candidates.

Refer to:

Server Side Request Forgery

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Look for fields such as:

filename
path
directory
template
archive
export_path

Example:

message DownloadRequest {

    string filename = 1;

}

If the service directly joins this value with a filesystem path:

Potential path traversal

Refer to:

Path Traversal

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
gRPC has its own status model.

Common gRPC status codes include:

OK
CANCELLED
UNKNOWN
INVALID_ARGUMENT
DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
NOT_FOUND
ALREADY_EXISTS
PERMISSION_DENIED
RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
FAILED_PRECONDITION
ABORTED
OUT_OF_RANGE
UNIMPLEMENTED
INTERNAL
UNAVAILABLE
DATA_LOSS
UNAUTHENTICATED

docs.title: UNAUTHENTICATED vs PERMISSION_DENIED
docs.text:
A useful conceptual distinction is:

UNAUTHENTICATED
→ Valid authentication credentials are absent or invalid

PERMISSION_DENIED
→ Identity is known but lacks permission

Applications should use status codes consistently.

docs.title: HTTP Status Is Not the Whole Story
docs.text:
Do not evaluate a gRPC call using only the HTTP status.

gRPC communicates RPC status separately.

Conceptually:

HTTP transport
       |
       v
gRPC protocol
       |
       v
grpc-status
       |
       v
RPC result

Therefore:

HTTP 200

does not necessarily mean:

RPC succeeded

docs.title: grpc-status
docs.text:
gRPC status information may appear in trailers.

For example:

grpc-status: 0

means:

OK

A non-zero status indicates a gRPC error.

Always inspect:

gRPC status
gRPC message
Response data
Trailers

rather than relying only on HTTP status.

docs.title: Error Information Disclosure
docs.text:
Poor error handling may reveal:

Stack traces
Database errors
Filesystem paths
Internal hostnames
Service names
Package names
Source paths
SQL statements
Internal object IDs
Debug information

Example:

rpc error:
code = Internal
desc = database connection failed:
postgres://db-internal:5432/users

This can expose useful internal information.

docs.title: Error Testing
docs.text:
Send controlled invalid values:

Missing required business value
Invalid identifier
Out-of-range value
Invalid enum
Malformed application data

Observe:

gRPC status
Error description
Metadata
Trailers
Server stability

Do not deliberately crash production services.

docs.title: Transport Security
docs.text:
Production gRPC services should generally use TLS where network trust cannot otherwise be assured.

Conceptually:

Client
   |
   | TLS
   v
gRPC Server

Without appropriate transport protection:

Credentials
RPC messages
Metadata
Tokens
Business data

may be exposed to network attackers depending on the environment.

docs.title: Testing TLS
docs.text:
Normal secure connection:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  list

Plaintext connection:

grpcurl \
  -plaintext \
  target.example:50051 \
  list

If an externally reachable sensitive production service accepts plaintext gRPC unexpectedly, investigate the architecture and impact.

docs.title: Mutual TLS
docs.text:
mTLS means:

Server proves identity to client
+
Client proves identity to server

Conceptually:

Client Certificate
        |
        v
      Server
        ^
        |
Server Certificate

mTLS is commonly useful for:

Service-to-service authentication
Internal infrastructure
Zero-trust architectures
High-trust backend services

docs.title: grpcurl With Client Certificates
docs.text:
A controlled mTLS test may use:

grpcurl \
  -cert client.crt \
  -key client.key \
  -cacert ca.crt \
  target.example:443 \
  list

Protect client private keys carefully.

docs.title: mTLS Is Not Authorisation
docs.text:
Even when mTLS is used:

Authenticated service

does not automatically mean:

Authorised for every method

The application may still require:

Service identity checks
Method permissions
Object permissions
Tenant permissions

docs.title: Deadlines
docs.text:
gRPC supports deadlines.

A deadline tells the system how long the client is willing to wait for an RPC.

Conceptually:

Client
  |
  | Request
  | Deadline: 2 seconds
  v
Server

If the deadline is exceeded:

DEADLINE_EXCEEDED

may be returned.

docs.title: Why Deadlines Matter
docs.text:
Without appropriate deadlines:

Slow requests
Long-running operations
Blocked dependencies

can consume resources unnecessarily.

Security and reliability overlap here.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text:
gRPC supports cancellation.

A client or server may cancel an RPC.

Important:

Cancellation does not automatically roll back
application changes already performed.

Therefore application developers must consider transactional behaviour carefully.

docs.title: Cancellation Testing
docs.text:
For state-changing operations, understand:

When does the state change?

What happens if the client disconnects?

Is the operation idempotent?

Is partial state possible?

Do not intentionally create inconsistent production data.

Use controlled test objects.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
gRPC endpoints need rate limiting just like other APIs.

Potential abuse includes:

Login attempts
OTP verification
Password reset
Search
Resource enumeration
Expensive calculations
Streaming
File operations
Administrative methods

Refer to:

Rate Limiting and Anti-Automation

when that page exists.

docs.title: Rate-Limit Scope
docs.text:
Test whether limits are applied by:

IP
Account
Token
Method
Tenant
Service
Connection

Weak implementations may only rate-limit:

HTTP connection

while allowing many RPC streams over another connection.

docs.title: HTTP/2 Multiplexing
docs.text:
Because HTTP/2 supports multiple concurrent streams:

One connection
       |
       +-- RPC 1
       +-- RPC 2
       +-- RPC 3
       +-- RPC 4

rate limiting should not assume:

One connection
=
one request

docs.title: Resource Exhaustion
docs.text:
gRPC services should protect against excessive resource consumption.

Potential areas include:

Large messages
Many concurrent RPCs
Long-lived streams
Large metadata
Expensive methods
Unbounded repeated fields
Unbounded search results
Compression
File uploads

Testing these areas can affect availability.

Use conservative tests.

docs.title: Message Size Limits
docs.text:
Servers and clients can configure message size limits.

A service accepting unexpectedly large messages may consume:

Memory
CPU
Bandwidth

Do not perform large-volume denial-of-service testing without explicit permission.

A normal pentest should generally identify configuration and demonstrate risk using minimal safe input.

docs.title: Metadata Size
docs.text:
Metadata also consumes resources.

Applications and infrastructure should enforce reasonable metadata limits.

Do not send extremely large metadata values to production services unless explicit stress-testing permission exists.

docs.title: Streaming Resource Exhaustion
docs.text:
Potential problems include:

Unlimited streams
Unlimited messages per stream
No idle timeout
No deadline
No per-user stream limit
Expensive processing per message

A safer assessment asks:

What controls exist?

before attempting high-volume validation.

docs.title: Authentication During Streams
docs.text:
Consider:

Stream opened at 10:00

Token expires at 10:05

Stream remains open until 15:00

Ask:

Should the stream remain authorised?

Are permissions re-evaluated?

What happens if account is disabled?

What happens if role changes?

The correct answer depends on the application's security model.

docs.title: Per-Message Authorisation
docs.text:
Suppose a bidirectional stream accepts:

message Command {

    int64 object_id = 1;

    string action = 2;

}

The server should not merely authorise:

Stream creation

and then trust every later:

object_id

Each security-sensitive operation may require appropriate authorisation.

docs.title: Server Reflection Security
docs.text:
Reflection can reveal:

Hidden services
Administrative methods
Internal message fields
Debug methods
Deprecated methods
Service structure

Example:

admin.InternalAdminService
debug.DebugService
migration.MigrationService

These are useful reconnaissance findings.

But again:

Discovery
≠
Exploit

docs.title: Health Checking
docs.text:
gRPC has a standard health-checking service.

You may encounter:

grpc.health.v1.Health

Example:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  grpc.health.v1.Health/Check

Depending on the schema/tool invocation, a service name may be supplied.

Health endpoints can reveal:

Service availability
Service names
Internal architecture

but exposure is not automatically a high-severity vulnerability.

docs.title: Debug and Administrative Services
docs.text:
Pay special attention to service names containing:

Admin
Debug
Internal
Management
Test
Dev
Health
Reflection
Migration
Maintenance
Diagnostics

Example:

admin.AdminService
debug.DebugService

Test whether they are:

Reachable
Authenticated
Authorised
Intended for the environment

docs.title: Deprecated Methods
docs.text:
A .proto definition may contain older methods still reachable by clients.

For example:

LoginV1
LoginV2
LegacyLogin
OldUpdateUser

Older methods may lack security controls added to newer versions.

Always compare:

Current method
vs
Legacy method

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
gRPC APIs may encode versions in:

Package names
Service names
Method names

Examples:

users.v1.UserService
users.v2.UserService

Test whether older versions remain accessible.

docs.title: Business Logic
docs.text:
gRPC applications can have the same business logic vulnerabilities as REST applications.

Examples:

Negative quantity
Duplicate coupon
Invalid state transition
Repeated refund
Bypassed approval
Skipped workflow step
Unexpected object state

Refer to:

Business Logic Vulnerabilities

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Concurrent RPCs may create race conditions.

Example:

RPC A:
RedeemCoupon()

RPC B:
RedeemCoupon()

If both execute before shared state is updated:

Coupon redeemed twice

HTTP/2 multiplexing and gRPC concurrency make race-condition testing relevant.

Refer to:

Race Conditions

Use controlled accounts and minimal concurrency.

docs.title: Authentication Bypass Through Alternate Services
docs.text:
A common architectural risk is inconsistent security between services.

For example:

Public Gateway
    |
    +-- Authentication enforced
    |
    v
UserService

but:

Direct Internal gRPC Port
    |
    +-- No authentication
    |
    v
UserService

If the internal service becomes reachable from an untrusted network, gateway-only authentication may be bypassed.

docs.title: Trusting the Gateway
docs.text:
Some architectures assume:

Only gateway can reach gRPC service

and therefore trust metadata such as:

x-user-id
x-role

This can be safe only if the network and service architecture genuinely enforce that trust boundary.

If an attacker can directly reach the backend:

Gateway security may be bypassed

docs.title: Network Exposure
docs.text:
During reconnaissance identify gRPC ports.

Common examples may include:

443
50051
50052

but gRPC can run on any configured port.

Do not rely solely on default ports.

docs.title: TLS / ALPN
docs.text:
Native secure gRPC commonly negotiates HTTP/2 using TLS ALPN.

During service identification, look for:

h2

support.

For example:

openssl s_client \
  -connect target.example:443 \
  -alpn h2

This only demonstrates HTTP/2 negotiation capability.

It does not prove the endpoint is gRPC.

docs.title: nmap Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Basic authorised service reconnaissance:

nmap \
  -sV \
  -p 443,50051 \
  target.example

If HTTP/2 is detected, investigate further.

Again:

HTTP/2
≠
gRPC

docs.title: grpcurl Discovery Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow:

Target
  |
  v
Is port reachable?
  |
  v
TLS or plaintext?
  |
  v
Try reflection
  |
  +-- Reflection works
  |       |
  |       v
  |   Enumerate services
  |
  +-- Reflection unavailable
          |
          v
    Obtain .proto / protoset
          |
          v
    Enumerate schema

docs.title: grpcurl Quick Recon
docs.text:
TLS:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  list

Plaintext:

grpcurl \
  -plaintext \
  target.example:50051 \
  list

Describe:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  describe package.Service

Methods:

grpcurl \
  target.example:443 \
  list package.Service

Invoke:

grpcurl \
  -d '{"id":"123"}' \
  target.example:443 \
  package.Service/GetObject

docs.title: Authenticated grpcurl Workflow
docs.text:
Set a shell variable:

TOKEN='REDACTED'

Then:

grpcurl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  target.example:443 \
  list

Invoke:

grpcurl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"id":"123"}' \
  target.example:443 \
  users.UserService/GetUser

Avoid putting sensitive real tokens into:

Shell history
Screenshots
Git repositories
Reports

without appropriate redaction.

docs.title: Two-Account Testing
docs.text:
For authorisation testing use:

Account A
Account B

Set:

TOKEN_A='REDACTED'
TOKEN_B='REDACTED'

Controlled object owned by A:

1001

Controlled object owned by B:

2001

Test:

grpcurl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN_A" \
  -d '{"id":"1001"}' \
  target.example:443 \
  objects.ObjectService/GetObject

Then:

grpcurl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN_A" \
  -d '{"id":"2001"}' \
  target.example:443 \
  objects.ObjectService/GetObject

Expected:

Denied

for the second request unless Account A legitimately has access.

docs.title: grpcurl Verbose Mode
docs.text:
grpcurl provides verbose output options.

Check:

grpcurl -help

for the exact options supported by your installed version.

Verbose output can help inspect:

Headers
Response metadata
Trailers
Timing
Status

docs.title: Burp Suite and gRPC
docs.text:
Burp Suite is fundamentally an HTTP testing platform.

Because native gRPC uses HTTP/2 and binary protobuf messages, the workflow is not always as straightforward as editing JSON REST traffic.

Burp can still be valuable for:

HTTP/2 inspection
Metadata
Gateway traffic
gRPC-Web
Authentication
CORS
Headers
Protobuf-assisted workflows

docs.title: Burp Proxy
docs.text:
When the client supports proxying and TLS interception, Burp can help observe:

HTTP/2 requests
Metadata
Authorization headers
Content-Type
gRPC-Web traffic
Gateway requests

Native gRPC client proxy support varies by implementation.

Do not assume every gRPC client honours:

HTTP_PROXY
HTTPS_PROXY

in the same manner as a browser.

docs.title: Burp and Binary Protobuf
docs.text:
Raw protobuf data is not naturally human-readable.

Conceptually:

Burp
  |
  v
Binary protobuf
  |
  v
Need schema / decoder

Having:

.proto files

greatly improves your ability to understand messages.

docs.title: Burp Extensions
docs.text:
Check the current BApp Store:

https://portswigger.net/bappstore

Potentially useful categories include:

Protobuf decoding
gRPC-Web decoding
HTTP/2 tooling

One known BApp is:

Protobuf Decoder

which can help decode and beautify protobuf responses.

Because extensions are third-party software, review their current status and source before relying on them.

docs.title: gRPC-Web Coder
docs.text:
For applications using:

gRPC-Web

a gRPC-Web-specific Burp extension may help decode or encode traffic.

Always confirm:

Native gRPC
or
gRPC-Web

before selecting tooling.

Do not apply gRPC-Web tooling blindly to native gRPC traffic.

docs.title: Burp Is Not Always the Primary Tool
docs.text:
For native gRPC:

grpcurl

is often more practical than trying to force every interaction through Burp.

A useful combination is:

grpcurl
    +
.proto files
    +
Burp
    +
Source review
    +
Application client

docs.title: Mobile Applications
docs.text:
Mobile applications frequently use gRPC.

Useful artefacts may include:

Generated protobuf classes
Service stubs
Descriptor data
API hostnames
Authentication metadata
Certificate configuration

Search decompiled applications for:

grpc
protobuf
proto
Channel
ManagedChannel
Authorization
Bearer

Only assess applications you are authorised to test.

docs.title: Source Code Review
docs.text:
When source code is available, search for:

service
rpc
grpc
RegisterService
interceptor
metadata
authorization
role
tenant
permission

Also inspect generated code carefully.

Generated protobuf code can be large, so locate:

.proto

sources first where possible.

docs.title: Interceptors
docs.text:
Search for authentication and authorisation interceptors.

Examples vary by language.

Conceptually:

UnaryInterceptor
StreamInterceptor
ServerInterceptor

Important question:

Are unary and streaming RPCs protected consistently?

An application might secure unary methods while forgetting streaming handlers.

docs.title: Unary vs Streaming Security
docs.text:
Build separate matrices:

Unary methods

and:

Streaming methods

because middleware registration can differ.

Example:

RPC Type Authentication Authorisation GetUser Unary Yes Yes WatchUsers Server stream Yes ? Upload Client stream Yes ? Chat Bidirectional ? ?

docs.title: Server-Side Validation
docs.text:
The service should validate:

Field format
Field length
Allowed values
Object relationships
Business rules
Authorisation

Do not rely only on:

protobuf type

for validation.

docs.title: Integer Boundary Testing
docs.text:
For numeric fields, safe controlled tests can include:

0
1
-1
Expected minimum
Expected maximum
Just outside expected range

Avoid intentionally causing resource exhaustion.

docs.title: String Boundary Testing
docs.text:
For string fields test:

Empty string
Normal value
Whitespace
Unexpected Unicode
Reasonable boundary length

Then apply vulnerability-specific tests only when the field reaches a relevant sink.

docs.title: Boolean Fields
docs.text:
Test:

true
false
absent

where field presence semantics matter.

Security-sensitive examples:

admin
enabled
verified
approved
internal

should never be trusted merely because the client sends them.

docs.title: Sensitive Fields
docs.text:
Pay particular attention to:

admin
role
permissions
owner_id
user_id
account_id
tenant_id
organisation_id
verified
approved
status
price
balance
discount
internal
is_staff

These fields are not vulnerabilities by themselves.

They are:

Authorisation and business-logic candidates

docs.title: Secrets in Protobuf Definitions
docs.text:
.proto files may reveal:

Internal service names
Hidden administrative functionality
Deprecated fields
Internal identifiers
Comments
Architecture

Do not place secrets directly in schema comments or generated client packages.

docs.title: Sensitive Data in Metadata
docs.text:
Metadata may accidentally contain:

JWTs
API keys
Session identifiers
Internal tokens
Tracing data
User identifiers

Review logging systems to ensure metadata is not unnecessarily recorded.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
gRPC services should log security-relevant events such as:

Authentication failures
Authorisation failures
Administrative actions
Sensitive state changes
Rate-limit events
Suspicious method use

but should avoid logging:

Passwords
Access tokens
Private keys
Full sensitive request bodies

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Useful telemetry can include:

Service
Method
Status
Latency
Authentication identity
Authorisation decision
Request volume
Error rate
Stream count

This helps detect abuse.

docs.title: gRPC and JWT
docs.text:
JWTs are commonly transported through metadata:

authorization: Bearer TOKEN

All normal JWT security concerns still apply:

Signature verification
Algorithm handling
Issuer validation
Audience validation
Expiration
Key management
Claims
Authorisation

Refer to:

JSON Web Token Security

docs.title: gRPC and OAuth
docs.text:
OAuth access tokens may also be passed through gRPC metadata.

The gRPC service must validate:

Token signature or introspection
Issuer
Audience
Scope
Expiration

as appropriate.

Refer to:

OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Security

docs.title: gRPC and API Security
docs.text:
Many standard API security issues apply directly:

Broken Object Level Authorisation
Broken Authentication
Broken Function Level Authorisation
Unrestricted Resource Consumption
Business Logic Vulnerabilities
SSRF
Security Misconfiguration

Refer to:

API Security

docs.title: gRPC-Web and CORS
docs.text:
Because gRPC-Web is browser-facing, CORS becomes relevant.

Inspect:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Access-Control-Allow-Headers
Access-Control-Allow-Methods

Refer to:

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

docs.title: gRPC-Web and CSRF
docs.text:
Whether CSRF is relevant depends on:

Authentication mechanism
Cookie behaviour
Request format
CORS
Gateway

docs.title: Example Finding: Missing Object-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Finding:
Broken Object Level Authorisation in gRPC GetInvoice Method

Affected service:
billing.InvoiceService

Affected method:
GetInvoice

Observed:
The GetInvoice RPC accepts an invoice identifier in the request message.

Testing was performed using two controlled accounts.

Account A owned invoice 1001.
Account B owned invoice 2001.

Using Account A's valid authentication token, changing the invoice identifier from 1001 to 2001 caused the service to return Account B's controlled invoice.

Impact:
An authenticated user can access invoice objects belonging to another user by modifying the invoice identifier supplied to the RPC.

Recommendation:
Perform server-side object-level authorisation for every requested invoice. Derive the authenticated user from trusted authentication context and verify that the user is authorised to access the requested invoice before returning it.

docs.title: Example Finding: Missing Function-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Finding:
Standard Users Can Invoke Administrative gRPC Method

Affected service:
admin.AdminService

Affected method:
ChangeRole

Observed:
A standard controlled user account was able to invoke the ChangeRole RPC successfully.

The method accepted a target user identifier and role value and did not enforce the expected administrator requirement.

Impact:
A standard user may be able to modify user privileges, potentially resulting in privilege escalation.

Recommendation:
Enforce server-side function-level authorisation before executing administrative RPC methods. Do not rely on client-side UI restrictions or knowledge of method names.

docs.title: Example Finding: Unauthenticated gRPC Method
docs.text:
Finding:
Sensitive gRPC Method Accessible Without Authentication

Affected service:
users.UserService

Affected method:
GetUser

Observed:
The method returned user information when invoked without authentication metadata.

The same method was expected to require an authenticated application user.

Impact:
An unauthenticated attacker with network access to the gRPC service may retrieve user information.

Recommendation:
Require authentication for the affected RPC and ensure authentication middleware or interceptors are applied consistently across all sensitive services and methods.

docs.title: Example Finding: Reflection Exposure
docs.text:
Finding:
Production gRPC Service Exposes Server Reflection

Observed:
The externally reachable production gRPC endpoint exposes the gRPC reflection service.

An unauthenticated client was able to enumerate service and method definitions.

The exposed schema included administrative and internal service names.

Impact:
Reflection significantly simplifies reconnaissance by exposing the gRPC API surface and message schemas.

No direct unauthorised access to administrative functionality was demonstrated through reflection alone.

Recommendation:
Disable or restrict gRPC reflection in production where runtime schema discovery is not required. If reflection is operationally required, restrict access according to the application's trust model.

Severity should be based on:

Actual exposure
Sensitivity
Environment
Attack-chain value

Do not automatically classify reflection as high severity.

docs.title: Example Finding: Sensitive Metadata Trusted
docs.text:
Finding:
Client-Controlled gRPC Metadata Influences Authorisation

Observed:
The service accepts an x-role metadata value from the client.

Changing:

x-role: user

to:

x-role: admin

caused the controlled account to gain access to an administrative method.

Impact:
An authenticated user can manipulate client-controlled metadata to influence the server's authorisation decision and escalate privileges.

Recommendation:
Do not trust client-supplied role or identity metadata. Derive identity and permissions from validated authentication credentials or a trusted upstream identity mechanism protected by an enforced network trust boundary.

docs.title: Example Finding: Excessive Error Disclosure
docs.text:
Finding:
gRPC Error Responses Disclose Internal Infrastructure Information

Observed:
Invalid input to the affected RPC caused the service to return detailed internal error information.

The response exposed internal service names and database connection details.

Impact:
An attacker may use the disclosed information to map internal infrastructure and identify additional attack targets or technologies.

Recommendation:
Return generic client-facing gRPC error descriptions while logging detailed diagnostic information only to appropriately protected server-side logging systems.

docs.title: Example Finding Titles
docs.text:
Useful titles include:

Broken Object Level Authorisation in gRPC GetInvoice Method

Missing Function-Level Authorisation in Administrative gRPC Service

Sensitive gRPC Method Accessible Without Authentication

Production gRPC Service Exposes Server Reflection

Client-Controlled gRPC Metadata Enables Privilege Escalation

gRPC Error Responses Disclose Internal Infrastructure Details

Sensitive gRPC Service Exposed Over Unencrypted Transport

Missing Rate Limiting on gRPC Authentication Method

gRPC Streaming Method Does Not Enforce Object Authorisation

Legacy gRPC Service Bypasses Current Authorisation Controls

Cross-Tenant Access Through gRPC Object Identifier Manipulation

docs.title: Discover Services and Methods
docs.text:
Start by identifying the transport, endpoint, authority, authentication mechanism, and whether the service is intended for browser, mobile, internal, or service-to-service clients. Where available, obtain the approved .proto files, generated client code, API gateway configuration, service registry entries, and deployment documentation.

Reflection can expose service and method definitions to a client, which makes discovery easier. Its absence does not prove that methods are protected or undiscoverable: clients, descriptors, gateway routes, logs, generated code, and documentation may still reveal the interface. Conversely, enabled reflection is not automatically a vulnerability; the security consequence depends on exposure, authentication, and the sensitivity of the definitions.

Build an inventory containing:

Service
Method
Unary or streaming type
Request and response message
Authentication metadata
Required role or tenant
Referenced object or resource
Expected side effect

Use grpcurl, an approved generated client, Burp Suite where the traffic is visible through an HTTP/2-capable proxy, or the application's own test client. Do not infer a complete attack surface from one collector or reflection result.

docs.title: Authentication and Authorisation
docs.text:
Test authentication metadata separately from authorization. Record whether the call is accepted with no metadata, an invalid token, a valid low-privilege token, and an approved higher-privilege token. Then compare the same method with:

  • a resource owned by the caller;
  • a resource owned by another controlled account;
  • an object in another tenant;
  • an administrative method;
  • an equivalent gateway or REST operation, if one exists.

An authenticated RPC proves only that the server accepted an identity. A successful method call does not by itself prove object access, tenant access, administrative rights, or code execution. A directory or service-discovery relationship is a candidate until the actual operation and consequence are validated.

docs.title: Messages and Streaming
docs.text:
Review protobuf fields, enum values, repeated fields, nested messages, field masks, resource names, pagination, timestamps, and optional fields for server-side validation. Test one controlled field at a time and compare the gRPC status, response message, trailers, and resulting state. Client-side generated types and field comments are useful context, not a substitute for server enforcement.

For client, server, or bidirectional streams, document the expected lifecycle and test only approved small sequences. Check authentication at stream creation and, where relevant, per message; check whether cancellation, deadlines, replay, ordering, message size, and idle timeouts are enforced. Avoid high-volume or long-lived resource tests against production.

docs.title: TLS and Transport Observations
docs.text: Record whether TLS is used, how the server identity is validated, whether mutual TLS is required, and which gateway or proxy terminates the connection. A certificate or protocol observation establishes transport properties, not application authorization. Test metadata forwarding and identity propagation only with approved accounts and controlled endpoints.

docs.title: Tool-Assisted Validation
docs.text:
Tools can assist with discovery and request construction:

Reflection / grpcurl -> service and method inventory
.proto files -> message and field interpretation
Generated client -> normal application workflow
Burp or HTTP/2 proxy -> request comparison and evidence
Server logs -> approved correlation of method and identity

Use the sequence:

Observation -> Candidate -> Validation -> Evidence -> Security Conclusion

Reflection output, a decoded message, an unusual status, or a proxy finding is not automatically a vulnerability. Confirm the baseline, repeat the changed request, and establish the smallest protected resource or state transition that demonstrates impact.

docs.title: Expected Results and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Observation What it establishes What still requires validation Reflection responds Definitions are available to that caller Whether sensitive methods or data are exposed Method returns OK The request was accepted Object ownership, tenant scope, and side effect UNAUTHENTICATED Authentication was rejected Whether another path accepts the identity PERMISSION_DENIED A policy decision denied the call Which policy layer made the decision Different response through a gateway Transport or routing differs Whether the application security decision differs

For inconsistent results, check authority and SNI, ALPN/HTTP2 support, proxy decoding, channel credentials, token expiry, clock skew, trailers, retries, deadlines, gateway translations, generated-client version, and whether the call is asynchronous. Re-establish a normal baseline before changing another variable.

docs.title: Evidence, Remediation, and Retesting
docs.text:
Capture the service, method, transport, client identity, tenant, redacted metadata, request message, response/status/trailers, baseline comparison, timestamp, and safe read-back or side effect. Preserve .proto or reflection evidence only where authorised and redact sensitive fields.

Remediation may include enforcing method and resource authorization server-side, restricting reflection, validating message fields and resource ownership, requiring appropriate TLS and metadata validation, limiting streams and message sizes, and aligning gateway and backend policy. Retest unauthenticated, low-privilege, cross-object, cross-tenant, administrative, unary, and relevant streaming cases, including equivalent gateway paths.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
A strong gRPC security model combines multiple controls.

                    gRPC SECURITY
                         |
        +----------------+----------------+
        |                |                |
        v                v                v
     Transport      Authentication    Authorisation
        |                |                |
       TLS              JWT            Method
       mTLS             OAuth          Object
                                         Tenant
        |                |                |
        +----------------+----------------+
                         |
                         v
                    Validation
                         |
             +-----------+-----------+
             |                       |
             v                       v
        Input Safety            Business Rules
             |                       |
             +-----------+-----------+
                         |
                         v
                  Resource Controls
                         |
               +---------+---------+
               |         |         |
               v         v         v
             Rate      Size      Streams
             Limit     Limit     Deadlines
                         |
                         v
                  Safe Error Handling
                         |
                         v
                 Logging / Monitoring

docs.title: Use TLS
docs.text: Protect sensitive production traffic with appropriate transport security.

docs.title: Consider mTLS for Service Identity
docs.text:
Where architecture requires strong service-to-service identity:

mTLS

can provide mutual authentication.

Still enforce application-level authorisation.

docs.title: Authenticate Every Sensitive RPC
docs.text:
Do not assume:

Internal network
=
trusted user

Apply authentication according to the service trust model.

docs.title: Authorise Every Sensitive Operation
docs.text:
Check:

Method permission
Object permission
Tenant permission
Business permission

server-side.

docs.title: Do Not Trust Client Metadata
docs.text:
Values such as:

x-user-id
x-role
x-tenant-id

must not be trusted unless they come through a genuinely enforced trusted boundary.

docs.title: Validate Application Data
docs.text:
Protobuf types are not sufficient security validation.

Validate:

Length
Range
Format
Relationships
Allowed state
Ownership

docs.title: Limit Resources
docs.text:
Configure appropriate:

Message size
Metadata size
Concurrent RPCs
Streams
Rate limits
Deadlines
Idle timeouts

docs.title: Restrict Reflection
docs.text: Disable or appropriately restrict production reflection when runtime schema discovery is unnecessary.

docs.title: Protect Administrative Services
docs.text:
Administrative and debugging services should have strong:

Network restrictions
Authentication
Authorisation
Monitoring

docs.title: Handle Errors Safely
docs.text:
Return enough information for legitimate clients without exposing:

Stack traces
Database strings
Internal hostnames
Source paths
Secrets

docs.title: Secure Streaming Separately
docs.text:
Do not assume security applied to unary RPCs automatically protects streams.

Review:

Stream creation
Each sensitive message
Long-lived authentication state
Resource consumption
Cancellation
Timeouts
