docs.title: Final Mass Assignment Testing Model
docs.text:
APPLICATION
                            ↓
                   IDENTIFY ENDPOINTS
                            ↓
                  POST / PUT / PATCH
                            ↓
                    CAPTURE REQUEST
                            ↓
                    BURP REPEATER
                            ↓
                  ESTABLISH BASELINE
                            ↓
                 DISCOVER OBJECT MODEL
                            ↓
       ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
       ↓                    ↓                    ↓
 API RESPONSES          JAVASCRIPT          API SCHEMA
       ↓                    ↓                    ↓
 READ-ONLY FIELDS       MODEL NAMES        GRAPHQL /
                                            OPENAPI
       └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                            ↓
                  CANDIDATE PROPERTIES
                            ↓
                     PRIORITISE SAFELY
                            ↓
                 ADD ONE PROPERTY ONLY
                            ↓
                     SEND REQUEST
                            ↓
                  PROPERTY RECOGNISED?
                     ↓             ↓
                    NO            YES
                     ↓             ↓
                 CONTINUE      RETRIEVE OBJECT
                                    ↓
                              VALUE PERSISTED?
                               ↓          ↓
                              NO         YES
                               ↓          ↓
                           CONTINUE    SHOULD CLIENT
                                      CONTROL FIELD?
                                       ↓         ↓
                                      YES        NO
                                       ↓          ↓
                                   EXPECTED    SECURITY
                                              BOUNDARY
                                              BROKEN
                                                 ↓
                                    SECURITY-SENSITIVE?
                                       ↓         ↓
                                      NO        YES
                                       ↓         ↓
                                  LOW / NONE   VERIFY WITH
                                              MINIMAL IMPACT
                                                 ↓
                                    ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                                    ↓            ↓            ↓
                                  ROLE       OWNERSHIP    VERIFICATION
                                    ↓            ↓            ↓
                               PRIVILEGE      IDOR /       WORKFLOW
                               ESCALATION      BOLA         BYPASS
                                    └────────────┼────────────┘
                                                 ↓
                                         COLLECT EVIDENCE
                                                 ↓
                                              REPORT

The central principle is:

A client should only be able to modify properties that the application explicitly intends that client to control. Do not treat a field as safe simply because it is hidden from the user interface, difficult to discover, or undocumented. Map the server-side object model, identify the intended write boundary, and verify that unexpected properties cannot cross it.

docs.title: Web Application Testing Methodology
docs.text:
A structured web application penetration test follows a repeatable process for discovering the attack surface, identifying vulnerabilities, validating their impact and documenting the results.

The exact methodology depends on the application, architecture, technologies and assessment scope.

Authorised Security Testing

The techniques documented in these notes are intended for authorised security assessments, lab environments, security research and responsible vulnerability disclosure.

docs.title: Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Reconnaissance
      ↓
Technology Identification
      ↓
Attack Surface Mapping
      ↓
Content Discovery
      ↓
Parameter Discovery
      ↓
Authentication Testing
      ↓
Authorisation Testing
      ↓
Input Validation
      ↓
Server-Side Testing
      ↓
Client-Side Testing
      ↓
Business Logic Testing
      ↓
Validation
      ↓
Reporting

The workflow should not be treated as strictly linear. Discoveries made during later stages frequently require returning to earlier stages.

docs.title: 1. Reconnaissance
docs.text: The first stage is understanding the application's externally accessible attack surface.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
Identify:

  • Domains and subdomains
  • IP addresses
  • Web applications
  • APIs
  • Administrative interfaces
  • Development and staging environments
  • Authentication portals
  • Exposed services
  • Historical endpoints
  • Third-party integrations

docs.title: Typical Activities
docs.text:
Domain
  ↓
Subdomain Enumeration
  ↓
DNS Resolution
  ↓
HTTP Probing
  ↓
Technology Identification
  ↓
Crawling
  ↓
Content Discovery
  ↓
Parameter Discovery
  ↓
Attack Surface

Reconnaissance should continue throughout the assessment as new infrastructure and application components are discovered.

docs.title: 2. Technology Identification
docs.text:
Understanding the technologies used by the target helps determine which testing techniques are relevant.

Identify where possible:

  • Web server
  • Application framework
  • Programming language
  • CMS
  • JavaScript frameworks
  • Reverse proxies
  • CDN
  • WAF
  • Authentication technologies
  • API technologies
  • Third-party components
  • Software versions

Technology identification can also reveal outdated or unsupported components requiring further investigation.

docs.title: 3. Attack Surface Mapping
docs.text:
The discovered assets should be converted into an organised attack surface.

Map:

  • Applications
  • Hosts
  • Ports
  • Endpoints
  • Parameters
  • APIs
  • Authentication boundaries
  • User roles
  • Administrative functionality
  • Upload functionality
  • Import and export functionality
  • External integrations

The objective is to understand where user-controlled input enters the application and where security boundaries exist.

docs.title: 4. Content Discovery
docs.text:
Content discovery identifies resources that may not be directly linked from the application's normal interface.

Look for:

  • Directories
  • Files
  • Backup files
  • Configuration files
  • Administrative panels
  • API endpoints
  • Debug interfaces
  • Development endpoints
  • Documentation
  • Source maps
  • Temporary files
  • Old application versions

Automated discovery should be combined with manual inspection and crawling.

docs.title: 5. Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Parameters represent potential input points into the application.

Investigate:

  • GET parameters
  • POST parameters
  • JSON properties
  • XML elements
  • HTTP headers
  • Cookies
  • Path parameters
  • Multipart fields
  • API parameters
  • WebSocket messages

Parameters discovered through JavaScript, historical URLs and API documentation can reveal functionality that is not immediately visible.

docs.title: 6. Authentication Testing
docs.text:
Authentication testing evaluates how the application verifies user identities.

Review:

  • Login functionality
  • Username enumeration
  • Password policies
  • Account lockout
  • Brute-force protections
  • Password reset
  • Multi-factor authentication
  • Remember-me functionality
  • OAuth
  • SSO
  • Authentication tokens
  • Authentication bypass opportunities

Authentication should also be tested across different application components and APIs.

docs.title: 7. Authorisation Testing
docs.text:
Authentication establishes identity. Authorisation determines what that identity is permitted to access.

Test for:

  • Horizontal privilege escalation
  • Vertical privilege escalation
  • Insecure Direct Object References
  • Missing access controls
  • Administrative endpoint exposure
  • Forced browsing
  • Role manipulation
  • API authorisation weaknesses

Where possible, use multiple accounts with different privilege levels to compare application behaviour.

docs.title: 8. Session Management Testing
docs.text:
Review how sessions are created, maintained and destroyed.

Investigate:

  • Session cookies
  • Cookie attributes
  • Session identifiers
  • Session fixation
  • Session expiration
  • Logout invalidation
  • Concurrent sessions
  • Token rotation
  • JWT handling
  • Session replay

Session handling should be tested alongside authentication and authorisation.

docs.title: 9. Input Validation
docs.text:
Identify locations where user-controlled input is processed.

Potential input sources include:

URL parameters
POST bodies
JSON
XML
Cookies
HTTP headers
File names
Uploaded files
WebSocket messages
API parameters

Trace how these values are validated, transformed, stored and returned.

Input points become candidates for more specialised vulnerability testing.

docs.title: 10. Server-Side Testing
docs.text:
Server-side testing focuses on vulnerabilities processed by the application or supporting infrastructure.

Test for areas such as:

  • SQL Injection
  • Command Injection
  • Server-Side Request Forgery
  • Server-Side Template Injection
  • XML External Entity Injection
  • Path Traversal
  • File Inclusion
  • File Upload
  • Deserialization
  • HTTP Request Smuggling

Pay particular attention to functionality that interacts with operating system commands, databases, file systems, parsers and internal network resources.

docs.title: 11. Client-Side Testing
docs.text:
Analyse functionality executed or processed within the browser.

Test for:

  • Cross-Site Scripting
  • DOM-based vulnerabilities
  • Cross-Site Request Forgery
  • CORS weaknesses
  • Open Redirect
  • Prototype Pollution
  • Browser storage issues
  • Web messaging
  • Client-side access controls

JavaScript should be reviewed for hidden endpoints, parameters, secrets, API calls and client-side security logic.

docs.title: 12. Business Logic Testing
docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities often require understanding how the application is intended to operate.

Investigate:

  • Workflow bypass
  • State manipulation
  • Price manipulation
  • Quantity manipulation
  • Race conditions
  • Repeated actions
  • Coupon or discount abuse
  • Multi-step process bypass
  • Trust assumptions
  • Limit bypasses

These vulnerabilities are difficult to detect using automated scanning alone.

docs.title: 13. API Testing
docs.text:
APIs should be treated as a separate attack surface even when they support the same web application.

Review:

  • Endpoint discovery
  • Authentication
  • Object-level authorisation
  • Function-level authorisation
  • Input validation
  • Mass assignment
  • Excessive data exposure
  • Rate limiting
  • API versioning
  • GraphQL
  • REST
  • SOAP

Compare API behaviour between unauthenticated users and users with different privilege levels.

docs.title: 14. Validation
docs.text:
Potential vulnerabilities should be manually validated before reporting.

Determine:

  • Is the behaviour reproducible?
  • What conditions are required?
  • Which users are affected?
  • What privileges are required?
  • What data or functionality is exposed?
  • Can the vulnerability be chained with another weakness?
  • What is the realistic security impact?

Avoid relying solely on scanner classifications.

docs.title: 15. Impact Assessment
docs.text:
Technical findings should be translated into realistic security impact.

Consider:

  • Confidentiality
  • Integrity
  • Availability
  • Required privileges
  • User interaction
  • Exploitability
  • Scope
  • Business impact
  • Potential attack chains

Where appropriate, CVSS can be used as one component of the severity assessment.

docs.title: 16. Reporting
docs.text:
Each confirmed vulnerability should contain enough information for another tester or developer to reproduce and understand the issue.

A finding should normally include:

Title
Description
Affected Component
Technical Details
Steps to Reproduce
Evidence
Security Impact
Severity
Recommendation
References

Screenshots, HTTP requests and responses should be included where they improve reproducibility.

docs.title: 17. Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation, previously identified vulnerabilities should be tested again.

Verify that:

  • The original vulnerability is resolved
  • The fix applies to all affected endpoints
  • Alternative attack paths are addressed
  • The remediation did not introduce another vulnerability
  • Related functionality remains secure

A vulnerability should only be considered resolved after the remediation has been validated.

docs.title: Continuous Discovery
docs.text:
Web application penetration testing is iterative.

A useful mental model is:

Discover
   ↓
Map
   ↓
Test
   ↓
Validate
   ↓
Discover More
   ↓
Test Again
   ↓
Report

New endpoints, parameters, roles and technologies discovered during testing should continuously feed back into the assessment methodology.

flowchart TD
      A["Reconnaissance"] --> B["Attack-surface mapping"]
      B --> C["Authentication and authorization"]
      C --> D["Input and workflow testing"]
      D --> E["Validate candidate behavior"]
      E --> F["Assess impact and evidence"]
      F --> G["Report and retest"]

docs.title: Related Notes
docs.text:
• Web Application Security Overview
  • Pentesting Checklist
  • Reconnaissance

docs.title: Multi-Factor Authentication Security
docs.text:
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) strengthens authentication by requiring users to prove their identity using more than one independent authentication factor.

A typical authentication flow is:

Username
   ↓
Password
   ↓
First Factor Valid
   ↓
MFA Challenge
   ↓
Second Factor Valid
   ↓
Fully Authenticated Session

MFA becomes ineffective when an attacker can bypass the second factor through weaknesses in:

Workflow state
Session management
OTP validation
Rate limiting
Recovery mechanisms
Remember-device functionality
API endpoints
Direct URL access
Response handling
Account recovery
SSO integration
Trusted-device tokens
MFA reset
Backup codes
Race conditions

The central testing question is:

Does the server independently enforce MFA
before granting access to protected functionality?

Authorised Security Testing

Perform MFA testing only against accounts and authentication factors that are explicitly authorised for the assessment. Use controlled test accounts, controlled phone numbers, controlled authenticator applications, and controlled email addresses wherever possible. Avoid locking real users out, consuming genuine recovery codes, generating excessive SMS messages, or performing high-volume OTP guessing unless specifically authorised.

docs.title: Authentication Factors
docs.text:
Authentication factors are generally divided into:

Something You Know
Something You Have
Something You Are

Examples:

Factor Examples Knowledge Password, PIN Possession Authenticator app, hardware token, phone Inherence Fingerprint, facial recognition

MFA should combine independent factors.

For example:

Password
+
TOTP

is MFA because it combines:

Knowledge
+
Possession

Using:

Password
+
Security Question

does not provide the same assurance because both are knowledge factors.

docs.title: MFA Architecture
docs.text:
A common MFA workflow looks like:

User
  ↓
POST /login
  ↓
Password Verified
  ↓
Temporary Authentication State
  ↓
MFA Challenge
  ↓
POST /mfa/verify
  ↓
OTP Verified
  ↓
Authentication State Upgraded
  ↓
Fully Authenticated Session

The critical transition is:

Partially Authenticated
        ↓
Fully Authenticated

This transition must occur only after successful MFA verification.

docs.title: Authentication State Machine
docs.text:
Think of MFA as a state machine:

STATE 0
Unauthenticated
    ↓
Correct Password
    ↓
STATE 1
Password Verified
MFA Pending
    ↓
Correct MFA
    ↓
STATE 2
Fully Authenticated

The application must enforce:

STATE 0
Cannot access authenticated resources

STATE 1
Cannot access fully authenticated resources

STATE 2
Can access authorised resources

A common MFA vulnerability occurs when:

STATE 1

is mistakenly treated as:

STATE 2

docs.title: MFA Testing Methodology
docs.text:
Use a structured workflow:

Create Controlled Account
        ↓
Enable MFA
        ↓
Record Normal Login
        ↓
Map Every MFA Request
        ↓
Identify Authentication State
        ↓
Inspect Cookies / Tokens
        ↓
Test Direct Resource Access
        ↓
Test Workflow Manipulation
        ↓
Test OTP Validation
        ↓
Test Account Binding
        ↓
Test Rate Limiting
        ↓
Test Remember-Device
        ↓
Test Recovery Codes
        ↓
Test MFA Reset
        ↓
Test Password Reset Interaction
        ↓
Test Session Behaviour
        ↓
Test API Enforcement
        ↓
Verify Minimal Impact
        ↓
Report

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
First perform a completely normal login.

Record:

Login request
Login response
Cookies before MFA
MFA challenge request
MFA verification request
Cookies after MFA
Redirects
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
Protected resources

This baseline becomes essential when comparing bypass attempts.

docs.title: Burp Proxy Workflow
docs.text:
Use Burp Proxy to capture:

POST /login
        ↓
302 /mfa
        ↓
GET /mfa
        ↓
POST /mfa/verify
        ↓
302 /dashboard
        ↓
GET /dashboard

Pay particular attention to:

Set-Cookie
Location
Authorization
JWTs
Hidden parameters
CSRF tokens
MFA identifiers
Challenge IDs

docs.title: Before and After MFA Comparison
docs.text:
Record the authentication material before MFA.

Example:

Set-Cookie: session=PRE_MFA_SESSION

After successful MFA:

Set-Cookie: session=POST_MFA_SESSION

Questions:

Does the session rotate?

Does the server track MFA completion?

Is MFA status embedded in a token?

Does the same pre-MFA session become privileged?

Can the pre-MFA session access protected endpoints?

docs.title: Direct Endpoint Access
docs.text:
One of the highest-value MFA tests is extremely simple:

Authenticate with password
        ↓
Stop at MFA
        ↓
Request /dashboard directly

Example:

GET /dashboard HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=PRE_MFA_SESSION

Expected:

Redirect to MFA

or:

403 Forbidden

Potential vulnerability:

200 OK
Protected content returned

docs.title: Do Not Trust Redirects Alone
docs.text:
Suppose:

GET /account HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=PRE_MFA_SESSION

returns:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /mfa

Check the response body.

Occasionally applications return:

302 Redirect
+
Sensitive HTML

The browser follows the redirect, but the protected data was still disclosed.

Inspect the raw response.

docs.title: Test Multiple Protected Resources
docs.text:
Do not test only:

/dashboard

Also consider:

/account
/profile
/settings
/admin
/api/me
/api/account
/api/orders
/api/messages
/api/documents
/api/admin

The UI may enforce MFA while APIs do not.

docs.title: API MFA Enforcement
docs.text:
A common architecture is:

Web Frontend
    ↓
MFA Check
    ↓
API

But the API may trust the session without checking MFA state.

Test:

Password Valid
MFA Pending
      ↓
Direct API Request

Example:

GET /api/account HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer PRE_MFA_TOKEN

Expected:

Denied

docs.title: Partial Authentication Tokens
docs.text:
Applications sometimes issue a token after password verification.

Example JWT:

{
    "sub": "1001",
    "authenticated": true,
    "mfa": false
}

After MFA:

{
    "sub": "1001",
    "authenticated": true,
    "mfa": true
}

Every sensitive backend endpoint must understand the distinction.

docs.title: JWT MFA State
docs.text:
Look for claims such as:

mfa
mfa_verified
amr
acr
auth_level
authentication_level
loa
otp_verified

Example:

{
    "sub": "1001",
    "amr": [
        "pwd"
    ]
}

After MFA:

{
    "sub": "1001",
    "amr": [
        "pwd",
        "otp"
    ]
}

Refer to:

JSON Web Token Security

for JWT-specific testing.

docs.title: Authentication Method Reference
docs.text:
OpenID Connect commonly uses:

amr

to describe authentication methods.

Conceptually:

pwd

may indicate password authentication.

otp

may indicate an OTP mechanism.

Do not assume every application implements these claims correctly.

docs.title: MFA Workflow Bypass
docs.text:
A typical vulnerable workflow:

POST /login
    ↓
Password Correct
    ↓
GET /mfa
    ↓
POST /mfa/verify
    ↓
GET /dashboard

Try:

POST /login
    ↓
Password Correct
    ↓
GET /dashboard

If successful:

MFA is only enforced by application navigation

rather than by the server-side authorisation layer.

docs.title: Skipping MFA Verification
docs.text:
Another workflow may be:

/login
   ↓
/mfa/send
   ↓
/mfa/verify
   ↓
/mfa/complete
   ↓
/dashboard

Test whether:

/mfa/complete

can be accessed before:

/mfa/verify

Security-relevant workflow transitions must be validated server-side.

docs.title: Client-Side MFA Enforcement
docs.text:
Look for JavaScript such as:

if (response.mfaVerified) {
    window.location = "/dashboard";
}

Changing the response locally may reveal the dashboard route.

That alone is not a vulnerability.

The real question is:

Does the server allow protected actions?

docs.title: Response Manipulation
docs.text:
Suppose the server returns:

{
    "success": false,
    "mfaVerified": false
}

Changing it in the browser to:

{
    "success": true,
    "mfaVerified": true
}

may cause the frontend to navigate to:

/dashboard

This only becomes a security vulnerability if:

/dashboard

or the underlying APIs accept the partially authenticated session.

Important:

Frontend Bypass
      ≠
Authentication Bypass

docs.title: Burp Match and Replace
docs.text:
Burp Match and Replace can help investigate client-side response handling.

For example, in a controlled environment you might temporarily modify:

"mfaVerified": false

to:

"mfaVerified": true

This can reveal:

Client-side workflow assumptions
Hidden routes
Additional API calls

Always verify server-side access separately.

docs.title: Hidden MFA Parameters
docs.text:
Look for parameters such as:

mfa=true
mfa=false
verified=true
otpVerified=true
step=2
stage=complete
authLevel=2
challengeComplete=true

Example:

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "username": "controlled-user",
    "password": "CONTROLLED_PASSWORD",
    "mfa": true
}

Security state must not be derived from attacker-controlled values.

docs.title: Hidden Form Fields
docs.text:
Example:

<input
    type="hidden"
    name="mfaVerified"
    value="true">

Never trust:

Hidden form fields

for authentication decisions.

docs.title: MFA State in Cookies
docs.text:
Inspect cookies for values such as:

mfa=true
verified=true
auth_level=2

Example:

Cookie: session=ABC; mfa_verified=true

Test whether the server trusts an unsigned client-controlled cookie.

Expected:

Server-side verification

not:

Trust arbitrary cookie value

docs.title: MFA State in LocalStorage
docs.text:
Search:

localStorage
sessionStorage

for:

mfa
verified
authenticated
authLevel

Example:

localStorage.setItem(
    "mfaVerified",
    "true"
);

This may control the UI but must not control server-side access.

docs.title: OTP-Based MFA
docs.text:
One-time passwords are commonly delivered through:

Authenticator application
SMS
Email
Hardware token

Common formats:

6-digit numeric
8-digit numeric
Alphanumeric

docs.title: TOTP
docs.text:
Time-based One-Time Passwords are commonly generated using:

Shared Secret
+
Current Time
+
Cryptographic Function

Conceptually:

Shared Secret
      ↓
Time Window
      ↓
TOTP Algorithm
      ↓
One-Time Code

The server independently calculates acceptable codes.

docs.title: HOTP
docs.text:
HMAC-based One-Time Passwords use:

Shared Secret
+
Counter

rather than time.

The counter must remain synchronised.

docs.title: OTP Validation
docs.text:
Test:

Correct OTP
Incorrect OTP
Expired OTP
Previously used OTP
OTP from another controlled account

docs.title: Two-Account OTP Binding
docs.text:
Create:

User A
User B

Both with MFA enabled.

Generate:

OTP_A
OTP_B

Test:

OTP Session Expected OTP A User A Allow OTP A User B Deny OTP B User B Allow OTP B User A Deny Invalid OTP User A Deny

This verifies:

OTP
    ↓
Correct Account / Challenge

binding.

docs.title: MFA Challenge IDs
docs.text:
Some applications use:

challengeId
transactionId
mfaId
verificationId

Example:

{
    "challengeId": "829192",
    "code": "123456"
}

Test whether:

Challenge A

can be used with:

Session B

using two controlled accounts.

docs.title: Challenge Binding
docs.text:
Secure design:

Challenge
   ↓
Account
   ↓
Session
   ↓
Authentication Attempt

should be securely associated.

docs.title: OTP Replay
docs.text:
After successful OTP verification:

OTP
 ↓
Accepted

test whether the same OTP can be submitted again.

For TOTP, a small acceptance window may exist because of clock skew.

Whether replay is prevented within the same TOTP time step depends on the application's risk model.

For high-security applications, preventing reuse can provide additional protection.

docs.title: OTP Expiration
docs.text:
Test whether old codes remain accepted beyond the intended window.

Do not assume:

Six digits

means:

30-second TOTP

The implementation may be custom.

docs.title: Time Window
docs.text:
TOTP implementations commonly tolerate neighbouring time windows for clock drift.

Conceptually:

Previous Window
Current Window
Next Window

An excessively large acceptance window weakens security.

docs.title: OTP Brute Force
docs.text:
A six-digit numeric code has:

1,000,000

possible combinations.

MFA security therefore depends heavily on online protections.

Look for:

Attempt limits
Rate limiting
Challenge invalidation
Account lockout
Progressive delays
Risk-based controls

docs.title: Safe OTP Rate-Limit Testing
docs.text:
Start with a very small number of incorrect codes:

000001
000002
000003

using a controlled account.

Observe:

HTTP status
Response
Delay
Headers
Challenge state
Account state

Do not attempt exhaustive brute force unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Rate-Limit Scope
docs.text:
Determine whether rate limiting applies to:

IP address
Account
Session
Challenge
Device
OTP
Combination

A control based only on:

IP address

may not adequately protect the account.

docs.title: Rate-Limit Reset
docs.text:
Check carefully whether obtaining a new challenge resets:

Failed attempt counter

Example:

Challenge A
3 failures
      ↓
Request Challenge B
      ↓
Attempt counter = 0?

Use only a few attempts.

docs.title: Header-Based Rate-Limit Bypass
docs.text:
Do not automatically assume headers such as:

X-Forwarded-For
X-Real-IP
Forwarded

can bypass a rate limit.

Whether they matter depends on trusted proxy configuration.

For authorised testing, a small controlled comparison may identify whether attacker-controlled forwarding headers improperly influence rate-limit identity.

docs.title: Burp Intruder for OTP Testing
docs.text:
Burp Intruder can be useful for:

Small controlled OTP sets
Response comparison
Rate-limit verification
Challenge-binding testing

Example payload position:

POST /mfa/verify HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "code": "§000001§"
}

Use a small payload list:

000001
000002
000003
VALID_CONTROLLED_CODE

This is usually sufficient to understand basic behaviour.

docs.title: Intruder Grep Match
docs.text:
Useful response indicators:

invalid
incorrect
expired
locked
too many
success
verified

Also compare:

Status
Length
Redirect
Set-Cookie

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer is useful for:

Valid vs invalid OTP
Expired vs invalid OTP
User A vs User B
Pre-MFA vs post-MFA responses

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Repeater should be the primary tool for MFA testing.

Use it for:

Workflow bypass
Direct endpoint access
OTP replay
Challenge manipulation
Session comparison
Account binding
MFA reset
Remember-device testing

docs.title: Burp Sequencer
docs.text:
Sequencer can analyse the statistical quality of:

Recovery tokens
Trusted-device tokens
Challenge identifiers

when enough samples can be safely collected.

It is generally less useful for standard TOTP codes because those are intentionally generated from a deterministic cryptographic algorithm.

docs.title: MFA Code Leakage
docs.text:
OTP values may leak through:

API responses
Logs
Analytics
Debug endpoints
HTML
JavaScript
Push notification metadata

Example vulnerability:

{
    "message": "OTP sent",
    "debugOtp": "381922"
}

Always inspect raw responses.

docs.title: OTP Returned by API
docs.text:
Development or test functionality sometimes returns:

verificationCode
otp
debugCode

in the response.

Search JSON for:

otp
code
verification
challenge
token

docs.title: Information Disclosure
docs.text:
Error responses may reveal:

Correct account
MFA method
Phone number
Email address
Challenge state
MFA enabled status

Example:

SMS sent to +31******42

Partially masked information may still aid user enumeration.

Refer to:

Information Disclosure

docs.title: MFA Method Enumeration
docs.text:
The application may reveal:

This user uses SMS MFA

versus:

This user uses authenticator MFA

This may help attackers profile authentication controls.

Assess actual impact before reporting.

docs.title: SMS MFA
docs.text:
SMS-based MFA introduces additional risks beyond the web application itself:

SIM swapping
Telecom account compromise
Message interception
Phone number reassignment

During web application testing, focus primarily on:

Application workflow
Rate limiting
OTP binding
Recovery
Phone-number change
Session handling

Do not attempt attacks against telecommunications infrastructure.

docs.title: Email MFA
docs.text:
Email OTP security depends partly on:

Security of the email account

Application testing should focus on:

OTP entropy
Expiration
Binding
Replay
Rate limiting
Workflow

docs.title: Push MFA
docs.text:
Push authentication may use:

Approve
Deny

notifications.

Potential concerns include:

MFA fatigue
Repeated push generation
Weak number matching
Unclear transaction context

Testing should avoid generating excessive push notifications.

docs.title: MFA Fatigue
docs.text:
An attacker may repeatedly trigger:

Push Notifications

hoping the user eventually approves one.

Applications can reduce this risk with:

Number matching
Rate limiting
Transaction context
User reporting
Temporary lockout
Risk detection

During testing:

Do not spam real users.

Use only controlled devices.

docs.title: Number Matching
docs.text:
A stronger push flow may display:

42

in the login browser and require:

42

to be selected or entered on the trusted device.

This helps reduce accidental approval.

docs.title: MFA Enrollment
docs.text:
MFA setup itself is a sensitive workflow.

Typical flow:

Authenticated User
      ↓
Enable MFA
      ↓
Generate Secret
      ↓
Display QR Code
      ↓
Verify OTP
      ↓
MFA Enabled

Test:

Reauthentication
CSRF protection
Secret exposure
Activation state
Account binding
Recovery code handling

docs.title: TOTP Secret
docs.text:
The TOTP secret is effectively a long-term authentication credential.

Example representation:

otpauth://totp/Example:user@example.test?secret=...

Anyone possessing the secret may generate valid future OTPs.

Treat it like a password.

docs.title: QR Code Exposure
docs.text:
The QR code usually contains:

TOTP secret
Issuer
Account name
Algorithm
Digits
Period

Do not include real TOTP secrets in reports.

Redact them.

docs.title: MFA Enrollment Without Reauthentication
docs.text:
If an attacker steals an authenticated session, they may attempt to enroll their own MFA device.

Sensitive operations such as:

Enable MFA
Replace MFA
Add authenticator

may require recent authentication depending on the application's threat model.

docs.title: MFA Enrollment CSRF
docs.text:
If MFA setup can be triggered through CSRF, an attacker may potentially bind their own authenticator to the victim's account.

The exact exploitability depends on:

Enrollment flow
Secret generation
Verification step
Session state

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: MFA Secret Regeneration
docs.text:
Requesting the MFA setup page repeatedly may:

Reuse same secret
Generate new secret
Invalidate previous secret

Understand the lifecycle.

Secrets should not remain exposed longer than necessary.

docs.title: Activation Verification
docs.text:
MFA should not normally become active until the user demonstrates possession of the authenticator by providing a valid code.

Conceptually:

Generate Secret
      ↓
User Configures Device
      ↓
User Enters Valid OTP
      ↓
MFA Activated

docs.title: MFA Disable
docs.text:
Disabling MFA is security-sensitive.

Potential controls:

Current password
Existing MFA
Recent authentication
Recovery code
Security notification

Test whether a partially authenticated session can call:

POST /mfa/disable

docs.title: Direct MFA Disable Endpoint
docs.text:
Example:

POST /api/account/mfa/disable HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=PRE_MFA_SESSION

Expected:

Denied

docs.title: MFA Disable CSRF
docs.text:
If disabling MFA requires only an authenticated session and lacks CSRF protection:

Victim Browser
     ↓
Attacker-Controlled Request
     ↓
MFA Disabled

may be possible.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: MFA Reset
docs.text:
Applications often provide:

Lost your authenticator?

or:

Reset MFA

This recovery path must provide equivalent security.

Conceptually:

Strong MFA
   ↓
Weak MFA Reset
   ↓
Effective MFA Security = Weak

docs.title: MFA Reset Channels
docs.text:
Common recovery methods:

Email link
SMS
Recovery code
Support desk
Identity verification
Password
Alternative authenticator

Test each available route.

docs.title: Password-Only MFA Reset
docs.text:
A dangerous workflow may be:

Password
   ↓
Reset MFA
   ↓
Enroll New Device

If an attacker already has the password:

MFA provides little additional protection.

Whether this is a vulnerability depends on the intended security model.

docs.title: Password Reset Interaction
docs.text:
Password reset can unintentionally bypass MFA.

Test:

MFA-enabled controlled account
        ↓
Password Reset
        ↓
New Password
        ↓
What Happens Next?

Possible outcomes:

MFA still required
Fully authenticated automatically
MFA disabled
Trusted device created
Recovery state persists

Refer to:

Password Reset Security

docs.title: Automatic Login After Password Reset
docs.text:
A particularly important test:

Reset Password
      ↓
Application Automatically Logs User In
      ↓
MFA Required?

If not:

Password Recovery

may become an MFA bypass.

docs.title: Recovery Codes
docs.text:
Recovery codes provide an alternative authentication path.

Example:

ABCD-EFGH
JKLM-NPQR
STUV-WXYZ

They should normally be:

Random
Single use
Account bound
Stored securely
Revocable
Protected from disclosure

docs.title: Recovery Code Replay
docs.text:
Use a controlled recovery code:

Code A
  ↓
Authenticate
  ↓
Try Code A Again

Expected:

Rejected

docs.title: Recovery Code Binding
docs.text:
With two controlled accounts:

Recovery Code A
+
Account B Session

must fail.

docs.title: Recovery Code Storage
docs.text:
Recovery codes should ideally be stored similarly to passwords:

Hash(Code)

rather than plaintext where practical.

docs.title: Recovery Code Disclosure
docs.text:
Check whether codes appear in:

API responses
Page source
JavaScript
Logs
Browser storage
Analytics

after initial generation.

docs.title: Regenerating Recovery Codes
docs.text:
When new recovery codes are generated:

Old Recovery Codes

should normally become invalid.

docs.title: Downloadable Recovery Codes
docs.text:
Applications may allow:

Download Recovery Codes

Check:

Cache-Control
Content-Disposition
Authentication
Reauthentication

and whether the file contains unnecessary sensitive information.

docs.title: Remember Device
docs.text:
Many MFA implementations support:

Remember this device

or:

Trust this browser for 30 days

This usually creates a long-lived token.

Architecture:

Successful MFA
      ↓
Remember Device Selected
      ↓
Trusted Device Token
      ↓
Future Login
      ↓
MFA Skipped

That token effectively becomes:

An MFA bypass credential

and must be protected accordingly.

docs.title: Trusted Device Cookie
docs.text:
Example:

Set-Cookie: trusted_device=TOKEN

Inspect:

Entropy
Expiration
Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
Domain
Path
Account binding
Device binding
Revocation

docs.title: Predictable Trusted Device Tokens
docs.text:
Do not assume a long cookie is secure.

Check whether it contains:

User ID
Timestamp
Username
Static hash

Burp Decoder can help inspect its structure.

docs.title: Trusted Device Account Binding
docs.text:
With controlled accounts:

Trusted Token A
+
Login as User B

must not suppress User B's MFA.

docs.title: Trusted Device Token Replay
docs.text:
Copy the trusted-device cookie to:

Another browser profile

using your own controlled account.

Determine whether the token is simply a bearer credential.

This may be expected.

The important questions are:

Is it sufficiently unpredictable?

Is it securely stored?

Can it be revoked?

Is it account bound?

Does it expire?

Does password reset invalidate it?

docs.title: Trusted Device Lifetime
docs.text:
Check whether:

Trust this device for 30 days

is actually enforced server-side.

Do not rely only on cookie expiration.

docs.title: Trusted Device Revocation
docs.text:
Test whether trusted-device tokens become invalid after:

Password change
Password reset
MFA reset
MFA disable
Account security reset
Manual device revocation

depending on intended policy.

docs.title: Trusted Device and XSS
docs.text:
If a trusted-device token is accessible to JavaScript because:

HttpOnly

is missing, an XSS vulnerability may potentially steal it.

However:

HttpOnly

cannot protect against every consequence of XSS.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Scripting

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
MFA is tightly connected to session security.

Compare:

Pre-MFA Session
Post-MFA Session

Look for:

Session rotation
Authentication level
Expiration
Privilege state

Refer to:

Session Management

docs.title: Session Fixation
docs.text:
A strong design often rotates authentication state when the user's authentication level increases.

Conceptually:

Anonymous Session
       ↓
Password Authentication
       ↓
New / Upgraded Session
       ↓
MFA
       ↓
New / Upgraded Fully Authenticated Session

Exact implementation varies.

docs.title: Pre-MFA Session Reuse
docs.text:
Capture:

PRE_MFA_SESSION

Then complete MFA.

Afterwards test whether the old pre-MFA session unexpectedly gained:

Full authentication

without being properly upgraded or rotated.

docs.title: Multiple Browser Test
docs.text:
Useful workflow:

Browser A
Password Login
Stop at MFA
Save Session A

Browser B
Use Same Account
Complete MFA

Return to Session A

Question:

Did Session A become fully authenticated merely because MFA was completed elsewhere?

The expected behaviour depends on how authentication challenges are bound.

This can reveal weak:

Account-level MFA state

instead of:

Session-level authentication state

docs.title: Challenge vs Account State
docs.text:
Dangerous implementation:

User.mfa_verified = true

globally after one successful challenge.

Safer model:

Authentication Session A
    ↓
MFA verified for Session A

Other login attempts should not automatically inherit that state.

docs.title: Parallel MFA Attempts
docs.text:
Create two controlled login attempts:

Session A
Session B

Both stop at MFA.

Complete MFA in:

Session A

Then test:

Session B

Session B should not become authenticated unless the application intentionally and securely binds both attempts.

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
MFA workflows may contain race conditions.

Example:

Recovery Code
     ↓
Request A validates
Request B validates
     ↓
Both execute before code marked used

Potential result:

Single-use code used twice

Refer to:

Race Conditions

docs.title: Safe Race Testing
docs.text:
Use:

Controlled account
Controlled recovery code
Two or a very small number of requests

Burp Repeater request groups are useful.

docs.title: Burp Repeater Parallel Requests
docs.text:
For appropriate endpoints:

Create request group
      ↓
Add two controlled requests
      ↓
Send in parallel

This can test:

Recovery code reuse
Single-use challenge
MFA reset race

without high request volume.

docs.title: Turbo Intruder
docs.text:
For specialised timing-sensitive MFA testing, Turbo Intruder can assist.

Useful cases may include:

Single-use token races
Recovery-code races
Challenge state races

Official BApp Store:

https://portswigger.net/bappstore/9abaa233088242e8be252cd4ff534988

GitHub:

https://github.com/PortSwigger/turbo-intruder

Use it conservatively.

Standard MFA testing rarely requires high request rates.

docs.title: Authentication Endpoint Discovery
docs.text:
Search JavaScript and source files for:

mfa
2fa
otp
totp
hotp
authenticator
verification
challenge
recovery
backup
trusted
remember
device
factor

Example:

grep -RniE \
'mfa|2fa|otp|totp|hotp|authenticator|verification|challenge|recovery|backup.?code|trusted.?device|remember.?device' \
.

docs.title: Common MFA Endpoints
docs.text:
Look for:

/mfa
/2fa
/otp
/mfa/verify
/2fa/verify
/otp/verify
/mfa/setup
/mfa/enable
/mfa/disable
/mfa/reset
/mfa/recovery
/mfa/backup-codes
/api/mfa
/api/auth/mfa
/api/auth/verify-otp

docs.title: JavaScript Analysis
docs.text:
Search frontend JavaScript for:

mfaRequired
mfaVerified
otpRequired
otpVerified
authLevel
challengeId
trustedDevice
rememberDevice

These may reveal:

Hidden API endpoints
Workflow states
Parameter names
Alternative MFA methods

Refer to:

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: API Documentation
docs.text:
Inspect:

Swagger
OpenAPI
GraphQL
Mobile API endpoints

for MFA functionality not exposed by the normal UI.

Examples:

POST /api/mfa/disable
POST /api/mfa/reset
POST /api/mfa/verify
POST /api/mfa/recovery

docs.title: GraphQL MFA
docs.text:
GraphQL applications may expose mutations such as:

mutation {
    verifyMfa(
        code: "CONTROLLED_CODE"
    ) {
        success
    }
}

or:

mutation {
    disableMfa {
        success
    }
}

Test the same:

Authentication
Authorisation
Workflow
Binding
Rate limiting

principles.

Refer to:

GraphQL API Security

docs.title: WebSocket Authentication
docs.text:
If an application uses WebSockets after login, determine whether:

Pre-MFA session

can establish an authenticated WebSocket connection.

Refer to:

WebSocket Security

docs.title: Mobile APIs
docs.text:
Mobile applications may use a different authentication flow.

Potential issue:

Web Login
Requires MFA

Legacy Mobile API
Does Not Require MFA

All authentication channels should enforce the intended security policy.

docs.title: Legacy APIs
docs.text:
Look for:

/v1/login
/v2/login
/mobile/login
/api/legacy/auth

A legacy endpoint may accept:

Username
Password

and return a fully authenticated token without MFA.

docs.title: Alternative Login Methods
docs.text:
Test available authentication mechanisms:

Password
SSO
OAuth
Magic link
API login
Mobile login
Recovery

MFA may be enforced on one path but missing from another.

docs.title: OAuth and MFA
docs.text:
Applications using OAuth or OpenID Connect may delegate MFA to an identity provider.

Architecture:

Application
    ↓
Identity Provider
    ↓
Password
    ↓
MFA
    ↓
OIDC Token
    ↓
Application

The application may rely on claims such as:

amr
acr

to determine authentication strength.

Refer to:

OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Security

docs.title: SAML and MFA
docs.text:
Enterprise applications may use SAML assertions to communicate authentication context.

The application should not simply assume:

SSO Login
=
MFA Completed

unless that assurance is provided and validated according to the intended architecture.

docs.title: MFA Downgrade
docs.text:
Look for ways to change:

TOTP

to a weaker mechanism such as:

Email OTP
SMS
Security question

without adequate verification.

A downgrade may undermine the stronger factor.

docs.title: Alternative Factor Selection
docs.text:
Example:

Use another method

may expose:

SMS
Email
Recovery code
Push

Test each independently.

The overall security is often determined by:

Weakest Available Recovery Factor

docs.title: MFA Factor Replacement
docs.text:
Changing the registered:

Phone number
Email
Authenticator
Hardware key

is security-sensitive.

Test whether replacement requires:

Current factor
Password
Recent authentication

according to application policy.

docs.title: Phone Number Change
docs.text:
A chain may be:

Session Compromise
      ↓
Change Phone Number
      ↓
Receive MFA OTP
      ↓
Permanent Account Access

Phone number changes deserve strong verification.

docs.title: Email Change
docs.text:
If email is an MFA factor:

Change Email

can become:

Change MFA Destination

Refer to:

Business Logic Vulnerabilities

and:

Password Reset Security

docs.title: Factor Deletion
docs.text:
Applications supporting multiple factors may allow:

Delete Authenticator
Delete Hardware Key
Delete Phone

Test whether the last strong factor can be removed without appropriate verification.

docs.title: WebAuthn and Passkeys
docs.text:
WebAuthn provides phishing-resistant public-key authentication.

Conceptually:

Server Challenge
      ↓
Authenticator
      ↓
Private Key Signature
      ↓
Server Verifies Public Key

Unlike OTPs:

Private key

does not leave the authenticator.

docs.title: WebAuthn Testing Areas
docs.text:
Relevant areas include:

Registration
Authentication
Challenge randomness
Challenge expiration
Challenge binding
Origin validation
RP ID validation
Credential binding
User verification
Credential deletion
Recovery

docs.title: WebAuthn Challenge
docs.text:
The server sends a random challenge.

Example conceptual structure:

{
    "challenge": "RANDOM_VALUE",
    "rpId": "target.example"
}

The challenge should be:

Unpredictable
Short-lived
Single-use
Bound to authentication ceremony

docs.title: WebAuthn Origin
docs.text:
The server validates the origin associated with the authentication ceremony.

This helps make WebAuthn resistant to traditional phishing.

docs.title: WebAuthn RP ID
docs.text:
The relying party identifier defines the domain scope of the credential.

Incorrect RP ID validation can undermine the security model.

docs.title: Passkeys
docs.text:
Passkeys use WebAuthn credentials and may be:

Device-bound
Synced across trusted devices

depending on provider and platform.

Application testing should focus on:

Registration
Authentication
Credential management
Recovery
Account binding

rather than attempting to attack the authenticator platform itself.

docs.title: Hardware Security Keys
docs.text:
Hardware security keys commonly use:

FIDO2
WebAuthn

They provide strong phishing resistance.

However, the application's:

Recovery path
Factor removal
Alternative factor

may still weaken overall security.

docs.title: Step-Up Authentication
docs.text:
Some applications require additional authentication only for sensitive actions.

Example:

Normal Session
     ↓
View Dashboard
     ↓
Transfer Money
     ↓
Require MFA

This is:

Step-Up Authentication

docs.title: Step-Up Bypass
docs.text:
Test whether the protected action can be called directly.

Example:

POST /api/payment HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=VALID_SESSION

without completing the step-up challenge.

Expected:

Denied

docs.title: Step-Up State
docs.text:
Do not trust:

UI navigation

to enforce step-up authentication.

The backend should verify:

Recent MFA
Authentication strength
Transaction context

docs.title: Step-Up Lifetime
docs.text:
Determine how long:

Recently MFA Verified

remains valid.

Potential issue:

MFA completed months ago

still satisfies a sensitive transaction requiring recent authentication.

docs.title: Transaction Binding
docs.text:
For high-risk operations, MFA may need to be bound to:

Specific transaction
Amount
Destination
Action

rather than simply:

User authenticated with MFA at some point

docs.title: Transaction Authorisation
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Transfer €100
to Account B
      ↓
MFA Challenge
      ↓
Authorise
      ↓
Transfer €100
to Account B

A vulnerability may exist if the attacker can change:

€100

to:

€10,000

or change the destination after MFA approval.

This is broader than login MFA and relates to transaction authorisation.

docs.title: MFA and IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
MFA endpoints may contain:

userId
factorId
challengeId
deviceId

Test whether these objects are correctly authorised.

Example:

DELETE /api/mfa/factors/812

A user must not be able to delete another user's factor.

Refer to:

IDOR and BOLA

docs.title: MFA and Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Example:

{
    "code": "123456",
    "verified": true,
    "authLevel": 2
}

Unexpected fields should not alter authentication state.

Refer to:

Mass Assignment

docs.title: MFA and Race Conditions
docs.text:
Relevant targets include:

Recovery codes
One-time challenges
MFA disable
MFA enrollment
Factor replacement

Refer to:

Race Conditions

docs.title: MFA and CSRF
docs.text:
High-value MFA-related CSRF targets include:

Enable MFA
Disable MFA
Replace MFA factor
Change MFA phone number
Generate recovery codes
Trust device

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: MFA and XSS
docs.text:
XSS may potentially:

Perform actions in authenticated session
Manipulate MFA enrollment
Access non-HttpOnly tokens
Alter transaction context

MFA does not eliminate XSS risk.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Scripting

docs.title: MFA and Business Logic
docs.text:
MFA is fundamentally a stateful business workflow.

Ask:

Can steps be skipped?

Can another session inherit MFA state?

Can factors be downgraded?

Can recovery bypass the factor?

Can the target account change?

Can MFA be disabled directly?

Can trusted-device state be forged?

Can the transaction change after approval?

Refer to:

Business Logic Vulnerabilities

docs.text:

It can help identify requests that remain accessible using:

Lower-privileged
Unauthenticated
Partially authenticated

contexts.

For MFA testing, manual verification is still essential because the important distinction may be:

Password-authenticated session

versus:

Fully MFA-authenticated session

rather than simply authenticated versus unauthenticated.

docs.text:

docs.title: False Positive: UI Access
docs.text:
Seeing:

/dashboard

after modifying frontend behaviour does not prove MFA bypass.

You need:

Protected server-side data

or:

Protected server-side action

to demonstrate impact.

docs.title: False Positive: Different Session Cookie
docs.text:
A new cookie after MFA is not automatically secure.

Verify what each cookie can actually access.

docs.title: False Positive: Same Session Cookie
docs.text:
Using the same session identifier before and after MFA is not automatically vulnerable either.

The server may securely store:

Authentication Level

server-side.

Test behaviour rather than assuming.

docs.title: False Positive: OTP Reuse During Same Time Window
docs.text:
TOTP implementations may intentionally accept the same code more than once during a short validity window.

Assess:

Threat model
Transaction type
Application design

before reporting.

docs.title: False Positive: SMS MFA
docs.text:
SMS is generally considered less phishing-resistant than stronger mechanisms such as WebAuthn.

Its use alone is not necessarily an application vulnerability.

Report concrete implementation weaknesses.

docs.text:

Normal login flow
Pre-MFA session
Protected request
Protected response
MFA verification request
Post-MFA session
API request
State comparison
Screenshots
Burp history
Timeline

For OTP findings:

Challenge identifier
Small controlled attempt set
Rate-limit behaviour
Account state

Redact:

Passwords
TOTP secrets
Recovery codes
Session tokens
Personal information

where not required.

docs.title: Example Finding: MFA Workflow Bypass
docs.text:
Finding:
Multi-Factor Authentication Can Be Bypassed Through Direct Endpoint Access

Observed:
A controlled account with MFA enabled was used during testing.

After submitting the correct username and password, the application redirected the browser to the MFA verification page.

Before supplying the second authentication factor, the partially authenticated session was used to request the authenticated account endpoint directly.

The server returned the protected account data without requiring successful MFA verification.

Impact:
An attacker who obtains a user's password can bypass the configured second authentication factor and gain access to the user's account.

This defeats the primary security objective of MFA.

Recommendation:
Track MFA completion as part of server-side authentication state and enforce the required authentication level on every protected endpoint. Partially authenticated sessions must not be authorised to access normal authenticated functionality.

docs.title: Example Finding: MFA Missing from API
docs.text:
Finding:
Application API Does Not Enforce Multi-Factor Authentication

Observed:
The web interface correctly required MFA after password authentication.

However, the access token issued before MFA completion could be used directly against authenticated API endpoints.

The API returned protected user information while the account remained in the MFA-pending state.

Impact:
An attacker possessing valid account credentials can bypass MFA by interacting directly with the backend API.

Recommendation:
Enforce authentication assurance consistently at the backend API layer. Tokens issued before MFA completion should either have limited scope or be rejected by endpoints requiring fully authenticated users.

docs.title: Example Finding: Cross-Account OTP
docs.text:
Finding:
MFA Verification Codes Are Not Bound to the Target Account

Observed:
Two controlled MFA-enabled accounts were used.

A valid OTP generated for User A was submitted using the MFA authentication session belonging to User B.

The application accepted the OTP and completed authentication for User B.

Impact:
An attacker able to obtain a valid MFA code for their own account may be able to use that code to satisfy another user's MFA challenge.

This may allow bypass of multi-factor authentication and account takeover.

Recommendation:
Bind each MFA challenge and verification code to the correct account, authentication session, and authentication attempt. The server should derive the target identity from trusted authentication state rather than client-controlled parameters.

docs.title: Example Finding: MFA OTP Lacks Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Finding:
MFA Verification Endpoint Lacks Effective Rate Limiting

Observed:
Multiple incorrect OTP values were submitted against a controlled account.

The application continued accepting verification attempts without meaningful delay, challenge invalidation, temporary lockout, or other effective attempt restrictions.

Impact:
An attacker who obtains a user's password may be able to systematically guess the second authentication factor.

For short numeric OTPs, insufficient online guessing protections can significantly reduce the effective security provided by MFA.

Recommendation:
Apply strict server-side attempt limits to MFA challenges. Bind limits to the account and authentication challenge, use short challenge lifetimes, invalidate challenges after excessive failures, and implement additional abuse detection where appropriate.

docs.title: Example Finding: Password Reset Bypasses MFA
docs.text:
Finding:
Password Reset Workflow Bypasses Multi-Factor Authentication

Observed:
A controlled account with MFA enabled was used.

After completing the password reset process, the application automatically established a fully authenticated session without requiring the configured second authentication factor.

Impact:
An attacker who gains access to the password recovery channel can bypass MFA entirely.

Recommendation:
Ensure password recovery does not automatically satisfy independent MFA requirements unless the recovery process itself provides equivalent assurance. Require the configured second factor before establishing a fully authenticated session.

docs.title: Example Finding: MFA Reset Requires Only Password
docs.text:
Finding:
Multi-Factor Authentication Can Be Reset Using Only the Account Password

Observed:
A controlled account with MFA enabled was used.

After authenticating with the account password, the MFA recovery functionality allowed the existing authenticator to be removed and a new authenticator to be registered without requiring the existing factor or an equivalently strong recovery mechanism.

Impact:
An attacker who obtains the user's password can remove the protection provided by MFA and register an attacker-controlled authentication factor.

Recommendation:
Protect MFA reset and replacement using a recovery mechanism that provides assurance appropriate to the account risk. Consider requiring an existing factor, recovery code, verified recovery channel, recent strong authentication, or additional identity verification.

docs.title: Example Finding: Recovery Code Reuse
docs.text:
Finding:
MFA Recovery Codes Can Be Reused

Observed:
A recovery code generated for a controlled account was successfully used to satisfy MFA.

The same recovery code remained valid and could be used again.

Impact:
An attacker who obtains a previously used recovery code may retain persistent access to the account.

Recommendation:
Treat recovery codes as single-use authentication credentials. Invalidate each code atomically after successful use and provide users with functionality to regenerate and revoke recovery codes.

docs.title: Example Finding: MFA State Shared Across Sessions
docs.text:
Finding:
MFA Verification State Is Incorrectly Shared Across Authentication Sessions

Observed:
Two independent login sessions were created for the same controlled account.

Both sessions successfully completed password authentication and stopped at the MFA challenge.

MFA was then completed only in Session A.

Without submitting an MFA code in Session B, Session B subsequently gained access to protected application functionality.

Impact:
An attacker who knows a user's password may be able to maintain a partially authenticated session and have it automatically upgraded when the legitimate user completes MFA in another session.

Recommendation:
Bind MFA completion to the specific authentication session and challenge that successfully completed verification. Do not maintain MFA verification as a global account-level flag for independent login attempts.

docs.title: Example Finding: Trusted Device Token Not Account Bound
docs.text:
Finding:
Trusted Device Token Can Suppress MFA for Other Accounts

Observed:
A trusted-device token was generated after successfully completing MFA for controlled User A.

The same trusted-device token was subsequently supplied while authenticating as controlled User B.

The application suppressed User B's MFA challenge.

Impact:
An attacker who obtains or creates a trusted-device token may be able to bypass MFA for other accounts.

Recommendation:
Cryptographically bind trusted-device tokens to the intended account and security context. Tokens should be unpredictable, revocable, time-limited, and validated server-side.

docs.title: Reporting Titles
docs.text:
Useful titles include:

Multi-Factor Authentication Can Be Bypassed Through Direct Endpoint Access

Password Reset Workflow Bypasses Multi-Factor Authentication

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on actual impact.

Examples:

Minor MFA information disclosure
→ Low

Weak security notification
→ Low

Long trusted-device lifetime
→ Low / Medium

Missing reauthentication for MFA settings
→ Medium / High

Recovery code reuse
→ Medium / High

Weak MFA recovery
→ High

OTP brute force
→ High

Direct MFA bypass
→ High / Critical

API MFA bypass
→ High / Critical

Cross-account OTP acceptance
→ Critical / High

Legacy login bypass
→ High / Critical

The most important question is:

Can an attacker with only the first factor
obtain access that should require MFA?

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
A secure MFA implementation should enforce:

Server-side authentication state
Session-specific MFA state
Challenge binding
Account binding
Short challenge lifetimes
Attempt limits
Strong recovery
Secure trusted-device tokens
Secure enrollment
Secure factor replacement
Secure factor removal
Consistent API enforcement
Consistent alternative-login enforcement

docs.title: Enforce MFA Server-Side
docs.text:
Every protected backend endpoint should verify the required authentication assurance.

Do not rely on:

Frontend routing
JavaScript
Hidden fields
Client-controlled cookies
LocalStorage

docs.title: Separate Partial and Full Authentication
docs.text:
Model authentication explicitly:

Unauthenticated

Password Authenticated

MFA Authenticated

Each state should have clearly defined privileges.

docs.title: Restrict Pre-MFA Sessions
docs.text:
A pre-MFA session should normally be able to access only functionality required to:

Complete MFA
Cancel login
Recover MFA
Logout

It should not have general account access.

docs.title: Bind Challenges
docs.text:
Bind MFA challenges to:

Account
Authentication session
Authentication attempt
Purpose
Expiration

docs.text:
Protect OTP verification with:

Server-side rate limiting
Attempt counters
Challenge invalidation
Monitoring

docs.title: Protect Recovery
docs.text: Recovery should not be significantly weaker than MFA itself.

docs.title: Secure Trusted Devices
docs.text:
Trusted-device tokens should be:

Cryptographically random
Account bound
Time limited
Revocable
Securely stored

and protected using appropriate cookie attributes.

docs.title: Secure Enrollment
docs.text:
Protect MFA enrollment with:

Authenticated session
Recent authentication where appropriate
CSRF protection
Verification of new factor
Security notification

docs.title: Secure MFA Disable
docs.text:
Protect MFA removal using:

Strong authentication
Existing factor where appropriate
Recent authentication
CSRF protection
Security notification

docs.title: Protect Recovery Codes
docs.text:
Recovery codes should be:

Random
Single use
Securely stored
Revocable
Regeneratable

docs.title: Preserve MFA During Password Reset
docs.text:
Password reset should not automatically:

Disable MFA
Create fully authenticated session
Create trusted device

unless the recovery process intentionally provides equivalent assurance.

docs.title: Enforce MFA Across APIs
docs.text:
Apply the same policy to:

Web
REST APIs
GraphQL
WebSockets
Mobile APIs
Legacy APIs

docs.title: Protect Step-Up Authentication
docs.text:
Sensitive operations should verify:

Recent authentication
Required authentication strength
Transaction context

server-side.

docs.title: Monitor MFA Events
docs.text:
Log:

MFA success
MFA failure
MFA reset

New factor
Removed factor
Recovery code use
Trusted device creation
Repeated failures

without logging:

TOTP secrets

OTP values

MFA enabled

Web Authentication specification.
