The key question during a pentest is not simply:

"Can I send many requests?"

Instead ask:

"Can an attacker automate this security-sensitive or business-sensitive operation at a scale that defeats its intended security controls or causes meaningful abuse?"

For each sensitive action, determine:

What is being protected?

Who is performing the action?

Who or what is being targeted?

Which identifier does the limiter use?

How many attempts are allowed?

Over what period?

What happens when the threshold is reached?

What resets the counter?

Does changing session reset it?

Does changing token reset it?

Does changing endpoint reset it?

Does requesting a new challenge reset it?

Are distributed attempts considered?

Are concurrent attempts handled atomically?

Are long-term quotas present?

Is abuse detected and logged?

What actual security impact does bypassing the control create?

That produces a much stronger rate-limiting assessment than simply sending requests until a 429 appears.

docs.title: SAML Security
docs.text:
Security Assertion Markup Language, or SAML, is an XML-based standard used to exchange authentication and authorisation information between security domains.

SAML is commonly used for enterprise Single Sign-On:

User
  ↓
Service Provider
  ↓
Identity Provider
  ↓
Authentication
  ↓
SAML Assertion
  ↓
Service Provider
  ↓
Authenticated Session

Common environments include:

Enterprise SSO
Microsoft Entra ID
AD FS
Okta
Ping Identity
Shibboleth
Keycloak
Google Workspace
Salesforce
SaaS applications
Internal corporate applications

A vulnerability in a SAML implementation can potentially result in:

Authentication bypass
Account takeover
Identity impersonation
Privilege escalation
Cross-tenant access
Replay attacks
Session confusion
Information disclosure
XML-based attacks

SAML security depends heavily on:

Cryptographic signature validation
Assertion validation
Issuer validation
Audience validation
Recipient validation
Destination validation
Time validation
Replay protection
Identity mapping
Secure XML processing
Trust configuration

Authorised Security Testing

Perform SAML testing only against applications and identity providers explicitly authorised for assessment. Use dedicated test accounts and test tenants wherever possible. Avoid impersonating real users, modifying production identity-provider configuration, extracting private signing keys, disrupting SSO infrastructure, or testing assertions against accounts outside the approved scope.

docs.title: SAML Terminology
docs.text:
The three most important parties are:

Principal
Identity Provider
Service Provider

docs.title: Principal
docs.text:
The principal is usually:

The User

who wants to access an application.

docs.title: Identity Provider
docs.text:
The Identity Provider is commonly abbreviated:

IdP

The IdP authenticates the user.

Examples include:

Microsoft Entra ID
AD FS
Okta
Keycloak
Ping Identity
Shibboleth

Conceptually:

User
 ↓
IdP
 ↓
Authentication

docs.title: Service Provider
docs.text:
The Service Provider is commonly abbreviated:

SP

The SP is the application the user wants to access.

Example:

https://app.example.com

The SP trusts assertions issued by an authorised IdP.

docs.title: Basic SAML SSO Flow
docs.text:
A simplified SAML flow:

User
 ↓
Service Provider
 ↓
Authentication Required
 ↓
SAML AuthnRequest
 ↓
Identity Provider
 ↓
User Authentication
 ↓
SAML Response
 ↓
Service Provider ACS
 ↓
Assertion Validation
 ↓
Session Created

docs.title: SAML Roles
docs.text:
Conceptually:

┌─────────────┐
│    User     │
└──────┬──────┘
       ↓
┌─────────────┐
│     SP      │
│ Application │
└──────┬──────┘
       ↓
┌─────────────┐
│     IdP     │
│   Identity  │
└─────────────┘

The SP normally does not directly authenticate the user's password.

Instead:

IdP
 ↓
Authenticates User
 ↓
Issues Assertion
 ↓
SP Trusts Assertion

This makes the trust relationship critical.

docs.title: SAML Components
docs.text:
Important SAML components include:

SAMLRequest
SAMLResponse
Assertion
Issuer
Subject
NameID
Conditions
AudienceRestriction
SubjectConfirmation
AuthnStatement
AttributeStatement
Signature
RelayState

docs.title: SAMLRequest
docs.text:
A Service Provider may send:

SAMLRequest

to the Identity Provider.

The request can contain information such as:

Request ID
Issuer
Destination
Assertion Consumer Service URL
Requested authentication context

docs.title: SAMLResponse
docs.text:
After authentication, the IdP returns:

SAMLResponse

to the Service Provider.

A common HTTP POST looks conceptually like:

POST /saml/acs HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

SAMLResponse=BASE64_ENCODED_XML&RelayState=...

docs.title: Assertion Consumer Service
docs.text:
The endpoint receiving the SAML response is usually called:

Assertion Consumer Service

or:

ACS

Examples:

/saml/acs
/sso/saml
/auth/saml/callback
/login/saml2/sso/provider

The ACS is one of the most important endpoints during SAML testing.

docs.title: SAML Assertion
docs.text:
The assertion contains claims made by the IdP.

Conceptual example:

<saml:Assertion>

    <saml:Issuer>
        https://idp.example.com
    </saml:Issuer>

    <saml:Subject>

        <saml:NameID>
            test-user@example.com
        </saml:NameID>

    </saml:Subject>

    <saml:Conditions>

        <saml:AudienceRestriction>

            <saml:Audience>
                https://app.example.com
            </saml:Audience>

        </saml:AudienceRestriction>

    </saml:Conditions>

</saml:Assertion>

Real assertions normally contain additional:

Namespaces
IDs
Timestamps
Signatures
SubjectConfirmation
Authentication statements
Attributes

docs.title: NameID
docs.text:
NameID often represents the authenticated identity.

Example:

<saml:NameID>
    alice@example.com
</saml:NameID>

Possible formats include:

Email address
Persistent identifier
Transient identifier
Unspecified identifier

Do not assume NameID always contains an email address.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Assertions may contain additional user information.

Example:

<saml:Attribute
    Name="role">

    <saml:AttributeValue>
        user
    </saml:AttributeValue>

</saml:Attribute>

Other attributes may include:

email
username
firstName
lastName
role
groups
department
tenant
organisation
employeeID
entitlements

docs.title: Authentication vs Authorisation
docs.text:
SAML can transport information used for both.

Authentication:

Who is the user?

Authorisation:

What is the user allowed to do?

For example:

NameID
→ Authentication Identity

groups
→ Authorisation Input

role
→ Authorisation Input

A dangerous application may trust authorisation attributes without sufficient control.

docs.title: RelayState
docs.text:
RelayState commonly preserves application state across the SSO flow.

Example:

User requests:

/admin/reports

↓

Redirect to IdP

↓

Authenticate

↓

Return to:

/admin/reports

RelayState may carry this destination.

It should not automatically be trusted as:

Authorisation

docs.title: RelayState Security
docs.text:
Potential issues include:

Open redirect
State confusion
Cross-flow substitution
Untrusted destination handling
Session mix-up

Refer to:

Open Redirect

docs.title: SAML Bindings
docs.text:
Common SAML bindings include:

HTTP Redirect Binding
HTTP POST Binding
SOAP Binding
Artifact Binding

The Web Browser SSO profile commonly uses:

Redirect
+
POST

docs.title: HTTP Redirect Binding
docs.text:
An AuthnRequest may be sent in a URL:

https://idp.example.com/sso?
SAMLRequest=...
&RelayState=...
&SigAlg=...
&Signature=...

The SAMLRequest may be:

DEFLATE compressed
Base64 encoded
URL encoded

docs.title: HTTP POST Binding
docs.text:
The IdP commonly returns a SAMLResponse through an automatically submitted HTML form.

Conceptually:

<form
    method="POST"
    action="https://app.example.com/saml/acs">

    <input
        type="hidden"
        name="SAMLResponse"
        value="BASE64_DATA">

    <input
        type="hidden"
        name="RelayState"
        value="...">

</form>

docs.title: SAML Metadata
docs.text:
SAML environments often publish metadata.

Potential paths include:

/saml/metadata
/saml2/metadata
/metadata
/federationmetadata/2007-06/federationmetadata.xml

Metadata can contain:

Entity ID
SSO endpoints
ACS endpoints
Bindings
Signing certificates
Encryption certificates
Logout endpoints

docs.title: Metadata Example
docs.text:
Conceptually:

<EntityDescriptor
    entityID="https://idp.example.com">

    <IDPSSODescriptor>

        <KeyDescriptor use="signing">
            ...
        </KeyDescriptor>

        <SingleSignOnService
            Binding="..."
            Location="https://idp.example.com/sso"/>

    </IDPSSODescriptor>

</EntityDescriptor>

docs.title: Public Certificates
docs.text:
SAML metadata commonly contains:

Public X.509 Certificates

This is normally expected.

Do not report:

SAML signing certificate exposed

merely because the public certificate appears in metadata.

The private signing key is the secret.

docs.title: SAML Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Useful strings to search for:

SAML
SAMLRequest
SAMLResponse
RelayState
AssertionConsumerService
SingleSignOnService
NameID
EntityDescriptor
IDPSSODescriptor
SPSSODescriptor

docs.title: Application Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Look for endpoints such as:

/login/saml
/saml/login
/saml/acs
/saml2
/sso
/sso/login
/auth/saml
/auth/sso
/federation

docs.title: JavaScript Analysis
docs.text:
Search JavaScript for:

saml
sso
identityProvider
relayState
acs
metadata

Refer to:

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: SAML Testing Methodology
docs.text:
A comprehensive workflow:

Identify SAML SSO
       ↓
Map SP and IdP
       ↓
Capture Complete Login Flow
       ↓
Identify SAMLRequest
       ↓
Identify SAMLResponse
       ↓
Decode Assertion
       ↓
Map Signed Elements
       ↓
Identify Identity Attributes
       ↓
Test Signature Enforcement
       ↓
Test Assertion Integrity
       ↓
Test Audience
       ↓
Test Recipient
       ↓
Test Destination
       ↓
Test Issuer
       ↓
Test InResponseTo
       ↓
Test Time Conditions
       ↓
Test Replay
       ↓
Test Identity Mapping
       ↓
Test XML Parser Behaviour
       ↓
Test RelayState
       ↓
Test Session Creation
       ↓
Test Logout
       ↓
Assess Impact

docs.title: Test Accounts
docs.text:
Ideally use at least two controlled accounts:

Account A
Account B

If role testing is authorised:

Account A
→ Standard User

Account B
→ Different Controlled Role

This makes identity substitution testing much safer.

docs.title: Capture the Full SAML Flow
docs.text:
Use Burp Proxy while performing a normal SSO login.

Record:

Initial SP request

SP → IdP redirect

SAMLRequest

IdP authentication

SAMLResponse

ACS POST

SP session cookie

Post-login redirect

Do not begin mutation before understanding the normal flow.

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Record:

IdP hostname
SP hostname
ACS endpoint
Entity IDs
NameID
Audience
Issuer
Destination
Recipient
NotBefore
NotOnOrAfter
SessionIndex
InResponseTo
RelayState
Signature location

docs.title: Decode SAMLResponse
docs.text:
A POST-bound SAML response is often Base64 encoded.

Using Python:

python3 - <<'PY'
import base64

value = input("SAMLResponse: ").strip()

decoded = base64.b64decode(value)

print(
    decoded.decode(
        "utf-8",
        errors="replace"
    )
)
PY

docs.title: Pretty Print XML
docs.text:
If xmllint is installed:

echo 'BASE64_VALUE' |
base64 -d |
xmllint --format -

docs.title: URL-Decoded SAML
docs.text:
If copied directly from HTTP traffic, URL encoding may also need handling.

Example Python helper:

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import sys
import base64
import urllib.parse


value = sys.stdin.read().strip()

value = urllib.parse.unquote_plus(
    value
)

decoded = base64.b64decode(
    value
)

print(
    decoded.decode(
        "utf-8",
        errors="replace"
    )
)

Usage:

cat saml.txt |
python3 decode_saml.py

docs.title: Burp SAML Raider
docs.text:
SAML Raider is one of the most useful Burp extensions for SAML assessments.

It provides:

SAML message decoding
SAML message editing
Certificate management
Signature manipulation
XML Signature Wrapping helpers
XXE testing helpers
XSLT testing helpers

Official BApp Store:

https://portswigger.net/bappstore/c61cfa893bb14db4b01775554f7b802e

Install from:

Burp Suite
    ↓
Extensions
    ↓
BApp Store
    ↓
SAML Raider

docs.title: SAML Raider Workflow
docs.text:
Recommended flow:

Capture SAMLResponse
       ↓
Send to Repeater
       ↓
SAML Raider Tab
       ↓
Inspect XML
       ↓
Inspect Signature
       ↓
Inspect Certificate
       ↓
Modify Controlled Attribute
       ↓
Send
       ↓
Observe Validation

docs.title: SAML Raider Certificate Management
docs.text:
SAML Raider can help inspect and manage:

X.509 certificates
Certificate chains
Public keys
Private keys used for controlled testing

It can also generate controlled certificates for signature validation testing.

Never treat:

Ability to create a certificate

as evidence that the SP trusts it.

The vulnerability exists only if:

SP Accepts Untrusted Signature

docs.title: SAML Editor
docs.text:
The BApp Store also contains:

SAML Editor

which provides SAML decoding and encoding functionality.

SAML Raider is generally more useful for a full SAML security assessment because it additionally supports:

Signature testing
Certificate handling
XSW testing

docs.title: SAMLReQuest
docs.text:
Another BApp Store extension is:

SAMLReQuest

which assists with viewing, decoding, and modifying SAML requests and responses.

Use the tool that best fits your workflow.

Avoid installing several extensions that perform identical transformations unless needed.

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Repeater remains essential even with SAML Raider.

Use it to:

Replay assertions
Modify attributes
Modify NameID
Remove signatures
Change conditions
Change audience
Change issuer
Change recipient
Change destination
Modify RelayState

Make one controlled change at a time.

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer is useful for:

Account A assertion
vs
Account B assertion

Compare:

NameID
Attributes
Audience
Issuer
SessionIndex
Conditions
Signature structure

This helps identify which fields actually control application identity.

docs.title: Burp Decoder
docs.text:
Decoder can assist with:

Base64
URL encoding
XML

SAML Raider is normally more convenient for SAML-specific transformations.

docs.title: Signature Validation
docs.text:
One of the most important SAML security questions is:

What exactly is signed?

Possible structures include:

Signed Response

Signed Assertion

Signed Response + Signed Assertion

The application must validate the signature appropriate to its trust model.

docs.title: XML Signature
docs.text:
A SAML signature may contain:

<ds:Signature>

    <ds:SignedInfo>

        <ds:Reference
            URI="#ASSERTION_ID">

            ...

        </ds:Reference>

    </ds:SignedInfo>

    <ds:SignatureValue>
        ...
    </ds:SignatureValue>

    <ds:KeyInfo>
        ...
    </ds:KeyInfo>

</ds:Signature>

The important relationship is:

Signature
   ↓
Reference URI
   ↓
Specific XML Element ID

docs.title: Signature Enforcement Test
docs.text:
A safe initial test with your own account:

Valid Signed Assertion
        ↓
Accepted

Remove Signature
        ↓
Send Again

Expected secure behaviour:

Rejected

If accepted:

Signature Enforcement Failure

may exist.

docs.title: Modified Assertion Test
docs.text:
Using your own controlled account:

Capture Valid Assertion
        ↓
Modify Non-Sensitive Controlled Attribute
        ↓
Leave Existing Signature
        ↓
Send

Expected:

Signature Validation Fails

If the modified assertion is accepted, investigate whether the modified element is actually covered by the signature.

docs.title: Do Not Begin With Administrator
docs.text:
Do not immediately change:

role=user

to:

role=admin

against a production system.

Start with:

Controlled identity attributes

and determine whether integrity validation exists.

Privilege testing should follow only where authorised.

docs.title: Signature Exclusion
docs.text:
A vulnerable implementation may accept:

Unsigned Assertion

or:

Unsigned Response

when a signature should be mandatory.

Testing flow:

Valid Signed Message
       ↓
Remove Signature
       ↓
Replay
       ↓
Accepted?
   ↓         ↓
  NO        YES
   ↓         ↓
Secure    Investigate

docs.title: Signature Wrapping
docs.text:
XML Signature Wrapping is commonly abbreviated:

XSW

The core problem is a mismatch between:

Element Verified by Signature

and:

Element Used by Application

Conceptually:

XML Document
   ↓
Signature Validator
   ↓
Validates Assertion A

Application Logic
   ↓
Processes Assertion B

If:

Assertion A
≠
Assertion B

authentication may be compromised.

docs.title: XSW Concept
docs.text:
Example concept:

<Response>

    <Assertion ID="SIGNED">
        Signed legitimate identity
    </Assertion>

    <Assertion>
        Attacker-controlled identity
    </Assertion>

</Response>

A secure parser and SAML library must ensure the application consumes the exact assertion that was cryptographically validated.

docs.title: SAML Raider XSW Testing
docs.text:
SAML Raider supports multiple common XML Signature Wrapping transformations.

Workflow:

Controlled Valid Assertion
        ↓
SAML Raider
        ↓
Apply XSW Variant
        ↓
Send to SP
        ↓
Observe

Only perform this using:

Controlled identities

until the validation weakness is established.

docs.title: Duplicate Assertions
docs.text:
Test whether the SP handles:

Multiple Assertions

securely.

Potential parser disagreement:

Validator
→ First Assertion

Application
→ Second Assertion

or the reverse.

docs.title: Duplicate IDs
docs.text:
XML signature validation relies on element identifiers.

Duplicate IDs should be rejected.

Conceptually:

<Assertion ID="abc">

appearing multiple times can create ambiguity.

Modern SAML libraries should defend against this.

docs.title: Signature Reference Validation
docs.text:
The application should verify:

Signature reference

points to:

The exact expected SAML element

and not merely accept:

Any valid signed element somewhere in XML

docs.title: Certificate Trust
docs.text:
A critical question:

Which certificate is trusted?

Secure model:

SP Configuration
      ↓
Known IdP Certificate
      ↓
Signature Verified

Dangerous model:

SAML Message
      ↓
Embedded Certificate
      ↓
Automatically Trusted

The application must not blindly trust arbitrary signing certificates supplied by the assertion itself.

docs.title: Self-Signed Certificate Test
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Create Test Certificate
       ↓
Sign Modified Assertion
       ↓
Send

Expected:

Rejected

because:

Certificate
≠
Trusted IdP Certificate

If accepted:

Broken Certificate Trust

may permit assertion forgery.

SAML Raider can assist with this controlled test.

docs.title: KeyInfo
docs.text:
XML signatures may contain:

<ds:KeyInfo>

The application should not automatically trust attacker-supplied key information.

Trust should be anchored in:

SP-side trusted configuration

docs.title: Algorithm Validation
docs.text:
Inspect:

SignatureMethod
DigestMethod
CanonicalizationMethod

Example:

<ds:SignatureMethod
    Algorithm="..."/>

The implementation should use supported secure algorithms and reject unsafe or unexpected algorithm combinations.

docs.title: Assertion Conditions
docs.text:
Important assertion conditions include:

NotBefore
NotOnOrAfter
AudienceRestriction

Example:

<saml:Conditions
    NotBefore="2026-08-28T10:00:00Z"
    NotOnOrAfter="2026-08-28T10:05:00Z">

docs.title: NotBefore
docs.text:
The assertion should not be accepted before:

NotBefore

subject to a small configured allowance for legitimate clock skew.

docs.title: NotOnOrAfter
docs.text:
The assertion should not be accepted after:

NotOnOrAfter

Test:

Valid Assertion
     ↓
Wait Until Expired
     ↓
Replay

Expected:

Rejected

docs.title: Clock Skew
docs.text:
Small clock-skew allowances are normal.

Example concept:

1 to several minutes

depending on architecture.

Do not report a small legitimate tolerance as a vulnerability without security impact.

docs.title: Excessive Assertion Lifetime
docs.text:
An assertion valid for:

Hours

or:

Days

may increase the impact of token theft.

Prefer:

Short-lived assertions

appropriate to the SSO flow.

docs.title: Audience Validation
docs.text:
The assertion may specify:

<saml:Audience>
    https://app.example.com
</saml:Audience>

This identifies the intended relying party.

The SP should verify:

Audience
=
Expected SP

docs.title: Audience Confusion
docs.text:
Consider:

IdP
 ├── App A
 ├── App B
 └── App C

An assertion issued for:

App A

should not automatically be accepted by:

App B

docs.title: Audience Test
docs.text:
If you have two authorised test applications using the same IdP:

Authenticate to App A
        ↓
Capture Assertion
        ↓
Submit to App B ACS

Expected:

Rejected

If accepted:

Audience Validation Failure

may exist.

docs.title: Recipient Validation
docs.text:
SubjectConfirmationData may contain:

Recipient="https://app.example.com/saml/acs"

The SP should verify the assertion is intended for the current recipient.

docs.title: Destination Validation
docs.text:
The SAML Response may contain:

Destination="https://app.example.com/saml/acs"

The SP should validate this according to the protocol and implementation requirements.

docs.title: Issuer Validation
docs.text:
Example:

<saml:Issuer>
    https://idp.example.com
</saml:Issuer>

The SP must verify that the assertion was issued by:

A Trusted IdP

not merely:

Any syntactically valid issuer

docs.title: Multi-IdP Environments
docs.text:
Some applications support:

Customer A IdP
Customer B IdP
Customer C IdP

This creates additional trust-boundary complexity.

Test:

Tenant A Assertion
       ↓
Tenant B Login Endpoint

Expected:

Rejected

docs.title: Cross-Tenant SAML Confusion
docs.text:
A severe vulnerability may occur if:

Tenant A
controls its own IdP

and the application incorrectly allows:

Tenant A assertion

to authenticate:

Tenant B identity

This can create:

Cross-Tenant Account Takeover

docs.title: Identity Mapping
docs.text:
The SP must map SAML identities safely.

Possible identifiers:

NameID
email
username
employeeID
persistent ID
external ID

Ask:

Which attribute uniquely identifies the account?

docs.title: Email-Based Identity Mapping
docs.text:
A common pattern:

SAML email
    ↓
Find Local Account By Email
    ↓
Login

Potential problems include:

Unverified email claims
Case normalisation
Unicode normalisation
Aliases
Domain confusion
Duplicate identities
Tenant confusion

docs.title: Case Sensitivity
docs.text:
Test controlled variations such as:

Test.User@example.com
test.user@example.com

depending on how the application treats identity values.

The IdP and SP should agree on canonical identity mapping.

docs.title: Unicode and Normalisation
docs.text:
Identity comparison should be consistent.

Potential edge cases include:

Unicode characters
Whitespace
Trailing spaces
Normalisation differences

Do not perform large identity mutation sets against real accounts.

Use controlled identities.

docs.title: NameID vs Attribute Identity
docs.text:
Some applications may receive:

NameID = account-A

but:

email = account-B@example.com

Determine:

Which value controls authentication?

A mismatch between:

Signed / validated identity

and:

Application lookup identity

can create security issues.

docs.title: Duplicate Attributes
docs.text:
An assertion might contain:

email=A
email=B

or multiple attribute elements with the same name.

Different components may interpret duplicates differently.

Conceptually:

SAML Library
→ First Value

Application
→ Last Value

Parser disagreement can create identity confusion.

docs.title: Attribute-Based Roles
docs.text:
Example:

<saml:Attribute
    Name="role">

    <saml:AttributeValue>
        user
    </saml:AttributeValue>

</saml:Attribute>

If roles are taken directly from SAML:

IdP
 ↓
role=admin
 ↓
SP
 ↓
Administrator

then the IdP becomes part of the application's authorisation trust boundary.

docs.title: Role Manipulation
docs.text:
Using a controlled role account:

role=user

change:

role

while invalidating the existing signature.

Expected:

Assertion Rejected

If accepted:

Assertion Integrity Failure

may exist.

docs.title: Group Mapping
docs.text:
SAML may transport:

groups

Example:

Administrators
Finance
Developers
Security

Test whether:

Unknown groups
Duplicate groups
Case changes
Unexpected group values

affect authorisation.

Refer to:

Authorisation Testing

docs.title: Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Potential SAML privilege escalation paths:

Unsigned role attributes
Weak signature validation
XSW
Duplicate attributes
Cross-tenant identity mapping
Improper group mapping
Trusting user-controlled IdP claims

docs.title: InResponseTo
docs.text:
A SAML response may contain:

InResponseTo

linking it to the original authentication request.

Conceptually:

AuthnRequest ID=ABC
       ↓
SAMLResponse
InResponseTo=ABC

This helps bind:

Request

to:

Response

docs.title: InResponseTo Testing
docs.text:
Capture two controlled authentication flows:

Flow A
Flow B

Attempt to cross-use responses where appropriate.

Expected:

Response A
should correspond to
Request A

The exact requirements depend on:

SP-initiated
vs
IdP-initiated

SSO.

docs.title: SP-Initiated SSO
docs.text:
Flow:

User
 ↓
SP
 ↓
AuthnRequest
 ↓
IdP
 ↓
SAMLResponse
 ↓
SP

Here:

InResponseTo

normally has clear relevance.

docs.title: IdP-Initiated SSO
docs.text:
Flow:

User
 ↓
IdP
 ↓
Select Application
 ↓
SAMLResponse
 ↓
SP

There may be no preceding SP AuthnRequest.

IdP-initiated SSO changes some request-correlation assumptions.

docs.title: Unsolicited Responses
docs.text:
Determine whether the SP accepts:

Unsolicited SAML Responses

If not required:

Rejecting them

can reduce attack surface.

docs.title: Replay Attacks
docs.text:
A valid SAML assertion should not necessarily be reusable indefinitely.

Test:

Authenticate
 ↓
Capture SAMLResponse
 ↓
Complete Login
 ↓
Replay Same SAMLResponse

Observe whether:

New Session Created

docs.title: Replay Context
docs.text:
Replay severity depends on:

Assertion lifetime
One-time enforcement
Session state
Exposure likelihood
Authentication sensitivity

docs.title: OneTimeUse
docs.text:
SAML supports:

<saml:OneTimeUse/>

as a condition indicating the assertion should not be reused.

Not every implementation uses it.

Regardless, replay risk should be assessed according to the application's SSO design.

docs.title: Replay Cache
docs.text:
A Service Provider can maintain a cache of consumed:

Assertion IDs
Response IDs

for the relevant validity period.

Conceptually:

Assertion ID
    ↓
Seen Before?
 ↓        ↓
NO       YES
 ↓        ↓
Accept   Reject

docs.title: Session Creation
docs.text:
After successful SAML validation:

SAML Assertion
      ↓
SP
      ↓
Local Session

Inspect:

Session cookie
Session rotation
Session lifetime
Authentication level
User identity

Refer to:

Session Management

docs.title: Session Fixation
docs.text:
The SP should establish a fresh authenticated session after SSO.

Test whether:

Pre-auth session ID

remains unchanged after:

SAML authentication

where the session architecture makes this relevant.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:
SAML environments may implement:

Local logout
Single Logout

commonly abbreviated:

SLO

docs.title: Local Logout
docs.text:
Local logout may terminate:

SP Session

while leaving:

IdP Session

active.

The user may immediately SSO back in.

This is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: Single Logout
docs.text:
SAML Single Logout can coordinate logout between:

SP
IdP
Other SPs

It introduces additional:

SAMLRequest
SAMLResponse
Signature validation
Redirect handling

attack surface.

docs.title: Logout Testing
docs.text:
Verify:

SP session invalidated
Session cookie unusable
Back button behaviour
IdP session behaviour understood
Other applications unaffected unless expected

docs.title: RelayState Testing
docs.text:
Capture:

RelayState

and determine whether it contains:

Path
URL
Opaque identifier
State token

docs.title: Open Redirect via RelayState
docs.text:
Example:

RelayState=https://example.org/

If the SP redirects to arbitrary external locations after SSO:

Open Redirect

may exist.

Refer to:

Open Redirect

docs.title: RelayState Integrity
docs.text:
If RelayState carries security-sensitive state:

Account
Tenant
Destination
Transaction

determine whether modification changes server-side behaviour.

RelayState should not become an unsigned authorisation mechanism.

docs.title: SAML and CSRF
docs.text:
SSO endpoints can interact with:

Login CSRF
Session swapping
Unsolicited assertions

The application should correctly bind authentication responses to intended flows where appropriate.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: Login CSRF
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Attacker Authenticates
       ↓
Attacker SAML Response
       ↓
Victim Browser
       ↓
Victim Becomes Logged In
As Attacker

This can cause:

Data entered into attacker account
Account confusion
Sensitive activity associated with wrong identity

The practical feasibility depends on the SAML flow and SP protections.

docs.title: XML Parsing
docs.text:
SAML is XML.

Therefore the SAML processing stack may potentially expose XML-related attack surface.

Examples:

XXE
XSLT processing
XML Signature Wrapping
Parser differentials
Namespace confusion

docs.title: XXE
docs.text:
If the SAML XML parser allows unsafe external entity resolution:

XXE

may become possible.

Refer to:

XML External Entity Injection

docs.title: SAML Raider XXE Support
docs.text:
SAML Raider provides functionality to insert XXE test structures.

Use:

Controlled external interaction

or:

Non-sensitive local proof

according to the authorised scope.

Do not attempt sensitive file extraction merely to prove parser behaviour.

docs.title: SAML and XSLT
docs.text:
XML signatures can involve transformations.

Unsafe XSLT processing in vulnerable implementations can create additional risk.

SAML Raider includes functionality to assist with XSLT-related testing.

Use these tests only when:

Relevant
Authorised
Controlled

docs.title: XML Comments
docs.text:
XML parsing and identity extraction can sometimes behave unexpectedly around:

<!-- comments -->

Testing parser consistency may be useful when assessing older or custom SAML implementations.

The important security question remains:

Does the identity consumed by the application
match the identity protected by the signature?

docs.title: Namespace Handling
docs.text:
SAML relies heavily on XML namespaces.

Examples:

saml:
samlp:
ds:

Custom or inconsistent XML parsing may introduce:

Namespace confusion
Element confusion
Parser differentials

Prefer mature SAML libraries rather than custom XML processing.

docs.title: XML Canonicalisation
docs.text:
XML signatures rely on canonicalisation.

Conceptually:

XML
 ↓
Canonical Representation
 ↓
Digest
 ↓
Signature

Do not implement SAML signature validation manually.

Use established libraries.

docs.title: SAML and XXE Relationship
docs.text:
Do not report:

SAML uses XML

as:

XXE vulnerability

You must demonstrate unsafe XML parser behaviour.

docs.title: SAML and Host Header Attacks
docs.text:
SSO implementations may construct:

ACS URLs
Redirect URLs
Metadata URLs
Entity IDs

using request-derived host information.

If untrusted headers influence these values:

Host Header Attack

may become relevant.

Refer to:

HTTP Host Header Attacks

docs.title: Dynamic ACS URLs
docs.text:
Look for SAML requests where:

AssertionConsumerServiceURL

changes according to:

Host
X-Forwarded-Host
Forwarded

A manipulated callback location can have serious consequences if the IdP accepts attacker-controlled destinations.

docs.title: ACS Allow-Listing
docs.text:
Identity Providers should restrict ACS destinations to:

Pre-registered trusted endpoints

rather than trusting arbitrary URLs supplied in authentication requests.

docs.title: SAML and Open Redirects
docs.text:
Redirect handling appears in several places:

RelayState
Login endpoint
Logout endpoint
IdP discovery
Post-authentication redirect

Open redirects can support:

Phishing
SSO flow manipulation
Token leakage in badly designed implementations

docs.title: SAML and Information Disclosure
docs.text:
Potentially exposed information includes:

User email
Name
Groups
Roles
Department
Employee ID
Tenant ID
Internal domain names
IdP identifiers
Internal URLs

Some assertion attributes may be unnecessarily exposed to the SP or browser.

Apply:

Data Minimisation

docs.title: Browser Exposure
docs.text:
With HTTP POST binding, the SAMLResponse passes through the browser.

Therefore:

Browser history
Extensions
Logs
Debugging tools
Analytics
Proxy logs

may become relevant to token exposure.

Sensitive assertions should have:

Short lifetimes
Secure transport
Replay protection

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Authentication responses should not be unnecessarily cached.

Review:

Cache-Control
Pragma

on SAML endpoints where relevant.

Refer to:

HTTP Security Headers

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text:
SAML endpoints should use:

HTTPS

including:

IdP SSO
SP ACS
Metadata retrieval where appropriate
Logout endpoints

Transport security protects SAML messages while in transit.

docs.title: SAML Certificate Expiration
docs.text:
Inspect signing certificate:

Subject
Issuer
Serial
Not Before
Not After
Fingerprint
Key algorithm

Expired or soon-to-expire certificates may create:

Availability risk

rather than direct exploitation.

docs.title: Certificate Rotation
docs.text:
A secure operational design should support:

Certificate rollover

without disabling signature validation.

Dangerous workaround:

Certificate expired
      ↓
Disable signature verification

Never recommend this.

docs.title: SAML and MFA
docs.text:
The IdP may enforce:

MFA

before issuing the assertion.

The SP may receive information about:

Authentication context

or assurance level.

Refer to:

Multi-Factor Authentication Security

docs.title: AuthnContext
docs.text:
SAML can include:

AuthnContextClassRef

representing the authentication context.

An SP may require stronger authentication for:

Administrative functions
Financial actions
Sensitive operations

docs.title: Step-Up Authentication
docs.text:
Potential flow:

Normal SSO
   ↓
Standard Assurance
   ↓
Sensitive Action
   ↓
Require Stronger AuthnContext
   ↓
IdP MFA

Test whether sensitive operations genuinely require the intended authentication level.

docs.title: MFA Bypass Through SAML
docs.text:
A flawed application might:

Trust any valid SAML assertion

without checking:

Required authentication context

This could bypass intended step-up authentication.

The actual requirement must be confirmed before reporting.

docs.title: SAML and Password Reset
docs.text:
Password reset may bypass federated identity controls.

For example:

SAML-only account
     ↓
Local Password Reset
     ↓
Local Password Login

If local authentication was intended to be disabled, this can create an alternate authentication path.

Refer to:

Password Reset Security

docs.title: Alternate Authentication Paths
docs.text:
For SAML-enabled accounts test:

Normal password login
Password reset
Magic link
Mobile API
Legacy login
Basic authentication
OAuth login
Recovery flow

The strongest SAML configuration is irrelevant if:

A weaker alternative login path

bypasses it.

docs.title: SAML and OAuth
docs.text:
Applications sometimes support both:

SAML
OAuth / OIDC

Do not confuse the protocols.

SAML:

XML Assertions
Enterprise Federation

OIDC:

OAuth 2.0 Based
JWT / JSON
Identity Layer

Refer to:

OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Security

docs.title: SAML vs OIDC
docs.text:
SAML OIDC XML JSON/JWT Assertions ID Tokens IdP OpenID Provider SP Relying Party ACS Redirect URI Entity ID Client ID SAML metadata OIDC discovery

Both require strict:

Issuer
Audience
Destination
Token integrity
State

validation.

docs.title: SAML and JWT
docs.text:
Some architectures:

SAML
 ↓
Gateway
 ↓
JWT
 ↓
Application

A vulnerability may occur during:

SAML-to-JWT claim mapping

Review:

Identity
Role
Groups
Tenant
Audience

Refer to:

JSON Web Token Security

docs.title: SAML and IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
SAML establishes identity.

IDOR/BOLA concerns:

What objects that identity can access

A secure SAML login does not guarantee secure object authorisation.

Refer to:

IDOR and BOLA

docs.title: SAML and Mass Assignment
docs.text:
SAML attributes should not automatically become arbitrary writable application properties.

Dangerous conceptual flow:

SAML Attributes
      ↓
Generic Object Mapper
      ↓
Local User Object

Potential sensitive fields:

role
admin
tenant
permissions
accountType

Refer to:

Mass Assignment

docs.title: SAML and Business Logic
docs.text:
SAML may affect:

Account provisioning
Tenant assignment
Role assignment
Licence assignment
Organisation membership
Account linking

These are business logic boundaries.

Refer to:

Business Logic Vulnerabilities

docs.title: Just-In-Time Provisioning
docs.text:
Many SAML applications use:

JIT Provisioning

Flow:

Valid SAML Identity
       ↓
No Local Account
       ↓
Automatically Create Account

Test:

Which attributes control account creation?

docs.title: JIT Provisioning Risks
docs.text:
Potential issues:

Untrusted role assignment
Wrong tenant assignment
Duplicate account creation
Email collision
Domain confusion
Unexpected administrative privileges

docs.title: Account Linking
docs.text:
An application may link:

Existing local account

to:

SAML identity

using:

Email
Username
External ID

Incorrect account linking can result in account takeover.

docs.title: Domain-Based Trust
docs.text:
Dangerous pattern:

email ends with @example.com
      ↓
Automatically trusted

The application must ensure the SAML assertion originates from the correct trusted IdP and tenant.

An email suffix alone is not a secure trust boundary.

docs.title: IdP Discovery
docs.text:
Applications supporting many IdPs may ask:

Enter email

then determine:

Which IdP?

Potential issues:

Tenant enumeration
Open redirect
Incorrect IdP selection
Cross-tenant confusion
Domain takeover implications

docs.title: Tenant Enumeration
docs.text:
Responses such as:

SSO configured

versus:

No organisation found

may reveal customer organisations.

Assess whether this information is sensitive.

docs.title: SAML Fuzzing Strategy
docs.text:
Avoid random large XML fuzzing initially.

Use structured changes:

Baseline
   ↓
One Field Changed
   ↓

Suggested order:

NameID
Issuer
Audience
Recipient
Destination
NotBefore
NotOnOrAfter
InResponseTo
RelayState
Attributes
Signature

docs.text:
Test Expected Secure Result Remove signature Reject Modify signed NameID Reject Modify signed role Reject Untrusted signing certificate Reject Wrong audience Reject Wrong recipient Reject Wrong issuer Reject Expired assertion Reject Future assertion Reject Invalid InResponseTo Reject where required Replay Reject where one-time semantics apply XSW Reject Duplicate ambiguous assertions Reject Untrusted tenant assertion Reject

docs.title: Controlled SAML Mutation Script
docs.text:
For basic analysis, the following script decodes a SAML response and prints important values.

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import argparse
import base64
import urllib.parse
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET


NS = {
    "saml": (
        "urn:oasis:names:tc:"
        "SAML:2.0:assertion"
    ),
    "samlp": (
        "urn:oasis:names:tc:"
        "SAML:2.0:protocol"
    ),
}


def text(element):

    if element is None:
        return None

    return element.text


def main():

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description=(
            "Decode and inspect a SAMLResponse "
            "for authorised security testing."
        )
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "file",
        help=(
            "File containing the encoded "
            "SAMLResponse value."
        )
    )

    args = parser.parse_args()

    with open(
        args.file,
        "r",
        encoding="utf-8"
    ) as handle:

        encoded = handle.read().strip()

    encoded = urllib.parse.unquote_plus(
        encoded
    )

    xml_data = base64.b64decode(
        encoded
    )

    root = ET.fromstring(
        xml_data
    )

    print(
        ET.tostring(
            root,
            encoding="unicode"
        )
    )

    print()
    print("=" * 70)
    print("SAML SUMMARY")
    print("=" * 70)

    issuer = root.find(
        ".//saml:Issuer",
        NS
    )

    name_id = root.find(
        ".//saml:NameID",
        NS
    )

    audience = root.find(
        ".//saml:Audience",
        NS
    )

    conditions = root.find(
        ".//saml:Conditions",
        NS
    )

    confirmation = root.find(
        ".//saml:SubjectConfirmationData",
        NS
    )

    print(
        "Issuer:",
        text(issuer)
    )

    print(
        "NameID:",
        text(name_id)
    )

    print(
        "Audience:",
        text(audience)
    )

    if conditions is not None:

        print(
            "NotBefore:",
            conditions.get(
                "NotBefore"
            )
        )

        print(
            "NotOnOrAfter:",
            conditions.get(
                "NotOnOrAfter"
            )
        )

    if confirmation is not None:

        print(
            "Recipient:",
            confirmation.get(
                "Recipient"
            )
        )

        print(
            "InResponseTo:",
            confirmation.get(
                "InResponseTo"
            )
        )

    print()
    print("Attributes")
    print("-" * 70)

    for attribute in root.findall(
        ".//saml:Attribute",
        NS
    ):

        name = attribute.get(
            "Name"
        )

        values = []

        for value in attribute.findall(
            "./saml:AttributeValue",
            NS
        ):

            values.append(
                value.text
            )

        print(
            f"{name}: {values}"
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: SAML Response Comparison Script
docs.text:
A small helper can compare two controlled assertions.

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import argparse
import base64
import urllib.parse
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET


NS = {
    "saml": (
        "urn:oasis:names:tc:"
        "SAML:2.0:assertion"
    ),
}


def load(path):

    with open(
        path,
        "r",
        encoding="utf-8"
    ) as handle:

        value = handle.read().strip()

    value = urllib.parse.unquote_plus(
        value
    )

    xml_data = base64.b64decode(
        value
    )

    return ET.fromstring(
        xml_data
    )


def extract(root):

    result = {}

    issuer = root.find(
        ".//saml:Issuer",
        NS
    )

    name_id = root.find(
        ".//saml:NameID",
        NS
    )

    audience = root.find(
        ".//saml:Audience",
        NS
    )

    result["Issuer"] = (
        issuer.text
        if issuer is not None
        else None
    )

    result["NameID"] = (
        name_id.text
        if name_id is not None
        else None
    )

    result["Audience"] = (
        audience.text
        if audience is not None
        else None
    )

    for attribute in root.findall(
        ".//saml:Attribute",
        NS
    ):

        name = attribute.get(
            "Name"
        )

        values = [
            value.text
            for value in attribute.findall(
                "./saml:AttributeValue",
                NS
            )
        ]

        result[
            f"Attribute:{name}"
        ] = values

    return result


def main():

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()

    parser.add_argument(
        "first"
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "second"
    )

    args = parser.parse_args()

    first = extract(
        load(args.first)
    )

    second = extract(
        load(args.second)
    )

    keys = sorted(
        set(first)
        |
        set(second)
    )

    for key in keys:

        left = first.get(
            key
        )

        right = second.get(
            key
        )

        if left != right:

            print(
                f"[DIFF] {key}"
            )

            print(
                f"  A: {left}"
            )

            print(
                f"  B: {right}"
            )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

xmllint --format -

HTTPS

rather than necessarily a SAML flaw.

docs.title: Self-Signed IdP Certificate

A self-signed SAML signing certificate is not automatically insecure.

SAML trust can be established through:

Explicit certificate pinning / metadata

rather than a public CA hierarchy.

Stop

where possible.

Demonstrate:

Tenant boundary violation

without accessing unrelated customer data.

docs.title: Example Finding: SAML Signature Not Validated
docs.text:
Finding:
SAML Assertions Are Accepted Without Valid Signature Verification

Observed:
The Service Provider accepts SAML assertions after the cryptographic signature has been removed or invalidated.

Testing was performed using a controlled account. A valid assertion was captured, a controlled identity attribute was modified, and the original signature was removed or rendered invalid.

The Service Provider nevertheless accepted the assertion and established an authenticated session based on the modified assertion data.

Impact:
An attacker able to submit a crafted SAML response may be able to forge authentication assertions and impersonate application users.

Depending on the application's identity and role mapping, this may result in complete account takeover or privilege escalation.

Recommendation:
Require cryptographic signature validation for every SAML message or assertion relied upon for authentication. Validate the signature using the explicitly configured trusted Identity Provider certificate and ensure the exact XML element consumed by application logic is the element protected by the validated signature.

docs.title: Example Finding: XML Signature Wrapping
docs.text:
Finding:
SAML Authentication Is Vulnerable to XML Signature Wrapping

Observed:
The Service Provider validates the cryptographic signature of one SAML assertion but processes identity information from a different assertion within the same XML document.

Using a controlled account, a modified SAML response containing both the valid signed assertion and a separate controlled assertion was accepted.

The resulting session reflected identity information from the unsigned assertion.

Impact:
An attacker possessing a valid SAML assertion may be able to alter the identity or attributes processed by the Service Provider without invalidating the cryptographic signature.

This may permit user impersonation or privilege escalation.

Recommendation:
Use a mature SAML implementation that securely binds XML signature verification to assertion processing. Reject ambiguous XML documents, duplicate IDs, unexpected assertions and unsupported structures. Application logic must consume the exact assertion element whose signature has been successfully validated.

docs.title: Example Finding: Assertion Replay
docs.text:
Finding:
SAML Assertions Can Be Replayed to Create New Authenticated Sessions

Observed:
A previously consumed SAML response could be submitted again to the Assertion Consumer Service and resulted in the creation of another authenticated session.

The assertion remained reusable during its validity period and no effective replay detection was observed.

Impact:
An attacker who obtains a valid SAML assertion may be able to reuse it to create authenticated sessions for the affected account.

The practical risk depends on how assertions may be exposed and the duration of their validity.

Recommendation:
Use short assertion validity periods and implement replay protection appropriate to the SAML profile. Track consumed assertion or response identifiers for the relevant validity period and reject unexpected reuse. Consider OneTimeUse where appropriate.

docs.title: Example Finding: Audience Validation Missing
docs.text:
Finding:
SAML Assertions Issued for Another Service Provider Are Accepted

Observed:
The application accepts a valid SAML assertion whose Audience value identifies a different Service Provider.

Testing was performed between authorised test applications using the same Identity Provider.

The assertion intended for the first application was accepted by the second application and resulted in an authenticated session.

Impact:
An attacker who obtains a valid assertion for another Service Provider may be able to reuse that assertion to authenticate to the affected application.

This breaks the intended separation between SAML relying parties.

Recommendation:
Strictly validate AudienceRestriction and require the assertion audience to match the expected Service Provider identifier.

docs.title: Example Finding: Cross-Tenant Identity Confusion
docs.text:
Finding:
SAML Identity Mapping Allows Cross-Tenant Account Impersonation

Observed:
The application maps SAML users to local accounts using an identity attribute without correctly binding the assertion to the originating tenant or trusted Identity Provider.

Using two controlled tenants, an assertion originating from one tenant could be modified or configured to resolve to an account belonging to the second tenant.

Impact:
A malicious tenant administrator may be able to impersonate users belonging to another organisation.

This could result in cross-tenant account takeover and unauthorised access to customer information.

Recommendation:
Bind every federated identity to the trusted Identity Provider, tenant and immutable external subject identifier. Do not perform global account lookup solely by mutable attributes such as email address.

docs.title: Example Finding: SAML Role Manipulation
docs.text:
Finding:
Unsigned SAML Attributes Control Application Privileges

Observed:
The application derives local privileges from SAML role attributes that are not effectively protected by the validated XML signature.

Using a controlled user, the role attribute was modified and the Service Provider accepted the modified value.

Impact:
An authenticated attacker may be able to modify SAML attributes to obtain privileges that were not granted by the trusted Identity Provider.

Recommendation:
Ensure every identity and authorisation attribute consumed by the application is contained within the cryptographically validated assertion. Apply server-side allow-listing and mapping for security-sensitive roles and groups.

docs.title: Example Finding: Expired Assertion Accepted
docs.text:
Finding:
Expired SAML Assertions Remain Valid

Observed:
The Service Provider accepted a SAML assertion after the assertion's NotOnOrAfter validity condition had expired.

The replayed assertion resulted in a new authenticated session.

Impact:
The effective lifetime of stolen SAML assertions is increased, allowing authentication tokens to remain useful beyond the period intended by the Identity Provider.

Recommendation:
Validate all SAML temporal conditions, including NotBefore and NotOnOrAfter, using a small and explicitly configured clock-skew allowance. Reject assertions outside their permitted validity period.

docs.title: Reporting Titles
docs.text:
Useful titles include:

SAML Signature Validation Can Be Bypassed

Unsigned SAML Assertions Are Accepted

SAML Assertions Can Be Replayed

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity should be based on demonstrated impact.

Examples:

Metadata disclosure
→ Informational

Weak hardening
→ Low

Assertion replay with limited exposure
→ Medium

Role manipulation
→ High

Authentication bypass
→ High / Critical

Arbitrary user impersonation
→ Critical

Administrator impersonation
→ Critical

Cross-tenant account takeover
→ Critical

Do not rate based only on:

SAML Misconfiguration

Determine:

What security boundary can actually be crossed?

docs.text:

SAML Parsing
Canonicalisation
Trust Processing

from scratch.

Use:

Mature
Maintained
Well-tested

SAML libraries.

docs.title: Validate Signatures
docs.text:

Validate using:

Explicitly trusted IdP certificate

rather than arbitrary certificate information contained in the message.

docs.title: Validate the Correct Element
docs.text:
After signature verification:

Application

must consume:

The exact signed assertion

not another similarly named or positioned XML element.

docs.title: Reject Ambiguous XML
docs.text:
Reject:

Duplicate IDs
Unexpected assertions
Duplicate security-sensitive attributes
Unsupported structures
Unexpected namespaces

docs.title: Validate Issuer
docs.text:

Issuer
=
Configured Trusted IdP

docs.title: Validate Audience
docs.text:
Require:

Audience
=
Expected Service Provider

docs.title: Validate Recipient
docs.text:
Require:

Recipient
=
Expected ACS

where applicable.

docs.title: Validate Destination
docs.text:
Require the response destination to match:

Expected ACS endpoint

according to the SAML profile being used.

docs.title: Validate Time
docs.text:
Check:

NotBefore
NotOnOrAfter
SubjectConfirmationData expiry

with only the necessary clock-skew allowance.

docs.title: Short Assertion Lifetime
docs.text:
Prefer:

Minutes

rather than unnecessarily long assertion validity.

Exact lifetime depends on architecture.

docs.title: Replay Protection
docs.text:
Where appropriate:

Assertion ID
Response ID
      ↓
Replay Cache
      ↓
Previously Seen?

Reject reused assertions according to the intended protocol semantics.

docs.title: Request Correlation
docs.text:
For SP-initiated flows:

AuthnRequest ID
       ↓
InResponseTo

should be validated appropriately.

docs.title: Secure Identity Mapping
docs.text:
Prefer an immutable mapping:

Trusted IdP
+
Tenant
+
Stable Subject Identifier

rather than relying only on:

Email address

docs.title: Secure Role Mapping
docs.text:
Do not blindly map arbitrary IdP strings to internal administrative roles.

Use:

Explicit role mappings
Allow-listed groups
Tenant-specific configuration

docs.title: Protect ACS Configuration
docs.text:
ACS URLs should be:

Preconfigured
Allow-listed
HTTPS

Do not construct them from untrusted Host headers.

docs.title: Protect Metadata
docs.text:
Retrieve metadata from:

Trusted locations

and validate configuration changes.

Do not dynamically trust arbitrary metadata URLs supplied by users.

docs.title: Certificate Rotation
docs.text:
Implement controlled:

Signing certificate rollover

without disabling validation.

docs.title: Secrets Exposure
docs.text:
Secrets exposure occurs when credentials, tokens, private keys, signing material, connection strings, or other security-sensitive values are disclosed to an unauthorised party or placed where an unintended party can retrieve them.

Authorised assessment

Test only systems, repositories, storage locations, and accounts included in the engagement scope. Do not use a discovered secret against production or a third party merely to prove that it works. Redact secrets in notes and reports, preserve the original value only in an approved secure evidence store, and follow the incident process when a live credential is encountered.

The assessment model is:

Observation
    -> Candidate secret
    -> Controlled validation
    -> Minimum necessary evidence
    -> Security conclusion

A scanner match, a string that looks like a key, or a public file containing a token is a candidate, not automatically a finding. Establish what the value is, who could obtain it, whether it is active, what it authorises, and whether the exposure is in scope.

docs.title: Discovery Sources
docs.text:
Review both the application and the places that support its delivery:

  • HTML, JavaScript bundles, source maps, mobile configuration, and public API documentation
  • HTTP responses, error pages, debug output, logs, cookies, local storage, and downloaded files
  • Repository history, branches, tags, pull requests, build artifacts, package manifests, and CI logs
  • Environment files, deployment manifests, container images, IaC, backups, archives, and shared drives
  • Cloud secret stores, object storage, registries, monitoring systems, ticket attachments, and documentation
  • Server configuration, application configuration, database connection strings, and integration settings

Use targeted searches rather than only generic keyword searches. Search for provider-specific prefixes, private-key markers, JWT-like values, connection-string schemes, and references to environment variables. Tools such as secret scanners can accelerate discovery, but their output requires manual classification and validation.

Related workflows:

  • Attack Surface Analysis
  • Third-Party JavaScript
  • Information Disclosure
  • Burp Suite Testing Workflows
  • Burp Suite Extensions
  • Secret-scanning source review

docs.title: Secret Types and Classification
docs.text:
Classify a candidate by both its function and its exposure:

Type Examples Questions to answer Authentication Password, API key, session token, refresh token Which identity does it represent? Authorisation Cloud access key, service token, deploy token Which actions and scopes are allowed? Cryptographic Private key, signing key, encryption key Can it forge, decrypt, or impersonate? Integration Webhook secret, SMTP credential, database string Which external system or data does it reach? Recovery material Backup code, reset token, recovery link Is it single-use, time-limited, or already consumed? Internal configuration Debug key, test credential, feature flag secret Is it security-sensitive in this deployment?

Record classification, location, intended owner, apparent scope, exposure duration, and whether the value is unique to the environment. A public identifier, a salted hash, and a bearer token must not be reported as equivalent.

docs.title: Candidate Triage
docs.text:
For every candidate, record:

Location and access path
Value type and owning system
Environment: development, test, staging, or production
Likely principal and permissions
First and last known exposure
Rotation or expiry metadata
Whether the value is duplicated elsewhere

Common false positives include example values, test fixtures, documentation placeholders, public identifiers, revoked values, and encrypted material without an available key. A value that matches a regular expression is only an observation until these questions are answered.

docs.title: Controlled Validation
docs.text:
Prefer non-authenticating checks first:

  1. Compare the candidate with approved documentation, configuration, and ownership records.
  2. Check metadata such as expiry, revocation, last-used time, scope, and environment.
  3. Ask the system owner or use an approved read-only introspection endpoint to confirm status.
  4. If active validation is explicitly authorised, use the least privileged, least destructive request possible.
  5. Use a dedicated test identity or harmless read-only operation where available.
  6. Stop when the security conclusion is established; do not enumerate unrelated resources.

Distinguish these outcomes:

Result Establishes Does not establish Secret-shaped string found Possible exposure That it is valid or privileged Authentication succeeds The value is accepted for an identity Broad resource access or administrative rights Read-only identity metadata returned Identity and some scope Write, delete, or code-execution capability Expired or revoked value rejected The value is not currently usable That historical exposure had no impact Owner confirms rotation Current use may be prevented That copies, logs, forks, or caches are gone

Never place a discovered bearer token in a third-party scanner, public URL, issue, or chat transcript. Redact it before using screenshots or HTTP examples.

docs.title: Active, Expired, and Revoked Secrets
docs.text:
An inactive secret can still represent a security issue when it was exposed while active, remains in backups or history, or indicates a broader secret-management failure. Establish the timeline where possible:

Exposed -> Active during exposure? -> Used? -> Revoked/expired -> Copies removed? -> Retested

Do not infer inactivity solely from a failed request. Failure may indicate a wrong endpoint, missing scope, network restriction, malformed request, clock skew, or an already-invalidated session. Capture the response category without retaining the secret value and ask the owner to verify lifecycle state through an authoritative control plane.

docs.title: Evidence and Impact
docs.text:
Evidence should prove exposure and consequence without unnecessarily reproducing the credential:

  • File, URL, response, repository commit, artifact, or log location
  • Redacted excerpt showing the secret type and surrounding context
  • Identity, scope, environment, and lifecycle status
  • Timestamp and account used for any approved validation
  • Request and response metadata with values and personal data redacted
  • Owner confirmation, revocation record, or control-plane result

Explain impact as a chain:

Observed secret
    -> Unauthorised party can obtain it
    -> Secret is accepted by a scoped service
    -> Permitted action or data access
    -> Security boundary crossed

Do not claim account takeover, tenant compromise, data exposure, or code execution unless the evidence supports that conclusion. Authentication success is not equivalent to authorisation or execution.

docs.title: Remediation and Retesting
docs.text:
Immediate actions may include revocation, rotation, session invalidation, certificate replacement, removal from public locations, and review of access logs. Longer-term controls include secret managers, short-lived scoped credentials, environment separation, pre-commit and CI scanning, protected logs, least privilege, and prevention of secrets in client-delivered assets.

Retest the complete exposure path:

  1. Confirm the old value is rejected or no longer grants the previously demonstrated capability.
  2. Confirm the replacement is scoped and stored in the intended secret-management system.
  3. Remove copies from repositories, artifacts, caches, logs, and backups according to retention policy.
  4. Re-run discovery searches and inspect the deployment actually served to users.
  5. Record residual historical risk separately from current exploitability.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP Web Security Testing Guide
  • OWASP Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • GitHub Secret Scanning documentation
  • NIST SP 800-57 Recommendation for Key Management

docs.text:
