docs.title: Web Cache Deception
docs.text:
Web cache deception is a vulnerability where an attacker tricks a shared web cache into storing a sensitive, dynamically generated response that should never have been cached.

The attacker then retrieves the cached response and gains access to information belonging to another user.

The core attack pattern is:

Victim
  ↓
Attacker-Controlled URL
  ↓
Application Treats Request as Dynamic
  ↓
Sensitive User-Specific Response Generated
  ↓
Cache Treats Request as Static / Cacheable
  ↓
Response Stored
  ↓
Attacker Requests Same URL
  ↓
Cached Victim Response Returned

Potentially exposed information includes:

Account details
Email addresses
Personal information
API responses
CSRF tokens
Session-related data
Order information
Billing information
Private messages
Authentication metadata
Internal identifiers
Application secrets exposed to the user

Web cache deception usually exists because:

Origin Server

and:

Cache / CDN

interpret the same request differently.

Authorised Security Testing

Web cache deception testing can cause sensitive authenticated responses to be stored in shared infrastructure. Use controlled test accounts and unique cache-busting paths. Never intentionally cache unrelated users' information. Avoid testing sensitive production endpoints without understanding the caching behaviour and assessment scope.

docs.title: What Is a Web Cache?
docs.text:
Web caches improve performance by storing responses so they can be reused.

Common caching layers include:

Browser Cache
CDN
Reverse Proxy
Edge Cache
Application Cache
Load Balancer Cache

Architecture:

Client
  ↓
CDN / Cache
  ↓
Reverse Proxy
  ↓
Application

Without caching:

Request
  ↓
Application
  ↓
Generate Response
  ↓
Return Response

With caching:

Request
  ↓
Cache
  ↓
Cached Object Exists?
  ↓
 YES ───────────────→ Return Cached Response
  ↓
 NO
  ↓
Application
  ↓
Generate Response
  ↓
Store Response
  ↓
Return Response

docs.title: Shared vs Private Caches
docs.text:
Understanding the distinction between:

Private Cache

and:

Shared Cache

is essential.

A browser cache is normally private to a user.

A CDN or reverse proxy cache may be shared between:

Thousands

or:

Millions

of users.

The dangerous situation is:

Authenticated Response
        ↓
Shared Cache

docs.title: Dynamic vs Static Content
docs.text:
Dynamic content commonly includes:

/account
/profile
/dashboard
/orders
/messages
/settings
/api/user

Static content commonly includes:

/style.css
/app.js
/logo.png
/image.jpg
/fonts.woff2

Caches frequently treat requests ending in static-looking extensions differently.

Examples:

.css
.js
.jpg
.jpeg
.png
.gif
.svg
.ico
.woff
.woff2

This becomes important when the cache and origin disagree about what resource is being requested.

docs.title: Web Cache Deception Core Concept
docs.text:
Suppose:

https://target.example/account

returns:

Alice's private account information

and is correctly not cached.

But the application also accepts:

https://target.example/account/test.css

and internally interprets it as:

/account

while the cache sees:

/test.css

and assumes:

Static CSS File

The result may be:

Victim requests:

/account/test.css
        ↓
Origin sees:
/account
        ↓
Returns victim's account
        ↓
Cache sees:
.css
        ↓
Stores response
        ↓
Attacker requests:
/account/test.css
        ↓
Victim's cached account returned

This is web cache deception.

docs.title: The Fundamental Discrepancy
docs.text:
Web cache deception commonly requires a discrepancy between:

Cache Interpretation

and:

Origin Interpretation

For example:

Request:
/account/test.css

Cache:
"Static .css resource"

Origin:
"/account endpoint with extra path information"

That disagreement creates the vulnerability.

docs.title: Cache Rules
docs.text:
Caches may decide whether to cache based on:

File extension
Path
Directory
HTTP method
Status code
Response headers
Query parameters
Cookies
Authentication headers
Configured route

Examples of potentially cacheable patterns:

*.css
*.js
*.jpg
*.png
/static/*
/assets/*
/images/*

Never assume a specific rule exists.

Determine actual behaviour.

docs.title: Origin Routing
docs.text:
Applications may interpret URLs using:

Framework routing
Path parameters
Path info
Rewrites
Reverse proxy rules
URL normalization

For example:

/account
/account/
/account/test
/account/test.css

may all route to the same application handler.

docs.title: Example Routing Behaviour
docs.text:
Suppose:

GET /profile

returns:

Current user's profile

Try a harmless unique path:

GET /profile/am-test-001

If the same profile is returned, the application may tolerate additional path segments.

Then test:

GET /profile/am-test-001.css

using only your controlled account.

If the same sensitive response appears, investigate caching behaviour.

docs.title: Web Cache Deception vs Web Cache Poisoning
docs.text: These vulnerabilities are related but fundamentally different.

docs.title: Web Cache Poisoning
docs.text:
The attacker causes:

Attacker-Controlled Response

to be cached and served to:

Victims

Flow:

Attacker
  ↓
Manipulates Response
  ↓
Cache Stores It
  ↓
Victim Receives Poisoned Response

docs.title: Web Cache Deception
docs.text:
The attacker causes:

Victim's Sensitive Response

to be cached and later retrieved by:

Attacker

Flow:

Victim
  ↓
Sensitive Response
  ↓
Cache Stores It
  ↓
Attacker Retrieves It

docs.title: Quick Comparison
docs.text:
Vulnerability Cached Content Main Victim Web Cache Poisoning Attacker-influenced response Other users Web Cache Deception Victim-specific response User whose response was cached

Remember:

Poisoning:
Attacker → Cache → Victim

Deception:
Victim → Cache → Attacker

Refer to:

Web Cache Poisoning

docs.title: Testing Methodology
docs.text:
A structured methodology is:

Identify Sensitive Dynamic Endpoint
        ↓
Confirm Authentication Dependency
        ↓
Understand Origin Path Handling
        ↓
Add Unique Path Segment
        ↓
Compare Response
        ↓
Add Static-Looking Extension
        ↓
Inspect Cache Behaviour
        ↓
Repeat Without Authentication
        ↓
Cached Response Returned?
        ↓
Confirm With Controlled Account
        ↓
Determine Impact
        ↓
Report

docs.title: Step 1: Identify Sensitive Endpoints
docs.text:
Prioritise authenticated endpoints containing:

Personal information
Account information
Orders
Messages
Documents
Tokens
Billing information
Administrative data

Examples:

/account
/profile
/dashboard
/settings
/orders
/messages
/api/me
/api/user

docs.title: Step 2: Establish the Baseline
docs.text:
Using a controlled authenticated account:

GET /account HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=CONTROLLED_SESSION

Record:

Status
Response body
Response length
Cache headers
Age
Cookies
Cache-Control
Vary
ETag

docs.title: Step 3: Test Additional Path Segments
docs.text:
Try:

/account/am-wcd-001

If the response becomes:

404 Not Found

the route may not tolerate extra path information.

If it still returns:

Account Page

then investigate further.

docs.title: Step 4: Test Static Extensions
docs.text:
Using a unique controlled path:

/account/am-wcd-001.css

Other extensions may include:

.js
.jpg
.png
.svg
.ico

Start with one or two common extensions.

Do not blindly generate large extension lists against production infrastructure.

docs.title: Step 5: Compare the Response
docs.text:
Compare:

/account

with:

/account/am-wcd-001.css

Ask:

Same status?
Same account information?
Same page?
Same user?
Same sensitive data?

If the origin returns the same authenticated content, a prerequisite may exist.

docs.title: Step 6: Determine Whether It Is Cached
docs.text:
Request the modified URL repeatedly.

For example:

/account/am-wcd-001.css

Observe cache-related headers.

Common examples include:

Age
X-Cache
X-Cache-Hits
CF-Cache-Status
Via
X-Served-By
Cache-Control
Vary

Possible responses:

X-Cache: MISS

followed by:

X-Cache: HIT

This strongly indicates shared caching.

docs.title: Cache Header Examples
docs.text:
Example:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
Age: 27
X-Cache: HIT

Another CDN may return:

CF-Cache-Status: HIT

Another might use:

X-Cache: HIT
X-Cache-Hits: 1

Header names vary between providers.

docs.title: Age Header
docs.text:
The Age header indicates approximately how long a response has been stored in a cache.

Example:

Age: 42

If repeated requests produce:

Age: 1
Age: 5
Age: 9

this may indicate the same cached object is being served.

Do not rely on Age alone.

docs.title: Cache HIT / MISS
docs.text:
A useful sequence is:

First request:
MISS

Second request:
HIT

Third request:
HIT

This provides much stronger evidence of caching than a single response.

docs.title: Step 7: Test Without Authentication
docs.text:
After caching a controlled account response, request the exact same unique URL without the session cookie.

For example:

GET /account/am-wcd-001.css HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

If the response contains:

Controlled Account Data

then a shared-cache disclosure may exist.

This is strong evidence of web cache deception.

docs.title: Controlled Account Workflow
docs.text:
Always prefer:

Your Test Account

rather than:

Real Victim

Workflow:

Authenticated Controlled Account
        ↓
Request Unique Cache URL
        ↓
Response Cached
        ↓
Remove Authentication
        ↓
Request Same URL
        ↓
Controlled Account Data Returned?

This demonstrates the issue without exposing unrelated users.

docs.title: Unique Cache Keys
docs.text:
Use a unique identifier:

am-wcd-847291

Example:

/account/am-wcd-847291.css

This reduces the chance of interacting with an existing cache object.

docs.title: Why Unique Paths Matter
docs.text:
Testing:

/account/test.css

repeatedly may collide with:

Previous tests
Other testers
Existing cache entries

Instead use:

/account/am-wcd-20260828-847291.css

or another unique random value.

docs.title: Cache Keys
docs.text:
The cache must determine which requests correspond to the same cached object.

A simplified cache key might be:

Host
 +
Path
 +
Query String

Conceptually:

https://target.example/account/test.css

may become:

target.example|/account/test.css

But real cache keys vary considerably.

docs.title: Cache Key Components
docs.text:
Potential components include:

Scheme
Host
Path
Query parameters
HTTP method
Selected headers
Cookies

Potentially excluded inputs include:

Some headers
Some cookies
Some query parameters

The exact configuration matters.

docs.title: Cookies and Caching
docs.text:
Authenticated pages normally use:

Cookie: session=...

A safe cache should not accidentally serve one user's personalised response to another user.

However, a cache may:

Ignore Cookie

for paths classified as static.

For example:

/account/am-test.css

might be considered static despite the origin returning personalised content.

docs.title: Vary
docs.text:
The Vary header tells caches that a response varies based on specific request headers.

Example:

Vary: Accept-Encoding

Another example:

Vary: Origin

However:

Vary

is not a universal solution for sensitive authenticated content.

Highly sensitive personalised responses often should not be stored in shared caches at all.

docs.title: Cache-Control
docs.text:
Important directives include:

private
public
no-store
no-cache
max-age
s-maxage

docs.title: private
docs.text:
Example:

Cache-Control: private

indicates that the response is intended for private caches rather than shared caches.

docs.title: no-store
docs.text:
Example:

Cache-Control: no-store

instructs caches not to store the response.

This is commonly appropriate for highly sensitive responses.

docs.title: public
docs.text:
Example:

Cache-Control: public

explicitly permits shared caching.

This is dangerous for user-specific responses unless the cache key safely separates every relevant user context, which is usually unnecessary complexity for sensitive pages.

docs.title: s-maxage
docs.text:
Example:

Cache-Control: s-maxage=300

controls freshness specifically for shared caches.

A response may therefore behave differently in:

Browser Cache

versus:

CDN

docs.title: Browser Cache vs Shared Cache
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

Browser caching

with:

CDN caching

If your browser shows a cached response, this does not prove another user can retrieve it.

Strong evidence requires:

Shared cache behaviour

and preferably:

Unauthenticated or second controlled session retrieval

docs.title: Static Extension Rules
docs.text:
Caches frequently classify resources by extension.

Examples:

.css
.js
.png
.jpg
.jpeg
.gif
.svg
.ico
.woff
.woff2

A rule might conceptually say:

IF extension == .css
THEN cache

without considering that:

/account/test.css

is actually handled dynamically by the application.

docs.title: Static Directory Rules
docs.text:
Caches may also cache specific directories.

Examples:

/static/
/assets/
/images/
/scripts/
/css/

A discrepancy may occur if the origin normalises or rewrites the path differently.

Conceptually:

Cache sees:
/static/../account

Origin sees:
/account

Whether this is possible depends heavily on:

Normalization
Encoding
Reverse proxies
Framework routing

docs.title: Path Mapping Discrepancies
docs.text:
Important differences may involve:

Path delimiters
Static extensions
Encoded characters
Path traversal normalization
Semicolon handling
Matrix parameters
URL decoding
Case normalization

The general model is:

Cache Parses URL
       ↓
Interpretation A

Origin Parses URL
       ↓
Interpretation B

If:

A != B

investigate whether the difference creates a security boundary.

docs.title: Path Delimiters
docs.text:
Different systems may interpret delimiters differently.

Characters of interest can include:

;
?
#
/
.

as well as encoded forms.

For example:

/account;test.css

might be interpreted differently by:

CDN
Reverse Proxy
Application Framework

Do not assume this behaviour exists.

Test incrementally.

docs.title: Semicolon Handling
docs.text:
Some frameworks treat:

;

as a path parameter delimiter.

Conceptually:

/account;test.css

might be routed by the origin as:

/account

while another component interprets:

.css

as part of the path.

This parser discrepancy can become relevant to cache deception.

docs.title: Path Parameters
docs.text:
Some application servers support:

Matrix Parameters

or similar syntax.

Example:

/account;foo=bar

The application may ignore:

;foo=bar

while the cache considers it part of the resource path.

docs.title: Encoded Delimiters
docs.text:
Different layers may decode URLs at different stages.

For example:

%2F
%3B
%3F
%23

may be handled differently by:

CDN
Reverse Proxy
Web Server
Framework

Testing should focus on identifying real parser differences rather than blindly trying encoding combinations.

docs.title: URL Decoding
docs.text:
Architecture:

Raw Request
    ↓
CDN Decoding
    ↓
Proxy Decoding
    ↓
Framework Decoding

If one layer decodes once and another layer decodes again:

Different interpretations

can occur.

This is relevant not only to cache deception but also:

Path Traversal
Access Control
Routing Bypass
Request Smuggling

docs.title: Path Normalization
docs.text:
Normalization can include:

Removing ../
Collapsing //
Decoding characters
Removing dot segments
Resolving semicolons
Canonicalising paths

If the cache and origin normalize differently:

Cache Key

may refer to a different conceptual resource than the origin response.

docs.title: Normalization Example
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Request:
/static/../account

Cache may treat:

/static/../account

as a static route.

Origin may normalize:

/static/../account

to:

/account

and return sensitive content.

Whether this occurs depends entirely on the infrastructure.

docs.title: Cache Deception Using Static Directories
docs.text:
Suppose a CDN caches:

/static/*

and the application accepts a path that normalizes to:

/account

A discrepancy could result in:

Cache:
Static resource

Origin:
Sensitive account endpoint

This is another form of web cache deception.

docs.title: Cache Deception Through Path Confusion
docs.text:
The central question is:

Can I create a URL that the cache believes is cacheable while the application believes it references a sensitive dynamic resource?

That is the core of path-based cache deception testing.

docs.title: Origin Cache-Control Behaviour
docs.text:
Check whether the application returns:

Cache-Control: no-store

for the original endpoint.

Then compare the modified path.

Example:

/account

versus:

/account/test.css

A reverse proxy or CDN may override origin caching rules depending on configuration.

docs.title: Authentication Responses
docs.text:
Sensitive authenticated endpoints should generally not become publicly retrievable from shared caches.

Test:

Authenticated request

then:

Unauthenticated request

using the exact same unique cache URL.

docs.title: Second Controlled Account
docs.text:
An even stronger test uses:

Account A
Account B

Workflow:

Account A
 ↓
Request unique URL
 ↓
Cache Account A response
 ↓
Account B
 ↓
Request same URL
 ↓
Account A data returned?

This demonstrates:

Cross-user cache exposure

without involving real users.

docs.title: Session-Specific Data
docs.text:
Look for:

Username
Email
Account ID
CSRF token
Orders
Messages
Address
Subscription
Billing data

Use a unique controlled marker in the account profile where possible.

For example:

AM-WCD-CANARY-8472

If this appears in another controlled session:

Cross-user disclosure confirmed

docs.title: CSRF Tokens
docs.text:
Some dynamic pages contain:

CSRF tokens

If the page is cached, the token may also be exposed.

Whether this creates additional impact depends on:

Token binding
Session binding
Token validation
Action being protected

Do not automatically claim CSRF bypass merely because a token is disclosed.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: API Endpoints
docs.text:
Web cache deception is not limited to HTML.

Sensitive JSON endpoints can also be affected.

Example:

/api/me

Modified:

/api/me/test.js

If the application still returns:

{
  "email": "controlled@example.com",
  "accountId": "12345"
}

and a shared cache stores the response, sensitive API data may be exposed.

docs.title: API Testing Model
docs.text:
/api/me
   ↓
Sensitive JSON
   ↓
/api/me/am-test.js
   ↓
Same JSON?
   ↓
Cached?
   ↓
Unauthenticated retrieval?

docs.title: Content-Type
docs.text:
Do not assume the response must actually be:

text/css

for the cache to store it.

Some cache rules rely primarily on:

URL

rather than:

Content-Type

A response such as:

Content-Type: text/html

may still be cached if the CDN configuration treats the path as static.

docs.title: Status Codes
docs.text:
Caches may cache:

200
301
302
404

and other responses depending on configuration.

Do not assume only:

200 OK

is cacheable.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
Suppose an authenticated endpoint redirects:

/account
 ↓
/users/alice

If a manipulated path causes the redirect itself to be cached, this may expose:

Usernames
Internal identifiers
Sensitive paths

or create other cache-related behaviour.

docs.title: Cache Deception and Open Redirect
docs.text:
Open redirects can sometimes interact with caching.

For example:

User-specific endpoint
       ↓
Redirect
       ↓
Cache

Investigate whether:

Redirect target

or:

redirect response

becomes incorrectly cached.

Refer to:

Open Redirect

docs.title: Cache Deception and Authentication
docs.text:
A common assumption is:

Authentication required
      ↓
Response is safe

But if:

Authenticated Response
      ↓
Shared Cache

authentication may be bypassed indirectly because subsequent requests are served by the cache before reaching the application.

docs.title: Cache Before Authentication
docs.text:
Architecture:

Request
 ↓
CDN
 ↓
Cache HIT?
 ↓
YES
 ↓
Return Response

The request may never reach:

Authentication Middleware

on the origin.

This is why shared caching of private responses is dangerous.

docs.title: Cache Deception and Authorisation
docs.text:
Suppose:

/admin/profile

requires administrative privileges.

If an administrator is tricked into requesting a cacheable variant:

/admin/profile/am-test.css

and that response is stored publicly, the cache may effectively bypass:

Origin Authorisation

for subsequent requests.

Refer to:

Authorisation Testing

docs.title: High-Privilege Victims
docs.text:
Impact increases substantially when the cached response belongs to:

Administrator
Support staff
Finance staff
Privileged employee
Tenant administrator

However, during testing:

Do not target real privileged users.

Use controlled privileged test accounts where available.

docs.title: Victim Interaction
docs.text:
Many web cache deception attacks require:

Victim requests attacker-crafted URL

This may happen through:

Link
Image
Redirect
Email
Embedded resource
Social engineering

The exact user interaction requirement should be reflected in severity.

docs.title: Safe Victim Simulation
docs.text:
During testing:

Controlled Account
       ↓
Act as Victim
       ↓
Request Crafted URL

Then:

Unauthenticated Session
       ↓
Act as Attacker
       ↓
Retrieve Cached Response

This provides complete proof without involving third parties.

docs.title: Cache Busters
docs.text:
Cache busters help isolate testing.

Example:

/account/am-wcd-847291.css

or where appropriate:

/account/test.css?cb=847291

However, query strings may be:

Included in cache key
Ignored
Normalized
Removed

depending on cache configuration.

A unique path is often easier to reason about.

docs.title: Query String Behaviour
docs.text:
Determine whether:

?a=1

and:

?a=2

produce:

Different cache objects

or:

Same cache object

Do not assume.

docs.title: Cache Key Discovery
docs.text:
A useful process:

Baseline URL
 ↓
Change One Component
 ↓
Observe HIT / MISS
 ↓
Repeat
 ↓
Infer Cache Key

Components to investigate include:

Path
Query
Host
Cookies
Headers

docs.title: Detecting Shared Cache Behaviour
docs.text:
Useful indicators:

Age increases
MISS → HIT
Stable cached response
Different session receives same content
Origin changes not immediately visible
CDN-specific headers

The strongest proof remains:

Controlled Account A Response
          ↓
Returned to Account B / Unauthenticated Session

docs.title: Burp Suite
docs.text:
Burp Suite is particularly useful for cache deception testing.

Useful components:

Proxy
Repeater
Comparer
Logger
Intruder

docs.title: Burp Repeater Workflow
docs.text:
Start with:

Authenticated Request

Example:

GET /account HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=CONTROLLED_SESSION

Send to Repeater.

Then test:

/account/am-wcd-001

and:

/account/am-wcd-001.css

Compare responses.

docs.title: Repeater Tabs
docs.text:
A useful layout is:

Tab 1:
Original authenticated request

Tab 2:
Modified authenticated request

Tab 3:
Modified unauthenticated request

Tab 4:
Second controlled account

This makes comparison easier.

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Compare:

/account

with:

/account/am-test.css

Check whether:

Sensitive content

is substantially identical.

Then compare:

Authenticated modified response

with:

Unauthenticated cached response

docs.title: Burp Logger
docs.text:
Logger can help identify:

Repeated requests
Cache headers
Redirect chains
CDN behaviour
Unexpected background requests

docs.title: Burp Intruder
docs.text:
Intruder can help test a small set of path suffixes.

For example:

.css
.js
.jpg
.png
.svg
.ico

Do not use large extension lists unnecessarily.

The objective is to understand:

Cache rules

rather than brute-force every possible extension.

docs.title: Param Miner
docs.text:
Burp Suite's:

Param Miner

is primarily known for discovering:

Hidden parameters
Unkeyed headers
Cache-related behaviour

and is particularly useful for web cache poisoning research.

It can still be useful while analysing cache architecture, but web cache deception usually requires careful manual testing of:

Path interpretation
Cache rules
Origin routing

rather than only hidden parameter discovery.

PortSwigger BApp Store:

https://portswigger.net/bappstore/17d2949a985c4b7ca092728dba871943

Always manually verify automated findings.

docs.title: Burp Cache Deception Scanner
docs.text:
When performing web cache research, check the current:

BApp Store

for extensions related to:

Web Cache Deception
Web Cache Poisoning
Cache Analysis

Extensions can help identify candidate behaviour, but manual confirmation is essential because cache rules are highly application-specific.

docs.title: curl Testing
docs.text:
A baseline request:

curl -i \
  -b "session=CONTROLLED_SESSION" \
  https://target.example/account

Modified path:

curl -i \
  -b "session=CONTROLLED_SESSION" \
  https://target.example/account/am-wcd-847291.css

Repeat:

curl -i \
  -b "session=CONTROLLED_SESSION" \
  https://target.example/account/am-wcd-847291.css

Then remove authentication:

curl -i \
  https://target.example/account/am-wcd-847291.css

Look for:

Controlled account data
Age
X-Cache
CF-Cache-Status
Via
Cache-Control

docs.title: Header Inspection
docs.text:
Useful command:

curl -s -D - -o /dev/null \
  https://target.example/account/am-wcd-847291.css

This displays response headers without printing the response body.

docs.title: Browser Testing
docs.text:
Browser testing is useful when:

Authentication state
Redirects
JavaScript
Cookies
Frontend routing

affect the request.

Use:

Browser
 ↓
Burp
 ↓
Application

rather than relying only on curl.

docs.title: Browser DevTools
docs.text:
Inspect:

Network

for:

Status
Cache headers
Request URL
Redirects
Cookies
Response

Be careful with browser-local caching.

Disable browser cache during analysis where appropriate so that:

Browser Cache

does not get confused with:

Shared Cache

docs.title: CDN Identification
docs.text:
Response headers may reveal:

Cloudflare
Fastly
Akamai
CloudFront
Varnish
Cloud CDN
Azure Front Door

This can help explain caching behaviour.

However:

CDN detected

does not mean:

Web Cache Deception exists

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Caches
docs.text:
Caching may also occur at:

Nginx
Varnish
Apache
Application Gateway
Reverse Proxy

Therefore lack of an obvious CDN does not eliminate the vulnerability.

docs.title: Framework Routing
docs.text:
Different frameworks handle additional path information differently.

During testing determine whether:

/profile/test

is:

404

or:

Same as /profile

This is more important than guessing the framework's behaviour.

docs.title: Static File Middleware
docs.text:
Applications may combine:

Static File Handler
       +
Dynamic Router

Ordering can create unexpected behaviour.

For example:

CDN
 ↓
Static Rule
 ↓
Reverse Proxy
 ↓
Dynamic Framework

Each component may interpret the path differently.

docs.title: Encoded Path Testing
docs.text:
Only after basic path testing, consider whether encoded delimiters produce different behaviour.

Examples:

%2F
%3B
%2E

Use controlled paths and one mutation at a time.

Do not indiscriminately fuzz complex encoding combinations against production systems.

docs.title: Cache Deception and Path Traversal
docs.text:
Both may involve:

Path normalization

but the vulnerabilities are different.

Path traversal:

Attacker manipulates path
 ↓
Access unintended filesystem resource

Cache deception:

Attacker manipulates path
 ↓
Cache and origin disagree
 ↓
Sensitive response cached

Refer to:

Path Traversal

docs.title: Cache Deception and Request Smuggling
docs.text:
HTTP request smuggling can sometimes create cache-related effects.

However:

Request Smuggling

and:

Web Cache Deception

are separate vulnerability classes.

Request smuggling concerns disagreement about:

HTTP request boundaries

whereas cache deception typically concerns disagreement about:

URL interpretation / cacheability

Refer to:

HTTP Request Smuggling

docs.title: Cache Deception and Information Disclosure
docs.text:
The ultimate impact of web cache deception is often:

Information Disclosure

But the root cause is:

Sensitive response stored in shared cache

A report should normally describe:

Web Cache Deception

and explain the resulting data disclosure.

Refer to:

Information Disclosure

docs.title: Cache Deception and Session Management
docs.text:
If a cached page contains:

Session-related information
CSRF tokens
Account state
Authentication metadata

review whether those values can be reused.

Do not assume that disclosure automatically results in:

Session Hijacking

Validate independently.

Refer to:

Session Management

docs.title: Cache Deception and Business Logic
docs.text:
Some cached information may not appear technically sensitive but may have significant business value.

Examples:

Private pricing
Unreleased products
Internal account status
Order history
Private reports
Subscription information
Customer-specific configuration

Assess impact based on:

Application context

rather than data type alone.

docs.title: Path Testing Matrix
docs.text:
Request Purpose /account Baseline /account/AMTEST Extra path handling /account/AMTEST.css Static extension /account/AMTEST.js Static extension /account/AMTEST.jpg Static extension /account;AMTEST.css Delimiter behaviour /account/AMTEST.css?cb=123 Query/cache behaviour

Do not send every variation automatically.

Proceed based on observed behaviour.

docs.title: Cache Testing Matrix
docs.text: Request Session Expected Purpose Original endpoint Account A Baseline Unique static path Account A Populate candidate cache Same static path Account A Detect HIT Same static path None Test public exposure Same static path Account B Test cross-user exposure

docs.title: Cache Indicators Matrix
docs.text:
Header Possible Meaning Age Time stored in cache X-Cache: HIT Cache served response X-Cache: MISS Cache did not have object CF-Cache-Status Cloudflare cache status X-Cache-Hits Number of cache hits Via Intermediate proxy/cache Cache-Control Caching policy Vary Request headers affecting representation

Headers are indicators.

Actual cross-session behaviour is stronger evidence.

docs.title: Vulnerability Confirmation
docs.text:
A strong confirmation sequence is:

1. Account A requests unique modified URL

2. Sensitive Account A response is returned

3. Response indicates MISS

4. Repeat request indicates HIT

5. Remove Account A session

6. Request exact same URL

7. Account A data is still returned

This demonstrates:

Sensitive Response
      ↓
Shared Cache
      ↓
Unauthorised Retrieval

docs.title: False Positive: Browser Cache
docs.text:
If:

Same browser

returns cached content but:

Separate client

does not, the behaviour may simply involve:

Private browser caching

Do not report shared-cache deception without validating the shared aspect.

docs.title: False Positive: Public Data
docs.text:
If the cached response contains only:

Public content

there may be no meaningful confidentiality impact.

docs.title: False Positive: Dynamic Reprocessing
docs.text:
Suppose:

/account/test.css

returns Account A's data while logged in.

Then when unauthenticated it returns:

Login page

This means the application may simply be dynamically processing both requests.

If there is no shared cached response:

Web Cache Deception is not confirmed.

docs.title: False Positive: Cache Header Alone
docs.text:
A response containing:

X-Cache: HIT

does not automatically prove a vulnerability.

Static resources are supposed to be cached.

The important condition is:

Sensitive user-specific response
      ↓
Shared cache
      ↓
Unauthorised user

docs.title: Impact Analysis
docs.text:
Consider:

What data is cached?
How long?
Who can retrieve it?
Is victim interaction required?
Does the attacker need to know the exact URL?
Can privileged users be affected?
Are tokens exposed?
Can cached data enable further attacks?

docs.title: Cache Lifetime
docs.text:
A cache TTL may be:

30 seconds
5 minutes
1 hour
24 hours

Longer TTLs may increase:

Exposure window

but even short TTLs can be exploitable.

docs.title: Predictable vs Unique URLs
docs.text:
If the attacker must know:

Exact random path

that they themselves supplied to the victim, this is often practical.

For example:

/account/ATTACKER-CONTROLLED.css

The attacker already knows the URL because they created it.

docs.title: Victim Interaction Requirements
docs.text:
Document whether exploitation requires:

Victim clicking a link
Victim loading a page
Victim being authenticated
Specific user role
Specific timing

These conditions affect severity.

docs.title: High-Impact Data
docs.text:
Examples include:

API tokens
Password reset tokens
Private messages
Financial information
Personal information
Authentication secrets
Administrative data
Confidential documents

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a confirmed finding record:

Original endpoint
Crafted endpoint
Cache-busting identifier
Account used
Authentication state
First response
Second response
Cache headers
Unauthenticated response
Cross-account response
Sensitive marker
Cache lifetime
CDN / cache indicators
Reproduction steps

docs.title: Recommended Evidence Sequence
docs.text:
Capture:

1. Authenticated baseline

2. Authenticated crafted URL
   X-Cache: MISS

3. Authenticated repeat
   X-Cache: HIT

4. Unauthenticated crafted URL
   X-Cache: HIT
   Controlled account data visible

This creates a clear narrative for the report.

docs.title: Example Finding: Account Information Disclosure
docs.text:
Finding:
Web Cache Deception Allows Unauthenticated Access to Authenticated Account Information

Affected Endpoint:
GET /account

Observed:
The authenticated account endpoint returned the same user-specific response when an additional static-looking path segment was appended to the URL.

A unique controlled URL ending in .css was requested while authenticated to a test account.

The response was stored by the shared caching layer.

When the exact same URL was subsequently requested without authentication, the cached response containing the controlled account's information was returned.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to cause authenticated users to cache sensitive account responses and subsequently retrieve those responses without authentication.

Recommendation:
Prevent shared caching of authenticated and user-specific responses, ensure the cache and origin interpret request paths consistently, and configure sensitive endpoints with appropriate Cache-Control directives.

docs.title: Example Finding: API Data Exposure
docs.text:
Finding:
Web Cache Deception Exposes Authenticated API Responses

Affected Endpoint:
GET /api/me

Observed:
The application continued to process requests containing additional static-looking path segments as requests for the authenticated /api/me endpoint.

The caching layer classified the modified URL as cacheable.

After the controlled authenticated response had been cached, the same response could be retrieved without the session cookie.

Impact:
An attacker may obtain user-specific API data by causing a victim to request a specially crafted cacheable URL.

Recommendation:
Ensure authenticated API responses are never stored in shared caches and configure routing and caching rules using consistent canonical paths.

docs.title: Example Finding: Cross-User Disclosure
docs.text:
Finding:
Web Cache Deception Causes Account Data to Be Shared Between Users

Observed:
A unique cacheable URL was requested using controlled Account A.

The response contained the marker:

AM-WCD-ACCOUNT-A-8472

When the same URL was subsequently requested using controlled Account B, the response still contained Account A's marker.

Impact:
Sensitive user-specific responses may be disclosed across account boundaries through the shared caching layer.

Recommendation:
Disable shared caching for personalised responses and ensure user-specific resources cannot be classified as static cacheable objects through manipulated request paths.

docs.title: Example Finding: Administrative Data
docs.text:
Finding:
Web Cache Deception Allows Exposure of Privileged Administrative Responses

Observed:
Using a controlled administrative test account, an administrative endpoint accepted an additional static-looking path component.

The resulting user-specific administrative response was stored by the shared cache and could subsequently be retrieved from an unauthenticated session.

Impact:
An attacker capable of causing a privileged user to request a crafted URL may obtain sensitive administrative information.

Recommendation:
Prevent caching of authenticated administrative responses, strictly canonicalise application routes and ensure cache rules cannot classify dynamic administrative paths as static resources.

docs.title: Reporting Titles
docs.text:
Useful titles include:

Web Cache Deception Allows Disclosure of Authenticated Account Data

Web Cache Deception Exposes User-Specific API Responses

Shared Cache Stores Sensitive Authenticated Responses

Web Cache Deception Allows Cross-User Information Disclosure

Web Cache Deception Exposes Administrative Information

Path Interpretation Discrepancy Causes Sensitive Responses to Be Cached

Avoid vague titles such as:

Caching Issue

CDN Problem

Cache Vulnerability

Describe the demonstrated impact.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

Data sensitivity
Victim interaction
Authentication requirements
Victim privileges
Cache lifetime
Exploit reliability
Additional attack chains

For example:

Minor account preference disclosure

may be:

Low / Medium

while:

Private account data

may be:

Medium / High

and:

Administrative secrets
Authentication tokens
Highly sensitive personal data

may justify:

High / Critical

depending on the actual impact.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
The fundamental objective is:

Sensitive Dynamic Response
        ↓
Never Enter Shared Cache

docs.title: Do Not Cache Authenticated Responses
docs.text:
Where appropriate:

Cache-Control: private, no-store

can help ensure sensitive responses are not stored by shared caches.

The exact policy should be selected based on application requirements.

docs.title: Use private
docs.text:
For personalised responses:

Cache-Control: private

indicates that shared caches should not store the response.

docs.title: Use no-store
docs.text:
For highly sensitive content:

Cache-Control: no-store

prevents storage.

Examples may include:

Account pages
Sensitive API responses
Authentication flows
Financial information
Private messages

depending on application requirements.

docs.title: Do Not Rely Only on File Extensions
docs.text:
Dangerous cache rule:

IF URL ends in .css
THEN cache

without considering:

Origin response
Authentication
Route
Cache-Control

Prefer cache policies based on explicitly defined static resources.

docs.title: Explicit Static Paths
docs.text:
Instead of broadly caching:

*.css

consider caching known static locations:

/assets/
/static/
/dist/

provided those paths cannot route to dynamic sensitive handlers.

docs.title: Consistent Path Interpretation
docs.text:
Ensure:

CDN
Reverse Proxy
Web Server
Framework

agree on:

Path
Normalization
Encoding
Delimiters

Avoid architectures where:

Cache sees static file

while:

Origin sees sensitive route

docs.title: Reject Unexpected Path Information
docs.text:
If the valid route is:

/account

then:

/account/random.css

should normally return:

404

rather than silently resolving to:

/account

unless the routing behaviour is intentionally required.

docs.title: Canonical Routing
docs.text:
Prefer deterministic routing:

/account

rather than allowing arbitrary suffixes such as:

/account/*

for endpoints that do not require them.

docs.title: Respect Origin Cache-Control
docs.text:
CDNs and reverse proxies should respect appropriate origin caching directives.

Avoid configurations that override:

private
no-store

for dynamic authenticated responses.

docs.title: Separate Static and Dynamic Content
docs.text:
A cleaner architecture is:

/static/*
    ↓
Static Content
    ↓
Cache

/account/*
    ↓
Dynamic Content
    ↓
No Shared Cache

rather than attempting to infer content type from arbitrary extensions across the entire application.

docs.title: Authentication-Aware Cache Configuration
docs.text:
If a request contains:

Authorization

or:

Session Cookie

carefully evaluate whether the response should be stored at all.

Do not assume cache keys based on authentication data are sufficient for every sensitive use case.

docs.title: Avoid Sensitive Data in Cacheable Responses
docs.text:
Where possible:

Public Cacheable Shell
       +
Authenticated API Request

may be safer than caching a complete personalised HTML page.

For example:

Public SPA HTML
      ↓
Browser
      ↓
Authenticated API
      ↓
Private Data

provided the authenticated API itself is securely configured.

docs.title: Purge Existing Cached Responses
docs.text:
After remediation, purge potentially affected objects from:

CDN
Reverse proxy
Edge caches
Application caches

Fixing the origin alone may not remove previously cached sensitive responses.

docs.title: Test After Remediation
docs.text:
Repeat:

/account

then:

/account/unique.css

Expected behaviour should be one of:

404

or:

Dynamic response not stored in shared cache

Then verify:

Unauthenticated request

cannot retrieve authenticated data.

docs.title: Remediation Validation
docs.text:
Checklist:

[ ] Sensitive endpoint not shared-cacheable
[ ] Unexpected suffix rejected
[ ] Static extension does not change cacheability
[ ] Cache respects Cache-Control
[ ] Authenticated response not publicly retrievable
[ ] Account A response not returned to Account B
[ ] Encoded path variants behave consistently
[ ] CDN and origin normalize paths consistently
[ ] Previously cached objects purged

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
[ ] Identify CDN / cache
[ ] Identify cache headers
[ ] Identify sensitive authenticated endpoints
[ ] Identify static cache rules
[ ] Identify tolerated path suffixes
[ ] Identify framework routing behaviour

docs.title: Baseline
docs.text:
[ ] Request original endpoint
[ ] Record response
[ ] Record Cache-Control
[ ] Record Age
[ ] Record X-Cache
[ ] Record Vary
[ ] Record cookies

docs.title: Path Testing
docs.text:
[ ] Add unique path segment
[ ] Add static extension
[ ] Test delimiter behaviour
[ ] Test normalization where justified
[ ] Test encoded delimiter where justified

docs.title: Cache Confirmation
docs.text:

[ ] Repeat request HIT
[ ] Age behaviour observed
[ ] Exact URL reused
[ ] Browser cache excluded

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
[ ] Controlled Account A
[ ] Unauthenticated retrieval
[ ] Controlled Account B
[ ] Cross-user response comparison

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
[ ] Username
[ ] Email
[ ] Account ID
[ ] Personal information
[ ] Orders
[ ] Messages
[ ] Tokens
[ ] Administrative data

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
[ ] HTML endpoints
[ ] JSON endpoints
[ ] Account APIs
[ ] User APIs
[ ] Administrative APIs

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
[ ] Sensitive data exposure

docs.text:

docs.title: Decision Tree
docs.text:
SENSITIVE AUTHENTICATED ENDPOINT
            ↓
       ADD UNIQUE PATH
            ↓
SAME SENSITIVE RESPONSE?
      ↓             ↓
     NO            YES
      ↓             ↓
  DIFFERENT      ADD STATIC
  TECHNIQUE      EXTENSION
                    ↓
            SAME RESPONSE?
              ↓          ↓
             NO         YES
              ↓          ↓
          REASSESS     REPEAT
                         ↓
                   CACHE HIT?
                    ↓      ↓
                   NO     YES
                    ↓      ↓
                REASSESS  REMOVE
                          SESSION
                            ↓
                    SAME RESPONSE?
                       ↓       ↓
                      NO      YES
                       ↓       ↓
                  NOT YET   CONTROLLED
                  CONFIRMED  ACCOUNT B
                               ↓

                        NO      YES

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
WEB CACHE DECEPTION

Sensitive Dynamic Endpoint
        ↓

Origin Still Returns Sensitive Content?
        ↓
YES

YES

        ↓

Remember:

Cache Poisoning:

Attacker Response
      ↓
Cache

Victim


Cache Deception:

Victim Response

Cache

docs.title: Recommended Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Burp Proxy

Find Sensitive Endpoint
     ↓
Burp Repeater

Baseline
     ↓
Unique Path
     ↓
Static Extension
     ↓
Check Cache Headers

Repeat Request

MISS → HIT?

Remove Session

Document Minimal Proof

docs.title: Final Web Cache Deception Testing Model
docs.text:
CLIENT
                                ↓
                         AUTHENTICATED USER
                                ↓
                    SENSITIVE DYNAMIC ENDPOINT
                                ↓
                         /account
                                ↓
                       MODIFY REQUEST PATH
                                ↓
                /account/AM-WCD-8472.css
                                ↓
                 ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
                 ↓                             ↓
               CACHE                         ORIGIN
                 ↓                             ↓
          SEES STATIC .CSS              SEES /account
                 ↓                             ↓
          CACHEABLE RESOURCE           AUTHENTICATED PAGE
                 ↓                             ↓
                 └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                                ↓
                       SENSITIVE RESPONSE
                                ↓
                          SHARED CACHE
                                ↓
                       ┌────────┴────────┐
                       ↓                 ↓
                 ORIGINAL USER       ATTACKER /
                                      OTHER USER
                                           ↓
                                  SAME CACHED RESPONSE
                                           ↓
                                   SENSITIVE DATA
                                      DISCLOSED
                                           ↓
                                  WEB CACHE DECEPTION

The key principle is:

Web cache deception is fundamentally an interpretation discrepancy. The cache believes it is storing a safe, reusable resource while the origin believes it is serving sensitive dynamic content. During testing, first determine how the origin handles modified paths, then determine how the caching layer classifies those same paths, and finally prove the security impact using controlled accounts and unique cache keys. A cache header or unusual route alone is not enough: the strongest evidence is a sensitive response generated in one controlled authenticated context and subsequently returned from a shared cache to another context that was not authorised to receive it.

docs.title: Web Cache Poisoning
docs.text:
Web cache poisoning occurs when an attacker causes a web cache to store a malicious or unintended response that is subsequently served to other users.

Modern web applications frequently use caching infrastructure to improve:

Performance
Scalability
Latency
Availability
Bandwidth usage

Caching may occur at several layers:

Browser
CDN
Reverse proxy
Load balancer
Application cache
API gateway
Web server

A simplified architecture is:

User
  ↓
CDN / Cache
  ↓
Reverse Proxy
  ↓
Application

Normally:

Request
   ↓
Cache Lookup
   ↓
Cached Response Exists?
   ↓
YES → Return Cached Response

If no cached response exists:

Request
   ↓
Cache MISS
   ↓
Application Processes Request
   ↓
Response Generated
   ↓
Response Stored
   ↓
Returned to User

Web cache poisoning becomes possible when attacker-controlled input affects the generated response but is not correctly represented in the cache key.

Conceptually:

Attacker-Controlled Input
          ↓
Application Response
          ↓
Cache Stores Response
          ↓
Victim Requests Normal Page
          ↓
Victim Receives Poisoned Response

Potential impact includes:

Cross-Site Scripting
Malicious redirects
Content manipulation
JavaScript injection
Sensitive information exposure
Denial of service
Authentication workflow manipulation
Cache-based persistence

Authorised Security Testing

Web cache poisoning can affect users other than the tester. During authorised assessments, use unique cache busters and controlled resources wherever possible. Do not deliberately poison shared production cache entries unless this has been explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Why Web Cache Poisoning Happens
docs.text:
A cache needs to determine whether two requests should receive the same cached response.

It does this using a:

Cache Key

A simplified cache key might consist of:

Scheme
Host
Path
Query string

For example:

https://target.example/products?id=123

may produce a cache key based on:

target.example
/products
id=123

However, the application may also use other request data when generating the response.

Examples include:

X-Forwarded-Host
X-Forwarded-Proto
X-Original-URL
X-Rewrite-URL
User-Agent
Accept-Language
Origin
Cookies
Custom headers

If the application uses a value that the cache ignores, a discrepancy can occur.

docs.title: Cache Key vs Application Input
docs.text:
This is the central concept behind web cache poisoning.

Consider:

CACHE KEY

Host
Path
Query

while the application also processes:

X-Forwarded-Host

If X-Forwarded-Host changes the response but is not part of the cache key:

Attacker Request
       ↓
X-Forwarded-Host: controlled.example
       ↓
Application Generates:
https://controlled.example/script.js
       ↓
Cache Stores Response Under:
target.example/
       ↓
Victim Requests:
target.example/
       ↓
Victim Receives Cached Response
Containing controlled.example

The unkeyed input has poisoned the cached response.

docs.title: Cache Keys
docs.text:
A cache key determines which requests are considered equivalent.

Potential components include:

Host
Path
Query parameters
HTTP method
Selected headers
Cookies
Protocol

The exact implementation depends on:

CDN
Reverse proxy
Application
Cache configuration
Framework

docs.title: Keyed Inputs
docs.text:
A keyed input contributes to the cache key.

Suppose:

Accept-Language

is part of the cache key.

Then:

Accept-Language: en

and:

Accept-Language: nl

may produce separate cache entries.

This prevents one language variant from being incorrectly served to another.

docs.title: Unkeyed Inputs
docs.text:
An unkeyed input affects the application response but does not contribute to the cache key.

This is particularly interesting during testing.

Conceptually:

Unkeyed Input
     ↓
Changes Response
     ↓
Cache Does Not Distinguish Request
     ↓
Modified Response Stored
     ↓
Normal Users Receive It

docs.title: Cache Poisoning Testing Methodology
docs.text:
A structured workflow is:

Identify Cache
      ↓
Find Cacheable Endpoint
      ↓
Understand Cache Key
      ↓
Add Unique Cache Buster
      ↓
Identify Unkeyed Inputs
      ↓
Determine Whether Input Changes Response
      ↓
Determine Whether Response Is Cached
      ↓
Request Same Cache Key Without Input
      ↓
Check Whether Modification Persists
      ↓
Assess Security Impact
      ↓
Report

The most important rule during testing is:

Avoid contaminating cache entries used by real users.

docs.title: Identifying a Cache
docs.text:
Look for response headers such as:

Age
X-Cache
X-Cache-Hits
CF-Cache-Status
Via
X-Served-By
X-Proxy-Cache
X-Varnish
Cache-Control
Expires
ETag
Last-Modified

Examples:

X-Cache: HIT

X-Cache: MISS

CF-Cache-Status: HIT

Age: 120

These can indicate caching behaviour.

docs.title: Cache HIT
docs.text:
A response may contain:

X-Cache: HIT

This generally indicates that the response was served from cache.

Another common indicator is:

Age: 42

If the value increases between requests, this may indicate that the same cached object is being reused.

docs.title: Cache MISS
docs.text:
A response may contain:

X-Cache: MISS

This generally indicates that the cache did not contain a suitable response and forwarded the request to the backend.

A common sequence is:

First Request
    ↓
MISS

Second Request
    ↓
HIT

docs.title: Dynamic Cache Headers
docs.text:
Different providers use different terminology.

Examples include:

HIT
MISS
BYPASS
DYNAMIC
STALE
REVALIDATED
EXPIRED

Do not rely on header names alone.

Confirm behaviour through repeated requests.

docs.title: Establishing a Baseline
docs.text:
Start with a normal request.

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Record:

Status code
Response length
Cache headers
Age
ETag
Response body
Response time

Send the same request again.

Compare the responses.

docs.title: Cache Busters
docs.text:
A cache buster creates a unique cache entry for testing.

For example:

/?cb=AM123456

Request:

GET /?cb=AM123456 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

This reduces the chance that testing affects ordinary visitors.

docs.title: Why Cache Busters Matter
docs.text:
Without a cache buster:

Tester
  ↓
Poisons /
  ↓
Cache
  ↓
Real Users Request /
  ↓
Poisoned Response

With a unique cache buster:

Tester
  ↓
Poisons /?cb=AM123456
  ↓
Unique Cache Entry
  ↓
Normal Users Request /
  ↓
Different Cache Entry

This is much safer during authorised testing.

docs.title: Verify That the Cache Buster Is Keyed
docs.text:
Do not assume every query parameter is part of the cache key.

Some caches ignore selected parameters.

Test:

/?cb=AM111

and:

/?cb=AM222

Compare:

Cache status
Age
Response

Ensure the values create separate cache entries before relying on them for safe testing.

docs.title: Query Parameter Handling
docs.text:
Caches may:

Include all query parameters
Ignore all query parameters
Ignore selected parameters
Normalise parameter order
Remove tracking parameters
Sort parameters

For example:

utm_source
utm_campaign
fbclid
gclid

may sometimes be excluded from cache keys.

Do not use a parameter as a safety cache buster until you know it is keyed.

docs.title: Unkeyed Header Discovery
docs.text:
Headers are common candidates for unkeyed inputs.

Interesting examples include:

X-Forwarded-Host
X-Forwarded-Proto
X-Forwarded-Port
X-Original-URL
X-Rewrite-URL
X-Host
X-Forwarded-Server
X-HTTP-Host-Override
X-Original-Host
Forwarded
Origin
Referer
Accept-Language
User-Agent

Not every application processes these headers.

Test systematically.

docs.title: Harmless Canary Testing
docs.text:
Start with a unique harmless marker.

Example:

X-Forwarded-Host: am-cache-001.example

Then search the response for:

am-cache-001.example

Possible reflection points include:

Absolute URLs
Canonical links
Script sources
Stylesheets
Redirects
Forms
API responses
Meta tags

docs.title: Example Reflection
docs.text:
Request:

GET /?cb=AM001 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
X-Forwarded-Host: am-cache-001.example

Response:

<script src="https://am-cache-001.example/resources/app.js"></script>

This establishes that:

X-Forwarded-Host

influences the response.

The next question is:

Is this response cached without X-Forwarded-Host being part of the cache key?

docs.title: Confirming Unkeyed Behaviour
docs.text:
Send:

GET /?cb=AM001 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
X-Forwarded-Host: am-cache-001.example

Then request:

GET /?cb=AM001 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

If the second response still contains:

am-cache-001.example

and is served from cache, this suggests that the header affected the cached response while not being represented in the cache key.

docs.title: Safe Proof Model
docs.text:
The safest useful proof is often:

Unique Cache Buster
       ↓
Harmless Canary
       ↓
Response Modified
       ↓
Response Cached
       ↓
Same Cache-Busted URL Requested Normally
       ↓
Canary Still Present

This demonstrates cache poisoning without injecting executable content.

docs.title: X-Forwarded-Host
docs.text:
One of the most important headers to test is:

X-Forwarded-Host:

Example:

GET /?cb=AM002 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
X-Forwarded-Host: controlled.example

Look for:

https://controlled.example/

in the response.

docs.title: Why X-Forwarded-Host Is Interesting
docs.text:
Applications behind proxies may use:

X-Forwarded-Host

to reconstruct the original hostname.

Architecture:

Browser
   ↓
CDN
   ↓
Reverse Proxy
   ↓
Application

The application may assume:

X-Forwarded-Host

was generated by trusted infrastructure.

If external clients can supply it directly, this assumption may fail.

docs.title: X-Forwarded-Proto
docs.text:
Another interesting header is:

X-Forwarded-Proto:

For example:

X-Forwarded-Proto: http

or:

X-Forwarded-Proto: https

It may affect:

Absolute URLs
Redirects
Canonical links
Cookie behaviour
Generated resources

docs.title: Forwarded
docs.text:
The standard Forwarded header may contain:

Forwarded: host=controlled.example;proto=https

Test whether it affects the response.

Support varies significantly between applications and proxies.

docs.title: X-Original-URL and X-Rewrite-URL
docs.text:
Some infrastructure supports headers such as:

X-Original-URL:

and:

X-Rewrite-URL:

These may affect request routing.

For example:

X-Original-URL: /admin

If such a header changes the generated response and the cache does not account for it, interesting discrepancies may arise.

docs.title: Web Cache Poisoning via Host Headers
docs.text:
Host-related headers are a classic cache poisoning source.

Refer to:

HTTP Host Header Attacks

A common pattern is:

Unkeyed Host Override
        ↓
Application Generates Absolute URL
        ↓
Modified URL Enters Response
        ↓
Response Cached
        ↓
Victims Receive Modified URL

docs.title: Cache Poisoning to Cross-Site Scripting
docs.text:
Cache poisoning can sometimes amplify another weakness into stored-like XSS behaviour.

Conceptually:

Unkeyed Input
      ↓
Unsafe Reflection
      ↓
Executable Browser Context
      ↓
Response Cached
      ↓
Victims Receive Cached Response
      ↓
JavaScript Executes

The important chain is:

Input controllable
+
Unsafe rendering
+
Cache persistence
+
Victim delivery

Refer to:

Cross-Site Scripting

docs.title: Harmless Validation Before XSS
docs.text:
During authorised testing, first establish:

Reflection
Cache persistence
Cache key behaviour

using a harmless canary.

You usually do not need executable JavaScript to prove the cache poisoning primitive.

Only escalate testing when necessary and authorised.

docs.title: Cache Poisoning via Cookies
docs.text:
Cookies may influence application responses.

Example:

Cookie: language=en

If:

Cookie affects response

but:

Cookie is not part of cache key

one user's response variant may potentially be served to another.

This can create:

Content poisoning
Information disclosure
User-specific cache leakage

docs.title: User-Specific Data and Caching
docs.text:
A particularly serious configuration error occurs when authenticated or personalised responses are cached incorrectly.

Conceptually:

User A
  ↓
Authenticated Request
  ↓
Personalised Response
  ↓
Shared Cache
  ↓
User B
  ↓
Receives User A Response

This may be better classified as:

Sensitive data exposure through shared caching

rather than classic attacker-controlled cache poisoning.

Report the root cause accurately.

docs.title: Cache-Control
docs.text:
Review:

Cache-Control:

Common directives include:

public
private
no-cache
no-store
max-age
s-maxage
must-revalidate

docs.title: public
docs.text:
Example:

Cache-Control: public

indicates that a response may be stored by shared caches.

This can be dangerous for personalised responses.

docs.title: private
docs.text:
Example:

Cache-Control: private

indicates that the response is intended for private caches rather than shared caches.

This is commonly appropriate for personalised content.

docs.title: no-store
docs.text:
Example:

Cache-Control: no-store

instructs caches not to store the response.

This is useful for highly sensitive responses.

docs.title: s-maxage
docs.text:
Example:

Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=300

s-maxage applies to shared caches.

It may override other caching lifetimes for CDN or proxy caching.

docs.title: Vary
docs.text:
The Vary response header tells caches that selected request headers influence the response.

Example:

Vary: Accept-Encoding

or:

Vary: Origin

Conceptually:

Response Changes Based On Origin
        ↓
Vary: Origin
        ↓
Cache Stores Separate Variants

docs.title: Missing Vary
docs.text:
Suppose an application changes its response based on:

Origin:

but does not return:

Vary: Origin

Depending on the caching architecture, responses intended for one origin may potentially be reused for another.

This can interact with:

CORS
Cache poisoning
Cross-origin data exposure

Refer to:

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

docs.title: Cache Poisoning and CORS
docs.text:
Consider:

Request Origin
       ↓
Application Reflects Origin
       ↓
CORS Response
       ↓
Shared Cache

If:

Origin

is not correctly represented in caching behaviour, an incorrect CORS policy may be cached.

Always inspect:

Vary: Origin

when CORS responses are dynamically generated.

docs.title: Cache Poisoning and Redirects
docs.text:
A cacheable redirect influenced by unkeyed input can potentially poison navigation.

Example:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://controlled.example/login

If cached:

Victim
 ↓
Requests Normal URL
 ↓
Receives Cached Redirect
 ↓
Sent Elsewhere

This can overlap with:

Open Redirect
Host Header Attacks
Cache Poisoning

Refer to:

Open Redirect

docs.title: Cache Poisoning and Error Responses
docs.text:
Some caches store error responses.

Potential status codes include:

301
302
404
403
500

depending on configuration.

This can sometimes produce:

Cache poisoning
Denial of service
Unexpected content persistence

docs.title: Cacheable 404 Responses
docs.text:
Suppose attacker-controlled input changes how a route is resolved and causes:

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

If the response is cached under a legitimate cache key, users may receive the cached error instead of valid content.

This can create a denial-of-service style cache poisoning condition.

docs.title: Cache Poisoning Denial of Service
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Attacker Request
       ↓
Application Generates Error
       ↓
Error Cached
       ↓
Victims Request Resource
       ↓
Cached Error Returned

The impact depends on:

Cache duration
Affected endpoint
Number of users
Ease of reproduction
Recovery behaviour

docs.title: Web Cache Poisoning vs Web Cache Deception
docs.text:
These are different vulnerability classes.

Web cache poisoning:

Attacker influences cached response
        ↓
Victims receive attacker-influenced response

Web cache deception:

Victim requests sensitive content
        ↓
Cache incorrectly stores it
        ↓
Attacker retrieves victim's cached response

Simplified:

POISONING
Attacker → Cache → Victim

DECEPTION
Victim → Cache → Attacker

A separate page should cover:

Web Cache Deception

docs.title: Cache Poisoning vs Stored XSS
docs.text:
Stored XSS:

Payload
 ↓
Application Storage
 ↓
Victim

Cache poisoning:

Payload
 ↓
Cache
 ↓
Victim

The persistence layer is different.

A cache-poisoning vulnerability can nevertheless deliver an XSS payload.

docs.title: Cache Poisoning vs HTTP Request Smuggling
docs.text:
HTTP request smuggling exploits disagreement about HTTP message boundaries.

Web cache poisoning exploits disagreement about:

Which request inputs define a cached response?

The two can sometimes interact, but they are separate vulnerability classes.

Refer to:

HTTP Request Smuggling

docs.title: Cache Key Normalisation
docs.text:
Caches may normalise request components before constructing a key.

Examples include:

Lowercasing hostnames
Normalising paths
Removing default ports
Sorting query parameters
Ignoring selected parameters
Decoding characters
Normalising duplicate slashes

The backend may perform different normalisation.

This can create discrepancies.

docs.title: Path Normalisation
docs.text:
Consider:

/products
/products/
/products//

Different components may treat these as:

Same resource

or:

Different resources

Differences between cache and origin behaviour can create unusual cache conditions.

docs.title: Query Parameter Normalisation
docs.text:
Consider:

?a=1&b=2

and:

?b=2&a=1

The application may consider these equivalent.

The cache may or may not.

Understanding parameter handling can help map the cache key.

docs.title: Parameter Exclusion
docs.text:
Some caching systems deliberately ignore selected query parameters.

Examples may include analytics parameters:

utm_source
utm_medium
utm_campaign

If an ignored parameter affects the application response, it may become an unkeyed input.

docs.title: Parameter Cloaking
docs.text:
Applications, proxies and caches may parse query strings differently.

For example, different components may disagree about:

Parameter delimiters
Duplicate parameters
Encoded delimiters
Parameter ordering

Conceptually:

Cache Parser
    ↓
Interpretation A

Application Parser
    ↓
Interpretation B

Parser discrepancies can sometimes allow attacker-controlled values to affect the backend response without changing the cache key as expected.

docs.title: Duplicate Parameters
docs.text:
Example:

?lang=en&lang=nl

Possible interpretations:

First value
Last value
Array
Combined value

If the cache and application disagree, cache behaviour may become interesting.

This overlaps with HTTP parameter pollution.

docs.title: Cache Key Injection
docs.text:
Some advanced cache vulnerabilities involve manipulating data used to construct the cache key itself.

The general question is:

Can attacker-controlled input cause the cache to confuse one request with another?

This can occur through:

Header parsing differences
Delimiter handling
URL normalisation
Port handling
Host parsing
Query parsing

Such issues require careful manual analysis.

docs.title: Fat GET Requests
docs.text:
Some applications accept request bodies with GET requests.

Example:

GET /search HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 9

q=example

A cache may key the response based on:

GET + path

while ignoring the body.

If the application uses the body, this can create a cache discrepancy.

docs.title: GET Body Model
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Cache
 ↓
GET /search
 ↓
Ignores Body

Application
 ↓
GET /search
 ↓
Processes Body

If the body changes the response:

Unkeyed Request Body

may exist.

Support for GET bodies varies significantly.

docs.title: HTTP Method Handling
docs.text:
Check whether:

GET
HEAD
POST

share unexpected cache behaviour.

For example, some caches may derive HEAD responses from cached GET responses.

Method handling should be understood before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: HEAD Requests
docs.text:
A HEAD request normally returns the same headers as GET without the body.

Test whether:

HEAD

and:

GET

interact unexpectedly with cache state.

docs.title: Static vs Dynamic Resources
docs.text:
Caching is common for:

JavaScript
CSS
Images
Fonts
Static HTML
Public API responses

Dynamic resources may also be cached.

Prioritise endpoints where:

Response is cacheable
+
Input influences response

docs.title: JavaScript Resources
docs.text:
Cached JavaScript is particularly sensitive.

Conceptually:

Attacker Influences JavaScript Response
          ↓
Response Cached
          ↓
Victims Load Script
          ↓
Attacker-Controlled JavaScript Executes

This can have widespread impact.

Use harmless markers during initial testing.

docs.title: CSS Resources
docs.text:
CSS may also be cached for long periods.

While CSS injection usually has different impact from JavaScript injection, poisoning shared static resources can still affect many users.

docs.title: API Caching
docs.text:
APIs may be cached by:

CDNs
API gateways
Reverse proxies
Application caches

Check whether responses vary by:

Authentication
Tenant
Role
Language
Origin
Device
Region

and whether those dimensions are represented correctly in the cache key.

docs.title: Authentication and Caching
docs.text:
Authenticated responses deserve special attention.

Ask:

Is this response cacheable?

Is the session cookie part of the cache key?

Is Authorization part of the cache key?

Does the CDN bypass authenticated requests?

Can a private response enter a shared cache?

docs.title: Authorization Header
docs.text:
Requests may contain:

Authorization: Bearer TOKEN

Shared caches should handle authenticated responses carefully.

A serious issue can occur if:

Response varies by Authorization

but:

Shared cache does not distinguish users

docs.title: Cookie Handling
docs.text:
Caches often bypass requests containing session cookies.

But this is configuration-dependent.

Check rather than assume.

Example:

Cookie: session=CONTROLLED_SESSION

Observe whether:

X-Cache: HIT

still appears.

docs.title: Tenant Caching
docs.text:
Multi-tenant applications may vary responses by:

Host
Tenant header
Cookie
JWT claim
Query parameter

If tenant identity is not properly represented in caching:

Tenant A
   ↓
Cached Response
   ↓
Tenant B

cross-tenant data exposure may occur.

docs.title: Language Caching
docs.text:
Applications may vary by:

Accept-Language:

or:

?lang=

If the cache ignores the relevant value, users may receive another language variant.

This is usually low impact unless the variation also contains security-sensitive or user-specific data.

docs.title: Device-Specific Caching
docs.text:
Applications may vary responses based on:

User-Agent
Device headers
Mobile detection

If the cache does not account for this, different clients may receive incorrect variants.

Again, impact depends on the content difference.

docs.title: Geographical Caching
docs.text:
CDNs may vary responses based on:

Country
Region
Edge location
IP-derived information

Custom geographic headers should generally be trusted only when generated by known infrastructure.

docs.title: Cache Poisoning via X-Forwarded-Scheme
docs.text:
Some frameworks recognise headers that influence URL scheme.

Examples may include:

X-Forwarded-Proto
X-Forwarded-Scheme
X-Forwarded-SSL

If these change response content and are unkeyed, investigate further.

docs.title: Cache Poisoning via Port
docs.text:
Generated URLs may use:

X-Forwarded-Port

or the port included in:

Host:

Example:

https://target.example:8443/

Check whether port values influence cached responses.

docs.title: Multiple Cache Layers
docs.text:
Applications may have several caches.

Example:

Browser
   ↓
Cloud CDN
   ↓
Reverse Proxy Cache
   ↓
Application Cache
   ↓
Origin

A response may therefore show confusing behaviour.

For example:

CDN MISS

does not necessarily mean:

Origin application generated response

because another downstream cache may have served it.

docs.title: Cache Layer Mapping
docs.text:
Useful headers may reveal cache layers:

Via
X-Cache
Age
Server
CF-Ray
X-Served-By
X-Varnish

Build a mental model:

Client
 ↓
CDN
 ↓
Proxy
 ↓
Origin

before attempting advanced cache analysis.

docs.title: Cache TTL
docs.text:
TTL means:

Time To Live

It controls how long an object remains fresh in cache.

Example:

Cache-Control: max-age=300

means:

300 seconds

for relevant caching behaviour.

Long TTLs can increase the persistence of a poisoning issue.

docs.title: Age Header
docs.text:
Example:

Age: 120

This can indicate how long the object has been stored by a cache.

Repeated requests may show:

Age: 120
Age: 121
Age: 122

providing useful evidence that the same cached object is being served.

docs.title: Cache Revalidation
docs.text:
Caches may revalidate content using:

ETag
If-None-Match
Last-Modified
If-Modified-Since

Example:

ETag: "abc123"

Client:

If-None-Match: "abc123"

Response:

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified

Revalidation behaviour can complicate cache testing.

docs.title: Cache Poisoning and CDN Behaviour
docs.text:
CDNs often have provider-specific caching rules.

Potential considerations include:

Query parameter handling
Cookie bypass rules
Cacheable status codes
Host handling
Forwarded headers
Origin configuration
Custom cache keys
Edge functions

Do not assume all CDNs behave identically.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
A practical Burp workflow is:

Proxy
  ↓
Browse Application
  ↓
HTTP History
  ↓
Identify Cached Responses
  ↓
Send to Repeater
  ↓
Add Cache Buster
  ↓
Establish MISS → HIT
  ↓
Test Candidate Unkeyed Input
  ↓
Insert Canary
  ↓
Request Same Cache Key Normally
  ↓
Check Persistence
  ↓
Assess Impact

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Repeater is particularly useful because cache testing requires precise control over:

Headers
Query parameters
Cookies
Request order

Example baseline:

GET /?cb=AM100 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Then:

GET /?cb=AM100 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
X-Forwarded-Host: am-cache.example

Then again:

GET /?cb=AM100 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Compare all three responses.

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer can help identify subtle differences between:

Baseline response
Modified response
Cached response

Compare:

Headers
Body
URLs
Script sources
Redirects
Length

docs.title: Burp Decoder
docs.text:
Decoder can assist when cache-related values appear:

URL encoded
Base64 encoded
HTML encoded

Understand how the application transforms the input before it reaches the response.

docs.title: Param Miner
docs.text:
A particularly useful Burp extension for web cache poisoning research is:

Param Miner

Param Miner can help identify:

Hidden parameters
Unkeyed headers
Unkeyed cookies
Cache behaviour

It is widely used when testing web cache poisoning.

docs.title: Installing Param Miner
docs.text:
In Burp Suite:

Extensions
   ↓
BApp Store
   ↓
Search:
Param Miner
   ↓
Install

After installation, relevant functionality becomes available through Burp's extension interfaces and context menus.

docs.title: Param Miner Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

Interesting Request
      ↓
Send to Repeater
      ↓
Establish Cache Behaviour
      ↓
Param Miner
      ↓
Guess Headers
      ↓
Interesting Header Found
      ↓
Manual Repeater Validation
      ↓
Canary Reflection
      ↓
Cache Persistence
      ↓
Impact Assessment

docs.title: Guess Headers
docs.text:
Param Miner can assist with identifying headers that affect application behaviour.

Conceptually:

Candidate Headers
      ↓
Application
      ↓
Response Difference
      ↓
Interesting Candidate

A detected header should always be manually verified.

docs.title: Param Miner Findings
docs.text:
Treat extension findings as:

Leads

rather than:

Confirmed vulnerabilities

You still need to establish:

Input affects response
Input is unkeyed
Response is cached
Normal request receives poisoned response
Security impact exists

docs.title: Web Cache Poisoning Testing With curl
docs.text:
curl can help inspect basic cache behaviour.

Example:

curl -k -i \
  "https://target.example/?cb=AM200"

Repeat:

curl -k -i \
  "https://target.example/?cb=AM200"

Compare:

Age
X-Cache
CF-Cache-Status

docs.title: Header Canary With curl
docs.text:
curl -k -i \
  -H "X-Forwarded-Host: am-cache.example" \
  "https://target.example/?cb=AM201"

Then:

curl -k -i \
  "https://target.example/?cb=AM201"

Search for the harmless canary.

docs.title: Response Comparison
docs.text:
Useful shell tools include:

diff
grep
sha256sum

Example:

curl -sk \
  "https://target.example/?cb=AM300" \
  -o baseline.html

Then compare against a modified response.

docs.title: Automated Testing Considerations
docs.text:
Automation can help identify:

Headers affecting responses
Cacheable endpoints
Cache status changes
Response differences

However, aggressive automated cache testing can accidentally affect shared cache entries.

Therefore:

Use unique cache busters
Limit request volume
Prefer controlled endpoints
Verify manually

docs.title: Safe Testing Strategy
docs.text:
A strong authorised workflow is:

1. Identify cache

2. Select low-risk endpoint

3. Create unique cache buster

4. Verify cache buster is keyed

5. Establish cache MISS/HIT behaviour

6. Introduce harmless canary

7. Determine whether canary changes response

8. Remove candidate input

9. Request identical cache-busted URL

10. Determine whether canary persists

11. Stop once cache poisoning primitive is demonstrated

12. Assess potential impact without affecting normal users

docs.title: Cache Discovery
docs.text:
[ ] Check Age
[ ] Check X-Cache
[ ] Check CF-Cache-Status
[ ] Check Via
[ ] Check Cache-Control
[ ] Check ETag
[ ] Repeat request
[ ] Establish HIT/MISS behaviour

docs.title: Cache Safety
docs.text:
[ ] Create unique cache buster
[ ] Verify cache buster is keyed
[ ] Avoid normal production cache keys
[ ] Use harmless markers
[ ] Limit testing volume
[ ] Stop after sufficient evidence

docs.title: Cache Key
docs.text:
[ ] Host
[ ] Path
[ ] Query string
[ ] Query parameter order
[ ] Selected headers
[ ] Cookies
[ ] HTTP method
[ ] Scheme
[ ] Port

docs.title: Candidate Unkeyed Inputs
docs.text:
[ ] X-Forwarded-Host
[ ] X-Forwarded-Proto
[ ] X-Forwarded-Port
[ ] Forwarded
[ ] X-Original-URL
[ ] X-Rewrite-URL
[ ] Origin
[ ] Accept-Language
[ ] User-Agent
[ ] Cookies
[ ] Custom headers

docs.title: Response Effects
docs.text:
[ ] Absolute URLs
[ ] Script sources
[ ] Stylesheets
[ ] Canonical URLs
[ ] Redirects
[ ] HTML
[ ] API responses
[ ] Error messages

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
[ ] Modified request sent
[ ] Response modified
[ ] Response cached
[ ] Candidate input removed

docs.title: Authentication

[ ] Check session cookies
[ ] Check Authorization
