docs.title: Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Parameter discovery is the process of identifying input parameters accepted by a web application or API.

Parameters are important because they represent locations where user-controlled input enters the application.

They may influence:

Database queries
File operations
Redirects
Authentication
Authorisation
API requests
Templates
Operating system commands
Server-side HTTP requests
Application state
Business logic

A parameter that appears insignificant may expose important functionality when its value is modified.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform parameter discovery and subsequent testing only against systems for which you have explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
The objective is to identify as much of the application's input surface as possible.

Parameters may exist in:

URL query strings
POST bodies
JSON requests
XML requests
HTTP headers
Cookies
Path parameters
Multipart forms
GraphQL requests
WebSocket messages

A practical workflow is:

Endpoint Discovery
        ↓
Historical URL Collection
        ↓
Parameter Extraction
        ↓
Active Parameter Discovery
        ↓
JavaScript Analysis
        ↓
API Analysis
        ↓
Burp Suite Analysis
        ↓
Deduplication
        ↓
Classification
        ↓
Manual Verification
        ↓
Vulnerability Testing

The objective is not simply to collect thousands of URLs.

The objective is to understand:

Where does user-controlled input enter the application?

docs.title: What Is a Parameter?
docs.text:
Consider:

https://target.example/product?id=123

The parameter is:

id

and the value is:

123

Multiple parameters may exist:

https://target.example/search?q=test&page=2&sort=date

Parameters:

q
page
sort

Values:

test
2
date

These parameters may behave very differently internally.

For example:

q
 ↓
Search functionality
 ↓
Database query

while:

sort
 ↓
Query construction
 ↓
Database ordering

Understanding the parameter's purpose is therefore just as important as discovering it.

docs.title: Parameter Locations
docs.text: Parameters are not limited to URLs.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
Example:

GET /product?id=123&category=books HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Parameters:

id
category

docs.title: Form Parameters
docs.text:
Example:

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=user&password=password

Parameters:

username
password

docs.title: JSON Parameters
docs.text:
Modern APIs frequently use JSON.

Example:

POST /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "username": "test",
  "email": "test@example.com"
}

Parameters:

username
email

docs.title: XML Parameters
docs.text:
Example:

<user>
    <username>test</username>
    <email>test@example.com</email>
</user>

Potential input points:

username
email

docs.title: Path Parameters
docs.text:
Some frameworks encode parameters directly into paths.

Example:

/users/123

The value:

123

may represent:

user_id

Another example:

/api/orders/8472

Conceptually:

/api/orders/{order_id}

Path parameters are particularly important when testing access controls.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Applications may process user-controlled headers.

Examples:

Host
Origin
Referer
User-Agent
X-Forwarded-For
X-Forwarded-Host
X-Original-URL
X-Rewrite-URL
Forwarded

Headers should therefore be considered part of the application's input surface.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Cookies can also contain application-controlled parameters.

Example:

Cookie: session=abc123; language=en; role=user

Potential values:

session
language
role

Never assume a cookie is safe simply because the browser normally manages it.

docs.title: Start With Burp Suite
docs.text:
Before using automated tools, inspect the application through Burp Suite.

Use:

Proxy
→ HTTP history

and:

Target
→ Site map

Look for requests containing:

?
=
POST bodies
JSON
XML
Cookies
Custom headers
Path identifiers

For example:

GET /account?id=1001 HTTP/1.1

or:

POST /api/search HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "administrator",
  "limit": 20
}

Burp often reveals parameters that automated URL collection tools cannot see.

docs.title: Browser Developer Tools
docs.text:
Browser Developer Tools are also useful.

Open:

Developer Tools
→ Network

Interact with the application.

Look for:

XHR
Fetch
API
GraphQL
WebSocket
Form submissions
Background requests

Modern applications may make numerous API requests that are not visible in the page URL.

docs.title: Historical Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Historical URL sources are extremely valuable for parameter discovery.

An application might currently expose:

/search

but historical data could reveal:

/search?q=test
/search?query=test
/search?keyword=test
/search?category=1

Even if some URLs are old, the parameters may still be recognised by the current application.

Useful tools include:

waybackurls
gau
urlfinder

docs.title: Waybackurls
docs.text:
Collect historical URLs:

echo target.example | waybackurls

Save the output:

echo target.example | waybackurls > wayback.txt

Remove duplicates:

sort -u wayback.txt -o wayback.txt

Find URLs containing parameters:

grep '=' wayback.txt

Or:

grep '?' wayback.txt

Save parameterised URLs:

grep '=' wayback.txt > wayback-params.txt

docs.title: GAU
docs.text:
GAU can collect URLs from multiple public sources.

Example:

gau target.example

Save output:

gau target.example > gau.txt

Find parameterised URLs:

grep '=' gau.txt

Save them:

grep '=' gau.txt > gau-params.txt

docs.title: URLFinder
docs.text:
URLFinder can also collect URLs associated with a domain.

Example:

urlfinder -d target.example

Save results:

urlfinder -d target.example -o urlfinder.txt

Extract parameterised URLs:

grep '=' urlfinder.txt > urlfinder-params.txt

docs.title: Combine Historical Sources
docs.text:
Combine the results:

cat wayback.txt gau.txt urlfinder.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > all-urls.txt

Then extract URLs containing parameters:

grep '=' all-urls.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > parameters.txt

Quick count:

wc -l parameters.txt

This produces an initial parameter attack surface.

docs.title: Extract Parameter Names
docs.text:
Suppose the collected URLs contain:

https://target.example/search?q=test&page=1
https://target.example/product?id=100
https://target.example/redirect?url=https://example.com

The interesting parameter names are:

q
page
id
url

A simple shell pipeline can help extract names:

cat parameters.txt \
  | grep -oE '[?&][^=]+' \
  | sed 's/^[?&]//' \
  | sort -u

Potential output:

id
page
q
url

This can quickly reveal recurring parameter patterns.

docs.title: ParamSpider
docs.text:
ParamSpider is designed to discover parameters from web archives.

Basic usage:

python3 paramspider.py -d target.example

Depending on the installed version, output is typically written into an output directory.

For example:

output/
└── target.example.txt

Inspect:

cat output/target.example.txt

Potential results:

https://target.example/search?q=FUZZ
https://target.example/product?id=FUZZ
https://target.example/redirect?url=FUZZ
https://target.example/download?file=FUZZ

This format is useful because parameter values are replaced with:

FUZZ

making the URLs ready for further testing.

docs.title: ParamSpider Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow might be:

python3 paramspider.py -d target.example

Then:

cd output

Review:

cat target.example.txt

Count:

wc -l target.example.txt

Deduplicate:

sort -u target.example.txt -o target.example.txt

The output can then be fed into specialised analysis tools.

docs.title: Active Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Historical sources only reveal parameters that have previously appeared publicly.

Applications may also accept undocumented parameters.

Active parameter discovery attempts to identify them.

Useful tools include:

Arjun
FFUF
Burp Intruder
Param Miner

docs.title: Arjun
docs.text:
Arjun is designed to discover hidden HTTP parameters.

Basic example:

arjun -u https://target.example/page

Potential result:

parameter detected:

debug

The application might therefore accept:

https://target.example/page?debug=true

even though the parameter never appeared in the application's normal interface.

docs.title: GET Parameter Discovery With Arjun
docs.text:
Example:

arjun \
  -u https://target.example/search \
  -m GET

Possible discovered parameters:

q
query
search
page
limit
sort

Always manually verify interesting results.

docs.title: POST Parameter Discovery With Arjun
docs.text:
Arjun can also test POST parameters.

Example:

arjun \
  -u https://target.example/api/search \
  -m POST

This can help identify parameters accepted by endpoints where the request structure is not fully documented.

docs.title: Parameter Discovery With FFUF
docs.text:
FFUF can fuzz parameter names.

Suppose:

https://target.example/page

You want to determine whether undocumented GET parameters are accepted.

Example:

ffuf \
  -u 'https://target.example/page?FUZZ=test' \
  -w parameters.txt

Possible wordlist entries:

id
page
debug
admin
user
file
url
redirect
callback
lang

Look for changes in:

Status
Response size
Word count
Line count
Redirect
Headers

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Before fuzzing parameter names, understand the normal response.

Request:

curl -i https://target.example/page

Then:

curl -i 'https://target.example/page?randomparameter123=test'

Compare the responses.

If the application ignores unknown parameters, both responses may be identical.

A valid parameter may produce a different:

Response size
Status code
Header
Redirect
Page content
Timing

This difference can be used during discovery.

docs.title: FFUF Response Filtering
docs.text:
If the baseline response size is:

4242

filter it:

ffuf \
  -u 'https://target.example/page?FUZZ=test' \
  -w parameters.txt \
  -fs 4242

Other useful filters:

-fs    Response size
-fw    Word count
-fl    Line count
-fc    Status code

This can significantly reduce false positives.

docs.title: Burp Param Miner
docs.text:
Burp Suite's Param Miner extension is useful for identifying hidden parameters.

It can test:

Query parameters
Headers
Cookies

This is particularly useful for discovering behaviour associated with:

Caching
Routing
Proxy behaviour
Hidden application functionality

Use the extension carefully because parameter guessing can generate a significant number of requests.

docs.title: JavaScript Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
JavaScript files frequently reveal parameter names.

For example:

fetch("/api/users?id=" + userId)

reveals:

/api/users
id

Another example:

axios.get("/api/search", {
    params: {
        query: searchTerm,
        limit: 20
    }
})

reveals:

query
limit

Search JavaScript files for patterns such as:

?
&
=
params
query
search
id
url
redirect
callback
file
path

docs.title: Grep JavaScript
docs.text:
If JavaScript files have been downloaded:

grep -RniE \
  'id|user|url|uri|redirect|callback|file|path|query|search|page|limit' \
  javascript/

This is noisy but can reveal useful parameter names.

You can also search for API routes:

grep -RniE \
  '(/api/|/graphql|/admin|/internal|/upload|/download)' \
  javascript/

Combine endpoint discovery with parameter discovery.

docs.title: API Documentation
docs.text:
API documentation can provide the most accurate parameter inventory.

Look for:

Swagger
OpenAPI
Postman collections
GraphQL documentation
Developer portals
API reference pages

Common endpoints include:

/swagger
/swagger-ui
/swagger.json
/openapi.json
/api-docs
/v2/api-docs
/v3/api-docs

An OpenAPI specification might describe:

parameters:
  - name: id
    in: query
    required: true

This immediately identifies:

Parameter: id
Location: query
Required: yes

docs.title: Swagger and OpenAPI Analysis
docs.text:
When API documentation is available, record:

Endpoint
Method
Parameter
Parameter location
Data type
Required/optional
Expected format
Authentication

For example:

Endpoint Method Parameter Location Type /api/users GET id Query Integer /api/search GET q Query String /api/files POST file Multipart File /api/orders/{id} GET id Path Integer

This provides an excellent starting point for later testing.

docs.title: GraphQL Parameters
docs.text:
GraphQL handles input differently from traditional REST APIs.

Example:

query {
  user(id: 123) {
    username
    email
  }
}

Input:

id

Another example:

query Search($term: String!) {
  search(query: $term) {
    title
  }
}

Input:

term
query

GraphQL variables may therefore represent important user-controlled input.

docs.title: JSON Parameter Mapping
docs.text:
Consider:

{
  "user": {
    "name": "test",
    "email": "test@example.com"
  },
  "preferences": {
    "language": "en"
  }
}

The input surface includes:

user.name
user.email
preferences.language

Do not only record top-level JSON keys.

Nested parameters can behave differently.

docs.title: Mass Assignment Awareness
docs.text:
JSON APIs sometimes accept more fields than the user interface sends.

For example, the UI may send:

{
  "name": "Asif"
}

while the backend model contains:

name
email
role
status
verified

Parameter discovery may therefore involve understanding which additional fields the API accepts.

This becomes particularly relevant during later business logic and authorisation testing.

Do not modify security-sensitive properties outside the authorised scope.

docs.title: Parameter Classification
docs.text:
Once parameters have been discovered, classify them.

A useful classification is:

Identifiers
Search
Files
URLs
Redirects
Paths
Commands
Templates
Authentication
Authorisation
Pagination
Sorting
Filters
Callbacks
Language
Debug
API control

For example:

id
user_id
account_id
order_id

could be classified as:

Identifiers

while:

url
uri
target
dest
destination
callback

could be classified as:

URL-like input

Classification helps determine what type of testing should happen next.

docs.title: Interesting Parameter Names
docs.text: Certain names deserve additional attention because they may indicate particular functionality.

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
id
uid
user
user_id
account
account_id
order
order_id
document
document_id

Potential testing areas:

Authorisation
IDOR
Object-level access control

docs.title: URL Parameters
docs.text:
url
uri
target
dest
destination
redirect
redirect_url
return
return_url
next
continue
callback
callback_url

Potential testing areas:

Open redirect
Server-Side Request Forgery
Callback handling

docs.title: File Parameters
docs.text:
file
filename
filepath
path
document
download
template
page
include

Potential testing areas:

Path traversal
File inclusion
File handling
Download authorisation

docs.title: Search Parameters
docs.text:
q
query
search
keyword
filter
term

Potential testing areas:

SQL injection
Cross-Site Scripting
Search logic
Input validation

docs.title: Command-Like Parameters
docs.text:
cmd
command
exec
execute
process
host
ip

Potential testing areas:

Command injection
Argument injection
Server-side processing

docs.title: Template Parameters
docs.text:
template
view
name
message
content
format

Potential testing areas:

Template injection
HTML injection
Cross-Site Scripting

docs.title: Debug Parameters
docs.text:
debug
test
dev
verbose
trace
preview
internal

Potentially interesting because they may expose:

Debug information
Alternative application behaviour
Development functionality
Verbose errors

docs.title: Parameter Wordlists
docs.text:
SecLists contains parameter-related wordlists.

Search:

find /usr/share/seclists \
  -iname '*param*'

You can also create a target-specific parameter wordlist from discovered application terminology.

For example, if the application contains:

customer
invoice
contract
document
organisation

create:

customer
customer_id
invoice
invoice_id
contract
contract_id
document
document_id
organisation
organisation_id

Target-specific wordlists can be more effective than generic ones.

docs.title: Build a Custom Parameter Wordlist
docs.text:
Suppose reconnaissance identifies:

/users
/accounts
/orders
/documents

A custom list could contain:

user
userid
user_id
account
accountid
account_id
order
orderid
order_id
document
documentid
document_id

This can then be tested with:

ffuf \
  -u 'https://target.example/page?FUZZ=1' \
  -w custom-parameters.txt

docs.title: Deduplicating URLs
docs.text:
Historical sources often produce many duplicates.

For example:

https://target.example/product?id=1
https://target.example/product?id=2
https://target.example/product?id=3

These represent the same basic attack surface:

/product?id=

Testing every historical value is usually unnecessary.

Instead, normalise URLs based on:

Host
Path
Parameter names

docs.title: uro
docs.text:
The uro tool can help reduce duplicate URLs.

Example:

cat all-urls.txt | uro

Save results:

cat all-urls.txt \
  | uro \
  > unique-urls.txt

This can significantly reduce noisy historical URL collections.

docs.title: qsreplace
docs.text:
qsreplace can replace query-string values.

For example:

echo 'https://target.example/search?q=test&page=1' \
  | qsreplace FUZZ

Result:

https://target.example/search?q=FUZZ&page=FUZZ

This can make parameterised URLs easier to process with later testing tools.

docs.title: Parameter Discovery Pipeline
docs.text:
A useful passive pipeline is:

echo target.example | waybackurls > wayback.txt

gau target.example > gau.txt

urlfinder -d target.example -o urlfinder.txt

Combine:

cat wayback.txt gau.txt urlfinder.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > all-urls.txt

Reduce noise:

cat all-urls.txt \
  | uro \
  > unique-urls.txt

Extract parameterised URLs:

grep '=' unique-urls.txt \
  > parameterised-urls.txt

Count:

wc -l parameterised-urls.txt

docs.title: Parameter Discovery With ParamSpider
docs.text:
A second workflow can use ParamSpider directly:

python3 paramspider.py -d target.example

Then:

cd output

Review:

cat target.example.txt

Deduplicate:

sort -u target.example.txt \
  -o target.example.txt

The resulting URLs can then be manually reviewed or passed into specialised analysis tools.

docs.title: XSS Candidate Discovery With kxss
docs.text:
After collecting parameterised GET URLs, kxss can help identify parameters where supplied input is reflected in responses.

For example:

cat parameterised-urls.txt | kxss

Or with ParamSpider output:

cat output/target.example.txt | kxss

This does not automatically mean an endpoint is vulnerable to Cross-Site Scripting.

It identifies locations where input reflection may deserve further investigation.

A useful workflow is:

Parameter Discovery
        ↓
Parameterised URLs
        ↓
kxss
        ↓
Reflection Candidates
        ↓
Manual Burp Testing
        ↓
Context Analysis
        ↓
XSS Testing

Always manually verify results.

docs.title: Live URL Verification
docs.text:
Historical URLs may no longer exist.

Before extensive testing, determine whether endpoints are still reachable.

For example, URL lists can be reviewed using HTTP probing tools such as:

httpx

A conceptual workflow is:

Historical URLs
      ↓
Deduplicate
      ↓
Probe
      ↓
Keep Relevant Live Endpoints
      ↓
Parameter Analysis

This can prevent spending time testing obsolete endpoints.

docs.title: GET Versus POST Parameters
docs.text:
GET parameters are easier to discover because they frequently appear in:

Browser history
Search engine indexes
Web archives
JavaScript
Logs
Links

POST parameters are less visible.

They are more commonly discovered through:

Burp Suite
Forms
JavaScript
API documentation
Source code
Mobile applications
Active parameter discovery

Do not assume a complete GET parameter inventory represents the complete input surface.

docs.title: Hidden Form Fields
docs.text:
HTML forms may contain hidden inputs.

Example:

<input type="hidden" name="user_id" value="123">
<input type="hidden" name="action" value="update">

Parameters:

user_id
action

Hidden does not mean trusted.

The browser can modify these values before submission.

Review all form fields through Burp Suite rather than relying only on visible page elements.

docs.title: Disabled Form Fields
docs.text:
Disabled fields can also reveal interesting application parameters.

Example:

<input name="role" value="user" disabled>

Although the browser may not normally submit the field, the backend may still accept it if manually included.

Record these parameters for later validation.

docs.title: HTTP Method Analysis
docs.text:
The same endpoint may behave differently depending on the HTTP method.

For example:

GET /api/user
POST /api/user
PUT /api/user
PATCH /api/user
DELETE /api/user

Each method may accept different parameters.

When documentation or application behaviour suggests multiple methods, map the parameter set independently.

docs.title: Content-Type Analysis
docs.text:
Parameter parsing may also depend on the content type.

For example:

application/x-www-form-urlencoded
application/json
multipart/form-data
application/xml
text/xml

An endpoint may process:

{"id":123}

differently from:

id=123

Record the expected content type alongside each parameter.

docs.title: Parameter Behaviour Analysis
docs.text:
Discovery alone is not enough.

For each important parameter, determine:

Is it required?
What data type does it expect?
Does it accept empty values?
Does it accept multiple values?
Does it affect the response?
Does it trigger a redirect?
Does it reference an object?
Does it reference a file?
Does it reference a URL?
Is it reflected?
Is it stored?
Does it change application state?

This creates context for later vulnerability testing.

docs.title: Duplicate Parameters
docs.text:
Applications may behave unexpectedly when the same parameter appears multiple times.

Example:

?id=1&id=2

Different frameworks may:

Use first value
Use last value
Create an array
Concatenate values
Reject request

This behaviour can become relevant during later validation and access-control testing.

Record it when observed.

docs.title: Case Sensitivity
docs.text:
Parameter names may be case-sensitive.

For example:

id
ID
Id
userId
userid
userID

Do not automatically assume these are equivalent.

Application frameworks and custom parsing logic may treat them differently.

docs.title: Parameter Relationships
docs.text:
Parameters should not always be analysed independently.

Consider:

/account?user_id=100&organisation_id=5

The relationship may be:

organisation_id
      ↓
Defines organisation

user_id
      ↓
Defines user inside organisation

Testing the parameters together may reveal behaviour that testing each one independently misses.

This is particularly important for:

Business logic
Authorisation
Multi-tenant applications
Object-level access control

docs.title: Parameter Inventory
docs.text:
Maintain a structured parameter inventory.

For example:

Endpoint Method Parameter Location Type Purpose /search GET q Query String Search /product GET id Query Integer Product identifier /redirect GET url Query URL Redirect destination /download GET file Query String File selection /api/user POST email JSON String User email /api/order/{id} GET id Path Integer Order identifier

Add additional columns when useful:

Authentication required
Role required
Reflected
Stored
Interesting behaviour
Testing status
Notes

docs.title: Prioritising Parameters
docs.text:
Not every parameter deserves equal attention.

A useful priority order is:

Object identifiers
        ↓
URL parameters
        ↓
File/path parameters
        ↓
Authentication parameters
        ↓
Search/filter parameters
        ↓
Template/content parameters
        ↓
Debug parameters
        ↓
Pagination/display parameters

However, context matters.

For example:

?page=2

might appear harmless.

But:

?page=../../etc/passwd

would indicate that page is actually being used as a file path.

Parameter names are hints, not proof.

docs.title: Mapping Parameters to Testing Areas
docs.text:
Once parameters have been classified, map them to likely testing categories.

Parameter Pattern Testing Areas id, uid, account_id Authorisation, IDOR q, search, query XSS, SQLi, input validation url, uri, target SSRF, open redirect redirect, next, return Open redirect, authentication flows file, path, page Path traversal, file handling template, view SSTI, file inclusion cmd, command, exec Command injection callback Redirects, SSRF, JSONP role, admin, privilege Authorisation, mass assignment debug, test, dev Debug functionality sort, order, filter SQLi, business logic host, domain, ip SSRF, command injection, network functionality

This mapping should guide testing, not replace manual analysis.

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text: A complete parameter discovery workflow could look like this.

docs.title: 1. Browse the application
docs.text:
Use:

Browser
Burp Suite
Developer Tools

Record:

GET parameters
POST parameters
JSON keys
Cookies
Headers
Path identifiers

docs.title: 2. Collect historical URLs
docs.text:
echo target.example | waybackurls > wayback.txt

gau target.example > gau.txt

urlfinder -d target.example -o urlfinder.txt

docs.title: 3. Combine results
docs.text:
cat wayback.txt gau.txt urlfinder.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > all-urls.txt

docs.title: 4. Reduce duplicates
docs.text:
cat all-urls.txt \
  | uro \
  > unique-urls.txt

docs.title: 5. Extract parameterised URLs
docs.text:
grep '=' unique-urls.txt \
  > parameterised-urls.txt

docs.title: 6. Run ParamSpider
docs.text:
python3 paramspider.py -d target.example

Review:

cat output/target.example.txt

docs.title: 7. Review JavaScript
docs.text:
Search for:

API endpoints
Parameter names
Fetch requests
Axios requests
GraphQL queries
Hidden functionality

docs.title: 8. Active parameter discovery
docs.text:
For interesting endpoints:

arjun -u https://target.example/page

or:

ffuf \
  -u 'https://target.example/page?FUZZ=test' \
  -w parameters.txt

docs.title: 9. Identify reflection candidates
docs.text:
For authorised GET-based testing:

cat parameterised-urls.txt | kxss

docs.title: 10. Verify manually
docs.text:
Send interesting requests to Burp Repeater.

Determine:

What does the parameter control?
What data type is expected?
How does the response change?
Where is the value processed?
What should be tested next?

docs.title: Example Attack Surface
docs.text:
Suppose reconnaissance produces:

/search?q=test
/product?id=123
/download?file=document.pdf
/redirect?url=https://example.com
/api/user?user_id=100

The parameters can be mapped as:

q
 ↓
Search
 ↓
XSS / SQLi investigation

id
 ↓
Object identifier
 ↓
Authorisation / IDOR investigation

file
 ↓
File reference
 ↓
File handling / path traversal investigation

url
 ↓
URL
 ↓
Redirect / SSRF investigation

user_id
 ↓
User object
 ↓
Authorisation investigation

This demonstrates why parameter discovery is a bridge between reconnaissance and vulnerability testing.

docs.title: Recommended Output Structure
docs.text:
Keep reconnaissance output organised.

For example:

recon/
├── urls/
│   ├── wayback.txt
│   ├── gau.txt
│   ├── urlfinder.txt
│   ├── all-urls.txt
│   └── unique-urls.txt
│
├── parameters/
│   ├── parameterised-urls.txt
│   ├── parameter-names.txt
│   ├── paramspider.txt
│   ├── arjun.txt
│   └── reflection-candidates.txt
│
└── javascript/
    └── endpoints.txt

This makes later testing considerably easier.

docs.title: Parameter Discovery Checklist
docs.text:
[ ] Review Burp HTTP history
[ ] Review Burp site map
[ ] Review browser Network requests
[ ] Record GET parameters
[ ] Record POST parameters
[ ] Record JSON parameters
[ ] Record XML parameters
[ ] Record path parameters
[ ] Review cookies
[ ] Review interesting headers
[ ] Collect Wayback URLs
[ ] Collect GAU URLs
[ ] Collect URLFinder URLs
[ ] Run ParamSpider
[ ] Deduplicate URLs
[ ] Extract parameter names
[ ] Review JavaScript
[ ] Review Swagger/OpenAPI
[ ] Review GraphQL requests
[ ] Check hidden form fields
[ ] Check disabled form fields
[ ] Perform active parameter discovery
[ ] Establish baseline responses
[ ] Review response differences
[ ] Identify reflection candidates
[ ] Classify parameters
[ ] Prioritise interesting parameters
[ ] Record parameters in an inventory
[ ] Manually verify important findings

docs.title: Passive Discovery
docs.text:
echo target.example | waybackurls > wayback.txt

gau target.example > gau.txt

urlfinder -d target.example -o urlfinder.txt

python3 paramspider.py -d target.example

docs.title: Combine URLs
docs.text:
cat wayback.txt gau.txt urlfinder.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > all-urls.txt

docs.title: Deduplicate
docs.text:
cat all-urls.txt \
  | uro \
  > unique-urls.txt

docs.title: Parameterised URLs
docs.text:
grep '=' unique-urls.txt \
  > parameterised-urls.txt

docs.title: Extract Parameter Names
docs.text:
cat parameterised-urls.txt \
  | grep -oE '[?&][^=]+' \
  | sed 's/^[?&]//' \
  | sort -u \
  > parameter-names.txt

docs.title: Active Discovery
docs.text: arjun -u https://target.example/page

docs.title: FFUF Parameter Names
docs.text:
ffuf \
  -u 'https://target.example/page?FUZZ=test' \
  -w parameter-names.txt

docs.title: Reflection Candidates
docs.text: cat parameterised-urls.txt | kxss

docs.title: Key Principle
docs.text:
Parameter discovery should not be treated as:

Collect URLs
     ↓
Find ?
     ↓
Done

A better approach is:

Discover Endpoint
        ↓
Identify Inputs
        ↓
Understand Input Location
        ↓
Determine Purpose
        ↓
Classify Parameter
        ↓
Observe Behaviour
        ↓
Prioritise
        ↓
Test

The important question is not:

How many parameters did I find?

The important questions are:

What does each parameter control?

and:

Where does this input go?

A good parameter inventory transforms reconnaissance from a collection of URLs into a structured map of the application's user-controlled input surface.

docs.title: Subdomain Enumeration
docs.text:
Subdomain enumeration is the process of identifying subdomains associated with a target domain.

During a web application penetration test, subdomain enumeration can reveal additional applications, APIs, administrative interfaces, development environments, staging systems and other assets that may not be linked from the primary website.

The goal is not simply to collect as many hostnames as possible. The objective is to produce a validated and organised list of assets that can be investigated during the rest of the assessment.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform subdomain enumeration only against domains and systems that are within the authorised scope of the security assessment.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
A practical subdomain enumeration workflow can be organised as:

                         Target Domain
                              |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
          |                   |                   |
      Subfinder             Amass             Assetfinder
          |                   |                   |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
                              |
                       CT / Passive Sources
                              |
                              v
                       Combine Results
                              |
                              v
                         Deduplicate
                              |
                              v
                        DNS Resolution
                            dnsx
                              |
                              v
                         HTTP Probing
                            httpx
                              |
                              v
                       Live Web Targets
                              |
                              v
                    Further Reconnaissance

Using multiple sources is important because different tools and data sources frequently discover different subdomains.

docs.title: 1. Create a Workspace
docs.text:
Keeping reconnaissance output organised makes it easier to reproduce the assessment and use the results in later stages.

mkdir -p recon/subdomains
cd recon/subdomains

A typical directory may eventually contain:

recon/
└── subdomains/
    ├── subfinder.txt
    ├── amass.txt
    ├── assetfinder.txt
    ├── ct.txt
    ├── subdomains.txt
    ├── resolved-subdomains.txt
    └── alive-hosts.txt

docs.title: 2. Subfinder
docs.text:
Subfinder performs passive subdomain enumeration using multiple online data sources.

Basic usage:

subfinder -d example.com -silent

Save the results:

subfinder -d example.com -silent -o subfinder.txt

For broader passive enumeration:

subfinder -d example.com -all -recursive -silent -o subfinder.txt

The results may look like:

www.example.com
api.example.com
portal.example.com
login.example.com
dev.example.com

Subfinder is often a good first source because it is fast and integrates multiple passive data providers.

docs.title: 3. Amass
docs.text:
Amass can be used as another independent source for discovering subdomains.

Passive enumeration:

amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt

Passive mode is useful when direct enumeration against the target should be minimised.

The results can later be combined with Subfinder and other sources.

docs.title: 4. Assetfinder
docs.text:
Assetfinder provides another lightweight source of subdomain information.

assetfinder --subs-only example.com

Save the results:

assetfinder --subs-only example.com > assetfinder.txt

Using several independent tools increases coverage because each may use different sources.

docs.title: 5. Certificate Transparency
docs.text:
Certificate Transparency logs are an important source of historical and current hostname information.

Certificates issued for an organisation may contain hostnames such as:

www.example.com
api.example.com
vpn.example.com
portal.example.com
mail.example.com

Certificate Transparency data can therefore reveal subdomains that are not easily discovered through other passive sources.

Useful sources include:

  • crt.sh
  • Certificate Transparency search services
  • Search engine certificate datasets
  • Passive DNS platforms

When reviewing Certificate Transparency results, remember that a hostname appearing in a certificate does not necessarily mean the hostname still exists.

Always validate discovered assets.

docs.title: 6. crt.sh from the Command Line
docs.text:
Certificate Transparency information can also be collected from the command line.

For example:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json"

If jq is available, names can be extracted with:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" \
  | jq -r '.[].name_value' \
  | sed 's/\*\.//g' \
  | sort -u

Save the results:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" \
  | jq -r '.[].name_value' \
  | sed 's/\*\.//g' \
  | sort -u > ct.txt

Certificate Transparency should normally be treated as another discovery source rather than as proof that a host is currently active.

docs.title: 7. Combine Results
docs.text:
After collecting results from multiple sources, combine them into one list.

cat subfinder.txt amass.txt assetfinder.txt ct.txt > combined.txt

Then remove duplicates:

sort -u combined.txt > subdomains.txt

This can also be performed directly:

cat subfinder.txt amass.txt assetfinder.txt ct.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > subdomains.txt

Count the discovered hostnames:

wc -l subdomains.txt

Example:

842 subdomains.txt

At this point, the list represents discovered candidate hostnames.

It does not mean that all of them currently resolve or expose a web service.

docs.title: 8. Scope Filtering
docs.text:
Before performing active validation, make sure the discovered hostnames remain within the authorised scope.

For a scope limited to:

*.example.com

you can review the list using:

grep -E '(^|\.)example\.com$' subdomains.txt

Save the filtered list:

grep -E '(^|\.)example\.com$' subdomains.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > scoped-subdomains.txt

Scope

A hostname being related to an organisation does not automatically mean it is authorised for testing. Always follow the defined engagement scope.

docs.title: 9. DNS Resolution with dnsx
docs.text:
The next stage is determining which discovered hostnames currently resolve.

dnsx -l scoped-subdomains.txt -silent

Save resolving hosts:

dnsx -l scoped-subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  > resolved-subdomains.txt

Count them:

wc -l resolved-subdomains.txt

The workflow is now:

Discovered Subdomains
        |
        v
   Scope Filtering
        |
        v
   DNS Resolution
        |
        v
Resolving Subdomains

This removes many historical or stale hostnames before HTTP probing.

docs.title: 10. Inspect DNS Records
docs.text:
DNS information can reveal useful infrastructure relationships.

For example:

dnsx -l scoped-subdomains.txt \
  -a \
  -aaaa \
  -cname \
  -resp

Interesting records include:

A
AAAA
CNAME
MX
TXT
NS

CNAME records are particularly interesting because they can reveal:

  • Cloud services
  • CDNs
  • SaaS platforms
  • Third-party hosting
  • External application platforms

Example:

portal.example.com
        |
        v
customer.vendor-platform.example

This helps identify where applications are actually hosted.

docs.title: 11. HTTP Probing with httpx
docs.text:
A resolving hostname does not necessarily expose a web application.

Use httpx to identify HTTP and HTTPS services:

httpx -l resolved-subdomains.txt -silent

Save live web targets:

httpx -l resolved-subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  > alive-hosts.txt

Count the results:

wc -l alive-hosts.txt

The pipeline now becomes:

Candidate Subdomains
        |
        v
      dnsx
        |
        v
Resolving Subdomains
        |
        v
      httpx
        |
        v
Live Web Applications

docs.title: 12. Collect Useful HTTP Metadata
docs.text:
Instead of collecting only URLs, httpx can collect additional information.

httpx -l resolved-subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect

Additional useful options include:

httpx -l resolved-subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect \
  -server \
  -ip \
  -cname

Example output might look like:

https://portal.example.com [200] [Customer Portal] [nginx] [React]
https://api.example.com [403] [Forbidden] [nginx]
https://dev.example.com [302] [Login] [Apache]

This makes prioritisation much easier than working from a plain hostname list.

docs.title: 13. Do Not Ignore Interesting Status Codes
docs.text:
A common mistake is to focus only on HTTP 200 responses.

Other responses can also reveal valuable targets:

200    Application available
301    Permanent redirect
302    Redirect
401    Authentication required
403    Access forbidden
404    Host exists but requested path not found
500    Server-side error

For example, a 403 response may indicate:

  • Administrative functionality
  • IP restrictions
  • Authentication controls
  • Reverse proxy restrictions
  • Access control at the web server

Therefore, avoid discarding hosts solely because they do not return HTTP 200.

docs.title: 14. Redirects
docs.text:
Redirects can reveal application relationships.

For example:

portal.example.com
        |
        v
login.example.com
        |
        v
sso.example.com

Following redirects can help identify:

  • Central authentication services
  • SSO infrastructure
  • Canonical applications
  • External identity providers
  • Legacy domains

When appropriate:

httpx -l resolved-subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  -follow-redirects \
  -status-code \
  -title

docs.title: 15. Wildcard DNS
docs.text:
Wildcard DNS can create misleading enumeration results.

For example, if:

random-does-not-exist.example.com

still resolves, the domain may use wildcard DNS.

Test with a random hostname:

dig random-does-not-exist-12345.example.com

or:

nslookup random-does-not-exist-12345.example.com

If random hostnames consistently resolve to the same infrastructure, enumeration results should be interpreted carefully.

Wildcard DNS does not necessarily make discovered hosts useless, but it changes how they should be validated.

docs.title: 16. Duplicate Applications
docs.text:
Different subdomains may point to the same application.

For example:

www.example.com
portal.example.com
app.example.com

may all redirect to:

https://login.example.com/

HTTP metadata can help identify these relationships.

Useful comparison points include:

  • IP address
  • CNAME
  • Page title
  • Response size
  • Redirect destination
  • Server header
  • Technology fingerprint

This can reduce unnecessary duplicate testing.

docs.title: 17. Development and Staging Systems
docs.text:
Subdomain enumeration frequently reveals environments such as:

dev.example.com
development.example.com
test.example.com
testing.example.com
stage.example.com
staging.example.com
uat.example.com
qa.example.com
preprod.example.com
demo.example.com

These environments may differ from production in important ways.

Things to review include:

  • Authentication
  • Debug functionality
  • Test accounts
  • Error handling
  • Software versions
  • Exposed documentation
  • Administrative functionality
  • Security controls

These systems should only be tested when they are explicitly within scope.

docs.title: 18. Interesting Subdomain Names
docs.text:
Certain names may deserve additional attention during triage.

Examples include:

admin
api
auth
backup
beta
cms
console
dashboard
demo
dev
developer
files
git
internal
jenkins
login
manage
monitor
old
portal
preprod
qa
sso
stage
staging
test
uat
upload
vpn

Search the discovered list:

grep -Ei \
'admin|api|auth|backup|beta|console|dashboard|dev|internal|login|portal|qa|stage|staging|test|uat|upload|vpn' \
subdomains.txt

This is useful for prioritisation, but hostnames should not be considered vulnerable based on their names alone.

docs.title: 19. Recursive Enumeration
docs.text:
A discovered subdomain may itself contain additional subdomains.

For example:

example.com
   |
   +-- dev.example.com
          |
          +-- api.dev.example.com
          |
          +-- admin.dev.example.com

This means enumeration can become iterative:

Initial Enumeration
        |
        v
Discover Subdomains
        |
        v
Identify Interesting Subdomains
        |
        v
Enumerate Deeper
        |
        v
New Subdomains

Recursive discovery can be particularly useful in larger environments.

docs.title: 20. Search Engine Discovery
docs.text:
Search engines can sometimes reveal subdomains through indexed content.

A basic search pattern is:

site:example.com

Results may reveal:

  • Applications
  • Subdomains
  • Documents
  • Login portals
  • Development environments
  • Cached pages

Search engine results should be validated before being added to the active attack surface.

docs.title: 21. Public Code Repositories
docs.text:
Public repositories may contain references to infrastructure.

Look for:

example.com
*.example.com
api.example.com
dev.example.com
internal.example.com

Potential sources include:

  • Configuration files
  • Documentation
  • CI/CD configuration
  • Deployment scripts
  • Environment templates
  • JavaScript
  • Infrastructure-as-code files

The purpose is asset discovery. Any discovered asset must still be checked against the authorised scope before active testing.

docs.title: 22. Historical Data
docs.text:
Historical URL sources may reveal additional subdomains.

For example:

waybackurls example.com

or:

gau example.com

Extract hostnames:

waybackurls example.com \
  | awk -F/ '{print $3}' \
  | sort -u

These results can then be added to the candidate list and validated.

A hostname found in historical data may no longer exist, so DNS resolution remains important.

docs.title: 23. Combining Historical Discovery
docs.text:
Historical sources can be incorporated into the enumeration pipeline.

For example:

waybackurls example.com \
  | awk -F/ '{print $3}' \
  | sort -u \
  > wayback-subdomains.txt

Then combine:

cat \
  subfinder.txt \
  amass.txt \
  assetfinder.txt \
  ct.txt \
  wayback-subdomains.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > subdomains.txt

This creates a broader candidate set.

docs.title: 24. One Practical Passive Pipeline
docs.text:
A simple workflow can be:

subfinder -d example.com -all -recursive -silent -o subfinder.txt

amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt

assetfinder --subs-only example.com > assetfinder.txt

cat subfinder.txt amass.txt assetfinder.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > subdomains.txt

dnsx -l subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  > resolved-subdomains.txt

httpx -l resolved-subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect

Conceptually:

subfinder ────┐
              |
amass ────────+──> sort -u
              |        |
assetfinder ──┘        v
                  subdomains.txt
                        |
                        v
                      dnsx
                        |
                        v
             resolved-subdomains.txt
                        |
                        v
                      httpx
                        |
                        v
                Live Web Targets

docs.title: 25. Extended Pipeline
docs.text:
For broader reconnaissance:

subfinder -d example.com -all -recursive -silent -o subfinder.txt

amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt

assetfinder --subs-only example.com > assetfinder.txt

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" \
  | jq -r '.[].name_value' \
  | sed 's/\*\.//g' \
  | sort -u \
  > ct.txt

waybackurls example.com \
  | awk -F/ '{print $3}' \
  | sort -u \
  > wayback-subdomains.txt

cat \
  subfinder.txt \
  amass.txt \
  assetfinder.txt \
  ct.txt \
  wayback-subdomains.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > subdomains.txt

dnsx -l subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  > resolved-subdomains.txt

httpx -l resolved-subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect \
  -server \
  -ip \
  -cname \
  > alive-hosts.txt

This creates a useful starting dataset for the next reconnaissance stages.

docs.title: 26. Analyse the Results
docs.text:
Do not stop after generating alive-hosts.txt.

Review the output and ask:

  • Which hosts return 200?
  • Which return 401 or 403?
  • Which hosts redirect?
  • Are there administrative interfaces?
  • Are there development environments?
  • Are there staging environments?
  • Are there APIs?
  • Are there authentication portals?
  • Which technologies are exposed?
  • Are different software versions present?
  • Are there unusual CNAME records?
  • Are multiple applications hosted on the same IP?
  • Are any hosts significantly different from the primary application?

Reconnaissance becomes valuable when the results influence what you test next.

docs.title: 27. Prioritisation
docs.text:
A simple prioritisation approach is:

                    Discovered Hosts
                           |
             +-------------+-------------+
             |             |             |
          Production   Development     Legacy
             |             |             |
             +-------------+-------------+
                           |
                           v
                    Authentication?
                           |
                           v
                       API / Admin?
                           |
                           v
                  Technology / Version
                           |
                           v
                    Testing Priority

Interesting targets may include:

  • Administrative portals
  • APIs
  • Development systems
  • Staging systems
  • Legacy applications
  • Authentication services
  • File-processing applications
  • Applications running unusual technologies

docs.title: 28. Feed Discoveries Back into Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Subdomain enumeration should not be treated as a one-time task.

Suppose JavaScript analysis later reveals:

https://internal-api.example.com

That hostname should be added to the reconnaissance dataset and validated.

Similarly, a discovered application may reveal:

api.eu.example.com
auth.eu.example.com
files.eu.example.com

These discoveries can lead to additional enumeration.

The process therefore becomes:

Enumerate
    |
    v
Validate
    |
    v
Investigate
    |
    v
Discover More
    |
    +---------> Enumerate Again

docs.title: 29. Recommended Output Files
docs.text:
A useful structure is:

recon/
└── subdomains/
    ├── subfinder.txt
    ├── amass.txt
    ├── assetfinder.txt
    ├── ct.txt
    ├── wayback-subdomains.txt
    ├── combined.txt
    ├── subdomains.txt
    ├── scoped-subdomains.txt
    ├── resolved-subdomains.txt
    └── alive-hosts.txt

Each file represents a specific stage of the reconnaissance pipeline.

This makes troubleshooting and reproducing results much easier than continuously overwriting a single file.

docs.title: 30. Tool Summary
docs.text:
Tool Purpose Subfinder Passive subdomain enumeration Amass Asset and subdomain discovery Assetfinder Passive subdomain discovery crt.sh Certificate Transparency discovery dnsx DNS validation and record inspection httpx HTTP probing and metadata collection waybackurls Historical URL discovery gau Historical and indexed URL discovery jq JSON processing sort Deduplication and organisation

No single source provides complete coverage.

The strongest workflow combines multiple sources and validates the results.

docs.title: Subfinder
docs.text: subfinder -d example.com -all -recursive -silent -o subfinder.txt

docs.title: Amass
docs.text: amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt

docs.title: Assetfinder
docs.text: assetfinder --subs-only example.com > assetfinder.txt

docs.title: Certificate Transparency
docs.text:
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" \
  | jq -r '.[].name_value' \
  | sed 's/\*\.//g' \
  | sort -u \
  > ct.txt

docs.title: Combine
docs.text:
cat subfinder.txt amass.txt assetfinder.txt ct.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > subdomains.txt

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text: dnsx -l subdomains.txt -silent > resolved-subdomains.txt

docs.title: HTTP Probing
docs.text:
httpx -l resolved-subdomains.txt \
  -silent \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect \
  -server \
  -ip \
  -cname

docs.title: 32. Final Workflow
docs.text:
The complete process can be summarised as:

                         example.com
                              |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
          |                   |                   |
      Subfinder             Amass             Assetfinder
          |                   |                   |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
                              |
                         CT / Archives
                              |
                              v
                         sort -u
                              |
                              v
                       subdomains.txt
                              |
                              v
                            dnsx
                              |
                              v
                 resolved-subdomains.txt
                              |
                              v
                            httpx
                              |
                              v
                       Live Web Targets
                              |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
          |                   |                   |
     Technology           Content            JavaScript
    Identification        Discovery            Analysis
          |                   |                   |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
                              |
                              v
                     Expanded Attack Surface

Subdomain enumeration is therefore not an isolated reconnaissance task. It is the first stage in building a broader understanding of the target's web attack surface.

docs.title: Ownership, Scope, and Takeover Triage
docs.text:
Treat every discovered hostname as a candidate asset:

Candidate hostname
  -> Normalize and deduplicate
  -> DNS validation
  -> Service and HTTP validation
  -> Ownership and authorised-scope validation
  -> Security relevance and evidence

Normalize case, trailing dots, wildcard records, internationalized names, ports, schemes, redirects, and aliases before deduplicating. A hostname resolving to a CDN, SaaS provider, cloud load balancer, or shared platform is not automatically owned by the assessed organization or in scope. Confirm ownership through the engagement scope, DNS authority, asset inventory, certificate context, application behavior, and the responsible provider where appropriate.

docs.title: Wildcard DNS and Historical Records
docs.text:
Query known-random labels to detect wildcard DNS before treating a resolved hostname as a real asset. Compare the answer, wildcard target, HTTP response, certificate, and application content with a known valid hostname. Wildcard resolution can make nonexistent names appear live and can produce misleading HTTP or takeover signals.

Historical, certificate, repository, search-engine, and passive-source results may identify retired or reassigned names. Preserve the source and timestamp, then revalidate DNS, HTTP, certificate, ownership, and scope before prioritising the asset.

docs.title: Takeover Candidate Versus Confirmed Condition
docs.text:
Do not treat an NXDOMAIN, dangling CNAME, provider-branded error page, or third-party service as a confirmed takeover. Validate the complete dependency:

DNS dependency
  -> Provider or service state
  -> Ownership and control validation
  -> Safe provider-specific confirmation
  -> Evidence and security conclusion

Use a harmless, provider-approved confirmation method only when explicitly authorised. Do not claim control, register a resource, or modify third-party infrastructure merely because a record appears dangling. Record DNS answers, CNAME chain, TTL, resolver and timestamp, HTTP/TLS behavior, provider error, scope decision, and the reason the condition is confirmed or remains a candidate.

docs.title: Evidence and Retesting
docs.text:
Store normalized candidate lists with source, discovery time, resolution result, HTTP status/title, technology indicators, ownership decision, scope status, and follow-up action. Keep raw tool output separately from the deduplicated assessment dataset. Troubleshoot inconsistent results by checking resolver differences, caching, split DNS, wildcard records, CDN behavior, rate limits, redirects, virtual hosts, and stale certificates.

Retest prioritized hosts after DNS, deployment, provider, or ownership changes. Confirm that a removed asset no longer resolves or serves the previous application, and confirm that legitimate assets remain in scope and reachable. Continue with Content Discovery, Technology Identification, HTTP Probing, and the relevant Web Attack Surface Analysis.
