docs.title: Why Signature Freshness Matters
docs.text:
Outdated security intelligence may reduce the endpoint's ability to detect known threats.

However, modern Defender protection also incorporates cloud and behavior-based capabilities, so signature age should not be treated as the entire protection model.

docs.title: Defender Version Information
docs.text:
Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object AMProductVersion,
                  AMEngineVersion,
                  AntivirusSignatureVersion,
                  AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated

docs.title: Example Evidence
docs.text:
Capture:

Product version

Engine version

Security intelligence version

Last update time

docs.title: Defender Service
docs.text:
Check:

Get-Service WinDefend -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Status   Name       DisplayName
------   ----       -----------
Running  WinDefend  Microsoft Defender Antivirus Service

docs.title: Important
docs.text: A running service alone does not prove all security features are correctly configured.

docs.title: Security Center
docs.text: On supported client systems, Windows Security Center can provide information about registered security products.

docs.title: Query Antivirus Products
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/SecurityCenter2 -ClassName AntivirusProduct -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object displayName,pathToSignedProductExe,pathToSignedReportingExe,productState

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
root/SecurityCenter2 is not available or meaningful in every Windows environment, particularly some server configurations.

Failure to query this namespace does not prove that no antivirus product exists.

docs.title: Third-Party Antivirus
docs.text:
A third-party antivirus product may change Defender's operating mode.

Therefore establish whether another security product is registered before interpreting Defender status.

docs.title: Defender Operating Mode
docs.text:
Depending on the endpoint configuration, Defender may operate differently when another antivirus product is installed.

Do not automatically report reduced Defender status as a vulnerability without establishing:

Whether another AV is active

Whether Defender for Endpoint is deployed

Whether passive mode is intentional

What the enterprise baseline requires

docs.title: Defender Exclusions
docs.text: Exclusions are one of the highest-value configuration areas to review.

docs.title: Why Exclusions Matter
docs.text:
Defender can exclude:

Paths

Processes

File extensions

IP addresses

depending on configuration and platform capabilities.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
Defender Protection
       |
       v
Exclusion
       |
       v
Reduced Inspection
       |
       v
Security-Sensitive Location?
       |
    +--+--+
    |     |
   No    Yes
    |     |
    v     v
Context  Investigate

docs.title: Path Exclusions
docs.text: (Get-MpPreference).ExclusionPath

docs.title: Process Exclusions
docs.text: (Get-MpPreference).ExclusionProcess

docs.title: Extension Exclusions
docs.text: (Get-MpPreference).ExclusionExtension

docs.title: IP Exclusions
docs.text:
Where available:

(Get-MpPreference).ExclusionIpAddress

docs.title: Combined Exclusion Summary
docs.text:
$pref = Get-MpPreference

[PSCustomObject]@{
    ExclusionPath      = ($pref.ExclusionPath -join '; ')
    ExclusionProcess   = ($pref.ExclusionProcess -join '; ')
    ExclusionExtension = ($pref.ExclusionExtension -join '; ')
    ExclusionIPAddress = ($pref.ExclusionIpAddress -join '; ')
}

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Access to exclusion information can be restricted by Defender configuration.

An empty or unavailable result does not always prove:

No exclusions exist

docs.title: Path Exclusion Assessment
docs.text:
For each path exclusion ask:

Why is it excluded?

Who can write there?

What files are stored there?

Do privileged applications execute from there?

Can standard users introduce content?

Is the exclusion broader than necessary?

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Cache

If this path is excluded, inspect:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Cache"

docs.title: Security Correlation
docs.text:
Defender Exclusion
       +
Standard-User Write Access
       +
Privileged Execution
       =
High-Value Review

docs.title: Do Not Report Every Exclusion
docs.text:
Some applications require documented exclusions for compatibility or performance.

The finding should be based on:

Unnecessary scope

Unsafe filesystem permissions

Security-sensitive use

Missing business justification

docs.title: Process Exclusions
docs.text:
A process exclusion should be reviewed carefully.

Ask:

Which executable is excluded?

Where is it installed?

Who can modify it?

Why is exclusion required?

Does it process untrusted content?

docs.title: Extension Exclusions
docs.text:
Broad exclusions such as an entire executable or script extension can materially reduce scanning coverage.

Review whether the exclusion is:

Necessary

Narrowly scoped

Centrally managed

Documented

docs.title: Wildcards and Broad Paths
docs.text:
Broad exclusions deserve additional scrutiny.

Conceptually:

C:\*

would be far more significant than a narrowly defined application cache directory.

docs.title: Filesystem Correlation
docs.text:
Always correlate security-sensitive exclusions with:

Windows Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Attack Surface Reduction
docs.text: Attack Surface Reduction - ASR - rules are designed to reduce common behaviors associated with malware and intrusion activity.

docs.title: ASR Configuration
docs.text:
Check:

Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids,
                  AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

docs.title: Display Rules
docs.text:
$pref = Get-MpPreference

for ($i = 0; $i -lt $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids.Count; $i++) {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        RuleId = $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids[$i]
        Action = $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions[$i]
    }
}

docs.title: Why Pair IDs and Actions?
docs.text:
The arrays correspond by index:

Rule ID 1 -> Action 1

Rule ID 2 -> Action 2

Rule ID 3 -> Action 3

docs.title: ASR Actions
docs.text:
ASR rules can support operating modes such as:

Disabled

Block

Audit

Warn

with exact supported behavior depending on the rule and platform.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not treat:

Audit

as equivalent to:

Block

docs.title: ASR Assessment Questions
docs.text:
For each rule determine:

Is it configured?

Which action applies?

Is it centrally managed?

Does the endpoint support it?

Is the rule producing events?

Does the organisation expect enforcement?

docs.title: ASR Exclusions
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-MpPreference).AttackSurfaceReductionOnlyExclusions

docs.title: Review Exclusions
docs.text:
ASR exclusions should be evaluated similarly to antivirus exclusions:

Business justification

Scope

Filesystem permissions

Privileged use

User-controlled content

docs.title: ASR Policy Matrix
docs.text:
A useful assessment table is:

Rule ID Configured Action Intended Action Result <GUID> Block Block Match <GUID> Audit Block Review <GUID> Not configured Block Review

docs.title: Avoid Memorising GUIDs in Reports
docs.text:
Where possible, map each rule GUID to its documented Microsoft rule name.

This makes findings easier to understand and maintain.

docs.title: Network Protection
docs.text:
Check:

Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object EnableNetworkProtection

docs.title: Security Purpose
docs.text: Network Protection extends Microsoft Defender SmartScreen-style reputation and network protection capabilities to supported applications and processes.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Determine whether the configured state matches the organisation's intended endpoint baseline.

docs.title: Controlled Folder Access
docs.text: Controlled Folder Access can help protect designated folders against unauthorized modifications by untrusted applications.

docs.title: Check Configuration
docs.text:
Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object EnableControlledFolderAccess

docs.title: Protected Folders
docs.text: (Get-MpPreference).ControlledFolderAccessProtectedFolders

docs.title: Allowed Applications
docs.text: (Get-MpPreference).ControlledFolderAccessAllowedApplications

docs.title: Assessment Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Is Controlled Folder Access enabled?

Which folders are protected?

Which applications are allowed?

Are exceptions broader than necessary?

Does the organisation require this feature?

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Controlled Folder Access being disabled is not automatically a vulnerability.

It must be evaluated against:

Threat model

Security baseline

Endpoint role

Other ransomware controls

docs.title: Defender Firewall
docs.text: Microsoft Defender Firewall is separate from Defender Antivirus but is part of the Windows security posture.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Get-NetFirewallProfile |
    Select-Object Name,Enabled,DefaultInboundAction,DefaultOutboundAction

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Name    Enabled
----    -------
Domain  True
Private True
Public  True

docs.title: Detailed Rules
docs.text:
Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName,Direction,Action,Profile

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
A complete firewall assessment deserves its own methodology.

For Defender assessment, record whether host firewall protection is active and whether obvious policy gaps affect the endpoint threat model.

docs.title: Defender Event Logs
docs.text:
The primary Defender operational log is:

Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational

docs.title: Recent Events
docs.text:
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational' -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,LevelDisplayName,Message

docs.title: List Defender Logs
docs.text:
Get-WinEvent -ListLog '*Defender*' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object LogName,RecordCount,IsEnabled

docs.title: Why Event Logs Matter
docs.text:
Events can provide evidence of:

Threat detection

Configuration changes

ASR actions

Protection changes

Scan activity

Security intelligence updates

docs.title: Event IDs
docs.text:
Microsoft documents specific event IDs for Defender Antivirus and ASR activity.

When reporting an event:

Record event ID

Timestamp

Message

Affected resource

Relevant policy

Do not rely on memorised event numbers without validating their meaning for the relevant Windows/Defender version.

docs.title: Defender Threat History
docs.text:
Query known threats:

Get-MpThreat -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Detection History
docs.text: Get-MpThreatDetection -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Selected Fields
docs.text:
Get-MpThreatDetection -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object InitialDetectionTime,
                  LastThreatStatusChangeTime,
                  ThreatID,
                  ActionSuccess,
                  Resources

docs.title: Sensitive Evidence
docs.text:
Detection history may contain:

Usernames

File paths

Network locations

Sensitive filenames

Handle assessment evidence appropriately.

docs.title: Scan Configuration
docs.text:
Review:

Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object ScanParameters,
                  ScanScheduleDay,
                  ScanScheduleTime,
                  RandomizeScheduleTaskTimes

docs.title: Scan Status
docs.text:
Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object QuickScanAge,
                  QuickScanStartTime,
                  QuickScanEndTime,
                  FullScanAge,
                  FullScanStartTime,
                  FullScanEndTime

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Scheduled scanning is one part of protection.

Real-time and behavior-based controls remain important even when periodic scans are configured.

docs.title: Safe Detection Validation
docs.text: A standard harmless validation mechanism for antivirus products is the EICAR anti-malware test file.

docs.title: EICAR
docs.text: The EICAR test file is specifically designed for antivirus testing and contains no malicious executable code.

docs.title: Recommended Approach
docs.text:
Use the official EICAR test mechanism only when:

The assessment scope permits antivirus validation

Operational teams understand the test

Alerting impact is acceptable

Evidence handling is agreed

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
A successful EICAR detection demonstrates:

The antivirus detection pipeline responded to the standard test pattern.

It does not prove:

Every real-world threat will be detected.

docs.title: Prefer Official Source
docs.text:
Use the official EICAR test file documentation rather than copying untrusted variants from random websites.

See the references at the end of this page.

docs.title: Detection Validation Model
docs.text:
Approved Test
     |
     v
Defender Inspection
     |
  +--+--+
  |     |
Detect No Detect
  |     |
  v     v
Capture Investigate
Event   Configuration

docs.title: Validation Evidence
docs.text:
Capture:

Test timestamp

Test location

Defender status

Detection event

Action taken

Relevant policy

Cleanup state

docs.title: Do Not Use Live Malware
docs.text: There is no need to deploy real malware merely to validate that Defender is operating.

docs.title: Defender and PowerShell
docs.text:
Defender can inspect PowerShell-related activity through multiple security mechanisms.

The endpoint may also use:

AMSI

Script scanning

ASR

PowerShell logging

Application control

EDR

docs.title: AMSI
docs.text: The Antimalware Scan Interface allows applications and services to integrate with antimalware products.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
Script / Content
      |
      v
AMSI-Aware Application
      |
      v
AMSI
      |
      v
Antimalware Provider
      |
      v
Allow / Detect

docs.title: Assessment Principle
docs.text:
Determine whether the endpoint's protection architecture is operating as intended.

Do not disable or patch AMSI as part of routine control validation.

docs.title: PowerShell Logging
docs.text:
PowerShell security monitoring can include:

Script Block Logging

Module Logging

Transcription

depending on enterprise policy.

docs.title: Registry Policy Review
docs.text:
Relevant PowerShell policy locations can be inspected where permitted.

Example:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Module Logging
docs.text: Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Transcription
docs.text: Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
PowerShell logging is not Defender Antivirus itself.

It is included here because endpoint detection quality frequently depends on several complementary Windows controls.

docs.title: Defender and Application Control
docs.text:
Defender and application control provide different security layers.

Application Control
       |
       v
Should this code run?

while antivirus/EDR asks questions more like:

Is this content or behavior malicious or suspicious?

docs.title: Combined Model
docs.text:
Executable
    |
    v
AppLocker / WDAC
    |
Allowed?
    |
    v
Defender / EDR
    |
Malicious?
    |
    v
Execution / Block / Alert

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Application Control

docs.title: Defender and Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
A Defender exclusion becomes much more important if:

The excluded directory is writable by standard users.

Check:

icacls "C:\ExcludedPath"

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Defender and Services
docs.text:
Security products operate through privileged services and drivers.

Do not modify Defender service permissions or service configuration during routine testing.

docs.title: Check Service
docs.text: Get-Service WinDefend -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Services

docs.title: Defender and Registry
docs.text:
Defender configuration can be influenced by:

Local policy

Group Policy

MDM

Microsoft security management platforms

Defender configuration

Avoid treating a single Registry key as the complete source of truth.

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Registry Security

docs.title: Enterprise Management
docs.text:
Defender settings may be centrally controlled through technologies such as:

Group Policy

Microsoft Intune

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Configuration Manager

Security management for Defender for Endpoint

docs.title: Assessment Principle
docs.text: Determine the authoritative management source before recommending configuration changes.

docs.title: Local vs Effective Configuration
docs.text:
A Registry value may exist locally but be overridden or protected by enterprise policy.

Prefer observed effective configuration where possible.

docs.title: Standard User Modification
docs.text:
An important security question is:

Can a standard user weaken Defender?

docs.title: Safe Assessment
docs.text:
Do not attempt to turn protections off.

Instead review:

ACLs

Policy ownership

Tamper protection

Command authorization

Observed configuration

docs.title: Expected Security Boundary
docs.text: Standard users should not be able to arbitrarily disable enterprise endpoint protection.

docs.title: Administrative Access
docs.text:
An administrator naturally has significantly greater system control.

The existence of administrator-accessible configuration is not by itself a vulnerability.

docs.title: Security Boundary
docs.text:
Focus on:

Unexpected lower-privileged control

rather than:

Administrator can administer the machine

docs.title: Defender Configuration Summary
docs.text:
A useful assessment summary:

$status = Get-MpComputerStatus
$pref = Get-MpPreference

[PSCustomObject]@{
    AMServiceEnabled              = $status.AMServiceEnabled
    AntivirusEnabled              = $status.AntivirusEnabled
    RealTimeProtectionEnabled     = $status.RealTimeProtectionEnabled
    BehaviorMonitorEnabled        = $status.BehaviorMonitorEnabled
    IoavProtectionEnabled         = $status.IoavProtectionEnabled
    NISEnabled                    = $status.NISEnabled
    TamperProtected               = $status.IsTamperProtected
    SignatureVersion              = $status.AntivirusSignatureVersion
    SignatureLastUpdated          = $status.AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated
    DisableRealtimeMonitoring     = $pref.DisableRealtimeMonitoring
    DisableBehaviorMonitoring     = $pref.DisableBehaviorMonitoring
    DisableScriptScanning         = $pref.DisableScriptScanning
    PUAProtection                 = $pref.PUAProtection
    NetworkProtection             = $pref.EnableNetworkProtection
    ControlledFolderAccess        = $pref.EnableControlledFolderAccess
}

docs.title: Exclusion Summary
docs.text:
$pref = Get-MpPreference

Write-Host "`n=== PATH EXCLUSIONS ==="
$pref.ExclusionPath

Write-Host "`n=== PROCESS EXCLUSIONS ==="
$pref.ExclusionProcess

Write-Host "`n=== EXTENSION EXCLUSIONS ==="
$pref.ExclusionExtension

Write-Host "`n=== ASR EXCLUSIONS ==="
$pref.AttackSurfaceReductionOnlyExclusions

docs.title: ASR Summary
docs.text:
$pref = Get-MpPreference

Write-Host "=== ATTACK SURFACE REDUCTION RULES ==="

if ($pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids) {
    for ($i = 0; $i -lt $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids.Count; $i++) {
        [PSCustomObject]@{
            RuleId = $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids[$i]
            Action = $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions[$i]
        }
    }
}
else {
    Write-Host "No ASR rules returned by Get-MpPreference."
}

docs.title: Comprehensive Read-Only Assessment
docs.text:
The following script collects useful Defender posture information without modifying Defender configuration.

Write-Host "========================================"
Write-Host " MICROSOFT DEFENDER SECURITY ASSESSMENT "
Write-Host "========================================"

Write-Host "`n=== CURRENT USER ==="
whoami

Write-Host "`n=== GROUPS ==="
whoami /groups

Write-Host "`n=== DEFENDER SERVICE ==="
Get-Service WinDefend -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Format-Table Status,Name,DisplayName -AutoSize

Write-Host "`n=== DEFENDER STATUS ==="

$status = Get-MpComputerStatus -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

if ($status) {
    $status |
        Select-Object AMServiceEnabled,
                      AntivirusEnabled,
                      AntispywareEnabled,
                      RealTimeProtectionEnabled,
                      BehaviorMonitorEnabled,
                      IoavProtectionEnabled,
                      NISEnabled,
                      OnAccessProtectionEnabled,
                      IsTamperProtected,
                      AMProductVersion,
                      AMEngineVersion,
                      AntivirusSignatureVersion,
                      AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated |
        Format-List
}
else {
    Write-Host "Get-MpComputerStatus did not return Defender status."
}

Write-Host "`n=== DEFENDER PREFERENCES ==="

$pref = Get-MpPreference -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

if ($pref) {
    $pref |
        Select-Object DisableRealtimeMonitoring,
                      DisableBehaviorMonitoring,
                      DisableIOAVProtection,
                      DisableScriptScanning,
                      DisableBlockAtFirstSeen,
                      MAPSReporting,
                      SubmitSamplesConsent,
                      PUAProtection,
                      EnableNetworkProtection,
                      EnableControlledFolderAccess |
        Format-List

    Write-Host "`n=== PATH EXCLUSIONS ==="
    $pref.ExclusionPath

    Write-Host "`n=== PROCESS EXCLUSIONS ==="
    $pref.ExclusionProcess

    Write-Host "`n=== EXTENSION EXCLUSIONS ==="
    $pref.ExclusionExtension

    Write-Host "`n=== ASR EXCLUSIONS ==="
    $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionOnlyExclusions

    Write-Host "`n=== ASR RULES ==="

    if ($pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids) {
        for ($i = 0; $i -lt $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids.Count; $i++) {
            [PSCustomObject]@{
                RuleId = $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids[$i]
                Action = $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions[$i]
            }
        }
    }
    else {
        Write-Host "No ASR rules returned."
    }
}
else {
    Write-Host "Get-MpPreference did not return Defender preferences."
}

Write-Host "`n=== DEFENDER EVENT LOG ==="

Get-WinEvent -ListLog 'Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object LogName,RecordCount,IsEnabled |
    Format-Table -AutoSize

Write-Host "`n=== RECENT DEFENDER EVENTS ==="

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational' -MaxEvents 20 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,LevelDisplayName,Message |
    Format-List

Write-Host "`n=== APPLICATION CONTROL CONTEXT ==="

Write-Host "PowerShell Language Mode:"
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Write-Host "`nAppLocker Collections:"

try {
    [xml]$appLocker = Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml -ErrorAction Stop

    $appLocker.AppLockerPolicy.RuleCollection |
        Select-Object Type,EnforcementMode |
        Format-Table -AutoSize
}
catch {
    Write-Host "Unable to retrieve effective AppLocker policy."
}

Write-Host "`n=== COMPLETE ==="

docs.title: What the Script Does
docs.text:
The script performs read-only collection of:

Identity

Groups

Defender service status

Antivirus status

Real-time protection

Behavior monitoring

Tamper protection

Engine/version information

Security intelligence information

Defender preferences

Exclusions

ASR configuration

Defender logging

PowerShell language mode

AppLocker context

docs.title: What the Script Does Not Do
docs.text:
It does not:

Disable Defender

Modify exclusions

Change ASR rules

Disable tamper protection

Change application-control policy

Create persistence

Modify security settings

docs.title: Evidence Collection Model
docs.text:
For every relevant Defender observation capture:

Configuration
      |
      v
Runtime Status
      |
      v
Relevant Policy
      |
      v
Validation Result
      |
      v
Event Log
      |
      v
Security Conclusion

docs.title: Finding - Real-Time Protection Disabled
docs.text:
Possible evidence:

RealTimeProtectionEnabled : False

Further validate:

Is another AV active?

Is Defender in passive mode?

Is this temporary?

Is the setting centrally managed?

What does the enterprise baseline require?

docs.title: Possible Finding Title
docs.text: Real-Time Antivirus Protection Is Not Active

docs.title: Do Not Overstate
docs.text:
Do not report:

The endpoint has no antivirus protection.

unless you have established that no alternative protection exists.

docs.title: Finding - Tamper Protection Disabled
docs.text:
Possible observation:

IsTamperProtected : False

docs.title: Further Validation
docs.text:
Determine:

Is Defender for Endpoint deployed?

Is tamper protection required by policy?

Can a standard user alter security settings?

Are settings protected through another management mechanism?

docs.title: Possible Finding Title
docs.text: Microsoft Defender Tamper Protection Is Not Enabled

docs.title: Finding - Broad Defender Exclusion
docs.text:
Example:

ExclusionPath:
C:\CompanyData

and:

BUILTIN\Users:
Modify

docs.title: Further Validation
docs.text:
Determine:

What is stored there?

Why is it excluded?

Does executable content exist there?

Do privileged processes consume content there?

Can the exclusion be narrowed?

docs.title: Possible Finding Title
docs.text: Microsoft Defender Exclusion Covers a Standard-User-Writable Directory

docs.title: Finding - ASR Audit Instead of Block
docs.text:
Observation:

Required ASR rule:
Audit

Enterprise baseline:

Block

docs.title: Possible Finding Title
docs.text: Attack Surface Reduction Rule Is Configured in Audit Mode Instead of Block Mode

docs.title: Finding - Outdated Security Intelligence
docs.text:
Observation:

AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated:
Significantly older than expected baseline

docs.title: Further Validation
docs.text:
Check:

Internet/connectivity status

Update infrastructure

Management policy

Platform update status

Cloud protection

docs.title: Possible Finding Title
docs.text: Microsoft Defender Security Intelligence Is Outdated

docs.title: Finding - Defender Logging Disabled
docs.text: If the operational log required by the organisation is unavailable or disabled, this can reduce detection and investigation capability.

docs.title: Possible Finding Title
docs.text: Microsoft Defender Operational Logging Is Not Available

docs.title: Finding - Weak Exclusion and Privileged Consumer
docs.text:
Strong chain:

Standard User
      |
      v
Writable Directory
      |
      v
Defender Exclusion
      |
      v
Privileged Service Dependency
      |
      v
Reduced Security Inspection

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
The exclusion itself does not automatically prove privilege escalation.

You must still establish the privileged execution or processing path.

docs.title: False Positive - Defender Disabled Because Another AV Is Active
docs.text: If enterprise-approved third-party antivirus is providing primary protection, Defender Antivirus may intentionally operate differently.

docs.title: False Positive - Controlled Folder Access Disabled
docs.text: Controlled Folder Access is not mandatory in every endpoint architecture.

docs.title: False Positive - No ASR Rules Returned
docs.text:
This requires investigation.

Possible explanations include:

No ASR policy configured

Insufficient visibility

Different management architecture

Unsupported configuration

Policy not applied

docs.title: False Positive - Empty Exclusions
docs.text:
An empty result does not always guarantee there are no exclusions.

Access and management architecture can affect visibility.

docs.title: False Positive - FullLanguage PowerShell
docs.text:
FullLanguage

does not mean:

Defender is disabled

PowerShell language mode and antivirus protection are separate security controls.

docs.title: False Positive - Defender Service Running
docs.text:
Likewise:

WinDefend = Running

does not prove:

All protections are enabled

docs.title: False Positive - One Detection Test Succeeds
docs.text:
A successful standard antivirus test proves that specific detection path worked.

It does not establish comprehensive endpoint security effectiveness.

docs.title: Alternative Explanations
docs.text:
Unexpected Defender configuration may result from:

Third-party antivirus

Passive mode

Troubleshooting

Legacy compatibility

Application vendor exclusions

VDI configuration

Server workload requirements

Performance requirements

Central security policy

docs.title: Reporting Principle
docs.text:
Do not report:

Configuration differs from personal preference

as:

Security vulnerability

Compare observations against:

Vendor guidance

Organisational baseline

Threat model

Compensating controls

Actual security impact

docs.title: Remediation - Real-Time Protection
docs.text: Where Defender is the intended primary antivirus, ensure real-time protection is enabled and centrally managed.

docs.title: Remediation - Tamper Protection
docs.text: Enable tamper protection where supported and appropriate to the organisation's endpoint security architecture.

docs.title: Remediation - Exclusions
docs.text:
Remove unnecessary exclusions.

Where exclusions are required:

Keep them narrow

Document the business justification

Protect excluded paths with strong ACLs

Avoid excluding broad executable locations

Review them periodically

docs.title: Remediation - ASR
docs.text:
Deploy appropriate ASR rules based on:

Microsoft guidance

Application compatibility

Enterprise risk

docs.title: Remediation - Cloud Protection
docs.text: Where supported by organisational requirements, configure cloud-delivered protection and related security intelligence capabilities according to Microsoft's security baseline guidance.

docs.title: Remediation - Security Intelligence
docs.text: Ensure Defender security intelligence updates occur through the approved enterprise update mechanism.

docs.title: Remediation - Logging
docs.text: Forward relevant Defender events to central monitoring where appropriate.

docs.title: Remediation - Least Privilege
docs.text: Standard users should not be able to weaken endpoint security controls.

docs.title: Remediation - Filesystem
docs.text:
Secure directories covered by Defender exclusions.

Review:

Windows Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: Remediation - Application Control
docs.text:
Use application control as a complementary control.

Review:

Windows Application Control

docs.title: Remediation - Central Management
docs.text: Manage Defender through the organisation's authoritative security-management platform where applicable.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: Retesting should reproduce the original observation under the same security context.

docs.title: Step 1 - Identity
docs.text: whoami

docs.title: Step 2 - Defender Status
docs.text:

    Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,
                  RealTimeProtectionEnabled,

                  IsTamperProtected

docs.title: Step 3 - Preferences

docs.title: Step 4 - Exclusions
docs.text:
$pref = Get-MpPreference

$pref.ExclusionPath
$pref.ExclusionProcess
$pref.ExclusionExtension

docs.title: Step 5 - ASR
docs.text:
$pref = Get-MpPreference

for ($i = 0; $i -lt $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids.Count; $i++) {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        RuleId = $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids[$i]
        Action = $pref.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions[$i]
    }
}

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational' -MaxEvents 20 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,LevelDisplayName,Message

docs.title: Step 9 - Safe Detection Validation
docs.text: Where explicitly approved, repeat the standard harmless antivirus validation used during the original assessment.

docs.title: Step 10 - Business Functionality
docs.text: Confirm that required applications continue to function after Defender hardening.

Check status and configuration

Get-MpComputerStatus and Get-MpPreference answer different questions. Review both so that configured preferences can be compared with the endpoint's observed protection state.

Prioritise exclusions

Defender exclusions deserve careful review, particularly when an excluded path is writable by standard users or contains content consumed by privileged applications.

Correlate Defender with application control

Defender Antivirus, AppLocker and WDAC provide different security functions. Evaluate them together rather than assuming that one control replaces the others.

Distinguish audit from enforcement

ASR rules operating in audit mode provide useful telemetry but should not be described as actively blocking the associated behaviour.

Do not disable protection to test protection

A normal endpoint assessment does not require disabling Defender, tamper protection, AMSI or EDR. Configuration inspection, event analysis and approved harmless validation provide stronger and safer evidence.

Defender status requires context

Defender Antivirus may intentionally operate differently when another enterprise antivirus product is active or when Defender is deployed in a different operating mode. Establish the complete endpoint protection architecture before reporting a configuration as vulnerable.

docs.title: Windows Enumeration
docs.text:
Windows enumeration is the process of systematically identifying the configuration, security context, software, services, network exposure, permissions, security controls, and other characteristics of a Windows host during an authorised security assessment.

The objective is not to execute every available command. The objective is to understand the system well enough to identify meaningful security relationships and determine which areas require deeper investigation.

A useful Windows enumeration process should answer questions such as:

  • Which user context am I operating under?
  • Is the process elevated?
  • Which groups and privileges are assigned?
  • Which Windows version and architecture are running?
  • Is the host joined to Active Directory?
  • Which users and groups exist?
  • Which processes and services are running?
  • Which ports are listening?
  • Which software is installed?
  • Which scheduled tasks exist?
  • Which directories and files are writable?
  • Which security controls are active?
  • Are credentials or secrets exposed?
  • Can a lower-privileged user influence resources used by privileged processes?

docs.title: Enumeration Methodology
docs.text:
A structured approach reduces missed attack surface.

Current Security Context
        |
        v
Operating System
        |
        v
Domain Membership
        |
        v
Users and Groups
        |
        v
Privileges
        |

        |

        |

        |
        v
Filesystem and Registry

        |

        |

Privilege Escalation Analysis

Enumeration should progressively build a model of the host rather than produce disconnected command output.

docs.title: 1. Current User
docs.text:
Start by determining the current identity.

whoami

Example:

corp\asif

Display the SID:

whoami /user

Display group membership:

whoami /groups

Display assigned privileges:

whoami /priv

Display everything:

whoami /all

PowerShell alternatives:

$env:USERNAME
$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:COMPUTERNAME

Windows identity:

[System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()

Current Windows principal:

$identity = [System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
$principal = New-Object System.Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal($identity)
$principal

docs.title: 2. Determine Administrative Context
docs.text:
Do not assume that membership in the local Administrators group means the current process is elevated.

Check group membership:

whoami /groups

Look for:

BUILTIN\Administrators

PowerShell:

$principal = New-Object Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal([Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent())
$principal.IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)

Possible output:

True

or:

False

Administrative membership and process elevation are related but not identical because User Account Control can result in filtered access tokens.

docs.title: 3. Integrity Level
docs.text:
The integrity level helps determine the security context of the current process.

whoami /groups

Look for entries such as:

Mandatory Label\Low Mandatory Level
Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level
Mandatory Label\High Mandatory Level
Mandatory Label\System Mandatory Level

Typical interpretation:

Integrity Level Typical Context Low Restricted or sandboxed process Medium Standard interactive user High Elevated administrator System SYSTEM-level process

Integrity level should be recorded when validating privilege escalation findings.

docs.title: 4. Operating System Information
docs.text:
Basic system information:

systeminfo

Useful information includes:

OS Name
OS Version
System Type
Hotfixes
Domain
Logon Server
Boot Time

PowerShell:

Get-ComputerInfo

Focused output:

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsBuildNumber, OsArchitecture

CIM:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem

Focused CIM output:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture

Simple version check:

ver

docs.title: 5. Architecture
docs.text:
Command Prompt:

echo %PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE%

PowerShell:

$env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE

Check whether the operating system is 64-bit:

[Environment]::Is64BitOperatingSystem

Check whether the current process is 64-bit:

[Environment]::Is64BitProcess

The distinction can matter when interacting with registry redirection, filesystem redirection, and architecture-specific applications.

docs.title: 6. Hostname
docs.text:
hostname

PowerShell:

$env:COMPUTERNAME

Alternative:

[System.Net.Dns]::GetHostName()

docs.title: 7. Domain Membership
docs.text:
Determine whether the computer is domain joined.

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain

Useful environment variables:

$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:LOGONSERVER

Command Prompt:

echo %USERDOMAIN%
echo %LOGONSERVER%

System information:

systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"Domain"

If PartOfDomain is True, continue domain-specific enumeration using the Active Directory Enumeration notes.

docs.title: 8. Local Users
docs.text:
Command Prompt:

net user

PowerShell:

Get-LocalUser

Detailed output:

Get-LocalUser | Format-Table Name, Enabled, LastLogon, PasswordRequired, PasswordExpires

Specific user:

Get-LocalUser -Name "Administrator"

Useful properties include:

Enabled
LastLogon
PasswordRequired
PasswordExpires
UserMayChangePassword
SID

Look for:

  • Unexpected local accounts
  • Enabled built-in Administrator accounts
  • Support accounts
  • Deployment accounts
  • Service-related accounts
  • Accounts with unusual password configuration

The presence of an account alone does not constitute a vulnerability.

docs.title: 9. Local Groups
docs.text:
Command Prompt:

net localgroup

PowerShell:

Get-LocalGroup

Enumerate administrators:

net localgroup Administrators

PowerShell:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators"

Other groups that may be relevant include:

Remote Desktop Users
Remote Management Users
Backup Operators
Hyper-V Administrators
Event Log Readers
Performance Log Users

Enumerate a particular group:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Remote Desktop Users"

docs.title: 10. Windows Privileges
docs.text:
Enumerate privileges:

whoami /priv

Privileges worth understanding include:

SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege
SeBackupPrivilege
SeCreateTokenPrivilege
SeDebugPrivilege
SeImpersonatePrivilege
SeLoadDriverPrivilege
SeManageVolumePrivilege
SeRestorePrivilege
SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege
SeTcbPrivilege

Example output:

Privilege Name                Description                          State
============================= ==================================== ========
SeChangeNotifyPrivilege       Bypass traverse checking             Enabled
SeImpersonatePrivilege        Impersonate a client after auth      Enabled

A privilege being listed does not automatically mean that exploitation is possible.

Consider:

Privilege
    |
    v
Enabled or Disabled?
    |
    v
Current Account
    |
    v
Current Integrity Level
    |
    v
Relevant Service / Resource
    |
    v
Practical Security Impact

docs.text:
Command Prompt:

set

PowerShell:

Useful individual values:

$env:USERNAME
$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:COMPUTERNAME
$env:USERPROFILE
$env:APPDATA

Any discovered secret should be handled as sensitive assessment evidence.

Get-NetAdapter

  • Multiple interfaces
  • VPN adapters
  • Management networks
  • Virtual interfaces
  • Internal-only networks
  • DNS servers
  • DHCP configuration
  • Default gateways

docs.text:
Command Prompt:

route print

Get-NetRoute

The routing table can reveal networks reachable from the compromised or assessed host that may not be reachable directly from the tester's original network position.

arp -a

The ARP or neighbour cache can help identify recently contacted systems on directly connected networks.

docs.title: 15. DNS Configuration
docs.text:
ipconfig /all

Get-DnsClientServerAddress

ipconfig /displaydns

PowerShell:

Get-DnsClientCache

Get-DnsClient

Domain environments often expose useful infrastructure relationships through DNS.

docs.title: 16. Proxy Configuration
docs.text:
WinHTTP proxy:

netsh winhttp show proxy

User-level proxy configuration can also be reviewed through Windows settings and relevant registry locations where authorised.

PowerShell environment variables:

Get-ChildItem Env: | Where-Object Name -Match 'proxy'

Proxy configuration can affect:

  • Outbound connectivity
  • Tool behaviour
  • Application traffic
  • Update mechanisms
  • Security monitoring

docs.title: 17. Listening Ports
docs.text:
Command Prompt:

netstat -ano

Listening ports only:

netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING

PowerShell:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

Display useful fields:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

Map listeners to processes:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        LocalAddress = $_.LocalAddress
        LocalPort = $_.LocalPort
        PID = $_.OwningProcess
        Process = (Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).ProcessName
    }
}

This helps answer:

What is listening?
        |
        v
Which process owns it?
        |
        v
Which service owns the process?
        |
        v
Which account runs the service?
        |
        v
Who can reach the port?

docs.title: 18. Active Network Connections
docs.text:
netstat -ano

PowerShell:

Get-NetTCPConnection

Established connections:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established

Useful output:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, RemoteAddress, RemotePort, OwningProcess

Active connections can reveal:

  • Management servers
  • Database servers
  • Proxy infrastructure
  • Internal applications
  • Monitoring systems
  • Domain controllers
  • Backup infrastructure

docs.title: 19. Windows Firewall
docs.text:
Command Prompt:

netsh advfirewall show allprofiles

PowerShell:

Get-NetFirewallProfile

Enabled firewall rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True

Allow rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True -Action Allow

Block rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True -Action Block

Firewall rules should be interpreted together with actual listeners and network reachability.

An allow rule without a listening service may have little immediate security impact.

docs.title: 20. Running Processes
docs.text:
Command Prompt:

tasklist

Verbose output:

tasklist /v

PowerShell:

Get-Process

Selected properties:

Get-Process | Select-Object Id, ProcessName, Path

Some process paths may require elevated permissions.

Process enumeration can identify:

Endpoint security software
Backup agents
Management agents
Web servers
Database software
Development tools
Remote access software
Custom applications
Administrative tools

Correlate processes with services and network listeners.

docs.title: 21. Process Command Lines
docs.text:
CIM can provide process command lines:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CommandLine

Search for a particular process:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object Name -Like "*java*" | Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CommandLine

Command lines can expose:

  • Configuration file locations
  • Service arguments
  • Application paths
  • Network endpoints
  • Operational parameters

Treat credentials or tokens exposed in command lines as sensitive information.

docs.title: 22. Services
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-Service

CIM provides more useful security information:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service

Focused output:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, StartName, PathName

Running services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object State -eq "Running" | Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

Services running as LocalSystem:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object StartName -eq "LocalSystem" | Select-Object Name, State, PathName

Other highly privileged contexts can include:

LocalSystem
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
LocalService
NetworkService
Privileged domain service accounts

A privileged service is not automatically vulnerable.

The key question is whether a lower-privileged user can influence:

Service configuration
Executable
Executable directory
DLL
Configuration file
Script
Registry key
Other consumed resource

See Windows Services.

docs.title: 23. Service Paths
docs.text:
Display service paths:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

Filter for non-empty paths:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object PathName | Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

When reviewing service paths, investigate:

  • Executable permissions
  • Parent directory permissions
  • Service configuration permissions
  • Quoting
  • Arguments
  • Referenced configuration files

Do not report a suspicious-looking service path without confirming the required conditions and practical impact.

docs.title: 24. Service Permissions
docs.text:
Windows service security descriptors can be queried with:

sc sdshow ServiceName

Example:

sc sdshow Spooler

The output uses Security Descriptor Definition Language.

For assessment purposes, determine whether untrusted principals have permissions capable of modifying the service or influencing its execution.

Potentially sensitive service rights include the ability to:

Change configuration
Start service
Stop service
Delete service
Modify security

Use tools such as Sysinternals AccessChk where permitted for easier interpretation.

docs.title: 25. Installed Software
docs.text:
Registry-based enumeration is usually preferable to Win32_Product.

64-bit applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

32-bit applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

Current-user applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

Review software for:

  • Unsupported applications
  • Old management clients
  • Backup software
  • Database software
  • Development tools
  • Remote management utilities
  • Deployment software
  • Custom enterprise applications

Version information should be validated before associating software with a vulnerability.

docs.title: 26. Hotfixes
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-HotFix

CIM:

Get-CimInstance Win32_QuickFixEngineering

Basic system information also displays hotfix information:

systeminfo

Patch enumeration can help prioritise investigation, but missing individual KB identifiers should not automatically be treated as proof of vulnerability because Windows servicing and cumulative updates can complicate direct KB comparisons.

docs.title: 27. Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Command Prompt:

schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

Display task names and paths:

Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object TaskPath, TaskName, State

Actions:

Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        TaskName = $_.TaskName
        TaskPath = $_.TaskPath
        User = $_.Principal.UserId
        RunLevel = $_.Principal.RunLevel
        Actions = ($_.Actions | ForEach-Object { "$($_.Execute) $($_.Arguments)" }) -join "; "
    }
}

Investigate tasks that:

Run with elevated privileges
        +
Reference modifiable files
        =
Potential privilege boundary

Confirm filesystem permissions before reporting.

docs.title: 28. Startup Programs
docs.text:
CIM:

Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select-Object Name, Command, Location, User

Common registry locations:

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce

PowerShell:

Get-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Also consider Sysinternals Autoruns for comprehensive startup analysis.

docs.title: 29. Filesystem Drives
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Command Prompt:

fsutil fsinfo drives

fsutil functionality may depend on the current privileges and Windows configuration.

CIM:

Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk | Select-Object DeviceID, DriveType, FileSystem, Size, FreeSpace

Additional drives may contain:

  • Application data
  • Backups
  • Deployment files
  • Configuration
  • User data
  • Logs
  • Sensitive operational information

docs.title: 30. Directory Permissions
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Path"

Readable format:

(Get-Acl "C:\Path").Access

Example:

Get-Acl "C:\ProgramData\Example" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Command Prompt:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Example"

Look for permissions assigned to broad principals such as:

Everyone
BUILTIN\Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Users

Potentially important rights include:

Write
Modify
FullControl

The presence of write access should lead to additional analysis rather than an immediate vulnerability conclusion.

docs.title: 31. Writable Directory Validation
docs.text:
A controlled write test can confirm whether the current user can actually create files.

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID.tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Host "[+] Write succeeded: $file"
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}
catch {
    Write-Host "[-] Write failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}

This test only validates write access.

It does not prove privilege escalation.

Continue by determining whether a privileged process consumes resources from the writable location.

docs.title: 32. Search for Writable Service Locations
docs.text:
Enumerate service paths first:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

For a candidate service, inspect the executable and its parent directory:

Get-Acl "C:\Program Files\Example"

or:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Example"

Assessment logic:

Writable directory?
      |
      v
Privileged service resource?
      |
      v
Can current user modify relevant content?
      |
      v
Does service actually consume that content?
      |
      v
Can impact be safely demonstrated?

docs.title: 33. Interesting Files
docs.text:
Potentially relevant file types include:

*.config
*.ini
*.xml
*.json
*.yml
*.yaml
*.ps1
*.bat
*.cmd
*.vbs
*.txt

Search should be targeted rather than indiscriminately scanning an entire host.

Example:

Get-ChildItem "C:\ProgramData\Example" -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Search filenames within an authorised application directory:

Get-ChildItem "C:\Application" -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object Name -Match 'password|credential|secret|token|config'

Avoid unnecessarily exposing sensitive data during broad searches.

docs.title: 34. PowerShell History
docs.text:
Determine the PSReadLine history location:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Read the history:

Get-Content (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Common history location:

%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt

Potentially interesting history entries include:

Administrative commands
Deployment commands
Network paths
Authentication operations
Configuration changes
Application administration

Any credentials or secrets discovered should be handled carefully.

docs.title: 35. User Profiles
docs.text:
List profiles:

Get-ChildItem C:\Users

Profile information:

Get-CimInstance Win32_UserProfile | Select-Object LocalPath, Loaded, Special

User profiles can contain:

PowerShell history
Application configuration
SSH configuration
Browser data
Scripts
Logs
Development configuration
Cloud CLI configuration

Access should remain within the authorised assessment scope.

docs.title: 36. Credential Manager
docs.text:
List stored credentials:

cmdkey /list

This can reveal the existence and target of stored credentials.

Do not assume that listed credentials are directly recoverable.

Assess:

Credential target
Credential type
Current user context
Associated application
Potential security relevance

See Windows Credentials.

docs.title: 37. Registry
docs.text:
List registry drives:

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider Registry

Common locations:

HKLM:\SOFTWARE
HKLM:\SYSTEM
HKCU:\Software

Example:

Get-ChildItem HKLM:\SOFTWARE

Specific key:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion"

Registry enumeration can identify:

Application configuration
Startup configuration
Service configuration
Security settings
Installed software
Paths
User preferences

docs.title: 38. Registry Permissions
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-Acl "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example"

Readable access entries:

(Get-Acl "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example").Access

The relevant question is whether an untrusted principal can modify configuration that influences a more privileged security context.

docs.title: 39. PowerShell Version
docs.text:
$PSVersionTable

Important fields include:

PSVersion
PSEdition
BuildVersion
CLRVersion
WSManStackVersion

PowerShell version can affect available features, logging capabilities, and compatibility with assessment commands.

docs.title: 40. PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible values:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

FullLanguage should not automatically be reported as a vulnerability.

Language Mode should be assessed together with:

WDAC
AppLocker
PowerShell policy
Endpoint security
User privilege level
System purpose

In hardened environments, Constrained Language Mode may form part of a broader application-control strategy.

docs.title: 41. PowerShell Execution Policy
docs.text:
Get-ExecutionPolicy

All scopes:

Get-ExecutionPolicy -List

Execution Policy is primarily a script-execution safety feature and should not be treated as a strong security boundary by itself.

Do not report RemoteSigned, Unrestricted, or another execution policy as a standalone vulnerability without relevant security context.

docs.title: 42. Microsoft Defender Status
docs.text:
Where available:

Get-MpComputerStatus

Focused output:

Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AntivirusEnabled, AntispywareEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, BehaviorMonitorEnabled, IoavProtectionEnabled

Additional useful properties:

Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMServiceEnabled, AntivirusEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, NISEnabled

Defender preferences:

Get-MpPreference

During normal assessment, prefer inspection over modification of defensive controls.

docs.title: 43. Microsoft Defender Version Information
docs.text:
Where supported:

Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMProductVersion, AMEngineVersion, AntivirusSignatureVersion, AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated

This can help document:

Platform version
Engine version
Signature version
Signature age

Version information alone does not demonstrate a vulnerability.

docs.title: 44. Defender Exclusions
docs.text:
Where permissions allow:

Get-MpPreference | Select-Object ExclusionPath, ExclusionProcess, ExclusionExtension

Exclusions should be assessed carefully.

An exclusion may be legitimate, but overly broad exclusions can reduce endpoint protection coverage.

Do not alter exclusions during routine enumeration.

docs.title: 45. Attack Surface Reduction Rules
docs.text:
Where Microsoft Defender cmdlets are available:

Get-MpPreference | Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids, AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

For easier inspection:

$p = Get-MpPreference

for ($i = 0; $i -lt $p.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids.Count; $i++) {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        RuleId = $p.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids[$i]
        Action = $p.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions[$i]
    }
}

Interpret the returned actions in the context of the Windows version and management platform being used.

ASR should be considered together with endpoint protection and application control.

docs.title: 46. AppLocker Effective Policy
docs.text:
Retrieve the effective policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Rule collections:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections

Summary:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections | Select-Object CollectionType, EnforcementMode

Possible collection types include:

Exe
Msi
Script
Dll
Appx

A collection being present does not necessarily mean it is effectively restricting the file being tested.

docs.title: 47. AppLocker File Testing
docs.text:
Test a specific executable:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective | Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\wscript.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Test a script:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective | Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:TEMP\test.ps1" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Detailed result:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:TEMP\test.ps1" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME" |
    Format-List FilePath, PolicyDecision, MatchingRule

Possible results may include:

Allowed
Denied
DeniedByDefault

Always evaluate the effective decision for the current user and exact path.

docs.title: 48. AppLocker Path Rules
docs.text:
Inspect effective rules:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections | ForEach-Object {
    $_.Rules
}

Path-based allow rules deserve particular attention.

For example, an administrator may intentionally allow:

%WINDIR%\*
%PROGRAMFILES%\*

The presence of a broad path rule does not automatically represent a bypass.

Determine whether lower-privileged users can write into locations covered by the rule.

The important relationship is:

Allowed path
      +
User-writable location
      +
Executable content
      =
Potential application-control weakness

All conditions should be validated.

docs.title: 49. Windows Defender Application Control
docs.text:
WDAC configuration can vary significantly by Windows release and enterprise management configuration.

Potential indicators can be inspected through Windows security and Code Integrity configuration.

Useful areas include:

Code Integrity policies
Event logs
Application Control policies
Enterprise management configuration

Do not assume that the absence of one PowerShell class or utility means WDAC is not deployed.

Evaluate multiple sources of evidence.

docs.title: 50. Code Integrity Event Logs
docs.text:
List relevant logs:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *CodeIntegrity* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

A commonly relevant log is:

Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational

Inspect recent events:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational" -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Code Integrity events can provide useful evidence regarding application-control enforcement and blocked execution.

docs.title: 51. AppLocker Event Logs
docs.text:
List AppLocker logs:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *AppLocker* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Relevant channels can include:

Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL
Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script
Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/Packaged app-Deployment
Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/Packaged app-Execution

Example:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL" -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Event logs can help confirm whether application-control decisions are actually being enforced.

docs.title: 52. AMSI Context
docs.text:
AMSI should be evaluated as one component of the Windows defensive architecture.

Relevant areas include:

PowerShell
Microsoft Defender
Third-party endpoint security
Script hosts
Application control
Logging

Avoid interpreting AMSI as a binary "enabled" or "disabled" control solely from whether a particular command executes.

Observed behaviour should be correlated with endpoint-security configuration and telemetry.

docs.title: 53. Windows Event Logs
docs.text:
List logs:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *

Security log:

Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -MaxEvents 20

System log:

Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 20

PowerShell operational log:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" -MaxEvents 20 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Relevant logging areas can include:

Authentication
Process creation
PowerShell
Service creation
Scheduled tasks
Application control
Code Integrity
Endpoint security

Access to some event logs may require additional privileges.

docs.title: 54. PowerShell Logging
docs.text:
PowerShell logging configuration may include:

Script Block Logging
Module Logging
Transcription
Operational event logging

Relevant registry locations can include:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell
HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell

Inspect where accessible:

Get-ChildItem "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell" -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Do not conclude that PowerShell is unmonitored solely because one logging mechanism is absent.

Enterprise EDR products may provide additional telemetry.

docs.title: 55. SMB Configuration
docs.text:
Server SMB configuration:

Get-SmbServerConfiguration

Client configuration:

Get-SmbClientConfiguration

Shares:

Get-SmbShare

Command Prompt:

net share

Relevant security properties can include:

SMB signing
Encryption
Protocol versions
Share permissions
Filesystem permissions
Guest access

For domain-specific SMB testing, see SMB.

docs.title: 56. Local Shares
docs.text:
net share

PowerShell:

Get-SmbShare

Share access:

Get-SmbShareAccess -Name "ShareName"

Share permissions must be considered together with NTFS permissions.

Effective access is influenced by both layers.

docs.title: 57. Remote Desktop Configuration
docs.text:
Determine whether Remote Desktop services are present:

Get-Service TermService

Listening port:

Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3389 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Relevant group:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Remote Desktop Users" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

RDP exposure should be assessed in the context of:

Network reachability
Authentication requirements
NLA configuration
User permissions
Firewall rules
MFA or gateway controls

docs.title: 58. WinRM
docs.text:
Service status:

Get-Service WinRM

Configuration:

winrm get winrm/config

Listeners:

winrm enumerate winrm/config/listener

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem WSMan:\localhost\Listener -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

WinRM is commonly used for legitimate remote administration and is not inherently a vulnerability.

Assess access controls and network exposure.

For domain use, see WinRM.

docs.title: 59. WMI and CIM
docs.text:
Operating system:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem

Computer system:

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem

Processes:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process

Services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service

Logical disks:

Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk

CIM is generally preferable to older WMI cmdlets for modern PowerShell usage.

docs.title: 60. Named Pipes
docs.text:
Named pipes can expose useful information about applications and services.

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem \\.\pipe\

Named pipes may reveal:

Database software
Browser components
Remote administration tools
Security software
Application IPC

A named pipe being present does not imply that it is exploitable.

Permissions and application behaviour must be investigated separately.

docs.title: 61. Current Sessions
docs.text:
Command Prompt:

query user

Alternative:

qwinsta

These commands can reveal currently logged-on interactive or remote users where permissions permit.

Session information may help identify:

  • Administrative activity
  • RDP usage
  • Multi-user systems
  • Operational context

Avoid disrupting active user sessions during testing.

docs.title: 62. Logged-On User
docs.text:
whoami

Console user information may also be available through:

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object UserName

The current process identity and console user may differ.

This distinction can matter on servers and systems accessed through remote administration mechanisms.

docs.title: 63. Time and Time Zone
docs.text:
time /t
date /t

PowerShell:

Get-Date

Time zone:

Get-TimeZone

Accurate host time is important when correlating:

Assessment actions
Event logs
EDR telemetry
Network logs
Authentication events
Screenshots

Record time-zone differences during evidence collection.

docs.title: 64. Security Products
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender:

Get-MpComputerStatus -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Running services can provide additional indicators:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object State -eq "Running" | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, StartName

Running processes:

Get-Process | Select-Object ProcessName, Id

Do not attempt to terminate, disable, or tamper with security software unless the assessment scope explicitly authorises that activity.

docs.title: 65. Automated Enumeration
docs.text:
Automated tools can improve coverage.

Useful tools include:

Seatbelt
SharpUp
PrivescCheck
WinPEAS
Sysinternals

docs.title: Seatbelt
docs.text:
Seatbelt

Seatbelt can collect information about:

Operating system
Users
Processes
Services
Security controls
Interesting files
Windows configuration

docs.title: SharpUp
docs.text:
SharpUp

SharpUp focuses on Windows privilege escalation enumeration.

docs.title: PrivescCheck
docs.text:
PrivescCheck

PrivescCheck performs extensive PowerShell-based privilege escalation checks.

docs.title: WinPEAS
docs.text:
PEASS-ng

WinPEAS provides broad Windows enumeration.

Automated results should always be manually validated.

docs.title: 66. Sysinternals
docs.text:
Microsoft Sysinternals provides several useful assessment and troubleshooting utilities.

Microsoft Sysinternals

Useful utilities include:

Tool Purpose Autoruns Startup and persistence enumeration AccessChk Permission analysis Process Explorer Process investigation Process Monitor Runtime filesystem, registry, and process monitoring TCPView Network connection analysis Sigcheck File signature and metadata inspection Strings String extraction PsExec Administrative remote/process execution utility

Use tools only where authorised and appropriate to the assessment.

docs.title: 67. AccessChk
docs.text:
AccessChk can assist with permission analysis.

Examples of resources that may be reviewed include:

Files
Directories
Registry keys
Services
Named pipes
Processes

AccessChk

Automated permission output should be correlated with the actual security context and resource usage.

docs.title: 68. Correlating Enumeration Results
docs.text:
The most important part of enumeration is correlation.

Example:

Service Enumeration
        |
        v
Service runs as SYSTEM
        |
        v
Executable located in custom directory
        |
        v
Directory ACL inspected
        |
        v
Standard user has Modify
        |
        v
Service consumes modifiable resource
        |
        v
Potential privilege escalation

Another example:

Listening Port
        |
        v
Owning PID
        |
        v
Process
        |
        v
Service
        |
        v
Service Account
        |
        v
Configuration / Permissions

Individual observations become meaningful when relationships are established.

docs.title: 69. What Not to Report Automatically
docs.text:
Avoid automatically reporting observations such as:

PowerShell FullLanguage is enabled
rundll32.exe exists
wscript.exe exists
A directory is writable
A service runs as SYSTEM
An application is installed
A firewall allow rule exists
A scheduled task runs elevated
An AppLocker path rule is broad

These observations may be useful starting points, but they require additional security context.

For example:

Writable directory

becomes significantly more important when:

Writable directory
        +
Privileged process
        +
Privileged process consumes modifiable resource
        =
Potential privilege escalation

docs.title: 70. Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each relevant observation, record:

Host
Timestamp
Current user
Integrity level
Relevant groups
Relevant privileges
Resource
Permissions
Process/service context
Security control state
Command
Output
Practical impact

Example:

Host:
WS01

User:
CORP\standarduser

Observation:
The user has Modify permission on C:\ProgramData\Vendor\App.

Related service:
VendorService

Service account:
LocalSystem

Service executable:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\App\service.exe

Validation:
The service configuration references the executable located inside the
user-writable directory.

Security relevance:
A lower-privileged user can influence a resource consumed by a
higher-privileged service.

This is substantially stronger evidence than simply reporting that a folder is writable.

docs.text:
• [ ] Correlate findings
  • [ ] Validate permissions
  • [ ] Validate execution context
  • [ ] Validate security boundary
  • [ ] Confirm practical impact
  • [ ] Collect reproducible evidence

A compact first-pass collection:

docs.title: 74. Reporting Enumeration Findings
docs.text:
Enumeration results should be converted into evidence-based findings.

Weak finding:

PowerShell is installed.

Better observation:

PowerShell is available to standard users and operates in FullLanguage mode.
Application-control configuration should be evaluated to determine whether
this behaviour is consistent with the intended endpoint-hardening model.

Weak finding:

C:\ProgramData\Example is writable.

Better finding:

Standard users have Modify permission on C:\ProgramData\Example. A service
running as LocalSystem loads its executable from this directory. The
permission relationship therefore allows a lower-privileged user to
influence a resource consumed by a privileged process.

Weak finding:

rundll32.exe is allowed.

Better observation:

The effective application-control policy permits rundll32.exe for the tested
user context. This should be evaluated together with application-control
objectives, writable locations, permitted content, and monitoring controls
before determining whether the configuration creates a practical security
weakness.

docs.title: 75. Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
Use enumeration as the foundation for subsequent Windows testing.

Windows Enumeration
        |
        +----------------------+
        |                      |
        v                      v

        |                      |
        +----------+-----------+
                   |
                   v
          Filesystem / Registry
                   |
                   v
             Credentials
                   |
                   v
        Privilege Escalation
                   |
                   v
              Validation
                   |
                   v
               Reporting

Continue with:

  1. PowerShell
  2. Windows Services
  3. Windows Credentials
  4. Windows Privilege Escalation

For domain-joined hosts:

  • Active Directory Enumeration
  • Active Directory
