docs.title: Windows Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Windows filesystem permissions determine which users and groups can read, create, modify, delete or otherwise control files and directories.

During a Windows security assessment, insecure NTFS permissions are particularly important because privileged services, scheduled tasks and applications frequently execute code or consume configuration from the filesystem.

A common privilege escalation pattern is:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Writable File or Directory
        |
        v
Privileged Process Dependency
        |
        v
SYSTEM / Administrator Execution

The important question is not simply:

Can I write to this directory?

Instead ask:

Can a lower-privileged user modify something
that a higher-privileged process trusts?

Authorised Security Testing

Perform filesystem permission testing only on systems included in the authorised assessment scope. Prefer ACL inspection and harmless probe files. Do not replace legitimate executables, scripts, DLLs or configuration files merely to demonstrate write access.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Security Principal
       |
       v
NTFS ACL
       |
       v
File / Directory
       |
       v
Privileged Consumer
       |
       v
Security Impact

A writable file or directory alone is not necessarily vulnerable.

A meaningful privilege escalation path normally requires:

Lower-privileged write capability
+
Security-sensitive resource
+
Privileged consumer
+
Reachable execution or processing path

docs.title: NTFS Security Components
docs.text:
NTFS permissions involve:

Owner

Discretionary ACL - DACL

Access Control Entries - ACEs

Allow entries

Deny entries

Inheritance

User and group membership

Effective permissions

docs.title: Current Security Context
docs.text:
Always establish the current identity before interpreting permissions.

whoami

docs.title: Group Membership
docs.text: whoami /groups

docs.title: Privileges
docs.text: whoami /priv

docs.title: PowerShell Identity
docs.text: [System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().Name

docs.title: Why Group Membership Matters
docs.text:
A file may not explicitly grant permission to your username.

Instead, access may come from:

BUILTIN\Users

Authenticated Users

Everyone

Domain Users

A local group

A domain group

A custom application group

docs.title: Basic Permission Enumeration
docs.text:
The primary built-in command-line tool is:

icacls.exe

docs.title: Inspect a File
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Example\worker.exe"

docs.title: Inspect a Directory
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Example"

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text: Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Example'

docs.title: Detailed PowerShell View
docs.text: Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Example' | Format-List *

docs.title: Access Entries
docs.text: (Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Example').Access

docs.title: Compact ACL View
docs.text:
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Example').Access |
    Select-Object IdentityReference,FileSystemRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited,InheritanceFlags,PropagationFlags

docs.title: Common icacls Permissions
docs.text:
Common abbreviations include:

Permission Meaning F Full control M Modify RX Read and execute R Read W Write

docs.title: Common Advanced Permissions
docs.text:
PowerShell may display more granular rights such as:

FullControl

Modify

ReadAndExecute

Read

Write

CreateFiles

CreateDirectories

AppendData

WriteData

Delete

DeleteSubdirectoriesAndFiles

WriteAttributes

WriteExtendedAttributes

ChangePermissions

TakeOwnership

docs.title: High-Value Permissions
docs.text:
During privilege escalation analysis, pay particular attention to:

FullControl

Modify

Write

WriteData

CreateFiles

CreateDirectories

Delete

DeleteSubdirectoriesAndFiles

ChangePermissions

TakeOwnership

docs.title: File vs Directory Permissions
docs.text:
This distinction is extremely important.

A file may be protected:

C:\ProgramData\Company\service.exe

while its parent directory is writable:

C:\ProgramData\Company

docs.title: Analysis Model
docs.text:
Target File
    |
    +--> File ACL
    |
    +--> Parent Directory ACL

Always review both.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
icacls "C:\ProgramData\Company\service.exe"

Then:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Company"

docs.title: Why Parent Permissions Matter
docs.text:
Depending on the exact permissions and application behaviour, directory access may allow:

Creating new files

Creating subdirectories

Deleting files

Replacing files

Renaming files

Introducing supporting dependencies

docs.title: Do Not Infer Replacement Automatically
docs.text:
Being able to create:

test.txt

in a directory does not necessarily prove the user can overwrite:

service.exe

The target file's ACL and directory permissions must be evaluated together.

docs.title: File Owner
docs.text:
PowerShell:

(Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Company\service.exe').Owner

docs.title: Directory Owner
docs.text: (Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Company').Owner

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Ownership can matter because an owner may have the ability to alter the object's security descriptor under applicable Windows security semantics.

However:

Ownership != automatic exploitability

Evaluate actual effective control.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
NTFS permissions are commonly inherited from parent directories.

PowerShell:

(Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Company').Access |
    Select-Object IdentityReference,FileSystemRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
IdentityReference : BUILTIN\Users
FileSystemRights  : ReadAndExecute
AccessControlType : Allow
IsInherited       : True

docs.title: Why Inheritance Matters
docs.text:
Weak permissions applied to:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor

may affect:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\App1

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\App2

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Scripts

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Plugins

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text: When one insecure directory is identified, inspect related child directories and files rather than treating the problem as a single isolated object.

docs.title: Inheritance Flags
docs.text:
PowerShell may display:

ContainerInherit

ObjectInherit

docs.title: Conceptually
docs.text:
ContainerInherit
    |
    v
Child directories

ObjectInherit
    |
    v
Child files

docs.title: Deny ACEs
docs.text:
Explicit deny entries can affect effective permissions.

Example:

BUILTIN\Users:
Allow Modify

DOMAIN\User:
Deny Write

Do not interpret a single Allow ACE without considering the complete ACL.

docs.title: Effective Access
docs.text:
Effective access depends on:

User SID

Group SIDs

Allow ACEs

Deny ACEs

Inheritance

Ownership

Token privileges

docs.title: Read Permissions
docs.text:
Read access may expose:

Configuration files

Credentials

API keys

Connection strings

Scripts

Source code

Backups

Logs

Command history

Read access should therefore be assessed independently from write access.

docs.title: Write Permissions
docs.text:
Write access becomes especially important when the resource is trusted by:

SYSTEM services

Administrator processes

Scheduled tasks

Backup agents

Monitoring agents

Deployment agents

Software updaters

Web services

docs.title: Writable Directory Discovery
docs.text: A practical assessment frequently involves identifying directories writable by the current user.

docs.title: Safe Manual Check
docs.text:
For a known directory:

Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Example' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Harmless Write Probe
docs.text:
Where the engagement permits it:

$folder = 'C:\ProgramData\Example'
$probe = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID.tmp"

try {
    'permission-test' | Set-Content -LiteralPath $probe -ErrorAction Stop
    Write-Host "[+] Writable: $folder"
    Remove-Item -LiteralPath $probe -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}
catch {
    Write-Host "[-] Not writable: $folder"
}

docs.title: What This Proves
docs.text:
Successful creation proves:

The current security context can create this test file
in this directory.

It does not automatically prove:

Existing executable overwrite

Existing script overwrite

File deletion

Privileged code execution

docs.title: Test the Exact Capability Required
docs.text: Security conclusions should correspond to the permission actually needed by the attack path.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose a SYSTEM service executes:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.exe

You identify:

Directory creation:
Allowed

but:

agent.exe modification:
Denied

This does not automatically prove executable replacement.

Further analysis is required.

docs.title: Writable Files
docs.text: A direct writable executable or script is generally a stronger candidate than merely having limited write access somewhere in its parent tree.

docs.title: Check File ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.exe"

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.exe').Access |
    Select-Object IdentityReference,FileSystemRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited

docs.title: Strong Candidate
docs.text:
Example:

BUILTIN\Users:(M)

on:

agent.exe

when the file is executed by a SYSTEM service.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Model
docs.text:
Standard User
      |
      v
Modify agent.exe
      |
      v
SYSTEM Service
      |
      v
Executes agent.exe
      |
      v
SYSTEM Context

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not replace the executable during discovery.

First establish:

Service identity

Executable path

ACL

Trigger

Application control

Operational impact

docs.title: Services
docs.text: Services are one of the highest-value consumers of filesystem content.

docs.title: Enumerate Services
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

docs.title: Find Non-Windows Paths
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object {
        $_.PathName -and
        $_.PathName -notmatch '^"?C:\\Windows\\'
    } |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Name      : VendorAgent
StartName : LocalSystem
State     : Running
PathName  : "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.exe"

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Review:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.exe"

and:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

docs.title: Service Security
docs.text:
Filesystem permissions are only one component.

Also review:

Service object permissions

Service configuration

Registry configuration

docs.title: Related Notes
docs.text:
See:

Windows Services

and:

Windows Registry Security

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks frequently execute:

EXE files

PowerShell scripts

Batch files

VBScript

JavaScript

Administrative scripts

docs.title: Enumerate Actions
docs.text:
Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    $task = $_

    foreach ($action in $task.Actions) {
        [PSCustomObject]@{
            TaskPath         = $task.TaskPath
            TaskName         = $task.TaskName
            User             = $task.Principal.UserId
            Execute          = $action.Execute
            Arguments        = $action.Arguments
            WorkingDirectory = $action.WorkingDirectory
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
TaskName  : BackupJob
User      : SYSTEM
Execute   : powershell.exe
Arguments : -File C:\ProgramData\Backup\backup.ps1

docs.title: Check Script
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Backup\backup.ps1"

docs.title: Check Directory
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Backup"

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Scheduled Tasks

docs.title: Script Files
docs.text:
High-value extensions include:

.ps1
.bat
.cmd
.vbs
.js
.py

docs.title: Search ProgramData for Scripts
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem 'C:\ProgramData' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object Extension -in '.ps1','.bat','.cmd','.vbs','.js','.py' |
    Select-Object FullName

docs.title: Do Not Assume Vulnerability
docs.text:
A script's existence under:

C:\ProgramData

does not imply insecure permissions.

Check the ACL.

docs.title: Script Consumer
docs.text:
Also determine:

Who executes it?

When?

Under which privilege?

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Privileged applications may consume configuration files such as:

.ini

.conf

.config

.xml

.json

.yaml

.yml

.properties

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Can modifying the configuration influence:

Executable path

Command

Script

Plugin

Module

Service endpoint

Update source

Authentication behaviour

File location

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.ini

Check:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.ini"

docs.title: Writable Config != Automatic Code Execution
docs.text:
Suppose the user can change:

LogLevel=Debug

That may not cross a privilege boundary.

But:

PluginPath=C:\Somewhere\plugin.dll

may deserve deeper investigation.

docs.title: Establish the Sink
docs.text:
Ask:

How does the privileged application use this value?

docs.title: Plugin Directories
docs.text:
Applications may load extensions from directories such as:

plugins

modules

extensions

providers

drivers

addons

docs.title: Example
docs.text: C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Plugins

docs.title: Check ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Plugins"

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
Writable Plugin Directory
        |
        v
Privileged Application
        |
        v
Loads Plugins
        |
        v
Potential Privileged Execution

docs.title: Important
docs.text: You must confirm that the privileged process actually loads content from the writable directory.

docs.title: DLL Dependencies
docs.text:
A protected executable may load DLLs from other directories.

A possible security path is:

Privileged EXE
     |
     v
Loads DLL
     |
     v
Writable Search Location
     |
     v
Potential DLL Hijacking

docs.title: Do Not Infer DLL Hijacking from Writability Alone
docs.text:
DLL loading depends on:

Application behaviour

DLL name

Load method

Search order

Known DLL handling

Safe DLL search mode

Application directory

PATH

Explicit paths

docs.title: Required Validation
docs.text:
Establish:

Which DLL is requested?

Where Windows searches?

Whether the legitimate DLL exists?

Which location is selected?

Whether the attacker can control that location?

Which privilege loads it?

docs.title: Program Files
docs.text:
Typical application locations include:

C:\Program Files

C:\Program Files (x86)

docs.title: Expected Security Posture
docs.text:
Standard users should generally have:

Read

ReadAndExecute

rather than:

Modify

FullControl

over installed application executables.

docs.title: Check Application Directory
docs.text: icacls "C:\Program Files\Example"

docs.title: ProgramData
docs.text:
C:\ProgramData is widely used for application data.

Some subdirectories legitimately require user write access.

Therefore:

Writable ProgramData directory

is not automatically a finding.

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Determine whether the directory contains or controls:

Privileged executable content

Scripts

Plugins

Modules

Security-sensitive configuration

docs.title: Users Public Directory
docs.text:
Review privileged dependencies referencing:

C:\Users\Public

because it may contain locations intentionally shared between users.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Again:

Location != vulnerability

The ACL and privileged consumer determine the security impact.

docs.title: Temporary Directories
docs.text:
Common temporary locations include:

C:\Windows\Temp

%TEMP%

%TMP%

User profile Temp directories

docs.title: Security Concern
docs.text: Privileged applications should not blindly execute code from broadly writable temporary directories.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Check:

$env:TEMP
$env:TMP

docs.title: System Temp
docs.text:
Often:

C:\Windows\Temp

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
A writable temporary directory alone is expected in many environments.

The vulnerability requires a privileged process that unsafely trusts content from it.

docs.title: Missing Files
docs.text: An interesting case occurs when a privileged process expects a file that does not exist.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Privileged task expects:

C:\ProgramData\OldVendor\update.exe

Check:

Test-Path -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\OldVendor\update.exe'

docs.title: If Missing
docs.text: False

docs.title: Next Check
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\OldVendor"

docs.title: Security Pattern
docs.text:
Privileged Consumer
       |
       v
Missing Dependency
       |
       v
Writable Parent
       |
       v
Potential File Planting

docs.title: Required Conditions
docs.text:
You still need to establish:

Exact expected filename

Writable location

Consumer privilege

Consumer execution

Trigger

docs.title: Existing File vs Missing File
docs.text:
These are different permission problems.

Existing File
    |
    v
Can user modify / replace it?

Missing File
    |
    v
Can user create it?

docs.title: CreateFiles Permission
docs.text: Directory permissions that allow file creation may become relevant when a privileged application expects a missing file.

docs.title: Delete Permissions
docs.text: Delete rights can be security-sensitive even when direct write access is absent.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
In some configurations, a user may be able to:

Delete existing object
+
Create replacement

depending on parent and target permissions.

docs.title: Do Not Simplify ACL Analysis
docs.text:
Windows delete semantics can involve rights on both:

File

Parent directory

Inspect the actual permissions before reaching a conclusion.

docs.title: Rename Behaviour
docs.text:
Similarly, directory permissions may permit operations that are not obvious from a simple:

Write = Yes/No

classification.

docs.title: Use Granular ACL Analysis
docs.text:
PowerShell:

(Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Example').Access |
    Format-Table IdentityReference,FileSystemRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited -AutoSize

docs.title: Network Shares
docs.text:
Files may also be consumed from UNC paths:

\\server\share\script.ps1

A complete review requires both:

Share permissions

NTFS permissions

docs.title: Share Permissions vs NTFS
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Network Access
     |
     v
Share Permissions
     |
     v
NTFS Permissions
     |
     v
Effective Access

docs.title: Important
docs.text: The most restrictive applicable access usually determines what the remote user can actually do.

docs.title: Privileged UNC Dependency
docs.text:
Example:

SYSTEM scheduled task
        |
        v
\\fileserver\automation\backup.ps1

Ask:

Who can modify the share?

Who can modify the file?

Which identity accesses the share?

Does the task successfully authenticate?

docs.title: Local vs Remote Context
docs.text:
A local SYSTEM account accessing a remote resource may authenticate differently from an interactive user.

Do not assume your own network access proves the task's access behaviour.

docs.title: Sensitive Files
docs.text: Filesystem permissions also affect confidentiality.

docs.title: Common Sensitive Locations
docs.text:
Examples include:

Application configuration

Backup files

Database configuration

Web configuration

Deployment scripts

Automation scripts

Logs

Exported Registry files

Credential files

Private keys

API configuration

docs.title: Search by Filename
docs.text:
Targeted examples:

Get-ChildItem 'C:\ProgramData' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Name -match 'password|credential|secret|token|backup|config'
    } |
    Select-Object FullName

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Filename matching is only candidate discovery.

A file called:

password-policy.txt

does not necessarily contain a password.

docs.title: Configuration File Search
docs.text:
Examples:

Get-ChildItem 'C:\ProgramData' -Recurse -File -Include *.ini,*.config,*.xml,*.json,*.yml,*.yaml -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object FullName

docs.title: Avoid Excessive Collection
docs.text:
Do not indiscriminately read every configuration file.

Prioritize:

Assessment-relevant applications

Privileged services

Known deployment tooling

Backup software

Web applications

Management agents

docs.title: Credential Search
docs.text:
When specifically authorised, targeted searches may look for terms such as:

password

passwd

secret

token

apikey

connectionstring

docs.title: PowerShell Example
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem 'C:\ProgramData\ExampleVendor' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password|passwd|secret|token|api.?key|connectionstring' -CaseSensitive:$false -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Protect Evidence
docs.text:
If credentials are discovered:

Do not expose them unnecessarily

Do not paste full secrets into reports

Redact screenshots

Follow evidence-handling requirements

docs.title: Backup Files
docs.text:
Common backup patterns include:

*.bak

*.old

*.backup

*.save

*.copy

*.orig

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem 'C:\ProgramData' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Extension -in '.bak','.old','.backup','.save','.orig'
    } |
    Select-Object FullName

docs.title: Security Relevance
docs.text:
Backups may contain:

Old credentials

Previous configuration

Database strings

API keys

Source code

Historical secrets

docs.title: Log Files
docs.text:
Logs may expose:

Tokens

URLs containing secrets

Usernames

Internal paths

Application errors

Authentication details

docs.title: Log Access
docs.text:
Readable logs are not automatically a vulnerability.

Determine whether they expose information that the user should not be able to access.

docs.title: Web Applications
docs.text:
Windows-hosted web applications may contain:

web.config

appsettings.json

connection strings

deployment configuration

application secrets

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem 'C:\inetpub' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Name -in 'web.config','appsettings.json','appsettings.Production.json'
    } |
    Select-Object FullName

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Access should be evaluated relative to the expected trust boundary.

An administrator being able to read application configuration is different from a standard user being able to read a privileged service account credential.

docs.title: IIS
docs.text:
Typical IIS content may exist under:

C:\inetpub\wwwroot

Review:

Application pool identity

Directory ACLs

Upload directories

Configuration files

Writable web roots

docs.title: Writable Web Root
docs.text:
A writable web root may create security impact when:

User can introduce server-executable content

and

The web server processes that content

This depends on:

IIS configuration

Handler mappings

Application framework

Application pool identity

Application control

docs.title: Do Not Assume Execution
docs.text:
Being able to write:

test.txt

to a web root does not prove server-side code execution.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Filesystem write access may be constrained by:

AppLocker

Windows Defender Application Control

Antivirus

EDR

PowerShell policy

docs.title: Security Layers
docs.text:
User Writable File
       |
       v
Privileged Consumer
       |
       v
Execution Control
       |
   +---+---+
   |       |
 Allow    Block
   |       |
   v       v
Impact   Reduced

docs.title: Important Reporting Distinction
docs.text:
If application control prevents execution, distinguish between:

Underlying insecure ACL

and:

Demonstrated privilege escalation

Do not claim successful privileged code execution when an effective control prevents it.

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
Where accessible:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

docs.title: Application Control Does Not Replace ACL Security
docs.text:
A privileged executable directory should not become user-writable merely because AppLocker currently blocks unsigned executables.

Controls can:

Change

Be misconfigured

Have allowed execution paths

Apply differently to scripts, DLLs, MSI or packaged applications

docs.title: Reparse Points
docs.text:
Windows filesystems can contain reparse points such as:

Symbolic links

Junctions

Mount points

docs.title: Enumerate Reparse Points
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem 'C:\ProgramData\Example' -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object Attributes -match 'ReparsePoint' |
    Select-Object FullName,Attributes,LinkType,Target

docs.title: Security Relevance
docs.text:
Reparse points can affect path resolution.

They become security-sensitive when a privileged application performs filesystem operations on paths that a lower-privileged user can redirect.

docs.title: Do Not Infer Vulnerability
docs.text:
The presence of a junction or symbolic link alone is not a security finding.

You need a privileged filesystem operation that follows or otherwise mishandles the redirected path.

docs.title: Hard Links
docs.text:
Hard-link behaviour may also matter in specific privileged file-operation scenarios.

Again, this requires application-specific validation rather than assuming exploitability from filesystem capabilities alone.

docs.title: TOCTOU
docs.text:
Time-of-check to time-of-use issues can occur when a privileged application:

Checks a file
      |
      v
Time passes
      |
      v
Uses the file

and an attacker can change the relevant filesystem object between those operations.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
Check Trusted Path
      |
      v
Attacker Changes Object
      |
      v
Privileged Use

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
TOCTOU testing can be timing-sensitive and potentially disruptive.

Perform only when relevant to the application and explicitly permitted.

docs.title: Installer Directories
docs.text:
Installers and update agents may use:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Updates

C:\Windows\Temp

Application cache directories

Package staging directories

docs.title: Security Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Who can write packages?

Who verifies package integrity?

Which account installs them?

Are filenames predictable?

Are signatures validated?

Can configuration redirect package sources?

docs.title: Update Security
docs.text: A writable update directory is not automatically exploitable if the updater cryptographically validates packages before execution.

docs.title: Validate the Complete Trust Model
docs.text:
Writable Package
      |
      v
Signature Validation?
      |
  +---+---+
  |       |
 Yes      No
  |       |
  v       v
Reduced   Investigate

docs.title: Backup Agents
docs.text:
Backup software often operates with significant privileges.

Review directories containing:

Scripts

Hooks

Plugins

Pre-backup commands

Post-backup commands

Configuration

docs.title: Monitoring Agents
docs.text:
Monitoring software may execute:

Custom checks

Plugins

Scripts

Health checks

Review whether lower-privileged users can modify these dependencies.

docs.title: Deployment Agents
docs.text:
CI/CD and deployment software on Windows can be high-value because it may run with elevated rights.

Review:

Agent directory

Workspace permissions

Script directories

Package cache

Service identity

Credential files

docs.title: Workspace Writability
docs.text:
A writable workspace may be intentional.

The key question is whether:

Privileged agent executes untrusted workspace content

without an appropriate trust boundary.

docs.title: Software Installation Directories
docs.text:
Enumerate potentially interesting non-standard directories:

Get-ChildItem 'C:\' -Directory -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object FullName

docs.title: Do Not Recursively Scan Everything Blindly
docs.text:
Recursive ACL enumeration across an entire system can be:

Slow

Noisy

Difficult to interpret

Operationally expensive

Prioritize likely privileged dependency locations.

docs.title: Recommended Priority
docs.text:
1. Privileged service executables

2. Scheduled task scripts

3. ProgramData application directories

4. Privileged application configuration

5. Plugin/module directories

6. Update directories

7. Backup/monitoring/deployment agents

8. Sensitive configuration files

docs.title: ACL Candidate Function
docs.text:
For assessment assistance, a PowerShell helper can summarize explicit ACL entries for a known path.

function Get-PathAclSummary {
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$Path
    )

    if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $Path)) {
        Write-Warning "Path does not exist: $Path"
        return
    }

    $acl = Get-Acl -LiteralPath $Path

    [PSCustomObject]@{
        Path  = $Path
        Owner = $acl.Owner
    }

    $acl.Access |
        Select-Object IdentityReference,
                      FileSystemRights,
                      AccessControlType,
                      IsInherited,
                      InheritanceFlags,
                      PropagationFlags
}

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: Get-PathAclSummary -Path 'C:\ProgramData\Example'

docs.title: Why This Is Better Than "Writable = True"
docs.text:
Security assessment benefits from retaining:

Identity

Exact rights

Allow/Deny

Inheritance

rather than reducing complex ACLs to a single Boolean value.

docs.title: Broadly Privileged Groups
docs.text:
Potentially interesting ACL principals include:

Everyone

BUILTIN\Users

Authenticated Users

Domain Users

but their presence is not automatically insecure.

docs.title: Example Safe Permission
docs.text:
BUILTIN\Users:(RX)

This generally provides:

Read and execute

without modification.

docs.title: Example Candidate
docs.text:
BUILTIN\Users:(M)

on a privileged executable directory deserves investigation.

docs.title: Everyone
docs.text:
Modern Windows permissions involving:

Everyone

should be evaluated carefully.

The security impact depends on the exact rights and object.

docs.title: Authenticated Users
docs.text:
Likewise:

Authenticated Users:(RX)

may be expected.

But:

Authenticated Users:(M)

on privileged executable content is more concerning.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Do not report:

Users has access

without specifying the exact access.

The difference between:

ReadAndExecute

and:

Modify

is fundamental.

docs.title: Full Control
docs.text:
FullControl is especially significant because it can include:

Read

Write

Modify

Delete

Change permissions

Take ownership

docs.title: Modify
docs.text:
Modify generally permits substantial control over file content and deletion.

For privileged executable content, this is a strong candidate.

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
Write requires more careful interpretation.

Determine which granular rights are present and whether they permit the operation required by the attack path.

docs.title: CreateFiles
docs.text: CreateFiles can be security-sensitive when a privileged application expects a missing predictable file.

docs.title: CreateDirectories
docs.text: This can matter when a privileged application expects a missing directory or searches recursively through user-controlled paths.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text: Delete rights may enable replacement patterns depending on parent directory and target permissions.

docs.title: ChangePermissions
docs.text: A lower-privileged user able to change permissions on a privileged dependency may be able to grant themselves additional control.

docs.title: TakeOwnership
docs.text:
Similarly, ownership control may enable further ACL modification.

Treat it as a high-value permission requiring careful validation.

docs.title: Integrity Levels
docs.text:
Windows also uses mandatory integrity control.

Processes can operate at integrity levels such as:

Low

Medium

High

System

docs.title: Current Integrity Context
docs.text:
One useful view is:

whoami /groups

and inspect the mandatory label entry.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level

docs.title: Security Boundary
docs.text:
Filesystem ACLs and integrity controls are related but distinct.

A user may appear to have discretionary permissions while another Windows security mechanism affects the actual operation.

docs.title: UAC
docs.text:
An administrator running with a filtered token may operate at medium integrity until elevation.

Do not assume:

Member of Administrators

means every process is currently executing with unrestricted administrative rights.

docs.title: Planned Related Note
docs.text: Windows User Account Control

docs.title: Safe Validation Workflow
docs.text:
Use this sequence:

1. Identify privileged consumer

2. Identify exact dependency

3. Inspect file ACL

4. Inspect directory ACL

5. Determine current identity/group rights

6. Determine exact required filesystem operation

7. Use harmless write test where appropriate

8. Confirm consumer privilege

9. Confirm execution/processing path

10. Evaluate application control

11. Establish security impact

12. Capture evidence

docs.title: Why Start With the Consumer?
docs.text:
Starting from random writable directories often produces large numbers of irrelevant results.

A stronger approach is:

Privileged Process
      |
      v
What does it trust?
      |
      v
Can I control any of those resources?

docs.title: Consumer-First Methodology
docs.text:
SYSTEM Service
      |
      +--> EXE
      |
      +--> DLL
      |
      +--> Config
      |
      +--> Plugin
      |
      +--> Script
              |
              v
          Check ACL

docs.title: Scheduled-Task-First Methodology
docs.text:
SYSTEM Task
     |
     v
PowerShell
     |
     v
backup.ps1
     |
     v
helper.exe
     |
     v
config.json

Review each security-sensitive dependency.

docs.title: Filesystem-First Methodology
docs.text:
Sometimes a writable directory is discovered first.

Then reverse the analysis:

Writable Directory
       |
       v
What uses this?
       |
       +--> Service?
       |
       +--> Scheduled Task?
       |
       +--> Privileged Application?
       |
       +--> Updater?
       |
       +--> Backup Agent?

docs.title: Process Enumeration
docs.text:
Running processes can help identify applications of interest.

Get-Process | Select-Object ProcessName,Id,Path -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Important
docs.text: Access to process paths may vary depending on privilege and process protection.

docs.title: Service Correlation
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

docs.title: Installed Software Correlation
docs.text:
Registry inventory can identify applications associated with unusual writable directories.

See:

Windows Registry Security

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text: For a filesystem privilege escalation finding, capture the complete chain.

docs.title: 1. Current User
docs.text: whoami

docs.title: 2. Group Membership
docs.text: whoami /groups

docs.title: 3. Privileged Consumer
docs.text:
Example:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='VendorAgent'" |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

docs.title: 4. File ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.exe"

docs.title: 5. Directory ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

docs.title: 6. PowerShell ACL
docs.text:
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.exe').Access |
    Select-Object IdentityReference,FileSystemRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited

docs.title: 7. Runtime Evidence
docs.text: Establish that the privileged consumer actually uses the dependency.

docs.title: 8. Safe Write Validation
docs.text: If required and permitted, create a separate harmless test file rather than altering the dependency.

docs.title: 9. Application Control
docs.text: Document relevant execution restrictions where they affect exploitability.

docs.title: Evidence Chain
docs.text:
Standard User
      |
      v
Group Membership
      |
      v
Modify Permission
      |
      v
Privileged Dependency
      |
      v
SYSTEM Consumer
      |
      v
Execution / Processing
      |
      v
Privilege Boundary

docs.title: Strong Finding
docs.text:
A strong finding establishes:

1. Current user is lower privileged.

2. The user or one of their groups has relevant write rights.

3. The affected file is security-sensitive.

4. A higher-privileged process consumes it.

5. The dependency is reachable.

6. Relevant controls do not invalidate the path.

7. Security impact follows from the user-controlled dependency.

docs.title: Weak Finding
docs.text:
This is insufficient:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor is writable.

It does not establish:

What is writable?

Which exact permission exists?

What uses the directory?

Which privilege is involved?

What security boundary is crossed?

docs.title: Better Finding
docs.text: The BUILTIN\Users group has Modify permission over C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.exe. The executable is launched by the VendorAgent Windows service running as LocalSystem. A standard local user can therefore modify executable content trusted by a SYSTEM-level service.

docs.title: Finding Titles
docs.text:
Suitable titles include:

Insecure Filesystem Permissions Allow Local Privilege Escalation

or:

Standard Users Can Modify a SYSTEM Service Executable

or:

Writable Privileged Application Directory Allows Local Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Sensitive File Finding
docs.text:
For confidentiality issues:

Sensitive Application Configuration Accessible to Standard Users

docs.title: Severity Factors
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

Required local access

Current privilege

Exact filesystem rights

Consumer privilege

Execution frequency

Trigger requirements

User interaction

Application control

Reliability

Operational conditions

docs.title: High-Risk Pattern
docs.text:
Standard User
+
Modify on EXE
+
SYSTEM Service
+
Automatic Start
+
No Effective Execution Restriction

docs.title: Lower-Risk Pattern
docs.text:
Writable Directory
+
No Privileged Consumer
+
No Security-Sensitive Content

This may not represent a vulnerability at all.

docs.title: False Positive - Writable ProgramData
docs.text:
Observation:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Data

is writable.

If it contains only user-generated data and no privileged process interprets that data as code or trusted configuration, privilege escalation is not established.

docs.title: False Positive - Writable Log
docs.text: A privileged process writing to a log that users can also write does not automatically provide code execution.

docs.title: False Positive - Same User Consumer
docs.text:
Current user:
UserA

Consumer:
UserA

A writable script executed by the same security context normally does not cross a privilege boundary.

docs.title: False Positive - Read and Execute
docs.text:
Users:(RX)

does not provide modification capability.

docs.title: False Positive - Writable Config with Harmless Setting
docs.text:
If the only user-controlled setting is:

WindowSize=Large

there may be no security impact.

docs.title: False Positive - Writable Temp
docs.text:
A writable temporary directory is common.

You need a privileged application that unsafely trusts predictable content from it.

docs.title: False Positive - Missing File
docs.text:
A missing file alone is not exploitable.

The user must be able to create it at the exact expected location, and the privileged consumer must use it.

docs.title: False Positive - Application Control Blocks Execution
docs.text:
If modified code cannot execute because of an effective application-control policy, do not claim successful code execution.

Still assess whether the insecure ACL itself should be remediated.

docs.title: Alternative Explanations
docs.text:
Unexpected permissions may result from:

Vendor application requirements

Shared application data

Legacy software

Installer behaviour

Multi-user workstation requirements

Development tooling

Update staging

Backup software

Determine whether the permission is genuinely required.

docs.title: Reporting Principle
docs.text:
Do not report:

Permission is unusual

as equivalent to:

Permission crosses a security boundary

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: The primary remediation is to remove unnecessary write access from files and directories trusted by privileged processes.

docs.title: Protect Executables
docs.text: Privileged executables should generally be writable only by trusted administrative identities.

docs.title: Protect Scripts
docs.text: Scripts executed by privileged services or scheduled tasks should not be modifiable by standard users.

docs.title: Protect Configuration
docs.text: Security-sensitive configuration should be protected according to the privilege of the consuming application.

docs.title: Protect Plugin Directories
docs.text: Only trusted administrators or designated service identities should be able to modify privileged application plugins or modules.

docs.title: Protect Parent Directories
docs.text: Do not correct only the target file while leaving a replacement path through its parent directory.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text: Grant only the permissions required for normal operation.

docs.title: Avoid Broad Permissions
docs.text:
Avoid unnecessary:

Everyone:(F)

Users:(F)

Authenticated Users:(M)

on privileged application content.

docs.title: Separate Data and Executable Content
docs.text:
Where an application requires user-writable data, separate it from:

Executables

Scripts

Plugins

Security-sensitive configuration

docs.title: Example Design
docs.text:
C:\Program Files\Vendor\
    binaries
    administrators write only

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Data\
    application data
    limited user write where required

docs.title: Secure Update Mechanisms
docs.text:
Privileged updaters should:

Validate package integrity

Use protected staging locations

Validate signatures where appropriate

Avoid predictable unsafe file replacement

docs.title: Secure Temporary Operations
docs.text:
Privileged applications should:

Use secure temporary-file creation

Avoid predictable filenames

Validate ownership and permissions

Avoid trusting user-controlled paths

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Use:

WDAC

AppLocker

as defense in depth.

Do not use application control as justification for insecure NTFS permissions.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Monitor changes to:

Service executables

Scheduled task scripts

Privileged configuration

Plugin directories

Security tooling

Deployment agents

docs.title: Remove Obsolete Content
docs.text:
Remove:

Old scripts

Unused binaries

Legacy backups

Orphaned updater files

Deprecated configuration

when no longer required.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: Retesting should reproduce the original permission and consumer analysis.

docs.title: Step 1 - Same User
docs.text:
Use the same low-privileged identity.

whoami

docs.title: Step 2 - File ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\agent.exe"

docs.title: Step 3 - Directory ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

docs.title: Step 4 - Effective Capability
docs.text: Where permitted, repeat the harmless write test.

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
If write access is no longer required:

Access denied

docs.title: Step 5 - Consumer
docs.text: Confirm the legitimate service, task or application still works.

docs.title: Step 6 - Related Dependencies
docs.text:
Review:

Scripts

Plugins

Configuration

Helper executables

Sibling directories

docs.title: Step 7 - Inheritance
docs.text: Ensure insecure permissions are not still inherited from a parent.

docs.title: Step 8 - Variant Analysis
docs.text: Search for equivalent permissions created by the same installer or product.

docs.text: Test Expected After Fix Standard user modifies privileged EXE Denied Standard user modifies privileged script Denied Standard user modifies privileged config Denied unless explicitly required Standard user creates executable in protected directory Denied Standard user deletes privileged dependency Denied Legitimate service executes Success Legitimate scheduled task executes Success Application functionality Preserved Parent ACL Secure Related directories Secure
