docs.title: Windows Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Windows privilege escalation is the process of identifying security weaknesses that allow a lower-privileged user or process to gain additional permissions on a Windows system.

During an authorised assessment, the objective is not simply to obtain administrative privileges. The objective is to identify the underlying trust or permission relationship that makes the escalation possible, validate the security impact safely, and provide evidence that allows the weakness to be remediated.

Typical escalation paths involve:

  • Windows services
  • Weak filesystem permissions
  • Weak registry permissions
  • Scheduled tasks
  • Service configuration permissions
  • Unquoted service paths
  • DLL search behaviour
  • Stored credentials
  • User privileges
  • Application configuration
  • Installer policies
  • AutoRun locations
  • Vulnerable software
  • Credential reuse
  • Security-control misconfiguration

The central question is:

Can the current user influence something
that executes or operates with greater privileges?

docs.title: 1. Privilege Escalation Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Low-Privileged User
        |
        v
Enumeration
        |
        v
Identify Privileged Resource
        |
        v
Identify Controllable Component
        |
        v
Validate Permissions
        |
        v
Determine Execution Context
        |
        v
Confirm Security Boundary
        |
        v
Controlled Validation
        |
        v
Evidence
        |
        v
Remediation

Most meaningful privilege escalation findings contain three components:

Privileged Context
        +
Attacker-Controlled Resource
        +
Execution / Consumption Relationship
        =
Potential Privilege Escalation

For example:

SYSTEM Service
      +
User-Writable Executable
      =
Potential SYSTEM Execution

docs.title: 2. Initial Enumeration
docs.text:
Start by understanding the current security context.

whoami
whoami /user
whoami /groups
whoami /priv

Complete information:

whoami /all

PowerShell:

$env:USERNAME
$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:COMPUTERNAME

Check integrity level:

whoami /groups

Look for:

Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level
Mandatory Label\High Mandatory Level
Mandatory Label\System Mandatory Level

For broader host enumeration, see Windows Enumeration.

docs.title: 3. Determine Administrative Context
docs.text:
PowerShell:

$identity = [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
$principal = New-Object Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal($identity)
$principal.IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)

Possible output:

True

or:

False

Remember that local Administrators group membership does not necessarily mean the current process is elevated because User Account Control can provide a filtered token.

docs.title: 4. User Privileges
docs.text:
Enumerate privileges:

whoami /priv

Privileges worth investigating include:

Privilege Security Relevance SeBackupPrivilege Can permit reading protected files through backup semantics SeRestorePrivilege Can permit restoring or replacing protected resources SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege Can permit taking ownership of securable objects SeDebugPrivilege Provides powerful access to processes SeImpersonatePrivilege Allows impersonation in appropriate authentication contexts SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege Allows assignment of primary tokens in specific circumstances SeLoadDriverPrivilege Allows loading kernel drivers under applicable conditions SeManageVolumePrivilege Provides powerful volume-management capabilities SeTcbPrivilege Highly privileged operating-system capability

A listed privilege is not automatically exploitable.

Determine:

Privilege Present?
      |
      v
Enabled?
      |
      v
Relevant Resource Available?
      |
      v
Current Integrity Context?
      |
      v
Security Boundary Crossed?

docs.title: 5. Local Groups
docs.text:
Enumerate groups:

net localgroup

Administrators:

net localgroup Administrators

PowerShell:

Get-LocalGroup

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators"

Other potentially important groups include:

Backup Operators
Remote Desktop Users
Remote Management Users
Hyper-V Administrators
Event Log Readers
Performance Log Users

Membership should be interpreted according to the capabilities granted on the particular host.

docs.title: 6. Operating System Information
docs.text:
systeminfo

PowerShell:

Get-ComputerInfo

Focused:

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsBuildNumber, OsArchitecture

CIM:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture

Version information helps determine whether known vulnerabilities or configuration behaviours may be relevant.

Do not infer vulnerability solely from an operating-system build number.

docs.title: 7. Services
docs.text:
Windows services are one of the most important privilege escalation areas.

Enumerate services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service

Useful fields:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, StartName, PathName

Running services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object State -eq "Running" |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

Services running as LocalSystem:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object StartName -eq "LocalSystem" |
    Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, PathName

Other privileged identities may include:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
LocalSystem
NetworkService
LocalService
Privileged domain service accounts

A service running as SYSTEM is normal.

The important question is whether a lower-privileged user can influence something used by that service.

See Windows Services.

docs.title: 8. Service Executable Permissions
docs.text:
Suppose a service uses:

C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service\service.exe

Inspect the executable:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service\service.exe"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service\service.exe" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Inspect the parent directory:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Potentially dangerous permissions for broad principals include:

Write
Modify
FullControl

Potentially broad principals include:

Everyone
BUILTIN\Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Users

The combination matters:

Service runs as SYSTEM
        +
Standard user can modify service executable
        =
Potential privilege escalation

docs.title: 9. Writable Service Directories
docs.text:
Sometimes the executable itself is protected while its parent directory is writable.

Check:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service"

or:

(Get-Acl "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service").Access

A controlled write test can validate permissions:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID.tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Host "[+] Write succeeded: $file"
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}
catch {
    Write-Host "[-] Write failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}

This proves only that the user can write to the directory.

It does not prove privilege escalation.

docs.title: 10. Correlating Writable Directories with Services
docs.text:
If a writable directory is identified, determine whether a service references it.

Example:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object PathName -Match ([regex]::Escape($folder)) |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, State, PathName

This is significantly stronger than simply reporting a writable folder.

Assessment logic:

Writable Folder
      |
      v
Used by Service?
      |
      +--> No --> Record only if otherwise relevant
      |
      +--> Yes
             |
             v
       Service Privileged?
             |
             +--> No --> Lower priority
             |
             +--> Yes
                    |
                    v
             Controllable Resource?
                    |
                    v
               Validate Impact

docs.title: 11. Service Configuration
docs.text:
Inspect a service:

sc qc ServiceName

Example:

sc qc Spooler

PowerShell:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='Spooler'"

Important properties include:

BINARY_PATH_NAME
SERVICE_START_NAME
START_TYPE
DEPENDENCIES

CIM equivalents:

PathName
StartName
StartMode

docs.title: 12. Service Security Descriptors
docs.text:
Query the service security descriptor:

sc sdshow ServiceName

Example:

sc sdshow Spooler

The output uses Security Descriptor Definition Language.

Security-sensitive service rights can include the ability to:

Change service configuration
Start service
Stop service
Delete service
Modify service permissions

A lower-privileged user with service configuration rights may be able to alter how a privileged service operates.

Validate the exact access granted before reporting.

docs.title: 13. AccessChk for Services
docs.text:
Microsoft Sysinternals AccessChk can simplify permission analysis.

AccessChk

AccessChk can inspect:

Services
Files
Directories
Registry keys
Processes
Named pipes

Always interpret AccessChk output in the context of the current user and the actual resource.

docs.title: 14. Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
A service path containing spaces may require further review if the executable path is not quoted.

Example:

C:\Program Files\Vendor Application\Service.exe

The important conditions are not simply:

Path contains spaces

A meaningful issue generally requires:

Unquoted service path
        +
Path parsing ambiguity
        +
Attacker-writable candidate location
        +
Privileged service
        =
Potential privilege escalation

Enumerate service paths:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object {
        $_.PathName -and
        $_.PathName -notmatch '^"' -and
        $_.PathName -match '\s'
    } |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

This is a candidate-generation technique only.

Each result requires manual validation.

docs.title: 15. Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Enumerate scheduled tasks:

schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

Useful summary:

Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        TaskName = $_.TaskName
        TaskPath = $_.TaskPath
        User = $_.Principal.UserId
        RunLevel = $_.Principal.RunLevel
        Actions = ($_.Actions | ForEach-Object {
            "$($_.Execute) $($_.Arguments)"
        }) -join "; "
    }
}

Look for tasks that:

Run as SYSTEM / Administrator
        +
Execute modifiable file
        =
Potential privilege escalation

docs.title: 16. Scheduled Task File Permissions
docs.text:
Suppose a task executes:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\maintenance.ps1

Inspect:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\maintenance.ps1"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\maintenance.ps1" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Also inspect the directory:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

Do not modify production scripts simply to demonstrate the issue.

Permission evidence combined with task configuration may already provide sufficient proof.

docs.title: 17. Startup Applications
docs.text:
Enumerate startup commands:

Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand |
    Select-Object Name, Command, Location, User

Registry locations include:

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce

PowerShell:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

A startup entry becomes security-relevant when a lower-privileged user can influence content that executes in a higher-privileged context.

docs.title: 18. Registry Permissions
docs.text:
Inspect a registry key:

Get-Acl "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Vendor"

Access entries:

(Get-Acl "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Vendor").Access

Look for broad write access such as:

SetValue
CreateSubKey
WriteKey
FullControl

Again, the permission alone is not enough.

Determine whether the registry value influences:

Privileged service
Privileged application
Startup mechanism
Security configuration
Executable path
DLL path

docs.title: 19. Autoruns
docs.text:
Microsoft Sysinternals Autoruns provides broad visibility into automatic execution locations.

Autoruns

It can enumerate areas such as:

Logon entries
Services
Drivers
Scheduled tasks
Explorer extensions
AppInit entries
Winlogon entries
Known DLLs
Boot execution

During privilege escalation analysis, investigate whether privileged automatic execution references lower-privileged writable resources.

docs.title: 20. Installed Applications
docs.text:
Enumerate installed applications through the registry.

64-bit applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

32-bit applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

Investigate:

Unsupported applications
Old management software
Backup agents
Deployment clients
Custom enterprise applications
Privileged helper services

Do not associate a version with a CVE without verifying the affected version range and applicable configuration.

docs.title: 21. Application Directory Permissions
docs.text:
Custom software is often installed outside the standard protected directories.

Common locations include:

C:\ProgramData
C:\Vendor
C:\Apps
C:\Tools
C:\Company

Inspect:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\ProgramData\Vendor" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

If writable, determine what uses the directory.

Search services:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object PathName -Match ([regex]::Escape($folder)) |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

Search scheduled tasks manually or through their actions.

The directory's consumers determine the actual impact.

docs.title: 22. DLL Search Behaviour
docs.text:
Applications may load DLLs from multiple locations.

Privilege escalation risk can arise when:

Privileged Process
       |
       v
Attempts DLL Load
       |
       v
Searches Attacker-Writable Location
       |
       v
Attacker Controls DLL Resolution

Do not assume that the absence of a DLL automatically means a hijack is possible.

Validate:

  • Actual DLL load attempt
  • Search order
  • Writable location
  • Process privilege
  • Architecture
  • Application behaviour
  • Existing mitigations

Process Monitor is useful for analysing runtime file and DLL activity.

Process Monitor

docs.title: 23. PATH Environment Variable
docs.text:
Inspect PATH:

echo %PATH%

PowerShell:

$env:PATH

Split entries:

$env:PATH -split ';'

Potential security concerns arise when:

Privileged application
        +
Searches PATH for executable or library
        +
PATH contains user-writable directory
        =
Potential execution-control issue

A writable PATH entry alone does not prove privilege escalation.

docs.title: 24. Environment Variables
docs.text:
Enumerate:

set

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Environment variables may reveal:

Custom application paths
Temporary directories
Development tools
Deployment configuration
Proxy configuration
Runtime paths

These can provide clues to applications and resources worth investigating.

docs.title: 25. Stored Credentials
docs.text:
List Windows Credential Manager entries:

cmdkey /list

This can reveal credential targets.

The presence of a credential entry does not necessarily mean the underlying credential can be extracted or reused.

Assess:

Target
Type
Current user
Associated service/application
Potential reuse context

See Windows Credentials.

docs.title: 26. PowerShell History
docs.text:
History location:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Read:

Get-Content (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

History may reveal:

Administrative commands
Network shares
Deployment commands
Application configuration
Operational paths
Authentication-related commands

Handle any discovered secrets as sensitive assessment evidence.

docs.title: 27. Configuration Files
docs.text:
Applications may store sensitive configuration in:

*.config
*.ini
*.xml
*.json
*.yml
*.yaml
*.conf

Search should be scoped to relevant application directories.

Example:

Get-ChildItem "C:\ProgramData\Vendor" -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object Extension -Match '\.(config|ini|xml|json|yml|yaml|conf)$'

Inspect configuration for:

Service accounts
Connection strings
API endpoints
Database configuration
Network shares
Credential references
Certificate locations

Avoid unnecessarily collecting sensitive content.

docs.title: 28. User Profiles
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-ChildItem C:\Users

Profiles:

Get-CimInstance Win32_UserProfile |
    Select-Object LocalPath, Loaded, Special

Interesting areas may include:

Documents
Desktop
Downloads
AppData
PowerShell history
SSH configuration
Cloud CLI configuration
Development configuration
Application configuration

Only access data permitted by the assessment scope and current account permissions.

docs.title: 29. AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
Windows Installer policies should be reviewed carefully.

Relevant registry values are traditionally associated with:

HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer
HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer

Inspect:

Get-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Focused query:

Get-ItemPropertyValue "HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-ItemPropertyValue "HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

A meaningful AlwaysInstallElevated condition historically requires the relevant policy to be enabled in both user and machine context.

Do not change the policy during routine testing.

docs.title: 30. UAC
docs.text:
User Account Control influences administrative token behaviour.

Basic information about the current token can be gathered through:

whoami /groups

and:

whoami /priv

Relevant registry configuration exists under:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System

Inspect:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Important values can include:

EnableLUA
ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin
ConsentPromptBehaviorUser
PromptOnSecureDesktop
FilterAdministratorToken

UAC configuration should be interpreted in the context of administrative membership and endpoint security requirements.

docs.title: 31. Application Control
docs.text:
Application control can significantly affect privilege escalation opportunities.

Relevant technologies include:

AppLocker
Windows Defender Application Control
Microsoft Defender
Attack Surface Reduction
PowerShell Constrained Language Mode

AppLocker effective policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Collections:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Select-Object CollectionType, EnforcementMode

PowerShell Language Mode:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Defender:

Get-MpComputerStatus -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Application-control testing should focus on effective policy rather than the mere existence of individual Windows utilities.

docs.title: 32. AppLocker Allowed Paths
docs.text:
Path-based rules require particular attention.

Retrieve effective rules:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections | ForEach-Object {
    $_.Rules
}

The important relationship is:

AppLocker Allows Directory
          +
Standard User Can Write There
          =
Potential Application-Control Weakness

For example, an allowed %WINDIR%\* path does not automatically create a weakness because standard users normally cannot modify most protected Windows directories.

The correct next question is:

Can the assessed user write to any location covered by the allow rule?

docs.title: 33. Test Effective AppLocker Decisions
docs.text:
Test a file:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "C:\Path\file.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Detailed output:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "C:\Path\file.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME" |
    Format-List FilePath, PolicyDecision, MatchingRule

This is preferable to assuming that a file is allowed because its parent directory appears in a rule.

docs.title: 34. PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible modes:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

FullLanguage is normal on many Windows systems.

It should not be reported as a vulnerability by itself.

In hardened environments, determine whether the expected design requires Constrained Language Mode through application control.

docs.title: 35. Security Products
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender:

Get-MpComputerStatus -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Preferences:

Get-MpPreference -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Running services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object State -eq "Running" |
    Select-Object Name, DisplayName, StartName

Do not disable or tamper with endpoint security during ordinary privilege escalation enumeration.

The goal is to understand the defensive environment.

docs.title: 36. Network Services
docs.text:
Listening ports:

netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING

PowerShell:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

Map to processes:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        Address = $_.LocalAddress
        Port = $_.LocalPort
        PID = $_.OwningProcess
        Process = (Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).ProcessName
    }
}

Local-only administrative applications may expose functionality that becomes security-relevant when accessible from a lower-privileged context.

docs.title: 37. Named Pipes
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-ChildItem \\.\pipe\

Named pipes can expose inter-process communication used by:

Services
Databases
Browsers
Management software
Security software
Custom applications

A named pipe is not inherently vulnerable.

Further analysis requires understanding its permissions and protocol behaviour.

docs.title: 38. Network Shares
docs.text:
net share

PowerShell:

Get-SmbShare

Permissions:

Get-SmbShareAccess -Name "ShareName"

Local shares may expose:

Scripts
Backups
Deployment packages
Configuration files
Application data

Evaluate both share permissions and NTFS permissions.

docs.title: 39. Process Enumeration
docs.text:
tasklist /v

PowerShell:

Get-Process

Command lines:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process |
    Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CommandLine

Processes may reveal:

Privileged applications
Management agents
Backup software
Database services
Deployment agents
Custom applications

Correlate interesting processes with:

Executable path
Service
User context
Filesystem permissions
Network listeners
Configuration

docs.title: 40. Process Ownership
docs.text:
CIM can help correlate processes and services, but access to owner information may depend on permissions.

For service-backed processes, start with:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object State -eq "Running" |
    Select-Object Name, ProcessId, StartName, PathName

This provides:

Service
PID
Service account
Executable path

which can then be correlated with filesystem permissions.

docs.title: 41. Hotfix and Patch Analysis
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-HotFix

or:

Get-CimInstance Win32_QuickFixEngineering

Patch analysis should not rely solely on the absence of a particular KB.

Modern Windows servicing uses cumulative updates, supersedence, and servicing-stack behaviour that can make simple KB checks misleading.

Validate:

Windows version
Build
Revision
Installed updates
Affected product
Vulnerability prerequisites

before reporting a missing patch.

docs.title: 42. Automated Privilege Escalation Enumeration
docs.text:
Automated enumeration can improve coverage.

Useful tools include:

WinPEAS
PrivescCheck
SharpUp
Seatbelt
AccessChk
Autoruns
Process Monitor

Automated results are candidate findings, not final findings.

Every meaningful result should be manually validated.

docs.title: 43. WinPEAS
docs.text:
PEASS-ng

WinPEAS can identify:

System information
Users
Privileges
Services
Scheduled tasks
Applications
Credentials
Interesting files
Registry settings
Permissions
Security controls

Its output can be extensive.

Use it to identify areas for manual validation rather than treating every highlighted result as a vulnerability.

docs.title: 44. PrivescCheck
docs.text:
PrivescCheck

PrivescCheck provides PowerShell-based checks for common Windows privilege escalation conditions.

Potential areas include:

Services
Scheduled tasks
Registry
Credentials
Applications
Permissions
Security configuration

Manual verification remains necessary.

docs.title: 45. SharpUp
docs.text:
SharpUp

SharpUp focuses on identifying Windows privilege escalation opportunities.

Use tool findings as leads for deeper inspection.

docs.title: 46. Seatbelt
docs.text:
Seatbelt

Seatbelt performs broad Windows host reconnaissance and can help identify:

Security controls
Users
Processes
Services
Interesting configuration
Credentials
System information

It is particularly useful when privilege escalation analysis requires broader environmental context.

docs.title: 47. AccessChk
docs.text:
AccessChk

AccessChk is useful for identifying permissions on:

Files
Directories
Services
Registry keys
Processes
Named pipes

Permission output should always be correlated with resource usage.

docs.title: 48. Process Monitor
docs.text:
Process Monitor

Process Monitor can help investigate:

Filesystem access
Registry access
Process activity
DLL loading
Configuration access
Missing files

It is particularly useful when determining what resources a privileged application actually consumes.

docs.title: 49. Autoruns
docs.text:
Autoruns

Autoruns can help identify privileged automatic execution paths that reference modifiable resources.

This is often more useful than manually checking a small number of startup registry keys.

docs.title: 50. Manual Validation
docs.text:
Automated tools may report:

Writable directory
Unquoted service path
Interesting privilege
Weak registry ACL
Scheduled task
Stored credential

The next step should always be manual validation.

Example:

Tool reports writable service directory
             |
             v
Identify service
             |
             v
Determine service account
             |
             v
Inspect exact ACL
             |
             v
Confirm current user has write access
             |
             v
Determine what service consumes
             |
             v
Establish practical impact

docs.title: 51. Safe Validation
docs.text:
Privilege escalation testing can alter privileged resources.

Where possible, demonstrate the condition without modifying production executables or configurations.

Preferred evidence can include:

ACL showing write permission
        +
Service configuration showing privileged execution
        +
Current user identity
        +
Controlled write test using temporary file
        =
Strong evidence

A destructive or persistent payload is usually unnecessary.

docs.title: 52. Controlled Write Test
docs.text:
For a candidate directory:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID-$(Get-Random).tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Host "[+] Write access confirmed: $file"
}
catch {
    Write-Host "[-] Write access denied: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}
finally {
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}

This demonstrates write capability without replacing an application file.

docs.title: 53. Permission Analysis
docs.text:
When a candidate resource is discovered, document:

Owner
ACL
Inherited permissions
Current user's effective group membership
Resource type
Privileged consumer

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Path" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Detailed:

(Get-Acl "C:\Path").Access |
    Format-Table IdentityReference, FileSystemRights, AccessControlType, IsInherited

Command Prompt:

icacls "C:\Path"

docs.title: 54. Important Permission Relationships
docs.text:
Common relationships worth investigating include:

Privileged Resource Controllable Component SYSTEM service Executable SYSTEM service Executable directory SYSTEM service Configuration file SYSTEM service Registry key Elevated scheduled task Script Elevated scheduled task Executable Privileged application DLL search directory Startup mechanism Referenced executable Deployment agent Package or script directory

The presence of the relationship is more important than either component individually.

docs.title: Writable directory without privileged consumer
docs.text:
User can write to:
C:\ProgramData\Example

but nothing privileged uses the directory.

Result:

Not sufficient for privilege escalation.

docs.title: SYSTEM service with protected executable
docs.text:
Service runs as SYSTEM.

but:

Executable protected
Directory protected
Configuration protected
Service configuration protected

Result:

Normal privileged service configuration.

docs.title: Unquoted service path without writable location
docs.text:
C:\Program Files\Vendor App\Service.exe

but the current user cannot write to any relevant candidate location.

Result:

No demonstrated privilege escalation path.

docs.title: FullLanguage PowerShell
docs.text:
LanguageMode = FullLanguage

Result:

Not inherently a vulnerability.

Evaluate against the intended hardening model.

docs.title: Allowed Windows utility
docs.text:
rundll32.exe = Allowed

Result:

Not inherently a vulnerability.

The practical security impact depends on what content can be executed, application-control objectives, writable paths, and other controls.

docs.title: 56. Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a privilege escalation finding, capture:

Host
Current user
SID
Groups
Privileges
Integrity level
Affected resource
Resource owner
Resource permissions
Privileged consumer
Consumer identity
Configuration
Controlled validation
Security impact

Example:

Host:
WS01

Current user:
CORP\standarduser

Integrity:
Medium

Affected directory:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Service

Permission:
BUILTIN\Users - Modify

Service:
VendorService

Service account:
LocalSystem

Service executable:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Service\service.exe

Validation:
The current standard user successfully created and removed a temporary
file in the service directory.

Impact:
A lower-privileged user can modify resources within the directory used by
a LocalSystem service. The exact executable and service behaviour should
be validated to determine whether privileged code execution is possible.

docs.title: 57. Severity Assessment
docs.text:
Severity depends on practical impact.

A useful model:

Exploitability
     +
Privileges Gained
     +
User Interaction
     +
Reliability
     +
Scope
     =
Severity

Examples:

Condition Typical Importance Writable unused directory Informational / no finding Writable privileged application config Potentially significant Writable SYSTEM service executable High impact Weak task file permissions with SYSTEM execution High impact Stored privileged credential Potentially critical depending on reuse Broad AppLocker rule without writable allowed location Usually not sufficient alone

Use the organisation's agreed severity methodology for final ratings.

docs.title: 58. Remediation Principles
docs.text:
Privilege escalation remediation usually focuses on removing the trust relationship.

Common approaches include:

Restrict filesystem permissions
Restrict registry permissions
Protect service configuration
Protect scheduled task resources
Remove unnecessary local privileges
Remove unnecessary local administrators
Secure application directories
Quote service paths
Protect secrets
Patch vulnerable software
Harden application control
Monitor privileged execution

Remediation should target the root cause rather than only the demonstrated technique.

docs.title: 59. Service Remediation
docs.text:
For vulnerable services:

Protect executable
Protect executable directory
Protect configuration
Restrict service permissions
Use least-privileged service account where practical
Quote executable paths
Remove unnecessary user write access

A typical secure relationship is:

SYSTEM Service
      |
      v
Executable
      |
      v
Administrators / SYSTEM Modify
      |
      v
Standard Users Read and Execute Only

docs.title: 60. Scheduled Task Remediation
docs.text:
For privileged tasks:

Protect task definition
Protect executable
Protect script
Protect parent directory
Review task principal
Use least privilege
Remove obsolete tasks

Privileged scheduled tasks should not execute content writable by ordinary users.

docs.title: 61. Credential Remediation
docs.text:
If credentials are exposed:

Remove plaintext secrets
Rotate affected credentials
Use managed identities where possible
Use Windows Credential Manager appropriately
Use gMSA for applicable domain services
Restrict configuration-file permissions
Avoid credentials in command lines
Review credential reuse

For Active Directory service accounts, see gMSA.

docs.title: 62. Application Control Remediation
docs.text:
Where application control is part of the security design:

Review AppLocker / WDAC policy
Review broad path rules
Identify user-writable allowed locations
Restrict script execution where appropriate
Apply PowerShell controls
Enable relevant logging
Review ASR configuration

Application control should be designed as a complete policy rather than as isolated executable blocks.

docs.title: 66. Testing Model
docs.text:
The strongest privilege escalation findings follow this model:

1. Identify current security context

2. Identify a more privileged process or execution mechanism

3. Identify a resource consumed by that mechanism

4. Confirm the lower-privileged user controls the resource

5. Confirm the relationship crosses a security boundary

6. Validate safely

7. Collect reproducible evidence

8. Recommend removal of the underlying trust relationship

Avoid:

Observation
    |
    v
Immediate vulnerability conclusion

Prefer:

Observation
    |
    v
Correlation
    |
    v
Permission validation
    |
    v
Execution-context validation
    |
    v
Practical impact
    |
    v
Finding

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Standard Users Can Modify Resources Used by a LocalSystem Service

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A Windows service running as LocalSystem references resources stored in a
directory where standard users have Modify permissions.

This permission relationship allows a lower-privileged user to influence
content consumed by a privileged service and may result in privilege
escalation depending on the affected resource and service behaviour.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Current user:
CORP\standarduser

Service:
VendorService

Service account:
LocalSystem

Service path:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Service\service.exe

Directory permissions:
BUILTIN\Users:(M)

Controlled write test:
Successful

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
A standard user may be able to influence execution performed by a service
running with LocalSystem privileges, potentially resulting in elevation of
privileges.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Remove unnecessary write and modify permissions for standard users from
directories and files consumed by privileged services.

Restrict modification rights to trusted administrative and service
identities, and review similar application directories for equivalent
permission relationships.

docs.title: Windows Registry Security
docs.text:
The Windows Registry is a hierarchical configuration database used by Windows, applications, services and users.

It stores information related to:

Operating system configuration
Services
Drivers
Applications
User profiles
Authentication
Security policies
Startup behaviour
File associations
Environment variables
Installed software
Application settings

During a Windows security assessment, Registry permissions and configuration can reveal privilege escalation opportunities, sensitive information and insecure application behaviour.

The key security question is not simply:

Can the user write to the Registry?

Instead ask:

Can a lower-privileged user modify a Registry value
that influences a higher-privileged security context?

Authorised Security Testing

Perform Registry testing only on systems included in the authorised assessment scope. Prefer permission inspection and non-destructive validation. Do not modify production service configuration, startup entries, security controls or other operational Registry values unless explicitly permitted.

docs.title: Registry Security Model
docs.text:
A typical privilege escalation path looks like:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Writable Registry Key
        |
        v
Privileged Configuration
        |
        v
SYSTEM / Administrator Process
        |
        v
Attacker-Controlled Behaviour

A writable Registry key alone is not necessarily a vulnerability.

A meaningful security issue normally requires:

Lower-privileged write access
+
Security-sensitive Registry value
+
Higher-privileged consumer
+
Demonstrable security impact

docs.title: Registry Hives
docs.text:
The primary Registry hives include:

Hive Abbreviation Purpose HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE HKLM System-wide configuration HKEY_CURRENT_USER HKCU Current user's configuration HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT HKCR File associations and COM registration view HKEY_USERS HKU Loaded user profiles HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG HKCC Current hardware configuration

docs.title: PowerShell Registry Drives
docs.text:
PowerShell exposes common Registry hives as drives:

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider Registry

Typical output:

Name Used (GB) Free (GB) Provider Root
---- --------- --------- -------- ----
HKCU                     Registry HKEY_CURRENT_USER
HKLM                     Registry HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE

docs.title: Registry Paths
docs.text:
PowerShell example:

Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE'

Traditional Registry path:

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE

reg.exe representation:

HKLM\SOFTWARE

docs.title: Core Registry Tools
docs.text:
Useful built-in tools include:

reg.exe
regedit.exe
PowerShell Registry provider
Get-Item
Get-ItemProperty
Get-Acl

docs.title: reg.exe
docs.text:
Query a key:

reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion"

docs.title: Query a Value
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion" /v ProgramFilesDir

docs.title: Recursive Query
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Example" /s

docs.title: PowerShell Query
docs.text: Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion'

docs.title: List Subkeys
docs.text: Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE'

docs.title: Specific Property
docs.text: Get-ItemPropertyValue -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion' -Name 'ProgramFilesDir'

docs.title: Current Identity
docs.text:
Before analysing Registry permissions, identify the current security context.

whoami

docs.title: Group Membership
docs.text: whoami /groups

docs.title: Privileges
docs.text: whoami /priv

docs.title: PowerShell Identity
docs.text: [System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().Name

docs.title: Why Identity Matters
docs.text:
An ACL may grant access to:

Users

Authenticated Users

Everyone

A local group

A domain group

You need to determine whether the current user belongs to the relevant security principal.

docs.title: Registry ACLs
docs.text:
Registry keys have security descriptors similar to filesystem objects.

Use:

Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example'

docs.title: Detailed ACL
docs.text: Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example' | Format-List *

docs.title: Access Entries
docs.text: (Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example').Access

docs.title: Compact View
docs.text: (Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example').Access | Select-Object IdentityReference,RegistryRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited

docs.title: Important Registry Rights
docs.text:
Common rights include:

Right Meaning QueryValues Read values SetValue Modify values CreateSubKey Create child keys EnumerateSubKeys Enumerate child keys Delete Delete key ChangePermissions Modify ACL TakeOwnership Change ownership ReadKey Read access WriteKey Write-related access FullControl Full access

docs.title: High-Value Write Rights
docs.text:
Pay particular attention to:

SetValue
CreateSubKey
WriteKey
FullControl
ChangePermissions
TakeOwnership

docs.title: ACL Example
docs.text:
RegistryRights    : SetValue, CreateSubKey, ReadKey
AccessControlType : Allow
IdentityReference : BUILTIN\Users
IsInherited       : False

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This establishes that:

BUILTIN\Users

has meaningful write access.

It does not yet establish a vulnerability.

Next determine:

What consumes this key?

Which privilege does that process use?

Can modification influence execution or security behaviour?

docs.title: High-Value Registry Areas
docs.text:
Useful areas to review include:

Services

Startup configuration

Application configuration

Installer policy

Environment configuration

COM registration

Protocol handlers

File associations

Security product configuration

Stored application secrets

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Windows service configuration is represented under:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services

Enumerate:

reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services"

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text: Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services'

docs.title: Specific Service
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\ExampleService"

docs.title: Important Service Values
docs.text:
Common values include:

ImagePath
DisplayName
ObjectName
Start
Type
DependOnService

docs.title: ImagePath
docs.text:
Query:

reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\ExampleService" /v ImagePath

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text: ImagePath    REG_EXPAND_SZ    C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe

docs.title: Security Analysis
docs.text:
Determine:

Who can modify the service key?

Who can modify ImagePath?

Who can modify the referenced executable?

Who can modify the executable's parent directory?

Which account runs the service?

docs.title: Service Registry ACL
docs.text: Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\ExampleService' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Access Entries
docs.text: (Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\ExampleService').Access | Select-Object IdentityReference,RegistryRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited

docs.title: Potential Pattern
docs.text:
Standard User
      |
      v
Writable Service Registry Key
      |
      v
ImagePath
      |
      v
Privileged Service
      |
      v
Potential Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Registry ACLs are only one part of service security.

Also review the service object's permissions.

See:

Windows Services

docs.title: Service Security Context
docs.text:
Check:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='ExampleService'" | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
Name      : ExampleService
StartName : LocalSystem
State     : Running
PathName  : C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If:

Service account:
LocalSystem

and:

Standard user can modify ImagePath

this is a strong privilege escalation candidate.

However, establish whether the user can actually change the value and whether the service can subsequently execute the modified configuration.

docs.title: Safe Validation
docs.text:
Prefer:

ACL inspection

Current-user access analysis

Service configuration review

before attempting any Registry modification.

docs.title: Autorun Registry Keys
docs.text: Windows and applications may use Registry values to start programs during user logon.

docs.title: Common Run Keys
docs.text:
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce

HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce

docs.title: Query HKCU Run
docs.text: reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"

docs.title: Query HKLM Run
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text: Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Machine-Wide Run
docs.text: Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Security Context Matters
docs.text:
An HKCU autorun normally executes as:

That user

It does not automatically provide privilege escalation.

docs.title: Machine-Wide Configuration
docs.text:
An insecure machine-wide startup configuration can be more significant when:

Standard user can modify it

and

A higher-privileged user or process consumes it

docs.title: Startup Command Dependencies
docs.text:
Example:

Updater    REG_SZ    C:\ProgramData\Vendor\update.exe

Review:

Registry ACL

Executable ACL

Parent directory ACL

Execution context

docs.title: Startup Folder Relationship
docs.text:
Registry autoruns are not the only startup mechanism.

Also consider:

Startup folders

Scheduled tasks

Services

when reviewing Windows persistence and privilege escalation.

docs.title: Winlogon
docs.text:
Security-sensitive configuration exists under:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon

docs.title: Query
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon"

docs.title: Common Values
docs.text:
Examples include:

Shell
Userinit

docs.title: Typical Values
docs.text:
Common legitimate values may resemble:

Shell:
explorer.exe

Userinit:
C:\Windows\system32\userinit.exe,

docs.title: Security Assessment
docs.text:
Review unexpected modifications and ACLs.

Do not modify Winlogon configuration during routine assessment validation.

Incorrect values can prevent normal user logon.

docs.title: Safe Check
docs.text: Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Installer Policies
docs.text: Windows Installer policy deserves attention during privilege escalation reviews.

docs.title: AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
Two Registry values are relevant:

HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer

HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer

docs.title: Query Current User
docs.text: reg query "HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" /v AlwaysInstallElevated

docs.title: Query Local Machine
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" /v AlwaysInstallElevated

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Get-ItemPropertyValue -Path 'HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer' -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-ItemPropertyValue -Path 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer' -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The security-relevant configuration is when the policy is enabled in both applicable locations.

Example:

HKCU:
AlwaysInstallElevated = 1

HKLM:
AlwaysInstallElevated = 1

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not report the condition based on only one value without understanding the effective Windows Installer policy.

The finding should be based on effective behaviour and the applicable policy configuration.

docs.title: Safe Reporting
docs.text: For an authorised assessment, configuration evidence is often sufficient to report the unsafe policy without executing an installer package.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Machine and user environment configuration can be stored in the Registry.

docs.title: Machine Environment
docs.text: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Environment

docs.title: Query
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Environment"

docs.title: User Environment
docs.text: HKCU\Environment

docs.title: Query
docs.text: reg query "HKCU\Environment"

docs.title: PATH
docs.text:
Pay attention to:

Path

but do not automatically treat writable PATH directories as exploitable.

docs.title: PATH Security Model
docs.text:
Privileged Process
       |
       v
Executes Relative Command
       |
       v
PATH Search
       |
       v
Writable Directory
       |
       v
Potential Hijack

docs.title: Required Conditions
docs.text:
A meaningful PATH-based privilege escalation generally requires:

Privileged process
+
Relative executable invocation
+
Attacker-controlled search location
+
Predictable execution

docs.title: Machine PATH
docs.text:
PowerShell:

[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','Machine')

docs.title: User PATH
docs.text: [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User')

docs.title: Split PATH
docs.text: [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','Machine') -split ';'

docs.title: Review Directory ACLs
docs.text:
For each relevant directory:

Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\Example\bin' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
A writable PATH entry is not sufficient by itself.

You still need a privileged application that resolves an executable through that path.

docs.title: Application Configuration
docs.text:
Third-party software frequently stores configuration under:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Vendor

HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Vendor

HKCU\Software\Vendor

docs.title: Enumerate Installed Vendor Keys
docs.text: Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE' | Select-Object PSChildName

docs.title: 32-bit Software
docs.text: Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object PSChildName

docs.title: Security Questions
docs.text:
For interesting application keys ask:

Who can modify the key?

Which process reads it?

Which account runs that process?

Does it contain executable paths?

Does it contain script paths?

Does it contain plugin paths?

Does it contain command-line arguments?

Does it contain credentials?

Does it contain network locations?

docs.title: Application Command Configuration
docs.text:
Example:

ExecutablePath = C:\ProgramData\Vendor\worker.exe

If a privileged service consumes this value, inspect both:

Registry permissions

Filesystem permissions

docs.title: Registry-to-Filesystem Relationship
docs.text:
Registry Value
     |
     v
Executable Path
     |
     v
Filesystem Object
     |
     v
Filesystem ACL

Both layers matter.

docs.title: Credentials in the Registry
docs.text:
Applications sometimes store sensitive information in Registry values.

Search should be targeted and authorised.

docs.title: Common Keywords
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

password
passwd
pwd
credential
secret
token
apikey
api_key
connectionstring
username
user

docs.title: Targeted PowerShell Search
docs.text:
For a known application subtree:

Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\ExampleVendor' -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
    try {
        $item = Get-ItemProperty $_.PSPath -ErrorAction Stop
        $item.PSObject.Properties | Where-Object {
            $_.Name -match 'password|passwd|pwd|secret|token|api.?key|credential|connection'
        } | ForEach-Object {
            [PSCustomObject]@{
                Path  = $_.PSParentPath
                Name  = $_.Name
                Value = $_.Value
            }
        }
    } catch {}
}

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Avoid indiscriminately dumping the entire Registry.

Large-scale searches can:

Generate unnecessary data

Expose unrelated secrets

Create evidence-handling issues

Consume significant time

docs.title: Scope Searches
docs.text:
Prefer:

Known application keys

Assessment-relevant vendor keys

Specific configuration paths

docs.title: Credential Interpretation
docs.text:
Finding a value named:

Password

does not prove it contains plaintext credentials.

Determine whether it contains:

Plaintext

Encrypted data

Hash

Reference

Placeholder

Empty value

docs.title: DPAPI
docs.text:
Some Registry values may contain data protected using Windows Data Protection API.

Encrypted data should not be described as plaintext credentials.

docs.title: Reporting Sensitive Data
docs.text:
Do not place full passwords, API keys or tokens in screenshots or reports.

Use redaction such as:

Password = Sup***********

docs.title: Uninstall Information
docs.text:
Installed application information is commonly stored under:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall

HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall

docs.title: Query
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall" /s

docs.title: PowerShell Inventory
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
    Get-ItemProperty $_.PSPath -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
} | Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher,InstallLocation

docs.title: Include 32-bit Applications
docs.text:
$paths = @(
    'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*',
    'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*'
)

Get-ItemProperty $paths -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object DisplayName |
    Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher,InstallLocation

docs.title: Security Use
docs.text:
Application inventory can support:

Patch review

Attack-surface identification

Service correlation

Vendor configuration discovery

Do not assume a version is vulnerable without verifying the applicable advisory and product configuration.

docs.title: Current User Software
docs.text:
Also consider:

HKCU\Software

for per-user application configuration.

docs.title: File Associations
docs.text:
Windows file associations may involve:

HKCR

and underlying user/machine class registration.

docs.title: Example Query
docs.text: reg query "HKCR\.txt"

docs.title: Handler
docs.text: reg query "HKCR\txtfile\shell\open\command"

docs.title: Security Relevance
docs.text:
File association hijacking can matter when:

A privileged process opens a registered file type

and

A lower-privileged user controls the applicable handler

Do not infer privilege escalation from a user-controlled association alone.

docs.title: HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT
docs.text:
HKCR is a merged view involving machine and user class registration.

This distinction matters during security analysis.

Conceptually:

Machine classes
+
User classes
     |
     v
Merged HKCR view

docs.title: COM Registration
docs.text:
COM configuration can be security-sensitive.

Relevant locations include class registration under:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes

HKCU\Software\Classes

docs.title: CLSID
docs.text:
Example structure:

Software\Classes\CLSID\{GUID}

docs.title: InprocServer32
docs.text:
COM servers may reference:

InprocServer32

or other server registration.

docs.title: Example Query
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes\CLSID\{GUID}\InprocServer32"

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
A COM-related privilege escalation requires much more than discovering a writable registration.

You need to establish:

Which component instantiates the COM object?

Which registration view applies?

Which user context is involved?

Which process privilege is involved?

Can the lower-privileged user influence the effective registration?

Does the behaviour cross a privilege boundary?

docs.title: Do Not Overstate COM Findings
docs.text:
COM registration is complex.

Avoid reporting:

Writable HKCU COM key = SYSTEM privilege escalation

without demonstrating the relevant privileged consumer and registration behaviour.

docs.title: Protocol Handlers
docs.text:
Applications may register URI schemes such as:

example://

Registry configuration can determine which application handles the scheme.

docs.title: Security Questions
docs.text:
Review:

Command path

Arguments

Quoting

User control

Privilege of invoking application

Input handling

docs.title: Shell Commands
docs.text:
Registry locations may contain command strings such as:

shell\open\command

Analyse:

Executable path

Arguments

User-controlled substitutions

Execution context

docs.title: Safe Inspection
docs.text:
Query only:

reg query "HKCR\Example\shell\open\command"

Avoid changing handlers on production systems during routine validation.

docs.title: Registry AutoRun Review
docs.text:
A consolidated PowerShell view:

$runKeys = @(
    'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run',
    'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce',
    'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run',
    'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce'
)

foreach ($key in $runKeys) {
    if (Test-Path $key) {
        Write-Host "`n[$key]"
        Get-ItemProperty $key
    }
}

docs.title: ACL Review for Run Keys
docs.text:
$runKeys = @(
    'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run',
    'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'
)

foreach ($key in $runKeys) {
    if (Test-Path $key) {
        Write-Host "`n[$key]"
        (Get-Acl $key).Access |
            Select-Object IdentityReference,RegistryRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited
    }
}

docs.title: Important HKCU Distinction
docs.text:
The current user is expected to control much of:

HKCU

That alone is not a security weakness.

Look for situations where per-user configuration unexpectedly influences a more privileged security context.

docs.title: HKLM Distinction
docs.text:
Write access to security-sensitive:

HKLM

locations is generally more interesting because HKLM contains machine-wide configuration.

Still, validate the actual consumer and impact.

docs.title: Registry Inheritance
docs.text:
Registry permissions may be inherited from parent keys.

Inspect:

(Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example').Access | Select-Object IdentityReference,RegistryRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited

docs.title: Why Inheritance Matters
docs.text:
An insecure permission may originate from:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Vendor

and propagate to many application subkeys.

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
After finding one insecure key, inspect sibling keys.

Example:

Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Vendor'

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text: If several keys inherit the same weak ACL, fixing one child key may not resolve the root cause.

docs.title: Registry Ownership
docs.text:
Inspect owner:

(Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example').Owner

docs.title: Ownership Security
docs.text:
Unexpected ownership can be relevant when it permits a lower-privileged identity to change permissions.

Do not equate ownership alone with immediate write access without examining effective rights.

docs.title: Deny ACEs
docs.text:
Explicit deny entries can override or constrain allow entries.

Example:

Users:
Allow SetValue

SpecificUser:
Deny SetValue

Effective access must account for the complete security descriptor and token membership.

docs.title: Effective Access
docs.text:
Registry ACL interpretation should consider:

Direct ACEs

Inherited ACEs

Allow entries

Deny entries

Group membership

Ownership

Privilege

docs.title: Safe Write Validation
docs.text:
When the engagement permits validation, avoid altering operational values.

If you control a dedicated test key, a harmless value can be used to validate effective write access.

docs.title: Example Test Key
docs.text:
Only use this against a location explicitly approved for testing:

$path = 'HKCU:\Software\SecurityAssessmentTest'

New-Item -Path $path -Force | Out-Null
New-ItemProperty -Path $path -Name 'WriteTest' -Value 'test' -PropertyType String -Force | Out-Null
Get-ItemProperty -Path $path -Name 'WriteTest'
Remove-Item -Path $path -Recurse -Force

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Testing write access to:

HKCU:\Software\SecurityAssessmentTest

does not prove write access to an unrelated target key.

For actual target keys, use ACL analysis or a specifically authorised non-operational value where appropriate.

docs.title: Do Not Modify Production Values Just to Test ACLs
docs.text:
Avoid changing:

Service ImagePath

Winlogon Shell

Security product settings

Authentication settings

Startup commands

Installer policies

unless explicit validation requires it.

docs.title: Remote Registry
docs.text:
Registry access can also occur remotely when:

Remote Registry service is available

Network access permits it

Authentication succeeds

Registry ACL permits access

docs.title: Security Relevance
docs.text:
Remote Registry exposure is not automatically a vulnerability.

Evaluate:

Network segmentation

Authentication

Authorization

Administrative requirements

Firewall policy

docs.title: Remote Registry Service
docs.text:
Check locally:

Get-Service RemoteRegistry -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
Status   Name            DisplayName
------   ----            -----------
Stopped  RemoteRegistry  Remote Registry

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A stopped Remote Registry service is common.

Do not report it merely because the service exists.

docs.title: Registry Backups
docs.text: Registry hives and exported .reg files can contain sensitive configuration.

docs.title: Search Relevant Filesystem Locations
docs.text:
During an authorised assessment, look for files such as:

*.reg
*.hiv
*.save
registry-backup*

in assessment-relevant directories.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not indiscriminately copy Registry hives.

Credential-bearing system hives are sensitive evidence and should only be collected when required by the assessment scope.

docs.title: Registry and UAC
docs.text:
Some UAC-related configuration is represented in the Registry.

Relevant policy configuration can exist under:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System

docs.title: Query
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System"

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not interpret individual UAC Registry values in isolation.

UAC behaviour depends on:

Account type

Token state

Integrity level

Policy combination

Executable behaviour

UAC deserves separate analysis.

See the planned note:

Windows User Account Control

docs.title: Registry and Application Control
docs.text:
Security controls may also expose configuration through Registry-backed policy.

Examples include:

AppLocker

Windows Defender

Windows Defender Application Control related policy/configuration

PowerShell policy

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Registry configuration visibility does not necessarily mean the current user can change the effective security policy.

Policies may be:

GPO-managed

MDM-managed

Locally enforced

Protected by security software

docs.title: Group Policy
docs.text:
Values under policy-related Registry locations may be applied by Group Policy.

A local modification, even if technically possible, may be:

Reverted

Overwritten

Ignored

Protected

docs.title: Determine Source of Truth
docs.text:
When analysing security policy, distinguish:

Observed Registry value

Effective policy

Policy management source

docs.title: WOW64 Registry Redirection
docs.text:
On 64-bit Windows, 32-bit and 64-bit applications can observe different Registry views.

Relevant paths may include:

HKLM\SOFTWARE

HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node

docs.title: Security Relevance
docs.text:
When investigating a third-party application, determine whether it is:

32-bit

64-bit

and inspect the applicable Registry view.

docs.title: PowerShell Architecture
docs.text:
Check:

[Environment]::Is64BitProcess

and:

[Environment]::Is64BitOperatingSystem

docs.title: Registry Value Types
docs.text:
Common Registry data types include:

Type Purpose REG_SZ String REG_EXPAND_SZ Expandable string REG_DWORD 32-bit number REG_QWORD 64-bit number REG_MULTI_SZ Multiple strings REG_BINARY Binary data

docs.title: Expandable Values
docs.text:
Example:

%SystemRoot%\System32\example.exe

may be stored as:

REG_EXPAND_SZ

docs.title: Expand Environment Variables
docs.text: [Environment]::ExpandEnvironmentVariables('%SystemRoot%\System32\example.exe')

docs.title: Do Not Assume Current User Expansion
docs.text:
A privileged service may execute with a different environment.

Consider the consuming process's security context.

docs.title: Interesting Registry Value Patterns
docs.text:
During targeted review, values containing these concepts may deserve attention:

Path

Executable

Command

Script

Plugin

Module

Handler

Service

Update

Backup

Temp

Config

Password

Secret

Token

Key

docs.title: Targeted Value Search
docs.text:
For a known vendor key:

$root = 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\ExampleVendor'

Get-ChildItem $root -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
    try {
        $item = Get-ItemProperty $_.PSPath -ErrorAction Stop

        foreach ($property in $item.PSObject.Properties) {
            if ($property.Name -match 'path|exe|command|script|plugin|module|handler|password|secret|token') {
                [PSCustomObject]@{
                    Key   = $_.Name
                    Name  = $property.Name
                    Value = $property.Value
                }
            }
        }
    } catch {}
}

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Treat keyword searches as:

Candidate discovery

not:

Vulnerability confirmation

docs.title: Registry-to-Execution Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose you find:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\ExampleVendor

WorkerPath =
C:\ProgramData\ExampleVendor\worker.exe

docs.title: Step 1 - Registry ACL
docs.text: Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\ExampleVendor' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Step 2 - File ACL
docs.text: Get-Acl 'C:\ProgramData\ExampleVendor\worker.exe' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Step 3 - Directory ACL
docs.text: Get-Acl 'C:\ProgramData\ExampleVendor' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Step 4 - Consumer
docs.text:
Determine which process uses:

WorkerPath

docs.title: Step 5 - Security Context
docs.text:
Determine whether that process runs as:

Current user

Administrator

SYSTEM

Service account

docs.title: Step 6 - Trigger
docs.text:
Determine:

When is WorkerPath consumed?

docs.title: Step 7 - Security Boundary
docs.text: Only then determine whether a privilege escalation exists.

docs.title: Complete Analysis Model
docs.text:
Registry Key
    |
    v
Registry Value
    |
    v
Consumer
    |
    v
Security Context
    |
    v
Referenced Resource
    |
    v
Filesystem / Network ACL
    |
    v
Trigger
    |
    v
Security Impact

docs.title: Application Update Configuration
docs.text:
Update mechanisms deserve particular attention.

Registry configuration may contain:

Update URL

Updater path

Package directory

Command

Installation path

docs.title: Security Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Does updater run privileged?

Can user modify updater path?

Can user modify package directory?

Can user influence update source?

Is package integrity verified?

docs.title: Important
docs.text: A writable update-related Registry value is only one part of the update trust model.

docs.title: Backup Configuration
docs.text:
Backup agents may store:

Executable paths

Script paths

Credential references

Network shares

Destination directories

in the Registry.

docs.title: Security Context
docs.text:
Backup software frequently runs with elevated privileges.

Therefore, writable configuration can be high-value.

docs.title: Monitoring Agents
docs.text:
Monitoring and management agents may use Registry configuration for:

Plugins

Scripts

Commands

Configuration directories

Review whether standard users can influence these values.

docs.title: Development Software
docs.text:
Developer tooling may create machine-wide Registry configuration.

Examples include:

Build tools

Package managers

IDE integrations

Local web servers

Automation agents

Do not assume development software is low risk when services run privileged.

docs.title: Registry and Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks may execute applications whose configuration is stored in the Registry.

Analysis can therefore become:

Scheduled Task
      |
      v
Privileged Application
      |
      v
Registry Configuration
      |
      v
User-Writable Value
      |
      v
Controlled Dependency

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Scheduled Tasks

docs.title: Registry and Services
docs.text:
Similarly:

Service
   |
   v
Application
   |
   v
Registry Configuration
   |
   v
Executable / Plugin / Script

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Services

docs.title: Registry and Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Registry write access may redirect a privileged process to a filesystem location.

Always evaluate both security descriptors.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Registry:
Executable = C:\ProgramData\App\worker.exe

Registry ACL:
Users = SetValue

Filesystem:
C:\ProgramData\App = Administrators only

Even though the current executable is protected, changing the Registry path may still allow redirection if the privileged application trusts that value.

docs.title: Conversely
docs.text:
Registry:
Administrators only

Filesystem executable:
Users = Modify

The privilege escalation may exist through the filesystem even though Registry permissions are secure.

docs.title: Multiple Control Points
docs.text:
PRIVILEGED PROCESS
                     |
          +----------+----------+
          |                     |
          v                     v
     Registry Path          Fixed Path
          |                     |
          v                     v
   Registry ACL          Filesystem ACL
          |                     |
          +----------+----------+
                     |
                     v
               User Control?

docs.text:
• [ ] Current user identified
  • [ ] Group memberships identified
  • [ ] Token privileges reviewed
  • [ ] Administrative status understood

docs.title: Registry Structure
docs.text:
• [ ] Relevant HKLM keys reviewed
  • [ ] Relevant HKCU keys reviewed
  • [ ] 32-bit Registry view considered
  • [ ] 64-bit Registry view considered
  • [ ] Inheritance considered

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
• [ ] Key owner reviewed
  • [ ] ACL entries reviewed
  • [ ] SetValue identified
  • [ ] CreateSubKey identified
  • [ ] WriteKey identified
  • [ ] FullControl identified
  • [ ] ChangePermissions identified
  • [ ] TakeOwnership identified
  • [ ] Deny ACEs considered
  • [ ] Group membership correlated

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
• [ ] Service Registry keys reviewed
  • [ ] ImagePath reviewed
  • [ ] Service account identified
  • [ ] Service object permissions considered
  • [ ] Executable ACL reviewed
  • [ ] Parent directory ACL reviewed

docs.title: Startup
docs.text:
• [ ] HKCU Run reviewed
  • [ ] HKLM Run reviewed
  • [ ] RunOnce reviewed
  • [ ] Winlogon configuration reviewed where relevant
  • [ ] Startup execution context established
  • [ ] Referenced files reviewed

docs.title: Installer Policy
docs.text:
• [ ] HKCU AlwaysInstallElevated checked
  • [ ] HKLM AlwaysInstallElevated checked
  • [ ] Effective policy interpreted correctly

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• [ ] Vendor keys reviewed
  • [ ] Executable paths reviewed
  • [ ] Script paths reviewed
  • [ ] Plugin paths reviewed
  • [ ] Configuration paths reviewed
  • [ ] Update configuration reviewed
  • [ ] Backup configuration reviewed
  • [ ] Referenced filesystem ACLs reviewed

docs.title: Sensitive Information
docs.text:
• [ ] Relevant application keys searched
  • [ ] Plaintext distinguished from encrypted data
  • [ ] Tokens handled as sensitive evidence
  • [ ] Credentials redacted in reports
  • [ ] Unrelated secrets not collected unnecessarily

docs.title: Advanced Areas
docs.text:
• [ ] File associations considered where relevant
  • [ ] Protocol handlers considered
  • [ ] COM registration considered where relevant
  • [ ] Environment configuration considered
  • [ ] PATH-based behaviour validated rather than assumed
  • [ ] WOW64 view differences considered

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Consumer identified
  • [ ] Consumer privilege identified
  • [ ] Trigger identified
  • [ ] User write access established
  • [ ] Security boundary established
  • [ ] Alternative explanations excluded
  • [ ] Non-destructive validation preferred

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• [ ] Exact Registry path recorded
  • [ ] Exact value recorded
  • [ ] ACL evidence recorded
  • [ ] Consumer identified
  • [ ] Privileged context identified
  • [ ] Security impact explained
  • [ ] Sensitive values redacted
  • [ ] Root cause identified

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
• [ ] Registry ACL retested
  • [ ] Referenced filesystem ACL retested
  • [ ] Original modification path closed
  • [ ] Legitimate application still operates
  • [ ] Parent-key inheritance reviewed
  • [ ] Equivalent vulnerable keys reviewed

docs.text: Goal Command Query key reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Example" Recursive query reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Example" /s Query value reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Example" /v ValueName PowerShell properties Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example' List subkeys Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example' Registry ACL Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example' ACL entries (Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Example').Access Current identity whoami Groups whoami /groups Privileges whoami /priv Services Get-CimInstance Win32_Service Machine PATH [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','Machine') User PATH [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User')
