docs.text: Purpose Path Services HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services Machine Run HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run User Run HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run Machine RunOnce HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce User RunOnce HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce Winlogon HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon Machine environment HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Environment User environment HKCU\Environment Installed software HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall 32-bit installed software HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall Machine classes HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes User classes HKCU\Software\Classes UAC policy HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System

docs.title: Candidate Prioritization Matrix
docs.text: Registry Condition Consumer Priority Writable service ImagePath SYSTEM service Critical review Writable privileged application path SYSTEM process Critical review Writable privileged script path Administrator/SYSTEM Critical review Writable plugin path Privileged application High review Writable updater configuration Privileged updater High review Writable backup configuration Privileged backup agent High review Writable HKCU autorun Same user Usually no privilege escalation Writable user application preference Same user Low Readable plaintext privileged credential Applicable privileged account Critical review Writable unused vendor key No consumer Low

docs.title: Interpretation Matrix
docs.text: Observation Interpretation User can write HKCU Usually expected User can write arbitrary sensitive HKLM key Investigate Users have SetValue on service key Strong candidate ImagePath references protected EXE Registry redirection may still matter Registry protected but EXE writable Filesystem path may remain vulnerable AlwaysInstallElevated only in one location Do not assume exploitable configuration Both relevant AlwaysInstallElevated policies enabled Significant insecure policy Plaintext password found Sensitive information exposure Encrypted Registry blob found Requires correct classification Writable PATH directory Requires privileged relative execution Writable COM registration Requires privileged consumer validation Writable autorun executes as same user Persistence, not necessarily privilege escalation

docs.title: Writable HKCU
docs.text:
A user being able to modify their own:

HKCU

is expected.

Do not report this without a cross-privilege impact.

docs.title: Writable Application Preference
docs.text:
A user may control:

Theme

Window size

Recent files

UI preferences

These are normally not security-sensitive.

docs.title: Registry Value Contains "Password"
docs.text: A property name alone does not prove credential exposure.

docs.title: Writable PATH Entry
docs.text: A writable PATH directory does not prove privilege escalation unless a privileged process resolves a predictable executable through it.

docs.title: Writable COM Key
docs.text:
COM behaviour is contextual.

A writable registration does not prove privileged COM hijacking without a relevant privileged consumer.

docs.title: Service Key Exists
docs.text:
The existence of:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\ServiceName

is normal.

The security issue requires inappropriate control.

docs.title: Alternative Explanations
docs.text:
When an unusual Registry permission is discovered, consider:

Application installer requirement

Legacy software compatibility

Per-user customization

Group Policy management

Vendor update mechanism

Development environment

Temporary migration configuration

These explanations do not automatically make the permission safe, but they help establish why it exists and whether it is security-sensitive.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
A strong Registry finding should capture:

Current user

Group membership

Exact Registry path

Exact value

Registry ACL

Relevant filesystem ACL

Consuming process

Process security context

Trigger

Observed impact

docs.title: Example Evidence Sequence
docs.text:
whoami

(Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\ExampleVendor').Access | Select-Object IdentityReference,RegistryRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited

reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\ExampleVendor"

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object PathName -match 'ExampleVendor' | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

icacls "C:\ProgramData\ExampleVendor"

docs.title: Evidence Chain
docs.text:
Standard User
     |
     v
Registry SetValue
     |
     v
Security-Sensitive Configuration
     |
     v
SYSTEM Process
     |
     v
Controlled Execution

docs.title: Strong Finding
docs.text:
A strong finding might establish:

1. Current user is a standard user.

2. BUILTIN\Users has SetValue on a vendor Registry key.

3. The key controls an executable path.

4. A SYSTEM service reads that value.

5. The user can redirect the path to a controlled location.

6. The service subsequently uses that configuration.

7. The result crosses the local privilege boundary.

docs.title: Weak Finding
docs.text:
This is insufficient:

Users have write access to a Registry key.

It does not explain:

Which key?

Which value?

Which consumer?

Which privilege?

Which impact?

docs.title: Better Reporting
docs.text: The BUILTIN\Users group has SetValue permission on HKLM\SOFTWARE\ExampleVendor\Service, which contains the executable path used by a service running as LocalSystem. A standard local user can therefore modify security-sensitive service configuration that is consumed in a higher-privileged context.

docs.title: Finding Titles
docs.text:
Possible titles include:

Insecure Registry Permissions Allow Local Privilege Escalation

or:

Standard Users Can Modify Privileged Application Configuration

or, when service-specific:

Writable Service Registry Configuration Allows Privileged Execution

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

Current user requirements

Registry rights

Consumer privilege

Trigger reliability

Application behaviour

Filesystem permissions

Application-control policy

User interaction

Operational conditions

docs.title: Do Not Inflate Severity
docs.text:
If the Registry key is writable but:

No privileged consumer exists

or

The value cannot influence security-sensitive behaviour

then privilege escalation has not been established.

docs.title: Correct Registry ACLs
docs.text: Remove unnecessary write permissions from standard users on security-sensitive machine-wide configuration.

docs.title: Principle
docs.text:
Privileged configuration should generally be writable only by:

SYSTEM

Administrators

Explicitly required trusted service identities

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Do not grant:

FullControl

when only:

Read

is required.

docs.title: Protect Parent Keys
docs.text: If insecure permissions are inherited, correct the appropriate parent key rather than only individual children.

docs.title: Protect Referenced Files
docs.text:
Registry ACL remediation alone is insufficient when the referenced:

Executable

Script

Plugin

Configuration file

remains user-writable.

docs.title: Secure Application Design
docs.text: Applications running with elevated privileges should not trust mutable per-user Registry configuration for security-sensitive decisions.

docs.title: Validate Paths
docs.text:
Privileged applications should use:

Explicit paths

Protected locations

Secure ACLs

for executable content.

docs.title: Avoid Secrets
docs.text:
Do not store plaintext:

Passwords

API keys

Tokens

Connection credentials

in broadly readable Registry values.

docs.title: Use Appropriate Secret Storage
docs.text: Where secrets must be stored locally, use platform-appropriate protected storage and restrict access according to the application security model.

docs.title: Group Policy
docs.text: Where appropriate, enforce machine security settings centrally using managed policy.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Use:

WDAC

AppLocker

as additional execution-control layers where appropriate.

They should complement secure Registry and filesystem permissions.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Monitor changes to security-sensitive keys such as:

Service configuration

Machine startup configuration

Security tooling configuration

Privileged application settings

docs.title: Remove Legacy Configuration
docs.text:
Delete obsolete:

Vendor keys

Service keys

Startup entries

Update configuration

Application remnants

when no longer required.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: Retesting should reproduce the original security chain.

docs.title: 1. Confirm Identity
docs.text:
Use the same privilege level as the original finding.

whoami

docs.title: 2. Recheck Registry ACL
docs.text: (Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\ExampleVendor').Access | Select-Object IdentityReference,RegistryRights,AccessControlType,IsInherited

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
The affected standard user or group should no longer possess inappropriate:

SetValue

CreateSubKey

WriteKey

FullControl

docs.title: 3. Recheck Configuration
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\ExampleVendor"

docs.title: 4. Recheck Filesystem
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\ExampleVendor"

docs.title: 5. Confirm Application Operation
docs.text: Ensure the legitimate application or service continues to function.

docs.title: 6. Review Inheritance
docs.text:
Check whether weak permissions remain on:

Parent keys

Sibling keys

Related vendor keys

docs.title: 7. Variant Analysis
docs.text: Search for equivalent configurations created by the same product or installer.

docs.title: Retest Matrix
docs.text: Test Expected After Fix Standard user modifies sensitive key Denied Standard user creates sensitive subkey Denied Standard user redirects privileged executable Denied Referenced executable modification Denied Legitimate application operation Success Parent key inheritance Secure Equivalent vendor keys Secure

Writable Registry Key

Not Enough

        +------ No ------> No PrivEsc Finding

docs.title: Final Testing Principle
docs.text:
Registry testing is not:

Find writable Registry key
        |
        v
Report privilege escalation

It is:

FIND WRITABLE KEY
        |
        v
UNDERSTAND VALUE
        |
        v
IDENTIFY CONSUMER
        |
        v
IDENTIFY CONSUMER PRIVILEGE
        |
        v
TRACE DEPENDENCIES
        |
        v
VERIFY USER CONTROL
        |
        v
ESTABLISH SECURITY IMPACT

docs.title: Final Questions
docs.text:
For every interesting Registry key ask:

Who owns this key?

Who can read it?

Who can modify values?

Who can create subkeys?

Are permissions inherited?

Does the current user belong to a permitted group?

What values exist?

Which values are security-sensitive?

Does a value contain an executable path?

Does it contain a script path?

Does it contain a plugin path?

Does it contain a command?

Does it contain credentials?

Does it contain a network location?

Which application reads the value?

Which service reads the value?

Which account runs that process?

Is that account more privileged than the current user?

When is the value consumed?

Can the user trigger the consumer?

Does the Registry value reference a file?

Who can modify that file?

Who can modify the parent directory?

Does application control affect execution?

Is the value machine-wide or per-user?

Does WOW64 Registry redirection matter?

Is the configuration managed by Group Policy?

Could the value be automatically restored?

Does the observed permission represent intended functionality?

Does modification actually cross a privilege boundary?

Can the issue be validated non-destructively?

What evidence proves the complete chain?

What is the root cause?

Does remediation need to occur at a parent key?

Are sibling keys affected by the same ACL?

Does the legitimate application still function after remediation?

Follow the consumer

A writable Registry key becomes security-relevant when you understand which process consumes it. Identify the process, its privilege level, the trigger and any referenced files before deciding whether the configuration creates a security boundary violation.

Correlate Registry and filesystem permissions

Registry configuration frequently points to executables, scripts, plugins and configuration files. Review both Registry ACLs and filesystem ACLs because either layer may provide the actual control point.

Use variant analysis

When one vendor key has insecure permissions, inspect related keys created by the same installer. Weak Registry ACLs frequently originate from a shared parent key or installation process.

Writable does not automatically mean vulnerable

Standard users are expected to control many HKCU settings. Even writable HKLM configuration does not automatically prove privilege escalation. Establish the privileged consumer and resulting security impact.

Do not modify operational Registry values unnecessarily

Changes to services, Winlogon, security controls and startup configuration can cause system instability or outages. Prefer ACL analysis and non-destructive validation during authorised assessments.

docs.title: Windows Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Windows Task Scheduler provides a mechanism for executing programs, scripts and system actions automatically based on configured triggers.

Scheduled tasks are commonly used for:

System maintenance
Software updates
Backup operations
Administrative scripts
Monitoring
Log rotation
Application maintenance
User logon actions
Security tooling

From a security assessment perspective, scheduled tasks are important because they may execute with privileges different from those of the current user.

A task running as:

SYSTEM

or another privileged account can become a privilege escalation path when an unprivileged user can modify something that influences what the task executes.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform scheduled task testing only on systems included in the authorised assessment scope. Prefer permission inspection and controlled proof files over modifying production tasks. Do not replace legitimate executables, scripts or task definitions unless the engagement explicitly permits it and the operational impact is understood.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
The important relationship is:

Scheduled Task
      |
      v
Security Context
      |
      v
Action
      |
      v
Executable / Script
      |
      v
Supporting Files
      |
      v
Directory Permissions

A privileged scheduled task is not a vulnerability by itself.

The security question is:

Can a lower-privileged user influence
what the privileged task executes?

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Model
docs.text:
Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Writable Task Dependency
        |
        v
Privileged Scheduled Task
        |
        v
Task Executes Dependency
        |
        v
Higher-Privilege Execution

A defensible finding therefore normally requires several conditions:

Privileged execution context
+
Attacker-controlled dependency
+
Task execution path
+
Demonstrable security impact

docs.title: Task Scheduler Components
docs.text:
Windows Task Scheduler consists of several relevant components:

Task Scheduler service

Task definitions

Triggers

Actions

Principals

Settings

Task folders

Task files

docs.title: Task Scheduler Service
docs.text:
The service is:

Schedule

Check it with:

Get-Service Schedule

Example:

Status   Name      DisplayName
------   ----      -----------
Running  Schedule  Task Scheduler

docs.title: Task Definitions
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks are logically organized under:

\

and may appear in folders such as:

\Microsoft\Windows\
\Company\
\Maintenance\
\Backup\

docs.title: Task Files
docs.text:
Task definitions are normally stored under:

C:\Windows\System32\Tasks

Do not assume direct filesystem write access to these files merely because the tasks can be enumerated.

docs.title: Core Task Properties
docs.text:
For each interesting task, identify:

Task name

Task path

State

Principal

Run level

Logon type

Trigger

Action

Executable

Arguments

Working directory

Last run time

Next run time

Last result

docs.title: Initial Enumeration
docs.text:
Start with the built-in PowerShell cmdlets.

Get-ScheduledTask

docs.title: Compact View
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,State

docs.title: Sort by Path
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTask | Sort-Object TaskPath,TaskName | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,State

docs.title: Enabled Tasks
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object State -ne 'Disabled' | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,State

docs.title: Running Tasks
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object State -eq 'Running' | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName

docs.title: Task Details
docs.text:
For a specific task:

Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'ExampleTask' | Format-List *

docs.title: Task Information
docs.text:
Runtime information can be retrieved using:

Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName 'ExampleTask'

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
LastRunTime        : 07/09/2026 20:00:00
LastTaskResult     : 0
NextRunTime        : 07/09/2026 21:00:00
NumberOfMissedRuns : 0
TaskName           : ExampleTask
TaskPath           : \

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Useful fields include:

Field Meaning LastRunTime Most recent execution LastTaskResult Result code from last execution NextRunTime Next expected execution NumberOfMissedRuns Missed scheduled executions

docs.title: Task Actions
docs.text:
The action is one of the most important properties.

Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    $task = $_
    foreach ($action in $task.Actions) {
        [PSCustomObject]@{
            TaskPath         = $task.TaskPath
            TaskName         = $task.TaskName
            Execute          = $action.Execute
            Arguments        = $action.Arguments
            WorkingDirectory = $action.WorkingDirectory
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Compact One-Liner
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object { $t=$_; foreach($a in $t.Actions){ [PSCustomObject]@{TaskPath=$t.TaskPath;TaskName=$t.TaskName;Execute=$a.Execute;Arguments=$a.Arguments;WorkingDirectory=$a.WorkingDirectory} } }

docs.title: Why Actions Matter
docs.text:
An action may execute:

Executable

PowerShell script

Batch file

VBScript

JavaScript

Administrative utility

Application updater

Backup script

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
TaskName         : BackupJob
Execute          : powershell.exe
Arguments        : -File C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ps1
WorkingDirectory : C:\ProgramData\Company

The important security question becomes:

Can the current user modify backup.ps1?

docs.title: Task Principals
docs.text:
Enumerate the configured execution identity.

Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        TaskPath = $_.TaskPath
        TaskName = $_.TaskName
        UserId   = $_.Principal.UserId
        RunLevel = $_.Principal.RunLevel
        LogonType = $_.Principal.LogonType
    }
}

docs.title: Compact One-Liner
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object { [PSCustomObject]@{TaskPath=$_.TaskPath;TaskName=$_.TaskName;UserId=$_.Principal.UserId;RunLevel=$_.Principal.RunLevel;LogonType=$_.Principal.LogonType} }

docs.title: Interesting Principals
docs.text:
Pay particular attention to:

SYSTEM

Administrators

Administrator

Service accounts

Backup accounts

Deployment accounts

Privileged domain accounts

docs.title: SYSTEM Tasks
docs.text:
Filter tasks configured for SYSTEM:

Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.Principal.UserId -match 'SYSTEM' } | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,State

docs.title: Highest Run Level
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.Principal.RunLevel -eq 'Highest' } | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,@{N='User';E={$_.Principal.UserId}},@{N='RunLevel';E={$_.Principal.RunLevel}}

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
A task configured as:

SYSTEM

or:

RunLevel = Highest

is not automatically vulnerable.

It only becomes security-relevant when a lower-privileged user can control a task dependency or task configuration.

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text:
Triggers determine when the task executes.

Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    $task = $_

    foreach ($trigger in $task.Triggers) {
        [PSCustomObject]@{
            TaskPath = $task.TaskPath
            TaskName = $task.TaskName
            Trigger  = $trigger.CimClass.CimClassName
            Enabled  = $trigger.Enabled
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Common Trigger Types
docs.text:
Examples include:

Time trigger

Daily trigger

Weekly trigger

Boot trigger

Logon trigger

Event trigger

Registration trigger

Idle trigger

docs.title: Security Relevance
docs.text:
A vulnerable task triggered:

Every minute

may provide a much easier privilege escalation path than one triggered:

Once per month

However, frequency affects exploitability rather than determining whether the underlying permissions are insecure.

docs.title: schtasks.exe
docs.text:
Windows also provides:

schtasks.exe

docs.title: List Tasks
docs.text: schtasks /query

docs.title: Verbose Output
docs.text: schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

docs.title: CSV Output
docs.text: schtasks /query /fo CSV /v

docs.title: Specific Task
docs.text: schtasks /query /tn "\ExampleTask" /fo LIST /v

docs.title: Useful Fields
docs.text:
Look for:

TaskName

Next Run Time

Status

Logon Mode

Last Run Time

Last Result

Author

Task To Run

Start In

Run As User

Schedule Type

docs.title: Representative Output
docs.text:
TaskName:                             \BackupJob
Status:                               Ready
Task To Run:                          powershell.exe -File C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ps1
Run As User:                          SYSTEM
Schedule Type:                        Daily

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This tells us:

Privileged principal:
SYSTEM

Dependency:
C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ps1

The next step is not to modify the script.

The next step is:

Inspect permissions.

docs.title: XML Task Definitions
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks can be represented as XML.

Export a task:

schtasks /query /tn "\ExampleTask" /xml

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text: Export-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'ExampleTask'

docs.title: XML Components
docs.text:
Relevant XML elements may include:

<Principals>
<Triggers>
<Actions>
<Exec>
<Command>
<Arguments>
<WorkingDirectory>

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
<Actions Context="Author">
  <Exec>
    <Command>powershell.exe</Command>
    <Arguments>-File C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ps1</Arguments>
  </Exec>
</Actions>

docs.title: Why XML Helps
docs.text: XML can expose configuration details that are difficult to interpret from compact command output.

docs.title: Enumerating Non-Microsoft Tasks
docs.text:
Windows contains many legitimate Microsoft tasks.

During assessments, custom tasks are often higher-value review targets.

Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskPath -notlike '\Microsoft\*' } | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,State

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Custom tasks are more likely to reference:

Custom scripts

Application directories

ProgramData

Vendor software

Deployment tooling

Backup locations

Temporary paths

docs.title: Do Not Ignore Microsoft Paths Completely
docs.text:
Third-party software or administrators may still create unusual tasks under other locations.

Use filtering for prioritization, not as a security boundary.

docs.title: Find PowerShell Actions
docs.text:
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object {
    $_.Actions.Execute -match 'powershell'
} | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,@{N='Execute';E={$_.Actions.Execute}},@{N='Arguments';E={$_.Actions.Arguments}}

docs.title: Find Script References
docs.text:
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object {
    $_.Actions.Arguments -match '\.(ps1|bat|cmd|vbs|js)'
} | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,@{N='Arguments';E={$_.Actions.Arguments}}

docs.title: Find ProgramData References
docs.text:
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object {
    $_.Actions.Execute -match 'ProgramData' -or
    $_.Actions.Arguments -match 'ProgramData'
} | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,@{N='Execute';E={$_.Actions.Execute}},@{N='Arguments';E={$_.Actions.Arguments}}

docs.title: Find Temp References
docs.text:
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object {
    $_.Actions.Execute -match '\\Temp\\' -or
    $_.Actions.Arguments -match '\\Temp\\'
} | Select-Object TaskPath,TaskName,@{N='Execute';E={$_.Actions.Execute}},@{N='Arguments';E={$_.Actions.Arguments}}

docs.title: High-Value Paths
docs.text:
Pay attention to dependencies under:

C:\ProgramData\

C:\Users\Public\

C:\Temp\

C:\Windows\Temp\

User profile directories

Application data directories

Custom installation directories

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Location alone does not prove writability.

Always inspect the ACL.

docs.title: File Permission Review
docs.text:
For a referenced file:

Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ps1' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: icacls
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ps1"

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
BUILTIN\Administrators:(F)
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(F)
BUILTIN\Users:(M)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If:

BUILTIN\Users

has:

Modify

on a script executed by SYSTEM, this may create a privilege boundary violation.

docs.title: Common Permission Abbreviations
docs.text:
icacls commonly displays:

Permission Meaning F Full control M Modify RX Read and execute R Read W Write

docs.title: Directory Permission Review
docs.text:
Even if the target file itself appears protected, inspect the parent directory.

Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Company' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: icacls
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Company"

docs.title: Why Parent Directories Matter
docs.text:
A user may not be able to directly modify:

backup.ps1

but may have directory permissions allowing:

Create files

Delete files

Rename files

Replace files

docs.title: File vs Directory Permissions
docs.text:
Evaluate both:

Target file ACL

Parent directory ACL

docs.title: Effective Access
docs.text: ACL output should be interpreted in the context of the current identity.

docs.title: Current Identity
docs.text: whoami

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: whoami /groups

docs.title: Privileges
docs.text: whoami /priv

docs.title: PowerShell Identity
docs.text: [System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().Name

docs.title: Writable Dependency Model
docs.text:
Task
 |
 v
Runs as SYSTEM
 |
 v
Executes backup.ps1
 |
 v
backup.ps1 ACL
 |
 +--> Users Read Only
 |        |
 |        v
 |      Safe from this path
 |
 +--> Users Modify
          |
          v
     Potential PrivEsc

docs.title: Safe Write Validation
docs.text:
Permission output can sometimes be complicated by:

Inheritance

Deny ACEs

Group membership

Integrity levels

Application control

Filesystem virtualization

If the engagement permits a non-destructive write test, use a separate probe file rather than modifying the production dependency.

docs.title: Example Directory Write Test
docs.text:
$path = 'C:\ProgramData\Company'
$probe = Join-Path $path "write-test-$PID.tmp"

try {
    'test' | Set-Content -LiteralPath $probe -ErrorAction Stop
    Write-Host '[+] Directory is writable'
    Remove-Item -LiteralPath $probe -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}
catch {
    Write-Host '[-] Directory write test failed'
}

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Creating a harmless temporary file proves:

Directory write capability

but does not automatically prove:

Ability to replace the scheduled task dependency

Further ACL analysis may still be required.

docs.title: Executable Dependencies
docs.text:
A task may execute:

C:\Program Files\Vendor\App\updater.exe

docs.title: Check File
docs.text: icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\App\updater.exe"

docs.title: Check Directory
docs.text: icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\App"

docs.title: Expected Secure Configuration
docs.text: Ordinary users should generally not have modification rights over executables launched by privileged tasks.

docs.title: Script Dependencies
docs.text:
Common examples:

.ps1

.bat

.cmd

.vbs

.js

.py

docs.title: Example
docs.text: powershell.exe -File C:\Scripts\maintenance.ps1

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
icacls "C:\Scripts\maintenance.ps1"
icacls "C:\Scripts"

docs.title: Interpreter Security
docs.text:
When a task launches an interpreter, review both:

Interpreter

Script

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
powershell.exe -File backup.ps1

The primary controllable dependency may be:

backup.ps1

rather than:

powershell.exe

docs.title: Relative Paths
docs.text:
Relative paths deserve additional review.

Example:

Execute:
backup.exe

rather than:

C:\Program Files\Company\backup.exe

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text: How does Windows resolve the executable?

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Working directory

PATH

Application search behaviour

Task configuration

docs.title: Working Directory
docs.text:
Example:

WorkingDirectory:
C:\ProgramData\Company

docs.title: Relative Script Paths
docs.text:
Example:

powershell.exe -File .\backup.ps1

docs.title: Security Relevance
docs.text: The task's working directory becomes important when resolving the script.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Task actions may reference:

%ProgramData%

%TEMP%

%USERPROFILE%

%APPDATA%

%PATH%

docs.title: Example
docs.text: %ProgramData%\Company\backup.exe

docs.title: Expand Variables
docs.text:
In PowerShell:

[Environment]::ExpandEnvironmentVariables('%ProgramData%\Company\backup.exe')

docs.title: Environment Differences
docs.text:
Remember that a task running as:

SYSTEM

may have different environment values from the current user.

docs.title: Quoting
docs.text:
Review paths containing spaces.

Example:

C:\Program Files\Company App\updater.exe

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not automatically treat an unquoted scheduled task command as equivalent to an unquoted Windows service path vulnerability.

Task Scheduler stores the executable and arguments as structured action fields in many configurations.

Inspect the actual task action before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: Action Separation
docs.text:
PowerShell helps show this distinction:

$task = Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'ExampleTask'
$task.Actions | Format-List Execute,Arguments,WorkingDirectory

docs.title: Shell Invocation
docs.text:
Different reasoning applies if the task explicitly invokes:

cmd.exe /c ...

powershell.exe ...

wscript.exe ...

cscript.exe ...

docs.title: Example
docs.text: cmd.exe /c C:\ProgramData\Company\maintenance.cmd

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
The security dependency includes:

maintenance.cmd

and any files that script subsequently executes.

docs.title: Dependency Chains
docs.text:
A task may execute:

Task
 |
 v
backup.ps1
 |
 v
helper.exe
 |
 v
config.json

docs.title: Review the Entire Chain
docs.text:
Do not stop at the first script.

Inspect whether it loads:

Executables

DLLs

Modules

Configuration files

Scripts

Templates

Plugins

Writable data interpreted as code

docs.title: PowerShell Script Review
docs.text:
For a task executing:

maintenance.ps1

inspect the script:

Get-Content -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\Company\maintenance.ps1'

docs.title: Look For
docs.text:
Invoke-Expression

Start-Process

& operator

Import-Module

Dot sourcing

Relative paths

Environment variables

External executables

Configuration imports

docs.title: Example Dependency
docs.text: & '.\helper.exe'

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Can the current user replace:

helper.exe

or influence how it is resolved?

docs.title: Batch Files
docs.text:
Inspect:

type C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.cmd

docs.title: Look For
docs.text:
Relative executable names

CALL statements

Other scripts

Writable configuration

Environment-variable expansion

Network paths

docs.title: Network Paths
docs.text:
A scheduled task may execute content from:

\\server\share\script.ps1

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Share permissions

NTFS permissions

Authentication

Availability

Who can modify the remote file?

docs.title: Security Boundary
docs.text: A SYSTEM task executing a script from a network share can be dangerous if unprivileged users can modify that share.

docs.title: UNC Path Example
docs.text: \\fileserver\automation\maintenance.ps1

docs.title: Test Share Access
docs.text: Get-Item '\\fileserver\automation\maintenance.ps1'

docs.title: Review ACL Where Accessible
docs.text: Get-Acl '\\fileserver\automation\maintenance.ps1' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Task Credentials
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks may run under:

SYSTEM

Service accounts

Domain accounts

User accounts

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not attempt to extract stored scheduled-task credentials merely because a task uses a privileged account.

Focus on whether the task configuration or dependencies expose an authorized security weakness.

docs.title: Logon Types
docs.text:
Task principals may use different logon types.

Examples include:

InteractiveToken

Password

S4U

ServiceAccount

docs.title: Enumerate
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object TaskName,@{N='User';E={$_.Principal.UserId}},@{N='LogonType';E={$_.Principal.LogonType}}

docs.title: Run Whether User Is Logged On
docs.text:
Tasks may be configured to execute independently of an interactive user session.

This can increase the reliability of a privilege escalation path if a vulnerable dependency exists.

docs.title: Boot Tasks
docs.text: Tasks triggered at startup may execute before normal user interaction.

docs.title: Security Relevance
docs.text: A writable dependency used by a boot-triggered SYSTEM task may create persistent privileged execution after restart.

docs.title: Do Not Restart Production Systems
docs.text: Never reboot a production system solely to trigger a task unless the engagement explicitly permits it.

docs.title: Logon Tasks
docs.text:
Tasks may execute:

At logon

for specific users or groups.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Determine:

Which user's logon?

Which execution principal?

Which action?

docs.title: Event-Based Tasks
docs.text: Tasks may trigger from Windows Event Log events.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Event log

Provider

Event ID

Filter

Frequency

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Can an unprivileged user legitimately generate the triggering event?

Even if yes, this is only relevant when the task executes something the user can improperly influence.

docs.title: Manual Task Execution
docs.text:
A user may have permission to start a task manually.

Example:

schtasks /run /tn "\ExampleTask"

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Being able to start a privileged task is not necessarily a vulnerability.

If the task performs a fixed, safe privileged operation, manual execution may be intentionally permitted.

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Can the user:

Modify what the task executes

or:

Abuse the fixed privileged action

to cross a security boundary?

docs.title: Task Modification
docs.text: Task security descriptors determine who can modify task definitions.

docs.title: Safe Approach
docs.text: Prefer inspection rather than changing a task during discovery.

docs.title: Export Definition
docs.text: schtasks /query /tn "\ExampleTask" /xml

docs.title: Task File ACL
docs.text:
Where permitted:

icacls "C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ExampleTask"

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Direct filesystem permissions are not the only relevant authorization layer.

Task Scheduler also applies task security semantics through its APIs and service.

docs.title: Existing Task Update Rights
docs.text:
If a lower-privileged user can legitimately modify a task that executes as a more privileged principal, investigate carefully.

The finding should demonstrate the actual permitted modification path rather than relying only on assumptions from task-file ACLs.

docs.title: User-Created Tasks
docs.text:
Not every scheduled task is privileged.

Example:

Run As User:
DOMAIN\StandardUser

If the current user already controls that identity, modifying its task generally does not create privilege escalation.

docs.title: Compare Privileges
docs.text:
Current User
     |
     v
Task Principal
     |
     v
Higher Privilege?

If:

No

then it may not represent a privilege escalation path.

docs.title: Task Scheduler GUI
docs.text:
The graphical interface is available through:

taskschd.msc

docs.title: Useful GUI Areas
docs.text:
Review:

Task Scheduler Library

Triggers

Actions

Conditions

Settings

History

Security options

docs.title: Task History
docs.text:
Task history can help determine:

Whether task executes

How frequently

Whether it succeeds

Whether the dependency is active

docs.title: Event Logs
docs.text:
Task Scheduler operational events are available under:

Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational

docs.title: PowerShell Event Log Query
docs.text: Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -First 30 TimeCreated,Id,LevelDisplayName,Message

docs.title: Filter by Task Name
docs.text: Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object Message -match 'ExampleTask' | Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,Message

docs.title: Why History Matters
docs.text:
A task definition may exist but:

Never run

Be disabled

Consistently fail

Reference removed software

This affects exploitability and severity.

docs.title: Last Result
docs.text:
Retrieve:

Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName 'ExampleTask'

docs.title: Success Code
docs.text:
A last result of:

0

commonly indicates successful task execution.

docs.title: Do Not Rely on Last Result Alone
docs.text:
Verify:

Actual action

Current task configuration

Relevant event history

docs.title: Disabled Tasks
docs.text: Disabled tasks can still be security-relevant as latent configuration, but they generally do not provide immediate scheduled execution.

docs.title: Report Carefully
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Active exploitable path

from:

Dormant insecure configuration

docs.title: Missing Dependencies
docs.text:
A task may reference a file that no longer exists.

Example:

C:\ProgramData\OldVendor\update.exe

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Test-Path -LiteralPath 'C:\ProgramData\OldVendor\update.exe'

docs.title: Missing File
docs.text: False

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text: Can a lower-privileged user create the missing file at the expected location?

docs.title: Check Parent
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\OldVendor"

docs.title: Potential Pattern
docs.text:
Privileged Task
     |
     v
Missing Executable
     |
     v
Writable Parent Directory
     |
     v
Potential Privilege Boundary Violation

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
A missing dependency alone is not a vulnerability.

The user must be able to create or control the expected dependency.

docs.title: Writable Working Directory
docs.text:
A task may have a protected executable but a writable working directory.

Review whether the application loads:

DLLs

Configuration

Plugins

Relative files

from that location.

docs.title: DLL Loading
docs.text: If a privileged scheduled executable loads DLLs from user-writable locations, this can create another privilege escalation path.

docs.title: Separate Analysis
docs.text: DLL loading behaviour should be validated independently rather than assumed from directory writability.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Example:

backup.exe --config C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ini

docs.title: Check
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ini"

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Does modifying the configuration allow:

Command execution

Executable path changes

Plugin loading

Script loading

or only harmless operational settings?

docs.title: Data vs Code
docs.text:
Writable data consumed by a privileged task is not automatically exploitable.

Example:

Writable log file

is different from:

Writable script

docs.title: Establish the Sink
docs.text:
Ask:

How does the privileged process use this file?

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Even when a user can write an executable or script, controls such as:

AppLocker

Windows Defender Application Control

Constrained Language Mode

Antivirus

EDR

may affect whether the modified dependency can execute.

docs.title: Important
docs.text: These controls can reduce exploitability, but they do not necessarily correct the underlying unsafe filesystem permissions.

docs.title: AppLocker Policy
docs.text:
Where accessible:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

docs.title: Test a Specific Existing Path
docs.text: When evaluating application-control policy, use appropriate policy inspection and harmless test artifacts rather than modifying the scheduled task.

docs.title: WDAC
docs.text: Windows Defender Application Control may enforce code integrity independently of AppLocker.

docs.title: Layered Model
docs.text:
Writable Dependency
       |
       v
Task Executes Dependency
       |
       v
Application Control
       |
   +---+---+
   |       |
 Allow    Block
   |       |
   v       v
Impact   Reduced

docs.title: Important Reporting Distinction
docs.text:
If application control blocks exploitation:

Writable privileged dependency

may still represent a hardening or defense-in-depth weakness, depending on architecture.

Do not claim successful privilege escalation unless privileged execution is actually demonstrated or otherwise conclusively established.

docs.title: Safe Validation Strategy
docs.text:
Prefer this sequence:

1. Identify privileged task

2. Identify action

3. Identify dependency

4. Inspect ACL

5. Confirm effective write capability safely

6. Confirm task actually executes

7. Evaluate application control

8. Use non-destructive proof if permitted

9. Restore any test artifacts

10. Capture evidence

docs.title: Non-Destructive Proof
docs.text:
Where permitted, a controlled proof should avoid:

Reverse shells

Persistence

Credential access

Destructive commands

Disabling security controls

docs.title: Preferred Evidence
docs.text:
For many assessments, sufficient evidence can be:

Task runs as SYSTEM

Task executes file X

Standard user has Modify on X

Task executes regularly

Application control does not prevent the relevant file type

Whether actual replacement is required depends on the engagement's evidence standard.

docs.title: Marker-Based Validation
docs.text:
If explicit execution proof is required and modification is permitted, use a harmless action such as creating a marker file in an approved test location.

The production dependency should be backed up and restored immediately if modification is authorized.

docs.title: Avoid Destructive Validation
docs.text:
Do not use:

Create administrator

Disable Defender

Dump credentials

Install persistence

Delete production data

to prove scheduled-task privilege escalation.

docs.title: Task Dependency Inventory
docs.text:
A useful assessment table:

Task Principal Action Dependency Writable? Trigger Risk BackupJob SYSTEM PowerShell backup.ps1 Yes Hourly Review VendorUpdate SYSTEM EXE update.exe No Daily Low UserCleanup Standard user Script cleanup.ps1 Yes Logon No privilege boundary

docs.title: Prioritization
docs.text:
Prioritize tasks where:

Principal is privileged
+
Action references non-Windows path
+
Dependency is user-writable

docs.title: Quick PowerShell Inventory
docs.text:
Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    $task = $_

    foreach ($action in $task.Actions) {
        [PSCustomObject]@{
            TaskPath         = $task.TaskPath
            TaskName         = $task.TaskName
            State            = $task.State
            User             = $task.Principal.UserId
            RunLevel         = $task.Principal.RunLevel
            Execute          = $action.Execute
            Arguments        = $action.Arguments
            WorkingDirectory = $action.WorkingDirectory
        }
    }
} | Format-Table -AutoSize

docs.title: Export Inventory
docs.text:
Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    $task = $_

    foreach ($action in $task.Actions) {
        [PSCustomObject]@{
            TaskPath         = $task.TaskPath
            TaskName         = $task.TaskName
            State            = $task.State
            User             = $task.Principal.UserId
            RunLevel         = $task.Principal.RunLevel
            Execute          = $action.Execute
            Arguments        = $action.Arguments
            WorkingDirectory = $action.WorkingDirectory
        }
    }
} | Export-Csv -NoTypeInformation -Path '.\scheduled-tasks.csv'

docs.title: Filter Interesting Paths
docs.text:
Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    $task = $_

    foreach ($action in $task.Actions) {
        if (
            $action.Execute -match 'ProgramData|Users|Temp' -or
            $action.Arguments -match 'ProgramData|Users|Temp'
        ) {
            [PSCustomObject]@{
                TaskPath  = $task.TaskPath
                TaskName  = $task.TaskName
                User      = $task.Principal.UserId
                Execute   = $action.Execute
                Arguments = $action.Arguments
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Manual Review Beats Blind Automation
docs.text:
Automated enumeration can identify candidates, but final validation requires understanding:

Task principal

Dependency resolution

Filesystem permissions

Trigger behaviour

Application-control policy

Actual security boundary

docs.title: False Positive - Privileged Task Exists
docs.text:
Observation:

Task runs as SYSTEM

Conclusion:

Expected administrative behaviour

unless an unprivileged user can influence it.

docs.title: False Positive - Writable Directory Nearby
docs.text:
Observation:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor

is writable.

But the task executes:

C:\Program Files\Vendor\service.exe

and does not load anything from the writable directory.

Conclusion:

No scheduled-task privilege escalation established.

docs.title: False Positive - Writable Script Runs as Same User
docs.text:
Current user:
DOMAIN\UserA

Task principal:
DOMAIN\UserA

A writable script does not create a privilege escalation boundary if the task executes with the same effective privilege.

docs.title: False Positive - Disabled Task
docs.text: A disabled task referencing a writable file may represent poor configuration but does not automatically provide active execution.

docs.title: False Positive - Application Does Not Interpret Writable File as Code
docs.text:
Writable:

config.txt

does not prove code execution.

Determine how the privileged process consumes it.

docs.title: False Positive - ACL Appears Writable
docs.text:
Group membership and deny ACEs may change effective access.

Validate the current user's actual effective capability where necessary.

docs.title: Alternative Explanation - Installer Leftovers
docs.text:
An old scheduled task may reference software that has been removed.

Determine whether:

Task is enabled

Trigger remains active

Parent directory exists

User can recreate dependency

docs.title: Alternative Explanation - Vendor Updater
docs.text:
A task executing from ProgramData may be intentional.

The issue is not:

ProgramData used

but:

Unprivileged modification of privileged executable content

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text: Capture the complete evidence chain.

docs.title: 1. Current Identity
docs.text: whoami

docs.title: 2. Group Membership
docs.text: whoami /groups

docs.title: 3. Task Definition
docs.text: schtasks /query /tn "\ExampleTask" /fo LIST /v

docs.title: 4. Task XML
docs.text: schtasks /query /tn "\ExampleTask" /xml

docs.title: 5. Dependency ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ps1"

docs.title: 6. Parent ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Company"

docs.title: 7. Task Runtime Information
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName 'ExampleTask'

docs.title: 8. Application Control
docs.text:
Where relevant and accessible:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

docs.title: 9. Safe Validation
docs.text: Capture only the minimum additional evidence required by the engagement.

docs.title: Evidence Chain
docs.text:
Standard User
     |
     v
Writable Dependency
     |
     v
Scheduled Task
     |
     v
SYSTEM Principal
     |
     v
Task Executes
     |
     v
Security Boundary Crossed

docs.title: Strong Finding
docs.text:
A strong scheduled-task privilege escalation finding demonstrates:

1. Current user is lower privileged.

2. Scheduled task runs under higher privilege.

3. Task executes a specific dependency.

4. Current user can modify that dependency.

5. Task is active or can legitimately be triggered.

6. Privileged execution follows from that dependency.

7. Relevant mitigations do not invalidate the path.

docs.title: Weak Finding
docs.text:
This is weak:

A SYSTEM scheduled task was identified.

That is normal Windows behaviour.

docs.title: Better Finding
docs.text: A scheduled task named BackupJob executes C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ps1 as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. The BUILTIN\Users group has Modify permission on the script, allowing a standard local user to alter code that is subsequently executed in the SYSTEM security context.

docs.title: Finding Title
docs.text:
A suitable title:

Writable Scheduled Task Dependency Allows Local Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Alternative Title
docs.text: Insecure Permissions on Privileged Scheduled Task Script

docs.title: Short Description
docs.text: A scheduled task executes a user-writable script with SYSTEM privileges. A local standard user can modify the script and influence code executed by the privileged task.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Potential impact:

Local privilege escalation

SYSTEM-level code execution

Security-control modification

Credential access

Persistence

Only include consequences supported by the demonstrated security boundary and assessment context.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

Required local access

Current privilege

Task principal

Dependency permissions

Trigger frequency

Trigger control

Application control

User interaction

Reliability

Operational conditions

docs.title: Example Severity Reasoning
docs.text:
A task may represent high risk when:

Standard user
+
Writable executable/script
+
SYSTEM task
+
Frequent automatic trigger
+
No effective execution restriction

docs.title: Lower Risk Example
docs.text:
Risk may be reduced when:

Task disabled
+
Requires administrator to enable
+
Application control prevents modified code

although the insecure ACL may still warrant remediation.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: The primary remediation is to remove unprivileged write access from all files and directories that influence privileged scheduled tasks.

docs.title: Protect Executables
docs.text: Privileged task executables should generally be writable only by trusted administrative identities.

docs.title: Protect Scripts
docs.text: Scripts executed by privileged tasks should not be modifiable by standard users.

docs.title: Protect Parent Directories
docs.text: Review directory permissions as well as file permissions.

docs.title: Use Secure Locations
docs.text: Prefer protected locations such as appropriately ACLed application directories rather than broadly writable paths.

docs.title: Avoid Temporary Locations
docs.text:
Do not execute privileged task dependencies from directories such as:

C:\Temp

C:\Windows\Temp

User-controlled temporary directories

unless permissions and execution semantics are deliberately secured.

docs.title: Use Absolute Paths
docs.text:
Prefer explicit absolute paths for:

Executables

Scripts

Configuration

where appropriate.

docs.title: Review Working Directory
docs.text: Ensure the working directory cannot introduce user-controlled dependencies.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Do not run tasks as:

SYSTEM

when the operation requires only a less privileged service identity.

docs.title: Dedicated Service Accounts
docs.text: Where appropriate, use a dedicated account with only the permissions required by the task.

docs.title: Remove Obsolete Tasks
docs.text:
Delete:

Unused tasks

Legacy updater tasks

Orphaned tasks

References to removed software

when no longer required.

docs.title: Secure Network Dependencies
docs.text:
If a privileged task uses a UNC path:

Protect share permissions

Protect NTFS permissions

Restrict modification rights

Monitor changes

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Use application control as an additional layer.

Examples:

Windows Defender Application Control

AppLocker

Application control should complement secure filesystem permissions rather than replace them.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Monitor changes to:

Scheduled task definitions

Privileged scripts

Privileged executables

Task directories

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text: After remediation, repeat the original evidence chain.

docs.title: 1. Verify Task
docs.text: schtasks /query /tn "\ExampleTask" /fo LIST /v

docs.title: 2. Verify Dependency
docs.text: Confirm the task still executes the intended protected dependency.

docs.title: 3. Verify File ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Company\backup.ps1"

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
Standard users should no longer have inappropriate:

Write

Modify

Full Control

docs.title: 4. Verify Directory ACL
docs.text: icacls "C:\ProgramData\Company"

docs.title: 5. Repeat Safe Write Test
docs.text: If permitted, attempt creation of a harmless temporary file in the directory using the original low-privileged identity.

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
Access denied

when the user no longer requires write access there.

docs.title: 6. Verify Legitimate Operation
docs.text: Ensure the scheduled task still completes successfully.

docs.title: 7. Verify Last Result
docs.text: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName 'ExampleTask'

docs.title: 8. Review Equivalent Tasks
docs.text:
Do not stop after fixing one instance.

Search for other tasks using the same:

Directory

Installer

Vendor

Script pattern

Permission model

docs.text: Test Expected After Fix Standard user modifies task script Denied Standard user replaces executable Denied Standard user writes parent directory Denied unless explicitly required Legitimate task executes Success Task principal unchanged As intended Application control Enforced as designed

docs.title: Final Questions
docs.text:
For every interesting scheduled task ask:

Who does the task run as?

Is that identity more privileged than the current user?

What exactly does the task execute?

What arguments are supplied?

What working directory is used?

Does the action use an absolute path?

Does it invoke a script interpreter?

Which script does it execute?

Can the current user modify the script?

Can the current user modify the executable?

Can the current user modify the parent directory?

Can the current user create a missing dependency?

Does the action use relative paths?

Does it rely on PATH resolution?

Does it load configuration from a writable location?

Does it load plugins or modules?

Does it execute another script?

Does it execute helper programs?

Does it use a network share?

Who can modify the network dependency?

When does the task run?

Is it enabled?

Has it executed recently?

Can the current user legitimately trigger it?

Does triggering it alone create a security boundary?

Does AppLocker affect execution?

Does WDAC affect execution?

Does another application-control mechanism apply?

Does the dependency actually execute as code?

Is the finding active or merely dormant?

Can the issue be demonstrated safely?

Can a harmless write probe prove the required permission?

What evidence establishes the complete chain?

What is the least invasive remediation?

Does the remediation protect both the file and parent directory?

Does the legitimate scheduled task still work after remediation?

Were equivalent scheduled tasks reviewed?
