      v
CHECK INTEGRITY LEVEL
      |
      v
CHECK UAC CONFIGURATION
      |
      v
CHECK CONSENT POLICY
      |
      v
CHECK SECURE DESKTOP
      |
      v
CHECK REMOTE TOKEN FILTERING
      |
      v
VALIDATE EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR
      |
      v
INTERPRET
      |
      v
REPORT
      |
      v
RETEST

docs.title: Establish Current Identity
docs.text:
Start with:

whoami

docs.title: User SID
docs.text: whoami /user

docs.title: Group Membership
docs.text: whoami /groups

docs.title: Privileges
docs.text: whoami /priv

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Before analysing UAC, establish whether the account is:

Standard user

Local administrator

Domain administrator

Built-in Administrator

Another privileged identity

docs.title: Local Administrators Group
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Alternative
docs.text: net localgroup administrators

docs.title: Domain Considerations
docs.text:
A domain account may obtain local administrative privileges through:

Direct local group membership

Nested domain groups

Group Policy

Endpoint management

Privileged workstation policy

Therefore do not rely solely on the username.

docs.title: Token vs Group Membership
docs.text:
Being a member of:

BUILTIN\Administrators

does not necessarily mean the current process is elevated.

docs.title: Split Token Model
docs.text:
An administrator may have:

Administrator account
       |
       +--> Filtered token
       |
       +--> Full administrator token

docs.title: Current Process Integrity Level
docs.text:
A convenient check is:

whoami /groups

Look for a mandatory integrity label such as:

Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level

or:

Mandatory Label\High Mandatory Level

docs.title: Common Integrity Levels
docs.text:
Windows integrity levels commonly include:

Low

Medium

High

System

docs.title: Simplified Interpretation
docs.text: Integrity Level Typical Context Low Restricted/sandboxed process Medium Normal interactive user process High Elevated administrator process System Highly privileged system service/process

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Integrity level and user identity are related but different security concepts.

A process can run as an account that belongs to Administrators while the process itself remains at:

Medium Integrity

docs.title: Check Integrity Label
docs.text: whoami /groups | Select-String 'Mandatory'

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: For a local administrator, this commonly indicates that the current process is using the filtered token rather than the elevated administrator token.

docs.title: Elevated PowerShell
docs.text:
An elevated administrative PowerShell session commonly shows:

Mandatory Label\High Mandatory Level

docs.title: Administrative Token Check
docs.text:
A useful PowerShell test is:

$identity = [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
$principal = [Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal]::new($identity)

$principal.IsInRole(
    [Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator
)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
True

This evaluates whether the current token has the Administrator role enabled.

docs.title: Compact Token Summary
docs.text:
$identity = [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
$principal = [Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal]::new($identity)

[PSCustomObject]@{
    User          = $identity.Name
    IsAdminToken  = $principal.IsInRole(
        [Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator
    )
}

docs.title: Determine UAC Configuration
docs.text:
Core UAC policy is stored under:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System

docs.title: Query All UAC Settings
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System"

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text: Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System'

docs.title: Important Values
docs.text:
Common UAC-related values include:

EnableLUA

ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin

ConsentPromptBehaviorUser

PromptOnSecureDesktop

FilterAdministratorToken

EnableInstallerDetection

EnableVirtualization

ValidateAdminCodeSignatures

EnableSecureUIAPaths

docs.title: Focused UAC Summary
docs.text:
$uac = Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System'

[PSCustomObject]@{
    EnableLUA                  = $uac.EnableLUA
    ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin = $uac.ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin
    ConsentPromptBehaviorUser  = $uac.ConsentPromptBehaviorUser
    PromptOnSecureDesktop      = $uac.PromptOnSecureDesktop
    FilterAdministratorToken   = $uac.FilterAdministratorToken
    EnableInstallerDetection   = $uac.EnableInstallerDetection
    EnableVirtualization       = $uac.EnableVirtualization
    ValidateAdminCodeSignatures = $uac.ValidateAdminCodeSignatures
    EnableSecureUIAPaths       = $uac.EnableSecureUIAPaths
}

docs.title: EnableLUA
docs.text:
One of the most important values is:

EnableLUA

docs.title: Query
docs.text: (Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System').EnableLUA

docs.title: Typical Values
docs.text:
1 = UAC enabled

0 = UAC disabled

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Disabling EnableLUA affects more than the appearance of elevation prompts.

It changes important Windows security and application behavior.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
If:

EnableLUA = 0

determine:

Why UAC is disabled

Whether enterprise policy requires UAC

Which users have local administrator rights

Whether compensating controls exist

docs.title: Administrator Consent Behavior
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System').ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This value controls how elevation requests are handled for administrators operating in Admin Approval Mode.

docs.title: Possible Behaviors
docs.text:
Depending on configuration and Windows version, policies can represent behaviors such as:

Elevate without prompting

Prompt for credentials

Prompt for consent

Prompt for credentials on secure desktop

Prompt for consent on secure desktop

Prompt for consent for non-Windows binaries

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
When documenting the setting, record:

Numeric value

Resolved policy meaning

Windows version

Observed runtime behavior

Do not rely solely on a memorised numeric value when producing formal evidence.

docs.title: Standard User Consent Behavior
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System').ConsentPromptBehaviorUser

docs.title: Standard User Model
docs.text: A standard user normally requires administrative credentials for operations requiring elevation.

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
Determine whether the endpoint:

Prompts for credentials

Automatically denies elevation requests

Uses another enterprise workflow

docs.title: Secure Desktop
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System').PromptOnSecureDesktop

docs.title: Typical Values
docs.text:
1 = Elevation prompt uses secure desktop

0 = Prompt appears on interactive desktop

docs.title: Secure Desktop Model
docs.text:
Normal Desktop
      |
      v
Elevation Requested
      |
      v
Secure Desktop
      |
      v
Consent / Credentials
      |
      v
Elevated Process

docs.title: Why Secure Desktop Matters
docs.text: The secure desktop isolates the elevation prompt from ordinary user applications, reducing the ability of normal desktop processes to interact with the prompt.

docs.title: Admin Approval Mode for Built-In Administrator
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System').FilterAdministratorToken

docs.title: Security Purpose
docs.text: This setting controls Admin Approval Mode behavior for the built-in Administrator account.

docs.title: Built-In Administrator
docs.text:
The built-in Administrator account can behave differently from other accounts in the local Administrators group.

Therefore establish whether the tested account is actually the built-in Administrator.

docs.title: Current SID
docs.text: whoami /user

docs.title: Local Built-In Administrator SID
docs.text:
The built-in Administrator account has a SID ending in:

-500

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
The account may have been renamed.

Therefore identify it by SID rather than assuming the account is literally named:

Administrator

docs.title: Find Local Administrator Account
docs.text:
Get-LocalUser |
    Where-Object { $_.SID.Value -match '-500$' } |
    Select-Object Name,Enabled,SID

docs.title: Installer Detection
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System').EnableInstallerDetection

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Installer detection helps Windows identify certain installer applications that may require elevation.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Installer detection is not an application-control boundary.

It should not be confused with:

AppLocker

WDAC

MSI policy

docs.title: UAC Virtualization
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System').EnableVirtualization

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: UAC virtualization can redirect certain legacy application writes from protected locations to per-user locations.

docs.title: Conceptual Example
docs.text:
A legacy application attempts to write to:

C:\Program Files\LegacyApp\config.ini

Windows may redirect compatible writes to a user-specific virtualized location rather than granting administrative write access.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
UAC virtualization is primarily an application compatibility mechanism.

Do not treat it as a substitute for correct filesystem permissions.

docs.title: Signed Elevation
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System').ValidateAdminCodeSignatures

docs.title: Security Purpose
docs.text: This policy can require executables requesting elevation to be signed by a trusted publisher.

docs.title: Important
docs.text: The organisation must evaluate compatibility before enabling strict signed-elevation requirements.

docs.title: UIAccess Security
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System').EnableSecureUIAPaths

docs.title: UIAccess
docs.text: Windows includes special handling for accessibility applications that require interaction with higher-integrity user interfaces.

docs.title: Assessment Principle
docs.text: UIAccess-related configuration should remain aligned with Microsoft security guidance and enterprise requirements.

docs.title: UAC Policy Through Local Security Policy
docs.text:
UAC settings are also represented through security policy interfaces such as:

Local Security Policy
    |
    v
Local Policies
    |
    v
Security Options

docs.title: Common Policy Names
docs.text:
You may encounter policies beginning with:

User Account Control:

Examples include:

Run all administrators in Admin Approval Mode

Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators

Behavior of the elevation prompt for standard users

Switch to the secure desktop when prompting for elevation

Detect application installations and prompt for elevation

Virtualize file and registry write failures

Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account

docs.title: Group Policy
docs.text: Enterprise environments may centrally configure UAC using Group Policy.

docs.title: Resultant Policy
docs.text:
Useful commands include:

gpresult /r

docs.title: HTML Report
docs.text:
Where permitted:

gpresult /h "%TEMP%\gpresult.html"

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text: gpresult /r

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Local Registry state may be the result of:

Local policy

Domain Group Policy

MDM

Security baseline

Determine the authoritative management source before recommending local changes.

docs.title: UAC Notification Level
docs.text:
Windows exposes familiar Control Panel notification levels such as:

Always notify

Notify only when apps try to make changes

Notify only when apps try to make changes without secure desktop

Never notify

These user-facing levels correspond to combinations of underlying policy settings.

docs.title: Important
docs.text: For assessment reporting, prefer the underlying effective policy values rather than relying only on the slider position.

docs.title: Token Inspection
docs.text: Understanding the token is central to UAC analysis.

docs.title: Full Identity Information
docs.text: whoami /all

docs.title: This Includes
docs.text:
User information

Group membership

Privileges

Integrity label

docs.title: Privilege State
docs.text: whoami /priv

docs.title: Example Privileges
docs.text: An elevated administrator token may expose additional privileges compared with a filtered medium-integrity token.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not determine elevation from one privilege alone.

Use multiple signals:

Group membership

Integrity level

Administrator role

Process context

docs.title: Process Integrity
docs.text:
PowerShell can inspect the current process:

Get-Process -Id $PID |
    Select-Object Id,ProcessName,Path

docs.title: Parent Process
docs.text:
Where available:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "ProcessId=$PID" |
    Select-Object ProcessId,ParentProcessId,ExecutablePath,CommandLine

docs.title: Why Parentage Matters
docs.text:
During testing, knowing whether PowerShell was started from:

Explorer

Windows Terminal

cmd.exe

Another administrative console

can help explain the current token context.

docs.title: Harmless Elevation Validation
docs.text:
A simple manual validation is to launch a legitimate administrative Windows utility that requires elevation and observe the expected UAC behavior.

The objective is to establish:

Was elevation requested?

Was consent required?

Were credentials required?

Was the secure desktop used?

Did the resulting process run elevated?

docs.title: Do Not Modify Security Settings
docs.text: The validation does not require actually changing the protected setting.

docs.title: Start-Process RunAs
docs.text:
PowerShell provides the normal Windows elevation mechanism:

Start-Process powershell.exe -Verb RunAs

docs.title: Expected Behavior
docs.text:
Depending on policy and user type:

Consent prompt

Credential prompt

Automatic denial

Elevation according to configured policy

docs.title: Important
docs.text: This is a normal Windows elevation request, not a UAC bypass.

docs.title: Elevated Validation
docs.text:
Inside the newly elevated PowerShell session:

whoami /groups

docs.title: Expected
docs.text:
An administrator session will typically show:

Mandatory Label\High Mandatory Level

docs.title: Compare Tokens
docs.text:
Before elevation:

whoami /all

After elevation:

whoami /all

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Capture the differences in:

Integrity level

Enabled groups

Privileges

docs.title: Standard User Test
docs.text:
For a standard user, an elevation request may result in:

Credential prompt

or:

Automatic denial

depending on policy.

docs.title: Do Not Supply Unauthorised Credentials
docs.text: During an assessment, do not use administrative credentials unless explicitly provided and authorised for the test.

docs.title: UAC and Local Administrators
docs.text: Local administrator membership is a high-value endpoint security consideration.

docs.title: Enumerate Administrators
docs.text: Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Which users are local administrators?

Which domain groups are included?

Are privileges required?

Are administrative accounts separated from normal accounts?

Is UAC enforced for those accounts?

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text: UAC should not be used as justification for giving ordinary users local administrator rights.

docs.title: Weak Model
docs.text:
User is Local Administrator
        +
UAC Prompt
        =
Least Privilege

This is incorrect.

docs.title: Stronger Model
docs.text:
Standard User
      +
Separate Administrative Identity
      +
UAC
      +
Application Control
      +
Endpoint Protection

docs.title: UAC and Application Control
docs.text:
Application control answers:

Should this application be allowed to execute?

UAC answers:

Should this operation execute with administrative privileges?

docs.title: Combined Model
docs.text:
Application
    |
    v
AppLocker / WDAC
    |
Allowed?
    |
    v
Normal Execution
    |
Requires Admin?
    |
    v
UAC
    |
    v
Elevation Decision

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Application Control

docs.title: UAC and Defender
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender provides another independent layer.

Application
    |
    +--> Application Control
    |
    +--> Defender / EDR
    |
    +--> UAC
    |
    v
Runtime Security Decision

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Microsoft Defender Security Assessment

docs.title: UAC and Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
A high-integrity process can modify resources that a medium-integrity process normally cannot.

However, insecure filesystem ACLs may allow a medium-integrity user to modify sensitive resources without elevation.

docs.title: Security Question
docs.text:
If a standard user can modify:

C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service.exe

the root problem is not:

UAC

It is likely:

Filesystem permissions

possibly combined with a privileged execution path.

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Filesystem Permissions

docs.title: UAC and Services
docs.text:
Windows services frequently execute with privileged identities such as:

LocalSystem

LocalService

NetworkService

Service accounts

UAC does not protect insecure service configuration from a user who already has permission to modify the relevant service resource.

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Services

docs.title: UAC and Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Scheduled tasks can be configured to run:

Only when user is logged on

Whether user is logged on or not

With highest privileges

A task running with highest privileges represents a privileged execution path that must be protected independently of UAC.

docs.title: Related Note
docs.text:
See:

Windows Scheduled Tasks

docs.title: UAC and Registry Permissions
docs.text:
Insecure Registry permissions can create privileged modification paths independently of UAC.

Review:

Windows Registry Security

docs.title: Remote UAC Restrictions
docs.text: Windows applies additional UAC-related behavior to some remote administrative connections.

docs.title: LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy
docs.text:
A relevant Registry value is:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy

docs.title: Query
docs.text: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Get-ItemPropertyValue `
    -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System' `
    -Name 'LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy' `
    -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Security Purpose
docs.text: Remote UAC restrictions can filter administrative tokens for local accounts connecting remotely.

docs.title: Important
docs.text: Do not change this value during assessment merely to enable remote administrative behavior.

docs.title: Domain Accounts
docs.text:
Remote token filtering behavior differs depending on:

Local account

Domain account

Group membership

Administrative share access

Remote management technology

Enterprise policy

docs.title: Assessment Principle
docs.text:
When remote administration behaves differently from local administration, investigate token filtering before assuming:

Credentials are invalid

or:

The service is broken

docs.title: Built-In Administrator and Remote Access
docs.text:
The built-in Administrator account can have special behavior depending on:

Admin Approval Mode

Remote UAC restrictions

Local security policy

docs.title: UAC and Network Logons
docs.text:
UAC primarily concerns interactive administrative elevation.

Network logons and remote administrative access involve additional Windows authentication and token rules.

docs.title: Do Not Conflate
docs.text:
UAC

NTLM

Kerberos

WinRM

SMB

Remote Desktop

Remote token filtering

are related in some scenarios but are distinct mechanisms.

docs.title: Auto-Elevation
docs.text: Windows includes trusted components that can support elevation behavior as part of normal operating system functionality.

docs.title: Security Assessment
docs.text:
The useful questions are:

Is UAC configured according to the security baseline?

Are users unnecessarily local administrators?

Are privileged execution paths protected?

Are trusted Windows components intact?

Is application control configured?

Are endpoint protections operational?

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not build an assessment around collecting arbitrary UAC bypass techniques.

A more durable security assessment evaluates the underlying security architecture.

docs.title: UAC Bypass Classification
docs.text:
When a UAC-related technique is discussed during a penetration test, classify it correctly.

A typical UAC elevation scenario assumes:

User already belongs to Administrators
        |
        v
Current process is Medium Integrity
        |
        v
Technique obtains High Integrity

This is different from:

Standard User
        |
        v
Local Administrator

The second case crosses a stronger privilege boundary.

docs.title: Reporting Consequence
docs.text:
Do not report:

Standard user privilege escalation

when the tested account was already a member of:

Administrators

docs.title: Integrity Transition
docs.text:
The actual transition may be:

Administrator
Medium Integrity
       |
       v
Administrator
High Integrity

docs.title: Why This Distinction Matters
docs.text:
It affects:

Severity

Impact

Root cause

Remediation

Executive reporting

docs.title: UAC and Credential Theft
docs.text:
UAC elevation can expose administrative operations, but UAC should not be treated as the primary credential-protection mechanism.

Credential security should be evaluated separately.

See:

Windows Credentials

docs.title: UAC and Process Elevation
docs.text: Processes started from an elevated parent can inherit an elevated context depending on how they are launched.

docs.title: Assessment Example
docs.text:
Elevated PowerShell
       |
       v
Launch cmd.exe
       |
       v
High Integrity cmd.exe

Therefore always establish the current shell context before interpreting command results.

docs.title: Windows Terminal
docs.text:
A Windows Terminal session may contain shells running under different privilege contexts.

Do not assume:

Windows Terminal

itself tells you whether the active shell is elevated.

docs.title: Check Every Relevant Shell
docs.text:
Use:

whoami /groups

inside the actual shell being tested.

docs.title: Process Explorer
docs.text:
Administrative tools such as Microsoft Sysinternals Process Explorer can also help inspect:

Integrity levels

Process tokens

Parent-child relationships

User identities

when GUI tooling is available and permitted.

docs.title: UAC Virtualization Status
docs.text:
For legacy application troubleshooting and assessment, virtualization state may be relevant.

A modern application with an appropriate manifest normally should not depend on UAC virtualization for secure operation.

docs.title: Application Manifests
docs.text:
Windows executables can declare requested execution levels such as:

asInvoker

highestAvailable

requireAdministrator

docs.title: asInvoker
docs.text: The application runs using the caller's current token.

docs.title: highestAvailable
docs.text: The application requests the highest privilege level available to the user.

docs.title: requireAdministrator
docs.text: The application requests administrative elevation.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
An application requesting:

requireAdministrator

is not automatically vulnerable.

Determine whether administrative privileges are genuinely required.

docs.title: Excessive Administrative Requirements
docs.text: An application that unnecessarily requires administrative privileges can increase security risk.

docs.title: Assessment Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Why does the application require elevation?

Can it function as standard user?

Which protected resources does it need?

Can permissions be redesigned?

Does every user need the elevated functionality?

docs.title: Potential Finding
docs.text: Application Requires Unnecessary Administrative Privileges

docs.title: Security Impact
docs.text: Unnecessary elevation increases the amount of code executing with administrative rights and can increase the impact of application vulnerabilities.

docs.title: UAC and Software Installation
docs.text:
Software installation frequently requires elevation because installers may modify:

Program Files

HKLM

Windows services

Drivers

System-wide configuration

docs.title: Assessment Principle
docs.text:
Do not weaken UAC simply because an installer requires administrative access.

Use appropriate software deployment mechanisms.

docs.title: Enterprise Deployment
docs.text:
Managed environments may install applications through:

Intune

Configuration Manager

Group Policy

Enterprise software deployment platforms

without granting permanent local administrator rights to end users.

docs.title: UAC Configuration Collection Script
docs.text:
The following read-only script collects useful UAC posture information.

Write-Host "===================================="
Write-Host " WINDOWS UAC SECURITY ASSESSMENT"
Write-Host "===================================="

Write-Host "`n=== CURRENT USER ==="
whoami

Write-Host "`n=== USER SID ==="
whoami /user

Write-Host "`n=== GROUP MEMBERSHIP ==="
whoami /groups

Write-Host "`n=== PRIVILEGES ==="
whoami /priv

Write-Host "`n=== TOKEN ADMINISTRATOR STATUS ==="

$identity = [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
$principal = [Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal]::new($identity)

[PSCustomObject]@{
    User = $identity.Name
    IsAdministratorToken = $principal.IsInRole(
        [Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator
    )
} | Format-List

Write-Host "`n=== UAC CONFIGURATION ==="

$policyPath = 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System'
$uac = Get-ItemProperty $policyPath -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

if ($uac) {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        EnableLUA                   = $uac.EnableLUA
        ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin  = $uac.ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin
        ConsentPromptBehaviorUser   = $uac.ConsentPromptBehaviorUser
        PromptOnSecureDesktop       = $uac.PromptOnSecureDesktop
        FilterAdministratorToken    = $uac.FilterAdministratorToken
        EnableInstallerDetection    = $uac.EnableInstallerDetection
        EnableVirtualization        = $uac.EnableVirtualization
        ValidateAdminCodeSignatures = $uac.ValidateAdminCodeSignatures
        EnableSecureUIAPaths        = $uac.EnableSecureUIAPaths
        LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy = $uac.LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy
    } | Format-List
}
else {
    Write-Host "Unable to retrieve UAC policy configuration."
}

Write-Host "`n=== BUILT-IN ADMINISTRATOR ==="

Get-LocalUser -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.SID.Value -match '-500$' } |
    Select-Object Name,Enabled,SID |
    Format-Table -AutoSize

Write-Host "`n=== LOCAL ADMINISTRATORS ==="

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object Name,ObjectClass,PrincipalSource |
    Format-Table -AutoSize

Write-Host "`n=== POWERHELL LANGUAGE MODE ==="
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Write-Host "`n=== APPLICATION CONTROL ==="

try {
    [xml]$appLocker = Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml -ErrorAction Stop

    $appLocker.AppLockerPolicy.RuleCollection |
        Select-Object Type,EnforcementMode |
        Format-Table -AutoSize
}
catch {
    Write-Host "Unable to retrieve effective AppLocker policy."
}

Write-Host "`n=== DEFENDER STATUS ==="

Get-MpComputerStatus -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,
                  RealTimeProtectionEnabled,
                  BehaviorMonitorEnabled,
                  IsTamperProtected |
    Format-List

Write-Host "`n=== COMPLETE ==="

docs.title: Script Purpose
docs.text:
The script collects:

Current identity

SID

Groups

Privileges

Administrator-token status

UAC policy

Built-in Administrator state

Local Administrators membership

Remote token-filtering configuration

PowerShell language mode

AppLocker context

Defender context

docs.title: Script Safety
docs.text:
The script does not:

Change UAC

Trigger elevation

Modify Registry settings

Disable Defender

Modify AppLocker

Create persistence

Change local group membership

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
The heading in the script:

POWERHELL LANGUAGE MODE

can be changed to:

POWERSHELL LANGUAGE MODE

if you want the output heading perfectly spelled.

The functional PowerShell command itself is unaffected.

docs.title: When This Applies
docs.text:
Use this methodology when:

Assessing Windows endpoints

Reviewing local administrator exposure

Testing workstation hardening

Reviewing Windows privilege boundaries

Validating security baselines

Investigating administrative execution

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Record:

Windows version

User identity

Local administrator membership

Domain membership

Management architecture

Assessment authorization

docs.title: Step 1 - Identify User
docs.text: whoami

docs.title: Step 2 - Identify Groups
docs.text: whoami /groups

docs.title: Step 3 - Identify Privileges
docs.text: whoami /priv

docs.title: Step 4 - Determine Integrity
docs.text: whoami /groups | Select-String 'Mandatory'

docs.title: Step 5 - Determine Administrator Token
docs.text:
$identity = [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
$principal = [Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal]::new($identity)

$principal.IsInRole(
    [Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator
)

docs.title: Step 6 - Retrieve UAC Configuration
docs.text: Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System'

docs.title: Step 7 - Identify Local Administrators
docs.text: Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Step 8 - Identify Built-In Administrator
docs.text:
Get-LocalUser |
    Where-Object { $_.SID.Value -match '-500$' } |
    Select-Object Name,Enabled,SID

docs.title: Step 9 - Check Remote Token Filtering
docs.text:
Get-ItemPropertyValue `
    -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System' `
    -Name 'LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy' `
    -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Step 10 - Validate Normal Elevation
docs.text:
Where permitted:

Start-Process powershell.exe -Verb RunAs

Observe the normal Windows elevation workflow.

docs.title: Representative Result
docs.text:
Example:

Current account:
CORP\User1

Local Administrators:
Yes

Current integrity:
Medium

Administrator token enabled:
False

EnableLUA:
1

PromptOnSecureDesktop:
1

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This supports a conclusion similar to:

The tested account belongs to the local Administrators group but the current interactive process is operating at medium integrity under a filtered token. UAC is enabled and elevation requests are configured to use the secure desktop.

docs.title: Positive Security Result
docs.text:
A hardened representative configuration may include:

UAC enabled

Administrative accounts operate using Admin Approval Mode

Elevation requires appropriate consent or credentials

Secure desktop enabled

Standard users cannot silently elevate

Built-in Administrator appropriately controlled

Local administrator membership restricted

Remote token filtering configured appropriately

docs.title: Negative Security Result
docs.text:
Further review may be required where:

UAC is disabled

Administrators elevate without prompting contrary to baseline

Secure desktop is disabled contrary to baseline

Users unnecessarily hold local administrator rights

Built-in Administrator configuration is weak

Remote administrative token filtering has been weakened without justification

docs.title: Alternative Explanations
docs.text:
Before reporting, consider:

Kiosk endpoint

Server role

Dedicated administrative workstation

Application compatibility requirement

Enterprise management tooling

Legacy system requirement

Alternative privileged access controls

docs.text:
Capture:

docs.text:
EnableLUA:
0

docs.title: Further Validation
docs.text:
Determine:

Is this required for a legacy workload?

Is the endpoint a workstation or server?

Which users have administrator rights?

Is the setting centrally managed?

Does the security baseline require UAC?

docs.title: Possible Finding Title
docs.text: User Account Control Is Disabled

docs.title: Reporting Conclusion
docs.text:
Example:

User Account Control is disabled on the tested Windows endpoint. As a result, the normal Admin Approval Mode protections and elevation workflow are not applied to administrative users. The configuration should be reviewed against the organisation's Windows security baseline.

docs.title: Finding - Elevation Without Prompt
docs.text:
If effective policy permits administrator elevation without prompting and this conflicts with the intended baseline:

Administrator Elevation Does Not Require User Consent

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: This reduces the visibility and explicit user interaction normally associated with administrative elevation.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not describe this automatically as:

Standard-user-to-SYSTEM privilege escalation

The tested user may already be an administrator.

docs.title: Finding - Secure Desktop Disabled
docs.text:
Observation:

PromptOnSecureDesktop:
0

docs.title: Possible Finding Title
docs.text: UAC Elevation Prompts Do Not Use the Secure Desktop

docs.title: Further Validation
docs.text:
Determine whether:

The organisation requires secure desktop

Another control compensates

The setting is intentionally disabled for accessibility or compatibility

docs.title: Finding - Excessive Local Administrator Rights
docs.text:
Observation:

Ordinary user:
Member of BUILTIN\Administrators

Possible finding:

Standard User Accounts Have Unnecessary Local Administrator Privileges

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
This is primarily a:

Least privilege

issue rather than a UAC configuration issue.

docs.title: Finding - Built-In Administrator Enabled
docs.text:
The built-in Administrator account being enabled is not automatically a vulnerability.

Review:

Business need

Authentication controls

Password management

Remote access

Admin Approval Mode

Monitoring

docs.title: Finding - Remote Token Filtering Weakened
docs.text:
If configuration changes remote UAC restrictions, determine why.

Do not report the Registry value alone.

Establish:

Affected accounts

Remote management exposure

Network access

Administrative privileges

Enterprise requirement

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
A strong UAC finding should contain:

Affected endpoint

Affected identity

Administrator membership

Current integrity level

Relevant UAC policy

Observed behavior

Security consequence

Compensating controls

Recommended policy

docs.title: Weak Finding
docs.text:
Avoid:

UAC can be bypassed.

This does not explain:

Which user was tested?

Was the user already an administrator?

Which configuration was weak?

What boundary was crossed?

What actual impact was demonstrated?

docs.title: Better Finding
docs.text: The tested user account is a member of the local Administrators group and normally operates at medium integrity. The effective UAC configuration permits administrative elevation without a consent prompt, reducing the user interaction normally required before administrative operations execute at high integrity.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
UAC remediation should be based on:

Least privilege

Microsoft security guidance

Organisational security baseline

Application compatibility

Endpoint role

docs.title: Enable UAC
docs.text:
Where organisational policy requires UAC:

EnableLUA

should remain enabled.

docs.title: Configure Admin Approval Mode
docs.text: Administrative users should use appropriate Admin Approval Mode settings rather than operating continuously with unrestricted administrative execution.

docs.title: Secure Desktop
docs.text: Use the secure desktop for elevation prompts where required by the security baseline.

docs.title: Standard Users
docs.text: Prefer standard-user accounts for normal daily activity.

docs.title: Separate Administrative Accounts
docs.text:
Where appropriate:

Normal Account
      |
      v
Daily Activity

Administrative Account
      |
      v
Privileged Administration

docs.title: Reduce Local Administrators
docs.text:
Remove unnecessary users and groups from:

BUILTIN\Administrators

docs.title: Manage Local Administrator Passwords
docs.text: Use appropriate enterprise mechanisms such as Windows LAPS where local administrative accounts are required.

docs.title: Application Compatibility
docs.text: Applications that unnecessarily require administrative privileges should be redesigned or reconfigured where possible.

docs.title: Central Management
docs.text:
Apply UAC configuration through the organisation's authoritative management platform:

Group Policy

MDM

Security baseline

Endpoint management

docs.title: Do Not Rely on UAC Alone
docs.text:
Combine UAC with:

Application control

Defender

Secure ACLs

Least privilege

Credential protection

Patch management

Security monitoring

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
Retesting should verify both:

Configuration

Observed behavior

docs.title: Establish the Security Context
docs.text:
Record the account type, local Administrators membership, current process integrity level, token elevation state, linked token information where authorised, and whether the test is local, remote, interactive, service-based, or scheduled. A standard user and a member of Administrators may receive different prompts and tokens.

Useful observations include:

Standard user + medium integrity token
Administrator + filtered medium integrity token
Administrator + elevated high integrity token
System or service context

Use whoami /all, token inspection, Get-TokenInformation-style approved tooling, process properties, and local policy inspection as appropriate. Configuration and token output establish state; they do not prove that a lower-privileged user can cross a boundary.

docs.title: Policy and Runtime Interpretation
docs.text:
Review the effective settings for EnableLUA, consent behavior, secure desktop, administrator and standard-user prompt behavior, installer detection, virtualization, built-in Administrator handling, and remote token filtering. Group Policy and registry values may differ from local defaults, and policy presence does not prove runtime enforcement for every execution path.

Perform a harmless, approved elevation workflow and compare the requesting account, parent and child process integrity levels, token privileges, prompt behavior, and resulting operation. A medium-to-high transition for an account already in Administrators is an elevation within that administrative identity, not automatically standard-user privilege escalation.

docs.title: Candidate and Validation Model
docs.text:
Observed policy or executable behavior
    -> Candidate elevation path
    -> Identify account and token boundary
    -> Confirm prerequisites and intended trigger
    -> Perform minimum harmless validation
    -> Capture resulting identity and operation
    -> Security conclusion

An auto-elevated binary, permissive setting, prompt behavior, or failed prompt is a candidate. Validate the required account type, file and registry permissions, trusted path, command-line or input influence, and whether the resulting process actually obtains a higher security context. Do not weaken UAC or alter policy to create the test condition.

docs.title: Evidence, Remediation, and Retesting
docs.text:
Capture effective policy source, account membership, process integrity, token state, elevation sequence, executable path and permissions, prompt behavior, and the minimum harmless operation. Redact usernames or host details where necessary. Explain whether the observation affects standard users, local administrators, remote administration, or only user experience.

Remediation may include removing unnecessary local administrator membership, applying the intended UAC policy and secure desktop settings, protecting trusted paths, correcting writable dependencies, and aligning remote administration controls. Retest standard and administrator accounts, local and approved remote paths, normal elevation, denied elevation, and relevant application-control interactions.

Establish administrator membership first

Before interpreting a UAC elevation result, determine whether the tested account already belongs to the local Administrators group. Moving from a filtered medium-integrity administrator token to a high-integrity administrator token is not equivalent to a standard user becoming an administrator.

Record both policy and behavior

Registry and Group Policy values show configuration, while an approved normal elevation test shows runtime behavior. Strong assessment evidence uses both.

Treat least privilege separately

If ordinary users are unnecessarily members of the local Administrators group, report the underlying least-privilege problem rather than relying on UAC prompts as the primary mitigation.

Correlate with other Windows controls

UAC is only one layer. Application control, Defender, filesystem permissions, service security, scheduled tasks and credential protections determine the broader endpoint security posture.

UAC is not a security boundary

Do not automatically classify a medium-to-high integrity transition for an account already in the Administrators group as a standard-user privilege escalation. Document the actual identity, token and privilege transition.

Do not weaken UAC during validation

Normal assessment does not require changing EnableLUA, consent behavior, secure desktop configuration or remote token filtering. Inspect the effective configuration and use the standard Windows elevation workflow where runtime validation is authorised.
